title: The New Congress Just Revealed Its Plan For Seniors, But 6 Dates Will Hit Your Wallet First

segments.text: The new Congress cannot change a single
dollar of your bills today. It has not
even been sworn in. And yet, six dates
are coming that will change what you
pay, what you collect, and what you owe
before it casts one vote. Almost nobody
on television is mentioning those dates.
They are busy with three big promises.
Cheaper health insurance, an end to the
AI program inside Medicare, and no tax
on your Social Security check. Here is
the part the headlines skip. Every one
of those promises has a wall in front of
it. A vote count, a veto, or a calendar
that does not work the way people think.
I will show you exactly where each wall
stands. And before this video ends, I
will run one couple's numbers on that
social security promise. You will see
what it would be worth to them, to the
dollar, and the one word that decides
whether they ever see it. I am Kevin.
The facts in this video come from the
Associated Press, the Congressional
Research Service, KFFF, Medicare, and
the Social Security trustees. Their
names are in the description. Check me
on any number. First, what actually
happened. In last week's midterms,
Democrats won control of both the House
and the Senate. Their House majority is
expected to land above 250 seats. A
couple of Senate races are still being
counted. The majority is already
secured. The new Congress is sworn in on
January 3rd. Hakeem Jeff is in line to
become speaker of the House. Chuck
Schumer is lining up support to become
Senate Majority Leader. Within days of
the win, Jeff laid out what his majority
wants to do first. Undo the Medicaid
cuts in last year's tax and spending
law. Bring back the expired health
insurance tax credits. Roll back
tariffs. According to the Associated
Press, the first House votes are
expected in the months after they take
their seats. Now, the part that matters
before any of that. A majority in the
House can pass almost anything it wants
in the House, but in the Senate, most
bills still need 60 votes, and President
Trump still holds the veto. On election
night, he posted a picture of a hat that
simply said veto. So, keep two lists in
your head as we go. Things that are
already set, which happen no matter
what, and things that are promised,
which have to get past 60 votes, and a
veto pen. Start with the calendar. Date
1 is December 7th. That is the last day
of Medicare's open enrollment, and it is
the first date on this list where the
decision is entirely yours. Here is why
it matters more than usual this year. On
January 1st, Medicare's negotiated
prices kick in for 15 more drugs. Ompic
and WGO are on that list. So are the
inhalers Trellogy and Brio, the cancer
drugs and IBR, and the diabetes pill
Janu. According to AARP, about 5.3
million people on Medicare use these
drugs. Out-ofpocket savings are
estimated at around $685 million a year,
spread across all of them. But the price
only reaches you through your plan. So
before December 7th, look up your exact
drugs in the plan you have for next
year. Check the tier, the co-ay, and
whether it is still covered at all. On a
Medicare Advantage plan, check your
doctors, too. Networks change on January
1st, and the plan does not have to call
you about it. And two numbers changed
for 2027. The most anyone can pay out of
pocket for covered drugs in a year rises
and the standard deductible rises to
$700. If you take an expensive drug
every month, you will likely hit that
ceiling earlier in the year than you
expect. Every drug plan has to offer a
way to spread those costs into monthly
payments instead. It is called the
Medicare prescription payment plan and
you have to opt in. And one more date
hides inside this one. By November 30th,
Medicare has to publish the prices for
its next round of negotiated drugs. For
the first time, that round can include
drugs given in a doctor's office, like
infusions and injections, not just
pharmacy prescriptions. Those prices
start in 2028. Date 2 is December 11th.
That is when government funding runs out
unless the outgoing Congress passes
another spending bill. As of this week,
lawmakers are not close to a deal. So,
if you hear the word shutdown, here is
what it does and does not mean for you.
Social Security checks keep going out on
schedule. They are paid from mandatory
spending, not the yearly budget fight.
Medicare keeps paying for your doctor
visits, hospital stays, and
prescriptions. The Medicare phone line
keeps running, too. What slows down is
service. In past shutdowns, Social
Security stopped giving benefit
verification letters by phone or in
person. Medicare card replacements were
online only. So, if you will need a

of IRA money into one. That money drops

every year until somebody spots it. None

road usually ends in one place. your
children writing checks to the IRS out

the year nobody plans for, the year one
of you dies. If your spouse dies before
taking that year's required withdrawal,
it still has to come out. It does not
vanish. The owner owed it and now the
beneficiary owes it. The final IRS rules
give you some breathing room here. You

talked about earlier. The required
withdrawal stays about the same size.
The space it lands in gets cut in half.

exactly half the couple's line. That is
why so much of this planning has to
happen while both of you are still here.

the search charge can often be lowered.
The income tax cannot. And your children

where does all of this leave you and in

For some of you, that is far too much.

over the line. If nothing changes, that

2028 for interest she was told nobody
would ever touch. Her December options
are not dramatic. She is over 70 and a
half, which opens a door I will show you
in a moment, a way to give from her IRA
that pulls her income down directly. Her
next CD or Treasury bill can be set to
mature in January rather than late
December.
And next year, she can ask whether those
bonds still make sense for someone whose
Medicare bill they quietly raise. Let me
add up only the last few minutes.
Cornelius, about $3,500
for a withdrawal he never knew existed.
Lorraine, around $1,100 a year for
interest she was promised nobody would
touch. Ambrose and Winifred, a penalty
that one phone call in December can
erase. None of that money bought
anything. It is simply what a rule costs
when you meet it one month too late. I
would much rather you meet these rules
early in a quiet hour with the dates in
front of you. The Quiet Rules was
written for exactly that hour, and you
will find it at kevinexplains.shop.
Point your phone's camera at the square
code on your screen or scroll down and
the link is in the description and again
in the comment I pinned. Take 7 days. If
it is not found a home in the drawer
with your tax papers by then, you get a
refund because the other way the bill
shows up in 2028 inside a Medicare
letter charging you for a CD you renewed
this December. Now, the rule I promised
you at the start, the one that has never
existed in any December before this one.
The same law created a charitable
deduction for people who take the
standard deduction beginning with this
tax year.
A single filer can deduct up to $1,000
of gifts and a married couple filing
together up to 2,000.
For most retirees, decades of church
envelopes never touched their tax
return. This is the first year those
envelopes can.
But the details are where people will
trip in April. Only money counts,
meaning cash, checks, or card payments.
A bag of clothes for the thrift store
does not.
The gift has to reach the charity
itself, like a church, a food bank, or a
hospital foundation.
Money parked in a donor-advised fund is
excluded. And any single gift of $250 or
more needs a written acknowledgment from
the charity in your hands before you
file.
So this month, ask your church office
for a year-end giving letter. People who
itemize got the opposite surprise.
Starting this year, the first half
percent of their income in donations no
longer counts at all.
If you are 70 and a half or older and
own an IRA though, the new deduction is
only the second best way to give. You
have probably heard of sending money
straight from the IRA to a charity. It
is called a qualified charitable
distribution. What matters this month is
the fine print. First, the age. You must
already be 70 and a half on the actual
day the money leaves the account.
Turning 70 and a half later in the year
does not rescue an earlier transfer.
Second, the deadline. The transfer has
to be completed by December 31st, and
many IRA companies stop taking these
requests in the middle of December. Call
this week, not Christmas week.
Third, the check. It must be payable to
the charity. If it is made out to you,
even for a day, it becomes an ordinary
taxable withdrawal. For 2026, the limit
and it counts toward your required
withdrawal. Here is the payoff for a
couple like Ambrose and Winifred who
give about $5,000 a year to their
church. Sent straight from the IRA
instead of by check, that 5,000 never
appears as income. More than $4,000 of
their social security drops out of the
taxable column. Even after the new
deduction, the IRA route leaves them
close to $900 ahead.
One more December habit deserves a
second look. Plenty of grandparents
write year-end checks to the family. The
IRS lets you give up to $19,000 to each
person this year without even filing a
gift tax form.
But Medicaid does not care what the IRS
allows. If you ever need Medicaid to pay
for a nursing home, it looks back five
years at every gift you made. A generous
December can turn into a stretch years
later when Medicaid will not pay. That
does not mean stop giving. It means keep
a record of every gift. And if long-term
care is a real possibility for you, talk
with an elder law attorney about how
much you give and how.
Now, if you hold mutual funds in a
regular taxable account, December has a
trap that looks like good news. Most
funds pay out their capital gains for
the year in December. The fund's price
drops by the same amount and you owe tax
on the payout. It counts in your income
for Social Security and for Medicare
exactly like interest does. So if you
are about to put new money into a mutual
fund in a taxable account this month,
check the fund's website for its
distribution date first. Buy the week
before that date and you pay tax on a
full year of gains you never enjoyed.
Wait a few days and you avoid it.
And if some of your investments are
down, December 31st is the last trading
day to sell them at a loss and count
that loss for 2026. Losses cancel out
gains and up to $3,000 more can offset
ordinary income including your interest.
Just do not buy the same investment back
within 30 days or the IRS disallows the
loss.
Before we leave the bank behind
completely, one thing to check while
your CD statements are spread out on the
table. The FDIC insures $250,000
per depositor per bank for each type of
ownership. But since April 2024,
accounts with named beneficiaries,
payable on death accounts, and many
trust accounts are counted differently.
They can be insured up to $250,000
for each beneficiary, up to five
beneficiaries. So think about a widow
with $600,000 at one bank, all in her
own name, no beneficiaries. $350,000 of
that is not insured. Now suppose she
names her two children as payable on
death beneficiaries on most of it. Her
coverage at that same bank can rise high
enough to cover every dollar without
moving any of it elsewhere. But be
careful. A beneficiary on an account
decides who inherits that money outside
of your will. Match it to your estate
plan before you sign anything. The FDIC
has a free online calculator called EDIE
that shows exactly how much of your
money is covered. It takes about 10
minutes.
Now the piece of December mail that
almost everyone gets.
On October 14th, the Social Security
Administration announced a 3.6% cost of
living increase for 2027. The notice
showing your new amount is either
already in your online My Social
Security account or it will arrive by
mail in December. Open it. If you
receive SSI, expect two payments in
December this year.
The increased January payment is being
sent early on December 31st because
January 1st is a holiday. It is not a
bonus. It has to last you through
January. If you are still working and
collecting before your full retirement
age, the new year also moves your
earnings limit. For 2027, it rises to
and above it, Social Security holds back
$1 for every two you earn. For everyone
else, do not stop at the new benefit
amount. Look at the line for your
Medicare premium because that comes out
before the money ever reaches your bank.
If that line shows a surcharge, it is
based on your 2025 tax return. And this
is where a lot of people leave money on
the table. If your income has dropped
since 2025 because of what Social
Security calls a life-changing event,
you can ask them to use your newer,
lower income instead. The events are
specific. You stopped working or cut
back your hours. Your spouse died. You
married or divorced. You lost a pension.
Or you lost income-producing property to
a disaster or to fraud.
If one of those happened, the request is
form SSA-44
and you can file it as soon as you see
that surcharge. What does not count
matters just as much. Selling a house, a
big one-time IRA withdrawal or a large
stock sale are not life-changing events.
Those have to be planned before they
happen, which is the whole point of
doing this in December instead of
discovering it later. And a warning
about that notice. Every winter,
scammers call and text seniors saying
they must verify a bank account to
release the new increase.
Your increase does not need releasing.
It is automatic. If anyone asks for your
account details to unlock your raise,
end the call. Then reach Social Security
yourself using the number on the notice
itself. While that letter is in your
hand, one date comes before all the
others. Medicare's open enrollment
period ends on December 7th. Drug plans
and Medicare Advantage plans are allowed
to change their premiums, their covered
drugs, and their pharmacies every
January. Your plan mailed you a notice
of those changes in the fall. If it is
still sealed in a pile somewhere, open
it before the 7th. After that, most
people are locked in for the year. If
you are in a Medicare Advantage plan,
you do get one more chance to switch
between January 1st and March 31st, but
that window is narrower than the one
closing now, so do not count on it. Now,
how do you make sure next January does
not look like this one? Social Security
will withhold federal tax from your
check if you ask. The form is called
W-4V and it is one page. You can choose
7, 10, 12, or 22% of each payment. It
usually takes a month or two to start,
so it will not rescue 2026, but it can
end the penalty problem for good.
Ambrose and Winifred would pick 10%.
With $52,000 of benefits, that alone
would cover their entire federal bill.
And if you take regular IRA withdrawals,
your IRA company will withhold from
those too at whatever percentage you
choose. So here is how I would spend one
afternoon this week. Four phone calls
and the sentence to say on each one.
Call one is your IRA company. Say, I
would like my December withdrawal to
have this many dollars of federal tax
withheld. Givers over 70 and a half get
a second sentence. Please send part of
my required distribution directly to my
church as a qualified charitable
distribution. If you are converting part
of an IRA to a Roth this year, that also
has to be finished by December 31st. The
same withholding rule can cover its tax
without a penalty. And while they are on
the line, ask who is named as the
beneficiary on each account. That form
overrides your will, and outdated ones
are far more common than people think.
Call two is your bank if you have CDs.
Say, when does each of my CDs mature?
Does it pay its interest at maturity?
And what happens if I do nothing during
the grace period? Call three is your
church or charity. Say, please send me a
written statement of everything I gave
this year. Call four is only for some of
you. If you inherited an IRA from a
parent, call that IRA company with two
questions. Was the person I inherited
from already taking required
withdrawals? And what was my required
amount for 2025 and 2026? And if your
Social Security notice shows a Medicare
surcharge and you stopped working in the
last two years, there is a fifth call.
That one goes to Social Security about
form SSA-44.
If your situation does not fit neatly
into any of these, and plenty do not,
write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
Put the word December in the subject
line so it finds me quickly. Give me
your age, roughly what you hold in
savings and IRAs, and which of these
dates is worrying you. If any of this
was new to you, subscribe because the
new year brings a whole new set of
dates, and I will walk you through those
too. And tell me something in the
comments. In all your years of banking,
has a bank ever withheld a single dollar
of tax from your interest? I would love
to know if Ralph's number holds up
across all of you. And if you would
rather have every one of these rules in
one place, you can open again next
December without hunting for this video.
The quiet rules is at
kevinexplains.shop.
Right now, your bank is still writing
that form. Every interest payment
between now and New Year's Eve adds
another line. At midnight on December
31st, the pen goes down for good.
What you do before then, you get to
decide. What comes after, you only get
to pay. I am Kevin. Thanks for
[clears throat] watching. Do not forget
to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: Trump’s New Tax Law: Retirees Already Lost 1 Year. Don’t Waste the Last 3

segments.text: You were told you had four years.
When President Trump signed the new tax
law in the summer of 2025, retirees got
a window, a new deduction, lower
brackets, and four tax years to use
one of those years is already gone. The
second one closes on December 31st,
which is now only a few weeks away, and
many retirees have not used a single day
of it. So you do not have four years
anymore. You have three. And what you do
before New Year's Eve may decide how
much tax you pay for the rest of your
life, not just this year, the rest of
your life, and in many cases, your
spouse's life after you are gone. In
this video, I am going to show you
exactly what the window is, the three
moves that make it worth something, and
three traps that quietly take the
benefit back. One of those traps hits
widows and widowers harder than almost
anyone else, and almost nobody plans for
it. I will walk you through it with real
numbers. I am Kevin. The figures in this
video come from the amounts the IRS
published for 2026 and from public
guides by firms like Schwab. Every
source is listed in the description so
you can check it.
This is general information, not tax
advice. Your own numbers will be
different, and that is exactly why I am
going to show you how to find them.
First, what actually changed in plain
English? Before this law, the tax cuts
from 2017 were set to expire at the end
of 2025. Brackets would have gone back
up. The 12% bracket would have become
15. The 22 would have become 25. The
standard deduction would have been cut
roughly in half. The new law stopped
that. The lower brackets and the bigger
standard deduction are now permanent,
and they keep rising with inflation
every year. So the permanent part is
good news, and you do not need to do
anything to get it. But the law also
added a few temporary pieces on top. And
for retirees, the biggest one is the new
senior deduction, $6,000 for each person
65 or older. $12,000 for a married
couple when both are 65 or older. If
only one of you has reached 65, the
couple gets $6,000 and it is only
available for tax years 2025 through
2028. After that, unless Congress acts,
it disappears. Here is what that looks
like when you stack it all together for
this year.
For 2026, according to the IRS, the
standard deduction for a married couple
filing jointly is $32,200.
If both of you are 65 or older, you each
add another $1,650.
Then the new senior deduction adds
$12,000 more. Put it together and a
married couple over 65 can have about
of income that is never taxed at all.
For a single person over 65, it is
And now here is a number worth knowing.
For 2026, the 12% tax bracket for a
married couple ends at $100,800
of taxable income. Add the $47,500
of deductions on top. Now a couple over
65 can have about $148,000
of adjusted gross income and still never
pay more than 12% federal tax on any
dollar. And that lands just under
which is exactly where the senior
deduction starts to shrink. Whether that
is by design or by coincidence, it is a
useful zone to know about. Now, before
you get excited, there is something the
headlines got wrong. You may have heard
this law called no tax on Social
Security. That is not what it does. The
senior deduction lowers your taxable
income. It does not change the formula
that decides how much of your Social
Security is taxable in the first place.
That formula uses something called
provisional income. It is your other
income plus half of your Social
Security. For a married couple, once
that number passes $32,000,
part of your Social Security starts
taxable. Past 44,000 up to 85% of it can
be. And those levels have never been
adjusted for inflation. The new
deduction did not touch them.
Why does that matter? Because every
extra dollar you take from a traditional
IRA can do two things at once. It is
taxed itself and it can drag up to 85
cents of social security into your
taxable income along with it. Planners
call this the tax torpedo. In the 12%
bracket, it can feel more like a 22%
tax. In the 22% bracket, it can feel
like 40. Keep that in mind because it
changes which move makes sense for you.
Let me show you how this plays out for a
real household. Bernard and Colette are
a made-up couple, but their numbers are
typical. He is 67, she is 66. Together,
they get $52,000 a year from social
security. They have about $900,000 in
traditional IRAs and they take $40,000 a
year out of them to live on. Here is
their 2026 tax return using the IRS's
own brackets. About $24,700
of their social security becomes
taxable. Their adjusted gross income
lands around 64,700.
Subtract the 47,500 of deductions and
their taxable income is about 17,200.
Their federal tax is about $1,720.
That is all. Most people would look at
that and say, wonderful, we are done.
And that is the mistake because Bernard
and Colette are sitting on $900,000
that has never been taxed. Every dollar
of it will be taxed someday. The only
question is when, at what rate, and on
whose tax return? In 2025, they did
nothing. That year is closed. You cannot
go back and convert money in a year that
has ended. But 2026 is still open until
December 31st. Bernard and Colette's
money will be taxed someday, no matter
what. The only part they still control
is when and at what rate. That is the
kind of decision the quiet rules is
built for. The quiet decisions that
never send you a warning, where the cost
only shows up years later. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
Scan the code on your screen or use the
link in the description or the one
pinned at the top of the comments. Take
seven days with it. If it does not show
you something your family did not know,
you get a refund. Because the person who
pays for a skipped December is usually
not the one who skipped it. It is the
one left behind, sitting at the kitchen
table in April, holding a tax bill twice
as big as the year before.
Which brings me to move one, the Roth
conversion. A Roth conversion means
moving money from a traditional IRA into
a Roth IRA. You pay income tax on the
amount you move this year, but once it
is in the Roth, it grows tax-free and
qualified withdrawals are tax-free. And
Roth IRAs have no required minimum
distributions during your lifetime. So
[clears throat] how much could Bernard
and Colette convert this year and still
stay in the 12% bracket? Using the 2026
numbers, about $64,000.
That fills their bracket right up to
line. Their federal tax would go from
about $1,720
to about $11,600.
So converting $64,000 costs them about
in extra tax, roughly 15%. 15%, not 12.
That extra 3% is the tax torpedo I just
told you about. Converting pushed more
of their social security into taxable
income. That is why you never estimate a
conversion with the bracket alone. You
run the whole return. And there are a
few rules on conversions that catch
people every year. A conversion has to
be completed by December 31st to count
for that year. There is no extension and
no going back to April like with an IRA
contribution. Once you convert, you
cannot undo it. And it is usually better
to pay the tax with money from outside
the IRA. If you have the tax withheld
from the conversion itself, less money
actually lands in the Roth. Also, the
tax is due. If you convert in December,
plan to pay it, either through
withholding or an estimated payment due
in mid-January. And one detail that
works in your favor. If you have never
had a Roth IRA before, the five-year
clock that decides when your earnings
come out tax-free starts on January 1st
of the year you first convert. So a
conversion in December of 2026 counts as
if you started on January 1st. And here
is how that adds up. Say Bernard and
Colette do something similar in 2026,
2027, and 2028. They could move close to
into Roth accounts at around 15%. That
is not the whole IRA. It does not need
to be. It is the slice that could
otherwise be taxed later at higher
rates, especially once one of them is
filing alone. And one worry I hear a
lot. Will a conversion count against me
under the Social Security earnings
limit? No. That limit only looks at
wages and self-employment income. A Roth
conversion is not earned income, so it
does not reduce your Social Security
check. Now, why would anyone pay 15%
today when they are paying so little
right now? Because of what happens next.
Bernard was born in 1959. Under current
law, his required minimum distributions
begin at 73. If you were born in 1960 or
later, they begin at 75. At that point,
the IRS forces money out every year,
whether you need it or not. If that
900,000 keeps growing, those forced
withdrawals grow with it, and the
percentage the IRS requires you to take
rises as you age. For a couple with a
large IRA, that can climb into higher
brackets with the torpedo on top. But
that is not even the real risk. That
brings me to trap number one. What
happens when one of them dies? Let me
introduce Ophelia. She is another
made-up name, and her story is the one I
promised you at the start. Ophelia was
married for 43 years. When her husband
died, a lot of things changed. But one
change nobody warned her about was her
tax bracket. In the year her husband
dies, a surviving spouse can usually
still file jointly.
After that, unless she has a dependent
child at home, she files as single. And
single means smaller brackets, about
half the standard deduction and one
senior deduction instead of two. Here is
what that looks like with numbers. Say
Ophelia and her husband had the same
setup as Bernard and Colette, $52,000 of
social security between them, $40,000
from IRAs, about $1,720
of federal tax. When her husband dies,
Ophelia keeps the larger of the two
social security checks. So her household
social security drops to about $30,000.
She still takes $40,000 from the IRA,
which is now all hers. Her income went
down by about $22,000
and her federal tax went up to about
Less income, more than double the tax.
And once her required minimum
distributions start on the combined IRA,
the numbers can climb from there. This
is called the widow's penalty. It is not
a separate law. It is just what happens
when one household's income meets single
brackets. And the three years left in
this window are some of the best years a
married couple will ever have to soften
it. They can move money into Roth
accounts while they still file jointly
at 12% with two senior deductions. If
this is useful, subscribe. I go through
these rules every week in plain English
so you do not have to read the tax code
yourself. Now, trap number two,
Medicare. Your Medicare Part B premium
depends on your income. Above certain
levels, you pay an extra charge called
IRMAA.
For 2026, the first level starts above
of modified adjusted gross income for a
single person and $218,000 for a married
couple. These levels rise a little every
year. The first surcharge adds about $81
a month to Part B for each person and it
gets bigger at higher levels. On top of
that, there is a separate surcharge on
Part D. And here is the part that
surprises people. IRMAA looks back two
years. Your income in 2026 sets your
Medicare premiums in 2028. So, if you do
a big Roth conversion this December, you
may not feel the cost until a Medicare
letter shows up in late 2027. And IRMAA
works like a cliff, not a ramp. Go $1
over a level and you pay the whole
surcharge for that level for the whole
year. For a married couple, that $1 can
cost close to $2,000 in Part B
surcharges alone. Bernard and Colette at
are safely below the married threshold,
but a single person hits that wall at
So, before you convert, find the IRMAA
line for your filing status and stay a
comfortable distance below it. Do not
aim for $1 under. Leave room because a
surprise dividend or capital gain can
push you over.
Trap number three, the phase-out zone.
And this one hits people who are still
working past 65. Sterling is another
made-up name. He is 66, single, and
still working, earning about $110,000 a
year. He assumed he gets the $6,000
senior deduction, but for a single
filer, the deduction shrinks by 6% of
every dollar of income above $75,000.
At $110,000, Sterling loses $2,100
it is gone completely.
For married couples, the shrinking
starts at $150,000 and ends at $250,000.
What that means in practice is that
every extra dollar Sterling earns in
that zone is taxed at his bracket plus a
little more because it also shrinks his
deduction. In the 22% bracket, that adds
about 1 and 1/3 %. But Sterling has an
easy fix that most people in his
position overlook. Money he puts into a
traditional 401k at work through payroll
lowers his adjusted gross income. That
lowers the income that counts for the
phase-out. So, every extra dollar he
defers before December 31st can save tax
twice, once on the dollar itself and
once by giving back part of his senior
deduction. That only works through
payroll. So, if you are still working,
talk to your employer's benefits office
this month, not in April. And two more
rules on the senior deduction that costs
people money. First, you need a valid
Social Security number. Second, if you
are married, you generally have to file
a joint return to claim it. And you must
be 65 by the end of the tax year. If you
turn 65 on December 31st, you count for
that year.
Married couples who file separately for
other reasons can lose it entirely. If
you file separately, run the numbers
both ways before you do it again. Now,
move number two. Harvesting games at 0%.
Say you have stocks or funds in a
regular taxable brokerage account that
have gone up in value.
You may be able to sell them and pay no
federal tax on the gain at all.
For 2026, long-term capital gains are
taxed at 0% while your taxable income
stays below $98,900
for a married couple. For a single
person, it is $49,450.
Add those big senior deductions on top.
A married couple over 65 can then have
of income on their return before those
gains start being taxed. You sell, you
pay nothing. And if you want to keep the
investment, you can buy it right back.
Your new cost is the higher price. That
means less tax later when you sell for
real.
With gains, unlike losses, there is no
wash sale rule to stop you from buying
back right away. Two cautions. Capital
gains also count in that provisional
income formula. So, they can make more
of your Social Security taxable. Run the
whole return, not just the gain. And if
you plan to hold that investment for the
rest of your life, your heirs may get a
stepped-up cost when they inherit it
anyway. Gain harvesting helps most for
money you expect to sell while you are
alive.
Now, move number three. And this one is
for anyone 70 and a half or older who
gives to charity. It is called a
qualified charitable distribution.
Instead of writing a check from your
bank account, you have your IRA send
money directly to a charity. For 2026,
you can give up to $111,000
this way. The money never shows up in
your adjusted gross income at all. And
if you are already taking required
minimum distributions, it counts toward
them. Why is that better than a regular
donation? Because most retirees take the
standard deduction and get no tax break
for giving. A qualified charitable
distribution lowers your income
directly, and a lower income can mean
less of your social security taxed, more
of your senior deduction kept, and a
better chance of staying under that
Medicare cliff. One move, four benefits.
And starting this year, there is a new
rule for people who do not itemize. You
can deduct cash gifts to qualifying
charities up to $1,000 for a single
person or $2,000 for a married couple.
This one is permanent. It does not apply
to gifts to donor-advised funds, and it
does not stack with the qualified
charitable distribution on the same
dollars. But if you give and take the
standard deduction, keep your receipts.
Now, let me bring this back to Ophelia
because this is the part that stays with
me.
Her husband did everything right. He
saved for 40 years. He never missed a
payment.
But nobody ever showed them that the 12%
years while they were both alive were
the cheapest years they would ever have
to pay tax on that IRA.
Once he was gone, every dollar of it
moved to her single tax return at higher
rates with one deduction instead of two.
Over the next 15 years, that difference
can easily add up to tens of thousands
of dollars that did not have to be paid.
The quiet rules is written for couples
who still have both names on the tax
return while those choices are still
open. You can find it at
kevinexplains.shop
through the code on your screen, the
pinned comment, or the link in the
description.
You have seven days to decide if it is
worth keeping. If it is not, you get a
refund because the cost of waiting does
not arrive with a warning. It arrives in
a widow's mailbox in a tax form with
only one name on it. And there is one
more person who pays for a skipped
window, and it is usually your children.
Under the rules passed in 2019, most
adult children who inherit a traditional
IRA must empty it within 10 years. And
if the parent had already started
required distributions, many of them
must also take money out along the way.
Those 10 years often land right in their
highest earning years, stacked on top of
their own salaries. A Roth IRA still has
to be emptied within 10 years by most
heirs, but the withdrawals are generally
tax-free. So converting at 12% now can
mean your children are not paying 24 or
32% on the same dollars later. Now, how
do you find your own numbers? You do not
need special software to start. Pull out
last year's federal tax return. Find the
line labeled adjusted gross income and
the line labeled taxable income. If you
are married and over 65, the 12% bracket
for 2026 ends at $100,800
of taxable income. The gap between your
taxable income and that number is
roughly the room you have. Then adjust
for anything that changed this year, a
new pension, a bigger required
distribution, a capital gain. And
remember the tax torpedo, which can make
that room smaller than it looks. That is
a rough first pass. A tax professional
or good tax software can then run the
exact return. And one more trick for
paying the tax that many retirees do not
know.
Taxes withheld from an IRA distribution
are generally treated as if they were
paid evenly through the year, even if
you take the distribution in December.
So if you are behind on estimated
payments, having extra tax withheld from
a December IRA distribution can help you
avoid an underpayment penalty. Talk to
your IRA custodian before mid-December
because they get busy.
And if a Medicare surcharge does hit
you, know which appeals work. Social
Security lets you ask for a lower
premium after certain life-changing
events, like retirement, a big drop in
work hours, or the death of a spouse.
You use a form called SSA-44.
But a Roth conversion you chose to do is
not one of those
So the planning has to happen before you
convert, not after the letter arrives.
Now, a few other temporary pieces of the
law you should know about briefly. If
you itemize and pay a lot in state and
local taxes, the cap on that deduction
rose from $10,000 to $40,000 for 2025.
It rises a little each year through
2029. It shrinks for people with income
above about half a million dollars, and
in 2030 it is scheduled to drop back to
If you bought a new car with a loan, you
may be able to deduct up to $10,000 a
year of the interest through 2028.
The vehicle needs its final assembly in
the United States, and the deduction
shrinks at higher incomes. That one only
applies to new vehicles bought for
personal use, and you need the vehicle
identification number on your return.
And if you are still working, two other
temporary deductions may apply to you
through 2028. Qualified tips can be
deducted up to $25,000 a year, and the
extra half of pay you get for qualified
overtime can be deducted up to $12,500
or 25,000 on a joint return. Both shrink
at higher incomes. For a retiree working
a part-time restaurant or hourly job,
they can matter more than you would
expect. Before the calendar, let me give
you the mistakes I see most often in
December because each one can wipe out
the benefit of everything else. Mistake
one, converting before taking your
required minimum distribution.
If you are already at the age where
required distributions apply, the first
dollars you take out of your IRA each
year count toward that requirement,
and a required distribution cannot be
converted to a Roth. So take your
required amount first, then convert on
top of it.
Do it in the wrong order, and you can
end up with an excess contribution
problem in your Roth.
Mistake two, converting in the same year
as a big one-time event.
Selling a home is the most common. A
married couple can usually exclude up to
$500,000 of gain on a home they have
lived in, and and person up to 250,000.
But anything above that is taxable and
it lands in the same year as your
conversion. A large sale of investments,
a severance payment, or a big
inheritance from a traditional IRA can
do the same.
In a year like that, convert less or
skip it. Mistake three, converting too
much in one year. The whole point of
this window is to fill the low brackets.
If you convert so much that you jump
into the 24% bracket, cross the Medicare
cliff, and lose your senior deduction,
you may pay more than you would have
later. Spread it across the three years.
Mistake four, forgetting your spouse. If
one of you is younger, the senior
deduction, Medicare, and required
distributions all happen on different
clocks. Plan it as one household, not
two people who happen to share a tax
return. And here is what the end of the
senior deduction would mean for a couple
like Bernard and Colette. In 2029, if
nothing changes, they lose $12,000 of
deductions. At 12%, that is roughly
more federal tax every year without a
single dollar of new income. That is not
a disaster, but it is a reason to use
the cheap years while they exist. So let
me put all three years on one calendar.
Before December 31st of this year, 2026,
decide on a Roth conversion and finish
it before the deadline.
If you are 70 and 1/2 or older and you
give to charity, send your qualified
charitable distribution directly from
the IRA. If you have taxable investments
with gains and your income is low,
consider harvesting them. If you are
still working, increase your 401k
contributions through payroll. And if
you converted, plan how you will pay the
tax by mid January. And on the
conversion itself, here is how it
usually works in practice. You call or
log in to the company that holds your
IRA. If you do not already have a Roth
IRA there, you open one, which usually
takes a few minutes. You ask to convert
a specific dollar amount, not shares by
guesswork.
You decide whether any tax should be
withheld. And, in January, you will get
a form called a 1099 R showing the
conversion. Keep it with your tax
papers.
One warning.
Many companies set their own internal
cutoff in mid or late December, so the
legal deadline of December 31st is not
the one to aim for. Aim for early
December.
In 2027, do it again with fresh numbers.
The IRS adjusts the brackets and the
standard deduction for inflation every
year, so the space will move a little.
Check the IRMAA levels before you act.
And remember, your 2027 income sets your
Medicare premiums in 2029. In 2028, the
last year of the senior deduction under
current law, this is the year to finish
anything you planned because in 2029,
unless Congress extends it, the extra
deduction is gone. A [clears throat]
married couple over 65 would lose up to
$12,000 of deductions overnight. And
will Congress extend it? Nobody knows
yet. Democrats just won control of
Congress this week, and the White House
is still Republican. Extending a
temporary tax break needs both, and they
may not agree on how. I would not plan
on an extension, and I would not plan
against one. I would plan for the law as
it is written and treat anything better
as a bonus. Now, here is the strongest
argument against everything I just said.
Some people should not convert at all.
If you need that money to live on soon,
paying tax early can leave you short. If
your income will drop a lot later, you
may already be in a lower bracket then.
If your heirs are in low tax brackets,
they may pay less tax on your IRA than
you would. If you live in a state with a
high income tax, the state bill can
change the math. And if you would have
to pay the conversion tax out of the IRA
itself, the benefit shrinks. Those are
real reasons, and for some households,
they win. And there is one more
argument. Nobody knows future tax rates.
If Congress cuts rates in 2030, paying
tax today may turn out to be a mistake.
That is fair, but here is how I see it.
The government is spending far more than
it collects, and Social Security's trust
fund is projected to run short in the
early 2030s.
I would not bet my retirement on tax
rates being lower for retirees 10 years
from now than they are today. And for a
married couple, the bigger certainty is
not tax policy. It is that someday one
of you will be filing alone. And there
is one more quiet advantage of money in
a Roth that matters most later in life.
Qualified Roth withdrawals do not count
in the formula that decides how much of
your Social Security is taxed, and they
do not count toward the Medicare
surcharge either. So a widow drawing
from a Roth instead of a traditional IRA
can keep her taxable income low, keep
her Social Security from being pulled
into tax, and stay under the Medicare
cliff. That flexibility is worth
something, even if you cannot put an
exact number on it today. So my view is
simple. If you are married, over 65 and
holding a large traditional IRA, the
next three years may be the cheapest
years you will ever have to pay tax on
that money. Do not waste them by doing
nothing, and do not overdo it either.
The goal is to fill the low brackets,
not to jump into the high ones. I want
to hear from you. Are you planning a
Roth conversion before December 31st or
did you not know this window existed
until today?
Tell me in the comments. It helps me
decide what to cover next. If you are
trying to work out how much to convert
or what your own numbers look like as a
couple, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
Tell me your ages, your rough income,
and what is in your IRAs. I read every
message, and I will tell you which
question I would answer first. And if
this channel has saved you money, the
description has a small way to support
the research behind it. You were told
you had four years. You now have three,
and the first of them ends in a few
weeks. Bernard and Colette still have
time. Ophelia's husband ran out of it.
The difference was never how much they
saved. It was whether anyone sat down
with them before December and showed
them the numbers. The quiet rules is
there for that, and the pinned comment
will take you straight to it. I am
Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: Democrats Won Congress: Seniors Who Panic Claim Social Security Now Could Lose Thousands

segments.text: You woke up this week to the news that
Democrats won control of Congress and
somewhere in your head a question
started. What happens to my Social
Security check now? Should I file early
before anyone in Washington can touch
it? Before you call Social Security or
fill out a single form, give me the next
few minutes because the people who make
the most expensive Social Security
mistakes are rarely the ones who wait.
They are the ones who panic. Here is
what actually happened. In Tuesday's
midterm elections, Democrats won
majorities in both the House and the
Senate according to news organizations
including the Associated Press. A few
races are still being counted, but both
majorities are secured. The new Congress
takes its seats in early January. And
within hours of the results, the same
three words were showing up everywhere
online. Claim it now. So, in this video,
I am going to answer the six questions
people are asking this week in the order
they are asking them. What really
changes? What does not? What each party
has actually proposed? And what history
says about who gets protected when
Social Security changes? And I will tell
you about one change from 2015 that gave
some families only 6 months to act. Most
people have never heard of it and it is
the best clue we have about what the
next change could look like. I am Kevin.
Every number in this video comes from
Social Security's own reports and other
public sources and they are all listed
in the description so you can check
every word. This is not about which
party you voted for. It is about your
check. And this is general information,
not financial advice. Question one. Can
a Democratic Congress change Social
Security on its own? The short answer is
no, not by itself. A majority in the
House is enough to pass a bill there,
but in the Senate, most major
legislation still needs 60 votes to get
past a filibuster. Democrats won a clear
majority, but nowhere near 60 seats. And
even if a bill made it through both
chambers, President Trump can veto it.
Overriding a veto takes 2/3 of both the
House and the Senate.
There is one exception people forget.
Some budget bills can pass the Senate
with a simple majority through a process
called reconciliation.
But there is a long-standing rule that
keeps Social Security changes out of
those bills. So, for the next 2 years,
any real change to Social Security needs
votes from both parties and a signature
from the White House. What a majority
does give you is control of the agenda.
The majority party chairs every
committee. It decides which bills get
hearings, which officials get called to
testify, and which problems get a
spotlight. And there is one more thing
the majority controls that touches you
directly. Congress sets Social
Security's operating budget every year.
Not your benefit, which is paid
automatically, but the money for staff,
phone lines, and field offices. That
budget decides how long you wait on hold
and how fast your claim gets processed.
A new majority writes the first draft of
that budget. So, the change you will
notice first is not in your check. It is
in what gets talked about in Washington
starting in January.
Question two, is the trust fund still
running out? Yes, and no election
changes the math. In June, Social
Security's trustees released their
yearly report. The trust fund that pays
retirement and survivor benefits is now
projected to run out of reserves in the
fourth quarter of 2032. That is about 6
years from now. Once those reserves are
gone, incoming payroll taxes would cover
only about 78% of scheduled benefits.
That is roughly a 22% cut for everyone
at once, unless Congress acts. There is
one more line in that report most news
stories skipped. Starting this year,
2026, Social Security's total cost is
projected to be higher than its total
income every year. The program is
already drawing down its savings. So,
let me put that cut in real money. The
average retired worker's check will be
about $2,170
a month in January after the new raise.
A 22% cut on that is about $477
a month. That is about $5,700
a year.
Now, here's the part that matters for
this week. That cut, if it ever happens,
would apply to everyone collecting
benefits. It does not matter when you
started. Someone who filed at 62 would
be cut. Someone who filed at 70 would be
cut. Filing early does not get you out
of it. It just means the cut lands on a
smaller check. And it helps to
understand why that cut would be
automatic. Social Security is not
allowed to borrow. It can only pay
benefits from what is in its trust funds
and what comes in through payroll taxes.
So, if the reserves run out, nobody has
to vote for a cut. The law simply does
not let the agency pay more than it has.
That is why this is a deadline, not a
debate. But, here is the other side of
this. It has almost happened before.
In 1983, Social Security was projected
to be unable to pay full benefits within
months.
Congress, a Democratic House, and a
Republican Senate, and a Republican
President made a deal just in time.
Nobody wanted to be the party that let
checks shrink. History suggests the
pressure will be just as strong this
time. The question is not whether they
act, it is what they choose and who pays
for it. And that brings me to the person
this video is really for.
Rosemary is a name I made up, but I have
heard her story many times. She is 63.
She had planned to wait until her full
retirement age of 67. Then, the election
results came in and her neighbor told
her to grab her benefits before Congress
took them away. So, she filed online
that same night. What Rosemary did not
know is that at 63, her check is
permanently reduced. Not for a few
years, for life. For someone with a full
retirement age of 67, filing at 62 cuts
the check by 30%. At 63, it is about
And if her husband dies first, the
widow's benefit she could receive later
can also be affected by when each of
them filed. A single panicked night can
follow a family for decades. That is why
I wrote The Quiet Rules. Not to tell you
what to do with your benefits, but so
that when everyone around you is
shouting, "Claim it now!" you already
know the questions to ask before you
click submit. It is waiting for you at
kevinexplains.shop.
Scan the code on your screen or tap the
link in the description or the one
pinned at the top of the comments. Give
it 7 days. If it does not settle your
mind, you get a refund. Because a
decision like Rosemary's does not happen
in an office. It happens at 11:00 at
night, alone, at a laptop with the news
still on in the next room. And if you
have already done what Rosemary did,
there is still a door. Social Security
lets you withdraw your application
within 12 months of first becoming
entitled. You use a form called SSA-521.
The catch is that you must pay back
everything you and your family received
on that record, including any spousal
benefits. But once you do, it is as if
you never filed. Your future check grows
again. You only get to do this once in
your life, so do not use it lightly. But
if you filed in a panic this week, you
have time to think.
Question three. What do Democrats
actually want to do? Here, I am going to
stick to what has been written down and
put in bills, not what anyone said in a
campaign ad. The best-known Democratic
plan is called the Social Security 2100
Act from Representative John Larson of
Connecticut. Its core idea is raising
more money from higher earners. Right
now, you only pay Social Security tax on
wages up to a cap. In 2027, that cap is
Every dollar earned above that is not
taxed for Social Security at all.
Larson's plan would remove that cap, and
it also adds a tax on investment income
for people making more than $400,000.
It also includes benefit increases for
current beneficiaries.
Other Democratic proposals over the
years have gone further. Some would
change the inflation measure used for
your yearly raise to one built around
what older Americans actually spend
money on, like health care and housing.
Some would raise the minimum benefit for
low earners.
These ideas share one direction. More
money in, and in most cases, more money
out. Question four. What do Republicans
actually want to do? Same rule, written
proposals only.
The Republican Study Committee is the
largest group of House Republicans. In
its budget plan released in March of
2024, it called for modest adjustments
to the retirement age for future
retirees to account for longer life
expectancy. It also suggested changing
how benefits are calculated for higher
earners. The group said these changes
would not affect people at or near
retirement. And there is one idea that
has had supporters in both parties,
which tells you it could come back. It
is called chained CPI. It is a different
way of measuring inflation, and it
usually grows a little more slowly than
the measure used today. Switching your
yearly raise to it would mean slightly
smaller raises every year, and over a
long retirement, that adds up. President
Obama included it in one of his budget
proposals, and many Republicans have
supported it, too. It was later dropped.
So, when you hear about changing how
your raise is calculated, ask one
question. Is the new measure bigger or
smaller than the one we have now? The
answer tells you whether it is an
expansion or a cut.
And there is the president himself.
President Trump has said publicly that
he will not cut Social Security. He has
also said, in an earlier interview, that
there is a lot you can do in terms of
entitlements. Since he holds the veto
pen, his position matters as much as
anything Congress writes. Now, here is
something you may not have heard because
it does not fit the usual story.
Raising or lifting the payroll tax cap
is not only a Democratic idea anymore.
This June, Senator Elizabeth Warren, a
Democrat, and Senator Bernie Moreno, a
Republican from Ohio, wrote together in
the New York Times calling on Congress
to lift the cap. And, according to
Representative Larson's office, two
senior House Republicans, Tom Cole and
Lloyd Smucker, have joined calls to have
higher earners pay more. That matters
because a change that needs 60 votes and
a presidential signature is only going
to come from ideas that have friends on
both sides. If you were trying to guess
what eventually passes, watch the ideas
that both parties are already saying out
loud.
If you want to know when any of these
proposals actually moves, subscribe. I
read the bills so you do not have to,
and I will explain each change in plain
English as it happens. And here is one
more thing worth knowing about how these
ideas get judged. Before any serious
Social Security bill moves, Social
Security's own chief actuary usually
scores it. That office estimates how
many years each plan would keep the
program fully funded. When you see a
headline about a new plan, look for that
score. A plan without one is usually
still a talking point. Question five. If
Congress changes Social Security, will
people already collecting be protected?
This is the question that decides
whether you should do anything at all.
And the honest answer is, mostly, but
not always. You will hear people say
"Lawmakers always protect current
retirees." History says it is more
complicated than that. Go back to the
biggest rescue in Social Security's
history.
In April of 1983, President Reagan
signed a set of amendments to save the
program from running out of money. Some
of those changes were phased in very
slowly. The full retirement age started
rising from 65 towards 67, but the
increase did not begin until the year
2000. 17 years of warning. That is the
part people remember. But the same law
did two things to people who were
already retired. It delayed that year's
cost of living raise by 6 months, and
for the first time, it made part of
Social Security benefits subject to
federal income tax for people above
certain income levels. Retirees who had
never paid tax on their checks suddenly
could. 10 years later, in 1993, another
law raised the taxable share to as much
as 85% for higher income retirees. And
here is the detail almost nobody knows.
Those income levels for taxing benefits
were set at $25,000 for a single person
and 32,000 for a married couple. They
have never been raised for inflation. In
1983, only a small share of retirees
paid that tax. Today, Social Security
itself says about 40% of the people
getting benefits have to pay federal
income tax on them. That share grew
because the numbers stood still while
incomes rose. Now, the story I promised
you at the start. In November of 2015,
Congress passed a budget bill that ended
two popular claiming strategies married
couples used to collect more. One was
called file and suspend. People who had
not used it yet had about 6 months until
the end of April 2016 to get in before
the door closed. The other was called
restricted application. That one was
allowed to continue only for people born
in 1953 or earlier. Everyone born in
1954 or later lost it. And changes do
not only go one way. In January of 2025,
President Biden signed the Social
Security Fairness Act, which passed with
votes from both parties. It ended two
rules that had reduced benefits for many
teachers, firefighters, police officers,
and other public workers with pensions.
And it applied backward to benefits
starting in January of 2024. Social
Security later reported sending more
than 3.1 million retroactive payments,
about $17 billion in all. People who
were already retired got a raise from a
law most of them had given up on. So,
when Congress changes Social Security,
current retirees can feel it in either
direction. So, look at the pattern. Big
changes to the retirement age come
slowly with years of warning. But
changes to taxes, raises, and claiming
rules can land on current retirees,
sometimes with only months of notice.
That is why the right answer is not
panic, and it is not ignoring the news
either. It is knowing which kinds of
changes reach people already collecting
and watching for those. Let me show you
what that looks like for a real
decision. Rupert and Gwendolyn are a
made-up couple. Rupert is 65, Gwendolyn
is 62. Rupert was the higher earner.
After the election, Gwendolyn wanted
them both to file right away to lock
things in. But here is what was at
stake. If Rupert dies first, Gwendolyn's
survivor benefit is based largely on
Rupert's check. If Rupert files early,
her widow's check can be permanently
smaller, too. If Rupert waits until 70,
his own check grows by 8% for every year
past his full retirement age. And that
larger check can follow Gwendolyn for
the rest of her life. Now, waiting is
not free. Rupert gives up 5 years of
checks between 65 and 70. If they both
die early, waiting costs them years of
checks. That is the honest trade.
Waiting is a bet on a long life. For a
married couple, it is really a bet that
at least one of you lives a long time,
which is far more likely than either one
alone. So, the real question for that
couple was never what will Congress do.
It was who is likely to live longer and
whose check needs to be bigger when only
one is left. The election did not change
that answer. It only made it louder.
Think about what that decision is worth.
On a check of $3,000 at full retirement
age, waiting to 70 adds about $720 a
month. For a widow who lives to 90, that
can add up to well over $100,000
over her lifetime. That is the kind of
money a rushed decision can leave on the
table. And you never get a letter
telling you it happened. The Quiet Rules
is built for that moment. The
conversation at the kitchen table before
anyone files. You can find it at
kevinexplains.shop
through the code on your screen, the
pinned comment, or the link in the
description. You have 7 days to decide
if it belongs in your home. If it does
not, you get a refund. Because the cost
of guessing wrong does not show up this
year. It shows up years from now in a
smaller envelope in the hands of the
person who outlived you. Before the
calendar, let me make this practical by
age, because the same election means
different things depending on where you
are. If you are already collecting, the
changes most worth watching in the next
2 years may not be to your benefit
amount. They may be to how your benefit
is taxed, how your yearly raise is
measured, and how well the agency
answers your calls. Those are the things
to watch. And there is one move many
people already collecting do not know
about. If you claimed early and have now
reached your full retirement age, you
can ask Social Security to suspend your
benefit. While it is suspended, your
check grows by 8% a year up to age 70.
It is not right for everyone because you
get no check during that time and anyone
collecting on your record is paused,
too. But for a healthy person who
regrets filing early, it is a second
chance most people never hear about. If
you are between 62 and your full
retirement age and have not filed yet,
you are the group most tempted to rush.
You are also the group with the most to
lose from rushing because an early claim
is permanent and a law that does not
exist yet cannot be planned around. Get
your three numbers at 62, full
retirement age, and 70 and make the
decision on those. And if you are
planning to collect a spousal benefit on
your husband's or wife's record, know
this. A spousal benefit stops growing at
your full retirement age. Waiting past
that point adds nothing to it. So, the
rules for when to file on your own
record and when to file as a spouse are
different and mixing them up can cost a
couple real money. If you are in your
50s, you are the group most likely to
feel any change to the retirement age or
benefit formula. Past reforms have
usually protected people near retirement
and phased in for everyone younger. This
is where saving a little more outside
Social Security gives you the most room
later.
Question six. So, what should you
actually watch for over the next 2
years? Here is my calendar. Six things.
But before the six, there is something
happening this month that matters more
to your check than anything Congress
will do this year. Your raise for 2027
is already set at 3.6%.
Social Security says your notice showing
your new amount will appear in your
online account's message center starting
in late November. If you want it online
instead of waiting for the mail, you
need to choose paperless notices by
November 18th. Your Medicare Part B
premium for next year shows up there,
too, and it usually comes out of your
check. Look at both numbers together
because the raise you actually see in
your bank can be smaller than the
headline. Then, in January, you will get
a form called [snorts] the SSA-1099,
showing what you received in 2026 for
your taxes. Keep it. You will need it in
the spring. None of that depends on who
won this week. First, January. The new
Congress is sworn in during the first
days of January. Watch which committees
hold hearings on Social Security. A
hearing does not change your check, but
it tells you which ideas are being taken
seriously and which ones have support
from both sides. Second, watch the
agency itself. Social Security has gone
through major staff cuts and office
changes over the last 2 years. A new
majority usually means more oversight
hearings on phone wait times, field
offices, and how quickly claims and
appeals get processed. That kind of
attention can affect your experience
long before any law changes your
benefit. Third, watch the tax side. The
new senior deduction from last year's
tax law, the extra $6,000 for people 65
and older, is temporary. It is scheduled
to end after the 2028 tax year. Whether
it gets extended, changed, or allowed to
expire will be decided by a Congress
that looks very different from the one
that passed it. If you have been
counting on that deduction to lower your
tax bill, mark 2028 on your calendar.
Fourth, watch for the headlines that are
not real. After every election, videos
and posts appear claiming a new law will
cut your check next month or that you
must claim before some date. Here's the
simple test I use. A real change to
Social Security has a bill number, and
you can look it up on congress.gov.
It gets a score from Social Security's
actuaries, and it gets covered by Social
Security's own website once it becomes
law. If a claim has none of those, it is
not news. It is fear. Fifth, next year's
Trustees report, usually out in the
spring or early summer. If the date
moves closer, the pressure on both
parties grows. If it moves further out,
Washington will feel less urgency. And
sixth, after the 2028 election. Many
analysts expect any real Social Security
fix to come closer to the deadline when
the cost of waiting becomes im- possible
to ignore. Which party holds the White
House and Congress then may matter more
than what happened this week. So, should
you do anything differently because of
this election? Here is my view. Your
claiming decision should be built on
things you can actually know. Your
health, your family history, your
spouse's age and benefits, your savings,
whether you are still working. Not on a
guess about what a Congress might do on
a bill that does not exist yet. And
there is one more reason not to rush. If
you claim before your full retirement
age and keep working, Social Security
can hold back part of your check. In
2027, if you are under full retirement
age all year, it holds back $1 for every
$2 you earn above $25,560.
You get credit for that money later, but
plenty of people file early, keep
working, and then feel like their check
disappeared. Leopold is one more made up
name. He is 63 and earns about $45,000 a
year at a hardware store. He filed early
after the election, thinking he would
bank some extra money. But he earns
almost $20,000 over the limit. So,
Social Security will hold back almost
$10,000 of his benefits next year. He
gets a reduced check for life, and for
now, he barely sees it. If he had waited
until he stopped working, none of that
would have happened. And it helps to
know roughly where the math breaks even.
Studies of claiming usually find that
waiting from 62 to full retirement age
pays off if you live past about your
late 70s.
Waiting from full retirement age to 70
pays off if you live past about your
early 80s. Those are rough numbers and
your own will differ.
But if you are healthy and your parents
lived long, the odds are often on the
side of waiting.
Here is the strongest argument on the
other side. Some people say, "Take it
early because a bird in the hand is
worth two in the bush." If the trust
fund runs short, at least you collected
more years of checks first.
And for some people, that is a
reasonable choice. If your health is
poor, if you need the money now, or if
you are single with no one depending on
your benefit, filing earlier can make
sense. But that is a decision about you.
It is not a decision about this
election. And here is what I believe is
true no matter who wins any election.
Social Security is going to change. The
trustees' numbers do not leave room for
nothing to happen. There is no fix where
nobody pays more and nobody gets less
than promised. Every option is some mix
of the two. And the longer Washington
waits, the bigger and faster that mix
has to be.
I want to hear from you. Did this
election make you rethink when to claim?
Tell me in the comments and tell me your
age. I read them and it helps me decide
which part of this to cover next. Before
you go, here is your short list for this
month. One, if you filed in a panic this
week, remember form SSA-521.
You have 12 months to withdraw your
application as long as you can repay
what you received. Two, log in to your
Social Security account and look at your
estimated benefit at 62, at full
retirement age, and at 70. Write all
three numbers down. It is much harder to
panic when you know what each choice is
worth.
Three, if you are married, have one
conversation about who is likely to live
longer and what the survivor will live
on. Four, if you are still working and
thinking about claiming early, check the
earnings limit before you file. And
five, ignore anyone online who tells you
to claim it now. They do not know what
Congress will do and neither does anyone
else yet. If you are trying to decide
when to claim or you already filed and
are wondering whether to withdraw, write
to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
Tell me your age, your spouse's age, and
what you are weighing. I read every
message, and I will tell you what I
would want to know before deciding. And
if this channel has helped you sleep a
little easier, the description has a
small way to support the research behind
it. Elections change who holds the pen.
They do not change the math, and they do
not change the one decision that is
still yours. When to claim. Make it with
your numbers in front of you, not the
headlines. The Quiet Rules is there to
help you do that calmly, and the pinned
comment will take you straight to it. I
am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check The Quiet Rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: Medicaid Warning for Every Homeowner With a Paid Off House: The Letter Your Kids Get After You Die

segments.text: You paid off your house. 30 years of
payments and now it is yours, free and
clear. And if you ever need long-term
care, that house is the one big thing
Medicaid lets you keep while you are
alive. That is exactly why it is the
thing the state comes looking for after
you die. Not a bank, not the IRS, your
own state with a letter your children
open after the funeral. I want to show
you how that letter works line by line
because almost every family who gets one
says the same thing. "Nobody told us."
And the truth is, it was written down
the whole time. Let me start with a
family. Lucinda is a name I made up, but
her story is one I have seen told again
and again. She is 81. Her house is worth
and it has been paid off since the year
her husband retired. Her husband passed.
She lives alone. Her son Everett lives
40 minutes away. One winter, Lucinda
falls in her kitchen. Hospital, then
rehab. Then the doctor says she cannot
go home alone anymore. So, she moves
into a nursing home. Within a year, her
savings are gone and Medicaid starts
paying her bill. Everyone is relieved.
"The house is safe," the caseworker
tells Everett. "The house does not
count." And the caseworker is right.
While Lucinda is alive, the house does
not count. 22 months later, Lucinda
dies. Six weeks after the funeral,
Everett opens an envelope from the
state. It says the state has a claim
against his mother's estate. The amount
and the only thing in that estate worth
anything is the house. So, how does a
paid off house, a house everyone said
was safe, end up owing almost its whole
value to the state? There are three
lines in that letter that decide
everything. The amount, the deadline,
and one word, estate. By the end of this
video, you will know how to read all
three and what actually keeps a house in
the family. And there is one mistake
married couples make, a one, that hands
the house to the state even after the
law protected it. I will show you that
one, too.
I am Kevin. Every rule and number in
this video comes from government and
research sources, and you will find each
one listed in the description so you can
check every word. This is general
information, not legal advice, and the
rules change from state to state. First,
why this happens at all? Long-term care
means help with ordinary daily things:
bathing, getting dressed, getting out of
bed, getting to the bathroom. And it is
expensive. According to the latest cost
of care survey from CareScout, a shared
room in a nursing home now costs about
a year. A private room is about
Now, here is where most families get
blindsided. Medicare does not pay for
that. Medicare covers a short stretch in
a skilled nursing facility after a
hospital stay, up to 100 days, and only
while you need skilled care. When you
just need help living, Medicare stops.
And even those 100 days come with a
trap. Medicare generally covers that
nursing facility stay only after at
least 3 days as an admitted hospital
patient, not 3 days in a hospital bed
under what is called observation status.
Those can look exactly the same from the
bed. So, if a parent is in the hospital,
ask the staff one direct question. Is my
mother admitted or is she under
observation? The answer can decide who
pays for the rehab that comes next.
Medicaid is the program that pays for
long stays in nursing homes, and
Medicaid is the one with a memory. Since
1993, federal law has required every
state to try to recover what Medicaid
spent on long-term care for people 55
and older. The money comes back from the
person's estate after they die. The
agency Dr. Oz runs, the Centers for
Medicare and Medicaid Services,
describes this on its own website. And
Medicare does not do this, only
Medicaid. So, think of it this way.
Medicaid long-term care works a lot like
a loan against your house with one
difference. A real loan comes with
paperwork that says loan in big letters.
This one comes with an application form
where the warning is in the fine print
and a bill that shows up after you are
gone. And here is why the house feels so
safe while you are alive. Medicaid has
strict limits on savings, often around
$2,000 for a single person. But your
home is usually not counted against you
as long as you say you intend to return
to it or a spouse or dependent still
lives there. There is a cap on home
equity, but in 2025, that cap ranged
from about $730,000
to over 1 million depending on the
state. For most families, the house
never blocks Medicaid at all. So the
house sits there untouched while
everything else gets spent. And by the
end, it is the only thing left in the
estate. The rules that protect the house
during your life are the same rules that
make it the target after. Now, line one
of the letter, the amount.
When Everett saw $187,000,
he did the math. 22 months in a nursing
home. Medicaid usually pays a nursing
home far less than the private price.
So, how did the number get that big?
Because the federal rule is only the
minimum. States must go after nursing
home care, care at home, and the
hospital and prescription costs that
came with it. But according to KFF, 32
states go further. They go after every
Medicaid dollar spent on a person from
age 55 on. Doctor visits, checkups,
everything. And there is a piece almost
nobody has heard of. These days, a lot
of Medicaid runs through private
insurance companies. The state pays the
company a fixed amount every month to
cover you. KFF found that 30 states can
bill your estate for those monthly
payments. And in 10 of them, the state
can recover the whole monthly premium
for every enrolled person, whether you
used any care that month or not. So the
bill is not a list of what your mother
used. In many states, it is a list of
what the state paid on her behalf. That
is how a number grows faster than anyone
expects. And that is why the first thing
Everett should do, and the first thing
you would do, is ask for an itemized
statement, month by month, service by
service. Mistakes happen, and you cannot
challenge a number you cannot see.
Lucinda did everything people tell you
to do. She worked, she paid off her
home, she let Medicaid help when her
money ran out. What she never had was
the one page that says which of her
choices would follow her house after she
was gone. That page is what I wrote The
Quiet Rules for. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
Point your phone at the code on the
screen, or use the link in the
description, or the one in the pinned
comment. Take 7 days with it. If it does
not give your family something it did
not have, you get a refund. Because the
worst time to learn these rules is at
the kitchen table after a funeral, with
a state envelope open, and a house full
of your mother's things.
Line two of the letter, the deadline.
Everett's letter gave him 60 days, and
60 days sounds like a countdown to
losing the house. Usually, it is not.
That window is often the time you have
to respond, ask questions, or apply for
a waiver. And this is the line most
families read wrong. Federal law says
states must waive recovery when it would
cause undue hardship. Federal law does
not define hardship, so every state
writes its own version. KFF looked at
all of them. 49 states offer some kind
of hardship waiver. 35 will waive it
when the property is the family's only
way of earning a living, like a family
farm or a small business run out of the
home. And 15 states offer a waiver for a
home of modest value. Seven of those
states, including California, Michigan,
New York, and Virginia, define a modest
home as one worth half or less of the
average home in that county. So, in some
places, a small paid-off house in a
pricey county may not be chased at all.
But you have to ask. Nobody grants a
waiver you never applied for. And the
odds are better than people think. The
group that advises Congress on Medicaid
is called the Medicaid and CHIP Payment
and Access Commission. When it studied
10 states, hardship approval rates
ranged from about 29% in New York to 95%
in Iowa. Same federal law, very
different outcomes, which is one more
reason to know which state you were
dealing with before you answer that
letter. And while you are reading that
letter, look for one more thing. Every
state has to set a threshold where
chasing an estate is not worth the cost.
Smaller states are often left alone. Ask
what your state's threshold is.
Sometimes the answer ends the
conversation. There is also something
the letter cannot do. It cannot touch
the house while certain people are still
alive. Federal law says the state cannot
recover while there is a surviving
spouse or a child under 21 or a child of
any age who is blind or disabled. That
sounds like the house is safe if you are
married. It is not quite that simple. In
many states, the bill is not erased. It
waits. When the surviving spouse dies,
the claim can come due. And while a
person is still alive in a nursing home,
some states can place a lien on the
house if they decide that person is not
coming home. But they cannot do it if a
spouse, a young child, a disabled child,
or a brother or sister who co-owns the
home lives there. And there is a quieter
problem families face while a parent is
still alive in a nursing home. The house
sits empty.
Someone still has to pay the property
taxes and the insurance and keep the
pipes from freezing. And many homeowners
policies limit coverage once a house has
been vacant for a stretch, often 60
days. Call the insurance company and
tell them the house is vacant. A burst
pipe in an empty house with the wrong
policy can cost more than the state ever
will.
And what if the family decides to sell
the house while the parent is alive on
Medicaid? Then the house turns into
cash. Cash counts. The parent can lose
Medicaid until that money is spent down,
often on the nursing home itself.
