Renting it out is not a clean fix,
either. In most states, that rent counts
as the parent's income and most of it
goes to the nursing home bill. None of
this means you should never sell. It
means you decide with the rules in front
of you, not after. Here is the part
where most videos stop. They tell you
about the letter, and they tell you to
get a lawyer. I want to go further,
because the most important line in that
letter is the third one. One word,
estate.
When you hear estate, you probably think
of what goes through probate after you
die. The things in your name alone with
no beneficiary. In some states, that is
all the state can reach. California
narrowed its rules in 2017, so it now
recovers only from the probate estate,
and it stopped going after the estates
of surviving spouses. Massachusetts cut
its program back to the federal minimum
in 2024. But federal law gives states
the option to use a much wider
definition. Under that wider definition,
the estate can include a house that
passed to your children outside probate,
a home in a living trust, a home held
jointly with a right of survivorship,
even a home that passed by a transfer on
death deed. Things families were told
would skip probate, and they do. They
just may not skip this. So, before you
count on any paperwork, ask one
question. Does my state use the probate
definition or the wider one? The answer
changes which plans actually work. And
that brings us to the plans people count
on. Three of them usually fail. The
first is a will. A will does not protect
assets from estate recovery. A will just
says who gets the house. It does not say
the state goes second. The second is a
regular living trust, the kind most
people set up so their family can skip
probate. While you are alive, Medicaid
treats that trust as if everything in it
is still yours, because you can change
it or take it back. And after you die,
in a state using the wider definition,
the house inside it can still be
reached. The trust did its job. It
skipped the court. It just was not built
for this.
The third is giving the house to your
children. This is the one I hear most.
Just put it in the kids' names. But
Medicaid looks back 5 years at anything
you gave away. If you gave the house
away inside that window, you get a
penalty. A stretch of time when Medicaid
will not pay for your care at all. Here
is how the math works. Your state
divides the value of the gift by its
average monthly cost of a nursing home.
So, say you gave your children a house
and your state uses about $9,600
a month. That is 25 months with no
Medicaid help. 25 months of a bill
nobody budgeted for. And the clock on
that penalty does not start until you
have applied and otherwise qualify. And
there is a hidden cost. When you gift a
house, your children usually inherit
your original purchase price for tax
purposes. When they inherit it after you
die, the cost is usually reset to the
value at your death. So, a gifted house
can carry a much bigger capital gains
tax bill when they sell. Two problems,
one signature. And there is a fourth
plan that is not really a plan. Waiting.
[clears throat]
According to the federal government's
own long-term care website, someone
turning 65 today has almost a 70% chance
of needing some kind of long-term care.
And nobody gets a 5-year warning before
a fall or a diagnosis. The look-back is
5 years. The warning is usually 5
minutes. If this is helping you see your
own house differently, subscribe. These
rules are moving and I will keep walking
through every change as it happens in
plain English. So, what does work? Let
me give you the moves that elder law
attorneys actually use and the catch on
each one. The first is the one almost
nobody has heard of and it might be the
most powerful. It is called the
caregiver child exception. Let me tell
this one as a story, too.
Percival is another made-up name. He is
56. Three years ago, his father started
forgetting the stove was on. So,
Percival moved back into his childhood
home. He cooked, he managed the pills,
he drove his father to every
appointment. For more than 2 years, he
was the reason his father did not need a
nursing home. Federal law has a rule for
exactly that son. Say a child lived in
the parent's home for at least 2 years
right before the parent went into a
nursing home. And say that child's care
is what kept the parent at home. Then,
the parent can transfer the house to
that child. No penalty, no 5-year wait.
And once the house is his, there is
nothing in his father's name for the
state to recover. But here is the catch,
and it is the reason this story has two
endings. In the first ending, Percival
kept nothing on paper. No doctor's
letter, no care log, nothing showing he
lived there. When his father needed a
nursing home, the state asked for proof.
He could not give it. The exception was
there. He could not use it. In the
second ending, Percival kept a simple
notebook. The date, what he did, the
medicine, the appointments.
He changed his driver's license to his
father's address. And he asked his
father's doctor for a letter saying that
without his care, his father would have
needed a facility. Same son, same
father, same house. The only difference
was a notebook and a letter. If someone
in your family is already doing this
kind of care, start that notebook this
week. There are a few more transfers
federal law allows without a penalty.
The second move is an irrevocable trust.
That is a trust you cannot change or
take back once you sign it. If it is set
up correctly and the house goes into it
more than 5 years before you apply for
Medicaid, the house is generally no
longer yours in Medicaid's eyes.
The catch is in the wording. If you keep
too much control, the state may still
treat it as yours.
This is not a form you download. This is
work for an elder law attorney. The
third move is a long-term care
partnership policy. Most states have a
partnership program. These are private
long-term care insurance policies that
come with a special promise. Every
dollar the policy pays for your care
protects a dollar of your assets from
Medicaid. That protection applies when
you apply, and in most states, when the
state looks at your estate later, too.
So, if your policy pays 150,000 dollars
toward your care, about 150,000 dollars
of what you own is shielded. The catch
is that these policies are easier to buy
when you are younger and healthier. The
fourth move only exists in a few states.
Florida, Texas, and Michigan are the
best known. It is called a ladybird
deed. You keep full control of the house
while you live and it passes to your
children automatically when you die
outside probate.
In a state that only recovers from the
probate estate, that can matter a great
deal. In a state with the wider
definition, it may not. The catch is
that it all depends on your state's law
and some states do not allow the deed at
all.
And the fifth move costs nothing. Write
down what is true right now. Who lives
in the house? Who takes care of whom?
Who owns what share? Because almost
every exception I just described depends
on proof and proof is easiest to collect
before anyone needs it. I want to go
back to Everett for a moment. $187,000.
When he called a lawyer, the first
question was whether anyone had ever
lived with his mother and cared for her.
Nobody had.
The second was whether the house was
worth less than half the county average.
It was not.
The third was whether she ever bought a
partnership policy. She had not.
Three doors. All three closed years
before the letter came. If your family
could open even one of them, now is when
it happens, not after.
The Quiet Rules is written for the years
before that letter [snorts] when every
door is still open. You can find it at
kevinexplains.shop
through the code on your screen, the
pinned comment, or the link in the
description. You have 7 days to read it.
If it is not worth keeping, you get a
refund because the alternative is a
stack of family photos in boxes and a
for sale sign on the lawn of the house
your mother paid off. And this is where
I promised you the mistake married
couples make. A transfer to a spouse has
no penalty. So, when one spouse goes
into a nursing home, many couples move
the house into the healthy spouse's
name. That part is right. But then
nobody updates the healthy spouse's
will. And sometimes the healthy spouse
dies first, which happens more often
than families expect. If that will still
leaves everything to the spouse in the
nursing home, the house goes straight
back into the name of the person on
Medicaid. Now, it can count against
them, and later it can land in the
estate the state recovers from. The fix
is a new will for the healthy spouse,
written with an elder law attorney that
does not leave the house outright to the
spouse in care. One meeting, one
signature. It can be the difference
between keeping the house and losing it.
To a spouse, to a child under 21, to a
child who is blind or disabled, and to a
brother or sister who already owns part
of the home and lived there for at least
a year before you went into care.
Now, something changed in the last year
and a half that makes all of this more
urgent. In July of 2025, President Trump
signed the law most people call the one
big beautiful bill. KFF's analysis of
the Congressional Budget Office
estimates puts the cut to federal
Medicaid spending at about $911
billion over years. That law did not
change estate recovery itself, but it
changed two things around it. The first
starts this January. Right now, Medicaid
can usually pay bills from up to 3
months before you applied. It is called
retroactive coverage. Starting January
1st, 2027, for most people 65 and older,
that window drops to 2 months. One less
month of bills covered. At about $315 a
day for a shared room, 1 month of
nursing home care is roughly $9,500.
So, if your family waits to apply after
a parent goes into a nursing home, that
is how much more of the bill can be left
behind. If a parent is heading into
care, apply quickly. And who pays a
nursing home bill that Medicaid will not
cover? The resident's savings. And when
the savings are gone, the facility
starts asking the family. The second
change starts in 2028. Today, each state
sets a cap on how much home equity you
can have and still get Medicaid
long-term care. 12 states, including
California, New York, and New Jersey
currently allow more than $1 million.
Starting in 2028, no state can go above
$1 million. And that number does not
rise with inflation. Not next year, not
in 20 years, unless a spouse, a child
under 21, or a disabled child lives in
the home. Now, think about what that
means over time. A cap that never moves
on houses that keep rising. Every year,
more paid-off homes will cross that
line. And when the home is worth more
than the cap, the owner may have to
borrow against it or sell it before
Medicaid helps at all. One detail
matters here. The cap is on equity, not
on the price of the house. Equity is
what the house is worth minus what is
owed on it. So, a paid-off house hits
that limit first. A house with a
mortgage, a home equity line, or a
reverse mortgage has less equity and may
stay under it. That does not mean you
should borrow against your home to
qualify. It means that if your house is
worth close to a million dollars, this
is a conversation to have with an elder
law attorney before 2028, not after.
Here is my view, and I want to be clear
that this part is opinion. States are
about to have less federal Medicaid
money. Estate recovery is one of the few
ways a state can raise money without
cutting care for someone who is still
alive. So, I expect the states that
already do this to lean on it harder.
Some states are going the other way,
like California and Massachusetts, but
the pressure points in one direction,
toward the house. And there is one more
thing that shows up in the news around
this time of year. You may have seen
posts claiming that a new rule in
January will force adult children to pay
for their parents' nursing home care.
There is no new federal rule like that.
But, here is what is real, and few
people know it. Many states still have
old laws on the books called filial
responsibility laws. They say adult
children can be responsible for an
indigent parent's basic care. Usually,
they sit unused, but not always. In
2012, a Pennsylvania court upheld a
ruling that made a son responsible for
about $93,000
of his mother's nursing home bill. The
case is known as Pittis.
His mother had moved out of the country.
The nursing home sued the son and won.
That case is rare, but it is a reminder
that when nobody plans, the bill does
not disappear. It looks for the nearest
family member with a bank account. Now,
I want to give you the other side
because this rule has real defenders.
Medicaid paid for that care. That is
taxpayer money. The people who defend
estate recovery say it keeps the program
alive for people who truly have nothing.
They say it is fair that someone with a
valuable house pays something back
instead of passing that house on while
taxpayers covered the nursing home. That
is a serious argument. And here is the
other side of that argument. Estate
recovery raises very little. According
to KFF, states collected about $733
million in 2019, which is still the most
recent national count. That covered
about 1/10 of 1% of Medicaid spending.
And in 2021, the commission that advises
Congress on Medicaid recommended making
estate recovery optional for states.
Their concern was who it hits hardest.
Families with money and a lawyer tend to
find legal ways around it. Families
whose only real asset is the house
usually do not. That is the part that
bothers me. A rule meant to be fair ends
up landing on the families who did
everything right, paid off their homes,
and never heard the rule exists.
In January of this year, Representative
Jan Schakowsky reintroduced a bill to
end the federal estate recovery
requirement. Whether it ever moves, I
cannot tell you. I would not plan your
house around it. And if a parent on
Medicaid has already passed, here is
what the first month should look like.
First, do not sell, transfer, or rent
out the house in a hurry. Moving it
before the state's claim is settled can
create a bigger problem than the claim
itself. Second, find the Medicaid
application your parent signed. It
usually included a notice about estate
recovery, and it shows which state
program you are dealing with. Third,
keep every receipt for what the family
pays for the house and the funeral. In
many states, reasonable funeral costs
and certain expenses of handling the
estate are paid before the state's
claim. Fourth, if a spouse, a young
child, or a disabled child is still
living, tell the state right away. That
alone can pause everything. And fifth,
write down every date on every letter.
Deadlines in estate recovery are real,
and missing one can cost you a waiver
you would have won. I want to know where
you stand. Tell me in the comments. Has
your family ever received a letter like
Everett's? Or are you planning ahead
right now? I read every comment, and it
helps me decide what to cover next. So,
let me turn all of this into something
you can do, not a lecture. Five
questions to ask at your own kitchen
table this month. Question one, whose
name is on the house and how? Alone,
joint, in a trust, or with a
transfer-on-death deed? Write it down.
It decides what the word estate means
for your family. Question two, does our
state use the probate definition of
estate or the wider one? Your state
Medicaid agency's estate recovery page
will usually tell you, or an elder law
attorney can answer it in one meeting.
Question three, is anyone already doing
the caring? A child living in the home,
a sibling who co-owns it? If so, start
the notebook, the address change, and
ask for the doctor's letter now.
Question four, is there time? If you are
healthy and more than 5 years away from
needing care, the irrevocable trust and
the partnership policy are still on the
table. Every year you wait, one of those
options gets harder. Question five, if a
letter ever comes, who reads it first?
Make sure someone in your family knows
three words: itemized statement,
hardship waiver, and deadline, so they
answer inside the window. And if you are
a family that already received a letter,
do not ignore it, and do not panic. Ask
for the itemized bill. Ask about every
waiver and every deferral your state
offers, and speak to an elder law
attorney before the response window
closes. If your family is facing one of
these letters, or you are trying to
figure out which of these moves fits
your house, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
Tell me your state and what you are
dealing with. I read every message, and
I will tell you which question I would
ask first. And if this channel has ever
saved your family a hard surprise, the
description has a small way to support
the research behind it. Lucinda's house
was safe for 22 months. It was safe
right up until the day it was not, and
everything that could have kept it in
the family had to happen years earlier
while she was still standing in her own
kitchen. The house you paid off can
still be the house you leave behind. It
just needs a plan before it needs a
lawyer. The Quiet Rules is there for
that planning, and the pinned comment
will take you to it. I am Kevin. Thanks
for watching. Do not forget to check The
Quiet Rules at kevinexplains.shop.

title: 5 THINGS THAT MAKE BANKS QUESTION YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY DEPOSIT: Is Yours One of Them?

segments.text: Your social security lands in your bank
on the same day every month. In most
months, nothing happens. But since June,
every bank and credit union in America
has had to watch incoming electronic
payments for fraud. Not every payment,
the ones that look wrong. And there are
five ordinary, completely honest
situations that make a social security
deposit look wrong to a bank's computer.
If you are in one of them, your deposit
can be slowed down, questioned, or sent
back to the government. Nobody mails you
this list. So I made one. Recently, I
made a video about banks flagging social
security deposits, and it has been
watched close to half a million times.
Some of you asked a sharp question in
the comments. Does this rule even apply
to social security? You deserve a
precise answer. So here it is before
anything else. The rule does not name
social security. Your bank is not
required to screen every deposit one by
one. And I found nothing in the rule
that carves social security out either.
So the real question was never whether
banks flag social security. It is which
deposits look wrong to a machine and how
to make sure yours never does. And this
matters more than it did a few years
ago. In March of 2025, President Trump
signed an executive order telling the
Treasury to stop issuing paper checks
for federal payments starting September
30th of that year with limited
exceptions. So almost every social
security payment now travels
electronically through exactly the
system this rule watches. Here is how
this works. I am going to walk you
through five situations. Keep count as
we go. Every situation that describes
you or a parent whose money you help
with is one point.
At the end, I will tell you what your
number means and what to do this week if
it is two or more. And after the fifth
one, I will show you the one thing this
rule tells your bank to do that it never
tells you. I am Kevin. Every rule and
number in this video is listed with its
source in the description so you can
check every word. This is general
information about how the rules work,
not or financial advice, and your own
bank's policies have the final say.
First, what a flag actually is, because
the word sounds scarier than the thing.
A flag is not a frozen check. It is an
alert. Some pattern in your account
trips a rule and the alert lands in a
review queue at your bank. The Federal
Reserve even offers banks a service that
sends alerts like these based on
thresholds each bank sets for itself.
Then a person or another rule takes a
look. And a flag is about patterns, not
people. The system does not know you are
74 and honest. It only knows what your
account did this month compared with
every month before. An alert can end
right there with nothing happening to
you at all. Some end with a call or a
text. A few end with a delay or a
payment sent back. What changed this
year is who has to do the watching. In
March, the rule started with the biggest
banks. Since June, it covers every bank
and credit union in the country, no
matter how small.
Situation one. The deposit lands in an
account without the right name on it.
This one usually starts with love. Your
mother stopped driving to the bank or
never trusted online banking, so her
social security goes into your account
and you pay her bills from there. It
feels practical. It is also against the
rules. Federal Treasury rules say a
federal benefit payment must go into an
account in the name of the person being
paid.
The regulation uses those exact words,
in the name of the recipient.
A joint account with your mother's name
on it qualifies. An account with only
your name on it does not.
And notice where that rule comes from.
Nacha's own guidance says the new bank
rule does not require a formal name
matching process at all.
The name rule is the Treasury's and it
applies whether your bank checks or not.
Now look at that account from the bank's
side. Nacha, the organization that
writes the rules for these electronic
payments, gave banks a short list of
patterns to watch. One of them, in its
own words, is a series of similar credit
entries received within a short period
of time, such as multiple payroll or
benefit payments. Now look at what lands
in your account every month. Your own
paycheck or benefit, your mother's
social security, maybe your father's
too. Several people's federal money
arriving in one person's account. That
is the kind of pattern the rule tells
banks to notice because it is also what
an account collecting stolen benefits
looks like. And the bank can see the
names. The electronic payment that
carries your mother's social security
also carries her name, not yours.
Want to check your own setup in 30
seconds? On most bank statements, a
social security deposit shows the
letters SSA, then the word trez, short
for treasury, then the number 310. Count
how many of those land in your account
each month and whose money each one is.
Marguerite is a name I made up for a
very common family. She is 58. For two
years, both of her parents' social
security payments went into her own
checking account. Then her bank's fraud
team called. Why were federal deposits
for two other people landing in her
account every month? She could explain
it. She could not prove it on that call.
While they reviewed it, the account was
restricted and that week the aide who
helps her father did not get paid on
time. There is a second risk families
rarely see coming. If a parent passes
away and a payment still lands in that
account, the government will take it
back from whatever account it reached.
It is not part of the estate. It has to
be returned. And if you are thinking, I
have power of attorney, so I am covered,
you are not. A report from the
Congressional Research Service spells it
out. A power of attorney does not give
you authority over someone's social
security payments unless social security
also appoints you as their payee. When
Marguerite's bank called, she did not
need a lawyer. She needed the rules
already in her head before the phone
rang. So a bank review would feel like a
question and not like an accusation. If
you help a parent with money or a grown
child helps you, keep the quiet rules
within reach. It lives at
kevinexplains.shop.
Aim your phone's camera at the code on
your screen or tap the first link in the
description, or the one I pinned under
this video. Look through it for seven
days. If you would not hand it to your
own family, you get a refund.
The fraud team's call never comes at a
good time. It comes when the aid is
standing at the door waiting to be paid.
So here is the clean way to set this up.
If your parent can still make decisions,
add them as an owner of the account the
money lands in. Then the account is in
the recipient's name and the rule is
satisfied. But treat that as a real
decision. A joint owner generally has
rights to the whole account, and in some
situations, one owner's creditors can
reach it. Ask your bank which kind of
account fits your family before you
sign.
If your parent can no longer manage
money, the official route is to become a
representative payee through Social
Security. Its own staff manual spells
out how that account should be titled.
The beneficiary's name, then the word
by, then the payee's name, then the
words representative payee. The manual's
own example is Peter Rock by Mary Stone,
representative payee.
Being a payee also comes with duties.
Social Security expects the money to be
spent on the beneficiary, any extra to
be saved for them, and records to be
kept. Some payees have to report how the
money was used, and a payee can be made
to repay money that was misused. And one
detail that trips up families. A husband
or wife who is the payee and lives in
the same home can sometimes use their
own checking account. A grown son or
daughter generally cannot. Their account
has to carry the parent's name. If you
and your spouse both get Social Security
and both payments go into your joint
account, relax. Both names are on it.
That is exactly what the rule expects.
If your parent has no account at all,
open one in their own name. A basic
account at a bank or credit union works,
and so does the Treasury's Direct
Express card. And if your parent lives
in a nursing home, the rules even allow
the payment to go into the facility's
resident trust account, which exists for
exactly this purpose.
Situation two. The deposit that is
suddenly much bigger than usual. The
second pattern on Naha's list is a high
dollar transaction that is atypical for
the receiving account. In plain English,
a deposit that looks nothing like what
that account usually gets. Your normal
monthly payment will never do this, not
even January's raise. Social Security
announced a 3.6% increase for 2027. On a
$2,000 check, that is $72 a month. No
computer blinks at that, but some Social
Security deposits are big. Back pay
after a disability approval that took a
year,
survivor benefits that took months to
process. Last year, Social Security sent
more than 3.1 million retroactive
payments under the Social Security
Fairness Act, about $17 billion in all.
For a lot of retired teachers,
firefighters, and their spouses, that
was one of the biggest deposits their
account had ever seen.
And one more that surprises people. If
you are already past your full
retirement age when you apply, you can
ask for up to 6 months of benefits paid
back in one lump sum. The cost is a
smaller monthly check for life because
those months count as if you had started
earlier. Here is how that plays out for
a man we will call Augustus. He applied
at 68 and asked for the 6 months back.
His regular deposit is about $2,400.
One Wednesday, $14,400
lands instead. That same week, he moves
most of it into an investment account he
had just opened online because he read
that money should never sit idle. To a
fraud system, that week has two warning
signs. A deposit unlike anything that
account has seen and money leaving for a
brand new destination. His bank paused
the transfer and called him.
Augustus did nothing wrong. He just did
two unusual things in the same week. The
fix is simple and almost nobody does it.
Keep the letter.
When Social Security approves a lump sum
or back pay, it mails you a notice that
explains the amount. Keep the paper with
your checkbook and a photo of it on your
phone. If your bank calls, you are not
explaining a mystery. You are reading
from a letter.
And when a big deposit lands, give it a
few days before you move it somewhere
new.
One more thing about a big back payment
because it can follow you to tax season.
The IRS says that when a lump sum covers
earlier years, you can figure the
taxable part using your income from
those earlier years instead of piling it
all onto this year.
It is called the lump sum election and
it is in IRS publication 915.
Your form from Social Security for that
year breaks the payment down by year. So
whoever does your taxes has what they
need. And if you get supplemental
security income, there is one more rule
worth knowing.
SSI has a strict limit on how much you
can have in the bank.
But Social Security's own manual says
retroactive SSI and Social Security
payments are left out of that count for
nine calendar months after the month you
receive them. So a big back payment does
not knock you off SSI right away. You
have nine months to use it.
Mark the date on your calendar because
on month 10, whatever is left starts to
count.
Situation three. The deposit that lands
in a brand new account or in an old one
that has been asleep for years. Not just
list names both, a new account and a
dormant account. The reason is blunt. A
new account or one nobody has used in
years is where stolen money tends to be
sent. That is also why Social Security
tightened its own side in 2025 and made
its identity checks stricter. The surest
ways to change your direct deposit are
through your own online account after
proving who you are or in person at an
office.
Millicent and Thurston are a made-up
couple with a very real story.
They moved this summer to be near their
son, opened accounts at a credit union
near his house and switched their Social
Security. They closed their old bank the
same afternoon.
When the first deposit landed in the new
account, they spent it that same day on
the movers, the first month's rent, and
a new mattress. A brand new account, its
first federal deposit, and almost all of
it gone within hours. The credit union
system did exactly what it was built to
do. It looked twice. If you are
switching banks, do it in this order.
Open the new account. Change your direct
deposit yourself with your own login or
in person. Leave the old account open
until one full payment has landed in the
new one. If a payment lands in an
account you already closed, it bounces
back to the government and you wait
while Social Security sends it again.
And when you open the new account, tell
the bank your Social Security will be
arriving there. A note on your file
costs nothing and it gives the person
reviewing an alert something to read.
And if you are pointing your deposit at
an old account you have not touched in
years, wake it up first. Use it for a
month. A small deposit, a small bill
paid. An account that suddenly comes
back to life with federal money is one
of the patterns these systems watch. One
more lock on this door. If you have
never created your own online Social
Security account, do it before someone
else does. Criminals have opened
accounts in other people's names to
redirect their payments. Once yours
exists with your own phone and email on
it, that door is much harder to use. And
for the strongest lock, Social Security
lets you block electronic access to your
record. It also shuts you out of your
own online account until you lift it. So
it is a tradeoff.
If you want this kind of warning before
your bank surprises you, subscribe now.
These rules are still changing and I
will keep explaining each change in
plain English as it happens.
Situation four. The deposit that leaves
as fast as it arrived. Nacha's list also
warns about an account acting as a mule.
A mule account is one that takes in
money and passes it on, usually for
criminals. And here is the cruel part.
Some of the people running these
accounts have no idea they are doing it.
They are older Americans who were told
they were protecting their own money.
The Federal Trade Commission looked at
reports from older adults who lost
$10,000 or more to imposters.
In 2020, there were 1,790
of those reports. In 2024, there were
more than four times as many. The FTC
found these calls tend to open with one
of three lies. Someone is using your
accounts. Your information is being used
to commit crimes or there is a security
problem with your computer.
Then comes the instruction. Move your
money and we will keep it safe. And the
money leaves in a few predictable ways.
In those reports of $10,000 or more, a
third went out as cryptocurrency, most
often through Bitcoin machines. One in
five went by bank transfer. About one in
six was handed over as cash. And among
losses of $100,000 or more, about one in
five was paid in gold. D'Amelda is not
her real name. She is 76. A man who said
he worked in her bank's fraud department
called her on a Monday. He said
criminals were going to take her social
security the moment it landed and he
would walk her through moving it to a
protected account. On Wednesday, her
payment arrived. By lunchtime, she had
sent it along with part of her savings,
$18,000 in all, to the account he gave
her. To her bank system, her account
suddenly looked like a pass through. To
D'Amelda, she was simply following her
bank's instructions. The next morning,
the caller told her to send the rest.
This time, her bank stopped the transfer
and called her. The flag could not save
the first $18,000. It saved everything
that was left. The FTC's advice is one
short sentence. Don't move money to
protect it. Make that your rule today,
not on the day of the call. No real bank
and no government office will ever ask
you to move your money to keep it safe.
If anyone does, hang up and call the
number printed on the back of your card.
A real fraud department may ask you to
confirm a transaction, yes or no. It
will not ask you for a code it just
texted you and it will not ask you to
move your money. And if it has already
happened, minutes matter. Call your
bank's fraud line right away and ask
them to try to stop or recall the
transfer. Then report it to the FBI at
ic3.gov
and to the Federal Trade Commission at
reportfraud.ftc.gov.
And if someone asks you to receive money
and send it on for them, a sweetheart
online, a new employer, a stranger with
a prize, anyone, stop. Police warnings
list exactly where these requests come
from. Online job ads, social media,
investment pitches, prize notices, and
dating sites. That is how ordinary
people end up running a mule account.
The Boston Police Department warned in a
public alert last year that being a
money mule is illegal, regardless of age
or intent. People who move money for
criminals can face charges and can be
held responsible for paying the victims
back. And when a bank closes an account
for that, the record can follow you to
the next bank. $18,000.
Imelda did not lose it because she was
careless. She lost it because the one
rule that would have saved her was not
in her head when a calm voice told her
to move it.
I put the rules for moments like that. A
voice on the phone, a bank account under
pressure, a family's money at stake into
the quiet rules. You can find it at
kevinexplains.shop.
The code on the screen is the quickest
way in, and the same link sits in the
description and in the comment pinned at
the top.
Read it over seven days at your own
pace. If it does not change what you
would say on that call, you get a
refund.
A call like Imelda's never sounds like a
scam. It sounds like your bank on a
quiet Monday telling you it is there to
help.
Situation five. The deposit that lands
on a card or an app instead of at a
bank. Millions of people now get their
social security on a prepaid card or
inside a finance app on their phone.
That is allowed. But the Treasury
attaches four conditions, and one of
them surprises people. The account has
to be held at an insured bank or credit
union. It has to be set up so the
insurance covers your money, not just
the company's. It has to give you the
same protections the law gives any
prepaid account. And it cannot be tied
to a loan that repays itself
automatically when your benefit arrives.
In other words, no lender is allowed to
stand at the door of your deposit and
take its cut first. That condition goes
back to a Treasury rule from 2010,
written so a lender could not hand out
an advance and then repay itself from
your next benefit the moment it arrived.
Why does the bank behind the app matter
so much? In 2024, a company called
Synapse, which sat between dozens of
finance apps and the banks holding their
customers' money, went bankrupt.
That summer, about $158 million owed to
customers was still frozen, and tens of
millions could not be accounted for at
all. People who thought they had a bank
account found out they had an app.
So, if your Social Security lands in an
app, find the name of the actual bank
that holds the money. It is in the fine
print, usually near the words member
FDIC. If you cannot find it, that tells
you something.
For most people, the safest home for a
Social Security deposit is a bank or
credit union with a phone number that a
person answers. Mortimer is not his real
name. He is 71, and he moved his Social
Security to a finance app because it
paid him two days early. One month, the
app's system put his account under
review. There was no branch to visit and
no phone number, only a chat window that
answered in two days. His rent was due
in one. Nothing he did was wrong. He had
simply put his only income somewhere
with no door to knock on. And if you use
the Direct Express card, a change is on
the way. The paper check order pushed
almost everyone toward electronic
payment, and that card is one of the
main ways people without a bank account
get paid. The Treasury chose Fifth Third
Bank to run the program, and current
cardholders are being moved over in
phases. Keep using your current card
until the new one arrives. Then activate
the new card right away so you can reach
your next deposit. And if you would
rather have your payment go to a bank
account, you can ask to switch to direct
deposit at any time. If you have
questions about the move, the Direct
Express number today is 1-800-333-1795.
Now, what really happens when one of
these deposits gets a second look? This
is where a lot of videos, mine included,
can make it sound worse or better than
it is. So, here are the facts as the
rules state them. One, your bank is not
required to inspect each deposit before
it reaches you. NACHA says plainly that
the rule does not require monitoring
before posting. So, a review can happen
after the money is already in your
account when a pattern shows up.
Two, if a bank does suspect a deposit,
it is allowed to slow the money down
while it looks, but it is expected to
act promptly, either releasing the money
or sending it back, and the delay is
supposed to be short and on the record.
It does not get to quietly keep it.
Three, if the deposit is sent back, it
returns to the government, not to you.
Then Social Security has to send it
again, and that can take a while. Four,
and this is the part I promised you at
the start. When a bank delays a payment
it suspects, NACHA tells it to promptly
notify the bank that sent the money, the
other bank. NACHA's guidance on that
notice does not say a word about telling
you. So, you may learn about a flag only
when your money does not show up. That
is why the most useful thing you can do
when a deposit is late is call your bank
first at the number on the back of your
card. Ask one question. Did a federal
benefit payment arrive for me and was
any of it held or returned? Write down
who you spoke to and the date. If it was
returned, call Social Security next and
tell them exactly what the bank told
you. And if the bank says a payment is
being held, ask for two dates, the date
it arrived and the date it will be
released or returned. A bank may not be
able to tell you why it flagged
something. It should be able to tell you
when. And if your bank calls you first,
expect a few plain questions. Do you
recognize this payment? Did you make
this transfer yourself? Is anyone
telling you what to say right now?
Answer them honestly, even if a voice on
another phone has told you not to.
Anyone who coaches you to mislead your
own bank is the criminal in the room.
The person asking those questions is
trying to keep your money where it
belongs. While you are at it, build what
I call a two-minute folder, one envelope
or one folder on your phone with
everything a bank could ask about your
deposits. A benefit verification letter,
which you can download from your online
social security account anytime, showing
exactly what you receive. Any award
notice for back pay or a lump sum.
If you are someone's payee, the letter
from social security naming you. The
name of each bank your benefits go to
and the last four digits of each
account. And the fraud number from the
back of your card written in ink. If
your bank offers it, add a trusted
contact to your account. Someone the
bank may call if it cannot reach you or
if it is worried about you.
When a bank calls with a question, the
person with that folder answers in two
minutes. The person without it can spend
days proving who they are. Keep it
somewhere a family member could find it,
too. One more thing these rules cover,
and almost nobody connects it to
retirees.
The same rule book now tells banks to
watch for payments sent under what it
calls false pretenses.
That means someone pretending to be a
person you already pay.
A contractor emails new bank details for
the final payment. A lawyer's office
says the closing money should go to a
different account.
A grandchild's college sends a new
payment link.
If any payment instruction changes by
email or text, call the person or the
office at a number you already had
before a single dollar moves.
The bank on the receiving end is now
supposed to watch for these, and your
own bank may slow a payment like that
down, too.
When it does, it is doing you a favor.
So, what is your number? Count it now.
Situation one, someone else's money in
your account or yours in someone else's.
Two, a big one-time deposit. Three, a
new account or one that has been quiet
for years. Four, money that leaves as
fast as it lands.
Five, a card or an app.
If your number is zero, your deposit
looks exactly like what it is, and you
can stop worrying about this rule. Just
keep the bank's number by your phone and
build the folder anyway.
If your number is one, fix that one
thing before January. Not all five, just
the one. One is not a warning sign. It
is a to-do item. If your number is two
or more, your deposits fit the patterns
these systems were built to notice even
though you have done nothing wrong. Pick
the fix that matches each situation. For
situation one, the right name on the
account. For two, the letter in your
folder. For three, the right order when
you switch. For four, the FTC's rule.
Don't move money to protect it. For
five, the name of the real bank behind
your card or app. Then make one call to
your bank this week. Ask whether they
can note on your account why your
deposits look the way they do. Then
build the folder this weekend. You are
