wrong house.
Where does that leave you?
If you live in a market that is still
rising, take your time and do it right.
If you live in one that is falling,
decide quickly and price honestly.
Either way, the worst choice is the one
made for you by a buyer who knew more
than you did. Before anyone puts a sign
in your yard, ask any agent you are
thinking of hiring five questions and
get the answers in writing.
One,
will my home be on the multiple listing
service on the first day where every
buyer and every website can see it?
Two,
will you bring me every offer in
writing, even the ones you think are an
insult?
Three, if we have no offer in 2 weeks,
what exactly happens next? I want that
plan now, not later. Four, will you or
anyone in your office also represent the
buyer? When one agent works both sides,
Zillow found sellers lost about $2,165
per home on average. That added up to
nearly 1 and 1/2 billion dollars over 3
years. Where it is allowed, it usually
needs your written consent, and you are
allowed to say no.
Five, how long is this agreement, and
how do I get out of it if it is not
working? And while you are at it, ask
how the buyer's agent will be paid.
Since a national settlement in 2024,
that fee is no longer automatically
offered through the listing service. In
a slow market, many buyers will ask you
to cover it inside their offer. So,
decide your answer before the offer
arrives. One warning about choosing the
agent. The one who quotes the highest
price is not automatically the best. In
a slow market, a flattering number can
win the listing, and the price cuts come
later after your house has gone stale.
Ask every agent to show you the recent
sales behind their number. Then, do one
more thing alone at your kitchen table.
Write down three numbers and keep them
to yourself. The lowest price you will
accept, what it costs you each month to
keep the house, and the date you need to
be settled somewhere else. When the
offers come, you will not be deciding
under pressure. You will be checking a
number you already chose on a calm day.
If you are in the middle of this right
now, I would like to hear from you.
Maybe there is an offer on the table, a
cash buyer calling, or a parent's house
to sell.
Send me the details at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
Your state, the offer, and how soon you
need to be out. I answer those myself,
and I will tell you the first thing I
would check. And if one of these videos
ever kept you from signing something you
would have regretted, the description
has a quiet way to support the work.
Buyers walked into this season with a
coach. You deserve one, too. For the
moments when someone wants your
signature fast, or a check is about to
land in your name, that is where the
quiet rules earns its keep, and you will
find it in the comment I pinned at the
top. Ask your five questions before
anyone hands you a listing agreement.
And when the first low offer comes, do
not take it personally. Counter it. I am
Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: SENIORS: Never Tell Your Bank These 3 Things or Your Account Gets Frozen

segments.text: You are standing at the counter with
your own money, and the teller asks one
small question. What is this for?
Whatever you say next gets typed into a
box, and that answer can decide whether
your account is frozen by the afternoon
or empty by the end of the week. Most
videos about this give you the same
warnings. Do not mention $10,000. Do not
say the word crypto. Those warnings are
real, and I've covered them before, but
they are not the sentences costing
people the most right now. Here are the
three that are. They sound polite. They
sound reasonable. Two of them are
usually said in complete honesty. The
first makes your bank treat the person
helping you as a suspect. The second can
close your account and put your name on
a list other banks check for 5 years.
The third switches off the only
protection standing between your savings
and a stranger on the phone. And stay to
the end because there is a fourth
sentence. It is the one you need if the
money is already gone, and the words you
choose on that call can decide whether
you ever see it again. My name is Kevin,
and I read the fine print so you do not
have to. If you want the next one of
these, subscribe because banks change
these rules quietly and nobody mails you
the new version. I have put every source
in the description, so nothing here has
to be taken on my word. None of this is
legal or financial advice. It is how the
rules work, and your own bank's policies
have the final say. First, understand
the question itself. When a teller asks
what a withdrawal is for, it is not
small talk. In June of 2022, the
Treasury's financial crimes office,
called FinCEN, issued banks a written
list of warning signs for elder
financial exploitation. Banks train
their staff on signs like these. Three
of them matter for everything in this
video. An older customer who is not
allowed to speak for himself. A customer
who seems to be taking direction from
someone on a cell phone. And a customer
who cannot answer basic questions about
their own account. Hold on to those
three. Each sentence I am about to give
you walks straight into one of them. The
first sentence sounds like the most
natural thing in the world. Talk to my
son, he handles all of this. Picture a
woman I will call Henrietta. She is 81,
sharp, and tired of paperwork. Her son
Garrick drives her to the bank every
month, and lately he does most of the
talking. Today, she wants to move
$40,000 out of savings to pay for a new
roof. The teller asks what it is for.
Henrietta waves a hand and says, "Ask
Garrick. He handles all of that."
Garrick explains, and every word he says
is true. Then, the teller excuses
herself. A manager comes back and says
the transfer is on hold for review.
Garrick is not on the account, and he
has no paperwork.
Two days later, a case worker from adult
protective services calls the house.
Garrick realizes his mother's bank has
reported a concern about him. Now, look
at that afternoon from the other side of
the glass. A new relative or friend
suddenly conducting transactions for an
older customer without proper
documentation is, almost word for word,
one of the red flags on FinCEN's list. A
federal law from 2018, the Senior Safe
Act, protects trained bank employees who
report suspected exploitation in good
faith. In some states, reporting is not
even optional. In California, every
officer and employee of a financial
institution is a mandated reporter of
suspected financial abuse of an elder.
And a growing number of states let a
bank pause the transaction itself while
it looks into it. So, the teller was not
deciding whether Garrick seemed like a
nice man. She was choosing between one
phone call and her own legal exposure.
The phone call wins every time. And
notice what caused it. Nobody lied.
Henrietta was honest, and so was
Garrick. The sentence did the damage.
Those two words, "Ask Garrick," told the
bank two things at once, that she might
not understand her own transaction, and
that somebody else was running it. There
was a gentler ending available, too. If
Henrietta had named a trusted contact,
the bank's first call could have gone to
someone she chose, not to the state. And
on the phone, the rules are even
tighter. A bank usually cannot discuss
your account with anyone who is not on
it until you say so yourself. If that
[snorts] call from adult protective
services ever comes to your house, know
two things before you panic. It is not
the police, and a report is not a
verdict. The national association that
sets standards for those programs puts
it plainly in its ethical principles.
Adults have the right to accept or
refuse services. And adults are presumed
to have decision-making capacity unless
a court decides otherwise. You can
answer their questions, show them you
understand your own money, and decline
any help you do not want. There is a
second trap in Henrietta's story, and it
catches families who try to fix this in
a hurry. Another item on FinCEN's list
is a sudden change in who manages an
older customer's money, such as a new
power of attorney. Picture a son who
rushes to a lawyer on Monday. On
Tuesday, he walks into the bank with a
brand new power of attorney and a large
transfer. To the bank, that can look
exactly like the thing it is trained to
stop. The paperwork that protects you is
the paperwork that was already on file
before anyone needed it. So, what should
Henrietta have said? One sentence, in
her own voice, before Garrick said a
word. "I am moving $40,000 to pay for my
roof, and my son is here to help me.
That is all." She speaks first. She
names the amount and the reason. Then
Garrick can fill in details, and the
bank hears a customer who is in charge
of her own money with help standing
beside her.
The same rule works on the phone. Do not
just hand over the phone and say, "Talk
to my daughter." Say who you are and
what you want first. Then tell the bank
you would like your daughter to help
with the call. One sentence fixes the
counter. But the paper behind that
sentence has to be in the file long
before the day anyone needs it. And most
families find that out at the worst
possible moment. If you were the one who
helps a parent with money, or the parent
who leans on a grown child, that moment
is is
what the quiet rules was built for. It
is at kevinexplains.shop.
Hold your phone up to the code on the
screen or tap the link pinned at the top
of the comments or the one in the
description. You have 7 days to decide
whether it deserves a place in your
drawer. If it does not, you get a refund
because nobody should learn this at the
counter with their own mother looking at
them like a stranger. Henrietta's money
did move, eventually. It took 11 days, a
signed letter, and Garrick waiting in
the car while his mother went inside
alone. So, put the helper on paper now
and know that three different papers do
three different jobs. The first is a
trusted contact. That is only a name and
a phone number the bank may call if it
is worried about you. It cannot touch a
dollar. The second is an authorized
signer, sometimes called a convenience
signer, which some banks offer.
That person can sign and make
transactions for you, but the money
stays yours. The third is a durable
power of attorney. That is legal
authority to act for you, and it matters
most if a day comes when you cannot act
for yourself. If you have money at a
brokerage, you may already have been
asked about the first one. Since 2018, a
FINRA rule has required brokerage firms
to make a reasonable effort to get a
trusted contact for each account. It is
one line on a form and it is easy to
skip. Go look for it. And one detail
about that power of attorney that most
families never hear. Many states have
adopted a uniform version of the power
of attorney law, and West Virginia is
one of them. Under rules like that, you
present a properly signed and notarized
power of attorney on the state statutory
form. The bank then generally has 7
business days to accept it or to ask for
a certification or a lawyer's opinion.
It cannot simply demand that you sign
its own form instead. If it refuses
without a valid reason, a court can
order it to accept and can make it pay
the legal fees. There is one important
exception. If the bank has reported a
good faith concern about the agent to
adult protective services, it can say
no. What you should not do is solve all
of this by adding your son as a joint
owner. That makes him an owner of the
account, and I explained in an earlier
video how his creditors and even his
divorce can then reach it. Help is a
role. Ownership is something else
entirely and if you are the son or
daughter in this story, three habits
keep you from looking like the problem.
Let your parents speak first every time,
even when it is slower. Never answer a
question the teller asked your parent.
And if the bank says no, do not argue.
Ask one question instead, "What document
would you accept?" Then go and get
exactly that and come back. And if a
case worker ever does call about you, do
not take it as an insult. Bring the
papers that show your role. Let your
parent talk to the case worker alone if
they ask. A helper with nothing to hide
usually ends that conversation quickly
and your parent's own voice is the
strongest evidence you have. The second
sentence sounds even more honest than
the first. "They sent me too much. I am
just sending the rest back." Take
Cornelius. That is not his real name. He
is 76, a retired machinist and careful
with every dollar.
One evening, a warning filled his
computer screen with a phone number to
call. The man who answered was patient
and kind. He said Cornelius was owed a
refund of $200 and asked him to log into
his bank so it could be sent.
The screen went dark for about a minute.
When it came back, his checking account
The man sounded panicked. He had typed
an extra zero, he said, and he would
lose his job. Could Cornelius please
send the difference back today? Here is
what happened during that dark minute.
Nothing came in from anywhere. The man
was inside Cornelius's online banking
and he moved $20,000 from Cornelius's
own savings into his own checking. On
the screen, it looked exactly like a
deposit. Credit unions have written
about this exact trick and one of them
called it the savings switcheroo. In
July of 2023, the FBI warned that refund
scammers were telling older adults to
send the difference back in cash wrapped
inside magazines by shipping company.
Every dollar Cornelius was about to send
was already his. He did not lose it. And
the reason is the twist in this story.
The next morning he said those exact
words at the counter. They sent me too
much. I am just sending the rest back.
The teller asked where the money had
come from. He could only say the refund
people and he could not name the
company. That is the third warning sign
on FinCEN's list. A customer who cannot
answer basic questions about his own
account. So, she pulled up his accounts
and saw a transfer from his own savings
the night before. She refused to send
the wire and her manager put a hold on
it. Cornelius was furious with his bank
for about an hour. Then he was grateful
for the rest of his life. You do not
need a teller to catch it though. The
test takes 1 minute. Before you send a
single dollar back to anyone, log in by
yourself with nobody on the phone and
nobody on your screen and look at your
savings. If it dropped by the same
amount, there was no refund. There was
only you about to pay a stranger with
your own money. And the real answer to
anyone who says they sent you too much
is one sentence. Then reverse it from
your end. Any real company can take back
its own payment. Only a scammer needs
you to do it for them. If someone has
already been on your screen, call your
bank using the number on your card and
tell them someone had remote access.
Change your banking password from a
different device. Then have the computer
cleaned by someone you chose, not
someone who called you. There is a phone
app this sentence too. A stranger sends
you money on a payment app then messages
you. Sorry, wrong person. Could you send
it back? Regions Bank describes how this
often works. The payment came from a
stolen card. When the real cardholder
disputes it, the money is pulled back
out of your account. If you already
returned it, you have lost it twice. The
advice is the same rule. Do not follow
return instructions from a stranger. Ask
the app to reverse it. The same goes for
a buyer who overpays you by check for
something you sold. The check can bounce
after the bank has already let you spend
the money, and then the bank takes it
back from you. Now, the darker version
of this sentence, where the money really
is someone else's. A new friend online,
or a work-from-home job, asks you to
receive a payment and pass most of it
on. Maybe you keep a small fee. Maybe
you are just being kind. The FBI has a
name for the person in the middle, a
money mule. In a public warning in
December of 2021, it said, "Mules can
face prison, a fine, or community
service, even if they were unwitting."
And it listed one consequence most
people never think about, the inability
to open bank accounts in the future.
Here is how that happens. Money arriving
and leaving again quickly, sent on to
someone you have never met, is one of
the oldest patterns banks watch for. The
account can be frozen while they look.
If that money was stolen from another
victim, that victim's bank can ask for
it back, and your bank can take it out
of your account, even though you already
sent it on. That can leave you negative
by thousands of dollars. Then, a letter
may arrive saying the bank has decided
to close your account. And that closure
can be reported to the screening
companies banks use, like ChexSystems
and Early Warning Services. Early
Warning, by the way, is the same company
that runs the Zelle network. And do not
expect an explanation. Banks can
generally close an account under their
own account agreement, and if one has
filed a suspicious activity report,
federal law forbids it from telling you
that the report exists. According to the
help site run by the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency, negative
information generally stays on those
reports for 5 years. Many banks look at
them when you try to open a new account.
So, if the account they closed was the
one your social security lands in, you
are now shopping for a new bank with a
mark next to your name.
You're entitled to a free copy of your
ChexSystems report every 12 months, and
you can dispute anything wrong in it. If
a bank ever closed an account on you and
never explained why, that report is the
first place to look.
The third sentence is different from the
first two. It is the only one that is a
lie. It is also the most boring sentence
you could ever say at a bank, and that
is exactly why somebody else picks it
for you. It is for renovations. AARP
reported the case of a woman in
Connecticut who believed she was helping
federal agents.
The man on the phone told her exactly
what to say at the counter. "I wish to
withdraw $20,000 from my money market
account. And if they ask why, say it is
for renovations." He also told her not
to discuss it with anyone. She even
called ahead, the way careful people are
told to, and asked the bank to have
$20,000 ready for the next day. Calling
ahead is good advice. Here, it was
turned against her. She made nine
withdrawals over 6 weeks. She lost
Every one of those visits was a chance
for someone to stop it. Every time, a
sentence somebody else wrote for her
closed that chance. Go back to that list
of warning signs. A customer who seems
to be taking direction from someone on a
cell phone. Scammers know banks watch
for exactly that. So, they rehearse you
before you walk in. They hand you a
reason that sounds dull and believable.
Home repairs, a new car, a gift for a
grandchild. Some of them stay on the
line the entire time. The Federal Trade
Commission says keeping you on the phone
is designed to keep you from talking to
anyone who could help. The lies are
nearly always a version of the same
three.
Your account is being misused. Your
identity is tied to a crime. Your
computer has been hacked. And the fix
they offer is always the same. Move your
money to keep it safe. The FBI even
named one version the phantom hacker
scam. It comes in three waves. First, a
fake tech support call. Then, a fake
call from your bank's fraud department.
Then, a fake government official who
insists your money is still not safe.
Victims are told not to tell anyone.
In just the first half of 2023, the FBI
counted more than $542 million dollars
lost to tech support schemes like this.
Nearly half the victims were over 60 and
they carried two-thirds of the losses.
Now, here is why this sentence is worse
than the other two. Every protection
your bank has depends on one thing.
Somebody at that bank being able to see
that something is wrong. The trusted
contact you named, the tellers training,
the hold your state allows, all of it
waits for a reason to act. The words "It
is for renovations." take that reason
away. This is the one place in this
whole video where a frozen account is
the happy ending. So, here is the
sentence that saves you and it is simply
the truth. "Someone on the phone told me
to say this is for renovations." That is
all you have to say. You do not have to
know whether it is a scam. You do not
have to be sure of anything. That one
sentence turns the person behind the
glass from an obstacle into the best
ally you have that day. And here is the
rule I want you to keep for the rest of
your life. If anyone tells you what to
say to your bank, the person telling you
is the scam. Think about the woman in
Connecticut for one more moment. Nine
trips to the counter. $165,000.
She was not foolish. She was frightened
and she was obeying someone she believed
was protecting her.
What she was missing was not
intelligence. It was one rule already in
her head before the phone rang. That is
what I want the quiet rules to be for
you. The voice that is already there
when a calm stranger starts telling you
what to say. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
The code on your screen opens it and the
link is pinned at the top of the
comments and waiting in the description.
You have 7 days with it. If it is not
worth keeping, you get a refund and that
is the end of it. Because the next call
will sound calm and it will come on an
afternoon when you are home alone. One
more layer because the calls are getting
better. This October, the American
Bankers Association launched a campaign
called "Banks Never Ask That." Two of
its points belong right here. A real
bank will never ask you for the one-time
passcode you use to log in and a real
bank will never tell you to move your
money to a different account. The
association also warns that scammers may
send a fake fraud alert first, then call
pretending to be your bank, and your
caller ID can even show the bank's real
number. One of its executives put the
difference simply. A real bank is never
going to instill urgency or fear. So, do
not argue with the caller and do not
test them. Hang up and dial the number
on the back of your card yourself. And
here is a twist on the word frozen. Some
[clears throat] of these calls open by
telling you that your account has been
frozen or is about to be. That claim is
the bait. A real hold comes from your
own bank, and you can confirm it with
one call to the number on your card. If
a caller says your account is frozen and
the cure is moving your money somewhere
else, the freeze is fiction and the
caller is the thief.
And this is not a rare problem.
According to the FBI, Americans over 60
reported losing $7.7 billion to internet
crime last year, about 60% more than the
year before.
In August of last year, the FTC reported
that complaints from older adults who
lost $10,000 or more to impersonators
had more than quadrupled since 2020.
Losses of $100,000 or more went from $55
million to $445 million in 4 years. And
where does the money go? In the FTC's
data on older adults who lost $10,000 or
more, cryptocurrency was the most common
payment, and most of those reports
mentioned Bitcoin machines.
Bank transfers came next, then cash.
Among losses over $100,000, roughly one
report in five involved gold. The FBI
has warned about couriers who come to
people's homes to collect cash and gold
after the victim is told it will be kept
safe in a protected account. More than
$55 million was lost that way in just 8
months of 2023.
The FBI says plainly that the government
and legitimate businesses will never ask
you to buy gold. At crypto kiosks alone,
Americans reported more than $333
million dollars last year.
In the FBI's report the year before,
people over 60 carried more than 85% of
those kiosk losses. AARP counts 24
states that have taken some action on
these machines. Notice the one
instruction every one of these scams
shares. Do not tell anyone. Not your
bank and not your family. That
instruction is the tell. A real bank, a
real investigator, and a real government
office never need your silence. So,
before any large withdrawal or transfer,
ask yourself three quick questions. Who
first told me I needed to do this? Is
someone hurrying me? And would I give my
reason out loud with my daughter
standing next to me? If the answer to
the first is a caller, a pop-up, or a
stranger, stop right there. A real
emergency survives a one-day pause. A
scam usually does not. Now, the fourth
sentence. The one for the worst day. The
money is already gone and you are
calling your bank. What you say in the
first minute of that call matters more
than almost anything that comes after
it. If someone tricked you into reading
them a code and then they moved the
money themselves, say exactly that. I
did not make this transfer. Someone else
made it after tricking me into giving
them a code. Do not say you authorized
it. Do not say it was your fault. The
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has
published answers on the federal
electronic transfer rules. According to
those answers, when a person is tricked
into sharing access information and a
third party then makes the transfer, it
counts as unauthorized. And your
carelessness cannot be used to make you
pay more than the rule allows.
Speed matters here, too. Under the same
federal rules, if your card or your
login details were stolen and you report
it within two business days of finding
out, your loss is generally capped at
$50. Wait longer and that cap goes up.
Those same answers say the bank must
begin investigating promptly. It cannot
make you file a police report first and
it cannot hold off until you send more
paperwork. Use the word fraud on that
call and ask for a claim number before
you hang up. If anyone tells you
otherwise, write down their name, the
date, and the time. And if the bank
investigates and says no, you are not
finished. Under those same rules, the
bank generally has 10 business days to
investigate. If it needs longer, up to
45 days, it usually has to credit your
account provisionally while it keeps
looking. If it denies your claim, it
must explain why in writing and tell you
that you can ask for the documents it
relied on. Ask for them. Then, if it
still looks wrong, file a complaint with
the Consumer Financial Protection
Bureau. If you pressed send yourself,
the honest truth is that the federal
rules are much weaker. Banks are
generally not required to refund a
payment you made yourself, even when you
were lied to. But tell them exactly who
the scammer pretended to be in your very
first sentence. In 2023, after pressure
from Washington, the Zelle network began
reversing payments for people tricked by
someone claiming to be from a government
agency or a bank. Who they pretended to
be can decide which rules apply to you.
And whatever kind of payment it was,
move fast. Call your bank and ask them
to try to recall the money today, not
tomorrow. Then, file a report at
ic3.gov, the FBI's internet crime site,
and report it to the FTC as well. The
FBI has a recovery team that contacts
the receiving bank and asks it to freeze
the money before it disappears. In 2025,
by the FBI's own figures, that process
handled 3,574
cases and froze more than $507 million.
That is about 61% of the money reported
lost in those cases. A freeze, for once,
working for you. And be ready for the
second wave. The FBI has warned about
fake law firms and recovery services
that contact scam victims, promising to
recover what you lost for a fee.
A real recovery never starts with you
paying a stranger again. And if the
scammer had your personal details,
freeze your credit at all three bureaus.
It has been free by federal law since
2018, and it makes it very hard for
anyone to open new credit in your name.
Put the four together and you have this
whole video in one breath. Talk to my
son becomes I am doing this and my son
is helping me. They sent me too much
becomes then reverse it from your end.
It is for renovations becomes someone
told me to say this and on the worst day
I authorized it becomes I did not make
this transfer when that is the truth. So
what do you actually do this week? Not a
long list. Five small moves and one
promise. Tonight find the phone number
on the back of your bank card and write
it on a piece of paper by your phone.
That is the only number you ever call
about your account. Tomorrow decide who
helps you with money and put that person
on paper in the right role before anyone
needs it. This weekend say one sentence
out loud until it feels natural. Someone
told me to say this. Ask your bank
whether it lets you name a trusted
contact on your checking and savings not
only at a brokerage and sometime this
year pull your check systems report. The
promise is simple. Nobody gets onto your
screen while your bank is open. Not a
technician, not a refund department, not
anyone. And if your bank has already
frozen something or closed an account
and will not tell you why write to me.
The address is
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
Tell me what the letter said and what
you were told at the counter. Every
message gets read and if this channel
has been useful to you there is a small
link in the description where you can
support the research. Each of these
takes many hours to check and that
support keeps them coming. Where do I
come down on all of this? Somewhere
uncomfortable. Banks hold transactions
because the law now protects them when
they do and most of the time that
protects you too. A teller who asks too
many questions is annoying. A teller who
asks none can cost you everything. When
a hold lands on you it feels like an
accusation and sometimes it really is a
mistake. But a question from your bank
is a far better phone call than a
question from the police about where the
money went. So, I am not angry at the
teller. What bothers me is bigger. Look
at what every scam in this video is
really after. Not your password, your
permission. Because in this country, the
moment you authorize a payment, most of
your protection walks out the door with
it. An executive at the Bankers
Association said it plainly this fall.
Banks never want to see you lose money,
but in the end, it is your money. He
meant it as advice. I hear it as the
whole problem. It does not have to work
that way. Since October of 2024, banks
in Britain have been required to
reimburse most victims of these
authorized payment scams up to 85,000
pounds.
Here, the same Bankers Association
running the Banks Never Ask That
Campaign also opposes proposed federal
laws that would require banks to
reimburse customers tricked into wire
transfers. The argument on the other
side is serious. Guaranteed refunds
could invite more fraud and push the
cost onto every customer. But until that
changes, the most important protection
you have is not a law. It is the
sentence you choose at the counter.
Everything from today is laid out in The
Quiet Rules. The three sentences, the
three papers, the words for the worst
day, and the order to do it all in. The
link sits at the top of the pinned
comment. Write that bank number down
tonight. And the next time a calm voice
tells you what to say at the counter,
say the true sentence instead. I am
Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check The Quiet Rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: Homeowners Over 60: File These 5 Documents Before It’s Too Late

segments.text: The IRS can take your home. You have
probably seen that sentence on a
thumbnail and feel your stomach drop a
little. Here is the part those videos
leave out. Before the IRS can seize the
house you actually live in, a federal
judge has to approve it in writing. That
has been the law since 1998. And if the
tax debt is $5,000 or less, the IRS
cannot take your residence at all. So,
why am I making this video? Because the
IRS almost never needs that judge. It
does something much quieter. It files
one page with your county, and that page
sits on your house until the debt is
gone. You cannot sell it clean, you
cannot refinance, your children cannot
inherit it free and clear. And here is
what surprised me most when I dug into
this. The IRS is not even the most
likely thing to come for a paid-off
house. A forger is. Then, a creditor
with a court judgment. Then, your own
county tax office. Then, a probate court
after you are gone. Five takers. Five
pieces of paper that stop them. Most of
them cost nothing, and most people over
60 have filed none of them. And I am
going to give you the order to file them
in, because the order matters more than
the papers. One of the five is a form
you sign at your own retirement account,
and it stops the IRS problem before it
starts. One is a single notarized page
that, in at least one big state, stops a
county from selling your home even after
you have fallen behind. And there is a
Supreme Court case from 1983 that
explains why your homestead protection
does not stop the IRS, which almost
nobody knows.
My name is Kevin. I read the rules so
you do not have to. If that is useful to
you, subscribe, because these rules
change, and the letters about them are
written to be skipped. Every source I
used today is listed in the description,
so you can check every word I say. This
is education, not legal or tax advice,
and your own state's rules are the ones
that count. Let Let with the one on the
thumbnail, because the truth about it is
more useful than the fear. When you owe
the IRS and do not pay after the bill, a
lien attaches automatically to
everything you own. That includes your
house. Nobody has to file anything for
it to exist. It simply arises by law.
What the IRS files is a public notice of
that lien, and under its own manual, it
generally files one once the balance
reaches about $10,000.
That notice lands in the same county
records as your deed. From that moment,
every buyer, every lender, and every
title company can see it. So, the real
danger is not a sheriff at your door. It
is the day you try to sell, downsize, or
refinance, and the title company tells
you the IRS gets paid first. The same is
true of a reverse mortgage. Those loans
require existing liens to be paid off at
closing. So, an IRS lien can quietly
decide whether you qualify at all. Now,
how does a careful retiree end up owing
the IRS in the first place? I see the
same three ways again and again. The
first is a withdrawal from an IRA with
too little tax taken out. Unless you
tell them otherwise, an IRA custodian
generally withholds 10% on a one-time
withdrawal. 10% sounds responsible, but
if that money lands in the 22% bracket,
you are short more than half the tax.
The second is a Roth conversion, where
nobody set money aside for the bill. The
third is the letter nobody opened. The
IRS sends a notice called a CP2000 when
the forms it receives do not match your
return. It is a proposal, not a bill,
and you get 30 days to respond. Ignore
it, and the proposal becomes a balance
you owe. The letters come in an order,
and the order is your warning system. A
balance due notice, then reminders, then
a notice of intent to levy, then a final
notice that gives you 30 days to ask for
a hearing. That final letter is the one
with real teeth. Inside those 30 days,
you can request what the IRS calls a
collection due process hearing, and
collection generally pauses while it is
heard. Let me tell you about a man I
will call Prentice. He is 73, retired
from a water utility, and his house has
been paid off for 11 years.
Two years ago, he took $40,000 out of
his IRA to replace the roof. The
custodian took out the standard 10%.
Nobody told him that was not enough. At
tax time, he owed about 4,000 more plus
penalties, and he did not have it. He
put the letters in the drawer with the
appliance warranties. By last spring,
the balance had grown, and a lien notice
was recorded at his county. Then, his
wife's health changed, and they decided
to sell and move near their daughter.
The buyer's title company found the lien
in one afternoon. Nothing could close
until the IRS was paid from the
proceeds, and the closing slipped 3
weeks waiting on a payoff letter. They
kept their house money. They lost the
condo they had picked to another buyer.
Before I go on, three things the IRS
cannot do because the scary videos get
these wrong.
It cannot seize the home you live in
over a small debt of $5,000 or less. It
cannot seize it over a bigger one
without a federal judge signing off
first. And the IRS generally has to show
the court that other ways to collect
will not work. And it cannot keep
collecting forever. The general limit is
10 years from the date the tax was
assessed.
For most homeowners, the lien is the
whole story. It does not take your
house. It takes your freedom to do
anything with it.
One more thing about how the IRS reaches
you because scammers copy it. The real
IRS starts with mail, paper letters with
a notice number in the corner. It does
not open with a phone call threatening
arrest, and it never asks for gift cards
or a wire. If a call scares you about
your house, hang up and call the number
printed on a letter you already have.
Here is what Prentice needed, and it was
not a lawyer.
It was the order of those letters
written down in front of him with the
deadline each one carries and the exact
sentence to say when he called. That is
why I wrote the quiet rules. It is for
exactly this kind of moment when the
letters arrive in an order nobody
explains and the windows close while
they sit in a drawer. It is at Kevin
Explains.shop.
The code is on your screen if you want
to point your phone at it and the link
is pinned at the top of the comments and
in the description. Take 7 days with it.
If it does not show you something you
can use, you get a refund. Now, back to
the paper that would have kept Prentiss
out of this entirely. Paper number one
is the withholding form for your IRA
withdrawals. The IRS calls it form W-4R
and your custodian hands it to you with
any one-time withdrawal.
Most people never fill it in, so the
custodian uses 10%. Fill it in. The form
itself prints a small rate table to help
you pick a number. If your other income
already puts you in the 22% bracket, 10%
will leave you short every single time.
Regular monthly withdrawals use a
different form, but the idea is the
same. Pick the rate on purpose and if
you already owe, the paper changes. For
balances of $50,000 or less, an
individual can usually set up a payment
plan online without talking to anyone.
A plan in good standing keeps the IRS
from moving toward levy. If you owe
$25,000 or less and pay by automatic
debit, you can ask the IRS to withdraw
the public lien notice. That cleans up
your county record once the plan is
running. And if you are selling and a
lien is in the way, there is a form that
asks the IRS to discharge the lien from
that one property so the sale can close.
Your title company has seen it many
times. The rule underneath all of it is
boring. Open the IRS envelope on the day
it arrives. Every protection I just
described has a clock that starts on the
date printed on the letter, not the day
you finally read it. The second taker
does not send letters at all. He sends a
forged deed to your county recorder.
Here is how it works. A paid-off house
has no lender watching the title. Your
name, your address, and the fact that
there is no mortgage are all public. A
forger prepares a deed transferring your
house to himself or to a company, fakes
your signature and a notary stamp and
records it. In most counties, the clerk
checks the formatting, not the truth.
Then, he borrows against your house or
sells it to someone who never met you.
There is a newer version that worries
title companies even more. It is called
seller impersonation. The forger does
not record a fake deed first. He
pretends to be you, lists your property
for sale, and tries to close the sale
himself, usually by email and a remote
notary. The targets are houses with no
mortgage and no one living there. A
rental, a lot you bought decades ago, a
second home, or the house you left empty
when you moved closer to your children.
If you own any property you do not live
in, that is the one to watch first. The
FBI's latest internet crime report put
reported real estate fraud losses at
about $275 million last year, up from
about $173 million the year before.
People over 60 filed about one in five
of those complaints, but they carried
about 45% of the money lost. That is the
number I keep coming back to. Paper
number two costs nothing. It is your
county's property fraud alert. Many
recorders now offer a free sign-up. You
enter your name, and the county emails
you whenever a document is recorded
under it. San Diego County started one
in 2022. Dallas County has one. Search
your county name and the words property
fraud alert. If your county has none,
ask the recorder whether one is coming,
and look up your own deed online twice a
year. While you are looking at your own
records, check one thing most paid-off
owners never check. When you made the
last mortgage payment, the lender was
supposed to record a release, sometimes
called a satisfaction of mortgage.
Search your name and look for it. If it
is missing, the old loan still shows as
open on your title. It will surface on
the worst possible day, when you try to
sell or when your children settle the
estate. Call the old lender or whoever
bought the loan and ask them to record
the release. If they have merged or
disappeared, your title company can help
you clear it. It is far easier to fix
now while you are here to sign than
after. And if you ever get that alert
and see a deed you did not sign, move
the same day. Call the recorder's office
and ask how to flag the document. File a
police report and report it to the FBI's
Internet Crime Center. Then call a real
estate attorney because the fix is
usually a court order that cancels the
forged deed. A forged deed passes no
real ownership, but it leaves a mess on
your title that gets more expensive
every week it sits there.
Now, the warning because this is where
people waste money. You have probably
seen ads for title lock services at 15
or $20 a month. In August of 2024, the
Federal Trade Commission warned that
these services are not insurance and do
not prevent title theft. They watch the
records and tell you after something is
filed. Your county's free alert does the
same job. While we are on the recorder's
office, watch your mailbox for one more
thing.
Every year, letters arrive that look
official, often with a seal and a
deadline, offering a certified copy of
your deed for close to $100.
Several state attorneys general have
warned about them. Your county will sell
you the same copy for a few dollars and
you almost never need one. A real
government office does not ask you to
pay a private company by a deadline to
protect your deed.
And one thing to find, not file. Dig out
the owner's title policy from when you
bought the house. A plain owner's policy
mostly looks backward at problems from
before you bought. Some newer homeowners
policies also cover certain forgeries
recorded after you bought. Read which
one you have so you know before you ever
need it.
The third taker has a court judgment, a
medical bill that went to collections, a
credit card that sued, a lawsuit over a
fall on your front steps. When a
creditor wins a judgment, it can usually
record it as a lien against real estate
in your county. That is where homestead
protection comes in and it is wildly
different from state to state. Florida
and Texas protect the value of a primary
home with no dollar cap, though both
limit the land. In Florida, it is half
an acre inside a city. Massachusetts
protects up to $500,000
with a recorded declaration, and up to a
million dollars when an owner is 62 or
older. Some states protect only a few
thousand dollars.
And there is a detail almost nobody
knows. In some states, the protection
follows the money for a while after you
sell. In Texas, the cash from selling
your homestead stays protected from
ordinary creditors for 6 months, so you
can buy your next home with it. If you
are planning to downsize and you have an
old judgment hanging over you, that
window can decide whether you keep the
money. Ask about it before you list the
house, not after. Here is the part most
videos get backwards. In many states,
the basic protection is automatic. You
do not have to file anything. In others,
the stronger protection only exists
after you record a homestead declaration
at the county.
Massachusetts is the classic example.
So, paper number three is not the same
everywhere. The question to ask your
county recorder or a local attorney is
simple.
Is homestead protection automatic here,
or do I have to record a declaration to
get the full amount? If you have to
record it, it is usually one page,
notarized, and filed for a small fee or
none. Now, the limit, and this is the
Supreme Court case I promised. The case
is United States against Rogers from
The court ruled that the IRS can ask a
federal court to force the sale of a
home for a tax debt. That held even
though a widow who did not owe the tax
lived there under Texas homestead law.
She had to be paid for her share out of
the sale, but the sale could happen. A
homestead protects you from ordinary
creditors. It does not protect you from
the IRS, and it does not protect you
from your own mortgage. That is exactly
why paper one comes before paper three.
The fourth taker is the one that has
actually taken the most homes from older
Americans, your own county, over
property tax. In 2023, the Supreme Court
heard the case of Geraldine Tyler. She
was 94. She owed about $15,000 in
property tax, penalties, and interest on
her Minneapolis condo. The county took
it, sold it for about 40,000, and kept
the other 25,000.
All nine justices said that was
unconstitutional, and counties now have
to return the surplus.
But notice what the ruling did not do.
It did not stop the sale. Geraldine
still lost her home. The ruling only
decides who keeps the leftover money.
So, paper number four is the one that
stops it happening in the first place.
It is your county's senior relief
application, and it comes in three
kinds. An exemption that lowers the
taxable value, a freeze that caps it,
and a deferral that lets you postpone
the tax entirely while you live there.
The deferral is the one almost nobody
knows about. In Texas, a homeowner 65 or
older can file a one-page notarized
affidavit with the appraisal district.
Collection of the tax on that home is
then deferred for as long as it stays
your homestead. Interest still builds at
5% a year, and the tax is paid when the
home is sold or the estate settles.
But a deferral filed in time stops a
pending tax sale or lawsuit, and a
surviving spouse who is at least 55 can
continue it.
Texas also gives owners over 65 a
$200,000 exemption on school taxes.
Florida, California, Washington, and
many other states have their own
versions, each with its own rules and
deadlines. There is one more Texas paper
that most owners over 65 never hear
about. You can pay the property tax on
your homestead in four installments
through the year instead of one lump in
January, without penalty, as long as you
make the first payment on time. A bill
that feels impossible in one check is
often manageable in four.
Ask your tax office whether your state
has anything like it. Many do, and they
rarely put it on the front of the bill.
And if a sale has already happened, do
not assume it is over. Many states give
the former owner a window to redeem the
property by paying what was owed. Since
the Tyler case, you also have a right to
claim any surplus from the sale. Both of
those have deadlines and the county is
not required to chase you to tell you.
Call the tax office and ask two
questions. Is there still a redemption
period and how do I file a claim for the
surplus? Let me tell you about a woman I
will call Odessa. She is 79, a retired
[clears throat] school secretary in
Texas, widowed four years. Her husband
always handled the tax bill. After he
died, the bill came and so did a new
roof and a new furnace and one year
behind turned into two. By the time she
called the tax office, the county had
filed suit and a sale was being
discussed. She was sure she would lose
the house she raised three children in.
The clerk on the phone mentioned, almost
in passing, that she could file a
deferral. One page, notarized. The sale
stopped. The back taxes did not
disappear and the interest keeps
running, but she is still in her own
kitchen. And here is what bothers me.
She had qualified for that page every
single day since her 65th birthday.
Odessa's problem was never really money.
It was that the one page that saved her
has a name she had never heard and
nobody is paid to tell you it exists.
That is the gap the quiet rules was
written to close. It puts the name of
that page in your hand before the letter
arrives, so you are not learning it from
a clerk in passing. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
Scan the code on your screen or use the
link pinned at the top of the comments
or in the description. Give it 7 days.
If it is not worth your time, you get a
refund. Then, come back for the fifth
paper because it decides who gets your
house after you and how long they wait
for it. The fifth taker is slower than
the others. It is the probate court and
it only arrives after you are gone. If
the house is titled in your name alone
when you die, it usually has to pass
through probate before your family can
sell it or live in it. That means a
court process, filing fees, often an
attorney, and time. In many states, it
takes the better part of a year,
sometimes much longer. And while it
drags, somebody has to keep paying the
tax, the insurance, and the utilities on
an empty house.
Paper number five is a deed that moves
the house outside probate. There are two
main kinds. The first is a revocable
living trust, where you deed the house
into a trust you still control
completely. The second is cheaper and
far less known. It is a
transfer-on-death deed, sometimes called
a beneficiary deed. More than half the
states now allow it. You record a deed
naming who gets the house when you die.
Nothing changes while you are alive. You
can still sell it, refinance it, or
cancel the deed. When you die, your
beneficiary records the death
certificate, and the house passes
without probate. Now, three corrections,
because I have heard every one of these
said wrong. First, a trust does not make
you invisible. If your trust is named
after you, and most are, your name is
still right there in the county records.
Second, a trust does not protect the
house from your creditors or from the
IRS while you are alive. It is a probate
tool, not a shield. Third, before you
deed your house into a trust, call your
title insurer and your county assessor.
Some older title policies may not carry
coverage over to the trust, and some
counties want a fresh homestead
application. 5 minutes on the phone
first. And one more, for anyone in
Pennsylvania. The state's inheritance
tax charges children 4.5% of what they
inherit, and a surviving spouse pays
nothing.
Putting the house in a revocable trust
does not escape that tax. What does help
is paying within 3 months of the death,
which earns a 5% discount on the bill.
Here is the paper I have seen do the
most damage. The trust drawn up years
ago, signed, sitting in a folder, while
the deed was never actually moved into
it. A trust only controls what is titled
in its name. Pull up [clears throat]
your deed online and check whose name is
on it today. I get one question about
this more than any other. Why not just
put my son's name on the deed? It feels
simpler than a trust. Here's what
changes the moment you do it. Your son
now owns part of your house. If he is
sued, divorced, or owes the IRS, his
creditors can reach his share. You
cannot sell or refinance without his
signature. It may count as a gift that
needs a gift tax return. And the biggest
one is taxes on the sale. When you die,
your share of the house gets a fresh
cost basis, but the share you gave away
while alive does not. Your son can owe
tax on decades of growth he would
otherwise have avoided. A transfer on
death deed gets the house to him without
any of that. And one situation touches
all five papers at once, the month after
a spouse dies.
If the two of you owned the house
jointly with survivorship, it is already
yours. But the county record still shows
both names until you record the death
certificate or a short affidavit. Do it
before you ever need to sell. Your
senior exemption or deferral may need a
new application in your name alone. In
Texas, a surviving spouse who is 55 or
older can usually keep the over 65
benefits, but you may still have to
file. And update your homeowner's
insurance because a policy in the name
of someone who has died is a claim fight
waiting to happen. Odessa missed two
years of this. Not because she was
careless, but because the person who
always handled it was the person she
lost. So, let me put the five in order
because the order is the point. First,
paper one. Fill [snorts] in the
withholding form at your IRA custodian
before your next withdrawal. If you
already owe, set up the payment plan
this week. That handles the only taker
who can step over your homestead.
Second, paper two. Sign up for your
county's free property fraud alert. 5
minutes. Then, find your title policy
and read which kind it is.
Third, paper four. Call your county tax
office or appraisal district and ask one
question. What exemptions, freezes, or
deferrals am I eligible for at my age?
And what are the deadlines? Many states
have a spring deadline. Some let you
claim back a year or two if you missed
it. Ask. Fourth, paper three. Ask
whether homestead protection is
automatic in your state or needs a
recorded declaration. If it needs one,
record it.
Fifth, paper five, decide between a
transfer on death deed and a trust with
someone licensed in your state. Then,
check that your deed actually says what
you think it says. Notice I put the
homestead fourth. That is not because it
does not matter. It is because the IRS
and the county can both reach a house
that a homestead protects and those two
cost people the most. If you only do one
thing today, open every envelope sitting
in the drawer. The IRS letters, the
county letters, the assessment notice.
Every clock in this video starts on the
date printed on those letters. If you
are looking at your own house right now
and something does not fit, write to me
at kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
Tell me your state and what is going on.
I read everyone. And if these videos
have been useful to you, there is a
small support link in the description.
Research like this takes real hours and
that link keeps it going. Here is my
honest read. None of these five takers
is new. Counties have always been able
to sell a house for taxes. The IRS has
always been able to lien one. Forgers
have been filing deeds as long as there
have been deeds. What has changed is
that a paid off house owned by someone
over 60 is now the easiest target in the
system because nobody is watching it.
There is no lender checking the title,
no escrow account paying the tax, no
loan officer calling when something
looks wrong. You paid off the mortgage
to be free and you are, but that bank
was also quietly a watchman. When it
left, the watching became your job. Five
papers is what that job looks like. Most
of them take an afternoon. One takes a
phone call and none of them helps you
after the fact. Everything in this video
is laid out in the quiet rules with the
deadlines and the exact questions in
plain English and the link sits at the
top of the pinned comment. Pick one
paper this week, then the next one the
week after. By the new year, your house
is being watched again. I am Kevin.
Thanks for watching. Do not forget to
check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: Don’t Do a Roth Conversion: Do THIS Instead From Age 62 to 75

segments.text: If you are anywhere between 62 and 75
and someone has told you to convert your
IRA to a Roth, do not sign anything yet.
A conversion is a tax bill you choose to
pay today, and since 2018, it can never
be undone. For many retirees, there is a
better move in those exact years, and
almost nobody talks about it. Here is
what it looks like with real numbers.
Walter and Gloria are both 62 with $1.9
million in their IRAs and old 401k
plans. Their plan said, "Convert
a year into a Roth for 6 years." The tax
bill came to roughly $225,000
paid out of savings they will never see
again. The other plan had no big
conversions, just a different order for
spending the money they already have.
Under it, their first forced withdrawal
at 75 drops by almost half. Their Social
Security check ends up about 77% bigger
than if they had claimed at 62. And the
tax they pay along the way buys
groceries, not a one-way ticket to the
IRS. So, today, I will show you why a
Roth conversion is not the automatic
answer it has become, and exactly what
to do instead. From 62 to 75, you will
see the 2025 tax law change that quietly
shifted the math for anyone over 65, the
hidden widow's tax that almost no
conversion plan models. Four situations
where a conversion really does win, and
three questions to ask before you sign.
Stay for the third one. It is the one
advisors skip. Every rule and limit here
comes from the IRS, Social Security, and
Medicare's own published figures for
2026, and the sources are listed in the
description. And tell me in the
comments, has anyone pitched you a Roth
conversion yet? Type yes or no and your
age. First, the problem a conversion is
supposed to solve. Money in a
traditional IRA or 401k is not all
yours. You never paid income tax on it,
so part of every dollar belongs to the
IRS, and it will not wait forever. Under
the current law, if you were born from
1951 through 1959, your required minimum
distributions begin at 73. If you were
born in 1960 or later, they begin at 75.
After that, a minimum amount must come
out every year, whether you need it or
not. The IRS takes your balance from the
last day of the prior year and divides
it by a number from its uniform lifetime
table. At 75, that number is 24.6.
So, roughly 4% of the account has to
come out in year one, and the share
rises every year after. Now, watch what
time does to Walt and Gloria if they
touch nothing. $1.9 million
growing at 6% a year for the 13 years
from 62 to 75 becomes about $4.05
million.
Divide that by 24.6, and their first
required withdrawal is about $165,000.
