segments.text: Your Social Security deposit now gets
checked twice before you can spend it.
The first check happens at the Treasury
before the money is even sent. The
second happens at your own bank the
moment it lands. And since June, every
bank and credit union in America has to
run that second check. If either check
does not like what it sees, your deposit
can be held or sent back. And the
network's guidance lists what deserves a
closer look. In its own words, multiple
payroll or benefit payments. Benefit
payments. That is your deposit named on
the list. Now, nobody has put retirees
on a list of suspects, and nobody is
coming for your check. What has changed
is quieter than that, and it is
permanent. The patterns these systems
are built to catch look a lot like the
ordinary money life of a retired
household. So, in this video, I am going
to follow one Social Security payment
from the moment it leaves the Treasury
to the moment you spend it. Five
checkpoints. At each one, you will see
what can stop it, who is allowed to
touch it, and the one move that keeps it
flowing. And stay for the part about
January. It is the first raise that
every bank in the country is required to
watch arrive. Everything here comes from
the rulebooks themselves. Nacha's own
rule pages, the Treasury, Social
Security, and the federal regulations
that govern your account. You can check
every one of them through the sources
listed in the description. The names in
my examples are invented. The rules are
not. And this is education, not legal
advice. Before we start, tell me
something in the comments. Has a bank
ever held a deposit of yours, even for a
single day? Your answers decide what I
dig into next. Checkpoint one is the
Treasury. Your payment does not come out
of Social Security's own bank account.
Social Security tells the Treasury who
to pay and how much, and the Treasury
sends the money. On March 25th, 2025,
President Trump signed two executive
orders that changed how the Treasury
pays you. The first one got the
headlines. The second got almost none.
The first is called Modernizing Payments
to and from America's bank account. It
told the Treasury to stop issuing paper
checks for federal payments from
September 30th, 2025 with narrow
exceptions. If you have had direct
deposit for years, it barely touched
you. But it pushed hundreds of thousands
of people into new accounts and new
cards. Even this June, according to the
Motley Fool, more than 283,000
people still received Social Security by
paper check. And reporting this fall in
the Dallas Morning News says Social
Security plans to finish the switch to
electronic payments by the end of this
year. Why should that matter if your
deposit has gone to the same bank for 20
years? Because every account opened for
a check that stopped coming is a new
account with no history. And because it
handed scammers a true story to borrow.
Hold on to both of those. They come back
later. The second order is called
protecting America's bank account
against fraud, waste, and abuse. It told
the Treasury to verify who it is paying
before the money goes out. On October
6th, the Treasury published its report
on the year. It screened more than 1.1
billion federal payments worth about 3.7
trillion dollars. And it caught about
payments worth 175 million dollars that
were about to go to people who had died.
That screen runs on Social Security's
full death file. And it raises a
question nobody asks until it happens to
them.
What if the file is wrong about you?
Social Security has said in the past
that about 1/3 of 1% of the death
reports it receives turn out to be
wrong. That sounds tiny. Against roughly
2.8 million deaths reported a year, it
means thousands of living people.
And now, the Treasury checks that file
before it sends a payment. If you are
ever listed by mistake, your money can
stop before it is sent, and your bank
cannot fix it. Only Social Security can
correct its own record. So, if your
deposit ever stops without warning, call
or visit your local Social Security
office that same day and bring your
identification. Then comes the sentence
that matters for every living retiree.
The Treasury says it piloted new checks
to validate bank account ownership.
Those checks, it says, became fully
operational on September 30th of this
year. In the Treasury's own words, they
let it identify and return payments that
fail before funds are dispersed. In
plain English, the Treasury can now stop
a federal payment before it is sent when
the account does not check out as
belonging to the right person. And that
collides with a rule that has been on
the books for years, one that a lot of
loving families quietly break. Under the
Treasury's own regulation, a federal
benefit payment must go into an account
in the name of the person receiving it.
An account you share with your son with
your name on it meets that rule. An
account in your son's name alone does
not. Take Opal. She is 81. After a fall
last spring, her daughter Nadine started
handling the bills. To keep things
simple, Nadine had Opal's Social
Security sent straight to Nadine's own
checking account. It worked for months.
But it breaks the Treasury's rule, and
an account that belongs to someone else
is exactly what an ownership check is
built to notice. Nadine has power of
attorney, and she assumed that covered
it. It does not. Social Security's page
for payees says it in one line. The
Treasury Department does not recognize
power of attorney for negotiating
federal payments. The fix took one visit
to the bank. Opal's name went on to a
joint account with Nadine, and the
deposit moved there right after a
payment day. And if a parent truly
cannot manage money anymore, the tool
Social Security recognizes is not a
power of attorney. It is a
representative payee, and you apply to
Social Security to become one. Nadine
did everything out of love. The rule she
broke sits in a Treasury regulation she
had never heard of, and the warning she
needed sat on a Social Security page she
had no reason to open. Nobody at the
branch was going to mention it.
The Quiet Rules gathers the rules that
decide what happens to your money into
one place, so you meet them on a calm
afternoon instead of a bad morning. It
is at kevinexplains.shop.
Watching on a television? The QR code on
the screen takes your phone straight
there. On a phone or a computer, the
link is in the pinned comment and in the
description. It is covered by a 7-day
guarantee. If it does not help you, you
get a refund. Picture Opal on a
Wednesday morning, rent due tomorrow,
refreshing that app again and again, and
the balance not moving. Checkpoint two
is the road your payment travels. It
moves on the ACH network, the same
system that carries paychecks and
automatic bill payments. And before it
leaves, it gets a tag, two letters, X
and X. The federal garnishment rule
describes it exactly. A benefit payment
carries the characters XX in positions
54 and 55 of a field called the company
entry description. You will never see
that tag. Your bank does. And later in
this video, when we get to court orders,
you will see why those two letters may
be the most valuable thing about your
deposit. The rules of this road are
written by an organization called Nacha.
It is not a government agency. It
governs the ACH network, and every bank
and credit union that touches an
electronic payment agrees to follow its
rules. In practice, they work like law.
And this year, Nacha changed them.
Checkpoint three is your bank, and this
is the change behind the headlines.
Nacha phased it in. From March 20th, it
applied to the biggest receivers, banks
that took in 10 million or more of these
payments in 2023. From June 19th, the
size limit disappeared. Every bank and
every credit union now falls under it,
down to the smallest one in your town.
What does it require? Each bank must
have risk-based processes, in Nacha's
words, "reasonably intended to identify
credit entries suspected of being
unauthorized or authorized under false
pretenses." A credit entry simply means
money coming in. Banks have always
watched money leaving your account. This
rule points them at money arriving. And
each bank must review those processes at
least once a year. So, this is not a
crackdown that fades. It is the new
normal. False pretenses is a newly
defined term, and it is worth hearing in
full. It means getting someone to make a
payment by misrepresenting your
identity, your authority to act for
someone else, or the ownership of the
account being credited. That third piece
is the one that matters to you. It is
the legal description of a crime aimed
squarely at retirees. A criminal changes
where your benefit goes to an account he
controls. So, banks are told to look for
the fingerprints of that crime. In its
answers to banks' questions, Nacha gives
examples of what a bank might watch for.
A payment type that does not fit the
kind of account it lands in. A
high-dollar payment that is unusual for
that account. A series of similar
credits arriving in a short time, such
as multiple payroll or benefit payments.
And any of those landing in a new
account, a dormant account, or an
account acting as a money mule, meaning
one used to pass stolen money along.
Nacha's technical notes add the kinds of
signals a system can weigh. How fast
money moves in and out. Patterns that
break from the usual. And traits of the
account itself, like its age and its
average balance. So, a thin account that
suddenly fills up tells a story, whether
the story is true or not. Think about
why benefit payments made that list. A
thief who steals eight identities and
points eight social security deposits at
one account creates exactly that
picture.
Eight similar federal credits, one
destination, one week. The mule item
deserves a minute of its own because
retirees end up on both sides of it. The
FDIC's inspector general defines a money
mule as any person who transfers or
receives funds at the direction of
another.
That includes people who have no idea
the money is stolen. It says recruiters
target, among others, people on dating
websites and the elderly. The approach
sounds harmless. A friend you met online
or a new business contact asks you to
receive a payment into your account and
send it on. To your bank, money arriving
from strangers and leaving fast is the
mule pattern exactly. And the Inspector
General lists what can follow:
prosecution, personal liability for
repaying the victims, bank accounts you
can no longer use. So, keep one rule
with no exceptions. Never let anyone you
have not met in person route money
through your account. Not a payment, not
a refund, not a favor. Now, look at an
honest retired home through the same
lens. Vernon is 74 and Maxine is 72. His
Social Security arrives on the second
Wednesday. Hers arrives on the fourth.
His union pension lands on the first.
All three go into one joint checking
account. In August, their branch closed,
so they opened an account at a credit
union and moved everything in a single
week. Three similar credits arriving in
an account with almost no history.
Nothing about it is improper. All of it
is on the list. The calendar adds its
own twists. Most of you are paid on the
second, third, or fourth Wednesday,
depending on your birthday. If you
started benefits before May of 1997, or
you get Social Security and SSI
together, you are usually paid on the
third. And the holidays bunch things up.
This November, if your birthday falls
between the first and the 10th, your
payment comes on Tuesday the 10th,
because Wednesday the 11th is Veteran's
Day. SSI for November was paid early on
Friday, October 30th, because November
1st is a Sunday. December is the one to
know. SSI arrives on December 1st, and
January's SSI arrives early on Thursday,
December 31st, because of New Year's
Day. The group paid on the third gets
the same treatment. Their December
payment comes on the third, and
January's comes on the 31st. Two similar
benefit credits in one month. Exactly
the shape on Notch's list, and
completely normal. If you were in one of
those groups, the second deposit is not
extra money. It is January's early. Do
not spend it as a bonus.
Now, the part that should calm you down.
Notch just says plainly that banks do
not have to screen every single payment
one by one, and they do not have to
check a payment before it posts. Most of
this watching happens after your deposit
is already in your account. A flag is a
question. It is not a verdict. But here
is why this year is different. Before
June, most of the country's banks and
credit unions had never been required to
do this. A brand new monitoring program,
still being tuned, tends to raise more
false alarms than one that has run for
years. We are living inside that first
year right now.
If you want to hear about quirks like
these before they reach your account,
subscribe. Reading these rule books is
the whole job here, so you never have
to. Checkpoint four is what your bank is
actually allowed to do when your deposit
gets flagged. There are three moves, and
you should know all three. The first is
a delay. Under NACHA's rules, a bank may
hold back a credit it suspects is
unauthorized or sent under false
pretenses while it looks into it. Your
deposit can show in your account and
still not be spendable. If the bank does
that, it has to contact the bank that
sent the payment and tell it. And NACHA
adds something reassuring. A bank cannot
delay your money simply because it has
not gotten around to screening it. A
delay needs a flag. The second move is a
call to the sender to confirm the
payment is genuine. For Social Security,
the sender is the federal government, so
this usually ends well. But it ends in
business days, not minutes. And if your
mortgage, your insurance, and your
electric bill all draft the next
morning, a hold of a few days is not a
technicality. It is a stack of overdraft
fees. The third move is the serious one.
The bank can send the payment back using
a return code that is literally labeled
questionable. Under the network's rules,
that kind of return normally has to
happen within two banking days of the
payment date. If it happens, the money
heads back toward the Treasury, and the
payment has to be sent to you again once
Social Security is satisfied the account
really is yours.
That means phone calls, waiting, and a
month of bills that do not wait with
you.
One more thing clears up a lot of
confusion. You may have heard that a new
account means long holds. For checks,
that is true, but federal availability
rules say that even in an account less
than 30 days old, electronic payments
like your social security must be
available by the next business day. The
long holds on new accounts are about
paper checks. What can slow a direct
deposit is a fraud flag, not the age of
the account by itself. So, if a deposit
ever goes missing, the first question at
the counter is a simple one. Was it
posted and held, or was it returned?
Held means the money is in your account
and the bank needs something from you,
usually identification.
Bring your benefit verification letter,
too. You can print it from your My
Social Security account and it shows
exactly what Social Security pays you.
Returned means the money has left and
your next call is to Social Security,
not the bank.
Social Security's own instructions
follow the same order. For a missing
direct deposit, it says to contact your
bank first because the bank may be
having a delay posting your payment. If
the money still has not arrived, call
Social Security or your local office.
And if the payment is due, Social
Security says it will replace it.
Checkpoint five begins after your money
lands because not every short deposit is
your bank's doing. Four other hands can
reach into that payment, each under a
different rule book. When your deposit
looks wrong, knowing which hand it was
saves you weeks of calling the wrong
office. The first hand belongs to Social
Security itself. If the agency decides
it paid you more than you were owed, it
sends a notice. For notices sent since
April 25th of last year, the default is
to hold back half of each monthly
payment until the debt is repaid. For
SSI, the default stays at 10%. You can
ask for a lower rate. You can ask for a
waiver if it was not your fault and
repaying would be a hardship. And you
can appeal whether you were overpaid at
all, which is called a reconsideration.
Social Security's own operations manual
tells its staff to stop collection when
someone asks for a reconsideration or a
waiver. So, ask within 30 days of the
date printed on the notice, not the day
you finally open it. Wanda is 76. Her
notice said she had been overpaid $9,400
after a mix-up over her earnings in a
year she worked part-time.
It arrived in a plain envelope in a week
with four other envelopes, and it went
into the pile. When her deposit suddenly
shrank, she called her bank. The bank
had done nothing. Half of her $2,000
benefit, $1,000 a month, was being kept
before the payment ever left the
Treasury. Do the math on Wanda's year.
taken a thousand at a time for close to
10 months. All of it over one envelope
she could have answered in an afternoon
if she had known the window existed.
The Quiet Rules is written for exactly
that kind of afternoon. So, you know
[clears throat] which letter to send and
by when while the clock is still on your
side. It is at kevinexplains.shop.
On a TV, scan the QR code with your
phone. On a phone or a computer, it is
pinned at the top of the comments, and
it is the first link in the description.
The 7-day guarantee applies. So, if it
is not useful to you, you get a refund.
Wanda kept that envelope. The postmark
on it is 2 months older than the day she
opened it. The second hand holds a court
order. If a creditor wins a judgment
against you over an old medical bill or
a credit card, it can send a garnishment
order to your bank. This is where those
two letters, XX, earn their place. Under
a Treasury regulation, a bank that
receives an order like that must review
your account within two business days.
It looks back over the last 2 months.
Every tagged federal benefit deposit in
that window is protected. The bank must
automatically leave you the smaller of
two numbers, the total of those benefit
deposits or your balance that day. You
do not file anything. The bank must do
the math for you, and it cannot charge a
garnishment fee against that protected
amount. Within three business days of
its review, it must send you a notice
explaining what it did. Here is the
limit. The automatic protection covers 2
months of deposits, not your whole
cushion. Money above that line can be
frozen. Some of it may still be yours to
keep because Social Security money is
generally protected from creditors. But
above the line, you have to claim it,
and the bank's notice must tell you that
you have that right. Your bank
statements are your proof of where each
dollar came from. Keep them.
Two exceptions. Orders from the federal
government or from a state child support
agency that come with a special notice
attached, follow the bank's ordinary
procedures without the automatic two
months. And federal tax debts and child
support can also be collected from the
payment itself before it ever reaches
you.
One more detail from the same
regulation. If you have two accounts at
that bank, it must calculate the
protection separately for each account
in your name. The third hand is one
people forget, and it belongs to your
own bank. If you owe that same bank
money, can it simply take your deposit?
For one common debt, federal law says
no. Under the truth in lending rules, a
bank that issued your credit card may
not take money from your deposit account
at that bank to pay the card. Not while
the card is open, and not after it is
closed. The exceptions are narrow. You
signed up in writing for automatic
payments from that account. You gave the
bank a security interest in the money,
or the bank goes through a court the
same way any other creditor would. So,
if you were ever told your Social
Security went to pay a card balance at
the same bank, ask one question. Where
is my written authorization? Other
debts, like an overdrawn account, depend
on your account agreement. So, read the
part called setoff. The fourth hand
reaches in after a death. Social
Security does not pay for the month a
person dies. The payment that arrives
the following month covers that month,
so it has to go back. If it came by
direct deposit, the Treasury can reclaim
it from the bank, and the bank will
usually take it straight from the
account. If your own deposit sits in
that same joint account, the bank does
not stop to ask whose money it is. I
went through that in detail in an
earlier video, so here's the short
version. Report a death promptly, and do
not spend a federal payment that arrives
after it. Now, the deposit I promised
you at the start. January, your raise is
official 3.6%
for the average retired worker social
security puts the monthly check at about
now and about $2,170
from January. But the number that lands
will be smaller than the headline
because part B comes out first. The
premium is $202.90
this year. Medicare's trustees project
for 2027. And the official figure
usually comes out in November. Now
picture January through your bank's new
eyes. Within a few days every social
security deposit in America changes size
at once. A system that learns what
normal looks like for your account is
about to watch your normal change. Banks
that have run these programs for years
have lived through that before. For most
banks and credit unions this January
will be the first raise they are
required to watch arrive. I am not
predicting failures. I am telling you
which month deserves your attention. The
dates. If you are paid by birthday, your
first raise deposit comes on January
13th, 20th, or 27th.
If you are in the group paid on the 3rd
or you get SSI, it comes early on
December 31st. Write your date down and
build January's budget on the net number
after part B, not on the headline. You
can see that net number before the money
arrives. Social Security says your new
amount appears in your My Social
Security message center starting in late
November up to 3 weeks before the paper
notice comes in December. To see it
early, sign up for paperless notices by
November 18th. Then when January's
deposit lands, compare the two. If they
differ, you will know on day one, not
month three. Now the hand to fear most.
Not a bank and not an agency. A stranger
with a true story.
When millions of people hear that their
payment method is changing, a scammer
does not need to invent a crisis. He
borrows a real one. This year there are
two to borrow. Paper checks are ending
and the Direct Express card is changing
banks.
On May 18th, Social Security told
advocates that the Treasury had picked
Fifth Third Bank as the new bank behind
Direct Express.
New enrollments started there in May.
People who already have the card keep
using their Comerica card until it is
replaced. Social Security says they will
get notice before their accounts move,
later this year or early next year.
Reporting in CPA Practice Advisor puts
the number of people paid on the card at
about 3.6 million. So, the writes
itself. A call, a text, or an
official-looking letter. Your paper
check has been discontinued. Your card
is being replaced. Confirm your bank
details to avoid an interruption. The
premise is real, which is exactly why it
works. And when someone confirms, the
thief changes where the deposit goes.
That is the very crime the new bank
rules were written to catch. False
pretenses about who owns the account.
The same rules help you if you were ever
tricked into sending money out. Say a
caller convinces you to move savings to
a safe account that turns out to be his.
Call your bank the moment you realize
it, and ask it to request a return from
the receiving bank. Under NACHA's rules,
your bank can make that request, and the
receiving bank, which now has to watch
for exactly this kind of payment, can
send it back. It does not have to agree,
but the faster you call, the more likely
the money is still sitting there. Social
Security's own fraud page says it in one
sentence. Social Security will never ask
for sensitive or personal information
through social media, email, or text
message. If a phone call sounds
official, hang up and call the agency
back on a number you looked up yourself,
and report the attempt to the Inspector
General at oig.ssa.gov.
The stale explains why the rules
changed. The FBI says Americans 60 and
older reported losing $7.7 billion to
fraud last year. And the Treasury's
Financial Crimes Enforcement Network
studied 1 year of bank reports from June
2022 to June 2023.
It found 155,415
reports of elder financial exploitation
tied to about 27 billion dollars of
suspicious activity. 80% involved scams
by strangers. 20% involved theft by
someone the older person trusted. And
about 40% of those theft reports named
the person's own children.
I am not telling you to distrust your
family. I am telling you that a second
person who can also see your accounts
protects everyone, including the honest
helper doing all the work. So, here is
what I would do in three places in one
afternoon. At Social Security, open your
my Social Security account or sign into
the one you have through login.gov or
id.me. An account you control is one a
criminal cannot quietly open in your
name. Check that your direct deposit
shows the bank you expect and look over
your payment history. Then, consider the
two blocks Social Security offers. The
first is the direct deposit fraud
prevention block. In the agency's words,
it prevents anyone, including you, from
enrolling in direct deposit or changing
your address or direct deposit
information through my Social Security
or a financial institution. Including
you. That is the whole point. That last
part matters more than it sounds. When
you open an account, many banks can sign
you up for direct deposit with Social
Security directly without you ever
calling the agency. Social Security
calls it auto enrollment. It is
convenient. It is also a door, and the
block closes it. Once the block is on,
you or your representative contact your
local office to lift it or to make any
later change. If your deposit has gone
to the same account for years and you
have no plan to move it, that
inconvenience costs you almost nothing.
The second is the e-services block. It
stops anyone, including you, from seeing
or changing your information online. It
suits people who will never use the
website. Ask Social Security about
either one. At your bank, make sure the
account your benefits land in carries
your name. If you changed your name
after a marriage or a divorce, make sure
your bank and Social Security have the
same one. Turn on an alert for every
incoming deposit, so you know the same
morning if a payment is missing or held.
If you have an old savings account you
never touch, use it now and then, or
close it, so it is not a dormant account
waiting to surprise you. If you ever
switch banks, open the new account
first, use it for a month or two, and
move your deposit right after a payment
arrives, never in the days before one. A
brand new account, a freshly changed
deposit, and a benefit landing in the
same week stacks three items from
Natasha's list at once. And if you are
expecting a back payment from Social
Security, say after winning an appeal,
it can be many times your usual deposit.
That is the high-dollar item on the
list. Call your bank before it arrives
and tell them it is coming and who is
sending it. At your kitchen table, write
one page. Your payment date. Your
expected deposit after part B. Your
bank's fraud department number. Social
Security's number, 1-800-772-1213.
And the name of one person besides you
who can see your accounts. If you or a
parent still gets a paper check, switch
this month. Waivers exist only in rare
cases through the Treasury. If anything
ever goes wrong, that one page turns a
frightening morning into three phone
calls. So, that is the journey. The
Treasury now checks who owns the account
before your money is sent. Two letters
mark it as a federal benefit on the way.
Your bank now watches it arrive, and a
series of similar benefit payments is
one of the patterns named in the
guidance. A flag can mean a short delay,
or in the rare serious case, a return
within two banking days. After it lands,
four other hands can reach in, and each
has its own rules and its own clock. And
January is the first raise every bank in
America is required to watch. Maybe your
situation has a twist I did not cover. A
payee, a joint account after a death, or
a deposit that is already being held.
Write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
Tell me what happened and when. I read
them, and they decide where my research
goes next. And a quick favor if you were
able. Every one of these videos means
days of reading rule books line by line.
If this one helped you, the support link
in the description keeps that work
going. And when you want these rules
within reach on a hard day, the quiet
rules is at kevinexplains.shop.
Scan the QR code on your screen or use
the pinned comment or the link in the
description. Before your next payment
day, open your banking app and read the
name on the account. Then, read the name
on your last letter from Social
Security. Make sure they match. I am
Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: Why Every Retiree Should Rethink the S&P 500 (Before It’s Too Late)

segments.text: If you own an S&P 500 fund, you probably
believe your money is spread across 500
companies. Look closer. Today, about 40
cents of every dollar in that fund sits
in just 10 of them. At the very top of
the dot-com bubble in 2000, it was about
26 cents. The index closed at a record
high on October 6th, and a record high
is exactly when nobody wants to ask what
is inside. But if you are retired, that
question matters more for you than for
anyone. Here is why. Two retirees each
put $1 million into the same S&P 500
fund. Each took out $40,000 a year. 10
years later, one had about $488,000
left. The other had about 2 million
Same fund, same withdrawals, the only
difference was the year they retired.
So, in this video, you will see what
changed inside the S&P 500 and why
artificial intelligence is the reason.
You will see what history says tends to
happen after a market gets this
lopsided. Then, you will see the moves
retirees can make about it without
selling in a panic and without paying a
dollar more in tax than you have to.
This is not a call to sell everything.
It is a call to know what you own before
the market decides for you.
Every number here comes from a source I
will name as we go, and you can check
them all through the sources listed in
the description. The people in my
examples are composites, but the market
returns are the real ones, and nothing
here is a prediction. Nobody knows what
the market does next. What you can know
is how much risk you are carrying and
whether it fits your age. Start with how
an S&P 500 fund actually works. It does
not split your money evenly. It weights
each company by its total market value.
The bigger a company gets, the more of
your dollar it receives. In plain terms,
the fund automatically buys more of
whatever has already gone up the most.
On the way up, that feels wonderful. On
the way down, it works in reverse.
When Tesla joined the index in December
2020, it was the largest company ever
added. Index funds had to buy it after
its shares had already risen several
hundred percent that year. For most of
history, this waiting barely mattered.
Forbes notes that the top 10 companies
have averaged about 24% of the index
over time. Today, based on the holdings
of the largest S&P 500 funds, the top 10
are about 40%. At the peak of the
dot-com bubble, research from Morgan
Stanley puts that figure at just over
26. Seven names do most of that work.
Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Amazon,
Alphabet, which owns Google, Meta, which
owns Facebook, and Tesla.
Wall Street calls them the Magnificent
Seven. Together, they're about 34% of
the S&P 500, according to Forbes.
Nvidia alone is worth about $5.2
trillion,
roughly 8% of the entire index. One
company, 8 cents of every dollar. To be
fair, that concentration is a big reason
the index did so well for a decade. The
giants earned their size. But look at
the arithmetic going the other way. If
the top 10 fell 40% and the other 490
did nothing at all, the whole index
would fall about 16%. Now, add what you
own outside the fund, because that is
where retirees get surprised. Murray and
Joan are 71 and 69 with $850,000
invested. $500,000 sits in an S&P 500
fund. Murray kept 120,000 in Apple stock
from his working years. Their son talked
them into 60,000 of Nvidia. And they own
a $90,000 technology fund full of the
same giants. Add it up and roughly half
of their entire nest egg rides on about
10 companies. They think they own 500.
On a bad day for big tech, they own 10.
If those giants fell 40%, about $170,000
of their savings would vanish on paper,
even if every other company held steady.
So, why did this happen? Mostly,
artificial intelligence. All seven of
those companies are tied to it in one
way or another. Amazon, Microsoft,
Alphabet, and Meta spent around $410
billion last year on buildings, chips,
and data centers. Their plans for this
year point to roughly $725 billion. And
that money moves in a circle. A large
share of what those companies spend on
chips goes to Nvidia, another member of
the same seven. So, when the spending is
strong, several giants rise together. If
it ever slows, they can fall together.
That spending could pay off. These are
some of the most profitable companies on
Earth, and artificial intelligence may
well change daily life. But when
investors all get excited about the same
idea at the same time, prices can run
far ahead of the profits. It happened
with the internet. In the late 1990s,
companies laid enormous amounts of fiber
optic cable for the coming boom. The
internet did arrive, but much of that
cable sat unused for years. And many of
the companies that paid for it went
broke. There is a well-known measure for
that, created by the Nobel Prize-winning
economist Robert Shiller. It compares
stock prices with 10 years of company
earnings, adjusted for inflation.
According to The Motley Fool, it
recently sat around 41. Only one stretch
in history saw it higher, at about 44,
at the end of 1999.
The Motley Fool is careful to say this
measure does not predict crashes, and it
can stay high for years. What it shows
is optimism is already built into the
price. Historically, very high readings
have tended to be followed by
below-average returns over the next
decade, though not every time. And you
know what came after 1999?
The internet really did change the
world. But from March 2000 to October
2002, the S&P 500 fell about 49%, and
the technology-heavy Nasdaq fell about
78. Even counting dividends, the S&P 500
ended that whole decade about 9% below
where it started. Murray and Joan never
chose to bet half their retirement on 10
companies. It happened one good year at
a time, and no statement ever flagged
it. That is the kind of quiet drift the
quiet rules is written to catch. So, you
spot it while there is still time to fix
it calmly. You can find it at
kevinexplains.shop.
On a TV, aim your phone's camera at the
QR code on the screen. On a phone or a
computer, the link sits in the pinned
comment and at the top of the
description. It carries a 7-day
guarantee. So, if it is not right for
you, you can get a refund. Murray still
checks the Apple price every morning on
the kitchen television. He calls it his
pension. Here is why this hits retirees
harder than anyone. When you were 40 and
still working, a 10-year slump hurts,
but you keep buying at lower prices.
When you are 70 and taking money out,
you are selling during the slump. Those
are the two retirees from the beginning.
Herbert retired in January 2000 with $1
million in an S&P 500 fund. He took out
$40,000 a year. Using the index's actual
yearly returns with dividends, his
account was down to about 540,000
after just 3 years. By the end of 2009,
it was about 488,000.
His withdrawals were not reckless.
$40,000 is 4% of a million, the classic
starting rate from William Bengen's
research in 1994. But, Bengen tested
portfolios that mixed stocks with bonds.
Herbert had every dollar in one index.
Floyd did exactly the same thing
starting in January 2010. Same fund,
same million, same 40,000 a year. After
10 years, he had about 2 million
Both men withdrew the same $400,000 over
their 10 years. Floyd was not smarter.
He was luckier with the calendar. J.P.
Morgan's Guide to Retirement has a
phrase for this. The greatest risk is
when wealth is greatest. The first few
years after you retire can decide more
than the next 20. A bad start forces you
to sell shares at low prices just to pay
your bills, and the shares you sold
never get the chance to recover. What
would have helped Herbert most was not a
hot stock. Suppose his next 2 years of
withdrawals had been sitting in cash and
bonds. He could have stopped selling
stocks in 2001 and 2002 and given them
time to come back. If this is the kind
of thing you want to hear before it
becomes news, subscribe because this
channel is built for exactly that.
History teaches a second lesson, too.
The leaders change. According to the UBS
Global Investment Returns Yearbook,
Britain was about a quarter of the
world's stock market at the start of
1900, the biggest of any country. The
United States was about 15%.
In the late 1980s, Japan was the market
everyone wanted. By some estimates,
around 40% of the world's total. Japan's
Nikkei Index hit a record on December
It did not close above that level again
until February 22nd, 2024.
34 [snorts]
years. Today, the United States is about
62% of the world's stock market value.
American companies earned that position,
and nobody can say they will lose it.
But last year offered a reminder.
According to Yahoo Finance, stocks in
developed markets outside the United
States returned about 32% in 2025, and
emerging markets about 34.
The S&P 500 returned nearly 18. Part of
that gap came from a weaker dollar,
which raises the value of foreign
holdings for American investors. And
currency can just as easily work the
other way. But that is exactly the
point. Nobody knows which country leads
the next 10 years, and a retirement plan
should not need to know. Herbert's
numbers are hard to look at. Roughly $2
million of difference between him and
Floyd, decided mostly by the year he
retired and by having every dollar in
one index when the storm hit.
Retirement rewards the people who
arrange things before the storm, not
during it. That is why I wrote The Quiet
Rules. It is at kevinexplains.shop.
If you are watching on a television, the
QR code on your screen opens it on your
phone. On a phone or a computer, tap the
link at the top of the comments or the
first line of the description. You have
7 days with it, and the 7-day guarantee
means a refund if it does not earn its
keep. Herbert still keeps his January
2000 statement in a folder. He has never
once opened the one from October 2002.
So, what can a retiree actually do about
all this? None of what follows means
selling everything, and none of it is
personal advice for your situation.
These are the moves people in your
position commonly look at. Take what
fits and leave the rest.
First, find out what you really own. Ask
your brokerage for a look-through view
of your holdings, or add up your largest
positions yourself, counting what sits
inside each fund.
If one company or one small group of
companies is a large share of your
total, you have found your
concentration. Many people find the same
few names three or four times. And if
you hold accounts at different firms, no
single statement will ever show you the
total. You have to add it up yourself or
ask someone to do it with you. Second,
match every dollar to when you will need
it. Money for the next one or two years
does not belong in stocks at all. If you
take 40,000 a year from savings, that
means keeping roughly 80,000 somewhere
steady. A common rule of thumb says
money you will need within 5 years
should not be in stocks, either. The
stock market is for money that can wait
out a bad decade. If a decade like the
one that started in 2000 would force you
to sell, part of your money is in the
wrong place. For that near money, think
short-term Treasuries, certificates of
deposit, and insured savings. Remember
that in 2022, stocks and the broad bond
market fell in the same year. So, near
money should be the kind whose value
barely moves. Third, look at how the
stock part is spread. The S&P 500 is a
fine index, but it is one index of large
American companies weighted toward the
biggest. There are funds that own the
total American market. There are funds
that hold the same 500 companies in
equal amounts, so each one gets roughly
the same small slice, about 1/5 of 1%.
And there are funds that own companies
outside the United States. Many target
date funds already blend these. The
point is not to pick the next winner. It
is to stop depending on one. And if the
market keeps rising, a more spread-out
mix may trail a little. Think of that
small gap as the price of insurance, the
same way nobody resents a fire policy in
a year without a fire. Fourth, rebalance
without handing the IRS a windfall.
Inside an IRA or a 401k, selling and
buying costs you no tax at that moment.
That makes it the easiest place to trim
what has grown too large. If you take
required minimum distributions, you can
take them from the holdings that grew
the most. That trims your concentration
while covering a withdrawal you owe
anyway. And if stock from your old
employer is still inside a 401k, ask
about a rule called net unrealized
appreciation before you roll it into an
IRA. Under that rule, the growth on
those shares can be taxed as a long-term
capital gain instead of as ordinary
income. Once the shares are rolled into
an IRA, that option is gone. As for how
often to rebalance, many people simply
check once a year on a date they pick in
advance. If any piece has drifted well
past the share they planned for it, they
trim it back. In a regular taxable
account, selling a winner can trigger
capital gains tax. But many retirees
overlook the 0% bracket. Kiplinger lays
out the 2026 numbers. Long-term capital
gains are taxed at 0% federally when
taxable income stays under $49,450
for a single filer.
For a married couple, the line is
Taxable income is what is left after
deductions, and the new $6,000 senior
deduction lowers it further. So, more
retirees fit under that line than they
realize, and some sell just enough
winners each year to fill that space at
no federal tax. Just remember that gains
still count toward how much of your
Social Security is taxed and toward
Medicare's income surcharge. Fifth, if
you inherited shares or your spouse died
owning them, check your cost basis
before you sell. Shares owned at death
generally get a new cost basis equal to
their value on the date of death. If the
two of you owned them jointly, in most
states the reset applies to the half
your spouse owned. In the nine community
property states like California and
Texas, the whole account can reset.
Edna's husband bought $40,000 of stock
decades ago all in his name. It was
worth $440,000 when he died. Her
statement still showed his old cost.
Selling on those numbers would have
reported $400,000 of gain that for tax
purposes no longer existed. One call to
update the basis fixed it. And if you
give to charity, giving shares that grew
a lot instead of cash lets the charity
sell them without anyone paying that
capital gains tax. And sixth, the
hardest one, do not let a scary week
make the decision for you.
JPMorgan tracks $10,000 invested in the
S&P 500 from 2006 through 2025. Staying
invested the whole time grew it to about
Missing just the 10 best days left about
And six of those 10 best days came
within two weeks of the 10 worst. People
who sell in a panic usually miss the
rebound. That is exactly why the time to
rearrange is now, calmly, at a record
high, and not in the middle of a drop.
One habit helps more than any forecast.
Write one page for yourself. What you
own, why you own it, how much stays safe
for the next two years, and the date
each year you will rebalance. When the
next scary week comes, you read your own
page instead of the headlines. And be
wary of anyone who pitches you gold,
crypto, or some product that is
supposedly safe from artificial
intelligence right after a video like
this.
Piling into a different single bet is
the same mistake wearing a new coat. So
here is where this leaves you. The S&P
500 is not broken. It holds some of the
finest businesses in the world, but it
is no longer the evenly spread basket
most retirees think they bought. And a
retiree no longer has decades to wait
out a bad stretch. Know what you own.
Match it to when you will need it. Trim
calmly with one eye on taxes.
If you work with an advisor, ask one
question at your next meeting. How much
of my total money depends on the 10
largest companies?
And let the decision happen on a quiet
afternoon, not on the worst day of the
year. Remember what you already have,
too. Your Social Security check rises
with inflation every year. And for many
retirees, it is the steadiest asset they
own. The more of your bills it covers,
the more patience you can afford with
everything else. If you would like a
second set of eyes on your own
situation, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
Tell me roughly how your money is split
and what worries you. I read these, and
they shape what I research next.
And one quick thing. Videos like this
one take days of checking every number
against its source. If this one helped,
there is a support link in the
description. It keeps this research
going. And if you want the rules behind
this kept where you can find them, The
Quiet Rules is at kevinexplains.shop.

applies. Tonight, open your latest
statement and circle every holding that

add up what you circled. Most retirees

to. I am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do

What if rates fall next year? Then, a

and the average money market account

And the most important question, Kevin,
is this not exactly what the scammers

Now, let us pull this together into your

Guaranteed income means money that

Social Security, a pension, and payments

any bank where one category passes
Then, look at every dollar above your
