title: Every Senior Must Check These 7 Benefits Before January 2027 or Lose Them

segments.text: Your January Social Security deposit is
going to be bigger and you will not fill
out a single form to get it. That part
is real and it is the part everyone is
talking about. What nobody is talking
about is who gets skipped. Seven things
change in your favor this January and
each one quietly passes over a group of
seniors. It passes over the couple who
files their taxes the wrong way. It
passes over the man who retired halfway
through last year. It passes over the
woman whose drug plan changed in a
letter she never opened. And the biggest
one passes over a great many people who
would qualify today because nobody ever
told them to ask. That one pays your
Medicare Part B premium for you. At this
year's price, that is $2,434
a year back in your check and next
year's price is projected to be higher.
Most people who qualify never apply for
one of three reasons. They think their
income is too high. They think their
savings are too big or they are afraid
the state will take their house when
they die. For a lot of people, all three
of those beliefs are wrong and I will
show you the federal law behind each
one. Every number in this video comes
from Social Security, Medicare, the IRS
or federal law itself and I will tell
you where each one comes from as we go.
You can check all of it through the
sources listed in the description. The
people in my examples are composites.
The rules and the dollar amounts are
real. Some of these seven arrive on
their own. Others only arrive if a form,
a tax return or a phone call says so. We
will start with the raise because even
the raise leaves a group behind. Number
one is the raise itself. According to
Social Security's own fact sheet for
2027, benefits go up 3.6%
starting with the January payment. For
the average retired worker, the monthly
check goes from $2,095
That is $75 more a month. For an aged
couple where both collect, the average
goes from $3,238
or $117 more. For a widow or widower
living on one check, it goes from 1,936
to 2,005. Now, here's the group this
raise leaves behind and it is bigger
than most people think. It is the people
whose raise gets quietly taxed. Up to
half of your Social Security becomes
taxable once your combined income
crosses $25,000 if you are single or
32,000 if you are married filing
jointly. Up to 85% becomes taxable above
34,000 single or 44,000 married. Those
lines were written into law in 1983 and
1993. They have never once been adjusted
for inflation. Your benefit is adjusted
every single year. The lines are not.
And combined income counts half of your
Social Security. So, the raise itself
helps push you toward them. The move for
this one starts this week. Social
Security says your new amount will
appear online in late November in the
message center of your my Social
Security account. But, only if that
account exists by November 18th. If you
have never set one up, do it now while
there is time. When the notice arrives,
set it next to last year's and compare
three lines. The gross benefit, the
Medicare deduction, and the amount
actually deposited. If that Medicare
line looks bigger than everyone else's,
you may belong to the group in number
two. Number two is the protection that
keeps Medicare from eating your raise.
Most people have their Part B premium
out of Social Security before the
deposit ever reaches the bank. This
year, the standard premium is $202.90
a month. In their June report,
Medicare's trustees projected about
for 2027. The official number usually
comes out in November. Either way, a
rule in the Social Security Act called
hold harmless says that for most people,
a Part B increase cannot make your net
check smaller than the year before. With
a $75 raise and a projected increase of
about $6.60,
the average retiree stays well ahead.
But hold harmless has three holes in it.
It does not cover people who are new to
Medicare in 2027.
It does not cover people whose premium
is billed to them directly instead of
taken from their check. And it does not
cover anyone who pays the income
surcharge Medicare calls IRMAA.
That third hole is where the real money
falls through.
According to Kiplinger, the surcharge
you pay in 2027 is based on your 2025
tax return, and that year is already
closed. In 2026, the surcharge started
of income for a single person and
$218,000 for a couple. Humana's 2026
tables show what the first level costs,
about $81 a month added to each person's
Part B premium, plus $14.50
on the drug plan.
And it works like a cliff. $1 over the
line triggers the whole amount. So, the
surcharge is really a bill for the
person you were 2 years ago. Otis and
Arlene know that person well. Otis ran a
regional sales office until June of
2025, then retired. His last 6 months of
salary, plus a final bonus, pushed their
2025 income past the line.
Today, they live on two social security
checks and a modest pension. And in
2027, Medicare will still add a
surcharge to both of their premiums
because of a paycheck that no longer
exists.
At this year's first level, that is
about $2,300
a year for the two of them. There is a
fix, and it has a plain name. Form
SSA-44 asks Social Security to use your
newer, lower income instead if your
income dropped because of a
life-changing event. The form lists
eight of them.
Marriage, divorce, and the death of a
spouse. Work stopping and work being cut
back. Losing a pension, losing property
that produced income, and a settlement
payment from an employer.
Choosing to sell stock or cash out an
account is not on that list. Otis
stopping work is. When their surcharge
letter arrives, they can file the form
with proof of his retirement date and
ask for a new decision. Here is what
bothers me about Otis and Arlene. The
surcharge will find them on its own. The
fix will not. It waits for them to know
its name.
That is exactly why I wrote the quiet
rules. It gathers the fixes that wait
for you to know their name, so you can
find the right one on the day the letter
shows up. You will find it at
kevinexplains.shop.
If you are watching on a television,
point your phone's camera at the QR code
on the screen. On a phone or a computer,
the link is in the pinned comment, and
it is also the first line of the
description.
You have 7 days to go through it, and if
it is not for you, the guarantee gets
you a refund.
In a few weeks, a letter from Social
Security will land on Arlene's kitchen
table. She will tuck it under the sugar
bowl beside the coupons. Otis will call
it the usual paperwork. Number three is
for anyone still working while
collecting before full retirement age.
Social Security's fact sheet puts the
2027 earnings limit at $25,560,
up from $24,480.
Above that line, Social Security holds
back $1 of benefits for every $2 you
earn over it. In the year you reach full
retirement age, the limit jumps to
and they hold back only $1 for every
three.
And only the earnings before the month
you reach that age count. If you were
born in 1960, 2027 is that year, because
your full retirement age is 67. After
that month, there is no limit at all.
This one leaves out the people who stop
working partway through a year and
assume the yearly number has already
ruined them.
There is a special rule for your first
year of retirement. In that year only,
Social Security can pay you a full check
for any month your earnings stay at or
under $2,130.
It does not matter how much you earned
earlier in the year.
Say you leave a full-time job in May
after earning $40,000, start your
benefits in June, and take a part-time
job paying $1,800 a month. On the yearly
test, you are far over. Under the
first-year rule, every month from June
on can be paid in full. And if money
does get held back, it is not gone. Once
you reach full retirement age, Social
Security recalculates your benefit to
give you credit for the months it held
back, and your check goes up from then
on. The move here is simple. When you
report your expected earnings, tell
Social Security the month you actually
stopped full-time work. That month is
what opens the door to the first-year
rule. If this is already useful to you,
subscribe. The official Part B premium
and next year's surcharge brackets come
out in November, and I will walk through
them the week they are published. Number
four arrives in late January when tax
season opens, and it is the one people
claim wrong most often. First, one thing
needs clearing up. Social Security did
not become tax-free. If your income is
high enough, part of it can still be
taxed, exactly the way we covered in
number one. What Congress did in the law
President Trump signed in July of 2025
is add a new deduction of $6,000 for
every person 65 or older. It applies to
tax years 2025 through 2028. It stacks
on top of the regular standard deduction
and the extra amount you already get for
age. Take your 2026 return, the one you
file this coming winter. A single person
over 65 can subtract $16,100
plus 2,050 for age plus the new 6,000.
That is $24,150
before the IRS taxes anything. For a
married couple who are both over 65, it
And unlike most breaks, you get the
6,000 whether you take the standard
deduction or itemize. So, who does it
skip? According to the National
Association of Tax Professionals, three
groups. First, married couples who file
separately. If you are married, you must
file jointly to get it. Second, anyone
without a valid Social Security number.
Third, higher earners. The deduction
shrinks by 6 cents for every dollar of
income above 75,000 for a single filer
or 150,000 for a couple. It is gone
entirely at 175,000 single or 250,000
joint. And here is the piece that
catches people off guard. This deduction
comes off after your adjusted gross
income is already figured. So, it does
not lower the combined income that
decides how much of your social security
gets taxed. And it does not lower the
income Medicare uses for the surcharge
in number two. It cuts your tax bill. It
does not move those two lines. When you
file, look for the enhanced deduction
for seniors by name on your return. And
if your income is low enough that you
think you can skip filing, check your
forms first. If any tax was withheld
from a pension or an account withdrawal,
filing is the only way to get it back.
If you want someone to check it for
free, the IRS runs a program called Tax
Counseling for the Elderly and AARP runs
one called Tax-Aide. The IRS line to
find the nearest site is 1-800-906-9887.
Number five lands on New Year's Day.
Medicare can now negotiate prices
directly with drug companies. The first
10 negotiated prices started this year,
and the second round, 15 more drugs,
takes effect January 1st, 2027.
According to Health Care Dive, Ozempic,
Wegovy, and Rybelsus drop from a list
price of $959
for a 30-day supply to $274.
Trilogy, a common inhaler, goes from 654
Breo goes from 397 to 67. Janumet, for
diabetes, goes from 526 to 80. The list
also includes Xtandi, Ibrance, Pomalyst,
Ofev, Linzess, Calquence, Austedo,
Xifaxan, Vraylar, Trajenta, and Otezla.
Medicare estimates people on drug plans
would have saved about 685 million
dollars out of their own pockets. The
yearly The keeps working, too. Once you
have paid $2,400
out of pocket for covered drugs in 2027,
you pay nothing more for them until the
year starts over. That cap was 2,100
this year, so it did go up. Now, who
gets left out of the price cuts? Anyone
who assumes a lower price means a lower
copay. Your cost still depends on how
your plan places the drug. If your plan
charges a flat copay, you may see no
change at all. And the deductible on a
standard drug plan rises in January to
$700, up from 615.
So, the first trip to the pharmacy in
January can be the most expensive one of
the year. If that worries you, call your
plan and ask about the Medicare
prescription payment plan. It lets you
pay your out-of-pocket drug costs in
monthly bills spread across the year
instead of all at once at the counter.
Thelma takes Trilogy and Janumet. In
September, her plan mailed its annual
notice of change. It moved her inhaler
to a higher tier and added a deductible
she did not have before. She never
opened it. On Medicare's Plan Finder,
another plan in her county covers both
drugs for about $1,100
less for the year. She has until
December 7th to switch. After that, her
choices shrink to a few narrow
exceptions for the rest of the year.
That is the price of one envelope Thelma
meant to get to. The letter told her
everything. It just never told her it
mattered.
The quiet rules exist so the next
envelope like that one gets opened in
time by someone who knows why it
matters.
It is at kevinexplains.shop.
If the video is playing on a TV, the QR
code on your screen opens it on your
phone. On a phone or a computer, the
link is pinned at the top of the
comments and waiting in the description.
Give it 7 days. If you decide it is not
earning its place on your shelf, the
7-day guarantee means a refund.
Thelma's envelope is still in the basket
by the front door under the seed
catalogs. The postmark says September.
Number six actually shows up before
January does. Supplemental Security
Income, called SSI, is a separate
program for people 65 and older or
disabled who have very little income and
very few assets. Many people get both, a
small Social Security check with SSI
filling in on top. Social Security's
fact sheet puts the 2027 federal payment
a month for one person, up from 994.
For a couple, it is 1,544.
Because January 1st is a holiday, Social
Security says the first higher payment
goes out on December 31st. For the
people already on SSI, that date is a
trap. It means two payments arrive in
December and none at all in January. The
next one comes February 1st. If the
December 31st payment gets spent as a
holiday bonus, January will feel very
long. But the larger group SSI misses is
the people who never apply because they
assume they own too much. The limit is
$2,000 in countable resources for one
person and 3,000 for a couple. Those
numbers have not changed since 1989.
But the home you live in does not count.
One car generally does not count. And
since September 30th, 2024, Social
Security no longer counts food that
family or friends give you as income.
Before that change, a son dropping off
groceries every week could shrink his
mother's payment. Now, it cannot.
Lucille is 80. She worked part-time for
most of her life, so her Social Security
is small. She owns her little house
outright and keeps about $1,600 in the
bank. Her son brings groceries every
Sunday after church. Lucille assumed the
house and the groceries both ruled her
out. Neither one does. Her move is a
single phone call to Social Security at
asking to apply for SSI. And in most
states, SSI also opens the door to
Medicaid, which leads straight into the
biggest one. Number seven is the one I
promised you at the start. Medicare
Savings Programs are run by your state's
Medicaid office with federal rules
underneath. When you qualify, the state
pays your Part B premium. At this year's
price, that is $2,434.80
a year. At next year's projected price,
it is about $2,514.
That money stops coming out of your
Social Security check and stays in your
account instead. There are three main
levels. The National Council on Aging
lists the 2026 monthly income limits for
a single person about $1,350
for the first level, called QMB, $1,616
for the second, called SLMB, and $1,816
for the third, called QI. For a married
couple, the top level goes to $2,455
a month. The first level goes even
further. It also covers your Part B
deductible and the 20% you normally pay,
and providers who take Medicare are not
allowed to bill you for those amounts.
Now, the three beliefs that keep people
away. Belief one, my income is too high.
A single person with about $1,800 a
month can still qualify. There is also a
rule that rarely gets mentioned. Federal
Medicaid law tells states to set aside
your January raise when they check your
income until the new federal poverty
numbers are published early in the year.
Texas spells this out in its own
Medicaid handbook. So, the 3.6% raise
does not knock you out in January.
Belief two, my savings are too big. The
federal limit for 2026 is $9,950
for one person and $14,910
for a couple. Your home and one car do
not count. And, according to Medicare
Interactive, run by the Medicare Rights
Center, 11 states plus Washington D.C.
have no asset limit at all. They include
New York, Massachusetts, Connecticut,
Arizona, Oregon, Louisiana, and Alabama.
Belief three, the state will take my
house.
Since January 1st, 2010, federal law has
required states to exempt Medicare
Savings program benefits from a state
recovery. The agency that runs Medicaid
spelled that out in a letter to every
state. The help with your premium does
not turn into a claim against your home.
Two more things make January the month
to act. The third level, QI, is paid
first come, first served each year. So,
applying early in the year matters. And
qualifying for any of these programs
automatically qualifies you for extra
help, which drops your drug plan
deductible to zero and keeps your copays
to a few dollars. It works the other
way, too. Under a law passed in 2008,
when you apply for extra help through
Social Security, your information goes
to your state. The state must then treat
it as an application for these programs.
And the second and third levels, SLMB
and QI, can often reach back up to 3
months before the month you apply. If
premiums were already taken out for
months the state ends up covering, that
money generally comes back to you. Della
and Rudy are 76 and 79. Between their
two Social Security checks, they bring
in about $2,300
a month. They have $12,000 at the credit
union and a paid-off house. For years,
Rudy would not apply because his father
lost the family farm to a county nursing
home bill. At the top level, both of
their Part B premiums stop coming out of
their checks. That is close to $4,900
a year at this year's price, and their
house is not on the hook for a penny of
it. The move is to call your state
Medicaid office and ask for the Medicare
Savings Program application by that
exact name. Ask whether your state uses
higher limits than the federal ones. And
if you were turned down, ask for the
reason in writing because you can
appeal. So, before you close this video,
find yourself in one of these. If you
have no my Social Security account, make
one before November 18th. If you are on
SSI, set the December 31st payment aside
for January. If your 2025 income
included a last paycheck, a big bonus,
or the loss of a spouse, keep form
SSA-44 handy for when the surcharge
letter comes. If you are working and
collecting early, tell Social Security
the month you stopped full-time work. If
you are married, file jointly and look
for the senior deduction by name. If you
take a brand name drug, open your plan's
September letter before December 7th.
And if your income is anywhere near
$1,800 a month or 2,455
for a couple, apply for a Medicare
savings program. Let the state tell you
no instead of telling yourself. If one
of these seven fits your life, but you
are not sure how, write to me. Tell me
your situation in a few sentences at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read these and your questions decide
what I research next. And one quick
favor. Every video like this one takes
days of reading federal rules and
checking each number against its source.
If this one helped you, there is a
support link in the description. It
keeps this research going. And if you
would like the rules behind all seven
kept in one place, the quiet rules is at
kevinexplains.shop.
The QR code is on your screen. The link
is pinned in the comments and listed in
the description. And the 7-day guarantee
still stands. Tonight, look for the
password to your My Social Security
account or for the letter that proves
you never made one. Your January notice
is already being written. November 18th
decides whether you get to read it
first. I am Kevin. Thanks for watching.
Do not forget to check the quiet rules
at kevinexplains.shop.

title: BREAKING: Congress Has a New Plan for All Homeowners Over 60

segments.text: Your house is paid off and it's still
costs you more every single year. The
tax bill climbs, the insurance bill
climbs faster and right now the rules
around that house are being rewritten in
three places at once. In Congress,
inside the Treasury and in seven states
where voters decide on November 3rd. One
law starts on January 7th and almost
nobody selling a house has heard of it.
One bill would let some owners over 65
sell with up to a million dollars of
profit tax-free and one sentence inside
it leaves most of you out. A law signed
last year quietly puts a ceiling on how
much home you can own and still get help
paying for a nursing home and a
Bloomberg analysis published on October
20th found that in about two-thirds of
American counties the insurance bill is
now bigger than the property tax bill.
So, here is how I am going to take it. A
paid-off house still sends you four
bills. The bill when you sell it, the
bill to insure it, the bill if you ever
need long-term care and the tax bill.
Congress and the states just changed all
four. For each one you will hear what is
already law, what is only a bill and
what you can do about it this week. I am
starting with the bill Congress is
fighting over right now. One question
for the comments first. What did your
homeowner's insurance do at renewal this
year? Went up, went down or dropped you?
One word is enough. Your answers tell me
where to dig next. If you own a home,
subscribe now because the vote results
and Treasury's final rule are coming in
the next few weeks and I will cover them
as they land. Every number here comes
from a source I name as I go. From
Bloomberg and Ballotpedia to the IRS,
the Treasury and the bills themselves on
congress.gov. All of them are listed in
the description. I am not a lawyer, a
tax preparer or an insurance agent. This
is general education and your state and
your policy can change the answer. The
first bill is the one that arrives when
you sell. Under the law today you can
exclude up to $250,000
of profit on your main home if you are
single. If you are married filing
jointly, $500,000.
You have to have owned it and lived in
it for two of the last five years. Those
limits were written in 1997, and they
have never been raised for inflation.
Not once in almost 30 years. So, more
people cross them every year without
moving an inch. The Budget Lab at Yale,
measuring actual profits, estimated that
about one homeowner in 10 was over the
limit in 2022, and said the share is
likely higher now. The National
Association of Realtors, counting home
equity instead, puts about 29 million
homeowners, roughly a third, above the
single-person limit, and projects 70% by
2035. For people who are over the line,
the Budget Lab estimated that ending the
tax would save them about $100,000 each,
on average. So, this is not a plan for
everyone, but for the people it touches,
the number is very large. That is the
problem Congress is circling, and there
are four bills on the table. The one
getting the headlines is the Nest Egg
Protection Act, HR 9064,
introduced on June 1st by Representative
Nicole Malliotakis of New York. If you
are 65 or older, it would let you
exclude up to $1 million of profit, the
same for single people and couples.
Now, the sentence that leaves most
people out. You must have owned the home
for at least 25 years. Buy at 50, and it
does nothing for you until 75.
A second bill, the More Homes on the
Market Act from Representative Jimmy
Panetta, would raise the limits to
500,000 and 1 million, and finally tie
them to inflation. A third, the No Tax
on Home Sales Act from Representative
Marjorie Taylor Greene, would end the
tax on selling your main home
altogether. A fourth, from
Representative Craig Goldman, would do
the same for anyone who lived in the
home at least two years. The White House
has been circling it, too. In July of
last year, President Trump told
reporters, "Quote, we are thinking about
no tax on capital gains on houses."
This August, Larry Kudlow said on Fox
Business that the president was very
interested in changing it. The National
Economic Council's Kevin Hassett said
new tax breaks were being looked at
before the midterms. But, here is the
status, plainly. All four bills are
still sitting in a House committee.
Experts quoted by CNBC called passage
before the midterms unlikely.
Until something passes and is signed,
the 1997 limits are the law. What
catches people is not the capital gains
tax by itself. It is the ripple. The
taxable part of a home sale counts as
income for that year. It can push more
of your Social Security into the taxable
column. It can shrink or erase the new
senior deduction, which starts shrinking
of income for a couple. Above $250,000
for a couple, the taxable gain can also
face a 3.8% tax on investment income.
And 2 years later, Medicare reads that
same tax return to set your premiums. A
home sale is not on Social Security's
list of life-changing events. So, that
surcharge generally cannot be appealed
away. Picture a couple I will call
Randall and Peggy, with the numbers
rounded to keep the math simple. Both
72, outside Worcester, Massachusetts.
They bought in 1986 for $110,000,
then put about 70,000 into a roof, a
kitchen, and an addition. Next spring,
they sell for 950,000.
After about 57,000 in selling costs,
their profit is about 713,000.
500,000 of it is tax-free.
At today's federal rates, that is
roughly $26,000 of capital gains tax,
plus about 2,200 in investment income
tax. Most of their senior deduction is
gone for the year.
Two years later, Medicare charges each
of them about $240 a month more for Part
B and drug coverage, close to $5,800
for 1 year. And during the garage
cleanout, Peggy threw away a shoebox of
old receipts. Without proof of those
improvements, the same sale cost them
roughly $17,000
more. Randall and Peggy knew about the
$500,000 exclusion. Everybody knows that
number. What nobody put in front of them
was the Medicare surcharge that trails a
big income year by 2 years. Or the fact
that a sale is not a reason Social
Security will accept to lower it. The
Quiet Rules is where I wrote rules like
that one down in plain English. So, a
big decision gets made with the whole
bill in view instead of half of it. You
can find it at kevinexplains.shop.
On a television, point your phone's
camera at the QR code on your screen. On
a phone or a computer, the link is in
the pinned comment and on the first line
of the description. It comes with a
7-day guarantee, so you have a full week
to decide if it is worth keeping.
Their new condo still smells of fresh
paint. The Medicare letter will not be
printed for 2 more years. Here is what
those four bills would mean for one
person. Picture a widow who bought her
house in 1990 for $150,000.
After costs, it would sell today for
700,000. Her profit is 550,000.
Under today's law, as a single person,
300,000 of that is taxable. Under the
Nest Egg bill, she is over 65 and has
owned the house more than 25 years, so
all of it would be tax-free. Under the
More Homes on the Market bill, 50,000
would be taxable. Under the No Tax on
Home Sales bill, none of it. Same house,
four very different tax bills, and only
one of them is the law today. Before you
sell, there are three rules in today's
law that work in your favor, and all
three come from IRS Publication 523.
First, keep every receipt for
improvements. A new roof, a kitchen, an
addition, a deck, they raise what the
tax code calls your basis, which shrinks
your taxable profit. Repairs and
repainting generally do not count.
Improvements do.
Second, if a husband or wife dies, the
survivor can still use the $500,000
exclusion. The house has to be sold
within 2 years of the death, and the
survivor cannot have remarried. After
that, it drops to 250,000.
Third, the one families most often miss.
If you become unable to care for
yourself and move into a licensed care
facility, such as a nursing home, the
time you spend there counts as time
living in your home. You only need to
have lived in the house at least 1 year
out of the five before the sale. And if
your health forces a move before you
reach 2 years in a home, the IRS allows
a partial exclusion based on how much of
the 2 years you completed. One more
planning point. Because a sale is taxed
in the year it closes. If you can choose
between closing in late December or
early January, you are choosing which
year carries that income, and which
year's Medicare premium it touches. Talk
to whoever does your taxes before you
sign the listing agreement, not after
you sign the closing papers. Now, the
law that starts on January 7th. The 21st
Century Road to Housing Act passed the
Senate 85 to 5, and the House 358 to 32.
The president neither signed nor vetoed
it, and it became law on July 11th. The
part that touches sellers limits large
institutional investors, meaning
companies that control 350 or more
single-family homes.
According to the National Association of
Realtors, starting January 7th, 2027,
those companies generally may not buy
more unless the purchase fits an
exception. Treasury released its
proposed rules on October 22nd. The law
firm Allen Matkins notes that the limit
runs for 15 years with penalties of up
to a million dollars per violation or
three times the purchase price,
whichever is greater. Homes they already
own do not have to be sold. What does
that mean if you are selling? For most
of you, very little because most homes
are bought by families. But if you live
in a market where the big rental
companies have been buying, one kind of
cash buyer mostly steps back from
existing homes after January 7th.
Smaller investors, the ones with fewer
than 350 homes, are not covered at all.
And there are exceptions worth knowing.
A large investor can still buy a home
that fails key building code standards
if it spends at least 15% of the price
fixing it. Newly built homes for rent
are exempt and so is qualifying housing
for people 55 and older. So, if a letter
offers cash for your house as is, the
law does not tell you who sent it. Ask.
The second bill is the one that now
outweighs the tax. Bloomberg
Intelligence compared insurance and
property taxes in every county using
census data and records from state
insurance regulators. In about
two-thirds of counties, the average
homeowner's premium is now higher than
the average property tax bill. After
adjusting for inflation, average
premiums rose about 45% over a decade.
In Nebraska, 79%.
In the Southeast, where property taxes
are low, insurance can run two and a
half to four times the tax. Across all
counties, owners now pay about 14% more
for insurance than for property tax on
average. Bloomberg flagged two quieter
shifts as well. Deductibles are rising,
so more of each repair comes out of your
pocket first. And over the last two
decades, Washington paid roughly 90% of
the cost of recovering from disasters.
That split is moving toward 50/50, which
leaves local budgets and in the end,
local taxpayers carrying more. So, when
a candidate promises to cut your
property tax, ask what is happening to
the other bill. Then, open your own
policy because three lines in it may
have changed while you were not looking.
The first is your roof. Many policies no
longer pay for an older roof at
replacement cost. They pay actual cash
value, meaning the insurer subtracts
depreciation for age, or they use a
payment schedule that pays less each
year the roof gets older, sometimes only
for wind and hail. United Policyholders,
a consumer group, walks through an
example. A $20,000 roof, 10 years old,
losing a $1,000 of value a year with a
$1,000 deductible. At replacement cost,
the owner pays 1,000. At actual cash
value, about 11,000. The second line is
your deductible for wind, hail, or
hurricanes. Many policies now state it
as a percentage of the home's insured
value instead of a dollar amount. 2% of
home is $6,400
before the policy pays anything. The
third line is the renewal itself.
Changes like these usually arrive inside
the renewal packet as an endorsement,
and paying the renewal generally means
the new terms apply. Lorna is a blend of
several households with rounded numbers.
She is 76 outside Kearney, Nebraska, and
her roof is 17 years old. Two renewals
ago, her policy moved to a roof payment
schedule for wind and hail. It was on
page 11. In June, hail took the roof.
The quote to replace it was $24,000.
Her schedule pays about 30% for a roof
that age, 7,200.
Her hail deductible is 2%, 6,400.
Her check came to $800. Tonight, there
is a blue tarp on her roof, held down at
the corners with bricks. So, before your
next renewal, find the declarations page
and ask your agent three questions. Is
my roof paid at replacement cost, actual
cash value, or on a schedule? What is my
wind and hail deductible in dollars?
And what changed at my last renewal?
Then, get at least two other quotes
because the same house can be priced
very differently from one company to the
next. Ask about discounts for a newer
roof, roof straps, or storm shutters.
In Florida, insurers are required to
offer credits for wind mitigation
features, and an inspection can pay for
itself.
If you have savings, a higher deductible
for everyday claims can lower the
premium, but only if you could write
that check tomorrow.
And one warning for paid-off homes.
Once the mortgage is gone, no lender
checks that you are insured or that your
coverage has kept up with the cost of
rebuilding.
That is how people end up underinsured
without ever deciding to be.
Check the dwelling coverage on that same
page. It should match what it would cost
to rebuild the house today, not what the
house would sell for.
Many companies offer extended
replacement cost, which adds a cushion
if building prices jump after a
disaster. And remember that a standard
homeowner's policy does not cover
flooding. Flood coverage is separate,
usually through the National Flood
Insurance Program, and a new policy
generally has a 30-day waiting period.
It cannot be bought once the storm is
already on the radar.
One last habit. Think twice before
filing small claims. Several small
claims can raise your premium or put a
renewal at risk. So, many owners keep
insurance for the losses they could not
absorb on their own. The third bill is
the one nobody wants to think about.
Long-term care.
A long nursing home stay can cost far
more than most retirement incomes, and
Medicaid is the biggest payer of long
stays once savings run low.
Here is how Medicaid looks at your house
today. While you live there, or your
husband or wife does, the home is
generally protected when you apply. But
for a single person, there is a limit on
how much home equity you can have and
still qualify. Equity means the value
minus anything you still owe on it.
According to Elder Law Answers, the
federal minimum limit in 2026 is
States can choose to go as high as about
The Tax and Spending Law President Trump
signed in July of 2025 changes that.
Starting in January 2028, no state may
protect more than $1 million of home
equity, and that million is frozen. It
does not rise with inflation while home
values do.
12 states and Washington D.C. currently
allow more, including California, New
York, Massachusetts, Colorado, and
Hawaii, and they will have to come down.
The cap does not apply when a spouse, a
child under 21, or a blind or disabled
child lives in the home. Homes on land
zoned for agriculture keep the old
rules. States must offer a hardship
waiver. And after death, Medicaid's
estate recovery rules still apply to the
house, whatever the equity limit was.
Here is who that cap reaches. I will
call her Rosalie, and her details are
blended and her numbers rounded. She is
81, a widow [clears throat] outside
Pasadena, California.
Her house is paid off and worth about
Under California's limit today, that
equity would not block her from
Medi-Cal's long-term care coverage. Her
daughter remembers that when Rosalie's
husband needed nursing care, the house
was never a problem. That was because
Rosalie was still living in it. Now, she
lives alone. If she needs that care in
2028 or later, her equity would be about
$50,000 over the new cap, and that cap
grows every year the house gains value
because the cap does not. Nothing about
this was hidden. It sits in a law that
was mostly reported as a tax cut, but it
changes what Rosalie's family may need
to weigh and when. Selling, borrowing
against the house, asking for a hardship
waiver, or simply knowing the rule
before a hospital discharge planner
brings it up. The Quiet Rules walks
through Medicaid planning in plain
English. So, a family meets rules like
this one on a quiet afternoon instead of
in a hospital hallway. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
The QR code is on your screen. The same
link is pinned at the top of the
comments and sits first in the
description. There is a 7-day guarantee
on it, and you will not have to explain
yourself to use it. Rosalie's daughter
has a sticky note on the dashboard of
her car. It says, "Call about mom's
house." It has been there since August.
Two more Medicaid rules sit right next
to the new cap. In most states, Medicaid
looks back 5 years at gifts. Give the
house to your children within 5 years of
applying, and you can face a penalty
period with no coverage. There are
exceptions. One is a transfer to a
husband or wife. Another is a transfer
to a son or daughter who lived in the
home for at least 2 years and gave care
that kept you out of a nursing home.
And if you sell the house before you
need care, it stops being a protected
home and becomes cash that Medicaid
counts.
Some families reduce home equity with a
reverse mortgage or a home equity loan.
Each comes with costs and rules of its
own. So, that is a decision for an elder
law attorney, not a brochure. Before the
last bill, one rule about what happens
to the house after you are gone, because
it changes whether selling now even
makes sense.
When someone inherits a home, its tax
basis generally resets to its value on
the date of death. The profit built up
over your lifetime is wiped clean for
tax purposes.
For married couples, at the first death,
usually half the house gets that reset.
In the nine community property states,
Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana,
Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington,
and Wisconsin, the whole house can
reset. That is why adding a son or
daughter to your deed while you are
alive can backfire. The share you hand
them keeps your old basis, and they can
lose the reset on it. Talk to an estate
attorney before you sign anything that
changes the deed. If your house is
already in a living trust, check one
more thing. Make sure your homestead and
senior exemptions survived the move into
the trust. In many states they can, but
only when the paperwork was filed the
way your assessor requires. Now, put two
of today's rules together and look at
Randall and Peggy's house again.
If one of them dies first, half the
house resets to its value at that death.
The survivor then still has 2 years to
sell with the $500,000 exclusion.
Together, those two rules can erase most
or all of the taxable profit. Selling
sooner is not automatically the smarter
move.
The fourth bill is the tax bill and on
Tuesday, November 3rd, voters in seven
states decide 13 property tax measures.
That count comes from Ballotpedia, which
tracks every measure on every ballot. If
you're watching after the vote, the
results will be on your state's election
website. What matters is what each one
does and when it starts. Florida's
Amendment 3 is the biggest. For every
property tax except school taxes, it
would exempt the first $150,000
of a homestead's value in 2027.
In 2028, the first 250,000.
Inflation adjustments would start in
If it passes, the larger exemption would
first show up on the tax bills mailed in
November of 2027.
Today, the homestead exemption is up to
50,000. It would also cut the yearly cap
on assessment increases for property
that is not a homestead from 10% to
five. It needs 60% of the vote. Keep in
mind that it does not touch school
taxes, which are often a large part of
the bill.
And there is a catch for newcomers.
Anyone who was not a Florida resident on
December 31st, 2026 would get the larger
exemption only from their fifth
qualifying year. Wyoming's Initiative 1
would exempt half the value of a primary
home, the house itself, not the land,
with no cap. It stacks on top of the
exemption Wyoming passed in 2025, which
covers a quarter of the first million
dollars of value.
You would need a year of residency and 6
months of living in the home.
Opponents say the biggest savings would
go to the most expensive homes, and that
counties and schools would face
shortfalls. Oklahoma's State Question
847 deserves a careful look if you are
over 65, because it gives with one hand
and takes with the other.
It would lower the yearly cap on
assessment increases for homesteads from
3% to 1 and 3/4, but the full value
freeze that Oklahomans 65 and older can
get today would become income-based. At
or below your county's median income,
the freeze stays. Above it, your home's
value could rise each year by about a
third of a percent up to 1 and 3/4%
depending on your income. If it passes
and you are near that line, ask your
county assessor how your freeze would be
handled. Louisiana has five measures,
and two are aimed at seniors.
Amendment 6 would add an exemption for
owners 65 and older who already qualify
for the state's income-based freeze.
It starts at $6,000 of assessed value at
65 and rises to 30,000 at 81.
It begins with tax year 2028, and each
parish has to approve it in its own
local vote.
Amendment 9 would raise the freeze's
income limit from $100,000 to $150,000,
also starting in 2028.
North Carolina would put limits on how
fast local property tax levies can grow,
with the actual limits set later by
lawmakers, who could also allow
exceptions.
Tennessee would ban a statewide property
tax, which it does not have, so local
bills would not change. And Georgia's
measure is about farm and timberland, so
homeowners generally would not see a
difference. Even if you do not live in
one of these states, watch the results
because ideas like these tend to travel
and keep the caution critics raise in
every state. A cap on your home's
assessed value is not a cap on your bill
because local governments can still
raise the rate. Now, the money that is
already law in a few big states and none
of it is automatic. In Texas, voters
approved two changes last November. The
school tax homestead exemption rose from
The extra exemption for owners 65 and
older or disabled rose from 10,000 to
60,000. Together, that can take up to
off your home's value for school taxes.
Texas also freezes the school tax for
owners 65 and older at the amount in the
year they qualify. And the senior
exemption counts for the whole year in
which you turn 65. You apply through
your county appraisal district. Call and
confirm both increases are on your
account. And if you move within Texas,
that senior school tax freeze can follow
you to the new home as a percentage. One
more rule for every state. After a
husband or wife dies, call the
assessor's office. Some exemptions have
to be applied for again in the
survivor's name. And Texas lets a
surviving spouse who is at least 55 keep
the senior freeze. In New York, a law
Governor Hochul announced last December
lets towns, counties, and school
districts raise the senior exemption
from 50% of assessed value to as much as
Her office said the old ceiling had not
been raised in decades. But each
locality has to choose to adopt it and
each sets its own income limit. Ask your
assessor two things. Did my town adopt
the higher exemption and do I need to
reapply?
In New Jersey, one form called the PAS-1
covers three programs: Anchor, Senior
Freeze, and StayNJ.
StayNJ is for homeowners 65 and older
with income up to $500,000.
It reimburses half of the property tax
bill up to $6,500
after the other two programs are
counted. For tax year 2025, senior
freeze required total income of $172,475
or less.
The deadline for this round is November
2nd. If you are watching before then,
file this weekend. And in Florida, tax
bills go out around the 1st of November.
Pay in November and state law gives you
a 4% discount, 3% in December, 2 in
January, 1 in February. On a $5,000
bill, paying in November instead of
March is worth $200.
Florida also lets counties and cities
offer an extra exemption to owners 65
and older with limited income. So, ask
your property appraiser whether yours
does. In California, Proposition 19 lets
homeowners 55 and older move their
property tax base value to a replacement
home anywhere in the state up to three
times. If the new home costs more, only
the difference is added. In
Pennsylvania, the property tax and rent
rebate program pays up to $1,000 a year
to homeowners 65 and older with
household income of $45,000 or less.
Only half of your Social Security counts
toward that limit. And wherever you
live, read the assessment notice when it
arrives. If the value is higher than
what your home would actually sell for,
you can appeal.
The window is usually short, often 30 to
60 days, so the date on that notice
matters more than anything else on it.
When the bill itself comes, look for the
exemption lines. If an exemption you
qualify for is not printed on the bill,
it is not being applied. Many states
also let older owners defer property tax
until the house is sold, with the
deferred amount and interest repaid from
the sale or the estate. It keeps you in
the house, but it eats equity. So, ask
the interest rate first. And if anyone
you love ever falls behind, there is a
Supreme Court ruling from 2023, Tyler
against Hennepin County. A county that
takes a home for unpaid taxes generally
cannot keep more than what was owed. The
surplus belongs to the owner, though in
many places it has to be claimed. One
more tax item from Washington for those
of you who itemize.
The same law signed in July of 2025
raised the cap on deducting state and
local taxes, including property tax,
from $10,000 to $40,000. Kiplinger puts
it at 40,400 for 2026, rising 1% a year
through 2029. It shrinks once income
passes about $505,000,
but never below 10,000. And in 2030,
unless Congress acts again, it falls
back to 10,000. If you still carry a
mortgage, the same law made the $750,000
limit on deductible mortgage debt
permanent. And starting with 2026
returns, premiums for private mortgage
insurance can be deducted again as
mortgage interest. It also took one
homeowner break away. The federal tax
credits for home energy improvements,
like efficient windows, heat pumps, and
solar panels, ended for work done after
December 31st, 2025.
If a contractor this year still promises
you a 30% federal credit, ask them to
show you where it is written.
Three things to watch in the next few
weeks.
The results on November 3rd. Treasury's
comment period on the investor rule,
which runs 30 days from publication. And
Medicare's official premiums for next
year, which usually come out in
November, along with the income lines
that decide who pays the surcharge we
talked about.
If you are deciding whether to keep a
house, sell it, or pass it on, and the
numbers will not line up, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
Tell me your state, the year you bought,
and roughly what the house is worth
today.
Leave out account numbers and anything
like your social security number. Nobody
needs those to look at a decision. Here
is what strikes me after laying all four
bills side by side. Every one of them
has the same shape. The rule is written
down, often years ahead, and it gets
explained to you on the worst possible
day. After the storm, after the closing,
after the diagnosis, after the vote.
Lorna's roof clause was in her packet
for 2 years. Randall and Peggy's
Medicare surcharge was set the day they
signed. Rosalie's cap was written into
the law before most people had heard of
it. None of these rules is secret. They
are just quiet, and quiet rules are
cheapest to learn while the house is
still quiet, too. And most of it comes
down to three pieces of paper you
already own. The declarations page of
your insurance policy, your property tax
bill with its exemption lines, and the
folder of receipts for everything you
ever improved. Find all three this week,
and you will know more about your house
than most people who sell one. If you
want rules like these gathered in one
place, the Quiet Rules is pinned at the
top of the comments. The QR code is on
your screen, the link is in the
description, and the same 7-day
guarantee applies. Tonight, find your
insurance declarations page and look
next to the word roof for two words,
replacement cost. If you cannot find
them, that is your first phone call
tomorrow. I am Kevin. Thanks for
watching. Do not forget to check the
Quiet Rules at kevinexplains.shop.

title: Born Before 1966? 4 Social Security Deadlines Hitting Your Birth Year in 2027

segments.text: Put your finger on the year you were
born. It is on your screen right now in
one of four rows. Between now and your
birthday next year, that row will decide
things your savings, your health, and
your hard work never will. Group one,
born 1960 through 1965.
One birth year in your row reaches an
age no American has ever had to wait
for. Another gets a first Medicare bill
priced off a paycheck many of them have
already stopped earning. Group two, 1955
through 1959. One birth year in your row
is the last one that waiting pays for
and anyone in your row who leaves a job
next year starts three clocks at once.
Group three, 1950 through 1954. One
birth year has a deadline on New Year's
Eve and missing it can stack two years
of withdrawals onto one tax return.
Group four, 1949 and earlier. If you
carry the supplement millions of people
your age bought, its price is now set by
a pool of customers that only gets
older. Nobody new has been allowed to
join it since 2020. So, I am not going
through this group by group. I am going
through it the way it will actually
reach your mailbox, one date at a time.
Four dates, December 7th, New Year's
Eve, January 1st, and your birthday next
year. At every date, I will tell you
which groups it hits. Stay for the dates
that are not yours, too. If you are
married, the person across the table may
sit in a different row and two rows
under one roof is where a lot of money
quietly leaks out. Before the first
date, do one thing in the comments. Type
the year you were born. If you are
married, add your husband's or wife's
year right after it. Two years, one
comment. It shows me how many houses
have two groups under one roof and by
the end, you will see why that matters.
If any of these dates belongs to you,
subscribe now. Medicare's official
premium for next year and the new tax
lines come out in the next few weeks and
I will go through them the week they
land. Everything in this video comes
from Social Security's own fact sheet
for next year, the IRS, Medicare's
website and trustees, and research on
drug plans from KFF. Every source is
listed in the description, so you can
check it yourself. I am not a lawyer, a
tax preparer, or a financial advisor.
This is general education, and your own
numbers can change the answer. The first
date is December 7th. That is the last
day of Medicare's open season, and
whatever you choose by then starts on
the 1st of January. Most years, people
treat it as optional. This year, one
large group of Medicare customers should
not. If you have original Medicare with
a supplement, your drug coverage usually
comes from a separate stand-alone drug
plan. About 25 million people had one of
those this year, according to KFF, the
health research group. For the last 2
years, a temporary federal program kept
those plans from raising premiums too
fast. In 2025, no more than $35 a month.
This year, no more than 50. Medicare has
ended that program for 2027. KFF warns
that some people in these plans could
see bigger premium increases next year
than they have seen in recent years.
Your own number is in a letter your plan
mailed in September called the annual
notice of change. If it went out with
the junk mail, call the number on your
plan card and ask one question. What
will my premium be on January 1st? While
you have that letter open, check three
more things. The deductible, whether
each of your medicines is still on the
plan's list, and whether your pharmacy
is still in the network. Then, put your
prescriptions into the plan finder on
medicare.gov and compare. If you would
like a person beside you while you do
it, every state has a free Medicare
counseling program called SHIP, and its
counselors are not paid by any insurance
company. If you have a Medicare
Advantage plan with drug coverage built
in, the federal help that just ended
only covered stand-alone drug plans.
Your plan can still change, so read its
notice, too. Now, groups three and four,
and this is the one I promised in the
first minute. If you were born in 1954
or earlier, there is a good chance your
supplement is plan F. For years, it was
the plan people bought when they wanted
every bill covered. Then, a federal law
closed it. Since the 1st of January
2020, nobody new to Medicare has been
allowed to buy plan F. The people who
already had it could keep it. Think
about what that does to the pool. No
younger customers come in. Every year,
the people still in it are a year older,
and older customers file more claims.
Consumer guides like NerdWallet say it
plainly. Because plan F is closed to new
members, its pool is aging, and that can
[clears throat] lead to larger premium
increases. There is a plan right next
door to it. Plan G covers everything
plan F covers except one thing, the part
B deductible. This year, that deductible
So, here is a simple test. Look up the
plan G premium for your age and zip
code, and compare it with what you pay
for plan F. If plan G saves you more
than about $24 a month, it comes out
ahead, even after you pay that
deductible yourself. In many areas, the
gap is bigger than that. But switching
is not automatic, and this is where
people get hurt. In most states, once
your first 6 months on Medicare have
passed, a supplement company is allowed
to ask health questions and turn you
down. A few states give you a yearly
window around your birthday, including
California and Oregon. Your state's SHIP
office knows your state's rule. And
never cancel the old policy until the
new one has been approved in writing.
Betty is a made-up name for a very
common situation, and her numbers are
rounded. She is 82 and lives outside
Chattanooga. She bought plan F the year
she turned 65 and never looked back,
because it paid everything. Every
renewal came with a higher premium, and
every year she paid it. Her
sister-in-law, the same age in the same
county, switched to plan G at 75. She
pays about $75 a month less, covers the
deductible herself, and still keeps
roughly $600 a year. Betty kept meaning
to make the same call. Last spring, she
had heart surgery. Now, the health
questions on a new application are a
wall she cannot climb. The door was open
for years. Nobody marked it, so nobody
noticed when it closed. Betty never
needed a lecture about Medicare. She
needed someone to mark that door while
it was still open.
The Quiet Rules is built to mark doors
like that one. Which ones close, when
they close, and what to say on the phone
while they are still open. It lives at
kevinexplains.shop.
If you are watching on a television,
hold your phone up to the QR code on the
screen, and the page opens.
On a phone or a computer, the pinned
comment at the top has the link, and so
does the first line of the description.
Take a full week with it. The 7-day
guarantee covers every one of those
days. Betty still writes every bill by
hand in her checkbook register. The new
premium is in there now, in blue ink on
the line under last year's. Back to
December 7th for one moment, because
groups one and two read it differently.
Group two, almost all of you turned 65
in 2020 or later, so plan F was never
sold to you. If you have a supplement,
it is probably plan G or plan N, and the
part B deductible is yours to pay. It
usually rises a little every January.
Group one, if you were born in 1961,
this is your first open season on
Medicare. If you were born in 1962, your
own Medicare window is about to open,
and I will come back to you at the last
date. And for every group, if your
medicines are expensive, ask your drug
plan about the Medicare prescription
