up to a cap, and next year that cap
rises to $192,300,
If you earn above it, that is up to $483
more in tax as an employee, and about
967 if you are self-employed. If you are
self-employed, the combined rate is
Medicare tax has no cap at all, 1.45% on
every dollar, plus 9/10 of a percent
more above 200,000 for a single person
or 250,000 for a couple. Most of you
will never come near that ceiling. But
underneath it sits a rule that matters
to anyone who still earns anything.
There is no age at which Social Security
tax stops. If you work at 75, you pay
it. And there is something you get back
for it that almost nobody explains.
Every year, Social Security reviews the
earnings of everyone who collects and
still works. If your newest year is one
of your 35 best, it refigures your
benefit and pays the increase on its
own. No application. If you work in
2026, any increase is paid in December
of 2027, backdated to that January.
Whether a new year beats an old one
comes down to a quirk. Social Security
does not compare plain dollars. Every
paycheck [snorts] you earned before 60
is multiplied up to match how much wages
have grown since. For most people
between 65 and 70, a paycheck from 1982
counts at three to five times its face
value. So, a $20,000 year back then
counts as roughly 60 to 100,000. Every
dollar you earn after 60 counts at face
value only. That is why a part-time job
at 70 usually changes nothing. Usually.
Here is the exception, and it matters
for a lot of women watching. Your
benefit is built on your 35 best years.
If you worked fewer than 35, the missing
years count as zeros. Years spent
raising children, years caring for a
parent. Any paycheck now, even a modest
one, replaces a zero. Picture a woman of
68 who stayed home for 12 years and now
works at a garden center for $18,000 a
year. Each year she works knocks out one
of those zeros, and it might add
somewhere between 15 and $40 a month to
her check. It will not change her life,
but it is permanent. It grows with every
future cost of living increase, and if
hers is the larger check in her
marriage, it passes to her husband after
she is gone. The fifth change looks like
the most boring number on the whole
sheet, the price of a work credit. Next
year, one credit takes $1,970
of earnings. You can earn at most four
in a year, so $7,880
gets you all four. It does not matter
which months you earn it in. Four
credits can come from one busy season.
Here is why it made this list. 40
credits is the line for your own
retirement check. It is also the line
for something most people assume is free
for everyone, Medicare Part A, your
hospital coverage. With 40 credits, Part
A costs nothing. With 30 to 39, this
year's premium is $311 a month. Under
a month. The amounts for 2027 come out
in November. Look at what happens at 30.
One more credit, $1,970
of work, can cut that premium by about
a month every month you pay it. 10 more
credits can take it to zero. For one
credit's worth of work, that is hard to
beat. Who does this hit? People who came
to this country later in life. People
who stayed home through most of their
working years. People who spent a career
in a government job that did not pay
into Medicare. Before anyone in your
family pays that premium, know there is
a second door. Part A can be free
through a husband's or wife's work
record, and in many cases through a
former or late spouse's record, too. Ask
Social Security to check every record
you might qualify on. And if you do have
to pay for Part A, and you sign up late,
Medicare adds 10% to the premium for
twice the number of years you waited.
Change six is the biggest check Social
Security pays. For someone reaching full
retirement age next year, the top is
a month, up 36. Each year you wait past
full retirement age adds about 8%, and
waiting until 70 pushes the top check
past 5,000. Only about 2% of people ever
collect the maximum. The formula behind
every new check moved, too. For people
turning 62 next year, Social Security
replaces 90% of the first $1,340
of their average monthly earnings. Then,
32% of earnings up to $8,077.
Then, only 15% of anything above that.
That tilt is deliberate. It is why the
lower earner in a marriage often gets
more back for each dollar paid in, and
why one more high earning year adds less
than people expect. That number hides a
lesson for every married couple. Your
own check grows every month you wait,
all the way to 70. A spouse's benefit
does not. It tops out at half of the
worker's full amount, and it stops
growing at the spouse's own full
retirement age. So, if you are
collecting only on your husband's or
wife's record, waiting past your full
retirement age earns you nothing, not
$1. People do it every year, convinced
they are being patient. And one trap at
the top of the ladder. If you file after
your full retirement age, Social
Security may offer you up to 6 months of
back pay in a lump sum. It sounds like
found money. It is not. Taking it means
your benefit is figured as if you had
started 6 months earlier. So, you give
up the delayed credits for those months,
and your check is smaller for life. If
you were the bigger earner in your
marriage, it can shrink your survivor's
check, too.
Sometimes, the lump sum is still the
right call. Just know it is a trade, not
a gift. There is one more piece of your
check that was never indexed to
anything, the tax on it. Take your other
income, add any tax-free interest, and
add half of your Social Security. That
total decides whether any of your
benefit is taxed. For a single person,
the first line is $25,000.
For a married couple, $32,000. Above
those lines, up to half of your benefit
can be taxed. Above 34,000 single or
44,000 married, up to 85%.
Those lines were written into law in
1983 and 1993, and they have never been
raised. Social Security's own
researchers have written that the lines
are not indexed to prices or wages. That
is why the share of retired families
paying tax on their benefits grew from
fewer than one in 10 to more than half.
So, every raise, including this one,
pushes more people toward a line that
does not move. The one cushion is
temporary. For tax years 2025 through 20
2028, people 65 and older get an extra
each. It starts to shrink once income
passes 75,000 for a single person or
150,000 for a couple. After 2028, unless
Congress acts, it is gone. If you are
near one of those lines, December is the
time to look. A withdrawal moved into
January can keep a dollar off the
return. So can a gift to charity sent
straight from your IRA if you are 70 and
a half or older. One record can also pay
several people at once. The worker, a
current husband or wife, children, and
former husbands or wives if the marriage
lasted at least 10 years. This is the
part that surprises people in second
marriages. Whatever a former spouse
collects does not reduce your check or
your current spouse's. Social Security's
own booklet says so in one sentence.
There is a ceiling on all of it. Social
Security limits the total paid on one
record, usually to between 150 and 180%
of the worker's own benefit. If the
family's checks add up to more, the
spouses and children's checks are cut,
never the worker's. Now the rule that
costs divorced people the most. While
your former husband or wife is alive,
you may get up to half of their full
benefit if you are at least 62,
unmarried, and the marriage lasted 10
years. If your own check is bigger than
that half, the answer is no. Plenty of
people hear that no once and never ask
again. But the day that former spouse
dies, the rule changes. You may now be
owed a survivor's benefit of up to 100%
of what they were getting. If you
remarried after 60, you keep that right.
And here is the catch. Social Security
does not go looking for you. If you are
not already collecting on that record,
nobody is required to call. Inez is a
composite as well. 69, in Albuquerque,
married 22 years, divorced long ago. At
66, she asked about her former husband's
record and was told no. Her own check,
$1,600, was bigger than half of his,
which was 1,450.
2 and 1/2 years ago, he died. Inez found
out last month when a cousin texted her
a photo of an obituary from 2 and 1/2
years ago. On his record, she is owed
his full check, $2,900.
That is $1,300 more than she gets now,
every month. She applied that same week.
Social Security can pay a survivor up to
6 months back. The other 2 years are
simply gone. About $31,000
lost to a phone call nobody was required
to make. Nothing Inez did was a mistake.
The no she got at 66 was correct on the
day she got it. Nobody mentioned that it
had an expiration date. That is exactly
the kind of rule I wrote down in the
quiet rules. Not only what Social
Security tells you on the day you call,
but what changes later, and when to go
back and ask again. You will find it at
kevinexplains.shop.
If you are watching on a television,
point your phone's camera at the QR code
on the screen. On a phone or a computer,
tap the pinned comment or the first link
in the description. There is a 7-day
guarantee on it, which gives you a full
week to read it next to your own
letters. Inez saved the cousin's text,
the photo of the obituary, and one line
typed underneath it. Did you know?
Change seven is the one I promised was
the most expensive, the one that looks
like it has nothing to do with you. It
is not a rule at all. It is two averages
printed on Social Security's own fact
sheet for next year. An aged couple,
both collecting $3,355
a month. An aged widow or widower living
alone, 2005.
Those are different households, so this
is not one family before and after. But
the rule behind the distance is exact.
When a husband or wife dies, the
survivor keeps the larger of the two
checks and the smaller one stops. For an
average couple, that is a drop of about
40%. The more equal your two checks are,
the more you lose. Two checks of 2,000
each, the survivor keeps 2,000 and half
the income in the house is gone. 3,000
and 1,000? The survivor keeps the three
and a quarter is gone. Now ask, which
bills drop by 40% when one person is
gone? The property tax does not. The
homeowner's insurance does not. The car
insurance, the internet, and the heating
barely move. And after the year of the
death, the survivor usually files taxes
as a single person against lower lines
for taxing Social Security and for
Medicare's income surcharge. Less income
measured against tighter lines. If you
are both still here, the fix is a
conversation and I will come back to it
before we finish. If you are already
widowed, you have a choice that most
other people lost years ago. The fix has
a date on it. If the higher earner files
early, the survivor's check can be
permanently smaller. The law keeps it
from falling below the larger of what
that spouse was actually receiving or
82.5% of the full amount. If the higher
earner waits, every year of waiting up
to 70 is added to the check the survivor
will keep. That is why the higher
earner's filing date is partly a
decision about whoever outlives them.
For anyone who turned 62 after the start
of 2016, filing for one retirement or
spouse benefit means filing for everyone
you qualify for. Survivors are the
exception. A widow [clears throat] or
widower can take one benefit first and
switch to the other later. AARP lays it
out plainly. Here is what that looks
like with round numbers. Picture a widow
who is 62. Her late husband's full check
Her own record pays about 1,100 at 62.
If she takes the survivor benefit now,
it is reduced to about 2,230
and it stays reduced for life. Or, she
takes her own 1,100 now and switches to
the full 2,800 at 67.
That second path gives up about $68,000
over 5 years. Then, it pays her $570
more every month for the rest of her
life. It catches up at around 77. Which
path is right depends on her health, her
savings, and what she needs this year.
And if her own benefit at 70 would be
bigger than the survivor benefit, she
flips the order. Survivor check first
and let her own grow until 70. What
matters is knowing there are two doors
and asking to see both of them in
writing before you sign anything. A
survivor benefit can start as early as
60 at about 71 and 1/2%. And you cannot
apply for it online. It takes a phone
call or an appointment. Two small rules
for the first weeks after a death
because families miss both. First,
Social Security does not pay for the
month a person dies. A check that
arrives the month after a death is the
check for the month of the death and it
has to be sent back.
If it came by direct deposit, the bank
may take it back on its own, so do not
spend it. Second, there is a one-time
payment of $255
to a surviving spouse who lived in the
same household or who was already
collecting on that record. If there is
no spouse, it can go to a child who
qualifies. It has been $255 since 1954
and you have 2 years to apply. It will
not cover a funeral, but it is owed to
you and nobody calls to mention it. If
you are standing in front of a choice
like that or you simply want someone to
look at your own numbers, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
Tell me your ages, the amounts on your
benefit letters, and the decision in
front of you. I read every message and
if your situation needs a closer look, I
will tell you what that involves. One
rule for me and for anyone else who
asks, never email your Social Security
number, a bank account number, or a
password. Nobody needs them to look at
your numbers. Changes eight and nine are
the disability limits. If you get Social
Security Disability, next year you can
earn up to $1,770
a month and still be treated as unable
to work. If you are blind, the limit is
Any month you earn more than $1,270
counts toward a 9-month trial work
period. And if you are on disability
when you reach full retirement age, your
check simply becomes a retirement check
and those limits stop applying to you.
For many people watching though, that
line is about somebody else, a son or a
daughter. If you have a child of any age
whose disability began before 22, that
child may be able to collect on your
record. Social Security calls it the
Disabled Adult Child Benefit. It can
start when you begin your own retirement
or disability benefit or after you die.
While you are living, it can be up to
half of your full benefit. After you are
gone, up to 75%.
After 24 months on it, your son or
daughter qualifies for Medicare. In most
cases, they must be unmarried and their
earnings must stay under that 1770 line.
According to the Congressional Research
Service, about 1.2 million people were
receiving it in May and the average
check was $1,105.
Here is a detail that changes the math
for some parents. The child's benefit is
figured from your full benefit, not the
reduced one. So, if you file early, your
own check is smaller, but your son's or
daughter's check on your record is still
based on your full amount within a
family limit. For some parents, that is
worth weighing before they pick a filing
date. Bonnie is a composite built from a
story parents tell over and over. She is
72 in Knoxville. Her son Kyle is 47. He
was hurt in a car accident at 19 and has
not worked since.
For decades, he lived on SSI, the
needs-based check. Bonnie started her
own Social Security 5 years ago and
never connected her claim to Kyle. Last
spring, his case worker asked one
question. "Has your mother started
collecting?" Kyle now gets a check on
Bonnie's record that is larger than his
SSI ever was. Most of those 5 years of
checks are gone. And someday, after
Bonnie is gone, his check rises to as
much as 75% of her benefit. Every parent
asks the same thing next. Does the
bigger check cost him his Medicaid?
Usually, it does not have to. When SSI
ends because this exact benefit started
or went up, there is a protection. It
was written into federal law in 1986,
and it can keep Medicaid going as if he
still had SSI. It is often called the
disabled adult child Medicaid
protection, and the Congressional
[clears throat] Research Service
published a fresh explanation of it this
month. Some states apply it more
strictly. So, when the switch happens,
call your state's Medicaid office and
ask for it by name. Change 10 is SSI
itself. The top federal payment rises to
a month for one person and 1,544
for a couple. But one number in that
program did not change, and it has not
changed since 1989.
To qualify, a person can have no more
than $2,000 in countable savings, $3,000
for a couple. The National Academy of
Social Insurance points out something.
If the limit set in 1972 had simply kept
up with inflation, it would be around
My own view is that a savings limit
frozen since 1989 punishes exactly the
people who try to put something aside.
One recent change does help. Since
September of 2024, help with food no
longer reduces an SSI payment. Help with
rent or utilities still can. Here is why
that matters to you, even if you will
never need SSI. If you want to help a
son, a daughter, or a grandchild who
depends on it, be careful.
A well-meaning gift of $5,000 can cut or
stop their check until the money is
spent down. There are two safer routes.
A special needs trust drawn up by an
attorney, or a special savings account
called an ABLE account. Since January,
anyone whose disability began before age
46 can open one. It used to be 26.
Social Security ignores the first
$100,000 inside it, and anyone can put
money in, including a grandparent.
Families like Bonnie's lose years of
checks because the rule sits where
nobody thinks to look. If you want rules
like that one gathered in a single
place, The Quiet Rules is the guide I
wrote for exactly that. The QR code is
on your screen, the link is pinned in
the comments and listed first in the
description, and the same 7-day
guarantee applies.
Bonnie carries Kyle's award letter in
her purse, folded around his insurance
card, so it is with her at every
appointment. Before I close, the part of
next year's numbers that comes out of
this very same check, Medicare. In June,
the program's trustees projected the
Part B premium at $209.50
a month next year.
They put the Part B deductible at about
The official figures are due in
November.
Social Security says the exact premium
will appear in your My Social Security
message center starting in late
November, up to 3 weeks before the paper
notice arrives in December.
To see it early, you need an account and
you need to sign up for paperless
notices by November 18th. If the premium
is a strain, ask your state's Medicaid
office whether you qualify for a
Medicare Savings Program. Ask for it by
that name.
In some states, it pays your Part B
premium for you. If you skipped Part B
at 65 and had no coverage through a job,
the penalty is 10% for every full year
you waited. It lasts as long as you have
Part B. And the surcharge on higher
incomes, called IRMAA, is set by your
tax return from 2 years back. What you
earn this year decides what you pay in
2028. This month, more than 20 million
people on original Medicare received a
one-time $90 Part B payment from the
Medicare Improvement Fund. It does not
repeat, so do not budget around it. Then
there is your pharmacy counter. On
January 1st, the most a drug plan can
make you pay out of pocket in a year
rises to $2,400,
up from $2,100.
The highest deductible a plan may charge
rises to 700 from 615.
And a temporary federal program that
held down drug plan premiums this year
has ended. On the same day, Medicare's
negotiated prices begin on 15 more
drugs. Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus go
to a negotiated price of $274
for a month's supply, down from 959 in
2024. The inhaler Trelegy goes to 175.
Linzess, for chronic constipation, to
Two common diabetes pills, Tradjenta and
Janumet, to 78 and $80. That negotiated
price is what Medicare pays, not
necessarily what you pay at the counter.
What you pay depends on your plan, but
it is the number your plan is now
working from. If any of your medicines
is on that list, ask your plan or your
pharmacist how your cost changes on
January 1st. All of those drug numbers
are in the letter your plan mailed in
September called the annual notice of
change. Open it. Find each of your
medicines by name and check that your
pharmacy is still in the network. Open
enrollment runs until December 7th. 20
minutes with that letter before then is
the cheapest comparison you will make
all year.
One more item, and it is not a Social
Security change at all, but it is good
news that barely made the papers.
Medicare's flexible telehealth rules let
you see a doctor by video from your own
kitchen instead of driving to a clinic.
Congress has extended them through the
end of 2027. If the drive has been the
reason you keep putting off an
appointment, you have another full year
of that option. And one thing that is
not on the list because a lot of people
are frightened of it, there is no cut to
the Social Security checks in 2027.
Social Security's trustees project that
the retirement trust fund can pay full
benefits until late in 2032.
After that, if Congress does nothing,
incoming taxes would cover about 78%
That is a real deadline, and it is about
6 years away. It is not next year's
check.
One habit makes every one of these
numbers safer. Open your My Social
Security account and read your earnings
record year by year.
Every one of your 35 best years is on
that page, and a missing year or a wrong
number there becomes a smaller check for
life. If a Social Security letter says
something that does not match what you
know, you generally have 60 days from
the day you receive it to ask them to
look again.
Write the date it arrived on the
envelope and keep the envelope. Here is
where I land after going through every
line of next year's numbers. The raise
is real, and it is welcome. But nearly
every dollar in this video was lost or
saved by one conversation held in
[clears throat] time or not at all. Dale
needed it before he signed. Inez needed
it the week her former husband died.
Bonnie needed it the day she filed her
own claim. So, if you are married, put
both of your benefit letters on the
kitchen table this week. Find out whose
check is larger. Say out loud what stops
when one of you is gone and which bills
do not. If neither of you has claimed
yet, decide the bigger earners start
date together. If you were married 10
years or more and later divorced, write
down your former spouse's full name and
date of birth and keep it with your
papers. If that person dies, call Social
Security that month. If you have a son
or daughter who has been disabled since
before 22, ask about the disabled adult
child benefit on the same day you file
for your own. And if you are still
working before your full retirement age,
do the earnings math in December, not in
April. If you would like those rules
written out in one place, the quiet
rules is in the pinned comment and at
the top of the description. The QR code
is on your screen. It comes with the
same 7-day guarantee. Before you do
anything else tonight, find the oldest
envelope from Social Security or
Medicare that you have not opened and
open it. I am Kevin. Thanks for
watching. Do not forget to check the
quiet rules at kevinexplains.shop.

title: Every Senior Must Move Their Cash Before November 1 Or Lose Out

segments.text: Your bank got a raise last month, and it
has not shared one penny of it with you.
On September 16th, the Federal Reserve
raised interest rates for the first time
in 3 years. The very next morning, the
big banks raised their prime rate, the
number credit cards and home equity
lines are built on, automatically. And
savings? The national average went from
of a point. That was your share. On
October 28th, the Fed decides again. 4
days later, on November 1st, the
government resets the one savings rate
in this country that has to follow
inflation. And this time, it is on track
to be the best in about 4 years. So,
yes, some of your cash should move. Not
all of it. In a lot of homes watching
this, there is a stack of paper that
loses almost half of what it is
guaranteed to be worth if you move it
too soon. And right now, people are
calling retirees with a bank's name on
the caller ID, telling them to move
everything tonight. So, every dollar you
own goes under one of three lights.
Green means move it this week. Yellow
means wait for a date. Red means do not
touch it, no matter who is asking. By
the end, you will know which light every
account in your name sits under. Quick
favor before the first light. Open your
bank app or find your last statement and
look for three letters next to your
savings. A P Y. Then, put that number in
the comments. Not the balance, the rate.
I want this audience to see how far
apart the answers are, because I think
it will shock a lot of people. If you
are new here, this channel reads the
fine print on retirement money out loud
before it costs you. And subscribing is
how the next deadline reaches you in
time. Every number in this video comes
from the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the
Treasury, the SEC, the FTC, and the FBI.
All the sources are listed in the
description. I am not a financial
advisor or a lawyer. This is general
education, and your own situation may
need its own answer. Green light first.
This is money sitting in savings or
checking that pays almost nothing. Here
is why the raise never reached it. A
savings account is what the rules call a
variable rate account. Under the federal
truth in savings rules, a bank has to
warn you 30 days before most changes
that hurt you. But the regulation carves
out one exception. Changes to the
interest rate on a variable rate account
need no notice at all. So the bank can
lower your rate without telling you and
it owes you nothing when the Fed raises.
One tracker followed 87 savings accounts
for 10 days after the September hike.
79% did not move at all. The incentive
runs one way. Your deposit is the
cheapest money a bank can get and it
lends that same money out at rates built
on the new 7% prime rate. Every dollar
you leave at 1/100 of a percent is a
dollar it never has to compete for and
many of the biggest banks in the country
still pay 1 100th of 1% on their
standard savings. Put that on $100,000.
At 1/100 of a percent, you earn $10 a
year. At the top online savings rates
right now, about 4 and 1/4%, the same
money earns about 4,250.
Same insurance, same access. And with
prices up 3.7% over the past year, the
account paying $10 is losing about
of buying power every year. It looks
safe. It is shrinking. So where does
green money go? Keep one or two months
of spending in checking where your
social security lands. In January, that
check grows by 3.6%.
If it lands in an account paying
nothing, even the raise starts shrinking
the day it arrives. The rest can go
somewhere that actually follows the Fed.
An online savings account at an FDIC
insured bank. Read the fine print on the
very top advertised rates though. Some
are introductory and drop after a few
months, and some only apply up to a
balance cap. A money market deposit
account, which is a bank account and is
insured, or Treasury bills, which are
short loans to the government paying
about 4 to 4 and 1/2% right now for
terms from 4 weeks to 1 year. Treasury
bills are not FDIC insured because they
do not need to be. They are backed by
the government itself, and the interest
is free from state and local income tax.
One warning on names. A money market
fund at a brokerage is not the same as a
money market account at a bank. The fund
is an investment, usually a very safe
one, but it is not FDIC insured. If this
were my mother's money, I would not
chase the single highest rate on a list.
I would pick an insured bank I can look
up on the FDIC's free bank find tool, a
rate within a few tenths of the top, and
a phone number where a human being
answers. The last tenth of a percent is
not worth a bank you cannot reach.
Lenora is a composite built from letters
I get every week.
79, a retired church secretary outside
Dayton. $212,000
in the savings account her husband
opened in 1971.
1/100 of a percent, about $21 a year.
When a neighbor asked what she was
earning, she did not know, so she called
the branch. The banker told her, very
politely, that they had a high yield
savings account. It had been on their
own website the whole time. Nobody moved
her into it because nobody has to. Over
the five years since her husband died,
the gap between what she earned and what
that same bank paid on its better

normal. So, unless something changes,
his surcharge should fall away in 2028.
One heavy year, one expensive echo. The
third hand is reaching in right now and
it has a deadline. December 7th.
Medicare's open enrollment runs from
October 15th through December 7th. In
September, your drug plan or your
Medicare Advantage plan sent you a
letter called the annual notice of
change. It lists everything your plan
changes on January 1st. A lot of people
never open it. For 2027, some of those
changes are bigger than your raise. The
highest deductible a drug plan is
allowed to charge goes from $615
to $700. That is almost 14%.
The yearly cap on what you pay out of
pocket for covered drugs goes from
About 14% again. Your raise is 3.6. On
top of that, a temporary federal program
that held down some drug plan premiums
for the past 2 years has ended. Medicare
projects the average standalone drug
plan premium will barely move to about
$36 a month.
But an average hides the plan that
jumps, the medicine that moves to a
pricier tier, and the pharmacy that
drops out of the network. When you open
that letter, it takes a few minutes.
Check the premium and the deductible.
Find every one of your medicines by name
and the tier it lands in. Make sure your
pharmacy is still in the network. And if
you have Medicare Advantage, make sure
your doctors and your hospital are still
in. And look at the most you could pay
out of pocket in a year. Twila opened
her letter. Her premium was rising, and
one of her heart pills was moving to a
more expensive tier. So, she called her
state's free Medicare counseling program
called SHIP and sat down with a
volunteer and her list of prescriptions.
They put her exact drugs, doses, and
pharmacy into the Plan Finder at
medicare.gov, and they compared the
total yearly cost, not just the monthly
premium. She switched. Next year, she
will pay about $300 less than if she had
stayed put. Clyde's letter is still in
its envelope under the fruit bowl. His
plan rolls over on its own. His premium
rises $18 a month, and the new $700
deductible is waiting for him in
January. About $300 more for the same
pills. Two more doors here. If January's
pharmacy bill is the part that scares
you, every drug plan now has to offer
something called the Medicare
prescription payment plan.
It spreads your out-of-pocket drug costs
into monthly bills across the year with
no interest and no fees. You ask your
drug plan to sign you up. And if
December 7th slips past you, there is
one smaller door. If you are in a
Medicare Advantage plan, you can switch
to another Advantage plan or go back to
original Medicare once between January
1st and March 31st.
If you have a stand-alone drug plan, you
are mostly locked in for the year. So,
if your mother or your neighbor is on a
drug plan, call this week and ask one
question. Did you open the letter from
your plan in September? Score so far.
Twila keeps $68.40
of her monthly raise and her drug costs
stay about where they were.
Clyde has already lost more than his
whole raise and the new year has not
started yet. The fourth hand waits until
April. Taxes. According to Social
Security, about 40% of people who get
benefits pay federal income tax on them.
Here is how the line works. Take your
other income, add any tax-free interest,
and add half of your Social Security.
Social Security calls that total your
combined income. If it passes $25,000
for a single person or 32,000 for a
married couple, up to half of your
benefits can be taxed. Above 34,000
single or 44,000 married, up to 85% can
be. Those lines were written into law in
They have never been raised, not once.
When Congress first taxed benefits, it
expected roughly one retiree in 10 to
owe. If that first line had grown with
prices, it would be somewhere around
$80,000 today. Instead, half of every
raise you get is added to a total that
is is against a line that never moves.
There is a cushion, for now. On tax
returns for 2025 through 2028, people 65
and older get an extra deduction of
$6,000 each. A married couple where both
qualify can get 12,000. It works whether
you itemize or not. Married couples have
to file jointly to claim it. And it
starts shrinking once income passes
$75,000 for a single person or 150,000
for a couple. It lowers the tax. It does
not move the line. And unless Congress
extends it, it disappears after 2028.
Depending on where you live, there can
be a second tax line, too.
As of this year, eight states still tax
some Social Security: Colorado,
Connecticut, Minnesota, Montana, New
Mexico, Rhode Island, Utah, and Vermont.
Most of them exempt lower and middle
incomes, and the cutoffs vary a lot from
state to state. So, check your own
state's rules before you assume either
way. Clyde's pension and his required
withdrawals already make 85% of his
benefit taxable. So, 85% of his raise is
taxable, too.
In his bracket, that is about $90 a
year.
Twila's other income is small, and after
her deductions, she owes nothing.
One more piece. If you have tax taken
out of your Social Security, you picked
a percentage on a form called the W-4V:
That percentage now applies to a bigger
check, so the dollars withheld go up on
their own. To change that percentage or
to start or stop withholding, you file a
new W-4V with Social Security. If you
owe tax on your benefits and nothing is
withheld, the raise quietly makes
April's bill bigger.
Better to know that in January than to
find it out in April. Now, add up
Clyde's year. $79 to the Part B
increase, about 1,150 to the surcharge,
about 300 to a plan letter he never
opened, about 90 to the IRS, a $900
raise, and he finishes 2027 roughly $700
behind where he started. Nothing he did
was foolish. Paying off a house is a
good decision. Letting a plan roll over
is what most people do. What cost him
was not knowing which day each decision
was due. I wrote The Quiet Rules so you
meet rules like these before they meet
you, in plain English with the dates up
front. You can find it at
kevinexplains.shop.
The QR code is on your screen right now
if your phone is close by. If not,
scroll down. The link is pinned in the
comments and sits at the very top of the
description. You get 7 days to look
through it. If it has not pointed you to
a date you were about to miss, you get a
refund. Clyde found out on January 20th
at the bank machine by the hardware
store. The first deposit, with his raise
in it, printed on the slip, $25 less
than December. Here is the day your
first bigger deposit lands, as promised.
The raise applies to your December
benefit, and the December benefit is
paid in January. So, your December
deposit will look like every other
month. In January, most people are paid
by birthday. If you were born on the 1st
through the 10th, your deposit comes
Wednesday, January 13th. The 11th
through the 20th, January 20th. The 21st
through the 31st, January 27th. If you
get SSI or you have been collecting
since before May of 1997,
January's payment arrives early. It
comes on Thursday, December 31st,
because New Year's Day falls on a
Friday. For those groups, that means two
deposits in December and none in
January. It is not a missing check. And
if a payment ever fails to show up on
its date, Social Security asks you to
wait three mail days before you call.
And one warning about comparing
deposits. In October, about 20 million
people on original Medicare received a
one-time $90 Part B rebate from
something called the Medicare
Improvement Fund. People in Medicare
Advantage, people paying the surcharge,
and people who get Medicaid help with
premiums did not qualify. It does not
repeat. So, if your January deposit
looks small next to October's, that is
why. Compare January with December, not
with October. A few other checks move
with this raise. Military retirees get
the same 3.6%.
Veterans disability pay rises by the
same amount once Congress passes its
yearly bill for it. Federal retirees
under the older CSRS system get the full
Under the newer system, called FERS,
retirees 62 and older get 2.6 because
that system trims any raise above 3% by
a full point. And Federal News Network
reported that federal health insurance
enrollees will pay about 11% more toward
their premiums in 2027.
For many federal retirees, the premium
is rising several times faster than the
raise. Back to November because one date
there protects you. Social Security now
sends a simplified one-page notice about
the raise. It shows your new benefit,
the exact payment dates, and every
deduction in dollars. If you have a My
Social Security account, the notice
appears online starting in late
November, up to 3 weeks before the paper
one. If you do not have an account and
want to see it online, Social Security
says you need to create one and sign up
for paperless notices by November 18th.
Otherwise, it comes by mail in December.
There is a second reason to open that
account. In Social Security's own words,
it takes away the risk of someone else
trying to create one in your name. Go
only to ssa.gov/myaccount.
Type it in yourself. Never use a link
from a text message. When the notice
arrives, check four lines. Your new
benefit before deductions, your Medicare
premium, and whether a surcharge is
hiding in it. Any drug or Advantage Plan
premium that comes out of your check and
any tax being withheld. If something
looks wrong, you generally have 60 days
to ask Social Security to take another
look. So, do not let it sit in a drawer.
If you get help with rent, food, or
Medicare costs from a program with an
income limit, the raise counts as income
there, too. When that office rechecks
your file, report the new amount and ask
whether their limit went up for the new
year, as well, because many of those
limits rise every year. And if your
notice shows a number you cannot explain
or a surcharge you think should not be
there, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
Tell me what the letter says and what
changed in your life. I read every
message and a good question often turns
into the next video. Then there is a
hand that has no business in your
envelope at all. Every year, the raise
brings scammers with it. Social
Security's Inspector General has warned
about letters on fake letterhead telling
people to call a number to activate a
benefit increase. Remember the sentence
I asked you to hold on to. The raise is
automatic. There is nothing to activate.
In the Inspector General's words, Social
Security will never threaten, scare, or
pressure you to take an immediate
action. Anyone asking for a fee, a gift
card, your bank login, or your full
Social Security number to release a
raise or a rebate is not the government.
Hang up and report it at oig.ssa.gov.
And during open enrollment, guard your
Medicare number like a credit card. Give
it only to a plan you called yourself or
to the SHIP counselor you sat down with.
And the warning I promised at the start
for anyone who has not started
collecting. Every fall, some people file
early just to grab the new raise. They
think if they are not collecting, they
miss it. They do not. Social Security's
own booklet says you are eligible for
cost of living increases starting with
the year you turn 62. That is true even
if you do not take benefits until full
retirement age or even 70.
Every raise since that birthday is
already being built into your future
check. Filing early to catch this one
trades a 3.6% raise for a permanent cut.
If your full retirement age is 67 and
you start at 62, your check is reduced
by 30% for life.
And every year you wait past full
retirement age, up to 70, adds about 8%.
If you were born in 1960, you were the
first group whose full retirement age is
the full 67 and you reach it in 2027.
And if you are already on Medicare but
have not claimed Social Security yet,
your Part B premium comes as a bill
instead of a deduction. The surcharge
rules from earlier apply to you exactly
the same way.
If you are working while collecting
before full retirement age, the earnings
limit for 2027 is $25,560.
Only wages and self-employment income
count toward it. Pensions, IRA
withdrawals, interest, and dividends do
not. Above that limit, Social Security
holds back $1 for every two you earn.
In the year you reach full retirement
age, the limit is $67,920.
There, they hold back $1 for every
three, counting only what you earn
before the month you reach it. That
money is not gone for good. Your benefit
is recalculated later to credit you for
it, but it surprises people every
spring. So, why does a 3.6% raise so
rarely feel like one? Because
[clears throat] of whose prices it
measures. The raise is based on an index
built from the spending of urban wage
earners, people who are mostly still
working. The Bureau of Labor Statistics
also built an experimental index for
households where someone is 62 or older.
In that older basket, medical care took
about 11% of spending. In the workers
basket, under six. Housing took a bigger
share, too. Over nearly 30 years, the
older Americans index rose about 3.1% a
year, while the workers index rose about
2.9. A fraction of a point sounds like
nothing. Compounded over a retirement,
it is the difference between keeping up
and slowly slipping behind. Medicare's
trustees expect that squeeze to tighten.
After this year's gentle increase, they
project the Part B premium at $224.50
That is more than 20% in 3 years, coming
out of the same check the raise goes
into. One Social Security analyst told
Kiplinger that retirees should not read
a higher raise as more spending money.
It is there to protect what your check
can buy, not to add to it. Twila does
one simple thing with hers. The day her
January deposit lands, she moves $68.40
into a separate savings account she
calls her Medicare jar. She does it
every month. By December, the jar holds
about $820,
enough for her Part B deductible and
most of her drug deductible before
either one shows up. The raise ends up
paying for the very costs it was meant
to cover. So, here is the scoreboard I
promised you. Clyde, you already know. A
$900 raise and he ends the year about
$700 behind. Twila, same 900. $79 to the
Part B increase, nothing to a surcharge,
nothing extra to her drug plan because
she switched, nothing extra to taxes.
She ends the year about $820 ahead. Same
street, same check, about $1,500 apart,
bigger than the raise itself. And the
difference was never income or
intelligence. It was which envelopes got
opened and on what day. Here are the
days to keep by the phone. November
18th, the last day to set up your online
account if you want to read the notice
early. In November, the new Medicare
premium. Late November, your notice
online and for some people a letter
about Irma. December 7th, the last day
to change your drug or Advantage plan.
December, the paper notice in your
mailbox. December 31st, the early
January payment for SSI. January 13th,
20th, or 27th, your first deposit with
the raise depending on your birthday.
January 1st through March 31st, one more
chance to switch if you are in Medicare
Advantage and April when the tax side of
the raise comes due. Twila's year
started with one envelope opened on
time. If you want the rules behind this
raise on your table before your own
envelope start arriving, the quiet rules
is waiting in the pinned comment. It is
also the first link in the description.
I am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: Seniors, STOP Writing Checks Until You Know About This New Scam

segments.text: The last check you mailed probably
cleared, and that is exactly why you
would never know if it was stolen.
Cleared only means the money left your
account. It does not mean the money
reached the name you wrote on it. Right
now, thieves are pulling checks out of
home mailboxes and blue collection
boxes, dissolving the ink with chemicals
that cost a few dollars, and writing in
a new name. Sometimes a bigger number,
too. Your bank pays it. Your statement
shows the check number, and very often
the exact amount you wrote. Nothing
looks wrong. And from that moment, a
clock is running that almost nobody has
heard of. It is written into the account
agreement you accepted when you opened
your account, and it is usually 30 or 60
days. Miss it, and your bank can refuse
to return the money. You lose the money,
and you still owe the bill. And this is
the worst time of year for it. The next
90 days are when the biggest checks of
the year go into the mail. Property
taxes in November and December. Checks
tucked inside Christmas cards for
grandchildren. Year-end gifts to
charity. And the January estimated tax
payment to the IRS, which, if you mail
it, carries your Social Security number
on the memo line, because the IRS asks
you to write it there. So today, I am
going to follow one check from your pen
to the moment that clock runs out. Seven
stops. At every stop, I will show you
what thieves do there, and the one move
that shuts them out. And near the end, I
will show you why the federal government
itself stopped mailing almost all of its
own checks last year, in the White
House's own words. When the people who
print the money stop trusting paper,
that should tell you something. Before
we start, tell me in the comments how
you pay your property tax. A check in
the mail, online, or in person. One word
is enough. I read them, and it shows me
how many people this touches. My name is
Kevin. If you are new here, this channel
reads the rules that banks and agencies
write, so you are not the last one to
find out. Subscribing costs nothing, and
it is how the next warning reaches you
first. Everything I cite today comes
from the agencies and news reports
listed in the description. So, please
check them. I am not a lawyer or a
financial advisor. This is general
education, not advice about your own
account. Stop number one is your pen.
Most people grab whatever pen is nearest
the checkbook. A cheap ballpoint sits on
top of the paper, and that is exactly
the kind of ink washing lifts off. New
York's Consumer Protection Division puts
it plainly. Gel pens may have ink that
thieves have greater difficulty erasing.
So, use a black gel pen for every check.
It costs almost nothing, and it makes
the thief's job harder before the check
even leaves the table. Then, look at the
empty space. Write the payee's full
name, not initials. Start the amount at
the far left edge of the box and draw a
line through whatever space is left on
both the number and the written amount.
A blank gap is room for a new word or an
extra zero. And look at the bottom edge
of the check. Those numbers are your
bank's routing number and your account
number. A thief does not even need to
wash a check to use them. When the
Treasury's Financial Crimes Unit,
FinCEN, studied check fraud tied to
stolen mail, it found that about a
quarter of stolen checks were used as
templates for counterfeits. Your real
numbers on a fake check with a fake
signature. Stop number two is your own
mailbox. A raised red flag on a mailbox
is a sign that says there is outgoing
mail in here. It is one of the first
things thieves look for. Never leave
outgoing mail in your box overnight, and
never with the flag up for hours. And
think about what December mail looks
like. A card-shaped envelope addressed
by hand to a young person with your last
name.
Thieves know what is inside a lot of
those. There is also a free tool for the
mail coming in. The Postal Service has a
service called Informed Delivery. Every
morning, it emails you a picture of the
outside of each letter that is on its
way to your house that day. So, if an
insurance refund or a new debit card is
coming, you know it before the carrier
arrives. If the picture shows up and the
envelope never does, report it that same
day. And when you order new checks, ask
your bank whether you can pick them up
at the branch. That beats having a box
of blank checks with your name on them
left in your mailbox. Stop number three
is the blue collection box and the
person who empties it. This is where
most people think they are being
careful. They drive to the post office
and drop the check in the box out front.
But criminals fish envelopes out of
those boxes and in a growing number of
cases, they open them with a stolen key.
Letter carriers carry a master key
called an arrow key. According to the
Postal Service's own figures, 82% of
robberies of letter carriers are
motivated by arrow key theft. The Postal
Service has been installing
high-security boxes and replacing old
locks with electronic ones, but not
every box in the country has been
replaced. In a case reported earlier
this year, a Bay Area couple's property
tax check was stolen and the mailbox
they used was later sealed off because
of the number of thefts from it. So, the
move at stop three is simple. Hand your
envelope to the clerk inside the post
office or to your own letter carrier. If
you must use a blue box, use it before
the last pickup time printed on the
front, never on a Friday evening and
never over a weekend. A check that sits
in a box overnight is a check that sits
there for whoever comes along with a
key. Harlan learned this one with a $46
water bill.
81 A retired railroad dispatcher in
Toledo, Ohio. He dropped the check in
the box outside his post office on a
Saturday afternoon after the last
pickup. It cleared for $4,600
payable to a name he had never heard.
Harlan does not read his statement every
month. His daughter found it 71 days
later. His bank's account agreement gave
him 60. The answer was a form letter and
it said, "No."
If that sounds extreme, it is not. In
Cicero, Illinois, an 88-year-old woman's
$62 gas bill check was turned into
That was money she and her husband had
set aside for their funerals. She told
CBS Chicago, "We tried to have money to
be buried when it's our time." 60 days.
Harlan had accepted that number decades
ago in an agreement nobody reads and
nobody ever said it out loud to him
until the day it was used against him.
That is the whole trap. The theft took
one night. The real loss came from a
deadline he did not know existed. The
Quiet Rules exists for exactly that gap.
It is where the windows and the first
moves are written down in plain English,
so they are sitting next to your phone
before an envelope ever goes missing.
You can find it at kevinexplains.shop.
There is a QR code on your screen right
now and your phone's camera will open
it. The same link is pinned as the first
comment under this video and it is the
first line of the description. Take 7
days with it. If it is not for you, you
get a refund. Harlan keeps that bank
letter on top of the refrigerator under
a magnet in the margin in his daughter's
handwriting. Day 71.
Too late. Stop number four is the
thief's table and this is where the
check changes. FinCEN describes it this
way. Check washing involves the use of
chemicals to remove the original ink on
a check. Then a new payee goes on and
often a new amount. There is a newer
version, too, called check cooking.
Instead of soaking the paper, the thief
photographs it and builds a digital
copy, then prints a fresh one. David
Maimon, a fraud researcher at Georgia
State University, told CBS News that the
criminals have all the right hardware,
all the right printers, all the right
inks. And your check may not stay with
the person who stole it. FinCEN warned
banks that stolen and washed checks are
sold to other fraudsters on the dark web
and encrypted social media platforms.
Your check with your signature can end
up in the hands of a stranger in another
state. The numbers explain why this is
not rare. In 2022, banks filed more than
reports of suspected check fraud. That
was nearly double the year before. Then,
FinCEN looked at just 6 months of
reports tied specifically to stolen
mail. More than 15,000 reports from more
than 800 financial institutions
describing more than 688 million dollars
in suspicious activity. 44% of those
stolen checks were altered and
deposited. 26% were used as templates
for counterfeits, and 20% were simply
signed with a fake signature and
deposited. And it is not only small
checks. Fortune reported on a business
owner whose wife mailed a $310,000
estimated tax payment to the IRS. It
cleared.
Months later, the IRS asked for a copy,
and the copy showed the check had been
washed and made out to a stranger.
His advice afterward was short. Don't
use checks for anything.
Stop number five is a stranger's bank.
The washed check has to be deposited
somewhere, and the people doing it work
hard to avoid looking anyone in the eye.
FinCEN noted that many of them tried to
avoid interaction with bank personnel.
So, the deposit happens at an ATM or
through a phone app, often into an
account opened for nothing but this.
The Bay Area couple's check was mailed
in California. It was deposited at an
ATM at a US bank branch in Minnesota.
Here is something worth knowing about
that second bank, because it changes how
hard you should push later. Under the
Uniform Commercial Code, the rules
almost every state uses for checks, the
bank that accepts a deposit makes a
promise to the bank that pays it. A
promise that the check has not been
altered. That promise is called a
warranty. So, when your bank pays a
washed check, it is usually not stuck
with the loss. It has someone up the
chain to go after. That is why a flat no
from your bank is not always the end of
the conversation. Before we leave stop
five, there is a mirror image of this
scam and it is aimed straight at
retirees. Sometimes the stolen or
counterfeit check does not leave your
mailbox. It arrives in it. A prize you
supposedly won. A buyer for something
you listed online who sends too much and
asks you to send back the difference. A
mystery shopper job. The check looks
real, your bank accepts it, and the
money shows up in your account within a
day or two. That is exactly where people
get caught. The Federal Trade Commission
explains it this way. By law, banks have
to make deposited funds available
quickly. Even if you see the funds in
your account, that doesn't mean it's a
good check. It can take weeks for a bank
to figure out that the check is a fake.
By then, whatever you sent back is gone
and the bank takes the full amount of
the bad check back out of your account.
So, here is the rule. Never return part
of the money to anyone who sent you a
check. Not by gift card, not by wire,
not by an app. No real buyer, employer,
or prize works that way.
Stop number six is your own bank the
moment it pays. This is where the word
cleared fools people. You log in, you
see the check number, you see the
amount. It cleared. Done. But the Bay
Area couple said their monthly statement
showed only the date and the amount, not
the name of who got paid. The stranger's
name was there the whole time, but only
on the picture of the check. So, here is
the move at stop six and it takes about
1 minute. When a check clears, open your
bank's website or app and tap on it. You
will see an image of the front and the
back. On the front, read the payee line.
Is that the name you wrote in your
handwriting? On the back, look at the
endorsement and at the stamp showing
which bank took the deposit. If you paid
your county and the back shows a
personal name or a bank in a state you
have never been to, call that same day.
FinCEN gave banks a list of warning
signs, and you can use the same list on
your own checks. Faded handwriting
underneath darker handwriting. A payee
line in writing that is not quite yours.
A name squeezed into the space where
your words used to be. The San Jose
woman in the Wells Fargo case described
her check to ABC7 this way, "They kind
of fit their name into those letters."
And set up an alert for every check over
an amount you choose. Many banks offer
that for free. Some banks have started
writing this duty into their agreements.
Since those cases, Wells Fargo has
updated its account agreement to also
call for reviewing check images, not
just the statement. The bank said the
images had always been available, which
is exactly the point. Available is not
the same as looked at. There is also a
move for a check that has not cleared
yet. Say your grandson tells you the
birthday card never came, or the county
says your payment never arrived. Call
your bank and stop payment on that check
number. But know this, under the check
rules most states use, a stop payment
you only give over the phone can lapse
after 14 days unless you confirm it in
writing.
A written stop payment generally lasts 6
months. Banks usually charge a fee. It
is still far cheaper than a washed
check. Stop number seven is the clock.
This is the one that decided Harlan's
case.
The rules for checks give you up to 1
year to report an altered check. After 1
full year, the door closes completely.
But inside that year, there are two
shorter traps. First, you are expected
to review your statements with
reasonable promptness. Second, say the
same thief hits you more than once. If
you do not report the first one within a
reasonable time, never more than 30
days, you can lose your claim on the
later ones.
And then there is your account
agreement. The law lets banks and
customers shorten those deadlines by
contract. Consumer advocates told ABC7
that banks usually allow 30 to 60 days.
In 2014, New York's highest court even
upheld a 14-day window for a business
account. When a San Jose woman asked why
her claim was denied, she put it simply,
"They denied it because I waited too
long." So, find your agreement on your
bank's website or by asking at the
branch and look for the section about
reviewing your statements. Write the
number of days on a sticky note and put
it inside your checkbook cover. That
single number decides more than the
thief does. Rosalind found out what it
costs.
72, a retired pharmacist outside
Sarasota, Florida. Every November, she
mails her property tax check early
because Florida takes 4% off if you pay
in November. $9,800
payable to the county tax collector. It
cleared.
In April, a delinquency notice arrived.
The check had been washed and deposited
under a man's name. Her bank's window
was 30 days and it had been 5 months.
She paid the tax a second time without
the discount with the late charges on
top. All in, a little over $10,500
gone twice for the same house. $10,500.
And the cruel part is that Rosalind did
nothing reckless. She paid early. She
paid in full. She used the post office.
What she did not have was one sheet of
paper. A sheet telling her that the day
a large check clears, it needs to be
looked at and that the bank's patience
runs out long before the county's notice
arrives. That missing sheet is what the
quiet rules was written to be. Not scary
stories. A plan that sits behind the
next envelope you mail before anything
goes wrong. It is waiting at
kevinexplains.shop.
Point your camera at the QR code on the
screen or tap the link pinned in the
comments or the first link in the
description. You have seven full days to
decide. If it has not earned a place in
your drawer, you get a refund. Rosalind
still has the image of that check saved
on her phone. Her handwriting on the
date, her signature at the bottom, and
on the line where she wrote the county's
name, a stranger's. Now, the day it
happens to you, because if you write
checks, it can happen to anyone, and the
first 48 hours matter more than anything
after. First, call your bank the moment
you see it, and then put it in writing
the same day. A secure message in the
app, an email, or a letter you keep a
copy of.
Write down the date, the time, and the
name of the person you spoke to. A phone
call alone is easy to lose. Second, the
bank will usually send you an affidavit,
a sworn form saying the check was
altered or forged. Fill it in and return
it fast. In the Cicero case, the bank
asked for a police report and a fraud
affidavit before it moved. Third, file a
police report and report the stolen mail
to the Postal Inspection Service at
uspis.gov.
Fourth, if the bank says no, do not
accept the first letter as final. Appeal
in writing.
The San Jose woman appealed with a
television station behind her, and Wells
Fargo refunded her.
The Cicero couple waited 5 months, and
the money came back within 24 hours of
CBS calling the bank.
A Long Island man named Roger Kaufman
had two washed checks. One for his town
taxes, and one for a $10 lab bill turned
His bank refunded all $5,937
after News 12 got involved. He said, "I
think without you, it doesn't happen."
You may not have a reporter,
but you do have regulators. If your bank
is a national bank, complaints go to the
Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency through a site called
helpwithmybank.gov.
If it is a state bank or a credit union,
your state's banking regulator or the
credit union regulator takes complaints,
too.
Banks answer those letters. Fifth,
remember that the original bill is still
unpaid. The county, the IRS, the utility
never got a cent. The Bay Area couple
ended up paying their taxes again with
penalties and said they were out $60,000
in total. Pay the bill, but ask in
writing for the penalty to be removed
and include the police report. The IRS
can remove penalties when you show
reasonable cause and a stolen check with
a police report is about as reasonable
as it gets. Many county tax collectors
have a process for this, too. In
California, for example, the law allows
penalties to be canceled when the late
payment was caused by circumstances
beyond your control. And sixth, if the
stolen check went to the IRS, it carried
your Social Security number. Ask the IRS
for an identity protection PIN. It is a
six-digit number that changes every year
and without it, nobody can file a tax
return in your name. Then, freeze your
credit at all three credit bureaus. It
is free and it takes about 10 minutes
each. And ask the bank one more
question. Should this account be closed
and a new one opened with new numbers?
The thief still has your routing number
and account number printed right on the
stolen check. A new account number makes
every copy of the old checks worthless.
If you do it, first make a list of
everything that pays in or draws out
automatically. Social Security, a
pension, insurance premiums, utilities.
Move each one and keep the old account
open for a few weeks until everything
has landed in the new one. If you are
dealing with something like this right
now or you are not sure whether
something on your statement is right,
write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
Tell me what happened and what the bank
said. I read everyone myself and many of
these videos started with exactly that
kind of email. Now, a piece of this that
almost nobody explains. A check, a debit
card, and a credit card are protected by
three different rule books and they are
not equal. A paper check falls under the
Uniform Commercial Code and your account
agreement. That is the 30- or 60-day
window we just talked about. The federal
rules that protect electronic payments
specifically leave paper checks out. A
debit card or an electronic withdrawal
from your account falls under federal
electronic transfer rules. If a debit
card is lost or stolen and you report it
within two business days, the most you
can lose is $50. Wait longer and it can
rise to 500. And if no card was involved
at all and you report an unauthorized
withdrawal within 60 days of the
statement that shows it, you generally
owe nothing. And here is the twist. If a
thief takes the numbers off the bottom
of your stolen check and types them into
an online payment form, that withdrawal
is electronic. The stronger federal
rules apply to that part. A credit card
has the strongest protection of the
three. Under the Fair Credit Billing
Act, your liability for unauthorized
charges is capped at $50 and you get 60
days after the statement to dispute in
writing. Most cards go further and
charge you nothing at all. The money in
your checking account is never touched
while the dispute is open. So, the
payment method you choose for a big bill
is not a small decision. It decides
which rule book protects you on your
worst day. Which brings us to what to
use instead, bill by bill. For the IRS,
use IRS Direct Pay on the IRS website.
It is free, it comes straight out of
your checking or savings account, you do
not need to register, and you get a
confirmation number on the spot. You can
schedule a payment ahead of time, so
your January estimated payment can be
set up now and never travel through a
mailbox. In the IRS's own words, the IRS
requests that whenever possible, you
make a payment online.
For property taxes, almost every county
now takes payments on its own website.
Paying from your bank account on the
county site is usually free, while
paying by credit card usually carries a
fee of a few percent. Or, pay in person
at the tax collector's office and ask
for a stamped receipt. In Florida, an
online payment in November still gets
the full 4% discount. For utilities, set
up automatic payment through the
utilities own website, so nothing is
mailed at all. And one warning about
your bank's online bill pay. It looks
electronic, but if the company you are
paying is not set up to receive
electronic payments, your bank simply
prints a paper check and mails it for
you. Same mailbox, same risk. Ask your
bank how each payee is paid. For
grandchildren, hand the check over in
person when you see them, or have it
deposited the same week, and look at the
image when it clears.
If you mail it, mail it from inside the
post office. And if you travel for the
holidays, do not let mail pile up in
your box while you are gone. The postal
service will hold your mail for free for
up to 30 days. You can set it up online
or at the counter. For charities, give
through the charity's own website, or
hand it to the office. And if you give
from an IRA through a qualified
charitable distribution, ask the company
that holds your IRA how the check
travels. Some mail it straight to the
charity. Some mail it to you to deliver.
Either way, find out where it goes and
confirm with the charity that it
arrived. And for the checks that still
come to you, a refund, a dividend, a
birthday check from a relative, do not
let them travel again. Deposit them
through your bank's app if you can, the
same day they arrive. Many banks ask you
to write for mobile deposit only,
followed by the bank's name, under your
signature on the back. Then, keep the
paper check in a drawer for a couple of
weeks until the deposit is final, and
shred it. A deposited check left lying
around is just another check for someone
else to wash. Now, the reason I promised
at the start. On March 25th, 2025,
President Trump signed an executive
order called Modernizing Payments to and
from America's bank account.
It told the Treasury to stop issuing
paper checks for federal payments as of
September 30th, 2025, with limited
exceptions for people without access to
banking.
Tax refunds, social security, and most
other federal payments move to
electronic. And the White House gave its
reason in plain numbers. It said,
"Treasury checks are 16 times more
likely to be reported lost or stolen
than electronic payments."
It also cited the 680,000 reports of
check fraud in 2022.
The same order said payments to the
government should move to electronic,
too, wherever the law allows.
You can still mail a check to the IRS
today, but the government has already
decided that paper is the weak link for
its own money. And one warning that
comes with that change, scammers love a
transition. No federal agency will call
you, text you, or email you to ask for
your bank login so they can switch your
payments. If anyone does, hang up and go
directly to ssa.gov or irs.gov typed in
yourself.
So, let me replay the journey one more
time, the safe way. Your next check is
written in black gel ink with no empty
space and no social security number
unless it is truly required. It does not
sit in your mailbox, and it does not
spend a night in a blue box. It goes
into a clerk's hand, or it is not mailed
at all, because the bill is paid on the
payee's own website instead.
When it clears, you open the image and
read the name on the front and the bank
on the back. And taped inside your
checkbook is one number, the days your
bank gives you. If anything is wrong,
the bank hears from you in writing that
same day. None of that takes more than a
few minutes. The thieves are counting on
the fact that most people will never do
any of it. If you want all of this kept
in one place, next to your checkbook,
the quiet rules is pinned at the top of
the comments and linked in the
description. And if someone you love
still mails checks, send them this video
before their property tax goes in the
mail. I am Kevin. Thanks for watching.
Do not forget to check the quiet rules
at kevinexplains.shop.

title: Seniors Over 65: 7 Bills You Legally Don’t Owe, Most Pay Them Anyway

segments.text: Some of the bills on your kitchen table
this year have your name on them. The
right address, the right amount, and
they are still not yours to pay. Not
because somebody made a mistake, because
a law says so, and the office that
mailed the bill has no duty to mention
it. After 65, that gap gets wider every
single year. More of the money you are
asked for comes with a waiver, an
exemption, or a rule that moves the bill
to somebody else. And almost none of
those switch on by themselves. You have
to recognize the bill first. So, today I
am going to walk you through seven of
them. And for each one, the exact words
printed on the paper that tell you it
may be a bill you do not owe. A few are
worth a couple of hundred dollars. One
is worth tens of thousands, and it is
not even mailed to you. It is mailed to
your children. And the last one arrives
in the hardest week of a person's life.
It is addressed to a husband or a wife
who has already died, and the people who
send it are counting on the one left
behind to pay it out of habit. If you
watched my video a few weeks ago on
bills you no longer have to pay after
65, this is not that list again. That
one was about bills you can pay less of.
This one is about bills that should
never have reached you at all, or never
at that size. Only one item even touches
the new senior deduction, and only to
check that it was actually applied.
Before the first one, a quick question
for the comments. Have you ever paid a
bill and found out later that you never
owed it? Just yes or no. I read those
comments, and the stories in them have
shaped more of these videos than you
would think. My name is Kevin. I read
the fine print so you do not have to.
And if you would like the next one of
these, subscribe so it reaches you
before the envelope does. Every rule in
this video comes from the agency or the
regulation that sets it, and all of the
sources are listed in the description.
So, please check me. I am not a lawyer,
a tax preparer, or a financial advisor.
This is education, not advice about your
own situation. Bill number one comes
from the IRS, and it can arrive in three
different shapes. The first one is not a
bill at all. It is a refund you never
got. If you were 65 or older by the end
of last year, you were given something
new. The law President Trump signed in
July of last year created a deduction of
up to $6,000 on top of everything you
already had, $12,000 for a married
couple when both of you qualify. It
phases out once income passes $75,000
for a single person or $150,000 for a
couple. So, most people watching get all
of it, but it does not appear on the
main page of your return. It lives on a
brand new page called schedule 1A. So,
here are the words to look for. Pull out
the return you filed this spring and
look for schedule 1A and on it the line
for the enhanced deduction for seniors.
If that page is missing or the line is
blank and you were 65 by the 31st of
December, the deduction may never have
been claimed and there are three ways it
gets missed. The age was entered wrong
in the software. The return was filed as
married filing separately, which shuts
this deduction off completely. Or one of
you does not have a valid social
security number on the return. If it was
simply missed, the fix is an amended
return called form 1040X and you
generally have 3 years from the date you
filed to claim that refund. One more
thing, the IRS says plainly in its own
guide for older taxpayers, you can claim
this deduction whether you take the
standard deduction or itemize. So,
itemizers, it is yours too. The second
shape is a penalty notice, a late filing
penalty or a late payment penalty. Here
is the line most people never read on
that notice. Near the top right corner,
there is a phone number. The IRS has a
policy called first time abate. If you
filed on time and had no penalties for
the 3 years before, the IRS will usually
remove a late filing or a payment
penalty just because you ask. Your
returns do need to be filed and the tax
paid or on a payment plan. You do not
need a reason. You do not need a lawyer.
On its own penalty relief page, the IRS
tells you to call the toll-free number
found in the top right corner of your
notice. The interest on the tax itself
stays, but the penalty and the interest
on the penalty can come off. And the
third shape is the one that costs the
most. It is a penalty for missing a
required withdrawal from your IRA.
For most people, that starts at 73. If
you miss one, the penalty is 25% of the
amount you should have taken out. It
drops to 10% if you fix it within about
2 years. And it can drop to nothing. The
IRS can waive it entirely if the miss
came from a reasonable error and you
take the money out as soon as you find
it. You ask on form 5329 and you attach
a short letter explaining what happened.
The words to look for here are on that
form. Additional tax on excess
accumulation. If you see those words on
your return and nobody attached a
letter, somebody chose to pay the
penalty instead of asking. That is what
happened to Clement.
77. A retired insurance adjuster outside
Dayton, Ohio. For 20 years, his wife
handled every withdrawal from his IRA.
She died in the spring of 2024.
The reminder letters from the IRA
company went into a drawer with the
sympathy cards.
He missed that year's withdrawal and the
next one. About $40,000 each. His
preparer caught it this spring, took the
money out, filled in form 5329, and
worked out the penalty at the reduced
Clement wrote a check for $8,000.
Nobody attached a single page saying
that the person who ran that account had
died. One page. That was the distance
between $8,000 and possibly nothing at
all. Not a lawyer, not a fight, not an
appeal.
A page in plain English sent with the
form. And the hard part was never
writing it. The hard part is knowing it
exists while you are sitting at a table
in the worst year of your life with a
stack of mail you cannot face. I wrote
the quiet rules for that table. It is
where rules like this one are written
down ahead of time so the person holding
that stack does not need to already know
them. You will find it at
kevinexplains.shop.
Point your phone at the QR code on your
screen and it opens the page. The link
is pinned at the top of the comments and
it is in the description as well. Keep
it for 7 days. If by then it has not
shown you something you would have paid
for later, you get a refund. Clement
still has the carbon copy from that
check, $8,000, and on the memo line, in
his own handwriting, three letters, I R
S. If you are in that spot right now and
nothing has been filed yet, take the
missed withdrawal out first. Then file
the form and send the letter with it. Do
not simply pay the number the software
prints. And one more IRS penalty because
this one was written specifically around
retirement. Say you owe a penalty for
underpaying your estimated tax. If you
retired after reaching age 62 in that
year or the year before, the tax code
lets the IRS waive it when the
underpayment had a reasonable cause.
People who had taxes withheld from a
paycheck for 40 years, then stopped
working and had no idea they needed to
send in quarterly payments, are exactly
who that rule was written for. It is
requested on form 2210. Most tax
software never asks you the question, so
you have to raise it. Bill number two is
one you never actually see because it
comes out of your social security before
the money reaches your bank. It is a
surcharge on your Medicare premium. The
standard part B premium this year is
a month, but if Medicare decides your
income is above a certain line, you pay
more. Medicare calls it the
income-related monthly adjustment
amount. Most people just call it IRMAA.
The words to look for are exactly those,
income-related monthly adjustment
amount, and they appear on the letter
Social Security sends you, usually near
the end of the year. For this year,
according to the Centers for Medicare
and Medicaid Services, the surcharge
starts once income passes $109,000
for a single person. For a married
couple, the line is $218,000.
At the first step up, your Part B
premium becomes $284.10
a month, and your drug plan adds $14.50
on top. At the highest level, Part B
alone is $689.90 every month. And these
are cliffs, not ramps. $1
over the line puts you in the next tier
in full. Now, here is the rule that
makes this a bill you may not owe.
Medicare does not look at your income
now. It looks at your tax return from 2
years ago. This year's surcharge is
based on your 2024 return. So, the bill
you are paying today may be measuring a
life you are no longer living, a salary
you stopped earning, a pension that was
cut, a husband or wife who is no longer
here. Social Security keeps a form for
exactly that. It is called the SSA-44,
and it lists eight life-changing events
that let you ask them to use a newer,
lower year instead. Marriage, divorce or
annulment, death of your spouse, work
stoppage, work reduction, loss of
income-producing property, loss of
pension income, and a settlement payment
from a former employer. If one of those
happened, and your income dropped
because of it, you fill in the form, you
give your new estimate, and you attach
proof. A death certificate, a letter
from your old employer, a statement from
your pension plan. Picture a couple
whose joint income on their 2024 return
Over the married line, so each of them
pays the first surcharge. Early this
year, he dies. Her own income this year
will be about $96,000
under the single line. But, Medicare is
still billing her from that old joint
return. With one SSA-44 and a copy of
the death certificate, she can ask them
to use this year's estimate instead.
That takes her back to the standard
premium, $95.70
a month, more than $1,100 a year that
she was paying on income that no longer
exists. And one warning that runs the
other way because people with savings
get caught by it. Selling a house at a
big gain, a large Roth conversion,
cashing in investments, none of those is
a life-changing event. If a one-time
sale pushes your income over a line, the
surcharge arrives 2 years later, and the
form cannot fix it. So, if you are
planning something big, look at the
lines first, and if you can, spread it
over two tax years. Hold on to that idea
of a bill measuring the wrong thing
because it comes back. Bill number four,
one mailed to your children, is the
largest dollar amount in this video. But
first, the bills from your doctor and
