the hospital. Bill number three is the
medical bill that should have been zero.
And the most common one comes from a
visit that Medicare covers in full. Once
every 12 months, you're entitled to an
annual wellness visit, and you pay
nothing for it if your doctor accepts
Medicare's approved amount as full
payment. But read the fine print on
Medicare's own page. It says, "It isn't
a routine physical exam." And it says,
"The Part B deductible may apply if your
provider performs additional tests or
services during the same visit." So,
here is how a free visit turns into a
bill. You mention your knee, or your
sleep, or a new pill that makes you
dizzy. The doctor deals with it, which
is good medicine, and then bills a
second, separate office visit on the
same day. Now, you owe the deductible,
$283 this year, or your co-insurance.
The words to look for are on your
Medicare summary notice or the bill
itself. Two lines with the same date.
One says annual wellness visit or
preventive. The other says office visit
or established patient. If you did not
expect that second line, call the office
and ask what it was for. Sometimes it is
fair. Sometimes it was a coding habit
and it comes off when you ask. And next
time, when you book the appointment, use
the exact words annual wellness visit.
If you want to bring up a new problem,
ask the front desk before you go in
whether that will be billed separately.
While we are here, a one-line reminder
that saves people real money. Since
2023, the vaccines recommended for your
age, the shingles shot among them, have
no copay under a Medicare drug plan.
Some people still end up paying, often
because the shot was given in a doctor's
office that is not set up to bill their
drug plan. A pharmacy in your plan's
network is usually the simplest place to
get it at no cost. Call your plan first
and ask which pharmacies those are. The
second medical bill is for something
Medicare refused to pay. If you are on
original Medicare, there is a form your
provider is supposed to hand you before
a service when they have reason to
believe Medicare will not cover it. It
is called an advanced beneficiary
notice. You sign it and by signing, you
agree to pay if Medicare says no. Now
look at what happens when they skip it.
According to the Medicare Rights Center,
you may not have to pay if four things
are true. You did not get that notice
before the service. Your provider had
reason to believe it would not be
covered. The service is not something
Medicare excludes entirely. And Medicare
denied it. You may have to appeal to
prove it, but the bill can be turned
back to the provider. So, the words to
look for are on a denial, not covered.
And the question to ask yourself is
simple. Did anyone give me a form to
sign before this was done? And the third
medical bill is the big one, the
hospital. [clears throat]
Even with Medicare, a hospital stay
starts with a part A deductible of
this year. And without a supplement, the
co-insurance after that can stack up
fast. This next rule lives mostly inside
hospital billing offices. More than half
of the hospitals in this country are
nonprofits. And under a section of the
tax code known as 501R, every nonprofit
hospital must have a written financial
assistance policy. It must limit what
eligible patients are charged, and it
must accept your application for at
least 240 days after the first bill it
sends you after you go home. 240 days. 8
months. Many of these policies reach
well into middle incomes, often several
times the federal poverty line. And some
take your savings into account, and some
do not. So, the words to look for are at
the bottom of the hospital bill, often
in small print. Financial assistance,
charity care, or a plain language
summary. Ask for the application, even
if you assume you earn too much. The
answer is written in their policy, not
in your guess.
Bill number four is the one I promised.
It is mailed to your children, and it is
the largest bill in this video. When
someone is admitted to a nursing home,
the family is handed a stack of papers
at a table, usually on the worst day of
the month. Somewhere in that stack,
there is a line for a signature, and
above it are the words responsible
party, or guarantor, or financially
responsible person. Those are the words
to look for before anybody signs. Here
is what federal rules say. Any nursing
home that takes Medicare or Medicaid,
which is almost all of them, must follow
a federal regulation. It reads, "The
facility must not request or require a
third-party guarantee of payment to the
facility as a condition of admission or
expedited admission or continued stay in
the facility." In plain English, they
cannot make your son or your daughter
promise to pay your bill out of their
own money. They can ask a person who
manages your money to sign as your
representative and agree to pay the bill
from your income and your savings, but
that person is not supposed to take on
personal liability for doing it. And in
the last 2 years, Medicare's own agency
tightened this further. New guidance for
the inspectors who check nursing homes
took effect in April of last year.
According to the National Consumer Law
Center, it treats a whole set of
workarounds as illegal. Making the
representative jointly responsible with
the resident, making them personally
liable if a Medicaid application is
late, or hinting that the resident could
be discharged unless the family pays.
Courts have not always seen it the same
way, and some families have still been
sued over the wording they signed, which
is exactly why the words on that line
matter so much. This is Kurt, 61, a
retired machinist from western
Pennsylvania. The day his mother was
admitted, he signed 11 pages at a
folding table. On page six, under the
words responsible party, he signed his
own name. Her Medicaid application then
stalled for 5 months over one missing
bank statement. When it finally went
through, the home said the earlier
months were still unpaid, and a
collection firm sent the bill to Kurt.
He believed his signature made it his
debt. He settled for $26,000
taken out of his own IRA and then paid
income tax on that withdrawal on top.
for a word, representative instead of
responsible party. That was the whole
difference, and nobody at that folding
table was ever going to point it out to
him. And this is the bill that never
arrives at your house. It arrives at
your children's house after you no
longer have any say in it. That is the
reason I put a book together called The
Quiet Rules. Not for the day you were
reading the bill, but for the day
before, so the people you love walk into
that room already knowing which line to
cross out and which word to write
instead. You can get it at
kevinexplains.shop.
The QR code on your screen will take you
straight there, and the same link sits
in the pinned comment and in the
description. Read it for 7 days. If you
decide it does not belong on your shelf,
you get a refund. Kurt still keeps that
admission packet in the glove box of his
truck. Page six folded back. His
signature on the line and a sticky note
on top with one number on it in his own
handwriting. 26,000.
So, what do you actually do? If you or
someone you love is going into a nursing
home, read the agreement before the day
of admission if you can. Wherever it
says responsible party or guarantor, the
person signing can write the word
representative or agent under power of
attorney next to their name and sign
only in that role. If the home insists
on a personal guarantee, ask them to put
that in writing and call your state's
long-term care ombudsman. Every state
has one and it costs nothing. And if a
bill like Kurt's has already reached
your child, do not let them pay it
before they show that page to a lawyer
or a legal aid office. One caution.
These federal protections cover nursing
homes. Assisted living is governed by
state law and the rules there can be
very different. If your own family is in
the middle of something like this or
anything else in this video, write to me
at kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com
and tell me what is happening. I read
them myself. It may take me a few days
in a busy week, but I do answer and many
of these videos began with somebody's
email.
Bill number five has not arrived yet. It
is the property tax bill on your next
home. If you ever plan to downsize or
move closer to your children, this one
can be decided years before the bill
exists. In most states, your senior
exemption and any freeze on your taxes
stays with the house, not with you.
When you sell, it is gone and you start
over at full price.
But the three states with the most
retirees in the country each have a way
to carry it with you and each one has a
form that you must file yourself. In
California, the rule is called
Proposition 19. If you are 55 or older,
you can take the taxable value of your
old home with you to a new one anywhere
in the state. You can do it up to three
times in your life as long as you buy
within two years of selling. If the new
home costs more, only the difference is
added on top. The words to look for are
on the county assessor's form, transfer
of base year value. It is not automatic.
In Florida, the protection is called
save our homes and the part that moves
is called portability.
Picture a couple who bought in Florida
decades ago. Their house is worth
on the market, but because of save our
homes, it is assessed for tax at just
The gap between those numbers is
They sell and buy a smaller condo for
Because the condo is worth 75% of the
old house, they can carry 75% of that
gap, about $262,000.
So, the condo is taxed as if it were
worth about 158,000
instead of 420. At a typical Florida tax
rate, that is more than $4,000 a year.
Every year they live there. The most
anyone can carry is $500,000
and you have to establish the new
homestead within about three years of
leaving the old one. The words on the
form are transfer of homestead
assessment difference and it is filed
alongside the homestead application.
And in Texas, the freeze on your school
taxes that begins at 65 can move to a
new home in Texas as a percentage. You
ask the appraisal district in your old
county for a tax ceiling certificate and
you hand it to the district where your
new home is. Without that one piece of
paper, the new house starts with a full
unfrozen school tax. Bill number six is
the funeral bill. Nobody likes this
part, and that is the whole problem
because funeral homes are some of the
only businesses where people buy in a
hurry, in grief, without comparing a
single price. According to the National
Funeral Directors Association, the
median cost of a funeral with a viewing
and burial is around $8,300
before the cemetery. And a good part of
that can be things nobody was required
to buy. There is a federal regulation
called the Funeral Rule, enforced by the
Federal Trade Commission, and it gives
you rights that almost no family uses.
You can call any funeral home and get
prices over the phone without giving
your name. When you walk in, they must
hand you a written, itemized price list
that you keep. The words to look for at
the top of it are general price list.
You can buy only the items you want, not
a package, apart from one basic services
fee that every home charges. And here is
a sentence straight from the Federal
Trade Commission. The funeral provider
cannot refuse to handle a casket or urn
you bought online, and under the same
rule, they cannot charge you a fee for
doing it. Caskets sold online and at
large warehouse stores often cost a
fraction of the showroom price. And one
more line from the same rule.
No state law requires routine embalming
for every death. Some states require
embalming or refrigeration if the burial
is delayed, and a home may require it
for a public viewing, but it is not
required just because someone died. If
you choose cremation, you do not need a
casket at all. The home must offer a
simple container.
So, the words to look for on the final
statement are anything described as
required. If a line says required by
law, ask which law, and ask to see it in
writing. Before you pay, you are
entitled to a written statement of
exactly what you chose and what each
item costs. And if you or your husband
or wife served in the military, ask
about this before you buy a single
cemetery plot. A veteran with a
qualifying discharge can be buried in a
VA national cemetery at no cost to the
family. The grave site, opening and
closing the grave, the headstone or
marker, and care of the grave for as
long as the cemetery exists. And the
spouse of that veteran can be buried
there as well, even if the spouse dies
first. Many families pay several
thousand dollars for a private plot
without ever knowing that choice
existed. Your local funeral home can
arrange it, but you may have to bring it
up. Bill number seven is the one I
mentioned at the very beginning. It
arrives after a death, addressed to the
person who died, and it is meant to be
paid by the person still living in the
house. A credit card balance, a medical
bill, a personal loan, sometimes a
polite letter, sometimes a phone call
from someone who sounds kind and patient
and says the family will want to take
care of this. Here is what the Federal
Trade Commission says. By law, family
members do not usually have to pay the
debts of a deceased relative from their
own money.
Debts do not vanish when someone dies.
They are paid by the estate, meaning
whatever money and property the person
left behind. And if the estate does not
have enough, many of those debts simply
go unpaid, not by you. There are
exceptions, and you need to know which
side of them you are on. If you
co-signed the loan, it is yours. If it
was a joint account with both your names
on it as owners, it is yours. If you
were only an authorized user on your
husband's card, that is different. Being
able to use a card is not the same as
owing on it. And if you live in a
community property state, debts taken on
during the marriage can be shared. There
are nine of those states. Arizona,
California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada,
New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and
Wisconsin. Some other states make a
spouse responsible for certain medical
bills. And if you are the executor, you
can become liable if you pay things out
of the estate in the wrong order. So,
ask before you write a single check from
that account. Two more things that
protect the person left behind. Money in
a life insurance policy generally goes
straight to the person named on it. So
does an IRA or a bank account with a
named beneficiary. It does not pass
through the estate, which means the
ordinary creditors of the estate usually
cannot reach it. And if your husband or
wife received Medicaid for nursing home
care, the state has a right to recover
some of that cost from the estate. But,
under federal law, it cannot do that
while the surviving spouse is still
alive. If a letter about Medicaid
recovery arrives while you are living,
do not pay anything until a legal aid
office has looked at it. The words to
look for are at the top of the letter.
If it says estate of, followed by the
name of the person who died, it is a
bill to the estate, not to you. A
collector is allowed to contact the
spouse and the executor. What they are
not allowed to do is tell you or suggest
that you have to pay it out of your own
money when you do not. If you want the
calls to stop, the Federal Trade
Commission says to put it in a letter,
keep a copy, and send it by certified
mail with a return receipt. The phone is
not enough. And so that this list is
fair, here is one payment after a death
that you do have to make. Social
Security pays one month behind. So, a
payment that lands in the month after
someone dies is for the month they died,
and it must be returned. Social
Security's own example is simple. If the
person died in July, the payment
received in August has to go back. And
there is one small amount that goes the
other way. A surviving spouse can apply
for a one-time death payment of $255,
and the application has to be made
within 2 years. It is not much, but it
is yours, and it is not paid unless you
ask. So, that is seven bills. Here is a
way to use all of it that does not
involve memorizing anything. The next
time an envelope you do not like lands
on the table, put it in one of three
piles before you pay it. The first pile
is never pay before asking. A penalty
notice from the IRS, a Medicare
surcharge letter, a nursing home bill
with your child's name on it, any bill
addressed to someone who has died. Each
one of those has a waiver, a form, or a
rule that can change the number, and
none of them comes with a reminder.
The second pile is pay, but only the
honest number. The doctor's bill with
two lines on the same date, the hospital
bill with financial assistance printed
somewhere in small type, the funeral
statement with the word required on it.
Those bills are often partly real. Your
job is to find the part that is not. And
the third pile is for paper that has not
arrived yet. The return you will file
next spring with schedule 1A on it, the
SSA-44 you may need after a death or a
retirement. The portability form if you
ever move, the admission papers you or
your children may sign one day. Those
are the cheapest bills of all to fix
because nothing has been paid yet. Most
people who sort a month of their own
mail this way find at least one envelope
that belongs in the first pile. Not
because anyone was sloppy, because every
one of these systems sends the bill
automatically and waits for you to come
asking for the exception. If you want
these written down in one place with the
exact words to look for and the forms by
name, the quiet rules is linked in the
description and pinned at the top of the
comments. And if this helped, send it to
one person over 65 who handles the mail
in their house. I am Kevin. Thanks for
watching. Do not forget to check the
quiet rules at kevinexplains.shop.

title: Every Senior Must Do This In November Or Pay All Year

segments.text: Some of the money you have already paid
this year is about to disappear. Not
stolen, not lost, reset. At midnight on
New Year's Eve, a set of counters you
have been filling up since January goes
back to zero. What you have paid toward
your Medicare costs, what you have spent
toward your drug plan's yearly limit,
the amount you are allowed to give each
person you love without a single form,
the new tax breaks in the law signed
last summer, the yearly room in the new
accounts the government just opened for
your grandchildren. Every one of them
starts over on the 1st of January, and
whatever you did not use is simply gone.
And here is what makes November the
month that matters. Most of these
counters cannot really be used in
December. The appointments are booked,
the paperwork takes weeks, and the
offices close for the holidays. So,
today I am going to walk you through
each counter, how to see where yours
stands right now, and what to do before
the 30th of November. And there is one
counter in this video that never resets
at all. It runs for 5 years, and it is
the one that can turn a Christmas gift
into a $70,000 bill. Why the 30th of
November and not the 31st of December?
Because almost everything on this list
needs somebody else to do something
first. A doctor has to write a
prescription, a surgery center has to
find an opening, a retirement
[clears throat] account company has to
process a request, and most of them set
their own cutoff dates well before New
Year's Eve. Medicare's own enrollment
window closes on the 7th of December,
and the last week of the year is
Christmas week when doctors' offices,
pharmacies, and account companies run on
holiday hours and skeleton staff. If you
treat the end of November as your
deadline, you finish with room to spare.
If you treat the end of December as your
deadline, you are relying on everybody
else being fast in the busiest month of
their year. Before the first counter,
one quick question for the comments.
Have you already reached your Medicare
drug plan's yearly limit this year? Just
yes, no, or not sure. Most people will
type not sure. And by the end of this
video, you will know exactly where to
look. I am Kevin. This channel goes
through the rules that decide what
happens to your money after 65. If that
is useful to you, subscribe so the next
one finds you. Every source I use today
is listed in the description, so you can
check it yourself. This is education,
not personal advice, and some of it
depends on your state and your plan. The
first counter is your health care, and
for most people watching, it is really
three counters. The first is your Part B
deductible. In 2026, it is $283.
Once you have paid it, Medicare pays 80%
of covered doctor and outpatient care
for the rest of the year. And if you
have a supplement like Plan G, that
supplement usually pays the other 20. In
January, it starts over, and Medicare's
trustees project it will rise to about
The second is the limit on your drug
costs. This year, the most anybody in a
Medicare drug plan can pay out of pocket
for covered drugs is $2,100.
Once you reach that line, your covered
prescriptions cost you nothing for the
rest of the year. Zero. On the 1st of
January, the counter resets, and next
year, the limit rises to $2,400
with a deductible of up to $700 before
your plan starts sharing the cost. The
third counter is for anybody in a
Medicare Advantage plan. Every one of
those plans has a yearly maximum
out-of-pocket for covered care in its
network. In 2026, Medicare allows plans
to set it as high as $9,250,
and according to KFF, the average is
around 5,400.
Once you reach your plan's maximum, the
plan pays 100% of covered care in its
network for the rest of the year. Every
office visit, every scan, every
outpatient procedure. And then, at
midnight on New Year's Eve, it all
starts again from nothing. If your plan
is a PPO, it actually has two maximums,
one for care inside the network and a
higher one for care inside and outside
combined. So, ask which one you are
close to. If you have the high
deductible version of plan G, you have
one more counter of your own, just under
$3,000, and it resets the same night.
There is one Medicare counter that does
not follow the calendar, and people get
it wrong in both directions. The part A
deductible, the one for a hospital stay,
this year, but it is not charged once a
year. It is charged once per benefit
period, which starts when you are
admitted and ends after you have been
out of the hospital and out of skilled
nursing care for 60 days in a row. So, a
hospital stay in December and another in
February can mean two deductibles if
they fall in separate benefit periods,
and two stays a month apart can mean
only one. New Year's Day has nothing to
do with it. Maud reached her plan's
maximum in September. A fall in the
spring, a broken wrist, surgery, and
weeks of therapy, and by the end of
summer she had paid $5,900,
the most her plan could charge her. In
October, her eye doctor told her she was
ready for cataract surgery in both eyes.
The scheduler offered two dates, the
18th of December or the 8th of January.
Maud picked January, so the holidays
would be quiet. Nobody in that office
mentioned her counter because nobody in
that office knew about it. In January,
her counter was back at zero. The
surgery center co-pays, the follow-up
visits, and the specialist charges added
up to about $1,100.
In December, the same two surgeries
would have cost her nothing. Maud did
not choose wrong. She chose without one
piece of information that her plan had
and her surgeon's office did not. The
scheduler was thinking about the
calendar. The plan was not going to
call, and Maud had no reason to know
that a single date on that calendar was
worth $1,100.
The Quiet Rules is for that exact gap,
the moment when two reasonable choices
look the same and one of them quietly
costs you a month of groceries. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
Point your phone camera at the code on
the screen or tap the link in the pinned
comment or the description. You are
[clears throat] covered by a 7-day
guarantee and if it is not useful, you
get a refund.
The day Maud's bill came, she was
standing at the front desk of that
surgery center in January with a patch
over one eye being asked for her card
before they would take her back. So,
here is how to read your own health
counters this week. For a Medicare
Advantage plan, log in to your plan's
website or call the number on your card
and ask one question. How much have I
paid toward my maximum out-of-pocket
this year? They have the number.
For a drug plan, look at the monthly
statement your plan mails you, usually
called an explanation of benefits.
Somewhere on it is a line for your total
out-of-pocket costs so far this year. If
it says $2,100,
you are at the limit. And if you change
drug plans partway through this year,
the amount you paid under your old plan
generally follows you to the new one for
the rest of the year, so do not assume
you started over. For part B, your
Medicare Summary Notice or your account
on Medicare's website shows whether your
deductible has been met. Then, if you
are at or near any of those limits,
think about what you've been putting
off. A procedure your doctor has already
said you need, a scan, physical therapy,
hearing tests, new glasses if your plan
covers them. Not care you do not need.
Care you were going to get anyway, just
in January. Call this month because
surgery centers and specialists often
book 4 to 6 weeks out and if your plan
requires permission in advance, that
approval can take time, too. The drug
counter needs a little more care because
there are rules about refills. If you
have reached the limit, ask your doctor
this month to write your regular
prescriptions for a 90-day supply if
that is appropriate for you. Most plans
let you refill once you have used most
of your current supply, often somewhere
around 3/4 of it. So, time your last
refill of the year to land before the
31st and you can carry several months of
medicine into January at no cost. I want
to be precise about what that does. If
your drug costs land you near the limit
every year, moving a few months of
medicine into a year you have already
paid for can genuinely lower what you
pay next year. If your costs are far
above the limit every year, you will
probably reach next year's limit anyway.
So, it mostly changes when you pay
rather than how much. But, even that
helps because January is when the new
deductible hits all at once. And if you
are switching drug plans on the 1st of
January, check whether your new plan
covers the same drugs before you stock
up so you are not left mid-supply on a
medicine your new plan treats
differently.
One more health counter, and this one
belongs to people in Advantage plans
with extras. Dental allowances, vision
allowances, hearing aid allowances, and
those cards loaded with money for
groceries or over-the-counter items.
Those almost never roll over. If you
have $500 of dental coverage left, that
cleaning and filling are worth booking
now. Dentists fill up in December for
exactly this reason. Now a word for
anybody who is about to leave for the
winter because November is when a lot of
you pack the car and head south.
Original Medicare works with any doctor
or hospital in the country that takes
Medicare. A Medicare Advantage plan
usually does not work that way. Many
Advantage plans, especially the ones
called HMOs, cover routine care only
inside your home network. Away from
home, they generally cover emergencies
and urgent care and not much else. So,
before you leave, call your plan and ask
what it covers in the state where you
will be spending the winter and whether
it has a travel or visitor program. Ask
your drug plan whether your pharmacy
chain is in network down there or set up
mail order to your winter address. And
if you are traveling outside the country
for the holidays, know that original
Medicare generally does not pay for care
abroad. Several supplement plans,
including plan G and plan N, include a
foreign travel emergency benefit, and
some advantage plans do, too. Find out
before you board, not in a foreign
emergency room. The second counter is
the one people misunderstand most, and
it is the one that comes out in
December. Gifts.
Every year, the IRS lets you give a
certain amount to any one person without
filing anything at all. For 2026, that
amount is $19,000 per person. A married
couple can each give it, so together you
can give $38,000 to each child, each
grandchild, anyone you like without a
single form. And that allowance does not
carry forward. If you give nothing this
year, you do not get to give 38,000 next
year. On the 1st of January, the counter
resets. Two things almost nobody tells
you about that number. First, going over
it does not mean you owe tax. It means
you file a gift tax return, form 709,
and the extra is subtracted from a
lifetime amount. Under the law President
Trump signed last summer, that lifetime
amount is $15 million per person
starting this year. Very few families
will ever pay a dollar of gift tax.
Second, there are payments that do not
count toward the 19,000 at all. If you
pay a grandchild's college tuition
directly to the school or pay someone's
medical bill directly to the hospital or
doctor, there is no limit for gift tax
purposes. The money has to go straight
to the school or the provider, not to
the grandchild. And if you are helping a
grandchild with college, one rule
changed recently in your favor. On the
newer financial aid form, money that a
grandparent pays out of a college
savings plan is no longer counted as the
student's income.
For years, a grandparent's generosity
could quietly shrink a grandchild's aid.
That trap is largely gone.
There is also a way to use 5 years of
the gift allowance at once, but only for
college savings. You can put up to 5
years worth into a grandchild's college
savings plan in a single year. $95,000
from one person or $190,000 from a
married couple and spread it across 5
years on your gift tax return.
Hold that thought because of what I am
about to tell you about the counter that
never resets. One timing detail about
the gift counter itself. A gift by check
generally counts in the year the check
is deposited and paid, not the year you
wrote it. A check written on the 28th of
December and cashed on the 3rd of
January can land in next year's counter.
If the year matters, give early or ask
the person to deposit it right away.
Now, the newest place grandparents can
give and it opened only weeks ago. The
law signed last summer created a new
kind of account for children, officially
called Trump accounts. On the 1st of
October, the Treasury announced it had
automatically opened accounts for more
than 60 million children under 18.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bassent put it
this way. Over 60 million more eligible
children now have an account ready to be
claimed.
Ready to be claimed is the important
part. The account cannot receive a
dollar from anyone until a parent claims
it in the Trump accounts app or on the
official website by verifying who they
are and that the child is theirs. And
there is money waiting in the system
that many families are going to miss. A
child who is a United States citizen
born from the beginning of 2025 through
the end of 2028 can receive a $1,000
deposit from the government, but it is
not automatic. A parent has to choose
it, usually on a form called form 4547
or through the online system. Before the
Treasury stepped in, only about 5.6
million sign-up forms have been
processed for more than 70 million
eligible children. So, if you have a
grandchild born last year or this year,
the single most valuable thing you can
do this Thanksgiving maybe to ask your
son or daughter one question. Have you
claimed the account and did you elect
the $1,000? If they have, family and
friends can contribute up to $5,000 a
year per child combined and that limit
resets every January, too. The money
must be invested in low-cost funds that
track the American stock market until
the child turns 18.
Two honest cautions. Your contribution
is not tax deductible for you and the
Treasury is still finishing some of the
rules including how gifts of stock will
work. So, some advisors suggest starting
small until the final rules are written.
A modest holiday contribution is a fine
way to begin. A very large one can wait
for the details. And if your grandchild
is a little older, born from 2016
through 2024, check one more thing.
Michael and Susan Dell pledged $6.25
billion
to put $250 into the accounts of about
25 million children that age in zip
codes where the typical household earns
a year. No application is needed, but
the account still has to be claimed
before anyone can see it. The money
generally cannot come out until the year
the child turns 18 and after that, it
follows rules much like an IRA. Now,
here is the counter that never resets
and it is the one that turns all of that
generosity into danger. Medicaid. If you
or your husband or wife ever need
long-term care in a nursing home and
apply for Medicaid to help pay for it,
the state looks back at every gift you
made during the previous 5 years. In
California, it is shorter, 30 months and
California brought its asset test back
this year. But for most of the country,
it is 5 years. And here is the sentence
I most want you to hear today.
The $19,000 IRS allowance means nothing
to Medicaid. Nothing. A gift can be
perfectly fine with the IRS and still
count fully against you for Medicaid.
The same is true of tuition you paid
directly to a college. Medicaid
generally treats it as a gift. And so is
that 5-year lump sum into a college
savings plan. One generous afternoon at
the bank can sit inside the look-back
window for the next 5 years. The penalty
works like this. The state adds up the
gifts made inside the look-back window.
Then, it divides that total by what a
month in a nursing home costs in your
state, a figure each state sets. The
answer is the number of months Medicaid
will refuse to pay for your care.
And here is the cruel part. That penalty
does not start the day you made the
gift. Under federal rules, it starts
only when you are already in care, your
savings are already spent down, and you
would otherwise qualify. It lands at the
worst possible moment on the people
least able to absorb it. And notice the
difference between giving and spending.
Medicaid penalizes transfers for less
than their value. It does not penalize
you for spending your own money on
yourself. Repairing your own roof,
paying off your own mortgage, buying a
reliable car you will use. In most
[snorts] states, prepaying your own
funeral through an arrangement that
cannot be canceled within the state's
limits. Those are generally not gifts.
Giving a grandchild the money to fix
their roof is. Josephine gave each of
her four grandchildren $19,000
two Christmases ago.
A teller at her bank told her that was
the legal limit, and she believed she
was being careful.
to four young people she adored for
houses and school and fresh starts.
Last spring, she had a stroke. After
rehab, she needed full-time care.
Her savings went quickly, and when her
daughter applied for Medicaid, the case
worker found the four gifts.
In her state, a month in a nursing home
was counted at about $11,000.
became almost 7 months with no Medicaid
payment for her care.
Her family had two choices. Ask four
grandchildren to return the money or
find $76,000 themselves. Josephine did
everything she was told. The problem is
that she was told about the wrong rule.
The IRS line and the Medicaid line are
two different lines written by two
different parts of the government and
nobody at the bank counter was ever
going to explain the second one. The
Quiet Rules was put together for exactly
that kind of rule. Not the rules
everybody repeats, but the ones that
only show up years later in a case
worker's office. If there is a gift you
are planning this season, read it before
the check is written. You can get it at
kevinexplains.shop.
The code is on your screen right now and
the link is in the pinned comment and
the description below. The guarantee
