beneficiary. Most banks add one while
you wait, and it costs nothing. Lowell
knew exactly where his money should go.
What he did not know is that wanting it
and having it on file at the bank are
two completely different things in the
eyes of the law. That is the kind of
difference the Quiet Rules was put
together to catch. Not the big decisions
people already think about, but the
small forms and settings that quietly
decide what your family can reach and
how fast. If you have an account like
Lowell's or a parent who does, this is
the week to look. The Quiet Rules is at
kevinexplains.shop.
The code on your screen opens it, and
the same link sits in the pinned comment
and in the description below. If within
7 days it has not shown you something
you would have missed, you get a refund.
Rhonda's 10 months started at a teller's
window with her father's death
certificate in her hand being told very
politely that the account was not hers
to touch.
The next layer is the one most people
already know a number for. $250,000.
That is the limit of federal deposit
insurance at a bank, and the same limit
applies at federally insured credit
unions. If the bank fails, you are
covered up to that amount. But the full
rule is $250,000 per owner, per bank,
per type of ownership. Accounts in your
name alone are one type. Joint accounts
are another, where each owner is covered
So, a A couple's joint account is
covered up to 500,000. Retirement
accounts at the bank are a third, and a
fourth type changed in April of 2024.
Accounts with payable on death
beneficiaries and accounts owned by a
living trust are now covered at $250,000
for each beneficiary, but only up to
five beneficiaries. That puts a ceiling
per owner at each bank. Under the old
rules, a grandparent who named eight
grandchildren could be covered for more.
Today, the sixth name adds nothing.
There is also a clock. When two banks
merge, the money you had at each one
stays separately insured for only 6
months. After that, it counts as one
bank. If you spread your money across
two banks to stay under the limit, and
those banks combine, you can end up over
the limit without moving a dollar.
That merger notice usually arrives
looking like routine paperwork. Open it.
Then there is money that sits right next
to insured accounts, but is not insured
at all. A money market fund at a
brokerage is not a money market account
at a bank. The fund is an investment. It
is usually very stable, but it is not
deposit insurance.
The SIPC protection on a brokerage
statement covers you if the firm fails
and your holdings go missing, not if an
investment loses value. Annuities are
backed by your state's guarantee
association, not by the FDIC. And then,
there are apps. In 2024, a go-between
company called Synapse, which sat
between several money apps and the banks
behind them, collapsed.
More than 100,000 people were locked out
of over $265 million.
Some of them for many months.
The banks underneath were insured, but
insurance only pays when a bank fails,
and the banks had not failed. The
records showing who owned what had.
A court-appointed trustee found a
shortfall of 65 to 95 million dollars.
So, the rule for this layer is short.
Never keep more than your insured amount
at one bank for each type of ownership.
Check again whenever a bank you use
merges, and never keep money in an app
that you could not live without for 6
months. The last layer has nothing to do
with how much you have. It is about how
long you leave it alone. Every state has
an unclaimed property law. If an account
shows no activity from you for a set
number of years, usually three to five
depending on the state, the bank has to
treat it as abandoned and send the money
to the state. And in many states,
interest the bank adds on its own does
not count as activity from you. An
account earning interest every single
month can still be called abandoned. You
can recover it, and every state runs a
free search. Missingmoney.com searches
many states at once, but it takes forms,
and it takes months. And if the account
held a certificate of deposit, the state
may already have cashed it in.
Gus's old account is exactly this kind.
Nobody has logged in for years, and the
statements still go to an address they
left. That one quiet account is carrying
three layers at once. It is over the
probate line, it is drifting toward the
state, and nobody is watching it. Before
I fix Gus and Lorraine's accounts, there
is one cost of keeping too much in the
bank that no one ever sends you a letter
about. The interest you are not earning.
According to the FDIC, the national
average savings rate is under 4/10 of
1%, and many of the biggest banks still
pay 1/100 of 1% on a basic savings
account. At the same time, after the
Federal Reserve raised rates again last
month, plenty of insured high-yield
savings accounts and Treasury bills are
paying around 4%. On Gus and Lorraine's
the difference between those two rates
is about $2,600
a year. That is more than their Medicare
surcharge would cost them if they ever
cross the line. So, money in checking
above what you need does not just sit in
the wrong layer. It also earns almost
nothing while it sits there. One quick
word for anybody who receives SSI or
helps a parent who does.
SSI has its own line, $2,000 for one
person and 3,000 for a couple, and those
limits have not moved since 1989.
Social Security checks the balance at
the first moment of each month. A gift
that lands on the 28th and is still
sitting there on the first can cost a
whole month of benefits.
If that is your family, spend or set
aside the gift before the month turns
and ask Social Security how to report
it. So, here is what Gus and Lorraine
did. Same money, different places.
They brought checking down to about
Two months of their checks plus a little
room for a bill that lands early.
Every dollar in that account now sits in
the layer nobody can reach. They also
wrote a note to themselves that if one
of them dies, checking comes down again
that same month because the protected
amount shrinks to one check. Out of the
extra in checking, they paid off the
on the car loan. That closed the set-off
door at the national bank completely.
The rest went into savings, and they
moved all of their savings to a credit
union across town where they owe
nothing. No loan, no card, nothing
anybody can set off against. It sits in
a high-yield savings account at around
4% titled jointly with their two
children named as payable on death
beneficiaries.
Joint ownership plus beneficiaries keeps
every dollar well inside the insured
limits. The certificate matures in
December. The grace period to change it
after maturity is usually only 7 to 10
days, so the date is on their calendar.
If they do nothing, it rolls into a new
certificate at whatever rate the credit
union decides to offer that week.
They are putting part of it into
treasury bills, which New York cannot
tax, and timing the rest so the interest
lands in the year that suits them, well
under the Medicare line. And Gus's old
account. He went into that bank, logged
in for the first time in years, updated
the address, made a small deposit, and
named Lorraine as the payable on death
beneficiary. It took about 15 minutes.
It is no longer over the probate line,
the dormancy clock has started over, and
somebody is watching it again. Before, a
creditor with a judgment could have
frozen $37,800
of their money. Their own bank could
reach 72,000,
and a court would have held up 58,000
after Gus died. After, every one of
those numbers is zero. They did not
spend a dollar to get there, and their
savings now earn more than they did. Now
your turn, and you do not need a
spreadsheet. Open the statement for the
account where your check lands and ask
it three questions. First, how much is
sitting above two months of the benefits
that land here? That extra is in the
creditor's layer, so give it a separate
home. Second, do I owe this bank or
credit union anything at all? A loan? A
line of credit? A loan I co-signed for
somebody? If the answer is yes, my
savings should live somewhere else.
Third, if I died tonight, who would this
account go to? If the answer is my
estate, add a beneficiary this week,
especially if the balance is above your
state's small estate limit. Then, once a
year, maybe on your birthday, do three
smaller checks. Log into every account
you own, including the quiet ones. Add
up half your social security plus all
your other income and interest, and see
how close you are to the tax lines and
the Medicare line.
And if any bank you use has merged in
the last 6 months, add up what you keep
there. If your situation does not fit
neatly into any of this, a trust account
at a bank that just merged, a parent's
account with no beneficiary, a
certificate maturing right before a big
tax year,
write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
Tell me what you were looking at. I read
every message, and the The ones often
turn into videos. Almost everything we
covered today is fixed with a form, a
phone call, or one visit to a bank.
The hard part is knowing which form and
getting it done before somebody else's
paperwork arrives first. If you want
that worked out ahead of time, the quiet
rules is waiting at the link in the
description and the pinned comment, and
the code is back on your screen. Set it
up while the account is still yours to
arrange, not on the morning a teller
turns the screen around to show you a
balance that is suddenly smaller than
the one you remember.
I am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: Do Not Throw Away These 5 Letters Arriving Before January

segments.text: The letter you are waiting for is the
one you can do the least about. Your new
Social Security amount is on its way,
and when that envelope arrives, you will
open it the same afternoon. But, the
letters that cost retirees real money
over the next 3 months will not look
like that one. One will look like
paperwork from a human resources office.
One will look like a newsletter from
your hospital. One will look like a
thank you note from your insurance
company. One will look exactly like a
scam. And one will look so final that
most people never think to question it.
Each of them has one sentence inside
that decides what you pay next year. A
couple of them decide it for the rest of
your life. So, today, I am going to show
you all five. What each one looks like
on the outside, the single line inside
it you cannot afford to miss, and what
silence costs you if it ends up in the
recycling. The second one comes from
somebody who is not your insurance
company, which is exactly why its
deadline gets missed. And the last one
can be undone in a way almost nobody
uses. But first, the raise, because the
number on the news is not the number
that lands in your account. Social
Security announced it on the 14th of
October, 3.6%
starting with the payments you receive
in January. For the average retired
worker, that is roughly $75 more a
month, about $900 over the year. SSI
rises by the same percentage, starting
with the payment at the very end of
December. But that raise applies to your
benefit before anything is taken out of
it. What lands in your account is what
is left after Medicare
The Part B premium for next year has not
been announced yet. It usually comes in
November. Medicare's own trustees
projected $209.50
a month, up $6.60.
If that holds, the premium eats only a
small slice of most raises. Your
personal letter usually arrives in
December. If you have a My Social
Security account, and you switch on
digital notices by the 18th of November,
you can read it online up to 3 weeks
before the paper copy reaches you. When
it comes, look at the Medicare line. If
it is far above that $210 figure, that
is a surcharge based on your income, and
it is the fifth letter on today's list.
And if your state normally pays your
Part B premium for you, and that line
suddenly shows a premium, call your
state Medicaid office that same week.
One thing before the first letter. Tell
me in the comments which of these five
is sitting in your house right now,
unopened. Just the number.
I am Kevin, and this channel translates
the rules behind your money after 65
into plain English. If that is useful to
you, subscribe so the next one finds
you.
Every source for today is listed in the
description. This is education, not
personal advice, and some of it depends
on your state and your plan, so check
your own details before you act. The
first letter should already be in your
house because it had to be sent before
the 15th of October.
It comes from an employer, a union, or a
retiree benefits office, and it usually
arrives inside an envelope stuffed with
other benefits paperwork. It's title is
something like important notice about
your prescription drug coverage and
Medicare.
Most people file it with everything else
or throw it out. Here is what it is. If
you have drug coverage through a job,
your spouse's job, a union, or a former
employer's retiree plan, that plan has
to tell you every year whether its drug
coverage is creditable. Creditable means
it is at least as good, on average, as a
standard Medicare drug plan. That one
word decides whether you can safely stay
out of Medicare's drug program. If your
coverage is creditable, you can skip a
Medicare drug plan for as long as you
have it and join later with no penalty.
If it is not creditable, and you go 63
days or more without coverage that
counts, Medicare adds a late penalty
when you finally join. 1% of a national
base premium for every month you went
without. Next year, that base premium is
And the penalty does not end. It is
added to your drug premium every month
for as long as you have Medicare drug
coverage, and it grows whenever the base
premium grows. A 3-year gap, for
example, is 36% of that base, about $15
a month, which sounds small until you
remember it is added every month for as
long as you live, and it rises almost
every year. This year, that letter
matters more than it has in a long time.
For 2027, Medicare raised the bar that
most employers use to call their
coverage creditable. Under the simpler
test, a plan used to qualify if it was
designed to pay about 60% of its
members' drug costs. Now, it has to pay
about 73%.
Benefits advisers have been warning
employers all summer that a meaningful
number of plans that were creditable
this year will not be next year. So, the
letter you receive this fall may say
something it has never said before.
Calvin learned what that letter is worth
the year he finally needed it. He kept
the drug coverage from his old phone
company job for 6 years after he turned
65. Every October, a notice came saying
it was creditable, and every October, it
went out with the recycling. Then the
retiree plan ended, and he joined a
Medicare drug plan.
A few weeks later, the new plan sent him
a form asking about his coverage
history. He could not remember the
dates, the plan decided he had a gap,
and when he asked for a review, he was
asked for proof. The proof was those six
October letters. The benefits office he
got them from had been sold twice. 72
months without proof became 72% of the
base premium, nearly $30 a month added
to his bill for life. So, think about
this for a second. If a plan sent you
that same form tomorrow, where are your
last six October letters? Most people
know exactly where their tax returns
are. Almost nobody knows where the one
page is that keeps a penalty off their
bill for the rest of their life. The
quiet rules exist so that the next time
a form like that lands on your table,
you are holding the answer instead of
hunting for it. You can get it at
kevinexplains.shop.
Aim your phone camera at the code on the
screen or use the link in the pinned
comment or the description. The
guarantee is 7 days long and if it is
not been useful to you by then, you get
a refund. Calvin's form gave him 30
days. He spent them in the garage
opening boxes looking for a letter he
had thrown away six times. So, what to
do with yours? Find it and read the one
word. If it says creditable, put it in a
folder you will never throw away and add
every year's copy for as long as you
rely on that coverage. If it says not
creditable or you cannot find it, call
the benefits office this week and ask in
writing. If your coverage will not count
next year, you can join a Medicare drug
plan between now and the 7th of December
and it starts on the 1st of January. If
your old coverage counted right up until
then, there is no gap and no penalty.
But do not drop anything until you ask
one more question. Some employer and
retiree plans bundle drug and medical
coverage together and dropping the drug
part can drop the medical part as well,
sometimes with no way back. Get that
answer in writing before you change a
thing. And if your drug coverage comes
from the VA, from Tricare or from the
Federal Employees Health Program, it
generally counts as creditable. Keep the
letter anyway. While you have that
benefits office on the phone, ask about
part B, too, because the same mistake
carries a bigger price there. If you are
still working or covered through your
spouse's current job at a larger
employer, you can usually put off part B
without a penalty. But coverage from a
former employer does not count for that.
Retiree coverage does not count. Cobra
does not count. People who keep a
retiree health plan and skip part B
because they feel fully covered can find
out later that the retiree plan only
pays after Medicare would have paid. For
many of them, it then pays very little.
And Medicare adds 10% to the part B
premium for every full year they could
have had it and did not for the rest of
their lives. If you are past 65 on a
retiree plan and you do not have part B,
ask your plan in writing whether it
expects Medicare to pay first. The
second letter looks like a newsletter.
It comes from your hospital, your
doctor's group, or your cancer center,
not from your insurance company.
Sometimes it is just an email. The
headline says something gentle, like an
important update about your insurance.
And the sentence that matters is in the
middle of a paragraph. Starting the 1st
of January, we will no longer be in
network with your Medicare Advantage
plan. There are a lot of these this
fall. According to a tracker kept by
Becker's Hospital Review, more than 30
health systems have ended or are
preparing to end their contracts with
one or more Medicare Advantage
companies. Ohio State's Medical Center
has already left Humana's Individual
Advantage plans. Lee Health in Fort
Myers is leaving United Healthcare at
the end of this year. Endeavor Health
near Chicago is ending its Aetna
Advantage contract after this year.
Fairview in Minneapolis stopped
scheduling United Healthcare Advantage
patients in January. Those are only a
few names on a long list. Here is why it
matters that this letter comes from the
hospital. Your plan's notice of changes
was printed months ago and it is mostly
about premiums, copays, and drugs.
A hospital leaving the network often is
not in it at all. The hospital's letter
may be the clearest warning you ever
get. And losing your hospital usually
does not give you a special window to
change plans. A plan ending its contract
with a hospital is not the same as the
plan itself ending. Medicare can open a
special window when a plan's network
shrinks dramatically, but that is
decided case by case and nobody can
promise you one. So the deadline that
matters is the ordinary one, the 7th of
December. Switch by then and the new
plan starts on the 1st of January. If
you miss it, there is one more door.
From the 1st of January to the end of
March, if you're in an Advantage plan,
you can make one switch either to
another Advantage plan or back to
original Medicare with a drug plan. But
here is the trap inside that door. Going
back to original Medicare in March does
not guarantee you a supplement to cover
what Medicare does not. In most states,
a supplement company can ask health
questions and turn you down unless you
are in a protected situation like your
plan leaving your area or the trial year
after you first tried an Advantage plan.
So, if a hospital you depend on is
leaving, the safest time to act is now
while every option is still open. And if
the letter you got this month says your
whole plan is ending, not just one
hospital, you are in better shape than
you think but only for a while. United
Healthcare and Humana alone are closing
plans that cover more than a million
people for next year. If yours is one of
them, you get extra time. You can choose
a new plan through the end of February
and for a limited window, you have a
guaranteed right to buy certain
supplements with no health questions at
all.
That right generally runs for 63 days
after your plan coverage ends. Miss it
and the supplement companies can start
asking about your health again. If you
do nothing, you land in original
Medicare on the 1st of January with no
supplement and possibly no drug plan. If
you are in the middle of treatment, a
round of chemotherapy, a surgery already
on the calendar, ask your plan in
writing about continuity of care. Some
companies will keep covering a current
course of treatment with a departing
provider at in-network cost for a period
of time. Get the answer in writing with
an end date on it.
And in an emergency, go to the nearest
hospital. Emergency care is covered
wherever you are.
To check where you stand, do not rely on
the plan's online directory alone.
Medicare's own reviews have found those
directories full of errors. Call the
billing office of the hospital or the
practice and ask one exact question.
Will you be in network for this plan,
using its full name, on the 1st of
January? Write down who told you and the
date. And if you do decide to switch,
expect your mailbox and your phone to
get busy because the rules for selling
Medicare plans loosened on the 1st of
October. Until this year, after you
agreed to talk with an agent about
plans, there generally had to be a
48-hour wait before the actual sales
pitch.
That waiting period is gone. An agent
can now take your permission and sell
you a plan in the same phone call. One
sentence will tell you who you are
dealing with. Agents and marketing
companies have to tell you that they do
not offer every plan available in your
area. If you see or hear those words, it
is a sales call, not Medicare. That does
not make it bad. It means you should
compare their answer with the free plan
finder on Medicare's website or with
your state health insurance assistance
program, which gives free counseling and
sells nothing. The third letter looks
like a thank you note. It comes from
your Medicare supplement company, the
policy that pays what original Medicare
leaves behind. It thanks you for being a
valued member. And somewhere below that,
it gives you your new monthly premium.
Supplement premiums are climbing faster
than they used to. KFF Health News has
reported this year that brokers now see
increases of 10 to 15% as routine. And
early filings from several large
companies showed Plan G increases from
just over 12% to more than 26%.
There are three things that letter will
never tell you. The first is how your
price is built. Supplements are priced
in one of three ways. Some companies
charge everyone the same, regardless of
age. That is called community rated.
Some set your price by the age you were
when you bought the policy. That is
issue age rated. And many charge by the
age you are now. That is attained age
rated. And it means your premium climbs
every year simply because you had a
birthday on top of any increase for
rising costs. If yours is priced by
attained age, this year's letter is not
the last big one. The way it is priced
is printed in your policy and the
company will tell you if you ask. And do
not assume the increase can only come on
your policy anniversary.
KFF reported that in August of last
year, one company raised premiums for
some Illinois customers by 45%
effective immediately rather than on the
policy anniversary. The second is that
every Plan G is the same Plan G. Outside
of three states, Massachusetts,
Minnesota, and Wisconsin, supplements
are standardized by federal law. A Plan
G from one company pays exactly the same
bills as a Plan G from another. The only
differences are the price, how the
company handles its increases, and its
service. So, two neighbors with
identical coverage can be paying very
different premiums and neither one knows
it. The third is whether you are allowed
to switch without health questions. In
most states, once your first 6 months on
Medicare have passed, a new supplement
company can ask about your health and
turn you down.
But a growing list of states have what
is called a birthday rule. Each year, in
a window around your birthday, you can
move to a supplement with the same or
fewer benefits without answering health
questions. Each state sets its own
details and a few limit it by age. This
summer, that list included California,
Nevada, Oregon, Idaho, Illinois,
Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland,
Oklahoma, Utah, Virginia, West Virginia,
Wyoming, and Delaware. And New Mexico
joins in 2027. In California and Nevada,
the window is 60 days starting on your
birthday. In Illinois, 45 days. In Idaho
and Louisiana, 63. And in Connecticut
and New York, you can buy a supplement
without health questions at any time of
year. Outside those states, there are
still two quiet moves. Ask your company
whether it gives a household discount,
which many do when two people in the
same home are covered. And ask about the
high deductible version of plan G. It's
deductible is just under $3,000 a year,
but the monthly premium is often a
fraction of the regular plan.
It is not right for everybody. For some
healthy people, the premium savings
cover most of the deductible. And one
warning before anybody acts on a rate
letter, do not drop a supplement to join
an advantage plan just because of one
premium increase. If you leave and want
to come back later, in most states you
face those health questions again, and a
supplement you dropped at 72 may not be
offered to you at 76. Bernadette lives
in Sacramento. Her plan G went up 3
years in a row, and each time she paid
it because changing insurance at 74
sounded like a medical exam she might
fail.
By this year, she was paying $312
a month. Her neighbor down the hall, 2
years older, was paying $208 for plan G
with a different company. Same coverage,
line for line. And Bernadette had a
60-day window after every birthday to
make that exact switch without a single
health question. She had let four of
those windows pass. Add it up, the
difference between what she paid and
what she could have paid came to roughly
And nothing Bernadette did was careless.
A window opened every year on her
birthday and closed 60 days later. And
the one company that knew about it had
every reason to stay quiet. That is the
kind of rule the quiet rules was written
to put in front of you. The yearly
windows and the polite sentence in a
polite letter that sets what you will
pay for the next 12 months. If you want
it in your hands before your next
birthday instead of after it. Your copy
is at kevinexplains.shop.
The code on your screen goes straight
there, and the link is in the pinned
comment and in the description below. It
comes with a 7-day guarantee and a
refund if it is not what you hoped. For
4 years, the most expensive thing in
Bernadette's apartment was a birthday
card on the refrigerator, hanging right
above a thank you letter from her
insurance company. The fourth letter
looks like a scam, and that is exactly
why careful people ignore it. It is a
bill from Medicare itself, a plain
document titled Medicare premium bill
with a payment coupon at the bottom.
Most people never see one because their
premiums come straight out of their
Social Security,
but more and more people are on Medicare
before they ever claim Social Security
because they are waiting until 67 or 70
for a bigger check. Some people's check
is too small to cover the premium, and
some people owe the income surcharge on
their drug plan while they are not yet
collecting benefits. All of them get
billed directly, often every 3 months.
And that drug plan surcharge has a trap
of its own. It is not paid to your drug
plan. It is paid to Medicare.
If it goes unpaid long enough, Medicare
can remove you from your drug plan
entirely, and that gap can bring the
late penalty from the first letter along
with it. Here is what makes this one
dangerous. Scammers send fake Medicare
bills, too. So, careful people have
learned to ignore anything that asks for
money in Medicare's name. The real bill
gets ignored right along with the fakes.
If a real bill goes unpaid, the next one
carries the past due amount. And if a
bill marked delinquent is not paid in
full by its due date, your Medicare
coverage can end. Getting Part B back
after that can mean waiting for the
general enrollment period from January
through March, with coverage starting
the month after you sign up, and
possibly a permanent late penalty on
top. So, here is how to tell the real
one. It has your name and your Medicare
number on it. It tells you to pay
through your secure Medicare account
online, through your bank's own bill
pay, or by mailing the coupon to the
address printed on the bill. It will
never ask for a gift card, a wire
transfer, cryptocurrency, or a payment
over a phone call somebody else started.
If you are unsure, call Medicare at the
number printed on your own Medicare
card, never a number printed on the
letter itself. And the simplest fix is
free. Medicare Easy Pay takes the
premium straight from your bank account
every month, so the bill becomes a
statement instead of a deadline. If you
are delaying Social Security to get a
bigger check, set it up now. The day
your benefits do start, the premium
simply moves to a deduction from your
check. The fifth letter looks final, and
that is its disguise. It comes from
Social Security, often around the same
time as your raise letter, and it says,
in careful government language, that
based on your income, you will pay more
for Medicare next year. It is the
surcharge called IRMAA.
This year, it starts when income goes
for a single person or $218,000 for a
married couple. The first step alone
adds $81.20
a month to part B per person, plus a
separate surcharge on your drug plan.
Put those two together, and $1 over the
line costs about $1,148
for the year per person. For a married
couple, more than 2,200.
The lines for next year come out with
the new premiums in November. The letter
is called an initial determination.
Initial, which means it can be changed.
And there are three ways to change it
that most people never use. The first is
the one people have heard of. If your
income has dropped because of a
life-changing event, you file a form
called the SSA-44.
The events it accepts are marriage,
divorce, the death of a spouse, stopping
work, cutting back your work, losing a
pension, losing income-producing
property through a disaster or fraud,
and a settlement payment from a former
employer. It is one page. The second,
almost nobody knows. Next year's
surcharge is based on your 2025 tax
return. If that return was not in the
IRS system when Social Security ran the
numbers because you filed late or used
an extension, they may have used your
2024 return instead. If your income in
2025 was lower, you can ask for a new
determination by sending Social Security
a signed copy of that return. They will
not do it for you. You have to ask, and
the sooner you ask after that return is
filed, the better.
The third is a plain mistake. A return
counted twice, an amended return that
lowered your income, a figure that is
simply wrong. Those you can appeal, and
you generally have 60 days from the date
on the letter to do it. You can ask for
that review by phone, at a local office,
or on a form called the SSA-561.
Whichever way you choose, send copies,
keep the originals, and write down the
date you asked. Now, here is what does
not count, and this is where people burn
their 60 days. Selling a house, a large
Roth conversion, a big withdrawal from
an IRA to pay for a new roof, a one-time
gain from selling investments. None of
those is a life-changing event in Social
Security's eyes, no matter how much they
felt like one. If the high income was
real, the surcharge stands for that
year. The good news is that it lasts 1
year at a time. It is recalculated every
year from a newer return. So, a single
big year costs you 1 year of surcharge,
not the rest of your retirement. And if
you know a big year is coming, a home
sale, a large withdrawal, spreading it
over two tax years can sometimes keep
you under the line in both. Two traps
that create a big year without anybody
planning one. If you turn 73 this year,
your first required withdrawal from your
IRA can be delayed until the 1st of
April next year.
Many people take that delay because it
sounds like free time. But the second
year's withdrawal is still due by the
end of that same year. So, delaying the
first one puts two withdrawals on one
tax return. And 2 years later, that
return is the one Medicare reads.
And if you give to charity anyway, and
you are 70 and a half or older, you can
send money straight from your IRA to the
charity. It is called a qualified
charitable distribution, up to $111,000
this year. It counts toward your
required withdrawal, but it never shows
up as income, which means it never shows
up on the line Medicare uses to decide
your surcharge. Three smaller letters
before I show you what to do with all of
them. If you use Medicare's prescription
payment plan, the one that turns big
pharmacy bills into monthly payments
instead of paying everything at the
counter, it now generally renews on its
own each year as long as you stay in the
same drug plan. But if you switch drug
plans during open enrollment, it does
not follow you. You have to sign up
again with the new plan, or January's
first big prescription lands on you all
at once. If your Advantage plan gave you
a card loaded with money for groceries,
over-the-counter items, or dental work,
look for a reminder letter about your
balance. Those allowances generally do
not roll over. Whatever is left on the
card on the 31st of December usually
disappears. And if your plan is
shrinking or ending that benefit next
year, this is the last season to use it.
Plans have even been required to mail
some members a midyear notice about
benefits they have not used. And that
notice is very easy to mistake for an
advertisement. And if you help a parent
who gets extra help with drug costs,
watch the color of the paper.
Medicare mails those notices on colored
paper on purpose. A gray letter means
your parent will lose extra help next
year unless they apply again. A plain
white form from Social Security mailed
in the fall is a review of whether they
still qualify. And if it is not
returned, the help ends. An orange
letter means their co-pays are changing.
A blue letter means Medicare is about to
move them into a different drug plan
unless they pick one themselves. The
color is the message. Do not let it sit
in a pile. Now, here is what I would do
with every letter that comes between now
and the end of January. Not a list of
chores, three folders. The first folder
is forever. The credible coverage
letters, every year of them. Your Social
Security award letter. Your first
Medicare enrollment letter. Any letter
that says you were given a penalty or
that one was taken away. These are the
papers that prove something about your
past and nobody else is required to keep
them for you. When a question comes up
10 years from now, this folder is your
memory. The second folder is this tax
year. Your Social Security raise letter.
The tax form Social Security mails in
January called the SSA-1099.
Interest forms from the bank. And forms
from your retirement accounts. Any
surcharge letter. Keep these until your
return is filed and then for at least
three more years. The third folder is
the clock. Anything that starts a
deadline goes in here. A surcharge
letter you want to challenge, 60 days. A
hospital letter about your network, the
7th of December. A supplement rate
letter. Your birthday window if your
state has one. A Medicare bill marked
delinquent, the due date printed on it.
When a letter goes into this folder,
write its deadline on the outside of the
envelope in big thick numbers. Then,
look at that folder every Sunday until
it is empty. And one habit that ties all
three together, open government and
insurance mail on the day it arrives,
even if that means reading it standing
at the mailbox, and ask one question
before anything else. Does this letter
start a clock? If it does, it goes in
folder three tonight. Everything else
can wait for the weekend. Most of the
letters people regret are not
complicated. They're ordinary. A notice
from an old employer, a note from a
hospital, a premium change, a bill that
looked fake, a determination that looked
final. What makes them expensive is that
each one is written to be filed rather
than read, and each one quietly assumes
that if you say nothing, you agree.
If a letter arrives that does not fit
any of these, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com
and tell me what it says. Leave out your
Medicare number and anything else
private. I read every message, and the
strange letters are usually the ones a
lot of other people are getting, too.
None of these letters is hard to answer
once you know what it is. The trouble is
always the one you did not recognize in
time. If you would like to be the person
in your family who knows what each
envelope means before the deadline does,
The Quiet Rules is linked in the
description and in the pinned comment,
and the code is back on your screen.
Because the most expensive piece of
paper in most houses is not a bill. It
is a letter sitting under the fruit
bowl, still sealed while its 60 days run
out. I am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do
not forget to check The Quiet Rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: Born Before 1966? Social Security Has Bad News For All 4 Groups In 2027

segments.text: You are about to get a letter with your
new Social Security amount on it, and
the year you were born decides which
line on that page should worry you. Four
people born in four different decades
will open the same letter and read four
very different stories. Group one is the
youngest, born 1960 through 1965.
Group two, 1955 through 1959. Group
three, 1950 through 1954.
And group four, 1949 and earlier. Those
are the groups on your screen in that
exact order. Group one, there is a tax
break that two birth years in your own
group will never see. And next year, a
retirement age no American has ever
reached before.
Group two, one birthday in your group
next year is the last day waiting pays
you a single cent more.
Group three, the Medicare number on your
letter can be set by something you did
last year, and only a short list of
reasons will get it lowered. Group four,
an insurance company may already be
leaving your county, and for a few short
months you can buy coverage you might
never be approved for again. And one
rule reaches every group on the day a
husband or wife dies. It is not new, it
is simply the most misunderstood rule in
the whole system. And in some families,
it has been costing money every month
for years. Along the way, I will answer
six of the questions you left in the
comments. And at the end, every group
gets its own short list. Before we
start, put your group number in the
comments and one word after it, married,
widowed, divorced, or single.
Last time, hundreds of you typed your
birth year, and the questions you left
are the reason this video exists. Many
of you also told me the group numbers on
that picture ran in the opposite order
from the video. You were right, and
thank you. Today, every group I name
matches the picture on your screen.
If you were born in 1966 or later, stay
two. Almost everything I say to group
one applies to you, and I will point out
the one place it does not.
My name is Kevin. If you want each of
these changes explained the week it
lands, subscribe now. Everything today
comes from Social Security's own rules,
Medicare, the IRS, and the government's
own announcements. And every source is
listed in the description, so you can
check it.
I am not a financial advisor or a
lawyer, and this is education, not
advice about your own money. First, the
letter itself, because it reaches every
group. Social Security mails it in
December, and if you have an online
account, a copy often shows up in your
message center sooner.
Only three numbers on it really matter.
Your new amount before anything comes
out,
what comes out for Medicare,
and what actually lands in your bank.
If you have never set up that online
account, do it before December. Signing
in now takes login.gov or id.me, and it
is worth the 20 minutes. The size of the
raise is set by the inflation report
released on the 14th of October.
Most forecasts this fall put it in the
middle 3% range, which for the average
retired worker is somewhere around $70
to $75 more a month.
If it lands there, it is the biggest
raise since 2023.
Medicare's standard Part B premium is
projected to rise from about $203 a
month to about $210.
So, for most people, the raise covers
the Medicare increase many times over.
That part is good news.
Now, each group's line on that letter.
Group one, if you have not claimed yet,
you still got this raise. Every increase
since the year you turned 62 is quietly
added to the check you will start later.
If you did claim early and you are still
working, read the first number
carefully. Earn more than the yearly
limit, which is $24,480
this year, and Social Security holds
back $1 for every two you go over.
It usually collects that by holding back
whole checks at the start of the year.
So, for some of you, January is the
month nothing arrives. And a line for
every group because it starts with this
same letter.
If Social Security decides it paid you
too much for earnings or anything else,
you get an overpayment notice. Since
April of last year, the standard is that
it takes half of your check every month
until the debt is repaid. You do not
have to accept that.
Within 30 days of the notice, you can
ask for a smaller monthly amount on a
form called SSA-634
or ask to have the debt forgiven if it
was not your fault on SSA-632.
Filing inside those 30 days pauses the
collection while they decide.
Group two.
By the end of this month, every one of
you will have reached full retirement
age. From then on, there is no earnings
limit at all. Work as much as you like
and nothing is held back. Group three.
Your line is the Medicare number.
If your income two years ago was above
roughly $109,000
as a single person or $218,000
as a couple, Medicare adds a surcharge
and next year's surcharge is based on
your 2025 tax return.
Selling a house, a large IRA withdrawal,
a one-time bonus, all of it counts.
You can ask for a lower number only
after certain life changes like the
death of a husband or wife, a divorce,
or stopping work using a form called
SSA-44.
A one-time sale is not on that list and
whatever you do between now and the 31st
of December lands on your Medicare bill
Group four.
Your line is the Medicare number two for
a very different reason.
For many of you, that number may not
need to be on the letter at all because
your state may be willing to pay it.
I will show you exactly who qualifies in
a few minutes. But, the biggest Medicare
change this year is not on that letter.
It came in a separate envelope around
the 1st of October, and a lot of people
put it in a pile. Wilma is 79, a retired
cafeteria manager in Lubbock. Last fall,
her Medicare Advantage Plan mailed a
notice saying it would no longer be
offered in her county.
It looked like every other piece of plan
mail, so she set it on the hall table.
On the 1st of January, she landed in
Original Medicare with no supplement. In
April, she applied for one.
The company asked about her health, saw
her heart condition, and said no.
For 63 days after her plan ended, she
had a legal right to buy that supplement
with no health questions at all. She
found out on day 90. There were maybe 40
envelopes on that hall table.
One of them was worth more than the
other 39 put together, and nothing on
the outside told her which one.
That is the whole trouble with these
rules. They do not arrive with a warning
label. They arrive with a return
address.
The Quiet Rules is built to be that
label, so you know which envelope to
open first, and what to do inside the
window it gives you.
You will find it at kevinexplains.shop.
The QR code on your screen takes you
straight there, and the same link is in
the pinned comment and in the
description below.
Use it for 7 days, and if it is not
helping you, you get a refund.
Wilma's envelope is still on that table.
It is open now. 90 days late. So, here
is what this year's Medicare season
actually looks like. Open enrollment
runs from the 15th of October through
the 7th of December, and whatever you
choose starts on the 1st of January.
Some of you wrote that Advantage Plans
are going extinct. They are not.
Medicare says there will be about as
many plans next year as this year, and
the average Advantage premium is falling
to about $12 a month. But, plans are
pulling out of particular counties. One
of the biggest insurers, Humana, told
investors its exits for next year touch
about 600,000 members. If your plan sent
a notice that it is leaving, two things
happen. You get extra time through the
end of February to pick a new plan, and
you get the rare right Wilma missed.
From 60 days before your plan ends until
63 days after, a Medigap company has to
sell you certain supplement policies
without asking a single health question.
And if you missed December, there is one
more door. From the 1st of January
through the end of March, anyone in an
Advantage plan can make one switch to a
different Advantage plan or back to
original Medicare with a drug plan. That
second door does not come with a no
question supplement, though. Drug costs
move, too.
The most you can pay out of pocket in a
year for covered drugs rises from $2,100
to about $2,400, and the deductible can
go up to about $700.
On the other side, on the 1st of
January, Medicare's negotiated prices
start for 15 more drugs. Among them are
Ozempic, Trulicity, Janumet, Trajenta,
Linzess, Breo, Xtandi, and Ibrance.
If you take one of those, compare plans
with the new prices before you choose.
And if you want someone to sit with you
while you compare, every state has a
free Medicare counseling program called
SHIP.
Those counselors are not paid by any
insurance company, which is more than
you can say for most of the voices on
television this time of year.
Now, each group. Group one, those of you
born in 1961 turned 65 this year, and
those born in 1962 turn 65 next year.
Your sign-up window is 7 months long.
The 3 months before your birthday month,
the month itself, and the three after.
Miss it without other coverage from a
current job, and Part B carries a
penalty of 10% for every full year you
waited, added to your premium for as
long as you have it. If you join an
Advantage plan when you first get
Medicare, you also get a trial year.
Leave within the first 12 months and you
can buy a supplement with no health
questions. After 12 months that door
closes and if you skip drug coverage
because you take no medicines today,
Medicare adds a penalty later. 1% for
every month you went without. One of you
raised this in the comments and it is
worth repeating. A cheap plan you do not
need today can cost less than a penalty
you pay forever. If you are on
disability, you most likely have
Medicare already and open enrollment is
your chance to check your plan like
everyone else.
Group two.
Your job is the drug list.
Plans change which medicines they cover
every year and those changes were in the
notice that came in September.
Put your exact prescriptions into
Medicare's plan finder before the 7th of
December.
10 minutes there can be worth hundreds
of dollars.
And if you dropped a supplement within
the last year to try an advantage plan
for the first time, you can go back to
that same supplement if it is still sold
as long as you leave within 12 months.
Group three.
If you take expensive medicines, ask
your plan about something called the
Medicare prescription payment plan.
It does not lower the cap, but it
spreads what you owe across the year in
monthly bills instead of hitting you
with most of it in January and February.
It costs nothing to join. Group four,
this is the one I promised you.
If your income is modest, there are
programs called Medicare savings
programs run by your state that pay your
part B premium for you. That is more
than $2,400 a year that stays in your
pocket.
Under this year's federal standard, a
single person with income up to about
a month can qualify and a couple up to
about $2,455.
Many states also have a savings limit
about $9,950
for a single person, but more than a
dozen states have no savings test at
all.
If you qualify, you also get extra with
your drug plan automatically. That help
keeps most prescription co-pays to a few
dollars, and it erases the late penalty
I just mentioned for group one. You
apply through your state's Medicaid
office, and a great many people who
qualify have simply never applied. Apply
even if you think you are a little over.
Some states count income more generously
than the federal standard.
The second thing is about taxes, and it
starts with a promise. Last July, as
President Trump's big tax law was
passing, Social Security sent an email
to millions of people. It said the law
eliminates federal income taxes on
Social Security benefits for most
beneficiaries, and that nearly 90% would
no longer pay federal income tax on
their benefits.
A lot of you read that and took it at
its word.
Here is what the law actually did. It
did not touch the tax on Social Security
itself. It added a new deduction, up to
$6,000 a person for anyone 65 or older
for the tax years 2025 through 2028.
For many people with modest income, that
deduction is enough that they owe
nothing. For others, it is not. And the
formula that decides how much of your
Social Security is taxable is exactly
what it was before. That formula has a
quiet problem. The income lines it uses,
$25,000 for a single person and $32,000
for a couple, were set back in 1983 and
have never once been raised for
inflation.
Your raise goes up every year. Those
lines never move. So, every year, a
little more of your check slides over
the line and becomes taxable.
One thing to keep straight, because a
few of you asked, no matter how high
your income goes, no more than 85% of
your Social Security is ever taxable.
Nobody pays federal tax on the whole
check.
And on top of the federal rules, eight
states still tax Social Security in some
way.
Colorado, Connecticut, Minnesota,
Montana, New Mexico, Rhode Island, Utah,
and Vermont.
Most of them excuse people under certain
incomes, so check your own state's line.
Now the deduction group by group. To get
it for a given year, you have to be 65
by the end of that year. Married couples
have to file jointly, and it shrinks
once your income passes $75,000 single
or $150,000 for a couple by 6 cents for
every dollar over.
Group one is the split group. Born in
1960, you get all four years. Born in
1961, three years. 1962, two years.
1963, one year, 2028. And born in 1964
under the law as it is written today,
you get none of it.
There is one odd exception. If your
birthday is the 1st of January 1964,
the tax rules count you as 65 a day
early, and you get the last year. And if
you were born in 1966 or later, this is
the one place where you are not like
group one. You get none of it. Groups
two, three, and four, you qualify for
all four years as long as your income is
under those lines.
Group two. If you are still working, the
deduction lowers the tax on your wages,
too. So look at the W-4 at your job, or
you may be overpaying all year.
Group three. Your required IRA
withdrawals count toward the income line
where the deduction starts shrinking. So
a large extra withdrawal can cost you
part of it. Group four.
Many of you may not need to file at all.
If Social Security is your only income,
you very likely owe nothing.
But if tax was taken out of a pension or
an IRA payment, file anyway to get it
back.
For everyone who does file, your job is
the same.
Pull out the return you filed this
spring for 2025 and look for a page
called schedule 1A. That is where the
deduction lives. If it is not there and
you qualified, you can still fix it. The
IRS generally gives you 3 years to amend
a return and claim money you missed. If
paying a preparer is out of the
question, the IRS runs a free program
called Tax Counseling for the Elderly
and AARP volunteers do the same through
Tax-Aide. Both are free.
One more for married couples in every
group. The deduction is per person.
While you are both alive and filing
jointly, it can be $12,000.
In the year after one of you dies, the
survivor files as a single person and it
drops to six.
The tax lines for single people are
lower, too. So, the same income can
bring a bigger tax bill for the widow
starting the year after the funeral.
And one more line for every group. If
you have federal tax taken out of your
Social Security, you chose that on a
form called W-4V
After that email, some people called and
stopped it. Ray is 70, a retired
machinist outside Altoona, and a
widower.
When the email came, he called Social
Security and stopped the 12% he had
taken out for years.
His Social Security, his union pension,
and his IRA withdrawal stayed exactly
the same.
The deduction helped. It did not help
enough.
In April, he owed about $1,900
plus a penalty for paying too little
during the year.
And because nothing has come out of his
check all of this year, next April's
bill is on track to be about twice that.
Ray did nothing careless. He read an
official email from the agency that pays
his check, and he believed it.
That is the danger with rules that
change by headline. The headline moves
faster than the law, and the bill
arrives a year later.
The Quiet Rules is written from the
rules themselves, not from the
announcements about them, so you can
check a claim before you act on it.
It is at kevinexplains.shop.
Scan the QR code on your screen, or tap
the link in the pinned comment, or use
the one in the description.
7 days, start to finish, to decide.
If it is not for you, you get a refund.
Ray printed that email, by the way. It
sits on top of his tax folder now, right
above next April's estimate.
Before the part about husbands and
wives, six quick answers to questions
you left last time. The first,
one of you wrote that you paid in for 50
years, but only get credit for 35.
Here is how it really works.
Social Security figures your check from
your highest 35 years of earnings,
adjusted for wage growth.
Your other years were not thrown away.
Each one was compared, and any year
higher than one of your 35 replaced it.
And if you are still working while you
collect, and this year's earnings beat
one of your old years, Social Security
recalculates your check upward on its
own, every year.
It is worth opening your statement, and
making sure every year you worked
actually shows up. The second, two
questions about charity.
Can you give from a 401k instead of an
IRA?
Not directly. Those tax-free gifts
straight to a charity only work from an
IRA, and only after 70 and a half.
If your money is in a 401k, it has to be
moved into an IRA first. And no, nobody
should give away $20,000 to save tax on
6,000. That only makes sense if you were
already planning to give.
The third, several of you said you
receive SSI.
SSI is a separate program from Social
Security for people with very low income
and savings. You get the same raise, and
because New Year's Day falls on a Friday
this time, your January SSI payment
arrives on the 31st of December. That is
not a bonus. It is January's money, so
it has to last until February. The
fourth.
One of you is retiring overseas and
asked why you should keep paying for
Medicare you cannot use there.
That is your decision to make, but know
the price of coming back.
Drop part B. Return years later, and
that 10% for every full year without it
is added to your premium for life.
The fifth.
If you are on disability, the raise
applies to your check exactly as it does
to a retirement check, and at your full
retirement age, your disability check
becomes a retirement check
automatically.
I will come back to that in group one's
birthday part. The sixth, and the one
under almost every comment, is Social
Security going to run out? No. Here is
the actual number. Social Security's own
trustees reported in June that the
retirement funds reserve is expected to
run dry late in 2032.
After that, the taxes still coming in
would cover about 78% of scheduled
checks unless Congress acts first. That
cut would hit every group by the same
percentage. The youngest group would
simply live with it the longest. The
third thing is not a new law. It is a
change inside your household, and it is
the question I get asked more than any
other.
What happens to the checks when a
husband or a wife dies? Here is the rule
in one sentence. The household goes from
two checks to one, and the survivor
keeps the larger of the two, not both.
If your own check was the smaller one,
Social Security does not add them
together. It pays you the bigger amount,
made up partly of your own benefit, and
partly of the survivor benefit.
Several of you wrote that your own
Social Security was eliminated when your
husband died. It was not taken. It is
inside the bigger check,
but it means the household just lost the
smaller check completely and nothing
replaces it. How big the survivor check
is depends on two things: what the one
who died was entitled to and how old the
survivor is when that benefit starts.
You can start it as early as 60 at about
71 and 1/2% or wait for the full amount
at your survivor full retirement age.
You apply by phone or at an office. If
you claimed early, there is a cap on
what you can get, the larger of what he
was actually receiving or 82 and 1/2% of
his full amount. If he died before he

title: Banks Can Now Freeze Your Money After 65 For Months (Most Don’t Know)

segments.text: You ask for your own money, and nobody
says no. They say, "Wait."
And the length of that word just
changed.
If you are 65 or older, a bank or a
brokerage can now hold a payment you
asked for without a judge and without
your permission, and the law protects
them from being sued for it as long as
they acted in good faith.
In most states, these holds used to
start at 15 business days, about 3
weeks. This summer, one state gave its
banks up to 60 business days, about 3
months. And a federal regulator has
until the 24th of this month to act on a
rule that would let investment firms
hold a 65-year-old's money for up to 145
business days. That is roughly 7 months.
Your bills do not wait 7 months. Some of
them will not wait 30 days. So, this is
a briefing on four changes that landed
this year, almost none of them announced
to the people they affect. The first is
that clock. The second is that banks now
watch the money coming into your
account, not just the money going out.
So, the house you sell or the policy
that pays out can get stuck on the way
in. The third is a list of things a bank
can now refuse that are not money at
all, including your power of attorney
and your change of beneficiary. And the
fourth is the phone call. When a hold
lands, the bank is supposed to tell
somebody. In a lot of families, the
person you trust most is the one person
they are allowed to skip. Along the way,
I will show you the one bill that, if it
bounces during a long hold, you may
never be allowed to buy back. And I will
finish with the questions that can get a
hold lifted early. Before we go further,
answer one thing in the comments. Has

do not even remember being asked. And I
I to see if that holds true for you.
My name is Kevin. My job on this channel
is to tell you when a rule about your

If that is useful, subscribe now because
the federal decision I just mentioned
could land within the next 2 weeks and I
will cover it when it does. Today, I am
working from the regulators own filing,
the state laws themselves, the rulebook
of the network that moves money between
banks, Medicare's own guidance, and the
FBI's latest elder fraud report.
Every source is listed in the
description so you can check me. I am
not a lawyer or a financial advisor.
Hold rules differ from state to state
and this is education, not advice about
your own account. Start with Y65.
In these laws, your age is not a detail.
It is the switch.
FINRA, the organization that writes the
rules for brokerage firms, calls you a
specified adult the day you turn 65.
North Carolina's law says older adult,
65 or older.
Georgia's says eligible adult, same age.
Before that birthday, a firm needs a
reason to think something is wrong.
After it, the firm only needs a
reasonable belief that someone may be
taking advantage of you. Not proof, a
belief. And if it acts on that belief in

reason is real. The FBI's latest report

by people 60 and older last year,
roughly 60% more than the year before.
Every lawmaker who voted for these holds
had a number like that in front of them.
So the states moved.
The Federal Trade Commission's own chart
of these hold laws listed 24 states.
One count this year puts it at 33 or

Now the clock. Georgia's version took

days, then 15 more if the bank's review
still supports the concern, and a court
can stretch it further. That is 6 weeks
before anyone needs to see a judge.
North Carolina went further. Its
governor signed the change on the 7th of
July.
30 business days to start and up to 30
more.
60 business days is about 12 weeks on
the calendar, and it covers banks and
credit unions, not just investment
firms. Brokerage accounts, where a lot
of you keep an IRA, already run longer
than most people think.
FINRA's rule today allows 15 business
days, then 10 more, then 30 more once
the firm has reported the matter to a
state agency or a court.
55 business days in all, 11 weeks.
And it does not only stop withdrawals.
Since 2022, it can also stop a sell
order. In August, FINRA formally asked
the Securities and Exchange Commission
to approve a longer version.
It adds up to three more extensions of
30 business days each, which takes the

Each extra extension requires the firm
to have chased the agency it reported
to, heard nothing useful back, and still
believe exploitation is happening.
And if an agency or a court asks for
more time, the hold can run past even
that on a request that does not have to
be in writing.
The same filing creates a brand new
delay of up to 10 business days for any
customer 18 or older when the firm
suspects fraud.
FINRA first proposed five days. It
doubled that after the comments came in.
The SEC has until the 24th of October to
approve it, reject it, or open
proceedings. And it can push that date
to the 8th of December. Why so long?
FINRA's own survey answers that. More
than half of the firms that had placed

The hold is not the slow part. The slow

often by adult protective
And one national estimate puts the
typical investigation at about 5 weeks.
Your hold lasts as long as the slowest
office in that chain. This is how it

Glenda is 71 and lives outside
Asheville.
Her husband's memory care community
finally had a room.
She asked her brokerage to send $46,000
for the entrance fee to an account she

cried on every phone call.

signs at once.
A large sum, a new payee, and a customer
under strain.
The hold went on.
The community kept the room for 10 days.
On the 11th, it went to the next family
on the list.
The firm was right to be careful.
It was also wrong about Glenda.
Both are true, and the law only protects

in it. The one the firm writes in its
file in the first few minutes, and the

Glenda's second story was a strong one.
A diagnosis, a waiting list, a husband

Glenda still drives past that building.
The light in that window belongs to

change is the one almost nobody has
heard about because it lives inside the
rulebook of the network that moves money
between banks. That network is called
the ACH.
Your social security, your pension, your
tax refund, and most transfers between
your own accounts travel on it. The
group that writes its rules is called
NACHA, and this year it changed them.
Starting in March for the biggest banks,

credit union, the bank receiving a

For years, the watching happened mostly

And if it decides the payment is

Third, ask the sender how they plan to

When the bank knows what is coming, it

So, if you keep savings at a brokerage,

The third change.
When people hear the word hold, they

It may refuse instructions given under a

And it may stop a change of beneficiary.
In other words, your paperwork can be
