For survivor benefits born in 1960, it
is 66 and 8 months. Born in 1961, 66 and
10 months.
Born in 1962 or later, 67. You can start
a survivor benefit as early as 60 at
about 71 and 1/2% of the full amount.
And because survivor benefits and your
own retirement benefit can be taken one
after the other, many widows in this
group take one first and switch to the
other later.
Ask Social Security to show you both
numbers before you sign anything.
And if you remarry after 60, you keep
your right to that survivor benefit.
Now, the tax break with a birth year
cliff.
The senior deduction, up to $6,000 a
person, runs only from 2025 through 2028
under the law as written. To get it for
a given year, you have to be 65 by the
last day of that year.
Do the math by birth year. Born in 1962,
you get it for 2027 and 2028. Born in
1963, you get exactly 1 year, 2028.
you get none of it at all, unless
Congress extends it.
And remember the New Year's Day rule I
promised? The IRS has its own version.
It treats you as turning 65 on the day
before your birthday. So, if you were
born on the 1st of January 1964,
you count as 65 on the last day of 2028,
and you squeeze in for that one final
year. One day of birth, $6,000 of
deduction. If you are still working in
group four, there are two rules about
retirement savings that changed
recently.
If you are 60, 61, 62, or 63 during a
year, many workplace plans now let you
put in an extra catch-up amount. In
2026, that is up to $11,250
on top of the regular limit, instead of
the usual $8,000.
Your plan has to offer it, so ask. Once
you turn 64, it drops back.
And if you earned more than $150,000
in wages from your employer last year,
your catch-up money now has to go into
the Roth side of the plan. You pay the
tax now, not later. A lot of paychecks
already look different because of that
rule, and almost nobody was warned. And
if anyone in group four is buying health
insurance on the marketplace before
Medicare, there are two changes you need
to know about right now. The extra help
that kept premiums down for older buyers
expired at the start of this year.
That means the old cliff is back.
If your household income goes even $1
above four times the poverty line, the
help can disappear completely.
For a couple in their early 60s, that
can be thousands of dollars a year.
And here is the connection almost nobody
makes. For marketplace help, the income
they count includes your social
security, even the part that is not
taxed. So, claiming social security at
62 or 63 can be the very thing that
pushes a household over that line, and
the lost help can cost more than the
check brings in.
And the window to sign up for next year
is shorter.
On healthcare.gov, open enrollment runs
from the 1st of November to the 15th of
December. The January backstop is gone.
State-run marketplaces set their own
dates, but they all have to close by the
end of December. Now, something for
every group that uses Medicare drug
coverage, which is most of you. Next
year, the most you can pay out of pocket
for covered drugs in a Part D plan rises
The highest deductible a plan can charge
goes up to $700. And on the 1st of
January, Medicare's negotiated prices
kick in for 15 more drugs, including
Ozempic and Wegovy.
A lower negotiated price does not
automatically mean a lower copay for
you. That depends on your plan. And you
only get to change your plan until the
7th of December. If you take any brand
name drug, put it into the plan finder
on medicare.gov before then, every year,
because your plan is allowed to change
its list every January. And if you are
in a Medicare Advantage plan, and
January goes badly, there is a second
window. From the 1st of January to the
31st of March, you can make one switch
to a different Advantage plan or back to
original Medicare. One more rule reaches
every group at once, and it lands in
January. Your raise for 2027 is set by
the inflation report released on the
14th of October. Forecasters have been
expecting around 3 and 1/2%. Medicare
takes its share first, and the standard
Part B premium is projected to rise from
to about $209.50.
Your real raise is the line after
Medicare, not before it.
Your new amount usually shows up in your
online Social Security account in early
December before the paper letter
arrives. So, that is the fastest place
to check it. And there is one date that
is the same for every group.
The retirement trust fund, according to
Social Security's own trustees, runs
short in the last months of 2032.
At that point, everyone's check in all
four groups would be cut by about 22%
unless Congress acts.
For group one, that is in your 80s. For
group four, it lands right around the
age you were planning to claim. If you
are in group four and still deciding
when to claim, remember that any cut
would be a percentage. A larger check
before the cut is still a larger check
after it.
If your situation crosses two groups, a
husband in group two and a wife in group
four, or survivor benefit and your own
benefit and a pension all at once, write
to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
Tell me both birth years. That one
detail changes the answer more than
anything else you could send me. So,
here is what I would do this month, one
line per group. Group one, if you are
married, find out what age the higher
earner claimed at and what the survivor
will actually receive.
If you are 70 and a half or older and
you give to charity, give from the IRA.
Group two, if you were born in 1954,
decide now whether your first withdrawal
comes out in 2027 or doubles up in 2028.
Group three, if you are the lower
earner, look hard at whether you are
waiting on a spousal benefit that has
already stopped growing.
Group four, if you were born in 1962,
mark your Medicare window on the
calendar today. And if Cobra is your
plan, call Social Security about part B
before you do anything else.
And every group, check your drug plan
before the 7th of December. Your birth
year already sorted you into a group.
What you do with the rules of that group
is still up to you.
The quiet rules is where I would start,
and it is linked in the description and
pinned at the top of the comments.
I am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: The Truth About Trump’s Secret Plan For Your Social Security Check

segments.text: You have heard the promise so many times
you could finish the sentence for him.
Nobody is going to touch your social
security. So for the next 25 minutes,
set the promise aside and look only at
what has actually been done. Because
this week on the south lawn of the White
House, the president told reporters that
in his first term, he wanted social
security fully invested in the stock
market. And in his own words, quote, "I
wanted to do it so badly." Two days
before that, his treasury secretary, the
official the law names as managing
trustee of your trust fund, spoke at an
event in Pennsylvania and described a
new government investment account as the
way to build an ownership economy in
which all citizens are shareholders.
Last summer, that same man called those
same accounts, quote, a backdoor for
privatizing social security. Then he
took it back within hours. In June, the
speaker of the house said social
security has to be quote adjusted and
fixed. And then he said, quote, "We have
a plan to do that next year." And this
week, about 20 million people on
Medicare found $90 in their bank account
that none of them asked for. So, is
there a secret plan for your check? I'm
not going to tell you who to vote for,
and I'm not going to tell you what to
think of any politician. I am going to
do something more useful than that. I am
going to lay out 10 decisions. What was
said, what was done, and what each one
means for the money that lands in your
account. Then I will show you the one
date no president of either party has
managed to move. And somewhere in the
middle, there is a 15-minute task that
protects your check from the risk almost
nobody is talking about. Before I start,
give me one word in the comments. Plan
or no plan. That is all. Do you believe
there is a plan for social security that
has not been shown to the public yet? I
read every answer and I want to see
where you land before you hear the
evidence and after. My name is Kevin. I
read the rules so you do not have to. If
you want to hear about changes to your
check while there is still time to act
on them, subscribe now because the next
few months are going to be busy.
Everything in this video comes from the
Social Security trustees, the
Congressional Budget Office, the AY's
own Inspector General, court filings,
and the public statements of the people
involved. And every source is listed in
the description, so you can check it
yourself. I am not a financial adviser
or a lawyer. This is education and it is
not an endorsement of any party.
Decision one is the stock market and it
deserves the most time because it is the
one that would change the most. Start
with what was actually built. Since the
1st of October, the Treasury has
automatically opened what are called
Trump accounts for nearly 70 million
American children. Children born during
this term are eligible for a $1,000
starting deposit from the government.
Families can add up to $5,000 a year. At
18, the account becomes an IRA.
According to reports of Wednesday's
exchange, the president pointed to those
accounts as a version of what he had
wanted for Social Security. His Treasury
Secretary said this week that the
accounts will complement Social
Security, not replace it. And he
projected that a kindergartener starting
with a couple of thousand dollars could
reach 500,000 by retirement age. And the
Treasury has said in writing that Social
Security, quote, is a critical safety
net for Americans and always will be.
Those are the facts on both sides. Now,
here is what almost nobody explains when
the words stock market and social
security show up in the same sentence.
Those words can mean two completely
different things. The first version is
that the trust fund itself buys stocks
the way Canada's National Pension Fund
does. Senators from both parties have
floated versions of that idea. Your
check would still be your check. Today,
the trust funds hold about $2.5
trillion, and every dollar of it sits in
special government bonds that cannot
lose value. Supporters of putting some
of it in stocks point out that over long
stretches, stocks have earned far more
than those bonds. Critics point to years
like 2008 when the broad stock market
lost more than a third of its value, and
they ask who would decide which
companies the government owns. The
second version is very different. It is
personal accounts where a slice of each
worker's payroll tax goes into an
account in that worker's name. President
George W. Bush proposed exactly that in
2005. He wanted to let workers move up
to four percentage points of their
payroll tax into their own accounts. And
this is the part that matters to you.
Your check this month is not paid from
an account with your name on it. It is
paid mostly by the payroll taxes of
people working right now. Roughly nine
of every $10 the program takes in comes
from those taxes. So the moment a
worker's tax goes into his own account
instead, the money that was going to pay
your check has to come from somewhere
else. That gap has a name, the
transition cost. For the Bush plan,
estimates at the time ran into the
trillions of dollars. The plan promised
that anyone 55 or older would not be
touched. It never even got a vote in
Congress. And personal accounts carry a
risk the current system does not. Two
neighbors who retire a year apart could
end up with very different incomes just
because one of them retired the month
after a crash. So every serious version
of this idea so far has promised to
protect people who are already retired.
But a promise is not a law and nobody
has written that law yet. That is the
honest picture and it lands in an
uncomfortable place. Nobody watching
this will be in the room where that
decision gets made. What you do control
is the set of rules that already decides
how much of your check you actually keep
under any president. And most people do
not read those rules until a letter
arrives. I put those rules together in
one guide, the quiet rules for people
who would rather know first. You will
find it at kevinexplains.shop.
The QR code is on your screen right now.
The same link sits in the pinned comment
and again in the description below this
video. spend seven days with it and if
it is not worth keeping, you get a
refund. Now stay with me because the
next decision has a year attached to it
and that year is next year. Decision two
belongs to the speaker of the house, not
the president and it may matter most for
In an interview in early June, Speaker
Mike Johnson said that most federal
spending runs on what he called
autopilot. He named Medicare, Medicaid,
and Social Security. He said they quote
have to be adjusted and fixed. and he
said, quote, "We have a plan to do that
next year." After the backlash, he said
his words were taken out of context and
that his focus is waste, fraud, and
abuse. And to be fair, neither party's
ideas are truly secret. Members of the
largest group of House Republicans, the
Republican Study Committee, have
proposed in past budgets raising the
full retirement age for younger workers.
Many Democrats have proposed applying
the payroll tax to wages above $400,000,
far above today's cap of $184,500.
Both of those ideas are written down.
What has not been written down is the
plan for next year. So next year means
2027 after the midterm election on the
3rd of November. As of this recording,
no written plan has been released. Here
is the rule that matters more than any
interview, and it protects you no matter
who wins. Congress has a fast track for
budget bills called reconciliation. It
needs only a simple majority in the
Senate and it is how the big tax law
passed last summer. But the law that
governs that fasttrack specifically
forbids using it to change Social
Security. That means any real change to
your benefit needs 60 votes in the
Senate. In practice, that means votes
from both parties unless one party holds
60 seats, and neither does. No single
party can quietly rewrite your check on
a partyline vote. That is not a promise
from anyone. It is written into the
budget law itself. Decision three is the
tax law the president signed on the 4th
of July last year. It gave every
American 65 or older an extra deduction
of up to $6,000 a year or 12,000 for a
married couple when both qualify. It
starts shrinking above $75,000 of income
for a single person or 150,000 for a
couple. and it ends after the 2028 tax
year. The White House said that 88% of
seniors on Social Security would now pay
no tax on their benefits. The same White
House material acknowledged that about
64% were already paying none before the
law. Both numbers are real. And here is
the part the headlines skipped. The
deduction lowers your tax bill, but it
does not touch the formula that decides
how much of your Social Security counts
as taxable in the first place. That
formula still starts counting at $25,000
of income for a single person and 32,000
for a couple. Those starting points were
written into law in 1983 and they have
never once been raised for inflation. So
every year more retirees cross them. The
deduction is temporary. The thresholds
are permanent. Now the second thing
almost nobody connected. Part of the
income tax people pay on their benefits
does not go to the general treasury. it
flows straight back into the Social
Security and Medicare trust funds. So
when that tax goes down, the trust funds
take in less. In their 2026 report, the
trustees listed the 2025 tax legislation
as one of the reasons the program's long
range picture got worse this year. So
the same law put money in many seniors
pockets now and took a little runway off
the program later. For you, the
practical step is simple. If you are 65
or older, make sure whoever prepares
your return claims it because you get it
whether or not you itemize. It goes on a
new form called schedule 1A. Decision 4
is the agency that sends your check.
Early last year, the Social Security
Administration announced it would go
from about 57,000 employees down to a
target of 50,000, about 7,000 jobs. Then
in October of last year, the
commissioner Frank Bizignano was also
named chief executive of the IRS, a
position that did not exist before while
keeping his job at Social Security. One
man now runs the agency that pays you
and helps run the agency that taxes you.
Here is the fair version of what
happened next. The commissioner told
lawmakers this year that phone wait
times are down 75% and the agency is
serving 50% more people. and he says no
field offices have closed. His critics,
including a group of senators, say staff
were pulled from disability work to
answer phones, that each field office
worker now covers nearly 4,000
beneficiaries, and that the improvement
is a bottleneck being moved around. The
agency's own inspector general found
both things at once. Real progress on
the phones and continuing errors in how
benefits are handled. So, here is how
you get through, whichever side is
right. Call the national number early in
the morning, as close to 8 as you can,
local time. Avoid Mondays. Later in the
month is usually quieter than the first
week. If the wait is long, ask for a
call back instead of holding. If you
need a field office, call first and make
an appointment because walk-ins wait the
longest. And for anything that changes
your money, your address, your bank, or
your tax withholding, ask for a written
confirmation because a phone call leaves
no trail. Tell me in the comments if you
have called the agency this year and how
long you waited. I want to know if the
numbers match what people are living.
One more change from this agency because
it reaches people who did nothing wrong.
When Social Security decides it paid you
too much, it now takes half of your
monthly check by default until the money
is back. Before last spring, the default
was 10%.
And many overpayments start with the
AY's own mistake. If you ever get one of
those letters, the clock that matters is
30 days. If you ask for a
reconsideration or a waiver within 30
days, the agency generally waits to
collect until it decides. miss that
window and the withholding can start
while you are still arguing. Decision
five is your data and this is the one I
would act on this week. In 2025, a team
from the Department of Government
Efficiency was given access to Social
Security's records which hold the name,
birth date, and number of nearly every
living American. In January of this
year, a Justice Department court filing
corrected the AY's earlier statements.
It said members of that team had used a
third-party service that was not
approved for social security data. And
it said quote, "SA has not been able to
determine exactly what data were
shared." In March, the AY's inspector
general told Congress it was reviewing a
complaint about possible misuse of
Social Security data by a former member
of that team. News reports said the
complaint alleged he kept copies of
sensitive databases. The agency says
those allegations have been strongly
refuted. Nobody has shown your record
was misused.
But you do not need to wait for an
investigation to protect yourself. Meet
Merl, a retired dairy farmer outside
Oaklair, Wisconsin. Merl never set up an
online social security account. He did
not trust computers. Somebody else did
it for him using his name and number and
changed where his deposit goes. Two
monthly payments, about $3,900,
went to an account he had never seen. It
took him five months and three trips to
the field office to straighten it out.
If anything like that happens to you,
report it to the agency's inspector
general at oig.sa.gov
and keep a copy of the report. $3,900
because a stranger made the account that
Merurl never got around to making. No
speech fixes that. Agencies get cut,
records get copied, promises get made,
and the job of protecting your own check
has quietly landed on you. The quiet
rules is how I would hand that job to
someone I love with the rules laid out
before they cost anything. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
Hold your phone up to the code on your
screen or tap the link in the pinned
comment or use the one in the
description. Give it 7 days and if it
does not earn its place in your house,
you get a refund. And if you do not have
that online account yet, pause me after
this sentence and go make one. It takes
about 15 minutes. I will be right here.
Here is the full protection in the order
I would do it. First, create your own my
social security account at ssa.gov
so nobody else can create it for you.
Second, if you truly never want to go
online, call the agency and ask for what
it calls an electronic access block.
That shuts off online and automated
phone access to your record, including
your own. So, pick one or the other, not
both. Third, freeze your credit at all
three credit bureaus. It is free.
Fourth, ask the IRS for an identity
protection PIN. Anyone can get one now,
and it stops someone from filing a tax
return in your name. And fifth, once a
year, open your earnings record inside
that online account and read it line by
line. If you see wages from a job you
never had, someone is working under your
number and that can tangle your benefits
later. If you have already had something
strange happen, a letter you did not
expect, a deposit that moved, write to
me at kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com
and tell me what the letter says. I read
those myself. Decision six is the story
about dead people. In his address to
Congress in March of last year, the
president said government databases
listed millions of people between 100
and 150 years old and that money was
being paid to many of them. The AY's own
acting commissioner had already said
that those records were people with no
date of death on file, not people
receiving checks. An earlier inspector
general review found about 44,000 people
born in 1920 or earlier with no death
record who were still being paid. a real
problem, but 44,000 is not millions.
Then in April of last year, the agency
moved about 6,300 living immigrants into
its death records on purpose to cut off
their ability to work and bank here.
Whatever you think of that decision, it
shows you how powerful one database is.
When your name lands in it, your deposit
stops, and banks that check that list
can freeze your accounts, and mistakes
already happen. An older inspector
general audit found about 12,000 living
people a year were wrongly added to it.
If your deposit ever fails to arrive, do
not just wait a month. Go to a field
office in person with your photo ID. Ask
them to correct the record and ask for
that correction in writing to take to
your bank. Decision seven is
immigration. And I am only going to talk
about the social security math, not the
politics. The Institute on Taxation and
Economic Policy estimated that people
living here without legal status paid
about $25.7 billion into Social Security
in a single year, 2022. Most of them
cannot collect benefits on it. In their
2026 report, the trustees lowered their
assumption for immigration and they
counted that change as one of the
reasons the long range shortfall grew.
Supporters of tougher enforcement say
the program should not depend on that
money and they have a point about the
principle. The trustees are simply
counting the dollars. Fewer workers
paying in means less money for the
people being paid. Decision 8 is prices
and it shows up next week. On the 14th
of October, the government releases the
inflation number that sets your raise
for 2027. Forecasters are estimating
about 3.5% which would be around $73 a
month for the average retired worker.
Some analysts call it the Trump bump
because tariffs and the jump in fuel
prices after the fighting with Iran
pushed prices up this year. A bigger
raise sounds good and for your budget it
is, but the trustees assume smaller
raises when they made their forecast.
Bigger raises mean the trust fund pays
out faster than planned and Medicare
takes its share first. The standard part
B premium is $22.90
this year and it is projected to rise to
about $29.50 50s in 2027. When your new
benefit letter shows up in your online
account in December, look at the line
after Medicare, not before it. That is
your real raise. There is one protection
worth knowing. For most people who have
the premium taken straight out of their
check, a federal rule called hold
harmless says the part B increase cannot
be bigger than the dollar amount of the
raise. Your net check cannot go down
because of it. Decision nine is the $90.
Earlier this month, the president
announced a one-time payment of $90 to
offset the October Medicare premium. The
money comes from a fund Congress set up
years ago to improve traditional
Medicare called the Medicare Improvement
Fund. About $2 billion of it. More than
20 million people qualify. About 40
million on Part B do not. If you are in
a Medicare Advantage plan, you pay a
higher premium because of your income or
you get help with your premium through
Medicaid, you are left out. Most
payments arrived by direct deposit
around the 8th of October. Some people
will get a paper check from the Treasury
later this month. The AY's information
line for this payment opens on the 15th.
And please hear this. Nobody from the
government will call, text, or email you
asking for anything to release your $90.
Anyone who does is a thief.
And to put $90 in perspective, it covers
a little less than half of one month's
Part B premium. It is also close to the
size of next year's projected premium
increase added up over 12 months, about
$79. Decision 10 is the promise itself.
In the State of the Union this February,
the president said, quote, "Under this
administration, we will always protect
Social Security and Medicare." In that
same speech, he announced a federal
match for workers without a retirement
plan at their job up to $1,000 a year.
That match, called the savers match,
actually comes from a bipartisan law
passed in 2022, and it starts with
savings made in 2027. An executive order
this spring also created a government
website, trumpir.gov,
set to open on the 1st of January.
Supporters say a federal match and
simple accounts could finally help the
half of workers with no plan at their
job. Critics say none of it does
anything for people already counting on
a social security check. Both can be
true. What the speech did not address
was the date I promised to show you.
Here it is. The trustees, the officials
who report on social security every
year, say the retirement trust fund runs
dry in the last 3 months of 2032. At
that point, by law, the program can only
pay what comes in, about 78% of
scheduled benefits, a cut of about 22%
to everyone, including people who
retired decades ago. The Congressional
Budget Office looked at the same program
in September and came out worse. It says
mid 2032 in a cut of about 26%. Nobody
has pushed that date back, not under the
last president and not under this one.
If anything, it crept closer this year.
Now, make it your number. The average
retired worker gets about $2,071
a month. A 22% cut takes about $456 a
month off that check. A 26% cut takes
about $538. For a married couple with
two average checks, it is roughly $900
to $1,100 a month. And for a widow
living on one check of $1,800, a 22% cut
is about $396 a month, close to $4,800 a
year with no second check to lean on.
There is one lever Congress has pulled
before without much fuss. In 1994 and
again in 2015, it moved money between
the retirement fund and the disability
fund. If it does that again, the
Congressional Budget Office says the
combined funds last into 2033 and the
cut shrinks to about 23%. That buys a
year, not a fix. And if you have not
claimed yet, remember that any cut would
be a percentage. A bigger scheduled
check is still a bigger check after the
cut. Here is the one planning step I
would take, whichever party you trust.
Take your fixed bills, the ones that
arrive every month, no matter what, and
ask whether 78 cents of every social
security dollar would still cover them.
If the answer is yes, 2032 is a
headline. If the answer is no, you have
about six years to change that. And six
years is a long time if you start now.
The last time Congress actually fixed
Social Security was 1983. A Republican
president, Ronald Reagan, and a
Democratic speaker, Tip O'Neal, signed
off on a deal from a bipartisan
commission. That was 43 years ago. No
law since then has closed the gap. So,
here is my comment on the plan. Is there
a secret one? On the public record, I
cannot find a written plan from the
White House to close that gap. What I
can find is a president who says he will
always protect the program and also says
he wanted it in the stock market. a
treasury building investment accounts
for children and a speaker who says a
plan is coming next year. People who
support the administration will point to
a real tax cut for millions of seniors,
faster phone service, and the argument
that stocks have historically earned
more than the trust fund does. People
who oppose it will point to 7,000 lost
jobs, questions about your data, and a
tax law that took Runway off the
program. Both lists are made of real
facts. Where I land is this. Do not
judge any plan from either party by how
it sounds. Judge it by one question.
What happens in 2032 to the check of
someone who is already retired. Any
politician who cannot answer that in a
sentence does not have a plan yet,

and the labor department is honest about

only the plan administrator can tell you

treat a match as a lead, not a check.
One more limit worth knowing. You can
only search your own social security

a benefit. Many people file it away

your old tax records. On an old W2, box
12 with the letter D next to it means

before you call a single plan, here is

Divorced in 1997, never remarried. His
will left everything to his son and

The beneficiary form on file was from

decided by a form from 1989 that nobody

miss it and the penalty is about $1,500

Before you can move anything, you have

Plans use different months and different

for staying two extra months to be

missingmoney.com.
You never have to pay anyone to search

because every account you find and every

here is how I would use the rest of this

her household income has already fallen

writing for the coming year. keep it. If

from your online account today and it

on dates, it helps to know what moves
these projections because every year the

their assumption for how many children
American families will have to about
1.75 per woman. They lowered their

It is simply why the date can move a few

to the next. What it has not done in a

four is sorting your income into what is
in this fund and what is not because a
surprising amount of it is not.
Supplemental security income. The
needsbased program known as SSI is paid

So, if the Social Security check were

and are not part of this cut. A pension
from a former employer, a military or
federal civil service pension, veterans
disability compensation, an annuity you

draw on the Social Security trust fund.
One group should know the opposite. If

after the law that ended the two offsets
in January of 2025, that larger check is

people. A smaller check does not only

would quietly reopen questions that may

who are just over a line today would

it is taxable. None of that replaces the

only the people who apply for those

is the second clock, and I have almost
never seen anyone put it next to the

According to Medicare's trustees, that
fund runs out of reserves in the spring
of 2033, a few months after the

costs. Now, this does not work like your
social security check. You do not get a

health agencies, and Medicare Advantage
plans are paid partly out of this fund
as well. The law does not spell out

decade away, many times since it was
created. And every time, Congress acted
before the money ran out. But think
about what this calendar actually means.
Somewhere around the winter of 2032,
Congress would be facing two shortfalls
in the two programs most people over 65
depend on most within months of each
other. Two very large bills on the same
desk at the same time. Nobody can tell
you today what a deal like that would

know both dates and not just one. Now,
let me give you a way to see this cut
that changes how people react to it.
Turn it into savings. Social Security is
income that rises with inflation and
lasts as long as you do. Buying that
kind of income with your own money is
expensive. By my own rough arithmetic,
replacing $100 a month of
inflationadjusted income for 20 years
takes something like $20,000 of savings,
depending on interest rates and your
age. So, take your own cut. On the
average check, 22% is about $456 a
month. That is a little over 4 and a
half of those $100 blocks. Something
like $90,000 of savings for one person
to replace it for 20 years. For a
couple, both on average checks, close to
twice that. Even on a $1,400 check, the
cut is about $38 a month, which works
out to something like $60,000 of
savings. And because the cut is still
some years away, the amount you would
need to set aside today is a little
smaller, but only by something like an
eighth. Put it that way, and it stops
sounding like a headline. It is a
decision sitting in Washington about
whether a household's retirement loses
the equivalent of a sizable savings
account for many couples, a six-f
figureure one. And that is exactly why
this subject draws salesmen. Burl is 71,
a retired [clears throat] plumber near
Tulsa, Oklahoma. Two years ago, a
postcard invited him and his wife to a
free steak dinner. The title of the talk
was, "Social Security is running out.
Protect yourself now." The man at the
front put the trustes date on a big
screen and said the only safe move was
to put their retirement savings into a
product that would replace the coming
cut. That same week, at a follow-up
meeting in a rented office, Burl moved
from his IRA into an annuity. What the
man mentioned once quickly was the
surrender schedule. For 10 years, taking
out more than a small amount each year
would cost a penalty starting at about
10%. This summer, they decided to sell
the house and buy a smaller one near
their daughter, and they needed most of
that money to do it. Getting to their
own money cost them about $17,000 in
surrender charges before taxes. All to
protect them from a cut that has not
happened. When federal and state
securities regulators examined these
free meal seminars, they found that
every single one they looked at was a
sales presentation, and half made
exaggerated or misleading claims. An
annuity can be a perfectly reasonable
thing for the right person. What Burl
bought that night was not really a
product. It was a fear with a 10-year
lock on it. $17,000
paid to reach money that was already
his. Nobody at that dinner was going to
hand Burl the three questions that would
have stopped it. How long is my money
locked up? What does it cost to take it
out early? And who is paid how much if I
sign tonight? The quiet rules puts
questions like those in your hands
before the postcard arrives so that the
next time somebody uses a real
government date to sell you something,
you already know what to ask and you
know you are allowed to go home and
think. It is at kevinexplains.shop.
The code is on your screen right now.
The link is the first thing in the
pinned comment and it is in the
description underneath. You have 7 days
to look through it and if it is not for
you, you get a refund. Burl kept the
postcard. It is on his refrigerator
under a magnet where he sees it every
time he reaches for the milk. So, if
this cut is the equivalent of a large
account, what do careful people with
savings actually do about it? Not one
dramatic move, a few quiet ones. The
first is to name the money. Decide now
which part of your savings, if any,
would cover the gap and roughly how
much. Most people never do this, so the
cut stays a vague fear instead of a
figure with an account attached to it.
If your price tag came to $90,000, you
might decide that one particular account
is the one that answers for it. You do
not have to move anything. You simply
stop treating that money as spare. The
second is timing. If you want money that
arrives when the cut would, the Treasury
sells inflationprotected securities
called TIPS, which come due on set
dates. A latter of them maturing in the
years after 2032, lines up the money
with the risk, and the principle is
adjusted for inflation along the way.
Ibonds are another inflationprotected
option, limited to $10,000 per person
per year, and the fixed rate on new ones
resets on the 1st of November. Neither
of these is a recommendation for you.
They are simply the tools that were
built for this kind of problem. The
third applies only if you have not
claimed yet. Waiting raises your check
for life and the cut, if it comes, is a
percentage of a larger number. For
married couples, the higher earnner's
age at claiming also sets the survivor
check. And as you saw with Leola, that
is the check that really decides how the
last years go. Two details there that
very few couples know. If the higher
earner claims early, the survivor's
check can be permanently smaller as
well, although the law keeps it from
falling below about 82 1.5% of that
spouse's full benefit. And if the
survivor starts the survivor benefit
before her own full retirement age, it
is reduced too to as low as about 71 12%
at 60. Those reductions happen to people
every year with no trust fund involved
at all, and the cut would come on top of
them. And the fourth is what not to do.
Do not pay a certain cost today to avoid
an uncertain one later. Cashing out a
large IRA to get ahead of this means
taxes this year and possibly a Medicare
sir charge 2 years from now. Claiming
early locks in a smaller check for life
and any cut lands on top of it. Locking
savings into a long surrender period
means paying to reach your own money.
Every one of those costs is guaranteed.
The cut is not. And one more because it
rises every time this subject is in the
news. The impostor calls. Somebody
claiming to be from Social Security says
your benefit is about to be cut or
suspended and that you can protect it by
moving money, buying gift cards, or
confirming your details. Social
Security's own inspector general warns
that the agency will never threaten you,
never demand an immediate payment, and
never ask for gift cards, a wire
transfer, or cryptocurrency. Hang up.
Look up the agency's number yourself and
call it. One question comes up every
time I cover this. What would the first
month actually look like? The plain
truth is that the law does not say
social security cannot borrow and it
cannot legally pay out more than it has.
The trustees and the budget office both
assume checks would simply be reduced
across the board to whatever incoming
revenue can cover. And that is how
almost everyone describes it. But the
Congressional Research Service has
pointed out that the law does not spell
out the method. And one possibility is
that full checks would be paid late
whenever enough money had come in.
Either way, nobody in Washington wants
to find out. And that is the main reason
every past shortfall has been dealt with
before the date arrived. Now, what is
Washington actually doing? More than the
news suggests and less than you would
want. In July, a bipartisan group of
senators led by two Democrats and two
Republicans introduced a bill called the
Promise Act. It does not change
anybody's benefit. What it does is force
a process. It would have the Social
Security Advisory Board gather public
input and send Congress draft
legislation and then require both
chambers to take up a Social Security
bill on a set timetable with
three-fifths of the Senate needed to
pass it. In the House, a bipartisan pair
has a separate bill to create a
commission. Neither one has passed. And
here is the date that matters more than
either bill. The midterm elections are
on the 3rd of November. Every seat in
the House and about a third of the
Senate is on the ballot, which makes
this one of the few stretches when they
are actually listening. So, here is a
single question that cuts through every
speech and it does not ask anybody to
pick a side. If you are elected, will
you vote for a plan that stops the
automatic cut for people already
collecting before 2032? Yes or no? Write
down the answer you get. And if you want
to check what a sitting member has done
rather than said, you can look up any
bill on congress.gov and see the list of
co-sponsors. A name on a bill is worth
more than a promise at a podium. After
the election, there are three things
worth watching. whether the new Congress
brings the Promise Act or a commission
bill back because any bill that is not
passed expires when this Congress ends
in January, whether either party puts a
specific social security plan into its
first budget, and the next trustees
report, which tells you whether the date
moved again. When any of those happens,
I will cover what it means for people
already collecting. So, here is your
page, five lines. Line one, your check
and your deposit and what the deposit
becomes at 22% and at 26. Line two, if
you are married, the survivor deposit at
both percentages set beside what the two
of you receive today. Line three, the
price tag, your monthly cut divided by
100 times roughly 20,000. Line four, the
income lines you are close to, the
Medicare savings programs, extra help,
your county's senior property tax rules.
Line five, the answer you got to that
one question, and who gave it to you.
For line one, use the December notice or
the benefit verification letter from
your online account. For line two, call
Social Security and ask what the
survivor benefit would be on your
spouse's record. They will tell you, but
only if you ask. And if you were married
for at least 10 years and later
divorced, you may be entitled to a
survivor benefit on your former spouse's
record, even if they remarried. That
belongs on line two as well. One sheet
of paper.
Most people who fill it in find that
line two is the number nobody ever
showed them. And if your situation does
not fit neatly on that page, a pension
you are not sure how to count, a
survivor benefit you suspect was
calculated wrong, an annuity somebody is
pressing you to buy, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com
and tell me what is going on. I read
everyone myself. In a busy week, it can
take a few days, but I do answer. And a
good number of these videos began with
exactly that kind of email. Where do I
come down on all of this? I do not
believe the full cut is ever allowed to
land on people already collecting. Every
incentive in Washington runs against it.
And in 1983, with only months to spare,
they did not let it happen. But the date
has sat in the early 2030s for years
now, while the hole behind it kept
getting deeper. And every year of
waiting means the same gap has to be
closed in less time. So the outcome I
worry about is not the 22%. It is the
version in between. A deal struck late
in a hurry with two trust funds on the
table at once where the pain is placed
on whoever is least organized to object.
People who know their own numbers are

something. People who only know the

an ordinary morning standing at the
counter with the bank app open reading a
