title: 3 New Rules Quietly Taking Money From Your Check Starting October

segments.text: Your social security check is about to
be squeezed from three directions at
once. And the first one is being handed
to you as good news. You have probably
already heard it. Social Security is not
taxed anymore. It was on the news. It
came in an email from the government
itself. And a lot of careful people did
the sensible thing with that news. They
stopped having tax taken out of their
check. That is the first change and it
is going to show up as a bill in April
that nobody warned them about. The
second one reaches backward. a search
charge on your Medicare that is being
decided right now, this month, from
money you made last year. And the letter
telling you about it arrives just in
time for Christmas. And the third one is
the quietest and the most expensive of
all. It comes from the same law
President Trump signed last July. It
starts counting in October. And for one
family in this country after another, it
will turn a single late phone call into
a bill of nearly $10,000.
Two of these three can be stopped with
the right piece of paper. And one of
them has a door that is open right now
and closes for good on New Year's Day.
Before this video is over, I will tell
you which one and exactly what to do
while that door is still open. Now, do
me one small favor first. In the
comments, tell me which of these you had
already heard about. Just type 1, 2, or
three, or none. That tells me how far
the news has actually reached, and I
read them. My name is Kevin. I read the
rules so you do not have to. And if you
want to hear about the next one of these
while there is still time to act,
subscribe now. And the honest note, I am
not a financial adviser or a tax
preparer. And this is education, not
advice about your own money. Tax rules
and dollar limits change, so check the
current figures before you act. The
first change, the tax break that
everybody heard about and almost nobody
read. Last July, the big tax and
spending law President Trump signed was
sold loudly as the end of taxes on
Social Security. The Social Security
Administration itself sent an email to
millions of people saying that nearly
nine and 10 beneficiaries would no
longer pay federal income tax on their
benefits. A former deputy commissioner
of the agency called that email
misinformation. And I think he was right
because here is what the law actually
did. It did not change a single word of
the rules that decide how much of your
social security is taxable. Those rules
are exactly the same as they were
before. What it did was create a new
deduction for people 65 and older, up to
$6,000 each, up to 12,000 for a married
couple who are both 65. It shrinks once
your income passes $75,000 for a single
person or $150,000 for a couple. and it
disappears completely at 175,000 single
or 250,000 for a couple. And it is
temporary. It runs for four tax years,
2025 through 2028, and then it is gone
unless Congress extends it. Now, a
deduction is not nothing. For a lot of
middle-income retirees, it is real
money, somewhere in the hundreds of
dollars a year, sometimes more than a
thousand. I am not going to pretend it
is a trick, but a deduction and tax-free
are two very different animals. And the
difference is where people are getting
hurt. Here is the first difference. A
deduction lowers your taxable income. It
does not lower the income figure the
government uses for almost everything
else. That figure is called your
adjusted gross income. And this
deduction sits below it. So the formula
that decides whether up to 85% of your
social security is taxable does not
change at all. The income lines in that
formula, $25,000 for a single person and
$32,000 for a couple, are the same lines
they have been since the 1980s. They
have never been adjusted for inflation,
and this law did not touch them. And the
income figure Medicare uses to decide
whether you pay a search charge does not
change either. Hold on to that. It is
the bridge to the second change. Here is
the second difference. If your only
income is social security or close to
it, you probably were not paying federal
income tax on your benefits in the first
place. So the deduction saves you
nothing because there was nothing to
save. The people it actually helps are
in the middle. Some pension, some
withdrawals from an IRA, some interest.
Those are exactly the people who had tax
withheld from their checks. And those
are the people who heard the headline
and stopped. Three small details that
decide how much of it you actually get.
First, the shrinking is gradual. For
every $1,000 of income above the line,
you lose $60 of the deduction. So, a
single person with an income of $100,000
is $25,000 over the line loses $1,500 of
it and keeps a deduction of $4,500.
Second, you get it whether you itemize
or take the standard deduction. So,
nobody has to change how they file. And
third, it goes by each person's age at
the end of the year. If you are 66 and
your wife turns 65 in January, only one
of you gets it this year and the joint
amount is 6,000, not 12. Raleigh did
exactly that. 70, a retired lineman for
the power company in Eastern Tennessee
with a small pension and a required
withdrawal from his IRA every December.
For years, he had 10% withheld from his
social security, so he never owed in
April. In August of last year, after
hearing that Social Security was no
longer taxed, he called and cancelled
the withholding. He thought he was
getting a raise. When he filed this
spring, the new deduction had helped. It
had just not helped nearly enough. He
still owed about $1,800 plus a small
penalty for not paying enough during the
year. Nothing he did was reckless. He
simply acted on the headline instead of
the law. So, here's what I would do this
month. If you or your preparer filed an
extension on last year's return, the
deadline is the 15th of October, make
sure that deduction is actually on it
because it is new and it is easy to
miss. It goes on a new schedule attached
to the return and you need a valid
social security number. And if you are
married, you must file jointly to get
it. Then look at this year. If you
stopped your withholding because of the
headline, you still have a few checks
left in this year to catch up. The form
is called the W4V.
You can choose to have 7, 10, 12, or 22%
withheld from each social security
payment, and you can change it whenever
you like. It takes a few weeks to kick
in, which is exactly why October is the
time to do it, and January is too late.
Raleigh did not need more news. He had
plenty of news. What he needed was one
calm place to check a headline against
the actual rule before he picked up the
phone and changed something. That is why
I wrote the quiet rules. So the next
time a headline promises you something,
you can open a page and see what the law
really says in plain words before you
act on it. It is at kevinexplains.shop.
Point your phone camera at the code on
your screen or tap the first link in the
pinned comment. It is in the
description, too. Keep it for 7 days. If
it has not been worth it by then, you
can get a refund and you keep whatever
you learned. Because the other way to
find this out is Righy's way. At the
preparers's desk in April, watching her
turn the screen toward him and seeing a
number he had been told would never
exist again. The second change. And for
this one, I need you to think back a
full year because that is where it
starts. Medicare has a sir charge for
people it decides can afford to pay
more. The official name is the income
related monthly adjustment amount and
most people just call it Irma from its
initials. If your income is over a
certain line, you pay more for part B
and more for your drug coverage and the
extra comes straight out of your social
security check every month for the whole
year. Here is the part that catches
people. Medicare does not look at what
you earn now. It looks at your tax
return from 2 years earlier. So, the
search charge you pay in 2027 is set by
your income in 2025. And the reason this
is an October story is that 2025 returns
are being finished right now. The last
extended returns are due on the 15th of
October. After that, the numbers flow
from the IRS to Social Security. And
late in the year, often in November or
December, the letters go out right next
to the letter telling you about your
raise. And 2025 was exactly the kind of
year that pushes careful people over the
line. Think about what happened in it.
The stock market had a strong year, and
a lot of people finally sold shares they
had been sitting on for a decade. Some
people took a bigger withdrawal from
their IRA for a new roof or a car. Some
did what advisers love to recommend and
converted part of a traditional IRA to a
WTH. Some sold a rental property or a
second home. Every one of those can be
perfectly sensible, and every one of
them adds to the income figure Medicare
reads. Now, here's where the first
change and the second change meet. That
new senior deduction does not lower the
number Medicare uses. Neither does the
bigger deduction for state and local
taxes in the same law. They both come
off below the line. Medicare looks above
it. And Medicare adds something back
that surprises people with conservative
portfolios. Interest from municipal
bonds, the tax-free kind, is not taxed,
but it is counted for this search
charge. So, a retiree who carefully
built a tax-free bond portfolio to keep
their taxes low can still find that
interest pushing them into the search
charge. Let me give you the numbers as
they stand for this year because next
year's lines will only move up slightly
with inflation when they are announced.
For a single person, the search charge
starts once that income figure passes
For a married couple filing jointly,
at the first step. Part B goes from
a month to $28410.
And your drug coverage picks up $14.50
50 on top. That is about $95 a month per
person. For a married couple both paying
it, that is roughly $2,300
a year. And the steps keep climbing. At
the highest levels, Part B alone is more
than $680 a month. And this is the part
I find hardest to defend. It is not a
slope. It is a cliff. If your income is
$1 over the line, you pay the full
search charge for that step, not $1
more. the whole step for the whole year.
I cannot think of another part of the
tax system where $1 of income can cost
you more than a thousand. I think it is
bad design and I think it survives
because the people it hits rarely know
it exists until the letter arrives and
there is a quieter version of the same
cliff for married couples who file
separately. If you live together and
file separate returns, the steps
collapse. Your sir charge can jump from
nothing straight to one of the highest
levels once your income passes $19,000.
Some couples file separately for good
reasons. Just make sure somebody has
done this arithmetic first. Marietta
found her cliff the expensive way. 68, a
retired court stenographer in suburban
Atlanta, and her husband, 71. Last year,
they sold shares they had bought back in
the 1990s to help their daughter with a
down payment. It was one sale, one time.
It pushed their joint income about
$6,000 over the first line. When the
letter came, both of them were paying
the search charge for the whole year,
about $2,300
to help a daughter with a house. And
because selling stock is not one of the
life events Medicare accepts, they had
no way to ask for it back. That point
matters. So, let me be precise about
what you can do and what you cannot.
There is a form called the SSA44.
It asks Social Security to use a more
recent year because your income has
dropped for a reason on its list. The
list is specific. You stopped working or
cut your hours. You married, divorced,
or lost your spouse. You lost a pension.
You lost income producing property
through no choice of your own, like a
disaster or a theft. Selling your house
is not on the list. Selling stock is not
on the list. Taking a big IRA withdrawal
is not on the list. A lot of videos tell
people to file that form after a home
sale and it simply does not work that
way. But there are two other doors
people miss. The first is a mistake in
the numbers. If Social Security used the
wrong return or the IRS data is wrong or
you later filed an amended return that
lowered your income, you can ask them to
redo the calculation with the correct
figures. Send a copy of the amended
return and the IRS confirmation. The
second is timing. If your search charge
was set using an older return because
your newest one was not available yet,
you can ask them to use the newer one
once it is filed. Every year there are
people paying a sir charge based on a
year that no longer reflects their life.
And the only reason is that nobody
asked. And for widows and widowers, one
detail that is almost never explained.
In the year your spouse dies, you can
usually still file a joint return. The
single person line comes the following
year and that is when the search charge
tends to appear sometimes on the very
same income. The death of a spouse is on
the list. So if a search charge shows up
after that loss, that form is exactly
the right tool and you should file it
the week the letter arrives. A few more
facts about this search charge that
people tend to learn one at a time,
usually the hard way. It is recalculated
every single year. One unusual year
means one year of search charge, not a
life sentence. So do not rearrange your
whole retirement around a single letter.
It applies to people in Medicare
Advantage plans too. You still pay the
part B premium. So you still pay the
part B sir charge. And if your plan
includes drug coverage, the drug
searchcharge comes along with it. It is
charged per person. If your spouse is
not on Medicare yet, only you pay it,
even though it was your joint income
that triggered it. And if you disagree
with the letter, you have 60 days from
the date you receive it to ask for a
reconsideration. So, do not put it in a
drawer until after the holidays. And
when the letter does come, check it
before you argue with it. It will name
the tax year it used and the income
figure it took from that year. Put it
next to your own return. Is it the right
year? Is it the right number? Did it
count a joint return when you had
already lost your spouse? A surprising
number of these letters are built on the
wrong year simply because the newest
return was not available when the
calculation ran. that takes five minutes
to check and it is the cheapest five
minutes in this whole video. And one
trap that is aimed squarely at people in
their early 70s. Your first required
withdrawal from a traditional IRA can be
delayed until the 1st of April of the
following year. A lot of people take
that delay because it sounds like free
time, but the second year's withdrawal
is still due by the 31st of December of
that same year. So, you end up taking
two withdrawals in one tax year. two
years of income stacked into one return.
And that is one of the most common ways
a perfectly ordinary retiree steps over
a sir charge line without ever meaning
to. If you are approaching your first
required withdrawal, ask whoever does
your taxes whether taking it this year
is cheaper than delaying it. For many
people, it is. Now, let me give you the
part that actually saves money because
it is about this year, not last year.
Your income in 2026 sets your search
charge in 2028 and 2026 still has three
months left. If you are close to a line,
those three months matter. Look at last
year's return and find the line for
adjusted gross income. Then add any
tax-free interest. That is roughly the
number Medicare reads. If you are within
a few thousand dollars of a step, there
are real moves still available before
the 31st of December. If you are 70 and
a half or older and you give to charity,
a qualified charitable distribution sent
straight from your IRA to the charity
counts toward your required withdrawal
and never shows up in that income figure
at all. This year, you can send up to
that way. If you are planning a Roth
conversion, you can size it to stop just
under a line instead of just over it. If
you have investments that have lost
value, selling some of them can offset
gains you have already taken. None of
these are exotic. They just have to
happen before the calendar runs out.
for a year when they help their daughter
buy a house. That is what a single sale
cost Marietta and her husband. And the
only thing that would have changed it
was one question asked before the sale
instead of after. Where is the line? And
how close are we to it? That is the kind
of question the quiet rules is built
around, not investment tips, the quiet
thresholds, the forms that work and the
ones that do not, and the deadlines that
decide which year a dollar lands in. You
can find it at kevvenexplains.shop
or scan the square code on your screen
or use the link pinned at the top of the
comments. It is in the description as
well. You have 7 days to go through it
and if it does not earn its place, you
get a refund. Simple as that. Because
the other version of this story is
Marietta opening that letter at
Christmas, reading that both of them
will pay more every month for a whole
year and realizing it was decided by a
sale they made in the spring. The third
change, the one I said starts counting
in October. And I want to start with
something almost everybody believes
about Medicare because this whole change
is built on top of that belief. Most
people think Medicare pays for a nursing
home. It does not. Not in the way people
imagine. Medicare pays for a short stay
in what is called a skilled nursing
facility for rehabilitation after you
have been formally admitted to a
hospital for at least 3 days. Not kept
overnight for observation. Admitted.
Many people spend three nights in a
hospital bed on observation status and
never know it did not count. Two
protections exist here that almost
nobody uses. If you are kept in the
hospital under observation for more than
a day, the hospital has to give you a
written notice saying so. Read it
because it tells you the stay may not
count. And since early last year, people
in original Medicare who are formally
admitted and then switch to observation
by the hospital, get a written notice of
that change and the right to a fast
appeal. If you have been there 3 days or
more, that appeal can decide whether
Medicare pays for the rehab stay that
comes next. So, the question to ask at
the bedside every day is this one. Is my
mother admitted or is she under
observation? Ask the nurse, ask the case
manager, and write down the answer and
the name of whoever gave it. If you do
qualify, Medicare covers the first 20
days in full. From day 21, you pay $217
a day this year, and the coverage ends
the moment you stop needing skilled
care, which is often long before the
100th day. What Medicare never pays for
is the long stay. Help with bathing,
dressing, eating, the care most people
actually need in a nursing home for
months or years. That is paid for by
you. By long-term care insurance if you
have it, or by Medicaid once your
savings have been spent down to your
state's limit. And that is where the
change comes in. For more than 50 years,
Medicaid has been able to reach
backward. If you applied in a given
month and you would have qualified
earlier, Medicaid could pay your medical
bills for up to three months before the
month you applied. That rule has saved
countless families because nobody
applies for Medicaid on the day their
mother moves into a nursing home. They
are dealing with the hospital, the
paperwork, the house, the grief. They
apply weeks later, sometimes months
later, often after Medicare's rehab
coverage runs out, and the facility's
business office finally tells them how
much they owe. The law signed last July
cuts that reach for applications made on
or after the 1st of January. Medicaid
for people who are aged, blind, or
disabled can only reach back 2 months,
not three. For working age adults who
get Medicaid through their state's
expansion, only one month. A few states
had already narrowed it on their own.
Now it is narrower everywhere. Now, let
me show you why this is an October
problem. The national median cost of a
shared room in a nursing home is now
about $315 a day. Call it $9,600
a month. Imagine somebody's care starts
to be paid privately in October. If the
family applies in December under the old
rule, Medicaid can reach back to
September and October is covered as long
as they would have qualified. If the
family applies in January instead, the
reach only goes back to November.
October falls off the edge. That is one
month and one bill of nearly $10,000
lost to nothing but the calendar. And
every month that passes from here moves
that edge along with it. Roa's family
lived a version of this. 84, a retired
seamstress in Toledo, Ohio. She fell at
home, spent a few days in the hospital,
and went to a nursing facility for
rehab. When the rehab ended, she was not
able to go home, so she stayed. Her son
assumed Medicare was still paying. It
was not. Her savings went first and by
the time the business office sat him
down, the unpaid balance covered more
than three months. Under the rule in
force at the time, Medicaid reached back
3 months and covered most of it. What
saved them was a social worker who
pushed him to file the application that
same week even though he did not have
half the documents. Under the rule that
starts in January, one of those months
would have been his families to pay. So,
here's what I would do, and it is
simple, even though it is not easy. If
someone you love is in a nursing
facility now or likely to be soon and
their savings are running down, do not
wait for Medicare to say no before you
think about Medicaid. Ask the facility's
business office this week exactly what
Medicare is covering and on what date it
expects that to end. Ask the social
worker about the Medicaid application in
your state and file it as early as the
rules allow, even if it is incomplete.
Every elder law advocate I have read on
this says the same thing. An application
filed on time without every document is
better than a perfect application filed
a month late. You can usually send the
missing papers afterward. And if there
is a husband or wife still living at
home, say so on the very first page. The
spouse who stays home is allowed to keep
the house and a protected share of the
couple's savings and a portion of the
income. And those protections are only
calculated properly if somebody asks for
them at the start. The same law also
puts a new limit on how much home equity
someone can have and still qualify for
long-term care Medicaid starting in 2028
capped at $1 million. That will not
touch most families watching this. But
if your home is worth a great deal, it
is one more reason to plan early rather
than late. And if there is any chance an
application will be needed around the
turn of the year, filing it in December
rather than January keeps the old
3-month reach. And for anybody between
50 and 64 who gets Medicaid through
their state's expansion or for your
adult children, the same law brings two
more changes at the end of this year.
Most states have to start a work
requirement, roughly 80 hours a month of
work, volunteering, or school with
exemptions for people who are medically
frail, people caring for someone, and
several others. And coverage has to be
renewed every 6 months instead of every
year. Every renewal is a letter and a
missed letter can mean a gap in
coverage. If that is you, make sure your
state Medicaid office has your current
address and open everything that comes
from them. Here is my honest opinion on
this one. Of all three changes, this is
the one that bothers me most. The first
change is a headline that promised too
much. The second is a clumsy cliff. This
one saves money by counting on families
being slow at the single worst moment of
their lives. It does not cut anybody's
benefit on paper. It simply shortens the
time you have to ask for it. And it
lands on people who are sitting in
hospital corridors, not reading the
federal register. If you would like the
questions for that business office and
the order to do things in when a parent
goes into care, they are written out in
the quiet rules at kevinexplains.shop.
The link is in the description and the
pinned comment and the code is on your
screen. 7 days to decide and a refund if
it is not for you. Because nobody should
learn about a two-month rule from a
collections letter lying on their
mother's kitchen table. Before I pull
all this together, there is one more
thing taking money out of checks this
fall and you will not find it on
anybody's October list. It has no date
attached to it. It can arrive in any
month to anybody. That is exactly what
makes it dangerous. It is a letter from
Social Security saying you were
overpaid. Sometimes it is right. Very
often it is about something the agency
itself got wrong. A wage report entered
twice. A change you reported that was
never recorded. A benefit calculated on
the wrong figures. And since the spring
of last year, the default way Social
Security collects on retirement survivor
and disability benefits has changed. For
a stretch before that, it took 10% of
your check each month. Now, unless you
do something, it takes 50%. Half. For
people on supplemental security income,
it stayed at 10. For everybody else, a
single envelope can cut the next deposit
in two. Ernestine got one of those
envelopes in the spring. 76. A widow
outside Kansas City living on her
survivor benefit of about $1,900 a
month. The letter said she owed a little
over $6,000 because a part-time job she
had held years earlier had been recorded
twice. Half her check month after month
for more than half a year. What saved
her was the date printed at the top of
the letter and a neighbor who knew what
it meant. Here's what that date means.
From the date on the notice, you have 30
days. If you file within those 30 days,
collection is paused while they review
your case. Not after, within. And there
are three different forms for three
different situations. If you believe the
overpayment is wrong or the amount is
wrong, the form is the SSA 561, a
request for reconsideration. If the
overpayment is real, but it was not your
fault, and paying it back would leave
you unable to meet ordinary expenses or
would simply be unfair, the form is the
SSA 632, a request for a waiver. An
approved waiver does not reschedule the
debt. It cancels it. And if you accept
that you owe it, but half your check is
impossible, the form is the SSA 634,
which asks for a lower monthly amount.
You can file more than one of these at
the same time. And there is a shortcut
worth knowing. If the overpayment is
$2,000 or less and you are not at fault,
Social Security can often wave it with
far less paperwork, sometimes over the
phone. You just have to ask for it.
Ernestine's neighbor helped her file the
reconsideration and the waiver together
within the 30 days. Collection stopped.
The double counted job was found. Her
check never lost a dollar. And a word on
keeping these letters from ever
arriving. Most overpayments start with a
change that Social Security did not
record in time. A new pension, a
part-time job, a marriage, a move, a
death in the family. When you report a
change, do it in a way that leaves a
trail through your online account where
you can save the confirmation or by
letter with a copy kept in that folder
or in person with a receipt. If you
report it by phone, write down the date,
the time, and the name of the person you
spoke with. When an overpayment notice
arrives years later, that one line of
notes is often the difference between
owing the money and proving you were
never at fault. So, let me keep the
promise I made at the very beginning. I
said two of these three can be stopped
with the right piece of paper, and one
has a door that closes on New Year's
Day. The paper is the first two. For the
tax change, it is the W4V to put your
withholding back before the year runs
out. For the Medicare sir charge, it is
the life event form if yours is on the
list or a request to recalculate if the
numbers are wrong or out of date. The
door is the third. Any Medicaid
application that might be needed around
the turn of the year keeps the old
3-month reach if it is filed by the 31st
of December. From the 1st of January,
that reach is shorter everywhere for
good. If there is a family in your life
with a parent in a nursing facility and
savings running low, that is the call to
make this month, not next. Now, let me
turn all of that into one thing you can
do this weekend. Get a single folder,
write October on the front, and put
three pieces of paper in it. The first
is last year's tax return. Find the line
for adjusted gross income and write it
on the front of the folder. Add any
tax-free interest. compare it with the
lines I gave you and check whether that
new senior deduction is actually on the
return. If it is not, ask why before the
15th. The second is your most recent
social security statement or the deposit
on your bank statement. Look for two
things. Is federal tax being withheld
and is it enough? And what is being
deducted for Medicare? When the new
amount arrives in December, you will
have this month's figure right there to
compare it with. The third is a sheet of
paper with two names and two phone
numbers on it. The business office and
the social worker at any facility where
somebody you love is staying or might
stay. And if a letter from social
security ever lands on your table
claiming an overpayment, it goes in this
folder, too, with a 30-day date circled
in red ink. That is the whole plan.
Three papers, one folder. It sounds
almost too small to matter. It is not.
Every story in this video, Raleigh at
the preparer's desk, Marietta at
Christmas, Roda's son in that business
office, Ernestine in her envelope, came
down to a piece of paper that was either
in front of somebody at the right moment
or it was not. And if your own situation
does not fit neatly into any of this, a
sir charge letter you do not understand,
an overpayment notice with the clock
already running, a parent heading into
care. Write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com
and tell me what is going on. I read
them myself and in a busy week it may
take me a few days to answer, but I do
answer. More than a few videos on this
channel started with one of those
emails. I will leave you with what I
actually think about all of this. None
of these three changes cuts your social
security on paper. Not one. The benefit
amount on your record is exactly what it
was. And that is precisely why they
work. A cut that shows up on paper makes
the news and people fight it. A change
that works through a headline, a
two-year delay, or a shorter window does
not make the news because there is
nothing to point at. There is just a
bill in April, a letter at Christmas, a
month that falls off the edge in
January. I do not think anybody sat in a
room and designed these to hurt you. But
I do think the system has learned that
the quiet way of collecting is the one
nobody complains about. So, the only
real defense is to be one of the people
who knows. You are watching this at the
start of October. That puts you months
ahead of the letters. And if you want
every one of these rules in one place
before the next headline arrives, the
quiet rules is linked in the description
and pinned at the top of the comments. I
am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevexplains.shop.

title: 7 Places Seniors Should Never Keep Their Cash Before December

segments.text: Somewhere in your house, there is a
statement with an interest rate on it.
And that rate was chosen for a world
that ended three weeks ago. For more
than a year, almost everybody told
retirees the same thing. Rates are
coming down. Lock in what you can before
they fall. Move fast. And a lot of
careful people did exactly that. Then
the Federal Reserve did the one thing
nobody on the television was preparing
you for. It raised rates. Not cut,
raised. the first increase in more than
3 years by a unanimous vote. And 16 of
the 18 officials who set those rates now
expect to raise them again before the
year is out. That one change quietly
flipped the right answer on at least
four places where retirees keep their
cash. And there are three more places
that were never what they looked like in
the first place. One of them is the
account a life insurance company hands a
widow the week of the funeral. One of
them is a box in a bank vault that the
bank does not insure. and one of them is
a place where waiting until November
could pay you more for the next 30
years. So, in this video, I'm going to
walk through all seven and then the
three dates between now and December
that decide what you do about them.
Before we go any further, tell me in the
comments whether your bank has raised
the rate on your savings since the
middle of September. Just yes, no, or I
have not checked. I read them and the
answers will tell everybody watching
which banks are passing it on. My name
is Kevin. I read the rules so you do not
have to. And if you want to hear about
the next rate decision before it lands
on your statement, subscribe now. Every
figure in this video comes from the
Federal Reserve, the Treasury, or the
regulators themselves. And every source
is listed in the description, so you can
check all of it. I am not a financial
adviser, and this is education, not
advice about your own money. Nothing in
this video involves picking stocks. Here
is what actually happened in plain
words. On the 16th of September, the
Federal Reserve raised its benchmark
rate by a quarter of a point to a range
of 3 and 3/4 to 4%. The chairman, Kevin
Walsh, no relation, said inflation is
too high and has been for too long.
According to the Fed's own projections,
the typical official expects one more
increase before the end of the year.
There are two meetings left to do it,
the 27th and 28th of October and the 8th
and 9th of December. And in between
those two, on the 1st of November, the
Treasury resets the rate on its
inflation protected savings bonds. Three
dates. Keep them in mind because every
one of the seven places connects back to
at least one of them. Place number one
is a savings account that ignored the
increase. For the last 2 years, you have
heard on this channel that when rates
fall, banks pass the cut on to you
within days. And when rates rise, the
increase takes its time arriving. Well,
now we get to watch that second half
happen in real time. Some banks raise
their savings rates within a week of the
decision. Some have not moved at all.
According to FDIC data, the national
average savings account still pays about
37 hundreds of 1%. Meanwhile, the best
federally insured savings accounts are
paying 4 and a4% and more, and 3-month
Treasury bills are paying about 4%. Same
insurance, same access, more than 10
times the interest. Here is a simple
test that takes 2 minutes. Find your
savings statement from August. Find the
one that arrives in October. Compare the
rate printed on each. If the number has
not moved since the Fed raised rates,
your bank has made a decision about your
money and you have just found out what
it is. Then call and ask one question in
these words. What is the highest rate
you pay on savings to any customer and
what do I need to do to get it? not what
am I earning, what is the highest you
pay. Banks very often have a better
account one page away on their own
website that they never offer to the
customers they already have. Place
number two is the one I think costs
retirees the most right now and almost
nobody talks about it. It is cash
sitting in savings while you carry a
debt whose rate just went up. When the
Fed raised rates, the prime rate, which
is what banks base most variable loans
on, went up with it to 7%. According to
Bank Rate, the average rate on a home
equity line of credit is now about 7.3%.
Credit cards are usually far higher than
that. So, think about what it means to
have money in a savings account, paying
a few ten of 1% while you owe a balance
at seven or more. In effect, you are
paying the bank far more to borrow than
it is paying you to save. And often, it
is the very same bank. Paying down a 7%
debt is the same as earning 7%
guaranteed with no risk at all. And
unlike the interest you earn in savings,
it never shows up on your tax return as
income. Now, one warning, because this
is where careful people overcorrect. Do
not empty your savings to zero to pay
off a home equity line, thinking you can
always borrow again from the line if an
emergency comes. Banks can freeze or cut
home equity lines. Many did exactly that
during the housing crash without much
warning to people who had never missed a
payment. So keep a real emergency fund
in an insured account and then use the
cash above that to pay down the variable
debt. Ask your lender what the rate on
your line is today, not what it was when
you opened it because on most lines it
moves every time prime moves and it will
move again if the Fed raises again in
October or December. Cyrus learned that
math the slow way. 70, a retired
electrician outside Columbus, Ohio. He
and his wife kept about $60,000 in a
savings account at a big bank, paying
almost nothing because it felt safe. At
the same time, they carried a balance of
about $45,000 on a home equity line they
had used for a new roof and a car. When
their accountant laid the two numbers
side by side this spring, the line was
costing them more than $3,000 a year in
interest. The savings were earning them
about 240. They had been paying the
difference every single year for the
comfort of seeing a bigger number in
savings. More than $3,000 a year for a
feeling. Cyrus and his wife were not
reckless. They did what their parents
taught them, which is to keep a cushion
and never touch it. Nobody had ever
shown them that a cushion sitting next

out on paper. which of your accounts are

It is at kevin explains.shop.
Point your phone at the code on your

with it. If it does not show you

Place number three is money you think of
as cash that is actually sitting in a
bond fund. This one surprises people
every time rates go up and they just
went up. Inside a lot of retirement
accounts, the part people call the safe

with a name like short-term income,
total bond, or conservative income.
Those funds hold bonds, and bonds have a
simple rule that FINRA, the regulator
for brokerage firms, explains on its own
website. When interest rates rise, bond
prices fall. And the size of the fall
roughly equals something called
duration, which every fund lists on its
fact sheet. A fund with a duration of 6
years loses about 6% of its value for
every onepoint rise in rates on
That is about $6,000 gone from the
balance in a fund you were told was the
conservative choice. And unlike a bank
account or a certificate, a bond fund
has no maturity date. There is no day
when it promises to hand you back
exactly what you put in. Over time, a
bond fund does start earning the new
higher rates. So this is not a reason to
panic and sell, but it is a very good
reason never to keep money you might
need within the next year or two in one.
That money belongs in an insured savings
account, a money market fund, or
treasury bills where a rise in rates
helps you instead of hurting you. And
while we are here, one distinction that
confuses almost everybody. A money
market account at a bank is a bank
deposit insured up to the federal limit.
A money market fund at a brokerage is
not a deposit and is not FDIC insured.
Money market funds are among the safest
places in the financial world and almost
never lose value. But they are a
different thing with a different
protection and you should know which one
you own. Place number four is a long
certificate of deposit you locked in for
a falling rate world. A great many
retirees last year and earlier this year
did what they were told and locked money
into three, four, and five-year
certificates before rates could fall.
Now, the one-year Treasury bill pays
about 4 and a/4% and the 5-year Treasury
pays about five. So, some of those
certificates are now paying less than
you could get almost anywhere else for
years to come. Here's the question
nobody asks. Is it worth breaking it?
Most people assume never because of the
penalty, but the penalty is a number and
you can do the arithmetic. On a 5-year
certificate, the typical penalty is
somewhere between 12 and 24 months of
interest, depending on the bank. So,
take $50,000 in a 5-year certificate,
paying 3.5% with a 12-month penalty.
Breaking it costs $1,750.
If you can get about a point more by
moving it, that is roughly $500 a year
of extra interest. With four years left,
you come out about $250 ahead. Barely
worth the trouble. With an 18-month
penalty, you lose money. That is my own
arithmetic, and it changes with every
bank. So, ask your bank for the exact
penalty in dollars before you decide.
And be aware that at some banks, the
penalty can come out of your original
deposit if you have not earned enough
interest yet. And if the certificate you
own was bought through a brokerage
rather than directly from a bank, there
may be no early withdrawal at all. A
brokered certificate can only be sold to
another investor. And when rates have
risen, it sells for less than you paid.
So check which kind you own before you
plan around breaking it. Now, the
mistake I would really like you to avoid
because it is the mirror image of the
one people made last year. Do not now
rush to lock everything into the longest
certificate you can find because the
news says rates are going up. Nobody
knows how far rates will go, including
the people who set them. They were wrong
in one direction last year. They can be
wrong in the other. The sensible answer
is not a single bet. It is a ladder.
Split your money into pieces that come
due at different times. three months,
six months, a year, two years, so that
something is always maturing and you are
never locked into one rate for
everything. Now, we leave the rate story
behind because the next three places
have nothing to do with the Fed. They
are places where cash is not what it
looks like. Place number five is a safe
deposit box. A great many people of this
generation keep cash in one and savings
bonds and sometimes the deed and the
will. And almost all of them believe
that because the box is inside the bank,
it is protected like the bank. It is
not. The FDIC is very clear that deposit
insurance does not cover the contents of
a safe deposit box. Cash in a box is not
a deposit. If there is a fire, a flood,
or a theft, the bank's own rental
agreement usually limits what it will
pay. And many agreements say it will pay
nothing unless you can prove the bank
was negligent. and you cannot easily
prove what was inside a box that nobody
else has seen. There are two more
problems people discover at the worst
moment. Access to the box is limited to
the bank's business hours, so it is no
place for anything you might need on a
weekend or in an emergency. And when the
owner dies, in many states, the box can
be sealed or restricted until the right
paperwork is produced. So, the family
may not be able to get the will out of
the box that the will says how to open.
If you keep cash in a box, look at your
homeowners or renters's policy under a
heading called special limits. Most
policies cover only a few hundred of
cash, wherever it is. Some insurers will
cover box contents with a rider for a
small extra cost. And if the box holds
paper savings bonds, keep listening
because those may have stopped paying
you years ago. Place number six is the
one I most want widows and widowers to
hear. When a life insurance company pays
out a death benefit, it often does not
send a check. Instead, it opens an
account in the beneficiary's name and
sends a book of drafts that look exactly
like checks. It feels like a bank
account. It has a statement. It pays a
little interest, but in most cases, it
is not a bank account at all. These are
called retained asset accounts. And the
National Association of Insurance
Commissioners explains that when the
money is held by the insurer rather than
a bank, it is not covered by FDIC
insurance. It is backed by the insurance
company. And if that company fails by
your state's insurance guarantee fund,
which has its own limits that vary by
state, and the rate is whatever the
insurer decides to pay, which is often a
fraction of what an insured savings
account pays, while the insurer invests
that same money at far more. The NIC's
own advice is that you should not feel
rushed and that you may be able to earn
more by choosing a different payout.
Both are true. The account is not a scam
and it gives a grieving person time, but
nobody should leave a life insurance
payout sitting there for years by
default. So, if you have one of these,
here is what to do, and you can do it
calmly. Call the insurer and ask three
questions. What rate is this account
paying today? Is it held by you or by a
bank? and how do I take the full balance
out? In almost every case, you can write
a single draft for the whole amount or
ask for a check and move it to an
insured account at your own bank. One
thing to know about tax while you are
deciding, the death benefit itself is
generally not taxable income, but the
interest it earns while it sits in that
account is. So, even the small amount it
pays will show up on a form at tax time.
And one more thing for any family that
has just lost somebody. If you are not
sure whether your husband, wife, or
parent had a life insurance policy at
all, the NIC runs a free service called
the life insurance policy locator. You
submit a request with the death
certificate information. Participating
insurers search their records and if
they find a policy where you are the
beneficiary, they contact you. It is
free and policies that nobody claims
every year are worth a great deal of
money. Mavis did exactly that. 73. A
retired church secretary near
Louisville, Kentucky. When her husband
died, his policy paid $380,000,
and the insurer opened one of these
accounts and mailed her a draft book.
She assumed it was a bank account
because it looked like one, and she was
in no state to think about it. It sat
there for a little over 2 years, earning
about half of 1%. At the rates an
insured high yield savings account was
paying over the same stretch, that money
would have earned roughly $28,000 more.
Her daughter only noticed when she saw
the insurers's name, not a banks, at the
top of the statement. $28,000
lost to a book of drafts that looked
like a checkbook. Mavis did nothing
wrong. She was grieving and the account
was designed to look familiar so that
grieving people would leave it alone.
That is the kind of trap I put in the
Quiet Rules plainly with the exact
questions to ask an insurer, a bank, or
a brokerage about where your money is
really held and what it is really paying
written. so that a son or daughter can
work through it with you at the kitchen
table. You will find it at
kevinexplains.shop.
The code is back on your screen and the
link is at the top of the pinned comment
and in the description underneath. 7
days to decide whether it is worth
keeping. And if it is not, you get a
refund. Mavis keeps the old draft book
in a kitchen drawer now, unused with a
note on the cover in her daughter's
handwriting, not a bank. Place number
seven is new and it is aimed squarely at
people who are careful, not people who
gamble. Dollar coins in an app. You may
have seen them advertised as digital
dollars or stable coins, sometimes
paying four or 5%, sometimes with a
picture of a bank vault on the screen.
Each coin is meant to be worth exactly
$1, so it feels like cash. Last July,
President Trump signed a law called the
Genius Act that for the first time set
federal rules for these coins. Two parts
of that law matter to you. The companies
that issue these coins are not allowed
to pay you interest on them. And the
coins are not federally insured
deposits. So, when an app offers you a
return on dollar coins, the money is
coming from somewhere other than the
coin itself, usually the app, calling it
a reward. Congress's own research
service published a paper this year on
whether those rewards should even be
allowed. I am not telling you these
coins are a fraud. Some of them are run
by large regulated companies. I am
telling you they are not a savings
account. They carry none of the
protection of one and they are exactly
the kind of products scammers love
because the word dollar is in the name.
According to the FBI, Americans over 60
reported losing more than $4 billion
dollar last year in schemes involving
cryptocurrency. And a great many of
those started with something that was
described as safe, stable, and paying a
little more than the bank. If anybody on
the phone or online suggests you move
your savings into digital dollars for
safety, hang up. A real bank and a real
government agency will never ask you to
do that. And before I get to where the
money should go, one more place as a
bonus because it may be sitting in your
house right now. Paper savings bonds
that have stopped paying you. Series E
and Series I savings bonds stop earning
interest exactly 30 years after the
issue date printed on the front. The
older series HH bonds stop at 20. After
that, the bond is still worth what it
was worth on that day, but it never
earns another cent. According to
reporting this year, the Treasury is
holding roughly $29.7 billion in savings
bonds that have reached final maturity
and never been cashed. About 80 million
bonds. Treasury's own online search for
them was shut down last year. So, the
simplest check is the one in your hands.
Look at the issue date. If it is more
than 30 years ago, take it to your bank
or contact the Treasury about cashing
it. And if you know a bond existed but
cannot find it, the Treasury has a form
to replace lost, stolen, or destroyed
bonds.
One tax note to raise with your
preparer. The interest on a matured bond
is generally taxable in the year the
bond reached final maturity, whether or
not anybody cashed it. And one timing
rule on the newer series EE bonds, the
electronic ones bought in the last 20
years or so. The Treasury guarantees
they will double in value at 20 years.
Most of that doubling arrives on the
20th anniversary itself. Cash one a few
months early and you can walk away from
a large part of the gain. So before you
cash any EE bond that is close to 20
years old, check the date first.
So where should the money actually go?
Think of your cash in two piles because
almost every mistake in this video comes
from treating it as one. The first pile
is anything you might need within a
year. emergencies, a car, the gap
between your income and your bills. That
pile belongs somewhere insured and fully
available. A high yield savings account
at an FDIC insured bank or an NCUA
insured credit union paying a real rate,
which right now means 4% or more. Or
Treasury bills, which according to the
Federal Reserve's latest figures pay
about 4% for 3 months and a little over
four for 6 months and a year. Treasury
bills are backed by the government
directly. There is no insurance limit to
worry about and the interest is free of
state and local income tax. You can buy
them directly from the Treasury or
through any brokerage. And when rates
are rising, short bills have a quiet
advantage. Every few months they come
due and you roll them into whatever the
new higher rate is. One thing to check
before you move because the headline
rates have fine print. Some of the
highest savings rates you see advertised
only apply to the first few thousand or
only if your social security is
deposited there or only for the first
few months before they drop to an
ordinary rate. Before you move a large
balance, ask three things. Does this
rate apply to my whole balance? Does it
require anything from me? And is it a
promotional rate? And if so, when does
it end? The second pile is money you
will not need for at least a year. And
this is where the three dates matter.
The first date is the 28th of October
when the Fed announces its next
decision. Whatever it does, it will not
change much about your savings that
week. Where it matters most is debt. If
you are carrying a balance on a home
equity line or a credit card and you
have cash above a real emergency fund,
this is the month to pay it down before
any second increase reaches your
statement. The second date is the 1st of
November. And here is where I want to
change the advice you may have heard,
including from me. The Treasury resets
the rate on series 1 savings bonds twice
a year. Each IBond has two parts to its
rate. An inflation part that changes
every 6 months and a fixed part that
stays with that bond for its entire life
up to 30 years. Right now, the fixed
part is 9/10 of 1%. According to the
analysis at TipsWatch, which has tracked
this formula for years, the fixed rate
set on the 1st of November looks likely
to rise to around 1.2 or 1.3%.
Because the market yields it is based on
have climbed sharply this year. If that
happens, someone who buys an Ibond in
October locks in 9/10 for 30 years.
Someone who buys in November locks in
the higher figure for 30 years. So, if
you are thinking of Ibonds as long-term
money, the better move this year is
probably to wait for the new rate. The
exception is someone who only plans to
hold them for a year or two because the
bond bought in October earns the current
rate of 4.26% for its first 6 months.
And for a short hold, that can matter
more than the fixed part. And remember
the rules. $10,000 per person per year
through Treasury Direct, no cashing at
all for the first 12 months, and three
months of interest given up if you cash
before 5 years. The third date is the
9th of December, the last Fed decision
of the year and the one that comes with
fresh projections for next year. By
then, you will know where the October
decision landed and what the new Ibond
rate is. That makes early December the
right time to set up a ladder for the
second pile. some in treasury bills,
some in certificates of different
lengths, and if it suits you, some in
Ibonds at the new rate, not all at once,
and not all in the longest term on
offer. And there is one product built
almost exactly for a year like this one,
which most people have never heard of, a
no penalty certificate. It pays a fixed
rate like an ordinary certificate,
usually a little lower than the best,
but after the first week or so, you can
take your money out at any time without
paying a penalty. So, if rates rise
again after you open it, you simply
close it and move to the higher rate.
Many online banks and credit unions
offer them. Ask for it by name because
branches rarely mention it. And one
caution that applies to every dollar in
both piles, which I have covered in
detail in earlier videos, so I will keep
it short. Interest is income. Moving a
large balance from almost nothing to 4%
can push more of your social security
into taxable territory and two years
later it can show up in the income
Medicare uses for its search charge.
That is not a reason to keep earning
nothing. Earning a real rate and paying
some tax on it beats earning nothing
every single time. It is a reason to
know roughly where you stand before you
move a large sum and to notice that
Ibonds and Treasury bills both give you
some control over which year that income
lands in. So, here's the whole thing as
a calendar, not a checklist. This week,
compare your August and October savings
statements and call your lender and ask
the rate on any variable debt. Before
the 28th of October, use cash above your
emergency fund to pay down that debt and
move any money you need within a year
out of bond funds. Before the 31st of
October, if you planned to buy ibonds
for the long haul, wait on the 1st of
November, look up the new rate. And any
day between now and the 9th of December,
do the three quiet ones. Call the
insurer about any life insurance
account. Look in the safe deposit box
and check the dates on any savings
bonds. And check what kind of
certificates you own and what it would
really cost to break them. And if your
situation does not fit neatly into any
of this, a large insurance payout, a
certificate you are not sure about, a
parents bonds you have just found in a
drawer, write to me at kevin explains
official@gmail.com
and tell me what is going on. I read
everyone myself. In a busy week, it may
take a few days, but I do answer. And
many of these videos started with
exactly that kind of email. Here is what
I actually think about all of this. A
surprise is the most expensive moment in
a retireese's financial life. And it is
expensive in both directions. Last year,
people rushed to lock everything in
because rates were supposed to fall.
This year, the temptation will be to
rush the other way. Both are the same
mistake. The rate increase is good news
for savers, the best in a while. But it
only reaches the people who go and
collect it. Your bank will not move you.
The insurer will not call. The bond in
the drawer will not tell you it stopped.
Every one of the seven places in this
video comes down to the same thing.
Somebody else made a default decision
about your money, and it stays made
until you look. If you want every one of
these places and the exact questions to
ask at each on paper in one place, the
quiet rules is linked in the description
and pinned at the top of the comments. I
am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: The Amount Seniors Should NEVER Leave in Checking | IRS Watching in 2026

segments.text: Your checking account is being watched
right now by five different parties. The
IRS is one of them and here is what
nobody putting a red warning on a bank
screen will tell you. Of all five, the
IRS is the one that sees the least. It
does not see your balance. It never has.
The one that sees the most has no badge,
no letterhead, and no rules at all. And
in between are three others most people
have never thought about. One that only
sees cash, one that can freeze
everything above a certain line the day
a judgment lands, and one that will one
day read five full years of your
statements line by line, every check and
every cash withdrawal, and ask you to
explain them. So, the amount you should
never leave sitting in checking is not
one number. It is the smallest of four
numbers and by the end of this video you
will know all four and which one is
yours. Along the way, I will show you
the one IRS report that actually arrives
with a letter telling you it was filed.
And why the people who get that letter
so often make the worst decision of
their year the week it arrives. Before
we start, tell me in the comments
roughly how much you keep in checking.
Not the dollars, just whether it is
under one month of bills, one to three
months, or more than three. I will use
the answers in a future video and I read
them. My name is Kevin. I read the rules
so you do not have to. And if you want
the next one of these, subscribe now.
Everything I quote today comes from the
agency's own published rules and every
source is listed in the description. So,
if you want to check me, please do. I am
not a financial advisor, a tax preparer,
or a lawyer. This is education, not
advice about your own money. Let me
start with the one in the title because
it is the one that frightens people most
and sees the least. The IRS does not
receive your checking account balance.
There is no form for it. There is no
report a bank files when your balance
crosses a line.
A few years ago, there was a proposal in
Washington to make banks report the
total money flowing in and out of
accounts above $600 a year. It caused an
uproar. It never became law. If anybody
tells you the IRS is looking at your
balance, they are describing a rule that
does not exist. The same goes for
payment apps.
The tax law President Trump signed last
July put the reporting line for apps
like PayPal and Venmo back at $20,000
and 200 payments a year. So, selling a
few things online or splitting a dinner
bill does not put you on any list. What
the IRS does receive about your checking
account is much smaller and much more
useful to understand. It is a slip. If
your bank pays you $10 or more in
interest in a year, it sends the IRS a
form called the 1099-INT
and it sends you a copy.
That is the requirement in the IRS's own
instructions for that form. $10, not a
balance, interest. A computer at the IRS
takes every one of those slips and
matches it against your tax return.
When a slip says you earned interest and
your return does not show it, a letter
goes out, usually more than a year
later, proposing extra tax. That
matching machine is the real IRS
watching.
It is not interested in how much you
keep. It is interested in whether every
slip with your social security number on
it shows up on your return. And there
are three places those slips come from
that catch careful retirees every year.
The first is an old account you forgot
about. A small savings account at a bank
you left years ago still paying a few
dollars of interest, still mailing the
slip to an address you moved away from.
You never see it. The IRS does. The
second is the IRS itself. When the IRS
takes too long to pay your refund, it
pays you interest on it and that
interest is taxable and the IRS sends a
slip for it like any bank would. People
are always surprised to get a tax form
from the IRS for money the IRS paid
them. The third is a certificate of
deposit longer than a year. On most
multi-year certificates, the interest is
taxed each year as it builds up, even
though you cannot touch it until the
certificate matures. You see nothing in
your hand, and you still owe tax on it
every April. So, can the IRS ever look
inside your account itself? Yes, in two
situations, and both come with warning.
During an audit, the IRS can issue a
summons to your bank for your records,
and in most cases you are told about it.
And if you owe tax and have ignored the
letters, the IRS can levy the account
and take the money. But that is the end
of a long trail, not the beginning of
one. Before any levy, the law requires a
final notice of intent to levy, sent by
certified or registered mail, and it
gives you 30 days to ask for a hearing.
That hearing request, on a form called
stops the levy while it is heard. Nobody
wakes up to a levy out of nowhere. They
wake up to one after a stack of
envelopes that went unopened. Now, the
one IRS report that does involve big
money, and the one that comes with a
letter, if you pay a business more than
$10,000 in cash, the business has to
report it to the IRS on a form called
the 8300. Car dealers file more of them
than almost anybody. And here is the
part that surprises people. For that
report, a cashier's check or a money
order of $10,000 or less counts as cash.
So does a group of them added together.
Paying for a car with two cashier's
checks of $9,000 each does not keep you
off the report. It puts you on it. And
unlike almost every other report in this
video, the business is required to send
you a written statement by the 31st of
January saying it reported the payment
to the IRS. That is in the IRS's own
guidance for car dealers. Myrtle got one
of those statements in January '74, a
retired school secretary outside Omaha.
She had bought a used car the summer
before, paying with cashier's checks
from her savings, every dollar of it
already taxed. Then the statement
arrived saying her payment had been
reported to the Internal Revenue
Service. She did not sleep that night.
By the end of the week, she had found a
company on television promising to
protect her from the IRS, and she paid
them a retainer of $2,900. They
sent her a folder of forms and stopped
returning her calls. There had never
been anything to protect her from. The
report was routine. It required nothing
of her at all. $2,900 spent defending
against a letter that was only ever a
receipt. Myrtle did not need a defense.
She needed somebody to tell her in plain
words what that letter meant before she
picked up the phone. I wrote the Quiet
Rules for moments exactly like that one.
Inside it is what the routine notices
actually mean. Which ones need an
answer, and which ones need nothing at
all. So a frightening envelope gets read
calmly at the kitchen table instead of
answered in a panic. You can find it at
kevinexplains.shop.
Scan the code on your screen or tap the
first link in the pinned comment, and it
is in the description, too. Take 7 days
with it, and if it does not earn its
place, you can get a refund. Otherwise,
the next envelope gets the same week
Myrtle had. A routine receipt from a car
dealer in one hand, a stranger's
contract in the other, and a phone line
that nobody answers anymore. The second
watcher only sees cash, and it is not
the IRS. It is a small office inside the
Treasury called FinCEN, the Financial
Crimes Enforcement Network. Its job is
money laundering, not your tax return,
although the IRS and other agencies can
search what it collects. I have covered
this one in depth before, so here is the
short version, and then the parts I have
never told you.
When you deposit or withdraw more than
$10,000 in cash in one business day,
your bank files a currency transaction
report. Withdrawals count, not just
deposits, which surprises a lot of
people.
Several smaller cash transactions on the
same day are added together.
And breaking cash into smaller pieces on
purpose to stay under that line is a
federal crime of its own called
structuring, even when every dollar is
honest. Deposit it in one go, explain
where it came from, and let the bank
file its routine report. Now the parts
most people never hear. That $10,000
line was set in 1970 and has never been
adjusted for inflation. In today's
money, it would be somewhere above
So a cash amount that was rare and
remarkable when the law was written is
now an ordinary used car or a roof. Last
October, a group of senators introduced
a bill to raise the line to $30,000
and index it for inflation from then on.
As of today, it has not passed. So the
old line still stands. And there is a
smaller line almost nobody knows about.
If you walk into a bank with cash and
buy a cashier's check or a money order
for $3,000 or more up to 10,000, the
bank has to log your name, the date, and
the serial number of every check and
keep that record for 5 years.
Several purchases on the same day can be
added together.
That is the Treasury's own record
keeping rule. Nothing is wrong with
doing it. Just understand that the
cashier's check you bought to pay a
contractor in cash is not invisible. And
a pattern of them just under 10,000
looks exactly like the pattern I just
told you to avoid. One more piece of
news from this year for anybody thinking
of buying a home with cash. A new
Treasury rule was set to make the
closing agent report cash purchases of
homes bought in the name of a trust or a
company, which is exactly how many
retirees buy through a living trust. In
March, a federal court in Texas threw
that rule out. The Treasury has
appealed. So, for now, no report is
required, but it may come back. And if
you are planning a cash purchase through
a trust next year, ask your title
company where that case stands. The
third watcher is the one people only
discover in the worst week of their
life, a creditor with a court judgment,
a credit card company that sued you, a
medical bill that went to collections
and then to court. When a creditor like
that sends a garnishment order to your
bank, the bank can freeze your account.
But, federal benefits get a special
shield, and the details of that shield
are the most practical number in this
whole video.
Under a Treasury rule, when a
garnishment order arrives, your bank has
two business days to look back over the
previous 2 months.
Any Social Security, Veterans Benefits,
Federal Retirement, or Railroad
Retirement that was directly deposited
in that period is protected
automatically, and you keep access to
it. That is the rule, written word for
word for banks to follow. Read that rule
carefully, though, because the
protection has an edge. It covers
roughly 2 months of your benefits, not
everything in the account. Money above
that line can be frozen on the spot, and
getting it released can mean going to
court to prove where it came from. So,
if your Social Security is $2,000 a
month, about 4,000 of it is protected
automatically.
If you keep $20,000 in that same
account, the other 16,000 is exposed the
moment an order arrives. And there are
two kinds of orders the shield does not
apply to at all.
Orders from the federal government
itself, such as an IRS levy, and state
orders for child support. So, that is
the second of our four numbers. Anything
above about 2 months of your benefits
sitting in checking has no automatic
protection. The fourth watcher is the
one that will read the most, and it is
the one nobody expects, Medicaid. If you
or your spouse ever need long-term care
in a nursing home and apply for Medicaid
to pay for it, the state will look back
over the previous 5 years of your
finances. 60 months. In most states,
that means statements, and case workers
go through them. Every check written to
a grandchild, every transfer to a son,
and every cash withdrawal. Here is the
part that turns ordinary habits into a
penalty. A check leaves a trail. You can
show who it went to and what it was for.
Cash leaves no trail at all. Many states
presume that a large cash withdrawal you
cannot explain went to somebody as a
gift, and a gift inside those 5 years
can make you ineligible for Medicaid for
a period of months.
The penalty is worked out by dividing
the amount by the average monthly cost
of a nursing home in your state. Think
about how many retirees run their lives
in cash. A few hundred out of the
machine every week. Cash for the
grandchildren's birthdays, cash to the
neighbor who cuts the grass. None of
that is wrong. But 5 years from now, a
case worker may be looking at it with no
receipts and no memory to explain it. My
view on this is simple. Pay by check or
card where you can. Write a word in the
memo line, and keep a small envelope of
receipts for anything you pay in cash
over a few hundred dollars. It costs you
nothing today, and it can be worth
months of nursing home care later. And
if you watched my last video about
Medicaid reaching back only 2 months
instead of 3, this is the other side of
the same coin. Medicaid will look back 5
years to judge your spending, and only 2
months to help pay your bills. And then,
the fifth watcher, the one that sees the
most because it is not looking at a
report or a statement. It is looking for
a way in. In its latest report, the FBI
says Americans age 60 and older reported
losing $7.75 billion
to scams and online crime in 2025.
That was up 59% in a single year, more
than 200,000 complaints, and the average
loss per victim was about $38,500.
For a great many of those people, that
number was not a loss of savings, it was
the checking account. Because checking
is the account with every door attached
to it, the debit card, the paper checks
with the account number printed along
the bottom, the app on the phone that
can send money to anybody in seconds,
the automatic payments. Savings accounts
usually have none of those doors,
checking has all of them. I talked a
while ago about the gap in protection
when a scammer talks you into sending
money yourself. So, I will only add two
things you have not heard from me. The
first is about paper checks. Mail theft
and check washing, where a stolen check
is chemically erased and rewritten for a
larger amount, have become one of the
most common bank frauds in the country,
and the clock on reporting it may be
shorter than you think. The general rule
is that you have to report a forged or
altered check with reasonable promptness
after your statement arrives. Many bank
account agreements tighten that to as
little as 30 or 60 days from the
statement date, and there is an outer
limit of 1 year, no matter what. If you
do not open your statements, you can
lose the right to have the bank cover
it. The second is a simple structural
fix that almost nobody uses. Keep your
larger savings at a different bank from
your checking account. No debit card
attached, no payment app connected. If
somebody gets into your checking
account, the most they can take is what
is in checking. Think of it as a moat.
And three things a real bank will never
do, so you can recognize the call that
is not your bank. A real bank will never
ask you to move your money to a safe
account to protect it. There is no such
thing. A real bank will never ask you to
read back a code that it just texted to
your phone. That code is the key to your
account, and the person asking for it is
trying to turn it. And a real bank will
never mind if you hang up and call the
number printed on the back of your own
card. A scammer always does. The caller
ID can be faked to show your bank's
name. The number on the back of your
card cannot. Lyndon is why I care about
that mode. 71, a retired surveyor near
Spokane, Washington. He kept about
$60,000 in checking because he liked
seeing it when he logged in. One
afternoon, a man called claiming to be
from his bank's fraud department with
his bank's name showing on the caller
ID. He said Lyndon's account had been
compromised and walked him through
moving the money to a safe account to
protect it. Lyndon is careful and
intelligent, and he did it in two
transfers, about $41,000 in total,
before his daughter called back and
stopped the third. Because he had made
the transfers himself, his bank treated
them as authorized. They recovered
nothing. $41,000
gone in one afternoon from an account
that never needed to hold more than a
few thousand. Lyndon did not lose it
because he was careless. He lost it
because his checking account was holding
money it had no reason to hold, and a
stranger knew exactly where to look for
it. I wrote the quiet rules so that the
people who watch this channel set things
up the other way around before the phone
ever rings, so that one bad afternoon
can never reach their savings. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
The code on your screen takes you
straight there, and the link is pinned
in the comments and in the description
below.
You have 7 days to see whether it is
worth keeping, and if it is not, you get
a refund. Lyndon's daughter still has
the screenshot of his balance from that
evening. Two numbers on a phone screen,
the morning figure and the night one,
and $41,000 of difference between them.
Now, there is one more cost to checking
that has nothing to do with any of the
five watchers. It is quiet. It is
arithmetic, and it happens every month
whether anybody is looking or not.
According to the Bureau of Labor
Statistics, prices were up 3.4% over the
year to August.
According to the FDIC, the national
average savings account pays 37/100 of
1% and most checking accounts pay less
than that or nothing at all.
So, $20,000 sitting in checking for a
year loses roughly $680
of buying power.
That is my own arithmetic from their
numbers. The balance on the screen does
not move, which is exactly why nobody
notices it. Nobody sends a letter. There
is no fee. It is simply money that buys
a little less every month it sits there.
So, let me give you the four numbers I
promised and how to put them together.
The first number is what checking is
actually for. One month of your regular
bills plus a buffer, so a payment
landing a day late never leaves you
short and a bill landing a day early
never bounces.
If your bills run about $4,000 a month,
that might be somewhere between five and
six thousand. That is not a government
rule. It is a working rule of thumb, and
I am telling you plainly that is what it
is. The second number is the garnishment
shield, about two months of your federal
benefits. Anything above that in the
account where your benefits land has no
automatic protection if a creditor ever
gets a court order.
The third number is the moat. Ask
yourself plainly, how much could I lose
in one bad phone call and still sleep at
night?
Whatever that number is, checking should
never hold more than that because
checking is the account with every door
attached. And the fourth is the ceiling
that most people already know.
per person, per bank, per type of
ownership is the limit of federal
deposit insurance. Above that, at a
single bank in a single kind of account,
your money is not insured. Let me run
that for a typical couple, so you can
see it work. Their bills come to about
$5,000 a month. So, the first number, a
month plus a buffer, is around 6 and 1/2
thousand. Their social security together
is about 4,000 a month. So, the
garnishment shield covers around 8,000.
Asked what they could lose in one bad
phone call and still sleep, they say
5,000. And the insurance ceiling is
nowhere close. So, their number is
5,000, the smallest of the four.
When they looked, they had $38,000 in
checking.
33,000 of it was doing nothing except
waiting for one of the five watchers.
The amount you should never leave in
checking is whichever of those four is
smallest. For most people watching this,
that turns out to be the first one,
somewhere between one and two months of
spending. For somebody with a large
balance and a habit of answering the
phone, it may be the third. And it is
almost never the fourth because by the
time you get anywhere near the insurance
ceiling, the other three have been
broken for a long time. So, where does
the rest go? Not anywhere exotic. The
money just above checking is your
emergency fund. And the usual guidance
is three to six months of expenses.
The two rules that matter most are that
it is separate from checking and that
you can reach it quickly without a
penalty. A high-yield savings account at
an FDIC-insured bank or an NCUA-insured
credit union does both and pays many
times the national average.
Put it at a different institution from
your checking and leave the debit card
off it. That is your moat. Beyond that,
money with a date on it, a roof in two
years, a car next spring, can go into
something that pays a fixed rate for a
fixed time, a certificate of deposit,
Treasury bills, which are free of state
income tax. Just remember what I said
earlier about multi-year certificates
and expect to pay tax on that interest
each year, even though you cannot touch
it yet. And keep one more thing in mind
as your interest grows. Every dollar of
interest is income. It is counted in the
formula that decides how much of your
Social Security is taxed and in the
income Medicare uses for its surcharge,
which I went through in my last two
videos. US savings bonds are the one
common exception that works differently.
The interest on series I and series EE
bonds is not taxed until you cash them
in, so it does not land on your return
year after year. They have their own
limits and you cannot cash them in
during the first year, so they suit
money you truly will not need soon, not
your emergency fund. And everything
beyond that, the money you will not need
for years, deserves a conversation with
somebody who can see your whole picture,
your pension, your IRA, your required
withdrawals, your health. I cannot see
any of that and neither can anybody else
on the internet. Two warnings for the
day. A big amount of money moves because
that is when checking accounts get hurt
the most. The first is about holds. When
you deposit a large check from a home
sale, an insurance payout, or a life
insurance policy after a death, your
