bank is required to make only the first
portion available quickly. Under the
Federal Reserve's rule on funds
availability, once a check deposit
passes $6,725
in a day, the bank can hold the amount
above that line for an extra stretch of
time, often a week or more. People write
checks against that money the same
afternoon, the checks bounce, and the
fees start. If a large check is coming,
ask the bank on the day you deposit it
exactly when every dollar will be
available and write the date down. The
second is about wires. If you are
selling a house, the proceeds usually
arrive by wire, and if you you buying
one, you usually send one. Criminals
watch for exactly that moment. An email
arrives that looks like it came from
your title company or your lawyer with
new wiring instructions, often marked
urgent. In its latest report, the FBI
says people over 60 lost more than half
a billion dollars in a single year to
schemes built on fake business emails
like that. A wire, once sent, is almost
impossible to pull back. So, before you
send or accept any wire, call the title
company or the lawyer on a phone number
you already had, not a number in the
email, and confirm the instructions out
loud. And a word on keeping too little
in checking, because that costs money,
too. A federal rule that would have
capped overdraft fees at the largest
banks was overturned by Congress last
year in a resolution President Trump
signed, so the fees remain whatever your
bank decides. An account run right down
to zero the week before Social Security
lands is an account that pays overdraft
charges.
That is the other reason the first
number includes a buffer. Let me take
three questions I get asked about this
almost every week. The first, does the
IRS see my Social Security deposits? It
already knows the total. Every January,
Social Security sends you a statement of
your benefits for the year, and the IRS
gets the same figures.
That is not watching your account. That
is the same agency's records being
shared with another part of the
government. Nothing about where you keep
the money changes it. The second, if I
take out $10,000 in cash to pay for
something, will I be reported? Only if
it is more than 10,000 in cash in one
business day. Exactly 10,000 does not
trigger it. More than that does, whether
it is coming in or going out. And if you
are withdrawing that much cash because
somebody on the phone told you to, stop
right there, hang up, and call somebody
you trust, because that is one of the
most common ways people lose money right
now. The third, can my bank close my
account for no reason? It can close an
account under the terms of your account
agreement. And if the closure follows a
report the bank filed, the law forbids
it from telling you about that report.
That is frustrating, but it is how the
system is built. The protection is not
avoiding banks. It is making sure that
nothing you do with your money looks
like something it is not.
One clear deposit with an explanation
instead of five small ones without. And
two questions that came up so often I
want to add them.
Is it safer just to keep cash at home? I
understand the instinct, especially for
anybody who remembers a bank failing.
But cash at home has no deposit
insurance. It is the first thing a
burglar or a fire takes, and it creates
every problem I have described today the
day you finally need to deposit it.
A large amount walking into a bank at
once means a report.
Walking in a piece at a time looks like
structuring. And if Medicaid ever
reviews your finances, money that moved
in and out of a coffee can leaves no
trail at all.
A modest amount for emergencies, a few
hundred dollars, a week of groceries, is
sensible.
Thousands in a closet is not. And should
I add my son or daughter to my checking
account so they can help?
There is a better tool. Most banks now
offer a way to give a family member view
only access or to name a trusted person
who can be called if something looks
wrong without making them an owner. When
you make a child a joint owner, the
account becomes partly theirs. And their
creditors, and in some cases the IRS if
they owe back taxes, can reach it. I
have gone through that one in an earlier
video. Ask your bank what view only and
trusted contact options it has before
you add anybody's name to the account
itself. One last quiet rule about the
second account that a lot of you keep
and never touch. The old savings account
at a bank from 20 years ago.
If you do not make any contact with an
account for a few years, usually three
to five depending on the state, the bank
is required to turn the money over to
the state as unclaimed property. You can
claim it back for free through your
state's unclaimed property office, but
you have to know to look.
Log in to every account you own or make
one small transaction in it at least
once a year. Now, if I could get you to
do one thing after this video, it would
not be moving money. It would be the
two-minute habit. Once a month, when
your statement arrives, look for three
things. Any check you did not write or
any amount that looks different from
what you remember writing. Any interest
line at all, so you know what that
account actually earned. And the balance
compared with the first of my four
numbers. If it is more than about two
months of spending, move the extra to
your savings across the moat. That is
all. Two minutes every month. That
single habit covers the check fraud
clock, the IRS slip, the garnishment
shield, and the quiet cost all at once.
And if something in your own situation
does not fit any of this, a notice you
are not sure about, a large amount of
cash you need to deposit, a parent's
accounts you are suddenly responsible
for, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com
and tell me what is happening. I read
them myself. It can take a few days to
reply in a busy week, but I do reply.
And a good number of these videos
started as somebody's email. Here's what
I actually believe after going through
all of this.
The fear in the title, the IRS watching
your balance, is the least of your
problems. It is a story that sells
because it gives a shapeless worry a
face.
The real risks to a checking account are
far less dramatic and far more common.
A slip from an account you forgot, a
routine notice answered in a panic, a
garnishment above the line,
five years of cash with no receipts,
a phone call from somebody who sounds
exactly like your bank.
None of those come with a red warning on
a screen. All of them are easier to
prevent than to fix.
And every one of them is smaller if the
account that has every door attached
only holds what it needs to hold.
If you want all of this written down in
one place, the four numbers, the
notices, and the phone rules, the quiet
rules is linked in the description and
pinned at the top of the comments. I am
Kevin. Thanks for watching.
Do not forget to check the quiet rules
at kevinexplains.shop.

title: Seniors 65+: 5 Bills You No Longer Have to Pay, Most Keep Paying Anyway

segments.text: There are five bills coming to your
house this year that the law says you no
longer have to pay in full once you are
65. And not one of the offices that
collects them is required to tell you.
They just keep sending the bill. Being
exempt and actually paying less are two
completely different things. And the
only bridge between them is a form that
you have to file yourself. Nobody files
it for you. But here is what makes this
list different from the ones you have
probably already seen. On four of these
five bills, the number most people have
been told is already out of date. Texas
changed its numbers last November.
Florida has a catch that almost every
list leaves out. The Medicare figure
everybody quotes is last year's. And the
list of states that tax your Social
Security shrank again in January. An old
number is not harmless. It is the most
common reason people look at a benefit,
decide it is not for them, and keep
paying a bill they do not owe. So, on
every one of these, I will give you the
current number and tell you exactly
where it comes from. And stay to the end
for this.
If you have lost a husband or a wife or
you are ever going to sell a house you
shared, there is a 2-year clock that
almost nobody is told about. On the
right side of it, the sale can cost you
nothing in federal tax. One day past it,
the very same sale can cost tens of
thousands of dollars. I will show you
exactly how it works before we finish.
Before we start, tell me your state in
the comments. On two of these five
bills, the answer depends entirely on
where you live, and I read every one of
them. My name is Kevin. I read the rules
so you do not have to. And if you would
like the next one of these before it
lands in your mailbox, subscribe now.
Every figure in this video comes from
the agency that sets it. And every
source is listed in the description. So,
if you want to check me, please do. I am
not a tax preparer, a lawyer, or a
financial adviser. This is education,
not advice about your own money. One
more thing before bill one. As we go, I
will put one of two labels on each item.
Age only or income tested. Age only
means nobody asks what you earn. You
qualify by having a birthday.
Incomeested means there is a limit. And
I will give you the real limit because
they are almost always higher than
people expect. That way, nobody watching
has to guess whether this is for them.
Bill number one is your federal income
tax, and this one is age only, up to a
point. Since last year, someone 65 or
older gets three separate deductions
stacked on top of each other. And the
most common mistake is getting two of
them and stopping. The first is the
regular standard deduction. for this
year. According to the IRS, it is
for a single person and 32,200 for a
married couple. The second is the extra
amount for being 65 or older, which has
been in the tax code for decades. For
this year, $2,50 if you are single and
$1,650 for each spouse who is 65 if you
are married. And the third is the new
one from the law President Trump signed
last July, up to $6,000 for each person
65 or older. Add them together, a single
person over 65, can have $24,150
of income before a single dollar is
taxed. A married couple, both over 65,
And if you have seen those numbers
quoted a little lower, 15,750
those were last year's figures. They
went up in January. Now, the label I
promised. The first two are age only.
The third, the new 6,000 has an income
limit. It starts to shrink once your
income passes $75,000 single or 150,000
for a couple and it is gone completely
single or 250,000 for a couple. For most
people watching, that limit never
touches you and it is temporary. It runs
through the 2028 tax year and then
disappears unless Congress extends it.
Here are two details I have not heard
anybody else explain. The first is for
people who itemize. If you have large
medical bills or big property taxes and
you itemize instead of taking the
standard deduction, you lose the old age
65 addition because it is part of the
standard deduction, but you do not lose
the new 6,000. That one can be claimed
either way. A lot of itemizers assume
none of the senior breaks apply to them
and they are leaving that money on the
table. The second is about whether you
need to file at all. If your only income
is social security and none of it is
taxable, you generally do not have to
file a federal return. And for everybody
else, the line that decides whether you
must file is your standard deduction
plus the age addition. For a single
person over 65 this year, that is
of income that counts. The new senior
deduction does not raise that line. So,
some people who owe nothing still have
to file, and some people who have been
paying somebody $200 or $300 every
spring to file a return never needed to
file one at all. If you are not sure
which you are, the IRS has a free tool
on its website that asks you a handful
of questions and tells you. It is called
plainly enough, do I need to file a tax
return? Bill number two is your property
tax. And this is where the largest
amounts hide because it is not one
break, it is three stacked. and very few
homeowners have all three on file. The
first is the homestead exemption, which
takes a slice off your home's value
before the bill is calculated. The
second is the senior exemption, a
separate application layered on top. And
the third, in the states that have it,
is a freeze. Once it is on file, part or
all of your bill or your home's taxable
value stops going up, no matter what
your neighborhood does. Texas is the
clearest example and the most out ofd on
most lists. Last November, Texas voters
approved two changes and they took
effect this January. The general
homestead exemption for school taxes
And the extra exemption for homeowners
65 and older or disabled went from
$10,000 to 60,000. So, a Texas homeowner
over 65 now has $200,000 of value taken
off before the school district
calculates its share. And on top of that
sits the over 65 ceiling, which freezes
your school tax at the amount it was in
the year you qualified. Age only. Texas
does not ask about your income for any
of it. And there is a Texas rule that is
worth real money to anybody who turned
65 a while ago and never filed. Under
the Texas Tax Code, you can file a late
application for those exemptions up to
two years after the date the taxes
became delinquent and get a refund of
what you overpaid. 2 years, not five,
not forever. Vera learned that rule a
year too late. 71, a retired dental
hygienist in a suburb of San Antonio.
She turned 65, retired, and assumed that
because she already had her homestead
exemption, the senior one came with it
automatically. It does not. For 6 years,
her school taxes kept climbing on a
house that had more than doubled in
value. When her nephew finally looked at
the tax statement, the over 65 line was
blank. She filed that week. The county
refunded what the law allowed, roughly 2
years. The four years before that, a
little over $9,000 were gone for good.
And the only thing between Vera and that
money was one form she did not know was
separate from the other one. That is the
whole problem with these bills. The
exemption exists. The county has the
form and nobody whose job it is to
collect the tax is going to point out
that you are paying too much of it. The
quiet rules is my answer to that. It
holds the list of what to ask for by
name and the deadlines that decide how
far back you can still recover laid out
before the money is gone instead of
after. You can get it at
kevinexplains.shop.
Scan the code on your screen or tap the
first link in the pinned comment. It is
in the description as well. Give it
seven days and if it is not worth
keeping, you can get a refund. Vera
still has the tax statement her nephew
circled. One empty box on page one and
six years of bills that were bigger than
they ever had to be. Now, Florida,
because this is the catch most lists
leave out. Florida's homestead exemption
can take up to $50,000 off your home's
value. And that part has no income test.
But the extra senior exemption you hear
about, another 50,000 off for people 65
and older, is not automatic and not
statewide. Each county and city decides
whether to offer it, and it has an
income limit. According to the Florida
Department of Revenue, for this year,
your household income has to be no more
It also only applies to county and city
taxes, not to school taxes. So, if
somebody told you that in Florida, age
is the only test. For this one, it is
not. There is a second larger version,
too. If you are 65, have lived in your
home at least 25 years, the home is
worth less than $250,000,
and you are under that same income
limit, some counties exempt the entire
value from their portion of the tax.
Your county property appraisers office
can tell you in one phone call which of
these your county offers, and in the
rest of the country, the pattern is the
same three layers under different names.
Some states freeze the assessed value.
Some offer a credit based on your
income, often called a circuit breaker.
And several, including California,
Washington, and Oregon, let older
homeowners postpone their property tax
entirely, with the unpaid amount simply
settled when the house is eventually
sold. That last one is income tested,
and it is not for everybody, but for a
widow on a fixed income in a house that
has tripled in value, it can be the
difference between staying and selling.
So, the one call for bill two is to your
county assessor or property appraiser.
Ask by name. Is my homestead exemption
on file? Is the senior exemption on
file? And is there a freeze, a ceiling,
or a deferral I qualify for. If
something is missing, ask how far back
you can still file? And write the answer
down. And one timing rule worth knowing
if your birthday is coming up. In Texas
and a number of other states, the senior
exemption applies to the whole tax year
in which you turn 65, not just the
months after your birthday. So, someone
who turns 65 in November can still get
the full year's exemption. Ask your
county whether yours works the same way.
Bill number three is your Medicare Part
B premium, and the number most people
have in their head is last year's. For
this year, according to the Centers for
Medicare and Medicaid Services, the
standard part B premium is $22.90
a month. Last year, it was $185.
It comes straight out of your Social
Security check, so most people never
actually see it leave. This one is
income tested and the limits are higher
than almost anybody guesses. There are
three Medicare savings programs and if
you qualify for any of them, your state
pays that premium for you every month
from then on. The most generous one
called QMB pays the premium and most of
your deductibles and co-pays as well.
For this year, the income limit is about
a month for one person or $1,824
for a couple. The middle one pays only
the premium with a limit of about $1,616
for one person and $2,184
for a couple. And the third goes up to
about $1,816
for one person and $2,455
for a couple. And those are not quite
the hard lines they look like. The first
$20 of most income is not counted. And
many states use their own higher limits.
There is an asset limit as well.
Federally, it is a little under $10,000
for one person and roughly 15,000 for a
couple. And your home, one car, and
certain burial funds do not count toward
it. And about a dozen states, plus
Washington DC, do not count assets at
all. New York, Massachusetts,
Connecticut, Arizona, and Oregon are
among them. If you live in one of those,
your savings simply do not matter for
this. And here is why this one is worth
the call. Even if you think you are
close to the line, qualifying for any
Medicare savings program automatically
qualifies you for extra help with your
drug plan, which lowers your premiums
and co-pays for prescriptions. Two
benefits from one application. And for
everybody, whatever your income, one
more drug cost change worth knowing.
This year, the most you can be charged
out of your own pocket for covered drugs
on a Part D plan is $2,100 for the whole
year. After that, you pay nothing for
covered drugs for the rest of the year.
And if a big prescription hits all at
once in January, there is a free option
called the Medicare prescription payment
plan. Your plan spreads those costs into
monthly amounts across the year instead
of making you pay them at the pharmacy
counter. You have to ask your plan to
sign you up. It is not automatic. The
call for bill 3 is to your state's free
Medicare counseling program called SHIP
or your state Medicaid office. Ask them
to screen you for a Medicare savings
program and extra help. It costs nothing
and the counselors do this all day. Bill
number four is state income tax on your
social security and your retirement
income. And this list has changed again.
Right now only eight states still tax
social security in any form. Colorado,
Connecticut, Minnesota, Montana, New
Mexico, Rhode Island, Utah, and Vermont.
West Virginia finished phasing its tax
out for this year. So if you see it on a
list, the list is old. And every one of
those eight has exemptions that protect
many retirees. Minnesota, for example,
exempts social security entirely for
single people with income up to about
So if you live in one of those states,
do not assume you owe it. Look up your
state's exemption or ask whoever does
your return to show you the line where
it was applied. But here is the bigger
opportunity, and almost nobody talks
about it. Social Security is only part
of your income. Your pension, your IRA
withdrawals, your annuity, those are
where most of the state tax actually
lands. And a lot of states have
exclusions for retirement income that
most people never claim properly.
Illinois, Mississippi, and Pennsylvania
do not tax most retirement income at
all. Georgia lets each person 65 or
older exclude up to $65,000 of
retirement income. New York excludes up
to $20,000 of pension and annuity income
for each person over 59 and a half.
These exclusions are age-based and they
are claimed on the state return line by
line. If your return is prepared by
software, make sure your date of birth
is entered correctly because that single
field is often what turns these on.
Before bill five, let me keep the
promise I made at the start because this
one is worth more than everything else
in this video put together for the
people it applies to. The 2-year clock
on the house. When you sell a home you
have owned and lived in for at least two
of the last 5 years, you can exclude a
large part of the profit from federal
tax. Up to $250,000 of gain for a single
person, and up to $500,000 for a married
couple filing jointly. That much most
people have heard. Here is the part they
have not. If your husband or wife dies,
you do not drop to the single limit
straight away. Under the rules the IRS
lays out in its own guide to selling
your home, a surviving spouse who is not
remarried can still use the full
$500,000 exclusion if the house is sold
within 2 years of the date of death. 2
years. On day 731, the limit falls to
And there is a second rule working in
your favor at the same time. When a
spouse dies, their half of the house
gets a new cost basis equal to what it
was worth on the day they died. In
community property states, which include
California, Texas, Arizona, and
Washington, the whole house can get that
new basis. Either way, a big chunk of
the old gain simply disappears. Put the
two together and look at what the
calendar can do. Royce and his wife
bought their house in New Jersey in the
When she died, it was worth about
Her half got the new basis. His half
kept the old one. So, the gain on a sale
came to roughly $475,000
inside 2 years under the $500,000 limit.
The federal tax on that sale was zero.
Royce was in no state to make decisions
that first year, and nobody pushed him.
He sold about 2 and 1/2 years later.
same house, nearly the same price.
of that gain was now taxable, and his
federal bill came to more than $33,000.
paid for 6 months of grief that nobody
warned him had a deadline attached. I am
not saying anybody should sell a home in
the first year after losing a spouse.
Often the wisest thing is to change
nothing at all for a while. But the
decision should be made knowing that the
clock exists, not discovered afterward
on a tax return. That is the kind of
rule I put in the quiet rules, the ones
with a date attached, written down
plainly, so the person going through the
worst year of their life does not also
have to find them alone. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
The code on your screen opens it and the
link is pinned in the comments and in
the description. You have 7 days to
decide whether it earns its place. And
if it does not, you get a refund. What
Royce kept from that year was a closing
statement and a second envelope from his
accountant with one number on it he
still cannot quite believe. If that is
you, or it might be someday, there are
two things to do now, not later. Get an
appraisal of the house as of the date of
death while it is easy to establish, and
put the 2-year date on the calendar
where you will see it. Then decide
calmly with that date in front of you.
Bill number five is not one bill. It is
the small monthly ones that nobody ever
audits and together they can add up to
more than any single item on this list.
Start with your car insurance because
this one is age only and almost nobody
asks for it. According to CNBC, 34
states in Washington DC require insurers
to give a discount to older drivers who
complete a state approved defensive
driving course. The discount is often up
to 15%. It usually lasts 3 years before
you retake the course. And many of the
courses can be done online in an
afternoon. For a 60-year-old with full
coverage, Bank Rate estimated a 15%
discount at a little over $300 a year.
And while you are on the phone with the
insurer, tell them how many miles you
actually drive now. A lot of retirees
are still being priced on the commute
they stopped making years ago. Next,
your phone or internet bill. A federal
program called Lifeline takes $9.25 a
month off one phone or internet service
and more in some states that add their
own discount. It is income- tested and
if you are already on Medicaid, food
assistance, or supplemental security
income, you usually qualify
automatically. And a correction on this
one because it still comes up in the
comments. The larger internet discount
from a few years ago, the affordable
connectivity program, ran out of money
and ended in 2024. If somebody calls
offering to sign you up for it, that
call is not real. And heating. The
federal home energy program known as Lee
HEAP helps pay heating and cooling bills
for households under its income limits
and older households get priority in
most states. Here is why I am mentioning
it this month in particular. The program
was fully funded for this winter, about
$4 billion, after Congress turned down a
proposal to eliminate it. But the
administration has proposed eliminating
it again for next year. Most states hand
out this money first come, first served.
And when a state share runs out, it runs
out. If you think you might qualify,
apply this fall, not in February. And
one last small one that applies to
almost everybody, look at your bank
account. Many banks have a checking
account for customers over a certain
age. often 55 or 62 with no monthly fee
and free checks. Your bank will not move
you to it on its own. You have to ask.
And a word for anybody who rents. You
are paying property tax, too. It is just
folded into your rent. And several
states give older renters a share of it
back. Pennsylvania, for example, refunds
up to $1,000 a year of property tax or
rent to older residents under its income
limit. Minnesota has a renters's credit,
and a few other states have their own
versions. These are income tested. They
usually require an application every
year and they are among the least
claimed benefits in the country simply
because renters assume property tax
relief is only for owners. If you rent,
search your state's name and the words
renter rebate or ask your local area
agency on aging. And one more property
tax move that has nothing to do with
your age and that people over 65 use far
less than anybody else. Your exemptions
come off your home's assessed value. But
if that value is wrong to begin with,
every exemption is being subtracted from
a number that is too high. Every county
lets you appeal your assessment, usually
within a short window after the notice
arrives, often 30 to 60 days, and in
Texas, generally by the 15th of May. You
do not need a lawyer. You need the
assessor's record of your house to check
that the square footage, the number of
bathrooms, and the condition are right.
and the sale prices of three or four
similar homes nearby. Errors on those
records are common. A house recorded
with a finished basement it does not
have or a bathroom that was never built
gets taxed for them every year until
somebody objects. And keep the
assessment notice when it comes. It is
the one piece of mail that starts that
clock. Now, getting these benefits is
only half of it. Here are three ways
people lose them after they already have
them, usually without noticing for a
year or two. The first is a new deed. If
you move your house into a living trust,
add a child to the title, or refinance
and sign new paperwork, in many
counties, the exemptions can drop off
the rolls until you file again. The tax
office does not always tell you. The
first sign is a bigger bill. So, anytime
the paperwork on your house changes,
call the assessor afterward and ask one
question. Are all my exemptions still on
file? The second is the yearly renewal.
The income tested programs, the Medicare
savings programs, extra help, the
Florida senior exemption, the renter
rebates have to be renewed. Florida, for
example, asks for a statement of
household income every year to keep the
senior exemption. Medicaid offices mail
renewal forms for the Medicare savings
programs, and if the form is not
returned, the help simply stops and the
part B premium starts coming out of your
Social Security check again. Open
anything that arrives from your state's
Medicaid office or your county the week
it comes. The third is a move. Every one
of these property breaks is tied to the
house you live in. Move across the
county and you start again with the new
house. Move in with a son or daughter
for a while or into assisted living. And
some states keep your exemption on the
old house and some do not. If a move is
coming, ask before you go, not after. So
those are the five bills. Now, for those
of you who have built up savings, a
house, a retirement account, a
portfolio, here are three more doors,
and they tend to be worth the most. The
first is a tax rate of zero on your
investment gains. For this year, a
single person with taxable income up to
or a married couple up to $98,900
pays nothing in federal tax on long-term
capital gains. That is taxable income
after deductions. And this is where the
new senior deduction quietly helps in a
way I have never heard anybody point
out. It lowers your taxable income,
which is the exact number that decides
whether your gains fall into that zero
bracket. So, a couple over 65 has
$12,000 more room in the zero bracket
than they had 2 years ago. If you have
shares you have been meaning to sell or
a fund you want to rebalance, the years
when your income is low are the years to
do it and the room is bigger now than it
has ever been. One caution, this is the
exact place where one rule can work
against another. Capital gains still
count in the income Medicare uses for
its search charge and in the formula
that decides how much of your social
security is taxed, which I covered in
detail in my last two videos. So, the 0%
bracket is real, but a large sale can
still push you over a Medicare line. Run
both numbers before you sell. The second
door is for anybody who claims Social
Security in the last 12 months and
wishes they had not. There is a form
called the SSA521.
It lets you withdraw your application
completely as if you had never filed.
You repay what you have received. There
is no interest charged and your benefit
then keeps growing for every month you
wait up to age 70. You can only do this
once in your lifetime and only within 12
months of when you first became
entitled. If you are inside that window
and you rushed into claiming because of
a scary headline, this is the one form
that lets you take it back. The third
door is for widows and widowers. Again,
if your husband or wife paid into Social
Security, you may be entitled to a
survivor benefit on their record as
early as age 60. And you can sometimes
take one benefit first and switch to the
other later. For example, the survivor
benefit now and your own at 70 if yours
grows larger. Social Security will
process whichever one you apply for, but
it is not their job to tell you which
order pays you the most over your
lifetime. Ask them to show you both
numbers in writing before you sign
anything. And for anybody 70 and a half
or older who gives to charity, the gift
can come straight from your IRA up to
this year and it counts toward your
required withdrawal without ever showing
up as income. Most people who give
simply write a check from their checking
account and get no tax benefit at all
because they take the standard
deduction. The same gift sent directly
from the IRA lowers the tax bill. And if
your return is fairly simple, social
security, a pension, some IRA
withdrawals, do not forget that there is
free help. The IRS runs a program called
tax counseling for the elderly for
people 60 and older. And the largest
version of it is AARP tax aid. You do
not have to be an AARP member to use it.
Every item I have described today on
your federal return, the volunteers
there have been trained to look for.
Now, here is what I would like you to do
with all of this. Not five phone calls
this afternoon, just a single sheet of
paper with five lines on it, one for
each bill. On each line, write the
number you had in your head before this
video. Then next to it, write the
current number, the deduction for
someone your age. And if last year's
return did not include the new senior
deduction, it is not too late. You can
generally file an amended return, the
form 1040x, within 3 years and claim it.
the exemptions on your property tax
statement, the Medicare premium and the
limits for help with it, your state's
rule on your social security and your
pension, and the small bills: insurance,
phone, heat, bank. Anywhere the two
numbers do not match, that line becomes
your call this month. Most people who do
this find at least two lines where they
had been working from an old number or
no number at all. And if your own
situation does not fit neatly into any
of this, a property tax statement you
cannot make sense of, a house you
inherited from a spouse, a social
security claim you are not sure about,
write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com
and tell me what is going on. I read
them myself. In a busy week, it may take
me a few days to answer, but I do
answer. And quite a few of these videos
started with somebody's email. Here is
what I actually think about all of this.
Not one of these breaks was hidden on
purpose. They are all written into law
in public with forms you can download.
But the system is built so that the bill
arrives automatically and the exemption
does not. Your tax bill comes to you.
The senior exemption waits for you to
come to it. And every year that goes by
without the form, the money is not
delayed. It is gone except for whatever
narrow window the law allows you to
reach back. That is why the old numbers
matter so much. A person who thinks the
Texas exemption is $10,000 or that
Florida does not care about income or
that the Medicare premium is 185 makes a
perfectly reasonable decision based on
bad information and pays for it every
year after. If you want all of this in
one place with the deadlines and the
exact forms by name, the quiet rules is
linked in the description and pinned at
the top of the comments. I am Kevin.
Thanks for watching. Do not forget to
check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: Check Your Mailbox. 600,000 Seniors Are Losing Their Medicare Plan

segments.text: Check your mailbox this week because
600,000 people are about to find out
their Medicare plan is gone. Not
changed, gone. The letters go out by
Friday, the 2nd of October, and every
one of those 600,000 comes from a single
company. And here is what worries me.
Most people who open that letter will
read the first line, see the same
company name printed on a brand new
plan, and sign it without reading
another word. That is exactly what the
company is counting on. But the 600,000
are not even the people I am most
worried about. At least they get a
letter. The people I am worried about
get no letter at all. Their plan
survives, so nobody writes to them, but
their hospital walks out of it. Or the
extra money their plan was quietly
adding to their social security check
stops on the 1st of January. And the
only way they find out is a smaller
deposit. So, in this video, I'm going to
show you the three kinds of people this
fall is going to hurt and which one you
are. The exact window, 123 days long,
where no insurance company in the
country can turn you down for a
supplement, the line on your social
security statement that can shrink in
January without anybody telling you why.
And near the end, the one protection the
government put into its own draft rules
and then quietly deleted in April.
Nobody has explained that one. I will.
Before we go any further, tell me
something in the comments. Did your
letter come yet? Just type yes or not
yet. It helps me see how many of you are
in this, and I read every one. I am
Kevin. I spend my weeks reading the
rules so you do not have to. And if you
want the next one of these the week it
matters, hit subscribe now. One honest
note first. I do not sell insurance. No
plan and no agent pays me. And this is
education, not advice about your own
coverage. Plans change from one county
to the next. So check yours before you
act. Here is why this is happening.
Because once you see it, you stop taking
it personally. Next year, the government
is actually paying these private
Medicare plans more money, not less,
about 2.5% more, which works out to
roughly 13 billion. And the companies
are cutting anyway. Humanana has told
investors it wants a profit margin of at
least 3% by 2028. And the plans it is
closing are mostly the ones rated three
and a half stars or lower, the ones that
do not earn enough. United Healthcare
shrank by roughly a million Medicare
members over the course of this year.
And one study found that in 2026 about
2.9 million people, roughly 1 in 10
people in these plans were forced out of
the plan they had. When plan executives
were surveyed this summer, nearly seven
in 10 said they expect benefits to be
less generous next year. So, I want to
be plain about my own view. This is not
Medicare falling apart. Your Medicare
card works exactly the same as it did
last week. This is a group of companies
deciding which customers are worth
keeping. And once you understand that,
you stop waiting for them to look after
you and you start reading their mail the
way they wrote it carefully. So, the
three kinds of people. The first kind is
the easiest to spot because they get the
letter. If your plan is ending, federal
rules say you must be told in writing by
the 2nd of October. The letter is
usually titled something like a plan
non-renewal notice. It will tell you
your plan is not continuing next year
that your coverage ends on the 31st of
December. And in most cases, it will
suggest a replacement plan from the same
company. Humanana expects about four in
every 10 of the people it is dropping to
sign up for another Humanana plan. That
is 240,000 people. And I understand why.
The name is familiar. The card looks the
same. It feels like staying put, but it
is not the same plan. A different plan
can have a different list of doctors and
hospitals. Your drugs can land on a
different tier or suddenly need
permission first. And the most you can
be made to pay in a year can be
thousands of dollars higher. Next year,
an advantage plan can make you pay up to
for care inside its network. And a plan
that also covers care outside its
network can go up to 14,800 combined.
So, if you sign the replacement, sign it
because you checked it, not because it
looked like home. Now, here's the good
news for this first group, and it is
real good news. When your plan ends, the
rules hand you rights that almost nobody
else gets. The first is time. You get
the normal window everybody gets from
the 15th of October to the 7th of
December. And on top of that, you get a
special window of your own from the 8th
of December to the last day of February.
The second right is the valuable one.
Because your plan is ending and it was
not your choice. You have a guaranteed
right to buy a Medicare supplement
policy with no health questions. They
cannot turn you down for your heart.
They cannot charge you more for your
diabetes. And the timing of that right
is the part almost everybody gets wrong.
It does not start when your plan ends.
It starts 60 days before. Your plan ends
on the 31st of December. So, your window
opens on the 1st of November, and it
stays open until 63 days after your
coverage ends, which is the 4th of
March, 123 days. The supplement plans
covered by that guarantee are lettered
A, B, D, G, K, and L, plus C, and F if
you were eligible for Medicare before
2020. Plan N, which a lot of people ask
about, is not on that federal list. And
keep that letter. When you apply, the
insurance company may ask for proof that
you qualify, and that letter is the
proof. Without it, your application can
be treated like anybody else's with the
health questions included. And now, the
trap inside the good news. That special
window running into February sounds like
extra time. It is not free time. If your
plan ends on the 31st of December, and
you have not chosen anything, you do not
stay covered while you think. You are
moved back to original Medicare on the
1st of January. No drug plan, no
supplement, just Medicare, paying its
share and leaving you with the rest.
Nowhere found out what that costs.
73. A retired dental hygienist in
Western Pennsylvania. She got her letter
in October, read that she had until
February, and decided to wait until
after the holidays when things were
calmer. In the second week of February,
she picked a new plan. It started on the
1st of March. For January and February,
she had no drug coverage at all. She
paid full price for an inhaler and two
maintenance drugs, about $900 in 8
weeks. And she was lucky on one thing
she did not even know about. The gap was
just under 63 days, which is the point
where a lifetime late penalty on drug
coverage begins. She missed it by a
handful of days, entirely by accident.
The extra time was never a gift. It was
a lifeline for people who find out late.
If you already have the letter, use the
normal window and choose by the 7th of
December. So, your new coverage starts
on the 1st of January, the same morning
the old one ends. That single decision
about the calendar is worth more than
any comparison chart you will ever look
at. That is the whole reason the quiet
rules exists, not to hand you another
brochure, but to put the order of things
in front of you before a company's
deadline decides it for you. Because
Lenor did not need more information. She
had the letter in her hand. She needed
somebody to tell her which date actually
mattered. You can open it at
kevinexplains.shop
or point your phone camera at the square
code on the screen right now or tap the
first link in the pinned comment. It is
in the description as well. Take a full
7 days with it. If it has not saved you
more than it cost, you can get a refund
and that is the end of it. Because
otherwise, February looks like it did
for Lenor. sitting at her kitchen table
with a pharmacy receipt in one hand and
a phone in the other on hold with a plan
that had not even started yet. The
second kind of person is the one I think
about most because nothing about this
looks like an emergency. Your plan is
continuing no non-renewal letter.
Instead, by the 30th of September, you
get the thick one, the annual notice of
change. It lists everything that is
different next year, and most of it is
buried on page four and after in
language written to be skimmed. This
year, there is one line in it I want
every one of you to find, and it
connects straight to your Social
Security. Some Advantage plans pay part
of your Medicare Part B premium for you.
The industry calls it a give back. In
the notice, it is usually listed as a
Part B premium reduction. You never see
it arrive as a check. It shows up as a
smaller part B deduction, which makes
your social security deposit a little
bigger every month. $10 in some places,
50 or 100 in others. And after a year or
two, you stop noticing it. It just
becomes what your deposit is. The give
back is one of the first things insurers
are cutting for next year. So, if your
plan drops it, that extra money stops on
the 1st of January, and nobody from
Social Security will write to explain
why your deposit went down. The plan
told you once on page four. Now watch
what January does to that. On the 14th
of October, Social Security announces
next year's raise. The forecasts are
around 3.5%.
On a $2,000 monthly benefit, that is
about $70. Then the Part B premium comes
out. Medicare's trustees project it
rising from $22.90
to about $29.50.
So, you are down to about 63. Now, take
away a $50 give back that ended. Your
raise is about $13. And the cruel part
is the timing. It all lands in the same
deposit. So, most people assume the
raise was simply smaller than the news
said and never connect it to their
health plan at all. One more thing about
timing. Changes like this can take
Social Security a month or more to catch
up. So, if your January deposit looks
untouched, do not spend the difference
yet. Check February and March, too.
There is a second Social Security trap
for anyone who leaves an Advantage plan
for original Medicare with a separate
drug plan. You can have that drug plan's
premium taken out of your Social
Security, but it can take up to 3 months
to start. Until it does, the plan sends
you a bill. People who ask for the
deduction assume those bills are a
mistake and put them in a drawer. They
are not a mistake. Unpaid premiums can
get you dropped from the plan after a
grace period. So pay the bills until you
see the deduction on your statement with
your own eyes. The give back is not the
only thing shrinking. Most plans are
keeping their $0 premium next year
because that is the number on the
advertisement. What moves instead is
everything around it. Dental allowances
getting smaller, grocery and
over-the-counter cards cut back,
specialist co-pays going up. And here is
my honest opinion on that. The zero
premium is the bait. The out-ofpocket
maximum is the price. When you compare
plans this year, look at that maximum
first and your own drug second and the
extras last. Almost everybody does it in
the opposite order. And one small
practical thing about those extras
because this is the time of year it
pays. Most dental allowances and
over-the-counter card balances do not
roll over. Whatever is left on the 31st
of December simply disappears. And if
your plan is ending or its allowance is
shrinking, next year's version may be
smaller or gone. So, if you have a
cleaning, a filling, or a pair of
glasses you have been putting off, book
it now while this year's allowance still
exists, check the balance on your card
this week. It is money you have already
been promised, and the plan will not
remind you that it is about to expire.
And one detail for anybody who is in the
middle of treatment and thinking of
switching when you move to a different
plan, the permission your old plan gave
you for a surgery, a scan, or a course
of therapy does not come with you. The
new plan can make your doctor ask again.
There is one real protection. If you
join a new advantage plan while you are
in an active course of treatment, that
plan must give you at least 90 days
before it can require new permission for
that treatment. 90 days, not forever.
So, if you switch, have your doctor's
office send the new plan your treatment
records in the first week of January,
not the week you run out. The third kind
of person has it worst, and they are the
least likely to know it. Their plan is
fine, their premium is fine, but the
hospital they trust has just walked out
of it. This fall, at least 33 health
systems around the country have ended or
are about to end contracts with one
Medicare Advantage insurer or another,
and the list keeps growing. On the 1st
of October, Ohio State's hospitals and
its cancer center go out of network for
people on Humanana's individual
advantage plans in Columbus. In
Southwest Florida, Lee Health is leaving
United Healthc Care's Advantage plans at
the end of the year. In Minneapolis,
Fairview stops scheduling United
Healthcare Advantage patients on the 1st
of January. Mayo Clinic is already out
of network with most United Healthcare
and Humanana Advantage plans. None of
those people got a non-renewal letter.
Their plans are continuing. So, in the
eyes of the rules, nothing happened to
them. Here is what you are actually owed
when a provider leaves your plan. A
written notice at least 30 days ahead or
45 days if it is your primary care
doctor. Emergency care is still covered
at the in network rate anywhere. And
that is almost the whole list. You do
not get a special window to leave. You
do not get the guaranteed right to a
supplement. Losing your hospital on its
own is not a qualifying event. And that
brings me to the thing I promised you at
the start. Last November, the government
published its draft rules for next
year's Medicare plans. In that draft was
a brand new special enrollment period, a
way out for people whose doctors and
hospitals leave their plan. Hospital
groups supported it. In April, the final
rules came out. That protection was not
in them. It was dropped with no
explanation. The same final rules also
removed a requirement that agents point
callers to the free government-f funed
counselors in every state. So when
people say the system is being made
simpler, I would ask simpler for whom?
Put those two facts next to each other
and something strange falls out. If your
hospital leaves your plan and you stay,
you get a notice and nothing else. But
if you are in active treatment and you
switch to a new plan that does include
your hospital, you get that 90-day
protection I mentioned a moment ago. In
other words, the rules protect the
person who moves, not the person who
waits. The open window from the 15th of
October to the 7th of December is your
one clean chance to act on that. And the
only question worth asking about any
plan you are handed is this. Is my
hospital in it on the 1st of January in
writing, not is it in the directory.
Directories are wrong often enough that
you should call the hospital's own
billing office and ask them which plans
they will accept next year. They know.
They are the ones who walked out. And if
you truly cannot leave, there is one
more lever. If your plan no longer has
any doctor in its network who can
provide the care you need within a
reasonable distance, the plan is
supposed to arrange that care outside
the network at your in-et network cost.
Most people never ask. Ask in writing
and keep the reply. Ambrose learned what
that gap costs. 69. A retired
electrician in southern Minnesota. For
six years, his cardiologist and his
hospital were in his plans network last
fall. The hospital system and his
insurer could not agree on a contract.
He got a notice. He assumed it was the
kind of standoff that always gets
settled at the last minute and he kept
the plan. It was not settled. This
February, he needed a planned procedure
on his heart, booked with the same
cardiologist at the same hospital. And
because his plan was an HMO, care
outside the network that was not an
emergency was simply not covered. The
bill was a little over $11,000.
And the notice that could have saved it
arrived months earlier in a plain
envelope in language that never once
said you should leave. I wrote the quiet
rules for exactly that kind of letter.
The one that is technically honest and
practically useless. It walks you
through what a notice actually means for
you and which calls to make while you
still have a window to use the answer.
The address is kevvenexplains.shop.
You can also scan the code on your
screen with your phone or use the link
pinned at the top of the comments and it
sits in the description, too. You have 7
days to decide it was worth it. And if
it was not, you get a refund. No
questions. Because the alternative is
sitting where Ambrose sat in March at a
billing office window holding a
statement for a heart procedure being
told politely that his plan had no
obligation to pay a hospital it no
longer had a contract with. Now I want
to talk about help because every one of
these letters sends you looking for it.
And the help you are most likely to find
this month is an insurance agent often
advertised as a free service. Many of
them are good at their jobs. But free to
you is not the same as unpaid. Agents
are generally paid by the insurance
company when you enroll. And some plans
pay them more than others. That is not a
scandal. It is simply how it works. And
it is worth knowing before you sit down.
This year, agents can also meet you and
enroll you in a single visit since the
old 48 hour waiting rule is gone and the
new rules cut how long sales calls have
to be kept on record from 10 years to
three. So, here is what I would do.
Before you speak to any agent, call your
state health insurance assistance
program. Every state has one. It is
funded by the federal government. The
counselors are trained and they do not
earn a commission on anything you
choose. Some states call it by a
different name. The easiest way to reach
yours is to call 1800 Medicare and ask
for the state health insurance
assistance program in your state. In the
busiest weeks, you may wait for an
appointment, which is one more reason to
call in early October rather than the
first week of December. And whoever
helps you, agent or counselor, ask for
your plan comparison in writing with
your doctors and your drugs listed by
name. [clears throat] A written
comparison is something you can hold
them to. A conversation is not. There is
one more thing coming in October that
almost nobody watches, and I think it is
the most useful early warning on this
whole list. In the first half of the
month, Medicare publishes its new star
ratings for every plan from one star to
five. Most people treat stars like
restaurant reviews. They are more than
that. Remember who is being cut this
year. Mostly plans at three and a half
stars or lower. Low ratings mean lower
bonus payments from the government. And
lower bonus payments are exactly what
pushes a company to close a plan. So,
when the new ratings appear, look up
your own plan. If it has slipped, that
is not a reason to panic. It is a reason
to think about whether you want to be in
it when next year's letters go out. And
the top of the scale has a rule of its
own. If a plan in your area earns five
stars, you are allowed to switch into it
once almost any time between the 8th of
December and the end of the following
November outside the normal windows.
Five-star plans are rare. For this year,
there were only 18 advantage contracts
with drug coverage rated five stars in
the whole country. But if one covers
your county, that is a door that stays
open nearly all year. Now, how to
compare plans without drowning because
the planfinder can show you 40 options
in a single county and most people give
up after the third. Here is the method I
would use. First, make a free account on
the Medicare website or ask a family
member to set it up with you. The reason
is simple. Once you are logged in, you
can type your drugs in once with the
exact dose and how often you take them
and it remembers them. Without an
account, you end up retyping them every
time and people quietly stop checking.
Second, pick your pharmacy inside the
tool because the same drug can cost very
different amounts at a preferred
pharmacy and a standard one. Third, sort
the results by what the site calls the
estimated total drug and premium cost.
That single number is far more honest
than the premium alone. Then, and only
then, cross off every plan that does not
include your doctors and your hospital.
What survives is usually three or four
plans, not 40. Print that page or ask
someone to print it for you and put it
next to your letter. Let me go through
the questions I get asked most about all
this because they come up every single
fall. The first, can I just go back to
original Medicare in October? Yes.
Between the 15th of October and the 7th
of December, anybody in an advantage
plan can switch back. The catch is the
supplement. Unless your plan is ending
or you are within the first year after
trying an advantage plan for the very
first time or you live in one of the few
states with year- round protections, the
supplement company is allowed to ask
health questions and to say no. So,
never cancel anything first. Apply for
the supplement, wait until it is
approved in writing, and only then make
the switch. Do it in the other order,
and you can end up with original
Medicare alone, paying 20% of every bill
with no ceiling. And while we are on
supplements, there is one question
almost nobody knows to ask, and it
matters more at 75 than at 65. How is
this policy priced as I get older? There
are three ways. Some policies are priced
by your age today and go up as you get
older, which is often called attained
age. Those can look cheapest right now
and climb every birthday. Some are
priced by the age you were when you
bought it, called issue age. So, your
age alone does not push the price up
later. And some charge everybody in the
area the same price regardless of age,
which is called community rated. All
three can still go up with inflation and
rising medical costs, but the difference
over 10 or 15 years can be thousands of
dollars, and it is almost never
mentioned when the first quote is read
out to you. So, ask it by name and ask
whether there is a household discount if
your spouse buys from the same company
because many companies offer one and
very few people ask. The second, my
letter says my plan is being combined
with another one, not ended. Do I get
the supplement guarantee? Usually not.
When your plan is folded into another
plan from the same company, the rules
treat you as moved, not dropped. You get
the normal window everybody gets and
nothing extra. The words on the first
page decide your rights, so read which
word they used. The third, I already
have a supplement and a separate drug
plan. Is any of this about me? The
advantage part is not, but your drug
plan changes every year, too. The
temporary federal program that held down
drug plan premiums has ended. The most
your plan can make you pay before
coverage kicks in rises to $700 next
year. And the yearly ceiling on your
drug costs rises to 2,400.
Your drug plan can also drop a medicine
from its list or move it to a costlier
tier. Compare your plan this fall, even
if everything else in your life is
staying exactly the same. Another one I
get every year. My coverage comes
through my old employer or my union.
Should I switch to one of these plans?
Be very careful here. Retirey coverage
often plays by different rules. In
Columbus, for example, the dispute that
pushed Ohio State's hospitals out of
network hit people on Humanana's
individual advantage plans. While the
group plans that come through employers
kept Ohio State in network, and if you
drop retiree coverage to join an
individual plan, in many cases, you can
never get it back. And sometimes your
spouse loses it, too. Before you touch
it, call your former employer's benefits
office and ask one question. If I leave,
can I ever come back? And another, "What
if I'm in the hospital on New Year's
Eve, the night my old plan ends?" There
is a specific federal rule for that. If
you are admitted as an inpatient while
your old advantage plan is still in
force, that plan stays responsible for
the hospital stay itself until the day
you are discharged, even if it runs well
into January. The new coverage picks up
from there. The hospital's billing
office knows this rule, but it helps to
know it, too, so nobody tells you that
you were uninsured on the morning of the
first. The fourth, what if no letter
ever came? The notice about next year's
changes should have reached you by the
30th of September and non-renewal
letters by the 2nd of October. If yours
has not arrived by the end of the first
week of October, call the member
services number on your card and ask for
it or ask them to email it. You can also
look up your plan on the Medicare
planinder once next year's plans appear
on the 1st of October. Do not assume
that no mail means no change. one
warning before the calendar because
every fall that brings plan
cancellations also brings a wave of
phone calls. Somebody rings and says
they are from Medicare, that your plan
has been cancelled or that your card is
being replaced and they only need to
confirm your Medicare number. Hang up.
Medicare does not call you out of the
blue to ask for your number. And it
never asks you to pay anything to keep
your coverage. Your real letter comes by
mail from your plan with your plan's
name on it. If a call worries you, hang
up and dial the number on the back of
your own card, not a number the caller
gives you. And the letter itself is
worth a second look, too. A few scammers
have copied the look of plan notices. If
anything in yours asks you to call a
number that is not on your card or to
act the same day, check it first. Now,
let me turn all of this into a calendar
because that is where these things are
actually won or lost. By the 2nd of
October, non-renewal letters arrive. If
you get one, put it somewhere you will
not lose it because it is your proof. In
the first half of October, the new star
ratings come out. Look up your own plan.
On the 14th of October, next year's
Social Security raise is announced.
Write the percentage down. You will want
it in January. On the 15th of October,
the window to change plans opens. Call
your state's free counseling program in
that first week before the rush. On the
1st of November, the supplement
guarantee opens for anyone whose plan is
ending. If you want a supplement, apply
in November with your letter attached.
So, it starts on the 1st of January. On
the 7th of December, the main window
closes. If your plan is ending, this is
the date I would treat as your real
deadline, not February. On the 31st of
December, the old plans end in January
and again in February and March. Look at
your actual social security deposit line
by line. Is the part B deduction what
you expected. Did a give back disappear?
Did a drug plan premium start or not
start? The last day of February, the
special window for people whose plans
ended closes. The 4th of March, the
supplement guarantee closes. And the
31st of March, the one change allowed to
people already in an advantage plan
closes as well. If something in your own
situation does not fit anything on that
calendar, maybe you got a letter you
cannot make sense of or your hospital is
in a dispute with your plan right now,
write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com
and tell me what is going on. It can
take me a few days in a busy week, but I
do reply and more than one video on this
channel began with somebody's email.
Here is where I have landed after
spending the last couple of weeks inside
these letters. For years, Medicare
Advantage was sold to people as the easy
choice. One card, no premium, extras
thrown in, and nothing to think about.
And for a lot of people, for a lot of
years, it really was fine. What has
changed is not the promise on the
advertisement. It is who carries the
risk when the promise gets expensive.
When the company's numbers go wrong, the
company can close the plan, trim the
extras, or let a hospital walk away. and
you are the one who finds out in a
mailbox or at a billing window or in a
January deposit that is a few dollars
short. I do not think that makes these
plans bad. I think it makes them a
contract you have to reread every single
fall the way you would reread a lease.
The people who come through this well
are not the smartest ones or the
richest. They are the ones who open the
envelope in October instead of in March.
You're watching this at the end of
September. That puts you ahead of almost
everyone who is going to get that
letter. And if you want all of it in one
place before the 15th, the quiet rules
is linked in the description and pinned
at the top of the comments. I am Kevin.
Thanks for watching. Do not forget to
check the quiet rules at
kevvenexplains.shop.

title: ⚠️ WARNING: The Real October Changes Hitting Your Social Security And Savings

segments.text: You're going to hear two words over and
over this week. October 1st. On the
evening news, in your email, from a
neighbor leaning on the fence, big
changes. And most of what you hear will
be wrong in the same direction. Too
frightening about the wrong things and
completely silent about the right ones.
Because the biggest change to your money
this fall did not happen on October the
1st at all. It already happened on a
Wednesday afternoon 2 weeks ago in a
room in Washington. 12 people voted the
same way and almost nobody watching this
saw it on the front page. Since that
afternoon, your bank has been charging
more to lend money. And in most cases,
it is paying you exactly what it paid
you before. Every day your savings sit
where they are. That gap costs you
something. Then on the 14th of October
at half past 8:00 in the morning, a
number comes out that sets your raise
for next year. If the forecasts hold, it
will be the biggest raise since 2023 and
a slice of it is already spoken for
before it ever reaches your account. So,
here is what we are going to do. First,
I'm going to clear away the five October
rumors you are most likely to hear this
week because every one of them is either
false or out of date. Then I will take
you through the five real changes
between now and the end of October,
ranked from the one that costs you least
if you ignore it to the one that costs
you most. The one at the top is not the
one on the news. And stay for the part
near the end about the 11th of December
because that is the date I would
actually circle on your calendar. Before
any of that, do me a small favor. Tell
me in the comments the wildest thing you
have heard about October the 1st, the
strangest version. I read them and the
best ones will get a straight answer in
a future video. I am Kevin. I read the
rules so you do not have to. And if you
want the next one of these the week it
happens, subscribe now because October
is going to be a busy month. The usual
honest note, I am not a financial
advisor and this is education, not
advice about your own money. Rates and
rules move quickly, so check the current
numbers before you act on any of them.
Rumor number one, your Social Security
check gets cut on October the 1st. It
does not.
Nothing in any law changes the amount of
your benefit on that day.
October the 1st is simply the first day
of the government's budget year, which
is why so many things get scheduled
around it and why so many videos use it
as a headline.
Your October payment arrives on your
normal day for your normal amount.
If you receive Supplemental Security
Income, you will actually see two
payments in October, one on the 1st and
one on the 30th because the 1st of
November falls on a Sunday.
That second payment is simply November's
money arriving early. It is not a bonus,
so please do not spend it as one.
And a small coincidence worth noticing,
the 14th of October, the morning next
year's raise is announced, is also
payday for everybody whose birthday
falls between the 11th and the 20th of
the month. Rumor number two, the
government shuts down on October the
1st. It does not and that one was
settled at the start of this month. On
the 2nd of September, President Trump
signed a stopgap funding law that keeps
the government open through the 11th of
December. I will come back to that date
because it matters far more than October
does, but for now, the offices stay open
and the checks keep coming.
Rumor number three, $2,000 tariff checks
go out in October. They do not. The idea
has been floated by the White House and
bills have been introduced, but Congress
has not approved any such payment. There
is no application. There is no sign up.
There is no fee that gets you one. If
anybody calls, texts, or emails offering
to process your tariff check, it is a
scam every single time. The government
does not call you, text you, or email
you asking for a fee or your bank
details in order to send you money. That
one rule will protect you from most of
what arrives this fall. Rumor number
four, and this one is a little more
complicated. An automatic 4% cut to
Medicare is coming in January. You may
have heard that from people who were
right to worry about it a year ago. An
old budget rule could have triggered an
automatic cut to what Medicare pays
doctors and hospitals because of how
much last year's tax law added to the
deficit. But when Congress reopened the
government last November, it quietly
reset that rule's tally to zero. That 4%
cut is not coming.
A smaller 2% trim that has been in place
for years does continue, but it comes
out of what providers are paid, not out
of your pocket. Rumor number five, banks
will lock older people out of their
accounts on October the 1st. There is no
such rule. What is true is much
narrower, and it is genuinely worth
knowing. Under federal law, banks and
brokerage firms that report suspected
financial exploitation of an older
customer in good faith are protected
when they do it. And brokerage firms are
allowed to place a temporary hold on a
specific withdrawal for a matter of
weeks if they reasonably believe
somebody is taking advantage of you.
That is a pause on one transaction, not
a lock on your account. And there is a
way to make that system work for you.
Brokerage firms are required to ask
whether you want to name a trusted
contact person, somebody they may call
if they cannot reach you or if something
looks wrong.
That person cannot touch a cent of your
money. They are simply a phone number.
If you have not named one, do it. It may
be the cheapest protection in this whole
video. I want to say one thing about all
five of those. Fear is the easiest thing
in the world to sell in October. Every
one of those rumors has somebody behind
it who benefits from you being
frightened. A video that wants your
click, a A who wants your Medicare
number, a salesman who wants you to move
your money in a hurry.
And frightened people make expensive
decisions. Lavinia is a good example.
71, a retired school librarian outside
Cleveland. In August, she watched a
video warning that banks would lock
older customers out of their accounts on
October the 1st. There was no such rule,
but she believed it, and she went to her
bank and broke two certificates of
deposit early to get her money out. The
early withdrawal penalties came to about
Then she did not know where to put the
money, so it went into her checking
account where it earns almost nothing.
The certificates she broke were paying
more than 4%, and 2 weeks later rates
went up. She did everything a careful
person would do with the information she
had. The information was simply wrong.
What Lavinia needed that afternoon was
not courage. It was one calm, reliable
place to check a rumor against the
actual rules before she acted on it.
That is the job I wrote The Quiet Rules
to do. It sits on your shelf so that the
next time somebody tells you something
frightening about your money, you have
somewhere steady to look it up before
you pick up your car keys. Open
kevinexplains.shop
on your phone, or point your camera at
the square code on your screen, or tap
the link at the top of the pinned
comment. The same link sits in the
description below. Take 7 days with it.
If it has not earned its place in that
week, you can get a refund, and nobody
will ask you why. Because the
alternative is Lavinia's afternoon.
Sitting across a desk from a bank
officer, signing a penalty form for
money that was perfectly safe exactly
where it was. So that is what is not
happening. Here is what is. Five real
changes between now and the end of
October, and I am going to count them
down from the one that costs you least
if you ignore it to the one that costs
you most. I will be honest with you.
When I started putting this list
together, I expected the Medicare
changes to land at the top. They did not
come close. Number five. The two changes
that genuinely start on October the 1st
both come from the tax and spending law
President Trump signed in July of last
year, and both reach a narrower group
than the headlines suggest. The first is
food assistance. From October the 1st,
states have to pay 3/4 of the cost of
running the program, up from half. The
benefits themselves are still paid by
Washington, and the maximum for a person
living alone rises to $306 a month. But
the offices that process your
application and your renewal are now
paid for mostly by your state. If your
state trims staff, those applications
may slow down. So, if you get food help
and your renewal is coming up, send it
in early and keep a copy of everything.
And if you were turned down for food
help in the past, it is worth asking
again this month. The income limits
reset every October, and for anybody 60
or older, the test is kinder than most
people realize. You skip the first
income test all together, and medical
costs above $35 a month come off your
income before they decide. The second
change is to Medicaid. From October the
1st, certain lawfully present
immigrants, such as refugees and people
granted asylum, lose eligibility for
federally funded coverage. If you are a
citizen or you hold a green card, it
does not reach you. I am telling you
exactly who it touches, so you can stop
worrying if it does not touch you, and
help somebody if it does. Number four.
Medicare selling season opens, and this
year it opens with the brakes off. I
went through the envelope from your plan
in detail in my last video. So, here is
the short version with the parts that
matter most this week. On October the
1st, the official plan finder switches
over to next year's plans, and the
advertising begins. And the rule that
made an insurance agent wait 48 hours
between agreeing to meet you and sitting
down to sell you a plan is gone from
that same day. An agent can now meet you
and enroll you in a single visit. On the
2nd of October, letters arrive for
people whose plans are ending.
Humana alone is ending plans that cover
about 600,000 people. If one of those
letters is addressed to you, it also
gives you a guaranteed right to buy a
supplement policy with no health
questions for a limited time. So keep it
somewhere safe. On the 15th of October,
the window to change opens and it closes
on the 7th of December. And if you have
a standalone drug plan, the temporary
program that held those premiums down
has ended. So compare before you let it
renew. And the numbers you will see when
the plan finder switches over are bigger
than this year's. The most a drug plan
can make you pay before its coverage
starts rises to $700.
The yearly ceiling on your drug costs
rises to $2,400.
And the most an Advantage plan can make
you pay for care inside its network
rises to $9,850.
My own view on that 48-hour rule is
simple. Losing it is not a disaster, but
it removes the one built-in moment to
think. So build it back yourself. Never
enroll in anything on the same day you
first hear about it. Number three, the
bill nobody is putting in the October
headlines. And for a lot of you, it is
the one you will feel first, energy.
Over the last 12 months, according to
the government's own price figures,
gasoline is up more than 27%.
Fuel oil, the heating oil so many homes
in the Northeast still burn, is up 52%.
Electricity is up nearly 4% and piped
natural gas a little over four. Most of
that jump traces back to the war
involving Iran earlier this year, which
sent crude oil past $118 a barrel at its
peak at the end of March. Prices eased
after that, then climbed again over the
summer. If you heat with oil, that is
not an inconvenience. It can mean
hundreds of extra dollars before
Christmas. In early October, the
government's energy agency publishes its
forecast for this winter's heating
bills, and that is the number your local
news will quote. Do not wait for it.
Here is what to do now. If you heat with
oil or propane, your dealer is probably
offering a fixed price or a capped price
contract for the winter right about now.
For a fixed income, a cap is usually the
safer of the two because you are
protected if prices rise, but you are
not stuck paying the high price if they
fall. Read the fee for the cap before
you sign. If your electric or gas
company offers budget billing, where the
year's cost is spread into equal monthly
payments, it will not lower the total,
but it takes the shock out of January.
While you are on the phone, ask whether
they have a discount rate for older or
lower income customers. Many utilities
do, and very few of them advertise it.
And learn two protections most people
only discover in an emergency. Many
states restrict winter shutoffs, usually
starting in November or December. And in
many states, a signed letter from your
doctor saying that losing heat or power
would endanger your health can hold off
a disconnection for a period of time.
Call your utility this week and ask how
its medical certificate works while it
is still mild outside and nobody is in a
hurry. And if money is tight, the
federal heating assistance program opens
applications in most states this fall.
Apply early because in many states the
money runs out before the cold does.
Number two, the change that already
happened.
On the 16th of September, the Federal
Reserve raised interest rates for the
first time since 2023.
The vote was 12 to nothing. The new
chairman said inflation is too high and
has been for too long. Prices overall
are running about 3.4% higher than a
year ago, and 16 of the 19 officials
around that table expect at least one
more increase before the end of this
year.
The next decision is on the 28th of
October.
Now, rate increases are usually reported
as bad news for people buying a house or
a business borrowing money. For a
retiree with savings and a paid-off
home, it is the reverse. You are the
lender now. The only question is whether
you are being paid like one.
I think this is the change that will
separate who come out of this winter
ahead from the people who fall quietly
behind, and here is why. When the Fed
raises rates, banks move in two
directions at two very different speeds.
What they charge you moves almost at
once. The prime rate, which credit cards
and home equity lines are built on, went
up to 7% by the next morning. What they
pay you moves slowly, if it moves at
all. The national average rate on a
savings account, according to the FDIC,
is 37/100 of 1%. The best widely
available savings accounts are paying
more than four. On $100,000, that is the
difference between about $370 a year and
more than 4,000. Same safety, same
federal insurance, as long as the bank
is FDIC insured. The only difference is
which building your money sleeps in.
Many of you know that part already,
because I have talked about savings
accounts before. So, here are three
places money hides that even careful
people miss. The first is inside your
investment account. If you have an IRA
or a brokerage account at one of the big
firms, the cash in it from a dividend, a
fund you sold, or a required
distribution you have not taken out yet,
is often swept automatically into a
holding account. At some large firms,
those sweep accounts have paid a small
fraction of 1%, while the money market
funds at the very same firm paid many
times more.
It has been the subject of lawsuits and
federal investigations. You We not have
to change firms. Log in, find the line
that says cash, and see what it is
earning. If it is close to zero, ask
what money market options you have. Very
