often, it is a single click.
The second is the tax on your interest.
If you live in a state with an income
tax, interest from Treasury bills, the
short-term loans you make to the federal
government, is exempt from state and
local income tax. Bank interest is not.
In a high-tax state, that alone can make
a Treasury bill the better deal, even
when the posted rates look the same. You
can buy them directly from the
Treasury's own website or through most
brokerage accounts, with terms as short
as 4 weeks. The third is timing. If more
increases are coming, locking every
dollar into a long certificate of
deposit today means you cannot catch the
next one. Here is my own view. This is a
moment for shorter terms or for a
ladder, where you split the money across
several maturities, so that some of it
comes free every few months.
Nobody knows what the 28th of October
will bring. A ladder means you do not
need to know. And if you already own a
certificate of deposit, find out today
when it matures. Most of them renew
automatically into a new certificate at
whatever rate the bank chooses, and you
usually get a short grace period, often
around a week to 10 days, to move the
money without a penalty.
Miss that window, and your money can be
locked up for another year at a rate you
never agreed to. Two warnings before you
move a single dollar. First, a money
market fund and a money market account
are not the same thing, even though the
names are nearly identical. A money
market account is a bank account, and it
is FDIC insured. A money market fund is
an investment, usually a very
conservative one, but it is not insured
by the FDIC.
Neither is a bad choice, just know which
one you are holding. Second, be careful
with apps. A couple of years ago, a
company called Synapse, which sat
between several popular money apps and
the banks behind them, went bankrupt. A
great many customers were locked out of
their savings for months, and tens of
millions of dollars could not be
accounted for because FDIC insurance
protects you when an insured bank fails,
not when the company in the middle
fails. If you open a higher rate
account, open it directly with an FDIC
insured bank or a federally insured
credit union, and look the bank up on
the FDIC's own website before you send
it anything. And if you are moving a
large sum, keep the insurance limit in
per person, per bank, per type of
ownership. A joint account covers each
owner, so a married couple is covered up
to half a million dollars at one bank.
And since the rules changed in 2024, an
account with named beneficiaries, a
payable on death account, is covered up
for each beneficiary, up to five of
them. That is as much as one and a
quarter million dollars for a single
owner at a single bank, simply by naming
the people who will inherit it. Fenton
and his wife are the reason I care so
much about this one.
76, a retired pipefitter in New Jersey,
careful with money his whole life. When
they sold the family house and moved
somewhere smaller, about $220,000
of the proceeds went into the savings
account at the big bank they had used
since the 1980s.
It felt like the safest thing in the
world, and it was safe. It was also
earning a few hundredths of a percent
while insured banks a short drive away
were paying four and five.
When their son finally sat down with the
statements, the difference over three
years came to more than $25,000.
Nobody stole it. Nobody broke a rule.
The bank never mentioned that the rate
had not moved, and Fenton never thought
lost to a question nobody asked. That is
the kind of money I wrote The Quiet
Rules to protect. Not with a clever
trick, but by putting the right
questions in front of you before the
years slip by. Head to
kevinexplains.shop
or aim your phone at the code on the
screen or use the first link in the
pinned comment. It is waiting in the
description, too. You have 7 days with
it. If in that week it has not shown you
something worth far more to you than
what you paid, you can get a full
refund. Because the other ending to this
story is Fenton's son at the dining room
table running a finger down 3 years of
statements and understanding that the
money was never lost. It was simply
never earned. Here is what Fenton's son
did in a single afternoon and it is
worth copying. He left enough in
checking to cover 2 months of bills. He
moved a large part of the rest into a
high rate savings account at an FDIC
insured online bank in both his parents'
names and he put the remainder into a
ladder of Treasury bills coming due
every 3 months so a piece of the money
comes back to his parents at the start
of every season. None of it needed a
salesman. None of it was risky. It
simply needed somebody to ask. There is
a second half to this change and it is
the half the banks will be quiet about.
If you carry any debt with a variable
rate, it just became more expensive and
it may become more expensive again on
the 28th. Credit cards are the obvious
one. The average rate is already close
to 21% and most cards are tied to that
prime rate. So the increase flows
through within a statement or two.
Home equity lines of credit are the ones
people forget because many retirees
opened one years ago as a safety net and
then drew on it for a roof or a car.
Most of those are variable, too. So here
is the simplest piece of arithmetic in
this whole video. If you have money
sitting in savings earning almost
nothing and a balance on a card at 21%,
you are paying the bank twice. Keep a
real emergency cushion, always. But
money beyond that cushion does more for
you, paying off a 21% balance than it
will ever do sitting anywhere else.
And ask. Call the number on the back of
your card and ask for a lower rate. It
sounds too simple to work, but card
companies lower rates for long-standing
customers who ask far more often than
people assume, and a no costs you
nothing. If you carry a larger balance
you cannot clear quickly, a balance
transfer card with an introductory 0%
rate can buy you a year or more of
breathing room.
There is usually a transfer fee of a few
percent, so do the arithmetic and only
do it if you will stop adding to the
balance. And one twist for homeowners
with a reverse mortgage. If you have the
adjustable kind with an unused line of
credit, that line grows every month at a
rate tied to your loan's interest rate.
When rates rise, the unused part of the
line grows faster. It is one of the few
places where higher rates quietly work
in your favor, and most people who have
one have no idea it is happening. And
number one, the raise. On the 14th of
October at half past 8:00 in the morning
Eastern time, the government publishes
September's inflation figures, and
Social Security's raise for next year is
calculated from those numbers the same
morning. The two best known forecasts
right now are 3.5% and 3.6%.
Either one would be the largest raise
since 2023. The same morning, Social
Security also publishes next year's
earnings limit for people who still work
before their full retirement age. So if
you have a part-time job, look for that
number, too. But I want you to see the
raise for what it is, because it changes
how you plan. It is not a gift, it is a
receipt. It pays you back in January for
price increases you have already been
paying for months. And this year, look
closely at what drove those prices.
Gasoline and heating oil did most of the
pushing. Medical care rose only about
1.5% over the year, and housing about
three. There is a detail behind that
worth knowing. The raise is calculated
from a price index built around working
households, not retirees. It gives more
weight to gasoline and commuting, and
less to doctors and prescriptions. In
most years, that works against you. This
year, for once, it may tilt slightly
your way. So, here is my honest read of
that. If you drive less than you used
to, and you do not heat with oil, this
may be one of the rare years when the
raise covers more than your real
increase in costs. If you heat with oil,
or you drive a lot, it will not come
close. Then comes what is taken out
before you ever see it. Your Part B
premium is deducted from your check, and
Medicare's trustees have projected it
will rise from $202.90
to about $209.50
next year.
The official figure usually arrives in
November.
So, on a $2,000 monthly benefit, a 3 and
1/2% raise is $70. Take away the higher
premium, and you keep about 63.
If you pay the income-related surcharge
on Medicare, you keep less than that.
So, and there is a link here to number
two that almost nobody makes. The
interest you earn on savings and
Treasury bills is income. Federal tax
applies to all of it. It counts in the
formula that decides how much of your
Social Security is taxable. And it
counts toward Medicare's income
surcharge, which looks at your tax
return from two years earlier.
Moving your cash to a higher rate is
still almost always the right call. But,
if you sit close to one of those lines,
a big jump in interest can nudge you
over. So, plan it, rather than stumble
into it. There is a slow relief, too,
and I will admit this one frustrates me
more than anything else on this list.
The income levels at which your Social
Security becomes taxable, $25,000 for a
single person, and 32,000 for a married
couple have never once been adjusted for
inflation. They are the same numbers
they were decades ago. So, every raise
you receive pushes a little more of your
benefit over the line where the IRS can
tax it. A raise that looks like 3 and
1/2% on the news can arrive as quite a
bit less once April comes around. Nobody
voted for that in any recent year. It
simply happens quietly because nobody
changed the numbers. Two things you can
do about it. First, if you have been out
by a tax bill in April, you can ask
Social Security to withhold federal tax
from each payment at 7, 10, 12, or 22%.
The form is called the W-4V
and you can change it whenever you like.
Second, do not plan around the headline.
In early December, your new benefit
amount is posted in your online Social
Security account and a letter follows in
the mail. Look at the actual deposit
after every deduction, not the
percentage on the news, and build your
January budget around that number. And
if your drug plan premium also comes out
of your Social Security, remember what I
said about stand-alone drug plans. The
program that held those premiums down
has ended, so a jump in that deduction
could eat into your raise as well.
Check it now during open enrollment, not
in January. If there is one thread
running through all five of these, it is
that the changes are announced loudly
and the consequences arrive quietly
months later in a deposit smaller than
you expected or a statement you never
opened.
The Quiet Rules is where I keep the
quiet part. kevinexplains.shop,
the code on your screen, the first link
in the pinned comment, or the
description. 7 days to look it over, and
if it is not for you, you get a refund.
Better that than a morning in January
staring at a deposit smaller than the
one on the news trying to work out where
the difference went. Now, the question
on the thumbnail, big changes ahead?
Yes. And here is where I would actually
be looking. The 15th of October comes
first. If you asked for an extension on
last year's tax return, that is your
deadline. And last year's return is the
first one where people 65 and older can
claim the new deduction of up to $6,000
each on top of the standard deduction
whether or not they itemize. A married
couple who are both 65 or older can
claim up to 12,000. It shrinks above
$75,000 of income for a single person
and 150,000 for a couple.
If a preparer filed your extension, ask
them directly whether that deduction is
on your return. The 28th of October, the
Fed decides again, and most of its own
officials expect another increase before
the year is out. If you are going to
move cash or pay down a variable
balance, doing it before that date costs
you nothing and may save you something.
The 3rd of November is the midterm
election. Several proposals to change
Social Security's future are sitting in
Congress, and none of them has passed.
Anything you read about your benefit
being changed by an election result
before a law is actually signed is
guesswork dressed up as news.
The 7th of December closes Medicare's
window to change plans. And then the
11th of December. That is the date I
would circle. It is when the stopgap
funding runs out. If Congress has not
acted by then, the government can shut
down again a couple of weeks before
Christmas. Your Social Security payments
would continue through a shutdown.
Medicare would keep paying claims. The
agencies themselves do slow down though.
Last year Social Security sent home
roughly one in eight of its staff for
the duration, and phone lines and
offices felt it. And last year's
shutdown, the longest in the country's
history, ran for 43 days, and food
assistance for November was thrown into
chaos with the The at one point saying
it would pay only half. So, if you or
somebody you care about relies on food
help, keep a little extra in the pantry
going into December. That is not panic.
That is simply learning from last year.
After that, the 31st of December is the
deadline for most required minimum
distributions from retirement accounts.
If you take yours in cash, do not let it
sit in a sweep account earning nothing
while you decide what to do with it. And
if you are 70 and a half or older and
you give to charity, a qualified
charitable distribution sent straight
from your IRA counts toward your
required amount without being counted as
income.
So, let me turn this whole month into
five questions you can ask before
Halloween, each one to a different
person.
Ask your bank what your savings account
is paying today as an actual number and
whether it offers a higher rate account
for the same money. If the answer is
under 1%, you already know what to do
next.
Ask your brokerage or look it up in your
online account where the cash inside
your IRA sits and what it earns. That
takes about 5 minutes and it can be
worth thousands of dollars a year. Ask
your utility or your heating oil dealer
two things. What winter protections you
qualify for, including their medical
certificate process, and what fixed or
capped price plans they offer. And ask
yourself, with your latest statements in
front of you, what you owe at a variable
rate. Every card, every home equity
line. Write each rate down. Then decide,
before the 28th of October, what gets
paid down first. And ask one person you
trust whether they will be your trusted
contact at your brokerage and at your
bank if it offers one.
Then call and add them. It takes 10
minutes and it is the one item on this
list that protects you from people
rather than from rates. And one more
date for later. In the second week of
December, log into your social security
account and look at your new deposit
amount, not the headline. If it
surprises you, there is still time to
change your tax withholding before
January. And if you have never set up
that online account, do it now in
October because the identity checks can
take a while and December is when
everybody else tries. If something in
your own situation does not fit neatly
into any of this, a certificate coming
due, a home equity line you are unsure
about, a heating bill that already
worries you, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com
and tell me what you are facing. Replies
can be slow in a busy week, but they do
come and a good number of these videos
started life as somebody's email. Here
is what I believe after spending these
last few weeks inside all of this. For
most of the last 15 years, people who
saved carefully were punished for it.
Rates sat near zero and the reward for
doing the responsible thing was nothing
at all.
Right now, for the first time in a long
while, the tide has turned a little
toward the saver. The raise is bigger,
the interest on cash is real, but none
of it comes to you on its own. The bank
will not call, the brokerage will not
email, Social Security will not explain
what the raise is really worth once the
deductions are taken. The benefit of
this particular October goes to the
people who move and the cost of it lands
on the people who wait for somebody to
tell them. You do not have to wait any
longer. This month, the people who ask a
few plain questions will be paid better
than the people who stay polite and
quiet. I would like you to be one of the
ones who asks. And if you would like
these rules in one place, on paper,
before the next rumor arrives, The Quiet
Rules is linked in the description and
pinned at the top of the comments. I am
Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check The Quiet Rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: Every Senior Must Open This Before September 30 Or Pay All Of 2027

12 months. Not until you notice, not
until you complain. 12 months. And this

down what drug plans could charge you.

600,000 people, and others are being

counter change. Medicare's price on 15

not sell insurance. No plan pays me and

your own before you act. If you have a
drug plan, this is you. If you have one

If you have a supplement with a separate

In 2025 and 2026, a temporary federal

because a plan that does not earn them

The third is the calendar. From the 1st

plan can go up. The yearly cap on your
drug costs goes up and 15 more brandame
drugs move to prices Medicare negotiated
itself. Every one of those shows up
somewhere inside that envelope. So let
us open it in the order that actually
protects you. Start with a single line
near the top of the very first page
before the premium before the drug list.
It tells you which of three things is

plan may be ending. or your plan may be
combined with a different plan from the
same company and you are being moved

catches people because the company name

What the letter does not spell out is
this. When your plan is ending, the

to buy a supplement with no health
questions. When your plan is combined

were moved. So, in the eyes of the

to the 7th of December. A retired bus

Sentences like that one are what the

So the first page tells you something

kevinexplains.shop.

envelope
because the other way to learn this is

Your plan is required to get that notice

Some of you agreed to receive it by
email years ago and forgot. So, look
there, too. Do not wait for it to find
you. The fuller booklet that lists every
benefit follows by the 15th of October.
When it arrives, do not read it front to
back. Turn to the table near the start
that compares this year with next year.
It is usually called a summary of
important costs. This year's figures sit
in one column, next year's in the other.
Take a pen and circle every number on
the right that is bigger than the one on
the left. That takes about a minute and
those circles are the only parts of the

Everything else is paperwork the law
requires them to send. Once you have

at is your premium. And this year, if
you have a standalone drug plan, the
kind people buy alongside a supplement,
look at this line before anything else.
In 2026, that temporary program lowered
the average standalone drug plan premium

The government's own benchmark premium

of the house and lived there for at

And the one that would have saved
Odile's family.
A son or daughter who lived in your home
for at least 2 years right before you
entered a nursing home and who provided
the kind of care that kept you at home
instead of in a facility.
If that describes your situation, the
house can be put in that child's name,
and Medicaid treats it as a permitted
transfer.
The care has to be real, and it has to
be documented. A doctor's letter,
records of what was done.
But, it is written into federal law, and
hardly any family has heard of it.
Number two, your spouse's share. This is
the one that should take the most fear
out of the room for married couples,
because the single most common nightmare
I hear is this.
One of us goes into a nursing home, and
the other one is left with nothing.
The law was changed decades ago
specifically to stop that from
happening, and most couples still do not
know how it works. When one spouse needs
long-term care and applies for Medicaid,
the spouse who stays at home is allowed
to keep a protected share of the
couple's savings.
This year, that protected amount can be
as much as $162,660,
and it is never less than $32,532.
That money is not spent down. Medicaid
is not allowed to count it against the
spouse who needs care.
And it comes on top of the house, the
car, and everything else on this list.
How much of the range you get depends on
your state.
In many states, the spouse at home keeps
half of what the couple owns on the day
long-term care begins, as long as that
half falls inside those limits.
In others, the spouse simply keeps
everything up to the maximum. That one
difference can be worth more than
$100,000 to the spouse at home. So, it
is worth knowing which kind of state you
live in before that day arrives. And
there is protection for income, too,
which is the part people really miss.
The income that is paid in the name of
the spouse at home belongs to that
spouse. It is not handed to the nursing
home. And if the spouse at home has very
little income of their own, they are
allowed to keep part of the other
spouse's income, as well. Enough to
bring them up to a monthly minimum. From
July of this year, that minimum is
a month in most states, and it can go as
So, the picture of the wife at home
living on nothing while her husband's
whole pension goes to the nursing home
is, in most cases simply not what the
law allows. But none of this is applied
automatically in your favor. You have to
ask for it. And in some cases, a spouse
needs a hearing to get the higher
amount. Number three, the car in your
driveway and everything inside your
house. When Medicaid looks at what you
own, in most states one vehicle is not
counted and it does not matter what that
vehicle is worth as long as it is used
to get you or member of your household
around. And your household goods and
personal effects, your furniture, your
wedding ring, your clothes, the things
in your kitchen are not counted either,
regardless of value.
Nobody from Medicaid is coming to value
your China cabinet. The IRS has its own
version of this. By law, it cannot levy
the clothing you and your family need
and it cannot take your household
furniture, provisions, and personal
effects up to a set value, which for
this year is $11,980.
That list in the tax code also shields
certain income entirely. Unemployment
benefits, workers compensation,
veteran's service-connected disability
payments,
supplemental security income.
The IRS is written out of every one of
those. Number four, your funeral.
This sounds like an odd thing to
protect, but it is one of the most
useful rules in the whole Medicaid
system and it is the one families most
often get wrong by being too slow.
A burial plot, a crypt, a headstone, a
casket bought in advance for you or your
close family are not counted as assets
at all, whatever they cost. And a
prepaid funeral contract that is
irrevocable, meaning you cannot cancel
it and take the money back, is generally
not counted either.
On top of that, a small burial fund of
up to $1,500 can be set aside.
Some states put a ceiling on how much an
irrevocable funeral contract can hold,
so check yours.
But think about what that means. Money
spent on your own funeral while you are
well is money that is not counted later.
And it is money your children will not
have to find in the worst week of their
lives.
It is one of the few ways to spend down
that leaves nobody worse off. And these
last two items lead to the single most
useful idea in the whole Medicaid
system, one that almost no family is
told.
Spending money is not the same as giving
it away.
If savings would push you over the
limit, you are allowed to turn countable
money into things that do not count, and
it is not treated as a gift.
Paying off the mortgage on the home you
live in, replacing the roof, the
furnace, the windows, replacing an old
car with a reliable one, buying hearing
aids, dental work, new glasses,
prepaying the funeral. Every one of
those moves money out of the column
Medicaid counts and into the column it
does not, and it leaves you better off
rather than poorer. It is the difference
between spending down on a nursing home
bill and spending down on your own life.
Number five, what you leave behind. And
this one is bigger than most people
realize because the law changed last
year.
The federal estate tax only reaches
estates worth more than $15 million per
person this year, and under the law
passed last summer, that threshold is
now permanent and rises with inflation.
A married couple can pass on 30 million.
For almost every family watching, the
IRS takes nothing at all when you die.
More than a dozen states have their own
estate or inheritance tax with much
lower thresholds. So, check yours. But
federally, it is simply not an issue for
most people. And there is a second
protection inside this one, and it is
worth far more.
When your children inherit your house,
or your shares, or your mutual funds,
the tax value of those assets is reset
to what they are worth on the day you
die.
Every dollar the house gained while you
owned it over 30 or 40 years disappears
for tax purposes. Your son can sell the
next month and owe little or nothing.
The IRS never taxes that lifetime of
growth, not you, not him. For married
couples, there is a version of this at
the first death, too.
When one spouse dies, their half of a
jointly owned house or portfolio gets
that reset in value. In the handful of
community property states, including
California and Texas, the whole of it
does, both halves.
That is why a widow can often sell the
family home soon after her husband's
death and owe far less tax than she
feared, which brings me to the most
expensive mistake on this whole list
because it destroys two of these
protections at once. A great many
parents, afraid of the nursing home,
give the house to their children while
they are still alive. It feels like
protecting it. Here is what it actually
does. First, Medicaid looks back five
full years at everything you gave away.
A gift of the house inside that window
creates a penalty, a period during which
Medicaid will not pay for your care.
The length of that penalty is the value
of what you gave divided by what a month
of nursing home care costs in your
state.
And the cruelest part is when it starts,
not the day you made the gift. The
penalty only begins when you are already
in the nursing home, have already spent
your money down, and would otherwise
qualify.
At the exact moment you have nothing
left to pay with. And second, the house
loses that reset in tax value. A gift
carries your original purchase price
with it. So, your children take on your
old cost, and when they sell, they pay
tax on the entire lifetime gain.
There is a quieter version of the same
mistake, and it is even more common,
adding a child's name to the deed.
People do it to avoid probate. In the
eyes of the law, that is usually a gift
of part of the house, so it can start
the Medicaid clock. And that part of the
house loses its reset in value, too.
In roughly 30 states, there is a better
tool for avoiding probate, a
transfer-on-death deed, which passes the
house to your child when you die, keeps
the full reset in value, and does not
count as a gift while you are alive.
Whether Medicaid can still reach a house
passed that way depends on your state's
recovery rules, so ask. But it avoids
both of the traps I just described. And
a word about the number of people think
protects them. You will hear that you
can give $19,000 a year to anyone
without tax. That is true for the IRS.
It means nothing at all to Medicaid.
Medicaid does not care what the IRS
allows. A $19,000 gift to a grandchild
is still a gift inside the 5-year
look-back. People mix up those two rules
all the time, and it costs them months
of coverage. A retired machinist I will
call Delbert signed his house over to
his son when he was 81 on the advice of
a friend at church to keep it away from
a nursing home. He and his late wife had
paid $90,000 for it in the 1970s. By
then, it was worth about 400,000.
3 years later, Delbert needed full-time
care. The gift was inside the 5-year
window. In his state, a month of care
was counted at roughly $10,000.
So, a $400,000 gift meant about 40
months with no Medicaid at all, starting
only once he had spent everything else.
His son had to sell the house to pay for
his care. And because it was a gift, the
son's tax cost was the $90,000 his
parents paid, not the 400,000 it would
have been worth if he had inherited it.
At the most common rate, that is well
over $40,000 in federal tax on a sale
made to pay a nursing home. If Delbert
had kept the house, it would not have
counted against him while he lived. The
state might still have made a claim on
it after his death, and that is a real
cost.
But whatever was left would have reached
his son at full value, with no tax on
the gain, and with the hardship waiver
and every other protection still on the
table,
giving it away early did not avoid the
nursing home bill. It added a tax bill
on top of it. And the part that hurts
most is that under federal law, if a
gift like that is handed back in full,
the penalty is lifted. Nobody told the
family that either. 40 months without
coverage, a house sold anyway, and more
than $40,000 handed to the IRS on top.
All because of one piece of advice from
a friend who meant well.
Delbert did not need a lawyer to avoid
that. He needed to know three rules
before he signed anything.
The five-year lookback, the reset in tax
value at death, and the fact that the
house was already protected while he
lived in it. Those are exactly the kind
of rules the quiet rules lays out in
plain English, in large print, for the
family conversation that happens before
the crisis, rather than after it. It is
at kevinexplains.shop.
The code is back up on your screen. The
pinned comment has the link right at the
top, and you will also find it in the
description. Give it 7 days. If it has
not earned its place on your kitchen
table by then, return it and I will
refund you without a single question.
Because the alternative is Delbert's son
sitting across from a buyer signing away
the house his parents paid off to cover
a bill his father's gift was supposed to
prevent. Number six, and the last two
are both about the IRS. Your retirement
account when the debt is with the IRS.
Here is something almost nobody knows.
The IRS does have the legal power to
levy an IRA or a 401K, but its own
manual tells its collection officers not
to, unless the person has engaged in
what it calls flagrant conduct. Things
like hiding assets or continuing to pay
into a retirement account while claiming
they cannot pay their taxes.
And even then, the officer is told not
to levy the account if the person
depends on that money for their living
expenses, now or in the near future.
For a retiree drawing on an IRA to pay
the bills, that is exactly the
situation. It is not a guarantee written
into the law itself, so I will not tell
you it is absolute, but it is the IRS's
own written rule, and if an officer ever
threatens your IRA, it is the first
thing you or your representative should
raise. Medicaid is a different story,
and I want to be clear so nobody walks
away with the wrong idea.
For long-term care, most states do count
an IRA as an available asset. Some treat
it differently once you are taking
regular payments from it. So on this
one, the IRS is mostly kept out, and
Medicaid mostly is not. Number seven, a
tax debt that is more than 10 years old.
The IRS generally has 10 years from the
date a tax is assessed to collect it.
When that date passes, the debt is gone,
not reduced, gone. The IRS cannot
collect it, cannot levy for it, and has
to stop. Now, I want to be careful here
because this is where people get caught.
That 10-year clock stops running during
certain events, while a request for a
payment plan is being considered,
while an offer to settle for less is
pending,
during a bankruptcy and for 6 months
after it,
while you are living outside the United
States for 6 months or more at a
stretch.
So the date is not always 10 years from
the bill,
but the IRS keeps a record of exactly
when it runs out, and you are entitled
to ask for it. A tax professional can
request your account transcript and tell
you the date.
I have seen people pay off debts in
their 70s that were weeks from expiring
because nobody told them the clock
existed, and there is a combination here
that tax professionals know and almost
nobody else does.
If paying the IRS would leave you unable
to cover basic living expenses, rent,
food, medicine, you can ask the IRS to
mark your account as currently not
collectible.
When it does that, it stops actively
collecting. No levies, no seizures,
although it can still keep any future
tax refund.
And here is the key. While your account
sits in that status, the 10-year clock
keeps running.
For an older person on a fixed income
with an old debt, that can mean the debt
simply expires legally while nobody is
chasing. Now the eighth thing, the one I
promised you, the one people guard least
and lose first, and it is not the house,
and it is not the savings account. It is
your Social Security check.
Almost everybody believes Social
Security cannot be touched. Against a
credit card company or a hospital or a
debt collector, that is largely true.
Private creditors are generally barred
from taking it, but the government is
not a private creditor, and there are
three ways it reaches into that check,
and all three catch people who had no
idea. The first is the IRS. If you owe
back taxes and do not respond, the IRS
can take up to 15% of every Social
Security payment automatically month
after month through a program that
simply intercepts it before it reaches
you. No court is involved. The IRS sends
a notice first, and that notice is your
window. The way to stop it is to get
into a payment arrangement or to show
the IRS that the levy is causing you
economic hardship, in which case the law
requires it to be released.
People lose 15% of their check for years
when a single phone call would have
stopped it. The second is Social
Security itself. If the agency decides
it overpaid you, sometimes years ago,
sometimes because of its own mistake, it
will now, by default, hold back half of
your monthly check until the overpayment
is repaid. Half. For years, the default
was the entire check. It was cut to 1/10
in 2024 and raised to half in April of
last year.
You do not have to accept it. You can
ask for a lower rate of withholding. You
can ask for a waiver if the overpayment
was not your fault and repaying it would
be a hardship. And you can appeal
whether you were overpaid at all.
But if you say nothing, the 50% simply
starts.
Always read a letter from Social
Security about an overpayment the day it
arrives because the deadlines to stop
the withholding are short. And the
third, the largest of all, is the
nursing home.
When you go into a nursing home on
Medicaid, almost all of your monthly
income, including your Social Security
and any pension, is paid to the nursing
home each month toward the cost of your
care.
You keep what is called a personal needs
allowance. The federal minimum is $30 a
month. Most states set it higher, but
not by much. That is the money you have
left for a haircut, a newspaper, a
birthday card for a grandchild. Your
spouse at home can keep a share under
the rules I described earlier. But the
check you spent 40 years earning mostly
goes to the facility. That is the eighth
thing. Not the house, the income. And
there is a change coming on the 1st of
January that makes timing matter more
than ever.
Right now, when you apply for Medicaid,
it can reach back and pay for care you
received up to 3 months before the month
you applied.
From the 1st of January next year, for
older people and people with
disabilities, that shrinks to 2 months.
That matters because of a pattern that
happens in every hospital in the
country.
Somebody moves into a nursing home after
a hospital stay. The family assumes
Medicare is paying. Medicare's coverage
runs out, the bills keep coming, and by
the time somebody applies for Medicaid,
months have passed. Under the new rule,
one of those months simply disappears.
At the median cost of a private room, a
single month is more than $10,000.
So if a parent of yours goes into a
nursing home and the money is running
down, do not wait for the Medicare days
to end before you apply. Start the
application early. So if I had one
afternoon with my own parents, here is
the order I would go through this in.
First, the house.
Find out whether your state recovers
only from what passes through probate or
reaches further, and whether a child who
has been caring for you at home might
one day qualify under the caregiver
rule. If so, start keeping a record of
that care now. Second, if you are
married, find out what your state lets
the spouse at home keep, both in savings
and in income, so neither of you is
making decisions out of a fear the law
does not support.
Third, if you are thinking of pre-paying
a funeral, make it irrevocable and keep
the paperwork where your children will
find it. Fourth, if anybody in the
family is talking about putting the
house in a child's name, stop and speak
to an elder law attorney first because
of everything that happened to Delbert.
Fifth, if you have an old tax debt, ask
for the date its collection clock runs
out before you pay another cent. And
sixth, open every letter from the IRS
and from Social Security the day it
arrives because the eighth thing, your
check, is only ever taken from people
who do not answer. If your situation has
a wrinkle I have not covered, a parent
already in care, a house with a child
living in it, a letter you do not
understand, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com
and tell me what is going on. I read
them and the questions people send are
what decide what I cover next. Here is
what I have come to believe after
spending a long time with these rules.
The fear of losing everything is almost
always bigger than the facts.
The law protects a great deal more than
people think. The house while you live
in it, your spouse's share, the car, the
funeral, the funeral, your retirement
account from the IRS in all but the
worst cases, a debt passed its 10 years,
what you pass on at death, and the
growth inside it.
That is a long list and it was written
deliberately by people who did not want
older Americans left with nothing.
But every protection on that list has a
condition and the conditions all come
down to the same thing. Timing.
The caregiver has to have been living
there before. The funeral has to be
arranged before. The gift has to have
been made more than 5 years before or
not at all. The application has to go in
before the months are lost.
The people who lose things are rarely
the people the law failed. They are the
people who found out one step too late.
So, go back to that envelope on the
counter. Only this time, you already
know the answer to the question in your
head. You know what they can touch, what
they cannot, and what they can only
reach with a judge's signature. And if
you want every one of these rules in one
place before anybody in your family
needs them, the quiet rules is linked in
the description and the pinned comment.
I am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: ⚠️ Every Senior Must Make These 5 Calls Before October 1. Almost Nobody Does.

segments.text: You were told no once. Maybe it was a
phone call. Maybe a letter. Maybe a
woman behind a window who glanced at one
number on your form and shook her head.
Over the limit. So, you stopped asking
and you have not asked since. Here is
what nobody went back to tell you. That
limit is gone. It was deleted. Every
year on the 1st of October, the numbers
behind several kinds of help are thrown
out and replaced with new ones. And the
answer you were given was an answer to a
question nobody is asking anymore. And
it is worse than that. The number they
looked at that day is very often not the
number that decides it at all.
Especially once you are past 60 when a
handful of rules quietly turn in your
favor and nobody behind the window is
required to mention a single one of
them. So today is five phone calls. Five
offices whose numbers reset on or around
the 1st of October. What actually
changed? what they really count and what
they do not and the exact sentence to
open each call with so that you are not
the person who talks themselves out of
money in the first 30 seconds. One of
these calls is worth well over $1,000 a
year to people who are certain they earn
too much. Another one is for homeowners
and it has a deadline that one popular
video this month got wrong. If you want
the next change covered the week it
happens, press subscribe now. That is
what this channel is for. A quick honest
note, I am not a financial adviser or a
benefits lawyer and this is education
rather than advice about your own case.
States said a great deal of this
themselves, so your figures may differ
from the ones I use. I will tell you
where. I am Kevin and I read the rules
nobody reads out loud. Before the first
call, you need one idea because every
office you will ring this fall runs on
it and almost nobody understands it.
When you ask for help, the office is
really asking you three questions, not
one. What comes in, what goes out, and
what you own. The trouble is that people
only ever hear the first one. They are
asked what comes in each month. They say
a number. They compare it in their own
head to a limit they half remember and
they hang up. But for most of these
programs, what goes out is subtracted
before anybody decides anything. your
medical bills, your rent or your
property tax, your heating, and what you
own is often counted far more generously
than you would guess with whole
categories left out entirely. A person
who only answers the first question has
refused themselves on a rule they have
never read. So, as we go through the
five calls, listen for the second and
third questions. That is where the money
is. Call one, the food help office.
Officially, it is called SNAP, and the
new year for it started on the 1st of
October. The maximum monthly amount for
a person living alone rises to $36. For
a couple, it is $562.
That is a modest rise, and I am not
going to dress it up. But the ceiling is
not the interesting part. The
interesting part is who they let through
the door because this is where the rules
change completely at 60. For most
households, there are two income tests.
a gross test on everything that comes in
and a net test on what is left after
deductions. If your household includes
somebody who is 60 or older, the first
test does not apply to you at all. You
skip it. You only have to pass the
second one, the one that comes after the
subtractions. And the subtractions for
older households are far more generous
than for anybody else. Every dollar of
out-of- pocket medical cost above $35 a
month comes off. That includes your
Medicare Part B premium, which on its
own is over $200 a month. It includes
drug co-pays, dental bills, glasses,
hearing aids, even the cost of getting
to appointments. And your housing costs,
rent or mortgage, property tax,
insurance, heating come off, too. And
for an older household, there is no cap
on how much of that can be subtracted.
For everyone else, there is. Now, what
you own. For households with somebody 60
or older, the limit on savings in the
states that still use one is now $4,750.
But look at what does not count toward
it. Your home does not count. Your
retirement accounts do not count. Your
IRA, your 401k left out. In most states,
one car does not count. And a great many
states have dropped the savings test
altogether for most applicants. So the
person who says, "I have money in my
IRA. I could never qualify." is usually
answering a question the office never
asked. Let me show you what that does
with real numbers because this is where
people are genuinely stunned. A woman I
will call Filamina, 71, widowed, gets
about $1,900 a month from Social
Security. She applied once a few years
ago was told she was over the income
limit and never tried again. And on the
gross test alone, she was over it. But
she should never have been given the
gross test. She is over 60. So, take her
$1,900. Take off the standard amount
everybody gets, $217.
Take off her medical costs above $35,
which with her Part B premium and her
prescriptions come to nearly 300. Then
her rent and utilities well over $1,000
a month. And because she is over 60 with
no cap by the time the arithmetic is
finished, her countable income is under
$600 a month, well inside the limit.
Depending on her state's figure for
utilities, she qualifies for somewhere
around $128 a month in food help. That
is over $1,500 a year. [snorts] She
turned it down for years because
somebody once looked at the wrong line.
And she is not unusual. She is typical.
Of all the adults over 60 in this
country who qualify for food help, only
about half are actually receiving it.
Not because they were refused, because
they refused themselves. often on a
memory of one conversation years ago
against numbers that have since been
replaced several times over. Half. Think
about what that means in your own
street. And the reason is almost always
the same. They were never told that 60
changes the test. The office is not
built to tell you. It is built to
process what you bring it. Nobody is
going to ring Filyamina and tell her the
arithmetic changed. That is the gap the
quiet rules was written for. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
Point your phone at the code on the
screen now or use the link at the top of
the pin comment or the one in the
description. It lays out the rules that
decide what you are owed in plain
English and in large print so you know
which question is really being asked
before you pick up the phone. Take 7
days with it. If it has not shown you
something you were missing, send it back
and that is the end of it. Because the
alternative is exactly where Filamina
was. Standing at the checkout, putting
things back on the shelf with help she
was entitled to sitting unclaimed in a
program that never called her. Before
you pick up the phone, one more rule in
this office and it changes everything
for older people who share a roof. You
might assume that if you live with your
grown son or daughter, their income gets
added to yours and that finishes it. Not
necessarily. For food help, a household
is the people who buy and prepare their
meals together. If you live in your
daughter's house, but you buy your own
food and cook it separately, you can
generally apply as your own household on
your own income. Spouses are always
counted together, and there are special
rules for parents living with children.
So, ask how your state treats your
arrangement. But a great many older
people living with family never apply at
all because they assume the whole house
is counted when only their own kitchen
is. So, here is how call one opens, and
the words matter. Do not start with what
you earn. say this, I am over 60 and I
would like to file an application today.
There is a reason for both halves of
that sentence. Over 60 tells them which
rules apply. And today matters because
of a rule most people have never heard
of. You have the right to file an
application on the very first day you
contact the office with nothing more
than your name, your address, and your
signature. The paperwork, the interview,
the proof, all of that can follow. And
if you are approved, your help is
generally counted from the date you
filed, not the date they finished. So
every week you spend gathering papers
before you apply is a week of help you
simply do not get back. File first,
prove it after. And when they interview
you, say clearly that you want your
medical expenses counted and bring
whatever you have. Many states will also
give older households a shorter form and
let them go up to 3 years before they
have to renew.
There is one more thing about food help
that changes this October and it affects
how fast any of this happens. Starting
on the 1st of October, states have to
pay 3/4 of the cost of running the
program instead of half. That is a large
new bill landing on state budgets. And
the groups that watch this closely are
warning about thinner staffing and
slower processing, which is one more
reason to get your application in early
in the season rather than in the middle
of winter when the queue is longest. And
a correction because you will hear this
one repeated a great deal. There is a
video going around saying that on the
1st of October, people between 55 and 64
suddenly became subject to work rules
for food help and that if they fall
short, they are cut off for 3 years.
Neither half of that is quite right. The
change is real, but it was not new this
month. It came in with the tax and
spending law signed in July of last
year, and states were told to apply it
straight away. And it is not three years
of nothing. The rule is that an adult in
that age group without an exemption can
receive food help for three months in a
three-year period unless they are
working, volunteering, or in training
for 80 hours a month. But a person who
loses it can generally get it back by
meeting that 80 hours for 30 days.
Volunteering counts in most places. So
does training. And there are exemptions
that people never ask about, including
being medically unable to work and
looking after somebody who cannot look
after themselves. I will come back to
this because it is really a call you
make for somebody else. Call two, the
heating help office. There is federal
money that pays part of a household's
heating bill and in most states it is
called Lee HEP. Its new year also begins
around the 1st of October. And here is
the detail that matters most to anybody
watching this. In some states, older
people are allowed in first. In Illinois
this year, for example, applications
opened on the 1st of October for people
over 60, people with disabilities,
families with very young children, and
households facing a shut off. Everybody
else waits until the 1st of November.
The money runs until it runs out. So, a
month's head start is not a courtesy. In
a cold winter, it can be the difference
between getting help and hearing that
the money is gone. That priority window
is set state by state. So, do not assume
yours has one, but do ask and ask about
the income limit because this is the
program where people misjudge themselves
most. In Illinois, this season, a person
living alone can have close to $4,000 a
month coming in and still be eligible.
$4,000. A great many retirees who assume
heating help is only for the very poor
are comfortably inside that line. Most
states do not look at your savings for
this program at all. Now, the funding,
because you deserve the honest picture.
Last winter, most of the federal heating
money was not released to the states
until the end of November, weeks later
than usual. The White House has proposed
eliminating the program entirely for
next year, as it did the year before,
and Congress refused that time and
actually increased it. For now, the
government is funded at last year's
level until the 11th of December. Nobody
can tell you for certain what happens
after that, which points in one
direction only. Apply early. Money that
is already committed to your household
is money that does not depend on a vote
in December. And here is the piece that
almost nobody connects and it is worth
real money. The heating program and the
food program talk to each other. If your
household receives even a small heating
payment, many states will then give you
a larger allowance for utility costs in
your food help calculation, which raises
your food benefit. Last year's law took
that link away from most households, but
it kept it for households that includes
somebody 60 or older or somebody with a
disability. So, for an older household,
getting approved for heating help can
raise your food help, too. Two offices,
one application feeding the other, and
not one of them will ring to tell you.
While you are on with the heating
office, ask about two things they rarely
volunteer. The first is protection from
shut off. Many states limit when a
utility can disconnect an older
household in the coldest months. And in
many places, a note from your doctor
saying that somebody in the home has a
serious medical condition can hold off a
disconnection for a period while you
arrange payment. The second is
weatherization. There is a separate
federal program that pays for
insulation, sealing drafts, and
sometimes repairing or replacing a
failing furnace at no cost to eligible
households, and older households are
given priority. The heating payment
helps with one winter. A repaired
furnace and a sealed house help with
every winter after it. People qualify
for both and only ever hear about one.
So, call 2 opens like this. I am over 60
and I would like to apply for heating
assistance for this winter. Is there a
priority window for older adults in the
state and when does it close? Then let
them tell you the income limit. Do not
tell them first. Before the third call,
let me clear away the fear that is doing
the rounds this week because a great
deal of what you are hearing is simply
out of date. Nothing collapses on the
1st of October. The government was
funded through a stop gap signed at the
start of September and it runs until the
11th of December. Social Security keeps
paying. Medicare keeps paying. Food help
keeps paying. Anybody telling you the
country changes overnight on the 1st is
selling a fear that was settled weeks
ago. and they are usually selling
something else alongside it. If you want
a date to watch, it is the 11th of
December. Even then, Social Security and
Medicare are paid under permanent law
and do not stop. Call three, the county.
And this is the one for homeowners,
which is most of you, and it is the call
with the most money in it for the people
who least expect to get anything.
Nearly every state offers some kind of
property tax relief for older
homeowners, a senior exemption that
lowers the taxable value of your home. A
freeze that locks your tax or part of it
at the level of the year you qualified.
A deferral or postponement which lets
you put off paying some or all of the
tax until the house is sold. Or a refund
based on how much of your income goes on
property tax and almost none of it
arrives by itself. You have to claim it
inside a window. And the windows are set
locally and they are all different. Some
examples so you can see how different.
In California, the state program that
lets homeowners 62 and older or blind or
disabled postpone their property tax
opens its filing period on the 1st of
October every year and closes on the
10th of February. It has an income limit
and requires a good amount of equity in
the home and the postponeed tax becomes
a lean that is repaid when the home is
sold. In New Jersey, the combined
application for the senior freeze anchor
and the newer State New Jersey credit
has a deadline this year of the 2nd of
November, not the 31st of October, which
is what you will hear in at least one
popular video this month, the 2nd of
November. In Texas, the over 65
exemption freezes your school district
taxes at the level of the year you
qualify. And it is not applied just
because you had a birthday. You have to
file for it. And if you missed it, Texas
generally lets you file late and have it
applied going back up to two years. And
do not skip this call because you rent.
Several states, Pennsylvania and
Minnesota among them, send older renters
a refund or rebate calculated on the
rent they paid on the reasoning that
part of every rent check is the
landlord's property tax passed along to
you. Some of these accept claims late
into the year. You may never have heard
of yours because it arrives through a
form nobody has sent. And while you are
dealing with the county, look at the
number the tax is based on, not just the
tax. Your home's assessed value is set
by an assessor who has usually never
been inside it. If that value is too
high, every exemption you claim is being
taken off the wrong starting figure.
Most counties allow you to challenge an
assessment inside a short window each
year, often with nothing more than
recent sale prices of similar homes
nearby. It costs nothing to ask when
your window is. Two cautions because
these tools are not all free money. A
deferral or postponement is a loan
against your house, not a gift. The tax
still has to be paid, usually with
interest, when the home is sold or
passes to your heirs. For somebody who
is house rich and cash poor and plans to
stay put, that can be exactly right. But
it is a decision to make with your
family in the room, not one to discover
later in the estate. And second, relief
programs almost never renew themselves
forever. Some need a fresh application
every year. Some need you to confirm
your income every year. People qualify
once, stop filing, and lose it without a
single letter telling them why. So, call
three opens like this. I am a homeowner
over 65. What senior exemptions,
freezes, deferrals, or refunds does this
county or state offer, and what are the
filing windows this year? Ask for all
four by name. The clerk will usually
tell you about the one you ask about,
and only that one. Here's how that plays
out in one house. A retired lineman I
will call Lyall in Texas turned 65 and
assumed the county would simply know.
Counties know your age. Surely they
would apply it. They did not. For three
years, his school taxes kept climbing
with the value of his home when they
should have been frozen at the level of
the year he turned 65. His neighbor
mentioned her ceiling over the fence. He
called the appraisal district and filed
the form in an afternoon. He got two of
the three years back. The third was
gone. Well over $1,000 that was simply
his lost because nobody told him the
exemption needed a signature. Lyall's
missing year cost him more than $1,000.
and all it needed was a form he did not
know existed. That is the kind of rule
the quiet rules puts in front of you.
The ones that are published, perfectly
legal, and never mentioned to the person
they are meant for. Your copy is at
kevinexplains.shop.
The code is back up on your screen. The
link sits at the top of the pinned
comment and it is also in the
description. You have 7 days to look
through it and if it is not paid for
itself in what it shows you, return it
and there are no questions. It is a
great deal cheaper than the year Lyall
will never get back. Sitting in the
county's accounts paid by a man who was
entitled to keep it. Call four. And this
one is really two calls about Medicare.
One short and one that most people never
make. The short one first. If you are in
a Medicare Advantage plan or a drug
plan, a booklet from your plan had to
reach you by the end of September
setting out everything that changes in
January. Your premium, your drugs, your
doctors. It does not come from the
government. It comes from the insurance
company. And it looks almost exactly
like the advertising they send you the
rest of the year, which is why so many
of them go straight into the recycling.
And the timing is built to trip you. The
bad news lands in September. You are not
allowed to act on it until the 15th of
October, and the window closes on the
7th of December. So people read it, feel
a flicker of worry, put it on a pile,
and the pile is cleared long before the
window opens. find it this week and put
it somewhere you will see it on the
15th. If it has gone, call the number on
your plan card and ask them to send
another. They have to. Now, the call
almost nobody makes, and for the right
person, it is worth more than every
other call in this video. Your state
runs something called the Medicare
Savings Programs. There are several
levels, and at the most common levels,
they pay your Part B premium for you.
This year, that premium is $22.90
a month. That is over $2,400 a year put
back into your Social Security deposit
every year you qualify. At the fullest
level, they also cover your Medicare
deductibles and co-pays. And there is a
quiet bonus attached. If you qualify for
any level of it, you are generally made
eligible for extra help with your drug
costs as well, which cuts your drug plan
premium and your co-pays down to a few
dollars. So, why does almost nobody
apply? for the same reason as everything
else in this video. People assume they
have too much. They look at their
savings and think that rules me out. But
more than a dozen states have dropped
the savings test for these programs
altogether. In those states, it does not
matter what you have in the bank. And
even where there is still a limit, the
income rules have allowances built in
that people never hear about. Your
state's Medicaid office handles the
application and you can apply at any
time of year. There is no October window
for this one, but the fall, when you are
already looking at next year's Medicare
costs, is the time people finally sit
down and do it. Two details make this
even better than it sounds. At some of
these levels, the help can reach back up
to 3 months before the month you apply,
and Social Security refunds the Part B
premiums it already took out of your
check for those months. And at the
fullest level, doctors and hospitals are
not allowed to bill you for the Medicare
cost sharing at all. If one does, you
show them the letter and the bill goes
away. So, call four opens like this. I
am on Medicare and I would like to apply
for the Medicare savings programs.
Please screen me for every level. Every
level matters because the clerk may only
check the first one. Decide you are over
it and stop there. And one more thing
about timing, which connects calls 1
through 4. On the 14th of October,
Social Security announces next year's
cost of living raise, currently
estimated at around three and a half
percent. That raise nudges your income
up, and a few people will drift over a
line they were just under. So, people
ask me whether they should wait until
after the announcement to apply. No.
Apply now on this year's figures while
you know you qualify. Your case will be
updated when the raise arrives, and many
of these programs adjust their own
limits upward in the new year, too.
Waiting only costs you the months in
between. And a warning that belongs with
all four of these calls. Every one of
these programs is free to apply for. Not
one of them charges an application fee,
and not one of them will ever ask you to
pay anything upfront to receive help.
So, when a letter arrives offering to
file your Homestead exemption for a fee,
or a caller says they can speed up your
heating assistance if you pay a
processing charge, or somebody wants
your Medicare number to check whether
you qualify for extra benefits, that is
not the program. It is somebody standing
between you and the program with their
handout. You make these calls yourself
to numbers you looked up yourself. Call
five. And this is the call you make for
somebody else. Because the people who
most need these calls are very often the
least able to make them. A brother of 58
living in your spare room. A mother of
87 who will not use the phone anymore. A
neighbor who is proud and alone.
[clears throat] Most of these offices
let you act for another person. For food
help. You can be named what is called an
authorized representative, which lets
you apply, talk to the caseworker, and
even shop on their behalf. For Medicare
and Social Security, a signed permission
form lets you speak for them. You
[clears throat] do not need a lawyer for
any of it. And that brother of 58 is
exactly who that work rule from earlier
lands on. If he is between 55 and 64 and
receiving food help, he may now need to
be working, volunteering, or training 80
hours a month to keep it past 3 months.
that is under 20 hours a week and
volunteering counts in most states. But
before he assumes he has to ask about
the exemptions because this is where
people give up money they could keep. A
person whose doctor says they are not
fit to work is exempt. So is somebody
caring for a person who cannot care for
themselves. So in most places is anybody
already meeting work rules through
another program. And here is the piece
that catches whole households. If he
loses his food help, it is not only his
plate that gets smaller. It was feeding
your kitchen, too. And the rule does not
apply to anybody 65 or over. So, the
older person in the house is never the
one it lands on and is very often the
one who pays for it. So, call 5 opens
like this. I am calling on behalf of my
brother or my mother, and I would like
to be added as their authorized
representative.
Then ask exactly what they need from you
and what counts toward the 80 hours in
your state. The list is almost always
longer than people assume. Whichever
call you make, two things will save you
weeks. First, gather the papers before
the interview, not before the
application. Your social security award
letter, a recent bank statement, your
rent receipt, mortgage statement, or
property tax bill, a utility bill, and
your medical costs. That last one sounds
like a mountain of receipts, but it is
not. Your pharmacy can print every co-ay
you paid this year on a single sheet.
Ask at the counter. Your Medicare
statement shows the rest. That one print
out is often the difference between
qualifying and not. Second, if you are
refused, do not accept it on the phone.
Ask for the decision in writing with the
reason. You have the right to that and
you have the right to appeal. For food
help, you generally have 90 days to ask
for what is called a fair hearing. And a
surprising number of refusals are simply
arithmetic done wrong, a medical cost
left out, a housing cost missed, the
wrong test applied to somebody over 60.
Filamina's first refusal would not have
survived a hearing. She just never asked
for one. If one of these five calls does
not fit your situation neatly, a state
whose rules you cannot find, a refusal
you think was wrong, a parent you are
trying to help from three states away,
write to me at kevinexplains
official@gmail.com
and tell me what is going on. I read
every one and the difficult ones are
usually what I cover next. So here are
the five sentences again because the
sentence is the whole point to the food
help office.
I am over 60 and I would like to file an
application today. Please count my
medical expenses
to the heating help office. I am over 60
and I would like to apply for heating
assistance this winter. Is there a
priority window for older adults
to the county? I am a homeowner over 65.
What exemptions, freezes, deferrals, or
refunds do you offer? And what are this
year's filing windows?
to the Medicaid office. I would like to
apply for the Medicare savings programs
and please screen me for every level.
And for somebody you love, I would like
to be added as their authorized
representative. Five sentences. Not one
of them begins with what you earn. Here
is what I have come to believe after
reading far too many of these rule
books. The most expensive thing a lot of
retired people own is not their house or
their car. It is a memory. the memory of
one refusal from one office on one day
years ago. They carry it around as
though it were a permanent fact about
their lives when it was only ever an
answer to one question measured against
numbers that have since been replaced
again and again. The offices are not
trying to hide anything. Every figure in
this video is published, but an office
waits for you to walk in. It does not
come looking for you. and the rules that
favor older people, the medical
deduction, the uncapped housing costs,
the savings that do not count, the
priority windows, the exemptions, all
sit in the part of the conversation you
only reach if you keep talking past the
first question. So, if you were told no
once, that is not a reason to stay away.
It is the best reason to ring again. The
numbers have changed since then. Very
possibly your age has changed the rules
since then. and the person on the other
end of the line this time may be the one
who finally does the arithmetic
properly. The only way to find out is to
make the call and not decide the answer
for them before they have had the
chance. And if you want every one of
these rules in one place before you
start dialing, the quiet rules is linked
in the description and in the pinned
comment. I am Kevin. Thanks for
watching. Do not forget to check the
quiet rules at kevinexplains.shop.

title: 🚨 October 1 Starts The 92 Days That Change Your Retirement Forever

segments.text: You wake up on the first morning of next
year, and five things about your money
are already different. Your Social
Security deposit, your Medicare plan,
the price of the pills in your cabinet,
what you owe the IRS, and whether your
doctor still takes your card.
Not one of those was decided in January.
Every single one was decided in a
stretch of 92 days that starts this
October the 1st and ends on New Year's
Eve. And here is what should bother you.
Most of those decisions will be made for
you, automatically, by default, by
companies and agencies that are not
thinking about you at all, unless you
make them first. The people who wake up
in January to a smaller check, a missing
doctor, or a pharmacy bill that makes no
sense are almost never the people who
did something wrong. They are the people
who did nothing during the only 92 days
of the year when doing something
counted. So, that is what today is, not
a list of headlines, a walk through
those 92 days, one date at a time, in
the order they arrive, with the money
attached to each one. Some dates open a
door, some dates close one. A couple of
them are traps dressed up as good news,
and I'm going to correct several things
you have probably already heard this
month, because a surprising amount of
what is going around about this fall is
simply wrong, including some of the
numbers in videos with a great many
views. If you want the next 92 days
covered as they happen, press subscribe
now, because I will be updating this as
each of these dates lands. The honest
note before we start, I am not a
financial advisor or a tax professional,
and this is education rather than advice
for your situation. Where a figure is a
projection rather than a final number, I
will tell you so. I am Kevin, and my job
is reading the part of the announcement
that comes after the headline. Day one,
October the 1st. On the calendar, it
looks like nothing, no announcement, no
ceremony, but three things switch on
that morning, and the first one is going
to reach your mailbox and your telephone
within days. October the 1st is the day
private insurance companies are allowed
to start marketing next year's Medicare
plans, which means that from that
morning your mailbox fills up. The
glossy envelopes with the
government-looking eagle on them. The
television commercials with the former
football player. The phone calls that
say you may be eligible for extra
benefits you are not receiving. Every
one of them is selling. None of them is
the government. And a great many of them
are paid a commission for each person
they move. Know one rule before that
phone starts ringing because it will
protect you better than any caller ID.
Under Medicare's own marketing rules, a
plan or an agent is not allowed to call
you out of the blue to sell you a plan.
They cannot knock on your door
uninvited. They need your permission
first. So, if a stranger calls you this
fall, says they are with Medicare, and
wants to go over your benefits, one of
two things is true. Either it is a
salesperson breaking the rules, or it is
somebody trying to steal your Medicare
number. Medicare itself does not call
you to sell anything, and does not call
asking for your number. Your Medicare
number is as valuable to a thief as your
bank card because it can be used to bill
for equipment and services you never
received in your name. So, the rule for
the next 92 days is simple. Nobody gets
your Medicare number over the phone on a
call you did not make. The second thing
that switches on is the government's own
tool. On October the 1st, the Medicare
Plan Finder on the official Medicare
website changes over to next year's
plans, next year's premiums, next year's
deductibles, next year's drug prices,
drug by drug at your own pharmacy. For
the first time, you can see exactly what
next year will cost you before anybody
has a chance to sell you anything. That
is the tool the commercials would rather
you did not use because it is neutral.
It is free, and it does not pay anybody
a commission. And the third thing is a
letter that should already be sitting in
your house. If you are in a Medicare
Advantage plan or a drug plan, the
company was required to mail you
something called the annual notice of
change by the end of September. It is
usually a plain-looking booklet and it
is the most important piece of mail you
will receive all year. And most people
put it straight in a drawer. That
booklet is your plan telling you in
writing everything it is changing for
next year. What your premium will be,
whether are moving to a more expensive
tier, whether your co-pays are going up,
whether benefits you rely on are being
cut. The plan is not required to call
you. It is not required to highlight the
bad news. It is only required to tell
you in that booklet. So, if you do
nothing else this week, find it and read
the first two pages because here is what
that booklet is carrying this year and
why this fall is not a normal fall.
Medicare Advantage plans are cutting.
Not a few of them. The industry.
The largest insurers in the country,
including United Healthcare and Humana,
have told their investors plainly that
they are trimming plans and pulling out
of areas to protect their profit
margins. A survey of the people who
design these plans found that nearly
seven in 10 expected their benefits for
next year to be less generous than this
year.
That shows up in exactly the places
people do not look. The dental allowance
that shrinks. The specialist co-pay that
goes up and the giveback. The plan that
has been quietly paying part of your
Part B premium for you and is now either
reducing that or dropping it entirely.
If your plan has been giving you money
back on your Social Security check and
it stops in January, your deposit gets
smaller and you may not connect the two
for months. So, day one gives you three
things to do and none of them involves
picking up the phone to anybody who
called you. Find the booklet, read what
is changing, and sit down with the plan
finder or with somebody neutral before a
sales person sits down with you. And for
that last part there is somebody neutral
and almost nobody uses them. Every state
has a free Medicare counseling program,
usually called SHIP. They are trained,
they are not selling anything, and they
are not paid by any insurer. You can
find yours through the Medicare website
or by calling Medicare directly. In a
fall like this one, a single hour with
them is worth more than every glossy
envelope in your recycling bin put
together. Now, if there is one person
this fall is built to catch, it is the
person who reads nothing, trusts that
last year's plan will still be last
year's plan, and discovers in February
that it is not.
That is precisely the person the quiet
rules was written for.
It is on kevinexplains.shop.
The code is on your screen now if you
want to point your phone at it. The link
sits at the top of the pinned comment
and you will find it in the description,
too. It is written so that the rules
deciding your money are in front of you
in plain English in large print before
somebody else decides them on your
behalf. Have it for 7 days and if it has
not changed what you do with this fall,
send it back and I will not ask you why.
Because the alternative is standing at
the pharmacy window in January being
told your plan no longer covers what it
covered in December with the easy way
back already closed behind you. Day 14,
October the 14th. This is the one
everybody knows about and it is the one
most badly misunderstood. At half past
8:00 that morning Eastern time, the
government releases its September
inflation figures and the Social
Security Administration announces next
year's cost of living adjustment. The
Senior Citizens League currently
estimates it at around 3 and 1/2%. Other
estimates sit a touch higher. It is a
projection until that morning, so treat
it as one. On a $2,000 check, 3 and 1/2%
is $70 a month. Now, here is where the
headline stops and your actual check
begins. The raise is applied to your
gross benefit. But, most people never
see their gross benefit. They see what
lands after Medicare Part B is taken
out. And the Part B premium goes up
every January, too. This year, it is
a month. And I want to correct something
here, because I have heard it said in
more than one video this month that Part
B is about $22.
It is not. It is 202.
The official figure for next year does
not come until November, but the
Medicare trustees projected it at about
So, on that $2,000 check, roughly $6.60
of your $70 raise is gone before it
reaches you. You are left with a little
over 63. And that is only the first
thing that eats it. The second is
quieter, and it is the one that has been
creeping up on retirees for 40 years.
Whether your Social Security is taxed
depends on what the IRS calls your
provisional income. Roughly, your other
income plus half your Social Security.
Above $25,000 for a single person, or
32,000 for a married couple, part of
your benefit becomes taxable. Those two
numbers were written into law in the
1980s. They have never been raised for
inflation, not once.
Your benefit goes up every year. The
line stays exactly where it was. So,
every cost of living raise pushes more
people across a line that was drawn when
a gallon of milk cost $2.
A raise that moves you over it means
part of that raise, and part of the
money underneath it, goes back to the
government in April.
Nobody announces that on October the
14th. It shows up the following spring.
So, on the 14th, do not just hear the
percentage. Take your own check, add the
raise, subtract a little under $7 for
Part B, and then ask whether the new
total with your other income puts you
near those two lines. And watch for one
more thing in early December. Social
Security posts a personal notice showing
your exact new benefit and your exact
deduction. If you have an online account
with them, it appears in your message
center before the paper letter arrives.
If you do not have an account, the fall
is a good time to set one up before
somebody else tries to set one up in
your name. Day 15, October the 15th. The
door opens. Medicare's annual enrollment
period runs from the 15th of October
through the 7th of December, 7 and 1/2
weeks. Whatever plan you are in on the
7th of December is, with narrow
exceptions, the plan you are in for next
year. And this year there are more
moving parts inside that window than
there have been in a long time. So, let
us go through them properly. Start with
the drug plan numbers because they
changed and the change matters. Next
year, the most anybody in a Medicare
drug plan can pay out of pocket for
covered drugs is $2,400
for the year. This year, it is $2,100.
So, the ceiling went up by $300. And the
standard deductible, the amount you can
be asked to pay before the plan starts
sharing costs, goes up to $700 from
If you take anything expensive, you will
