hit that deductible in January, and your
first pharmacy visit of the year will
feel like a mistake. It is not a
mistake. It is the new deductible. And
there is a detail inside that cap which
catches people every single year. The
ceiling only counts drugs your plan
actually covers. A drug that is not on
your plan's list does not count toward
the cap at all. And your monthly premium
does not count toward it either. You pay
that on top every month all year, which
is why the cheapest looking plan on the
screen can be the most expensive plan
you could possibly choose. A low premium
plan that does not cover one of your
drugs means paying full price for that
drug all year with no ceiling to stop
it. That is the single worst outcome in
this whole enrollment period and it is
completely avoidable by typing your
actual drugs into the plan finder before
you compare anything. If you do take
something costly, there is also a
program that lets you spread what you
owe across the months of the year
instead of paying most of it in January.
It is called the Medicare prescription
payment plan. It does not lower what you
pay. It changes when you pay it. For
somebody on a fixed income, that
difference can decide whether the first
quarter of the year is manageable. You
have to ask your plan for it. It does
not switch itself on. And while you have
the plan finder open, check one thing
that has nothing to do with which plan
you pick. There are two programs that a
great many people qualify for and never
apply to. The first is called extra
help. If your income and savings are
modest, it pays most or all of your drug
plan premium and cuts your co-pays down
to a few dollars. The second is the
group of Medicare savings programs run
by your state which can pay your part B
premium for you. That is more than
$2,400 a year going back into your
social security deposit. The limits are
higher than most people assume. Some
states do not count your home or your
car at all and a few do not look at
savings for certain levels. The raise on
the 14th may nudge some people's income
so do not assume you are over the line.
Apply and let them tell you. The worst
they can say is no and a surprising
number of people who assumed they were
too comfortable to qualify turn out to
be wrong. Now the good news and the trap
folded inside it. On the 1st of January,
the prices Medicare negotiated directly
with drug makers take effect for 15 more
drugs. They include Ozempic and Wegovy,
along with drugs for COPD and asthma,
type 2 diabetes, and prostate and breast
cancer. Medicare estimates the net
savings on those drugs at around 44%.
That is real, and it will help a great
many people. But understand what it does
and does not do. It lowers the price
Medicare pays. What you pay at the
counter still depends on your plan, your
deductible, and which tier your plan
puts the drug on. So, if you take one of
those 15, do not assume your costs fall
on their own. Check what your specific
plan will charge you for it next year,
and compare it against the other plans
in the plan finder, because they will
not all treat it the same way. And then
there is the decision that looks
simplest and is anything but. A great
many people this fall are going to read
that their Medicare Advantage plan is
cutting benefits, get angry, and decide
to leave Advantage and go back to
original Medicare with a supplement
policy. That can be a very good
decision, but there is a door on that
path that closes quietly, and almost
nobody warns you. When you first join
Medicare, you had a window where any
supplement company had to sell you a
policy, whatever your health. That
window is long gone for most of you.
Outside of it, in most states, a
supplement company is allowed to ask
about your health, and it is allowed to
charge you more or turn you down because
of it. So, a person who has been in
Advantage for 6 years, who now has a
heart condition and diabetes, can switch
to original Medicare in December, and
then find that no supplement company
will sell them a policy at a price they
can live with. And original Medicare
without a supplement has no ceiling on
what you can spend. A few states protect
you from that. New York and Connecticut
require supplement companies to sell to
you, whatever your health, all year
round. A handful of others, including
California, Oregon, Illinois, Idaho, and
Nevada, have rules that give you a
yearly window to switch supplement
policies without health questions.
Everyone else, check before you leave,
not after. Apply for the supplement
first, get the approval in writing, then
drop the Advantage plan, in that order.
There is one exception that is worth a
great deal this particular year. If your
Advantage plan is leaving your area or
ending altogether, you receive a
guaranteed right to buy certain
supplement policies, whatever your
health. That right has a time limit,
generally 63 days after your coverage
ends. With the number of plans pulling
out this year, more people will have
that right than usual, and most will not
know they have it. If your booklet or a
letter tells you your plan is not
continuing, that is not only bad news.
It may be the one chance you get to buy
a supplement without a health question.
Use it. Here is how that plays out when
nobody reads anything.
A woman I will call Winifred, 73, stayed
in the same Advantage plan for 5 years
because it had always been fine. The
booklet arrived in September. She did
not open it. Inside it said two things.
Her plan was dropping the giveback that
had been adding $90 a month to her
social security, and the cardiologist
she saw every quarter was leaving the
plan's network. She found out about the
first when her January deposit came in
$90 short. She found out about the
second at the reception desk of her
cardiologist's office in February.
$90 a month is over $1,000 a year, and
the specialist, out of network, was
going to cost her considerably more than
that. Winifred did not lose that money
because she made a bad decision. She
lost it because she never made one. The
booklet was in a drawer, the window came
and went, and the default made the
decision for her. The Quiet Rules was
built for exactly that moment, for the
person who would rather know which
letter matters before the window closes
than after. You can find it at
kevinexplains.shop.
Point your phone at the code on the
screen, tap the first link in the pinned
comment, or go through the description.
Keep it a full 7 days. If you close it
at the end of that week thinking it did
nothing for you, it comes back, no
conversation needed. Because the
alternative is the version Winifred
lived through, finding out about the cut
at the cardiologist front desk, holding
a plan card the office no longer
accepts. Day 32, November the 1st. This
one is for everybody watching who is not
on Medicare yet. If you are 60, 62, 64,
retired early, and buying your own
health insurance through the
marketplace, this date matters more to
your budget than anything else in this
video. Open enrollment for marketplace
coverage opens on the 1st of November,
and on the federal site, healthcare.gov,
it now closes on the 15th of December.
That is a full month shorter than it
used to be.
A few states run their own exchange with
their own dates, so check yours, but do
not count on January the way you may
have in past years. And the ground under
those plans has moved. The extra premium
help that kept marketplace coverage
affordable for the last few years
expired at the end of last year, and it
was not extended. So, the old cliff is
back. Once your household income goes $1
over four times the federal poverty
level, you lose all help with your
premium, not some of it, all of it. And
there is a second change that is
catching early retirees completely by
surprise. It used to be that if your
income came in higher than you
estimated, the amount of premium help
you had to pay back at tax time was
capped. That cap is gone. So, if you
estimate your income low, take the help
all year, and then sell some stock or
take a larger IRA withdrawal in
December, you can owe back every dollar
of it in April. Which means that for a
63-year-old, this fall's decisions are
tangled together in a way nobody warns
you about. A Roth conversion, a large
IRA withdrawal, selling an investment
property, any one of those done in
December to save tax can knock you over
the cliff and cost you your entire year
of premium help. Before you move any
money this fall, if you are on a
marketplace plan, work out where that
line is for your household. It is the
single most expensive dollar in your
finances. There is one more thing for
this age group and it lands at the end
of the 92 days. If you are between 19
and 64 and covered by Medicaid through
the expansion that most states adopted,
new federal work requirements begin by
the 1st of January. Roughly 80 hours a
month of work, volunteering, school, or
job training with exemptions for
caregivers and people with certain
conditions.
States are rolling this out on their own
timelines and their own paperwork and
some started earlier.
If you or somebody in your family is in
that group, do not wait for the letter.
Call your state Medicaid office this
fall and ask exactly what they will need
from you and when. Day 34, November the
3rd, the midterm elections.
I am not going to tell you how to vote
and I never will, but understand what is
on that ballot for your money, whichever
way you lean. The Social Security Trust
Fund is projected to run short in the
early 2030s and when that happens,
benefits are cut automatically unless
Congress acts first. The Congress
elected on the 3rd of November is very
likely the one that will face that
choice or let it pass them by. There are
bills sitting in Congress right now that
would change how the annual raise is
calculated, how the payroll tax works,
and how the retirement earnings test
treats people who keep working. None of
them has passed. Whichever you favor,
the people deciding what happens to them
are chosen that Tuesday. That is the
whole of what I will say about it. Then
comes the middle of November and the
second announcement, the one that gets a
fraction of the attention and costs a
great many people more than the raise
gives them. Medicare publishes next
year's official Part B premium, the
deductible, and the income brackets for
the surcharge called IRMAA.
And this is where I want to slow down
because this surcharge is one of the
least understood numbers in retirement.
And this fall is when you can still do
something about it. If your income is
above a certain level, Medicare charges
you more for Part B and Part D. For this
year, that first line sits at $109,000
for a single person and $218,000 for a
married couple. And it is a cliff, not a
slope. Go $1 over and you pay the full
surcharge for the entire year. At the
first level, that is a little over
$1,000 a year for one person and more
than 2,000 for a couple for $1. Now,
here is the part that matters for these
92 days. Medicare does not look at this
year's income. It looks at your tax
return from 2 years earlier. So, what
sets next year's premium is already
done.
But what you do with your income before
the 31st of December decides what you
pay for Medicare 2 years from now. A
Roth conversion, selling a rental,
cashing in a large chunk of an IRA done
this December, it can land on your
Medicare bill in 2 years' time, long
after you have forgotten why.
So, if you are planning any of those,
find out where the line is before you
move the money, not after. And if your
income dropped because life changed,
there is a form almost nobody knows
about. If you retired, lost a spouse,
divorced, or lost pension income, you
can ask Social Security to use your
current income instead of the old
return.
The form is called the SSA-44.
People pay the surcharge for 2 full
years without ever hearing that it
exists. Day 68, December the 7th, the
door closes. Whatever plan you are in at
the end of that day is your plan for
next year. And if you miss it, here is
what you should know, because it is not
quite as final as the commercial
suggests.
If you are in a Medicare Advantage plan,
there is a second, smaller window from
the 1st of January to the end of March.
During it, you can switch to a different
Advantage plan once, or leave Advantage
for Original Medicare and pick up a drug
plan.
It is narrower than the fall window, and
the supplement warning from earlier
applies just the same. But it exists,
and a surprising number of people who
got a nasty surprise in January never
learn they had until March to fix it.
Day 72, December the 11th. And this is
one almost nobody is talking about.
Congress did not pass a full budget for
the new year. At the start of September,
it passed a stopgap that keeps the
government funded through the 11th of
December. So there was no shutdown on
the 1st of October. But that means there
is another deadline sitting right in the
middle of the holidays. So let me take
the fear out of it in advance.
If the government does shut down in
December, your Social Security payment
keeps coming. So does Medicare. Those
are paid under permanent law and do not
depend on that yearly vote.
What can slow down is the service around
them. Local offices, phone lines,
replacement cards, certain appeals. So
if you have any business with Social
Security that needs a human being, a
question about your record, a new card,
an appeal, try to get it done before the
2nd week of December rather than after.
Day 76, December the 15th. The last day
to pick a marketplace plan on the
federal site for anybody not yet on
Medicare. After that, on healthcare.gov,
the door is shut until next year unless
something in your life changes. If you
are 64 and your Medicare starts partway
through next year, that does not excuse
you from choosing. You still need
coverage for the months in between.
There is a person I think about on this
date. A man I will call Orville, 63,
retired early from a utility company. He
estimated his income low, took his
premium help all year, and in December
his financial advisor suggested a Roth
conversion to use up a low tax bracket.
Sensible advice on its own. Nobody put
the two together. The conversion pushed
his household over the cliff, and in
April he owed back every dollar of
premium help he had received, a little
One good idea, one missing piece of
information, and a whole year of help
reversed. That missing piece is what the
quiet rules is meant to supply, before
December rather than after April.
It is at kevinexplains.shop,
the code is up on your screen, the first
link in the pinned comment takes you
there, and so does the description. 7
days to decide it was worth it,
otherwise it goes back. It will cost you
a good deal less than Orville's letter
from the IRS, the one that arrived in
April asking for his whole year back.
Day 92, December the 31st, New Year's
Eve. The last day of the 92, and the day
more money is decided than any other,
because a whole list of things only
count if they are finished before
midnight. And this is also where the
most confident wrong information is
being passed around this fall. So, let
me go through it carefully. Start with
the new senior deduction, because almost
everybody is describing it slightly
wrong. The tax law passed last year gave
people 65 and older an extra deduction
of up to $6,000 each, or $12,000 for a
married couple where both qualify. It
runs for four tax years, last year
through 2028. So, this is the second of
the four. It starts shrinking once your
income passes 75,000 for a single
person, or 150,000 for a couple. And it
disappears entirely a good deal above
that. You can take it whether you
itemize or not. All of that is right,
and it is genuinely helpful. Here is the
part that keeps getting said wrong. You
will hear that this deduction lowers
your adjusted gross income, and so it
might keep you under the line where your
Social Security gets taxed, or under the
Medicare surcharge line. It does not. It
is taken after your adjusted gross
income is worked out. It lowers the
income you pay tax on. It does not lower
the income those two tests look at. So,
it will not rescue you from the Social
Security tax line, and it will not
rescue you from the Medicare surcharge.
If you have been counting on it for
either of those, you need a different
tool. And that different tool is the one
I most want you to hear about if you are
70 and a half or older, and you give
anything at all to charity.
It is called a qualified charitable
distribution. Instead of taking money
out of your IRA, and then writing a
check to your church or your charity,
you have your IRA send the money
straight to the charity. For this year,
you can do that with up to $111,000.
And here is why it matters so much. That
money never counts as your income at
all. It does not appear in your adjusted
gross income. So, unlike the senior
deduction, it does lower the number that
decides whether your Social Security is
taxed, and the number that decides your
Medicare surcharge 2 years from now. And
if you are old enough to have required
withdrawals, it counts toward those,
too. The same gift given one way raises
your income. Given the other way, it
does not. Most people give the expensive
way for years without knowing there was
a choice. The one warning is timing. The
money has to leave your IRA by the 31st,
and a check that goes out in the last
week of December and is not cashed until
January can end up counting in the wrong
year. So, if you are going to do it, ask
your IRA company about their year-end
cutoff this month, not on Christmas Eve.
And there is something new for people
who do not itemize, which is most
retirees. Starting with this tax year,
even if you take the standard deduction,
you can deduct cash gifts to charity up
to $1,000 for a single person and 2,000
for a married couple. It has to be cash
to an ordinary public charity and it has
to be given by the 31st.
Small, but it is new and a great many
people who give every Sunday will never
hear about it. Next, the required
withdrawals.
If you are 73 or older, the minimum you
are required to take out of your
traditional IRAs and old workplace plans
has to come out by the 31st. Miss it and
the penalty is 25% of what you should
have taken, which drops to 10% if you
fix it quickly.
There is one wrinkle for people taking
their very first one. You can delay that
first withdrawal until April of next
year, but then you take two in the same
year, which can push your income, your
tax bracket, and your Medicare surcharge
up all at once. And if you have several
IRAs, you can add up the requirement and
take it from any one of them. But
workplace plans each have to be handled
on their own. That trips people every
year. And one more that is new this year
because the tax authorities stopped
being lenient about it. If you inherited
an IRA from somebody who had already
started their required withdrawals and
you are not their spouse, you generally
have to take something out every year
and empty the account within 10 years.
For several years, the IRS waived the
penalty while it finished writing the
rules. That grace period is over. If you
inherited an account in the last few
years and you have been leaving it alone
because somebody told you that you had
10 years, check this before the 31st.
And if you are the one leaving an IRA to
your children, tell them. Finally, Roth
conversions. If you convert part of a
traditional IRA to a Roth, it counts for
this year only if it is done by the
31st. There can be very good reasons to
do it, particularly in a year where your
income is lower than it will be later.
But every dollar you convert is income.
It counts toward the social security tax
line. It counts toward the Medicare
surcharge 2 years from now. And for
anybody under 65 on a marketplace plan,
it counts toward that subsidy cliff. Do
the arithmetic on all three before you
convert, not just the first. And then
you wake up
the 1st of January.
Your new cost of living raise shows up
in your January deposit minus the new
Part B premium. Your drug plan's new
deductible starts counting from zero.
The negotiated prices on those 15 drugs
switch on at the pharmacy. And your
plan, whichever one you ended up in on
the 7th of December, is the plan in your
wallet. Everything I described at the
start of this video is now simply true.
The only question is whether it is true
because you chose it or because nobody
did. So, here is what I would actually
do tonight, and it takes about 10
minutes.
Take the calendar that hangs in your
kitchen and write on it. On the 1st of
October, find the booklet. On the 14th,
work out your real raise after Part B.
Between the 15th of October and the 7th
of December, put in your drugs and
compare plans with a SHIP counselor if
you can. If you are under 65, circle the
15th of December. In the middle of
November, check the Medicare surcharge
lines against any money you plan to
move. And on the first week of December,
not the last, make your gifts, your
withdrawals, and any conversion. That is
the whole thing. Six marks on a
calendar. Most people will make none of
them. And if something in your own
situation does not fit neatly into any
of this, a plan that is leaving your
area, a surcharge you think is wrong, an
inherited account you are not sure
about, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com
and tell me what is going on. I read
them all, and the questions people send
in are what decide what I cover next.
Here is my own view of these 92 days,
for whatever it is worth.
Almost none of what happens this fall is
a secret. Every date I have given you is
published. Every number is public. The
booklet is mailed to your own house. And
yet every January, a great many people
are genuinely shocked by what happened
to their money. It is not because
anybody hid anything. It is because the
system is built to run on defaults, and
a default is simply a decision somebody
else made for you. Usually somebody with
a different interest from yours. The
insurer's default is the plan that suits
the insurer. The tax default is
whichever way costs you most. The only
way to beat a default is to show up
before it is applied. That is all these
92 days are, a window where showing up
is worth money, and after which it is
not. So when you wake up on the 1st of
January, I hope the check, the plan
card, the pharmacy price, and the tax
bill all look exactly the way you
expected, because you chose each one of
them.
If you want all of these rules in one
place, in your hands, before the first
of those dates arrives, the quiet rules
is linked in the description and the
pinned comment. I am Kevin. Thanks for
watching. Do not forget to check the
quiet rules at kevinexplains.shop.

title: The Bank Account A Judge Freezes Before You Even Know

segments.text: Your card gets declined at the pharmacy
counter. There is money in that account.
You know there is because your social
security landed 4 days ago. You try it
again. Declined again. And the young man
behind the register is looking at you
the way people look when they are trying
very hard not to. Here is what happened.
A few days before that moment, a
one-page court paper arrived at your
bank. Not at your house, at your bank.
Somebody there opened it, did exactly
what it said, and froze your account.
You were the last person in the entire
chain to find out. And the part that
should bother you most is this. Some of
that money was never allowed to be
frozen at all. Some of it was. And which
is which has nothing to do with whether
you owe anybody a penny today. It
depends on a few small decisions about
how your account was set up. Most of
them made years ago by people who
thought they were being sensible.
Because it does not only happen to
people in trouble. It happens to people
whose grown son is on their checking
account and just lost a lawsuit. It
happens to people whose own bank took a
missed car payment straight out of
checking. And it happens to careful
people who did everything right with
their social security and then did one
tidy, responsible thing that quietly
switched the protection off. So today we
are going to sit on the other side of
the counter at the desk inside the bank
where that paper lands. I am going to
walk you through what that desk does in
order in the first two business days
because every step is a place where your
money either stays yours or does not. By
the end, you will know how to build an
account a private creditor's order
cannot empty and the mistakes that break
it for people who were sure they already
had one. If that is useful, press
subscribe now because when the rules at
that desk change, this is where you will
hear about it first. One quick word, I
am not a lawyer and this is education
rather than legal advice. Some of this
comes from your state and states vary,
but the most important part is federal.
It applies everywhere and almost nobody
has had it explained to them. I am
Kevin, and the fine print is my whole
job. So, it is a Tuesday morning and the
paper arrives. It might be called a writ
of garnishment, a bank levy, a
restraining notice. The name changes
from state to state. What it says never
changes. A court has decided you owe
somebody money, and the bank must hold
what is in your account so they can
collect it. and understand the people at
that desk. They are not on your side.
They are not on the creditor's side.
They are on the side of the bank not
getting sued. They will follow the rules
to the letter and not one inch further.
So the rules are the only protection you
have in that room. Let us go through
them in the order the desk does. Step
one, who sent it? If the order came from
a private creditor, a credit card
company, a debt buyer, a hospital, a
landlord, then what happens next is
governed by a federal rule written to
protect people who receive federal
benefits. But if the order came from the
United States government itself or from
a state child support agency, that rule
steps aside and the bank simply freezes
what it is told to freeze. So what we
are building today is a wall against
private creditors. The government has
its own limits and we will get to them.
For everybody else, the desk moves to
step two. Step two, the desk looks back
two months. This is the most important
thing in this video, so go slowly with
me. The bank system opens your account
and searches the previous two months for
one kind of deposit. A federal benefit
payment sent electronically straight
into that account: Social Security,
supplemental security income, veterans
benefits, railroad retirement, federal
civil service, and federal employee
pensions. When those arrive by direct
deposit, they carry a small electronic
marker telling the bank's computer
exactly where they came from. The desk
is required to look for it. You do not
have to ask. You do not fill in a form.
You do not even have to know it is
happening. Whatever total of federal
benefits landed in that account by
direct deposit in those two months, the
bank must leave available to you. It
cannot freeze it. It cannot send it to
the creditor. It cannot even charge its
own garnishment fee against it. Private
creditors have never been allowed to
take social security. That goes back to
the original act in 1935. But for
decades, it only worked on paper because
banks froze everything first and left
the retiree to prove it in court. In
2011, the Treasury moved that burden
onto the bank. The bank does the
arithmetic itself automatically,
generally within two business days. That
sounds like the end of the story. It is
not because three things about how your
account is built decide whether that
protection covers all of your money or
only a slice of it. The first is how the
money arrives. The automatic protection
is for direct deposit. A paper check you
carry in and deposit yourself carries no
marker. It is still legally social
security, but the desk will not protect
it on its own. It freezes it and proving
what it was becomes your job. If any
federal payment still reaches you on
paper, that is the first setting to
change and it takes one phone call. The
second is how much has piled up. The
protected amount is the smaller of two

segments.text: There is a date being shouted at you

in this exact month, on this exact

number.

Now, here is what genuinely does happen

for Medicaid.

immigrant.
Those are people who came here legally,

legally today.
Their status is not changing. Their

I am telling you plainly who it reaches,

One provision, one group. Everything

the first clock. The 31st of December

The second is the person under 65 who is

If your daughter left a job to look

There is an exemption for caregivers in

But an exemption is not automatic. It is
a the you have to claim with
documentation inside a window.
And the entire history of programs like

Most of the people who lose coverage are

They are people who qualified and failed

Paperwork, not eligibility. Let me tell

Noreen is not on Medicaid. She has

It gets paid for out of her account

And that is precisely the situation I

Get your copy at kevinexplains.shop.
There is a code on the screen right now.

What is inside it for a month like this

That is exactly why she is the one who
pays.

Medicaid. So when a state's Medicaid

And a very large share of the home and

That is the mechanism that reaches you,

You will never receive a notice about

From January, states have to recheck

That is the entire change. It sounds

A letter arrives. It goes to the last

The letter has a deadline on it, usually

Doubling the frequency of that does not
double the paperwork. It roughly doubles

it.
And there is a second thing landing on
the same date that has had almost no
attention, and it is worth understanding

genuine crisis.
Retroactive coverage is being cut back.
The way it has worked for decades is
that if you were eligible for Medicaid
and did not happen to be enrolled when

program could reach backwards up to 3

that protection was built for. It is for
the person who has a stroke on a Tuesday
and is not in a position to fill in an
application for a fortnight.
It is for the family dealing with a

coming home, working out the paperwork
afterwards.
3 months was the margin for the fact
that catastrophes do not wait for your
filing to be in order.
1 month is a much thinner margin and the

And a third piece on that same date,

So, the fallback that everybody assumes
exists, the idea that you would simply
buy a policy instead, is closed off for

first thing.
That is not a gap. That is a door being
held shut behind the first door.
Now, the third clock, and this is the
Medicare one, and it is the 4th of
January.
On that date, the Social Security
Commissioner is required to terminate
Medicare eligibility for the same
categories of lawfully present
immigrants that the October provision

Refugees, people granted asylum, people
admitted on humanitarian grounds.
And I want to be exact about what that
means rather than vague because vague is
how people get frightened about things
that are not happening to them. It means
somebody who is here legally, who has
worked and paid Medicare tax out of
every paycheck for years, and who is
currently enrolled, has that enrollment
terminated on a date set by statute. Not
phased, not means tested, terminated.
And that is the first time I can recall
an eligibility category being removed
from people already receiving Medicare
rather than applied going forward to new
applicants. If that is not your
household, it costs you nothing to know.
And the reason I want you to know it is
this. A person in that position is going
to be terribly vulnerable in December
and January to somebody offering to fix
it for a fee.
There is no fix that costs money. If it
reaches somebody you know, the right
answer is free legal help for people 60
and over, which exists in every state
under federal law, and I will come back
to that at the end. And if you are a
citizen or a long-term permanent
resident, and you have been lying awake
about this one, put it down. It does not
reach you.
Now, the fourth clock, and I have to be
straight with you about this one because
it is the only item in this video where
I cannot tell you what is going to
happen. When Congress passes a law that
adds a great deal to the deficit, an old
rule can trigger automatic
across-the-board cuts to certain federal
programs, and Medicare is one of them.
There is a cap on how deep it can go for
Medicare, and the figure being discussed
is 4%. Now, here is what you need to
hold in your head about it in two parts.
The first part is what it actually cuts
because this is misreported constantly.
It does not cut your benefit. It does
not reduce your check, raise your Part B

reduces what the government pays
doctors, hospitals, and other providers.
Your entitlement is untouched. The
second part is why that still reaches

paid to see a Medicare patient drops,
some of them stop taking new Medicare
patients. That is the mechanism. Not a
cut to you, a cut to the number of
people willing to see you, and it shows
up in rural areas and in specialties
first. The honest position on the timing
is that this has been triggered, that
Congress has historically found a way to
postpone it every single time it has
come up, that there is legislation
pending to exempt Medicare from it, and
that as I record this, it has not been
resolved. So, anybody telling you with
confidence that your Medicare is being
cut by 4% is overstating it. And anybody
telling you it is definitely going to be
waived is guessing, too.
What I would do is not worry about it,
and instead do the one practical thing
it suggests, which is to confirm now,
this month, that your own doctor is
still accepting Medicare assignment, and
to know the name of one other practice
in your area that does. That is a
5-minute phone call, and it is worth
making whether this lands or not.
Now, I want to turn this around, because
there is something in this same law that
hands money to a very large number of
people watching this, and it has been
buried under the noise about everything
else.
This one is not a threat. It is a
deduction, and it is yours if you are 65
or older, and it has a date on it, too,
which is the part that is going to catch

The law created an additional deduction
of up to $6,000 per person aged 65 and
over.
Per person.
So, a married couple where both of you
are 65 or over is looking at up to
and that sits on top of the standard
deduction you already get, and on top of
the extra amount that people over 65
have always received. Three separate
things stacking, not one replacing
another. And here are the details that
decide whether you actually get it,
because almost every version of this you
will have heard has left at least one of
them out.
It begins to phase out once your
modified income passes $75,000
as a single person, or $150,000 on a
joint return, and it disappears entirely
single, or $250,000 joint.
You have to reach 65 by the last day of
the tax year, not at some point during
it.
And here is the one that surprises
people, because it is the opposite of
how these things usually work.
You do not have to take the standard
deduction to get it. If you itemize
because you have large medical costs or
you give a lot to charity, you can
itemize and still take this on top.
That is unusual, and a great many people
are going to leave it on the table
because they assume itemizing
disqualifies them.
There is one exclusion to know.
A married person filing separately is
not getting this at any income level,
which is one more entry on the growing
list of things that filing status
quietly costs the household.
And now the date, which is the whole
reason this belongs in a video about
clocks. This deduction is temporary. It
covers the tax years 2025 through 2028,
and unless a future Congress extends it,
it ends after that. So, there are three
more tax years of it, including this
one, and then it is gone, which turns it
from a nice surprise into a planning

what that actually means, because this
is where the real money is, and almost
nobody is treating it this way.
If you have been considering converting
some of a traditional retirement account
into a Roth, the years where you were
holding an extra six or twelve thousand
dollars of deduction are cheaper years
to do it in than the years afterwards.
If you have a capital gain you have been
putting off taking, the same logic
applies. If your income sits just above
one of the lines that decides how much
of your Social Security gets taxed, this

And if you are close to that
seventy-five thousand or hundred fifty
thousand figure, then the ordering of
your income across these years genuinely
matters, because a dollar that pushes
you over the line does not just get

That is a conversation worth having with
somebody who can see your actual
numbers, and it is worth having it this

because most of the moves that use this

Let me tell you about a man I will call
Wendell, seventy-four, a retired site

exactly the kind of income where this

Their preparer took the deduction

and say, "There is a window open, and it

each year, and he will never once use
the window for the thing it is actually
good for.
Wendell's window is exactly what I put

same as a window that was never open.
Your copy is at kevinexplains.shop.
The code is back on your screen. The

What it does for something like this is
put the timing in front of you.
Which of these changes has a deadline?
Which has a window? And what has to be

whenever you get to it? Written plainly
rather than in the language these things
arrive in. 7 days to look through your

back, and we part on perfectly good
terms. Nobody in Wendell's life did

the year behind him, which is the job,

of it. Now, there is one more thing in
this law, and it is the single most
relevant item in the whole video for the
ordinary American senior, and it has had

I have left it until now because it
needs the context I have just given you.
It does not take a benefit away from
anybody. It takes away a door that was
about to open. Here is the background.
There are programs run through your
state called the Medicare Savings

pay your Medicare Part B premium for

There are several levels of it, and the
upper levels exist specifically for

For years, the problem with these

that hardly anybody knew they existed,
and the application was its own small
ordeal. So, millions of people who
qualified never enrolled.
So, a rule was written to fix exactly

apply.
This law stops that rule being enforced.
And the estimate attached to it is that
something in the region of 1.3 million
people with Medicare, people who
genuinely qualify, will now not be
enrolled who otherwise would have been.
Read that again, because it is not the
shape people expect. Nobody is being
denied. Nobody is losing anything they
currently have. The door simply stays
shut instead of opening, and you will
never receive a letter about a thing
that did not happen to you. There is no
notice for this. There is no appeal for
this. The only way anybody ends up on
the other side of it is by applying the
old way, on their own initiative, having
somehow found out it exists, which is
why I am telling you now. If your income
is modest, and modest here is a great
deal higher than most people assume,
because these limits are tied to a
federal figure that moves every year,
then the most valuable phone call you
can make this autumn is to ask to be
screened for the Medicare savings

which is free and sells nothing, will
walk you through the application.
That is a call that can raise your
monthly deposit, and it exists whether
this law had passed or not.
What the law changed is only whether
anybody was going to come and find you.
They are not. So, you go and find it.
And there is a companion to that one,
which reaches a different group, and it
is the same shape. A second rule,
written to make it easier for people to
enroll in Medicaid and the related
programs, is also stopped.
The estimate on that one runs into the
millions over the coming years. Same

shut.
I want to name that pattern clearly
before I move on. Because once you see
it, you will spot it in everything that
comes out of Washington for the rest of
your life.
There are two ways to reduce what a
program costs. You can take something
away from people who have it, which is
visible, which makes the news, and which
somebody has to defend on television.
Or, you can make it slightly harder to
get in the first place, which is
invisible, which generates no story at

because you cannot send somebody a
letter about a benefit they were never
told about. Now, the last provision, and
this one is for anybody with a parent in

There was a federal rule setting a

It had a phase-in period, and the

for a year or two.
The moratorium runs until the 30th of
September, 2034.
Nine years. So, there is no federal
minimum staffing floor for a nursing
home for the next nine years. And I want
to be careful and fair here, because
there is a genuine argument on the other
side of it. Rural facilities in
particular argued they could not hire to
the standard at any price, and that a
rule they could not meet would have
closed them. And a closed nursing home
in a county with one nursing home is not
a better outcome for anybody. That
argument is real. I am not going to
pretend it is not, but here is what it
means for you practically, and this is
the only thing I want you to take from
it. There is no national number you can
rely on. So, when you or your family are
choosing a facility, the staffing
question is yours to ask, and it is not
a rude question. Ask what the actual
nursing hours per resident per day are.
Ask what the turnover rate among staff
has been. Ask how many agency staff are
used, meaning temporary people who do
not know the residents. Those three
answers tell you more about how somebody
will be cared for than the building, the

And you can look at a facility's own
reported staffing figures publicly
before you ever walk in.
There is also $50 set aside in this law
for rural health, distributed to states,
meant to soften the effect on rural
hospitals.
Whether it is enough is an argument for
somebody else's video. What matters at
your kitchen table is narrower. If you
live rurally, the hospital nearest to
you is having a difficult few years, and
services get thinned before buildings
close.
The obstetric unit goes first, then the
specialty clinic, then the emergency
department's overnight cover.
So, it is worth knowing now, while
nothing is wrong, where the nearest
emergency department is that will
definitely be open at 2:00 in the
morning, and how long that drive
actually takes.
Not because I expect your hospital to
close, because the answer to that
question is worth having before the
night you need it.
And there is one more date in this
autumn that has nothing to do with this
law at all, which is exactly why I want
to name it, because it is going to get
lost in the noise about everything else,
and it is the one with your name on it.
Medicare open enrollment runs from the
15th of October to the 7th of December
every year.
And the reason it matters this
particular year is that a great many
people are going to spend these weeks
reading frightening things about a bill
in Washington and miss the window where
they could have actually changed
something about their own coverage.
Your drug plan is allowed to change its
list of covered medications every single
year.
The pharmacy it prefers can change. What
you pay at the counter for the same
tablet you have taken for 9 years can
change. And the plan is required to send
you a notice about it in an envelope
that looks exactly like every other
envelope they send you in September.
So, while everybody is arguing about
October the 1st, the genuinely useful
thing sitting on your table is that
notice. And the question it answers is
whether the medication you take is still
on the list for next year.
If you do nothing at all during those
weeks, you are automatically kept in the
same plan under next year's rules, which
people mistake for safety.
It is not safety. It is a decision to
accept changes you have not read.
That is a 20-minute job with your list
of medications in front of you and the
free help I mentioned earlier. Your
state health insurance assistance office
will sit and do it with you at no cost
and with nothing to sell. Two dates, 3
weeks apart.
One of them is a headline about other
people. The other one is your own
prescriptions next year.
Spend your attention accordingly. And
while you have that notice out, there
are two other things on it worth 30
seconds each.
Look at whether your plan's deductible
has moved because that is the amount you
pay entirely yourself before the
coverage does anything at all, and it is
a number that moves more often than
people expect.
And look at whether your own pharmacy is
still in the preferred group because the
same plan can charge you one price at
one chemist and a different price at
another one two streets away for the
identical prescription purely because of
which one it has an arrangement with.
People change plans over a monthly
premium and lose more than they saved on
that one detail. So, let me put the
whole thing on one page because 30
minutes of detail is worth nothing if
you cannot hold it.
Four dates. October the 1st, Medicaid
eligibility ends for certain lawfully
present immigrants. The 31st of
December, work reporting requirements
begin for adults under 65 in the
expansion group. The 1st of January,
eligibility checks double in frequency,
the backwards protection narrows from 3
months to 1, and the marketplace
fallback closes behind the work rules.
The 4th of January, Medicare enrollment
is terminated for the same immigration
categories.
Then the one still unresolved, the
automatic cut that reaches what
providers are paid rather than what you
receive.
Then the deduction, up to $6,000 a
person running through 2028 and then
gone.
And then the two quiet ones, the
enrollment rule that would have found
you stopped. And the staffing floor in
nursing homes suspended for 9 years.
Now here is your list, and it is six
things, and most of them are phone
calls.
One, ring your own doctor's office and
confirm they are still accepting
Medicare assignment, and get the name of
one other practice in your area that is.
Five minutes, and it matters whether or
not that automatic cut ever lands.
Two,
ring your area agency on aging or your
state health insurance assistance office
and ask to be screened for the Medicare
savings programs.
Nobody is coming to find you for this
one, and it is the item on this list
most likely to put money back into your
monthly deposit.
Three, if there is anybody under 65 in
your family on Medicaid, a son, a
daughter, the person caring for you, sit
down with them this month and make sure
the address on their file is the address
they actually live at, and that they
know which exemption applies to them and
what documents prove it. The coverage
that gets lost is almost never lost over
eligibility. It is lost over a letter
that went somewhere else.
Four, if you are 65 or over, ask whoever
prepares your return one specific
question.
Given this deduction runs out after
2028, is there anything I should be
doing in these three years that I should
not wait to do?
That is a different question from do my
taxes, and you will get a different
answer.
Five. If anybody in your family is in a
facility or may be soon, ask the three
staffing questions.
Nursing hours per resident per day,
staff turnover, and how much agency
cover they use.
And go and look at the reported figures
yourself before you ask, so you know
whether the answer matches.
Six.
And this is the one to hold on to for
the next 6 months.
Nobody legitimate is going to ring you
about any of this.
If a call or a letter tells you that you
need to verify, confirm, re-enroll, or
pay a fee to protect your benefit
because of this law, it is a fraud
without exception.
Hang up.
And if somebody in your life is in one
of the groups genuinely affected, the
free legal help for people 60 and over
exists in every state under federal law,
and it is a far better answer than
anybody charging a fee to help. If you
have a question about your own
particular situation after all this,
write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read every one that comes in, and what
people send me is genuinely what decides
the next video. Now, my honest read, and
it is not the one you were expecting
from a video with this title.
The reason a law like this is difficult
to understand is not that it is
complicated. It is that it was written
to land in pieces. If every one of these
changes had taken effect on the same
morning, there would have been one
enormous news story, one set of
hearings, and a great deal of pressure
on a great many people. Instead, there
is a date in October, a date in
December, two in January, one that has
not been settled, a deduction that
quietly runs out 3 years from now, and a
pair of rules that were simply never
switched on. No single one of those is a
story, and a person only ever sees the
one that reaches them, which means
nobody ever sees the shape of it. I am
not telling you that to make you angry
because anger is not useful to you at
your kitchen table. I am telling you
because it tells you exactly how to
behave for the next 6 months. Not by
watching the news, which will have moved
on. By knowing your own four dates,
checking the one or two that actually
touch your household, and ignoring the
rest with a completely clear conscience.
And notice something about the list of
things to do. Almost none of it is about
this law. Confirming your doctor takes
Medicare, asking to be screened for a
program that pays your premium,
making sure your daughter's address is
right on a form,
asking a preparer a forward-looking
question, asking a nursing home what its
staffing actually is.
Every one of those was worth doing last
year and will be worth doing next year.
The law did not create those tasks. It
just removed the assumption that
somebody else was going to handle them
for you.
Last thought. There is a version of this
subject that exists purely to frighten
you, and it is going to be everywhere
for the next several weeks because fear
travels further than a date does.
The truthful version is duller and far
more useful.
Your check is not being cut. Your card
still works.
Four things are changing on four days.
Most of them will not reach you, and the
two that most likely will are a
deduction you should be using and a
program nobody is going to enroll you
in. That is the whole of it, and none of
it requires you to be frightened. It
requires you to make about three phone
calls. I am Kevin. Thanks for watching.
Do not forget to check the quiet rules
