segments.text: You can pay no income tax at all on a
dollar this year and still have that
same dollar cost you money. That
sentence does not make sense to most
people and it is the reason a great many
careful retirees end up paying more than
they needed to while doing everything
they were told. So before I give you a
single asset, I want to give you the
thing that makes the whole list make
sense. Because without it, you will hold
the right assets and still get caught.
Every dollar that touches your life in
retirement faces two separate tests, not
one. The first test is whether the tax
is charged on it. That is the one
everybody knows about and the one every
video on this subject stops at. The
second test is whether it gets counted.
Counted toward the figure that decides
how much of your social security becomes
taxable. Counted toward the figure
Medicare looks back at two years later
to set what you pay every month. And
here is the part that catches people. An
asset can pass the first test and fail
the second. It can be genuinely legally
untacked and still push part of your
social security check onto the tax
return and still raise your Medicare
premium 18 months later. So, there are
seven assets the tax code will not tax.
Five of them are invisible, which means
they pass both tests and cost you
nothing anywhere. Two of them are
untacked but counted. And those two are
where the damage happens because people
hold them believing they are safe. I am
going to go through all seven, tell you
which are which and give you the
condition attached to each one because
every single one of them has a condition
and that is where these things quietly
break. If you are not subscribed, do
that now because this is the channel
that reads what the rules actually say
rather than what everybody repeats about
them. One thing before we start, I am
not a tax adviser and this is education
rather than advice for your particular
return. Every rule here comes with a
condition and your own situation will
have details I cannot see from here. My
name is Kevin and I read the rules so
you do not have to. The first asset is
your own social security benefit and it
goes first because it is the thing the
second test is measuring which makes it
the one people get backwards. Plenty of
people assume every dollar of that check
is taxed the way a paycheck was. It is
not. The rule is that your benefit is
not taxable at all unless a particular
figure crosses a line. That figure is
built by taking all of your other
income, adding any tax exempt interest,
and then adding half of your Social
Security benefit. If the total stays
under $25,000 as a single person or
$32,000 on a joint return, then none of
your Social Security is taxable. Not a
dollar of it. Now, two things about
those lines that almost nobody is told
and both of them matter enormously. The
first is that crossing the line does not
put the whole check on the table. It is
graduated. Part of your benefit becomes
taxable. And even at the very top of the
scale, the most that can ever be counted
is 85% of it, which means at least 15%
of your social security is untouchable,
no matter how large your income gets.
There is no version of this where the
entire benefit is taxed. The second is
the one that should annoy you. Those two
figures, the 25,000 and the 32,000, were
written into law in 1983, and they have
never been adjusted for inflation. Not
once in over 40 years. Every other
number in the tax code moves with
prices. These two do not, which means
that every single year, on purpose, a
slightly larger share of ordinary
retirees crosses a line that was
originally drawn to catch only the
wealthy. That is not an accident and it
is not an oversight. A number that stays
still in a world where prices do not is
a tax increase nobody has to vote for.
And there is one row in that rule that
works completely against a particular
household. So listen for it. If you are
married, filed separately, and lived
with your spouse at any point during the
year, your base amount is not 25,000 and
it is not 32,000. It is zero. the
protection simply is not there for that
return. If that describes your
situation, that is worth a conversation
with somebody who can look at your
actual filing status because the gap
between filing jointly and separately in
that case is not a small adjustment. So
that is asset one and it belongs in the
counted column which I want you to start
keeping in your head as we go. The
second asset is the Roth account, and
this is the only thing on the entire
list that passes both tests cleanly with
nothing attached to it at all. Money
went into a Wroth after tax was already
paid on it. What comes out later once
the conditions are met is not taxed.
That much most people have heard. What
almost nobody has been told is the
second half, which is worth more than
the first. A qualified withdrawal from a
Wroth is not income, not reduced income,
not lightly taxed income. It is not
income at all for the purpose of any of
those calculations, which means it does
not appear in the figure that decides
how much of your Social Security is
taxable. And it does not appear in the
figure Medicare reads 2 years later to
set your premium. So, two retirees can
take the identical amount of money out
in the identical year, one from a
traditional account and one from a
Wroth. and one of them can trigger tax
on their social security and a higher
Medicare premium 18 months later while
the other triggers neither. Same money,
same month. Completely different
consequences everywhere else on the
return. There are two conditions and you
should know both precisely. The account
has to have satisfied a 5-year period
counted from the first year anything
went into a Roth for you and you have to
be past the age condition, which nearly
everybody watching this already is. Let
me tell you about a woman I will call
Marcine, 72, a retired school
administrator, and she has done
everything right for 40 years. Last
autumn, she needed $11,000 for a new
roof. She had the money in two places, a
traditional account and a wroth, and she
took it from the traditional one because
it was the larger balance, and that felt
like the sensible place to draw from. It
was not a foolish decision and nobody
would have flagged it. But she was
sitting just under one of the lines and
that withdrawal crossed it which made
part of her social security taxable for
the first time in her life. And the
following year it also moved her
Medicare premium. The roof cost her more
than the roof and the money to avoid all
of it was sitting in the other account
the entire time. That is the exact thing
this guide was built to stop. It is
called the quiet rules. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
There is a code on the screen now if you
want to point your phone at it. The link
is at the top of the pin comment and it
is in the description underneath. What
is in it for a video like this one is
the two column sheet. Every asset on
this list written out in large print
with a straight answer in each column,
taxed or not taxed, counted or not
counted, and the condition that has to
hold for each one. So that when you need
$11,000 for a roof, you can look at one
page and know which account to take it
from. 7 days with it. If it does not
show you something about your own
accounts you did not know this morning,
send it back and that is the end of it.
Marcine was not careless. She reached
for the bigger pile, which is what
anybody does, because nobody had ever
shown her that the two piles behave
completely differently once the money
leaves them. And here is the wrinkle on
that 5-year rule that catches people who
are new to it. It is not 5 years from
when you open that particular account.
It runs from the first year you had any
Roth at all. So somebody who opened one
years ago and forgot about it may have a
clock that started long ago. And
somebody who has just opened their first
one has a clock that starts now. There
is one more feature of a Roth that
matters enormously and it is about what
does not happen. Nobody forces money out
of it. A traditional account starts
pushing money at you on a schedule once
you reach a certain age whether you want
it or not. And every one of those forced
dollars counts everywhere. A Roth does
not do that to you. You can leave it
entirely alone for as long as you live,
which makes it the one account in this
entire subject that you control rather
than the other way around. The third
asset is a health savings account, and I
am including it because a great many
people in this audience have one sitting
somewhere from a job they left years ago
and have genuinely forgotten about it.
Money in that account was not taxed
going in. The growth inside it is not
taxed, and what comes out is not taxed
either, provided it goes to a qualifying
medical expense. That is the only thing
in the entire tax code that is untaxed
at all three stages. Nothing else does
that. And the withdrawal does not count
as income either, which puts it in the
invisible column alongside the Roth. Two
things about it that people get wrong in
opposite directions. The first is that
leaving the job did not close it. That
account is yours and it travels with you
and the balance sits there whether you
think about it or not. The second is the
one that catches people and it involves
a particular age. past 65, you can take
money out of that account for any reason
at all without the extra penalty that
would otherwise apply. And a lot of
people hear that and conclude the money
has become free to use however they
like. It has not. Take it out for
something that is not medical and it is
ordinary income counted everywhere like
any other income. The penalty
disappeared. The tax did not. So, the
useful way to hold this in your head is
that it stays invisible only while it is
paying medical bills. And it becomes a
fully counted withdrawal the moment it
pays for anything else. And here is the
part worth knowing if you have one and
are past 65. Medicare premiums are
generally a qualifying expense you can
pay from it, which means the very
deduction coming out of your Social
Security every month can be paid from an
account that cost you nothing in tax to
use if you have the balance sitting
there. The fourth asset is the one that
breaks the pattern. And this is the one
I most want you to hear because it is
the reason the whole two test idea
exists. A bond issued by a state or a
city. The kind people call a municipal
bond. The interest on those is exempt
from federal income tax. That is real
and it is not a loophole and it is
printed plainly in the rules. And for a
great many retirees, that is where the
understanding stops. Here is what does
not stop. That interest, exempt as it
is, is added right back in when the
calculation for your social security
runs. It is written into the rule in
plain words. You take your other income,
you add tax exempt interest, and you add
half your benefit. So, the interest the
government will not tax is interest the
government still counts, and it can push
part of your social security check onto
your return all by itself. Think about
what that means for somebody who bought
these specifically because somebody told
them it was the tax-free option for
retirees. They bought a product to
reduce tax and it can increase the tax
on their benefit. Not because anybody
misled them, but because they were
answering the first test and there was a
second one nobody mentioned. And it can
reach your Medicare premium the same
way. So municipal bonds are not a
mistake. And I want to be careful here
because they do a real job for the right
household. Particularly somebody in a
high bracket in a state with its own
income tax, but they belong in the
counted column. And anybody holding them
because they believe they are invisible
is holding them for a reason that is not
true. There is one more thing worth
seeing on that same line and it is
almost the mirror image. Interest from
Treasury securities works the opposite
way round. It is taxed federally and it
is exempt from state and local income
tax. So those two things people
constantly confuse with each other are
in fact opposites. The municipal one
avoids the federal tax. The government
one avoids your state's tax. If you live
somewhere with no state income tax at
all, half of that advantage is worth
nothing to you. And it is worth knowing
which half you are actually buying. And
there is one more thing about these
bonds that hardly anybody is warned
about because it only shows up if you
buy them a particular way. A bond bought
secondhand at a discount to its face
value can produce a gain when it
matures. And that gain is not exempt
from anything. It is taxable. So
somebody can buy what they were told was
a tax-free bond and end up with a
taxable amount at the end of it purely
because of the price they paid rather
than anything about the bond itself. And
there is a version of these bonds that
can reach an alternative calculation
that applies to a small number of
households. which is another reason the
phrase tax-free is doing more work in
the sales conversation than it is doing
in the rules. And if you hold these
through a fund rather than individually,
look at what is actually inside it.
Because a fund holding bonds from all
over the country only gives you the
federal exemption. The state exemption
on top of it generally applies only to
bonds issued in the state where you
live. So somebody in a state with a
meaningful income tax holding a national
fund is getting half the benefit they
think they are getting and paying their
own state on the rest of it. And one
small thing because it worries people
every single year when that exempt
interest appears as a line on your
return. Nothing has gone wrong.
Reporting it is an information
requirement and it does not turn it into
taxable interest. It is being reported
precisely because it gets counted in
that other calculation which is the
whole point I have been making. The
fifth asset is life insurance seen from
the side of the person who receives it.
If your name is on a policy as the
beneficiary and the person insured dies,
that payment is generally not included
in your income and there is nothing to
report on it. In the hardest month
somebody will ever have, that money
arrives and the tax return does not
change. There are two edges on it and
both are worth knowing before you need
them. The first is that any interest the
insurance company adds while it holds
the money is taxable and is reported as
interest. So the payment itself is clean
and the interest sitting on top of it is
not. The second is one that catches
families and it is a thing people do
with good intentions. If a policy is
handed over to somebody else in exchange
for money, that exclusion is limited to
roughly what was paid for it, which is a
very different outcome from simply being
named on it. Now, two practical things
about this asset that matter more than
the tax rule does. The first is that the
payment goes to whoever is named on the
policy, not to whoever your will says,
not to whoever everybody in the family
assumes. The name on the form wins. And
the form was very often filled in
decades ago, sometimes before a divorce,
sometimes before a second marriage,
sometimes naming somebody who has since
died. That happens more than anybody
would believe. And it is entirely
preventable by looking. So the task
attached to this one is not tax planning
at all. It is reading the beneficiary
line on every policy you own and on
every account that has one and
confirming out loud that it says what
you think it says. The second is that
you should tell somebody the policy
exists. A payment that costs no tax is
worth nothing at all if the family never
files a claim because nobody knew there
was anything to claim. That happens and
there is no system anywhere that reaches
out to tell them. The sixth asset is
anything given to you or left to you. In
most cases, property you receive as a
gift, a bequest, or an inheritance is
not included in your income. A house
left by a parent, savings left by an
aunt, money given to you while somebody
is alive, none of that arrives as
taxable income to you. And when a gift
is large enough for gift tax to come
into it at all, the person giving it is
generally the one responsible, not the
person receiving it. What that property
earns after it reaches you is a
different matter entirely. interest,
dividends, and rent produced by it once
it is yours are taxable to you like
anything else. And there are two things
in this area that are worth more than
most people realize because they sit
completely outside the gift rules. The
first is that an amount under the yearly
exclusion is simply outside the whole
system. And that figure is per person
per year, which means a couple giving to
a child and that child's spouse is
working with several of those at once
without touching anything complicated.
The second is the one hardly anybody
uses. Tuition or a medical bill paid
directly to the school or the provider
is not a taxable gift at all in any
amount and it does not use up anything.
Paid directly. That is the condition and
it is the entire difference. Money
handed to your grandson to pay his
hospital bill is a gift. The identical
amount paid straight to the hospital is
not. And one thing I want to say plainly
here because it is where the largest
mistakes in this whole subject get made.
When somebody dies and leaves you
something that has grown in value, a
house, shares, land, the value generally
resets to what it is worth on the day
they died, which means the growth of an
entire lifetime can pass without capital
gains tax ever touching it. Now compare
that to the same asset given to you
while they are alive, where you
generally inherit their original cost
instead, and the gain comes with it.
Same house, same family, same intention.
The timing changes the tax by an
enormous amount. And this is exactly the
decision people make at a kitchen table
without knowing a decision is being
made. That one is worth a conversation
with somebody who can look at the actual
numbers before anybody signs anything.
Let me tell you about a man I will call
Hollis. 78 widowed and every December
for 11 years he has given his church
$4,000. He takes his required withdrawal
from his traditional account. The tax is
taken out of it and then he writes the
check from his bank account the way he
has always done it. 11 years. And every
one of those years, that $4,000 was
counted as his income first because it
landed in his account before it left it,
which lifted the figure that decides how
much of his social security is taxable.
He gave away money and paid tax on it on
the way past. Nothing he did was wrong.
He simply used the route he had always
used. Hollis's 11 years is the number I
want you sitting with, because nothing
went wrong in any of them. That is the
whole reason the quiet rules exists.
Same place, kevinexplains.shop.
The code is back on your screen. The
link is at the top of the pinned comment
and in the description below. What it
gives you here is the routing. Which
account a dollar should leave from, in
what order, in which route to use for
the things you already do every year
anyway, so that the money you are going
to move moves the cheap way instead of
the expensive way. Seven days to look it
over. And if it does not earn its place
in the first hour, it goes back and we
part on good terms. Hollis was generous
for 11 years and paid for the privilege
because of the direction the check
traveled. That is the seventh asset and
it is the one that opens in your 70s. If
you are past 70 and a half and you have
a traditional account and you give to a
church or a charity at all, this is the
most valuable thing in this video for
you. Money normally comes out of a
traditional account as ordinary income
counted everywhere. There is one
exception. If the money goes directly
from the account to a qualifying charity
arranged by the custodian rather than by
you, it is generally not a taxable
distribution at all. It never becomes
your income. It never enters the
calculation for your social security. It
never reaches the figure Medicare reads
2 years later. The limit is substantial,
a little over $100,000 per person per
year. And if you file jointly, your
spouse can do the same from their own
account. And here is the part that
changes the arithmetic completely once
the forced withdrawals have started. It
counts toward what you were being forced
to take out anyway. So the withdrawal
the rules require can go to the charity
and stay off your income at the same
time. You were going to be forced to
take that money. You were going to give
that money. This does both in one
movement and the tax never touches it.
Now the conditions because there are
several and each one has caught
somebody. The money has to travel
directly. The moment it lands in your
bank account first, it is an ordinary
taxable withdrawal and writing the check
afterwards does not undo that. There is
an age condition of 70 and a half. And
note that this is a different age from
the one where force withdrawals begin,
which means there is a window of a few
years where you can do this before
anything is being forced on you at all.
And using that window shrinks the
account before the force withdrawals
ever start. It has to go to an operating
charity which means donor advised funds
and private foundations do not qualify.
You cannot receive anything of value
back for it. So the gayla ticket and the
auction item break it. It cannot come
from an ongoing employer funded account
of certain kinds. And a workplace
retirement plan cannot do this at all.
Only an individual retirement account
can. And you need the same written
acknowledgement from the charity that
any donation would require. The order
matters, too. And this is the one that
quietly ruins it. Once you have taken
your required withdrawal for the year,
that money cannot retroactively become
one of these. It has to go out this way
first, which means the person who takes
their withdrawal in January and thinks
about charity in December has already
closed the door for that year without
knowing it was open. So if you give
anything at all and you are past that
age, the single most valuable phone call
available to you is to your account
custodian asking them to send it
directly and making that call before you
take anything else out this year. Now
before I put the seven side by side, I
want to spend two minutes on the other
side of this because the things people
wrongly believe are untaxed cost more
than the things that genuinely are.
There are four of them and every one of
them lands somebody in an unpleasant
April. The first is the idea that money
from your own savings account is not
income because you already paid tax on
it. The money you deposited is not
income. That is correct. The interest it
earns is every dollar of it ordinary
income counted everywhere. Which is why
moving a large balance into something
paying a real rate is a decision with
two consequences rather than one. And I
have covered that properly in its own
video. The second is the belief that a
withdrawal from a retirement account is
somehow softer than a paycheck because
it is your own money and you are
retired. It is not softer. It comes out
as ordinary income at the same rates a
wage was taxed at and it stacks on top
of everything else you have that year
rather than sitting underneath it. The
third is one I hear constantly and it is
about the sale of a home. There is a
genuine exclusion on the gain from
selling the home you actually live in
and it is generous but it belongs to
your primary residence. A holiday place,
a cabin, a property you rented out,
those do not carry it and the gain on
them is exposed. The fourth is the most
expensive of the lot. A great many
people believe that because a debt was
forgiven, nothing happened. A canceled
debt is very often treated as income to
you and a form arrives saying so. And
people who genuinely had no money that
year discover they have income that
year. I am not going to work through the
exceptions here because they deserve
their own video. But if a letter has
ever arrived telling you a balance was
written off, that is not the end of the
story and it is worth knowing before the
spring. And I want to name one more
thing in the same family because it
catches households at the worst possible
moment. When somebody dies, the money in
their traditional retirement account
does not become untacked because they
are gone. It carries the tax with it to
whoever inherits it, and the rules on
how fast it has to come out changed in
recent years and are stricter than most
families expect. An inherited
traditional account is a tax bill with a
deadline attached. An inherited Roth is
not, which is one more reason the two
accounts that look similar on a
statement behave nothing alike once they
leave the family's hands. Now, let me
put the seven side by side because once
you see the shape of it, you will never
look at your own accounts the same way.
Five of them are invisible, meaning
untaxed and uncounted, the Roth, the
health account while it pays medical
bills, the life insurance payment, the
gift or the inheritance, and the
charitable distribution straight from
the account. Money can move through any
of those, and nothing else on your
return moves at all. Two of them are
untaxed, but counted, and those two are
the ones that catch careful people. your
own social security benefit, which is
what the counting is measuring, and the
municipal bond, which is exempt from the
tax and added straight back into the
calculation. And notice something about
how they split because it tells you
where your effort should go. Three of
them are about where money is kept. Two
of them are about money arriving from
somebody else, which you mostly do not
control. And two of them, the benefit
and the charitable route, are about how
money is counted in which direction it
travels. Those last two are the ones you
can change this year without buying
anything, without moving an account, and
without anybody's permission. That is
where the money is. Now, my honest read
on all of it. The reason ordinary
retirees get caught by this is not that
the rules are hidden. Every one of them
is published and public and anybody can
read it. It is that the rules are
written in separate places by separate
people and they do not refer to each
other. The page that tells you a Roth
withdrawal is not taxed does not mention
Medicare. The page that tells you
municipal interest is exempt does not
sit next to the page that adds it back
in. So somebody can read everything
relevant to their situation, understand
all of it correctly, and still get
caught because the trap is not in any
one rule. It is in the space between two
of them. And nobody owns that space. Not
your bank, not your broker, not the
person who sold you the bond, and not
the agency that sends your check. The
retirees who do well here are not more
sophisticated than you. They just
happened to learn once that untaxed and
uncounted are two different words. So,
here is your list. Seven items, one for
each asset. One, if you hold a Roth,
confirm the 5-year clock has been
satisfied. And remember that when you
need a lump sum, it is the cheapest
place in your house to take it from.
Two, if you have a health account from
an old job, find out what is in it. And
if you are past 65, ask whether your
Medicare premium can be paid from it.
Three, if you hold municipal bonds,
understand that the interest gets
counted in the social security
calculation even though it is not taxed
and decide whether you still want them
on that basis. Four, read the
beneficiary line on every policy and
every account you own and check that the
name on it is the name you would choose
today.
Five, if anybody in your family is
planning to hand over a house or shares
while they are alive, get advice before
it happens because the timing changes
the tax enormously.
Six, if you help a grandchild with
tuition or a medical bill, pay the
institution directly rather than handing
over the money. Seven, if you are past
70 and a half and you give to a church
or a charity at all, ring your account
custodian and set up the direct route
before you take anything else out this
year. And if you have a question about
your own particular situation, write to
me at kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read everyone that comes in and the
questions people send are what decide
the next video. If this was useful,
subscribe because the pieces that cost
people money are almost never the famous
ones. Last thought, nobody is going to
send you a letter explaining which of
your dollars are counted and which are
not. There is no office that holds both
halves of this at once and no person
whose job it is to put them side by side
for you. It is one afternoon with a pen
and a list of your own accounts and the
whole thing becomes visible. Most people
never get that afternoon, not because
they could not have understood it, but
because nobody ever told them the second
test existed. You know now I am Kevin.
Thanks for watching. Do not forget to
check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: 6 Places Seniors Should Never Keep Their Cash Before Nov 1

segments.text: Your money is sitting somewhere right
now and whatever that place is paying
you, it did not ask your permission to
pay you that and it will not ask your
permission to pay you less. There are
two dates coming 11 days apart and
between them almost every rate in this
country gets reset. The first is the
27th and 28th of October when the
Federal Reserve meets and decides. The
second is the 1st of November when the
government resets the rate on the one
savings product built to keep pace with
inflation. And whatever it announces
that morning is locked for the next 6
months for everybody who buys after it.
Neither of those dates is going to be
explained to you by the institution
currently holding your savings. And here
is the part that should bother you. A
rate cut reaches your savings account
within days. The bank does not need to
notify you, does not need your
signature, and in most cases, does not
need to announce it anywhere you would
look. A rate increase, on the other
hand, has a way of taking weeks to
arrive. That asymmetry is not a
conspiracy. It is simply the direction
the incentive runs. So, today, I am not
going to hand you another list of places
to put your money. I'm going to count
down from the worst to the best the six
places retirees are actually keeping
cash right now. Starting with the one
where I would move the money this

ask before you sign is simply whether it
is callable, and a straight answer is
easy to get. The third is that early
withdrawal penalties vary enormously,
and this occasionally works in your
favor. If rates have risen substantially
since you locked yours in, it is
sometimes worth breaking a certificate,
paying the penalty, and reinvesting at
the higher rate. The arithmetic is
simple enough to do on a piece of paper,
and almost nobody does it because the
word penalty stops people before they
run the numbers. And the same
variability is a reason to compare
penalties rather than only rates when
you buy. Two certificates paying the
same rate, one charging three months of
interest to break and the other charging
12 are not the same product. And one
arrangement worth knowing about if you
are holding a large balance, and the
idea of splitting it across several
institutions sounds like a chore. Some
banks participate in networks that
spread your deposit across many other
insured institutions behind the scenes
so that a single account can be covered
well beyond the ordinary limit without
you opening accounts everywhere. You
deal with one bank, one statement, one
relationship. The network handles the
distribution. It is a legitimate
arrangement and it exists precisely for
this problem. Two things to check before
using one. Confirm which institutions
your money is actually placed with
because you cannot be insured twice at
the same bank. And if you already hold
money at one of them, there can be an
overlap. And understand that the rate is
usually somewhat lower than chasing the
best individual offers yourself, which
is the price of the convenience. For
somebody with a large amount who does
not want to manage five relationships,
that trade is frequently worth making.
For somebody with $200,000, it is
unnecessary. Now, a distinction that
trips up an enormous number of people,
and it is the difference between insured
and not insured. A money market account
and a money market fund sound like the
same thing. They are not. A money market
deposit account is a bank product. It is
federally insured exactly like a savings
account to the same limits in the same
categories. A money market fund is an
investment product usually held through
a brokerage and it is not covered by
deposit insurance at all. Now government
money market funds are genuinely
conservative and they are held by an
enormous number of institutions and
individuals. I am not telling you they
are dangerous. I am telling you that
very conservative and federally insured
are two different sentences and only one
of them comes with a government
guarantee. So if anybody offers you a
money market anything, there is one
question that settles it. Is this an
insured bank account or is this an
investment fund? And there is a related
confusion worth clearing while I am here
because people conflate two protections
that do completely different jobs.
Deposit insurance protects your money if
the bank fails. The protection that
covers brokerage accounts is a different
thing entirely. It protects you if the
brokerage firm fails and your assets go
missing. It does not protect you against
an investment losing value. Those are
not the same risk and the coverage is
not interchangeable. Now, the option
that a great many older households
overlook completely, and it is
particularly useful if you are holding a
large amount, lending money to the
government directly. Treasury bills and
notes are backed by the government
itself. They currently pay in the region
of 4% and there are two advantages that
matter enormously for the situation this
video is about. The first is that there
is no insurance ceiling to work around
because there is no insurance involved.
It is the government's own obligation
which makes it genuinely well suited to
protecting a large balance without
splitting it across five banks. The
second is tax and this is the part that
almost nobody mentions. Interest from
Treasury securities is exempt from state
and local income tax. If you live
somewhere with a meaningful state income
tax, that is a real advantage over a
bank account paying the identical rate.
And it costs you nothing to capture. You
can buy them directly with no middleman
and no commission through the
government's own system or through a
brokerage. And here is the piece I have
genuinely never heard anybody explain to
an ordinary retiree. And it is the
reason treasury bills deserve a place in
this video rather than a footnote. A
treasury bill of less than a year does
not pay interest along the way. You buy
it at a discount and it matures at full
value. And the interest is reported in
the year it matures, which hands you
something you almost never get with a
bank account. Control over which tax
year the income lands in. A bill bought
in November that matures in February
puts that interest in next year rather
than this one, which matters a great
deal if you are sitting close to a
threshold. And I will come to those
thresholds in a moment. And the same
idea applies more powerfully to savings
bonds designed to track inflation. Those
have a limit on how much you can buy in
a year. They cannot be touched at all
for 12 months. And cashing them in
before 5 years costs you 3 months of
interest, but the interest accumulates
inside them and is not taxed until you
cash them in, which means no annual form
arrives. Nothing lands on your return
each year, and you decide the year the
income appears. For a retiree, that is
not a small technicality. That is the
ability to hold money productively for
years without it touching the
calculation that decides how much of
your social security gets taxed and then
to realize it in a year of your
choosing. Let me tell you about a woman
I will call Verene 70 in Michigan
widowed. She did exactly what everybody
told her to do, which was move her
savings out of an account paying almost
nothing into one paying 4%. It was the
right decision and I would have told her
to do it. What nobody mentioned was what
it would do to the rest of her return.
The interest pushed her past a threshold
and a portion of her social security
became taxable for the first time in her
life and the following year her Medicare
premium reflected it. The additional
cost was a meaningful fraction of the
extra interest she had earned. She still
came out ahead, but she came out
considerably less ahead than the advice
she had been given suggested, and she
found out in the spring. Verene's
situation is why the tax section of the
quiet rules sits right next to the
section on where to put money because
the two questions are the same question
and almost nobody treats them that way.
Scan the code or go to
kevinexplains.shop
or use the link at the top of the pinned
comment. 7 days to look it over and if
it does not earn its place, send it
back. Verene was not given bad advice.
She was given half of the advice, which
in this particular subject is a
different thing. So, let me give you the
other half now. And I am going to keep
it tight because I have covered the
mechanics in full elsewhere on this
channel. Interest is ordinary income,
every dollar of it, and it counts toward
the figure that decides how much of your
social security is taxable, which for a
great many households sits on thresholds
that have not been adjusted since the
1980s. And it counts toward the income
figure Medicare reads 2 years later to
set your premium, where crossing a line
by a single dollar costs you the entire
step rather than a portion of it. Which
means moving a large balance from almost
nothing to 4% is not only a decision
about interest. It is a decision that
can move you across two separate lines
and the second one does not show up for
2 years. None of that is a reason not to
do it. Earning 4% and paying some tax on
it is better than earning nothing. I
want to be completely clear about that
because this is exactly the sort of
thing that gets used to frighten people
into doing nothing. It is a reason to
know roughly where you sit before you
move a large sum and to consider whether
some of it belongs somewhere that gives
you control over the timing, which is
precisely what treasury bills and
inflation bonds do. And one warning
about a thing that gets recommended
constantly in this context and is
frequently misunderstood. Municipal bond
interest is exempt from federal income
tax, which people know. What they do not
know is that it still counts toward the
calculation that decides how much of
your social security is taxed. So, a
product bought specifically to be
tax-free can still increase the tax on
your benefit. That surprises people
every single time and it is written
plainly in the rules. Now, the fifth
question, which is who gets paid when
you say yes? And this is where the last
product on the list belongs, the
annuity. And I want to handle this
fairly because annuities are not evil
and the people who tell you they always
are have their own reasons for saying
so. An annuity is a contract with an
insurance company. And for certain
people in certain situations, it does a
real job, which is turning a lump sum
into income that cannot run out. If your
fear is outliving your money rather than
losing it, that is a genuine problem,
and this is a genuine tool for it. But
run it through the five questions and
you can see exactly why it is being
pushed at you rather than offered.
Question one, is it insured? Not by the
federal government. There is no deposit
insurance on an annuity, and anybody who
implies otherwise is doing something
wrong. There is a state level
arrangement, a guarantee association,
which provides a backs stop if an
insurance company fails. It is real and
it has paid out, but the limits vary by
state. They are generally lower than
people assume, and it is not the same
thing as federal deposit insurance and
should never be described as though it
were. Question two, does it lock? Yes,
and frequently for a long time. Many
carry a surrender period of six to eight
years, sometimes longer. And taking
money out during that window triggers a
charge that can begin around seven or
eight% and step down each year. And
there is a second mechanism attached to
some of them that people have never
heard of, which adjusts what you receive
based on what interest rates have done
since you bought it. So the amount you
get back can be reduced by something
beyond the stated surrender charge.
Question three, what does it do to my
tax? growth inside it is not taxed until
it comes out, which is genuinely useful
and works in the same direction as the
savings bonds I described earlier. But
when it does come out, it comes out as
ordinary income rather than at the
gentler rates that apply to investments
and the earnings come out first.
Question four, can they change the rate?
On some of them, yes, after an initial
period, and that is where a great deal
of disappointment lives. And question
five, who gets paid when you say yes?
Somebody is paid a commission,
frequently a large one, and frequently
entirely upfront. And that commission is
part of why this product is marketed
harder at your age group than anything
else in this video. None of that makes
it wrong for you. It makes it a decision
that deserves more scrutiny than a
savings account, not less, which is the
opposite of how it is usually sold. So,
here is the only rule I would give
anybody on this, and I would give it to
my own family. Never sign an annuity
contract in a single meeting. If
somebody has created urgency, that
urgency is the warning rather than the
reason. A product that genuinely fits
your life will still fit it in a
fortnight after somebody with no stake
in the sale has read the contract. And
that second opinion is available. An
adviser paid a flat fee, who earns
nothing from what you buy, will read it
and tell you plainly. There are free
directories of them. One conversation
costs a few hundred at most and can
prevent a decision that is very
difficult and very expensive to undo.
And the same applies to the free dinner
because it is running right now and it
is aimed at exactly this audience. The
education portion is frequently
accurate. The destination is a product
with a commission attached. If an
evening about protecting your savings
ends with paperwork, you were not the
audience that night. Two more things
before the list and both are about what
happens to this money rather than what
it earns. The first is that every
account you hold should have a named
beneficiary on it. And I raised this
earlier for insurance reasons, but the
other reason matters just as much. An
account with a named beneficiary passes
directly to that person on production of
a death certificate. No probate, no
waiting, no court. An account without
one becomes part of an estate, which
means it is frozen until somebody has
legal authority. And that authority
takes time to obtain in the exact weeks
when a funeral has to be paid for. So
the same 10-minute form does three jobs.
More insurance coverage, faster
transfer, and it keeps a surviving
spouse out of a situation where the
money exists and cannot be reached. The
second is about spreading money across
institutions, which I have recommended
twice in this video, and there is a cost
to it nobody mentions. Every additional
bank is another login, another
statement, another set of paperwork, and
another thing somebody will have to find
and unwind one day. Which means there is
a genuine argument for consolidating
rather than scattering, particularly as
people get older. And the right answer
is a balance rather than a maximum. If
you do hold accounts at several
institutions, keep a single written list
of where everything is and tell somebody
where that list lives. Not the
passwords, just the institutions. The
number of families who have discovered
an account 18 months after a death or
never discovered one at all is far
larger than people imagine. And every
state runs an unclaimed property office
precisely because of it. Here is your
list. Six things. One, find out what
your cash is actually earning right now.
Not what it earned when you opened the
account and not the rate on the
advertisement. What is on this month's
statement? Two, if you have cash at a
brokerage, ask what it is being swept
into and what else is available inside
the same account. That one call recovers
more money for more people than anything
else on this list. Three, work out your
insurance coverage properly using the
categories rather than assuming a single
limit. And if you are near it, add
beneficiaries to an account. 10 minutes,
more coverage, and it avoids probate at
the same time. Four, before moving a
large balance into something paying 4%,
know roughly where you sit against the
thresholds that tax your social security
and consider whether some of it belongs
in something that lets you choose the
tax year. Five, before you buy any
certificate, ask two questions. Is it
callable? And is it a bank certificate
or a brokered one? Both answers change
what you are holding. Six. If anybody is
selling you anything, ask who pays them
and how much. It is not a rude question
and the answer is frequently the whole
story. If any of that landed close to
home, all of it is laid out in order in
the quiet rules link pinned at the top
of the comments. And if you have a
question about your own situation, write
to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read everyone, my honest read. There
is a belief that has done more damage to
careful savers than almost anything
else, which is that safe and productive
are opposites. For a generation, people
your age were told that the responsible
thing to do with cash was to leave it
alone, and that anything paying a real
return must involve risk. That was never
quite true, and it is plainly not true
now. Every single option in this video
is either federally insured or backed by
the government itself. The difference
between the household earning 4/10en of
1% and the household earning 4% is not
appetite for risk. It is knowing which
door to walk through. And the reason so
many people are on the wrong side of
that gap is not a lack of intelligence
or discipline. It is that the
institution holding your money has no
incentive to tell you. And the only
people with an incentive to telephone
you are the ones selling something that
pays a commission. So the field is left
to whoever happens to hear the right
thing from a neighbor. Last thought.
Money sitting still in a retirement is
not neutral and it is not safe. It is
making a decision every month and it is
making it in favor of somebody else. The
five questions in this video take about
20 minutes to run against wherever your
money currently sits insured and to what
limit locked or not, what it does to my
tax, whether the rate can move, and who
gets paid. That is not investing and it
is not risk. It is finding out what has
already been decided on your behalf and
deciding whether you agree with it. I am
Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: 4 Medicare Changes Hitting In 2027, One Costs You $300 More

segments.text: There is a headline going around saying
Medicare drug coverage is ending and it
is false. It is not ending. It is not
being cut. Nothing about the program is
going away. What is actually happening
is more specific than that. It affects
one particular group of people rather
than everybody on Medicare. And if you
are in that group, nobody is going to
write and tell you. So, let me give you
the true version because the true
version is both less frightening and
more useful than the headline. On the
28th of July this year, the agency that
runs Medicare announced that a temporary
program most people had never heard of
will not continue into next year. It
ends on the 31st of December. That
program has been quietly holding down
the monthly cost of standalone drug
plans for 2 years. When it stops,
roughly 25 million people lose a cushion
they never knew they had. And here is
the number that matters. The agency
itself says around 75% of people in
those plans should expect their premium
to rise. 3/4 of one specific group. Now,
that group is not everybody. This is the
part that almost every video on this
subject gets wrong. So, let me be
precise about who is affected and who is
not. If you have a standalone drug plan,
meaning you are on ordinary Medicare and
you bought drug coverage separately,
this is about you. If your drug coverage
is bundled inside a Medicare Advantage
plan, the program that is ending never
applied to you in the first place. You
have other things to watch this year and
I will get to those, but this specific
change is not one of them. So, the first
useful thing you can do in the next 10
seconds is work out which of those two
you are. If you have a separate card for
your drug plan from a different company
than your medical coverage, you are in
the first group. I am not an insurance
agent. I do not sell any plan and I have
nothing to gain from what you choose.
Everything in this video comes from what
the agency has published and I will tell
you where the published figures end and
where the estimates begin. My name is
Kevin. I read the rules so you do not
have to. If that is useful, subscribe.
Let me explain what this program
actually did because understanding it
tells you exactly how much of a change
to expect. A few years ago, the law was
rewritten to cap what you pay out of
pocket for covered drugs. That cap is
genuinely good and I will come back to
it because it is still there and it is
not going anywhere. But a cap on what
you pay is not a cap on what the drugs
cost. It moved a much larger share of
that cost onto the insurance companies
running the plans and those companies
responded the way you would expect by
proposing sharp premium increases. So
the government created a temporary
arrangement to cushion the transition.
It paid the plans additional money in
exchange for holding premiums down. and
the mechanics of it were specific, which
is how you can estimate your own
exposure. In the first year,
participating standalone plans received
a $15 reduction applied to the premium
calculation and a limit of $35 on how
much any single plan could raise its
premium from one year to the next. In
the second year, this year, that support
dropped to $10 and the increase limit
loosened to $50. Across this year, the
average reduction worked out to
somewhere around $16 a month. And the
whole thing cost roughly $9.8 billion,
which is the number the current
administration pointed at when they
described it as a bailout for insurance
companies that is no longer needed. So
that is the first change and here is how
to think about the size of it. The AY's
own estimate is that most people will
see an increase of less than $10 a
month. Independent analysts have warned
that some plans could jump considerably
more than that. And both of those things
can be true at once because the effect
is not uniform. It depends on your plan,
your insurance company, and where you
live. Now, the protection that survives,
which almost nobody reporting on this
has mentioned, there is still a cap on
how fast the base premium figure can
grow from year to year and it is 6%.
That is a genuine limit and it means
this is not open season. But read it
carefully because that cap applies to a
base calculation rather than to what any
individual plan charges you. Your
specific plan can still move more than
6%. The ceiling constrains the system,
not your bill. So, the honest summary is
this. Most people in standalone plans
will pay somewhat more. A minority will
pay considerably more. Some will pay the
same or less because plans compete, and
some will use this as an opportunity to
take customers. And nobody knows which
of those you are until the numbers are
published. The second change is one that
almost nobody is reporting at all, and
it is a straight number that you can act
on immediately.
The standard deductible on drug coverage
is rising from $615 this year to $700
next year, $85, and it is the money you
pay first before the plan pays anything.
Now, plans are allowed to charge less
than the standard deductible, and many
do. Some charge nothing at all on
certain tiers. So this is a ceiling
rather than a bill everybody receives.
But it matters more than the size of it
suggests because of who it hits.
Somebody with very high drug cost blows
through a deductible in January
regardless. Somebody with no regular
medications never reaches it at all. The
person this actually lands on is the one
in the middle with two or three ordinary
prescriptions who reaches the deductible
sometime in the spring and then notices
their costs change. That is a very large
group and it is the group least likely
to be watching for it. Let me tell you
about a man I will call Cleveland 71 in
Ohio. He has been in the same standalone
drug plan for 5 years and he has never
once changed it because every autumn the
post arrives. He glances at it and
nothing looks urgent enough to act on.
His plan has quietly changed around him
every single year. Different premium,
different deductible. Two of his
medications moved tears and one now
requires his doctor to get approval
first. He has not chosen any of that. He
has simply not opted out of it. And this
year, unlike the last five, the cushion
underneath his premium is being removed
at the same time. Cleveland is the
reason there is a chapter in the quiet
rules on exactly this because his
problem was never that he could not
understand a plan comparison. It was
that nothing in his life ever told him
the comparison was worth doing. It is at
kevexplains.shop.
The code is on the screen now or the
link is pinned at the top of the
comments and in the description below.
It has the four things to check in that
autumn envelope. What each change
actually costs you and the dates that
close 7 days with it. If it does not
change what you do this month, send it
back. Now, the third change, and this is
the one with the biggest single number
attached, which is why I put it in the
title. The cap on what you pay out of
pocket for covered drugs is rising from
$2,100 this year to $2,400 next year.
$300 more before the protection kicks
in. And I want to be careful here
because this one is easy to present
dishonestly and I am not going to. That
cap is one of the best things to happen
to older Americans in a generation.
Before it existed, somebody on a
specialty medication could face costs
running into five figures every single
year with no ceiling at all. The cap put
a lid on that and the lid is still
there. It started at $2,000, went to
21,00 and goes to 2400. It is indexed,
so it rises. That is not a cut. It is
the normal operation of a protection
that still protects you. But $300 is
$300. And if you are somebody who
reaches that cap every year, you will
pay it. Now, the limitations on that cap
because this is where people get
genuinely caught out and almost nobody
explains it. Your monthly premium does
not count toward the cap. You pay that
separately on top all year regardless.
And medications your plan does not cover
do not count toward it either. Not $1.
If a drug is not on your plan's list,
everything you spend on it sits
completely outside the protection. Which
means somebody can spend $4,000 in a
year and still not have reached the cap
because a portion of it went on
something the plan does not cover. That
is the single most important sentence in
this section. The cap protects covered
drugs only. And whether your drugs are
covered is decided by a list that is
rewritten every year. So checking the
list is not a small administrative task.
It is what determines whether the
protection applies to you at all. And
there is one thing that becomes
considerably more useful now that the
cap is higher and hardly anybody uses
it. You can ask to have your
out-ofpocket costs spread evenly across
the months of the year rather than
paying them as they hit. Think about why
that matters more at 2400 than it did at
2000. The way the year resets, somebody
with high costs can face a very large
bill in January and February, which is
exactly when the heating bill is at its
worst. Spreading it turns a brutal two
months into a predictable monthly
amount. You have to ask your plan for it
by name. Nobody enrolls you. And one
honest caution. So, I am not selling you
something that fits everybody. If your
drug costs are modest, this does nothing
for you except add a bill to keep track
of. It is aimed at people with high
costs concentrated early in the year.
Two more things about the drug side that
matter more this year than they usually
do because of how the changes stack. The
first is how your plan handles the
deductible because plans have real
freedom here and almost nobody checks
it. A plan can apply the deductible to
every drug you take, or it can exempt
certain tiers from it entirely. A great
many plans do not apply it to the
cheapest generic tiers at all. [snorts]
Which means two plans showing the same
deductible on paper can behave
completely differently. One charges you
nothing until you have spent the full
amount. The other starts covering your
ordinary generics from the 1st of
January and only applies the deductible
to the expensive tiers. For somebody
taking three common generics and one
brandame drug, that distinction is worth
more than the premium difference between
the two plans, and it appears nowhere in
any advertisement. So when you compare,
look at whether the deductible applies
to all tiers or only to some. That
single line separates plans that look
identical. The second is preferredies,
and it is the cheapest fix available to
anyone. Plans have networks ofarmacies,
and they are not all treated the same. A
plan will have preferredies where your
share of the cost is lower and standard
ones where it is higher and both are in
network. So you can be using a pharmacy
that is perfectly in network being told
nothing is wrong and paying more than
you would two streets away at a
preferred one. Nobody at the counter is
going to raise it. The comparison tool
shows it when you enter your pharmacy
and changing where you fill costs you
nothing and changes nothing about your
coverage. for somebody on several
regular medications that is frequently a
few hundred a year for one decision made
once. Now the fourth change and this one
is for everybody in the other group. The
people whose drug coverage is bundled
into a Medicare Advantage plan. Nothing
I have described so far applied to you
directly. This does insurance companies
running those plans have been under real
financial pressure for the last few
years. And when a company decides a
particular plan in a particular county
is not working for them, they have
several options and none of them require
your agreement. They can reduce the
extra benefits. They can shrink the
network. They can raise what you pay at
the doctor. They can stop paying agents
to sell it which quietly makes it
invisible. Or they can stop offering the
plan altogether. That last one is the
one to understand properly because what
happens next depends entirely on which
version of it you get. And most people
have never heard the distinction. If
your plan is being discontinued, the
company is required to tell you in
writing, usually more than once, in the
autumn, and then one of two completely
different things happens. The first is
that the company moves you on to another
plan of theirs automatically. It is
called crosswalking. And if you do
nothing at all on the 1st of January,
you are simply in a different plan you
did not choose. That new plan may be
fine. It may also have a different
network, different costs, and a
different drug list. The point is that
nobody asked you and doing nothing
counts as agreement. The second version
is that the plan is terminated outright
with nothing to move you on to. And
here, the consequence is severe if you
ignore it. On the 1st of January, you
are on ordinary Medicare with no
supplemental coverage and no drug
coverage at all. Not reduced coverage,
none. So, if a letter arrives this
autumn telling you your plan is ending,
the single most important thing to
establish is which of those two is
happening. And that letter will say, now
if your plan is being terminated, you
have three routes and the third one
carries a right that is genuinely
valuable and timelmited. The first route
is choosing another plan of the same
kind. That is what most people do. And
when you compare, look past the extra
benefits. The dental allowance and the
card with money on it are real, but the
things that decide a bad year are the
network, what you pay at the doctor, the
drug list, and the maximum you can be
asked to pay in a year. The second route
is returning to ordinary Medicare and
buying standalone drug coverage. The
third is that plus a supplemental
policy. And here is the part to write
down. Normally, buying a supplemental
policy later in life means answering
medical questions. And depending on your
health history, you can be charged more
or declined outright. That is the
one-way door I have talked about before
on this channel. But when your plan is
terminated, you get a guaranteed right
to buy certain supplemental policies
with no medical questions at all. Your
health cannot be used against you. That
is a genuine protection and it exists
precisely because you did not choose to
lose your coverage. Three things about
it though, and each one matters. It does
not cover every supplemental plan. Some
popular ones are not available through
this route. And if you want one of
those, you are back to answering health
questions. It is time limited.
Generally, you have 63 days from when
your coverage ends. Miss that window and
the protection is gone. And it does not
come back. And it is not automatic.
Nobody applies it for you. You have to
act inside the window and say what you
are doing. So, if this is happening to
you, that 63-day count is the most
important number in your year. Let me
tell you about a woman I will call
Ramona, 74, in Florida. Her plan was
discontinued and the letter arrived in
October and she read it and she
understood that she needed to pick
something new. What she did not
understand was that the letter had also
handed her a right that expired.
She chose another bundled plan, which
was a perfectly reasonable decision. And
by the time her health changed two years
later and she wanted ordinary Medicare
with a supplement, the guaranteed right
she had held for 63 days was long gone.
And she was asked about her health.
Ramona's letter contained the most
valuable thing she would ever be offered
on a clock. And it was written in a
paragraph that looked like every other
paragraph. That is why the quiet rules
exists in the form it does with the
windows and the exact deadlines laid out
rather than the rules explained in the
abstract. Scan the code or go to
kevinexplains.shop
or use the link at the top of the pinned
comment. 7 days to look it over and if
it does not earn its place, send it
back. Ramona did not make a mistake. She
made a decision without being told that
one of her options came with an expiry
date.
And there is a fifth thing happening
that is not a rule change at all, which
is why most videos on this subject leave
it out. It is a market trend and it is
affecting a large group. The most
comprehensive supplemental policies are
seeing rate increases in many parts of
the country that are steeper than
anything in recent memory, which is
pushing people toward two alternatives.
One is a slightly less comprehensive
policy that leaves you paying a share of
certain costs. The other is a
highdeductible version of the
comprehensive plan where the monthly
cost is dramatically lower and you carry
a substantial deductible before it pays.
Some people pair that highdeductible
version with a separate policy that pays
a cash benefit if something serious
happens on the theory that the cash
covers the deductible. I am not going to
tell you that is right for you because
for a great many people it is not and it
is genuinely more complicated than it
sounds. What I will tell you is that it
exists. that almost nobody was
discussing it a few years ago and that
if your supplemental premium has jumped
and you assumed your only option was to
pay it, there are other shapes available
and they are worth asking about. And two
more things about plan changes that
catch people every year and both are
worth knowing before the letters arrive.
The first is that a plan does not have
to disappear entirely to become a
different product. The most common
change is not termination. It is a plan
that continues under the same name with
a smaller network, a higher amount you
pay at the doctor, or benefits that
quietly shrank. There is no letter
announcing that in the way there is for
a termination. It is simply listed in
the autumn notice among everything else.
Which means the people who get caught
are frequently not the ones whose plan
ended. They are the ones whose plan
continued and changed underneath them
because a termination at least forces a
decision and a quiet change does not.
The second is about the extra benefits
specifically because they are what the
advertising sells and they are the
easiest thing for a company to reduce. A
dental allowance can be cut in half. A
card for over-the-counter items can drop
in value or change what it can be spent
on. A transport benefit can disappear
entirely. None of that changes your
medical coverage, and none of it is a
scandal. But if you chose your plan
largely because of those benefits and
they are the reason you stayed, it is
worth checking whether the thing you
chose it for is still there at the level
you expected. And a practical note that
saves money every year regardless. Those
allowances expire. They do not roll
over. Whatever is unused on the 31st of
December is simply gone. And an enormous
number of people never use theirs at all
frequently because they do not know they
have one. Now, let me spend real time on
what is not changing because the fear
circulating about this is doing more
damage than the change itself. The cap
on out-ofpocket drug spending is not
going away. It rises to $2,400 and it
continues to protect you above that. The
$35 monthly limit on insulin is not
going away. Recommended vaccines remain
available at no cost to you. The
negotiated prices on certain drugs
remain in effect. And the program
itself, the thing the headlines say is
ending, is not ending in any sense. A
temporary subsidy paid to insurance
companies is ending. The coverage
continues exactly as it is.
I am laboring this because I have
watched people make genuinely bad
decisions out of a belief that their
coverage was disappearing. It is not. If
somebody telephones you this autumn
suggesting you must act urgently because
drug coverage is ending, you now know
more than they do. And that call is not
an honest one. Now, who is protected
from all of this entirely? Because there
is a group and it is larger than people
think. If you receive the low-income
subsidy for drug coverage, sometimes
called extra help, the premium change
largely does not reach you. That subsidy
covers the premium for qualifying plans,
which means the cushion being removed
was never the thing holding your cost
down in the first place, and the
eligibility for it was widened. So more
people now qualify for the full subsidy
than did a few years ago,
which makes this exactly the right
autumn to check whether you qualify
because if you do, most of this video
stops applying to you. You apply through
Social Security and you can do it at any
time of year. The same is true of the
programs where your state pays your
Medicare premium. Those are worth asking
about in the same conversation and I
have covered them in detail elsewhere.
And now something almost nobody knows
about which runs in the opposite
direction. There is a search charge on
drug coverage for people above certain
income levels just as there is on
medical coverage. Most people know that
higher earners pay more for the medical
part. Far fewer know there is a separate
amount added to drug coverage as well
calculated from income 2 years earlier
and deducted from your social security
rather than build by the plan.
which means somebody can switch to a
cheaper drug plan, feel like they have
solved the problem, and still see an
amount coming out that has nothing to do
with the plan they chose. If that
describes you and the income behind it
has since ended because you retired or
lost a spouse or had a one-off event,
there is a form to have it recalculated
on your current circumstances. It is
free and it works on both parts at once.
And one more thing that belongs here
because it is the free route through all
of this and it is used by a fraction of
the people who could use it. Every state
runs a counseling service with trained
counselors who will sit with your
medication list and your doctors and run
the comparison with you. It is free. It
is funded to be independent. And the
part that matters most is that they do
not sell insurance and earn nothing
based on what you choose. That is the
only advice in this entire landscape
with no product attached to it.
In this year specifically, their
calendars will fill faster than usual
because a change this size produces a
wave of people wanting help. Book the
appointment in the first week of October
and you get a calm hour. Book it in late
November and you are competing with
everybody who waited for a letter to
frighten them into it. The same is true
of a good independent agent. And there
is an honest distinction worth making.
An agent is paid a commission by
whichever plan you enroll in, and
different plans pay differently. That
does not make anybody dishonest, and
there are excellent agents doing careful
work. But there are two questions that
separate a comparison from a sales call,
and you are entitled to ask both. Will
you run my actual medication list and
show me the annual total alongside two
alternatives? And how many plans in this
county do you actually represent?
Somebody contracted with three plans
cannot show you the best option if it is
the fourth. Not because they are hiding
it, but because they cannot sell it.
Now, the dates because everything here
runs on a calendar and the calendar is
not obvious. Plan prices for next year
are published in late September and the
complete data goes live on the 1st of
October, which means you can see every
premium, every deductible, every drug
list, and every network two full weeks
before anyone is permitted to enroll.
Enrollment runs from the 15th of October
to the 7th of December. And whatever you
choose takes effect on the 1st of
January. And here is what happens if you
do nothing, which for this year in
particular is worth stating plainly. You
are not dropped. You are renewed into
next year's version of your plan with
the higher premium, the higher
deductible, and whatever changed on the
drug list.
In an ordinary year, that default costs
people a little. This year with the
cushion removed underneath standalone
plans, it will cost some people
considerably more than a little. There
are two windows after that and both are
narrow. If you are in a bundled plan,
you get one more change between the 1st
of January and the 31st of March. One
change, not several, and only if you are
already in that kind of plan. And if
your plan was discontinued, there is a
separate window that runs into the new
year, which is different from the
ordinary one and gives you longer One
more thing before the list and it is the
question I expect in the comments. So
let me answer it directly. Should you
switch or should you stay? There is no
general answer to that and anybody
giving you one is not looking at your
situation. But there is a way to decide
and it takes one number.
Run the comparison and produce two
figures. What your current plan will
cost you across next year including the
premium, the deductible, and what you
will pay at the counter on your actual
medications. and the same figure for the
best alternative in your county. If the
difference is small, stay. Switching has
a real cost that nobody mentions, which
is that you have to check your doctors
again, learn a new drug list, and
occasionally sort out a pharmacy that is
not caught up. If the difference is
several hundred or more across the year,
switch and do it early rather than in
the final week when the phone lines are
worst. And there is one situation where
the answer is almost always to look
closely regardless of the arithmetic
which is if a medication you depend on
has moved tears or had a requirement
added to it. That is not a cost
question. That is a question about
whether you can get the medication at
all without a fight in January.
Here is what to do and I have kept it to
five because a list of 15 is a list
nobody starts. One, establish which
group you are in. standalone drug plan
or drug coverage bundled inside a bigger
plan. Everything in this video sorts on
that one question. Two, find the notice
that arrived in the autumn and find four
things in it. The premium, the
deductible, your medications on the drug
list, and your doctors in the network.
Everything else in that document is
required padding. Three, on or after the
1st of October, run your actual
medications and your actual pharmacy
through the official comparison tool and
look at the total annual cost rather
than the premium. Two plans with the
same monthly price can differ by over
$1,000 a year once your specific drugs
go through them.
Four, if a letter says your plan is
ending, establish immediately whether
you are being moved automatically or
terminated outright. and if it is
terminated, note the 63-day window on
the guaranteed right. Five, check
whether you qualify for the low-income
subsidy before assuming any of this
applies to you because if you do, most
of it does not. If any of that landed
close to home, all of it is laid out in
order in the quiet rules link pinned at
the top of the comments. And if you have
a question about your own situation,
write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read everyone my honest read. I think
the subsidy ending is defensible and I
think the way it was communicated was
not. The argument for ending it is
straightforward. It was always
temporary. It was designed to cushion a
transition that has now happened and
$9.8 billion a year going to insurance
companies is a genuine cost to
everybody. The argument against is
equally straightforward. The transition
it was cushioning is not finished from
the point of view of the person paying
the premium. And removing it in the same
year the deductible rises and the cap
rises means three increases landing on
the same household at once. Both of
those are real arguments and reasonable
people land in different places. What is
not defensible is that a change
affecting 25 million people was
announced in July will show up on bills
in January and not one of those people
received a letter explaining it. The
information exists. It is published. It
is accurate. And it reaches whoever
happens to be reading. Last thought.
Almost everything frightening about this
year comes from a headline that is not
true. And almost everything expensive
about it comes from a default that
nobody chose.
The program is not ending. Your coverage
is not disappearing. And if you do
nothing at all, nothing dramatic happens
to you either. which is precisely the
problem because the number on your
January payment will simply be different
and nobody will have asked. Two weeks
from the 1st of October with your own
medication list in front of you settles
all of it. I am Kevin. Thanks for
watching. Do not forget to check the
quiet rules at kevexplains.shop.

title: New Income Rules For Seniors Start October 1, One Erases Your Denial

segments.text: If somebody at an office told you your
income was too high, that answer was
produced by a test your household does
not take. Not a test you failed, a test
that does not apply to you and has not
applied to you since the day somebody in
your house turns 60. And the numbers
behind that answer, every single one of
them get thrown out and replaced on the
1st of October. the income limits, the
deductions, and the benefit amounts, all
of them, on one date every year on
schedule. Nobody wrote to you the first
time. Nobody is going to write to you
this time either. So, here is what this
video is. Four ways the government
counts your money differently once
somebody in the household is 60 or older
than the date all four of those numbers
change and what that does to a denial
letter sitting in a drawer right now.
And before anybody clicks away because
they assume this is not about them, let
me be specific about the amount because
a wrong figure is circulating about this
and it is doing damage. For one person,
the maximum benefit runs to roughly
across a year paid onto a card monthly,
not 35,000, 3 and a half. That is still
a year of car insurance or most of a
heating season or the entire gap that a
lot of households are quietly covering
out of savings. and it does not shrink
because you live alone. And here is the
fact that this entire video rests on.
The reason most older Americans never
claim a dollar of it has almost nothing
to do with what they earn. I am not a
lawyer and I am not your financial
adviser. Rules here vary by state more
than in almost any subject I cover. And
I will tell you exactly where that
matters. My name is Kevin. I read the
rules so you do not have to. If that is
useful, subscribe. Let me start with the
first way the counting changes because
nothing on this list costs people more.
Most households in this country have to
pass two separate income tests. The
first looks at everything coming in
before a single dollar is subtracted.
Gross. The second looks at what is left
after the agency subtracts what it
agrees to subtract, net. Fail either one
and you are out. A household with
somebody 60 or older in it does not take
the first test at all. Read that again
because it is the whole reason people
disqualify themselves. Your household
skips the gross test entirely. The box
is still on the form. The answer written
in it changes nothing about the
decision. Which means the number most
people compare themselves against, the
one they saw on a website or heard from
a neighbor or were told over the phone
is the wrong number for their household.
It is the gross number. And your
household is measured after the
subtractions rather than before them.
And the subtractions are large. That is
the rest of this video. So, when a
caseworker looked at your paperwork and
said no, that decision was built out of
numbers that expire and they expire in a
matter of days. A denial is not a
status. It is the answer to a question
asked in one particular year using that
year's arithmetic. The second way the
counting changes is medical spending.
And this one moves more older households
across the line than anything else in
the program. Once somebody in the
household is 60 or older, out-ofpocket
medical spending above $35 a month comes
off the income being counted. The
