spending is not reimbursed. Nobody sends
you the money. What shrinks is the
income the office measures you against,
which is the number that decides
everything. And the list of what counts
is considerably wider than people
assume. prescriptions, dental work,
including dentures, hearing aids, and
the batteries for them, eyeglasses, and
contact lenses, insurance premiums,
including supplemental coverage,
transport to and from medical
appointments, including mileage,
over-the-counter medication, a doctor
recommended, nursing care and attendant
care at home, even the cost of
maintaining a service animal. And here
is the line that catches almost
everybody. Your Medicare premium counts.
That is deducted from your Social
Security before the payment ever reaches
your bank, which means most people have
never once thought of it as money they
spend. The program counts it as money
you spend because you do. That single
line on its own clears the $35 floor for
very nearly every household on Medicare
in this country, which means the medical
deduction is available to almost
everybody watching this before you have
added a single prescription to it. Now,
three things about this deduction that
almost nobody is told, and each one
matters. The first is that a great many
states offer a standard medical
deduction instead of itemizing. Rather
than documenting every receipt, a
household that can show medical costs
above the threshold, gets a flat amount
subtracted, frequently well over $100 a
month with far less paperwork. Which
means the objection people raise most,
that they could never keep track of all
those receipts, is often solved by one
question. Does this state have a
standard medical deduction and do I
qualify for it? The second is that these
expenses can be averaged forward. You
are not limited to what you spent last
month. Costs that recur or that are
reasonably anticipated across your
certification period can be counted
across it. So a dental bill in March is
not wasted because you applied in June.
The third is that unpaid medical bills
count too if you are responsible for
them, not only bills already paid. So
the envelope you are building is not
just receipts. It is the premium notice,
the pharmacy printout, the dental
estimate, the outstanding bill, and a
note of what the trips to appointments
cost. One envelope, and for a great many
households, it is the entire difference
between over the line and under it. Let
me tell you about a man I will call
Rayburn, 72, in Kentucky, living on a
social security payment and a small
pension from a lumberm mill. He applied
once, four years ago, was told he was
over the limit, and never went back.
What had happened was that somebody read
his gross income off the top of the form
and compared it to a number that did not
apply to his household. Nobody asked him
about a single medical cost. He had a
supplemental premium, four
prescriptions, and a set of dentures
being paid off. He was not over the
line. He was never measured properly.
and the four years in between do not
come back because this pays forward from
the date you apply and not one day
earlier. Raburn's problem is the reason
I wrote the chapter in the quiet rules
that covers this because his answer was
never a judgment about his income. It
was a sentence somebody said quickly at
a counter and he carried it for four
years. It is at kevinexplains.shop.
There is a code on the screen now or the
link is pinned at the top of the
comments and in the description below.
It has the exact words that get the
senior rules applied to your file on the
first call, the envelope of documents
that moves the number, and the window
you have to challenge a decision once a
notice is dated. 7 days with it. If it
does not change what you do this month,
send it back. The third way the counting
changes is about savings rather than
income. And this is where the largest
number of people wrongly disqualify
themselves. There is a limit on what you
can have and still qualify. For most
households, that ceiling sits at $3,000.
Once somebody in the house is 60 or
older, it rises to $4,500.
And the things older people actually own
mostly do not count toward it. Your home
does not count. The land it sits on does
not count. Your vehicle in most cases
does not count. And most retirement and
pension accounts do not count at all.
That last one stops people every time.
Somebody with a pension behind them
owning their house outright can still
sit inside the resource limit because
the program is not measuring what you
built across a lifetime. It is measuring
what is sitting in a checking account
this month. But here is the part that
matters far more than the federal number
and it is the single most common reason
people are wrong about their own
eligibility. Most states have raised or
eliminated the asset test entirely.
There is a mechanism that allows a state
to set its own limits well above the
federal ones or to remove the resource
test altogether. And the large majority
of states have done exactly that. Which
means the honest answer to whether
savings disqualify you is that it
depends entirely on where you live. And
the only way to find out is to ask the
state agency that would hold your file.
And that federal ceiling is itself on
the list of numbers being rewritten on
the 1st of October. The fourth
difference is the one that costs the
most and gets explained the least. So
stay with me through this one. Your
housing costs come off your income, too.
Rent counts. Mortgage interest counts.
Property taxes on the place you live
count. Heating, cooling, electricity,
water, and the basic fee on one
telephone all count. And anything you
spend on shelter above half of what is
left after the other subtractions comes
off as well. That is called the excess
shelter deduction. For most households
in this country, there is a cap on how
much of that can be subtracted. It sits
somewhere around $740
regardless of what the heating bill
actually came to. For a household with
somebody 60 or older, there is no cap at
all. The entire excess comes off. Take a
moment with what that does in practice.
Picture an older household in a cold
state in an old house with a heating
bill that doubles in January and a
property tax bill that arrives in the
autumn. Every single dollar of that
comes off the income being counted. A
younger household one street over with
identical bills stops subtracting at the
cap. Two homes, two completely different
arithmetics, and only one of those
households is ever told about it. And
there is a companion rule here that is
worth knowing by name because it is one
of the strangest and most useful
provisions in the whole program. In a
number of states, a household that
receives even a token amount of heating
assistance. in some cases as little as
$21 in a year is automatically credited
with a standard utility allowance rather
than having to document actual utility
costs. It is sometimes called the heat
and eat arrangement. And the effect is
that a small heating benefit can
substantially increase the food benefit
by changing how the shelter costs are
calculated. Which means the two programs
I am always telling people to apply for
in October are not separate. One of them
can increase the other. So, if your
state runs that arrangement, applying
for heating assistance is not only worth
what the heating assistance pays, it is
worth what it does to this calculation.
That is four separate provisions inside
one program, and every one of them
exists specifically for households like
yours. The resource limit alone puts the
program out of reach for a great many
younger households that would otherwise
qualify.
And here is the thing that ties them
together and that I want stated plainly.
Nobody at any office is required to walk
you through any of them. The application
does not ask whether the senior rules
should be applied to your file. The form
assumes you already know. And there is a
fifth difference that is not one of the
four, but belongs beside them because it
removes the objection people raise most
often after eligibility. The way the
benefit amount itself is calculated
works in favor of a household with high
deductions. The arithmetic is roughly
this. The agency takes your net income,
the figure left after every subtraction
in this video, and expects you to
contribute about 30% of it toward food.
The benefit makes up the difference
between that contribution and the
maximum for your household size, which
means the deductions are doing two
separate jobs at once, and people only
ever hear about the first. The first job
is getting you under the line at all,
that is eligibility. The second job is
that every dollar of deduction also
lowers the net income the benefit is
calculated from which raises the benefit
itself. So the medical envelope is not
only deciding whether you qualify, it is
deciding how much you receive every
month for the length of your
certification. A household that scrapes
in with no deductions claimed receives
the smallest possible amount. The
identical household that documented its
medical and shelter costs properly
qualifies more comfortably and receives
more from the same income. That is worth
saying plainly because it changes what
the envelope is worth. It is not
paperwork to prove you are poor enough.
It is the thing that sets the amount.
Now the date because everything above is
about to move. The standards in force
right now cover the period that runs
from last October through the end of
this September. That is the window we
are standing in and it closes in days. A
new set of standards takes its place on
the 1st of October and it lands in three
specific ways. The income limits go up.
For a household measured under the
senior rules, the net figure for one
person currently sits somewhere just
over $1,300 a month and for two people
somewhere in the region of 1,700.
Those are the numbers your file was
measured against. They are replaced next
month and they move with the cost of
living and the cost of living has not
gone down. Which means households that
were a little over the line stop being
over it without doing anything at all.
The deductions go up as well. The
standard deduction that comes off every
household's income before anything else
rises. So does the shelter cap for the
households that have one. And the
benefit itself goes up because the
maximum amounts are recalculated
annually and take effect on the same
date. Now, put those three things
together against a denial letter. A no
issued in the spring of this year was
measured against numbers that stop
existing in a matter of days. Nothing
about that decision carries forward. No
case worker reruns it for you. The file
sits closed at the state agency until
somebody opens it again. And the only
person who can do that is the person it
belongs to. An application filed after
the 1st of October is not the same
application you filed before. It is the
same household measured against
different arithmetic. And one more
consequence of that date that nobody
connects, which matters if you are
already receiving something. Households
already on the program did not
automatically get recalculated the
moment the new numbers land. The new
maximum amounts generally flow through,
but the deductions on your file are
whatever was documented the last time
somebody looked. which means a household
certified 18 months ago whose medical
costs have risen since is being paid on
the strength of an 18-month-old
envelope. You are permitted to report a
change in medical expenses
mid-certification. And in most cases,
that triggers a recalculation of the
benefit rather than a fresh application.
So, if you are already receiving this
and your prescriptions, your premiums,
or your dental costs have gone up since
you last documented them, that is a
phone call rather than a reapplication,
and it can raise the monthly amount for
the rest of your certification period.
Almost nobody makes that call because
people assume the amount is fixed once
it is set. It is not. It is fixed to the
last set of numbers anybody was given.
Now, three things about the process
itself that almost nobody knows, and
each one removes a reason people give
up. The first is that a great many
states run a simplified process
specifically for households with
somebody elderly or disabled in them.
Shorter application, in many places, no
interview requirement at all. And a far
longer certification period, in some
states, 3 years rather than one. That
last part matters more than it sounds
because the reertification paperwork is
what causes people to fall off these
programs even when they still qualify. A
three-year certification is 3 years of
not having to prove anything again. So,
the question to ask by name is whether
your state runs a simplified application
for elderly households. The second is
about work requirements and it removes a
fear people hold quietly. There are time
limits and work requirements attached to
this program for certain adults. They do
not apply to people 50 or older and the
age threshold has been rising. So, if
you have avoided applying because you
assumed you would be required to work or
to prove you were looking for work, that
is not your situation. The third is the
one I would most like to put in front of
anybody living in a multigenerational
house because it overturns what people
assume completely. The default rule is
that people who live together and buy
and prepare food together are one
household and everybody's income is
counted. Which is why an older parent
living with an adult child frequently
assumes there is no point applying
because the child's income would be
counted against them. There is an
exception written specifically for this
situation. An elderly person who lives
with others and who is unable to
purchase and prepare their own meals
separately because of a disability can
in certain circumstances be treated as a
separate household. And when that
applies, the income of the others in the
house is largely left out of the
calculation. The rules around it are
specific and they involve the income of
the people you live with. So this is
genuinely one to ask about rather than
assume. But the number of older parents
living in a child's home who have never
applied because they assumed the answer
was obvious is enormous. And for some of
them, the answer is not what they
assumed at all. Let me tell you about a
woman I will call Leavonne, 69, in
Michigan, living in her daughter's house
since a fall 2 years ago. She never
applied for anything because her
daughter and son-in-law both work and
she assumed their income would simply be
counted as hers. Nobody had ever told
her that the rule about separate
households existed or that her Medicare
premium alone would have cleared the
medical threshold or that her state had
removed its asset test entirely. She had
been told once informally by somebody at
a community center that she would not
qualify. That was the entire basis of 2
years of not applying. Leavonne's
situation is exactly why the chapter on
this in the quiet rules is written as
questions to ask rather than rules to
memorize because the rule that applied
to her is one she would never have found
on her own. Scan the code on the screen
or go to kevinexplains.shop
or use the link at the top of the pinned
comment. 7 days to look it over and if
it does not earn its place, send it
back. What Leavonne had was not a
decision. It was somebody's guess
delivered kindly at a community center
and she treated it as final for two
years. Before the practical part, three
more provisions that sit in the same
place and that are worth real money to
specific households. The first is for
anybody who has been told their benefit
would be so small it is not worth the
paperwork. There is a minimum monthly
benefit for one and twoerson households.
It is not large, somewhere in the region
of $23 a month. And I know how that
sounds when you have just sat through 20
minutes about arithmetic, but hear what
it actually unlocks because the dollar
amount is the least valuable part of it.
Being enrolled in this program is
automatic qualification for a number of
other things. The telephone and internet
discount runs off it. In many states,
the heating assistance program treats it
as automatic eligibility. The farmers
market coupon program frequently runs
off it. Some utility companies use it to
qualify people for their own discounted
rates. So, the household that shrugs at
$23 a month is frequently turning down a
key rather than a payment. That is the
same unlocking pattern I keep running
into, and it works the same way here.
The second is about how often you have
to prove any of this again. Ordinary
households reertify every year.
Households with somebody elderly or
disabled in them are frequently
certified for 24 months and in states
running the simplified process up to 36,
which means the paperwork is a
front-loaded cost rather than an annual
one. One envelope, one interview, and in
some states you are not asked again for
3 years. The third is for anybody whose
income changes across the year, which
describes a great many older households.
You are generally required to report
changes, but the reporting rules for
households like yours are lighter than
the ordinary ones. And in many states,
you are only required to report when
income crosses a specific threshold
rather than every time something moves.
So the fear that this becomes a monthly
obligation to report every small change
is usually not the arrangement that
applies to your household. Ask what the
reporting requirement actually is for an
elderly household in your state before
assuming the worst version. So what does
a household actually do with this? The
first thing is the envelope because that
is what moves the number. Every medical
cost in one place. The premium notice,
the pharmacy printout, the dental bill,
the outstanding balance you have not
paid yet, and a note of what the trips
to appointments cost. That envelope is
the single most commonly omitted thing
in this entire process. And it is the
thing that decides the answer. The
second is to apply through your own
state agency rather than through a
website that offers to check for you.
Every state runs its own application and
holds its own files. The federal agency
does not process applications and does
not hold your case. And if getting to an
office is difficult, you can name
somebody in writing to apply and be
interviewed on your behalf. That is
built into the rules rather than a favor
anybody is doing you. A daughter can do
the entire process for a parent with one
authorization form. The third is to say
the words out loud when you apply. Tell
them somebody in the household is 60 or
older and ask in those words for the
senior rules to be applied to the file.
Then ask three specific questions. Has
the medical expense deduction been
taken? Were the housing costs counted
without the cap? And does this state
have a standard medical deduction? Those
questions are not clever and they are
not aggressive. The form simply never
asks them for you. The fourth is timing
and it is doing work for you right now
that no amount of paperwork can do. An
application filed after the 1st of
October is measured against the new
standards rather than the ones that
produced a no.
Now what happens after the form goes in?
Because the waiting is where people give
up. The agency has 30 days to process an
answer. There is an interview inside
that window, usually by telephone rather
than in person. But there is a faster
track that a great many people qualify
for and never ask about. If your income
and resources are very low, or if your
housing and utility costs exceed your
income and resources combined, the
application must be processed on an
expedited basis in a matter of days
rather than a month. That second
condition catches people. Housing costs
exceeding income is not an unusual
situation for an older household in an
expensive rental and it triggers
expedited handling by rule. So ask
whether you qualify for expedited
processing. Nobody volunteers it. And
whatever the answer turns out to be,
benefits run back to the day you
submitted the form rather than the day
somebody approved it. Which is the
plainest possible argument for filing
early in a month rather than late in one
because the date you file is the date
the clock starts. In one situation that
is worth its own 30 seconds because it
catches a specific and growing group. If
you are caring for a grandchild, the
arithmetic changes again. A grandparent
raising a grandchild is a household with
a child in it, which changes the
household size, changes the maximum
benefit, and in many cases opens a
completely separate set of programs
alongside this one. And the child's own
situation matters less than people
assume. You do not need legal custody or
adoption to include a child you are
actually feeding and housing in your
household for this purpose. That
describes a great many households right
now and a great many of those
grandparents have never applied for
anything because they are thinking about
their own eligibility as a single older
person rather than as the household they
actually are. If that is your house, say
it plainly on the application because
household composition is the first thing
the arithmetic is built on and nobody
will guess it for you. Now, let me take
away four fears because each of these
stops people and none of them is true.
It is not a loan and it is not repaid.
There is no lean on your house, no claim
against your estate, and nothing your
children inherit as a debt. It is not
taxable income. It does not appear on
your return and it does not affect the
taxation of your social security. It
does not reduce your social security,
your Medicare or any other benefit you
receive. These are separate systems. And
the card itself works exactly like an
ordinary bank card at the till. The
concern people hold about standing in a
queue with something that marks them out
is genuinely out ofd and has been for
years. And two things that are available
specifically to your age group that
almost nobody knows about. Online
ordering and delivery are now available
in every state, which matters enormously
for anybody who has difficulty getting
to a shop. And a number of states run a
restaurant program where people who are
elderly, disabled, or homeless can use
the benefit at participating restaurants
because a household without the ability
to prepare meals still has to eat. It
exists in a minority of states and where
it exists almost nobody uses it. Now,
the last piece and it is for anybody
holding a recent denial. There is a
window to challenge a decision and it is
counted in days from the date printed on
the notice, not from the day you open
the envelope. That distinction matters
because letters sit in drawers. And here
is the part that is genuinely worth
knowing. If you appeal within a certain
period and you were already receiving
benefits that are being reduced or
stopped, those benefits generally
continue while the appeal is decided.
Appeals of this kind go through several
levels. And the first level is a fair
hearing that you can attend by
telephone. And the same free legal
assistance I have mentioned on this
channel before, funded for people 60 and
older, handles benefit denials
specifically. That is what it is for. It
costs nothing. One more thing before the
list, and it is the one I would want
somebody to tell my own mother. The
people who end up receiving this are
almost never the ones with the most
need. They are the ones who applied
twice. Agencies deny a substantial share
of first applications and most of the
time it is not because somebody did not
qualify. It is a missing document, a box
completed differently than a clerk
expected, an expense nobody asked about,
or a rule that was never applied to the
file. Which means the single most useful
thing in this entire video is not any
individual provision. It is knowing that
the first no is frequently a paperwork
outcome rather than a verdict and that
the correct response to it is a specific
question rather than acceptance. Ask in
writing for the denial to state the
exact reason. That one page turns a
closed door into a task. And in a
startling number of cases, the task is
producing a document nobody ever asked
you for. Here is your list. Six things.
One, stop comparing yourself to the
gross income figure. your household does
not take that test. Two, build the
envelope. Every medical cost, including
the Medicare premium that comes out
before you ever see your payment. Three,
find out whether your state has removed
its asset test, because most have, and
whether it runs a standard medical
deduction and a simplified elderly
application. Four, if you live with
family, ask specifically about separate
household status before assuming their
income disqualifies you. Five, file
after the 1st of October, early in the
month rather than late, because the
benefit runs from the date you file.
Six, if you hold a denial, check the
date on it and the appeal window. And
understand that the numbers it was
measured against no longer exist. If any
of that landed close to home, all of it
is laid out in order in the quiet rules
link pinned at the top of the comments.
And if you have a question about your
own situation, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read everyone, my honest read. About
one in three older Americans who could
receive this help never applies at all.
And a good share of the rest stopped
after a single no. That is not an
eligibility problem. It is the lowest
participation rate of any age group in
the country. And the reason is not
income. Part of it is pride. And I am
not going to lecture anybody about that
because it comes from the same place
that made these households save
carefully and pay their own way for 40
years. But a larger part of it is
simpler and it makes me angrier. It is
that the rules written specifically for
older households are not printed on the
form, not raised at the counter, and not
mentioned in the letter that says no.
Four provisions exist exclusively for
people your age. And not one of them is
triggered unless the applicant already
knows to ask. Last thought. Somebody
said a sentence to you or to somebody
you love and it has been treated as a
permanent fact ever since. It was not a
fact. It was one year's arithmetic run
against the wrong test without the
subtractions that exist specifically for
your household by somebody who was not
required to mention any of them. And in
a matter of days, every number in that
sentence stops existing. So the only
thing that has to happen is that
somebody files again after the first
with the envelope. I am Kevin. Thanks
for watching. Do not forget to check the
quiet rules at kevinexplains.shop.

title: Every Senior Must Do This Before October 15 Or Pay More All Year

segments.text: There are two weeks in October that
decide what you pay for the whole of
next year and almost nobody uses them
because almost nobody knows they exist.
Here is the fact that this entire video
is built on and I have never once seen
it explained anywhere. Enrollment opens
on the 15th of October. Everybody knows
that date. It is on every advertisement
and every piece of post you have
received this month. But the complete
data for next year, every plan, every
premium, every drug list, every network
goes live on the 1st of October, two
full weeks earlier, which means there is
a 14-day window where you can see
exactly what next year costs, compare
every option available in your county,
and decide precisely what you are going
to do before a single other person in
the country is allowed to enroll. And in
those same two weeks, something else is
happening that is aimed directly at you.
And it is also not a coincidence. It is
also the 1 of October. And I will get to
that because understanding why your post
box filled up this month changes how you
read every piece of it. So this video is
about three things in this order. What
opens for you on the 1st of October,
what opens on you on the same day, and
what closes permanently on three dates
after that. Most people experience
October as noise. It is actually the
only month in the year where you hold
more information than the people selling
to you and it lasts 14 days. I am not an
insurance agent. I do not sell any plan
and I have no stake in what you choose.
This is educational plans and rules vary
and you confirm your own details before
acting. My name is Kevin. I read the
rules so you do not have to. If that is
useful, subscribe. Let me start with the
head start because this is the part with
actual money attached. On the 1st of
October, the official comparison tool
loads next year's information, not this
year's. Next year's premiums, next
year's deductibles, next year's drug
lists, and next year's networks for
every plan available where you live. And
here is how to use it properly, because
there is a right way, and almost
everybody does it the wrong way. Do not
search by premium. The premium is the
least important number in the entire
exercise, and it is the only number the
advertising ever mentions. Instead,
enter your actual medications, every
single one with the exact dose, and
enter the pharmacy you actually walk
into. The tool then produces an
estimated total cost for the year for
every plan in your area, combining what
you pay monthly with what you will pay
at the counter across 12 months. That
total is the number that matters. And
two plans with an identical monthly
premium can differ by well over $1,000 a
year once your specific medications are
run through them. There is no way to see
that from a brochure, from an
advertisement, or from a conversation
with an agent who has not entered your
drug list. And the pharmacy matters more
than people expect. Plans have
preferredies, and the same plan charges
different amounts depending on which
shop you use. Changing where you fill
your prescriptions can lower your cost
without changing anything else about
your coverage. So, the exercise is your
real medication list, your real
pharmacy, and the annual total. It takes
about 20 minutes. Now, what to actually
look for once the data is in front of
you? Because there are four changes that
cost real money and people only check
the first one. The first is the premium.
Fine, check it. It takes a second. The
second is your medications, and there
are four different things that can
happen to each one. It can be removed
from the list entirely. It can be moved
to a higher tier, which is the most
common and the one nobody notices in
advance. It can have a requirement added
where your doctor has to get approval
before the plan pays. Or it can have a
requirement added that you try a cheaper
alternative first and have it fail. That
last one genuinely upsets people. And I
understand why. Somebody stable on a
medication for 9 years being told they
must try something else before the plan
continues covering it is a real thing
that happens every January. The third is
the network. And this one is harsher
than the price. The list of doctors and
hospitals in a plan is rewritten every
year. The specialist you have seen since
your surgery can simply not be in it
next year. And here is the practical
instruction on that. Because the
directories are frequently out of date,
do not rely on the plan's own list.
Telephone the practice directly and ask
whether they are contracted with that
specific plan for next year. Not this
year, next year. The person at the desk
knows before the directory does. The
fourth is the maximum you can be asked
to pay in a year, which applies if you
are in a plan that bundles everything
together. That number changes annually.
It can rise substantially and it varies
enormously between plans in the same
county. It is the number that decides
what a genuinely bad year costs you and
the advertising never mentions it. Four
things: premium, medications, network,
annual maximum. If you check those four
against your own situation in the first
two weeks of October, you have done more
than the overwhelming majority of people
receiving this information. And there is
one more thing that becomes available on
the 15th rather than the first. And it
is worth knowing the difference. The
document you received in September was a
summary of changes. The full document,
the one that spells out every benefit in
detail, becomes available on the 15th.
The summary tells you what is different.
The full one tells you what you actually
have. Most people never open either. The
four checks above are drawn from the
first one, and that is enough for the
decision. Let me tell you about a man I
will call Ellery, 73, in Kentucky. He
had been in the same plan for 4 years,
and every October, he did what most
people do, which was wait until the
advertising told him it was time and
then let the automatic renewal happen.
Two things changed for last year. A
medication he had taken since 2018 moved
to a higher tier and the cardiologist he
had seen since his bypass left the
network. He found out about the
medication in January at the pharmacy
counter and about the cardiologist in
March at a front desk. By then, the
window had been closed for 3 months. He
spent the rest of the year paying more
for a drug and driving further to a
doctor he did not know. And every single
one of those changes was published in
writing available to him on the 1st of
October. Ellery is the reason the quiet
rules exists in the first place. It is
at kevin explains.shop. There is a code
on the screen now. So hold your phone up
to it or use the link pinned at the top
of the comments or the one in the
description below. It covers what to
check and buy when in plain English in
large type in the order you would
actually work through it. You have 7
days with it. If it does not change
something about what you do this month,
send it back and we are done. Ellery was
not careless. He simply believed the
advertising was the starting gun and by
the time the advertising starts, the
head start is already half gone. Now,
the second thing that happens on the 1st
of October, and this is the part that
reframes everything sitting on your
kitchen table right now, the reason your
postbox filled up this month is not that
companies happen to get organized at the
same time. The 1st of October is the
date agents and insurers are permitted
to begin marketing next year's plans.
Before that date, they legally cannot.
On that date, all of them start at once
in every county in the country. So, the
flood is regulatory, not coincidental.
And knowing that tells you something
useful, which is that every single piece
of that post and every one of those
advertisements was produced by somebody
who was waiting for a starting gun and
none of it was triggered by anything
specific about you. Now, the protections
because there are real ones and almost
nobody knows they have them. An agent
generally cannot telephone you out of
the blue if you have not asked them to.
Unsolicited calls about your Medicare
options are at best somebody breaking
the rules and frequently they are not
agents at all. Nobody from the
government telephones people to sell
them a plan. That call does not exist in
any legitimate form. And here is the
protection that surprises people the
most and it is genuinely powerful. if
you know to use it. Before an agent can
sit down with you and discuss specific
plan types, they are required to have
documented what you agreed to discuss in
advance. It is called a scope of
appointment. And in most circumstances,
it has to be completed before the
meeting rather than at the start of it.
What that means practically is that an
agent cannot arrive to discuss one thing
and then pivot to selling you something
else entirely. If you agree to talk
about drug coverage, they are supposed
to stay on drug coverage. So, if
somebody is in your living room steering
the conversation somewhere you did not
agree to, you are permitted to stop it.
And there is a rule behind you when you
do. There are two more things about
these conversations that are worth
knowing. Calls with agents about plan
enrollment are generally required to be
recorded and retained. Which means if
you are ever told something on a call
that turns out not to be true, there is
a recording of it and that is worth
saying out loud on the call itself. And
every agent is paid a commission by
whichever plan you enroll in. and
different plans pay different amounts.
That does not make anybody dishonest and
there are excellent agents doing careful
work. It does mean the incentive exists
and you are allowed to ask directly
whether the plan being recommended pays
more than the alternatives. Now, the
advertising itself, and I want to be
specific about what it leaves out rather
than just complaining about it, the
advertisements offering extra benefits,
cards with money on them, dental and
vision allowances, are describing real
features of real plans. Those things
exist. What a 30- secondond
advertisement never mentions is the
network, the approval requirements, or
the annual maximum, which are the three
things that decide what happens to you
in a bad year, and which are precisely
the three things in the data that went
live on the 1st of October. So, the
advertising and the data are describing
the same plans. One of them is complete,
and the scam version is straightforward
once you know the rule. Nobody
legitimate needs your Medicare number on
a call you did not initiate. Nobody
needs your bank details to check
eligibility. No plan requires payment to
enroll you. If that call comes, put the
phone down, then look the number up
yourself from a statement or the
official site and call them back. Never
the number the caller gave you. And
there is one free route that exists
specifically to solve all of this. And
it is used by a small fraction of the
people who could use it. Every state
runs a counseling service with trained
counselors who will sit with your
medication list and your doctors and run
the comparison with you and explain the
differences. It is free. It is funded to
be independent. And the crucial part is
that they do not sell insurance and earn
nothing based on what you choose. That
is the only advice in this entire
landscape with no product attached to
it. And October is exactly when their
calendars fill up, which is another
reason the first two weeks matter. Book
the appointment in the first week of
October and you get a calm hour. Book it
in late November and you are competing
with everybody who waited. And one more
thing about those October conversations
that I want to put plainly because it is
the single most useful sentence you can
say to any agent. Ask them to run your
medication list, not to describe the
plan, not to explain the benefits, to
enter your actual prescriptions and your
actual pharmacy and show you the annual
total for the plan they are recommending
alongside the annual total for at least
two others. A good agent does that
without being asked and frequently
offers it first. Somebody who talks
around it, who keeps returning to the
premium and the extra benefits and the
card with money on it, has told you
something important about how that
conversation is going to go. And you can
ask one more question that almost nobody
asks. How many plans in this county do
you actually represent? Some agents are
contracted with most of what is
available. Others are contracted with
two or three, which means the best plan
for you may simply not be on their list.
Not because they are hiding it, but
because they cannot sell it. Neither of
those questions is rude and neither
requires any expertise to ask. They are
the two questions that separate a
comparison from a sales call. and
October is when you have the most
leverage to ask them because you have
already seen the data yourself. Now, the
third thing that happens on the 1st of
October and it has nothing to do with
Medicare at all and hardly anybody
connects it. The federal fiscal year
starts on the 1st of October, which
sounds like an accounting detail and is
not because of what it does to a
specific set of programs. The assistance
that helps pay heating and cooling bills
is funded as a block grant and states
receive their allocation at the start of
the fiscal year. So, the money for this
coming winter becomes available in
October. And here is the part that
matters. In a great many states, that
money is finite and it runs out partway
through the season. When it is gone, it
is gone until the next fiscal year. So,
the household that applies in October is
applying into a full account. The
household that waits until a January
bill arrives is applying into whatever
is left. And in some states, that is
nothing. Same eligibility, same
paperwork, same household. Completely
different outcome based entirely on the
month. And the program that sits
alongside it, the one that sends people
to your house to insulate the attic and
seal the air leaks and repair an unsafe
furnace rather than paying your bill,
runs on the same fiscal calendar with
the same finite allocation and the same
queue. that one is worth considerably
more over time because it lowers every
winter's bill rather than this winter's.
And the work done on a single home
commonly runs into thousands of dollars.
I covered both of those in full in
another video, so I am not going to
repeat the detail here. What matters
today is the date. If you are going to
apply, the first week of October is the
best week of the year to do it and
January is the worst. And the same
fiscal reset affects a handful of other
things worth asking about in the same
call. Some housing assistance opens
lists at the start of a fiscal year.
Some transport and meal programs have
annual capacity that resets. If you were
told no in the spring because something
was full. October is when it may not be.
That is a genuinely useful sentence.
Being told no in March and being told no
in October are not the same no. Now the
announcement everybody is waiting for
which lands in the middle of the month.
The cost of living adjustment for next
year is announced in mid-occtober once
the September price figures are
published. And I want to give you the
one instruction that matters about it
because everybody does the opposite.
When the percentage is announced, do not
write it down and do not budget on it.
The reason is that if you are on
Medicare, your premium is deducted from
your payment before it reaches you and
that premium is set separately by a
different process and announced weeks
later in November. So the sequence every
single year is that people feel good
about a raise in October and then open
their first payment of January and find
the number is nothing like what they
expected. Every year there is a wave of
people who believe a mistake has been
made. There was no mistake. The raise
was real. It simply went somewhere on
its way to them. So the number that
actually matters is the announced raise
in dollars minus the increase in the
premium. Whatever survives that
subtraction is your real raise and
nobody publishes it because it is
different for every person. Which means
October gives you half the equation and
November gives you the other half. And
the only sensible thing to do in October
is wait. And there is one more piece of
that November news that catches a
specific group. So I want you ready for
it. If your income 2 years ago was above
certain thresholds, there is a sir
charge added to your premium and those
determination letters go out in
November. Here is what to do if one
arrives and the income behind it no
longer exists. If you retired, stopped
working, lost a spouse, or had a one-off
event like a property sale that is over,
you can ask for the calculation to be
redone on your current circumstances
rather than a year that no longer
reflects your life. There is a form for
it. It is free and it takes an
afternoon. And the number of people
paying a search charge right now who
could have it removed is not small
because nobody tells them the door is
there. Let me tell you about a woman I
will call Dovey 79 in Ohio. [snorts] She

or use the link at the top of the pinned

Now, the third part of this video, which

very hard. If you filed an extension on

extended deadline is the 15th of

regardless. So, if that is you, that

December, and it is the big one.
Everything I described in the first half
of this video, every change you might

the 7th of December to take effect on
the 1st of January. On the 8th of
December, the ordinary route closes for
a full year. And I want to be precise
about what happens if you do nothing
because doing nothing is not neutral.
You are not dropped and nothing lapses.
You are automatically enrolled in next

The third closes on the 31st of

the tax side. A gain realized on the

And if you use a checkbook feature,
actually cashed by the charity before

on that last one for anybody who gives

happen before you take anything else
out. Order matters and it cannot be
reversed afterward. Now, one piece of

insurer, you get one more change once.
You can move to a different plan of that

people discover problems in January at
the pharmacy counter or at a front desk.
But read the limits carefully. It is one
change, not several, and it only applies
if you are already in that kind of plan.
If you are on ordinary Medicare in
January and want to move, that window is
not yours. And there is a separate one
hardly anybody has heard of. If there is
a plan in your county rated at the top
of the fivepoint scale, you can switch
into it once during the year almost any
time outside every other window. It
depends entirely on whether such a plan
exists where you live, and many areas do
not have one, but it costs nothing to
check and almost nobody does. Now, three
more things that land in the same
stretch and that nobody puts in the same
calendar and each one reaches a
different household. The first is for
anybody whose spouse is younger than 65.
A separate open enrollment period for
ordinary health coverage opens on the
1st of November and runs into January.
And it is a completely different system
with completely different deadlines from
everything else in this video. So, a
household where one person is on
Medicare and the other is 62 has two
enrollment seasons running almost on top
of each other with two sets of dates and
the coverage for the younger spouse
generally has to be selected by the
middle of December to start on the 1st
of January. People confuse the two
constantly and the confusion always runs
the same direction. They handle the
Medicare side, feel finished, and let
the other one lapse or renew badly. If
that describes your house, write both
deadlines down separately because
nothing in either system will remind you
about the other. The second is your
property tax. And the timing on this
varies enormously, but the pattern is
consistent enough to be worth naming. A
great many counties have autumn
deadlines attached to their exemption
and freeze filings. and a great many

with a payment date in the winter, which

age, frequently have to be filed or

automatically. And the deadline is set
by your county rather than by anything
federal. So, the single question worth
asking is whether there is a senior
exemption or a freeze you are not
receiving and whether whatever you
already have needs renewing and by when.
The number is printed on the bill
itself. I have covered those properly in
their own video because they deserve
more room than I can give them here.
What belongs in an October video is only
the timing, which is that autumn is when
those deadlines cluster, and spring is
when people discover they missed one.
The third is a piece of paper that
arrives in this stretch and gets thrown
away almost universally. If you or your
spouse are still working and covered by
an employer plan, that employer is
required to send you a notice once a
year stating whether the drug coverage
counts as creditable. It arrives in the
autumn, it looks like junk, and it goes
in the bin. Keep it. That notice is the
only proof you have that you were
covered, and it is what protects you
from a permanent penalty if you enroll
in drug coverage later. The penalty is
calculated by the month, and it never
comes off once it is applied. one page
once a year and it is the cheapest
insurance in this entire video. And two
more things worth doing in the same
sitting because you will already have
the paperwork out. The first is the
annual look at your account deductions.
Whatever is coming out of your payment
automatically, the drug plan premium, a
supplemental plan, anything else is
being deducted on the strength of a
decision you made at some point and have
probably not revisited. October and
November are the only weeks in the year
when those can be changed. The rest of
the year, you simply pay them. The
[clears throat] second is your
beneficiary designations. And I raise it
here only because this is the one time
of year when people voluntarily look at
their financial paperwork. Every account
and every policy has a named
beneficiary. And that name overrides
your will completely. A will drafted
last year does not correct a form
completed in 1991. The form wins every
time. Checking the primary and the
contingent on everything is an afternoon
with a telephone, and it is the highest
return afternoon available to most
households. while the folder is open. Do
it. And one last piece of relief for
anybody who reaches December and
realizes they have missed everything.
Missing the 7th of December is not
always final. There are circumstances
that open a window regardless of the
calendar, moving to an area where your
plan is not offered, losing other
coverage, including employer coverage,
your plan ending its contract in your
county, entering or leaving a nursing
facility, qualifying for the assistance
programs that help with premiums and
drug costs. Each of those opens a period
during which you can change outside
every window in this video. So if
something significant changes in your
life, the question to ask is whether it
opened a door. And the answer is more
often yes than people assume. Here is
your list. Six things in date order.
One. This week before anything else,
open the comparison tool and enter your
real medications and your real pharmacy.
Look at the annual total, not the
premium. That is 20 minutes and it is
the whole exercise. Two, telephone every
doctor you actually see and ask whether
they are contracted with your plan for
next year, not this year. The directory
is frequently wrong and the front desk
is not. Three, book your free counseling
appointment in the first week of October
rather than late November because their
calendars fill and you want the calm
hour. Four, if you use heating or
cooling assistance or you have ever been
told a program was full, apply now. The
fiscal year restarted on the 1st of
October and the accounts are full for
the first time since last autumn. Five,
when the raise is announced midmon,
write down nothing. Wait for the premium
in November, subtract it and then you
have your real number. Six, put the 7th
of December on a calendar today and the
31st alongside it. One closes your

everything on the tax side. If any of

link pinned at the top of the comments.
And if you have a question about your
own situation, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read everyone that comes in, my honest
read. Nothing in this video is hidden.
That is the part I keep coming back to.
The data goes live on the 1st of October
and it is free and public. The
counseling service is free and exists in

The deadlines are printed. And yet, the
shape of the month is that the

experience only the second of those two

then filled with noise. And noise beats
availability every single time for
anyone who does not know what day to

Same information, same county, same

title: 9 Programs. One Call. Nobody Ever Tells You.

segments.text: Your state has already set aside this
money. It is sitting in an account with
a program name on it this month,
appropriated, budgeted, waiting. And not
one item on that list gets mailed to
anybody. Every single one waits for a
person to ask for it by name. Which
means the deciding factor is not your
income and it is not your need. It is
whether you know the words. Let me prove
that with the thing that actually
happens on the phone because this is the
part nobody explains. Call your county
and say, "I need some help." and you
will get whatever the person on the
other end happens to think of first.
They are not withholding anything. They
are answering a vague question with
whatever comes to mind. Call the same
office, same person, same afternoon, and
read them nine program names off a piece
of paper and they will check each one
against your file and tell you yes or no
on every single item. Identical call,
completely different outcome. And the
difference between remembering four of
them and reading all nine is measured in
hundreds of dollars a month. So this
entire video is that list. Get a pen
because at the end you are going to read
these out loud to somebody. And I am
giving you the phone number now rather
than holding it to the end because I
would rather you had it than watched
politely to get it. Every county in the
United States is covered by something
called an area agency on aging. There
are hundreds of them. They exist under
federal law and their entire function is
to be the front door to everything I am
about to describe. You do not have to
know which program you want. That is the
whole point of them. You describe your
situation and they tell you what your
county and your state actually have. The
national line that routes you to yours
is called the elder care locator.
One call, not one call per program.
Write that down now. And before the
list, let me take away the two things
that stop people from ever dialing it.
The first is the word that comes to mind
when somebody hears state program. And
for a lot of people, that word is
welfare. And they have paid their own
way for 60 years, and they tune out
immediately. I understand that
completely. But several items on this
list have no income test whatsoever. Not
one. and the ones that do have limits
set considerably higher than people
assume because they are usually tied to
a percentage of a federal figure rather
than to a number that sounds poor. The
second is the assumption that if you
qualified for something somebody would
have told you by now that is the
expensive one and I want to take it off
you directly. Nobody is assigned to tell
you. There is no agency whose job it is
to call. The system does not look
outward at all. It processes what
arrives and it waits. I am not a lawyer
and I am not your financial adviser and
the rules on this vary by state more
than almost any subject I cover. I am
giving you the categories that exist
everywhere and the door that leads to
your own state's version. My name is
Kevin. I read the rules so you do not
have to. If that is useful, subscribe.
Now the list nine names and I am leading
with the one that does the opposite of
what anybody expects from a government
program. The first one pays people 55
and older to work. It is called the
Senior Community Service Employment
Program. Federal money administered
through your state, placing people 55
and up in part-time positions at
libraries, senior centers, food banks,
and public agencies. You are paid at
least the local minimum wage for those
hours, typically around 20 hours a week.
There is an age floor of 55 and no
ceiling at all. And the design of it
matters. It is not charity work and it
is not volunteering. It is built to fill
a gap on a resume and move somebody into
ordinary employment at the end of it.
Now write down two words because this is
the part that makes the phone call work.
Title five. That is the section of the
law it comes from and a number of states
run it under their own local name
instead. So if the program name draws a
blank on the phone, say title five
instead and it will land. And I want to
be clear about who this is genuinely for
because most people watching this are
long retired and will skip it. It is for
the person who retired earlier than they
planned and needs some income. It is for
somebody whose spouse died and who
suddenly needs both money and a reason
to leave the house. And it is for the
person watching this on behalf of a
brother or a neighbor who is 57 out of
work and being told repeatedly that they
are too old to be hired. That last
situation is common and it is brutal and
this program exists precisely for it.
The second one is the largest number in
this entire video for a household in the
middle of it and almost nobody knows the
category exists. Your state can pay a
family member to be the caregiver. Every
state runs its Medicaid program with
something called home and community
based services. And the arithmetic
behind it is simple and the state worked
it out a long time ago. A nursing home
costs the state an enormous amount every
month. Keeping somebody at home costs a
fraction of that. So, the state would
rather pay for care at home. And in a
great many states, the person paid to
provide that care can be an adult child.
In some states, it can be a spouse. I
want to be honest that the rules vary
enormously here, more than anything else
on this list, but the category exists in
every single state. sit with what that
means for a household where a daughter
dropped a part-time or left a job
entirely to look after a parent. That is
happening in millions of homes in this
country right now unpaid. And in a large
number of those homes, there is a
program that would pay for some of those
hours. Here is what is actually
involved. So, nobody goes in expecting
it to be simple. There is an assessment
of the parents care needs, which is
about what help they genuinely require.
There is an income and asset test. And
here is the important part. It is
applied to the parent rather than to the
child. The adult child's own income is
generally irrelevant to whether the
parent qualifies. And in many states,
there is a waiting list, sometimes a
long one, which is exactly why the phone
call matters more than anything else
about it. Getting on to a list early is
the single most important action in this
entire category because the list does
not care when you started needing help.
It cares when you applied. Let me tell
you about a woman I will call Ardell. 68
and she rented the same secondf flooror
apartment for 19 years. Her heating bill
one January was $310 and she left the
envelope unopened on the table for 2
days because she already knew roughly
what was inside it. She had heard
somewhere that there was help with
heating bills. She called the number on
a flyer, was told she needed a different
office, called that one, got a
recording, and gave up. She told her
sister she had called and they did not
have anything for her. What she had
actually done was call about one
program. Three years later, her sister
called the elder care locator on her
behalf, four or five questions, and the
person came back with three things. The
heating program, which she had qualified
for the entire time, her state's renter
rebate, which she had never heard of and
had been eligible for since the day she
turned 65, and a note that her building
might qualify for weatherization.
None of the three years in between came
back. Not a dollar. These programs pay
forward from the date of approval and
not one day earlier. That is the reason
I put together the quiet rules. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
There is a code on the screen now. So,
hold your phone up to it or use the link
pinned at the top of the comments or the
one in the description below. It has
this entire list in it in print in large
type with the exact words to say on the
call and what each program is called in
different states. You have seven days
with it. If it does not change something
about what you do this week, send it
back and we are done. Ardell was not
lazy and she was not uninformed. She did
the thing almost everybody does, which
is call one office about one problem,
get told no, and conclude that no was
the answer for all of it. That is what
this system punishes, not ineligibility,
delay. And there are two things sitting
underneath that second program that
nobody covers. And both are worth more
than most items on this list. The first
is for married couples, and it is the
reason a great many people wrongly
believe they could never qualify for
care at home. When one spouse needs
long-term care and the other does not,
there are rules that exist specifically
so the healthy spouse is not left with
nothing. They are sometimes called the
spousal impoverishment provisions and
that name tells you exactly what they
were written to prevent. Under them, the
spouse who remains at home is allowed to
keep a substantial share of the couple's
assets and there is a floor and a
ceiling on that amount that adjusts
every year. The house is generally
protected entirely while that spouse
lives in it. And the atome spouse is
allowed to keep a minimum monthly
income, which in some cases means income
is actually shifted from the spouse
receiving care to the one at home. So
the picture people have in their heads
where a couple has to be reduced to
nothing before any help arrives is not
how it works when one spouse is still at
home. And that misunderstanding stops
people from applying for years. The
second is a program that exists in most
states and that hardly anybody has heard
of. And for the right person, it is the
best arrangement available anywhere. It
is called PACE, the program of
all-inclusive care for the elderly. It
is for people 55 and older who need a
nursing home level of care but want to
stay at home. What it does is unusual.
It combines everything into one
organization. Your doctors, your
specialists, your prescriptions, your
therapy, transportation, day services,
home care, all coordinated by one team
that is responsible for the whole
picture rather than billing separately
for pieces of it. It is available in
roughly 30 states. For somebody on both
Medicare and Medicaid, it typically
costs nothing at all. And for somebody
on Medicare only, there is a monthly
premium. The reason it matters is that
it is the one arrangement in this entire
landscape where somebody is actually
responsible for coordinating everything
rather than a family member being handed
a list of phone numbers. Ask whether
there is a PACE program in your county.
In a great many places there is and
almost nobody applies. And one more
piece of that category that people never
ask about because they assume the answer
is obvious and it is not. If somebody is
already in a nursing home paid for by
Medicaid, that is not necessarily
permanent. There is a federal initiative
built specifically to move people out of
facilities and back into the community
with the funding following the person
rather than staying attached to the
building. It pays for the transition
itself, setting up a home, a deposit,
the equipment somebody needs to live
independently again, and the services
once they are back. Which means a family
who was told 2 years ago that a parent
needed a facility and has assumed ever
since that the decision was final may
have a route back that nobody mentioned
because nobody at the facility has any
reason to mention it. Ask about it by
name if that describes your household.
Money following the person out is a very
different conversation from money
following them in. The third one is
prescriptions, and this one is
geographic in a way that is genuinely
unfair. Roughly 20 states run their own
pharmaceutical assistance program. These
sit on top of Medicare drug coverage and
help with premiums, deductibles, or the
cost of the medication itself. Some of
them are substantial. If you live in one
of those states and you are paying out
of pocket for medication, you may be
paying for something your state was
already prepared to cover. And if you
live in a state that does not run one,
you need to know that, too. So, you stop
looking for it and put your attention on
the federal program instead, which
reduces what you pay for drug coverage
and is worth asking about in the same
call. Now, two additional routes on
medication that almost nobody uses, and
both matter if your state has nothing.
Most drug manufacturers run assistance
programs that provide medication at no
cost or heavily reduced cost to people
below certain income levels. They are
longestablished. They are real and they
are underused because you have to find
them and apply usually with your
doctor's office helping. And if you
receive care at a community health
center, ask about their pharmacy
specifically because those centers
frequently access drug pricing
dramatically below retail. The fourth
one is your utility bill. And there are
three completely separate things here
that people collapse into one. And the
second of the three is worth the most.
The first is the program that helps pay
heating and cooling bills directly.
Depending on your state, it commonly
runs somewhere between a few hundred
dollar and 1,500 a year. And many states
also have a crisis component for an
emergency. A furnace failing in February
or a dangerous heat wave. The critical
thing about that one is timing. It is
funded as a block. And in a number of
states, the money for the season
genuinely runs out. Apply early rather
than when the bill arrives. The second
is separate, much larger, and hardly
anybody knows it exists. It does not pay
your bill. It fixes the reason the bill
is high. It sends people to your house
to insulate the attic, seal the places
air is escaping, and repair or replace
an unsafe or failing heating system with
a safety inspection of your appliances.
It is done at no cost to an eligible
household. And the value of the work on
a single home commonly runs into
thousands of dollars. Think about the
difference between those two. One pays
this winter's bill. The other lowers
every winter's bill for as long as you
live in that house. and approval for the
first frequently makes you automatically
eligible for the second, which is that
unlocking pattern you will see again and
again on this list. The third is your
own utility company, and it is the
easiest phone call in this video. Most
gas and electric companies run their own
discounted rate for older or lower
income customers, and they do not
advertise it. One question while you
have them on the phone, do you have a
senior or low-income discount program,
and am I on it? The fifth one is for
renters. And I want to say that clearly
because almost every video about
benefits for older people talks
exclusively to homeowners. Several
states run a rebate for renters.
Pennsylvania has run one for decades.
Others have their own version, sometimes
called a renter credit, sometimes
bundled into a property tax and rent
rebate. The logic behind it is that your
landlord's property tax is built into
your rent, so the state rebates a share
of it back to you directly. It is
usually claimed on a state form once a
year, which means two things. It is
genuinely easy to claim and it is the
single most commonly missed item for
renters because it lives with tax forms
rather than with benefit offices and
nobody connects the two. And there is a
detail about it that cost Ardell 3
years. Those rebates are claimed for a
specific year and the years you never
filed for close on their own schedule
and are finished. Some states allow you
to go back a year or two. most do not.
So the question for your state is not
only whether one exists but whether you
can still claim a prior year and that is
worth asking in the same call. The sixth
is food and I am going to be direct
about why this one goes unclaimed
because it is not eligibility. The share
of eligible older adults who actually
receive food assistance is far lower
than for any other age group in the
country and the reason is that people
who worked their whole lives will not
apply. I am not going to tell anybody
how to feel about that. I will give you
two facts. The first is that for a
household with somebody 60 or older, the
rules are different and considerably
more generous than most people know.
Medical costs above a small monthly
threshold come off your income before
eligibility is calculated, which pulls
in a great many people who assume their
income is too high. That includes your
Medicare premiums, your supplemental
premium, co-ayments, prescriptions,
dental work, and transport to
appointments. And in most states, there
is no asset limit at all for these
households, which removes the other
thing people disqualify themselves over.
The second fact is that a great many
states run a separate seasonal program
issuing coupons for fresh produce at
local farmers markets with a simple
application and a low bar. It is small,
it is genuinely pleasant, and it is
almost entirely unclaimed. And there is
one more thing about that food program
that is worth 30 seconds because it
removes the last objection. A great many
people picture standing at a checkout
with something that marks them out. That
is not how it works anymore and has not
been for years. It arrives as an
ordinary card that works exactly like a
bank card at the till. And nobody in the
queue behind you knows the difference
between yours and theirs. I mention it
because that specific worry, not the
paperwork and not the eligibility, is
what actually stops people in this age
group from applying. The dignity concern
is real and it is also out of date. The
seventh is transportation and this is
the one people are most embarrassed to
ask about. Every area agency on aging in
the country funds transportation and it
is one of the most heavily used services
they have. Rides to medical appointments
to the pharmacy to the grocery store to
dialysis. Some of it is a scheduled van,
some of it is a volunteer driver. Some
of it is a voucher for a taxi or a ride
service. And there is usually no income
test on it at all. The qualification is
age. I am spending time on it because
giving up driving is one of the hardest
things that happens to a person and the
fear underneath it is almost never about
the car. It is about becoming a burden
about having to ask a son or a daughter
for permission to go to every single
errand. A scheduled ride to the doctor
that does not require asking anybody for
a favor is worth considerably more than
its dollar value and it is sitting
unused in most counties in this country.
The eighth is meals and there are two
different programs here that people
constantly confuse. The first is home
delivered meals which most people know
by the name of the best known
organization doing it. That one is for

the year, whether you sold anything or
not. So, somebody holding a fund in a
taxable account can receive a taxable
gain in December on a fund they never
touched in a year when the fund itself
went down.
That happens regularly and it infuriates
people.
Those distributions are announced in
advance, usually in late autumn. Which
means two things are possible. If you
were going to sell a fund anyway,
selling before the distribution date
avoids receiving a gain you did not
want. And if you were going to buy a
fund, buying just before a distribution
means paying for somebody else's gain
and immediately owing tax on it. So,
waiting until after is simply better.
Nobody tells you the date. It is
published and almost no ordinary
investor has ever looked it up. And this
only matters outside retirement
accounts. Inside one, a distribution is
invisible. Now, let me deal with the
reason none of this is happening in most
households because it is not laziness
and it is not ignorance. It is that the
person who prepares your tax return is
looking backward and cannot help it. By
the time your paperwork reaches a
preparer in February, the year is over.
Every sale happened. Every withdrawal
happened. Every one of the decisions in
this video was made or not made months
earlier. A preparer's job at that point
is to report accurately what already
occurred. They are not doing anything
wrong. There is simply nothing left to
change. So, the entire industry that
touches your taxes touches them at the
one moment when nothing can be done, and
everybody involved knows that, and
almost nobody says it out loud. And
there is a second gap alongside it. The
person managing your investments and the
person preparing your return are usually
two different people who have never
spoken.
One knows what you own and does not see
your return. The other sees your return
and does not know what you own.
Every single item in this video sits
precisely in the space between those two
people. Which asset to sell, in which
account, in which year, in whose name.
That is why it goes undone. Not because
it is difficult, but because it is
nobody's job, and nobody is paid for the
space between two roles, which means
somebody has to be looking at both, and
by default, that is you.
Or you pay somebody once for a review
rather than a product, and it is one of
the few fees in this whole landscape
that reliably pays for itself.
And one more that belongs with the
timing question, because it is the
version of all of this that has an
actual deadline on it.
Almost everything in this video has to
happen before the 31st of December. A
sale on the 30th of December is in this
year. On the 2nd of January, it is in
the next one.
A gain harvested in December fills this
year's zero band. A loss taken in
December offsets this year's gains.
There is exactly one significant thing
you can still do after the year ends,
and that is fund a retirement account
for the prior year, which most retirees
are not doing anyway.
Everything else closes at midnight on
the 31st permanently, and the next
chance is 12 months away.
Which means the useful month for all of
this is November, not April.
In November, you know almost everything
about your year, and you still have 6
weeks of room to act on it.
In April, you know everything and can do
nothing.
That single shift, looking in November
instead of at tax time, is worth more
than any individual item on this list,
because it is the thing that makes any
of them possible.
Here is your list. Six things. One, find
out whether you are inside the zero rate
band for long-term gains. That single
fact changes everything else, and most
people have no idea which side of it
they are on.
Two, if you are inside it, consider
deliberately realizing gains and
rebuying immediately.
The wash sale rule does not apply to
gains, and every year you do not do it
is a year that does not come back.
Three,
check whether you have a capital loss
carry forward on your return. If you do,
understand that it disappears when you
do, and think about how to use it faster
than $3,000 a year.
Four,
look at where your bonds and your growth
investments actually sit across your
three types of account.
Moving them around inside a retirement
account costs nothing and improves every
year from here. Five,
look at your beneficiary designations
with one question in mind. Is the
retirement account going to the
recipient who pays no tax, and are the
taxable investments going to the people
who receive them with the gain wiped
clean?
Six,
if you have a trust holding investments,
find out whether income is being
retained inside it, because a trust hits
the top rate at a level that would shock
you.
If any of that landed close to home, all
of it is laid out in order in the Quiet
rules. Link pinned at the top of the
comments. And if your own arrangement is
complicated, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read everyone, my honest read. There
is a version of this subject that gets
sold constantly, and I want to be clear
that this is not it.
Nobody in this video is using a
loophole. There is no offshore anything,
no aggressive structure, no clever
entity.
Everything here is the ordinary
operation of rules that were written
openly and are applied to everybody.
What separates the household that pays
less from the one that pays more is
almost never sophistication.
It is that somebody looked.
And here is what genuinely bothers me
about it. Every one of these advantages
is largest for people with moderate
incomes. The zero rate on gains is a
middle income provision. The favorable
brackets are widest at the bottom. The
beneficiary arrangement matters most
when the amounts are modest enough that
a tax bill actually hurts.
And those are exactly the households
least likely to be paying anybody to
look at this, because paying for advice
feels like something wealthy people do.
So the benefits that were designed for
ordinary retirees are used most reliably
by the ones who can afford somebody to
notice them.
That is not a conspiracy, it is just how
it lands.
Last thought. You spent 40 years with
almost no control over your taxable
income. It was decided by an employer,
reported by a computer, and deducted
before you ever saw it. That ended the
day you stopped working, and nobody sent
a letter explaining what had changed.
Now the number is largely yours. Which
account, which year, whose name, which
asset? Four choices made over and over
that add up to a great deal across a
retirement. Most people go on behaving
as though the number is still being
decided somewhere else.
That is the whole mistake, and it is a
habit rather than an error. So look
once, find out which side of the zero
rate you are on, and look at whose name
is on what.
That is an afternoon, and it is the
afternoon that changes the rest of it. I
am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: Bad News For US Veterans: 3 Checks Most Never Claim

segments.text: Everyday you wait to file, the
department is not holding your place in
line. It is deleting it. That is the
single most expensive misunderstanding
in the entire veterans benefit system,
and almost nobody is told at a
discharge, at the clinic, or anywhere
else.
Here is what it means in practice. When
a claim is finally approved, payment
does not begin on the day somebody signs
off on it. It begins on what is called
your effective date, and in most cases,
that is the date the department received
your claim.
Everything between those two dates gets
paid at once, in a single deposit. So, a
claim that took 18 months to process is
not 18 months of waiting for nothing. It
is 18 months of compensation you were
legally owed arriving together. Which
means every month you spend deciding
whether to file, gathering one more
record, or waiting to see how you feel,
is a month permanently removed from that
calculation. Not delayed, removed. It
never gets paid. And here is the part
that makes it worse. There is a form
that stops the clock. It takes about
four minutes. It claims nothing, and
hardly anybody outside the system has
heard of it. It is called an intent to
file. Filing it does not start a claim.
It does not commit you to anything. What
it does is lock in your effective date
for a full year while you gather medical
records, get an opinion, or simply work
out what you were doing. So, somebody
who files that form today and submits
the actual claim 11 months from now is
paid as though the claim had been filed
today. 11 months of compensation
preserved by a form that takes less time
than a phone call. And a veteran who
spends those same 11 months gathering
evidence without filing it, loses every
one of those months permanently, having
done exactly the responsible thing. I
want that to be the first thing you take
from this video, before anything else.
If you are considering filing anything
at all, file the intent to file today,
and then take your time. I am not a
lawyer, and I'm not accredited to
represent anybody on a claim. This is
