educational. The details vary enormously
by situation, and every one of these
should be checked with an accredited
service officer, which is free.
My name is Kevin. I read the rules, so
you do not have to. If that is useful,
subscribe. Now, let me go through the
three checks, and I'm starting with the
one that produces the largest single
deposits because the rules around it are
the ones most worth understanding.
The first is retroactive compensation,
back pay.
I have explained the basic mechanism.
Effective date to approval date, paid in
one sum.
Now, the details that decide how large
that sum is. The first is the discharge
rule, and it is worth tens of thousands
of dollars to anybody it applies to. If
your very first claim is filed within 1
year of leaving active service, your
effective date can reach back to the day
after your discharge, rather than the
day you filed.
So, somebody who separates in March and
files the following January is paid from
March.
Somebody who files 14 months after
separating is paid from the date of
filing, and those first 10 months are
simply gone.
1 year.
That is the line, and it is the reason
every advocate pushes people to file
immediately, rather than waiting to see
whether something settles down.
The second is the rule for increases,
and this one surprises people who
already have a rating.
If your condition worsens and you claim
an increase, the effective date is not
automatically the date you filed. It can
reach back up to 1 year before you filed
if the medical evidence shows the
worsening had already happened by then.
Read that carefully because it changes
what you should do before filing. It
means the evidence in your file is what
determines how far back it reaches. A
veteran whose records document the
deterioration 8 months before they filed
can be paid from that point. A veteran
whose records only show it on the day of
the examination cannot.
So, if you are filing for an increase,
the most valuable thing you can do is
get the older records into the file.
The visits from last year, the notes
from the specialist, the physical
therapy that started 14 months ago.
Those documents are not background. They
are the difference between a payment
starting today and one reaching back a
year. The third piece is dependents and
it catches an enormous number of people.
Compensation is paid at a higher rate
when you have a spouse or children above
a certain rating level.
But that higher rate is only applied if
the form declaring your dependents was
actually on file during the period being
paid.
So somebody who was married the whole
time, who never submitted that form,
receives back pay calculated at the
single rate.
For a multi-year retroactive award, that
difference is substantial. And if you
filed it late, there is generally a
window of 1 year from the date of the
grant to add dependents and have the
retroactive amount adjusted. Which means
if a decision came through in the last
12 months and your dependents were not
on file, that is a thing to fix this
month rather than next year.
The fourth is that these decisions are
not permanent in the way people assume.
If a past decision contains what is
called a clear and unmistakable error,
meaning the outcome would have been
different had the correct rule been
applied, that decision can be revised
and the effective date corrected and
there is no time limit on it. A decision
from 1992 can be challenged. I want to
be honest about the standard because it
is high. It is not enough that the
decision was arguable or that you
disagree or that a different examiner
might have seen it differently. The
error has to be undebatable and it has
to have changed the result.
Most old decisions do not qualify, but
the ones that do can produce back pay
covering decades and the only way to
know is to read the decision rather than
remember it. And there is one
consequence of a retroactive rating that
has nothing to do with the compensation
itself
and it is one of the most commonly
missed refunds in the entire system.
The home loan funding fee.
When you use a veteran's home loan,
there is a fee charged at closing and it
can run into the thousands or tens of
thousands depending on the size of the
loan and whether it is your first.
Veterans receiving disability
compensation are exempt from that fee.
Now put the two things together.
Somebody buys a house, pays the fee at
closing, and 18 months later a claim is
approved with an effective date that
falls before the closing date. Under the
rules, they were exempt on the day they
closed. They just did not know it yet.
That fee is refundable and it is not
automatic. Nobody at the lender is going
to notice because the lender was paid
and closed the file years ago. So, if
you have ever used a veteran's home loan
and later received a disability rating
with an effective date before the loan
closed, that is a refund sitting there.
You raise it with the regional loan
center and people have recovered five
figures this way. Almost nobody knows to
look because the two things happen years
apart in completely different parts of
the system. Let me tell you about a man
I will call Roscoe, 68 in Georgia, Army,
and he filed an increase for a back
condition that had been getting steadily
worse for years. The claim took 16
months. When it came through, he was
paid back to a date almost a year before
he had filed because his records
happened to document the deterioration
clearly.
What he did not know was that he had
bought his house 11 months before that
effective date and had paid the funding
fee at closing. He found out from
another veteran at a coffee morning,
raised it, and was refunded. Nobody in
the process connected those two facts
for him. There is nobody whose job it is
to. If you are watching this and any of
what I have just described sounds like
your paperwork, the practical problem is
usually not eligibility. It is that
nobody has ever laid the rules out in
one place in language you can actually
work from. That is what the quiet rules
is for. It is at kevinexplains.shop
and there is a code on the screen now or
the link is pinned at the top of the
comments and sitting in the description.
7 days to look at it. If it does not
change what you do next, send it back.
Roscoe's refund was sitting there for a
year and a half. The only reason he
received it is that somebody at a coffee
morning happened to mention it. Two more
things about back pay before I move on
because both change the number. The
first is that retroactive compensation
is not taxed. Disability compensation is
tax-free, and that does not change
because it arrives in one deposit rather
than across 4 years. A five-figure
retroactive award is not a five-figure
taxable event, and people set money
aside for a tax bill that never comes.
The second is what that deposit can do
to other things, and this is the piece
to actually plan around. It is not
taxable income, so it does not touch
your tax return. But a large sum landing
in a bank account can matter for any
program that looks at your assets rather
than your income. For most people, that
is irrelevant. For somebody receiving a
needs-based payment with an asset limit,
it is not. And there are protections and
exclusion periods that apply to exactly
this situation. If that describes you,
raise it before the deposit rather than
after because unwinding it afterward is
considerably harder.
Now, the second check, and this one is
for career retirees specifically, and it
involves a choice most people do not
know they are making.
For decades, the rule worked like this.
If you retired from the military after
20 or more years and also received
disability compensation, your retirement
pay was reduced dollar for dollar by
whatever the department paid you.
Two different payments from two
different systems compensating for two
entirely different things, and you
effectively received only the larger of
the two. There are now two separate
programs that undo that, and here is
what almost nobody understands. They are
different. You cannot receive both, and
you are supposed to choose. The first
restores your retired pay if you have 20
or more years of service and a combined
rating of 50% or higher.
It phases in. It is applied
automatically once you meet both
conditions, and it is taxable. The
second is for disabilities that are
combat related, and the rules are
completely different. There is no
20-year requirement. Medical retirees
with fewer than 20 years can qualify.
There is no 50% threshold. It can apply
at lower ratings. It is not automatic.
You have to apply for it. And
critically, it is not taxable. So, the
comparison is not simply which number is
bigger.
A smaller tax-free payment can be worth
more than a larger taxable one. And for
a lot of retirees, it is. And here is
the piece I most want you to have,
because it is genuinely valuable, and it
is almost never mentioned.
You are not locked into whichever one
you have. There is an open season once a
year in which retirees receiving one of
these can switch to the other. It
happens at the start of each year, and
notices go out about it. Which means
somebody who chose one of these 6 years
ago, whose rating has since changed, or
whose tax situation has changed, may be
in the wrong one right now and can move.
And a great many people have never
compared them once, because the
automatic one arrived without them doing
anything, and it never occurred to them
that there was a decision to make. And a
second thing about the automatic one
that catches people constantly,
automatic does not mean reliable. It
means no application is required. Those
are different. When a rating changes,
two separate systems have to
communicate, and they do not always do
it promptly or correctly.
Veterans whose rating crosses the 50%
threshold frequently find months later
that their retired pay never adjusted,
with no letter explaining anything. So,
the check here is specific. Pull your
retiree account statement, the actual
statement rather than the deposit in
your bank account, and compare it line
by line against your compensation
letter.
Confirm you are receiving both in full
rather than one reduced by the other.
If your rating changed and the pay has
not adjusted within a couple of months,
that is a phone call and corrections are
generally made retroactively when they
find the error.
And while I am on career retirees, there
is one more thing that belongs here and
it is one of the most under claimed
provisions in the entire system.
You do not need a 100% rating to be paid
at the 100% rate. If service connected
conditions prevent you from maintaining
substantially gainful employment, you
can be paid at the full rate even with a
lower combined rating.
It has its own application and its own
criteria and it is generally available
at a 60% single rating or a 70% combined
with one condition at 40.
The number of veterans sitting at 70%
unable to work because of those
conditions who have never heard of it is
very large.
And it matters beyond the monthly amount
because being paid at that rate opens
other doors that a lower rating does
not.
Now, the third check and this is the one
with the widest reach because it does
not require a service connected
disability at all. It is an enhanced
pension for wartime veterans and their
surviving spouses who need help with the
ordinary activities of daily life. And
the first thing that stops people is a
misunderstanding about what it is. They
hear veterans benefit and think it must
be tied to an injury from service. It is
not. It has nothing to do with how you
were hurt or whether you were hurt at
all. It has three requirements. Service
during a wartime period, a genuine need
for help, and income and assets under
the limits. Let me take the wartime one
first because this is where a lot of
people wrongly disqualify themselves.
Wartime period does not mean combat. It
does not mean deployment. It means you
served during a defined window and one
day inside that window is enough
alongside the general service
requirement. And here is the fact that
surprises almost everybody.
The Gulf War period for these purposes
opened in August of 1990 and has never
been closed, which means anybody who
served on active duty at any point from
1990 onward has wartime service under
this rule.
Not just people who deployed, not just
people who went anywhere near the
region. So a person who served in the
mid-90s entirely stateside has it.
A person who served after 2000 has it.
And a great many of them have assumed
for years that this could not possibly
apply to them.
The second requirement is need and it is
broader than people expect. It covers
needing help with bathing, dressing,
eating, or moving about. And it also
covers being in an assisted living
facility or a nursing home. And there is
a separate lower level for people who
are largely confined to the home.
And the third is the financial test. And
this is where the mechanism is genuinely
clever and almost nobody understands it.
There is a net worth limit and it sits
somewhere above $160,000
adjusted annually.
Critically, it excludes your home and a
vehicle. And on the income side, this is
the part that matters most. Your
countable income is reduced by
unreimbursed medical expenses, which
includes the cost of in-home care and
assisted living and a nursing facility
and insurance premiums including what
comes out of your benefit for health
coverage. So consider what that does
arithmetically. Somebody paying $4,000 a
month for care has $48,000 a year of
expenses off their income before
anything is calculated. Which means a
household that looks far too well off on
paper, that would never think to apply,
can qualify comfortably once the care
costs are applied. And that is exactly
the household least likely to apply
because they look at their income,
decide they are over the limit, and
never make the call. The payment is
monthly and it is tax-free. And the
rates run to somewhere around $2,800 a
month for a married veteran, somewhat
less for a single veteran, and a smaller
amount for a surviving spouse, all
adjusted each year. That last one
deserves emphasis. Surviving spouses
qualify. A widow of a wartime veteran
paying for her own care in her own home
or in a facility can receive this on his
service. And the number of widows who
have no idea that anything flows to them
from a war their husband served in 50
years ago is enormous. Two more things
about this one, and both are important.
There is a look back on transfers of
assets. Money given away before applying
can create a penalty period, and the
look back runs 3 years, which means this
is a thing to understand before you
start moving money around to qualify,
not after. And it is another reason to
start the conversation early rather than
when the need becomes urgent. And the
warning, which is serious. Where there
is a needs-based benefit with an asset
test, there is an industry. There are
companies that charge substantial fees
to help veterans and widows qualify,
frequently by restructuring assets into
products those companies happen to sell.
Understand two things about that.
Accredited representatives cannot charge
you for preparing an initial claim. That
is not a courtesy, it is the rule.
And your county or state service officer
does this for nothing as their actual
job without selling anything.
So, if somebody is offering to help you
qualify and there is a fee or a product
attached, you are in the wrong room.
Walk out and telephone the service
officer instead. Let me tell you about a
woman I will call Bernadine. 79 in Ohio,
widowed for 6 years. Her husband had
served in the '50s and never saw combat,
and never had a disability rating of any
kind. She was paying a little over
$3,000 a month for care in her own home
out of savings that were visibly running
down. She had never once considered that
anything from his service could reach
her because in her mind that had ended
when he did. It took a neighbor's
daughter who worked in a nursing
facility and had seen this before to
tell her to call the county service
officer.
If you are sitting there recognizing
your own situation in any of that, the
difficulty is almost never the
eligibility. It is that no single
document anywhere lays out which rule
applies to which situation and what to
do about it. That is what I built the
quiet rules to be and it is at
kevinexplains.shop
with the code on your screen and the
link pinned at the top of the comments.
7 days with it. If it does not earn its
place, send it back and that is the end
of it. Bernadine had been eligible for 6
years.
The money for those 6 years is gone and
cannot be recovered because this one
does not pay backward the way a
disability claim does.
One more thing about that rating
question because it decides more than
the monthly amount. A rating is not only
a payment, it is a key that opens other
things and most veterans think of it
purely as a number attached to a check.
At certain rating levels, health care
priority changes. At certain levels,
dependents become eligible for education
benefits and for health coverage of
their own.
Certain states waive property tax
entirely at particular thresholds and
partially below them.
Vehicle registration, park access,
hunting and fishing licenses, tuition at
state institutions, all of it is
frequently tied to a rating and
administered by somebody who will never
contact you. So, a veteran who moves
from 30% to 60% has not simply increased
a payment. They may have crossed into a
completely different set of entitlements
in their own state, none of which will
be mentioned in the decision letter
because the decision letter is a federal
document and those benefits are
administered locally.
Which means after any rating change,
there is a second call worth making that
nobody tells you about and it is to your
state Department of Veterans Affairs
rather than the federal one.
They administer an entirely separate
list and they will tell you what your
new number unlocked.
And one practical thing about the whole
process that saves people months, which
nobody tells you,
there is more than one route to file,
and they are not equally fast. Filing on
your own, without help, is the slowest
and the most error-prone because the
evidence that decides your effective
date has to be assembled by somebody.
And if that somebody is you, working
from memory, it usually is not complete.
An accredited service officer does this
for nothing, county, state, or through a
veteran's organization. They know what
evidence the decision actually turns on.
They know which examination the claim
will be routed to, and they file it in
the form the system expects.
And there is a specific version of a
claim that comes with a much faster
route where you gather your own evidence
up front and submit it complete, and the
claim moves considerably quicker because
there is nothing to go and request.
Which is worth knowing because the
length of the wait is not fixed. It
depends substantially on how complete
the file is on the day it arrives. So,
the sequence that actually works is
this.
File the intent to file immediately to
stop the clock.
Then, take the time you have just bought
to get the records together with a
service officer.
Then, submit it complete. That order
costs you nothing, and it is the
difference between a claim that takes 8
months and one that takes 2 years with
the same outcome at the end. Now, three
more that belong in this video because
they follow the same pattern, and each
one reaches a group that assumes it does
not apply to them.
The first is for surviving spouses, and
it is separate from the pension I just
described. There is a monthly payment
for the survivor of a veteran whose
death was connected to service. It is
tax-free, it is not needs-based, and it
is a considerably larger amount than the
pension. And there is a rule attached to
it that a great many widows have never
heard. If a veteran was rated totally
disabled from service-connected
conditions for a continuous period of 10
years before dying, the survivor can
qualify regardless of what the veteran
actually died of.
10 years at that rating. The cause of
death does not have to be connected at
all.
So, a widow whose husband held that
rating for years, and then died of
something entirely unrelated, who was
told or assumed there was nothing for
her, may be looking at a substantial
monthly payment she never claimed.
And there are shorter versions of that
rule for veterans who died closer to
their discharge.
The second is a set of additional
payments that exist above and beyond the
ordinary rating scale for specific
circumstances.
Loss of use of a limb, certain sensory
losses, needing regular aid and
attendance, being housebound.
They are paid on top of compensation
rather than instead of it. And they are
frequently missed because they are not
automatic, and the criteria are
specific. The one I want to name in
particular is that a veteran rated at
the highest level, whose spouse needs
help with daily activities, can receive
an additional amount for that. Not for
himself, for her care. That is a payment
tied to the health of the spouse on the
veteran's claim. And I would guess 95%
of the households it applies to have
never heard of it. And the third is
presumptive conditions, which have
expanded significantly in recent years.
Certain illnesses are presumed connected
to service if you served in particular
places at particular times.
That means you do not have to prove the
connection. The connection is assumed,
and the burden shifts.
The list has grown a great deal
recently, covering exposure to burn pits
and airborne hazards, and expanding the
locations covered for older exposures
well beyond where people assume,
including places a lot of veterans do
not associate with those conditions at
all, which matters enormously for two
groups.
Veterans previously denied for a
condition that has since been made
presumptive, who can file again under
the new rules. And survivors of veterans
who died of a condition that is now
presumptive.
So, a denial from 2099 is not
necessarily the end of that question.
The rule that produced the denial may no
longer be the rule.
And there is one more category that
belongs here because it applies to
people who never think of themselves as
having a claim at all. Conditions that
developed years after service.
A great many veterans assume that if
something did not appear until decades
later, the connection is gone.
That is not how it works.
There is no time limit on filing and a
condition that surfaces 30 years
afterward can still be connected if the
evidence supports it. And there is a
category called secondary conditions
that is missed constantly.
If a service connected condition causes
or worsens something else, that
something else can be connected, too.
The examples are ordinary rather than
exotic. A knee injury that changes how
somebody walks, which damages the other
knee or the hip or the back.
A medication for a connected condition
that causes another problem. Sleep
disruption from pain. The mental health
consequences of living with chronic pain
for 20 years.
Each of those can be its own claim and
each raises the combined rating. And
combined ratings do not add the way
people expect, which is a separate
frustration entirely.
So, the question is not only what
happened to you in service, it is what
has happened since as a consequence of
it. And that second question is the one
almost nobody has asked. Here is your
list. Six things and the first one takes
four minutes. One, if you are
considering filing anything at all, file
the intent to file today. It commits you
to nothing and it protects up to a year
of payments. This is the single highest
value action in this video and it costs
nothing. Two, if you are filing for an
increase, get your older medical records
into the file. The evidence of when the
worsening happened is what decides how
far back the payment reaches. Three,
check that your dependents are on file
and if a decision came through in the
last year and they were not, fix that
now while the window is open. Four, if
you are a retiree with 20 years and a
rating of 50% or more, pull the actual
statement and confirm you are receiving
both payments in full and find out which
of the two programs you are in because
you may be in the wrong one and there is
one chance a year to move. Five, if you
or a spouse served during a wartime
period and either of you is paying for
care of any kind, telephone the county
or state service officer. Do not
disqualify yourself on income before
somebody has applied the medical expense
rule to your numbers.
Six, if you have ever used a veteran's
home loan and later received a rating
with an effective date before the
closing, ask about a refund of the
funding fee.
If any of that landed close to home, all
of it is laid out in order in the quiet
rules. Link pinned at the top of the
comments. And if you have a question
about your own situation, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read every one. Though for a live
claim, what you want is an accredited
representative and I will say so.
My honest read, the system is not
withholding this. Every rule in this
video is published and the people
staffing the service offices are, in my
experience, genuinely trying to help and
are badly outnumbered. The problem is
that the whole thing is built to respond
rather than to reach out. It processes
what arrives. It answers what is asked.
It has no mechanism at all for noticing
that a widow in Ohio has been eligible
for six years and has not applied
because nothing in it is designed to
look outward.
So the benefit reaches whoever happened
to hear the words from another veteran,
from a daughter who works in a facility,
from somebody at a coffee morning.
That means it reaches the connected and
misses the isolated, which is very
nearly the opposite of who it was
written for.
And there is a particular unfairness in
that for this group specifically.
These are people who were told,
correctly, that their service earned
them something
and then handed a system that only gives
it to whoever knows the name of the
form.
Last thought, nearly everything in this
video comes down to one distinction.
Some of these pay backward and some do
not. A disability claim reaches back to
an effective date, which is why the
intent to file matters so much and why a
year of waiting is a year of money
rather than just a year of waiting. The
pension does not work that way. It
starts when you apply and every month
before that is simply gone.
Which means for one of these, filing
today protects the past. For the other,
filing today is the only thing that
protects the future.
Either way, the instruction is identical
and it is the only one that matters.
Make the call this week rather than next
year.
I am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: Most Retirees Pay Tax On Their RMD For No Reason

segments.text: If you have already taken this year's
required withdrawal, the move I am about
to describe is closed to you until
January. Not reduced, not partially
available, closed for the rest of the
year with no way to undo it. And almost
nobody knows that. Which is why the
single most common way people lose this
is by doing the responsible thing early
in the year and taking their withdrawal
in January the way they always have.
So before anything else, if you are
watching this and you have not yet taken
your withdrawal for this year, you are
in the best possible position and you
should not take it until you have
finished this video.
Here is what is at stake. There is one
way to move money out of a retirement
account that never appears on your tax
return at all. Not as income you then
deduct, not as a write-off. It simply
does not appear. And it satisfies the
withdrawal the government forces you to
take every year once you reach the
required age. The same withdrawal that
raises your tax, pulls more of your
social security into the taxable column,
and raises what you pay for Medicare two
years later. It exists. It is written
plainly into the code. It has been there
for years and the overwhelming majority
of people who could use it never have.
And there is a reason for that which I
want to say out loud because it is
uncomfortable and it is true.
This move takes money out of the
accounts that financial advisors are
frequently paid a percentage to manage.
Nobody has to be dishonest for that to
affect how often it gets mentioned. So
this one is yours to know. I am not a
lawyer, I am not an accountant, and I am
not your financial advisor. This is
educational and your situation is your
own. My name is Kevin. I read the rules
so you do not have to. If that is
useful, subscribe. Let me explain what
it actually is in about 90 seconds. It
is called a qualified charitable
distribution and it works like this.
Once you reach 70 and a half, you can
instruct the company holding your
individual retirement account to send
money directly to a charity. The money
goes from them to the charity. It never
touches your bank account and it never
touches your hands. And because of that,
it is excluded from your income
entirely, not deducted from it, excluded
before your income is even calculated.
And it counts toward the withdrawal you
were required to take anyway.
So, the forced withdrawal happens, the
requirement is satisfied, the charity
receives exactly what it would have
received, and the income never existed
as far as your return is concerned.
Now, let me explain why this is
dramatically better than writing a
check. Because this is the part that
surprises people and it is the reason
this matters even for small amounts.
Roughly nine out of 10 retirees take the
standard deduction rather than
itemizing. And if you take the standard
deduction, the check you write to your
church gives you no tax benefit at all.
None. Zero.
This is a completely different
mechanism. It does not care whether you
itemize, it never enters your income in
the first place. And that distinction
matters far more than it sounds because
of what your income controls.
Your income is the number that decides
how much of your Social Security becomes
taxable. It is the number Medicare reads
two years later to set your premium. It
is the number that determines whether
the additional deduction available to
people 65 and older starts phasing out.
And in many states, it is the starting
point for your state tax as well.
Lowering it does not just save you the
tax on that amount. It can pull you back
under thresholds that cost far more than
the amount itself. So, the same gift to
the same church in the same year does
two jobs when it goes through this door
and one job when it goes through your
checkbook. And now, let me kill the two
beliefs that stop people using it
because they are the reason this is so
underused. The first is that this is for
wealthy people giving away enormous
sums. It is the opposite. Somebody
living mostly on Social Security with a
modest retirement account benefits more
from keeping their income low than a
wealthy person does because they are the
ones sitting close to the thresholds
that decide whether their benefit gets
taxed. The second is that you have to
give a fortune for it to matter.
Also false.
A few hundred dollars routed this way
instead of by check lowers the number
that drives everything else.
And if you already give monthly, that
giving is already happening. The only
question is which door it goes through.
That is the whole point. This is not
about giving more. It is about the same
generosity taking a different route.
One more thing before the example
because it explains why this stays
hidden. Your giving in your retirement
account almost certainly live in two
different parts of your mind. The giving
comes out of the household money. It is
the envelope on Sunday, the standing
order, the check at the end of the year.
It sits with the electricity bill and
the groceries in your thinking.
The retirement account is something else
entirely. It is the long-term thing, the
serious thing, the one you do not touch
except when the rules make you.
Nothing about ordinary life ever
suggests those two things could be the
same transaction.
Nobody at the church has any reason to
raise it. Nobody at the custodian knows
you give. And the forced withdrawal
arrives as a piece of administration
rather than as a decision.
Let me tell you about a man I will call
Alton, 76 in Tennessee, retired from a
school district. He had given the same
amount to his church every month for 31
years out of his checking account
without ever thinking about it. And
every year he took his required
withdrawal in January because he liked
to have it done.
He had been eligible for this for six
years and had used it zero times because
the giving and the withdrawal were two
entirely separate things in his mind and
nobody had ever suggested they were
connected.
Six years of a withdrawal taxed in full
alongside six years of giving that
produced no tax benefit at all in a
household where the two amounts
overlapped considerably.
That is the reason I put together the
quiet rules.
It is at kevinexplains.shop.
There is a code on the screen now, so
hold your phone up to it or use the link
pinned at the top of the comments or the
one in the description below. It covers
the doors like this one that stays shut
only because nobody tells you they are
there in plain English with the exact
steps and the traps attached to each.
You have 7 days with it. If it does not
change something about what you do next,
send it back and we are done.
Alton gave the same money for 31 years.
For six of those years, it could have
been free and it was not because of
which account it left from.
And there is one more thing about that
comparison worth making concrete because
it is the piece that makes people
finally act. Think about a household
taking a required withdrawal of $12,000
a year who also gives 4,000 a year to
their church out of the checking
account. The ordinary way, all 12,000
lands as income.
The 4,000 of giving produces nothing at
tax time because they take the standard
deduction.
And that 12,000 of income is what the
social security calculation reads and
what Medicare will read in 2 years.
The other way, 4,000 goes directly to
the church and 8,000 comes to them.
The requirement is fully satisfied
because the 4,000 counts toward it.
The church receives exactly the same
amount on the same schedule
and only 8,000 ever appears as income.
Same household, same giving, same
church, same year.
A third of the income simply removed
from the calculation.
Now the rules and I want to go through
these carefully because getting any one
of them wrong does not reduce the
benefit. It destroys it entirely and you
find out the following spring.
The first is the age and it is more
precise than people expect. 70 and a
half. Not the year you turn 70, not the
year you turn 71, the actual half
birthday, 6 months to the day after your
70th. And here is something about that
age that has become genuinely valuable
and that almost nobody has noticed. The
age for this never changed. It is still
70 and a half. But the age at which
forced withdrawals begin was moved. It
is now 73 for most people and 75 for
anybody born in 1960 or later, which
means there is now a gap, a window of 2
and 1/2 years for some people and closer
to five for others, where you are old
enough to do this but not yet required
to take anything at all. And in that
window, every dollar you send this way
is a dollar permanently removed from the
account before the forced withdrawals
ever begin, which makes every future
required withdrawal smaller for the rest
of your life. So, if you are somewhere
between 70 and a half and the age your
withdrawals start and you give to
anything at all, you are standing in the
best version of this that exists.
The second rule is where the money comes
from. It has to be an individual
retirement account, a traditional one or
an inherited one if you yourself are old
enough, or an old workplace plan that
has already been rolled into an
individual account. It cannot come
directly from a workplace plan you still
have. If your money is sitting in an old
employer account, it has to be rolled
over first, and that rollover takes
weeks, which matters enormously if you
are watching this in December.
The third rule is who receives it, and
this is where people slip. It has to be
a qualified public charity, a church, a
school, a hospital, a food bank, a
veterans organization. It does not work
for a donor-advised fund, which is the
one that catches people who have been
advised well in other respects. It does
not work for a private foundation, and
it does not work for certain supporting
organizations.
So, if somebody has set you up with a
fund that you make grants out of over
time, that is a perfectly good
arrangement for other purposes and it
does not work for this. The fourth rule
is the one nobody mentions, and it is
the easiest way to lose the whole thing
without any idea you have done so.
You cannot receive anything in return,
anything at all. Not a ticket to the
fundraising dinner, not preferred
seating, not the tote bag, not a raffle
entry, not a round of golf at the
charity tournament, not membership
benefits. So, the gift has to be clean.
Nothing back, not even something
trivial. And this is why the
acknowledgement letter matters more than
people realize. You need a written
acknowledgement from the charity, and it
needs to state that you received no
goods or services in return. Get that
letter, keep it with your tax papers,
and make sure it says that sentence. If
the charity sends you something that
only thanks you, ask them for one that
includes it. Now, the timing. And this
is where I want to spend real time
because timing is what people actually
get wrong. The rule is that the first
dollars out of your account in a year
are what satisfy your required
withdrawal, which means if you take your
withdrawal in January, that requirement
is already satisfied by the time you get
around to the charity later in the year.
You can still do a charitable
distribution, and it is still excluded
from your income, which is good, but it
no longer replaces a withdrawal you
would have taken anyway because that
withdrawal already happened and was
already taxed. So, you have lost the
second half of the benefit for that year
permanently, and there is no way to
reverse it. The order is the entire
thing. Do the charitable distribution
first, early in the year, before you
touch the account for anything else.
And there is a second timing trap that
catches people specifically in December.
So, listen closely if you are watching
this late in the year.
Many custodians offer a checkbook
attached to the account, which lets you
write checks directly to charities. That
is convenient, and it is a legitimate
way to do this, but the transaction is
not complete when you write the check.
It is complete when the charity cashes
it. So, a check written on the 28th of
December posted to a small church that
processes its post in January does not
count for the year you meant it to. And
if it was supposed to satisfy your
required withdrawal for that year, you
have now missed the required withdrawal
entirely, which carries a penalty of its
own. So, if you are doing this in
December, do not use the checkbook.
Instruct the custodian to transfer
directly, and give yourself weeks rather
than days.
Better still, make this a thing you do
in the spring every year, and remove the
deadline from your life entirely.
Now, two provisions that almost nobody
outside the profession knows, and one of
them can quietly reduce or eliminate
your benefit without you ever seeing it.
The first applies to anybody still
working past 70 and 1/2. It used to be
that you could not contribute to a
traditional retirement account after
that age at all. That restriction was
removed, so somebody still earning can
contribute again.
But, there is a catch attached, and it
is severe. If you make deductible
contributions to a traditional account
after 70 and 1/2, those contributions
reduce the amount you can exclude
through this route, dollar for dollar.
And it is cumulative across all the
years, not year by year.
So, somebody who contributed $5,000 a
year for 3 years while still working
part-time has reduced their available
exclusion by $15,000
permanently, and it follows them. If
that describes you, that is a
conversation with a preparer about which
of the two is actually worth more in
your situation. And for a great many
people, it is the giving.
The second provision runs the other way,
and it is genuinely favorable, and it
applies to anybody who ever made
contributions they did not deduct.
Normally, when you take money out of a
traditional account that contains a mix
of taxed and untaxed money, every
withdrawal comes out as a proportional
blend. You cannot choose to take only
the taxed part. That rule frustrates
people constantly. This is the one place
that rule is reversed. A charitable
distribution is treated as coming from
the untaxed portion first. The part that
would have been fully taxable is the
part that goes out, which is exactly
what you would want, because the money
leaving is money that would have been
taxed at full rates and the already
taxed money stays behind for you.
Let me tell you about a woman I will
call Hedy, 79 in Iowa.
She had been doing this correctly for 4
years on advice from a friend and she
was pleased with herself.
Then one spring her preparer told her
she owed considerably more than
expected. What had happened was not her
fault. Her custodian's tax form reported
the distributions as ordinary
withdrawals, which is exactly what those
forms do. There is no box on that form
that says this went to a charity.
Her preparer, who was competent and
busy, entered the form as it was
written.
The money had gone to the charity
correctly. Every rule had been followed
and it was taxed anyway because the last
step, telling the preparer, had never
happened. Everything in this video is
written out in the quiet rules in the
order you would actually use it,
including the reporting step that Hedy
missed.
Scan the code on the screen or go to
kevinexplains.shop
or use the link at the top of the pinned
comment. 7 days to look it over and if
it does not earn its place, send it
back.
Hedy did everything right for 4 years
and paid tax on one of them because of a
conversation that never took place. So,
let me make that step explicit because
it is the one that gets missed most. The
form your custodian sends will show the
full amount as a distribution. It will
not identify any of it as charitable.
That is not an error and they are not
going to change it. It is on you or on
whoever prepares your return to report
the total distribution, then show that a
portion of it was not taxable and to
write the notation identifying it as a
charitable distribution beside it. Which
means you have to tell them. Say the
words.
I made a qualified charitable
distribution this year in this amount to
this organization and here is the
acknowledgement letter.
If you use software rather than a
preparer, look specifically for the
question about whether any of the
distribution went to charity. It is
there. It is easy to skip past. And
skipping it means paying tax on money
that was never supposed to be taxed.
And keep that acknowledgement letter
with the return. Not in a drawer
somewhere. With the return.
Now, a few smaller points that answer
the questions people always have. Each
spouse has their own limit and it comes
from their own account. So, a married
couple where both are old enough can do
this twice over, but the money has to
come from each person's own account. One
spouse cannot use the others. The annual
limit is generous. It runs well into six
figures per person and it rises a little
each year with inflation. So, the vast
majority of people will never approach
it. Check the current figure for the
year you are filing. There is a
once-in-a-lifetime option to direct a
portion of this into an arrangement that
pays you an income for life while
ultimately benefiting the charity.
It is capped at a much smaller amount.
It can only be done once and it is
genuinely complicated. I mention it only
so you know the tool exists and can ask
about it if you have a large account and
a real giving goal.
And your state may not treat this the
same way the federal rules do.
Most states start from your federal
income and so the benefit carries
through automatically, but not all of
them and a few have their own quirks.
That is a one-line question worth asking
your preparer.
Two more practical questions people
always ask and both are worth a minute.
The first is whether this has to be one
large gift or whether it can be spread
out. It can be spread out and for most
people that is the better way to do it.
If you already give monthly, the
arrangement can be set up so it
continues monthly straight from the
account and you simply stop giving from
your checking account. That is the
version I would encourage most people
toward because it removes the December
scramble entirely and it means the
requirement is being chipped away at all
year rather than dealt with in one
panic. The second question is what
happens if you give more than your the
amount, which a lot of people worry
about. Nothing bad happens. The excess
is still excluded from your income. It
simply exceeds what you were required to
take, which means you have removed more
from the account than the minimum, and
that is generally a good outcome rather
than a problem. What you cannot do is
carry an excess forward to satisfy next
year's requirement. Each year stands on
its own. Now, let me be honest about
when this is not the right move because
I would rather you trust the rest of it.
There are two situations where something
else beats it. The first is if you are
still itemizing, which some people do
because of large medical costs or a
mortgage.
If your charitable giving is already
producing a real deduction, the
advantage here is smaller, though the
effect on your income can still be worth
more than the deduction.
That is genuinely a numbers question
rather than a rule.
The second is if you own investments
outside your retirement accounts that
have grown substantially. Giving
appreciated shares directly to a charity
is its own powerful move. The charity
receives the full value, and you never
pay the tax on the gain that built up
inside them.
If you have a holding you have owned for
20 years that has quadrupled, that is
frequently the better thing to give.
So, the honest hierarchy for somebody
with both is roughly this.
Use appreciated shares for the giving
you are doing above and beyond, and use
this route for the giving that would
otherwise come out of your retirement
account anyway because that is where it
does the double job.
And there is a version of this I want to
raise for anybody being told to set up a
fund that they make grants out of over
time.
Those arrangements have real uses. They
let somebody bunch several years of
giving into one year for deduction
purposes and then distribute it slowly,
but they do not work for this. The money
has to reach an operating charity
directly. So, if you have been steered
toward one of those, and you are over 70
and a half and taking required
withdrawals, it is worth asking whether
it is actually serving you because it
may be closing this door for the money
that goes into it.
Here is your list. Six things, and the
first one takes a phone call. One,
confirm your exact date. Six months
after your 70th birthday to the day,
write it down.
Two, if you have not yet taken this
year's required withdrawal, do not take
it until this is arranged. The first
dollars out are the ones that satisfy
the requirement, and once they have left
as an ordinary withdrawal, that
opportunity is gone for the year.
Three,
telephone whoever holds your account and
ask for their charitable distribution
form.
Ask specifically for a direct transfer,
rather than a checkbook, if there is any
chance of doing this late in the year.
Four, confirm the recipient is an
ordinary operating charity, not a fund
you grant out of, and not a private
foundation. And take nothing in return,
no dinner, no tickets, no tote bag.
Five, get the acknowledgement letter and
make sure it says you received no goods
or services. Six,
tell your preparer in words that you did
this and how much. Their form will not
say it and they cannot see it. If any of
that landed close to home, all of it is
laid out in order in the quiet rules,
link pinned at the top of the comments.
And if you have a question about your
own situation, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read every one, my honest read. This
is one of the few provisions in the tax
code that I think is unambiguously good,
and it is one of the most underused
things in American retirement. It costs
the person using it nothing. It requires
no aggressive planning and no clever
structure.
The charity receives exactly what it
would have received anyway, and the only
thing that changes is which door the
money leaves by.
And yet, the take-up is a small fraction
of the people who could use it. And some
of it, I think, is simpler than either
of those.
Most people do not think of their giving
and their retirement account as related
to each other at all.
The giving is something they do out of
the checking account, from the household
money, the way they always have.
The retirement account is a separate
thing in a separate part of the mind.
Nobody ever suggested those two things
could be the same transaction, so they
never were.
Last thought, if you already give to
something and you are over 70 and a
half, and you have a retirement account,
then a portion of the tax you paid last
year was voluntary, not avoidable
through anything clever. Voluntary in
the sense that the same money going the
same place through a different route
would not have been taxed at all.
That is a difficult sentence, and I do
not say it to make anybody feel foolish.
Nobody told you.
That is the entire subject of this
channel.
But it means the fix is available this
year. It takes one phone call, and the
only thing that closes it is taking your
withdrawal before you make the call.
So, make the call first. That is the
whole thing.
I am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: 5 Things Retirees Buy That Cost Double

segments.text: Nothing you buy in retirement costs what
the tag says and the difference does not
show up for two years. That is the whole
problem in one sentence. When you were
working, a purchase costs what it cost.
You paid, you took it home, and that was
the end of the transaction. That is no
longer how it works. Now, a large
purchase sends bills to you on four
different schedules, and only the first
one arrives at the register. The second
arrives the following April on your tax
return. The third arrives the April
after that in the form of a piece of
your own social security becoming
taxable. And the fourth arrives two full
years later in a Medicare letter, at
which point nobody on earth connects it
to the boat. And for some of these,
there is a fifth bill that does not
arrive for a decade when you go to sell
the thing and discover it was never
protected the way you assumed it was.
So, by the time you learn what something
cost, the money is spent, the thing is
bought, and every decision is locked,
which means the only defense is seeing
all four bills at the moment of the
decision before anything is signed. That
is what this video is for. Now, let me
clear up the belief that does the most
damage here because it is the reason
most people stop watching. This is not
about wealthy people buying yachts. The
retirees who get hit hardest by every
single one of these are the careful
ones, the savers. The couple who finally
felt secure enough to buy the thing they
had promised themselves for 30 years.
The person who paid cash because that
felt responsible. Not one of these traps
is triggered by wealth. Every one of
them is triggered by an ordinary
decision made without knowing a rule
existed. I am not a lawyer. I am not an
accountant and I am not your financial
adviser. This is educational and your
situation is your own. So confirm
anything here before you move a large
sum. My name is Kevin. I read the rules
so you do not have to. If that is
useful, subscribe. Let me start with the
first one and it is the one that breaks
the most hearts because people buy it
out of pure joy. The second home, the
cabin, the place near the water, the
condo somewhere warmer, the house near
the grandchildren. Here is what almost
everybody believes. that when you sell a
home, there is a large tax break that
protects the gain. That is true. When
you sell your main home, a couple can
exclude up to $500,000 of gain from tax
entirely and a single person up to
And that break does not apply to a
second home. It never has. A second home
is treated as an investment. Sell it for
more than you paid and the entire gain
is taxable with no shield of any kind.
So, the cabin bought for 200,000 that is
now worth $350 carries $150,000 of fully
exposed gain. At the rate that applies
to most retirees, that is over $20,000
in tax. And if it stacks high enough on
your other income, more than that. And
here is the part that makes it sting.
You watch that number climb for years
and felt wealthier every time. In tax
terms, what was actually growing was a
liability, and nobody ever said so. Now,
people hear this and reach for the
obvious solution, which is to move into
it and make it their main home before
selling. And that does help, but it does
not work the way people assume. And this
is the detail almost nobody covers. You
cannot simply move in for 2 years and
wipe out the whole gain. The rules
divide the time you owned it into the
period when it was your main home and
the period when it was not. And the
share of the gain that corresponds to
the years it was a second home generally
stays taxable proportionally even after
you move in. So somebody who owned a
cabin for 16 years and then lived in it
for two does not get the full break.
They get a fraction of it roughly
matching the fraction of time it was
actually their home. That surprises
people badly because the advice to move
in first is given constantly and the
proration almost never is. What does
genuinely help is records. Every
improvement you ever made to that
property raises what it counts as having
cost you and reduces the taxable gain.
The new roof, the deck, the well, the
addition. Keep every receipt for as long
as you own it because that shoe box is
worth real money at the moment of sale
and reconstructing it later is
impossible. The second purchase is the
one that feels most like a reward and it
is the recreational vehicle, the boat or
the second car. The tax problem here has
two halves and most people know neither.
The first half is how it gets paid for
and I will come back to that properly
because it applies to everything in this
video. The second half is what happens
on the other end, and it is genuinely
one-sided. These things lose value and
quickly. Most of them are worth
substantially less the day after you buy
them and continue falling from there.
Now, if that were an investment, a loss
would at least be useful at tax time. It
is not. A loss on personal property, a
boat, a motor home, a car is not
deductible at all. So, the arrangement
runs entirely one direction. If you pull
money from a retirement account to buy
it, every dollar of that withdrawal is
taxable income to you. And when the
thing loses half its value, you get
nothing back. Taxed on the way in and no
relief on the way out. But I do not want
to leave that section without giving you
the two things that genuinely help
because both exist and both are missed
constantly. The first is that a
recreational vehicle or a boat can
qualify as a second home for the
purposes of deducting loan interest,
provided it has sleeping quarters,
cooking facilities, and a toilet. A
great many of them do, which means
somebody who finances part of it may be
able to deduct the interest in a way
they never expected, and that changes
the arithmetic of whether to pay cash.
The second is that in the year you make
a very large purchase, you may be better
off deducting the sales tax you paid
rather than state income tax if you
itemize. On a large motor home or boat,
that single choice can be worth a
meaningful amount, and it only applies
in the year of the purchase. Both of
those are things a tax preparer should
catch and frequently does not because
nobody tells them there was a large
purchase. Let me tell you about a man I
will call Marvin, 72, in Michigan. He
bought a motor home for $90,000 and paid
cash from his retirement account because
he had spent his whole life avoiding
debt and it felt like the right thing.
That 90,000 became $90,000 of income on
his return that year. He sold it four
years later for a little over 40. So he
paid tax on 90,000, watched the thing
fall to less than half, and received
nothing back for the loss. and he never
once considered financing part of it
because a loan felt irresponsible and
cash felt careful. That is the reason I
put together the quiet rules. It is at
kevin explains.shop.
There is a code on the screen now, so
hold your phone up to it or use the link
pinned at the top of the comments or the
one in the description below. It covers
what these decisions actually cost in
plain English with the questions to ask
before the money moves rather than
after. You have seven days with it. If
it does not change something about what
you do next, send it back and we are
done. Marvin did the responsible thing
according to everything he was ever
taught and it was the most expensive
route available to him. The third
purchase is the annuity and this one is
different from the others because it is
sold to you rather than chosen by you.
The pattern is consistent. Somebody
approaches a retiree around the time
they stop working and offers safety and
guaranteed payments. A large sum goes
in. For a while, it feels reassuring.
Then something changes. An emergency, a
health event, or simply the realization
that the terms were not what was
understood, and they try to get their
money back. That is where two separate
costs land at once. The first is the
surrender charge. Most of these lock
your money up for a number of years,
commonly 6 to 8. and taking it out early
triggers a charge that often starts
around 7% and steps down by roughly a
point each year until it disappears. So
pulling $50,000 out in the early years
can cost several thousand that goes to
the company and never comes back to you.
The second is the tax. And here is the
detail that catches everybody which
almost no video explains. When you take
money out of an annuity bought with
ordinary savings, the earnings come out
first, not the money you put in the
growth. That ordering is deliberate and
it means the most heavily taxed portion
is the first portion you touch. And it
is taxed as ordinary income at the same
rates as a paycheck, not at the gentler
rates that apply to investments. So
somebody who put in 100,000 and watched
it grow to 120 who takes out 20,000 is
taking out the entire 20,000 of growth
and paying full income tax rates on all
of it. And if that annuity was funded
with money from a traditional retirement
account, it is worse because then every
dollar coming out is taxable, not just
the growth. And if you are under 59 and
a half, there is an additional penalty
on top. Now, the thing almost nobody is
told, which is genuinely useful if you
already own one. If your complaint is
with the product rather than needing the
cash, you can generally move from one
annuity to another without triggering
tax at all through a specific type of
exchange. The tax is deferred and the
transfer is direct between companies.
That does not avoid the surrender
charge, which is a contract term rather
than a tax rule. But it means somebody
stuck in a poor product is not forced to
choose between staying and paying income
tax on everything. And if you are being
offered one right now, there is exactly
one question to ask out loud and to get
the answer to in writing. What will it
cost me in charges and in taxes if I
need my money back in year three? A good
agent will answer that plainly. Anybody
who moves past it quickly has told you
what you needed to know. The fourth is
not a purchase at all, which is why it
slips past people. It is a decision not
to sell. Somebody is moving to be nearer
family to somewhere smaller, somewhere
warmer, and instead of selling the house
they have lived in for 30 years,
somebody suggests renting it out. Keep
the asset, earn some income. That advice
sounds prudent and it can quietly
destroy the most valuable tax break a
homeowner ever gets. That exclusion I
described earlier, the $500,000 for a
couple requires that the home was your
main residence for at least two of the 5
years before you sell. The moment you
move out, a clock starts. Let me walk it
because the speed surprises everybody.
First year of renting, you have lived
there four of the last 5 years. Fine.
Second year, three of five. Fine. third
year, two of five, and you are exactly
at the edge. Cross into a fourth year,
and you have lived there one of the last
five, and the exclusion is gone
entirely. So, there is roughly a
three-year window after moving out. And
after that, a break worth potentially
$100,000 or more simply evaporates, and
almost nobody renting out the old family
home knows that clock is running. Then
there is a second cost layered
underneath it, and this one is genuinely
unfair. Every year you rent a property,
the tax code expects you to claim
depreciation. When you sell, all of that
depreciation is taxed back at a rate
that can reach 25%. And here is the
phrase that matters. It is taxed back
whether or not you actually claimed it.
So somebody who rented out the old house
for 6 years, never bothered with the
depreciation deduction because it seemed
like paperwork, still owes the tax on it
when they sell. They gave up the benefit
and kept the bill. Which means if you
are going to rent, claim it. You are
paying for it either way. The whole
thing is the crulest version of good
advice in this video. Hold the asset,
earn the income. Nobody attaches a
calendar to that sentence, and the
calendar is the entire point. And there
is one more thing about renting it out
that people discover far too late, which
is what it does to the house itself as
an inheritance. If you keep the property
until death, whoever inherits it
receives it valued at that date. And
every dollar of gain that built up
across 30 years simply disappears for
tax purposes. That is enormously
valuable and it applies whether it was a
rental or not. So the choice is not
really rent it or sell it. It is three
choices. Sell it now while the break is
intact. Rent it briefly and sell inside
the window or keep it permanently and
leave it. In which case the gain is
wiped clean at the end and the rental
years were paid for by the rent. What
does not work is the middle path most
people fall into by accident, which is
renting it for 6 or 8 years, losing the
break, and then selling because the
upkeep became too much. That is the
version that costs the most, and it is
the version nobody chooses deliberately.
It is the one that happens when there
was never a decision at all. The fifth
is the one nobody in this genre ever
covers, and I think it is the most
regretted purchase in American
retirement, the time share. And I want
to be careful here because plenty of
people genuinely enjoy theirs and use it
every year. And I am not going to tell
those people they made a mistake. The
problem is not the weeks, it is the
exit. A time share is one of the very
few things you can buy that has almost
no resale market. Many of them sell for
nothing. And I mean that literally.
People give them away and struggle to
find takers. And the reason is the
maintenance fee which continues every
year regardless of whether you use it
which rises every year and which is a
permanent obligation attached to the
deed rather than to your enjoyment of
it. So somebody in their 70s who no
longer travels is paying an annual fee
forever for something they cannot sell
and cannot easily give away. And that
obligation does not end when you do. It
can pass to your estate and in some
circumstances to your children. which is
why families sometimes discover after a
death that they have inherited an annual
bill attached to a week in a place none
of them want to go. There is a route out
of that one and it is worth knowing. A
beneficiary is generally not obliged to
accept an inheritance. There is a formal
process for refusing it and it has
strict requirements and deadlines and it
is exactly the sort of thing to raise
with an attorney rather than to attempt
from a video. Now the tax side briefly
because it follows the same pattern as
everything else here. Sell a time share
at a loss which is the usual outcome and
that loss is not deductible because it
is personal use property. Sell one at a
gain which almost never happens and the
gain is taxable. One Direction again and
the maintenance fees are not deductible
either in the ordinary case. But the
reason I have put this in the video is
not the tax. It is what has grown up
around it. There is an entire industry
selling time share exit services and it
is aimed with precision at people your
age. The advertising runs on the same
stations at the same hours as everything
else aimed at retirees. The shape is
consistent. A large upfront fee, often
several thousand, and a promise to get
you out. And a meaningful share of those
companies take the fee and do very
little. And some have been shut down by
regulators for exactly that. So here is
the rule. Before you pay anybody a fee
to exit a time share, telephone the
resort directly and ask about their own
exit or deedback program. Many of them
have one. A great many people do not
know it exists, and it frequently costs
nothing or very little. Ask the company
that sold it to you before you pay a
stranger to negotiate with them. Let me
tell you about a woman I will call Dia,
69, in Arizona, widowed. She and her
husband had bought a time share in the
'90s and used it happily for 20 years.
After he died, she stopped traveling,
and the fee kept arriving every January,
and it had roughly doubled since they
bought it. She paid a company nearly
$4,000 to get her out of it. 14 months
later, she was still paying the annual
fee, and the company had stopped
returning her calls. The resort had a
deedback program the entire time. She
found out from another owner in a queue
at a pharmacy. Everything in this video
is written out in the quiet rules in the
order you would actually use it with
what each of these actually costs and
what to ask before you sign. Scan the
code on the screen or go to
kevinexplains.shop
or use the link at the top of the pinned
comment. 7 days to look it over and if
it does not earn its place, send it
back. Dileia paid $4,000 to be told
about something the company she already
owned from would have done for nothing.
Now, one more that belongs here because
it comes attached to a purchase and it
catches an enormous number of people
every year. Buying a place in another
state. A great many retirees end up with
two homes in two states or move to a
state with no income tax and keep a
property behind them. And what almost
nobody thinks about is which state
considers them a resident because states
do think about it and some of them think
about it very carefully. Moving to a
state with no income tax does not make
you a resident of it. What makes you a
resident is a combination of where you
actually live, how many days you spend
where, and where your life is genuinely
centered. And several states are known
for examining that closely when somebody
with meaningful income claims to have
left. They look at where you registered
to vote, where your license was issued,
where your doctors are, where your bank
accounts sit, where your possessions
are, and how many days you were
physically present. So the retiree who
spends half the year in each place,
keeps a house behind them, keeps their
doctors, keeps their voter registration,
and files as a resident of the low tax
state is in a genuinely weak position if
anybody looks. And the consequence is
not small. It can mean owing income tax
to a state you thought you had left for
years with interest. If you are going to
split time between two states, the move
is to actually make the change rather
than to claim it. license, registration,
voting, accounts, doctors, and the mail.
And keep a record of the days because in
a dispute, the burden of proving where
you were tends to land on you. That is
not a tax trick. It is simply doing
properly the thing most people do
halfway. Now, let me deal with the thing
that sits underneath four of those five,
which is where the money comes from. I
have covered the full chain on this
channel before, and I am not going to
repeat it thinly. So, here is the short
version. Money pulled from a traditional
retirement account is ordinary income.
That income can push you into a higher
bracket can pull more of your social
security into the taxable column and can
raise your Medicare premium 2 years
later. And that Medicare threshold is a
cliff rather than a slope. So $1 over
cost you the entire step. Money from a
Roth does none of that. Money from
ordinary savings you already paid tax on
does none of that. So, the same purchase
at the same price from the same shop can
cost thousands of dollars more depending
purely on which account the payment came
out of. Nobody at the dealership will
ever mention it because it was never
their job and it is not on the sticker.
The single most useful question before
any large purchase is this. Where is
this money coming from? And what does
pulling it trigger? And one thing about
that ordering that is worth saying
plainly because people get it backwards.
The instinct is to spend from savings
last and to protect the retirement
account. That instinct came from the
accumulation years and it is frequently
wrong. Now, ordinary savings that you
have already paid tax on are the
cheapest dollars you own because
spending them creates no income at all.
The Roth is the most valuable and should
generally be spent last because it grows
and comes out clean and passes cleanest
of everything you have. And the
traditional account sits in between. And
the goal there is not to avoid it
entirely, but to draw from it
deliberately in measured amounts in
years you choose. Which means for a
large purchase, the ordinary answer is
to reach for taxed savings first, then a
measured amount from the traditional
account if needed, and to leave the Roth
alone unless there is a specific reason.
Almost everybody does it in exactly the
opposite order because the traditional
account is the biggest number on the
page. Now, let me give you three things
that genuinely help. And the first one
is the most underused opportunity in
retirement. There is a rate of tax on
long-term investment gains that a great
many retirees have never heard of, and
it is zero. If your taxable income sits
below a certain level, and for a married
couple, that level is considerably
higher than people expect. Long-term
gains are taxed at nothing at all, not
reduced, zero. which matters enormously
here because it means somebody in a
lowinccome year before social security
has started and before forced
withdrawals begin may be able to sell an
appreciated investment and pay no
federal tax on the gain whatsoever. So
the retiree funding a purchase from a
brokerage account in a quiet year may be
in a completely different position from
the one they assume and it is worth
finding out before reaching for the
retirement account instead. The second
is timing and it is free. If a large
purchase is coming and the money has to
come from a taxable source, splitting it
across two calendar years rather than
one is frequently the difference between
staying inside a bracket and crossing it
and between staying under a Medicare
threshold and going over. December and
January are 11 days apart and can be in
different tax years. That is a lever
nobody uses. And the third is the one
that feels wrong and is often right.
Financing part of a large purchase can
be cheaper than paying cash. That is
genuinely counterintuitive and it goes
against everything most people your age
were taught. But run the comparison
properly. If pulling $90,000 in one year
would push you into a higher bracket,
expose more of your benefit, and trip a
Medicare threshold, the total of those
three can exceed the interest on a
modest loan spread over a few years. I
am not telling anybody to take on debt
for a toy. I am telling you that paying
cash is not automatically the cheapest
option once tax is counted. And the
assumption that it always is has cost a
lot of careful people a great deal. Here
is your list. Six things. One, before
any large purchase, trace the money back
to its source and ask what pulling it
triggers. That question alone prevents
four of the five regrets in this video.
Two, never let one purchase create one
enormous taxable year. Split it across
two if you can. Three, ask the exit
question at the entrance, not the exit.
for anything you are buying. What
happens tax-wise when I sell this, cash
it in, or leave it to somebody? A second
home, an annuity, a rental, and a time
share all have an exit cost, and the
time to learn it is before you sign.
Four, if you are thinking of renting out
the family home rather than selling it,
understand that a break potentially
worth six figures expires roughly 3
years after you move out and that
depreciation is taxed back whether you
claimed it or not. Five, if you own a
time share you no longer want, telephone
the resort about their own exit program
before you pay any company a fee. Six,
if you split time between two states,
actually make the move rather than
claiming it and keep a record of the
days. If any of that landed close to
home, all of it is laid out in order in
the quiet rules link pinned at the top
of the comments. And if you have a
question about your own situation, write
to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read everyone, my honest read. Every
person in the chain of a large purchase
is paid before the tax bill is printed.
The dealership is paid the day you drive
away. The agent selling the annuity is
paid the day you sign. The estate agent
is paid at the closing table. The time
share company was paid decades ago.
Every one of them has completed their
job and collected before the first of
the four bills in this video has even
been calculated. So there is nobody in
that entire chain whose role is to stop
and say, "Wait, here is what this
actually costs you in 2 years. That
person does not exist unless you become
that person or you pay somebody whose
only job is your numbers." And the
reason this catches careful people
specifically is that every instinct they
were raised with points the wrong way
here. Pay cash. Avoid debt, hold the
asset, do not sell. Every one of those
is good general advice, and every one of
them is the expensive choice in at least
one section of this video. The tax code
does not reward the instinct. It rewards
knowing the rule. Last thought, the
price on the tag is a down payment on
the real cost. The rest arrives on a
schedule nobody shows you from four
different directions over two years,
long after the excitement has faded and
every decision is locked. And the only
place any of it can be changed is at the
beginning in the 10 minutes before you
sign when the only thing standing
between you and the full price is a
question nobody thinks to ask. So ask
it, where is this money coming from?
What is that trigger? And what does it
cost me to get out of this later? Three
questions before the pen moves. That is
the whole defense. I am Kevin. Thanks
for watching. Do not forget to check the
quiet rules at kevinexplains.shop.

title: Every Senior Must Open This Before September 30 Or Pay All Year

segments.text: There is an envelope arriving at your
house this month that decides what you
pay for your health care for the whole
of next year. It is not a bill. It is
not an advertisement. It is required by
law to be in your hands by the 30th of
September. And it is the single most
expensive piece of post you will receive
all year. Most people throw it away. It
is thick. It is gray. It looks like the
sort of thing insurers send constantly.
And it arrives in a month when nothing
feels urgent. And here is what makes
that so costly. If you do nothing about
what is inside it, everything in it
happens to you automatically on the 1st
of January. And you are locked in for 12
months. Not until you notice. Not until
you complain. 12 months. Your premium
can rise. Your deductible can rise. What
you pay at the pharmacy counter can
change completely. A medication you have
taken for 9 years can be removed from
the list your plan covers or moved to a
tier that costs several times more or
given a new requirement that makes you
get permission before they will pay for
it. And your doctor can be gone from
your network entirely which you will
discover at the front desk in February.
Every one of those is disclosed in that
envelope in advance in writing. None of
it happens without notice. The notice
simply arrives in a form that almost
nobody reads. So, this video is about
the seven weeks that decide your next
year. What actually has to happen in
each of them and the doors that close
permanently at the end of it. And there
is one door in here that closes for good
that most people do not know exists. And
that decides whether you can ever go
back to a different kind of coverage for
the rest of your life. I will get to
that one and it is the most important
thing in this video. I am not an
insurance agent. I do not sell any plan
and I have nothing to gain from what you
choose. This is educational. Plans vary
enormously and you confirm your own
situation before acting. My name is
Kevin. I read the rules so you do not
have to. If that is useful, subscribe.
And I want to be clear about who this
reaches because a lot of people assume
it is somebody else's problem. If you
have a drug plan, this is you. If you
have a bundled plan through a private
insurer, this is you. If you have a
supplement, parts of this are you. The
only people for whom none of it applies
are those on original Medicare with no
drug coverage at all. And that is a
small group and most of them are in that
position by accident rather than by
choice. So if you are on Medicare in any
form, an envelope is coming or has
already come and the changes in it apply
to you on the 1st of January, whether
you read it or not. Let me start with
what is actually in the envelope because
knowing what to look for turns 40 pages
into about 10 minutes. The document is
called the annual notice of change.
Every plan has to send one and it has to
reach you by the end of September. Its
entire purpose is to compare next year
against this year. What it costs now,
what it will cost, and what is
different. And there are exactly five
things in it that matter. Everything
else is legally required padding. The
first is your premium, what you pay
every month. The second is your
deductible and any change to what you
pay when you actually use the plan. your
co-ayment at the doctor, at the
specialist, at the hospital. The third
is the drug list, which medications the
plan covers next year and at what tier.
