The fourth is the network, which doctors
and which hospitals are in it. And the
fifth, if you are in a plan that bundles
everything together, is the maximum you
can be asked to pay out of pocket in a
year. Five things. If you find those
five and compare them against this year,
you have done the work and you have done
more than the great majority of people
receiving that envelope. Now, let me
explain the default because the default
is the whole trap. If you read that
notice and do nothing, you are not
dropped and nothing lapses. You are
automatically enrolled in next year's
version of your plan with all of the
changes applied. That sounds convenient
and it is exactly what the system is
counting on because the plan that was
right for you in the year you chose it
may be a completely different product by
the time you have been in it four years
and at no point were you asked to agree
to any of it. People say they have been
in the same plan for 6 years. Frequently
they have not. They have been in six
versions of a plan each one slightly
different from the last and they agreed
to all of it by not opening an envelope.
Now let me go through the changes that
actually cost people money. Starting
with the one that catches the most, your
medications. Every plan has a list of
what it covers, and that list is
rewritten every year. And there are four
different things that can happen to a
drug you take. It can be removed
entirely, and then the plan does not pay
for it at all. It can be moved to a
higher tier, which is the most common
one, and the one nobody notices in
advance. Same drug, same pharmacy, same
prescription, and your share of the cost
goes up substantially because of which
shelf it now sits on. It can have a
requirement added called prior
authorization, which means the plan will
not pay until your doctor submits a
justification and it is approved. That
is not a refusal, but it is a delay and
it happens at the counter when you are
trying to collect a refill. Or it can
have step therapy added, which means the
plan requires you to try a cheaper
alternative first and to have that fail
before they will cover the one you are
on. That last one genuinely upsets
people, and I understand why. Somebody
stable on a medication for years can be
told they must try something else before
the plan will continue paying for what
is working. So when you look at that
notice, do not skim the drug section.
Take your actual list of prescriptions,
every one of them, and find each one.
That is the single highest value 10
minutes in this entire video. And if
something has changed, you are not stuck
with it. That is exactly what the next
seven weeks are for. Now, one thing
about that drug list that is worth
understanding before you panic about
anything in it. Plans are not allowed to
change the list however they like at any
moment. There are protections. Certain
categories of medication get extra
protection and midyear removals are
restricted with notice requirements
attached to them. So, the changes you
see in the September notice are the
changes for next year disclosed in
advance, which is the system working as
intended. The problem has never been
that they are hidden. it is that they
are disclosed in a format nobody reads.
And here is the practical point. Almost
every change in that document is
something you can respond to. A drug
move to a higher tier is not a sentence.
It is a reason to look at whether a
different plan covers it better. That is
the entire purpose of the weeks that
follow. The second change that costs
real money is the network. And this one
is harsher in some kinds of coverage
than others. If you are in a plan that
manages your care through a network, the
list of doctors and hospitals in that
network is rewritten every year too. And
it can also change during the year. So
the doctor you have seen for 11 years
can simply not be in it next year.
Nobody telephones you. It appears in the
notice and in the plan directory and you
find out at the front desk when somebody
says they no longer take that plan. And
the consequence depends entirely on what
kind of coverage you have. On original
Medicare, this issue barely exists. Any
provider who accepts Medicare accepts
you anywhere in the country and there is
no network to be in or out of. On a plan
that bundles everything together through
a private insurer, the network is the
product. Out of network can mean paying
substantially more or in some plan types
paying the entire cost yourself, which
is why the network section of that
notice matters as much as the price. A
cheaper premium with your specialist
removed is not cheaper. So take your
list of doctors, the ones you actually
see, including the specialist you only
see twice a year, and check everyone
against next year's directory, not this
year's, next year's. And a piece of
practical advice that saves people a
great deal of grief. Do not rely only on
the printed or online directory because
those are frequently out of date.
Telephone the practice directly and ask
whether they are contracted with that
specific plan for next year. The person
at the desk will know before the
directory does. Let me tell you about a
man I will call Lel, 74, in Ohio. He had
been in the same plan for 5 years and
had never once opened the September
envelope because it looked like the
other post from the same company. Two
things changed for the coming year. His
blood pressure medication moved to a
higher tier and the cardiologist he had
seen since his surgery left the network.
He found out about the medication in
January at the pharmacy and about the
cardiologist in March when the office
told him at check-in. By then, the
window to change anything had been
closed for 3 months. He spent the rest
of that year paying more for a drug and
traveling to a doctor he did not know
over an envelope on a hall table. That
is the reason I put together the quiet
rules. It is at kevinexplains.shop.
There is a code on the screen now, so
hold your phone up to it or use the link

it. If it does not change something
about what you do next, send it back and
we are done. Lel did not choose any of
what happened to him. He simply did not
open an envelope and the system treated
that as agreement. The third thing to
look at and this one is genuinely

the maximum you can be asked to pay in a

a cap. Once you have spent that amount

kind of coverage. But that number
changes every year and it can rise
substantially and it varies enormously
between plans in the same area. And here
is the comparison people never make.
Original Medicare on its own has no such

people who choose it also buy a

there is no ceiling on what a bad year

two options is not premium against
premium. It is what you pay every month
plus what you would pay in a genuinely
bad year against the same two numbers on
the alternative. A low premium with a
high ceiling is a bet and it is a bet
you make with your own health. Two more
things about how these plans actually
operate because the differences between
them matter more than the marketing
suggests. The first is the type of plan
and there are two main shapes. One
requires you to stay inside the network
and in many cases to get a referral from
a primary doctor before seeing a

a real friction and people underestimate

The other allows you to go outside the

flexibility, generally a higher premium.
Which one you have is written in the

knows which they are in. It is worth
knowing before you need something
urgently. The second is permission.
Plans that bundle everything are allowed
to require approval before covering
certain services. Scans, procedures,
hospital stays, care in a rehabilitation
facility. That is legal and it is a

often it applies and what to do when the

A denial is not final. You can appeal

would harm your health, which produces
an answer in a matter of days rather
than weeks. And appeals succeed far more

denials are overturned when somebody

to a denial is never to accept it

to ask for the expedited route if the

That is also when the full detailed
document for next year becomes
available, the long one that spells out

the summary. That one is the whole

ordinary route is gone until the

January everything you did or did not do
becomes real. And there is one more

more change once. You can move to a

for it. Everything I have described so

every autumn for the rest of your life.
There is one decision that is not. Here
it is. Moving from original Medicare

easy, and you can do it every year.
Moving back the other way is easy, too.

its own leaves you with no ceiling on

Once that period ended, in most states,
that protection ended with it. apply
after that and the insurer can ask about
your health, can charge you more, or can

what that means for somebody who chose a

reasonable choice that millions of
people make. At 76, their health has
changed. They are seeing more
specialists and they want to move to
original Medicare with a supplement so
they can see anyone anywhere. and they
may discover that the only reason they
want to switch their health is the exact
reason they can be turned down. That is
why I call it a one-way door. Not
because you cannot leave the plan. You
can leave any time because you may not
be able to buy the thing that makes the
alternative work. Now, there are
exceptions and they matter enormously.
So, listen for whether any of these is
you. The first is a trial right. If you
joined one of those bundled plans when
you first became eligible at 65 and it
is your first year in it, you generally
have 12 months to change your mind and
go back to original Medicare with a
guaranteed right to buy a supplement. No
health questions, 12 months from when
you joined. If you are inside that
window right now, you are holding a
right that expires and does not come
back. The second is if you dropped a
supplement to try one of these plans for
the first time. In that case, you can
generally return to the policy you had
or to a similar one within 12 months.
The third is if your plan leaves your
area or ends its contract. That triggers
protections, including in many cases a
right to buy a supplement. And the
fourth is your state. A handful of
states have decided this should not be a
one-way door and require insurers to
sell to anybody during certain periods,
regardless of health. If you live in one
of those, this section may not apply to
you at all. And that is worth knowing
rather than assuming. So the instruction
is this. If you have ever thought you
might want original Medicare with a
supplement at some point, find out now
what your state allows and whether any
trial right applies to you. Not in 5
years when the answer may be no. Now a
second window that hardly anybody knows
about and that is genuinely useful.
Plans are rated on a fivepoint scale. If
there is a plan in your area rated at
the top of that scale, you can switch
into it once during the year outside the
ordinary enrollment period from early
December right through the following
November. One switch to a top rated plan
almost any time of year. That is a real
escape hatch for somebody who ends up in
a plan that is not working and has
missed every other window. It depends
entirely on whether such a plan is
offered where you live and many areas do
not have one, but it costs nothing to
check and almost nobody does. Let me
tell you about a woman I will call
Karen, 71, in Florida, and she chose a
bundled plan at 65 because it cost her
almost nothing every month and she was
healthy. For 6 years, it was the right
choice and she was happy with it. Then
she was diagnosed with something that

them. She wanted to move to original
Medicare with a supplement. She applied,
was asked about her health, and was
declined. She said she had assumed that
because she could change plans every
year, she could always change back.
Nobody had ever told her that one of
those directions had a lock on it.
Everything in this video is written out

the exact questions to ask. Scan the
code on the screen or go to
kevinexplains.shop
or use the link at the top of the pinned
comment. seven days to look it over and
if it does not earn its place, send it
back. Karen was not misinformed. She
simply assumed a door that opened one
way opened both ways, which is what
almost everybody assumes. Now, let me
give you the practical part because
knowing there is a window is useless if
comparing options is impossible and most
people find it impossible. There is a
free official tool that does this
properly and a startling number of
people have never used it. You enter
your actual medications, the exact ones
with the doses. You enter the pharmacy
you actually use, and it produces a
total estimated cost for the year for
every plan available where you live.
That total is the number that matters,
not the premium. Because two plans with
an identical monthly premium can differ
by well over $1,000 a year once your
specific drugs are run through them. And
there is no way to see that from a
brochure. And the pharmacy matters more

preferredies.
Changing which shop you walk into can

Your real drug list, your real pharmacy,
the annual total, 20 minutes. And if

counselors who do exactly this with you.
They will sit with your drug list and

because this is the season for it. From

the advertising is relentless.
Television, post, telephone, and a great

here is what is actually true about how

It does mean the incentive exists and

And the scam version is straightforward

an agent you chose. Before that, two

great many people do not know it exists,

plans and your pharmacy tells you

exception request. If your plan does not

can ask for an exception. Your doctor

plan has to decide within a set period
with a fast track available when waiting
would cause harm. And if they say no,
that decision can be appealed further
through several levels eventually to an
independent body outside the plan
entirely. Those two together mean that a
drug being dropped from a list is a
problem to be solved rather than a wall.
Most people treat it as a wall because
nobody has ever told them there is a
process. Now, a few things worth
checking while you have the paperwork
out because they are adjacent and this
is the season when people are actually
looking at it. The first is the star
rating of your own plan. Every plan has

There is a subsidy for people with

Losing other coverage you had, including
employer coverage, your plan leaving
your area or ending its contract.
Entering or leaving a nursing facility,
qualifying for the assistance programs I
just mentioned. Each of those opens a
period during which you can change
regardless of the calendar. So, if
something significant changes in your
life, the question to ask is whether it

expensive mistake. That is a different
video and I have made it. The fourth is
your premium itself which is set
separately and announced in the autumn.
And if you are paying a search charge on

and it works. One more thing that is
worth saying plainly because it is the

and people are afraid to ask it. Neither

otherwise is selling something. The
bundled plans genuinely do include

cap what you can be asked to pay in a
year and for a great many people they
cost less every month. Those are real
advantages and I am not going to pretend
they are not. What you are trading for
that is flexibility. A network
permission requirements and the fact
that going back may not be available
later. Original Medicare with a
supplement is the reverse. Any provider
anywhere, no referrals, no permission
and predictability. and you pay for that

Which one fits depends on your health,
on how much you travel, on whether you
already have doctors you will not give
up, and on how much uncertainty you can
tolerate. The honest answer is that
people who are healthy and settled in
one place frequently do very well with a
bundled plan. And people with complex
health or strong attachments to
particular specialists frequently do
not. And the group that gets hurt is the
one that chooses on the premium alone
without knowing that one of those
directions has a lock on it. Now, let me
make this small because a list of 20
things is a list nobody starts.
Everything in this video comes down to
one afternoon. And it is genuinely one
afternoon. Find the envelope. If you
have already thrown it away, and a great
many of you have, you can get another
copy by teleoning the number on the back
of your card or by looking in your
account on the plan's website. Then
write down three lists on one sheet of
paper. Every medication you take with
the dose, every doctor you actually see,

what you paid this year in premium and
in deductible. That single sheet is the
entire preparation. With it, the
comparison takes 20 minutes either on
the official tool or with a free
counselor. Without it, nobody can help
you, including you. Here is your list.
Seven things. One, open the notice and
find the five things: premium,
deductible and co-ayments, drug list,
network, and the annual maximum.
Everything else in that document is
required padding. Two, check every one
of your medications against next year's

removals, tier changes, and new

Do not trust the directory.
Four, run your real drug list and your

Five, book a free appointment with your

Six, if you have ever thought you might
want original Medicare with a
supplement, find out now whether you are

Seven, do all of it before the 7th of

link pinned at the top of the comments.
And if you have a question about your

I read everyone that comes in. my honest
read. I do not think there is a villain
in this. The disclosure requirements are

Somebody living alone at 82 opening that

nothing in this video is a rule you have

segments.text: One sentence at a family table can cost
more than a bad decade in the market.
Somebody asks how retirement turned out.
You were honest and a little proud
because you earned the right to be and
you say a number out loud. What you
meant was after 40 years of careful
choices, we finally have enough to be at
peace.
What the room heard was something else
entirely. They heard that you are set,
that there is room, and that from now on
when money gets tight in this family,
this is who we call.
But the social part is not what this
video is about and it is not where the
real money goes. There is a second cost
sitting underneath every favor you will
be asked for and almost nobody has ever
explained it, including most people who
make videos on this subject. It is that
handing somebody $10,000 can cost you
16. Not through generosity, through the
machinery your money has to pass through
to get to them. And there is a third
thing further down that is worse than
the tax and it can arrive 15 years later
at the exact moment you need help
yourself. That is what I want to spend
this video on, not the awkward dinners,
the arithmetic. Let me start with what
your money actually is because this is
the misunderstanding everything else
grows out of. When somebody hears a
large number, they picture a pile,
something sitting there whole with a top
to it that pieces can be taken off
without changing what it is. That is not
what you have. What you have is an
engine. It is not there to be spent. It
is there to produce an income for the
rest of your life and the size of the
number determines the size of the income
and nothing else. The common guideline
is that you can draw somewhere around 4%
a year and have a reasonable chance of
it lasting.
On a million dollars, that is roughly
40,000 a year before tax. That is the
whole thing. That figure covers your
housing, your food, your medical costs,
your car, your travel, your emergencies,
and any generosity you actually plan
for.
So when somebody looks at your number
and sees an enormous cushion and you
look at the same number and see a modest
annual income you cannot increase, you
are both looking at the same figure and
seeing two completely different objects,
and theirs is the one that feels true in
the room.
Now, watch what small favors do to that
engine, because this is the part nobody
runs the numbers on. Not the dramatic
six-figure request. That one people can
see coming, and most of you would never
say yes to it. The small ones.
5,000 to help a child through a rough
stretch. 8,000 so somebody does not miss
an opportunity. Picking up the family
trip because you are retired now, and
you can swing it. Each one is kind. Each
one feels like an exception. Add 10,000
a year of those to a plan built on
40,000, and you have not added a quarter
to your spending. You've taken your
withdrawal rate from 4% to 5. Add a
trip, an emergency, and a tuition bill
on top, and you are at 6 or 7% without
ever once making a decision that felt
large. That is the difference between
money that lasts 30 years and money that
runs out while you still need it. And
nobody in the family will ever see the
line being crossed.
And here is the part that makes the
timing so much worse than it looks.
Money taken out early in retirement is
the most expensive money you will ever
spend, and there is a specific reason
for that, which has nothing to do with
discipline.
Your engine has to survive whatever the
market does in the first several years.
If those years are poor, and you are
also withdrawing, you are selling into
weakness and permanently reducing what
is left to recover. People who study
this call it sequence risk, and it is
why two people with identical savings
and identical spending can end up in
completely different places based purely
on which decade they retired into. Which
means a dollar given away at 63 is not a
dollar. It is everything that dollar
would have become by the time you are
83, and it is being taken out at the
moment your plan is most fragile. A
market crash announces itself. This
never does. It simply narrows quietly,
one kind gesture at a time, in exactly
the years when narrowing costs the most.
And there is a second thing eating that
engine that nobody at the table is

they did not choose. There are two more
pieces of the 65 decision that carry
their own permanent consequences and
both are widely missed. The first is
drug coverage which has its own separate
penalty with its own separate rules. If
you go without creditable drug coverage
and enroll later, there is a permanent
increase to that premium too calculated
by the month rather than the year. And
here is the trap. Employer coverage is
usually creditable but not always. and
the employer is required to tell you in
writing once a year whether it is. That
notice arrives in the autumn, looks like
junk, and gets thrown away by almost
everybody. Keep it. It is the only proof
you have that you were covered, and it
is what protects you from that penalty
later. The second is larger, and it is a
one-time window that closes permanently.
When you first enroll at 65, there is a
six-month period during which you can
buy a supplemental policy with no
medical underwriting at all. They cannot
refuse you and they cannot charge you
more because of your health history.
Once that window closes, in most states,
that protection is gone. Apply later and
you can be asked about your health,
charged more, or declined outright. So,
somebody who chooses a different
arrangement at 65 entirely reasonably,
and then wants to switch at 73 after a
diagnosis may find the door has been
shut for 8 years without anybody
mentioning it. A handful of states have
rules that keep it open. Most do not,
which makes the choice at 65
considerably more consequential than it
appears at the time because one of the
two paths is reversible and the other
largely is not. Let me tell you about a
man I will call EMTT, 67, in Wisconsin,
still working 3 days a week at the firm
he had been at for 31 years with a
health plan he was happy with and a
company well over the 20 employee line.
He signed up at 65 because everybody
told him he had to. Nobody asked him a
single question about whether he was
covered because nobody was asking
questions by then. He paid a premium
every month for two years for coverage
that sat behind a plan already paying
his bills. He found out from a
conversation at a lunch counter, which
is where a great many people in this
country now find out things that used to
be explained to them at a desk. That is
the reason I put together the quiet
rules. It is at kevinexplains.shop.
There is a code on the screen now, so
hold your phone up to it or use the link
pinned at the top of the comments or the
one in the description below. It covers
the rules that quietly decide what
happens to your money in plain English
with the questions to ask before a
decision is made rather than after. You
have 7 days with it. If it does not
change something about what you do next,
send it back and we are done. EMTT did
not lose that money to a scam or a
market. He lost it because the question
nobody asked him used to be somebody's
job. There is one more thing about that
65 decision that is worth 30 seconds
because people ask about it constantly.
If you are still working past 65 and
covered at work, you can generally take
the hospital part which has no premium
for most people and delay the part that
costs money. That is what a great many
people do and it is usually reasonable.
The exception is the health savings
account because taking any part of
Medicare ends your ability to
contribute. So somebody still working,
still building that account may want to
delay everything rather than take the
free portion and somebody not
contributing to one has no reason to
delay it. That is the whole decision and
it turns entirely on one question about
one account which is exactly the sort of
question that used to get asked across a
desk. The second threat is not being
able to reach anybody at all. And I want
to be practical about it rather than
just complain because there are routes
that work and most people have never
been told about them. Here's what
changed on the phones. The systems that
answer now are conversational. You state
your problem out loud and it routes you.
And they genuinely do answer faster than
a human cue ever did. The difficulty is
that they route on keywords rather than
on what you actually mean. So, somebody
calling about an overpayment can find
themselves being told about voluntary
tax withholding because a word in their
sentence match something else. And there
is a call back option which sounds like
a solution and creates a specific
problem. You are offered a call back
rather than holding. Some people never
receive it. And in terms of how
performance is measured, that call was
answered promptly with almost no weight,
so it counts as a success. That is the
gap between the reported figures and the
experience. Both are real. So, here are
the routes that actually work in the
order I would use them. The first is to
do it in writing, in person, at a local
office with an appointment. Slower to
arrange and vastly more likely to end in
a resolution because a person is looking
at your file. Appointments can be booked
and the wait is often weeks, which is
why you book it now rather than when it
becomes urgent. The second is to know
that when you do reach somebody, the
first person is not always the right
person. These offices are large.
Different things are handled by
different areas and the person who picks
up may simply not handle your issue. Ask
politely who does and ask to be
transferred rather than accepting the
first answer. And the third is the one
almost nobody uses and it is the most
effective thing in this entire section.
Your representative in Congress has case
workers whose actual job is helping
constituents with federal agencies. Not
policy, casework. somebody with a direct
line into the agency who makes inquiries
on behalf of the people in that
district. It is free. It is a service
you already pay for and it is used
mostly by people who happen to know it
exists. You call the district office,
not the Washington one, and you say you
are a constituent with a problem
involving a federal agency and you would
like to speak to a caseworker. There is
a privacy release form to sign that
allows them to look at your file and
then somebody who deals with that agency
every week starts asking on your behalf.
For a genuinely stuck case, a claim
sitting for months, an appeal going
nowhere, an overpayment nobody will
explain, that is the single most
powerful thing available to an ordinary
person and it costs nothing. Write that
down. District office, caseworker,
constituent services. And there is one
thing about acting on somebody else's
behalf that almost every family in this
country gets wrong. So I am going to be
very direct about it. A durable power of
attorney does not work with this agency.
Read that again because people build
entire plans around a document that has
no authority here. You can hold a
properly drafted power of attorney
signed, notorized, accepted by every
bank and every hospital and that agency
will not recognize it for managing
benefits. It is not a mistake by the
person on the phone. It is their stated
policy. What they use instead is a
representative payee. Somebody formally
appointed by the agency to receive and
manage the payments on behalf of a
person who cannot manage them with an
application and a review. So the common
situation is a son or daughter holding a
power of attorney, discovering a problem
with a parents benefit, calling to sort
it out, and being told politely that
nothing can be discussed with them at
all. And by the time that is discovered,
the parent is frequently no longer able
to participate in appointing anybody.
There is a solution that takes 15
minutes and that almost nobody has heard
of. You can name in advance up to three
people you would want appointed as your
payee if it ever became necessary. It is
called advanced designation. You do it
yourself while you are entirely capable
and it costs nothing. It does not give
anybody authority now. It does not let
them touch anything. It simply records
your choice. so that if the day ever
comes, the agency starts from the name
you picked rather than from whoever
turns up. For anybody with a spouse or
children who might one day need to help,
that is 15 minutes that prevents a
genuinely awful few months. The third
threat is getting into your own account.
And this one is going to get harder
rather than easier. So, I want you ahead
of it. Online accounts with the agency
now require identity verification
through a separate service. And that
process asks for a government
identification document, sometimes a
photograph of your face. And it is
genuinely difficult for a lot of people,
particularly for anybody whose document
has an old address or whose name changed
at marriage and was never updated
consistently or who simply does not have
a smartphone that can take the
photograph. That verification is not
going away. It is tightening because the
pressure driving it is real. There are
automated attempts to break into these
systems constantly and the agency is
defending against them and every layer
of defense lands on you as well as on
the attacker. So the instruction is
straightforward. If you do not have an
account set up, set it up now. While you
have the capacity and the patience to
work through the verification, not in
the year you need it urgently. And once
you have one, use it. It shows your
earnings record, your estimates, and the
notices sent to you. which means a
letter that went to an old address is
still visible to you if you look. Now,
the specific danger underneath this and
it is the one that ends the worst.
Somebody filing on your record. If a
person has enough of your information,
they can attempt to claim benefits in
your name and redirect the payment. That
is not hypothetical. It is a known
category of fraud and it is a nightmare
to unwind because you are then arguing
about your own identity with an agency
that has already paid somebody. There is
a protection for this that hardly
anybody knows about. So listen closely.
You can ask the agency to block
electronic access to your record
entirely. That means no changes online,
no changes by telephone, not by anybody,
including you. Any change to your direct
deposit or your address has to be made
in person with identification at an
office. It is inconvenient by design.
That is the point. For somebody who is
settled, whose payment goes to the same
account it has gone to for a decade,
that inconvenience costs nothing and
closes the door completely. You request
it by contacting the agency and asking
to block electronic access to your
record. And you can lift it later if you
need to in person. For a great many
people watching this, that one request
is worth more than anything else in this
video. Let me tell you about a woman I
will call Juny, 73, in Georgia, and her
payment stopped one month with no letter
and no warning. Somebody had changed her
direct deposit, not by breaking into
anything sophisticated, with her details
through an automated channel in about 4
minutes. It took her 11 weeks to
resolve. And during those 11 weeks, she
borrowed money from her sister to cover
her rent, which she described as the
most humiliating thing that had happened
to her in her adult life. The block on
electronic access existed the entire
time. Nobody had ever mentioned it to
her. Everything in this video is written
out in the quiet rules in the order you
would actually use it with the exact
words to ask for on each call. Scan the
code on the screen or go to
kevinexplains.shop
or use the link at the top of the pinned
comment. 7 days to look it over and if
it does not earn its place, send it
back. Juny lost 11 weeks to a 4-minute
change that one free request would have
made impossible. Now, the three
structural ones and here I am going to
be more careful than most people are on
this subject because this is where the
frightening version and the accurate
version separate sharply. The fourth
item is the trust fund and you have
heard about it constantly, usually
badly. Here is what is actually true.
The system is largely pay as you go. The
great majority of what arrives in your
account each month comes from people
working right now and paying in. Only a
portion comes from the reserve. That
reserve is being drawn down and every
year a slightly larger share of the
total comes out of it. On current
projections, it runs out sometime in the
early 2030s. Now, the important part,
and this is where both popular versions
get it wrong. The version that says the
money runs out and payments stop is
false. When the reserve is exhausted,
the money still coming in from people
working still arrives. Every projection
has the great majority of the benefit
continuing to be funded. The figure most
commonly used is that roughly 3/4 of
scheduled benefits would still be
payable, which means a reduction
somewhere around 23% if absolutely
nothing is done. And the version that
says there is nothing to worry about is
also wrong because a reduction of that
size is not a rounding error to anybody
living on it. So the honest position is
that this is a real problem with a known
date and a known size and it has always
been fixed before every previous time,
usually late and usually with a
combination of unpleasant adjustments.
What I would say to somebody planning is
this. Do not plan on a cut because the
political cost of allowing one is
enormous.
But do not build a plan that only works
if nothing changes either. Some of the
fixes that have been discussed for
decades involve the retirement age, the
taxable wage ceiling, and the way the
annual increase is calculated. And any
of those affect somebody's numbers. And
there is a genuine new pressure that
does not get discussed properly. The
system is funded by wages, not by
profits, not by investment returns, not
by machines, by people receiving a
paycheck and paying in from it. which
means anything that reduces the number
of people earning wages or moves work
into forms that do not generate payroll
tax puts pressure on the funding side
that the projections were not originally
built around. I am not going to tell you
what happens with automation over the
next 15 years because nobody knows and
anybody claiming certainty is selling
something. But the structure of the
funding is worth understanding because
it explains why this is a wages question
rather than an economy question. The
economy can do very well while the wage
base does not. And it is worth knowing
what the fixes actually look like
because the conversation is usually
conducted as though nobody has any ideas
and that is not the case at all. There
is a ceiling on the wages that get taxed
for this. Income above that ceiling
contributes nothing. Raising or removing
that ceiling is one option and it closes
a substantial share of the gap on its
own. Adjusting the age at which full
benefits begin is another which has been
done before and which is effectively a
reduction for anybody it applies to.
Changing the index used for the annual
increase is a third which sounds
technical and compounds into a large
number across a retirement. And a
broader tax base is a fourth meaning
applying the tax to forms of income it
currently does not touch. Every one of
those is unpopular with somebody which
is precisely why nothing has been done
for four decades. But the point worth
holding on to is that this is not an
unsolvable problem. It is a solved
problem that is politically expensive
and those get addressed late rather than
never. The fifth item is what your
retirement money is actually invested
in. And I want to be careful because I
do not give investment advice and I am
not about to start. So I will make one
structural point and then stop. A great
many people have their retirement money
in a fund that tracks a broad market
index or in a target date fund that
holds those index funds. That has been
an entirely reasonable place to be and
it has served people well. What has
changed is what is inside the index. The
largest companies in it now make up a
considerably larger share of the whole
than they did historically. And those
companies are heavily concentrated in
one industry which is currently spending
enormous amounts on one bet. Which means
somebody who believes they are broadly
diversified may be considerably less
diversified than they think. That is not
a prediction about whether that bet
works. It is a statement about
concentration. And concentration is a
description rather than a forecast. So
the only thing I will say is this. Open
the statement and find out what you
actually hold, not the name of the fund.
What is inside it and in what
proportions. And if that concentration
is more than you would knowingly choose
at your age, that is a conversation with
a fee only adviser, meaning one who is
paid by you rather than by commission on
what they sell you. The sixth is the
security of the institutions holding
your money. And here I want to bring the
temperature down rather than up. Yes,
financial institutions are under
constant automated attack. And yes, that
has intensified. Their security spending
has risen accordingly and their systems
are considerably more defended than they
were and your deposits at an insured
bank or credit union remain insured
within the limits which for most
households covers everything they have
there. That protection has not changed
and is not in question. What has changed
is where the weak point sits. It is not
the vault. It is the account holder
because it is far easier to convince a
person to authorize a transfer than to
break into a bank. Which is why the
practical defenses are personal rather
than institutional. Two-step
verification on every financial account
and on the email address those accounts
recover to because that email is the key
to all of them. Alerts on transactions
so you learn about something within
minutes rather than at the end of the
month. And a credit freeze at all three
bureaus which is free and permanent
until you lift it. And there is one more
piece of identity protection that sits
alongside all of this and belongs in the
same conversation. Separately from your
benefits, there is a protection
available against somebody filing a tax
return in your name to steal a refund.
It is a six-digit number issued to you,
changed every year, without which a
return filed under your social security
number will not be accepted. It used to
be available only to people who had
already been victims. It is now open to
anybody who wants one. It takes a few
minutes to request through the tax
agency's online account, and once you
have it, you simply include it when you
file. Nobody can file as you without it.
Given how much of the information needed
to impersonate somebody is already
circulating from old data breaches, that
is a strong protection for very little
effort, and hardly anybody outside the
profession knows it is open to everyone
now. And now, the scam, because every
single one of the subjects in this video
has one attached to it already. The
shape is always the same. Somebody hears
about a threat from a video like this
one or from a neighbor and a few days
later a call arrives. The caller says
they are from the agency or from a
benefits protection service or a
verification department. They reference
the very thing you have been worrying
about. They offer to secure your account
or verify your record or protect your
benefit from the new system. Here is
what ends every version of it. That
agency does not telephone people out of
nowhere to ask them to confirm a social
security number or bank details. They
already have your number. Real contact
comes as paper through the post. There
is no service, no fee, and no third
party that can protect your record on
your behalf. The protections I described
in this video are free and you request
them yourself. And nobody legitimate
will ever ask you to resolve anything
with a gift card, a wire, a payment
application, or a cryptocurrency
machine. Not once, not ever in any
circumstance. So, if that call comes,
put the phone down. Then look up the
number yourself from a statement or the
official site and call them, never the
number the caller gave you. Before I get
to what to do, one more thing that
belongs with the recordkeeping because
it is the version of this that reaches
families rather than individuals.
When somebody dies, there is a benefit
payable to a surviving spouse and it has
to be claimed. It is not large and it is
not automatic in every case and there is
a time limit on applying for it. More
importantly, survivor benefits
themselves are frequently claimed late
or not at all because people do not
realize they are eligible or assume
somebody would have told them. A widow
or widowerower can generally claim on a
late spouse's record from 60 and earlier
in some circumstances.
Divorced people can claim on a former
spouse's record where the marriage
lasted long enough, and doing so takes
nothing away from anybody else. A great
many people have no idea that last one
is true and never ask, and nobody is
going to raise it. The record exists,
the eligibility exists, and the
application does not happen until
somebody makes it. Now, let me give you
the practical answer to the whole video
because there is one, and it is not
complicated. If the person who used to
catch a mistake is not there anymore,
then the checking has to happen before
the decision rather than after it. That
is the entire adjustment. Everything
else follows from it. Which means three
specific things. The first is your
earnings record. And I would put this
above almost everything else in this
video. Your benefit is calculated from a
record of what you earned across your
working life. If a year is missing from
that record or understated, your benefit
is calculated from the wrong number
permanently. Employers make errors.
Companies close and records get lost.
Names change at marriage and a year
lands under the wrong one. Somebody
works under a slightly different name
for a season. Here is why the urgency
matters. There is a period after which a
year generally cannot be corrected. It
is a little over 3 years and after that
the record is treated as conclusive
except in specific circumstances which
means for most people the older years in
that record are already fixed and cannot
be argued with. And every year that
passes another year moves out of reach.
So looking at that record is not
something to do when you are about to
claim. By then a great many of the years
are closed. It is something to do now
and then annually. It takes 10 minutes
in the online account. Compare each year
against your own recollection and
against tax returns if you kept them.
Anything missing, raise it immediately
because the clock on that specific year
is running. The second is that you now
need to arrive at any interaction
knowing what you are entitled to. That
is a genuine change and it is not fair
and I would rather say that plainly than
pretend it is empowering. The burden
shifted on to you and nobody asked
whether you wanted it. But the shift
happened. So the response is
preparation. Before any call, know which
benefit you are asking about by its
name. Know the year involved. Know the
amount. And know what you believe the
correct answer is. If you arrive with a
general question, you will get a general
answer. And the third is that for
anything genuinely important, get it in
writing and keep the confirmation. Every
request, every change, every
conversation, note the date and the name
of the person. Keep the confirmation of
anything filed. In a system where fewer
people can see your whole history, your
own file is increasingly the only
complete record of what happened. One
more thing before the list and it
applies to everything I have described.
Every protection in this video has the
same property, which is that it has to
be set up before it is needed and it is
nearly worthless afterward. The block on
electronic access does nothing after
somebody has already redirected your
payment. The advanced designation does
nothing once capacity is gone. The
supplemental policy window does nothing
once it is closed. The correction to
your earnings record does nothing once
the year has passed out of reach. That
is not a coincidence and it is not bad
design. It is simply what protections
are. They are things you install while
nothing is wrong, which is the exact
moment when nobody has any motivation to
install them. Which is why the honest
instruction for this entire video is a
single afternoon rather than a plan.
Four phone calls and one online session
done in one sitting while everything is
fine. The people who do that afternoon
are not better informed than everybody
else. They just happen to hear the words
once from somewhere. Here is your list.
Seven things. One, if you or your spouse
are near 65 and still working, find out
how many employees that plan covers
before anybody enrolls in anything. 20
is the line, and the rule reverses on
either side of it.
Two, if you are contributing to a health
savings account and plan to enroll at
any point, stop contributing 6 months
beforehand and keep the letter your
employer sends every autumn confirming
your drug coverage is creditable because
that letter is your proof.
Three, understand that the choice you
make at 65 about supplemental coverage
is largely one way. The six-month window
with no medical questions does not come
back.
Four, set up your online account now
while the verification is merely
annoying rather than urgent. Then check
your earnings record every year because
the older years close permanently. Five,
ask the agency to block electronic
access to your record. It takes one
request. It is free and it makes the
direct deposit change that ruined Juny's
year impossible.
Six, for anything genuinely stuck,
contact the district office of your
representative in Congress and ask for a
caseworker. It is free and it is the
most effective route most people have
never used. Seven, open the statement
for your retirement account and find out
what is actually inside the fund you
own. Not the name, the contents. If any
of that landed close to home, all of it
is laid out in order in the quiet rules
link pinned at the top of the comments.
And if you have a question about your
own situation, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read everyone that comes in. My honest
read briefly. I do not think automation
is the villain here. And I am not going
to pretend otherwise for the sake of a
better story. A phone system that
answers immediately is genuinely better
than a queue that never ends. And there
are people getting help this year who
would have waited months a decade ago.
The problem is not the tool. It is the
sequence. The experience left the
building first and the systems arrived
second. And in the gap between those two
things, a category of protection quietly
disappeared that nobody had ever named
because nobody knew it was a service.
Nobody was employed to ask a 65-year-old
whether he still had coverage at work.
It was not in a job description. It
happened because somebody had done that
job for 19 years and recognized the
situation across a desk. You cannot put
that in a specification, which means
nobody noticed when it stopped. And
there is no line item anywhere measuring
what it cost. That is what I think is
actually happening and it is less
dramatic than a robot taking your money
and considerably more expensive. Last
thought, every single item in this video
has the same shape. There was a person
and now there is a process. And the
process does exactly what it was built
to do and nothing more. It will not warn
you. It will not ask the question. It
will not notice that your situation does
not fit the box because noticing is not
something a box does. So the checking is
yours now. That is not fair and I would
not pretend it is, but it is true. And
knowing it is true is the entire
defense. Make the calls while nothing is
wrong. Ask the questions before the
decision and write down what you were
told. I am Kevin. Thanks for watching.
Do not forget to check the quiet rules
at kevexplains.shop.

title: Retirees Are Being Fined For Paying Their Taxes On Time

segments.text: You can pay the IRS every dollar you owe
on time in April and still be fined for
it. Not for paying late, you did not pay
late. Not for filing late, you filed on
time. Fined for the timing of money you
already handed over in full. And here is
the part that makes it genuinely unfair.
Nobody tells you the fine is coming. It
is not on a notice. Your preparer very
often does not mention it until it is
already sitting on the return calculated
added to the bottom line in the same
conversation where you find out it
exists. For a great many people watching
this, the first year it happens is the
year after they retire. And there is a
reason for that which nobody explains
and which I'm going to make very clear
in the next 2 minutes. There is also a
fix for it that takes about 20 minutes
in December and can erase the entire
penalty retroactively for a whole year.
Even if you have paid nothing at all up
to that point, I am going to give you
that fix. But you have to understand
what is actually happening first or you
will apply it wrong. Here is the rule
underneath all of this. The tax system
in this country is not a bill you settle
once a year. It is a pay as you go
system. The government expects to
receive your tax across the year in
roughly the periods you earned the
income. And if it arrives later than
that, there is a charge for the delay.
While you were working, this was
invisible to you. Your employer took tax
out of every paycheck and sent it in.
You never thought about it because
somebody else was doing it every two
weeks automatically for 40 years. Then
you retired and that machinery stopped.
And this is the thing almost nobody is
told. Nothing replaced it. Not
automatically. Your social security has
no tax withheld from it unless you
specifically ask. That is not an
oversight. It is the default. And the
vast majority of people receiving it
have never asked. Money coming out of a
traditional retirement account has a
default withholding rate, and that rate
is very often far too low for the person
taking it. Interest from savings and
certificates has nothing withheld at
all. Dividends have nothing withheld.
Capital gains from selling anything have
nothing withheld. So somebody who spent
four decades never once thinking about
this suddenly has a household income
arriving from four or five sources and
not one of those sources is sending
anything to the government on their
behalf unless they went and arranged it.
And the year it bites hardest is the
first full year of retirement because
the year before had a paycheck in it and
this one does not. Now before I go
further let me clear up the belief that
causes most of the damage. People assume
this only applies to business owners and
the self-employed. That is the whole
reason nobody watching this thinks it is
about them. It is not about employment.
It is about whether enough tax reach the
government during the year. A retired
postal worker with a pension, a benefit,
and a certificate of deposit paying real
interest for the first time in 15 years
can be squarely inside this while a
self-employed neighbor is not. The
trigger is a gap between what you owe
and what arrived on time. That is all it
has ever been. I am not a lawyer and I
am not your accountant. This is

increase. Neither felt like a problem.
Both looked like good news.
The following spring, part of her social
security was taxable for the first time
in her life.
The additional tax was several times the
size of the bonus that helped trigger
it.
She said something I have not been able
to shake. She said, "So, I was punished
for shopping around?"
Effectively, yes. Not by design, but
that is the result.
All of this is written out in the quiet
rules, in the order you would actually
use it, including how to work out your
own number before you move money rather
than afterward.
Scan the code on the screen or go to
kevinexplains.shop
or use the link at the top of the pinned
comment. 7 days to look it over and if
it does not earn its place, send it
back.
Ruth Ann did the thing every financial
article in the country tells retirees to
do, which is shop around for a better
rate, and it cost her more than it paid
because nobody mentioned the second half
of the arithmetic. Now, a few situations
that sit outside the simple test and
each one catches a specific group of
people. The first is anybody who owns a
rental property or does any consulting
or small business work, and a great many
people watching this do.
When you buy something for that activity
and deduct it and you receive cash back
on that purchase, the cash back reduces
what the item cost you, which means your
deduction is smaller. Nothing is added
to your income, but you cannot deduct
the full price and keep the rebate
untouched. The two net against each
other and what you deduct is what the
thing actually cost you after the
reward. For small amounts, nobody is
going to build a case around it. For
somebody putting $15,000 of materials on
a card for a rental renovation, the
reward is meaningful and the correct
treatment is to reduce the cost, not to
ignore it. The same logic reaches two
other places people never think about.
If you pay a medical expense with a card
and get cash back on it, the amount you
actually paid is lower and if you are
deducting medical expenses, that
matters. And if you make a charitable
donation on a card and earn rewards on
it, you did not really give the full
amount. You gave the amount minus what
came back to you. Nobody is coming after
your church donation over a 2% rebate,
but if you are giving in serious amounts
and deducting it, that is a real
adjustment. The second situation is one
that catches almost everybody at some
point and it has nothing to do with
whether something is taxable. It has to
do with paperwork.
Every one of those forms goes to two
places, to you and to the agency.
Their system matches what was reported
against what you filed. If a form exists
that you did not include, the mismatch
is caught automatically. It is not a
person deciding to look at you. It is a
computer comparing two lists. And this
is one of the single most common notices
sent in this country because interest is
exactly the kind of income people
forget. It arrives on small forms from
institutions you may have used once,
sometimes online only. And if you close
the account, you may never see the form
at all. So, the practical instruction is
short. If you opened an account or moved
money for a bonus at any point last
year, expect a form and go looking for
it in January rather than waiting for it
to find you.
Check the online statements of every
institution you dealt with, including
ones you have since closed.
And a wrinkle on timing that catches
people. The year a bonus is reported is
the year the bank credited it, not the
year you signed up. If you opened the
account in November and the bonus posted
in February, it belongs to the following
year.
People reported in the wrong year and
create a mismatch out of an honest
attempt to do it right. There is a
version of this that is genuinely unfair
and it happens regularly, so I want you
to see it coming.
Every one of those bonus offers has a
condition attached about keeping the
account open. Usually 6 months,
sometimes 12. Close it early or let the
balance drop below the required level
and the bank takes the bonus back. Here
is the problem. The form was already
issued for the year you received it, so
you can end up reporting income you no
longer have. The bank clawed the money
back in March, the form covering the
previous year is already sitting in the
agency system and the two do not
automatically reconcile themselves. It
is fixable, but it requires you to
notice and to ask the bank for a
corrected form and most people never
realize the two events are connected at
all. So if you are moving money for a
bonus, write down the date you can close
the account without penalty and do not
touch it before then. It is the simplest
possible protection and it removes the
whole problem.
There is also a question about whose
name the form comes in when an account
is joint. It generally goes to the
primary holder, whoever that is on the
paperwork.
If you have added a child to an account
for convenience or if a joint account
has a spouse listed first, the income
may be reported against one person
rather than split and that can matter a
great deal when the two people are in
different positions against those
thresholds. And one specifically for
anybody paying a tax bill by card to
earn rewards, which people do. The
processing fee runs somewhere
approaching 2%. If the rewards on that
card are less than the fee, you are
paying to earn points. And for an
individual, that processing fee is not
deductible.
Run the arithmetic before you do it,
rather than assuming the rewards win.
Third, if a form arrives and the number
is wrong, and this happens more than you
would think, do not simply leave it off
your return. That guarantees a notice.
Contact the institution and ask for a
corrected form.
If they will not issue one in time, that
is a situation to put in front of
somebody who prepares returns, because
there is a right way to report it and an
explanation attached. And doing it that
way is a completely different experience
from staying silent.
The worst possible response to any tax
form is to ignore it and hope. That is
the one approach that turns a small
number into a long correspondence. One
last thing that belongs in a video on
this channel and that you will not hear
anywhere else on this subject. Points
and miles are not an asset your family
reliably inherits. Every one of those
programs is governed by an agreement
that says, in one form or another, that
the points have no cash value and belong
to the program rather than to you.
What happens at death is up to the
program. Some will transfer a balance to
a spouse or an estate on request,
sometimes with a fee attached. Some
forfeit the balance entirely on
notification of death. And a great many
people have discovered which kind they
were dealing with at the worst possible
moment. So, if you have been carefully
accumulating a large balance for years
towards some future trip, understand
what you are holding. It is not money
and it is not property. It is a promise
that can be changed or ended by the
other side without notice. If there is
something you have been saving them for
and it is roughly possible now, use
them.
And if a balance is significant, find
out what your specific program does at
death and put that answer with your
papers so somebody knows to ask.
Now, let me give you my read on this
briefly because I do not think there is
a villain here. The rules are not
unreasonable. A discount is not income
and money paid for the use of your money
is. Those are both defensible and I
would not argue with either. What
bothers me is who carries the
consequence.
Every one of these offers is designed
and advertised by an institution that
knows exactly which of them generates a
tax form.
They know it before they print the
offer.
There is no requirement to say so
anywhere in the advertising and none of
them do.
And the person who ends up with the
letter is very often somebody who moved
a few thousand dollars to a better rate
because that is what everybody tells
retirees to do. Here is your list, five
things. One, apply the test to anything
you are offered. Did I have to spend
money to get this? If yes, it is a
rebate. If no, expect a form. Two,
before you move money for a bonus, know
roughly where you sit against the social
security thresholds. Your other income
plus tax-exempt interest plus half your
benefit. If you are close to a line, the
offer is worth less than it says.
Three, in January, go looking for forms
from every institution you dealt with
last year including accounts you closed.
Do not wait for the post. Four, if you
have a rental or do any work on the
side, reduce the cost of anything you
deduct by the reward you received on it.
Same for medical and charitable amounts
you are deducting. Five, if a form is
wrong, ask for a correction and get help
reporting it. Never leave it off and
hope. If any of that landed close to
home, all of it is laid out in order in
the quiet rules, link pinned at the top
of the comments. And if you have a
question about your own situation, write
to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read everyone.
Last thought, the offers themselves are
usually fine. Some of them are genuinely
good and I am not telling anybody to
leave money on the table.
But every one of those advertisements is
written by somebody who knows precisely
which side of that line their offer
falls on and every one of them is aimed
at people who do not.
You know the test now, one question
asked before you sign anything and you
will know what is coming in January
instead of finding out from a letter in
October.
I am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: The Way You Hold Real Estate Can Erase Your Kids' Tax Break

segments.text: Two people own identical rental
properties. Same street, bought the same
year, worth about the same today. Both
of them die. Both leave the property to
their children. One family owes nothing
at all when they sell it. The other
family owes well over $100,000.
Neither of those people made a mistake.
Neither was careless. Neither got bad
advice. And neither did anything the
other did not do. The only difference
between them is a piece of paper filed
at the courthouse decades ago that
neither of them has thought about since.
And here is the part that makes this
genuinely cruel. The family that owed
nothing did not do anything clever. The
family that owed a h 100,000 did not do
anything wrong. The second family lost
that money because of a single election
that had to be made on a tax return in
one specific year by an accountant who
did not know to make it on behalf of
children who had never heard of it at a
moment when the one person who could
have explained it was already gone. That
is what this video is about. Not a
trust, not a will, not who you leave it
to, how the thing is held. Because that
decides whether your children inherit an
asset or inherit a tax bill wearing the
same clothes. I am not a lawyer. I am
not an accountant and I am not your
financial adviser. This is educational.
It is genuinely technical in places. And
this is exactly the kind of subject
where you confirm everything with a
licensed professional before you act. My
name is Kevin. I read the rules so you
do not have to. And I bring you the ones
that quietly decide what happens to your
money before they cost you anything. If
that is useful, subscribe. Let me start
with what is actually supposed to happen
because it is one of the most generous
provisions in the entire tax code and
most people only half understand it.
When you die and something passes from
you to your children, the tax code
resets what that thing cost, not what
you paid for it, what it is worth on the
day you die. Say you bought a rental
property in 1991 for $80,000. It is
worth $600,000 now. If you sold it while
you were alive, you would owe tax on
more than half a million dollars of gain
plus the recapture of every dollar of
depreciation you claimed over 30 years.
If your children inherit it instead,
their cost becomes 600,000. If they turn
around and sell it for 600,000, the gain
is zero, not reduced, zero. Every dollar
of appreciation across 30 years and
every dollar of depreciation you took
simply disappears for tax purposes at
the moment of death. That is called a
step up in basis and it is the single
most valuable thing most families will
ever inherit. It is not a loophole and
it is not aggressive planning. It is
written plainly in the code and it has
been there for generations. Now one
thing quickly because it is the reason
most people click on videos like this
one and I want to clear it and move on
to what actually matters. A revocable
living trust does not create this. It
does not improve it. It does not protect
it. Everything I just described happens
with a trust, without a trust, with a
will, and with no will at all. Property
passing from somebody who died gets
valued at the date of death either way.
Revocable trusts are often worth having.
They keep the estate out of probate,
which saves time and legal fees, and
they keep your affairs private. Those
are real benefits, and they are the
reasons attorneys recommend them. They
are simply not tax reasons. And anybody
telling you a revocable trust reduces
the tax on what you leave behind has
taken a real thing and attached it to
the wrong mechanism. So set the trust
question aside. It is not where the
money is won or lost. Here is where it
is won or lost. And this is the part
almost nobody explains to ordinary
families. When you hold real estate or a
business inside any kind of entity,
there are not one but two different
basis numbers in play and they can move
independently of each other. There is
the basis in the thing you own on paper,
your interest in the company or your
shares, and there is the basis in the
actual property that the company owns,
the building itself. People assume those
are the same number or that they move
together. They are not, and they do not.
And here is the whole video in one
sentence. When you die, the first one
steps up automatically in every case.
Whether the second one steps up depends
entirely on what kind of entity is
holding it. Your children can inherit
shares that stepped up beautifully in a
company that still owns a building with
your 1991 cost sitting inside it. And
when they sell the building, that old
number is the one the tax is calculated
from. The paperwork stepped up. The
property did not. Let me walk you
through the ways this can be held from
the cleanest to the worst so you can
find yours. The first way is the
simplest. You own it in your own name or
through a single member limited
liability company that is treated as a
sole proprietorship for tax purposes.
That is most people watching this. The
rental house is in your name or it is in
an LLC you set up years ago because
somebody told you it was safer and that
LLC has one owner which is you. For tax
purposes, there is no separate entity at
all. It is you. So when the property
passes at your death, it steps up
directly. The building itself gets the
new value. Your children inherit it with
a fresh cost equal to what it is worth
that day. If they sell, there is
nothing. If they keep it and rent it
out, they begin depreciating it all over
again from the new higher number, which
is a benefit that runs for years
afterward and that almost nobody
mentions. Let me tell you about a man I
will call Vernon, 79, in Missouri, and
he owned two rental houses he had bought
in the early 90s and managed himself for
30 years. He fixed the furnaces. He knew
the tenants. Both houses were in his own
name. No entity, no company, nothing
complicated because in 1991, nobody was
telling ordinary people to put a rental
in an LLC. When he died, his daughter
inherited both. She sold one within the
year and kept the other. She paid
nothing on the sale. Not a reduced
amount, nothing. And on the one she
kept, she started depreciating it from
the new value, which lowered her taxable
rental income for years afterward. And I
want to be honest about what happened
there. Vernon did not plan that. He did
not know the rule. He simply never got
around to putting the houses into
anything. And the simplest possible
arrangement turned out to be the best
one available. That is the reason I put
together the quiet rules. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
There is a code on the screen right now,
so hold your phone up to it or use the
link pinned at the top of the comments
or the one in the description below. It
covers the rules that quietly decide
what your family actually receives in
plain English, including what to check
about how your property is held and the
exact words to leave for the people who
will handle it. You have seven days with
it. If it does not change something
about what you do next, send it back and
that is the end of it. Vernon got the
best outcome available by accident. The
next two ways of holding property do not
have accidental good outcomes and that
is where I am going next. The second way
of holding property is a partnership and
in practice that usually means a limited
liability company with more than one
owner. This is extremely common and most
people in it do not think of themselves
as being in a partnership at all. You
and your brother own a duplex together
through an LLC. You and your wife formed
one and depending on your state, it may
be treated as a partnership. You went in
with two other people on a small
commercial building in 1998.
Here is what happens when one owner
dies. The interest in the partnership
steps up. That is automatic and it
always happens. Your children's stake in
the company is now valued at what it was
worth the day you died. The property
inside the partnership does not step up.
Not automatically, not at all. So, the
company still owns that building
carrying the old cost from 1998. And it
still has all the depreciation you
claimed sitting against it. And when
that building is sold, the gain is
calculated from the old number and
passed through to the owners. Your
children hold an interest that stepped
up beautifully in a company that owns a
building that did not. Now, there is a
fix. It exists. It is legitimate, and it
is written into the code specifically
for this situation. It is an election
the partnership makes, and it is known
by its section number, which is 754.
When that election is in place, the
partnership adjusts the basis of its
assets specifically for the person who
inherited. So the building for that
person's share is treated as though it
stepped up along with everything else.
That is the difference between a family
owing nothing and a family owing a great
deal. And it is one line on a tax
return. And here is why I am spending
time on this rather than mentioning it
in passing because this is the part that
should genuinely worry you. You are not
the person who makes that election. It
is made on the partnership's tax return
for the year the death occurred. Which
means it is made after you are gone by
your children or more accurately by
whoever prepares that partnership return
who may be an accountant who has handled
this small LLC for 11 years and has
never once encountered this situation.
There is nobody whose job it is to raise
it. The tax software will not prompt
anybody. Your children will not know the
words. And the one person in the family
who might have known to ask is the
person the return is being filed because
of. So it gets missed quietly in a year
when nobody is thinking about tax
returns and it does not announce itself.
The family finds out years later when
the building sells and the gain is
enormous and somebody finally asks why.
There is one more thing worth knowing
about that election and it cuts both
ways. Once a partnership makes it, it
generally stays in place for the future,
applying to later transfers as well.
That is usually a good thing, but it is
a decision with a long tail, and it is
exactly the sort of thing to raise with
a professional rather than tick a box
on. And there is relief if it was
missed. Under the regulations, there is
an automatic extension available in
certain circumstances to make a late
election, generally within a window
after the original due date. It is not
unlimited and it is not guaranteed. But
it means that a family who discovers
this within a reasonable time may not be
finished. So if you are watching this
and a parent died in the last year or
two and there was a partnership
involved, that is a question worth
putting to a professional this month
rather than next year. The third way of
holding property is inside a
corporation, either kind. And this is
the difficult one. Some people put real
estate into a corporation decades ago,
often on advice that made sense for
other reasons at the time. Small family
businesses that own their own building
are frequently structured this way. Here
is what happens at death. The stock
steps up. Your children's shares are
valued at what they were worth the day
you died. The property inside the
corporation does not step up. And unlike
a partnership, there is no election that
fixes it. There is no 754 for
corporations. It does not exist. The
mismatch is simply the outcome. So your
children own shares worth 600,000 in a
company that owns a building the tax
code still thinks cost 80,000. If the
company sells the building, the gain is
calculated from 80,000. And with a fully
depreciated property, the basis can be
close to nothing at all. There is a
technique that can address it and I want
to describe it carefully because it is
the kind of thing that needs a
professional in the room. Broadly, if
the corporation sells the property and
is then liquidated in the same year, the
gain on the property and the loss on the
stock can land in the same tax year and
offset each other. The stock was stepped
up to a high value. The company
distributes out what is left and the
loss on the shares comes back against
the gain. The result can be roughly what
the family would have had if the asset
itself had stepped up. But it depends
heavily on which kind of corporation it
is because one of them taxes the gain at
the company level first and then again
on the way out which is a very different
picture from the other. It has to be
done in one year in the right order and
getting it wrong is expensive. This is
not a home project. If a corporation
holds appreciated property in your
family, this belongs in front of an
accountant who has done it before and it
is worth finding one who has rather than
assuming yours has. Let me tell you
about a woman I will call Margarite, 73,
and her father had run a small heating
and plumbing business in Ohio,
incorporated in 1984, and the company
owned the building it operated out of on
a corner lot that had become genuinely
valuable as the town grew around it.
When he died, she and her brother
inherited the shares. Nobody explained
the difference between the shares and
the building. Why would they? They
inherited a company, and the company
owned a building, and that seemed like
one thing rather than two. Four years
later, they sold the property. The
building had been fully depreciated over
decades. The gain that came out was
almost the entire sale price. She said
the sentence that made me want to build
this video. She said, "We thought we had
already inherited it. They had inherited
it. They had inherited the shares, which
had stepped up perfectly, and none of
that helped them because they sold the
building rather than the company four
years after the only window that
mattered had closed. Everything I am
walking through here is written out in
the quiet rules in the order you would
actually work through it, including what
to check about your own arrangement and
the exact question to put to an
accountant. Scan the code on the screen
or go to kevinexplains.shop
or use the link at the top of the pinned
comment. 7 days to look it over and if
it does not earn its place, send it
back. Margarit's family lost that money
four years after her father died to a
rule none of them had ever heard the
name of. There are families watching
this right now sitting in exactly that
position and not one of them knows it.
Now there is a second layer underneath
all of this that has nothing to do with
entities and for married couples it may
be worth more than everything I have
said so far. It is how the property is
titled between the two of you. Here is
the situation. A married couple owns a
property together. One of them dies.
What steps up? In most of the country
the answer is half. The half belonging
to the person who died steps up to
current value. The surviving spouse's
half keeps the original cost from
whenever it was bought. So the property
ends up with a blended basis, part new
and part very old. Which means if the
survivor sells it 5 years later, there
is still a substantial gain sitting
inside that other half. But in a group
of states, something different happens.
In community property states, when one
spouse dies, the entire property can
step up. both halves, not just the
deceased spouse's share. That is a
completely different outcome from the
same death, the same marriage, and the
same house. And the only difference is
which state the property sits in and how
the title is written. There are nine
community property states and a small
number of others that allow couples to
elect similar treatment through a
specific arrangement. And here's the
part that catches people even inside
those states. It depends on how the deed
actually reads. A couple in a community
property state can hold a property as
joint tenants rather than as community
property and in doing so give up the
double step up without ever realizing
there was a choice. The words on the
deed are doing work. Most people have
never read theirs. So if you are married
and you own appreciated property, there
are two questions worth asking a
professional in your state. What is my
property titled as right now? And given
where I live, is that the arrangement
that produces the best result for
whichever of us is left? That is a
15-minute conversation. And for some
couples, it is worth more than every
other item in this video combined. Now,
let me tell you why all of this matters
far more for rental property than for
anything else you own. Because there is
a piece here that people miss. When you
own a rental, you claim depreciation
every year. That is the deduction that
makes rental property so effective while
