you are alive. But depreciation is not
free. It reduces your cost in the
property. And when you sell, all of it
comes back as taxable income at a rate
of its own. People are frequently
shocked by that bill. Here is what the
step up does to it. It wipes it out.
Every dollar of depreciation you claimed
across 30 years disappears at death and
never gets recaptured. Which is why for
somebody who has held rental property
for decades and does not need to sell,
holding it to the end is often
extraordinarily powerful. You took the
deduction every year and the obligation
attached to it evaporates. And it is
precisely why the entity question
matters so much for these specific
properties. The asset where the stepup
is worth the most is the one most likely
to be sitting inside an LLC or a
corporation where the stepup may not
reach it. The place where the prize is
biggest is the place where it is most
often lost.
Now let me give you the thing I actually
want you to do and it costs nothing and
takes one afternoon. Everything I have
described has a common feature that
should bother you. The person who has to
act is not you. The election is made
after your death by your children or by
an accountant they hire in a year when
the family is dealing with a funeral and
a house and a hundred other things. And
that accountant may be excellent and
still not think of it because a small
partnership return for a family duplex
is not where people expect this to come
up. So write it down now while you are
here to write it. It does not need a
lawyer and it does not need to be
formal. A single page in an envelope
with the property documents. It should
say what the property is, what kind of
entity holds it, and that in the year of
your death, the person preparing the
return should be asked specifically
whether a section 754 election is
appropriate. If it is a corporation, it
should say that the shares and the
underlying property are treated
differently and that a professional
experienced in this should be consulted
before anything is sold. Then tell
somebody in your family where the
envelope is. That page is worth more
than most of the estate planning
documents people spend real money on
because it is the only one that speaks
at the exact moment the decision has to
be made to the exact person who has to
make it and there is a reason to write
it today rather than when it seems
relevant. You are the only person who
can explain your own arrangement. That
is not a permanent condition. Let me
tell you about a man I will call Cyrus.
69 in Georgia and he and his brother had
owned a small commercial property
together through an LLC since 2001.
He watched something like this video and
rather than doing anything dramatic, he
did the small thing. He called his
accountant and asked one question, which
was whether their arrangement would need
an election at either of their deaths.
The accountant said yes almost certainly
and that he was glad to have been asked
because in his words, "Nobody ever asks
in advance, and he is usually finding
out about it a year late.
Cyrus wrote the page. He put it in the
file with the deed and the operating
agreement. And he told his daughter and
his brother's son where it was, and then
he did not think about it again. He
described the whole thing as the
cheapest useful thing he had ever done
because it cost him one phone call and a
sheet of paper. And that is genuinely
all it takes. This is not a subject
where you need to become an expert. You
need to know that the question exists
and you need somebody who will be there
afterward to know it, too. Now, let me
give you my honest read and it is only
that there is something uncomfortable
about this whole subject and I would
rather say it plainly than pretend
otherwise. The step up in basis is one
of the most generous provisions in the
tax code and it applies to everybody
equally on paper. Rich, ordinary,
whoever you are, property passing at
death gets valued at death. But whether
you actually receive it depends on
paperwork, on which entity somebody put
the property into 20 years ago, on how a
deed was worded, on whether an
accountant knows to make an election in
a particular year, and who has the
paperwork right, people who paid
somebody to get it right. So, a
provision that is written to be
universal is delivered unevenly and it
is delivered worst to exactly the
families who were told to form an LLC by
somebody who was thinking about
liability and not about what happens at
death, which is nearly everybody with a
rental house in this country. Notice
that Vernon, who did the least, got the
best result. He never formed anything.
And that produced a cleaner outcome than
a family who did what they were advised
to do and put the property into a
company. That should tell you something
about how this works. It is not
rewarding sophistication. It is
rewarding whoever happened to end up in
the right structure. And a great many
people ended up in the wrong one
following perfectly reasonable advice
about something else entirely. And there
is nobody in the system whose job it is
to look at your arrangement and say this
will not work the way you think. At the
end, the attorney set up the entity. The
accountant files the return each year.
Neither of them is being paid to look 15
years ahead at a death that has not
happened. That gap is where this money
goes. Here is your list. Five things and
the first three take one afternoon. One,
find out exactly how each property you
own is held. Your own name, a single
member company, a company with more than
one owner, or a corporation. Do not
guess. Look at the documents and if you
are not certain, ask whoever files the
return. Two, if anything is held in a
partnership or a multi-owner company,
ask your accountant one question. Will a
section 754 election be needed at my
death? And does whoever handles this
afterward need to know that? Ask it by
name. Three, if any appreciated property
is inside a corporation, either kind,
that needs a professional who has
handled it before, and it needs them
before anybody sells anything. That is
the most urgent item on this list for
the small number of people it applies
to. Four, if you are married and you own
appreciated property, ask how it is
titled and whether that is the right
arrangement in your state. In some
states, the difference is the entire
step up on the survivor's half. Five,
write the page. What the property is,
what holds it, what question needs
asking in the year you die, and where
the documents are. Put it with the deed.
Tell somebody where it is. If any of
that landed close to home, all of it is
laid out in order in the quiet rules
link pinned at the top of the comments.
And if your own arrangement is tangled,
if you are looking at an operating
agreement and cannot work out what you
have, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read everyone and they shape what gets
covered next. Last thought, everything
in this video comes down to a single
mismatch that almost nobody is told
about. When you die, the paperwork you
hold steps up in value. The property
behind it might not. For most people,
those two things are the same and
nothing goes wrong. For anybody holding
property inside a company with more than
one owner or inside a corporation, they
are two different things. And the gap
between them is where an inheritance
quietly turns into a tax bill. You
cannot fix it afterward. Your children
cannot fix it afterward because in most
cases, they will not know there was
anything to fix. The only person who can
put this right is the person who
understands the arrangement and that is
you and only for as long as you are
here. So do the small version this week.
One phone call and one page in an
envelope. I am Kevin. Thanks for
watching. Do not forget to check the
quiet rules at kevinexplains.shop.

title: Every Senior Must Do This Before September 30: The 2027 COLA Rule Nobody Explains

segments.text: There is a number being calculated on
you right now this month and it decides
what you live on for the whole of next
year.
Nobody is going to write to you about
it. It will not appear on a statement.
There is no form to fill in and no
office to call. It is being assembled
quietly out of data that has nothing to
do with you personally and when it is
finished in October, it will be
announced on the news for one day and
then everybody will move on. And by
then, it will be closed permanently.
There is no appeal, no review and no way
to be reconsidered. What almost nobody
understands is that the window it is
calculated from closes on the 30th of
this month.
Three months of data decide it. Two of
those three are already locked and
cannot be changed. The third is being
recorded right now this week in grocery
stores and gas stations and rent
payments all over the country and on the
30th of September, the door shuts on it
for good.
That is your raise for 2027.
It is being decided this month and you
are not in the room.
Now, most people hear that and assume
there is nothing to be done and that is
exactly the wrong conclusion and it is
the reason I'm spending the next half
hour on this. Because you cannot change
the number, that is true, but there are
four separate things that happen between
the announcement of that number and the
amount that actually lands in your
account and every one of those four is
something you can do something about and
every one of them has a deadline
attached that nobody tells you about.
People spend September arguing on the
internet about whether the raise will be
That argument is worth nothing. The
difference between those two figures on
a typical benefit is a few dollars a
month. The four things I'm going to show
you are worth vastly more than that
difference and every single one of them
is inside your control. I am not a
lawyer, I am not an accountant and I am
not your financial advisor. This is
educational based on the rules as they
stand today, and your situation is your
own. So, confirm anything here before
you act on it. My name is Kevin. I read
the rules so you do not have to. Every
week I go looking for the thing that
quietly decides what happens to your
money, and I bring it here before it
costs you anything. If that is useful,
subscribe because the fourth item in
this video has a clock on it that starts
the day a letter arrives, and most
people let it run out without knowing it
existed. Let me start with how that
number is actually built because almost
everything people believe about it is
wrong, and the wrongness costs them.
Here is the first thing. The raise is
not based on inflation for the year.
That is what nearly everyone assumes.
Prices went up this much, so the benefit
goes up by that. It is not how it works
at all. The calculation uses one
specific measure over one specific
3-month window compared against the same
3 months from the previous year, July,
August, September. That is the entire
measurement period. Nine months of the
year are not counted at all, which means
something strange and important. If
prices spiked in February and settled by
June, that spike does not exist as far
as your raise is concerned. It happened
outside the window. You paid it, and it
does not count. And if prices climb in
October, right after the window closes,
you absorb every bit of that for 15
months before any adjustment reaches it.
That is not an accident or a flaw. It is
simply how the law was written, and it
has been written that way for decades.
But, it means the raise you receive was
measured during one quarter of the year
and then applied to a full year of your
life. The second thing people get wrong
is which measure of prices is used.
There is more than one. The one used for
your benefit is called the Consumer
Price Index for urban wage earners and
clerical workers. Read the name of it
again because the name tells you the
problem. Urban wage earners.
Clerical workers. It measures the
spending pattern of working people in
cities,
what working people buy in the
proportions they buy it. You are not a
working person in a city. Your spending
looks nothing like theirs.
Working households spend a large share
on transportation, on getting to a job,
on the things a working life requires.
Retired households spend a far larger
share on medical care and on housing,
and those two categories have generally
risen faster than the overall basket for
very long time. There is an index that
measures older households specifically.
It exists. It has existed for decades.
It is called the experimental index for
Americans 62 and older, and it weights
medical care and shelter much more
heavily, closer to how you actually
live. It is not used. Your raise is
calculated from the working person's
basket, not yours, and proposals to
change it have gone nowhere for 30
years. So, when your raise arrives and
it does not feel like it covered what
your year actually cost, you are not
imagining that, and you are not bad with
money. You are being measured against
somebody else's shopping list. Now, here
is where September sits in all of this,
and why this month specifically.
The August figures were published on the
11th of this month. That gave two of the
three months.
Two-thirds of the calculation is now
fixed and cannot move. The third month,
September itself, is being recorded
right now and closes on the 30th.
Those figures get published in the
middle of October, and that is when the
official number is announced,
which means everything you are reading
online in the meantime is a projection.
As of the end of August, the estimates
were running somewhere in the region of
3 and 1/2% with different organizations
landing on slightly different figures.
Those are forecasts. They are not the
number.
And I want to be careful here because
every year, without fail, there are
channels and websites that publish a
projection as though it were confirmed,
and people plan around it, and then the
real figure lands somewhere else.
Do not budget on a projection. Wait for
October.
And there is a reason the projections
tend to run high, which is worth knowing
so you can read them properly. The
organizations publishing them are mostly
advocacy groups for older Americans, and
they are not lying to anybody. But a
forecast built in August has only one of
the three months in hand, and the third
month has historically had a way of
coming in softer than the summer months
did. So, the pattern most years is that
the September estimate is a little above
where the final figure lands. Not
always, but often enough that you should
treat any number you see this month as a
ceiling rather than a promise.
Let me tell you about a man I will call
Otis, 74 in Alabama, retired from a
lumber yard where he worked for 26
years.
Otis follows this every year. He is not
a passive person about it. Every
September he reads what the projections
are, and he tells his wife what to
expect. And by the time October comes,
he already has a number in his head. Two
years ago, the projection he read in
September was noticeably higher than
what was eventually announced.
He had already told his wife they could
handle a particular expense in the new
year on the strength of it.
It was not a catastrophe. They adjusted.
But he described the feeling of having
to walk it back, and it was not about
the money. He said, "I felt like I had
been careless, and I had not been
careless. I had read something that was
printed like a fact."
That is the reason I put together the
quiet rules.
It is at kevinexplains.shop.
There is a code on the screen right now,
so hold your phone up to it, or use the
link pinned at the top of the comments,
or the one sitting in the description
below.
It covers how these numbers are actually
built, and what happens to them on the
way to your account, in plain English,
printed large enough to read without
hunting for your glasses. You have 7
days with it. If it is not change
something about what you do next, send
it back, and that is the end of it.
Otis was not careless. He was reading a
projection that had been dressed up as
an announcement, which happens every
single September, and it is happening
right now while you are watching this.
Now, the first of the four things that
stand between that number and your bank
account, and it is the largest one.
Your raise is announced as a percentage.
What arrives in your account is not that
percentage, and for a great many people,
it is barely half of it.
Here is why.
If you are on Medicare, your Part B
premium is deducted from your Social
Security payment before it reaches you.
You never see that money. It moves from
one federal agency to another, and you
get the remainder. And the Part B
premium is set separately, by a
different process, on a different
timetable, and it goes up almost every
year. So, the sequence goes like this. A
raise is announced in October, and
everybody feels good about it for a few
days. Then, in November, the new
Medicare premium is announced. And in
January, when the first payment of the
year arrives, the number is nothing like
what people expected. Every year,
without exception, there is a wave of
people who believe a mistake has been
made. There was no mistake. The raise
was real. It simply went somewhere on
its way to you. In some years, the
premium increase has consumed the
majority of the raise for people on
modest benefits. Understand what that
means in practice. Somebody with a
smaller benefit receives a smaller
dollar raise because it is a percentage.
But, the premium increase is a flat
dollar amount, identical for everyone at
the standard rate. So, the same premium
increase eats a much larger share of a
small raise than a large one. The person
with the least is hit the hardest by the
same dollar. That is not a conspiracy.
It is arithmetic.
But, it is arithmetic that nobody
explains, and it means the announced
percentage and the experienced
percentage are two different things, and
the gap between them is widest for the
people who can least afford it.
Now, here is the protection that exists,
and I want to explain it properly
because it is genuinely valuable and
almost everybody who has heard of it
misunderstands what it does.
It is called the hold harmless
provision.
What it does is this.
For most people who have their Part B
premium deducted directly from their
Social Security payment, the premium
increase cannot be larger than the
dollar amount of their raise.
In plain terms, your net payment cannot
go down because of a Part B increase.
If the premium would rise by more than
your raise, your premium rise is limited
so that the net stays flat.
That is a real protection and it has
saved a lot of people from an outright
cut. But look closely at what it does
not promise. It does not promise you
keep your raise. It only promises the
number does not go backward. So, in a
year where the premium jump is large,
hold harmless can mean your entire raise
disappears into the premium and your
payment stays exactly where it was.
Nothing was taken from you, nothing was
given either. And there are groups it
does not cover at all. And this is the
part almost nobody knows, so let me name
them. It does not cover you in your
first year of Medicare. If you are
enrolling for the first time, you are
not protected and you pay the full new
premium.
It does not cover you if your income is
high enough that you are paying the
income-related surcharge. Those payers
are excluded entirely. It does not cover
you if your Part B premium is not being
deducted from a Social Security payment.
If you are paying Medicare directly by
bill, you are outside the protection.
And it does not cover you if a state
program is paying your premium because
in that case the state absorbs the
increase rather than you.
So, if you turn 65 this year or if you
are paying Medicare by bill rather than
deduction, or if you are in a surcharge
tier, you are exposed in a way most
people around you are not. And nobody
sends a letter to tell you which group
you are in.
Here's what I want you to actually do
about it and it is not complicated.
When the raise is announced in October,
do not write down the percentage. Write
down nothing.
Wait for the Medicare premium
announcement, which follows within
weeks. Then take the new premium,
subtract this year's premium, and
subtract that difference from your
dollar raise.
Whatever survives that subtraction is
your actual raise.
That is the only number that matters,
and it is the one nobody publishes
because it is different for every single
person. And then, before January, look
at whatever is automatically deducted
from your payment and decide whether it
still fits because there is something
people do that quietly cost them for
years. Medicare Part D premiums,
supplemental plan premiums, and Medicare
Advantage arrangements all change
annually, and the annual enrollment
window falls in October and November,
right when the raise is being announced.
So, the exact weeks when you are being
told about your raise are the exact
weeks when you can change what comes out
of it.
And most people spend those weeks
reading about the percentage instead of
looking at their own deductions. The
percentage is decided. Your deductions
are not. One of those two is worth your
attention in October, and it is not the
one the news is talking about. There is
one more piece to this that catches
people, and it involves the surcharge I
mentioned. That surcharge is calculated
from your income 2 years earlier.
So, the premium you will pay in the year
ahead was decided by a tax return you
filed two springs ago and have not
thought about since.
Which means if something unusual
happened in that year, a property sale,
a large withdrawal, a conversion, the
loss of a spouse that moved you to
single filer thresholds, it may be about
to show up in your premium for the first
time.
And if the income behind it has since
ended, there is a form that lets you ask
for it to be recalculated based on your
current circumstances rather than a year
that no longer exists. It is free, it
takes an afternoon, and the number of
people paying a surcharge they could
have removed is not small.
Now, the second of the four, and this is
the one that makes people genuinely
angry when they understand it because it
turns the raise itself into the problem.
A cost of living increase can push you
across a tax threshold and cause more of
your benefit to become taxable. Here is
the mechanism and it is not complicated
once somebody draws it for you. There is
a figure the government calculates that
decides how much of your Social Security
is taxed. It is your other income plus
any tax-exempt interest plus half of
your Social Security benefit. Notice
that last part. Half of your benefit
counts toward the number that determines
whether your benefit gets taxed. So,
when your benefit rises, that figure
rises with it automatically without you
doing anything at all. For a single
person, once that figure crosses
up to half your benefit becomes taxable.
Cross 34,000 and up to 85% of it does.
For a married couple, those two lines
And here is the part that should stop
you cold. Those dollar figures were
written into law in the early 1980s with
the second tier added in the early 90s
and they have never been adjusted for
inflation. Not once. Not in 40 years.
Every other number in this system moves.
The benefit moves every year, the
earnings limit moves, the taxable wage
base moves, the premium moves. Those
four thresholds do not move. They have
sat perfectly still since before most
people watching this retired. So, think
about what a raise actually does to
somebody sitting just below one of those
lines.
The raise arrives, meant to keep you
level with rising prices. Your benefit
is now larger. Half of a larger benefit
is a larger number. That larger number
pushes your calculation across a line
that has not moved since 1984.
And now a portion of your benefit that
was not taxed last year is taxed this
year. You did not earn more. You did not
withdraw more. You did nothing at all.
Inflation raised your benefit and the
frozen line did the rest. The increase
meant to protect you from inflation
triggered a tax because of inflation on
a threshold that ignores inflation. And
every single year that happens to a new
group of people who have never had their
benefit taxed before and who will never
be told why it started. When these
thresholds were created, this tax was
described as reaching a small fraction
of beneficiaries. Today, it reaches a
majority of them. Nobody voted for that
expansion. It expanded on its own, one
raise at a time, by standing still while
everything else moved. Now, what do you
actually do with that? If you are
anywhere near one of those lines, and a
great many people watching this are, the
raise you receive in January can matter
to your tax bill in a way that has
nothing to do with the raise itself,
which means the last months of this year
are the time to look at what else is
landing on your return.
A withdrawal you were planning, interest
from a certificate of deposit that
renewed at a much better rate than the
last one, a distribution you were going
to take in December that could just as
easily be taken in January. Small timing
choices made before the 31st of December
decide which side of a frozen line you
land on. And here is a piece that almost
nobody connects to this.
Interest rates. A great many older
households have money in savings
accounts and certificates of deposit
that were paying almost nothing for a
decade and are now paying a great deal
more.
That interest counts. It counts fully
toward the calculation.
So, there are people who will cross one
of those thresholds for the first time
this coming year purely because their
savings finally started paying them
something combined with a raise they did
not ask for. Nobody warned them. The
bank certainly did not. The bank is
delighted about the rate.
Let me tell you about a woman I will
call Clementine, 71, a widow, in a small
town in Kentucky, living on her social
security and a modest amount of interest
from money she and her husband had put
aside over 40 years. For most of her
retirement, none of her benefit was
taxable. She was comfortably under to
line and she had never once thought
about it, because there had never been a
reason to.
Two things happened in the same year.
Her benefit rose with the annual
increase, and the money she had sitting
in a certificate of deposit renewed at a
rate several times higher than the old
one.
Neither of those things felt like a
problem. One was a raise, the other was
her savings finally earning something
after years of earning nothing. Both
looked like good news.
The following spring, part of her Social
Security was taxable for the first time
in her life, and she did not understand
why. And the person who prepared her
return explained it in about 90 seconds
and moved on to the next client.
What she said to me afterward is the
reason this section exists. She said,
"So, the two good things that happened
to me are what caused it?" Yes, that is
exactly right, and that is the design.
All of this is written out in the Quiet
Rules, in the order you would actually
work through it, where the frozen lines
sit, how to work out your own number
before the year closes, and what can be
moved between December and January. Scan
the code on the screen, or go to
kevinexplains.shop,
or use the link at the top of the pinned
comment. 7 days to look it over, and if
it does not earn its place, send it
back. Clementine crossed the line drawn
in 1984, because her savings finally
paid her something. There are people
watching this who are going to do the
same thing in about 4 months and have no
idea it is coming. Now, the third of the
four, and this one is about how the
money physically reaches you, which
sounds dull until it does not reach you.
Federal benefit payments are now
required to be made electronically. That
means direct deposit into a bank or
credit union account, or onto a prepaid
card provided for exactly this purpose,
for people who do not have a bank
account. Paper checks have been going
away for years, and the transition is
largely finished. But, there are still
people receiving them, and there are
more people than you would think who
have an account on file that they no
longer use, or one at a bank that was
bought by another bank, or one that was
closed when a spouse died and the joint
account was reorganized.
Here is why this matters more than it
sounds.
A payment that cannot be delivered does
not sit patiently and wait for you. It
goes back. And getting it reissued is a
phone call and a wait. And if you are
living on that payment, the wait is the
whole problem. So, the practical
instruction is short. If you are still
receiving a paper check, or if the
account your payment goes into is one
you have not looked at recently, or one
that belonged to a bank that has changed
names, verify it now rather than in
January when a raise and a new premium
are both landing. January is the worst
month of the year to discover a delivery
problem because it is the month with the
most moving parts. And there is a card
option for anybody who does not have a
bank account and does not want one. It
exists specifically for this and it is
free to receive payments onto.
If somebody in your family has been
receiving paper checks and is uneasy
about banks, that is worth knowing
rather than letting the payments become
a problem.
Now, a warning attached to this because
every single time a rule about bank
accounts and federal payments gets
attention, something attaches itself to
it within days and it is running right
now. The shape is always the same.
Somebody hears about a change involving
Social Security and bank accounts from a
video or a neighbor or something half
remembered from the news. A few days
later a call comes. The caller says they
are from a verification department or a
benefits compliance office or a federal
payments services team.
They explain that because of the change,
your account details need to be
confirmed or updated or re-registered
and that they can handle it for you
today over the phone.
Here is the sentence that ends every
version of this.
That agency will never telephone you out
of nowhere and ask you to confirm your
Social Security number or your bank
account details in order to comply with
a rule change.
They already have your number.
When they need something from you, it
arrives as paperwork and written notice,
not as a surprise call demanding you act
today. And what the caller is after is
almost never a payment. It is the number
itself or a verification code read out
loud. So, if that call comes, put the
phone down. Then, if you have a real
question about your own situation, look
the number up yourself from a statement
or from the official website and call
them. Never the number the caller gives
you because in a great many of these,
that number is theirs. Now, the fourth
thing, and I have held it until last
deliberately because it is the one with
an actual clock on it, and it is where I
see the most damage done.
If a letter ever arrives saying you have
been overpaid, there is a clock that
starts the day it lands, and most people
do not know it is running. An
overpayment happens for all sorts of
ordinary reasons that have nothing to do
with anybody doing anything wrong.
Earnings reported late, a change in
circumstances processed months after it
happened, a calculation adjusted
retroactively, a wage figure that
arrived from an employer after the fact.
And the letter is frightening. It
arrives with a number on it that can be
very large because it covers a period
that may go back years, and it explains
that recovery will begin from your
future payments.
Here is what almost nobody understands.
That letter is not the end of the
conversation. It is the beginning of
one, and there are three separate things
you can do, and two of them have
deadlines. The first is a
reconsideration. That is what you file
if you believe the overpayment is wrong,
either that it did not happen or that
the amount is incorrect. There is a form
for it, and there is a limited window
from the date of the notice to file it,
generally around 60 days. The second is
a waiver.
That is what you file if you accept that
the overpayment happened, but it was not
your fault, and paying it back would
cause you hardship.
That is a different form, and here is
the part worth writing down.
There is no time limit on requesting a
waiver. You can request one at any
point. And the third is a payment
arrangement, which is what you file if
you accept the debt but cannot survive
the rate at which they intend to take it
back.
That rate is negotiable.
People do not know it is negotiable.
And filing something matters for a
reason beyond the merits. Filing
generally pauses collection while the
request is being considered.
Doing nothing does not pause anything.
So, the instinct, which is to be
frightened, put the letter down, and
hope it resolves itself, is exactly
backwards.
The clock only runs against you while
nobody is doing anything.
Let me tell you about a man I will call
Harlan, 81, in Pennsylvania, a widower
living alone in the house he raised four
children in.
The letter came in the spring, and the
number on it was over $4,000,
and it referred to a period he could not
reconstruct from memory. He read it
three times. He was going to ask his son
about it when he came at the weekend.
Then the weekend came, and something
else was going on.
The letter moved from the table to the
counter, and from the counter into a
drawer with the warranty paperwork.
He was not defying anybody. He wanted to
give a correct answer rather than a
wrong one, and he wanted help doing it,
and the help was busy.
By the time the family found it, the
window to challenge the amount had
closed. He could still request a waiver,
and eventually did, and it took months.
What cost him was not the overpayment,
it was the silence. One sentence filed
on time saying that he was looking into
it would have changed the entire shape
of the next year of his life. I have
seen far more damage done by an
unanswered letter than by anything
anybody ever disclosed.
If one of these arrives at your house or
at the house of somebody you look after,
the rule is simple. Answer it the week
it arrives, even if all you can say is
that you are reviewing it.
And there is one more thing about these
letters that I want you to have because
it changes how you read them.
The number on that letter is not always
right. Overpayment calculations are
produced by systems reconciling records
from employers, from other agencies, and
from your own reporting, sometimes years
after the fact. Errors happen in both
directions, which means asking them to
show their work is not being difficult.
You are entitled to see how the figure
was calculated, and asking for that in
writing is a normal request that gets
made all the time. So, when the letter
arrives, the first move is not to panic
about the total, and it is not to start
planning how to pay it. It is to ask, in
writing, for the breakdown of how the
amount was arrived at, and for the
specific months involved. A great many
people pay back numbers they never
checked, out of a sense that a letter
from a federal agency must be correct by
definition. It is a calculation
performed by a system, and systems are
wrong sometimes, and there is a process
precisely because everybody involved
knows that.
Now, let me give you my honest read, and
it is only that, and you are welcome to
disagree with me in the comments.
There is something being said about this
system constantly right now, and I want
to handle it properly rather than either
frightening you or waving it away. You
have almost certainly heard that the
trust fund runs short sometime in the
early 2030s,
and that if nothing is done, benefits
could be reduced by something in the
region of 20% or more. That projection
is real. It comes from the system's own
trustees and from the Congressional
Budget Office, and the date has been
moving slightly closer rather than
further away. Here is what I want you to
understand about it, because both of the
popular versions are wrong. The version
that says the money runs out and payment
stop is false. Payments are funded on an
ongoing basis by people currently
working. Even in the worst modeled case,
the great majority of the benefit
continues to be funded. And the version
that says there is nothing to worry
about is also wrong, because a reduction
of that size is not a rounding error to
anyone living on it. But here is my
actual position, and it is not about the
trust fund at all. Nothing in this video
required a crisis to hurt anybody.
The measurement window that ignores 9
months of the year is current law. The
index that measures a working person's
basket rather than yours is current law.
The premium that quietly consumes the
raise is current practice. The four tax
thresholds frozen since the 1980s are
current law.
Not one of those is a future risk. Every
one of them is happening this year to
people watching this, and every one of
them was working perfectly the entire
time.
When people argue about the 2030s, they
are arguing about something that may be
legislated away long before it arrives.
And there is a reasonable case that it
will be because every previous shortfall
in this system's history was addressed
before it landed.
Meanwhile, the things in this video need
no legislation and no crisis. They are
already running.
So, I would spend far less worry on the
date in the headlines and considerably
more on the four months between October
and January because that is where your
actual income for next year gets
decided. And there is a pattern
underneath all of it that I keep running
into on this channel. Everything that
pays out gets adjusted. The benefit
rises every year, the premium rises
every year, the wage base rises every
year. Everything that decides whether
you qualify or whether you get taxed
tends to stay frozen. The provisional
income lines have not moved in 40 years.
The resource limits on the needs-based
program have not moved since the late
1980s. So, the numbers that move keep
pushing you toward the numbers that do
not, and the space between them shrinks
a little every single year without
anybody voting on anything. That is not
a conspiracy. It is what happens when a
system is built in pieces across four
decades and nobody is responsible for
looking at all of it at once. But, the
practical result is the same as if it
had been designed, which is that a
person who did everything right ends up
on the wrong side of a line that was
drawn before their grandchildren were
born and finds out about it in a spring
from a stranger.
Here is your list. Six things and none
of them take more than an afternoon.
One, ignore every projection you read
this month.
The official number arrives in the
middle of October and everything before
that is a forecast, however confidently
it is printed.
Two, when the raise is announced, do not
write down the percentage. Wait for the
Medicare premium announcement that
follows, subtract the increase from your
dollar raise and write down what
survives. That is your actual raise and
nobody will calculate it for you. Three,
use October and November properly. That
is when your drug plan and any
supplemental coverage can be changed and
it is the only window in the year when
they can.
The percentage is already decided, your
deductions are not.
Four, before the 31st of December, work
out your own provisional income. Other
income plus tax-exempt interest plus
half your benefit. Then see how close
you are to a line and look hard at any
interest or withdrawal that could land
on either side of the new year.
Five, check that your payment is going
somewhere that still exists. The right
bank, the right account, no paper check
sitting in the wrong post box. Do it now
rather than in January.
Six, if a letter ever arrives from that
agency, answer it the week it comes.
Reconsideration has a window of roughly
60 days. A waiver has no time limit at
all. And filing something generally
pauses collection while doing nothing
pauses nothing. If any of that landed
close to home, all of it is laid out in
order in the quiet rules. Link pinned at
the top of the comments.
And if your own situation is tangled, if
you are looking at a letter or a number
and cannot work out what it means, write
to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read everyone that comes in and they
decide what gets covered next. Last
thought, on the 30th of this month a
window closes on a calculation you were
never invited to participate in and in
October a number will be announced and
for one day everybody will talk about
whether it was generous or stingy. That
conversation is almost entirely beside
the point. By the time that number
reaches your account it will have passed
through a premium that rises on its own
schedule, past a tax threshold that is
not moved since the 1980s and through
whatever deductions you set up years ago
and have not looked at since.
Every one of those things is decided
somewhere between October and January.
Not one of them is announced on the news
and every one of them is something you
can actually reach. So do not spend this
month arguing about a percentage you
cannot change. Spend the next three
months on the four things you can. I am
Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: Your Pension Just Made Your Social Security Taxable

segments.text: You have a pension, which means almost
every piece of retirement advice you
have ever been given was written for
somebody else. Not badly written, just
written for a different person. Somebody
whose income in retirement moves up and
down depending on what they withdraw.
Somebody who can choose to have a low
year. You cannot have a low year. Your
pension pays what it pays on the first
of the month, whether you need it or
not, whether it helps you or hurts you.
And that one fact, the fact that your
income has a floor under it that never
drops, changes the answer to almost
every question that matters after 60. It
changes how much of your social security
gets taxed. It changes whether a
conversion makes sense. It changes what
your Medicare costs. It changes how your
investment should be positioned. And it
changes one decision that gets made
once, usually in a single afternoon,
that determines what happens to your
husband or wife after you are gone.
Here's what makes this so strange. You
are in a shrinking minority and the
advice industry has quietly stopped
writing for you. Only around 15% of
private sector workers still have access
to a traditional pension. Among state
and local government workers, it is the
large majority. So if you have one, you
are either a public servant or you are
one of the last people in the private
sector holding something that has mostly
disappeared. which means the retirement
books, the calculators, the standard
withdrawal sequence, the 4% rule, all of
it was built around the person without a
pension because that is now nearly
everybody. You inherited a rule book
that was written for a different game. I
am not a lawyer. I am not an accountant
and I am not your financial adviser.
This is educational. Your situation is
your own and you confirm anything here
with somebody licensed before acting on
it. My name is Kevin. On this channel, I
take the rules that quietly decide what
happens to your money in retirement and
lay them out in plain English while
there is still time to use them. If that
sounds useful, subscribe. I'm going to
do this differently than most videos on
this subject. Instead of listing what
the tax system does to you, I am going
to walk through the standard advice you
have been given piece by piece and show
you exactly where it breaks for somebody
with a pension. Six pieces of advice.
Every one of them is correct for most
retirees. Every one of them is wrong for
you. The first piece of advice is this.
Manage your income in retirement to
control how much of your social security
gets taxed. That is genuinely good
advice. And for somebody without a
pension, it is one of the most valuable
things they will ever hear. For you, it
is close to meaningless. And I want you
to understand exactly why. There is a
number the government calculates on you
called provisional income. It is not the
number on your tax return. And it is not
what you would call your income if a
neighbor asked. It is your other income
plus any taxexempt interest plus half of
your social security benefit. And that
number decides how much of your social
security becomes taxable. For a single
person, cross $25,000 and up to half
your benefit is taxed. Cross $34,000 and
up to 85% of it is. For a married
couple, those lines sit at $32,000 and
Now, here is the part specific to you.
Pension income counts fully toward that
number. Every dollar, there is no
exemption for it. No reduction, no
special treatment. Which means your
provisional income does not start at
zero the way it does for somebody else.
It starts at whatever your pension pays
before you touch a single dollar of
savings. Let me make that concrete. Say
your pension pays $30,000 a year and
your social security is 24,000. Add the
pension, 30,000, plus half the social
security, $12,000. That is $42,000 of
provisional income. You have not
withdrawn $1 from an account. You have
not earned a dollar of interest. And you
are already well past the second
threshold, which means up to 85% of your
social security is taxable. Now, compare
that to your neighbor. Same social
security, no pension, but $30,000 a year
coming out of a retirement account. On
paper, they look identical to you. In
practice, they are in a completely
different position because in any given
year, they can decide to withdraw less.
They can pull from a Roth instead. They
can spend from savings and take nothing
from the account at all. They have a
dial. You have a switch that is welded
on. And this is where the second effect
kicks in. The one that turns an
annoyance into something with real money
attached because your social security is
being taxed at the top of that range
already. every additional dollar you
pull out of a retirement account behaves
strangely. For most people, an extra
$1,000 of withdrawal is taxed at their
bracket and nothing else happens. For
somebody sitting where your pension put
you, that same $1,000 can also drag more
of your social security into the taxable
column at the same time. So, you are
taxed on the thousand and taxed on the
social security it pulled along with it
from one withdrawal. People who study
this call it the tax torpedo and pension
holders sail into it earlier than
anybody else because the pension carried
them into the zone before they made a
single decision of their own. And there
is a third effect underneath both of
them that hardly anybody connects to the
pension at all. Medicare premiums are
not the same for everybody. Above
certain income levels, there is a sir
charge on top of the standard premium
and it is calculated from your income 2
years earlier. Most pension holders will
never reach those thresholds on the
pension alone. But your pension is the
floor that everything else stacks on. So
when a larger conversion happens or a
property sells or a spouse dies and the
single filer thresholds cut themselves
roughly in half, you are starting that
climb from higher up than the person
next to you. Three effects, one cause,
the floor. And notice what none of them
required. None of them required you to
make a mistake. And the thing that makes
this genuinely unfair is that those
dollar thresholds were written into law
in the early 1980s with the second tier
added in the early9s and they have never
been adjusted for inflation. Not once in
40 years. $25,000 meant something
entirely different then. Today, a modest
pension alone can carry you past it
before social security is even counted.
So the first standard piece of advice,
manage your provisional income, is not
something you have the ability to do in
the way it is meant. Your floor already
puts you where you are going to be,
which does not mean nothing can be done.
It means the moves that work for you are
different, and I will get to them. Let
me tell you about a man I will call
Dale. 68, retired from a county water
department in Ohio after 31 years with a
pension he was rightly proud of and a
wife who taught elementary school. The
first spring after they both retired,
they took their paperwork to the same
preparer they had used for years, and
the number came back higher than either
of them had expected. Dale asked the
question that everybody asks. He said,
"We make less than we did when we were
working. How is the tax bigger?" And the
answer was that his social security had
gone from being mostly untacked in the
partial year to being taxed at the
maximum [clears throat] permanently
because the pension had lifted the floor
and it was never going back down.
Nobody had explained that when he
elected the pension. Nobody had
explained it at the retirement seminar.
He had a folder from his employer that
covered the health insurance in enormous
detail and did not mention provisional
income once. That is the reason I put
together the quiet rules. It is at kevin
explains.shop. There is a code on the
screen right now, so hold your phone up
to it or use the link pinned at the top
of the comments or the one in the
description below. It covers the rules
that decide what happens to your
retirement money in plain English,
including the ones that work completely
differently when a pension is involved.
You have 7 days with it. If it does not
change something about what you do next,
send it back and that is the end of it.
Dale found out from a stranger with a
calculator in the spring after the
decisions were already made. That is the
worst possible order to learn any of
this in.
The second piece of advice is this. Use
your lowinccome years between retirement
and required withdrawals to move money
into a WTH. For most retirees, that is
the single best move available to them.
There is a stretch after they stop
working and before the forced
withdrawals begin where their income
drops to the lowest it will ever be, and
they can move money out of a traditional
account cheaply during those years. You
do not have that stretch. Your pension
started, your income floor went up, and
it never came back down. There is no low
year to exploit. So the standard
conclusion is that you missed the
window. That conversions are not for you
because why would you pay 22% to convert
when somebody else gets to do it at 12.
And that conclusion is wrong, but for a
reason nobody explains properly. Here is
what actually happens to you if you do
nothing. At 73 for most people retiring
now and 75 for anyone born in 1960 or
later, you are required to start
withdrawing a minimum amount from your
traditional accounts every single year.
Those forced withdrawals do not replace
your other income. They land on top of
it. Your pension does not pause. Your
social security does not pause. The
forced withdrawal stacks on both of
them. And the percentage you are forced
to take climbs every year you age. So
somebody with a pension of 30,000,
social security of $24,000, and $400,000
in a traditional account is looking at a
first forced withdrawal in the
neighborhood of $15,000
on top of everything else. And that
number grows every single year afterward
while the account keeps growing, too.
Add it up and you are looking at 60 or
$70,000 of fully taxable income in your
70s. A large share of it forced on you
whether you wanted it or not. And here
is the piece that reframes the entire
question. You are not converting to find
a low rate. You do not have one and you
never will. You are converting to shrink
the pile before the forced withdrawals
turn a manageable situation into an
impossible one. Converting 20,000 a year
in your 60s at a rate that stings is
unpleasant. Being forced to recognize
40,000 a year in your 80s at the same
rate or higher while a pension and fully
taxed social security are already
sitting underneath it is considerably
worse. The math is not about finding a
bargain. It is about paying while you
still choose the amount. And there is
one more thing that is specific to you
and almost never mentioned. Roth money
does not count toward provisional income
and it does not count toward the
Medicare calculation. Which means for a
pension holder, every dollar moved into
a Wroth is a dollar that will never
again participate in the cascade that
your pension already started. You cannot
lower the floor. You can stop adding to
what sits on top of it. Now, the third
piece of advice, and this is the one I
would ask you to stay for, even if you
skip everything else in this video, the
advice is this. When you elect your
pension, take the option that pays the
most per month. On its face, that sounds
like arithmetic. More money is more
money. Here is the decision it is
actually attached to. When you retire
with a pension, you generally choose
between a single life option, which pays
a higher amount and stops the day you
die, and a joint and survivor option,
which pays less every month, but
continues to your husband or wife for
the rest of their life. Most people
compare the two monthly numbers, see
that one is bigger, and take it. And a
great many of them do it without ever
modeling what happens on the other side.
So let me model it because the
arithmetic is brutal and it is not what
people assume. When one spouse dies, the
household expenses do not fall by half.
The mortgage or the taxes are the same.
The utilities are almost the same. The
insurance on the house is the same.
Realistically, expenses drop by
something like 20 to 25%. But the income
does not drop by 25%. The household
loses one entire social security check,
not part of it. The survivor keeps the
larger of the two and the smaller one
stops. And if the single life option was
elected, the pension stops completely on
the same day. So the survivor is left
with roughly 75% of the expenses and
very often less than half of the
guaranteed income. That gap is what
ruins people. And it does not show up
immediately, which is what makes it so
cruel. It shows up 3 or four years later
when a retirement account that was never
sized to support one person alone has
been carrying the entire shortfall month
after month and it starts running out.
There is something else about this
decision that people do not realize
until it is too late. It is usually
permanent. Once the election is made and
the window closes in most plans it
cannot be changed. Not if circumstances
change, not if health changes, not if
you simply change your mind. And here is
a protection that exists specifically
for this which you should know about
whichever side of it you are on. In most
plans, waving the survivor benefit
requires your spouse's written consent
and in many cases it must be notorized.
That requirement exists because this
decision was being made unilaterally and
the person who paid for it was not in
the room. So here is the exercise and if
you are married and have not retired
yet, do it this month. Take your fixed
expenses and subtract about a quarter.
That is your surviving spouse's floor.
Now list what guaranteed income would
still be arriving if you died first. The
surviving social security check plus
whatever pension survivor benefit you
elected, which is zero if you chose
single life. If that number sits well
below the floor, then the higher monthly
payment is not a better deal. It is a
bet on the order in which two people die
made by the person who is not going to
have to live with the answer. The joint
and survivor option is not a worse
payout. It is insurance and the premium
is the difference between the two
monthly figures. Let me tell you about a
woman I will call Lorraine, 77. Her
husband spent his career at a utility
company and retired at 63 with a good
pension. They had a comfortable ordinary
retirement for 11 years. Cruises with
another couple, a camper for a while. He
elected the single life option. The
difference was a few hundred a month and
it made the early years feel easier. And
I do not think for one second that he
was being selfish. I think nobody sat
him down and drew the second picture. He
died at 74. Her social security dropped
to just his since his was the larger.
And on the first of the following month,
the pension simply did not arrive. Her
expenses fell by almost nothing because
she was still in the same house with the
same taxes and the same insurance. She
has been covering the difference out of
a retirement account for 3 years, and
she can tell you exactly how many years
are left in it because she has counted
more than once at the kitchen table at
night. She said the thing that made me
want to make this video. She said, "I do
not think he knew. I think if anybody
had shown him this on paper, he would
have taken the smaller check without a
moment's thought." Everything in this
video is written out in the quiet rules
in the order you would actually work
through it, including the survivor
election and the exact numbers to run
before you sign anything. Scan the code
on the screen or go to
kevinexplains.shop
or use the link at the top of the pinned
comment. 7 days to look it over and if
it does not earn its place, send it
back. Lorraine is 3 years into a
shortfall that was decided in one
afternoon in an office by a man who had
never been shown the second picture.
That decision is still ahead of some of
you. The fourth piece of advice is this.
When you think about state taxes in
retirement, look at whether the state
taxes social security. Most people do
exactly that because that is the
comparison every article makes. And for
a pension holder, it is close to the
wrong question. Pension income is
treated as its own separate category by
states, and the variation between them
is far wider than anything on the Social
Security side. Some states do not tax
pension income at all. Pennsylvania and
Illinois both exempt it entirely.
Mississippi does as well, and several
states have no income tax whatsoever,
which handles it by default. Other
states tax it as ordinary income at
their full rate. California treats
pension income as regular income, and
the top rates there are high. New York
exempts a limited amount of pension
income for people past a certain age and
taxes everything above it. And a number
of states in the middle have partial
exclusions. Exclusions that phase out
with income or special treatment
specifically for government pensions
that does not apply to private ones. Run
one comparison in your head. A $40,000
pension in a state with no pension tax
versus the same pension in a state
taxing around 9%. That is roughly $3,600
a year in difference. Over a 25-year
retirement, that is approaching $90,000.
Same pension, same house, same life. I
am not telling you to move. Moving
because of taxes alone is usually a poor
reason, and people underestimate what
leaving their community costs them. But
if you were already considering it, and
a great many retirees are, this is a
much larger number than the Social
Security comparison you have probably
been reading, and it deserves to be part
of the decision rather than an
afterthought. The fifth piece of advice
is this. As you get older, shift your
investments to be more conservative.
That is the most universally repeated
rule in retirement. It appears on every
chart, and for you, it may be actively
costing you money. Here is the thinking
behind it. As you age, you have less
time to recover from a downturn. So, you
should hold less in stocks and more in
bonds because your portfolio has to
survive you. But that entire logic rests
on an assumption. It assumes your
portfolio is what feeds you. For a
pension holder, very often it is not.
So, do the exercise properly. Add up
your fixed expenses, not your spending,
your fixed expenses. housing, utilities,
food, insurance, basic transportation,
health premiums, the things that arrive
whether you feel like it or not. Now add
up your guaranteed income, your pension
plus your social security. If the second
number covers the first, something
important is true about you that is not
true about most retirees. Your survival
is already funded. Your portfolio is not
keeping you in your house. It is paying
for travel, for grandchildren, for a car
when this one dies, for a cushion
against a health event. Those are
different jobs. And money doing a
different job should be invested
differently. Financial planners have a
term for this. They call it asset
liability matching, which sounds
technical and simply means you line up
guaranteed income against the expenses
that must be paid and then the rest of
your money is free to do something else.
And here is the part that surprises
people. Your pension is already
functioning as an enormous bond position
in your overall picture. It is a stream
of fixed payments that does not care
what the market does. That is what a
bond is. So when you put a large bond
allocation inside your retirement
account on top of it, you are counting
the same safety twice. You are buying
protection you already own and paying
for it in growth you gave up. I am not
telling you what your allocation should
be. That depends on far more than a
video can know. And it is exactly the
kind of thing to sit down with a fee
only planner about. But I am telling you
that the standard rule get more
conservative with age was written for
somebody whose portfolio is their
survival. If your pension is your
survival, that rule was not written
about you. And following it without
thinking may be the most expensive habit
in this entire video. Now the sixth and
final piece of advice. Your pension is
guaranteed income for life. So it is the
safe part of your retirement. It is
guaranteed. That part is true and it is
worth a great deal. But guaranteed and
protected are not the same word. And
here is where the difference lives. Most
pensions have no cost of living
adjustment. Some public plans do, often
capped. Most private plans have none at
all. Which means the amount that arrives
in your first year is the same amount
that arrives in your 20th. The number
never moves. Everything around it does.
At 3% inflation, $36,000 of purchasing
power today is worth roughly 27,000 in
10 years and closer to 20,000 in 20
years. The check is identical. What it
buys is not. Notice what this does over
time. Social Security has a cost of
living adjustment built into it. Your
pension mostly does not. So the longer
you live, the more your guaranteed
income quietly shifts from being pension
dominant to being social security
dominant in real terms without a single
thing changing on paper. This is
precisely why the investment account
still matters even for somebody whose
pension covers their expenses
comfortably today. That account is not
only for wants. It is your inflation
defense and it is the thing that will be
closing a widening gap in your 80s.
There is one more thing under the word
guaranteed that hardly anyone knows and
I want you to have it. If you have a
private sector pension, it is generally
backed by a federal insurance program in
the event that the plan fails. That
protection is real, but it is capped and
the cap is meaningfully lower for people
who retired early. And if you have a
public sector pension, a state or local
government plan, that federal program
does not cover you at all. public plans
are backed by the state or the
municipality and by whatever their
funding position happens to be. There is
also something happening in the private
sector right now worth watching where
companies transfer their pension
obligations to an insurance company.
When that happens, the payments usually
continue exactly as before, but the
federal protection is replaced by state
insurance guarantee coverage, which
works differently and has its own
limits. None of this is a reason to
panic. Pensions pay overwhelmingly and
the systems mostly work. But if a letter
ever arrives telling you your pension is
being transferred to an insurer, that is
not junk mail and it is worth reading
closely rather than filing. Before the
list, there is one decision I have not
touched yet and it belongs here because
it is the one moment when a pension
holder can buy back the flexibility this
entire video has been about. Some plans
offer a lump sum instead of a monthly
payment. You take the value, roll it
into a retirement account, and manage it
yourself. Most discussions of this treat
it as a return question. Will you earn
more managing it? Will you live long
enough for the monthly payment to win
the tax angle almost never gets
mentioned? And it is the more important
one. If you take the monthly payment,
every dollar is fully taxable every year
forever and you cannot move any of it.
Your provisional income floor is set for
life. If you take the lump sum, you have
bought back the dial. You choose when to
withdraw and how much and which year to
convert and whether to stay under a
Medicare threshold this year and catch
up next year. Everything a pension
holder cannot normally do becomes
possible again. But, and this is the
whole thing, the lump sum is only better
if you actually use that flexibility. If
you take it, roll it over and then
withdraw a steady amount every month
exactly as the pension would have paid
you, you have given up guaranteed income
for nothing. you took on market risk.
You took on the risk of living longer
than the money and you captured none of
the tax control that was the entire
reason to do it. If yes, the lump sum
can be worth a great deal. If you know
you will not, the monthly payment is
almost certainly the better answer and
there is no shame in that. And here is
an option most people are never told
about. A number of plans allow a partial
lump sum alongside a reduced monthly
payment. That is often the right shape.
Take enough monthly income to cover the
fixed expenses, the ones that arrive
regardless, and take the rest as a lump
sum for flexibility on everything else.
Security for the needs, control for the
rest. Ask your plan administrator
whether it is available. Most people
never ask because nobody tells them
there is a third option on a form that
appears to have two. Let me tell you
about a man I will call Everett because
he is the version of this that goes
well. 64, two years out from retiring
from a state agency. And the only reason
he learned any of this was that his
sister-in-law lost her husband and went
through what Lorraine went through. He
asked for the survivor election numbers
and sat with them properly. The joint
and survivor option cost about $400 a
month against the single life figure.
His first instinct was that 400 a month
was a lot to give up. Then he did the
exercise. He wrote down what his wife's
expenses would be alone and what income
would still arrive and the gap was not
small. He took the survivor option. He
also asked about the partial lump sum,
which nobody had mentioned. And it
turned out his plan offered one. And he
did one more thing that costs nothing
and that I would put on everybody's
list. He asked for a copy of the plan's
summary description and the actual
election form in writing a full year
before he needed to make the decision so
that he was reading it calmly at his
kitchen table instead of in an office
with somebody waiting. He described it
as the only major financial decision of
his life he did not make in a hurry. Now
my honest read on this I do not think
anybody is hiding this from pension
holders. I think something quieter
happened which is that the advice
industry followed the money. Traditional
pensions have been disappearing from the
private sector for 40 years. The people
writing retirement content, building
calculators, and producing the standard
guidance are writing for the
overwhelming majority, and the
overwhelming majority no longer has one.
So, the content that reaches you was
built around somebody with a flexible
income and a portfolio that has to feed
them. Almost none of it applies cleanly
to you, and none of it announces that.
And the group left holding pensions is
largely public servants, teachers,
firefighters, county workers, people at
utilities and water departments and
school districts. People who took lower
pay for 30 years in exchange for
security later. They got the security.
What they did not get was anybody
explaining that the security itself
creates a completely different set of
problems and that the standard playbook
would quietly work against them. Here is
your list. Six things. One, find out
what your provisional income actually
is. Your pension plus other income plus
half your social security. Most pension
holders have never calculated it and it
explains their entire tax picture. Two,
if you are not yet retired, get your
election options in writing now, all of
them, including whether a partial lump
sum exists. Read them at home, not in a
meeting. Three, if you are married, run
the survivor exercise. fixed expenses
minus about a quarter against the income
that would still arrive. Do it on paper.
This is the highest stakes item on this
list. Four, add up your fixed expenses
against your guaranteed income. And if
the guaranteed income covers them, ask a
fee only planner whether your investment
allocation is duplicating safety you
already own. Five, ask whether your
pension has a cost of living adjustment.
If it does not, plan on the number
shrinking in real terms every year for
the rest of your life and size the rest
of your money accordingly. Six, if force
withdrawals are still ahead of you, ask
what a measured conversion would cost
and ask specifically what it does to
your Medicare calculation 2 years out
because your pension is already sitting
underneath it. If any of that landed
close to home, all of it is laid out in
order in the quiet rules link pinned at
the top of the comments. And if you have
a question about your own situation,
write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read them and they shape what gets
covered next. Last thought, a pension is
a genuinely good thing to have. I want
to say that plainly because nothing in
this video was an argument against them.
And a guaranteed check for life is
something most Americans will never see.
But it comes with a second half that
nobody hands you a folder about. It sets
a floor under your income that never
moves. and everything above that floor
behaves differently because of it. The
taxes, the Medicare, the conversions,
the investments, and the one election
that decides what your spouse lives on.
You traded higher pay for security over
decades on purpose. The least the system
could have done was explain how the
security actually works. It did not. So
now you know, and there is still time to
use it. I am Kevin. Thanks for watching.
Do not forget to check the quiet rules
at kevinexplains.shop.

title: Millions Of Seniors Are Overpaying On A House They Already Paid Off

segments.text: Your house is paid off and your property
tax bill went up again this year. That
is the part that never made sense to
anybody. You spent 30 years paying off a
mortgage so that the house would finally
stop costing you money. And the one bill
that never goes away is the one that
keeps climbing. And here is what almost
nobody realizes. For a great many of
you, that bill is higher than it legally
has to be. Not because anybody cheated
you, because there are four separate
layers of protection available to older
homeowners in this country. and the
average person over 65 has claimed
exactly one of them. Most people get the
first layer, feel relieved, and stop.
They never learn that the second one
exists. The third one, almost nobody has
heard of, and it is the one that can
stop a tax bill from being collected at
all. And the fourth one is a federal
bill sitting in Congress right now that
would put real money behind the thing
you are probably already planning to do
to that house. Let me be direct about
why you have not heard this from anyone.
It is not a conspiracy. It is simpler
and more permanent than that. Your
county assessor's office is not a
benefits agency. It is a valuation
office. Their job is to determine what
your house is worth and produce a bill.
Nobody in that building is assigned to
call you and say, "We noticed you turned
65. Here are three additional programs
you have not applied for." Think about
how different that is from almost
everything else in your financial life.
Your bank tells you when a certificate
matures. Your insurer tells you when a
policy renews. Medicare sends you a
handbook every single year whether you
want one or not. The property tax system
sends you exactly one thing which is the
bill. And each of those programs is
usually a separate application filed at
a separate time, sometimes with a
separate office. Some of them have to be
refiled every single year. And if you
forget one year, it silently stops. So
the system is not hiding anything from
you. It is simply built on the
assumption that you already know what to
ask for and nobody ever told you what to
ask for. I am not a lawyer. I am not an
accountant and I am not your financial
adviser. This is educational. The rules
vary enormously by state and county and
you confirm everything with your own
assessor before you act on it. My name
is Kevin. On this channel, I take the
rules that quietly cost older Americans
money and lay them out in plain English
while there is still time to act on
them. If that is useful, subscribe. Let
me lay out the four layers first so you
know where you are in this and then we
will go through them one at a time. The
first layer is an exemption that reduces
the value your tax is calculated on. The
second layer is a ceiling, sometimes
called a freeze that locks something in
place so it stops climbing. The third
layer is a deferral that stops the
collection of the bill entirely for as
long as you live in the house. And the
fourth is the federal accessibility
credit that is being debated right now,
which is about the money you spend to
stay in the house safely. Four layers:
exemption, freeze, deferral, credit.
Most people have layer 1 and do not know
layers 2, three, and four exist. Let me
start with the first because you need to
be certain you actually have it before
anything else matters. The first layer
is the exemption, and it comes in more
than one piece. Nearly every state has a
general homestead exemption for the home
you actually live in. And on top of
that, most states have an additional
exemption specifically for homeowners 65
and older, which is separate and which
is very often not applied automatically.
That word automatically is where the
money gets lost. People assume that
because the county knows their date of
birth, the senior exemption simply
switches on the year they qualify. In
most places, it does not. It requires an
application, and if you never file it,
nothing happens. and no letter arrives
explaining what you missed. Let me show
you the size of this using one state as
the example because the numbers there
are dramatic and recent. In Texas, the
general homestead exemption for school
district taxes was raised to $140,000
and a homeowner 65 or older gets an
additional $60,000 on top of that. That
is $200,000 of value removed before the
school rate is even applied for a home
appraised at or below that figure. the
school portion of the bill effectively
disappears and those increases were made
retroactive to the previous tax year
which matters enormously and I will come
back to why. Now I am not telling you
this because you live in Texas. Most of
you do not. I am telling you because it
demonstrates the principle that applies
everywhere. The senior piece is separate
from the general piece. It is usually
not automatic and it is frequently much
larger than people expect. And here is a
detail that applies in a great many
places and that people miss entirely. If
you should have had it and did not file,
you can often go back. In Texas, a late
resident's homestead application,
including the age 65 piece, can
generally be filed up to 2 years after
the deadline, which means somebody who
turned 65 3 years ago and never applied,
may still be able to recover part of
what they overpaid. Not every state
allows that and the number of years
varies, but almost nobody asks because
it does not occur to anybody that a tax
office would give money back. Ask the
question. The worst answer you get is
no. There is also a widow and
widowerower exemption in many states and
a disabled veteran exemption and a
general disability exemption. These
frequently stack with the senior
exemption rather than replacing it.
Though the rules on stacking vary and in
some places you must choose, which is
exactly the kind of thing that requires
you to ask specifically because a form
that says senior exemption on the front
does not mention the other three. And
the widow and widowerower exemption
deserves a moment of its own because of
when it becomes relevant. It becomes
available in the year somebody loses
their husband or their wife, which is to
say, it becomes available in the single
worst year of that person's life at the
exact moment they are least likely to be
researching county tax forms. Nobody at
the funeral home mentions it. It is not
in the paperwork the hospital gives you,
and it is not going to be triggered by
anything the county does on its own. So,
if you know a widow or a widowerower,
that is the thing worth mentioning to
them gently at some point when the worst
of it is passed.
Let me tell you about a woman I will
call Wifred, 73, widowed at 68, still in
the house she and her husband bought in
1984 in a suburb outside Kansas City.
Her husband had always handled the tax
bill. After he died, she simply kept
paying whatever the envelope said, the
way you do when you were getting through
a year you did not plan for. She had the
general homestead exemption because he
had filed it decades earlier and it
carried over. She did not have the
senior exemption. She had turned 65 8
years earlier and no one had ever
mentioned there was a second form. She
did not have the widow exemption either.
When a neighbor finally asked her about
it and she called the county, the woman
on the phone was perfectly pleasant and
told her exactly what to file. It took
20 minutes. The part that stayed with
her was not the money. It was that in 8
years across eight bills, nobody had
ever once told her there was a form.
That is the reason I put together the
quiet rules. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
There is a code on the screen right now,
so hold your phone up to it or use the
link pinned at the top of the comments
or the one in the description below. It
covers the programs older homeowners are
entitled to and almost never claim in
plain English, including what to ask for
by name and in what order. You have 7
days with it. If it does not change
something about what you do next month,
send it back and we are finished.
Winifford paid eight years of bills that
a 20-minute phone call would have
lowered. Some of you are in year two of
that same phone call not being made.
Now, the second layer, and this is the
one I most want you to hear because it
is where the real long-term money is,
and it is the layer people stop before
reaching. An exemption and a freeze are
two completely different things, and the
words get used interchangeably by people
who should know better. An exemption
reduces the value your tax is calculated
on. It is a one-time reduction that
helps every year, but it does not stop
anything from rising. [clears throat] A
freeze locks something in place.
Depending on where you live, it locks
the assessed value of your home or it
