locks the actual tax amount at whatever
it was the year you qualified. Which
means that while home values in your
neighborhood keep climbing and your
neighbors bills climb with them, yours
does not move. Every year that passes,
the gap between what you pay and what
you would have paid gets wider. An
exemption saves you a fixed amount. A
freeze saves you a growing amount
forever. Let me put that difference in a
way you can feel. Two neighbors,
identical houses, both 65. One has the
exemption only. The other has the
exemption and the freeze. In year 1,
their bills are close enough that
neither of them notices anything. By
year 8, the neighborhood is appreciated.
The assessments have climbed with it,
and one of those two bills has been
climbing the whole time, while the other
has not moved at all. Neither of them
did anything different with the house.
One of them filed a second form. Roughly
a third of states have some version of a
freeze mechanism, and they work very
differently from one another. So, let me
give you the two main shapes. In Texas,
once you qualify at 65, the school
district portion of your tax is capped
at what you paid that year. The market
value of the house can double. The
school portion does not move. That is
the largest slice of a Texas tax bill,
but it covers only the school portion.
The city, the county, the hospital
district, and the special districts are
separate, and those can and do still
climb. Local governments can adopt their
own senior ceilings, and some do, and
many do not, and nobody sends you a
notice either way. In Cook County,
Illinois, the freeze works differently.
If your household income is at or below
the equalized assessed value of your
home gets frozen where it stands. And
here is the part that costs people the
most. So listen closely. That one has to
be applied for every single year. It
does not renew itself. There is no
automatic continuation. If you file it
at 68 and then have a hard year or you
are in the hospital in the spring or the
mail gets lost, it simply stops and your
value unfreezes and nothing warns you
until the bill arrives. That is not
unique to one county. A number of these
programs require annual reertification
and a number of them do not. And the
only way to know which kind you have is
to ask the specific question. So write
these words down because they are what
you actually need to say. Does this
renew automatically or do I have to
refile every year? and what month is the
deadline? Now, here is something that is
almost never discussed anywhere, and it
can erase a freeze that somebody has
held for a decade. There are ordinary,
well-intentioned things people do to a
house that quietly cancel these
protections. Adding an adult child's
name to the deed. People do this
thinking it simplifies the estate.
Depending on the state and how it is
done, it can change the ownership status
the exemption depends on, and it can
undo the freeze, transferring the house
into certain kinds of trusts. Some
trusts preserve the exemption and some
do not and the difference is technical
and completely invisible from the
outside. Moving. In many places, the
freeze does not walk with you. In some
states, there is partial portability
where a percentage of the benefit
transfers to the new home. In others,
there is none, and downsizing at 78
means starting over at whatever the new
value is. And in some jurisdictions,
renting out a portion of the property or
being away from the home for an extended
period can affect whether it still
counts as your primary residence. None
of those things are wrong to do, but
every one of them should be a
conversation with your assessor's office
before it happens rather than after
because after is when you find out, and
after is not reversible. Let me tell you
about a man I will call Alvin, 79, in
the same house on the same street in a
Chicago suburb since 1976.
He had the low-income senior freeze, and
he had held it for 6 years running. His
wife had a bad winter 3 years ago, two
hospital stays, and a spring where
nothing got done except keeping her
comfortable. The renewal form came in
the spring and went into a stack on the
kitchen counter with everything else. He
did not discover it until the following
year's bill arrived and the number was
several hundred higher than he expected.
He called and they were kind about it
and he refiled and it took effect going
forward, but the year in between was
simply gone. He said something that I
have thought about since. He said, "I
did not lose that because I could not
afford it or because I did not qualify.
I lost it because my wife was sick in
April." That is the whole design flaw in
one sentence. These programs quietly
assume that every year of your life is a
normal year. Everything I am walking you
through is written out in the quiet
rules in the order you would actually
work through it. What each layer is
called, the questions that get a real
answer out of an assessor's office and
what to check before you touch the deed.
Scan the code on the screen or go to
kevinexplains.shop
or use the link at the top of the pinned
comment. 7 days to look it over and if
it does not earn its place, send it
back. Alvin lost a year to a form on a
kitchen counter during the worst spring
of his life. That is not carelessness.
That is a system that does not account
for people being human. Now, the third
layer, and this is the one that hardly
anybody in America knows about,
including a lot of people who very much
need it right now, it is called a
deferral. Here is what it does. If you
are over a certain age, usually 65, you
can file one form that stops the
collection of your property taxes
entirely for as long as you own and live
in that home. Not reduce, stop. The tax
still occurs. It is a postponement, not
a cancellation. But collection halts and
critically so does any foreclosure
action over unpaid property tax. Roughly
a third of states offer some version of
this. Let me use Texas again because the
mechanics there are clean and well
documented. A homeowner 65 or older
files a single form with a county
appraisal district called a tax deferral
affidavit. Once it is accepted,
collection stops. The unpaid balance
acrru interest at 5% a year, which is
dramatically lower than the penalties
and interest that pile on to ordinary
delinquent taxes. The balance comes due
when the home is sold or when you move
out or from the estate after death,
generally within about 6 months of that
event. A surviving spouse who is at
least 55 can continue the deferral
rather than having it come due and you
file it once. It does not require annual
renewal. Now, I want to be honest with
you about this one because it is not
free money and I am not going to present
it as if it were. Every dollar you defer
plus the interest comes out of what the
house is eventually worth to you or to
your children. It reduces the
inheritance. That is real and you should
not file this without talking it through
with your family. And there is a second
thing worth knowing before you file.
Once a deferral is in place, some
lenders will not write a new loan
against the property because the
deferred taxes sit ahead of them as a
claim. If a reverse mortgage or a home
equity line is anywhere in your
thinking, ask about that interaction
first. But hold the two options side by
side honestly. Deferring at a low rate
of interest against penalties and
interest on delinquent taxes that run
several times higher plus the risk of
losing the house entirely is not a close
comparison for somebody who is genuinely
stuck. But look at who this is actually
for. It is for the widow who is sitting
on a paidoff house she cannot afford the
taxes on. choosing between the tax bill
and her prescriptions, watching
penalties build, genuinely frightened of
losing the only thing she has left. For
that person, a deferral is not a clever
strategy. It is the difference between
staying in the house and not. And there
are people watching this right now,
today, who are behind on a property tax
bill and are quietly terrified about it
and who have never once been told that a
one-page form exists that stops the
whole process. If that is you or
somebody you love, call the county
appraisal district or the tax office and
ask this exact question. Does this state
offer a property tax deferral for
homeowners 65 and older? And what form
do I file? That is the sentence. Nothing
else needs to be said. Now, the fourth
layer, and this one is different from
the other three because it is federal
and because it has not happened yet.
There is a bill in Congress called the
Senior Accessible Housing Tax Credit
Act. What it proposes is a federal tax
credit of up to $10,000 a year for
homeowners 60 and older for money spent
making the home safer to live in as they
age. And the list of what counts is
broader than people assume. Grab bars,
widening a doorway for a walker or a
wheelchair, converting a tub into a
walk-in shower, non-slip flooring, a
stairlift, a raised toilet, and
importantly, the labor to install any of
it, not only the materials. Here is why
this matters more than it first sounds.
Most people assume that if a doctor says
you need a modification, Medicare covers
it. Medicare will generally cover
certain equipment, a walker, a
wheelchair. It does not pay to widen
your doorway or build a ramp. The only
existing route is to deduct some
modifications as a medical expense, and
that requires itemizing and requires
your total medical costs to exceed 7 12%
of your income. Most people never reach
that, which means most people get
nothing. This bill would replace that
with a direct credit, which is a
completely different thing. A deduction
reduces the income you are taxed on. A
credit reduces the tax itself, dollar
for dollar. Now, I need to be straight
with you because I am not going to let
you plan around something that has not
happened. This is a proposal. It sits in
committee. It has been introduced before
and has not passed. And there is no
guarantee this session is different. Do
not restructure anything around it. But
if you are already thinking about a
walk-in shower or a stairlift in the
next year or two, there is a practical
thing worth doing. When you get the
estimate, ask the contractor to break
out labor and materials as separate line
items. And keep that paperwork. If this
ever passes, that breakdown is what a
credit gets calculated from. And
reconstructing it 2 years later from a
single lumpsum invoice is close to
impossible. That cost you nothing today.
And it protects you if the rules change.
And while we are on federal proposals,
there is a separate one about the tax
when you sell the home. And I covered
that in full in another video on this
channel, so I am not going to repeat it
here. What matters for today is that the
sale side and the stay side are two
different conversations and everything
in this video is about staying. Now, let
me give you the part that actually turns
all of this into money because
information is not the same as action.
And I know that a lot of people will
finish this video, agree with all of it,
and never make the call. So, let me make
the call easy. You are going to phone
your county assessor's office or the
equivalent in your state, and you are
going to ask five specific questions.
Write them down now. One, am I currently
receiving the senior exemption on this
property? And if not, what is the form
and can I file it retroactively? Two,
does this county or state have a senior
tax freeze or a tax ceiling? and is it
separate from the exemption I already
have? Three, if I have one, does it
renew automatically or do I have to
refile and what is the deadline month?
Four, is there a property tax deferral
available to homeowners my age? Five,
are there widow, disability, or veteran
exemptions that stack with what I
already have? Five questions. That is
the whole thing. And I want to say
something about how that call goes
because a lot of people avoid it out of
a feeling that they are asking for a
favor or that they will sound like they
do not know what they are doing. You are
not asking for a favor. You are asking
about programs that were written into
law specifically for you. The person
answering the phone deals with these
questions all day. And in my experience,
they are usually glad when somebody asks
the right one because most people call
to complain about a number rather than
to fix it. Ask plainly. Write down the
answers. Get the form numbers. And two
practical notes about making that call
because they matter more than they
sound. Call early in the morning and
early in the week if you can. These
offices get buried in the weeks around a
deadline. And the answer you get from
somebody who has time is a different
answer from the one you get from
somebody with 11 people on hold. And if
the first person you speak to does not
know, that is not your answer. These
offices are large. The programs are
handled by different desks. And the
person who picks up is not always the
person who knows. Ask politely who
handles exemptions and call that desk
directly. There is one more thing
standing between you and all four of
these layers and it is not eligibility.
It is a date. Almost every one of these
programs has a filing deadline and it is
very often in the spring. In Texas, it
is the end of April for the homestead
and senior exemption. Other states
cluster around similar months and some
are earlier. And here is what makes
deadlines so expensive in this specific
area. Missing one usually does not cost
you the program. It cost you the year.
You file in May instead of April. And
depending on where you are, you may
simply not receive it until the
following tax year. One month of delay,
12 months of the higher bill. Which is
why the single most useful thing some of
you will do after this video is not a
phone call at all. It is writing one
line on next year's calendar in whatever
month your county uses that says check
the property tax filings. And if you are
watching this in a month when the window
is closed, do not wait for spring to
make the call. Ask now, find out the
date, and be ready. The people who get
these benefits are not smarter than the
people who do not. They are just the
ones who called in the right month. Let
me tell you about a woman I will call
Rosland because she is the version of
this that ends well. And I want you to
see what that looks like. 76 in Arizona,
in the same house for 29 years, living
on social security and a small pension
from a hospital where she worked in
medical records. She had the general
exemption. That was all. Her
daughter-in-law watched a video very
much like this one and pushed her to
call. and Rosalyn resisted for a while
because she did not want to be a bother
and she assumed if there were something
available somebody would have said so.
She made the call in February. It took
under half an hour. She learned she
qualified for a valuation protection
program she had never heard of, which
locks the assessed value of her home in
place as long as she keeps
re-qualifying.
She learned there was a separate widow
exemption she had been eligible for
since her husband died in 2017. and she
learned the deadline for both and wrote
it on the calendar in the kitchen, which
is where it still is. What she said
afterward is the reason I'm telling you
this. She said she had assumed for years
that the reason her neighbors seemed to
manage better was that they had planned
better than she and her husband did.
They had not. They had made a phone call
she had not made. Now, let me give you
my honest read on this. I do not think
anybody designed this to be hard on
purpose, but I do think the structure of
it produces a result that nobody would
defend out loud if you asked them
directly. Here is what I mean. The
benefits are real. They are written into
law and they are genuinely generous in
some places, but they are entirely
opt-in. And they are opt-in for a
population that includes people in their
80s, people recovering from surgery,
people who have just lost a spouse,
people who do not use a computer, and
people who have never in their lives
thought of a government office as
somewhere you call to ask for something.
So the money goes to the people who are
organized, connected, and comfortable
making phone calls. And it does not go
to the people who are isolated,
grieving, or overwhelmed, which is very
nearly the exact opposite of who these
programs were written for. There is a
phrase that gets used about programs
like this. They call it uptake. Low
uptake. It sounds like a technical
problem with a chart attached to it. It
is not a technical problem. It is a
widow in Kansas City paying eight years
of bills nobody told her she could
lower. Here is your list. Six things.
And the first one takes half an hour.
One, make the call. Five questions, the
ones I gave you, assessor's office or
county tax office. Two, get form numbers
for anything you are not currently
receiving and ask specifically whether
you can file for prior years. Three,
find out whether anything you already
have needs to be refiled annually and
put that month on the calendar
permanently, not just this year. Four,
if you are behind on a property tax bill
or heading that way, ask about a
deferral before you miss another
payment. That is the single most urgent
item on this list for anyone it applies
to. Five, if you are considering putting
a child's name on the deed, moving the
house into a trust, downsizing, or
renting out part of the property, call
the assessor first and ask what it does
to your exemptions before, not after.
Six, if an accessibility renovation is
on your horizon, have the contractor
separate labor and materials on the
estimate and keep it. If any of that
landed close to home, all of it is laid
out in order in the quiet rules link
pinned at the top of the comments. And
if you have a question about your own
situation, write to me at
kevinexplainsofficial@gmail.com.
I read them and they shape what gets
covered next. Last thought, you bought
that house so it would be the one thing
that eventually stopped costing you
money. And for the mortgage, that came
true. The tax bill was never going to
stop, but it was never supposed to be
running at full price either. And for a
great many of you, it currently is. For
no reason other than that, the second
form was never mentioned. Nobody is
coming to tell you. There is no letter
and there is no reminder. And the office
that sends your bill is not the office
that would think to say anything. It is
one phone call, five questions, and
about half an hour of a Tuesday. That is
genuinely all that separates the people
who pay the lower number from the people
who do not. I am Kevin. Thanks for
watching. Do not forget to check the
quiet rules at kevinexplains.shop.

title: 12,400 Retirees Lost Over $100,000 Last Year For One Reason

segments.text: Somebody in your life already knows
roughly what you have and you probably
cannot remember telling them. It might
have been at a retirement lunch. It
might have been a comment to a neighbor
while you were both standing in a
driveway. It might have been one
sentence to your son over dinner said
with pride because you had earned the
right to say it. You were not careless.
You were being normal. You told the
people around you that after 40 years of
work, you were finally all right. And
that sentence, the harmless one, is the
most valuable piece of information
anybody could have about you. Because
from the moment it leaves your mouth, it
is no longer yours. It travels. It gets
repeated. It sits in the memory of every
person who heard it. And it quietly
shapes every financial conversation you
will ever have with them for the rest of
your life. Here is the part almost
nobody understands. You are not selected
at random. Nobody pulls names out of a
phone book. You are selected by signal.
And the strongest signal a retiree can
send is the one that says there is money
here. Let me kill the belief that does
the most damage before I go any further.
People watch a video like this and
quietly think that happens to gullible
people, to the confused, the frail, the
ones who are slipping. That is wrong and
it is dangerous because it makes you
feel safe. The people this happens to
are hospital administrators, retired
engineers, school teachers, business
owners, people who managed budgets
bigger than their own for 30 years.
Sharp people, careful people, people who
would tell you they are far too smart to
fall for anything. They are not targeted
because they are foolish. They are
targeted because they are worth
targeting. And being sharp is no defense
at all against a person who spent six
months earning your trust before they
ever mentioned money. I am not a lawyer.
I am not an accountant and I am not your
financial adviser. This is educational
and your situation is your own. So
confirm anything here with somebody
licensed before you act. My name is
Kevin. On this channel, I take the
things that quietly go wrong for
retirees and lay them out in plain
English while there is still time to do
something. If that is worth something to
you, subscribe. Let me start with the
scale because until you see the size of
it, you will not take it seriously
enough. The FBI runs a reporting center
for exactly this. And in the most recent
full year of data, Americans aged 60 and
older reported more than 7.7 billion
dollars in losses, not million, billion,
from one age group in one year. That was
a 59% increase over the year before.
More than 201,000 complaints were filed
by people over 60. And more than 12,400
of those people each lost over $100,000.
12,400 people, each of them losing six
figures in a single year. Now, hold on
to one more thing because it changes how
you read every number I just gave you.
People over 60 filed about one complaint
in five, but they accounted for roughly
37% of every dollar lost in the entire
country across every age group. You are
a fifth of the reports and more than a
third of the money. That is not a
coincidence and it is not bad luck. That
is a system that has figured out where
the money is. And the FBI says plainly
that these numbers are only a fraction
of what is really happening because most
people never report it at all. Some are
embarrassed. Some believe nothing can be
recovered and a great many do not report
because the person who took the money is
someone they love and they cannot bring
themselves to file a report against
their own child. That last one is not a
footnote. Hold on to it because it is
the first category. Let me explain how
the targeting actually works because
once you see it, you cannot unsee it.
Information about your finances
functions as intelligence. That is the
honest word for it. When you mention
that you have a good retirement account,
that the house is paid off, that you
have a pension on top of social
security, that your mother left you
something when she passed, every one of
those is a data point. And every one of
them tells a listener two things. That
there is money and roughly how much. And
that information does not stay where you
put it. The person you told mentions it
to somebody. A remark at a dinner
becomes a known fact in a social circle.
A post reaches people you have not
spoken to since the 80s. A comment in a
parking lot gets overheard by somebody
you never noticed. You cannot call it
back. There is no mechanism for taking
it back. It is simply out permanently
and working. There are four categories
of people who use it. I'm going to walk
you through all four. And the first one
is the one nobody wants to talk about.
The first category is family. I want to
say this carefully because I am not
accusing anybody's children of anything.
But the research on this is not
ambiguous and pretending otherwise would
not be doing you any favors. The
majority of financial exploitation of
older adults happens inside families.
Most often in a home where the older
person is living by somebody who has
legitimate access and it very rarely
begins as theft. It begins as need.
There is a name that elder law attorneys
use for one version of this. They call
it inheritance impatience. An adult
child who knows what the parent has, who
is under real financial pressure of
their own, who watches that parent spend
money on travel or a new roof or medical
care, and who slowly begins to think of
that money as already spoken for. It
starts with a loan that is never repaid.
Then another request. Then a suggestion
that you do not really need to spend
that much on something. Then a growing
role in your decisions. Then in the
worst cases, a power of attorney and a
gradual distance from anyone who might
ask questions. And here is the thing I
most need you to understand because it
applies even when nobody in your family
is anything but good. When your child
knows the exact number, the texture of
every difficult conversation changes
forever. You feel a pressure not to say
no that you would not otherwise feel.
They calibrate what they ask for to what
they know is sitting there. Neither of
you is being dishonest. It is simply
what knowledge does to a room. The
parent who cannot say no is not weak.
They are responding to a real dynamic
that they created by accident years
earlier with one sentence. Let me tell
you about a man I will call Roland. 71,
retired from a county road department in
Indiana, widowed and rightly proud of
what he had put together. Paid off
house, a retirement account that was
better than he ever expected it to be.
He told his two children the whole
picture the year he retired. He thought
he was being open with them. He thought
secrecy between a father and his kids
was a kind of insult. Nothing dramatic
happened. Nobody stole anything. That is
exactly why I want to tell you about
him. What happened was that over four
years, in small pieces, he became a
source. A loan for a truck that was
never mentioned again, help with a
bathroom renovation, a co-signed note,
and a slow shift where his own spending
started getting quiet commentary from
people who were counting on what was
left. He stopped mentioning things he
wanted to do. He talked himself out of a
trip he had been planning for 11 years.
And when he described why, he could not
point to anyone who had actually told
him not to go. He said, "I do not think
they did anything wrong. I think I told
them something I should not have, and
everything after that was just people
being people. That is the honest version
of this problem, and it is far more
common than outright theft. That is the
reason I put together the quiet rules.
It is at kevinexplains.shop.
There is a code on the screen right now,
so hold your phone up to it or use the
link pinned at the top of the comments
or the one in the description below. It
covers the structures that protect what
you built in plain English in the order
you would actually set them up, what to
sign, what never to sign, what to tell
people, and what to keep between you and
a professional. You have seven days with
it. If it does not change something
about how you handle this, send it back
and we are done. Roland did not lose his
money. He lost the ability to make a
decision without an audience. Some of
you know exactly what that feels like.
The second category is the one that
comes through people you already trust.
These are adviserss, salespeople,
neighbors, people from your church,
somebody from a club or a community
group. They are not strangers. That is
the entire point. The most expensive
version of this is investment fraud and
it is now by a wide margin the costliest
thing happening to retirees in this
country. In the most recent year of FBI
data, investment fraud alone accounted
for over $3.5 billion dollars in losses
among people over 60. That is nearly
half of all elder fraud losses from one
category. And the victims are not who
you would picture. They are educated.
Many of them are financially
experienced. They did not fall for a
stranger. They trusted somebody who was
introduced to them by somebody they
already trusted. That is called affinity
fraud. And the mechanism is beautiful in
the worst possible way. The person
builds credibility through a shared
community first before money is ever
mentioned. By the time the pitch comes,
you do not think of them as a salesman.
You think of them as somebody from
church or somebody your neighbor vouched
for. And the thing that made you worth
approaching in the first place was
information you shared in the most
ordinary way possible. Here is the
single clearest warning sign and I want
you to memorize it because it is the one
that catches educated people. Guaranteed
returns. If somebody tells you an
investment is guaranteed to return 10%
or 12% or anything meaningfully above
what a government bond pays, that is not
an aggressive investment. That is not a
special opportunity. It is not real.
Guaranteed and high do not exist in the
same sentence. They never have. Anyone
offering both is either lying to you or
has been lied to themselves. And either
way, your money goes to the same place.
There is a version of the second
category that is growing faster than
anything else. And it deserves its own
moment because of who it targets. It is
called confidence fraud. Sometimes
romance fraud. And the setup never
changes. Somebody enters your world who
appears to be a peer, successful, warm,
financially comfortable, interested in
you through a dating site, a community
group, a shared interest, a message that
seemed like a wrong number. The
relationship builds over weeks or
months. Nothing is asked for. That is
the investment they are making. Then
eventually the conversation turns to
money. They have been doing well on a
platform you have never heard of. They
offer to show you. The account shows
your returns going up in real time. you
put in more and then one day the
withdrawal requires a fee or the
platform will not load or the person is
simply gone. I want to be very careful
about how I describe these victims
because the usual word is wrong. They
are not naive. They are lonely. Those
are completely different things.
Retirement creates real isolation
especially after losing a spouse or
moving somewhere new. That isolation is
as real a vulnerability as anything
medical. And the people running these
operations know it precisely. They will
spend four months being kind to somebody
before they ever mention a dollar. The
third category is strangers who contact
you directly. Government impersonators,
fake technology support, the call that
says your account has been compromised.
Let me give you the rules that end all
of these and they are short. The
Internal Revenue Service does not call
you. Social Security does not call to
verify your account information.
Medicare does not call asking for a bank
account number. No government agency
will ever ask you to resolve anything
with a gift card, a wire, a
cryptocurrency machine, or a payment
application. Any call claiming to be a
government agency that involves money,
personal information, or a threat is a
scam every time without exception. There
is no version of that call that is real.
And there is a piece of this that is new
and genuinely frightening. And I would
rather you hear it from me than
experience it. Artificial intelligence
voice cloning. The technology now needs
only a few seconds of somebody's
recorded voice to reproduce it
convincingly. And there is a great deal
of recorded voice available. A video
your grandchild posted. A voicemail
greeting. A clip from a family event
somebody put online. So the call comes
and it is your grandson's voice panicked
crying. he has been in an accident or
arrested and he needs money right now.
And please do not tell his parents. In
the most recent FBI data, seniors
reported over $350 million in losses
tied to fraud involving artificial
intelligence. It is now large enough
that the report has a dedicated section
on it for the first time. The urgency in
that call is not incidental. It is the
whole design. It exists specifically to
stop you from thinking because if you
have 30 seconds to think it falls apart.
So here is the counter measure and it
costs nothing. Pick a code word with
your family. One word, something no
stranger could guess and nothing that
appears anywhere online. Anybody calling
you with a financial emergency has to
say the word. If they cannot, you hang
up and you call that person back on the
number you already have saved, not the
number that called you. And if the
person on the phone tells you there is
no time to verify, that is the
confirmation. A real emergency survives
a five-minute phone call. A scam does
not. This only works if you set it up
before the call. In the moment, you will
not think of it. That is the entire
point of the moment. And here is a small
one that almost nobody does. Change your
voicemail greeting so it is not your
voice. Use the automated one your phone
came with, the one that just reads your
number back. Your outgoing greeting is a
free, permanently available recording of
you speaking, sitting there for anyone
who dials the number. It takes 2 minutes
to change it, and it removes you from
the easiest source of cloning material
there is. Let me tell you about a woman
I will call Glenda, 67, widowed for 2
years, in a town in Missouri where she
had lived her entire adult life. She was
not isolated in the way people picture.
She had friends, she went to things, but
she had lost the person she talked to at
the end of every day. And that is a
specific kind of alone that people who
have not been through it do not
understand. A man began talking to her
in a group online for people who had
lost a spouse. He had lost his wife,
too. He was kind. He was consistent. And
for 5 months, he asked her for
absolutely nothing. It was almost half a
year before money came up at all. And
when it did, it came up as something he
was doing for himself, not as a request.
She had to ask him about it. She lost
$41,000 before it stopped. and she has
never told her children. What she said
afterward has stayed with me. She said,
"I would like people to know that I was
not stupid. I was just so glad somebody
was there at 9:00 at night. Everything I
am walking through here is written out
in the choir rules in the order you
would actually put it in place. The
exact language for a power of attorney
that protects you, the forms to file,
the accounts to lock, and what to say
when somebody asks you a question you
should not answer. Scan the code on the
screen or go to kevinexplains.shop shop
or use the link at the top of the pin
comment. 7 days to look it over and if
it does not earn its place, send it
back. Glenda had every protection in
this video available to her. Free and
nobody had ever told her a single one of
them existed. The fourth category is not
a person at all. It is time. Every
decision you make today about who knows
what about your money is still in force
in 15 years. The neighbor you told about
your retirement account in 2026 still
knows in 2041. The son who knows your
estate plan still knows. The adviser
with full visibility into your accounts
still has it. And here is the
uncomfortable part. The person
evaluating those relationships in 15
years is not you as you are today. The
specific mental functions that detect
deception and weigh risk tend to decline
faster with age than general
intelligence does. Which means somebody
can be entirely sharp, entirely capable,
still doing the crossword, still
managing their own affairs, and be
measurably less able to spot a
manipulation than they were at 65. That
is not an insult, and it is not a
prediction about you personally. It is
simply the reason the strongest
protections are the ones built early by
a clear mind before anybody needs them.
The version of you at 82 will be living
inside every decision the version of you
at 68 made about who to tell and who to
trust. Build the fence now while you are
the one holding the hammer. Now, let me
give you something that is almost never
mentioned anywhere and it costs families
a great deal. Obituaries. When somebody
dies, the family writes an obituary and
it is published online where it stays
permanently. And what does a standard
obituary contain? the deceased person's
full name and age, the surviving
spouse's full name, the town, the
children's names, and often their
cities, sometimes the employer, the
church, and the funeral date, which
tells anyone reading exactly when the
house will be empty. That is a complete
targeting profile published voluntarily
at the single most vulnerable moment in
a person's life, and it is indexed and
searchable forever. There is a
documented pattern of new widows
receiving a wave of calls, letters, and
visits within weeks, fake debts
belonging to the deceased, urgent
insurance matters, investment help,
somebody who says they had an
arrangement with your husband. You do
not have to skip an obituary, but you
can write one that honors somebody
without publishing an intelligence file.
Leave out the survivors full names and
towns. Leave out the specific service
time if the house will be empty. Do not
mention what anyone did for a living or
what they left behind. And if you have
lost somebody in the last 2 years and
the calls started, now you know why. It
was not a coincidence and it was not the
universe. It was a search result. The
same goes for property records, which
most people do not realize are public.
Your name, your address, what you paid
for the house, the assessed value, and
in many states, whether there is still a
mortgage on it, are sitting in a county
database that anybody can search from a
laptop. which means somebody can know
that you own a home outright without
ever speaking to you. That is exactly
why people over 62 get the reverse
mortgage mail, the refinancing offers,
and the home equity pitches at rates far
above what younger homeowners see. The
equity is visible and the age is
inferable. You cannot remove yourself
from those records. What you can do is
treat every unsolicited contact about
your house, your equity, or your
mortgage as what it is, which is
somebody who read a public file and
decided you were worth a phone call.
Now, here is the part I think matters
most because everything so far has been
about what not to say. Let me give you
what to say instead. People struggle
with this. They do not want to lie and
they do not want to be rude. And so they
end up telling the truth because they
cannot think of a third option in the
moment. So here are four sentences.
Learn them now and they will be there
when you need them. When somebody asks
how your retirement is going, you say,
"We are comfortable. We planned
carefully and we are doing fine." That
is completely true. It says nothing.
When somebody asks a direct number
question, and people do, you say, "I
keep the details between me and my
accountant. Nobody argues with that
sentence. It is polite. It is final. and
it does not accuse anyone of anything.
When an adult child asks about the
estate, you say everything is set up
properly. It is documented and you are
taken care of. Notice what that does. It
gives real reassurance about the thing
they actually need to know without
giving a number that changes how they
behave. And when an investment
opportunity comes from somebody you
know, you say, "I do not make financial
decisions the same day I hear about
them, and I run everything past my
adviser first." That one sentence ends
nearly every scam that exists because
none of them survive a delay and none of
them survive a second opinion. Say it
kindly and say it every time. Now, the
structures. These are the things that
protect you whether or not you say the
right sentence on a given day. And most
of them are free. The first is a trusted
contact at every financial institution
you use. Federal rules now require
investment firms to ask you to name one,
and most banks offer it, too. A trusted
contact cannot move a dollar. They have
no access and no authority. All they can
do is receive a phone call from your
bank if the bank sees something strange
or cannot reach you. It is one of the
strongest and most ignored protections
available. And it takes one phone call.
And be deliberate about who it is. It
should be somebody with no financial
stake in your estate, a sibling, a
longtime friend, a professional, not the
person who inherits. The second is the
durable power of attorney. And I need to
be very direct about this one because it
cuts both ways. You need one. Without
it, if something happens, your family
may have to go to court to get authority
over your affairs. And that process is
slow, expensive, and public. But a power
of attorney is also the single legal
instrument through which more elder
financial exploitation happens than any
other because it hands somebody broad
authority over your accounts and your
property, and actions taken under it are
extremely hard to undo. So, be
deliberate. Consider a springing power
of attorney, one that only activates
under specific conditions rather than
one that is live the day you sign it.
Consider naming two people who must both
agree above a certain dollar amount.
Tell your bank who your agent is and ask
them to flag unusual requests to your
trusted contact and apply three tests to
whoever you are considering. Are they
currently under financial pressure? Have
they asked you for money recently? Do
they stand to gain from moving your
money faster? Those are uncomfortable
questions to ask about people you love.
Ask them anyway. It is far more
uncomfortable to have not asked. The
third is a credit freeze at all three
credit bureaus. It is free. It is
permanent until you lift it and it stops
somebody from opening an account in your
name. If you are not applying for
credit, there is no reason not to have
one in place today. The fourth is
verification and it takes 5 minutes.
Before you give anyone access to your
money, you can check them. Any
legitimate broker or firm in the United
States appears in a free public database
called broker check run by the industry
regulator along with their entire
disciplinary history. Investment
advisors appear in a similar database
run by the Securities and Exchange
Commission. If the person you are
considering does not appear or appears
with complaints and sanctions attached,
that is your answer. free 5 minutes and
it has prevented more losses than any
warning ever written. And the fifth is
the simplest and possibly the best. A
rule about time. No money leaves your
accounts in under 72 hours. Ever for
anyone, no exceptions, including family.
Write it on a card and put it where you
take phone calls. Every scheme in this
video depends on speed. The panicked
grandchild, the closing window on the
investment, the agent who needs it
resolved today. Not one of them survives
three days of sunlight. And a legitimate
opportunity is still legitimate. On
Thursday, let me tell you about a man I
will call Merryill because I want you to
see what this looks like when somebody
gets it right. 74, retired from
engineering in Michigan, married. He
told his wife and his accountant the
complete picture. And that was the
entire list. Not his three children, not
his brother, not the men he golfed with
twice a week for 11 years. His children
know he is comfortable. They know there
is a will and they know they are in it.
They know it has been handled properly.
They do not know a single number. He
decided this deliberately the year he
retired and the way he explained it has
stayed with me. He said he did not want
anybody in his family making decisions
about their own lives based on what they
expected to get from him. He wanted them
building their own things and he wanted
to be able to spend his own money
without a committee. In six years,
nobody has asked him for a large loan.
Nobody has suggested he does not need to
buy something. Nobody has raised the
subject of his estate documents. He is
honest that he cannot prove those things
are connected. He also does not
particularly care. He describes the
freedom of making a financial decision
without an audience as one of the better
things about his retirement. And here is
the part worth sitting with. Merryill is
not secretive with his family. He is
close to them. He simply understood that
there is a difference between being open
about your life and publishing your
balance sheet. Now, let me give you my
honest read on this. There is a norm
that wealthy families have passed down
for generations that almost nobody in an
ordinary middle-class retirement was
ever taught. It is very simple. You do
not discuss your net worth socially. Not
the number, not the breakdown, not the
inheritance, not the sale. You discuss
what you are doing and how everyone is.
The financial details stay with your
adviserss. That did not develop because
those families are ashamed of their
money. It developed because generation
after generation learned the same
lesson, which is that financial
disclosure creates dynamics with family,
with friends, with strangers that almost
never work in favor of the person who
disclosed. And here is the thing I find
genuinely unfair about it. Nobody
teaches this to the people who need it
most. If you inherited money, somebody
taught you these rules at 19. If you
built it yourself over 40 years of work,
nobody taught you anything because the
people who would have taught you were
also working. So, an entire generation
reached retirement with real money for
the first time in their family's history
and no cultural instruction whatsoever
on how to hold it quietly. And then we
call them careless when it goes wrong.
They were not careless. They were never
told. There is a real difference and it
matters. One more thing before the
checklist and I want to say it plainly
for a specific group of people watching.
If some of this has already happened to
you, I want you to hear something
clearly. It was not your fault and the
shame you are carrying is doing more
damage than the loss. The FBI is
explicit that most of this never gets
reported and embarrassment is the main
reason. Which means the same people get
to do it again to somebody else next
month. If it involved a stranger or an

There is a filling phase and there is an
emptying phase and almost everybody
pours enormous care into the first one
and gives no thought at all to the
second.
The emptying is where it is quietly won
or lost. Your partner is not going to
write to you. There is no notice, no
deadline, no reminder in the mail. They
are simply going to wait patiently while
you keep doing the responsible sounding
thing until the day the choice is no
longer yours.
The window is open right now. It is the
only part of this you actually control
and it closes one December at a time.
I am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: After 60, The IRS Has 5 Ways To Take Your Money Back

segments.text: Something changes about your money the
year you turn 60, and nobody sends you a
letter about it. Your balance looks the
same, your check arrives on the same
day, nothing on any statement anywhere
tells you that a clock started. But, it
did.
From that point forward, there are five
separate mechanisms sitting between you
and the money you spent 40 years
building. Not one of them is a penalty.
Not one of them is triggered by anything
you did wrong. They are triggered by the
fact that you saved. That is the part
people cannot get their heads around it
first. If you had spent it all, most of
this would never touch you. Because you
were careful, all five of them are
pointed directly at you.
Let me clear up the thing that does the
most damage before I go one more
sentence. There is a belief sitting in a
lot of living rooms right now that this
is a wealthy person's problem. That if
you are living on a modest pension and a
social security check, none of this
reaches you. That is backwards,
completely backwards. Every single one
of these five mechanisms was designed
decades ago to touch only people with
real money. Every single one of them now
reaches straight into the middle of an
ordinary retirement, and it happened
without a single vote, without a single
new law, purely because the lines were
frozen and everything else kept rising.
It catches the retired teacher, the
nurse who worked nights for 30 years,
the couple who paid off the house and
thought that was the end of the hard
part. So, stay with me because the
difference between the person who keeps
this money and the person who hands it
over is not income. It is
[clears throat] knowing what is coming
while there is still time to move. I am
not a lawyer, I am not an accountant,
and I am not your financial advisor.
Everything here is educational and based
on the rules as they stand right now.
Your situation is your own, so confirm
anything here with somebody licensed
before you act on it. My name is Kevin.
On this channel, I take the rules that
decide what happens to your money after
60, the ones nobody explains until it is
too late to use them, and I lay them out
in plain English. If that is useful to
you, subscribe because these five things
are running against honest retirees
every single year, and the only defense
is seeing them coming.
Let me start with the first one, and it
is the one that makes people angriest
when they finally understand what
happened. The first thing is this, up to
85% of the Social Security you already
paid for gets pulled back into your
taxable income and taxed a second time.
Sit with that because most people do not
believe it the first time they hear it.
Depending on your income, as much as 85%
of your benefit gets counted as taxable
income and taxed all over again. Not 8%,
not 18, 85% of the thing you already
funded. Here is the mechanism, and here
is the part that should genuinely make
you angry.
There is a number the government
calculates on you that you have almost
certainly never heard of. It is called
your provisional income. Some people
call it combined income.
It is not the number on the bottom of
your tax return, and it is not what you
would call your income if somebody asked
you at church.
It is your other income plus any
tax-exempt interest plus half of your
Social Security benefit.
For a single person, if that number
crosses $25,000,
up to half your benefit becomes taxable.
Cross 34,000 and up to 85% of it does.
For a married couple, those two lines
Now, here is the outrage.
Those dollar figures were written into
law in the early 1980s.
The second tier was added in the early
'90s, and they have never been adjusted
for inflation, not once, not in 40
years. Think about what $25,000 meant in
A retiree with that kind of income was
doing genuinely well.
This tax was sold to the public as
something that would touch about one
retiree in 10, and at the time that was
true. Today, $25,000 is a tight
retirement. And because the line never
moved while everything else in your life
did, this now reaches more than half of
everyone collecting a benefit. And here
is the cruelest turn inside that. Every
year your Social Security gets a cost of
living increase, a small raise meant to
help you keep up. That raise increases
your benefit. Your benefit is half of
the provisional income calculation. So,
the raise pushes your provisional income
up, which can push you over a line,
which makes more of your benefit
taxable. The raise that was supposed to
protect you from inflation can be the
exact thing that triggers a new tax on
you. For a household sitting just under
one of those lines, the cost of living
adjustment gives with one hand and takes
with the other in the same month. Let me
put real numbers on it so you can feel
how low these lines actually sit.
Picture a woman living alone collecting
around $24,000 a year in Social
Security. That is 2,000 a month, which
is not a comfortable life anywhere in
this country. She pulls another 18,000
from a traditional retirement account to
cover the rest. Watch the arithmetic.
18,000 from the account plus half her
Social Security, which is 12,000. That
is $30,000 of provisional income. She
has already blown past the first line. A
meaningful chunk of her Social Security
is now taxable. This is a woman living
on about $42,000 a year total before
taxes. And the government is reaching
into her Social Security anyway. That is
how low those frozen lines are. Not a
wealthy person, not close. And there is
a version of this that is worse and
almost nobody talks about it. So, I want
you to hear it now rather than the hard
way.
When one spouse in a married couple
dies, the survivor does not keep the
married thresholds. The very next tax
year, that person files as a single
filer.
The lines drop from 32 and 44,000 down
So, income goes down slightly and the
thresholds go down enormously, which
means a widow can be pushed into a
higher effective tax situation in the
worst year of her life on less money
than the household had before.
There was a woman I will call Lurline,
67, widowed 18 months, living in the
same house she and her husband bought in
1981. Her income did not change much
when he died. She went from two social
security checks down to one, but it was
the larger one and his pension continued
at half. On paper, she lost maybe $400 a
month. That first spring, she took the
paperwork to a preparer and the number
at the bottom was almost $1,100 more
than the couple had ever paid in a
single year on less income. There was no
mistake. She had simply become a single
filer and the lines had cut themselves
in half around her while she was
grieving.
She said the thing I hear more than any
other sentence in this line of work,
"Somebody should have told me."
And nobody had.
Not the preparer, not the agency, not
the pension office.
Every one of them was doing its job
correctly. Not one of them had the job
of warning her. And she is right.
Somebody should have.
This is why I put together the quiet
rules. It is a plain English reference
for the rules that quietly decide what
happens to your money after 60.
Not theory, not a seminar, not
somebody's pitch. The actual lines,
where they sit, what crosses them, and
how to check your own position at your
own kitchen table in an afternoon.
It is at kevinexplains.shop.
There is a code on the screen right now,
so hold your phone up to it or use the
link pinned at the very top of the
comments or the one sitting in the
description under this video.
You have 7 days with it. If it does not
change something about what you do next
month, send it back. No argument, no
questions from me.
I would much rather you found your own
line while you can still stand on the
right side of it then find it the way
Lurleen did in a spring from a stranger
with a calculator. Now, let me give you
the second thing and this one is more
direct because it does not just tax your
money, it reaches in and takes it out of
the account whether you want it out or
not. The second thing is this, at a
certain age the government forces you to
withdraw your own savings and then taxes
every dollar it forced out. Your whole
working life you were told to save in a
traditional account. An individual
retirement account, a workplace plan,
whatever your employer offered. What was
left out of that sentence is who decides
when later is.
Once you reach the required age, the
government forces you to start pulling a
minimum amount out of those accounts
every single year for the rest of your
life.
These are called required minimum
distributions and required is not a
figure of speech. The government waited
decades to tax that money and now it
forces it out into the open where it
becomes ordinary income taxed at the
same rate as a paycheck. Now, here is
something that almost every video on
this subject gets wrong and it matters
enormously to anyone watching this who
is in their early 60s right now. The
required age is not 73 for everyone. For
people already in their 70s, it is 73.
But for anyone born in 1960 or later,
the age is 75. If you are 66 today, your
first forced withdrawal is nine years
away, not seven. That is two additional
years of the most valuable planning
window of your life. And a great many
people are working off the wrong number
and shortening their own runway for no
reason. Check your birth year. That
single fact changes the size of
everything I am about to tell you.
And if you are already past that age,
the window is behind you. But the
sourcing move and the charitable move I
will get to later both still work and
they work well. And the amount you are
forced to take is not fixed. It is a
percentage of your account balance, and
that percentage climbs every year you
age. Somebody with $800,000 in a
traditional account can be forced to
recognize around $30,000 of income in
the very first year, and more the year
after that, and more after that. Now,
understand what actually happened here,
because this is the part that should
change how you look at that account
statement. For decades, you thought of
that balance as your money. It is mostly
yours.
But, the government has always quietly
held a claim on a slice of it, which is
the tax you deferred every year you
contributed. And there is a threat
behind it, because of course there is.
Miss a required withdrawal, and there is
a penalty on the amount you should have
taken and did not. It can be reduced if
you correct it quickly, but it is real
and it is steep. There is one specific
trap inside this that catches people in
the very first year, and I want you to
have it now rather than discover it.
Your first required withdrawal has a
delayed deadline. You are allowed to
postpone that one into the following
April. It sounds like a kindness. It is
a trap. Because the second year's
withdrawal is still due that same
December. So, if you take the delay, two
forced withdrawals land inside one
calendar year, stacked on top of each
other, doubling the income that hits
your return.
That single choice can push somebody
through a threshold they would never
have crossed otherwise, and it walks
them straight into the third thing on
this list. The third thing is this.
The government uses the income it forced
you to take to raise the price of your
own health care. This one is sneaky
because it does not arrive looking like
a tax. It arrives looking like a
Medicare bill. Your Medicare premiums,
the parts that cover doctors and
prescriptions, are not the same for
everybody.
Above certain income levels, you pay a
surcharge on top of the standard
premium.
Your income sets it off.
And what raises your income in
retirement is the forced withdrawal we
just discussed, and the social security
that became taxable before that. So,
watch the trap close. The government
forces the withdrawal. The withdrawal
raises your income. The higher income
crosses a Medicare surcharge line. Your
premium jumps, sometimes by hundreds of
dollars a month.
Right now, those lines started around
for a single person, and around $218,000
for a couple.
Most people watching this will never see
those numbers, and that is exactly why I
need you to hear the next part. Because
there are two situations where ordinary
households hit them anyway. The first is
a single large event, selling a rental
property, cashing a stack of savings
bonds that finally matured, a large
one-time conversion. Any of those can
spike a single year's income far above
what your life actually looks like.
The second is the widow situation again.
The single threshold is roughly half the
married one, so the surviving spouse is
measured against a line that just fell
while her income barely moved.
And here is the detail that makes this
almost impossible to see coming.
The surcharge is based on your income
from 2 years ago.
The premium you pay this year was
decided by a tax return you filed two
springs back and have not thought about
since.
So, a one-time event today quietly
raises your health care costs 2 years
from now, long after you have forgotten
what caused it.
People open the letter, cannot connect
it to anything, and simply pay. And it
is not a gradual slope. It is a cliff.
$1 over the line and you owe the entire
surcharge for that tier, not a portion
of it. $1 of interest, $1 of extra
withdrawal, and the price of the whole
step lands on you. Now, I am going to
give you something here that I almost
never see covered, and it is the single
most useful thing in this section,
especially for anybody watching who has
already been hit.
If the income that triggered your
surcharge came from something that is
over, you can ask them to look again.
There is a form for it. It is Social
Security form SSA-44,
and it exists specifically for what they
call a life-changing event. Retiring
counts. Stopping work counts. The death
of a spouse counts. Divorce counts.
Losing a pension counts. You do not have
to simply accept that. You file the
form. You show what actually changed,
and they can recalculate using your
current situation instead of a year that
no longer exists. It is free. It takes
one afternoon, and the number of people
paying a surcharge right now that they
could get removed is not small, because
nobody tells them the door is there.
There is no deadline that closes this
forever, either. If your circumstances
changed, you can ask. And if they say
no, you can appeal the answer. Write
that down. SSA-44.
Let me tell you about a man I will call
Hollis.
69 years old, retired from a utility
company, careful with everything his
entire life.
He and his wife sold a rental duplex
they had owned since the '90s.
One transaction, one year, one large
gain. He knew the sale was taxable. He
planned for that part. He paid the
capital gains, and he did not complain
about it. What he did not plan for
arrived 22 months later in an envelope
with no explanation he could follow.
His Medicare premium and hers had both
jumped. Together, it came to a little
over $4,000 across the year for exactly
the same coverage they had the year
before. Not the sale. That one was real.
But he had also stopped working in that
window, and nobody ever mentioned that a
form existed to say so. $4,000 because
of one sheet of paper nobody handed him.
The Quiet Rules is my attempt to be the
person who tells you. Scan the code on
the screen or go to kevinexplains.shop
or use the link at the top of the pinned
comment. 7 days to look it over. If it
does not earn its place, send it back,
and that is the end of it.
Hollis paid $4,000 to learn a form
number. You can learn it tonight for
nothing at all before the envelope shows
up with your name on it. Now, let me
give you the fourth thing, because this
is the one that almost nobody
understands, including a fair number of
people who prepare taxes for a living.
The fourth thing is this. The government
takes far more out of each additional
dollar than the bracket you think you
are in.
This one is subtle, so let me make it
plain because it is costing people money
they never see leave. You probably
believe you know your bracket. You
think, "I am in the 12% bracket, so an
extra $1,000 cost me 120 in tax."
Here is why. Remember that the taxation
of your Social Security depends on your
provisional income. So, every extra
dollar you pull out does two jobs at
once. It gets taxed itself, and it drags
more of your Social Security into the
taxable zone alongside it.
$1 out of the account can create almost
$2 of new taxable income. Let me walk
the math slowly. Say you take an extra
$1,000 out of a traditional account, and
you believe you are in the 12% bracket.
You expect that to cost about $120.
But, that thousand also raised your
provisional income, which can pull, say,
another $850 of your Social Security
into taxable territory,
money that was not being taxed the day
before.
So, you are not being taxed on $1,000.
You are being taxed on 1,850.
At the same 12%, that $1,000 withdrawal
did not cost you 120. It cost more than
double that.
People who study this call it the tax
torpedo, and it is a good name because
it hits below the waterline where nobody
is looking.
Inside a certain income range, every
additional dollar can carry an effective
cost of 22, 30, in some cases over 40%
once you count the Social Security it
dragged along with it. And there is a
second version of the same effect
running right now that is brand new.
There is a special additional deduction
available to people 65 and older worth
$6,000 per person sitting on top of the
standard deduction. It is real, it is
available now, and it runs through 2028.
But it phases out above $75,000 for a
single filer and 150,000 for a couple.
And while it is phasing out every extra
dollar of income is also shrinking that
deduction. So in that band you are taxed
on the dollar, taxed on the Social
Security it pulled in, and losing part
of your deduction all at the same time
from the same dollar. Now here is the
fifth thing and in some ways it is the
hardest one because it is not a tax at
all. It is an opportunity that gets
quietly taken from you. The fifth thing
is this. The government takes your best
tax planning years simply by staying
quiet while the clock runs out. Here is
the situation and I want you to find
yourself in it. Between the day you
retire, often in your early or middle
60s, and the day the forced withdrawals
begin, there is a window. In those years
you may not have claimed Social Security
yet or you claimed only part of what you
will eventually get. You are not being
forced to take anything out of your
accounts. Your income is very likely the
lowest it will ever be again for the
rest of your life. That window is the
single greatest tax planning opportunity
you will ever have and for most people
it is somewhere between 8 and 13 years
long. And here is what actually happens
to most people. Then they reach the
required age. The forced withdrawals
begin. The Social Security tax arrives.
The surcharge arrives two years behind
it. And every one of those quiet years
is gone and cannot be bought back at any
price. This is what makes the fifth one
different from the other four. The first
four are things the system does to you.
It taxes. It forces. It surcharges. It
stacks.
The fifth one requires the system to do
absolutely nothing at all. It only has
to stay quiet and let the calendar run.
The window does not announce itself. No
letter arrives saying this is the year.
It opens silently the day you stop
working, stays open through your 60s,
and closes for good at 73 or 75, whether
you used a single day of it or not. So,
those are the five. Your social security
taxed a second time on lines frozen for
40 years. Your own savings forced out
and taxed on somebody else's schedule.
>> [snorts]
>> Your health care made more expensive by
the income they forced. More taken from
each extra dollar than any bracket table
admits.
And your best years quietly lost while
nobody says a word. Now, let me show you
how to fight all five because every one
of them bends and two of them can be
avoided almost entirely. And here is the
good part. It is nearly the same handful
of moves against all five because they
are not really five separate problems.
They are one machine with five arms.
The forced withdrawal feeds the social
security tax. Those two together feed
the Medicare surcharge. The stacking
multiplies whatever the other three
produce. And the lost window is what
leaves you standing there without a
defense while it happens.
The first move, and the most powerful
one by a distance, is a conversion done
inside that window.
Here is the idea in plain language.
During your low income years, you
deliberately move money out of a
traditional account where it will
someday be forced out and taxed at
whatever rate the future decides and
into a Roth account.
But you pay it now at a low rate on an
amount you chose in a year you picked
instead of later at a higher effective
rate on an amount somebody else picked
in a year you did not choose. And once
that money is in a Roth, three things
become true at once. It grows without
tax, it comes out without tax, and it It
not count toward your provisional
income, which means it cannot drag your
Social Security into the taxable zone,
and it does not push you toward a
Medicare line. You have moved that money
outside the reach of three of the five
mechanisms permanently by paying a small
controlled amount now instead of a large
forced amount later.
But it has to be done with your eyes
open, and here is the trap inside the
solution that I do not hear anyone
mention.
A conversion is income in the year you
do it, which means a large conversion at
63 shows up on the Medicare calculation
at 65. People convert aggressively in
their early 60s, feel good about it, and
then get a surcharge letter in their
first year of Medicare, and have no idea
what they did. Convert in measured
amounts. Watch that line as carefully as
you watch the bracket, and it never
happens to you.
There is also a 5-year holding rule on
converted money before it can come out
clean. So, a conversion made at 68 is
not spending money at 69. It is money
for later, on purpose.
The second move, if you give to a church
or a charity at all, is a qualified
charitable distribution.
Starting at 70 and 1/2, you are allowed
to send money directly from a
traditional retirement account to a
qualified charity.
It counts toward your required
withdrawal for the year, but it never
touches your taxable income. Compare the
two versions. The ordinary way, you take
a forced withdrawal of $15,000, it lands
in your income, it gets taxed, it pushes
more of your Social Security into the
taxable zone, it nudges you toward a
Medicare line, and then you write your
check from what survived.
The direct way, the same 15,000 goes
straight to the charity. The requirement
is satisfied. The charity gets exactly
the same amount, and not $1 of it ever
entered your income, so not one link in
that chain ever fires.
Notice the ages, too. You can start this
at 70 and 1/2 before the forced
withdrawals begin at 73 or 75.
So, there is a gap of 2 to 4 years where
you can be shrinking that account
without being required to take anything
at all.
The third move is simply controlling
which bucket you reach into and when.
Because Roth money, and for the most
part money you already paid tax on, do
not count toward provisional income, the
source of a withdrawal matters as much
as the size of it. Say you need a
certain amount to live on this year.
Take all of it from a traditional
account and every dollar pushes you
toward those lines.
Take part of it from a traditional
account and part from a Roth or from
savings, and only the traditional part
counts against you. Same money in your
pocket, same life, very different
result, purely because you chose which
door to open.
The fourth move is the senior deduction
I mentioned earlier.
$6,000 per person 65 and older on top of
the standard deduction, available now
and scheduled to end after 2028.
Ask directly whether it was applied to
yours.
If the person doing your taxes
hesitates, press.
If you already filed without it, an
amended return is available for a
limited number of years back. And the
fifth move is the one Hollis missed. If
a surcharge has already hit you and the
income behind it came from something
that has ended, file that form, SSA-44,
free and available whether you are 66 or
86. Let me tell you about a couple I
will call Odessa and her husband because
this is where all five arrive in one
life.
Both in their late 60s when they
retired, they did everything right. They
saved hard into traditional accounts
their entire careers, and by the end
they had well over a million dollars
between them, plus a pension, plus two
social security checks.
And during those years, nobody told them
anything. Nobody explained that the low
tax bills were not a reward, they were
an opportunity running on a timer.
So, they did what felt responsible. They
left it alone and let it grow. Here is
the quiet tragedy inside those
comfortable years. Every one of them was
a wasted one. Every year the balance
rose felt like success, and every year
the balance rose, the eventual forced
withdrawal grew larger. Their good
discipline was building the thing that
was going to hit them. Then the required
age arrived, and all five landed at
once.
The forced withdrawal was enormous, far
more than they needed to live on because
the account was so large. That income

The combination put them in a higher
bracket than either of them had ever
been in while working full-time.
And 2 years later, the Medicare letters
came. Every one of the five in a
cascade, all traceable to a single
decision that was never actually made.
They simply did not act in the years
when acting was cheap.
Now, let me give you my honest read on
this, and it is only that. I do not
think there is a room somewhere where
people design this to catch careful
savers. I think something worse
happened, which is that nobody designed
it at all. Nobody ever sat down and
asked what all of it does when it lands
on the same person in the same year. And
that is precisely why it lands hardest
on the people who followed the rules.
Someone who spent everything and saved
nothing walks past all five of these
untouched. It is the saver, the careful
one, the person who did what they were
told, who ends up standing at the

of unrelated law making.
The system does not punish you for being
irresponsible. It has no mechanism for
that. It only has mechanisms that
trigger on savings, and you have
savings. And because no single person
built it, no single person is going to

There is nobody to write to. There is
only the calendar and what you do inside

Three, if you are inside the window

one.

Same gift and it never touches your
