title: Your Social Security Drops 22% Unless Congress Does One of These 5 Things

segments.text: The date just moved. Last year the
government said the retirement fund
would run dry in 2033.
This year they said 2032, a full year
closer in 12 months. And the single
largest reason is something that was
sold to you as a benefit to you. I will
come back to that. But first, the number
itself, 22%.
That is the automatic cut that lands on
every retirement check in this country
if Congress does nothing at all.
Not a proposal, not a threat, it is what
the law already says happens. Now,
before anybody's heart stops, let me say
the thing that most coverage of this
never gets around to saying, Social
Security is not going away. Nobody is
coming to shut off your check. If you
hear somebody tell you the program is
ending, they are either misinformed or
they want something from you. Depleted
does not mean gone. It means the savings
account hit zero and the program pays
out only what comes in.
And what comes in covers about 78 cents
on the dollar. That is a serious cut. It
is not zero. But here is what almost
nobody tells you and it changes the
entire picture.
Social Security does not have one trust
fund, it has two. They are legally
separate and they are in completely
different condition. One of them is in
trouble. The other one is genuinely
healthy, growing, and projected to pay
every dollar it owes for the next 75
years.
Almost every headline you have read
merges those two into one number and
merging them is how a manageable problem
starts sounding like a collapse. So here
is what we are doing today. First, what
depleted actually means and the two
funds nobody separates. Second, the last
time this country was in this exact
position and it was worse, considerably
worse. The fund was months from empty
rather than years and what they did
about it is still shaping your check
today, right now, this year.
Third, the five things Congress can
actually do, not opinions. The five
levers that exist, what each one closes,
and who each one costs. And I will tell
you plainly which combination is most
likely and roughly when, because the
timing is more predictable than people
think. My name is Kevin. I read the
rules so you do not have to. Every week
I go looking for the thing that quietly
decides what happens to your money, and
I bring it here before it costs you
anything.
If that sounds useful, subscribe and
turn on the bell, because the last part
of this video is the only part that
involves anything you can personally do,
and it is the part nobody covers.
Let me start with how this actually
works, because you cannot judge any of
it without the mechanism. Every paycheck
in this country has a Social Security
tax on it. 6.2% from you, 6.2% from your
employer, 12.4% total. That money does
not go into an account with your name on
it. There is no vault. It goes out
almost immediately to the people
collecting benefits right now. Today's
workers pay today's retirees. That is
the design, and it always has been. When
more comes in than goes out, the surplus
goes into reserves held in Treasury
securities that earn interest. When more
goes out than comes in, the program
draws on those reserves, and that is
exactly where we are. Since 2010, costs
have exceeded income excluding interest.
Since 2021, costs have exceeded total
income including interest. The reserves
are being drawn down every single year.
In 2025 alone, the combined reserves
fell by $160 billion
to 2.56 trillion. Now, the two funds.
The first is the Retirement and
Survivors Fund. That is the one that
pays your retirement check, your
spouse's check, and survivor benefits to
widows and widowers. It is the big one,
and it is the one in trouble. It is
projected to be depleted in the final
quarter of 2032.
At that point, incoming money covers 78%
of scheduled benefits, hence 22%.
The second is the Disability fund, and
this one is a genuinely different story.
It is projected to pay 100% of what it
owes through at least the year 2100.
Every year of the projection.
It passes both of the financial tests
the trustees apply.
The retirement fund fails both.
So when somebody says Social Security is
going bankrupt, they are describing one
of two funds and quietly attaching it to
the whole program. And there is a third
number worth knowing. If Congress passed
a law allowing the two funds to share
reserves, which it has done before, the
combined depletion date moves out to
2034, and the payable share rises from
Two extra years and five extra points
from a single piece of legislation that
does not raise anybody's taxes or cut
anybody's benefit.
It just permits two government accounts
to lend to each other. That is not a
solution. It is a delay.
But it is the cheapest delay available,
and it is almost certainly part of
whatever eventually happens.
Now, back to what I opened with.
Why did the date move a year closer?
Several things, but the largest single
contributor is this.
In 2025, legislation reduced the tax
that Social Security beneficiaries pay
on their benefits.
Now, that sounds like good news, and for
individual households it is. Less tax on
your benefit means more money in your
pocket. But the tax collected on Social
Security benefits does not go to the
general treasury. It flows back into the
Social Security trust funds. It is one
of the program's revenue sources. So
reducing that tax put money in
beneficiaries' pockets and took it out
of the fund that pays those
beneficiaries. And the depletion date
moved a year closer. I am not saying
that was the wrong decision. Reasonable
people disagree about it, and I am not
here to referee that. I am pointing out
something that essentially nobody
explained at the time, which is that the
two things are connected, and that a tax
cut on benefits is also, mechanically, a
reduction in the money available to pay
benefits. And there is one more figure
in that report that tells you more than
the headline date does. So, let me give
it to you.
The trustees measure the gap over 75
years as a percentage of taxable
payroll.
This year, that figure is 4.42%.
Last year, it was 3.82%.
That is the number to actually watch
because it is the size of the hole
rather than the date it becomes visible.
And it grew by more than half a
percentage point in a single year, which
is a substantial move. What it means in
plain terms is this: To close the entire
gap through payroll tax alone, you would
need to raise the combined rate by about
4 and 1/2 points, from 12.4 to roughly
starting immediately and permanently.
Nobody is going to do that in one move.
But that figure is the honest measure of
the problem. And it is worth knowing
because every proposal you hear about
from here on can be measured against it.
When somebody says their plan fixes
Social Security, the question is what
share of 4.42% it actually closes. Most
of the popular ones close a quarter or a
half. Very few close all of it, and that
is why the eventual answer will be a
combination rather than a single idea,
no matter how good any single idea
sounds. Let me tell you about Willard.
Willard is 67, and he retired in March.
He's been reading about this for 2
years, and he made a decision based on
it. He claimed at 62, early, permanently
reduced, roughly 30% less every month
for the rest of his life. And when his
daughter asked him why, he gave her the
reason a great many people give. He said
he wanted to get some of it before it
ran out. Willard is in good health. His
father lived to 89. On any ordinary
calculation, he was a candidate for
waiting, and waiting would have paid him
considerably more over his lifetime.
He took a certain permanent 30% cut to
protect himself against an uncertain 22%
cut that has never once happened in the
program's history.
And nobody at any office was going to
stop him because claiming early is
completely legitimate and it is his
decision to make. That is what the Quiet
Rules was built for.
Plain English, printed large enough to
read without hunting for your glasses,
on the things that quietly decide what
happens to your money.
What the actual risk is. What the actual
arithmetic is. And how to think about a
decision like Willard's before you make
it rather than afterward. You can find
it at kevinexplains.shop.
The link is below this video and in the
pinned comment at the top. And there is
a code on the screen if you are watching
on a television. 7-day guarantee. If it
does not help you, ask for a refund and
nobody will argue with you.
Now, the second part. And this is the
part that should genuinely lower your
blood pressure.
This country has been here before.
And it was much worse.
In the early 1980s, the retirement fund
was not years from depletion. It was
months.
Projections had it running out as early
as August of 1983.
Checks would have been missed that
summer, not reduced, missed.
So, President Reagan set up a commission
chaired by Alan Greenspan, who later ran
the Federal Reserve.
It included members from both parties
and that was deliberate. Neither side
could blame the other for whatever came
out of it.
And what came out of it came down in the
end to a private agreement between two
men who did not like each other
politically.
Reagan and the Democratic Speaker of the
House, Tip O'Neill.
They shook hands on a compromise where
both sides swallowed something they
hated.
Here is what that deal actually
contained and one piece of it is
affecting you personally this year.
First, they raised the full retirement
age from 65 to 67.
But they phased it in so gradually that
it did not fully take effect until this
year.
2026 is the first year everybody reaches
full retirement age at 67.
43 years to phase in one change, and I
want to be honest about what that change
was.
It was a benefit cut.
You collect for fewer years. It was
simply a benefit cut delivered so slowly
that most of the people that affected
never experienced it as one.
Second, they taxed Social Security
benefits for the first time in history.
Before 1983, benefits were entirely
tax-free. The deal made up to half of
benefits taxable for higher income
recipients. And here is where it becomes
your problem, rather than a history
lesson.
The thresholds they set were $25,000 for
a single person and 32,000 for a couple.
In 1993, a second tier was added at
34,000 and 44,000, taxing up to 85%.
Neither set of thresholds has ever been
adjusted for inflation. Not once. Not in
43 years. So, a figure designed to
capture higher income retirees in 1983
now captures a person with $25,001
of income.
Around 40% of all beneficiaries now pay
tax on their benefits, up from
essentially nobody in 1984.
And that did not happen because anybody
voted to tax more people. It happened
because the line stopped moving while
everything else kept going.
If those thresholds had simply been
indexed, the way every other figure in
the system is, the first tier would
begin somewhere around $80,000 for a
single person, rather than 25,000.
Third, they brought new workers in.
Federal employees hired after January of
1984 and all nonprofit employees were
pulled into Social Security for the
first time.
>> [clears throat]
>> That expanded the tax base immediately.
And fourth, they accelerated payroll tax
increases that were already scheduled,
pulling revenue forward. The result was
that the chief actuary estimated the
program was solvent for another 75
years. And it was, until now.
Notice the shape of that deal because it
is the whole lesson. Republicans
accepted tax increases. Democrats
accepted a benefit cut. Both sides took
something home they had to defend to
their own voters. That is what a fix
looks like and it is exactly why nothing
has happened yet this time.
And there is a piece of that history
worth pausing on because it is the
single best predictor of what happens
next.
The commission was bipartisan by design
and that design was the entire point.
Not because bipartisanship is virtuous,
because it was the only structure in
which either side could survive voting
for something unpopular.
Reagan could not raise taxes alone.
O'Neill could not cut benefits alone.
Either of them attempting it in
isolation would have been destroyed in
the next election and both of them knew
it. So, the commission existed to give
both sides cover.
When the deal was announced, neither
party could attack it without attacking
its own members who had signed on.
That is what made it possible to pass
something that genuinely hurt.
Now, look at where we are.
There is no commission.
There has been no serious bipartisan
process.
What there is instead is each side
introducing bills the other will not
support and using the resulting failure
in fundraising letters.
And I want to be careful here because it
would be easy to say both sides are
equally to blame and leave it there. And
that is lazy.
What I will say is narrower and I think
defensible.
The structure that produced the last fix
does not currently exist and nobody has
built a replacement for it, which is why
I would watch for one. If you ever see a
bipartisan commission announced on this,
that is the signal that something real
is about to happen. Not a bill, not a
press conference, a commission with
names from both parties on it. That is
the tell and it came about 18 months
before the last fix passed. And there is
one more thing from 1983 worth knowing
because it is genuinely reassuring in a
way nothing else in this subject is.
That deal passed in April of 1983.
The fund was projected to be unable to
pay full benefits that July.
They fixed it with roughly 3 months to
spare in an era with less data and
slower government than we have now. So,
when people tell you Congress will never
get this done in time, the historical
record says otherwise. They will almost
certainly leave it far later than
anybody is comfortable with. That is
different from not doing it. Let me tell
you about Elna. Elna is 71 and she has a
folder.
In it are printouts of every article she
has read about this since 2023.
She keeps them in date order.
She has not been on a holiday in 3
years. Not because she cannot afford
one, because she is convinced that at
some point she will need that money and
she does not know when.
She lives on a benefit that has arrived
on schedule every single month for 9
years in a program that has never missed
a payment in its 90-year history,
including through a Great Depression, a
World War, and multiple recessions.
And the actual worst case, which almost
certainly will not happen, is that in 6
years her payment becomes 78% of what it
is now.
That is worth planning for.
It is not worth 3 years of not seeing
your grandchildren because you are
frightened of a headline. The cost of
this coverage is not just
misinformation. It is fear that produces
bad decisions in people who have very
little room to make bad decisions.
That is the gap this guide is meant to
close.
Not to make anybody an expert in trust
fund accounting, to put the actual
numbers in one place in plain language
so that a person can tell the difference
between something worth preparing for
and something worth being afraid of.
Same place, kevinexplains.shop.
Link below and in the pinned comment or
the code on your screen.
7-day guarantee and you will not be
asked to explain yourself.
Now, the third part, the five options.
The debate is not about whether this can
be fixed. Mathematically, it can,
easily. The debate is entirely about who
pays. So, here are the five levers, what
each one actually accomplishes, and who
it costs. Option one, lift or eliminate
the cap on taxable wages. Right now, the
Social Security tax applies only to the
of income. Above that, nothing. So,
somebody earning 90,000 pays on every
dollar. Somebody earning 500,000 pays on
less than 40% of theirs. Eliminating
that cap entirely would close roughly
half of the 75-year shortfall. Half,
from one change. The politics. This
polls extremely well. Most people like
the idea of taxing income above their
own. The objection is structural rather
than partisan. Social Security was built
as an earned benefit, where what you pay
in determines what you get out. Taxing
income above the cap without also
increasing benefits above the cap
converts part of it into a transfer,
which changes what the program is. That
argument is real, and it is not just
made by wealthy people. Option two,
raise the tax rate on everybody. The
combined rate is 12.4%.
Raising it by one percentage point
closes about a quarter of the shortfall.
Closing the whole thing this way alone
would require roughly four and a half
points, taking the combined rate to
about 17%. The politics. Difficult for
everybody. Republicans oppose it as a
broad tax increase. Democrats are
uncomfortable because it hits lower and
middle-income workers hardest, since
they pay the rate on all of their income
rather than part of it. This appears in
a package as a fraction of a point, not
as a standalone fix. Option three, raise
the retirement age again. Straight from
the 1983 playbook. Moving it from 67 to
68 closes about 12% of the shortfall.
Moving it to 70 closes roughly a third.
And I want to be blunt about what this
is. It is a benefit cut. You collect for
fewer years. That is the entire
mechanism. It also lands hardest on
people with shorter life expectancies
and less ability to keep working, which
correlates with lower incomes and
physical work. Research consistently
shows most people stop working around
62, regardless of what they intended,
because of health, job loss, or caring
for somebody. Telling people to work
longer only functions if they are able
to. The politics. Almost certainly part
of any deal. A gradual move to 68 over
15 or 20 years is far more plausible
than anything reaching 70. Option four,
adjust the benefit formula. The formula
that calculates your benefit is
progressive by design. It replaces a
higher share of income for lower
earners.
Congress can change those rates for
future retirees without touching anybody
currently receiving a check. The
politics. This is the most acceptable
option for anybody already retired,
because by construction it does not
touch you. The savings arrive slowly,
which limits how much it helps in the
near term, but it is nearly always in
the package because it is the least
painful thing to vote for.
Option five, change how the annual
increase is calculated. Your cost of
living adjustment is calculated using a
particular price index. Switching to a
slightly different one, called the
chained index, produces marginally
smaller increases each year. Marginally.
And that is the point. It compounds. 10
or 20 years of slightly smaller
increases produces a meaningfully
smaller benefit, and the people most
affected are the oldest retirees who
have been collecting longest and are
frequently the most financially exposed.
It appeals to budget analysts precisely
because it is almost invisible in any
single year.
Advocacy groups oppose it hard for the
same reason, and there is a fair
objection worth naming. The index
currently used is built around the
spending of working households, and it
does not weight the things older people
actually spend money on, particularly
medical care.
So, the argument that the current
adjustment already understates senior
inflation is a legitimate one, and
switching to a slower index makes that
gap wider.
So, what actually happens?
Before I answer that, there is a sixth
thing worth mentioning that is not on
most lists, because it is not a cut or a
tax at all.
Invest a portion of the reserves. Right
now, every dollar in those trust funds
sits in Treasury securities, extremely
safe, and the return is correspondingly
modest.
Several proposals over the years have
suggested investing some fraction in a
broad market index instead, the way
essentially every public pension fund in
this country already does. The argument
for it is straightforward. Over long
periods, a diversified equity position
has returned considerably more than
Treasury securities, and the trust funds
have a very long horizon.
The arguments against are also real and
worth stating. It exposes the program to
market downturns at exactly the moments
when people need it most. It would make
the federal government a very large
shareholder in American companies, which
raises genuine questions about how those
shares get voted. And a bad decade would
deepen the hole rather than filling it.
I mention it because it comes up
periodically. It has never gone
anywhere, and it is the only option on
any list that does not involve somebody
paying more or receiving less,
which is precisely why it keeps
resurfacing, and precisely why it is
never passed. Now, what actually
happens? History is a good guide here.
The 1983 deal came together within weeks
of missed checks. There is no obvious
reason to expect anything different this
time, which points to action somewhere
in the 2029 to 2031 window. And between
now and then, you are going to hear
about this constantly. Both parties
benefit from the fear this generates. It
moves voters. Expected in every election
cycle between now and whenever they act.
When they do act, it will almost
certainly be a package because no single
option is both mathematically sufficient
and politically survivable.
The realistic shape is something like a
fraction of a point on the payroll tax
rate, a partial lift of the cap applying
above some higher threshold, a gradual
retirement age increase to 68 phased
over a decade or more, benefit formula
adjustments for higher earning future
retirees, and permission for the two
funds to share reserves. Notice who that
package protects, current retirees
almost entirely, and notice who pays,
today's workers and tomorrow's retirees.
That is not an accident. It is who
votes.
Now, before the last story, there is a
practical question almost nobody
answers, and I get asked it constantly.
If the cut did happen, what would it
actually look like? Here is the honest
answer, and it is worth knowing. The law
does not currently specify a mechanism.
There is no provision saying benefits
shall be reduced by a set percentage
across the board.
What the law says is that the fund
cannot pay out more than it has, which
leaves two possibilities, and legal
scholars genuinely disagree about which
would occur.
One is an across-the-board reduction.
Every check shrinks by roughly the same
percentage on the same date. Simple,
terrible, and immediately visible to 70
million people. The other is delayed
payments, full checks sent late with a
delay growing as the shortfall grows.
So, your payment arrives on time in
January, 4 days late by June, and
further behind after that. Nobody knows
which. And that uncertainty is itself an
argument that it will not be allowed to
happen because neither outcome is
survivable politically, and both would
be catastrophic administratively. There
is also a question about what would
happen to Medicare premiums, which are
deducted from most benefits before they
reach you.
A smaller check with the same premium
taken out of it produces a much larger
effective cut for people with modest
benefits.
Nobody has addressed that, either.
I am telling you this not to alarm you,
but because it is genuinely unresolved.
And anybody who tells you confidently
exactly how the cut would be
administered is telling you something
nobody actually knows. Let me tell you
about Rayford. Rayford is 59. He is not
retired, and he is not close. And he is
the person this actually lands on.
Every proposal that protects current
beneficiaries protects them by shifting
the cost onto him.
The higher retirement age applies to
him.
The adjusted benefit formula applies to
him.
The payroll tax increase comes out of
his check for the next 8 years. And he
is completely fine with that, which is
what I find interesting about talking to
people his age. Most of them are. They
want their mother's check protected.
What they object to is not the cost, it
is that nobody has ever put the trade in
front of them honestly and asked. That
is the actual debate underneath all of
this, and it is a generational one, and
it is almost never described that way
because describing it that way makes it
harder to win votes.
Now, let me give you my honest opinion,
and it is only that. I do not think
benefits will be cut 22% in 2032. I
would be surprised if it happened, and
here is my reasoning rather than just my
confidence. 70 million people receive
these benefits. They vote at higher
rates than any other group in the
country.
There is no version of American politics
where Congress allows an automatic 22%
cut to land on 70 million voters in an
election cycle.
Whatever else you believe about the
people in that building, they respond to
that.
So, my genuine expectation is that
something passes late, in a hurry, and
that it is a compromise nobody is happy
with, which is what happened last time
and the time before.
Where I do get frustrated is the honesty
of the conversation. The 1983 deal is
described as the fix that saved Social
Security. It was.
It was also a benefit cut that took 43
years to fully arrive and a tax on
benefits with thresholds that were never
indexed so that a tax aimed at the
wealthy quietly became a tax on ordinary
retirees over four decades.
Both of those were in the same bill.
Only one of them gets talked about.
And that pattern is what I would watch
for in whatever comes next.
The parts that are announced will be the
parts that sound like protection. The
parts that actually cost you will be
phased in slowly enough that nobody
experiences them as a change and index
to nothing so that they grow on their
own while you are not looking.
That is not a conspiracy. It is simply
how difficult legislation gets passed.
But knowing it is how it works means you
read the next deal differently. And
there is one more thing I want to say
because I think it is the most important
idea in this entire video and it gets
lost underneath the arithmetic.
Everything about how this problem is
communicated is designed to produce
urgency rather than understanding.
The headline is a date. The date is
frightening and the natural response to
a frightening date is to do something.
But almost every action available to an
individual person in response to this
fear makes them worse off, not better.
Claiming early makes you worse off.
Cashing out investments makes you worse
off. Buying a product from somebody who
telephoned you about it makes you
dramatically worse off.
Not taking a holiday for 3 years makes
your life smaller for no financial gain
whatsoever.
The correct response to this particular
problem is almost entirely passive.
Understand it. Plan conservatively. Do
not make a permanent decision based on a
temporary uncertainty.
And then get on with your life. That is
a genuinely unsatisfying answer and I
think that is exactly why so much of the
coverage avoids it. There is no product
to sell attached to calm down and wait.
There is enormous money in the
alternative.
So, if you take one thing out of this
video, let it be that. The people making
you most afraid of this are almost
always the people with something to sell
you, and the thing they are selling
almost always costs you more than the
cut they are warning you about.
Now, one warning before your list,
because this fear is monetized
aggressively. If anybody contacts you
offering to protect your benefits from
cuts, to lock in your current amount, or
to move your money somewhere safe before
2032, that is a sales approach and
frequently a fraud. There is nothing to
lock in. There is no product that
protects a Social Security benefit.
Nobody can opt you out of a change in
federal law, and the agency will not
telephone you about any of this. If it
happens, it comes through written
notice, the way everything else does.
All right, here is your list, five
things. One, if you have not claimed
yet, do not claim early out of fear of
this. That converts an uncertain future
cut into a certain permanent one, and
the permanent one is usually larger.
Two, if you are already receiving
benefits, understand that the realistic
worst case is 78% of your current amount
in about 6 years, and that even that is
unlikely. Plan around it, do not panic
around it. Three, if you are still
working and building a retirement plan,
stress test it. Run your numbers
assuming Social Security comes in at 85
or 90% of what is currently projected.
If the plan survives that, you are fine.
Four, watch what actually passes rather
than what is announced. Specifically,
look for anything phased in over decades
and anything not indexed to inflation.
Those two features are where the real
cost always hides. Five, ignore anybody
selling you protection from this. There
is no such product, and if your own
situation is tangled, if you are trying
to decide when to claim and this is
weighing on it, write to me. The address
is on your screen and in the description
below and I read every one.
One last thing before you go. Willard
took a certain 30% cut to avoid an
uncertain 22% one and he will live with
that decision for the rest of his life.
Elna has not seen her grandchildren in 3
years because of a folder full of
headlines about something that has never
happened.
And Raiford is going to pay for most of
whatever fix arrives and nobody has ever
asked him about it. None of the three
did anything unreasonable. Every one of
them responded sensibly to the
information they were given. The
information was just built to frighten
rather than to explain.
So, here is what I would hold on to. The
number is real. The date is real. The
program has never missed a payment in 90
years and it has been in worse shape
than this within living memory and was
fixed inside a single year.
Prepare for 78% expect better
and do not let a headline talk you into
a permanent decision about a temporary
problem. I am Kevin. Thanks for
watching. Do not forget to check the
quiet rules at kevinexplains.shop.

segments.text: A woman in Minneapolis owed $2,300 in
property tax. By the time the county was
finished, that number had become 15,000.
So, they took her home and sold it for
And then they kept all of it. Not the 15
they were owed. All 40. Every dollar of

stop you. None of that was illegal. It
was the written law in a dozen states,

her family wanted her somewhere safer.
She did not sell it. The taxes piled up.
Interest and penalties turned $2,300
into 15,000 and the county took the
whole thing. Now, three years ago, the
Supreme Court of the United States
looked at that case and ruled against
the county unanimously. Every single
justice. They said that keeping a
person's equity beyond what they
actually owed is a taking under the
fifth amendment and the government
cannot do it. That decision changed the
law in about a dozen states overnight
and states have been rewriting their
statutes ever since and almost nobody in
this audience has heard of it, which is

built to protect is sitting in this

second half about something scheduled

So, here is what we are doing today.
First, what that court decision actually

limitation inside it that nobody
mentions. Second, the thing that stops

every county in this country, in which
almost nobody applies for. Third, the

does not cover. And underneath all of

better, no matter what any court says.
My name is Kevin. I read the rules so
you do not have to. Every week I go

bring it here before it cost you

the protection in the second part of
this video has an application deadline

a full year. Let me start with what the

forecloses on a property for unpaid
taxes and sells it, it may keep what it

is anything above that. The surplus, the

it is a taking under the constitution.
So, in the Tyler case, the county was

and enormous improvement over what
Geraldine Tyler experienced. It is not

somewhere in the paperwork is a notice

So, the practical instruction if this
ever touches anybody in your family is a
single sentence. After a tax foreclosure
sale, ask the county in writing whether
there is surplus and how to claim it.
That sentence is worth whatever the
equity in that house was. And there is a
piece of good news buried in the reform
wave that followed, which is worth
knowing. A number of states have used
this as an occasion to lengthen

of time after a foreclosure begins
during which you can still pay what is

$15,000 in the first place. That varies
enormously by state, and it is worth

thing about that ruling that almost
nobody has picked up on, which matters

this. The decision was handed down three

nothing. Several states when they

in your family lost a property to tax

is not automatically a closed matter. It
is worth one conversation with a legal

on without charging anybody because this

money. I am saying that a great many
families wrote this off as finished and
in some states it is not finished and

is 82 and she has lived in the same
house in a small city for 41 years. Her

one, and there were two years where the

She has never been more than a year
behind. What Lys does not know is that
her county offers a program that would

been in that building four times. And I
want to be careful about how I say the

not somebody who cannot afford her
house. She owns it outright. It is worth
well over $200,000. She is a woman with

The link is below the video and in the

this is the one I actually want you to
act on because it prevents everything I
have just described. There is a program
in most of this country called a
property tax deferral and it is
genuinely different from an exemption.
So let me draw the distinction clearly.
An exemption reduces what you owe. A
deferral postpones it entirely. Here is
how it works. If you qualify generally
on age and sometimes on income, you can
stop paying property tax on your home.
Not reduce it, stop. The county records
a lean against the property for the
amount deferred. Interest occurs at a

and the whole balance becomes due when

making the payment that has been the
tightest thing in her budget for a
decade. She keeps the house. Nobody
forecloses. The county gets paid

eligibility varies, and I will not
pretend otherwise. Some states set it at
65, some at 70. Some have income limits

And a handful of states do not offer it

better. There is one honest caution, and
I would rather you hear it from me. A

twiceearly bill is the problem rather

It is frequently as simple as asking.
And there is a third thing worth asking

all of it called a circuit breaker. The

a share of your income. Rather than
reducing your assessment, it looks at

well because a portion of rent is

a check for tax you already handed over.
Now, a few honest complications because

and I would rather you heard it in
advance. If you have a mortgage, a

additional penalties from acrewing while

In others it runs to two or three years.
and a number of states lengthen theirs

And the exact length is a single

is not taking with him on terms the

outright over a program designed for

this guide is meant to close. Not to

The governor's office estimates that at

your county offers or whether you

below, and I read everyone that comes

Geraldine Tyler was 94 and lost $25,000
of her own equity, and it took a
unanimous Supreme Court to say that was
wrong.
Merritt has gone without things for 11
Februaries in a house he owns outright
over a program he qualified for the
entire time. An artist has overpaid for
22 years on a form that takes about 10
minutes. None of them did anything
careless. Not one was refused by
anybody. Every single one of them was on

this week, make the telephone call. Not

Thanks for watching. Do not forget to

closes. Document one, the long-term care
premium increase. Let me explain what is
actually happening here because the
scale of it is genuinely remarkable and
almost nobody outside the industry
understands why. In the 1980s and '90s,
insurers began selling long-term care
policies. The pricing was built on four
assumptions, and all four of them turned
out to be wrong in the same direction.
They assumed roughly 4% of policy
holders would drop their policies each
year. The real figure turned out to be
about 1%. They underestimated how long
people would live. They underestimated
how much care would cost and they
assumed interest rates that never
materialized. Now think about what the
first of those means. If you sell
100,000 policies expecting 80% of them
to lapse over 20 years, you are planning
to pay claims on 20,000 people. Instead,
80,000 policies are still active. Four
times the claims you priced for. So the
insurers went to state regulators and
asked for permission to raise rates. and
the regulators, whose job is to make
sure the company can actually pay the
claims it promised, largely said yes. A
survey of 17 major insurers found the
average approved increase across states
was around 28%. But that is an average.
Some states, including Nebraska and
Texas, have approved increases exceeding
100%. And because these arrive in waves
rather than once, policy holders who
bought in their 50s are now facing
cumulative increases of 150 to 250% over
the life of the policy. This year
specifically, letters going out are
commonly in the 20 to 50% range with
plenty above that. So here is where
somebody in this audience actually finds
themselves. You bought a policy at 58
because you watched your mother go into
a facility and you decided that would
never happen to your children. you have
paid every year for 19 years and a
letter arrives telling you the premium
is going from $325 a month to $471. That
is $146 more a month, $1,752
a year on a fixed income. And you have
about 30 days to respond. Now, the
options, and this is where the money is,
so stay with me. Almost everybody
assumes there are two. Pay it or cancel.
Both of those are bad and there are at
least five. The first is to pay the
increase. Sometimes that is genuinely
correct, particularly if you bought an
unusually generous policy that nobody
sells anymore. The second is to reduce
the daily benefit. If your policy pays
$200 a day toward care, you can often
reduce that to $150 and hold the premium
near where it was. You keep the policy.
You keep the catastrophic protection.
You accept a smaller daily figure. The
third is to shorten the benefit period.
A policy that pays for 3 years can often
be compressed to two with the same
effect on premium. The fourth is to
lengthen the elimination period, which
is the waiting time before benefits
begin. Going from 90 days to 180 means
you cover more of the front end yourself
and the premium falls. And there is a
fifth, the one I open this video with.
It is called contingent non-forfeite.
And here is what it does. If your
premium has increased by a substantial
percentage and you decide you simply
cannot pay it anymore, you can elect
this rather than letting the policy
lapse. Your coverage converts to a paid
up policy with a benefit equal to what
you have already paid in premiums. You
stop paying forever and you keep a pool
of money for care equal to everything
you contributed. Now, think about the
difference between that and simply
stopping payment. Somebody who has paid
$4,200 a year for 19 years has put in
around $80,000. If they let it lapse,
they have nothing. 19 years of premiums
gone in exchange for the coverage they
had during those years and did not use.
If they elect contingent non-forfeite
instead, they walk away from all future
premiums and retain a benefit pool worth
roughly what they paid in. Same decision
to stop paying. Two completely different
outcomes. This is not a loophole. It is
a consumer protection that regulators
required precisely because they knew
these increases were coming. It is
described in the letter. It is described
in one paragraph in the language of an
insurance contract in the middle of a
document whose first page contains a
number that made your stomach drop. Let
me tell you about Verice. Verice is 74.
She and her husband bought policies
together in 2004, the year after his
mother died in a facility that took most
of what she had. Her husband died 6
years ago. She kept paying hers. It is
the last thing they decided together and
she was not going to be the one who let
it go. The letter came in March. 43%
increase. She read the first page. She
looked at the number and she made a
decision that a great many people in her
position make, which is that she would
deal with it later because looking at it
again that week was more than she could
manage. Later turned into 8 weeks. By
then the response window had closed. The
increased premium had gone into effect
and the option to elect anything else
was no longer on the table. She is now
paying an amount she cannot really
afford for a policy she is not going to
use for years. And the alternative that
would have let her stop paying and keep
something was printed on page three of a
letter she never got to. Verice is not
careless. She is a woman who was handed
a distressing piece of paper about a
decision she made with a husband who is
no longer here and she put it down,
which is what almost anybody would have
done. That is the whole reason the quiet
rules exists. plain English printed

you can point your phone camera at.
7-day guarantee always. If it does not

question worth sitting with. Is there a
letter in your house right now that you
started reading and put down? Document
two, the annual statement on a permanent
life insurance policy. This one is
quieter than the first and in some ways
worse because there is no dramatic
number and no deadline printed anywhere.
Here is the mechanism and you need it to
understand why this happens. If you own
whole life or universal life insurance,
part of your premium goes toward the
actual cost of insuring you and part
accumulates as cash value inside the
policy. The cost of insuring you rises
every year as you get older. That is not
a trick. That is simply what insurance
costs. In a universal life policy, when
the premium you are paying is no longer
enough to cover that rising cost, the
difference comes out of the cash value
quietly automatically without anybody
telephoning you. And that works for a
while until the cash value runs down.
And when it reaches zero, the policy
lapses. So somebody can pay faithfully
for 35 years, receive no warning that
anything is wrong, and lose the entire
death benefit in their 80s. Not because
they missed a payment, because the
payment they were making stopped being
enough, and the reserve that was
covering the gap ran out. The
information is in the annual statement.
It is not hidden. It is a line, usually
somewhere in the middle, showing the
cash value or the account value. And a
policy in trouble shows that figure
falling year overear. That is the entire
diagnostic. One number compared against
the same number last year. If it is
going down and you are still paying the
same premium, that policy is on a timer
and nobody is going to tell you how long
is left. So, here is what to do and it
takes one telephone call. Ring the
insurer and ask for an inforce
illustration. That is the actual term
and it matters that you use it. An
inforce illustration projects forward
from where the policy stands today and
tells you the year it will lapse if
nothing changes and what premium would
be required to keep it going to age 100
or beyond. It is free. You are entitled
to it. And it converts a vague worry
into a specific date. And if the answer
is bad, there are options and they are
far better than doing nothing. You can
increase the premium to whatever the
illustration says is sustainable. You
can reduce the death benefit which
lowers the cost of insurance and can
stabilize the whole thing. You can use
accumulated cash value to purchase a
smaller fully paid up policy which is
called reduced paid up and then never
pay another premium. And there is one
more that people find genuinely
surprising. A policy you no longer want
or can afford may be sellable. There is
a regulated market for this called a
life settlement where a third party buys
the policy, takes over the premiums, and
pays you a lump sum. Now, it is
generally worth considering for older
policy holders with larger policies, and
the amount is frequently several times
the cash surrender value the insurer
would offer you. I am not recommending
it. It has real tax consequences and it
is not right for everybody. I am telling
you it exists because a great many
people surrender a policy for its cash
value having never been told there was
another buyer. And there are two more
things about these policies that catch
people. So let me name them both
quickly. The first is the grace period
and it is shorter than people assume. If
a policy does run out of value, you
generally get somewhere around 31 to 60
days before it terminates. That letter
is the last warning you will ever
receive and it frequently looks like
every other envelope from that company.
If you do miss it, ask about
reinstatement. Most insurers allow a
lapsed policy to be reinstated within a
window of several years, provided you
pay the back premiums and can
demonstrate you are still insurable.
That second condition is the difficult
one at 80, but the window exists and
people assume a lapsed policy is simply
gone when it may not be for a few more
years. The second is a policy loan,
which is where this quietly goes wrong
for a lot of families. If you ever
borrowed against the cash value, that
loan acrus interest and the interest is
added to the loan balance rather than
build to you. So it compounds silently
against the same cash value that is
holding the policy up. A loan taken out
at 60 to help with a roof or a wedding
can entirely on its own be the reason a
policy collapses at 85. And there is a
genuinely unpleasant tax outcome
attached to that. If a policy with a
large outstanding loan lapses, the
forgiven loan amount can become taxable
income to you, which means somebody can
lose the death benefit and receive a tax
bill in the same year on money they
borrowed decades earlier and long since
spent. So when you telephone for that
inforce illustration, ask two additional
questions. Is there a loan against this
policy? And what is the balance? And
what happens tax-wise if this policy
lapses with that loan outstanding? Those
two questions take 30 seconds and they
surface the single worst outcome
available in this entire category. Let
me tell you about Alton. Alton is 81. He
bought a universal life policy in 1987
with a $200,000 death benefit. He has
paid the same premium every year since
and he has always thought of it as the
thing he is leaving his daughter. He
does not read the statements. They
arrive. They look like the previous one
and they go in a folder in the same
drawer as his tax returns. The cash
value in that policy has been falling
for 6 years. On the current path, it
will reach zero when he is 84, and the
policy will lapse, and the $200,000 his
daughter has been counted on receiving
will not exist. Alton has paid roughly
40 years of premiums. He has done
nothing wrong. He is not behind on
anything, and unless somebody opens that
statement and reads the middle of the
page, the entire thing simply
evaporates, and his daughter finds out
about it after he is gone. That is
exactly the gap this guide closes. Not
to make anybody an insurance expert, to
point at the specific line on the
specific page and give a person the
exact sentence to say on the telephone
so that 40 years of payments do not
disappear because a document looked like
the one before it. Same place,

link in the description and in the
pinned comment at the top and the code
on your screen if you are watching this
on the television. 7-day guarantee, no
argument. Document three, the
non-renewal notice from your home
insurer. This one has become genuinely
serious in the last few years and it is
different from a premium increase in a
way that matters enormously. A premium
increase says we will still cover you
and it will cost more. A non-renewal
says we will not be covering you at all
after a certain date. And the reason it
belongs in this video is the timing.
Depending on your state, you may receive
somewhere between 30 and 60 days of
notice. That is the entire window to
find replacement coverage. Now, here is
why this is worse than it sounds for
somebody in this audience. If you have a
mortgage, your lender requires
insurance. If your policy lapses and you
have not replaced it, the lender will
place coverage for you. It is called
forceplaced insurance, and it is
dramatically more expensive than

several times the cost. And it typically
protects the lender's interest rather
than your possessions or your liability.
So, a letter that goes in a drawer for 6
weeks can end with a mortgage payment
that has jumped by hundreds of dollars a
month for coverage that is worse than
what you had. And here is the piece
almost nobody knows. Every state has a
backs stop. It is generally called a
fair plan, which stands for fair access
to insurance requirements. It exists
specifically for people who cannot
obtain coverage in the ordinary market.
It is usually more expensive and more
limited than a standard policy. And it
is a great deal better than nothing, and
it is a great deal better than
force-placed coverage. Most people who
receive a non-renewal have never heard
of it. They telephone two or three
companies, get declined, and conclude
they are out of options. So, the
sequence, if that letter arrives, is
this. Start the day you open it, not the
week before the deadline. Ask your
existing insurer directly whether
anything would make them reconsider
because sometimes a roof replacement or
removing a particular structure changes
the answer. Contact an independent agent
who works with multiple carriers rather
than telephoning single companies
yourself. And if the market genuinely
will not take you, ask about your
state's fair plan by name. Two more
things worth knowing here. Check whether
the letter says non-renewal or
cancellation because those are different
and the difference matters. A
non-renewal means they are choosing not
to continue at the end of your term,
which is ordinary business and gives you
the full notice period. A cancellation
means they are ending the policy
midterm, which insurers can generally
only do for specific reasons like
non-payment or a material
misrepresentation. If you receive a
cancellation and you do not believe
either applies to you, that is worth
challenging with your state insurance
department, which is free to contact and
exists precisely for this. And be
careful what you ask your current
insurer before the non-renewal arrives.
Telephoneoning to ask a hypothetical
question about whether something would
be covered is sometimes logged as a
claim inquiry. And claim inquiries can
appear in the industry database that
other insurers check. So a person who
telephoned twice to ask about a leak,
never filed anything, and never received
a dollar can find themselves harder to
insure. Ask questions of an independent
agent rather than of your own carrier
where you can. Document four, the
property assessment notice. This is the
one people are most likely to throw away
because it is not a bill. It arrives. It
says what your home is now considered to
be worth and it does not ask you for
money. So, it feels informationational.
It is notformational. It is the number
your tax bill will be calculated from
and it comes with a window to challenge
it that is frequently as short as 30
days. And the challenge is not about
whether your house is nice. It is a
narrow technical question. Is this
assessment accurate compared to similar
properties? Which means the grounds that
actually succeed are specific errors in
the record. And these are common. The
county has your house listed with four
bedrooms when it has three or a finished
basement that was never finished or
square footage that is simply wrong.
comparable sales that came in below your
assessment or condition issues that the
assessor could not see from the street
because assessments are frequently done
from the outside or from a computer.
That last one matters for this audience
specifically. An older house with an
aging roof, outdated systems, or
deferred maintenance can be assessed as
though it were in the same condition as
a renovated house on the same street.
The assessor never came inside. Nobody
told them. So, if you get that notice
and the number looks high, the useful
response is not outrage. It is three
specific things. Request the property
record card, which is free, and check
every physical detail on it for errors.
Find three or four comparable sales in
your area, and photograph anything
genuinely wrong with the property. That
is an afternoon of work against a figure
that determines your tax bill every year
until the next reassessment. And there
is one more thing about that notice
specifically which is separate from the
appeal and frequently worth more. A
reassessment is the moment to check
whether you are receiving every
reduction you are entitled to at your
age. Most places offer something. A
senior exemption, a homestead reduction,
an assessment freeze that locks your
value in place, a deferral that
postpones payment entirely until the
property changes hands. The critical
detail is that these almost never apply
themselves. there is generally an
application. It generally has to be
filed by a specific date and in many
places it has to be renewed rather than
continuing automatically. So there are
people who applied at 65, qualified,
received the reduction for several years
and then quietly stopped receiving it
because a renewal form went unreturned.
The bill went up. Nobody explained why.
They assumed it was rising values. So,
when that notice arrives, make one
telephone call to the assessor's office
and ask a single question. What
reductions am I currently receiving on
this property? And what else am I
eligible for at my age? That is a
2-minute call. It costs nothing, and the
person on the other end deals with it
all day. Let me tell you about Delma.
Delma is 77 and has lived in the same
house since 1981. Her assessment notice
arrived and showed a value that had
jumped substantially because three
houses on her street had sold in the
previous year. All of them fully
renovated by people who bought them,
gutted them, and resold them. Delma's
house has the original kitchen. The roof
is 19 years old. The bathroom has not
been touched since her husband tiled it
himself. She was assessed as though she
lived in the renovated version of her
own house because from the street and
from a satellite image, that is exactly
what it looks like. She did not appeal
because she did not know she could
because the notice did not say appeal in
large letters. It said notice of
assessment and it stated a number and it
read like something that had already
been decided and that is the thread
running through all four of these
documents. Now let me give you my honest
opinion which is only that I have been
doing this long enough to notice
something about these letters and I want
to say it plainly rather than dance
around it. Every one of them is
technically compliant. The long-term
care letter does disclose the
non-forfeite option. The insurance
statement does show the declining cash
value. The assessment notice does state
the appeal window. Nobody is breaking
any rule. But look at how the
information is arranged. The number that
frightens you is at the top in large
type. The option that helps you is in
the middle in small type in technical
language. The deadline is somewhere near
the bottom in a sentence that does not
begin with the word deadline. Now, I do
not think there is a room somewhere
where people design these letters to be
missed. Most of them are written by
compliance departments whose job is to
satisfy a regulator, not to communicate
with a 74 year old woman at her kitchen
table. The lawyer's question is, did we
disclose it? Nobody's job is to ask
whether anybody actually understood it,
but the effect is identical either way.
And the effect is that the people who
successfully use these protections tend
to be the people with a financially
confident son or daughter who opens the
mail with them. And the people who lose
out tend to be the ones going through it
alone. And the second thing which is
less comfortable to say, every document
in this video arrives at a moment of
stress. A premium doubling, a policy in
trouble, losing your insurer, your home
being reassessed. Each one delivers
difficult news first and the solution
second. So the natural human response
which is to put it down and come back to
it when you feel steadier is precisely
the response that costs the money. The
system does not account for the fact
that a person receiving distressing news
needs a day before they can absorb the
details. Which is why I would rather you
hear about all of this now on an
ordinary afternoon when nothing has
arrived and nothing is at stake. Because
knowing what to look for before the
envelope comes is a completely different
experience from learning it while your
hands are shaking. All right, here is
your list. Five things. One, go and find
any letter you started reading and put
down. That is the one today. Two, if you
hold a long-term care policy and have
received an increase notice, telephone
and ask specifically about contingent
non-forfeite, reduced daily benefit,
shortened benefit period, and a longer
elimination period. four options by
name. Three, if you own permanent life
insurance, telephone and request an
inforce illustration. It is free and it
tells you the year the policy lapses if
nothing changes. Four, if you receive a
non-renewal from your home insurer, act
the day it arrives. Contact an
independent agent and ask about your
state's fair plan by name if the market
declines you. Five, when your assessment
notice arrives, request the property
record card and check every physical
detail for errors before the appeal
window closes. And if your own situation
is tangled, if you are holding one of

telling you, write to me. The address is

put down a letter about a decision she

Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not

regulated entry point into a federal

That means the person serving you has
obligations that have nothing to do with
customer service.
When a transaction is unusual, they are
required to ask about it. When you
answer, that answer goes into a field,
