6 months or more pauses it. Having an
offer in compromise under consideration
pauses it plus 30 days afterward.
Requesting a collection due process
hearing pauses it. A pending innocent
spouse request pauses it as well. Which
means, and this is genuinely
uncomfortable, some of the relief
options in this very video will extend
your clock while they are pending. That
is not a reason to avoid them. For most
people, an approved offer or a granted
innocent spouse claim is worth far more
than the months added. But, it is a
reason to know where you stand on that
clock before you file anything. The
right move for somebody with 9 years
elapsed is frequently different from the
right move for somebody with two. And
you can find out. You are entitled to
request your account transcript, which
shows the assessment dates. That is the
starting point for the arithmetic. And
it costs nothing. Let me be practical
about how you actually get that, because
it is simpler than people expect, and it
is the single most useful thing anybody
watching this can do today.
You want what is called an account
transcript for each year in question,
not a return transcript, which just
shows what you filed. The account
transcript shows the activity on the
account, including the date the tax was
assessed. That is the date the clock
started. You can request it through your
own online account with the agency, or
by telephone, or by posting in a form.
It is free in every case. When it
arrives, the line you are looking for
shows an assessment with a date beside
it. 10 years from that date is your
starting figure,
>> [snorts]
>> before accounting for anything that
paused it. And if the transcript is
difficult to read, and they genuinely
are not written for ordinary people,
that is exactly the kind of thing a free
taxpayer clinic will walk through with
you in 20 minutes. Now, before I move
on, there is a distinction here that
confuses an enormous number of people
and costs some of them real money. Let
me draw it clearly. Innocent spouse
relief, which I have just described, is
about a tax debt that you should not be
held responsible for. There is a
completely separate thing called injured
spouse relief. Despite the similar name,
it addresses an entirely different
problem. That one is for when you file
jointly, you are owed a refund, and the
government seizes the whole refund to
pay a debt that belongs only to your
spouse. Their student loan, their child
support, their older tax debt. In that
situation, you are not disputing
responsibility for anything. You are
saying that part of that refund was
mine, from my income and my withholding,
and it should not have been taken for
somebody else's debt. There is a form
for it, and it can be filed alongside
your return or afterward. So, the
shorthand is this: Innocent spouse means
I should not owe this. Injured spouse
means that refund was partly mine.
People routinely file the wrong one, and
the wrong one gets rejected, regardless
of how strong the underlying situation
was. Let me tell you about Bertram.
Bertram is 69. He is owed roughly
$26,000 since a business failed in a
year he would rather not talk about. He
has never filed anything, never
requested anything, never spoken to
anybody about it. He has simply lived
with it quietly for a long time, the way
people do with things that frighten
them. And the thing Bertram does not
know is that he is inside the last 2
years of his 10-year window on most of
that balance. He has spent nearly a
decade in a low-level state of dread
over something that is, on the current
trajectory, going to expire on its own.
Now, I want to be careful here because I
am not telling anybody to hide from a
tax debt and wait it out. That is not
advice, and it is not what I am saying.
The agency has real collection powers,
and it uses them.
And a debt in its final years is exactly
when collection activity tends to
intensify. What I am saying is that
Bertram made a decision 10 years ago to
know nothing, and that decision meant he
could not tell the difference between a
situation that was genuinely dangerous
and one that was nearly over. He carried
the same fear either way. That is
exactly the gap this guide closes. Not
to make anybody a tax professional, to
put the handful of facts that tell you
where you actually stand in one place in
plain language, so that a person is
never afraid of the wrong thing for a
decade. Same place, Kevin explains.shop.
Link in the description and in the
pinned comment at the top. And the code
on your screen if you are watching this
on the television.
7-day guarantee, no argument. Now, the
third thing. What happens when you
genuinely cannot pay anything at all?
There is a formal status for this. It is
called currently not collectible. Here
is what it means. If paying anything
toward the debt would leave you unable
to cover basic living expenses, the
agency can determine that you cannot pay
and it stops active collection.
No levy on your bank account, no
garnishment. Collection simply pauses
until your situation improves.
This is enormously relevant to people on
a fixed income and a great many of them
have no idea it exists. They assume the
only options are pay it or be pursued.
There is a third door. How you get it?
You ask and you prove it.
The agency will generally want a
collection information statement, which
is form 433F
for most individuals or form 433A. You
show your income, your expenses and your
assets with documentation. The agency
compares your figures against published
standards for housing, food, transport
and medical costs. If your necessary
expenses consume your income, you
qualify. Now, three honest things about
it because I will not sell you half a
rule. First, the debt does not
disappear. It sits there. Interest and
penalties continue to accrue on the
balance while you are in this status.
Second, the agency reviews it. This is
not permanent. If your income improves,
they can revisit and start collecting
again. Third, and this is the piece that
connects it to everything else in this
video. The 10-year clock keeps running
the entire time you are in this status.
It does not pause for currently not
collectible. Put those two facts
together and you have one of the
genuinely powerful positions available
in this entire subject. Somebody with a
modest fixed income and a debt that is 7
years old can potentially be placed in
this status, protected from collection
while the remaining 3 years of the clock
run out on their own. That is not a
trick. It is the plain interaction of
two published rules. It is the reason
knowing about the clock matters so much.
Two more practical things about this
status that people ask about constantly.
The first is what happens to a federal
tax lien. Being placed in currently not
collectible does not automatically
remove a lien if one has already been
filed. A lien is a claim against your
property and it can remain in place. So,
somebody in this status is protected
from active collection, from levies and
garnishment, and may still have a lien
sitting on record. If a lien is causing
you a specific problem, that is a
separate conversation with its own
routes and it is worth raising by name
rather than assuming the status handles
everything. The second is social
security. A great many of you are
wondering whether your benefit can be
taken for a tax debt. The honest answer
is that it can be through a program that
can take a percentage of a monthly
payment, but hardship matters enormously
here and this status is precisely the
argument against it.
If your benefit is what keeps you housed
and fed, that is exactly the case you
are making when you file the financial
statement, which is why doing nothing is
so expensive in this particular
situation. The person who never files
the paperwork has never made the
argument and an argument that was never
made cannot be accepted. Now, the fourth
thing,
penalties. An enormous share of what
people owe is not tax at all. It is
penalties plus interest calculated on
those penalties.
Failure to file, failure to pay, both
accumulating month after month. It is
entirely ordinary for penalties to
represent a substantial portion of a
balance and penalties come off far more
easily than tax does. There are two
routes. The first is the one almost
nobody knows about and it is the easier
of the two by a wide margin. It is an
administrative waiver, commonly called
first time abatement. It has nothing to
do with hardship, nothing to do with
your circumstances, nothing to do with
having a good excuse. You qualify on
three conditions. You had no significant
penalties for the three tax years before
the one in question. You have filed all
currently required returns. You have
paid or arranged to pay any tax due.
That is it. Meet those three and the
penalties for that year can be removed.
You can request it by telephone. One
call. The reason so few people get it is
simply that the agency does not offer
it. You have to ask by name. The second
route is reasonable cause. This is for
situations where something genuinely
prevented compliance.
Serious illness,
a death in the immediate family, a
natural disaster, records destroyed,
incorrect advice from a tax professional
you reasonably relied on. Reasonable
cause requires you to explain in writing
what happened, when it happened, and how
it prevented you from meeting the
obligation. Documentation helps
enormously. Hospital records, a death
certificate, correspondence with the
professional who advised you. And here
is the sequencing that saves people
money, which almost nobody gets right.
If you qualify for first-time abatement,
and you also have a genuine reasonable
cause argument, ask for reasonable cause
first, because first-time abatement can
only be used once in a stretch of years.
If you spend it on a year where you had
a legitimate reasonable cause argument
anyway, you have wasted it. Save the
automatic one for a year where you have
no story to tell. Now, the fifth thing,
settling for less than you owe. This is
the one everybody has heard of, mostly
through advertisements, and it is the
one most badly misrepresented. It is
called an offer in compromise. Here is
what it genuinely is. The agency can
accept less than the full balance when
it concludes that the amount offered
represents the most it can realistically
expect to collect from you within the
time it has left to collect. That last
part is the whole thing, and it is why
the 10-year clock keeps reappearing in
this video.
The calculation is fundamentally about
what they can get before the clock runs
out. How it works in practice. You file
form 656, along with a detailed
financial statement, form 433-A for
individuals. There is an application fee
and an initial payment, typically 20% of
your offer if you are paying in a lump
sum.
And here is the piece that matters most
to this audience. Both the fee and the
initial payment are waived entirely if
you qualify as a low-income taxpayer,
generally defined as income at or below
of the federal poverty guidelines. A
great many people watching this qualify
for that waiver and have no idea. The
agency looks at three things:
your income, your expenses, the equity
in your assets. It values assets at
roughly 80% of market value on the
theory of a quick sale minus what is
secured against them. Now, the honest
parts. Review takes 6 to 24 months.
Collection is generally suspended while
it is pending, which is a real benefit.
But the 10-year clock is also paused
during that time, plus 30 days.
You must stay completely compliant
throughout, filing, paying, everything.
Falling out of compliance while an offer
is pending is among the fastest ways to
have it rejected. And most offers are
rejected. That is the truth, and you
should hear it from me rather than from
an advertisement. The people who succeed
are generally those with genuinely
limited income, minimal asset equity,
and a realistic offer. Which means for a
great many retirees, an offer in
compromise is not actually the best
route. Currently not collectible status,
combined with a clock that keeps
running, frequently achieves a better
outcome with less paperwork, less cost,
and no pause on the expiration date. Let
me tell you about Corrine. Corrine is
71. She owed about $19,000.
She saw an advertisement on television
promising to settle tax debt for pennies
on the dollar. She telephoned. She paid
$4,000 up front to a company that
promised to handle everything. They
filed an offer. It was rejected because
her situation was never a good fit for
one. The company kept her $4,000.
What she actually qualified for, on the
numbers she had all along, was currently
not collectible status. It would have
cost her nothing. It would have stopped
collection just as effectively. It would
not have paused her clock. She did not
do anything foolish.
She did what a frightened person does
when somebody on television offers to
make a frightening thing go away.
Now, the warning. Because this industry
is full of people like the ones who took
Corrine's money, every genuine program
in this video is free to apply for.
Innocent spouse relief is free.
Currently not collectible is free.
Penalty abatement is free. The offer in
compromise has a fee of $205,
which is waived for lower incomes. And
that fee goes to the government, not to
a company. Nobody has special access.
There is no insider route, no
relationship, no expedited channel. A
company charging you thousands is
filling in the same free forms you can
fill in. That does not mean professional
help is never worth it. A genuinely
complicated innocent spouse case or a
large offer can absolutely justify
hiring somebody qualified. But the
qualified person is an attorney, a
certified public accountant, or an
enrolled agent. And they will tell you
honestly whether you have a case before
taking your money. And there is a
completely free option almost nobody
knows about. Low income taxpayer clinics
exist across the country specifically to
represent people in disputes with the
agency. They are free or nearly free.
They are staffed by qualified
professionals. They handle exactly these
cases. Also, and this is important, the
agency will not telephone you out of
nowhere demanding immediate payment,
threatening arrest, or asking for
payment by card or gift card. Contact
begins by post. If you get that call,
put the phone down. Now, let me give you
my honest opinion, which is only that. I
do not think the collection system is
unfair in its design. A country that
cannot collect tax does not function.
And every one of these relief provisions
exists precisely because Congress
recognized that rigid collection
produces cruel outcomes. My objection is
about who finds out. Every provision in
this video is published. All of them are
free. None of them are secret. And the
agency does not proactively tell you
about a single one. The letter that
arrives tells you what you owe and how
to pay. It does not say, you may qualify
for relief as a spouse who is kept in
the dark.
It does not say, this debt expires in 3
years. It does not say there is a status
for people who pay anything. So, the
person who gets relief is not the person
who most deserves it. It is the person
who found out, which means it flows
toward people with resources, education,
and confident family members. And away
from a 74-year-old widow who assumes a
letter is the final word. And the same
silence is exactly what companies like
the one that took Corrine's money depend
on. They are not selling access. They
are selling the information itself,
which was always free, to people nobody
bothered to inform. All right, here is
your list. Five things. One, if you
signed joint returns and the debt came
from your spouse's income and decisions,
file form 8857.
Being widowed or divorced makes your
case stronger, not weaker.
Two, request your account transcript and
find out your assessment dates. You
cannot make a sensible decision about
any of this without knowing where you
sit on the 10-year clock.
Three, if paying anything would leave
you unable to cover basic living costs,
ask for currently not collectible status
by name. It stops collection and it does
not pause your clock. Four, ask for
penalty abatement by name. Ask about
first-time abatement. And if you also
have a genuine reasonable cause story,
use that one first and save the
automatic waiver. Five, before paying
any company anything, telephone a
low-income taxpayer clinic. They are
free and they will tell you honestly
what you qualify for. And if your own
situation is tangled, if you are holding
a letter and cannot work out which of
these fits you, write to me.
The address is on your screen and in the
description below, and I read every one
that comes in. One last thing before you
go. Ruth Ann signed where her husband
pointed every spring for 31 years. She
found out 4 months after his funeral
what those signatures meant. Bertram
spent almost a decade afraid of
something that was quietly running out
of time the entire while.
Because he decided it was safer not to
look, and Corinne paid $4,000 for
something that was free to a company
that knew exactly what she qualified for
and sold her something else. None of the
three did anything a reasonable person
would not have done. Not one of them was
treated unfairly by any individual
person. Every one of them was on the
wrong side of a system where the relief
is real, the relief is free, and nobody
whose job it is to tell you about it
actually exists. So, go and find out
where you stand this week while there is
still time to choose. Get the
transcript. Learn the dates. Ask for
things by name. Because in this system,
the difference between the person who
pays and the person who does not is
almost never the size of the debt. It is
whether anybody ever told them what was
available. I am Kevin. Thanks for
watching. Do not forget to check the
quiet rules at kevinexplains.shop.

title: The 5 IRS Red Flags Silently Targeting Retirees

segments.text: Nobody at the IRS is reading your tax
return. Not this year, not last year,
probably not ever. A computer is.
And that computer is not looking for
anything you did wrong. It is looking
for two numbers that should match and do
not. That is the whole thing. That is
what an audit actually is for somebody
in retirement. Not an investigation, a
mismatch. And there are five places
where retirees numbers routinely fail to
match. And four of the five involve
money you never received or money you
already paid tax on years ago.
So let me say the important part now,
rather than at the end. The single most
dangerous idea in this entire subject is
that following the law protects you. It
does not. Following the law is necessary
and it is not sufficient. Because when
that letter arrives, the agency does not
have to prove you did anything wrong.
You have to prove you did it right. That
is called the burden of proof and it
sits on you, not on them. They ask one
question.
Can you show me? And if you cannot, a
completely legal, entirely correct
position collapses anyway. Not because
it was wrong, but because you could not
document it. Which means the goal is not
to avoid the letter. Some of you are
going to get one no matter what you do.
The goal is to be somebody who opens
that letter, pulls one folder out of a
drawer and is finished in an afternoon.
So here are the five flags. What each
one is, why the computer catches it and
the single piece of paper that ends the
conversation before it starts. My name
is Kevin. I read the rules so you do not
have to. Every week I go looking for the
thing that quietly decides what happens
to your money and I bring it here before
it costs you anything. If that sounds
useful, subscribe and turn on the bell.
Because the first flag on this list
carries a penalty that shrinks by more
than half if you catch it inside a
specific window and grows if you do not.
Flag number one, the distribution you
did not take. Once you reach 73, you are
required to withdraw a minimum amount
from your traditional retirement
accounts every year. Not suggested,
required. It is calculated from your
account balance on the last day of the
previous year. Divided by a figure from
a table based on your age. Here is why
this is the easiest one for a computer
to catch. Your account custodian files a
form with the government every year
reporting your balance. So, the agency
can calculate what you were required to
withdraw before you do and they can see
what you actually withdrew.
Because that gets reported, too.
Two numbers, theirs and yours. If they
do not match, the computer notices
without a human ever being involved and
the penalty used to be brutal. 50% of
whatever you failed to take out.
That has been reduced to 25% which is
still severe on a fixed income.
But, here is the part almost nobody
knows and it is worth real money. If you
correct the shortfall inside what the
rules call the correction window,
generally through the end of the second
year after the one you missed, that
penalty drops from 25% to 10% and if you
had a genuinely reasonable cause,
illness, a death in the family, bad
advice from a custodian, you can request
that it be waived entirely. The form is
Form 5329.
You take the missed amount out as soon
as you realize, you file that form, and
you attach a short written explanation.
That is the difference between a $2,500
penalty and a $500 one on the same
mistake decided entirely by whether you
acted before you were contacted. Let me
tell you about Lonnie. Lonnie is 76. He
has three retirement accounts because he
changed employers twice in the 80s, and
he genuinely believed that taking a
distribution from the largest one
covered all three. It does not work that
way for employer plans. Each one has to
be calculated and satisfied on its own.
He was short by about $6,000 for 2 years
running before anybody noticed. His
preparer never asked because his
preparer only ever saw the one statement
Lonnie brought in.
He was not hiding anything. He brought
in every document he thought was
relevant. Nobody ever told him there
were three conversations to have instead
of one. That is the whole reason the
quiet rules exists. Plain English,
printed large enough to read without
hunting for your glasses, on the things
that quietly decide what happens to your
money. Which forms actually matter, what
the computer is comparing them against,
and the exact question to ask before you
hand your papers to anybody. So that a
mistake nobody warned you about does not
become a penalty nobody warned you
about, either. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
The link is in the description below and
in the pinned comment at the top. And if
you are watching this on a television
right now, there is a code on the screen
you can point your phone camera at.
7-day guarantee, always. If it does not
hand you something you did not have
before, you send it back. Flag number
two, the money you moved. This is the
most common retiree mismatch there is,
and it catches people who did absolutely
nothing wrong. You move an account from
one institution to another or from an
old employer plan into an IRA.
Perfectly [clears throat] ordinary,
perfectly legal. The institution you
moved it from is required to report that
as a distribution. A form goes to you,
and a copy goes to the government
showing that a large sum left a
retirement account. If that money went
into another retirement account within
60 days, it is a rollover and none of it
is taxable, But but the form does not
say that. The form says money came out.
So, the computer sees a large
distribution and looks at your return to
see it reported.
If your return does not account for it
properly, the mismatch is automatic and
the letter that follows treats the
entire amount as taxable income. The fix
is straightforward and it has to happen
when you file, not afterward.
The distribution gets reported on your
return and the word rollover gets
entered next to it and the taxable
amount shows as zero. Keep the paperwork
from both institutions. The statement
showing it left and the statement
showing it arrived. Those two pages
together end this conversation in about
90 seconds.
Flag number three. The business that
never makes money. A great many people
start something in retirement.
Consulting, woodworking, selling at
markets, photography, and a great many
of those things lose money, especially
at the start. Losses are the single
loudest signal in this entire system.
When a return shows a loss that reduces
other income, attention follows. That is
true for everybody and it is
particularly true for small, informal
operations run by one person. The rule
underneath it is what people call the
hobby loss rule.
If an activity shows a profit in three
of the last five years, it is generally
presumed to be a business. If it does
not, the agency can decide it is a hobby
and hobby expenses cannot be deducted
against your other income at all.
Now, three of five is a presumption, not
a law of physics.
Plenty of genuine businesses lose money
for longer than that, but if you are
outside it, you are the one who has to
demonstrate you are running a real
business.
What demonstrates it is not passion. It
is behavior. A separate bank account,
actual books, a written plan, records
showing you changed something when it
was not working, evidence you were
trying to make money rather than
enjoying yourself and deducting it. Let
me tell you about Sybil.
Sybil is 69 and she has sold her pottery
at craft fairs for 6 years. She has
never once made a profit, mostly because
she gives most of it away to family.
She has deducted her kiln, her
materials, her booth fees, and the
mileage to every fair against her
pension income every year. She has no
separate account. The money goes into
her regular checking. She has no books
beyond a notebook. And she has said out
loud at more than one fair that she does
not really care whether it makes money.
Every one of those things is true and
reasonable and human. Together, they
describe a hobby and 6 years of
deductions rest on it. That is exactly
the gap this guide closes. Not to turn
anybody into an accountant, to put the
handful of things that separate a
defensible position from an indefensible
one in plain language so that a person
doing something perfectly honest is not
caught out by paperwork nobody
explained. Same place,
kevinexplains.shop.
Link in the description and in the
pinned comment at the top.
And the code on your screen if you are
watching this on the television. 7-day
guarantee, no argument. Flag number
four, generosity that does not match the
income.
Retirees frequently give a considerably
larger share of their income to church
and charity than working people do. That
is genuinely admirable and it is also
statistically unusual and statistically
unusual is exactly what a computer is
built to find. A charitable deduction
that is large relative to your reported
income invites a question, not an
accusation. A question. Two things
protect you completely. For anything
over $250,
you need a written acknowledgement from
the organization, and it must state
whether you received anything in return.
A cancelled check is not enough on its
own. Your church will produce that
letter if you ask. And for anybody over
70 and a half, there is a better route
entirely.
You can send money directly from an IRA
to a charity. It counts toward your
required distribution, and it never
appears in your income at all. That
matters more than it sounds. Because it
never enters your income, it cannot push
more of your social security into being
taxable, and it cannot raise your
Medicare premium 2 years later. A
deduction cannot do either of those
things for you. This can.
And there is one more thing here that
catches genuinely generous people.
If you donate property rather than cash,
a car, furniture, anything valued above
$5,000, you generally need a qualified
written appraisal. Not your estimate.
Not the charity's estimate. An
appraisal. Skip it, and the entire
deduction can be disallowed regardless
of how valuable the item actually was.
Flag number five, the casino. When you
win above certain thresholds, the
establishment reports it. A form goes to
you, and a copy goes to the government.
So, those winnings arrive on the
computer side of the ledger, whether you
mention them or not. Now, you can deduct
losses, but only up to your winnings,
only if you itemize, and only if you can
prove them.
And the government has been explicit for
decades about what proof looks like. A
contemporaneous log, dates, locations,
amounts won and lost, kept as you go. A
shoebox of losing tickets is not a log,
and courts have said so repeatedly. So,
the arithmetic that catches people is
this. Somebody wins $1,200 on one
machine, and loses it all back across
the year. The 1,200 is reported. The
losses are not documented, and they are
taking the standard deduction anyway.
So, the deduction is unavailable. They
pay tax on the entire 1,200, having
ended the year down. And there is a
second cost people never see coming.
Those winnings count as income for every
other purpose, too. So, a good night at
a casino can push more of your social
security into being taxable. And it can
raise your Medicare premium 2 years
later.
Entirely separately from the tax on the
winnings themselves. Most players card
programs will produce a win and loss
statement for the year on request, and
it takes one phone call. It is not a
perfect substitute for a log, and it is
far better than nothing at all, which
brings me to the thing that protects you
against all five at once.
Timing. Documentation created after a
letter arrives has almost no weight.
Courts have a name for explaining your
intentions after the fact, and it is not
a flattering one. What carries weight is
what was written down when the thing
actually happened. So, the protection is
not a strategy.
It is a folder.
One folder for the year with the
acknowledgement letters, the rollover
statements, the distribution records,
and anything else showing what a number
was and why. And two more things worth
knowing about how this actually unfolds,
because the fear people carry is usually
worse than the reality.
Most of what people call an audit is not
a person coming to your house. It is a
letter asking you to post in proof of
one specific item.
That is called a correspondence audit,
and it is the overwhelming majority of

once.

six. So, the folder for this year is

objection is that it treats an
80-year-old with three retirement

corporation with an accounting
department. The same mismatch, the same

to prove yourself, and no allowance
anywhere for the fact that one of those

the other has a drawer in the kitchen.
All right. Five things. One, if you are
73 or older, confirm you took the full

one.
Two, if you moved any money between

Four, get written acknowledgement for

Five, if you gamble at all, keep a

that comes in. One last thing, Lonnie

undermines her.
And 6 years of deductions rest on a
notebook. Neither of them did anything

anyway, because in this system, the
question is never whether you were
truthful. It is whether you can show it.
So, build the folder this week while
nothing has happened, because the people

because most coverage of this subject

long enough that the money you saved by

And there is one more thing about that

because it tells you something useful

owed. They accepted $2,800. He borrowed

question worth sitting with. If an
unfamiliar tax form arrived in January,
would you recognize it as something that

and this is the most valuable section of
this video, so stay with me. It is

that moment. By the tax code's own

some or all of it. Let me walk through
the arithmetic because it is simpler
than people expect. Add up everything
you owed immediately before the
cancellation. every credit card balance,
any mortgage, any car loan, medical

being cancelled, your mortgage if you

including any you took out for a child,
money owed to family members if there is
genuine documentation of it, past due
utility bills, any tax you owed at that

every one you leave out makes you look
less insolvent than you actually were.
On the asset side, use fair market

it and not what it is insured for. A
12-year-old car is worth what a
12-year-old car sells for. Household
furniture is worth almost nothing on the

your home is worth what comparable homes

minus nothing because the mortgage
against it is already counted on the

surprises people and it is the single

because a person with a modest
retirement account and a manageable

Suppose your total debts were $80,000

the entire 12,000 is excluded because it

You owe nothing on it. But if the
canceled amount were 35,000, you could

for most ordinary cases involving a

because bankruptcy carries consequences

When your return does not account for

instruction is straightforward. If that

received a cancellation of debt form and
I believe I may have been insolvent at

single sentence spoken in March is the
difference between owing nothing and

entire difference between Roxy's outcome

That is exactly the gap this guide

That is the single most useful thing in

14 months after the relief in the form

There is simply a number and a name and
a great deal of silence. And the people

the people who were in financial
difficulty. That is why the debt was

I want to say because it is the part

Something as simple as you may not owe

subject. Not concealment, not malice,

rather than either paying it or ignoring

senior deduction which appears
separately. If your total shielded
income does not come anywhere near what
I just described and your income was
under the threshold, something was
missed. And if something was missed, you
are not stuck with it. You can amend a
return for roughly 3 years after filing.
So a mistake made on the last two
returns is money that can still be
recovered rather than money that is
gone. Let me tell you about Fern. Fern
is 71 and she has used the same preparer
at the same office for 11 years. She
likes him. He is pleasant. He remembers
her husband's name and he charges her a
couple of hundred. Her income is small,
social security and a modest pension
from a hospital where she worked in the
records department for 26 years. She
paid federal income tax last year, not
much, a few hundred. And she paid it
without a second thought because she has
paid tax every year of her adult life.
and it never occurred to her that a year
might come when she simply would not owe
any. Her income was under the threshold.
All three deductions applied to her.
Only two of them appeared on her return.
Nobody cheated her. A busy man in a busy
office in March missed one line on one
form, and Fern paid a bill that was
never hers, and she will do it again
next year unless somebody tells her to
look. That is the whole reason the quiet
rules exists. plain English printed
large enough to read without hunting for
your glasses on the things that quietly
decide what happens to your money, which
line to look at, what the number should
be, and the exact question to ask the
person who prepares your return so that
nobody pays a bill that was never theirs
simply because it was easier not to
check. It is at kevinexplains.shop.
The link is in the description below and
in the pinned comment at the top. And if
you are watching this on a television
right now, there is a code on the screen
you can point your phone camera at.
7-day guarantee always. If it does not
hand you something you did not have
before, you send it back. So, here is a
question worth sitting with. When did
you last actually read your own tax
return rather than just sign it? Bill
number two, your bank. This one has no
income test whatsoever. It takes one
conversation, and I would guess 90% of
you have never had that conversation.
Most banks in this country charge a
monthly maintenance fee on a current
account. Somewhere between $5 and $20 a
month, depending on the bank and the
account. It comes out automatically. It
appears on a statement most people
glance at, and over a year, it adds up
to real money for something you are not
receiving any service for. And most
banks wave it. for people over a certain
age, usually 62 or 65, sometimes 55.
Some of them call it a senior account.
Some of them call it a 55 plus account
or a golden account or something equally
cheerful. Some of them do not advertise
it at all and simply have a code a
teller can apply if somebody asks. Here
is what makes this worth 2 minutes of
your life. You do not qualify by being
old. You qualify by asking. A bank that
has been charging you a fee for nine
years will keep charging you for nine
more because there is no obligation
anywhere for them to look at your date
of birth and move you to a cheaper
product. So walk in or telephone and say
exactly this. I am over 65. What
accounts do you offer that wave the
monthly fee and can you switch me today?
That sentence has in my experience about
a 70% hit rate and the whole thing takes
10 minutes. While you are having that
conversation, ask about three more
things because they are usually
available at the same time and nobody
offers them either. Ask about the fee
for a cashier's check or a money order,
which many banks wave on senior
accounts. Ask about overdraft charges
and specifically whether they will link
your savings account so a shortfall
pulls from your own money rather than
triggering a $35 fee. And ask about safe
deposit box rental, which some banks
discount or wave. And one more thing
which is not a fee at all but belongs in
the same conversation. Ask what your
savings account is actually paying. A
great many people have money sitting in
an account paying almost nothing while
the same institution offers considerably
more on a different product across the
counter. Nobody moves you. You have to
ask. None of this is dramatic on its
own. Add up the fee waiver, the check
fees, and one avoided overdraft, and you
are typically looking at $2 to $400 a
year, every year, for one conversation
you have once. And while we are on the
subject of things that arrive every
month and never get questioned, there
are three more in the same category, and
they work exactly the same way, your
mobile phone. Most of the major carriers
run a plan priced specifically for
customers over 55. And in several cases,
it is roughly half what a standard plan
costs for the same service. Almost
nobody gets moved on to it automatically
because a phone company that moves you
to a cheaper plan without being asked is
a phone company earning less money.
Telephone them and ask what plan they
offer for customers over 55 and what it
would cost compared to what you pay now.
Your internet. There is a lowcost home
internet program run by most major
providers, generally priced somewhere
around $ 20 to $30 a month, and
eligibility is usually tied to
participation in another program such as
Medicaid, food assistance, or the
prescription subsidy I will describe
shortly. If you qualify for one of
those, you very likely qualify for this,
and the two are almost never mentioned
in the same conversation by anybody. and
your car insurance. If you are retired
and driving considerably less than you
were when you commuted every day, your
premium is frequently still priced on
the mileage you reported years ago.
Telephone them. Tell them your actual
annual mileage now and ask whether that
changes anything. Ask separately whether
they offer a discount for completing a
defensive driving course for older
drivers because a great many insurers
do. Several states require them to and
the course is often available online in
an afternoon. Here is the pattern I want
you to notice across all four of those.
Not one of them is a benefit somebody
has to grant you. They are all products
a company already sells at a lower price
to people in exactly your position. And
the only barrier between you and the
lower price is a telephone call in which
you ask a direct question.
[clears throat] So make an afternoon of
it. Bank, phone, internet, insurance.
Four calls. Realistically somewhere
between $400 and $1,000 a year. and the
entire cost is one afternoon and a
willingness to ask a stranger for a
better price. Bill number three, your
utility bill. This one surprises people
because they think of the power company
as a company rather than something with
rules and it has more rules attached to
it than almost any business you deal
with. There are three separate things
available here and they stack which is
the part almost nobody understands. The
first is a senior or fixed income rate
discount offered directly by the
utility. Many companies, particularly
municipal ones, offer a monthly credit
or a reduced rate for customers over 60
or 62. Some are income tested and some
are simply age tested. The bill has to
be in your name, which catches people
out where a bill is still in a late
husband's name years afterward. The
second is worth knowing about even if
you are comfortably off because it has
nothing to do with income at all. Many
utilities offer what is often called a
medical baseline rate. If somebody in
the household uses medical equipment
that consumes electricity, an oxygen
concentrator, a nebulizer, certain
monitors, a powered bed, or has a
condition requiring the house to be kept
at a particular temperature, you can
qualify for a reduced rate or a larger
allowance at the cheaper tier. That one
requires a form signed by a doctor and
it is not means tested. If somebody in
your house is on oxygen and you are
paying a standard rate, that is money
going out every month for no reason. The
third is the federal assistance program
that operates in every state which helps
with heating and cooling costs. It is
income based and the limits are higher
than most people assume, generally set
against a percentage of the state median
income rather than a small fixed figure.
Benefits commonly run between $400 and
$1,500 a year. And there is a separate
crisis component for anybody facing a
shut off. And here is the timing detail
that matters, which is why this is in a
video I am publishing now rather than in
January. These programs are funded with
a fixed pot of money each year. When a
state runs out, it stops taking
applications until the next cycle,
regardless of whether you qualified.
Applications for the heating season open
in the autumn in most states. The people
who get help are frequently just the
people who applied early. One phone
number covers all of this. If you do not
know where to start, dial 211 from any
phone in the country and you reach a
local service that will tell you what
exists in your area and how to apply for
it. It is free. It is not a government
agency selling you anything. And it is
the single most useful telephone number
in this entire video. Let me tell you
about Odell. Odell is 76 and his wife
has been on oxygen at night for 4 years.
Their electricity bill went up when the
machine arrived and they absorbed it the
way people do. It was not a crisis. it
was $30 or $40 a month and they simply
stopped eating out. There is a rate on
their own utility's own website
requiring a form and a doctor's
signature that would have covered a
large part of that from the first month.
Nobody at the hospital mentioned it
because that is not their job. Nobody at
the utility mentioned it because they
had no way of knowing and the equipment
supplier did not mention it either. So
for four years, a household on a fixed
income quietly paid for something they
were entitled to have discounted and
every party involved behaved reasonably
and the money is gone. That is exactly
the gap this guide closes. Not to turn
anybody into an expert on utility
tariffs. To put the handful of things
that exist and the words that unlock
them in one place so that the difference
between paying and not paying is a form
rather than a piece of luck about who
happened to mention it. Same place,
kevin Kevin expplains.shop. Link in the
description and in the pinned comment at
the top and the code on your screen if
you are watching this on the television.
7-day guarantee, no argument. A woman on
oxygen, a machine running every night
and a discount sitting on a website
nobody in that house had a reason to
visit. Bill number four, your
prescription drug costs. This is the
largest dollar figure in the video for
the people it fits, and the income
limits are considerably higher than
almost anybody assumes. The program is
called Extra Help, officially the
lowincome subsidy, and it works
alongside Medicare prescription
coverage. Here is what it does. It pays
your prescription drug plan premium. It
removes the deductible entirely, and it
caps what you pay at the pharmacy
counter at roughly $5 for a generic and
about 12 or 13 for a brandame drug,
regardless of what that drug actually
costs. The government's own estimate of
what this is worth to the average person
who qualifies is around $5,700
a year. Now, the limits, and listen
closely, because this is where people
rule themselves out incorrectly. The
income limit this year is about $23,475
for one person and about $31,725
for a married couple. Not 2,000, not
some tiny welfare figure. Over 23,000
for one person. The resource limit is
around $18,90
for a single person and $36,100 for a
couple. And here is the part that
changes who qualifies. So hear this
properly. Your home does not count. Your
car does not count. Your household goods
do not count. Your burial plot and a
burial fund do not count. Life insurance
does not count. So the house you own
outright, the car in the driveway, and
the plot at the cemetery are all
invisible to this calculation. An
enormous number of people take one look
at the resource limit, think about their
house, and decide it is not for them.
Their house was never in the equation.
Two more things, and then I will move
on. The partial version of this no
longer exists. It used to be that some
people qualified for a reduced subsidy.
Now, everybody who qualifies receives
the full amount. And if you are already
receiving help from your state with your
Medicare premiums, you should be
enrolled in this automatically. If you
are in that position and have never seen
a letter confirming it, that is worth a
telephone call because being eligible
and being enrolled are not always the
same thing in practice. The application
takes about 10 minutes. You can do it
online, by telephone, or in person. You
do not need to send bank statements with
it. It is free and there is no penalty
of any kind for applying and being told
no. That last point matters more than
any figure I have given you. The worst
outcome of applying is a letter saying
you do not qualify. Nobody has ever been
made worse off by asking. Bill number
five, property tax, and specifically the
version that sends you a check. Now, a
lot of people know that senior property
tax exemptions exist. That is not what
I'm covering here because that is the
well-known one. What I am covering is
the second program that most states run
alongside it, which works completely
differently and which very few people
ever claim. An exemption reduces the
taxable value of your home before the
bill is calculated. Useful and it only
helps if you own and it only helps going
forward. The other kind is usually
called a circuit breaker. The idea
behind the name is that it trips when
your property tax becomes too large a
share of your income. Rather than
reducing the assessment, it looks at
what you actually paid against what you
actually earned and it sends money back.
That difference produces three things
worth knowing. First, because it is
based on income rather than assessment,
the income limits are frequently far
more generous than people expect,
running into the tens of thousands
rather than being restricted to the
poorest households. Second, in a number
of states, renters qualify, too. A
portion of rent is treated as property
tax paid on your behalf, and that
portion counts. So, somebody who has
never owned a home and assumed every
property tax program was irrelevant to
them may be leaving money on the table
every year. Third, and this is the one
that makes it worth acting on today, it
frequently arrives as an actual payment
rather than a reduction, a check or a
direct deposit for tax you already paid.
And several states allow you to claim it
for prior years. So, a person who has
qualified for 3 years and never applied
can in some places claim all three. The
deadlines vary and a great many of them
fall in the autumn, which is precisely
why this is the last item and why I
would not leave it until the new year.
Here is what to do. Telephone your
state's revenue department, not the
county, the state, and ask whether they
operate a property tax credit or circuit
breaker for older residents, what the
income limit is, whether renters
qualify, and whether you can claim for
previous years. Four questions, one
call. Let me tell you about Winona.
Winona is 80 and she rents a small flat
above a shop. And she has rented her
whole life. Every time property tax came
up in conversation, she stopped
listening because she does not own
anything and it obviously had nothing to
do with her. Her state runs a credit
that treats a share of rent as property
tax paid. She has qualified every year
for about 11 years. She has never
claimed a penny of it. And what gets me
about Winona is that she was not
misinformed. Nobody told her anything
wrong. She drew an entirely sensible
conclusion from an accurate fact, which
is that she does not own property. And
the conclusion happened to be wrong for
a reason nobody had any occasion to
explain to her. Now, let me give you the
thing that connects all five, which is
what I promised at the start. Look at
what these five have in common because
it is not what people assume. It is not
that they are hidden. [clears throat]
Every one of these is published. The tax
figures are on the revenue services own
website. The bank's senior account is on
a leaflet at the counter. The medical
rate is on the utilities site. The
subsidy has its own application page.
The property credit is in the state tax
booklet. It is not that they are hard to
get either. The longest application in
this entire video takes about 10
minutes. The thing they share is this.
Every single one is triggered by asking,
and not one of them is triggered by
qualifying. There is no organization
anywhere whose job it is to look at your
date of birth and your circumstances and
tell you what you have become eligible
for. That job does not exist. Your bank
does not do it. Your utility does not do
it. Your tax preparer does it only for
the things he happens to remember. Your
county does not do it. Nobody does it.
So the entire system works on the
assumption that you already know. And
the only people who reliably know are
the ones who happen to be told by
somebody. That is the whole thing. And
once you can see it, you stop waiting to
be informed and you start asking a very
simple question of every organization
that takes money from you every month.
What do you offer people my age? And am
I on it? Now, let me give you my honest
opinion, which is only that, and you are
welcome to disagree with me in the
comments. I do not think there is a
conspiracy here, and I want to say that
plainly because it would be easy and
dishonest to sell you one. A bank is not
hiding the senior account. It is simply
a business and businesses do not
generally telephone customers to offer
them a cheaper product. A tax preparer
working through a queue in March is not
defrauding anybody. A utility genuinely
does not know what medical equipment is
in your house. Every one of these gaps
has an ordinary explanation and none of
them requires anybody to be a villain.
My objection is about the design rather
than the people. When a government
creates a benefit and does not create
any mechanism for finding the people who
qualify, it has made a choice and it has
made it knowing exactly what the result
will be. The result is that the benefit
reaches the people with the most
confidence, the best information, and
the most persistent family members. And
it does not reach the 80-year-old who
rents a flat above a shop and has no
reason to think any of it is about her.
That is not a small thing. It means a
program designed to help the people in
the most difficulty systematically works
best for the people in the least. And
nothing about that is going to change
because I am annoyed about it. So the
practical response is the only one
available, which is to go and ask. One
warning before the list because a video
like this one creates exactly the
opening somebody looks for. Every
program in this video is free to apply
for. Every single one. There is no fee
to claim a tax deduction. no charge to
apply for the prescription subsidy, no
cost to request a utility rate, and no
such thing as a company authorized to
claim a property tax credit on your
behalf for a percentage. So, if somebody
telephones you in the next few weeks
offering to check what benefits you
qualify for or to file an application
for you for a fee or asking you to
confirm your social security number so
they can see what you are owed, put the
phone down. The people who run these
programs do not cold call. And the only
thing a stranger needs to steal from you
is the number you are about to read out
loud. If you want help and you would
rather not do it alone, the free version
already exists. Dial 211
or telephone your local agency on aging,
which every county has and which employs
people whose entire job is helping older
residents apply for exactly these things
at no cost whatsoever. All right, here
is your list. Five things. and everyone
is a phone call or a form. One, pull out
last year's tax return and look at the
deduction line. If you were over 65 and
under the income threshold and you paid
federal tax on a modest income, ask your
preparer specifically whether the new
senior deduction was applied. You can
amend roughly 3 years back. Two,
telephone or visit your bank and ask
what account they offer that waves the
monthly fee for somebody your age and
ask them to switch you today. While you
are there, ask about check fees,
overdraft linking, and what your savings
is actually paying. Three, telephone
your utility and ask three questions. Do
you offer a senior or fixed income rate?
Do you offer a medical rate for
households using medical equipment? And
what assistance program do you refer
people to? If you would rather make one
call than three, dial 2 1 1. Four, apply
for extra help even if you are certain
you will not qualify. Remember, the
house, the car, and the burial fund are
not counted, and the income limit is
over 23,000 for one person. Being told
no cost you nothing at all.
Five, telephone your state revenue
department and ask whether they run a
property tax credit or circuit breaker,
what the income limit is, whether
renters qualify, and whether you can
claim for prior years. And if your own
situation is tangled, if you are not
sure which of these fits you, write to
me. The address is on your screen and in
the description below, and I read every
one that comes in. Tell me your age and
roughly what your income is made up of,
because those two things determine
almost everything on this list. One last
thing before you go. Fern has paid a tax
bill that was never hers for at least
two years because one line was missed by
a decent man in a busy month. Odell
watched his electricity bill rise when
the oxygen machine arrived and simply
absorbed it 4 feet from a discount he
was entitled to. And Winona stopped
listening every time property tax came
up for 11 years. And she was right about
the fact and wrong about the conclusion.
None of the three did a single thing a
sensible person would not have done. Not
one of them was refused anything by any
person. Every one of them was waiting to
be told about something nobody had any
duty to mention. So go and ask this
week. Ask the bank. Ask the power
company. Ask whoever does your return.
And when they tell you what you qualify
for, ask the second question that almost
nobody asks, which is whether you can
claim it for the years you already paid.
I am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: 3 Changes Quietly Hitting Every Senior's Check Starting September

segments.text: The next time you need Social Security
to answer a question for you, there will
be fewer people on the other end than at
any point since 1967.
Not fewer than last year, not fewer than
before the cut started, fewer than 1967,
back when the agency did not yet run the
disability program at all and served 52
million fewer people than it serves
today. That is not a projection or
somebody's opinion about the future. It
is the staffing number and it is already
true while you are watching this. Now I
want to be careful and precise here
because this subject attracts a great
deal of noise and you deserve better
than noise. Your check is not stopping.
Nobody is losing a benefit because of
anything in this video. Every dollar you
are owed is still owed to you and it is
still coming. If somebody has told you
otherwise, they were wrong and I want
that settled in the first minute rather
than the last. What has changed is not
the money. It is whether there is
anybody available when something goes
wrong with it. And that distinction
matters more than almost anything else I
could tell you. Because in this system,
nothing gets fixed on its own. A wrong
amount, a missing payment, a form that
needs signing, a letter you do not
understand. Every one of those requires
a human being to look at your file. That
has always been true. What is different
now is how many human beings there are.
So here are the three things happening
right now. and every one of them touches
you regardless of which benefit you
receive or how long you have been
receiving it. One, the staffing. More
than 8,000 people have left that agency
in 15 months, the largest single-year
reduction in its history, and it has
landed on every state in the country
rather than a few. Two, the doors. The
AY's own operating plan for this year
sets a target of cutting field office
visits roughly in half. Not visits that
were unnecessary, visits. Rural offices
have already closed for lack of anybody
to staff them. Three, September the
30th. That is the last day of the
federal budget year. And what happens on
that date determines how the agency
operates going into winter. I will tell
you exactly what that does and does not
mean for your payment. Because last time
this came around, a great many seniors
were frightened by people who either did
not know or did not care. And I will
finish with the one figure that tells
you whether to believe any official
statement about this at all. It is not a
number about staffing. It is about
something that was supposed to be
published and quietly was not. My name
is Kevin. I read the rules so you do not
have to. Every week I go looking for the
thing that quietly decides what happens
to your money and I bring it here before
it costs you anything. If that sounds
useful, subscribe and turn on the bell
because the practical advice in the
second part of this video works far
better if you act on it before the
autumn rather than during it. Change
number one, there are 8,000 fewer people
at that agency than there were 15 months
ago. Let me put that in proportion
because a big number on its own means
nothing. That is roughly 14% of the
entire workforce and it happened in a
little over a year. It is the largest
reduction in a single year that the
agency has ever recorded. And it did not
happen in one region or a handful of
offices. 42 states and the District of
Columbia lost more than 10% of their
Social Security staff between the start
of last year and this spring. So
wherever you live, this is your state.
There is no version of this that is
happening somewhere else to other
people. Now here is what actually
matters, which is what those people were
doing. Almost nothing at that agency is
automatic once your situation stops
being ordinary. Your monthly payment is
automatic. Your annual increase is
automatic. Those run on computers and
they will keep running no matter how
many people leave. But everything else
needs a person. Somebody has to review
an appeal. Somebody has to correct an
earnings record. Somebody has to look at
why a payment stopped. Somebody has to
process a claim after a spouse dies.
Somebody has to make a determination on
a waiver. Every one of those is a human
sitting at a desk making a judgment
about your specific file. Take out 14%
of the desks and the work does not
shrink to match. It cues and cues in
this system do not distribute themselves
evenly. They land hardest on the most
time-sensitive things because the most
time-sensitive things are also the most
complicated and complicated work is what
gets pushed back when there are too few
people. Which means the person who feels
this first is not somebody with a simple
question. It is a widow trying to switch
on to a survivor payment. It is a family
whose parent has just died. It is
somebody whose payment stopped for a
reason nobody has explained. Those are
precisely the situations where waiting 3
months instead of 3 weeks is not an
inconvenience. It is rent. Now the
agency has responded to this criticism
directly and I am going to give you
their side properly because you should
hear it. The commissioner has stated
publicly that service has improved
substantially. The figures cited include
field office wait times down by around
30%, the backlog of initial disability
claims reduced by more than 30% from
nearly 1.3 million to around 853,000
and hundreds of millions of transactions
moved online. Those are real claims made
on the record and some of them are
supported. The disability backlog
reduction in particular is a genuine
achievement if the numbers hold. And I
am not going to pretend otherwise for
the sake of a better video. But
independent analysts looking at the same
period have reported that telephone wait
times are considerably longer than what
is advertised publicly, that weights for
appointments are hitting widows and
berieved families hardest, and that
local offices are struggling to function
with the staff they have left. So you
have an agency reporting improvement and
outside observers reporting strain. in
the same months about the same offices.
Both can produce true statements because
they are counting different things. And
I will come back at the end of this
video to the one piece of information
that tells you which picture to trust.
Let me tell you about Rosco. Rosco is 72
and his wife of 44 years died in
February. He did the correct thing. He
reported it. He was told what he needed
to bring and then he waited for an
appointment to make a claim that in an
ordinary year would have been handled in
a few weeks. He is a practical man. He
assumed there was a queue and that Q's
move. What he did not know is that his
own payment stayed exactly the same the
entire time he waited because switching
on to the higher survivor amount does
not happen until somebody processes the
claim. So every month of waiting was a
month at the lower figure in a household
that had just lost one of its two
incomes. in the year that is already the
most expensive year of most people's
lives. Nobody did anything wrong to
Rosco. There was simply nobody free to
reach his file and nothing in the
process he went through ever told him
that the delay itself had a price
attached to it. That is the whole reason
the quiet rules exists. Plain English
printed large enough to read without
hunting for your glasses on the things
that quietly decide what happens to your
money. what has to be claimed rather
than granted, which delays cost you
money and which do not, and the exact
words that move a file to the front of a
queue, so that nobody in your family is
waiting quietly for something they
should have been pushing on. It is at
kevin explains.shop.
The link is in the description below and
in the pinned comment at the top. And if
you are watching this on a television
