Getting to work, a car and the fuel for
it, a mortgage rather than a paid-off
house, clothes for a job, children.
Now, think about your own month and how
little of it looks like that. The
largest and fastest growing thing in
most retired households is medical care,
premiums, prescriptions, the specialist,
the dentist, which nothing covers. After
that, housing costs that do not fall
just because the mortgage is gone,
property tax, insurance, the roof,
heating a house you are now inside all
day rather than out of it for 9 hours.
Medical care and housing carry less
weight inside the working person's index
because working households genuinely do
spend a smaller share on them.
So, when medical costs run ahead of
everything else, that shows up in your
life at full strength and in the index
at a discount.
And medical costs do run ahead.
That is not a feeling. It is one of the
most consistent patterns in the whole
economy.
Over most stretches of the last few
decades, the cost of medical care has
climbed faster than the general price
level and the cost of prescription drugs
has climbed faster still in many years.
Now, put that next to how a retired
household actually spends.
For a working family, medical care is a
payroll deduction they barely look at
and a copay a few times a year.
For a household in its 70s, it is often
the second largest line after housing
and in a bad year, it is the largest.
So, the thing rising fastest in your
life is the thing counted lightest in
your raise.
And the further into retirement a person
gets, the wider that gap tends to open
because medical spending generally rises
with age while the index weighting does
not move at all.
That is the whole argument in one
sentence and it is why this is not a
small technical quibble about
statistics.
It is a compounding difference between
the life the index describes and the
life you are actually living.
Now, here is the part that makes this
worth a section rather than a complaint.
The government already builds a second
index. It is called the Consumer Price
Index for the elderly, and it is
designed around the spending patterns of
Americans aged 62 and over.
Medical care carries more weight in it.
Housing carries more weight in it. It
exists. It is published. It has existed
since the 1980s. It is not used to set
your raise. The law names the other one,
and only Congress can change which index
the law names. And over most of the
years since it was created, the elderly
index has run higher than the wage
earner index. Not enormously higher in
any one year, a fraction of a percentage
point, but a fraction of a percentage
point compounded across a 25-year
retirement is not a small thing at all.
It is the difference between a benefit
that roughly holds its ground and one
that quietly loses it. Now, let me give
you the honest case on the other side,
because I do not think you are well
served by only hearing one. The elderly
index is officially experimental.
It is built from a smaller sample of
households, and a smaller sample means
more statistical noise.
Using it properly would cost money to do
the survey work correctly, and there is
a fair argument that you should not
attach 75 million people's income to a
measurement that was never funded to
carry that weight.
And there is a straightforward second
argument. Using a higher index means
paying out more from a program whose
trust fund is already on a timetable
everybody can see.
Every dollar of a larger raise has to
come from somewhere, and the people
making that decision are looking at that
timetable.
So, this is not villains against
victims. It is a genuine trade-off that
has been settled the same way for
decades, quietly, without most of the
people affected ever being told there
was a choice being made. And there is a
third index in this conversation that
you should know exists, because it comes
up in Washington regularly, and it moves
in the opposite direction. It is called
the chained index. The idea behind it is
substitution. If the price of beef
rises, people buy chicken instead. So,
the argument goes that measuring the
price of beef alone overstates what it
actually costs a household to get
through the week. A chained index
accounts for that swapping. As a piece
of economics that is defensible, as a
rule applied to your raise, it produces
a smaller number year after year because
it assumes you adjust. And this is where
I want to be careful and also honest.
Substitution assumes there is something
to substitute to. You can move from beef
to chicken. You cannot move from your
heart medication to a cheaper heart
medication because the price went up.
You cannot substitute a different
specialist. You cannot buy less of the
property tax. That is the objection
people make to it, and it is not a
partisan objection. It is a practical
one about whether the assumption behind
the arithmetic describes an
80-year-old's month.
Proposals to switch to that index have
been raised more than once from more
than one direction. Usually as part of a
larger package aimed at the funding
shortfall everyone can see coming. None
has passed. It remains live, and it will
come around again. And now you know what
it means when you hear the phrase,
rather than having to take somebody's
word for what it does.
So, there are three indexes in play.
The one measuring working households,
which is the one your raise uses. The
one measuring older households, which
exists and is not used and would
generally have paid more.
And the one accounting for substitution,
which is not used and would generally
pay less.
Nobody at that agency chose among them.
Congress named one in the law decades
ago, and it has been that one ever
since. If nothing else in this video
sticks, let that be the thing you carry.
Not anger, just the knowledge that the
number is a design, and designs have
authors, and the authors are reachable
by anybody who knows the design exists.
And if you want the plain version of all
of this on paper, the guide is at
kevinexplains.shop
or the code on your screen. Now, the
second thing, and this is the one that
will affect the most people watching
this in January. A raise can arrive and
your deposit can still get smaller. Here
is why. Most people have their Medicare
Part B premium taken directly out of
their Social Security payment before it
reaches them. You never see it leave.
You see the remainder. So, there are two
numbers moving every year, not one. The
raise decided in October by one agency
and the premium decided in November by a
completely different agency on its own
timetable using its own data about
medical spending. This year, the
standard Part B premium is $202.90.
The trustees have projected next year at
around $209.50
and some independent forecasters put it
higher in the range of 216 to 219.
Nothing is confirmed until the autumn.
If the premium rises by less than your
raise, your deposit goes up by the
difference. If it rises by more, the
arithmetic goes the other way.
Now, there is a protection and I want to
describe it accurately because it is
real and it is also narrower than its
reputation. It is called the hold
harmless provision.
What it does is straightforward. If the
increase in the standard Part B premium
is larger than the dollar amount of your
raise, the premium increase gets capped
so that your net payment cannot fall
below what it was the year before. Your
check does not shrink. Before I go
through who it leaves out, I want you to
notice something about the timing
because it explains why this catches
people every single year. The raise is
announced in October. The premium is
announced in November. Two agencies, two
releases, four to six weeks apart, and
the news cycle has completely moved on
by the time the second one lands. So,
every October, seniors across this
country hear a percentage, do the
multiplication, and form a picture of
next year.
And every November, the number that
actually determines their deposit is
published to almost no coverage at all.
By December, the notice arrives with the
real figure in it, and by then the
expectation has been sitting in
somebody's head for 2 months.
That gap between the two announcements
is where most of the disappointment in
this subject gets manufactured.
Not by anybody misleading anybody, by a
schedule. So, mark the November release
as the one that matters.
When the standard premium for next year
is published, that is the moment you can
actually work out your own arithmetic,
and not 1 day before.
And there is a second thing published at
the same time, which is the set of
income brackets for the surcharge I
mentioned. Those brackets shift a little
each year, and a person who is just
inside one can find themselves just
outside it, or the reverse, without
their own income changing at all.
Now, here is who the protection leaves
out, because these five groups do not
receive a letter explaining that they
are outside it. One, anyone new to
Medicare Part B. If you did not have a
premium deducted last year, there is no
prior figure to protect, so you pay the
full standard amount, whatever it turns
out to be. Two, anyone paying the
income-related surcharge. That surcharge
is calculated separately from the
standard premium, so hold harmless
simply does not reach it. And remember,
that surcharge runs on a 2-year delay,
so next year's is based on the tax
return you filed for the year before
last.
Three,
anyone who does not have Part B taken
out of a Social Security payment.
If you are billed directly quarterly,
because you have not claimed your
benefit yet, you absorb the whole
increase.
Four, certain retired public servants
who never paid into Social Security, and
therefore have no payment for the
premium to come out of. They are billed
directly, and they carry every increase
in full, and there has been legislation
proposed to change that, which has not
passed.
Five, people enrolled in a state program
that pays the premium on their behalf.
Different arrangement, different rules.
And then there is a limitation that
applies to absolutely everybody,
including the people who are protected,
and it is the one that catches the most
households.
Hold harmless covers the standard Part B
premium and nothing else. It does not
cap the hospital deductible. It does not
cap what you pay for prescription
coverage. It does not cap a supplement
premium. It does not cap the co-pays
inside an Advantage plan. So the check
is protected in a narrow way, and the
costs it has to cover are not protected
at all. And that is why so many people
can look at an announced raise, know it
is real, and still find that January is
harder than December was.
Now, if you think you might be in one of
those five groups, here is what to do
about it rather than simply worrying.
Find out for certain first, and there is
a simple way.
Look at what actually arrived in your
account last January against what
arrived the December before.
If the deposit went up, you were not
being held harmless, because hold
harmless only ever activates when the
premium increase would have pushed you
down.
Most people in most years never touch it
at all. Then, if you are billed directly
rather than having it deducted,
understand that you are carrying the
full increase every year and always will
be, and budget for it in November when
the figure is published rather than
being surprised in January.
If you pay the income-related surcharge,
the appeal route is real, and I will
come back to the form for it shortly.
And if you are newly enrolled, you are
outside the protection for 1 year only.
Next year, you will have a prior figure
on your record, and the ordinary rules
apply from then on.
That is genuinely worth knowing, because
people hear they are unprotected and
assume it is permanent. It is not. It is
a first-year gap.
Let me tell you about Bernice.
Bernice is 67, and she enrolled in
Medicare last year, which is the entire
story right there, though she does not
know it yet, she has friends. Her
friends have been on Medicare for a
decade and when the subject comes up at
the table, one of them says the check
never goes down. They cannot let it go
down. There is a rule.
And that friend is right about herself.
Bernice has no prior year premium on her
record. She is outside the rule she has
been reassured about by somebody who
loves her and is describing their own
situation accurately.
She will find this out in January
standing in her kitchen with her phone
in her hand looking at a deposit that
does not match what she was told twice
by people she trusts.
Nobody misled her.
The most dangerous information in this
whole subject is not the false kind.
It is a true statement about somebody
else's situation repeated warmly at a
kitchen table to a person it does not
apply to. That is precisely what the
guide exists for. Not to make anybody an
expert in Medicare financing, to let a
person work out in 10 minutes which of
these rules is actually theirs rather
than inheriting somebody else's answer
and finding out in January it was never
their answer at all. Same place,
kevinexplains.shop.
Link in the description and in the
pinned comment at the top and the code
on your screen if you are watching this
on the television. 7-day guarantee, no
argument. A woman standing in a kitchen
in January holding a phone looking at a
number two people she trusts told her
could not happen.
Now the third thing, the one September
can quietly trigger without you noticing
and here is the figure I promised you at
the start. When your raise arrives, it
can make more of your Social Security
taxable.
Not because Congress passed a new tax,
because of a line that is not moved
since 1984. Here is how the tax on
benefits works. The government
calculates something called your
provisional income. It is your other
income plus any tax-free interest plus
half of your Social Security.
Then it compares that figure to a
threshold. For a single person the
threshold is $25,000.
For a married couple filing together,
32,000. Cross it and up to half your
benefit becomes taxable. There is a
second threshold at 34,000 and 44,000.
And above that, up to 85% of your
benefit can be taxed.
Now, here is the figure.
25,000 and 32,000 were set in 1984.
34 and 44,000 were added in 1993.
Not one of those four numbers has been
adjusted since. Not for inflation, not
once. In 42 years.
Think about what has happened to every
other number in this system in that
time. Your benefit has been adjusted
every single year. The taxable maximum
has been adjusted every year. The
earnings limits have been adjusted every
year. The part B premium changes every
year. Everything moves except the line
that decides whether you are taxed.
Which produces a result nobody ever
voted for. When that rule was written,
it was aimed at a small number of people
at the top. Because the line stayed
still while every benefit climbed past
it, the share of households paying tax
on their Social Security has grown every
year automatically, with no vote taken
and no debate held. And it means
something specific about September,
because September is the month the raise
is finished.
For some households, this raise is the
one that carries them across the line
for the first time. They will get an
increase, and part of what they gain
will come back out as tax. And the
letter announcing the raise will not
mention any of that. Let me put a real
household on that, because the
arithmetic is easier to see than to
describe.
Take a single person with a benefit of
$22,000 a year and a small pension of
Half the benefit is 11,000.
Add the pension, and the provisional
income comes to 24,000.
Under the line by a thousand dollars, so
none of the benefit is taxable. Now
apply a raise of 3 and 1/2%. The benefit
goes up by roughly $770.
Half of that is 385,
which pushes the provisional income to
about 24,385.
Still under this year.
Do it again next year and the year
after. Somewhere in there the line gets
crossed and it gets crossed by a person
whose real circumstances have not
improved by a single day of comfort.
Their pension did not grow. Their
savings did not grow. The only thing
that moved was an adjustment designed to
keep them level with rising prices.
That is the mechanism. And once you can
see it working, you can see why the
share of households paying this tax has
climbed every year for four decades
without a single vote. So, here is what
to actually do about it. Because unlike
the index, this one you can act on. Work
out roughly where you sit. Take your
other income for the year. Add any
tax-exempt interest.
Add half of your annual Social Security.
Compare it to 25,000 if you are single
or 32,000 if you are married filing
together.
If you are within a couple of thousand
dollars on either side, this raise is a
live question for you and it is worth an
hour with whoever does your taxes before
January.
And know that you can have tax withheld
directly from your payments rather than
facing it in one piece in April.
The form is W-4V,
the voluntary withholding request, and
it lets you choose from a short list of
percentages.
Nobody offers you this. It is entirely
your choice and it can be started or
stopped or changed whenever you like.
And for a great many people, it turns an
unpleasant April into something that
never needs thinking about. All right,
what else can you actually do between
now and the end of the year? There are
four things and every one of them has a
date on it. The first is the notice that
arrives in December. Every year the
agency sends a letter setting out your
new payment amount for the coming year.
Most people glance at the big number and
put it down. Do not do that this year.
Check three things: what the raise came
to in dollars, what is being deducted
for Part B, and what the net figure is,
which is what will actually appear in
your account. If any of those three
surprises you, that is a phone call to
make in December rather than a discovery
to make in February. The second is the
7th of December, and this one is a hard
deadline. That is when the window to
change your prescription drug coverage
closes for the whole year. Those plans
rewrite their terms annually. The drug
list changes, the tiers change, and the
specific medication you take can move
from one tier to another with the plan
name staying identical. That is a
genuine opportunity rather than a
warning because the money people save by
moving to a better plan is frequently
larger than the entire raise we have
been discussing.
So, if you take regular medication,
spend an evening on it before the 7th.
The third applies if your income has
dropped. If you are paying that
income-related surcharge and it is based
on a year when you were still working or
when you sold something and your
circumstances have since changed, there
is a form to have it recalculated. It is
SSA-44,
and it covers events like retiring,
losing a job, a spouse dying, or a
divorce.
People pay that surcharge for a full
year without knowing this form exists.
The fourth applies if you are still
working and drawing your benefit before
your full retirement age.
The earnings limits are adjusted every
year, and they are announced at the same
time as the raise.
If you are anywhere near that limit, you
want the new figure when it comes out in
October, not when it catches you in the
spring.
Let me tell you about Talmadge. Talmadge
is 80 and lives on his benefit plus a
small pension from a plant that closed
in 2004. For 3 years, he has been within
a few hundred dollars of the threshold,
drifting up toward it because the raise
climbs every year and the line does not.
The year he crossed it, nothing
announced itself. He received a larger
raise than usual and he was pleased
about it.
The consequence turned up the following
April in a bill he had never had before
and he assumed he had made a mistake on
the form.
He had not made a mistake.
He had received a raise exactly as
designed and part of it had been
reclaimed by a rule written when he was
38 years old and never revisited.
He still cannot really explain it to his
daughter and I do not blame him because
the whole thing depends on a number
nobody ever mentioned to him in his
life.
Now let me give you my honest opinion,
which is only that and you are welcome
to disagree with me in the comments. I
do not think the raise is a swindle. It
is a real adjustment. It is applied
automatically to every record every year
and a system that adjusts 75 million
payments annually without anybody having
to apply is a genuine achievement. Most
countries do not manage it.
And I want to be fair about the index
question because it is easy to be cheap
about it.
The wage earner index is a serious
measurement. It is not manipulated and
the argument that the elderly index is
not robust enough to carry this weight
is an honest argument made by serious
people, not a cover story.
My objection is narrower than any of
that and it is the same objection I keep
arriving at on this channel.
Every part of this machine that moves in
the government's favor moves
automatically and every part that moves
in yours requires you to know something.
The raise is automatic, the premium
increase is automatic, the tax threshold
staying frozen is automatic and it works
against you every single year without
anybody deciding anything.
But the withholding form is not
automatic. The surcharge appeal is not
automatic. Checking the December notice
is not automatic. Changing your drug
plan before the 7th of December is not
automatic. Look at the pattern.
Everything a computer can apply to every
record at once gets applied. Everything
requiring a person to know a thing
exists does not happen unless that
person already knew.
And nobody is assigned to tell them.
That is the whole gap and it is the
reason a channel like this one has
anything to do at all. And one more
thing on that because September is
exactly the month it happens. Every
autumn as this announcement approaches a
particular kind of message starts
circulating. A text, an email, sometimes
a call. It says the raise requires you
to confirm something. It says your new
payment amount needs verifying. It
offers to calculate your increase if you
supply a few details.
None of that exists. There is no
confirmation step. There is no form to
complete to receive your raise. There is
nothing to verify, nothing to register
for, and no fee anywhere in it.
The adjustment is applied automatically
to every record in the system and the
first legitimate communication you
receive about it is a letter in December
telling you what it came to.
So, if anything reaches you between now
and Christmas asking you to confirm,
verify, or unlock your increase, that is
somebody attempting to take it from you.
Put the phone down and if you have a
real question, look the number up
yourself rather than using one you were
given. All right, here is your list.
Five things and everyone has a date
attached. One, on the 14th of October,
write down the announced percentage.
Then wait for the part B figure in
November because the second number is
what determines your actual deposit.
Two, when the December notice arrives,
check three lines rather than one. The
raise in dollars, the part B deduction,
and the net. Query anything that
surprises you in December, not in
February.
Three, before the 7th of December,
review your prescription drug coverage
against the medications you actually
take. For many people, the saving there
is larger than the raise itself.
Four, work out your provisional income.
Other income plus tax-free interest plus
half your Social Security. If you are
near 25,000 single or 32,000 married,
get advice before January and look at
form W-4V for withholding.
Five, if your income has fallen because
you retired or a spouse died or you were
divorced and you were paying the income
related surcharge, file form SSA-44
rather than carrying it for a year.
And if your own situation is tangled, if
you cannot work out whether you are
inside or outside any of these rules,
write to me. The address is on your
screen and in the description below and
I read everyone that comes in.
One last thing before you go. Cordell
has written a percentage in a notebook
every October for 11 years and not once
has anybody explained why the figure he
writes down is never the figure that
arrives.
Bernice is going to discover in January
that a rule two people she loves told
her about was true for them and never
applied to her.
And Talmadge crossed a line that has not
moved since 1984, got a raise for doing
it and paid for the privilege the
following April. Not one of the three of
them did anything a sensible person
would not have done. Not one was cheated
by any person. Every one of them was on
the wrong side of a design that nobody
was ever assigned to explain. So, go and
look this September while the number is
still being finished and there is time
to prepare for whatever it turns out to
be. Know how it is built, know what
comes out of it before it reaches you
and know which of these rules is
actually yours rather than somebody
else's answer passed to you across a
table.
I am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: $92,000 Mistake: Why Some Trusts Cost Your Kids More Than No Trust At All

segments.text: You have spent decades being told to
fear a tax that was never coming for
your family. The estate tax. It comes up
at Thanksgiving like a wolf at the door.
Fewer than one estate in a hundred in
this country will ever owe a dollar of
it. It was almost certainly never going
to touch you. And while everybody's
attention was fixed on that door, a
completely different one was left
standing wide open. And it is the one
that is actually going to walk off with
your children's money. In March of 2023,
the tax authority issued a ruling that
quietly rewrote what happens inside the
exact kind of trust a great many
families built for the most protective
reason there is, to keep a house safe
from nursing home costs. And I want to
say the next part slowly because it is
the reason this video exists. The ruling
says that when a person puts property
into an irrevocable trust and that
property is not counted as part of their
estate when they die, their children do
not get the tax reset that inherited
property is supposed to receive. No
reset means your children take on
whatever you originally paid for the
house from decades ago and they pay tax
on every single dollar it has grown
since. Now, before anybody panics, I am
going to be straight with you the way I
always am because there are two versions
of this going around and both are wrong.
The first version says irrevocable
trusts are a trap and anybody who has
one has been sold something harmful.
That is not true and I'm going to show
you exactly why. The second version says
this is a technicality that only matters
to wealthy families with complicated
arrangements. That is also not true and
it is the more expensive of the two
because the people it actually reaches
are ordinary families whose only real
asset is a house that quietly grew for
30 years while they lived in it. Here is
the accurate version and it is three
things. One, why property transferred at
death is treated so much better than
property given away which is the single
most counterintuitive rule in this
entire area and the foundation for
everything else. Two, exactly what makes
one irrevocable trust preserve that
treatment and another destroy it. It is
not the name of the trust. It is not the
attorney's reputation. It comes down to
a specific kind of authority you either
kept or gave up. and I will tell you
what it is called so you can go and look
for it. Three, the four questions to put
to whoever drafted it in writing and
what a bad answer sounds like so you
know one when you hear it. And here is
the part I want you holding on to for
the next 20 minutes because it is the
whole reason to keep watching rather
than to worry. You are very likely not
choosing between protecting the house
and protecting your children from the
tax. A properly built version of this
does both at the same time. Most people
have never been told that is possible,
so they assume they made a trade they
never actually had to make. My name is
Kevin. I read the rules so you do not
have to. Every week, I go looking for
the thing that quietly decides what
happens to your money, and I bring it
here before it costs you anything. If
that sounds useful, subscribe and turn
on the bell because there is a 5-year
clock attached to the fix at the end of
this video, and it only runs forward.
Let me start with the foundation because
if you do not have this piece, none of
the rest will make sense. Everything
here turns on one idea, basis. Your
basis in your house is essentially what
you paid for it plus what you spent
improving it. When somebody sells a
house, they do not pay tax on the sale
price. They pay tax on the difference
between the sale price and the basis.
That difference is the gain. So, a house
bought for $210,000
and sold for $700,000 has a gain of
At the long-term rate of 15%, that is
in federal tax. If the seller's income
is high enough to trigger the additional
investment income charge of 3.8%,
add another $18,620.
That is the $92,000 in the title of this
video. And if their income puts them in
the 20% bracket instead, it climbs well
Now, here is the rule that decides
everything. And I want you to sit with
how strange it is. If you give your
house away while you are alive, the
person receiving it takes your basis.
Whatever you paid in 1990, that becomes
their number. Every dollar the house
grew while you owned it stays taxable
and it becomes their problem. But if
that same house passes at your death and
it counted as part of your estate, the
basis resets to what the house was worth
on the day you died. Section 1014 of the
tax code. 30 years of growth simply
vanishes from the calculation. Not
deferred, not reduced, gone. So the
house bought for 210,000 and worth
700,000, inherited rather than given has
a basis of 700,000. sold the following
month for 700,000. The gain is nothing
and the tax is nothing. Same house, same
children, same sale price. One route
costs $92,000 and the other costs
nothing. And I want to name the stranges
out loud because it is what makes people
get this wrong. In almost every other
part of life, doing something early and
generously is the better version.
[clears throat] Here, it is the
opposite. The tax code rewards property
that transfers at death and penalizes
property that was handed over during
life. That runs against every instinct a
parent has, which is precisely why so
many well-meaning people walk directly
into it. Now, the trust, and here is the
trap in one sentence. The tax reset at
death does not follow ownership. It
follows whether the property counted as
part of your estate when you died. Those
two are not the same thing. And that gap
is where families lose $90,000. Before
the ruling in 2023, there was a
widespread assumption that assets in
these trusts got the reset anyway
because the person who set it up was
still treated as the owner for income
tax purposes. Attorneys said it,
beneficiaries claimed it. The authority
looked at that and said, "No, if the
property was given away completely and
was not counted in the estate at death,
then there is no reset." Now, here what
that ruling did not say, because this is
the part that matters most. It did not
say irrevocable trusts lose the reset.
It said trusts where the property is
outside the estate lose it. Which means
a trust deliberately built so the
property stays inside the estate keeps
it. And this is the piece almost nobody
explains. Keeping the house inside your
estate for tax purposes does not undo
the protection from care costs. Those
are two separate legal tests. You can be
outside the reach of one and inside the
other at the same time. That is not a
loophole. It is how these are supposed
to be drafted. Let me tell you about
Hollis. Hollis is 79 and lives in the
house he bought in 1986 with a workshop
out the back that he built himself. 6
years ago, his wife spent 14 months in a
care facility before she died. And the
cost of it took most of what they had
saved. Afterward, he did what a person
does after watching that happen. He went
to a lawyer and he said, "I do not want
this house going the same way. Protect
it for my son." He signed everything. It
cost him a few thousand and he
considered it the best money he ever
spent. And he told his son, "So the
house cost him $104,000 in 1986. It is
worth about $630,000 now." Nobody in
that office ever used the words cost
basis in front of him, not once. He was
asked about care costs and he answered
about care costs and the question that
would have cost 20 extra minutes to ask
never came up. Hollis is not going to
find out. His son will in a year neither
of them has picked yet from an
accountant. That is the whole reason the
quiet rules exists. Plain English
printed large enough to read without
hunting for your glasses on the things
that quietly decide what happens to your
money. what the paragraph is called,
where to look for it, and the exact
questions to put to whoever holds your
file. So that a document you already
paid for is a document you actually
understand. It is at kevin
explains.shop.
The link is in the description below and
in the pinned comment at the top. And if
you are watching this on a television
right now, there is a code on the screen
you can point your phone camera at.
7-day guarantee always. If it does not
hand you something you did not have
before, you send it back. So, here is a
question worth sitting with. When was
the last time anybody read your trust to
you? Now, before I tell you what to look
for, let me explain why people set these
up in the first place. Because I am not
here to suggest anybody was foolish for
doing it. Nursing home care in this
country runs to many thousands of
dollars a month. Most families cannot
carry that for long out of savings. And
the program that covers it for people
who cannot is Medicaid, which is
needs-based. It looks at what you own.
And critically, it looks backward 5
years at anything you gave away. That
5-year look back is the whole reason
these get done early. Anything
transferred inside that window creates a
penalty period, and the penalty is
calculated by dividing what you gave
away by the average monthly cost of care
in your state. On a house worth
$400,000, that can leave a person
ineligible for two or three years,
during which they are paying for care
out of their own pocket at exactly the
moment they have nothing left. So, a
transfer done in a panic after a
diagnosis frequently makes the situation
worse rather than better. Done 6 years
earlier, calmly, it works. So, the
strategy is legitimate. You move the
house into an irrevocable trust. Once
the 5 years pass, that house is
generally no longer counted as yours for
that purpose. You have protected the
roof over your head from being consumed
by care costs and protected what is left
of it for your children. And the reason
people choose an irrevocable trust
rather than an ordinary living trust is
exactly the thing that creates the tax
problem. Irrevocable means you gave
something up. You cannot simply take the
house back out whenever you like. That
surrender is what makes it protected in
the first place. Which is why the fix is
so specific. You cannot solve this by
keeping more control. Because control is
what you traded away to get the
protection. You have to keep exactly the
right kind of authority and no more.
Now, let me give you what to actually
look for because this is the useful part
and I want you to be able to do it.
There is a specific kind of authority
that if you kept it pulls the property
back into your estate for tax purposes
and preserves the reset. In these
documents, it is usually called a
limited power of appointment. Sometimes
a special power of appointment. Here is
what it means in plain terms. It is a
right you kept to change at your death
which of your family members ends up
with the property and in what shares.
That is all it is. You cannot take the
house back. You cannot sell it and spend
the money. You cannot give it to
yourself or your creditors. All you kept
is the ability to redirect it among a
defined group. And because you kept no
ability to get at the property for your
own benefit, it does not break the care
cost protection. But because you kept
the power to determine where it lands,
the tax rules count it as part of your
estate, which triggers the reset. That
is the entire mechanism, one paragraph
doing two jobs. There are other features
that can accomplish the same thing. A
retained right to live in the house for
the rest of your life. A retained right
to the income the property produces.
Certain powers over how and when
beneficiaries receive things. A
well-drafted version of this often has
more than one. So, here are the four
questions. Put them in writing in an
email so the answer comes back in
writing, too. One, will the property in
my trust be included in my gross estate
for federal estate tax purposes at my
death? Two, will my beneficiaries
receive a step up in basis under section
1014 when I die? Three, did I retain a
limited power of appointment? And if so,
where is it in the document? Four, if
the answer to the first two is no, what
can be done now to change that. Write
those down. Send them exactly as I have
said them. And here is how to read the
answer you get back. Because the answer
tells you more than the content of it
does. A good answer is short and it is
specific. It names the paragraph. It
points to a section number in the tax
code. It says yes or it says no.
Somebody who built this deliberately
will answer in two sentences without
reaching for anything because it was a
decision they made on purpose while
drafting. A bad answer is long and it is
general. It reassures you about how
wellprotected everything is without
answering what you asked. It talks about
the excellent job the trust does on care
costs, which is not the question. or it
says something like the trust is a
granter trust so the treatment should be
fine which is precisely the assumption
the ruling in 2023 overturned if you get
the second kind of answer that is not
proof that anything is wrong. It is a
reason to have somebody else read the
document and I want to be fair to the
profession here because I am not
accusing anybody of anything. A great
many of these were drafted before that
ruling existed by people doing competent
work under the understanding that
everyone shared at the time. The ruling
changed what a careful draft looks like.
It did not make anybody dishonest. And
now the part that should genuinely lift
some weight off you. It can very often
be fixed. These are called irrevocable.
And that word makes people assume the
door is welded shut. It is frequently
not. Many of these documents include a
person, sometimes called a trust
protector, with authority to make
exactly this kind of amendment. Many
states allow a process called decanting
where the contents of one trust are
poured into a newly drafted one with
better terms. Some states permit
modification by agreement among everyone
involved or by asking a court. And there
are documents that already contain a
power to substitute assets which opens a
different route entirely. Not every one
of these is available in every state or
in every document. But the assumption
that nothing can be done is wrong far
more often than it is right. And it is
the assumption that keeps people from
asking. Two practical notes about that.
The first is cost. Reviewing a trust and
answering the four questions is a modest
piece of work for somebody who does this
daily. And a great many attorneys will
confirm whether the paragraph is in
there without charging you much of
anything because it takes them minutes.
Amending or decanting one costs more and
it is still a fraction of the tax at
stake. Set the two numbers next to each
other before you decide it is too
expensive to look into. The second is
timing, and it is the harder one. If the
fix involves moving property or
restructuring in a way that counts as a
new transfer, that can restart the
5-year clock for care purposes. That is
not always the case, and a properly done
amendment frequently does not. But it is
precisely the question to ask before
anybody signs anything. Ask it in these
words. Will this change restart my look
back period? If the person cannot answer
that immediately, stop and find somebody
who can. Because getting the tax right
and losing the protection is not a trade
worth making. And this is why age
matters here in a way it does not
elsewhere. At 72 with reasonable health,
there is room to fix something and still
clear a 5-year window. At 86, it is a
different calculation entirely. And the
right answer may be to leave the
protection alone and plan around the tax
instead. There is no single answer. and
anybody who gives you one without asking
how old you are and how you are keeping
is not actually advising you. There is
also one route that avoids the whole
question for some families and it is
worth naming because almost nobody
mentions it. If your children are going
to live in the house rather than sell
it, the arithmetic changes completely. A
person who owns a home and lives in it
as their main residence for at least two
of the five years before selling can
exclude up to $250,000 of gain or
500,000 for a married couple filing
together. That exclusion belongs to them
regardless of what basis they inherited.
So a son who moves into his mother's
house and lives there for 2 years before
selling can wipe out a great deal of
gain even without any reset at all. The
conditions are strict. he has to
actually live there. Renting it out does
not qualify, and leaving it empty does
not qualify, and the two-year clock does
not begin until he moves in. But for the
family where somebody is going to take
the house on rather than sell it, this
can matter more than everything else in
this video. Let me put the number behind
the fear I open this video with because
I promised you it and I want it in your
hands precisely rather than roughly. The
federal estate tax exemption this year
is $15 million for one person and $30
million for a married couple. Your
estate has to exceed that before the
federal government takes a single
dollar. Keeping your house inside your
estate for tax purposes, which is what
buys your children the reset, costs
almost every family watching this
exactly nothing against that threshold.
So hold the two numbers side by side.
The tax you were taught to fear starts
at 15 million. The tax that is actually
going to reach your children starts the
moment a house you paid $200,000 for is
worth $700,000 and the wrong box was
checked in a document you never read. I
will add one honest note. A number of
states run their own estate or
inheritance taxes with far lower
thresholds than the federal one and a
handful have no exemption worth speaking
of. So it is a fair question to ask
about your own state. But even in those
states, the reset on an inherited home
usually saves considerably more than the
state tax costs. Let me tell you about
Vesta. Vesta is 82. Her trust was drawn
up 11 years ago by an attorney her
church recommended, and she has never
opened it since the day she signed it.
It lives in a fireproof box with her
marriage certificate. Her granddaughter,
who works in accounting, asked her one
Sunday whether the trust kept the step
up. Vesta did not know what that meant,
which is not a failing because nobody
had ever said it to her. So they sent
the four questions. The answer came back
in one paragraph and it named the
section and the section was there. Her
attorney had built it correctly 11 years
ago without ever explaining to her that
she had made a choice. And here's what
struck me about it. Vesta spent one
evening genuinely afraid. And the fear
was for nothing. and she only carried it
because in 11 years nobody had ever told
her what her own document did. That is
exactly the gap this guide closes. Not
to make anybody an expert in trust law.
To put the questions and the plain
meaning in one place so that finding out
where you stand takes an evening rather
than a decade. And so that whatever the
answer turns out to be, you are the one
who knows it. Same place
kevinexplains.shop.
link in the description and in the
pinned comment at the top and the code
on your screen if you are watching this
on the television. 7-day guarantee, no
argument. An 82y old woman sitting up at
night with a fireproof box afraid of a
document she paid for and was never
shown. Now, before the other ways this
goes wrong, there is one more
arrangement worth knowing about because
for a certain kind of family, it is the
simplest answer in this entire video. It
is called a life estate deed. You
transfer the house to your children now,
but you keep written into the deed
itself the legal right to live there for
the rest of your life. Nobody can put
you out. You are not a guest in your own
home. Here is why it matters for
everything I have been describing.
Because you kept that lifetime right,
the tax rules count the property as part
of your estate at your death. So, your
children get the reset. And because the
transfer already happened, the house
passes to them automatically without
going through the court process, which
is what most people were trying to
achieve in the first place. It is
simpler than a trust, and it costs
considerably less to set up. Now, the
honest side of it, because this one has
a real edge to it, once that deed is
signed, you cannot sell the house
without your children's agreement. Every
one of them has to sign. If you decide
at 83 that the stairs have become too
much and you want to move somewhere
smaller, you need everybody on board and
families are families. It is also a
transfer for care purposes. So, the
5-year clock applies to it exactly as it
does to a trust. So, it is a real
option. It is not the right one for
everybody, and it is worth knowing
exists rather than hearing about it
after the fact. Now, three other ways
the same thing goes wrong and they are
quicker. The first is a trust that was
never actually filled. This happens more
than anybody would guess. The document
gets drawn up, it gets signed, everybody
feels the matter is settled, and the
deed to the house is never changed into
the trust's name. So, the trust exists
and it is empty. It controls nothing.
When the person dies, the house goes
through exactly the process the trust
was meant to avoid. And the family
discovers this while grieving. The check
takes 10 minutes. Look at your deed or
look up your property record with the
county and see whose name the house is
in. If it is still in yours personally
and you believe it is in a trust, that
is a conversation to have this week. The
second is putting a child on the deed. I
will keep this short because it is the
version most people already half know.
Adding your son or daughter as a joint
owner while you are alive gives away
part of the house, which means part of
it carries your old basis forever, and
that portion never resets no matter how
long you live afterward. It also exposes
that share to their divorce, their
creditors, and their lawsuits. And it
usually requires a gift tax filing that
almost nobody makes. It feels like the
simple option. It is the expensive one.
The third is genuinely good news for
people in nine states. In community
property states, which are Arizona,
California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada,
New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and
Wisconsin, when one spouse dies, the
entire property gets the reset, not just
the deceased spouse's half. The
surviving spouse gets a full new basis
on the whole house. Everywhere else,
only the deceased spouse's half resets.
The survivor keeps their original basis
on their own half permanently. And that
difference can easily be worth tens of
thousands of dollars when the survivor
eventually sells. Which leads to
something worth knowing if you are a
widow or widowerower watching this. If
you inherited a halfinterest in your
home when your spouse died, part of your
basis was reset on that day. What the
house was worth at that moment matters.
And if you never had it valued, that is
worth raising with whoever prepares your
taxes because reconstructing a value
from years ago is possible and it gets
harder every year. Let me tell you about
EMTT. Emmett is 74 and his wife died 5
years ago. They lived in Ohio, which is
not one of the nine. He is thinking
about selling the house now and moving
nearer his daughter. He has assumed all
along that because he inherited his
wife's share, the whole house was reset
when she died. half of it was his own
half is still carrying what they paid in
Nobody told him wrong. He simply
extended a rule he had heard correctly
into territory it does not cover which
is what every single person in this
video did including the lawyers. Now let
me give you my honest opinion which is
only that and you are welcome to
disagree with me in the comments. I do
not think anybody engineered this. There
is no villain in it. An attorney sitting
across from a frightened person after a
spouse has died in a care facility is
being asked one question and it is not a
tax question. It is please make sure
this does not happen to me. And they
answer that question competently. And
the person leaves relieved. The
conversation about what happens to the
basis afterward is a different
conversation. It is dry. It concerns a
moment neither person wants to discuss
and it happens after the client has
already exhaled. My objection is
narrower than blame. It is that a
document like this makes a decision on
your behalf that you were never told was
being made. You were not offered a
choice between protection and the tax
reset. You were not told the choice
existed or that in most cases it is not
even a choice because a well-built
version delivers both. You simply signed
and a paragraph either was or was not
included and you will not find out which
for years and you will not be the one
who finds out. And that is the thread
running through everything on this
channel. Not that anybody is hiding
things from you. That the moment when a
decision gets made and the moment when
its consequence arrives are separated by
20 years and nothing in the system
connects them. All right, here is your
list. Five things and none of them takes
longer than an evening. One, find the
document. Physically find it. If you
cannot, ask whoever drafted it for a
copy today because everything else on
this list depends on having it in your
hands. Two, check that the house is
actually in it. Look at the deed or the
county record and see whose name is on
the property. A trust with nothing in it
protects nothing. Three, send the four
questions in writing. Will the property
be in my gross estate? Will my
beneficiaries get the step up under
section 1014? Did I retain a limited
power of appointment and where is it?
And if not, what can be done now? Four,
if the answer is unclear or evasive,
have a second person read the document.
That is not disloyalty to anybody. It is
the same thing you would do with a
diagnosis. Five, know your numbers. What
you paid for the house, roughly what it
is worth now, and the difference.
Multiply that difference by 15% and that
is roughly the tax your children either
pay or do not pay decided by one
paragraph. And there is a sixth thing
that is not on the list because it is
not urgent, but it will matter
enormously to somebody one day. So do it
while you are thinking about it. Write
down what you paid for the house and
when and put it with the deed. Then add
whatever you can remember spending on it
that was an improvement rather than a
repair. A new roof, the addition, the
kitchen you did in 98, central air.
Improvements add to your basis, which
means they reduce the taxable gain, and
almost nobody keeps the receipts for 30
years. If the reset applies, none of
that matters. But if it turns out it
does not apply, every one of those
numbers is worth real money to your
children. and you are the only person
alive who knows them. An index card in
an envelope with the deed is enough.
Nobody needs perfection. They need a
starting point that is not a blank page.
And if your own situation is tangled, if
you are holding a document and cannot
tell what it says about any of this,
write to me. The address is on your
screen and in the description below, and
I read everyone that comes in. One last
thing before you go. Hollis paid a
lawyer to protect the house he built a
workshop behind, and he will die
believing he succeeded. and he may well
have, and neither he nor I can tell you
which without reading the paragraph.
Vesta was afraid for one evening about a
document that turned out to have been
drafted properly 11 years earlier. And
the only thing wrong was that nobody had
ever told her so. And EMTT is about to
sell a house carrying a basis from 1981
on half of it, believing the whole thing
was reset. All three of them did the
responsible thing. All three of them
paid somebody. Every one of them ended
up holding a document that made a
decision on their behalf without ever
presenting it as a decision. And I want
to say one thing to the people watching
this who are now worried they have got
it wrong because I know there are some
of you. You may not have got it wrong. A
large share of these were drafted
properly. The whole point of the four
questions is that you do not have to
guess and the answer is very often the
one you were hoping for the way it was
for Vesta. Worry is not information. A
one paragraph reply from the person who
holds your file is information and it
cost you an email. And if the answer
does come back badly, you have found out
at the only point in your life when
finding out is useful. Nobody has died.
Nothing has been sold. There is a
document. And documents can be amended
far more often than the word irrevocable
suggests. The version of this that ends
in a $90,000 tax bill is not the version
where somebody found a problem. It is
the version where nobody ever looked. So
go and read yours this week while there
is time to change it. Find the
paragraph, send the four questions, and
get the answer in writing because in 20
years, you will not be the one who needs
it. I am Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do
not forget to check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop. shop.
