segments.text: Your name is on somebody else's bank
account. Your grandson's so you could
help him when he was starting out. Your
sister's so somebody could reach her
money if she ever went into hospital.
You have never taken a dollar out of it.
It is not your money and everybody in
your family knows it. As far as the
Social Security Administration is
concerned, every dollar in that account
belongs to you. That is not a mistake
somebody made. It is the default rule
written into the policy manual and it
has been the rule for years. Here is
what changed. For a long time, that rule
only mattered if somebody found the
account. And the agency generally did
not go looking. They asked you what you
had, you told them, and if the number
you gave was small, that was usually the
end of it. That is over. As of this
year, the agency runs an electronic
search of financial institutions on
essentially every new claim, regardless
of what you report. It does not wait for
a red flag. There is no longer a dollar
figure you can stay under to avoid it.
And the search does not only confirm the
account you named, it goes looking for
the ones you did not. Now, I am going to
be straight with you the way I always am
because there are two versions of this
circulating and both are wrong. The
first version says the government is now
reading everybody's bank account and
your retirement check is at risk. That
is not true and I'm going to tell you
exactly who this reaches and who it does
not. The second version says this is
routine paperwork and anybody discussing
it is frightening seniors for clicks.
That is also not true and it is the more
expensive of the two because there are
people watching this right now who are
one forgotten account away from losing a
payment they live on. Here is the
accurate version and it is three things.
One, what this system actually is, what
it can see and precisely who it reaches
this year. Two, the five kinds of money
it finds that people never think of as
theirs. Starting with the account your
name is on for somebody else's benefit.
Three, what is genuinely protected?
Because there is a real list of things
this search cannot touch and almost
nobody knows the whole list. And knowing
it is the difference between panicking
and being fine. And I am going to close
with one number that explains why so
many decent, careful people fall over
this line. It is not a number about
fraud. Once you hear it, the entire
situation makes a different kind of
sense. My name is Kevin. I read the
rules so you do not have to. Every week,
I go looking for the thing that quietly
decides what happens to your money, and
I bring it here before it cost you
anything. If that sounds useful,
subscribe and turn on the bell because
there is a timing rule in the fourth
part of this video that decides whether
a deposit costs you an entire month's
payment or cost you nothing at all. And
it comes down to what day of the month
it is. Let me start with what this
actually is. The tool is called access
to financial institutions. Inside the
agency, everybody just says AFI. It is
an electronic system that lets the
agency ask banks and credit unions
directly what is in your accounts and
get an answer back without anybody
sending you a letter about it. It is not
new. It has existed for years. What
changed is two things and neither of
them was announced in a way designed to
reach you. The first is the threshold.
There used to be a dollar figure. If
what you reported was under it, a full
financial search often did not happen.
That figure worked like a speed bump. It
is now gone. Starting in August of last
year for people 65 and older and
expanded in April of this year, the
agency operates on what it calls a 0
tolerance. That means the search runs
regardless of what you say you have.
Report nothing at all and it still runs.
The second is the reach. The instruction
was expanded to cover essentially all
new claim approvals, claims that get
reopened, and appeals that end up
granting eligibility. Not a sample, not
the suspicious ones, all of them. Now,
what can it actually see? It can run up
to 10 geographic searches based on your
address and the identifying information
tied to you. And if you have somebody
managing your payment on your behalf, it
can search on the information tied to
them as well. Roughly 96% of financial
institutions in this country participate
in the automated system. It covers all
50 states, the District of Columbia, and
the territories. For the small number of
institutions that do not participate,
there is a slower paper process, but the
coverage is close to national. And what
it looks for is what the rules call
liquid resources. checking accounts,
savings accounts, money market accounts,
certificates of deposit, credit union
share accounts, and the ones people
never think of, like a Christmas club or
a holiday club account with a couple of
hundred in it that somebody opened at a
branch that no longer exists. Now, here
is the part where I have to be precise
about scope because plenty of channels
are being vague about this on purpose.
This applies to the needs-based program,
Supplemental Security Income. That is
the program with the resource limit and
resources have always been part of
qualifying for it which is why the
verification machinery gets built there
first. If you receive a regular
retirement benefit on your own work
record or disability insurance on your
own record, there is no resource limit
on those and this search is not reaching
your accounts today. So why should you
stay for the next 20 minutes? Two
reasons and they are both real. The
first is that a great many of you are
one degree away from somebody this
reaches. A brother, a grown child with a
disability, a neighbor you drive to
appointments, and nobody is going to
explain any of this to them. The second
is what the machinery represents. Every
serious proposal to means test other
benefits, and there are several in both
parties, requires one thing before it
can function. Somebody has to be able to
see inside the accounts. That capability
is being built and tested right now in
the one program where checking resources
is already permitted. I am not telling
you it is coming for your retirement
check. I am telling you that if it ever
does, it will not need to be invented
first. Let me tell you about Olla. Olla
is 77. She receives the needs-based
payment. She lives in one room of her
daughter's house and her entire life
fits in a chest of drawers. 11 years
ago, her brother was diagnosed with
something that scared everybody. And the
family put Olla's name on his savings
account so that somebody could get to
his money if he ended up unable to
handle it himself. He recovered. Nobody
ever took her name off. There is about
$9,000 in that account. Not $1 of it is
hers. She has never had a card for it.
She could not tell you which bank it is
at. The search does not weigh any of
that. It finds an account with her name
attached and the default rule says the
whole balance is a resource belonging to
her. She is not hiding anything. She has
never hidden anything in her life. She
simply does not know that the favor she
did her brother 11 years ago is sitting
inside a government computer with her
name on it. That is the whole reason the
quiet rules exists. plain English
printed large enough to read without
hunting for your glasses on the things
that quietly decide what happens to your
money, what counts, what does not, what
to check before anybody checks it for
you, and the exact words to use if you
have to explain that money is not yours
so that nobody in your family finds out
how the rule works from a letter. It is
at kevinexplains.shop.
The link is in the description below and
in the pinned comment at the top. And if
you are watching this on a television
right now, there is a code on the screen
you can point your phone camera at.
7-day guarantee always. If it does not
hand you something you did not have
before, you send it back. So, here's a
question worth sitting with. Whose
accounts is your name on that you have
not thought about in years? Now, let me
give you the five kinds of money this
finds that people do not think of as
theirs. And I want you to listen to
these against your own life rather than
against somebody you imagine is cheating
because not one of these involves
anybody cheating. The first is the one I
opened with a joint account. The rule is
this. If your name is on an account with
somebody else, the AY's starting
position is that the entire balance
belongs to you. Not half, not your
share, all of it. The reasoning is that
a joint owner can walk in and withdraw
the lot. So the money is available to
you. and availability is what the
resource test measures. Now, here is the
part that actually helps you and it is
the part nobody mentions when they tell
this story to frighten people. That is a
presumption, not a verdict. You are
allowed to rebut it. If you can show
that you did not contribute the money
and that it is not really yours, the
agency can remove it from your
resources. And when a rebuttal succeeds,
it applies going backward as well as
forward, not only from the day you
argued it. What rebutts it is
documentation.
deposit records showing where the money
came from, withdrawal records showing
you never touched it, a written
statement from the actual owner
explaining the arrangement, and ideally
a corrected signature card from the bank
showing your name removed. And that last
one is the real answer for most people.
If your name is on somebody's account
purely as a convenience, and there is
any chance you will ever need the
needs-based program, get your name off
it. It is a 15-minute conversation at a
branch. Arguing the money is not yours
after the fact is a fight you can win
and it is a fight you did not have to
have. And if you cannot get your name
off it for whatever reason, then write
the statement now rather than later. It
does not need a lawyer. It needs to say
who actually put the money in, why your
name was added, on what date, that you
have never made a withdrawal, and it
needs to be signed by the person whose
money it is. Attach a few bank
statements showing the deposits coming
from them and no withdrawals going to
you. Then put the whole thing in an
envelope with the account details on the
front and tell somebody in your family
where it is. The reason to do it today
rather than when it is asked for is
simple and slightly uncomfortable. The
person who can explain that arrangement
is a person and people become unwell and
people die. A statement signed by your
brother this month settles the question
permanently. a statement nobody can sign
next year does not exist. There is a
particular version of this that catches
the most careful people of all. If you
serve as somebody's representative payee
or you are the guardian for a grandchild
and there is an account holding their
money with your name on it as the person
responsible, that account can appear in
a search as yours. Those funds are
supposed to be kept separate and
identified as belonging to the
beneficiary. And if they are, the
situation is defensible. if they are
mixed in with your own money in one
account, it becomes very hard to
untangle. The second kind is money your
family gives you to help. When somebody
deposits money into your account to help
you out, it is treated as income in the
month it arrives, and then whatever is
still sitting there after that becomes a
resource. So the $200 your son sends
every month because he worries about you
does not simply disappear. If it
accumulates, it counts. And there is a
straightforward way around it that cost
your family nothing. Rather than
depositing money into your account, have
them pay the bill directly. Petting the
electric company in your name is treated
differently from handing you the cash to
pay it. If somebody in your family is
helping you, that one change in how they
help can be the difference between
staying eligible and not. The third is
an account you genuinely forgot. A
savings account at a bank that was
bought by another bank which was bought
by a third one and the statement stopped
coming to an address you left in 2009. A
credit union account opened decades ago
to get a car loan with $60 still in it.
A certificate of deposit an aunt set up
for you when you were young. These are
not rare. They are extremely common and
the system does not care whether you
remembered. The fourth is a lump sum you
already spent in your head, an
inheritance that has not been
distributed yet, a settlement, a
retroactive payment. Money is a resource
the month after you receive it. And
people plan around money for months
before the paperwork catches up. And the
fifth, which is the one that produces
the most anger, is the timing. And I am
going to give you that one in full a
little later because it is the single
most useful thing in this video and it
deserves its own place. Now, let me give
you the other side. Because a video that
only lists what counts is doing half the
job and leaving you frightened for no
reason. Here is what this search cannot
touch, and it is a longer list than
almost anybody realizes. Your home does
not count. The house you live in and the
land it sits on are excluded entirely,
regardless of what it is worth. A
paidoff house does not disqualify you.
One vehicle does not count regardless of
value if it is used for transportation
by you or somebody in your household.
Your household goods and personal
effects do not count. Your furniture,
your wedding ring, the things in your
house are not being toted up against
you. Your burial plot does not count.
And the plots for your immediate family
do not count either. A burial fund of up
does not count. And here is the
condition that trips people. So, listen
to this one closely. It has to be
identified as a burial fund and kept
separate from your other money. If that
$1,500 is sitting in your ordinary
checking account mixed with everything
else, it counts against you. Move it
into its own account. Tell them what it
is for and it stops counting. That
single step can be the entire difference
between being over the line and being
under it. Life insurance with a small
face value is excluded within limits. A
federal tax refund does not count for 12
months after you receive it. 12 full
months. That includes the earned income
credit. So, a refund arriving in spring
does not put you over the line that
summer. Retroactive payments from Social
Security or the needs-based program
itself do not count for 9 months after
you receive them, which matters
enormously because those back payments
are frequently large and people have
been terrified by their own back pay.
And then there is one more that is worth
a video of its own. So, I will give you
the short version. If a person's
disability began before they turn 26,
they can hold an ABLE account and money
in it is excluded from the resource test
$100,000 rather than 2,000. If that
describes anybody in your family, that
is the single most valuable sentence in
this video for them. Now, before I move
on, there is one more thing you need to
understand about what actually happens
if you do go over the line. Because the
difference between the two outcomes is
enormous and almost nobody explains it.
Going over does not immediately end your
benefit forever. What it does is suspend
it. You are ineligible for the months
you are over and when your resources
come back under the limit, your payment
resumes. That is unpleasant and it is
survivable. But there is a second door
behind that one. If you stay ineligible
for 12 consecutive months, the case does
not stay suspended. It terminates. And a
terminated case is not something that
switches back on when your circumstances
improve. You have to apply again from
the beginning as a brand new applicant
with the whole process and the whole
weight that comes with it. Set that
against real life. Somebody receives an
inheritance, goes over the limit,
assumes the matter is settled and there
is nothing to be done and simply stops
engaging for a year. At month 13, they
are not suspended. They are out. And
getting back in is a different and far
harder task than never leaving. So if
you ever go over, the instruction is the
opposite of what instinct says. Stay in
contact, report accurately, keep the
file open, and get your resources back
under the line before that 12-month
stretch runs out. The clock only runs
while nobody is doing anything. And one
more piece that catches people living
with family because a great many of you
are. There is a rule about what the
agency calls inind support and
maintenance. If somebody provides your
food or your housing without you paying
for it, your payment can be reduced by
up to roughly a third. That is not about
your bank accounts at all, but it comes
up in exactly the same conversation. And
people who moved in with a daughter to
save money are frequently surprised by
it. If your living arrangement has
changed, that is worth asking about
specifically by name. Let me tell you
about Dorcas. Dorcas is 69. She gets the
needs-based payment. And last spring,
her tax refund arrived, $1,100. She had
been carrying a fear about that money
for two years because somebody at a
community center had told her that
anything over the limit would end her
payment. And $1,100 plus what she
already had put her over. So every year
she rushed to spend it, not on anything
she wanted, on getting rid of it. She
bought things she did not need to make
the number go down before anybody
looked. Her refund was never countable
for 12 months. She could have simply
left it in the account. She spent 3
years frightened of money that the rules
had already protected and she made
herself poorer doing it. Nobody lied to
her. A well-meaning person at a
community center knew half a rule. That
is exactly the gap this guide closes.
Not to make anybody an expert in the
regulations, to put the whole rule in
one place in plain language, so that a
person is never making frightened
decisions about their own money on the
strength of half of something somebody
told them at a table. Same place, kevin
explains.shop. Link in the description
and in the pinned comment at the top and
the code on your screen if you are
watching this on the television. 7-day
guarantee, no argument. A woman spending
money she did not want on things she did
not need to stay under a line she was
never over.
Now the timing rule I promised you and I
have held it deliberately because it is
the most useful thing in this entire
video and I want you awake for it. Your
resources are not measured continuously.
They are measured at one moment. The
first moment of the first day of the
month. That is it. That is the test.
What is in your countable accounts at
the start of the first day of the month
is the number that decides that month.
Think about what that means in practice.
If a payment lands in your account on
the 28th and you use it during those
last few days on your rent, your food,
your medication, your electricity, then
on the first of the next month, it is
not there and it is not counted. You did
nothing clever. You spent your own money
on your own life in the order the rules
already anticipate. But if that same
money is sitting there at the start of
the first, it counts. And if it puts you
over the line, the payment for that
month is gone. So the practical
instruction is this. Know what is in
your accounts at the end of every month.
Not roughly, actually. Because in this
program, the calendar is doing something
to you whether you are watching or not.
And a warning attached to it because I
will not give you half a rule the way
that community center did. Do not give
money away to get under the line.
Transferring resources for less than
they are worth to qualify carries its
own penalty and its own period of
ineligibility.
Spending your money on your own needs is
entirely different from handing it to
somebody to hold for you. The first is
fine. The second creates a problem worse
than the one it solves. Now, the scam
because every time one of these rules
gets attention, something attaches to it
within days. And this one is already
running. Here is the shape of it.
Somebody hears about a new bank
verification rule from a video or a
neighbor. A few days later, a call
comes. The person says they are a
verification specialist or a benefits
compliance officer or from a federal
account review service. They explain
that because of the new rule, your
accounts have to be verified or
pre-clared and that they can handle the
process for you or protect your accounts
from the search for a payment. Sometimes
a few hundred, sometimes a share of your
monthly benefit. Here is the single
sentence that ends this every time.
There is no fee, no service, and no
third party anywhere that can shield
your accounts from official verification
or handle it on your behalf. The search
is run by the agency directly. Nobody
can opt you out of it, pre-clar you, or
protect you from it for money. Anybody
offering that is describing something
that does not exist. And what they are
usually after is not the fee. It is your
social security number or your account
number or a verification code read out
loud over the telephone. The fee is the
story. The number is the point. So hold
on to this. The agency will not
telephone you out of nowhere and ask you
to confirm your social security number
or your bank details in order to comply
with a new rule. They already have your
number. When they need something
verified, it comes through your
application, your redetermination
paperwork, and written notices, not
through a surprise call demanding you
act today. If that call comes, put the
phone down. Then, if you have a real
question about your own situation, look
the number up yourself and call them.
Never use the number the caller gives
you because in a great many of these,
the number is theirs. All right, what do
you actually do about all of this?
First, build the list. every account
with your name on it anywhere. Not the
one your payment arrives in. All of
them. Your checking, your savings,
anything at a credit union, anything at
a bank that changed its name, any
certificate of deposit, any club
account, and critically, any account
belonging to somebody else that has your
name attached for convenience. If you
are not sure whether an old account
still exists, telephone the institution
and ask. You want to know what a search
would turn up before it turns it up,
because a surprise you already know
about is not a surprise. Second, deal
with the joint accounts specifically.
For each one, decide whether your name
needs to be there. If it does not, go
and have it removed. If it genuinely
does, start the evidence file now, while
the person whose money it is can still
explain it. Deposit records, a written
statement, anything showing the money's
source. Building that file takes an
afternoon today and can take months
later. Third, separate your burial fund
if you have one. Its own account clearly
identified. $1,500 that stops counting.
Fourth, know your number on the first of
the month and understand what is
protected. The refund for 12 months, the
back payment for nine, the house, the
car, the plot, and fifth, when a
verification notice or a redetermination
notice arrives, answer it on time,
honestly, and keep a copy of everything
you send. The worst thing anyone does
with these is put them in a drawer. and
I have seen more damage done by silence
than by anything anybody ever disclosed.
Let me tell you about Isham. Isham
[clears throat] is 81. When the
redetermination notice came, he read it,
understood roughly 9/10en of it, and got
stuck on one question about an account
he could not remember. So, he did
nothing, not out of defiance. He was
going to ask his nephew about it at the
weekend, and then the weekend came and
went, and the notice moved from the
table to the shelf, and from the shelf
to a drawer. The account was a credit
union account with $41 in it. $41.
It would not have moved the calculation
by a hair. What cost him was the
silence. A question he could have
answered in one sentence turned into a
file with no response in it, and the
process that followed took months, and a
great deal of worry over an amount of
money that was never a problem at all.
Now, let me give you the number I
promised at the start, and it is not a
number about fraud. The resource limit
for one person on this program is
$2,000. For a couple, 3,000. That figure
was last changed in 1989. 1989.
It has not moved since. It is not
indexed to inflation unlike almost every
other figure in the entire social
security system, all of which adjust
every single year. If that $2,000 had
been indexed the way everything else is,
it would sit somewhere above $5,000
today. which means the real value of
what a person on this program is
permitted to keep has fallen by roughly
2/3 while nobody changed a word of the
law. So when you hear that inspectors
found nearly $199,000 people had
received a combined $718 million in
payments tied to accounts that were not
disclosed. Hold both things in your head
at once. Yes, that is a real amount of
money and the agency is right that it
has to be addressed. And also the line
those people crossed is a line drawn in
1989 and never redrawn on a program
where the maximum monthly payment is
under $1,000. It is very difficult to
keep $2,000 and no more for years while
living on that and never once be over
the line on the first of a month. Now,
let me give you my honest opinion, which
is only that, and you are welcome to
disagree with me in the comments. I do
not object to the verification. I want
to say that plainly because it would be
easy to sell you outrage here and I am
not going to. The agency is legally
required to pay the right amount to the
right person. An overpayment is not a
windfall. It is a debt with your name on
it that turns up later, usually much
later, and gets taken back out of a
payment you were living on. Inspectors
estimated that checking accounts more
often could have prevented around $2
billion of overpayments in a single
year. Every one of those dollars was
going to become somebody's letter
eventually. finding it in month one is
genuinely kinder than finding it in
month 20. So the scanning on its own is
defensible. My objection sits somewhere
else entirely. It is that the
enforcement was modernized and the rule
was not. The tools to find money got
faster, more automated, and nearly
nationwide. The limit those tools
measure against has not been touched in
37 years.
So, we have built an extremely precise
instrument for detecting a line that
stopped making sense a long time ago.
And underneath that is the thing this
channel keeps running into. Nothing
about any of this arrives at anybody's
house. There is no letter explaining
that the threshold was removed or that a
joint account counts entirely or that a
refund is protected for 12 months or
that the first of the month is the only
moment that matters.
The system simply started running
differently and the people it runs on
found out afterward or not at all. All
right, here is your list. Five things
one afternoon. One, write down every
account with your name on it, including
accounts belonging to other people, and
telephone the institutions about any you
are unsure of. Two, for every joint
account, either get your name removed or
build the evidence file now while the
owner can still explain where the money
came from.
Three, move your burial fund into its
own clearly identified account up to
$1,500 so it stops being counted.
Four, know what is in your accounts at
the end of each month. And remember what
is protected. Tax refund 12 months. Back
payment 9 months. House, car, household
goods, burial plot, always.
Five, answer every notice from that
agency the week it arrives. Even if all
you can say is that you are looking into
one question. Silence costs more than
any answer you could give. And if your
own situation is tangled, if you are
looking at an account and cannot work
out whether accounts against you, write
to me. The address is on your screen and
in the description below and I read
everyone that comes in. One last thing
before you go. Olla did a kindness for
her brother 11 years ago and it is
sitting in a government computer with
her name on it and she has no idea.
Dorcas made herself poorer every spring
on purpose to escape a rule that had
already protected her. And Aishim lost
months to a question about $41 because
he wanted to get the answer right before
he replied. None of the three of them
did a single thing a reasonable person
would not have done. Not one was
breaking a rule. Every one of them was
operating on a picture of the rules that
nobody had ever corrected. So go and
correct yours this week while nothing is
wrong. [snorts] Find out whose accounts
your name is on. Find out what is
actually protected. And answer the
letter the day it comes, even if all you
have is half an answer. I am Kevin.
Thanks for watching. Do not forget to
check the quiet rules at
kevvinexplains.shop.

title: Seniors Over 60: These 5 Forms Decide What Happens To Your SSA Check

segments.text: You have a document in a drawer that you
believe protects your family, a power of
attorney. You paid a lawyer for it. You
signed it in front of a witness. And
when it comes to your Social Security
check, it does almost nothing. The
Treasury Department does not recognize a
power of attorney for the purpose of
handling federal benefit payments. Not
Social Security, not the needs-based
payment. That is not my opinion. It is
written on the AY's own website in plain
letters where almost nobody goes
looking. So if the day ever comes when
you cannot manage your own affairs, the
person you chose, the one you sat down
with a lawyer to name, walks into that
office holding a document the agency is
not permitted to act on. I want to say
the next part slowly because it is the
reason this video exists. There is a
separate form for that. There is a
separate form for almost everything in
this system and not one of them is going
to arrive in your mailbox because the
entire program is built to answer what
you submit and nothing else. Today I am
going to give you five of them. Five
forms in the order they will actually
matter to you. Two of them decide who is
allowed to speak for you and one of
those two you can only file while you
are still perfectly capable which is
exactly why nobody files it. One of them
is the difference between paying $22.90
a month for the rest of your life and
paying a permanent penalty on top of
that forever. And the window to use it
is 8 months wide and it does not reopen.
One of them is worth roughly $5,700
a year to the average person who
qualifies and it takes about 10 minutes
to fill in. And the last one is a form
that lets you undo a decision you
already made about your own social
security, which almost nobody knows is
possible. And it is the one with the
hardest clock on it. So stay with me for
that one. My name is Kevin. I read the
rules so you do not have to. Every week
I go looking for the thing that quietly
decides what happens to your money, and
I bring it here before it cost you
anything. If that sounds useful,
subscribe and turn on the bell because
the fifth form on this list closes 12
months after you file for benefits. and
after that it is gone permanently. Form
number one, the one that fixes the
drawer problem. It is called SSA1696,
the appointment of representative. And
it is the form that actually does what
most people believe their power of
attorney already does. Let me explain
the gap first because until you see it
clearly, the rest of this will not land.
A power of attorney is a state law
instrument. You create it, you name
somebody, and banks and hospitals and
title companies generally honor it. that
is real and it works. Social Security is
federal and it runs on its own rules.
The AY's position, which it states
openly, is that a power of attorney does
not make a finding about whether you are
capable and does not by itself grant
anybody the right to handle your
payments. And the Treasury regulations
that govern how federal payments are
made do not recognize it for that
purpose at all. So, what happens in
practice is this. Your daughter
telephones the agency to sort out a
problem with your check. She has the
document. She reads them the relevant
paragraph and the person on the other
end who is not being difficult and is
following the rules they are given tells
her they cannot discuss your record with
her. That is the moment families
discover this and it is always the worst
possible moment to discover it. The 1696
closes that gap. It is you while you are
fully capable formally naming somebody
to act for you in your dealings with
that agency. They can then receive
information about your record. They can
be present. They can help with an
application or an appeal, and they can
receive copies of the notices the agency
sends. Now, here is what it does not do,
and I want to be exact rather than
encouraging because this is where people
misunderstand. The 1696 does not hand
your money to anybody. It does not take
a single decision away from you. You
remain entirely in charge of your own
affairs. The person you name is standing
beside you, not in front of you. And you
can name almost anybody. It does not
have to be a lawyer. It can be your son,
your sister, a friend from church. If
they are a lawyer or a professional
representative, there are rules about
fees and any fee has to be approved by
the agency, which is a genuine
protection. But a family member helping
a family member does not charge a fee.
And that is what most of these are. Two
practical points before I move on. The
form is free. You can get it from the
agency's website or by teleoning and
asking them to post one to you. And both
of you sign it. You sign to a point and
the person you name signs to accept.
Send it in and keep a copy. And if you
hand it in at an office, ask them to
stamp your copy in front of you. And
name somebody younger than you. I say
that plainly because a great many people
in this audience name a spouse of the
same age, which is entirely natural and
also means that on the day it is needed,
the person named may be in exactly the
same position you are. Name your spouse.
if you want to name a second person
after them. Now, let me tell you about
Berdine. Berdine is 83. She had a
stroke, recovered most of the way, and
now has good days and days where the
words do not come out in the order she
wants them to. Her son Rey handled
everything after it happened. The bank
was fine, the hospital was fine, the
insurance company was fine, he had the
power of attorney, and every one of them
accepted it. Then a letter came from
social security about her payment and
Ray telephoned and for the first time in
8 months of managing his mother's entire
life, somebody told him they could not
talk to him. He thought he was being
stonewalled. He was not. He was holding
the wrong piece of paper. And there had
never been a moment in his life when
anybody told him a right piece of paper
existed. Berdine could still sign. She
was capable on a good day in the morning
sitting at her own table. So they filed
the form. It cost nothing and it took an
afternoon. But there was a version of
that story where the stroke was worse
and there was no good morning and the
form was no longer available to her at
all. That is what the quiet rules is
for. The plain list of what you need in
place before anything happens printed
large enough to read without hunting for
your glasses with the form names and
what each one actually does so that
nobody in your family is standing in a
hallway with a document in their hand
being told it does not count. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
The link is in the description below and
in the pinned comment at the top. And if
you are watching this on a television
right now, there is a code on the screen
you can point your phone camera at.
7-day guarantee always. If it does not
hand you something you did not have
before, you send it back. Form number

you are watching this on a television,
there is a code on the screen you can
point your phone camera at. 7-day
guarantee, always. If it does not put
something in your hands you did not have
before, send it back.
Now, two things that get missed inside
this same section, and both of them are
worth real money to the right person.
The first is survivor benefits, and the
number there is not 62, it is 60. A
widow or widower can start a survivor
benefit at 60 and can start at 50 if
they are disabled.
Every year I run into people who waited
until 62 because 62 is the number
everybody knows and gave away two full
years of payments they were entitled to
and can never recover.
The second is smaller and stranger and
almost nobody knows it. Your full
retirement age for a survivor benefit is
not the same as your full retirement age
for your own retirement benefit.
The two schedules are written separately
and they do not line up.
For most people caught in the transition
years, the survivor age arrives a few
months earlier than the retirement age.
So, if you are planning to claim a
survivor benefit at your full retirement
age and you use the retirement number,
you will hand back several months of
payments believing you are being
patient. Ask specifically. Say the words
survivor full retirement age, not just
full retirement age, because those are
two different answers and the system
will give you exactly the one you asked
for.
All right, that is the sort. Now, let me
get to the thing I actually made this
video for.
Your benefit was not decided by a
person. It was calculated one time by a
computer using a list. The list is every
year you worked and what was reported
for you in that year, going all the way
back to your first job.
The formula takes your highest 35 years,
indexes them, averages them, and
produces a number. So, the check is not
a judgment about your career. It is
arithmetic performed on a list, which
means that the list is wrong, the check
is wrong, and it has been wrong every
month since the day it started, and it
will keep being wrong until somebody
says something.
And the list is wrong more often than
anybody at that agency enjoys admitting.
Here is what it looks like when it is
wrong. You pull up your earnings record
and you see a column of years with
dollar figures beside them. 40,000,
41,000, 40,000. Then one year sitting at
zero, then 40,000 again.
Inside the agency they call that a gap
year. And a gap year is not always an
error because people do stop working.
There are years for illness, for raising
a child, for a layoff, for a move.
But if you look at a zero and you can
remember going to the same job that year
that you went to the year before and the
year after, then that zero is not your
life. It is a clerical problem.
And that zero is not neutral. This is
the part people underestimate. The
formula uses your highest 35 years. And
if you did not work a full 35, the empty
slots get filled with zeros anyway. So a
wrongly reported year does not just go
missing. It sits inside your average as
a zero and drags the whole figure down.
And it does that for as long as you
receive a check. So where do these come
from and why are there so many?
Almost none of it is anybody being
careless with your file specifically. It
is the volume. Every year employers in
the tax system send in hundreds of
millions of wage reports and each one
has to be matched to a name and a number
that already exists in the records. If
the name and the number do not agree,
the wages cannot be posted to anybody.
They do not get thrown out. They get set
aside. That is the file I mentioned at
the start. Officially, it is the
earnings suspense file. In practice, it
is a room full of money nobody can find
the owner of. More than 1 trillion
dollars in reported wages have
accumulated in it since the program
began and it grows by billions every
single year.
And the reasons your wages might be
sitting in it are ordinary, which is
exactly why nobody suspects them.
A digit transposed. Somebody typed 12
where the number reads 21 at a payroll
desk in 1997 and nobody ever noticed.
A name that changed at marriage and got
updated with one office and not the
other. So the wages posted under a name,
the records no longer recognized.
A small employer doing payroll by hand,
a company that closed, a nickname on one
form and a legal name on another, a
hyphen. And the crucial thing about that
file, which is the reason I built a
section of this video around it, is that
wages can be pulled back out of it at
any time. There is no expiration on the
wages themselves. If proof shows up that
connects a name and a number to
something sitting in that file, it can
be moved to your record decades after
the fact.
So, how do you actually do this? First,
you need to see the list. And that means
going to the Social Security website and
setting up your own account there. It
takes a while and it is deliberately
awkward. And I want you to understand
that the awkwardness is the point. An
account that is difficult for you to
open is also difficult for somebody else
to open in your name. That protection
only works if you claim your account
before a stranger does. And every year
people discover the hard way that they
went to set theirs up and one already
existed. While I am on that, a small
piece of housekeeping somebody in my
audience passed along and it is
genuinely good. If you are about to
change your phone number, go into your
account and get everything settled and
updated while the old number is still
working. People change their phone
first, then find they cannot get back
into the account to change it and the
whole thing becomes a project.
Once you are in, look at every line, not
just the total. Look for zeros in years
you know you worked. Look for a year
that is suspiciously smaller than the
two on either side of it. And look
hardest at the early years, the 1970s
and 80s, because that is when the
records were most manual and the
mistakes are most common.
Then, if you find something, here is
what to do about it. And here is where
most people give up because they are
told something that is technically
accurate and functionally misleading.
You will hear that there is a time
limit. That is real. The written rule
says an earnings record can be corrected
up to 3 years, 3 months, and 15 days
after the year the wages were paid. That
sounds like a locked door on anything
older, and a great many people hear that
sentence, conclude that 1997 is
unreachable, and stop. Do not stop. The
exceptions are written into the rules.
They are published, and they cover very
nearly every situation a real person
actually walks in with. The record can
be corrected after the deadline to match
a tax return that was filed with the tax
authorities. It can be corrected when an
employer reported wages for you, and
they simply are not showing in the
records. It can be corrected for errors
that can be seen on the face of the
record itself. And it can be corrected
where wages were left out of a report
that was otherwise processed. Read that
list again against your own situation.
If you filed the tax return that year,
you are very likely inside an exception.
If your employer sent in a report, and
your name is not on it correctly, you
are inside an exception. The deadline is
real, and the exceptions swallow most of
it. And the sentence people hang up the
phone after hearing is the first half of
a rule with a second half. The form is
called SSA-7008,
the request for correction of earnings
record. It is free. It is short. Bring
what you have.
A W-2 from that year is the strongest
thing you can carry. A tax return for
that year, pay stubs, and if you have
none of that, which after 30 years is
completely normal, you are still not
finished. Because a written or spoken
statement from the employer can serve as
evidence of your wages.
So can the name of the company, the
address, the dates you worked there, and
your supervisor's name. And here is the
sentence I want you to actually say,
because it changes what happens next.
Tell them, "I have a year on my record
showing zero, and I worked for the same
employer the year before, and the year
after. I would like the suspense file
checked under that employer's
identification number for that year."
That sentence does two things at once.
It shows you know the wages might not be
lost, but misfiled, and it points at
exactly where to look. The employer
identification number is the key that
opens that file.
It is on your old W-2, right at the top.
Let me tell you what this is worth,
because the number surprises people. If
your record gets corrected and you are
already receiving benefits, they
recalculate, and then they go back and
pay you the difference for the months
you were underpaid, and every cost of
living increase that has been applied
since then is applied to the corrected
figure, not the old one. So, a
correction that raises your monthly
check by $20 is not $20. It is $20 a
month for as long as you live, plus
every increase that is compounded on top
of it, plus a deposit covering the
stretch behind you.
A woman I will call Zelma found this out
at 79.
Zelma worked in a laundry, then a school
cafeteria, then 19 years for a small
building contractor who did payroll
himself at a desk in the back.
Her granddaughter set up the online
account for her, mostly to stop the
paper statements piling up, and read the
list out loud to her at the kitchen
table. 1986 was zero.
Zelma remembered 1986 clearly. Her
second grandchild was born that spring,
and she did not miss a week of work. It
took two visits and a shoebox. The
contractor had been dead for 11 years,
and the company was long gone, but the
tax return existed, and the tax return
was enough.
Zelma had been paid a little less every
month for 14 years over a typing error
made in a back office by a man who meant
her no harm and never knew he had done
it.
And that is the version of this that
bothers me most, because there is no
villain anywhere in it.
There is only a list that nobody was
assigned to check, and a woman who
assumed the check was the check, because
why on earth would it not be? That is
precisely what the guide exists for, not
strategy. The plain sequence of what to
look at, what to bring, and the exact
words that turn a shrug at a counter
into a search of a file, so that an
afternoon of paperwork is a task with a
beginning and an end, instead of 2 years
of assuming the number is simply the
number.
Same place, kevinexplains.shop,
link in the description and in the
pinned comment, and the code on your
screen if you are watching this on the
television.
7-day guarantee, no argument. An
80-year-old woman with a shoe box on a
folding chair, proving that she went to
work in 1986.
Now, the third thing, and this one has
the clock on it. There is a group of
people watching this who are being paid
the wrong benefit right now, and not
because of any error at all. They are
being paid exactly what they applied
for. The problem is, they applied for
the smaller one, and nobody has told
them the other one grew. Here is the
situation.
A husband dies. His widow is 63, 65, 68.
She files for a survivor benefit because
that is the larger check at that moment,
and she is correct, it is.
And then she stops thinking about it
because the matter feels closed.
But her own benefit, the one built on
her own working life, did not stop. It
kept growing.
It grew every year she did not claim it,
all the way to 70, and somewhere in
there, for a great many women, it
quietly passed the survivor benefit.
Nothing happens when it passes. No
letter arrives. Nobody calls. The system
does not switch you to the higher one on
its own. And I want to be blunt about
this because I have watched people
assume otherwise.
It is not automatic at 70. It is not
automatic ever.
You have to file an application, and
until you file it, they keep paying you
the smaller one, and there is nothing
improper about that because you never
asked for the other. Now, you may have
heard that the rules about switching
between benefits were tightened years
ago, and that this kind of thing is not
allowed anymore. That is true for
spousal benefits between two living
people. It was never true for survivors.
Survivor benefits were left out of that
change on purpose, and the ability to
take one benefit and move to the other
later is one of the last genuine choices
remaining in the entire system. Here is
the ceiling, and this is why I asked you
to turn the bell on at the beginning.
When you finally do file, they will pay
you retroactively, but only 6 months.
Six. That is the whole window. So,
consider what that means for a woman who
is 82 and has been on a survivor benefit
since she was 66.
If her own record has been the higher of
the two since she turned 70, she has
been underpaid for a dozen years. She
can recover 6 months of it. The rest is
simply gone, and it is gone because of a
letter that either never went out or
arrived in an envelope she reasonably
mistook for junk.
So, here is what I want you to do, and
it is one phone call.
If you receive a survivor benefit and
you have never checked your own record
against it, call and say, "I am
receiving a survivor benefit, and I have
never had my own retirement benefit
compared to it. I would like that
comparison run today."
And if that is not you, then think for a
moment about who it is. Your mother,
your aunt, the widow two doors down who
has been getting the same check since
her husband died. Ask them the question.
It takes 15 seconds, and I have seen it
change what people live on. Two more
things in this area because both of them
are where people get told no
incorrectly.
The first is a rule with an ugly name
and a real effect, the widow's limit. If
your spouse claimed his own benefit
early before his full retirement age,
then your survivor benefit is capped. It
cannot be more than the larger of what
he was actually receiving or 82 and 1/2%
of what his full retirement age amount
would have been. That matters in two
directions. It means his early decision
follows you, which is worth knowing
before either of you claims anything,
and it is one of the strongest arguments
for the higher earner in a a waiting.
But, it also means there is a floor. If
he claimed at 62 and was drawing 70%,
you are not stuck at 70%. The floor
lifts you to 82 and 1/2. Ask which of
the two numbers is being used on your
record by name because it is not obvious
from the check. And the second is
divorce where the amount of money left
on the table is genuinely hard to
believe.
If you were married 10 years or longer,
you can receive a benefit on your former
spouse's record. He does not have to
have filed for anything. He only has to
be 62. Your claiming does not reduce his
check by a penny and he is never
notified. It has no effect on him
whatsoever. One more piece of that. If
the marriage ended more than two years
ago, you do not have to wait for him to
file at all. That is a separate
provision with its own name and it
exists precisely so that one person
cannot hold another person's benefit
hostage by refusing to retire.
A number of people have been sitting on
their hands for years waiting for an
ex-husband to make a decision he was
never required to make. Now, if you
called once and were told you do not
qualify, understand what that answer
actually was. It was a comparison of two
numbers on one particular day and it was
almost certainly correct on that day. It
was not a permanent ruling and the
person delivering it is not allowed to
explain to you what would change it. So
when you are told no, ask two more
questions and do not hang up before you
get them out. First, if he is still
working, his own benefit may still be
rising and if it rises far enough, the
comparison flips. Ask whether you are
close. They can tell you that much
without telling you his figures. Second,
and this is the one nobody thinks to
ask. The rule that blocked you is the
50% rule which governs benefits taken on
a living former spouse. If he dies, a
completely different rule takes over and
it goes up to 100%.
Ask them directly whether you would
qualify under that rule instead. They
will tell you and if the answer is yes,
you now know something enormously
important about your own future that you
would otherwise have learned by accident
or not at all.
And if you have lost track of him
entirely, which happens after 30 years,
call once every 6 months or so and ask
the question again. Circumstances
change, and this system will never,
under any conditions, call you to tell
you that they did.
A woman I will call Marvis was told no
in her 50s and believed it for 22 years.
She had raised two children mostly alone
after a marriage that ended badly. And
honestly, she was relieved to be told
she was not entitled to anything of his.
It felt clean. She did not want his
money. Her daughter made the second
call, not to argue, just to ask the two
questions. And what came back was that
the situation had changed years earlier
and had been sitting there changed
waiting for somebody to ask. She
recovered 6 months.
22 years of it were beyond reach, not
because anybody refused, but because the
question had a shelf life and nobody had
told her there was a clock attached to a
thing she had been told did not apply to
her.
Now, let me draw a line under all of it
because there is a pattern here, and
once you can see it, you will never need
me to point it out again. Some things in
this system happen to you automatically
without you doing anything at all. Your
cost of living increase is automatic,
applied to every record every year. And
if somebody tells you they did not get
theirs, what they mean is the Medicare
premium moved at the same time and the
deposit looked flat. The underlying
amount went up. It always goes up. If
you keep working after you claim, that
is automatic, too. Every year your
earnings get compared against your
highest 35, and if the new year beats
one of them, they swap it in,
recalculate, and back pay you to
January. Nobody has to request it. Now,
compare that list to the other one.
Correcting a wrong record is not
automatic. Switching from a survivor
benefit to your own is not automatic.
Claiming on a former spouse is not
automatic. Getting the 6 months of back
pay you were owed for filing after your
full retirement age is not automatic and
you have to ask for it by name when you
apply. Look at what separates the two
lists. Everything the computer can do to
every record at once, it does.
Everything that requires a human being
to look at your specific file and make a
judgment, it does not do unless you make
it. And I want to be fair here because
the easy version of this is to say
somebody is hiding your money and that
is not what is happening. The people at
that agency are handling a case load
that has grown while the staff has not.
There was a time when a claims
representative would print your earnings
record, slide it across the desk and
walk through it line by line with you
before you signed anything. That was
standard. It was not generosity, it was
the job. It largely does not happen now
and it is not because anybody stopped
caring, but the effect is the same for
you either way.
The review that used to be built into
the process has quietly become something
you have to bring to the process
yourself. And nobody sent a notice
explaining that the arrangement had
changed. So, bring it yourself. Here is
exactly what that looks like. One, find
your full retirement age precisely with
the months, not rounded. Then, find your
survivor full retirement age separately
because it is a different number.
Two, open your account on the Social
Security website today before somebody
else opens one in your name and read
your earnings record line by line rather
than looking at the total.
Three, for any year showing zero or an
amount that does not match what you
remember, ask them to check the suspense
file under that employer's
identification number and do not accept
the 3-year deadline as the end of the
conversation because the exceptions are
written down and published. Four, if you
receive a survivor benefit and have
never had it compared against your own
record, make that call this week. 6
months is the entire window and it does
not extend for good reasons.
Five. If you were ever married for 10
years or more and were told you did not
qualify on that record, call back and
ask the two questions. Am I close? And
what happens under the other rule?
And if your own situation is tangled, if
you are looking at a record with three
suspicious years in it and cannot work
out where to start, write to me. The
address is on your screen and in the
description below and I read everyone
that comes in.
One last thing before you go. Wendell
filed on the exact day he believed was
the right day and was two months early
on a chart that has been public since
before his children finished school.
Zelma went to work every day in 1986 and
was paid for it and a typing error meant
the government never knew. And Marvis
was told the truth once, 22 years ago,
and was never told that the truth had an
expiration date on it.
Not one of those three did anything a
sensible person would not have done. The
failure was never in their judgment. It
was that the thing each of them needed
to know had no route to reach them and
no one whose job it was to carry it.
So go and get it yourself. One phone
call, one website, one list read slowly
on a quiet morning before there is any
reason to read it. I am Kevin. Thanks
for watching. Do not forget to check the
quiet rules at kevinexplains.shop.
