kevexplains.shop.
The link is in the description below and
in the pinned comment at the top. And if
you are watching this on your
television, there is a code on the
screen you can point your phone camera
at. 7-day guarantee. no argument. If it
does not put something in your hands you
did not already have, send it back. Now,
how to actually do it? Because it is far
simpler than it sounds, and there are
three ways people get it wrong. Ring the
company holding your account. The large
ones all handle this constantly and have
a form for it. Tell them you want to
make a qualified charitable
distribution. Give them the name and
address of the charity and the amount.
They send the money. You never touch it.
The three mistakes. The first, and it is
by far the most common, is having the
money sent to you and then writing the
check yourself. That does not qualify.
If the money passes through your hands,
it is an ordinary taxable withdrawal,
and no amount of explaining afterward
changes it. The second is the
destination. Donor advised funds do not
qualify. Private foundations do not
qualify. It has to go to an operating
public charity. And if you are not
certain, ask the charity directly
whether they can accept a qualified
charitable distribution. They will know.
The third is the age, and it is stricter
than people expect. You must have
actually reached 70 and a half on the
day the money leaves. Not turn 70 that
year, not 70 in 4 months, 70 and a half
precisely. Work out your own date before
your first one. Two more practical
points because they remove the two
reasons people put this off. The first
is that you do not have to give
everything this way and you do not have
to decide anything permanent. There is
no election, no form filed with your
return, no commitment. You can do one
transfer of $200 this year and nothing
next year. It is simply a way of moving
money available whenever you want it.
And using it once does not oblige you to
anything. The second is the receipt
because this is where people get caught.
You need written acknowledgement from
the charity stating the amount and
stating that you received nothing in
return. That last part matters. If the
charity gives you dinner, a raffle
ticket, or event seats in exchange, the
transfer can be disqualified entirely.
So, the sentence to say when you arrange
it is simply that you need a receipt
confirming no goods or services were
provided. Any charity that handles these
regularly will know exactly what you
mean. and keep that receipt with your
tax papers rather than in a drawer
because the paperwork sent by your
account provider will show the money
left. The letter from the charity is
what shows where it went. Now, the
second door, and this one is a gap that
Congress created by accident and never
closed. The age for this is 70 and a
half. It has always been 70 and a half,
and it still is, but the age at which
forced withdrawals begin was moved. It
is now 73 for people born between 1951
and 1959 and 75 for anybody born in 1960
or later. So there is now a gap of
between 2 and 4 1/2 years where you can
do this and nothing is being forced out
of your account yet. That gap is worth
understanding properly because it is
where the real money is. Your forced
withdrawal when it eventually starts is
calculated from your account balance on
the 31st of December of the previous
year. The larger the balance, the larger
the forced withdrawal permanently for
the rest of your life. So every dollar
you move out during those gap years is a
dollar that is not in the balance when
the calculation runs. And it is not just
a one-time saving. It reduces every
single forced withdrawal you will ever
take. Somebody who routes 15,000 a year
in giving through this during a 4-year
window has removed $60,000 from the
balance. The formula reads their first
forced withdrawal is a couple of
thousand dollar smaller and everyone
after it is smaller too which keeps
their income figure lower which keeps
social security taxation lower which
keeps them further from the Medicare
search charge every year forever. And
the whole thing was funded entirely by
giving they were doing anyway. And there
is a version of this that applies even
if you give nothing to charity at all,
which is worth saying because a lot of
people watching are in that position and
have been waiting for me to acknowledge
it. The gap years are still the most
important years in your account and the
principle is identical. Whatever leaves
that account during them is not there
when the formula reads the balance. For
a charitable household, the tool is the
one I have described. For everybody
else, the same window is when a
conversion to a tax-free account does
the most good. when a deliberate
withdrawal at a low rate beats a forced
one at a higher rate later and when
spending down that account rather than
another one is very often the right
order. I am not going to run through
those here because they each deserve
their own treatment and getting the
amount wrong on some of them is
expensive. But the underlying fact is
the same for everybody. There is a
stretch of 2 to 4 and 1/2 years once
when the government is not yet
participating in your account and almost
nobody uses it because nothing about
that stretch announces itself. That is
the part I want to land. This is not
asking you to give more. It is not
asking you to give at all if you do not
already. It is saying that if money is
leaving your account and going to a
charity, the route it takes decides
whether it also cost you tax. And there
is a second quieter reason those gap
years matter, which has nothing to do
with charity at all. During that window,
your income is generally at the lowest
it will ever be again. No forced
withdrawal is inflating it. If you
delayed social security, you may not
even be collecting yet. That lowinccome
year is the cheapest year you will ever
have for anything that adds to your
income. Which means the gap years are
not only the best time to shrink the
account. They are the best time to do
almost anything deliberate with it. And
once forced withdrawals begin, that
flexibility does not vanish, but it
narrows every single year because the
required amount grows as a percentage as
you age. At 75, it is one figure. At 85
it is considerably larger and it fills
the low brackets before you get to
decide anything. So the gap years are
the only stretch where you are genuinely
in control of your own income figure.
Before it you were working. After it the
formula participates 2 to 4 and 1/2
years once and then never again. Burl is
72 and he has an account of about half a
million dollars and no idea what is
coming. He is a retired equipment dealer
and he is not careless with money. But
his forced withdrawals do not start for
three years and so he has not thought
about them because nothing about his
life is currently prompting him to. He
gives 10,000 a year mostly to a veterans
organization and a hospice that cared
for his brother. 3 years of that rooted
properly is $30,000 off the balance. The
formula will read it changes the size of
every forced withdrawal for the rest of
his life and it costs him nothing
whatsoever because that money was going
out the door regardless. Instead, it
will sit in the account until the
formula finds it and then come out on a
schedule set by somebody else taxed at
his rate, raising his income figure
every year. He has 3 years. He does not
know he has 3 years. That is precisely
what the guide is built for. The windows
that are open right now and close on a
date written plainly and in large type
so that a three-year advantage is
something you use rather than something
you find out about afterward. For
somebody in Burl's position, the
difference between knowing this now and
knowing it at 75 is measured in tens of
thousands of dollars across the rest of
his life. Same place, kevin Kevin
explains.shop in the description and in
the pinned comment. And the code is on
your screen if you are watching on the
television. 7-day guarantee every single
time. A man with three years of open
window and no reason on earth to know it
exists. Now, the third door, and this
one is genuinely new, and almost nobody
has heard of it. There is a
once-in-a-lifetime option to send money
from your retirement account into an
arrangement that pays you income for
life and leaves whatever remains to a
charity when you die. The vehicles are a
charitable gift annuity, which the
charity itself issues, or a charitable
remainder trust. For this tax year, the
limit on that is $55,000,
up from 54,000 last year. Here is what
makes it unusual. Normally funding
something like that with retirement
money means withdrawing the funds,
paying income tax on the withdrawal, and
contributing what is left. This lets it
go directly with no income tax on the
transfer. So, you convert a portion of a
taxable retirement account into a
guaranteed income stream for the rest of
your life without the tax event that
would normally accompany it and a cause
you care about receives what remains.
Now, two things I have to tell you
because the coverage of this is
frequently wrong. It is once, not once a
year, once in your entire life. You
elect it in a single tax year and once
used in any amount, the option is
finished. And this is the one people get
wrong constantly. That 55,000 comes out
of the 111,000 annual limit. It is not
on top of it. If you use the full 55,000
this way, you have 56,000 of ordinary
capacity left for that year, not 111.
This is not for everybody. The payments
you receive back are taxable. The rules
are fussy. It requires working with a
charity that runs a planned giving
program, and universities and large
hospitals do this routinely, while a
small local charity may not. But for
somebody with a large traditional
account who is already charitably
inclined and would like guaranteed
income, there are very few things in the
tax code that do this much at once. One
more thing about it worth saying plainly
because I do not want anybody rushing at
this. A charitable gift annuity is not
an investment and it should not be
compared to one. You are handing money
to a charity in exchange for a promise
of payments and that promise is backed
by the charity's own finances rather
than by an insurance guarantee fund. A
large university or hospital system with
a long history is a very different
proposition from a small organization
and the payment rate is generally lower
than a commercial annuity would offer
because the whole point is that the
charity keeps the remainder. So the
honest framing is that this is a way of
giving that happens to pay you back
rather than a way of investing that
happens to be charitable. If you would
not have given the money away
regardless, this is probably not the
right tool. And because the election is
once in a lifetime, there is no undoing
it and no second attempt.
That is a strong argument for using it
later rather than sooner once you
actually know what your situation looks
like rather than using it on the first
charity that mentions it to you. Now,
the fourth door, and this is the timing
rule I mentioned at the start, and it is
the one that costs people the entire
benefit. This applies once your forced
withdrawals have begun. The rule is that
the first money out of your account in a
calendar year counts towards satisfying
your required withdrawal first dollars
out in order. Which means that if you
take your forced withdrawal in February
and then make your charitable transfer
in November, the transfer is still
tax-free, but it did not satisfy
anything. Your required withdrawal
already happened and you already paid
tax on it. The transfer simply sits on
top. Do it the other way round and the
transfer itself satisfies the
requirement dollar for dollar and the
tax on that portion is zero. Same two
transactions, same amounts, same year
reversed order and one version costs you
thousands and the other costs you
nothing. So the instruction is one
sentence. If you are past the age where
withdrawals are forced, make your
charitable transfer in January before
anything else comes out of that account,
not in December. Almost everybody does
it in December because that is when
people think about giving and December
is when the entire year's advantage has
usually already been lost. There is no
way to fix it afterward. A distribution
that has already happened cannot be
reclassified. The money that came out in
February was an ordinary withdrawal and
it stays one. And there is a related
ordering point that catches people in
the other direction. If you intend to
give more than your required withdrawal
that is completely permitted. The annual
limit is $111,000,
regardless of what your required
withdrawal happens to be. So, somebody
with a small required amount and a large
charitable intention, can transfer far
beyond it, and all of it stays out of
their income. What you cannot do is go
backward. A withdrawal already taken
cannot be converted into a charitable
transfer afterward, no matter how
quickly you send the money on to the
charity. The character of that
distribution was set the moment it left
the account. So the whole thing reduces
to one habit and it is worth building it
deliberately. Decide your charitable
giving for the year in January, arrange
it in January and let everything else in
your financial year happen afterward.
That single sequencing change is worth
more than most of the tax planning
people spend money on. And the fifth
door, which is not a strategy at all. It
is a piece of paperwork that finally got
fixed and it may mean the government
owes you money. For years, there was a
genuine problem with how these were
reported. Your account provider sends a
form at the end of the year showing what
came out. Until recently, there was no
way on that form to indicate that a
distribution had gone to a charity. It
looked identical to an ordinary
withdrawal, which meant tax software
read it as taxable income. The exclusion
had to be entered manually by you or by
whoever prepared your return. And a
great many people did it correctly and
had it taxed anyway because the person
preparing the return did not know to
make the adjustment or the software did
not prompt for it and nothing on the
form said otherwise. That has been
fixed. There is now a specific code on
that form that identifies a distribution
as having gone to a charity and software
reads it automatically. Here is why that
matters beyond convenience. If you made
one of these in a previous year and it
was included as taxable income on your
return, you paid tax you did not owe.
And a return can generally be amended
for 3 years. So the practical
instruction is this. Pull your forms
from the last 3 years. If you made a
charitable transfer and the amount
appears in the taxable portion of your
return, that is recoverable and it is
worth putting in front of somebody who
prepares returns. That is a refund, not
a strategy. It is money already paid
that should not have been. And while you
are pulling those forms, there is a
second thing worth checking on the same
afternoon because it is the other place
this quietly goes wrong. Look at whether
the amount that left your account
matches the amount the charity actually
received. Transfers get split, sent to
the wrong entity, or arrive after the
31st of December and land in the
following tax year. That last one is the
common failure. A check posted by your
provider on the 28th of December that
the charity does not deposit until
January can end up counted in a year you
did not intend. So if you are doing this
near the end of a year, start it in
November rather than the final week.
Providers are slow in December. The post
is slow in December and the deadline is
not when you gave the instruction. It is
when the money moved. And keep it simple
where you can. Fewer larger transfers to
fewer charities produce fewer
opportunities for something to go astray
than a dozen small ones scattered across
a year. Now, let me come back to why
this year specifically. New rules took
effect this year that reduced the value
of ordinary charitable deductions for a
great many people. The mechanics differ
depending on your situation and this is
genuinely a question for a professional
rather than a video. What was not
touched at all is the route I have just
described. So the distance between the
ordinary way and this way widened this
year. It did not narrow. Anybody who
looked at this a few years ago decided
the difference was not worth the phone
call and moved on was making a
reasonable judgment about a different
set of rules than the ones enforced now.
So where do I come out on all five? What
strikes me is not any single provision.
It is the silence. Every one of these
has been sitting in the tax code
available free for years. Not one of
them is aggressive. Not one is a
loophole. And everyone exists because
Congress deliberately put it there. And
the reason almost nobody uses them is
not complexity. It is that there is no
party anywhere in the chain whose job it
is to tell you. Your account provider
earns fees on the balance. Moving money
out of it tax-free to a charity is the
opposite of their interest. And I do not
think they are hiding it, but nobody is
going to ring you about it either. The
charity would benefit enormously and
most small ones have never heard of it.
And the tax authority has no obligation
to inform anybody of anything they have
not asked about. So it sits there and
every year another cohort of people turn
70 and a half in complete silence. And
most of them go the rest of their lives
writing checks from the wrong account.
And I want to be clear about one thing
before the list because I do not want
this to land as an accusation. If you
have been giving by check from your
current account for 20 years, you have
not done anything wrong. That is how
everybody does it. It is how it was done
before this provision existed. And
nobody in your life has had any reason
to mention an alternative. The only
thing worth taking from this video is
that there is a different route
available from a specific age and that
the route is worth money every year you
use it. Not that you should have known.
So, here is what to do and it is four
things. One, work out the exact date you
reach or reached 70 and a half. Not your
birthday, the precise date. Write it
down. Two, if you give to charity in any
amount, ring the company holding your
retirement account this week and ask how
to set up a qualified charitable
distribution. The words are exactly
those. It takes about 15 minutes and it
saves money every year for the rest of
your life. Three, if forced withdrawals
have already started for you, do it in
January before anything else comes out.
That single decision about which month
decides whether the tax on that portion
is zero. Four, pull your tax forms from
the last 3 years. If you made one of
these transfers and it was included as
taxable income, that is money you can
get back with an amended return. And if
you are looking at your own situation
and cannot work out whether any of this
applies to you, email me. The address is
on your screen and in the description
below. I read everyone that comes in.
Olita has been paying tax on money she
gave away for 8 years because nobody
said five words to her. And Burl has
three years of open window in front of
him and no reason on earth to know it is
there. Neither of them was careless.
Both of them were doing the ordinary,
sensible, generous thing in the only way
anybody had ever described to them. 70
and a half is the one age nobody writes
to you about. So write it down yourself.
Make one phone call this week and turn
the only silent milestone in the entire
system into the one that actually pays
you something. I am Kevin. Thanks for
watching. Do not forget to check the
quiet rules at kevinexplains.shop.

title: What the Big Beautiful Bill Actually Did to YOUR Social Security and Medicare

segments.text: A year ago, you were told the government
was about to cut Medicare by 4%
automatically with no vote required. It
did not happen and almost nobody has
told you why.
That prediction was correct when it was
made. The arithmetic behind it was real.
The law that triggered it was real and
the people warning you about it were not
making it up. It simply did not arrive
and the reason it did not arrive is the
single most useful thing in this entire
video.
But four other things from that same law
did arrive quietly without headlines and
three of them have dates attached that
land in January.
So this is not another video predicting
what a bill might do. That bill is a
year old. It is signed. It is law and
enough time has passed that we can check
the receipts.
Here is what I found when I went back
through it and it is the pattern I want
you to carry through the next 27
minutes. The predictions that failed and
the predictions that came true split
along one line and it is not a political
line. Everything that got cancelled had
an industry standing behind it.
Hospitals, doctors, insurers,
organizations with offices in Washington
and people whose job it is to make phone
calls. Everything that survived lands on
an individual filling out a form at a
kitchen table. That is the whole
pattern. Not one party protecting its
friends. A system that responds to
whoever has representation and a great
many of you do not have any. My name is
Kevin. I read the boring documents so
you do not have to sit with them. Every
week I bring one of these here in plain
English with the actual move attached.
If that is useful to you, subscribe and
turn the bell on because the third item
in this video takes effect on the 1st of
January and the failure mode has nothing
to do with whether you qualify. So, the
Medicare cut. Let me give you the whole
story because it is genuinely
instructive. When that law passed, it
added enormously to the federal deficit
and there is a separate law on the books
since 2010 called statutory
pay-as-you-go which says that when
Congress increases the deficit,
automatic cuts must follow. It runs on
its own. Nobody has to vote for the
cuts. They simply happen.
Social Security is exempt from that
process. Medicaid is exempt. Most
low-income programs are exempt. Medicare
is not. And the reductions to Medicare
are capped at 4%. So, the arithmetic was
straightforward, and the Congressional
Budget Office ran it. Roughly $45
billion out of Medicare in the first
year, and something in the region of
half a trillion across the following
decade. That is where the warnings came
from. They were not invented, and they
were not exaggerated. And then in
November of last year, during the
negotiation that reopened the
government, a provision was included
that wiped the pay-as-you-go scorecard
clean. Not reduced it, erased it. Which
meant the trigger never fired. The 4%
cut that providers had been preparing
for did not materialize, and the half
trillion dollars over a decade went with
it. Now, I want to be careful and fair
here, because there is more than one way
to read that. If you were a hospital, a
doctor, or somebody on Medicare who
would have felt those cuts as fewer
accepting physicians and thinner
services, this was straightforwardly
good news. It is difficult to argue
otherwise.
If you care about the deficit, this was
the second time in recent memory that a
scorecard designed to enforce discipline
was simply erased rather than met. And
the Committee for a Responsible Federal
Budget said so plainly at the time.
There were offsets available. None were
used. Both of those are honest readings.
What is not in dispute is the mechanism,
and the mechanism is the lesson.
>> [clears throat]
>> The Medicare cut disappeared because the
people it would have hit had somebody
making the case for them continuously in
the building where it was decided.
And I want to spend a moment on how that
provision actually got there, because it
explains a great deal about how these
things work. It was not a stand-alone
vote. Nobody stood up and proposed
protecting Medicare from the sequester
as its own bill.
There was a bill introduced to do
exactly that and it went nowhere.
What happened instead is that the
scorecard eraser was included inside the
enormous negotiated package that
reopened the government after the
shutdown.
It was one provision among dozens in a
bill that had to pass for entirely
unrelated reasons and it was attached in
a moment when nobody was going to vote
the whole thing down over it. An
amendment was submitted to strip that
provision out. It was never scheduled
for a vote.
So a half trillion dollar change to
Medicare over a decade was made without
a single debate on the subject inside a
bill about keeping the lights on.
I am not saying that is corrupt. That is
how nearly everything of consequence
gets done now by both parties and it has
been that way for a long time. But it is
worth understanding because it is the
reason predictions about legislation are
so unreliable in either direction.
The thing you were warned about can
vanish in a paragraph you never heard of
in a bill about something else at 3:00
in the morning.
Which is also why the correction never
reaches anybody. The warning was a
story. The cancellation was a line item.
And there is a second thing worth
knowing about it, which is that it is
not permanent. The scorecard was wiped
as of the end of that year. It did not
repeal the underlying law.
So the same mechanism still exists,
still applies to future legislation, and
could produce the same threat again the
next time a large deficit increasing
bill passes.
So the correct summary is not that
Medicare is safe from this. It is that
this particular trigger from this
particular law was diffused once in a
negotiation and the device it was
attached to is still sitting there.
Velma is 76 and she spent last autumn
genuinely frightened. She had watched
the coverage. She understood it
correctly, which is more than most
people manage, and she reached the
conclusion that her Medicare was about
to be cut and there was nothing anybody
could do because no vote was required.
So she did what a sensible frightened
person does. She started delaying
things. She put off a procedure she had
been advised to have because she wanted
to see what her costs looked like in
January before committing to anything.
The cut never came.
She delayed that procedure for 5 months
for a reason that had stopped being true
in November and nobody told her because
the announcement that something is not
happening is not a story anybody covers.
She did not act foolishly. She acted on
the best information available and the
correction never reached her.
That gap between the warning that
travels and the correction that does not
is exactly why the quiet rules exist.
Not clever strategy.
A plain current account of what is
actually true right now in large print
so that nobody delays a procedure or a
decision for months on the strength of
something that stopped being accurate.
The scary version of the news is always
louder than the update. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
The link is in the description below and
in the pinned comment at the top. And if
you are watching this on your
television, there is a code on the
screen you can point your phone camera
at. 7-day guarantee, no argument. If it
does not put something in your hands you
did not already have, send it back. Now
the four things that did survive and the
first three all begin on the same day,
the 1st of January. Number one is the
work requirement for Medicaid. Adults
covered through the expansion, meaning
people between 19 and 64 who qualify on
income, will have to demonstrate 80
hours a month of qualifying activity.
That is roughly 20 hours a week and it
can be met by paid work, by half-time
schooling or training, by community
service, or by combining them. It
reaches across 43 states and the
District of Columbia and touches roughly
20 million people. Now before anybody
switches off, two things. There are real
exemptions. Caregivers of dependent
children, veterans with disabilities,
pregnant women, people with serious
mental health or substance use
conditions. And if you are over 65, you
are not in the expansion group at all.
So, this does not apply to you directly.
And on the policy itself, I am not going
to tell you what to think.
Supporters argue a work or community
engagement expectation is reasonable for
able-bodied adults and exists in other
assistance programs.
Opponents point to states already
running it and argue the coverage losses
come overwhelmingly from paperwork
rather than from anybody refusing to
work.
Both are honest positions held by
serious people.
What is not a political question is the
failure mode. And this is where the
pattern from the top of the video comes
back. Georgia has been running this
since 2023.
Nebraska started in May, Montana and
Arkansas in July.
Those states are the preview and the
consistent finding across all of them is
the same. The people who lose coverage
are overwhelmingly not people refusing
to work. They are people who were
working and could not prove it in the
format required or whose notice went to
an old address or who did not know they
had been flagged until the coverage was
already gone.
There is a 30-day window to provide
proof of activity or of an exemption.
30 days is not long when the letter went
to a house you moved out of.
And I want to give you the specific
mechanics because the difference between
keeping coverage and losing it is almost
entirely procedural. States are required
to check automatically first using data
they already hold.
Payroll records, wage reporting,
anything already flowing into a state
system.
For somebody with one steady employer
and regular pay, that check usually
succeeds and the person never hears
about any of it.
Where it breaks is everybody else and
everybody else is a large group.
Somebody paid in cash, somebody working
several small jobs, somebody
self-employed, somebody doing seasonal
work, somebody caring for a parent which
qualifies in many circumstances and
appears in no payroll system anywhere in
the country. Those are precisely the
people who have to actively document and
report, and precisely the people least
likely to have a clean way of doing it.
And there is a timing detail inside it
that catches people who are otherwise
fine. The requirement is monthly. So, a
person who works 50 hours a week for 8
months and nothing for four can fail in
the four, even though their annual total
is far above what anybody would consider
part-time.
Construction, landscaping, agriculture,
anything weather-dependent, anything
tied to a season.
The requirement does not average across
a year, and it does not care that you
worked double the standard in July.
There are hardship provisions in some
circumstances, and states have some
flexibility in how they administer this,
which is genuinely worth asking about
rather than assuming. But, the default

already spent it in your head. Working
it out beforehand takes one quiet
afternoon. Finding out afterward cost
you the whole winter. It is at
kevinexplains.shop.
The link is in the description below and
in the pinned comment at the top. And if
you are watching this on your television
right now, there is a code on the screen
you can point your phone camera at.
7-day guarantee always. No argument. If
it does not put something in your hands
you did not already have, send it back.
Which brings us straight to the second
date because this is the other half of
Delia's arithmetic. Sometime in
November, the Medicare Part B premium
for next year gets announced. And that
premium comes directly out of your
Social Security payment before it is
deposited. This year, the standard
premium is $22.90
a month. Projections for next year put
it somewhere around $213,
which would be an increase of roughly
5%. Now, watch what that does. Take
somebody with a benefit of $2,000. A 3%
increase is $60. The part B increase is
about $10. So, the actual change in the
deposit is about $50, not 60. That is
not a scandal and nobody is stealing
from you. Part B is a premium for
medical insurance and it has always been
deducted this way. But it means the
headline percentage and the deposit
almost never agree. And the smaller your
benefit, the harder that bites because
the premium is a flat dollar amount that
does not scale down for people with
less. Somebody with a benefit of $900
gets the same $10 premium increase as
somebody with a benefit of $4,000. On
the smaller check, that eats a far
larger share of the raise. So, the
practical instruction is short. When the
October number comes out, do not do the
multiplication. Wait until November,
take the premium increase off and then
do it. That is your actual figure and it
will be the one that shows up. There is
one protection worth knowing about here
and it does not apply to everybody.
There is a provision that generally
prevents your Part B premium increase
from being larger than your dollar
increase from the adjustment so that
your net payment does not go down
year-over-year.
It has exceptions and it does not apply
to everyone. But in years when the
premium rises faster than the
adjustment, it is what stops a great
many people from actually losing ground
in cash terms. There is a second thing
about part B that catches people every
year and it has nothing to do with the
standard premium. If your income is
above a certain level, you pay more than
the standard amount. That search charge
is called the income related monthly
adjustment amount and it is calculated
using your tax return from two years
earlier. 2 years earlier. So the premium
you pay next year is based on what your
income looked like two tax years ago,
which produces a genuinely unfair
situation that happens constantly.
Somebody sells a house or takes a large
withdrawal from a retirement account or
receives a one-time payment. 2 years
later, long after that money is spent, a
search charge arrives based on an income
they no longer have. And here is the
part people do not know. There is a form
for exactly this. If you have had a
qualifying life-changing event, and that
list includes retirement or reduced work
hours, the death of a spouse, divorce,
and several others, you can ask for the
search charge to be recalculated using
your current income instead of the
2-year-old figure. People pay that
search charge for a full year without
ever knowing the form exists. If your
income dropped for one of those reasons
and you are paying a search charge, that
is worth a phone call this month. Now,
the third date, and this is the one I
told you at the start, is worth more
than the first two for a lot of you. The
15th of October to the 7th of December.
That is the Medicare annual enrollment
period. During those eight weeks, you
can change your Medicare Advantage plan,
change or add a prescription drug plan,
or move between advantage and original
Medicare. Whatever you choose takes
effect on the 1st of January. Here is
why this window is worth more than the
adjustment. The adjustment is a fixed
formula. You cannot change it by a
single dollar no matter what you do. It
is arithmetic happening to you. This
window is the opposite. It is 8 weeks in
which your decisions actually change
what you pay for the next 12 months. And
the differences involved are frequently
in the hundreds or thousands rather than
the tens. And the reason it matters more
some years than others is that your plan
does not stay the same. Advantage plans
and drug plans are one-year contracts.
On the 31st of December, your plan as it
currently exists ends. What arrives on
the 1st of January is a new one, often
with the same name and the same card and
different terms underneath. Which is why
the single most important piece of mail
you will receive this autumn is a
document called the annual notice of
change. Your plan is required to send it
before this window opens. It tells you
exactly what is changing about your
specific plan for next year. the
premium, the deductible, what you pay
for a hospital stay, which drugs are
still on the list, which doctors are
still in the network. Almost nobody
reads it because it arrives looking like
every other envelope from an insurance
company, and there is nothing on the
outside saying that this one determines
what a hospital night cost you next
year. So, here is what to do, and it
takes about 20 minutes. Find that
notice. Go to the section listing what
changes. Check four things specifically.
Is my prescription still covered and at
what tier? Is my doctor still in
network? What is my out-ofpocket maximum
next year compared to this year? And
what does an inpatient hospital day
cost? Now, if any of those moved in a
direction you do not like, this window
is when you can do something about it.
And after the 7th of December, you
generally cannot until the following
year. And there is free help for this
that almost nobody uses. Every state has
a health insurance assistance program
funded federally. staffed by trained
counselors who do not sell anything and
do not earn a commission. They will sit
with you and compare your options
against your actual medication list. It
costs nothing. It is not a sales call.
And in most states, the appointments
fill up in November, which is why the
useful move is to ring them in October.
Two more things about that window
because they are what separate a useful
20 minutes from a wasted one. The first
is the mistake nearly everybody makes,
which is comparing plans on the monthly
premium. The premium is the most visible
number, and it is very often the least
important one. A plan with a lower
premium and a higher hospital day rate
or a worse drug tier for the one
medication you actually take costs more
over a year than the plan you left.
Compare on your own medication list and
your own doctors, not on the headline
price. The second is that if you take
prescriptions, bring the actual bottles
or a written list with the exact dosages
when you compare, not the general name
of the drug, the specific one with the
strength. Drug lists are built at that
level of detail. And a plan that covers
your medication at one dose can treat a
different dose entirely differently. And
one thing worth knowing, if you have an
advantage plan, there is a second window
from the 1st of January to the 31st of
March in which you can switch advantage
plans once or return to original
Medicare. So if January arrives and
something is badly wrong with the plan
you have, that is not the end of it. But
it is narrower than the autumn window
and it does not apply to everybody. So
it is a safety net rather than a plan.
The fourth date is the 1st of January,
and this one is a number moving in a
direction that surprises people. The cap
on what you pay out of pocket for
prescription drugs under Part D is going
up. This year, the cap is $2,100.
Next year, it becomes $2,400.
Read that carefully because it is the
opposite of how a cap increase usually
sounds. This is not more protection. It
is the ceiling moving further away. It
means you have to spend $300 more of
your own money before the point where
your plan starts covering everything.
For most people, that changes nothing at
all because most people never approach
the cap. But for somebody on an
expensive medication, that is $30
additional dollars out of pocket,
arriving in the early months of the year
at exactly the time of year when heating
bills are highest. The cap is still an
enormous improvement on what came before
it, which was no ceiling at all, but it
adjusts upward every year. And the
direction of that adjustment is worth
understanding rather than being
surprised by in March. And if that $300
matters to your household, that is the
strongest possible reason to look at the
program called Extra Help, which is a
separate federal subsidy that can cover
your premium, wipe out your deductible,
and cut your co-pays down to a few
dollars. It has income and resource
limits. They are more generous than
nearly everybody assumes and your home
and your car do not count toward them.
The fifth date is also January and this
one only touches you if you are still
working. The maximum amount of earnings
subject to social security tax goes up.
This year it is $184,500.
The trustees projected at $190,200
next year. In practical terms, an
additional $5,700 of earnings becomes
taxable, which for somebody earning
above that line is roughly $353 more in
payroll tax over the year with the
employer paying the same. Again, if you
earn below that cap, and the
overwhelming majority of people do,
nothing about this changes anything for
you. You were already paying on every
dollar. I include it because this is the
number at the center of the entire
national argument about how to fix the
program and it is worth knowing what it
actually is rather than what people say
it is. The sixth date is January as well
and this one matters if you are drawing
benefits and still working which is a
larger group than people think. There is
an earnings test. If you are under full
retirement age for the whole year and
you earn above a certain amount benefits
get withheld $1 for every $2 over the
line. This year that line is $24,480.
In the calendar year you actually reach
full retirement age. The rules loosen
considerably. The line jumps to $65,160
this year, projected at around $67,200
next year, and the withholding drops to
$1 for every three over. And from the
month you reach full retirement age
onward, the earnings test disappears
entirely. You can earn any amount at all
with no effect on your benefit. Now,
here are the two things about this that
people get badly wrong, and both of them
cost real money. The first is that money
withheld under the earnings test is not
gone. It is not a penalty, and it is not
confiscated. When you reach full
retirement age, your benefit is
recalculated upward to account for the
months that were withheld. You get it
back, spread across the rest of your
life. A great many people believe they
lost it permanently and made an entirely
different decision about working because
of that belief. The second is that in
your first year of claiming, there is a
monthly test as well as an annual one.
So, somebody who earned a great deal in
the first half of the year, then
retired, can often still receive
benefits for the remaining months based
on their monthly earnings, regardless of
what the annual total says. People
assume they have to wait until January
and lose several months of payments they
were entitled to. There is a third piece
of this worth knowing, and it applies to
people who have not claimed yet. The
earnings test only exists before full
retirement age. So the decision about
working and the decision about when to
claim are connected in a way people
miss. Somebody who intends to keep
working substantially and who has not
yet reached full retirement age may find
that claiming early produces very little
actual income because the earnings test
withholds much of it while permanently
reducing the benefit amount. That
combination is genuinely poor
arithmetic. And it happens because
people think of the two decisions
separately. And a related point that
catches surviving spouses in particular.
The earnings test applies to survivor
benefits as well. Somebody widowed at 62
who is still working full-time and
claims survivor benefits may see most of
those payments withheld when waiting
would have preserved them entirely. None
of that means do not claim. It means the
earnings test belongs in the
calculation. And for a great many
people, nobody ever put it there. Clovis
is 64 and he turned down a part-time job
last spring because of exactly that
first misunderstanding. It was 20 hours
a week at a hardware store. Work he
would have enjoyed with people he knew.
He had heard from somebody at church
that if you go over the limit, Social
Security takes the money and you never
see it again. So he did the arithmetic
on losing benefits permanently and
concluded it was not worth it and he
stayed home. He was working from a fact
that was wrong, not a small detail, the
central fact of the decision. And the
thing about it that bothers me is that
the correct information would have taken
one page and 4 minutes to read. And
instead it cost him a year of work he
wanted income he needed and something
harder to price which is somewhere to go
on a Tuesday. That is what the guide is
for. Not complicated strategy. The
handful of things that are simply not
true corrected plainly in large type so
that nobody makes a year-long decision
out of something they overheard. The
cost of not having it is not abstract.
For Clovis, it was roughly $15,000 of
work he turned down for no reason at
all. Same place, kevinexplains.shop.
The link is in the description and in
the pinned comment, and the code is on
your screen if you are watching on the
television. 7-day guarantee every single
time. A man of 64 sitting at home for a
year because of something somebody told
him after a church service. Now, the
seventh date, and this one is the
largest change on the whole list in
terms of how many people it reaches, the
1st of January, and it is a work
requirement for Medicaid. Here is what
it is. Adults covered through the
Medicaid expansion, meaning people aged
19 to 64 who qualify on income, will be
required to demonstrate 80 hours a month
of qualifying activity in order to keep
coverage. States must have this in place
by the 1st of January. 80 hours a month
works out to about 20 hours a week. It
can be met by paid work, by half-time
enrollment in school or technical
education, by an approved job training
program, by community service, or by any
combination of them added together. It
can also be met by earning at least a
certain monthly amount, which at the
federal minimum wage works out to
roughly $580.
This applies across 43 states and the
District of Columbia and reaches roughly
20 million people. Now, two things I
want to say clearly because this is a
live political argument and I have
people watching from every position on
it. First, the exemptions because a
great many people who assume this hits
them are exempt. There are exemptions
for caregivers of dependent children,
for veterans with disabilities, for
pregnant women, and for people with
serious mental health or substance use
conditions. Being over 65 means you are
not in the expansion group at all, and
this does not apply to you. Second, the
argument on both sides. Supporters make
the case that a work or community
engagement expectation is reasonable for
able-bodied adults and that similar
requirements exist in other assistance
programs. Opponents point to the states
that have already run this and argue
that the coverage losses come
overwhelmingly from paperwork failures
rather than from people refusing to
work. Meaning the people removed are
largely people who were in fact working
and failed to document it correctly.
Both of those are real positions held by
serious people and I am not going to
tell you which to hold. What I will tell
you is the practical fact which is not
political at all. Several states have
already been running this. Georgia has
since 2023. Nebraska began in May of
this year. Montana and Arkansas began in
July. Those states are the preview. And
the consistent lesson from every one of
them is the same. The failure mode is
almost never somebody refusing to work.
It is a notice going to an old address
or a reporting portal that did not
accept the documentation or somebody not
knowing they had been flagged until the
coverage was already gone. There is a
30-day grace period to provide proof of
activity or of an exemption before
coverage terminates. 30 days is not long
if the notice went to the wrong house.
So, if this touches anybody in your
family, the single most valuable thing
you can do this autumn has nothing to do
with work at all. It is making sure the
address, the phone number, and the email
on file with the state Medicaid agency
are current and that somebody in the
household knows to open mail from them
immediately rather than setting it
aside. And there is a practical detail
about proving compliance that the states
already running this have made very
clear. The systems are generally
designed to verify your hours
automatically wherever they can by
checking payroll data and other records
the state already holds. For somebody
with a steady job at a single employer,
that often works and no action is needed
at all. Where it breaks is everybody
else. Somebody paid in cash, somebody
working several small jobs, somebody
doing seasonal work, somebody caring for
a parent, which is qualifying activity
in many circumstances, but does not
appear in any payroll system anywhere.
Those are precisely the people who have
to actively document and report and
precisely the people least likely to
have a straightforward way of doing it.
So the practical instruction for anybody
in that situation is to start keeping
the record now rather than in January. A
simple written log of dates and hours,
payubs kept rather than discarded, a
letter from whoever you help care for,
enrollment paperwork if it is school or
training. It sounds excessive. It is the
difference between a portal accepting
your documentation in an afternoon and a
30-day clock running while you try to
reconstruct 6 months of work from
memory. The eighth date is the same day
and it is the quieter half of the same
law. Two other things change for that
same group on the 1st of January.
Renewals move to every 6 months instead
of every 12. That is twice as many
opportunities in a year for a form to go
astray. And the failure mode is
identical to the one I just described.
And the retroactive coverage window
shortens. That is the provision that
allowed coverage to reach backward to
cover medical bills incurred shortly
before you applied. it is being
narrowed, which means the gap between
getting sick and getting approved
becomes a gap you may be responsible
for. There is a third consequence that
almost nobody has reported, and it is
the one that concerns me most. Beginning
on the 1st of January, somebody who
loses or is denied Medicaid solely for
failing to meet the work requirement
will not be eligible for marketplace
subsidies either. Normally, losing
Medicaid is the thing that qualifies you
for help buying a plan on the
marketplace. In this specific
circumstance, it will not. So the
ordinary safety net underneath losing
Medicaid does not catch this particular
fall. That is a significant detail and
it is worth knowing before January
rather than after. And the ninth item
which is not being covered anywhere and
which is not next year. It is now. If
you have a defaulted federal student
loan, the government can withhold up to
15% of your monthly social security
payment to collect it. retirement
benefits, survivor benefits, disability
insurance benefits, all of them.
Collections were paused for years during
the pandemic, restarted, then paused
again in early this year, while the
Department of Education rolled out its
new repayment system. That system
launched on the 1st of July, and
involuntary collections, including
Social Security offsets, are restarting
on that timeline. About 452,000 people
receiving Social Security are currently
in default and within reach of this. And
I want you to understand who these
people actually are because the picture
in most people's heads is wrong.
Government analysis of older borrowers
subject to this found that about 43% had
held those loans for 20 years or more.
3/4 had borrowed only for their own
education. Most owed less than $10,000
when the offset began. The typical
monthly amount taken was a little over
$140 and almost half were subject to the
full 15%. And an enormous number of the
rest are grandparents and parents who
took out or co-signed loans for a
child's education decades ago. There is
a floor and it matters. Your check
cannot be reduced below $750 a month. So
the amount taken is the lesser of 15% or
whatever amount would bring you down to
that floor. If your entire benefit is
under $750,
nothing can be taken at all and
supplemental security income is fully
protected and cannot be offset. Now,
here is the part that actually matters
because there are three ways out and
most people know about none of them. The
first, and it is the most effective for
the majority of people, is loan
rehabilitation.
Nine on-time monthly payments made
within a 10-month period removes the
default status entirely and stops the
offset. The payments are based on your
income, and for somebody on a modest
benefit, they can be very small indeed.
The second is a hardship reduction.
Under federal law, the department can
determine that the standard offset
amount would cause hardship and reduce
it. and the agencies involved have
historically been more willing to grant
reductions on social security offsets
than on tax refunds. The third applies
if you are receiving disability. Total
and permanent disability discharge can
eliminate the federal loans entirely.
You are also supposed to receive a
warning letter at least 30 days before
an offset begins telling you when it
starts and how much. If you act inside
that window, you can often stop it
before it ever touches a payment. And if
you are looking at a letter like that
right now or you think you might be in
this category and cannot work out where
you stand, email me. The address is on
your screen and in the description
below. I read every single one that
comes in. There is one more thing here
that matters enormously and almost
nobody says it, so I want to be direct
about it. There is a difference between
being behind on a loan and being in
default. Default happens after roughly
270 days of missed payments. A loan that
is late or in forbearance or in a
repayment plan you are struggling with
is not in default and none of this
applies to it. So if you are worried the
first question is not how much do I owe.
It is what is the actual status of the
loan and you can find that out in one
place at the federal student aid website
which lists every federal loan in your
name and its current status. That
matters because the fear is frequently
larger than the situation. People assume
that being behind means the worst thing
is already happening, avoid finding out,
and lose the window in which it was easy
to fix. And if the loan genuinely is in
default, the new repayment plan that
launched in July calculates payments as
a percentage of income with a minimum of
$10 a month. For somebody living on a
modest benefit, the payments involved in
rehabilitation may be far smaller than
anything they have imagined. Reeba is 68
and she signed for her son's loans in
1996. He finished the degree. Life went
in the direction lives go. The loans
came back to her and by the time she
understood that they had, she was not
working anymore and the balance had
grown in the way these balances grow.
What she said to me was not about the
money. She said that for 11 years she
has been afraid to open certain
envelopes and that she has a drawer and
that she knows exactly which drawer it
is and how full it is. The offset had
not even started when she wrote to me.
The fear had been running for a decade
on its own and rehabilitation nine
payments based on what she can actually
afford would end the entire thing. It
has been available the whole time.
Now let me tell you what is not changing
because a fair amount of what circulates
online about next year is simply false
and you deserve the correction. Full
retirement age is not going up. It is 67
for everybody born in 1960 or later.
That transition is complete and there is
no scheduled increase. The Social
Security resource limit for supplemental
security income has not changed. $2,000
for an individual, 3,000 for a couple.
There is no fourth stimulus payment.
There is no special bonus check. And
there is no new benefit being paid to
seniors that requires you to sign up
through a website you have never heard
of. Every one of those is currently
circulating. And every one of them is
false. And your benefits are not being
cut next year. The projected reduction
from the trust fund is in the next
decade, not next January. And nothing
about that changes anybody's check in
the year we are talking about. So here
is where I come out on all nine. And you
may see this differently. What strikes
me looking at the list is not any single
item. It is that eight of the nine were
produced by formulas or by laws already
passed. And only one of them, the
enrollment window, is a place where you
get to make a decision. That is the
actual shape of this. Nearly everything
on this calendar is happening to you.
One thing on it is available to you. And
people spend the autumn worrying about
the parts that are arithmetic, which
cannot be changed by anybody, and
letting the 8week window go by, which
can change what they pay for an entire
year. I understand why. The arithmetic
is the part that gets announced. The
window is the part that arrives in an
envelope that looks like junk. on a
Medicaid changes specifically. I am not
going to give you a political position
because the argument about whether a
work expectation is appropriate is a
genuine disagreement and it is not mine
to settle for you. What I will say is
narrower and I think it holds regardless
of where you sit. Whatever the rule is
meant to do, a rule administered through
notices, portals, and documentation
deadlines will remove people who
complied but reported it wrongly. And
the states already running it show that
clearly. That is not an argument against
the policy. It is an argument for making
absolutely certain that anybody you love
in that category has a current address
on file. So nine dates and what to do
about each one. The 14th of October, the
adjustment is announced. Write it down
and do not multiply yet. In November,
the part B premium is announced.
Subtract that increase then multiply.
That is your real number. The 15th of
October through the 7th of December is
the enrollment window. Find your annual
notice of change. Check your drugs, your
doctor, your out-ofpocket maximum, and
your hospital day rate, and ring your
state's free counseling service in
October before they fill up. On the 1st
of January, the drug cap rises to
If that matters to you, apply for extra
help now rather than in the spring. The
taxable maximum and the earnings limits
both rise. If you are working while
claiming, remember that withheld money
comes back to you at full retirement age
and remember the monthly test in your
first year. The Medicaid work
requirement, the six-month renewals, and
the shortened retroactive window all
begin on the 1st of January. Update the
address, the phone, and the email with
the state agency this month and tell
whoever is affected to open that mail
the day it arrives. And if there is a
defaulted student loan anywhere in your
household, look into rehabilitation now
before an offset starts because nine
affordable payments ends it. Delphia
planned her winter around a number that
was never going to reach her account.
Clovis turned down a year of work he
wanted because of one sentence that was
not true. And Reeba spent 11 years
afraid of a drawer over something that
nine payments would have ended at any
point in those 11 years. Every one of
those three was careful. careful their
whole lives. They were simply working
from a picture that was slightly wrong
in a way that cost them something real.
So spend one morning with the calendar
instead. Nine dates, four of them before
Christmas. Most of this list you cannot
change, and that is genuinely fine
because knowing which parts those are is
what frees you to spend your attention
on the one part you can. I am Kevin.
Thanks for watching. Do not forget to
check the quiet rules at
kevinexplains.shop.

title: 4 Credit Card Changes Every Senior Needs to Know Before Their Next Statement

segments.text: That is what a large bank is permitted
to charge you for being one day late on
a credit card payment. Not 30 days late,
one day. And if it happens a second time
inside the same year, that is the amount
for the second one, sitting on top of
the first. Two years ago, you were told
that number was becoming $8. Every
outlet carried it. $10 billion a year
coming back out of the banks and into
ordinary accounts. It never happened.
Not for one day, not for one customer,
not once. And that is only the first of
four things sitting between you and the
statement that arrives in your mailbox
this month. The second is a protection
almost everybody believes is federal law
and is not. The third has already
lowered the credit scores of people who
did nothing at all differently from the
year before. And the fourth is something
you may have been carefully saving up
for years that can be reduced to nothing
without anybody asking you. Here is what
connects all four. And once you see it,
you will not be able to stop seeing it.
Not one of these four protections is
legally binding on anybody. That is the
thread. Every single one of them exists
because a company chose it or an agency
proposed it or a court permitted it. Not
one of them is a law that somebody would
be breaking if they took it away
tomorrow. They can each be withdrawn
without your consent, without notice,
and without anybody doing anything
wrong. which sounds bleak and it is not
and I want to say why before we go any
further. Because there are protections
in this that are absolutely binding and
they are the ones you build yourself, a
setting you switch on, a phone call you
make, a report you pull. Those cannot be
taken away by a court ruling or a policy
change. And by the end of this, you will
have four of them. My name is Kevin. I
read the fine print so you do not have
to sit with it. Every week I take one of
these apart in plain English with the
actual move attached because knowing a
rule changed has never once put a dollar
back in anybody's account. The setting
does. The phone call does. If that is
useful, subscribe and turn the bell on
because the third item in this video is
the one nobody is warning older people
about and it works quietly. So, the late
fee, let me give you the whole story
because the ending is not where most
people think it is. A federal rule was
finalized in March of 2024 that would
have capped late fees at $8 for the
largest credit card issuers, meaning
those with more than 1 million open
accounts. The reasoning was that the
existing amounts, $30 for a first late
payment and 41 for any after that, were
far above what it actually costs a bank
to process a late payment and were
functioning as a revenue line rather
than a penalty. The estimate was $10
billion a year. Within days, the Chamber
of Commerce, the American Bankers
Association, and several other trade
groups sued in federal court in Texas.
And here is where it gets genuinely
unusual. And I want you to understand it
because it is not what people assume
happened. The rule was not simply struck
down by a judge over the objection of
the government. What happened is that
after the change in administration, the
agency that wrote the rule switched
sides. It filed a joint motion together
with the industry groups that were suing
it asking the court to vacate its own
rule. In that motion, the agency agreed
with the plaintiffs that its own rule
had violated the law. The judge granted
it on the 15th of April, 2025. So, the
$8 cap is not delayed and it is not
under appeal. It was vacated by
agreement and the agency that created it
conceded the case. Now I am going to
give you both sides of that properly
because this is a live political
argument and I have people watching who
sit on every side of it. The legal
argument that one is not frivolous.
There is a law from 2009, the card act
which says card issuers may charge
penalty fees that are reasonable and
proportional to the violation. The court
held that dropping the amount to $8 did
not allow issuers to actually impose
penalty fees in any meaningful sense and
therefore conflicted with the statute
Congress had written. [clears throat]
Whatever you think of the fees, that is
a real legal question about whether an
agency exceeded what Congress authorized
it to do. The argument on the other side
is equally real. The gap between what a
late payment costs a bank to handle and
what it is charged for is enormous. And
that gap falls hardest on people who are
late because the money was not there
rather than because they forgot. I am
not going to tell you which of those to
hold. What I will tell you is the
practical fact. And the practical fact
is that at most large banks, your late
fee today is $30 for the first one and
41 after that. Now, what happened last
month? Because this is genuinely new. In
early July, multiple financial outlets
reported that the same agency has
submitted a request for information
about credit card late fees to the White
House office that reviews these things.
A request for information is often the
first formal step before a new
rulemaking begins, which is a striking
turn given that the same agency spent
last year working to kill its own rule
on this exact subject. Be careful about
what that means. It is not a rule. It is
not a proposal. It is a request for
information. And analysts who follow
this closely are openly skeptical that
anything binding comes out of it given
how the last attempt ended in court. So
the honest status is this. Your fee is
$30 to $41 today. Something may be
underway. Nothing has changed and you
should not arrange a single thing in
your life around the possibility that it
will. Wilburn is 76 and he has never
missed a payment on anything in his
life. He is quite proud of that and he
has earned it. Last October, he was in
hospital for 11 days for a hip he had
been putting off. His daughter brought
him the mail. Nobody thought about the
card because there was nothing on it.
$70 for a prescription and a tank of
petrol. $41 in fees on a $70 balance.
And then interest began because paying
late also ends the grace period on a
card most months he had cleared in full.
The fee was more than half of what he
had actually spent. And here is the part
that stayed with me. When I told him he
could have called and asked them to
remove it, he said, "I did not know you
were allowed to ask." That sentence is
the reason the quiet rules exists. Not
clever strategy. The short list of
things you are simply allowed to ask
for, written plainly and in large print,
so that a hospital stay cost you a
hospital stay and not a hospital stay
plus a fee plus interest plus a year of
a higher balance. Reading it on an
ordinary afternoon cost you nothing at
all. Finding out about it afterward from
a stranger is how most people learn it.
It is at kevinexplains.shop.
The link is in the description below and
in the pinned comment at the top. And if
you are watching this on your
television, there is a code on the
screen you can point your phone camera
at. 7-day guarantee. No argument. If it
does not hand you something you did not
already have, send it back. So, let me
give you the two things that actually
protect you here because these are
binding in the only way that matters,
which is that nobody can vote them away.
The first is automatic minimum payment,
not automatic full balance, the minimum.
Go into your account online or telephone
the number on the back of the card and
set the automatic payment to the minimum
amount due on every card you hold. It
takes a few minutes per card. Understand
what that does and does not do. It does
not stop interest. If you carry a
balance, you still pay interest on it.
What it does is make it structurally
impossible to be charged a late fee
because the minimum goes out on its own
whether you are traveling, unwell,
distracted, or in hospital for 11 days.
And you can still pay the full balance
manually the way you always have. The
automatic minimum sits underneath as a
floor. Most months it never triggers
because you have already paid. The one
month it matters, it saves you $41 and
the loss of your grace period. The
second is the phone call, and it works
far more often than anybody expects. If
you are charged a late fee, ring the
number on the back of the card and ask
them to remove it. That is the whole
request. Most major issuers will wave a
first late fee on an account with a
clean history. And a great many will do
it on a long-standing account, even when
it is not the first. You do not need a
story, and you do not need to be upset.
The words are simply, "I have had this
card a long time, and I have not been
late before. would you remove that fee
for me? The person answering usually has
the authority to do it without asking
anybody. The reason this works is not
generosity. It is that a customer who
has paid on time for 15 years is worth
vastly more than $41 and the person on
the phone knows it. Almost nobody tries.
Two things that make it work better, and
neither of them is a trick. The first is
when you call, ring within a few days of
the fee appearing rather than waiting
for the next statement. A fee that is
still sitting in current activity is
easier for the person on the phone to
reverse than one that has already closed
into a prior statement and had interest
calculated on top of it. The second is
what to do if the first person says no.
Ask politely whether a supervisor is
able to review it, not angrily and not
as a threat. The authority to wave a fee
sits at different levels at different
institutions, and the person who answers
first does not always hold it. A calm
second ask succeeds surprisingly often.
And if the answer is still no, you have
lost four minutes. And one thing not to
do, do not close the card in
frustration. Closing a long-held card
removes its age from your credit history
and reduces your total available credit,
which can lower your score on both
counts. A card you have had for 20 years
is worth far more sitting open and
unused than it is worth as a gesture.
Now, the second item, and this is the
one where the gap between what people
believe and what is actually true is
doing real damage. Medical debt on your
credit report. You have very likely seen
headlines saying medical debt is being
removed from credit reports. That is
partly true and the part that is not
true is costing people. Here is what
actually exists. The three credit
bureaus, Equifax, Experian, and
TransUnion, adopted voluntary policies
between 2022 and 2023.
Under them, paid medical collections
come off entirely, regardless of the
amount. Medical collections with an
original balance under $500 do not
appear at all, paid or unpaid. And a
medical collection cannot appear on your
report until at least 12 months after
the first missed payment. Those three
changes removed roughly 70% of medical
collection entries from credit files
across the country. That is enormous and
it is real. Now look carefully at what
is not on that list. An unpaid medical
collection with an original balance
above $500 that is more than 12 months
old can still appear on your credit
report and can still lower your score.
Estimates put that at somewhere around
15 million Americans. And here is the
part that matters most. Those three
protections are not law. They are
policies the bureaus adopted voluntarily
and continue by choice. There was a
federal rule finalized in January of
2025 that would have banned medical debt
from credit reports entirely and barred
lenders from using it in decisions. It
was challenged in federal court in Texas
and in July of 2025 it was vacated on
the finding that the agency had exceeded
the authority Congress gave it under the
Fair Credit Reporting Act. So, there is
no federal regulation banning medical
debt from credit reports. What protects
you is a decision three companies made
and could unmake. Now, two pieces of
genuinely good news that almost nobody
mentions. And the first one may apply
directly to you. 15 states have passed
their own laws restricting or banning
medical debt on credit reports. State
law is law. If you live in one of those
states, your protection does not depend
on any bureau's goodwill, and it did not
disappear when that federal rule was
vacated. That is worth 10 minutes of
your time to find out because it changes
what you can insist on. On those 15
states, one practical note, the list has
been growing. States have been adding
themselves yearbyear, and the
protections differ. Some ban medical
debt from credit reports outright.
Others restrict how and when it can be
reported or bar collectors from
furnishing it at all. So, the question
to ask is specific rather than general.
Search for your own state's name
together with the words medical debt
credit reporting law or ring your state
attorney general's consumer protection
office, which exists in every state and
answers questions like this at no cost.
And if you are in one of those states
and a medical collection is on your
report anyway, that is not just
something to be disappointed about. That
is a violation of your state's law and
your state attorney general is the place
that complaint goes. The second is about
scoring. The newer models FICO 9, FICO
10, and Vantage score 4 ignore paid
medical collections completely and weigh
unpaid medical collections considerably
less than other kinds of collections.
Older models do not. Which lender uses
which model is out of your hands, but
the direction is moving in your favor.
There is one more thing about that
12-month window, and I think it is the
single most valuable protection still
standing in this whole area. 12 months
is a long time. A medical bill that goes
to collections today cannot appear on
your credit report for a full year. That
is not a grace period in the sense of
hoping nobody notices. It is a working
window in which you can do something.
And there is a great deal you can do
inside it. You can request an itemized
bill which hospitals must provide and
which catches errors at a rate that
would astonish you. You can ask whether
the charge should have gone to insurance
and did not. You can apply for the
hospital's financial assistance program,
which nonprofit hospitals are required
to have and which very few people know
to ask for by name. And you can
negotiate the amount directly with the
collector in writing. Any one of those
resolving means the collection never
appears at all. So the practical
instruction is this. The moment a
medical bill goes to collections, that
is not the moment to be embarrassed and
put it in a drawer. That is the start of
a 12-month clock during which the thing
is still fixable and invisible. The
people at damages are almost always the
ones who did not know the clock existed.
Nadine is 69 and she found out about
hers from a car dealership. Her rate
came back higher than she expected on a
modest used car. And the finance
manager, who was decent about it, turned
the screen round and showed her a
medical collection from a hospital stay
four years earlier. She had paid that
bill. She was certain of it. And she was
right. and she had the record at home in
a folder. What had happened is that the
account was reported to one bureau and
never updated after payment. Her other
two reports were clean. She had never
looked at any of them because nothing in
her life had ever suggested she needed
to. What she asked me afterward is the
question I get most on this subject. How
was I supposed to know? And the honest
answer is that she was not under the
system as it works. Nobody writes to
tell you that a company failed to update
a record about you. There is no
notification. The only mechanism that
exists for finding out is you going and
looking on purpose at something you have
no particular reason to suspect is
wrong. That is a strange arrangement
when you think about it plainly. A file
is kept about you. It affects the price
of nearly everything you borrow and the
entire responsibility for its accuracy
sits with the person least equipped to
audit it. It took one dispute letter and
about 5 weeks and it came off. 5 weeks,
one letter, and it had been sitting
there for four years, silently costing
her money on every rate she was ever
quoted. That is exactly what the guide
is built to prevent. Not complicated
strategy. The three or four things worth
checking once a year in plain English
and large type so that a mistake
somebody else made gets caught by you in
an afternoon rather than by a stranger
with a computer screen at the worst
possible moment. Same place,
kevinexplains.shop.
The link is in the description and the
pinned comment and the code is on your
screen if you are watching this on the
television. 7-day guarantee every single
time. A woman of 69 in a dealership
being shown a bill she had already paid.
So, here is how you check and it is free
and it is the highest value hour in this
entire video. Go to
annualcreditreport.com.
Say the name out loud to yourself
because that is the only site authorized
under federal law to give you your
reports for free. Everything else
advertising free credit reports is
selling something. Pull all three.
Equifax, Experian, TransUnion. This
matters enormously and Naen is the
reason. An error very often sits on one
bureau and not the others and each one
must be disputed separately. Checking
one and assuming the rest are fine is
the most common mistake people make. You
can now pull all three free every week
and that is permanent. When you have
them, go to the collection section and
look for four specific things. Any
medical collection under $500, which
should not be there at all. Any medical
collection you have already paid, which
should not be there either. Any medical
collection less than 12 months old. And
any account where the date of the
original missed payment looks later than
when you actually missed it because a
debt that has been redated stays on your
report longer than it legally should. If
you find any of those, dispute it with
that bureau. Disputes are free. They
must be investigated, and the
investigation has a deadline of 30 days.
And if you look at your reports and
cannot work out whether something is
wrong or simply unflattering, email me.
The address is on your screen and in the
description below. I read everyone that
comes in. Now, the third item, and this
one is genuinely a trap because the
product was sold on the exact opposite
promise. Buy now, pay later. You have
seen these at checkout online and
increasingly in shops. Split this into
four payments. No interest. The names
are a firm, CLA, Afterpay, and the pay
later option inside PayPal. For years,
one of the loudest selling points was
that these were invisible to the credit
bureaus. That was accurate. A person
could open several of them and none of
it touched a credit file. That is over.
A firm began voluntarily reporting to
Experian and TransUnion. CLA began
reporting to TransUnion and the scoring
company itself has built two new models
specifically designed to include this
activity. So the thing that was sold as
leaving no trace now leaves a trace. Why
this matters more for the people
watching this than for anybody else and
this is the part nobody is saying.
Somebody in their 30s with a thin file
may actually benefit. Ontime payments
become positive history where they had
none. That is a fair argument and I will
not pretend otherwise. But consider
somebody who has spent 45 years building
a score in the high 700s or above. That
score rests on a long average account
age, a spotless payment record, and very
few new accounts. Now, open three of
these in a single autumn, buying
presents for grandchildren. Each one can
be a new account. New accounts lower
your average account age. Several opened
close together looks like a burst of new
borrowing. And a payment missed by a
fortnight on a purchase you had already
forgotten about can now be reported as a
