title: File These 5 Documents Before Someone Else Legally Takes What Is Left of Your Home

segments.text: The deed to your house is not proof that
you own it. I know how that sounds. Let
me say it more precisely because the
distinction is the entire reason this
video exists. That deed is a record. It
sits in a filing cabinet at a county
office and it says you own your house
and everybody involved treats that as
true. But a record is not a fact. A
record is a thing that can be added to.
In most counties in this country, a
person can walk into the recorder's
office, hand the clerk a document about
your property, pay the filing cost, and
have it entered into the public record
that same day. Nobody verifies that it
is true. Nobody calls you. Nobody checks
whether the signature on it is really
yours. And I want to sit on that for a
moment because when people hear it the
first time, they assume they have
misunderstood something. There is no
fraud department at the county recorder.
There is no verification desk. There is
no step where somebody compares a
signature against anything or telephones
the owner listed in the system or pauses
a filing to ask a question. The clerk
checks that the document is the right
kind of document, that it is formatted
correctly, that the fee is paid. Then it
goes into the record, that is not
incompetence and it is not underfunding.
It is the actual legal role of that
office and it has been since these
offices were created. A recorder is a
librarian of documents, not a judge of
them. Deciding whether a document is
truthful is what courts are for. And
courts only get involved when somebody
brings them a case, which produces a
situation most homeowners have simply
never considered. The public record of
who owns your house is maintained by an
institution that has no mechanism and no
obligation to determine whether what it
contains is true. That is not a scandal
and it is not a loophole somebody found.
That is the design. The recorder's job
is to record. It has never been to
investigate. Which means the record of
who owns your house can be wrong. It can
be added to by a stranger and it can sit
there being wrong for years. And in any
dispute, that record is what everybody
works from until you prove otherwise at
your own expense on your own time. So
here are five documents that decide what
happens when the record and the truth
stop agreeing. Most of them are free.
Two of them take 5 minutes. Now let me
tell you why the person watching this is
the specific target. because it is not
random and it is worth understanding.
Picture what a paidoff house looks like
from the outside to somebody who is
looking. It is searchable. Property
records are public in this country and
anybody can pull yours up online in
about 30 seconds without leaving their
chair. They can see the address, the
assessed value, when you bought it, and
what you paid. There is no lender on it.
When a bank holds a mortgage, that bank
is watching. It has a financial interest
in the ownership chain staying clean,
and it employs people whose entire job
is monitoring exactly that. When you
paid off your mortgage, you gained
enormous freedom. And you also quietly
lost your only unpaid security guard.
And the owner of a paidoff house in this
country is very often over 60, sometimes
living alone, and has almost certainly
never had a reason to look at their own
property record. So, a house with
equity, no lender, and an owner who is
not watching. That is not a fortress.
That is a vault nobody is standing next
to. My name is Kevin. I read the rules
so you do not have to. Every week, I go
looking for the thing that quietly
decides what happens to your money. And
I bring it here before it costs you
anything. If that sounds useful,
subscribe and turn on the bell because
the fourth document on this list
involves a Supreme Court case most
homeowners have never heard of and a
follow-up case being decided this year.
Document number one, and this is the one
I would do first today before you do
anything else in this video, property
fraud notification. Most counties in
America now run a free alert program.
You go to your county recorder website.
You find the property fraud alert or
recording notification signup. You enter
your name and your property information
and you are done. It costs nothing. From
that moment forward, anytime anybody
records anything at all against your
property, a deed, a lean, a transfer, a
claim of any kind, you get an email
usually within a day. That is the entire
program. It does not stop anything from
being recorded. What it does is tell you
the same day instead of the same decade.
And that distinction is everything
because these situations are almost
never discovered early. They are
discovered at a closing table or during
a refinance or by the children of
somebody who has died, which is years
later and after the trail is cold. Now,
let me tell you how the thing it
protects against actually works because
most people picture it wrong. They
imagine somebody breaking in. It is
nothing like that. A person searches
public records for properties with no
mortgage on them. That is free and it
takes seconds. They look for older
owners, which is also visible from
public information. They prepare a deed
transferring the property. They sign
your name to it and they walk it in and
record it. The county accepts it because
the county accepts documents. That is
the job. And now the public record says
somebody else owns your house. Not
truthfully, but officially. From there,
they either borrow against it through a
lender who does not look closely or
attempt to sell it to somebody who has
no idea. And you find out much, much
later, and you are the one who has to
prove the negative. Let me tell you
about Adeline. Adeline is 73. She taught
elementary school for 31 years in a
midsized county, and she has lived in
the same house since 1986.
It has been paid off since 2009.
She found out something was wrong when a
letter arrived from a lender she had
never heard of about a loan she had
never taken, secured by her house. A
deed had been recorded transferring her
property to a person she had never met.
It had her name on it and a signature
that was not hers, and the county had
accepted it and filed it because that is
what the county does. Nobody stole
anything physically. Nobody came near
her house. Somebody typed her address
into a public database, printed a form,
and walked it into a government office,
and it took her months and several
thousand dollars in legal fees to
establish in writing that she still
owned the house she was sitting in. And
I want to be specific about what those
months were actually like, because the
dollar figure is the smallest part of
it. Every institution she dealt with
worked from the record. The lender
worked from the record. Her own bank,
when she went to explain, worked from
the record. The record said something
had happened to her property and her
word that it had not was procedurally
just a claim she was making. She was in
the position of proving a negative about
her own house to people who were not
being unreasonable and who simply had a
document in front of them that said
otherwise. And here is the part that
stayed with me when I looked into how
these actually resolve. It is almost
never a dramatic fight. There is no
villain in a room somewhere. It is forms
and waiting and a title company that
will not proceed until the cloud is
cleared and a person in her 70s making
the same explanation to the sixth person
who has no authority to fix it. She got
it resolved. Most people do eventually,
but she spent a season of her life on it
at an age when seasons are not something
anybody has in unlimited supply. Now, I
want to stop here because Adeline is
exactly why I built the thing I am about
to tell you about. The program that
would have caught this was free. It was
on her county's website the entire time.
It would have emailed her within a day
of that deed being recorded. And one
phone call to the recorder that same
week would have ended the whole thing
before a single dollar was spent. Her
county has her name. They have her
address. They know she owns that house.
They have never once sent her a letter
about the program. That is what the
quiet rules is. It is the free things
nobody tells you about written large and
written plain in the order to do them so
a person can sit down on a Saturday with
a cup of coffee and actually close the
doors that are standing open. You can
find it at kevinexplains.shop.
The link is in the description below and
in the pinned comment at the top. And if
you are watching this on a television
right now, there is a code on the screen
you can point your phone camera at.
7-day guarantee always. If it does not
hand you something you did not have
before, you send it back. Ask yourself
one thing. Would you know today if
somebody recorded a document against
your house last Tuesday? Document number
two, and this is the one where most
people find out they have been carrying
the wrong coverage for 20 years. Title
insurance. And the difference between
the kind that looks backward and the
kind that looks forward. When you bought
your house, you almost certainly paid
for title insurance at closing. It was a
line item. Somebody explained it in
about 11 seconds and you signed. Here is
what a standard owner's policy actually
does. It protects you against defects
that existed before you bought the
property. A forged signature somewhere
back in the chain. An unpaid lean from a
previous owner. An heir nobody knew
about. Problems that were already there
sitting in the history waiting. That is
genuinely valuable and it is why the
policy exists. But notice the direction
it faces. Backward. It covers the past.
If somebody forges a deed on your
property next year, that is not a defect
that existed when you bought it. That is
a new event. And a standard policy
generally does not cover it. An enhanced
owner's policy faces the other way.
Depending on the policy and the state,
it can cover forgery occurring after
closing, fraudulent transfers, identity
theft affecting your title, and
critically the legal costs of fighting
it. Those legal costs are the part
people underestimate. Clearing a
fraudulent deed is not a form. It is a
case and cases are expensive. Now, this
one is not free. It costs money to
upgrade. And I am not going to pretend
otherwise. But here's the question worth
one phone call. Call whoever handled
your closing or the title company named
on your policy and ask two things. Is my
policy standard or enhanced? And if it
is standard, what would an enhanced
policy cost? That is a 5-minute call and
you will have an answer. And there is a
related thing worth knowing that costs
nothing at all. Pull your policy out and
actually look at it. A great many people
have never read the document they
bought. Some of you will find you
already have an enhanced policy and can
stop worrying about this section
entirely. Some will find the policy is
in the name of a person who has died,
which is a separate problem I am going
to get to. And I want to add one more
thing about this that people almost
never consider because it is genuinely
counterintuitive.
Your title insurance policy does not
expire. It has no renewal date and no
premium after the first one. You bought
it once at closing and it has been
sitting there quietly ever since for as
long as you own the property. That
sounds like good news, and in one sense
it is. But think about what it means in
practice. It means the coverage you are
relying on today was purchased under
whatever the standard product was in the
year you bought your house. If you
bought in 1986, the policy protecting
your house is a 1986 product written
before online property databases
existed. Before anybody could search
your county's records from a kitchen
table in another state and before this
particular kind of fraud was a category
anybody was thinking about. The threat
changed. Your coverage did not because
nothing about a title policy prompts you
to revisit it. There is no annual
statement, no renewal notice, no agent
calling to review your needs. It is the
one insurance product in your life that
nobody ever tries to upsell you on after
the day you buy it. And that is
precisely why so many people are
carrying coverage that was appropriate
decades ago and has not been
reconsidered since. Let me tell you
about Bernard. Bernard is 69. He has
retired from a career in heating and
cooling and he lives in a house he
bought in 1994. He did everything right
on the front end. He bought title
insurance at closing. He kept the
paperwork in a folder and he could have
told you exactly where that folder was.
When a problem surfaced on his title
decades later, he pulled out that folder
with complete confidence and then found
out that the policy he had been counting
on for 30 years was built to protect him
against things that happened before
1994. He was not underinsured because he
was careless. He was underinsured
because nobody at any point in three
decades ever told him there were two
kinds. and the one he had was pointed in
the wrong direction. Document number
three, the trust that exists on paper
and does not exist in the record. A
revocable living trust is a genuinely
useful tool and I am not going to
oversell it. Here is what it actually
does. Your home is currently titled in
your personal name, which means the
public record shows your name attached
to that address. When a house is held in
a trust, the trust name appears in the
record instead. You still own it. You
still live in it. You can still sell it.
refinance it or change the trust
entirely at any time. Nothing about your
daily life changes at all. Two real
benefits come from that. The first is
that when you die, a house held in a
trust passes to whoever you named
without going through the court process.
No probate on that asset. That saves
months and it saves whatever probate
costs in your state. The second is
quieter and it matters for everything
else in this video. Your personal name
is no longer the thing sitting in the
public record next to that address,
which makes the property meaningfully
less attractive to somebody running a
quick search for older owners with no
mortgage. Now, here is the failure I
actually want to warn you about because
it is enormously common and almost
nobody checks. An extraordinary number
of people have a trust document sitting
in a drawer, professionally drafted,
properly signed, and their house was
never actually transferred into it. The
trust exists, the house is not in it.
Creating a trust and funding a trust are
two separate acts. The attorney drafts
the document. Then a deed has to be
prepared transferring the property into
the trust and that deed has to be
recorded at the county. If that second
step never happened or happened for one
property and not another or was prepared
and never filed, then the trust is an
empty container and you will not find
out. The document in your drawer looks
exactly the same either way. your family
finds out at the worst possible moment
when the house goes through probate
anyway and somebody has to explain why
the trust did not work. That is a
15-minute check. Call your county
recorder or search their online records
and find out whose name is currently on
the deed to your house. If it says your
personal name and you believe it should
say your trust, that is a phone call to
your attorney this week, not next year.
And I want to be honest and say a trust
is not free. It typically runs somewhere
from around $1,000 to a few thousand
depending on your state and your
situation and it requires an attorney to
do properly. There are situations where
it is genuinely not worth it and a
transfer on death deed accomplishes the
probate part alone for a fraction of
that in many states. What is not
defensible is paying for a trust and
never funding it. That is the worst of
every option. You paid the cost and got
none of the benefit. And there is a
second version of this failure that
catches people who did fund the trust
correctly, which is worth 30 seconds
because it is entirely invisible. People
refinance. Somewhere in the last 10 or
15 years, a great many households
refinanced a mortgage. And when they
did, the lender required the property to
be taken out of the trust temporarily.
That is normal, and it is not anybody
behaving badly. Lenders often will not
write a loan against a property held in
a trust. So, the deed comes out of the
trust, the loan closes, and the property
is supposed to go back in. Sometimes it
does not. The closing is over, everybody
moves on, and the step that puts the
house back into the trust is somebody's
job in a way that means it is nobody's
job. And the homeowner has no idea. They
funded their trust correctly the first
time. They remember doing it. They have
no reason to think anything changed
because from their side, nothing did.
So, if you have a trust and you have
refinanced at any point since you set it
up, that check is not optional. It is
the single most likely way for a
correctly created trust to be quietly
empty. Document number four, and this
one comes from a Supreme Court case that
changed the law for every homeowner in
this country, and almost nobody knows it
happened. Let me tell you about
Geraldine Tyler because this is a real
person and a real case. She was 94 years
old. In 1999, she bought a one-bedroom
condominium in Minneapolis and lived
there alone for over a decade. As she
got older, she and her family decided
she would be safer in a senior
community, and she moved there in 2010.
Nobody paid the property taxes on the
condo after she left. By 2015, the
unpaid taxes had reached about $2,300.
With interest and penalties on top, the
total was around 15,000. The county
foreclosed and sold the condominium for
$40,000. It kept all of it. It took the
15,000 it was owed and it kept the
remaining $25,000 as well because under
that state's law, the former owner had
no way to recover the surplus. She sued.
And in May of 2023, the Supreme Court of
the United States ruled for her
unanimously. every justice. The chief
justice wrote the opinion and said that
property rights cannot be manipulated
that easily and that keeping the excess
was a classic taking under the
constitution. And I want to point out
something about that case that I find
genuinely remarkable. The organizations
that filed briefs supporting a 94 year
old woman against her county came from
across the entire political spectrum.
Groups that agree on almost nothing
else. There was no side to be on.
Everybody looked at it and saw the same
thing. So the law is now clear. A county
cannot keep the equity above what it is
owed. Here is why this still matters for
you rather than being a closed story.
States are implementing that ruling at
wildly different speeds. Some rewrote
their statutes promptly. Others have
moved slowly. The mechanism for actually
claiming your surplus, who you file
with, what form, and by when varies
enormously. And in a lot of places, it
is a claim you have to make rather than
a check somebody mails you. And there is
a question the court left open that is
being argued right now. When a house
sells at a tax auction for far less than
it is worth, is the surplus measured
against the auction price or against
what the property was actually worth. A
follow-up case on exactly that is before
the court this year. It matters
enormously because auction prices are
frequently a fraction of real value. So
the right you now have is real and it is
also incomplete. And the practical
version for you is this. Know your
state's redemption period. That is the
window during which you can pay the back
taxes and reclaim the property. And it
has a hard deadline. If you receive a
delinquency notice, that notice is the
beginning of a clock. And the people who
lose houses this way are almost always
people who set the notice aside. That is
exactly the situation the guide is built
around. Every document in this video is
a small piece of paper standing between
an ordinary life and a very bad year.
And every one of them is easier to
handle in advance than to fix afterward.
Same place, kevinexplains.shop,
link in the description, pinned comment
at the top, and the code on your screen
if you are watching this on the
television. 7-day guarantee. No
questions, no argument. a 94 year old
woman in a senior community and a
condominium she still owned being sold
out from under her for less than it was
worth. While we are here, a related
thing that costs nothing and that far
too many people miss. Nearly every state
offers some form of property tax
reduction for older homeowners.
Exemptions, freezes, deferrals, credits,
the names vary. They are not automatic.
Nobody enrolls you when you turn 65. The
reason I am putting it in this section
rather than treating it separately is
that unpaid property taxes are how the
situation in that Supreme Court case
begins. And a household that is not
receiving an exemption it qualifies for
is paying a larger bill than it owes
every year, which makes falling behind
more likely rather than less. So, one
phone call to your county assessor does
two things at once. It lowers the bill
and it makes the worst outcome in this
video less likely to ever start.
Document number five, and this one is
for anyone who has lost a spouse or who
will. The document that removes a
deceased person from the deed. Here is
what most people believe. If a house is
held by a married couple with what is
called right of survivorship, then when
one spouse dies, the house passes
automatically to the survivor. And that
belief is correct. It does pass
automatically. That part is true. Here
is what is also true. And almost nobody
knows. The public record does not update
itself. Your husband's name or your
wife's name is still sitting on that
deed at the county. The law says you own
the house outright. The record still
shows two owners, one of whom died years
ago. Nothing goes wrong for a long time.
You live there, you pay the taxes, you
have no reason to think about it at all.
Then somebody needs the title to be
clean. you go to sell or refinance or
take a reverse mortgage or you die and
your children try to sell and now there
is a dead person on the deed and
clearing that requires a document
usually a certified death certificate
recorded at the county often along with
a sworn affidavit and the exact
requirements vary by state. Doing that
in the year after a death is
straightforward. The death certificate
is right there. You have already ordered
several copies. It is one more errand in
a period that is already full of
errands. Doing it 15 years later is a
different task. Doing it after the
surviving spouse has also died by
children who were not involved in any of
it is a considerably harder task and it
happens constantly. Let me tell you
about Eta. Eta is 80. Her husband died
in 2012. They had owned their house
together since 1978 and it was paid off
long before he passed. She handled
everything correctly by every ordinary
measure. She notified the bank. She
notified the pension. She changed the
insurance and the utilities and the
vehicle registration. She did the entire
list that people give you. Nobody on
that list said anything about the deed.
It is not on most of the lists. So for
over a decade, the record at her county
has shown two owners of that house, one
of whom has been gone since 2012. She is
not in any danger. She owns it. But the
day her daughter has to deal with that
property, there will be an extra problem
waiting. and the person who could have
resolved it in 10 minutes with a
document she already had in her hand
will not be there. That is the whole
shape of this video in one story.
Nothing was wrong. Something was simply
never finished. And I want to say one
more thing about Eta's situation because
there is a version of this that is
considerably worse and it is worth
knowing about. Everything I just
described assumes the house was held in
a way that passes automatically to the
surviving spouse. Most married couples
own their homes that way. And if you do,
the only problem is the paperwork lag I
described. But not every deed is written
that way. Some couples hold property as
what is called tenants in common, which
means each person owns a share and that
share does not automatically pass to the
other. It goes wherever that person's
will directs or through the court
process if there is no will. People end
up in that arrangement for all kinds of
ordinary reasons. A second marriage
where each person brought their own
children into it. a property one spouse
owned before the marriage and added the
other two later. A deed prepared by
somebody who used a standard form
without asking. And the surviving spouse
frequently has no idea because it never
came up in 40 years of living in the
house. So the check I am describing is
not only about clearing a dead person's
name. It is about finding out what the
deed actually says in the words it
actually uses while both people are
still here to do something about it if
the answer is not what either of you
assumed. That is a 10-minute look at a
public record. And for a small number of
you, it will be the most important 10
minutes in this entire video. Now, let
me give you my honest opinion, and it is
only that. I do not think anybody
designed this to hurt anyone. The
recorder records. The title company
sells the product you asked for. The
attorney drafts what you paid for. Every
person in this chain is doing their job
correctly. But look at what it adds up
to. The single largest asset most
American families will ever own sits
inside a system where nobody is
responsible for telling you anything and
where the default outcome of doing
nothing is that the record slowly drifts
away from the truth. And I think the
thing that bothers me most is how cheap
the fixes are. The fraud alert is free.
Checking whose name is on your deed is
free. Reading the policy you already
paid for is free. Recording a death
certificate costs almost nothing. Four
of the five things in this video cost
less than a tank of gas combined. This
is not a wealth problem. Wealthy people
are not protected here because they have
money. They are protected because
somebody on their payroll does this as a
matter of routine and hands them a form
and says, "Sign here." Nobody hands you
the form. So, the difference between the
household that keeps everything and the
household that has a very bad year is
not income. It is whether one afternoon
ever got spent. All right, here is your
checklist. Five things and you could
genuinely do most of them before dinner.
One, sign up for property fraud alerts
through your county recorder. Free five
minutes and it is the single highest
value thing in this video. Two, call
your title company and ask whether your
policy is standard or enhanced and what
an upgrade would cost. Then read the
policy you already have. Three, look up
your own deed in the county records and
find out whose name is actually on it
right now. If you have a trust, confirm
the house is in it. If you have lost a
spouse, see whether they are still
listed. Four, call your county assessor.
Ask what senior property tax relief you
qualify for and whether you are
currently receiving it and confirm you
are not delinquent on anything. Five, if
a spouse has died and their name is
still on the deed, record the death
certificate now while you are the one
holding it. Let me leave you with this.
Adeline had a free program available to
her the entire time and nobody in her
county ever mentioned it. Bernard bought
insurance in 1994 and kept the folder
for 30 years without knowing it pointed
the wrong direction. And Eta did every
single thing on the list somebody handed
her and the deed was not on the list.
Not one of them was careless. Every one
of them was let down by the same thing,
which is that the record of what you own
is a document somebody else maintains.
And it is nobody's job to keep it honest
for you. So go look at your own record
this week. It is public. It is free. And
it will take you 10 minutes to find out
whether it still says what you think it
says. I am Kevin. Thanks for watching.
Do not forget to check the quiet rules
at kevinexplains.shop.

title: 5 Changes Could Affect Every US Veteran Who Served Before 1990

segments.text: Right now, tonight, there are
advertisements running on television
telling veterans to call about Camp
Leune. You have almost certainly seen
one. I need to tell you something before
you pick up that phone because almost
nobody is saying it plainly. That claim
window closed. It closed on the 10th of
August, 2024. The Navy is no longer
accepting new claims. It cannot grant
exceptions to that deadline. And as of
this year, there has been no move in
Congress to reopen it. More than 400,000
people filed before it shut. If you did
not, that particular door is closed. But
here is the part that made me want to
make this video. There is a second door.
It was never the same door. It has no
deadline. And it is wide open right now.
Most veterans have no idea there are
two. That is the pattern in every single
thing I am about to show you. Five
changes, all of them real, all of them
sitting there unused. And in almost
every case, the reason people miss them
is that they were told no once years ago
under a rule that has since changed.
None of these require combat service.
None of them require a lawyer. And two
of them apply even if you have never
filed a claim in your life. Let me start
with the one I just opened because I
want to be genuinely useful about it
rather than just alarming. Change number
one. The Camp Lleune lawsuit closed. The
Camp Lleune benefit did not. Between
1953 and 1987, the water supply at that
base in North Carolina was contaminated
with industrial solvents. Anyone who
lived or worked there for at least 30
days during that window was exposed.
That includes family members, spouses,
children who grew up on base. Two
entirely separate things came out of
that and people confused them constantly
and the confusion is costing veterans
real money. The first was a lawsuit
against the government. That was the
Camp Lleune Justice Act. It was a legal
claim. It produced settlements and it
had a hard two-year deadline that is
passed. The second is a disability
benefit through the Veterans
Administration. Completely different
system, different application, different
rules, no deadline at all. The agency
recognizes eight conditions as
presumptively connected to that water.
adult leukemia, alastic anemia, bladder
cancer, kidney cancer, liver cancer,
multiple myyoma, non-hodkkins lymphoma,
and Parkinson's disease. Presumptive
means you do not have to prove the water
caused it. If you were there for the
required time in the required window and
you have one of those conditions, the
connection is assumed. And there is a
second longer list of conditions that
qualifies a person for health care
through the agency even without a
disability rating. That list includes
breast cancer, lung cancer, esophageal
cancer, and several others. Family
members who lived on that base can
qualify for reimbursement of certain
health care costs, which almost no
family knows. So, if you or your spouse
or your parent was on that base and has
one of those conditions, the fact that
you missed a lawsuit deadline 2 years
ago is close to irrelevant. That was
never the benefit that keeps paying
every month. Now, let me tell you what
else changed, and this one is the
largest. My name is Kevin. I read the
rules so you do not have to. Every week
I go looking for the thing that quietly
decides what happens to your money and I
bring it here before it costs you
anything. If that sounds useful,
subscribe and turn on the bell because
the fourth thing on this list pays a
member of your own family every month.
And I have never once heard anybody talk
about it. Change number two. The burden
of proof moved and old denials did not
move with it. For decades, a veteran who
got sick after exposure to something
toxic had to prove the connection. You
had to demonstrate that your cancer or
your respiratory illness came from Agent
Orange or from a burn pit or from
wherever you served. That was
extraordinarily difficult and an
enormous number of those claims were
denied. The Pacted Act flipped that. If
you served in a recognized location
during a recognized period and you have
one of the listed conditions, the
connection is now presumed. You do not
prove it. The agency assumes it. That
covers Vietnam era locations, certain
periods of service along the Korean
demilitarized zone, and a long list of
other sites going back decades. And here
is the change inside the change that
matters most for people watching this.
Hypertension was added to the
presumptive list for Agent Orange
exposure, high blood pressure. That
single edition covers an enormous number
of Vietnam veterans who spent years
unable to connect a blood pressure
condition to their service because
before that you simply could not. Now,
here is the sentence I most want you to
hear in this entire video. Your old
denial did not update itself. If you
filed a claim in 2008 or 1999 or any
year before the rules changed and you
were denied because you could not prove
the connection, that denial was correct
under the standard that existed then.
The standard has changed. Your file did
not move with it. Nobody at that agency
went back through the archive, found
your name, and reopened it. That is not
how it works, and it never has been. So,
an enormous number of veterans are
walking around right now saying, "I
already tried that." When what they
actually mean is they tried it under a
rule that no longer exists. Let me tell
you about Clifton. Clifton is 78. He
lives outside Kingsport, Tennessee. He
was in country in Vietnam for 14 months
in 1969 and 1970. And he came home and
went to work at a chemical plant and
stayed there 31 years. He developed high
blood pressure in his 50s like a great
many men do. He filed a claim in the
early 2000s because somebody at a
veterans hall told him to. It was
denied. The reason was straightforward
and at the time correct. He could not
establish that his blood pressure was
caused by his service. He took that as
an answer. He was a little embarrassed
about it if I am honest, the way men of
that generation often are about asking
for something and being told no. And he
never filed again. 20 years later, the
rule that denied him no longer exists.
He does not know that. Nobody told him.
There is no letter that goes out to
everyone who was ever denied under an
old standard. And the men most likely to
have been denied are the least likely to
go back and check. And I want to say
something about that last part because
it is the whole reason a video like this
is worth making. The men of that
generation who came home from that
particular war did not come home to a
welcome. A lot of them learned very
early to stop bringing it up, to not ask
for anything, and to treat a no from the
government as confirmation of something
they already suspected about how they
were regarded. So when a man like
Clifton files once and gets a denial
letter, that letter does not land on him
as a technical determination about the
medical evidence in a file. It lands as
an answer about him. And a man who has
taken that answer once is very unlikely
to volunteer for it a second time. That
is not stubbornness, and it is not
pride. It is a completely reasonable
response to how a lot of these men were
actually treated. But the thing I need
him to understand is that the denial he
is carrying around was never about him.
It was about a rule. And that rule was
repealed by an act of Congress while he
was not paying attention because he had
no particular reason to be. Now I want
to stop here because Clifton is exactly
why I built the thing I am about to tell
you about. He does not need a lawyer. He
does not need to understand federal
regulation. He needs one person once to
tell him that a no from 2004 is not a no
today. That is what the quiet rules is.
It is plain English written large on the
things that quietly decide what your
money does, what changed, what to check,
and which no answers are worth going
back and testing again. So, a man at a
kitchen table with a folder can find out
in an afternoon instead of never. You
can find it at kevvenexplains.shop.
The link is in the description below and
in the pinned comment at the top. And if
you are watching this on a television
right now, there is a code on the screen
you can point your phone camera at.
7-day guarantee always. If it does not
hand you something you did not have
before, you send it back. Ask yourself
something. Is there a claim you filed
once, got a no, and never touched again?
There is a survivor's half of this, too,
and it is the part I find most
overlooked. If a veteran died from a
condition that is now on the presumptive
list but was not recognized as connected
to service at the time of death, a
surviving spouse may be able to file for
dependency and indemnity compensation.
Now that is a monthly payment and it can
apply even if a claim was filed and
denied years before the person passed
away. So, there are widows in this
country living on a reduced income whose
husbands died of something the
government now formally recognizes as
caused by their service who were told no
once and have never been told the rules
changed. And I want to slow down on that
group specifically because I think they
are the most overlooked people in this
entire subject. Consider what her
situation actually looks like. Her
husband served, came home, worked, got
sick somewhere in his 60s or 70s, and
died at the time. and whatever killed
him was not recognized as connected to
his service. Maybe he filed and was
denied. Maybe he never filed at all
because he did not believe there was any
connection either. So she buried him as
a man who happened to get sick, not as a
man who died from something he was
exposed to in uniform. And then years
later, a law passed that formally
recognized that exact connection as
service connected. That recognition
applies to him. It does not stop
applying because he is gone. But nobody
at any agency knows to look for her. She
is not in a queue. She is not on a list
of people to notify. There is no
mechanism anywhere in the federal
government whose job is to identify
widows whose husbands died of conditions
that were added to a list after the
funeral. The only way she finds out is
if somebody tells her. And a monthly
survivor payment is not a small thing to
a woman living alone on one income in
her 80s. It is the difference between a
household that is tight and a household
that is comfortable permanently for the
rest of her life. So if you are watching
this and you are a widow of somebody who
served or if you have a mother or an
aunt or a neighbor in that position,
that is the single highest value phone
call in this entire video. One honest
caution on all of this before we move
on. Presumptive does not mean automatic.
You still have to establish that you
were in the right place during the right
window, which means your discharge
paperwork, your deployment records, and
your duty station history are the
foundation of everything. Locate those
first, not after you file, first. And
here is something that will save some of
you real money. You do not need to pay
anybody to help you file. Every state
has accredited veterans service officers
who do this at no cost through
organizations like the Veterans of
Foreign Wars, the American Legion, and
your county or state Veterans Affairs
Office. They are trained, they are
accredited, and they are free. Anybody
charging you a large fee to file an
initial claim is selling you something
you can get for nothing. Change number
three, the money you were told you had
to choose between. This one is for
military retirees and it confuses people
who have been drawing benefits for
decades. If you retired after 20 years
of service, you receive retired pay. If
you also have a service connected
disability rating, you receive
disability compensation. For a long
time, federal law required an offset
between those two. Every dollar of
disability reduced your retired pay by a
dollar. You were not getting both. You
were getting one divided in half.
Concurrent retirement and disability
pay, which everybody calls CRDP, phased
that offset out for retirees with a
rating of 50% or higher. And here is
where people lose money without knowing
it. Ratings change. A man told 15 years
ago that he was at 30% and did not
qualify, maybe at 60% today after a
condition worsened or after a new
presumptive condition was added. The
threshold did not move. He did. There is
a second program alongside it called
combat related special compensation
which works differently. It applies when
the disability is tied to combat to
hazardous duty or to an instrument of
war and it can apply at ratings below
50%. It is also paid tax-free which the
other one is not. You cannot collect
both for the same disability you pick.
And an enormous number of retirees were
placed into one of them years ago and
have never once compared them since.
that is worth an actual phone call
because when your rating changes, the
answer to which one pays more can
quietly flip and nobody calls to tell
you. And I want to be concrete about how
much money is actually sitting in that
comparison because retirees hear the
acronyms and their eyes glaze over. The
difference between the two programs is
not a few dollars. One of them is
taxable income and the other is not. So,
two retirees with identical ratings and
identical service can end up with
meaningfully different amounts landing
in the account every month depending
purely on which program they happen to
be enrolled in and what their tax
situation looks like. And the enrollment
decision for most people was made once a
long time ago by whoever was handling
the paperwork at the time based on a
rating that has since changed. Nobody
reruns that comparison for you annually.
The office that pays your retirement is
not modeling your tax return. The agency
that rates your disability does not talk
to the office that pays your retirement
about which program suits you better
this year. The comparison exists.
Somebody has to ask for it. And the
somebody is you. So, here is the
specific thing to ask for, and I would
write this down. Call the finance office
that handles your retired pay and ask
them to run a sideby-side comparison of
what you would receive under each
program at your current rating. not what
you are receiving, what you would
receive under each. Those are two
different questions and only one of them
gets you a useful answer. And there is a
piece of this for surviving spouses that
I want to make sure lands because for
decades it was one of the ugliest
arrangements in federal benefits. A
widow receiving both a survivor benefit
plan annuity from the military and
dependency and indemnity compensation
from the agency used to have the first
one reduced dollar for dollar by the
second. People in military families
called it the widows tax. You paid
premiums for years into an annuity for
your spouse and then it got cut because
of a separate benefit she was
independently entitled to. That offset
has been eliminated. But listen to this
part carefully. Older cases were not
always corrected automatically. There
are widows still receiving a reduced
amount who were told long ago the
reduction was permanent and who have
never called to check. Let me tell you
about Leona. Leona is 83. She lives in a
coastal town in Florida. Her husband was
a chief petty officer for 26 years and
he has been gone since 2011. For years,
her annuity payment was reduced. She was
told why. She understood the reason and
she filed it away as one of the facts of
her life. She is not a complainer and
she did not consider it an injustice. It
was simply the rule. The rule ended. Her
payment did not change because her case
was old and the correction did not reach
her automatically. She found out two
years after the fact from a woman at
church whose husband had also served.
She made one phone call and her monthly
amount went up and stayed up. Nothing
about Leona changed. Not her situation,
not her paperwork, not her eligibility.
Only the rule changed. And the rule
changing did not reach into her mailbox
and tell her. That is exactly what the
guide exists to catch. Not to make you
an expert on federal benefits, to make
sure you are not the person still living
under a rule that was repealed while you
were not looking. Same place, kevin
explains.shop. Link in the description,
pinned comment at the top, and the code
on your screen if you are watching this
on the television. 7-day guarantee, no
questions, no argument. An 83-year-old
widow finding out at a church social
that she had been underpaid for 2 years.
Change number four, and this is the one
almost nobody covers, and I think it is
the most valuable thing in this video.
There is a program that pays a member of
your family a monthly stipend to take
care of you. Not a reimbursement, not a
service voucher, a monthly payment made
directly to your spouse or your adult
child or your sibling for the care they
are already providing. It is called the
program of comprehensive assistance for
family caregivers. And depending on the
level of care needed and where you live,
the stipen generally runs somewhere from
around $900 a month up into the low
thousands. It is tax-free and it comes
with health coverage for the caregiver,
respbit care, mental health counseling,
and training. Now, here is why almost
nobody in this audience knows about it.
When it was created, it was only
available to veterans who served on or
after the 11th of September, 2001. If
you served in Vietnam or Korea, you were
excluded, flatly, not eligible. That
changed. It opened first to one earlier
group and then a few years ago to
veterans of every era. Korea, Vietnam,
all of it. So, a caregiver who applied
and was turned down or who was simply
told this is for the younger ones was
told something that was true at the time
and has not been true for years. The
requirements are real and I am not going
to soften them. The veteran has to have
a serious service connected injury or
illness, has to need in-person care for
at least six continuous months, and has
to be enrolled in agency healthcare. It
is not a program for someone who needs
occasional help. And I will tell you
honestly that denial rates on it are
high. But if you have a spouse or a
child who has genuinely reorganized
their life around caring for you, they
may be entitled to be paid for it. And
the odds are extremely good that nobody
has ever told them the program exists.
And I want to speak directly to the
caregivers watching this for a moment
because there are more of you here than
anybody thinks. You are very likely a
wife in her 70s or a daughter in her 50s
who cut back her hours and you have been
doing this for years without ever once
considering that it might be a thing
somebody pays for because it never
occurred to you that it was work. It was
just what you do. The government does
consider it work. That is the entire
reason the program was built. Somebody

birthday is predictable. You know it is
