applies to everybody equally. A referral
is not predictable. It depends on who is
watching you, what they think they saw,
and whether they act on it. And the
person most likely to file one is
somebody who loves you and is
frightened, which is a very human thing
and also means it can happen in a year
when nothing is actually wrong. That is
not an argument against the new system.
It is an argument for knowing it exists
because the old system announced itself
and the new one does not. There is one
more thing I want to say about this and
it is for the people watching who are
quietly worried that this video is about
them. Losing a license is not the only
outcome and it is not even the most
common one. The far more common outcome
of a medical review is a restriction.
Daytime driving only, no highways, a
limited radius from home, corrective
lenses required. Those are not defeats.
Those are the system finding a version
of your independence that still works,
which is a very different thing from
taking it away. And most people never
learn that because they only ever hear
about the worst case. And there is
something else worth knowing because it
removes a specific fear that keeps
people from ever engaging with any of
this. Giving up driving does not mean
giving up your identification. Nearly
every state offers a reduced cost or
free identification card for older
adults, and several offer one
specifically to somebody who voluntarily
surrenders a license. Illinois issues a
free non-expiring photo card at 65.
California issues a free senior
identification card at 62. Washington
now offers one at no cost after a
voluntary surrender. I mentioned that
because I have seen people hold on to a
license they were genuinely no longer
able to use past the point of safety
because they believed the alternative
was having no identification at all and
becoming a person the world could not
verify. That is not the choice. It has
not been the choice for a long time. And
knowing that is the difference between a
decision made calmly and a decision made
under pressure after something has
already gone wrong. All right, here is
your checklist. Five things and none of
them take an afternoon. One, pull your
license out of your wallet right now and
look at the expiration date. Put it on a
calendar and on a phone because the
renewal cycle at your age is very likely
shorter than the one you remember. Two,
spend 10 minutes on your state's
licensing website and find three things.
the age vision testing starts, whether
you can still renew online at your age,
and how long your next license will be
good for. Three, ask your eye doctor
whether they can complete and submit
your state's vision form for license
renewal. That one question can eliminate
the trip entirely in several states.
Four, confirm the licensing agency has
your current mailing address. A notice
you never receive still has a deadline
on it. Five. Open every piece of mail
from that agency the day it arrives.
Everyone, every time. No exceptions. Let
me leave you with this. Audis had a
clean record going back to the 1990s,
and a letter arrived because his
daughter was frightened for him.
[clears throat]
Wanda drove her granddaughter to school
for 19 days on a license that had
already expired and found out afterward.
Neither of them did anything wrong.
Neither of them was a bad driver. One
had a form filled out about him and the
other had a website that would not load.
That is what this whole subject actually
is, not a test you fail. A piece of
paper you did not know was coming. So,
go look at the date on your card and
open the next envelope the day it
arrives. That is the whole thing. I am
Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevexplains.shop.

title: Millions of Seniors Could Lose 22% of Their Social Security Check Soon, Unless They Do This

segments.text: Go get a calendar. An actual one, not a
figure of speech. Because the thing I am
about to tell you only lands properly
once you count it yourself. And almost
nobody has ever counted it. This year,
the government published its own report
on the condition of Social Security. Not
a think tank, not a website, the
trustees of the program in writing
signed by the commissioner and three
cabinet secretaries. And that report
says the retirement trust fund runs out
of reserves in the fourth quarter of
Now, here is what everyone does with
that number, and here is why it never
changes anybody's behavior. They leave
it as a year. And a year sounds like a
thing that happens to somebody else
later in a news story you have here in
another room. So, let me convert it into
the only unit that actually means
anything to a person living on this
money. Checks. Count the months between
the check that lands this month and the
last quarter of 2032.
You will get somewhere in the
neighborhood of 75.
75 more checks at the full amount, then
unless Congress acts, the amount
changes, not to zero. I want to be
extremely clear about that. And I am
going to spend real time on it. But it
changes by about 22% for everybody,
current retirees included, not future
retirees, you. 75 is not a number you
file away for later. 75 is a number you
can count on your fingers if you have
enough of them and enough patience. It
is closer than a mortgage. It is closer
than most car loans. And the reason I am
starting here instead of with outrage is
that the outrage version of this story
has been playing for 30 years and it has
changed exactly nothing while the number
got closer every single year. So let me
do something different. I'm going to
tell you precisely what is true,
precisely what is not. What the actual
options are without telling you which
one to pick. how to make yourself heard
in a way that is not immediately
dismissed and then the part almost
nobody covers which is what you do with
your own money regardless of what any of
them decide because both of these things
are true at the same time. This can only
be fixed in Washington and you should
not build the rest of your life on the
assumption that Washington will fix it
on schedule. First, the most important
sentence in this entire video and if you
take nothing else, take this. Social
Security does not go bankrupt. It
cannot. The trust fund is not the
program. The trust fund is a savings
account sitting next to the program.
Money comes into Social Security every 2
weeks from every working person in this
country. And that never stops as long as
people are working. The trust fund is
the extra that got built up over
decades. And it is what covers the gap
between what comes in and what goes out.
Right now, that reserve is around $2.5
trillion. And it dropped by roughly 60
billion last year. It is being drawn
down on purpose because that is what it
was there for. When it is empty, the
program does not close. Payroll taxes
keep arriving. Those taxes cover about
78% of what is scheduled to be paid. 78%
is where the 22% comes from. That is the
entire arithmetic. It is not a
punishment and it is not a policy
decision. It is what happens
automatically when the money coming in
is less than the money going out and
there is nothing left in the savings
account to make up the difference. So
anybody who tells you the check stop is
wrong and anybody who tells you nothing
happens is also wrong. What happens is
that everybody's check gets smaller on
the same day. My name is Kevin. I read
the rules so you do not have to. Every
week I go looking for the thing that
quietly decides what happens to your
money and I bring it here before it
costs you anything. If that sounds
useful, subscribe and turn on the bell
because in a few minutes I'm going to
walk through the specific things people
are told about this that are simply not
accurate. And one of them is probably
something you believe right now. Let me
tell you what changed this year because
the date moved and it is worth knowing
why. Last year's report put the
retirement funds depletion one quarter
later than this year's does. So the
deadline came closer by 3 months in the
space of 12. Part of that is the long
slow thing that has been happening since
2009, which is that payroll taxes have
not covered annual costs for that entire
stretch. Fewer workers per retiree,
people living longer, which is a good
thing that costs money. Wages growing
more slowly than anybody projected. And
part of it is more recent and more
specific. The tax law passed last year
reduced the amount of tax that many
seniors owe on their benefits. Some of
that tax money flows back into the trust
funds. Less tax collected on benefits
means less revenue going back in. Now, I
want to be careful and fair here because
this is exactly the kind of thing that
gets turned into a political weapon by
both sides within about an hour. That
tax change genuinely helped a lot of
people in this audience. If you got the
senior deduction, that was real money
and I am not going to pretend otherwise.
It also mechanically reduced revenue
flowing to the trust funds. Both of
those statements are true. They are not
in conflict. That is simply what the
trade-off was. And the longerterm
picture got worse in a way that got less
attention. The size of the shortfall
over the next 75 years measured against
payroll grew by about 16% in a single
year's report. So the honest summary is
this. The date is close. It moved closer
and the size of the problem underneath
it grew. Let me tell you about Clyde.
Clyde is 69. He lives outside Marian,
Ohio, and he ran a two-truck excavating
outfit for most of his working life. He
sold the equipment when his back gave
out and he retired on social security, a
small amount from the sale and whatever
he had managed to put aside. He does a
thing that a lot of careful people do.
He has a sheet of paper handwritten that
projects his income out yearbyear, and
he uses it to decide what he can afford.
And every year on that sheet, the social
security number is the same, adjusted
upward a little for the cost of living
increase. That sheet has him fine,
comfortable even, right through his 80s.
He built it that way because that is
what he was told the number was. Nobody
handed him a report. Nobody at any point
in his life sat him down and said, "By
the way, the figure you are writing on
that line is scheduled through a certain
year and after that it is a different
figure unless something happens." His
plan is not wrong because he made a
mistake. His plan is wrong because he
was given one number and there were two.
And I want to be precise about what that
actually costs somebody like him because
it is not abstract. If a household is
running close to the line, a reduction
of roughly a fifth is not a matter of
eating out less. For a couple where both
people receive an average benefit, the
reduction would run somewhere in the
range of $10,000 a year off the
household. That is a figure from the
analysis of this year's report, not
something I estimated. $10,000 a year is
a car. It is a year of a supplement
premium and a good deal of the
medication that goes with it. For a lot
of households, it is the entire margin
between comfortable and careful or
between careful and something worse. And
here is the part about Clyde that I keep
coming back to. He is not a man who
avoids bad news. He ran a business. He
handled equipment loans and payroll and
the year the work dried up. If somebody
had put the real figure in front of him
10 years ago, he would have planned
differently and he would have had 10
years to do it in. Nobody did. And the
reason nobody did is not a conspiracy.
It is that this information lives inside
a 400page actuarial report. And the
version of it that reaches ordinary
people has been converted into an
argument before it arrives. Now, I want
to stop right here because Clyde is
exactly why I built the thing I'm about
to tell you about. He does not need
somebody to tell him to be angry at
Washington. He has that covered. What he
needed was for one person once to
explain what the number on that line
actually is so he could plan around the
real thing instead of around a headline.
That is what the quiet rules is. Plain
English written large on the things that
quietly decide what your money does and
what you can actually control about
them. So, a person can sit at a kitchen
table with a pencil and a sheet of paper
and be working from the truth. You can
find it at kevinexplains.shop.
The link is in the description below and
in the pinned comment at the top. And if
you are watching this on a television
right now, there is a code on the screen
you can point your phone camera at.
7-day guarantee always. If it does not
hand you something you did not have
before, you send it back. Go look at
whatever sheet of paper or spreadsheet
you plan from, if you have one. Does it
have one number on that line or does it
have two? Now, let me go through the
things people believe about this that
are not true because you will hear every
single one of these and you cannot have
a useful conversation with anybody until
they are cleared away. The first one,
the government stole the money and the
trust fund is full of worthless paper.
No. By law, every surplus dollar that
came into social security was required
to be invested in United States Treasury
securities. That is not a scheme. That
is a statute and it has worked that way
since the beginning. Those securities
pay interest and the trust funds earned
real interest last year in the tens of
billions. Now, is it fair to say that
the government borrowed the money and
spent it on other things? Yes, that is
exactly what happens when anybody buys a
Treasury bond. That is what a Treasury
bond is. It is also what your pension
fund did, what banks do, and what most
of the governments on Earth do with
their reserves. If those securities were
worthless, the problem would not be
social security. The problem would be
everything. And there is a version of
this belief that is more sophisticated
and that I want to address separately
because thoughtful people land on it.
Some people say, "Fine, the bonds are
real, but the interest on them has to be
paid out of general tax revenue. So, it
is all just the same pot in the end."
That is a legitimate observation about
federal accounting, and I am not going
to wave it away. But notice what it does
and does not mean. It does not mean the
money was taken. It means the federal
government borrowed from itself the way
it borrows from everybody else and owes
itself back with interest. Every dollar
has been accounted for annually in
public for decades. The reason this
matters is not academic. If you believe
the money was stolen, then the only fix
that makes sense to you is to get it
back. And there is nothing to get back.
If you understand the actual mechanism,
then you can evaluate the actual
options, which are the four I am going
to lay out in a few minutes. Being angry
at the wrong thing feels identical to
being angry at the right thing and it
accomplishes considerably less. The
second one, it is a Ponzi scheme and it
will collapse. A Ponzi scheme is a fraud
built on secrecy that dies the moment
new money stops coming in. Social
Security publishes its books every year.
The report I have been quoting is public
and anyone can read it. It promises
modest, defined benefits rather than
extraordinary returns. and it has not
missed a payment since payments began.
It is a pay as you go system which is
genuinely different from a scheme.
Whether pay as you go is good design is
a real argument that reasonable people
have. It is not the same argument as
calling it a fraud. The third one,
immigrants are draining it. People who
are not authorized to be in the country
cannot collect retirement benefits.
Proof of lawful status is part of the
application and it is verified and a
substantial amount of payroll tax gets
paid every year under numbers that will
never result in a benefit being claimed.
That is money going in that does not
come out. You can hold any view you like
about immigration policy generally. That
is your business and it is a legitimate
debate. But as an explanation for the
trust fund's condition, it does not hold
up and it is worth knowing that before
somebody uses it on you as a reason
nothing else needs to be done.
The fourth one, it is riddled with fraud
and cleaning that up would fix it. There
is fraud. There is fraud in every
program of this size. But the category
people are usually pointing at is
improper payments. And the large
majority of those are not fraud at all.
They are overpayments to people who kept
working and crossed the annual earnings
limit or who moved or whose paperwork
lagged behind their life. Those get
recovered. Improper payments run at a
very small fraction of what the program
pays out. Recovering every dollar of
them would not close a gap measured in
trillions. That does not mean they
should be ignored. It means they are not
the answer to this particular question.
And the fifth one, which is the one I
find most corrosive. Relax. Congress
always fixes it at the last minute.
Historically, that is not wrong. In the
early 1980s, this program came within
months of the same wall. and a
Republican president and a Democratic
speaker cut a deal that held for
decades. But look closely at what that
deal actually contained because this
matters enormously. They raised the full
retirement age from 65 to 67. They began
taxing benefits. Those changes were not
applied to the people who were already
retired and already voting. They were
applied to the people who were younger.
That is what a lastminute fix looks
like. It is not painless. It is a set of
cuts aimed at whoever is least able to
object at the moment the deal is struck.
So yes, they will probably do something.
The question is what and to whom. And
the later it happens, the fewer good
options are left on the table. And I
want to spend one more minute on that
because the timing point is the single
most important thing in this entire
video. And it is the thing nobody
explains properly. Every year that
passes, the same shortfall has to be
closed with fewer remaining years to
close it in. That means each option gets
more severe, not less. Think about it in
terms of a tax increase. whichever way
you feel about tax increases. If the
payroll rate had been raised by a very
small amount 30 years ago, phased in
slowly, almost nobody would have
noticed. Done today all at once, the
increase required to keep the program
solvent is a great deal larger because
it has to do the same work in less time.
The same is true on the benefit side. A
gradual adjustment starting decades ago
applied to people with 30 years to plan
around it is a completely different
thing from an adjustment applied to
somebody who is 74 next year. That is
what delay actually costs. Not the
debate, not the arguing. Every year of
waiting converts a manageable adjustment
into a painful one. And it does that
automatically whether anybody in
Washington ever votes on anything or
not. So when somebody tells you there is
plenty of time, they are describing the
calendar. They are not describing the
arithmetic. Let me tell you about
Maybel. Maybel is 74. She lives in a
small town in Georgia. She raised three
children, mostly alone, and she worked
in a school cafeteria and then at a
fabric store. And her benefit is not
large. She heard the 22% figure on
television. And she did what a lot of
people did, which is nothing, because
she assumed it meant the program was
ending and there was no point. Then a
few months later, she heard someone say
it was all made up and nothing was
happening at all. and she believed that
too and felt relieved. Both of those
things cannot be right and neither of
them is. And this is what I think the
actual damage is. It is not that people
panic. It is that they are handed two
versions. One hysterical and one
dismissive. They cannot tell which is
which. So they stop listening entirely.
And then no letter and no vote and no
plan ever happens. Her benefit is small
enough that a 22% reduction is not an
inconvenience. It is the heating bill.
That is exactly the gap the guide exists
to close, not to make you an expert. To
give one plain version of what is
actually true so you can act on it
instead of being pushed back and forth
between two people yelling. Same place
kevin Kevin explains.shop link in the
description, pinned comment at the top
and the code on your screen if you are
watching this on the television. 7-day
guarantee. No questions, no argument. a
woman in Georgia sitting in front of a
television told twice in one year that
opposite things were true and deciding
it was easier to stop paying attention.
Now, let me lay out the actual options
on the table and I want to be very clear
about how I am going to do this. I am
going to describe each one accurately,
including who it helps and who it costs.
I am not going to tell you which to
support. I have an audience that spans
every political position in this
country. And I think you are all
perfectly capable of deciding what you
believe once somebody puts the choices
in front of you. Honestly, there are
really only four levers. Everything
anybody proposes is some combination of
them. Lever one, bring in more money by
raising or removing the cap. Right now,
Social Security tax applies to earnings
up to about $184,500.
above that, no more social security tax
is owed on the additional earnings. So,
a person earning that amount and a
person earning several million pay the
same amount into the program. Removing
that cap entirely would close a very
substantial share of the long-term gap
on its own. Supporters say the cap is
why the program is short in the first
place, given how much income has moved
above that line over 40 years. Opponents
say it is a large tax increase on a
group that is already paying a great
deal. that it breaks the link between
what you pay in and what you get out and
that the money will simply be spent
elsewhere. Both of those are real
arguments made by serious people. Lever
two, raise the retirement age. This is
what was done in the 80s and it is on
the table again. Supporters say people
live considerably longer than they did
in 1935 and the program should reflect
that. Opponents make a point I think
everybody should understand regardless
of which side they land on. Raising the
retirement age is a benefit cut. It is
not a neutral adjustment. If you have to
wait longer for the full amount, you
either lose those years of payments or
you claim early and take a permanently
reduced check for the rest of your life.
And it falls hardest on people whose
work was physical who often cannot keep
doing it and do not live as long. Lever
three, means testing or changing the
benefit formula at the top. This means
reducing or eliminating benefits for
people with high income or high lifetime
earnings. Supporters say the program
should concentrate on people who need
it. Opponents say it turns an earned
benefit into a welfare program, that
everybody paid in under the same rules,
and that programs perceived as welfare
lose political support and get cut
further later. Lever four, change how
the increases are calculated. Every
year, benefits rise by a cost of living
adjustment. There is a version of that
calculation that would grow more slowly,
which saves money gradually and
enormously over decades. There is
another version built around what older
households actually spend money on,
which would generally grow faster and
cost more. Whichever direction you
favor, understand that this lever
compounds. A small annual difference
becomes an enormous difference across a
25-year retirement, which is precisely
why it is fought over so hard by people
who understand it. That is the whole
menu. Every serious proposal is some
mixture of those four and the arithmetic
is not actually the hard part. Somebody
has to be told no and no one wants to be
the one to say it. There is a fifth
thing that gets raised and I want to
mention it because you will hear it
which is investing part of the trust
fund or part of individual contributions
in the stock market rather than in
treasury securities.
Supporters point out that market returns
over long periods have exceeded what
Treasury securities pay and that the
current arrangement is leaving money on
the table. Opponents point out that
social security is the one piece of a
retirement that is supposed to be there
regardless of what markets do and that
anyone who retired into a bad stretch
would find out exactly why that
guarantee mattered. I am not going to
resolve that for you either. But I would
ask you to notice that it is a genuinely
different kind of proposal from the
other four. The other four adjust the
size of the promise. This one changes
what kind of promise it is.
Now the practical part, how to actually
be heard in a way that is not
immediately discarded.
The capital switchboard connects you to
the offices of the people who represent
you. You give your zip code and they
connect you. You have three people, one
representative and two senators. Each
call takes a few minutes. And here is
the part that actually matters because
most people do this in a way that gets
them politely thanked and forgotten.
Say you are a constituent and say where
you live. That is the single thing that
determines whether your call gets
counted. Offices tally contacts from
their own district. A passionate call
from outside it is noise to them. Be
specific about what you want. Not save
social security, which everybody says
and which commits nobody to anything.
Name a lever. Say you want the cap
raised or you do not. Say you oppose
raising the retirement age or you
support it. Whatever you actually
believe. Specific positions get tallied.
General sentiment does not. Ask a
question and wait for the answer. Ask
where that member stands on the trust
fund shortfall and what they intend to
vote for. Then be quiet and let them
answer. A question requires a response
in a way that a statement does not. Be
brief and be civil. The person on that
phone is usually young, underpaid, and
keeping a tally. They are not the
villain in this story, and being
unpleasant to them accomplishes nothing
except that your call gets categorized
differently. And write as well as call.
A letter or an email in your own words
gets weighted more heavily in most
offices than a signature on somebody
else's petition. Now, the part almost
nobody covers and the reason I made this
video rather than just pointing at
Washington. You cannot control the vote.
You can control everything else. And a
plan that only works if a specific
political outcome happens on schedule is
not a plan. So, here is what to actually
do. And none of it requires knowing what
Congress will do. First, find out your
actual number. Not the general figure,
yours. Your statement is available
through your online account with the
agency and it shows what you are
receiving or projected to receive. Then
do the arithmetic that nobody does. Take
that number and multiply by 78%. Write
the second number next to the first one.
That is not a prediction. I am not
telling you that is what you will get
and I genuinely do not believe that is
the most likely outcome. I think
something passes. But that second number
is the floor if nothing does. And
knowing your own floor is different from
knowing a percentage on the news.
Second, look at what that second number
does to your fixed costs. Not your
lifestyle, your fixed costs. The
mortgage or rent, the utilities, the
insurance, the medication. If the floor
still covers those, you have a
manageable problem. If it does not, you
have a real one, and you would rather
know that now with years to work with
than find out in a month when it
happens. Third, understand which of your
money is exposed to this and which is
not. Social Security is exposed. A
pension is a separate promise from a
separate entity. Money in your own
accounts is yours regardless of what any
vote says. That mix matters and most
people have never looked at it as a mix.
Fourth, and this is the one people skip,
if you are married, run the numbers for
the survivor. When one spouse dies, the
household does not keep both checks. It
keeps the larger one. A household living
on two checks becomes a household living
on one. And that shift is far larger
than 22%. And it is not a projection or
a policy debate. It is arithmetic that
applies to nearly every married couple
watching this eventually. If your plan
survives that, it will survive most
things. And there are two more things
worth knowing while you are looking at
all of this because they are decisions
you actually control and most people
make them without connecting them to any
of this. The first is when you claim, if
you have not yet. Claiming early
permanently reduces the monthly amount.
Waiting increases it. That trade-off
exists regardless of anything in this
video, and it is a real calculation
involving your health, your work, your
savings, and your spouse. What I will
say is that people sometimes hear about
a trust fund shortfall and conclude they
should grab benefits as early as
possible before something happens to
them. I understand the instinct
completely, but think it through. If a
reduction eventually applies across the
board, it would apply to a permanently
reduced check just as much as to a full
one. Claiming early to outrun a cut
mostly means locking in a smaller number
and then having the reduction applied to
that smaller number, too. That is not
advice about what you should do. It is a
warning about a specific piece of
reasoning that sounds sensible and is
not. The second is the part of your
income that is entirely yours. Anything
in your own accounts is not subject to a
vote in Washington. Nobody in Congress
adjusts it. That does not make it safe
from everything since markets do what
markets do. But it does mean it sits in
a different category of risk than the
check does. Understanding which of your
income is politically exposed and which
is not is genuinely useful and almost
nobody has ever sorted it that way. Now,
let me give you my honest opinion, and
it is only that, and you are welcome to
disagree in the comments. I do not think
either party is going to be honest with
you about this before an election. I
think the incentives run entirely the
wrong way. Every one of the four levers
I described takes something from
somebody who votes, and there is no
version of a fix that does not, which is
why the delay is not an accident and not
incompetence. Delay is the rational
strategy for anybody who wants to keep a
job because the cost of acting is
immediate and the cost of not acting
arrives after the next election and then
the one after that. And I want to say
one more thing that I think gets lost in
every version of this discussion. The
most likely outcome is not the 22% cut.
I want to be honest about that. Even
though a scarier version would probably
get more people to watch. This program
is politically enormous. Something
almost certainly passes. But something
passing does not mean nothing happens to
you. In 1983, something passed and what
passed raised the retirement age and
started taxing benefits. Everybody said
it was saved and it was for a while by
taking something from a group that was
not paying attention at the moment. So
the question worth asking is not whether
they act. It is which group is not
paying attention this time. All right,
here is your checklist. One, count your
own checks. Look at a calendar. Find the
last quarter of 2032 and count the
months. That number is real and it
belongs to you. Two, find your actual
benefit amount, multiply it by 78% and
write both numbers down side by side.
Check whether the smaller one covers
your fixed costs. Three, if you are
married, do the same exercise for the
surviving spouse living on one check
because that is a larger change than the
one this video is about. Four, call all
three of your people. Say you are a
constituent. Name where you live. Name a
specific position. Ask a direct
question. And be brief and decent about
it. Let me leave you with this. Clyde
has a handwritten sheet with one number
on a line where there should be two.
Maybel heard two opposite things in one
year, could not tell which was true, and
stopped listening. And her benefit is
small enough that this is her heating
bill. Neither of them was foolish. Both
of them were handed a political argument
when what they needed was arithmetic.
So do the arithmetic. It takes 10
minutes and a calculator and it belongs
to you no matter what anybody in
Washington decides. Then make the calls
because that part belongs to you too. 75
checks. That is the number. Go count it
yourself and see if I am right. I am
Kevin. Thanks for watching. Do not
forget to check the quiet rules at
kevvenexplains.shop.

title: Congress Already Passed the Social Security Tax Cut, Most Seniors Don't Know If They Actually Got It

segments.text: The tax cut is real. It passed. It is
law right now, and it is sitting on the
tax return you filed this spring,
whether you noticed it or not. That is
not a rumor. It is not a proposal, and
nobody in Washington is arguing about
whether it exists. But, here is what
almost nobody has told you plainly. It
is not the tax cut that was promised. It
is a different one. It has an age
requirement. It has an income ceiling.
It has one filing status that
disqualifies you completely, no matter
how old you are or how little you make.
And it has an expiration date already
written into the law, right now, today.
And depending on which side of some very
specific numbers you happen to fall on,
you either received $6,000 of it, or a
fraction of it, or absolutely none of it
at all. Most people watching this do not
know which of those three happened to
them.
>> [clears throat]
>> That is not a criticism. Nobody sent a
letter. There was no announcement. It
arrived quietly inside a return that a
preparer or a piece of software handled,
and the number at the bottom was
whatever it was. So, let me do the thing
nobody has done for you, which is walk
you through exactly which group you are
in, exactly what it was worth, and
exactly what you can still do about it.
Let me start with the difference between
what was promised and what passed,
because that gap is the source of nearly
all the confusion.
During the campaign, the promise was
simple, and it was repeated constantly.
No tax on Social Security.
Four words. Everybody understood them,
and everybody understood what they would
mean. That is not what became law. What
became law inside the One Big Beautiful
Bill Act is a new deduction for people
aged 65 and older. Up to $6,000 per
qualifying person, or up to 12,000 for a
married couple where both spouses are 65
or older. Social Security benefits are
still taxable. The old rule is
completely untouched. Up to 85% of your
benefit can still be included in your
taxable income, depending on your total
income, exactly the way it worked
before, using the exact same formula.
Now, I want to be fair here, because
there are two honest ways to look at
that, and you deserve both.
The people who wrote it will tell you
this version actually delivers more
money to lower and middle-income seniors
than a straight exemption would have,
and that it does less damage to the
trust funds.
Those are real arguments, and there is
genuine analysis behind them. The people
who objected will tell you that it is
not what was promised, that it leaves
out the poorest seniors entirely, for
reasons I will explain in a moment, and
that it expires in a few years. Both of
those are accurate. I am not going to
tell you which one to be angry about. I
am going to tell you what it does to
your return, which is the part that
actually affects your kitchen table.
My name is Kevin. I read the rules so
you do not have to. Every week I go
looking for the thing that quietly
decides what happens to your money, and
I bring it here before it costs you
anything. If that sounds useful,
subscribe and turn on the bell, because
there are three specific ways to be
disqualified from this deduction, and
two of them are things you could
accidentally do to yourself next year
without ever knowing it. So, let me
explain what this deduction actually is,
mechanically, because it stacks in a way
that surprises people. This is a brand
new deduction. It is not a replacement
for anything that already existed. It
sits on top.
Here is what that means in practice for
a single person aged 65 or older. You
take the regular standard deduction,
which everyone gets, then you add the
additional standard deduction for being
over 65, which has existed for years and
runs around $2,000, and then, on top of
both of those, you add this new one, up
to 6,000 more. Three separate
deductions, stacked, all in the same
year.
And here is a detail that matters and
that almost nobody mentions. This new
one is available whether you itemize or
not. The old additional senior deduction
only helps people taking the standard
deduction. This one does not care.
If you itemize because of large medical
expenses, which a great many people in
this audience do, you still get it. For
a married couple where both people are
65 or older, both qualify separately,
6,000 each. $12,000 of new deduction on
one return.
Now, what is that actually worth in
dollars? Because a deduction is not a
check, and I want to be honest about the
difference.
A deduction reduces the income you are
taxed on. It does not hand you money.
So, the value depends entirely on your
tax bracket.
For a household in the 12% bracket,
$6,000 of deduction is worth about $720
of actual tax.
For 12,000, roughly 1440.
That is real money.
On a fixed income, that is a property
tax bill, or several months of a
supplement premium.
But, it is not $6,000 in your pocket.
And anybody telling you otherwise is
either confused or selling something.
And let me put the whole stack together
on one person, so you can actually see
it. Because this is where it stops being
abstract. Take a single woman aged 67
who is not a surviving spouse. For the
current tax year, she gets the regular
standard deduction, which is somewhere
around $16,000.
She adds the additional deduction for
being over 65, which is a little over
2,000. And then she adds this new one,
6,000. That is roughly $24,000 of income
shielded from federal tax before she has
done a single clever thing, before she
has itemized anything, and before she
has hired anybody.
For a married couple where both are over
65, the equivalent stack runs
considerably higher than that. And that
is the honest reason a great many
seniors are going to end up owing
nothing at all this year.
Not because Social Security stopped
being taxable, because the pile of
deductions sitting in front of it got
tall enough to cover the whole thing.
There is also a mechanical detail worth
knowing if you file your own return.
This new deduction is claimed on a
schedule that did not exist before,
added specifically for it. If you use
software, it handles this without your
involvement. If you fill out paper forms
yourself, or if somebody in your family
does it for you, that is a form that has
to actually get attached, and a return
that omits it does not get corrected by
anybody. Nobody at the agency is going
to write to you and say, "We noticed you
qualified for a deduction you did not
claim." Let me tell you about Orville.
Orville is 71. He lives outside Bowling
Green, Kentucky, and he spent 36 years
as a lineman for a rural electric
cooperative. His wife is 68. Between the
two of them, they have Social Security,
his pension from the cooperative, and a
modest amount they pull from a
retirement account each year. Their
combined income lands comfortably under
the threshold, which means both of them
qualified for the full amount.
$12,000 of new deduction on top of
everything they were already getting.
And here is the part I find genuinely
striking. Orval did not know it
happened. His return was prepared by the
same woman who has done it for 19 years.
She applied it correctly because she is
competent, and it is in her software.
The refund was larger than the year
before. He assumed that was because of
something to do with his withholding,
mentioned it to nobody, and got on with
his spring.
He found out what it was in June from a
man at the co-op retirees breakfast.
Now, I want to stop here because Orval
is the reason I built the thing I'm
about to tell you about. Nothing went
wrong for him. That is exactly the
point. He got every dollar he was
entitled to, and he still could not have
told you what he received, why he
received it, whether he would receive it
again, or what would take it away. And
you cannot protect something you cannot
name. That is what the Quiet Rules is.
It is plain English, written large on
the things that quietly decide what your
money does, what you are entitled to,
what disqualifies you, and what question
to ask the person who prepares your
return before you sign it. So, you are
not learning about your own tax return
at a breakfast in June.
You can find it at kevinexplains.shop.
The link is in the description below and
in the pinned comment at the top. And if
you are watching this on a television
right now, there is a code on the screen
you can point your phone camera at.
7-day guarantee, always. If it does not
hand you something you did not have
before, you send it back. Ask yourself
one question before we go on. Do you
actually know whether this appeared on
your last return, or are you assuming
somebody handled it?
Now, let me get to the income ceiling,
because this is where a great many
people in this audience are going to
find out they got less than they
thought.
The full deduction is available up to
of modified adjusted gross income for a
single filer and $150,000 for a married
couple filing jointly.
Above that, it does not stop. It
shrinks. For every dollar of income
above that line, the deduction is
reduced by 6 cents. That is the
mechanic. 6 cents on the dollar,
steadily, until it is gone entirely.
So, a single filer at $82,000
is 7,000 over the line. 7,000 * 6 cents
That person's deduction is not 6,000. It
And it keeps going. A single filer
reaches zero at 175,000.
A married couple filing jointly, where
only one spouse is 65 or older, reaches
zero at 250,000.
Now, here is why this matters far more
than it sounds like it should. It is not
a cliff. That is genuinely good news,
and I want to say so because a cliff is
what Medicare surcharges do to people,
and it is brutal.
$1 over a Medicare threshold and the
whole surcharge lands. This is not that.
This one slides. But a slope has its own
problem, and the problem is that it is
invisible. With a cliff, you can at
least see the edge. With a slope, every
additional dollar of income you take in
a year quietly shaves 6 cents off a
deduction you may not even know you
have. There is no letter. There is no
notice. There is no line on anything
that says, "This withdrawal cost you $60
of deduction." And I need to tell you
about the part that makes this genuinely
worse than it first appears, because a
single dollar of extra income in
retirement almost never does only one
thing. Think about what one large
withdrawal actually sets in motion for
somebody over 65. It is taxable income,
which is the obvious part, and it is the
only part most people are told about. It
also raises the figure that decides how
much of your Social Security benefit is
taxable. So, the withdrawal does not
just get taxed. It reaches sideways and
drags a portion of your benefit into
taxation along with it. It now also
shaves this new deduction, 6 cents on
every dollar, if you are above the
threshold. And 2 years later, that same
income figure is what the Medicare
system looks at to decide your monthly
premium. So, one decision made in one
afternoon touches four separate things
across three different years. And
exactly one of those four is visible to
the person making the decision at the
moment they make it. That is not a
conspiracy. Nobody designed it to ambush
anyone. It is what happens when four
different systems each use a version of
the same income number, and nobody is
responsible for showing you the combined
picture. And I want to name who is not
going to show it to you, because the
list is longer than people expect. Your
retirement account custodian will not.
Their job is to send money when you ask
for it. The person on that phone is
processing a request, not modeling your
tax year.
Your bank will not. Your insurance agent
will not. Your tax preparer very likely
would have if you had asked in October,
but you saw them in April after the year
had already closed and every decision in
it had already hardened into a fact.
That is the whole structural problem
with retirement tax planning in one
sentence. The people qualified to help
you are looking backward at a year you
can no longer change and the moment you
actually needed them was a Tuesday in
the fall when nothing seemed important
enough to call about. Let me tell you
about Winifred. Winifred is 69. She
lives in a suburb of Columbus and she
was a school administrator. So she has a
pension that is better than most along
with social security and a retirement
account. Her ordinary income sits a
little above the line already which she
knew and she had made peace with.
What she did not know was that the roof
mattered. She needed a roof. It was not
optional and it was not a luxury and the
estimate was a number that required her
to take money out of her retirement
account. So she took it in one
withdrawal in October the way anybody
would. That withdrawal raised her income
for the year by a meaningful amount and
every dollar of it on top of income that
was already past the threshold shaved 6
cents off her senior deduction.
By the time the return was filed, a
deduction that would have been $6,000
was a fraction of that.
Now I want to be careful here because I
do not want anybody hearing this and
refusing to fix their roof. She needed
the roof. Taking the money was correct.
Here is what was avoidable.
She took the entire amount in a single
tax year in October with no idea that
the timing of it touched anything other
than the income tax on the withdrawal
itself.
Splitting it across two calendar years,
part in December and part in January was
available to her.
It was the same money, the same roof,
the same contractor.
It would have kept more of her deduction
in both years and it would have cost her
nothing but a conversation. Nobody had
that conversation with her because the
roofer's job is the roof and the
custodian's job is to send the money and
the tax preparer sees all of this in
April, 5 months after every decision has
already been made.
And I want to say something about
Winifred that goes past the arithmetic
because it is the part that stayed with
me when I looked at this.
She is not a person who was careless
with money.
She ran a school building. She managed
budgets. She read contracts. She was the
person other people came to when a form
was confusing.
If you had told her there was a rule she
should know about, she would have gone
and learned it that evening.
The problem was never her capacity.
The problem was that nothing in her life
ever told her the rule existed. And that
is true of nearly everybody in this
audience.
This is not a knowledge gap that gets
closed by being smarter or more careful.
It gets closed by somebody once saying
the sentence out loud. Here is the
sentence for the roof and for everything
like it.
Before you take a large amount of money
out of a retirement account, ask whether
it can be split across two calendar
years and ask what taking it does to
your income for that year beyond the tax
on the withdrawal itself.
Two questions asked before, not after.
That is the entire difference between
Winifred's return and the one she could
have had.
And there is a version of this for
almost every large decision in
retirement. Selling a piece of property,
cashing in something that has grown,
taking a lump sum instead of payments.
In every one of those, the amount is
usually fixed and the timing usually is
not and the timing is the part nobody
discusses.
That is exactly the gap the guide exists
to close. Not to make you a tax expert,
to make sure you know which decisions
have a second price tag attached before
you make them instead of after. Same
place, kevinexplains.shop,
link in the description, pinned comment
at the top and the code on your screen
if you are watching this on the
television. 7-day guarantee, no
questions, no argument. A woman signing
a roofing contract in October with no
idea that the month she signed it was
worth money.
Now, let me give you the three ways to
be disqualified entirely because these
are absolute, not reduced, zero.
The first one is age and it is stricter
than people assume. You must be 65 or
older by the last day of the tax year,
December 31st.
Not 65 sometime during the following
spring, not 65 by the time you file,
which means if your birthday falls on
January 1st, you missed the previous
year by one day.
That is not a technicality somebody
invented for a video. That is how the
rule reads.
The second disqualifier is the one that
catches people completely off guard and
I want you to pay close attention if it
applies to you.
You cannot claim this deduction if your
filing status is married filing
separately.
Not reduced, not partial, zero for both
spouses regardless of age and regardless
of income. Now, most married couples
file jointly and this will never touch
them, but some file separately and they
usually have a reason. Sometimes it is a
large medical expense that works out
better separately. Sometimes it is a
business liability. Sometimes it is a
marriage where the finances have been
kept apart for decades, which is more
common in this age group than people
think.
And sometimes a preparer simply ran both
ways and separate came out ahead on the
software's own math.
If that software was not accounting for
the loss of $12,000 of senior deduction,
then separate may have come out ahead by
a few hundred dollars and cost more than
a thousand. So, if you file separately,
that is a specific question to ask out
loud before the next return is signed.
Run it both ways and make sure this
deduction is in the comparison. The
third disqualifier is a documentation
one. Every person claiming it must have
a valid work authorized social security
number on the return. A taxpayer
identification number does not qualify.
For most of you, this is automatic and
you will never think about it, but on a
joint return, both people need one.
And I want to add one more scenario that
does not fit neatly into any of those
three, but catches people every year,
which is the year somebody turns 65.
That first year feels like it should be
simple and it very often is not.
If your birthday is in November, you are
65 by December 31st and you qualify for
that entire tax year, including the 11
months when you were 64.
That surprises people and it surprises
them in a good way and a fair number of
them never claim it because they assume
it starts the following year. If your
birthday is in early January, the
opposite is true. You were 64 on the
last day of the year and you get nothing
for that year at all, no matter that you
turn 65 3 weeks later.
Two people born 5 weeks apart, one gets
$6,000 of deduction and one gets zero
for the same calendar year. That is not
unfair exactly. Every line has to be
drawn somewhere, but it is worth knowing
which side of it you were on, especially
if you turn 65 recently and had somebody
else prepare the return. And if you find
out you should have claimed it and did
not, that is fixable.
There is a process for amending a return
and there is a window on it measured in
years, not weeks.
This is one of the more straightforward
things to correct because there is no
judgment call in it. Either you were 65
on the last day of the year or you were
not. Now, here is the fourth group and
this is the group nobody in Washington
talks about and I think it deserves to
be said clearly.
This is a deduction. It is not a
refundable credit.
A deduction reduces the income you pay
tax on. If you already pay no federal
income tax, reducing your taxable income
further does nothing at all. There is no
check. There is no payment. 0 - 6,000 is
still zero. And a very large number of
Americans over 65 already owe no federal
income tax because their income is
modest enough that the standard
deduction already covered it. Which
means the seniors with the least money
got nothing from this, mathematically,
by design. Let me tell you about Buford.
Buford is 77. He lives in a small town
in Alabama and he worked in and around a
paper mill for most of his life.
His income is his social security and a
very small amount from a savings
account. He does not owe federal income
tax. He has not for years. He heard
about the tax cut. Everybody heard about
the tax cut. He assumed something was
coming the way people assume and he
mentioned it to his daughter over the
summer and she looked into it and she
had to explain to her father that a
deduction only helps somebody who owes
tax to deduct it from.
And I want to be very clear about
something because this is where a lot of
channels would tell you he was cheated.
He was not cheated. Nobody took anything
from Buford. The law worked exactly the
way it is written but he spent a year
believing a benefit was coming to him
that was never structured to reach him
and nobody ever corrected that. And that
is a genuine cost even though it is not
a dollar cost. And there is something I
want to say about Buford's situation
that I think gets lost every time this
gets discussed. The reason a deduction
cannot reach him is not an oversight. It
is arithmetic.
A deduction works by removing income
from the pile that gets taxed and if the
pile was already small enough to owe
nothing, there is nothing left to
remove.
The tool that would have reached him is
a different tool entirely. A refundable
credit pays out whether you owe tax or
not.
That is how some other benefits in this
country are built and it is a deliberate
choice each time. This one was not built
that way.
Whether it should have been is a policy
argument I will leave to you and there
are people on both sides of it who are
arguing in good faith. But here is the
practical version for anyone in Buford's
position watching this because I do not
want to leave you with nothing. If you
owe no federal income tax, this
particular provision does not help you,
and no amount of paperwork will change
that.
What can help you are the programs built
specifically for lower-income
households, which are a completely
separate system with completely separate
rules. Property tax relief at the county
level,
help with Medicare premiums and
prescription costs, utility assistance,
food benefits with medical expense
deductions for people over 60.
Every one of those is real. Every one of
those has an income test rather than a
tax bill test, and every one of those is
an application nobody sends you. That is
the entire reason I mention it here. The
people this deduction could not reach
are frequently the people with the most
unclaimed help sitting in front of them
somewhere else. Now, let me answer the
question underneath this entire video,
because it is the one I get most.
Is Social Security still taxed? Yes. The
rule did not change. Here is how it
actually works, and it is worth
understanding because it has not moved
in a very long time.
You take your adjusted gross income, you
add any tax-exempt interest, and you add
half of your Social Security benefit.
That total is your provisional income.
Depending on where it lands, up to 50%
or up to 85% of your benefit becomes
taxable.
Every part of that formula is exactly
what it was before this law passed.
What changed is that a larger deduction
sitting on top means more people end up
owing nothing after the math is done.
Their benefits are still technically
taxable. Their tax bill is just zero,
and that distinction is the entire
reason for the confusion.
When the government says a large
majority of seniors will owe no tax on
their benefits, that is a statement
about the bottom line, not about the
rule.
The rule stands. It was simply out of
reach for more people this year, and I
want you to understand why that
difference is not just semantics,
because it matters for what happens
next.
If the rule itself had been repealed,
your benefits would be permanently
outside the tax system, and nothing
about your other income could drag them
back in.
That is what the four words described.
What actually exists is different. Your
benefits are still inside the system,
still subject to the same formula, and
still perfectly capable of becoming
taxable again the moment your income
rises or the deduction shrinks or the
law expires.
So, the protection you have is not a
wall. It is a cushion.
And a cushion has a thickness, and yours
depends on your income this year and on
whether the deduction still exists in
the year you are asking about. That is
why I keep saying the phrase and the
thing are not the same. Not to score a
point because one of them would have
been permanent and the one you actually
got is temporary and conditional, and
you should plan around the one you
actually got.
And that leads directly to the thing I
most want you to write down. This
deduction expires. It is written into
the law. Tax years 2025 through 2028, 4
years. After that, it is gone unless
Congress extends it, and Congress
extending something is a thing that may
happen and may not. And I want to be
straight with you about that because
there is a genuine temptation for
somebody in my position to tell you it
is definitely going away so you feel
urgency about it. I do not know. Nobody
does. Temporary tax provisions in this
country get extended all the time,
sometimes repeatedly, sometimes at the
last minute. This one might.
There is also a real budget cost
attached to extending it, and that
argument will be had.
What I can tell you is what the law says
today, and what it says today is 4
years. So, there is a window. And a
window changes what you should be
thinking about. If you have been
considering moving money from a
traditional retirement account into a
Roth, these are the years where that
cost the least because you have an extra
six or twelve thousand dollars of
deduction absorbing income that would
otherwise be fully taxed.
That window closes after 2028.
If you are choosing when to take a large
distribution, whether to sell something,
or when to realize any income you have
discretion over, these four years are
structurally different from the years
that follow. And I want to be honest and
say plainly that this is exactly the
kind of decision where a licensed
professional earns their fee. Because
the interaction between this deduction,
your Social Security taxation, and your
Medicare premiums 2 years later is
genuinely complicated. And it depends on
numbers I do not have.
Now, let me give you my honest opinion,
and it is only an opinion.
I do not think the design of this is the
scandal.
Reasonable people can argue about
whether a targeted deduction is better
policy than a blanket exemption, and
there are serious arguments on both
sides, and I am not the person to settle
that.
What I object to is the distance between
the phrase and the thing. Four words
were repeated for a year. No tax on
Social Security.
Millions of people over 65 heard those
four words, and reasonably concluded
that their benefits would stop being
taxed. What passed is a temporary
deduction with an age test, an income
slope, a filing status trap, and an
expiration date. It helps a lot of
middle-income seniors meaningfully,
helps higher-income seniors partially,
and does nothing whatsoever for the
poorest ones.
That is not the same thing. And the gap
between the two is not a technicality.
It is the difference between a person
planning correctly and a person planning
around something that was never there.
And nobody is required to close that gap
for you. Not the agency, not your
preparer, and certainly not the people
who said the four words. All right, here
is your checklist. Four things, and none
of them take long. One, pull out your
most recent tax return and find out
whether this deduction actually appeared
on it. If you use a preparer, call and
ask them directly whether the new senior
deduction was applied and for how much.
Do not assume. Ask. Two,
find out roughly where your income sits
relative to 75,000 single or 150,000
married filing jointly. If you are near
or above it, every dollar of
discretionary income you take costs you
6 cents of deduction, and that is worth

Three, if you file married filing

the right call now that this deduction

you will see it. That is when this
expires as the law currently stands, and
if you have any flexibility about when
you take income, these four years are
not like the ones that follow.
Let me leave you with this.
Orville got every dollar he was entitled
to and could not have told you what it

Winnifred signed a roofing contract in

segments.text: Your car has a title sitting in a state
database with your name on it. Your bank
account has a signature card. Your
retirement account has a beneficiary
form that somebody made you fill out on
the day you opened it, whether you
wanted to or not. Your house has one
piece of paper recorded once, possibly
before your children were born. And from
that day forward, the county has never
asked you for another thing. That is not
an oversight. That is exactly how the
system is built. And there are four
forms sitting at that county office
right now that could decide what your
house cost your family. And nobody there
will ever mention a single one of them
to you. I want to explain why. Because
once you understand it, everything else
in this video makes sense. The county
recorder's office is a filing cabinet.
That is the whole job. It records what
people hand it. It stamps the date and
it files it. What it does not do and
what it has never done and what it is
not funded or staffed or expected to do
is tell you what you ought to be handing
it. Nobody there is going to call you
and say you have owned this house for 31
years and you have never filed the one
form that keeps it out of court. So
every single thing in this video is a
piece of paper that you have to walk in
and hand somebody. Not one of them is
automatic. Not one of them is triggered
by anything. And every one of them costs
less than a tank of gas. and any one of
them can be worth more than a year of
your income. Now, let me be honest about
the number in the title because I do not
like it when other people are vague
about theirs. $50,000 is not a promise
and it is not a threat. It is what it
looks like when a household misses
several of these at once. Probate on a
house, the equity that was not protected
when a judgment landed, years of a tax
exemption nobody applied for, and a
title problem that took a lawyer to
untangle. Most of you will not have all
four. If you have one, this video pays
for the time you spend on it many times
over. My name is Kevin. I read the rules
so you do not have to. Every week, I go
looking for the thing that quietly
decides what happens to your money, and
I bring it here before it cost you
anything. If that sounds useful,
subscribe and turn on the bell because
the first of these four is a form that
most people have never heard the name
of, and it does something that a will
cannot do. Form number one, the transfer
on death deed. Now, most of you have a
will. That is good. And most of you
believe that because you have a will,
your house goes to your children the way
you wrote it down. That part is true.
And it is also the source of the
misunderstanding. Your will does not
move your house. Your will tells a court
what you wanted and then the court moves
your house. That process is called
probate. And probate on real estate is
not fast and it is not free. The court
has to open a case. Someone has to be
appointed. Notice has to be given.
Creditors get a window. In many places,
there are attorney fees and court costs
and a timeline measured in months,
sometimes considerably longer, before
your children have the legal authority
to sell or rent or in some cases even to
make a decision about the roof.
Meanwhile, the property taxes are still
due, the insurance is still due, the
lawn still grows. And I want to be
specific about that because probate is
one of those words people have heard
their whole lives without anybody ever
describing what it actually feels like
from the inside. It is not a trial.
Nobody is accusing anybody of anything.
In the overwhelming majority of cases,
there is no argument at all and everyone
involved agrees on exactly what should
happen. That is what makes it so strange
to live through. What it is is a cue.
Your family joins a line at a courthouse
and waits for a system that was built to
handle disputes to process a situation
where there is no dispute. The paperwork
has to be filed. A judge has to sign. A
window has to open for creditors who
almost never appear. And every step of
that has a clerk, a calendar, and a fee
attached to it. And the house sits there
the whole time generating expenses and
generating nothing. The insurance
company, by the way, deserves a mention
here because this catches families
constantly. A homeowner's policy on a
house where nobody lives is not the same
product it was the week before. Many
policies restrict coverage on a vacant
property and a house can sit through an
entire winter in a court queue with a
furnace nobody is checking. So the cost
of probate is not only the fees, it is
the fees plus the carrying costs plus
the months plus the risk of an empty
house in weather. And the person paying
all of that is usually a son or daughter
in their 50s who has a job and a family
and now has a second unpaid job managing
a property they do not yet legally
control. Now, here's the form almost
nobody has heard of. A transfer on death
deed lets you name a beneficiary on your
house the same way you name a
beneficiary on a life insurance policy.
You record it while you are alive. When
you die, the property passes directly to
the person you named without probate,
without a court, and in most states
without an attorney. It is also called a
beneficiary deed in some states and in a
few places an enhanced life estate deed,
which people call a ladybird deed.
Different names, same essential idea.
And I want to be clear about what it
does not do because this is where people
get nervous. You keep everything.
Complete control. You can sell the house
tomorrow. You can refinance it. You can
rent it out. You can change your mind
and name somebody else or cancel the
whole thing entirely. And you do not
have to tell the beneficiary you did it.
The person you name has no rights, no
access, and no say in anything until the
day you are gone. The cost to record one
runs from about $15 to a couple hundred
depending on the county. Compare that to
what a living trust costs, which is
commonly a,000 to $3,000 or more, and a
trust is genuinely the better tool for a
complicated situation. But for a person
who owns one house and wants it to go to
one or two people, this is the shortest
distance between those two points that
exists in American law. Let me tell you
about Delmare. Delmare was 76. He lived
in a town in southern Missouri and he
had owned the same house since 1984.
He had a will. He had written it himself
years ago and had it witnessed and it
said in plain language that the house
went to his daughter. He died in
February. The will was completely valid.
Nobody contested it. His daughter was
named clearly and there was no dispute
of any kind from anyone at any point.
And it still took 9 months. 9 months of
a court file. nine months of paying the
property taxes and the insurance on a
house nobody lived in out of her own
pocket because the estate account was
not accessible in the way she needed it
to be. 9 months of a lawyer's clock
running in a state where that is simply
how it works. When it was over, she
owned the house exactly as her father
intended. She had also spent a number in
the low five figures getting to a result
that was never in doubt for one single
day. And here is the part that made me
sit down and look this up properly. Her
father's county recorder had a transfer
on death deed form available. It was on
their website. It would have cost him
about $40. 9 months and thousands of
dollars against $40 in an afternoon for
the identical outcome. Now, I want to
stop here because Delmare is the exact
reason I put this thing together. He was
not disorganized. He wrote a will that
is more than most people do. He did the
thing everyone tells you to do and it
worked. And it still cost his daughter
almost a year and a great deal of money
because the one form that would have
made the difference is not something
anybody ever mentions. That is what the
quiet rules is. It is the paperwork
nobody hands you written large and
written plain in the order you need it.
what to file, where it goes, what it
costs, and what question to ask when you
get to the counter so that a person can
sit at a kitchen table on a Saturday and
actually finish something. You can find
it at kevinexplains.shop.
The link is in the description below and
in the pinned comment at the top. And if
you are watching this on a television
right now, there is a code on the screen
you can point your phone camera at.
7-day guarantee always. If it does not
hand you something you did not have
before, you send it back. $40 against
nine months. That is the entire
argument. Now, let me give you the sharp
edges on this form because it has some,
and I am not going to pretend otherwise.
First, and most important, it is not
available everywhere. Roughly 30 states,
plus the District of Columbia recognize
some version of it. Some do not. Florida
does not use a standard transfer on
death, but does have the enhanced life
estate deed I mentioned. Pennsylvania
does not permit them at all. So, the
very first thing you do is find out
whether your state is one of them. And
the county recorder's office can tell
you that in one phone call. Second, it
beats your will. If your will says the
house goes to three children and your
recorded deed names one, the deed wins.
The most recently recorded document
controls, which means if you file one of
these, your will and your deed have to
agree with each other, and somebody
needs to actually look at both of them
side by side. Third, and this is the one
I most want you to hear because there is
a great deal of bad information about
it. This form does not protect the house
from Medicaid estate recovery in most
states. It does not erase leans. It does
not wipe out debts attached to the
property. Your beneficiary inherits the
house along with whatever is already
sitting on it. A handful of states treat
this differently, and Texas under
current law does exclude it from a state
recovery, but do not assume yours is one
of them. So, this is not a shield. It is
a shortcut. It moves the house quickly
and cheaply to the person you chose. It
does not make anything about the house
disappear. And fourth, a practical one,
name a backup. If the person you name
dies before you do and there is no
alternate named, the whole thing can
fail and the house lands right back in
the court process you were trying to
avoid. Form number two, and this one is
not about what happens after you die.
This one is about what happens if
somebody sues you while you are alive.
The homestead declaration. Almost
everybody has heard the word homestead
in the context of property taxes. That
is a different thing and I am going to
get to it. And the fact that two
completely separate protections share
the same word is responsible for an
enormous amount of confusion. This one
is about creditors. Nearly every state
has a law that protects some amount of
the equity in your primary home from
being taken to satisfy a judgment. If
somebody wins a lawsuit against you, if
a medical debt goes to collection and
then to court, if a business obligation
follows you into retirement, the
homestead protection is the wall that
stands between that judgment and the
roof over your head. The amount varies
wildly. A few states protect 100% of the
equity in your home without limit,
including Florida, Texas, Kansas,
Oklahoma, South Dakota, and Iowa. Others
protect a modest figure. Illinois
protects $15,000.
New Jersey has no state homestead
exemption at all. The federal figure for
people who use it sits around $31,000.
Now, here is the part that costs people
everything. In some states, that
protection is automatic. You live in the
house. It is your primary residence. You
are covered. Texas and Florida work that
way, and most people in those states
never think about it. But in other
states, the protection does not exist
until you record a declaration. Read
that again. In those states, a homeowner
who never filed the form has no
protection. Not reduced protection,
none. The wall is not there until you
build it. And you build it by walking
into the county recorder and filing a
piece of paper. And nobody tells you
which kind of state you live in.
I want to slow down on that because it
is genuinely one of the strangest things
in American property law and almost
nobody knows it exists. Two people can
own identical houses with identical
equity in identical circumstances in two
different states. One of them is
protected automatically and has never
thought about it once in their life. The
other one has exactly nothing and has
also never thought about it once in
their life. And neither of them has any
idea which one they are. There is no
letter. Your title company does not tell
you at closing. Your mortgage lender has
no reason to raise it. Your homeowner's
insurance agent is selling you something
else entirely. And a great many
attorneys who handle a routine house
purchase do not bring it up either
because the closing is a transaction and
this is not part of it. So the
protection either exists or it does not.
And which one you have was decided by a
state legislature you have never thought
about and the only way to find out is to
ask. And there is a second layer to this
that trips up people who do know about
it. The amount of equity protected is
set by state law. And in a great many
states, that number has not been
meaningfully updated in a very long
time. Illinois protects $15,000.
That number might have covered a house
once. It does not cover a house now.
Which means in some states, the honest
answer is that the protection exists and
is mostly symbolic. And you should know
that, too, because it changes what else
you might want to do. This is exactly
the situation where a conversation with
an actual attorney is worth the hour it
costs. And I would rather tell you that
plainly than pretend a form solves
everything. And I want to name the
confusion directly one more time because
I get more mail about this than almost
anything. The Homestead Declaration
protects your equity from creditors. The
Homestead Tax Exemption reduces your
property tax bill. They share a word and
they are administered by two different
offices. The declaration goes to the
recorder. The tax exemption goes to the
assessor. Having one does not give you
the other, and in most places, filing
for one does not put you on any list for
the other. People routinely tell me they
already have homestead, meaning they got
the tax break, and they have no creditor
protection at all. Let me tell you about
Fern. Fern is 68. She lives in a state
that requires the declaration, which she
did not know, and which nobody in her
life knew either. Her situation was not
dramatic. Her husband had run a small
contracting business for years and it
closed the way small businesses close
slowly and with some loose ends. One of
those loose ends turned into a claim and
the claim turned into a judgment several
years after the business itself had
stopped existing. The house was paid
off. That was the whole point of her
life in a sense. 30 years of payments
and it was theirs and there was equity
in it. And equity in a house in a state
that requires a declaration from a
homeowner who never filed one is
exposed. It did not go the worst
possible way. It rarely does. There was
a negotiation and a settlement and a
lean and she is still in the house. But
she paid a number she did not have to
pay out of equity she thought was
untouchable because a piece of paper
that costs almost nothing to file was
never filed. Here is what makes it worse
and what I want you to sit with. If she
had filed that declaration years earlier
before any of this began, the protection
would have been standing there waiting.
Filing it after a judgment already
exists does very little. The timing is
the entire value of it. This is a form
whose worth is measured by how long
before the trouble it was filed. And I
want to say something about firm that
goes past the paperwork because it is
the part that stayed with me. She did
not think of herself as somebody who
could be sued. That is the thing. She
had never been sued in her life. She had
no debts of her own. no judgments, no
history of anything remotely like it.
The claim did not come from her behavior
at all. It came from a business that had
been closed for years attached to a
spouse surfacing long after everybody
had stopped thinking about it. And that
is genuinely how most of these arrive at
a house, not from recklessness, from a
co-signed loan for a grandchild. From a
car accident where the other driver's
costs ran past the policy limit, from a
medical bill that got sold to a
collection company that eventually went
to court, from a business that closed
with a loose thread. Nobody noticed.
Every one of those is ordinary. None of
them is a character flaw. And every one
of them can end up in front of a judge
with a number attached years after the
fact pointed at the only large thing a
retired household owns. That is why the
timing on this form matters more than
anything else about it. You are not
filing it because you expect trouble.
You are filing it because the day
trouble is expectable is the day it is
already too late to help. That is the
exact idea behind the guide. Every one
of these is worth the most on a
completely ordinary Tuesday when nothing
is wrong and nobody is threatening
anything, which is precisely the day
nobody thinks about it. Same place,
kevin Kevin explains.shop link in the
description, pinned comment at the top,
and the code on your screen if you are
watching this on the television. 7-day
guarantee. No questions, no argument.
Picture a woman standing in her own
paidoff kitchen in a house she and her
husband spent 30 years buying, reading a
letter about equity she was certain
nobody could touch. Here is your action
on this one and it is two questions
long. Call your county recorder or your
state bar's public information line and
ask one question. Does my state require
a recorded homestead declaration for
creditor protection or is it automatic?
That is it. That single answer tells you
whether you have homework. If the answer
is that it is required, file it today if
you can. Not because anything is wrong,
because the value of this particular
form is measured entirely in how far
ahead of the trouble it was recorded.
And know what it does not cover because
this is where people get a false sense
of safety. Homestead protection does not

the Internal Revenue Service. It does

who worked on the house. and it does not
