wall against everybody. Form number
three. This one does not protect you
from anything. This one just quietly
gives you money back every year. And a
startling number of people who qualify
have never claimed it. The senior
property tax exemption. Almost every
state has some version of a break on
property taxes for older homeowners.
Depending on where you live, it might be
called a senior exemption, a senior
freeze, a circuit breaker, or a deferral
program. The mechanics differ. Some
reduce your assessed value. Some freeze
it so it stops climbing. Some let you
postpone the tax entirely until the
house is sold. The amounts are real. For
a lot of households, this is somewhere
between several hundred and a few
thousand a year, every year, for the
rest of the time you own the house. And
here is why so many people are not
getting it. It is an application. Nobody
enrolls you. Turning 65 does not trigger
anything anywhere. Your county does not
have a system that watches birthdays and
adjusts bills. And there are three
specific traps in it that catch even
people who did apply. The first is that
in many places it does not automatically
renew. You file once, you get it, and
then a year or two later it quietly
requires a reertification that arrives
in an envelope that looks exactly like
every other envelope from the county.
and if you miss it, the exemption comes
off and your bill goes up and you assume
the taxes just went up. The second is
that it does not follow you. People
downsize, they move across town into
something smaller and they do not
realize the exemption belonged to the
old parcel. New house, new application,
and a surprising number of people never
file the second one. The third is the
one I find genuinely sad. There is often
an age or income-based version that a
widow qualifies for after a spouse dies
that she did not qualify for before
because the household income dropped.
The county does not know that. The
county knows somebody died only if
somebody told it. Let me tell you about
Elma. Elma is 81. She has lived in the
same house for 44 years. Her husband
handled the mail for most of their
marriage, which is not unusual for that
generation. And after he passed, she
took it over and did it carefully. She
had been eligible for a senior exemption
on her property taxes for 11 years and
had never filed for it. Not because she
was told no, not because she was denied,
because she had never once heard of it.
And nothing in 11 years of envelopes
from that county had ever said the word
to her. When her grandson finally asked
the assessor's office directly, she was
approved in about 3 weeks. her bill
dropped by a real amount immediately.
And she asked the question everybody
asks, which is whether she could get
back the 11 years? Mostly, no. Some
jurisdictions allow a limited
retroactive claim. Most do not. That
money is simply gone, and it was gone
one year at a time, quietly in a bill
she paid without complaint because she
assumed the number on it was the number.
Here is your action. Call your county
assessor, not the recorder, the
assessor, and ask them to tell you every
exemption or deferral program available
to a homeowner your age and whether you
are currently receiving any of them. Ask
that second part specifically out loud
because a great many people believe they
already have it and have not had it for
years. And then ask one more thing. Ask
whether it renews automatically or
whether you have to reertify. And if you
have to reertify, write the month on a
calendar you actually look at. And while
you have that office on the phone, ask
them one more question that costs
nothing and that almost nobody thinks to
ask. Ask what your home is currently
assessed at. Not what it is worth, what
they have it down as. Those are two
different numbers, and the second one is
the only one that generates your bill.
Assessments are made by people and
sometimes by software working from
records that can be years out of date
and occasionally simply wrong. A house
can be carrying square footage it does
not have, a bedroom that was never
built, a finished basement that was
never finished. Every one of those
inflates a bill that arrives every year
for as long as you own the place. And
the correction process for that is
usually free and usually has a deadline
that runs a matter of weeks after the
assessment notice goes out, which is
another envelope that looks like every
other envelope. So, it is one call and
two questions. What exemptions am I
eligible for and am I getting them? And
what am I currently assessed at? 15
minutes once and it can change a bill
you will pay for the rest of your life
in that house. Form number four, and
this one is not really a form you file.
It is a form you make sure somebody else
filed and it is the quietest problem in
this entire video. The release of your
mortgage. When you pay off a mortgage,
something has to happen at the county.
The lender is supposed to record a
document releasing their claim on your
property. Depending on the state, it is
called a satisfaction of mortgage, a
release of lean, or a reconveyance. When
that document is recorded, the public
record shows your house is clear. When
it is not recorded, the public record
still shows a lean on your house held by
a bank for a loan you finished paying
years ago. And here's the thing about
that. Nothing happens. Not for years.
You live in the house, you pay the
taxes. Nothing about your daily life
indicates any problem whatsoever.
Because there is no problem until the
day somebody has to prove that title is
clean. That day is the day you sell or
refinance or the day your children try
to. And now you are trying to get a
document from a lender that may have
been acquired, merged, renamed, or
dissolved sometime in the intervening
decade. Records get moved, departments
get closed, and a title company will not
close a sale on a property with an
unresolved lean on record, which means
everything stops until it is cleared,
which can take weeks and sometimes a
lawyer. This one shows up most often in
a specific situation, which is worth
naming. Somebody dies. The family goes
to sell the house and a lean from 1996
that everybody in that family would have
sworn was paid off is sitting on the
record and now the person who could
explain it is not available to explain
it. The fix is almost insultingly simple
and it takes one afternoon. If you have
ever paid off a mortgage on your home,
go and check whether the release was
recorded. You can call your county
recorder's office and ask them to look
up your property and tell you what leans
are currently on record against it. Many
counties now have this searchable online
for free. If the release is there, you
are done and you have spent 20 minutes
buying certainty. If it is not there,
start now while the lender may still be
findable and while you are the one who
remembers the loan rather than leaving
it for somebody who never saw the
paperwork. And while you have that
office on the phone, do not stop at the
mortgage. Have them read you the entire
list of what is recorded against your
property because there are two other
things that sit on a title record
quietly for decades. The first is an old
home improvement lean. A contractor did
work. There was a dispute or a slow
payment. They filed a mechanics lean to
protect themselves and then the two of
you worked it out between yourselves
like reasonable people. The handshake
ended the argument. It did not clear the
record. That lean is still sitting there
unless somebody went back and recorded a
release and almost nobody does. The
second is a home equity line of credit
that was closed. People pay these down
to zero, stop using them, and quite
reasonably assume that closed means
gone. But closing the account and
releasing the lean are two separate acts
by two separate departments, and the
second one does not always follow the
first. Neither of these will trouble you
for a single day while you live in the
house. Both of them will stop a closing
cold. And let me give you the practical
version of what to do if you find one
because I do not want anybody hearing
this. and panicking about a house they
have lived in happily for 30 years.
Start with whoever filed it if they
still exist. Most of the time this is a
records request and a form handled by a
person whose actual job it is and it
takes a few weeks rather than a lawyer.
Gather whatever you have that shows the
thing was paid because the burden of
demonstrating that lands on you rather
than on them and a canceled check from
2004 is worth a great deal in that
conversation. If the institution is
gone, merged, or dissolved, that is the
situation where a title company or a
real estate attorney genuinely earns
their fee. And it is far cheaper and far
calmer to pay that fee on an ordinary
Tuesday of your own choosing than in the
two weeks before a closing that four
other people are waiting on. Now, let me
give you my honest opinion, and it is
only that I do not think any of this is
a scheme. Nobody designed the county
recorder's office to trap people. It
genuinely is a filing cabinet and it
genuinely does its job. But I think we
have built something strange without
meaning to and I think it deserves to be
said out loud. The house is the largest
asset most American families will ever
own. And it is the only major asset in a
person's life with no institution
attached to it whose business it is to
talk to you. Your bank calls you. Your
insurance company calls you constantly.
Your retirement account sends statements
four times a year with a beneficiary
line printed on them. Every one of those
institutions has a commercial reason to
stay in contact. The county has no such
reason. It is not selling you anything.
It does not want your business. It has
no marketing department and no retention
problem. And so the largest thing you
own sits inside the one system in your
life that has absolutely no incentive to
ever speak to you. That is not
corruption. That is just what an
incentive vacuum looks like from the
inside. And the practical result is that
home ownership in this country quietly
rewards people who happen to know
somebody. A daughter who works in real
estate, a neighbor who sold a house last
year and learned the hard way. A

I'm going to show you today are not

segments.text: You finally wrote that last check to the
bank. Maybe it was last month. Maybe it

your bank, not your lender, the Internal
Revenue Service. And these traps do not

probably never warned you because CPAs

three IRS traps that destroy paidoff

Real sections of the tax code, real

number one is the capital gains bomb.

switch to direct deposit or the Direct
Express card. If you are changing banks,
update the VA first. Wait for one
payment to land, then close the old
account. Turn on deposit alerts so you
know the day the money arrives, and
never answer a conversation about your
money. Start it yourself with a number
you looked up or a login you opened on
your own. Save 1 800-827-1000
and the VSAE number 833-38VSAE
in your phone. Confirm that the account
the VA has on file is in the name of the
person receiving the payment. And if you
help a parent, set up form 21-0845
so you can ask questions and look at the
fiduciary program if they truly cannot
manage their money anymore. The
connecting thread across all three rules
is this: paper is fading, the order of
your steps matters, and the moment you
update your information is the moment
you are most exposed. None of that
enforces itself, and nobody hands you a
pamphlet about it. But, knowing the
order, knowing who to call, and knowing
that the VA will never ask for your
password puts you in a very different
position than you were in a few minutes
ago. That is the difference between
Harold getting paid on the 30th and
Harold waiting on a paper check in the
mail. Go and get what you earned. I am
no licensed expert, so make sure to
check all information with verified
sources before you make a move. Now I
want to hear from you. In the comments,
tell me which of these three rules
surprised you most and whether you have
already had a payment go missing. And if
you want your own numbers instead of the
averages in this video, I built a free
check. Six questions, two minutes, and
it shows you what you have put away, how
long it has to last, and where the gap
sits. If you're watching on a
television, point your phone's camera at
the square in the corner of the screen.
On a phone or tablet, tap the link right
under this video.
SmartSavingsBlueprint.com.

title: If You Were Born in the 40s, 50s and 60s, These New SSA Rules Could Affect You Right Now

segments.text: If you were born in the 1940s, the
1950s, or the 1960s, the Social Security
you think you have is not quite the
Social Security you have now. Six things
changed. Some of them land in your
mailbox, some land in your bank account,
and one of them may be money the
government already owes you. Most people
have only heard about the first one. By
the end of this video, you will know all
six, plus one simple habit that protects
you from the scams that follow every
rule change. Stay with me for number
four. I'm Lana Mains. I'm not with any
agency, and nobody pays me to point you
anywhere. What I do here is read what
these programs publish and put it in
plain words before the deadline runs
out. So, if that sounds useful, hit
subscribe because this is exactly what I
do here every single week. I follow this
calendar so you don't have to. I want to
be clear about what this video is
because there is a lot of noise on this
subject, and you deserve better. I am
not going to tell you Social Security is
about to disappear, and I am not going
to tell you to panic. Everything I
describe comes from official sources,
and most of it is genuinely
well-intentioned. What I will tell you
is that these rules change quietly, and
nobody from the government calls to warn
you. So, this is a video about where the
lines moved, who they hit first, and the
one thing to do about each. Let me start
with the idea underneath all six,
because once you see it, the rest
becomes obvious. Social Security does
not run on fairness or on good
intentions. It runs on dates, ages, and
forms. Your birth year decides your full
retirement age. The month you claim
decides the size of your check for the
rest of your life. The way you verify
your identity decides whether a payment
arrives or stalls. None of that is
personal and none of it bends because
you worked hard for 40 years. The people
who do well are not the ones who know
the most. They are the ones who find out
where the lines are before they cross
them. As we go through these changes,
keep one question in mind. Does this
apply to my record and what can I check
myself? Some rules affect new claimants,
others affect people who have collected
for years. Change number one, the ages
have a new name and your full retirement
age is locked at 67. Start with the age
itself. If you were born in 1960 or
later, your full retirement age is 67
flat. No more months added. If you were
born in 1959,
you are the last group with a slightly
lower bar, which is 66 and 10 months. If
you were born in the 1940s or early
1950s, your full retirement age has
already passed and your question is no
longer when to claim, but whether your
record is right. If you are turning 62,
you can still start your check. Nobody
is stopping you, but starting at 62
locks in a permanent cut of about 30% on
every check for the rest of your life.
It is not a one-time hit. It is forever.
On the other side, every year you wait
past 67 up to age 70 adds about 8% to
your monthly benefit. Wait the full 3
years and your check is about 24% larger
before any cost of living raise. Those
extra amounts are called delayed
retirement credits and they stop the
month you turn 70. So, there is no
reason to wait past that birthday. Now,
here is the new part. On the 29th of
September, the Senate passed a
bipartisan bill called the Claiming Age
Clarity Act and it has been headed to
the president's desk. Check whether it
has been signed by the time you watch
this. It does not change the ages, it
does not change your benefit, it changes
the names. Age 62 becomes the minimum
monthly benefit age. Age 67 becomes the
standard monthly benefit age. And age 70
becomes the maximum monthly benefit age.
The Social Security Administration would
have about a year after signing to make
the switch. Why does that matter?
Because the phrase full retirement age
has fooled people for decades. It sounds
like a finish line and it isn't. People
hear full and assume that claiming
anything earlier is a mistake or that
claiming at 67 is the best you can do.
Neither is true. The new words are
clearer, but even they only tell you the
size of the check. They do not tell you
whether it is the right choice for you.
That depends on your health, your
savings, whether you are still working,
and whether a spouse will rely on your
record someday. That last point deserves
a moment because it changes the math for
married couples. If you are the higher
earner and you pass away first, your
surviving spouse can step up to your
benefit, including those delayed
credits. So, for a couple, waiting is
not only about your check. It can be
about the check your spouse lives on for
the last 10 or 15 years of their life. A
widow whose husband claimed at 62 may be
living on a permanently reduced amount
and she never had a say in the decision.
So, here's what to do. Log in to your My
Social Security account at ssa.gov
and look at your estimated benefit at
62, at 67, and at 70 side by side. The
gap tends to shock people. While you are
in there, scroll to your earnings record
and read it year by year. Your benefit
is built from your highest 35 years of
earnings and a missing or wrong year
quietly lowers it. Errors can be
corrected, but the paperwork gets harder
the longer you wait. That side by side
look at your numbers is exactly the kind
of one-page habit that saves people real
money. And it is only the beginning of
what I put together. There is a whole
book of them. The five bills seniors
overpay and how to cut each one, the one
property tax form most seniors never
file, the three phone calls that cut
fees from your monthly bills, 50 states,
the exact form, the exact office. It's
called the senior exemption playbook. If
you're watching on a television, point
your phone's camera at the square in the
corner of the screen and it opens the
page. On a phone or tablet, tap the link
right under this video. lonamains.com.
Change number two. The new identity
rules. This one has caught a lot of
older people off guard and it hits the
oldest group the hardest, the ones born
in the 1940s. Since April of 2025,
Social Security has tightened how you
prove who you are. I want to be accurate
here because this rule has been
described wrongly in a lot of places. If
you want to change the bank account your
check goes into, you can no longer do
that over the phone. You have to do it
through your online my Social Security
account or in person at a field office.
That part is firm. If you are applying
for retirement or survivor benefits, you
can still start the claim by phone, but
if the agency flags the call as a fraud
risk, it can require you to verify your
identity in person. And if you cannot
use the online account, the agency has
advised people to call and schedule an
in-person appointment so the whole claim
can be done in one visit. Why did the
agency do this? Because redirecting a
retiree's deposit to a criminal's
account is one of the most common ways
seniors lose their monthly income. A
scammer calls, pretends to be the
beneficiary, and asks to change the
direct deposit. The check goes somewhere
else and the real owner finds out when
the rent is due. The new rules are aimed
at that. The cost of the protection is
paid by honest people who have always
done everything by phone. Let me tell
you about Gerald. Gerald is 81, a
retired machinist in Ohio, and he has
handled his own paperwork by telephone
since 1998. When his bank merged with
another one last spring, he assumed he
could call Social Security, read off the
new numbers, and be done in 10 minutes.
He was told he could not. The next field
office appointment was almost 3 weeks
out, and his old account was closing in
two. He spent a stressful month making
sure one deposit did not bounce. Nothing
was lost in the end, but only because
his daughter drove him in and sat with
him the whole morning. The rule did not
target Gerald. It simply did not know
him. So, do this on a calm afternoon,
not the week you urgently need
something. Set up your own my Social
Security account. If that isn't
realistic, call 1-800-772-1213,
and ask how to book an in-person
appointment before you need one. And a
bonus, an account you have set up
yourself is one of the best protections
against a criminal setting one up in
your name. Change number three. Paper
checks are going away for good. If you
or your mother or father still get a
Social Security check in the mailbox,
lean in because this one has a clock on
it. Under an executive order signed in
September of 2025, federal benefits are
moving to electronic payment only. The
phaseout began on the 30th of September
2025, and the agency has said it plans
to complete the transition in 2026. As
of this past June, about 99.6%
of beneficiaries were already paid
electronically, But, roughly 283,000
people were still getting paper checks.
There's no guarantee the last ones will
get a gentle reminder before their check
stops arriving. You have two ways to
keep your money flowing. The first is
direct deposit into a bank or credit
union account. The second, for people
who do not use a bank, is the Direct
Express card, a prepaid debit card from
the Treasury. Either way, the money
comes on the same schedule it always
did. For most people, that is the
second, third, or fourth Wednesday of
the month, depending on your birthday,
or the third of the month if you started
benefits before May of 1997.
There is a narrow exception. If you
truly cannot go electronic, perhaps
because you live somewhere remote or you
have a mental impairment, or you are 90
or older, you can ask the Treasury for a
waiver. That line is 1-855-290-1545.
it down because that number has been
given wrong in some places. There is a
real reason behind all this. A paper
check is far more likely to be lost,
stolen, or forged than an electronic
payment. Mail theft from curbside boxes
has become a serious problem, and a
stolen Social Security check can be
altered and cashed before you ever know
it is missing. Electronic payments also
arrive faster and cannot be misplaced
behind a couch cushion. So, here is a
favor to ask. If you have a parent in
their late 70s or 80s who is still
waiting on a check in the mail, pause
this video and call them tonight. Help
them set up direct deposit and sit with
them while they do it. Don't let this be
the thing that interrupts their money.
The announcement may be national, but
changing payment methods often falls on
one family member helping another. The
next change matters for a different
reason. It may involve money that should
already have arrived. Change number
four, the repeal almost nobody filed for
and the back pay that came with it. This
is the one I promised you. For more than
40 years, two rules quietly shrank or
wiped out Social Security checks for
people who also had a public pension.
Teachers, firefighters, police officers,
postal workers, and other public
employees in certain states. The rules
had clunky names, the windfall
elimination provision and the government
pension offset, but the effect was
simple and it was harsh. You worked a
public job, you also paid into Social
Security through other work or your late
spouse did and when you went to collect,
the government docked you, sometimes by
hundreds of dollars a month. Sometimes
it wiped out a survivor's check
completely. That is over. The Social
Security Fairness Act was signed in
January of 2025 and it repealed both
rules reaching back to benefits for
January 2024. Then the agency did
something it rarely does quickly. It
started sending money. By the middle of
last year, more than 3 million people
had received back payments, around $17
billion
in total. Many arrived as a lump sum in
a single deposit. For most people, there
is nothing to file. If Social Security
has your current information, the
adjustment and the back pay are
automatic. But most is not all. If you
moved, if your bank changed, if your
record was complicated or if you never
claimed a spouse or survivor benefit
because the old rule made it pointless,
you might be sitting on money the system
has not routed to you. That last group
is the one I worry about. Many widows
and widowers were told years ago that
they would receive nothing, so they
never applied. The agency cannot adjust
a claim that was never filed, and nobody
sends a letter to a person who is not in
the system. It also helps to know what
to look for. Your award letter should
say whether your benefit was
recalculated. If you were never
affected, there is nothing to find. But
if you or your late spouse worked for a
school district, a city, a county, or a
state that did not pay into Social
Security, you should ask. And if a
spouse or survivor claim was denied or
reduced under the old offset, ask for it
to be reviewed under the new law. And if
you want the one property tax form most
seniors never file, it is in the
playbook, and the square in the corner
takes you there. Let me tell you about a
woman I'll call Dolores. She is 69, a
retired school teacher, and she lives
outside Dayton, Ohio. She taught for
nearly 30 years on a state pension. When
her husband died, she went to claim a
survivor benefit on his record, and the
old offset rule reduced it to nothing.
For years, she assumed that was simply
the law, and she got on with her life.
Then the rule was repealed. Her survivor
benefit switched on at a little over
$1,100 a month. A few weeks later, a
back payment appeared in her account.
She had no idea it was coming. If you or
your late spouse ever worked a job with
a public pension, check your status. Log
in to ssa.gov
One phone call can be worth a year of
checks. And one more detail for widows
and widowers, survivor benefits can
start as early as age 60, which is
earlier than most people realize. If you
are in that group, ask what you are
eligible for before you assume anything.
Do not assume a small monthly amount is
too small to pursue. A recurring payment
can matter for years. Ask Social
Security to check your own record rather
than guessing from someone else's story.
Change number five. Your raise came in
and Medicare took a bite before you saw
it. In January, every Social Security
recipient got a cost of living raise of
For the average retiree, that was about
$56 more a month. Real money. But, the
standard Medicare Part B premium jumped
a month. An increase of nearly $18. And
because that premium comes straight out
of your Social Security check before it
reaches your bank, a big slice of the
raise disappeared on the way in. For
many people, close to a third of the
2026 raise was gone before it landed.
Now, here is what is new. The 2027 raise
has been announced and it is 3.6%.
For the average retired worker, that is
about $75 more a month. It takes effect
with your December benefit and shows up
in your bank account in January. But,
look at the other half. The 2027 Part B
premium has not been announced yet. The
Medicare trustees projected about
which would be roughly $6.60 more than
this year. Some private forecasters
expect it to come in higher. The
official number usually arrives in
November. So, please don't plan your
budget around the headline.
Do the simple subtraction. Take your
raise in dollars, which is your current
benefit * 0.036.
When the premium is announced, subtract
the increase. What is left is your real
raise. Write both numbers on the same
sheet of paper because most people only
remember the first one. There is a
second Medicare detail that surprises
people and it is worth knowing before
you open your January statement. If your
income from two years ago was above a
certain level, you pay an extra charge
on top of the standard Part B premium.
It is called IRMAA, short for
income-related monthly adjustment
amount. It is based on your tax return
from 2 years earlier, which means a
one-time spike, like selling a house or
cashing out a retirement account, can
raise your Medicare premiums for a year.
If your income dropped because you
retired or lost a spouse, you can file a
form with Social Security to ask them to
use a more recent year. Most people
never know the option exists. And since
it is the end of October, one date
matters right now. Medicare open
enrollment runs from October 15th
through December 7th. This is the window
to review your Part D drug plan or
switch your Medicare Advantage plan for
next year. Plans change their prices,
their formularies, and their pharmacy
networks every single year. And a drug
that cost you $10 in 2026 can cost 40 in
2027. Spending an hour on the Medicare
Plan Finder at medicare.gov can save you
hundreds. One more thing, for anyone in
their 50s and 60s who is still working,
if you are under full retirement age all
of 2026, you can earn up to $24,480
before Social Security starts holding
back $1 for every two you earn over the
line. In 2027, that limit rises to
In the year you reach full retirement
age, the limit is much higher. 65,160
this year and 67,920
next year. And the holdback eases to $1
for every three. And once you reach full
retirement age, the limit disappears
completely. Here is the part people
panic over for no reason. The money held
back isn't gone. Once you reach full
retirement age, Social Security
recalculates and gives it back to you
over time in a permanently higher check.
It feels like a penalty. It is really a
delay. Change number six, the new senior
tax deduction. This one is actually in
your corner. There is a new tax break
written for older Americans and it began
with the 2025 tax year. If you are 65 or
older, you can claim an extra deduction
of up to $6,000 per person. That is
for a married couple where both of you
are 65 or older. You can take it whether
you claim the standard deduction or
itemize. As the law stands, it runs
through the 2028 tax year. It does fade
out at higher incomes. It starts
shrinking when your modified income
passes $75,000 for a single filer or
for a couple and it is gone entirely at
single or $250,000
for a couple. But for a lot of retirees
living on a Social Security check and a
modest pension, that is real money
staying in your pocket. If you were
eligible for 2025 and nobody claimed it,
ask your tax preparer whether an amended
return makes sense. Many retirees who
filed late or filed on extension only
found out about it afterward. And if you
want the five bills seniors overpay and
how to cut each one, it is in the
playbook and the square in the corner
takes you there. Let me tell you about a
man I'll call Vernon. He is 76.
His wife died in the winter and his tax
return was the last thing on his mind.
His son helped him sort it out later in
the year and they discovered he
qualified for the new deduction. The
return they filed was much better than
the one they had feared. Deductions like
this do not announce themselves. You
have to ask. While we are on taxes,
there is one more piece that catches
retirees by surprise. Part of your
Social Security can be taxable,
depending on your other income, up to
50% and for many people up to 85% of
your benefit can be counted as taxable
income. Those thresholds, $25,000 for a
single filer and 32,000 for a couple at
the low end, were set in 1983 and have
never been adjusted for inflation. So,
each year more retirees cross them. In
January, you will receive a form called
the SSA-1099,
which shows what you were paid. Keep it
with your tax papers. If you owe tax at
the end of the year, you can ask Social
Security to withhold a percentage from
each check using a form called the W-4V
instead of paying it all at once in
April. Two things I need to say in the
same breath. First, why you keep hearing
about reform. On the 9th of June, the
Social Security Trustees released their
annual report. The main retirement trust
fund, the one that pays retirement and
survivor benefits, is now projected to
run short in the fourth quarter of 2032.
If Congress does nothing before then,
incoming payroll taxes would cover about
78% of scheduled benefits. That is the
number you will hear again and again.
The combined retirement and disability
funds are projected to last until 2034
with about 83% payable. Let me be clear
about what that means. It does not mean
Social Security goes broke. It does not
mean checks stop. It means that without
action by Congress, benefits would be
reduced to match incoming revenue.
Nothing changes today. Your check is
safe right now, but that date is why the
claiming decision deserves real thought.
If you are 62 and deciding whether to
wait, the answer should not come from a
headline. It should come from your own
numbers. Second, and please hear me on
this one, every time Social Security
changes its rules, the scammers go to
work because confusion is their best
friend. Right now, the biggest one is a
phone call. Somebody says they're from
Social Security, tells you your number
has been suspended over fraud, and says
the only way to fix it is to confirm
your number or pay them, sometimes with
gift cards.
It is all fake. Social Security will not
call you out of the blue and threaten
you. They will never ask you to fix
anything with a gift card. Hang up, then
call Social Security yourself at
on a number you looked up. You can
report the call to the Inspector General
at oig.ssa.gov
or by phone at 1-800-269-0271.
And to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
There is also a simple protection most
people forget. You can freeze your
credit for free at all three bureaus,
and it takes about 15 minutes. A freeze
means that even if a criminal gets your
number, they cannot open an account in
your name. Be the person in your family
who knows it's fake. Now, let me clear
the air on three things that are not
happening. First, your benefit is not
being cut in January. The 3.6% is a
raise, and it is automatic. You don't
have to apply or call anyone to get it.
Second, the new names don't change your
age or your check. The Claiming Age
Clarity Act only changes the words used
to describe the ages. It does not raise
the retirement age. Third, nobody will
phone you to verify your raise, your
account, or your new card. If someone
does, it is not Social Security. Before
the checklist, remember this. Good news
can still require action. If a claim was
never filed or an account detail is
outdated, silence does not prove
everything has been handled. The
checklist. One, look at your estimated
benefit at 62, 67, and 70 in your My
Social Security account. Check your
earnings record and don't decide
anything until you have seen all three
numbers. Two, set up your own online
account or call 1-800-772-1213
book an in-person appointment before you
need one. Three, if you or a parent
still gets a paper check, switch to
direct deposit or Direct Express. Use
the Treasury waiver line,
only if you truly cannot go electronic.
Four, if you or your late spouse ever
worked a job with a public pension, call
Social Security and ask whether your
benefit was adjusted and whether any
back pay is owed. Five, write down your
2027 raise in dollars, then subtract the
Part B increase when it is announced in
November, and before December 7th,
review your Medicare drug plan. Six, if
you are 65 or older, ask your tax
preparer whether the $6,000 senior
deduction was applied. And seven, if
someone calls claiming to be from Social
Security, hang up and call
yourself. My honest read, not one of
these changes is a trick and none of
them is a threat. They are rules and the
rules have moved, but I do have one
objection and it is about how people
find out. Almost nothing here arrives
with a letter that says this affects
you. The identity rule surfaces when a
call is refused. The paper check change
surfaces when a deposit is missing. The
pension repeal surfaces when a neighbor
mentions it over the fence. The system
is built for people who read the Federal
Register, not for a 79-year-old widow at
her kitchen table. And that gap is where
money gets lost. So, this is my ask for
this month, and it takes about an hour.
Write down your birth year, your benefit
at 62, 67, and 70, how you get paid, and
whether you or a spouse ever worked for
a public pension. Put it on one sheet of
paper, and keep it where your family can
find it. The rules never come looking
for you, but now you know exactly where
they landed. Until then, know your
numbers, check your account, and I'll
see you in the next one. I am no
licensed expert, so make sure to check
all information with verified sources
before you make a move. Tell me in the
comments which decade you were born in,
the '40s, the '50s, or the '60s. I read
every one, and they decide what I cover
next. And if you want your own numbers
instead of the averages in this video, I
built a free check. Six questions, two
minutes, and it shows you what you have
put away, how long it has to last, and
where the gap sits. If you're watching
on a television, point your phone's
camera at the square in the corner of
the screen. On a phone or tablet, tap
the link right under this video.

title: 3 Questions From VA Most Veterans Answer Wrong

segments.text: The VA can make a decision months from
now based on a sentence you say today. A
casual I'm fine, a vague answer about
work, or a letter left unopened can
become part of the record that
determines what happens to your
benefits. That does not mean you should
hide anything or be afraid of every
phone call. It means your words matter
because they may outlast the
conversation. Most veterans have heard
one warning like this, but there are
three kinds of sentences to watch for.
I'm Lana Mains. I'm not with any agency
and nobody pays me to point you
anywhere. What I do here is read what
these programs publish and put it in
plain words before the deadline runs
out. So if that sounds useful, hit
subscribe because this is exactly what I
do here every single week. I follow this
calendar so you don't have to. I want to
be clear about what this video is
because there is a lot of noise on this
subject and veterans deserve better. I
am not going to tell you the VA is out
to take your benefits and I would never
tell you to hide anything from it.
Everything I describe is published,
legal, and in most cases honestly
well-intentioned. What I am going to
tell you is that the benefits system
runs on a written record and a written
record captures wording. It does not
capture your service, your character, or
what you meant. An honest veteran who
phrases something badly can end up with
the same paperwork as a careless one. So
this is a video about how to speak to
the VA. Three kinds of sentences to
avoid, why each one causes trouble, and
what to say instead. Let me start with
the principle underneath all three
because once it clicks, the rest is
easy. Whenever you deal with the VA,
whether at a claims exam, on the phone,
at a regional office, or on a form at
your kitchen table, you are not having a
conversation. You are creating evidence.
The examiner writes what you said into a
report. The call center representative
types a note into your file. A form you
signed becomes a dated statement. Months
or years later, a rater who has never
met you opens that file and decides
based on those words. They cannot recall
your tone or the fact that you were
trying to be polite. For programs that
depend on income, the VA also checks
what you told it against records from
other federal agencies like the IRS and
Social Security. Here's why that
distinction matters in practice. The
person speaking with you today may
understand exactly what you meant, but
the person reviewing the file later may
only see a short note or a few lines in
an examination report. A phrase that
felt ordinary in the moment can look
much more definite on paper. You do not
need to speak like a lawyer. You need to
make the facts clear enough that someone
who has never met you can understand the
situation without guessing. That is the
thread connecting all three mistakes.
So, being decorated does not protect you
and 30 years of service does not protect
you. The file speaks and you don't. The
right way to talk to the VA is the way
you would write to any official body.
Polite, specific, accurate, and aware
that a stranger will read it later. One
note on language. When veterans say a
check got frozen, it usually means one
of three things. A payment was
suspended, a reduction was proposed, or
money was withheld to repay a debt. I'll
use freeze as shorthand for all of them.
The first sentence to avoid is the one
nearly every veteran has said, "I'm
fine." or its cousins, "It's not that
bad. I get by. I just push through.
Other guys have it worse." If you
served, you were trained to say exactly
those things. Mission first, complaints
never. It is an admirable instinct and
at a claims exam, it is quietly
expensive. The trap is that I'm fine can
mean two completely different things. In
everyday conversation, it can mean you
are coping, refusing to complain, or
trying to reassure the person asking. In
a disability examination, it can be read
as a description of your current
functioning. Those are not the same
thing. You are not there to prove
toughness, and you are not there to
perform suffering. You are there to
describe what your condition actually
does to your life, including what
happens on the difficult days and how
often those days occur. Disability
ratings are not a one-time decision. The
VA can schedule a re-examination when it
believes a condition may have improved,
and many decision letters even say a
future exam is planned. At that exam,
the examiner has a form and roughly the
length of a doctor's visit. Whatever you
say about how often, how severe, and how
it affects daily life goes into the
report, and the rater uses those words
to decide whether your percentage still
fits. If the report reads, "Veteran
states he is managing well and pushes
through," that sentence can be read as
improvement, no matter how many nights a
week you are awake at 3:00 in the
morning. There are real protections. A
rating in place 5 years or more is
considered stabilized, and the VA
generally needs evidence of sustained
improvement before reducing it. A rating
in place 20 years is protected from
reduction except in cases of fraud.
Service connection itself is protected
after 10 years, and the VA generally
does not order routine re-exams once you
turn 55. But none of that helps a
veteran whose rating is young, or one
who gets a reduction letter and then
sits on it. Do not mistake these
protections for a reason to say less.
They are important safeguards, but they
do not make every proposed reduction
disappear automatically, and they do not
mean you should ignore a notice. Read
the decision letter, look at the dates,
and respond to what the VA is actually
asking. If you are unsure whether a
protection applies to your rating, get
help from an accredited representative
rather than trying to work it out from
memory. The goal is not to panic, it is
to make sure the record reflects the
full picture. Let me tell you about
Frank, a name I'm using for a man like
thousands of others. He is 67, Army,
rated 50% for his back and
post-traumatic stress, a rating granted
3 years earlier. A re-exam notice
arrived, and he went. The examiner asked
how things were going, and Frank, a man
raised never to complain, said, "I'm
fine. I get by. Some days are rough, but
I push through." Every word was true.
Two months later, a letter arrived
proposing to cut his rating to 30%,
roughly $500 a month less. The examiner
did nothing wrong. She recorded what he
said. It took Frank 4 months, treatment
records, and a written statement from
his wife to get it corrected. What
protects a man like Frank costs nothing.
Write a one-page worst day sheet. List
each condition, how often it flares,
what you cannot do on those days, and
what you have stopped doing because of
it. Be concrete. Not, "My back hurts,"
but, "Three or four days a week, I can't
stand more than 10 minutes, and I no
longer drive longer than half an hour."
Date it, keep a copy, and hand it to the
examiner at the exam. You can also
submit it on VA form 21-4138,
the statement in support of claim, so it
sits in your file in your own words. And
one caution, never exaggerate. A false
statement to the VA is a federal
offense, and examiners are trained to
spot inconsistent reporting. Be accurate
about the bad days and honest about the
good ones. That one-page sheet is
exactly the kind of small paper step
that keeps real money in a household,
and there is a whole book of them. The
five bills seniors overpay and how to
cut each one. The one property tax form
most seniors never file. The three phone
calls that cut fees from your monthly
bills. 50 states, the exact form, the
exact office. It's called the senior
exemption playbook. If you're watching
on a television, point your phone's
camera at the square in the corner of
the screen and it opens the page. On a
phone or tablet, tap the link right
under this video, lanemanes.com.
Before moving on, notice the pattern.
Frank did not need a clever argument or
a dramatic story. He needed a specific
description of frequency, limits, and
consequences.
"I pushed through" tells the reviewer
almost nothing about what pushing
through costs him. A useful statement
answers practical questions. How often
does it happen? What can you no longer
do? What do you have to stop, change, or
ask someone else to do? Write those
answers in ordinary language. If your
condition varies, say that it varies.
Accuracy is more useful than either
minimizing or exaggerating. That is the
first mistake, making a real problem
sound smaller than it is. The second
mistake can look like the opposite
because it sounds harmless and ordinary.
Never give the VA a rounded, casual, or
half-complete answer about work, money,
or your household. In real life, it
sounds like this. "I do a little work on
the side." "I haven't really worked in
years." "My wife helps out." "We're sort
of separated." "A relative gave me some
money." None of those is a lie, but each
one is vague, and vagueness invites
follow-up. If your benefit depends on
income, work, or who lives in your home,
a vague answer gets treated as an open
question. Consider where this matters.
Some veterans receive individual
unemployability, known as TDIU, which
pays at the 100% rate for a veteran
rated lower who cannot hold
substantially gainful work. Earnings
above roughly the federal poverty level
for one person can end that eligibility,
though marginal work below that line or
in a protected setting generally does
not. The VA sends an annual employment
questionnaire, Virginia form 21-4140,
and then compares your answers with tax
and Social Security records. Other
veterans and surviving spouses receive
needs-based pension, including aid and
attendance where income and net worth
decide the amount, and any change must
be reported. And for everyone, marital
status and dependents change the amount
you are paid. A divorce, a death, or a
child turning 18 and not being in school
all need to be reported. The point is
not that every job or every household
change automatically ends a benefit. The
rules differ by program, and the details
matter. The risk comes from giving an
answer so loose that it cannot be
compared with the records the VA uses.
If a form asks about employment, do not
assume that a short job is too small to
mention. If it asks about income or
assets, do not assume a transfer is
irrelevant because it was meant to help
family. Read the question, answer to the
question, and keep the paperwork that
explains the answer. Gene is 70, Navy,
on unemployability. When the
questionnaire arrived, he wrote, "Some
part-time work," and mailed it. In
truth, he had worked 3 months at a
garden center and earned $9,400,
well under the line. But the VA's
records showed wages from an employer,
the form showed nothing specific, and a
letter arrived proposing to stop his
unemployability payment unless he could
document his earnings. Gene had not done
anything wrong. His answer just did not
match the data in a way anyone could
verify at a glance. The sentence that
would have protected him was simple.
Seasonal work, 3 months, $9,400
in total, W-2 attached. It would have
been dull, specific, and closed. So, the
rule is exact numbers, exact dates, in
writing. When something changes, report
it promptly on the right form, VA form
C for changes in marital status or
dependents. If a dependent child turns
18 and is still in school, the school
form, VA form 21-674,
keeps them on your award until 23. And
before you take any job at all while on
unemployability, call and ask if a gift
or transfer might affect pension, ask
first because the VA reviews asset
transfers in the 36 months before you
apply and can impose a penalty period of
up to 5 years. It is a cousin of the
Medicaid look-back, and it catches the
same families for the same reason. A
well-meant transfer made without knowing
the rule. Here is what an unreported
change costs. The VA does not fix it
quietly. It calculates an overpayment,
sends a debt letter, and can withhold
some or all of your monthly payment to
recover it. One late report can turn
into months of a shrunken check, plus a
bill for money you already spent. If the
overpayment was not your fault, you can
ask for a waiver, and I'll come back to
that. But the cheapest fix is reporting
early. And if you want the five bills
seniors overpay and how to cut each one,
it is in the playbook, and the square in
the corner takes you there. If you
receive a notice about an overpayment,
do not assume the amount is correct, but
do not put the letter aside either.
Compare the period and amount with your
own records. Keep the envelope and every
page, and ask for help if you cannot
tell what the VA is counting. A waiver
is not automatic, and asking for one is
different from ignoring the debt. The
important thing is to act within the
dates on the letter, because a problem
that can be explained is harder to fix
after the response window has passed.
The first mistake minimizes what is
happening. The second leaves important
details fuzzy. The third can be even
more costly because it says nothing at
all. Never go silent. The silent version
sounds like, "I'll deal with that letter
later. I'm not going to that exam.
That's none of their business." Or, most
often, no sentence at all, just an
envelope on the counter that nobody
opens. The VA does not read silence as
privacy. It reads silence as a missing
answer. The consequences are written
into the rules. If you fail to report
for a scheduled re-examination without
good cause, the VA can reduce or
discontinue your benefit. If you do not
return the annual employment
questionnaire, the same applies to
unemployability. If the VA's mail comes
back undeliverable, payment can be
suspended until it finds you. A proposed
reduction letter generally gives you 60
days to submit evidence, and if the 60
days pass, the change takes effect. A
debt letter gives you a short window,
about 30 days, to respond before
collection actions begin. And a waiver
request generally must be filed within
180 days. Check your own letter for the
exact dates because they can differ.
This is why opening mail is not a minor
administrative chore. A letter can be a
request for information, a notice of a
proposed change, or a decision that
starts a review deadline. Until you open
it, you do not know which one it is. You
do not have to solve the whole problem
that day. The first job is simply to
identify what the letter says, mark the
deadline, and make sure it reaches the
person who can help. That small first
step preserves options that silence can
close. Silence usually comes from one of
two places. The first is fear. You open
the envelope, it sounds like trouble,
and you set it aside. The second is
pride. I earned this, they can wait.
Both feelings are completely human. But
a letter that sits unopened for 50 days
costs you the very window the law gave
you to protect yourself. Let me tell you
about Teresa, 66, Navy, who moved in
with her daughter after a hip
replacement. She never updated her
address, so a re-exam notice went to her
old apartment and was returned. A month
later, a second letter went there, too,
and her payment was suspended. She
learned about it when her deposit did
not arrive. Nobody was cruel. The mail
simply went where she no longer was. A
phone call and a signed address change
restored it, but she waited 5 weeks with
a car payment due. A 2-minute change on
va.gov would have prevented the whole
thing. So, here is what to do. Open
every VA envelope the day it arrives and
write the date on it. If you cannot make
an exam, call and reschedule rather than
skip it. A good reason on the record is
good cause. If a letter proposes a
reduction, respond in writing before the
deadline, even if you only say, "I am
gathering evidence. Please confirm my
deadline." If you receive a debt notice,
respond within the first window, and if
the overpayment was not your fault,
request a waiver. Keep your address,
phone, email, and direct deposit current
on va.gov. And if your bank account
changes, update it immediately because a
payment sent to a closed account bounces
back. And if you disagree with any
decision, you generally have 1 year from
the date on the decision letter to
choose a review option such as a
supplemental claim or a higher level
review. And keep your original effective
date. When you respond, make it easy to
prove what you did, keep a copy of the
form or letter, note when you sent it,
and save any confirmation you receive.
If you call, write down the date and
time and what the representative told
you. If you mail something, keep the
mailing record. If you submit something
online, save the confirmation screen or
number. These habits are not about
expecting a fight. They are about making
sure you can show what happened if the
file later appears incomplete. There are
two other habits that cost nothing.
First, file an intent to file Virginia
form 210966
before you gather paperwork for any new
claim because it can lock in your start
date for up to a year. If the PACT Act
expanded coverage for something you were
denied before, such as certain cancers
or respiratory conditions tied to burn
pits and toxic exposure, that intent to
file can matter a great deal. Second,
log every call. Date, time, the name of
the person, and any reference number. If
a dispute comes up, a log is worth more
than a memory. There is one more danger
to watch for before we get to the form I
promised, scammers. A frozen benefit is
exactly the kind of worry they exploit.
Nobody from the VA will demand payment
in gift cards, ask you to wire money to
unfreeze a check, or require you to pay
a fee to file an initial claim. If
someone calls claiming to be the VA and
pressures you, hang up and call the VA
yourself at 800-827-1000.
Now, the thing I promised you at the
start, the single most useful item in
this video, there is a form called VA
Form 21-22,
the appointment of Veterans Service
Organization as claimant's
representative. It lets you name an
accredited representative from an
organization like the American Legion,
the VFW, DAV, or your county veterans
service office to act on your claim.
They can see your claims file, speak to
the VA for you about your case, and
receive copies of correspondence. It
takes about 4 minutes to complete, it
costs nothing, and the help is free.
What it does not do is give them access
to your bank account or the power to
sign away your money. It is a
representative for your claim, nothing
more. A representative does not replace
your responsibility to read your mail or
tell the truth. Think of the appointment
as adding another set of eyes, not
handing over control of your life. You
still decide what information to
provide, and you should understand what
you are signing. The value is that
someone familiar with the process can
help you understand a notice, organize
evidence, and choose the right next step
before a deadline becomes urgent. That
is why setting this up while things are
calm is so much better than searching
for help during a crisis. Almost nobody
fills it in until there is a crisis, but
think about what it does. When a letter
arrives proposing a reduction, you are
not alone with a 60-day clock. Someone
who knows the rules reads it with you.
When an exam is scheduled, someone helps
you prepare the worst day sheet. And
when the VA needs to reach someone, it
has more than one door to knock on. Look
up an accredited representative on the
VA's website, and if you ever hear of
someone charging to prepare an initial
claim, walk away. One more piece of
preparation costs only an afternoon.
Introduce yourself to your county
veteran service officer before you need
anything. Walk in on a quiet day, say
who you are, what you receive, and that
you want to know your deadlines. You are
not asking for a favor. You are building
a relationship so that when a letter
lands, you already have someone to call.
While you are protecting the benefit,
make sure you are claiming everything
that comes with it. Many states offer a
property tax exemption or reduction to
disabled veterans. And in a number of
states, a veteran rated 100% permanent
and total can pay little or no property
tax on a primary home. The same applies
to some surviving spouses. Vehicle
registration fees, state park passes,
and hunting and fishing licenses are
other places where states build in
discounts, and almost nobody applies
unless someone tells them. And if you
want the one property tax form most
seniors never file, it is in the
playbook, and the square in the corner
takes you there. Let me give you my
honest opinion, which is only that I do
not think these rules are wrong. The VA
has to verify that people are paid
correctly because overpayments and fraud
are real, and the system exists so that
benefits go to veterans who qualify.
Review is not an insult. I also
understand that examiners and raters
work through enormous caseloads, and
most of them are trying to do the job
right. My objection is narrower. The
rules are published, and they are
accurate, but they are written for
adjudicators, not for the 68-year-old
man standing at a counter or opening an
envelope. No letter says the wording you
choose matters as much as the facts.
Nobody mentions form 21-22 at your first
visit. And the culture the military
builds in us never complain, never ask,
handle it yourself is exactly the
culture that produces I'm fine and an
unopened envelope. A system that rewards
specifics and a population trained to be
modest will keep producing the same
outcome. That is not anyone's villainy.
It is a gap and the person who falls
into it is usually the one who can least
afford the several months it takes to
climb out. That is the uncomfortable
middle ground. The system needs accurate
information and you need a fair chance
to make sure the information is
understood. Both things can be true at
once. You do not have to assume bad
intentions to prepare carefully. You can
respect the people doing the review and
still keep copies, ask questions, use
the right forms, and get assistance.
Preparation is not hostility. It is
simply making sure your side of the
record is complete. So, let me put it
all together. Harold is 69, a retired
Marine rated 70%. He did four things
differently from the old Harold. He
signed form 21-22
with his county veterans service
officer. He updated his address and bank
information on va.gov. He wrote a worst
day sheet and kept a copy. And when a
re-exam notice arrived, he opened it the
day it came and wrote the date on it. At
the exam, when the examiner asked how
things were going, the old Harold would
have said, "Fine. I get by." The new
Harold said, "Four nights a week I sleep
under 5 hours and I don't drive after
dark anymore." He handed over the sheet.
The report came back detailed and
accurate and his rating stayed where it
was. He did not say anything clever. He
just avoided the three wrong sentences.
So, let me recap. One, never say I'm
fine or any version of it. Describe your
worst days with specifics and bring a
worst day sheet to every exam. Two,
never give a rounded or vague answer
about work, money, or your household.
Give exact numbers and dates in writing
and report changes promptly on the right
forms. Three, never go silent. Open
every letter the day it arrives, respond
before the deadline, keep your address
and direct deposit current, and
reschedule an exam rather than skip it.
Four, sign VA form 21-22
and name an accredited representative.
It takes 4 minutes and costs nothing.
Five, keep a call log and copies of
everything you send. One last thing
before you go. Frank told the exact
truth about his back and was nearly cut
by $200 a month for it. Gene told the
exact truth about his job and was asked
to prove it. Teresa told the VA nothing
because she never knew where her mail
was going. None of them did anything a
reasonable person would not do. All of
them were honest and honesty in the
wrong wording or no wording at all
produced the same result carelessness
would have. So, this week do one small
thing. Write three sentences on a piece
of paper and put it in your wallet. One
describing your worst day, one stating
your current income and work, and one
with your current address and the name
of your representative. Make each one
specific, short, and true. The day you
need them, you will be glad you wrote
them before you needed them. I am no
licensed expert, so make sure to check
all information with verified sources
before you make a move. And if your own
situation is tangled, if a payment has
stopped, and you cannot work out why,
tell me in the comments. I read every
single one, and if you want your own
numbers instead of the averages in this
video, I built a free check. Six
questions, 2 minutes, and it shows you
what you have put away, how long it has
to last, and where the the sits. If
you're watching on a television, point
your phone's camera at the square in the
corner of the screen. On a phone or
tablet, tap the link right under this
video. smartsavingsblueprint.com

transfer, which is why the old rules
often left you carrying the loss. That
changed on the 7th of October 2024.
Under rules set by the payment systems
regulator, if you're tricked into
sending money through faster payments or
CHAPS, your bank must reimburse you
unless you were grossly negligent. The
sending bank and receiving bank share
the cost equally. The bank that received
the money can no longer simply sit back
and shrug. The maximum you can claim is
85,000 pounds per claim. In most cases,
the bank has five working days to refund
you. More complicated claims requiring
investigation can take up to 35 working
days. And here's the important change.
The bank now has to prove gross
negligence. You don't have to prove your
innocence. Consider Doreen, 79, who
lives on her own. She receives a call
that appears on her phone screen to come
from her bank's fraud line. The caller
knows her name, her branch, and the last
four digits of her card. Believing the
caller is genuine, Doreen transfers
£11,000 to a so-called safe account.
Under the old rules, she might have been
left with a loss. Under the rules that
now apply, her bank had to replace the
money because she hadn't been grossly
negligent. She had been deceived by
someone who had done their homework. But
there are two details you need to
understand before assuming every claim
will be paid in full. First, banks are
allowed to deduct an excess of up to
£100 from a refund, although they don't
have to. Customers the bank recognizes
as vulnerable are exempt from that
excess. Second, you have 13 months from
the last payment to make a claim. That's
the outside limit, not a reason to wait.
If you believe you've been scammed,
contact your bank immediately. And don't
assume this protection applies to every
way money can leave your account. The
reimbursement rules cover faster
payments and CHAPS, which include most
everyday bank transfers. Card payments,
cash, international payments, and
transfers between your own accounts are
treated differently. A dispute with a
genuine seller over goods that never
arrived is also different from an
authorized push payment scam. The gross
negligence test matters, too. If you
ignored multiple clear warnings from
your bank or refused to take part in a
scam check the bank was required to
carry out, you could lose the
protection. The right response is not to
stay silent and hope. Engage with the
bank, answer questions honestly, and
keep a record of what happened. Before
we go further, one thing straight,
reimbursement rules are a real
protection, but they aren't a promise
that every loss will be refunded. The
type of payment, the circumstances of
the scam, and your response to the
bank's warnings all matter.
Now, consider why these rules also
affect legitimate payments. Because
banks may have to reimburse customers
who are scammed, they have a stronger
incentive to stop suspicious transfers
before the money leaves. That's useful,
but it can also mean a perfectly
legitimate payment is held while the
bank makes inquiries. If your payment is
delayed, ask one direct question. Is
this an automated security check or a
formal hold? Then ask what information
you need to provide to release the
payment. Those are different situations
and you deserve to know which one
applies to you. If you've been scammed,
act the same day. Call your bank using a
number you trust and explain that you
believe you've been the victim of an
authorized push payment scam. Ask for a
reference number. Report the incident to
the police through the national fraud
reporting service. Keep every message,
call log, and screenshot that might help
explain what happened. If you disagree
with the bank's final answer, you can
take the case to the Financial Ombudsman
Service. It is free and you generally
have 6 months from the bank's final
response to do so. Banks don't always
get these decisions right. The Ombudsman
has the power to overturn them. There
are also two simple precautions worth
taking before anything goes wrong. Turn
on transactional alerts if your bank
offers them. An alert that tells you
when money leaves your account can help
you identify a problem while there's
still time to respond. Then write a
short instruction and keep it by your
phone. If somebody claiming to be my
bank asks me to move money, I will hang
up, call 159, and tell someone I trust.
Make that decision while you're calm.
Scammers are counting on you having to
make it while you're frightened. Let's
bring the three changes together. First,
your bank can change your account terms
without phoning you because a posted
notice can be enough. Read your bank
letters, check your fees, and ask
whether a basic account would cost you
less. Second, confirmation of payee
helps you spot mismatched account names
before sending money. Never override a
warning without independently checking
the details. Third, reimbursement rules
can protect you after certain authorized
push payment scams up to 85,000 pounds
per claim, but eligibility depends on
the payment method and the
circumstances. So, report a suspected
scam immediately. And remember the
overdraft rule. Fixed daily and monthly
overdraft charges were banned in April
2020. If you're being charged a flat fee
for going overdrawn, ask your bank to
explain it. So, what would I actually do
this week? I'd check the last three bank
statements for unfamiliar charges. I'd

third-party access. I'd open every bank

rule never to override a name mismatch
without checking. I'd also review my
savings interest against my personal
savings allowance. And I'd make sure I
knew exactly how to contact my bank's
genuine fraud team. These aren't
complicated tasks. They're small steps
that put you back in control of
decisions affecting your own money. And
that's what this is really about, not
becoming an expert in every banking
rule, and not living in fear of every
phone call or letter. It's about keeping
your independence, protecting the money
you've worked for, and making sure that
a change in a bank's rules doesn't catch
you completely unprepared. You weren't
asking for favors. You were collecting

the law changes with them. The people

careless. Sometimes they're simply

title: 7 Things the IRS Lets You Do After 70½ (Most Retirees Don't Know)

opportunity comes from combining three
rules that most retirees treat
separately, and that combination can
bring a $70,000 retirement year down to
zero federal income tax. The difference
is not how much you receive. It is how
you arrange the money you already have.
I'm Lana Mains. I'm not with any agency
and nobody pays me to point you
anywhere. I read what these programs

that's useful to you, subscribe. I do
this every week. Number one is the
qualified charitable distribution and it

entire list. If you give money to

you can send money directly from your
traditional IRA to a qualifying charity
without counting that money as income.
For 2026, the limit is $111,000 per
person and it rises with inflation every

have your own IRA, each of you gets that

your checking account never gets added

That is a separate process.

or CPA who specializes in retirement
taxation and ask them directly which of

which one to implement first. That
single question, asked with the right
documents in front of the right
professional, is what turns everything
in this video from information into
actual protection. Here's the number
worth remembering. The IRS has collected
over $4 trillion
in the last decade and most retirees

You now know all seven. A retiree who
only knows the Roth IRA is protecting
one position. A retiree who stacks even

different terms, legally, permanently,
on the rules the IRS itself into the tax
code. None of these seven ask you to
hide money, misreport income, or take on
risk with the law. Every one of them is
sitting in plain sight in the federal
tax code waiting for someone to actually
use it the way it was written. Tell me
in the comments which of these seven you
already own and which one surprised you
most. I read every single one. And next
week, I'm walking through the one Social
Security filing mistake that quietly
costs married couples tens of thousands
of dollars over a lifetime
and how to check in about 5 minutes
whether you're about to make it. I am no
