title: The Extra VA Check Thousands of Veterans Qualify For — and Never Claim

segments.text: That VA check, landing in your account
every month, may not be the only check
you qualify for. Some veterans are
already sitting at 100%
and are still missing a separate
recurring payment that stacks directly
on top of what they already receive. Let
that go unclaimed for years and several
thousand dollars can turn into tens of
thousands that never reaches your
account. This is not a raise. It is not
a one-time payout and you do not need a
higher rating to qualify. By the end of
this video, you will know exactly what
the second payment is called, the five
situations that can trigger it, the
forms that matter, and the evidence that
can make or break the claim. Pay special
attention to number four. That is the
category that can push a veteran already
rated at 100% to a combined monthly
total well above $5,000. And stay with
me after that because one paperwork
mistake causes veterans who may actually
qualify to get denied anyway. I'm Lana
Mains. On this channel, I break down the
financial and legal benefits most people
never hear about until it is too late.
If you want that kind of information in
your corner, subscribe now because
understanding this one benefit could
change your monthly check for the rest
of your life. The payment is called
special monthly compensation or SMC. And
before we go any further, understand
what SMC will not do. It will not change
your percentage from 90 to 100. It is
not another disability rating. It sits
above your regular disability
compensation as an entirely separate
category of payment for specific
situations Congress decided deserved
extra support. You can already be rated
at the maximum 100%
and still qualify for SMC on top of it.
That misunderstanding costs people
money. And if you are wondering why the
VA does not simply call veterans who
qualify, the answer is not some dramatic
conspiracy.
The problem is how the system works. The
VA is claims driven, not entitlement
driven. An entitlement driven system
would monitor your circumstances and
adjust your payment when you qualified
for more. A claims driven system waits.
It processes what you file. There is no
employee whose job is to comb through
your file and call you saying, "Based on
your condition, you might qualify for
another payment. Have you thought about
applying?" That job does not exist
inside the VA.
Under Title 38 of the United States
Code, Sections 1114 and 1115, Congress
created this program because a
percentage rating cannot capture
everything a service connected condition
costs a veteran. A rating measures
severity. SMC measures something
different. It looks at what those
conditions force you to live with
day-to-day and what additional help they
require. The VA's duty to assist under
Title 38, Section 5103A,
only activates once a claim has been
filed. It does not require the VA to
tell you which claims you should file in
the first place. When the original
disability claim closes, that duty
closes with it. If a separate benefit
applies, a separate claim is required.
If nobody tells you that second layer
exists, that second claim may never
happen. So, here are the five situations
you need to recognize. Number one, loss
or loss of use. This category includes
the loss of a hand or foot, blindness,
deafness in both ears, and similar
serious losses. But, here is what most
veterans get wrong. They hear the word
loss and assume something must
physically be gone. That is not what
loss of use means. If a service
connected condition leaves a hand or
foot so damaged that it no longer
functions in any meaningful way, that
can count under the law even when the
limb is still attached. Picture the test
in everyday life. The hand is still
there, but between nerve damage and lost
grip strength, you cannot button a
shirt. You cannot hold a coffee cup.
That is the difference. The wrong move
is waiting for the condition to match
some dramatic picture of complete
physical loss. The right question is
whether meaningful function remains. The
same logic applies to feet, eyes, and
ears. Look at what the body part
actually lets you do. Do not judge it
only by whether it is physically
present. Function, not appearance, that
is the test that matters. Number two is
part of that same loss of use family,
but it gets skipped more than almost
anything else. Loss of use of a
reproductive organ. In plain terms, this
very often means erectile dysfunction. I
am going to say this plainly because
embarrassment keeps a lot of men silent
about it. A significant number of
veterans develop this condition as a
side effect of medications prescribed
for other service-connected issues,
including pain management, blood
pressure treatment, or mental health
conditions. If the service-connected
condition or the treatment for it caused
this, it can qualify a veteran for an
additional monthly payment. The wrong
move is leaving it off the paperwork
because it feels too personal to
discuss. That silence can cost money
month after month. This is a recognized
compensable condition under federal law.
There is no shame required to claim a
benefit you earned. If treatment for a
service-connected condition changed this
part of your life, document what
actually happened. Embarrassment does
not protect your benefits. Documentation
does. Number three, housebound status.
This is where the 100% myth starts
costing veterans again. If you carry a
single disability rated at 100%
plus an additional separately rated
disability that adds up to a certain
threshold on top of that, or if your
service connected conditions effectively
confine you to your home, you may
qualify for an additional housebound
payment. The wrong assumption is simple.
I'm already at 100%. There is nowhere
higher to go. But your rating and your
ability to leave your home are two
different questions. This tends to creep
up on older veterans. There is rarely
one dramatic morning where somebody
suddenly says, "Now I am housebound."
The world just gets smaller. First
certain errands disappear, then driving
becomes harder, then leaving the house
becomes rare. Room by room, year by
year, life moves inside four walls. That
change matters. Do not ask only what
percentage on your award. Ask what your
service connected conditions have done
to the physical size of your life.
Rating and housebound status are
separate questions. Treat them that way.
Number four, aid and attendance. This is
the category I told you to stay for. One
service connected conditions progress to
the point where you regularly need
another person's help with basic
activities of daily life, that need
itself is compensable. And it is
compensable at a significantly higher
rate than the categories above it. Those
activities include bathing, dressing,
eating, and getting around safely. Here
is what most families get wrong. They
think the veteran must be completely
helpless. Under 38 CFR 3.352,
you do not need help with every single
activity to qualify. Needing regular
assistance with even one or two can be
enough to meet the standard. A veteran
can still cook, a veteran can still
drive, but if that same veteran cannot
safely bathe or dress without help, that
can meet the bar. A veteran may even
live alone, but if moving through the
home creates a real risk of falling,
that can matter, too. The wrong approach
is describing only the diagnosis. The
right approach is describing function.
Can the person get into the shower
safely? Can they dress without another
set of hands? Can they move around the
home without a real risk of falling?
Those details are what turn a medical
condition into an understandable daily
limitation. And if you are the spouse,
adult child, or caregiver watching this,
you may notice those limitations before
the veteran ever admits them. Maybe you
help your father get dressed every
morning. Maybe you make sure your
husband does not fall in the shower.
Maybe you keep his medication straight
because he cannot manage them anymore.
That daily help has a name inside this
system. Naming it correctly can mean a
meaningfully larger monthly check.
Bringing it up is not complaining. It is
making sure the person you care for
receives what he earned. Daily function
is the evidence. Do not hide it behind
pride. Number five, dependence. This one
rarely gets grouped with the others, but
in practice, it creates the same
problem. Under section 1115, a veteran
rated at 30% or higher receives an
additional monthly amount for each
eligible dependent. That can include a
spouse, a child, or in some cases a
dependent parent. And again, it does not
necessarily activate on its own. If you
married after your rating was
established, had a child, or took on the
care of a parent, the wrong move is
assuming the VA already knows. If you
never went back and reported that
change, you are very likely receiving
less every month than the law says you
are owed right now. 30% or higher.
Eligible dependent, report the change.
Simple facts, real monthly consequences.
Now, before we get into the filing
mistakes, see whether you recognize
yourself in these conditions.
Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is one of
the most common paths into the loss of
use category when it progresses to the
point where a veteran cannot feel or
safely use their feet. Many veterans
think of neuropathy as just numbness.
The important question is what the
numbness has done to function. Traumatic
brain injury frequently qualifies
veterans for aid and attendance when
cognitive or balance problems make
independent daily functioning unsafe.
Even when the veteran can still hold a
conversation perfectly well. Severe PTSD
can also support an aid and attendance
claim when it reaches the point where a
veteran cannot safely manage their own
medication schedule or cannot be left
alone for extended periods without risk.
That category is frequently under
documented because the symptoms are
behavioral rather than physical. Spinal
cord injuries, severe COPD requiring
supplemental oxygen, and advanced
Parkinson's disease connected to Agent
Orange exposure also repeatedly show up
in approved SMC claims. If one of those
sounds like your situation or like
somebody you served with, do not stop at
the name of the diagnosis.
Look at function. What can the person
safely do today that they could once do
alone? That recognition is often the
missing piece. Now, we need to kill one
myth completely. A combined rating of
does not mean the math is finished.
Combined ratings and special monthly
compensation run on entirely separate
tracks. Your combined rating comes from
the VA's formula for stacking multiple
service connected conditions against
each other. That calculation caps at
100%. SMC does not run through that
formula. It is a flat, statutorily
defined addition, layered on top of
whatever your combined rating already
produced. That is exactly why somebody
can be sitting at the maximum rating and
still see monthly compensation increase
substantially once SMC is added
correctly. And there is another detail
veterans rarely hear. These payments can
stack. Qualifying under one category
does not automatically cancel
eligibility under another. A veteran
with more than one qualifying condition
can, in the right circumstances, receive
more than one additional payment at the
same time. This is one of those details
the system will not sit down and explain
to you. A good accredited claims
representative can catch it. Now, put
actual money behind the words. Based on
the VA's published compensation rate
tables, a veteran rated at 100% who also
qualifies for SMC at the aid and
attendance level, can see a combined
monthly total well above $5,000 for a
single veteran with no dependents. Add a
spouse or children and that number
climbs further. At the lower SMCK tier,
loss of use of a single limb or organ
adds a smaller but still meaningful
fixed amount every month on top of the
existing check. And it stacks regardless
of overall rating. Veterans who
successfully file for aid and attendance
typically see monthly compensation
increase by several hundred dollars,
often somewhere between $400 and $900 a
month depending on prior rating and
dependency status.
Run that over 1 year, several thousand
dollars. Run it over a decade, tens of
thousands. That money either reaches the
veteran or it quietly disappears, one
unfiled month at a time. And none of it
is taxable. VA VA
compensation and special monthly
compensation are excluded from gross
income under title 26 of the federal tax
code. Whatever you claim, you keep in
full. Now, picture Gerald. Gerald is 67
years old, retired Army infantry, living
in Knoxville, Tennessee. He has a 70%
combined rating for knee damage, a lower
back injury, and documented hearing
loss. Gerald has collected his monthly
disability check for 11 years. He walks
with a cane. On his worst pain days, he
cannot safely bathe without help. But,
he never filed for special monthly
compensation because he assumed the
existing rating already accounted for
everything he was owed. Gerald did
nothing wrong. He is exactly the veteran
this program exists for. And, he has
been leaving money on the table for more
than a decade because nobody told him
the second layer existed. Now, compare
him with Walter. Walter is 79 and rated
at 100% for a combination of
service-connected conditions, including
severe COPD. He stopped driving 3 years
ago because his oxygen levels dropped
too fast outside the house. On bad air
quality days, he does not leave his
bedroom. His daughter checks on him by
phone every morning instead of in
person. And, Walter's explanation is
painfully common. There wasn't anything
more the VA could give me anyway. I'm
already at the top. Walter is wrong.
And, he is far from alone. A 100% rating
tells the VA how severe his conditions
are. It does not answer whether those
conditions have confined him to his
home. The housebound category exists
specifically for that second fact.
Walter never filed because nobody
explained that his rating and his
housebound status are two different
questions. That is the pattern. You
cannot file for a benefit you were never
taught to recognize. So, here's what I
want you to do. The exemptions, the
breaks, the refunds most seniors already
qualify for but never claim. I've put
them all in one place, state by state,
form by form, so you don't waste hours
digging through government sites.
Everything's laid out fast and simple,
so any senior can find exactly what
applies to them. No matter what state
you're in, there's money you're leaving
on the table. It's called the Senior
Exemption Playbook. It's in the first
pinned comment right below this video.
Just tap it once and you'll have
everything you need. Now, stay with me
because knowing that SMC exists is only
half the battle. The paperwork is where
good claims get lost. Most veterans who
get denied on their first SMC attempt
did not necessarily fail to meet the
eligibility rules. They failed to submit
the specific documentation the VA
requires to prove those rules are met.
That distinction is enormous. A denial
letter is not necessarily saying you do
not qualify. It is saying the evidence
submitted at that particular moment did
not establish eligibility. Those are
different things, and the second one can
be fixed. Take Miriam. Miriam is 72, a
retired Army nurse from Albuquerque, New
Mexico, carrying a 70% combined rating
for bilateral knee replacements. Her
daughter Patricia moved in 3 years ago
after two falls made living alone
unsafe. Miriam filed for Aid and
Attendance on her own. She was denied.
The rejection letter said her medical
records did not establish a need for
regular assistance with daily
activities, not because she did not need
the help. Her paperwork simply never
documented which activities she could
not safely perform alone. Then Miriam
brought in a VA accredited claims agent.
The agent helped her obtain a detailed
functional statement from her
orthopedist and a written buddy
statement from Patricia describing
exactly what daily help she provided. On
appeal, Miriam's claim was approved. Her
monthly compensation rose by over $500.
Nothing about Miriam's condition changed
between the denial and approval. Only
the paperwork did. That is the lesson.
Do not make the VA guess. A medical note
saying a veteran has difficulty with
daily activities is not enough by
itself. What moves the claim forward is
a statement from a physician, nurse
practitioner, or another licensed
provider naming the exact activities the
veteran cannot safely perform without
help and tying those limitations
directly to a service-connected
condition. Buddy statements matter, too.
Under 38 USC 5107,
the VA must weigh lay evidence. That
means a spouse, adult child, or neighbor
with firsthand knowledge of a veteran's
daily limitations can submit a written
statement that genuinely strengthens the
claim. Describe what actually happens,
not vague difficulty. What help? Why is
it unsafe alone? Specific beats vague
every time. Once the claim is filed, the
VA typically schedules a compensation
and pension exam, or C&P exam. That exam
may be performed by a VA physician or a
contracted examiner. Its purpose is to
evaluate the functional limitations
connected to the claim. So, do not walk
into that room and describe only your
best day. Many veterans minimize
symptoms out of pride or habit. If a bad
day means you need help getting out of
the shower, describe the bad days
accurately. The examiner is trying to
capture your actual limitations, not
your toughest performance for a
stranger. After the exam, a rating
officer reviews the full file including
the physician's statement, buddy
statements, and C&P findings. Then a
decision is issued. This entire process
commonly takes several months, and that
is why the filing date matters. Every
month between filing and decision
becomes retroactive back pay once the
claim is approved, but only counting
from the date you filed. Write that date
down. Do not trust yourself to remember
it 6 months later. Before we get to the
exact filing steps, there are four
distinctions that can save you from
going down the wrong road. First,
special monthly compensation is not
special monthly pension. The names sound
almost identical. The programs are not.
SMC is paid on top of service connected
disability compensation and requires no
income limit. Special monthly pension is
a needs-based benefit for wartime
veterans with limited income and net
worth. It runs under completely
different rules. Veterans and families
confuse the two, apply for the wrong
program, and get frustrated by a denial
that may have nothing to do with their
actual eligibility. Make sure the form
matches the program. If you are unsure,
a free accredited representative can
answer that question in a single phone
call before you file. Second, these
benefits are not limited to living
veterans. Surviving spouses of veterans
who died from a service-connected
condition may qualify for dependency and
indemnity compensation. Within that
program, a surviving spouse who needs
regular help with daily activities can
qualify for an aid and attendance
addition of their own. That addition is
calculated on a separate schedule from
the veteran's original SMC. Families
dealing with the loss of a veteran
rarely think about benefit research in
the middle of everything else. Grief
does not leave much room for paperwork.
If you are a surviving spouse, or you
know one, this is worth a phone call to
a VSO on its own. Third, understand what
filing will and will not do. You do not
need a lawyer to file a first claim,
though one can help with a denied claim
if you prefer that route. There is no
deadline that permanently closes SMC
off. You can file at any point in your
life, even decades after the original
rating was established. Applying does
not put your existing disability rating
at risk of being reduced or reviewed. An
SMC claim is additive, not a
reevaluation of what you already have.
And none of this requires exaggeration.
It requires documentation. Your medical
providers and your daily life should
show the truth. Document that truth.
Fourth, a denial is not the final word.
Under the Appeals Modernization Act,
veterans have three separate paths
forward. A supplemental claim lane
allows new evidence. A higher-level
review lane requests a fresh look at the
existing evidence. And the third path is
an appeal directly to the Board of
Veterans Appeals. Each path has its own
timeline and procedure. All three exist
so a first denial does not automatically
become permanent. And be careful about
who offers to recover this money for
you. You never have to pay anyone a fee
up front to pursue any of this. VA
accredited attorneys handling SMC claims
and appeals are regulated under 38 USC
and 38 CFR 14.636.
They are legally barred from charging
anything before a decision is made. They
collect a fee from retroactive back pay
only after a favorable outcome, and that
fee is capped by federal regulation.
Veteran service organizations such as
the DAV, the VFW, the American Legion,
and state-level veterans agencies
provide claims assistance completely
free of charge. That help can continue
from the first application through a
full appeal. If somebody outside those
accredited channels offers to recover
the money for a percentage, walk away.
The people doing this correctly can help
through the accredited system. Military
retirees need one more distinction.
Special monthly compensation is not
concurrent retirement and disability pay
or combat-related special compensation.
Those programs deal with how military
retirement pay interacts with VA
disability pay when a veteran also
receives a pension. They run through the
Department of Defense rather than the
VA's disability rating system. A retired
veteran can potentially qualify for SMC
in one of those retirement pay programs
at the same time because they solve
different problems. But, the
applications and rules are separate. If
somebody mentions concurrent receipt, do
not automatically fold that into an SMC
claim. It deserves a separate
conversation with an accredited
representative. Now, here are the seven
filing moves I want you to remember.
Step one, build the package before you
open a form. Pull together your most
recent VA rating decision letter, your
discharge paperwork, and any VA or
private medical records that speak
directly to the condition you believe
qualifies you. The wrong approach is
filing something incomplete and planning
to fill the gaps later. Build the
package first. Open the folder and look
at it. Rating decision, discharge
paperwork, medical evidence. If one
piece is missing, you know before the
claim starts. Complete first, submit
second. Step two, use the right forms.
For aid and attendance and housebound
status, the primary form is VA form
Your treating physician completes it and
you submit it with the claim. If you are
[clears throat] adding SMC onto an
existing disability rating, you will
also likely need VA form 21-526EZ,
the standard application used to
initiate or update a disability
compensation claim. Both forms are
available directly on va.gov by
searching the exact form numbers. Do not
guess at the form 21-2680-21526EZ.
Match the paperwork to what you are
actually claiming. Step three, call a
veteran service organization before you
submit. The DAV's toll-free line is
And the VFW maintains accredited
benefits specialists in every state.
Tell them plainly that you are filing
for special monthly compensation. Name
the specific category you believe
applies. Then ask them to review your
documentation package before you send
it. The call is free, and it
dramatically reduces the odds of a
preventable denial. One review before
submission can expose a gap you did not
know was there. Step four, make the
physician describe function, not just
diagnosis. Ask your treating physician
to complete form 21-2680
with a written narrative. The narrative
should name the specific daily
activities you cannot safely perform
without help. Then it should tie those
limitations directly to your service
connected condition. A diagnosis alone
leaves the rating officer to connect the
dots. Specificity removes the guesswork.
Bathing, dressing, eating, moving
safely. Say what actually requires help.
Step five, submit the claim and record
the exact filing date. You can submit
through the va.gov online portal or in
person at your regional office. Then,
write down the date. That is the date
your potential back pay begins counting
from. If the claim takes 6 months to
process and is approved, you receive 6
months of retroactive payment on top of
your new ongoing monthly amount, but it
counts from the date you filed, not the
date your condition originally began.
The filing date starts the clock. Do not
lose it. Step six, keep a paper trail.
Save copies of every document you
submit. Log the date and name of every
phone call. If the VA requests
additional evidence, respond within the
deadline stated in the letter. A missed
response window can produce a denial
even when the underlying proof exists.
The proof simply never reached the file
in time. You should be able to put your
hands on every document you sent. If you
cannot, rebuild that record now. Paper
trail, every time. Step seven, keep
documenting even after approval. Aid and
attendance is not always treated as
permanent, especially when it is tied to
a condition that could theoretically
improve. The VA may schedule a future
reexamination to confirm that the need
for regular assistance still exists. So,
do not throw the paperwork into a drawer
and forget about it. Keep documenting.
If the condition changes, better or
worse, update the file proactively. That
can protect against an unexpected
reduction. And if the situation
genuinely worsens, updated evidence can
support a higher payment. Treat approval
as the beginning of an ongoing record,
not a one-time transaction. So, here is
the whole method. First, understand that
SMC is separate from your disability
percentage. Then, identify the actual
trigger, loss or loss of use, loss of
use of a reproductive organ, housebound
status, aid and attendance, or eligible
dependents. Look at function, not just
diagnosis. Document the exact daily
limitation. Use the correct form. Have
an accredited representative review the
package. Record your filing date. Keep
the paper trail. And if you are denied,
read what evidence was missing before
assuming the answer is no. Every piece
is now in front of you. The program
name, the legal authority, the payment
structure, the triggers, the
documentation, the appeals process, the
forms, but none of that changes anything
while it sits on a screen. The value
appears when somebody acts on it. That
is what self-reliance looks like inside
a system built around claims. Not
knowing every law by heart, knowing
enough to ask the right question, keep
the right paperwork, and make sure a
benefit somebody earned does not
disappear simply because nobody told
them to file for it. There are veterans
in every state, at every rating, sitting
on eligibility for this right now. Some
of them for years. The VA is never going
to call and tell them. The check does
not arrive because it is deserved. It
arrives because someone files for it
correctly with the right paperwork
behind it. Before you leave, tell me
something specific in the comments.
Which part of this was new to you? Loss
of use, housebound status, aid and
attendance, dependents, or the fact that
SMC can stack above a 100% rating. And
if you are helping a parent, spouse, or
another veteran navigate this, tell me
that, too. I read every single one. That
single piece of paper can tell you far
more than most people realize. I am no
licensed expert, so make sure to check
all information with verified sources
before you make a move.

connecting thread across all three rules
is this: The institutions processing
your direct deposit, your bank, your

Patricia paying $172
she never owed and Patricia keeping it.

challenging the referral before his next
payday. A question I get constantly is
whether closing an account and opening a

account hold exceptions rather than
avoiding them. Offsets are tied to your

itself, not to any particular bank or

a different bank doesn't remove you from
the Bureau of the Fiscal Service
database. The only thing that actually

kitchen table. She doesn't use a banking
app. 2 days after that test charge, the
real draining began. An electronics
purchase, a batch of online gift cards,
a transfer to an offshore payment
processor. Over roughly 3 weeks, $8,400
moved out of her account while she
tended her garden and visited her
grandchildren completely unaware. Her
statement cut on the 15th was processed
and printed by the bank and arrived in
her mailbox on the 20th, five full days
after it was even generated. On top of
the three weeks that had already passed
while the theft was underway, by the
time she sat down at her kitchen table
on a quiet Sunday afternoon and traced
her finger down the column of charges,
the damage was already done. She called
the number on the back of her card, sat
through an automated menu, and was told
a fraud investigation would open with a
federally mandated window of up to 10
business days before any provisional
credit would even be considered. In the
meantime, her property tax check
bounced, her automatic electric bill
payment failed, her account was frozen
while the investigation proceeded, and
she had to borrow grocery money from her
daughter. And here's the part that
matters most for this record
specifically. Because her savings was
linked to checking for overdraft
coverage, the bank had already begun
quietly pulling from that savings
balance to keep the fraudulent charges
clearing before she ever picked up the
phone. What should have been a contained
loss, limited to whatever cash sat in
checking that month, became a much
larger one simply because of a setting
she'd agreed to years earlier and never
thought about again. Updating this
particular record takes one phone call.
You tell your bank you want to formally
opt out of any overdraft coverage that
draws from a linked savings account.
Under the Electronic Funds Transfer Act,
that request is a right you already
have, and the bank cannot legally refuse
it. They will read you a script warning
about declined transactions and returned
item fees. Let them read it.
A declined charge at the register is a
minor inconvenience you can solve on the
spot. A drained retirement account is
not something you solve on the spot. A
declined transaction in this specific
situation is quite literally your last
working line of defense once every other
safeguard has already failed. The second
record most people never think to
revisit is the list of automatic
payments still quietly running on a
debit card. Think for a moment about how
many companies actually have your card
numbers sitting on file for a
set-it-and-forget-it
payment. The electric company, the cable
or internet provider, a streaming
subscription you signed up for years
ago, maybe a Medicare supplemental
premium, or a life insurance policy.
It's convenient, which is exactly why
almost nobody revisits it. But merchant
databases get breached constantly, and
when a retailer or subscription platform
gets hit, hackers rarely walk away with
just one card number. They walk away
with millions all at once in bulk.
Because your card is already tied to
recurring charges on that account, a
fraudulent transaction sized to resemble
a normal utility bill or a routine
subscription renewal can slide right
past a bank's automated fraud filters
without tripping a single alarm. It
blends in with everything else on the
page. By the time anyone actually
notices, the reporting window has
frequently already closed, and the money
is simply gone for good. There's also a
slower quieter version of the same
problem. Banks periodically reissue
debit card numbers, sometimes after any
reported breach, and every single
merchant with your old number on file
has to be updated one at a time manually
by you. Miss even one, and either a bill
silently fails to pay, generating its
own late fees and the risk of a service
interruption, or worse, an old number
that should have been fully deactivated
still has just enough life left in the
system
to be exploited before the bank finishes
closing it out completely. A quieter
version of this same problem has nothing
to do with hackers at all. And it's
worth mentioning here because it hides
in the exact same list. A free trial
signed up for years ago converts into a
small monthly charge that nobody
remembers agreeing to. A streaming
service raises its price a dollar or two
every year and the increase never gets
questioned because the total still looks
roughly like what it always looked like
on the statement. None of that is fraud
in the legal sense, but it lives on the
same debit card buried in the same list
and it compounds in exactly the same
way. A little at a time, unnoticed,
until a full accounting of the list
turns up. Two or three subscriptions
nobody actively uses anymore, sometimes
adding up to 50 or 60 dollars a month in
charges nobody would actively choose to
keep paying if they were looking at the
list fresh. Fixing this record is a
Sunday afternoon project, not a phone
call. Pull your last three statements
and physically list every company
drafting your account automatically. For
anything currently pulling from a debit
card, log into that account directly and
switch the payment method over to a
credit card instead. A fraudulent charge
there draws against the bank's money
first, not yours, while any dispute gets
sorted out and you're never actually out
the cash while it's being investigated.
For anything that has to pull directly
from a checking account by routing
number, such as certain insurance
premiums or mortgage, consider routing
those specific payments through a small
separate checking account that holds
only enough to cover that month's bills,
kept entirely apart from your primary
savings. If that secondary account is
ever compromised, a thief can only reach
whatever happens to be sitting in it for
the month and your actual life savings
never enters the picture at all. It's
worth asking, honestly, why a bank would
ever let a setting this risky stay
switched on by default for years without
a single check-in call. The answer isn't
complicated once you look at the
incentives involved. A debit card
transaction is enormously profitable for
a bank because it collects a swipe fee
from the merchant on every single
purchase while carrying almost none of
the risk itself. A credit card is the
opposite. The bank is lending you its
own money for 30 days. So, if that card
gets stolen, the loss lands on the
bank's balance sheet, not yours. That's
exactly why debit cards get handed out
by default the moment you open a
checking account. Why banks dangle cash
back offers and round up savings
programs to keep you swiping them daily.
And why so few institutions ever
proactively call a long-time customer to
say, "You may want to revisit that
overdraft link you set up back in 2004."
There's simply no financial incentive on
their end to start that conversation.
Closing these gaps has always quietly
been left to the account holder, whether
or not anyone ever explained that up
front. The Federal Trade Commission's
own fraud data backs this up plainly.
Consumers lose billions of dollars to
fraud every year in this country, and
bank transfers and direct payments
consistently account for some of the
largest total losses of any category
tracked. Older adults are
disproportionately targeted for a fairly
straightforward reason. Decades of
steady saving means there's simply more
sitting in the account to take. And a
continued reliance on paper statements
over real-time banking apps builds in
exactly the kind of reporting delay that
a 60-day liability clock is practically
designed to exploit. None of that
reflects poorly on anyone's judgment or
attentiveness. It's simply how the
incentives line up on both sides of this
equation. And understanding that is most
of the battle when it comes to deciding
to close the gap yourself instead of
waiting on someone else to do it. A bank
will always meet its minimum legal
obligation once fraud has already
happened. It has far less reason to help
you prevent that fraud in the first
place. And that gap between the minimum
required response and genuine prevention
is exactly where these three records
tend to sit unnoticed for years at a
time. So, here's what I want you to do.
The exemptions, the breaks, the refunds
most seniors already qualify for but
never claim. I've put them all in one
place state by state, form by form, so
you don't waste hours digging through
government sites. Everything's laid out
fast and simple, so any senior can find
exactly what applies to them. No matter
what state you're in, there's money
you're leaving on the table. It's called
the Senior Exemption Playbook. It's in
the first pinned comment right below
this video. Just tap it once and you'll
have everything you need. Now, stay
right here because the third record is
the one that quietly costs families the
most money of all. And it's the reason I
made this whole video. Before we get to
the third record, it helps to understand
why this problem even exists in the
first place because the answer explains
almost everything else in this video. A
credit card and a debit card sit side by
side in your wallet, look identical,
weigh the same, and slide into the exact
same machine at checkout. But legally,
they are governed by two completely
different laws written a decade apart
with two completely different
assumptions baked into them. Congress
passed the Truth in Lending Act back in
when credit cards were expanding rapidly
and built it around a simple idea. A
credit card represents the bank's money.
If a criminal steals a credit card
number, they're taking an unsecured loan
from a major financial institution, and
that institution has every incentive in
the world to chase it down because every
dollar stolen comes straight off its own
bottom line. Liability for the card
holder was capped at $50 permanently. A
decade later in 1978, Congress wrote a
separate law for the new world of ATMs
and point of sale terminals, the
Electronic Funds Transfer Act. But a
debit card doesn't move the bank's
money, it moves yours. The bank is a
custodian here, not a lender, and its
legal obligation is procedural rather
than financial. That one difference in
the underlying law is the reason one
card in your wallet protects you almost
completely, and the identical looking
card right next to it does not. That
difference is exactly what happened to a
retired teacher I'll call Harold. He had
$22,000 sitting in his checking account
after selling a classic car. A hotel
reservation database breach exposed his
debit card number, and on the 10th of
the month a hacker ran a small $20 test
charge against a fake online charity. It
landed on a statement mailed out on the
15th, buried on page three between a
hardware store receipt and a grocery
bill. Harold missed it completely.
Federal law gives him 60 calendar days
from that statement date to catch and
report an unauthorized charge before his
liability protection expires.
And that clock quietly started ticking
the moment the statement went out, not
the day he opened the envelope. The
hacker did nothing for two months
because professional fraud rings
understand this exact deadline better
than most consumers ever will. Six days
after Harold's protection lapsed, they
came back and moved $19,000 out of his
account in under 48 hours. Because he
had missed that first $20 charge, on
paper every dollar taken after the
60-day mark was gone for good, with the
bank under no legal obligation to return
a single cent of it. Run that identical
scenario with a credit card instead of a
debit card, and the math flips entirely.
Same hacker, same hotel breach, same $20
test charge, same $19,000 theft. 2
months later, under the Truth in Lending
Act, Harold's liability stays capped at
$50, regardless of how many days have
passed. Because a credit card draws on
the bank's money, not his own. And the
law treats it accordingly. There's a
second layer of protection built on top
of that cap as well. Under the Fair
Credit Billing Act, Harold would have
had the right to formally dispute the
charges and withhold payment on the
disputed amount while the investigation
ran its course. Meaning, he never has to
hand over a single dollar of his own
cash while the matter gets sorted out.
His checking account and the $22,000
sitting inside it would never have been
touched at all. That's the entire
difference between the two cards sitting
side by side in the same wallet. One
asks the bank to absorb the risk it's
actually built to absorb, and the other
quietly hands that same risk straight
back to you. That brings us to the third
record, and it isn't a number or a
linked account at all. It's how your
bank is actually allowed to reach you
when something goes wrong. If your bank
is only mailing you a single paper
statement once a month, you are, by
design, always going to be closer to
that 60-day cliff than you realize.
Because an entire billing cycle can pass
before you even see the first sign of
trouble. Call your bank and turn on
real-time transactional alerts by text
message or email for any withdrawal
above a small threshold you set
yourself, something like $25 or $50.
Most banks can set this up during the
very same call as the overdraft change,
without requiring you to download or
learn a new mobile app if that isn't
something you're comfortable with. A
plain text alert sent to an ordinary
cell phone works exactly as well as a
push notification through an app. That
single change turns a 2-week blind spot
into a same-day notice, and it costs
absolutely nothing to set up. It is
quite simply the fastest and cheapest
fix on this entire list. While we're on
the subject of staying ahead of a
problem instead of cleaning up after it,
a few more things are worth knowing
because they rarely come up in the same
conversation as a bank statement. You're
entitled to a completely free credit
freeze with each of the three major
credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian, and
TransUnion, which stops new accounts
from being opened in your name without
your direct approval, and it costs
nothing to place or lift whenever you
need to. Each bureau has to be contacted
separately, since freezing one does not
automatically freeze the other two. The
Federal Trade Commission runs a
dedicated reporting portal for exactly
this kind of theft at
reportfraud.ftc.gov,
and filing a report there creates an
official record that can matter a great
deal later if a bank drags its feet on
an investigation it's required to
complete. The Department of Justice also
operates a national elder fraud hotline
staffed specifically to help older
adults navigate reporting and recovery
after this kind of theft, entirely at no
cost, and staff there can often point
you toward the correct next step faster
than a general customer service line
will. And if a bank denies a legitimate
claim outright or slow walks a
Regulation E investigation past its own
10 business day window, the Consumer
Financial Protection Bureau accepts
direct complaints against the
institution itself, a route that tends
to get a bank's compliance department
moving considerably faster than a second
call to the regular customer service
line ever will. Keep a simple written
log of every call you make during any of
this. The date, the representative's
name, and what was promised since the
bank's own notes on a file are rarely as
complete as the record you can keep
yourself. One more record is worth
mentioning briefly, even though it falls
just outside our main three. Most banks
and brokerage firms now let you
designate what's called a trusted
contact on the account. Someone the
institution is permitted to reach out to
if they notice unusual activity or a
sudden pattern that looks like
exploitation without granting that
person any access to the money itself.
It costs nothing to add, takes about 5
minutes over the phone, and gives your
bank one more legitimate way to catch a
problem early instead of watching it
unfold in silence for 2 months. Two
related records get overlooked just as
often and they deserve a mention here as
well. If you've added an adult child to
a checking account as a joint owner
years ago, purely for convenience during
an illness or a trip, that person
retains full access and full liability
exposure on the account indefinitely,
long after the original reason for
adding them has passed. It's worth
revisiting whether a joint account is
still the right tool or whether a
limited power of attorney would
accomplish the same convenience without
leaving another name permanently
attached to every dollar in the account.
And if a power of attorney is already on
file at your bank, it's worth confirming
the branch actually has the current
version. Banks sometimes hold on to an
outdated copy for years after a family
updates the document with an attorney,
which can create real delays exactly
when a family member needs to step in
and help. A quick call to ask the branch
to pull up whatever document they
currently have on file and compare it
against the most recent copy in your own
records. Takes only a few minutes and
closes a gap that otherwise tends to
surface at the worst possible moment,
usually during a hospital stay when
nobody has the time or the composure to
sort out paperwork discrepancies with a
bank. A quick example of what it looks
like when these three records actually
get fixed in time is worth mentioning
here. A retired postal worker I'll call
Ruth had the exact same overdraft link
Margaret did. The exact same forgotten
debit card auto pays and the exact same
paper only statement preference, but her
daughter had watched a video almost
identical to this one and spent a
Saturday afternoon walking her through
all three changes. Four months later, a
merchant Ruth had a streaming
subscription with was breached and a
fraudulent charge appeared against her
card within days. Because real-time
alerts were switched on, she saw the
text message the same afternoon and
called her bank before the sun went
down. Because overdraft coverage from
savings had been turned off, the charge
simply declined once it exceeded what
was left in checking and nothing beyond
that ever moved. The entire incident
cost her roughly $40 and about 20
minutes on the phone. Nothing about her
situation was different from Margaret's
except that the three records had
already been updated before the fraud
ever arrived. So, let's put the whole
thing back together into a sequence you
can actually follow this weekend.
Because updating three records is
genuinely a single afternoon of work,
not a project that drags on for weeks.
Begin with a single phone call to your
bank about overdraft settings. Tell the
representative directly that you want to
opt out of any overdraft coverage that
draws from a linked savings account and
ask them to confirm the change in
writing either by email or through your
online account messages, so there's a
clear record the request was actually
processed and not just noted verbally.
Move next to your automatic payments and
treat it as a short audit rather than a
memory exercise. Pull your last three
statements side by side and write down
every company drafting your account
automatically along with the amount and
the data typically hits. For anything
currently pulling from a debit card, log
in to that specific merchant account and
switch the payment method over to a
credit card. For anything that legally
must stay tied to a checking account and
routing number, move that particular
payment to a small separate checking
account holding only enough to cover
that month's bills kept entirely apart
from where your real savings lives.
Finish with your alert preferences and
be specific rather than general when you
set them up. Ask your bank to enable
real-time text or email alerts for any
single withdrawal above a threshold you
choose yourself, whether that's $25,
$50, or whatever number makes sense for
your typical spending. While you're on
that same call, ask whether a trusted
contact can be added to the account
since it costs nothing and takes only a
few extra minutes once the
representative already has your file
open. None of these calls costs a fee,
none of them requires a lawyer or a
financial advisor to carry out on your
behalf. Every single one of them shifts
risk away from your family and back onto
the institution that is actually
equipped, staffed, and legally
positioned to absorb it. None of this is
about distrusting your bank and it isn't
about assuming the worst of anyone
behind the counter. It's about
recognizing that the default settings on
your account were written for a version
of banking that existed decades ago.
Back when a stolen wallet was something
you'd notice the very same afternoon and
a monthly paper statement was the
fastest way anyone had to check their
own balance. Banking has changed
dramatically since those settings were
first put in place, but the settings
themselves rarely get revisited once
they're switched on, especially on an
account that's been open for 20 or 30
years and has quietly outlived the
branch manager who originally opened it.
Nobody is coming to update these three
records for you, and no employee at your
branch is measured on how much risk they
found and removed from your file before
you walked in the door. That part has
always quietly been the customer's job,
whether or not anyone ever bothered to
say so out loud. This matters most at
exactly the moments in life when it's
hardest to think about, right after a
spouse passes away and the mail starts
piling up on the dining room table,
during a hospital stay when statements
sit unopened for weeks, or during a long
winter trip when mail forwarding runs
behind schedule. Those are precisely the
gaps a 60-day clock is built to exploit,
and they're also precisely the moments
when nobody has the bandwidth to think
about a banking setting from 2004.
That's exactly why this is worth doing
now on an ordinary week while nothing
urgent is happening and there's nothing
competing for your attention. You've
spent decades building what's sitting in
those accounts. An hour this weekend
made on a calm day rather than a hard
one is genuinely all it takes to make
sure three old settings can't quietly
undo it later. Take care of yourselves
and go check those three settings this
week.

title: Disabled Veteran Over 60? Your VA Check Could Freeze When You Die — How to Protect Your Spouse

segments.text: Somewhere inside a VA file right now,
there's a check with your name on it.
Not one you're collecting, one your
spouse is supposed to collect the day
you die. Except most spouses never see a
single dollar of it. Not because they
don't qualify, because nobody ever sat
the veteran down and explained what to
file, when to file it, or why the clock
on this benefit is already running right
now while he's still alive. My name is
Lana Maines. I'm no expert, but I spend
my time breaking down the financial side
of veterans benefits. The parts nobody
explains at the rating exam, the parts
that only show up as a problem after
it's too late to fix them. I am here to
give you the kind of financial
information that actually protects the
people who depend on you. So, if that's
useful, hit subscribe because I cover
exactly this. One benefit, one form, one
mistake at a time, every single week.
Let's start with the part that catches
almost every veteran off guard. Under
federal law, VA disability compensation
is paid to you, the veteran, for your
service-connected disabilities. It is
not a household benefit. It is not a
joint payment. It is not part of your
estate. Title 38 of the United States
Code is explicit about this. The legal
authority for that payment exists only
as long as you're alive to receive it.
The moment you die, it terminates. Not
reduced, not paused, terminated. It does
not matter if you're rated at 100%.
It does not matter if you're permanently
and totally disabled. It does not matter
if that check has been hitting your
account every month for 30 years. The
day you die, it stops, and your spouse
does not inherit what's left of it,
because there is nothing left of it to
inherit. Look at what that means in real
numbers. A veteran rated at 100%
receives somewhere around $3,830
a month in 2025, depending on dependent
status. A veteran at 70% is closer to
A lot of veteran households run on that
income as their primary source. Some run
on it as their only source. And the day
the veteran passes, that number goes to
zero without warning, without a
transition period, without so much as a
phone call. The VA will not call your
spouse to walk her through what happens
next. There is no letter that arrives in
advance explaining the process. If a
payment happens to get deposited after
the date of death, the VA will actually
require that money to be returned. The
system is built to pay the veteran while
the veteran is alive. What happens to
the family after that is an entirely
separate program with an entirely
separate application that somebody has
to know to file. You will not hear this
explained at your compensation and
pension exam. You will not find it laid
out clearly on the VA's main benefits
page. That's not a conspiracy. It's just
how the system is built. It processes
what gets filed in front of it. Nobody
there is evaluated on how well they
prepared your family for the day you're
gone. Now, here's the part that matters
most because it's also the part that
gives you room to act. Your spouse is
not without options. There's a federal
program called Dependency and Indemnity
Compensation, DIC for short,
administered by the VA and paid monthly
to qualifying surviving spouses. The
current base rate sits somewhere around
a month, and it's tax-free. That's over
$20,000 a year your spouse would never
owe a dollar of tax on. DIC also isn't
needs-based and isn't tied to your
spouse's income or assets. A wealthy
household and a struggling one receive
the exact same base amount if they
qualify. But qualifying is the catch,
and it's the catch that quietly costs
families everything. Your spouse does
not receive DIC automatically because
you were a veteran. She does not receive
it automatically because you died.
Qualification comes down to one of two
specific paths, and both of those paths
depend on decisions you make while
you're still alive. That's the entire
structure of this problem in one
sentence. The benefit is real, the
qualification depends on you, and you
will not be here to fix it once it's
missed. Let's go through both paths
because most veterans have only ever
heard of one if they've heard of either
at all. Path one is what's commonly
called the 10-year rule, and it comes
from 38 USC Section 1318. If a veteran
has been continuously rated at 100%
or at the combined level that meets the
statutory threshold for 10 or more
consecutive years immediately before
death, the surviving spouse qualifies
for DIC no matter what actually caused
the death. Read that again. No matter
what caused the death. Your spouse does
not have to prove your death connects to
your service in any way. The length of
time you carried that rating creates the
qualification entirely on its own.
Picture a veteran currently rated at 80%
who's held that rating for 7 years. His
spouse does not qualify under path one
yet. Three years remain on that clock,
and the clock only moves forward. It
never runs backward, and it never gives
back time a veteran spent underrated
because he never filed the claim that
would have gotten him there sooner.
Here's where veterans lose that window
without ever realizing it. A veteran
reaches 60 or 70% feels grateful for
what he has and stops filing. He doesn't
want to look like he's working the
system, so the clock never starts
because the rating never reaches the
level that starts it. Every condition
that's real, service connected in fact,
but never claimed on paper is a
condition that isn't counted. If it
isn't filed, it isn't rated. If it isn't
rated, it doesn't count toward that
10-year window. Open your va.gov account
today. Not last year's letter, the
actual current rating sitting in your
file right now, and find the effective
date on your combined rating. That date
is when your clock started ticking,
whether you knew it or not. Path 2
doesn't require 10 years at all, which
is exactly why most veterans need to
hear about it. This one comes from 38
USC section 1310. If a veteran dies from
a condition the VA has already
recognized as service connected, the
surviving spouse qualifies for DIC. Your
rating percentage at the time of death
doesn't matter here. The number of years
you carried that rating doesn't matter
either. If the condition that caused
your death was on your service connected
list before you died, your spouse
qualifies. Full stop. Heart disease is
the leading cause of death among men in
the United States, and it isn't close.
It rarely shows up announced.
Hypertension feeds into it. Untreated
sleep apnea feeds into it. Chronic
stress and elevated cortisol from
something like PTSD feed into it.
Diabetes accelerates it. Weight gain
from medications prescribed for other
service connected conditions can feed
into it, too. There is substantial
research tying each of these to military
service. The physical toll, the
disrupted sleep cycles, environmental
and toxic exposures, and the sustained
psychological load that comes with the
job. So, ask yourself the same three
questions I ask every veteran who
watches this.
Do you have high blood pressure? Is it
service connected? Do you have sleep
apnea? Is it service connected? Do you
have any cardiac condition at all?
Arrhythmia, coronary artery disease, a
prior heart attack? Is it service
connected? If the answer to the first
part of any of those is yes and the
second part is no, path two currently
offers your spouse zero protection.
There's a version of this most people
never think to check. Ischemic heart
disease is a presumptive condition tied
to certain toxic exposures including
Agent Orange. If you served in a
qualifying window and location and
you've since developed a heart
condition, the connection may already be
legally presumed under the law. You may
not even need to build a causal case
from scratch. Most veterans never look
because nobody ever tells them to. Take
a veteran named Gerald. He's 64, a
retired Army infantry sergeant from
outside Fayetteville, North Carolina.
He's been rated 70% for a back condition
and a knee condition since 2017. He's
also had hypertension for 11 years,
medicated daily and never once filed a
claim for it. Because he figured a blood
pressure prescription wasn't worth the
paperwork. Gerald hasn't reached 10
years on a qualifying rating. So path
one doesn't cover his spouse yet. And if
Gerald has a fatal cardiac event
tomorrow, path two won't cover her
either because the condition that would
have killed him was never on his service
connected list. Gerald didn't do
anything wrong. He just never filed the
one claim that would have closed the
gap. Now let's talk about a piece almost
nobody brings up because it isn't the
headline benefit, it's the one stacked
quietly on top of it. Under 38 USC
section 1311, there's a supplemental DIC
payment available to surviving spouses
who meet one additional condition. If
the veteran was rated at 100% or the
qualifying combined threshold for a
continuous period of at least eight
years immediately before death and the
veteran and spouse were married to each
other for that entire eight-year
stretch, the surviving spouse receives
an extra payment of roughly $360 a month
on top of the base DIC amount every
month for the rest of her life. This
bonus doesn't require 10 years. It
doesn't require that the death itself be
service connected. It requires eight
continuous years at the qualifying
rating, an unbroken marriage through
that period, and a surviving spouse who
actually knows to claim it because the
VA does not calculate this automatically
and apply it for her. It has to be
requested on the application itself in
writing. And here's where it compounds.
If your spouse qualifies under path one
and also meets the 8-year marriage
requirement, she receives both amounts
together. The base DIC payment plus the
$360 supplement stacked. That's
meaningful monthly income for someone
who may be managing a household
completely on her own for the first
time. There is also a version of this
most families never think to ask about.
What happens if you have a claim sitting
open unresolved the moment you die? It
doesn't just vanish. There's a process
called substitution where your spouse
can legally step into your place and
continue the exact claim you already
started using VA form 21-0847,
request for substitution of claimant.
She has 1 year from your date of death
to file it. If that claim gets approved
after you're gone, she can collect the
retroactive back pay that would have
been yours, and an approved rating from
that claim can also help establish her
DIC eligibility. Almost nobody knows
this form exists until they need it, and
by then the clock is already running.
Before we get to the exact steps,
there's a second program worth knowing
about, mainly because families confuse
it with DIC constantly. It's called the
VA survivor's pension, and unlike DIC,
it's needs-based, tied to your spouse's
income and assets with a net worth limit
currently sitting around $163,000
not counting the home or one vehicle.
There's also a 3-year look-back period
on asset transfers. So giving assets
away right before applying can trigger a
penalty. If your spouse happens to
qualify for both DIC and the survivor's
pension, the VA automatically pays
whichever benefit is higher. And in
almost every case, that's DIC. The
survivor's pension exists as a backstop,
not the primary target. Everything you
do now should be aimed at securing DIC
first. One more detail spouses need
before anything else, remarriage. If
your spouse remarries before age 55, she
loses DIC entirely. If she remarries at
55 or older, she keeps it. That
threshold surprises almost everyone the
first time they hear it. And it's worth
saying out loud now rather than letting
her discover it by accident later. If
there are dependent children involved,
there are separate DIC provisions that
apply to them as well on top of whatever
your spouse receives. DIC isn't the only
thing sitting behind that qualification,
either. Once a spouse is approved for
DIC, a whole second layer of benefits
often opens up that almost nobody
explains at the same time. If a
surviving spouse needs regular help with
daily activities, bathing, dressing,
managing medication, simply getting
around the house safely, she may qualify
for an additional aid and attendance
allowance on top of the base DIC payment
similar in concept to the special
monthly compensation a veteran can
receive while alive. The exact phrase
aid and attendance has to appear in the
written application for the review to
trigger, the same way it does on a
veteran's own claim. Leave that language
out and the extra allowance frequently
never gets evaluated at all. Healthcare
is the next piece families miss.
A surviving spouse who qualifies for DIC
is generally eligible for CHAMPVA, a
health insurance program that covers a
large share of medical costs for spouses
and dependent children of veterans who
died from a service-connected condition
or who were rated permanently and
totally disabled at the time of death.
For a spouse who loses access to a
veteran's other coverage the same month
she loses his income, this alone can be
the difference between manageable
healthcare costs and a financial
emergency layered on top of a loss she's
still processing. Education benefits
carry forward, too, and this one
surprises almost every family who hears
it for the first time. Under the
Survivors and Dependents Educational
Assistance Program, commonly called
Chapter 35, a qualifying spouse or
dependent child can receive up to 45
months of financial for college,
technical training, or an
apprenticeship. There's a newer,
generally more generous version called
the Fry Scholarship tied to veterans who
died in the line of duty or from a
service-connected condition.
And in many cases, a spouse or child can
choose whichever program pays out better
for their situation. Neither of these
arrive automatically. Both require a
separate application most families never
realize exists until years after they
would have been useful. Home loan
benefits also extend to a portion of
surviving spouses. If your spouse
qualifies for DIC, she may be eligible
for a VA backed home loan certificate of
eligibility in her own name. The same
zero down payment competitive rate
benefit veterans use now available to
her directly. For a spouse who needs to
relocate, downsize, or simply refinance
after losing your income, that's a
resource that rarely gets mentioned in
the middle of DIC paperwork, even though
it's directly tied to the same
qualification. Then there's the piece
nobody wants to think about, but every
family eventually needs: burial.
Veterans who meet basic service
requirements are generally eligible for
burial in a VA national cemetery at no
cost to the family, along with a
headstone or marker, and in some cases,
a burial flag and presidential memorial
certificate. A spouse or dependent child
can often be buried in the same plot. If
your family prefers a private cemetery
instead, a partial VA burial allowance
may still apply. None of this is
complicated when someone knows to ask
for it, but in the middle of a funeral,
it's exactly the kind of detail that
gets missed if it isn't written down
somewhere in advance. Several states
layer their own benefits directly on top
of DIC eligibility as well. A number of
states offer full or partial property
tax exemptions specifically for
surviving spouses of veterans who were
rated 100%
or who died from a service-connected
cause. And some extend that exemption
for as long as the spouse doesn't
remarry. A handful of states go further,
offering reduced vehicle registration
fees, hunting and fishing license
waivers, or preference points on state
employment applications. These benefits
live entirely outside the federal DIC
system, which means qualifying for DIC
doesn't automatically trigger them. Your
spouse has to know they exist and file
for them separately through your state's
Department of Veterans Affairs. Consider
a spouse named Patricia, married to a
veteran named Walter for 38 years before
he passed from a service-connected
respiratory condition tied to burn pit
exposure. Patricia's DIC claim was
approved within a few months because
Walter's condition had already been
rated before he died. What Patricia
didn't know, because nobody told her at
the time, was that she also qualified
for ChampVA, for a property tax
exemption in her home state, and for a
home loan certificate of eligibility she
ended up using two years later to
downsize into a smaller house near her
daughter. None of that arrived
automatically alongside her DIC approval
letter. She found out about each one
separately, months apart, mostly by
accident, through conversations with
other veteran spouses in a support
group. Walter had done everything right
on his end. The gap wasn't in his
paperwork. It was in nobody ever handing
Patricia a complete map of everything
his service had already earned her.
That's exactly why step five in a minute
isn't just about the DIC form. It's
about making sure your spouse has the
entire picture in front of her, not just
the first piece of it. Now, since I
brought it up earlier, every veteran
family loses money to the same root
cause. Benefits that exist on paper, but
never get filed, because nobody flags
them. So, here's what I want you to do.
The exemptions, the breaks, and the
survivor protections most veteran
households already qualify for, but
never claim. I've put them all in one
place, state by state, form by form, so
you don't waste hours digging through
government websites trying to piece it
together yourself. Everything's laid out
fast and simple, so any veteran or
spouse can find exactly what applies to
them. No matter what state you're in,
there's money you're leaving on the
table. It's called the VA Survivor
Protection Playbook, and it's in the
first pinned comment right below this
video. Just tap it once, and you'll have
everything you need. Stay right here,
because the last one is the biggest
bonus most spouses never claim, and it's
the reason I made this whole video. Take
a veteran named Dennis. He's 67, a
retired Marine from outside
Jacksonville, Florida. He reached 100%
combined back in 2014 and has held it
continuously ever since. He's been
married to his wife for 31 years. Dennis
has already cleared the 8-year bonus
threshold. If he passed away today, his
wife would qualify for that extra $360 a
month automatically. But path one, the
full 10-year rule, depends entirely on
his exact effective date clearing a full
decade, not just close to it. Dennis
needs to check that date precisely
because the difference between 9 years
and 10 years on paper is the difference
between his wife having an automatic
unquestioned qualifier and having to
fight for one. Dennis didn't do anything
wrong, either. He just never checked the
exact date. For a lower-income veteran
household living primarily on that VA
check, closing these gaps is the
difference between a spouse maintaining
stability after a death and facing a
financial cliff the same month as the
funeral. For a more financially
comfortable household, this isn't
survival money. It's protection that was
already earned through decades of
service and shouldn't sit unclaimed
simply because nobody connected the dots
in time. Before we get to the exact
steps, let's clear up a handful of
misconceptions that trip up almost every
family I talk to because getting these
wrong is just as costly as never filing
at all. The first is thinking DIC and
Social Security Survivor Benefits work
the same way or that one cancels out the
other. They don't. DIC comes from the VA
and is entirely separate from Social
Security. A surviving spouse can
generally receive both at the same time
in full without one reducing the other.
Families sometimes assume applying for
one disqualifies them from the other and
that assumption alone has kept spouses
from filing for months or years longer
than necessary. The second misconception
is around divorce and prior marriages.
DIC eligibility is tied to the marriage
at the time of death, not to how many
marriages came before it. If you were
previously divorced and have since
remarried, your current spouse is the
one whose eligibility matters for DIC,
provided the marriage requirements,
including the 8-year continuous marriage
window for the bonus payment, are met
from your current marriage forward. If
you have questions about a specific
situation involving a prior marriage, a
former spouse with dependent children,
or a marriage that was interrupted and
later resumed, that's exactly the kind
of detail an accredited veteran service
officer can walk through with you
individually at no cost. The third
misconception is assuming that because a
veteran's cause of death is listed as
something like natural causes or a
general term on a death certificate,
path to is automatically closed. It
isn't. What matters legally is whether a
service-connected condition caused or
substantially contributed to the death.
And a knowledgeable veteran service
officer, or in some cases a private
medical opinion, can help establish that
connection even when the death
certificate itself is vague. Don't
assume the door is shut just because the
paperwork from the hospital or coroner
used general language. The fourth
misconception, and maybe the most
damaging one, is veterans assuming that
because they're young and healthy right
now, none of this applies to them yet.
The 10-year clock and the 8-year clock
don't start when a veteran feels ready
to think about mortality. They start on
the effective date of the qualifying
rating, whenever that happens to be. A
veteran who reaches 100% at 45 and lives
to 85 has had that clock running quietly
for four decades, but only if the rating
was filed and locked in early. Waiting
until retirement age to deal with this
someday is often the single biggest
reason families end up short of both
thresholds when it matters most. One
last piece worth knowing before you
start, you don't have to navigate any of
this alone, and you shouldn't pay anyone
to help you with the initial steps.
Accredited veteran service officers
through organizations like the American
Legion, the VFW, the DAV, or your
state's Department of Veterans Affairs
review files like yours every single day
free of charge, and can usually tell
within a single conversation exactly
where you stand on both clocks and which
conditions are worth pursuing. The VA
maintains a searchable directory of
accredited representatives directly on
va.gov. Nobody accredited through that
system is permitted to charge you a fee
for help filing an initial claim. And
any request for upfront payment to
expedite your case is a signal to walk
away, not a shortcut worth taking. So,
here's the exact sequence in order
starting this week. Step one, confirm
your current rating and your effective
date. Log in to va.gov, pull up your
disability rating, and find the
effective date tied to your current
combined rating. Write it down and
calculate how many years that puts you
on both the 10-year path, one clock, and
the 8-year bonus clock. No va.gov
account yet? Call 1-800-8
and request your current rating decision
letter with all effective dates listed.
Step two, audit your service-connected
conditions against your actual medical
diagnoses. Pull your full list of
service-connected conditions from va.gov
or your regional office. Then get a
current problem list from your primary
care provider. Lay them side by side.
Anything on the medical list that isn't
on the service connected list is a claim
that's never been filed. Pay particular
attention to cardiovascular conditions,
hypertension, sleep apnea, and diabetes.
Step three, file for any high mortality
condition that isn't service connected
yet. Use VA form 21-526EZ
filed online, by mail to your regional
office, or in person with a veteran
service organization representative. For
hypertension or cardiac conditions,
request a nexus letter from your
treating physician connecting the
condition to your service or to another
condition already rated. The VA has a
duty to help you gather evidence once a
claim is filed, but identifying which
claims to file in the first place is
still on you. Step four, gather marriage
documentation for the 8-year bonus. The
VA will require proof of continuous
marriage across that qualifying window.
So, pull your marriage certificate now,
and if you've been married more than
once, make sure the documentation
clearly shows your current marriage date
and that it predates or coincides with
your qualifying rating's effective date.
Step five, tell your spouse what DIC is,
what form covers it, and where your
paperwork lives. She'll file using VA
form 21P-534EZ,
Survivor's Application for Dependency
and Indemnity Compensation, and that
application can only be submitted after
your death. Make sure she knows the form
number, knows where your rating decision
letters and marriage certificate are
kept, and has a contact name at a
veteran service organization. The
American Legion, the VFW, or the DAV all
provide this kind of claims help for
free, at no cost to her, ever. Step six,
set a yearly reminder to reassess.
Ratings can change, medical situations
change, the thresholds themselves
haven't moved, but where you stand
against them shifts every year, and if a
combined rating ever drops below the
qualifying level, the continuous year
count resets to zero. Revisit this every
12 months and protect the rating you've
already earned. That's the whole
picture. The check stops the moment you
die. DIC exists to replace part of it.
Aid and attendance, CHAMPVA, education
benefits, and state-level protections
all sit stacked on top of it once she
qualifies. And whether your spouse
actually receives any of it depends
entirely on paperwork you either file
now or don't. None of it requires a
lawyer, none of it requires a fee. It
requires an afternoon on va.gov, a
folder with the right documents in it,
and a conversation with your spouse you
may have been putting off simply because
it's uncomfortable to have. She can't
file any of this on your behalf while
you're still here to do it yourself, and
she won't know where to start the day
she needs to if you haven't shown her
first. This is yours to finish, and the
only window that exists to finish it is
open right now, today, whether or not
you were planning on thinking about it.

title: 4 Provisions Home Owners Qualify For After 60 (But Most People Don't Know)

segments.text: Right now, there's a bill sitting on the
books with four provisions that affect
your home, your costs, and your future.
And almost nobody over 60 has heard a
word about it. This isn't a proposal. It
isn't stuck in committee. It already
passed. Those four provisions decide
whether you can afford to stay in your
home, whether your home holds its value,
and whether your neighborhood changes in
ways nobody ever asked you about. Some
of it is moving right now with deadlines
running anywhere from 180 days out to 5
years. So if you're 55, 65, or 75, part
of this already applies to your life.
Hey, I'm Lana Mains. I'm no expert, but
I share financial information that helps
you protect and improve your quality of
life. So if that sounds useful to you,
hit subscribe. I break down exactly this
kind of thing every single week. The
crisis this bill was built to answer is
worse than most reporting admits. About
three out of four adults over the age of
50 say they want to stay in their homes
as they age. That's the preference.
Aging in place, the house they know, the
neighborhood they know, the doctors
nearby, the routines built up over
decades. The system has made that
preference nearly impossible for
millions of them. Roughly 25% of
homeowners nationally are
costbururdened, meaning they spend more
than 30% of their income on housing
costs alone. Property taxes, insurance,
maintenance, utilities. For renters,
that number climbs closer to 50%. Half
of all renters in this country are
costburdened. Reporting on the housing
shortage gets sloppy fast, so let's be
honest about the range. You'll hear
figures anywhere from roughly 1 million
homeshort to 10 million homeshort
depending on who's counting and what
they include. The conservative estimates
sit around 1 million. The higher
estimates come from researchers who fold
in shadow demand, suppressed household
formation and migration pressure. Both
numbers point the same direction. There
isn't enough housing, and for older
adults on fixed incomes, the shortage
hits hardest at exactly the price points
they can afford. What makes this bill
different from earlier housing
legislation is how it actually became
law. It cleared Congress by landside
margins almost never seen anymore, and
it still didn't get a signing ceremony.
A separate unrelated policy fight became
the sticking point and rather than sign
it or veto it, the bill was left to sit.
Because Congress stayed in session and
no action was taken within the
constitutional window, the legislation
