for that second death. The joint account
protects you while both of you are
alive. It does not protect your children
when the last of you is gone. The second
assumption is that joint ownership
eliminates the need for a POD entirely.
It does not. Survivorship handles the
first death in the couple. The POD
handles the second. You need both.
Before we go further, here is something
I want you to have. Every form, every
designation, every protection like this,
one that most seniors are never told
about. The beneficiary forms, the
exemptions, the breaks you already
qualify for, but no one ever pointed you
to. I have put them all in one place,
state by state, form by form, so you are
not digging through government websites
trying to figure out what applies to
you. It is called the Senior Exemption
Playbook, and it is in the first pinned
comment right below this video. Tap it
once, and it is yours. Now, stay right
here, because the next part is the one
that quietly undoes everything. The five
mistakes that make this form completely
worthless, and your bank will not tell
you about a single one of them until it
is too late. Mistake one, naming a minor
child as a direct beneficiary. If your
beneficiary is under 18 when you die,
the bank cannot legally release funds to
them. A court must appoint a guardian of
the property first, a separate
proceeding that creates a brand new
freeze. The fix, name a trusted adult or
set up a custodial account under the
Uniform Transfers to Minors Act. Mistake
two: Naming your estate as the
beneficiary. This is one of the most
common errors, and it defeats the entire
purpose. The funds route straight back
into probate, the exact system the form
was designed to bypass. The fix: Name a
living person or a properly funded
living trust, never the estate itself.
Mistake three: Failing to update the
form after a divorce or remarriage. A
POD does not automatically void when a
marriage ends. If you named a former
spouse and never updated it, that former
spouse receives the money regardless of
what your will says, regardless of your
divorce decree. The bank follows the
contract on file. The fix: Update it the
moment your family situation changes.
Mistake four: Listing a beneficiary who
dies before you. If your named
beneficiary predeceases you and you
never updated the form, the account
reverts to the frozen state as if no
designation existed. The fix: Always
name both a primary and a contingent
beneficiary, so someone is still in line
if the first person is gone. Mistake
five: Filing the form without getting
the bank's acknowledgement. Some banks
process these through online portals
that occasionally fail to record them.
If there is no confirmation copy, there
is no proof it was ever filed. The fix:
Always request a printed or emailed
confirmation that the designation is on
file, and keep it with your estate
documents. Now, here is exactly how to
do it correctly. This week, at any US
bank, go to your bank in person. Do not
rely only on the online portal for the
initial filing. Tell the representative
you want to add or update a payable on
death beneficiary on your account. If
the teller does not know what you mean,
ask for the branch manager. Every
insured bank is required to offer it.
Bring your government photo ID and the
account numbers for every account you
want to designate because you will
complete a separate form for each one.
And this next part is where people lose
money without realizing it. One form
does not cover all your accounts
automatically. Your checking, your
savings, and every single certificate of
deposit are each their own contract and
each one needs its own POD on file. If
you hold three CDs at the same branch
where you filed a POD on your checking
account, those three CDs are still
completely unprotected until you file
three more forms. Do not assume the bank
rolls them together. They do not. On
every form, name a primary beneficiary
and a contingent beneficiary with full
legal names, dates of birth, and social
security numbers because incomplete
information can delay the transfer. The
social security number is how the bank
verifies identity at the moment of
payout. Sign it in front of the
representative. Ask them to witness it
and leave with an acknowledged copy for
your records. Put that copy in the same
folder as your will and tell your
beneficiaries where that folder is. Now,
the POD covers your bank accounts, but
there are three more places your money
lives that it does not automatically
reach and each one has its own trap. The
first is your brokerage account, your
stocks, bonds, and mutual funds. Those
use the transfer on death form filed
with your brokerage firm, not your bank.
If you hold investments with no TOD on
file, they go through probate exactly
like an undesignated bank account. Same
fix, different institution. The second
is your retirement accounts, your IRA,
your 401K, your 403B. These already run
on a transfer-on-death principle by
federal design, so most people assume
they are safe. Here is the danger. Most
people filled out that beneficiary line
when they opened the account decades ago
and have never looked at it since. And
under federal law, the named beneficiary
on a retirement account overrides any
conflicting will or divorce decree. Let
me say that plainly. If your former
spouse is still listed on an IRA you
opened in 1995, they may legally collect
the entire balance when you die,
regardless of what your will says,
regardless of the divorce, regardless of
how many years have passed. Pull those
designations up and check every one of
them this week. The third is the safe
deposit box, and this one catches almost
everyone by surprise. Many seniors store
their will, their deeds, and their
valuables inside a box and hand a spare
key to a family member, believing that
solves it. That key grants nothing after
your death. Federal regulations require
the bank to seal the box the moment it
is notified of the owner's passing, and
your family will be denied entry even
with the key in their hand. And here is
the cruel loop. If the original will is
sitting inside that sealed box, your
family needs the will to open the
probate case, but they need a probate
order to open the box. The fix costs
nothing. Add your child or your
beneficiary as a joint renter on the box
contract at the branch. You both sign
together and they keep access no matter
what happens to you. And if you own real
estate, a vehicle, or anything without a
direct account designation, that is
where a revocable living trust comes in.
When a trust is properly drafted and
funded, meaning your assets are legally
retitled into it, the successor trustee
takes control the moment you die with no
probate and no waiting period. Put it
all together and the picture is simple.
POD designations on every bank account,
TOD designations on every brokerage
account, updated beneficiaries on every
retirement account, a joint renter on
your safe deposit box, and a funded
living trust for the real property that
has no designation option. When all of
that is in place at once, your death
becomes financially invisible to the
banking system. No freeze, no probate,
no waiting period, every asset moving to
the person you chose. Most estate
attorneys bill each of these as a
separate service and rarely explain how
they fit together because the incentive
is for the complexity to stay
compartmentalized. Here is what few
people realize. Most banks bury the POD
option in the fine print of a 40 to 60
page account agreement you signed
without reading. So, take the
initiative, walk into your bank and ask
in writing for the beneficiary and
transfer designation options available
on your account. Ask for the answer in
writing, too, and keep it with your
records. If a representative tells you
your account cannot have a POD
designation,
ask them to put that in writing, as
well. That simple paper trail is often
all it takes to get the designation
properly filed. And if a branch ever
refuses outright, you can raise it with
your state banking regulator, whose
contact information is free and public.
Had Eleanor filed a POD on her account,
even without the trust, even without
changing anything else, Diane would have
walked into that bank on Friday,
presented a death certificate, and had
access to every dollar within 72 hours.
The 11 months did not have to happen.
The fees did not have to happen. The
credit card debt did not have to happen.
What the family lost during those
months, the space to grieve without a
financial emergency pressing in from
every side cannot be recovered. One form
could have preserved it. So, here is
what you do right now, today. Log into
every bank account you hold and check
whether a beneficiary is on file. A
blank field means no POD. Go to your
bank in person this week and request the
payable on death form for every account
with a blank field. And remember to file
one for every certificate of deposit
separately. Bring the full legal name,
date of birth, and social security
number for both the primary and a
contingent beneficiary. Complete each
form, get it acknowledged, and leave
with a copy. Then do the same with the
transfer on death form on your brokerage
accounts and pull up every retirement
account to confirm the beneficiary line
is current and not still pointing at
someone from a past chapter of your
life. Add a joint renter to your safe
deposit box. And if you own real
property, talk to an estate attorney
about a revocable living trust. And
specifically ask how POD, TOD, and the
trust work together, not as three
separate bills.

quietly sorted you into are losing

every single year. Not tomorrow, not
next year, right now. A lifetime of
paying in would not protect you. Filing

There is one thing, one that decides

Knowing which group you're in and
claiming what's yours before the next
payment cycle passes. And the reason
most people have never been told these
rules changed is simple. Nobody whose
job depends on the current system has
any incentive to tell you. My name is

directly in front of the Internal
Revenue Service. If this kind of

subscribe because every week I break
down the financial and legal facts that

Here is the one idea that connects

volunteer information. The law does not

to chase you down. You have to know it
exists and you have to go claim it. The

American senior into one of four

to claim or are currently turning 65.

four is the safe group. And by the end
of this video, you will know exactly
which group you are in and exactly what
to do about it. The group losing the
most money right now is not who you
would expect. It is not the lowest

mistakes. It is people who spent 30
years serving the public. Group one,
public sector retirees. Take a woman
named Marlene. She is 67, a retired
school teacher from outside of Columbus,
Ohio. 31 years in the classroom. She has
a pension. She applied for Social
Security when she retired and was told
her benefit would be significantly

that date repealed both the windfall

pension offset in full. These were two

title: Banks Changed These Joint Account Rules — Seniors Need To Know

And when she called the bank, they told
her there was nothing they could do
because under the account agreement she
signed, he had every right to take it.
Carol is not a rare case. This plays out

Financial exploitation tied to shared
account access costs Americans $28
billion
every single year. 70% of that

the victim already knew and trusted. In

documented victims lost an average of

the account. You will never be told any

Every single person at that counter
whose job it is to open that account has
a direct financial incentive to keep the
conversation simple. That leads directly
into the first thing you need to
understand because the legal mechanics
are where everything goes wrong. When
you add someone to a joint account, you
are not adding an authorized user. You
are not adding a helper, you are

both signatures are on the document, the
other person owns that money in full.
Not 50%, not their half, all of it. Each

Banks present this as a convenience

The most common scenario follows a

The bank does not describe it that way,
but under federal banking law and the
account agreement, that is exactly what

makes all three rule changes I am about
to explain so dangerous. Rule change
number one, the survivorship clause
override. Stay with this one because it
is the rule change that erases something
you may have already put in writing.
Most joint accounts in the United States
are structured as joint tenancy with
right of survivor ship. When one account
holder dies, the surviving account
holder receives the entire balance
automatically. No probate, no delay, the
money transfers by operation of law the

not new. What has changed is how banks
document and enforce that survivorship
language, and it now routinely overrides
written wills in ways that are final and
irreversible. Here's the situation that

account wins every time. Your will is

account. The Consumer Financial

a growing source of estate disputes. The
account agreement signed at opening
supersedes testamentary documents for
assets held in joint tenancy under
established state probate law. Banks
have tightened the survivorship language
in updated agreements over the past
several years, making these outcomes
harder to challenge after the fact. What
makes this especially dangerous is that
most people sign these agreements years
or even decades ago. The language in
that original document is not the
language governing your account today.
Banks are permitted to update account
agreements and are only required to
notify you in writing, typically buried
inside a mailing most people never open.
You did not sign the new version, but
you are bound by it, whether your
primary asset is a single checking
account or a formally drafted estate
plan, the survivorship clause reaches in
and overrides it at the account level.
That is rule change number one. Rule
change number two, creditor access
expansion. This one surprises people
more than the first because it does not
require anyone to die. Updated banking
policies and state-level legal shifts
have expanded the window in which a
co-owner's personal creditors can reach
the shared balance in a joint account.
This surprises people most because the
instinct is to think of it as your
money. You deposited it. You earned it.
You saved it. Under joint account law,
that reasoning does not hold. The other
account holder's creditors can treat the
full balance as their debtor's asset.
Take a woman named Patricia. She is 67,
a retired [clears throat] licensed
practical nurse from Knoxville,
Tennessee. After her husband passed, her
adult son encouraged her to add him to
her checking account to help manage her
bills. Patricia deposited her pension,
her social security, and 31 years of
careful savings into that account. Her
son had taken on a business partnership
that went wrong. When his partner filed
a civil judgment against him, the
creditor reached directly into
Patricia's joint checking account and
placed a garnishment on $44,000.
Patricia did nothing wrong. That money
was legally hers in every practical
sense, but under the joint tenancy
structure, her son's creditor had the

garnishment was enforced before Patricia

She recovered a portion, she did not
recover all of it. The IRS operates
under the same access rules for tax

under updated state garnishment
statutes. This is also where Medicaid

joint account complicates this

in that account may be counted as

purposes of that look-back period, even
if only one person ever deposited a
single dollar into it. Families who
added a child to an account for
convenience without realizing the
Medicaid implications sometimes face
penalties, delays, or disqualification
periods at the exact moment they need
those benefits most. Every dollar in
that joint account is exposed if the
co-owner carries any unresolved debt,
judgment, or federal liability. The
larger the balance, the larger the
target. That is rule change number two.
Right now, open your bank's account
summary page and look at every name
listed on every joint account you hold.
Not from memory, the actual account.
Look at each name and ask yourself one
question. Do you know the current state
of that person's debts and liabilities,
your answer determines how exposed you
are. So, here's what I want you to do.
The exemptions, the breaks, the refunds
most seniors already qualify for but
never claim, I've put them all in one
place, state by state, form by form, so

what state you're in, there's money
you're leaving on the table. It's called
the Senior Exemption Playbook. It's in
the first pinned comment right below
this video. Just tap it once and you'll
have everything you need. Now, stay
right here because the last rule change
is the one that catches people who have
done everything else right, and it is
the reason I made this entire video.
Rule change number three, the
exploitation access window. Banks have
adjusted internal monitoring thresholds
and dispute resolution timelines for
joint accounts, creating a wider window
in which withdrawals by a co-owner can
drain an account before the other holder
can stop it. You will never be told this
threshold changed. A co-owner on a joint
account has legal access by definition.
When that co-owner begins making unusual
withdrawals, the bank's fraud detection
software does not flag it the same way
it would flag an outside actor. The
transaction looks authorized because it
is authorized. The exploitation is
invisible to the system
until the balance is already gone. Under
older joint account agreements, a
co-owner disputing unauthorized
withdrawals could trigger an internal
review within 10 business days. Updated
agreements now route these disputes into
a contractual gray zone because both
parties have equal legal ownership. The
resolution process can take 90 days or
longer. In some documented cases, banks
have declined to resolve the dispute at
all, citing the co-owner's legal access
as a complete defense. 70% of financial
exploitation is carried out by a known
and trusted party. The CFPB received
tens of thousands of complaints matching
this exact pattern in a single reporting
year. The average loss was $35,000.
And under updated monitoring and dispute
rules, the window between the first
withdrawal and the moment the account
holder can intervene has grown
considerably. There is another version
of this that catches married couples
specifically, and it is becoming more
common. A husband and wife share a joint
checking account the same way they have
for decades. They trust each other
completely, but later in life one spouse
begins showing early signs of memory
loss. Around that same time, a caller

the account has been compromised and
that funds need to be moved immediately
to a safe account. The spouse with
memory difficulties, wanting to do the
right thing, follows the instructions
and transfers a large sum before anyone
else knows what happened. Because it is
a joint account, the other spouse had
every legal right to that money, but in
the moment had no idea the call was
happening and no chance to intervene.
The bank had no reason to flag it
because an authorized owner approved the
transfer. Scammers have become
significantly more sophisticated in
recent years, using technology that can
mimic familiar voices or spoof official
caller identification. The combination
of a wider bank dispute window and
faster moving fraud makes this the
highest risk moment for joint account
holders in a generation. That is rule
change number three. Here is what you do
about it. Five steps. Starting this
week, step one, request the current
account agreement in writing. Call your
bank's main service line and ask for the
current joint account agreement for
every account you share. Not the
original you signed, the current one.
Banks update these agreements and are
required to notify account holders, but
those notifications are buried in the
fine print. Get the document and read
the survivorship clause specifically.
Step two, compare the survivorship
clause to your will. Take both documents
to an estate attorney or at minimum your
state's legal aid office. Search your
state name plus joint tenancy
survivorship override will on your state
bar association's official website to
find a licensed estate attorney in your
county. Many people discover the
conflict for the first time at this
step. A short consultation, often

1 hour what might otherwise take years
of family conflict to untangle after the
fact. Step three, ask your bank about

account. They can pay your bills, handle

yours. It is protected from their
creditors and legal troubles, and it
passes according to your will when you

happened to be added to the account.

access buffer account. Keep a modest

genuine convenience. Keep your primary

your intended beneficiaries directly.
This separates access from exposure. The
co-owner can still help when needed.
Your core savings sit outside their
reach, and outside the reach of their
creditors. Step five, search your state
name plus joint account garnishment
exemption rules on your state attorney
general's official website. Some states

deposited from social security or
pension income, even in a joint account.

losing them. This step costs nothing.
Most people never take it. Banks are
also starting to roll out something
called a trusted contact designation,
which is worth knowing about. This is
not someone who can access your money at
all. It is simply a person the bank is
authorized to call if they notice
unusual activity on your account, signs
of possible fraud or red flags that
something might be wrong. It is an extra
layer of protection that costs nothing
and changes nothing about who owns your
money, but it gives your bank one more
way to catch a problem early before real
damage is done. Ask your bank directly
whether they offer one. And beyond all
the paperwork, there is one more habit
that catches what every other safeguard
misses. Check your own statements, not
once a quarter, every month. Banks are
required to flag certain types of
suspicious activity, but the line

problematic one is often invisible from
their side. A family member taking out
small amounts regularly does not usually
trigger any fraud alert because nothing
about it looks unusual to a bank system.
The only person who can catch that
pattern early is you. Simply by glancing
at your own statement every month,
knowing roughly what should be coming in
and going out, and asking questions the
moment something feels even slightly
off, that single habit is the safety net
that catches what every other protection
might miss. It costs nothing. It takes
minutes. The account you opened for
convenience is not the account it was
when you signed it. Three rules changed.
The survivorship clause now overrides
your will. Your co-owner's creditors now
have a wider path to your balance. And
the bank's updated policies give bad
actors more time before the account can
be frozen or disputed. None of this
required your signature again. None of
it came with a notice you were likely to

convenient time to become your problem.
Take the five steps this week before
something else decides the timing for
you.

title: Born Before 1966? Your Bank Account Could Freeze After You Die

segments.text: Right now, your family cannot touch a
single dollar in your bank account if
you died tonight, not tomorrow, not next
week. A will would not help them. A
notary would not help them. An attorney
drafted estate plan would not help them.
There is one free form, one, that
bypasses all of it. And the reason most
people have never been told it exists is
simple. Nobody whose job depends on the
current system has any incentive to tell
you. My name is Lona Mains. I represent
taxpayers directly in front of the
Internal Revenue Service. I sit across
the table from the IRS and from bank
compliance officers on behalf of real
people. If this kind of information is
useful to you, hit subscribe because
every week I break down the financial
and legal facts that protect your money
and your family and I make sure you
actually understand them. The single
most preventable financial disaster I
see is not a bad investment. It is not a
tax mistake. It is a family standing at
a bank counter the week after a death
being told they cannot access a cent of
money that was legally theirs because
one form was never filed. That form
takes 10 minutes. It costs nothing. It
requires no attorney and you will never
be told about it unless someone like me
tells you. The legal framework that
still controls your money, the Uniform
Probate Code finalized in 1969 by the
National Conference of Commissioners on
Uniform State Laws, established
something that most Americans have never
been told. It classified financial
accounts held at banks and credit unions
as contractual instruments sitting on a
completely separate legal track from
your will. States adopted this framework
over the following decades and every
state in the country now operates under
some version of it. Courts have
reinforced it in case after case ever
since. What that means, in plain terms
is this. The contract between you and
your bank, not your will, not your
trust, not your estate plan, governs
what happens to your money when you die.
A signed beneficiary designation on a
bank form overrides a notarized,
witnessed, attorney drafted will every
time, without exception. The will
controls your furniture, your car, your
jewelry, the physical property in your
home. The bank contract controls your
cash. If you die without a named
beneficiary on your bank account, the
account does not transfer to your heirs.
It transfers to your estate, and the
moment it transfers to your estate,
probate is triggered automatically.
Probate is the court-supervised process
of validating your will and distributing
your assets under judicial oversight.
Most states set probate thresholds
between $50,000 and $100,000. If your
account balance exceeds that threshold,
and for most retirees it does, your
family waits. The court moves on the
court's schedule, not yours and not
theirs. Here's what people do not
understand about probate. It is not a
fast administrative process. In most
states there is a mandatory creditor
waiting period of 3 to 6 months built
into the law. Unknown creditors, medical
providers, credit card companies, anyone
who might have a claim against the
estate must be given time to come
forward before any distribution can
occur. Your family cannot receive a
dollar until that window closes,
regardless of how clean your finances
were. And during that entire period,
your bills keep running. The funeral
does not wait. Grief does not come with
a financial timeout. That leads directly
into Dorothy's story. Asterisk, she did
everything right. It did not matter.
Dorothy was 71 years old. She was a
retired school teacher from Illinois who
had sold the family home and walked into
her local bank with $350,000
from the proceeds. She opened a standard
savings account, hired an estate
attorney for $800,
and had a comprehensive will drafted,
witnessed, notarized, and clearly naming
her two adult children, Michael and
Sarah, as equal beneficiaries. She put
the will in a lock box under her bed and
called Michael to tell him everything
was handled. It was not. Dorothy
suffered a stroke and died. Michael and
Sarah flew in, received a $11,500
funeral invoice, and Michael took the
death certificate and notarized will to
the bank. The branch manager looked at
the account screen, looked at the will,
and slid the documents back. Dorothy had
never filed a payable on death
beneficiary designation. The account
held only her name. Because the balance
exceeded the state's small estate
threshold, the bank had no legal
authority to release a single dollar. A
will is a letter of instruction
addressed to a probate judge. It carries
no weight at a bank counter. The bank's
obligation runs to the contract on file,
and the contract on file named no
beneficiary. The account was frozen.
Michael and Sarah walked out of the bank
with nothing. They put the $11,500
funeral bill on their own credit cards,
paying interest rates that were running
well above 20% at the time, rates
typical of consumer credit cards, while
of their mother's money sat 20 ft away
behind a counter they could not legally
cross. Then the probate process began.
The court filing fee to open the estate
A secondary publication filing required
by Illinois law to notify unknown
creditors through a local newspaper for
three consecutive weeks cost $250.
The executor bond premium cost $1,000.
These were just the entry fees. The
probate attorney charged a percentage of
the gross estate, which is standard
practice in many states. On an estate of
this size, that came to over $10,500.
The mandatory creditor waiting period
held the case open for months. From
start to finish, the family waited 14
months to access their mother's money.
They lost over $12,000 in documented
fees, and the interest accumulating on
the credit card they used for the
funeral kept running the entire time.
Dorothy did nothing wrong. She had the
will, the notary, the attorney. None of
it reached inside a bank contract. Her
situation was not a legal error. It was
not unusual. It was the entirely
predictable result of a system working
exactly as it was designed to work, and
it has three specific entry points where
families fall into it. Before I walk you
through those three failure points, open
your online banking right now, or pull
out your most recent bank statement.
Look for a beneficiary field. If you
cannot find one, or if it is blank, that
is already your answer. Write down what
you see, because what you find
determines exactly which of these traps
you are sitting in.
Three ways people accidentally lock
their own money. The first failure point
is no beneficiary designation on file at
all. This is the most common situation I
encounter. You open the account years or
decades ago. Nobody at the bank asked
you to name a beneficiary. You signed
the signature card and left. You assumed
your will would handle it. It will not.
Under the contractual framework now
codified in state law across the
country, a will has no authority over a
bank account. The account defaults to
the estate. Probate opens automatically.
For a lower income retiree, this is
often catastrophic. A 6-month probate
process on a $60,000 account can consume
a meaningful slice of that balance in
filing fees, attorney fees, and
publication costs before a single dollar
reaches the family. For the comfortable
middle-class retiree, the assumption is
usually that the estate attorney already
handled it. Most estate attorneys draft
wills. They do not file bank beneficiary
forms. Those are two completely separate
documents at two completely separate
institutions, and almost no one explains
that to you when you write the check for
the estate plan. The second failure
point is an outdated beneficiary
designation. This one is more dangerous
than no designation at all because it
gives you a false sense of security. You
named someone 20 years ago, an
ex-spouse, a parent who has since died,
a sibling you no longer have a
relationship with. That name is still on
the form. That is who the bank sends the
money to. The will says something
entirely different. It does not matter.
The Uniform Probate Code in every state
that has adopted it are clear. The
designation on file at the bank
controls, period. Courts have
consistently ruled against surviving
spouses, adult children, and estate
executors who believed a current will
would override an old bank designation.
It will not. The bank looks at the form
on file, not the document in your
lockbox. The third failure point is the
joint ownership assumption. Many married
couples believe that because they are
married, all accounts automatically
transfer to the surviving spouse. In a
number of states, that is simply not
true. Joint tenancy with right of
survivorship is a specific legal
arrangement that must be explicitly
created and documented at the bank.
Marriage alone does not establish it.
The account structure, the title on the
account, and the state specific
treatment of marital property all
determine what happens, not the marriage
certificate. And there is a trap hidden
inside the most common attempt to fix
this. Many seniors add an adult child
directly to their account as a joint
owner, thinking it gives their child
easy access to pay bills if something
goes wrong. The intention is good. The
legal consequence is severe. The moment
you add another person to your account
as a joint owner, the law in most states
treats that money as partly theirs,
right now while you are still alive. If
your child is in a car accident and
faces a lawsuit, the plaintiff can
pursue your bank account. If your child
goes through a divorce, their spouse can
claim a portion of your savings in the
settlement. If your child has a tax
debt, the IRS can levy your account to
satisfy it. Joint ownership transfers
your exposure to every liability your
child carries immediately and
completely. The POD designation avoids
all of this. It grants your beneficiary
zero ownership rights while you are
alive. Your money stays entirely yours,
entirely protected from their creditors,
until the moment you pass. Then the
transfer happens cleanly on contract
with no court involved. All three of
these failures have the same fix, one
form, free, available at your bank right
now.
So, here's what I want you to do. The
exemptions, the breaks, the refunds most
seniors already qualify for but never
claim. I've put them all in one place,
state by state, form by form, so you
don't waste hours digging through
government sites. Everything's laid out
fast and simple, so any senior can find
exactly what applies to them. No matter
what state you're in, there's money
you're leaving on the table. It's called
the senior exemption playbook. It's in
the first pinned comment right below
this video. Just tap it once and you'll
have everything you need. Now, stay
right here because the last section
covers the one form that makes all of
this go away and it's the reason I made
this whole video. The form that makes
probate irrelevant. The form is called a
payable on death designation or POD. The
concept traces to a New York court
decision called Matter of Totten in
1904, which established that money could
transfer directly to another person upon
death without a formal trust or court
involvement. That principle was codified
in the Uniform Probate Code section 6 to
101 and adopted in some form across all
50 states. It is not a will. It is not a
trust. It is a contractual instruction
to your bank operating on the exact same
contractual track that froze Dorothy's
accounts. Because it operates on that
track, it bypasses probate entirely. The
bank never looks at the probate court.
It looks at the designation on file.
When a valid POD is recorded, your
beneficiary presents a certified death
certificate at the bank. The designation
is verified, the transfer is processed,
no judge, no attorney, no filing fees,
no mandatory waiting period. Processing
time varies by institution. Smaller
banks may handle it the same day or next
business day. Larger institutions
typically take three to five business
days. What it does not take is 14
months. The cost of filing a POD
designation is zero. Every FDIC insured
bank in the country is required to offer
it. Every federally insured credit union
offers an equivalent. There is no fee to
file it. There is no annual fee to
maintain it. It costs nothing because it
generates nothing for the bank. It
serves only you and the people you name
on it. What the POD form does not cover
and what to file instead. Here is where
most people stop and where most people
leave gaps. The POD designation covers
your individual bank accounts, checking,
savings, money market. It does not
automatically extend to every financial
instrument you hold, even at the same
institution. Certificates of deposit
require a separate designation. A CD
sitting at the same branch where you
filed your POD for your checking account
is not covered by that form. Each
account is its own contract. Each
contract requires its own beneficiary
designation. If you hold three CDs at
the same bank, each one needs its own
POD filed separately. Brokerage accounts
use a different form entirely,
called a transfer on death designation
or TOD. It operates on the same legal
principle as a POD, direct contractual
transfer outside of probate, but it is
filed with your brokerage firm, not your
bank. If you hold stocks, bonds, or
mutual funds in a brokerage account with
no TOD on file, those assets go through
probate just like an undesignated bank
account. Retirement accounts, IRAs,
already operate on a transfer on death
principle by design under federal law.
But most people filled out their
beneficiary designation when they first
opened the account decades ago and have
never revisited it. An outdated name on
a retirement account carries the same
consequence as no name and sometimes
worse. Under federal law, a named
beneficiary designation on a retirement
account controls over any conflicting
will or divorce decree. If your former
spouse is still listed on an IRA you
opened in 1995. They may legally collect
the entire balance regardless of what
your will says, regardless of your
divorce agreement, and regardless of how
many years have passed. Review those
designations today. There is one more
asset worth addressing, the safe deposit
box. Many seniors store their will,
deeds, and valuables inside one and hand
the spare key to a family member. That
key grants nothing after your death.
Federal regulations require banks to
seal safe deposit boxes upon
notification of a customer's death, and
your family will be denied entry even
with the key in hand. Worse, if the
physical will is inside the box, they
face a circular problem. They need the
will to open the probate case, but they
need a probate order to open the box.
The fix costs nothing.
Add your child as a joint renter on the
safe deposit box contract at the branch.
Both of you sign together and they
retain access regardless of what happens
to you. What to do before you close this
video. Step one, go to your bank this
week in person or through your online
portal and request the payable on death
beneficiary designation form. Every FDIC
insured bank is required to provide it.
If the teller does not know what it is,
ask for the branch manager. Step two,
name a primary beneficiary using their
full legal name, date of birth, and
social security number. Do not write
nicknames or vague terms like my
children. The social security number is
how the bank verifies identity at the

can be delayed. Step three, name a
contingent beneficiary as a backup. If
your primary dies before you and no
contingent is named, the account

again. Step four, submit the form in
person and request written confirmation
that the designation has been recorded.
Keep that confirmation with your
important documents. Step five, check
every account separately. Your checking,
savings, and each CD all require their
own designation. One form does not cover
all of them. Step six, contact your
brokerage and file a transfer on death
designation for any non-retirement
investment accounts. Step seven, review
your retirement account beneficiary
designations and update any outdated
names immediately through your plan
administrator. Step eight, revisit all
designations every three years or after
any major life event. A death, a
marriage, a divorce, a new grandchild.
Tonight, your family still cannot touch
a single dollar in your account. That is
true tonight. Unless you file this form.
The probate system is not broken. It is
working exactly as it was designed to
work under the framework adopted from
the Uniform Probate Code. The POD
designation is the one mechanism that
operates on the same contractual track
and wins. Go to your bank this week, ask
for the POD form. It costs nothing. It
takes 10 minutes, and if you found this
useful, subscribe.

title: Cash Reporting Rules Banks Follow – 2026 Information

segments.text: If you have more than $25,000
sitting in any single checking or
savings account right now, you are
losing money in three separate ways at
the exact same time. And the most
dangerous one has nothing to do with
overspending, bad investments, or market
risk. It is a federal reporting system
your bank is already running on your
account, and the law forbids them from
telling you about it. The other two
dangers are quieter, but just as
destructive. They are draining your
purchasing power every single month
while your balance sits there looking
perfectly fine. My name is Lana Mains. I
represent taxpayers directly in front of
the Internal Revenue Service. What I am
about to walk you through is the same
conversation I have with clients before
they make any major decision about where
their savings live. There is no version
of this your bank will ever start with
you. Your bank earns money while your
money sits idle. That incentive has
never changed, and it never will. The
first danger, the reporting system. The
first danger is the one most people have
heard about and almost nobody actually
understands. Under the Bank Secrecy Act
of 1970, every financial institution in
the United States is required by law to
file a currency transaction report
anytime a customer makes a cash
transaction exceeding $10,000 in a
single business day. That report is
filed on FinCEN Form 100 and goes
directly to the Financial Crimes
Enforcement Network, a bureau inside the
US Treasury Department. Your bank files
it. You do not sign anything. You will
never see a copy, and the bank is
legally prohibited from telling you it
was filed. The report contains your full
legal name, your Social Security number,
your date of birth, your home address,
the exact amount, and the time of the
transaction down to the minute. It sits
in a federal database shared between
FinCEN, the IRS Criminal Investigation
Division, the Drug Enforcement
Administration, the Department of
Homeland Security, and roughly 400 other
federal, state, and local agencies. Once
your name is in that database, it stays
there for 5 years, and every future
transaction is cross-referenced against
your history. But, it does not stop at
cash transactions. The software your
bank runs is watching your balance and
your habits continuously, looking for
anything that breaks your normal
pattern. A sudden large deposit, a
sudden large withdrawal, money moving in
a way it has not moved before. You do
not have to do anything wrong to get
flagged. You only have to do something
different, and the bigger the pile
sitting in that one account, the more
attention it draws. Now, here is the
part that costs people everything. When
most people hear about the $10,000
threshold for the first time, they have
the same instinct. They think, "If
$10,000 triggers a report, I will just
deposit $9,000,
or break it into smaller amounts across
a few days." That instinct has a name.
It is called structuring, and under
Title 31, United States Code Section
structuring is a federal felony, not a
fine, not a warning, a federal crime
carrying up to 5 years in federal
prison, and forfeiture of the entire
amount, even if every dollar of that
money is completely legal. Carol Hinders
ran a restaurant in Iowa for 38 years
and made deposits below $10,000
because her insurance policy capped on
premises cash. The IRS seized her entire
account, $33,000
in operating capital, with no criminal
charges filed. It took 2 years of
litigation and a pro bono law firm to
get it back. Carol did nothing wrong.
She never committed fraud. She made
deposits in a pattern the software
recognized and the government took her
money. In 1994, the Supreme Court ruled
in Ratzlaf versus United States that the
government must prove you knew the
reporting requirement existed and that
structuring itself was illegal. That is
an important legal protection. But if
you are watching this video, you now
know both things. Do not hand a
prosecutor that argument. The simplest
way to reduce this exposure is to stop
keeping so much sitting in the one place
that is doing the watching. The second
danger, inflation erosion. This one
requires no government report. It is
happening to every account automatically
every single month. At a 4% annual
inflation rate, $50,000 sitting in a
standard savings account paying less
than half a percent loses approximately
$2,000 in real purchasing power every
single year. Not from withdrawal, not
from fees, not from any mistake, simply
from sitting there. Here is the part
that should make you angry. Your bank is
taking your money and lending it back
out to other people at 7 and 8%. And
paying you back less than half a
percent. That is not an accident. That
is the business model. Your money is
doing all the work and the bank is
keeping all the reward. If you are
carrying $80,000 or $100,000
in a traditional savings account, you
are losing
in real purchasing
power every single year. One account
decision recovers most of that. We are
going to get to exactly which one. Right
now, open your account, not last month's
statement, the actual balance today and
the actual interest rate. Look at both
numbers because what comes next depends
on where they land. The third danger,
FDIC exposure. This is the one that
catches the people who did everything
right. FDIC insurance covers $250,000
per person per institution. That is not
per account, it is per institution. A
retiree with a checking account, a

insured accounts. She has one covered
pool capped at $250,000.
Any amount above that cap at a single
institution is uninsured. If that bank

People think bank failures are something

The people who were under the limit were

You never want your life savings to

protected is so easy to arrange. And the

numbers. Patricia is 71, a retired

Six months after consolidation, she

institution never flagged it. Patricia

If you have saved diligently over
decades, this gap is the one that can

single bank failure. Now for the

That is your cushion, your emergency

Here are the five places careful people
actually move it. One, a high yield

available.
Three, Series I savings bonds. These are
built for exactly this kind of
environment because the interest rate
adjusts along with the cost of living.
By design, your money does not lose its

a regular account. You buy them from the
same government website up to $10,000
per person each year. The one rule to

that every dollar stays under the

5%. It is completely liquid, no lockup

to do this week. Step one, find your

or CD ladder through treasurydirect.gov
or brokerage account. Step five, verify

at FDIC.gov
to confirm every dollar you have is
protected. Before I give you the final
piece, one quick thing. Everything I

unprotected. This is just one part of
what most seniors are walking past

exact qualifier. Filing a return, even
when you owe nothing, is the mechanism
that unlocks the refund. No one
finishing this video should walk away
believing this does not apply to them.
Both groups reach the same conclusion
through different logic, and both
conclusions are incorrect. That leads
directly into the exact numbers, because
the figures are the fastest way to prove
the point to yourself. Here is the win
for each group. The IRS sets maximum
credit amounts by filing category. For a
single filer with no qualifying
children, the maximum credit in the
current tax year is $632.
For a filer with one qualifying child,
For a filer with three or more
qualifying children, $6,960.
The income thresholds for qualification
are under $18,591
for a single filer, and under $49,084
for married filing jointly. There is
also an investment income cap. If your
investment income exceeds $11,600
in the tax year, you do not qualify,
regardless of your earned income level.
That number is specific. Check it
against your actual account statements,
not your estimate. One thing seniors
miss constantly, Social Security alone
does not count as earned income for this
credit, but it does not disqualify you
either. If you have any earned income on
top of Social Security, even part-time
work, babysitting grandchildren for pay,
occasional handyman jobs, or selling
items online, you may qualify, and the
calculation must be run. Small amounts
of self-employment income open the door.
If you are a lower-income senior, the
floor for a filer with no qualifying
children is the minimum, not the ceiling
for your situation. Your actual credit
depends on your specific earned income
calculation. And for many seniors in the
low-income bracket, the number lands
significantly above $632.
If you are a more comfortable retiree,
married threshold means this is not
exclusively a program for seniors in
financial hardship. A retired couple
receiving pension distributions, modest
social security, and some interest
income may still fall within qualifying
range. Run the actual numbers before you
self-disqualify. Right now, pause and
open your last tax return or your most
recent social security statement, not
your estimate of your income, the actual
number on the document. Look at the
adjusted gross income line, because what
comes next depends on where that number
lands against $18,591
The first form is schedule EIC, and it
attaches to your standard federal
return, form 1040. You do not file
schedule EIC as a standalone document,
it attaches to the 1040 and triggers the
IRS eligibility calculation. Both forms
are available free at irs.gov.
You do not need a third-party service,
you do not need to pay a filing fee to
access these documents. The second form
most seniors never hear about is
schedule R, the credit for the elderly
or disabled. This credit has existed
since 1976,
and it was designed specifically for
seniors on fixed incomes. It is one of
the least claimed credits in the entire
tax code, not because few seniors
qualify, but because most preparers
never navigate to it as part of a
standard return. If you are 65 or older,
schedule R should be on your return. If
it is not there, ask why. The 2025 tax
year includes a new senior bonus
deduction that reduces your adjusted
gross income. That reduction can push
seniors who previously calculated out of
the schedule R credit back into
qualifying range, particularly in the
$20,000 to $35,000 income bracket. If
your preparer has not mentioned this,
ask them directly. Did you run schedule
R with the updated AGI after applying
the senior bonus deduction? A preparer
current on 2025 tax law will answer that
immediately. A preparer who is not will
give you a vague answer or look
confused. That answer tells you
everything you need to know. There are
three sections on schedule EIC where
seniors most frequently make errors. The
first is the earned income calculation.
Earned income for this credit means
wages, self-employment income, and
certain disability payments. Social
Security benefits alone do not count as
earned income for EIC purposes. If your
only income is Social Security, you do
not qualify. If you have any earned
income in addition to Social Security,
even a small amount from part-time work
or self-employment, you may qualify and
the calculation must be run correctly.
The second common error is leaving the
investment income line blank or under
reporting it. If your investment income
exceeds the cap, the credit is zeroed
out entirely. That number must be
accurate. The third error is filing
status. Your filing status on the 1040
must match your status on schedule EIC
exactly. Mismatches trigger processing
delays and in some cases automatic
disqualification that requires an
amended return to correct. If you need
filing assistance, two free programs
serve seniors specifically. VITA, the
Volunteer Income Tax Assistance Program,
and TCE, Tax Counseling for the Elderly.
Both are IRS certified and available at
no cost. TCE through AARP Tax-Aide
specializes specifically in retirement
tax questions, pension income, social
security taxation, Schedule R, and EITC
for seniors. It does not require AARP
membership. Search IRS.gov
for VITA locations near you or call
to find the closest TCE site. That is
the form. Here is the deadline. And this
is where the people who thought they
were safe find out they are not. The IRS
operates on a strict three-year
look-back window for unclaimed refunds.
Once that window closes on a specific
tax year, the refund is permanently
forfeited. It transfers to the US
Treasury. There is no appeals process.
There is no exception for seniors. There
is no hardship waiver. The window closes
and the money is gone. The 2021 tax year
deadline falls in April 2025. If you did
not claim the earned income tax credit
or the Schedule R credit on your 2021
return and you qualified, that window is
closing right now, not next year. Now,
figure cited by IRS data is the average
unclaimed amount recovered by seniors in
this exact filing window when they filed
before the deadline. If you used a paid
preparer in 2021 and the credit was not
claimed, you are entitled to file an
amended return on Form 1040-X.
Here is the catch that costs everyone.
Most seniors assume the preparer's
silence means they did not qualify. That
is not what the silence means. Many
preparers will file an amended return at
no additional charge if the original
oversight was theirs. Ask directly. If
they decline, the amended return can be
filed independently through irs.gov. You
can also use the IRS interactive tax
assistant tool, available free at
irs.gov,
to check your eligibility for any prior
year in under 5 minutes using your
actual income figures. If it shows you
qualified for a credit that is not on
your return, you have a confirmed missed
credit and a clear basis for filing the
You will never be told by the IRS that
your window is closing. Here is exactly
what to do before the deadline. Step
one, confirm your filing status for tax
years 2021, 2022, and 2023. Pull the
returns or confirm non-filer status for
each year. If you filed, check whether
schedule EIC and schedule R were
attached. If either is missing, an
amended return is available. Step two,
run the IRS EITC assistant tool. Search
irs.gov for EITC assistant. Enter your
information for each tax year in
question, and the tool returns a clear
eligibility answer in under 5 minutes.
Use the actual numbers from your return,
not estimates. Step three, gather three
documents before you open the form.
Proof of earned income for the tax year,
your social security statement, and your
prior year return if filing an amended
return. Step four, for the 2021 tax year
specifically, confirm the exact deadline
for your situation at irs.gov under the
unclaimed refund section. The standard
window closes in April 2025. Do not
assume you have more time than that.
Step five, submit the completed 1040X
or original return directly through
irs.gov or mail it to the IRS address
listed for your state on the form
instructions. Keep a copy of everything
you submit and note the date. The IRS
has your money. The forms exist. The
deadline is real. The only remaining
variable is whether you file before the
window closes. Now you know. If someone
in your life is over 60 and has not
heard about this, send them this video
today. It may be the one thing that gets
their money back before the deadline.

title: Your Old Job May Owe You More Money — Most Seniors Don't Know They Qualify

segments.text: If you worked a job for 10, 15, or 20
years and you are now 60 or older, there
is a very good chance your former
employer still owes you money and nobody
ever told you to go claim it. The
average combined recovery when a senior
goes through all four categories is
That is not a lottery. That is not a
projection. That is what the numbers
look like when someone actually searches
every bucket instead of just one. A 2023
study by Capitalize found there are more
than 29 million forgotten 401k accounts
sitting in the American retirement
system right now. The total value is
estimated at over $1.65 trillion.
That is not a rounding error. That is a
systemic problem that nobody in that
system has a financial incentive to fix.
The average forgotten account holds
roughly $56,000.
That is not Diane's number. That is the
average, which means the headline of
this video is not a best-case scenario.
It is what a typical forgotten account
looks like before anyone even goes
looking. And the reason most people
never collect it has nothing to do with
eligibility. It has everything to do
with the fact that the institutions
holding this money are not legally
required to find you. They wait. And if
you never ask, they keep it. If this is
the kind of information nobody ever told
you, hit subscribe. We cover this every
week. My name is Laura Haines. I am here
to represent taxpayers directly in front
of the Internal Revenue Service. What I
see over and over again is not fraud. It
is not negligence. It is honest people
in their 60s and 70s who worked their
entire careers, changed jobs, moved
states, raised families, and never went
back to ask what was left behind. The
money did not disappear. The system just
stopped reminding you it was there. Here
is why it stays unclaimed. The American
retirement system was built in layers.
Pension plans, employer 401k matches,
group life insurance policies, state
wage accounts. Each layer has a
different administrator, a different
claim process, and a different silence
incentive. When you leave a job, the
employer transfers administrative
responsibility to a plan custodian or a
state agency, and then closes the file
on their end. Nobody at that institution
has a financial incentive to search for
you. Under the Employee Retirement
Income Security Act, Title 29, United
States Code, plan administrators are
required to make reasonable efforts to
locate missing participants. Reasonable
efforts. That phrase does the least
possible work in the English language.
It means a letter to your last known
address. If the letter comes back
undelivered, the search is over. The
money goes dormant. The administrator
keeps collecting fees. That is the
entire incentive structure. Whether you
are a lower income retiree living on a
fixed monthly check or a comfortable
retiree with savings already set aside,
this applies to you. An $8,000 or
$12,000 recovery from a forgotten
account is a material change for one
person. A $25,000 pension payout from a
job held in the 1990s is still money
that belongs to the other. This is not
income tested. There is no ceiling. The
only question is whether you ever worked
there and whether you ever claimed it.
That leads directly into the four
categories because you need to know
exactly what you are looking for before
you start searching. There are four
separate buckets of money tied to former
employment. Most people know about one.
Here is what the other three look like.
The first bucket is unclaimed pension
benefits from defined benefit plans.
These are the old-style pensions where
your employer promised you a monthly
payment based on years of service. If
you worked somewhere for 10 years in the
vested, and then left, that pension may
still be sitting there. The Pension
Benefit Guaranty Corporation,
established under 29 U.S.C. Section
1302, insures most private sector
defined benefit plans. When a company
goes bankrupt or terminates a plan, the
PBGC takes over and holds those benefits
until the participant claims them. Right
now, the PBGC is holding benefits for
tens of thousands of people who have
never filed. And since 2018, the PBGC's
Missing Participants Program was
expanded to also cover defined
contribution plans like 401(k)s, not
just old-style pensions. So, even if you
left a 401(k) behind and your plan later
terminated, the PBGC may be holding that
money, too. The second bucket is
abandoned 401(k) and defined
contribution accounts. When you change
jobs and leave a 401(k) behind, the
account does not vanish. If the balance
was above $5,000, the plan administrator
is required to hold it. If it was under
they were permitted to roll it to an IRA
in your name, or in some cases transfer
it to the state as unclaimed property.
There is a specific risk here for
smaller balances. If your forgotten
401(k) held under $7,000,
the plan administrator was legally
permitted to force roll it into a
default IRA, often a low-yield account
with ongoing maintenance fees. Those
fees do not stop. Every year the account
sits unclaimed, the balance shrinks. You
are not losing it all at once. You are
losing it slowly, quietly, with no
notification. As of December 2024,
the Department of Labor launched a brand
new tool specifically for this, the
retirement savings lost and found
database created under the secure 2.0
Act. It is the first centralized
government database that lets you search
for forgotten retirement accounts across
plans nationwide. It is free, it is run
by the federal government, and it is the
most powerful tool available right now
for recovering a lost 401k. The third
bucket is unpaid wages and severance
held by state labor boards. Every state
has an unclaimed property office. Unpaid
final paychecks, unused vacation
payouts, and unreturned deposits land
there when the employer cannot locate
the former employee. These amounts are
smaller on average, but they add to the
total. The fourth bucket is
employer-sponsored group life insurance.
This is the most overlooked of all four.
Many employers provide life insurance as
a standard benefit. When an employee
dies, beneficiaries are not always
notified, but this also affects living
retirees directly. If you are a named
beneficiary on a former colleague's or
spouse's workplace policy, and the
insurer never located you, that payout
is either sitting with the insurer or
has escheated to the state. Four
buckets. Most people search one and
stop. Now, pause for a moment. Open a
browser on your phone or computer right
now, not later. Here are the five free
searches you need to run, in order.
First, go to the Department of Labor's
Retirement Savings Lost and Found
Database at
retirementlostandfound.dol.gov.
This launched in December 2024 and is
the most comprehensive free tool
available for finding forgotten 401ks
and defined contribution accounts. You
will need a login.gov account to access
it, which is free to set up. Second, go
to pbgc.gov
and search the PBGC's unclaimed
retirement benefits database using your
last name and the last four digits of
your social security number. This covers
terminated pension plans and since 2018
also covers terminated 401k plans whose
funds were transferred to the PBGC.
Third, go to
unclaimedretirementbenefits.com,
the National Registry of Unclaimed
Retirement Benefits. Search your social
security number. It is free and former
employers submit participant data
directly to it. Fourth, go to
missingmoney.com, which is the
multi-state unclaimed property database
operated in partnership with NAUPA, the
National Association of Unclaimed
Property Administrators. Search every
state where you ever worked or lived,
not just your current state, every
state. Fifth, if you're searching for a
terminated plan whose custodian has gone
out of business, use the Department of
Labor's abandoned plan search, also at
dol.gov. Those five searches cost
nothing and take less than 45 minutes
total. Do not pay anyone to do this for
you before you have done it yourself.
That matters and I will come back to it.
Here is where the $56,000
figure comes from. It is not one
account, it is the stack. Take a woman
named Diane. She is 67, a retired
administrative coordinator from Dayton,
Ohio. She worked four jobs over her
career, a manufacturing firm in the
1980s, a hospital system in the 1990s, a
school district, and a private medical
office. When she ran all five database
searches, here is what she found. A
vested pension from the manufacturing
firm, which had been acquired and whose
plan was now held by the PBGC, worth
in back benefits. A forgotten 401k from
the hospital system with a current
balance of $18,700.
Unpaid vacation wages from the medical
office held by the Ohio unclaimed
property office totaling $4,200.
And an employer life insurance payout
from the school district where her late
husband had also worked held by the
insurer totaling $11,600.
Diane's total recovery was $56,900.
She did nothing wrong. She simply never
knew to look. That is exactly what the
stack produces when someone goes through
every bucket. Finding the money is the
first problem. Claiming it correctly is
the second. And the second one is where
most of the damage happens. Mistake
number one is using a paid recovery
service before searching the free
databases yourself. These companies
charge between 20 and 40% of your total
recovery. They are legal, but they are
charging you a four-figure fee for a
45-minute search you can do yourself at
no cost on government-operated websites.
Do the free search first. If you find
nothing, you owe no one anything.
Mistake number two is missing the 60-day
rollover window on recovered retirement
funds. Under Internal Revenue Code
Section 402,
if you take a direct distribution from a
recovered 401k instead of rolling it
directly into an IRA, the plan
administrator is required to withhold
20% for federal taxes immediately. You
then have 60 days to deposit the full
original amount including the withheld
20% out of your own pocket into an IRA
to avoid treating the entire amount as
taxable income. Miss that window and the
IRS taxes the full distribution as
ordinary income in the year you receive
it. A 10% early withdrawal penalty may
also apply depending on your age at
distribution. Request a direct rollover
to an IRA custodian before any funds are
dispersed to you personally. Mistake
number three is submitting a life
insurance claim without the correct
documentation. Insurers are legally
permitted to delay or deny claims where
the beneficiary cannot produce required
proof. That typically means a certified
copy of the policy or plan summary, a
certified death certificate if claiming
as a beneficiary, and written proof of
your relationship to the insured.
Without those documents in hand before
you file, the claim goes into a review
queue that can take 12 to 18 months.
Gather the documents first. File
complete. One submission, clean records.
Here is the action sequence. Step one,
run all five free database searches
today. The DOL retirement savings lost
and found at
retirementlostandfound.dol.gov.
The PBGC unclaimed benefits database at
pbgc.gov
using your last name and last four
digits of your social security number.
The national registry of unclaimed
retirement benefits at
unclaimedretirementbenefits.com.
Missing money.com across every state you
have worked or lived in. And the DOL
abandoned plan search also at dol.gov.
Step two, pull your complete social
security earning statement from ssa.gov.
It lists every employer who ever
reported wages in your name. That is
your road map. Step three, contact each
former employer's HR department or plan
administrator in writing. Request your
current vesting and benefit status. Keep
every response. Step four, before you
accept any distribution from a recovered
retirement account, open a rollover IRA
at your bank or custodian and request a
direct trustee-to-trustee transfer.
Never take the check. Step five, for any
life insurance claim, request the full
plan summary from the insurer or from
your state's Department of Insurance. If
the insurer is unresponsive, gather your
documentation and file a complete
written claim with all supporting
documents attached. One more thing, this
money does not expire, but it does move.
Small balances get force rolled, dormant
accounts get escheated to the state.
Every transfer makes it one step harder
to find and one step closer to being
gone in practice, even if not on paper.
The time to look is not when you get
around to it. The time is now because
the account you find today may not be in
the same place next year. You will never
be told this money is waiting. The
institution holding it has no obligation
to call. The search takes 45 minutes.
The claim takes a weekend. The money has
been there for years. If someone you
love is still working toward retirement,
share this with them now. What they do
not know will cost them.

title: Bank Account Activity Seniors Should Be Aware Of in 2026

segments.text: If you have moved money between your own
bank accounts, received a large cash
gift, helped a child with a down
payment, or kept more than $10,000 in a
single checking account, there are seven
specific bank account moves the IRS and
federal regulators are flagging right
now in 2026. Most seniors have made at
least three of them in the past 12
months, and not one of them was told.
Here is what makes this dangerous. These
are not moves that look suspicious. They
are moves that look careful. They look
responsible, they look exactly like what
a financially cautious person would do,
and that is precisely why they trigger
automatic federal reports, account
freezes, and in the worst cases the
seizure of money you spent decades
earning. My name is Laura Haines. I am
here to represent taxpayers directly in
front of the Internal Revenue Service.
What I am going to walk you through
today is the same information I go over
with clients before they make any
significant financial move in
retirement. There is no version of this
conversation your bank will ever start
with you. Move one is the $10,000
threshold. Under the Bank Secrecy Act of
1970, every financial institution in the
United States is required to file a
currency transaction report with the
Financial Crimes Enforcement Network
anytime a customer makes a cash
transaction exceeding $10,000
in a single business day. You do not
sign it, you do not see a copy, you will
never be told it was filed. The report
includes your full legal name, Social
Security number, date of birth, address,
and the time of the transaction down to
the minute. That report sits in a
federal database shared between FinCEN,
the IRS Criminal Investigation Division,
the DEA, the Department of Homeland
Security, and approximately 400 other
agencies. It stays there for 5 years. A
currency transaction report by itself is
not an accusation. It is routine
paperwork. The CTR is not the danger,
what people do next is the danger. Move
two is structuring. Under Title 31,
United States Code Section 5324,
it is a federal felony to break up any
transaction for the purpose of staying
below the $10,000 reporting threshold.
Up to 5 years in federal prison, up to
in fines, and forfeiture of the entire
amount, even if every cent is legal.
Consider a woman named Patricia, a
67-year-old retired postal worker from
Dayton, Ohio. She sold her late
husband's truck for $14,000 in cash. A
neighbor told her to deposit it in two
separate transactions to avoid the
hassle. Patricia deposited 7,000 on a
Monday and 7,000 the following Thursday.
The bank's software flagged two
below-threshold deposits from the same
account within 7 days and filed a
suspicious activity report. The IRS
opened a review. The money was never
seized, but that review took 4 months
and required documentation going back 2
years. The fix is simple. Deposit the
full amount in one transaction. Bring
your documentation. Let the currency
transaction report file. Move three is a
suspicious report. This is the report
with no floor. A bank can file a SAR on
a transaction of any size. The decision
is made entirely by the bank's internal
compliance software based on whether
your behavior fits a pattern the
algorithm flags as unusual. The bank is
legally prohibited from telling you it
was filed. A bank employee who tips you
off has committed a federal crime
carrying up to 5-years in prison. The
bank faces zero penalty for filing a SAR
incorrectly. A bank that fails to file
when it should have can be fined
millions. That is the entire incentive
structure. Right now, open your bank
account and look at your last 60 to 90
days of transactions. Not the amounts,
the pattern. Consistent small
withdrawals followed by one large one,
multiple transfers to accounts that did
not previously receive them. That is
what the software is reading. Move four
is the 15-day senior account freeze.
Under elder financial protection
regulations adopted across most states,
a bank that suspects financial
exploitation of a senior can place a
hold on account disbursements for up to
15 calendar days without your consent
and without a court order. The bank's
software does not know why you are
making a large withdrawal. During a
15-day freeze, your scheduled bills do
not get paid and your debit card does
not work. The solution is the same
regardless of your balance. Notify your
bank in writing before any large
transaction. Give them the reason, the
recipient, and the amount. One call to
your branch manager before the
transaction eliminates the flag
entirely. Move five is the $250,000
FDIC insurance cliff. The FDIC insures
deposits up to $250,000
per depositor per institution. In 2023,
three major US banks failed within
approximately 10 weeks. Seniors who kept
more than $250,000
at a single institution faced real
exposure above that limit. The solution
is to distribute balances across
multiple FDIC insured institutions
keeping each account at or below the
insured threshold. Distributing savings
for insurance purposes is a documented
lawful financial practice. Keep records
of each account and each transfer. Move
six is the gift that triggers a federal
filing. In 2025, the annual gift tax
exclusion is $19,000 per recipient per
year. Above that amount, the giver is
required to file IRS form 709.
If the giver breaks a larger gift into
smaller transfers across multiple
accounts or multiple weeks to stay below
the threshold, that pattern can trigger
a suspicious activity report on both
accounts. A single clean transfer with a
written gift letter and a copy of form
709 filed by the giver closes the issue
completely. The gift letter takes 10
minutes. The SAR review takes months.
Move seven is the joint account change.
Adding a family member to your bank
account as a joint owner is treated by
the IRS as a partial transfer of
ownership, which can trigger gift tax
reporting under form 709. It also gives
that person immediate and total legal
access to every dollar in the account,
meaning their creditors, their divorce
proceedings, and their financial
judgments can reach your savings
directly. Banks also flag sudden
ownership changes on senior accounts as
potential elder financial exploitation,
which can trigger a SAR and a 15-day
freeze simultaneously. A woman named
Sandra, a 71-year-old retired nurse from
Phoenix, added her son's name to her
$38,000 savings account to simplify
things after her husband died. The bank
flagged the change. A SAR was filed. A
15-day freeze followed. Sandra did
nothing wrong. The clean alternative is
a durable financial power of attorney
reviewed by an estate attorney, which
grants access without transferring
ownership and without triggering a bank
flag. Here is the action checklist. Step
one, confirm your current account
balances today. If any single
institution holds more than $250,000,
plan a documented transfer to a second
FDIC insured institution. Step two,
before any transaction above $5,000,
notify your bank branch in writing,
state the amount, the reason, and the
recipient. Keep a copy. This protects
you against both a SAR filing and a
15-day freeze. Step three, never break a
deposit into smaller amounts to avoid
the $10,000 threshold. Deposit the full
amount, bring your documentation, let
the currency transaction report file.
Step four, if you have gifted or plan to
gift more than $19,000 to any one person
in 2025, confirm that the giver files
IRS form 709 before the tax deadline.
Step five, if a family member has
suggested adding their name to your bank
account, stop before you sign anything.
Consult a licensed estate attorney about
a durable financial power of attorney
instead. Step six, pull your last 90
days of bank transactions and review the
pattern from the outside. If you see
structured deposits, below threshold
transfers, or sudden activity changes,
bring those records to an enrolled agent
or tax attorney before the bank software
flags them first. You will never be told
these rules when you open an account.
You know them now. Share this with the
woman in your life who manages her own
finances and has never heard the words
currency transaction report. That one
conversation could save her everything
she spent a lifetime building.

title: Notable 2026 Rule Changes Affecting Seniors

segments.text: If you were born before 1960, the IRS is
sending out a specific letter right now,
and most people who receive it have no
idea what it actually means or what they
are legally required to do next. That
letter has a response window. Miss it
and the IRS does not wait for you to
figure it out. They assess, they
collect, and by the time you understand
what happened, the penalty is already
final. My name is Laura Haynes. I am
here to represent taxpayers directly in
front of the Internal Revenue Service.
What I see across the table from the IRS
over and over is not fraud. It is not
evasion. It is ordinary retirees,
careful people in their late 50s and 60s
and 70s, sitting with penalties they
never saw coming because the rules
changed and nobody told them. That is
what this video is here to fix. Here is
