Social Security benefits, this applies
to you directly. If you are a surviving
spouse whose own benefit was reduced
because of your late partner's
government pension, this applies to you
directly. If you were ever told your
Social Security would be zero or near
zero because of a government pension
offset, this applies to you directly.
They are not going to call you. That has
not changed. What has changed is that
you now know exactly why, and you know
the three steps that move your account
from the queue to a corrected payment.
The law is enacted. The retroactivity
date is January 2024. The average lump
sum owed is $6,710.
The average permanent monthly increase
The only remaining question is whether
your account gets corrected or stays in
that queue unchallenged. If someone you
know was a teacher, a firefighter, a
government worker, or a surviving spouse
who lost benefits they earned, send this
to them today. It may be the one
conversation that finally gets their
money corrected.

title: The Banking Mistake That Can Get Your Account Reported (Most Don't Realize It)

segments.text: If you have ever taken out cash in
amounts under $10,000 because you
thought that was the safe way to do it,
you need to stop and watch this. That
habit, the one you followed to protect
yourself, is the exact behavior the
banking system is built to detect. It is
not the large transaction that puts you
on the IRS radar. It is the pattern of
small ones. And if you are a retiree who
has helped a grandchild with rent, paid
a contractor in cash, or spread out a
large withdrawal across a few trips to
the bank, there is a real chance a
report has already been filed on your
account. You were never told, you were
never warned. The law forbids it. My
name is Laura Haynes. I am here to
represent taxpayers directly in front of
the Internal Revenue Service. The
clients I sit across from are not
criminals. They are retired teachers,
widows, and tradespeople who handled
their own money the way they always had,
and one day found themselves explaining
their bank account to a federal
compliance officer. The pattern I see in
almost every one of those cases starts
with the same misunderstanding about a
rule most people have heard of, but
almost no one actually understands. Here
is the rule. Under the Bank Secrecy Act
of 1970, every financial institution in
the United States is required by law to
file a currency transaction report, a
CTR, anytime a customer makes a cash
transaction that exceeds $10,000 in a
single business day. That report goes
directly to the Financial Crimes
Enforcement Network, known as FinCEN, a
bureau inside the United States
Treasury. It is filed on FinCEN Form
104. It includes your full legal name,
your Social Security number, your date
of birth, your address, the exact
amount, the type of transaction, and the
time it occurred down to the minute. The
bank has 15 calendar days to submit it.
You will never see a copy. The bank is
legally prohibited from telling you they
filed it. Now, here is the
misunderstanding that costs people
everything. Millions of Americans heard
the $10,000 number and drew the wrong
conclusion. They decided that staying
under it was the cautious move. So, they
withdrew 9,000,
then 8,000, then 9,000 again, a few days
apart. They thought they were being
careful. They were building a federal
case against themselves. That leads
straight into what the law actually
calls this behavior because the name for
it changes everything. The federal
statute is title 31, United States Code,
section 5324.
It defines structuring as deliberately
breaking a transaction into smaller
amounts for the purpose of evading the
reporting requirement. That is the
crime, not the money. The pattern. You
do not need to be hiding income. You do
not need to be evading taxes. You do not
need to have done a single dishonest
thing with a single dollar. If the money
is completely clean, legally earned,
legally inherited, legally gifted, and
you broke it into smaller deposits or
withdrawals to stay under 10,000, you
have committed a federal offense under
section 5324.
The penalties are not small. For
violations under $100,000
in a 12-month period, the statute
carries up to 5 years in federal prison
and fines up to $250,000.
For violations over $100,000 or
connected to other activity, up to 10
years and fines up to $500,000.
And in both cases, the government can
seize the funds through civil forfeiture
before a single charge is filed. Here is
something worth holding on to for both
groups watching this. If you are a lower
income retiree handling modest amounts
of cash, the dollar thresholds may seem
distant. They are not. Forfeiture cases
in the public record involve amounts as
low as $7,000.
If you are a comfortable retiree
managing larger sums, the exposure is
proportionally greater, and the legal
costs of reclaiming seized funds scale
with the amount involved. This rule does
not spare either group. Now, here is the
part that makes this different from
almost any other financial risk. No
human at your bank is watching your
account and making a judgment call. That
is not how this works. Pause for a
moment and think about the last three
cash withdrawals you made. Not the
amounts, the timing. Were any of them
within a few weeks of each other? Each
one under $10,000?
Hold that thought because what comes
next depends entirely on whether that
pattern exists. The banking software
your institution uses runs pattern
detection continuously. It does not
sleep. It does not take holidays, and it
does not care why you needed the money.
When your transaction history fits the
profile of structuring, the software
does not send a manager to ask you about
it. It files a suspicious activity
report, a SAR, directly with FinCEN.
That filing happens automatically. No
human at the bank authorizes it. No one
reviews it before it goes. FinCEN shares
that SAR with IRS Criminal Investigation
within hours of the filing. There is no
phone call to you. There is no letter.
There is no warning. And under federal
tipping off rules, any bank employee who
tells you a SAR was filed on your
account has committed a federal crime
carrying up to 5 years in prison. That
is why your bank cannot tell you. It is
not policy. It is federal law. Here is
the catch that costs everyone. A
currency transaction report, the CTR,
filed on a transaction over $10,000 is
routine. It goes into a database. Almost
nothing happens. But a suspicious
activity report is different. A SAR is a
targeted flag. It goes to the same
database and to the same agencies, but
it signals a pattern of evasion, not a
large transaction. CTRs are paperwork.
SARs are investigations. And the
behavior that generates a SAR is not a
big deposit. It is the repeated small
ones. Now, let us talk about who is
actually triggering these reports
because it is not who most people
imagine. Take a woman named Dorothy. She
is 71, a retired bookkeeper from
Knoxville, Tennessee, who raised four
children on one income and saved
carefully her entire life. When her
furnace failed last October, she hired a
contractor who worked for cash only. She
withdrew
Two weeks later, she withdrew 2,500 for
the second phase of the work. Three
weeks after that, 2,200 for the final
materials. Three withdrawals, same
payee. Rolling 90-day window. The
software flagged a structuring pattern.
Dorothy did nothing wrong. Dorothy paid
a contractor. That is the entire story
and it became a federal compliance file.
Dorothy is not unusual. Retirees deal in
cash more than any other demographic and
they do it for completely ordinary
reasons. There are five situations that
appear in forfeiture cases and
compliance investigations more than any
others. The first is helping family with
cash. Slipping a grandchild money for a
security deposit, a car repair or a
medical bill. The amounts feel modest.
The timing is whatever the crisis is.
The pattern is not visible to the person
making the withdrawals. The second is
paying contractors. Plumbers, painters,
handymen, landscapers, cash-preferred
tradespeople are common in every
retirement community in the country.
Multiple jobs, multiple withdrawals, all
legitimate, all flaggable. The third is
spreading out a large cash purchase. A
used car bought privately, a piece of
furniture, a repair that runs over
budget. The buyer breaks it into two or
three withdrawals across a week or two,
each one comfortably under $10,000. The
fourth is funeral expenses. A family
death generates multiple urgent cash
needs in a compressed window. Flowers,
travel, a deposit at the funeral home, a
reception. The withdrawals cluster in
days, not weeks. The software sees the
cluster. The fifth is cash gifts for
milestones. A grandchild's wedding, a
college graduation, a new baby. The
giver makes several withdrawals over a
few weeks thinking they are being
thoughtful. The pattern recognition does
not know what the envelope was for. In
every one of these cases, the money is
clean. The person is doing nothing
wrong. That is what makes the next part
so consequential. Under civil asset
forfeiture law, the United States
government has the authority to seize
funds from a bank account based on a
finding of probable cause. Not a
conviction, not an arrest, not even a
formal charge. Probable cause. A SAR
filing combined with a transaction
pattern consistent with structuring
under Title 31 can be sufficient to
establish probable cause for seizure.
Once the funds are seized, the burden of
proof does not fall on the government to
prove you did something wrong. It falls
on you to prove you did not. That is the
legal structure. You are proving
innocence, not the government proving
guilt, and you are doing it while your
money is inaccessible, while legal fees
accumulate, and in some cases while you
are managing the very life circumstances
that caused the withdrawals in the first
place. The Institute for Justice
documented this pattern extensively in
its reporting on structuring seizures.
In one case, a convenience store
operator in North Carolina lost $17,000.
In another, a restaurant owner in Iowa
had $33,000 seized. In both cases, no
criminal charges were filed. In both
cases, the money was legally sourced. In
both cases, recovery required years of
litigation. If you are a lower income
retiree, a seizure of even several
thousand dollars is a financial
emergency. If you are a comfortable
retiree, the legal fees alone in a
protracted forfeiture case can easily
exceed the amount being contested.
Neither group is insulated from this.
Now, here is the part that matters most
because everything up to this point is
reversible going forward. Three changes
eliminate this risk entirely. The first
is consolidation. Make one transaction
instead of several. A single $12,000
cash withdrawal triggers a CTR. That is
routine paperwork that goes into a
database and almost never results in any
further action. Three $4,000 withdrawals
over 3 weeks triggers a SAR. That is a
targeted federal investigation flag. One
large transaction is safer than several
small ones. That is the precise opposite
of what most people believe, and it is
the central point of this entire video.
The second is documentation. If you must
make multiple cash transactions for a
legitimate reason, create a paper record
before you go to the bank. Write down
the date, the amount, the purpose, and
who received the money. Keep the
contractor's invoice. Keep the bill of
sale, keep the gift note, keep the
funeral home receipt. Documentation does
not prevent a SAR from being filed, but
it is the evidence that resolves an
investigation quickly when one opens.
The third is electronic transfer over
cash, wherever possible. A Zelle
transfer, a wire transfer, a personal
check, a cashier's check, any traceable
electronic method creates a permanent
record, eliminates the cash pattern
entirely, and gives you documentation by
default. There is nothing for the
pattern software to flag. You started
this video thinking that keeping
transactions under $10,000 was the
cautious move. Now you know it is the
opposite. The system is not watching for
one large transaction. It is watching
for the pattern of someone who learned
about the $10,000 rule and tried to stay
beneath it. That pattern has a name in
federal law. The name is structuring.
And the consequences reach your account
before a single charge is filed. You
will never be told when a report is
filed. You will never be warned that a
flag was entered. The law forbids it.
What you can do is stop the pattern
before it forms. Here is what to do now.
Step one, review your last 90 days of
cash withdrawals. Open your statement
and look at every cash transaction. If
you see three or more withdrawals, each
under $10,000, within any rolling 90-day
window, note the amounts and dates. Step
two, consolidate future cash needs into
single transactions. Before your next
cash withdrawal, add up the full amount
you need and take it in one trip. A CTR
on a single large transaction is safer
than a SAR on three smaller ones. Step
three, open a written log for any
ongoing cash situation. If you are
paying a contractor over multiple
visits, keep a single document with
every payment, the date, the amount, the
purpose, and the contractor's name.
Update it at each payment and keep the
receipts. Step four, switch to
electronic payment for any recurring
cash recipient. Ask your contractor,
your landscaper, your regular service
providers whether they accept Zelle,
check, or bank transfer. Most do. One
conversation eliminates the risk
permanently for that payee. Step five,
if you have already made a series of
cash withdrawals in a pattern that
concerns you, consult an enrolled agent
or a tax attorney before your next
transaction. Do not make another
withdrawal in the same pattern while the
issue is unresolved. The consultation is
the protective move. If someone you love
handles their own banking and has never
heard this explained, send this to them
today. It may be the one piece of
information that keeps their money
exactly where it belongs.

title: 3 Social Security Checks in 2026

segments.text: If you or someone you love receive
Social Security, there are three
government changes hitting in 2026, and
most seniors have no idea any of them
are coming. One of them could cut your
monthly check in half, starting as soon
as next month. Not a rumor, not
speculation. The Social Security
Administration has already been mailing
the notices. The Treasury has already
frozen payments for people caught off
guard. And the third change has a hard
deadline of July 1st, 2026, that almost
no one is talking about. Three changes:
the overpayment clawback, the paper
check elimination, and the student loan
garnishment deadline. Stay through all
three because the last one is the one
that is going to hit people who have not
thought about a student loan in 30
years. And when it hits, it hits
automatically. Here is what this video
covers: the overpayment letter and
exactly what it can take from you, the
90-day window you have to fight back,
and the three forms that do it. The
paper check elimination and what happens
to your money if you have not acted. The
identity verification rule that now
makes your phone call useless, the
student loan garnishment that is already
affecting 452,000
Social Security recipients, the three
ways to stop it before July 1st, 2026,
and the exact steps to protect yourself
before any of these deadlines pass. My
name is Laura Haynes. I am here to
represent taxpayers directly in front of
the Internal Revenue Service. What I see
across the table from real seniors every
week is the same pattern. The money
disappears first, the explanation
arrives weeks later, and the window to
fight back is already closing. You will
never be told about any of this until
after it starts. So, let us start with
the one that is already in motion. The
letter that steals half your check. The
Social Security Administration has been
mailing overpayment letters since 2024.
An overpayment letter tells you that SSA
believes it paid you more than you were
entitled to and that it now intends to
collect the difference directly from
your monthly benefit. Here is what most
people do not know. In 2022, 73,000 of
those overpayment notices were caused by
SSA's own calculation errors, not fraud,
not misreporting. The agency made the
mistake and then sent you the bill. And
on notices dated after April 25th, 2025,
the default withholding rate is 50% of
your monthly benefit. If your check is
SSA can now reduce it to $900
automatically. For SSI recipients, the
withholding rate is 10%, but the
mechanism is identical. Here is the
catch that costs everyone. You have 90
days from the date of that letter to
act. After 90 days, the withholding
begins and the money comes out without
any further notice. The agency will not
call you. Nobody mails you a second
warning. The burden is entirely on you
to respond in time. There are three
forms and each one does something
different. Form
is a request for
reconsideration. You use it when you
believe SSA made a calculation error,
which in thousands of cases it did. Form
SSA 632 is a waiver request. You use it
when you agree money was overpaid, but
you cannot afford to pay it back and
repayment would cause financial
hardship. Form SSA
is a request to reduce the repayment
rate. You use it when you accept the
debt, but 50% withholding is more than
your budget can absorb. Here is what
each of those forms can actually do for
you. If you are a lower income senior
living on a fixed benefit, form SSA 632
is your most powerful tool because a
hardship waiver can eliminate the
repayment obligation entirely. Here is
the win for each group. For the lower
income senior, that waiver removes the
debt. For the comfortable retiree with
other income coming in, Form SSA 561
is where to start because if SSA made
the error, the debt itself may not be
valid and reconsideration can get it
reversed before withholding ever begins.
And here is one more fact you will not
be told. If your alleged overpayment is
$2,000 or less, you may be able to
request a waiver by phone without filing
a paper form at all. SSA will not offer
this. You have to ask for it by name.
Take Francis. She is 72, a retired home
health aide from Akron, Ohio, who
received an overpayment letter in
February 2025 stating she owed $3,400
from a benefit recalculation 3 years
earlier. Francis did nothing wrong. The
recalculation was an SSA administrative
correction on their end. Francis called
to ask questions and was told to repay
the balance. She was not told she could
request reconsideration. She was not
told she could request a waiver. She was
not told she had 90 days. Six weeks
later, half her check was gone. That gap
between what SSA tells you and what SSA
is required to allow you to do is
exactly what these three forms exist to
close. Now, knowing how to fight a
clawback only helps you if the check
actually arrives because the government
just eliminated paper checks entirely.
And people already on direct deposit are
finding their payments frozen without
any warning. No check, no phone call, no
warning. The US Treasury has moved
approximately 69 million beneficiaries
to electronic payments. Anyone not
enrolled in direct deposit or the Direct
Express card is now at risk of having
their payment frozen entirely, not
delayed. Frozen. And it can happen
without any notification arriving before
the money fails to appear. Here is what
changed about identity verification. And
this is the part catching people who
thought they were already safe. You can
no longer change your banking
information by phone. That option is
gone. To update your direct deposit
account, you now must verify your
identity either online through login.gov
or id.me or in person at a Social
Security Administration office. A phone
call to SSA will not accomplish it. Here
is the win for each group. If you are a
lower-income senior who has been
reluctant to go online, setting up a my
Social Security account with login.gov
is free, takes less than 30 minutes, and
is the only way to update your
information from home. If you are a
comfortable retiree who assumed your
direct deposit was already set and
protected, know this. Fraud filters are
now actively flagging and holding
deposits even for accounts that have
been receiving payments for years. A
bank merger, an account number update
from your institution,
any unusual change can be enough to
trigger a hold with no notice to you.
Right now, go to your most recent Social
Security payment and confirm it
deposited in the amount you expected.
Not last month, today. If the number is
different or if no deposit appears where
one should, that is not a bank error to
wait out. That needs to be addressed
directly with SSA. If you are genuinely
unable to complete the online
verification process, there is one
specific number. Call the US Treasury
electronic payment solution center at 1
to request a hardship waiver for paper
checks. That waiver exists. It is not
advertised. You have to ask for it.
Getting your payment method squared away
is not optional anymore. But even if
your check arrives on time and in the
right account, there is a third group of
seniors who are about to watch up to 15%
of it disappear automatically. And the
window to stop it closes on July 1st,
This is the change with the hardest
deadline of the three and the one that
is going to blindside people who have
not thought about a student loan in
decades. The student loan time bomb
under the Treasury offset program, the
federal government has the legal
authority to seize up to 15% of your
monthly Social Security benefit to
collect on defaulted federal student
loans. There is a floor of $750
per month. Below that floor, your
benefit cannot be touched. Above it, up
to 15% comes out automatically before
the check ever reaches you. No separate
bill, no collection call. The offset
happens at the Treasury level before the
deposit is made. Approximately 452,000
Social Security recipients are currently
subject to this. Many of them are
retirees who borrowed decades ago. Many
of them co-signed loans for a child or
grandchild and the underlying borrower
stopped paying. The co-signer is equally
liable. Collections under this program
were paused twice. The most recent pause
began January 16th, 2026. That pause
ends when the repayment assistance plan,
the wrap, launches on July 1st, 2026.
After that date, garnishment can resume
for anyone in default who has not taken
action. July 1st, 2026 is not a soft
guideline. It is the restart date.
Consider Marlene. She is 67, a retired
bookkeeper from Louisville, Kentucky who
co-signed a $28,000 federal loan for her
daughter in 2009.
Her daughter made payments for several
years and then stopped. Marlene had no
idea the loan was in default. She
received no direct notice. In 2024, she
discovered that 15% of her Social
Security benefit had been withheld for
four consecutive months before she
realized the deposits were short.
Marlene did nothing wrong. By the time
she understood what had happened, the
offset had already taken $1,260
from her account. There are three ways
to stop this before the deadline, and
all three must be started before July 1,
2026. Here is the win for each group. If
you are a lower-income senior who cannot
sustain 15% coming off the top of your
only income, loan rehabilitation is your
most powerful path. If you are a
comfortable retiree with assets and
other income, a hardship objection filed
directly with the Department of
Education gives you the strongest
immediate lever to delay the offset
while your case is reviewed. Federal
student loan rehabilitation requires
nine on-time payments over 10 months.
The monthly payment amount during
rehabilitation can be set as low as $5
depending on your income. Once those
nine payments are complete, the default
is removed from your record entirely,
and the Treasury offset is terminated.
If you have a qualifying medical
condition, a total and permanent
disability discharge through the
Department of Education may eliminate
the debt entirely. You do not have to be
completely incapacitated. You must meet
the Department of Education's definition
of total and permanent disability, which
is a documented condition expected to
continue indefinitely. A third option is
a hardship objection, which is a formal
challenge to the garnishment filed
directly with the Department of
Education before collections resume. The
hardship objection does not eliminate
the debt, but it can delay or reduce the
offset while your case is reviewed. Here
is the sequence that matters. Check your
federal loan status first. Go to
studentaid.gov and log in. Look for any
loans listed as in default. If you see
them, the time to act is now, before
July 1st, 2026. If collections resume
before you have started rehabilitation
or filed a discharge application, the
offset restarts and your check is short
again with no further warning. That is
the deadline. That is the exposure, and
that is exactly the kind of fact you
will never be told by the agency
collecting from you. Your action
checklist before the deadlines pass here
is every step in the order you need to
take them. Step one, check your mail and
your SSA account for any overpayment
notice. If a letter has arrived, look at
the date. If the date is after April
your 90-day window is already running.
Do not wait. Step two, if you received
an overpayment letter, decide which form
fits your situation. If you believe SSA
made the error, file form SSA 561 for
reconsideration. If you cannot afford to
repay, file form SSA 632 for a waiver.
If you accept the debt but cannot absorb
50% withholding, file form SSA 634 to
request a lower rate. If your debt is
$2,000 or less, call SSA directly and
ask for a waiver by phone before filing
anything. Step three, go to ssa.gov
and set up or log in to your My Social
Security account. Verify your identity
through login.gov or id.me, confirm your
direct deposit information is current
and matches an active account. If you
cannot complete this online, call
to request a paper check hardship waiver
from the US Treasury Electronic Payment
Solution Center. Step four, go to
studentaid.gov and check whether any
federal loans are listed in your name as
defaulted. Include loans you co-signed.
Step five, if you find a defaulted loan,
contact the Department of Education
before July 1st, 2026. Request loan
rehabilitation,
a total and permanent disability
discharge if you qualify, or file a
hardship objection to contest the
garnishment. All three require you to
initiate contact. None of them are
offered to you automatically. Step six,
confirm your next Social Security
deposit after completing these steps.
Verify the full expected amount arrived.
If it is short, act immediately. Do not
assume it will correct itself. Three
changes most seniors have no idea. Now
you do. And more
know exactly what to do about each one
before the deadlines close. If you have
a parent, a grandparent, an aunt, an
uncle, or a neighbor receiving Social
Security, this video is the phone call
the government has not made to them.
Send it to them today.

title: Seniors over 65 STOP Overpaying Property Tax — Check These 5 Bills

segments.text: There are at least five legal forms the
average American homeowner over the age
of 65 is sitting on right now that can
stop, lower, or permanently freeze the
property tax bill they pay every single
year. Five forms. And before I go one
sentence further, I need to clear
something up because this is the single
biggest misunderstanding about property
tax exemptions. And it is the reason
most seniors who legally qualify never
file a single one. People assume a video
like this is only for one kind of
homeowner. Either they think it is only
for lowincome retirees who are
struggling. So if they are comfortable
and their home is paid off, they tune
out. Or they think it is for people
whose accountants handle everything. So
if they already have a tax preparer,
they assume it is covered. Both of those
assumptions are wrong. And I am going to
tell you exactly why on every single
form your accountant does not
automatically handle these. These are
county level filings, not federal tax
filings. Two completely separate
systems. Your accountant files with the
IRS. Nobody files these forms with the
county unless you do it yourself. And
most of these exemptions are not
incomebased. They are age triggered. You
turn 65, you own the home you live in,
and the entitlement exists whether you
earn $30,000 a year or $130,000 a year.
Income does not disqualify you. The
national median property tax bill is
about $4,800 a year. For a 65year-old
who lives in their home another 20
years, that is nearly $100,000
going out the door on a bill that for
many of you should be a fraction of what
you are paying. or in some cases zero.
Here is what this video covers. First,
the exact reason the county will never
notify you and why that is not an
accident. Second, the senior homestead
exemption and what it actually does to
your bill. Third, the property tax
freeze, a separate filing that most
people who claim the exemption still
never touch. Fourth, three underused
exemptions that stack on top of the
first. Fifth, the appraisal cap, the one
form that compounds against you the
longest if you never file it. And sixth,
the exact steps to find out right now
whether any of this has been applied to
your account. Stay to the end because
the last form I am going to show you is
the one that quietly costs people the
most money and it is one of the easiest
to claim. My name is Laura Haynes. I
represent taxpayers directly in front of
the Internal Revenue Service. And what I
am about to walk you through is the same
conversation I have had with clients who
came in for something entirely
unrelated. Estate planning, a trust
review, an IRS notice, and it came out
that they had owned their home for 20
years and had never filed a single one
of these forms. Not one. Every single
time, the pattern is the same. Nobody
told them. Not their bank, not their
county, not their tax preparer, nobody.
Here is why. County appraisal districts
are funded by property tax revenue.
Every dollar and exemption they hand out
is a dollar their own office does not
collect next year. There is no fraud
here. There is no conspiracy. There is a

deduction and the provisional income
mechanism are two separate systems.
Saving money in one does not protect you
in the other. And because the IRMAA
look-back period is 2 years, the
interest income you are earning in 2024
and 2025 is determining your Medicare
premium costs in 2026 and 2027. The
decisions happening right now and the
accounts you have open right now are
setting your costs 2 years forward. Here
is the calculation framework so you can
run your own numbers. Step one, add your
adjusted gross income, your tax-exempt
interest income, and 50% of your annual
Social Security benefit. That total is
your provisional income. Step two,
identify your gap to the nearest
threshold. If you are single, the
thresholds are $25,000
If you are married filing jointly, the
thresholds shift up. Calculate the
distance between your current
provisional income and the next
threshold above you. Step three, divide
your gap by your current API as a
decimal. That gives you the maximum
balance you can hold in an
interest-bearing account without
crossing the threshold. If your gap is
$3,000 and your API is 5%, your maximum
safe balance at that yield is $60,000.
Any balance above that will generate
interest that crosses the line. That
number is your threshold, not the IRS's
threshold, yours. If you are a
lower-income retiree and your
provisional income is currently below
your gap may be small and a modest
savings account balance may already be
pushing you toward the line. Knowing
your exact gap tells you exactly how
much room you have. If you are a
comfortable retiree already above
your priority is the distance to $34,000
because that is where the 85% social
security taxability bracket begins and
where most RMD exposure originates. Here
is where to move the money instead.
Municipal bond interest is excluded from
the provisional income calculation
entirely. Interest earned from
qualifying municipal bonds does not
count toward the number the IRS uses to
determine your social security
taxability. If you are holding a balance
above your personal threshold in a
taxable high-yield account, moving a
portion into a municipal bond fund
produces comparable yield without
inflating provisional income. Roth IRA
distributions are also excluded from
provisional income. The IRS does not
count Roth distributions as income for
this calculation. If you have money in a
traditional IRA that could be converted
to a Roth during a low-income year and
your provisional income currently sits
below a threshold, a strategic partial
conversion can shift future
distributions outside the calculation
permanently. The conversion itself
creates taxable income in the year it
happens. So, the math has to be run
carefully, but the long-term protection
is real. Series I bonds and Series EE
bonds allow you to defer the interest
recognition to the year of redemption
rather than the year it accrues. If you
hold these bonds and do not redeem them
in a given year, the interest does not
appear in your provisional income
calculation for that year. That gives
you direct control over which tax year
the income lands in. These are not
workarounds. They are the legal
structure the IRS has built. Using them
is the point. Run your personal numbers
with a licensed CPA or enrolled agent
before making any moves. What I have
shown you here is the framework.
The professional confirms the math for
your specific income picture, your
specific filing status, and your
specific threshold position.
The money in your checking account and
your savings account right now is not
dangerous because of fraud. It is not
dangerous because of bank failure. It is
not dangerous because of inflation. It
is generating a number, and that number
is interacting with three separate
federal mechanisms that your bank will
never explain to you, that the IRS will
not warn you about in advance, and that
most advisers have never walked through
with you in a single conversation. Now
you know what the number is. Now you
know how to calculate yours. Now you
know where the line is and what sits on
the other side of it. The rule is not
complicated. It is just hidden. And now
it is not hidden from you. If someone
you love is earning interest on their
savings without knowing what it is doing
to their Social Security tax and their
Medicare premium, send this to them
today because the 2026 costs are being
set right now.

title: Seniors Over 65: You Could be Exempt From These Bills (Most Don't Know)

segments.text: There are five bills that the average
American over 65 still pays every single
year that they are not legally required
to pay. Five bills. And before I go one
sentence further, it does not matter
whether you are scraping by on a fixed
income or sitting comfortably in
retirement. Both groups are overpaying.
And the reason most people never find
out is not an accident. Every
institution whose job it is to collect
these bills has a direct financial
incentive to keep their mouths shut.
Your county does not call you and say
the tax bill just got smaller. The IRS
does not send a letter explaining you no
longer owe what you used to. And the tax
preparer charging you $300 does not open
by telling you there's a way to make
their work simpler. These exemptions
exist. They are written into federal and
state law. They apply to you right now.
But being legally exempt from a bill and
actually not paying it are two
completely different things. The law
does not refund you automatically.
Nobody mails you a check. You have to
know the rule exists and you have to
claim it. Stay to the end because bill
number four is the one I have watched
cost ordinary retirees the most money
and it is the most invisible of all
five. My name is Laura Haynes. I am here
to represent taxpayers directly in front
of the Internal Revenue Service. The
most painful pattern I see is not people
who cheat. It is honest, careful people
in their 60s and 70s paying bills they
never owed year after year simply
because no one told them they could
stop. There is no notice. There is no
penalty. There is just money quietly
leaving your account every year that
never had to. That is the most expensive
kind of mistake there is. Bill number
one is federal income tax withholding on
your Social Security check. The mistake
here is not complicated. It is a single
form that millions of seniors filled out
years ago and never touched again.
When people apply for Social Security,
they are offered the option to have
federal tax withheld automatically. The
form is a W-4V.
Many check that box to avoid a surprise
bill at tax time. Reasonable, but
whether your social security is even
taxable depends on your provisional
income. Your adjusted gross income plus
non-taxable interest plus half your
annual social security benefit. If you
are single and that number comes in
0% of your social security is taxable.
If you are married filing jointly, the
threshold is 32,000. Below those lines,
not $1 is subject to federal income tax.
If you are a lower income retiree living
mostly on social security, there is a
strong likelihood you owe nothing. And
if you filed a W-4V years ago and never
updated it, the government holds your
money all year at zero interest and
returns it as a refund the following
spring. If you are a comfortable retiree
with a pension and investment income,
you are almost certainly
over-withholding what you actually owe.
The fix is the same for both groups.
File a new W-4V. Look at your real
provisional income number and right-size
the withholding to match what you will
actually owe. Not 1 cent more. That is
bill number one. That leads straight
into bill number two because it lives
inside a statement most seniors assume
they have no power over. Your property
tax. That is not the whole picture.
Nearly every state has a senior property
tax exemption, a freeze or a circuit
breaker credit. The income-based circuit
breaker targets lower and fixed income
seniors and can reduce your taxable home
value dramatically or defer the tax
until the property is sold. The flat
senior exemption removes a fixed chunk
of assessed value regardless of income.
And the age-based freeze, which
comfortable retirees consistently assume
does not apply to them, locks your
property tax at the level it was when
you turned 65 with no income test at
all. In Texas, once you turn 65, your
school district property taxes are
frozen permanently. Your home can double
in value, the frozen portion does not
move. The lower income retiree gets
income based relief that can eliminate
most of the bill. The comfortable
retiree who assumed they were too well
off for any program still qualifies for
the age-based freeze that requires
nothing except their birthday. None of
these are automatic. Your county does
not see that you turned 65 and apply the
discount. You have to file, and almost
every program has a hard annual
deadline. Miss it, and you pay the full
bill for another year. Look up your
county assessor's office online. Search
for senior exemption or senior freeze
and apply before that deadline. That is
bill number two. That leads straight
into bill number three, because it
arrives inside a statement you already
expect and never question. It is called
IRMAA, income-related monthly adjustment
amount. It is a surcharge on top of your
Medicare Part B and Part D premiums,
triggered when your income in a prior
year crossed certain thresholds. Social
Security looks at your tax return from 2
years ago to set your current premium.
The misconception that costs people
money is this. They assume once IRMAA is
applied, it is fixed until the next
annual review. It is not.
If your income drops significantly due
to retirement, divorce, death of a
spouse, loss of pension income, or
reduced work hours, you can file form
SSA-44
directly with Social Security and
request a reduction based on your
current income. If you are a lower
income retiree who recently retired and
your income dropped sharply, the IRMAA
AA surcharge may no longer apply at all.
If you are a comfortable retiree whose
income dropped after a spouse passed or
a pension ended, you may qualify for a
lower surcharge tier. The 2025 income
thresholds start at $85,000 for single
filers and $170,000
for married couples under 42 USC chapter
7. The standard Part B premium is $245
per month. The top IRMAA tier adds over
$400 on top of that per person per
month. File form SSA-A44
with your local Social Security office
with documentation of the life-changing
event and your current income estimate.
That is bill number three. That leads
straight into bill number four, the one
I told you to stay for because it hides
inside the return you already file every
year without anyone flagging what is
missing. There is an additional standard
deduction for seniors already written
into the tax code under Internal Revenue
Code section 63F. Every person 65 or
older receives an additional standard
deduction on top of the base amount. For
2025, that additional amount for seniors
per person or $3,200
for a married couple where both spouses
are 65 or older. If you are married and
both spouses are 65 or older, that is
That amount stacks on top of your
regular standard deduction and on top of
the existing extra standard deduction
seniors already receive. You do not have
to itemize. It applies based on filing
status and age. If you are a
lower-income senior, stacking these
deductions pushes your taxable income
down, in many cases to zero. If you are
a comfortable middle-class retiree, this
deduction is available in full to single
filers up to $75,000
and married couples up to $150,000.
It only begins to phase out above those
numbers. The only people this truly
leaves out are the genuinely wealthy. Go
to your tax preparer and ask one direct
question. Did you apply every senior
additional deduction available under
current law. Go to your tax preparer and
ask one direct question. Did you apply
the senior bonus deduction? If they
hesitate or look it up, you have your
answer. That is bill number four. That
leads straight into bill number five
because it is the most invisible of all.
You will never see it as a line item on
any statement. It is state income tax on
retirement income and depending on where
you live, you may be paying it on income
the state has no legal right to touch.
13 states currently exempt all pension
and retirement account income from state
income tax entirely. Several more exempt
social security specifically. Illinois,
Mississippi, and Pennsylvania exempt
virtually all retirement income. Iowa
recently phased out taxation on
retirement income for residents 65 and
older entirely. If you live in one of
those states and never verified your
state's current rules, you may have been
filing and paying a tax that does not
apply to you. If you are a lower income
retiree living on social security and a
small pension, your state may owe you
nothing. If you are a comfortable
retiree with a larger pension, IRA
distributions, and investment income,
the difference between a state that
taxes retirement income and one that
does not can be several thousand dollars
per year. Go to your state's Department
of Revenue website and search for
retirement income exemption. Several
states change their laws between 2020
and 2024. The rule that applied when you
filed last year may not be the rule that
applies today. That is bill number five.
Three more and at least one of them
applies to you right now. The first, if
your income is modest, you qualify for
the extra help program under Medicare
Part D. It can eliminate or sharply
reduce prescription drug costs. The
income limit for full subsidy in 2025 is
approximately $22,000
for a single person. Apply through
Social Security directly. LIHEAP
provides utility bill relief to
qualifying seniors, and many states have
utility discount programs reaching well
into middle-income territory. Contact
your state's energy assistance office.
And this one connects directly back to
bill number one. If you are still over
withholding on Social Security or
pension income, file a corrected
withholding form today. Not next
January. Every month you wait is another
month the Treasury holds your money at
zero interest. Every single person I
have sat across from who walked away
from this money was not careless. They
were simply never told. You now know the
senior bonus deduction exists and
expires in 2028. You now know your
property tax freeze requires an
application with a deadline. You now
know Irma A can be appealed with a
single form if your income dropped. You
now know your state may not tax your
retirement income at all. The law does
not refund you automatically. Nobody
mails you a check. But now you know to
ask.

title: Seniors: 7 Pieces of Good News for Your Medicare in 2027

segments.text: Next year, the average Medicare
Advantage premium is going down, not up.
Medicare just announced it drops from
a month to $12. And the drug coverage
inside those plans drops even more by
And believe it or not, that is not even
the biggest piece of good news coming
for your Medicare in 2027. For the last
few weeks, almost everything you have
heard about Medicare has been bad news.
Plans being dropped, deductibles going
up, warnings about prior approvals and
surprise bills. Some of that is real and
I have covered it on this channel, but
today is different. Today, I am going to
walk you through seven pieces of
genuinely good news for your Medicare.
Real benefits written into federal law
and published by Medicare itself. For
each one, I will show you exactly what
it is, who gets it, what it is worth in
dollars, and the one thing you do so it
does not slip past you. And I want you
to stay with me for number seven. Number
seven is worth up to $2,500
a year and most families who qualify for
it have never even heard its name. It is
not a discount and it is not a rebate.
It is help that Medicare pays for for
one of the hardest situations a family
can go through. Your own doctor may not
have mentioned it because it only
started recently and it is run through
special programs. I will show you
exactly who qualifies and the one
question that starts it when we get
there. Every rule and dollar figure in
this video comes straight from Medicare
and the federal government. in my
examples are made up, but the rules and
the dollars are real. Here is why this
matters right now. Medicare open
enrollment started on October 15th and
it runs until December 7th. That is the
window when everybody is shouting about
what is going wrong. Your mailbox is
full of plan flyers, your phone is
ringing with sales calls, and almost
nobody is telling you about the things
that are going right. But a lot of these
good things only work if you use them.
Medicare will not call you up and remind
you. Some of these benefits have been
sitting there, paid for, for years, and
millions of people on Medicare have
never once used them. Therefore, think
of this video as a checklist. By the
end, you will know which of these seven
you already have, which ones you need to
ask for, and exactly who to ask. Let's
start with the one that costs you
nothing at all, and that most people use
the wrong way. Number one, Medicare pays
for a yearly checkup visit that costs
you $0.
It is called the yearly wellness visit.
Once every 12 months, Medicare Part B
pays for a visit with your doctor to go
over your health and build a plan to
keep you well. If your doctor accepts
Medicare's approved amount, which most
do, you pay nothing, not a copay, not
coinsurance, and the Part B deductible
does not apply. That matters because in
2026, the Part B deductible is $283.
For most things, you pay that first
before Medicare starts paying its share,
but not for this visit. This one is free
from the very first dollar. And if you
are brand new to Medicare, there is a
separate visit just for you. It is
called the welcome to Medicare visit,
and you can get it anytime in your first
12 months on Part B. It is also free
when your doctor accepts assignment.
After that first year, you get the
yearly wellness visit every 12 months.
Here is what happens in that visit. Your
doctor reviews your medical history and
your family history. They go over every
prescription you take. They check your
height, your weight, and your blood
pressure. They do a quick check of your
memory and thinking. They offer to talk
with you about your wishes for future
care, and they give you a written
schedule, a checklist of which
screenings and which shots you are due
for over the next several years.
Meet Frank. Frank is 73. He worked 30
years as a mail carrier, and he has not
had a real checkup since he retired
because he figured every visit would
cost him money. When his daughter
finally booked him a yearly wellness
visit, it cost him nothing. The memory
check came back fine, but the written
checklist showed he was years overdue
for two screenings Medicare also covers
for free. He got both done that spring,
but here is the part most people get
wrong. The yearly wellness visit is not
the same thing as a full physical exam.
Medicare does not cover a routine
head-to-toe physical. And if during your
free visit, the doctor starts treating a
new problem or orders extra tests, those
extra pieces can come with a bill.
Therefore, when you book it, use these
exact words. Say, "I am calling to
schedule my yearly wellness visit." And
when you are in the room, if the doctor
wants to add something, it is perfectly
fine to ask, "Will this part cost me
anything?"
That one question keeps a free visit
free.
But a free checkup is only the first
piece of good news.
The second one is a shot in the arm,
literally.
Number two, your vaccines now cost you
zero dollars.
For years, this was one of the most
frustrating things about Medicare.
Some vaccines were free and some were
not. The flu shot was free, but the
shingles vaccine, which comes in two
doses, could cost you a real chunk of
money at the pharmacy because it was
covered under your drug plan with a
copay and sometimes a deductible.
That changed. Under a federal law that
took effect on January 1st, 2023, adult
vaccines that are recommended by the
government's vaccine experts are now
free under your Medicare drug plan. No
deductible, no copay, zero dollars.
That includes the shingles vaccine, both
doses. It includes the RSV vaccine,
which protects against a lung virus that
sends thousands of older adults to the
hospital every winter. And it includes
the tetanus, diphtheria, and whooping
cough booster, which a lot of
grandparents get before a new baby
arrives in the family.
On top of that, Medicare Part B already
covers the flu shot, the pneumonia
vaccines, and the COVID vaccine at no
cost to you.
And the hepatitis B vaccine is free
under Part B for people at higher risk.
Here is how big this is.
In the first year alone, more than 10
million people with Medicare drug
coverage got a recommended vaccine
without paying a penny. And the number
of people getting the shingles vaccine
went up by 42% because the price stopped
scaring them off.
Meet Joan. Joan is 69. Her sister had
shingles a few years ago and described
it as the worst pain of her life. Joan
always meant to get the shot, but the
last time she asked at the pharmacy,
they quoted her a price that made her
walk out. This fall, she asked again.
Both doses, $0.
But there is one catch you need to know
about. The free shingles, RSV, and
whooping cough shots come through your
drug coverage. That means you need a
Medicare drug plan, either a separate
Part D plan or a Medicare Advantage plan
that includes drug coverage. And it
works best at a pharmacy that is in your
plan's network. Therefore, here is what
you do.
Bring your Medicare drug plan card, not
just your red, white, and blue Medicare
card to the pharmacy. Ask the
pharmacist, "Which vaccines am I due
for, and are they covered at $0 under my
plan?" If the price on the screen is not
zero, ask them to run it through your
Part D plan. But vaccines help you stay
healthy. The third piece of good news is
for millions of people who already have
a condition they live with every single
day. Number three, your insulin is
capped at $35 a month.
If you or someone you love has diabetes,
you already know how expensive insulin
used to be. Before the cap, it was not
unusual for someone on Medicare to pay
hundreds of dollars a month for the
insulin they needed to to alive. Now
there is a hard ceiling. Under Medicare,
you pay no more than $35 for a 1-month
supply of each covered insulin. If you
get a 3-month supply, the most you pay
And here is the part that surprises
people. There is no deductible for
insulin. Even in January, when you have
not paid anything towards your drug plan
yet, the cap still applies. Think about
what that means over a year. $35 a month
is $420 a year for that insulin at the
very most. For a lot of families, that
is less than they used to pay in a
single month. The cap covers insulin
through your drug plan, which includes
pens, vials, and inhaled insulin. And if
you use an insulin pump that Medicare
covers as medical equipment, the insulin
for that pump falls under part B, and
the same $35 cap applies there, too.
Meet Earl. Earl is 71, and he has been
on insulin for 11 years. He remembers
standing at the counter, doing math in
his head about which bills to pay late
that month. Now, his insulin costs $35 a
month, and the January price shock that
used to wipe out his first check of the
year is gone. But here is where people
still get caught. The cap is per insulin
product for a 1-month supply. If you
take two different kinds of insulin,
each one has its own cap. And the cap is
for insulin itself. Some supplies, like
needles and test strips, are handled
differently and can cost extra.
Therefore, if your pharmacy ever charges
you more than $35 for a 1-month supply
of a covered insulin, do not just pay
it. Ask the pharmacist to check the
claim, and if it is still wrong, call
your drug plan, because the law is on
your side.
Now, before I get to number four, a
quick note. If this video is helping
you, I put every bill seniors are
legally allowed to stop paying after 65
into one guide called the Senior Exempt
Playbook. Scan the code on your screen
now, or tap the link in the description.
Number four, Medicare Advantage premiums
are going down in 2027. This is the good
news I opened with and it comes straight
from Medicare's own announcement for
next year. If you are in a Medicare
Advantage plan, the average monthly
premium is dropping from $14.37
in 2026 to $12 in 2027. That is a drop
of 16 and a half percent.
And it gets better. For Medicare
Advantage plans that include drug
coverage, the average part of the
premium that pays for your drugs is
falling from $11.32
to $7. That is a 38% drop. Medicare also
says about eight out of 10 people in
Medicare Advantage can stay in their
current plan next year and pay the same
premium or less. More than 99 out of 100
people have at least one Medicare
Advantage plan available where they live
and 97 out of 100 can choose from 10 or
more. And Medicare expects the extras
that many of these plans offer, like
dental, vision, and hearing, to stay
stable.
If you are on original Medicare with a
separate drug plan, your news is
steadier. The average premium for a
standalone drug plan goes from $35.09
to about $36. That is less than a $1
change. And Medicare says most people
can find a basic drug plan for about
$10.30 a month or less. But here is the
twist and it is important. Those are
averages. Your own plan could go up, go
down, or change its drug list and its
doctors. And you will not know until you
look. Your plan already mailed you a
letter called the annual notice of
change. It lists every change for 2027.
A lot of people throw it away without
opening it.
Meet Linda. Linda is 76 and has been in
the same Medicare Advantage plan for six
years. She almost tossed her annual
notice of change. When her son read it
to her, they saw her plan was moving one
of her heart medicines to a more
expensive tier. They compared plans
together, found one that covered the
same medicine for less with the same
doctors, and switched before the
deadline.
Therefore, here is your action. Find
that letter. If you cannot find it, call
your plan and ask them to send it again.
Then compare your plan against others on
the Medicare website or call
1-800-MEDICARE.
And if you want a person to sit down and
go through it with you, every state has
a free counseling program called SHIP.
They do not sell anything and they do
not earn a commission. You can find
yours at shiphelp.org.
And remember the deadlines. You can
switch until December 7th. If you are in
Medicare Advantage and change your mind,
there is a second chance from January
1st to March 31st when you can make one
change. But lower premiums help your
monthly budget. The fifth piece of good
news fixes a problem that hits people at
the pharmacy counter every January.
Number five, you can now spread your
drug costs out over the whole year with
zero interest. Here is the problem it
solves. Every January, your drug plan
resets. If your plan has a deductible,
you pay that first before the plan
helps. In 2027, the standard deductible
for a Medicare drug plan is $700. For
someone on an expensive medicine, that
whole amount can land in the very first
trip to the pharmacy of the year, right
when holiday bills are still sitting on
the counter. Now, there is a program
called the Medicare Prescription Payment
Plan. It started in 2025 and anyone with
a Medicare drug plan can join it. That
means a stand-alone drug plan or a
Medicare Advantage Plan with drug
coverage. Instead of paying the pharmacy
all at once, you pay zero dollars at the
counter for covered drugs and your plan
sends you a monthly bill that spreads
the cost across the rest of the year.
There is no interest, there are no fees,
it does not lower the total amount you
owe, but it turns one painful bill into
smaller, steady ones you can plan
around. Meet Gus. Gus is 74 and takes a
brand name blood thinner and an inhaler.
Last January, his first pharmacy trip
cost him almost $700 and he had to put
it on a credit card. This year, he
signed up for the payment plan. Instead
of one big hit, his costs are spread
into monthly bills he can actually
budget for with no credit card interest
at all.
And here is a newer piece of good news.
Once you are in the program, Medicare
now requires your plan to renew you
automatically for the next year if you
stay in the same plan. You do not have
to sign up all over again every January.
If you ever want out, you just tell your
plan. But this program is not for
everyone. If your drug costs are small
and steady, it does not help much and it
just adds another bill to keep track of.
It helps the most when you have one or
two expensive prescriptions, especially
early in the year. And if you miss a
payment, your plan can remove you from
the program after a grace period.
Therefore, if January drug bills hurt
you last year, call the number on your
drug plan card and say, "I want to join
the Medicare prescription payment plan."
The best time to call is before your
first expensive fill of the year, not
after.
But money is not the only thing that
wears seniors down. The sixth piece of
good news is about the kind of help
Medicare used to refuse to pay for.
Number six, Medicare now pays for more
kinds of help, including help for the
family member who takes care of you. For
decades, if you wanted to talk to a
counselor on Medicare, your choices were
limited. Medicare paid psychiatrists,
psychologists, and clinical social
workers, but two of the most common
kinds of counselors in America, marriage
and family therapists and licensed
mental health counselors, could not bill
Medicare at all. That changed on January
1st, 2024. Under a federal law passed by
Congress, marriage and family therapists
and mental health counselors can now
treat people on Medicare, and Medicare
pays its share. After your part B
deductible, you pay 20% of the Medicare
approved amount, just like most other
doctor visits. Many of these counselors
can also see you by video, so you do not
even have to drive. That matters more
than people think. Losing a spouse,
moving out of the family home, caring
for someone who is sick, feeling alone
after retirement. These are some of the
hardest years of a person's life, and
now there are thousands more
professionals who can help you through
them under Medicare.
And here is the second part of this good
news, which almost nobody knows about.
Starting in 2024, Medicare also began
paying for something called caregiver
training. If you have a health condition
and a family member helps take care of
you, your doctor or therapist can now
bill Medicare to train that family
member how to help you move safely, how
to manage difficult behaviors, how to
keep up with your treatment plan at
home, and you do not even have to be in
the room for the training. Meet Tom and
Carol. Carol had a stroke last year, and
Tom, who is 78, became her caregiver
overnight. He did not know how to help
her out of a chair without hurting his
own back. Her physical therapist set up
caregiver training sessions just for
Tom, billed to Carol's Medicare. Tom
says it was the first time anyone showed
him what to actually do.
But these services are still new, and
not every office offers them yet. Some
counselors are not signed up with
Medicare, and some therapists have never
billed for caregiver training.
Therefore, ask directly. When you call a
counselor, ask, "Do you accept
Medicare?" And at your next appointment,
if someone in your family is helping
take care of you, ask your doctor, "Can
you set up caregiver training for my
family member under Medicare?" But if
you are a caregiver, or you are worried
about becoming one, number seven is the
one I promised you, and it is worth up
a year. Number seven, Medicare now helps
pay for a break for families caring for
someone with dementia. If you have ever
cared for someone with Alzheimer's
disease or another kind of dementia, you
know it is not a 9-5 job. It is every
hour of every day. Caregivers miss their
own doctor visits. They stop seeing
friends. Many of them are in their 70s
themselves and they wear down to the
point where their own health starts to
fail. For years, Medicare did almost
nothing for the caregiver. That started
to change in July of 2024 when Medicare
launched a program called GUIDE. That
stands for Guiding an Improved Dementia
Experience. It is run by Medicare's own
Innovation Center and it is set to run
for 8 years. Here is what GUIDE gives a
family. A care navigator who helps
coordinate the doctors, the medicines,
and the services. A support line you can
call any hour of the day or night, every
day of the year. Training and education
for the caregiver. And help connecting
to meals, transportation, and other
community services.
And here is the part I promised you at
the start. For people whose dementia has
moved into the moderate or severe stage
and who have a family caregiver, GUIDE
can pay for respite. Respite means
someone else steps in to provide care so
the caregiver can rest. That might be a
trained aid coming to the home for the
day, time at an adult day center, or a
short overnight stay somewhere safe.
Medicare pays for up to $2,500
of respite a year per person. And for
the family, there is no copay and no
coinsurance on that respite. $2,500 of
care is not a small thing. For a
caregiver who has not had a full day off
in a year, it can mean a weekend to
sleep, a trip to see grandchildren, or
simply time to go to their own doctor.
Meet Maria. Maria is 72 and her husband
was diagnosed with Alzheimer's 3 years
ago. She had not left him alone for more
than an hour in over a year. When his
neurologist office joined a GUIDE
program, Maria got a care navigator, a
phone number she could call at 2:00 in
the morning, and paid respite. The first
time an aid came to the house for a full
day, Maria went to the hairdresser, had
lunch with her sister, and took a nap.
She said she had forgotten what that
felt like.
But, this is the part where you need to
listen closely because GUIDE has rules.
The person with dementia has to be on
original Medicare with both part A and
part B, and Medicare has to be their
main insurance. People in Medicare
Advantage plans are not eligible right
now. They also cannot be in hospice, and
they cannot live full-time in a nursing
home. Living at home with family or in
assisted living is fine, and they have
to get care through a doctor or
organization that is part of a GUIDE
program. Those programs are now running
in many parts of the country, but not in
every town.
Therefore, here is the one question that
starts it. At the next appointment, ask
the doctor, "Are you part of a GUIDE
program?" And if not, is there one near
us? You can also call the Alzheimer's
Association Helpline, which is open
around the clock at 1-800-272-3900,
and ask them to help you find a GUIDE
program in your area. And if your loved
one is in Medicare Advantage, and you
are thinking about switching to original
Medicare, talk to your free SHIP
counselor first so you understand
everything that changes before December
7th. So, let's put all seven together.
Here is your Medicare good news
checklist for 2027.
One, book your yearly wellness visit. It
costs $0 when your doctor accepts
assignment. Call it by its name and ask
before anything extra is added. Two, get
your vaccines. Shingles, RSV, and the
whooping cough booster are free under
your drug plan. Flu, pneumonia, and
COVID shots are free under part B.
Three, if you take insulin, you should
never pay more than $35 for a 1-month
supply of each covered insulin with no
deductible. Four, Medicare Advantage
premiums are dropping to an average of
$12. Read your annual notice of change
and compare plans before December 7th
with free help from SHIP if you want it.
Five, if big drug bills hit you in
January, join the Medicare prescription
payment plan. Zero interest and it
renews automatically. Six, Medicare now
covers marriage and family therapists,
mental health counselors, and training
for the family member who cares for you.
Seven, if someone you love has dementia
and is on original Medicare, ask their
doctor about a guide program. It can pay
up to $2,500
a year for respite so the caregiver gets
a break.
For help finding a guide program, call
the Alzheimer's Association at
And for anything else about your
Medicare, call 1-800-MEDICARE.

title: Seniors: 7 Pieces of Good News for Your Money in January (Most Don't Know)

segments.text: Starting in January, the average retired
couple on Social Security will get $117
more every single month. That is $1,404
more over the year without filling out a
single form. And believe it or not, that
is the smallest piece of good news
coming for your money this January. For
the last few months, almost everything
you have heard about retirement money
has been bad news. Prices going up,
Medicare plans being dropped, warnings
about your savings, your taxes, and your
check. Some of that is real, and I've
covered it on this channel. But today is
different. Today I'm going to walk you
through seven pieces of genuinely good
news that land in January. Real dollars
written into federal law and published
by Social Security, Medicare, and the
IRS. For each one, I will show you the
exact number, who gets it, and the one
thing you do so it does not slip past
you.
And I want you to stay with me for
number seven. Number seven is worth
about $2,400
a year back in your Social Security
check every year for as long as you
qualify. Millions of seniors qualify for
it right now and have never once applied
because they assume their income is too
high, or they have simply never heard
the name. I will show you exactly who
qualifies and the one phone call that
starts it when we get there. Every
number in this video comes from a
federal agency. The people in my
examples are made up, but the rules and
the dollars are real. Here is why this
matters right now. Some of this good
news shows up automatically. You do not
have to lift a finger, but some of it
only shows up if you ask. And if you do
not ask, nobody is going to call you to
remind you. The government is very good
at announcing increases. It is not
nearly as good at telling you how to
collect the ones you have to claim.
Therefore, think of this video as a
checklist. By the end, you will know
which of these seven are already coming
to you and which ones you need to go and
get. Let's start with the one everybody
is talking about because there is more
to it than the headline. Number one,
your Social Security check goes up 3.6%
in January. Every October, Social
Security looks at how much prices rose
over the past year, and it raises
benefits to match. It is called the cost
of living adjustment. For 2027, Social
Security has confirmed it will be 3.6%.
Here is what that looks like in actual
dollars, using Social Security's own
estimates. The average retired worker
gets $2,095
a month right now. In January, that goes
That is $75 more a month, or $900 more
over the year. For a retired couple who
are both collecting, the average goes
from to $3,355.
That is the $117 a month I opened with.
And if you are a widow or widower living
on one check, the average goes from
That is $69
more every month. And if you worked at
the top of the pay scale and waited
until full retirement age, the maximum
benefit goes to $4,188 a month.
Meet Walter and Ruth. Walter is 74 and
spent 30 years driving a delivery truck.
Ruth is 71 and worked in a school
cafeteria. Between them, they get almost
exactly the average couple's benefit. In
January, their deposit goes up by about
Over the year, that is $1,404
they did not have before, and they did
not have to ask for a penny of it. Now,
here is the part most people miss. You
do not have to apply for this raise. It
is automatic, but you should check it.
Before the end of the year, Social
Security posts a notice showing your new
amount. If you have an online My Social
Security account, it shows up in your
message center. If not, it comes by
mail. Read that notice. It shows your
new gross benefit, and it shows what is
being taken out for Medicare. If the
numbers look wrong, you have the right
to ask Social Security to explain them.
Therefore, when that notice arrives, do
not throw it in the drawer. Put it next
to last year's letter and compare them
line by line. That one habit catches
mistakes that can cost you money for
years. But a lot of seniors are already
worried about one thing taking that
raise right back. And that brings us to
the second piece of good news. Number
two, there is a rule that stops Medicare
from shrinking your check. Here is the
worry. Most people on Medicare have
their part B premium taken straight out
of their Social Security check before it
ever reaches the bank. In 2026, the
standard part B premium is $202.90
a month. For 2027, Medicare's own
trustees project it will go up to about
The official number comes out later this
fall. So, a lot of people ask, is
Medicare going to eat my raise? For most
people, the answer is no. And there is a
law that guarantees it.
It is called the hold harmless rule. It
is written into the Social Security Act.
It says that for most people, an
increase in the part B premium is not
allowed to make your Social Security
check smaller than it was the year
before. If the premium goes up more than
your raise, the increase in your premium
is limited, so your net check does not
go down. In practice, this year it will
not even come close. If the average
retiree gets $75 more, and the projected
premium goes up by about $6.60,
that retiree is still ahead by roughly
Meet Dolores. Dolores is 78 and lives on
one check. Every January for years, she
has braced herself for the letter,
expecting Medicare to swallow her raise.
This year, her raise is about $69. The
premium increase is a fraction of that,
and the hold harmless rule stands behind
her no matter what.
But here is the twist, and this is where
I need you to pay attention. The hold
harmless rule does not protect
everybody. It does not cover you if you
are new to Medicare this year. It does
not cover you if your premium is not
taken out of your Social Security check.
And most importantly, it does not cover
you if you pay the higher income
surcharge called IRMAA.
IRMAA is an extra charge on top of your
Part B premium for people whose income
was above a certain level. And here is
the trap. Medicare does not look at your
income today. It looks at your tax
return from two years ago. So a one-time
event like selling a house, cashing out
an account, or a big required withdrawal
can trigger a surcharge years later,
long after the money is gone.
If that happened to you and your income
has since dropped because you retired,
lost a spouse, or stopped working, you
can ask Social Security to use your
newer, lower income instead. The form is
called SSA-44.
It is free and it can lower your
surcharge, sometimes all the way to
zero. How do you know if you are paying
it? Look at the Medicare line on your
notice. If the amount taken out is
higher than the standard premium, the
difference is almost always IRMAA.
Social Security also sends a separate
letter explaining it. And that letter
tells you which year of income they
used. Therefore, if your January notice
shows a Medicare charge that looks too
high, do not just accept it. Ask whether
you are paying IRMAA.
And if your income has dropped, file
form SSA-44.
But Medicare is not the only thing
people worry about in January. If you
are still working, there is a different
rule that has been quietly holding your
money back and it just loosened.
Number three. If you are still working,
you get to keep more of your check. This
one surprises a lot of people. If you
start Social Security before your full
retirement age and you keep working,
Social Security can hold back part of
your benefit if you earn too much. It is
called the earnings test. For 2026, the
limit is $24,480.
In January, it goes up to $25,560.
That is $2,130
a month you can earn before Social
Security holds back a single dollar.
Above that, they hold back $1 of
benefits for every $2 you earn over the
limit. So, that higher limit means
of extra earnings that are now safe, and
$540 less held back from your check. And
in the year you actually reach full
retirement age, the limit is much
higher. It goes from $65,160
And they only hold back $1 for every
three you earn over it. For anyone born
in 1960 or later, full retirement age is
67. For people born a little earlier, it
is a few months sooner. Now, here is the
best part. Once you reach full
retirement age, the earnings test
disappears completely. There is no limit
at all. You can earn as much as you want
and keep every dollar of your Social
Security. Meet Hank. Hank is 63. He took
Social Security early, then got bored
and went back to work part-time at a
hardware store. Last year, Hank earned a
little over the limit, and Social
Security held back part of his check.
Hank was furious. He thought that money
was just gone.
But, here is what almost nobody tells
you. That money is not lost. When Hank
reaches full retirement age, Social
Security recalculates his benefit and
gives him credit for every month they
held money back. His check goes up from
then on. Therefore, if you are working
and collecting early, look at the new
limit and plan your hours around it. And
if money has been held back, do not
panic. It is not gone. It comes back to
you in a higher check later. But, the
next piece of good news has nothing to
do with work. It has to do with taxes.
And the filing season that opens in
January is the first time a lot of
seniors will see how big it really is.
Now, before I get to number four, a
quick note. If this video is helping
you, I put every bill seniors are
legally allowed to stop paying after 65
into one guide called the senior exempt
playbook. Scan the code on your screen
now or tap the link in the description.
Number four, tax season opens in January
and seniors get the biggest deductions
they have ever had. Let me clear
something up first because there is a
lot of confusion out there. Social
Security did not become tax-free. You
may have heard that on the news or seen
it online. It is not true. If your
income is high enough, part of your
Social Security can still be taxed. But
here is the good news. Congress created
something that for a lot of seniors gets
them to the same place. When you file
your taxes for 2026 starting in late
January, you get three separate breaks
just for being over 65. First, the
regular standard deduction. For a single
filer, that is $16,100.
Second, the extra amount for being 65 or
older. For a single filer, that is
$2,050 more. And third, the brand new
senior deduction. That is $6,000 for
every person 65 or older and it runs
through 2028. Add those up and a single
senior can subtract $24,150
from their income before the IRS taxes a
single penny. For a married couple who
are both over 65, it is $32,200
plus $1,650
each for age plus $6,000 each for the
senior deduction. That is $47,500.
And here's what makes the senior
deduction different from almost every
other tax break. You get it whether you
take the standard deduction or itemize.
Most deductions make you choose. This
one does not.
Meet Betty. Betty is 68 and a widow. She
has a small pension, some interest from
her savings, and her Social Security.
She has been paying a little income tax
every year since her husband passed.
This year, with all three of these
breaks stacked together, a lot of her
taxable income simply disappears.
Depending on her exact numbers, she may
owe much less than last year, or nothing
at all. But, there is a catch. The
senior deduction starts to shrink if
your income is above $75,000 for a
single filer, or $150,000
for a married couple. And, it only helps
you if it actually ends up on your
return. I have seen seniors use cheap
tax software, or a rushed preparer, or
skip a question about their age, and
miss money they were entitled to. The
IRS is not going to call you and say you
forgot something. Therefore, when you
file this winter, look for the senior
deduction by name. Make sure the extra
amount for age is there for every person
on the return who is 65 or older. And,
if you want someone to check it for
free, the IRS runs a program called Tax
Counseling for the Elderly. You can find
the nearest site by calling
But, taxes are only one bill that gets
smaller in January. The next one shows
up at the pharmacy counter. And, for
some people, it is the biggest drop of
all.
Number five. On January 1st, the price
Medicare pays for 15 of the most
expensive drugs drops. For the first
time ever, Medicare was allowed to
negotiate directly with drug companies.
The first round of lower prices started
this year. The second round starts on
January 1st, 2027, and it covers 15 more
drugs.
Here are a couple of examples from
Medicare's own numbers. Ozempic, along
with Wegovy and Rybelsus, had a list
price of about $959
for a 30-day supply. The new negotiated
price is $274.
Trelegy, a common inhaler for breathing
problems, goes from $654
The full list includes drugs for
diabetes, cancer, breathing problems,
and more, including Xtandi, Ibrance,
Linzess, Breo, Tradjenta, Janumet, and
Otezla. Medicare estimates people on
drug plans will save about $685 million
out of their own pockets.
