Now, I want to be honest with you. Your
exact copay depends on your plan. A
lower price for Medicare does not
automatically mean the same discount for
you at the counter, but a lower
negotiated price pushes everything in
your direction.
And there is another protection that
keeps working in January. Your
out-of-pocket costs for covered drugs on
a Medicare drug plan are capped. For
2027, the cap is $2,400
for the whole year. Once you hit it, you
pay nothing more for covered drugs until
the year starts over. And insulin is
capped at $35 a month.
Meet Ray. Ray is 70 and takes three
brand-name medications, one of them on
the negotiated list. A few years ago,
there was no cap at all, and Ray was
spending thousands of dollars a year at
the pharmacy. Now, his worst-case for
the whole year has a ceiling, and one of
his drugs just got a lot cheaper for
Medicare to buy.
Therefore, if you take any of these
drugs, look at your plan's notice for
next year, and call your plan in January
to ask what your copay is now. And if
you are still deciding on a plan, you
have until December 7th to compare and
switch. Plans change their drug lists
every single year, so a drug that is
covered today may not be covered next
year. 5 minutes on the phone now can
save you a very expensive surprise in
January. But the next piece of good news
is for the people who need it most, and
it arrives before January even starts.
Number six, SSI goes up and the January
payment arrives early. SSI stands for
Supplemental Security Income. It is a
separate program from regular Social
Security, and it is for people 65 and
older or disabled who have very little
income and very few assets. A lot of
seniors get both a small Social Security
check and an SSI payment on top of it.
In January, the federal SSI payment goes
up. For an individual, it from $994 a
month to $1,029.
For a couple, it goes from $1,491
And here is a little bonus. Because
January 1st is a holiday, the January
SSI payment is actually sent out on
December 31st. So, the raise shows up
before the new year even begins. Now,
here is the part that matters most. A
lot of seniors who qualify for SSI have
never applied because they think they
own too much. The limit is $2,000 in
countable resources for an individual
and 3,000 for a couple. But the home you
live in generally does not count. One
car generally does not count. Many
personal belongings do not count. Meet
Marie. Marie is 81. Her Social Security
is small because she spent years at home
raising five children. She owns her
little house, an old car, and has about
$1,500 in the bank. Marie always assumed
owning a home meant she could not
qualify for anything. She was wrong.
Therefore, if your income is very low
and your savings are under those limits,
not counting your home and car, call
Social Security and ask to apply for
SSI. The number is 1-800-772-1213.
Even a small SSI payment can open the
door to other help, including help with
medical bills. But the biggest piece of
good news on this list is not SSI. It is
the one I promised you at the beginning.
The one worth about $2,400
a year. Number seven, a program that
pays your Medicare premium for you.
Remember that Part B premium I talked
a month taken right out of your Social
Security check. Over a year, that is
There is a set of programs that will pay
that premium for you. They are called
Medicare Savings Programs. When you
qualify, the premium stops coming out of
your check, and that money goes straight
back into your pocket. That is the
$2,400 a year I promised you. And here
is why most people never apply. They
think these programs are only for people
with almost no income. That is not
[clears throat] true. There are three
main levels. The first, called QMB, pays
your Part B premium, and also your
deductibles, co-insurance, and co-pays.
For this year, the income limit for an
individual is about $1,350
a month.
The second, called SLMB, pays your Part
B premium. The income limit is about
a month for an individual. And the
third, called QI, also pays your Part B
premium. The income limit is about
a month for an individual, or $2,455
for a couple. Think about that. A single
person with about $1,800
a month of income can still qualify to
have their Medicare premium paid. That
is a lot of retirees. There is usually
an asset limit, too, about $9,950
for an individual, and $14,910
for a couple. But your home and your car
generally do not count. And some states
set the limits higher, or drop the asset
test completely.
But wait, because it gets better. If you
qualify for any of these Medicare
Savings Programs, you automatically
qualify for another program called Extra
Help, which lowers what you pay for
prescription drugs. In 2027, the
standard deductible on a Medicare drug
plan can be as high as $700. With Extra
Help, your deductible is zero, and your
co-pays are capped at $5.80 for a
generic, and $14.40
for a brand-name drug. Let's go back to
Marie. Her income is well under those
limits. Once she qualifies for a
Medicare Savings Program, $202.90
a month stops coming out of her Social
Security check. On top of her raise,
that is about $2,400
a year back in her pocket, plus a $0
drug deductible from extra help. And for
a married couple where both spouses
qualify, the premium savings can be
close to $4,900
a year.
That is real money. That is groceries, a
car repair, a gift for the grandkids, or
simply not worrying about the next bill.
Therefore, if your income is anywhere
near those limits, apply. Do not decide
for yourself that you are over. Let them
tell you. Medicare savings programs are
run through your state Medicaid office,
and you can apply even if you have never
been on Medicaid and never will be. When
you call, ask for the Medicare savings
program application by name, and ask
whether your state uses higher limits
than the federal ones. If you are turned
down, ask for the reason in writing
because mistakes happen and you can
appeal. So, let's put all seven
together. Here is your January
checklist. One, your social security
goes up 3.6% automatically. When the
notice comes, compare it line by line
with last year's. Two, the hold harmless
rule protects most people from Medicare
shrinking their check. If you pay the
IRMAA surcharge and your income has
dropped, file form SSA-44.
Three, if you are working and collecting
early, the earnings limit rises to
Money held back is not lost. It comes
back later. Four, when you file your
taxes, make sure the $6,000 senior
deduction and the extra amount for age
are on your return. Five, if you take
one of the 15 negotiated drugs, call
your plan in January and ask what you
pay now. Your yearly drug costs are
capped at $2,400.
Six, if your income and savings are very
low, apply for SSI even if you own your
home. Seven, if your income is under
about $1,800 a month, apply for a
Medicare Savings Program. It can put
about $2,400 a year back in your check,
and it opens the door to extra help.
You can call Social Security at
And for help with Medicare, including
how to reach your state's Medicare
Savings Program, call 1-800-Medicare.

title: After 70½, the IRS Lets You Do These 7 Things (Most Don't Know)

segments.text: This year, the IRS lets a married couple
over 65 take $47,500
off the top of their income before a
single dollar of it is taxed. A couple
in their 50s gets 32,200.
That is $15,300
of income the government is quietly
letting you keep just because of your
age. And that is not a loophole. It is
written into the tax code, and it is
printed in the IRS's own instructions.
The problem is that nobody calls you to
tell you it exists. That is the pattern
with everything in this video. Once you
pass 70 and a half, the IRS gives you a
handful of permissions that younger
people simply do not have. Some of them
lower your tax bill. Some of them
protect you from penalties. And a couple
of them let you take money out of your
retirement accounts in ways most people
assume are against the rules.
Today, I'm going to walk you through
seven of them. For each one, I will show
you the exact rule, the exact dollar
amount, and the one thing you do to
actually use it. And stay with me for
number four. Number four lets you pull
money out of your IRA, satisfy the IRS
completely, and never pay one penny of
income tax on it. Not later. Not ever.
It can also keep your income low enough
that less of your social security gets
taxed. It has been in the law for years,
and most retirees who could use it never
do. I will show you exactly how it
works, and the one mistake that cancels
it when we get there. Every rule and
dollar figure here comes straight from
the IRS. The people in my examples are
made up, but the rules are real. Here is
why this matters right now. We are in
the last quarter of the year. A lot of
what I am about to show you only counts
if it happens before December 31st. Wait
until tax season in April, and for most
of these, it is too late for this year.
But here is what most people get wrong.
They think the IRS only has rules that
take money from you after 70.
Withdrawals you are forced to make,
penalties if you forget, taxes on your
social security, and those rules are
real. Therefore, the people who come out
ahead are not the ones with the most
money. They are the ones who know which
permissions to use.
Let's start with the one that surprises
people the most. Number one, the IRS
lets you keep putting money into an IRA
at any age.
For decades, there was a hard stop. Once
you turn 70 and a half, you were not
allowed to put another dollar into a
traditional IRA, even if you were still
working. A lot of people still believe
that rule is in place. It is not.
Starting in 2020, Congress removed the
age limit. The IRS says it plainly,
there is no age limit on making regular
contributions to traditional or Roth
IRAs.
For 2026, you can put in up to $7,500
plus a catch-up of $1,100 because you
are over 50. That is $8,600
a year. Meet Ed. Ed is 72, retired from
the post office, and he works three
mornings a week at a hardware store. He
earns about $9,000 a year there. Ed
assumed his IRA days were over. They are
not. Because Ed has earned income, he
can put up to $8,600
into an IRA this year. If it goes into a
traditional IRA, he may be able to
deduct it, which lowers his taxable
income. If it goes into a Roth IRA, it
grows, and he can later take it out
tax-free. And here is the part almost
nobody knows. If you are married and
file jointly, your spouse can put money
into their own IRA based on your
paycheck, even if they have no job at
all. So, Ed's wife, Carol, can
contribute, too.
There is one catch. It has to be earned
income, wages from a job or money from
self-employment. Social security,
pensions, and interest do not count. And
you cannot put in more than you earned.
Therefore, if you or your spouse earn
anything from work, even part-time, ask
yourself whether some of it should be
going into an IRA instead of sitting in
checking. You have until the tax filing
deadline next April to make a
contribution for this year, but putting
money in is only half of it. The bigger
wins come from what the IRS lets you
subtract.
Number two, the IRS gives you a bigger
standard deduction just for being over
65. The standard deduction is the amount
of income the IRS lets you subtract
before it starts taxing anything. For
2026, a single filer gets $16,100.
A married couple filing jointly gets
But once you turn 65, the IRS adds an
extra amount on top. If you are single,
you get $2,050 more. If you are married,
each spouse who is 65 or older adds
So, a married couple who are both over
65 starts at $35,500.
A single senior starts at $18,150.
You do not have to apply for this, but
you do have to make sure it is actually
on your return. I have seen people fill
out their own taxes, check the wrong
box, or skip the age question, and lose
the extra amount without ever knowing.
There is also a tax form built just for
you. It is called form 1040SR.
It is the same return as the regular
1040 with larger print and a chart of
the standard deduction right on the
form, including the extra amount for
age. If you do your own taxes on paper,
ask for the SR version.
Therefore, this year, look at your
return before you sign it. Find the line
for the standard deduction, and make
sure it includes the extra amount for
every person on that return who is 65 or
older. But that extra amount is small
compared to the next one, and the next
one is brand new.
Number three, the IRS now lets you take
a separate $6,000 senior deduction. In
2025, Congress created a new deduction
just for people 65 and older. It is
$6,000 per person. It stacks on top of
everything I just showed you, and it
runs from 2025 through 2028. If you and
your spouse are both over 65, that is
Here is what makes it different. You get
it whether you take the standard
deduction or itemize. Most deductions
make you choose. This one does not.
So, let's add it all up. A married
couple, both over 65, now gets $32,200,
plus $1,650
for each spouse, plus $6,000 for each
spouse. That is $47,500
that is not taxed. That is the number I
opened with. Meet Frank and June. Frank
is 71, June is 69. Between their
pensions, some IRA withdrawals, and part
of their social security, they have
about $60,000 of income that the IRS
counts. Before this deduction existed,
most of that would have been taxed. Now,
of it is not. But, there is a limit. The
new $6,000 deduction starts to shrink
once your modified adjusted gross income
goes over $75,000
if you are single, or $150,000
if you are married. Above that line, it
gets smaller as your income rises.
And this is temporary. Under the current
law, it ends after 2028. That means you
have four tax years to use it, and the
first one is already behind you.
Therefore, if you filed for 2025 without
this deduction, talk to a tax preparer
about whether you can still amend that
return. And for this year, make sure it
is on there. But, here is the real
problem with all of these deductions.
They only help if your income stays
under the lines. And the next permission
is how you keep it there. Number four,
the one I promised you at the start.
Once you turn 70 and a half, the IRS
lets you send money straight from your
IRA to a charity, and none of it counts
as income. It is called a qualified
charitable distribution. Most people
just call it a QCD.
Here is how it normally works without
it. Say you are 75, and the IRS requires
you to take $10,000 out of your IRA this
year. That $10,000 is taxable income.
You pay income tax on it, even if you
turn around and give some of it to your
church. Now, here is how it works with a
QCD. You tell your IRA company to send
part of that money directly to your
church or charity. The money never
touches your bank account. And because
it went straight to the charity, it is
not counted as your income. Not taxed
now, not taxed later, not taxed at all.
And it still counts toward the
withdrawal the IRS requires. So, you
satisfy the IRS, and you pay nothing on
that part. For 2026, you can do this
with up to $111,000
a year. If you are married and you each
have an IRA, you each get your own
limit. Meet Walter. Walter is 76, and he
has given $3,000 a year to his church
for as long as he can remember. He
writes the checks out of his bank
account, and every year his required IRA
withdrawal adds to his taxable income.
Here is what Walter does not know.
Because he takes the standard deduction,
he gets no tax break at all for those
$3,000 of giving. They come out of money
he already paid tax on. If Walter sends
the same $3,000 to his church straight
from his IRA, it becomes a QCD. His
church gets the same gift, but Walter's
taxable income drops by $3,000 every
year. And here is why that matters more
than it looks. Your income does not just
decide your income tax. It decides how
much of your social security gets taxed.
It decides whether you stay under the
line for that new $6,000 deduction. And
it decides whether Medicare charges you
a higher premium. A lower income on
paper can help with all of them at once.
Think about what that means for Walter
over 10 years. $30,000 of giving that he
has been paying income tax on turned
into $30,000 that never touches his tax
return. Same church, same gift, same
Walter. The only thing that changed is
which account the check came from. That
is why I called this the permission most
retirees never use. Now, the one mistake
that cancels it. The money has to go
directly from your IRA to the charity.
If your IRA company sends the money to
you first and you write a check to your
church, it is not a QCD. It is a regular
taxable withdrawal. You cannot fix it
afterward by giving it away. There are
three more details. It only works from
an IRA, not straight from a workplace
plan like a 401k. You need a written
receipt from the charity, and when you
file, your tax form from the IRA company
will not mark it for you. You or your
preparer write the letters QCD next to
the line for IRA distributions, so the
IRS knows that part is not taxable.
Therefore, if you give to a church or
charity and you are 70 and a half or
older, call your IRA company before
December. Ask for a qualified charitable
distribution form. Many of them will
send a check made out directly to the
charity. Now, before I get to number
five, a quick note. If this video is
helping you, I put every bill seniors
are legally allowed to stop paying after
65 into one guide called the senior
exempt playbook. Scan the code on your
screen now or tap the link in the
description. Number five, the IRS lets
you wait longer than you think to take
money out. Most people still think
withdrawals are forced at 70 and a half
or at 72. Those were the old ages.
Congress has raised them twice. Today,
if you were born between 1951 and 1959,
your required withdrawals start at 73.
If you were born in 1960 or later, they
start at 75. That means a lot of people
in their early 70s have more time than
they realize to let that money grow or
to move some of it on their own terms.
But there is a trap hiding in the first
year. The IRS lets you delay your very
first withdrawal until April 1st of the
following year. It sounds like a gift,
but if you take that delay, you still
have to take your second withdrawal by
December 31st of that same year. So you
take two withdrawals in one tax year.
Meet Margaret. Margaret turned 73 last
year and she waited until March to take
her first withdrawal of $22,000.
Then in December, she has to take her
second one, another $22,000. That is
$44,000 of extra taxable income in one
year. It can push her into a higher
bracket and it can push more of her
social security into the taxable column.
Therefore, for most people, taking the
first withdrawal in the year you
actually turn 73 is the safer move. Run
the numbers both ways before you take
the delay. There is one more permission
here. If you are still working past 73
and you have a retirement plan at that
job, the IRS lets you hold off on
withdrawals from that employer's plan
until the year you retire. That
exception does not apply to IRAs and it
does not apply if you own more than 5%
of the company. But for a lot of people
working into their 70s, it means no
forced withdrawals at all from that
plan. And there is a lesser-known
option. The IRS lets you move up to
of your retirement money into a special
kind of annuity called a qualifying
longevity annuity. That money is left
out of your required withdrawal math
until the annuity pays out, which has to
start by age 85. It is not for everyone
and anyone selling one should explain
every fee, but it exists. But taking
money out raises a different headache
because once those withdrawals start,
the IRS wants its tax on time and that
brings me to the permission almost
nobody uses. Number six.
The IRS lets you pay your whole year of
taxes in December and treats it as if
you paid all year. Here is the problem.
Once you retire, nobody is taking tax
out of a paycheck anymore. If you owe
tax on your pension, your IRA
withdrawals, or your social security,
the IRS expects you to pay it during the
year, usually through estimated payments
every few months. If you pay too little,
too late, you can owe an underpayment
penalty, even if you pay everything in
full by April. A lot of retirees hate
estimated payments. They forget a
deadline. They mail the voucher late.
They guess wrong. But there is a rule in
the tax code that changes everything.
When tax is withheld, the IRS treats it
as if it was paid in equal parts
throughout the year, no matter when it
was actually taken out. That is
different from an estimated payment,
which only counts on the day you send
it.
So you can do this. Skip the quarterly
payments. Then in December, take an IRA
withdrawal and ask your IRA company to
withhold a large chunk of it for federal
tax. The IRS treats that withholding as
if it came in a little at a time all
year long. Meet Margaret again. Her tax
[clears throat] bill for the year is
about $4,800.
Instead of writing four checks to the
IRS, she has her IRA company withhold
from her December withdrawal. As far as
the penalty rules are concerned, she
paid on time all year. Therefore, if you
are making estimated payments and you
have an IRA, call your IRA company and
ask how to set up federal withholding on
a year-end withdrawal. Ask your preparer
how much to withhold so you you covered.
But what if you already got it wrong?
What if you missed one? Number seven,
the IRS lets you fix a missed withdrawal
and sometimes erase the penalty
completely.
This is the one that scares people. If
you miss a required withdrawal, the
penalty used to be 50% of the amount you
should have taken out, half of it gone.
Congress cut that. Today, the penalty is
25% and if you fix the mistake within
the correction window, which is
generally about 2 years, it drops to
10%. But, here is the part most people
never hear. The IRS can waive the
penalty completely if the shortfall came
from a reasonable error and you are
taking steps to fix it. You take the
missed withdrawal as soon as you catch
it. Then, you file form 5329
with a short letter explaining what
happened. Meet Carol. Carol's husband
always handled the accounts. After he
passed, she missed a $10,000 withdrawal
from his old IRA that had rolled over to
her. At 25%, that is a $2,500
penalty. Fixed quickly, it is $1,000.
With a waiver approved, it is zero.
Carol did not cheat anybody. She was
grieving and the account was new to her.
That is exactly the kind of situation
the waiver exists for. Therefore, if you
discover a missed withdrawal, do not
hide from it and do not wait. Take the
money out now, file form 5329
and ask for the waiver in writing.
So, let's put all seven together. Here
is what to do before December 31st. One,
if you or your spouse earn any wages,
ask whether some of it should go into an
IRA. There is no age limit anymore.
Two, make sure your return includes the
extra standard deduction for every
person 65 or older. Three, make sure you
are claiming the new $6,000 senior
deduction and ask about amending last
year if you missed it. Four, if you give
to a church or charity and you are 70
and a half or older, give it straight
from your IRA as a qualified charitable
distribution. Never let the money pass
through your own account first.
Five, know your real starting age for
required withdrawals and think twice
before stacking two of them into one
year.
Six, if you hate estimated payments, use
withholding on a December IRA withdrawal
instead.
Seven, if you ever miss a withdrawal,
take it right away and file form 5329
asking for the waiver. And you do not
have to figure any of this out alone.
The IRS runs a free program called Tax
Counseling for the Elderly built for
people 60 and older and it specializes
in pension and retirement questions.
They are volunteers, they are trained by
the IRS, and they are not selling you
anything. To find the nearest site, call

title: 7 Medicare Changes Hit Seniors in 2027 — #4 Quietly Takes More of Your Check

segments.text: Starting January 1st, your Medicare drug
plan is allowed to make you pay $700 out
of your own pocket before it covers a
single penny of your prescriptions. And
the most it can make you pay in a year
is going up by $300 to $2,400.
That is not a rumor. That is the
official number Medicare published for
2027. And it is only one of seven
changes coming at you on January 1st.
Some of these changes will cost you
money. A couple of them will actually
save you money if you know they exist.
And one of them is already sitting in
your mailbox right now in an envelope a
lot of people throw away without
opening. Today, I'm going to walk you
through all seven. For each one, I will
show you the exact rule, the exact
dollar amount, and the one thing you
should do about it before the window
closes.
And stay with me for number four because
number four is the one that quietly
takes more of your Social Security
check. Social Security just announced a
3.6% raise for 2027. But for a lot of
retirees, number four starts eating that
raise before it ever reaches your bank
account. It does not show up as a bill.
It just comes out of your check. And the
people it hits hardest are not rich. I
will show you exactly who it catches and
the one form that can stop it when we
get there. Every rule and dollar figure
here comes straight from Medicare and
the Social Security Administration. When
a 2027 number is still a projection, I
will tell you. The names are examples,
but the rules are real.
Here is why this matters today. Medicare
open enrollment started on October 15th,
and it ends on December 7th. That is the
one window each year when you can change
your Medicare Advantage plan, switch
your drug plan, or move back to Original
Medicare. Your plan has to receive your
request by December 7th. But here is
what most people miss. If you do
nothing, Medicare does not leave you
where you are. Your plan rolls you into
whatever it looks like next year with
next year's prices, next year's drug
list, and next year's doctors. Doing
nothing is still a choice. It is just a
choice somebody else makes for you.
Therefore, the seven changes in this
video are not news to watch and forget.
They are the seven things you need to
check before December 7th. Let's start
with the one that is already in your
mailbox. Number one, your Medicare
Advantage plan may be going away.
For the third year in a row, insurance
companies are pulling Medicare Advantage
plans off the market. Humana says about
600,000 of its members are in plans it
is cutting for 2027. United Healthcare
says about 390,000 of its members are in
plans being dis- continued. And
according to one industry count reported
this week, more than 3 million people on
Medicare Advantage need to find a new
plan for next year.
When a plan is leaving, federal rules
require it to mail you a written notice.
For 2027, those letters went out dated
October 2nd. And a lot of them are
sitting unopened on kitchen counters
right now.
Meet Dorothy. Dorothy is 73, and she has
been in the same Medicare Advantage plan
for 6 years. In early October, a letter
from her plan arrives, and she tosses it
in the pile with the other insurance
mail.
That letter says her plan will not exist
on January 1st. If Dorothy does nothing,
she does not lose Medicare. But she gets
sent back to original Medicare
automatically with no drug plan unless
she picks one.
Now, here is why that matters. In
original Medicare, if Dorothy goes into
the hospital, the Part A deductible this
year is $1,736
for each benefit period. And original
Medicare has no yearly limit on what you
can pay out of pocket for doctor and
hospital care.
So, if Dorothy lands back in original
Medicare without a supplement and
without a drug plan, one bad winter can
cost her thousands.
But Dorothy has protection she does not
know about. Because her plan is the one
leaving, she gets something called a
guaranteed issue right.
That means she can buy a Medigap
supplement policy, plan A, B, D, or G,
and the insurance company cannot turn
her down or charge her more because of
her health.
Normally, after your first few years on
Medicare, a Medigap company can ask
about your health and say no.
This is one of the few times they
cannot.
But the clock on that right is short.
She can apply as early as 60 days before
her plan ends and no later than 63 days
after her plan coverage ends.
Miss that window and the right is gone.
She also gets extra time to pick a new
Advantage plan or a drug plan.
Besides open enrollment, people whose
plan is ending get a special window that
runs from December 8th through the end
of February. Therefore, the first thing
you do this week is find every piece of
mail from your Medicare plan since late
September and open it. Look for two
words, not renewing or non-renewal. If
you see either one, your plan is ending
and your clock has started. But even if
your plan is staying, it is changing.
And the next two changes are inside your
drug plan. Number two, your drug
deductible is going up to $700. The
deductible is the amount you pay for
your prescriptions yourself at the
counter before your drug plan starts
paying its share. This year, the
standard Medicare drug deductible is
On January 1st, it goes to $700. That is
$85 more out of your pocket before your
plan pays a single penny.
Meet Frank. Frank is 69 and he takes a
brand-name blood thinner and a
brand-name inhaler. Every January, his
first refill of the year costs him
hundreds of dollars and it feels like a
mistake. It is not. That is the
deductible resetting on January 1st. In
2027, Frank's January shock gets $85
bigger. Here is the part most people
miss. $700 is the most a standard plan
can charge first, but not every plan
uses it. Some charge less and some skip
the deductible on certain drugs. The
plan with the lowest monthly premium is
not always the plan that costs Frank the
least over a full year.
Therefore, before December 7th, write
down every drug you take, the exact name
and the exact dose, and put that list
into the Medicare Plan Finder on the
official Medicare website, or bring it
to a free counselor. I will give you
that number at the end. The Plan Finder
adds up your premium, your deductible,
and your co-pays for a full year, so you
see the real total. But, the deductible
is only the front door. The next change
is the ceiling. Number three, the most
you can pay for drugs in a year is going
A couple of years ago, a new law put a
hard ceiling on what you pay for
prescriptions in a Medicare drug plan.
Once you hit that ceiling, you pay
nothing for your covered drugs for the
rest of the year, zero. This year, that
ceiling is $2,100.
On January 1st, it goes to $2,400.
That is $300 more that you can be asked
to pay before the protection kicks in.
To be fair, the ceiling is still real
protection. Before the law changed,
there was no ceiling at all. But, here
is what the ceiling does not cover. It
does not count your monthly plan
premium. Your premium is separate, and
you pay it every month, no matter what.
And it only counts drugs that are on
your plan's list. If your drug is not on
the list, what you pay for it does not
count toward the Helen. Helen
is 71, and she takes a brand name drug
for her heart. Her plan covered it this
year, but her plan sent her a notice
this fall that says the drug is coming
off its list for 2027.
Helen did not read it closely.
On January 1st, every dollar Helen pays
for that drug stops counting toward her
ceiling. She could pay full price for
months, and never get the protection she
thinks she has.
That notice is called the annual notice
of change. Every plan has to send one
every fall listing next year's premium,
deductible, copays, and drug list. It is
the most important piece of Medicare
mail you will get all year, and most
people never read it. Therefore, find
your annual notice of change, turn to
the drug section, and check every drug
you take. If even one of them is moving
to a higher price tier or coming off the
list, that is your signal to shop before
December 7th.
But, the drug changes are the ones
people expect. The next change is the
one almost nobody sees coming because it
comes out of a different check entirely.
Number four, the Medicare change that
quietly takes more of your Social
Security check. This is the one I
promised you at the beginning.
Social Security just announced a 3.6%
raise for 2027. That is real money, and
it is the law. But, for most people on
Medicare, the first thing that happens
to that raise is that Medicare takes its
cut. Because for most retirees, your
Part B premium does not come as a bill.
It comes straight out of your Social
Security check before the money ever
reaches your bank account. This year,
the standard Part B premium is $202.90
a month. Medicare's own trustees project
it will go up to about $209.50
in 2027. The final number comes out
later this fall.
That increase alone comes off the top of
your raise. Now, there is a rule that
protects most people here. It is called
the hold harmless rule. It says a Part B
premium increase is not allowed to make
your Social Security check smaller than
it was the year before. For a lot of
retirees, that rule means the raise
shrinks, but the check does not go down.
But, here is what nobody tells you. The
hold harmless rule does not protect
everyone. It does not protect you if
your Part B premium is not taken out of
your Social Security check. It does not
protect you if you are new to Medicare.
And it does not protect you at all if
you pay the income surcharge that
Medicare calls IRMAA.
And IRMAA
is where this gets expensive. IRMAA
is an extra charge on top of your Part B
premium, and on top of your drug plan
premium for people whose income passes a
certain line. This year, that line is
for a single person and $218,000
for a married couple.
You might be thinking, that is not me.
But here is the trap. Medicare does not
look at what you make this year. It
looks at your tax return from 2 years
ago. So your 2027 premium is based on
your 2025 tax return. And that number
includes things that happen once. The
year you sold the house and had a gain
over the tax-free amount. The year you
took a big withdrawal from your IRA to
fix the roof or help a grandchild. The
year you sold some stock. The year your
spouse passed away and you filed one
last joint return. One big year and 2
years later, Medicare sends you the
bill.
Meet Linda. Linda is 70. She is single
and she lives on about $45,000 a year.
In 2025, she pulled extra money out of
her IRA to pay for her husband's final
medical bills and her income for that
one year came out to $120,000.
At this year's rates, that one year puts
Linda in the first surcharge bracket.
Instead of paying $202.90
cents a month for Part B, she pays
That is $81.20
more every month. And she pays an extra
a month on her drug plan on top of that.
Over a year, the Part B surcharge alone
taken straight out of her Social
Security check for income she does not
even have anymore.
Therefore, if your income jumped in 2025
for any one-time reason, watch for a
letter from Social Security late this
year that sets your 2027 premium. And
here is the form that can stop it. It is
called form SSA-44.
If your income went down because of a
life-changing event, you can ask Social
Security to use your newer, lower income
instead. Life-changing events include
marriage, divorce, the death of a
spouse, stopping or cutting back work,
losing a pension, and certain employer
settlement payments. You can file it
online through your My Social Security
account, by mail or fax, or call Social
Security at 1-800-772-1213.
Linda qualifies because her husband
died. If she files that form with proof,
Social Security can look at her current
income of about $45,000,
and her surcharge can go away. But most
people never file it because nobody
tells them it exists. Now, before I get
to number five, a quick note. If this
video is helping you, I put every bill
seniors are legally allowed to stop
paying after 65 into one guide called
the Senior Exempt Playbook. Scan the
code on your screen now or tap the link
in the description.
So far, every change on this list has
been about money. But number five is
different. Number five is about whether
Medicare says yes to your care in the
first place. Number five, Original
Medicare now needs permission first in
six states. For decades, one of the
biggest reasons people chose Original
Medicare over Medicare Advantage was
simple. In Original Medicare, if your
doctor ordered something that Medicare
covers, you got it. No asking permission
first. Prior authorization, the process
where someone has to approve your care
before you get it, was something
Medicare Advantage plans did, not
Original Medicare. That is changing.
Medicare is now running a new pilot
program that adds prior authorization to
Original Medicare in six states.
Arizona, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma,
Texas, and Washington. It started this
year, and it is scheduled to run through
the end of 2031. So, it is fully in
place for 2027. For a list of selected
services, private technology companies
review the request first using computer
tools to help decide. The list includes
things like skin substitutes for wounds,
nerve stimulator implants for pain, and
knee scopes for arthritis. Medicare says
a licensed clinician must make the final
call before any denial, and that the
program does not change what Medicare
covers. But, here is what it means for
you in real life. Your procedure can be
delayed while the paperwork moves. And
if a service is not approved, and you go
ahead with it anyway, you can be on the
hook for the bill.
Meet George. George is 74. He lives in
Ohio, and his doctor wants to scope his

your benefits. It is equal to the state
tax rate times the taxable part of your
social security. Take Walter again and
move him to Utah. $11,300
of taxable social security times Utah's
rate of about 4 and 1/2% gives him a
credit of about $500. That cancels the
tax on his social security.
But, here is the catch. That credit
starts to melt the moment a single
person's income passes $54,000.
For a married couple, the line is
$90,000, and it does not melt slowly.
For every single dollar you earn over

cents of your credit. So, Walter's $500
credit shrinks a little with every

the credit is gone completely. Meet

year, Ray takes an extra $20,000 out of
the IRA to replace the roof.
That one withdrawal pushes them $20,000
over the line. At 2 and 1/2 cents per
dollar, that takes about $500 off their
Social Security credit in a single year,
on top of the regular state tax on the
$20,000 itself. Utah did raise those
lines last year, and lawmakers voted to
trim the tax rate again, but lawmakers
did not pass the full repeal of the
Social Security tax that the governor
asked for. So, the melting credit is
still the law. Therefore, if you live in
Utah, try to keep big one-time
withdrawals spread out across more than
one year when you can, and ask a
preparer to run the Social Security
credit worksheet before you take the
money. But, so far, we are talking about
a few hundred dollars. Starting with
number three, a single extra dollar of
income can cost you hundreds. And by the
time we reach number seven, your
children get a bill for tens of
thousands of dollars. Stay with me.
Number three, Connecticut.
Connecticut has one of the most generous
Social Security breaks on this list,

outside Hartford. She gets $30,000 a

At that level, she pays nothing to
Connecticut on her Social Security.
Then one year, her required withdrawal

condo, same Social Security check, but
now 25% of her benefits, $7,500,

she owes zero. At $80,000, she owes $412
on top of the tax on the extra income
itself. That is what a cliff does. And
here is the part that stings. Those
75,000 and 100,000 dollar lines are
written into the law as flat numbers. As
your Social Security goes up every year
with the cost of living raise, more
Connecticut retirees drift toward that
line without doing anything at all.
Therefore, if you live in Connecticut
and your income is close to the line, a
few thousand dollars of planning can be
worth hundreds of dollars a year.
Things like timing a withdrawal or

after 70 and a half, which keeps that
money out of your income, can keep you
under it. But Connecticut at least
starts its line at $75,000.
The next state starts much lower, and it
is the lowest line of any state that
taxes Social Security. Number four,
Vermont. In Vermont, a single person's
Social Security is fully exempt only if
their income is $55,000 or less. For a
married couple, the line is $70,000.
Above that, the exemption shrinks fast.
And by $65,000 for a single person or
$80,000 for a couple, there is no
exemption left at all.
A couple with two average Social
Security checks and a modest IRA can
blow right through $80,000 without
feeling rich at all. Meet Frank. Frank
is 71 and single. And he lives in a
farmhouse outside Burlington that he has
owned for 40 years.
His income is $66,000,
and $20,000 of his Social Security is
taxable on his federal return. Because
Frank is over $65,000,
Vermont gives him no Social Security
exemption at all. $20,000 * Vermont's
rate of 6.6%
a year.
If Frank's income were $60,000 instead,
half of that would be exempt, and he
would pay about $660.
So, the last $6,000 of Frank's income
cost him $660 of extra Social Security

income.
And Vermont does not stop there. Its
income tax rates go up to 8.75%,
and Vermont has its own estate tax on
what you leave behind, starting at $5
million
at a flat 16%. Keep that idea in your

are alive, plus again on what you leave,

Therefore, if you live in Vermont, the

Security. It is your total income. Every

single, costs you part of your

Number five, Minnesota. Minnesota is

Minnesota does give a Social Security
break, and its lines are higher than

about $108,000 of income. A single

But above that line, Minnesota takes

$4,000 you earn, not every $4,000 of
Social Security, every $4,000 of total

Jim retired from the hospital with a

their income is $130,000
and $40,000 of their Social Security is

They are about $21,000 over the line.
That is six steps of $4,000. So
Minnesota takes away 60% of their

is taxed at 6.8%. That is $1,632
a year. And Minnesota's top income tax
rate is 9.85%,
one of the highest in the country. But
here is the part Carol and Jim never

to federal estate tax line this year is

Minnesota's is 1/5 of that. $3 million

the way the state does. The house, the

Add a family farm or a small business

cross that line. Therefore, if you live
in Minnesota and your estate could get
anywhere near $3 million,
that is a conversation to have with an
estate planning attorney now, not later.
Because Minnesota's line is set in state
law and it does not follow the federal
increase. But Minnesota at least gives
everyone the same deal at 65. Number six
has a rule that quietly skips right over
the people who just retired. Number six,
Rhode Island. On paper, Rhode Island
exempts social security for retirees,
but to qualify, you have to pass three
tests, and almost nobody reads the
second one.
Test one, you have taxable social
security.
Test two, you have reached your social
security full retirement age.
Test three, your income is under the
line.
Here is the trap in test two. Full
retirement age is not 65. For anyone
born in 1960 or later, it is 67. Rhode
Island's own tax guide uses an example
of a 65-year-old man named Benjamin, and
it says plainly that he does not qualify
because he has not reached full
retirement age. Meet Joyce. Joyce turned
65 this year, and she lives in Warwick.
She claimed social security early, and
she has the same income as Walter from
Montana, $24,000 of social security and
$30,000 from her IRA. $11,300
of her benefits are taxable federally.
Because Joyce is 65, not 67, Rhode
Island gives her no exemption. $11,300
is about $424 a year for 2 years until
she reaches full retirement age. And
that IRA? Rhode Island has a pension
break of up to $50,000 per person, but
its own guide says IRA withdrawals do
not qualify for it. Joyce's $30,000 is
taxed in full. Now, test three. For last
year, the income line for a single
person was $107,000,
and this one is a hard cliff. There is
no partial exemption above it.
Meet George. George is 70, single, and
gets $40,000 a year from social
security. So, $34,000 of it is taxable
federally. If George's income is
Rhode Island exempts all of it. If his

dollars, Island exempts none of it.
34,000 dollars times 4.75%
is about 1,615
dollars. One extra dollar of income,
dollars of extra tax. And Rhode Island

dollars. That is less than 1/8 of the
federal line. Therefore, if you live in
Rhode Island and you are between 65 and
67, plan for state tax on your social
security until your full retirement age.
And if your income is anywhere near the
line, watch it like a hawk because 1
dollar over costs you everything.
But every state so far has taxed you.
The next state sends the bill to your
children. Number seven, Pennsylvania.
Pennsylvania is actually kind to
retirees while they are alive. It does
not tax social security. It does not tax
most retirement income. That is why so
many people retire there. But
Pennsylvania has an inheritance tax, and
it is one of only five states that still
have one. And here's what makes it
different. In most inheritance tax
states, your children pay nothing. In
Pennsylvania, your children and
grandchildren pay 4 and 1/2% starting
from the very first dollar. There is no
exemption amount for them. None.
Brothers and sisters pay 12%. Nieces,
nephews, and friends pay 15%. Only a
husband or wife pays zero. Meet
Margaret. Margaret is a widow in
Allentown. She owns her house outright,
worth 600,000 dollars, and she has an
IRA worth 200,000 dollars. She leaves
everything to her two children, split
evenly. 800,000 dollars times 4 and 1/2%
is 36,000 dollars. Her children owe it
to the state, and it is due quickly. The
tax is due at death, and it becomes late
after 9 months. Some families have to
sell the house just to pay it, or they
have to pull the money out of the IRA,
which can create income tax, too. Now,
here's the part almost nobody knows.
Pennsylvania gives a 5% discount if the
tax is paid within 3 months of death. On
Margaret's estate, that saves $1,800
and the bill drops to $34,200.
And there are a few things Pennsylvania
does not tax. Life insurance is not
subject to the inheritance tax. Property
owned jointly between a husband and wife
is exempt. And debts, funeral costs, and
the costs of settling the estate are
deductible. But a joint bank account
with one of your children is a different
story. If Margaret puts her daughter on
her checking account, Pennsylvania still
taxes the daughter on half of that
account when Margaret dies. In Florida,
Margaret's children would owe zero. In
Ohio, zero. Federally, zero. Because the
federal estate tax line this year is $15
million.
Therefore, if you live in Pennsylvania,
sit down with an estate attorney and ask
about two things: how your family will
pay the inheritance tax within 3 months
to get the discount, and whether life
insurance makes sense to cover it. But
Pennsylvania only takes once after you
are gone. The last state on this list
takes twice. And this is the one I
promised you at the beginning. Number
eight, Oregon. Oregon looks friendly at
first. It does not tax social security
at all, but that is where the good news
ends. Oregon taxes the money you pull
out of your IRA, your 401k, and most
pensions. And its rates are some of the
highest in the nation. For a single
person, Oregon's 8.75%
rate kicks in at only about $11,000 of
taxable income. So, almost every dollar
of a normal retirement income lands
right in that 8.75%
bracket. Oregon does have a retirement
income credit, but to get it, a single
person's social security has to be
a year or less. And their household
income plus social security has to stay
Those lines have not been raised for
inflation. Almost nobody who collects a
normal social security check qualifies.
Meet Ed. Ed is 67, single, and he
retired to Bend. Like Walter, he gets
$24,000 from Social Security, and he
pulls $30,000 a year from his IRA.
Oregon ignores his Social Security, but
it taxes the IRA. Oregon's own tax table
shows close to $1,900 of tax on $25,000
of taxable income before credits every
year. If Ed lived across the Columbia
River in Washington, his state income
tax would be zero because Washington has
no income tax. That is the first time
Oregon takes. Here is the second. Oregon
has its own estate tax, and its line is
$1 million.
The lowest estate tax line in the entire
United States. It has sat at $1 million
since 2012, and it has never been raised
for inflation, not once. Earlier this
year, a bill to raise it died in
committee. The federal line is $15
million. Washington's line is $3
million. Massachusetts is $2 million.
Oregon is $1 million, and it is not
going anywhere.
Meet Ed's sister, Barbara. Barbara and
her late husband bought a house in
Portland in 1991. Today, it is worth
She also has $300,000 left in her IRA.
One house and one retirement account.
That is $1 million $200,000.
$200,000 over Oregon's line. At Oregon's
10% starting rate, her children owe the
Federally, they owe nothing. In
Washington, nothing. In Massachusetts,
nothing. So, that is the answer to the
promise I made at the beginning. The
worst state on this list is Oregon
because it taxes your retirement savings
every year while you are alive. After
you are gone, it taxes what is left
before your children can have it with a
line so low that a paid-off Portland
house and a modest IRA can cross it.
Therefore, if you live in Oregon and
your house plus your accounts are
anywhere near $1 million,
which in much of Oregon today means most
homeowners, talk to an estate planning
attorney now because Oregon's line is
fixed in state law, and every year that
home prices rise, more ordinary families
cross it. So, here is what to do, no
matter which state you live in. One,
look up your own state's rule for Social
Security, IRA withdrawals, and pensions.
42 states and Washington, D.C. do not
tax Social Security at all, but check
whether your state taxes your IRA. Two,
if you live in Connecticut, Rhode
Island, Vermont, Minnesota, or Utah,
know your income line and watch it

Three, spread large IRA withdrawals

Four, if you are 70 and 1/2 or older and

Five, if you live in Rhode Island and

Six, if you live in Pennsylvania,

Seven, never put a child on your bank
account just to make things easier until
you know how your state taxes it.
Eight, get free help. The IRS runs a

title: The IRS Flags These 7 Things After 65 (Most Don't Know)

segments.text: Every January, the IRS receives a copy
of every tax form your bank, your
brokerage, your IRA, and Social Security
send you. Then, a computer compares
every one of those forms against your
tax return, line by line. And if a
single number is missing, the IRS can
mail you a bill for the tax plus
interest plus a penalty of 20%. No agent
ever looks at your face. No one calls
you. A machine finds the gap, and a
letter shows up in your mailbox. Here is
why that matters after 65. When you were
working, you had one simple form from
your employer. Now, you might have a
form from Social Security, a form from
your IRA, a form from every bank that
holds your savings, and a form from your
brokerage. Every one of those forms is a
chance for the numbers to disagree, and
the IRS computer is built to catch
exactly that. But, this is not about
cheating. Almost every senior who gets
one of these letters never tried to hide
a single dollar. They simply did not
know the rule.
So, today, I'm going to walk you through
the seven things the IRS flags most
often after 65. Each one has a real form
behind it, a real rule, and a real
dollar amount. And stay with me all the
way to number seven because one of these
seven is brand new this year. It is
worth up to $12,000 off your taxes for a
married couple, and the IRS is watching
it in both directions. People who claim
it wrong get flagged, and millions of
people who qualify are going to leave it
on the table. I will show you exactly
where the line is at the end. First, let
me be clear about one thing. Every rule
in this video comes straight from the
IRS and federal tax law. The names I use
are examples, but the rules and the
dollar amounts are real. Number one, the
interest you forgot about. Banks are
paying real interest again. Certificates
of deposit, high-yield savings accounts,
money market accounts. That is good news
for seniors with savings, but it comes
with a form.
Any bank that pays you $10 or more in
interest during the year has to send a
form called the 1099-INT,
and it does not just send it to you. It
sends the exact same form to the IRS.
Meet Helen. Helen is 74. Two years ago,
she moved $40,000 into a certificate of
deposit at a small online bank because
the rate was so much better than her
local branch. That account earned her
about $1,800 of interest last year. The
bank mailed the form to her old address.
Helen never saw it, so she left the
interest off. Here is what she did not
know. The IRS did see the form. About a
year and a half later, a letter arrived.
It is called a CP2000.
It said the IRS had received income that
was not on her return, and it proposed a
new bill for the tax she owed on that
$1,800 plus interest from the original
due date. The IRS says plainly that
interest is taxable, whether you receive
the form or not. Losing the form is not
a defense. Therefore, before you file,
make a list of every bank and credit
union that holds your money, including
the ones you forgot about. Log in to
each one in February and download the
form yourself. Do not wait for the mail.
But interest is the small one. Number
two is the one that surprises almost
everybody because it involves money you
were told was safe. Number two, your
Social Security check. Every January,
Social Security mails you a form called
the SSA-1099.
It shows every dollar of benefits you
received during the year, and just like
your bank, Social Security sends a copy
to the IRS.
Now, a lot of seniors heard on the news
last year that Social Security is no
longer taxed. That is not what the law
did. The new tax law created a separate
deduction for seniors, and I will get to
that at number seven. But it did not
change the rule that taxes Social
Security. That rule is still on the
books. Here is how it works. The IRS
adds up your other income plus half of
your Social Security. If you are single
and that total goes over $25,000,
part of your benefits become taxable.
For a married couple, the line is
And here is the shocking part. Those two
numbers were written into the law in
1983. They have never been raised for
inflation, not once. Back then, almost
no one crossed them. Today, a retiree
with a modest IRA crosses them easily.
Meet Walter. Walter is single. He gets
$24,000 a year from Social Security.
Last year, he also pulled $20,000 out of
his IRA to fix the roof and replace his
car. Walter assumed his Social Security
was tax-free because it always had been.
But here is the math. Half of his Social
Security is $12,000. Add the $20,000
from his IRA and Walter is at $32,000.
That is $7,000 over the line. So, $3,500
of his Social Security became taxable
income. Walter never reported it. The
IRS computer had both forms and it did
the math for him. Therefore, any year
you take a bigger withdrawal from your
IRA, sell investments, or earn extra
income, assume part of your Social
Security may now be taxable and run the
worksheet in the IRS instructions or ask
a preparer before you file.
But here is where it gets more
expensive. Numbers one and two can cost
you a few hundred dollars. Number three
can cost you a quarter of the money in
one shot and the deadline is less than
three months away. Number three, the
withdrawal you were required to take.
Once you reach a certain age, the IRS
stops letting your traditional IRA grow
untouched. You are required to take out
a minimum amount every year. This is
called your required minimum
distribution. For most people today, it
starts at age 73. If you were born in
1960 or later, it starts at 75. And the
deadline for this year is December 31st.
Here is the trap. Your IRA company
already reports to the IRS that you owe
a required withdrawal. It is printed on
a form called the 5498. So, the IRS
knows the withdrawal was due before you
even think about it. If the money never
comes out, the gap is easy for them to
spot.
Meet Ruth. Ruth turned 74 this year. Her
husband always handled the money, and he
passed away last spring. Ruth did not
know the IRA had a required withdrawal.
Her amount for the year was $8,000, and
December came and went. Here is the
penalty. The IRS charges an excise tax
of 25% of the amount you failed to take.
For Ruth, that is $2,000, and that is on
top of the regular income tax she still
owes when she finally takes the money
out. But, there is good news, and almost
nobody hears it. Congress lowered that
penalty a few years ago. If you take the
missed withdrawal and fix it within the
correction window, generally about 2
years, the penalty drops from 25% to
10%. For Ruth, that turns $2,000 into
And it gets better. If you missed it
because of a reasonable error, like Ruth
losing her husband, you can file form
5329, take the withdrawal right away,
and write a short explanation asking the
IRS to waive the penalty. The IRS has
the power to waive it completely.
Therefore, if you are 73 or older, call
your IRA company this month and ask one
question. Have I taken my full required
withdrawal for this year? If the answer
is no, you still have until December
31st. But, what if you do not need that
money at all? What if you would rather
give it away? That brings us to number
four, and it is one of the most generous
rules in the tax code. It is also one of
the easiest to get flagged on. Number
four, the gift to your church that the
IRS taxes anyway.
If you are 70 and a half or older, the
IRS lets you send money straight from
your IRA to a qualified charity. Your
church, the food bank, your old school.
This is called a qualified charitable
distribution. The money is not counted
as income at all. And once you reach the
age for required withdrawals, it counts
towards your required minimum. You can
give more than $100,000 a year this way.
It is a wonderful rule, but here is the
problem. When your IRA company sends the
form showing the withdrawal, it usually
reports the full amount as a regular
distribution. The form does not tell the
IRS that it went to a church. That part
is your job. On your tax return, you
report the full amount on the line for
IRA distributions. Then, on the line for
the taxable amount, you put zero, and
you write the letters QCD right next to
it. Meet George. George is 76, and for
years he has given $5,000 a year to his
church straight from his IRA. But, the
person who did his taxes saw the form
from the IRA company, saw $5,000, and
entered it as taxable income. Nobody
wrote QCD. So, George paid tax on money
he gave to his church. At his tax rate,
that was about $600 a year. And because
George takes the standard deduction like
most seniors, he never got a charity
deduction either. He lost both ways. And
here is one more rule that trips people
up. The check has to go straight from
the IRA company to the charity. If the
IRA company writes the check to you, and
you hand it to the church, that is not a
qualified charitable distribution. It is
a regular withdrawal, fully taxable.
Therefore, if you give from your IRA,
tell your tax preparer in writing. Keep
the receipt from the charity, and look
at your return before you sign it. Find
the IRA line. If you do not see the
letters QCD, stop and ask. Before I get
to number five, a quick note. If this
video is helping you, I put every bill
seniors are legally allowed to stop
paying after 65 into one guide called
the Senior Exempt Playbook. Scan the
code on your screen now, or tap the link
in the description. Now, number five.
And this is the one that can turn a
small sale into a giant tax bill on
profits you never actually made. Number
five, the old stock with no price on it.
When you sell stock or a mutual fund,
your brokerage sends you and the IRS a
form called the 1099-B. It shows how
much you sold it for. But for older
investments, there is a hole in that
form.
Brokerages are only required to report
what you originally paid for stock
bought in 2011 or later. Anything older,
like shares you bought decades ago or
shares you inherited from your parents,
may show up with a blank where the
purchase price should be. Meet Margaret.
Margaret is 71. Her mother left her some
shares of a utility company years ago,
and last year Margaret sold them for
$40,000 to help pay for her
granddaughter's wedding. Her real cost
was about $30,000, so her actual profit
was only $10,000. But the form showed
$40,000 sold and nothing in the purchase
price box. Margaret thought cashing out
an inheritance did not count as a sale,
so she left it off. Here is what the IRS
computer saw: $40,000 of sales and zero
cost. To the computer, that looks like
$40,000 of pure profit, and the letter
she got proposed tax on all of it, four
times what she actually owed.
And there is a special rule for
inherited stock that makes this even
more painful to miss. When you inherit
shares, your cost is usually the value
on the day the person died, not what
they paid decades ago. That is called a
stepped-up basis, and it can wipe out
most of the gain. But you only get it if
you report it. Therefore, every time you
sell an investment, check the form for a
blank purchase price, find the real
number, and report the sale. Do not
leave it off. But stocks are one thing.
Number six involves the biggest thing
most seniors own, and the dollar amounts
are much larger. Number six, selling the
family home. When you sell your main
home, the IRS lets you keep up to
of profit tax-free if you are single,
and up to $500,000 if you are married
and file together. You have to have
owned it and lived in it for two of the
last five years.
For most families, that covers
everything. But, here is the problem.
Those numbers have not been raised since
and a lot of seniors bought their homes
in the 1970s and '80s when houses cost a
fraction of what they do now. Meet Joan.
Joan and her husband bought their house
Her husband passed away, and 3 years
later, Joan sold the house for $750,000
to move closer to her daughter. That is
a profit of $630,000.
As a single person, Joan can only
exclude $250,000.
That leaves $380,000
that may be taxable, and the sale does
not stay quiet. The title company
usually files a form called the 1099-S
with the IRS. If that form is filed, the
IRS expects to see the sale on your
return, even if you owe nothing. But,
here's what Joan did not know, and it
could have saved her a fortune. If a
surviving spouse sells the home within 2
years of the date their husband or wife
died, the IRS generally still lets them
use the full $500,000 limit. Joan waited
3 years. If she had sold within two, her
taxable amount would have dropped from
And your cost is not just what you paid.
Major improvements, like a new roof or
an addition, get added to it. And when a
spouse dies, their half of the house
usually gets a stepped-up value as of
the date of death. Therefore, before you
sell the house, gather every receipt for
improvements. Find out what the house
was worth when your spouse died. And if
you are widowed, sit down with a tax
professional before you list it. The
2-year window matters.
But, I promised you that number seven
would be brand new, and that the IRS is
watching it in both directions. Here it
is. Number seven, the new senior
deduction.
Last year, Congress passed a new tax
law. Inside it is a brand new deduction
just for people 65 and older. It is
$6,000 per person. For a married couple
where both spouses are 65 or older, that
It runs for four tax years from 2025
through 2028. And here is the best part.
You get it whether you itemize or take
the standard deduction. Meet Bill and
Linda. They are both 66. And together,
they have about $90,000 of income from
pensions, Social Security, and their
IRAs. They get the full $12,000
deduction. At their tax rate, that is
roughly $1,400 less in federal tax every
year for 4 years.
But here is why the IRS is flagging it.
The deduction has an income line. For a
single person, it starts shrinking once
your modified income goes over $75,000.
For a married couple filing together,
the line is $150,000.
Above that, you lose 6 cents of the
deduction for every dollar you go over.
So a single retiree with $95,000 of
income is $20,000 over the line. 6% of
that is $1,200. So their deduction is
And once a single person reaches
it is gone completely. There are other
rules, too. You have to be 65 by the
last day of the tax year. You need a
valid Social Security number on the
return. And if you are married, you have
to file jointly to get it.
And because this deduction never existed
before, the IRS is checking it closely.
People who claim the full amount when
their income is over the line, or who
claim it for a spouse who has not turned
65 yet, are exactly the kind of mismatch
the computer is built to catch. But here
is the other direction, and this is the
one I really wanted you to hear.
Millions of seniors who do qualify will
never claim it because it is new, and it
goes on a brand new form called schedule
1A. If you copy last year's return, you
can miss it completely, and nobody from
the IRS is going to call you and tell
you that you left $6,000 on the table.
So, that is the answer to the promise I
made at the beginning. The newest flag
after 65 is the new senior deduction.
Claim it wrong, and you get a letter.
Forget to claim it, and you simply lose
up to $12,000 a year.
Now, what if one of those letters shows
up in your mailbox? Here's what most
people do not know. A CP2000 is not a
bill. It is a proposal. The IRS is
telling you what it thinks you owe, and
it is asking you to agree or disagree.
You can disagree. Margaret, with her old
stock, could send in the real purchase
price and cut her bill by
three-quarters. But, you have to answer
it. The letter gives you a deadline,
usually 30 days. If you ignore it, the
IRS assumes you agree, and the bill
becomes final. And one more warning, the
IRS starts these conversations by mail.
It does not first contact you by text
message, by email, or on social media.
If someone calls or texts you about a
flagged return and demands payment by
gift card, it is a scam. Hang up. So,
here are your seven steps before you
file your next return. One, download
your interest forms from every bank
yourself in February. Do not wait for
the mail. Two, in any year you take a
big IRA withdrawal, check whether part
of your social security became taxable.
Three, if you are 73 or older, confirm
your required withdrawal is done before
December 31st. If you missed one, take
it now and file form 5329.
Four, if you give to charity from your
IRA, make sure the letters QCD are on
your return.
Five, never leave an investment sale off
your return, and fill in a blank
purchase price with the real number.
Six, if you are widowed and thinking of
selling the house, talk to a
professional before the 2-year mark.
Seven, claim the new senior deduction on
schedule 1A and check the income line
first.
And if you get a letter you do not
understand or you cannot get an answer
from the IRS, call the Taxpayer Advocate
Service. It is a free independent office
inside the IRS. The number is

title: Never Give Your Kids More Than This After 65 (Most Don't Know)

segments.text: This year, the IRS lets you hand each of
your children $19,000 without filling
out a single form. But if you need a
nursing home in the next 5 years,
Medicaid can go back and count every one
of those gifts. And for roughly every
you gave away, you can lose about 1
month of nursing home coverage at the
exact moment you need it most. That is
not a scam. It is federal law. And most
grandparents who write those loving
checks have never heard of it. Here is
why it matters to you. According to the
Department of Health and Human Services,
someone turning 65 today has about a 70%
chance of needing some kind of long-term
care before the end of their life. And
one in five will need it for more than 5
years. So the money you give your family
today does not just leave your account.
It can follow you all the way to the
front door of a nursing home. But giving
money to your kids is not the problem.
The problem is that there are seven
rules about giving that almost nobody
explains. And every one of them has a
number attached to it. And stay with me
all the way to number seven. Because
there is one way to give your kids or
grandkids as much money as you want.
$50,000, even $100,000. And the IRS does
not count a single penny of it as a
gift. It is written right into the tax
code. Almost nobody uses it. and I will
show you exactly how it works at the
end. First, let me be clear about one
thing. It is your money and you are
allowed to give it to anyone you want.
Every rule in this video comes from
federal law and federal agencies. The
names I use are examples, but the rules
and the dollar amounts are real. Number
one, the number the IRS is watching. The
IRS calls it the annual exclusion. For
this year, it is $19,000.
That means you can give up to $19,000 to
any one person in a single year and the
IRS does not want to hear about it. No
form, no report, nothing. And it is per
person. If you have three children and
four grandchildren, each one could get
$19,000 this year. And if you are
married, you and your spouse together
can give $38,000 to each person. But
here is where most people get scared for
the wrong reason. They think that if
they give more than $19,000,
somebody owes a big tax. Usually, nobody
does. Meet Dorothy. Dorothy is 72, and
last spring, she gave her son $30,000 to
help with the down payment on his first
house. Then, a neighbor told her the IRS
was going to take a huge bite out of it.
Dorothy did not sleep for a week. Here
is the truth. Dorothy went $11,000 over
the line. That means she has to file one
form with the IRS called form 709, the
gift tax return. It is due by the
regular tax deadline in April of the
following year. But she does not owe a
single dollar of tax. Why? Because the
extra $11,000 simply gets subtracted
from her lifetime exclusion. And
starting this year under the new tax law
Congress passed, that lifetime number is
$15 million per person. Unless you plan
to give away more than $15 million in
your lifetime, you will almost certainly
never pay gift tax at all. And one more
thing the IRS makes very clear. When a
gift tax is owed, it is the person
giving the money who is responsible for
it, not the child who receives it. Your
son does not report your gift as income.
He does not pay tax on it.
Therefore, if you go over $19,000 to one
person in one year, do not panic and do
not hide it. file the form. It keeps
your records clean, but that is the IRS
number, and the IRS number is the one
everybody talks about. Number two is the
number nobody talks about, and it is the
one that actually costs families money.
Number two, Medicaid has no safe number
at all. Most people believe that if they
stay under $19,000, their gifts are
safe. For the IRS, that is true. For
Medicaid, it is not true at all. When
you apply for Medicaid to help pay for a
nursing home, federal law requires the
state to look back at every dollar you
gave away in the last 60 months. That is
five full years. This is called the look
back period, and it is written right
into the Social Security Act. And here
is the part that shocks families. There
is no $19,000 safe zone in the look
back. A $10,000 check to your grandson
counts. A $5,000 wedding gift counts. In
most states, any money you gave away for
less than its value inside that 5-year
window can be added up and held against
you. Then the state does a simple piece
of math. It takes the total amount you
gave away and it divides it by the
average monthly cost of a nursing home
in your state. The answer is the number
of months Medicaid will refuse to pay
for your care. Each state sets its own
number, but nationally a private nursing
home room now costs about $127,000
a year or about $10,600
a month.
Meet Walter. Walter is 79 and he loves
his grandkids. Over 4 years, he gave
them $60,000, some for college, some for
a used car. He never gave any one of
them more than $19,000 in a single year.
So he never filed a single form. He
thought he did everything right. Then
Walter had a stroke and needed full-time
nursing care. His savings ran out within
a year and he applied for Medicaid. The
state looked back 5 years and found
$60,000 in gifts. In Walter's state, the
monthly number was about $10,000. So
Walter was hit with 6 months of no
Medicaid coverage for his nursing home.
And here is the crulest part. That
penalty does not start the day he wrote
the checks. It starts on the day he is
already in the nursing home, already out
of money, and would otherwise qualify.
So, his family had to come up with about
$60,000 to cover those 6 months, the
exact same amount Walter had given away.
There are a few important exceptions.
Money you give to your spouse does not
count against you. And money given to a
child who is blind or disabled is
protected, too. But for most gifts to
most children and grandchildren, the
look back applies. Therefore, if there
is any chance you might need long-term
care in the next 5 years, talk to an
elder law attorney before you give away
any large amount of money, not after.
Before once the check is cashed, the
5-year clock has already started. But
the checks you write are only part of
the story. Before I get to number three,
let me tell you who I am. I'm Mark
Callaway and on this channel I dig
through the federal rules that decide
what happens to your money after 65. So
you hear it from me before you hear it
from a letter in your mailbox. If that
is worth something to you, stick around
because number seven is the one every
grandparent needs to hear.
Now the biggest gift most seniors ever
give their children is not cash at all.
It is the house. Number three, never
give your kids the house while you are
alive until you hear this. A lot of
parents think the smartest move is to
sign the house over to the kids now. It
feels safe, but the tax code treats a
house you give away very differently
from a house you leave behind. When you
give your children property while you
are alive, they take over your original
cost. The IRS calls this carryover
basis. Whatever you paid for the house
decades ago becomes their starting
number for taxes. But when your children
inherit that same house after you pass
away, the law resets the cost to what
the house is worth on the day you die,
that is called a stepped up basis. And
that one difference can be worth tens of
thousands of dollars. Meet Ed and Linda.
They bought their home in 1985 for
$60,000. Today, it is worth $400,000.
Last year, they deeded it to their
daughter to keep it in the family.
Here's what that means. If their
daughter sells the house someday for
$400,000, the IRS will say her cost was
only $60,000. That is a taxable gain of
At the common federal capital gains rate
of 15%, that is about $51,000 in federal
tax before her state takes its share.
Now, imagine Ed and Linda had simply
left the house to her in their estate
instead. Her cost would reset to
$400,000. If she sold it for that, her
taxable gain would be close to zero.
Same house, same family, about $51,000
of difference. And there is more. A
house worth $400,000 is far over the
$19,000 line. So Ed and Linda also had
to file a gift tax return, and the house
now falls right inside the Medicaid
5-year look back. If either of them
needs a nursing home in the next 5
years, that house can be treated as a
gift they gave away. Therefore, do not
sign the deed over to your kids without
talking to a professional first. There
are other tools that can pass the house
to your family while keeping that
stepped up basis. And there is one
Medicaid exception worth knowing. If an
adult child lived in your home for at
least 2 years and cared for you so you
could stay out of a nursing home, the
house can sometimes go to that child
without a penalty. But the house is a
big decision and most people think about
it carefully.
Number four is a small decision that
families make in 5 minutes at the bank
and it can quietly unravel your entire
plan.
Number four, adding your child's name to
your bank account. A parent gets older
and wants a son or daughter to help pay
the bills, so they add that child as a
joint owner on the account. It takes one
signature. Here is the good news first.
Under IRS rules, simply adding your
child's name to a regular bank account
is usually not a gift by itself. The
gift happens later when your child takes
money out for their own use. But here is
the bad news. A joint account with your
child is not just a helping hand. In
most states, when you pass away,
everything in that account goes straight
to the other owner. It skips your will
completely.
Meet Carol. Carol is 80 and she has
three children. She added her oldest son
to her $90,000 savings account so he
could help with her bills. Her will says
everything gets split three ways. But
when Carol passed away, that $90,000
went entirely to her oldest son because
his name was on the account. Her other
two children received nothing from it
and her son had no legal duty to share.
And in many states, if your child owes
money or gets sued, an account with
their name on it can be exposed to their
creditors. Therefore, if you just want
help paying bills, ask your bank about
other options. Many banks offer a
convenient signer or you can sign a
durable power of attorney. those let
your child help you without making them
an owner of your money.
Before I get to number five, a quick
note. If this video is helping you, I
put every bill seniors are legally
allowed to stop paying after 65 into one
guide called the senior exempt playbook.
Scan the code on your screen now or tap
the link in the description.
But some parents try to avoid every one
of these problems with one simple idea.
They say it is not a gift. It is a loan.
And that leads to number five.
Number five, the loan to your kids that
the IRS calls a gift. Lending money to
your children feels safer than giving
it. And many parents charge no interest
because charging your own child interest
feels wrong. But the tax code has a rule
for this. Under federal law, if you lend
your child $10,000 or less, the IRS
generally leaves it alone. But once a
family loan goes above that amount and
you charge less than a minimum interest
rate the IRS publishes every single
month, the IRS can treat the interest
you did not charge as if you gave it
away.
There is some relief for loans up to
$100,000 where the extra interest is
limited based on your child's investment
income. But above $100,000, that
protection is gone. Meet Jim. Jim is 74.
He lent his daughter $150,000
to buy a home. No interest, no
paperwork, just a handshake. A few years
later, Jim told her not to worry about
paying it back. In the eyes of the IRS,
that loan was never really a loan. The
moment Jim forgave it, the balance
became a gift. That is far over $19,000.
So Jim needed to file a gift tax return.
And for Medicaid, that forgiven loan is
a transfer that falls inside the 5-year
look back.
Therefore, if you lend your kids real
money, treat it like a real loan. Put it
in writing, sign a promisory note,
charge at least the minimum IRS interest
rate called the applicable federal rate,
and keep a record of every payment. If
