you want to forgive it someday, do it
slowly in pieces of $19,000 or less per
year. But what if you want to help a
grandchild pay for college? That brings
us to a shortcut that most grandparents
have never heard of. Number six, the
5-year college shortcut. A 529 plan is a
savings account for education. The money
grows and when it is used for qualified
school costs, the growth comes out free
of federal tax. And there is a special
rule that lets you put in 5 years of
gifts all at once. Instead of $19,000,
you can put up to $95,000 into a
grandchild's college plan in a single
year. If you are married, you and your
spouse can put in up to $190,000
together. The IRS treats it as if you
spread it over 5 years, but this is the
one time where you must file the gift
tax return even though you owe nothing.
You have to make the election on form
709. If you skip that form, the IRS can
treat the whole amount as a gift in a
single year. And for the next five
years, you cannot give that same
grandchild any more gifts without going
over the line.
Now, here is some good news that changed
recently. For years, money a grandparent
paid from their own college plan could
hurt a grandchild's financial aid. It
was counted as the students income. But
under the new federal student aid form,
money from a grandparents plan no longer
has to be reported as student income.
So, grandparents can help again without
cutting the grandchild's federal aid.
and one warning. If you might need
Medicaid, how your state treats a
college plan you own can vary. Some
states count it as your asset. Ask
before you open one. Therefore, the
college shortcut can move up to $95,000
out of your hands in one year. Just file
the form, but even the college plan has
limits. Number seven has no dollar limit
at all, and it is the one I promised you
at the very beginning. Number seven, the
gift the IRS never counts. Buried in the
tax code is a rule that says certain
payments are simply not gifts, not small
gifts, not gifts at all. Here it is. If
you pay someone's tuition directly to
the school, or you pay someone's medical
bills directly to the doctor, the
hospital, or the insurance company, the
IRS does not count it as a gift. There
is no dollar limit. It does not use up
any of your $19,000, and you do not have
to file form 709. Meet Helen. Helen is
77 and her granddaughter got into a
state university. The tuition was
$40,000 for the year. Helen could have
written her granddaughter a check for
$40,000. That would have been $21,000
over the line, and she would have needed
to file a gift tax return.
Instead, Helen sent the $40,000 straight
to the university's tuition office. Then
that same year, she gave her
granddaughter a separate gift of $19,000
in cash for books, an apartment, and a
car to get to class. That is $59,000 to
one person in one year. And the IRS did
not count a single dollar of the tuition
as a gift. No form, no tax. The same
rule works for medical care. If your son
needs surgery, you can pay the hospital
directly. If your daughter cannot afford
her health insurance, you can pay the
insurance company directly. As long as
the money goes straight to the provider,
it does not count against your $19,000.
But there are two catches and they
matter. First, it has to be direct. If
you give your grandchild the money and
she pays the school, that is a regular
gift. If you pay her back for a bill she
already paid, that is a regular gift,
too. The check must go to the school or
the provider. Second, it only covers
tuition, not books, not dorm rooms, not
meal plans. for those use your $19,000
exclusion. And here is the final
warning. This rule is an IRS rule.
Medicaid does not follow it. If you pay
$40,000 of tuition for a grandchild and
need a nursing home within 5 years,
Medicaid can still count it in the look
back. So, how much should you give your
kids after 65? For the IRS, $19,000 per
person per year and no limit at all on
tuition and medical bills paid directly.
But for Medicaid, there is no safe
number. Inside five years, every gift
counts. So, here are your seven steps
before you give your kids another
dollar.
One, keep gifts to $19,000 or less per
person per year if you want to avoid IRS
paperwork. Two, if you go over, file
Form 709 by the April deadline. You will
almost certainly owe nothing. Three, if
a nursing home is possible in the next 5
years, talk to an elder law attorney
before you give away any large amount.
Four, do not deed the house to your kids
without professional advice. You could
cost them the stepped up basis. Five, do
not add a child as a joint owner just to
pay bills. Ask about a power of attorney
or a convenient signer instead. Six, if
you lend money, put it in writing and
charge at least the IRS minimum rate.
Seven, pay tuition and medical bills
directly to the school or provider. The
IRS does not count it as a gift. If you
need help finding an elder law attorney
or free legal help near you, call the
Elder Care Locator from the Federal
Administration for Community Living at

title: Never Keep More Than This in Cash at Home After 65 (Most Don't Know)

segments.text: Over 10 years, one federal agency seized
more than $4 billion in cash from
ordinary Americans. And according to the
Justice Department's own Inspector
General, about $3.2 billion of it was
taken without anyone being charged with
a crime and without a single judge ever
looking at the case. Most of that cash
was not taken from drug dealers in back
alleys. It was taken at airports, at bus
stations, and at train stations from
people who were simply carrying their
own money. Now, here's why that matters
to you. Millions of Americans over 65
keep cash at home in a coffee can, in a
shoe box on the closet shelf, in an
envelope taped under a drawer. It feels
like the safest money you have. Nobody
can freeze it. No bank can charge you a
fee on it. And no computer glitch can
make it disappear. But cash at home has
seven enemies, and most seniors have
never thought about a single one of
them. Some of them want to steal it.
Some of them quietly shrink it. And some
of them are federal rules that can count
it against you or take it from you the
moment it leaves your house. And stay
with me all the way to number seven
because there is one number printed
inside your homeowner's insurance policy
that tells you the most cash you should
ever keep at home. It is a shockingly
small number. Almost nobody has read it,
and I will show you exactly where to
find it at the end. First, let me be
clear about one thing. There is no
federal law that limits how much cash
you are allowed to keep in your own
home. It is your money, and keeping it
is legal. But legal and safe are two
very different things. Every rule in
this video comes from federal agencies
and federal law. The names I use are
examples, but the rules and the dollar
amounts are real.
Number one, the scammers who come to
your door to collect it. Every year, the
FBI publishes a report on internet and
phone crime. In the newest report,
Americans 60 and older filed more than
200,000 complaints and reported about
$7.7 billion in losses. That is more
than any other age group in the country.
The average loss for an older victim was
And there is one scam the FBI and the
Federal Trade Commission keep warning
about because it goes straight after
cash. It works like this. Your phone
rings. The caller says he is from your
bank, or from the government, or from
the Federal Trade Commission itself. He
tells you your accounts have been
hacked, your identity has been stolen,
and your money is in danger. He sounds
calm. He sounds official. And he has a
solution. Take your money out in cash,
or gather the cash you already have, and
he will send a secure courier to pick it
up and keep it safe.
Meet Helen. Helen is 76, and she lives
alone. She had about $40,000 in savings,
part in the bank and part in a lockbox
in her bedroom. When the call came, the
man knew her name, her address, and the
last four digits of her Social Security
number. He told her not to tell anyone,
not even her family, because the
criminals might be watching.
Over 2 days, Helen withdrew the rest of
her savings, added it to her lockbox,
and handed $40,000 to a polite young man
in a car at her curb. She never saw it
again. The FBI says that in one recent
year, it received 525 complaints about
these courier schemes for cash and gold,
and the losses came to almost $219
million.
But here is why cash at home makes this
so much worse. When a scammer tries to
wire money out of your bank account, the
bank can stop it. A teller can ask
questions. A fraud team can freeze the
transfer. But cash in your house has no
fraud department. Once you hand it over,
it is gone in seconds, and there is no
way to call it back. Therefore, write
this rule down and put it by your phone.
No real bank, no real government agency,
and no real police department will ever
send a courier to your home to pick up
your cash. The Federal Trade Commission
says it plainly. It will never ask you
to hand cash or gold to anyone. The
moment you hear the word courier, hang
up the phone. But the scammer on the
phone is a stranger.
Number two is someone you already know,
and that makes it much harder to see
coming.
Number two, the people inside your own
home. In 2024, the Financial Crimes
Enforcement Network, the part of the
Treasury Department that tracks
suspicious money, looked at 1 year of
reports from banks about elder financial
exploitation. It found more than 155,000
reports covering about $27 billion
in suspicious activity. And here is the
part that stings. When the government
studied theft from older Americans as
opposed to scams by strangers, the
people most often responsible were
family members and caregivers. The same
people who know where you keep things.
FinCEN also warned that this kind of
theft is often never detected and never
reported. Think about why. If an adult
child or a home helper takes money from
your bank account, there is a statement.
There is a record. Someone can see it.
But if they take a few hundred dollars
from a shoe box on the closet shelf,
there is nothing. No statement, no
record. Just a box that seems a little
lighter than you remember.
Meet Frank. Frank is 81, and he kept
about $12,000 in a shoe box in his
closet, money he had saved up over years
from his Social Security checks. After a
fall, his family hired a helper to come
in 4 days a week. Frank liked her. She
was kind to him. Months later, when his
son helped him count the box, there was
a little over $4,000 left. Nearly $8,000
was missing, and there was no way to
prove who took it or when. And it is not
always a hired helper. Sometimes it is a
struggling grandson or a neighbor who
checks in. And very often, nobody ever
says a word. Therefore, if you keep cash
at home, keep a written count and update
it every time you add or remove money.
Date it, sign it, and never keep it in
the obvious places, like the bedroom
closet, the dresser drawer, or the
freezer. Those are the first three
places anyone looks.
But even if nobody ever touches your
cash, there is a thief that gets into
every single coffee can in America, and
it never has to open the lid. Before I
get to it, let me tell you who I am. I'm
Mark Callaway and on this channel, I dig
through the federal rules that decide
what happens to your money after 65. So,
you hear it from me before you hear it
from a letter in your mailbox. If that
is worth something to you, stick around
because number seven is the one every
senior with cash at home needs to hear.
Number three, the quiet thief called
inflation. Every month, the Bureau of
Labor Statistics measures what everyday
things cost. Since early 2020, prices
are up nearly 30%. In the latest report,
prices were up 3.4% in just the last 12
months.
Here is what that means for cash in a
coffee can. Say you tucked away $10,000
at the start of 2020. It still says
$10,000 when you count it, but measured
by what it actually buys, using the
government's own price index, it only
buys about what $7,700
bought back then. More than $2,000 of
your savings disappeared and nobody ever
touched the can.
Meet Walt. Walt is 73 and he does not
trust banks. He was raised by parents
who lived through the depression and he
keeps about $30,000 in a fireproof box
in his basement. Walt thinks his money
is perfectly safe, but in buying power,
that box has lost thousands of dollars
since 2020 while a basic insured savings
account would have been earning
interest.
And Walt's fear about banks is
understandable, but it is outdated.
Deposits at a federally insured bank are
protected by the FDIC up to $250,000
per depositor per bank for each type of
account ownership. Since the FDIC was
created in 1933, no depositor has lost a
single penny of insured money.
Therefore, ask yourself one question
about every dollar you keep at home. Do
I need this money in my hand in the next
few weeks? If the answer is no, it is
losing value every single day it sits
there. But, inflation only shrinks your
cash slowly. Number four can wipe out a
whole month of income at once, and it
catches people who have no idea it even
applies to them. Number four,
Supplemental Security Income counts
every dollar under your mattress.
Millions of older Americans with low
income and few assets receive
Supplemental Security Income, which most
people call SSI. It is run by the Social
Security Administration. In 2026, the
federal SSI payment for one person is
$994 a month. But, SSI has a strict
limit on what you can own. For one
person, your countable resources cannot
be more than $2,000. For a married
couple, the limit is $3,000. And those
limits have not gone up since 1989, not
once in more than 35 years. Your home
does not count. One car does not count.
Your furniture and household goods do
not count. But, cash counts, every
dollar of it. It does not matter whether
it sits in a bank, in a jar, or in a
shoebox. Under federal rules, cash is a
countable resource.
And here is the detail that trips people
up. Social Security looks at what you
have at the very first moment of each
month. If your countable resources are
over the limit on the first of the
month, you are not eligible for SSI for
that month.
Meet Margaret. Margaret is 78, and she
gets SSI. She is careful with money, and
she has been tucking away a little cash
each month in an envelope in her kitchen
drawer for emergencies. Together with a
few hundred dollars in her checking
account, her total crept up to about
She thought she was being responsible,
but in the eyes of the SSI program, she
was $600 over the limit. Now, if Social
Security discovers that, it can decide
she was not eligible for those months.
And when that happens, it can ask her to
pay back the SSI she received. That is
called an overpayment, and for some
people, it adds up to thousands of
dollars.
But, here is the part most people never
hear. Many people believe that cash at
home is invisible, and that if it is not
in a bank, nobody will ever know. That
is a dangerous mistake. When you apply
for SSI, and when Social Security
reviews your case, you are asked about
your cash, and you are required to
report it honestly. Hiding it is not a
loophole. It can turn a simple
overpayment into a fraud problem.
Therefore, if you receive SSI, or
someone in your family does, count your
cash at home, and add it to your bank
balances before the 1st of every month.
If you are getting close to the limit,
talk to Social Security or a local legal
aid office about the allowed ways to
spend down, like prepaying for a
funeral, or buying things you actually
need. But, SSI is not the only program
that counts the cash in your house.
Number five is the one that matters if
you or your spouse ever needs a nursing
home.
Number five, Medicaid will count it,
too, if you ever need long-term care.
For most families, the way they pay for
a nursing home after the savings run out
is Medicaid. And Medicaid for long-term
care has an asset test, just like SSI.
In most states, a single person can have
only about $2,000 in countable assets
and still qualify. The rules vary by
state, but the idea is the same
everywhere. And just like SSI, cash at
home is a countable asset. When you
apply, the application asks for your
bank accounts, your investments, and
your cash on hand. You sign it under
penalty of law. Now, here is where
people get into real trouble. Some
families panic when a parent needs care,
and they start moving cash around. They
hand it to the kids. They hide it with a
relative. They tell themselves that cash
leaves no trail.
But, Medicaid has a look-back period.
When you apply for nursing home
coverage, it can look at any gifts or
transfers you made in the past 5 years,
which is 60 months. If you gave away
money for less than it was worth,
Medicaid can make you wait before it
starts paying. And for many families,
that waiting period means paying the
nursing home out of pocket. Meet Ruth.
Ruth is 84. When her doctor said she
would likely need a nursing home, her
son took the $15,000 in cash she kept in
her cedar chest and put it in his own
safe, thinking it would protect her
savings. It did the opposite. That
transfer was exactly the kind of thing
the look-back is designed to find. And
if the family had simply left it off the
application, they would have been
signing a form that was not true.
Therefore, if anyone in your family
might need long-term care in the next 5
years, do not move cash around on your
own. Talk to an elder law attorney
first, because there are legal ways to
plan for this, and the illegal ways can
cost you far more than they save. Before
I get to number six, a quick note. If
this video is helping you, I put every
bill seniors are legally allowed to stop
paying after 65 into one guide called
the Senior Exempt Playbook. Scan the
code on your screen now or tap the link
in the description. But numbers four and
five are about cash sitting still.
Number six is about what happens the
moment you try to move it, and it is
where the government can take it from
you directly. Number six, putting it
back in the bank the wrong way.
Here is a rule most people have heard
about, but almost nobody understands.
When you deposit or withdraw more than
$10,000 in cash in one day, your bank
files a report with the Treasury
Department called a currency transaction
report. That report is routine. Banks
file millions of them every year. It
does not mean you did anything wrong,
and you do not have to fill out anything
yourself. If you walk into your bank
with $15,000 in cash from a coffee can,
the bank files a form, and you go on
with your day. But a lot of seniors are
afraid of that form, so they try to be
clever. Instead of depositing $15,000 at
once, they deposit $9,000 one week and
$6,000 the next, or they spread it
across a few different branches, so the
bank never has to file the report.
And that is the trap. Breaking up cash
deposits to avoid that report has a
name. It is called structuring, and
under federal law, structuring is a
crime by itself, even if every single
dollar of the money is honest and legal.
The penalty can be up to 5 years in
federal prison. Meet Bill. Bill is 70, a
retired contractor, and over the years
he saved about $27,000 in cash from side
jobs he had already reported on his
taxes. When he decided to put it in the
bank, his brother-in-law told him the
government flags anything over $10,000.
So, Bill deposited $9,000 3 weeks in a
row. Clean money, taxes paid, but the
pattern itself is exactly what bank
compliance teams are trained to spot.
For years, this was how the IRS took
money from honest people. Agents could
seize an entire bank account just
because the deposits were all a little
under $10,000, even with no other sign
of any crime. After a wave of cases
involving small business owners and
families, the IRS changed its policy in
2014, and in 2019, Congress passed the
Taxpayer First Act, which now requires
the IRS to show probable cause that the
money came from an illegal source or was
connected to some other crime before it
can seize money for structuring. It also
gives you the right to a hearing within
30 days. That protection matters. But,
structuring itself is still a federal
crime.
And it is not just the bank. Remember
the airport seizures from the very
beginning of this video. If you travel
with a large amount of cash, it can be
questioned and even seized on suspicion
alone, and the burden falls on you to
fight to get it back. And if you carry
more than $10,000 into or out of the
United States, federal law requires you
to report it to customs on a form called
FinCEN Form 105. Fail to report it and
the government can take the money.
Therefore, if you ever move cash from
your home into the bank, do it the
honest way. Deposit it all at once, let
the bank file its routine form, and keep
a simple note of where the money came
from. The report is not the danger.
Trying to avoid the report is the
danger. But everything so far has been
about people and rules. Number seven is
about the one thing no lock, no hiding
place, and no rule can stop. And it is
where I keep my promise from the
beginning of this video.
Number seven, a fire, a flood, or a
break-in, and the number hidden inside
your insurance policy. Most homeowners
believe that if their house burns down,
insurance will cover what was inside.
Your furniture, your clothes, your
television. And for most of that, they
are right. But almost every standard
homeowner's policy in America has a
short list called special limits. These
are categories of property where the
insurance company will only pay a small
fixed amount, no matter how much you
actually lost. And at the very top of
that list is money, cash, banknotes,
coins. Here is the number I promised
you. On the standard homeowner's policy
form used across the country, the
special limit for money is $200. $200.
That is the total for the entire loss,
not $200 per envelope, not $200 per
room. If you keep $2,000 in your
bedroom, or $20,000 in your basement,
and it burns, or floods, or a burglar
walks out the door with it, the most the
standard policy pays for that cash is
$200. Meet George. George is 79. He kept
about $15,000 in cash in a metal box in
his bedroom closet because he remembered
when banks failed during his parents'
lifetime. Last winter, a space heater
started a fire while he was at his
daughter's house for dinner. The
firefighters saved most of the house.
His insurance rebuilt the bedroom and
replaced his furniture. And when the
adjuster got to the line for the $15,000
in cash, the answer was $200. That was
all his policy would pay.
George lost $14,800
in one evening, and there was nobody to
blame and nothing to appeal. That is why
the answer to the question in the title
of this video is not a feeling, and it
is not a guess. It is in writing in your
own policy. Any cash you keep at home
above that special limit is cash you are
insuring yourself. If it is lost, it is
simply gone. Now, let me give you two
things that can help. First, some
insurance companies will let you raise
that limit with an add-on to your
policy, often up to around $1,000. It
usually costs very little. Call your
agent and ask about the special limit
for money on your policy. And while you
are there, pull out the declarations
page, because some policies are
different, and you deserve to know your
exact number.
Second, there is one free rescue that
almost nobody knows about. If your cash
is damaged, but not completely
destroyed, burned, soaked, or chewed by
mice, the Bureau of Engraving and
Printing, part of the United States
Treasury, will examine it and redeem it
for free. As long as more than half of
each bill can be identified as real
United States currency, they can send
you a Treasury check for it. It can take
anywhere from 6 months to 3 years, and
you have to pack the remains very
carefully. Do not throw away burned
money. Do not try to separate it. Box it
up exactly as it is and contact the
Treasury. So, how much cash should you
actually keep at home? The federal
government's own emergency planning
advice says to keep some cash on hand
because during a storm or a power
outage, ATMs and card readers may not
work. Enough for a few days of
essentials makes sense. Food, gas,
medicine.
But beyond that small emergency amount,
every extra dollar at home is exposed to
every single thing on this list. The
scammer on the phone, the person with a
key, inflation, the SSI and Medicaid
rules, the trouble of putting it back in
the bank, and the $200 limit in your
insurance policy. So, here are your
seven steps to protect your cash. One,
never hand cash to a courier, ever. No
real bank or government agency will ask
you to. Two, keep a written dated count
of any cash at home, and never store it
in the closet, the dresser, or the
freezer. Three, move any money you will
not need in the next few weeks into a
federally insured account, protected up
Four, if you get SSI, count your cash at
home before the first of every month.
The limit is $2,000 for one person.
Five, if long-term care might be coming,
do not move cash around. Talk to an
elder law attorney first. Six, when you
bring cash back to the bank, deposit it
all at once. Never break it up to avoid
the report. Seven, call your insurance
agent this week. Ask for the special
limit for money on your policy, and ask
what it costs to raise it. If someone
has already called you asking for cash,
or you think a scammer has targeted
someone you love, call the National
Elder Fraud Hotline from the Justice
Department at 1-833-372-8311.

title: The IRS Will Give You These 9 Things After 65 (But Only If You Ask)

segments.text: This spring, about $1.2 billion in tax
refunds became the permanent property of
the United States Treasury. Not because
anyone cheated, not because anyone broke
a rule. It belonged to more than a
million ordinary Americans and it
disappeared for one reason only. Nobody
asked for it. That is how the IRS works.
When you owe the IRS money, it finds
you. It sends letters, it adds
penalties, and it will chase you for
years. But when the IRS owes you
something, a refund, a credit, a waiver,
it usually just waits. If you never ask,
you never get it. So today, I am going
to walk you through nine things the IRS
will give you after 65, but only if you
ask. Some of them put cash back in your
pocket. Some of them erase penalties you
thought you were stuck with, and a
couple of them protect money you already
have from being taken.
Stay with me all the way to number nine,
because number nine is the big one. The
IRS has a program that can automatically
take up to 15% of your social security
check every single month without a judge
and without a court date. A federal law
says the IRS must stop in certain
situations, but it will not stop on its
own. You have to ask with the right
words, and I will give them to you at
the end. Every rule in this video comes
straight from federal law and from the
IRS itself. The names are examples, but
the rules and the dollar limits are
real. Number one, the IRS will give you
back the refund you never claimed, but
only for 3 years. Under federal law, you
generally have three years to claim a
tax refund. If you never filed a return
at all, the clock usually runs 3 years
from the original due date. After that,
the money goes to the Treasury and it
stays there forever.
That is exactly what happened this
spring. The IRS announced that about
$1.2 billion in refunds from the 2022
tax year was still sitting there
unclaimed. The typical refund was $686.
The deadline was April 15th, and once it
passed, every dollar became property of
the government. A lot of retirees fall
into this trap without knowing it. They
stop filing because their income
dropped, and they assume they do not
have to. Meet Walt. Walt is 68. He gets
a small pension and the pension company
has been withholding federal tax from
every check. In 2023, his income was low
enough that he did not think he needed
to file, so he did not. What Walt never
realized is that he had about $1,400
of tax withheld that he never owed. That
money is his, but the only way to get it
back is to file the return.
And here is the clock. For the 2023 tax
year, Walt has until April 15th, 2027.
After that, his $1,400
belongs to the Treasury. The same window
works for mistakes on returns you did
file. You can file an amended return on
form 1040X and ask for the difference
back. But if you owe the IRS, your
state, or certain other federal debts,
the government can apply your refund to
that debt first. Therefore, pull out
your last 3 years of tax paperwork. If
you skipped a year or you think
something was missed, file now. The IRS
will not send you a reminder. It will
just keep the money. But the second
thing on this list might be even bigger
and it is hiding inside a bill you
already pay every single month. Number
two, the IRS will let you deduct your
Medicare premiums and much more, but
only if you ask for it.
Most retirees pay Medicare Part B
straight out of their Social Security
check. In 2026, the standard part B
premium is $22.90
a month. That is $2,434.80
a year for one person and almost $4,870
for a married couple. Here is what most
people do not know. Under the tax code,
those premiums count as medical
expenses. So, do your Part D drug plan
premiums and your Medicare supplement
premiums. If you itemize your
deductions, you can deduct the medical
expenses that go over 7 and 12% of your
adjusted gross income. Now, I want to be
honest with you, this only helps if you
itemize. And for many retirees, the
standard deduction is bigger. So, for a
healthy couple with modest medical
bills, this one may not change a thing,
but it changes everything in one
situation, and that is long-term care.
According to IRS publication 502, if a
principal reason someone is living in a
nursing home is to get medical care, the
entire cost counts as a medical expense.
That includes the meals and the room.
Meet Ruth. Ruth is 84 and she has moved
into a memory care unit because of her
dementia. It costs about $8,000 a month.
That is $96,000 a year. Ruth still has
income from her pension and her IRA
withdrawals. And she is paying tax on
every dollar of it because nobody told
her family that most of those memory
care bills could be deducted. And if
Ruth has long-term care insurance, part
of her premiums can count, too. In 2026,
the IRS allows up to $6,200
of premiums for anyone 71 or older and
for anyone 61 to 70. Therefore, if you
or your spouse has heavy medical bills
this year, and especially if anyone in
your family is in assisted living or a
nursing home, keep every receipt and ask
your tax preparer to run the numbers
both ways. The IRS will not do that math
for you. But number three is a tax
credit that almost nobody has ever heard
of, and it was written specifically for
people over 65. Before I get to it, let
me tell you who I am. I'm Mark Callaway
and on this channel I dig through the
federal rules that decide what happens
to your money after 65. So you hear it
from me before you hear it from a letter
in your mailbox. If that is worth
something to you, stick around because
number nine is the one that protects
your social security check. Number
three, the IRS will give you a credit
just for being 65, but only if you file
one extra page. It is called the credit
for the elderly or the disabled and you
claim it on a form called schedule R.
Most people go their whole retirement
without ever seeing it. Here's how it
works. If you are single and 65 or
older, the IRS starts you with a base
amount of $5,000. If you are married and
you are both 65 or older, the base
amount is $7,500.
That base is reduced by untaxed social
security or pension money and by part of
your income. The IRS gives you 15% of
what is left as a credit. At the very
top, that is a credit of $750 for a
single person and $1,125
for a married couple. And remember, a
credit is not a deduction. A credit
comes straight off the tax you owe
dollar for dollar. But this credit has
tight limits. If you are single, your
adjusted gross income has to be under
and your untaxed social security and
pensions have to be under $5,000. If you
are married and you both qualify, the
limits are $25,000 of income and $7,500
of untaxed benefits. So, who actually
gets this? Usually, a retiree with
little or no social security who lives
mostly on a taxable pension or IRA
withdrawals. Many former teachers and
government workers fit that picture.
Meet Dorothy. Dorothy is 71, a retired
school secretary. She never paid into
Social Security, so she gets no social
security check. She lives on a modest
taxable pension, and every year she pays
a little federal tax on it. Dorothy
qualifies for this credit, and nobody
has ever told her it exists. Every year
she does not file schedule R is money
she simply hands back.
Therefore, if your income is on the
lower side and most of it is taxable,
ask whoever does your taxes one direct
question. Do I qualify for schedule R?
It takes one extra page and the IRS will
never fill it out for you. But what if
you cannot afford someone to do your
taxes at all? That is number four. And
most retirees have no idea the IRS will
actually help you for free. Number four,
the IRS will do your taxes for free, but
only if you go and ask. There is a
federal program called tax counseling
for the elderly. It was created by
Congress in 1978. It is funded through
the IRS and it exists for one purpose to
give free tax help to people 60 and
older. The volunteers are certified by
the IRS and they specialize in pensions,
IRA withdrawals and how social security
gets taxed. Next to it is a sister
program called VA for people with low to
moderate incomes. Between the two, there
are free sites in libraries, senior
centers, and churches all over the
country. Plenty of retirees pay a
preparer $300 or more every spring for a
simple return. Over 10 years, that is
$3,000 for something a volunteer would
have done for nothing. And a good
volunteer will ask about your medical
expenses, ask about schedule R, and help
you file a return you skipped. But these
sites are mostly open from late January
through the middle of April. And the
good ones fill up early. Therefore,
write this number down. To find a free
tax site near you, call 1 8009069887.
Ask for a tax counseling for the elderly
site and book your appointment the
moment they open in January. But now we
get to the part of this list where the
money gets serious because the next
three things are not about getting a
refund. They are about making a penalty
disappear. Number five, the IRS will
cancel the penalty for a missed required
withdrawal, but only if you write them a
letter.
If you have a traditional IRA or an old
workplace plan, the law forces you to
take money out each year, starting at
age 73 for most people today. These are
called required minimum distributions.
Miss one, and the penalty is brutal. The
IRS can charge an excise tax of 25% of
the amount you were supposed to take out
and did not. Meet Linda. Linda is 74.
Her husband always handled the
retirement accounts, and when he passed
away, nobody told her she had to take a
withdrawal from her own IRA that year.
Her required amount was $12,000. She did
not take it. The penalty on that is
$3,000. But here is what most people
never find out. The law has two escape
hatches.
The first one is automatic once you act.
If you take the missed withdrawal and
fix it within the correction window,
generally about 2 years, the penalty
drops from 25% to 10%. For Linda, that
cuts it from $3,000 to $1,200.
The second escape hatch is the one the
IRS will not mention. If the mistake was
due to a reasonable error and you are
taking reasonable steps to fix it, the
IRS can wave the penalty completely.
Zero for Linda, a grieving widow who did
not know the rule. That is exactly the
kind of situation the waiver was written
for. To ask for it, you take the missed
withdrawal as soon as you discover the
mistake. Then you file form 5329 and you
attach a short letter explaining what
happened and what you did to fix it. The
IRS is not hiding this. It is on its own
website, but it is not going to call
Linda and offer it. If she pays without
asking, the $3,000 is gone.
Therefore, if you ever miss a required
withdrawal, do not panic and do not just
pay. Take the money out right away. File
Form 5329 and write the letter. And if
you have just lost a spouse, check every
retirement account in both names this
year. But number six is a penalty almost
every new retiree walks right into,
usually in the very first year they stop
working. Before I get to it, a quick
note. If this video is helping you, I
put every bill seniors are legally
allowed to stop paying after 65 into one
guide called the senior exempt playbook.
Scan the code on your screen now or tap
the link in the description. Number six,
the IRS will wave your underpayment
penalty because you retired, but only if
you check the box and ask.
When you are working, your employer
withheld tax from every paycheck. The
moment you retire, that safety net
disappears. Unless you set up
withholding on your pension and IRA
withdrawals or send the IRS estimated
payments every quarter, you can end up
owing a big bill in April. If you owe
$1,000 or more when you file, the IRS
can add a penalty for underpaying during
the year. It works like interest and it
is charged on every quarter you came up
short. Meet Bob. Bob retired last year
at 64. He started taking money out of
his IRA to cover the bills until his
social security began and nobody told
him those withdrawals had no tax taken
out. When he filed in April, he owed the
IRS a little over $9,000 and the
software tacked an underpayment penalty
right on top. But here is the rule
buried in the tax code. Federal law says
there is no underpayment penalty if you
retired after reaching age 62 in the
year the payments were due or the year
before and the shortfall was due to
reasonable cause and not willful
neglect. That describes Bob almost
perfectly. He did not ignore anything.
He simply did not know that retirement
changed how his taxes worked. To ask for
it, you use form 2210. There is a
section where you request a waiver and
you attach a short explanation of when
you retired. Your tax software will
usually charge the penalty automatically
unless you tell it you are requesting
the waiver. Therefore, if you retired in
the last year or two and got hit with an
underpayment penalty, go back and look
at form 2210. And going forward, ask
your IRA provider and your pension to
withhold federal tax so you never face
this again.
But number seven is the penalty
forgiveness that works almost like a
free pass and the IRS hands it out every
day to people who simply know to ask.
Number seven, the IRS will forgive a
firsttime penalty, but only if you call
and use two words. Life happens. A
spouse gets sick, paperwork gets lost,
and suddenly you file late and the IRS
letter shows up with penalties attached.
Those penalties add up fast. The penalty
for filing late is 5% of the unpaid tax
for every month the return is late, up
to 25%. The penalty for paying late is
another half a% a month. If you owed
$8,000 and your return was 5 months
late, the penalties alone could be about
But the IRS has an administrative policy
called firsttime abate. The two words to
say on the phone are first time abate.
If you qualify, the IRS removes the
penalty, no long story required, no
proof of a hardship.
Here is how you qualify. You did not
have any penalties in the three tax
years before. You have filed all the
returns you are currently required to
file, or you have an extension, and you
have paid the tax, or you have set up a
plan to pay it. Meet Carol. Carol is 69.
The year her husband went into the
hospital, she filed late for the first
time in her life, and she got a notice
with $1,600
in penalties. She was about to write the
check. Instead, a friend told her to
call the number on the notice and ask
for firsttime abate. The agent checked
her record, saw a clean history, and
removed the penalty on the phone. Now,
this only works for one tax period, and
it does not cover every type of penalty.
If you have a real reason for being
late, like a serious illness, you can
ask for reasonable cause relief instead
and save firsttime abate for later.
Therefore, before you pay any IRS
penalty, call the number on the notice
and ask one question. Do I qualify for
firsttime abate? It costs you a phone
call. Not asking can cost you thousands.
But the next thing on this list is about
protection because the fastest way to
lose a refund today is to have somebody
else claim it before you do. Number
eight, the IRS will give you a secret
number that locks your tax return, but
only if you request it. Identity thieves
love retirees. If a thief gets your
social security number, they can file a
fake return in your name before you file
yours and collect your refund. Meet
Harold. Harold is 76. He went to file
his return in March, expecting a refund
and it was rejected. Someone had already
filed a return using his social security
number in February. Harold got his money
eventually, but it took months to prove
he was really himself.
Here is what the IRS offers, and almost
nobody uses it. It is called an identity
protection pin. It is a six-digit number
known only to you and the IRS, and you
get a new one every year. Once you have
it, any return filed with your social
security number without that PIN gets
rejected. Anyone with a social security
number who can verify their identity can
get one. It is completely free. You can
sign up through the IRS website, but be
very careful about one thing. The IRS
will never call, text, or email you
asking for your PIN. Only scammers do
that. You give it only to your tax
preparer or you type it into your tax
software yourself. Therefore, request
your identity protection PIN from the
IRS website before tax season starts. It
takes a few minutes and it closes the
door before the thief ever finds it. But
now, I owe you the big one, the one I
promised you at the very beginning.
Number nine, the IRS will stop taking
your social security check, but only if
you ask and only if you know the words.
Most people believe social security is
untouchable. For a credit card company,
that is mostly true, but the IRS is not
a credit card company. Through something
called the federal payment levy program,
the IRS can automatically take up to 15%
of your Social Security benefit every
single month for an unpaid tax debt. No
lawsuit, no judge, no court date. The
money is simply taken out before your
deposit ever reaches your bank.
Meet Eleanor. Eleanor is 73. A few years
ago, she cashed out part of an old
retirement account to fix her roof, and
nobody withheld enough tax. She owed the
IRS money she could not pay. She got
letters she did not fully understand and
she put them in a drawer. Then one
month, her $2,000 social security
deposit came in short. The IRS was
taking $300 a month. That is $3,600
a year, but there is a federal law
written for exactly her situation. It
says the IRS shall release a levy if the
levy is creating an economic hardship,
not may shall. And under the
regulations, economic hardship means the
levy leaves you unable to pay your
reasonable basic living expenses, your
rent, your food, your utilities, your
medicine. But the IRS does not check on
its own whether you can still afford
groceries. You have to tell them.
Here are the words. When you call, say,
"This levy is causing me an economic
hardship and I am requesting a levy
release and currently not collectible
status." Currently not collectible means
the IRS agrees you cannot pay right now
and it stops collecting. Be ready to
share your monthly income and your basic
expenses because the IRS will ask for
them. And this is not a theory. The
National Taxpayer Advocate has reported
cases exactly like this where the IRS
agreed to release a social security levy
for hardship, marked the account
currently not collectible, and even
returned levy payments it had already
taken. To be straight with you,
currently not collectible does not erase
the debt. interest can keep adding up
and the IRS can review your situation
later, but it stops the money leaving
your check while you cannot afford it.
And there is a warning sign you should
never ignore. Before the IRS starts
taking social security, it is supposed
to send a notice called a CP91, a final
notice before it levies your benefits.
If you ever see that letter, do not put
it in a drawer. That is the moment to
call. Therefore, if the IRS is already
taking part of your check or you have
received that notice, call the number on
the letter and ask for a hardship levy
release. If you cannot get anywhere,
call the Taxpayer Advocate Service, an
independent office inside the IRS whose
job is to help people facing exactly
this kind of hardship. So, here are your
nine things the IRS will give you, but
only if you ask. One, file any return
you skipped in the last 3 years or amend
one with a mistake. The 2023 window
closes April 15th, 2027. Two, if you
have big medical or nursing home bills,
keep every receipt and have your taxes
figured both ways.
Three, if your income is low and mostly
taxable, ask about schedule R. Four,
book a free tax counseling for the
elderly appointment the moment the sites
open. Five, if you missed a required
withdrawal, take it now. File form 5329
and write the letter. Six, if you
retired at 62 or later and got an
underpayment penalty, request the waiver
on form 2210. Seven, before you pay any
penalty, call and ask for firsttime
abate. Eight, request your free identity
protection pin before tax season. Nine,
if the IRS is taking your social
security, call and ask for a hardship
levy release. For the IRS, call
For free tax help, call 1-800906-9887.
And for the taxpayer advocate service,

title: If You're Over 65, STOP Doing These 7 Things With Your Money

segments.text: If you sign your house over to your
children while you are still alive, they
could owe the IRS more than $50,000
the day they sell it. If you leave them
the exact same house in your will
instead, they could owe almost nothing.
Same house, same kids, same sale price.
The only difference is one signature,
and millions of families get it
backwards because it feels like the
responsible thing to do. That is one of
seven things seniors do with their money
every single day out of habit, out of
love, or because somebody told them it
was smart. And every one of them quietly
hands money to someone else, the IRS, a
scammer, a lender, a nursing home. So
today, I am going to walk you through
seven things you need to stop doing with
your money if you are 65, 70, or 80. I
have split them by age because the
mistakes change as you get older. The
first two hit hardest around 65. The
next three hit around 70. And the last
two are the ones that hit people in
their 80s when there is the least time
left to fix anything. Number four is the
house, the one I just told you about,
and it costs families more than anything
else on this list. But stay with me all
the way to number seven because number
seven is something almost every
grandparent in America does out of pure
love. It is completely legal. The IRS
even gives you a dollar limit for it,
and it can still leave you with no way
to pay for a nursing home at the exact
moment you need one. I would stop that
one first. Every number in this video
comes straight from a federal source,
the IRS, Social Security, the Treasury,
or federal law. The names are examples,
but the rules are real. Let's start with
65. Number one, stop collecting Social
Security early while you are still
working. A lot of people turn 62 or 65,
sign up for Social Security, and keep
working at least part-time. But, if you
have not reached your full retirement
age yet, Social Security runs something
called the earnings test, and almost
nobody explains it until the money
stops. Here is how it works in 2026. If
you are under full retirement age for
the whole year, you can earn up to
from work. For every $2 you earn over
that line, Social Security holds back $1
of your benefits. For anyone born in
1960 or later, full retirement age is
67. So, if you were born in 1961, you
turn 65 this year, and you are still two
full years away from the finish line.
Meet Linda. She is 65. She started her
Social Security early, and her check is
$2,000 a month. She still works at a
dental office, and she earns $54,480
a year. That puts her $30,000 over the
line. Half of that, $15,000,
gets held back. Social Security does not
take a little out of every check. It
holds back whole checks, usually
starting at the beginning of the year,
until the amount is covered. For Linda,
that is about 7 and 1/2 months with no
Social Security deposit at all.
But, here's what makes it worse. Most
people never see it coming because they
never told Social Security what they
expected to earn. They find out when the
deposit does not show up, or when a
letter arrives saying they were overpaid
and now owe money back. Now, to be fair,
that money is not lost forever. When
Linda reaches full retirement age,
Social Security recalculates her benefit
and gives her credit for the months it
held back. So, her check goes up a
little from then on, but it comes back
slowly, a few dollars a month over many
years, and only if she lives long enough
to collect it. The rule loosens in the
year you actually reach full retirement
age. That year, the limit jumps to
Social Security only holds back $1 for
every $3 over, and it only counts what
you earned before the month of your
birthday. Once you reach full retirement
age, there is no limit at all.
Therefore, if you are still working and
you are under full retirement age, do
the math before you file. If your
paycheck is well above $24,480,
waiting may put far more money in your
pocket. And if you already filed, call
Social Security and give them an honest
estimate of this year's earnings, so you
get a smaller adjustment now instead of
a surprise bill later.
But the second thing on this list has
nothing to do with your paycheck. It is
a piece of paper most people filled out
once 20 or 30 years ago and never looked
at again.
Number two, stop trusting your will to
fix your beneficiary forms.
Here is something that shocks people.
For your IRA, your old workplace
retirement plan, your life insurance,
and many bank accounts with a payable on
death designation, your will does not
decide who gets the money. The
beneficiary form does. The company pays
whoever is named on that form, period,
and the will is never even opened.
The Supreme Court of the United States
settled this in a case called Kennedy
versus the plan administrator for
DuPont, decided in 2009. A man named
William Kennedy had named his wife as
the beneficiary of his retirement plan
at work. They divorced. The divorce
papers even said she gave up any claim
to his retirement plans, but he never
changed the beneficiary form. When he
died, the plan paid his ex-wife, not his
daughter. The case went all the way to
the Supreme Court, and the court ruled
unanimously that the plan did the right
thing by following the form.
Meet Frank. Frank is 66. He rolled his
old work plan into an IRA years ago, and
the account is worth $310,000
today. When he opened it, he named his
wife first and his two sons second. His
wife passed away 4 years ago. One of his
sons passed away last year and left
behind two young children.
Frank's will says everything goes
equally to his son and to his late son's
kids, but his IRA form still says his
two sons. And depending on the wording,
the share meant for his late son can go
entirely to the son who is still living.
Those grandchildren could get nothing
account and Frank would have no idea
because his will says exactly what he
wants. It gets worse if every name on
the form has died. Then the account
usually goes to your estate. That can
drag it into probate court. It can delay
your family for months and it can force
the money out of the tax-sheltered
account much faster than if a living
person had been named.
Therefore, this week call every company
that holds your retirement accounts,
your life insurance, and your bank
accounts and ask one simple question.
Who is listed as my beneficiary first
and second? If anyone on that list has
died, divorced you, or fallen out of
your life, change it. If you want a
share to pass down to grandchildren when
one of your children dies, ask the
company how their form handles that
because the wording matters. But now we
move up to 70 and this is where the
mistakes start getting bigger. Before I
get to number three, let me tell you who
I am. I'm Mark Callaway and on this
channel I dig through the federal rules
that decide what happens to your money
after 65. So you hear it from me before
you hear it from a letter in the
mailbox. If that is worth something to
you, stick around because number four is
coming and it is the one that costs your
kids the most. Number three, stop
mailing checks from the mailbox in front
of your house.
This one sounds small. It is not. Your
paper checks have become one of the
favorite targets of criminal rings in
this country and the federal government
has said so in writing. In February of
2023, the Financial Crimes Enforcement
Network, which is part of the United
States Treasury, put out a nationwide
alert about a surge in check fraud tied
to mail theft. Banks had filed about
350,000 reports of suspected check fraud
in 2021. In 2022, that number nearly
doubled to about 680,000.
Here is how it works. A thief takes
envelopes out of a home mailbox with the
little red flag up or out of a
collection box. They open the envelope
and pull out your check. Then they use
ordinary chemicals to wash the ink off
the payee line and the amount and they
write in a new name and a new number.
Meet Dorothy. She is 74 and she has paid
her water bill the same way for 40
years. She writes a check for $85, puts
it in the mailbox, and raises the flag.
Three days later, that same check clears
her account for $8,500
made out to a name she has never heard
of. And it does not stop with one check.
Treasury warned that once criminals have
your stolen mail, they can use the
personal information inside it for more
fraud down the road like opening credit
cards in your name. Whether Dorothy gets
her money back depends on how fast she
notices and reports it. Banks generally
expect you to review your statements and
report an altered check quickly.
Therefore, stop leaving outgoing checks
in your home mailbox. Hand them to your
mail carrier or drop them inside the
post office itself. Better yet, pay your
regular bills through your bank's bill
pay where the bank sends the payment and
no paper check ever sits in a box
overnight. And look at your bank account
online or on the phone at least once a
week so you catch anything strange in
days instead of months. But the next one
is the big one. It is the house. If this
video is helping you, here's a quick
note before number four. I put every
bill seniors are legally allowed to stop
paying after 65 into one guide called
the Senior Exempt Playbook. Scan the
code on your screen now or tap the link
in the description. Number four, stop
signing your house over to your kids.
I understand why people do it. You want
to make sure the house goes to your
children. You have heard that probate is
slow and expensive. So, you go down to
the county office, you sign a new deed,
and the house goes into your son's or
your daughter's name while you keep
living in it. But, the IRS treats that
as a gift. And when you give someone
property while you are alive, the IRS
rule is that they also take over your
original cost in it. The tax world calls
that your basis. If you bought the house
for $80,000 back in 1984, your
children's basis is now $80,000, too, no
matter what the house is worth today.
Now, compare that to what happens if
your children inherit the same house
when you pass away. Under federal tax
law, inherited property gets what is
called a stepped-up basis. The cost
resets to what the house is worth on the
day you die.
Meet Walt and June. They bought their
home for $80,000 in 1984. Today, it is
They are 72 and 70, and they signed the
deed over to their son, Mike. A few
years later, after they are gone, Mike
sells the house for $420,000.
Because the house came to him as a gift,
his cost is still Walt and June's
$80,000. That means a taxable gain of
Mike does not live in the house, so he
cannot use the home sale exclusion that
homeowners get. At the 15% capital gains
rate most families pay, that is a
federal tax bill of about $51,000
before any state tax.
Now, rewind. Suppose Walt and June had
kept the house in their own names and
left it to Mike in their will or through
a trust or a transfer on death deed
where their state allows one. When they
pass, Mike's cost resets to $420,000.
He sells for 420,000.
His taxable gain is about zero. His tax
is about zero. One signature, roughly
But the tax is only part of it. Once the
house is in Mike's name, it is Mike's
house. If Mike gets sued, goes through a
divorce, or runs into debt, that house
can be pulled into his problems. And as
you will see in number seven, giving
away your biggest asset can create a
completely different problem if you ever
need long-term care.
There is also paperwork. A house is
almost always worth more than the yearly
gift limit, which is $19,000 per person
in 2026. So, a gift like this usually
means filing a federal gift tax return.
Most families will not actually owe gift
tax because the lifetime limit is very
high, but the return still has to be
filed, and many people who sign over a
house never do. Therefore, if you are
thinking about putting the house in your
children's names, stop and talk to an
estate attorney first and ask one
question. Should this house pass to my
kids at my death so they get the
stepped-up basis? Many states now allow
a transfer on death deed, which can keep
the house out of probate and still pass
it at death. And if you already signed
the house over, get advice now because
there may still be ways to reduce the
damage. But the next thing on this list
is a favor. It is the kind of favor
grandparents do every single day. Number
five, stop co-signing loans for your
kids and grandkids. Your grandson needs
a car to get to work. Your granddaughter
needs a private loan to finish school.
The lender says they need a co-signer
with good credit. And who has better
credit than a grandparent who has paid
every bill on time for 50 years? So, you
sign. Here is what you actually signed.
The Federal Trade Commission requires
lenders covered by its rule to hand
co-signers a written notice. And the
wording is blunt. You are being asked to
guarantee this debt. If the borrower
does not pay the debt, you will have to.
You may have to pay up to the full
amount of the debt if the borrower does
not pay. You may also have to pay late
fees or collection costs. And the notice
says the creditor can collect this debt
from you without first trying to collect
from the borrower. Read that last line
again. They do not have to chase your
grandson first. They can come straight
to you.
Meet Harold. He is 71 and he co-signed a
$32,000 car loan for his grandson. 18
months later, his grandson loses his job
and stops paying. The lender calls
Harold. Harold is now responsible for
the remaining balance plus late fees
plus collection costs. And the missed
payments show up on Harold's credit
report, too. So, the score he spent 50
years building drops right when he might
need it to refinance or to rent an
apartment in a retirement community.
Now, here is one piece of good news
because I want you to know your rights.
Under federal law, a private lender
generally cannot garnish your Social
Security benefits to collect a debt like
this. And when Social Security is
directly deposited into your bank
account, federal rules protect up to two
months of those benefits from being
frozen by a private creditor's
garnishment order.
But that protection has limits. Money
you have saved from other places, like
your pension, your savings, or your
house, can still be at risk if the
lender sues and wins. Therefore, before
you co-sign anything, ask yourself one
question. Could I pay this entire loan
myself starting tomorrow without hurting
my retirement? If the answer is no, do
not sign. If you want to help, give a
smaller gift you can actually afford or
help them find a car or a school that
fits their own budget. And if you have
already co-signed, ask the lender for
online access so you can see every
payment and you will know the moment one
is missed. But now we get to 80. And the
first thing on the 80 list might
literally be sitting in a drawer in your
house right now. Number six, stop
holding savings bonds that stopped
paying you years ago. Millions of
Americans bought paper savings bonds
over the decades for themselves, for
their kids, or as gifts for
grandchildren.
Series EE bonds and Series I bonds stop
earning interest 30 years after the
issue date printed on the front. After
that, the bond is just a piece of paper
sitting in a drawer, losing value to
inflation every year. And here is a date
that matters right now. A bond issued in
1996 reaches 30 years in 2026. If you
bought bonds that year, they are
stopping this year. How big is this? In
a report to the president, the Treasury
said that about 80 million savings
bonds, worth about $29 billion,
had already matured and never been
cashed. That money belongs to someone.
But the part that really catches people
is the tax. Most people never paid tax
on their savings bond interest year by
year. They put it off. The IRS lets you
do that, but the IRS also says that if
you put it off, you must report all of
that interest in the year you cash the
bond, or the year the bond reaches final
maturity, whichever comes first.
Read that carefully. Whichever comes
first. If your bond hits 30 years this
year, the interest is taxable this year,
even if the bond never leaves your
drawer. Meet Evelyn. She is 81. She has
a stack [clears throat] of bonds she
bought for the grandkids in the 1990s,
and they are worth about $9,000 today.
About $4,500
of that is interest she has never paid
tax on. If those bonds reached 30 years
and she never cashed them, that interest
still belonged on her tax return. If she
misses it, the IRS can come back for the
tax, plus interest, plus possible
penalties. And if Evelyn passes away
with those bonds still in a drawer, her
family has to find them, prove they own
them, and sort out the tax on interest
that was piling up for decades.
Therefore, go find your bonds. Every
drawer, every safe, every envelope in
the closet. Look at the issue date on
each one. If it is 30 years old or
older, it is not earning a penny, and it
is time to cash it and report the
interest. If you think you or your
parents own bonds that are now lost,
Treasury has a form to replace lost,
stolen, or destroyed bonds, form 1048,
and and can start at treasurydirect.gov.
But now, the one I promised you at the
very beginning, the one almost every
grandparent does out of love. Number
seven, stop giving money away by the IRS
rules when the Medicaid rules are the
ones that matter. You have probably
heard about the gift limit. In 2026, you
can give up to $19,000
to as many people as you want, and you
do not even have to file a gift tax
return. Many grandparents hear that
number and think it is the safe amount.
The government said it is fine, right?
But that $19,000 number is an IRS rule,
and Medicaid, the program that pays for
nursing home care for people who run out
of money, does not use the IRS rule.
Medicaid has its own rule, and it is
much harsher. Under federal Medicaid
law, when you apply for long-term care,
the state looks back 60 months. That is
five full years. Every gift you made in
those five years, every dollar given
away without getting something of equal
value back, gets added up. The IRS limit
does not protect it. Then the state
divides that total by the average
monthly cost of a nursing home in your
state. The answer is the number of
months Medicaid will refuse to pay for
your care. And here is the cruelest part
of the rule. That penalty clock does not
start when you made the gift. Under
federal law, it starts only when you
have applied. You are already in need of
care, and you would otherwise qualify
for Medicaid. In other words, it starts
at the exact moment you have spent
nearly everything and need help the
most. Meet Ruth. She is 82, a widow, and
she adores her three grandchildren. For
2 years in a row, she gives each of them
$19,000 to help with school and a first
home. That is $114,000
in total, and every bit of it was within
the IRS limit. She did everything the
tax rules said she could. Then Ruth
falls and breaks her hip, and she needs
nursing home care. She spends down what
she has left, and she applies for
Medicaid. The state looks back 5 years
and finds $114,000
in gifts. In her state, the average
monthly cost of a nursing home is about
more than 11 months. For more than 11
months, Medicaid will not pay for Ruth's
care. At about $10,000 a month, that is
that somebody has to come up with at a
time when Ruth no longer has it. Often,
the only way out is asking the
grandchildren to give the money back if
they still have it.
This is also why number four can be such
a trap. A house signed over to the kids
within those five years can count as a
gift, too. And a house is usually the
biggest gift of all. Federal law does
carve out certain exceptions, like
transfers to a spouse or to a child who
is disabled or to a child who lived in
the home and cared for you for years.
But, you need a professional to tell you
whether any of those apply to you.
Therefore, if you are in your late 70s
or 80s, or if your health is changing,
stop making large gifts on autopilot.
And before you give away any large sum
or any property, sit down with an elder
law attorney in your state and ask how
it would look under Medicaid's five-year
look-back, not just under the IRS limit.
So, here are your seven things to stop
and exactly what to do instead. One, if
you are under full retirement age and
still working, run the earnings test
before you claim or tell Social Security
what you expect to earn.
Two, call every company that holds your
accounts and confirm your first and
second beneficiaries in writing.
Three, stop putting checks in your home
mailbox. Use bill pay, hand them to your
carrier, or drop them inside the post
office, and check your account every
week.
Four, before you sign your house over to
anyone, ask an estate attorney about the
stepped-up basis and a transfer on death
deed.
Five, never cosign a loan you could not
pay off yourself starting tomorrow.
Six, find every savings bond you own,
check the issue date, and cash anything
30 years old.
Seven, keep a 5-year record of your
gifts and check the Medicaid rules
before any large one.
To reach Social Security, call
For tax questions, call the IRS at

title: 7 New IRS Rules Quietly Taking Money From Seniors — Fix Them Before December

segments.text: If your income this year goes just $1
Medicare will charge you about $1,148
extra 2 years from now. For a married
couple, the line is $218,000
and the bill is about $2,296.
It comes straight out of your social
security check and the government uses
your tax return to decide it. $1. That
is all it takes. And that is only one of
seven rules quietly taking money from
seniors right now. Some of these rules
are brand new. They came out of the big
tax law that Congress passed in July of
2025 and they started hitting tax
returns this year. Others are older
rules the IRS has just started enforcing
after years of looking the other way.
And one of them is a rule almost every
senior in America thinks was changed
when it was not changed at all.
But here is the part that matters most.
Nearly every one of these seven can be
fixed and the deadline to fix most of
them is not April 15th. It is December
31st. After midnight on New Year's Eve,
the year is locked. The numbers are
final and the IRS and Medicare get to
take what the rules say they can take.
So today, I'm going to walk you through
seven new IRS rules quietly taking money
from seniors and exactly what to do
about each one before December 31st.
Number four is the one that costs the
most, and it is the one I just told you
about, the $1 rule. Wait until you see
how easy it is to trip. And stay with me
until the end because there is also one
brand new rule in that same tax law that
works in your favor. It hands money back
to millions of seniors who never
itemize. Almost nobody is talking about
it, and it only works if you act before
the end of this year.
Let's start with the one that sounds
like good news, because that is exactly
why it catches people. Number one, the
$6,000 that disappears. You may have
heard about the new senior deduction.
Starting with 2025 tax returns and
running through 2028, if you are 65 or
older, you get an extra deduction of
$6,000. If you are married and both of
you are over 65, that is $12,000. That
is on top of the regular standard
deduction and on top of the extra amount
seniors already got. It is real money
and you get it whether you itemize or
take the standard deduction. but it
comes with strings and the IRS spells
them out. First, if you are married, you
have to file a joint return to get it.
File separately and it is gone. Second,
the social security number of each
person claiming it has to be on the
return. And third, here is the one that
takes money. The deduction starts
shrinking once your modified adjusted
gross income goes over $75,000 if you
are single or $150,000 if you are
married filing jointly. For every dollar
you go over, you lose 6 cents of the
deduction. Go far enough over and it
disappears completely. Now, a lot of
seniors read that and think, "My income
is not that high. This is not about me."
But the income that counts is not just
your pension and your social security.
It is every dollar that lands on your
tax return this year, an extra
withdrawal from your IRA, a Roth
conversion, the gain when you sell some
stock or a rental property or a piece of
land.
Meet Margaret. She is 68, single, and
her normal income is about $72,000,
comfortably under the line. But in
November, her car dies, and she pulls an
extra $25,000 out of her IRA to buy a
new one. That pushes her income to
$97,000, which is 22,000 over the line.
At six cents per dollar, her new senior
deduction shrinks by $1320,
and she still owes ordinary income tax
on the whole 25,000 she withdrew. If she
had split that withdrawal, taking part
of it in December and part of it in
January, the extra income would have
been spread across two tax years instead
of piling into one. Therefore, before
December 31st, add up what you have
already taken out of every account this
year. If you are near the line, ask
yourself whether the next withdrawal can
wait until January. One date on a
calendar can be worth more than $1,000.
But the next rule is one that hits the
most generous people in this audience,
the ones who give. Number two, the
charity floor. For decades, the rule was
simple. If you itemized your deductions,
every dollar you gave to a qualified
charity could come off your taxable
income within the normal limits. That
changed this year.
>> [snorts]
>> Starting with 2026, if you itemize, the
first half of 1% of your adjusted gross
income in charitable gifts is no longer
deductible at all. The IRS says it
plainly. If you itemize, you can only
deduct the charitable contributions that
are more than half of 1% of your income.
Meet Bill and Carol. They are in their
70s. They have a paidoff house in a
state with high property taxes, so they
still itemize and they tithe to their
church every month. about $6,000 a year.
Their adjusted gross income is $120,000.
Half of 1% of that is $600. So this
year, the first $600 they give to their
church does not count. Nobody sent them
a letter about it. They will only find
out when they file. $600 is not the end
of the world. But it is a new rule
taking money from people who are doing
exactly what they are supposed to do.
And there is a better way for many
seniors to give.
It is called a qualified charitable
distribution. If you are 70 and a half
or older, you can have money sent
directly from your IRA to a qualified
charity. In 2026, each person can give
this way. That money never shows up in
your adjusted gross income in the first
place. So, the new floor does not touch
it, and it can count toward your
required minimum distribution for the
year. And here is the part people miss.
Because that money stays out of your
income, it also helps you stay under the
senior deduction line from number one
and under the $1 Medicare line from
number four. Therefore, if you give to
charity and you are over 70 and a half,
call your IRA custodian before December
31st and ask for a qualified charitable
distribution sent directly to the
charity. It has to go straight from the
IRA to the charity. If the check is made
out to you first, it does not count.
But the next rule is not about your
money. It is about your children's money
and what happens to it after you are
gone. I'm Mark Callaway and on this
channel I dig through the federal rules
that decide what happens to your money
after 65. So you hear it from me before
you hear it from a letter in the
mailbox. If that is worth something to
you, stick around because number four is
coming and it is the most expensive rule
on this list.
Number three, the inherited IRA your
kids do not know about. Here is how
inheriting an IRA used to work. Your
child would stretch the withdrawals out
over their entire life, a little each
year, paying a little tax each year.
Then a law called the Secure Act changed
it. For most adult children who inherit
an IRA today, the whole account has to
be emptied by the end of the 10th year
after the owner's death. That part a lot
of families have heard.
What most families have not heard is the
second rule hiding inside it. If the
parent had already started taking
required withdrawals before they died,
the child cannot just wait 9 years and
take it all at the end. They have to
take a withdrawal every single year
along the way and then empty the rest by
year 10. For four years, the IRS did not
enforce that. It issued notice after
notice waving the penalty for 2021,
2022, 2023, and 2024 because the rules
were confusing even to the
professionals. But the IRS said its
final regulations apply starting in
2025. The grace period is over and the
penalty for missing a required
withdrawal is an excise tax of 25% of
the amount you should have taken out. It
drops to 10% if you fix it within two
years. But either way, it is money that
simply disappears.
Meet Steven. He is 58 and he inherited a
$400,000 IRA when his mother passed away
at 84. She had been taking her required
withdrawals for more than 10 years.
Steven read online that he had 10 years,
so he left the account alone. But
because his mother had already started
her withdrawals, Steven owes a
withdrawal every year. this year that is
roughly $14,000.
If he misses it, the excise tax is 25%
about $3,500 for doing nothing. Now,
here is why this is in a video for
seniors. Steven's mother could have
prevented it with one conversation.
Therefore, if you have an IRA and you
have already started your required
withdrawals, sit down with your children
this year and tell them two things. One,
when they inherit it, they will likely
owe a withdrawal every single year, not
just at the end. And two, the deadline
each year is December 31st. And if you
are the one who already inherited an IRA
from a parent or a sibling, call that
custodian this week and ask one
question. Do I owe a withdrawal this
year? But everything so far has been a
few hundred or a few thousand. The next
one can be much bigger and it is the
rule I opened this video with. If this
video is helping you, here is a quick
note before number four. I put every
bill seniors are legally allowed to stop
paying after 65 into one guide called
the senior exempt playbook. Scan the
code on your screen now or tap the link
in the description. Number four, the $1
Medicare rule.
Here is how it works. Every year, the
IRS shares your tax return information
with Social Security. Social Security
looks at your modified adjusted gross
income from 2 years earlier and if it is
above a certain line, you pay an extra
charge on top of your normal Medicare
premiums. It is called the income
related monthly adjustment amount. Most
people just call it IRMA.
In 2026, the standard Medicare Part B
premium is $22.90
a month. According to Medicare, only
about 8% of people with Medicare pay
this extra charge. So, most seniors
assume it could never be them. And that
is exactly how one large withdrawal in
one year sneaks up on people who have
never paid it before. If your income 2
years ago was more than $19,000
as a single filer or more than $218,000
filing jointly, you pay more.
And here is the trap. IRMA is not a
gentle slope. It is a cliff. At the very
first tier, you pay an extra $8120
a month for part B and an extra $14.50
a month for your drug coverage. That is
about $1,148
a year per person. And it does not
matter whether you went over by $50,000
or by $1. $1 over the line costs you the
whole amount. At the top tier, the extra
charge reaches $487 a month for Part B
plus $91 a month for drug coverage. That
a year for one person. And it is taken
right out of your Social Security check
before it ever reaches your bank
account.
Now, here is why December 31st matters
so much. The income you report for 2026
is the income Medicare will use to set
your premiums in 2028. So every
withdrawal, every Roth conversion, every
stock sale you make between now and New
Year's Eve is quietly deciding your
Medicare bill 2 years from now. And here
is what catches people offguard. The
income that counts for IRMAa includes
your taxexempt interest. That municipal
bond interest you thought did not count
for anything, Medicare adds it right
back in.
Meet Ron and Diane. They are 71 and 69.
Their normal joint income is about
safely under the line, but this year
they need a new roof, and Ron pulls
$40,000 out of his IRA in one lump to
pay for it. their income jumps to
27,000 over the line. In 2028, at
today's rates, that one withdrawal cost
them about $2,296
in extra Medicare charges on top of the
income tax on the 40,000. If Ron had
taken 20,000 in December and 20,000 in
January, the income would have been
split across 2 years, and they might
never have crossed the line at all.
Therefore, before December 31st, ask
whoever does your taxes one question.
Where is my income for this year
compared to the IRMA
line? If you are close, a withdrawal can
wait until January or go to charity
directly through a qualified charitable
distribution. And if your income dropped
because of a life-changing event, like
you stopped working, your spouse passed
away, or you got divorced, you do not
have to wait 2 years for Medicare to
catch up. You can ask Social Security
for a new decision using form SSA44,
but the next rule is the one that sets
up most of the others because it decides
how much income you are forced to take
in the first place. Number five, the
double withdrawal year. Once you reach
73, the IRS requires you to start taking
money out of your traditional IRA and
most workplace retirement plans every
year. That is your required minimum
distribution. For people born in 1960 or
later, the age is 75. The deadline every
year is December 31st. Miss it and the
same excise tax from number three
applies to you. 25% of what you should
