have taken or 10% if you fix it within 2
years. But there is a special rule for
your very first year. And it sounds like
a gift. You are allowed to delay your
first withdrawal until April 1st of the
following year. Here is the catch nobody
explains. If you delay that first
withdrawal into the next year, you still
have to take your second withdrawal by
December 31st of that same year. Two
withdrawals, one tax year. Meet Gan. He
turned 73 in 2025, and his adviser told
him he could wait until April, so he
did. His first required withdrawal,
about $18,000, came out in March of
2026. His second one, about $19,000, has
to come out by this December 31st. That
is $37,000 of extra income stacked into
one year.
And look at what that stack does. It can
push Gan over the senior deduction line
from number one. It can push him over
the Medicare line from number four,
which shows up on his bill in 2028. And
it can push more of his social security
into the taxable column, which is
exactly what number six is about.
Therefore, if you turn 73 this year,
think hard before you use the April 1st
delay. For many people, it is better to
take the first withdrawal by December
31st and keep the income spread out. And
if you have more than one IRA, here is a
detail that saves people from penalties.
You can add up the required amounts from
all your IAS and take the total from any
one of them. But a 401k is different.
Each workplace plan has to pay out its
own required amount. But the next rule
is the one almost every senior in
America thinks was changed this year,
and it was not. Number six, the social
security tax that did not go away.
You may have seen the headlines this
year. No tax on social security. You may
have even heard people say the new law
eliminated federal income taxes on
social security for most seniors. Here
is what the tax code actually says. The
rules for taxing social security
benefits were not repealed. They are
exactly where they have been for
decades. Here is how it works. You take
half of your Social Security benefits
and you add all your other income,
including taxexempt interest. If that
total is more than $25,000 for a single
filer or $32,000 for a married couple
filing jointly, part of your benefits
become taxable. Go over $34,000 single
or $44,000 married, and up to 85% of
your benefits can be taxed.
And those lines have never been adjusted
for inflation. The $25,000 line was set
in 1983. The $34,000 line was set in
Every time your benefit gets a cost of
living raise, more of your check gets
pushed over a line that never moves.
What the new law did was add the $6,000
senior deduction from number one. That
can lower your tax bill, but it does not
change how much of your social security
counts as taxable. Those are two
different things and a lot of people are
mixing them up.
Meet Patricia. She is 70, single, and
she gets $28,000 a year from social
security plus $24,000 from a small
pension and her IRA. Half her benefits
is 14,000. Add 24,000 and her total is
$4,000 over the higher line. Under the
IRS worksheet, $7,900
of her social security is taxable.
Patricia was certain she would owe
nothing on her benefits this year. She
stopped her withholding in the spring
because of a headline. Therefore, before
December 31st, look at what you have had
withheld this year. If you stopped
withholding because you thought Social
Security was no longer taxed, you can
file form W4V with Social Security to
have 7, 10, 12, or 22% withheld from
your benefit going forward. And if you
pay estimated taxes, the last payment
for this year is due January 15th. But
the last rule is the newest one of all,
and it changes the way your refund
reaches you. Number seven, the refund
check that is not coming. For
generations, seniors got their tax
refund the same way. a paper check from
the United States Treasury in the
mailbox. That is ending. In March of
2025, an executive order directed the
Treasury to stop issuing paper checks.
And according to the IRS, it generally
stopped issuing paper refund checks to
individual taxpayers after September
30th of 2025. So, what happens if you
file your return and leave the bank
account section blank? The IRS says your
return will still be accepted, but your
refund will be held. You will get a
notice in the mail called a CP53E.
giving you 30 days to send your banking
information or explain why you cannot.
If you never respond and there are no
other issues, the refund is released as
a paper check after 6 weeks.
Meet Evelyn. She is 81. She has filed on
paper for 50 years and she has never
once put a bank account number on a tax
form. She is owed $1,800. Her refund
sits frozen for weeks while a notice
works its way through the mail. And
there is more changing at the same time.
The free direct file program the IRS ran
for two years is gone. It was not
offered in the 2026 filing season and
the IRS has set no date to bring it
back. And if you pay quarterly estimated
taxes through the system called EFTPS,
the IRS says those payment options will
be shut down for individual taxpayers in
late 2026. If you are one of those
seniors, you need a new way to pay
before your next payment is due in
January.
And here is the part that protects your
money the most. The IRS says it will
only ask for your missing bank
information by a letter in the mail, not
by phone, not by text. If anyone calls
or texts you about your refund and asks
for your bank account number, it is a
scam. Therefore, before December 31st,
set up your IRS online account at
IRS.gov. Get your direct deposit
information ready for when you file. And
if you use EFTPS, switch to IRS direct
pay or your online account before your
January payment. Now, I promised you one
brand new rule in that same tax law that
works in your favor. Most seniors do not
itemize. They take the standard
deduction, which means for years, the
money they gave to their church or their
favorite charity did nothing for them at
tax time.
That changes in 2026. Starting this
year, even if you do not itemize, you
can deduct up to $1,000 in cash gifts to
qualified charities. For a married
couple filing jointly, it is $2,000.
There are rules. It has to be a cash
gift, which includes a check or a card,
not clothing or stock. It has to go to a
qualified charity. And gifts to donor
advised funds do not count. But for
millions of seniors who give and never
itemize, this is new money back. And
here is why I saved it for last. It only
counts for gifts you actually make in
2026. The deadline is December 31st. A
gift you make on January 2nd goes on
next year's return. So, remember Bill
and Carol from number two? Their church
gets the same money either way. But for
a couple who does not itemize, making
those gifts before New Year's Eve and
keeping the receipts means up to $2,000
comes off their taxable income this
year.
So, here's what to do before December
31st. One, add up every withdrawal you
have taken this year and check it
against the senior deduction line of
$75,000 single or $150,000 married. Two,
if you are over 70 and a half and you
give to charity, ask your IRA custodian
for a qualified charitable distribution
paid directly to the charity. Three, if
you inherited an IRA, call the custodian
and ask whether you owe a withdrawal
this year and tell your own children how
the annual rule works. Four, check your
income against the Medicare line of
109,000 single or 218,000 married and
move any withdrawal you can into
January. Five, if you turn 73 this year,
think twice before delaying your first
required withdrawal into April. Six, if
you stopped withholding on your social
security because of a headline, look at
form W4V.
Seven, set up your IRS online account.
Have your bank information ready and
never give it to anyone who calls or
texts you. To ask Social Security for a
new Medicare income decision, call 1
For tax questions, call the IRS at 1

title: 7 Places Seniors Should Never Keep Their Money After 65

segments.text: Last year, about 700 American families
reported opening their front door to a
polite stranger and handing over cash
and gold worth a combined $311 million.
That is the FBI's own number. And the
FBI says the people being targeted are
very often over 60, not because they
were foolish, because somebody convinced
them the money was not safe where it was
and that it would be safer somewhere
else. And that is the whole story of
this video. Where you keep your money
after 65 matters almost as much as how
much you have. Because there are places
that feel safe, places your parents
used, places your bank or your phone or
a voice on the line will steer you
toward where the money can be taken from
you. Sometimes by a scammer, sometimes
by a company that fails, and sometimes
completely legally by the federal
government itself. So today I am going
to walk you through seven places seniors
should never keep their money after 65.
Number four is the one that lets them
take it and you would be the one who
moves it there with your own two hands
because you were told it was the safe
thing to do. But stay with me until the
end because I am also going to show you
the one place the federal government
actually guarantees your money and the
one form you can fill out at your own
bank that can raise that guarantee from
to more than $1 million at a single
bank. Almost nobody over 65 has filled
it out. Let's start with the oldest
hiding place there is because it is
where a lot of people keep the money
they trust the most. Number one, cash
and gold at home. I understand the
instinct. You remember bank runs from
your parents' stories. You remember
2008. You want some money you can put
your hands on. And a little emergency
cash at home is reasonable. But a lot of
seniors keep far more than a little.
Coffee cans, freezers, shoe boxes on the
top shelf of the closet, a gun safe in
the basement with gold coins in it. And
here is the first problem. Money in your
house is insured by nobody. The FDIC
ensures deposits at a bank. It does not
insure a shoe box. And many homeowners
insurance policies limit how much cash
they will pay back after a fire or a
burglary to a small amount. So read your
policy because the limit may be a
fraction of what you have hidden. But
fire is not the real danger anymore. The
real danger is the knock on the door. In
January of 2024, the FBI issued a public
warning about a scam that has exploded
since. Someone calls pretending to be
from tech support or your bank or a
federal agency. They tell you your
accounts have been hacked and that you
need to protect your money by turning
your savings into cash or gold. And then
they send a courier to your house to
pick it up for safekeeping. In the FBI's
own words, the government and legitimate
businesses will never ask you to buy
gold. But in 2025 alone, the FBI
received about 725 complaints about
these courier scams with $311.8
million in losses. Do the math on that.
The average family that got hit lost
more than $400,000.
Meet Dorothy. She is 79, a widow in a
quiet suburb, and she keeps about
$30,000 in cash in a cedar chest because
her late husband never trusted banks.
One afternoon, a man calling himself a
federal agent tells her that her name
has been linked to a moneyaundering case
and that her cash must be sealed and
held as evidence. Two hours later, a
young man in a delivery vest is standing
on her porch, and Dorothy hands him the
envelope. She never sees it again, and
because it was cash, there is no
transaction to reverse and no bank to
call. Therefore, keep only a small
emergency amount at home, enough for a
few weeks of groceries and medicine if
the power goes out. Keep the rest where
it is insured, and make yourself one
promise out loud right now. I will never
hand cash or gold to anyone who comes to
my door, no matter who they say sent
them. But the next place is one that
most people over 65 do not even realize
they are using as a bank. It is sitting
in your pocket right now. Number two,
the balance inside a payment app. Venmo,
PayPal, Cash App. Millions of seniors
started using them to send birthday
money to grandkids, split a dinner bill,
or pay the neighbor kid who mows the
lawn. And when someone pays you, the
money lands in the app and just sits
there as a balance. It feels like a bank
account. It has a number. It shows a
balance. But in June of 2023, the
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
published an analysis of these apps, and
its finding was blunt. Funds sitting in
payment app accounts often lack deposit
insurance, and if the company were to
fail, customers could lose their funds.
And this is not small money. The CFPB
found that peer-to-peer payment apps
moved about $893 billion in a single
year and projected about $1.6 trillion
by 2027. Some of that money just stays
parked in the apps. sometimes for
months. The CFPB's own advice was
simple. Consumers may need to take
action to move their balances into an
account with federal deposit insurance.
Meet Ry. He is 68 and he sells
woodworking pieces at craft fairs on
weekends. Customers pay him through an
app and over 2 years he lets the balance
grow to about $11,000 because it is easy
and he likes watching the number climb.
Then he gets an email from the app
saying his account is under review and
temporarily restricted. It takes him
weeks of calls to get access back. And
the whole time, there is no federal
agency standing behind that balance the
way there would be at an insured bank.
Therefore, treat every payment app like
a mailbox, not a safe. Money comes in
and you move it out to your insured bank
account the same week. Most of these
apps let you transfer to your bank for
free if you are willing to wait a day or
two. Do that every time. But the third
place is one where the money actually is
in a real financial company with a real
adviser and a real statement. And the
danger there is not that it disappears.
It is that somebody else quietly keeps
what it earns. I'm Mark Callaway and on
this channel I dig through the federal
rules and the federal warnings that
decide what happens to your money after
65. So you hear it from me before you
hear it from a stranger on the phone. If
that is worth something to you, stick
around because number three is costing
retirees thousands of dollars a year and
it is printed on a statement you already
get in the mail. Number three, the cash
sitting in your brokerage or retirement
account. When you have an IRA or an
investment account, there is almost
always some money in it that is not
invested. Maybe you sold a fund, maybe a
dividend came in, maybe you are keeping
cash on the side for your required
withdrawals. That uninvested cash goes
somewhere automatically into what is
called a cash sweep. And here is what
most people never notice. Many firms
sweep that cash into a bank that the
firm itself is connected to at a rate
that can be tiny. While the firm and its
bank earn far more on your money behind
the scenes. In January of 2025, the
Securities and Exchange Commission
charged two of the biggest names in the
business, Wells Fargo's Advisory Firms
and Meil Lynch, over how they ran these
cash sweep programs. The SEC said the
firms failed to have proper policies to
make sure clients cash was being handled
in their best interest. The firms agreed
to pay $60 million in combined
penalties,
and the gap they were fighting over was
not small. Reports on the case described
the difference between the default sweep
rate and other cash options, reaching
nearly 4 percentage points at times. On
$100,000, that is close to $4,000 a year
that never reached the account owner.
Now, one more thing people get wrong
here. Cash at a brokerage is generally
not protected by the FDIC unless
[clears throat] it is actually swept
into an insured bank. Instead, the
Securities Investor Protection
Corporation protects up to $500,000,
including up to $250,000 in cash if the
brokerage firm itself fails. But that
protection does not cover a low interest
rate, and it does not cover investments
going down.
Meet Frank and Linda, 71 and 69. They
roll Frank's old work retirement plan
into an IRA, and about $120,000 of it
sits in cash while they decide what to
do. They decide nothing for 3 years.
When their grandson finally looks at
their statement, the cash has been
earning a sliver of a percent the entire
time, while a money market option inside
the very same account was paying many
times more. Over 3 years, the difference
is more than $10,000.
Therefore, pull up your latest IRA or
brokerage statement this week and find
the line that says cash or sweep or
money market. Then call the firm and ask
one question. What rate is my uninvested
cash earning right now? And what other
cash options do you offer? You do not
have to change anything, but you should
know the answer. But the next place on
this list is different from all the
others. It is not a place you choose. It
is a place a stranger builds for you,
one phone call at a time. and it is the
reason the FBI is begging families to
have one conversation with their
parents. If this video is helping you,
here is a quick note before number four.
I put every bill seniors are legally
allowed to stop paying after 65 into one
guide called the senior exempt playbook.
Scan the code on your screen now or tap
the link in the description. Number
four, the safe account. This is the one
I promised you at the start. It is the
most dangerous place on this list
because it does not exist until someone
invents it for you and you move your
money into it yourself. The FBI calls it
the phantom hacker scam and in September
of 2023, it issued a public warning
describing it in three phases.
Phase one, a popup appears on your
computer or you get a call from someone
pretending to be tech support. They say
there is a virus or a hacker in your
computer and they ask to connect
remotely to fix it. While they are in,
they look at your bank and investment
accounts. Phase two, a second person
calls. This one says he is from your
bank's fraud department. He tells you a
foreign hacker has gotten into your
accounts and that you need to move your
money right away to a safe account to
protect it. Phase three, a third person
calls claiming to be from a federal
agency, sometimes even the Federal
Reserve. He confirms everything and he
tells you the money must be moved to a
new account under an alias for your
protection. Sometimes there is even an
official looking letter on government
letter head. Every voice on that call is
part of the same crew and the safe
account belongs to them.
In the first 6 months of 2023 alone, the
FBI says tech support scams like this
drew 19,000 complaints and more than
$542 million in losses. Almost half of
the victims were over 60 and they took
about 2/3 of the losses and it has only
grown. In 2025, people over 60 reported
more than $1 billion in losses to tech
and customer support scams. Meet Harold.
He is 73, a retired engineer, and he is
not a gullible man. A warning pops up on
his laptop with a phone number. The
polite young man who answers says his
bank account has been compromised and
transfers him to the bank's fraud
department. That person walks him
through moving $280,000,
his entire retirement savings, into a
safe account, a little at a time over
two weeks. and even coaches him on what
to tell the teller if she asks
questions. By the time his daughter
finds out, every dollar is gone.
Here is the rule that would have saved
Harold, and it comes straight from the
FBI's warning. The United States
government will never ask you to send
money by wire transfer to foreign
accounts, cryptocurrency, or gift cards.
And no real bank and no real federal
agency will ever tell you to move your
money to keep it safe. There is no such
thing as a government safe account.
Therefore, if anyone on any call on any
screen tells you to move your money to
protect it, that is the moment you know.
Hang up. Do not call back the number
they gave you. Pick up your bank card,
turn it over, and call the number on the
back yourself. And never let a stranger
connect to your computer. But here is
what makes this new wave so much worse
than the old scams. And it is the reason
number five even exists. The crooks no
longer want you to wire the money. They
want you to walk it into a gas station.
Number five, the crypto ATM.
You may have seen them and never
noticed. A tall machine in the corner of
a gas station or a convenience store
with a screen and a slot for cash and
the word Bitcoin on the side. The
government calls them convertible
virtual currency kiosks. Most people
just call them crypto ATMs. Here is how
they get used against seniors. The same
caller from number four, the fake fraud
department or the fake federal agent,
tells you to withdraw cash from your
bank and feed it into one of these
machines and then scan a code that he
sends you. That code sends the money
straight into his digital wallet. Once
it goes in, it is effectively gone.
There is no stop payment. There is no
chargeback. And the numbers are
staggering. The FBI's 2025 crime report
counted 13,460
complaints involving crypto ATMs with
389 million in losses. And people over
60 accounted for $6,188
of those complaints and about $257
million of the losses. That is two of
every $3 stolen through these machines
taken from people over 60. The Federal
Trade Commission found the same pattern.
People over 60 were more than three
times as likely as younger adults to
report losing money at one of these
machines. And in August of 2025, the
Treasury's Financial Crimes Office,
Fininsson, warned banks to watch for one
red flag in particular. An older
customer with no history of crypto,
suddenly pulling out large amounts of
cash after being told by someone on the
phone to take it to a kiosk.
Meet Barbara. She is 76. A caller says
he is from her bank, that her account is
being drained, and that she must
withdraw $15,000
and deposit it into a secure federal
system before the hackers take it. He
stays on the phone with her the entire
time while she drives to the bank while
she tells the teller it is for a home
repair. And while she stands at a
machine beside the coffee counter at a
gas station, feeding in $100 bills,
$15,000 gone in 20 minutes. Therefore,
write this down and put it on your
refrigerator. No bank, no government
agency, and no legitimate company will
ever tell you to pay with a crypto ATM.
If anyone does, it is a scam every
single time. And if a caller tells you
not to tell the teller the real reason
for a withdrawal, that alone tells you
everything. But the next one is not a
scam at all. It is something families do
out of love, and it can let the
government take your money for somebody
else's debt.
Number six, a joint account with your
adult child. It happens in almost every
family. A parent gets older and to make
things easier, they add a son or
daughter to their checking or savings
account. That way, the child can pay
bills if mom gets sick and the money
passes to the child without probate. It
sounds sensible, but the moment you add
your child as a joint owner, you have
given them more than help. You have
given them a legal right to withdraw
every dollar in that account. And that
right comes with their problems
attached.
In 1985, the United States Supreme Court
decided a case called United States
versus National Bank of Commerce. The
Internal Revenue Service had levied
joint bank accounts for taxes owed by
only one of the people named on them.
The court sided with the IRS. Its
reasoning was simple. If the person who
owes the tax has the right to withdraw
the money under state law, the IRS can
levy the account and the other owners
have to step forward and prove the money
is really theirs. So, think about what
that means. If your son owes back taxes
or your daughter's business goes under,
the money you saved for your own old age
can be frozen because their name is on
it. And depending on your state, other
creditors may be able to reach it, too.
Meet Ruth. She is 81 and she added her
son, Michael, to her savings account 5
years ago after her hip surgery. She has
about $40,000 in it, money from 40 years
of teaching. Michael falls behind on his
taxes after a bad year in his business.
One morning, Ruth's debit card is
declined at the pharmacy. The account
has been levied for her son's tax debt.
It takes her months, a stack of
paperwork, and help from a lawyer to
show the IRS that the money was hers all
along. And there is a quieter problem,
too. Because Michael is a joint owner,
the money is legally his the moment Ruth
dies, no matter what her will says about
splitting things equally with her
daughter.
Therefore, if you want a child to help
with your bills, ask your bank about
adding them as an authorized signer,
sometimes called a convenience serer
instead of a joint owner. And if what
you really want is for the money to pass
to them without probate, ask about a
payable on death beneficiary instead.
Hold on to that idea because that
beneficiary form is the key to the
protection I promised you at the
beginning. But first, the last place on
this list. It may be in your house right
now in a drawer you have not opened in
years, and it may have stopped earning
you a single penny a long time ago.
Number seven, old savings bonds in a
drawer. Millions of Americans bought
savings bonds through payroll deductions
at work or received them as gifts for a
birthday or a graduation. And a lot of
those paper bonds are still sitting in
desk drawers, safe deposit boxes, and
old filing cabinets. Here is the rule
most people never learn. A savings bond
does not earn interest forever.
According to Treasury Direct, the
government's own savings bond site. EE
bonds earn interest for 30 years and
then they stop. The same is true for
Ibonds. After that, the bond is frozen
at whatever it was worth on that day.
The government holds your money and it
pays you nothing more for it. And series
Ebonds, the kind sold for decades before
1980, have all stopped earning interest.
And it gets worse. Until recently, the
Treasury ran an online search tool
called Treasury Hunt that helped people
find bonds they had lost track of. But
according to Treasury Direct, as of
September 30th, 2025, that tool is no
longer available. So if you lose the
paper and nobody remembers it existed,
the money can sit unclaimed
indefinitely.
Meet George. He is 77. Cleaning out his
late mother's desk, he finds an envelope
of savings bonds she bought for him in
the 1970s and early 1980s with a
combined face value of about $5,000.
They stopped growing years ago, but they
are still worth well more than their
face value, and he can still cash them.
If he had thrown out that envelope with
the rest of the old papers, that money
would simply have gone unclaimed.
Therefore, go find every paper bond in
your house this month. Check the issue
date on each one. Any bond more than 30
years old has stopped earning. So, it is
time to cash it or move it. If you have
lost a bond, the Treasury has a claim
form for lost, stolen, or destroyed
bonds. And remember, the interest is
subject to federal income tax when you
cash it, but it is exempt from state and
local income tax. So, let's put the
seven together because this is where it
all connects.
cash at home, payment apps, brokerage
cash, the safe account, crypto, ATMs, a
joint account with your child, and
forgotten bonds in a drawer. Three of
these, the money can simply disappear
and nobody is standing behind it. Two of
them, someone else quietly keeps what
your money earns. And two of them, the
safe account and the crypto ATM, work
only because you are the one who moves
the money after a stranger frightens you
into it. Now, I promised you the one
place the federal government actually
guarantees your money and the form that
can stretch that guarantee past $1
million. The place is a plain deposit
account at an FDIC insured bank or an
insured credit union. Checking, savings,
money market deposit accounts,
certificates of deposit. The standard
insurance is $250,000
per depositor per insured bank for each
ownership category. And in the entire
history of the FDIC, no depositor has
ever lost a penny of insured deposits.
But here is the part almost nobody over
65 knows. In April of 2024, new FDIC
rules for trust accounts took effect,
and that includes ordinary accounts with
payable on death beneficiaries. Under
those rules, each owner is insured up to
for each beneficiary named up to five
beneficiaries. That means one person who
names five beneficiaries on a payable on
death account can be covered up to $1.25
million at a single bank. So remember
Ruth, a payable on death form, naming
her son and her daughter, would have
kept her son's tax problem away from her
savings while she was alive, passed the
money to both children without probate
and doubled her insurance coverage. One
form at her own bank in about 10
minutes. So here's what to do this week.
One, keep only a small emergency amount
of cash at home and never hand cash or
gold to anyone who comes to your door.
Two, move every payment app balance into
your insured bank account every single
week. Three, find the cash line on your
IRA or brokerage statement and ask what
rate it is earning. Four, if anyone
tells you to move your money to keep it
safe, hang up and call the number on the
back of your card. Five, never put money
into a crypto ATM because someone on the
phone told you to. Six, if your child is
a joint owner on your account, ask your
bank about an authorized signer and a
payable on death beneficiary instead.
Seven, find every paper savings bond in
your house and cash any that are more
than 30 years old. To check your deposit
insurance, call the FDIC at
And if you think someone is targeting
you or a parent for money, call the
National Elder Fraud Hotline at
One.

title: Banks Quietly Treat You Different After 65 (#4 Is Kept Secret)

segments.text: If the bank vault that holds your safe
deposit box floods, burns, or gets
robbed tonight, the amount of that box
the federal government insures is $0.
Not 250,000, not half, zero. And that is
only the first thing your bank does not
tell you. Because once you pass 65, your
bank starts treating you differently.
Not in a way they put on a poster in the
lobby, in the fine print, in the back
office, and in a few federal rules that
were written with people your age
specifically in mind. Some of those
rules protect you. Some of them are used
against you, and most seniors never find
out which is which until the day their
money is stuck. So, today I am going to
walk you through seven things banks
quietly do differently once you are over
65. Number four is the one that happens
without you ever being told. Not by a
letter, not by a phone call. The law
actually forbids the bank from telling
you it happened.
But stay with me until the end because I
am also going to give you the one page
you can fill out this week that keeps
your bank or investment firm from
sitting on your money for weeks after
something like number four happens. It
takes about 10 minutes, and almost
nobody over 65 has done it. Let's start
with the box in the basement because it
is where a lot of people keep the things
they think are safest. Number one, the
safe deposit box. Ask most people what
the FDIC insures, and they will tell you
And that is right for deposits,
checking, savings, money market deposit
accounts, certificates of deposit,
per depositor, per bank, for each type
of ownership. But the FDIC says it
plainly on its own website. The contents
of a safe deposit box are not deposits,
and they are not insured. Not the cash,
not the gold coins, not the jewelry your
mother left you, not the savings bonds.
Zero.
And here is the part that surprises
people even more. The bank itself
usually does not insure the box either.
Read the rental agreement for your box,
and you will often find a line saying
the bank's liability is limited,
sometimes to a small fixed amount,
sometimes to only what you can prove was
lost through the bank's own negligence.
And how do you prove what was inside a
box only you ever opened? Meet Walter.
He is 74, a retired machinist, and he
does not trust banks with his emergency
money. So, he keeps it where he thinks
it is safest, $40,000 in cash in a safe
deposit box at the branch 2 miles from
his house. Then a water main breaks
under the street, and the vault floods
overnight. Walter's cash is a wet brick
of paper. He calls the bank, and the
bank points him to the line in his
rental agreement. He calls the FDIC, and
the FDIC tells him the box was never
covered.
Therefore, think about the box
differently. It is a good place for
papers you can replace, like a copy of
your deed or your passport. It is a
terrible place for cash. If you keep
valuables there, take photos of
everything inside, keep a written list
somewhere else, and check whether your
homeowner's or renter's policy covers
the contents. Many do, but only if you
add it. But the box is not the only
thing in the bank building that is not
insured. The next one is usually sitting
at a desk upstairs with a friendly smile
and a name tag that says banker. Number
two, the desk upstairs. Here is how it
happens. You walk in to deposit a check.
The teller sees your balance, sees your
birthday, and says something like, "You
know, you could be earning more on that
money. Would you like to talk to our
investment specialist?" And she walks
you to a nicer office.
That person may work for a brokerage
firm that rents space in the bank or for
the bank's own investment arm. And what
they sell there, annuities, mutual
funds, stocks, bonds, is not a deposit.
The FDIC says it directly. These
products are not FDIC insured, not
guaranteed by the the and they can lose
value. Federal guidance even requires
that warning to be disclosed to you in
writing. But, most people do not hear it
because the conversation is happening
inside the same building where their
checking account lives. It feels like
the bank. It feels safe.
And the product most often sold to
people over 65 at that desk is the
deferred annuity. Now, an annuity can be
the right tool for some people, but it
comes with something the Securities and
Exchange Commission warns about by name,
a surrender charge. If you need your
money back in the first several years,
the company takes a percentage of it.
The SEC's own example shows a surrender
charge that starts at 7% in the first
year and declines a little each year.
And the SEC says those charge periods
often run 6 to 8 years, sometimes as
long as 10, before you can touch your
own money without paying to leave. Meet
Joan. She is 76. Her husband passed, and
she has $100,000 from his life insurance
sitting in savings. The specialist
upstairs moves it into a deferred
annuity. Two years later, Joan needs a
new roof and help with a hip
replacement, and she asks for the money.
The surrender charge takes about $6,000
of her husband's money before she sees a
dime. Therefore, before you sign
anything at that desk, ask three
questions out loud. Is this FDIC
insured? Is there a surrender charge,
and for how many years? And how are you
paid for selling this to me? Then, take
the paperwork home and wait a week. I'm
Mark Calloway, and on this channel I dig
through the federal rules that decide
what happens to your money after 65, so
you hear it from me before you hear it
from a letter. If that is worth
something to you, stick around because
number three is happening to millions of
seniors right now, and it happens while
they sleep.
Number three, the certificate of deposit
that quietly renews. Families over 65
are almost twice as likely to own a
certificate of deposit as the average
American family. According to the
Federal Reserve, the typical CD held by
families aged 65 to 74 is worth $53,000.
It makes sense. A CD feels simple. You
put the money in, you lock in a rate,
and you get it back with interest.
But here is what happens at the end.
Most CDs are set to renew automatically.
If you do nothing when it matures, the
bank rolls your money into a brand new
CD. And here is the catch. The new CD
does not have to get the special rate
you signed up for. It gets whatever rate
the bank is paying on the day it renews.
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
says it plainly. That new rate may be
higher or lower. And when you signed up
for a special or promotional rate, it
can be a small fraction of what you were
getting, or of what the bank down the
street is paying new customers.
Now, federal law does give you a
warning. Under the Truth in Savings
rules, if your CD is longer than a year,
and it renews on its own, the bank has
to send you a notice before it matures.
Usually at least 30 days before, or 20
days if the bank gives you a grace
period of at least 5 days after it
matures to pull your money out without a
penalty. But that notice is allowed to
say the new rate is not known yet, and
it often arrives in a plain envelope
that looks just like every other piece
of bank mail. Meet Frank and Marie. They
are 78 and 75. Three years ago, they
opened a $100,000 CD at a special rate
of 4 and 1/2%. It quietly renewed last
spring at the bank's standard rate of
1/2 of 1%. The notice came in the mail,
and it went straight into the pile with
the credit card offers.
a year. 1/2 of 1% is 500. They lost
$4,000 of interest in a single year, and
nobody broke a single rule. Then, their
grace period ended, and the money was
locked up again. If they want out now,
they pay an early withdrawal penalty on
top of it. Therefore, find the maturity
date of every CD you own and write it on
your calendar. When the notice arrives,
open it and in the days after it
matures, during the grace period, shop
the rate. You can walk across the street
or open an online account and move the
whole thing without paying a penny of
penalty. But the first three are about
money you can see, your box, your
annuity, your CD.
If this video is helping you, here's a
quick note before number four. I put
every bill seniors are legally allowed
to stop paying after 65 into one guide
called the Senior Exempt Playbook. Scan
the code on your screen now or tap the
link in the description. Now, the one I
told you about at the start, because if
numbers one through three surprised you,
number four is the reason I made this
video. Number four, the report you are
never told about. Every bank in America
is required by federal law to file
something called a suspicious activity
report when it sees a transaction that
looks wrong. For banks, the rule kicks
in on transactions of $5,000 or more
that the bank knows, suspects, or has
reason to suspect involve something
illegal or that have no apparent lawful
purpose. The report goes to a bureau
inside the Treasury Department called
the Financial Crimes Enforcement
Network. And in June of 2022, that
bureau sent every bank in the country an
advisory. It told them exactly what to
watch for in customers who are older.
Sudden large withdrawals, wire transfers
to people the customer just met,
cashiers' checks bought in a hurry, a
new friend or relative suddenly showing
up at the counter, even an older
customer who seems nervous or who has
someone answering questions for them.
Then, in 2024, the same bureau published
what all that watching produced. In just
one year, from June of 2022 to June of
2023, banks and other financial
institutions filed more than 155,000
reports tied to elder financial
exploitation. Reports involving roughly
$27 billion in suspicious activity.
About eight out of every 10 of them
involved a scam.
Now, a lot of those reports catch real
crimes, and the crimes are real. The FBI
says people over 60 reported losing more
than $7.7 billion
to fraud in 2025 alone, up more than
half from the year before. Scammers,
thieves, sometimes family. So, when a
bank catches one, that is good. But,
here is the sentence that changes
everything. Federal law says the bank
cannot tell you a report was filed. Not
the teller, not the branch manager, not
even if you ask them directly. The law
makes the report confidential, and a
bank employee who tells you about it is
breaking federal law. So, you never get
a letter, you never get a phone call.
You just notice that things at your bank
start to feel different. The teller asks
more questions, a withdrawal takes
longer, a wire you send every year
suddenly needs a supervisor. And
sometimes, a few weeks later, a letter
arrives saying the bank has decided to
close your account. No reason given,
because they are not allowed to give you
the reason. Meet Eleanor. She is 81,
sharp as a tack, and she has decided to
help her grandson buy his first house.
She walks in and asks for a $25,000
cashier's check. She is a little
flustered because she is excited, and
her grandson is standing right next to
her answering half the questions. To the
teller, that checks almost every box on
the list. Large sudden withdrawal, a
younger relative doing the talking, a
nervous older customer. The teller does
exactly what she was trained to do.
Eleanor gets her check two days later
after a supervisor calls her alone. She
thinks that was the end of it, but a
report with her name on it is now
sitting in a federal database, and she
will never know it exists. And the next
time she moves a large amount, the bank
already has her on its radar. But, here
is the part nobody tells you. The report
itself is not the danger. It is what the
bank does next when it cannot reach
anybody who can vouch for you. That is
when the hold start, and that is when
accounts get closed. And there is one
page that changes how all of that goes
for you. I will show you exactly what it
is in number five.
Therefore, for any large transaction, do
three things. Go in on a weekday morning
alone, and tell the teller plainly what
the money is for and who it is going to.
Bring paperwork if you have it, like a
closing statement for that house, and
never let anyone else do your talking
for you at the counter. You are not
being suspicious. You are being exactly
the customer the bank does not have to
worry about.
Now, number five, because here is where
it gets serious. Number four is a report
you never see. Number five is what
happens to your money while they decide.
Number five, the hold and the one name
they call.
If you have an investment account, a
brokerage account, an IRA at an
investment firm, or that annuity from
the desk upstairs, there is a rule
written specifically for people 65 and
older. This one is about investment
firms, not your checking account. The
industry regulator, called FINRA, lets a
firm put a temporary hold on money
leaving your account if it reasonably
believes you are being financially
exploited. The rule calls you a
specified adult. That means anyone 65 or
older automatically. The first hold can
last up to 15 business days. Then it can
be extended for another 10. And if the
firm reports the matter to state
regulators, adult protective services,
or a court, it can be extended again.
Put together, your money can sit frozen
for up to 55 business days, and longer
if a regulator or a court orders it.
That is close to 3 months of not being
able to touch your own retirement
savings. For banks, there is a federal
law called the Senior Safe Act. It
protects bank employees from being sued
when they report suspected exploitation
of someone 65 or older, as long as they
were trained and acted in good faith.
And many states have their own laws that
let banks delay a transaction for a
senior while they look into it. So, who
decides when the hold ends? Here is the
part that matters. Under FINRA's rules,
firms have to make a reasonable effort
to get the name of a trusted contact
person from you. One person they can
call if they are worried about you.
Someone who can confirm you are fine,
that the money is going where you say it
is, or tell them that something really
is wrong. But most people skip that line
when they open an account, or they
opened it so long ago, the form did not
exist yet.
Meet Harold. He is 79. He decides to
move $60,000 from his IRA to pay for his
wife's assisted living. The firm sees a
big sudden withdrawal, a confused phone
call, and a new address on the
paperwork, and it places a hold. They
try to reach someone who can vouch for
him. There is no trusted contact on
file. So, they report it to the state,
and the hold gets extended. Harold's
wife's facility wants the deposit now.
He ends up putting $12,000 on card at
22% interest to cover the gap while his
own money sits frozen. Remember the one
page I promised you at the beginning?
This is it. The trusted contact form.
And unlike the report in number four, a
hold is not a secret. The firm has to
notify your trusted contact or another
authorized person within two business
days, but only if you gave them one. And
that form does not give that person any
power over your money. They cannot
withdraw anything. They cannot sign
anything. It just gives the firm one
phone number to call before they lock
things up. And when Eleanor's bank or
Harold's firm can reach someone in 5
minutes who says, "Yes, she is fine.
Yes, he is paying for his wife's care."
the hold is usually lifted fast.
Therefore, call every brokerage, IRA,
and annuity company you have money with
and ask one question. "Do you have a
trusted contact person on file for me?"
If they say no, fill out the form this
week. Ask your bank the same question.
Many banks now have their own version.
Pick someone you trust who answers their
phone and who is not the person you are
sending the money to.
But a hold is temporary. Number six can
keep your family locked out for months
at the exact moment you need them most.
Number six, the power of attorney the
bank refuses. You did everything right.
You went to a lawyer, you signed a
durable power of attorney, so if you
ever have a stroke or dementia or a bad
fall, your daughter can pay your bills
and handle your accounts. You had it
notarized. You put it in the drawer.
Then the day comes. Your daughter walks
into your bank with that document and
the bank says, "No. We do not accept
outside forms. You need to fill out our
form." And you, the person who is
supposed to sign that bank form, are in
a hospital bed and cannot.
This happens so often that the national
group that writes model state laws, the
Uniform Law Commission, wrote a law to
stop it. It is called the Uniform Power
of Attorney Act and more than half the
states have adopted it in some form.
Under the version many states adopted,
when someone presents a properly
acknowledged power of attorney, the bank
has seven business days to either accept
it or ask for a certification or a legal
opinion. It is not allowed to demand its
own different form instead. A bank can
still refuse if it honestly believes the
document is not valid or if it has
reported suspected abuse. But if it
refuses without a good reason, a court
can order it to accept the document and
make it pay the family's attorney fees.
But many banks still say no at the
counter, and most families do not know
they can push back. So, they give up and
go to court for a guardianship instead,
which can take months, costs lawyer
fees, and puts a judge in charge of
decisions you already made yourself.
Meet Ruth and her son Michael. Ruth is
83 and has a stroke. Michael brings her
power of attorney to her bank to pay her
rent and her medical bills. The bank
refuses it because it is not on their
form. Michael pays the rent out of his
own pocket for 4 months, more than
$7,000, while a lawyer gets the bank to
accept the document. Therefore, do this
while you are well. Take your power of
attorney to every bank and investment
firm you use and ask them to review it
now and put it on file. Ask if they have
their own form, and if they do, sign
theirs, too, while you still can. And if
a bank ever refuses a valid power of
attorney, ask for the refusal in writing
and the reason, and talk to an elder law
attorney about your state's version of
this law. But the last one is the one
people almost never think about because
it happens on the other side of the
bank, not your savings, your credit.
Number seven, your credit after you
retire. Here is a fear a lot of people
have, and it is not crazy. You retire,
your paycheck stops, and the bank looks
at you and decides you are a risk now.
Your credit card limit drops, your home
equity line gets frozen, a loan you
apply for gets turned down because you
are 70.
But this one is different because here

a sentence on the phone, a sentence said
out of fear, grief, love, or shame. And
the next two are sentences you might say
this week without a second thought.
Number six, never say, "Sure, sign me up
for overdraft coverage." This one sounds
harmless. It sounds like protection. The
banker even calls it courtesy. Here is
the federal rule. Your bank is not
allowed to charge you an overdraft fee
on an ATM withdrawal or an everyday
debit card purchase unless you
affirmatively opted in. Yes means yes.
Without that yes, the bank generally
declines the purchase instead, and you
pay nothing. Now, look at what that yes
cost. The Consumer Financial Protection
Bureau found that the median overdraft
fee at the largest banks and credit
unions that charge them was $35, and
years earlier, the Bureau found that
most debit card overdrafts are for
purchases under $26, and they get paid
back within about 3 days. Picture Frank.
He buys a coffee, a prescription, and a
tank of gas on a day his pension deposit
is running late. Three small swipes,
three overdraft fees, $105 gone for
about $60 of purchases, all because he
once said, "Sure, sign me up."
But, the fix is just as simple. The same
federal rule says you can revoke that
consent at any time. One phone call.
Tell the bank you want to opt out of
overdraft coverage for ATM and debit
card transactions. Just know that opting
out does not refund the fees you have
already been charged. So, do it today,
not after the next surprise.
Number seven. Never say, "Sure, I will
deposit your check and send you back the
difference." Eleanor sold her late
husband's piano online. The buyer mailed
her a cashier's check for $4,850,
which was 1,800 more than the price. He
apologized, said his assistant made a
mistake, and asked her to deposit the
check and send the extra by gift cards
or a transfer. The next day, the money
showed up in her account, so she sent
it. Two weeks later, the bank told her
the cashier's check was fake, and she
owed the bank the entire amount,
including the 1,800 she had already sent
away.
Here's the rule that fools almost
everyone. Under a federal rule called
Regulation CC, banks must make the first
of many check deposits available by the
next business day, and the rest of the
money often follows within a day or two.
That is the law requiring the money to
be available. It does not mean the check
has cleared. It does not mean the check
is real. A fake check can bounce days or
even weeks after you have spent the
money, and when it does, you are the one
who owes it back. Therefore, never
accept a check for more than you are
owed. Never send back the difference.
And if a stranger insists on it, you are
looking at a scam every time. So, those
are the seven. All in cash with no
explanation, moving money to protect it,
using a spouse's account after death,
sharing your PIN, saying I sent it
before telling the whole story, saying
yes to overdraft coverage, and sending
back the difference on a check.
But, I promised you one more, the one
sentence you should say. Here it is in
plain words. I did not authorize this
transfer and I am disputing it as an
error. Those words switch on the error
resolution rules of Regulation E, and
they come with deadlines the bank has to
meet. First, the bank must receive your
notice within 60 days after it sends the
statement where the problem first shows
up. You can call, but the bank is
allowed to ask you to confirm in writing
within 10 business days. So, always
follow up with a letter or a secure
message. Second, once you report it, the
bank must investigate within 10 business
days. If it needs longer, it generally
has to put the money back into your
account temporarily, and then it can
take up to 45 days to finish. And while
that provisional credit is there, you
get full use of the money.
Third, and this is the part that changes
everything. The clock decides how much
you can lose. If your card or PIN is
lost or stolen, and you report it within
two business days of finding out, your
loss on unauthorized transfers is capped
at $50. Wait longer, and it can rise to
as much as $500. And if you ignore a
statement for more than 60 days, you can
be on the hook for later unauthorized
transfers with no cap at all. $50 versus
everything. The only difference is how
fast you say that one sentence. Remember
Walter? The moment his daughter spotted
the problem, if Walter had told the bank
in writing that his nephew was no longer
authorized, every transfer after that
point could have been protected. And
remember Ruth? If her first words had
been, "I did not authorize this
transfer, and here is exactly what
happened," the investigation would have
started on her side of the table. So,
here is what to do this week. One,
change any PIN or password you have ever
shared with anyone, and tell your bank
in writing who is no longer authorized.
Two, if someone helps you with money,
set them up the right way as an
authorized signer, an agent, or with a
power of attorney the bank accepts.
Three, call your bank and opt out of
overdraft coverage on ATM and debit card
purchases. Four, ask your bank whether
you can name a trusted contact they can
call if something looks wrong. Five,
open every bank statement the week it
arrives, and if you see anything you did
not do, say the sentence, I did not
authorize this transfer and I am
disputing it as an error. Six, never
move money because someone called to
warn you. Hang up and call the number on
the back of your own card. Seven, never
deposit a check from a stranger and send
back the difference.
If your bank will not follow the rules,
file a complaint with the Consumer
Financial Protection Bureau at
And if you or someone you love has
already been targeted by a scam, call
the National Elder Fraud Hotline at

title: The Government Quietly FLAGS You at These 7 Ages After 60

segments.text: If you turn 73 and forget one withdrawal
from your own retirement account, the
Internal Revenue Service can take 25% of
the money you forgot to take out. On a
$500,000 account, that one missed
withdrawal is about $18,800
and the penalty on it is about $4,700
charged to you for doing absolutely
nothing. Nobody mails you a warning.
Nobody from the government calls. The
rule simply switches on the year you
reach a certain age and it is waiting
for you whether you know about it or
not. And that is only one of seven ages
after 60 where the government quietly
flags you. At each one, a rule you have
never heard of turns on. And if you miss
it, the cost is usually not a one-time
fee. It is permanent. It follows you for
the rest of your life.
Number four on this list is the one most
seniors miss and it is the crulest of
the seven because the mistake feels like
the responsible choice. People make it
on purpose thinking they are being
careful with their money and then they
pay for it every single month until the
day they die. And before we are done, I
am going to show you something almost
nobody talks about. Two of these seven
ages are secretly connected. A decision
you make at one age can quietly trigger
a bill at a completely different age
years later from a completely different
agency. And by the time the bill
arrives, most people have no idea what
caused it. I will show you exactly how
that hidden chain works and the one
simple move that breaks it. Stay with me
because it is at the very end and it
could save you thousands.
First, you need to understand why these
ages exist at all because once you see
it, you will never look at a birthday
the same way again. These rules were not
written by one person at one time with
you in mind. They were written by
Congress over almost 90 years. The
Social Security rules came from laws
passed in 1935 and changed again in
1983. Medicare came in 1965. The
retirement account rules were rewritten
in 2019 and again in 2022. Each law set
its own clock and each clock is run by a
different agency.
Social Security runs one clock. Medicare
runs another. The Internal Revenue
Service runs a third. And here is the
problem. None of these agencies
coordinates with the others to warn you.
Social Security does not call you about
your Medicare deadline. Medicare does
not call you about your tax penalty. The
Internal Revenue Service does not call
you about anything except to collect.
The law assumes you know. And if you do
not, the default always favors them, not
you. My name is Mark Callaway, and on
this channel, I take the rules that
quietly cost seniors money and read them
to you in plain language, straight from
the federal agencies that wrote them. No
sales pitch and nothing to buy. Just the
rules, the numbers, and what to do about
them. So, let us walk through all seven
ages in order. Starting with the first
one the government flags at 62.
The first age the government flags you
is 62. This is the first year you can
claim your social security retirement
check. And for a lot of people, it feels
like the finish line. You have worked
for decades. You have paid in every
paycheck. And now the money is finally
available. Millions of Americans file at
62 for exactly that reason. But here is
what the Social Security Administration
says in its own benefit planner. If your
full retirement age is 67, which it is
for everyone born in 1960 or later, and
you start your check at 62, your benefit
is reduced by 30%. And that reduction is
permanent. It does not go away when you
turn 67. It does not go away at 70. It
is the size of your check for the rest
of your life. And every cost of living
raise you ever get is figured on the
smaller number. Let me show you what
that looks like in real money. Say your
check at full retirement age would be
$2,000 a month. If you claim at 62, it
becomes $1,400
a month. That is $600 less every month,
less every year for as long as you live.
If you live into your late 80s, like
millions of Americans do, the difference
can add up to well over $100,000.
Now, to be fair, there are good reasons
to claim early. If your health is poor
or you need the money now, 62 can be the
right decision. The problem is making it
without knowing the price. Most people
who file at 62 think the cut is
temporary and gets fixed later. It does
not. And there is a second trap at 62
that catches even more people. It is
called the earnings test. If you claim
your check before full retirement age
and you keep working, Social Security
can hold back part of your benefit. In
2026, the limit is $24,480.
For every $2 you earn above that, Social
Security withholds $1 of your benefit.
Think about a man I will call Ron. Ron
retired from his main job at 62 and
claimed his social security. Then he
took a part-time job at a hardware store
because he liked being around people and
the extra money helped. That year he
earned $34,480.
That is $10,000 over the limit. So,
Social Security withheld $5,000 of his
checks. Several months in a row, the
check he was counting on simply did not
arrive. Ron thought something was
broken. He thought he was being punished
for working. He almost quit the job he
loved. Hold on to Ron's story because I
am coming back to him at a later age.
And what happens to that $5,000 is
something almost nobody is told.
So that is the first age, 62, the
permanent cut and the earnings test. But
the second age the government flags you
is the one that surprises almost
everyone because it happens before you
are even on Medicare and it quietly
decides what Medicare will charge you.
The second age the government flags you
is 63. Most people have never heard
anyone say that 63 matters at all. It
does not show up on the Social Security
statement. There is no benefit that
starts. Nothing arrives in the mail. And
yet, 63 is the year that quietly sets
the price of your Medicare when you turn
Here is how it works. Medicare charges
most people a standard monthly premium
for Part B, the part that covers doctors
and outpatient care. According to the
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid
Services, the standard part B premium in
a month. But if your income is above a
certain level, Medicare adds a search
charge on top. The official name is the
income related monthly adjustment
amount. People in the industry just call
it Irma. And here is the part that
catches people. Medicare does not look
at your income this year. The Social
Security Administration, which figures
the search charge, looks at your tax
return from 2 years earlier. So, the
premium you pay at 65 is decided by the
income on your tax return from the year
you were 63.
In 2026, the search charge starts when
that income is above $19,000
for a single person or above $218,000
for a married couple filing together. At
the first level, it adds $81.20 20 cents
a month to each person's part B premium.
At the highest level, it adds $487 a
month per person on part B alone. And
there is a separate search charge on
your drug coverage, too. Now, think
about what people do at 63. It is one of
the most common years to sell a house
and downsize. It is a common year to
cash out a stock account, take a big
lump sum from a retirement plan, or
collect a final bonus or a severance
check on the way out of a job. Every one
of those things can push your income for
that single year over the line.
Think about a couple I will call Frank
and Linda. At 63, Frank took his final
year of salary plus a large severance
check when his company restructured.
That one year, their joint income came
in just over $218,000.
Two years later, when they both turned
65 and enrolled in Medicare, each of
them was charged the search charge.
$81.20 20 a month times two people times
12 months. That is $1,948.80
in one year for Medicare coverage
identical to what their neighbors paid
less for. By then, Frank was retired and
their income had fallen by more than
half. Medicare did not care. It was
looking at the year he was 63. The good
news is that there is a fix, and it is a
form most people have never heard of. If
your income dropped because of what
Social Security calls a life-changing
event, you can ask them to use a more
recent year. Life-changing events
include retiring or cutting back your
work hours, the death of a spouse,
marriage, divorce, and losing a pension.
The form is called SSA44.
Frank and Linda qualified because Frank
stopped working. They filed the form,
sent proof, and got the search charge
removed going forward. But they only
found out because a friend told them, "I
want to be honest about one thing.
Selling a house or taking a big one-time
withdrawal is not by itself a
life-changing event on that form. So, if
that is the reason your income spiked,
the better move is planning ahead. If
you know a big sale or withdrawal is
coming, think about which year it lands
in before you do it."
So that is the second age, 63, the year
that sets your Medicare price.
Therefore, you might think the next
thing to watch is 65 itself, and it is,
but there is a hidden age right before
it that almost nobody knows exists, and
it catches exactly the people who are
trying hardest to save. The third age
the government flags you is not a
birthday at all. It is the six months
right before your Medicare starts. And
it only matters if you have a health
savings account, which millions of
working Americans now do. A health
savings account is one of the best tax
deals in the whole system. Money goes in
without being taxed. It grows without
being taxed, and it comes out tax-free
for medical bills. Plenty of people who
work past 65 keep putting money into
their health savings account every
paycheck, right up until they retire. It
feels smart. It is smart right up to the
moment Medicare starts.
Here is the rule straight from Internal
Revenue Service publication 969.
Beginning with the first month you are
enrolled in Medicare, the amount you are
allowed to put into a health savings
account is zero, not reduced zero. And
the publication says this applies to
retroactive Medicare coverage too. And
here is the trap inside that rule. When
you sign up for Medicare Part A after
you turn 65, or when you apply for your
Social Security check after 65, which
automatically signs you up for Part A,
your Part A coverage is usually
backdated. It reaches back up to 6
months, but never earlier than the month
you turned 65. You did not ask for it to
be backdated. It just happens.
So, picture a woman I will call Carol.
Carol kept working until 67 and kept
putting money into her health savings
account through her job. The month she
retired, she applied for social
security. Her Medicare Part A was
automatically backdated 6 months, and
every dollar she had put into her health
savings account during those 6 months
instantly became what the Internal
Revenue Service calls an excess
contribution. She had put in about
$4,000 during those months. If that
money is not taken back out in time, the
Internal Revenue Service charges a 6%
tax on it, and it charges that tax again
every year the money stays in the
account. Carol had no idea until her
accountant caught it. The fix is simple
once you know it. If you have a health
savings account, stop putting money into
it 6 months before you plan to apply for
Medicare or for your Social Security
check. And if you already made
contributions during backdated months,
you can withdraw the excess along with
anything it earned before your tax
return is due and avoid the penalty.
Publication 969 explains exactly how.
And I want you to stop for a moment
right here because what I am about to
tell you raises the stakes for
everything else in this video. Every
rule we have covered so far costs you
money, but the next one does something
worse. It is the only mistake on this
list that cannot be undone. There is no
form to fix it. There is no appeal.
There is no withdrawal that makes it go
away. Once it attaches to you, it stays
with you for the rest of your life. And
every year, it quietly gets more
expensive. It is number four. It is the
one I warned you about at the very
beginning. And the reason most seniors
miss it is that they make it while doing
something they believe is responsible.
The fourth age the government flags you
is 65. And the rule is the Medicare
PartB late enrollment penalty. Here is
how it works straight from medicare.gov.
When you first become eligible for
Medicare, you get a seven-month window
to sign up for Part B. It starts 3
months before the month you turn 65 and
ends 3 months after. If you do not sign
up during that window and you do not
qualify for a special exception, you
will pay an extra 10% on your Part B
premium for every full year you could
have had part B but did not. And here is
the sentence that matters most. That
penalty lasts for as long as you have
part B, which for almost everyone means
for the rest of your life.
Let me show you the real numbers. The
standard part B premium in 2026 is
a month. Medicare's own example says if
you wait 2 years, your penalty is 20%,
which adds $40.58
a month for a total of $243.50.
Now, say you wait three years. That is a
30% penalty, $60.87
extra every month, about $730 a year.
And because the penalty is figured as a
percentage of the premium, every time
the premium goes up, your penalty goes
up with it. Over 20 years of retirement,
a three-year mistake at 65 can cost you
well over $14,000, and there is nothing
you can file to get it back. Now, you
might be thinking, I would never just
forget to sign up for Medicare. And you
are right. Most people who get this
penalty did not forget. They made a
decision.
There is an exception to the penalty. If
you are still working at 65 and you have
health insurance through that current
job or through your spouse's current
job, you can delay part B without a
penalty. And when that job or that
coverage ends, you get an 8-month
special window to sign up. That
exception is real and it protects
millions of people. But here is the
trap. That exception only covers
insurance based on current employment.
Medicare.gov says it in plain words.
Cobra and retiree health plans are not
considered coverage based on current
employment. Think about what that means.
You retire at 64. Your company offers
you COBRA which keeps the exact same
health plan or a retiree health plan
that feels like a benefit you earned.
Same doctors, same card in your wallet.
So you turn 65 and you think, "I already
have good insurance. I will sign up for
Medicare later.
Think about a retired union electrician.
I will call Walter. Walter had an
excellent retiree health plan from his
union. At 65, he skipped part B because
he was already covered and did not want
to pay two premiums. 3 years later, his
retiree plan changed its rules and told
him Medicare had to pay first. When he
went to sign up, he learned two things.
First, he had to wait for the general
enrollment period at the start of the
year. Second, because his retirey plan
never counted as current employment, he
owed a 30% penalty on his part B premium
for life. He did everything he thought
was responsible, and he will pay for it
every month for the rest of his life.
And the same trap exists with Cobra. The
8-month special window starts the day
you stop working, not the day your Cobra
ends. So, if you ride Cobra for 18
months after you retire, the window you
thought you had already closed while you
were still using it.
And Medicare drug coverage, called Part
D, has its own lifetime penalty. 1% of
the national base premium for every
month you went without coverage that
Medicare considers as good as its own.
So, here's the protection, and it is
simple. Before you turn 65, find out in
writing whether your health insurance
counts as coverage based on current
employment. If you are not sure, call
Medicare and ask them directly. If you
are retired and on COBRA or a retiree
plan, sign up for Part B during your
7-month window or within 8 months of the
day you stopped working, whichever
applies to you. That one phone call is
worth more than almost anything else in
this video. So, that is the fourth age.
65. the penalty that never leaves. But
the fifth age is different from all the
others. The fifth age is where the
government actually owes you something
and almost nobody claims it because
almost nobody knows it exists. The fifth
age the government flags you is your
full retirement age, which is 67 for
anyone born in 1960 or later. For people
born a few years earlier, it is a little
younger, between 66 and 67. Remember
Ron, the man from the hardware store? At
62, Social Security withheld $5,000 of
his checks because he earned over the
limit. Ron assumed that money was gone.
He thought it was a fine for working.
Most people think exactly the same
thing. But here is what the Social
Security Administration says in its own
publication on how work affects your
benefits. Benefits withheld because of
the earnings test are not lost. When you
reach full retirement age, Social
Security recalculates your monthly
benefit to give you credit for the
months your checks were withheld. Your
check goes up and it stays up for the
rest of your life.
Social Security's own example makes it
very clear. A person whose benefit was
$910 a month at 62 and who had 12 months
of benefits withheld because of work
would get $975
a month starting at full retirement age.
That is $65 more a month every month for
life. For Ron, whose withheld money was
larger, the increase was bigger. And
there is a second thing that happens at
full retirement age. The earnings test
disappears completely. From the month
you reach full retirement age, you can
earn any amount of money from any job
and Social Security will not withhold a
single dollar of your check. In the year
you reach full retirement age, the limit
is also much higher. In 2026, it is
And Social Security only holds back $1
for every $3 above that and only for the
months before your birthday.
Millions of people quit jobs they
enjoyed in their 60s because they
believed working would cost them their
social security when the government was
actually keeping score to pay it back.
Here is what to do at full retirement
age. Check your My Social Security
account online or call Social Security
and make sure your benefit was
recalculated for any months that were
withheld. The recalculation is supposed
to happen automatically, but it is your
money and it is worth one phone call to
confirm it happened. So that is the
fifth age, full retirement age, the year
the government pays you back. Therefore,
you might think the lesson is simple.
Wait as long as possible and your check
keeps growing. And that is almost true.
But there is a hard stop and people who
miss it lose money that can never be
recovered. The sixth age the government
flags you is 70. And the rule at 70 is
that your raise stops.
Here is how it works. For every month
you wait past full retirement age to
claim social security, your check grows.
The Social Security Administration calls
these delayed retirement credits. They
add up to about 8% a year. If your full
retirement age is 67, and you wait until
70, your check is 124% of what it would
have been at 67 on a $2,000 benefit,
that is $2,480
a month for life. For many people,
waiting to 70 is one of the smartest
financial moves available. But the
credits stop at 70 completely. Waiting
until 71 does not make your check any
bigger. Waiting until 72 does not
either. And here is the trap. Social
Security generally cannot pay you back
benefits for more than six months before
the month you apply.
Think about a widowerower I will call
George. George had heard for years that
waiting made his check bigger, so he
kept waiting. After his wife passed
away, he stopped paying close attention
to the mail and the calendar. He finally
applied at 71. His check was $2,480
a month, the same amount it would have
been at 70. Social Security paid him six
months of back benefits, but the other
six months between his 70th birthday and
the six-month limit were simply gone. 6
months times $2,480,
that is $14,880
he waited for, earned nothing extra for,
and will never get. The fix is almost
embarrassingly simple. If you are
delaying your Social Security to earn
the bigger check, put the month you turn
70 on your calendar now. Better yet,
apply a few months before your 70th
birthday and ask for your benefits to
start the month you turn 70. Social
Security allows you to apply up to 4
months before you want your benefits to
begin. So, that is the sixth age, 70,
when the raise stops. But the seventh
age is the one I opened this video with,
and it is the one where the Internal
Revenue Service is waiting for you. The
seventh age the government flags you is
73. And for anyone born in 1960 or
later, that age moves to 75.
Here is the rule. If you have a
traditional individual retirement
account or a traditional workplace plan
like a 401k, the money in it has never
been taxed. The government let you put
it in tax-free and let it grow tax-free
for decades. And at a certain age, the
government wants its share. That is why
it requires you to start taking money
out every year. It is called a required
minimum distribution. According to the
Internal Revenue Service, if you were
born from 1951 through 1959, you must
start these withdrawals at 73. If you
were born in 1960 or later, you must
start at 75. The amount is figured by
dividing your account balance by a
number from an internal revenue service
table. At 73, that number is 26.5.
So on a $500,000 account, the first
required withdrawal is about $18,868.
And if you do not take it or you take
too little, the Internal Revenue Service
charges an excise tax of 25% of the
amount you should have taken on that
$500,000 account. That is about $4,717.
If you catch the mistake and fix it in
time, the tax drops to 10%. That is
still about $1,887
for a mistake that most people make
simply because nobody told them the
date.
Think about a retired school teacher I
will call Eleanor. Eleanor rolled her
teacher's retirement savings into an
individual retirement account years ago
and never touched it. She had a pension
and her social security, so she never
needed the money. The year she turned 73
came and went. Nobody called her. Her
bank sent a notice she thought was
advertising. When her nephew finally
helped her with her taxes, they found
two years of missed withdrawals and a
penalty that took her breath away. She
had not spent a dollar. She had simply
let the money sit. Now, here is the part
I promised you at the very beginning,
the hidden chain that connects two of
these seven ages.
Remember the second age, 63. Medicare
looks at your income from 2 years
earlier to set your premium. Now look at
the seventh age. The Internal Revenue
Service gives you a small bit of
flexibility on your very first required
withdrawal. You can take it during the
year you turn 73 or you can wait until
April 1st of the following year. Most
people hear that and think, "Great, more
time." So they wait. But here is what
happens. If you take your first
withdrawal on April 1st of the next
year, you still have to take your second
withdrawal by December 31st of that same
year. That means two required
withdrawals land in one single tax year.
On a $500,000 account, that is roughly
$37,000 of extra taxable income stacked
into one year instead of $18,000.
And that one year of doubled income does
two things. First, it can push you into
a higher tax bracket and make more of
your Social Security taxable that year.
And second, two years later, Social
Security looks back at that exact tax
return to set your Medicare premium. The
same two-year look back that caught
Frank and Linda at 63 reaches forward
and catches you again at 75. A decision
you made about the Internal Revenue
Service turns into a sir charge from
Medicare from a different agency 2 years
later, and almost nobody ever connects
the two. And a doubled withdrawal is not
a life-changing event on form SSA44.
So, there is usually no form to fix it.
That is the chain. And here is how you
break it. Take your first required
withdrawal in the same calendar year you
reach the required age. Do not wait
until April. Spread the income out
instead of stacking it. It costs
nothing. It takes one phone call to the
company that holds your account. And it
can protect you from a tax bill and a
Medicare sir charge at the same time.
So, let us put it all together. Seven
ages, seven rules, and what to do about
every one of them. Step one, take one
sheet of paper and write down your seven
dates. The month you turn 62, the year
you turn 63, 6 months before you plan to
start Medicare or Social Security, the
first day of your 7-month Medicare
window around your 65th birthday, your
full retirement age, the month you turn
70, and the year you turn 73 or 75 if
you were born in 1960 or later. Put that
page on your refrigerator.
Step two, create your free My Social
Security account at ssa.gov. It shows
your full retirement age, your estimated
check at 62 at full retirement age and
at 70 and whether any benefits were
withheld. Step three, if you are within
a year of 65 and you are on COBRA or a
retiree health plan, call Medicare
before your birthday and ask one
question. Does my coverage count as
coverage based on current employment? If
the answer is no, sign up for part B on
time. Step four, if you have a health
savings account, stop contributing 6
months before you apply for Medicare or
Social Security. Step five, if your
income dropped because you retired, cut
back your hours, lost a spouse, or lost
