a pension, ask Social Security for form
SSA44, and request a lower Medicare
premium. Step six, at 73 or 75, take
your first required withdrawal in that
same calendar year, not the following
April.
Step seven, if you want free unbiased
help with any Medicare decision, every
state has a free counseling program
called SHIP. Medicare can connect you to
yours. Social Security is 1-8007721213.
Medicare is 1 800 Medicare.

title: Fed WARNING to Every Senior With Savings: Move It Before It's Too Late

segments.text: If you have $100,000 sitting in an
ordinary bank savings account tonight,
your bank is paying you about $370 a
year to hold it, while rising prices are
quietly eating about $3,400 of what that
money can buy. That is a loss of roughly
$3,000 a year every year. And on
September 16th, the Federal Reserve put
the reason in writing. In its official
statement the day it raised interest
rates for the first time in roughly
three years, the Fed used four plain
words. Inflation remains elevated. That
was the warning. It was not a press
conference aimed at you. And nobody from
your bank called to explain it. But if
you are over 65 and you keep your
savings where most seniors keep them,
that warning was written about your
money. And the slow leak in your savings
account is only the first of six places
where seniors keep their cash that are
costing them, exposing them, or quietly
setting them up to lose it. Number four
on this list is the one that surprises
almost everyone because it is something
millions of loving parents do on purpose
thinking they are being careful. And
before we are done, I am going to show
you one short form at your own bank. It
is usually a single line. Most seniors
have never been told it exists. And it
can raise the federal insurance
protecting your money at one bank from
And hand that money straight to your
family the day you die without it ever
going near a probate court. It costs
nothing. It takes about 10 minutes. Stay
with me because I will come back to it
and it may be the most valuable 10
minutes you spend this year. First, you
need to understand what actually
happened in September because the
headlines got it backwards. When the
Federal Reserve raises its rate, most
people assume their savings account
starts paying more. It does not work
that way. The Fed sets the rate that
banks charge each other overnight. It
does not set the rate your bank pays
you. Your bank sets that number on its
own and it can change it whenever it
likes for any reason without waiting for
the Fed and without asking you. So, here
is what the Fed's own numbers show. The
Federal Reserve's target rate is now
between 3 and 3/4 and 4%. The Bureau of
Labor Statistics reports that consumer
prices rose 3.4% over the past year. And
the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation, the agency that insures
your bank deposits, publishes the
national average rate that banks
actually pay savers. As of September
21st, the National Average Savings
Account, pays 0.37%.
The average interest checking account
pays 0.07%.
Read those two numbers again. Prices are
rising at 3.4%. 4%. The average savings
account is paying about onetenth of
that. That gap is not an accident. The
bank borrows your money at almost
nothing, puts it to work at far higher
rates, and keeps the difference. And the
Fed's warning that inflation remains
elevated means the gap is not closing on
its own.
My name is Mark Callaway, and on this
channel, I take the rules that quietly
cost seniors money and read them to you
in plain language, straight from the
federal agencies that wrote them. no
sales pitch and nothing to buy. Just the
rules, the numbers, and what to do about
them. So, let us go through the six
places one at a time. Starting with the
one almost everybody reading this has
right now. The first place you should
never keep a large amount of cash is an
ordinary savings account at a big bank
that pays the national average. I want
to be very clear because this is not
about panic. Your money in that account
is safe from the bank failing up to the
insurance limit. And I will get to that
limit in a moment. The problem is not
safety. The problem is that the money is
shrinking while it sits there. And the
statement makes it look like it is
growing.
Let me show you what that looks like
over a real retirement. I want you to
picture a couple I will call Walter and
June. When Walter retired, they put
into the savings account at the same
bank where they had banked for 40 years.
It felt responsible. It was insured. It
was local. And the teller knew them by
name. Every month, the statement showed
a few dollars of interest. And every
month the balance went up a little. For
years that felt like progress. But here
is the arithmetic the statement never
shows you. At the national average rate
earns about $666 a year. At 3.4%
inflation, that same $180,000
loses about $6,120
of buying power in the same year. So,
while the balance on paper went up by
what that money could actually buy at
the grocery store and the pharmacy went
down by more than $5,400
every single year. Over 10 years of
retirement, Walter and June did not lose
a dollar on paper, and they quietly lost
the buying power of tens of thousands of
dollars in real life.
Now, I am not telling you to empty your
savings account. You need money you can
reach in an emergency the same day with
no penalty. For most households, that is
a few months of expenses. The problem is
the big balance that sits there for
years because moving it feels like work
or because nobody ever explained that a
different equally safe place pays many
times more. I will show you exactly
where that place is later in this video.
And it is backed by the same federal
government that insures your bank. And
checking is even worse. The national
average interest checking account pays
on $100,000. That is $70 a year against
$3,400 of lost buying power. So that is
the first place, the slow leak. But the
second place is not slow at all and it
is where people with the largest savings
are exposed without realizing it. The
second place you should never keep your
cash is in one bank in one name above
This is the federal insurance limit and
it is one of the most misunderstood
numbers in all of personal finance. Here
is the rule straight from the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation. Your
deposits are insured up to $250,000
per depositor, perins insured bank, per
ownership category. Every word in that
sentence matters. Per depositor means
per person. Perins insured bank means
per separately chartered bank, not per
branch. And per ownership category means
the type of account such as an account
in your name alone, a joint account, or
a retirement account. If you are a
single owner and you have $400,000 in
accounts in your name alone at one bank,
the first $250,000
is insured. The other $150,000
is not.
Now, I want to be fair about the risk
because this channel does not deal in
fear for its own sake. Since the FDIC
began operating in 1934, no depositor
has ever lost a single penny of insured
money. Not one. That is an extraordinary
record. The operative word in that
sentence is insured. When banks do fail,
and banks do still fail, the insured
money is protected, and the uninsured
money is at the mercy of how the failure
is resolved. Most seniors who have more
than the limit at one bank have no idea
they are over it because the number grew
slowly through a house sale, an
inheritance, a pension rollover, or a
lifetime of careful saving. And nobody
at the bank ever pointed it out.
Think about a widow I will call
Margaret. When her husband died, his
life insurance and the sale of their
second home went into her account at the
bank they had always used. She now had
just over $400,000 there in her name
alone. She felt safer than she had ever
felt in her life. And she had $150,000
sitting uninsured in an account where it
was earning a fraction of 1% without a
single person ever telling her either
fact.
The fix is not complicated and it does
not require an adviser. You can spread
money across more than one bank. You can
use different ownership categories and
there is a free tool from the FDIC
itself called EDI, the electronic
deposit insurance estimator that will
tell you in a few minutes exactly how
much of your money is covered. But the
most powerful fix is the one I promised
you at the beginning. The single line at
your bank that can multiply your
coverage at that same bank by five. Hold
that thought. I am going to show you
exactly how it works because it also
solves the problem in number four. So
that is the second place. Therefore, you
might think the answer is to take the
cash out of the bank entirely and lock
it up somewhere you control. And that is
precisely how millions of seniors walk
straight into the third place. The third
place you should never keep your cash is
in a safe deposit box. This one
surprises people because a safe deposit
box feels like the safest place in the
whole building. It is behind the vault
door. It takes two keys. The bank checks
your identification. How could anything
be safer than that? Here is what the
FDIC itself says. A safe deposit box is
not a deposit. The contents of a safe
deposit box, including any cash you put
inside it, are not insured by the FDIC.
Not up to $250,000,
not up to any amount. If there is a
fire, a flood, or a theft, the federal
deposit insurance that protects your
checking account does not protect the
envelope of cash in your box. And the
bank's own rental agreement for that box
usually limits what the bank is
responsible for, sometimes severely.
Most people have never read that
agreement and they signed it decades
ago.
Think about what that means. Imagine you
keep $20,000 in cash in a safe deposit
box because you remember 1929 or your
parents did and you want money nobody
can freeze. That $20,000 has zero
federal insurance and it earns zero
interest. At 3.4% inflation, it loses
about $680 of buying power every year it
sits in that drawer. and it is protected
by nothing but a lock and the fine print
you signed. And there is a second
problem most families only discover at
the worst possible moment. In many
states, when the only person on a safe
deposit box dies, the bank restricts
access to the box until an executive is
appointed or a court process is
followed. Families have been unable to
get the will out of the box because the
will is inside the box. The cash that
was supposed to be there for an
emergency is locked away exactly when
the emergency happens.
A safe deposit box is a fine place for
papers and photographs. It is a poor
place for cash. But the fourth place on
this list is the one I warned you about
at the start because the danger does not
come from a bank, a fire, or a stranger.
It comes from love. The fourth place you
should never keep your cash is in a
joint bank account with one of your
adult children set up for convenience.
This is extraordinarily common. A parent
gets older, maybe after a fall or a
hospital stay, and a son or daughter
says, "Let me get on your account so I
can help pay the bills if something
happens." The bank adds the child as a
joint owner in 5 minutes. Everyone feels
relieved, and almost nobody in that room
understands what just happened legally.
Here is what the Consumer Financial
Protection Bureau explains in its
guidance for families. A joint owner on
a bank account generally has full legal
access to every dollar in it. Not half.
every dollar. Your child can withdraw
all of it at any time without your
permission. And in most cases, the bank
will simply let them because on paper,
it is their money, too. That is the
first problem. And in families that love
each other, it rarely comes up. It is
the second and third problems that catch
good families.
The second problem is that money in a
joint account can become reachable by
the other owner's creditors. If your son
is sued after a car accident, if he runs
up debt, if a business goes under, or in
some cases, if he goes through a
divorce, the account that has your name
on it and his name on it can be pulled
into his trouble. Money you saved over a
lifetime can be frozen or garnished to
pay a judgment that has nothing to do
with you. Your money was never meant to
be your child's money. But the moment
their name went on the account, the law
in most states started treating part or
all of it as if it were.
Think about a retired school teacher I
will call Dorothy. She added her son to
her savings account so he could help
with her bills after her knee surgery.
The account held about $60,000, which
was most of her emergency savings. Two
years later, her son was in a car
accident that was his fault, and the
other driver's lawyer won a judgment
against him. When they went looking for
his assets, they found a joint account
with $60,000 in it. Dorothy spent months
and legal fees proving that the money
was hers and had always been hers. Some
parents in that situation get it all
back. Some do not. Every one of them
wishes somebody had told them there was
a different way. And the third problem
is what happens when you die. A joint
account usually passes directly to the
surviving joint owner, no matter what
your will says. If you have three
children and only one of them is on the
account for convenience, that one child
can legally end up with the whole
balance. And the other two can end up
with nothing from that account, even if
your will divides everything equally.
That is how brothers and sisters stop
speaking to each other at the funeral.
Not out of greed most of the time, but
because the account said one thing and
the will said another and the account
wins.
Now, here is the part that matters. You
can get all the convenience you wanted
without any of these three problems.
Most banks allow you to name a person as
an authorized signer, sometimes called a
convenience signer, who can write checks
and pay bills for you without becoming
an owner of the money. A properly
prepared financial power of attorney can
do the same thing. And the single line I
promised you at the start of this video,
which I will show you in just a few
minutes, lets your children inherit the
account instantly when you die, while
giving them no access and no ownership
at all while you are alive. Ask your
bank exactly what your account agreement
says and what options they offer. The
difference between a joint owner and a
beneficiary is one word on a form and it
can decide whether your savings stay
yours.
So that is the fourth place. Therefore,
it is no surprise that some seniors
decide the only person they can trust
with their money is themselves and they
bring it home. But the fifth place is
where the people hunting for senior
savings are waiting. The fifth place you
should never keep a large amount of cash
is hidden in your own home. The coffee
can, the freezer, the shoe box in the
closet, the envelope under the mattress.
I understand exactly why people do it.
Cash at home cannot be frozen by a bank,
cannot be charged a fee, and is there in
the middle of the night if the power
goes out. For a small amount of
emergency money, that makes sense. For a
large amount, it is one of the most
dangerous places your savings can be.
Start with insurance. Most people assume
their homeowners policy covers
everything in the house. But the
standard homeowners policy form used
across the insurance industry sets a
special limit on money, banknotes, and
gold. In the standard form, that limit
is $200. $200. If you keep $15,000 in a
coffee can and the house burns or a
burglar finds it, your policy under that
standard form may pay you $200 of it.
Check your own policy because some are
different, but most people who check are
shocked.
And the second danger is worse than FIRE
because it is aimed directly at seniors
on purpose. The Federal Trade Commission
tracks the reports people file about
scams. Its own data shows that the money
lost by people 60 and older who were
robbed of $100,000 or more by criminals
pretending to be a business or a
government agency went from $55 million
in 2020 to $445 million in 2024. That is
eight times as much in 4 years. Reports
of seniors losing $10,000 or more than
quadrupled. And when the FTC looked at
how those seniors paid the criminals,
cash was one of the most common ways.
Here's how it works. And I want you to
listen carefully because it uses the
very news we started this video with.
The phone rings. The caller says they
are from your bank's fraud department or
from the Federal Trade Commission or
even from the Federal Reserve. They tell
you your accounts have been compromised,
that the government has issued a
warning, and that you need to withdraw
your cash to protect it. Then they send
a courier to your door to pick up the
cash or they tell you to buy gold or to
feed the money into a Bitcoin machine at
a gas station. They are calm,
professional, and very convincing. And
every senior who has lost their savings
this way thought they were being
careful. So, I want you to remember this
sentence from the Federal Trade
Commission. And I want you to say it out
loud to anyone in your family who is
over 65. No government agency will ever
tell you to move your money to protect
it. Not the Federal Reserve, not the
FTC, not Social Security, not the IRS.
No real government agency will ever ask
you to withdraw cash, buy gold, or hand
money to a courier. The Federal
Reserve's warning this fall was about
inflation. If anyone ever calls you
using that warning to tell you to move
your money, that is not the Fed. That is
a thief. Hang up and call your bank
yourself at the number printed on the
back of your own card. So, that is the
fifth place. But the sixth place is the
strangest one on the list because the
money in it belongs to you. It is backed
by the full faith of the United States
government and it has quietly stopped
growing without anyone telling you.
The sixth place you should never leave
your money is in old paper savings bonds
sitting in a drawer past the day they
stopped earning. Many seniors have
savings bonds. Some bought them through
a payroll plan decades ago. Some were
given them at birth or a wedding. Some
found them in a parents desk after a
funeral. And almost everyone assumes a
savings bond just keeps growing for as
long as you hold it. It does not. Series
E and Series I savings bonds stop
earning interest at 30 years. On the
30th anniversary, the interest stops
completely and permanently. The bond is
still worth what it grew to, and you can
still cash it, but from that day
forward, it is the same as money in a
coffee can, losing buying power to
inflation every single year.
And the scale of this is staggering. The
United States Treasury is holding
roughly $29.7 billion in savings bonds
that have matured and never been cashed.
That is about 80 million bonds earning
nothing owed to Americans who either do
not know they have them or do not know
they have stopped growing. And the old
federal search tool called Treasury Hunt
was shut down in September of 2025. So,
if you think there may be matured bonds
in your family, the search now runs
through Treasury Direct, the Treasury's
own website, and through your state's
unclaimed property office. So, pull out
that envelope tonight. Look at the issue
date on every bond. If it is more than
30 years old, it has stopped earning and
it is time to cash it or move it. If you
have lost the paper bonds, the Treasury
has forms to replace them and Treasury
Direct can walk you through it.
Those are the six places. the low-paying
bank account, more than the insurance
limit at one bank, the safe deposit box,
the joint account with a child, cash at
home, and matured savings bonds. But
knowing where not to keep your money is
only half of the answer. The other half
is where it actually belongs. And that
is where the Fed's warning turns into
good news for you. Remember what
happened in September? The Federal
Reserve raised its rate to between 3 and
3/4 and 4%. Your bank did not have to
pass that on to you, but the United
States Treasury does automatically every
single week because the Treasury sells
its own short-term savings called
Treasury bills. And the rate on those
bills moves right along with the rate
the Fed sets.
You can buy Treasury bills directly from
the government at Treasury Direct with
no broker and no fee in terms.
They are backed by the full faith and
credit of the United States. And here is
a quiet bonus most seniors never hear
about. Under federal law, the interest
on Treasury bills is exempt from state
and local income tax. So, if you live in
a state with an income tax, a Treasury
bill pays you more after tax than a bank
account paying the very same rate. On
$100,000, the difference between the
national average savings rate and a
Treasury bill paying close to the rate
the Federal Reserve just set can be well
over $3,000 a year. That is the $3,000
leak from the first place on this list
plugged.
There is a second option that was built
for exactly the warning the Fed gave. It
is called the series 1 savings bond and
its rate is tied directly to inflation.
For bonds bought between May 1st and
October 31st of 2026, the Treasury is
paying 4.26%.
You can buy up to $10,000 a year per
person electronically. You have to hold
it at least one year. And if you cash it
before five years, you give up the last
three months of interest. So, it is for
money you will not need right away. But
it is the one savings product whose rate
rises when inflation rises, which is
precisely the problem the Fed warned
about. And if you would rather keep
everything at a bank, that is fine, too.
Just shop. The FDIC's own figures show
the national average 12-month
certificate of deposit pays 1.73%
and many insured banks pay far more than
the average. The average is dragged down
by the biggest banks paying almost
nothing. You are not required to accept
the average. Moving a large balance to
an insured bank that pays more is not
risky. It is simply refusing to fund
somebody else's profit. Now, I promised
you at the very beginning that I would
show you one short form, usually a
single line at your own bank that can
raise the federal insurance on your
money at one bank from $250,000
and pass that money straight to your
family without probate. Here it is.
It is called a payable on death
designation. Sometimes the bank calls it
a POD beneficiary and sometimes it
appears as in trust for. All it does is
name the people who will receive the
money in the account when you die. That
is all. You stay the only owner. You
keep complete control. Your
beneficiaries cannot touch a dollar
while you are alive. They do not need to
sign anything. And in most cases, they
do not even need to be told.
But here is what almost nobody knows. On
April 1st of 2024, the FDIC changed its
rules for these accounts. Under the
current rule, an account with payable on
death beneficiaries is insured up to
for each beneficiary you name, up to
five beneficiaries for each owner at
each bank. Name one beneficiary and you
are covered up to $250,000.
Name three and you are covered up to
Name five, whether they are children,
grandchildren, or others you choose, and
you are covered up to $1,250,000
at that one bank from a single owner.
Go back to Margaret, the widow with
$400,000 in her name alone and $150,000
sitting uninsured. If Margaret walks
into her bank and adds her two daughters
as payable on death beneficiaries, her
coverage on that account can rise to
Every dollar she has is now insured at
the same bank with the same teller who
knows her by name and she did not have
to move a penny.
And now go back to Dorothy, the school
teacher who added her son to her account
for convenience. If instead of making
him a joint owner, she had named him as
a payable on death beneficiary and added
him as an authorized signer if she
needed help with bills, her son's car
accident could not have reached her
savings because it was never his money.
He would have had no ownership at all
while she was alive. And when she dies,
the account goes straight to him or to
all of her children equally if she names
all of them without waiting for a
probate court without a lawyer and
without the account and the will
fighting each other at the funeral.
That is the single line, one form,
usually one page, often done at the
teller window or online in a few minutes
and free at almost every bank. It fixes
the insurance limit problem from the
second place and it fixes the joint
account problem from the fourth place at
the same time. And most seniors have
never been told it exists because nobody
profits from telling you. So here is
exactly what to do starting tonight.
First, pull out your most recent bank
statement and find the interest rate. If
it starts with a zero, you are almost
certainly being paid less than onetenth
of the rate of inflation. Decide how
much you truly need to reach the same
day. keep that and look at moving the
rest to a treasury bill, an Ibond, or a
higherp paying insured bank.
Second, add up how much you have at each
bank in each type of account. If any
single bank holds more than $250,000 of
yours in one ownership category, use the
FDIC's free estimator at eddie.fdic.gov
or call the FDIC directly at
Third, ask your bank to add payable on
death beneficiaries to every account
that does not have them. If one of your
children is on your account as a joint
owner only for convenience, ask the bank
and your family attorney about switching
them to an authorized signer and a
beneficiary instead.
Fourth, open your safe deposit box and
your desk drawers. Move large amounts of
cash into insured accounts. Check the
date on every savings bond and cash any
that are more than 30 years old through
treasurydirect.gov.
Fifth, tell every senior you love the
sentence from the Federal Trade
Commission. No government agency will
ever tell you to move your money to
protect it. If anyone calls with that
request, hang up and report it to the
National Elder Fraud Hotline at 1833
The Federal Reserve told the whole
country in writing that inflation
remains elevated. Your bank was never
going to call and explain what that
means for your savings because the gap
between what they pay you and what your
money is worth is how they make theirs.
But you know now, six places your cash
is shrinking, exposed, or waiting to be
taken, and one line on one form that
protects up to 1,250,000
at a single bank. Start with the
statement in your own kitchen drawer
tonight. And if you have one question
about whether your money is covered,
call the FDIC at 1877-2753342.

title: 7 Retirement Assets the IRS Can't Touch After 65 (Most Don't Know)

segments.text: The Internal Revenue Service will
quietly collect more than $88,000
from a retiree who saved $400,000 in an
ordinary retirement account. And almost
none of those seniors ever learn that
seven different kinds of money sitting
in their own name are legally off limits
to the IRS entirely. Not reduced, not
deferred, off limits. The government
cannot tax them. And in one case at the
very end of this list, it cannot ever
collect a single dollar of the tax that
built up over an entire lifetime. Most
seniors protect exactly one of these
seven, if they protect any of them at
all, and they hand the rest straight to
Washington by accident. I am going to
walk you through all seven in plain
language with the exact dollar figures
and the exact federal rules behind each
one. And there is one move near the end
of this list, the seventh one, that does
something the others do not. It does not
just avoid a tax this year. It hands
your children a lifetime of growth on
your home and your savings. And the IRS
never collects $1 of the tax on it. But
it only works if you refuse to do the
single thing that almost every senior is
told to do by a well-meaning neighbor or
a late night radio show. do that one
thing and you forfeit the whole loophole
and hand your kids the tax bill instead.
Keep that in the back of your mind
because I will come back to it and it
may be the most important 90 seconds in
this entire video. First, understand why
this matters so much right now. The
rules that decide how much of your
retirement the IRS can take were written
decades ago and many of the numbers
inside them have never been updated for
inflation. That means every year quietly
more of your money drifts into the range
where it becomes taxable. Unless you
know which accounts and which kinds of
income the law has permanently walled
off. The seniors who keep the most of
their own money are not the ones who
earn the most. They are the ones who
knew where the walls were. So, let me
show you the walls one at a time. The
first asset the IRS cannot touch is
money inside a Roth account. This is a
Roth individual retirement account or a
Roth version of a workplace plan and it
is the cleanest, simplest protection in
the entire tax code. Here is the rule.
When you put money into a WTH, you
already paid the tax on it that year.
So, the government made a deal with you
because it already took its cut going
in. It agrees to never tax that money
again coming out. Not the original
amount you put in, and this is the part
people miss. not $1 of everything it
grew into over the years. Under the law,
once your Roth account has been open for
at least 5 years and you are older than
59 and a half, every withdrawal is what
the code calls a qualified distribution.
And a qualified distribution is
completely free of federal income tax.
Think about what that means at the scale
of a real retirement. Imagine you have
$400,000 saved. If that $400,000 sits in
a traditional retirement account, every
dollar you pull out is taxable and at a
modest 22% rate, you would hand the
Internal Revenue Service roughly $88,000
over the course of your retirement. If
that same $400,000 sits in a Roth
instead, the tax the IRS collects on
those withdrawals is zero. Nothing. That
is the same money, the same balance, and
the difference is $88,000
kept in your pocket instead of mailed to
Washington. I want you to picture two
men who retired on the same street in
the same year. Harold and Raymond. They
saved almost exactly the same amount,
but Harold's savings sat in a
traditional account, and every
withdrawal he took to fix his roof or
help a grandchild came with a tax bill
stapled to it.
Raymond had quietly moved a chunk of his
into a Wroth years earlier. And when he
pulled money out for the very same
reasons, the IRS got nothing. Same
street, same savings, same needs. One of
them spent his 70s handing a slice of
every withdrawal to Washington, and the
other did not, and the only difference
between them was that one man understood
this wall, and the other never had it
explained. There is one more quiet gift
buried in the Roth rules. A Roth
individual retirement account has no
required minimum distributions during
your lifetime. The government cannot
force you to pull money out at 73 the
way it can with a traditional account.
You leave it alone tax-free for as long
as you like. So why does almost everyone
only have the taxable kind? because for
years the traditional account was the
default and nobody sat these seniors
down and explained the trade. That is
the first wall. But the second wall is
even older, older than most of the
people watching this and even fewer
seniors ever use it. The second asset
the IRS cannot touch is the interest
from municipal bonds. A municipal bond
is simply a loan you make to a state or
a local government, a city, a county, a
school district, so they can build roads
and schools and water systems. In
exchange for lending them that money,
they pay you interest. And here is the
rule that has stood for more than a
century. Under the tax code, the
interest on most of these state and
local bonds is exempt from federal
income tax. The IRS cannot touch it. Let
me put a number on it. Say you earn
$10,000 of interest in a year. If that
$10,000 came from an ordinary savings
account or a certificate of deposit, it
is fully taxable. And at 22%, you would
owe the IRS about $2,200 on it. If that
same $10,000 came from qualified
municipal bonds, the federal tax you owe
on it is zero. It still shows up on a
form the bank sends you, but it is
walled off from your taxable income. For
a retiree who has moved money out of the
stock market and wants steady,
predictable income without feeding the
IRS every year, this is one of the
quietest and most durable protections in
the entire code. There are fine points
and I will always tell you the fine
points because I am not here to sell you
anything. Some specialized bonds can
interact with another tax and whether
your own state also exempts the interest
depends on where you live. But the core
federal rule is simple and it is real.
Municipal bond interest is federally
tax-free. Now, before I go any further,
let me finally do the thing I have been
putting off. My name is Mark Callaway. I
spend my days reading the parts of the
tax code and the benefits rules that
affect older Americans. The parts
written in language designed to be
skipped and I translate them into plain
English so that you can keep the money
that is legally yours. I do not sell
financial products. I do not manage
anyone's money. Everything I am telling
you today traces back to the Internal
Revenue Code, to Social Security's own
published rules, and to the Internal
Revenue Services own publications. And I
will point you to them at the end. What
I want you to feel by the time we are
done is not fear. It is the opposite. It
is the quiet relief of realizing how
much of your own money the government
was never allowed to take in the first
place. So, let us keep going because the
third wall is the one that almost nobody
outside of accountants ever hears about.
The third asset the IRS cannot touch is
money inside a health savings account.
Now, stay with me here because this is
the single most tax favored account that
exists in American law. And most seniors
either do not have one or do not
understand what they are holding. A
health savings account does something no
other account does. It is tax-free three
separate times. The money goes in and
you get to deduct it. So it lowers your
taxes that year. The money grows inside
the account and that growth is never
taxed. And when you pull the money out
to pay for a qualified medical expense,
that withdrawal is tax-free, too. In
grow out, three walls, not one. Most
accounts give you one tax break if you
are lucky. A traditional retirement
account lets the money grow untaxed, but
taxes you on the way out. A Roth taxes
you on the way in, but never again. But
the health savings account is the only
thing in the entire tax code that
refuses to tax you at any of the three
doors. And once you see that, you
understand why financial people quietly
treat it as the most valuable account a
person can own. For the year, a person
with self-only coverage can put in
A family can put in $8,550.
And if you are 55 or older, you can add
another $1,000 on top of that as a
catch-up. And here's the part built
specifically for seniors. As long as you
spend that money on a qualified medical
cost, and in retirement, that includes
your Medicare premiums, your dental
work, your vision, your hearing aids,
and your long-term care costs. The
withdrawal is never taxed at any age,
ever. There used to be a penalty if you
pulled the money out for something that
was not medical. But the moment you turn
65, that 20% penalty disappears
completely. After 65, a non-medical
withdrawal is simply treated like a
normal retirement account withdrawal.
So, at worst, it behaves like your
traditional account, and at best, for
anything medical, it is pure tax-free
money. For a senior facing years of
medical bills, that is a wall the IRS
built and then handed you the key to.
That is three. And I want you to notice
a pattern forming because it is going to
matter for the rest of this list. Every
one of these walls exists in writing in
federal law right now today. The
government is not hiding them exactly.
It is just counting on the fact that no
one reads the code and no one explains
it. Which brings me to the fourth one.
And the fourth one is the one I promised
was different. This is the move most
seniors have never heard of. and it is
the closest thing to a magic trick that
honest tax law allows.
The fourth asset the IRS cannot touch is
a qualified charitable distribution. I
know that sounds like accountant
language. So, let me tell you exactly
what it does because it is remarkable.
If you are 70 and a half or older, you
are allowed to send money directly from
your retirement account to a charity, a
church, a food bank, a veterans group,
whatever you choose. When you do it this
specific way, sending it straight from
the account to the charity without it
ever touching your own hands, that money
is completely excluded from your income.
The IRS acts as if you never received
it. But, and this is the part that makes
grown accountants smile, it still counts
as your required minimum distribution
for the year. The government forces most
seniors to pull a certain amount out of
their retirement account every year
after a certain age. And that force
withdrawal is normally taxable.
A qualified charitable distribution lets
you satisfy that requirement without the
money ever showing up as taxable income.
You can move up to $18,000
this way in a single year. and a married
couple can each do their own. Let me
show you why this is so much more
powerful than just writing a check to
your church. If you took $18,000
out as a normal withdrawal and then
donated it, that withdrawal would first
land on your tax return as income. At
22%, that is roughly $23,760
of tax you would owe before you gave a
penny. But because a qualified
charitable distribution never enters
your income at all, it does something a
normal donation cannot. It can lower how
much of your social security gets taxed
and it can keep you underneath a
Medicare premium sir charge that is
triggered by your income. You are not
just avoiding tax on the gift, you are
shrinking the income number that every
other senior tax trap is measured
against.
It is the one move on this list that
reaches out and protects the other
items, too. And almost nobody uses it
because almost nobody has ever had it
explained to them in plain words. I
think of a woman named Eleanor, a widow
who gave faithfully to her church every
single month out of her own checking
account, proud that she never missed.
She was also being forced to take a
withdrawal from her retirement account
every year and paying tax on all of it.
When someone finally showed her that she
could route that same giving straight
from her retirement account to her
church, the giving did not change by a
dollar, but her taxable income dropped.
Less of her social security got taxed
and her Medicare premium stopped
creeping upward. She had been doing the
right thing the expensive way for years
purely because no one told her the
freeway existed. That is what this
fourth wall is. It is generosity the IRS
is not allowed to tax.
Therefore, if you take only one new idea
out of this entire video and carry it to
whoever helps you with your taxes, let
it be those three words: qualified
charitable distribution.
Now, let me pause here right around the
middle because I want to make sure you
do not miss what is coming. We have
covered accounts and income so far. Roth
money, municipal interest, the health
account, the charitable move. But the
last three walls are different in kind.
And the very last one, the seventh, is
the one I opened this video with. It is
the loophole that lets the IRS lose an
entire lifetime of tax. And it is the
one that a single common mistake can
destroy. Most of the seniors watching
this have never been warned about that
mistake. And some of them are about to
make it this year with the best of
intentions.
So stay with me all the way to number
seven because the difference between
doing it right and doing it wrong can be
more than $50,000 handed to the
government that never had to be. The
fifth asset the IRS cannot touch is a
life insurance death benefit. This one
is short and it is a relief for the
people you love. Under the tax code,
when a life insurance policy pays out
because the insured person has died, the
money that goes to the beneficiary is
generally not counted as income. The IRS
cannot tax the death benefit. So, if you
carry a policy that will pay $250,000 to
your spouse or to your children, that
full $250,000 arrives in their hands
free of federal income tax at the exact
moment they need it most. when they are
burying you and trying to keep the
household running. There are narrow
exceptions and I will always be honest
about them. If the insurance company
holds the money and pays interest on it,
that interest can be taxable. And there
are unusual situations where a policy
was sold from one person to another. But
the ordinary case, the case that covers
almost everyone listening is clean.
The death benefit is tax-free to the
people you leave it to. That is a wall
the IRS cannot climb. Built specifically
to protect a grieving family. I once
heard from a daughter named Ruth, whose
father had carried a modest policy for
decades, worried the whole time that the
government would take a third of it
before she ever saw a penny. He was
wrong to worry. When he passed, the full
amount arrived in her account with
nothing withheld. And it was the thing
that let her keep her mother in the
family home instead of selling it in a
panic. He spent years quietly afraid of
attacks that the law never allowed in
the first place. Therefore, having
protected the money you leave behind,
let us protect the money you live on
right now. Because the sixth wall guards
the one check almost every senior in
this country depends on. The sixth asset
the IRS cannot touch is a large piece of
your social security itself, plus a
brand new deduction that Washington just
handed to seniors and that many have not
claimed. Let me take the social security
part first because there is a myth I
need to kill. A lot of seniors believe
the government taxes their entire social
security check. It does not. It cannot.
By law, no matter how high your income
climbs, the most of your social security
benefit that can ever be taxed is 85%.
Which means at least 15% of your benefit
is always permanently free of federal
tax for everyone. And it gets better at
the lower end. If your combined income
is below $25,000 as a single person or
below $32,000 as a married couple filing
together, then none of your social
security is taxed at all. Zero. The IRS
cannot touch a dollar of it.
Now, here is the quiet scandal inside
that rule. And I promised you I would
always tell you the truth. Those two
numbers, the $25,000 and the $32,000
were written into the law back in 1983.
and they have never once been adjusted
for inflation. They are frozen. So every
year, as ordinary cost of living raises
push seniors past those frozen lines,
more retirees get pulled into paying tax
on benefits that were never meant to be
taxed at their income level. That is
exactly why the fourth item, the
charitable move, is so powerful because
it lowers the income number that decides
whether you cross those lines. But there
is also good news, and it is new. For
the tax years running from this year
through the year 2028, any American who
is 65 or older can claim an additional
deduction of $6,000. A married couple
where both spouses are 65 can claim
$12,000 between them. You can take it
whether or not you itemize, and it sits
on top of the extra standard deduction
seniors already get. It does begin to
phase out for higher incomes above
$75,000 for a single filer and $150,000
for a couple. But for the great majority
of seniors, that is $6,000 of your
income. The IRS simply agreed to stop
taxing. And a lot of people have no idea
it exists. Check that you claimed it.
Check that whoever prepared your return
claimed it. It is real money. Therefore,
we arrive at the seventh wall. the one I
have been promising you since the first
30 seconds of this video. This is the
one that does not just save you a tax
this year. This is the one that can
erase an entire lifetime of tax. And it
is also the one that a single
well-intentioned mistake can throw away.
It is called stepped up basis. And once
you understand it, you will understand
why the truly wealthy have used it for
generations while ordinary families walk
right past it. Here's how it works. Say
you bought a home decades ago for
$50,000 and today it is worth $400,000.
That is $350,000
of growth. Normally, if you sold that
home, the IRS would want to tax that
gain. But under the tax code, when you
pass away and leave that home to your
children, something remarkable happens.
The cost basis of that home, the number
the gain is measured from, resets to
what the home is worth on the day you
die. It steps up. So, in the eyes of the
IRS, your children did not inherit a
$50,000 house that grew to $400,000.
They inherited a $400,000 house. Period.
of lifetime growth is simply erased from
the tax books. If your children turn
around and sell it, the taxable gain can
be zero.
at a 15% capital gains rate. That is
roughly $52,500
of tax that the Internal Revenue Service
will never ever collect. And it does not
only apply to your home. It applies to
your stocks, your mutual funds, your
brokerage account, all of it. But here
is the trap, and this is the mistake I
begged you to stay for, because seniors
make it every single day trying to be
helpful. Somebody tells them just add
your kids to the deed now or just give
them the stocks while you are alive. It
will make things simpler and it feels
generous and it feels smart. It is
neither. When you give an asset away
while you are still living, your
children usually take over your old low
basis, the $50,000, not the stepped up
value. So instead of the growth being
erased, the entire $350,000 gain lands
on your children, and the IRS collects
the tax it would otherwise have lost
forever. The exact move meant to help
them is the move that forfeits the
loophole. The step up only works if the
asset passes through your estate at
death, not before. For the overwhelming
majority of seniors, this costs nothing
to protect because the separate federal
estate tax does not even begin until an
estate is worth almost $14 million. So,
this is not a rich person's tool. It is
your tool. You just have to not give it
away by accident. Let me show you the
trap with two neighbors, George and
Frank. both widowers, both with a
paidoff home worth $400,000. Both
wanting to leave it clean to a single
son. George heard the popular advice and
added his son to the deed while he was
still alive, thinking he was saving
everyone trouble. Frank did nothing. He
simply left a will and kept the house in
his own name. When each man passed, the
difference was staggering. Frank's son
inherited the home at its stepped up
value, sold it, and owed the IRS nothing
on the gain.
George's son inherited his father's old
low basis along with half the deed. And
when he sold, the IRS handed him a
capital gains bill north of $50,000.
Two identical houses, two loving
fathers. One phone call to an attorney
would have told George exactly what it
told Frank's family for free, and it
would have kept more than $50,000 inside
his own bloodline instead of sending it
to Washington. And that closes the loop
I opened at the very beginning. The
seventh wall, stepped up basis, hands
your children a lifetime of growth
completely free of the tax the IRS would
otherwise collect, but only if you keep
the asset in your own name until death
instead of gifting it or adding them to
the deed early. The single most loving
mistake a senior can make is also the
one that quietly hands the government
tens of thousands of dollars that your
family should have kept.
So, let me bring all seven walls
together because I want you to leave
here able to act, not just able to
worry. Here is what to do, and none of
it requires a lawyer to get started.
First, pull your latest retirement
account statement tonight and find out
whether any of it is Roth money. If none
of it is, ask your adviser about
converting a portion because a dollar in
a Wroth is a dollar the IRS can never
tax again. Second, if you are 70 and a
half or older and you already give to a
church or a charity, stop writing
personal checks and ask your account
custodian to send it as a qualified
charitable distribution instead so it
satisfies your required withdrawal
without ever becoming taxable income.
Third, before your next big withdrawal,
find out where your combined income sits
against those frozen social security
lines, $25,000 single and $32,000
married, because staying underneath them
protects your benefit. Fourth, make
absolutely sure your 2025 tax return
claimed the new $6,000 senior deduction
because a great many people missed it.
Fifth, and I cannot say this strongly
enough, before you add a single child to
your deed or give away a single share of
stock, call an estate attorney and ask
the words, "Will this cost my children
the stepped up basis?" That one phone
call can be worth more than $50,000 to
your family.
You do not have to do all of this at
once, and you do not have to do it
alone. There is free help built for
exactly this. You can read every one of
these rules in the Internal Revenue
Services own publications at the
government website IRS.gov
spelled out in the same language I use
today. You can reach the Social Security
Administration directly with any
question about how your benefit is taxed
by calling 18007721213.
And if you want a real person to sit
down with your actual return for free,
seniors qualify for the tax counseling
for the elderly program and the AARP
Foundation tax aid program, both of
which cost nothing.
The walls are already there. The law
already built them. Nobody was ever
going to knock on your door and point
them out because the seniors who never
learn about them are the ones who
quietly overpay. And that overpayment is
somebody else's convenience. But you
know now seven kinds of money in your
own name that the government is not
allowed to take. Protect all seven, not
just the one. Start tonight. Start with
a statement in your own filing cabinet.
And if you only make one call this week,
make it the Social Security
Administration at 1-8007721
1213. Three.

title: Medicare Is DROPPING 1 Million Seniors in 2027 — Is YOUR Plan on the List?

segments.text: This fall, more than 1 million seniors
are being dropped from the Medicare
Advantage plan they trusted. And most of
them will not find out until they are
standing at a pharmacy counter that
suddenly wants full price or sitting in
a doctor's office that no longer takes
their card. It is already happening
quietly, plan by plan, and the letter
that would have warned them is sitting
in a stack of mail on the kitchen table,
unopened, because it looks like every
other piece of junk the insurance
companies send. Here's the part that
should stop you cold. If you are in the
wrong Medicare Advantage plan when
something serious happens, your share of
the bill in a single year can climb as
high as $9,350
before the plan pays everything. And
that is if you stay inside their
network, step outside it, and there may
be no limit at all. So before you do
anything else today, I need you to
understand something because it is the
whole reason I sat down to make this.
There are seven changes hitting Medicare
this year and into 2027, and six of them
can hurt you. But there is one change
hidden in the middle of that list that
most seniors never see coming. And it is
the crulest of them all. Because once it
happens to you, you can be locked into a
plan for the rest of your life with no
way back. I am going to show you exactly
what that trap is and how a small number
of people slip out of it. But not yet.
Because if I tell you now before you
understand the first three changes, you
will not believe how easily it happens.
Stay with me because the way out only
works if you act inside a window that
most people do not even know is open.
And I promise you this, by the end, you
will know the one letter to dig out of
that pile of mail tonight. The two
enrollment windows the plans hope you
sleep through and the single phone call
that costs you nothing and can undo
almost every mistake on this list.
Now, let me tell you who I am and
[clears throat] why I spend my days
buried in this. My name is Mark
Callaway. I am not a lawyer. I am not a
salesman. And I do not work for any
insurance company or for the government.
What I do is read the actual rules, the
ones written in the Code of Federal
Regulations and posted on medicare.gov.
The pages the plans count on you never
reading. And then I say them out loud in
plain English so an ordinary person can
protect themselves. I do not sell plans.
I have no plan to push on you.
Everything I am about to tell you, you
can confirm yourself with one free phone
call. And I will give you that number
before we are done. Because that is the
whole point. The people who lose the
most are not the people who made a bad
choice. They are the people who made no
choice at all. Who let the calendar
decide for them and by the time they
noticed the door had already closed.
So let us start with a change that is
already sweeping the country right now.
Change number one. Your plan can simply
be cancelled and you may be the last to
know. Every year, insurance companies
decide which Medicare Advantage plans
they will keep offering and which ones
they will quietly end. When a company
decides a plan is not profitable enough,
they do not fix it. They pull it. And
for the coming year, the companies are
pulling plans that cover more than 1
million seniors across the country. If
your plan is one of them, it does not
renew on January 1st. it is gone. The
federal rules that allow this are right
there in the regulations in the sections
that let a plan choose not to renew its
contract and let the company modify or
terminate what it offers. The insurance
company is allowed to walk away from
you. You are not allowed to walk away
from them whenever you please. And that
imbalance is the heart of almost
everything I am going to tell you today.
But here is what the plans do not put in
big letters. and it is the first piece
of good news. So hold on to it. When a
plan drops you, the government does not
leave you stranded. A plan cancellation
triggers something called a special
enrollment period. That is a protected
window written into the rules that gives
you time to choose a new Medicare
Advantage plan or to go back to original
Medicare with a separate drug plan
without being penalized for it. The plan
created the problem. So the law hands
you a door out. The catch, and there is
always a catch, is that the door does
not stay open forever. And if you ignore
the notices and let that window slide
shut, you can end up dumped back into a
version of Medicare with no drug
coverage and a late penalty waiting for
you. So, a canceled plan is not the
disaster. Ignoring the canceled plan is
the disaster. Let me tell you about a
man named Walter because his story is
the story of a million people this year.
Walter had the same Medicare Advantage
plan for six years. He liked it. He
never thought about it. Last fall, a
letter came. He assumed it was another
advertisement and it went in the
recycling bin with the grocery flyers.
What that letter actually said was that
his plan was ending on December 31st and
that he had a protected window to choose
a new one. Walter did nothing because
Walter never knew. On January 2nd, he
went to refill his blood pressure
medication and the pharmacy told him he
had no drug coverage at all. His plan
was gone. His special window had quietly
closed. And now he was staring at full
retail price for every prescription he
took, plus a late enrollment penalty
that would follow him for years. None of
that had to happen. The letter was in
his hands. The window was open. The only
thing missing was somebody telling
Walter the way I am telling you right
now that the letter is not junk and the
clock is real.
Therefore, the very first thing you have
to understand is that Medicare is not a
set it and forget it decision. It is a
yearly decision whether you want it to
be or not. And that brings us straight
to change number two, which is the one
that quietly costs people their favorite
doctor. Change number two, the network
can change underneath you in the middle
of the year. When you join a Medicare
Advantage plan, you are joining a
network, a list of doctors and hospitals
that plan has agreed to work with. What
almost nobody tells you at signup is
that the list is not frozen. Doctors
leave networks. Hospitals get dropped in
contract disputes. The cardiologist who
has known your heart for 15 years can be
in your network in the spring and out of
it by the fall. And you will find out
when the receptionist runs your card and
tells you they no longer accept your
plan. This is the difference that
matters most between the two roads in
Medicare. And I want to be fair about it
because Medicare Advantage is the right
choice for some people. Under original
Medicare, you can walk into almost any
doctor's office or hospital in the
country that accepts Medicare and the
overwhelming majority do. Under Medicare
Advantage, you are inside a fence and
the plan gets to move the fence. If your
doctor ends up on the wrong side of it,
you either switch to a doctor you have
never met or you go out of network and
pay for it. And going out of network is
where those enormous outofpocket numbers
come from. I think of a woman named Ruth
who wrote to me about this. Ruth had
been seeing the same oncologist all the
way through her cancer treatment. A
doctor who knew every detail of her
history and whom she trusted with her
life.
In the middle of her treatment year, her
advantage plan and the hospital system
where he practiced could not agree on a
contract. And just like that, he was out
of her network. Ruth was told she could
keep seeing him and pay out of network
or start over with a new oncologist in
the middle of fighting for her life.
That is not a choice anyone should have
to make. And it did not happen because
Ruth did anything wrong. It happened
because the fence moved and she was
standing in the wrong spot. This is the
quiet cost of a network that can change
underneath you. And it is the kind of
thing that never shows up in the
cheerful commercials with the dancing
seniors. Remember that figure I gave you
at the start? As high as $9,350
in a single year just for in network
care. Out of network, the plan's yearly
limit can be far higher, and some
services outside the network may not
count toward any cap at all.
The rules that set those maximum
out-of-pocket limits are published by
Medicare every single year, but the
plans are very good at advertising the
low monthly premium and very quiet about
the ceiling on what you could owe if you
get sick. So, change number one can take
your plan and change number two can take
your doctor. That brings us to change
number three, the one that turns a
covered benefit into a fight. Change
number three, prior authorization and
the wall of no. Prior authorization
means that before your Medicare
Advantage plan will pay for certain
care, a scan, a surgery, a stay in a
rehabilitation facility, your doctor has
to ask the plan for permission first.
And plans say no more often than most
people would ever guess. The federal
watchdog at the Office of Inspector
General studied this and found that
Medicare Advantage plans were denying
requests for care that would have been
covered under the regular Medicare
rules. Care your doctor ordered care the
government's own rules said you were
entitled to denied because saying no
saves the company money. But this is
another place where the law is quietly
on your side if you know to use it.
First, a new rule that took effect
recently forces Medicare Advantage plans
to follow the same coverage rules as
original Medicare to honor an approval
for a full course of treatment instead
of making you reask every few weeks and
to answer faster. Second, and this is
the part people forget in the moment of
panic, every single denial can be
appealed. There is a formal appeals
process written into the federal rules
level after level. And when your health
is on the line, you can demand a fast
decision. Here is the number that should
make you angry and then make you act. A
large share of the Medicare Advantage
denials that get appealed are
overturned. Overturned, which means the
plan said no to care you were owed and
only the people who pushed back got the
yes. The plan is betting that you will
hear no and go home. Do not go home.
File the appeal. Picture what that
actually looks like. Your doctor says
you need to stay in a rehabilitation
facility after a fall. The plan says no
and you are lying in a hospital bed
being told you have to go home before
you can safely walk. The instinct is to
give up because you are tired and scared
and the company sounds official. But the
doctor who ordered that care can request
a fast appeal in writing. And when your
health is at immediate risk, the plan
has to answer quickly, not in months.
Families who make that one phone call
and put it in writing win reversals
every single day. Care that was owed to
them all along. The denial is often just
the opening move, not the final answer.
The people who know that get the care.
The people who do not know it go home
and suffer. And the company keeps the
money it never should have kept. Now, if
you are still with me, take a breath
because we have arrived at the one I
promised you at the very beginning. The
trap in the middle of the list and it is
different from all the others.
Everything so far, a canceled plan, a
lost doctor, a denied service has a door
out. This next one is about the door
itself and how it can lock behind you.
This is change number four, and it is
the reason some seniors feel trapped for
the rest of their lives. Change number
four, the one-way door between Medicare
Advantage and a Metagap policy. Let me
explain this slowly because it is the
single most important thing in this
entire video and the insurance companies
would honestly prefer that I not say it
out loud. There are two roads in
Medicare. One road is original Medicare
and most people who take that road also
buy a supplement policy called metagap
that pays the gaps Medicare leaves
behind the deductibles and the co-
insurance so that a hospital stay does
not wipe out their savings. The other
road is Medicare Advantage the
all-in-one plans we have been talking
about. Now here is the trap. When you
first turn 65 and sign up for part B,
the law gives you a one-time golden
window, 6 months long, called your
metagap open enrollment period. During
those 6 months, an insurance company
must sell you a metagap policy, no
matter how sick you are. They cannot
turn you down. They cannot charge you
more for your diabetes or your heart
condition or your cancer history. It is
guaranteed. But that golden window
closes and for most people it never
opens again. If you choose a Medicare
Advantage plan when you turn 65 and then
years later you decide it is not
working. Your doctor got dropped, your
drugs are not covered, the denials wore
you down, and you want to go back to
original Medicare with a metagap policy.
You can find that the door is locked. In
most states, once that first window has
passed, a metagap insurer is allowed to
look at your health and medically
underwrite you. They can charge you far
more because of your conditions. They
can make you wait. Or they can simply
say no and refuse to sell you a policy
at all. So a senior who chose advantage
at 65 and developed real health problems
in their 70s exactly when they need
protection most can discover that they
are stuck. They cannot afford to go back
because original Medicare without a
supplement can expose them to unlimited
bills and no company will sell them the
supplement. That is what I mean by
locked in for life. It is not written on
the glossy brochure. It is written in
the federal metagap standards and it is
the most important sentence I will say
today. Let me make this real with two
neighbors because I have seen this exact
story play out more times than I can
count. Two men, same street, both turned
65 the same year. Both healthy, both
looking at the same mailbox full of
Medicare choices. The first man, call
him George, chose original Medicare and
bought a Medigap policy during his
golden six-month window when no company
could turn him down. It cost him a
little more every month. And for years,
his friends teased him that he was
paying for insurance he barely used. The
second man, call him Frank, chose a
Medicare Advantage plan with a 0
premium. And for years, he looked like
the smart one because he was paying
almost nothing. Then, in their mid70s,
both men got sick the way most of us
eventually do. George's Medigap policy
quietly paid the gaps, and he never saw
a frightening bill. Frank tried to
switch back to original Medicare so he
could finally buy a metagap policy of
his own. And every company he called ran
his health history and either quoted him
a price he could not possibly afford or
turned him down flat. Frank was trapped,
not because he was careless, but because
he made his one permanent decision on
the day he understood the least, and
nobody warned him it was permanent. The
teasing about George stopped after that.
The difference between those two men was
not luck. It was one window, 6 months
long, that opens once and in most states
never opens again. So, let me stop here
for a moment because I know some of you
just felt your stomach drop and you are
thinking that is me. I chose advantage
years ago. Is it too late? It may not
be. And this is the rehook, the part I
need you awake for. There are narrow
escape hatches the law leaves open and a
handful of states that throw the door
wide. The federal rules give you what
are called guaranteed issue trial
rights. For example, if you joined a
Medicare Advantage plan when you were
first eligible and you decide to leave
within the first 12 months, you may have
a guaranteed right to buy a metagap
policy. After all, if your plan is one
of the ones being cancelled this year,
that can open a guaranteed issue right
too. And a small number of states,
including New York, Connecticut,
Massachusetts, and Maine, have passed
their own laws that require metagap
insurers to sell to seniors every year,
regardless of health.
If you live in one of those states, the
trap I just described may not apply to
you at all. This is exactly why you
cannot take a stranger's word for your
situation, including mine. You have to
check your own state and your own
timing. And I will tell you the free way
to do that before we finish. Therefore,
with that trap in front of us, let us
keep going because change number five is
the one that hits your wallet every
single month without you ever seeing a
bill for it. Change number five, the
income sir charge called IRMAa.
Most people think everyone pays the same
for Medicare. They do not. There is a
standard part B premium. And in 2025,
that standard amount is $185 a month.
taken quietly out of your social
security check before you ever see it.
But if your income is above certain
lines, the government adds a search
charge on top called the income related
monthly adjustment amount, IR MA for
short, and it applies to both your part
B and your part D drug coverage. At the
highest tier, that sir charge can add
more than $400 a month on top of the
standard premium for part B alone. And
the income they use to decide is usually
your tax return from 2 years earlier.
So, a good year long ago can raise your
premium today.
Here is the trap inside the trap. If you
retired or your spouse passed away or
you stopped working and your income
dropped, the government may still be
charging you based on that old higher
income because their computer does not
know your life changed. Seniors overpay
this sir charge every year simply
because no one told them they could
challenge it. But you can challenge it.
There is a form, form SSA44,
built for exactly this situation, a
life-changing event. You fill it out,
you show that your income went down, and
Social Security can lower or completely
remove the search charge. That is
potentially thousands of dollars a year
going back into the pocket of someone
living on a fixed income. And almost
nobody files it because almost nobody
knows it exists. Now, you do. Think
about a widow named Eleanor. The year
before her husband passed, the two of
them had a strong income, a little
part-time work, some investments they
sold. Two years later, living alone on a
single social security check, Eleanor
was still being charged the high income
search charge on both her Part B and her
Part D, hundreds of dollars a month
based on a household and an income that
no longer existed. The government's
computer did not know her husband had
died. It only knew the number on an old
tax return. Every month it took money
she desperately needed for a life she
was no longer living. One form, the SSA
form I just named, sent to Social
Security with proof of her change
circumstances and that sir charge came
off. Nobody at the plan volunteered that
to her. The system does not correct
itself. It waits for you to know your
rights and use them. So we have covered
the plan being cancelled, the doctor
being dropped, the care being denied,
the door being locked, and the search
charge being hidden. Every one of those
is the system working against you.
Therefore, it is only fair that I give
you change number six, which for once is
the system finally working for you. And
it is money you may already have coming
that you are not using. Change number
six, the new cap on what you pay for
your medicine. For decades, seniors with
serious illnesses, cancer, autoimmune
disease, the expensive conditions, could
pay tens of thousands of dollars a year
out of their own pocket for prescription
drugs with no ceiling. That is over. A
new federal law put a hard annual cap on
what you pay out of pocket for covered
Part D drugs. In 2025, that cap is
$2,000, and it rises a little each year
after that. Once you hit that number,
your covered drugs cost you nothing for
the rest of the year.
That is not a rumor and it is not a
proposal. It is the law. It is in effect
right now and it is written into the
Social Security Act. The same law caps
the cost of insulin at $35 a month. So,
no senior should be paying $2 or $300
for the insulin that keeps them alive.
and recommended adult vaccines. The
shingle shot that used to cost a small
fortune are now free under part D. I am
telling you this for two reasons. First,
so you actually use protection you
already paid for. And second, so you
understand what is at stake when a plan
gets cancelled or you get talked into
switching. You want to make sure
whatever plan you land in carries these
protections and covers your specific
drugs because not every plan handles
them the same way. And the only way to
know is to check before you enroll, not
after. Which brings us finally to change
number seven. And this is where I close
the loop I opened at the very beginning,
the letter in the pile of mail. Because
change number seven is the one thing
that gives you power over all six of the
others. Change number seven, the annual
notice of change and the two windows the
plans pray you sleep through. Every year
by law, your Medicare Advantage plan and
your drug plan must mail you a document
called the annual notice of change, and
it must reach you before the fall
enrollment season begins, which in
practice means it lands in your mailbox
on or before September 30th. This is the
letter I told you to remember. It is not
junk. It is the single most important
piece of mail a senior receives all
year. And it spells out in black and
white everything that is changing about
your plan for the coming year. what the
premium will be, which of your drugs
they are dropping or moving to a higher
cost tier, whether your doctors are
still in the network, what your co-pays
will become. Every trap I have described
today shows up first in that letter
weeks before it can hurt you if you
simply open it and read it. And here's
why it is so powerful. Once you have
read what is changing, the law gives you
two windows to do something about it.
The first is the annual enrollment
period. And it runs from October 15th to
December 7th every single year. During
those weeks, you can switch to a
different Medicare Advantage plan,
change your drug coverage, or leave
Advantage entirely and go back to
original Medicare. And whatever you
choose takes effect on January 1st. The
second window is a safety net most
people have never heard of. It is called
the Medicare Advantage open enrollment
period, and it runs from January 1st to
March 31st. If you are already in an
advantage plan and once the new year
starts you realize it is not working,
that window lets you switch plans once
or drop back to original Medicare. Two
windows, one in the fall, one in the
winter. Miss them both and you are
locked into your plan's new terms for
the entire year, no matter how bad they
are.
That is the loop closed. The letter
warns you, the windows let you act, and
the plans make their money on the
millions of seniors who never open the
one or never use the other. And I want
you to notice the pattern running
through all seven of these because once
you see it, you will never be fooled
again. Every single one of these changes
is designed around the same quiet bet.
The plan bets you will not open the
letter. The company bets you will not
read the network list. They bet you will
hear the word no and stop asking. They
bet you do not know that door was ever
open or that this form exists or that
these two windows are on the calendar.
They are not betting that you are
foolish. They are betting that you are
busy and trusting and that nobody ever
sat you down and explained the rules the
way I just did. The default, the thing
that happens when you do nothing, always
favors them. The exception, the thing
that protects you, always requires you
to act. That is the whole game. And now
you know how it is played. So now, let
me tell you exactly what to do in plain
steps starting tonight. Because knowing
this changes nothing unless you act on
it.
Step one, go to that pile of mail and
find the annual notice of change from
your plan. If you already threw it out,
call your plan and ask them to send it
again or look at it in your online
account. Read the section that lists
your drugs and the section that lists
your doctors first. Those are where the
pain hides. Step two, make a short list
of the things that matter most to you.
The names of your doctors, the names of
your prescriptions, the pharmacy you
use. You are going to check any plan
against that list because an
advertisement means nothing if it does
not cover your doctor and your medicine.
Step three, before you keep, switch, or
drop anything, make one free phone call.
The number is 1-800med Medicare. That is
1800med Medicare, and it is the official
line staffed to answer these exact
questions at no cost to you. You can
also go to medicare.gov and use their
planfinder to compare plans against your
own list of drugs and doctors.
Step four, and write this one down
because it is the one almost nobody
uses. Ask for your state health
insurance assistance program called
SHIP. Every state has one. It gives
free, unbiased, one-on-one counseling
from people who do not earn a commission
and are not trying to sell you anything.
They will sit with you, look at your
specific situation, tell you whether
that metagap door is still open in your
state, and help you use the enrollment
windows correctly. Free, ask Medicare
for your local ship office or find it on
medicare.gov. Step five, if you have
been denied care, appeal it. And if your
income has dropped since your last tax
return, file form SSA44
to fight the search charge. Do not
accept the first no. The system is built
so that the people who push back are the
ones who win. Do this before December
7th because after that the fall window
is closed. Find the letter tonight. Make
your list. Call 1 800 Medicare.

title: The DMV Can TAKE Your License After 70 — #4 Happens Without Warning

segments.text: Starting this July in the state of
Illinois, a driver who is 87 years old
has to get back behind the wheel and
pass a full road test in person every
single year just to keep the license
they have carried safely for 70 years.
And Illinois is not alone in changing
the rules on older drivers this year.
Right now, there are 25 states that will
no longer let a senior renew a license
online or by mail. 33 states that force
a vision test at the counter and 24
states that quietly shorten how long
your license even lasts. Miss one of
these new steps and getting back on the
road can cost you more than $1,000 in
fines on top of losing the one thing
that keeps you independent.
Because that is what this is really
about. It was never about a piece of
plastic in your wallet. It is about
whether you can drive yourself to the
doctor, to church, to the grocery store,
to your grandchildren's ball games
without picking up the phone and asking
somebody to come get you. That freedom
has a price tag most people never stop
to add up. The American Automobile
Association says the true cost of owning
a car in 2026 has climbed to $12,863
a year. But the little license that lets
you use it is worth far more than that
number because the day it is gone, that
car in your driveway stops being
transportation and becomes a very
expensive lawn ornament you still have
to insure.
So here is what I need you to hear
before we go one step further because it
is the whole reason I made this. Out of
the five new rules I am about to walk
you through, there is one that seniors
are the most afraid of because they
believe it is the one that ends their
driving for good. It does not. It is
actually the only one of the five that
can save your license if you know the
two simple words to say the day the
letter arrives in your mailbox. I am
going to tell you exactly what those two
words are before we are done, but not
yet because you need to understand the
other four rules first, or you will not
recognize the moment when it is time to
use them.
Now, before I go any further, let me
tell you who I am and why I spend my
days digging into things like this. My
name is Mark Calloway. I am not a lawyer
and I am not with the government. What I
do is read the actual state statutes,
the actual motor vehicle rules, and the
actual renewal notices, so that you and
the people you love do not lose a
license over a form that nobody ever
bothered to explain. Everything I am
about to tell you comes straight from
the state licensing agencies, from the
Insurance Institute for Highway Safety,
and from the Federal Highway Traffic
Safety Administration. There is no
guessing in this video and there is
nothing made up. So, if this helps you
or if it helps somebody you care about,
do me one small favor and say so down in
the comments, because that is the only
way I know these are worth making.
Here's the first thing that catches
families completely off guard. There is
no such thing as a national driver's
license. There is no federal agency that
takes your keys on a certain birthday.
Every single one of these rules is
written by your individual state, which
means the age, the test, and the penalty
all change depending on which side of a
state line your house happens to sit on.
I want you to really picture that. Two
neighbors, the very same age, living on
