the very same street, can face
completely different driving rules if
that street happens to be a border
between two states. One of them renews
online from the kitchen table at 80. The
other one has to stand in line and read
an eye chart at 70. Same age, same
driveway, different fate decided
entirely by a line on a map.
And most seniors have no idea their own
state changed anything at all until the
renewal notice shows up in the mail
looking nothing like the one they got
four years ago. There is new language on
it. There is a line about appearing in
person. There is a box about a vision
screening. And by the time they read it
carefully, the clock is already running.
Therefore, let us go through all five of
these rules one at a time, slowly, so
that when your notice comes, you already
know exactly what your state can and
cannot do to you. The first new rule is
the one that traps the most people, and
it is also the simplest to understand.
It is called mandatory in-person
renewal. For most of your driving life,
renewing your license was the easiest
thing in the world. A notice came in the
mail, you paid online, or you sent a
check, and a fresh license landed in
your mailbox a couple of weeks later.
You never had to leave the house. But
there are now 25 states where the moment
you reach a certain age, that
convenience disappears completely and
permanently. You are no longer allowed
to renew online, and you are no longer
allowed to renew by mail. You have to
show up in person at the counter and
wait in line, almost like it is your
very first license all over again.
And the ages this kicks in are far lower
than you would ever guess. In Maine, it
starts at 62 years old. In Ohio, in
Utah, and in South Dakota, it starts at
65. In California, in Iowa, and in
Louisiana, it starts at 70. In
Massachusetts, in New Mexico, and in
Virginia, it starts at 75. In Illinois
and in Texas, it starts at 79, and in
Florida at 80. The California Motor
Vehicle Handbook puts it in plain
language that leaves no room to argue.
It says, "If you are 70 years old or
older when your driver's license
expires, you are required to renew it in
person and pass a vision test. No
mailing it in, no clicking a button. You
appear in person, or you do not drive."
>> the counter. Where's the harm in that?
But, here is exactly where the harm
hides. If you did not know the rule had
changed, you would naturally do what you
have always done. You set the notice on
the kitchen counter. You tell yourself
you will mail it next week. And next
week quietly becomes next month. Then
the deadline slides by and the license
expires. And now, you are driving on an
expired license without even realizing
it. And that is not a slap on the wrist.
Under California Vehicle Code 14601,
driving on a suspended or expired
license carries, on a first offense, a
fine of $300 to $1,000. And it can carry
up to 6 months in a county jail. Do it a
second time within 5 years and the fine
can climb to $2,000. All of that, every
dollar of it, because nobody told you
the mailbox option was gone.
Let me give you a picture of how
ordinary this is. Imagine a man named
Harold, 71 years old, sharp as a tack,
drives to the same diner every morning.
His renewal notice comes and for the
first time in his life, it says appear
in person. He does not read the fine
print. He mails the check like he always
has. The check comes back. He gets busy.
He sets it aside. And 3 weeks later, he
gets pulled over for a tail light. The
officer runs his license and it is
expired. Now, Harold, who has never had
an accident in his life, is looking at a
fine and a court date over a rule he
never knew existed. That is not a bad
driver. That is a good driver who missed
one line on one form. Therefore, the
very first move for every senior
watching this is simple. Find out the
exact age your state switches you to in
person renewal and mark it down today
because the notice will not warn you
ahead of time.
But, that is only the first rule. And
the second one ends more senior licenses
than any test on any road ever has. The
second new rule is the vision test at
every single renewal. Now, this one
sounds completely harmless, and that is
precisely what makes it so dangerous.
There are now 33 states that require a
vision screening tied directly to your
renewal once you reach a certain age. In
Oregon, it can begin as early as 50. In
Maine, at 62. In California, in
Illinois, and in Texas, the older driver
vision check is built right into that
in-person renewal we just talked about.
You walk up to the counter to renew, and
before they will hand you a new license,
you have to lean into the machine and
read the line of letters out loud.
And here is why this matters more than
any driving test they could ever give
you. A road test you can study for. You
can practice. You can go out with your
son on a Sunday and sharpen up. But, a
vision problem is different because most
of the time you do not even know you
have one. It came on so slowly, a little
blurrier each year, that your brain
quietly adjusted and filled in the gaps.
And the world still looks perfectly
normal to you. You feel like the same
driver you have always been. Then, you
fail the line at the counter, and in
that single instant, the clerk can add a
restriction to your license or hold it
entirely until an eye doctor signs off
on you. You did not do a thing wrong.
You simply got older, the exact way
every human being on Earth gets older.
And the cost of this rule is not just
the eye exam itself. It is everything
you keep paying while a vision hold sits
on your license, and that car sits cold
in the driveway. The average full
coverage car insurance premium,
according to the Automobile Association,
runs $1,694
a year. And that bill does not politely
pause just because the state paused your
ability to drive. You are paying to
insure a car you are not legally allowed
to move. Therefore, before your next
renewal, do this. Go get your eyes
checked by your own eye doctor first, on
your own schedule, in a quiet office, so
that you walk into that counter already
knowing for certain you are going to
pass. Do not let a stranger with a
machine be the first person to tell you
your eyes have changed in front of a
line of people on the one day it can
cost you your keys.
And I want you to understand what a
failed line at that machine can actually
do, because it is not always all or
nothing. Sometimes the clerk does not
take the license at all. Instead, they
stamp a restriction right onto it. It
might say "Corrective lenses required",
meaning you can never drive again
without your glasses on, or you are
breaking the law. It might say "Daylight
driving only", meaning the moment the
sun goes down, that license is no good.
A woman I read about, call her Ruth, 73,
failed the night vision portion by a
hair. She did not lose her license. She
got a daytime restriction she never
expected, and just like that, she could
no longer drive herself to her own
evening church group, the one thing she
looked forward to all week.
She was a safe driver. One line on one
machine quietly rewrote her whole
calendar. That is why you check your
eyes on your own terms first, so you are
the one in control of the news.
The third new rule is the quietest of
them all, and it is the one that almost
nobody notices until it has already cost
them. It is the shrinking renewal cycle.
For most of your life, a driver's
license was good for a nice long stretch
of time, six years, eight years,
sometimes even longer. You renewed it so
rarely, you could barely remember the
last time, but 24 states now shorten
that window the older you get, so that
the license you used to renew once a
decade suddenly needs renewing every
couple of years.
In Rhode Island, at 75, your license is
only good for 2 years. In Hawaii, at 80,
2 years. In Texas, at 85, 2 years. In
Missouri, starting at 70, 3 years. And
in Illinois, it drops to 2 years at 81.
And to a single year at 87.
Now, on the surface, a shorter renewal
cycle sounds like the smallest thing in
the world. So, what if I have to renew a
little more often, you might say. But,
stop and think about what that shorter
cycle actually means when you stack it
on top of everything else. Every single
renewal is another vision test you have
to pass. Another trip down to the
counter you have to make in person.
Another expiration date you have to
catch before it quietly slips past you.
You have gone from renewing once a
decade to renewing every year or every
other year. And each and every one of
those renewals is a brand new chance for
something to go sideways. It is not one
hurdle you clear and forget anymore. It
is a hurdle every single year, arriving
right at the age when your eyes and your
memory are the least forgiving they have
ever been.
And the stakes on missing even one of
those closer deadlines are enormous,
because that car is not sitting there
for free. Remember the number. The
Automobile Association pegs the real
all-in cost of owning a vehicle at
a year, and you are paying that whether
the car moves or whether it just sits.
Let it lapse, and you are paying $12,000
a year to own a machine you are not
allowed to drive, plus the fine on top
if you forget and drive it anyway.
Therefore, if you are over 70, do not
trust your memory for the expiration
date, not for 1 second. The day you get
each new license, take out a calendar
and write the exact expiration date on
it, because with these shorter cycles,
the next deadline is always, always
closer than you think it is. Now, I want
you to stop with for just a moment
because we are about to reach the rule I
warned you about at the very start. And
this is the one that changes the entire
picture. Everything I have told you so
far, the in-person rule, the vision
test, and the shrinking cycle, all three
of them are triggered by something you
can see coming from a mile away, a
birthday, a date on a calendar. And
anything triggered by a date, you can
plan for. You can prepare.
But the fourth rule is completely
different. And it is different in a way
that genuinely frightens families the
moment they finally understand it.
Because it is not triggered by your age
at all. It is triggered by another human
being. And it can strip your license
away before you ever set one foot in
front of a judge.
This fourth rule is the medical review.
And it is the single rule that quietly
takes more licenses than every renewal
in the country combined. So, let me show
you exactly how it works step-by-step.
Because this is the part nobody explains
until it is too late. In most states, a
doctor is allowed to report you to the
motor vehicle department. In California,
doctors are not just allowed to, they
are required by law to report a patient
who has been diagnosed with certain
conditions, such as dementia or any
lapse of consciousness. But it does not
stop with doctors. And this is what
shocks people. A family member can file
a report on you. A police officer who
pulls you over for something small can
file one. Even a clerk behind the
counter, if you seem the least bit
confused on a bad day, can flag you. And
the moment that report is filed, the
state opens up what they call a
re-examination.
And here is the part that catches every
single family off guard. In many states,
they do not wait for a hearing. They do
not wait to hear your side. In New York,
a single physician's form is enough to
let the motor vehicle department suspend
your license until a doctor certifies
that that are safe to drive again. In
Missouri, you receive a letter telling
you that your license will be revoked in
10 days unless you turn in new medical
information before the clock runs out.
In Wisconsin, a license can be canceled
immediately, the very moment a medical
professional reports the driver as
unsafe. Think about what that means. You
could be driving perfectly well, feeling
completely like yourself, running your
same errands on your same streets, and
open your mailbox to find a letter
saying your license is already
suspended. All because one person
somewhere filled out one form with your
name on it.
Let me make this real for you, the way
it plays out in living rooms all over
the country. Picture a woman named
Eleanor, 78, still driving to her church
every Sunday and to her doctor every
month. Her adult daughter, who lives
three states away and is worried,
mentions to a nurse that mom seems
forgetful on the phone. A form gets
filed. Two weeks later, Eleanor opens a
letter saying she has to be re-examined,
and until she is, she should not drive.
She is stunned. She has not had so much
as a fender bender in 50 years. She did
nothing wrong, and yet the burden is now
entirely on her to prove she is fit, and
the clock is already ticking. Now, I
know how frightening that sounds, and
I'm not telling you any of this to scare
you. I am telling you because this exact
moment, this letter in the mailbox, is
when those two words I promised you at
the beginning become the most important
words you will ever say to the motor
vehicle department.
But before I hand them to you, there is
one more rule, the fifth one, and it is
the freshest of them all, brand new for
this very year. The fifth new rule is
the return of the behind-the-wheel road
test, and the state of Illinois just
rewrote it this year in a way that made
national news. On the 18th of August
last year, Illinois signed something
called the Road Safety and Fairness Act,
and it took full effect on the 1st of
July this year. Under the new law, once
a driver reaches 87 years old, they must
demonstrate the ability to safely
operate a motor vehicle. That is not a
written quiz you take at a desk. That is
not a vision line you read at a machine.
That is a real, live road test from
behind the wheel with an examiner
sitting right there in the passenger
seat every single year for the rest of
your driving life. Every year at 87, at
88, at 89, you get back in that car and
you prove it all over again. Now, here's
the twist that most people got
completely wrong when this story hit the
news and I want you to hear it clearly
because it actually matters.
That very same law also raised the road
test age. It used to begin at 79 years
old. This year, Illinois moved it up to
87 and ended the mandatory road test for
everyone from 79 all the way to 86. So,
for a whole lot of older drivers in that
state, this new rule was actually good
news, a break they did not have before.
But, for the very oldest drivers,
Illinois still stands alone. It remains
the one state in the entire country that
will still put you back behind the wheel
to keep a license you have held safely
for a lifetime. Therefore, if you or
your mother or your father lives in
Illinois and is anywhere near that age,
you need to know the exact year it kicks
in and you need to actually practice the
drive because this is the one test in
all five rules that you cannot mail in,
cannot click through, and cannot talk
your way around. And that brings us all
the way back around to the promise I
made you at the very beginning of this
video. I told you that one of these five
rules is the one seniors fear the most
and yet it is actually the only one that
can save your license. So, here it is,
finally, in full. When that letter
arrives, the one from the medical
review, the one that says your license
is suspended or that you must come in
and be re-examined, most seniors do one
of two things, and both of them are
exactly the wrong thing. They either
panic, decide it is hopeless, and
surrender the license without a fight.
Or, they get angry, ignore the letter
entirely, and keep right on driving,
which turns a fixable problem into that
$1,000 criminal charge we talked about
way back at the start. But, there is a
third door in that room, and almost
nobody knows it is even there.
Those two words are restricted license.
You have the right to request a
restricted license instead of losing
your driving privileges entirely. A
restricted license lets you keep
driving, just with limits. It can let
you drive in the daylight hours only. It
can let you drive within a set number of
miles from your home. It can let you
drive on local roads while staying off
the freeway. In other words, it can
still get you to your doctor, to your
church, and to your grocery store on
your own without a single phone call for
a ride. The motor vehicle department
would genuinely rather keep you driving
safely with a restriction than take you
off the road completely, because their
job is safety, not cruelty. But, here is
the catch that cost so many seniors
everything. They will almost never offer
it to you. You have to ask for it by
name. Let me show you what that looks
like when a senior gets it right. Go
back to Eleanor, the 78-year-old whose
worried daughter set off the medical
review. When Eleanor got that letter,
she did not surrender, and she did not
ignore it. She called the number, she
requested the hearing before her
deadline, she brought a clean letter
from her own eye doctor, and she said
those two words, restricted license.
The state did not take her keys. They
gave her a daytime, local roads
restriction, and she drove herself to
church that very next Sunday, same as
she had for 50 years.
Nothing about her driving had actually
changed. The only difference between
Eleanor keeping her independence and
losing it was that she knew there was a
third door in that room, and she knew
what to say to open it.
That is the entire reason I am telling
you this today, so that you are an
Eleanor and not a cautionary tale.
And the second half of that protection
is just as important, and it is called
the re-examination hearing. You have the
right to request an administrative
hearing before the state takes anything
away from you. In California, for
example, you have 10 days to request
that hearing if the notice was handed to
you in person, and 14 days if it came to
you in the mail. And usually there is no
fee at all to be heard. That hearing is
your chance to sit down, explain your
situation, bring your own eye doctor's
letter, and make your case to a real
person before any final decision is
made. It is not a courtroom, and you are
not on trial. It is your opportunity to
be heard, and it exists specifically so
that a good driver does not lose
everything over a single form filed by
someone else. So, put those two
protections together, the hearing and
the restricted license, and you finally
understand the whole game the way the
state understands it. There is no
federal law anywhere that takes a
license away purely because of age. The
state cannot pull your keys just because
you had another birthday. Age, all by
itself, is not legal grounds to end your
driving. What the state is legally
allowed to do is check whether you can
still function safely behind the wheel.
And if there is a genuine question about
that, you have the right to a hearing.
And you have the right to ask for a
restriction instead of an outright
revocation. Knowing that, and saying
those two words at the right moment, is
the entire difference between a senior
who keeps their independence with a
small daytime restriction, and a senior
who loses it all over a letter they
simply did not know how to answer.
Now, let me give you the exact steps.
So, this is not just something you
watched and nodded along to, but
something you actually did today. Step
one, right now, before you forget, look
up your own state's older driver rule.
Search for the Insurance Institute for
Highway Safety License Renewal Table, or
go straight to your own state's Motor
Vehicle Department or Secretary of State
website and find four specific things.
The age at which you must start renewing
in person, the age at which they add a
mandatory vision test, whether your
renewal window shrinks as you get older,
and whether your state ever requires a
behind-the-wheel road test. Write those
four ages down on a card and keep that
card tucked right behind your license in
your wallet.
Step two, renew early and renew in
person if your state now requires it.
Never, under any circumstance, let an
older driver license lapse because the
moment it expires, driving on it stops
being a paperwork problem and becomes
that $300
offense we covered. Get ahead of the
date, not behind it. Step three, get
your own eye exam from your own eye
doctor before every single renewal so
that a vision hold can never ambush you
at the counter on the one day it matters
most. Step four, if a medical review
letter ever lands in your mailbox, do
not surrender the license and do not
ignore it. Pick up the phone, call the
Driver Safety Office at the number
printed right there on that letter.
Request the re-examination hearing
before your deadline runs out and ask,
out loud and by name, about a restricted
license.
And step five, the one I want you to do
before you even finish watching this.
Say those two words out loud right now,
wherever you are sitting, so that they
are already in your mouth on the day you
need them under a real pressure.
Restricted license. Now say it one more
time so it sticks. Restricted license.
Because the seniors who hold on to their
independence are not the lucky ones who
never got the letter. They are the ones
who knew exactly what to say the moment
it arrived. So look up your state's rule
today. Write those four A's on your card
and if you are not sure of anything,
call your state motor vehicle department
directly. The number is printed right on
the back renewal notice.

title: The IRS Is Watching These 7 Things in Your Bank Account After 65

segments.text: A retired dairy farmer in this country
once had his entire bank account,
$63,000 of it, frozen and seized by the
federal government. And he had not
committed a single crime, had not
cheated on a single tax return, and had
earned every dollar of it honestly
selling milk. His only mistake was the
way he carried his own cash to his own
bank. He had been making his deposits in
amounts a little under $10,000, the way
his father had taught him, never
dreaming that the pattern itself, not
the money, was the thing the government
was watching. And what happened to that
farmer is only one of seven things the
tax man and your own bank are quietly
watching for in your account once you
cross the age of 65. Seven separate
triggers that can freeze your money, tax
your money, or skim a piece of your
money before you ever see it. And here's
the part almost nobody understands.
Every single one of the seven has a
protection built into the law right
beside it. A line that shields you the
moment you know it is there and
completely fails the person who never
found out.
That is the thing I need you to hold on
to before we go one step further. Your
bank reports far more about you to the
IRS than you have ever been told. And
the tax man can reach into an account
faster than most people believe. But
being watched is not the same thing as
being guilty. And a reported deposit is
not a taken deposit. And there is one
protection in particular sitting inside
your account right now that almost no
senior knows about. It is a rule that
automatically shields part of your money
from being frozen even by a court order
without you filing a single form or
hiring a single lawyer. I am going to
tell you exactly what that rule is,
exactly how much of your money it
protects, and exactly how to make sure
it is working for you before the end of
this video. So stay with me all the way
through because that one protection
alone can be the difference between an
account that gets frozen to zero and an
account that keeps the roof over your
head. My name is Mark Callaway and I
spend my days reading the federal
statutes, the Treasury regulations, and
the IRS rules that quietly decide what
happens to the money in an ordinary
senior's checking account. I do that so
that you do not have to and so that when
the letter comes or the hold hits your
account or the bank asks you a strange
question at the counter, you already
know which line in the law is standing
between you and the people who want a
piece of what you saved. What I have
learned after all of it is simple and a
little bit hard to hear. The system that
takes money from seniors is almost never
built on cruelty. It is built on
silence. It counts on you not knowing
the rule.
I need you to understand one idea before
we begin because it runs underneath all
seven of these. And if you hold it in
your mind, the fear loses most of its
power. Your bank is not on your side and
it is not against you. Your bank is a
reporting machine. It is required by law
to tell the government about certain
movements of your money, certain
amounts, certain kinds of income. And it
does this automatically on millions of
accounts without any judgment about you
personally at all. So the moment you
understand that being reported is just
the machine doing what it is legally
required to do, you stop taking it
personally and you start doing the one
thing that actually protects you, which
is knowing which reports are harmless,
which ones have a protection attached
and which ones carry a deadline you must
not miss. Every senior who has ever been
hurt by one of these seven was hurt not
by the report but by reacting to it
without knowing the rule decided.
So, let me walk you through all seven of
the things the tax man and your bank are
watching for one at a time. Starting
with the one that scared that farmer
half to death, the famous $10,000
report. The first thing they are
watching is any cash movement over
$10,000. And the tool they use is
something called the currency
transaction report. Here is what it
means in plain language. Anytime you
deposit or withdraw more than $10,000 in
cash in a single day, your bank is
required by federal law to file a report
with the government's financial crimes
network. A report that names you, your
account, and the amount. This is not the
bank being nosy, and it is not the
teller judging you. It is a legal
requirement written into the federal
code, and the bank has no choice about
filing it. It applies to cash, physical
currency, and it can add up several
smaller cash transactions in the same
day to reach that $10,000 line. But here
is what almost nobody tells the seniors
who panic when they first hear about
this report. The report itself is
completely harmless to an honest person.
It is not an accusation. It is not a
tax. It does not freeze your money and
it does not cost you a penny. Every
single day in this country, people
deposit large amounts of perfectly legal
cash, the proceeds from selling a car,
the cash from selling a home, a lifetime
of savings pulled out from under a
mattress, an inheritance, a gift from a
family member, and the report is filed,
and absolutely nothing bad happens
because the money was legal and the
source was clear. Therefore, the correct
response to the $10,000 report is not
fear and it is not hiding. It is
documentation. If you are moving a large
amount of cash, you keep the paperwork
that shows where it came from, the bill
of sale, the closing statement, the
letter from the family member, and you
deposit it openly because an honest
deposit with a clear source is the
safest thing in the world, no matter how
large it is. Let me give you a concrete
picture of how this works, because the
abstraction hides how ordinary it really
is. Imagine a widow in her 70s who
finally sells the old family car that
has been sitting in the garage since her
husband passed and the buyer pays her in
cash $14,000 in an envelope. She walks
into her bank to deposit it and the
teller quietly fills out that currency
report and for a moment her heart drops
because she is certain she has done
something wrong. She has done nothing
wrong at all. She sold a car she owned.
She has the signed title and the bill of
sale in her purse. And the report that
gets filed is as harmless as a receipt.
Nothing happens. The money sits in her
account, hers to spend. Now, imagine the
exact same widow, but this time a
neighbor has scared her about that
report. So, instead of depositing the
$14,000 at once, she makes four separate
trips over 2 weeks, $3,500 at a time,
each one carefully under the line. She
thinks she is being smart. She has just
committed the one act in this entire
story that can actually cost her the
money and I will show you exactly why in
the very next rule. The second thing
they are watching is far more dangerous
and it is the exact thing that destroyed
that farmer because it punishes the
people who are trying hardest to stay
out of trouble. It is called structuring
and it is the single most misunderstood
financial crime in America. Here is how
the trap works. People hear about the
$10,000 report and their instinct is to
stay under it. They think, "I do not
want the government looking at my
account, so I will just make my deposits
in smaller amounts. 9,000 here, 8,000
there, and keep every single one under
that $10,000 line." That instinct feels
careful and responsible. It is also a
federal felony. Deliberately breaking up
your cash to keep the bank from filing
that report is itself a crime under
federal law, completely separate from
taxes. And the money involved does not
have to be dirty. It can be 100% legal,
honestly earned, already taxed. And the
act of splitting it up to avoid the
report is still against the law. And it
gets worse than a fine because
structuring is one of the offenses the
government can use to seize the money
itself through what is called civil
asset forfeite. That is what happened to
the farmer. Agents looked at his deposit
history, saw a long pattern of amounts
just under $10,000 and took the entire
account, tens of thousands of honest
dollars before he was ever charged with
anything at all. He was not laundering
money. He was not hiding income. He was
a man who had been told years earlier
that deposits over $10,000 get reported
and who quietly decided he would rather
stay under that line. His caution was
the crime. Now, I want to be fair and
tell you the rest of that story because
after enough of these cases hit the
newspapers, the outrage was loud enough
that the tax agency changed its own
policy and stopped seizing money from
people whose only sin was structuring
legal funds. And many of those victims
eventually got their money back after
long and painful fights. But understand
what those fights cost. Months and
sometimes years of a retired person's
life, lawyers they could barely afford
and an account they could not touch the
entire time. All because of a habit that
felt cautious. The policy softened, but
the farmer did not get those years back,
and the law itself never disappeared. I
do not tell you his story to frighten
you away from your own bank. I tell it
to you so that you never talk yourself
into the one behavior that turns
harmless, honest money into a target.
But the law against structuring is still
on the books. Therefore, the lesson
could not be simpler or more important.
Never ever break up a deposit to stay
under the $10,000 line. If you have
$12,000 in legal cash, you walk in and
you deposit $12,000 in one honest
transaction, and you let the harmless
report be filed. The reporting was never
the danger. The hiding was. The third
thing they are watching lives on your
phone. And most seniors have no idea it
reports to the IRS at all. It is the
world of the payment apps, Zel and Venmo
and PayPal and Cash App, the services
your children and grandchildren use to
move money around in seconds. Here is
the rule that is quietly changing under
everyone's feet. The companies that run
those apps are now required to report
certain payments you receive to the IRS
on a form called the 1099K. And the
dollar level that triggers that report
has been dropping toward a much lower
threshold than it used to be. Low enough
that an ordinary person selling a few
things or collecting money from friends
can suddenly get a tax form in the mail.
For years, the line was set high,
thousands of dollars and dozens of
transactions.
The law was changed to push it down
dramatically, and the tax agency has
been phasing that change in over several
years, which is exactly why the rules
have felt so confusing and why so many
seniors are getting forms they never got
before. But here is the part that stops
the panic, and you need to hear it
clearly. A 1099K is not a tax bill. It
is not proof that you owe anything. It
is simply a report that money moved. And
the most important truth about these
apps is that personal money is not
taxable income. When your daughter sends
you her share of the dinner bill, that
is not income. When a friend pays you
back for the concert tickets, that is
not income. When you sell an old couch
or a used lawn mower for less than you
paid for it, that is not taxable income
either because you sold it at a loss.
None of that is taxable no matter what
form shows up. Therefore, the way you
protect yourself in the world of these
apps is not to avoid them. It is to keep
them clean. Keep your personal transfers
and any real selling activities
separate. When you send or receive
personal money, label it as personal, as
a gift, as reimbursement, not as goods
or a sale.
Keep a simple record of anything you
actually sell and what you originally
paid for it. If a form comes and it
includes money that was never income,
you can show exactly what it was. The
app is watched, but watched money that
was never income is money the IRS cannot
tax.
Let me make this real because I have
watched it frighten good people over
nothing. A grandmother sells a few
pieces of old furniture and some of her
late husband's tools on an online
marketplace over the course of a year,
and she collects maybe $2,000 through a
payment app for things she and her
husband paid far more than that for
decades ago. In January, a tax form
arrives in her mailbox reporting that
$2,000. And she is terrified, certain
she now owes taxes she cannot afford on
money she thought was just cleaning out
the garage. She owes nothing. She sold
used personal belongings for less than
she originally paid, which is a loss,
not a profit. And a loss is never
taxable income. All she needed was a
simple note of what those items were and
roughly what they had cost when they
were new.
The very same week, her grandson sends
her $60 through the same app to pay her
back for a birthday gift she bought for
his sister. And that too shows up as
money moving through the app. And that
too is not income. It is a family
reimbursement. The form reports the
movement. It never decides what the
money was. Only you can prove that. And
proving it is easy when you keep it
clean.
The fourth thing they are watching is
the interest your own bank pays you. And
this one has quietly grown teeth again
after years of being asleep. Here is the
rule. Anytime a bank pays you $10 or
more in interest in a year on a savings
account, a certificate of deposit, a
money market account, it reports that
interest to the IRS on a form called the
1099 int. And it reports it whether or
not you ever remember to. For a long
stretch of years, interest rates were so
low that this barely mattered because a
senior savings earned almost nothing.
But rates climbed and suddenly the same
certificate of deposit that used to pay
pennies started paying real money,
hundreds or even thousands of dollars in
interest. And every dollar of it is now
being reported to the tax man with your
name attached. But the reported interest
is not even the most expensive part of
this. And here is the trap that catches
so many seniors by surprise. That
interest income does not just get taxed
on its own. It gets added into the
formula that decides how much of your
social security check itself becomes
taxable. The government uses something
called your combined income to decide
whether your benefits get taxed. And the
thresholds where that tax kicks in.
$25,000 for a single person and $32,000
for a married couple have not been
raised even $1 since the early 1980s.
They are frozen in time. So, when you
chase a higher interest rate and earn a
few thousand more, that extra interest
can quietly push more of your social
security into being taxed, and you can
end up losing far more than you
expected. Let me show you how the trap
closes. Picture a single widow whose
combined income sits just a little below
that $25,000 line, so that almost none
of her social security is being taxed.
She moves her savings into a certificate
of deposit that pays her $3,000 in
interest, delighted at the higher rate.
That $3,000 does not just get taxed by
itself. It lifts her combined income
above the threshold. And now a chunk of
her social security benefit that was
completely taxfree last year becomes
taxable this year. She reached for a few
thousand of interest and accidentally
handed the tax man a piece of her social
security check on top of it. She never
saw the second bill coming because
nobody ever told her the two numbers
were connected. Therefore, before you
move your life savings to chase the
highest advertised rate, you need to
know two things.
You need to know that the interest will
be reported and taxed. And you need to
know how close you already are to those
frozen thresholds. And you should know
that there is one kind of interest the
federal government does not tax at all.
the interest from municipal bonds, which
is exempt from federal income tax and is
one of the few tools a senior has to
earn a yield without feeding the very
formula that taxes their benefits. Now,
let me stop here for a moment because we
are far enough in that I want you to see
the pattern underneath every one of
these and it is the most important idea
in this entire video. In all of them,
your bank and the tax man are watching,
reporting, and keeping records. But
watching is not the same thing as
taking. And a report is not a bill. The
report over $10,000 does nothing to an
honest deposit. The payment app form
does nothing to money that was never
income. The interest report only matters
if you did not plan for it. The danger
in every single case is never the
watching itself. The danger is the
senior who does not understand the rule
and reacts out of fear. Like the farmer
who split up his own honest money, or
the widow who never learned what part of
her account could never be frozen at
all. And I want to show you exactly
that. Two women who banked at the very
same branch on the very same street who
got two completely different endings
because one of them knew the next three
rules and the other one did not. Hold on
to that because their story is where
this gets real. Let me tell you about
those two women because everything I'm
about to explain in the second half
lived or died in the difference between
them. They were neighbors, both widows
in their late 70s, both banking at the
same branch on the same street, both
living mostly on a social security check
and a small amount of savings. And
within the same year, both of them had
something frightening happen to their
accounts. One of them ended up frozen
down to nothing, terrified, borrowing
money from her children just to buy
groceries because she did not know the
rules I'm about to give you. The other
one had almost the exact same thing
happen and walked out of it with her
essential money completely protected
because she did. Same street, same bank,
same kind of account. Two completely
different endings. The only thing that
separated them was knowledge. The three
rules that make up the rest of this
video, starting with the one that
quietly skims money out of a senior's
account without any warning at all. The
fifth thing they are watching is whether
the name and number on your account
match the government's records. And when
they do not, the consequence is
automatic and it is expensive. It is
called backup withholding and most
seniors have never heard the phrase in
their lives. Here is how it works. When
your bank pays you interest, it normally
pays you all of it and simply reports
it. But if the social security number
you gave the bank does not match what
the IRS has on file, or if the tax
agency notifies the bank that you
underreported interest in the past, the
bank is required by law to start
withholding a flat 24% of your interest
and sending it straight to the IRS
before you ever touch it. 24% skimmed
off the top automatically on every bit
of interest you earn. And often the
first a senior hears about it is when
the interest they expected shows up
almost a quarter smaller than it should
be. And the reasons it gets triggered
are heartbreakingly ordinary. A woman
gets married or divorced and her name no
longer matches her social security card
at the bank. A senior transposes two
digits on a form. A bank has an old
maiden name or a typo in the system from
decades ago. A senior opens a new
account over the phone and the clerk
mishars one number. None of it is
dishonest and all of it can flip on that
automatic 24% skim quietly month after
month until someone finally notices that
the interest checks are coming up short.
But here is the good news and this is
why the second widow did fine. Backup
withholding is completely fixable and
the money is not lost. Therefore, the
protection is simple and you can do it
this week. You contact every bank where
you hold money and you confirm that the
name and social security number they
have on file for you exactly match your
social security card and your tax
records.
If a mismatch is found and corrected,
the withholding stops and any amount
that was already withheld is not gone
forever. It is credited to you when you
file your tax return, the same as any
other tax you prepaid. The first widow
lost a quarter of her interest for a
year because a clerk had fat-fingered
her social security number in 1990
something. The second widow made one
phone call and never lost a dime. That
is the whole difference. The sixth thing
they are watching is whether you owe the
tax man money because if you do, the IRS
has a power that no ordinary creditor
has. It can reach directly into your
bank account and freeze it. It is called
a levy and it is the single most
frightening thing that can happen to an
account because one day the money is
simply there and locked and you cannot
pay your rent or your medicine or your
electric bill. The IRS can order your
bank to freeze the funds in your account
up to the amount of tax it says you owe
and the bank must comply. That is real
and I am not going to soften it. But
here's the part the fear never mentions.
the part that is written into the very
same law and it is a gift of time that
most people waste because they never
knew they had it. When the IRS levies a
bank account, the bank does not hand
over your money that same day. Federal
law requires the bank to hold those
funds for 21 days before sending a
single dollar to the IRS. 21 days. That
waiting period is not an accident and it
is not the bank being slow. It is
written into the law on purpose and it
exists for one reason, to give you a
window to fix the problem before the
money is actually gone. And you have
real rights inside that window. Before
or after a levy, you have the right to
something called a collection due
process hearing. A formal chance to
challenge the levy, to prove a mistake,
to show hardship, or to set up a payment
arrangement that releases the freeze.
During those 21 days, you can call the
IRS, request that hearing, propose an
installment agreement, or claim that the
levy is creating a genuine hardship. And
any of those steps can stop the money
from ever leaving. Therefore, the 21-day
hold is not a delay to dread. It is a
right to use. The seniors who lose
everything to a levy are almost always
the ones who saw the notice, got scared,
and did nothing for 3 weeks. The ones
who keep their money are the ones who
understood that the clock was on their
side and picked up the phone. Let me
give you a picture of what using that
clock actually looks like. Imagine a
retired man who fell behind on his taxes
a few years back after his wife's long
illness drained everything. And one
morning he logs in and his account is
frozen over an old tax balance. His
first instinct is despair because the
rent is due in a week and now the money
is locked. but he knows about the 21
days. So instead of sitting in fear, he
calls the IRS that same afternoon. He
requests a collection due process
hearing and he explains that this levy
will leave him unable to pay for his
housing and his medicine. Because he
acted inside the window, the collection
can be paused. An affordable monthly
payment arrangement can be put in place
and the freeze can be released before a
single dollar was ever sent to the
government. He did not need a fortune
and he did not need to win a court
battle. He needed to understand that the
law had handed him 3 weeks and a phone
number and to use them instead of
surrendering to them. And I will tell
you one more mercy written into the law.
Even when the IRS goes after a social
security check itself through its
automatic levy program, it is limited to
taking no more than 15% of that benefit.
And certain benefits for the poorest
seniors cannot be touched at all. Which
brings me to the seventh thing and the
promise I made you at the very
beginning. The protection that sits
inside your account right now that
almost no senior knows is there. Here it
is. When money comes into your account
as a direct deposited federal benefit,
your social security, your disability,
your veterans benefits. Federal law
automatically protects a portion of it
from being frozen by a creditor's
garnishment. And the bank must apply
that protection on its own without you
filing anything at all. Here is exactly
how much is protected. If a creditor
with a court judgment sends a freeze
order to your bank, the bank is required
to look back over the previous two
months and automatically protect an
amount equal to all of the federal
benefit payments that were deposited
during those two months. That protected
amount stays available to you. You can
still take it out, still spend it on
your groceries and your medicine, even
while the rest of the account is frozen.
And the bank has to do this look back
automatically by law the moment the
freeze order arrives.
This is the rule that saved the second
widow. When a old debt collector with a
judgment froze both women's accounts,
the first widow did not know this
protection existed. So when the bank
told her the account was frozen, she
believed every dollar was gone and she
spent weeks borrowing from her children
in a panic. The second widow had her
social security coming in by direct
deposit. And because of that automatic
two-month protection, the essential
money she lived on was never frozen at
all. The bank ran the look back,
shielded her benefits, and she kept
paying her bills the entire time. Same
freeze, same bank. One knew the money
was protected and one did not. Now, I
have to be honest with you because
honesty is the whole point of this
channel. And there is one important line
to understand. This automatic shield is
designed for garnishment by ordinary
creditors, the credit card companies,
and the debt buyers. It works
differently against the tax man and
against child support, which is exactly
why the 21-day levy window and your
hearing rights from a moment ago are the
tools that matter most against the IRS.
But against the ordinary creditor who
freezes a senior's account, this rule is
a wall. And the single most important
thing you can do to keep that wall
standing is to make sure your social
security and any federal benefits come
to you by direct deposit, not by paper
check. Because it is the direct deposit
that lets the bank see them and protect
them automatically. Think for one moment
about what that difference meant in the
daily lives of those two women. The
first widow spent the worst month of her
life believing she was destitute. She
skipped a medication to make it last
longer. She sat at her kitchen table,
too ashamed to tell her son, until
finally she had to borrow grocery money
from him, a woman who had never asked
her children for a dime. And the cruel
part is that the essential money she
needed was very likely protected the
entire time under this exact rule,
sitting there available to her, if only
she had known to ask the bank the right
question. The second widow got the same
frightening letter, felt the same jolt
of fear, but she made one call, learned
that her social security deposits were
automatically shielded, and kept buying
her groceries and her medicine without
missing a single week. Two women, the
same street, the same bank, the same
frozen account. And the only thing that
stood between panic and peace was
whether they knew that this protection
existed. That is this entire channel in
a single story. The law was already on
the side of both of them. It only ever
spoke up for the one who knew to listen
for it. So, let me give you the steps,
the specific things to do, because
knowing the rule is only half of it, and
the widow who kept her money is the one
who acted. Step one, never ever break up
a cash deposit to stay under the $10,000
line. If the money is legal, deposited
whole. Keep the paperwork that shows
where it came from and let the harmless
report be filed. The splitting is the
only crime. Step two, this week, contact
every bank where you keep money and
confirm that your name and social
security number on file exactly match
your social security card so that no
automatic 24% backup withholding ever
touches your interest. Step three, make
sure your social security and every
federal benefit you receive arrives by
direct deposit, not by paper check, so
that the automatic protection against an
account freeze attaches to your money
the way the law intends. Step four, if a
levy notice or an account freeze ever
arrives, do not freeze yourself. Mark
the date and use the 21-day window to
call the IRS, request a collection due
process hearing, and stop the money
before it moves. And step five, before
you chase the highest interest rate you
see advertised, remember that the
interest is reported, that it can push
more of your social security into being
taxed against thresholds frozen since
the 1980s, and that municipal bond
interest is the one kind the federal
government does not tax at all.
Where do you start today? You start at
IRS.gov,
where you can read about levies, the
collection due process hearing, and
backup withholding in plain language.
You go to social security.gov to set up
or confirm your direct deposit. And you
call the records department at every
bank where you hold money and confirm
your name and number match and confirm
your benefits are arriving as direct
deposits. Those three places and one
afternoon of phone calls are the entire
difference between the widow who was
frozen to zero and the widow who kept
every dollar she needed to live. The tax
man and the bank are watching. But
watching was never the danger. Not
knowing the rule

title: 7 Things They Can't Take From Your Home After 65 (Not Even Medicaid)

segments.text: A county in this country once took a
94-year-old widow's home over a tax debt
of about $15,000,
sold that home for roughly $40,000, and
then kept every single dollar of it,
including the $25,000 of her own equity
that she was still owed. That is not a
story from 100 years ago. It happened
recently in a state with courts and laws
just like yours, to a woman who had paid
on that home for decades. And it is only
one of seven things that someone can try
to take from your home once you cross
the age of 65. Whether that someone is a
nursing home, a Medicaid office, the
county tax collector, a probate court,
the taxman, or an ordinary creditor with
a judgment. Seven separate ways the roof
over your head can be threatened. And
here is the part almost nobody
understands.
Every one of the seven can be stopped,
blocked, or clawed back because federal
law, and even the highest court in the
land, have already drawn a line around
your home that most seniors never knew
was there. That is the thing I need you
to hold on to before we go one step
further. Your home is protected in far
more ways than you have ever been told,
but protection is not the same thing as
automatic. The nursing home is not going
to remind you that the house is exempt.
The county is not going to mail you the
form that freezes your tax bill. The
probate court is not going to skip its
own fees out of kindness. The
protections are real. They are written
into the law, and some of them were just
confirmed by the Supreme Court, but they
only ever help the person who knows they
exist and actually reaches out to claim
them. The seniors who lose their homes
are almost never the ones who did
something wrong. They are the ones who
never found out what was already theirs.
And there is one story in particular
that I want to promise you right now,
because it is the one that changes how
you will look at your own property tax
bill for the rest of your life. It is
the story of that 94-year-old widow, the
one whose home was taken and whose money
was kept. And it is the story of what
the highest court in the United States
did about it. I'm going to tell you her
name. I'm going to tell you exactly what
the court ruled, and I'm going to tell
you exactly what that ruling now means
for you and your home before the end of
this video. So, stay with me all the way
through because that one story alone is
worth more than the price of any lawyer
you will ever hire.
My name is Mark Callaway, and I spend my
days reading the federal statutes, the
Medicaid rules, and the court decisions
that quietly decide whether a senior
gets to keep the home they spent a
lifetime paying for. I do that so that
you do not have to, and so that when the
letter comes, or the diagnosis comes, or
the tax bill comes, you already know
which line in the law is standing
between you and the people who want your
house. What I have learned after all of
it is simple and a little bit hard to
hear. The system that takes homes from
seniors is not built on cruelty. It is
built on silence. It counts on you not
knowing. So, let me walk you through all
seven of the things they cannot take
from your home, one at a time, starting
with the oldest and most basic
protection of them all, the one that
stops an ordinary creditor from ever
putting your house on the auction block.
The first thing they cannot take is the
roof over your head to pay an ordinary
debt, and the protection that makes that
true is called the homestead exemption.
Here's what it means in plain language.
Nearly every state in this country has a
law that shields the equity in your
primary home from most creditors, so
that if you fall behind on a credit
card, a personal loan, or an old medical
bill, the person you owe generally
cannot force the sale of the house you
live in to collect. In a handful of
states, and Florida and Texas are the
famous ones, that protection has no
dollar limit at all for a primary home
on a normal lot, which means your home
equity is essentially untouchable by an
ordinary creditor, no matter how large
it grows. In most other states, there is
a set amount that is protected, and even
in bankruptcy, there is a federal
homestead exemption written into the
bankruptcy code with many states letting
you use the larger state figure instead.
But here is what the collectors count on
you never learning. When a debt
collector calls or when a judgment lands
in the mail, they speak as if your house
is on the table, as if everything you
own is fair game. For most seniors on
most ordinary unsecured debts, it simply
is not. The homestead exemption was
written precisely so that a person
cannot be made homeless over a consumer
debt. Therefore, the single most
important thing to understand about an
aggressive collector is that the threat
is very often bigger than the power
behind it. Before you ever panic, before
you ever drain a retirement account to
pay off a collector who is frightening
you, you find out what your state's
homestead exemption actually protects.
Because in many cases the answer is that
your home was never at risk in the first
place. I have to be honest with you here
because honesty is the whole point of
this channel.
The homestead exemption is set by your
state. So the exact amount protected
depends entirely on where you live and
it does not erase a voluntary mortgage
or a properly recorded tax lien. But
almost everywhere some version of it
stands between an ordinary creditor and
your front door.
Let me give you a concrete picture of
how this works because the abstraction
hides the power of it. Imagine a widow
in her 70s with a paid off home and an
old credit card balance that got away
from her after a hospital stay. A
balance that a collector bought for
pennies on the dollar and is now chasing
her for thousands of dollars. That
collector calls and calls again and
speaks as though the house is days away
from the auction block. In reality, in
most states that unsecured collector
cannot touch her homestead at all and
even if it went to court and won a
judgment, the equity in her primary home
is shielded up to her state's limit and
in a few states with no limit
whatsoever. The right response to that
frightening call is not to reach for the
checkbook.
It is to hang up, write down exactly who
is calling and what they claim you owe,
demand the debt in writing, and only
then find out what your state's
homestead exemption actually protects
before you part with a single dollar.
The collector is betting that your fear
moves faster than the facts. Do not let
it, because the home you were terrified
of losing was very likely never within
their reach in the first place.
The second thing they cannot take is the
home itself while your husband or wife
is still living in it. And this is the
one that terrifies married couples the
most, so I want to be very clear about
it. The fear goes like this. One spouse
gets sick, needs long-term care, needs a
nursing home, and the family is certain
that the moment Medicaid gets involved,
the house will have to be sold to pay
for that care, leaving the healthy
spouse with nowhere to live. For most
couples, that fear is simply wrong.
Under federal law, when one spouse needs
Medicaid for long-term care, the home is
treated as a non-countable asset, an
exempt asset, for as long as the other
spouse, the one still living at home,
remains there. Medicaid cannot force the
sale of that house out from under the
spouse who still lives in it.
It goes further than that, because the
same body of federal law was written
specifically to stop what used to happen
to the healthy spouse. There are rules
with a name, the spousal impoverishment
rules, and they exist so that the wife
or the husband who stays home does not
end up penniless while their partner is
in care. Those rules let the at-home
spouse keep a protected share of the
couple's income and a protected share of
their resources, an amount that runs
well into the tens of thousands of
dollars, and in many situations, far
higher, so that they are not stripped of
everything. And the home stays exempt
not only for a spouse, but also while a
child under the age of 21 or a blind or
disabled child of any age is living in
it. But here is the catch that costs
families dearly, and it is the same
catch that runs through this entire
video.
None of this protects you if you panic
and sell the house yourself, or sign it
away in fear before anyone ever told you
it was exempt. Families lose homes they
never had to lose because they acted on
the rumor instead of the rule.
Therefore, if a spouse ever needs
long-term care, the very first thing you
do, before you sell anything, before you
sign anything, is find out what is
actually exempt because the home you
were about to sacrifice is very often
the one asset the law was built to
protect. Here is what that looks like
for a real couple. So, the rule stops
being an abstraction. Say a husband
suffers a stroke and needs nursing home
care that costs many thousands of
dollars every month, and his wife is
still living in their paid-off home. The
family's instinct is to rush and sell
the house to pay for his care before
Medicaid can get near it. That instinct
is exactly backwards, and it is one of
the most expensive mistakes a family can
make. The home is exempt while she lives
in it, and on top of that, the spousal
impoverishment rules let her keep a
protected share of the couple's savings,
an amount that in recent years has run
in the range of roughly $30,000 on the
low end to more than $150,000
on the high end, depending on the state,
along with a minimum monthly income so
she can pay her own bills.
If that family had sold the house in a
panic, they would have taken a protected
exempt asset and turned it into a pile
of countable cash that then had to be
spent down before he could ever qualify.
Therefore, the exempt home is very often
the smartest thing to keep, not the
first thing to sell, and the family that
understands that keeps both the house
and the care.
The third thing they cannot take is the
home through what people call the
Medicaid clawback, at least not the way
most seniors fear it, and this is where
knowing the exact rule is worth a
fortune. There is a program called
Medicaid estate recovery, and it is
real. After a person who received
long-term care through Medicaid passes
away, the state can try to recover what
it spent on that care, and for many
families, the home is the largest thing
left. That is the part people have heard
about, and it frightens them into
terrible decisions. But almost nobody
hears the second half of the rule, the
half that is full of protections. First,
estate recovery can only happen after
death. It cannot touch your home while
you are alive. Not while you are in the
hospital, not while you are in care, not
ever while you are breathing. Anyone who
tells you the state is going to take
your house out from under you while you
live is simply wrong.
And it is hemmed in even after death by
a whole list of protections. Estate
recovery is barred or must be put off
while a surviving spouse is still alive.
It is barred while a child under the age
of 21 is living, and while a blind or
disabled child of any age is living, no
matter how old you were when you passed.
Every state is also required to have
what is called an undue hardship waiver,
a way for an heir to stop the recovery
when taking the home would cause real
hardship, such as an heir who lives in
the home and would be left with nowhere
to go. And in many states, recovery only
reaches assets that pass through
probate, which means assets you arrange
to pass outside of probate may be beyond
its reach entirely. And that is a door
I'm going to walk you through in just a
few minutes. Therefore, the Medicaid
clawback is not the unstoppable force it
is made out to be.
It is a narrow, delayed,
exception-filled process, and the
families who lose the most to it are
almost always the ones who never learned
where its limits were.
And there is one more limit worth
understanding on its own because it is
the one that quietly saves the most
homes. In many states, estate recovery
can only reach what passes through
probate, the assets that go through the
court after a death. That means an asset
arranged to pass outside of probate may
never be exposed to recovery at all.
This is not a trick, and it is not
hiding anything from anyone. It is
simply using the ordinary legal tools
that let property pass directly to the
people you choose without a court in the
middle. A home that transfers to your
child through a properly recorded deed
in a state that recovers only from the
probate estate can pass to that child
without ever becoming a target for
recovery. I want to be careful and
honest here because states differ and
some have expanded their recovery beyond
probate. So, whether this helps you
depends entirely on where you live, but
the principle holds everywhere.
Estate recovery is not a giant net that
catches everything you ever owned. In
many places, it only catches what falls
into the court's hands, and the entire
art of protecting a home is keeping it
from falling there in the first place.
The fourth thing they cannot take is
your home through the 5-year look back,
at least not for the transfers that
federal law specifically allows. And
this one corrects the single most
expensive myth in all of senior
planning. You have probably heard of the
look back. When you apply for Medicaid
long-term care, the state looks back
over the previous 5 years at gifts and
transfers you made, and it can impose a
penalty for assets you gave away, a
period of time during which Medicaid
will not pay for your care. That much is
true, and it is why people are told
never to give anything away. But here is
what they almost never tell you. Federal
law lists specific transfers of the home
that carry no penalty at all, not 1 day
of penalty, even inside that 5-year
window.
Let me tell you exactly what those
exceptions are because each one is a
home saved. You can transfer your home
with no penalty to your spouse. You can
transfer it with no penalty to a child
who is blind or permanently disabled.
You can transfer it to a child under the
age of 21. You can transfer it to what
the law calls a caregiver child, a son
or daughter who lived in your home and
personally provided care that kept you
out of a nursing home for at least 2
years before you entered care. And that
transfer is completely exempt because
that child quite literally saved the
state the cost of your care. And you can
transfer it to a sibling who already has
an ownership interest in the home and
lived there for at least a year. But, I
want to be honest and careful with you
because this is exactly the kind of
thing people misuse and get themselves
in trouble.
These are specific documented
exceptions, and the caregiver child rule
in particular requires real proof that
the child lived there and that the care
actually delayed a nursing home. This is
not a blanket permission to give the
house to anyone you like and call it
protected. Therefore, the right way to
think about the look-back is not as a
wall that traps your home, but as a rule
with named doors already built into it.
Doors that a family who plans ahead can
walk right through.
Now, let me stop here for a moment
because we are far enough in that I want
you to see the pattern underneath every
single one of these, and it is the most
important idea in this entire video. In
all seven of these, the home is
protected by default in some real and
specific way, but the protection is a
claim you have to make, not a gift the
system hands over. The creditor speaks
as if your house is theirs to take. The
nursing home does not sit you down and
explain that the house is exempt while
your spouse lives there. The state does
not send a friendly letter listing the
transfers that carry no penalty. The
county, as you are about to see, does
not remind you that you were owed money
back. Protected does not mean automatic.
Protected means the law is on your side
the moment you stand up and use it, and
completely silent for the person who
never does.
Hold that idea because it is the
difference between the widow who keeps
her home and the widow who loses it. And
I am going to show you two of them
living on the very same street in just a
moment. The fifth thing they cannot take
is your home through the probate court
if you use one simple document that most
seniors have never heard of. And this is
where you go from playing defense to
playing offense. When a person dies
owning a home in only their name, that
home usually has to pass through
probate, the court-supervised process of
settling an estate. Probate can take
many months, sometimes more than a year,
and it comes with court costs, filing
fees, and often attorney fees, all of
which come out of the very estate you
were trying to leave to your children.
For a paid-off home, probate can quietly
eat thousands of dollars and tie the
house up for a year while your family
waits, unable to sell it, unable to
settle it, sometimes struggling just to
keep the taxes and insurance paid in the
meantime.
But there is a document that skips all
of it, and in a majority of states, it
is available to you right now. It is
called a transfer on death deed,
sometimes called a beneficiary deed.
Here is what it does. You record a deed

senior can legally stop paying so that
you know they exist and you know the
right questions to ask. What this video
cannot do is file your return or your
applications for you because every one
of these depends on your income, your
state, your marriage, and your own
numbers. The social security threshold
depends on your combined income. The new
deduction phases out at higher earnings.
The home exclusion depends on how long
you lived there. The property tax break
depends entirely on your state and
county. This is not a place to guess and
it is absolutely not a place to try to
hide income or claim something you do
not qualify for because that is fraud
and it carries real penalties. The
exemptions are legal. Claiming ones you
do not qualify for is not. If you want
the tax by tax walkthrough with the
exact thresholds, the forms to ask for,
and a plain English checklist of what to
bring to a tax preparer and in what
order, that is exactly what I built the
senior exempt playbook to do. And the
link is in the description below. But
whether you use that or not, here is
what I need you to actually do starting
today. First, before you file another
tax return, sit down with a list of
these seven and check which ones apply
to you. Most seniors are already
qualified for several of them and are
simply not claiming them. And knowing
that is the first step to keeping the
money. Second, find out your state's
property tax rules for seniors because
that is the one that changes the most by
location and the one most people leave
completely unclaimed and it can be worth
the most every single year for the rest
of your life. Third, do not do this
alone if your situation is at all
complicated because the difference
between a tax you legally avoid and a
mistake on your return is often a single
line. And when you are ready to act, you
do not have to pay a fortune to get
help. The place to start is the Internal
Revenue Service itself at irs.gov
where the rules for every one of these
are written out in plain publications.
For free hands-on help, there are two
programs built specifically for older
Americans. The Tax Counseling for the
Elderly program and the AARP Tax Aid
Program, both of which help seniors file
for free. For your property tax, call
your county assessor's office directly
and ask what senior exemptions and
freezes you qualify for. Write those
down. IRS.gov
and your county assessor's office.

title: 5 Accounts Medicaid Can't Touch After 65 — Even in a Nursing Home

segments.text: A single month in a nursing home now
costs more than $9,000. And the way the
system is built, Medicaid can force you
to spend almost everything you own down
to nearly nothing before it pays a
single dollar of that bill. That is the
part nobody explains to seniors until it
is already happening. A lifetime of
saving, a paid-off home, the money you
meant to leave your children, all of it
can be drained in a matter of months.
And by the time most families call for
help, the money is already gone and the
door has already closed.
But here is what almost no one tells
you. There are specific accounts that
Medicaid legally cannot count and cannot
take, even when you or your spouse are
living in a nursing home. These are not
tricks. These are not loopholes. They
are real protections written into
federal and state law. And the people
who know about them keep their homes,
keep their savings, and still qualify
for the care they need. The people who
do not know about them lose almost
everything. And the difference between
the two is nothing more than
information.
There is one account in particular that
becomes completely invisible to Medicaid
when it is set up the right way. It can
hold your home. It can hold your
savings. And Medicaid cannot count it.
And in most states cannot recover
against it after you pass. But there is
a clock attached to it, a five-year
clock. And if you miss it, the
protection is gone. I am going to show
you that account and exactly how the
clock works before the end of this
video. So stay with me because getting
this one wrong is the single most
expensive mistake a senior can make.
Before 90 seconds are up, let me tell
you why this matters so much right now.
My name is Mark Callaway, and I spend my
days reading the federal rules that
decide what happens to a senior's money
so that you do not have to. And the
rules around Medicaid and long-term care
are the cruelest ones in the entire
system because they punish the people
who did everything right. They punish
the person who saved. They punish the
person who paid off the house. They
reward only the people who knew the
protections ahead of time.
So let me explain the trap first because
you cannot appreciate the protections
until you understand what they protect
you from. Medicare, the program almost
every senior has, does not pay for
long-term nursing home care. People
assume it does. It does not. Medicare
covers a short rehabilitation stay, and
then it stops. The program that actually
pays for a long nursing home stay is
Medicaid, and Medicaid is a program for
people with very few assets. To qualify,
a single person in most states can have
almost no countable assets to their
name. So, the government looks at
everything you own, and if you are over
the limit, it tells you to spend your
own money first. That is called the
spend down. That is how a family watches
a lifetime of savings disappear at more
than $9,000 a month.
But, not everything you own counts, and
that is the entire game. The law carves
out specific assets and specific
accounts that Medicaid is not allowed to
count against you, and that a nursing
home cannot force you to sell. Most
seniors know one of them, maybe. The
people who protect their families know
all five. So, let me give you all five,
starting with the one that surprises
people the most.
The first account Medicaid may not be
able to touch is your retirement
account. Your traditional individual
retirement account, your 401k, the money
you spent a working lifetime putting
away. In many states, once that account
is in what is called payout status,
meaning it is paying you the required
minimum distributions the law forces you
to take after a certain age, Medicaid
treats it very differently. It stops
looking at the whole balance as a
countable asset, and instead, it only
counts the monthly payment coming out of
it as income. Think about what that
means. You could have a retirement
account with a serious balance inside
it, and in the right state, Medicaid
does not count that balance at all. It
only counts the small monthly check it
pays you.
Now, I have to be honest with you,
because honesty is the only thing that
protects you here. This one is state
dependent. Roughly half the states in
this country exempt a retirement account
that is in payout status, and the other
half count it. Some states protect only
the at-home spouse's account and count
the other. So, this is not automatic,
and it is not universal. But, in a state
that allows it, putting a retirement
account into payout status can shield
tens of thousands of dollars, sometimes
far more, from the spend-down. That is
why the very first thing a good elder
law attorney asks is what state you live
in, because the answer changes
everything. Let me give you a picture of
how much this can matter. Imagine a
retirement account with $200,000 inside
it, sitting in a state that exempts a
payout status account. Left alone and
paying out its required monthly
distribution, that entire $200,000 can
sit outside the countable asset limit,
and only the small monthly check counts
as income. Now, imagine [clears throat]
that same senior, frightened by a
hospital stay, cashes the whole thing
out. In an instant, $200,000 of
protected retirement money becomes
$200,000 of countable cash sitting in a
checking account, and almost all of it
is now exposed to the spend-down.
Nothing changed except the form, and the
form is the entire game.
Therefore, if you take only one thing
from this section, take this. Do not
cash out your retirement account in a
panic when a health crisis hits. That is
exactly the wrong move, and it is the
move most families make. Cashing it out
can turn a protected income stream into
a countable pile of cash overnight, and
hand the nursing home the very money the
law would have let you keep. The account
is often more protected right where it
is, and the worst thing you can do is
touch it before you understand your own
state's rule.
The second account Medicaid cannot touch
is one that almost every single senior
can set up, no matter their income, no
matter their state. It is an irrevocable
funeral trust paired with a burial fund.
Here is why this matters. Medicaid does
not force you to spend your final
expenses money on nursing home bills.
The law specifically sets aside money
you have designated for your own funeral
and burial as an exempt asset. When you
prepay your funeral through an
irrevocable funeral trust, meaning the
money is locked in and assigned to the
funeral home and cannot be taken back,
that money is no longer counted against
you. In most states, you can protect
somewhere around $15,000 this way and a
separate smaller burial fund on top of
it.
$15,000 may not sound like the whole
battle, but think about it from the
other direction. That is $15,000 that
would otherwise be spent down at the
nursing home. It is $15,000 your
children do not have to scramble to find
in the worst week of their lives when
they are grieving and the funeral home
is asking for payment. And unlike some
of the bigger strategies, this one has
no 5-year clock. You can do it late. You
can do it close to the time of need. It
is the single easiest protection on this
list and it is the one the most people
leave on the table. But the funeral
trust only works if it is irrevocable.
If you can take the money back, Medicaid
can count it. Locked means protected.
Reachable means countable. Remember that
phrase because it is the theme that runs
through every real protection in the
law. The third account, or more
accurately, the third protection, is for
the married seniors watching this and it
is one of the most powerful and most
misunderstood rules in the entire
system. It is called spousal
impoverishment protection and it exists
for one reason. Congress decided it was
cruel to force a healthy spouse living
at home into poverty just because their
husband or wife needed nursing home
care. So, the law lets the at-home
spouse, the one still living in the
community, keep a protected share of the
couple's money.
In the year 2026, that protected share,
called the community spouse resource
allowance, lets the at-home spouse keep
in assets. The minimum a state must let
the spouse keep is $32,532
and states set their own number in
between. On top of the assets, the
at-home spouse can keep a monthly income
allowance of up to just over $4,000
every month. Medicaid cannot take that
protected money to pay for the other
spouse's care. It is walled off for the
spouse who is still at home, so that
person is not left destitute.
Now, here is the part that costs
families dearly when they do not
understand it. Those numbers are based
on a snapshot of everything the couple
owns on the day long-term care begins.
The state takes a picture of your assets
at that moment, and the protected amount
is calculated from it. Therefore, the
timing of when you apply and what your
assets look like on that exact day can
