swing how much your family keeps by tens
of thousands of dollars. This is not a
rule you want to learn about on the day
of the crisis. It is a rule you want to
understand long before. So, the snapshot
works in your favor instead of against
you. Let me stop here for a moment
because we are about halfway through,
and I want to make sure you understand
what is really going on. Let me tell you
about two men who lived on the same
street, both widowers, both with a
paid-off home, and about the same modest
savings. Both of whom ended up needing
nursing home care in the same year. The
first man had never heard any of this.
When his health failed, his family
panicked. They cashed out his retirement
account. They spent his savings straight
to the nursing home at more than $9,000
a month. And within about a year, almost
everything he had built was gone, and
his children inherited nothing but the
memory of watching it disappear. The
second man, same street, same money, had
sat down with an elder law attorney
years earlier while he was still
healthy.
His savings were protected. His home was
protected. His final expenses were set
aside. And when he needed care, Medicaid
paid for it while his family kept nearly
everything he wanted to leave them. Same
street, same money, two completely
different endings. The only difference
between those two families was that one
of them knew these rules in time, and
the other one did not.
And that is the thing I need you to
really feel because it is the reason I
make these videos. This is not about how
much money you have. A family with
modest savings can protect them, and a
wealthy family can lose everything. And
which one happens comes down almost
entirely to knowledge and timing. Every
single one of these protections has the
same shape. The money is protected only
if it is in the right form, set up the
right way, at the right time. The exact
same dollar can be completely exempt or
completely countable, depending on
nothing more than how it is titled and
when it was moved. That is the whole
secret. Medicaid is not really looking
at how much you have. It is looking at
what form it is in and how long it has
been that way. And that brings us to the
fourth account, which is the one that
takes countable money and legally
transforms it into protected money.
The fourth protection is the Medicaid
compliant annuity. Stay with me, because
this is the move that can save a family
the most and the one they understand the
least. Imagine a married couple where
one spouse needs a nursing home, and
after the protected spousal share is
counted, there is still a chunk of
savings sitting above the limit. Under
the normal rules, that extra money has
to be spent down, but there is another
option. That excess money can be placed
into a special annuity, and when it is
done correctly, that lump of countable
savings is converted into a stream of
monthly income for the at-home spouse.
And here is the key. Income to the
at-home spouse is not a countable asset.
The savings that would have been spent
down at $9,000 a month is turned into
protected income the healthy spouse can
actually live on. But, and this is the
biggest but in this entire video, the
annuity only works if it meets a very
strict set of federal conditions. It has
to be irrevocable, meaning you cannot
cash it back out. It has to be
non-assignable. It has to be actuarially
sound, meaning it pays out over a
reasonable life expectancy, and it has
to name the state as the remainder
beneficiary, up to the amount Medicaid
paid after both spouses have passed.
Miss any one of those conditions and it
is not a protected annuity at all. It
becomes either a countable asset or a
penalized transfer that actually delays
your care. This is the one that must be
done exactly right by someone who does
this every day or it backfires
completely. This is not a do-it-yourself
project.
Therefore, if there is a lot of savings
on the line and a spouse who needs care,
the Medicaid compliant annuity is often
the single most powerful tool in the
room. But, it is also the most dangerous
to attempt alone. The line between a
protection and a costly mistake is a
single clause in the contract. And now
we come to the fifth account, the hero
of this list, the one I promised you at
the very beginning. This is the account
that becomes completely invisible to
Medicaid when it is set up the right
way. And it is the one with the
five-year clock attached. It is called
an irrevocable trust and specifically
the version elder law attorneys call a
Medicaid asset protection trust. Here is
how it works and why it is so powerful.
When you place assets into a properly
drafted irrevocable trust, the law no
longer considers those assets to be
yours. You do not own them anymore. The
trust owns them. And because you do not
own them, Medicaid cannot count them
when it decides if you qualify. And in
most states, Medicaid cannot come after
them through estate recovery after you
pass away. This trust can hold your
home. It can hold your savings. It can
hold investments. And when it is drafted
correctly, the home inside it still
keeps its stepped-up basis, which means
your children are not hit with a giant
tax bill when they eventually sell it.
It protects the asset from the nursing
home and protects your children from the
tax at the same time.
This is the closing of the loop I opened
at the start. This is the account that
disappears from Medicaid's view. But,
now the clock. To get this protection,
the assets have to be moved into the
trust at least five years, 60 full
months, before you apply for long-term
care Medicaid. That is the look-back
period. Medicaid looks back five years
at every transfer you made, and anything
you moved inside that window triggers a
penalty, a period of time where they
will not pay for your care. So, the
trust does not protect you if you set it
up the week you need the nursing home.
It protects you if you set it up five
years and one day before. The clock is
not tied to your age, it is tied to your
health. The right time to do this is
while you are healthy and long-term care
is not yet on the horizon, because that
is the only time the five-year clock has
room to run.
And here is the mistake that undoes
everything, the one I have to warn you
about directly. A revocable living trust
does not do this. Millions of seniors
have a revocable living trust, the kind
you can change or cancel anytime, and
they believe it protects them from the
nursing home. It does not, because you
can still control it and take the money
back. Medicaid still counts it as yours.
Revocable means reachable. Only the
irrevocable trust, the one you can not
simply undo, gives you this protection.
Confusing the two is one of the most
common and most expensive
misunderstandings in all of elder law,
and now you will never make it.
So, let me be very clear and very honest
about what this video is and what it is
not, because that honesty is exactly
what protects you. This video is a map.
It shows you the five accounts and
protections the law provides, so that
you know they exist and you know the
right questions to ask. What this video
cannot do is set any of them up for you,
because every single one of these
depends on your state, your marriage,
your health, your assets, and the exact
wording of the documents. The retirement
account rule is different in every
state. The spousal numbers are set
within a federal range, but chosen by
your state. The annuity has to meet
strict federal conditions. The trust has
to be drafted correctly and funded in
time. This is not a place to guess, and
it is absolutely not a of to try to hide
money or lie on an application because
that is fraud and it carries real
penalties. The protections are legal.
Doing them wrong is not.
If you want the account-by-account
walk-through with your own state's exact
numbers for the spousal allowance and
the home equity limit and a plain
English checklist of what to ask an
attorney and in what order, that is
exactly what I built the Senior Exempt
Playbook to do and the link is in the
description below. But whether you use
that or not, here is what I need you to
actually do starting today.
First, write down which of these five
you already have and which you do not.
Most seniors have none of them set up
correctly and simply knowing that is the
first protection. Second, find out your
state's rules because half of this list
changes depending on where you live and
the retirement account rule alone can be
the difference between keeping a small
fortune and losing it. Third, and this
is the one that matters most, do not
wait for a health crisis because the
most powerful protection on this list,
the irrevocable trust, only works if the
five-year clock has already run. Every
month you wait is a month off that clock
and there is no way to buy that time
back once a crisis has started. The
families who win at this are simply the
ones who acted while everything still
looked fine.
And when you are ready to act, do not
call the nursing home and do not call a
general lawyer. Call an attorney who
does this specific work every day. The
place to find one is the National
Academy of Elder Law Attorneys at
naela.org
and your own state Medicaid office for
your local numbers. For general Medicare
coverage questions, you can call
1-800-MEDICARE.
Write those down. naela.org
and your state Medicaid office. That is
where the protection actually gets
built.

title: 7 Things They Can't Take From You After 65 — Not Even the IRS

segments.text: There are seven things the law says no
creditor, no debt collector, and no
nursing home can take from you after the
age of 65, no matter how much you owe.
And the biggest one on that list is the
single thing most seniors lie awake at
night afraid of losing. The roof over
their head worth hundreds of thousands
of dollars. Think about that for a
moment. Not a loophole, not a trick, not
some gray area a clever lawyer whispers
about behind a closed door. seven
categories of money and property that
federal and state law in plain black and
white put behind a wall that the people
coming after you cannot climb over. And
the reason almost no senior knows the
full list is simple. There's an entire
industry built on making you afraid on
making you believe that one lawsuit, one
hospital bill, one long stay in a care
home, and everything you spent a
lifetime building is gone. That fear is
profitable. The truth is not.
Before I go one inch further, I want you
to hold on to a single promise because
it is the whole reason to stay to the
very end. There is one thing on this
list that is protected more fiercely
than all the others. The thing you are
most afraid a nursing home or Medicaid
will swallow. And I am going to show you
exactly why in most cases it cannot be
taken from you while you are alive. And
the specific rule that keeps it in your
family. It is the last one I will name
because it is the most important and it
only makes sense once you understand the
six that come before it. So stay with me
all the way through.
Let me start with the one almost
everyone half knows because it is the
doorway to understanding all the rest.
Most seniors have a vague sense that
social security is somehow safe that
nobody can just take it. That instinct
is correct and it is written directly
into federal law. Under a section of the
United States Code, Social Security
benefits are protected from execution,
levy, attachment, garnishment, and any
other legal process. In plain English,
that means a credit card company, a
hospital, a debt collector, or any
private creditor who takes you to court
and wins a judgment against you still
cannot garnish your social security
check. They can win the case and still
walk away with nothing from that
benefit. It sits behind a federal wall.
But you have to know the honest
exceptions because half a truth in this
area can hurt you. That same protection
does not stop everyone. The federal
government can still reach your social
security for a few specific debts. The
IRS can levy up to 15% of your benefit
for unpaid federal taxes. Your check can
be tapped for child support or alimony
you owe. And a defaulted federal student
loan can reach it. So the honest rule is
this. Against a private creditor, your
social security is a fortress. against
the federal government itself for those
few specific debts it is not. Knowing
which is which is the difference between
panicking over a threat that is empty
and acting on one that is real.
Let me make that real with a person
because a rule floats away but a face
stays with you. Picture a woman I will
call Ruth, 71 years old, living on a
social security check of $1,900 a month
and not a dollar more. An old credit
card balance from a hard year finally
catches up to her. The company sues and
it wins a judgment against her in court.
The letters start arriving thick with
threats, warning that they will take
what she owes and Ruth stops sleeping.
She is certain that next month the check
will not come, that she will have to
choose between her heart medication and
her electric bill. But the first of the
month arrives and so does her check
whole exactly as it always has. That
judgment has no power over her social
security. The creditor spent good money
to win a case that bought them nothing
from that benefit. Ruth spent three
months of her life in terror over a
threat the law had already answered
before it was ever made.
That is the real cost of not knowing
this. It is not only the money, it is
the fear that eats the years you have
left over dangers that were never
coming. And here is the second thing
they cannot take. And this one surprises
almost everyone because it happens
automatically and no one ever told you
it exists. When money is deposited into
your bank account, you might think that
if a creditor freezes the account,
everything in it is frozen, including
your benefits. That is not true. Federal
rules require your bank, the moment it
receives a garnishment order, to
automatically protect the last two
months of federal benefits that were
directly deposited into that account.
Two full months of social security or
veterans benefits or a federal pension
are walled off before the bank hands a
single dollar to the creditor. You do
not file anything. You do not call
anyone. The bank is required by law to
do it for you. But, and this matters, it
only works for benefits that arrive by
direct deposit, which is one more reason
every senior watching should have their
benefits deposited straight into the
account and never taken by paper check.
Therefore, the money the government
sends you is protected both while it
travels and once it lands. And that
brings us to the third thing they cannot
touch, which for many of you is the
largest pile of money you will ever
have, your retirement savings. Money
held in an employer plan, a traditional
pension, or a workplace retirement
account carries a powerful federal
shield written into the law that governs
those plans. That shield means the funds
generally cannot be assigned to a
creditor or seized to pay a judgment
even in bankruptcy. A creditor can win a
lawsuit against you and still cannot
force open your workplace retirement
account. Picture a man who spent 40
years paying into a plan and built it up
to $300,000. A lawsuit lands on him at
70 and he is terrified that account will
be drained overnight. In the ordinary
case, it cannot be.
That federal wall was built on purpose
so that a person could not be stripped
of the very savings meant to carry them
through old age. But there is a
distinction inside this you need to hear
plainly because it is where people get
caught. An individual retirement
account, an IRA, is protected a little
differently from a workplace plan. In
bankruptcy, your IRA is shielded up to a
very high federal limit, currently more
a ceiling that is adjusted every few
years. Outside of bankruptcy, how well
your IRA is protected from a regular
creditor depends on the state you live
in. And some states guard it completely
while others guard it less. So, the
workplace plan is the stronger fortress,
and the IRA is strong, but with a
footnote. Both are far safer than the
ordinary savings account most people
fear for. But the exact wall around your
IRA is one worth checking for your own
state before you ever need it.
Now, I am Mark, and on this channel, we
do exactly one thing. We take the
protections that were written to shield
you, the ones buried under legal jargon
and quiet neglect, and we drag them back
into the daylight where you can actually
use them. And this list today may be the
most important I have ever handed you.
Because it is not about clawing back one
small fee. It is about the wall around
everything you have left. You know,
three of the seven. Now, let me give you
the other four. And remember, the
biggest and most protected one of all is
still coming.
Now, before I give you the fourth, I
want to stop for one moment and raise
the stakes on everything you are
hearing. Because it is easy to nod along
and forget why this matters so urgently
right now. The people who profit from
your fear are not sitting still. Every
single year, more seniors are frightened
into signing away their homes, cashing
out protected retirement accounts, and
handing over money they never had to
surrender because a phone call scared
them or a smooth salesman promised to
shield them from a danger that was never
real in the first place. The protections
I am naming today are only as strong as
your willingness to stand on them. A
wall does you no good at all if a
stranger can talk you into walking
around it. So, as we move into the
biggest protections on this list, hold
on to this single thought. Knowing the
rule is step one. Refusing to be
frightened out of it is step two. And
step two is the one that actually keeps
the house in your name. The fourth thing
they cannot take is the set of benefits
earned by the men and women who serve
this country. Veterans benefits carry
their own federal protection written in
plain terms. They are not assignable.
They are exempt from the claims of
creditors and they are exempt from
taxation. That means veterans disability
compensation is shielded from a creditor
coming after a judgment and it is not
counted as taxable income at all. A
veteran living on that compensation does
not report it on a tax return the way
wages are reported and a debt collector
cannot garnish it. And because those
benefits usually arrive by direct
deposit, they also get that same
two-month automatic bank protection I
described a moment ago. So for a
veteran, the protection stacks one wall
on top of another exactly as it should
for someone who already paid their
price.
Therefore, the money you earned in
service is guarded, coming and going.
And that leads us to the fifth thing
they cannot take. One that arrives at
the hardest moment a family ever faces.
When a person dies and leaves a life
insurance payout to a spouse or a child,
that death benefit is generally not
counted as taxable income. A $100,000
policy pays the beneficiary the full
$100,000. A4 million policy pays a full
million. The person receiving it does
not report it as income and does not
lose a slice of it to federal income
tax. In a season of grief, when a widow
is trying to figure out how to keep the
lights on, that whole untouched check
can be the difference between keeping
the home and losing it. And here is a
second layer many never learn.
The cash value that builds up inside a
life insurance policy or an annuity
while you are still living is protected
from creditors in many states. So, the
very savings tucked inside that policy
can sit behind a wall, too. It varies
from state to state, so it is worth
confirming where you live. But for a
great many seniors, that money is far
safer than they ever realized.
I have watched families sit frozen over
a life insurance letter, afraid to even
open it, whispering to each other that
the government is going to take a third
of it, so they had better set money
aside for the tax bill. And they set
aside money they did not need to set
aside, and they lived smaller than they
had to in the hardest year of their
lives over a tax that was never going to
arrive. So hear me clearly. In the
ordinary case, when a policy pays out
because someone has died, that money
reaches the beneficiary hole and the
savings built up inside it can be
shielded too. Telling the people you
love that simple truth while you still
can is one weight you can lift off their
shoulders before you ever go.
Now lean in because we have reached the
sixth and it sounds humble but it
protects your dignity in the worst case.
Both federal and state exemption laws
reserve a floor of basic property that
no creditor and no bankruptcy can strip
from you. Your household goods and
furniture, your clothing, the tools you
use for work, and equity in a car
protected under federal bankruptcy law
at around $4,450
with many states protecting far more
than that. The reason this matters is
simple and human. The law does not allow
a creditor to leave an older person with
nothing, sitting in an empty house with
no way to get to a doctor. There is a
line beneath which they cannot reach. A
reserve set of the basics of a life. And
most people never know that line is
drawn in their favor until the day they
desperately need it. Think of what that
means in practice.
A creditor cannot come into your home
and haul away your bed, your kitchen
table, your refrigerator, or the coat on
your back. They cannot take the reliable
car you need to get to the pharmacy and
the doctor. The law treats those things
not as prizes for a creditor to seize,
but as the floor of a dignified life
that a person is entitled to keep. And
in most states, that floor is higher
than the federal minimum, protecting
more of your property, not less. So even
in the very worst case, the picture of
an older person left with absolutely
nothing is not what the law allows. It
draws a line and it draws it on your
side. But everything I have named so
far, the benefits, the retirement
accounts, the life insurance, the basic
property, all of it circles around the
one thing you have been waiting for, the
thing you were most afraid of. And this
is the promise I made you at the very
start. The seventh thing they cannot
take is your home. And I need you to
hear this clearly because the fear
around it has been sold to seniors for
years. And it is mostly a lie. The story
goes like this. You get old. You need
long-term care. You go into a nursing
home and the nursing home takes your
house. So families panic. They rush to
give the house away. They make expensive
mistakes all to stop something that in
most cases the law already stops for
them. Here is the truth. A nursing home
is a private business. It bills you for
care. It cannot take your house. It has
no power to seize your property.
The real question is about Medicaid, the
program that pays for most long-term
care. And even there, the protections
are far stronger than the fear suggests.
While you are alive, your home is what
the rules call an exempt asset for
Medicaid purposes, up to a home equity
limit that runs, depending on your
state, from roughly $700,000 to over $1
million. That means you can qualify for
the help you need and still keep your
home. And the protection is even
stronger than that. If your spouse lives
in that home or a child under 21 or a
blind or disabled child of any age, the
home is fully exempt with no dollar
limit at all. Your husband or wife is
not going to be put out on the street so
the state can be paid. The law
specifically protects the spouse who
still lives there. So while you are
alive, in the ordinary case, that house
stays yours.
Let me put a face on this too because
this is the one that matters most.
Picture a couple married 50 years in the
house they raised their children in. a
house worth maybe $400,000 today that
they bought for almost nothing decades
ago. The husband has a stroke and needs
long-term care, and a well-meaning
relative tells the wife she has to sell
the house immediately or the state will
take it. She is 78 years old and
terrified, and she nearly signs a paper
handing the home to someone else in a
panic. But she does not have to sell,
and she must not sign anything. Because
her husband needs Medicaid to pay for
his care does not mean the home is lost.
She lives there. As the spouse living in
that home, her house is fully exempt
with no dollar limit at all while she is
alive. The very thing the relative told
her to give away in fear was the thing
the law was already holding safe in her
hands.
Therefore, the thing you feared most is
in fact the most protected item on this
entire list. And the only piece left to
understand is what happens after you are
gone because that is where the last of
the fear lives. After death, a state may
seek repayment for the long-term care
Medicaid paid through something called
estate recovery, and that can involve
the home. But even here, the law is full
of doors left open on purpose. There is
no recovery while a surviving spouse is
alive. There is no recovery while a
child under 21 or a blind or disabled
child is living, and there are specific
protections for a child who moved in and
cared for you and kept you out of a
nursing home for years, and for a
sibling with an ownership interest who
lived in the home. These are not
accidents. They are protections Congress
built into the law. And they exist
precisely so that the home can stay in
the family.
The tragedy is that most families never
learn them until after a crisis when the
expensive mistakes have already been
made. Learn them before and in most
cases the house is exactly where it
belongs.
Now, let me be honest with you about
what this video can do and what it
cannot because you deserve straight
talk. Everything I have told you is real
federal and state law. But every one of
these seven protections has conditions
and none of them is truly automatic in
the sense that you can ignore it and
assume it works. The bank protection
happens on its own, yes, but only for
direct deposit. The homestead protection
and the Medicaid rules depend heavily on
your own state and your own numbers and
states differ enormously. What I have
given you is the map, the knowledge that
the walls exist and roughly where they
stand. What I cannot do in one video is
fill in the exact form for your county,
your state's exact homestead figure, or
your family's specific situation. For
the people who want that, the exact
forms, the state-by-state numbers, and
the full checklist of every protection,
I put it all together in the senior
exempt playbook, and the link is in the
description.
But you do not need to buy anything to
act on what you learn today. You just
need to stop being afraid of threats
that the law already blocks and start
confirming the ones that are real. So,
here is exactly what to do in order.
First, make sure every federal benefit
you receive, your Social Security, your
veterans benefits, your pension arrives
by direct deposit into your bank account
because that single choice unlocks the
automatic two-month protection we talked
about. Second, if a debt collector ever
threatens to take your Social Security,
your retirement account, or your
veterans benefits, know that against a
private creditor, those are protected.
And do not let a threat frighten you
into a mistake. Third, if you are
worried about long-term care and your
home, do not give the house away in a
panic. Call your state Medicaid office
and ask specifically about the home
equity limit, the spousal protection,
and the estate recovery exemptions for
your state before you do anything.
Fourth, confirm your own numbers because
every figure I gave you is a federal or
typical figure, and your state may
protect you even more.
To reach the Social Security
Administration directly about your
benefits and your protections, call

title: 7 Bills the Government Can't Make You Pay After 65 (Most Seniors Only Escape One)

segments.text: A retired woman in this country was
handed a hospital bill for more than
And she did not pay a single penny of it
because a federal rule said the hospital
was not allowed to make her. She did not
hire a lawyer. She did not file for
bankruptcy. She filled out one form and
made one phone call and the entire
balance was erased to zero. And here is
the part that should make you angry.
That same rule protects most seniors
over the age of 65 in America. and
almost none of them are ever told it
exists because that is the quiet truth
about being older in this country. There
are bills landing in your mailbox every
single month that you have a legal right
to refuse, to freeze, or to erase. Not
by cheating, not by hiding, by law. But
the charge shows up anyway, printed and
stamped and due on the first because the
people sending it are counting on one
thing. They are counting on you
believing that if you owe it, you have
to pay it.
So today I am going to walk you through
seven of them. Seven bills that the
government cannot force you to pay after
65 and the exact office to call for each
one. And I'm going to be honest with you
the way most of these videos are not.
Most seniors watching this only managed
to escape one of the seven if that
because no one ever handed them the
list. By the time we are done, you will
have the whole list. And there is one
more thing I need you to stay for. One
of these seven is powerful enough to
wipe out a hospital bill you have
already been sent. even one that has
already gone to collections. It is the
strongest protection on this entire list
and I am saving it for last. I will name
it before we finish. So stay with me to
the end.
I am Mark Callaway. I spend my time
reading the federal rules that decide
how much of your money you actually get
to keep. And then I say them out loud in
plain language because the agencies that
write them will not. What I am about to
show you is not a loophole and it is not
a trick. It is written into federal law.
The only reason it feels like a secret
is that no one profits from you knowing
it.
Think for a moment about how strange
that really is. In almost every other
part of your life, when something is
free, you are told it is free. The store
puts up a sign. The advertisement shouts
it at you. But when the free thing is a
bill you are legally allowed to skip,
the silence is total. No letter arrives
to tell you the charge was never
required. No clerk stops you at the
counter to say you did not have to pay
that. The default is set to charge you
quietly month after month and the whole
design depends on you never questioning
the piece of paper in your hand. A
senior who trusts the paper pays. A
senior who questions the paper keeps
their money. That is the entire
difference. And by the end of this
video, you are going to be the second
kind. Let me start with the smallest one
because it is the fastest to fix and
once you see how it works, you will
understand how all seven work. Number
one is the overdraft fee on your bank
account. Here is what almost no one
realizes. Your bank is not allowed to
charge you an overdraft fee on an
everyday debit card purchase or an ATM
withdrawal unless you personally agreed
to let them. That agreement has a name.
It is called opting in. And a federal
rule called regulation E says the fee is
only legal if you said yes to it in
advance. The average overdraft fee in
this country is about $35. And the
households that get hit pay well over
$150 a year in these charges alone. But
if you never opted in or if you opt out
today, the bank simply declines the
transaction instead of charging you. No
fee, no permission to take your money.
Most seniors were opted in years ago at
a branch desk and never knew what they
were signing. Therefore, the single call
to make this week is to your bank. And
the words to use are, "Remove my
overdraft coverage. I want everyday
transactions declined instead." That one
sentence can save you a fee every single
month for the rest of your life. Picture
how this plays out in real life. A widow
on a fixed income buys her groceries on
the debit card and the balance runs a
few dollars short. In the old days, the
bank would quietly cover it and then
charge her $35 for the favor she never
asked for. Do that twice a month and she
is handing the bank the price of a full
week of groceries every year for
nothing. But the moment she opts out,
that same short transaction is simply
declined at the register. She puts one
item back and not a single fee is ever
charged again. The bank did not lose the
right to protect her. She lost the
obligation to pay them. Now watch what
just happened because this is the
pattern for the whole video. The charge
was never truly required. The bank
simply set it as the default and waited
to see if you would ask. That is exactly
how the next six work, too. Number two
is the surprise medical bill. And this
one makes people furious once they
understand it. If you go to the
emergency room or if you are treated at
a hospital that takes your insurance but
a doctor inside it does not, you have
very likely been sent a bill for the
difference. That difference has a name.
It is called balance billing. And since
the first day of 2022, a federal law
called the No Surprises Act has made
most of that balance billing illegal.
For emergency care and for out of
network care delivered inside an in-et
network facility, you owe only your
normal in-et network share. The rest is
not your responsibility. It never was.
But the hospital sends the full bill
anyway because they know that a
frightened person in their 70s will
usually just pay it. Think of the man
who goes to the emergency room with
chest pains gets the care he needs and 3
weeks later opens an envelope demanding
$2,000 because the on call doctor who
saw him for 10 minutes was not in his
plan. That $2,000 is exactly the kind of
balance the No Surprises Act was written
to erase. He owes his normal emergency
room share and nothing more. Do not pay
the rest. The federal government runs a
helpline for exactly this. And there is
a formal dispute process behind it.
Therefore, if you are holding a surprise
bill from an emergency room or a
hospital stay, that bill is very likely
one you cannot legally be forced to pay.
And there is a phone number staffed by
the federal government to prove it.
Number three is any bill at all for
Medicare preventive care. This is one
seniors pay by accident constantly.
Medicare covers a long list of
preventive services at zero cost to you,
not a reduced cost, zero. Your annual
wellness visit, a whole range of cancer
and heart screenings, and your vaccines,
including the shingle shot, which now
costs you nothing thanks to a change in
federal law. When the provider accepts
Medicare assignment, you should never
see a co-ay, a co- insurance, or a
deductible for these. But mistakes
happen and codes get entered wrong and a
bill for $40 or $60 shows up for a visit
that was supposed to be free. That is
not a bill to pay. That is a billing
error to dispute. Therefore, before you
write a check to any doctor for a
checkup or a screening or a shot, the
question to ask is simple. Was this a
Medicare preventive service? If the
answer is yes, the correct price is zero
and you hand it back.
Let me stop here for one moment because
I can already hear the objection forming
and it is the most expensive thought a
senior can have. The thought is this. If
I really qualified to skip this bill,
somebody would have told me. somebody
would have taken it off automatically. I
need you to throw that thought in the
trash because it is backwards. Nothing
on this list comes off automatically.
The entire system is built so that the
charge applies by default and the
protection only switches on when you ask
for it out loud. The bank does not
remove the fee to be kind. The hospital
does not erase the balance to be fair.
The county does not lower your tax
because you turn 65. You have to claim
it. And the ones who never learn to
claim it are the ones quietly handing
over thousands of dollars a year that
they were never required to pay.
Number four is medical debt on your
credit report. For years, an old medical
bill could wreck your credit score,
raise the interest on everything you
borrow, and follow you around for 7
years. But that has been changing fast
and in your favor. The national credit
bureaus have already pulled paid medical
collections and smaller medical debts
off of consumer credit reports and
federal regulators have moved to remove
medical debt from your credit report
altogether. The rule is still being
fought over in court. So, I'm going to
tell you the honest version. Medical
debt is being stripped out of credit
scoring and you have the right to
dispute any medical collection on your
report right now. Therefore, if a
medical bill is dragging down your
credit, you do not have to sit and
accept it. You dispute that line with
each of the credit bureaus and an
unverified or a paid or a small medical
debt should come off. Your score is not
the hospital's property. It is yours. I
want to pause here at the halfway point
and tell you about two neighbors because
their story is the whole point of this
video. They lived on the same street,
both retired, both on a fixed income,
and in the same year, each of them
landed in the same hospital with the
same kind of surprise bill waiting when
they got home. The first neighbor looked
at the paper, felt her stomach drop, and
paid it because that is what a lifetime
had taught her to do when a bill says
due. The second neighbor made two phone
calls. One asked about financial
assistance. One disputed the surprise
charge. And when the dust settled, the
second neighbor had paid nothing at all.
Same street, same hospital, same bill.
One of them lost thousands of dollars.
And the only thing that separated them
was that one of them asked and one of
them did not.
So, if you are watching this and a
number just flashed through your mind, a
bill you are paying right now that you
are starting to suspect you never owed,
then do this one thing for me. Say the
name of that bill out loud right now,
wherever you are sitting. Naming it is
how you stop being the person who pays
by default and start being the person
who asks because everything I am telling
you only works for the seniors who
actually pick up the phone. And that
brings me to the two that cost the most
and then to the one I promised you at
the beginning.
Number five is the penalty and the
search charge buried inside your
Medicare. There are two of these and
together they quietly drain more from
seniors than almost anything else on
this list. The first is the late
enrollment penalty, an extra amount
added to your premium forever because of
a gap in your coverage years ago. But
that penalty can often be removed
through something called equitable
relief when the gap happened because you
were given bad information or because
you had other qualifying coverage the
whole time. The second is the income
searchcharge. The one that raises your
premium based on a tax return from two
years in the past. If your income
dropped since then because you retired,
because a spouse passed away, because of
a divorce, or because you lost a
pension, you are very likely being
overcharged today on old numbers. But
there is a single federal form that
fixes the second one. It is called form
SSA44
and it tells social security to
recalculate your premium based on your
life today instead of your life 2 years
ago. Think about how quietly unfair the
old way is. A man retires, his income
falls by half, and yet for two full
years, his Medicare premium is still
calculated on the paycheck he no longer
earns. Nobody at the agency calls to fix
it. The higher charge simply keeps
coming out of his check every month
until he learns that one form exists.
Therefore, if a life-changing event has
lowered your income, that sir charge is
not a bill you are stuck with. It is a
bill you appeal on one form at your
Social Security office.
Number six is your property tax bill.
And I know some of you have been paying
this one faithfully on time for 40 years
without ever asking the one question
that changes it. Every state in this
country gives older homeowners a way to
lower this bill, to freeze it so it can
never rise again or to defer it
entirely. It goes by different names in
different places. A homestead exemption,
a senior freeze, a deferral, a circuit
breaker. In Texas, for one example, a
homeowner over 65 gets an additional
school tax exemption on top of the
normal one, and a ceiling that locks the
school portion of the bill so it cannot
climb.
But not one piece of that happens on its
own. You have to file for it with your
county. I have watched people pay a
rising tax bill on a paidoff home for a
decade, watching it climb a little
higher every single year, while a
neighbor on the very same block froze
theirs the day they turned old enough
and never paid another dollar of
increase. Same house, same street, same
law available to both of them. One asked
the county and one assumed the bill was
simply the bill. Therefore, the call to
make is to your county assessor and the
exact words are, "I want to apply for
the senior homestead exemption, the
freeze, and the deferral." Three
protections, one phone call. And for
many seniors, it is the difference
between keeping the house and losing it
slowly to a tax bill that never had to
keep rising.
Now, I told you at the very beginning to
stay to the end because one of these
seven is stronger than all the rest.
Strong enough to erase a hospital bill
you have already been sent. even one
that has already gone to collections.
This is number seven and it is the one
almost no one is ever told about. It is
called hospital charity care and it
comes from a federal rule with a plain
name section 501R of the tax code. Here
is what it means for you. Almost every
hospital in America is a nonprofit. And
in exchange for the enormous tax break
they receive, federal law requires them
to keep a written financial assistance
policy and to offer real help to
patients who cannot afford their bills.
That is the trade. The public lets these
hospitals skip a fortune in taxes every
year. And in return, they are supposed
to take care of the people who cannot
pay. Most of them meet that obligation
only when a patient walks in the door
and asks for it by name. The law says a
qualifying patient cannot be charged
more than the discounted amount an
insured patient would have paid. And for
a great many seniors on a fixed income,
the bill is reduced all the way down to
zero.
This is the one the retired woman used
at the start of this video. That $11,000
bill did not vanish by magic. She asked
the hospital billing office for the
financial assistance application. She
qualified and section 501R did the rest.
And this is the part that stuns people.
It works on a bill you already received.
It works on a bill that has already been
turned over to collections. As long as
that hospital is a nonprofit, which most
are, the door is open. Therefore, if
there is a hospital bill in your house
right now that you have been dreading,
do not pay it in a panic and do not run
from it. You call that hospital's
billing department and you say seven
words. I want the financial assistance
application and section 501R.
That sentence has erased more medical
debt for seniors than any lawyer ever
has.
So there it is, the whole list.
Overdraft fees you never opted into.
Surprise medical bills the no surprises
act made illegal. Preventive care that
is supposed to cost zero. Medical debt
being pulled off your credit. A Medicare
sir charge you can appeal away on one
form. A property tax bill you can freeze
for life. And a hospital charity care
rule that can wipe a bill down to
nothing. seven bills and the government
cannot force you to pay any of them once
you know how to ask.
I want to be straight with you about
what this video can and cannot do
because I respect your time too much to
pretend. In 17 minutes, I can prove to
you that each of these rights is real
and I can tell you which office to call
for each one. What I cannot do here is
read you the exact form to fill in, the
precise words to say to each agency, and
the version that applies in your
specific state because that would take
hours. So, I put all of it, every form,
every word for word phone script, all 12
of these exemptions instead of just
seven into a single plain guide called
the senior exempt playbook. And the link
is in the description and pinned at the
top of the comments if you want the done
for you version. But you do not need it
to start. You have enough right now
today to make the first call.
And I want to say one more thing to you
because I think you have earned the
right to hear it. You are not asking for
charity when you claim any of these. You
paid for them. You paid taxes into this
country for 50 years. You paid the
premiums. You paid every bill they ever
sent you on time without complaint.
These protections were written for you,
funded by you, promised to you. Claiming
them is not begging. It is collecting
what you are already owed. The only
people who lose out are the ones who
were never told. And after today, that
is no longer you. Because the seniors
who keep their money are never the ones
who knew the most. They are simply the
ones who picked up the phone and asked.
So this week, pick one. The overdraft
line at your bank, the county assessor,
the hospital billing office, any one of
the seven, and say the words out loud.
Start with the bill that scares you the
most. Call the hospital billing
department. Ask for the financial
assistance application and say the words
section 501R.

title: STOP Paying Tax When You Sell Your Home After 65 — You're Legally Exempt

segments.text: There is a rule buried in the federal
tax code that lets you sell your own
home after the age of 65 and hand the
government nothing on as much as
$500,000 of the profit. And almost every
senior in this country either forgets it
exists or is quietly frightened into
thinking the tax will swallow half their
house. It will not. In plain black and
white, the law says a married couple can
walk away from the sale of their main
home with half a million dollars of gain
and owe the federal government zero. A
single person can keep a quarter of a
million. And right now, while you are
watching this, lawmakers in Washington
are moving to make that number even
bigger or to erase the tax on your home
entirely.
Before I go 1 in further, I want you to
hold on to one promise because it is the
whole reason to stay to the end. There
is one specific move that a widow or a
widower has to make on a strict deadline
that decides whether they keep the full
$500,000 exemption or only half of it.
Miss the window and you cut your
protection in half overnight. I am going
to give you the exact deadline before we
are done, but it only makes sense once
you understand the rest. So, stay with
me all the way through.
Let me start with the rule itself
because it is the doorway to everything
else. When you sell your main home, the
profit you made on it, what the tax
people call the gain, would normally be
taxable. But, the tax code hands you an
exemption so large that most seniors
sell and owe absolutely nothing. If you
are single, you can exclude up to
of gain from federal tax. And if you are
married and filing jointly, you can
exclude up to $500,000.
That is not a deduction that shaves a
little off the top. That is the profit
becoming completely invisible to the
government as if it never happened.
Now, here is the first thing almost
nobody understands and it is where the
fear comes from. The exemption is not on
the price you sell the house for. It is
on the gain. The gain is what you sold
it for minus what the tax code calls
your basis. And your basis is what you
originally paid for the home plus the
cost of every improvement you ever made
to it. The new roof, the kitchen you
redid, the addition you put on when the
grandchildren started coming. All of it
gets added to your basis, which means
all of it lowers your gain.
Let me make that concrete because it is
where real money quietly hides. Say you
bought your home for $40,000, and over
the years you put on a new roof for
$15,000, remodeled the kitchen for
$30,000, and added a room for another
improvements, and every single dollar of
it gets added to your basis. So, your
basis is not $40,000 anymore. It is
And if that home sells for $440,000,
your gain is not 400,000, it is 315,000.
You just knocked $85,000 off the number
the tax is even measured against simply
by remembering the work you already paid
for. Most seniors never do this. They
look at the price they paid the year
they moved in, panic at the size of the
profit, and forget the decades of
receipts that shrink it.
Think about what that means for the
people who bought a modest house decades
ago. Say you and your spouse bought your
home years ago for $40,000, and today it
is worth $440,000.
On paper, that looks like $400,000 of
profit, the kind of number that would
terrify anyone into believing the tax
bill will be enormous. But, you are
married. Your exemption is $500,
and 400,000 is comfortably underneath
it. So, you sell the home you have lived
in your whole life, and you hand the
federal government nothing, not a
dollar. That is the law working exactly
the way it was written.
Now, I am Mark, and on this channel we
do one thing. We take the rules that
were written to protect you, the ones
that got buried under jargon and
silence, and we drag them back into the
daylight where you can actually use
them. And this rule, the one sitting
inside the home you already own, is the
single largest tax break most seniors
will ever touch in their lives. And it
is the one they most often forget they
even have because they only think about
it in the one year they finally decide
to sell. Therefore, let me tell you
exactly who qualifies because the rule
has one condition and it is worth saying
plainly so no one gets caught out. To
claim the exemption, you have to have
owned the home and lived in it as your
main home for at least two of the last
five years before you sell. That is 24
months of living there and they do not
even have to be back to back. For a
senior who has been in the same house
for 20 or 30 years, this is not a hurdle
at all. It was met many times over
decades ago. But, if you are thinking
about selling a place you moved into
only recently or a vacation home or a
rental property, the rules are different
and that is exactly the kind of thing
worth checking before you sign anything,
not after.
And here's the quiet tragedy of not
knowing this. Every single year, seniors
sit down to sell the family home and
somewhere in the back of their mind, a
voice says the government is going to
take a third of it. So, they had better
brace for a giant bill and that fear
does real damage. Some of them delay the
sale they needed to make. Some of them
price the house wrong or hand it to the
first buyer in a panic or set aside
money they never needed to set aside all
over a tax that in the ordinary case was
never going to arrive. The fear is the
enemy here and the fear is built
entirely on not knowing where the line
is drawn.
But, there is a real trap hidden inside
this rule and it is the reason I need
you to keep watching because this is
where a comfortable number turns into a
painful one for the people who least
expect it. Those two exemption amounts,
the quarter million for a single person
and the half million for a couple, were
written into law in the year 1997 and
they have never once been raised since.
Not for inflation, not for the fact that
the typical home has multiplied in value
many times over since then. The numbers
have sat frozen in place for more than a
quarter of a century while home prices
ran away from them.
Let that sink in for a moment. In the
year those numbers were written, the
typical American home cost a small
fraction of what it costs today. Wages
changed. Prices at the grocery store
changed. The cost of nearly everything
you buy changed over and over for 28
years. But the exemption on your home,
the one thing standing between you and a
tax bill the day you sell, did not move
a single dollar in all that time. It is
one of the quietest failures in the
entire tax code. And the people it
punishes hardest are not the wealthy
with lawyers and accountants who plan
around it. It is the ordinary senior who
bought one house, lived in it for 40
years, and is now sitting on a gain that
Congress of 1997 never once imagined.
For a married couple in a modest home,
that frozen number is usually still big
enough. But think about the single
person, the widow living alone in the
house she and her husband bought 50
years ago. The widower who never
remarried. They only get the $250,000
exemption because the half million is
only for couples filing together. And in
a lot of this country, a home that a
couple bought long ago for 30 or 40
thousand dollars is now worth well over
That single senior can blow right past
the quarter million dollar line and
every dollar of gain above it becomes
taxable.
Therefore, the very people this rule
should protect the most, the ones living
alone on a fixed income with a home that
quietly became their largest asset, are
the ones most likely to get caught by a
cap that Washington froze in place and
forgot about. And that brings me
straight to the promise I made you at
the very beginning. Because for a widow
or a widower, there is a window, and the
window closes.
Here it is, and it is the most important
timing decision on this entire list.
When your spouse passes away, you do not
lose the full $500,000 exemption
immediately. The law gives you a grace
period. If you sell the home within 2
years of the date your spouse died, and
you have not remarried, you can still
claim the entire $500,000
exclusion. exclusion, exactly as if you
were still filing jointly. But, the day
that 2-year window closes, you drop down
to the single person amount of $250,000,
and half of your protection vanishes.
So, the widow who sells 18 months after
losing her husband can shield $500,000
of gain. The widow who waits 3 years on
the identical house can only shield
Same home, same person. A quarter of a
million dollars of difference, decided
entirely by the calendar. And there is a
second gift that arrives at that same
painful moment, one that almost no one
tells a grieving spouse about. When your
husband or wife dies, the tax value of
their share of the home resets to what
it is worth on the day they passed. The
professionals call it a stepped-up
basis. So, if the two of you bought the
house for $40,000, and it is worth
the day your spouse dies, the deceased
spouse's half of that gain simply
disappears for tax purposes. Your basis
jumps up. Your taxable gain shrinks,
sometimes to nothing. In many states,
that step-up applies to their half of
the home, and in the community property
states, it can apply to the whole thing.
Between the stepped-up basis and the
2-year window, a widow who understands
both can very often sell the family home
and owe the government absolutely
nothing at the single hardest moment of
her life.
Now, I want you to lean in, because this
is where the story stops being only
about the rule you already have and
becomes about the rule that is coming.
Everything I have told you so far is
current law, sitting in the code right
now, waiting for you to use it. But,
while home prices have soared and those
1997 caps have stayed frozen, pressure
has been building in Washington to
finally fix it, and that pressure has
turned into real action this year.
There are two separate efforts moving
through Congress right now, and you
deserve to know about both. The first is
a bill that would double the exemption
outright, lifting it from $250,000 to
$500,000 for single filers, and from
$500,000 all the way to $1 million for
married couples. And then, for the first
time ever, tying those numbers to
inflation, so they can never again be
frozen and forgotten. Think about what
that one change alone would mean for the
widow we just talked about. Today, her
exemption is $250,000.
Under that bill, it would jump to
$500,000, the very same as a married
couple. And it would rise a little every
year with inflation, instead of sitting
frozen for another generation.
For a single senior in a home that has
quietly grown past that quarter
million-dollar line, that is the whole
difference between owing the government
a real tax bill on the sale and owing it
nothing at all. The second effort goes
even further. It is a proposal to
eliminate the federal capital gains tax
on the sale of your primary home
entirely, so that the profit on the
house you live in would never be taxed
by the federal government at all, no
matter the size. The president himself
has said publicly that the
administration is thinking seriously
about ending the tax on home sales. Now,
I have to be honest with you, the way I
always am on this channel, because that
honesty is exactly why you are here and
not listening to someone selling you
something. Neither of those changes is
law yet. They are bills that have been
introduced, and a position the White
House has floated. They would have to
pass before a single one of them
protects a single dollar of your money.
So, do not sell your house tomorrow,
believing the tax is already gone. But,
the direction is unmistakable, and here
is why it matters to you today. The
exemption you already have, the quarter
million and the half million, is real.
It is current, and it is enough for the
great majority of seniors to sell and
owe nothing. And if these changes do
pass, the protection only gets larger.
You are standing on solid ground right
now, and the ground may be about to get
wider.
Therefore, the worst possible thing you
can do is let the old fear, the fear of
attacks that probably does not even
apply to you, scare you out of a
decision you need to make about your own
home and your own life. The house you
have spent a lifetime paying off can
move with you or move to your children
far more intact than you were ever led
to believe.
So, let me put a real person on all of
this because numbers float away, but
people stay with you. Picture two
neighbors, same street, same kind of
house, each one bought decades ago for
around $40,000, each one now worth
The first neighbor sells and spends the
whole process terrified, sets aside
$100,000 for a tax bill she was sure was
coming, lives smaller and tighter
through a hard year, and only finds out
at tax time that the bill was zero the
entire time, and that the money she set
aside she never needed to touch. The
second neighbor learned the rule first.
She knew her gain of $400,000 sat
comfortably under her exemption. She
sold with confidence, kept every dollar
of the proceeds, and used them to do
exactly what she wanted with the years
she had left. Same house, same profit.
One of them handed her peace of mind to
a fear that was never real, and the
other kept it simply because she knew
where the line was drawn. And notice
what the second neighbor did not do. She
did not cheat. She did not hide
anything. She did not find some clever
loophole a tax collector could ever
knock on her door about. Every move she
made was written into the law in advance
waiting for anyone willing to learn it.
That is the part I need you to hold on
to. Keeping this money is not the reward
for being sneaky. It is the reward for
being informed. The government wrote
this door into the wall on purpose. It
just never hung a sign over it. So, now
let me give you the exact moves in order
because knowing this rule and using it
correctly are two very different things,
and the whole system quietly bets that
you will stop at knowing.
Move number one. Before you even think
about the tax, find your real gain, not
the scary sale price. Sit down and add
up what you originally paid for the home
and the cost of every major improvement
you ever made to it. The roof, the
kitchen, the additions, the new systems.
That total is your basis, and your gain
is only what the house sells for above
that basis. Most seniors discover their
real gain is far smaller than they
feared, and often it sits entirely
inside the exemption. Move number two.
Confirm you meet the ownership and use
test before you list the house. You need
to have owned it and lived in it as your
main home for at least two of the last
five years. For most long-time owners,
this is already met, but confirm it,
especially if the property is a second
home or one you moved into recently.
Move number three, and this is the one
to write down and never forget. If you
have lost a spouse, mark the date. You
have a two-year window from the day your
spouse died to sell the home and keep
the full $500,000 exemption. Do not let
that window close without knowing it is
there. If you are inside it, that alone
can be the difference of a quarter of a
million dollars in protected gain.
Move number four. If your gain is
genuinely larger than your exemption,
which can happen to a single senior in a
high-value home, do not panic and do not
assume the worst rate. Gain above the
exemption is taxed at the long-term
capital gains rate, which for many
retirees is zero or 15%, not the
frightening number people imagine. Let
me show you how gentle that can actually
be. Suppose you are a single senior, the
gain on your home is $300,000, and your
exemption covers 250,000 of it. That
leaves $50,000 of taxable gain. If your
total income for the year keeps you in
the lower brackets, and for a great many
retirees living on social security and a
modest pension, it does, the federal tax
on that $50,000 can be zero, or it can
be 15%, which is $7,500
on the sale of a home worth more than
half a million.
That is a very long way from the third
or the half that people picture in their
worst nightmares. The fear is almost
always far bigger than the bill. Talk to
a tax professional about your exact
bracket before you sign, not after. And
here is the one to keep, because these
rules can change at the edges, and the
numbers may be about to change in your
favor, and you want the truth from the
source and not from a stranger. The
Internal Revenue Service lays all of
this out in plain language in its own
guide, publication 523, Selling Your
Home, on its own website at irs.gov, and
its helpline is 800-829-1040.
Say that back to yourself so it sticks.
You worked your whole life to pay off
that home. You made the payments year
after year, decade after decade, through
every hard season, and you were promised
that when you finally owned it free and
clear, it would be yours to keep, or to
sell, or to leave to your children,
without the government reaching in and
taking a piece on the way out the door.
And quietly, in language they prayed you
would never sit down and read, the tax
code actually kept that promise. A
quarter of a million dollars of your
home's gain, tax-free if you are single,
a half million if you are married, a
two-year window that protects a widow, a
stepped-up basis that can erase decades
of gain in a single day, and a change
coming that may make all of it larger
still. Most seniors never learn any of
it. Starting today, you know all of it.
Find your real gain, confirm the
two-of-five-year test. If you are
widowed, watch the two-year window. And
when you want the rule in black and
white, you go straight to the source at
irs.gov, publication 523, or you call

title: 7 Types of Income the IRS Can't Touch After 65 (Most Seniors Only Know One)

segments.text: There are seven kinds of income the IRS
is legally not allowed to touch after
the age of 65. And one of them can
shield as much as $500,000 from federal
tax in a single afternoon. Yet almost
every senior in this country knows about
only one of the seven and quietly hands
the government money it was never
entitled to take. Think about that. Not
a loophole, not a scheme, not some gray
area a clever accountant whispers about
behind a closed door. seven categories
of money that the tax code itself in
plain black and white says you get to
keep in full. And the reason you were
never taught them is simple. Nobody
profits when you keep your own money.
There is no industry built around
telling a widow on a fixed income that
the check in her hand was tax-free the
whole time.
Before I go one inch further, I want you
to hold on to two promises because they
are the whole reason to stay to the end.
There is one type of income on this list
that can protect the single largest
amount far more than the rest. And I am
going to name it and show you the exact
dollar figure. And there is one specific
move, one decision you make with your
own money that determines whether the
IRS gets to tax your social security
check at all or whether it stays
completely untouched. I will give you
both before we are done. But the second
one only works if you understand the
first six. So stay with me all the way
through.
Let me start with the one type almost
everyone already half knows because it
is the doorway to understanding all the
others. Most seniors have heard
somewhere along the way that social
security is not fully taxed. That part
is true. What they never learned is
exactly how much of it is protected and
that is where thousands of dollars slip
through the cracks every single year.
Here is the hard rule straight from the
tax code. No matter how high your income
climbs, the absolute most of your social
security the government can ever tax is
85%. That means at least 15% of every
social security dollar you receive is
exempt from federal income tax for
everyone at every income level always.
It cannot be touched.
But that is only the ceiling. And for a
great many seniors, the real number is
far better than that. Whether the
government taxes your benefits at all
depends on something called your
provisional income. And the thresholds
are lower than most people fear and
higher than they hope. If you are single
and your provisional income sits below
$25,000, then 0% of your social security
is taxable. None of it. If you are
married and filing jointly and that
number sits below $32,000, again, 0% is
taxed. Above those lines, up to half
becomes taxable. And only once a single
filer passes $34,000 or a married couple
passes $44,000 does that 85% ceiling
ever come into play. So, the truth
almost no one tells you is this.
A large number of seniors living on
modest fixed incomes are paying tax on
social security they never actually owed
simply because no one showed them where
those lines are drawn. And here is the
quiet cost of not knowing it. Every
single year, a great many seniors sit
down with their tax paperwork or hand it
to someone in a hurry. and they include
social security income. The government
was never entitled to tax because nobody
ever showed them the $25,000 and $32,000
lines. They overpay by a few hundred
here, $1,000 there year after year, and
it adds up over a retirement into real
money. It is not a dramatic robbery. It
is a slow leak. And a slow leak sinks a
boat just as surely as a whole. The
tragedy is that it is completely
avoidable. And it starts with knowing
that the one rule everyone half
remembers has real numbers attached to
it.
Now I am Mark and on this channel we do
one thing. We take the rules that were
written to protect you, the ones that
got buried under jargon and silence and
we drag them back into the daylight
where you can use them. And today might
be the most valuable list I have ever
handed you. Because this is not about
clawing back one small fee. This is
about seven separate rivers of money
that can flow to you and your family
without the federal government ever
dipping its hand in. You know one of
them now. Let me give you the other six
and I promise the biggest one is still
coming. The second type of income the
IRS cannot touch is the money that comes
out of a Roth account. A Roth individual
retirement account or a Roth version of
a workplace plan is funded with dollars
you already paid tax on. And because you
already paid, the deal the government
made with you is permanent. Once you are
past the age of 59 and a half and the
account has been open for at least 5
years, every single dollar you withdraw
comes out completely free of federal
income tax. Not the money you put in,
not the growth, not the gains that built
up over 20 or 30 years. All of it
tax-free. Picture a retiree who put
money away quietly for decades and now
has a wroth worth $200,000. When she
draws on it, she owes nothing. While her
neighbor pulling from an ordinary
retirement account pays tax on every
withdrawal. Same money saved, two
completely different outcomes. The
difference is which bucket it sat in.
And there is a hidden second gift buried
inside that Roth, one that almost no one
talks about. Because those withdrawals
are not counted as income, they do not
push up that provisional income number
that decides whether your social
security gets taxed. So, a senior who
pulls from a Roth can cover her expenses
without accidentally dragging her social
security into the taxable zone. There is
a cruel little trap in the tax code that
professionals quietly call the tax
torpedo, where pulling money from the
wrong account raises your income just
enough to start taxing your social
security on top of it, so you get hit
twice from one withdrawal. The Roth is
one of the few tools that lets you step
around that torpedo completely. That is
why which bucket your money sits in is
not a small detail. It can decide your
tax bill for the rest of your life.
Therefore, the type of account your
money lives in matters just as much as
how much money you have. And this is
where the third category comes in
because it is the closest thing to true
magic the tax code allows. It is called
a health savings account. Money you put
into one of these was never taxed going
in. It grows without being taxed. And
when you pull it out to cover a
qualified medical expense, it comes out
without being taxed either. That is
three separate tax breaks stacked on a
single account which exists nowhere else
in the entire code. And here is the part
built for seniors specifically. Before
the age of 65, if you pull that money
out for something other than medical
care, the government hits you with a 20%
penalty on top of the tax. But the day
you turn 65, that penalty vanishes.
From that day forward, you can pull the
money out for anything at all. And if
you use it for medical costs, and
seniors face a mountain of medical
costs, it is still 100% tax-free. Let me
make this a real person for a moment
because numbers float away but people
stay with you. Picture a man and I will
call him Walter. 68 years old, careful
with a dollar his whole life. Walter
quietly built a health savings account
up to $40,000 over his working years.
Now in retirement, every prescription,
every doctor visit, every pair of
glasses and hearing aid and dental bill,
he pays straight from that account. And
not one cent of it is ever taxed. His
brother, who never opened one, pays for
the identical care out of a taxable
account and loses a slice to the
government every time. Same illnesses,
same bills. One brother handing money to
the IRS, the other keeping all of it.
Walter was never smarter. He was just
shown the door and he walked through it.
But the three we have covered so far,
social security, Roth, and the health
savings account, are all about income
you arranged for yourself. The fourth
type is different because it arrives at
the worst moment of a family's life and
the tax code for once shows a little
mercy. When a person dies and leaves a
life insurance payout to their spouse or
their children, that money, the death
benefit, is generally not counted as
taxable income at all. A $100,000 policy
pays $100,000. A4 million policy pays a4
million. The beneficiary does not report
it as income and does not lose a piece
of it to federal income tax. In a season
of grief, when a widow is trying to
figure out how to keep the lights on,
that full untouched check can be the
difference between keeping the house and
losing it. And most families brace
themselves for a tax bill on it that, in
the ordinary case, simply never comes. I
have watched families sit frozen over a
life insurance letter, afraid to cash
it, whispering to each other that the
government is going to take a third of
it, so they had better set money aside.
and they set aside money they did not
need to set aside and they lived smaller
than they had to in a hard year over a
tax that was never going to arrive. So
hear me clearly. In the ordinary case
when a policy pays out because someone
died, that money reaches the beneficiary
whole. That is one weight you can lift
off the shoulders of the people you love
just by telling them the truth about it
while you still can.
Now, I want you to lean in because we
have reached the fifth type. And this is
the giant I promised you at the very
beginning. This is the one that can
shield the largest single amount of
money from the IRS in one move. And it
sits inside something almost every
senior watching me owns, your home. When
you sell your main home, the profit you
made on it, the gain, would normally be
taxable. But the tax code hands you an
exemption so large that most seniors
sell and owe absolutely nothing. If you
are single, you can exclude up to
$250,000 of gain from tax. And if you
are married and filing jointly, you can
exclude up to $500,000.
$500,000 of profit on your own home,
completely invisible to the IRS, as long
as you owned it and lived in it as your
main home for at least two of the last 5
years.
Think about what that means for the
people who bought a modest house decades
ago for 30 or $40,000 and now it is
worth4 or $500,000. That is an enormous
gain on paper. The kind of number that
would terrify anyone into thinking the
tax bill will swallow half of it. And
yet, because of this one rule, a married
couple can walk away from that sale with
half a million dollars of profit and
hand the government nothing. This is the
one out of all seven that can protect
the most. And it is the one seniors most
often forget they even have because they
only think about it in the one year they
finally sell.
There is one condition you have to meet
and it is worth saying plainly so no one
gets caught out. You have to have owned
the home and lived in it as your main
home for at least two of the last 5
years. Those two years do not even have
to be backtoback. For a senior who has
lived in the same house for 20 or 30
years, this is not a hurdle at all. It
is already met many times over. But if
you are thinking about selling a place
you moved into only recently or a second
home or a rental, the rules are
different. And that is exactly the kind
of thing worth checking before you sign
anything, not after. Because getting
this one right can be the single largest
tax decision of your entire retirement.
and getting it wrong can cost you tens
of thousands of dollars that the law
would happily have let you keep.
Let me stop here at roughly the middle
of everything I have to tell you because
up to this point you might think these
are just seven nice little breaks, a bit
of money saved here and there. They are
not. Stacked together, they can shape
whether you spend your final decades
comfortable or squeezed and whether your
children inherit something whole or
something the government took a bite out
of first. So lean in because the sixth
type reaches past your own lifetime and
into what you leave behind and it is one
of the most misunderstood rules in the
entire code.
The sixth type of income the IRS cannot
touch is an inheritance. When you
receive money or property from someone
who has died, that inheritance is
generally not treated as taxable income
to you at all. There is no federal
inheritance tax reaching into an
ordinary family's pocket. And there is a
second piece to this that is worth more
than most people ever realize called the
stepped up basis. When you inherit an
asset, say a house or shares of stock
that the person bought long ago for very
little, the tax value of that asset
resets to what it is worth on the day
they died. So if your mother bought a
home for $40,000 and it was worth
$400,000 when she passed and you inherit
it and sell it, the decades of gain in
between are wiped clean. You are treated
as if you acquired it at $400,000 and
the tax on all that growth simply
disappears. Let me put a real picture on
that stepped up basis because it is
worth more than almost anyone realizes
and it is quietly one of the most
generous rules in the whole code. Say
your father bought shares of a company
long ago and paid $5,000 for them and by
the time he passed those shares were
worth $55,000. If he had sold them
himself the day before he died, he would
have owed tax on $50,000 of gain. But
because you inherited them instead, the
tax value resets to $55,000 on the day
he died. And that $50,000 of gain that
built up over his whole lifetime simply
evaporates for tax purposes. You could
turn around and sell those shares and
owe little or nothing. The same thing
happens with the family home, with land,
with almost any asset that grew in value
over the years. a lifetime of growth
handed to the next generation with the
tax scrubbed clean off it.
That is not a trick and it is not
aggressive planning. It is written
directly into the law and it is one of
the main reasons an ordinary family can
pass a home and a nest egg to their
children without the government taking a
bite on the way down. But people hear
the words estate tax and panic. So, let
me put that fear to rest with a real
number because this is where families
torture themselves for no reason. The
federal estate tax, the one everyone is
afraid of, does not touch a family until
the estate is worth more than 13,990,000
per person. $13 million and change. For
the overwhelming majority of seniors
watching me right now, that tax will
never ever apply. You have been
frightened of a monster that lives in a
mansion far down the road from your
house. the inheritance you leave and the
inheritance you receive in almost every
normal family passes free of that tax
entirely.
Therefore, the money you have spent a
lifetime building and the home you have
spent a lifetime paying off can move to
your children far more intact than you
were ever led to believe. Which brings
me to the seventh type on the list. And
this one is quieter than the rest
because it does not arrive as a windfall
or a sale or a death benefit. It arrives
as a steady trickle of interest month
after month and the government agreed
long ago to keep its hands off it
entirely.
I am talking about the interest paid by
municipal bonds. When you lend money to
a state, a city, a county, or a local
school district by buying what people
call a mun bond. The interest that bond
pays you back is exempt from federal
income tax. It is one of the oldest
bargains in the entire code. The
government wanted towns to be able to
build roads and schools and hospitals
cheaply. So, it made the interest on
those bonds tax-free to the people who
bought them. So, a retiree with money
parked in municipal bonds can collect
that interest year after year and never
report a dollar of it as federal taxable
income. For a senior who wants steady,
safe income without feeding the IRS,
this is a river that has been running
quietly the whole time. But let me be
honest with you about one wrinkle here
because I will never hand you half a
truth. That municipal bond interest,
while it is free of federal income tax,
does still get counted when the
government figures out whether your
social security is taxable in that
