provisional income formula we talked
about at the start. So it is a powerful
tool, but it is not a magic wand and you
use it with your eyes open. That honesty
is exactly why you are here and not
listening to someone selling you
something. Now, before I give you the
action steps, I promised you one
specific move. A lever you can pull on
purpose that decides whether the IRS
gets to tax your social security at all.
Here it is, and it is the most powerful
single action on this entire list. Once
you reach the age of 70 and a half, and
certainly once you are forced to start
taking required withdrawals from your
retirement accounts, the government
normally taxes every dollar of those
withdrawals as income. That forced
income can even push your other income
high enough to start taxing your social
security, the very thing we opened with.
But there is a tool called a qualified
charitable distribution. It lets you
send money up to $18,000 in a single
year directly from your retirement
account to a charity you care about. And
because it goes straight to the charity
and never lands in your hands as income,
it is not taxed. It never raises your
provisional income by a single dollar.
and it still counts toward the required
withdrawal the government was going to
force on you anyway. So for the seniors
who give to their church, their food
bank, their veterans group, this is the
move that turns a taxable forced
withdrawal into a gift that costs the
IRS its cut and can keep your social
security check completely untouched.
Exactly as I promised at the very
beginning.
Now, let me show you what all seven of
these look like when they sit in one
household at the same time. Because this
is where it stops being a list and
starts being a life. Imagine two
neighbors, same age, same street, same
amount of money to their names. The
first neighbor knows only the one rule
everyone knows that social security is
partly tax-free and lives the rest of
his retirement paying tax he did not
have to. He draws from a taxable account
and loses a slice. He sells his home and
worries the whole way through it. He
gives to his church out of his checking
account and gets nothing back for it.
The second neighbor draws from a wroth
and pays nothing. pays her medical bills
from a health savings account and pays
nothing. Sells the family home and
shields $500,000 of gain. Gives to her
church straight from her retirement
account and erases the tax on that
withdrawal. Leaves her children a home
with a stepped up basis that wipes out
decades of gain.
Same money, same street. One family
handed the government thousands it never
owed, and the other kept it all legally
in the daylight exactly as the code
allows. The only difference between them
was knowing the other six. And notice
what the second neighbor did not do. She
did not cheat. She did not hide money
offshore. She did not find some shady
adviser with a secret. She did nothing
that a tax collector could ever knock on
her door about because every single move
she made was written into the law in
advance, waiting for anyone willing to
learn it. That is the part I need you to
hold on to. Keeping this money is not
the reward for being sneaky. It is the
reward for being informed. The
government wrote these seven doors into
the wall on purpose. It just never hung
a sign over any of them.
So now, let me give you the exact moves
in order because knowing these rules and
using them are two very different things
and the entire system is quietly betting
that you will stop at knowing. Move
number one, sit down and find out your
provisional income, the number that
decides whether your social security is
taxed at all. If you are single and
under $25,000 or married and under
$32,000, your benefits should not be
taxed. And if you have been paying tax
on them, that is a conversation to have
with a tax professional right away
because you may be owed money back. Move
number two, learn which of your accounts
are taxable and which are not before you
pull a single dollar. If you have a
Roth, understand that after 59 12 and 5
years, those withdrawals are free. Draw
from the taxable buckets and the
tax-free buckets in the right order and
you can lower your tax for the rest of
your life.
Move number three. If you have a health
savings account and you are past 65, use
it deliberately for your medical costs
because every one of those dollars comes
out tax-free and there is no smarter
money you can spend in retirement. Move
number four. Before you ever sell your
home, remember the exclusion. $250,000
of gain protected if you are single,
$500,000 if you are married and filing
jointly as long as you live there two of
the last five years. Do not let anyone
frighten you into thinking the tax will
eat your home sale and confirm you meet
the ownership and use test before you
sign.
Move number five. If you give to charity
and you are past 70 and a half, ask
about the qualified charitable
distribution before you take your
required withdrawal, not after, sending
it straight from the retirement account
up to $18,000 a year keeps that money
off your tax return entirely and
protects your social security in the
bargain. And here is the one to write
down and keep because these rules change
at the edges every year and the numbers
get adjusted and you want the truth from
the source and not from a stranger. The
Internal Revenue Service publishes every
one of these rules in plain language on
its own website at IRS.gov and its
helpline is 8008291040.
Say that back to yourself so it sticks.
You worked your whole life. You paid
your taxes on every paycheck year after
year, decade after decade. And you were
promised that when you finally reached
the far side of all that work, the
system would not keep reaching into your
pocket for money it had no right to. and
quietly in language they prayed you
would never sit down and read. The tax
code actually kept a piece of that
promise. Seven kinds of income it cannot
touch. The portion of your social
security, the wroth you built, the
health savings account, the life
insurance that reaches your family, the
half million dollars of gain in your own
home, the inheritance you receive and
the one you leave, and the gift that
erases the tax on money you are going to
give anyway. Most seniors know one.
Starting today, you know all seven.
Find your provisional income. Draw from
the right accounts in the right order.
Use the home exclusion. Make the
charitable distribution before your
required withdrawal. And when you want
the rule in black and white, you go
straight to the source at IRS.gov GV or
you call them at 800829104.

title: 6 Social Security Changes Hit Seniors This Fall — #4 Quietly Takes Part of Your Check

segments.text: Social Security can now reach into your
monthly check and take up to half of it
back without a judge, without a court
order, and without asking your
permission first. That is not a rumor,
and it is not something being debated in
Congress for some future year. It is the
rule right now, this fall, and it is one
of six separate changes landing on your
Social Security check at the same time.
Most seniors [clears throat] have heard
about one or two of them. Almost nobody
has heard about all six together, and
there is one change on this list, one
single change, that can quietly cut your
payment in half the month it hits.
Here is what I need you to understand
before we go one step further. These six
changes are not spread out over the next
10 years. They are stacking up on the
very same check, in the very same
season, and they interact with each
other in ways the notices in your
mailbox will never explain. The letter
that tells you about your raise will not
mention the rule that can take that
raise away. The card that comes with
your new premium will not mention the
withholding that can swallow the rest.
So, I am going to walk you through all
six in plain language, in the order that
matters for your wallet. And somewhere
in the middle of this list is the one
that scares me the most, the one that
can take half your check in a single
month. I am also going to give you the
exact form and the exact phone call that
stops it cold. Stay with me all the way
to that part, because if you leave
early, you will miss the one piece of
paper that protects you. That promise is
the reason to watch to the end.
Let me tell you why all of this is
happening now, in the fall of 2026.
Three separate clocks are all striking
at once. The Social Security
Administration announces the new cost of
living raise for the coming year on the
14th of October, right after the
September inflation report is finalized.
The federal budget year turns over on
the 1st of October, which is when brand
new income rules and premium amounts
click into place. And a presidential
order signed last year set a hard
deadline for the way your money is
delivered, a deadline that already
passed on the 30th of September. Three
clocks, one check, six changes. That is
why this season, more than any other in
years, is the one where seniors quietly
lose money they never knew was at risk.
And here is the backdrop that makes all
of this hurt so much more than it
should. Independent researchers who
track senior spending have found that
Social Security has lost close to a
third of its buying power since the year
2000. A dollar of benefits back then
buys only about 67 cents of the things
seniors actually need today. So, even
before these six changes, the check was
already falling behind. A retiree who
felt comfortable 20 years ago is now
stretching the same benefit across rent
that has doubled, groceries that climb
every single month, and medicine that
costs more than a car payment used to.
That is the hole you are already
standing in. Now, imagine six new
changes landing on top of that all at
once, most of them quietly reducing what
reaches your account. This is why I am
not exaggerating when I say this fall is
the most important season in years for
you to understand your own check.
The difference between a senior who
knows these rules and one who does not
can be hundreds of dollars a month. Now,
I want to be clear about who this
affects because it is not a small group.
If you are already collecting Social
Security, this is you. If you are about
to file in the next year or two, this is
you. If you are still working past 65
and drawing a check at the same time,
this is very much you. And if you have a
husband or a wife or a parent who
depends on that monthly deposit to cover
the rent and the groceries and the
medicine, then this is them and you are
the one who needs to know this so you
can protect them. So, do not tune out
thinking this is for somebody else.
Every single one of these six changes
touches an ordinary retired household.
Let me give you the first change, and it
is the one that sounds like good news.
Your raise is coming. The projection for
the new cost of living raise is about 3
and 1/2 percent, which works out to
roughly $75 a month for the average
retiree. On paper, that looks like the
biggest raise in a few years, and the
The will tell you to celebrate. But,
here's the part the headlines leave out.
That raise is measured against the wrong
shopping cart. By law, your cost of
living raise is tied to an inflation
index built around young working people
in cities. The things they spend money
on, gas for a long commute, new
electronics, restaurant meals. It is not
tied to the index the government itself
already publishes for people 62 and
older. The one that weighs medicine and
rent and doctor visits much more
heavily. Those are the exact things that
eat a senior budget alive. So, your $75
raise is measured against a cart of
goods you do not even buy, which means
it is designed to fall short of your
real costs before it ever reaches your
bank account.
Let me make that real with two shopping
carts side by side. In the first cart,
the one the government uses to set your
raise, you have gasoline for a daily
commute, a new laptop, a gym membership,
and dinner out on Friday night. In the
second cart, the one that matches your
actual life, you have a bottle of
prescription pills, a copayment at the
doctor, a heating bill, and this month's
rent. When the price of gasoline drops,
the government's cart looks cheaper, so
your raise stays small. But your cart,
the medicine and the rent and the
doctor, keeps climbing no matter what
happens at the gas pump. That is the
trick hiding inside the very first
change. The raise is not built to keep
up with the life of a 70-year-old. It is
built to keep up with the life of a
25-year-old. And the gap between those
two carts is money that quietly leaves
your pocket every single year, a little
more each time, and it never comes back.
But the raise being too small is only
the beginning, because the second change
decides how much of your full benefit
you even get to keep, and it is quietly
costing early filers a fortune. For
everyone born in 1960 or later, the age
at which you get your full unreduced
Social Security benefit is now 67, not
65, the way it was for your parents. Not
66, 67. And if you claim your benefit at
62, the earliest age allowed, your check
is permanently reduced by as much as 30%
for the rest of your life. That is not a
temporary cut that fixes itself later.
That is a lower number stamped onto
every single payment you will ever
receive, month after month, year after
year. On a benefit that would have been
$2,000 at full retirement age, claiming
early can knock it down to around
That is a difference of $600 every
month, gone permanently, because of a
rule most people never had explained to
them before they signed.
I want you to sit with that number,
because $600 a month is not a small
thing. Over a single year, that is
Over a retirement that lasts 20 years or
more, that early claiming decision can
cost well over $100,000 in total
benefits. And the cruel part is that
most people who claim at 62 do it
because nobody ever showed them the
math. They see the earliest age, they
assume that is when they are supposed to
file, and they lock in the lower number
for life. Now, I'm not telling you that
waiting is always right, because
everyone's health and situation is
different. And for some people, claiming
early truly is the correct choice. But I
am telling you that this is a permanent
decision made with almost no guidance.
And the difference between choosing well
and choosing blindly is one of the
largest financial choices you will ever
make. Change number two does not take
your money the way the others do. It
just quietly locks in how much you were
ever allowed to have.
Now, the third change is the one that
catches working seniors completely off
guard, and it feels almost like a
punishment for staying employed. If you
are collecting Social Security before
you reach that full retirement age of
67, and you are still working, the
government limits how much you can earn
before it starts holding your check
back. In the current rules, once your
earnings pass roughly $23,400
in a year, Social Security withholds $1
of your benefit for every $2 you earn
above that line.
Think about that. You go to work, you
earn the money, you pay the taxes on it,
and after all of that, Social Security
reaches in and holds back part of the
check you already earned a right to.
Now, to be fair, that withheld money is
not lost forever. Once you reach full
retirement age, they recalculate and
give it back to you slowly over time.
But in the here and now, in the months
you are living on, it can feel like your
check simply shrank for no reason you
can see.
Many seniors do not even connect the
smaller deposit to the extra hours they
worked. Now, stop for a second because
this is the part I really need you to
hear, and it is the reason none of these
changes should be looked at alone. These
six changes do not take turns. They land
on the same check in the same month at
the same time. Picture one ordinary
retiree this coming winter. She gets the
raise, but it is too small against her
real costs. She claimed a little early,
so her base check is already reduced.
She picks up a part-time job to make
ends meet, so part of her benefit is
being withheld, and she has not even hit
the two changes I have not told you
about yet. The two that can take the
biggest bite of all. This is why seniors
keep saying the same thing to me. My
raise went up, so why is my check
smaller? The answer is that the raise is
the one number they show you, and
everything else is happening quietly
underneath it. So, let me pull back the
curtain on the change that scares me the
most.
Therefore, let us talk about the fourth
change, the one I promised you at the
very beginning. The single change on
this entire list that can take half your
check in one month. Here it is, plainly.
Social Security can now automatically
withhold up to half of your monthly
benefit, up to 50% to recover what it
calls an overpayment. An overpayment is
any amount the agency later decides it
paid you by mistake, even if the mistake
was entirely theirs, even if it happened
years ago. Even if you had no idea
anything was wrong. And here is how it
works in real life. A letter arrives in
your mailbox saying you were overpaid.
Maybe your income was reported a little
differently than expected. Maybe a work
record updated late. Maybe a survivor
benefit overlapped with something else.
You did nothing wrong and you may not
even understand the letter.
But if you do not respond within the
window they give you, the agency begins
pulling up to half of every single
monthly payment until the so-called debt
is repaid.
Let me put a real number on that so it
lands. Say your benefit is $1,800 a
month, which is close to the national
average. Under this rule, Social
Security can withhold $900 of it month
after month until the balance is
cleared. $900 gone from a check that was
already covering rent and food and
medicine. For a household living close
to the edge, that is not an
inconvenience. That is a crisis that
arises with no warning and no court and
no judge. And I want you to understand
how recently this got worse. Earlier in
the year, the agency actually moved to
take 100% of the check, the entire
payment, to recover these overpayments.
After an outcry, they pulled it back to
50% as the standard rate. 50% is the
rule you are living under right now. So
a change that most seniors have never
heard a word about can cut their income
in half overnight. And let me tell you
why this one is so much more dangerous
than it sounds. Because the word
overpayment makes it seem like it must
be your fault. Like you must have done
something wrong to owe the money. In
most cases, you did nothing at all. The
agency processes millions of payments
and when its own records update late or
a piece of information arrives out of
order, the computer can decide months or
even years later that it paid you too
much. The letter does not say we made an
error on our end. It says you were
overpaid, as if you reached into the
till. A widow can get one because her
survivor benefit and her own benefit
overlapped for a few months during the
paperwork. A working senior can get one
because a wage figure was estimated and
later corrected. A person on disability
can get one simply because their
situation changed and the notice moving
through the system lagged behind real
life. None of these people cheated. All
of them can wake up to a check cut in
half.
And the timing is the trap. These
letters come with a window, a set number
of days to respond, and if that window
closes before you act, the withholding
begins automatically. Many seniors set
the letter aside because they do not
understand it, or they assume it is a
mistake that will sort itself out, or
they are simply afraid to call. Then the
next deposit arrives and it is half of
what it should be, and now they are
scrambling to cover the rent with money
that is no longer there. That is the
exact sequence I want to help you avoid.
The rule is harsh, but the people who
get hurt worst are almost always the
ones who did not know they were allowed
to fight back. Now, here is the promise
I made you, and I am keeping it. You are
not helpless against this. There is a
specific set of steps that stops the
withholding, and I'm going to give them
to you in a moment in plain order,
because knowing the rule is only half
the protection. Knowing the form is the
other half. But, before I give you the
way out, you need the fifth change,
because it is already reaching into your
check every single month, and most
people never notice it. Your Medicare
Part B premium, the part that covers
doctors and outpatient care, is deducted
straight out of your Social Security
payment before the money ever reaches
your bank. It is taken first, off the
top, before you see a dime. In the
current year, that premium is about
a month, and the projection for the
coming year pushes it to around $209.50
a month, an increase of roughly $6.60.
That may not sound like much on its own,
but remember change number one, your $75
raise. A chunk of that raise is eaten by
this premium increase before it ever
lands. So, the raise you were told to
celebrate is quietly shaved down by the
premium you were never told to watch.
One hand gives, the other hand takes,
and both letters arrive in the same week
pretending to be unrelated.
And there is a quiet second layer to
this one that catches higher income
retirees completely by surprise. If your
income is above certain thresholds, you
do not pay the standard premium at all.
You pay a surcharge on top of it, an
extra amount added to your Part B
premium based on your tax return from 2
years ago. So, a retiree who had one
good year, maybe they sold a house or
cashed out an old account, can suddenly
find a much larger premium being pulled
from their check, all because of income
from a year that is already behind them.
If that has happened to you because of a
one-time event that will not repeat,
there is a form you can file to ask for
that surcharge to be reconsidered, and I
will point you to the right phone call
at the end. For most people, the lesson
is simpler. Watch the premium line on
your check as closely as you watch the
benefit line because the premium is
where a good chunk of your raise quietly
disappears before you ever get to touch
it.
And that brings us to the sixth change,
the one about how your money is even
delivered. And this one has a hard
deadline that already passed. Under a
presidential order signed last year, the
federal government is ending paper
checks. As of the 30th of September,
Treasury stopped issuing paper checks
for federal payments, and that includes
Social Security. Everything is moving to
electronic payment, either direct
deposit into your bank account or a
prepaid card. Now, if your check already
goes straight into your bank, you are
fine. Nothing changes for you. But if
you are one of the seniors still
receiving a paper check in the mail, and
there are still hundreds of thousands of
them, your payments can be disrupted if
you have not switched over. Imagine
depending on that envelope every month,
watching for the mail carrier, and one
day simply having nothing arrive. That
is the risk for anyone who has not moved
to electronic payment.
So, this is the one change on the list
where doing nothing is the dangerous
choice.
So, now you have all six.
The raise that is too small. The full
retirement age that punishes early
claims. The earnings limit that holds
back your check while you work. The
overpayment rule that can take half your
payment. The premium that gets deducted
first and the paper check that is
disappearing.
Six changes, one check, one season.
Now, let me give you the part I
promised, the protection, starting with
the big one.
If you ever get one of those overpayment
letters, do not panic and do not ignore
it, because ignoring it is exactly what
triggers the withholding.
You have three real options and they all
start with one phone call to Social
Security at 1-800-772-1213.
Option one, you can ask them to lower
the withholding rate. You do not have to
accept them taking half. You can request
a much smaller monthly amount that you
can actually afford. And by law, they
are supposed to work with you on a
payment you can live on.
Option two, if the overpayment was not
your fault and paying it back would
leave you unable to cover your basic
needs, you can file for a waiver using
form SSA-632.
A waiver asks them to forgive the debt
entirely. And while that waiver is being
reviewed, they are not supposed to keep
taking the money.
Option three, if you believe the
overpayment is simply wrong, that you
were not actually overpaid at all, you
can file for reconsideration using form
which is a formal appeal.
And again, the collection is supposed to
pause while your appeal is pending.
The single most important thing is to
act inside the window on the letter.
A phone call the week you get the notice
can be the difference between keeping
your full check and losing half of it.
Now, let me give you the simple action
steps for the rest of the list, because
every one of these six changes has
something you can actually do about it.
First, before the new amounts post in
December, log in to your account at
ssa.gov
and check your own numbers with your own
eyes. Do not trust the summary in the
letter. Look at your benefit amount,
look at the premium being deducted, and
make sure they match what you expected.
Second, if you are still receiving a
paper check in the mail, call Social
Security today and switch to direct
deposit or the prepaid card option, so
your payments are never interrupted.
Third, if you are still working and
collecting before your full retirement
age, know the earnings limit. Keep track
of what you make and understand that
going over it will hold back part of
your check until you reach 67.
Fourth, if you have not filed yet and
you are healthy, run the numbers on
waiting, because every year you delay
past 62 raises your permanent benefit,
and the difference over a lifetime can
be tens of thousands of dollars. And
fifth, watch your mail carefully this
fall for anything that says overpayment.
And if you see that word, make the phone
call immediately before the window
closes. Therefore, let me give you one
more layer of protection, because there
is a simple habit that guards you
against almost every one of these six
changes at once. Once a month, when your
deposit lands, take two minutes and
actually look at it. Not the letter, not
the headline, the real number in your
real account. Compare it to last month.
If it went down, ask yourself why before
you spend another dollar. Was there a
premium increase you expected? Fine. Was
there something you did not expect? A
sudden drop? A number cut nearly in
half? That is your early warning that an
overpayment withholding may have
started, and it means you need to call
that day, not next week. The seniors who
lose the most are not the ones who make
a mistake. They are the ones who never
look closely enough to notice the money
leaving. Two minutes a month is the
cheapest insurance you will ever buy on
your own income. And let me say a word
to the family members watching this, the
sons and daughters, because you have a
role here, too. If you have a parent who
lives on Social Security, sit down with
them this fall and go through these six
changes together. Help them log in and
check their numbers. Help them switch
off the paper check if they are still on
one. And if a letter shows up with the
word overpayment on it, do not let them
set it in a drawer out of fear. Pick up
the phone with them and make the call. A
single afternoon of your time can
protect a parent from months of a check
cut in half. This is exactly the kind of
thing that slips past an older person
living alone, and it is exactly the kind
of thing a caring family member can
catch in time. I also want you to know
your rights, plainly, because the agency
is not your enemy, and the people who
answer that phone are usually trying to
help. You are allowed to ask for a
smaller withholding you can afford. You
are allowed to ask for the debt to be
forgiven if it was not your fault. You
are allowed to appeal a decision you
believe is wrong. And you are allowed to
have all of it explained to you in
language you understand. None of these
are favors. They are protections written
into the law for exactly this situation.
The only way you lose them is by staying
silent until the window closes.
I want to leave you with one last
thought because it ties this whole thing
together. None of these six changes were
designed to be understood by the person
they happened to. They arrive as
separate letters on separate days in
separate envelopes. Each one written in
language that hides how much it costs

title: Your 2027 Social Security Raise Is Rigged to Fall Short — the Hidden Math They Won't Show You

segments.text: The Social Security raise coming to your
bank account in January of 2027 is
projected to be about $75 a month. And
before that money ever reaches you, the
government has already measured it
against the wrong prices on purpose.
That number, 3.6%, is being called the
biggest raise in years. It sounds like
good news. It is being decided right now
in the final weeks of the measuring
window, and the official figure will be
announced on October 14th. But here is
the part almost no one says out loud.
The raise is calculated using a
yardstick that was never built for you.
A yardstick that measures what a young
worker buys, not what a retired person
buys. And because of that single choice,
the raise is designed to fall short of
your real costs before the ink is even
dry. I want you to stay with me because
there is one line buried in federal law
that makes it illegal for the government
to take your entire raise, no matter how
high the Medicare premium climbs next
year. Almost no one knows to check
whether that protection is actually
working for them. I am going to name it
before we finish, and I'm going to tell
you exactly how to make sure it applies
to you. Because if it does not, you
could quietly lose money you are legally
entitled to keep. Hold that thought. We
will come back to it. For now,
understand what is happening this month.
The cost of living adjustment, the thing
everyone just calls the cola, is not
pulled out of thin air. It is set by
looking at a specific inflation index
over the months of July, August, and
September, and comparing it to the same
three months a year earlier. September
is the last month of that window. So the
number that decides how much you live on
for all of next year is being locked in
as this month ends. And the Social
Security Administration will announce it
officially on October 14th. The Senior
Citizens League, which tracks this every
year, projects the raise will land near
For contrast, the raise for 2026 was
2.8%. So on paper, 3.6% looks generous.
For the average retiree, 3.6% works out
to roughly $75 more each month.
$75 a month, write that number down
because everything I am about to tell
you is about where that $75 actually
goes and why so much of it is gone
before you ever get to spend it. Let me
tell you who I am talking to because
this affects some people far more than
others. If Social Security is the
foundation of your monthly income, if it
is the check that covers your rent or
your mortgage, your groceries, your
prescriptions, your electric bill, then
this is your money and this is your
fight. There are more than 70 million
Americans receiving Social Security. And
for a huge share of them, that check is
not extra money. It is the money. When
the raise falls short of real life, it
is not an abstraction on a government
report. It is a choice between filling a
prescription and filling the
refrigerator. So, let us look at exactly
how the raise gets measured and why the
measurement is rigged against the very
people it is supposed to protect.
Think about your last 12 months for a
second. Think about what actually went
up in your house. It was probably not
gasoline that hurt the most because you
are not commuting to a job five days a
week anymore. It was the health
insurance. It was the doctor who now
costs more for the same visit. It was
the prescription that jumped $40 at the
pharmacy counter with no warning. It was
the property tax bill or the rent notice
or the homeowners insurance that climbed
again. It was the electric bill in the
summer and the heating bill in the
winter. Those are the things that
quietly drained your check. And I want
you to hold that picture in your mind
because it is the whole argument. The
prices that hurt seniors the most are
not the prices the government uses to
size your raise. Your real life and the
government's measuring stick are two
different things and the gap between
them is where your money disappears.
Here is the heart of it. The index that
sets your raise is called the Consumer
Price Index for urban wage earners and
clerical workers. That is a mouthful, so
remember it by what it actually means.
It is a basket of spending built from
the lives of urban wage earners and
clerical workers. In plain English, it
is built from what working-age people
buy while they are still going to a job
every day. It is weighted toward things
like gasoline, commuting costs, and
consumer electronics. It is the shopping
cart of someone driving to work, not
someone who retired 10 years ago. Now,
think about your own shopping cart. If
you are retired, you are probably not
spending a fortune on gasoline to
commute 5 days a week. You are spending
it on medical care, on health insurance,
on housing, on prescription drugs. Those
are the categories that dominate a
senior budget, and those are exactly the
categories that rise the fastest year
after year. So, when the government
measures inflation using a worker's
shopping cart instead of a retiree's
shopping cart, it captures the wrong
prices. It undercounts the things you
actually spend money on, and it
overcounts the things you do not.
And here is the part that should make
you angry because it proves this is not
an accident. The government already
knows this. The Bureau of Labor
Statistics, the same federal agency that
produces the workers index, also
produces a separate index built
specifically for older Americans. It is
called the Consumer Price Index for the
Elderly, and it measures the spending of
Americans aged 62 and older. It weights
medical care and housing far more
heavily because that is where seniors
actually spend. The Bureau of Labor
Statistics has been publishing this
elderly index since 1982. Let me say
that again so it lands. There has been
an inflation index designed for seniors,
produced by the federal government,
sitting on the shelf for more than 40
years.
Let me make the difference concrete
because this is not a small technical
footnote. Picture two shopping carts
sitting side by side at the checkout.
The first cart belongs to a 40-year-old
who drives to an office every morning.
It is heavy with gasoline, with a car
payment, with a new phone, with
restaurant lunches, with the kind of
spending that fills a working person's
week. The second cart belongs to a
75-year-old. It is heavy with
prescription bottles, with a Medicare
supplement premium, with a home that
needs a new roof, with a heating bill
that does not care how old you are. Now,
imagine the government walks up, looks
only at the first cart, the working
person's cart, and announces, "Based on
this cart, here is how much more
everyone gets next year." That is
exactly what happens to your raise. It
is priced off the wrong cart.
And the items in your cart, medical care
and housing above all, are the ones
climbing fastest. So, the raise
consistently lands beneath the reality
you live in. Therefore, the obvious
question is, "Why is your raise not
calculated using the index built for
you?" The answer is that social security
is tied to the workers index by law.
Switching to the elderly index would
take an act of Congress. Bills to make
that switch have been introduced over
and over for years, and every single
time they have failed to become law. So,
the mismatch is not a glitch. It is
baked into the statute. Your raise is
measured with the wrong ruler, and it
stays that way because the law says so.
But, the story gets worse. And this is
where I need you to really pay
attention, because a one-year gap
between the workers index and the
elderly index might sound small. A
fraction of a percent here, a fraction
of a percent there, who cares? Here is
why you should care. That gap does not
happen once. It happens every single
year. And every year it happens, it
stacks on top of the year before.
The Senior Citizens League tracks this
exact problem in a study they run every
year. They measure how much buying power
a social security dollar has lost over
time, and their finding is staggering.
They estimate that social security has
lost roughly a third of its buying power
since the year 2000. Sit with that, a
third. That means a dollar of social
security benefits today buys about a
third less than it did at the start of
the century, even after every single
cost of living raise has been added in.
The raises have been happening the whole
time, and the buying power still
collapsed because the raises were
measured against the wrong prices, year
after year after year.
So, when you hear that your 2027 raise
is 3.6% the biggest in years, understand
what that really means. It is not the
government finally getting generous. It
is the government letting you tread
water for 1 year in a pool that has been
slowly draining for two decades. 3.6%
does not close a gap that big. It does
not even come close. It just keeps you
from sinking a little faster this year.
Let me put that a third in terms you can
feel because a percentage is easy to
shrug off. Imagine that back in the year
2000, your Social Security check covered
your rent, your groceries, and your
medicine with a small amount left over
at the end of the month. Now, imagine
that today, after 20-some years of
raises that were all measured against
the wrong prices, that same check,
adjusted for what a dollar actually
buys, has lost roughly a third of its
reach. That is not a check that
stretches a little less. That is a check
where one out of every $3 of purchasing
power has quietly evaporated, even
though the number printed on it went up
almost every year. The raises were real
on paper. The erosion underneath them
was also real, and it was bigger. That
is the con in one sentence. They showed
you a number going up while the value
underneath it was going down, and they
measured both with a ruler that was
never yours.
That $75 a month is starting to look
different now, is it not? It is not a
windfall. It is a partial patch on a
hole that keeps getting bigger. Now,
before I show you the trap inside the
trap, I want to remind you of the
promise I made at the start because we
are getting close to it. I told you
there is a line in federal law that
makes it illegal for the government to
take your entire raise. That protection
is real, and I am going to tell you its
name and how to use it in just a few
minutes. It is the single most important
thing you can check after watching this.
But first, you need to understand the
mechanism that makes the shortfall so
dangerous because it changes everything
about how you should think about this
raise.
Here is the mechanism, and it is the
part that most people never grasp. When
the raise is applied, it is not to some
fresh starting number every year. It is
applied to your current benefit amount.
That new, slightly higher amount then
becomes the permanent base that next
year's raise is calculated from. Every
year, the new number becomes the floor
for the next number. That is how
compounding works, and normally,
compounding is your friend. It is how
savings grow.
But when the raise itself is too small,
compounding turns against you. Think
about what that means. If your raise
falls short of your real inflation this
year, you do not just lose ground this
year. You lock in a lower base, and next
year's raise, however big or small it
is, gets calculated off that lower base.
And the year after that, off an even
lower base relative to where you should
be. The shortfall does not reset every
January. It never resets. It compounds.
A raise that falls short of true senior
inflation quietly lowers the size of
every single check you will receive for
the rest of your life, and it lowers the
starting point for every future raise on
top of it. Let me walk you through why
compounding cuts both ways, slowly,
because this is the single most
important idea in the whole video. When
your money is in a savings account
earning interest, compounding is a
miracle. A little bit of growth this
year sits on top of your balance. So
next year, you earn growth on the
growth, and over many years, a modest
start becomes a large sum. Everyone
loves compounding when it is working for
them. But compounding does not care
which direction it runs. It simply takes
whatever base you give it and carries
that base forward year after year. And
here is the cruel twist for a retiree.
Your benefit uses the same compounding
machinery, but the base it carries
forward has been shrunk against real
prices from the very first year. So
instead of growth stacking on growth,
you get shortfall stacking on shortfall.
Every year the raise comes in a little
light against your true costs. That
lighter number becomes the permanent
starting line for the next year. And the
year after that starts even further
behind where you should be. You are not
falling behind in a straight line. You
are falling behind on a curve that bends
against you. And it bends a little more
sharply every year you live.
That is the number three villain in this
whole story, and it is the one almost
nobody talks about. The problem is not
just that your raise is small this year.
The problem is that a small raise,
measured with the wrong yardstick,
permanently shrinks every check you will
ever get. It is not a one-year insult.
It is a lifetime sentence, applied
silently, and it grows heavier every
year you live. The longer you live, the
more it costs you. And the people it
hurts most are the ones who live the
longest, which means it falls hardest on
the oldest and often the most vulnerable
retirees, the ones who can least afford
to absorb it. So, let us add up the
bites so far. The raise is measured
against a worker shopping cart, not
yours, so it undercounts your real costs
from the very first day. That gap
compounds year after year, which is how
buying power fell by roughly a third
since the year 2000. And because each
raise becomes the permanent base for the
next, the shortfall locks in for life.
That is three strikes against your $75,
and I have not even mentioned the part
that gets deducted before the check
leaves the building.
Therefore, let me be quick about the
next bite, because you have heard about
this one before, but it matters here.
Before your Social Security check is
ever paid to you, the Medicare Part B
premium is pulled directly out of it.
This year, the standard Part B premium
a month. The projected premium for 2027,
based on the Medicare Trustees report,
is about $209.50
a month. And some private forecasters
think it could climb higher than that,
into the $216 to $219 range. When the
premium goes up in the same year your
raise goes up, the premium increase
quietly eats into the raise, because
both land in the same check at the same
time. So, the raise that was already too
small, already compounding against you,
now gets one more slice taken off the
top before you see a dollar of it.
At this point, you might be feeling like
there is nothing you can do. Like the
whole thing is designed so that you lose
no matter what. And I understand that
feeling. But, that is exactly why I told
you to hold on to the promise from the
beginning because now I am going to keep
it. And this is the part you can
actually act on.
There is a provision in federal law
called hold harmless. Remember that
name, hold harmless. Here is what it
does, and it is powerful. For most
people who have their Medicare Part B
premium deducted directly from their
Social Security check, the law says that
the dollar increase in your Part B
premium cannot be larger than the dollar
amount of your cost of living raise.
Read that carefully. It means the
premium increase is not allowed to
swallow your entire raise. It means your
net Social Security payment, the actual
number that hits your bank account,
cannot go down from one year to the next
just because Medicare raised its
premium. The floor under your check is
protected by law. The government can
take a bite of your raise, but under
hold harmless, it cannot take the whole
thing. The amount your net check is
allowed to fall because of a Part B
increase is zero.
That is the line in the law I promised
you. And here is why you have to check
it yourself because it does not protect
everyone. Hold harmless applies to the
majority of beneficiaries who already
have Part B deducted from their Social
Security check, but it does not protect
three groups, and you need to know if
you are one of them. It does not protect
people who pay the higher income
surcharge called IRMAA.
It does not protect people who are brand
new to Medicare this year. And it does
not protect people who do not have their
Part B premium deducted directly from
their Social Security check, meaning
people who pay Medicare separately by
bill. If you fall into one of those
groups, the shield does not cover you,
and you could see your net check drop in
a way that other people are legally
protected from.
Let me spend a moment on each of those
three groups because I do not want you
to walk away unsure of where you stand.
The first group is people who pay the
higher income surcharge called IRMAA.
That surcharge kicks in above certain
income levels, and it is based on your
tax return from two years ago. Here is
why that trips people up. You could have
had one unusually high income year.
Maybe you sold a house, maybe you took a
large withdrawal from a retirement
account one time, and that single year
can push you into the surcharge for a
year even though your income has since
dropped back to normal. If that is you,
the hold harmless shield does not
automatically cover you, but there is a
fix, and I will get to it in the action
steps, so stay with me. The second group
is people who are brand new to Medicare
this year. Because they were not
enrolled the year before, there is no
prior net check for the law to protect.
So, the shield does not apply the same
way in that first year.
The third group is people who do not
have their Part B premium taken directly
out of their Social Security check. The
people who instead get a separate
Medicare bill and pay it on their own.
That direct deduction is the very thing
that plugs you into the protection. So,
if you pay separately, you may be
standing outside the wall without
realizing it. Knowing which of these
three describes you, or knowing that
none of them do, is the difference
between guessing about your own check
and actually controlling it. So, here is
what to do, and I am going to make this
simple because this is the whole point
of the video. Step one, confirm that
your Medicare Part B premium is being
deducted directly from your Social
Security check, not paid separately.
That direct deduction is what puts you
under the hold harmless shield in the
first place. Step two, if you were hit
with the IRMAA income surcharge because
of a one-time spike in your income, or
because of a life-changing event like
retiring, losing a spouse, or losing
income, you do not have to just accept
it. You can file a form called form
SSA-44
and ask Social Security to recalculate
your surcharge based on your new, lower
income instead of the 2-year-old income
they used. That one form can pull you
back under the protection and put money
back in your check. Step three, log in
to your my Social Security account at
the website ssa.gov/myaccount
and check your earnings record line by
line.
Your entire benefit is built from your
highest earning years and if there is an
error in that record, a missing year, a
wrong amount, then your benefit is too
low, which means every cost of living
raise on top of it is also too low
forever. The compounding we talked about
works against an error, too. Fixing it
fixes every future check. Let me be
specific about how to read that record
because most people log in once, glance
at the big number, and log back out. Do
not do that. Go year by year down the
earnings column and compare each year
against your own memory. And if you
still have them, your old tax returns or
W-2 forms. You are looking for a year
that shows zero when you know you worked
or a year that shows far less than you
actually earned. Employers make
mistakes. Records get lost when
companies close or change hands.
A single missing year in your top
earning years can drag your whole
benefit down. And remember, Social
Security generally only lets you correct
the record going back about 3 years, 3
months, and 15 days after the wages were
earned with a few exceptions. So, an old
error can harden into a permanent loss
if nobody catches it in time. Your new
2027 benefit amount will post to that
same account in December. So, this is
the exact season to be looking while the
new number is landing and while you
still have time to question anything
that looks wrong.
Let me close the loop completely because
I promised I would. The reason the hold
harmless provision matters so much is
everything we covered before it. The
raise is measured with the wrong index.
The shortfall compounds for life. The
Part B premium takes a bite before you
see the money. Hold harmless is the one
legal wall standing between you and
losing the entire raise, and it only
works if you make sure you are actually
standing behind it. Most people never
check. They assume they are protected.
Some of them are wrong, and it costs
them every month. So, do not assume.
Verify, because the government built the
math to fall short, and the only defense
you have is knowing the rules better
than the people counting on you not to
read them.
I want to say something plainly here
because it matters. None of this is
about being angry for the sake of being
angry. It is about the fact that you
earned this. Every dollar of your Social
Security came out of your paycheck
across a working lifetime, decade after
decade, deducted before you ever saw it.
This was not a gift, and it was not
charity. It was your money set aside
under a promise. So, when the raise is
measured against the wrong prices, and
the shortfall compounds against you for
life, that is not some abstract policy
debate. That is a promise being quietly
trimmed a little smaller every year,
hoping you will not notice. The people
who notice, the people who make the
calls and check the boxes, are the ones
who keep what is theirs. The people who
assume it is all handled for them are
the ones who lose it a little at a time.
I am telling you all of this so you can
be the first kind of person, not the
second.
Here is exactly what to do this week
while the 2027 number is being
finalized, and before the new amount
posts in December. Call the Social
Security Administration directly at
and ask two questions. Ask whether the
hold harmless provision applies to you
this year, and ask them to confirm how
your Part B premium is being paid. Then,
for anything involving Medicare, the
premium, or the IRMAA surcharge, call
Medicare directly at 1-800-MEDICARE.
If a life-changing event lowered your
income, ask about form SSA-44,
and go to ssa.gov/myaccount
today. Create the account if you do not
have one and read your earnings record
before the year closes. Write these down
and make the calls this week before the
window closes and before the new number
posts. Your My Social Security account
is at ssa.gov/myaccount.
Medicare is at 1-800-Medicare.
And the one number to start with, the
number that can tell you today whether
hold harmless is protecting your check,
is the administration at 1-800-772-1213.

And the people it belongs to are almost

And I want you to understand something

Working people spend a big share of

You spend far more of yours on medicine,

keeping a roof over your head and the

That is why so many seniors feel like
they are quietly falling a little

before anyone tells you 3.6% is a

change because it is the one everybody

Now, I want to be careful and honest
with you because I never want to hand
you a number that is not real. That 3.6%
is a projection, not the final word. The

3.4% and that group nudged their

The official number does not exist until

But if that projection holds, 3.6% would

since 2023.
For comparison, the raise this year for

was 2.5% and the year before that was
3.2%. So this would genuinely be the

around $75 more every single month. On

Now, the second change, and this is the
