Medicare adds a surcharge on top of your
normal Part B premium, and on top of
your drug plan premium. It is an extra
charge tacked on for the crime of having
done a little too well. But, here is
what makes I-R-M-A-A so vicious, and why
it catches so many people completely off
guard. It is not based on what you earn
today. It is based on your tax return
from two years ago. So, the surcharge
you pay in 2026 is set by the income you
reported for 2024. Think about how many
people that ambushes. Somebody sells a
house, or cashes out an old investment,
or works one last big year before
retiring. And then two years later, long
after that income is gone, and they are
living on a fixed check, the government
reaches back in time and charges them
for it. Above about $109,000
for a single person, or about $218,000
for a married couple, the surcharge
kicks in. And at the higher brackets,
the Part B surcharge alone can run over
$400 a month for each person, with a
separate drug surcharge stacked right on
top of it.
For a couple, that can add up to more
than $7,000 over a single year. And the
first many people ever hear of it is a
smaller deposit landing in their bank
account one month with no explanation.
And there is a cruel little wrinkle
buried inside I-R-M-A-A that makes it
sting even worse. It works like a cliff,
not like a gentle slope. Cross one of
those income lines by even a single
dollar, and you do not pay just a little
bit more. You leap the entire surcharge
for that whole bracket all at once. One
extra dollar of income, $1, can cost you
hundreds of dollars a month for an
entire year. So, if you find yourself
anywhere close to one of those
thresholds, the timing of when you pull
money out of an account, or when you
sell an investment, can matter
enormously. But, almost nobody thinks
about it in the moment. And so, they
sail $1 over a line they never knew was
drawn, and the bill arrives two years
later when it is far too late to undo.
Therefore, here is the move that almost
nobody knows they are allowed to make,
and it is the whole reason I am telling
you about this now instead of after the
fact. If your income has dropped because
of a life-changing event, you do not
have to just accept that surcharge, and
the government's own list of
life-changing events is broad. It
includes retiring or cutting back your
work hours, or the death of a spouse, or
a marriage, or a divorce. If any of
those happened to you, you can file a
single form, and it is called form
SSA-44,
and you ask Social Security to throw out
that 2-year-old income and use your
current, lower income instead. People
wipe out thousands of dollars in
surcharges with that one form every
year, and most seniors have never even
heard its name. Now you have. Say it out
loud so you remember it. Form SSA-44.
Let me tell you about two men on the
same block, because this is exactly how
it plays out in real life. Both of them
retired the same year. Both of them had
one final strong year of income right
before they hung it up. 2 years later,
they both open their statements and see
the same ugly surcharge eating into
their Medicare. The first man shrugs,
assumes it is just the way things are,
and pays it month after month for years.
The second man had heard about that
little form. He fills out form S SSA-44,
attaches proof that he retired, and
mails it in. Within a couple of months,
his surcharge is gone because his real
income now is nothing like it was 2
years ago. Same situation, same
paperwork available to both of them. One
of them kept thousands of dollars simply
because he knew to ask, and the other
one never knew the door was even there
to open.
Now I am going to keep the promise I
made you at the very beginning, because
this is the moment it pays off. I told
you that one of these five changes was
not a threat at all, that it was brand
new, genuinely good news, and worth
thousands to the people who need it
most, but only if you switch it on in
time. Here it is. Starting recently,
Medicare finally put a hard ceiling on
what you can be forced to pay out of
your own pocket for prescription drugs
in a year. That ceiling is $2,000. Once
your covered drug costs hit $2,000 in a
calendar year, you are done. You pay
nothing more for your covered
prescriptions for the rest of that year.
For a senior on expensive medications,
the kind of drugs that used to cost
families 10 or $15,000 a year and wiped
out their savings, this is
life-changing. There used to be no limit
at all. Now there is a wall, and it
stands at $2,000. To understand how
enormous that wall really is, you have
to remember what it replaced. For
decades, there was a gap in Medicare
drug coverage that people bitterly
nicknamed the donut hole, a stretch
where your coverage suddenly dropped out
from under you, and you were left paying
huge amounts out of your own pocket with
no ceiling anywhere in sight. People
rationed their pills. People split their
tablets in half to stretch them. People
sat at their kitchen tables and chose
between their medicine and their
groceries because there was simply no
limit on how high that bill could climb.
That is the world this $2,000 cap just
ended. For someone on a specialty drug
that used to run 10 or 15,000 dollars a
year, the kind of cost that quietly
drains a lifetime of savings, this is
not a small convenience. It is the
difference between filling the
prescription and going without it.
Therefore, it deserves your attention
far more than any threat on this list
because for once, the change is entirely
in your favor.
But, and you knew there was a catch,
this only works the way it should if you
are in the right plan. And there is a
second piece of it you have to actively
turn on. Along with that cap, Medicare
created a new option that lets you
spread your drug costs out into smooth
monthly payments across the whole year
instead of getting hammered with one
enormous bill at the pharmacy counter in
January or February. It is called the
Medicare Prescription Payment Plan, and
here is the thing you must not miss. It
is not automatic. Nobody enrolls you in
it. You have to opt in yourself.
Therefore, this brings us right back to
that open enrollment window from October
15th to December 7th, because that is
your chance to pick the drug plan that
actually uses this new $2,000 cap in
your favor and to sign up for the
payment plan if spreading the cost would
help you. The protection is real and it
is finally there.
But like everything else on this list,
the government built the door and then
left it up to you to walk through it.
So, let me pull all five of these
together because the thread running
through every single one of them is the
same and it is the entire lesson of this
video. The senior deduction worth up to
$6,000, the Medicare window that closes
on December 7th, the retirement
withdrawal deadline with the 25%
penalty, the IRMAA surcharge you can
appeal with one form, and the new $2,000
drug cap you have to choose the right
plan to use. Not one of them is handed
to you automatically in the way that
helps you. Every one of them either
takes your money quietly if you sit
still or gives you money only if you
stand up and ask. The people who come
out of this fall thousands of dollars
ahead are not smarter than you and they
are not luckier than you. They simply
knew the deadlines and they made a few
phone calls.
And that is exactly what I'm going to
hand you right now in plain steps so
this does not become another video you
nodded along with and forgot by supper.
Step one, sometime before the October
filing deadline, whether you use a
preparer or do it yourself, make
absolutely sure you are claiming that
new senior deduction. Up to $6,000 for
you or 12,000 for a couple where both of
you are 65 or older. If a preparer does
your taxes, say the words new senior
deduction out loud and make them confirm
it is on your return. Step two, between
October 15th and December 7th, review
your Medicare plan. Do not let it auto
renew without a look. Pull out the
annual notice of change they mailed you.
Go to the website, which is
medicare.gov, or pick up the phone and
confirm your drugs and your doctors are
still covered at a price you can accept.
If they are not, switch plans before
December 7th.
Step three. If you are 73 or older, take
your required minimum distribution from
every traditional retirement account
before December 31st. Do not wait for
the last week of the year when everyone
is distracted. Call whoever holds your
account now and ask them to confirm the
exact amount and get it done so that 25%
penalty can never touch you. Step four.
Look at your Medicare statement and if
you see that IRMAA surcharge and your
income has fallen since two years ago
because you retired, lost a spouse, or
cut back your work, call Social Security
and request form SSA-44.
The number for Social Security is
Fill it out, attach your proof, and get
that surcharge reconsidered. Step five.
While you are inside that open
enrollment window, ask specifically
about the $2,000 prescription cap and
the Medicare prescription payment plan.
Make sure the plan you choose puts that
cap to work for your medications. And if
spreading your drug costs across the
year would help your budget, opt into
the payment plan because it will not
happen on its own. You do not need to
hire anyone to do a single one of these
things. You do not need to pay a fee to
any advisor to make these calls. Every
one of these is your own money, your own
benefit, earned by a lifetime of working
and paying in. The only thing standing
between you and every dollar of it is a
few dates on the calendar and the
willingness to pick up the phone before
those dates pass. So, do it this week
while the windows are still open and do
not let another year roll by on
autopilot, leaving your own money on the
table.
For your Medicare plan and the drug cap,
the number to call is 1-800-633-4227.

title: The $23,760 Social Security Bonus Most Retirees Never Claim

segments.text: Social Security will pay you up to
a year more every single year for the
rest of your life. And most retirees
never claim $1 of it. It is not a scam.
It is not some special fund you have to
drive down to a government office and
beg for. It is money the Social Security
Administration already owes you sitting
right there on the table. And the only
reason most people walk straight past it
is that nobody ever explained it to them
in plain English.
I want you to stay with me for the next
few minutes because there is a second
piece of this you need to hear even if
you already started your checks. Even if
you are 67, even if you are 70, even if
a payment already hit your bank account
this month, there is a second version of
this bonus that you can still switch on.
I'm going to show you exactly what it is
before we are done because it is the one
move that can lift a check that is
already started. But first you have to
understand the big one, the $23,760
one because once you see how simple it
really is, you will understand why the
government almost never says a word
about it.
Here's what this so-called bonus
actually is. When you reach what Social
Security calls your full retirement age,
which for everyone born in 1960 or later
is 67, you have a choice. You can start
your checks right then, or you can wait.
And for every single year that you wait
past that full retirement age, all the
way up to age 70, Social Security adds
8% to your monthly benefit. Not 8% one
time, 8% for each year you hold off and
it stacks on top of itself. Wait the
full 3 years from 67 to 70 and you have
locked in a permanent raise of 24% for
life that never goes away and that keeps
growing with every cost of living
increase piled on top of it. That 8% a
year has a real name inside the agency.
They call it the delayed retirement
credit.
And for a person who earned a strong
paycheck across their working years,
that credit is worth roughly $1,980
more a month, which comes out to about
a year. That is the bonus. It is not a
check in the mail. It is a raise you
turn on by waiting.
Let me slow this down and walk it year
by year, because when you see it move
one step at a time, it stops feeling
like a trick and starts feeling like the
plain arithmetic it really is. Say your
full retirement age check would be
$4,000 a month. You reach 67, and
instead of filing, you wait. At 68, the
government has added 8%, so now you are
owed about $4,320.
You wait again. At 69, another 8%, and
you are up around $4,640.
You wait one final year. At 70, you have
stacked the full 24%, and that $4,000
check has become right around $4,960 a
month.
Almost a thousand extra dollars every
month for the rest of your life for
doing nothing but waiting 3 years.
And every cost of living raise from that
day forward is calculated on the bigger
number. So, the gap between you and the
person who filed early does not stay the
same. It grows wider every year you both
live.
Now, let me prove the ceiling to you
with the real government numbers,
because I do not want you taking my word
for anything. The Social Security
Administration publishes the maximum
benefit for each claiming age. In 2026,
the most a person can receive if they
started age 62 is about $2,969
a month. If they wait until their full
retirement age of 67, that maximum jumps
to about $4,152
a month. And if they hold on until age
70, the maximum climbs to about $5,181
a month. Look at the distance between
those two ends. The person who waited
from 62 to 70 is collecting about $2,212
more every month than the person who
grabbed it early. Over a year, that is
more than $26,000.
Same worker, same lifetime of paying in.
The only difference is one of them
understood the bonus and one of them did
not. Therefore, the real question is not
whether the money is there. The money is
absolutely there, published by the
government itself. The real question is
why on earth so few people ever reach
out and take it. And the answer is the
part that should make you angry. The
single most common age for Americans to
start their Social Security is 62. It is
the earliest age you are allowed to
file, and year after year, it remains
the most popular choice. In the most
recent year of data, about 26% of the
more than 3 million people who filed for
the first time did it right at 62. That
is the biggest group of any age. Only a
small handful wait all the way to 70,
where the bonus is fully loaded. So,
when I tell you most retirees never
claim this money, I am not exaggerating
for effect. The majority of people file
early and permanently lock themselves
out of the largest raise the government
offers a human being.
But, filing at 62 does not just skip the
bonus. It cuts what you already had. If
your full retirement age is 67 and you
claim at 62, Social Security permanently
reduces your check by about 30%. Read
that again. 30% gone for the rest of
your life, on top of missing the 24% you
could have gained by waiting. Put those
two together and you start to see the
real size of the gap. The early filer
and the patient filer are not a few
dollars apart. They are living in two
completely different retirements, and
the difference between them can be the
price of a second pension you never knew
you qualified for.
Now, I have to be honest with you about
the other side of this, because plenty
of people hear the word wait and
immediately think they are being told to
gamble. So, let me answer the question
sitting in the back of your mind right
now. What if I wait and I do not live
long enough to enjoy it? That is a fair
question, and it deserves a real answer,
not a sales pitch. The way to think
about it is the break-even point. When
you wait, you give up checks in your 60s
in exchange for a much larger check
later. There is a point down the road
where the larger check has fully made up
for the ones you skipped, and after that
point, you are simply ahead more and
more with every passing month. For most
people, that crossing point lands
somewhere in the early 80s. And here is
the piece almost nobody tells you. A
person who has already made it to 65
today, on average, lives well into their
So, for a healthy person with normal
longevity in the family, waiting is not
a wild bet. It is the safer bet. The
gamble, statistically, is filing early
and hoping you were one of the unlucky
ones, which is a strange thing to hope
for. Before I show you how this plays
out with real people, I need to raise
the stakes on you, because if you are
married, this next part is worth double,
and most couples never see it coming.
The mistake we are talking about does
not just shrink your own check while you
are alive. It can quietly cut the income
your husband or wife has to live on
after you are gone for 10 or 15 years,
long after you cannot fix it for them.
Hold on to that, because it changes
everything about how a married couple
should think about this decision, and I
will come back to it.
Let me show you what this looks like on
a normal street with normal people,
because numbers on a page never land the
way a real story does. Picture two
neighbors who live across from each
other. They worked similar jobs. They
earned similar money. They both turned
62 in the same year. The first neighbor
files the very week she becomes
eligible, because a friend told her to
grab it while she still can. Her check
settles in at a reduced amount, and it
stays there for good. The second
neighbor does the harder thing. She
waits. She bridges those years with some
savings, a part-time job, and a tighter
budget, and she files at 70. When the
dust settles, the second neighbor is
collecting well over a thousand dollars
more every month than the first, and she
will collect that larger amount for the
rest of her life, and it will grow every
single year when the cost of living
raise lands, because that raise is
figured on the bigger number. Same
street, same paychecks. One of them is
quietly wealthier every month until the
day she dies. And the only thing she did
differently was understand the bonus and
have the patience to claim it. But here
is where I have to stop you before you
make the opposite mistake, because I
have watched people take this too far.
Waiting is not the right answer for
everybody, and anyone who tells you it
is has never sat across a kitchen table
from a real family. If your health is
poor, if the doctors have handed you a
serious diagnosis, if your family
history says the odds are simply not in
your favor, then claiming earlier can be
exactly the correct move. The bonus only
pays off if you live long enough to
collect it. So this is not me telling
you to wait no matter what. This is me
telling you to make the choice with your
eyes wide open, knowing that $23,760
a year is what sits on the other side of
the table, instead of finding out years
later that you gave it away for nothing.
And I want to name the real reason so
many people file early, because it is
not laziness and it is not stupidity. It
is fear. It is the voice that says
Social Security is going broke and you
had better grab yours before it
disappears. I understand that fear, but
let me give you the honest picture, the
one the news programs never take the
time to finish. Social Security is
funded by the payroll taxes of every
working person in the country, and those
taxes keep pouring in every payday,
whether the trust fund is full or
running low. The government's own
trustees say the combined reserve fund
runs short sometime in the middle of the
next decade, but here is the sentence
they never read you afterward. Even on
that day, with nothing fixed and no
changes made at all, the incoming
payroll taxes would still cover roughly
80 cents of every promised dollar, 80%
automatically, funded by workers who
have not even retired yet. It does not
go to zero.
It is never gone to zero in 90 years. So
the idea that you should permanently
slash your own check by 30% because the
whole system might vanish next year is a
fear talking, and it is a fear that has
cost American retirees more money than
almost any scam I could ever name. The
people selling you that panic are not
the ones who have to live on the smaller
check for the next 30 years. You are.
Now, I want to widen this out because
the delayed credit is the biggest bonus
most people miss, but it is not the only
money left lying on the ground. There
are several more, and they hit different
people. So, listen closely for the one
that sounds like your life.
The first is the spousal benefit. If you
are married, or if you were, and your
husband or wife earned more than you
across their life, you may be entitled
to a check based on their record instead
of your own. That spousal benefit can be
worth up to 50% of what the higher
earner would receive at their full
retirement age. 50%. Let me make that
real. If your spouse is owed $4,000 a
month at their full retirement age, your
spousal benefit could be worth as much
as $2,000 a month, even if your own work
record would only have paid you a few
hundred. I have met women who spent
years raising children instead of
building a work history, who assumed
they were owed almost nothing, and who
were sitting on a benefit worth half of
their husband's full amount and never
knew to ask. The agency does not always
volunteer it. You have to raise your
hand and say the words.
Therefore, if you are married and you
were the lower earner, or you never
worked long enough to build a big record
of your own, you owe it to yourself to
find out what half of your spouse's
benefit would be, because it may be far
larger than the check you are staring at
right now.
The second one is heavier, and I want
you to hear it with the seriousness it
deserves. It is the survivor benefit.
When a husband or a wife passes away,
the one left behind can step up to
receive up to 100% of what the person
who died was receiving, not half, all of
it, if it is larger than their own
check. Let me put a number on it so it
is not just words. If a husband was
collecting $3,000 a month and his wife
was collecting 1,500 on her own record,
when he passes, she does not keep her
1,500. She steps up to his 3,000. That
is double, at the very moment a
household has lost half its income. And
yet widows all across this country are
quietly collecting less than they are
owed, sometimes for years, because
nobody sat them down in the worst week
of their life and explained the rule. If
you have lost a spouse, or when that day
comes, this is the number that can keep
a household whole. It is up to 100% of
the higher check, and it does not switch
on by itself. Somebody has to ask. And
now I keep the promise I made you a few
minutes ago, the one about how this
decision is worth double for married
couples. Here it is, and it is the most
important thing I will tell you today.
When the higher earning spouse in a
marriage waits and builds up that
delayed credit, they are not just
raising their own check. They are
permanently raising the survivor benefit
that whichever one of them lives longer
will collect. Remember, the survivor
steps up to the larger of the two
checks. So, if the husband is the higher
earner, and he delays all the way to 70,
he pumps his check up by that full 24%,
and then when he passes, his widow does
not step up to his old full retirement
age amount. She steps up to the bigger
delayed amount, and she keeps it for the
rest of her life, which for a woman is
very often 10 or 15 years beyond her
husband.
That one decision made by the higher
earner can mean hundreds of extra
dollars a month flowing to a grieving
spouse for more than a decade.
Therefore, the smartest move for most
married couples is not for both people
to wait, and it is not for both to file
early. It is for the higher earner to
delay as long as they can stand it,
ideally to 70, so that the delayed
credit protects the survivor, while the
lower earner can often claim earlier to
bring some income in the door. That
single piece of coordination is worth
more to a surviving spouse than almost
any life insurance policy a couple could
buy, and it costs nothing but patience.
But, let me warn you about a trap on the
other side of the spousal benefit,
because it works the same way your own
retirement check does. If you claim a
spousal benefit before you reach your
own full retirement age, that spousal
amount gets permanently reduced, too,
just like an early retirement check. So,
the 50% I told you about is the amount
you receive if you wait until your full
retirement age to claim it. File for it
at 62, and you will get a good deal
less. That does not mean never claim
early. It means know the cost before you
do. So, nobody talks you into leaving
money behind by accident.
Let me stop right here and come back to
the promise I made you at the very
beginning, because this is the moment it
matters most. I told you there was a
second version of this bonus that you
can still switch on, even if you already
started your checks. Here it is. It is
called voluntary suspension. If you have
already reached your full retirement
age, even if your payments are already
arriving every month, you are allowed to
tell Social Security to pause your
benefit. And while it is paused, that
same 8% a year delayed credit starts
building all over again, month after
month, until you turn it back on at a
higher amount, or until you reach 70.
Think about what that means. Say you
filed at 65, a little early, and you are
now 67, and you realize you did not
actually need to start when you did.
You can suspend, let the credit stack
for 3 years, and restart at 70 with a
permanently bigger check worth
potentially hundreds of dollars more a
month.
So, the person who filed early, who
thought the door was shut and bolted
forever, is not actually stuck. Let me
give you one more picture because I have
watched this exact thing happen. A man
files at 65 because he was worried, like
everybody is worried. Two years later,
at 67, his part-time work has picked up,
and he realizes he does not actually
need the check right now. He walks in
and suspends it. For the next 3 years,
he collects nothing, but that 8% a year
quietly stacks up, and at 70, he flips
it back on. His check is now permanently
larger by nearly a quarter than it was
the day he he it, and it will stay that
way, growing with every cost of living
raise until the end of his life.
He did not need a lawyer. He did not
need a special program. He needed to
know the word suspension and be willing
to say it. That is the second bonus. It
is smaller than the full $23,760,
but it is real. It is yours, and almost
nobody knows it is even allowed. But,
there is one more piece of found money
that catches people completely off
guard, and it goes to anyone who kept
working while collecting early. Maybe
you filed at 63 or 64, and you were
still on the job, and Social Security
held back part of your check because you
earned over their yearly limit. Most
people believe that withheld money is
simply gone, taken, never to be seen
again. That is false, and it may be the
most common misunderstanding in the
entire program. When you reach your full
retirement age, the agency goes back,
recalculates your benefit, and returns
that money to you in the form of a
higher monthly check going forward. It
was never lost. It was parked. If they
withheld a year's worth of checks while
you worked, you get credited for those
months, and your ongoing payment goes up
to pay it back over time.
But, if you do not know to look for it,
you will never notice whether it was
actually returned to you. And mistakes
happen inside a system this large every
single day. Therefore, the lesson across
every one of these is the same, and it
is the whole reason I made this video.
Social Security is not a machine that
automatically hands you the most it
owes. It is a machine that pays what you
claim. The delayed credit worth up to
a year, the spousal benefit worth up to
50% of your partner's check, the
survivor benefit worth up to 100%, the
suspension move that restarts the
credits even after you filed, the
withheld earnings that come back to you
at full retirement age. Every one of
them requires the same thing from you.
You have to ask. And the people who ask
end up thousands of dollars a year
richer than the people who sit quietly
and wait for a letter that is never
going to come.
And I have to say one more hard thing
before I give you the steps because it
is the whole reason this money goes
unclaimed. Do not walk in expecting the
person on the other end of the phone to
hand you the best possible answer. That
is not their job. The representative you
reach is trained to process the claim
you ask for, not to sit you down and
design the smartest strategy for your
whole life. If you call and say you want
to file, they will help you file, even
if waiting one more year would have paid
you tens of thousands more. They are not
being simply answering the exact
question you asked. So, the burden is on
you to ask the right questions by name,
and that is precisely what I am about to
hand you. So, let me tell you exactly
what to do this week in plain steps so
this does not just become another video
you nodded along to and forgot by
supper.
Step one, go to the Social Security
website, which is ssa.gov,
and create your personal account. They
call it My Social Security. It is free,
it takes about 10 minutes, and once you
are inside, you can see your own
estimated benefit at 62, at your full
retirement age of 67, and at 70 laid out
side by side in real dollars for your
own record, not the maximums I quoted
you. That single screen will show you
the size of your own personal bonus in
plain black and white. And I promise you
it will get your attention far more than
anything a stranger like me could ever
say to you.
Step two, look hard at the gap between
the 67 number and the 70 number on that
screen. That gap is your delayed
retirement credit. That is your personal
version of the $23,760.
For some of you, it will be a few
hundred a month. For some, it will be
far more than that. Either way, now you
know what waiting is worth to you
specifically, and you can make the
decision like an adult with the facts in
front of you instead of out of fear
whispered by a neighbor. Step three, if
you are married or widowed, call Social
Security directly and ask two exact
questions. Ask what your spousal benefit
would be based on your partner's record.
And if you have lost a spouse, ask
whether your survivor benefit would be
larger than the check you are collecting
now. Say the words spousal benefit and
survivor benefit out loud, so there is
no confusion about what you are asking
them for. Step four. If you are already
past full retirement age, and you filed
earlier than you wish you had, ask them
directly about voluntary suspension. And
ask whether any earnings that were
withheld while you worked have already
been credited back to you. Those are two
separate questions, and you deserve a
clear answer to both of them. You do not
need to hire anyone. You do not need to
pay a single fee to a single advisor to
have this conversation. Everything I
described today is your own money, under
your own record, earned by your own
decades of showing up and working and
paying in. The people who are quietly
getting this money are not smarter than
you, and they are not one bit luckier
than you. They simply learned the words,
picked up the phone, and asked for what
was already theirs by name. Now you know
the words, too. So, make the call, ask
the four questions, and do not let
another year go by leaving your own
money sitting on that table.
The number to call is 1-800-772-1213.

title: They Can Now TAKE HALF Your Social Security Check in 2026 — Most Seniors Have No Idea

segments.text: Starting this year, the Social Security
Administration can quietly reach into
your monthly check and take up to half
of it. 50% of the money you live on to
recover a debt that in many cases the
government created by its own mistake,
and you have only 90 days to stop it
before the withholding begins. That is
one of five changes that hit Social
Security this year, and most seniors
have not heard about a single one of
them. Some of these changes shrink your
check. One of them resets the age you
are supposed to claim, and one of them
may be sitting on thousands of dollars
that belong to you right now. Money the
government owes you and will never call
to tell you about.
I want you to stay with me all the way
to the fifth change because that last
one is the good news hiding inside all
the bad news, and it could put a large
retroactive payment back in your bank
account if you know the two words to say
when you call. I am going to give you
those words and the exact phone number
to call before we are done. If you or
your spouse depend on Social Security,
the next 20 minutes are about the actual
dollars in your checking account this
year. Not politics, not predictions,
just what changed and what you have to
do about it.
Let us start with the change everyone
waits for every single year, the raise.
For this year, the cost-of-living
adjustment, the COLA, came in at 2.8%
for the average retired worker. That
adds up to roughly $56 more per month,
and on the surface, that sounds like
good news. A raise is a raise. But here
is the first thing nobody at the Social
Security office is going to explain to
you. That 2.8% is one of the smaller
raises retirees have seen in years, and
it is not really a reward. It is a
catch-up. The COLA is calculated on
inflation that you already lived through
and already paid for all of last year at
the grocery store, at the pharmacy, at
the gas pump. So by the time that $56
shows up, it is not putting you ahead.
It is trying, and often failing, to get
you back to where you already were.
And it fails for a simple reason. The
costs that hit seniors hardest are not
the costs the raise is measured against.
The formula the government uses tracks
the spending of younger working people,
but a retiree spends a far bigger share
of every dollar on the two things
climbing fastest of all, medical care
and housing. A doctor bill, a
prescription, a homeowner's insurance
premium, a property tax bill. These have
been rising much faster than that 2.8%
for years. So, even in a year when the
government hands you a raise, the
specific basket of things you actually
buy has often gone up more than the
raise did. That is why so many seniors
feel like they are falling behind even
as the official number says they got
more. They are not imagining it. The
raise is real and it is still not
keeping up with their real life.
Therefore, the real question is not how
big the raise is. The real question is
how much of it you actually get to keep.
And that brings us to the second change,
the one that quietly eats the raise
before it ever reaches your bank
account. Because for the vast majority
of seniors, Social Security and Medicare
are joined at the hip. Your Medicare
Part B premium, the one that covers
doctor visits and outpatient care, is
pulled directly out of your Social
Security check before the money is ever
deposited. You never touch it. And this
year, that Part B premium jumped to
a month. That is an increase of almost
$18 a month, close to a 10% jump in a
single year, far faster than the 2.8%
raise you just got.
Now, do the math the way the government
hopes you never will. You were handed a
raise of about $56 a month, but a big
piece of it was immediately clawed back
by that higher Medicare premium before
you saw a dime of it. Independent
researchers at Boston College found that
the rising Medicare premium eats up more
than a quarter of this year's entire
raise for the typical retiree. So, the
$56 you were promised is not $56. For
many people, it is closer to 40, and for
some, it is less than that. The raise is
real on paper, but the check that lands
in your account barely moved, and now
you know exactly why. It is not an
accident. It is the design. There is one
small piece of protection here, and I
want to be honest with you about it,
because I never want to leave you more
scared than the facts require. There is
a rule called the hold harmless
provision, and it means that for people
who have their Part B premium taken
straight out of their Social Security
check, the premium increase in a given
year is not allowed to be larger than
the dollar amount of their cola raise.
So, the higher premium cannot by itself
make your check go down from 1 year to
the next. That protection is real, but
notice what it does and does not do. It
stops your check from shrinking. It does
absolutely nothing to stop the raise
from being eaten. You were promised more
money, the premium quietly took most of
it, and the government calls that a good
year.
And for some of you, it is worse than
the standard premium because of a
surcharge most people have never heard
of until it hits them. If your income is
above a certain level, the government
adds an extra charge on top of your Part
B premium called the income-related
monthly adjustment amount. For this
year, that surcharge starts for a single
person with income above $109,000,
and for a married couple above $218,000.
And it is based on your tax return from
2 years ago. At the higher income
brackets, that surcharge can push the
total Part B cost to nearly $700 a month
per person, plus an extra charge on your
drug plan on top of that. And here is
the trap inside the trap. It looks at
income from 2 years back. So, a retiree
who had one good final working year, or
who sold a house, or who took a large
withdrawal, can get slapped with this
surcharge long after their income has
actually dropped.
If a life-changing event lowered your
income, a retirement, the death of a
spouse, a divorce, you can file a form
called SSA-44
to ask them to use your current income
instead. Almost nobody knows that form
exists, and it can save you thousands.
But, the Eaton raze is a paper cut
compared to the third change, and this
is the one I opened the whole video
with, because it is the one that can
genuinely take food off your table. This
year, the Social Security Administration
brought back one of the most aggressive
collection powers it has ever used
against ordinary retirees. If the agency
decides it has overpaid you at any
point, it can now withhold up to 50% of
your monthly benefit
half of the check you use to pay your
rent, your utilities, your medicine,
gone until the agency has recovered the
full amount it says you owe.
And here is what makes this so
frightening and so unfair. A Social
Security overpayment is very often not
your fault at all. The agency itself
makes the mistake. It miscalculates a
benefit, or it is slow to process a
change you reported months ago, or its
own computers pay you an amount that was
wrong from the start. You did nothing
except cash the checks the government
sent you, and trust that they were
correct. Then, sometimes years later, a
letter arrives saying you were overpaid,
that you owe thousands of dollars, and
that the agency is going to start taking
half of every future check until the
debt is square. People who did
absolutely nothing wrong suddenly find
their income cut in half because of a
bureaucratic error they never even knew
was happening.
Let me put a face on this, because it is
not a hypothetical. Picture a widow
living on about $1,800 a month from
Social Security. That is her entire
income. One day a letter comes saying
the agency overpaid her by $9,000 over
several years, an error in how a
survivor benefit was calculated, an
error she had no way of catching. And
the letter says that starting soon, they
will withhold half of her monthly
benefit until that $9,000 is repaid. Her
income just fell from $1,800 to $900 a
month overnight for a mistake the
government made. That is is a story from
the past. Under the rule that took
effect this year, that is exactly what
the 50% withholding does. Now, here is
the part you must burn into your memory
because it is the difference between
losing half your check and keeping it.
When one of these overpayment letters
arrives, you have a 90-day window, and
inside that window, you have real rights
that most people never use because they
are too frightened by the letter to open
it twice. You can ask the agency to
lower the withholding rate to something
you can actually live on. You can ask
for a reconsideration, which is a formal
request for them to look at the decision
again if you believe the overpayment is
wrong, and you can request a waiver,
which asks them to forgive the debt
entirely. And a waiver can be granted
when the overpayment was not your fault
and paying it back would cause you real
hardship. But every one of those doors
closes if you do nothing. If you let the
90 days pass without acting, the agency
simply starts taking up to half of your
check, and you have handed away rights
you did not have to lose.
Therefore, if you ever see an envelope
from the Social Security Administration
with the words overpayment or notice of
planned action on it, you do not set it
aside, and you do not panic and assume
it is hopeless. You open it that day.
You write down the date, and you call
the agency or an advocate immediately
because that 90-day clock starts whether
you read the letter or not. The single
worst thing you can do with that letter
is nothing. The people who lose half
their checks are almost never the people
who fought. They are the people who were
too afraid to open the envelope.
And let me give you the actual names of
the tools that fight this so you are not
calling in blind. There are three
specific requests you can make, and each
has its own form. To ask for a smaller
bite out of your check so they take a
little each month instead of half, you
request a change in the withholding
rate. To argue that the overpayment is
wrong in the first place, that you do
not actually owe it, you file for a
reconsideration. And to ask them to
forgive the debt entirely because it was
not your fault and repaying it would
cause you hardship, you file for a
waiver. That waiver is the powerful one,
and it is granted far more often than
frightened people expect, especially for
a retiree living on a fixed income who
never caused the error. You do not need
a lawyer to start any of these.
You can call the agency directly and say
you want to request a waiver of an
overpayment, and they must send you the
form and pause aggressive collection
while it is reviewed, as long as you act
inside that window. The government is
counting on you to be too intimidated to
ask. Ask anyway.
Now, let me give you the fourth change,
because it quietly rewrites one of the
most important decisions of your entire
retirement, the decision of when to
claim. This year, the full retirement
age has finished its long climb and has
officially reached 67 for everyone born
in 1960 or later. Your full retirement
age is the age at which you are entitled
to 100% of the benefit you earned, and
most people do not realize how brutally
the math punishes claiming early. If you
take your benefit at 62, the earliest
you can, you are not taking a small
trim. You are locking in a permanent cut
of roughly 30% for the rest of your
life. That reduced check never bounces
back. It follows you for 20, 30 years.
Wait until 67 and you get your full
amount. Wait even longer, all the way to
70, and the government actually pays you
delayed retirement credits that make
your check even larger.
The gap between claiming at 62 and
claiming at 70 can be hundreds of
dollars every single month for as long
as you live.
Let me put real numbers on that, because
30% is an abstraction until you see it
as a check. Say your full benefit at 67
would be $2,000 a month. Claim at 62
instead, and that permanent cut drops
you to roughly $1,400 a month for life,
a loss of about $600 every month, more
than $7,000 a year that you never get
back. Now, wait past full retirement age
to 70, and those delayed retirement
credits push that same benefit up to
roughly $2,480
a month. So, the very same worker with
the very same work record is looking at
$1,400 a month if they grab it early or
nearly $2,500 a month if they wait. That
is a difference of over $1,000 every
single month purely from the timing of
one decision. Over a 25-year retirement,
that choice is worth hundreds of
thousands of dollars.
And most people make it in an afternoon
based on fear or rumor without ever
seeing these numbers laid side by side.
But, the age is only half of this
change. The other half catches the
millions of seniors who keep working
while they collect and it surprises
almost everyone. If you claim Social
Security before your full retirement age
and you are still earning a paycheck,
there is a limit on how much you can
make before the government starts
holding back part of your benefit. This
year, if you are under full retirement
age for the whole year, that limit is
Earn more than that from working and the
agency withholds $1 of benefits for
every $2 you go over. In the year you
actually reach full retirement age, the
limit is much more generous, $65,160,
and they only hold back $1 for every $3
over. And once you are past full
retirement age, the limit disappears
completely and you can earn any amount
with no reduction at all.
Here is the good news buried in that
rule, the part that keeps it from being
a pure penalty and almost no one
explains it. The money they withhold
because you earn too much is not gone
forever. It is not a tax and it is not
lost. Once you reach full retirement
age, the agency recalculates your
benefit and gives that withheld money
back to you in the form of a higher
monthly check going forward. So, it is a
delay, not a robbery. But, you still
need to know the limit exists because if
you are working and claiming at the same
time without understanding this, a
sudden drop in your checks can feel like
a punishment out of nowhere when really
it is just this rule quietly doing its
job. And there is one more number to
know for the workers still building
their benefit.
The maximum amount of income taxed for
Social Security rose this year to
up from $176,000 the year before, which
means higher earners are paying Social
Security tax on a bigger slice of their
pay than ever. Therefore, before you
claim, before you assume you know your
own full retirement age, and before you
take a part-time job while collecting,
you owe it to yourself to run the actual
numbers for your situation. Because a
single wrong assumption here, claiming 3
years too early, or tripping the
earnings limit without knowing it, can
cost you tens of thousands of dollars
over a retirement. This is the one
decision you generally cannot undo, so
it is the one worth slowing down for.
And now we arrive at the fifth change,
the one I promised you at the very
beginning, the good news hiding inside
all the bad news. And for millions of
families, this is the one that actually
puts money back. For decades, two
obscure rules quietly robbed a specific
group of retirees. They were called the
windfall elimination provision and the
government pension offset. And what they
did was cut, and in many cases
completely wipe out the Social Security
benefits of people who had spent part of
their careers in public service.
Teachers, firefighters, police officers,
postal workers, state and local
government employees. Millions of people
who paid into Social Security at some
point in their working lives were told
their benefit would be slashed simply
because they also earned a government
pension. Widows and widowers of these
workers were hit especially hard,
sometimes losing a survivor benefit
entirely.
That injustice finally ended. A new law,
called the Social Security Fairness Act,
was signed at the start of last year,
and it repealed both of those provisions
completely. As a result, about 3.2
million people, public servants and
their spouses and their survivors, are
now entitled to higher monthly Social
Security checks. And this is the part I
want you to really hear because it is
where the real money is. The law is
retroactive to January of the year
before it passed, which means the agency
owes many of these people a lump sum of
back payments, thousands of dollars in
some cases, to make up for the benefits
that were wrongly withheld before the
fix took effect. Some people have
already received these payments
automatically, but the rollout has been
complicated, and as we sit here, a
portion of the more difficult cases are
still being worked through, which means
some of the people owed this money have
not yet received it, and many do not
even know to ask. Think about what that
back payment can actually look like
because these are not small sums.
Picture a retired teacher whose Social
Security had been cut by four or 500
dollars a month for years under the old
rules, on top of a survivor benefit from
her late husband that had been wiped out
entirely by the offset. When the repeal
made her whole, her monthly check jumped
by hundreds of dollars going forward,
and because the law reached back more
than a year, the agency owed her a lump
sum that ran into the thousands, in some
cases well over 10,000 dollars, all at
once, to cover the months she had been
shortchanged before the fix took hold.
For a household that had been quietly
getting by on less for years, that is a
life-changing amount of money, and it is
money the person earned and was always
owed.
The only thing standing between many of
these retirees and that payment is the
simple act of calling and asking the
right question because the harder cases
are exactly the ones the agency has not
gotten to yet.
So, here is how you claim what may
already be yours, and here are the words
to say. If you or your late spouse ever
worked in a job with a government
pension, a teaching job, a firefighting
job, a police job, any state or local
government work where you were told your
Social Security would be reduced, then
you need to contact the Social Security
Administration and say these exact
words. Ask them whether the repeal of
the windfall elimination provision and
the government pension offset applies to
your record and whether you are owed a
retroactive payment. Say the name of the
law, the Social Security Fairness Act,
out loud. That is the phrase that gets
you to the right answer. Do not wait for
them to call you because on the harder
cases they may not and every month you
wait is a month that money sits in the
government's account instead of yours.
Let me show you how differently this
whole [clears throat] year plays out for
two neighbors on the same street because
I have watched this exact contrast
happen. Both are retired, both in their
70s, both living mostly on Social
Security. The first neighbor treated
these five changes as real. When the
overpayment letter arrived, she opened
it the same day, called within the
90-day window, requested a waiver
because the error was not her fault, and
kept her full check. She had been a
school teacher for 15 years, so she
called and asked about the Fairness Act
by name and discovered she was owed a
retroactive payment she had never been
told about. She understood the earnings
limit before she took a part-time job,
so nothing surprised her. Her year got
better.
The second neighbor, same street, did
what most people do. He saw the
government envelope, felt his stomach
drop, and left it unopened on the
counter for two months because he could
not bear to read it. By the time he
finally called, the 90-day window had
closed and the agency was already
withholding half of his check. He had
also spent 20 years as a firefighter and
he was almost certainly owed money under
the Fairness Act, but he assumed the
government would contact him if he had
anything coming, so he never asked and
that back payment is still sitting there
unclaimed. Same street, same five
changes. The only difference was that
one neighbor acted and the other one
waited and waiting is what it costs you.
Therefore, here's exactly what to do
this week, in order, and I want you to
write these down. First, if you have
received any letter mentioning an
overpayment, call the Social Security
Administration immediately before your
90-day window closes and ask about a
lower withholding rate, a
reconsideration, or a waiver. Do not
wait, and do not assume it is hopeless,
because waivers are granted every day to
people who are not at fault. Second, if
you or your spouse ever worked a job
with a government pension, call and ask
whether the Social Security Fairness Act
entitles you to a higher benefit and a
retroactive payment. Use the name of the
law, and if the first person you speak
with is unsure, politely ask to speak
with someone who handles windfall
elimination provision and government
pension offset cases, because not every
representative is up to speed on this
yet.
Third, before you claim your benefit or
take a job while collecting, confirm
your real full retirement age, which is
now 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later,
and check this year's earnings limit of
so a paycheck does not shrink your check
by surprise. And if you have not yet
claimed, and you can afford to wait,
remember that every year you hold off
past 67, up to age 70, permanently grows
your check through delayed retirement
credits. So, the decision to wait is
often the single most valuable financial
move left in your retirement. Fourth,
create your free online account at the
Social Security website, so you can see
your own record, your own benefit
amount, and any notices the moment they
post, instead of finding out too late
through the mail. This one step protects
you against almost everything we talked
about today, because the overpayment
notice, the benefit amount, the record
of your earnings, all of it shows up
there first, often before the paper
letter ever reaches your mailbox, and it
gives you back the days that 90-day
clock tries to steal.
And do not keep this to yourself. Every
one of these five changes affects
someone you love, a spouse, a parent, a
neighbor, a friend from church who is
too proud to admit money is tight. The
overpayment letter that could take half
a check, the back payment a retired
teacher never claimed, the claiming
decision worth $100,000. These are not
rare edge cases, they are landing on
ordinary households on ordinary streets
this year. The people who come through
this year whole are simply the ones who
knew what to look for and were not
afraid to pick up the phone. For every
one of these, the number to call is the
Social Security Administration at

title: Signed Your House Over to Your Kids? The Nursing Home Can Still Take It

segments.text: The single most common thing families do
to keep the nursing home from taking the
house is to sign the house over to the
children. And that one move can lock you
out of paid care for more than two and a
half years and hand your kids a tax bill
of tens of thousands of dollars at the
same time. It feels like the smart
thing. It feels like the loving thing.
It is, in the eyes of every elder law
attorney in this country, the most
expensive mistake a senior can make with
a paid-off home. And almost nobody finds
out until it is far too late to undo.
Here is what I need you to understand
before we go one step further. There is
a right way to keep your home and your
family and out of the nursing home's
reach. And there is one specific
document that does it. A document that
makes your house invisible to Medicaid,
invisible to the taxman, and even
shielded from your own children's
divorces. But there is also a deadline
attached to it. And once that deadline
passes, that door slams shut for good
and no amount of money can reopen it.
I'm going to give you the name of that
document and the exact deadline before
this video is over. Keep it in the back
of your mind because it is the
difference between keeping the house and
losing it. Let me tell you who this
actually affects because it is not who
you think. This is not a problem for the
very wealthy. The very wealthy have
lawyers who handle this quietly years in
advance. This is the problem of the
ordinary middle-class family. The couple
who worked their whole lives, paid off a
modest home, and have that home as
almost the only real thing they own.
That house is the entire inheritance. It
is what they want to leave the kids. And
so when someone at church or a
brother-in-law or a well-meaning
neighbor says the words, "Just put it in
the kids' names so the nursing home
cannot get it." It sounds like common
sense. It is not common sense. It is a
trap. And the people who fall into it
are the honest, careful people who were
only ever trying to protect their
family. So let me show you the first way
it backfires. And this is the one nobody
sees coming. To have Medicaid pay for a
nursing home, and understand that a
nursing home is the one bill that can
wipe out everything. You have to apply
and qualify, and when you apply, the
state does not just look at what you own
today. It looks backward. It reviews
five full years of everything you gave
away or sold for less than it was worth.
Five years. That is called the look-back
period, and it is 60 months of your
financial life laid out on a table and
examined. If they find that you signed
your house over to your children inside
that window, they do not just say no.
They impose what is called a penalty
period. Here is how that penalty works,
and I want you to really hear the size
of it. The state takes the value of what
you gave away and divides it by the
average monthly cost of a nursing home
in your state. Whatever number that
division gives you is the number of
months Medicaid will refuse to pay for
your care, even though you now qualify
in every other way. The national average
cost of a nursing home for a shared room
in the year 2025 is about $9,197
a month. That is more than $110,000
a year. Now, picture a paid-off home
worth $300,000, which is an ordinary
house in much of this country. You
divide 300,000 by roughly 9,200,
and you get about 32 months. 32 months.
That is more than 2 and 1/2 years in
which you need care. The house is
already gone from your name, and
Medicaid will not pay a single dollar.
You are trapped between a home you no
longer own and a bill you cannot pay.
And do not assume the family can simply
pay their way through those months,
because almost no ordinary family can.
At more than $9,000 a month, 32 months
of private pay adds up to nearly
$300,000 out of pocket, which is the
entire value of the home you just gave
away. Therefore, the penalty is not a
fee you pay once and move past. It is a
wall. The money that would have covered
those months is the exact money you
locked up inside a house that is no
longer in your name, and the children
who now own that house are rarely in a
position to write a $9,000 check every
month, either. The family ends up
scrambling, borrowing, or bringing the
senior back home to be cared for by
relatives who are not equipped for it.
All because of a signature on a deed
that was only ever meant to help. But,
it gets worse because most families walk
straight into this while believing they
are being careful. And the reason they
believe that is a second trap hiding
right next to the first. You have
probably heard your whole life that you
are allowed to give away a certain
amount of money each year without any
tax. In the year 2026, that amount is
$19,000 per person. And so, people
think, "Well, I will just gift the house
slowly, or I will stay under the limit,
and I will be fine." Here is the
problem. That $19,000 figure is an
Internal Revenue Service rule. It has
absolutely nothing to do with Medicaid.
Medicaid does not care about the gift
tax limit at all. Any transfer of any
size inside that 5-year window counts
against you and triggers the penalty.
Believing that the tax rule and the
Medicaid rule are the same rule is one
of the single most costly
misunderstandings in all of elder law,
and it has cost families their homes and
their savings both. Therefore, before
you ever consider moving your home to
anyone, you have to understand that
these are two completely different
systems with two completely different
rule books. And staying under an
Internal Revenue Service limit protects
you from nothing when it comes to the
nursing home. The taxman and the
Medicaid office are not the same office,
and the thing that keeps one happy does
the other one no good at all.
Now, let me show you the second bomb
because even if you somehow dodge the
penalty, gifting your home during your
life quietly destroys something worth a
great deal of money to your children. It
is called the stepped-up basis, and it
is one of the most valuable things in
the entire tax code for an ordinary
family, and most people have never heard
of it. Here is what it means in plain
language. If you leave your home to your
children when you die, the tax value of
that home resets on the day you pass to
whatever it is worth on that day. All
the growth in value over the decades you
owned it simply disappears for tax
purposes. Your children could sell it
the next week and owe little or nothing
in capital gains tax.
But if you gift that home to them while
you are alive, that reset never happens.
Instead, your children inherit your
original cost, the price you paid for
the house decades ago, which might have
been 30 or 40 or 50 thousand dollars.
So, imagine that home is now worth 300
thousand dollars and your children go to
sell it after you are gone. Because you
gifted it instead of leaving it to them,
they could face capital gains tax on the
difference between what you paid long
ago and what it sells for now. On a home
that appreciated by a quarter of a
million dollars, that can be a tax bill
of tens of thousands of dollars, a bill
that would have been completely erased
if the house had simply passed at death
instead of being handed over early. You
gave the house away to protect your
children and in doing so, you handed
them a tax bill they never needed to
pay.
Let me put real numbers on that so it
lands. Say you and your husband bought
that home decades ago for 40 thousand
dollars and today it is worth 300
thousand dollars. If your children
inherit that home at your death, the tax
value resets to 300 thousand dollars and
if they turn around and sell it for
that, the taxable gain is essentially
nothing. But if you gifted that home to
them while you were alive, their tax
starting point stays frozen at that
original 40 thousand dollars. And when
they sell for 300 thousand, they can be
taxed on 260 thousand dollars of gain.
Depending on their own income, the tax
on that can climb into the tens of
thousands of dollars. That is a tax the
family would never have owed a single
penny of if the home had simply passed
at death, a tax created entirely by the
well-meaning decision to hand it over
early.
That brings me to the third way this
backfires and I saved it for here
because it is the one that frightens
people the most once they understand it
and it is the reason this deserves your
full attention right now. The moment you
sign that deed, the house is not yours
anymore. It is your child's, legally,
completely, it belongs to them. And that
means your home is now exposed to
everything that can happen in your
child's life, none of which you control.
Let me make that real, because it is
easy to say and hard to feel until you
picture it. Suppose you sign your home
over to your son to keep it safe. A few
years later, your son goes through a
divorce. In many situations, that house,
your house, the house you paid off over
30 years, is now a marital asset in his
divorce. And a share of it can walk
right out the door with a
daughter-in-law you barely [snorts]
knew. Or suppose your daughter is in a
car accident and gets sued, and there is
a judgment against her. Your home can be
a target for that judgment, because it
is her asset now, not yours. Or suppose
your child runs into serious debt or
files for bankruptcy. The home can be
pulled into that, too. Or, and this is
the one that breaks families, suppose
your child passes away before you do.
The home does not come back to you. It
passes to their heirs under their will,
which might mean it goes to a spouse who
remarries, and now strangers own the
house you are still living in.
And there is one more piece to losing
control that people forget entirely.
Once your children's names are on that
deed, you cannot sell the home, and you
cannot refinance it without every single
one of them agreeing and signing. If one
child says no, you are stuck. If the
children disagree with each other, you
are stuck. You have taken the one thing
you owned free and clear and made
yourself a guest in it, dependent on
your children's cooperation, their
marriages, their finances, and their
good health for the roof over your own
head. That is not protection. That is
handing away control of your own home
and calling it safety.
Now, I want to pause here, because we
are about halfway through, and I need
you to understand the pattern behind all
three of these, because the pattern is
the real lesson. Every one of these
disasters comes from the same instinct,
the instinct to just move the house,
quickly and quietly, to get it out of
reach. and that instinct is exactly
backward. The fast, free, kitchen table
move, the one that feels like taking
action, is the one that triggers the
penalty, destroys the tax break, and
exposes the home to your children's
lives. The thing that actually protects
the house is slower. It is done in
advance, and it does not involve simply
putting the kids' names on the deed at
all. Hold on to that because it is where
we are going.
And before we get there, I have to tell
you the hard truth about the house you
decide to keep, the one you do not sign
away. Because there is a myth here, too,
that costs families everything. Many
seniors believe that a paid-off home is
automatically safe. "I own it free and
clear," they say. "Nobody can touch it."
That is not true, either. While you are
alive and receiving care, yes, the home
is usually protected, and they will not
force you to sell it to qualify. But the
day you die, a federal program is
required by law to come after that exact
house to repay every dollar of care it
covered. It is called the Medicaid
Estate Recovery Program, and it is not
optional, and it is not some states
being greedy. A federal law passed in
the year 1993
requires every single state to try to
recover the cost of your care from your
estate after you are gone. And your
paid-off home is almost always the only
thing left in that estate, which makes
it the first and biggest target.
Paid-off does not mean protected.
Paid-off just means it is the only thing
left to take. So, now you understand the
full picture.
Sign the house to the kids, and you
trigger the penalty, the tax bomb, and
the exposure. Keep the house and do
nothing, and the state can recover
against it after you die. It can feel
like there is no way out. But there is,
and this is the promise I made you at
the very beginning. So, let me now close
that loop and give you the document and
the deadline.
The document is called a Medicaid Asset
Protection Trust. It is a special kind
of irrevocable trust, and it is the tool
the wealthy have quietly used for
generations.
Here's what it does, and I want you to
hear how completely different it is from
just signing the deed to your kids. You
place your home into this trust. You are
still allowed to live in it for the rest
of your life. That right is written
right into the trust. But because the
trust owns the home and not you, and not
your children directly, the house
becomes invisible to Medicaid. It is
shielded from a state recovery after you
die.
Your children keep the step up basis, so
they dodge that capital gains bomb. And
because your children never own it
outright, it is out of reach of their
divorces, and their creditors, and their
lawsuits. It solves all three problems
at once. The very three problems that
signing the deed created. But here is
the deadline, and this is the part you
cannot ignore, because it is the reason
procrastination is so dangerous. The
trust has to be set up and funded at
least five years and one day before you
apply for Medicaid. That is the same
five-year look back we talked about at
the start. Move the home into the trust
in time, and once that clock runs out,
the house is protected completely. Wait
too long, wait until a diagnosis, wait
until a fall, wait until the nursing
home is already a conversation, and the
clock has not run, and the protection is
gone. The deadline is not your age. The
deadline is your health. This only works
while you are still well, which is
exactly why the people who do it are the
ones who did it years before they
thought they needed to.
Now, I want to clear up a confusion that
trips up even careful people, because
you may have set up a trust already and
believe you have handled all of this.
There are two very different kinds of
trust, and only one of them protects you
here. A regular revocable living trust,
the common kind that most people set up
simply to avoid probate, does nothing at
all against the nursing home, because
you keep the power to pull the home
right back out of it. And as long as you
can take it back, Medicaid still counts
it as yours. Therefore, the trust that
actually protects your home has to be
the irrevocable kind, the Medicaid Asset
Protection Trust, the one where you give
up the power to casually undo it. That
surrender of some control is the very
thing that makes it work, and it is
exactly why this is not something to
attempt with a form printed off the
internet.
It has to be drafted correctly by an
attorney who does this for a living,
because a trust built the wrong way
protects nothing while making you feel
completely safe.
Now, not every state is the same, and
there is a second tool that is even
simpler in the five states that allow
it. It is called a Lady Bird Deed, or an
Enhanced Life Estate Deed, and right now
it is recognized in Florida, Michigan,
Texas, Vermont, and West Virginia. Here
is how it works. You keep complete
control of your home for your entire
life. You can sell it, you can refinance
it, you can change your mind and cancel
the whole thing, all without asking
anyone. Nothing changes while you are
alive, but the moment you pass, the home
transfers automatically and directly to
the children you named, outside of
probate, which in these states places it
beyond the reach of estate recovery. And
because you kept full control the whole
time, the government does not even treat
it as a completed gift, so there is no
gift, no penalty, and your children
still get that stepped-up basis. In
those five states, it is one of the
cleanest tools there is, and it costs a
fraction of what people fear.
>> But maybe you are watching this and
thinking, I do not have 5 years. The
nursing home is not a someday problem.
It is a right now problem. Do not give
up, because the law has built in a
handful of exemptions that let you
transfer the home penalty-free, even
when time is short, and almost nobody
knows they exist. The first is the
caregiver child exemption. If you have
an adult child who moved into your home
and provided care for you for at least 2
years, care that kept you out of a
nursing home during that time, you are
allowed to transfer the home to that
child with no penalty at all. The law
rewards the child who stepped up.
Think about how common that situation
really is. All over this country, there
is a daughter or a son who moved back
into the family home to look after an
aging parent, who gave up years of their
own life, their own career, sometimes
their own marriage, to keep mom or dad
out of a facility. The law actually sees
that sacrifice. If that child lived in
the home and provided that level of care
for at least 2 years, and a doctor can
confirm the care is what delayed the
move to a nursing home, the home can
pass to that child with no penalty at
all, even inside the 5-year window. It
is one of the very few places in this
entire system where the rules reward the
family that gave the most, and almost
nobody ever claims it, because almost
nobody knows it is there. The second is
for a child who is disabled or blind, of
any age, to whom you can transfer the
home penalty-free.
The third is for a sibling who already
has an ownership interest in the home
and lived there for at least 1 year
before you entered care. And the fourth
and biggest is your spouse. You can
transfer the home to a husband or wife
with no penalty whatsoever, and the
healthy spouse who stays in the
community is allowed to keep the house
plus up to 162,660
of the couple's other assets in the year
2026, so that the well spouse is not
left with nothing. Let me show you what
all of this looks like in two real
lives. Two neighbors on the same street.
Both are 72 years old. Both have a
paid-off home worth about 300,000
dollars. Both are terrified of the
nursing home taking it. The first
neighbor does the obvious thing. At the
kitchen table, with a form printed off
the internet, she signs the deed over to
her two children, and she feels a wave
of relief. Three years later, she needs
care. When her family applies for
Medicaid, the state finds the transfer
inside the look back and imposes a
penalty of about 32 months, during which
the family has to pay out of pocket or
scramble for care, even though the house
is already out of her name. Then, when
the home is eventually sold, her
children discover they owe capital gains
tax on decades of growth because the
house was gifted instead of inherited.
And in the middle of all of it, one of
her children goes through a rough
divorce and a piece of the home she
worked her whole life to pay off ends up
in the settlement.
The second neighbor, years earlier,
while she was still healthy and the
nursing home was nothing but a distant
worry, sat down with an elder law
attorney and set up a Medicaid asset
protection trust and moved her home into
it. She kept living in the house exactly
as before, but the five-year clock ran
out quietly in the background. When she
later needed care, the home was
invisible to Medicaid, so there was no
penalty and no wait. When she passed,
the home went to her children with a
full stepped-up basis, so there was no
capital gains bomb, and it went to them
protected outside the reach of anyone's
divorce or creditor. Same street, same
house, same $300,000.
One family lost years of care, a tax
bill, and a chunk of the home to a
divorce. The other kept all of it, and
the only difference between them was
that one acted early with the right
structure, and the other waited and
grabbed the fast, free, wrong one.
And understand, the first neighbor is
not foolish, and she is not careless.
She did exactly what most loving, honest
people do. She acted out of fear and
love. She did the thing that felt like
protecting her children, and she trusted
that a simple, obvious move would work.
That trust is the most expensive thing
she owned. The second neighbor was not
smarter and was not richer. She simply
learned in time that the obvious move is
a trap, and that the real protection is
a quiet, boring legal structure set up
years in advance. That is the entire
difference, not money, not luck, just
knowing before the crisis that the
kitchen table deed is the one thing you
must never do.
So, here is the assumption I need you to
throw away today because it is the
belief that causes all of this. The
assumption is that getting the house out
of your name by any means fast is
protection. It is not. Moving the house
the wrong way is worse than doing
nothing at all because it can cost you
the care, the tax break, and control of
your own home all at once. Real
protection is never the fast free move.
Real protection is the structure built
in advance that lets you keep living in
your home while quietly placing it
beyond the reach of the nursing home,
the taxman, and even your own children's
misfortunes. The government is not going
to hand you that structure. It has
simply made it legal for you to build
one, and then it stays very quiet about
how.
So, let me give you your action plan in
order, and I want you to write these
down or come back to this part of the
video. First, do not sign, gift, or add
anyone's name to your deed until you
have spoken with a professional.
Whatever you do, do not do the kitchen
table transfer. That single instruction
may save your family more than
everything else combined. Second, find
an elder law attorney, not a general
lawyer. An attorney who specifically
practices elder law and Medicaid
planning. And you can find one through
the National Academy of Elder Law
Attorneys at naela.org.
Third, ask that attorney about a
Medicaid asset protection trust. And if
you live in Florida, Michigan, Texas,
Vermont, or West Virginia, ask
specifically about a ladybird deed as a
simpler option. Fourth, if care is
needed soon and 5 years is not possible,
ask about the exemptions, the caregiver
child, the disabled child, the sibling,
and the spouse because one of them may
fit your family right now. And fifth,
for free help understanding your
options, call your state health
insurance assistance program, which
offers free counseling for seniors in
every state. Every one of those steps
protects the very thing the fast, free
move destroys. The wealthy have always
known that the secret is not to move the
house quickly, but to protect it
correctly years before anyone needs
care. Now you know it, too. This is your
playbook. Do not touch that deed and
make the call today. Start with the
National Academy of Elder Law Attorneys
at nela.org
and say the words Medicaid Asset
Protection Trust out loud when you call.

title: The Government Quietly ERASES These 5 Bills After 65 — Most Seniors Still Pay Them

a month. But for millions of seniors,
the government quietly adds a second
charge on top of that. And at the
highest level, it reaches $487
more every single month. That is almost
$500 taken from your check on top of the
premium you already pay. And here's the
part that should make you angry. That
charge is not a law of nature. It is a
setting. There is one free form that
erases it. The form takes about 20
minutes, and almost no senior in this
country has ever heard its name.
That form is one of five bills the
federal government has already given you
a legal way to wipe out, and you are
almost certainly still paying at least
one of them right now. Not because you
did anything wrong, because the system
was built to keep charging you until you
speak up, and no one is going to speak
up for you. So, before this video is
over, I'm going to give you the exact
program, the exact form, and the exact
phone number for each of these five
bills. But there is one of them, the
very first one, that the government adds
to your bill by default the moment you
turn 65. And it follows you for the rest
of your life unless you know the words
to make it stop. Keep that one in your
mind because most people watching have
already been hit by it and have no idea.
Let me tell you who this actually
affects because it is not who you think.
This is not about low-income seniors
filling out charity paperwork. Two of
the five bills I'm about to show you
have no income limit at all. They apply
to the middle-class retiree, the
homeowner, the couple who saved
carefully their whole lives and assumed
that because they were comfortable, none
of these programs were for them. That
assumption is exactly what the system
counts on. The wealthiest retirees in
America pay a financial advisor
specifically to file these forms. And
they save thousands every year doing it.
You are going to do the same thing today
for free by yourself.
So, let me start with the charge I told
you about, the one added by default,
because it is the one hiding in plain
