sight on the most Medicare bills. It is
called the late enrollment penalty, and
it works like a trap that snaps shut
quietly and then never lets go. Here is
how it happens. When you become eligible
for Medicare, you get a window of time
to sign up for Part B, which is your
doctor and outpatient coverage, and for
Part D, which is your prescription drug
coverage. If you miss that window, even
because you were still working, even
because you were confused by the
paperwork, even because no one told you,
the government adds a permanent
surcharge to your premium.
For Part B, that penalty is 10% of the
standard premium for every full 12-month
period you could have had it and did
not. Think about what that means. If you
signed up 2 years late, that is a 20%
surcharge, and it does not go away next
year. It lasts as long as you have
Medicare, which for most people means
the rest of their life. On a premium of
$202 a month, a 20% penalty is more than
$480 a year, forever, for a paperwork
mistake. For Part D, the drug penalty
works the same cruel way. It is 1% of
the national base premium, which is
in 2026, multiplied by the number of
months you went without coverage, added
to your premium for good.
Let me make that real, because a
percentage on a screen never feels like
anything until it is your money. Picture
a man who kept working past 65 because
he still had good coverage through his
job, or so he thought. He did not
realize his employer plan did not count
the way Medicare wanted it to. Three
years slip by. When he finally enrolls,
the government stacks a 30% penalty onto
his Part B premium. On a $202 premium,
that is more than $720
a year in penalty alone, and he will pay
it every year he lives. Over a 20-year
retirement, that single paperwork gap
can cost him more than $14,000.
All of it for a mistake he did not even
know he was making. And the letter that
told him he owed it did not mention, not
once, that there was any way to
challenge it. But here is what they do
not put on the letter. That penalty can
be erased. If you qualify for a program
called extra help, which is the
low-income subsidy for prescription
drugs, the entire Part D late penalty
disappears completely. Gone. And the
Part B penalty can be waived through
something called equitable relief. If
Medicare gave you the wrong information,
or avoided entirely if you had what is
called creditable coverage from an
employer. The people who fix this are
the ones who call and ask. Therefore,
the very first thing you should do after
this video is call your state health
insurance assistance program, which
offers free Medicare counseling in every
state, and ask them to check whether you
are paying a late enrollment penalty,
and whether you qualify to have it
removed. That one phone call has erased
hundreds of dollars a year for people
who thought the charge was set in stone.
Now, let me show you the second bill,
the one I opened this video with,
because this is the one that hits the
middle class the hardest, and the one
they hide the best. It is called IRMA,
and it stands for the income-related
monthly adjustment amount. That is a
deliberately boring name for something
that quietly drains real money. Here's
what it is. If your income is above a
certain line, the government adds an
extra charge to both your Part B and
your Part D premiums. In 2026, that line
starts at $109,000
for a single person, and $218,000
for a married couple filing together.
Now, you might be thinking, my income is
nowhere near that. This is not for me.
But stay with me, because this is where
the trap is. The government does not
look at your income today. It looks at
your tax return from 2 years ago. So,
the premium you pay in 2026 is based on
what you earned in 2024. Do you see the
problem? The year you retire, your
income drops. You are living on Social
Security and savings now, but the
government is still billing you based on
the year you were working full-time,
earning your highest paycheck of your
life. So, a newly retired senior gets
slapped with a surcharge calculated on
income they no longer have.
And that surcharge is not small. At the
top level, it raises the Part B premium
all the way to $689.90
a month and adds as much as $91 a month
on top of your drug plan. Even at the
lower levels, it is hundreds of dollars
a year you should not be paying. And
there is one more cruel piece to how it
is built. IRMAA works on what are called
cliffs, not a gentle slope. Go $1 over
the line and you do not pay a little
more. You jump to the entire next
surcharge tier. A retiree who sold a
house, cashed out an old account, or
took one large withdrawal in a single
year can be pushed over a cliff by a
one-time event that has nothing to do
with their normal income and then get
billed for it two years later when the
money is long gone.
Picture a married couple who both
retired last year. In their final
working year, they earned a good income,
the best of their careers, and they also
sold an investment to help pay for the
move to a smaller home. That single year
looks wealthy on paper. Now, living on
Social Security and their savings, they
open their Medicare statement and find
hundreds of dollars a month in extra
premiums charged on a year that will
never come again. They assume it is
simply what Medicare costs. It is not.
It is a surcharge on income they no
longer have, and it is exactly the
situation form SSA-44 was written to
fix. But, there is a form, and the form
fixes it. It is called form SSA-44, and
it exists for exactly this situation.
If your income went down because of a
life-changing event, and retirement
counts, and your spouse passing away
counts, and a divorce counts, and losing
a pension counts, you file form SSA-44,
and you ask Social Security to
recalculate your premium using your
current income instead of your old
income. Therefore, if you have retired,
reduced your work, lost a spouse, or
lost pension income in the last two
years, and you are paying any IRMAA
surcharge, that form can cut it or erase
it entirely. It is free. You get it at
ssa.gov or by calling Social Security,
and almost no one who is owed this
relief ever files it. Let me pause here
because we are about halfway through,
and I want to make sure you understand
what is really going on because it is
worse than five separate mistakes. Every
single one of these five bills has the
same design. The charge is automatic.
The removal is not. The government will
add the fee, add the surcharge, add the
penalty, all on its own without asking.
But, it will only ever take it back off
if you find the right program, say the
right words, and file the right form.
Nobody at Medicare is going to call you
and say, "We noticed you are overpaying.
Let us fix that." That call never comes.
And that is precisely why the wealthy
hire people to make these filings, and
everybody else just pays. You are about
to stop being everybody else.
And I want to correct something you may
have been told your whole life because
it is the belief that keeps most of
these bills in place. You were probably
raised to think that asking for help, or
claiming a program, or filing for relief
is something for other people. People
who did not save. People who did not
plan. That pride is admirable, and it is
also costing you thousands of dollars a
year. None of the five things on this
list are handouts. You paid into
Medicare out of every paycheck for your
entire working life. You paid the taxes
that funded these energy programs. You
paid property tax on that home for
decades. Claiming the relief that the
law attaches to your own money is not
taking charity. It is collecting on a
debt that is already owed to you. The
retiree with the financial advisor
understands that in his bones. It is
time you did, too.
So, now the third bill. And this one
touches almost every senior in America,
because almost every senior takes a
prescription. For years, the terror of
Part D was the cliff, the point where
your drug costs could climb into the
thousands with no ceiling. That is over.
As of the year 2025, there is now a hard
cap on what you can pay out of pocket
for covered prescription drugs under
Medicare Part D. In 2025, that cap was
And in 2026, it is $2,100.
Once your out-of-pocket drug spending
hits that number, your plan pays 100% of
your covered drugs for the rest of the
year. You are done paying.
Think about what that means for someone
with a serious condition. A senior on a
cancer drug or a specialty medication
for a heart or lung condition
used to face bills that ran into the
many thousands of dollars a year with no
ceiling at all. One prescription could
quietly eat an entire month of Social
Security. Now, no matter how expensive
the drug, no matter how many
prescriptions you take, the most you
will pay out of pocket for covered drugs
in the year 2026 is $2,100.
And then the meter stops. For the person
who was skipping doses to stretch the
pills or choosing between the medication
and the grocery bill, that cap is not a
small convenience. It is the difference
between taking the medicine and going
without.
But most seniors do not know that cap
exists. And even the ones who do are
missing a second tool that was built
right alongside it. It is called the
Medicare prescription payment plan, and
it started in January of 2025. Here's
what it does. Instead of getting hit
with a huge drug bill at the pharmacy
counter in one painful month, you can
choose to spread that out-of-pocket cost
across the the calendar year in smooth
monthly payments at zero interest with
no fee. You walk out of the pharmacy
paying nothing that day and the plan
bills you gently over the year. For a
senior on a fixed income who dreads the
January refill that costs a fortune,
this changes everything. But it is
opt-in. You have to ask your drug plan
to enroll you. They will not do it for
you.
And there is more inside this one.
Insulin is now capped at $35 a month for
each covered insulin with no deductible.
And every vaccine your doctor
recommends, the shingles shot, the RSV
shot, the tetanus booster, all of them
are now $0 under Part D. Zero. And yet
seniors are still being handed a bill
for a shingles shot at the pharmacy and
just paying it because they assume the
bill is correct. Therefore, if you were
charged for a recommended vaccine,
dispute it because by law it should have
cost you nothing. Call your plan, ask to
join the Medicare prescription payment
plan, and if money is tight, apply for
extra help at ssa.gov, which can drop
your co-pays to just a few dollars. Now,
the fourth bill is different from the
others and I want you to hear the
difference because this is not the
government helping you pay a bill. This
is the government paying to make the
bill smaller forever. I am talking about
your home energy costs. Most people have
heard of programs that help pay a
heating bill in the winter. This is not
that. Under a federal law passed a few
years ago, there is now money set aside
administered through your state to
actually pay for the upgrades that cut
your energy bill permanently.
Here's the scale of it. For a lower
income household, the home
electrification and appliance rebate can
pay up to $14,000
toward things like a new heat pump, a
heat pump water heater, an electric
stove, an upgraded electrical panel, and
new insulation. And the home efficiency
rebate can pay up to $8,000 for a whole
home efficiency retrofit. That is not a
discount on one month. That is the
government buying you a furnace so your
bill goes down every month for the rest
of the time you live there.
And the money is broken out by the exact
upgrade, so it is not one vague pot.
There is money set aside for the heat
pump itself, money for a heat pump water
heater, money for an electric stove,
money to upgrade the old electrical
panel that could not handle any of it,
money for wiring, and money for
insulation and sealing up the drafts.
For a senior in an older home with a
furnace on its last winter, this can
mean replacing the thing that has been
bleeding money for years and paying
little or nothing to do it. Now I have
to be honest with you because honesty is
the whole point of this channel. These
rebates are run by each individual
state, and not every state has opened
its program yet. So you have to check
whether yours is available where you
live.
But there is a second energy program
that has been running for decades and is
available right now in every state, and
it prioritizes you specifically. It is
called the Weatherization Assistance
Program, run by the Department of
Energy. If you are income eligible, it
sends trained workers to your home to
seal it up, add insulation, and fix what
is wasting your money, completely free.
And by law, it gives priority to the
elderly. They start with what is called
an energy audit, walking the home to
find exactly where the heat and the cool
air and the money are escaping, and then
they do the work. They seal the drafts
around the doors and windows. They add
insulation in the attic and the walls.
They check the heating system for
safety, and they do it all at no cost to
you.
For a senior in a drafty old house who
has been paying to heat the outdoors
every winter, this is real money back in
your pocket, month after month, year
after year. And it starts with a single
phone call to put your name on the list.
The Department of Energy says households
save, on average, $372
a year on energy after the work is done.
Therefore, if your energy bill feels
like it is eating your fixed income
alive, search for your state home energy
rebates and call your state
weatherization office, and ask them to
put a senior on the priority list, which
is you.
That brings me to the fifth bill, and I
saved it for last because it is the
biggest one on this list for a
homeowner, and it is the one seniors are
most likely to keep paying year after
year without ever questioning it. Your
property tax. If you own your home, and
especially if it is paid off, the
property tax bill is very often the
single largest bill you still receive
every year, and it climbs as your home
value climbs, even though your income
does not. But nearly every state in this
country has quietly built relief for
seniors into its tax code, and it is
almost never applied automatically.
Depending on where you live, you may be
eligible for a homestead exemption that
carves a chunk of value off the taxable
amount, or an assessment freeze that
locks your tax bill in place so it
cannot rise as your home value goes up,
or a deferral that lets you postpone the
tax, or a circuit breaker that caps your
property tax as a percentage of your
income. Let me give you a real example
so you know these are not vague
promises. In the state of Texas, a
homeowner who is 65 or older gets an
additional $60,000 knocked off the value
their school taxes are based on, and on
top of that, their school tax bill is
frozen at that year's amount and legally
cannot climb, no matter how high the
home's value goes. That is a permanent,
enormous reduction, and a homeowner has
to file for it. The state does not do it
for you. And here is the quiet injustice
buried in this one. The senior who paid
off the mortgage, who did everything
right, who owns the home free and clear,
is often the one most exposed to the
rising tax because there is no bank
escrow account smoothing it out anymore,
and the bill lands in full every year.
The value of the home climbs on paper,
the tax climbs with it, but the
retiree's income does not move at all. A
freeze stops that climb cold. An
exemption shrinks the base it is
calculated on. A deferral lets you
postpone it entirely. And a circuit
breaker says that once your property tax
passes a certain share of your income,
the state steps in. These are not
loopholes, and they are not charity.
They are written directly into the tax
code of most states specifically for
people your age. And the reason so few
claim them is simply that no letter ever
arrives telling you they exist. You have
to know to ask. So, here is the promise
I made you at the very beginning of this
video, and here is where I close the
loop. I told you the first bill, the
late enrollment penalty, was added by
default the moment you turn 65 and would
follow you for life unless you knew the
words to make it stop. Now you know. The
words are creditable coverage, equitable
relief, and extra help. And the phone
call is to your state health insurance
assistance program. But I want you to
understand the pattern behind all five
of these, because the pattern is the
real lesson. In every case, the machine
adds the charge on its own and removes
it only when you ask. Silence is read as
consent to keep paying. Let me show you
what that looks like in a real life with
two neighbors on the same street. Both
are 70 years old. Both retired two years
ago. Both own their homes. The first
neighbor opens every government letter,
assumes the amount printed on it is
final, and pays it. She is paying an
IRMAA surcharge based on her final
working year, a late enrollment penalty
on her drug plan from the months she was
confused about signing up, full price
property tax that rises every single
year, and full price at the pharmacy
every January. The second neighbor did
four things. She filed form SSA-44
and erased her IRMAA surcharge. She
called about extra help and wiped out
her drug penalty. She filed her senior
homestead exemption and froze her
property tax. And she joined the
Medicare prescription payment plan, so
her drug costs are spread out and
capped. Same street, same age, same
income. One of them keeps thousands of
dollars a year that the other one hands
back to the government for no reason but
silence. And understand, the first
neighbor is not foolish, and she is not
lazy. She is doing exactly what most
honest, careful people do. She trusts
that the bill is correct. She assumes
that a government agency, of all things,
would not overcharge her, and that if
she were owed something, a letter would
arrive to tell her. That trust is the
most expensive thing she owns. The
second neighbor is not smarter. She
simply learned, somewhere along the way,
that the amount printed on the letter is
only the starting point, not the final
word, and that a few free phone calls
can change it. That is the entire
difference between them. Not income, not
luck, just the knowledge that these
forms exist, and the willingness to pick
up the phone. You now have the
knowledge. The willingness is the only
thing left, and it is yours to decide
today. And this is the assumption I need
you to throw away today, because it is
the single most expensive belief a
senior can hold. The assumption is this:
If I qualified for something, surely
they would have told me, or surely they
would have taken it off automatically.
They will not. That is not how any of
this works. The default setting of every
one of these systems is that you pay
full price until the day you personally
stand up and claim [clears throat] what
the law already says is yours. The
government is not going to erase these
bills for you. It has simply made it
legal for you to erase them yourself,
and then it stays very quiet about how.
So, let me give you your action plan, in
order, and I want you to write these
down, or come back to this part. First,
call your State Health Insurance
Assistance Program, which is free
Medicare counseling in every state, and
ask them two things: Whether you are
paying a late enrollment penalty, and
whether you qualify for extra help.
Second, if you have retired, reduced
your work, lost a spouse, or lost
pension income in the last two years, go
to ssa.gov,
or call Social Security at
and file form SSA-44
to cut your IRMAA surcharge. Third, call
your prescription drug plan and ask to
enroll in the Medicare prescription
payment plan and ask them to confirm
your vaccines are showing at zero
dollars. Fourth, search for your state
home energy rebates and call your state
weatherization office and ask to be
placed on the senior priority list. And
fifth, call your county tax assessor and
ask by name for the over 65 homestead
exemption, the assessment freeze, and
the deferral. Every one of those calls
is free. Every one of those forms is
free and every senior who makes them is
quietly taking back money the system was
counting on them never to claim. The
wealthy have always known these forms
exist. Now so do you. This is your
playbook. Make the calls. Start with
your state health insurance assistance
program and your county tax assessor and
say the program names out loud when you
call.

title: They Can SELL Your Paid-Off Home Over a Small Tax Bill After 65 — Here's How to Stop It

segments.text: A 94-year-old woman in Minneapolis fell
about $15,000 behind on the property
taxes for her small one-bedroom
condominium. And so, the county took the
condo, sold it for $40,000, kept every
single penny, and handed her back
nothing. Not the difference, not the
$25,000 of value that was left over
after her debt was paid. Nothing. She
owned that home. She had paid it off,
and the government sold it out from
under her and pocketed the equity she
spent a lifetime building. Her name was
Geraldine, and if you own your home free
and clear right now, what happened to
her is the single most important warning
you will hear this year. Because the
same thing is legal, or was legal until
very recently, in about a dozen states
across this country. And almost no
senior over 65 sees it coming until the
notice is already taped to the door.
Here is what I need you to understand
before we go one step further, because
this is the part that will save your
house. There is one specific program,
one form you can file at your own county
office, that would have let Geraldine
keep her home and every dollar of that
equity. And it is sitting available
right now in state after state. And the
people who run these offices will almost
never mention it to you unless you walk
in and ask for it by its exact name. I
am going to give you that name. I am
going to tell you exactly what to say.
But I need to walk you through how they
take the house first. Because if you do
not understand the trap, you will not
understand why this one move stops it
cold. Stay with me, because the mistake
that ends with a family losing a
paid-off home is almost always made in
complete silence, years before anyone
knocks. Let me tell you what actually
happened to Geraldine, because the
details matter. She owned her condo
outright, no mortgage. That was supposed
to be the safe part. But she had fallen
behind on her property taxes, and over a
few years the unpaid bill, which started
at only about $2,300, grew with
penalties and interest and fees until it
reached roughly $15,000. So, Hennepin
County, Minnesota, did what the law at
the time allowed. It It her home. It
sold it at auction for $40,000. It took
the 15,000 it was owed, and then it kept
the other $25,000 for the county
treasury. She got a bill for zero and a
home she no longer owned. Now, here is
why this is not just one sad story in
one city. A legal group called the
Pacific Legal Foundation went and
counted. Between the year 2014 and the
year 2021, local governments in this
country took at least 8,950
homes this exact way. The families who
lost those homes lost around $860
million in equity. And on average, each
of those families lost 86% of the value
of their home over a debt that was often
a tiny sliver of what the home was
worth. 86% gone. Not because they
refused to pay a mortgage. Most of them
did not even have a mortgage. They lost
the whole house over a few thousand
dollars in property tax. And I want you
to sit with how strange that really is
because it is the opposite of how every
other debt in your life works.
If you fall behind on a car loan and the
lender repossesses the car and sells it
for more than you owe, they have to give
you the difference.
If a bank forecloses on a mortgage and
the house sells for more than the loan,
the leftover money comes back to you.
That is normal. That is how it is
supposed to work.
But for generations in a whole set of
states, property taxes were the one
glaring exception. Where the government
could take an asset worth hundreds of
thousands of dollars to satisfy a debt
of a few thousand and simply keep the
entire difference as if it had earned
it.
There was a man in Michigan, not long
before Geraldine's case, who underpaid
his property taxes by about $8.
$8. Interest and penalties pushed it
higher, and the county took his home and
sold it and kept roughly $24,000 of his
equity over that original $8 mistake.
That is not a story I'm exaggerating for
effect. That is the kind of case that
finally pushed this all the way to the
highest court in the country. Therefore,
you need to understand the machine
because it runs on a timeline and the
timeline is where you either lose
everything or stop it. It begins the
moment you miss a property tax payment.
You do not lose your house that day.
What happens that day is quiet. The
county places what is called a tax lien
on your home. That lien is a legal claim
for the money you owe. And here is the
part almost nobody knows.
In a lot of states, the county does not
wait around to collect it themselves.
They sell that lien. They hold a public
auction and investors show up and buy
the debt on your home.
Which brings me to something I promised
I would come back to and it is the part
that makes people the angriest when they
finally learn it. So, hold that thought.
Once the lien exists, the clock starts
on what is called the redemption period.
That is the window of time you have to
pay the back taxes plus the interest
plus the fees and get your home back
clean.
And this window is different in every
state, which is exactly why so many
people miss it. In Ohio, you might have
about 1 year.
In Texas, for a homestead, roughly 2
years. In New York and in Colorado,
about 3 years.
In some states that sell the deed
directly, it moves faster than that.
But, here is the trap inside the trap.
That clock is running whether or not you
understand it is running. The notices
come in dense legal envelopes that look
like junk mail or look like a scam and a
lot of seniors, especially anyone living
alone or dealing with failing eyesight
or memory, set them aside. And when the
redemption period ends and you have not
paid, the county or the investor who
bought your lien goes to court,
forecloses just like a bank would, takes
a tax deed, and sells your home at
auction. Minimum bid at that auction is
just the debt, which is how a home worth
$300,000 gets sold to settle a bill of
8,000. Now, let me tell you who this
actually happens to because it is not
who you think. It is not people who
cannot afford their homes.
The people this happens to almost always
own their homes free and clear.
They are seniors on fixed incomes and
they got hit by the one thing nobody
warned them about. Which is that
property taxes never stop and property
taxes keep going up. You paid off your
mortgage, you did everything right. You
thought the hard part was over. But the
assessed value of your home kept
climbing and every time it climbed, your
tax bill climbed with it. And one year
on a fixed social security income, the
bill simply became more than you could
pay on time.
That is not irresponsibility. That is
arithmetic. And here is why this is more
urgent right now than it has ever been.
Over the last few years, home values in
this country climbed faster than almost
anyone expected. And when home values
climb, county assessments climb right
behind them. And when assessments climb,
property tax bills climb, too. Millions
of seniors are opening their tax bills
this year and finding numbers that are
hundreds or even thousands of dollars
higher than they were just a few years
ago. On the exact same house, on the
exact same fixed income that has not
grown to match. So the gap between what
the county wants and what a retiree can
actually pay is widening in real time in
county after county. Which means more
paid off homes are sliding toward that
delinquency list than in any year in
recent memory. But the very same rising
values that are inflating your bill are
also inflating the equity in your home.
Which is precisely what makes your house
such a tempting target for the county
and for the investors who trail behind
it. The more your home is worth, the
more there is to lose over a bill of a
few thousand dollars. Therefore, waiting
is the one thing you cannot afford to do
because every year this trap gets a
little bigger and a little quieter at
the same time. And there is one more
piece of this trap that I have to say
plainly because it catches more paid off
homeowners than any other single thing.
And once you hear it, you will never
forget it. When you had a mortgage, you
almost certainly had an escrow account.
Every month, part of your payment went
into that account, and the bank used it
to pay your property taxes for you
automatically. You never had to think
about it. The bank handled it. But, the
day you make that final mortgage payment
and you own your home outright, that
escrow account closes. And now, nobody
is paying those property taxes for you.
You are. And if you did not realize the
responsibility just quietly shifted onto
your shoulders, your paid-off home can
slide into tax delinquency without you
doing a single thing wrong, just by not
knowing that the job changed hands. The
very moment your house becomes fully
yours is the exact moment it becomes
most exposed. Let me make this real for
you with two people who lived on the
same kind of street because I have seen
this exact contrast play out more times
than I can count. Picture two widows,
same age, both about 78, both living in
homes they had paid off decades ago,
both living on social security and a
small pension.
The first one got a thick envelope from
the county one winter. It was the
delinquency notice. The print was small,
and the language was the kind of legal
wording that makes your eyes slide right
off the page, and she was recently
widowed and overwhelmed and grieving,
and she set it on the counter with the
rest of the mail she would deal with
later. Later never came.
Three more notices arrived over the next
2 years, and each one went on the same
pile. And when the redemption period
closed, the county foreclosed, and her
home, worth well over $200,000,
was sold at auction to settle a tax debt
of about $9,000. She found out when
someone came to look at what was now
their property.
The second widow, on the very same fixed
income, did one thing differently.
When her husband passed and the mortgage
was long gone, her daughter made a
single phone call to the county assessor
and asked one question. "What does my
mother qualify for?"
Therefore, that home is still in the
family today, protected, the taxes
deferred, not $1 of equity lost. Same
age, same income, same size debt.
The only difference between keeping the
house and losing it was knowing that one
question existed to be asked. So, let me
come back to the thing I told you to
hold because at about this point in the
story, people always ask me the same
question. They ask, who actually buys my
tax debt? And the answer is the part of
this that feels almost unbelievable. In
many states, it is not the government
that ends up owning the claim on your
home. It is a private investor.
There are companies and individuals
whose entire business is showing up at
these county auctions and buying up the
tax liens on other people's houses.
They pay the county the back taxes,
which is why the county is happy to
sell.
And now that investor holds the debt on
your home, charges you interest on it,
sometimes double-digit interest, and if
you do not pay them back inside the
redemption window, that private party
has the legal right to foreclose on your
house and take it. A stranger who has
never met you, who found your address on
a delinquency list, can end up owning
the home your children were supposed to
inherit. That is not a loophole. In a
lot of places, that is the system
working exactly as designed. And think
about the incentive that creates because
it is chilling once you see it. That
investor does not actually want you to
pay them back on time. If you pay them
back, they collect their interest and
they move on. But, if you cannot pay
them back inside the redemption window,
they get to foreclose and take a home
worth many times what they paid for the
lien. So, there is real money in you
failing. There are investors who target
the tax liens on the homes of the
elderly for exactly this reason because
an older homeowner on a fixed income is
statistically more likely to fall behind
and stay behind, and the property
underneath is often a paid-off house
loaded with equity.
One unpaid tax bill of a few thousand
dollars can turn into a stranger holding
the deed to a home worth 300,000.
Therefore, the single most dangerous
thing you can do is treat a property tax
notice like ordinary mail because on the
other end of that notice, there may be
someone quietly hoping you never open
it. The good news, and I promise there
is good news, is that every one of the
protections I am about to walk you
through takes you off that list entirely
so that no investor is ever circling
your address in the first place. But
here is the story turns, and this is the
part I have been building toward, so
lean in. Because a woman named
Geraldine, 94 years old, did not just
lose her home quietly. She fought back.
Her case went all the way to the Supreme
Court of the United States, and in the
year 2023, the Supreme Court ruled. Not
five to four, not some narrow split down
party lines, nine to nothing. Every
single justice agreed. The court held
that when the government takes your home
for a tax debt and keeps more than you
actually owed, that is an
unconstitutional taking under the Fifth
Amendment. The Chief Justice wrote the
line that I want you to remember because
it is the whole case in one sentence. He
wrote that the taxpayer must give the
government what the government is owed,
but no more. No more. They can collect
the debt, they cannot keep your equity
on top of it. Therefore, if you are ever
caught in this, the law of the land now
says that the surplus, the money left
over after your debt is paid, belongs to
you. And after that ruling, states
started scrambling to rewrite their
laws. Nebraska, North Dakota,
Massachusetts, Idaho, and others passed
new rules so that homeowners get their
surplus back.
Wisconsin had already passed a bill to
end most of this. So if a home in your
family was this way and the government
kept the extra, that money may still be
legally claimable, and it is worth
calling to ask. But, and I need you to
hear this clearly, the ruling protects
your surplus. It does not stop them from
taking the home in the first place. If
you fall behind and you do nothing, you
can still lose the house. You will just
be owed the change afterward, and nobody
watching this wants to be owed the
change. You want to keep the home. So
let me finally give you the moves that
keep it. This is the promise I made you
at the very beginning, and here is the
name I told you I would give you.
The single most powerful protection for
a senior who is worried about property
taxes is called property tax deferral.
Write that down. Property tax deferral.
Here is what it does. If you qualify,
and in most of these programs you
qualify simply by being a certain age
and owning your home, the state lets you
postpone your property taxes.
You do not pay them right now.
The unpaid amount becomes a lien that is
quietly repaid later when the home is
eventually sold or passed on.
And while you are alive and living in
that home, they cannot foreclose on you
for those deferred taxes.
Let me say that again because it is the
whole point.
Deferral means the clock that ends in
foreclosure never starts.
The house is safe while you are in it.
And these programs are real, and they
are generous, and they are sitting there
unused. In Texas, under a section of the
state tax code, a homeowner who is 65 or
older can defer property taxes on their
homestead indefinitely. The unpaid tax
accrues interest at 5% a year, and it is
simply settled when the property is
later sold or transferred. In
California, the state runs a
postponement program for homeowners 62
and older who have at least 40% equity
and a household income at or below
roughly $55,000,
and the postponed tax becomes a lien at
5% interest. In Minnesota, the very
state where Geraldine lost her home, a
qualifying senior pays only 3% of their
household income toward property tax,
and the state covers the rest as a loan
at an interest rate that cannot exceed
5%. Oregon and Massachusetts run
deferral programs of their own, and
Vermont offers one at 0% interest. Think
about that. In some states, you can push
your entire property tax bill down the
road, protect your home completely, and
pay no interest at all. That is the move
Geraldine needed and never knew to ask
for. Let me show you what that actually
looks like in real dollars because I do
not want this to stay abstract. Say your
property tax bill runs about $5,000 a
year and you are 80 years old and on
some months choosing between that bill
and your medication is a real choice.
Under a deferral program, you stop
writing that $5,000 check. The state
records it as a lien and lets it sit.
Say you live another 10 years in that
home, which I hope you do and more. That
is roughly $50,000 in deferred taxes
plus some interest that gets settled
quietly out of the sale of the home much
later after you are gone from a house
that may be worth three or four hundred
thousand dollars by then. Your children
still inherit the overwhelming majority
of that value and in exchange, you got
to keep your home, keep your dignity,
and never once lie awake wondering if a
missed bill was going to cost you the
roof over your head. That is not a
handout. It is a program written into
state law specifically so that no senior
is ever forced out of a paid-off home by
a tax bill. But, it only works if you
enroll and it almost never happens
automatically. Somebody has to file the
paperwork. In most places, that somebody
is you or a son or daughter making one
phone call on your behalf. But, deferral
is only the first tool and you may want
to lower the bill itself, not just delay
it. So, let me give you the others.
The first is the homestead exemption.
This subtracts a fixed chunk of value,
commonly anywhere from $10,000 to
off the assessed value of your home
before the tax is even calculated. A lot
of seniors qualify for it and never
filed the one-page form to claim it. The
second is the senior exemption combined
with an assessment freeze. Many states
give you an extra exemption once you
turn 65 and even better, they will
freeze the assessed value of your home
so that when property values in your
area shoot up, your tax bill does not
follow them up. That freeze alone can be
the difference between affording your
home and falling behind. The third is
called a circuit breaker program. It
works like the circuit breaker in your
house. When your property tax bill takes
too big a bite out of your income, it
trips and the state refunds part of the
tax. In North Carolina, for example, the
program caps what you pay at 4 to 5% of
your household income and gives back the
rest. And let me put a real number on
that assessment freeze because it is the
quietest hero on this whole list and the
one people underestimate the most.
Imagine you bought your home years ago
and it was assessed at $150,000
and your tax bill was built on that
number. Now, imagine that over the years
the market went wild and your county
reassessed your home at $400,000.
Your home did not change. It is the same
house with the same roof and the same
kitchen. But, your tax bill just got
calculated on a number more than twice
as high and on a fixed income, that
increase alone is what tips thousands of
seniors into falling behind. A senior
assessment freeze locks your assessed
value back down at that lower figure and
holds it there. So, the rising market
cannot keep dragging your bill up year
after year. In some counties, that
freeze can save a homeowner one, two,
even $3,000 a year, every year for the
rest of their life in that home.
Therefore, the single afternoon it takes
to walk into the assessor's office and
file for the senior freeze and the
homestead exemption may be the highest
paid afternoon of your retirement. And I
want to be very clear about something.
These are not favors. You are not asking
anyone for charity. These are
protections that lawmakers put on the
books precisely for people in your
position and they are yours to claim.
The only reason they go unused is that
the offices that administer them are not
in the business of chasing you down to
hand them over. And there is fresh help
arriving right now that you should know
about. New Jersey just launched a
program for homeowners 65 and older that
reimburses up to half of your property
tax bill up to a cap of $6,500 a year.
Montana approved a new tiered homestead
system beginning this year that
officials estimate will cut the typical
qualifying homeowners bill by around
18%. These programs change and expand
almost every year, which is exactly why
you cannot assume you know what is
available. You have to ask this year
again. Therefore, let me tell you
exactly what to do in order so this
never happens to you or to your parents.
Step one. If your mortgage is paid off,
confirm today who is paying your
property taxes. Do not assume. Call your
county and ask if your account is
current and set up automatic payment or
your own escrow so a bill can never be
missed in silence. That one phone call
closes the most common trap there is.
Step two.
Call your county assessor's office and
use these exact words. Ask them, what
property tax relief do I qualify for as
a senior? Then ask for three things by
name. Ask for the senior homestead
exemption. Ask for the assessment
freeze. And ask for the property tax
deferral program. Make them tell you
about each one.
Step three.
If you are already behind, do not hide
from the notices.
Find out your state's redemption period
immediately because that is your window
and paying the back taxes plus interest
before that window closes gets your home
back clean.
Step four. If a home in your family was
ever taken over back taxes and the
government kept more than the debt, call
and ask about recovering the surplus
because the Supreme Court says that
money is yours. Because here is the
assumption I want to leave you with, the
one that costs people everything. Almost
every senior believes that once the
mortgage is gone and the home is paid
off, the home is finally safe. That no
one can take it. And that belief is
exactly backwards. A paid off home is
not the safest home. In the eyes of this
system, it is the richest target because
it holds the most equity to lose and it
has no lender in the background quietly
protecting the tax bill. The wealthy
know this. They defer, they exempt, they
set up the payments, they never miss. It
is ordinary people, people who did the
responsible thing and paid off their
house who lose it over a few thousand
dollars simply because no one ever told
them the one word that stops it. So, if
you do nothing else after today, do
this. Call your county assessor's
office. Ask what you qualify for as a
homeowner over 65. And say the words
property tax deferral out loud and make
them answer you.

title: Social Security Is Sitting On Money It Owes You — Here's How to Claim It

segments.text: Social Security's own internal watchdog
investigated the agency and found that
it had underpaid 82% of a group of
widows and widowers quietly for years
and never told a single one of them. And
the total came to about 131 million owed
to people who had no idea it was theirs.
Let me say that number again so it lands
because it is not a rumor and it is not
a headline someone invented. $131
million. That figure comes straight out
of a report by the Office of the
Inspector General for Social Security.
the office whose entire job is to catch
the agency's mistakes. They looked at
more than 13,000 people who were
entitled to two different kinds of
social security at the same time. And
they found that more than 11,000 of them
may have been shortchanged because
Social Security never told them about an
option they had every right to use. If
you are a widow, a widowerower, a
divorced spouse, or anyone who has ever
claimed a benefit, I need you to hear
the rest of this because the money that
is missing is not lost. It is sitting
there and almost nobody knows to ask for
it. Here is the promise I am making you
right now, and I want you to hold me to
it before this video is over. There is
one specific move, one benefit choice
that Social Security's own investigators
said the agency failed to explain to 82%
of those widows. And it is the single
reason so many of them were underpaid. I
am going to tell you exactly what that
move is in plain words, so that you or
someone you love can walk into a Social
Security office and use it. But I have
to build up to it because if I just say
it now, you will not understand why it
is worth thousands of dollars. So stay
with me because the biggest mistake
people make with Social Security is
assuming the agency is looking out for
them and will automatically hand them
the largest check they qualify for. That
assumption is exactly backwards and I am
going to prove it to you. Let me start
with how this even happens because most
people cannot believe a government
agency would underpay someone and just
say nothing. Social Security is not one
simple benefit. It is a stack of
different benefits and a single person
can be eligible for more than one of
them at the same time. You can have a
benefit based on your own work history.
You can have a benefit based on a
husband or a wife. You can have a
benefit based on a spouse who has passed
away. You can even have one based on an
ex-husband or an ex-wife you divorced
decades ago. And here is the quiet truth
at the center of all of it. When you
apply, Social Security generally pays
you the benefit you applied for. It does
not always sit you down and walk you
through every other door you could have
opened instead. The inspector general
said this plainly. The agency did not
have the controls in place to make sure
its own employees told widows and
widowers about their options. So, the
responsibility, whether that is fair or
not, lands on you to know what to ask
for. And before you tell yourself this
is old news or some one-time mistake
that has surely been cleaned up by now,
let me stop you because it is not. That
same inspector general issued another
report just this year again warning
Social Security that it still needs to
take steps to make sure widows and
widowers are actually paid correctly and
told their options. Just this year,
years after the first alarm was raised,
the watchdog is still saying the same
thing. Which means if you are sitting at
home assuming the problem got fixed and
the checks got corrected, you are making
the exact assumption that left 11,000
people short. Think about who this hits
the hardest. It is not the wealthy who
pay advisers to squeeze every dollar out
of these rules. It is ordinary widows,
many of them women in their 70s and 80s,
living alone on a fixed income, who
walked into an office during the worst
week of their lives right after losing a
husband and simply trusted the person
behind the desk to give them what they
were owed. But trust is not a claiming
strategy. And that is the hard lesson
buried inside that $131 million number.
Now, let me get to the heart of it, the
part that involves the most money for
the most people. And that is the
survivor benefit. When a husband or a
wife passes away, the surviving spouse
is entitled to a survivor benefit based
on what that person had earned. And this
can be a large amount. A survivor
benefit can be worth up to 100% of the
deceased spouse's full benefit if you
claim it at your own full retirement
age. 100%. The entire check your spouse
would have received. If you claim it
earlier, as young as age 60, it is
reduced down to about 71%. But at full
retirement age, you can step into the
full amount. For a lot of widows,
especially women who earned less over
their lifetimes or who stayed home to
raise a family, that survivor benefit is
dramatically larger than anything on
their own record. And that is where the
missing money begins. Let me put real
numbers on it so you can see the size of
what we are talking about. Say a husband
worked his whole life and earned a full
social security benefit of about $2,400
a month. and say his wife, who worked
part-time and raised their children,
earned a benefit on her own record of
about $900 a month. While they were both
alive, the household saw both checks.
But when he passes away, one of those
checks stops and she is left to live on
far less than the two of them planned
for. Here is where the survivor benefit
matters. As his widow, at her full
retirement age, she is entitled to step
up to 100% of his benefit, that full
in place of her own 900. That is a
difference of $1,500 a month. $1,500
every single month for the rest of her
life. Over just 10 years, that is well
Now, imagine she was never clearly told
to claim the survivor benefit and simply
kept collecting her own $900 because
that was the check she already had
coming. That is not a small clerical
error. That is a woman living in near
poverty while the money that would have
kept her comfortable sits unclaimed on a
record with her late husband's name on
it. But here is the part that Social
Security failed to explain. And this is
the move I promised you. So lean in.
When you are entitled to two benefits at
once, a survivor benefit and your own
retirement benefit, you do not have to
take them both at the same time. And you
do not have to take the bigger one
first. There is a rule most people have
never heard of. The rule that forces you
to take everything at once, which is
called deemed filing, does not apply to
survivor benefits. Let me translate
that. It means a widow or widowerower
can take one benefit now and switch to
the other one later whenever the other
one has grown larger. So, you could take
the survivor benefit first and let your
own retirement benefit keep growing in
the background because your own benefit
grows by about 8% for every year you
wait past full retirement age all the
way up to age 70. Then at 70, when your
own benefit has grown to its maximum,
you switch over to it or you flip it and
take your own smaller benefit early
while the survivor benefit waits. You
get to choose the order that pays you
the most over your life. And that single
choice, that switching strategy is
exactly what the inspector general said
Social Security failed to tell 82% of
those widows about. They took one
benefit, were never told they could have
optimized the order, and left thousands
of dollars on the table. Let me make
this real because numbers on their own
do not stick. Picture two widows who
live on the same street, both 70 years
old, both lost their husbands a few
years back. The first walked into the
office, grief still fresh, and simply
asked to start her benefits. The clerk
started the survivor benefit because at
that moment it was the bigger of the
two, and that was that. Nobody mentioned
that her own benefit was still sitting
there growing and that she could have
arranged things differently. She has
been collecting a smaller total ever
since and has no idea. The second widow
before she filed asked one question. She
asked, "I may be entitled to more than
one benefit, so which order should I
claim them in to get the most money over
time?" Therefore, the agent had to
actually run her options. She took the
survivor benefit first, let her own
retirement benefit grow to its maximum
at 70 and then switched to that. Over
the years ahead, she will collect tens
of thousands of dollars more than her
neighbor for one reason only. She knew
the switch existed and she asked for it.
Same age, same situation. The only
difference was one question. And I want
to make sure you understand why the
waiting works. Because it is not magic.
It is a rule written into the law that
rewards patience. When you delay taking
your own retirement benefit past your
full retirement age, Social Security
adds delayed retirement credits to it.
Worth about 8% for every year you wait
all the way until age 70. 8% a year
guaranteed. No risk. No stock market.
There is almost nowhere else on earth an
older person can get a guaranteed 8%
raise on their income just for waiting.
So a widow whose own benefit would be
say $1,600 at her full retirement age
could see that same benefit grow toward
roughly $2,000 a month by age 70 simply
by living on the survivor benefit in the
meantime and letting her own check
climb. Therefore, the switch strategy is
really two gifts stacked on top of each
other. You get income now from one
benefit and you get a bigger permanent
check later from the other because it
grew while you waited. That is the
machinery social security did not bother
to explain to 82% of those widows. And
it is the difference between just
getting by and living with real
breathing room. But survivor benefits
are just one of the doors. And there are
others standing open that people walk
right past. So let me keep going. The
next one is the spousal benefit. And
this one is for people whose husband or
wife is still living. If your spouse
worked and earned a social security
benefit, you can be entitled to a
spousal benefit of up to 50% of their
full retirement amount, up to half of
their check added to your household,
even if you personally never worked a
day under social security in your life.
A lot of spouses, again often women who
raise children or work jobs that did not
pay into the system, assume they get
nothing of their own. That is false. If
your husband or wife earned a benefit,
you may be owed up to half of it. And
plenty of people are collecting a tiny
benefit on their own record right now,
never realizing that the spousal benefit
on their partner's record would have
been larger. Let me give you a picture
of that one, too, because it is more
common than almost any other miss.
Imagine a wife who worked on and off
over the years and earned a benefit of
about $600 a month on her own record.
Her husband earned a full benefit of
about $2,200.
half of his benefit is $1,100.
So, her spousal benefit could lift her
from $600 up to that $1,100 level, an
extra $500 a month, because the rule
says she can receive up to 50% of his
full amount. But if she simply filed on
her own record years ago, and nobody ran
the comparison, she is sitting at $600,
leaving $500 a month on the table,
$6,000 a year, and she may not even know
the higher option exists. This is why
you cannot just look at your own
earnings and decide you do not qualify
for much. Your check is not only about
what you earn. It is about what your
[snorts] spouse earned too. And the law
let you claim the better of the two.
Now, here is the rehook, the part that
surprises people the most. So, do not
tune out even if you think none of this
applies to you. Because you might be
sitting there thinking, "My spouse is
gone and I never remarried or I got
divorced years ago so I am on my own."
And that is exactly the person this next
benefit is for. If you were married for
at least 10 years and you are currently
unmarried and you are at least 62 years
old, you can claim a benefit on your
ex-husband or your ex-wife's social
security record. Let me repeat that
because people do not believe me the
first time. You can collect on an
ex-spouse. A marriage that ended in
divorce 20, 30, 40 years ago can still
put money in your pocket today. up to
50% of their benefit while they are
living and up to 100% as a surviving
divorced spouse if they have passed away
as long as you did not remarry before
age 60. And here is the part that makes
it almost unbelievable. It does not
reduce their benefit at all. It does not
touch their new spouse's benefit. And
they are never even notified that you
filed. That ex who you may not have
spoken to in decades has no idea and no
say and loses nothing. The only person
who loses if you never claim it is you.
I have seen this one change lives
because so many people write themselves
off completely. Think of a woman who was
married for 12 years back in her 30s,
divorced, never remarried, and spent the
decades since supporting herself on
modest work. She has always assumed
social security would be a small check
because her own earnings were never
high. But her ex-husband went on to have
a long, well-p paid career, and his full
benefit today is substantial. Because
that marriage lasted more than 10 years
and because she never remarried, she can
claim on his record up to half of his
benefit while he is alive and up to the
full amount if he has since passed away.
A marriage that ended 30 years ago that
she rarely even thinks about anymore
could be worth hundreds of dollars a
month to her right now. And the
beautiful part is that it takes nothing
from him. He will never know. His
current wife can also claim on his
record fully at the same time. Social
Security does not make anyone choose.
There is no penalty, no notice, no
awkward phone call. The benefit is
simply there, tied to a decade of your
life you already lived, waiting for you
to claim it. Therefore, if you take
nothing else from this, understand this.
Social Security is a menu, not a vending
machine. It will not automatically serve
you the most expensive item. You have to
know what is on the menu and order it by
name. And there is one more item on that
menu that can put a lump sum of money in
your hand almost immediately. So, let me
give you that, too. When you finally do
claim certain benefits at full
retirement age or as a survivor, Social
Security can pay you up to 6 months of
benefits retroactively. That means a
lump sum check for the 6 months before
you even applied if you were eligible
during that time. For someone claiming a
survivor benefit, that can be thousands
of dollars paid all at once as backay.
It is not automatic in every case. and
claiming retroactively can affect your
ongoing amount. So, it is a conversation
to have carefully, but it is real money
that is available, and most people never
ask whether they qualify for it. Picture
what that lumpsum can mean. A widow
finally sits down to claim her survivor
benefit, and it works out to about
$2,000 a month. If she qualifies for the
full 6 months of retroactive back pay,
that is a single check for around
$12,000 handed to her right at the start
on top of her regular monthly benefit
going forward. $12,000 can be the
difference between a roof repair getting
done or not, between staying current on
medical bills or falling behind. But you
have to ask for it and you have to weigh
it because for some people taking those
6 months early can lock in a slightly
lower monthly amount. So it is not
always the right move. The point is that
it is a lever, a real one, and the only
way it works against you is if you never
even learn it is there. That is the
theme of this entire video. Every one of
these tools is neutral until you know
about it. Knowledge is the only thing
standing between you and the version of
your benefit that pays the most. And
there is one more place your money
hides, and this one is on you to go
check today. Your Social Security
benefit is calculated from your highest
35 years of earnings. If even one of
those years is recorded wrong or is
missing entirely because an employer
reported it incorrectly, your benefit is
permanently smaller than it should be
for the rest of your life. This happens
more than you would ever think. So, you
need to log in to your My Social
Security account at the website, pull up
your earnings record, and check it
yearbyear against your own memory and
your old tax records. If you find a year
that is wrong or blank, you can correct
it. And correcting it can raise your
check permanently. Do not assume the
record is right just because it is the
government's record. The same agency
that underpaid 11,000 widows keeps that
record, too. Here is how this quietly
robs people. Imagine you had a good
earning year, one of your best, but the
company you worked for that year
reported your wages under a wrong number
or went out of business and never filed
the paperwork correctly. That year shows
up on your record as a fraction of what
you actually made or as a blank because
your benefit is built from your highest
35 years. That one damaged year gets
baked into the formula and drags your
monthly check down a little forever. It
might be $20 a month. It might be 80. On
its own, it sounds small, but multiply
even $50 a month across a 20 or 25 year
retirement, and you are talking about
$15,000 or more that should have been
yours, lost because of a typo nobody
ever caught. The fix cost you nothing
but an afternoon. You pull your earning
statement, you find the bad year, and
you bring your old tax return or your
old payubs to Social Security to prove
what you really earned using their
correction form. They fix the record,
and your check goes up. This is the
least exciting item on the whole list.
And it may be the one that quietly earns
you the most because it corrects a
mistake that would otherwise follow you
every month for the rest of your life.
And I want you to notice something about
who ends up with all of this money and
who does not because it tells you
everything about how the system really
works. The wealthy almost never miss
these benefits. They have financial
advisers and attorneys whose entire job
is to sit down with the social security
rule book and run every combination, the
survivor switch, the spousal claim, the
divorced spouse benefit, the retroactive
lumpsum until they have squeezed out the
largest possible check. They treat it
like the serious money that it is. But
the ordinary retiree, the widow on a
fixed income, the divorced woman who
thinks she is on her own, the spouse who
assumes they earn too little to matter,
they get none of that guidance. They get
a busy office, a short appointment, and
whatever benefit they happen to know to
ask for. So the exact same rules that
quietly pay the wealthy every dollar
they are owed end up shortchanging the
people who need the money the most. Not
because the law treats them differently,
but because no one ever handed them the
playbook. Therefore, consider this video
your playbook. Everything an expensive
adviser would check, you can now walk in
and ask for yourself by name for free.
The rules do not care how much you paid
to learn them. They pay out exactly the
same. So, now let me close the loop I
open at the very beginning and tie this
all together because I promised you the
one move at the center of that $131
million failure. That move is the dy
entitled switch. It is the right of a
widow or widowerower who qualifies for
two benefits to take them in the
smartest order, one first and the other
later, instead of being quietly
defaulted into just one. Social
Security's own inspector general said
the agency failed to explain that choice
to 82% of the widows they examined and
issued a brand new report just this
year, again telling the agency it still
needs to do a better job making sure
widows and widowers are paid correctly
and told their options just this year.
which tells you the problem is not fixed
and the responsibility to ask is still
sitting squarely on your shoulders.
Nobody is going to knock on your door
and hand you this money. You have to go
get it. Therefore, let me give you the
exact steps in order so you can act on
this. Step one, make a list of every
social security record you might be
entitled to claim on. Your own, a
current spouse, a late spouse, and any
expouse you were married to for at least
10 years. Every one of those is a
possible door. Step two, before you file
for anything or if you are already
collecting, call Social Security at 1
and ask this exact question. Am I
entitled to more than one benefit? And
if so, what claiming order pays me the
most over my lifetime? Make them run it.
Do not accept a one-word answer. Step
three, if you are a widow or widowerower
already collecting, specifically ask
whether you are duly entitled and
whether switching benefits later would
pay you more because that is the exact
thing the agency admits it fails to tell
people. Step four, log into your my
social security account at the website
and check your earnings record for any
wrong or missing years and ask about up
to 6 months of retroactive back pay when
you claim. Step five. If any of this
feels overwhelming, bring an adult child
or a trusted friend to the appointment
with you because two sets of ears catch
what one set misses. And this is too
much money to leave to a rushed
conversation. And one more thing, if you
asked about any of this in the past and
were told no, ask again anyway with
these specific words because the answer
you got may have depended entirely on
who happened to be sitting across the
desk that day. Because here is the
assumption I want to leave you with. the
one that costs people the most.
Almost everyone believes that Social
Security, being the government,
automatically calculates and pays them
the largest benefit they are legally
owed, that it looks out for you. And the
AY's own watchdog has now proven in
writing twice that this is not how it
works. They pay what you applied for.
They often do not volunteer the bigger
option sitting right next to it. The
people who get every dollar they are
owed are not the people who trusted the
system to be generous. They are the
people who walked in knowing exactly
what to ask for and refused to leave
until they got an answer. So do this
today. Call 1 8007721213
or log in at the Social Security website
and ask them the one question the
government hoped you would never think
to ask. What else am I owed?

title: When Your Husband Dies, the IRS Quietly Raises Your Taxes — The Widow's Penalty

segments.text: The year after her husband died, a woman
I will tell you about sat down to do her
taxes, expecting a smaller bill because
her income had clearly gone down. And
instead, she discovered she owed the
government thousands of dollars more
than the year before on less money
coming in, simply because she was now
alone.
Her income had fallen by roughly a
quarter when her husband passed, and his
smaller Social Security check stopped.
And yet her federal tax bill went up by
more than $4,000.
And on top of that, her Medicare premium
quietly climbed by a few hundred dollars
a month.
Nobody had warned her. There was no
letter, no phone call, no notice from
anyone. The tax code had simply reached
into the worst year of her life and
decided that because she was a widow,
she should pay more.
This has a name among the people who
plan for it. They call it the widow's
penalty, and almost no ordinary family
has ever heard of it until it lands on
them. And here is the part I need you to
hold on to because it is the difference
between paying that penalty for the rest
of your life and sidestepping most of
it. There is a window that opens the
moment a spouse dies, a window measured
in months and a couple of short years.
And inside that window, there are two or
three specific moves that can save a
surviving spouse tens of thousands of
dollars over the years that follow. The
cruelest thing about it is that the
window is silent. It opens, it ticks,
and it closes, and nobody from the
government tells you it was ever there.
Stay with me all the way through,
because I am going to show you exactly
what the widow's penalty is, where it
hits the hardest, and the moves that
beat it. And at the very end, I am going
to show you the single assumption that
makes good people walk straight into it,
the belief that quietly does the most
damage of all. But first you have to
understand why this even happens,
because once you see the machinery,
every number I give you later will make
sense.
For your entire married life, the two of
you filed your taxes together as what
the government calls married filing
jointly. And that status is built for
two people. It gives you a wide of tax
brackets and a large standard deduction,
both roughly double what a single person
gets, because the system assumes that
income is supporting two lives.
When one spouse dies, the law lets the
survivor file jointly one final time for
the year of the death itself as a last
courtesy.
But, after that year is over, unless
that survivor is still raising a
dependent child, which almost no older
widow is, the government moves them onto
the single tax status. And single in the
eyes of the tax code is treated almost
exactly like a young person at the start
of their working life, even though this
is an 80-year-old woman living on the
same retirement income she and her
husband built together. So, let me show
you the first place it bites, because it
is the engine of the whole problem. The
single tax brackets are about half as
wide as the married brackets. What that
means in plain language is that the
exact same amount of income gets pushed
up into higher tax rates the moment you
go from joint to single. Picture a
retired couple with a comfortable but
ordinary retirement income. As a married
couple, a big slice of that income sat
in the lower brackets, taxed gently. The
husband dies, a year passes, and now
that very same kind of income, even a
little less of it, is being squeezed
through brackets half the size. So, more
of it is taxed at 12% instead of 10, and
more again at 22% instead of 12.
Not $1 of her spending changed. Her
grocery bill did not get cheaper because
she was grieving. But, the rate the
government charges her on the money she
lives on went up, purely because of a
checkbox on a form. Let me put real
numbers on that so it stops being
abstract, because the example is the
thing that makes people finally
understand. Picture a couple who
together brought in about $90,000 a year
in retirement, between their two Social
Security checks, a pension, and the
required withdrawals from their savings.
As a married couple, after their large
joint deduction, only a modest slice of
that was taxable, and most of it was
taxed in the lowest bracket, so their
federal tax was relatively gentle. Now,
the husband dies. His smaller Social
Security check, say around $1,800 a
month, stops. So, her income falls to
around $70,000 a year, which is
noticeably less money to live on. But,
she is now single. Her deduction is cut
roughly in half, so far more of that
70,000 is taxable than before, and the
bracket she is running it through are
half as wide. So, it climbs faster into
the higher rates. When the dust settles,
this woman, living on $20,000 a year
less than the couple did, can easily owe
four or five thousand dollars more in
federal income tax than the two of them
paid together. Less money coming in the
door, and a bigger check going out to
the government. That is the widow's
penalty in a single, concrete,
infuriating example. And just when that
would be painful enough on its own, the
second blow lands, because the standard
deduction collapses, too. The standard
deduction is the chunk of income the
government lets you earn completely
tax-free before any tax is calculated at
all.
For a married couple over the age of 65,
that protected amount is large,
somewhere in the range of 34 or 35,000
dollars, once you add the extra
deduction that older people receive. The
year after her husband dies, that
protected amount is cut roughly in half,
down near 17 or 18,000 dollars for her
as a single senior. So, tens of
thousands of dollars that used to be
shielded from tax entirely are now
exposed and taxable. Therefore, she gets
hit twice at the same time, with
narrower brackets pushing her income
into higher rates, and a smaller
deduction dragging more of that income
into the taxable pile in the first
place. Two cuts, one grieving person, in
the same brutal year. Now, I want to
show you a third hit that catches people
completely off guard, because it does
not come through the tax return at all.
It comes through Medicare. There is a
surcharge built into Medicare, an extra
amount that higher income retirees pay
on top of their normal premiums, and the
income line where that surcharge kicks
in is, once again, about twice as high
for a married couple as it is for a
single person. So, a couple could be
earning right up near that line for
years and never trigger a single dollar
of surcharge. The husband dies, the
survivor moves to single, and suddenly
that same household income is sitting
above the single line, and her Medicare
premiums jump, sometimes by a few
hundred dollars every single month,
which is a few thousand dollars a year
taken quietly out of the Social Security
check she has left. She did nothing
wrong. Her income did not rise. But, the
line she is measured against was cut in
half, and now she is on the wrong side
of it. There is even a quieter version
of this buried inside Social Security
itself, and it surprises almost everyone
who runs into it. The government decides
how much of your Social Security benefit
is taxable using an income calculation,
and the income thresholds inside that
calculation, just like all the others,
are far kinder to a married couple than
to a single person. So, when a widow
moves to single status, a larger portion
of the very Social Security check she
depends on can become taxable, even
though the check itself never grew by a
single dollar. Stack it all up, and she
is being taxed at a higher rate on her
income, taxed on a bigger slice of her
own benefit, and charged a higher
Medicare premium, all at the same time,
all because the number of names on the
tax return dropped from two down to one.
But, none of this ever shows up as a
headline or arrives in a notice. It
hides inside the arithmetic, and the
only people who see it coming are the
ones who go looking, or who have someone
in their corner who already knows it is
there.
And this is the moment the whole thing
turns truly cruel. So, lean in, because
here is the part that makes the widow's
penalty so unfair that once you see it,
you cannot unsee it.
When one spouse dies, the household's
income does not fall by half. It often
barely falls at all.
The survivor keeps the larger of the two
Social Security checks because the rule
is that the bigger benefit continues and
only the smaller one stops. So, the
household might lose only the lesser
check. She usually keeps the pension or
a survivor's portion of it. She keeps
every dollar of the investment income,
the dividends, and the required
withdrawals from the retirement
accounts.
So, her income might drop by only a
quarter while her tax brackets, her
deduction, and her Medicare line all get
cut nearly in half.
Therefore, the math is upside down.
The income falls a little, the tax
protections fall a lot, and the result
is a person living on less money while
handing a bigger share of it to the
government than she ever did when her
husband was alive. So, let me take you
to the largest single trap of all, the
one with the silent clock because this
is the open loop I promised you, and it
is about the house. Most of these
couples own a home that has grown
enormously in value over decades, and
the tax code lets you avoid tax on that
growth when you sell up to a limit. For
a married couple, that tax-free limit on
the gain is $500,000.
For a single person, it is cut in half
Now, here is the silent window. After a
spouse dies, the survivor is allowed to
keep the full $500 exclusion, the
married sized one, but only if she sells
the home within 2 years of the death. 2
years, and the clock starts the day he
passes, and nobody mails her a reminder.
If she sells inside that window, up to
$500,000 of the home's growth can be
tax-free. If she waits until 2 years and
1 day, her limit drops to $250,000,
and as much as a quarter million dollars
of that gain can suddenly become
taxable, costing her tens of thousands
of dollars she would have kept if anyone
had simply told her the clock was
running. And there is a companion rule
on that same house that you have to
understand because it can turn a
frightening tax bill into almost
nothing, but only if she acts in time.
When a spouse dies, the tax value of the
home, what the government counts as your
starting cost when it measures the gain,
gets reset upward to the home's value on
the day of death. In most of the
country, half of the home resets that
way, the half that belonged to the
spouse who passed. And in a handful of
states that treat marital property
differently, the entire home resets to
its date of death value. What that reset
does is erase much of the growth that
piled up over all those decades, so that
if the survivor sells reasonably soon,
there may be very little taxable gain
left at all. But, here is where it ties
right back to that silent clock. The
reset helps the most when it is paired
with the full $500,000 exclusion, and
that larger exclusion only survives for
2 years. A widow who sells inside the
window gets both the reset and the
bigger exclusion stacked together, and
very often pays no tax on the sale
whatsoever. A widow who waits past the
window keeps the reset, but loses half
the exclusion, and can owe tax she never
needed to owe. Therefore, the house is
not just an asset she lives in, it is a
ticking decision. And that 2-year clock
is the most expensive deadline most
widows have never heard of. So, now that
you see the damage, let me show you how
the people who plan for this actually
beat it, because there are real moves,
and the most powerful one happens in a
window that is open right now for
anybody whose spouse has recently
passed, or who is thinking ahead as a
couple. It is this: In the year a spouse
dies, the survivor can still file
jointly one final time at those wide
married brackets and that big married
deduction. That final joint year is a
golden opportunity to move money out of
a regular retirement account and into a
Roth account, what is called a
conversion, and to pay the tax on it at
the low married rate while it is still
available. Every dollar moved into the
Roth that year grows tax-free for the
rest of her life, and is never taxed
again on the way out. A family that does
a careful conversion in that final joint
year, and in any low income years that
follow, can pull tens of thousands of
dollars out of the higher single rates
forever. The wealthy do this on purpose.
Most widows never hear the word. Let me
make that conversion idea concrete
because it is the single most powerful
move on this entire list.
Say a couple has a few hundred thousand
dollars sitting in a traditional
retirement account, the kind where every
dollar is taxed on the way out. In the
year the husband dies, the wife can
still file at the wide married brackets
one final time, which means there is
room to move a meaningful chunk of that
money, perhaps 30 or 40 thousand
dollars, into a Roth account and pay the
tax on it at the lower married rate
while it is still available.
From that day forward, those dollars
grow without tax and they come out
without tax and they never again push
her into a higher single bracket or over
the Medicare line. If she instead does
nothing, that same money stays in the
account and the government forces her to
pull it out year after year as a single
filer, taxed at the higher single rates
for the rest of her life. Therefore, the
difference between converting in that
one quiet window and simply letting the
money ride can easily be 10 or 20
thousand dollars over a long retirement
and the chance to do it at the lowest
