possible rate is open only for that
final joint year and the lower income
years that follow it. And there are more
moves that stack on top of that one. So,
let me give you the rest of the toolkit
because every one of them is legal,
ordinary and sitting in plain sight.
First, that house. If selling the family
home is something she would consider
anyway, doing it inside that two-year
window protects the full 500 thousand
dollar exclusion. And combined with
another quiet rule that resets the
home's tax value at the date of death,
the taxable gain can often be erased
almost entirely.
Second, there is a way to satisfy the
required withdrawals from a retirement
account by sending that money straight
to a charity instead, which keeps it
from ever counting as income. And that
single trip can hold a widow underneath
the Medicare surcharge line and save her
thousands in premiums.
Third, if she is one of the rare older
people still raising a child or
grandchild, she may qualify to keep the
married brackets for two extra years.
And fourth, she should confirm with
Social Security that her surviving
benefit was correctly switched to the
higher of the two checks because errors
there are common. Therefore, the penalty
is real, but it is not unbeatable. And
almost every weapon against it depends
on acting early inside that quiet window
before the door swings shut. And there
is one more piece that almost nobody
thinks to check, which is the Social
Security itself. When a spouse dies, the
survivor does not get to keep both
checks. She keeps the larger of the two
and the smaller one ends. For a widow
whose own work record produced the
smaller benefit, this means she should
step up to her late husband's higher
amount, but only if the agency actually
makes that switch correctly and only if
she files for the survivor benefit,
which is not always automatic. Mistakes
here are common, and a widow can spend
years quietly collecting less than she
is owed simply because the change was
never properly made. On top of that, the
timing of the death inside the calendar
year shapes that final joint tax return.
Because no matter what month a spouse
passes, even in December, the survivor
is still allowed to file jointly for
that entire year. Therefore, two of the
most valuable things a grieving spouse
can do in those first hard months are
painfully simple.
Confirm with Social Security that the
surviving benefit is correct and is
truly the higher of the two. And treat
that final joint tax year as the rare
and closing opportunity that it is
before it disappears for good. Let me
stop for a moment and make sure you see
the pattern underneath all of this
because it tells you everything about
who this system is built for. The tax
code is generous to a married couple and
harsh to the survivor. And the people
who have advisors simply plan around it,
converting money in the right year,
timing the sale of the house, managing
their income to stay under the lines.
The family that has never heard the
phrase widow's penalty does none of it
and walks straight into every trap at
the worst possible time while grieving,
while overwhelmed, while assuming that
less income must surely mean less tax.
The rules are the same for everyone, but
the knowledge is not and that gap is the
whole game. The widow's penalty is not a
punishment for being poor or for being
rich. It is a punishment for not knowing
and not knowing is the one thing you can
fix today. And do not make the mistake
of thinking this is only a wealthy
person's problem because the truth is
the opposite. The widow's penalty
actually bites the ordinary middle-class
family the hardest. The couple with a
paid-off house that quietly grew to four
a pension, and a few hundred thousand
dollars in a retirement account. Because
that is exactly the family sitting right
near all of these invisible lines at
once. The bracket lines, the deduction
line, the Medicare line, and the home
gain line.
A truly wealthy family has advisors
watching every one of those thresholds
for them.
A family with very little income never
crosses them in the first place.
But the great middle, the people who did
everything right, saved steadily, paid
off the home, and built an ordinary
comfortable retirement are the very ones
who get pushed across those lines by the
simple fact of becoming single and who
then pay for it quietly every single
year afterward. Therefore, this is not
some exotic problem for a tiny few. It
is a tax that falls on the most ordinary
American retirement there is and it
falls on the survivor at the exact
moment she is least able to fight back.
Let me leave you with the picture that
all of this land. Two widows who lived
on the same street, both of whom lost
their husbands within a year of each
other, both living on almost identical
retirement incomes. The first woman had
a daughter who had heard about all of
this and together, in the year her
father died, they sat down and did the
work. They moved a portion of the
retirement savings into a Roth account
while the joint rates were still
available. They sold the family home 18
months later while the full $500,000
exclusion still applied, and they
arranged the yearly withdrawals to stay
just under the Medicare surcharge line.
Over the years that followed, that
planning saved her well over $30,000.
The second woman, on the same income,
did nothing because no one told her
there was anything to do. She paid the
higher single rates every year. She sold
her home 3 years after her husband died
and lost half of her exclusion, and her
Medicare premium climbed and stayed
there. Same street, same income, same
loss. The only difference between them
was that one family knew the window was
open, and the other never knew the
window existed at all. And that brings
me to the assumption I promised you at
the very start. The single most
dangerous belief in this whole
situation, the one that quietly does the
most harm,
it is the belief that less income
automatically means less tax. That
because money stopped coming in when
your spouse died, the government must be
taking a smaller share.
It is the most natural assumption in the
world, and it is exactly backwards.
The widow's penalty exists precisely
because the income falls a little, while
the tax protections fall a lot. So, the
rate climbs even as the dollars shrink.
A surviving spouse who assumes the tax
bill will simply go down is the
surviving spouse who never looks, never
plans, never converts a dollar or checks
a deadline, and who then opens a tax
bill a year later that is larger than
she ever imagined,
on less money than she has ever had.
The assumption that you are paying less
is the very thing that guarantees you
pay more. So, let me add up what is
actually at stake here, because the
total is the part that should really
land. Between the higher single tax
brackets, the standard deduction cut
nearly in half, the lost half of the
home sale exclusion, and the higher
Medicare premiums, a typical surviving
spouse can end up paying somewhere
between four and $10,000 more every
single year for the rest of her life on
the same retirement income she and her
husband built together. Over a widowhood
that can last 10, 15, even 20 years,
that is not a one-time loss. It is a
hole in the bottom of the boat that
drains tens of thousands of dollars that
should have stayed with her, paid for
her care, and gone to her children.
Therefore, the question was never
whether the widow's penalty is real. It
is. The only question is whether you
find out about the window while it is
still open or after it is already
closed. And if you are watching this and
your spouse died years ago, so that the
final joint year and the two-year window
are already behind you, please do not
feel that the door is shut because it is
not. The biggest trap of all, the higher
tax rate on every dollar you pull from a
retirement account, is still sitting in
front of you for every year you have
left, which means converting money into
a Roth account during your lower income
years still helps you. Sending your
required withdrawals straight to a
charity to stay under the Medicare line
still helps you. And carefully choosing
which year you realize income still
helps you. The widow's penalty is not a
single event that happens once and is
finished. It is a yearly leak, and a
leak can be slowed at almost any point
you decide to pick up the wrench.
Therefore, whether your loss was last
month or 10 years ago, the move is the
same. Stop assuming your tax bill is
already as low as it can possibly be and
go find out what it could actually be
instead. So, here is exactly what to do,
and none of it requires being wealthy or
hiring an army of advisers. Step one, if
you are part of a couple, understand
right now, while you both are here, that
the survivor will be pushed onto single
tax rates and plan for it together
because the best moves are made before
anyone passes and in the year of the
death.
Step two, if your spouse has recently
died, mark the two-year clock on the
calendar today because the full home
sale exclusion and the final joint tax
year are both deadlines you cannot get
back. Step three, look hard at moving
money into a Roth account during any
year you can still use the joint rates,
so that future withdrawals come out
tax-free instead of at the higher single
rate.
Step four, if required withdrawals are
pushing you near the Medicare surcharge
line, ask about sending that money
directly to a charity to keep it off
your income. And step five, before you
file that first return alone, read the
plain language guide the tax agency
publishes for survivors, which is
publication 559, available for free at
irs.gov,
and sit down with a qualified tax
professional for one honest
conversation, because that single
meeting can pay for itself many times
over. The number for the tax agency is 1

title: Your Social Security Check STOPS in 2026 Unless You Do This First (Most Don't Know)

segments.text: Last year, on the 30th of September, a
federal order quietly took effect that
ended something millions of older
Americans have relied on for their
entire lives, the paper Social Security
check. And almost nobody was told what
it really means for them. Around that
same time, the agency's own internal
watchdog finished an investigation that
found criminals were already exploiting
the changeover, quietly rerouting other
people's Social Security payments into
accounts the rightful owner had never
heard of. And in a single sample, those
thieves had diverted around 2.2 million
dollars in benefits, most of which was
never recovered. So, the money that
lands in your account every month, the
income you actually live on, is now
governed by a brand new set of rules
about how it gets paid, who is allowed
to change where it goes, and what
happens to you if you do nothing. And if
you are like most seniors in this
country, not one person has explained a
single word of it to you. And here is
the part that should make you sit up in
your chair. There is one step, one
account you can set up in about 15
minutes, that does two powerful things
at the very same time. It guarantees
your check keeps arriving without
interruption under these new rules, and
it slams the door shut on the exact scam
those criminals are using to steal
payments out from under people. Almost
no senior has done it. And on the other
side of that same coin, there is one
phone call, one perfectly ordinary
mistake that people make every single
day that can hand a complete stranger
the keys to your monthly benefit. Stay
with me all the way through, because I
am going to show you both, the one step
that protects you, and the one mistake
that quietly exposes you. And at the
very end, I am going to show you the
single assumption that is leaving good
people wide open right now, the one
belief that keeps this whole thing
dangerous. But first, you have to
understand what actually changed and
why. Because once you see it, every step
I give you later will make complete
sense.
For decades, the federal government
mailed out paper checks to anyone who
wanted one. And a great many seniors
trusted that paper check far more than
they trusted a bank because they could
hold it, walk it to the teller, and know
it was real.
That world is over.
A federal order signed at the start of
last year with a name about modernizing
the way the government pays people
directed the Treasury to stop printing
and mailing paper checks for nearly all
federal payments including Social
Security and it set the deadline at the
end of this past September.
The reason the government gives is
blunt. By its own numbers, a paper check
is 16 times more likely to be lost,
stolen, altered, or returned than a
payment sent electronically. Every
stolen check is somebody's grocery money
or rent and the Treasury decided the
paper check itself had become the weak
link. Now, you might be thinking that
this does not apply to you because you
already use direct deposit and for most
people that is true, but do not tune out
yet because the change runs much deeper
than just the people still getting
paper. By the time the deadline arrived,
fewer than one out of every 100
beneficiaries was still receiving a
paper check, which sounds tiny until you
remember that Social Security pays
roughly 72 million people more than 1.6
trillion dollars every year.
Fewer than 1% of 72 million is still
around half a million human beings, most
of them very old, many with no bank
account, suddenly told that the only
form of payment they ever trusted is
being shut off. Therefore, if you or
your mother or your father or a neighbor
you check on is still getting a paper
Social Security check in the mail, that
payment is living on borrowed time and
the worst thing you can do is wait until
it simply does not show up one month.
So, let me tell you exactly what the new
rules give you because there are only
two ways to be paid now and you get to
choose between them. The first way is
ordinary direct deposit where the money
goes straight into a checking or savings
account at a bank or a credit union, the
same way most paychecks have worked for
years. The second way exists
specifically for people who do not have
a bank account and do not want one and
it is called the Direct Express debit
card. It is a prepaid card issued
through the Treasury. There is no credit
check, there is no bank required, and
your social security simply loads onto
the card each month. So, you can spend
it, withdraw cash, or pay bills. Nobody
is being forced to open a bank account
they are uncomfortable with, but
somebody does have to make the choice.
And if the person receiving paper checks
makes no choice at all, they risk a gap
in the one income they cannot afford to
lose. Let me say a little more about
that Direct Express card, because it is
the option the government points to for
anyone without a bank, and a great many
seniors have never heard of it. It is a
prepaid debit card backed by the
Treasury. Your benefit loads onto it
automatically each month. You can use it
anywhere debit cards are accepted,
withdraw cash, and check your balance
anytime. And you do not need a bank
account, a minimum balance, or good
credit to qualify. You sign up through
the Social Security office or the
Treasury program for going direct, and
the number for that card is 1-800-333-
There is also a narrow exception for
people who genuinely cannot go
electronic, who can request a waiver to
keep a paper check. But, it is small,
and you have to ask for it. Therefore,
nobody is truly stranded by this change,
but everyone has to take an action. Pick
direct deposit, pick the card, or
request that hardship exception.
And doing nothing is the one option that
can cost you your payment. Now, here is
where it stops being a simple story
about switching to direct deposit.
Because the much bigger danger is not
whether you switch, it is how you
switch. And this is the part that
watchdog investigation exposed.
Think about it for a second. If the
government is moving everyone onto
electronic payments, then the single
most valuable thing in your whole
financial life is now one small piece of
information.
The bank account number where your
Social Security lands.
Anybody who can change that number can
quietly redirect your entire monthly
check into their own account, and you
might not even notice until the money
stops arriving.
That is no longer a hypothetical fear.
That is exactly what was already
happening on a large scale.
And the agency's own inspector general
put the numbers in writing. Here is what
they found, and it should make every
family in America pay attention.
The inspector general looked at a sample
of beneficiaries whose direct deposit
had been changed by a telephone call,
and found that around 38% of them,
nearly four in every 10, had their
payments misdirected, sent somewhere the
real person never authorized.
In that one review, criminals had
rerouted roughly 2.2 million dollars in
Social Security benefits, and about 2
million of it had still not been
recovered months later.
And when the investigators dug deeper
into a single month of phone calls, they
estimated that the agency's own staff
had failed to properly verify the
identity of more than 25,000 callers
before changing where the money went.
25,000 chances in 1 month for a thief on
the phone to point somebody else's check
at their own account. Therefore, the
government did not just change how you
get paid, it was forced to change who is
even allowed to move your money, and
that change is the heart of everything
you need to do this week. And you should
understand just how simple that theft
really was, because it tells you exactly
what you need to protect. A criminal did
not have to break into a bank vault or
hack a government computer. In a great
many cases, all they needed was a name,
a date of birth, and a Social Security
number. The very information that has
been stolen and resold in data breaches
over and over for years. And with those
few details, they could reach the
agency, pose as the real beneficiary,
and ask to send the monthly payment to a
different account. The rightful owner,
often elderly and simply trusting that
the check would appear like it always
had, had no idea anything was wrong
until the deposit failed to show up. And
it can be even more dangerous for the
millions of seniors whose benefits are
handled by someone else.
A person the agency calls a
representative payee because there are
more hands near that money and more
seams for a bad actor to slip through.
But, notice that every one of those
attacks relies on the very same
weakness, an account that the rightful
owner had never locked down. Therefore,
the entire defense against all of it
comes down to one thing, claiming and
securing your own record before a
stranger holding your stolen details can
get there first. And this is the moment
I really need you to lean in because
this next part is the new rule almost
nobody has heard about and it is the
difference between a check that is
protected and a check that is sitting
wide open. Faced with all that fraud,
the Social Security Administration
tightened the rules on proving who you
are. As of the spring of last year, you
can no longer simply call on the phone,
give a few personal details that a
scammer could easily have bought or
stolen, and change your direct deposit.
The agency eliminated phone identity
verification as a way to claim
retirement benefits or move your
payment. Instead, to change where your
money goes, you now have to prove your
identity in one of two secure ways,
either online through your own verified
account on the Social Security website
or in person at a Social Security
office. They also sped the process up,
so a legitimate change you make the
right way now takes about one business
day instead of being held for a month
like before. The fraud forced their hand
and the result is a system that is
safer, but only for the people who
understand how to use it. There is still
a way to make a change by phone, but
they built a lock onto it and you need
to know how that lock works. Starting in
the spring of last year, if you do want
to handle a direct deposit change over
the telephone, you first have to go to
the Social Security website and request
a one-time code, a short personal
identification number, and then read
that code to the representative on the
call. Without that code, the change does
not happen. On top of that, the agency
now runs every direct deposit request
through a Treasury verification service
that instantly checks whether the bank
account really belongs to you before any
money is pointed at it. So, the
protections are real and they are in
place. But, and this is the whole point,
none of those protections do you any
good if a thief gets to your account
before you do, or if you hand your
information to the wrong person on a
phone call you did not start. So, let me
show you the one step that ties all of
this protection together, the step I
promised you at the very beginning.
It is this.
Go and create your own personal account
on the Social Security website. The
account they call My Social Security.
And once it is yours, it is locked to
your verified identity and nobody can
quietly set one up in your name or
reroute your payment without getting
through that verified login.
This single account is where you choose
direct deposit or the Direct Express
card, where you check that your money is
going to the right place, where you can
see your benefit information, and where,
if you ever feel threatened, you can
even block all electronic and automated
access to your record, so that no one,
not even over the internet, can change a
thing without you unblocking it first.
It is free, it takes about 15 minutes,
and the cruel irony is that the seniors
who most need that protection are the
least likely to have set it up, which
leaves the door open for a criminal to
claim that account before they ever do.
Let me stop for 1 second and make sure
you see the pattern underneath all of
this, because it is the same truth that
runs through everything about Social
Security. The government changed the
rules to protect you, but it built those
protections so that they only switch on
when you take the action yourself. The
safer identity rules, the verified
account, the one-time phone code, the
account blocking, the bank verification
service, every one of them is sitting
there waiting, and not one of them
protects a person who never sets up the
account and never makes the choice. The
thief is counting on exactly that, on
the millions of seniors who hear about a
change like this, feel a little uneasy,
and then do nothing at all. Therefore,
the most powerful move you can make is
to stop being the person who waits and
become the person who has already
claimed and locked their own account
before anyone else can. Let me show you
two settings inside that account that
almost nobody ever turns on because
together they are the closest thing to a
deadbolt you will find. The first is the
ability to block all electronic and
automated access to your social security
record. When you switch that block on,
no one can change your direct deposit or
pull up your information through any
automated channel. Not over the
internet, not through the phone system,
not even you until you personally call
the agency and lift it. For a senior who
rarely needs to change anything from one
year to the next, that is an enormously
powerful way to freeze the account shut
so that a thief with your stolen details
simply runs into a locked door. The
second setting is to make sure the
contact information inside your account
is current and correct so the real
agency can always reach the real you.
But, understand clearly that the agency
will reach you through that secure
account and through the mail, never
through a surprise phone call demanding
your bank details on the spot.
Therefore, turning on that electronic
block and keeping your true contact
information current is what turns your
account from an open door into a locked
one. And the whole thing costs you
nothing but a few minutes of attention.
Now, I want to widen this out because
the direct deposit scam is only the most
expensive version of a much larger
problem.
And the same rule change has given
criminals a perfect script to scare you.
Whenever there is a big confusing
government change, the phone calls and
the text messages begin and they always
sound official.
Someone calls claiming to be from Social
Security, says that because of the new
payment rules your benefits are about to
be suspended and that to keep your check
coming you need to confirm your bank
account number or your Social Security
number or pay a small fee right now with
a gift card.
Every piece of that is a lie.
The real agency will not call you out of
the blue and threaten to cut off your
check. It will not demand that you pay
anything with a gift card or a wire
transfer, and it will not rush you into
reading off your bank details on a call
you did not place. But, the fear is
effective because the underlying change
is real, and a frightened person who
just heard that paper checks are ending
is exactly the person most likely to
believe that their payment is in danger
and hand over the very information the
thief needs. You have probably already
heard a version of this scam, even if
you did not know it had a name. The most
common one is a recorded phone call
warning that your Social Security number
has been suspended because of suspicious
activity, and that you must press a
number or call back right away, or you
will be arrested or lose your benefits.
Your Social Security number is never
suspended. That is simply not a thing
that can happen, and the real agency
does not threaten anyone with arrest.
Another version is a text message or an
email carrying an official-looking seal
telling you to click a link and confirm
your account because of the new payment
rules, where the link leads to a fake
page built only to harvest your login
and your banking details. And the newest
version leans directly on this very
change. A caller who offers to kindly
help you switch off paper checks and set
up direct deposit, and who only needs
your bank account number to get it
started. But, the real agency will never
call you out of the blue to set that up,
and it will never ask you to pay any
kind of fee with a gift card, a wire
transfer, or a prepaid card to keep your
benefits flowing. Therefore, the safest
habit you can build is to treat any
unexpected message about your Social
Security payment as a scam until you
have personally proven otherwise by
contacting the agency yourself. So, let
me add up what is actually at stake here
because the total is the part that
should really land. Your Social Security
check is very likely the largest and
most reliable source of income you have,
often somewhere around $2,000 a month
for a retired worker. A criminal who
reroutes that payment even once can
drain a month of it before anyone
notices, and the The
showed that most of the stolen money was
never given back. A senior who never
sets up their account leaves that entire
income stream guarded by nothing but an
outdated phone system that thieves had
already learned to beat.
Therefore, the question was never really
about paper checks at all. The paper
check ending is just the moment that
forces everyone to deal with the real
issue, which is whether your monthly
income is locked down under your own
verified control or left sitting out in
the open for whoever reaches it first.
Let me leave you with the picture that
makes all of this click. Two retired men
who live on the same street, both
widowers, both living almost entirely on
their social security. The first one
heard that the rules were changing, sat
down one afternoon with his daughter,
and together they set up his account on
the social security website, confirmed
his direct deposit was going to the
right bank, and turned on the extra
protection so that no change could be
made without his verified login. It took
them less than half an hour, and he
never thought about it again. The second
man heard the same news, felt that
familiar dread about anything to do with
computers and the government, and
decided he would deal with it later. A
few weeks afterward, he got a friendly
phone call from a man who said he was
with social security helping seniors
update their payment under the new
rules, and all he needed to confirm the
account was a few details. The second
man gave them. The next month, his check
did not arrive because it had been
quietly redirected [snorts] to a
stranger, and by the time he untangled
it, he had lost a payment he was never
fully repaid. Same street, same income,
same news. The only difference was that
one of them spent 30 minutes claiming
what was his, and the other one waited
for a letter and got a phone call
instead. And that brings me to the
assumption I promised you at the start.
The single most dangerous belief in this
whole situation,
the one that leaves good people exposed,
it is the belief that someone, the
government, the bank, a grown child,
somebody, is watching over your social
security and will catch it if something
goes wrong.
They are not.
The agency processes the change that
comes in with the right code or the
right login, and it cannot tell the
difference between you and a thief who
has your details.
That is the entire reason the fraud
worked in the first place.
The bank sees a deposit instruction and
follows it.
Nobody is sitting in an office somewhere
personally guarding your individual
check.
The only person who can truly protect
that money is you or someone in your
family acting with you.
And the protection only exists once you
have set it up. A senior who assumes
they are being watched over is precisely
precisely the senior a criminal is
hoping to find because that person has
left every door unlocked while believing
somebody else locked. So, here is
exactly what to do this week, and not
one of these steps cost you a single
dollar. Step one, and this is the most
important thing you will do. Go to the
Social Security website, which is
ssa.gov,
and create your personal my Social
Security account if you do not already
have one. Proving your identity through
their secure system so that the account
is locked to you and no one else can
claim it. Step two, once you are inside
that account, check that your payment
method is correct. And if you are still
receiving a paper check, choose either
direct deposit into your bank or credit
union or the Direct Express debit card
if you do not want a bank account. Step
three,
if you ever need to change your direct
deposit by phone, first go to
ssa.gov/pin
to get your one-time code before you
call, and never give your banking
information to anyone who calls you.
Step four, if you are worried about
fraud, log into your account and turn on
the block that stops all electronic and
automated access to your record so that
nothing can be changed without you
unblocking it yourself.
And step five, if you believe you have
been targeted or a payment has been
redirected, report it immediately to the
Social Security Inspector General at
or online at oig.ssa.gov.
The main Social Security number for
everything else is 1-800-772-1213.
And for the Direct Express card, it is
And let me give you one rule that will
keep you safe through every version of
this scam, no matter how official it
sounds. You contact them, they do not
contact you. If you ever need to do
anything with your Social Security, you
start the call or you start on the
website yourself, using the real numbers
and the real address.
If someone calls you or texts you or
emails you claiming there is a problem
with your payment under the new rules,
you hang up and you call the real number
yourself to check. A genuine issue will
still be there when you call back
through the front door. A scam will
evaporate the moment you refuse to stay
on their call. That one habit, that you
always start the contact and never trust
the contact that comes to you, will
defeat almost every fraud aimed at
seniors, because the entire scam depends
on catching you off guard on a call you
did not expect. And if you are watching
this for a parent rather than for
yourself, this may be one of the most
important afternoons you ever spend with
them. A great many older people will
never set up an online account on their
own. They find it intimidating, they
worry they will break something, or they
simply trust that the paper check will
keep coming the way it always has.
That second man, the one who lost a
month of his income to a friendly voice
on the phone, is real in millions of
homes right now, because the people most
comfortable with a paper check are
exactly the people least prepared for a
world without one.
So, sit down next to your mother or your
father, open the Social Security website
together, set up the account together,
confirm the direct deposit together, and
turn on the protections together. Half
an hour of your time may be the only
thing standing between a parent and a
thief who is already dialing. You work
your entire life and you paid into this
system out of every paycheck for
decades, exactly as you were told to,
and that monthly check is not a gift, it
is your own money coming back to you.
The money you earned and were promised.
The rules for how it reaches you have
changed. The paper check is gone, and
the criminals already know it. The only
thing that decides whether your income
stays safe is whether you take the few
simple steps to lock it down before
someone else tries the door. So, do not
wait for a letter that explains all of
this because that letter is not coming.
And the phone call that does come may be
the one you should never have answered.
Do one thing tonight. Go to ssa.gov
and start your account. Every week you
wait is a week your check is sitting out
in the open.

title: Your Social Security Check Could Be WRONG Without This One Form

segments.text: There is a single form sitting on the
Social Security website right now, a
form most seniors have never heard of.
And the people who fill it out often
watch their monthly check go up for the
rest of their lives, while the people
who never knew it existed keep getting
paid less than they actually earned. It
is one page. It costs nothing to file.
And it exists for a reason that should
make every retiree in this country stop
and pay attention, because the
government calculates your entire Social
Security benefit off a record of your
life's work. And that record is allowed
to be wrong. When it is wrong, your
check is smaller. Not for 1 month, but
for every month you have left. And the
agency will not fix it for you. They
wait for you to ask on this one specific
form. And almost nobody ever does. And
here is what almost no senior
understands about Social Security. Your
monthly check is not a fixed number
handed down from on high that you simply
have to accept. It is the result of a
calculation built on numbers in a file.
And there are specific legal named forms
you can file to change that calculation
in your favor. Millions of older
Americans are getting a smaller check
than they are entitled to. Month after
month, year after year. Not because they
did anything wrong, but because no one
ever told them which form to file or
which question to ask. The money is
real. It is theirs. And it stays with
the government until they reach out and
claim it. So here is what I'm going to
do for you tonight. I'm going to give
you the one form that can permanently
raise your check. The form I just
described. And I'm going to show you
exactly who it helps and exactly how to
file it. But stay with me all the way
through, because that one form is only
the beginning. There are several more
forms and requests that can each put
more money into your check, including
one that lets you undo a decision you
were told could never be undone. And
another that quietly stops the
government from taking an extra bite out
of your payment every single month. And
at the very end, there is one
assumption. The single most expensive
belief in all of Social Security, that
keeps every dollar of this money sitting
in the government's hands instead of
yours. I will show you that assumption
before we finish, and once you see it,
you will never make it again. But first,
you have to understand why this happens
at all, because once you see it,
everything else makes sense. Ask
yourself a simple question. If the
Social Security Administration is paying
you less than you are owed, whose job is
it to catch that and fix it? You would
assume the agency does. It does not. The
system was built so that the burden is
on you, the person receiving the check,
to know what you qualify for, to spot
the errors, and to file the right
paperwork to correct them. The agency
processes what you submit. It does not
go hunting for ways to pay you more. So,
when your record has a mistake in it, or
a benefit is available to you that you
never claimed, the result is not a phone
call from a helpful clerk. The result is
silence and a smaller check for as long
as you live. Therefore, the single most
powerful thing you can do is stop
waiting to be told and start filing the
forms that put the responsibility back
on them. Let me clear away three beliefs
that keep this money out of your hands,
because you may be holding one of them
right now. Belief one, if my check were
wrong, somebody would have noticed by
now. Nobody is checking. The computer
pays what the record says, and the
record can be wrong for 30 years without
a single person looking at it. Belief
two, the amount is the amount, there is
nothing I can do about it. That is false
for a great many people, because there
are real forms that can raise it,
sometimes by hundreds of dollars a
month. Belief three, all of this is too
complicated for me. Almost every step
I'm going to give you is one form or one
phone call, and the people on the other
end are legally required to help you.
Throw all three of those out, because
every one of them is the reason good
people leave money on the table for
years. Now, let me give you that first
form. The one form is called the request
for correction of earnings record, and
on the Social Security website, it is
listed as form number 7008. To
understand why it matters so much, you
have to understand how your check is
built. Social Security takes the highest
35 years of earnings from your entire
working life, adjust them, and runs them
through a formula to set your monthly
benefit. Every one of those 35 years
matters. So, what happens when a year is
wrong? What happens when a year of good
income was reported under the wrong
number, or posted to somebody else, or
never reported at all because an
employer made a mistake, or you were
self-employed and it slipped through?
That year shows up on your record as a
low number, or as nothing. And a low
year, or an empty year, in your top 35
drags your whole average down, which
means a smaller check, permanently, for
the rest of your life. And if you are
married, a smaller survivor benefit for
your spouse after you are gone. Let me
make that concrete, because people badly
underestimate how much one bad year
costs. Imagine a man who ran a side
business for 3 years in his 40s, and
earned a solid living doing it. But
because of how it was reported, those 3
years show up on his Social Security
record as almost nothing. Three strong
earning years replaced in his top 35 by
three nearly empty ones. That can pull
his benefit down by a real amount,
quietly, every single month, and he
would never feel it happen, because the
check simply arrives a little smaller
than it should, forever.
But the moment he opens his earnings
record and sees those blank years, he
can file form 7008, bring his old tax
returns or pay stubs as proof, and have
it corrected, which raises the benefit
going forward. Therefore, checking that
record and filing that one form is not
busy work. It is protecting the exact
number that every future payment is
built on, and it can mean hundreds of
dollars more a year for the rest of your
life. And here is the part that should
bother you most.
Most people have never once looked at
their earnings record.
They have no idea whether it is right,
because they assume the government got
it right. But the government is working
off numbers reported by every employer
you ever had, going back to your very
first job as a teenager, and across a
whole working life, errors are not rare.
They are common.
A missing year here, a year cut in half
there,
a stretch of self-employment that never
made it onto the books.
Each one is money shaved off your check.
Therefore, one of the most valuable
hours you will ever spend is logging
into your own account on the Social
Security website, reading your earnings
record line by line, year by year. And
if anything is wrong or missing, filing
form 7008 to fix it.
That single form is the hero of this
entire video, and we are going to come
back to it because there is one more
reason it matters that almost no one
realizes. Now, the second form is the
one I promised would surprise you
because it lets you undo something you
were probably told was permanent. A huge
number of seniors claim Social Security
the moment they could, at 62, often
because they needed the money or because
somebody told them to take it early
before it ran out. And the day they
filed, they locked in the smallest
possible check for life, reduced by as
much as 30% below what they would have
gotten by waiting. Most of them believe
that decision is carved in stone. It is
not always. There is a form called the
request for withdrawal of application,
listed as form 521, and it does
something remarkable. If you have been
receiving benefits for less than 12
months, you can withdraw your
application entirely, one time in your
life, pay back what you have received,
and then refile later at a higher age
for a permanently larger check. But, you
have to act inside that 12-month window,
and you have to be able to repay.
Therefore, if you started your benefits
in the last year, and you have come to
regret claiming so early, this is the
form that can hand you a do-over almost
no one knows exists. And even if that
12-month window is already closed for
you, there is a third move that does
something similar, and it works at any
point once you reach your full
retirement age. It is called voluntary
suspension. Once you hit your full
retirement age, you are allowed to tell
Social Security to suspend your
payments, to pause them on purpose. Why
on earth would anyone pause their own
check? Because for every year you
suspend, your future benefit grows by 8%
all the way up until age 70. That is a
guaranteed 8% increase per year,
something you cannot find anywhere in
the safe part of the financial world. A
person who suspends for a few years can
come back with a check that is 24%
larger for the rest of their life, and
they simply have to ask for it. But, the
agency does not call you at your full
retirement age and offer this.
Therefore, if you can afford to pause,
even for a year or two, suspending your
benefit is one of the most powerful
raises available to anyone in
retirement. Let me stop for 1 second
because I need you to see the pattern
before I give you the rest. An earnings
correction form, a withdrawal form, a
voluntary suspension. Three completely
different tools for three completely
different people. But, underneath every
single one is the exact same truth. Your
check is not fixed. It can be raised,
and the increase is legal, and it is
yours, but it stays out of reach until
you personally file for it or pick up
the phone and ask. The government is not
going to volunteer any of this. Hold
that thought because the next form is
the one that quietly affects the most
people of all, especially women. And it
is the one most often left completely
unclaimed. Now, here is the new stakes I
want to put in front of you, the thing
that should make you sit up because this
next part is where the largest amount of
money goes unclaimed in this entire
country. And the proof comes from inside
the government itself.
The Social Security Administration has
its own internal watchdog called the
Office of the Inspector General, and
that office audited how the agency
handles benefits for widows and
widowers.
What they found should make every family
in America angry. They found that 82% of
the people entitled to both a survivor
benefit and their own benefit were never
told they could claim the larger one or
claim them in the smarter order. 82%.
The audit estimated the agency had
underpaid around $131 million
to roughly 9,000 widows and widowers,
all of them age 70 or older, simply
because nobody informed them of their
options. These were not people who did
anything wrong. They were people the
system quietly failed. So, let me
explain exactly what those widows were
never told because understanding it can
put real money back in a person's
pocket. When you are a widow or a
widower, you often have two benefits
sitting there. Your own and a survivor
benefit based on your late husband or
wife. You do not get to stack them. You
get the larger one. But, here is the
strategy almost no one is shown. You can
choose to claim just the survivor
benefit first and let your own benefit
keep growing at that 8% a year all the
way to 70 and then switch to your own
benefit once it has grown larger.
That move, taking one now and letting
the other grow, is something you have to
request by name. But, by the agency's
own Inspector General, 82% of the time,
no one will tell you it is even
possible. Therefore, if you are a widow
or a widower, you do not wait to be
offered this. You call and you ask about
survivor benefits and about claiming
them in the order that lets your own
benefit grow. And right alongside that
is the spousal benefit, which millions
of people, especially women, never
claim. If you were married, you can be
entitled to a benefit of up to 1/2 of
your husband's or wife's full Social
Security, even if you worked very little
yourself. And you receive whichever is
higher, your own or that spousal amount.
And it does not end with marriage. If
you are divorced, but the marriage
lasted at least 10 years, you can claim
on your former spouse's record up to
that same 1/2. Your ex is never even
notified and it takes nothing away from
them. Think of all the women who spent
years out of the workforce raising
children, now collecting a tiny check on
their own small record, when a benefit
based on a husband's or former husband's
record could be far larger, but almost
no one in that situation knows to ask.
Therefore, if you are married or you
were married for 10 years or more before
a divorce, you ask the agency one direct
question, whether a spousal benefit
would pay you more than what you were
getting right now. Now, I promised you a
form that quietly stops the government
from taking an extra bite out of your
check every month. And this one catches
people completely off guard because it
is not about Social Security adding to
your check, it is about stopping a
deduction that is shrinking it. If you
are on Medicare, your Part B and Part D
premiums are pulled directly out of your
Social Security payment before it ever
reaches you. And for some retirees, the
government adds an extra surcharge on
top of those premiums called an
income-related adjustment based on your
income from 2 years earlier. Here is the
trap. That surcharge is based on old
income. So, if you have since retired,
lost a spouse, gotten divorced, or your
income is simply dropped, you may be
paying a surcharge based on money you no
longer make, and that surcharge is being
subtracted from your check every single
month. But, there is a form for exactly
this called Form 44, the life-changing
event form, and filing it can get that
surcharge reduced or removed. Therefore,
a smaller deduction means a bigger check
landing in your account. And Form 44 is
how you claim it when your life has
changed. Now, there is one more request
that puts cash in your hand right at the
start. And it is for anyone who is about
to file for Social Security or filed
only recently.
When you claim at or after your full
retirement age, you are allowed to ask
for up to 6 months of benefits paid
retroactively, handed to you as a single
lump sum the moment your benefits begin.
For many people, that is several
thousand dollars they never knew they
were allowed to request, simply given to
them because they asked.
Now, there is a trade-off you need to
understand, so you go in with your eyes
open.
Taking those 6 months up front means the
government treats you as though you
started 6 months earlier, which can very
slightly lower your ongoing monthly
amount.
For some people, especially those who
need the cash now, that trade is
absolutely worth it. For others, it is
not. But, the point is that it should be
your choice, made with a full picture in
front of you, not an option you were
simply never told existed.
Therefore, if you are about to file, ask
them to walk you through both sides, the
lump sum now against the slightly higher
check later, and decide for yourself.
And there is one more group owed a
payment so large it deserves its own
warning, the public servants.
For decades, two old rules with
complicated names, the windfall
elimination provision and the government
pension offset, cut down or wiped out
the social security of people who earned
a government pension, teachers,
firefighters, police officers, postal
and government workers, along with the
survivor benefits of their spouses.
But, a law signed at the start of last
year repealed both of those rules
completely, and it reaches all the way
back to the beginning of the year
before.
By the middle of last year, the agency
had already sent more than 3 million of
these payments, totaling around $17
billion,
with the average one-time back payment
landing somewhere between $4,000 and
$8,000, on top of a permanently higher
monthly check.
But, many people who are owed this still
have not claimed it because no one told
them the rule was gone. Therefore, if
you, or a husband or wife who has
passed, ever worked a job with a
government pension, and your social
security has always looked surprisingly
small, that is very likely your money,
and it is one phone call to claim. So,
let me add it up because the total is
the part that should really land. A
corrected earnings record can raise your
benefit by hundreds of dollars a year
for the rest of your life. A withdrawal
and refile, or a voluntary suspension,
can grow your monthly check by a quarter
or more. A survivor or spousal benefit
claimed the right way can be hundreds of
dollars more every single month. A
life-changing event form can stop a
surcharge that has been quietly draining
your payment. A retroactive request can
put several thousand dollars in your
hand at the start. And a repealed
pension rule can be thousands more in
back pay. Put it together and a senior
who learns these forms and actually
files them can recover and gain
thousands of dollars they were already
entitled to and raise their monthly
income for the rest of their retirement.
Therefore, the real question was never
whether the government owes this money
or whether your check can be higher. It
plainly can be. The only question is
whether you are going to be one of the
people who files the form or one of the
people who never knew to ask. Let me
leave you with the picture that makes
all of this click. Two retired neighbors
on the same street, both widowed, both
living on Social Security. The first one
watched something like this, spent one
afternoon on the phone and on the
website, and discovered three things.
That she had a missing year in her
earnings record she could fix with one
form. That she could switch to a larger
survivor benefit, and that she was
paying a Medicare surcharge based on
income she no longer earned. She filed
the forms. Her monthly income went up by
hundreds of dollars and it kept going up
because her own benefit grew while she
drew the survivor check. The second
neighbor, in nearly the identical
situation, assumed that if anything were
wrong, the government would have caught
it. So, she never looked, never called,
and never filed a single form. Same
street, same circumstances. The only
difference was that one of them filled
out the paperwork and the other one
waited for a letter that was never going
to come. Over 10 years of retirement,
that difference adds up to tens of
thousands of dollars. Real money that
one of them collected and the other one
simply left with the government. And
that brings me to the assumption I
promised you. The single most expensive
belief in all of Social Security. The
one that keeps every dollar we have
talked about sitting in the government's
hands. It is the belief that the Social
Security Administration will find what
it owes you and pay it to you
automatically. It will not. And you do
not have to take my word for it because
the government's own Inspector General
put it in writing when it found the
agency failed to tell 82% of eligible
widows about a larger benefit they had
every right to claim.
Understand what that means. A person who
is legally owed a higher check, but who
never files the form, is treated exactly
the same as a person who was never owed
anything at all.
Both of them get the smaller payment.
The only difference, almost every single
time, is that one of them filed and the
other one assumed. The agency is not
your advocate. It processes paperwork.
The advocate has to be you or someone in
your family acting for you. So, here is
exactly what to do this week and not one
of these steps cost you a dollar. Step
one, go to the Social Security website,
which is ssa.gov. Create or log into
your personal account and read your
earnings record from your very first job
to your last, looking for any year that
is wrong or missing. And if you find
one, file the request for correction of
earnings record, form 7008, with your
proof. Step two, if you started your
benefits within the last 12 months and
you regret claiming so early, ask about
form 521, the withdrawal of application,
before that window closes. Step three,
if you have reached your full retirement
age and you can afford to pause, ask
about voluntarily suspending your
benefit to earn that 8% a year. Step
four, if you are a widow, a widower,
currently married, or were married for
at least 10 years before a divorce, call
and ask whether a survivor or spousal
benefit, claimed in the right order,
would pay you more. And step five, if
your income has dropped since you
retired and you are on Medicare, ask
about form 44 to lower the surcharge
coming out of your check. And step six,
if you or a husband or wife who has
passed ever worked a government job with
a pension, a teacher, a firefighter, a
police officer, a postal or government
worker, ask specifically about the
repeal of the windfall elimination
provision and the government pension
offset because you may be owed thousands
in back pay.
The number to call for all of it is the
Social Security Administration at
And one tip that makes every one of
these calls easier so you never feel
lost or talked over on the phone.
You do not need to know the law and you
do not need to memorize a single form
number. You only need one sentence. Tell
whoever answers, "I want to make sure I
am receiving the highest benefit I am
entitled to and I would like you to
review my record and my filing options
with me." That one sentence puts the
responsibility where it belongs, on them
to check.
Write down the name of the person you
spoke to and the date. And if you are
told you do not qualify for something,
politely ask them to note in your file
exactly why.
The moment you ask the right questions,
the entire conversation changes because
now they know that you know. And if you
are watching this for a parent instead
of for yourself, this might be the most
valuable afternoon you ever give them. A
great many seniors will never make these
calls on their own. They do not want the
hassle. They do not want to feel like
they are begging or they simply assume
the government must have it right.
That second neighbor, the one who left
tens of thousands of dollars sitting
with the government, is real in millions
of homes. So sit down next to your
mother or your father, open the Social
Security website together, read the
earnings record together, and make the
calls together.
Putting a few hundred dollars a month
back into a parent's budget and filing
the one form that finally corrects a
lifetime of their work may be one of the
kindest and most practical things you
ever do for them. You worked your entire
life and you paid into this system out
of every single paycheck for decades,
exactly as you were told to. This is not
a handout and it is not charity. It is
your own money, a benefit you earned and
were promised. And the only thing
standing between you and the full amount
is the willingness to read your record
and file the form. So, do not keep
waiting for a letter that is never going
to arrive, because that letter is not
coming. To start, do one thing tonight.
Go to ssa.gov, create your account, and
look at your earnings record, and then
make the first phone call this week.
Every month you wait is money you were
owed and will never get back.

title: They Can Still Take Your Paid-Off Home After 65 — File These 6 Documents First

segments.text: You can spend 30 years paying off your
home, burn the mortgage, own every brick
of it free and clear, and still have it
taken right out from under your family
the moment you are gone for the simple
reason that paying off a house and
protecting a house are two completely
different things, and almost nobody is
ever told the difference.
A paid-off home with the wrong paperwork
around it can lose as much as $75,000 to
court costs, to a government recovery
program, and to a tax bill that never
had to exist before a single dollar of
it ever reaches the children you bought
it for.
Not because you owed anyone, not because
you did anything wrong, simply because
the deed sitting in your drawer is not
the thing that decides who gets the
house.
Six other documents decide that, and
most families have never filed a single
one of them. This is not a problem for
the rich. This is the trap that waits
specifically for the careful, ordinary
family that did the hard part right,
that sacrificed and saved and finally
owned a roof over their heads outright,
and quietly assumed that owning it was
the same as keeping it in the family. It
is not. The most painful losses I have
ever seen were not the families who owed
money. They were the families who owned
everything and protected nothing. So,
before I show you the six documents, I
want you to hold on to one promise
because it is the whole reason I made
this video. There is one document that
almost every family already has that
they believe is the very thing
protecting their house, and that
document actually does the opposite. It
quietly hands the house to a court in
public for months or years and drains
thousands of dollars out of it on the
way through. And there is one other
document, a quiet one that hardly anyone
files, that keeps the house out of that
court entirely and moves it to the
children in weeks instead of years. I am
going to tell you exactly which document
is the trap and exactly which one is the
shield, but first you need to understand
why a paid-off home is exposed in the
first place because everything else
hangs off of that. Here is the thing
nobody explains. The day you die, your
house does not simply pass to your
family the way you imagine it does. If
that home is titled in your name alone,
it has to go through a court process
called probate. Probate is the public
proceeding where a court proves who you
were, reads whatever paperwork you left,
pays off anyone with a claim against
you, and only then signs the house over
to your heirs. And probate is slow and
it is expensive. In most of the country,
it runs anywhere from 9 months to 2 full
years, and it eats roughly 3 to 7% of
the entire estate in court fees, legal
fees, executor fees, and appraisal
costs. On a modest $500,000 home and
savings, that is commonly $15,000 to
gone, paid out of the very inheritance
you spent your life building before the
children see a dime. But, probate is
only the first set of teeth because
there is a second one that is far more
frightening, and it is aimed directly at
the home. If you ever need long-term
care, a nursing home, memory care, the
kind of care that can cost around $9,000
a month, you will likely end up on
Medicaid to pay for it because almost no
ordinary family can carry $9,000 a month
for long. And here is what federal law
says in black and white. Every state is
required to try to recover what Medicaid
spent on your care after you die out of
your estate. They call it estate
recovery, and the single asset they come
after most often is the house. So, the
paid-off home you thought you were
leaving to your kids can instead be sold
to repay the government for the care
that kept you alive.
The family that did nothing to protect
that home can watch the entire thing
disappear into a recovery claim. I
watched this happen to a family two
doors down from where I grew up. The
father had passed years earlier, and the
mother lived alone in the little house
they had paid off together when they
were young. Her health failed slowly,
the way it often does, and eventually
she needed a nursing home, and the bills
ran somewhere around $9,000 a month.
Their savings were gone inside 2 years,
so Medicaid stepped in and paid for her
care, the way it is supposed to. The
children were grateful. They thought the
house was theirs, free and clear,
waiting for them because mom had owned
it outright for decades. But, when she
passed, a letter came from the state. It
was a claim for everything Medicaid had
spent on her care, more than $200,000,
and the state intended to collect it out
of her estate, which meant out of the
house. The children had to sell the home
their parents had spent a lifetime
paying off, hand most of the proceeds to
the government, and walk away with a
fraction of what they thought they were
inheriting.
Not one thing about it was illegal. It
was simply the law, working exactly as
written, on a family that was never
warned and never filed a single document
to stop it.
Therefore, you have to stop thinking of
a paid-off house as something you own,
and start thinking of it as something
you have to actively defend, because
between probate on one side and estate
recovery on the other, the house is the
most exposed thing you own, not the
safest. And the only thing standing
between those two sets of teeth and your
family is paperwork. Six documents.
Let me walk you through every one of
them in the order that matters. The
first document is the one I call the
shield, and it is a revocable living
trust. Now, I know the word trust sounds
like something only wealthy people have,
like a thing for mansions and yachts.
But, that is exactly the
misunderstanding that costs ordinary
families the most.
A revocable living trust is simply a
private container that holds your home
while you are alive. You still control
it completely. You can live in the
house, sell it, refinance it, change
your mind, tear the whole trust up
tomorrow. Nothing about your daily life
changes. But, when you die, the house
inside that trust does not go to
probate. It does not go to a court. It
passes privately, directly, to the
people you named, usually in a matter of
weeks, with no public proceeding, and
none of that 3 to 7% bleeding out in
fees. A house worth $500,000 that would
have lost $30,000 in two years to
probate instead moves cleanly to your
children in a fraction of the time for a
fraction of the cost. But, here is the
trap inside the shield, and this is the
open loop closing in part. So, pay close
attention. A living trust only protects
your house if you actually put the house
into it. The lawyer drafts the trust,
you sign a stack of papers, you pay your
two or three thousand dollars, and you
walk out feeling like you handled it.
But, if no one ever changes the deed to
move the house into the trust, the trust
is empty.
The house is still in your name, and
when you die, that house probates
anyway, exactly as if the trust never
existed, while your family stands there
holding a thick binder that did nothing.
This is the cruelest version of the
mistake, the family that paid for
protection and never got it. Because the
one step that mattered, retitling the
deed into the trust, the step they call
funding the trust, was never done. Let
me make this real with two men who lived
on the same block, because the
difference between them is the whole
lesson. Both did what their lawyer told
them. Both set up a revocable living
trust in the same year, paid about the
same money, walked out with the same
thick binder. The first man went home,
called the attorney back the next week,
and made absolutely sure the deed to his
house was re-recorded into the name of
his trust. He checked. He held the
recorded copy in his hand. The second
man set the binder on a shelf and felt
finished, and nobody ever moved his
deed. For years, on paper, the two
looked identical. Therefore, you would
think it made no difference at all. But,
when each of them passed, the difference
was enormous. The first man's house
moved to his children privately in a
matter of weeks, no court, almost no
cost. The second man's house, still
sitting in his own name because the
trust was never funded, went straight
into probate, public, slow, and
expensive, and his family lost the
better part of a year and tens of
thousands of dollars to a process he had
paid good money believing he had
avoided. Same block, same trust, one
recorded deed. Therefore, if you take
one thing from this entire section, take
this. A trust that does not hold your
deed is just expensive paper. The deed
has to go in or none of it counts. Now,
the second document is for the families
who hear the word trust and feel it is
too much, too complicated, too
expensive, and want something simpler
that still keeps the house out of court.
It is a special kind of deed, and
depending on your state, it is called a
transfer on death deed, a beneficiary
deed, or in a handful of states, a
ladybird deed, which is an enhanced life
estate deed. What it does is beautifully
simple. You record a deed today that
says, "While I am alive, this house is
100% mine to live in, sell, or change.
But, the moment I die, it passes
automatically to my named person with no
probate at all."
You keep total control for your entire
life. You can revoke it anytime. And the
day you pass, the house transfers
outside the court. The same clean way
the trust does, often for the cost of a
single recording fee instead of
thousands of dollars in legal work. But,
the ladybird version does something even
more powerful, and this ties straight
back to that estate recovery monster I
described earlier. Remember, federal law
lets states recover the cost of your
care out of your estate, but many states
are only allowed to reach into your
probate estate, the assets that actually
pass through the court. A house that
transfers automatically through a
ladybird deed never enters the probate
estate at all. Therefore, in those
states, that deed can keep the home not
just out of probate, but out of the
reach of Medicaid recovery as well,
shielding the very asset the program
would have come after. And it does one
more quiet thing that saves your
children a fortune. Because you held the
home until the day you died, your kids
inherit it with what is called a
stepped-up basis. The taxable value of
the house resets to what it is worth on
the day you pass. A home you bought
decades ago for around $80,000, worth
around $500,000 today carries more than
$400,000 of growth. And that entire gain
can be wiped clean off the tax bill when
the children sell.
But, if you had simply gifted them the
house while you were alive, they would
have inherited your old $80,000 cost
instead and gotten hammered with capital
gains tax on that whole $400,000 jump.
The deed, done right, erases a tax that
the gift, done wrong, creates. Now, I
want to stop here and raise the stakes.
Because if you were sitting there
thinking this is all about what happens
after you die,
the next document is about something
that can take your house away while you
are still very much alive, and it is the
one almost everyone forgets.
We have talked about death. Now, let me
talk about the years before death, the
ones that actually destroy more
families. Because there is a gap in your
protection that opens the moment you can
no longer make your own decisions, and a
house has been lost through that gap
more times than I can count. The third
document is a durable power of attorney
for your finances.
Here is the scenario that nobody plans
for.
You do not die.
You have a stroke or dementia sets in,
or an accident leaves you unable to
manage your own affairs.
The house still needs its property taxes
paid, the roof still needs fixing.
Maybe the house needs to be sold to pay
for your care.
But, you can no longer sign anything.
And here is the part that shocks people.
Your spouse cannot simply step in and
handle the house, either.
Not if both your names are not set up
correctly, and not for anything in your
sole name.
Without a durable power of attorney, no
one has the legal authority to act on
that house. Therefore, your family has
to go to court and ask a judge to
appoint a guardian or a conservator, a
public, humiliating, expensive process
that commonly costs several thousand
dollars, takes months, and afterward
puts a court in charge of your affairs
for the rest of your life, watching
every dollar, requiring permission for
major moves. A durable power of attorney
prevents all of it. The word durable is
the key because it means the document
stays in force even after you become
incapacitated, which is exactly when you
need it most. You name a person you
trust and the moment you cannot act,
they can step in and protect the home,
pay what needs paying, and make the hard
decisions without ever setting foot in a
courtroom. But, it has to be signed
while you are still of sound mind. You
cannot create one after the stroke.
Therefore, the window to get this
document is always now, while you still
can, because the entire purpose of it is
to be ready before the day you are no
longer able to make it. The fourth
document lives right beside the third,
and it covers the part of you the
financial power of attorney does not,
your medical care.
It is your advance health care directive
and it has two pieces.
The first names the person who makes
your medical decisions if you cannot
speak for yourself.
The second writes down what you actually
want, the living will. So, your family
is not left guessing and fighting at the
worst moment of their lives.
Now, you might wonder what your medical
directive has to do with the house, and
the connection is direct. The medical
decisions made in your final years,
whether you go into long-term care, how
long, what kind, are the very decisions
that determine whether you ever face the
$9,000 a month bills that trigger a
Medicaid spend down and put the home at
risk in the first place.
The person holding your health care
directive is steering the situation that
decides the fate of the house. But,
there is a small companion to this one
that families skip constantly and it
causes real damage.
It is a simple privacy authorization,
what the rules call a HIPAA release.
Under federal privacy law, doctors and
hospitals are forbidden from sharing
your medical information with anyone you
have not authorized in writing, and that
includes your own spouse and your own
adult children.
Therefore, families discover at the
worst possible time that they cannot
even get a straight answer from a doctor
about their own mother because no one
ever signed the one-page form that gives
them permission.
A few signatures now prevents that wall
from ever going up. Now we come to the
fifth document and this is where I close
the loop I opened at the very beginning.
So stay with me.
The fifth document is a last will and
testament and here is the truth that
catches almost everyone.
The will is the document I warned you
about at the start. The one that almost
every family believes is protecting
their house when it is actually the
document that hands the house to the
court.
Read that again. Your will does not
avoid probate. Your will is the
instruction sheet the probate court
reads.
It is the ticket into the courtroom, not
the way around it.
The families who proudly tell me they
are all set because they have a will are
in many cases the families whose homes
are headed straight for the very process
they think they avoided. So why is the
will on this list at all if it sends the
house to court? Because you still need
one as a backstop for everything the
trust and the deeds do not catch. A will
is what names the guardian for anyone
who depends on you. It is what directs
the odds and ends, the personal
belongings, the accounts you forgot to
title. And there is a special kind of
will, a pour-over will, that acts like a
safety net sweeping anything you
accidentally left out of your trust back
into it at the end. But understand its
real job. The will is the backup, not
the plan. If your house is sitting in a
will and nothing else, it is going to
probate. The trust and the deed are what
keep it out. The will just catches
whatever falls through. And if you have
no will at all, it is worse because then
the state's own formula decides who gets
everything. A rigid intestacy law that
can force your home to be sold and split
among relatives in shares you never
wanted. And roughly 2/3 of American
adults have no will at all, which means
2/3 of families are leaving that
decision entirely to the state. The
sixth and final document is not one
piece of paper, but the one nobody
checks and it quietly undoes all the
others if it is wrong. It is the deed
itself, the actual current title to your
home, and how that title is written.
Because here is what most people never
realize. The way your house is titled
overrides almost everything else you
have done. If the deed is in your name
alone, the house probates, no matter
what your will says. If it is held in
joint tenancy with right of
survivorship, it passes to the co-owner
automatically, which sounds wonderful,
but it exposes your home to that
co-owner's creditors, to their divorce,
to a lawsuit against them, and it can
accidentally cut your own children out
entirely if that co-owner is not who you
think will end up with it. Therefore,
the single most important housekeeping
task in this entire video is to pull
your actual recorded deed and confirm
exactly how your home is titled. Because
if the title does not match your plan,
the plan loses. And while you are
checking the deed, check the things that
travel with it, because they obey the
same hidden rule. Your beneficiary
designations, the payable on death and
transfer on death forms on your
accounts, your life insurance, your
retirement accounts, those forms
override your will every single time.
The Supreme Court has said as much. It
does not matter what your will
instructs, the money goes to whoever is
named on the form, and a stale form, an
ex-spouse, someone who has passed, or a
blank that defaults to your estate can
send a fortune to exactly the wrong
place, or straight into probate. I knew
a man who did almost everything right.
He had a will, he had a trust, he had
told his whole family exactly how he
wanted his money split evenly among his
three children. But decades earlier,
long before that second marriage ended,
he had named his first wife as the
beneficiary on his largest retirement
account, and he never once went back and
changed the form. He assumed his will
would sort it out, the way he assumed
everyone does.
It did not.
When he passed, that account did not
care what his will said, did not care
what he had told his children, did not
care that the marriage had ended a
lifetime ago.
The money went to the name on the form,
his first wife, in full, and there was
nothing his children could do about it.
Therefore, a single outdated form on a
single account undid a plan he believed
was airtight and split his family in the
process. Therefore, the deed and the
beneficiary forms have to be reviewed
together as one picture because a
perfect trust means nothing if the deed
never went in and the forms point
somewhere else.
And one last layer worth claiming, most
states give your primary home a
homestead protection that shields some
or all of its equity from creditors
while you are alive and a few states
protect it without limit, but several of
them require you to record a homestead
declaration to claim it. It is often
free, it takes one short form filed with
the county, and it is one more wall
around the most valuable thing you own.
A wall that costs you almost nothing and
that a creditor or a lawsuit cannot
climb over.
Most people never file it simply because
no one ever told them it existed. Now,
let me say the quiet part out loud
because once you see it, you cannot
unsee it.
Every single document I have just
described is already in place cold in
the homes of families with real money.
The wealthy do not let their houses go
through probate. They do not lose them
to estate recovery.
They funded their trusts the same week
they signed them, they recorded the
right deeds, they have powers of
attorney and directives sitting in a
drawer ready to go, and their
beneficiary forms are reviewed every
year by someone they pay to care.
The exact same paperwork that quietly
costs an ordinary family tens of
thousands of dollars and the house
itself is the paperwork that protects
the fortunes at the top down to the last
brick.
The documents are not secret, they are
simply silent and silence favors whoever
already knows to ask. Therefore, the
system is upside down because the family
that can least afford to lose the home
is the one no one ever warns and the
family that needs no help at all never
misses a step. The only thing standing
between those two families is
information and the willingness to act
on it before it is too late, but
information only helps the family that
uses it in time. So, let me turn this
into something you can actually do this
week. So, here are the action steps, the
specific things to actually do, because
understanding the trap is worthless if
you do not move on it. Here is what
protects your home. Step one, this week
pull your actual recorded deed from your
county recorder or register of deeds and
read exactly how your home is titled.
Sole name, joint tenancy, something
else. You cannot protect a house until
you know how it is currently held and
most people have never once looked. Step
two, sit down with an estate planning or
elder law attorney and have all of it
drafted as one coordinated plan, not
piece by piece. The trust, the deed that
funds it or a transfer on death deed,
the durable power of attorney, the
health care directive with a privacy
release, and the backup will. You can
find an elder law attorney through the
National Academy of Elder Law Attorneys
at naela.org.
One coordinated plan, not six
disconnected pieces. Step three, if you
set up a trust, fund it the same week.
Make sure the attorney actually records
a new deed moving your home into the
trust and get a copy of that recorded
deed in your hand. A trust without your
deed inside it does nothing. So, do not
leave that office until the house is in.
Step four, sign the durable power of
