the Social Security Fairness Act. For
decades, there were two old rules with
complicated names, the Windfall
Elimination Provision and the Government
Pension Offset. And what they did was
simple and harsh. If you worked a job
that gave you a government pension, a
teacher, a firefighter, a police
officer, a postal worker, many state and
federal employees, those rules cut your
social security down, and in many cases
wiped out the benefit you earned, or the
survivor benefit from a late husband or
wife, almost entirely. Millions of
public servants spent their whole
retirement getting a fraction of what
they had paid in. But in January of last
year, that law was signed, and it
repealed both of those rules completely.
And here is the part that matters most.
It is retroactive, all the way back to
January of 2024. So, the agency does not
just owe these people a bigger check
going forward, it owes them back pay for
every month their benefit was wrongly
cut. Let me put real numbers on that
because they are staggering. By the
middle of last year, the Social Security
Administration had already sent out more
than 3 million of these payments,
totaling around $17 billion.
The average one-time back payment landed
somewhere between $4,000 and $8,000,
paid as a single lump sum, and on top of
that, a permanently higher monthly check
from that point on. Picture being a
retired teacher who spent 30 years
watching your social security come in
tiny because of a rule you never
understood, and then learning that the
rule is gone, that you are owed
thousands in back pay, and that your
monthly check is going up for the rest
of your life. Therefore, if you, or a
husband or wife who has passed, ever
worked a public service job that came
with a pension, and your social security
has always looked surprisingly small,
this is very likely your money, and the
way to claim it is one phone call I will
give you at the end. Now, you may be
wondering how to know whether this one
applies to you, and it is simpler than
you would think. Ask yourself one
question. Did you, or a husband or wife
who has passed, ever spend years in a
job that did not take social security
out of your paycheck, but instead gave
you a government pension? That is the
tell. Public school teachers in many
states, firefighters and police
officers, postal workers, and many state
and federal employees from an earlier
era. For decades, those workers were
told that their own Social Security, or
the survivor benefit from a spouse,
would be cut down or erased, and they
accepted it because it was simply the
law. But, that law is now gone, repealed
and reversed back to the start of 2024,
which means the reduction that quietly
shrank their checks for all those years
is not only stopped going forward, it is
owed back to them in a lump sum. If that
describes anyone in your family, there
is very likely a payment with their name
on it that has not been claimed. The
second way you may be owed is the one I
promised would shock you, because the
proof comes from inside the government
itself. The Social Security
Administration has its own internal
watchdog called the Office of the
Inspector General, and a while back that
office audited how the agency handles
survivor benefits, the benefits a widow
or widower receives after a spouse dies.
What they found should make every family
pay attention. They found that 82% of
the people who were entitled to both a
survivor benefit and their own benefit
were never told that they could claim
the larger of the two. 82%. The audit
estimated that the agency had underpaid
around $131 million
to roughly 9,000 widows and widowers,
all of them aged 70 or older, simply
because no one informed them of their
options. These were not people who did
anything wrong. They were people the
system failed to tell. And think for a
moment about who those widows actually
are. They are women in their 70s and 80s
who lost a husband years ago, who were
often living alone on the smallest fixed
income of their lives, counting every
dollar. For many of them, an extra few
hundred dollars a month is the
difference between covering the medicine
and skipping it, between keeping the
heat on and going without. And it was
theirs the entire time. The benefit
existed, the rule allowed it, and the
only thing missing was a single sentence
from the agency telling them the option
was there. But, that sentence never
came, and so the smaller check kept
arriving year after year, while the
larger one they were entitled to went
unpaid. That is not a small clerical
matter. That is real hardship sitting on
top of money that was owed. Now, stay
with me because understanding how this
one works can put real money back in a
widow's pocket, and it is not
complicated once someone explains it
plainly.
When you are a widow or widower, you
often have two benefits available, your
own and a survivor benefit based on your
late spouse. You do not get both stacked
on top of each other, you get the larger
one. But here is the strategy almost no
one is told about. You can choose to
claim just the survivor benefit first
and let your own benefit keep growing
because a social security benefit you
delay grows by about 8% every year up
until age 70. Then at 70, you switch to
your own benefit if it has grown larger.
That move, taking one benefit now and
letting the other one grow, is called
filing a restricted application. And it
can mean a meaningfully larger check for
the rest of your life. But the agency,
by its own Inspector General's finding,
very often will not tell you it is even
an option. Therefore, if you are a widow
or a widower, you do not wait for them
to mention it. You call and you ask
about survivor benefits and the
restricted application by name. The
third way you may be owed is a benefit
that millions of people, especially
women, never claim and it is called the
spousal benefit. Here's how it works. If
you are married, you can be entitled to
a benefit of up to 1/2 of your husband's
or wife's full Social Security. Even if
you worked very little yourself and you
receive whichever is higher, your own or
that spousal amount. And it does not
stop at marriage. If you are divorced,
but the marriage lasted at least 10
years, you can claim a benefit on your
former spouse's record up to that same
1/2. And your ex does not even have to
know you did it. It takes nothing away
from them. Think of all the women who
took years out of the workforce to raise
children who are now collecting a tiny
benefit on their own small earnings
record when a benefit based on their
husband's or former husband's record
could be far larger. Therefore, if you
are married or you were married for 10
years or more before a divorce,
you ask the agency one question, whether
a spousal benefit would pay you more
than what you are getting now. And do
not skip past the divorce part of that
because it is where some of the most
money goes unclaimed. Picture a woman
who was married for 15 years, divorced
long ago, and never remarried. She may
have spent those years raising children
and earning very little on her own
record. And she may believe that because
the marriage ended, she has no claim to
anything from her former husband. That
is wrong.
As long as the marriage lasted at least
10 years, she can claim on his record up
to 1/2 of his full benefit, and it takes
nothing away from him or from his
current wife, and he is never even
notified. But, almost no one in that
situation knows it, so she goes on
collecting a tiny check on her own small
earnings when a far larger benefit was
available to her the whole time.
Therefore, if you were married for a
decade or more, even if it ended in
divorce many years ago, that is a
question worth asking before you assume
the answer is no. Let me stop for 1
second because I need you to see the
pattern before I give you the rest.
A repealed pension rule, a survivor
benefit, a spousal benefit.
Three completely different situations,
three completely different people.
But underneath every single one is the
exact same truth.
The money is owed, it is legal, it is
yours, and it stays in the government's
hands until you personally reach out and
claim it.
Hold that thought because the next way
is one that quietly shrinks the check of
people who do not fit any special
category at all, just ordinary workers.
And it has been doing it for years
without them ever knowing. The fourth
way you may be owed comes down to a
mistake in your own record. Your Social
Security benefit is calculated from your
lifetime earnings, every year you worked
reported by every employer, but that
record is not perfect. It contains
errors. A year of your income reported
under a wrong number. A year that is
simply missing because an employer never
reported it correctly. A period of
self-employment that never made it onto
the books. And every dollar of earnings
that is missing from your record lowers
the benefit you receive. Not for 1
month, but permanently for the rest of
your life. Most people have never once
looked at their earnings record, so they
have no idea whether it is right. But
you can check it yourself, line by line,
year by year, in your own account on the
Social Security website. And if you find
a year that is wrong or missing, you can
have it corrected, which can raise your
benefit going forward. Therefore, one of
the most valuable things you can do this
week is simply read your own earnings
record and make sure the government got
your life's work right. Let me make that
concrete because people underestimate
how much one error costs. Imagine a man
who worked a side business for 3 years
in his 40s, earning a solid income. But
the way it was reported, those 3 years
show up on his record as almost nothing.
Social Security takes your highest 35
years of earnings to calculate your
benefit. So, three strong years replaced
by three nearly empty ones can pull that
average down and trim a real amount off
of every monthly check for the rest of
his life. And if he is married, off his
spouse's survivor benefit, too. He would
never feel it happen because the check
simply arrives a little smaller than it
should, forever. But the moment he opens
his earnings record and sees those three
blank years, he can bring the proof, his
old tax returns or pay records, and have
it corrected. Therefore, checking that
record is not busy work. It is
protecting the exact number that every
future payment is built on. And there is
a fifth way, a smaller one, but real
money for people who are filing soon.
When you claim Social Security at or
after your full retirement age, you are
allowed to request up to 6 months of
benefits retroactively, paid to you as a
single lump sum at the start. For many
people, that is several thousand dollars
they never knew they were allowed to ask
for. Simply handed over because they
requested it. Therefore, if you are
about to file or you filed recently,
that is one more question worth asking,
whether you qualify for that retroactive
lump sum. And here is a quiet detail
about that lump sum that catches people
off guard. So, I want you to understand
it before you ask.
When you take those 6 months as a single
check up front, the government treats it
as though you started your benefits 6
months earlier, which can very slightly
lower your ongoing monthly amount.
For some people, especially those who
need the cash now, that trade is
absolutely worth it because thousands of
dollars in hand today matters more than
a few dollars a month later.
For others, it is not. But, the point is
that it should be your choice made with
the full picture in front of you, not a
thing that simply happens to you or,
worse, an option you were never told
existed.
Therefore, when you call, do not just
ask whether you qualify. Ask them to
walk you through both sides, the lump
sum now against the slightly higher
check later, so you decide with your
eyes open. So, let me add it up because
the total is the part that should really
land. A WEP repeal back payment can be
thousands of dollars in a single lump
sum plus a higher check for life.
A corrected survivor or spousal benefit
can be hundreds of dollars more every
single month for as long as you live.
A fixed earnings record protects every
future payment. And a retroactive lump
sum is several thousand more for those
who ask. Put it together and a senior
who learns these and actually claims
them can recover thousands of dollars
they were already owed and raise their
monthly income for the rest of their
retirement.
Therefore, the real question was never
whether the government owes this money.
It plainly does. The only question is
whether you are going to be one of the
people who claims it or one of the
people who never knew to ask. Let me
leave you with a picture that makes all
of this click.
Two retired neighbors on the same
street, both widowed, both former public
servants, both living on Social
Security.
The first one watched something like
this, made a single afternoon of phone
calls, and discovered three things. That
she was owed a WEP repeal back payment
of several thousand dollars, that she
could switch to a larger survivor
benefit, and that a missing year in her
earnings record could be fixed.
Her income went up by hundreds of
dollars a month, and a lump sum arrived
that she never expected.
The second neighbor, in nearly the
identical situation, assumed that if she
were owed anything, the government would
have paid it. So, she never called,
never checked, and never claimed a dime
of it.
Same street, same career, same benefits
available to both.
The only difference was that one of them
picked up the phone, and the other one
waited for a letter that was never going
to come. Over 10 years of retirement,
that difference adds up to tens of
thousands of dollars. Real money that
one of them collected, and the other one
simply left with the government. And
that brings me to the mistake I
promised, the single most expensive
assumption in all of Social Security.
The one that keeps every dollar we have
talked about sitting in the government's
hands.
It is the belief that the Social
Security Administration will find what
it owes you and pay it to you
automatically.
It will not. And you do not have to take
my word for that, because the
government's own Inspector General put
it in writing when it found that the
agency failed to tell 82% of eligible
widows about a larger benefit they had
every right to claim.
Understand what that means. A person who
is legally owed more money by Social
Security, but who never files for it, is
treated exactly the same as a person who
is never owed anything.
Both of them get the smaller check. The
only difference, almost every single
time, is that one of them asked and the
other one assumed.
The agency is not your advocate. It
processes claims. The advocate has to be
you, or someone in your family acting
for you. So, here is exactly what to do
this week, and not one of these steps
cost you a dollar. Step one, go to the
Social Security website, which is
ssa.gov,
and create or log into your personal my
Social Security account, and then read
your earnings record from your first job
to your last, looking for any year that
is wrong or missing.
Step two, if you or a husband or wife
who has passed ever worked a job with a
government pension, a teacher, a
firefighter, a police officer, a postal
or government worker, call the agency
and ask specifically about the Social
Security Fairness Act and the repeal of
the WEP and GPO, because you may be owed
back pay.
Step three, if you are a widow or a
widower, call and ask about survivor
benefits and the restricted application
by name, and do not let them move you
along until they have explained your
options.
Step four, if you are married now or you
were married for at least 10 years
before divorce, ask whether a spousal
benefit would pay you more than what you
receive today. And step five, the number
to call for all of it is the Social
Security Administration at
And one tip that makes every one of
these calls easier, so you never feel
lost or intimidated on the phone, you do
not need to know the law. You only need
one sentence. Tell whoever answers, "I
want to make sure I am receiving every
benefit and every back payment I am
entitled to, and I would like you to
review my record with me." That one
sentence puts the responsibility where
it belongs, on them to check. Write down
the name of the person you spoke to and
the date, and if you are told you do not
qualify for something, politely ask them
to note exactly why in your file. The
moment you ask the right questions, the
entire conversation changes, because now
they know that you know. And if you are
watching this for a parent instead of
for yourself, this might be the most
valuable afternoon you ever give them. A
great many seniors will never make these
calls on their own. They do not want the
hassle, they do not want to feel like
they are begging, or they simply assume
the government must have it right. That
widow on the same street, the one who
left tens of thousands of dollars
unclaimed, is real in millions of homes.
So, sit down next to your mother or your
father, open the Social Security website
together, make the calls together, and
ask the questions together. Putting a
few hundred dollars a month back into a
parent's budget and a lump sum they
never expected into their account may be
one of the kindest and most practical
things you ever do for them. And if your
parents have already passed, or you are
not close with them, then do this for
someone else. The widow down the street,
the retired teacher at your church who
always seemed to get by on so little.
Anyone you know living quietly on a
Social Security check that may be
smaller than it should be.
This is the rare kind of help that costs
you nothing and can change a person's
entire month every month. Forward them
this video. Sit down at their kitchen
table. Because somewhere very close to
you, right now, tonight, there is
someone being underpaid by a system that
will never once knock on their door to
make it right. And one short
conversation from you might be the only
thing that finally gets them what they
were owed all along. You worked your
entire life and you paid into this
system out of every paycheck for
decades, exactly as you were supposed
to. This is not a handout and it is not
charity. It is your own money, benefits
you earned and were promised, and the
only thing standing between you and the
full amount is the willingness to check
your record and ask the questions. So,
do not keep waiting for a letter that is
never going to arrive, because that
letter is not coming. To start, do one
thing tonight. Go to ssa.gov, create
your account, and look at your earnings
record, and then make the first phone
call this week. Every month you wait is
money you were owed and will never get
back.

title: Paid-Off Home? Medicaid Can Still Take It After 65 — File This First

segments.text: Right now, the single most valuable
thing you own, the home you spent 30
years paying off, the house you finally
hold free and clear with no mortgage and
no payment, is the exact thing a federal
program is required by law to come and
take the day after you die. Not a bank,
not a scammer, the government itself
under a law that has been on the books
since before most of your grandchildren
were born. And it is aimed straight at
the one asset you were sure no one could
ever touch. And here's the part that
makes my stomach turn.
Most seniors believe the opposite.
They believe that a paid-off home is the
safest thing they have.
That because there is no mortgage on it,
because they own it outright, it is
locked away and protected and will pass
cleanly to their children.
That belief is wrong and it is the most
expensive wrong belief a homeowner over
the age of 65 can hold.
Because the very thing that makes the
house feel safe, the fact that it is
paid off and it is all you have left, is
exactly what makes it the first and
biggest target. So, here is what I am
going to do for you tonight. I am going
to show you precisely how this program
works,
why a paid-off home is not protected the
way you think,
and the specific tools that real
families use to make that house
invisible to it.
But stay with me all the way through
because there is one document that filed
in time can shield your home completely.
And one deadline that once it quietly
passes, slams that door shut forever and
there is no opening it again.
I will show you both before the end. And
I will show you the one ordinary
well-meaning mistake that hands your
house straight to the state even when
you were trying to protect your kids.
But first you have to understand why
this even exists because once you see
the logic of it, everything else makes
sense. When a senior needs long-term
care, a nursing home, years of it, the
cost is staggering. In this country
today, a semi-private room in a nursing
home averages around $9,000 a month.
That is over $110,000 a year for one
person for one year. Almost no family
can pay that out of pocket for long. So,
people turn to Medicaid, the only
program that covers long-term nursing
care. But, to qualify for Medicaid, you
have to be nearly broke. You have to
spend down almost everything you have
first. And when the dust settles, there
is usually one thing left standing that
they let you keep while you are alive,
the house. Now, here is where the trap
springs, and almost no one sees it
coming.
While you are alive and receiving that
care, your home is what they call
exempt.
They will not force you to sell it to
qualify.
And that is exactly why people relax.
They think, "See, the house is safe.
They let me keep it."
But, the moment you pass away, a
completely different law wakes up, and
it is called the Medicaid Estate
Recovery Program.
Under a federal law passed in 1993,
every single state is required, not
allowed, required to try to recover
every dollar Medicaid spent on your care
from your estate after you die. And
since you spent down everything else to
qualify, your estate is the house. That
quarter of a million dollars in care
they covered does not just disappear. It
becomes a claim against the one thing
you had left to give your children. Let
me make this real because some version
of it is happening to a family this
week. Picture a widow, 78 years old, in
a home she and her husband paid off two
decades ago. She has a stroke, she needs
nursing care, and the family does what
they are supposed to do. They apply for
Medicaid, it covers her care, and
everyone is relieved that the house was
allowed to stay in her name. She lives
another 3 years in that facility, and
Medicaid pays over $300,000 for her care
across those years. Then she passes, and
a few months later, her children open a
letter from the the a notice of estate
recovery with a balance due on it of
secured against the house. The home that
was supposed to be their inheritance now
has to be sold to pay the state back,
and the children walk away with whatever
is left after the government takes its
share. They never saw it coming because
every step along the way, someone told
them the house was safe.
That gap between what people believe
about a paid-off home and what the law
actually does to it is the exact gap I
am going to close for you right now.
Because here is the truth that changes
everything. Paid-off does not mean
protected. Paid-off in the eyes of this
program simply means it is the only
thing left to take. So, before we get to
the protections, let me clear away three
beliefs that keep families from acting
until it is too late because you may be
holding one of them right at this
moment. Belief one, my house is exempt,
so it is safe.
It is exempt while you are alive and
qualifying for care. It is fully exposed
to recovery after you die. Those are two
different rules at two different times,
and confusing them costs families the
house.
Belief two, I will just give the house
to my kids before I ever need care.
Problem solved. I will show you in a
moment why that single move can backfire
twice and cost more than doing nothing.
Belief three,
this only happens to people who plan
poorly or have a lot of money.
It is the opposite. This program hits
the modest, paid-off middle-class home
the hardest because that family has the
least cushion, and the house is 100% of
what they have. Throw all three of those
out because every one of them is the
reason good families lose homes they
thought were locked away. Now, you might
be wondering exactly how a state reaches
in and does this because it sounds
almost too aggressive to be real.
Here's the mechanism. After you pass,
before your heirs can cleanly inherit,
the state files a claim against your
estate in the probate process, and in
many states, it can place an actual lien
on the home itself, a legal hold that
has to be paid off before the property
can be sold or transferred free and
clear. So, your children cannot simply
move in, and they cannot sell and pocket
the proceeds until that claim is
satisfied. And how hard a state pushes
varies. Some states pursue only what
passes through probate. Others have
expanded their definition of your estate
to reach assets that would normally skip
probate entirely, which is why the same
paid-off house can be perfectly safe in
one state and fully exposed in another.
Therefore, the first thing any homeowner
needs to know is not a national rule. It
is what your own state does, because
that single answer decides how much
danger your house is actually in. Now,
let me show you why the most obvious
solution, the one almost everyone thinks
of first, is a trap. The instant, the
second a family senses care is coming,
is to simply sign the house over to the
children. Just put their names on the
deed, give it to them outright, and then
there is nothing left for the state to
recover. It sounds airtight. It is one
of the most costly mistakes in this
entire area of the law, and here is why.
There is a rule called the five-year
lookback. When you apply for Medicaid,
they do not just look at what you own
today. They look back 60 months, a full
five years, at everything you gave away
or transferred for less than it was
worth. And any gift inside that window,
including signing your house to your
kids, triggers what is called a penalty
period. They take the value of what you
gave away, divided by the average
monthly cost of nursing care in your
state, and that is the number of months
Medicaid will refuse to pay for your
care. Give away a house worth a few
hundred thousand dollars, and you can
disqualify yourself from paid care for
years, right at the moment you need it
most, with the house already out of your
hands and no money to pay the bill
yourself. The transfer that was supposed
to save you locks the door from the
inside. Let me put real numbers on that,
because the penalty is not a small slap.
It is brutal. Say your home is worth
$300,000, and a year before care, you
sign it over to your son. Then care
becomes necessary. Medicaid looks back,
sees that $300,000 gift, and divides it
by the average monthly cost of nursing
care in your state. Call it around
$9,000 a month. 300,000 divided by 9,000
is more than 30. That is over 30 months,
nearly 3 years, during which Medicaid
will pay nothing for your care, even
though you now own nothing and have
nothing to pay with, because you already
gave the house away. The family is left
scrambling to cover 3 years of nursing
bills out of thin air. Or worse, the
child has to sell the very house you
just gave them to pay for the care the
gift disqualified you from. Therefore,
the casual transfer does not just fail
to protect you. It actively creates the
exact crisis you were trying to avoid.
Now, stay with me, because the next
piece is the one that catches even
careful families, the ones who thought
they did their homework, and it is the
single most misunderstood rule in all of
this. People hear the words gift limit,
and they think of the IRS. They know the
IRS lets you give away a certain amount
each year with no tax. And in 2026, that
amount is $19,000 per person. So, they
think, "Fine. I will gift the house in
pieces, or I will gift under the limit,
and I will be safe." Therefore,
understand this clearly, because it is
the trap. The IRS gift limit and the
Medicaid lookback are two completely
different rules from two completely
different agencies. Staying under the
$19,000 IRS limit does absolutely
nothing to protect you from Medicaid. A
gift that is perfectly fine to the
taxman still triggers the full Medicaid
penalty.
Families lean on that $19,000 number
like it is a shield, and it is not a
shield for this at all. It is a
different rule for a different purpose.
And believing they are the same has cost
people the very house they were trying
to save. And there's a second way the
give-it-away move backfires, a quieter
one that shows up as a tax bill.
When you hand the house to your children
outright while you are alive, they take
it with your original cost basis, what
you paid for it decades ago.
So, when they eventually sell it, they
can owe capital gains tax on all that
growth on a house that may have
multiplied in value many times over
since you bought it.
That can be a tax bill of tens of
thousands of dollars. But, if that same
house passes to them the right way,
through the proper structure, they get
what is called a stepped-up basis. The
value reset to the day you passed, and
that capital gains tax can vanish almost
entirely. So, the casual deed transfer
manages to do the impossible. It
triggers the Medicaid penalty, and it
creates a tax bill. Two wounds from one
well-meaning mistake. Therefore, the
answer was never to give the house away
in a panic. The answer is structure, set
up in advance. And this is where I keep
my promise to you, because there is a
document that does exactly what people
wish a simple gift would do without
either of those backfires. It is called
a Medicaid Asset Protection Trust, an
irrevocable trust that holds your home.
You move the house into the trust, you
keep the right to live there for the
rest of your life, and once it has been
in that trust long enough, the home is
invisible to Medicaid and shielded from
estate recovery, while your children
still get that stepped-up basis and
avoid the capital gains hit.
It is the one move that protects the
house from the program, and protects
your kids from the tax at the same time.
But, here is the catch, and it is the
deadline I warned you about at the
start. That trust has to be funded at
least 5 years and 1 day before you apply
for Medicaid. That is the look-back
again. Set the trust up in time, while
you are healthy, and the 5-year clock
runs out quietly in the background, and
the house is safe.
Wait until care is already near, and the
clock is not run, and the protection is
not there when you need it. The deadline
on this is not a date on a calendar. The
deadline is your health. The trust only
works if it is done years before you
ever think you will need it, which is
exactly why so few families do it, and
exactly why I am telling you tonight
instead of next year. Now, the word
irrevocable scares people, and I
understand why, because it sounds like
you are handing your home to a stranger
and losing all control of it. So, let me
ease that fear, because it is the single
biggest reason people hesitate and lose
the clock.
A properly built trust still lets you
live in your home for the rest of your
life. That right is written right into
it. You can keep the property tax breaks
you already have. The income from the
home, if you ever rent or sell within
the trust, can still be directed to you.
What you give up is not the use of your
home, it is only the ability to suddenly
yank it back out and gift it away, which
is the very thing that would have broken
the protection anyway. But, the people
who let the word irrevocable scare them
into doing nothing end up with far less
control than the trust ever would have
cost them, because they lose the house
entirely. A little structure now, or the
whole thing later. That is the real
choice. Now, I know what some of you are
thinking. What if I do not have 5 years?
What if care is close or already here?
You are not out of options, and this is
the part almost nobody knows. So, listen
closely, because there are protections
that work even when the clock has run
out. There is something called the
caregiver child exemption. If you have
an adult child who moved in and took
care of you, who lived in your home and
provided the kind of care that kept you
out of a nursing facility for at least 2
years, you are allowed to transfer the
home to that child with no penalty at
all, even inside the look-back window.
The law rewards the child who showed up.
Think about how common that is. A
daughter who moves back in to care for
an aging mother, who cooks and bathes
and drives to appointments, and gives up
years of her own life, so her mother
does not have to go into a facility a
day sooner than necessary. The law sees
that, and it says that daughter has
already earned the house, and it lets
the home pass to her with no penalty,
even if care comes the very next month.
So, if there is a child in your family
who has been doing that quiet,
exhausting work, the home may already be
protected through them, and almost no
family realizes it. There is a similar
exemption for a child who is disabled or
blind at any age, the home can go to
them protected. There is an exemption
for a sibling who has an ownership
interest and lived in the home for at
least a year. And of course, there is
your spouse. You can transfer the home
to a husband or wife with no penalty
whatsoever, and the healthy spouse, the
one still living at home, is allowed to
keep a substantial amount of your
combined assets, up to about 162
thousand dollars in 2026, and the home
is protected as long as that spouse
lives there. And in a number of states,
there is one more tool, a special kind
of deed called a ladybird deed, an
enhanced life estate deed. With it, you
keep complete control of your home while
you are alive. You can sell it, you can
change your mind, no one can touch it.
But the moment you pass, it transfers
directly to your children outside of the
probate estate. And in many states, that
places it beyond the reach of a state
recovery with no look back penalty for
setting it up. It is not available
everywhere, but where it is, it is one
of the simplest, cleanest tools there
is. And there is one more protection
worth knowing about, a safety net, even
when nothing was set up in advance.
Federal law requires states to offer
what is called an undue hardship waiver
and to pause recovery in certain
situations. Most importantly, when a
surviving spouse still lives in the home
or a minor child, or a child who is
blind or disabled.
In those cases, the state cannot come
take the house out from under them.
But, and this is the part families
misread, and it is critical, in most
states, that protection is only a pause,
not an erasure. The claim does not
disappear. It can wait quietly in the
background, and when that spouse later
passes or that protected person moves
out, the recovery can wake back up and
come for the house then.
So, a pause is a breathing space to get
real structure in place. It is not the
finish line.
And the families who treat it like the
finish line are the ones blindsided
years later. So, let me close the loop I
opened at the very beginning. The
document I promised, the one that makes
your paid-off home invisible to this
program, is the trust, or in the right
state, that ladybird deed. And the
deadline I warned you about, the one
that slams the door shut for good, is
the 5-year clock that runs on your
health, not your calendar. The whole
game is timing. The families who keep
their homes are not richer or smarter.
They are simply the ones who set the
structure up while they still had the
years to spare. The ones who lose the
house are almost always the ones who
waited until it felt urgent. And by
then, the most powerful tool was already
off the table. Let me leave you with a
picture that makes all of this click.
Two widows on the same street in nearly
identical homes, both paid off, both
worth about the same.
The first one, years before she ever
needed care, sat down with an elder law
attorney and put her home into the right
structure.
The clock ran out. When she eventually
needed nursing care, Medicaid covered
it. And when she passed, the house went
to her children, clean, no recovery
claim, no forced sale, no capital gain
surprise.
The second widow did what felt natural.
She kept the house in her own name
because it was paid off, and she was
sure it was safe. And when care came,
the family was relieved the house could
stay.
Then she passed, and the state sent the
bill, and her children had to sell the
family home to pay back a quarter of a
million dollars in care. Same street,
same house, same paid-off home everyone
swore was protected. The only difference
was that one family understood the rules
early enough to act, and the other
believed the house was safe until the
day it was gone.
You are not behind because you did
anything wrong. You are behind because
no one ever explained that paid-off and
protected are two completely different
things. And that brings me to the
mistake I promised, the single most
expensive one, the one that hands your
house straight to the state even when
you were trying to do everything right.
It also comes in two parts.
The first is simply believing the house
is safe because it is paid off and
exempt, and therefore doing nothing at
all until care arrives and the best
options have already expired.
Doing nothing feels safe precisely
because the danger does not show up
until after you are gone. When it is
your children, not you, who open that
letter.
The second part of the mistake is the
panic move, the quiet deed signing,
handing the house to the kids at the
last minute, which, as you now know,
detonates the five-year penalty and the
capital gains bomb in one stroke.
Both halves of that mistake come from
the same root, the belief that a
paid-off home takes care of itself. It
does not.
A house is protected by structure and by
timing, never by the simple fact that
you finished paying for it. So, here is
exactly what to do, and the first three
steps do not cost you a dollar.
Step one, today stop assuming your
paid-off home is automatically safe and
find out one specific thing, whether
your state has an estate recovery
program that reaches the home, because
every state is required to have one, and
most aggressively pursue the house.
Step two, find out whether your state
allows a ladybird deed, because if it
does, that may be the simplest
protection available to you, and it can
often be done quickly.
Step three, pull out a calendar and look
honestly at the five-year clock. If you
are healthy now, you have the most
valuable thing there is in this area of
the law, which is time. And the worst
thing you can do with it is wait.
Step four, sit down with an elder law
attorney, specifically an elder law
attorney, not a general one, and ask
about a Medicaid asset protection trust,
and which exemptions apply to your
family. Many offer a first consultation
at little or no cost. And the place to
find a qualified one is the National
Academy of Elder Law Attorneys. And one
more thing, because this is the part
that matters most, if if are watching
this for a parent instead of for
yourself. The people most exposed to
this are the ones least likely to act on
their own. A widow living alone in a
paid-off home is not going to call an
attorney about a problem that does not
appear until after she is gone. She does
not want to think about it, and she does
not want to be a burden. So, if you have
a parent in a home they own, this
conversation may be the single most
valuable thing you ever do for your
family because the house they think they
are leaving you can be taken right back
if no one acts in time.
Sit down at the kitchen table together.
Find out how the deed is held. Ask the
questions while there are still years on
the clock because the one thing this
program counts on more than anything
else is that the family will assume the
house is safe until the moment it is too
late to protect it. You spent your whole
life paying that house off, every
payment for decades, so that you would
have something solid to pass on. That
was the entire point. Do not let a
program you never heard of and a
deadline you never knew was running undo
30 years of work in a single letter your
children open after you are gone. The
house can be protected. It just has to
be done in time. And time is the one
thing that only moves in one direction.
To start, do one thing this week. Find
out today whether your state can reach
your home after you pass and whether a
ladybird deed is allowed where you live.
Then make the call to an elder law
attorney, and you can find one through
the National Academy of Elder Law
Attorneys at naela.org.
Every year you wait is a year off the
only clock that protects you.

title: STOP Paying These 7 Fees After 65 — They're Illegal to Charge You (Most Don't Know)

segments.text: Right now, there is a fee sitting on a
bill in your home that a federal law
already made illegal to charge you. And
you are paying it anyway every month
because the company collecting it is
betting on one thing. That you will
never read the line, never question it,
and never pick up the phone. That is one
fee. There are seven seven separate fees
that millions of Americans over the age
of 65 are still paying even though the
law either bans them outright, caps them
at a fraction of what you are being
charged, or gives you the absolute right
to refuse them and walk away. Not a
loophole, not a scam. Real federal
consumer protections written
specifically because companies were
caught draining older people on fixed
incomes and then almost never explained
to the very seniors they were built to
protect. And the reason you are still
paying is almost never that the fee is
legitimate. It is that nobody told you
it was not. Let me make this real
because some version of it is happening
tonight in homes all over this country.
Picture a man 74 years old who just lost
his wife of 50 years. In the worst week
of his life, grieving and exhausted, he
walks into a funeral home and they hand
him a package and they add a handling
fee for the casket and a fee for this
and a fee for that. and he signs every
line because he cannot think straight
and he does not know he is allowed to
say no. He overpays by thousands of
dollars in a single afternoon. Money
that should have gone to his
grandchildren all because no one ever
told him that federal law was standing
right there in the room on his side.
That gap between what the law gives you
and what you actually know is the exact
gap I am going to close for you right
now. So here is what I am going to do. I
am going to walk you through all seven
fees, exactly which law protects you,
and exactly what to say to make each one
stop. But stay with me all the way
through because the fourth fee on this
list is the single most expensive
mistake a grieving family makes. The
seventh one is a charge I would bet
money is on your bill this very month
without you realizing it. And there is
one quiet mistake that hands every
dollar right back to these companies
even after the law says the money is
yours. I will show you that mistake
before the end. And once you see it, you
will never make it again. But first, you
need to understand why these fees
survive at all when so many of them are
already against the rules. Ask yourself
one simple question. If a company is
charging you a fee the law does not
allow, who has the incentive to tell you
to stop paying it? Not the hospital
billing office, not the bank, not the
cable company, not the funeral home.
Every single one of them makes more
money the longer you stay quiet. So the
entire system runs on one quiet rule. If
you do not object, you do not get it
back. There is no letter that arrives
explaining your rights. The burden is
100% on you to know, to catch it, and to
refuse. Now, before we start, let me
clear away three beliefs that keep this
money in their pockets instead of yours.
because you may be holding one right
now. Belief one, if the fee were really
illegal, they would not be allowed to
put it on my bill. They put it there
anyway every day because almost no one
challenges it. And a fee that 99 people
pay without a word is worth the one
person who fights it. Belief too, it is
only a few dollars. It is not worth my
time. One of these fees on a single
afternoon is worth more than $1,000. and
several of the small ones repeat every
month for the rest of your life, which
is how a few dollars quietly becomes
thousands. Belief three, fighting it is
too much hassle and they will never back
down. For most of these, it is one
sentence on one phone call and because
the company knows the law is against
them, they fold far faster than you
would ever expect. Throw all three of
those beliefs out because every one of
them was planted to keep you paying. Let
me show you the seven, starting with the
one that can cost you the most in a
single moment. Fee number one, the
surprise medical bill. If you have ever
gone to an emergency room or had a
procedure at a hospital that was in your
network and then weeks later a bill
arrives from some doctor you never met
charging you hundreds or even thousands
of dollars because that one provider was
out of network, you have been hit with
what is called balance billing. And here
is what almost no senior knows. As of a
few years ago, a federal law called the
No Surprises Act made that illegal for
emergency care, for air ambulance rides,
and for out of network providers working
inside an in-et network hospital, you
can only be charged your normal in-et
network cost. The same co-ay or co-
insurance you would owe anyway. The
thousands of dollars in the gap, the
part they try to stick you with, you do
not owe. Before this law, the average
surprise bill ran over $1,000 and
emergency ones climbed into the tens of
thousands. Picture getting that bill,
your stomach dropping, assuming you have
to drain your savings to pay it. You do
not. It is against the law for them to
send it. But the bill still arrives
because they are counting on you not
knowing. And if you pay it out of fear,
almost no one ever refunds you.
Therefore, if a surprise bill like that
shows up, you do not pay it. You dispute
it. And there is a federal helpline
built for exactly this that I will give
you at the end. Fee number two, bank
overdraft fees. When your account dips
below zero, your bank charges you what
is called an overdraft fee. And the
average one is about $35 for a single
transaction, sometimes for being short
by only a couple of dollars. A senior on
a fixed income who gets caught a few
times a year can lose well over $100 to
these charges alone. And for years,
banks deliberately arranged your
transactions largest first to trigger as
many of them as possible. But the rules
have turned hard against the banks.
Federal regulators have moved to rein
these fees in. Many of the biggest banks
have already dropped the related bounced
payment fee all the way to zero. And
here is the part that matters most. You
have the right to simply opt out of
overdraft coverage entirely, which means
the charge can never happen again. Your
card is just declined instead and you
pay nothing. One phone call to remove
overdraft coverage or to switch to one
of the many accounts that charge no
overdraft fee at all and that $35 trap
is gone for good. Therefore, no senior
should be feeding a bank $35 at a time
for the crime of being a little short
when one sentence to the bank shuts it
off forever. Fee number three, credit
card late fees. For years, if your
payment landed even one day late, the
credit card company hit you with a late
fee of 30, 35, sometimes over $40. And
for a senior who simply forgot a due
date or was traveling, it felt like a
punishment far bigger than the mistake.
But the Federal Consumer Bureau capped
that fee at just $8 for most of the
largest issuers, a fraction of what they
used to grab. And here's the part almost
nobody uses. Credit card companies will
very often wave your late fee completely
the first time you call and ask because
a longtime customer in good standing is
worth far more to them than one fee. So
you have two protections stacked
together. The legal cap that limits the
damage and a simple phone call that can
erase it. Picture calling saying you
have been a customer for years. you
missed one date and asking them to
remove the fee as a courtesy. More often
than not, it is gone before you hang up.
That is real money for one minute on the
phone. Money you would otherwise simply
hand over. Now, stay with me because the
next fee is the one I told you can cost
a grieving family the most. And it is
the one nobody is thinking clearly
enough to question at the moment it is
charged. Fee number four, funeral home
fees. This is the one that breaks my
heart because it press on people in the
worst week of their lives. When a spouse
dies and you walk into a funeral home,
you are exhausted. You are grieving and
you are in no condition to negotiate and
they know it. So, they hand you an
expensive package and they pat it with
extra charges. And one of the most
outrageous is a handling fee they try to
add when you bring in a casket you
bought somewhere cheaper. But there is a
federal rule called the funeral rule
that protects you with real teeth. The
funeral home is required by law to give
you an itemized price list of every
single item so you can see each charge
by itself and refuse the ones you do not
want. They cannot force you to buy a
package. And it is flatly illegal for
them to charge you a handling fee for a
casket or earn you purchase somewhere
else, which matters enormously because
the same casket a funeral home sells for
thousands can often be bought online for
a fraction of the price. The average
funeral in this country now runs over
$8,000. And a family that knows this
rule can cut that bill by thousands just
by asking for the itemized list and
saying no to what they do not need.
Therefore, before you or anyone in your
family ever signs a single funeral
document, you ask for that itemized
price list by name. And you remember
that the law is standing in that room on
your side. Let me stop for one second
because I need you to see the pattern
before I give you the last three. A
surprise medical bill, an overdraft fee,
a late fee, a funeral charge. Four
completely different industries, four
completely different companies, none of
them connected to each other. But
underneath every single one is the exact
same truth. There is already a law on
your side. You already have the right to
refuse or reduce the charge, and it
stays in their hands instead of yours
until you physically speak up and claim
it. Hold that thought because the next
two fees are ones almost nobody ever
thinks to question. And the very last
one is the charge I promised is sitting
on your bill right now. Fee number five,
the fees hidden on your phone bill.
There is a practice with an almost
comical name, cramming, and it means a
third party slips a small charge onto
your monthly phone bill for a service
you never ordered. A few dollars here, a
few dollars there, buried in the fine
print where you would never notice it.
It sounds too petty to matter, but it
has drained hundreds of millions of
dollars from Americans. much of it from
older people who pay the same bill on
autopilot every month and never read the
itemized charges. It is illegal. The
federal communications regulators and
the consumer protection agencies have
forced companies to refund enormous sums
over it. A charge of just $3 or $4 a
month for something you never signed up
for is over $100 a year, quietly gone.
Therefore, this month, you pull out your
actual phone bill, you read every single
line item, and any charge you do not
recognize, you call and dispute, and you
ask your carrier to block all
third-party charges going forward so it
can never happen again. Fee number six,
the hidden overcharge at the pharmacy
counter. This one is almost unbelievable
because for years, pharmacists were
actually gagged by their contracts.
Forbidden from telling you that the cash
price of your medication was lower than
what you were about to pay with your own
insurance. You would hand over your
card, pay a 20 or $30 co-pay, and never
know that if you had simply paid cash,
the very same pills would have cost you
less. A federal law put a stop to that
gag. And now the pharmacist is allowed
and supposed to tell you when paying
cash would save you money. But here's
the catch. They still will not always
volunteer it unless you ask because the
system does not run on them looking out
for you. So the protection only works if
you use it. Therefore, from now on, at
every single prescription you fill, you
ask one simple question. Is the cash
price lower than my co-ay? That one
sentence at the counter can save you 10,
20, $30 on a single prescription over
and over for the rest of your life. Fee
number seven, and this is the one with
the charge I promised is almost
certainly on your bill this very month.
Look at your cable or internet bill and
find the line where they charge you to
rent your equipment, the modem, the
cable box, the router. It is usually
around $15 a month and it never ends.
You pay it month after month, year after
year, renting a piece of equipment you
could simply buy once and own. $15 a
month is $180 a year for a box every
year forever. And the federal
communications regulators recently
forced these companies to show you the
true all-in price of your service
precisely because they were burying fees
like this where customers could not see
them. You are allowed to return that
rented equipment and buy your own
compatible device which usually pays for
itself in well under a year. And from
then on that $15 stays in your pocket.
Therefore, pull out the cable bill, find
the equipment rental line, and either
buy your own device or call and demand
they strip the add-on fees and put you
on their best available price. So, let
me add it up because the total is the
part that should really land. A single
surprise medical bill you no longer owe
can be thousands of dollars. The funeral
rule can save a family thousands more.
The overdraft trap, the late fee, the
phone cramming, the pharmacy overcharge,
and the equipment rental are each worth
$1 to $200 a year or more every year.
And they repeat for the rest of your
life. Put it together, and a senior who
learns these seven protections and
actually uses them, can easily keep
thousands of dollars that the system was
quietly counting on taking. Therefore,
the real question was never whether
these protections exist. It is whether
you are going to be one of the people
who actually uses them or one of the
people who keeps paying because no one
ever told them they could stop. And
those are just the seven big ones.
Before I give you the action steps, let
me hand you a quick bonus round because
once you start pulling this thread, the
junk fees aimed at you are everywhere.
First, hotel resort fees and event
ticket fees now have to be shown allin
upfront because regulators got tired of
the surprise charges at checkout. So,
you can see the real total before you
ever agree to it. Second, airline seat
and bag fees are negotiable far more
often than people think, and many are
waved for the asking. Third, those
convenience fees they tack on when you
pay a tax bill or a utility bill by
card. You can almost always dodge them
simply by paying by check or bank
transfer instead. And fourth, the outof
network ATM fee, where you get charged
twice, once by your bank and once by the
machine, can be avoided entirely just by
using your own bank's machines or
getting cash back at the store. None of
these will ever be refunded to you
automatically. Every one of them waits
for the person who finally asks. And
notice the real problem with that whole
list. Medical bills, bank fees, funeral
charges, phone fees, pharmacy prices,
cable rentals. None of them are
connected to one another. And none of
them are connected to the same agency.
They are scattered across a dozen
different industries that will never
once talk to each other. And that
scattering is exactly why it all goes
unchallenged. No single office is ever
going to hand you the complete list of
fees you are allowed to refuse because
no single office even has it. You are
the only person on earth who can pull
all of these together for your own life.
That sounds daunting, but it is actually
the opportunity because almost nobody
bothers which means almost every one of
these protections is sitting there
unused waiting for the person who
finally stands up and uses it. Let me
leave you with a picture that makes all
of this click. Two seniors living on the
same street in nearly identical
situations, same fixed income, same
stack of monthly bills, same surprise
charges landing in the same mailbox. The
first one watched a video like this,
learned the seven protections, and
started reading every bill and asking
one question at every counter. Over a
year, that person refused a surprise
medical bill, killed the overdraft trap,
erased a late fee, returned the cable
box, caught the phone charges, and saved
at every pharmacy visit. thousands of
dollars kept every year. The second one
meant to look into it, felt a little
overwhelmed, figured it was not worth
the trouble, and kept paying every fee
exactly as it came. Stretch that over 10
years, and it is tens of thousands of
dollars, real money, that one of them
kept, and the other simply handed over
for no reason except that they never
spoke up. You are not behind because you
were careless. You are behind because
the system was quietly built to keep you
that way, betting on confusion and
silence and the hope that you will
assume instead of ask. Today is the day
you stop betting with the house. And
that brings me to the mistake I
promised, the single most expensive one.
The one that quietly hands every dollar
on this entire list right back to them.
The mistake comes in two parts. The
first part is assuming that if a fee is
illegal or capped, it will simply come
off your bill on its own. It will not.
The charge still arrives every time, and
the law only helps the person who
catches it and objects. The second part
of the mistake is even more common and
honestly it is the painful one because
it is people paying out of fear. They
get the scary bill, they do not know
their rights and they pay it just to
make it go away. And once you have paid
it, getting it back is far harder than
refusing it would have been. Understand
this clearly. A senior who is legally
protected from a fee but pays it anyway
is treated by these companies exactly
the same as a senior who owed it. Both
of them are out the money. The only
difference almost every single time is
that one of them spoke up and the other
one stayed silent. I think of that
grieving widowerower at the funeral home
signing every line because he did not
know he could say no. The protection was
real. It was the law. It still cost him
thousands because the one thing a law
will never do is read your bill and
speak up for you. So, here's exactly
what to do this week. And not one step
cost you a dollar. Step one, for any
surprise medical or emergency room bill,
do not pay the balance and call the
federal no surprises helpline at 1
and tell them you were balanc build.
Step two, for your bank, call today and
say two things. Remove overdraft
coverage from my account and tell me
every monthly fee on this account and
how to wave it. Step three, for a credit
card late fee, call the number on the
back of the card and ask them to remove
it as a one-time courtesy. Step four,
keep the funeral rule in your back
pocket and tell your family now before
anyone needs it to always ask for the
itemized price list and never to sign a
package under pressure. Step five, pull
out your phone bill and your cable bill
this week. Read every line, dispute
anything you do not recognize, return
the rented equipment, and ask for third
party charges to be blocked. And step
six, the one people forget at every
pharmacy counter from now on, ask if the
cash price is lower than your co-ay. And
one tip that makes every one of these
calls easier so you never feel lost or
intimidated. You do not need to memorize
the names of the laws. You only need one
sentence. Tell whoever answers, "I
believe this fee is one I am protected
from and I want it removed." And then
let them check. Write down who you spoke
to and what they said. And if they
refuse, you say one more sentence. Then
I would like to file a complaint with
the Federal Consumer Protection Agency.
The moment you say that, you will be
amazed how quickly the fee disappears
because the company knows exactly who is
on your side. And if you are watching
this for a parent instead of for
yourself, this might be the most
valuable afternoon you ever give them. A
lot of seniors will never question these
fees on their own. That widowerower at
the funeral home is real in millions of
homes, and he will not call to dispute a
bill because he does not want to be a
burden or he simply assumes the company
must be right. So sit down next to your
mom or your dad, go through the bills
together at the kitchen table, make the
calls together. Putting a few thousand a
year back into a parents budget and
lifting the quiet fear of the next bill
off their shoulders may be the kindest
thing you do for them all year. And if
your parents have already passed or you
are not close with them, then do this
for someone else. The widow down the
street who waves to you every morning.
The veteran at your church. Anyone you
know living quietly on a fixed income
who is far too proud to ever question a
bill. This is the rare kind of help that
costs you nothing to give and can change
a person's entire month. Forward them
this video. Sit down at their kitchen
table and go through the bills together.
Because somewhere very close to you
right now, tonight there is someone
paying a fee they were never supposed to
pay. And one short conversation from you
might be the only thing that finally
gets them to stand up and refuse it. You
spent your entire life paying every bill
you ever owed on time in full like an
honest person. These protections are not
a handout. They are the law catching up
to companies that were caught taking
advantage of you. And the only thing
standing between you and that money is
the willingness to read the line and
speak up. So do not keep waiting for a
refund that is never going to arrive on
its own because that letter is never
going to come. To start, pull out one
bill tonight. Just one. Read every line
and call about the first fee you do not
recognize. Do it this week. Every single
month you wait is money you will never
get

title: Seniors STOP Paying Property Tax After 65 — You're Legally Exempt (Most Don't Know)

segments.text: Right now, all over this country, there
are seniors over the age of 65 writing a
property tax check every year for
thousands of dollars on a home they
already own free and clear when their
own state has already passed a law
saying they are exempt from a large
piece of that bill. They keep paying the
full amount for one reason, and it is
not that they do not qualify. It is that
nobody ever told them to ask. That is
one way they are quietly overpaying.
There are five. Five separate ways that
millions of Americans over 65 are
legally entitled to stop paying a big
part of their property tax. Freeze it so
it can never climb again, or even have a
chunk of it paid back to them. And
almost none of it happens automatically.
Not through a loophole, not through a
scam, through real exemptions and freeze
programs that your own state and county
created, funded with tax dollars, and
then quietly never mentioned to you. And
the reason you are still paying full
price is almost never that you earn too
much or own too much. It is that nobody
applies because nobody knows to ask. Let
me make this real because some version
of it is happening tonight in a paid-off
house on a quiet street. Picture a
widow, 73 years old, living alone in the
home she and her husband paid off 20
years ago. She owns it outright. There
is no mortgage. And yet every single
year that property tax bill arrives, and
every single year it is a little higher
than the year before. Even though her
house has not changed and her income has
only shrunk.
So, she does what so many seniors
quietly do. She cuts back somewhere
else. She keeps the thermostat low. She
skips the thing she wanted. She tells
her children she is managing just fine.
And the entire time her state offers a
senior exemption that would shield a
large piece of that home's value from
tax. And a freeze that would lock her
bill so it could never rise again.
Not one office ever called to tell her
because telling her was never their job.
Asking was hers.
That is the exact gap I'm going to close
for you right now. So, here is what I am
going to do. I'm going to walk you
through all five ways to stop
overpaying, exactly who qualifies, and
exactly who to call to claim each one.
But, stay with me all the way through
because the fourth one is a benefit your
own town has to switch on, and most
never tell you they did. The fifth one
has nothing to do with your income at
all, so nearly every homeowner watching
can use it. And there is one quiet
mistake that disqualifies eligible
seniors from every program on this list,
even when the money was already theirs.
I will show you that mistake before the
end. And there is a hard deadline tied
to one of these that, if you miss it,
costs you the entire benefit for the
year. Miss the date, lose the money. So,
stay with me. But first, you need to
understand why all this relief is just
sitting there unclaimed. Ask yourself
one simple question. If you are entitled
to pay less property tax, who has the
incentive to tell you? Not the county
that collects it. Not the taxing
district that spends it. Every one of
those offices takes in more money the
longer you stay silent. So, the entire
system runs on one quiet rule. If you do
not apply, you do not get it. There is
no letter that arrives on your 65th
birthday listing every exemption you are
now allowed to claim. The burden is 100%
on you to ask. Now, before we start, let
me clear away three beliefs that keep
this money in the county's hands instead
of yours because you may be holding one
of them right now. Belief one, if I
qualified, somebody would have told me.
They would not for the exact reason I
just gave you.
Belief two, I make too much or my house
is worth too much to qualify. Maybe for
one of these, but several have income
limits far higher than people assume,
and one of them has no income limit at
all. So, checking costs you nothing
while assuming costs you thousands every
year.
Belief three, it is too much paperwork
for too little. One form on the very
first exemption I am about to show you
can shield tens of thousands of dollars
of your home's value from tax for the
rest of your life. That is not
paperwork. That is the highest paid hour
you will work all year. Throw all three
of those out because every one of them
was built to keep you from claiming what
is already yours. Let me show you the
five starting with the one almost every
senior qualifies for. Number one, the
senior homestead exemption. This is the
foundation and it is the one that most
people leave on the table. Here is how
it works. Your property tax is
calculated on the assessed value of your
home. A homestead exemption simply
removes a chunk of that value from the
calculation before the tax is figured.
So, you are taxed on less, which means
you owe less.
Most states offer a basic homestead
exemption to anyone living in their own
home. But, here is the part they do not
advertise.
Many states offer a much larger
exemption once you turn 65. And the
senior version can be worth many times
the regular one.
Look at what Texas just did.
On top of the standard homestead
exemption, Texas raised its school tax
exemption for seniors all the way up to
And combined with the regular homestead
exemption, a senior homeowner there can
now shield up to $200,000 of their
home's value from school property tax.
Think about what that means in real
dollars. On a home that would otherwise
be taxed in full, shielding $200,000 of
value can cut a tax bill by thousands of
dollars a year, every single year for a
senior who simply files the form. And
the senior who lives right next door,
same street, same age, who never filed,
pays the full bill. Same house. Same
eligibility. The only difference is one
application. But, here is the part that
makes the second one so powerful because
it solves the problem that keeps seniors
up at night. It is not just that the
bill is high, it is that it keeps
climbing. Number two, the senior
assessment freeze. Even after you claim
your exemption, your home's assessed
value can keep rising year after year as
the housing market climbs and your bill
rises right along with it, which is
terrifying when you are on a fixed
income that does not climb at all. So
many states offer seniors something
called an assessment freeze, which locks
the taxable value of your home at the
level it was when you qualified. So that
no matter how high the market goes, the
value they tax you on cannot go up.
Illinois just made this dramatically
easier to get. The state raised the
income limit for its senior assessment
freeze to $75,000,
and it is set to climb higher in the
next couple of years. Which means a huge
number of retirees who assumed they
earned too much now land comfortably
under the line. Picture two neighbors
again. Both seniors, both in homes that
are quietly rising in value. The first
one files for the freeze and her taxable
value locks in place. Five years later,
her neighbor's bill has climbed by
hundreds of dollars, while hers has not
moved a dollar. She did not get lucky.
She filed one form on time and the climb
stopped. The other one assumed she would
not qualify, never asked, and watched
her bill rise every year for nothing.
Now, stay with me because we are about
to hit the one that does not just lower
your bill, it can actually pay money
back into your pocket. And there is a
hard deadline attached that most people
blow right past. Number three, the
senior property tax rebate, sometimes
called a circuit breaker or
reimbursement program. This one works
differently from the first two. Instead
of shrinking your bill before you pay,
it pays you back a portion after, like a
refund on the property tax you already
paid, aimed squarely at seniors on fixed
incomes. New Jersey just rolled out one
of the most generous versions in the
country. Through a program called Stay
New Jersey, eligible seniors can be
reimbursed for half of their property
tax bill, up to a maximum benefit of
a year. Read that number again. $6,500
back in a senior's pocket on a bill they
already paid, and it stacks on top of
the state's other senior property tax
breaks. To qualify, you generally need
to be 65 or older, own and live in your
home, and fall under a household income
limit that is set high enough to include
a great many ordinary retirees. But,
here [snorts] is the catch that cost
people the entire benefit. These
programs have a hard filing deadline,
and if you miss it, you do not get a
smaller benefit, you get nothing for
that year. For the New Jersey program,
that deadline lands in early November.
The senior who files by the date gets
thousands of dollars back. The senior
who meant to, who set the letter on the
kitchen counter and forgot, gets zero
and has to wait an entire year for
another chance. Same eligibility. One of
them simply mark the date. And I want
you to sit with how big that one is for
a moment. Because we have crossed from
saving money to getting money back. The
first two programs lower what you owe.
This third one can put an actual check
or a credit worth thousands back into
the hands of a senior who already paid.
For someone living carefully on a fixed
income, $6,500
is not a rounding error. It is a new
roof. It is a year of prescriptions. It
is the cushion that turns a scary month
into a manageable one. And it is sitting
there every single year for the people
who file by the deadline and evaporating
every single year for the people who do
not. Therefore, if you take only one
thing from this entire video, take this.
That the date on these programs matters
as much as the eligibility. And a
benefit you qualified for but filed one
day late is worth exactly the same as
one you never qualified for at all.
Nothing. Let me stop for 1 second
because I need you to see the pattern
before I give you the last two. And the
last two are the ones almost nobody
knows to ask for. The exemption shrinks
your bill. The freeze stops it from
climbing. The rebate pays part of it
back. Three completely different
programs, three completely different
offices, none of them connected.
quiet truth. The money is already set
aside. You already qualify. And it stays
in the county's hands instead of yours
until you physically file a form and
ask. Hold that thought because the
fourth one is a benefit your own town
has to vote to turn on and they will
never once tell you that they did.
Number four, the expanded senior
exemption that your local government can
adopt. Here is something the counties
would rather you not focus on. In many
states, the basic senior exemption is
just a floor and state law lets your
individual town, city, or county choose
to make it far more generous. New York
just did exactly this. The state passed
a law allowing local governments to
raise the senior citizen exemption from
the old limit of 50% of a home's
assessed value all the way up to 65%.
Think about that. In a town that adopts
the full amount, a qualifying senior
could have 65% of their home's value
wiped off the tax calculation entirely.
But here is the trap built into it. It
is not automatic on two levels. First,
your local government has to actually
vote to adopt the higher amount and many
seniors have no idea whether their town
did or not. Second, even where it is
adopted, you still have to apply for it
and you usually have to refile to keep
it. So the money can be sitting right
there, approved by your own town
council, and you will pay full price
anyway unless you call and claim it. The
seniors who win here are the ones who
pick up the phone and ask two questions.
Did my town adopt the higher senior
exemption and how do I apply for it?
That is the entire difference.
Therefore, let me give you the fifth
one, the one with no income limit at
all, the one that nearly every single
homeowner watching this can act on
today. Number five is actually two
rights that work together. The first is
the property tax deferral. Many states
let qualifying seniors legally postpone
paying some or all of their property tax
with the balance simply settled later
out of the home's value, which can mean
a senior who is genuinely cash strapped
is allowed to stop writing that check
now without losing the house. The
second, and this is the one with no
income test whatsoever, is your right to
appeal your assessment. Counties make
mistakes constantly and homes are very
often assessed for more than they are
actually worth which means the tax is
calculated on a value that is simply too
high. You have the legal right to
challenge that assessment and if you
win, your bill drops, sometimes by a
lot, for years to come. It does not
matter how much you earn or what your
home is worth. Every homeowner has this
right and almost nobody uses it because
they assume the number on the bill is
simply correct and final. It is not. It
is an opening offer and the senior who
calmly asked the county to review an
inflated assessment with a few
comparable home values in hand often
walks away paying hundreds or thousands
of dollars less every year on a bill
they used to think was carved in stone.
So let me add it up because the total is
the part that should really land.
A senior exemption shielding tens of
thousands of dollars of value, a freeze
that stops your bill from ever climbing
again, a rebate worth up to $6,500
a year, an expanded local exemption that
can erase most of your home's taxable
value. A deferral that lets you stop
paying now and an appeal that lowers the
bill for everyone. No income limit at
all.
Stack what you qualify for and a single
senior homeowner can knock thousands of
dollars off their property tax every
year and a couple even more. Year after
year after year. For nothing more than a
handful of phone calls and a few forms
filed on time.
And this is not some old program winding
down. States are racing to expand this
relief right now.
Montana just rolled out a new tiered
homestead system that hands qualifying
homeowners an average property tax cut
of around 18%.
The relief is growing, not shrinking.
The only thing standing between you and
it is whether you ask. And those are
just the five big ones, but before I
give you the action steps, let me hand
you a quick bonus round because once you
start pulling this thread, the property
tax breaks seniors are owed are
everywhere and they go unclaimed for the
exact same reason. First, if you are a
veteran or the surviving spouse of one,
most states stack an additional veterans
exemption right on top of your senior
exemption, and the two together can wipe
out a large share of your bill. Or, for
some disabled veterans, the entire
thing. Second, if you have a disability,
there is very often a separate
disability exemption that you can claim
alongside the senior one, not instead of
it. Third, the surviving spouse trap.
And this one quietly hurts widows the
most. When one spouse passes, the senior
exemptions and freezes do not always
carry over on their own. And the
survivor who never refiles can suddenly
find the bill jumping back up in the
worst year of their life, when a single
call to the assessor would have kept the
protection in place.
Fourth, ask whether your county lets you
pay in installments instead of one large
lump sum. Because, for a senior on a
fixed income, splitting the bill across
the year can be the difference between
paying it calmly and dreading it. And
fifth, if you still carry any mortgage
and your taxes are paid through escrow,
make sure your lender actually
recalculates that escrow after your
exemption is approved. Because, if they
do not, you keep overpaying every month
and the savings never reach you. And
notice how that bonus list works, too.
The veterans break, the disability
exemption, the widow's continuation, the
installment plan, the escrow
recalculation. Everyone sits in a
different office, and not one of them
happens on its own. That scattering is
the whole game. No single person is ever
going to assemble the complete picture
for your home, except you. That sounds
like a burden, but it is really the
opening, because almost no one does it,
which means almost all of this relief is
still sitting there for the senior who
finally decides to claim it. Let me give
you one more picture, because it is the
one that makes the appeal worth more
than people think. A retired couple gets
their tax bill, and like always, just
pays it, assuming the value on it is
simply correct. One year, their son
looks at it, pulls up what three similar
homes down the street recently sold for,
sees their house is assessed well above
all of them, and walks his parents
through a simple appeal at the county
office. The assessment comes down, and
