As of last year, there is now a hard cap
on what any senior pays out of pocket
for prescriptions in a single year, and
that cap is $2,000.
Let me make that concrete. There are
retirees who were paying 8, 9, $10,000 a
year out of pocket for the medications
keeping them alive, rationing doses,
skipping refills, choosing between pills
and groceries. For those people, the
bill is now capped at $2,000 by law, and
it can never go higher. That change
alone, for someone with serious health
costs, can free up thousands of dollars
a year, and most seniors still have no
idea the cap exists. They are still
bracing every January for bills that
legally can no longer happen. Let me be
clear about how big this is, because it
got almost no attention. That
prescription cap is the largest change
to Medicare drug coverage in roughly 20
years, and it arrived quietly with
almost no one explaining it to the
seniors it was built to protect. If you
have ever stood at a pharmacy counter
and quietly put a medication back on the
shelf because you could not afford it
that month, this is the change that was
meant to end that moment forever. But it
can only help you if you know it exists,
and you are enrolled in a plan that
actually applies it. Now, stay with me,
because we are about to hit the two
bills almost nobody thinks to question.
And the next one is the one I told you I
would bet you are overpaying right now.
Bill number three, your home energy
bill. Heating in the winter and cooling
in the summer is not a luxury when you
are older, it is a health issue, and for
a senior on a fixed income, the energy
bill can become a real choice between
staying warm and buying food. So, there
is a federal program called LIHEAP, the
Low Income Home Energy Assistance
Program, and it does exactly what it
sounds like. It pays a chunk of your
heating and cooling costs directly to
the utility company. And in many cases,
it will also stop an emergency shutoff
or help repair a broken furnace or air
conditioner. It is generally open to
households earning up to 150% of the
federal poverty level, which is a far
wider door than most people assume. Well
into the income range of a typical
retiree. But, here's the catch that
costs people the benefit. The funding is
limited. It runs out. And you have to
apply every single year during your
state's enrollment window. The seniors
who call early get hundreds of dollars
knocked off their bills. The ones who
assume they will not qualify or who wait
until the funds are gone pay full price
all winter long. Think about what that
really looks like in February. One
senior makes a 10-minute call in the
fall and has a few hundred dollars taken
straight off their winter heating bills.
Money that stays in the grocery budget
where it belongs. The senior right next
door, same income, same drafty house,
never calls and spends the coldest
months rationing the thermostat and
dreading the mailbox. Same eligibility,
completely different winter. The only
thing that separated them was one phone
call that one of them made and the other
one kept meaning to. Bill number four,
your phone and internet bill. This is
the one I promised you are almost
certainly overpaying because in a world
where you need a phone to reach your
doctor and the internet to manage your
Medicare, your bank, and your
prescriptions, these stopped being
luxuries a long time ago and they are
not cheap. There is a federal program
called Lifeline that takes $9.25
off your phone or internet bill every
single month. And more than that, if you
live on tribal lands. If you are already
on Medicaid, on food assistance, on
Supplemental Security Income, or on the
energy program I just described, you
automatically qualify for Lifeline. Now,
a month may not sound like it will
change your life, but that is over $100
a year for filling out a single form one
time, and it is money you hand back to
the phone company every month you do
not. The catch, like the others, is that
you have to recertify once a year, and
if you forget, the discount silently
falls off and your bill creeps right
back up while you are not looking. Let
me stop for 1 second because I need you
to see the pattern before I give you the
fifth one.
Your Medicare premium, your drug costs,
your energy bill, your phone bill.
Four completely different bills, four
completely different agencies, none of
them connected. But underneath every
single one is the exact same truth. The
money is already set aside, you already
qualify, and it stays in their hands
instead of yours until you physically
pick up a phone and ask. Hold that
thought because the fifth bill breaks
the one excuse most people use to talk
themselves out of all the others. Bill
number five, your bank fees.
And this is the one with no income limit
whatsoever.
Banks quietly drain seniors with monthly
maintenance fees, minimum balance fees,
and overdraft fees, and most people just
accept them as the price of having an
account. They are not. Nearly every
major bank and credit union offers a
senior checking account that waives the
monthly fee entirely, and many waive
overdraft fees on top of it. One large
bank drops the monthly fee completely at
age 60. Another offers free senior
checking with no monthly fee and free
checks at 62.
Another waives every maintenance fee for
customers 55 and older, free checks
included. And remember, this one has
nothing to do with your income. It is
based purely on your age. So, if you are
paying even 10 or 15 dollars a month in
account fees, that is well over 100
dollars a year, every year, that
vanishes with a single phone call asking
your bank to move you to their senior
account. No senior should be paying a
monthly fee on a checking account, and
the only reason most still are is that
no bank on earth is going to volunteer
to charge you less.
And do not wave this one off just
because it is the smallest number on the
list because this is the test. It is the
one that takes 5 minutes, no income
check, no application, just a phone call
or a tap in your banking app. If you
will not claim the easy one, you will
never claim the bigger ones. Therefore,
do this one today before you even start
on the others and let that first quick
win prove to you that the rest of this
money is every bit as real and every bit
is claimable. So, let me add it up
because the total is the part that
should really land.
The Medicare premium alone is more than
a year.
The prescription cap saves thousands
more for anyone with serious
medications.
The energy assistance is often several
hundred dollars a winter, the phone
discount is over a hundred a year, and
the bank fees are another hundred or
two.
Put it together and a single senior who
claims everything on this list can
easily put four to five thousand dollars
a year back in their pocket and a couple
even more. Year after year after year
for nothing more than a handful of phone
calls and a few forms.
Therefore, the real question was never
whether this money exists. It is whether
you are going to be one of the people
who actually asks for it. Therefore,
stop thinking of this as five separate
chores and start seeing it for what it
really is, a single afternoon that pays
you $4,000 and then quietly pays you
that same amount again every year you
stay enrolled.
There are very few hours left in your
life that will ever pay you that well
and this is one of them. And those are
just the five monthly bills. Before I
give you the action steps, let me hand
you a quick bonus round because once you
start pulling this thread, the discount
seniors are owed are everywhere and they
go unclaimed for the exact same reason.
First, your property taxes. Most states
give homeowners over 65 an exemption
that shields part of your home's value
or a freeze that locks your assessment
so the bill stops climbing every year
and some seniors cut that bill by
thousands just by filing one form at the
county office. Second, your income
taxes. The moment you turn 65, the IRS
gives you a larger standard deduction
than younger filers get automatically
just for your age, lowering the income
you are taxed on before you do anything
at all. Third, your medical costs. If
your out-of-pocket medical and dental
bills are large enough in a year, you
can deduct the portion above a set share
of your income. And for a senior with
real health expenses, that deduction is
far from small.
Fourth, if you love the outdoors, the
lifetime senior national parks pass
costs $80 one time and gets you into
every national park for the rest of your
life, when a younger visitor pays nearly
that for a single year.
And fifth, look at your everyday life
because seniors routinely qualify for
discounts on vehicle registration,
public transit, even trash and water
fees, none of which any agency will ever
apply for you. And notice the real
problem with that whole list. Property
taxes, income taxes, medical deductions,
park passes, transit and utility
discounts, none of them are connected to
each other and none of them are
connected to the five bills before them.
They are scattered across a dozen
different agencies that will never once
talk to one another. And that scattering
is exactly why it all stays unclaimed.
No single office is ever going to hand
you the complete list because no single
office even has it. You are the only
person on Earth who can pull all of
these together for your own life. That
sounds daunting, but it is actually the
opportunity because almost nobody
bothers, which means almost every one of
these is still sitting there untouched
waiting for the person who finally does.
Let me leave you with a picture that
makes all of this click. Two seniors
living on the same street in nearly
identical situations. Same modest social
security check. Same paid off little
house. Same rising bills. The first one
watched a video like this, spent one
single afternoon on the phone, and
claimed the Medicare savings, the
prescription cap, the energy help, the
phone discount, and drop the bank fees.
$4 to $5,000 a year back in their budget
every year.
The second one meant to look into it,
felt a little overwhelmed, decided they
probably would not qualify anyway, and
never made one call.
Stretch that over 10 years and it is 40
or 50,000 dollars, real money that one
of them kept and the other one simply
handed over for no reason except that
they never asked. You are not behind
because you were careless. You are
behind because the system was quietly
built to keep you that way, betting on
confusion and silence and the hope that
you will assume instead of call. Today
is the day you stop betting with the
house and that brings me to the mistake
I promised, the single most expensive
one, the one that quietly disqualifies
eligible seniors from every program on
this entire list. The mistake comes in
two parts. The first part is assuming
any of this is automatic. None of it is.
Every program requires an application
and several of them, the energy
assistance and the phone discount in
particular,
must be refiled every single year or
they silently expire and your bills
climb right back to full price while you
assume you are still covered. The second
part of the mistake is even more common
and honestly, it is the heartbreaking
one because it is people disqualifying
themselves. They hear there is an income
limit, they assume they must earn too
much and they never even pick up the
phone to check. When in reality, the
limits are higher than they believe and
the programs are wider than they expect.
Understand this clearly, a senior who
qualifies for thousands of dollars in
relief and never applies is treated by
the system exactly the same as a senior
who does not qualify at all. Both of
them pay full price for everything. The
only difference between them, almost
every single time, is that one of them
asked and the other one talked
themselves out of it. I think of a man
who saw the new prescription cap come
in, that $2,000 limit, and assumed it
would just happen on its own because it
was a law. So, he never reviewed his
plan or switched to one that applied it
correctly, and he kept overpaying for
another full year before his daughter
finally caught it. The benefit was real.
It was the law. It still cost him
thousands because the one thing a law
will never do is fill out your paperwork
for you. So, here is exactly what to do
this week, and not one step cost you a
dollar. Step one, for your Medicare
premium and your drug costs, call your
State Health Insurance Assistance
Program, often just called SHIP, which
gives free unbiased Medicare counseling,
and ask them to check whether you
qualify for a Medicare Savings Program
and extra help. They will walk you
through the whole application. Step two,
for your energy bill, search your
state's name followed by the word
LIHEAP, or call your local community
action agency and ask when the next
enrollment window opens. Step three, for
your phone and internet, ask your
current provider whether they offer the
Lifeline discount, or look up the
Lifeline program directly and apply.
Step four, for your bank fees, call your
bank today and ask one simple question,
"Do you have a senior checking account
with no monthly fee, and can you move me
to it?"
Step five, and this is the one people
forget. Put a note on your calendar to
reapply every year for the ones that
require it because these benefits expire
and the agencies are quietly counting on
you to forget.
And one tip that makes every single one
of these calls easier so you never feel
lost on the phone,
you do not need to memorize the program
names or the income rules. You only need
one sentence. Tell whoever answers, "I
am a senior on a fixed income and I want
to know every program I qualify for to
lower this bill." And then let them do
the work.
Write down what they tell you, ask them
to send the application, and ask for the
deadline.
That one sentence repeated to a few
different offices is the entire system.
You do not have to be an expert. You
just have to be the person who calls.
And if you are watching this for a
parent instead of for for
this might be the most valuable
afternoon you ever give them. A lot of
seniors will never make these calls on
their own. That widow I described at the
start is real in millions of homes, and
she will not phone a government office
to ask for help, because she does not
want to be a burden, or she simply
cannot believe a benefit this large
could really be sitting there with her
name on it. So, sit down next to her,
make the calls together, fill out the
forms at the kitchen table. Putting two
or three thousand dollars a year back
into a parent's budget, and lifting the
quiet fear of the next bill off their
shoulders, may be the kindest thing you
do for them all year. And if your
parents have already passed, or you are
not close with them, then do this for
someone else. The widow down the street
who waves to you every morning, the
veteran at your church, anyone you know
who is living quietly on a fixed income
and is far too proud to ever ask for
help. This is the rare kind of help that
costs you absolutely nothing to give,
and can change a person's entire month.
Forward them this video, sit down at the
kitchen table with them, and make the
calls together. Because somewhere very
close to you, right now, tonight, there
is someone splitting their pills in half
who does not have to be. And one short
conversation from you might be the only
thing that finally gets them to pick up
the phone and claim what was theirs all
along. You spend your entire life paying
into this system. These programs are not
a handout, they are money that was set
aside for you, sitting in an account
with your name on it, waiting for one
thing, for you to ask. So, do not keep
waiting for a letter that tells you it
is there, because that letter is never
going to come. To start, call your state
health insurance assistance program for
the Medicare savings, and your local
community action agency for the rest, or
just search your county name with the
words senior assistance programs. Make
those calls this week. Every single
month you wait is money you will never
get back.

title: If You Own Your Home and You're Over 60, File These 5 Documents Before a Nursing Home Takes It

segments.text: A single year in a nursing home now
costs more than $111,000.
And when your savings run out and
Medicaid finally steps in to pay, the
government does something most families
never see coming.
After you die, it comes back for your
house to get its money back. And the
family that thought they were inheriting
a paid-off home instead inherits a bill.
Let me make this real because it happens
to careful families every single day.
Picture a man who did everything right.
He worked 40 years, paid off his house,
saved a modest nest egg, and planned to
leave all of it to his two kids. Then at
81, he has a stroke and needs full-time
care. The nursing home is over $9,000 a
month, and within about two years, his
entire life savings is gone, spent down
to almost nothing just to qualify for
Medicaid to take over the bill. He
passes a year later, and his children,
grieving, go to handle the house, the
one asset he had left, the one thing he
was sure he was leaving them. And
waiting in the mailbox is a notice from
the state's Medicaid recovery program, a
claim for everything Medicaid paid,
secured against the house. They are
given a choice that is not a choice. Pay
the state back or sell the home. Every
dollar gone, and it was all avoidable.
That is the story these five documents
are designed to prevent. So, let us make
sure it is never yours. But, it does not
have to happen, and that is what this
video is about. There are five documents
that, put in place correctly and in
time, can protect your home and your
life savings from being drained by a
nursing home and then clawed back by the
state. Not a loophole, not a scam, real
legal tools that elder law attorneys use
every single day for the families who
know to ask. The problem is that almost
nobody knows to ask, and almost
everybody waits until it is too late.
So, here is what I am going to do. I am
going to give you all five documents,
what each one protects, and when you
have to have it in place. But, stay with
me because the fourth document is one
that even people who think they have
planned almost always miss. The fifth
one can still protect a huge chunk of
your savings even if you are already
staring down a nursing home with no time
left. And there is one mistake, the most
common one of all, that does the exact
opposite of what people think and
actually hands more of your money to the
state. I will show you that mistake
before the end. First, you have to
understand the trap because if you do
not understand it, you will walk right
into it. Someone turning 65 today has
almost a 70% chance of needing long-term
care at some point. That more comes
straight from the United States
Department of Health and Human Services.
And long-term care is staggeringly
expensive, more than $111,000
a year for a shared room in a nursing
home and over $127,000
for a private one according to the 2024
Genworth Cost of Care Survey. Almost no
family can pay that out of pocket for
long, so the money runs out and Medicaid
takes over. But Medicaid is not a gift.
Federal law under Title 42 of the United
States Code, Section 1396p,
requires every state to try to recover
what it spent on your care after you
pass away. And the single biggest asset
it comes after is your home. That is the
trap. You do not lose the house while
you are alive. You lose it after when
your children open a letter from the
state instead of a deed. These five
documents are how you close that trap
before it ever springs. And before I
give them to you, I have to clear away
three beliefs that keep families from
protecting themselves because you may be
holding one right now.
Belief one.
I do not have enough to bother.
If you own a home, you have enough.
Because the home is almost always the
single largest thing the state comes
after. And protecting it is the whole
ball game.
Belief two.
Medicaid will just take everything
anyway, so why fight it?
That is exactly what they are counting
on you to think and it is false.
The entire field of elder law exists
because the law is full of legal,
deliberate protections. And the families
who use them keep their homes while the
families who give up lose them.
Belief three. My will protects me. It
does not.
A will does nothing to stop a nursing
home from spending your savings while
you are alive and nothing to stop a
state recovery after you die. A will
just tells a probate court who gets
whatever is left. And if you do nothing
else, the answer will be almost nothing.
Throw those three beliefs out because
every one of them talks people out of
acting until it is too late. Document
number one, the lady bird deed, also
called an enhanced life estate deed.
This is a special kind of deed that lets
you keep complete control of your home
for the rest of your life. You can live
in it, sell it, mortgage it, change your
mind entirely, and then the moment you
pass, the home transfers directly to
your children outside of probate. Here
is why it is so powerful against a
nursing home. Because the house passes
outside of your probate estate, the
state generally cannot reach it a state
recovery. And because you kept full
control the whole time, the law does not
treat it as a gift, so it does not
trigger the penalty I am about to
explain. It is recognized in a handful
of states, including Florida, Michigan,
Texas, Vermont, and West Virginia. And
many other states offer a similar
transfer on death deed. For the right
homeowner, this one page is the
difference between your children keeping
the house and the state selling it. To
put a real number on it, on a home worth
$400,000, that single deed can be the
difference between your kids inheriting
$400,000 in equity and inheriting
nothing once the state takes its share.
One page against $400,000.
That is the trade you are making by not
signing it. Document number two, the
Medicaid Asset Protection Trust. And
this is the heavy artillery, the single
most powerful tool an elder law attorney
has.
You create an irrevocable trust and you
move your assets into it. Your home,
your savings, your investments. Once
they are in that trust, after a waiting
period, they are completely invisible to
Medicaid. Not reduced, invisible. If you
need care, Medicaid pays, and there is
nothing left in your name for the state
to recover from afterward. So,
everything inside that trust passes to
your family fully protected. But, here
is the catch that makes timing
everything. The trust has to be created
and funded at least 5 years and 1 day
before you apply for Medicaid. That is
the famous 5-year rule.
Money you move into the trust today does
not become protected until that clock
runs out. Therefore, the single most
valuable day to set up this trust is not
the day you get sick. It is today, while
you are healthy and the clock can start.
Let me show you what that protection is
worth. Say at 70 years old, in good
health, you move a paid-off home and
$150,000 of savings into the trust. 5
years and 1 day later, every dollar of
it, the house and the savings, is
invisible to Medicaid. If you need care
at 76, Medicaid pays the bill, and your
family still inherits the entire amount,
fully protected. And this is the right
moment to actually understand the 5-year
rule, because it confuses everyone. When
you apply for Medicaid, the state looks
back at every transfer you made in the
60 months before, and anything you gave
away or sold for less than it was worth
in that window creates a penalty. The
trust is simply a way to make a transfer
that, once the clock has run, the
look-back can no longer reach. That is
the entire reason starting early is
everything, because the only thing you
cannot buy later is time. Document
number three, a durable financial power
of attorney, but not the simple one most
people sign. It has to be a power of
attorney that specifically includes the
authority to do Medicaid and gifting
planning. Here is why that matters more
than almost anything. If you have a
stroke or develop dementia before your
planning is done, someone has to be able
to step in and protect your assets for
you. Move money into the trust, file the
paperwork, make the legal transfers. A
standard power of attorney often does
not grant those exact powers, and
without them, your family is frozen.
They cannot protect a single dollar, and
they have to go to court for permission
while the nursing home bill, more than
$9,000 a month, eats your life savings
in real time. Picture it for just a
second. Your spouse has a stroke on a
Tuesday. By Friday, your family wants to
move the savings into the trust to start
protecting it, and the bank says no,
because the only person who could
authorize that move is the one lying in
the hospital bed, and the simple power
of attorney you signed years ago does
not include the power to make those
transfers.
Now you are hiring a lawyer and waiting
on a judge for guardianship, which takes
weeks or months, and every single one of
those weeks the nursing home is billing
more than $9,000,
draining the exact money you were trying
to save.
The right document, signed years before
any of this happens, is what keeps that
door open instead of slamming it shut at
the worst possible moment. One correctly
written document keeps your family in
control instead of locked out. And let
me re-anchor you right here, because
this is the heart of the whole thing.
Every tool I am describing, the deed,
the trust, the powers of attorney, only
works if it is already in place before
the crisis. And the crisis gives no
warning. 70% of seniors will need this
kind of care, and not one of them got a
save the date for the stroke or the
diagnosis that started it. This
protection is not something you grab on
the way to the hospital. It is something
you build while the sun is still
shining, and that is exactly why so many
families miss it. They were not
careless. They simply believed they had
more time. Document number four. The
document almost everyone misses, even
people who thought they planned. And it
is the caregiver child agreement. Here
is the situation it solves. Medicaid
normally penalizes you for giving away
assets in the 5 years before you apply,
including your home, but there is a
powerful exception written into the law.
If one of your adult children moved in
and provided care for you for at least 2
years, care that kept you out of a
nursing home longer than you otherwise
would have been, you are allowed to
transfer the home to that child with no
penalty at all, even inside the 5-year
window.
The catch is that you have to be able to
prove it, and that is where the document
comes in.
A written caregiver agreement with dates
and duties created at the time is what
turns a loving child into a legally
protected transfer. The families who
write it down keep the house. The ones
who just assume mom helping will count
find out too late that the state does
not take their word for it. Let me show
you how close this comes for real
families. A daughter cuts back at work,
moves into her mother's home, and spends
2 years cooking, bathing, and driving to
doctor's appointments, doing the work
that would have cost a nursing home a
fortune.
When the mother finally needs full-time
care, the family assumes the house will
of course go to the daughter who gave up
2 years of her life for it. But Medicaid
looks at the transfer, sees a home
handed to a child, and gets ready to
apply a penalty.
Until the family produces a signed
caregiver agreement and a doctor's note
showing that her care is what kept her
mother out of a facility.
That single piece of paper is the only
thing standing between the daughter
keeping the home and the daughter losing
it. Same care, same sacrifice. The only
difference is whether somebody wrote it
down at the time. Document number five,
a Medicaid compliant annuity. And this
is the one I told you can still save
your money even when you are out of
time. Say a health crisis hits tomorrow
and you never set up the trust. You are
not out of luck. A Medicaid compliant
annuity lets you take a chunk of
countable savings, the money that would
otherwise have to be spent down to
almost nothing before Medicaid pays, and
convert it into a protected stream of
income instead. Done correctly, it does
not violate the 5-year rule. And for a
married couple, it can shield tens of
thousands of dollars that would
otherwise have gone straight to the
nursing home. It is the emergency tool,
the one your attorney reaches for when
the trust window has already closed. And
there are a few more protections worth
knowing because the system has more
doors than people realize. First,
understand that your home is actually an
exempt asset while you are alive and
intend to return to it up to an equity
limit that in 2026 ranges from about
to over $1 million depending on your
state. So, Medicaid generally does not
force you to sell the home to qualify.
The danger is almost entirely after
death through recovery, which is exactly
what the deed and the trust are for.
Second, there is a legitimate way to
spend down that has nothing to do with
going broke. Before you ever qualify,
you are allowed to spend your countable
savings on exempt things, paying off
your mortgage or other debt, making
needed home repairs, buying a reliable
car, or prepaying funeral and burial
costs through an irrevocable plan. Every
dollar moved from a countable account
into an exempt asset is a dollar the
nursing home cannot demand, and it is
completely allowed. Third, for those
already in a crisis, elder law attorneys
use a strategy often called half a loaf,
where you protect roughly half of your
remaining assets by gifting them and use
a Medicaid compliant annuity to cover
the penalty period the gift creates, so
that instead of losing everything, a
family keeps a meaningful share.
Therefore, even when it feels like it is
too late, it is almost never the case
that nothing can be done. There is
almost always a move left if you call
the right person. So, let me put the
whole picture together because the
stakes here are not abstract. Take a
typical situation, a home worth three or
four hundred thousand dollars and a nest
egg of one or two hundred thousand. With
none of these documents in place, a
multi-year nursing home stay can consume
the savings down to almost nothing and
then take the house through estate
recovery, leaving your children with
effectively zero. With the same
documents in place in time, that same
family keeps the home and most or all of
the savings while Medicaid still pays
for the care. Therefore, we are not
talking about shaving a little off the
edges. We are talking about whether the
entire estate you spent a lifetime
building survives intact or whether it
vanishes into the system in the last 2
years of your life. That is what is
actually on the table and that is why a
single afternoon in an elder law
attorney's office may be worth more than
any investment you have ever made. Now,
I have to clear up the most dangerous
myth in all of this because it is the
mistake I promised you and it is the one
that does the opposite of what people
think. People hear about the 5-year rule
and they panic and they decide the
simple fix is to just give the house and
the money to the kids now, today, to get
it out of their name. Please, do not do
this. Giving your assets away directly
is the single fastest way to disqualify
yourself. Every dollar you gift in those
5 years creates a penalty period, a
stretch of time where Medicaid will
flatly refuse to pay for your care,
calculated by taking what you gave away
and dividing it by the average monthly
cost of a nursing home in your state.
Give away $100,000 and you can lock
yourself out of paid care for the better
part of a year, right when you need it
most. And it gets worse because there is
no income limit forgiveness on this.
People also believe the IRS gift rule
protects them, that because you can give
$19,000 a year without a gift tax form
in 2026, that gift is safe. It is not.
That is an IRS rule and it has nothing
to do with Medicaid. A gift that is
perfectly fine to the IRS still triggers
the full Medicaid penalty. And one more
hidden cost because when you give the
house away outright instead of using a
deed or a trust, your children lose what
is called the stepped-up basis, which
can stick them with a capital gains tax
bill of tens of thousands of dollars
when they sell. So, the do-it-yourself
gift fails three different ways at once.
The tools in this video exist precisely
because the obvious move is the wrong
one. Let me re-anchor you on why the
timing matters so much because it is the
whole game. Remember that 70% chance of
needing care, and remember the 5-year
clock on the trust. Put those two facts
together, and the conclusion is
unavoidable. The protection only works
if it is already in place before the
crisis, and the crisis does not send a
warning. A stroke does not schedule
itself. So, the deadline on all of this
is not a date on a calendar. The
deadline is your own health, and it can
arrive without any notice at all. The
families who lose everything are almost
never the ones who did not care. They
are the ones who meant to get to it and
ran out of time. And here is the
protection for the spouse, because I do
not want to scare a married couple into
thinking they will be wiped out. Federal
law protects the healthy spouse. The
husband or wife who stays home can keep
the house while you are alive, and can
keep a share of the savings, called the
community spouse resource allowance,
which in 2026 can be as much as
So, even in a crisis, a married couple
is not left with nothing. But, notice
what that protection depends on, a
living spouse.
For the millions of seniors who are
widowed or single, those automatic
shields do not apply, and the documents
in this video become the only protection
there is. Let me leave you with a
picture that matters most. Two families
living on the same street in nearly the
same situation. Both have a paid-off
home and a lifetime of savings. Both
have a parent who needs a nursing home
at 80 years old. The first family did
nothing, because they meant to get to it
and simply never did, and 4 years later,
the savings are gone, and the state has
a claim on the house, and the children
inherit almost nothing but the cost of
the funeral. The second family sat down
with an elder law attorney years
earlier, put the deed and the trust and
the powers in place, and started the
5-year clock while their mother was
still healthy. Same illness, same bills,
same Medicaid paying for the same care
in the same facility. But, the second
family keeps the house and the savings,
hundreds of thousands of dollars, passed
down exactly as their parents intended.
Nothing separated those two families
except a few documents and the decision
to act in time. Do not be the first
family. So, here is exactly what to do,
and the first step is the most important
one.
Step one, find an elder law attorney,
specifically an elder law attorney, not
a general lawyer, because Medicaid
planning is its own specialty. Most
offer a free first consultation.
Step two, ask them the single most
important question. Given my age, my
health, and my state, what should I put
in place now, while I'm healthy, to
protect my home and my savings from a
nursing home?
Step three, if you own a home, ask
specifically about a ladybird deed or a
Medicaid asset protection trust, and
start the 5-year clock as early as you
possibly can, because that clock only
runs while you are well.
Step four, make sure your power of
attorney actually includes gifting and
Medicaid planning powers, because the
standard one usually does not.
Step five, if a child is caring for you,
write the caregiver agreement down now
with dates, not later from memory. And
if you are watching this for a parent,
rather than for yourself, understand
that this might be the most important
conversation you ever have with them.
And the hardest.
A lot of seniors will not do this on
their own. They do not want to think
about a nursing home, they do not want
to feel like a burden, and they do not
believe the state would really take the
house.
So, you may have to be the one who
gently starts it. You do not have to
have the answers.
You just have to get them in front of an
elder law attorney while they are still
healthy and the 5-year clock can still
run.
Making that one appointment and going
with them can be the difference between
your family keeping everything your
parents built and watching it disappear
into a system that was counting on no
one speaking up. You spend a lifetime
building what you have, so you could
pass it on, not hand it to a nursing
home in the state in the last chapter.
The tools to protect it are real, they
are legal, and they are sitting in an
elder law attorney's office waiting for
you. The only thing they require is that
you act while you still can. To find a
qualified elder law attorney near you,
go to NAELA.org,
the National Academy of Elder Law
Attorneys. NAELA.org.
Make the call while the five-year clock
can still start.

title: Your Will Is Worthless Without These 6 Documents (Most Seniors Skip #4)

segments.text: If you own your home and the only thing
protecting it is a will, the state can
still take up to 7% of everything you
leave behind before your children ever
see a single dollar. On a $500,000
estate, that is 15,000 to 35,000 dollars
gone to court costs and legal fees. And
most seniors have no idea it is even
happening until the day their family is
standing in a courthouse hallway holding
a will and being told it changes
nothing. I want you to picture something
because some version of this happens
somewhere in this country every single
day. A man works 40 years, pays off his
house, and leaves a simple will that
says the home goes to his daughter. He
dies believing he did everything right,
but his daughter does not get the keys.
She gets a court date. She gets a
lawyer's invoice. And 9 months later,
after the fees are finally paid, she
inherits a house that is worth less than
it was the day he died because nobody
ever told him the truth. A will is not
the document that protects your home. A
will is the document that sends your
home to court. There are six documents
that quietly decide who really gets your
house. And the fourth one on this list
is the single page that almost every
senior skips. It is the difference
between your paid-off home passing to
your children untouched and the state
quietly taking it back after you are
gone. I am going to get to document
four, but you need the first three in
place before it will even matter. So,
stay with me. Now, three quick promises
about what is coming so you know it is
worth your time. Two of these six
documents are completely free and you
can take care of them this week without
paying anyone a cent. There is one
mistake that erases all six even if you
do everything else perfectly, and I will
show you exactly what it is near the
end. And there is a hidden deadline on
document four, a deadline that has
nothing to do with any date on a
calendar, and missing it is the single
most common way careful families lose
the house anyway. Keep all three of
those in the back of your mind as we go.
Let me start with a number that should
stop you cold. 76% of Americans do not
even have a will. That figure comes from
the 2025 caring.com wills and estate
planning study, and it is the lowest it
has been in years. A separate 2026
report from Trust & Will found that 56%
of Americans have no estate plan at all.
So, more than half of the people
watching this right now have nothing in
place. But, here is what nobody tells
the other half, the ones who feel safe
because they once sat down and wrote a
will. Having a will is not the finish
line. A will does not avoid probate. A
will is simply your written instructions
to the probate court. And probate is the
slow, public, expensive court process
that decides how your property changes
hands after you die. According to the
National Center for State Courts, the
average estate takes about 9 months to
settle. Many drag on for 2 years or
longer, and the entire time your house
and your accounts sit frozen while the
fees come straight out of what your
family was supposed to inherit. Probate
is also completely public. Anyone, a
neighbor, a scammer, an estranged
relative looking for an opening, can
walk into the courthouse and read
exactly what you owned and exactly who
got it. Therefore, the real goal is not
just to have the right documents sitting
in a drawer. The goal is to keep your
house and your money out of probate
entirely. These six documents are how
you do exactly that. But, before I give
you the first document, I have to clear
away four myths because these are the
exact beliefs that cost families their
homes, and you may be holding on to one
of them right now without knowing it.
Myth one, a will avoids probate. It does
not. I just said it, but it is worth
repeating because it is the single most
expensive misunderstanding in this
country. Your will is your ticket into
probate, not your way around it. Myth
two, my spouse automatically gets
everything, so we are fine. Not
necessarily. Without the right titling
and the right documents, even a husband
or wife of 50 years can be forced
through probate, locked out of accounts,
and unable to sell the family home for
months while they wait on a judge. Myth
three, I do not have enough for any of
this to matter. If you own a home, you
have more than enough for it to matter.
The house is almost always the single
largest asset a family ever fights over.
And as you are about to see, it is the
asset the state targets first.
Myth four,
my home is my homestead, so it is
protected no matter what.
A homestead exemption can shield your
home from many creditors while you are
alive,
but in most states, it does not stop
your home from going through probate
when you die, and it does not
automatically stop Medicaid from
recovering against it afterward.
The protection you think you have can
disappear the very moment you pass away.
Clear those four out of your head right
now, because everything I'm about to
give you is built on the truth, not the
myth. Now, there is one more thing I
have to warn you about before document
one, because it is the trap good
families fall into when they try to
handle all of this themselves. Someone
tells them the simplest fix is to just
add their child to the deed as a joint
owner, so the house passes automatically
when they die. It sounds smart. It is a
disaster waiting to happen. The moment
you add your child as a joint owner, the
law can treat it as a gift of half your
home, which may legally have to be
reported to the IRS. Worse, that half of
your house is now exposed to your
child's entire life. If your child gets
sued, goes through a divorce, files for
bankruptcy, or simply falls behind on
their taxes, a creditor can come after
your home, the home you still live in
every day, because your child is now a
legal owner of it. And there is one more
hidden cost. When you give away part of
your home this way, the portion you gave
can lose the stepped-up basis I'm going
to explain later. And that can hand your
family a capital gains tax bill of tens
of thousands of dollars they never saw
coming.
Adding a child to your deed feels like
protection. It is the opposite of
protection. The documents I am about to
give you accomplish everything people
think joint ownership does without a
single one of those dangers. Document
one, the transfer on death deed, also
called a beneficiary deed.
This is a deed you sign and record now
while you are alive that names exactly
who your house goes to the moment you
pass. And the part that surprises people
most is how much control you keep. You
can live in the home, sell it, rent it
out, borrow against it, or change your
mind and name someone else entirely. All
without asking permission from anyone
because while you are breathing, it is
still completely your house.
The person you named has no rights, no
access, and no say until the day you
die. But the instant you pass, the home
transfers directly to them with no
probate, no court hearing, and no
9-month wait. Roughly 30 states now
allow some version of this deed. On a
$500,000 home, recording this one piece
of paper can save your family $15,000 to
$35,000 in fees. And it can save them a
year of their lives fighting paperwork
while they are still grieving you.
One page filed at the county recorder's
office can do what people wrongly
believe a will does. Document two, your
beneficiary designations. And this is
the one that shocks people the most
because it quietly overrules almost
everything else you have signed. The
beneficiary form on your retirement
account and your life insurance
overrides your will every single time.
The IRS treats your 401K, your IRA, and
your life insurance as contracts. And
the company is legally required to pay
whoever is named on that form no matter
what your will says. Let me make that
real. Imagine your will leaves
everything to your children. You signed
it last year. It is notarized. It is
airtight. Your lawyer says it is
perfect. But your old IRA still lists an
ex-spouse you divorced 20 years ago
because you opened that account back in
1990 and never touched the beneficiary
line again. When you die, your ex gets
that money, not your children. And no
will, no lawyer, and no judge can undo
it because the contract always wins. A
$200,000 account can land in the hands
of someone you have not spoken to in
decades, all because of one outdated
line on a form you forgot existed. And
it gets worse in two ways most people
never consider.
If the only beneficiary you named has
already died and you never updated the
form, that money can fall straight back
into your estate and go through probate
after all.
And if you named a young grandchild
directly, a minor cannot legally receive
it. So, a court has to appoint someone
to manage that money under court
supervision until the child grows up.
Which is exactly the kind of mess you
were trying to avoid.
So, here is your free action.
Pull up every retirement account and
every insurance policy you own. Read the
primary beneficiary out loud and make
sure there is a backup, what they call a
contingent beneficiary, named right
behind them.
Fixing this costs nothing and it is the
most common expensive mistake there is.
Document three, payable on death
registration on your bank and brokerage
accounts.
This is the second free document on the
list and it is a one-page form you can
get at your bank today. It does for your
cash exactly what the deed does for your
house. Without it, every dollar in your
checking, your savings, your money
market and your CDs is frozen inside
probate for 6 to 24 months. Think about
what that actually means for the people
you leave behind. The mortgage payment
still comes due, the property tax bill
still comes due, the funeral home still
wants to be paid and a funeral in this
country now averages well over $8,000.
But your spouse or your children cannot
legally touch the money you left
specifically to cover those exact things
because it is locked inside a
courthouse.
Families end up putting a funeral on a
credit card while tens of thousands of
dollars of their own inheritance sit
frozen a few miles away. With a payable
on death form, that same money becomes
legally theirs within days of your
passing. No court involved, no waiting.
The bank will hand you the form for free
if you simply ask. Almost nobody ever
asks because almost nobody knows to.
Now, before I give you document four,
understand this clearly. If you do
nothing else after this entire video, do
the next one. Because documents one,
two, and three keep your home and your
money out of probate. Document four is
what keeps them away from something far
more dangerous and far more aggressive
than probate will ever be. So, listen
closely. Document four, the one almost
every senior skips, and the one I
promised would have a hidden deadline. A
regular transfer on death deed keeps
your house out of probate, but it does
not always protect it from Medicaid. And
here is the trap that catches good,
careful, hard-working families every
single day. Someone turning 65 today has
almost a 70% chance of needing some form
of long-term care in their remaining
years. That is not a scare number I made
up. That comes directly from the United
States Department of Health and Human
Services, published on their own
website. And long-term care is
staggeringly expensive. According to the
2024 Genworth Cost of Care Survey, the
national median cost of a semi-private
room in a nursing home is now more than
a year. A private room runs over
a year. The average nursing home stay
lasts more than two years. Almost no
family can pay that out of pocket. So,
Medicaid steps in and covers the bill.
But after you die, federal law, under
Title 42 of the United States Code,
Section 1396P,
requires your state to try to recover
everything Medicaid spent on your care.
And the single biggest thing it comes
after is your house.
This is called estate recovery. It is
real. It is happening right now in all
50 states, and most people have never
even heard the term until the letter
shows up in the mailbox. Let me tell you
how it actually plays out, because it is
never what people imagine. Your parent
passes away. The funeral is over. The
family finally exhales and starts going
through the house. The house that has
been in the family for 30 years, the one
that was always supposed to go to the
kids. And then a notice arrives from the
state's Medicaid recovery program. It is
a claim against the estate for
everything Medicaid paid for that
nursing home care, often well over
$100,000, sometimes two or three times
that much. In many cases, the state can
place a lien directly on the home, and
the family is handed a choice that is
not really a choice at all. Pay the
state back in full, or sell the house to
satisfy the claim. Families who were
certain they were inheriting a home end
up writing a check to the government or
watching the home get sold out from
under them, simply because one deed was
the wrong kind of deed. Now, there are
some important protections written into
that same federal law, and you deserve
to know them.
The state cannot recover while a
surviving spouse is still alive.
It cannot recover if you are survived by
a child under the age of 21, or by a
child who is blind or disabled at any
age.
And in many cases, it cannot force a
sale when a caregiver child has lived in
the home for at least two years and
provided the care that kept you out of
the nursing home longer. Or when a
sibling with an ownership interest has
lived there for at least a year.
There is also an undue hardship waiver
families can apply for.
But notice what every one of those
protections has in common.
They depend on someone specific
surviving you or living in that home.
For the millions of seniors who are
widowed, or whose children are grown and
living their own lives elsewhere, none
of those shields apply, and the house is
fully exposed. So, here is the real
protection, and here is that hidden
deadline I promised. The shield is a
specific kind of deed called an enhanced
life estate deed, far better known as a
ladybird deed. Because you keep full
control of the property until the day
you die, the law does not treat it as a
gift, which means it does not trigger
Medicaid's five-year look-back penalty
the way simply giving the house away
would. And because the house passes
outside of your probate estate, the
state generally cannot reach it through
estate recovery. It is formally
recognized in Florida, Michigan, Texas,
Vermont, and West Virginia. And many
other states offer a transfer on death
deed that accomplishes part of the same
goal. But here is the deadline. None of
this works if you wait until you are
already sick, already in a crisis, or no
longer mentally able to sign. You can
only put these protections in place
while you are still competent and still
in control. The deadline is not a date.
The deadline is your health, and it can
arrive without any warning at all. The
families who lose the house are almost
never the ones who did not care. They
are the ones who waited 1 year too long.
Document five, a durable financial power
of attorney. And this one is not about
your death at all. It is about the years
right before it, which is where most
families actually get destroyed
financially, long before any inheritance
is ever discussed. If you have a stroke,
or you develop dementia, and you have
not signed this document first, then no
one, not even your spouse of 50 years,
can legally sell your house, refinance
your mortgage, move your investments, or
manage your money for you. People simply
assume a spouse automatically has that
power. They do not. Instead, your family
has to go to court and ask a judge for
something called guardianship, or
conservatorship, a process that
routinely costs $3,000 to $10,000 in
legal fees, takes months to complete,
and in many states drags your family
back into court for supervision every
single year for the rest of your life.
While that plays out, the bills go
unpaid, the house cannot be touched, and
your loved ones are filling out court
forms instead of sitting at your
bedside.
You should also pair this with a
healthcare power of attorney, sometimes
called a healthcare proxy, along with a
HIPAA release, so the person you trust
can actually speak to your doctors and
make medical decisions when you cannot.
All of it, every dollar and every delay
and every helpless moment is avoided by
a few pages signed in advance while you
are still healthy enough to sign them.
Now, I need to rehook you for a moment,
because here is a statistic that should
reframe everything I just told you.
Remember that 70% chance of needing
long-term care? For women, the need
lasts even longer, an average of nearly
4 years of care. Women also tend to
outlive their husbands. That means the
people most likely to be sitting alone
at the kitchen table making these
decisions as a widow managing a paid-off
home by themselves are the exact people
the system is most likely to come after
and the exact people with the fewest of
those family protections left. This is
not paranoia. This is simply the math of
how the system is built, which brings us
to the last document, the one that ties
every other one of these together into a
single plan, document six, the revocable
living trust. This is the master
document. You create the trust and then
you move your house and your accounts
into it while you are alive and in
complete control as your own trustee.
Nothing about your daily life changes at
all. You still own everything. You still
spend your money however you please. You
can still sell the house tomorrow if you
want to. But when you die, everything
held inside that trust passes to your
family privately and almost instantly
with no probate whatsoever. Therefore,
no court, no 9-month delay, no public
record of what you own for strangers to
read, and no $15 to $35,000
eating into the inheritance. A good
trust does even more than that. It can
include instructions for what happens if
you become incapacitated, so the person
you choose steps in immediately without
any guardianship court at all. And it
lets you control not just who inherits,
but how and when. You can say that a
child receives their share gradually
instead of all at once, which protects
the money from a bad marriage, a
lawsuit, or a child who is simply not
good with money. A will cannot do that.
And there is one more benefit most
people miss entirely. Your heirs receive
what the IRS calls a stepped-up basis.
Let me show you exactly what that is
worth. Say you bought your home decades
ago for $80,000, and today it is worth
$400,000. If you simply gave it to your
children while you were alive, they
would inherit your original $80,000
basis. And if they sold, they could owe
capital gains tax on $320,000 of growth.
But if that same home passes through
your trust at your death, the basis
resets to the full $400,000 value, and
that capital gains tax can disappear
entirely. That one feature, all by
itself, can save your family tens of
thousands of dollars. And now the
mistake I promised you at the very
beginning, the one that erases all six.
People hear about a living trust, they
go to a lawyer, they pay good money to
have one drawn up, they sign it, they
feel protected, and then they take it
home, put it in a drawer, and never fund
it. Funding the trust means actually
retitling your house and your accounts
into the name of the trust. A trust that
does not legally own your house does
absolutely nothing to protect your
house. It is an empty box with a fancy
lid. This is one of the most common and
most heartbreaking failures in all of
estate planning. Families who did the
responsible thing, who paid for the
document, who thought they were covered,
and who still marched straight into
probate because the deed on the house
was never actually changed. So, if you
remember only one thing about trust from
this entire video, remember this. The
trust is not finished when you sign it.
The trust is finished when your home is
titled in its name. There is one last
habit that protects everything else, and
it costs you nothing.
Tell the people you trust where these
documents are and what they say. A
beneficiary cannot claim what they
cannot find.
Every year families lose money simply
because no one knew an account or a
policy existed.
Keep the originals somewhere safe but
reachable. Give a trusted person a copy,
or at least a list, and review all of it
every 3 to 5 years, and especially after
any big life change. A death, a divorce,
a marriage, a new grandchild, or a move
to a new state. Because the rules and
the right deed can change when you cross
a state line. Here is exactly what to do
this week. One, call your bank and ask
for the payable on on form for every
account you have. It is free and it
takes about 10 minutes. Two, log in to
every retirement account and every
insurance policy, read the beneficiary
name out loud, fix any that are wrong,
and add a backup beneficiary behind each
one.
Three, find out whether your state
allows a ladybird deed or a transfer on
death deed. And if you own a home and
there is any chance you might one day
need care, talk to an elder law attorney
about which deed actually protects you.
Most offer a free first consultation.
Four,
ask that same attorney whether a
revocable living trust makes sense for
your house. And if you already have one,
ask the only question that truly
matters.
Is my home actually titled in the name
of my trust?
Five, sign a durable financial power of
attorney and a healthcare proxy now
while you are healthy and tell your
family where everything is kept. You do
not need all six in a single day.
But you do need to start because the one
thing none of us is ever promised is
time.
And as you now know, the deadline on the
most important document of all is your
own health.
To find a qualified elder law attorney
near you, go to naela.org,
the National Academy of Elder Law
Attorneys.
naela.org.
Start with document one.

title: 5 States Where The New Equity Tax Quietly Drains Your Home

segments.text: Five states are quietly putting in place
what amounts to a new equity tax on the
homes of older Americans. And in two of
those states, a senior who sells a
paid-off house this year can lose more
to the state before the proceeds ever
clear escrow. The mechanism is not
called an equity tax in any statute. It
is buried inside surtaxes, transfer
taxes, capital gains taxes, reassessment
triggers, and proposed wealth taxes that
piggyback on the value sitting inside
your home. But the practical result is
the same. The longer you have owned the
house, the more equity has built up, the
larger the bite the state takes on the
way out. The reason almost no one over
60 has heard of this is simple. These
taxes are written for income brackets
and asset thresholds that in any normal
year apply to nobody but the wealthy.
The trap is that selling a long-held
primary residence is not a normal year.
The capital gain on a house bought in
1985 and sold in 2026
is not a small number. It is often the
single largest taxable event of an
entire retirement. And in five specific
states, that one transaction is the
moment the equity tax fires. Consider a
composite scenario drawn from how this
commonly plays out for senior homeowners
in eastern Massachusetts. A couple in
their early 70s bought their home in
They paid the mortgage off by the late
1990s. They lived in the same house for
40 years. In 2025, they decided to sell,
downsize to a smaller condominium, and
use the equity to fund the rest of their
retirement. The home sold for
The check at closing, after the federal
capital gains exclusion for a married
couple, after the basis adjustment for
the modest improvements they had
documented, looked clean. They thought
the federal tax was the worst of it.
Then the Massachusetts return came due.
Between the regular state income tax on
the gain and the 4% surtax under the
fair share amendment that was triggered
by the size of the gain in a single tax
year, the Massachusetts Department of
Revenue collected close to $100,000
from that one transaction. The couple
had no idea any of that was coming.
Therefore, the question for any senior
homeowner in those five states is not
whether the equity tax exists. It is
whether you understand which trigger
applies to your situation, what range of
dollars is actually at risk, and what
filing made before the sale, before the
transfer, before the death of a spouse,
pulls the equity back out of the path of
the state. Most homeowners do not
realize that there is one set of forms
filed in a specific window of time that
limits the state's reach on equity in
all five of these states at once. By the
end of this video, the forms have a
name, the window has a deadline, and the
order has a sequence. But before that,
the five states. State number one is
Massachusetts.
Massachusetts voters approved something
called the Fair Share Amendment in 2022
by a thin margin. The amendment added a
4% surtax on top of the existing state
income tax for any taxpayer whose income
in a single year exceeds $1 million.
On its face, this is a wealthy person
tax. It was sold to voters as a
millionaire surtax. The governor's
office described it as a tax on the
rich. But here is the problem. The
Massachusetts Department of Revenue
defines income for this surtax broadly.
It includes the capital gain on the sale
of a home above the federal exclusion.
The federal exclusion lets a married
couple shield up to $500,000 of gain,
and a single homeowner up to 250,000.
After that, the gain counts as taxable
income. Therefore, consider the same
suburban Boston couple who bought their
home for 110,000
and sold it for 1,800,000.
The math the Department of Revenue runs
looks like this. Sale price, 1,800,000.
Original basis plus documented
improvements, roughly 200,000. Gross
Federal exclusion for a married couple,
500,000. Taxable gain at the state
That gain by itself, in a single tax
year, crosses the fair share threshold.
The 4% surtax applies. That is roughly
on top of the regular Massachusetts
state income tax of 5%, which is another
$55,000 on the same gain. Combined
Massachusetts tax on what looked like a
routine retirement downsize comes in
around $99,000.
But the part most retirees do not catch
is this. The 4% surtax does not apply
only to the dollars above 1 million in
income. It applies to the gain in a year
where total income exceeds 1 million. So
a senior with 50,000 in pension income,
25,000 in Social Security, and a
home gain ends up with 1,015,000
in income for that year. And the 4%
surtax fires on the slice above the
threshold. Therefore, the mitigation in
Massachusetts is real, and it is the
reason this section is worth your
attention. There are two strategies that
licensed Massachusetts tax attorneys
commonly use to soften the hit. The
first is to structure the sale as an
installment sale, where the buyer pays
over multiple years, and the gain is
recognized in pieces, never crossing the
1 million threshold in any single year.
The second is to file a Massachusetts
homestead declaration before the sale,
which is a separate state-level
protection that does not change the
surtax directly, but does protect equity
from creditor claims during the
transition. Some seniors also explore a
charitable remainder trust structure,
where the home is transferred to a trust
that sells it on tax-favored terms. None
of these are do-it-yourself moves. All
of them require a Massachusetts licensed
tax attorney or a certified public
accountant who specializes in real
estate transfers. The Fair Share
Amendment is the law as of recent
legislative reporting, but the income
brackets and exemption thresholds are
reviewed by the Massachusetts Department
of Revenue each year. Confirm the
current numbers with a Massachusetts
licensed professional before relying on
this video for any planning decision.
State number two is Washington. In 2021,
Washington passed the first state-level
capital gains tax in modern American
history. The state had no income tax
before this, and the new tax was
challenged in court for 2 years. In
the Washington Supreme Court upheld the
tax, classifying it as an excise tax
rather than an income tax, which
preserved its constitutionality under
the Washington State Constitution. The
structure looks simple at first. 7% on
long-term capital gains over $250,000
in a single year. Sale of a primary
residence is exempt. On paper, a senior
selling a primary home is safe. But the
exemption is narrower than retirees
expect. It applies only to the principal
residence, as defined under Washington
Department of Revenue rules. Vacation
homes do not qualify. Second homes do
not qualify. Inherited homes that were
never occupied by the heir do not
qualify. Investment properties,
including rental homes that a senior may
have used to fund retirement, are taxed
at the full 7%. And the threshold of
is per taxpayer, not per couple, which
means a single senior who inherits a
vacation home from a deceased spouse and
sells it within the same year can be hit
with the full 7% on every dollar of gain
over the threshold. The dollar exposure
adds up quickly. A senior in Washington
who inherited a beach property worth
with a stepped-up basis at the date of
death of 500,000 sells the property a
year later for 700,000. The gain is
200,000. That is below the threshold,
and the 7% does not apply. But add a
second sale, a brokerage account
distribution, an inherited investment
property in a trust that sells assets,
and the same senior crosses 250,000
in long-term gains across the year. The
7% surcharge then applies to every
dollar over the line. Therefore, the
mitigation in Washington is structural.
The first move is documentation. The
Department of Revenue requires sellers
to substantiate the cost basis of any
property sold, and inherited basis is
the date of death value, not the
original purchase price. Many seniors
lose money simply because no appraisal
was done at the time of the parents'
death, and the basis is treated as a
contested second move is timing. Spread
sales across multiple tax years if
possible, never recognizing more than
250,000 in gains in any one year. The
third move is exemption preservation.
Confirm in writing with a Washington
licensed tax professional that the
primary residence exemption applies
before relying on it. The Department of
Revenue audits these exemptions, and a
senior who has lived in two homes over
the past 5 years can find the exemption
challenged. There is also a separate
Washington tax that affects every home
sale regardless of equity. The
state-level real estate excise tax,
known as REET, is graduated. The first
of sale price is taxed at 1 and 1/10%.
Above that, the rate climbs in steps to
a top rate of 3% on portions of the sale
price above 3 million. A senior selling
a long-held home for 1 and 1/2 million
pays roughly $21,000 in REET alone,
separate from the capital gains tax,
separate from any federal taxes. That is
the equity tax embedded in the transfer
itself. State number three is
California. The California problem is
layered. There is no single equity tax
in California with a clean name. There
are three overlapping mechanisms that,
when combined, produce one of the
highest effective state-level equity tax
rates in the country on a long-held
home. The first mechanism is the regular
California state income tax. The top
marginal rate is 13 and 3/10%. When a
senior sells a long-held home and the
gain exceeds the federal exclusion of
500,000 for a couple, the entire excess
gain flows into California state income
tax at the senior's marginal rate. For a
retiree with substantial pension or
investment income, that marginal rate
often sits at 9 and 3/10% or higher. The
second mechanism is Proposition 19,
which California voters approved in
2020. Before Proposition 19, when a
parent transferred a home to a child,
the child inherited the parent's
property tax basis. That is the assessed
value used to calculate the annual
property tax. A home that had been on
the rolls at $120,000
in assessed value for 30 years could
pass to the children at that same
$120,000 assessed value, and the
children would continue paying property
tax on that low number rather than the
current market value. But Proposition 19
changed that. Under the new rules, when
a senior transfers a home to a child,
the assessed value resets to the current
market value unless the child moves in
within 12 months and uses the property
as a primary residence. And even then,
only up to $1 million of the assessed
value increase can be excluded. For a
Bay Area home worth $2.5 million,
the child can preserve the basis on
roughly $1 million, and the rest
reassesses at market. The practical
effect for a California senior planning
to leave the family home to children is
dramatic. A home in San Jose that has
been on the property tax rolls at
in assessed value for 40 years pays
roughly $3,000 a year in property tax.
That same home, reassessed to its
current market value of $2.2 million
when the parent dies, generates a
property tax bill of roughly $22,000
a year. The increase, year after year,
for the life of the child's ownership is
the equity tax in another form. Over 20
years, it can total nearly $400,000
in additional property tax that the
family would not have owed under the old
rules. The third mechanism is a series
of proposed state-level wealth taxes.
Assembly Bill 259 and related proposals
have been introduced multiple times in
the California legislature and would
impose a wealth tax on assets including
primary residence equity above defined
thresholds. As of recent legislative
sessions, these proposals have not
become law, but the structure has been
published and the trajectory is clear.
The thresholds in the most recent draft
begin around $50 million in net worth,
which excludes most seniors. But the
precedent matters because once a wealth
tax is in statute, the threshold can be
lowered in later sessions. Therefore,
the mitigation in California is filing
dependent. The single most important
form for any senior planning to transfer
a home to children is the BOE 19P, which
is the parent-to-child transfer
exclusion claim. It must be filed within
3 years of the transfer. Pair it with a
child who moves into the property within
12 months of the transfer and treats it
as a primary residence, and the basis
preservation rule activates. Without
that filing, the reassessment is
automatic. Talk to a California-licensed
estate attorney before any transfer.
State number four is New York. New York
has the largest stack of overlapping
real estate taxes of any state, and
seniors who have lived in the same home
or apartment for decades are the most
exposed. The first equity tax in New
York is the state-level real estate
transfer tax, which applies to every
home sale. The base rate is 4/10 of 1%
paid by the seller. On a home that sells
for $1 million, the transfer tax is
$4,000. That is a number most New York
sellers see at closing and treat as
routine. But on top of the state
transfer tax sits the New York City real
property transfer tax. For sales of
residential property within the five
boroughs above $500,000,
the tax is 1 and 425/1000
of 1%. So a senior who sells a Brooklyn
brownstone for $1.8 million pays roughly
in city-level transfer tax on top of the
$4,000 state level, on top of any
federal capital gains, on top of New
York state income tax on the gain. The
second equity tax is the New York state
mansion tax, which applies to the buyer.
While technically paid by the buyer, in
practice the cost is built into the
negotiated sale price, which lowers what
the seller nets. The base mansion tax is
1% of the sale price for residential
sales over $1 million. In New York City,
the rate is graduated upward, starting
at 1 and 1/4% on sales between $1
million and $2 million, climbing to 3
and 9/10% on sales above $25 million. A
senior selling a Manhattan apartment for
$2.4 million pays no mansion tax
directly, but the buyer pays roughly
which buyers typically negotiate as a
price reduction. The senior nets less.
The third equity tax in New York is the
proposed state-level wealth tax. State
Senator Liz Krueger and Assemblymember
Carmen De la Rosa have introduced wealth
tax legislation in multiple sessions of
the New York legislature. The most
recent versions would impose a tax on
net worth, including primary residence
equity above defined thresholds. As of
recent legislative reporting, these
proposals have not advanced to passage,
but the structure is published and
active. Combined with the existing
transfer taxes, the cumulative state
level equity exposure on a long-held New
York home is among the highest in the
country. The fourth piece is the New
York state estate tax, which kicks in at
a much lower threshold federal estate
tax. The federal estate tax exemption is
currently above $13 million per
individual. The New York estate tax
exemption sits around $7 million
depending on the year. Seniors with a
long-appreciated New York home, plus
retirement accounts, plus any other
assets, can find their estate above the
New York threshold while still well
below the federal one. The tax on the
excess can run into the hundreds of
thousands of dollars. Therefore, the
mitigation in New York is structural and
front-loaded. The first step is to
confirm the current state estate tax
exemption with a New York-licensed
estate attorney because the threshold
has shifted multiple times over the past
decade. The second step is to evaluate
whether the home should be held in trust
to remove it from the New York taxable
estate. The third step is to time the
sale carefully if downsizing is on the
horizon because layering a large home
sale gain on top of a year with high
pension income can push the senior into
both a higher New York state income tax
bracket and into a year that draws
scrutiny under the gift tax rules. State
number five is Minnesota. Minnesota is
the state where the Supreme Court of the
United States drew a line in the sand on
equity confiscation, but the state's
other equity taxes remain in place and
have expanded. Start with the case.
Geraldine Tyler was a 94-year-old
grandmother who owned a condominium in
Minneapolis. She fell behind on her
property taxes by roughly $15,000.
Hennepin County took the condominium
under state tax forfeiture law, sold it
and kept the entire $40,000. Tyler sued,
arguing that Minnesota law violated the
takings clause of the Fifth Amendment by
retaining the surplus equity above the
actual tax debt. In May of 2023,
the Supreme Court ruled unanimously,
nine to nothing, in her favor. States
can no longer keep surplus equity from a
tax foreclosure sale. The opinion was
written by Chief Justice John Roberts,
but the ruling did not eliminate
Minnesota's other equity taxes.
Therefore, the second equity tax to know
in Minnesota is the state estate tax.
Minnesota imposes its own estate tax
separate from the federal one. The
Minnesota exemption is $3 million per
individual. The federal exemption is
currently above $13 million. The result
is that a Minnesota retiree with a
paid-off home worth $1.2 million,
retirement accounts of $1.8 million, and
a vacation cabin worth $400,000 has a
taxable estate of $3.4 million at death,
which is below the federal exemption by
a wide margin and above the Minnesota
exemption by $400,000. Minnesota
assesses an estate tax on the excess at
rates that climb up to 16% for larger
estates. The tax on a moderately-sized
Minnesota estate is rarely zero. The
third Minnesota equity exposure is a
proposed state wealth tax. House File
was introduced in a recent legislative
session and would have imposed a wealth
tax on net worth above defined
thresholds, including the equity in a
primary residence above an exemption
amount. The proposal has not become law
as of recent reporting, but the
structure is documented and the
precedent is forming. The fourth piece
is the property tax burden itself.
Minnesota has one of the higher
effective property tax rates in the
Upper Midwest. A Minneapolis homeowner
with a home assessed at $350,000
typically pays between $4,500 and $5,500
per year in property tax. Over a 30-year
retirement, that is roughly $150,000
in property tax, which is itself a slow
drain on equity. The fifth Minnesota
issue is that the Tyler ruling, while it
ended outright equity confiscation going
forward, did not retroactively return
surplus equity to families who lost it
before 2023. Litigation continues across
multiple states to recover that surplus,
and Minnesota has been one of the slower
states to publish a clear claims
process. Families who lost a home to tax
forfeiture in Minnesota between 2010 and
should consult a Minnesota-licensed real
estate attorney because the path to
recovery exists, but the deadlines are
short and the documentation requirements
are specific. Therefore, the mitigation
in Minnesota stacks. Step one is to keep
property taxes current. Never let a
Minnesota property tax bill go more than
90 days past due because the forfeiture
process moves quickly. Step two is to
plan an estate at the $3 million
threshold, not the federal one. Step
three is to document the home's basis
and any improvements over the years
because Minnesota tax authorities can
challenge inherited basis without good
records. Five steps to take this week
before the equity tax in your state
quietly fires. Step one is the records
audit. Pull the last 3 years of property
tax bills for every property you own.
Look at the assessed value column. If
the assessed value has jumped more than
15% in a single year, the state has
already begun the reassessment process
that often precedes any new equity tax.
Pair those bills with the original
purchase records, including the closing
statement, every receipt for capital
improvements, and any prior appraisals.
The cost basis number is the single most
important number in any equity tax
calculation and most homeowners cannot
produce it on demand. Step two is the
threshold check. For your specific
state, write down on a single page the
current year exemption thresholds for
state income tax, state estate tax, and
any proposed wealth tax that has been
introduced in your state legislature.
Then, add up your projected income for
any year in which you might sell,
transfer, or inherit a home. If the
projected income crosses the surtax
