court involvement at all. The filing fee
commonly runs between $20 and $100. An
attorney can prepare the deed for
between $100 and $300.
And in many states, the form is
available at the county recorder's
office for no cost at all. Therefore, on
any home in a state that allows this
deed, the total cost of bypassing
probate under $100. But most parents
have never heard of this deed because
the attorneys who benefit from probate
have no incentive to explain it. This is
exactly why I put together a free
checklist for families who want to
protect their home from probate before
the end of this year. The checklist
walks through every one of the seven
mistakes in this video, but it also
covers the three core documents that
must be in place for the fix to hold up
in court, the exact language that needs
to appear on the deed, the deadlines
that trigger a forced sale if they are
missed, and the 5-year Medicaid
look-back rule that can undo every
protection if the timing is wrong. It is
a printable document. It is free. It is
the same kind of checklist that a family
would commonly pay an estate attorney
several hundred dollars to walk through
in a consultation. Therefore, it is the
fastest way to find out tonight whether
the home is actually protected or
whether the family is one court filing
away from a probate disaster. To get it,
go to mark-callaway.kit.com
/checklist
and enter the email address where the
checklist should be sent. It arrives
within 1 minute. There is nothing to
buy, nothing to sign up for beyond the
email, and no obligation of any kind.
Print it, take it to the kitchen table
this weekend, and go through it line by
line with whoever in the family will
inherit the home. One conversation this
weekend can protect everything the
family has spent a lifetime building.
Three final steps to take this week.
First, pull the current deed on the home
from the county recorder's website or
office, and read the ownership language
out loud. If the words right of
survivorship, tenants by the entirety,
or trust do not appear, the home is
exposed. Second, pull every life
insurance policy, every retirement
account, and every transfer on death
bank account, and write down every
beneficiary name on a single sheet of
paper. If a name on that sheet is an
ex-spouse, a deceased relative, or
anyone who is not supposed to inherit
that money, update it this week. Third,
confirm that a named executor exists in
the will, confirm that a backup executor
exists, and confirm that both of them
have been told they are being chosen. An
executor who is surprised at the funeral
is already behind schedule. Do not wait
for a diagnosis, a hospital visit, or a
family emergency to force the
conversation. Probate is not something
that only happens to other families.
Probate happens to every family that has
not taken these steps, and it is already
costing American parents billions of
dollars every single year.

title: 5 Ways Medicaid Takes Your Home After You Die

segments.text: Five ways Medicaid can take your house
after you die are hidden inside a
federal law most seniors have never
heard of, but every single state is
required to enforce it. Therefore, the
average family loses more than $300,000
of equity because nobody told them what
was coming. The law is called the
Medicaid Estate Recovery Program.
Congress passed it in 1993. It requires
every state to go after the estate of
anyone who received Medicaid long-term
care after age 55. That includes nursing
home care, assisted living, and in-home
care paid by Medicaid. Most seniors
assume that once they die, their house
passes to their children. But if
Medicaid paid for even a few months of
care before death, the state steps in
before the children see a single dollar.
In many cases, the house is sold, the
proceeds are sent to the state treasury,
and the family gets whatever is left.
Often, there is nothing left. One of
these five ways is the one almost nobody
sees coming because it reaches assets
your parents thought were completely
safe from the government. I will tell
you which one at the end. First, here is
how it actually works. The first way
Medicaid takes your house is the
simplest one. It is called the Probate
Estate Claim, and it happens in all 50
states without exception. When a
Medicaid recipient dies, the state opens
a claim against the deceased person's
probate estate. The probate estate is
everything that passes through a will.
If the house is titled in the deceased
person's name alone, it enters probate.
The state files its claim before the
will is honored. Therefore, the Medicaid
bill gets paid first. The children
inherit what is left. Here is the math.
If the parent received 3 years of
nursing home care at $120,000 per year,
the state claim is $360,000.
If the house is worth $400,000,
the state takes nearly the entire value
of the house. The children receive
$40,000 to split. This happens every
single day in every single state. The
state does not need a court order. It
does not need to sue the family. It
simply files a claim during probate, and
the probate court is required by federal
law to honor it ahead of the heirs.
There is one exception that almost
nobody knows about. The state cannot
recover while a surviving spouse is
alive, or while a child under 21 is
living, or while a child who is blind or
permanently disabled is living. But once
the last protected person dies, the
state comes back. It can wait 10 years,
20 years, 30 years. The claim does not
expire. Therefore, if your father dies
and leaves the house to your mother,
Medicaid cannot touch it while she is
alive. But when she dies, the state
sends a letter. It wants every dollar it
paid for your father's nursing home
care, plus every dollar it paid for
hers. It collects from whatever of the
house most families find out the day the
letter arrives. They had no idea the
state was waiting in the background for
the surviving parent to pass away. By
then, the house has already been
promised to the children in the will,
and the will is worthless against the
Medicaid claim. The only way to avoid
the first way is to move the house out
of the probate estate before either
parent needs care. Therefore, if the
house is still in a parent's name when
they die, the first way Medicaid takes
it is almost guaranteed. The second way
Medicaid takes your house happens while
your parent is still alive. It is called
a TEFRA lien, named after the Tax Equity
and Fiscal Responsibility Act of 1982.
The rule allows states to file a lien
against the home of a Medicaid recipient
who is permanently in a nursing home.
The word "permanently" is doing a lot of
work in that sentence. Here is how it
plays out. A parent enters a nursing
home for long-term care. Medicaid starts
paying the bills. The state assesses
whether the parent is likely to return
home. If the determination is permanent
institutionalization, meaning the parent
is not expected to return, the state
files a lien on the house. The lien does
not force a sale while the parent is
alive, but the moment the parent dies,
the lien becomes enforceable. The state
collects directly from the house before
probate, before the will, before the
family can do anything about it. This is
different from the probate claim because
the lien is already recorded on the
deed. Therefore, the family cannot sell
the house, refinance it, or transfer it
without first paying off the state. In
many cases, the lien amount grows by
$10,000 per month as Medicaid pays more
nursing home bills. If the parent is in
the nursing home for 4 years at $120,000
per year, the TEFRA lien grows to
If the house is worth $350,000,
the state takes the entire house, and
the family still owes a balance. A
family in Indiana found this out the
worst way possible. The father entered a
nursing home after a fall. Within 90
days, the state classified the admission
as permanent and recorded a lien on the
house. The daughter drove past the house
every week and had no idea a lien had
been filed. 3 years later, the father
passed away. The daughter went to list
the house for sale and discovered a
state lien of $270,000
already attached to the deed. She had
spent 3 years paying the property taxes
and the homeowner's insurance out of her
own pocket on a house she would never
inherit a single dollar from. There is
one narrow protection. If a sibling of
the Medicaid recipient has lived in the
house for at least 1 year before the
nursing home admission, the lien cannot
be filed. There is also a protection if
an adult caregiver child lived in the
house for at least 2 years providing
care that delayed the nursing home
admission. But these protections require
proof, and the proof must be submitted
in advance. Therefore, the second way
Medicaid takes your house is by
attaching itself to the deed while your
parent is still breathing. The third way
is the most aggressive. It only exists
in certain states, and if your parent
lives in one of them, assets they
thought were protected are not. is
called Expanded Estate Recovery. Federal
rules allow every state to go beyond the
probate estate and recover from assets
that normally bypass probate entirely.
More than 20 states have adopted
expanded recovery, including New York,
Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode
Island, Ohio, Tennessee, North Dakota,
Iowa, and others. Expanded recovery
reaches assets that seniors were
specifically told would avoid probate.
That includes jointly held property with
right of survivorship, life estate,
remainder interests, living trust
assets, transfer on death deeds, and
payable on death bank accounts. The life
estate interest is one of the most
misunderstood. Thousands of families
sign a life estate deed that lets the
parent live in the house until death, at
which point the house automatically
passes to the children. In a normal
probate state, this works, and the state
cannot recover against the remainder
interest. But in an expanded recovery
state, the state values the parent's
life interest on the day of death and
collects that percentage of the house's
value from the children. The older the
parent at death, the smaller that
percentage, but the claim is almost
never zero. Here's what that means in
practice. A parent puts the house into
joint tenancy with their child thinking
that when the parent dies, the child
automatically inherits the house, and
the state cannot touch it. In a normal
probate state, that works. In an
expanded recovery state, the state
calculates the parent's ownership share
at the moment of death and collects that
share from the child. If the parent
owned 50%, the state takes 50% of the
house's value from the child. The child
has to sell the house or take out a loan
to pay the state. The same thing happens
with a living trust. Families pay
attorneys thousands of dollars to set up
trusts specifically to avoid probate. In
an expanded recovery state, the trust
does not shield the house. The state
recovers from the trust assets just as
if they were in the probate estate. A
family in Connecticut learned this the
hard way. The parent set up a revocable
living trust, moved the house into it,
and believed the house was safe. The
father spent 2 years in a nursing home
on Medicaid before passing away. The
state filed a claim for $240,000
against the trust. The trust paid it.
The mother was forced to sell the house
to cover the remaining bill. She moved
in with her daughter at age 79.
Therefore, if your parents live in an
expanded recovery state, every strategy
they have been told protects the house
may not actually protect the house. The
only real protection is an irrevocable
trust set up more than 5 years before
Medicaid begins. Everything else is at
risk. The fourth way Medicaid takes your
house is by denying the one escape hatch
Congress wrote into the law, the
hardship waiver. It is supposed to
protect families when a state recovery
would cause undue hardship. On paper,
the waiver is available in every state.
In practice, it is denied the vast
majority of the time. To qualify for a
hardship waiver, the family must prove
two things. First, that the estate is
the heir's only source of income or
shelter. Second, that recovering the
estate would force the heir into poverty
or homelessness. Both conditions must be
documented with financial records, tax
returns, and sworn affidavits. Even when
families meet both standards, states
deny the waiver on technical grounds.
The paperwork was filed late. The proof
of residency was insufficient. The heir
owns another property that could
theoretically house them. The heir has a
job. Therefore, the heir is not
impoverished. One of the most common
denials happens to adult children who
moved in to care for a parent. Federal
law allows a caregiver child waiver if
the child lived in the house for at
least 2 years before the parent entered
the nursing home and provided care that
delayed the nursing home admission. But
states require the child to prove the
care directly prevented nursing home
placement. That proof is almost
impossible to produce. Therefore, most
caregiver child claims are denied. A
family in Ohio filed a hardship waiver
after their mother died. The son had
moved home to care for her for 18
months. The state denied the waiver
because 18 months is 6 months short of
the 2-year minimum. The son was forced
to sell the house for $290,000
and remit the full amount to the state.
He was 62 years old with no other
housing. There is a reason so few
waivers are granted. Every dollar a
state recovers from a deceased Medicaid
recipient is a dollar the state keeps.
Federal matching funds are calculated
after recovery. Therefore, the state
treasury has a direct financial interest
in denying as many hardship waivers as
possible. Some states process these
claims through a contracted recovery
firm that receives a percentage of every
dollar collected, which means the person
reviewing the waiver is paid more if the
waiver is denied. Therefore, the
hardship waiver is not a safety net. It
is a narrow door with a high threshold,
and the people on the other side of that
door have every incentive to keep it
closed. The fifth way Medicaid takes
your house is the one almost nobody sees
coming, and this is the one I promised
you at the start of the video. Most
families hear about the 5-year look-back
rule and assume it only applies before
Medicaid begins. Meaning, if a parent
transfers the house to a child and then
applies for Medicaid within 5 years, the
transfer triggers a penalty period where
Medicaid will not pay for care. Many
families accept the penalty period and
plan around it, but there is a second
version of the look-back rule that
applies after death. If a parent
transferred the house within 5 years of
receiving Medicaid and then died during
the penalty period, the state treats the
transfer as an attempt to defraud
Medicaid. The state can file a claim
against the child who received the
house, and the child becomes personally
liable for the Medicaid bill. Here is
how the trap works. transfers his house
to his daughter in 2021. In 2024, he has
a stroke and enters a nursing home. He
applies for Medicaid. Medicaid imposes a
penalty period of 30 months based on the
transferred house. The father dies in
2025, 18 months into the penalty period,
still owing Medicaid for care that
should have been penalized. The state
does not write off the bill. It files a
claim against the daughter for the 18
months of nursing home costs during the
penalty period. That is approximately
The daughter either pays it from her own
funds or loses the house to a lien filed
against her personally. This happens
because the look-back rule is not just a
waiting period. It is a penalty system
that survives the Medicaid recipient's
death. The state will chase the person
who received the transferred asset even
years later, and courts enforce it.
Therefore, the one asset transfer most
families do to protect the house, a
simple deed to a child, is the exact
transfer that triggers personal
liability for the child after the parent
dies. Here's what you need to do this
week. First, find out if your state is
an expanded recovery state. Call the
state Medicaid office or search for your
state's estate recovery policy. If the
policy includes joint tenancy, trust
assets, or transfer-on-death deeds, you
are in an expanded recovery state, and
every ordinary estate plan is at risk.
Second, stop the informal deed
transfers. Do not add a child to the
deed. Do not use a transfer-on-death
deed without an attorney. Do not assume
a living trust protects the house. These
are the exact strategies that trigger
the first, third, and fifth ways
Medicaid takes the house. Third, if a
parent is currently healthy and not yet
in need of care, consult an elder law
attorney about an irrevocable Medicaid
asset protection trust. The trust must
be funded more than 5 years before any
Medicaid application. After 5 years, the
house is legally outside the parent's
estate, and none of the five recovery
methods apply. Fourth, if a parent is
already in a nursing home, demand the
intent-to-return-home determination in
writing. If the nursing home admission
is classified as permanent, a TEFRA lien
can be filed. If it is classified as
temporary or rehabilitation, the lien
cannot be filed.
is not automatic. The family has to push
for it. Fifth, if a parent has already
passed away and the state has filed a
claim, do not pay it without a
consultation. Hardship waivers can be
negotiated. Recovery amounts can be
reduced. Some claims are invalid on
technical grounds. A single call to an
elder law attorney has saved families
hundreds of thousands of dollars. The
five ways Medicaid takes your house are
baked into federal law. The only way to
stop them is to move before the state
does.

title: Parents Are Losing Their Homes to These 5 Mistakes

segments.text: Five mistakes are costing your children
the house right now, and most parents
have already made at least two of them
without knowing it. The average American
home is worth $350,000.
For most families, it is the single
largest asset they will ever own. But
right now, five common mistakes are
quietly destroying the transfer from
parent to child, and the families who
make them do not lose a little money.
They lose the entire house, or they lose
in taxes and legal fees that did not
need to exist. But before I walk through
all five, I need to tell you about the
last mistake on this list. Mistake
number five is the only one on this list
that cannot be fixed after a parent
dies. There is no court order. There is
no appeal. There is no legal remedy of
any kind. Once the parent is gone and
this mistake is still in place, the
house goes to the wrong person
permanently. Therefore, stay through all
five because the last one is the one
your family cannot afford to miss.
Mistake number one, adding your child's
name to the deed. This is the single
most common estate planning mistake in
America, and it sounds completely
harmless. A parent drives to the county
recorder's office, files a quitclaim
deed, and puts their adult child's name
on the house. The logic is simple. If
both names are on the deed, the house
passes automatically when the parent
dies. No lawyer, no probate, no hassle.
It cost about $30 to file, and it feels
like you just solved the entire problem.
But that $30 form just triggered four
separate financial disasters that no one
at the county office warned you about.
The first disaster is the tax hit. When
a child inherits a home after a parent
dies, they receive what the IRS calls a
stepped-up basis. That means the home's
value for tax purposes resets to
whatever it was worth on the day the
parent died. Therefore, if a parent
bought a home in 1985 for $62,000, and
it is worth $430,000
when they die, the child's tax basis is
If they sell that home for $440,000,
they owe capital gains tax on $10,000.
At the current federal rate, that is
roughly $1,500. But when a parent adds a
child to the deed while they are still
alive, the IRS treats it a CA gift, not
an inheritance. Therefore, the child
does not get a stepped-up basis. They
inherit the parent's original purchase
price as their cost basis. That same
child selling that same house now owes
capital gains tax on $378,000
at 15%. That is $56,700
in federal capital gains tax alone. In
California, add another $37,000
in state tax. One quitclaim deed just
cost the family over $93,000 in taxes.
That would have been zero if the parent
had done nothing. But the tax bill is
not even the worst part. The moment your
child's name goes on that deed, your
home becomes their legal asset. If your
child gets sued, their creditors can
place alien on your home. If your child
files for bankruptcy, a trustee can
force a sale of your home to pay your
child's debts. If your child gets
divorced, a court can treat your home
ASA, marital assets subject to division.
A mother in New Jersey added her
daughter to the deed in 2016. When the
daughter divorced 7 years later, the
ex-husband's attorney argued the home
was marital property. The court agreed.
The mother was 74 years old and nearly
lost her home in her daughter's divorce
settlement. And if you ever need
Medicaid for long-term care, the
government reviews every financial
transaction you made in the last 60
months. Adding your child to the deed
counts as a gift. That gift triggers a
penalty period during which Medicaid
will not pay for your care. On a
home, the penalty in most states exceeds
20 months. At $9,000 per month for a
nursing home, that is over $180,000
out of pocket before Medicaid covers a
single day. Therefore, never put your
child's name on the deed while you are
alive. There are better ways to transfer
a home, and every single one of them
avoids these disasters. Mistake number
two, relying on a will to transfer the
house. Most parents assume their will
controls what happens to the home. You
go to an attorney, you write down who
gets what, you sign it in front of
witnesses, and you put it in a safe. But
a will does not avoid probate. It
guarantees probate. When a parent dies
and the home is titled in their personal
name, that house must go through probate
court before anyone can touch it.
Probate is a court-supervised process
where a judge validates the will,
notifies creditors, settles debts, and
eventually authorizes the transfer. The
process takes 12 to 18 months in most
states. In New York and California, it
regularly takes two years. During that
entire time, your children cannot sell
the home. They cannot refinance it, they
cannot rent it out, but they are
responsible for the mortgage, the
property taxes, the insurance, and the
maintenance. On a $350,000 home, the
carrying cost is roughly $24,000 per
year. If probate takes 18 months, your
children just spent $36,000
keeping a house that they are not
allowed to use. But the carrying cost is
only part of it. Probate fees run
between 3 and 7% of the estate value. On
a $400,000 home, that is $12,000 to
$28,000 in attorney fees, executor fees,
and court costs. Therefore, a parent who
thought their will would handle
everything just cost their children up
to $64,000 in probate expenses and
carrying costs combined. And probate is
a public proceeding. The will, the
estate value, and the names of the
beneficiaries all become public record.
Anyone can walk into the courthouse and
look up exactly what your family
inherited. That is how inheritance scams
work. Scammers monitor probate filings
and target grieving families within
weeks of a death. A revocable living
trust avoids all of this. When a home is
titled in the name of a trust, it passes
to the beneficiaries immediately. No
court, no waiting, no public filing, no
probate fees. The child can sell, move
in, or rent the home within days.
Therefore, if the home is your family's
largest asset, a trust is not optional.
It is the only document that actually
protects the transfer. Mistake number
three, holding the home in the wrong
type of joint ownership. This mistake is
invisible until the day someone dies,
and by then, it is permanent. There are
two common ways to hold property
jointly, joint tenancy with right of
survivorship and tenancy in common. Most
families do not know which one is
written on their deed. But the
difference between those two phrases
determines whether your family keeps the
house or lose it. With joint tenancy
with right of survivorship, when one
owner dies, their share automatically
passes to the surviving owner. No
probate, no court. The transfer happens
by operation of law the moment the death
occurs. But with tenancy in common, when
one owner dies, their share does not go
to the surviving owner. It goes into
their estate. Therefore, it goes through
probate, and it passes according to
their will, or if there is no will,
according to state intestacy law, which
may send it to people the family never
intended. Here is where families get
destroyed. A parent adds a child to the
deed as tenants in common because the
title company used the default language.
The parent assumes that when they die,
the child will own the home. But tenants
in common means each person owns a 50%
share. When the parent dies, the
parent's 50% goes into their estate and
through probate. It does not
automatically pass to the child. But the
more dangerous version works in the
other direction. If the child dies
before the parent, the child's 50% does
not go back to the parent. It goes into
the child's estate. Therefore, it can
pass to the child's spouse, the child's
creditors, or someone the parent has
never met. A mother in Florida added her
son to the deed as tenants in common.
Her son died at age 41. His 50% went to
his wife. When the wife remarried, she
wanted to sell. The mother was 78 years
old, still living in the home, and the
daughter-in-law had every legal right to
force a partition sale. The court
ordered the home sold. The mother got
half the proceeds and had to find
somewhere else to live. The cost to
change a deed from tenants in common to
joint tenancy with right of survivorship
is under $300. The cost of not doing it
was the house. Therefore, check your
deed today, not next week, today. The
exact words on the title determine
everything. Mistake number four, failing
to get a date of death appraisal. This
mistake does not happen while the parent
is alive. It happens after, and it is
the children who pay for it. Remember
the stepped-up basis from mistake number
one? When a child inherits a home, their
tax basis resets to the fair market
value on the date the parent died. But
the IRS does not automatically assign
that value. The family has to prove it,
and the way you prove it is with a date
of death appraisal. This is a formal
appraisal conducted by a licensed
appraiser that documents the home's fair
market value as of the exact date the
parent died. It cost between $300
and it is the single most important
document your family needs after a
parent passes away. But almost nobody
gets one. The family is grieving. They
are overwhelmed. Nobody tells them this
one document controls the entire tax
bill on the house. Therefore, they skip
it. And two, three years later, when
they finally sell the home, they have no
proof of what it was worth on the date
of death. Without that appraisal, the
IRS can use the parent's original
purchase price as the cost basis, and
the numbers are devastating. A parent
who bought a home in 1990 for $85,000
dies in 2026. The home is now worth
With a date of death appraisal, the
child's basis is $425,000.
They sell for $435,000.
Capital gains tax on $10,000,
roughly $1,500 in federal tax. Without
the appraisal, the IRS can argue the
basis is $85,000.
Capital gains on $340,000
at 15%. That is $51,000
in federal tax. Add state taxes, and the
total can exceed $65,000.
One appraisal, $400, saves over $63,000
in unnecessary taxes. And here is the
part that catches families off guard.
You can get a retroactive date of death
appraisal, even years after the parent
died. Appraisers can use historical
comparable sales to establish the value
at the date of death. But the longer you
wait, the harder it becomes to find good
comparables and the more vulnerable the
appraisal is to an IRS challenge.
Therefore, if you have inherited a home
from a parent in the last 5 years and
never got an appraisal, call a licensed
appraiser this week, not next month,
this week. Mistake number five, failing
to update estate documents after a major
life event. This is the mistake I warned
you about at the beginning, the one that
cannot be undone. Estate documents are
not permanent. They are a snapshot of
your family at the moment they were
signed. But most parents treat them like
they are carved into stone. They create
a will, they sign a deed, they set up a
trust, they name beneficiaries, and then
life changes and the documents do not. A
child gets divorced, a spouse dies, a
parent remarries, a child becomes
estranged, a grandchild is born. Every
one of these events can redirect who
receives the house, and most families
never update a single document after any
of them. Here is why this is the most
dangerous mistake on this list. Transfer
on death deeds, beneficiary
designations, and joint tenancy
arrangements all operate outside of
probate. They override the will. Most
families do not realize that the deed on
their home can contain the exact same
kind of override. A father in Ohio
remarried at age 67. He updated his will
to leave everything to his new wife. His
attorney reviewed the will carefully and
it was legally sound, but the home had a
transfer on death deed that the father
had filed during his first marriage.
That deed named his two adult children
from his first marriage as the
beneficiaries of the house. Nobody
reviewed it. Nobody remembered it
existed. When the father died, the will
clearly stated the house goes to his
wife, but the transfer on death deed
said it goes to his children. The deed
won. His widow, who had lived in that
home for 9 years, lost it entirely. She
hired an attorney, she fought it for 14
months, she spent over $22,000
in legal fees. The court ruled against
her. The transfer on death deed is a
legal instrument that operates outside
of probate and the will has no authority
over it. Once the father died with that
deed still in place, the outcome was
permanent. There was no appeal, there
was no remedy. The house went to the
children from the first marriage and his
wife had 30 days to vacate. Every other
mistake on this list has a fix. You can
remove a child from a deed, you can
create a trust, you can change the
ownership type, you can get an appraisal
retroactively, but this one is
permanent. If a parent dies with
outdated documents, the wrong person
receives the house and no court in the
country will reverse it. Therefore,
every time there is a marriage, a
divorce, a death, a birth, or an
estrangement, every document must be
reviewed. The will, the trust, the deed,
the transfer on death designations, the
beneficiary forms on every account.
Here's what you need to do this week.
Step one, pull up the deed to your home
from your county recorder's website or
office. Read the exact language. If your
child's name is on it, call an estate
attorney about removing ITANDD
using a trust or transfer on death deed
instead. Step two, check whether the
deed says joint tenancy with right of
survivorship or tenants in common. If it
says tenants in common, get it changed
immediately. The cost is under $300.
Step three, if you inherited a home in
the last 10 years and never got a date
of death appraisal, call a licensed
appraiser this week. The longer you
wait, the weaker the appraisal becomes.
Step four, if anything has changed in
your family since your estate documents
were signed, a marriage, a divorce, a
death, a birth, or an estrangement,
schedule a full review with an estate
attorney. Do not just update the will.
Review the deed, the trust, the transfer
on death designations, and every
beneficiary forms. Step five, if you do
not have a revocable living trust and
your home is worth more than $100,000,
get one. A trust costs between $1,500
and $3,000. Probate costs your family
five to 10 times that amount, plus a
year of their lives. One afternoon of
phone calls this week could save your
children over $150,000
and the roof over their head.

title: The 1 Form That Overrides Your Will Every Time

segments.text: There's one form that beats your will
every single time. And if you have not
checked it in the last 12 months, your
entire estate plan could already be
sending your money to someone you never
intended. It does not matter how much
your attorney charged you. It does not
matter how carefully your will was
drafted. It does not matter if you
updated your will last month. If this
one form says something different from
your will, this form wins. Not
sometimes, not in certain states, every
single time. Federal courts have ruled
on it. State courts have ruled on it.
The United States Supreme Court settled
it unanimously. The form beats the will.
But here is what your estate attorney
probably never told you. There is not
just one of these forms. There are at
least five different versions hiding
inside accounts you already own. And the
most dangerous one is inside an account
most seniors have not looked at in over
a decade. By the end of this video, you
will know exactly where all five are
hiding, what they control, and the one
mistake that turns a simple form into a
disaster for your family. This form is
called a beneficiary designation. You
filled one out the day you opened your
401k at work. You filled out another one
when you bought your life insurance
policy. Your bank may have asked you to
fill one out. Your brokerage may have
one on file. You signed these forms
years ago, probably never thought about
them again, and that is exactly where
the problem starts. A beneficiary
designation is a legal contract between
you and the financial institution that
holds your money. It tells that
institution one thing, who gets the
money when you die. And when you die,
the institution follows that form. Not
your will, not your trust, not your
handwritten letter, not a verbal promise
you made to your children at the kitchen
table. They follow the form because
legally, the form is a contract, and
contracts beat wills. And here is the
part that makes this so dangerous. The
financial institution does not
investigate. They do not call your
family. They do not check your will.
They do not uh ask whether the person on
the form is still the person you would
choose today. They see a name, they send
the money, and once that money is sent,
getting it back is nearly impossible.
This is not a loophole. This is federal
law. Let me show you how badly this can
go. A man named William Kennedy worked
for DuPont for over 20 years. He had an
employer retirement plan worth over
When he first enrolled in the plan, he
named his wife as the beneficiary. That
made sense at the time. They were
married, she was the obvious choice.
Years later, they divorced. After the
divorce, Kennedy did what most
responsible people do. He went to his
attorney and rewrote his entire will. He
made it crystal clear, everything goes
to his daughter. He signed it, it was
notarized, it was legally valid in every
way. But he never called DuPont to
update the beneficiary designation form
on his retirement plan. He may not have
even remembered the form existed. It was
a piece of paperwork he signed two
decades earlier on his first day
enrolling in the plan. When Kennedy
died, his daughter assumed the money was
hers. The will said so in plain
language. There was no ambiguity. But
DuPont sent the full $400,000 to the
ex-wife because the beneficiary form
still had her name on it. Kennedy's
daughter sued. She had the will. She had
her father's clear intent. The case went
through the federal courts and
eventually reached the United States
Supreme Court. The court ruled
unanimously. The beneficiary designation
form controls. The will is irrelevant.
The daughter received nothing. $400,000
gone because of one form he forgot to
update. And this is not rare. A study by
the American Association of Retired
Persons found that nearly 40% of
Americans with retirement accounts have
not updated their beneficiary
designations in over five years. 40%.
millions of seniors right now have forms
on file that do not reflect who they
actually want to receive their money.
Divorces happened. Remarriages happened.
Spouses passed away. Grandchildren were
born. Life changed in every possible
way. But the form stayed frozen in time
because nobody picked up the phone and
changed it. Therefore, the question
every senior needs to answer right now
is not whether your will is up to date.
The question is whether every
beneficiary designation across every
account you own matches what your will
actually says. Because if there is a
single conflict between the two, the
form wins and your family loses. Here
the five places these forms are hiding
right now. Number one, your 401k or
403b. If you ever worked for a company,
a school district, a hospital, or the
government, you have a retirement plan
with a beneficiary form on file. The
average 401k balance for Americans
between the ages of 60 and 69 is
That entire balance is controlled by the
beneficiary form. Your will does not
touch it. Your trust does not touch it.
The form is the only document that
matters. Number two, your IRA.
Traditional, Roth, SEP, it does not
matter. Every IRA has a beneficiary
designation. And here's the trap that
catches more retirees than almost
anything else. If you rolled your old
401k into an IRA when you retired, the
beneficiary designation did not roll
over with it. That old form stayed at
your old employer. When the money landed
in the new IRA, you signed a brand new
beneficiary form at the IRA custodian.
Maybe you filled it out carefully. Maybe
you checked a box in a rush because it
was one of 15 forms they handed you that
day. If you do not remember exactly who
you named on that new form, that is the
problem. Number three, your life
insurance policy. The average life
insurance death benefit in the United
States is $350,000.
That payout goes directly to whoever is
on the beneficiary form. And life
insurance policies are where this
problem gets the most painful because
people buy these policies young and hold
them for decades. A woman in Ohio lost
her husband after 32 years of marriage.
He had a $250,000
life insurance policy. She assumed it
was hers. They had been together for
over three decades. But her husband had
originally purchased the policy during
his first marriage and had listed his
first wife as the beneficiary. He never
updated it after the divorce. He never
updated it after the remarriage. For 32
years, that form sat in a filing cabinet
with the wrong name on it. His second
wife, the woman who spent 32 years by
his side, received nothing. The first
wife, who he had not spoken to in
decades, cashed the check within 60
days. Number four, your bank accounts.
Most banks offer a feature called
payable on death, and many seniors sign
up for it without fully understanding
what it does. A payable on death
designation sends your entire bank
balance directly to the named person
when you die. It skips probate entirely.
It also skips your will entirely. You
may have added this to your uh checking
or savings account years ago because the
bank suggested it as a simple way to
avoid probate. But if the person you
named is no longer the right choice, or
if your family situation has changed,
this form is quietly overriding your
entire estate plan right now, and nobody
knows it until you are gone. Number
five, this is the most dangerous one I
mentioned at the beginning of the video,
your brokerage account. If you have
stocks, bonds, mutual funds, or ETFs at
a firm like Schwab or Fidelity or
Vanguard, there may be a transfer on
death registration on file. Some of
these accounts hold 300,000, 500,000,
even over a million dollars. This form
sends the entire account balance
directly to whoever is listed with no
court involvement, no probate process,
and no input from your will whatsoever.
Seniors who set these up in their 50s
and never looked at them again are
sitting on a ticking time bomb for their
families. And because brokerage accounts
often grow significantly over the
decades, the amount at stake today may
be three or four times what it was when
you originally signed the form. Now, let
me show you the four mistakes that cost
families the most money. The first
mistake is naming your estate as the
beneficiary instead of a real person.
This sounds logical, but it is one of
the most expensive errors in estate
planning. When you name your estate, the
retirement account gets pulled into
probate. That means attorney fees, court
costs, and delays of six months to over
a year. But the real damage is the tax
hit. When a spouse inherits a retirement
account directly through a beneficiary
form, they can roll it into their own
IRA and keep deferring taxes for
decades. When the estate inherits it
instead, that spousal rollover option
disappears completely. On a $300,000
IRA, this one mistake can trigger over
in accelerated federal income taxes that
your family would not have owed if the
form had simply listed a name instead of
the estate. The second mistake is never
updating after a divorce. In most
states, a divorce does not automatically
remove your ex-spouse from a beneficiary
designation. Some states have laws that
revoke a spouse upon divorce for certain
types of accounts. But the rules are
wildly inconsistent, and they do not
apply to employer retirement plans that
are governed by federal ERISA law.
Federal law overrides state law in those
cases. If your ex-spouse is still on the
form, assume they are getting the money
until you call the institution and
confirm otherwise. The third mistake is
naming minor children or grandchildren
directly. If you list a child under 18
as a beneficiary, the financial
institution cannot legally hand them the
money. A court will have to appoint a
legal guardian to manage the funds on
the child's behalf. That triggers court
oversight, annual reporting
requirements, attorney involvement at
every step, and guardian fees that can
account before the child ever sees a
cent of it. The fourth mistake is the
one that turns all of this into a tax
emergency. Before the year 2020, if your
child inherited your IRA, they could
stretch the distributions over their
entire lifetime. A 45-year-old
inheriting a $500,000 IRA could take
small withdrawals over four decades and
let the rest of the money continue to
grow tax-deferred. But Congress changed
the rule. Now, most non-spouse
beneficiaries must empty the entire
inherited IRA within 10 years. Let me
put real numbers on this. Say you have a
$500,000 traditional IRA, and you leave
it to your son, who earns $120,000 a
year. Under the 10-year rule, he must
withdraw the entire $500,000 within a
decade. If he takes 50,000 per year,
that pushes his annual taxable income
At that level, he jumps from a 24%
federal tax bracket to 32% on those
distributions. Over 10 years, that 8%
difference alone costs him $40,000 in
extra federal taxes, and that does not
include the state income taxes on top of
it. Therefore, your beneficiary
designation does not just control who
gets the money. It controls how fast the
IRS takes their cut. If If If the form
is wrong or if the form names the wrong
person in the wrong way, your family
pays the maximum tax bill, and there is
nothing they can do about it after you
are gone. And here is one more thing
that surprises people. A power of
attorney does not fix this. Many seniors
assume that if they become
incapacitated, their power of attorney
can step in and update the beneficiary
designations for them. Most financial
institutions will not allow it. A power
of attorney typically authorizes someone
to manage your money and pay your bills
while you are alive. It does not
authorize them to change who receives
the money after you die. Therefore, the
only person who can fix a beneficiary
designation is you, and the only time to
do it is right now, while you are still
able to make that phone call. Here is
what to do this week. Step one, call
every financial institution where you
hold an account. Your 401k provider,
your IRA custodian, your life insurance
company, your bank, and your brokerage.
Ask them one question. Who is currently
listed as the primary and contingent
beneficiary on my account? Do not guess.
Do not rely on your memory of what you
think you filled out years ago. Get the
actual name that is on file right now.
Some institutions can tell you over the
phone. Others will mail or email you a
copy of the form. Either way, get it in
writing. Step two, compare every single
form to your current will or trust. Line
them up side by side. If any name on any
form does not match your estate plan,
the form is what the institution will
follow, not the will. Update the form
immediately. Step three, if you have a
revocable living trust, ask your
whether any of your retirement accounts
should name the trust as beneficiary
instead of an individual. This is not
always the right move because of the tax
implications I just explained, but it
must be a deliberate decision, not an
accident leftover from a form you signed
15 years ago and never looked at again.
Step four, if you have been divorced at
any point in your life, check every form
across every account, even the ones you
are certain you already updated,
especially the employer retirement plan
and the life insurance policy. Those are
the two that families fight over more
than any others, and those are the two
where the wrong name costs the most
money. Step five, do not name minor
children or grandchildren directly as
beneficiaries. Name a custodian under
your state's uniform transfers to minors
act, or name your trust with specific
provisions for how the money should be
managed until the child reaches the age
you choose. One phone call to the
institution that holds your largest
account could save your family $400,000.
Make that call before the end of this
week.

title: 7 IRS Rules That Cost Retirees $50,000

segments.text: There are seven IRS rules that change
the moment you retire and nobody at your
company, nobody at Social Security, and
nobody at the IRS is going to explain a
single one of them to you on your last
day of work. When you had a job, your
employer pulled taxes out of every
paycheck and sent the money to the IRS
before you ever saw it. You filed once a
year, maybe got a refund, maybe owed a
little, and the system ran itself. The
day you retire, that entire system shuts
off. There is no letter, there is no
checklist, there is no phone call. You
go from autopilot to a system where
every single tax decision is yours and
every single mistake has a price. But
here's what makes this dangerous. There
is one rule on this list, rule number
six, that opens a window the day you
retire and closes it the day you turn
73. Most retirees never hear about this
window until after it shuts. The ones
who use it save over $50,000. The ones
who miss it pay full price for the rest
of their lives. We will get there, but
first you need the full picture. Here
are all seven rules in the order the IRS
expects you to deal with them. Rule
number one, the IRS will charge you a
penalty every single quarter you do not
pay them on time. When your employer
withheld taxes from your paycheck, that
money went to the IRS throughout the
year. In retirement, your income comes
from Social Security, a pension, IRA
withdrawals, dividends, maybe rental
income, but most of those sources either
withhold nothing or withhold nowhere
near enough. Social Security only
withholds federal tax if you
specifically ask for it. IRA withdrawals
often default to 10% withholding, but
your actual tax rate might be 22%. If
the gap between what you owe and what
was withheld is too large, the IRS
charges an underpayment penalty. The
rate for the second quarter of 2026 is
6% calculated daily on the amount you
underpaid for each quarter. Here is what
that looks like. In dollars, say your
total tax bill for 2026 is $14,000. You
had $8,000 withheld from various sources
throughout the year. That leaves $6,000
short. You did not make estimated
payments because nobody told you to. The
IRS calculates the penalty on that
$6,000 across four quarters. You are
looking at $300 to $400 on top of the
$6,000 you already owe. The fix is
quarterly estimated tax payments. The
deadlines are April 15th, June 15th,
September 15th, and January 15th. You
can set them up at irs.gov. The safe
harbor rule says if you pay at least
100% of last year's total tax through
withholding and estimated payments
combined, you will not be penalized no
matter what you owe this year. If your
income was above $150,000,
that number is 110%. But here is the
part almost no new retiree knows. The
IRS has a specific waiver for people 62
and older who retired in the last 2
years. If you had reasonable cause for
underpaying, they can waive the entire
penalty, but they do not apply it
automatically. You have to file form
2210 with your return and check the box
yourself. If you just pay the bill
without filing that form, you will pay
the penalty and never know the waiver
existed. If that penalty surprises you,
the next rule is worse because it
affects money you thought was already
yours. Rule number two, up to 85% of
your Social Security can be taxed and
the formula that decides how much has
not been updated since 1993. Most
retirees find this out the hard way.
They get their first Social Security
check, assume it is tax-free, and then
April comes and they owe the IRS
thousands of dollars they did not
expect. The IRS uses something called
provisional income to decide how much of
your Social Security gets taxed. It is
your adjusted gross income plus any
tax-exempt interest plus half of your
Social Security benefits. If that total
is between $25,000 and $34,000
as a single filer, up to 50% of your
benefits are taxable. Above $34,000,
up to 85%. For married couples, the
thresholds are $32,000 and $44,000.
Those thresholds were set in 1983 and
1993. They have never been adjusted for
inflation. A combined income of $25,000
in 1983 meant you were comfortable.
Today, it is barely scraping by.
Therefore, this frozen threshold now
catches 56% of all Social Security
recipients. But the real trap is what
happens at the edges. Every extra dollar
of income you bring in does not just get
taxed at its own rate. It can push more
of your Social Security into the taxable
zone. The effective marginal tax rate
for retirees in this income range can
hit 40 to 50%. Not because the tax
bracket is that high, but because each
new dollar triggers tax on benefits that
were previously untaxed. The fix is to
file form W-4V with the Social Security
Administration. It takes 5 minutes. You
choose a flat withholding rate of 7, 10,
12, or 22% and that money comes out of
your check before you ever see it. It
does not solve the underlying formula,
but it stops the surprise bill in April.
You can also set it up online through
your My Social Security account. Now,
before we get to rule number three, I
need you to pay close attention because
this next one is brand new. It did not
exist until this year and most tax
software is not flagging it
automatically. Rule number three, there
is a brand new $6,000 deduction for
seniors and the IRS will keep every
penny of it if you do not specifically
ask for it on your return. The One Big
Beautiful Bill created a new deduction
specifically for taxpayers 65 and older.
It is $6,000 per person, $12,000 for a
married couple filing jointly where both
spouses qualify. This is on top of the
regular standard deduction and on top of
the existing additional standard
deduction for seniors. The income limits
are 75,000 for single filers and 150,000
for married couples. Below those limits,
you get the full amount. Above them, it
phases out. This deduction is available
for tax years 2025 through 2028. It goes
on the new schedule 1A, but here is the
problem. Not all tax preparation
software has been updated to include it.
Not all preparers are flagging it.
Therefore, if you already filed your
2025 return without it, you can amend
within 3 years and claim the money back.
If you have not filed yet, ask your
preparer specifically whether they
applied the senior bonus deduction on
schedule 1A. Do not assume they did. For
a married couple both over 65 and under
the income limit, this is $12,000 in
additional deductions over 4 years. At a
22% tax rate, that is $2,640
back in your pocket that the IRS will
keep if you do not ask for it. That is
free money sitting on the table, but the
next rule is about money the IRS will
take from you if you are even one day
late. Rule number four, your required
minimum distributions start at 73 and
the penalty for missing one is 25% of
whatever you fail to withdraw. If you
have a traditional IRA or a 401k, the
IRS requires you to start taking minimum
withdrawals at age 73. The amount is
based on your account balance on
December 31st of the prior year divided
by a life expectancy factor from the IRS
tables. You must take your first
required minimum distribution by April
1st of the year after you turn 73. Every
distribution after that is due by
December 31st of each year. If you miss
the deadline, the penalty is 25% of the
amount you should have withdrawn. It
drops to 10% if you correct it within 2
years, but that is still a massive
penalty on money you were going to take
out anyway. But here is where the real
damage happens and most retirees walk
right into it. If you delay your first
distribution to that April 1st deadline,
you will have to take two distributions
in the same calendar year. Your first
one before April 1st and your second one
before December 31st. On a $500,000
that is roughly $38,000
in withdrawals hitting your tax return
in a single year. That can push you into
a higher bracket, make more of your
Social Security taxable under the
formula I just explained, and trigger
the Medicare surcharge I am going to
cover in rule number seven. Take your
first distribution in the year you turn
73. Do not wait until April.
The deadline is a trap. Speaking of
those required distributions, there is a
way to satisfy them without paying a
single dollar in tax and almost nobody
does it. Rule number five, you can use a
qualified charitable distribution to pay
your required minimum distribution with
zero tax. If you are 70 and a half or
older, you can donate up to $111,000
directly from your IRA to a qualifying
charity. This is called a qualified
charitable distribution. The money has
to move directly from your IRA custodian
to the charity. If the check comes to
you first and you deposit it, the IRS
treats the whole thing as a regular
taxable withdrawal and the tax break
disappears. The donation counts towards
your required minimum distribution, but
it does not count as taxable income. It
does not increase your adjusted gross
income. It does not push your Social
Security into the taxable zone. It does
not trigger the Medicare surcharge. If
you were going to give to charity
anyway, routing it through a qualified
charitable distribution instead of
writing a check from your bank account
saves you thousands of dollars for the
exact same donation. Same money to the
same charity, but one way costs you
nothing in tax and the other way costs
you plenty. Now, we are at rule number
six. This is the one I told you about at
the beginning. This is the window that
opens the day you retire and closes the
day your required minimum distributions
begin. If you miss it, you cannot go
back. Rule number six, the years between
retirement and age 73 are the most
valuable tax planning window of your
entire life and most people waste every
single one of them. These are called the
gap years. During this window, your
income is often at its lowest point.
Your tax bracket is at its lowest point.
This is the optimal time to do Roth
conversions. When you convert money from
a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA, you pay
income tax on the amount you convert in
that year. But once it is in the Roth,
it grows tax-free, withdrawals are
tax-free, and there are no required
minimum distributions on a Roth during
your lifetime. The tax you pay now at a
lower rate saves you from paying a
higher effective rate later when Social
Security required distributions and the
Medicare surcharge all stack on top of
each other. Here is the math. Say you
convert $50,000 per year for 6 years
during your gap window. That is $300,000
moved from your traditional IRA to your
Roth at a 12 or 22% rate. If you had
waited until 73 when required
distributions force the money out
anyway, that same $300,000 comes out at
a 24 or 32% rate because it stacks on
top of Social Security and every other
income source. At a 10% difference in
tax rate, that is $30,000 saved, but the
Roth keeps growing tax-free for the rest
of your life and your heirs inherit it
tax-free. Over 20 years, the total
benefit can exceed $50,000. In a down
market like we have right now,
conversions are even more powerful. You
convert at a lower dollar amount, pay
less tax, and all the recovery growth
happens inside the Roth where the IRS
cannot touch it. But every year you wait
is a year of conversions you cannot get
back. The window closes at 73. Talk to a
tax advisor this week about filling your
current bracket with Roth conversions.
Do not wait until next year. There is
one more rule, and this one does not
come from the IRS. It comes from
Medicare, but it is triggered by
everything I just told you. And it is
the surcharge that blindsides more
retirees than any other. Rule number
seven, a single large withdrawal or
conversion can raise your Medicare
premiums by over $4,000 a year, and
Medicare will not warn you before it
happens. IRMAA is the income-related
monthly adjustment adjustment amount. If
your modified adjusted gross income
exceeds certain thresholds, Medicare
adds a surcharge to your part B and part
D premium. The surcharge is based on
your tax return from 2 years prior. This
is the part that catches retirees off
guard. The income that decides of your
2026 Medicare surcharge is the income
you reported on your 2024 tax return.
You can be fully retired with almost no
income today and still be paying the
highest surcharge because of one large
event 2 years ago. For 2026, the first
threshold is $106,000
for individuals and $212,000
for married couple. Above those levels,
your Medicare premiums can increase by
$70 to over $400 per month per person.
Therefore, a single large IRA
withdrawal, a Roth conversion that was
too aggressive, or a one-time capital
gain from selling a property can push
you over the threshold for 1 year and
raise your Medicare premiums for the
following 12 months. For a married
couple in the second IRMAA tier, the
surcharge is over $4,800 per year for
coverage that is identical to what
someone below the threshold pays. If
this happens because of a one-time event
like a retirement, a job loss, or the
death of a spouse, you can file form
SSA-44 with the Social Security
Administration to request a reduction,
but Medicare will not tell you this form
exists. You have to know to ask. Here is
what you do this week. First, check
whether you need to make quarterly
estimated tax payments. If you have any
income that does not have taxes
withheld, the answer is yes. Set them up
at irs.gov before the next deadline.
Second, file form W-4V with Social
Security to start withholding from your
benefit. Third, ask your tax preparer
whether they applied the $6,000 senior
bonus deduction. If they did not, amend
your return. Fourth, look up your
required minimum distribution start date
and plan to take your first one in the
calendar year you turn 73, not the
following April. Fifth, call a tax
advisor and ask specifically about Roth
conversions during your gap years. Every
year you wait is a year you lose. Sixth,
before making any large withdrawal or
conversion, check whether it will push
you over the IRMAA threshold and raise
your Medicare premiums for the next 12
months. The IRS is not going to call
you. Medicare is not going to warn you.
The system that ran on autopilot your
entire career just handed you the
controls, and the first mistake is the
most expensive one.

title: 6 Forms Seniors Forget That Cost Their Children The House

segments.text: There are six forms that every American
homeowner over 60 has to file, but most
never do. And the day they die, those
forms cost their children the house. I
am going to walk you through every
single one of them, the exact
[clears throat] dollar amount each one
saves, and the order to file them in.
The fifth form on this list is the one
that nine out of 10 seniors never even
hear about until their family is already
sitting in a probate court watching the
judge decide who gets their parents'
house. And we will get to that one in a
few minutes. But first, you need to
understand why this is happening at all.
The American probate system was not
designed to protect families. It was
designed to generate revenue for state
courts and fees for the attorneys who
work in them. Therefore, every single
year, hundreds of thousands of American
families lose tens of thousands of
dollars, sometimes the entire value of
the family home, because the people who
built the system never told them about
the six documents that would have
stopped it. Most of these forms cost
less than $200 to file. Some are
completely free. But if you do not know
they exist, the system takes the money
you would to your children, and there is
nothing your family can do to stop it
after you are gone. Here are the six
forms in the order you need to file
them. This first form is the difference
between your children paying $20,000 or
paying nothing. It is called a transfer
on death deed, sometimes shortened to
TOD. This document does one thing, but
it is the single most important thing on
this list. It allows you to name the
person who will inherit your house the
moment you die without that house ever
passing through probate court. Here is
why that matters. The average probate
case in the United States costs the
family between 3 and 7% of the entire
value of the estate. Therefore, on a
home worth $300,000, your children will
pay somewhere between $9,000 and $21,000
in court fees, attorney fees, and
executor fees before they ever see the
title to the house. But the money is not
even the worst part. In some states, the
probate process takes between 9 and 18
months to finish, during which the house
cannot be sold, cannot be refinanced,
and cannot even be cleaned out. Property
taxes still come due, insurance still
has to be paid. The mortgage, if there
is one, still has to be paid. All of
that comes out of your children's
pockets while they sit there and wait
for a court to give them permission to
touch their own parents' house. A
transfer on death deed eliminates the
entire process. You file it once with
your county recorder, and on the day you
die, the house transfers directly to
whoever you named on the form. There is
no court involvement, no attorney fees,
and no waiting period. The form is
available in roughly 30 states. You can
find out if your state allows it by
searching for the words transfer on
death deed and the name of your state.
fee in most counties is between 20 and
$60, but the transfer on death deed only
works if you actually file it before you
die. Most people find this out too late.
Therefore, this is not a document you
can put off until next year. The second
form is the one the federal government
does not want you to know about. It is
called a ladybird deed. This one is only
available in five states: Florida,
Texas, Michigan, Vermont, and West
Virginia. If you live in any of those
five states, pay very close attention to
the next 60 seconds because this single
document can protect your home from a
threat that wipes out families every
single day in this country. Here is what
it does. A ladybird deed allows you to
retain complete control of your home
during your lifetime, including the
right to sell it, refinance it, or rent
it out. But the moment you die, the
property automatically transfers to
whoever you named on the deed. It
functions almost identically to a
transfer on death deed, except for one
critical difference. A ladybird deed
protects the house from Medicaid estate
recovery. the Medicaid five-year
look-back rule in another video on this
channel, but here is the short version.
If you ever apply for long-term care
Medicaid in your final years, the
federal government has the legal right
to come back after your death and force
the sale of your house to repay every
dollar Medicaid spent on your care. On a
typical nursing home stay of three
years, that is somewhere between
the government can take from your
estate. This is where families lose
everything. The ladybird deed legally
removes your home from your estate the
instant you die. Therefore, there is
nothing for the government to recover.
Your children inherit the house free and
clear, even if you spent the last five
years of your life on Medicaid. But the
ladybird deed has to be filed and
recorded before you ever apply for
Medicaid. If you wait, the look-back
rule cancels the protection. Therefore,
if you live in one of those five states
and you own a home, this is a document
you need to talk to an estate attorney
about this month, not next year. By the
time you need it, the window is already
closed. The third document is the one
that saves families more money than
anything else on this list, but it is
also the one where people make the most
expensive mistake. It is called a
revocable living trust. A trust costs
more to set up than the first two
documents, somewhere between $1,500 and
$3,000, depending on the attorney. But
here is why it is worth every dollar.
When you put your home into a revocable
living trust, the house no longer
belongs to you on paper. It belongs to
the trust. You still have full control.
You can sell, refinance, or move at any
time. Nothing about how you live
changes. But because the house is
technically owned by the trust, it does
not belong to your estate when you die.
Therefore, it cannot be touched by
probate. On a $400,000 home, this single
move saves your family between $12,000
and $28,000 in probate fees alone. But
the trust does something even more
important than that. A trust gives you
specific instructions for how the house
is handled after you are gone. If you
have three children and one of them
lives in the house and the other two
want to sell, a trust can spell out
exactly what happens. If you want the
surviving spouse to live in the house
for the rest of their life and only then
have it passed to the children, a trust
can do that. If you want to protect the
house from a future divorce of one of
your children, a trust can do that, too.
A will cannot do any of these things. A
will gets read in a courtroom and the
judge decides what to do. A trust is
private. It bypasses the court entirely
and it does exactly what you wrote into
it. But here is where people destroy
everything they just paid for. The most
expensive mistake American families make
with a trust is creating one and then
forgetting to actually transfer the
house into it. The legal term for this
is funding the trust. If the trust
exists on paper, but the deed to the
house was never updated, the trust does
nothing. The house still goes to
probate. Every dollar you spent setting
it up is gone. Therefore, when you set
up a trust, the very next thing you do
is file a new deed transferring the
house from your name to the name of the
trust. Skip that step and the trust is
worthless. We are now halfway through
the list, but the fifth document is
still ahead, and that is the one almost
nobody knows about. It is the one that
will save your family the most, but it
is also the one with the smallest window
to act. Stay with me. The fourth
document is an updated will with
specific language about your house. If
you die without a will in the United
States, your state government decides
who gets your property. The legal term
for this is dying intestate, and the
rules are not what most Americans think
they are. In Texas, for example, if you
die without a will and you are married,
your surviving spouse only inherits 1/3
of your separate property. The other 2/3
go to your children, even if those
children are from a previous marriage
and have never spoken to your current
spouse. In California, if you die
without a will and you have children,
your spouse only gets 1/3 or 1/2 of the
community property, depending on the
situation. In Pennsylvania, the first
$30,000 goes to your spouse, and
everything beyond that gets split. These
intestate rules vary by state, but the
pattern is the same in all 50. The state
assumes it knows better than you do how
your property should be divided. And
unless you have a written will that says
otherwise, the state wins every single
time. The fix is simple. A basic will
costs between $200 and $800 to draft
with an attorney. Um some online
services do it for under $100. But if
you own a home, I do not recommend the
cheap online versions because the the
language about real estate has to be
specific to the state you live in. But
here is the part most people miss, and
this is the part that tears families
apart. A will must be updated every time
something changes in your family. If you
wrote your will in 1992 and you have not
looked at it since, the names on it are
probably wrong. Your spouse may have
died. Your children may have divorced.
Your grandchildren may have been born.
The executor you named is probably no
longer alive. Therefore, every will
needs a review every five years and
every time a major life event happens.
An out-of-date will is sometimes worse
than no will at all because the family
ends up in court fighting over which
version controls. And while they fight,
the house sits there bleeding money.
Now, we are at the fifth document. This
is the one I told you almost nobody
knows about. It is called a durable
power of attorney for finances. This is
the form that nine out of 10 seniors
never file, and it is the one that costs
their families the most. If you only
file one document after watching this
video, make it this one. Here is why. A
durable power of attorney is the
document that names someone you trust to
handle your finances if you become
unable to do it yourself. If you have a
stroke, develop dementia, or end up in
the hospital for an extended period,
this is the document that lets your
spouse or your child pay your bills,
manage your bank accounts, and most
importantly, handle anything related to
your house. Without a durable power of
attorney, your family cannot legally do
any of those things. They cannot touch
your accounts, they cannot pay your
mortgage, they cannot do anything. They
have to go to court and ask a judge to
appoint a guardian or a conservator. The
legal term for this is a guardianship
proceeding, and the average cost in the
United States is somewhere between
$3,000 and $10,000 in legal fees just to
get the appointment. After that, the
guardian has to file annual reports with
the court, which often costs another
$2,000 to $4,000 per year. But the worst
part is not the money. The worst part is
the time. A guardianship proceeding
takes between three and six months to
complete in most states. During those
months, nobody can pay your property
taxes. Nobody can sign for repairs to
the house. Nobody can sell the house if
you need to move into care. Nobody can
do anything, and the bills do not stop.
The mortgage company does not care that
the family is waiting on a court.
Therefore, families lose homes to
foreclosure during guardianship
proceedings every single year in this
country. And a single piece of paper
filed on a Tuesday afternoon would have
prevented every one of those losses. A
durable power of attorney costs between
$100 and $300 to draft. It takes about
an hour with an attorney. But here is
the part that makes this so urgent. It
has to be signed while you are still
mentally competent to sign it. The
moment a doctor questions your capacity,
the window closes permanently. sign it
from a hospital bed. Your children
cannot sign it for you. Once that moment
passes, the only path left is the
courtroom. And by then, the damage is
already done. The sixth and final
document is your homestead exemption
filing. This is the one that is costing
you money right now, today. Every single
month you do not have it. Almost every
state in the country offers a homestead
exemption to homeowners. But the rules
and the savings are completely different
in each one. In Florida, the exemption
removes up to $50,000 from the assessed
value of your home for property tax
purposes. It also caps how much your
property tax can increase each year, no
matter how much your home value goes up.
In Texas, as of 2024, the exemption
removes $100,000 from the assessed value
of your home for school district taxes
alone. The annual savings vary by state,
but for most senior homeowners, they
range from $1,000 to $3,000 per year.
Over 20 years of retirement, that is
between $20,000 and $60,000 in your
pocket instead of the state
government's. But here is what most
seniors do not realize. In many states,
the homestead exemption is not
automatic. You have to file an
application with your county tax
assessor's office, and you only have to
do it once. After that, the exemption
stays in place for the rest of the time
you own the house. The application is
usually free, and it takes about 15
minutes to fill out. Many states also
offer additional senior exemptions on
top of the regular homestead exemption
available the year you turn 65. These
add another 5,000 to 15,000 dollars in
lifetime tax savings, depending on the
state. Almost nobody who qualifies for
the senior exemption actually files for
it because the county does not send you
a letter telling you it exists. You have
to know to ask, and now you know. Here
is what you do this week. First, find
the deed to your house. It is in your
filing cabinet, your lock box, or your
county recorder's online portal. Second,
write down which of these six documents
you already have, and which ones you do
not. Third, for any document you do not
have, search the name of the document
plus the name of your state. Read the
first three results. Fourth, call an
estate attorney in your county and ask
for a 1-hour consultation specifically
about home protection documents. The
cost will be between $200 and $400. The
attorney will tell you which of the six
documents you actually need based on
your state, your family situation, and
the value of your house. Fifth, do not
wait. Every one of these documents has a
window, and every one of those windows
closes the moment something happens to
you. Once you are in the hospital, once
the court gets involved, once the state
steps in, none of these forms matter
anymore.

title: The Government’s 5-Year Rule Takes Your Home and Most Seniors Never Know

segments.text: The 5-year rule lets the government take
your house, and most seniors do not find
out until it is far too late to do
anything about it. If you are 65 or
older, if you own your home, if you have
any savings at all, you need to
understand exactly how this rule works
because the people who are supposed to
explain it to you have a very strong
reason to stay quiet. There is one
specific document that can stop the
entire process before it ever begins,
but most estate attorneys will not bring
it up unless you ask for it by name. I
will tell you what that document is
called before this video is over. The
rule itself is called the Medicaid
5-year look back, but the name is
misleading. It is not really about
looking back. It is about punishing you
for things you did when you had no idea
you were doing anything wrong. Here is
how it works. If you ever need long-term
nursing home care, and the average stay
in this country now costs over $108,000
per year, you will almost certainly run
out of money. Therefore, you will have
to apply for Medicaid to cover the bill.
But before Medicaid pays a single
dollar, a state case worker will pull
every bank statement, every property
record, and every gift you have made for
the previous 60 months. Every single
transfer, every check to a grandchild,
every car you signed over, every dollar
you moved. Then they calculate a
penalty. The penalty is not a fine. It
is something worse. The state takes the
total amount you transferred during
those 60 months, divides it by what they
call the regional penalty divisor, which
in most states sits between $10,000 and
$12,000. And the result is the number of
months you are locked out of Medicaid
coverage. During those months, you must
pay for the nursing home yourself at
over $9,000 per month, even though the
entire reason you applied for Medicaid
is that you do not have $9,000 per
month. This is the trap. You gave away
the money, therefore, you cannot pay.
But because you gave away the money, the
state will not pay either. So, who pays
the nursing home? The nursing home does
not care. They will sue, and the first
asset they will come for is your house.
Most people assume the rule only catches
large transfers. That is wrong. The look
back catches everything. A $400
Christmas check to your granddaughter
counts. Paying for your son's wedding
counts. Helping a grandchild with
college tuition counts. Forgiving a loan
to a family member counts. Selling your
car to your nephew for $1 counts. Even
charitable donations over a certain
threshold can count, depending on the
state. There is no birthday exemption.
There is no holiday exemption. There is
no I did not know exemption. The federal
annual gift tax exclusion, which
[clears throat] currently sits at
$19,000 per recipient, has nothing to do
with this. That is an IRS rule. Medicaid
is a completely separate system with its
own rules, and Medicaid does not care
what the IRS allows. A gift that is
perfectly legal under federal tax law
can still trigger a full Medicaid
penalty. Most seniors do not understand
this distinction. Therefore, they assume
their gifts are safe. They are not. Now,
here is where it gets worse, and this is
the part that destroys marriages from
beyond the grave. If you are married and
your spouse goes into a nursing home,
you might think the law protects the
healthy spouse who stays home. There is
a protection. It is called the community
spouse resource allowance, and in 2026,
it sits at $157,920.
That is the maximum amount of countable
assets the at-home spouse is allowed to
keep. Everything above that number must
be spent down before Medicaid will pay
sounds like a lot until you realize what
it actually has to cover. Property
taxes, home repairs, Medicare premiums,
food, gas, medications, emergencies for
the rest of the healthy spouse's life,
which could be 20 years, which works out
to roughly $657
per month. That is the math the state
expects you to live on while your
husband or wife is in a facility that is
charging over $9,000 per month for the
same time period. But the house, surely
the house is safe. The house is the one
thing they cannot touch. That is what
almost every senior in America believes,
and it is wrong. The house is exempt
while you are alive and using it.
Therefore, Medicaid will not force you
to sell it before you qualify. But the
moment the Medicaid recipient passes
away, a program called the Medicaid
Estate Recovery Program activates.
Federal law requires every state to
attempt to recover the cost of care from
the estate of any Medicaid beneficiary
who is over 55 at the time benefits were
