paid. The recovery target is the house.
The state files a claim against the
estate. The heirs are told they must
either pay the bill in full, often
hundreds of thousands of dollars, or
sell the home and turn over the
proceeds. The average estate recovery
claim in this country now exceeds
In some states, it is over $200,000, and
it is not optional. It is not
negotiable. The federal government
requires the state to come after the
house. Therefore, the house your parents
promised would go to the grandchildren
ends up going to the state of whatever
they happen to live in. And in 29
states, including Pennsylvania, North
Carolina, New Jersey, Connecticut, and
Georgia, there is an even older law on
the books called filial responsibility.
These laws say that adult children can
be held financially responsible for the
unpaid nursing home bills of their
parents. For decades, these laws sat
unused. But starting in 2012, after a
Pennsylvania appeals court ruled that a
nursing home could collect $93,000
from an adult son for his mother's care,
the floodgates opened. Therefore, the
trap is not just that the state takes
your house. The trap is that the nursing
home, after the state finishes its
recovery, can turn around and sue your
children for whatever is left. give you
a real example. A widow in Ohio, aged
78, transferred $45,000 to her daughter
over a 4-year period. Birthday gifts,
holiday checks, some help with a car
repair, nothing she considered unusual.
She entered a nursing home in month 47
of those 4 years. The state divided her
45,000 by the Ohio penalty divisor of
per month and locked her out of Medicaid
for 6 months. The nursing home billed
her $9,200 per month for those 6 months.
Total bill, $55,200.
She did not have it. The home placed a
lien against her house. She passed away
8 months later. The state then filed an
estate recovery claim for an additional
in care costs. Her daughter received a
letter informing her that the home she
grew up in was being sold by court
order. There is a strategy that some
attorneys use to soften the blow when
there is no time left. They call it the
half a loaf. The idea is that if you or
your spouse already needs care, you give
away half of your remaining assets and
use the other half to pay for care
during the penalty period that the gift
triggers. It saves something. It is
better than losing everything, but it
requires precision timing. It requires a
specialized attorney, and it has to be
done before the Medicaid application is
filed, not after. Once you apply, the
strategy is dead. The seniors who lose
everything are almost never the ones who
planned. They are the ones who were
never told planning was an option. They
sat in the hospital room, signed a power
of attorney, and started writing checks
to the nursing home with no idea that
with one phone call to the right kind of
lawyer 2 years earlier, they could have
protected the house, the savings, and
the inheritance. Now, I told you at the
start that there is one document most
estate attorneys will not bring up
unless you ask for it. Here is what it
is called. It is called a Medicaid Asset
Protection Trust. In five specific
states, including Florida, Texas,
Michigan, West Virginia, and Vermont,
there is also something called a lady
bird deed, which accomplishes part of
the same goal for the home specifically.
A Medicaid Asset Protection Trust is an
irrevocable trust. You move your house,
your savings, and your investments into
the trust. You no longer technically own
them. The trust does. But you can still
live in the house. You can still receive
the income from the investments. You
just cannot take the assets back out.
After the trust has been in place for 5
years, those assets are no longer
counted by Medicaid. The look back
cannot reach them. The estate recovery
program cannot reach them. The house is
protected. Savings are protected.
Everything inside the trust passes
directly to your heirs without going
through probate, without going through
estate recovery, and without being
touched by the state. The reason most
attorneys do not mention this is simple.
A Medicaid Asset Protection Trust costs
between $4,000 and $12,000 to set up
correctly. A standard will cost $200. A
senior walks in asking for a will. The
attorney sells them a will, and the
conversation about long-term care never
happens. Therefore, you must walk in
already knowing the right phrase. You
must say the words Medicaid Asset
Protection Trust out loud, and you must
ask whether you qualify, and you must do
it at least 60 months before any care is
needed because the 5-year clock does not
start until the trust is funded. Here is
what to do this week. First, pull every
bank statement from the last 60 months
and look for any transfer over $500 to a
family member. Make a list. You need to
know your exposure before you talk to
anyone. Second, find an attorney who is
certified in elder law specifically. The
certification is called CELA, which
stands for Certified Elder Law Attorney.
A general estate attorney is not enough.
You need someone whose entire practice
is built around Medicaid planning.
Third, ask that attorney by name about a
Medicaid Asset Protection Trust. And if
you live in Florida, Texas, Michigan,
West Virginia, or Vermont, also ask
about a lady bird deed for the home.
Fourth, get the trust funded immediately
because every day you wait is a day
added to the back end of your 5-year
clock. Fifth, tell every adult child in
your family to read this exact same
information because the rule does not
just affect you. It affects everything
you planned to leave behind. The 5-year
clock starts the day the trust is
funded, not the day you decide to plan,
not the day you call the lawyer, the day
the assets actually move. Therefore, the
most expensive day in your life is the
day after you should have started.

title: The IRS Is About to Keep $1.2 Billion Dollars on April 15

segments.text: The IRS is about to keep $1.2 billion in
refunds that belong to 1.3 million
Americans, and the deadline to claim
your share is exactly 7 days away. On
April 15th at midnight, that money stops
being yours. It does not roll over, it
does not get held in escrow, it does not
get returned to anyone. It becomes the
property of the United States Treasury
by federal law with no appeal and no
exception. The IRS itself published the
warning. The notice is sitting on their
website right now, but almost nobody is
talking about it because the people most
likely to be owed this money are not the
people the news covers. And there is one
specific group of seniors who are almost
certainly owed money from this exact pot
and have no idea it exists. I will tell
you exactly who they are and how much
they are most likely owed before this
video ends. This is a rule almost nobody
outside the IRS bothers to explain. It
is called the 3-year statute of
limitations on refund claims, and it has
been quietly emptying senior bank
accounts for as long as the federal
income tax has existed. Here is how it
works. When you pay federal income tax,
whether through a paycheck, a pension
withdrawal, or a one-time withholding on
an IRA distribution, the IRS holds that
money until you file a return and tell
them what you actually owe. If you paid
more than you owed, the difference is
your refund, but the IRS does not send
your refund automatically. You have to
file a return to claim it, and the law
gives you exactly 3 years to do it.
After 3 years, that money no longer
belongs to you. It belongs to the
Treasury. There is no extension, there
is no appeal, there is no waiver. The
IRS itself cannot give it back even if
they wanted to because the law forbids
it for tax year 2022. That 3-year window
closes on April 15th, 2026. That is 7
days from today. This rule was not
written by accident. Congress put it
into the tax code in 1942 during the
height of the Second World War when the
federal government needed a way to close
its books cleanly each year. The
argument at the time was that the
Treasury could not function if it had to
hold open refund claims forever.
Therefore, Congress gave taxpayers
exactly 3 years and not 1 day more. The
Supreme Court has upheld this rule
multiple times, and the most famous case
is from 1996 when a taxpayer who was
hospitalized and unable to file lost his
refund anyway because the court ruled
that the 3-year deadline applies
regardless of medical hardship. There is
no exception for sickness. There is no
exception for disability. There is no
exception for grief. The clock runs no
matter what. But the IRS released the
official numbers last month, and they
are larger than almost anyone realizes.
1.3 million Americans are owed refunds
for tax year 2022. The total sitting in
the Treasury right now is $1.2 billion.
The median refund is $686,
which means half of the people on the
list are owed more than that. Some are
owed thousands. A few are owed tens of
thousands. Therefore, the question is
not whether this money exists. The IRS
confirmed it. The question is who is on
the list and why. Most of them have no
idea. Look at where the money is sitting
right now. In California, 143,000
Americans are owed roughly $124 million.
In Texas, 126,000
Americans are owed roughly $111 million.
In Florida, the state with the highest
concentration of seniors in the country,
89,000 Americans are owed roughly $74
million. In New York, 73,000 Americans
are owed roughly $72 million.
In Pennsylvania, 53,000 Americans are
owed roughly $49 million. In Illinois,
51,000 Americans are owed roughly $47
million. In Ohio, 45,000 Americans are
owed roughly $38 million. Every state
has people on this list. The IRS
publishes the breakdown by state, and
every line on it represents real people
who are about to lose real money in 7
days. But the abstract numbers do not
capture what is actually happening. So I
want you to picture a specific person.
Her name is Eleanor. She is 69 years
old. She lives in a one-bedroom
apartment in Phoenix. Her only regular
income is her Social Security check,
which is $1,740
a month. That puts her below the federal
filing threshold for someone her age. So
she has not filed a tax return in years.
Her son told her she does not need to
file, and her son is technically
correct. But in February of 2022,
Eleanor took a $4,200 withdrawal from a
small IRA she inherited from her late
husband. She used the money to fix the
transmission on her car. The brokerage
that held the IRA with held $420 in
federal tax automatically because that
is the default on retirement account
distributions when you do not check a
box telling them otherwise. That $420 is
Eleanor's money. The IRS owes it back to
her because her actual tax liability for
that year was zero. All she has to do to
claim it is file a 2022 Form 1040, but
she does not know the money exists. She
never got a notice. She does not check
the IRS website. And in 7 days, that
$420 belongs to the United States
Treasury forever. Eleanor is not
unusual. Eleanor is the median case, and
there is a man in Ohio named Walter who
is owed almost 10 times as much as
Eleanor for the exact same reason.
Walter is 74. He retired from a
manufacturing job in 2021. In 2022, he
rolled over part of his pension into a
personal account, and the rollover was
processed incorrectly by the plan
administrator. 20% of the distribution,
around $4,100,
was withheld for federal tax even though
it should have gone directly into the
new account. Walter never filed a return
for 2022 because he assumed the rollover
was clean. It was not. That $4,100
is sitting in the Treasury right now
waiting for him to file a single piece
of paper. If he does not file by April
15th, the IRS keeps it. And then there
is Margaret. Margaret is 72, and she
lives outside Pittsburgh. Her husband
passed away in 2021, and the year after
he died, she finally cashed in a stack
of paper savings bonds that the two of
them had been collecting since the
1970s. The bonds had matured. The total
payout was a little over $11,000. The
Treasury withheld federal tax on the
accumulated interest portion
automatically, which came to about
$1,100. Margaret had never filed a tax
return on her own before. Her husband
had always handled it. She did not know
she needed to file in 2022 to claim that
$1,100 back. The bonds were her only
taxable event for the year, and her
actual tax liability was zero because
her total income was below the filing
threshold for a widow her age. But if
she does not file a 2022 return by April
15th, that $1,100 belongs to the
Treasury permanently. Multiply Eleanor
and Walter and Margaret by 1.3 million
people, and you get $1.2 billion. So who
exactly should be checking this week? If
you are a senior who did not file a
federal return for tax year 2022 and any
one of the following happened to you
that year, you are very likely owed
money. You took any distribution from an
IRA, a 401k, a pension, or an inherited
retirement account. You worked any
part-time job even for a few weeks where
the employer withheld federal tax from
your paycheck. You collected interest
from a bank account that issued you a
Form 1099-INT
with federal tax withheld. You sold any
investment that triggered backup
withholding. You cashed out a savings
bond. You received a one-time payout
from a life insurance annuity. Or a
relative who passed away that year had a
final pension or IRA distribution paid
out in your name. In every one of those
situations, federal tax was almost
certainly withheld from the payment even
if the amount looked small at the time.
And in every one of those situations,
that withholding is refundable to you
because most seniors who only collect
Social Security have a federal tax
liability of zero or very close to zero.
But here is the catch, and it is the
catch that traps almost everyone. The
3-year clock does not pause for any
reason. It does not pause if you are
sick. It does not pause if you did not
know. It does not pause if a family
member was handling your finances and
dropped the ball. The IRS published a
clear statement on this. By law,
taxpayers have only 3 years to claim a
refund. After that, the money becomes
property of the United States Treasury.
End of story. There is no grace period.
There is no late filing window. At
midnight on April 15th, 2026, every
dollar that has not been claimed is
gone. Now, I know what some of you are
thinking right now because I have heard
it from every senior I have ever
explained this rule to. There are three
objections that stop people from acting,
and I want to take them apart one at a
time. The first objection is, I do not
have my old paperwork. I lost the W-2. I
never kept the 1099. The brokerage
closed years ago, therefore I cannot
file. This is wrong. The IRS keeps a
copy of every single income document
ever issued in your name going back at
least 10 years. You can pull a free wage
and income transcript directly from the
IRS website in about 10 minutes. It will
list every W-2, every 1099-R, every
and every other reportable payment that
was made to you in 2022. You do not need
the original paper. You need the
transcript. The second objection is, it
is only a few hundred dollars. It is not
worth the trouble. I want you to think
about that for a moment. $686
is the median. That is roughly 1 month
of groceries for most seniors. It is
roughly half a month of rent in many
parts of the country. It is enough to
cover a heating bill, a car repair, or a
Medicare copay that would otherwise come
out of savings. The IRS is keeping that
money by default unless you take one
specific action. There is no scenario in
which leaving $600 sitting in the
Treasury is the smart choice. The third
objection is, I am scared to file. I do
not want to deal with the IRS. I do not
want them looking at my finances. This
one I understand, but I want you to hear
me clearly. Filing a refund claim is not
an audit. It does not put you on a list.
It does not invite scrutiny. The IRS
already has every document I just
described. They already know what was
withheld from you. All you are doing by
filing is asking them to send back what
they already owe you. The risk of filing
is essentially zero. The risk of not
filing is losing every dollar in 7 days.
And uh one more thing because almost
everyone gets this part wrong. Filing an
extension does not help you. An
extension gives you until October 15th
to file your 2025 return. It does
absolutely nothing for your 2022 refund.
The 3-year clock runs from the original
2022 filing deadline, and it cannot be
extended by anyone for any reason. You
might also be wondering where exactly
this money goes after April 15th. It
does not get held in a special fund. It
does not get returned to your state. It
does not get used to pay Social
Security. It is swept into the general
fund of the United States Treasury,
which means it pays for whatever
Congress decides to spend it on that
year. Defense contracts, foreign aid,
federal salaries, whatever the budget
calls for. Your refund becomes
indistinguishable from any other federal
tax dollar the moment the deadline
passes. There is no fund you can appeal
to and no office you can call to get it
back. So, here is exactly what to do
this week. Step one, go to irs.gov and
search for prior year forms and
instructions. Find form 1040 for tax
year 2022. Download both the form and
the instructions for that year. They are
free. Step two, gather every 2022 tax
document you can find. That means W-2
forms, 1099-R forms from any retirement
account distribution, 1099-INT
forms from your bank, the SSA-1099
from Social Security, and any other 1099
you might have received that year. If
you cannot find them, go to irs.gov and
search for get transcript. Request a
wage and income transcript for 2022. The
IRS keeps a copy of every form ever
issued in your name, and you can pull
the entire transcript online for free in
about 10 minutes. Step three, fill out
the 2022 form 1040 using the 2022
instructions. Not the current year
version, the 2022 version. The brackets,
the standard deduction, the senior
add-on, and the rules are different than
they are now. And using the wrong year
invalidates the return. Step four, sign
the return, attach copies of every
withholding document you gathered and
put it in an envelope. Prior year
returns this far back generally cannot
be filed electronically, so you will
need to mail a paper return. The mailing
address is printed in the 2022
instructions, and it depends on which
state you live in. Use that exact
address. Step five, postmark the
envelope by April 15th, 2026. The IRS
uses the postmark date, not the receipt
date. If the envelope is postmarked
April 16th, the refund is gone forever,
even if it arrives the next day. Do this
for yourself if you think you might be
on the list. But more importantly, do it
for any senior in your family who does
not normally file a return. Pick up the
phone today. Ask them whether they took
any retirement distribution, sold any
investment, cashed any savings bond, or
worked any part-time job in 2022. If the
answer to any of those questions is yes,
they are very likely owed money, and
they have 7 days to claim it. After
that, the IRS keeps it.

title: The IRS Rule That Just Took 25% From Retirees

segments.text: There is a rule the Internal Revenue
Service quietly enforced on April 1st
that takes 25% of your retirement
account and the deadline to act on it
was 5 days ago. If you turn 73 years old
at any point during 2025, you were
required to pull a specific amount of
money out of your retirement account by
April 1st of this year. April 1st has
come and gone. Therefore, if you missed
it, the federal government is now
legally entitled to take a quarter of
what you should have withdrawn on top of
the regular income tax you already owe.
I'm going to walk you through exactly
what that rule is and how to make the
entire penalty disappear with one short
form. But before I get to it, you need
to understand three other rules the
federal government either changed, hid,
or quietly enforced against retirees in
the last few months. All of them have
hard deadlines. None of them were
explained to the public in plain
English. Rule one, the social security
tax trap that should make every retiree
in America furious. Most retirees
believe their social security benefits
cannot be taxed. They paid into the
system with after-tax dollars for 40
years. Therefore, that money should be
tax-free on the way out. But the federal
government does tax it and the way they
do it is one of the cleanest examples of
a rule that was designed for one purpose
and is now used for another entirely.
The Internal Revenue Service uses
something called combined income to
decide how much of your social security
gets taxed. Combined income is your
adjusted gross income plus tax-exempt
interest plus half of your annual social
security benefit. If your combined
income is between $25,000 and $34,000 as
a single filer, up to 50% of your social
security becomes taxable. Above $34,000,
up to 85% of it becomes taxable. For
married couples filing jointly, the
thresholds are $32,000
and $44,000. Here is the part that
should make you furious. Those
thresholds were set in 1983 and 1990.
They have never been adjusted for
inflation, not once. In over 30 years,
because of inflation alone, those frozen
thresholds now hit an estimated 56% of
all social security recipients. The rule
was designed for the wealthy few.
Through congressional inaction, it now
hits the majority. Linda is 72, single,
with $24,000 a year in social security
and a $24,000 withdrawal from her
individual retirement account. Her
combined income is $36,000. She just
crossed the $34,000 line. Up to 85% of
her social security is now taxable. That
added to her taxable income. At a 22%
bracket, that is $4,488
in tax on benefits she thought she had
already paid for. Your social security
cost of living adjustment was 2.8% this
year. For some retirees, that raise is
exactly what pushed them across the line
for the first time. The raise triggered
the tax, the tax ate the raise. Rule
two, the brand new $6,000 senior
deduction that most filers will miss.
Last July, Congress passed a tax bill
called House Resolution 1. Buried inside
that bill is a brand new deduction for
anyone aged 65 and older. $6,000 per
qualifying person, $12,000 for a married
couple where both spouses qualify. It
sits on top of every other deduction you
already get, including the standard
deduction. This is the very first filing
season the deduction exists. Therefore,
tax preparation software is still
rolling out updates that include it.
Therefore, the paid preparer at the
storefront down the street has a real
chance of missing it and the federal
agency that collects the tax has every
financial reason in the world not to
remind you it exists, because every
senior who claims it sends less money to
the Treasury. Roughly 33 million
Americans qualify this year. The
deduction is worth between $600 and
$1,300 in actual tax savings for a
single filer, depending on bracket.
Twice that for a married couple. It
expires after 2028 unless Congress
extends it. Here is the trap. The
deduction phases out at higher incomes.
The full $6,000 applies if your modified
adjusted gross income is at or below
single or $150,000 married. Above those
thresholds, it shrinks fast. By $175,000
single or $250,000
married, it is gone entirely and a
required minimum distribution from your
retirement account flows straight into
that income calculation. Therefore, the
same withdrawal that triggers the
penalty I am about to walk you through
can wipe out your $6,000 deduction at
the same time. Action item, pull out
your 2025 tax return. Look for a line
labeled additional senior deduction or
new deduction for taxpayers age 65 and
over. If you do not see that line and
you qualify, your return is wrong. If
you already filed and the line is
missing, you can file form 1040X to
amend it. Rule three, the inherited
individual retirement account 10-year
rule that destroys families. If you
inherited a retirement account from a
parent, a sibling, or an aunt or uncle
in the last few years, the rules for
that account were rewritten under a law
called Secure 2.0. The rewrite is
brutal. Before the change, an heir who
inherited a traditional individual
retirement account could stretch
withdrawals over their entire life
expectancy, paying tax on small
distributions year by year. A
60-year-old who inherited a $500,000
account could spread that across 20-plus
years and never get pushed into a higher
bracket. That stretch option is gone for
almost every non-spouse heir. The new
rule requires the entire inherited
account to be drained within 10 years of
the original owner's death. And here is
the part the federal government is now
actively enforcing. If the original
account owner was already taking
required minimum distributions when they
died, the heir also has to take an
annual required distribution every
single year inside the 10-year window.
Most heirs have no idea this rule
exists. The penalty for missing those
annual distributions is the same 25%
excise tax I am about to walk you
through. On a typical inherited account,
missing a single annual distribution can
cost the heir more than $4,000 in
penalty alone plus the regular income
tax they still owe on the distribution
itself. Action item, if you inherited a
retirement account in 2020 or later, log
into that account this week. Check
whether you took a required distribution
last year. If you did not and the
original owner was over 73 when they
died, you may already be exposed. Rule
four, the 25% penalty I warned you about
in the first sentence, the required
minimum distribution rules force you to
start pulling money out of every
traditional retirement account you own
at a specific age. For most retirees
watching this, that age is 73. The
amount you have to withdraw each year is
calculated by formula using your account
balance and a federal life expectancy
table. If you fail to take the full
required amount by the federal deadline,
the Internal Revenue Service charges a
25% excise tax on the shortfall. That is
on top of the regular income tax you
also owe. Until 2023, the penalty was
actually 50%. Congress cut it to 25
under Secure 2.0. Most news coverage
framed that as good news. But here is
the part nobody covered. Reducing the
penalty also let the federal government
start enforcing it more aggressively
because 25% is easier to collect than
50. Notices for missed distributions
have actually increased since the law
passed, not decreased. Helen is 73. She
in a traditional individual retirement
account from a job she left in 2007. Her
required distribution this year is about
She forgot to take it. The penalty alone
On top of that, she still owes about
in regular income tax on the
distribution. By missing one deadline,
Helen loses $4,600 to the federal
government on money she never even
spent. And remember, the senior
deduction phase out from rule two, the
very same withdrawal that triggers this
penalty also raises your modified
adjusted gross income, which can wipe
out your $6,000 deduction at the same
time. Two penalties from one mistake.
Now, here is what the federal government
does not put on the front page of its
website. The penalty can be erased
entirely. There is one specific form,
three pages long, that does it. Form is
called form 5329. Part nine of that form
is the section for requesting a waiver
of the 25% penalty. To qualify, you have
to do two things. First, take the missed
distribution as soon as humanly
possible, even if the deadline has
already passed. Second, attach a written
statement explaining what the law calls
reasonable cause. Reasonable cause is
intentionally vague. It can include
serious illness, the death of a spouse,
an error by your financial advisor, a
recent move, or simply that you did not
know the rule applied to you. The waiver
is granted in the overwhelming majority
of cases where the form is filed
correctly and the missed amount has
actually been withdrawn. You do not have
to negotiate. You do not have to hire a
tax attorney. You file the form, you
write a short statement, you attach
proof that you finally took the
distribution, and the penalty almost
always disappears. For a typical
retiree, that is $4,000
saved on a single sheet of paper. But
you have to do this before the federal
government issues a formal notice. Once
they start collection, your odds of a
full waiver drop dramatically.
Therefore, the window for action is the
next few weeks, not the next year. After
everything I just told you, I want to
end with something good, something that
puts real money back in your pocket and
undoes the damage from several of these
rules in one move. It is called a
qualified charitable distribution. It is
one of the most powerful tools in the
entire retirement tax code and almost no
one talks about it. 70 and a half or
older, you can instruct the company that
holds your traditional individual
retirement account to send a
distribution directly to a qualified
charity instead of sending it to you
first. The distribution counts toward
your required minimum distribution for
the year, but because the money never
touches your bank account, it does not
count as taxable income on your return.
That single mechanic does three things
at once. It satisfies your requirement
of distribution, which means you avoid
the 25% penalty from rule four. It does
not raise your adjusted gross income,
which means it does not push you across
the social security threshold from rule
one, and it does not raise your modified
adjusted gross income, which means it
does not phase out your $6,000 senior
deduction from rule two. One move, three
traps avoided. The annual limit for 2026
is approximately $108,000
per person. For a married couple where
both spouses have individual retirement
accounts, that is over $216,000
per year that can be out of taxable
territory. Action item. If you give to
charity at all, even $500 a year to your
church, call your individual retirement
account custodian this week and ask
about qualified charitable
distributions. Many custodians let you
set up a recurring distribution that
handles it automatically every year. One
phone call can save thousands of dollars
over the next decade.

title: Millions Lost Money on Social Security Benefits | Check If You're One of Them

segments.text: 3 million Americans are sitting on a
government-backed payment they were
never told about, and some of them have
already lost part of it simply by
waiting too long. That number is not an
estimate. The Social Security
Administration confirmed it. 3 million
100,000 people received checks totaling
$17 billion
in retroactive Social Security payments
after Congress reversed one of the most
damaging benefit cuts in the history of
the program. The average check was
but here is the part nobody is talking
about. A significant number of those
payments came in short. Some people were
underpaid, and some people who should
have been in that group of 3 million
never received a single dollar. There is
also a trap buried inside the payments
that already went out that could quietly
cost you thousands more in Medicare
bills 2 years from now. In a moment, I'm
going to tell you exactly who's being
shorted, what the specific numbers look
like, and what you need to do before you
lose any more of this money. But first,
you need to understand how this cut
worked, because if you are a teacher, a
firefighter, a police officer, a federal
employee, or the spouse or surviving
widow of any one of those people, there
is a real chance you are in this story.
My name is Mark Callaway. I spent over a
decade inside the financial system
watching people leave money on the
table, not because they were careless,
but because the rules were written to be
confusing. This channel is the briefing
you should have gotten before you
retired. For 40 years, the federal
government ran two separate rules that
quietly reduced Social Security benefits
for millions of Americans who worked in
public service. The rules were called
the Windfall Elimination Provision and
the Government Pension Offset. Most
people who were affected never fully
understood what was happening to their
money. They just knew their Social
Security check was smaller than it
should have been, but the reduction was
not random. It was calculated, and in
many cases, it was severe enough to
change how people lived in retirement.
Here is how the Windfall Elimination
Provision worked. When Social Security
calculates your monthly benefit, it
takes your lifetime average earnings and
applies a percentage to different
portions of that history. For the first
portion of your earnings record, the
standard formula applies 90%. That first
portion is where most middle-income
workers receive the bulk of their
benefit. But if you also had a pension
from a government job that did not pay
into Social Security, the formula did
not apply 90% to that first portion. It
applied 40%. That one change slashed the
most valuable part of your benefit
calculation. The maximum reduction under
the 2024 formula was $587
every single month. $587
every month for the rest of your life.
The average reduction across everyone
affected was about $350 per month over a
20-year retirement. That is $84,000
in lost Social Security income. Most
people had no idea the rule existed and
no idea how much it was costing them.
The Government Pension Offset worked
differently, but the result was even
more extreme. This rule did not touch
your own earned benefit. It attacked
your spousal or survivor benefit. If
your spouse or your late spouse paid
into Social Security their entire
career, you are normally entitled to a
spousal benefit based on their earnings
record. The Government Pension Offset
subtracted 2/3 of your government
pension from that benefit. Therefore, if
your pension was large enough, 2/3 of it
wiped out your Social Security spousal
or survivor benefit completely, not
reduced it, eliminated it. Nearly 70% of
everyone affected by the Government
Pension Offset had their entire spousal
or survivor benefit reduced to zero. The
average government pension of those
people was $3,502
per month. 2/3 of that is $2,335.
That exceeds most spousal benefits.
Therefore, for millions of public
workers and their spouses, the Social
Security benefit they had earned and
expected simply disappeared. Now, here
is who this affects, because I want you
to be able to place yourself or someone
in your family in this story before we
get to what needs to be done. Teachers
are the single largest category. 15
states plus the District of Columbia
have public school systems where
teachers do not pay into Social Security
at all. Their retirement comes through a
separate state pension system. Those
states are Alaska, California, Colorado,
Connecticut, Georgia, Illinois,
Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine,
Massachusetts, Missouri, Nevada, Ohio,
Rhode Island, and Texas. If you were a
teacher in any of those states and you
also worked other jobs during your life
that paid into Social Security, the
Windfall Elimination Provision was
cutting your benefit every single month.
Federal employees hired before 1984 are
the second major group. The older Civil
Service Retirement System did not
include Social Security. Therefore, if
you spent your career as a federal
employee under that system and you also
had Social Security credits from earlier
work or a second job, those credits were
being quietly cut every month you
collected them. Police officers and
firefighters in many cities and counties
fall into this group as well. Many local
governments opted out of Social Security
and set up their own pension systems.
But if their employees also had Social
Security credits from other work, the
Windfall Elimination Provision applied,
and the spouses and widows of all of
these workers were subject to the
Government Pension Offset, which in
close to 70% of cases wiped out the
spousal or survivor benefit entirely. On
January 5th, 2025, Congress passed the
Social Security Fairness Act, and the
president signed it into law. Both
provisions were eliminated permanently,
and the restoration of benefits was made
retroactive to January of 2024. That
meant everyone affected was owed back
pay for every month their benefit had
been reduced since the start of 2024.
The Social Security Administration moved
faster than anyone expected. By July of
2025, they had already processed and
sent 3 million 100,000 payments totaling
$17 billion. The average retroactive
lump sum was $6,710
per person. People whose spousal or
survivor benefits had been eliminated
entirely saw their monthly checks go up
by an average of $1,190
per month going forward in addition to
the back pay they received. But this is
where the story gets more complicated,
and this is the piece that determines
whether you have received everything you
are actually owed. A large number of
people never filed for Social Security
benefits in the first place. They were
told years ago that the Government
Pension Offset would eliminate their
spousal or survivor benefit entirely.
Why file paperwork for a benefit that is
going to be zeroed out? So they never
applied. After the law passed in January
people filed new claims for the very
first time. Security Administration
applied a standard 6-month retroactive
limit to those new filers, not 12 to 13
months of back pay like everyone else
received, 6 months. Therefore, if you
filed a new claim in April of 2025,
instead of receiving retroactive
benefits going back to January of 2024,
you may have only received back pay
covering 6 months from your application
date. Depending on your benefit amount,
the difference can be $4,000 or more.
Senators and advocates have challenged
this interpretation. The argument is
that these people were locked out of
filing by the existence of the
Government Pension Offset itself.
Applying the standard 6-month limit
punishes them for following the advice
they were given at the time. As of
today, the ruling has not been reversed.
Therefore, if you filed a new claim
after the law passed and your
retroactive lump sum is smaller than the
full period back to January of 2024,
there is a formal reconsideration
process available to you. I will walk
you through it step by step at the end
of this video. But first, I need to tell
you about a trap sitting inside the
payments that already went out, because
this one is catching people completely
off guard. If you received a retroactive
lump sum in 2025, that payment was
counted as income for 2025. Up to 85% of
Social Security income can be subject to
federal tax depending on your total
income for the year. That is the
immediate issue, and it is manageable.
The IRS has a specific provision called
the lump sum election method described
in IRS Publication 915. That method lets
you calculate the taxable portion of the
payment by allocating it back to the
years in which it would have originally
been paid using each of those prior
years as the income baseline, rather
than forcing the entire amount into your
2025 return. It can significantly reduce
the tax bill on a large back payment,
but the Medicare impact is slower, and
it is sneaking up on people right now.
Medicare sets your premiums based on
your income from 2 years earlier. That
means your 2025 income determines your
2027 Medicare premiums, the same year
your retroactive lump sum arrived. If
that payment pushed your 2025 income
as a single filer or $222,000
as a married couple, your Medicare
premiums in 2027 will be higher. The
first surcharge tier alone adds
approximately $840 per person per year.
Crossing $1 over the threshold triggers
the full amount. There are two things
you can do. First, use the IRS lump sum
election method on your 2025 return
described in IRS Publication 915. That
method allocates the back payment across
prior years rather than landing it all
in 2025, which can reduce both the tax
bill and the income figure Medicare will
use. Second, file form SSA-44
with Social Security to request a
premium review with documentation
showing the income was a one-time,
non-recurring payment. It does not
always succeed, but it costs nothing to
file. Here is what you need to do right
now. Step one, if you were a teacher in
any of the 15 states listed in this
video, a federal employee under the
Civil Service Retirement System, a
police officer or firefighter in a
non-Social Security covered pension
system, or the spouse or surviving
spouse of any of those workers, log into
your My Social Security account at
ssa.gov and review your payment history
and your current monthly benefit amount.
If your monthly benefit increased and
you received a retroactive payment,
verify the numbers look correct. Step
two, if you were never in the system
because you were told the Government
Pension Offset would eliminate your
benefit and you still have not filed a
claim, call the Social Security
Administration at 1-800-772-1213.
Tell them you are calling about the
Social Security Fairness Act, and that
you want to file a new spousal or
survivor benefit claim. Every month you
wait is a month of retroactive pay you
cannot recover under the current
six-month rule. Step three, if you filed
a new claim after January 5th of 2025,
and your retroactive lump sum only
covers six months, rather than the full
period back to January of 2024, file
form SSA-561.
That is the request for reconsideration.
Submit it in writing. It creates a
formal record of your challenge and
gives you standing if this ruling is
ever corrected. Step four, bring your
2025 tax return to whoever prepares your
taxes and ask specifically whether they
applied the lump sum election method
from IRS publication 915 to your Social
Security back payment. If they did not,
have them recalculate. The savings can
be substantial, and it may also protect
your 2027 Medicare premiums. Step five,
if your new monthly benefit still does
not match what you calculated it should
be based on your earnings history,
request a written benefit calculation
breakdown from the Social Security
Administration. You are entitled to see
exactly how they arrived at your number.
If the math is wrong, file form SSA-561
and request a formal reconsideration in
writing. The money was taken from you
for 40 years. Congress gave it back.
Make sure you received all of it.

title: They Charged Seniors $2,850 and Didn’t Tell Them

segments.text: If your household income crossed
in 2024, Medicare is charging you an
extra $540
per month right now, on top of your
standard premium, and they were never
required to tell you before it started.
That is $6,480
this year alone for coverage that has
not changed, for income that may have
come from a single financial decision
made 2 years ago, and will never happen
again. Before I walk you through exactly
how this works, I need to tell you about
one specific move that millions of
American retirees have made in the last
few years on the direct advice of their
financial planners. It is widely
considered one of the smartest
retirement strategies available. Done at
the wrong income level in the wrong
year, it quietly triggers this rule and
adds thousands of dollars to your
Medicare bill 2 years later with no
warning and no notice from anyone. I'm
going to show you exactly what that move
is, and I'm going to show you how to
find out whether it has already cost you
this year. The rule is called Irma. It
stands for income-related
adjustment amount. It is a surcharge
that Medicare adds to your monthly
premiums when your income exceeds a
specific threshold. It applies to part
B, which covers your doctor visits and
outpatient care, and it applies to part
D, which covers your prescription drugs.
Both bills go up at the same time. In
2026, the standard Medicare part B
premium is $203 per month. Most people
on Medicare pay exactly that, but the
moment your income crosses the first
Irma threshold, your part B premium
jumps to $284
per month. At the second tier, it climbs
per month. The tiers continue upward
from there, all the way to $690
per month at the highest bracket. Each
tier is a cliff, not a slope. $1 of
income above the line and the entire
surcharge applies. For a married couple
where both spouses are on Medicare and
both hit the second tier, the additional
charge is $406 per month per person.
Combined, that is $812 per month in
Medicare surcharges before prescription
drug costs are added, nearly $10,000 per
year. For the exact same doctors, the
exact same coverage, not one additional
benefit. But here is what almost no one
explains when they describe this rule.
And this is the part that makes IRMA
genuinely dangerous for people who are
not actively tracking it. Medicare does
not look at your current income to set
your tier. It looks at your tax return
from 2 years ago. That means your 2026
Medicare premiums are based on your 2024
modified adjusted gross income, not what
you are earning today, not what you
earned last year, what you reported on
your federal return 2 years ago. For
most retirees, this creates a direct and
painful mismatch. You could have fully
retired in early 2025. Your income this
year could be $40,000. But if something
happened in your finances in 2024 that
caused a spike in your reported income,
Medicare is reading that spike right now
and billing you accordingly. Even though
that income is completely gone, even
though you have no way to go back and
undo it. There is no automatic
correction. There is no letter that
says, "Your income has dropped since we
ran this calculation." Medicare issues
an IRMA determination at the start of
each year based on the tax data the IRS
shares with them. And that determination
stands for the entire year unless you
file to challenge it. Therefore, the
group most likely to be overpaying IRMA
surcharges right now is not the wealthy.
It is recent retirees. People who had
one large income event in 2023 or 2024
whose income has since dropped to a
fraction of what it was. And by far the
most common cause of those spikes is the
transaction I told you about at the
start of this video. The transaction is
a Roth IRA conversion. A Roth conversion
is when you move money from a
traditional IRA or 401k into a Roth IRA.
The money grows tax-free inside the
Roth, and qualified withdrawals in
retirement are not taxed. Financial
planners have been recommending these
conversions aggressively, particularly
to people in the decade before
retirement, as a way to reduce future
required minimum distributions and
manage long-term tax exposure. The
recommendation is often exactly right,
but a Roth conversion counts as ordinary
income in the year you execute it. If
you converted $100,000 from a
traditional IRA into a Roth in 2024,
Medicare sees $100,000 of additional
income on your 2024 return. For a
married couple whose income was
otherwise below the Irma threshold, that
single conversion can push them from the
standard rate to the second tier in one
transaction. The result is that Medicare
is now charging them $812 per month in
2026 instead of $400. That is nearly
5,000 extra dollars this year for a
conversion they made two years ago, for
money that is now locked inside the Roth
and cannot be touched without
consequences. That is not a penalty for
doing something wrong. the rule working
exactly as designed, and it will run for
the entire year unless you file to stop
it. Roth conversions are not the only
trigger. There are three others that hit
seniors regularly and that almost no
financial planner thinks to mention
before the transaction happens. The
first is a home sale. If you sold your
primary residence in 2024 and your
profit exceeded the capital gains
exclusion, which is $250,000
for a single filer and $500,000 for a
married couple, the excess was reported
as income on your return. Medicare is
reading that number right now. The
second is required minimum
distributions. Once you reach the age at
which IRA withdrawals are required,
those distributions count as income. If
you inherited an IRA in 2024 or took a
larger distribution than usual for any
reason, it is sitting on your 2024
return and it raised your tier. The
third is what I call the combination
trap. Social Security benefits are not
directly taxed, but up to 85% of your
benefit becomes taxable once your
combined income crosses certain
thresholds. When you stack that on top
of pension income, investment income,
and IRA withdrawals, your reported
income can be significantly higher than
you expected. One year where multiple
income sources land on the same return
is often enough to push a household into
the first or second Irma tier. Now, I
want to come back to the number I told
you about at the opening of this video,
because the numbers in this rule are not
approximate. They are exact, and you
need to know where you stand. For a
single filer in 2026, below $109,000
in modified adjusted gross income, you
pay the standard rate of $203 per month
for Part B. Between $109,000
you pay $284
per month. Between $137,000
you pay $406 per month. The tiers
continue upward from there. For a
married couple filing jointly, every
threshold doubles. The Part D drug
coverage surcharges stack on top of each
tier. At the first tier, $14.50
per person per month. At the second
per person per month. These numbers
compound. A married couple at the second
tier for both Part B and Part D is
paying over $940
per month combined. The standard rate
for that same couple is just over $400.
The difference is $540 per month, $6,480
per year for coverage that is identical
in every respect to what they were
paying for before. But here is something
Medicare does not put in the notice it
sends when your premium goes up. You can
appeal this determination. And if your
income has genuinely dropped since the
year Medicare is reading, there is a
strong chance the appeal will succeed.
The Social Security Administration
handles Irma determinations. If your
income dropped because of a qualifying
life-changing event, you can request
that Medicare recalculate your premium
using a more recent income estimate. The
form is SSA-44.
It is available at ssa.gov at no cost,
no attorney required, no fee to file.
The qualifying events include retirement
or a significant reduction in work
hours, the death of a spouse, divorce,
loss of income from a rental property,
loss of pension income, and certain
employer settlements. If any of those
events occurred after the tax year
Medicare is currently using, you submit
form SSA-44
with documentation showing your current
or expected income, and Social Security
will recalculate. The recalculation is
not automatic. You have to file the form
yourself. Thousands of seniors overpay
every year because they received a
higher premium notice, assumed it was
correct, and never challenged it. The
SSA does not call you. They do not
follow up. The form has to come from
you. Therefore, if your income drops
significantly between 2024 and today
because you retired, because a spouse
passed, because a rental was sold, or
for any other qualifying reason, filing
form SSA-44
is the first thing you do after this
video ends. If you have not yet hit the
threshold, but you are planning a Roth
conversion, a large IRA withdrawal, or a
real estate sale in 2025 or 2026, model
the IRMAA impact before the money moves.
The conversion you execute this year
becomes Medicare's calculation 2 years
from now. A planner who walks you
through a conversion without showing you
the 2-year Medicare impact is giving you
half the picture. And if you have been
meeting with a financial advisor for
years, and the word IRMAA has never once
come up, that tells you something about
the kind of planning you have been
receiving. Here's exactly what to do
right now. Pull up your 2024 federal tax
return. Find line 11 on form 1040. That
is your adjusted gross income. Find line
2A, which shows your tax-exempt interest
income. Add those two numbers. The
result is your modified adjusted gross
income for IRMAA purposes. That is the
exact number Medicare used to set your
2026 premiums. If that number as a
single filer is above $109,000,
you are in a surcharge tier right now.
If you are a married couple and your
combined number is above $218,000,
you are in a tier now. If you qualify
for an appeal because your income has
dropped since 2024, download form SSA-44
at ssa.gov. File it before the end of
this year. ssa44.ssa.gov.

title: Congress Just Killed 12 Years of Medicare and Social Security Cuts Are Coming in 2032

segments.text: The United States Congress passed a law
last year that erased 12 years of
Medicare's financial survival, not
gradually, not theoretically, 12 years
gone, according to the non-partisan
Congressional Budget Office. And if
nothing changes between now and 2032,
the law also requires an automatic 24%
cut to Social Security benefits for
every retiree in America, regardless of
how long they paid in, regardless of
income, regardless of anything. The
people this will hurt most are the
people nobody in Washington is talking
about right now. And the detail that
makes this particularly alarming is one
I am going to walk you through in this
video because most people covering this
story are missing it entirely. Stay with
me because the number that matters most
is not the 12 years. It is a different
number that tells you exactly how this
affects your household. I will give you
that number in a moment. Let me start
with what actually happened. In July of
2025, Congress passed legislation called
the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The law
cut taxes and created a new deduction
for Americans age 65 and older on their
Social Security income. On the surface,
that sounds beneficial. For many
seniors, it genuinely does reduce their
tax bill in the short term. But here is
what the law also did. It dramatically
reduced the amount of revenue flowing
into the trust funds that pay for
Medicare and Social Security. Because
those programs are partially funded by
income taxes collected on Social
Security benefits, and because the new
law reduced those taxes, the money
flowing into the trust funds dropped
significantly. The Congressional Budget
Office published updated projections in
February of 2026. They found that the
Medicare Hospital Insurance Trust Fund,
which is the fund that pays for hospital
care, skilled nursing facility stays,
hospice care, and home health services,
is now projected to run out of money
entirely by 2040. One year earlier, in
March of 2025, the CBO projected that
same fund would last until 2052. 12
years of solvency erased in less than 12
months. But here is what the 12 years
actually means in practical And this is
the part that should concern every
single person watching this video. When
the Hospital Insurance Trust Fund runs
out of money, federal law does not allow
Medicare to borrow. It does not allow
Medicare to run a deficit. It does not
give Congress any flexibility. The law
requires that Medicare pay out only what
it collects in revenue at that moment,
nothing more. The CBO estimates that
when the fund is exhausted in 2040,
Medicare hospital payments will need to
be cut by 8% immediately. By 2056, that
cut grows to 10%. 8% does not sound
catastrophic until you realize what
Medicare Part A actually covers:
inpatient hospital stays, emergency
surgery, recovery in a skilled nursing
facility after a major illness, hospice
care. These are not optional benefits.
These are the benefits that seniors need
most at the most vulnerable moments of
their lives, and those benefits are now
14 years closer to an 8% automatic cut
than they were 1 year ago. Now, I told
you there was a second number that
matters more than the 12 years. Here it
is. The Social Security Trust Fund,
which is separate from Medicare, faces
an even more urgent timeline. The
Congressional Budget Office projects the
Social Security Retirement Trust Fund
will be exhausted by 2032. That is just
6 years from today. When that fund runs
out, federal law triggers automatic
across-the-board benefit cuts for every
retiree in America. The Committee for a
Responsible Federal Budget, which is a
non-partisan fiscal watchdog, calculated
what that cut looks like in real
dollars. For a typical couple retiring
in 2032 or shortly after, the automatic
cut equals $18,400
per year in lost benefits, not a
one-time reduction, every year for the
rest of their retirement. For a senior
currently receiving $2,000 per month
from Social Security, a 24% cut reduces
that check to $1,520
every single month, $340 gone. That is
not an abstraction. That is a utility
bill. That is a car payment. That is a
week of groceries. And it happens
automatically by law the moment the
trust fund hits zero unless Congress
acts to prevent it. The same legislation
that accelerated these timelines, the
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, reduced the
revenue flowing into these trust funds
by approximately $169 billion
over 10 years, according to the Social
Security Administration's own chief
actuary. The Social Security Fairness
Act, which was the bipartisan law passed
earlier in 2025 that expanded benefits
for certain government workers, added
another $200 billion to the shortfall
over 10 years. Together, these two laws
accelerated Social Security's insolvency
timeline by nearly a full year and made
the eventual benefit cut significantly
larger than it would have been
otherwise. Here's what I need you to
understand about how this mechanism
actually works because this is where
most coverage of this topic fails
seniors completely. These cuts are not a
political choice that Congress will make
in 2032. They are not a negotiation.
They are not something that gets voted
on when the time comes. They are
automatic. They are written into
existing law right now. The law says
that when the trust fund balance reaches
zero, the Social Security Administration
is legally prohibited from paying out
more than it collects in that month's
revenue. Congress does not have to vote
to cut your benefits. The cuts happen by
default unless Congress votes to stop
them. And the last time Congress
successfully passed legislation to shore
up Social Security was in 1983, 43 years
ago. But lifestyle inflation is only one
half of the trap. So, what can you
actually do with this information right
now? The first thing to understand is
that none of this is inevitable.
Congress can act. The options available
to lawmakers include increasing the
payroll tax rate, raising or eliminating
the cap on wages subject to Social
Security taxes, currently set at
in 2026, transferring general revenue
into the trust funds, modifying the
benefit formula, or some combination of
all of these approaches. These are
politically difficult decisions, but
they are available. The program has been
rescued from the brink before. The
second thing to understand is what this
means for your personal retirement
planning right now. Regardless of what
Congress does, if you are already
receiving Social Security benefits, your
payments are not changing today. The
trust fund still has reserves and is
projected to remain solvent through 2031
before the balance begins declining. You
have time, but you should be aware that
these projections exist and that they
are based on current law with no
Congressional intervention. If you are
between 55 and 65 and still deciding
when to claim Social Security, these
projections are directly relevant to
your decision. Delaying your claim to
build a higher base benefit gives you
more cushion against a future percentage
cut. Someone receiving $2,000 per month
loses $480 in a 24% cut. Someone who
delayed claiming and receives $3,000 per
month loses $720. The absolute dollar
loss is larger, but the lifestyle impact
depends entirely on what your other
income sources look like. If you are
younger and these timelines feel
abstract, the Committee for a
Responsible Federal Budget said
something in their most recent report
that cuts through the abstraction
completely. They wrote that the people
most harmed by an action are not the
retirees of 2032. They are the workers
in their 50s and early 60s right now who
are planning their retirement around
benefit levels that current law will not
be able to deliver without Congressional
action. There is one thing you can do
today, regardless of your age or your
political views, you can contact your
Congressional Representative and your
Senators and tell them you are aware of
the 2032 insolvency date, that you
understand automatic cuts are triggered
by existing law, and that you expect
them to be part of a solution. The
Capitol Switchboard number is
That number connects you to the
Congressional Switchboard, and you can
ask to be transferred to the office of
any representative or senator by name or
state. The 12 years Congress wiped off
Medicare's timeline last year cannot be
put back without legislative action. The
24% Social Security cut scheduled for
2032 will not be prevented without
legislative action. This is not a
partisan issue. It is an arithmetic one,
and the arithmetic has never been
clearer or more urgent than it is right

title: YOU ONLY HAVE 3 DAYS Before You Lose This Benefit

segments.text: In 3 days, a deadline closes that 42
million American seniors do not know
about. After March 31st, you will not be
able to make a single change to your
Medicare Advantage coverage until
October 15th. That is 6 and 1/2 months
from now. And here is what nobody is
telling you. There is one specific
situation where making a change before
that deadline could actually cost you
more money than staying put. I will tell
you exactly what that situation is
before this video ends. If your plan has
been quietly raising your costs,
dropping your doctors, or changing what
medications it covers,
this window is your only chance to fix
it before you are locked in for the rest
of the year. My name is Mark Callaway.
Every week on this channel, I cover the
financial rules and deadlines that the
government does not explain clearly
enough. The ones that cost seniors real
money when they are missed. And this
one, the Medicare Advantage open
enrollment period, is one of the most
overlooked deadlines in all of Medicare.
Most seniors on Medicare Advantage have
no idea this window even exists.
The insurance companies certainly are
not reminding you about it. So, let me
tell you exactly what this window is,
who it applies to, what you can do
before it closes,
and most importantly, whether you should
do anything at all. Medicare has two
main enrollment windows that matter
every year. The first is the big one.
The annual enrollment period that runs
from October 15th through December 7th.
That is when anyone on Medicare can make
major changes to their coverage for the
following year.
Most people have heard of that one.
But there is a second window that most
people do not know about. It is called
the Medicare Advantage open enrollment
period. It runs every year from January
1st through March 31st. Today is March
You have 3 days left. Here is the
critical thing to understand. This
window is not for everyone on Medicare.
It is specifically for people who are
already enrolled in a Medicare Advantage
plan, also called Medicare Part C. If
you are on original Medicare, meaning
traditional government Medicare, this
particular window does not apply to you
in the same way.
But if you have a Medicare Advantage
plan through a private insurer such as
Humana, United Healthcare, Aetna, Blue
Cross, or any other company, pay close
attention because this affects you
directly. During this window, you can do
one of two things. You can switch from
your current Medicare Advantage plan to
a different Medicare Advantage plan, or
you can drop your Medicare Advantage
plan entirely and go back to original
Medicare. You get one change. Just one.
And whatever change you make takes
effect on the first day of the following
month. So, if you make a change before
March 31st, your new coverage begins
April 1st. After March 31st, if you are
on Medicare Advantage and you want to
make a change, you will have to wait
until October 15th when the annual
enrollment period opens again. And any
change you make during that window would
not take effect until January 1st of
That is 9 months from now.
So, the question you need to be asking
yourself right now is this. Has anything
changed about your Medicare Advantage
plan since January 1st that is causing
you problems?
Here are the most common situations
where making a switch before March 31st
makes sense. The first situation is your
doctor left your network.
Medicare Advantage plans use networks,
meaning they only cover you fully when
you see doctors and hospitals that are
in their approved list. If your primary
care doctor, your cardiologist, your
orthopedic surgeon, or any specialist
you rely on regularly has left your
plan's network since the start of the
year,
you may be paying significantly more out
of pocket than you expected. That is a
legitimate reason to switch plans. The
second situation is your prescription
drug costs changed. Medicare Advantage
plans that include drug coverage, called
MAPD plans, can change their
formularies, meaning the list of drugs
they cover and what tier those drugs are
placed in. If a medication you take
every month moved to a higher tier, your
monthly cost for that prescription may
have jumped significantly.
If you are paying more for your
medications than you anticipated when
you chose this plan, comparing other
plans before March 31st could save you
hundreds of dollars over the rest of the
year.
The third situation is your premium or
out-of-pocket costs went up more than
you realized. Sometimes people allow
their existing plan to auto-renew at the
end of the year without carefully
reviewing the new terms.
Your plan may have increased its monthly
premium, raised its deductibles, or
changed its out-of-pocket maximum for
2026. If you are now paying more than
you budgeted for,
this window gives you one opportunity to
course correct. The fourth situation is
you enrolled in a Medicare Advantage
plan at the end of last year and you now
realize it was the wrong choice.
Maybe you were influenced by advertising
for extra benefits such as dental
coverage, vision, or grocery cards,
and the plan you signed up for turned
out to have a narrow network or high
cost for the services you actually use.
The Medicare Advantage open enrollment
period exists precisely for this kind of
situation. It is your one do-over
opportunity each year. Now, let me tell
you what you cannot do during this
window because this is where people get
confused. You cannot switch from
original Medicare to a Medicare
Advantage plan during this window. That
direction of switching is only available
during the annual enrollment period in
the fall. You cannot make changes to a
standalone Medicare Part D prescription
drug plan during this window unless you
are also making a change to your
Medicare Advantage coverage. And you can
only make one change.
If you switch to a new Medicare
Advantage plan and then change your mind
again before March 31st, you cannot make
a second switch during this window. Here
is what I want you to do right now if
any of what I just described applies to
your situation.
Step one. Go to medicare.gov and use the
Medicare Plan Finder tool. It is free.
It is run by the federal government. You
enter your zip code, your current
medications, and your preferred doctors.
And it shows you every Medicare
Advantage plan available in your area
along with the estimated annual cost
based on your specific situation. This
is the most important tool most seniors
never use. Step two. When you are
comparing plans, do not just look at the
monthly premium. The premium is what the
insurance company wants you to focus on
because a low premium can hide high
out-of-pocket costs, high deductibles,
and narrow networks.
Look at the total estimated annual cost
the Plan Finder calculates for you based
on your actual medications and health
needs. That number is far more
meaningful than the monthly premium
alone. Step three. Check the network.
Before you switch to any plan, call your
most important doctors, your primary
care physician, and any specialist you
see regularly and ask them directly
whether they accept that specific plan.
Do not assume.
Plans can list doctors as in-network on
their website and that information can
be outdated. A 2-minute phone call to
your doctor's billing department can
save you months of coverage headaches.
Step four. If you decide to make a
switch, do it through the official
Medicare website or by calling
That is 1-800-Medicare.
Making the change through official
channels gives you an additional
protection in 2026. If you were given
incorrect network information through
Medicare's official platform, you will
be granted a special enrollment period
to correct the mistake.
You do not get that protection if you
enrolled through a third-party broker or
insurance agent's website. Step five.
Here is the situation I told you about
at the beginning of this video. The one
where making a change could actually
cost you more money.
If you are considering dropping Medicare
Advantage entirely and going back to
original Medicare, there is something
critical you need to understand first.
Original Medicare does not cap your
out-of-pocket costs the way Medicare
Advantage does. To get that protection
with original Medicare, most people add

title: Never Keep More Than This in the Bank After 65 — Most Seniors Miss These

segments.text: Two retirees, both 68, both careful with
money, both kept everything in one bank.
One of them slept fine every night. The
other opened his banking app one morning
and found his account frozen with
nothing he could touch.
>> [music]
>> He had broken no law. He had made no
mistake. The difference between them was
one number that nobody ever told him to
watch. There is a small set of dollar
limits sitting in the background of
every retiree's life. They are not
secret, but they live in rule books that
almost nobody reads. And the moment your
balance crosses one of them, someone
else gets a say over your money. The
government, a creditor, or your own
bank. Today, I'm going to count down
seven of those limits, one at a time, in
plain [music] English. And at the end,
I'll give you the exact setup I would
