the right to receive the proceeds. Do
not rely on a universal January 1st
deadline. The relevant deadlines follow
the actual exchange. The fifth asset is
life insurance cash value, and this is
the most misunderstood asset in the
video. Permanent life insurance policies
can build cash value, but the tax
treatment depends on the contract, its
basis, whether it is a modified
endowment contract, how distributions
are taken, and whether the policy
remains in force.
>> [music]
>> Your basis is generally connected to the
premiums you paid, adjusted for previous
distributions and other policy activity.
In many non-modified endowment life
insurance contracts, withdrawals are
generally treated as a recovery of basis
first. That means a withdrawal may not
be taxable until total distributions
exceed the remaining basis.
Modified endowment contracts, commonly
called MECs, are different.
Distributions from a MEC are generally
treated less favorably, with taxable
gain coming out before basis, and
distributions before age 59 and 1/2 may
face an additional penalty unless an
exception applies. Policy loans are
different from withdrawals. A loan
against a policy generally does not
create immediate taxable income while
the policy remains in force.
>> [music]
>> But that does not make borrowing
automatically superior. The loan accrues
interest, reduces available cash value
and the death benefit, and can increase
the chance that the policy will lapse.
>> [music]
>> The lapse is where a large tax surprise
can appear. Suppose a retiree paid
$60,000 in premiums into a non-MEC
policy that now has $85,000 of cash
value. The policy also has a $30,000
outstanding loan. If the policy lapses
or is surrendered, the tax calculation
may treat the loan and remaining
proceeds as amounts received. A taxable
gain may result even when the owner
receives little or no cash at the moment
of lapse. That is why always borrow and
never withdraw is unsafe advice. A
modest withdrawal within basis may be
less risky than a growing loan on a
policy that is already struggling. In
another contract, a properly managed
loan may be appropriate. The answer
depends on the in-force policy values,
basis, loan interest, premium
requirements, death benefit, and whether
the policy is a MEC.
>> [music]
>> A section 1035 exchange may allow one
qualifying insurance or annuity contract
to be exchanged for another without
immediate recognition of gain. But an
exchange can bring new surrender
charges, different guarantees, higher
expenses, a new surrender period, and
loss of valuable provisions in the old
contract. It should never be treated as
an automatic solution. Before
withdrawing, borrowing, surrendering, or
stopping premiums, request an in-force
illustration and a written statement of
the current basis, outstanding loans,
surrender value, and projected lapse
date. Ask what happens under several
scenarios. The most expensive mistake is
often not reviewing the policy until
after it lapses. The sixth asset is your
Social Security benefit, not because
Social Security must be moved, but
because income generated by the other
assets can change how much of it appears
on your federal tax return. The federal
calculation uses what is commonly called
provisional income. In simplified terms,
it consists of adjusted gross income
plus tax-exempt interest plus 1/2 of
Social Security benefits subject to
applicable adjustments. For an
individual filer, the long-standing base
thresholds are $25,000 and $34,000.
For married couples filing jointly, they
are $32,000 and $44,000. These
thresholds are not indexed for
inflation. Above the first level, up to
50% of benefits may become taxable.
Above the second, up to 85% may become
taxable. That does not mean the IRS
takes 50% or 85% of your check. It means
that up to that share of the benefit may
be included in taxable income, after
which the ordinary income tax
calculation is applied.
>> [music]
>> Consider a married couple receiving
$36,000 of Social Security and $40,000
of pension income with no tax-exempt
interest in this simplified example.
Their provisional income is 40,000 plus
18,000, which equals $58,000.
It would be wrong to say that the full
85% of their Social Security or $30,600
automatically becomes taxable. The
statutory formula applies. In this
simplified case, the taxable benefit may
be approximately $17,900,
although the exact result depends on the
complete return. The important point is
that crossing 44,000 does not instantly
place the full 85% of the benefit into
income.
Traditional IRA distributions, pensions,
taxable bank interest, and realized
capital gains can all increase
provisional income. Qualified Roth IRA
withdrawals generally do not enter
adjusted gross income, but that does not
mean retirees should automatically spend
Roth money first. Roth assets may be
valuable later for large expenses,
surviving spouse planning, or heirs.
>> [music]
>> Every withdrawal strategy has a
trade-off. Deductions create another
source of confusion. The standard
deduction, additional age deduction, and
temporary senior deduction may reduce
final taxable income and the resulting
tax bill. They generally do not reduce
the provisional income calculation
itself. You must calculate how much
Social Security enters income first,
then apply deductions through the
broader tax return.
If you expect to owe tax, Form W-4V can
request voluntary federal withholding
from Social Security at available
percentage options. The form does not
reduce your tax. It simply prepays part
of it and may help prevent an April
surprise.
The seventh asset is your joint bank
account and its beneficiary
designations.
>> [music]
>> Unlike Roth conversions or gain
harvesting, reviewing this asset has no
universal December 31st deadline, but it
may be the easiest item on the list to
check. A joint account can provide
convenient access for both owners, but
it also creates legal ownership rights.
Adding an adult child as a joint owner
may allow that child to withdraw the
entire balance. It may also expose the
account to complications involving the
child's creditors, divorce, taxes, or
estate.
>> [music]
>> A payable on death designation generally
instructs the institution to transfer
the account to the named beneficiary
after the owner dies. It ordinarily
operates outside the will, which means a
beneficiary designation can override a
different instruction in the will. The
exact outcome still depends on state
law, account terms, and whether the
beneficiary survives the owner.
>> [music]
>> If one child is named on an account
while a will divides everything among
three children, the named child may
receive that account directly. Whether
that child has any legal obligation to
share it is a state law question and
should not be left to a family
assumption. Financial exploitation
protections also need accurate framing.
FINRA rule 2165 applies to qualifying
situations involving accounts at FINRA
member firms.
>> [music]
>> It permits a member firm to place a
temporary hold on certain disbursements
or transactions when it reasonably
believes financial exploitation of a
specified adult may be occurring. It
does not require every bank to freeze
every checking account after a large
withdrawal, and a legitimate transfer
does not automatically trigger a hold.
Banks may have their own fraud and
exploitation procedures under applicable
law. A hold can still be disruptive, but
it should not be described as an
automatic consequence of being 65 or
making a large payment. A trusted
contact is not necessarily an account
owner and generally does not receive
authority to transact merely by being
listed. A durable financial power of
attorney may authorize someone to act
for you, but institutions may have
review procedures. Some banks offer
convenience or agency accounts, but
their legal consequences vary by state
and institution. Your low-risk review is
straightforward. Ask the institution to
confirm the exact account title, all
owners, payable on death beneficiaries,
trusted contacts, and any power of
attorney documents on file. Make sure
every named person is alive, correctly
identified, and still part of your plan.
Then compare those forms with your will
and trust documents. Do not assume the
will controls an account with a separate
beneficiary designation. Now, let us
separate the checklist by deadline
because not every item belongs on the
same calendar.
Transactions that may have a true
December 31st tax year deadline include
a Roth conversion intended for 2026
and sales used for 2026 capital gain or
capital loss planning. Those
transactions need enough processing time
to complete before year end.
Waiting until the afternoon of December
31st is not a plan. Required minimum
distributions have their own deadlines.
Most annual RMDs are due by December
31st, but a first RMD may have the
special April 1st rule. Delaying that
first distribution may put two RMDs into
one year. So, check before choosing the
delay. A 1031 exchange does not operate
on a universal December 31st deadline.
Its 45- and 180-day clocks depend on the
transfer of the relinquished property
and the tax return deadline.
Reviewing savings rates, CD maturities,
life insurance contracts, bank
ownership, and beneficiaries is
important, but those items do not have
one federal year-end deadline that
applies to everybody. Review them now
because another year should not pass
with outdated information, not because
the IRS automatically takes money on
January 1st. Your seven-point review is
this. Check what your cash earns and
what protection each account or security
actually has. Confirm your RMD age and
deadline, then model any Roth conversion
before completing it. Review unrealized
brokerage gains, cost basis, and the
interaction with Social Security and
Medicare. If you are selling investment
property, discuss the transaction with a
qualified intermediary and tax
professional before closing. Request an
in-force illustration before changing a
permanent life insurance policy.
>> [music]
>> Estimate provisional income separately
from final taxable income. And confirm
every bank account owner and beneficiary
against your estate plan. That is also
where Claim Every Dollar, the Senior
Benefits Playbook, can give you a
clearer starting point for understanding
retirement-related decisions and senior
benefits. You can explore the book at
marcusretires.com,
and the link is in the description. Here
is my honest conclusion. Seven
retirement assets deserve a careful
review before the end of 2026.
Some decisions have real year-end tax
deadlines. Others can create expensive
problems when ignored. But moving money
without understanding the rules can
sometimes make the problem worse. Do not
retitle a brokerage account merely to
chase a basis adjustment. Do not convert
an IRA based only on your current
bracket.
>> [music]
>> Do not borrow from life insurance
without checking the lapse risk. And do
not enter a property exchange after you
have already taken control of the
proceeds. Review before you move, verify
before you sign, and make sure every
decision fits your personal tax and
retirement situation.
My name is Marcus, and this is Marcus
Retires. If this video helped, hit the
like button, and tell me in the comments
which of these seven assets you plan to
review first. Share it with someone
approaching a year-end retirement
decision, and subscribe with
notifications turned on for more plain
English retirement updates. Until next
time, know the deadline, understand the
trade-off, and never move an asset
solely because a headline frightened
you.

title: Never Keep More Than This in One Bank Account After 65 — 7 Rules Most Seniors Miss

segments.text: Two retired men, both 68, both receiving
Social Security, and both keeping a
large part of their savings in the same
checking account where their monthly
benefits arrive. One of them has never
experienced a problem. The other woke up
one Tuesday and discovered that $14,000
in his account had been restricted after
a creditor obtained a court order. He
could still access a portion of the
federal benefits the bank was required
to protect, but the rest of the account
became the subject of a legal process he
did not understand. He had not committed
a crime, and the bank had not randomly
taken his money. A lawsuit had been
filed, a judgment had been entered, and
a garnishment order had reached the
bank. The real problem was that he did
not understand the difference between
money protected automatically by federal
banking rules and money that might
require him to claim an additional
exemption under state law.
Your checking account may feel like a
private box with one key, and that key
belongs to you.
Legally, however, several different
rules can affect what happens to the
money inside it. Some rules only require
the bank to report information. Some
count your balance when deciding whether
you qualify for assistance. Some may
allow the bank to apply money toward a
debt you owe that same institution. And
some can temporarily restrict funds
after a court order arrives. Today, I'm
going to walk you through seven of those
rules in plain English. Number five
explains how a creditor can reach a bank
account after obtaining a valid
judgment.
>> [music]
>> And near the end, I will explain the
federal two-month look-back rule
accurately, what it protects, how the
bank calculates the protected amount,
and what it does not mean. My name is
Marcus, and this is Marcus Retires,
where we break down Social Security,
Medicare, retirement taxes, and money
rules without the confusing language.
If this information is useful, subscribe
and turn on notifications now, because
these dollar limits and procedures can
change, and I will cover the updates as
they happen. Nothing in this video is
individualized legal, tax, or financial
advice. Rules vary by state, account
type, debt type, and personal
circumstances, so confirm the details
before moving money or changing
ownership. And as you watch, tell me in
the comments which of these seven
banking rules surprises you most.
The first rule belongs to Supplemental
Security Income, commonly called SSI,
and it matters because SSI is a
needs-based program with strict resource
limits. It is different from a regular
Social Security retirement benefit.
>> [music]
>> Your retirement benefit is based
primarily on your earnings record and
claiming age.
>> [music]
>> SSI eligibility, on the other hand,
considers both income and countable
resources. Under the long-standing
federal limits, an individual generally
cannot have more than $2,000 in
countable resources, while the limit for
an eligible couple is generally $3,000.
Those limits were set decades ago and
have not kept pace with inflation.
>> [music]
>> Your primary home generally does not
count. One vehicle used for
transportation generally does not count.
Many household goods and personal
belongings are also excluded, but cash,
ordinary checking and savings accounts,
and certain investments usually do
count.
SSI eligibility is generally evaluated
based on the resources you own at the
beginning of the month. That means a
temporary increase in your balance can
matter even when the money came from an
innocent one-time event. Imagine a woman
I will call Vivian. She is 76 and
receives a small Social Security
retirement check plus an SSI payment.
>> [music]
>> She normally keeps around $1,500 in the
bank. After selling her late husband's
old pickup truck for $4,000, she leaves
the proceeds in checking while deciding
how to use them. If those sale proceeds
remain a countable resource into the
following month, Vivian may be over the
SSI resource limit and could become
ineligible for that month. The sale
itself is not wrongdoing. The issue is
what the proceeds become after the sale
and how long they remain available to
her. Social Security may verify
financial accounts during an eligibility
review through records, statements, and
authorized electronic verification
procedures. The exact verification
process can depend on the case and the
program's current procedures, so do not
assume an old or forgotten account is
invisible. There is another warning
here. Giving money away merely to get
below the resource limit may create a
separate SSI transfer penalty. Medicaid
long-term care rules also have their own
transfer rules and generally use a much
longer look back period. That means
handing money to a son or daughter is
not automatically a safe solution.
Legitimately spending money on your own
needs may be allowed depending on the
circumstances. Examples may include
necessary home repairs, medical or
dental care, hearing aids, paying valid
debts, replacing household items, or
properly arranged burial expenses. But
the timing and documentation matter. If
you receive SSI and expect to sell an
asset, receive an inheritance, or
receive a large payment, ask Social
Security or a qualified benefits
counselor how it will be treated before
moving or giving away the money.
The second rule belongs to the IRS, but
it is important to separate two
calculations that are often confused.
The first calculation determines how
much of your Social Security may become
taxable. The second determines whether
you ultimately owe federal income tax
after deductions. They are not the same
calculation. Banks and credit unions
generally report taxable interest to you
and the IRS when reporting requirements
are met. That interest can be included
in the provisional income formula used
to determine whether part of your Social
Security benefit is taxable. Provisional
income generally includes adjusted gross
income, tax-exempt interest, and one
half of your Social Security benefits.
For a single filer, the first federal
threshold is $25,000.
For a married couple filing jointly, it
A second level begins at $34,000 for a
single filer and $44,000 for a married
couple filing jointly. Depending on the
result, up to 50% or up to 85% of your
Social Security can become part of
taxable income. The critical word is up
to. An 85% inclusion does not mean the
government takes 85% of your benefit. It
means up to 85% of the benefit may be
included in the income on which your tax
is calculated.
>> [music]
>> Your actual tax depends on your taxable
income, deductions, credits, and tax
bracket. This is also where deductions
must be explained carefully. A standard
deduction, an additional deduction for
age, or another senior tax deduction may
reduce your final taxable income and
therefore reduce the tax you owe. But
those deductions do not normally lower
the provisional income figure used in
the earlier Social Security taxation
calculation. In other words, a deduction
may help reduce or eliminate your final
tax bill without moving you back below
the $25,000 or $32,000 provisional
income threshold.
That distinction matters because many
retirees began earning more bank
interest after years of receiving almost
nothing. More interest is usually good
news. Earning 4% and paying some tax is
generally better than earning almost
nothing solely to avoid tax. But the
interest can cause part of your Social
Security to become taxable, even if
deductions later reduce the amount of
tax you actually owe.
The right approach is not to fear
interest. It is to estimate both
calculations before the tax year ends.
Ask two separate questions.
>> [music]
>> How much of my Social Security may be
included in income, and after all
available deductions, how much federal
tax will I actually owe? Those questions
can produce very different answers. The
third rule belongs to the state agency
that administers Medicare Savings
Programs. These programs may pay your
Medicare Part B premium, and depending
on the program, may also help with
deductibles, co-insurance, co-payments,
or prescription drug expenses through
extra help. A Part B premium of roughly
$200 per month represents more than
over a full year. If a Medicare Savings
Program pays that premium, the money may
no longer be deducted from your Social
Security benefit. That can produce a
meaningful increase in the net deposit
reaching your bank account.
Eligibility is based on both income and,
in many states, countable resources.
Federal baseline figures are updated
over time, but states are permitted to
use different methods, higher limits, or
no resource test at all in some cases.
Your primary home, one vehicle, and
certain personal belongings generally do
not count in the same way ordinary cash
and savings may count.
The important lesson is not to reject
yourself before applying. A person with
savings above a federal baseline may
live in a state using more generous
rules. Another person may qualify after
the state applies deductions that are
not obvious from the monthly gross
income number. These programs are
especially valuable because they can
open the door to extra help with
Medicare prescription drug costs. That
may reduce or eliminate a drug plan
deductible and lower copayments.
Therefore, losing eligibility may cost
more than the Part B premium alone. If
your income or savings are anywhere
close to the public limits, contact the
state Medicaid agency or a free Medicare
counseling program and request an
official eligibility determination. Ask
what income is counted, what resources
are excluded, and whether the state has
eliminated or increased its resource
limit. Do not rely on a friend's
eligibility decision from another state
because these rules are not identical
nationwide. The fourth rule belongs to
your own bank. Many deposit agreements
contain a contractual right of setoff.
In general terms, this may allow a
financial institution to apply funds in
your checking or savings account toward
a delinquent debt you owe that same
institution. Whether and how this can
happen depends on the type of debt, the
language in your account and loan
agreements, federal law, state law, and
the source of the deposited funds. A
right of setoff is not the same thing as
a court-ordered garnishment. Setoff
usually concerns the relationship
between you and your own bank.
Garnishment generally involves an
outside creditor using a court judgment
and legal process.
>> [music]
>> Consider Ron, a in savings and a vehicle
loan at the same bank. After a long
hospital stay, he misses several loan
payments. Depending on his agreements
and applicable law,
the bank may have a right to apply some
account funds to the delinquent loan.
Ron may first discover the setoff when
he reads his statement. Credit card
debts have additional federal
restrictions, and Social Security
deposits may have protections that
depend on the particular facts and the
applicable law. That is why no
responsible video should promise that
one rule produces the same result in all
50 states.
Keeping savings at an institution where
you do not owe money may reduce exposure
to that institution's contractual setoff
rights, but it does not make the money
untouchable. A valid court-ordered
garnishment can potentially be sent to a
different bank as well.
Account separation is a risk management
tool, not a magic shield. Before moving
a large balance, ask each bank whether
its deposit agreement includes a right
of setoff, which debts it covers, and
how protected federal benefits are
handled under its procedures.
Everything I have explained so far shows
how easily one ordinary account can
become connected to several different
rules. Knowing those rules is useful,
but knowing what to check and which
questions to ask is where the money is
often protected. That is why I created
Claim Every Dollar, the Senior Benefits
Playbook. It is a plain English guide
designed to help older Americans
identify benefits, deadlines, and
questions that are easy to miss. You can
see it at marcus-retires-playbook.net
qualify.app, and the link is also in the
description. Before you buy it, review
the page and make sure it fits what you
need. Now, let us return to the fifth
rule because this is the one that can
temporarily restrict a bank account
after a court order arrives. The fifth
rule concerns creditor judgments and
bank garnishment. A private creditor
ordinarily cannot freeze an account
merely because it claims you owe money.
The creditor generally must sue, obtain
a valid judgment, and then use the legal
collection process available under state
law. You should normally receive notice
of the lawsuit. The problem is that
notices may go to an old address, may be
misunderstood, or may be ignored during
an illness or family emergency. If the
person does not respond, the court may
enter a default judgment. After that,
the creditor may ask for a garnishment
order directed to the bank.
The lawsuit notice, the garnishment
order sent to the bank, and the notice
you receive after funds are restricted
are different parts of the process. The
bank itself may not call you before
following the garnishment order.
Depending on state procedures, you may
first learn about the account
restriction when a transaction fails or
when the garnishment notice arrives. But
federal law gives certain directly
deposited federal benefits an important
layer of automatic protection. Imagine
Arthur, a 78-year-old retiree. Years
earlier, he fell behind on a credit card
while caring for his wife. A debt buyer
filed a lawsuit, court papers went to an
address Arthur had left, and a default
judgment was eventually entered. Arthur
later moved $14,000 of ordinary savings
into the checking account where his
social security arrived because keeping
one account seemed easier. When the
garnishment order reached the bank, the
bank was required to perform the federal
account review for qualifying benefit
deposits. The amount protected
automatically depended on the qualifying
federal benefits deposited during the
2-month lookback period and the balance
present when the bank reviewed the
account. Other money could be restricted
while Arthur asserted any additional
federal or state exemptions. This is
where the 2-month rule must be explained
precisely. When a private creditor's
garnishment order reaches a bank, the
bank generally reviews the account
history covering the previous 2 months.
It identifies qualifying federal
benefits that arrived by direct deposit,
such as social security, SSI, certain
veterans benefits, and certain federal
retirement payments. The automatically
protected amount is generally the lesser
of two figures, the total qualifying
benefits deposited during that lookback
period, or the account balance at the
time of the bank's review.
For example, suppose $4,000 of
qualifying Social Security benefits were
deposited during the look-back period,
but the account contains only $3,000
when reviewed. The automatically
protected amount would generally be
3,000 because that is the smaller
number. If the account contains $10,000,
but only 4,000 in qualifying benefits
was directly deposited during the
look-back, the automatic protected
amount would generally be 4,000. The
remaining balance is not automatically
declared collectible. It may still be
protected by other federal or state
exemptions. But, the bank's automatic
federal calculation is based on the
qualifying direct deposits and the
account balance at review.
This does not create a legal rule saying
retirees should keep only 2 months of
benefits in checking. It does not mean
every dollar above the protected amount
can automatically be taken. And it does
not mean moving every extra dollar to
another account will make it legally
unreachable. A creditor with a judgment
may be able to garnish another account
subject to applicable exemptions. The
practical lesson is to keep clear bank
records, use direct deposit for federal
benefits, understand which money
receives automatic protection, and
respond immediately to any garnishment
or exemption notice.
If an account is restricted, read every
notice the same day it arrives.
>> [music]
>> State deadlines for claiming exemptions
may be short. Gather your Social
Security award letter and bank
statements showing the source of
deposits. Contact Legal Aid, an elder
law attorney, or a consumer attorney
promptly. If you were never properly
served with the lawsuit, if the judgment
is mistaken, or if protected funds were
improperly restricted, legal remedies
may be available. Do not ignore the
notice, and do not assume the bank is
permitted to decide every exemption on
its own. Some protections have to be
claimed through the court process.
The sixth rule belongs to the state's
unclaimed property system. Bank accounts
that remain inactive for a legally
defined period may eventually be
classified as dormant and transferred to
the state as unclaimed property. The
relevant period and the type of activity
required to prevent dormancy vary by
state and by financial institution. That
is why the simple advice to log in once
or move $1 should not be presented as a
universal legal solution. A login may
count as customer contact at one
institution but not another. An
automated transaction may not count as
owner initiated activity under a
particular state's rules.
Consider Eileen who kept $23,000 in a
rainy day savings account and
intentionally left it untouched. She
later moved in with her daughter but
forgot to update the address on that
account. Statements and dormancy notices
continued going to the old house. Years
later, the balance was transferred to
the state's unclaimed property office.
>> [music]
>> The money was still hers and she
eventually recovered it but the process
required identity documents and proof of
ownership. The safe step is to ask each
financial institution what it considers
sufficient owner contact or activity to
keep an account active. Confirm the
address, telephone number, email, and
beneficiaries on file. Review every
account at least annually. You can also
search your state's official unclaimed
property database for your name and the
names of deceased relatives.
>> [music]
>> Filing a claim through the official
state process is generally free so be
cautious about paying a finder to
perform a search you can conduct
yourself.
The seventh rule belongs to the FDIC and
it concerns deposit insurance coverage
after an account owner dies. The basic
FDIC limit is generally $250,000 per
depositor, per insured bank, per
ownership category. That last phrase,
ownership category, is essential.
Individual accounts, joint accounts, and
certain trust or payable on death
accounts can be insured differently. A
married couple may receive up to
$500,000 of coverage on qualifying joint
deposits at the same insured bank
because each co-owner is insured up to
for the joint category. When an account
owner dies, FDIC rules generally
continue to calculate coverage as if the
deceased owner was still alive for 6
months.
>> [music]
>> This grace period gives the surviving
owner or estate time to restructure the
accounts. After 6 months, [music]
coverage is recalculated based on the
actual account ownership and beneficiary
arrangements then in place.
>> [music]
>> Imagine Margaret and her husband holding
in a qualifying joint account after
selling their home. While both were
alive and met the joint account
requirements, the balance was within
their combined $500,000 joint account
coverage.
After her husband died, the 6-month
grace period began. Once it ended,
coverage could be recalculated as
Margaret's individual ownership,
potentially leaving the balance above
$250,000 uninsured unless the account
structure or deposits had been changed.
The correct solution depends on all
deposits held at that bank, the
ownership categories, and the
beneficiary designations.
It may involve moving part of the money
to another insured institution or
restructuring the account. Do not assume
that adding beneficiaries always
produces a particular amount of
coverage. Ask the bank for an FDIC
insurance calculation or use an official
insurance estimator based on your
