directly into the Social Security Act,
and it says that for most people, an
increase in the Part B premium is not
allowed to make your Social Security
check smaller than it was the year
before. If the premium goes up more than
your raise, the premium increase is
limited, so your net check does not go
down. In practice this year, it will not
even come close. If the average retiree
gets $75 more and the premium goes up by
about $6.60,
that retiree is still ahead by roughly
$68 a month.
Let me tell you about Agnes. Agnes is 78
and lives on one check. Every January
for years, she has braced for the
letter, expecting Medicare to swallow
her raise whole. This year, her raise is
about $69. The premium increase is a
fraction of that, and the hold harmless
rule stands behind her no matter what.
But here is the twist, and this is where
I need you to pay attention. The hold
harmless rule does not protect
everybody. It does not cover you if you
are brand new to Medicare this year. It
does not cover you if your premium is
not taken out of a Social security
check. And most importantly, it does not
cover you if you pay the higher income
surcharge called IRMAA.
IRMAA is an extra charge on top of the
Part B premium for people whose income
was above a certain level. And here is
the trap inside it. Medicare does not
look at your income today. It looks at
your tax return from 2 years ago. So, a
one-time event like selling a house,
cashing out an account, or one large
required withdrawal can trigger a
surcharge years later, long after the
money is gone. If that happened to you
and your income has since dropped
because you retired, lost a spouse, or
simply stopped working, you can ask
Social Security to use your newer, lower
income instead. The form is called
SSA-44.
It is free, it is a real process, and it
can lower your surcharge, sometimes all
the way to zero. How do you know if you
are paying one?
Look at the Medicare line on your
notice.
If the amount taken out is higher than
the standard premium, the difference is
almost always IRMAA, and Social Security
sends a separate letter explaining it,
including which year of income they
used. So, if your January notice shows a
Medicare charge that looks too high, do
not just accept it. Ask whether you are
paying IRMAA, and if your income has
dropped, file the form. Number three.
[music]
If you are still working, you get to
keep more of your check. This one
surprises a lot of people. If you start
Social Security before your full
retirement age and you keep working,
Social Security can hold back part of
your benefit if you earn too much. It is
called the earnings test. This year, the
limit is $24,480.
In January, it goes up to $25,560.
>> [music]
>> That is just over $2,100 a month you can
earn before Social Security holds back a
single dollar. And above the limit, they
hold back $1 of benefits for every $2
you earn over it. That higher limit
means over $1,000 of extra earnings are
now safe, and about $540 less held back
from your check.
And in the year you actually reach full
retirement age, the limit is much higher
still, rising to almost $68,000.
And they only hold back $1 for every
three you earn above it. For anyone born
in 1960 or later, full retirement age is
67. For people born a little earlier, it
is a few months sooner. Now, here is the
best part. Once you reach full
retirement age, the earnings test
disappears completely. There is no limit
at all. You can earn as much as you want
and keep every dollar of your Social
Security. Let me tell you about Hank.
Hank is 63. He took Social Security
early, then got bored, and went back to
work part-time at a hardware store. Last
year, Hank earned a little over the
limit, and Social Security held back
part of his check, and Hank was furious
because he thought that money was simply
gone. But here is what almost nobody
tells you. That money is not lost. When
Hank reaches full retirement age, Social
Security recalculates his benefit and
gives him credit for every month they
held money back. His check goes up from
that point on permanently. [music]
So, if you are working and collecting
early, look at the new limit and plan
your hours around it. And if money has
been held back, do not panic. It is not
gone. It comes back to you in a higher
check later.
Real quick, before number four, because
everything I have given you so far is
the rule, and the rule is only half of
it.
>> [music]
>> The paperwork is where the money
actually moves, and I have put every
form from this channel into one book. It
is called The Retiree's Playbook, the
SSA-44 for the premium surcharge, the
Medicare Savings Program application,
the January checklist from this video on
paper in large print with the exact
words to say on every phone call. I
built it because the government
announces the money and then quietly
leaves the claiming to you. And that is
exactly where careful people lose money
every single year. It is at
marcusretires.com,
and the link is in the description.
>> [music]
>> If it does not hand you back one thing
you did not know this morning, there is
a full refund, and I will not ask you
why. It is there if you want it and I
will not bring it up again. All right,
[music] back to it. Number four, tax
season opens in January and seniors get
the biggest deductions they have ever
had. Let me clear something up first
because there is a lot of confusion out
there. Social Security did not become
tax-free. You may have heard that on the
news or seen it online. It is not true.
If your income is high enough, part of
your Social Security can still be taxed.
But here is the good news. Congress
created something that for a lot of
seniors gets them to the same place.
When you file your taxes for this year,
starting in late January, you get three
separate breaks just for being over 65.
First, [music] the regular standard
deduction, which is $16,100
for a single filer. Second, the extra
amount for being 65 or older, which is
just over $2,000 more. And third, the
brand new senior deduction, $6,000 for
every person 65 or older running through
Add those up and a single senior can
subtract about $24,150
from their income before the IRS taxes a
single penny. For a married couple who
are both over 65, it is $32,200
plus the extra age amounts plus $6,000
each, which comes to $47,500.
>> [music]
>> And here is what makes the senior
deduction different from almost every
other tax break. You get it whether you
take the standard deduction or itemize.
Most deductions make you choose. This
one does not. Let me tell you about
Betty. Betty is 68 and a widow. She has
a small pension, some interest from her
savings, and her Social Security. She
has paid a little income tax every
single year since her husband passed.
This year, with all three of those
breaks stacked together, a large part of
her taxable income simply disappears.
And depending on her exact numbers, she
may owe far less than last year or
nothing at all. But there is a catch and
it comes in two parts. The The deduction
starts to shrink once your income passes
$75,000 for a single filer or 150,000
for a married couple. And it only helps
you if it actually ends up on your
return.
>> [music]
>> I have seen seniors use cheap tax
software or a rushed preparer or skip a
question about their age and miss money
they were fully entitled to. The IRS is
not going to call and say you forgot
something. So when you file this winter,
look for the senior deduction by name.
Make sure the extra amount for age is
there for every person on the return who
is 65 or older.
And if you want someone to check it for
free, the IRS runs a program called tax
counseling for the elderly and you can
find the nearest site by calling 1 8009
Now, real quick, before the pharmacy
counter because the next one is where
some people see the biggest drop of all.
If this video has already shown you
money you did not know was coming, tap
the like button so it reaches more
people who have spent all year hearing
the bad news and share it with one
person who lives on that monthly
deposit. Somebody you know qualifies for
number seven right now and has never
even heard its name.
All right, number five. Number five. On
the 1st of January, the price Medicare
pays for 15 of the most expensive drugs
in the country drops.
>> [music]
>> For the first time ever, Medicare was
allowed to negotiate directly with drug
companies. The first round of lower
prices started this year. The second
round starts on January 1st and it
covers 15 more drugs.
Here are a couple of examples from
Medicare's own published numbers.
Ozempic, along with Wegovy and Rybelsus,
had a list price of about $959
for a 30-day supply.
The new negotiated price is 274.
Trelegy, a common inhaler for breathing
problems, goes from 654 to 175.
>> [music]
>> The full list includes drugs for
diabetes, cancer, breathing problems,
and more including Xtandi, Ibrance,
Linzess, Breo, Trajenta, Janumet, and
Otezla. And Medicare estimates the
savings to people's own pockets in the
hundreds of millions of dollars. Now, I
want to be honest with you.
Your exact copay depends on your plan,
and a lower price for Medicare does not
automatically mean the same discount
lands in your hand at the counter. But a
lower negotiated price pushes everything
in your direction, and there is another
protection that keeps working in
January.
>> [music]
>> Your out-of-pocket costs for covered
drugs on a Medicare drug plan are
capped. For 2027, the cap is $2,400 for
the whole year, and once you hit it, you
pay nothing more for covered drugs until
the year starts over.
>> [music]
>> And insulin is capped at $35 a month.
Let me tell you about Roy. Roy is 70 and
takes three brand-name medications, one
of them on the negotiated list. A few
years ago, there was no cap at all, and
Roy was spending thousands of dollars a
year at the pharmacy. Now, his
worst-case for the whole year has a
ceiling, and one of his drugs just got
dramatically cheaper for Medicare to
buy.
So, if you take any of these drugs, look
at your plan's notice for next year, and
call your plan in January to ask what
your copay is now. And if you are still
deciding on a plan, you have until
December 7th to compare and switch,
because plans change their drug lists
every single year, and a drug that is
covered today may not be covered next
year. 5 minutes on the phone now can
save you a very expensive surprise in
January. Number six, SSI goes up and the
January payment arrives early. SSI
stands for Supplemental Security Income.
It is a separate program from regular
Social Security, and it is for people 65
and older or disabled who have very
little income and very few assets. A lot
of seniors get both a small Social
Security check and an SSI payment on top
of it. In January, the federal SSI
payment goes up. For an individual, it
goes from $994 a month to $1,029.
For a couple, it goes from $1,491 to
And here is a small bonus. Because the
1st of January is a holiday, the January
SSI payment is actually sent out on
December 31st. So, the raise shows up
before the new year even begins. Now,
here is the part that matters most. A
lot of seniors who qualify for SSI have
never applied because they think they
own too much. The limit is $2,000 in
countable resources for an individual
and 3,000 for a couple. But, the home
you live in generally does not count.
One car generally does not count. Most
personal belongings do not count. Let me
tell you about Marie. Marie is 81. Her
social security is small because she
spent years at home raising five
children. She owns her little house, an
old car, and has about $1,500 in the
bank. Marie always assumed that owning a
home meant she could not qualify for
anything. She was wrong. So, if your
income is very low and your savings are
under those limits, not counting your
home and car, call Social Security and
ask to apply for SSI. The number is
Even a small SSI payment can open the
door to other help, including help with
medical bills.
Number seven, the one I promised you at
the beginning, a program that pays your
Medicare premium for you. Remember that
Part B premium I talked about earlier?
a month taken right out of your Social
Security check. Over a year, that is
There is a set of programs that will pay
that premium for you. They are called
Medicare Savings Programs, and when you
qualify, the premium stops coming out of
your check and that money goes straight
back into your pocket. That is the
$2,400 a year I promised you. And here
is why most people never apply. They
think these programs are only for people
with almost no income.
>> [music]
>> That is not true. There are three main
levels. The first, called QMB, pays your
Part B premium and also your
deductibles, co-insurance, and co-pays.
And the income limit is about $1,350 a
month for an individual.
The second, called SLMB, pays your Part
B premium with an income limit of about
$1,616 a month for an individual. And
the third, called QI, also pays your
Part B premium with an income limit of
about $1,816 a month for an individual
or about $2,455 for a couple.
Think about that. A single person with
roughly $1,800 a month of income can
still qualify to have their entire
Medicare premium paid. That is a lot of
retirees. There is usually an asset
limit, too, about $9,950 for an
individual and about $14,900 for a
couple. But your home and your car
generally do not count. And some states
set the limits higher or drop the asset
test completely. But wait, because it
gets better.
If you qualify for any of these Medicare
Savings Programs, you automatically
qualify for another program called Extra
Help, which lowers what you pay for
prescription drugs. Next year, the
standard deductible on a Medicare drug
plan can be as high as $700.
With Extra Help, your deductible is
zero, and your co-pays are capped at
just a few dollars for generics and
about $14 for a brand-name drug. Let's
go back to Marie. Her income is well
under those limits. Once she qualifies
for a Medicare Savings Program, $202.90
a month stops coming out of her Social
Security check. On top of her raise,
that is about $2,400 a year back in her
pocket, plus a zero-dollar drug
deductible from Extra Help. And for a
married couple where both spouses
qualify, the premium savings can be
close to $4,900 a year. That is real
money.
>> [music]
>> That is groceries, a car repair, a gift
for the grandkids, or simply not
worrying about the next bill. So, if
your income is anywhere near those
limits, apply. Do not decide for
yourself that you are over.
>> [music]
>> Let them tell you.
Medicare Savings Programs are run
through your state Medicaid office, and
you can apply even if you have never
been on Medicaid and never will [music]
be. When you call, ask for the Medicare
Savings Program application by name, and
ask whether your state uses higher
limits than the federal ones. And if you
are turned down, ask for the reason in
writing because mistakes happen and you
can appeal. So, let's put all seven
together because here is your January
checklist. One, your Social Security
goes up 3.6% automatically and when the
notice comes, compare it line by line
with last year's. Two, [music]
the hold harmless rule protects most
people from Medicare shrinking their
check and if you pay the IRMAA surcharge
and your income has dropped, file form
SSA-44.
Three, if you are working and collecting
early, the earnings limit rises to
and money held back is not lost. [music]
It comes back later. Four, when you file
your taxes, make sure the $6,000 senior
deduction and the extra amount for age
are actually on your return. Five,
[music] if you take one of the 15
negotiated drugs, call your plan in
January and ask what you pay now. And
remember your yearly drug costs are
capped at $2,400.
Six, if your income and savings are very
low, apply for SSI even if you own your
home.
And seven, if your income is under about
$1,800 a month, apply for a Medicare
savings program. It can put about $2,400
a year back in your check and it opens
the door to extra help. You can call
Social Security at 1-800-772-1213.
And for help with Medicare, including
how to reach your state's Medicare
savings program, call 1-800-MEDICARE.
And if you want that entire checklist on
paper with every form and every phone
script behind it, the Retiree's Playbook
is at marcusretires.com.
Here is my honest read on all of this
before you go. The bad news this year
was loud and most of it deserved the
attention it got. But January is not
only the month where bills reset and
premiums rise. It is also the month
where a surprising amount of money moves
in your direction. Some of it
automatically and a lot of it sitting
behind a phone call that takes 10
minutes. The government announced every
one of these seven items.
What it did not do is knock on your door
and tell you which ones belong to you.
That part has always been left to you
and it always will be. The seniors who
come out ahead every January are not the
lucky ones or the wealthy ones. They are
the ones who checked the notice, asked
the question, and made the call. So, be
one of them. I am Marcus and this is
Marcus retires. If this video gave you
even one number you did not know this
morning, do three things for me. Hit the
like button so it reaches more people
who have only been hearing the bad news.
Share it with one person in your life
who lives on that monthly deposit
because there is a very good chance they
qualify for number seven and have never
heard its name. And subscribe with the
bell turned on because next week I am
walking through the December notice from
Social Security line by line so you can
catch any mistake before it costs you a
full year.
Until then, keep the checklist, make the
calls, and I will see you in the next
one.

title: If You're Over 60, Aldi Will Give You These 14 Things (If You Ask)

segments.text: If you are over 60, and you shop at
Aldi, there are things the store will
give you that almost nobody at the
register will ever mention. Not because
they are secret, because Aldi runs a
store with a handful of workers, no
service desk, and a phone that nobody
answers. If you do not ask, nobody
offers. One of them gives you your money
back and the food again, both for
something you simply did not like.
One of them cuts a grocery delivery
membership in half if you are on food
stamps. And one card a lot of people on
Medicare carry gets refused at the
register, and they find out in front of
a line of people. Here are 14 things
Aldi gives you. Not all of them will
matter to you. But skip the one that
does, and you keep paying full price for
something the store was ready to give
you. One, your money back and the food
again. Aldi calls it the twice as nice
guarantee.
In Aldi's own words, "If for any reason
you are not 100% satisfied with the
quality of any product, we will gladly
replace the product and refund your
money." Not one or the other, both. Here
is what that means in a real kitchen. A
woman tries an Aldi coffee instead of
the name brand she has bought for 30
years. She does not like it. She takes
the bag back to the store with what is
left in it, and she walks out with her
money back and a new bag of coffee or
something to replace it. You bring the
packaging and whatever is left of the
product back to the store. If you have
the receipt, you get the refund in the
way you paid. If you do not, Aldi gives
you a store credit card for the current
price. So, keep your Aldi receipts in
one envelope in the kitchen drawer.
There are a few things it does not
cover. Non-food items from the special
buys aisle, national brand alcohol, a
product you already got as a
replacement, and problems that are not
about quality.
And it only applies to things you bought
in the store, not online. For someone on
a fixed income, this is the end of the
fear of trying something cheaper. If you
do not like it, the store pays for the
mistake, not you. And it is not only for
things that taste bad. Picture a man who
buys a frozen lasagna, cooks it, and
finds it dry and tasteless. He eats two
bites. He keeps the box and the rest of
the tray in the freezer, takes it back
on his next trip, and gets his money and
another frozen dinner. Opened, half
eaten, it does not matter. What matters
is that he brought back the packaging
and what was left. And if getting to the
store is the hard part, the next one is
for you. Two, if you get food stamps,
groceries delivered for less. You can
use your food stamp card at Aldi in the
store. But a lot of people do not know
you can also use it to order Aldi
groceries online for delivery or pickup
through Instacart.
Instacart lists Aldi among the stores
where food stamp customers can pay for
online orders. And here is the part
almost nobody tells you. Instacart
offers food stamp customers 50% off its
Instacart Plus membership for 1 year. To
get it, you have to have placed a food
stamp order on Instacart in the past 6
months. The membership gives you no
delivery fee on eligible Aldi orders of
$10 or more, though service fees still
apply.
One thing to know before you start, food
stamps can only pay for the food. You
also need a regular debit or credit card
on the account for fees, taxes, and
tips. Picture a man of 74 with a bad
hip. In January, when the parking lot is
ice, he is not going to push a cart.
With his food stamp card on Instacart,
the groceries come to his door. Now,
picture a couple on a small fixed income
who order every 2 weeks. With the
delivery fee gone on their orders over
$10, the only extra they pay is the
service fee and the tip. For them, that
can be cheaper than the gas in the
afternoon it takes to get to the store
and back. But if the app itself is the
problem, there is a phone number for
that. Three, a real person who will help
you order. Aldi stores do not answer the
phone. Aldi says so itself. Rather than
hire extra staff to answer phones, its
workers stay focused on shoppers in the
store.
But Instacart, which runs Aldi's online
orders, has a line for older customers.
Instacart says it offers senior and
specialized support for customers who
who extra help setting up an account or
placing an order. The number is
everyday from 8:00 in the morning to
11:00 at night Eastern time.
Picture a widow who has never ordered
anything online. Her daughter lives
three states away. One phone call and a
live person walks her through it. She
does not need to understand the app. She
needs to say, "I am a senior. I have
never done this and I want to order Aldi
groceries for pickup."
The person on the line takes it from
there.
Write that number on the inside of a
kitchen cabinet door where you will find
it again. And if you would rather pick
it up yourself, that is cheaper, too.
Four, pick up brought to your car. If
you order online and choose pickup, Aldi
says pickup fees start at $1.99
and every online order has to be at
least $10. You drive to the store, park
in the pickup spot, and someone brings
it out to you. Picture a woman who uses
a walker. Getting from the parking lot
to the door, through the store, back to
the car with a loaded cart takes
everything she has. With pickup, she
never leaves the driver's seat. She pops
the trunk and the groceries are in it.
There is a catch with online orders. On
top of the pickup or delivery fee,
service fees can apply. So, for a big
weekly shop, walking in may be cheaper.
Check the total on the screen before you
confirm. For a bad weather week or a bad
knee week, a couple of dollars can be
worth it. And if it is your very first
time ordering, the fees can be lower
still.
Five,
first time ordering. The first
deliveries can come with no delivery
fee. On its food stamp page, Instacart
says new customers get no delivery fee
on their first three grocery orders.
Read the conditions on the screen before
you order because fees and service
charges are not the same thing. But if
you are trying delivery for the first
time, those first three orders are the
time to test it. Picture a woman who has
never had groceries delivered in her
life. She uses her first order for the
heavy things only. Water, cat litter,
the big bag of potatoes, the laundry
soap, the things that hurt her back.
Then she decides whether it is worth
keeping. Now, there is something you
need to know before you ever reach the
register.
Six, the grocery card Aldi refuses at
the register. Some Medicare Advantage
plans give members a card with money on
it for groceries or health items. Aldi
says it does not accept insurance health
spending cards and it names United,
Aetna, and Humana cards. Picture a woman
who drives across town because her
plan's card has $60 on it, fills her
cart at Aldi, and gets told no at the
register with a line of people behind
her. Do not let that be you. Use that
card at a store your plan lists. Aldi
also does not accept checks and it does
not accept WIC. What it does accept is a
long list. Cash, most debit cards, Visa,
MasterCard, Discover, American Express,
food stamp cards, and tap to pay with
Apple Pay or Google Pay. So, if your
plan gives you a grocery card, keep it
for the stores that take it and bring
your regular card or your food stamp
card to Aldi. A 2-minute call to the
number on the back of your plan card
tells you exactly which stores take it.
And there is one more thing you can get
at that register.
Seven, cash back at the register.
When you pay with a qualifying card,
Aldi offers cash back at checkout in
amounts of 10, 20, 40, or $100. For a
lot of people over 60, cash is still how
the week works. Money for the
hairdresser, the church plate, a
birthday card for a grandchild. If you
are making a separate trip to an ATM or
paying a fee at a machine that is not
your bank's, ask for cash back while you
pay for your groceries instead. Say it
before you pay, "I would like $40 cash
back, please." Picture a widower hour
who used to drive to his bank every
Friday for $40 in cash. He buys his
groceries on Friday instead, asks for
the $40 at the register, and that is one
less trip in his week. And while you are
thinking about change in your pocket,
there is a quarter you always get back.
Eight, your quarter comes back. Aldi
carts are locked together and you put in
a quarter to unlock one. Aldi's own
words are simple. Lend us a quarter and
we will lend you a cart. When you bring
back the cart, you get your quarter
back. That quarter is not a fee. It is
how Aldi avoids paying someone to chase
carts around the parking lot. And that
saving is part of the shelf price.
If walking the cart back is hard for
you, hand it to someone walking in. They
give you their quarter, you give them
the cart, and you are done. The next one
is about the price on the shelf. Nine,
price drops. And this falls price cuts.
Aldi runs a program it calls price
drops. Extra low prices on certain
items. And in late September, Aldi
announced a round of price cuts for the
fall. In its announcement, honeycrisp
apples were $1.99 for a 2-lb bag and
family packs of chicken breast were
$1.99 a pound. Aldi itself says prices
can vary by store. Picture a couple who
buy chicken every week. At that price, a
family pack bought on the right week and
split into the freezer is three or four
dinners for the cost of one meal at a
drive-thru. Look for the price drop
signs in the store and check the weekly
ad. In plain words, look for that price
drops tag on the things you already buy
every week. A lower price on something
you buy every week is money saved every
week for as long as that price lasts.
And the price drops are only half of it.
The other half changes every single
week.
10. A new weekly ad and the special buys
aisle. Aldi puts out a weekly ad with
its deals and the middle aisle carries
what Aldi calls Aldi Finds products
available for a limited time only and
not always food. A space heater one
week, slippers the next. Here is the
rule to remember. Food from that aisle
is covered by the twice as nice
guarantee. Non-food items from that
aisle are not. So, for anything electric
or anything you wear, keep the box and
the receipt and read the return terms at
the store.
Picture a woman who buys a small space
heater from that aisle in November. It
stops working after a few weeks.
If she threw the box and the receipt
away on the first day, she has made it
much harder for herself. If they are on
the shelf in the closet, she takes it
back and asks for a refund or an
exchange. And watch out for deals that
say Aldi, but are not from Aldi at all.
11. Coupons that are real and the ones
that are scams.
Aldi does not offer online coupons. In
Aldi's own words, any coupon found
online or through social media is not a
legitimate Aldi coupon. Real Aldi
coupons are printed and handed out in
the store or mailed to you. So, if a
post on says, "Click here for a $50 Aldi
coupon." It is not from Aldi. And a fake
coupon is often a way to get your name,
your email, or your card number. Picture
a grandmother who sees a post from a
friend saying, "Aldi is giving away $100
coupons to seniors this week." All she
has to do is fill in a short form. That
form is the scam. Aldi has already told
you where real coupons come from, the
store or your mailbox. The same goes for
text messages that say you won an Aldi
gift card or that your Aldi order is on
hold and you need to click a link. If
you did not order anything, there is no
order. Delete it. And if you want to
give Aldi as a gift, there is a better
way. 12. Gift cards with no fees that
never expire. Aldi sells gift cards in
its stores from $5 up to 100. Aldi says
there are no fees and the balance never
expires. One thing to know, they cannot
be used for online orders. For a
grandparent on a budget, an Aldi gift
card is a practical gift for a grown
grandchild who is just starting out. And
for yourself, it is a way to set your
grocery money aside on payday. So, it is
there at the end of the month. And there
is one page on Aldi's website worth
knowing about before the next food
scare. 13. A recall list you can check.
Aldi keeps a product recalls page on its
company website.
If you hear on the news that a food was
recalled, that is where you check
whether it was an Aldi product. And if
you bought it, follow the recall notice
for how to return it or get your money
back. Picture a man who hears on the
radio that a brand of spinach was
recalled. He does not remember if his
bag came from Aldi or somewhere else.
Two minutes on the recall page or one
question to a grandchild with a phone
tells him whether to throw it out. And
one last thing about the calendar. 14
point, the days the doors are closed.
All these stores are closed on New
Year's Day, Easter Sunday, Thanksgiving
Day, and Christmas Day. Hours otherwise
vary by store. That matters more than it
sounds. Picture a man who plans to pick
up his Thanksgiving rolls on
Thanksgiving morning because it is close
by. The doors are locked. Shop the day
before and go early because everyone
else will have the same idea.
So, that is the list. What Aldi does not
give you is a senior discount. Aldi says
it does not offer discounts at its
stores. It does not do rain checks and
it does not price match. Its argument is
that the low price on the shelf is the
discount every day for everyone. But the
things on this list are real. Your money
back and the food again. Food stamp
delivery for less. A phone line with a
real person. And a register that will
not take your plan's grocery card so you
know before you get there. Write down
the three that matter to you and use
them on your next trip. This is
educational content and general
information only. It is not financial
advice and it is not affiliated with or
endorsed by Aldi or Instacart. Policies,
prices, fees, and offers can change and
vary by store. Confirm anything here
with your local Aldi store or on the
official Aldi and Instacart websites
before you rely on it. Take care of
yourself.

title: Seniors: Move These 7 Assets Before 2027 — The IRS Could Take $45,000

segments.text: January 1st, 2027 is not a deadline you
can negotiate. It is a hard calendar
line, and on the other side of it wait
the tax rules that land on seven
specific assets you are probably holding
right now. If those assets are still
sitting still when the calendar turns,
the combined cost in the first year
alone can reach $45,000 for a retired
couple with an ordinary portfolio. Not
because you did something wrong, because
you did nothing. Here is the number I
want you to memorize, $45,000.
And it is not a guess pulled from the
air. It is what the arithmetic comes to
when you put the seven pieces side by
side.
The biggest pieces are 2,000 in lost
savings yield, 6,000 in unnecessary IRA
taxes, 7,500 in capital gains that could
have been harvested at 0%, 20,000 in
real estate recapture, 4,000 in life
insurance lapse income, 3,000 in social
security taxation, and 2,500 in probate
and freeze costs. Some people will lose
more, some will lose less, but almost
everybody watching this holds at least
three of these seven assets, and every
one of those three quietly costs money
for as long as it sits still. Now, most
people hear a number like that and
assume it belongs to somebody else,
somebody richer, somebody careless,
somebody with a team of advisers. That
assumption is exactly what these seven
assets have in common. Not one of them
requires you to make a mistake. A
savings account paying half a percent,
an IRA nobody has touched since the
paperwork was signed,
a brokerage account titled the way the
bank suggested 20 years ago, a rental
property, an old life insurance policy,
a pension, a checking account with a
beneficiary form that was filled out
when the account was opened and never
looked at again. Ordinary things held by
careful people, and the calendar does
not care how careful you were. It only
cares what is still sitting still when
it turns. My name is Marcus, and this is
Marcus Retire. Every week I go looking
for the rule that quietly decides what
happens to your money, and I bring it
here before it costs you anything. If
that sounds useful, hit subscribe and
tap the bell right now because almost
everything in this video has a date
attached and the dates are doing more
damage than the rules are. The usual
honesty before we start. I am not a
lawyer, I am not an accountant, and I am
not your financial advisor. This is
education based on the rules as they
stand today and your situation is your
own. So, confirm anything here before
you act on it. The seven assets are
coming one at a time and each one is
worse than the last. The first one is
not stocks and it is not bonds. It is
the cash sitting in your savings account
right now. And the seventh does not feel
like an asset at all because it is just
your checking account. By the end, you
will know why that is the one I want you
to check first. And if you are watching
on behalf of a parent or a spouse, stay
till the end because the last section is
a list of seven phone calls and every
one of them is free. Asset number one is
cash. Not stocks, not bonds. The money
in your savings account, your checking
account, and the certificate of deposit
that rolled over last month without you
noticing that the rate dropped. Here is
how the trap works.
Banks are required to file a currency
transaction report with the Treasury
Department's Financial Crimes Network
for any cash deposit or withdrawal of
$10,000 or more. It happens
automatically. The bank does not ask
your permission and it does not send you
a copy. Your name simply goes into a
federal database. And if you try to
avoid the report by breaking a $15,000
deposit into two $7,500
deposits, files a suspicious activity
report instead and that is a federal
felony called structuring. You can go to
prison for breaking your own money into
smaller pieces to avoid a form you did
not even know existed. I think that is
one of the most insulting traps in the
entire banking system. You are not a
criminal. You are a retiree who sold a
car and deposited the cash. And the
government treats that deposit as a
potential crime because the amount
crossed a line drawn in 1970 and never
adjusted for inflation. $10,000 in 1970
would be roughly $80,000 today if it had
kept pace with prices. It is still
10,000, and banks are still filing
reports on retirees who have no idea the
report exists. But the reporting is not
even the biggest loss. The biggest loss
is the invisible tax of inflation on
cash that earns nothing. $50,000 in an
account paying half a percent with
inflation running at 3% loses about
$1,250 of purchasing power every single
year. Over 5 years, that is over 6,000.
Over 10 years, over 12,000. That is not
a fee you ever see on a statement. It is
a hole in your balance that gets bigger
while you sleep.
Here is what you do instead.
If the money does not need to be
immediately reachable, it can go into
government savings bonds through a
Treasury Direct account, which pay a
blended rate that tracks inflation plus
a fixed component, or into a Treasury
money market fund paying just over 4%
with no state income tax on the
interest. Both are backed by the full
faith of the federal government, and
neither involves a bank report at
$10,000 because you are buying
government securities, not pushing cash
through a teller window. If you need the
money absolutely liquid for emergencies,
use a high-yield savings account at an
online bank paying 4% or more. The
interest is taxable, yes, but the
after-tax return on 50,000 at 4% is
still around $1,700 net in the 12%
bracket, which beats losing purchasing
power every single year.
The difference between doing nothing and
moving the cash comes to close to $2,000
a year on the same balance. Cash that
sits still is cash that dies quietly.
Asset number two is your traditional IRA
or 401k, and this is the asset that
creates the largest tax cascade in
retirement. The government does not need
you to understand it. It needs you to
wait until age 73, take your required
minimum distribution, and pay whatever
tax rate happens to apply in that year.
Because whoever controls the timing
controls the rate. Under current law,
your first required distribution must
begin at age 73, and it is calculated by
dividing your December 31st account
balance by life expectancy factor from
the IRS uniform lifetime table. At age
73, that factor is 26 and a half. On a
$500,000 IRA, that is a first
distribution of about $18,800,
and every dollar of it is ordinary
income. But here is what most retirees
never see coming. The distribution does
not only create tax on itself, it
creates tax on your Social Security
benefits. It triggers Medicare
surcharges 2 years later. It pushes
capital gains out of the 0% bracket into
the 15% bracket. One distribution
touches every other income source you
have. That is the cascade, and the
cascade is where the real money is lost.
Let me show you the math on a worked
example. A married couple, both 69, with
a combined Social Security benefit of
36,000 a year, a $600,000 traditional
IRA, and 40,000 of pension income.
Before any IRA distribution, their
provisional income is the pension plus
half their Social Security. 40,000 plus
18,000 is 58,000, which is already above
the $44,000 married threshold where 85%
of Social Security becomes taxable. So
85% of their $36,000
which is 30,600, is already taxable.
Now, add the required distribution at
600,000 divided by 26 and a half is
about 22,600.
Their income becomes roughly 93,000, and
for a married couple, the 12% bracket
tops out just above 94,000. They are
sitting about a $1,000 away from the 22%
bracket where every marginal dollar is
suddenly taxed at nearly twice the rate.
But the real killer is what happens when
one spouse dies. The survivor files as a
single taxpayer, and the single 12%
bracket tops out at about 47,000.
The same stack of income that fit
comfortably inside the 12% bracket as a
couple now spills into the 22% bracket
as a single filer. And the difference
comes to roughly $10,000 of extra
federal tax every single year, purely
because the filing status changed from
married to single. The IRA distribution
that was manageable as a couple becomes
a bracket killer for the survivor. I
believe the traditional IRA is the most
dangerous asset in retirement because it
looks safe. It grows tax deferred, the
statement shows a big number, and you
feel wealthy. But every dollar in that
account is a future tax bill with an
unknown rate attached to it, and the
rate is determined by the year you are
forced to take the distribution, not the
year you would have chosen. So, here is
the move. If you are between 60 and 72,
and your taxable income sits in the 12%
bracket, you have a window to convert
traditional IRA dollars into Roth
dollars at 12 cents on the dollar. Every
dollar converted permanently exits the
required distribution calculation. It
never forces a future distribution, it
never pushes your Social Security into
higher taxation, it never feeds the
Medicare surcharge, and it grows
tax-free for the rest of your life and
your spouse's.
The conversion must be completed by
December 31st of the tax year. You
cannot convert in January and apply it
to the previous year. There are no
retroactive conversions.
Run the numbers on our example couple.
69 years old with 40,000 of taxable
income means roughly $54,000 of 12%
bracket space remaining. Converting
50,000 this year costs 6,000 in federal
tax, and that 6,000 is the price of
permanently removing 50,000 from the
cascade. That 50,000 would have
generated nearly $1,900 a year of forced
distributions starting at 73, stacked on
top of everything else, taxed at
whatever future rate applies. And there
is a second layer most preparers never
mention until it is too late. The extra
senior deduction of up to $6,000 per
person runs only through tax year 2028.
That deduction expands your 12% bracket
space, which means the conversion window
is cheapest right now while the extra
deduction is in effect. Every year you
wait, the conversion costs more because
the bracket space is smaller. Your
traditional IRA is a ticking clock. Move
it to Roth before the window narrows or
the IRS will move it for you at a rate
they choose.
Asset number three is your brokerage
account. The account with the stocks,
bonds, and index funds you have been
holding for years without selling. Most
retirees believe the strategy is to hold
forever and let the step-up in basis at
death eliminate the capital gains tax.
That strategy works if you die. It does
not work if you need the money while you
are alive and it does not work if the
account is titled incorrectly. If you
and your spouse hold the brokerage
account as joint tenants with right of
survivorship, in most states only half
of the account receives a step-up in
basis when the first spouse dies. The
other half keeps its original cost basis
because the surviving spouse already
owned that half. $200,000 of unrealized
gains on a joint account means 100,000
of those gains remain fully taxable when
the surviving spouse sells at 15%
federal plus state tax.
That is $15,000
of capital gains tax that simply does
not exist if the account had been titled
in one spouse's individual name. Let me
tell you about a widow I will call
Yvonne from Florida. She sold her
brokerage account six months after her
husband died. The account was joint. She
inherited his half with a stepped-up
basis, but her own half kept its
original basis from 1998. She owed over
$14,000 in capital gains tax on a sale
she made to pay medical bills. If the
account had been in her husband's name
alone, her basis would have been the
full value on the date he died and the
tax would have been zero. The retitling
costs nothing. The lack of retitling
cost 14,000. If you have a joint
brokerage account with significant
unrealized gains, retitle it into the
name of the older spouse or the spouse
in poorer health.
The transfer from joint to individual is
not a taxable event. It requires a
signature at your brokerage and it takes
about two business days. And there is a
second move on the same account that is
even more urgent because it expires
every December 31st, the 0% long-term
capital gains bracket. A married couple
filing jointly pays 0% federal capital
gains tax on long-term gains as long as
taxable income stays under the
threshold, which sits near $99,000.
If your taxable income is below that
line, you can harvest capital gains at a
0% federal rate. Sell the appreciated
stock, buy it back immediately, and the
gain is realized at zero, the new basis
is higher, and the future tax is lower.
There is no wash sale rule on gains.
That rule only applies to losses.
$30,000 of unrealized gains harvested at
0% this year permanently eliminates
about $4,500 of future tax.
Miss the date and the gains keep growing
and the tax bill keeps growing with
them. The 0% bracket is a use it or lose
it opportunity. It resets every January
1st and if your income rises in future
years, you may never see it again. Now,
real quick, before asset number four
because the dollar amounts are about to
get much bigger and real estate is where
careful people lose the most. If this
video has already put a number on
something you were guessing about, do me
one small favor. Tap the like button so
it reaches more people holding these
same seven assets and share it with your
husband or wife because the titling
decisions in assets three and seven are
decisions the two of you make together.
And half of the 45,000 in this video
hides in the space between how accounts
are titled and who actually survives.
All right, asset number four.
Asset number four is real estate. Not
your primary residence, your rental
property, your vacation home, or the
commercial building you inherited. This
is where the dollar amounts are largest
and the tax traps are deepest. When you
own rental real estate, you deduct
depreciation every year. Residential
property is depreciated over 27 and 1/2
years, commercial over 39, and that
depreciation reduces your taxable income
while you own the property. But when you
sell, the IRS wants that depreciation
back. Every dollar you deducted is
recaptured at a flat 25% federal tax,
regardless of your ordinary income
bracket. If you deducted $80,000 of
depreciation over 20 years, the
recapture tax on sale is 20,000, even if
you are retired, even if you are in the
12% bracket. And the 1031 exchange
deadline is what destroys most retirees
who own rentals.
A 1031 exchange allows you to defer all
capital gains and all depreciation
recapture by reinvesting the proceeds
into a similar property. You have 45
days to identify the replacement
property and 180 days to close, and the
exchange must be set up with a qualified
intermediary before the sale closes. If
you miss the 45-day identification
window, the exchange fails and the
entire tax bill becomes due immediately.
Let me tell you about a man I will call
Reuben, an investor in Arizona. He sold
a rental property in March without
setting up the exchange first because he
thought he could buy another property
and claim the exchange later.
He was wrong. The exchange must be
structured before the sale. He owed
34,000 in capital gains and 18,000 in
depreciation recapture, over 50,000 on a
property he sold for 280,000, an
effective tax rate near 19% on his gain.
If he had set up the exchange before
listing, the tax would have been zero
and the 50,000 would have stayed inside
the next property, growing tax deferred.
So, if you are considering selling a
rental, set up the 1031 exchange with a
qualified intermediary before you list
it, not after you accept an offer,
before you list. And if you are not
selling, but you want to protect the
step-up in basis for your heirs, the
property can be transferred into a
revocable living trust. The transfer is
not taxable. The property keeps its
character, and at death, the trust
distributes it with a full step-up. For
properties carrying significant
recapture, there are more advanced
trusts that let you keep living in the
property or receive income from it while
removing it from your taxable estate.
And those require an attorney who costs
$3 to $5,000 against tax savings that
can reach 30,000 or more.
Your real estate is a ticking clock, and
the depreciation recapture does not care
what your retirement income looks like.
Asset number five is your life insurance
cash value. Not the death benefit, the
cash value. The money that has been
building inside a whole life or
universal life policy for 20 or 30
years. Most retirees believe that cash
value is tax-free. It is not. It is
tax-deferred, and if you access it
incorrectly, it becomes taxable income
in the year you access it in a spike
large enough to push you into a higher
bracket, trigger Medicare surcharges,
and make 85% of your social security
taxable. Here is how the mechanics work.
The cash value grows tax-deferred, and
you can borrow against it or withdraw
it. But withdrawals are taxed last in,
first out, which means the gains come
out first, and your own basis comes out
last. If you have 50,000 of cash value,
and 30,000 of that is gain, the first
30,000 you withdraw is taxable income.
Withdraw 40,000, and 30 of it is
taxable, while 10 is a return of your
own money. But the real danger is the
lapse. If you stop paying premiums and
the policy lapses, the IRS treats the
lapse as if you received the cash value.
The entire gain becomes taxable in the
year of the lapse. 80,000 of cash value
with 50,000 of gain creates 50,000 of
taxable income in a single year, enough
to push almost any retiree into the 24%
bracket with a tax bill that can reach
And you do not even get the money. The
policy simply dies, and the IRS sends
you a bill for the privilege. Let me
tell you about a man I will call Curtis,
71, from Texas. He let his universal
life policy lapse because the premiums
had become too expensive for his budget.
65,000 of cash value, 42,000 of gain.
The lapse triggered 42,000 of taxable
income, and his tax bill that year
jumped by nearly $10,000.
He called the IRS and asked why he owed
so much, and they told him it was the
policy lapse. He had no idea. He thought
the cash value was his money, tax-free.
The insurance company never explained
the tax treatment. They just sent a
lapse notice and a tax form. So, if you
have a policy with significant cash
value, do not withdraw the gains. Borrow
against the cash value instead. Policy
loans are not taxable income. They do
not appear on your tax return. They do
not affect how your Social Security is
taxed, and they do not touch the
Medicare surcharge. The loan does accrue
interest, typically 5% to 8%, but that
is far below the 22% to 24% marginal tax
you would pay on a withdrawal. And if
the loan is still outstanding at death,
the death benefit pays it off. And if
you no longer need the death benefit,
there is a tax-free exchange into an
annuity called a 1035 exchange,
where the cash value keeps growing
tax-deferred and can later be annuitized
into a stream of payments that may be
only partially taxable.
Your life insurance cash value is not a
savings account. It is a tax-deferred
account with a trapdoor. Borrow it. Do
not withdraw it. And never let it lapse.
Asset number six is your Social Security
benefit. Not the amount you receive, the
amount the IRS taxes. Most retirees are
shocked to learn that up to 85% of their
benefit can be taxed as ordinary income.
Not because they are wealthy, but
because the thresholds that trigger the
taxation have not been adjusted for
inflation since 1983.
The lower threshold is 25,000 for single
filers and 32,000 for married couples.
The upper threshold is 34,000 single and
44,000 married. Those numbers were
written into law over 40 years ago. If
they had been indexed to inflation, the
lower threshold would sit near $80,000
today and the upper one well past
100,000. They are not indexed and
because they are not, almost every
retiree with a pension and a modest IRA
crosses them automatically. The
provisional income formula works like
this.
Take your adjusted gross income, add any
tax-exempt interest like municipal bond
interest, and add half of your Social
Security benefit. That total is your
provisional income. For a married couple
between 32 and 44,000, up to half the
benefit becomes taxable. Above 44,000,
up to 85%. And think about what is
actually being taxed. Money that was
already taxed when you earned it through
payroll deductions during your working
life.
Here is what it costs in practice using
our same couple. 36,000 in Social
Security and 40,000 of pension.
Provisional income is 58,000. So, 85% of
the benefit,
and in the 12% bracket, that inclusion
costs about $3,600 a year. If they had
no pension and lived only on Social
Security, they would be far below the
line and none of it would be taxable.
The pension itself is not what costs
them. The pension pushes their Social
Security into the taxable zone and that
push costs 3,600 a year. You manage this
by controlling what counts as income.
Every dollar of Roth IRA withdrawal is
tax-free and does not count toward
provisional income.
Every dollar of policy loan is tax-free
and does not count. Interest on those
government savings bonds does not count
until you cash the bond. The assets that
do not count toward provisional income
are the assets you want to live on first
and the ones that do count, pension,
traditional IRA distributions, taxable
interest, and capital gains, are the
ones to delay or minimize.
And if you are sitting above the
threshold, there is a form called a W-4V
that lets you have federal tax
voluntarily withheld from your Social
Security check.
It does not reduce the tax, but it
prevents a surprise bill in April, and
it keeps you staring at exactly how much
of your benefit is being consumed by a
law from 1983 that nobody has touched
since.
Asset number seven is your joint bank
account and your payable on death
designations. And this is the one that
does not feel like an asset at all. It
is just your checking account, the one
your Social Security deposits land in
every month. But if it is titled
incorrectly, or the beneficiary
designation is wrong, or the bank's
fraud algorithm flags it, this account
can lock your family out of money for
weeks. Under rules from the financial
industry's own regulator, institutions
are allowed to place a temporary hold on
disbursements from the account of anyone
65 or older if the firm reasonably
believes financial exploitation may have
occurred. The hold can last up to 15
business days, and it can be extended.
During that hold, you cannot access the
funds. Your checks bounce, your
automatic payments fail, your mortgage
does not go through. And the bank does
not need to prove that exploitation
occurred, they only need a reasonable
belief. A large withdrawal, a new name
on the account, a wire transfer to a
grandchild, any of those can trigger it.
Let me tell you about a woman I will
call Phyllis, 78 from Michigan.
She added her nephew to her checking
account so he could help pay bills while
she was in the hospital. The bank saw
the new joint owner and a $12,000
transfer to a contractor for home
repairs and placed a 15-day hold on the
entire account. Her Social Security
deposit landed two days into the hold
and froze with it. She could not pay her
rent. She could not buy her medication.
She spent three days on the phone with
the bank's fraud department before they
released the hold. The nephew was not a
fraudster. The contractor was
legitimate. The algorithm did not care.
So, if you have a joint account with an
adult child, ask your bank about a
convenience account instead, which lets
the child write checks and pay bills
without owning a penny of the balance.
At your death, the account passes to
your estate or your named beneficiary,
not to the child. If the child gets
divorced, a convenience account is not
marital property. If the child is sued,
it cannot be attached. A joint account
is all of those things. And for your
payable on death designations, verify
that the named beneficiary is still
alive, still competent, and still the
person you want to receive the money. If
your beneficiary is your spouse and your
spouse dies before you, the designation
can fail and the account goes to
probate. If the beneficiary is one child
and you have three, that one child
receives the entire account, no matter
what your will says, because the
designation overrides the will. And if
you named an ex-spouse 20 years ago and
never updated it, the ex-spouse gets the
money. The bank does not check your
divorce decree. They check the form on
file. The fix is free.
Call your bank, ask for the current
beneficiary designation on every
account, and if it is wrong, fill out a
new form. 5 minutes per account. The
wrong name on a form can cost your
family months of probate and thousands
in fees. The right name costs nothing.
Now, I want to bring the full picture
together, because seeing the seven
assets in isolation is not enough. You
need to see how they interact, because
the interaction is where the money is.
Take a married couple, both over 65,
with a $600,000 traditional IRA, 40,000
of pension, 36,000 of social security,
50,000 in cash earning half a percent, a
brokerage account with significant
unrealized gains, a rental property with
80,000 of accumulated depreciation, a
life policy with 40,000 of cash value
gains, and a joint checking account with
outdated beneficiary forms.
If they do nothing before January 1st,
the first-year cost is roughly $45,000.
The cash loses purchasing power. The
required distribution pushes 22,000 into
taxable income, which triggers
additional Social Security tax and
Medicare surcharges 2 years down the
road.
The brokerage gains never harvested at
0% wait in the wings to be taxed at 15
or 20. A rental sale triggers 20,000 of
depreciation recapture plus capital
gains. A lapse or careless withdrawal
turns policy gains into a spike of
taxable income. The Social Security is
already 85% taxable because the pension
pushed it over the line.
And the checking account with outdated
designations sends the balance through
probate while the family cannot pay
expenses.
Now, the same couple acting on all seven
before December 31st. The cash moves to
a Treasury money market earning a real
rate. The IRA converts 50,000 a year to
Roth at 12% permanently removing that
balance from the required distribution
calculation and cutting future Social
Security tax.
The brokerage is re-titled into the
older spouse's individual name
eliminating 15,000 of future capital
gains tax for the survivor and gains are
harvested at 0% this year. The rental
property either enters a 1031 exchange
or transfers to a revocable trust
deferring or eliminating the recapture.
The life insurance cash value is
borrowed, not withdrawn, creating zero
taxable income. The provisional income
is managed by living on Roth dollars and
policy loans first. And the beneficiary
forms are updated closing the probate
door. The difference between doing
nothing and doing all seven is not
45,000 once. It is 45,000 in the first
year plus 15 to 20,000 every year after
that for the rest of retirement. Over 20
years, the total cost of inaction runs
into the hundreds of thousands.
The total cost of action is a few phone
calls, a few forms, and a voluntary Roth
conversion tax paid now at 12% instead
of later at 22.
So, here are the seven actions, one per
asset, and every one of them is a free
phone call or a free form. One, log into
every bank account and check the
interest rate. If it is below 3%, move
the cash to a Treasury Direct account or
a high-yield account before the end of
December. Two, call your IRA custodian,
get your current balance, estimate your
taxable income, calculate your remaining
12% bracket space, and convert as much
traditional IRA to Roth as that space
allows before December 31st.
Three, call your brokerage and request
the cost basis report for every
position. If your taxable income is
under the 0% capital gains line, harvest
those gains before December 31st and ask
about retitling the account while you
have them on the phone. Four, if you own
rental real estate and are considering
selling, contact a 1031 exchange
intermediary this week, not after you
have a buyer.
Five, call your life insurance company
and request the in-force illustration.
If the cash value has significant gains,
ask about a policy loan instead of a
withdrawal, and ask what it would take
to keep the policy from lapsing. Six,
calculate your provisional income, your
pension plus half your Social Security
plus your taxable interest. If you are
above the threshold, file the W-4V to
have federal tax withheld from your
check so April does not surprise you.
And seven, call every bank where you
hold an account and verify the
beneficiary designation. If it is wrong,
update it the same day. Now, my honest
read, and you are welcome to disagree
with me in the comments, the IRS is not
your enemy. The banks are not your
enemy. The system is enormous. It is
automated, and it does not send you a
memo when a rule changes in your
disfavor. I do not believe anybody sat
in a room designing a way to take
$45,000 from retirees. I believe
something more ordinary happened, and
something more dangerous. Each rule was
written for its own moment. Each number
was left alone while everything around
it moved. And the machine now runs on
the quiet assumption that you will not
read the manual. The burden of knowing
these rules falls on you. The burden of
moving these assets falls on you. And
the burden of filing the right form
before the deadline falls on you.
January 1st, 2027 is coming and it is
not waiting for you to be ready.
The seven assets are in your portfolio
right now. Move them or the rules move
them for you.
I am Marcus and this is Marcus retires.
If this video put a number on something
you were guessing about, do three things
for me. Hit the like button so it

seven assets. Share it with your husband
or wife because four of these seven
decisions belong to both of you and half
the money in this video hides in the gap
between what the two of you have each

turned on because next week I am taking
the Roth conversion window from asset
number two and breaking it down in full.
Exactly how much to convert, which year

your house or against it. And in the

about the year an old form or a frozen
account caught your family off guard
because your story might be the thing

title: Born Before 1967? 4 Social Security Changes Hitting Your Birth Year In 2027

segments.text: Find your birth year on the screen right
now, because starting in January, the
rules for your Social Security, your
Medicare, and your taxes split into four
distinct groups. And the only thing that
decides which group you fall into is the
year you were born. Two people can do
exactly the same thing next year. Same
income, same choice, same paperwork
filed on the same day. One of them pays
nothing. The other one pays a penalty
every single month for the rest of their
life. The only difference between those
two people is a birthday. And this year,
the lines between the groups have moved
in ways that almost nobody has properly
explained. One birth year becomes the
first in the entire history of Social
Security to reach a full retirement age
of exactly 67. And that happens next
year. One tax break that Congress passed
recently ends at a specific birth year.
And if you were born 1 year too late,
you will never collect a single dollar
of it unless the law is extended. One
rule treats a person born on New Year's
Day as if they were born the year
before. And one group has a widow's rule
that can quietly hold her check below
what she was promised for the rest of
her life without anyone ever explaining
why.
I'm going to take each group in turn,
starting with the oldest. Stay with your
own group, of course, but do not skip
the others, because if you are married,
your husband or wife may be in a
completely different group from you. And
the space between two different groups
living under the same roof is exactly
where couples lose the most money.
I am Marcus from Marcus Retires. I read
the rules so you do not have to. If you
want to know what changes for your birth
year before it actually changes, hit
that subscribe button right now and tap
the bell icon, because I will be
covering each of these groups again
individually as the actual dates arrive
throughout the year. Everything I am
about to tell you comes directly from
the Social Security Administration, the
IRS, Medicare, and the federal health
insurance marketplace. I am not a
financial advisor or a lawyer, and this
is education, not advice about your
specific situation. Now, let me give you
the four groups. Group one is born 1950
or earlier. Group two is born 1951
through 1954.
Group three is born 1955 through 1959.
Group four is born 1960 through 1966.
But before I get into any of the groups,
I need to explain the New Year's Day
rule because it quietly moves people
between groups without ever telling
them. Social Security says that if you
were born on the 1st of January, your
benefit and your full retirement age are
calculated as if you were born in the
year before. So, a person born on the
1st of January 1960 is treated as a 1959
baby with a full retirement age of 66
and 10 months, not 67. And if you were
born on the 1st of any other month, you
are treated as being born in the month
before that one. It sounds like trivia
until it applies to you personally. For
the person it reaches, it can mean 2
months of their life on the calendar and
thousands of dollars over a lifetime.
Now, let me start with each group. Group
one is everyone born in 1950 or earlier.
Your full retirement age was 66 or
younger. You are past 70 and the
claiming decision is behind you. So, the
rules that still move real money for you
right now are about two specific things.
What happens to your check when a
husband or wife dies? And what comes out
of your IRA every single year? Let me
start with the first one because it
catches more widows than any other rule
I have ever seen. You have probably been
told your entire life that a widow gets
100% of her husband's benefit. But 100%
of what exactly? Here is the actual rule
and it is not what most people think. If
your husband claimed his benefit early
before for his full retirement age, then
your survivor check is limited. It is
capped at the larger of two numbers,
either what he was actually receiving at
the time of his death or 82.5% of what
his full benefit amount would have been,
not 100%. Let me make that real with
actual numbers.
Say his full benefit amount with every
raise since he claimed would be $2,400 a
month today.
But he claimed at 62, so he was actually
receiving about $1,800.
As his widow, you do not get $2,400. You
get the larger of 1,800 or 82.5% of
2,400, which is 1980. That is $420 a
month less than the number most widows
have in their heads when their husband
passes away. And it works in the
opposite direction, too. If he had
waited until 70, his check would have
grown by 32% to about $3,168,
and his widow keeps every penny of that
larger amount. The age he claimed at
follows you for the rest of your life.
Two more survivor rules that people get
wrong constantly. If your husband died
before he ever claimed his benefit, and
he was already past full retirement age,
the survivor benefit includes the
delayed retirement credits he earned for
every month he waited right up to the
month he died.
If he died before reaching full
retirement age without ever claiming,
the survivor amount starts from his full
benefit amount, not a reduced one.
Either way, you never get your own check
and his check added together. You get
the larger of the two.
When you sit down with Social Security,
ask for one specific thing. Ask them for
the survivor computation in writing
showing exactly which rule they used to
calculate your amount. That one request
has found mistakes that nobody else
would have caught. Let me tell you about
a woman I will call Loretta. She is a
retired school secretary from Oklahoma.
Her husband took his check at 62, the
first month he was eligible. When he
died last spring, Loretta had budgeted
the house, the car, and the property tax
payments based on the full survivor
amount she had been told about years
earlier.
The letter from Social Security said
She had planned on $2,400.
Nobody had done anything wrong. The rule
had simply never been put in front of
her in plain language before she needed
it. So, here is a question for every
married couple watching this video in
every single group.
Which one of you is likely to be the
survivor?
And what will that person actually live
on every month after the other one is
gone? Most couples have never said those
two numbers out loud to each other. They
hear them for the first time in a letter
that arrives in the worst month of their
lives.
Have that conversation at the kitchen
table while you can both still sit at
it. It takes one evening and it could be
the most important evening you ever
spend. Now, the second thing for group
one, and this reaches group two and part
of group three as well. Anyone who is 70
and a half or older can send money
straight from their IRA to a charity. It
is called a qualified charitable
distribution. In 2026, you can send up

toward your required minimum
distribution. And here is the part that
matters the most. The money never shows
up in your taxable income at all. That
used to matter mostly for keeping your

something additional. The extra senior
deduction of up to $6,000 per person
starts shrinking once your income passes
$75,000 for a single person or 150,000
for a married couple. It shrinks by 6
cents for every dollar over those
thresholds. So, picture a widow with
$95,000 of income.
She is $20,000 over the line, so she
loses $1,200 of her senior deduction. If
$20,000 of her required withdrawal goes

her IRA instead of passing through her

to 75,000 and she keeps the full $6,000

money to walk through. Two important
warnings about this. The money has to go

account first or it loses the benefit

That is exactly why I built Marcus
retires and your likes and shares are

through 1954.

And for one specific birth year in this

The one you postponed from 2027,

Double that up into one calendar year,

Ask whoever does your taxes to run the

Two more rules for group two.

Group three is everyone born 1955

for every year you were born after 1954.
And here is something new for 2027.
The very last people in this group,

October. So starting in January, every
single person in group three is past

Your benefit stops growing the month you

Not when your COBRA coverage ends. And

Raymond. Raymond retired from a

65. He kept his COBRA coverage because

The total bill was about $26,000.

Raymond owed approximately $20,800

Two more Medicare traps specifically for

And if you were born in 1960, you become

At that point, benefits for everyone in

I would do this month. One line for each

And share this video right now with your
