title: Every Senior Must Know The Real October Changes Hitting Social Security And Savings Or Lose Out

segments.text: October is the busiest month of the year
for anyone on Social Security and
Medicare. And this year, it is busier
than usual. In the space of 31 days,
there is a new federal budget year, a
new set of food assistance rules, an
announcement that sets your income for
next year, the opening of the window
that sets your health costs for next
year, a tax deadline a surprising number
of retirees forget, and a quiet deadline
for anyone with money in savings. And
alongside the real changes, there is a
flood of noise. videos and messages
claiming your social security is being
cut in October, that you must verify
your account or lose your benefits, that
a new rule is coming for your savings.
Most of that is wrong, and some of it is
designed on purpose to frighten you into
handing over information. So, this video
is a calendar. I am going to walk
through October date by date, and for
each date, I will tell you what is
actually changing, who it reaches, and
the one thing to do about it. And I will
finish with three things you may have
heard about that are not happening this
October at all so you can put them down
and stop worrying. My name is Marcus and
this is Marcus Retires. I have spent
years helping seniors and their families
work through rules exactly like these.
And I will tell you plainly what I am
not. I am not your lawyer, your
accountant, or your financial adviser.
And this is general education, not
advice for your personal situation. But
the dates are real and they do not move
just because nobody told you about them.
If this is useful, hit subscribe and tap
the bell right now. And then send this
video to one person who has been getting
frightening messages about October
because the noise this month is loud.
And a calm calendar is the only antidote
I know of. On the 1st of October, the
federal government's new financial year
began. And that single date matters for
three different groups of people. The
first group is anyone who receives food
assistance through SNAP. Every year on
the 1st of October, the program's
numbers reset. And this year, the
maximum benefit for a single person in
the lower 48 states rose to just under
$300 a month. The standard deduction for
small households rose to $217.
And the savings limit for households
with someone 60 or older or with a
disability rose from $4,500 to $4,750.
Those sound like small numbers, but a
handful of quiet rules like these decide
who keeps their benefits in retirement.
So, let me give you the two that matter
most. There is also a rule change many
people in their late 50s and early 60s
have not heard about at all. Under last
year's federal budget law, SNAP's work
requirement now reaches adults up to age
64 who do not have dependent children
and do not qualify for an exemption. If
that describes you, you generally need
to work, volunteer, or train for 80
hours a month to keep benefits beyond 3
months in a 3-year period. People 65 and
older are completely exempt from this.
And there are also exemptions for people
unable to work or caring for someone who
cannot care for themselves. But those
exemptions usually have to be claimed
and shown, not assumed. And here is the
SNAP rule I most want older viewers to
hear. If you are 60 or older, you can
deduct out-ofpocket medical costs above
$35 a month, and that includes your
Medicare Part B premium. A great many
older people on SNAP never report those
costs, and because of that, they receive
far less each month than they are
actually entitled to. If you take
nothing else from the 1st of October,
take that one. The second group touched
by the new fiscal year is certain
lawfully present immigrants such as
refugees and people granted asylum who
under the same budget law generally stop
qualifying for Medicaid from the 1st of
October unless they are lawful permanent
residents or fall into certain protected
groups. If you are a citizen, this does
not reach you. But if it describes
someone in your family, the first of the
month is when that clock started. And
the third group is everyone on Medicare
because the 1st of October was the day
insurance companies were allowed to
begin marketing next year's plans, which
means your phone, your mailbox, and your
television are about to fill up between
now and December. Remember one rule
through all of it. A legitimate agent
generally may not call you out of the
blue. If they came to you, be careful.
If you went to them, you are usually
fine. And there is one more thing tied
to the new federal year worth 10 minutes
of your afternoon. Heating assistance
for the coming winter through the
program called lie heap starts its new
year on the 1st of October. Many states
open applications in October or around
the 1st of November. And in a lot of
places, the money is handed out as
applications arrive until it runs out.
If you need help with heating bills this
winter, apply early, not after the first
cold snap. Dial 211 from any phone to
find where to apply where you live. On
the 14th of October, Social Security is
scheduled to announce next year's cost
of living adjustment on the same morning
the September inflation figures are
published. Here is where the estimates
currently stand. AP estimates 3.6%. The
Senior Citizens League estimates 3.5.
The analyst Mary Johnson, who has
tracked this number for years, estimates
3.4. On the average retirement benefit
of a little over $2,000 a month, a 3.5%
raise works out to about $70. But the
raise is not the only number announced
that morning, and this is the part most
people miss entirely. Social Security
also announces the new earnings limit
for people under full retirement age who
are still working, which this year is
It announces the new maximum amount of
wages subject to social security tax,
which this year is $184,500.
It announces the new SSI payment
amounts, which this year are $994 for an
individual. and it announces the maximum
retirement benefit. It is a full morning
of numbers and the news will only repeat
one of them. So, here is what to do with
the raise and it is the difference
between a January disappointment and a
January plan. Do not write down the
percentage. Write down the dollar amount
of your raise. Then wait for the
Medicare Part B premium for next year,
which is usually announced in November.
The Medicare trustees projected it at
about $29.50,
up from the $2290 you are paying now.
and some analysts expect it to come in
higher. Subtract the premium increase
from your raise and whatever is left is
your real raise. That is the only number
worth planning a budget around. Let me
tell you about a woman I will call
Loretta. Loretta is 70, a retired dental
assistant in Oregon. Every
[clears throat] year she tells her
children the raise percentage on the day
it is announced. And every January she
is disappointed when her check goes up
by less than the headline said. This
year she is going to wait for the
premium and do the subtraction first. It
sounds like a small thing, but it
changes the whole conversation from why
did I get less than they said to here is
exactly what I will have. Now, real
quick, before we get to the 15th,
because that date carries two deadlines
and most people only know one of them.
If this video has already sorted out
even one date for you, do me a small
favor. Tap the like button so it reaches
more people trying to make sense of a
loud month and share it with someone in
your family who watches the news and
worries because somebody you love is
about to see a headline saying social
security is being cut and you can hand
them the facts first. All right, back to
the calendar. The 15th of October is a
date with two completely different
deadlines attached to it and retirees
tend to remember only one. The first is
the opening of Medicare open enrollment.
From the 15th of October to the 7th of
December, you can change your Medicare
Advantage plan, change your drug plan,
or move between Medicare Advantage and
original Medicare with no health
questions and no explanations owed to
anyone. This year, that window matters
more than usual, and I want to be
straight with you about why insurers are
pulling back. One large insurer has said
its plan exits will affect about 600,000
members. And analysts estimate that
roughly 1 in 10 Medicare Advantage
members will need a new plan this fall,
whether they wanted one or not. Many
plans that are continuing are quietly
cutting the extras. Things like dental
coverage and the money some plans paid
back toward your Part B premium. And on
the drug side, two numbers are already
set for next year. The most a standard
drug plan can charge as a deductible
rises to $700 and the most you can pay
out of pocket for covered drugs in a
year rises from $2,100 to $2400. So the
action is this. Find the annual notice
of change your plan sent you probably in
September, probably unread. Open it.
Check whether your plan is continuing at
all. Check your doctors and your drugs
against next year's list and compare the
total yearly cost premium plus drugs
plus co-pays on the planfinder at
medicare.gov. gov or with your state's
free ship counselors who sell nothing
and are trained for exactly this. The
second deadline on the 15th has nothing
to do with Medicare and it is the one
that slips past people. It is the
deadline to file your tax return if you
ask the IRS for an extension back in
April. A surprising number of retirees
request an extension because a corrected
tax form arrived late or because a
spouse died and the paperwork was more
than anyone could carry in April and
then the October date arrives unnoticed.
If you filed an extension and have not
yet filed the return, the 15th is the
day. And while you are thinking about
that return, here is something worth
checking. Last year's tax law created an
extra deduction of up to $6,000 for each
person 65 or older for the tax years
2025 through 2028. If you were eligible
for 2025 and it was not claimed, it may
be worth asking your preparer about
amending the return. and an amended
return that finds a $6,000 deduction
pays for the conversation many times
over. Let me tell you about a man I will
call Vernon. Vernon is 76, a retired bus
mechanic in New Jersey. His wife died in
February and tax paperwork was the last
thing on his mind in April, so his son
filed an extension to buy time. In
September, the son realized the October
deadline was almost on top of them. When
they finally sat down with the preparer,
they found that Vernon qualified for the
new senior deduction and that he and his
late wife could still file jointly for
the year she died. The return they filed
was far better than the one they had
been afraid of. Deadlines are like that.
They look like threats until you sit
down with them. Now, the savings part of
the calendar, because October has a
quiet deadline for anyone with money set
aside, and it gets no headlines at all.
If you buy United States Series 1
savings bonds, the inflation linked
bonds sold by the Treasury, their
interest rate resets twice a year on the
1st of May and the 1st of November. A
bond bought by the end of October keeps
the current rate for its first 6 months.
A bond bought in November gets the new
rate. Nobody on this earth can tell you
in advance whether the new rate will be
higher or lower. So, I am not telling
you to rush. But if you were planning to
buy Ibonds anyway, it is worth checking
the current rate and the forecasts
before the end of the month because that
is the entire decision. The same
thinking applies to certificates of
deposit. If you have a CD maturing this
autumn, do not let it roll over
automatically into whatever the bank
offers because banks often renew a
maturing CD at a rate noticeably lower
than their best advertised one. And they
are perfectly allowed to. Look at what
your bank, other banks, and credit
unions are offering before it renews and
compare those rates with Treasury bills
whose interest is exempt from state
income tax. And here is the connection
almost nobody makes to their social
security. Interest from savings, CDs,
and Treasury bills counts as income, and
income affects your social security in
two separate ways. It counts toward the
calculation that decides how much of
your benefit is taxed using thresholds
that have not moved since the 1980s and
'90s. and it can raise your Medicare
premiums two years later through the
income related search charge. For most
people with modest savings, earning more
interest is still clearly worth it. And
I do not want anyone walking away
thinking otherwise. But if your income
sits close to one of those lines, the
timing of when interest lands, December
or January, can genuinely matter. Let me
tell you about a woman I will call
Doris. Doris is 73, a retired librarian
in Wisconsin. For 10 years, her savings
earned almost nothing. And then in the
last 2 years, her CDs renewed at much
better rates. And this spring, for the
first time, part of her social security
became taxable. She thought she had made
a mistake somewhere. She had not. Her
savings were finally earning something.
And that pushed her across a line that
has not moved since 1984. The new senior
deduction helps her a great deal, but
she now looks at the whole picture
before a CD renews instead of just the
rate. October is also the right month to
start two year-end tasks because both
have a hard deadline of the 31st of
December and both get harder the longer
you wait. The first is your required
minimum distribution. If you are 73 or
older and have a traditional IRA or an
old 401k, the IRS requires you to take a
minimum amount out each year. And if you
miss it, the penalty is 25% of the
amount you should have taken, reduced to
10% if you correct it in time. Financial
companies get very busy in December, and
the people who wait until the last week
are the people who discover problems on
the 30th. Ask yours now whether this
year's distribution has been taken or
scheduled, and write down the answer.
The second task, for anyone who gives to
a church or charity and is 70 and a half
or older, is a qualified charitable
distribution.
Instead of writing a check from your
bank account, you ask your IRA custodian
to send the gift directly to the
charity. That money counts toward your
required distribution, but it is never
added to your taxable income. For many
people, that is a better deal than any
deduction because it keeps your income
lower, which can reduce the tax on your
social security and help keep you below
the Medicare search charge lines 2 years
from now. The paperwork takes longer
than people expect. So, start in
October, not December. One more date
belongs on this calendar, even though it
falls just after October. If you or your
spouse are retired but not yet 65 and
you buy health insurance through the
marketplace, open enrollment for next
year begins on the 1st of November, and
this year it matters more than usual.
The extra premium help that many
marketplace buyers received from 2021
through 2025 expired at the end of last
year. Premium help is once again limited
to households with incomes up to 400% of
the federal poverty level, and many
people watch their premiums rise sharply
this year. As a result, insurers have
proposed further increases for next
year. If you are an early retiree, look
carefully at your options in November
and remember that the income you report
decides your help. So, the timing of
withdrawals and when you claim Social
Security can matter a great deal in the
years before 65. There is one more thing
worth doing in October, and it takes 10
minutes. Social Security has said it
will finish moving everyone off paper
checks by the end of this year. Fewer
than 1% of beneficiaries still receive
them. But if you or a parent are among
that 1%, do not wait for a final notice
to arrive in the mail because the final
notice is not guaranteed to arrive
gently. Set up direct deposit or ask for
the Direct Express prepaid debit card if
there is no bank account. And whether
you get a paper check or not, set up
your own My Social Security account
online if you have not already because
criminals have been creating accounts in
other people's names and redirecting
their payments. And the best protection
against someone opening your door is to
lock it yourself first. In early
December, your notice showing next
year's benefit and deductions will
appear in that account, too, often
before the paper letter reaches you.
There is one particular scam aimed at
savings that rises every autumn. And I
want to describe it word for word
because it works on careful people. It
starts with a call, a text, or a popup
on your computer saying there is a
problem with your bank account or that
your identity has been used in a crime.
you are passed to someone claiming to be
from your bank's fraud department or
from a federal agency. They tell you
your savings are at risk and that you
must move them to a safe account or
withdraw cash or buy gold and hand it to
a courier for safekeeping. And they tell
you not to tell anyone, not even your
bank, because the bank staff may be
involved. Every single part of that is a
lie. No real bank and no government
agency will ever ask you to move your
money to protect it, withdraw cash for a
courier, or keep it secret from your
family.
Your deposits are already protected by
federal deposit insurance up to $250,000
per depositor per bank for each
ownership category. The money is safe
where it sits. The only thing that has
to move is the phone away from your ear.
If anyone asks you to move money to keep
it safe, stop, hang up, and call your
bank on the number printed on your card
or call a family member first. Now, as
promised, three things you may have
heard about that are not happening this
month. First, your Social Security
benefit is not being cut in October.
There is no rule that reduces your check
this month. Your benefit goes up in
January with the cost of living
adjustment, not down in October with a
rumor. Second, there is no automatic 4%
Medicare cut coming from last year's
budget law, no matter how many times you
have heard it phrased that way. When
that law added to the deficit, an old
budget rule could have triggered
automatic cuts, including up to 4% to
Medicare payments to doctors and
hospitals. But last November, Congress
cleared that effect away as it has every
single time before. It is not happening,
and even if it had, it would have
reduced payments to providers, not your
benefits. Third, Social Security is not
running out of money this year. The
trustees report from June projects that
the retirement trust fund will run short
in late 2032.
If Congress did nothing at all before
then, benefits would continue, but at
about 78% of the scheduled amount. That
is a serious problem that Congress needs
to fix and the earlier it does the
better. But it is not an October problem
and anyone telling you your benefits are
disappearing this autumn is either
mistaken or selling something. And while
we are clearing the air, every October
brings the same seasonal scams. A call
or text saying your social security will
be suspended unless you verify your
account or that you must call to claim
your 2027 raise or that your Medicare
card is being replaced and you must
confirm your number. None of those are
real. The raise is automatic. There is
no new card. Social Security will not
call you out of the blue asking for your
Social Security number or bank details
ever. Hang up and call Social Security
yourself at 1 8007721213
or Medicare at 18006334227
using numbers you looked up, not numbers
that were read to you. Here is what I
think about October after all of that.
Almost nothing that matters this month
is a threat. Most of it is a decision.
The raise is a number to plan with. Open
enrollment is a chance to fix your
coverage before it fixes itself around
you. The tax deadline is a chance to
claim a deduction you may have missed.
The savings deadline is a chance to earn
more on money you already have. The
danger in October is not that something
will be taken from you. It is that you
will be so busy reacting to frightening
headlines that you miss the decisions
that were actually yours to make. So
here is the whole month as a checklist.
One, if you are on SNAP and 60 or older,
report your medical costs, including
your Medicare premium, because that
deduction is yours by rule and invisible
unless claimed. Two, if you need help
with heating this winter, apply for lie
heap early and dial 211 to find your
local office. Three, on the 14th of
October, write down your dollar raise,
not the percentage, and wait for the
Medicare premium before you plan. Four,
between the 15th of October and the 7th
of December, check whether your Medicare
plan is continuing and compare plans by
total yearly cost, not by premium alone.
Five, if you filed a tax extension, file
by the 15th and ask about the senior
deduction while you are at it. Six,
before the end of October, look at any
maturing CDs. And if you buy Ibonds,
check the current rate before November
arrives. And seven, set up your own My
Social Security account and hang up on
anyone who calls you about your
benefits. If you have a question about
your own situation, leave it in the
comments. I read every one of them and
they genuinely decide what I cover next.
Loretta will finally know her real raise
before January this year. Vernon filed a
better return than the one he feared.
Doris learned that good news on her
savings came with a tax line attached
and planned around it. October is loud,
but most of the noise is about things
that are not happening. And the real
changes are quieter and every one of
them comes with something you can do.
Take the calendar one date at a time. I
am Marcus and this is Marcus Retires. If
this video gave you even one date you
did not know was on it, hit the like
button so it reaches more people through
a noisy month. Share it with one person
who has been frightened by the headlines
and subscribe with the bell turned on
because when the cost of living
adjustment is announced on the 14th and
the Medicare premium follows in
November, I will be here with the plain
English breakdown of what both numbers
actually mean for your January deposit.
Until then, keep the calendar, ignore
the noise, and I will see you in the
next

title: UK Pensioners: 5 Bills You DON'T Have To Pay After 60 - Exempt By Age

segments.text: There are at least five bills the
average American retiree is still paying
year after year that the law says you
may not have to pay at all after a
certain birthday. Five of them. And most
people keep paying them for years. Not
because they owe them, but because no
one ever told them a birthday had
canceled them. And before I go a single
sentence further, I have to clear up the
misunderstanding that costs more than
all five combined. People see a title
like this and think it is for one sort
of retiree. If you live mainly on your
social security check, you think this
will be clever tax talk for people with
big portfolios. Not me, you think. And
if you have a decent pension, a paidoff
house, and a healthy 401k, you think
this will be about benefits for people
who are struggling. Not me either. You
are both wrong. Genuinely, both of you.
On some of these five, the bigger win
goes to the modest retiree. On others,
it is the comfortable one, overpaying
without the faintest idea. I will tell
you on every single one who it helps
most. So nobody gets to fold their arms
and say not me. Because here is the
uncomfortable truth. Retirees at every
income level in this country are
overpaying. They are just overpaying in
different ways. And the reason almost
nobody tells you is depressingly simple.
Your pharmacist does not call to tell
you a shot just became free. Your county
assessor does not call to say you
qualify for a freeze. The marketplace
does not volunteer a refund when
Medicare starts. The IRS will never send
a friendly note saying, "We have been
charging you for something and we did
not have to." The whole machine is built
so that what you are exempt from stays
quietly paid unless you stand up and ask
for it by name. I am going to take you
through all five one at a time in plain
English. How old you have to be, who it
helps, and the exact words to use. And
do stay to the end because the fifth
quietly costs the average household
several hundred a year and it is one of
the easiest of the lot to fix once you
know which questions to ask. Here is the
one idea that holds the whole thing
together. Being old enough and being
treated as old enough are two completely
different things in this country. The
law can say you are exempt from 59 and a
half, from 62, from 65. But the pharmacy
counter, the county office, the
insurance marketplace, and the Medicare
computer will carry on charging you
until you show your date of birth and
claim it. My name is Marcus, and this is
Marcus Retires. I am not with any
agency. No company pays me to point you
anywhere, and I am not selling a thing.
What I do here every week is read the
rules these programs actually publish
and put them into plain English before
the mistake gets made. If that sounds
useful, hit subscribe and tap the bell
right now because these rules keep
shifting and nobody is going to mail you
a summary of what changed. This channel
will do its best, too. So, five bills
canceled by birthdays. Starting with the
one that puts your own money back in
reach the day a half birthday arrives.
Bill number one, the 10% penalty on your
own retirement savings. It is canceled
at 59 and a half. And most people have
no idea what that birthday actually did.
For your entire working life, the deal
on your 401k or IRA was simple. The
money grows untaxed, but if you touch it
before 59 and a half, the government
takes a 10% penalty on top of the income
tax. No exceptions and no mercy. With a
few narrow escapes most people never
learn. That rule is the reason an entire
generation of careful savers learn to
treat their retirement account like a
museum exhibit. Look, but do not touch.
And here is what almost nobody explains.
The day you turn 59 and a half, that
rule is gone. Not reduced, not phased
out, gone. You can walk into your own
savings, withdraw what you need, pay
ordinary income tax, and not $1 of
penalty forever. It is your money again,
the way a paycheck was your money. So,
where does it go wrong? People carry the
museum exhibit fear a decade past the
birthday that ended it. Let me tell you
about a man I will call Gordon, 61, from
Ohio. His furnace died in February and
the replacement with the duct work came
He did not have that in checking, so he
financed it through the contractor at
11% over 5 years and he paid it every
month on time, the way careful people
do. What he did have was a 401k sitting
at just over $200,000 penalty-free for 2
years already on the day the furnace
died. He could have withdrawn 14,000,
paid the income tax, and owed nobody
anything. Instead, he handed the finance
company over $4,000 in interest for the
privilege of not touching his own money.
Nobody cheated him. He simply never
updated the rule in his head. Now, a few
useful details. If you leave a job in
the year you turn 55 or later, money
still inside that employer's 401k can
usually be withdrawn penalty-free even
before 59 1/2 under what is called the
rule of 55. That works for employer
plans, not for IAS. And if you are past
59 and a half, use these plain words
with your plan administrator or bank. I
am past the age-based penalty threshold.
Please confirm my withdrawal will be
processed without any early withdrawal
charge and send me the confirmation in
writing. One sentence and the museum
exhibit turns back into money. Who does
this help most? Both of you in different
ways. If you are modest, this is
emergency access without the 10% haircut
at the worst moment of your life. If you
are comfortable, this is the door you
walk through for every withdrawal, every
Roth conversion, every cash need from
here to the end, and every one of them
penalty-free.
That leads to bill number two, because
this is the one that arrives on the
biggest birthday of your retirement, and
it cancels what is usually the single
largest bill of your early 60s. Bill
number two, full price health insurance
premiums. They are cancelled or replaced
at 65 and the savings are enormous. Here
is the situation for most Americans
between 60 and 64. You are too young for
Medicare. So, if you retire before 65,
you buy your own coverage on the
marketplace. And marketplace insurance
for a person in their early 60s is
brutally expensive. Commonly 700 to well
over $1,000 a month before any subsidy.
Because insurers price for exactly the
age group that uses the most care, that
premium is often the biggest bill in a
retireese's entire budget. Then your
65th birthday arrives and the whole
structure changes. Medicare becomes
available. You get a seven-month
enrollment window that opens three
months before the month you turn 65,
runs through your birthday month, and
closes 3 months after. Part A, hospital
coverage, is free for anyone who worked
roughly 10 years. Part B, doctor and
outpatient coverage, has a standard
premium of a little over $200 a month,
and it is the same price whether you are
healthy or sick. No medical questions,
no age rating, nothing. Compare 200 a
month to a,000 a month and that is what
the birthday does. That is $800 a month,
nearly 10,000 a year, cancelled by
turning 65 and enrolling on time. So
where does it go wrong? In two places.
First, people enroll in Medicare and
then forget to cancel the marketplace
plan and the two cannot coordinate. Once
Medicare is active, a marketplace plan
cannot pay second, cannot fill
Medicare's gaps, cannot do anything
except keep charging you, and enrolling
in Medicare makes you ineligible for the
subsidies on top of it. Let me tell you
about a woman I will call Beverly, 66,
from Arizona. Her Medicare started on
the 1st of March. Her marketplace plan,
$640 a month, kept autocharging her card
until October because cancelling it
simply never appeared on any checklist.
eight months, over $5,000 for a plan
that could not pay a single claim. She
got a small part of it back after hours
of phone calls and only because she
asked. Second place it goes wrong.
People stay on COBRA or an employer plan
past 65 without signing up for Part B,
assuming the other coverage protects
them, and then discover the late
enrollment penalty, which is 10% added
to your Part B premium for every full
year you were late, and it follows you
for life. Now, one warning I owe you
before you cancel anything. Do not drop
any coverage until your Medicare start
date is confirmed in writing. And if you
are still working past 65 with employer
coverage, ask your HR department. In
those words, how does our plan
coordinate with Medicare before you
touch a thing? Because the answer
depends on your employer's size. The
plain words for the marketplace are
these. I now have Medicare. I need to
cancel my marketplace plan effective the
first of next month. Who does this help
most? If you are modest, that
marketplace premium may be the reason
you have not retired yet, and this
birthday removes it. If you are
comfortable, you are the one most likely
to be double paying out of pure
administrative momentum. Bill number
three is the one people get angriest
about because it is charged by an office
that has your date of birth on file and
never says a word. Bill number three,
property tax that never stops climbing.
At 65, in most states, a birthday can
freeze it, cut it, or postpone it, and
almost nobody claims it in the first
year they qualify. Property tax is the
quiet killer of fixed incomes. The house
is paid off, but the tax bill rises
every single year because the assessed
value rises, the local rate rises, or
both, and there is no paycheck rising
alongside it to keep pace. Over a
decade, a $4,000 bill can quietly become
six. And here is what most people never
learn. Most states offer some form of
senior property tax relief and it comes
in three different shapes. So, let me be
precise because this is exactly where
retirees at both ends get told they do
not qualify when very often they do. The
first shape is the senior exemption, an
extra slice knocked off your assessed
value or a flat dollar discount purely
for age. And in many states, there is no
income test at all. The second is the
freeze, and this is the one worth real
money over time. Once you are in, the
assessed value of your home is locked.
Your town can raise the rate, but the
value they multiply it against stops
climbing, and the longer you live, the
wider the gap grows between your frozen
bill and your neighbor's identical
house. On an expensive home, the freeze
can be worth more each year than the
exemption itself, which is why the
comfortable homeowner should be first in

your house, usually with interest,

lifesaver. For others, it quietly

which one you are signing. Now, here is
the catch, and it is the same catch as

not look at your file and apply the
freeze. You have to walk in or call or

71, from a small town in Ohio. Her
husband handled everything with the
county. After he passed, she kept paying
the full bill and kept paying for 6

exemptions for widows, veterans, or
disability? Those stack in many states.
Who does this help most? Both of you.
And this time I mean it literally. The
modest retiree can see a large slice,
sometimes all, of the bill reduced
through income based versions of these
programs. The comfortable retiree with
the big house should be claiming the
freeze because on a high-value home, the
freeze is worth more every single year.
Now, real quick before bill number four,
because this next one is the quietest
overpay on the whole list, and it is
happening to people who did everything
right. If this video has already named
one bill you might be paying for no
reason, do me one small favor. Tap the

person over 60, a parent, a neighbor,
the friend down the road you know is too
proud to ask. Somebody in your life is
paying at least one of these five right
now. And one share from you could be
worth more than any present you will
ever wrap. All right, back to it. Bill
number four. Medicare's hidden sir
charge based on your income from 2 years
ago canceled by one free form that most
people never learn exists. This is the
comfortable retirees silent overpay and
it deserves a slow walkthrough. Medicare

and part D. And the thresholds start
around the low 100,000s for a single

adjusted gross income from 2 years
earlier because that is the most recent
complete tax return the government holds

security maybe half of what you earned.
Your second year of Medicare should be
priced on your new smaller income.
Instead, the system reaches back and
prices your premium on the fat working
year income, and the sir charge follows

catches up with reality. Let me tell you
about a man I will call Richard, 67,
retired from an engineering firm. His
first Medicare year carried a sir charge
built on his final salary, and he
assumed that was simply the price of
having earned well. It was not. What he
had was a life-changing event in the
eyes of the rules. And there is a form
built for exactly this. It is called
form SS SA44. It is free. It is filed
with the Social Security Administration
and its purpose is to say, "My income
dropped for a qualifying reason,
retirement being one of the listed
reasons. Please recalculate my premium
on what I earn now. Richard filed it,
attached proof of his retirement date

charge came off. The plain words are
these. I have had a life-changing event,
retirement, and I would like to file
form SS SA44 to have my income related
Medicare premium recalculated. One form,
one stamp, and it can be worth close to
$1,000 a year every year for people in
the upper tiers. Two more things you
need to hear on this bill. If you did a
Roth conversion after retiring, that
conversion is income and it can trip the
search charge 2 years later. Which is
why the timing of conversions is a

And if you never receive the initial
notice and simply pay whatever is
deducted, you can be overpaying for
years. Because the search charge notice
goes to whatever address social security
holds, and we have all seen how that
goes. Who does this help most? By
design, the comfortable retiree. because
the thresholds only bite above certain
incomes. But the modest retiree is not
immune because a one-time event, a house
sale, an inheritance distribution, a
large withdrawal can spike a single
year's income and trigger a sir charge 2
years later on a household that cannot
afford it. One birthday does not cancel
this one. One piece of paper does. Bill
number five, the one I asked you to stay
for. Full price bills for things your
birthday already discounted. And this
one is everywhere once you see it. It is
not one bill. It is a whole category.
And the principle is identical to every
other item in this video. The discount
exists. The age threshold exists. And
nobody applies it for you. Let me walk
you through the big ones. First,
transit. Nearly every public transit
system in the country offers a reduced
senior fair, commonly half price or
better, from age 65. And most riders
simply tap the same full fair payment
they have used for a decade. If you ride
the bus four times a week, that discount
is worth hundreds of dollars a year, and
it requires asking one question at the
fair office or one setting changed in
the app. Second, the National Park
Senior Pass. At 62, for a onetime $80,
you get a lifetime pass covering
entrance fees at every national park and
federal recreation site in the country
for you and everyone in your car at per
vehicle sites standing. The math is
absurd. One week of park entrances can
exceed the lifetime price. Third, the
gym. Many Medicare Advantage plans and
some metagap plans include a free
fitness membership as a built-in
benefit, the kind of program with
locations in almost every town. And
retirees pay $40 or $50 a month for a
gym their plan was already covering
because the benefit is printed in the
evidence of coverage and never mentioned
by anyone. The words are these to your
plan's number on the back of your card.
Does my plan include a fitness or gym
benefit and how do I activate it?
Fourth, the shots. Under Medicare, the
flu shot, the shingle shot, the RSV
shot, and others are covered at no cost
to you, and the shingle shot alone is
worth well over $200 at full pharmacy
price. Yet, every autumn, people walk
intoarmacies and clinics and pay cash or
skip the shot over the price without
ever sliding their Medicare card across
the counter. The words are these: Is
this vaccine covered at no cost under my
plan? Fifth, the utilities. Many states
require or offer utility discount
programs and low-income energy
assistance that trim electric, gas, and
phone bills. And the phone program in
particular has an age and income
component most people never check. One
call to each utility asking what
discount programs do you offer is all it
takes. Let me tell you about a woman I
will call Glattis, 68. Her Medicare
Advantage plan had included a fitness
membership the entire time she had it.
She was also paying $46 a month at a gym
two blocks from the one the plan
covered. And she was paying full transit
fair to get there. Over $500 a year plus
fairs for a benefit her card in her
purse already owned. Who does this help
most? Everyone. Which is exactly why I
saved it for last because unlike the
other four, there is no income boundary,
no state boundary, no portfolio
requirement. There is only the question
and whether you ask it. So, let me draw
all of this together with the one idea
that matters more than any single rule.
I think of these exemptions like keys
cut for you on each birthday. At 59 and
a half, a key is cut that unlocks your
own savings without the penalty. At 62,
a key is cut for every national park in
the country. At 65, keys are cut for
Medicare, for the property tax freeze,
for the transit fair, for the vaccines,
for the fitness benefit hiding in your
plan. And the keys are real. They
already have your name on them. But no
one walks around and puts them in your
hand. They sit in a drawer at the county
office, at the plan administrator, at
the assessor, at the fair counter, until
you walk up, show your date of birth,
and ask for them by name. Being old
enough is worth precisely nothing until
you claim it. And one key works in
reverse, which is worth a sentence, so
it never surprises you. At 73, for most
people now, the IRS cuts a key that
opens a bill you did not have before,
the required minimum distribution. And
if you miss taking it, there is a
penalty on top. That is a video of its
own and I will make it. But for today,
know that the calendar cuts keys in both
directions and only one direction sends
you a reminder letter. So here is what I
ask of you and it costs you nothing.
Take one birthday, yours or your
spouse's, and ask what that birthday
canceled. Check the 401k rule, the
Medicare enrollment, the county
assessor, the plan's fitness benefit,
the transit office, the pharmacy
counter. Write down the answers. And
here is what that looks like in real
life. A man I will call Gus, 78, watched
a video much like this one that his
daughter sent him. The following week,
he made three phone calls. One to the
county about the senior exemption he had
never claimed in 9 years of eligibility.
One to Social Security about a premium
search charge built on income from
before he retired, and one to the number
on the back of his Medicare card about a
fitness benefit nobody had ever
mentioned. By the end of the month, he
was a little under $200 a month better
off. and he had not earned a penny more,
moved a dollar, or changed a single
thing about the way he lived. He had
simply gone and picked up the keys that
were already his. One more time, because
it matters. This video is general
education, not personal, legal, tax, or
financial advice. Rules differ from
stateto state. Thresholds and premiums
adjust every year, and your own
situation may be different. So, confirm
the details with the county, with Social
Security, with Medicare, or with a
qualified professional before you act.
And if this video helped you, do three
things for me. Hit the like button so it

overpaying. Share it with one person
over 60 because the odds are very good
they are paying at least one of these
five bills right now for no reason on

distribution rule, the penalty for
missing it, and the one move that
satisfies the requirement without adding

Marcus and this is Marcus Retires.

segments.text: Imagine sitting down at your kitchen
table on the morning your Social
Security payment is supposed to arrive.
You open your banking app, you refresh
the screen, and nothing is there. No
letter came in the mail. No one called.
No warning of any kind. Just an empty
space where your money should be. Here
is what makes this so frightening. In
most of these cases, the person did
nothing wrong. They did not ignore a
notice, and they did not break a rule.
They simply did not know that the way
government payments move has been
changing, and that a few small details
they never used to think about now
matter a great deal. In this video, I'm
going to walk you through three changes
that affect how your Social Security
money reaches you, and exactly what to
do about each one. Stay until the end
because the third change is the one
almost nobody is talking about, and it
can lock you out of your own account on
the very day you need it most. A quick
word about me before we start.
My name is Marcus, and this is Marcus
retires, the channel where I explain
money, Medicare, and Social Security in
plain English with no hype and no sales
pitch. I am not a licensed financial
advisor, attorney, or tax professional,
and nothing in this video is personal
advice. Rules and procedures change, so
use this video as a map and confirm your
details directly with the Social
Security Administration before you act
on any of it. If that kind of
information is useful to you, hit
subscribe and tap the bell right now
because these rules keep shifting, and
nobody is going to mail you a summary of
what changed. This channel will do its
best to. Here is the road map. Change
one is about the payment itself because
the paper check is on its way out.
Change two is about your bank
information and how carefully it needs
to be kept up to date because that is
where scammers like to strike.
And change three is about getting into
your own online account, which now has a
stronger lock on the front door. Let us
take them one at a time. Change number
one. The paper check is being phased
out. For generations, this was simple.
The government printed a check, put it
in an envelope, and mailed it to your
house. That system had its flaws, and
everyone who ever had a check go missing
in the mail knows them personally. But
it was the system, and millions of
people built their month around it. In
March of 2025, an executive order
directed the Treasury Department to move
federal payments away from paper and
toward electronic payment. Since the
fall of that year, the Treasury has been
winding down paper checks for most
federal payments, and Social Security is
part of that shift. Why is the
government pushing this so hard? The
Treasury's own position is that a paper
check is far more likely to be lost,
stolen, altered, or returned as
undeliverable than an electronic
deposit. Anyone who has ever had mail go
missing can understand that a check
sitting in a mailbox is a check anyone
can reach. A check in transit can be
washed and rewritten. An envelope
forwarded to an old address can sit in a
stranger's hands. An electronic deposit,
by contrast, moves bank to bank, never
touches a mailbox, and lands in an
account that only you control. The
reasoning is sound, but sound reasoning
at the system level does not always feel
sound at the kitchen table level, and
that is where most people are living.
Now, here is something many news stories
leave out. The government did not simply
cut everyone off overnight. There are
exceptions for people who genuinely
cannot use an electronic payment. That
can include someone with a documented
disability that makes electronic banking
impractical, someone dealing with a
serious health condition, someone living
in a remote area, or someone who has no
reasonable way to reach a bank at all.
If that sounds like you or someone in
your family, you can ask Social Security
or the Treasury about an exception, and
you should do it before you run into
trouble, not after. An exception
requested in advance is paperwork. An
exception requested after a missed
payment is a crisis with a waiting
period. But for most people watching
this video, the smart move is simply to
make sure you are set up for electronic
payment, and to make sure it is set up
correctly, because that is where I see
the real problems. Let me describe a
situation that is easy to picture,
because it is happening all over the
country right now. A A woman I will call
Alice, 76, has had her Social Security
deposited into the same small local bank
for over 20 years. Same branch, same
tellers who know her by name, same
account. She has never touched the setup
because it has always worked, and in
retirement, things that work are things
you leave alone. Then, last year, her
bank was bought by a larger bank. The
sign on the building changed. Letters
arrived with new account numbers, new
routing details, and in some cases, old
accounts were closed and reopened under
entirely new numbers. Alice filed the
letters somewhere because that is what
careful people do with bank letters.
But, it never occurred to her that
Social Security was holding a copy of
her old details and that those details
might no longer point to an open
account. She assumed everything
transferred. And mostly, in a bank
merger, things do transfer. But, not
always and not automatically, and the
moment they do not, her payment has
nowhere to land. And here is the part
that makes this genuinely new. In the
old days, if a direct deposit failed, a
paper check would eventually be printed
and mailed as a fallback. As paper
checks go away, that safety net goes
away with them. This is not a story
about carelessness.
It is a story about a perfectly
reasonable assumption meeting a changed
system. So, the first thing I want you
to do this week is check. Sign in to
your online Social Security account or
visit your local office or call the
agency directly and confirm that the
bank information on file matches the
account you are actually using today.
Not an account you used to have. Not an
account from a bank that has since
merged or changed its name. The account
that is open and active right now. If
you do not have a bank account at all,
ask Social Security what options are
currently available to you. There have
been prepaid card options for people
without a bank account, and there are
also low-cost bank accounts specifically
designed for people who want to receive
federal benefits electronically.
Because these programs have been
changing, ask for the current choices
instead of relying on what a friend told
you last year, and write down whatever
they tell you along with the date you
were
>> on what a friend told you last year, and
write down whatever they tell you, along
with the date you were told. And one
more habit that costs you nothing.
From now on, when your bank merges,
changes its name, or sends you a letter
about new account numbers, treat that
letter as a social security matter, too.
Update your direct deposit information
with the agency as soon as the new
details are official. A 5-minute update
today can prevent a very stressful
morning 6 months from now.
Alice eventually got her payment sorted.
It took 3 weeks, two office visits, and
a string of mornings spent refreshing a
screen that had nothing in it. 3 weeks
is survivable when you have savings
behind you. It is something else
entirely when that deposit is the month.
Change number two. Your bank information
is now a target, and the way changes get
processed matters more than ever. Here
is the reality of electronic systems.
They move fast. That is good news when
you are the one fixing a mistake,
because an update to your direct deposit
can go through quicker than it used to.
But, that speed works in both
directions.
If a criminal manages to change your
direct deposit information, that change
can move just as quickly, and the first
sign of it may be a payment that never
arrives. That is why protecting your
banking details has become one of the
most important things you can do for
your benefits. So, let us start with the
rule that has not changed and never
will. Social Security does not call you
out of the blue and ask you to confirm
your bank account number. It does not
text you a link and tell you to verify
your payment. It does not email you
asking for a code.
And it does not threaten to stop your
benefits unless you act in the next 24
hours. If someone contacts you and does
any of those things, that is not how the
agency operates. Investigators who track
this kind of fraud describe the same
pattern again and again, and once you
have heard it laid out, you will
recognize it for the rest of your life.
First, the caller or message claims to
be from Social Security, the Treasury,
or some other government office. The
caller ID may even say so, because phone
numbers can be faked. of your identity.
Third, they add pressure. You must act
within a day or by the end of the call,
or you will lose your payment entirely.
And fourth, only after you are worried
and rushing, they make the real request.
They want your account number, your
social security number, or a one-time
code that was just sent to your phone.
Let me tell you about that code, because
it is the most dangerous item on the
entire list. A one-time code is meant to
prove that you are the person trying to
sign into your own account. It is the
system asking, is this really you? If a
stranger calls you, triggers that code,
and then reads it back to you and asks
you to confirm it, they are not
confirming anything. They are handing
you the key to your own house and asking
you to hold the door. If you read that
code to them, you are not verifying your
identity. You are verifying theirs. So,
if you ever get a call or message like
this, here is exactly what to say. I do
not confirm account information over an
incoming call. I will contact you using
a number I already have. Then hang up.
Do not call back any number the caller
gave you, because the person on the
other end of that callback is the same
person who called you. Find the official
contact information yourself, either on
the Social Security Administration's own
website, typed in by hand, or on a paper
letter you already received in the mail,
and contact the agency that way. A real
agency will never punish you for being
careful. Now, let me give you a few
habits that make you much harder to
fool, and none of them require a
computer. First, know your payment date.
Social Security pays most beneficiaries
on a Wednesday, and which Wednesday
depends on the day of the month you were
born. If your birthday falls between the
1st and the 10th of the month, your
payment usually arrives on the second
Wednesday. If it falls between the 11th
and the 20th, it usually arrives on the
third Wednesday.
And if it falls between the 21st and the
end of the month, it usually arrives on
the fourth Wednesday. Some people who
who receiving benefits a long time ago,
before the schedule changed, are still
paid on the 3rd of the month instead.
Write your date down. Put it on the
refrigerator. Because knowing it cold
lets you tell the difference between a
normal delay and a real problem, and
that difference matters. Second, if a
deposit is a little late, do not panic.
Banking systems have hiccups. Payments
occasionally post a day or two behind
schedule for reasons that have nothing
to do with you. Give it a few business
days before you assume something is
wrong. Panic is exactly what scammers
are counting on. The moment you feel
rushed is precisely the moment to slow
down, because urgency is their product.
They cannot steal from a calm person.
Third, look at your bank statement every
single month. Not a glance, a look.
Make sure your deposit is arriving from
the right source, in the right amount,
on the right day.
If anything is off, you will notice it
within days instead of months, and every
day of early notice matters. And fourth,
build a simple safety agreement with
someone you trust. Tell a spouse, an
adult child, or a close friend which
bank your payment goes to, and agree on
one rule. If either of you ever gets a
call claiming to be from Social
Security, you check with each other
before doing anything. That one
agreement shuts down the most common
version of this scam completely, because
scammers rely on you being alone, under
pressure, with nobody to ask.
A target with a phone-a-friend is a much
harder target.
Now, real quick, before we get to change
number three, because this is the one I
teased at the start of the video, and it
is the one that catches completely
careful people. If this video has
already given you something useful, do
me one small favor. Tap the like button
so it reaches more people who depend on
this monthly deposit, and share it with
someone in your family or your
neighborhood. Somebody you know is going
to get one of those phone calls this
month, and a 2-minute video watched in
advance can be the difference between
hanging up and losing a payment. All
right, back to it.
Change number three.
There is now a stronger lock on the
front door of your online account. This
is the one almost nobody is talking
about, and it is the reason I made this
video. For years getting into your
online Social Security account meant
typing in a username and password that
you may have created a very long time
ago, probably on a deadline, probably
with a piece of paper you have since
lost. That was the old door. Social
Security has been moving away from that
system and today signing in is built
around identity verification through
approved government providers,
specifically login.gov and id.me. If you
set up your account years ago and never
updated how you sign in, your old
username and password may no longer work
the way you remember and the path back
in now runs through identity
verification. I want to be very clear
about something before I go further
because this part can cause needless
fear. Your payment itself does not
depend on any of this. Your benefit
arrives every month whether or not you
have ever touched an online account in

the door first. But think carefully

late, a deposit looks wrong, a letter

you want to see your own record. Every
hour matters on a day like that. And
that is the worst possible day to

that you now have to go through identity
verification for the first time in a
hurry while you are stressed, possibly
without the documents the process asks
for.
Let me paint that picture for a second
because it happens more than you would
think. A man I will call Raymond, 71,
has had an online Social Security
account since the office first
encouraged them, maybe a decade ago.
Username and password written in a
notebook, which is fine. That is what

Last month his deposit was late by two
days, not missing, just late, but he did
not know that yet. So he went to sign in

on file was a landline and the notebook

So, there he sat on the one morning he

That is the trap. Not the system itself,

wrong day. So, do it now while nothing
is wrong. Go to the official Social
Security website and choose to sign in
with login.gov or id.me. Type the web
address yourself or use a bookmark you
made earlier.
Do not click a link in a text message or
an email because fake sites that imitate
the real thing are common and they are
very good. Have your driver's license or

email. The process usually takes about
15 minutes. And in some cases, you may
be asked to take a photo of your
identification or complete a short video
check. It feels a little strange the
first time and that is normal. Once it
is done, you are set and the door opens
for you every time. When you create the
account, do three things. Use a strong
password that you do not use anywhere
else, and I mean anywhere else, because
a password reused is a password half
given away. Turn on the extra sign-in

it is offered, because that one setting

break-in attempts.
And save your backup code somewhere
safe, like a paper folder at home, not

because it is worth its own line. No

Security or anywhere else, will ever ask

this online feels like too much, I want
you to hear this clearly. You do not

sign-in. There is one more benefit to
