Owen is in trouble. This level is
measured in your essentials, not in your
income. A bigger lifestyle does not just
cost money. It moves the finish line.
Priya needs $19,200
for 6 months of safety. Owen needs
$33,000 for the same 6 months. same
protection, 72% more cash required
because his life costs more to keep
running. Owen reaches that $33,000 close
to year 13. The common mistake here goes
the other way. Somebody reads that
investments earn 7% and cash earns
almost nothing and decides the cushion
is a waste. It is insurance. The premium
is the gap between 7% and 1% on a few
thousand. and what it buys is never
having to sell your investments in the
month everyone else is selling too.
Level three, six months up to two years
of spending. For Priya, $19,200
The shock here is not an emergency at
all. It is a decision. A boss you cannot
stand, a job that is slowly wearing you
down, a better opportunity that pays
less at first, a career you want to
leave. The first two levels protect you
from things that happen to you. This is
the first level that gives you things to
do. With a year or two of spending
banked, you can walk away from a bad
situation, retrain, or take a role with
a 20% pay cut because it leads
somewhere. You can negotiate like a
person who is allowed to hear no. Priya
crosses $96,000 at month 57, a little
under 5 years. And this is where the
scoreboard gets interesting. Year 1,
Priya has $19,598.
Owen has $2,815.
Year three, Priya has $58,567.
Owen has $7,718.
Year five, Priya has $103,323.
Owen has $12,720.
Priya has passed level three. Owen is
still in the early part of level two. He
earns more than she does. He works as
hard and by every visible measure, he
looks like the one who is winning. That
brings me to the lever I promised you.
It is not your returns and it is not
your income. It is how much your
spending creeps upward as your income
grows. Here is what it does. Suppose
Priya gets a raise and upgrades her life
by just $500 a month. A better
apartment, a nicer car, nothing crazy.
Her spending goes to $4,500 a month,
which does two things at once. It raises
every finish line. The level three line
now sits at $18,000,
Level 6 moves from 1.2 million to 1.35
million to $150,000
further away because you now have a
bigger life to fund and it slows the
climb. She saves $1,000 a month instead
of $1,500. The $108,000 line arrives in
about 7.4 years instead of $4.8. Level 6
arrives in about $32.5 years instead of
25.7. A $500 a month upgrade pushes the
finish line back almost 7 years. That is
the crulest part of the system. Every
level is measured against your spending.
So when spending grows, the line you are
racing toward moves away from you. Level
four, 2 years up to 10 years of
spending. For Priya, $96,000 to
This is the level where the shock
changes from a personal one to a market
one. The shock is a crash. And this
level matters more than any other
because it is where something flips.
Look at the math. Priya saves $18,000 a
year. At $96,000,
7% growth is $6,720
a year. Her savings are still doing most
of the work, but at about $258,000,
7% growth is $18,000,
the same as her savings. That moment
arrives around month 124, a little past
year 10. After that, her money out earns
her effort. In a normal year, the
portfolio does more than she does. That
is the switch. Before it, you are the
engine. After it, you become a passenger
who still has to keep paying for the
fuel. But here is the trap, and I want
to be careful because it is the most
emotional trap in the whole video. A 7%
average does not arrive as a smooth 7%.
Imagine a $300,000 portfolio and a 35%
crash. That is $105,000
gone. On paper, that is about two years
and two months of Priya's entire
spending, vanishing in a handful of
months. Does that ruin her? If she is
still working, no, she does not need
that money this year. She keeps buying
and everything she buys is on sale. The
crash hurts her pride and her pride is
the real danger. What destroys people at
this level is not the drop, it is
selling during it. That is why level two
never goes away. The cash cushion she
built by month 12 is still there quietly
doing its job in the background. It
means she never has to sell a share in
the bad year. That is the whole reason
the boring step comes first. So the
worry at level four changes again. It is
no longer do I have enough? It becomes
do I have the nerve. The danger moves
from your bank balance into your
behavior. And the mistake that catches
people here is the opposite of panic.
The portfolio has had a great few years.
They look at the number and they decide
the market has this handled. They ease
off the contributions. Then a flat
decade arrives and they realize the only
reliable part of the machine was them.
Level four takes Priya from year 4.8 to
year 15.7 11 years. Level 5 10 up to 25
years of spending. For Priya, $480,000
to $1.2 million. The shock at this level
is time itself. Not a bill, not a job,
not a crash. The question is whether the
money lasts longer than you can work.
Here is the new feeling. At the start of
this level, 4% of $480,000
a year. Only 40% of Priya's spending. By
4% is $30,000. About 62% of what she
spends. Work stops being a necessity and
starts being a decision. She could scale
back. She could take a lower paying job
she likes. She could stop in a few years
if she wanted to. And this is where
something odd happens. The worry gets
quieter, but the swings get louder
because the numbers are bigger. A 30%
drop on $750,000
Nearly 5 years of Priya's entire
spending. The percentage is the same.
The feeling is not. This is also the
level where the order of your returns
starts to matter. and it is the least
understood idea in all of retirement.
Say Priya stopped working at $750,000
and withdrew $30,000 a year. If the
market fell 30% in her first year, her
balance becomes $525,000
before she takes anything out and
after the first withdrawal. Now, that
same $30,000 is a 6% withdrawal, not 4%.
A bad year early costs far more than a
bad year late because you are drawing
the portfolio down while it is low. The
fix is boring and it is the same boring
fix as level two. Keep one to two years
of spending in cash so you can spend
from the cushion while stocks recover
instead of selling at the bottom. People
who do this are not smarter. They are
insured. Level five takes Priya from
year 15.7 to year 25.7.
Another 10 years. Level six, 25 times
your spending and beyond. For Priya,
$1.2 million. The reasoning is simple.
If you can safely withdraw about 4% a
year, then your spending multiplied by
25 is the amount that covers it. Priya
spends $48,000 a year, 25 times that is
At 4%, that is exactly $48,000. Her
portfolio can pay for her entire life
with no paycheck. She crosses it at
month 308, a little under 26 years. Now,
I want to be honest about what level six
is and is not because this is where
people get the wrong idea. The first
thing it is not is a guarantee. The 4%
figure comes from historical US data. It
is a guideline, not a law. A long period
of poor returns, high inflation, or a
long retirement can all stretch it. Good
planners treat it as a starting point
and stay flexible, spending a little
less in a bad year. The second thing it
is not is the end of worry. This is the
part nobody puts on the thumbnail. At
level six, the worry changes shape
again. It stops being about whether the
money survives and starts being about
what it is for. Taxes, health care
before the age when public coverage
starts, leaving something behind,
deciding what you actually want to do
with Monday morning. These are better
problems and they are still problems.
And the third thing it is not is a
number you can compare across people.
Remember Owen? If he somehow reached
$1.2 million but still spent $8,000 a
month, he would need $2.4 million. His
finish line is twice as far because his
life is twice as expensive. Same
portfolio, completely different level.
That is why I measure everything in your
spending and not in dollars. The people
who feel free at this level are almost
always the ones who decided what enough
meant. Not a number someone handed them,
a number they chose based on a life they
wanted, the ones who keep moving the
finish line to 2 million. Then three,
never get to feel it. Here are the six
levels again in plain language. Level
one, under one month of essentials, a
bill can hurt you. Level two, 1 to 6
months, a layoff can hurt you less.
Level three, 6 months to two years. You
can say no. Level four, 2 to 10 years. A
crash cannot force you to act. Level
five, 10 to 25 years. Work is a choice.
Level six, 25 years or more. The
question becomes what the money is for.
Priya got through the first three levels
in 4.8 years, holding about 8% of the
dollars she will eventually need. The
other three levels took the remaining 21
years to build the other 92%. Here is
what that means, and I think it is the
most useful thing in this video. The
biggest drop in worry per dollar and per
year happens in the first three levels.
Those are the cheapest, shortest, least
glamorous stretch of the whole climb.
They are also the ones people skip
because a $1,000 buffer feels too small
to bother with, while the exciting part,
the investing, is waiting up ahead. If
you do one thing after this video, do
this. Find your level honestly. One,
work out your essentials. Rent or
mortgage, utilities, food, insurance,
transport, minimum debt payments, the
things that keep going if your income
stops. Write down the monthly total.
Two, work out what you actually spend in
a normal month, everything included.
Three, multiply. Your level one line is
one month of essentials. Level two is
six times your essentials. Level three
is 24 times your monthly spending. Level
four is 120 times. Level five is 300
times. Four. Add up your cash and
investments. Leave the house out. Five.
See where you land and look only one
level ahead. The next one is the only
one that matters. If you are in level
one, the next move is $1,000 in cash and
the next full month of essentials.
Ignore everything else for now. If you
are in level two, finish the 6 months,
then invest. If you are in level three
or four, protect your savings rate
because that is the lever that moves
every line and watch your spending like
the finish line is attached to it
because it is. If you are in level five
or six, keep a cushion so you never have
to sell in a crash and decide what
enough looks like. A few honest limits
because this does not describe everyone.
Priya and Owen are simplified. Real
incomes rise and fall. Real returns
arrive in lumps and nobody saves exactly
the same amount for 25 years. The 7% is
an average. Some decades will be far
worse and a long bad stretch early on
would push every level back. Cash
earning 1% is also an assumption. Rates
change. I left out the house. Debts
other than the card, children, health
costs, and any pension or social
security income, which can shrink the
level six number a great deal. A person
with a pension covering half their
spending needs far less than 25 times.
And the levels are a way of looking at
risk, not laws of nature. Your own
boundaries will sit somewhere different.
And that is fine. This is education, not
personal advice. Your numbers are yours,
and those are the inputs that decide it.
So, go back to that Tuesday and the $600
text. Priya did not pay it calmly
because she was rich. She had $1,500.
She paid it calmly because the shock was
smaller than the cushion. That is the
whole mechanism. Worry is not a feeling
about your balance. It is a feeling
about the gap between the biggest thing
that could go wrong and the cushion you
have against it. Owen's income was
higher. His cushion was smaller. So, the
same $600 landed on a different person.
You do not need level six to stop
worrying. You need to get ahead of the
next shock and then the next one level
at a time. The cheapest ones come first.
If this changed how you see your own
number, tell me in the comments which
level you are on and what the next shock
on your list is. I read them. And if you
want more of the math behind the money
decisions nobody explains properly,
subscribe to Mark Invests. I will see
you in the next

title: What a Study of 5 Million Retirees Found About Spending

segments.text: What if I told you the biggest
retirement number you've been chasing
might be completely wrong? A massive JP
Morgan study looked at the real spending
habits of more than 5 million retirees,
and they discovered something shocking.
Most retirees do not spend more and more
money every year. In fact, spending
often declines significantly as we get
older. The study showed that retirement
spending actually follows a hill-like
curve, peaking early and then dropping.
It starts with your active go-go years,
where you travel, explore, and check off
your bucket list. Then your slow-go
years, when you naturally slow down and
spend less on activities. And eventually
your no-go years, where you stay close
to home and expenses drop even further.
Watch the full video before you spend
another year chasing the wrong
retirement number.

title: NEVER DOWNSIZE YOUR HOME IN RETIREMENT: Your Province Charges You $5,000 for Moving

segments.text: Never downsize your home in retirement.
Your province charges you $5,000
for moving. Hello friends. The title of
this video isn't clickbait. Downsizing
is sold to retirees as the smart move.
Sell the big house, buy something
smaller, unlock your equity, and live
comfortably on the difference. Sometimes
that's exactly how it works out. But
very often, by the time the land
transfer tax, the real estate
commission, the lawyers, and the movers
have all been paid, a lot of that equity
is gone. And then there are the costs
nobody mentions until later. Condo fees,
special assessments, and a quiet hit to
your government benefits that can follow
you every year. Good, careful people
lose a small fortune this way. Not
because they're foolish, but because
nobody shows them the whole bill before
they sign. Now, let me be straight with
you right away, because I will never lie
to you. You may have seen a British
video saying the tax office charges
retirees thousands just for moving. In
Canada, the CRA generally doesn't take a
cut when you sell your home. If it's
been your principal residence every year
you've owned it, the gain is usually
tax-free. The $5,000 in our title comes
from your province, not the CRA. It's
the land transfer tax you pay when you
buy your next home. And when I say
never, I mean this. Never downsize on a
hunch, and never without adding up every

70. It grows by 0.6%
for every month you wait, up to 36%
more. When your January OAS arrives,
check that it rose. If you're 75 or
older and receive a full OAS pension,
check that you're getting the higher
amount. And if you're having OAS clawed
back, but your income has dropped, ask
your tax preparer about filing form
OAS. Benefit number three, the
guaranteed income supplement. If your
income is low, the GIS is the most
valuable benefit on this list. It's
tax-free and for October to December, a
single senior can receive up to 1,000
a month. Like OAS, it's adjusted for
inflation every January, April, July,
and October. Remember what counts as
income for the GIS. Your OAS itself
doesn't, but your CPP, workplace
pensions, RRIF withdrawals, and interest
do. If you work part-time, the first
$5,000 of earnings and half of the next
10,000 aren't counted. But here's what
January is really a reminder of. The GIS
is renewed each July based on your tax
return, which means you must file your
tax return by April 30th every year,
even if you have no income to report.
Skip it and your GIS can stop. If your
income dropped this year because you
retired or a pension was reduced or
stopped, Service Canada can set your GIS
based on an estimate of this year's
income instead of last year's. And if
you and your spouse now live apart for
reasons beyond your control, most often
because one of you moved into long-term
care, ask about form ISP-3040.
Your GIS may be calculated at the single
rate, which can mean hundreds of dollars
more each month. Call Service Canada at
and ask, "Am I receiving the GIS? If
not, do I qualify? And has anything
changed in my income or living situation
that I should report?"
Then, mark April 30th on your calendar.
That's your tax filing deadline.
Benefit number four, the Canada
Groceries and Essentials Benefit. This
is the new name for what used to be the
GST/HST
Credit. It changed names in July and it
was increased by 25% for 5 years.
It's tax-free, it's paid four times a
year, and the next payment is on January
5th. For the July 2026 to June 2027
benefit year, a single person can
receive up to $679
and a couple up to $890.
The exact amount depends on your family
income from your 2025 tax return.
The key thing to understand is that you
don't apply for it separately. You get
it by filing your tax return. And when
you file your 2026 return this spring,
that return will decide your payments
from July 2027 to June 2028.
Many provincial credits are paid along
with it, too.
Two details catch couples out. The
benefit is paid to only one spouse. So,
if you're married, check both of your
accounts before assuming it's missing.
And if your marital status changed in
2026, you were widowed, separated, or
you have a new partner, tell the CRA
because it changes the calculation. When
January 5th comes, check that the
payment arrived. If it didn't and you
expected it, sign in to your CRA account
or call the CRA's benefits line at
And if you didn't file a tax return for
2025, file it now. Late is far better
than never.
Benefit number five, your provincial
seniors top-up. This is the one I told
you to stay for. Most provinces have
their own benefit for low-income seniors
on top of the federal GIS. In Ontario,
it's called GAINS, the Guaranteed Annual
Income System. For the 2025 benefit
year, it was worth up to $90 a month for
a single senior with very low private
income, paid monthly and based on the
same information used for your federal
OAS and GIS. The full amount goes to
people with very little income beyond
OAS and the GIS. But smaller amounts can
be paid at somewhat higher incomes.
British Columbia has the Seniors
Supplement. Alberta has the Alberta
Seniors Benefit. And Saskatchewan has
the Seniors Income Plan. Other provinces
have their own programs, too.
Here's the catch. In some provinces, the
top-up is assessed automatically when
you receive the GIS. In others, you have
to apply separately. And many people who
qualify never do.
On top of that, Ontario homeowners 64
and older with low to moderate incomes
may be able to get the Ontario Senior
Homeowners Property Tax Grant worth up
to $500 a year by claiming it on their
tax return. And many Ontario seniors
also receive the Ontario Trillium
Benefit, which is usually paid monthly.
Again, only if you file your taxes.
Search for your province's name plus
seniors benefit or call your provincial
information line and ask, "I receive the
GIS. Is there a provincial top-up for
seniors? Do I receive it and do I need
to apply?"
In Ontario, make sure your tax preparer
claims the senior homeowners property
tax grant and the Trillium benefit if
you qualify.
Benefit number six, your new TFSA room
on January 1st. Every January, Canadians
18 and older who live in Canada get new
tax-free savings account room. The 2027
amount is announced in November and it's
expected to be at least $7,000.
And there's no upper age limit. You can
keep contributing in your 70s, 80s, and
90s. Why does this matter so much for
seniors? Because money inside a TFSA
grows tax-free and withdrawals aren't
counted as income. They don't reduce
your GIS. They don't trigger the OAS
clawback. And interest earned inside a
TFSA doesn't count either, unlike
interest in an ordinary savings account,
which can quietly reduce your GIS. Plus,
anything you withdrew from your TFSA
during 2026 is added back to your room
on January 1st. Two cautions. The room
figure in your CRA account is based on
information reported at the start of the
year. So, it may not include your most
recent deposits or withdrawals. Keep
your own record, too. And don't over
contribute. The penalty is 1% a month on
the excess. Ask your bank in January,
"How much TFSA room do I have for 2027?"
Or check it in your CRA account. If you
have savings sitting in an ordinary
account earning very little, ask whether
a TFSA savings account or a GIC inside a
TFSA at your own bank would make sense.
Do it yourself at your own bank, never
because someone called you about moving
your money.
Benefit number seven, the Canada Dental
Care Plan. For many seniors, this has
been one of the most valuable new
benefits in years. It's for Canadians
without access to private dental
insurance whose adjusted family net
income is under $90,000.
Below $70,000, there's no co-payment for
covered services. Between 70 and 90,000,
you pay a share of the cost. The plan
covers a wide range of care. Checkups
and cleanings, x-rays, fillings, root
canals, extractions, and dentures among
them. Though some services may need
approval in advance. Here's what to
check. Coverage runs in benefit years
and members need to renew. For the 2026
to 2027 year, the renewal window ran
from April 15th to June 1st and renewing
required having filed your 2025 taxes.
If you missed the renewal, your coverage
may have ended on June 30th. If you're
part of a couple, each of you has your
own coverage. So, check for both of you.
And always ask your dentist before
treatment whether a service is covered
and whether there's any extra charge
above what the plan pays. If you're not
sure whether you're covered, call the
Canada Dental Care Plan at
or check your My Service Canada account
and ask, "Am I covered right now? And
when do I need to renew?" Before any big
dental work, ask your dentist for a
written estimate showing what the plan
covers. And one bonus for February, your
tax slips start arriving. The T4A(P) for
your CPP, the T4A(OAS)
for your Old Age Security, slips from
your RRIF and your bank, and others.
Keep them together in one envelope. If
one is missing, you can usually find it
in your CRA account once it's been
issued or ask the payer for a copy. A
complete set of slips is the easiest way
to file on time and avoid a review
later. A quick warning, because January
is a favorite month for benefit scams.
You may get texts or emails saying your
January benefit increase is ready. Click
here to claim or confirm your banking
information to receive your new payment.
Those are scams. Increases to CPP, OAS,
and the GIS happen automatically. You
never have to click anything to get
them. Service Canada says the Canada
Dental Care Plan contacts seniors by
mail, not by text or email. And no
government agency will ever ask for a
fee, a gift card, or cryptocurrency to
release a benefit. Never share the
password or sign-in codes for your CRA
or My Service Canada account with anyone
who contacts you. If in doubt, hang up
and call the official number from
Canada.ca yourself. If you've already
given something away, call your bank,
your local police, and the Canadian
Anti-Fraud Centre at 1-888-495-8501.
Let me make this real with a quick
story. Picture a woman, call her
Bernice, 71, a widow in Sudbury. She
owns a small bungalow and she lives on
CPP, OAS, the GIS, and a tiny pension
from her years at a credit union. Last
January, her granddaughter sat down with
her for what they called the money
check. First, they compared her January
deposits with December's. CPP and OAS
both went up as they should. Then they
looked at Bernice's last tax return and
found two things missing. Bernice had
never claimed the Ontario Senior
Homeowners Property Tax Grant, even
though she'd paid property tax on her
bungalow for years. And her game stop up
from the province was smaller than they
expected because she'd forgotten to tell
Service Canada that her late husband's
small pension had stopped. One phone
call and her income was updated. Next,
they called the Canada Dental Care Plan.
Bernice hadn't been to a dentist in four
years because she was afraid of the
cost. She qualified with no co-payment.
By spring, she had new partial dentures
covered by the plan after her dentist
confirmed the costs in writing. "I'd
stopped smiling in photos," she told her
granddaughter. "I didn't even realize
how much it bothered me until it was
fixed." Finally, they looked at her
savings. Bernice had about $20,000
sitting in an ordinary savings account
at her bank, earning almost nothing. And
every dollar of interest it did earn
counted against her GIS. She had never
opened a TFSA in her life, so she had
plenty of room. That afternoon, at her
own branch, she moved the money into a
TFSA savings account. Same bank, same
teller she'd known for years, but now
the interest doesn't touch her GIS. Same
Bernice, same bungalow. One January
afternoon with her granddaughter and
several hundred dollars a year back in
her pocket, plus a smile she hadn't
shown in years. Be a Bernice. And if you
can, be the granddaughter for someone
you love. Let me answer the questions I
know you're thinking. Do I need to apply
for the January CPP and OAS increases?
No, they're automatic. You only need to
check that they arrived. When will we
know the exact January increase? The CPP
figure depends on inflation up to
October, so it's known in late fall. The
January OAS and GIS amounts are
announced in December. I have no income.
Do I really need to file a tax return?
Yes. The GIS, the groceries and
essentials benefit, provincial credits,
and the dental plan all depend on it.
File by April 30th. How much is the
groceries and essentials benefit? For
July 2026 to June 2027, up to $679
for a single person and 890 for a
couple, based on income. It's paid
quarterly, including on January 5th.
Does my province have a seniors top-up?
Most do, like GAINS in Ontario, the
Seniors Supplement in BC, the Alberta
Seniors Benefit, and Saskatchewan
Seniors Income Plan. Some are automatic,
and some require an application. Can I
still contribute to a TFSA at my age?
Yes, there's no upper age limit, and new
room arrives every January 1st. Will
TFSA interest reduce my GIS? No,
interest and withdrawals inside a TFSA
don't count as income for the GIS or the
OAS clawback. Am I eligible for the
Canada Dental Care Plan? If you don't
have access to private dental insurance,
and your adjusted family net income is
you may be. Remember to renew each year.
What if my January payment didn't go up?
Call Service Canada at 1-800-277-9914.
Have your social insurance number and
your bank statement ready. A text says I
need to confirm my banking details for
my January increase. Is it real? No,
it's a scam. Increases are automatic,
and you never need to click a link to
receive them.
Let's bring it all together. Seven
benefits to check for January 2027. One,
your CPP raise, automatic in your late
January deposit. Two, your OAS
adjustment, the 75-plus increase, and
form T1213 OAS if your clawback is too
high. Three, the GIS. File your taxes by
April 30th, report income drops, and ask
about the living apart rule. Four, the
Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit,
paid January 5th, and only if you file.
Five, your provincial top-up, which may
need its own application, plus Ontario's
Homeowner Grant and Trillium Benefit.
Six, your new TFSA room on January 1st,
where interest doesn't count against
your GIS. And seven, the Canada Dental
Care Plan. Check your coverage and renew
on time. Because here's the heart of it,
friends. The benefit system in Canada is
more generous than most people realize,
but it runs on paperwork, deadlines, and
the assumption that you'll check. Nobody
will phone you in January to say a
payment is missing. So, make it a
tradition. One afternoon, early in the
new year, a cup of coffee, your bank
statement, and a phone. It may be the
most profitable hour of your entire
year. Put a note on your fridge with
seven words: CPP, OAS, GIS, groceries,
provincial, TFSA, dental. Check them off
one by one. One honest note. This is
general information to help you
understand what's available. It is not
legal, financial, or tax advice. Benefit
amounts change regularly. Provincial
programs differ, and whether you qualify
depends on your income, your residence,
your marital status, and your own
situation. So, always confirm the
specifics for your own case with Service
Canada, the Canada Revenue Agency, your
provincial government, or the official
canada.ca website before you act on
anything here. If this helped you,
subscribe because I explain the rules
nobody else spells out for Canadian
seniors in plain English before they
cost you. And please, do one thing for
me. Share this with one senior who lives
alone and might not have anyone to help
with the money check. That one
conversation could be worth hundreds of
dollars a year to them. Take care of
yourself. Watch out for your money, and
I'll see you in the next one.

title: The CRA Is Watching: Avoid These 5 Red Flags Or You'll Be Investigated

segments.text: Hello friends. The title of this video
isn't clickbait. The CRA really is
watching and it sees far more of your
financial life than most people realize.
Before you ever sit down to file your
tax return, the CRA already has a copy
of almost every slip with your name on
it. Your Canada pension plan, your old
age security, your RRIF withdrawals, the
interest from your bank. Its computers
compare what you report with what it
already knows. When the two don't match,
or when you stop filing, stop answering,
or claim something you can't back up,
your file gets flagged. For most of us,
that doesn't mean a dramatic
investigation. It means a reassessment,
a bill with interest, a benefit that
stops, or a guaranteed income supplement
you're asked to pay back. On a fixed
income, any one of those can upend a
whole year. Now, let me be straight with
you right away because I will never lie
to you. The CRA is not reading your
Facebook page to see where you went on
holiday. Nobody is going to knock on
your door because you cashed in a GIC.
The frightening version with
investigators and courtrooms is about
deliberate fraud, and that is not the
people who watch this channel. Most
letters the CRA sends to seniors aren't
investigations at all. They're requests.
Send us this receipt. explain this slip.
Confirm this amount. But here is what is
true. Those letters are real. The
computer matching behind them is real.
And the mistakes that set them off are
small, ordinary, and almost always
avoidable. A missing slip, a credit
claimed on the wrong kind of income, a
tax return never filed because I don't
owe anything anyway, a letter left
unopened on the kitchen counter. Those
are the things that turn into money
taken back from you. So, today, the five
red flags that most often get a senior's
file a second look, what each one costs
you, and exactly what to say on the
phone or at the bank to clear it up.
Stay with me to the end because number
five is the one that catches people who
think their paperwork is perfect, and it
has nothing to do with money you earned.
Let's get into it. Let me tell you why
this matters so much for people like us.
When you're working, a tax mistake is an
annoyance. When you're retired, it's
something else. Your income is fixed and
you can't pick up a few extra shifts to
cover a surprise bill. Your guaranteed
income supplement, your old age security
clawback, the new grocery benefit, and
in some provinces, even your drug
coverage all depend on what's on your
tax return. So, one error doesn't cost
you once. It can ripple through every
benefit you receive for a whole year.
And if it's found later, you can be
asked to repay it all at once with
interest out of the same pension you
live on. And before we go on, do one
quick thing for me. Subscribe to this
channel. I'm not asking just to ask.
These rules are complicated. They change
every year. And nobody at the CRA is
going to phone you to say a slip is
missing before the reassessment arrives.
The people who are subscribed hear about
it while there's still time to fix it.
Hit subscribe, tap the bell, and let me
keep watch over your money with you. All
right, the first red flag. A quick word
before we go on. There are more of these
rules, slips, and quiet traps than I
could ever fit into one video. The
things the CRA and Service Canada never
bother to spell out. I gathered the
whole of it in plain English into one
handbook at waltercanada.com.
The video is the short version. The
handbook is the whole of it. If you want
it, it's there. I won't bring it up
again. Red flag number one. Income on
your return that doesn't match the slips
the CRA already has. Here's how it
works. Every organization that pays you
sends a slip to you and a copy to the
CRA. Service Canada sends one for your
CPP and one for your old age security.
Your bank sends slips for your RRIF
withdrawals, your interest, and your
investment income. A small pension from
an old employer comes with its own slip,
too. The CRA puts all of those together
and compares the total with what you put
on your return. Seniors rarely get
caught on this because they're hiding
anything. They get caught because they
have more slips than they used to,
scattered across more places. A Rif at
one bank, a GIC at another, a small
account a spouse opened years ago. One
slip goes to an old address or gets
thrown out with the flyers. The return
goes in without it. Months later, the
computer notices. What does it cost you?
First, the CRA adds the missing income
and reassesses you with interest on the
extra tax. That's the small part. The
bigger part is what the extra income
does to your benefits. Your guaranteed
income supplement is reduced by about 50
cents for every dollar of income. So a
forgotten slip for $2,000 of RNR income
isn't just a little more tax. It can
mean roughly $1,000 less GIS for that
benefit year. And if it's already been
paid, you may be asked to give it back.
At the other end, every dollar above the
clawback threshold, which for the 2026
tax year is $95,323,
cost you 15 cents of old age security.
One thing that is not a red flag, money
you take out of your TFSA, TFSA
withdrawals are not income. They don't
go on your return and they don't reduce
your GIS. Some people report them anyway
out of caution and end up hurting
themselves. Don't. Before you file, make
sure you have a slip from every place
you hold money. At each bank or credit
union, say these words. Please tell me
every account I hold here that will
issue a tax slip for 2026 and confirm
the address you'll mail them to. If
someone prepares your taxes, say,
"Before you file, please compare my
slips with what the CRA has on file for
me so nothing is missing." And if you
realize you've already left something
off a past return, don't wait for the
letter. Call the CRA at the number on
the official canada.ca website and say,
"I left a slip off my return and I'd
like to correct it. Please tell me how."
Fixing it yourself always goes better
than being found. Red flag number two,
not filing at all. This is the one I
worry about most because the people it
hurts are the ones who can least afford
it. Many seniors with modest incomes
stop filing because they think there's
no point. I only get CPP and OAS. I
don't owe anything. Why bother? To them,
silence feels safe. To the system,
silence is a red flag. Not the kind that
brings an investigator, the kind that
quietly switches things off. Here's what
it costs you. Your guaranteed income
supplement runs on a benefit year from
July to June. And it's based on last
year's tax return. no return, nothing to
calculate it from, and your GIS can stop
from July. Then there's the Canada
Groceries and Essentials Benefit, which
replaced the GST credit this past July.
It's 25% larger than the old credit for
5 years. For July 2026 to June 2027,
that's up to about $950 for a single
person. It's paid in January, April,
July, and October. and it does not
reduce your GIS, but it only goes to
people who file. On average, people who
don't file lose about $2,212
a year in benefits they were entitled
to. You may have heard that automatic
tax filing is coming for people with low
incomes. That's true. It begins with the
2026 tax year, and at the start, it's
expected to reach about a million
people. That's a good thing, but it's
beginning with a limited group. And you
shouldn't assume you're in it. Unless
the CRA tells you in writing that you're
covered, file yourself. And if you do
owe money, filing late adds a penalty on
top of the interest. File your 2026
return on time this spring. Even if your
only income is CPP and OAS, if you've
missed past years, file those, too. You
can still catch up and some of what you
missed may come back to you. If paying
someone to do your taxes is a strain,
call 211. It's free and open around the
clock. Say, "I'm a senior on a low
income and I need a free tax clinic near
me. Can you tell me where the closest
one is?" There are volunteers across the
country who do simple returns for
seniors at no cost. Red flag number
three, claiming credits you don't
qualify for or can't back up. This is
where honest [clears throat] people get
caught because the rules behind the
senior credits aren't obvious, and some
well-meaning advice gets them wrong. The
CRA systems check your claims against
your slips and your income. When a claim
doesn't fit, it gets questioned. The
most common one is the pension income
amount, a credit on up to $2,000 of
eligible pension income. Plenty of
people assume their CPP and OAS count.
They don't. What does qualify once
you're 65 is income from a RRIF or a
pension from a former employer. So, a
retiree with nothing but CPP and OAS who
claims that credit will have it taken
back. And here's the flip side. If
you're over 65 drawing from an RRI and
you haven't been claiming it, you've
been leaving money on the table. The
second is the age amount. For 2026, it's
a credit on up to $9,28
for people 65 and older, but it shrinks
by 15 cents for every dollar of net
income above $46,432.
Claim the full amount when your income
is above that line, and the computer
will spot it. The third is anything that
needs a receipt, medical expenses,
charitable donations, and so on. You
usually don't send receipts with your
return, so people think nobody will ask,
but the CRA can ask, sometimes years
later. If you can't produce the receipt,
the claim is disallowed and you pay the
difference with interest. When your
return is being prepared, ask these
exact questions. Where is my pension
income amount coming from, my RRIF or my
CPP? Because CPP doesn't qualify. and
has my age amount been reduced for my
income. Then keep every receipt in one
envelope per tax year and keep those
envelopes for several years. If a letter
ever asks for proof, you'll open a
drawer instead of panicking. Red flag
number four, going quiet, a balance you
don't deal with, a letter you don't
answer, an address the CRA doesn't have.
This is the one that turns small
problems into big ones. Most CRA files
that get ugly don't get ugly because of
the first mistake. They get ugly because
of what happened next. Nobody answered
the letter. Nobody paid the bill. The
letter went to a house that was sold 3
years ago. Start with the bill because
it surprises a lot of retirees. No
income tax is taken off your CPP or your
old age security by default. Not a scent
unless you ask. So someone with CPP,
OAS, and RRIF can reach the spring owing
more than they expected. A balance that
sits unpaid gathers interest, and one
that keeps showing up year after year
draws more attention to your file. Then
there's the mail. If the CRA asks a
question and gets no answer by the date
it gives, it doesn't wait forever. It
makes a decision based on what it has.
And when it decides for you, it doesn't
decide in your favor. Then there's
direct deposit. And this year it matters
more than ever. Since January 5th, the
CRA no longer issues checks. A refund,
the grocery benefit, anything the CRA
owes you needs direct deposit set up
with the CRA itself. And here's the
trap. Your pension deposit doesn't
count. Your CPP and your OAS and GIS
arrive tomorrow, October 29th, in two
separate deposits. But those come
through Service Canada. The CRA is
separate. Plenty of seniors have direct
deposit with one and assume it covers
the other. It doesn't. Action in three
parts. First, call Service Canada at
and say, "I'd like income tax deducted
from my CPP and from my Old Age
Security. Please send me forms
ISP-352-CP
and ISP-352-as.
Those are two separate forms, one for
each benefit. Ask for both. Second, call
the CRA at the number on the official
canada.ca website and say, "Please
confirm the mailing address you have for
me and confirm whether I have direct
deposit set up with the CRA, not with
Service Canada." Third, if you owe money
you can't pay all at once, call before
it grows and say, "I owe a balance I
can't pay in full. I'd like to set up a
payment arrangement." The CRA is far
easier to deal with when you call it
than when it has to come looking for
you. And if a letter does arrive, open
it the same day. Note the date it gives.
Send exactly what it asks for. And keep
a copy of everything you send. If you
don't understand it, say so. I don't
understand this letter. Can you tell me
what you need from me? A calm, complete
answer closes most of these within
weeks. Silence keeps them open. Red flag
number five, the one I told you to stay
for. Your marital status and the life
behind it not matching what's on file.
This is the red flag that catches the
tidy people, the ones whose slips are
perfect and whose receipts are filed by
year. It has nothing to do with money
you earned. It's about who you live
with. Your guaranteed income supplement
is calculated on a couple's income if
you're part of one and on your own
income if you're single. And the amounts
are different. The grocery benefit for a
couple is paid to one spouse, not both.
What decides all of that is the status
on your file. When life changes and the
file doesn't, the system is paying you
as someone you no longer are. Here are
the three ways this goes wrong. A spouse
dies and the survivor, grieving and
overwhelmed, never updates anything. A
widow or widowerower meets someone. That
person moves in and nobody stops to ask
whether that changes their status. Or
the reverse, and this one costs people
money. A husband or wife moves into a
long-term care home and the spouse at
home is still treated as half of a
couple. The rules for what's called
involuntary separation can mean you're
each assessed as a single person. For a
low-income couple, that can mean

credit card step-by-step? Canadian
seniors. Hello friends. The title of
this video isn't clickbait. Today, I'm
going to walk you through exactly what
happens in Canada when a credit card
goes unpaid step-by-step.
The first missed payment, the interest,
the credit report, the collection calls,
the lawsuit, and what happens to that
debt when you die. Because a lot of

The video is the short version. The
handbook is the whole of it. If you want
it, it's there. I won't bring it up
again. Step one. The first missed
payment. The due date passes and you
haven't made at least the minimum.
Here's what happens. Interest keeps
running at your card's full rate. You
lose the interest-free grace period on
new purchases until the balance is paid
in full. Some cards add a fee, and your
bank will start sending reminders and
maybe calling. But here's something
important that most people don't know. A
payment that's only a few days late is
usually not reported to the credit
bureaus yet. Lenders typically report it
once it's about 30 days past due. So, if
you catch it quickly, you can often
limit the damage. If you've missed a
payment, pay at least the minimum as

polite call from a long-time customer

expect. And to stop it happening again,
think about setting up an automatic
minimum payment from your bank account.
So, a busy month or a stay in hospital
never turns into a missed payment. Step
two, 30 days late and it goes on your
record. Once a payment is about 30 days
past due, it's typically reported to
Equifax and TransUnion, Canada's two
credit bureaus. A late payment can drop
a credit score sharply, and information
about late or unpaid credit cards can
stay on your credit report for up to 6
years.
You might be thinking, "Walter, I'm 75.
I don't need credit anymore." But your
credit report can still matter. When you
rent an apartment, move into some
retirement residences, set up a phone
plan, or need a loan for a car or a home
repair.
And here's the next trap, the one that
makes a hard situation worse. Many
credit card agreements in Canada say
that if you miss your minimum payment
twice in a 12-month period, your
interest rate jumps, often to around 25%
and stays there for at least 6 months.
On a large balance, that's real money,
and it lands at exactly the moment you
can least afford it. Find your

company and ask, "What happens to my

And how long does it last?" Knowing the

a year, get your own credit report from
both Equifax and TransUnion. You can get
it free from each of them. It shows you
exactly what lenders see, and it's also
one of the best ways to catch fraud in

Step three, two to six months, the
collectors. After about 60 to 90 days,
your bank's own collection department
usually takes over. Your card may be
frozen, and somewhere around the
six-month mark, the bank will often
close the account and write it off. Now,
written off does not mean forgiven. It's
an accounting step. It usually means the
debt is handed to a collection agency or
sold to a company that buys old debts.
Or, less often, the bank takes you to
court. Collection agencies are regulated
by your province, and they have rules
they must follow. In Ontario, for
example, an agency must first send you a
written notice and then wait six days
before contacting you. After that, it
can contact you only Monday to Saturday
between 7:00 in the morning and 9:00 at
night, and on Sundays between 1:00 and
5:00 in the afternoon. Never on a
holiday. It can contact you no more than
three times in a week unless you agree
to more. It cannot threaten, intimidate,
or harass you. It cannot charge you fees
beyond any interest you actually owe.
And it can contact your family, your
friends, or your neighbors only to get
your address or phone number. It's not
allowed to discuss your debt with them.
Other provinces have their own rules,
many of them similar. If a collector
calls, don't agree to anything on the
phone. Ask for the agency's name, its

the debt in writing. Write down the date

I'll tell you in a moment why even a

think. Step four, the one that can empty
your bank account. This is the one I

your account. Think about what that

and it can reach further than people

account. So if your adult son is a joint
holder on your account and he owes that
same bank money, your savings could be
exposed too.
If you're falling behind on a card,
don't wait for this to happen. Talk to a
non-profit credit counselor or a
licensed insolvency trustee about where
your pension is deposited. Many will
suggest having it paid into an
institution where you don't owe any
money. If you make that change, do it
yourself through Service Canada and a
bank you chose, never because someone
phoned you and told you to. Step five,
the lawsuit and the clock. If the debt
is big enough, the bank or the
collection agency may sue you. In
Ontario, small claims court now handles
claims up to $50,000.
You'll be served with court papers and
you'll have a short deadline to respond.
If you ignore them, the creditor can get
what's called a default judgment, a win
without you ever saying a word. With a
judgment, a creditor can ask the court
to garnish your wages if you're still
working, to garnish or freeze a bank
account, or to register a writ against
property you own, including your home. A
writ usually doesn't mean anyone forces
you out of your house, but it generally
has to be dealt with before the home can
be sold or refinanced. And whether
pension money sitting in your bank
account stays protected from a court
garnishment can depend on your province
and your circumstances, which is exactly
why you get advice the day court papers
arrive. Now, here's the good news about
time. A creditor can't sue you forever.
In most provinces, the limit is 2 years
from when you stopped paying. In Quebec,
it's three. In a few provinces, it's
longer. Once that time is past, they can
no longer take you to court. But listen
carefully, the debt itself doesn't
vanish. A collector can still ask you to
pay and it can stay on your credit
report for up to 6 years. And in many
provinces, making even a small payment
or acknowledging the debt in writing can
restart that clock. That's why you never
send a little something to show good
faith before you've had advice. Never
ignore court papers. Call a lawyer, a
community legal clinic, or a licensed
insolvency trustee the day they arrive.
The deadline to respond is short and
missing it costs you your chance to be
heard.
Step six, what happens to the debt when
you die?
Your credit card debt doesn't disappear
when you do. It becomes a debt of your
estate. Your executor pays it from what
you leave behind before your heirs
receive their inheritance, but your
children do not have to pay it out of
their own pockets unless they co-signed
or were joint holders on the card.
Someone who is just an authorized user
with a card on your account generally
isn't responsible for the balance. And
if the estate doesn't have enough to
cover it, the unpaid part is usually
written off. Collectors sometimes call
grieving families and make it sound as

don't. The right answer is simple.
Please send the details to the executor
of the estate. Make sure your executor
knows which cards you have. And if one
of your children is a joint card holder,
both of you should understand exactly
what that means before anything happens.
Now, the most important part of this
whole video, the way out. Because if
you're behind or worried you soon will
be, you have more options than the

call your card company before you miss a

payment plan. Banks would rather be paid

And if you've already been scammed, call

with them. Should I cash in my RRRIF to

your GIS, and in a bankruptcy, most

Refunds and benefits, like the groceries

Will the new fraud law refund me if I'm

Yes. Government of Canada checks never

At a CDIC member institution, eligible

Let's bring it all together. Rule one.
