title: 7 Things the CRA Lets You Do After 65 (Most Retirees Never Use Them)

segments.text: Hello, friends. The title of this video
isn't clickbait. The year you turn 65,
the Canada Revenue Agency quietly hands
you a set of tools that working people
don't get. Credits that lower your tax,
ways to move income between spouses,
money back on renovations to your own
home, and none of them arrive
automatically. They're boxes on a tax
return, forms nobody mentions, and rules
that only work if you know to use them.
Which is why a great many retirees go
year after year without using most of
them, and pay hundreds, sometimes
thousands of dollars more than they had
to. Now, let me be straight with you
right away, because I will never lie to
you. These aren't loopholes or secrets.
Every one of them is in the CRA's own
guides, and every one is perfectly
ordinary. And not all of them will apply
to you. Some depend on your income, some
on whether you're married, some on
whether you renovate or give to charity.
But in my experience, almost every
retiree is missing at least two of
these, and many couples are missing four
or five. And none of this is about
hiding income or bending rules. These
are lines on the same return you already
file every spring. You just have to know
they're there. So, today I'll walk you
through all seven in plain English. What
each one is, roughly what it's worth,
and the exact words to say to whoever
does your taxes. Stay with me for number
three, because for married couples, it's
often worth more than all the others put
together. Let's get into it. Let me tell
you why this matters so much on a fixed
income. When you were working, your tax
was mostly taken care of. Your employer
withheld it, and there wasn't much you
could do about it anyway. In retirement,
that changes. Your income comes from
several places: CPP, OAS, maybe a
workplace pension, maybe a RRIF. And how
those pieces fit together on your tax
return makes a real difference. The CRA
has written rules specifically to help
people over 65, but it assumes you'll
find them. And a tax return prepared in
a hurry at a storefront from last year's
file very often doesn't. Picture two
retired couples on the same street with
the same pensions and the same savings.
One couple splits their pension income,
claims the age amount, and
[clears throat] pension credit, and
keeps a log of every medical trip. The
other files the way they always have.
Year after year, the first couple can
keep a thousand dollars or more that the
second simply hands over. Over a 20-year
retirement, that can pass twenty
thousand dollars.
And before we go on, do one quick thing
for me. Subscribe to this channel. I'm
not asking just to ask. These numbers
change every year, and nobody at the CRA
is going to phone you to say you've been
missing a credit. I go through these
rules so you don't have to dig through
them yourself. The people who are
subscribed stay ahead of it. Hit
subscribe, tap the bell, and let me keep
watch over your money with you. All
right. Number one. A quick word before
we go on. There are more of these
credits, rules, and quiet provisions
than I could ever fit into one video.
The things the CRA never bothers to
spell out. I gathered the whole of it in
plain English into one handbook at
waltercanada.com.
The video is the short version. The
handbook is the whole of it. If you want
it, it's there. I won't bring it up
again.
Number one. The age amount. This is the
most basic of the seven, and it's still
missed more often than you'd think.
If you're 65 or older at the end of the
year, you can claim a non-refundable
federal credit called the age amount.
For 2026, the base amount is nine
thousand two hundred and eight dollars,
which reduces your federal tax by
roughly $1,300.
And provinces have their own age amount
on top of that.
There's a catch you need to understand
though. The age amount is income tested.
It starts to shrink once your net income
passes $46,432,
reduced by 15 cents for every dollar
above that line until it disappears
entirely at higher incomes.
So, for retirees in the middle, not
wealthy but comfortable, every extra
dollar of income in that range quietly
cost you a piece of this credit as well
as ordinary tax.
That's why the way income is split
between spouses, which I'll come to in
number three, matters so much.
Look at last year's return, line 30100,
and make sure the age amount was
claimed. And if your income sits
anywhere near 46,000,
ask your preparer whether moving income
to your spouse could keep more of your
age amount intact.
Number two, turning your RRIF into
pension income so you can claim the
pension income amount. Here's a credit
many retirees qualify for and never get.
You can claim a credit on up to $2,000
of eligible pension income each year,
worth roughly $280 of federal tax plus a
provincial credit. Workplace pension
payments qualify at any age. And here's
the part that matters for this video.
Once you're 65, withdrawals from a RRIF
and payments from an annuity also count
as eligible pension income. Notice what
doesn't count because this is where
people get confused. Your CPP and your
OAS are not eligible pension income for
this credit. So, a retiree whose only
income is CPP and OAS with savings
sitting in an RRSP gets nothing from
this credit even though a simple change
would unlock it. And here's that change.
If you're 65 or older and you don't have
a workplace pension, you can convert
part of your RRSP to a RRIF.
You don't have to wait until 71 and
withdraw about $2,000 a year from it.
That withdrawal is taxed, but the
pension credit cancels a good part of
that tax and it can open the door to
income splitting with your spouse as
well. Action. Ask your banker or
advisor, "If I convert part of my RRSP
to a RRIF at 65 and withdraw $2,000 a
year, can I claim the pension income
amount?" For many people with no
workplace pension, the answer is yes,
every year.
And now number three, the one I told you
to stay for, pension income splitting.
For married and common-law couples, this
is often worth more than every other
item on this list combined. Here's how
it works. If one of you receives
eligible pension income, a workplace
pension at any age, or RRIF or annuity
income once you're 65, you can choose to
report up to half of it on your spouse's
tax return instead of your own. No money
actually moves between accounts. It's an
election you make on your returns each
year using form T1032,
which both of you sign. Why is that so
powerful? Because Canada taxes
individuals, not couples. If one spouse
of income and the other has 20,000, the
higher earner is paying a higher rate on
their top dollars than the lower earner
would. Moving some of that income across
can lower the household's tax bill,
sometimes by $1,000 or more a year. But
the benefits go beyond the tax rate.
Lowering the higher spouse's income can
protect their age amount from being
clawed back. It can keep them under the
old age security recovery tax threshold,
which begins around $95,300
for 2026. And it can let both spouses
claim the pension income amount instead
of only one.
One caution, so you get the right answer
for your own situation. The best amount
to split is rarely exactly half. Move
too much and your spouse's income can
climb to the point where their old age
amount starts to shrink or the bar for
their medical expense claim rises. Good
tax software and a good preparer can
work out the best split to the dollar.
Make sure yours actually does. Action.
If either of you has a pension or RRIF
income, ask your preparer, "Are we
splitting pension income and have you
calculated the best amount to split this
year?" The right percentage changes as
your incomes change, so it should be
reviewed every year, not set once and
forgotten. And if you've never split,
ask whether earlier years can be
adjusted. Number four, the home
accessibility tax credit, where being 65
is the entire test. If you're 65 or
older, no disability required, you can
claim a credit on up to $20,000 a year
of eligible renovation expenses for work
that makes your home safer or easier to
live in. The credit is calculated at the
lowest federal tax rate, so on $20,000
of work, it's worth up to about $2,800
federally. What counts? Permanent
changes to the home. Grab bars and the
backing in the wall behind them. A
walk-in tub or a curbless shower. A
ramp. Widened doorways. Lowered
counters. A stair lift. Non-slip
flooring. Better lighting on the stairs.
What doesn't count? Furniture, household
appliances, and ordinary repairs or
maintenance. Materials and a
contractor's work count, but not the
value of your own labor and not work
done by a relative unless they run a
business registered for GST/HST.
And one more thing couples should know.
If two people 65 or older live in the
same home, the $20,000 limit is for the
home, not for each of you. Three details
that make it more valuable. A spouse or
a relative who supports you can
sometimes claim it instead if you don't
have enough tax to use it. If your
renovation also qualifies as a medical
expense, the CRA lets you claim it under
both credits. And a government grant for
the same work doesn't reduce this credit
at all. Action. Keep every invoice and
receipt for accessibility work with the
contractor's name and business number.
And say these words when you file, "I'm
over 65 and did accessibility
renovations. I'd like to claim the home
accessibility tax credit." Number five,
the multigenerational home renovation
tax credit for when the family wants to
bring you home. This one isn't something
you claim for your own house so much as
something your family claims to house
you. If a family builds a self-contained
secondary unit with its own entrance,
kitchen, and bathroom so that a relative
65 or older can live with them, the
renovation qualifies for a credit on up
to $50,000 of expenses worth up to about
$7,000 at the 2026 rate. And unlike most
of the credits on this list, it's
refundable, which means it pays out even
if no tax is owed. For many families,
this is the difference between a parent
moving into a care home and a parent
moving into the basement suite
downstairs with their own front door,
their own kitchen, and their
grandchildren upstairs. Action. If your
family is even considering it, talk to
an accountant before the work starts.
Keep every receipt and check zoning with
the municipality first. And remember two
rules. An expense you've already claimed
under the accessibility or medical
credits can't be claimed here as well.
So, pick the right credit for each cost.
And this one can only be used once in a
senior's lifetime. So, get it right the
first time.
Number six, the medical expense tax
credit and three rules that make it far
more valuable than people realize. Most
retirees know you can claim medical
expenses. Very few use these three
rules. First, you don't have to use the
calendar year. You can claim expenses
for any 12-month period that ends in the
tax year. So, you can pick the stretch
where your costs were highest. Second, a
couple can combine their medical
expenses and claim them together on one
return. And it's usually best on the
return of the spouse with the lower
income because the threshold you have to
pass is roughly 3% of net income or a
fixed amount of a little under $3,000,
whichever is less. On a modest income,
3% is a low bar. And third, the one
almost nobody knows, travel. If you have
to travel at least 40 km from home for
medical care that isn't available
closer, your transportation costs can
count. Travel 80 km or more and meals
and lodging can count, too. For seniors
in smaller towns who drive to a city for
cancer treatment, cardiology, eye
surgery, or specialist appointments,
that can add up to a great deal over a
year. What else counts? Prescriptions
and dispensing fees, dental work,
glasses and hearing aids, many medical
devices, and premiums you pay for
private health or dental insurance.
Action. Ask your pharmacy for an annual
printout of everything you've paid. Keep
a simple log of medical trips with dates
and distances. And say to your preparer,
"Can you check the best 12-month period
and whether our medical expenses should
be claimed together on the lower income
return?"
Number seven, giving to charity in a way
that costs you less.
If you give to your church or a charity
anyway, there are two things the CRA
allows that can make each gift go much
further. First, the donation credit
itself is more generous above the first
$200 in a year. So, couples can combine
their donations on one return to get
more of their giving above that line.
Second, if you own investments that have
grown in value, shares or funds in a
non-registered account, you can donate
them directly to a registered charity in
kind instead of selling them and
donating the cash. Do that and the
capital gain on those investments is
generally not taxed at all, and you
still get a donation receipt for the
full value. And for planning ahead,
outside Quebec, you can name a
registered charity as the beneficiary of
part of your RRIF or TFSA.
When you die, the donation credit on
your final return can offset a large
share of the tax on that RRIF money. So,
more of it reaches the charity and less
goes to the CRA.
Action. If charitable giving is part of
your life, ask your bank whether your
investments can be donated in kind and
mention charity beneficiary designations
to your lawyer when you next review your
will.
Now, seven is the list, but let me add
three smaller things the CRA lets you do
that also help retirees.
You can keep contributing to a TFSA at
any age. There's no upper age limit, and
every dollar inside it grows and comes
out tax-free without affecting your GIS
or your OAS.
If your income this year is lower than
last year, a one-time sale or big
withdrawal last year, for example, you
can ask the CRA to reduce the Old Age
Security recovery tax being taken from
your monthly payments with form T1213
OAS. And if you're facing a tax bill
every April because no tax is taken off
your CPP and OAS, you can ask Service
Canada to withhold tax at source using
forms ISP-3520-CPP
and ISP- 3520-OAS.
Two separate forms, one for each. And
here's the thread through all of it.
Every one of these seven depends on
filing a return and on someone looking
for them. If filing is hard, free tax
clinics run across the country for
seniors and lower-income Canadians with
trained volunteers. And if you've missed
some of these in past years, it's often
not too late. You can ask the CRA to
adjust a previous return. And for many
refunds, you can go back as far as 10
years. Bring the old notices of
assessment and ask. A quick warning
because tax lists bring out the
scammers. The CRA won't phone you to say
you're owed a seniors tax refund and ask
for your banking details or a fee to
release it. It never takes gift cards,
never threatens arrest, and never sends
a text link to claim a credit. And be
cautious of companies that offer to
recover credits for a percentage of the
refund. Your preparer or a free clinic
can do the same thing at a fraction of
the cost. If a call or message comes in,
hang up and contact the CRA yourself
using a number from the official
canada.ca website. And if you've already
given something away, call your bank,
your local police, and the Canadian
Anti-Fraud Centre at 1-888-495-8501.
Let Let this real with a quick story.
Picture a couple. Call them Bill and
Carol. Both 68 in a small town 2 hours
from Toronto. Bill has a workplace
pension from 30 years at a paper mill,
plus CPP and OAS, about $76,000 a year.
Carol stayed home with their children
and later worked part-time. She has OAS
and a small CPP, about 15,000.
For 3 years since retiring, they'd filed
their returns separately at the same
storefront and paid what they were told.
Their daughter-in-law, who's an
accountant, offered to look over their
returns one Christmas. Here's what she
found. They'd never split Bill's pension
income, and his income was high enough
that most of his age amount was being
clawed back. Splitting a portion of his
pension onto Carol's return lowered
their household tax, protected Bill's
age amount, and let Carol claim the
pension income amount, too. They'd also
been splitting their church donations
between their two returns. Combining
them on one return put more of their
giving above the $200 line, where the
credit is roughly twice as generous.
They'd spent $14,000
the year before on a walk-in shower and
grab bars after Bill's hip replacement,
and never claimed the home accessibility
tax credit. And Carol had been driving
Bill 130 km each way to a specialist in
the city 11 times. Those trips could
count as medical expenses, and together
with their pharmacy receipts claimed on
one return, they produced a real credit.
They asked the CRA to adjust the
previous years where they could. The
refunds paid for a new furnace. And
going forward, their household is better
off by well over a thousand dollars a
year on exactly the same income. Same
couple, same pension, same town. They
just started using the tools the CRA had
handed them at 65. Be a Bill and Carol,
with or without the accountant in the
family. Let me answer the questions I
know you're thinking. Do I have to apply
for these credits? They're claimed on
your tax return, mostly by entering the
right amounts and forms. Your preparer
should do it, but only if they know your
situation. So, tell them. What's the age
amount worth? For 2026, a base of
which reduces federal tax by about
It shrinks once net income passes
Do my CPP and OAS count for the pension
income amount? No. Workplace pensions
count at any age, and RRIF and annuity
income count once you're 65. Can we
split my CPP with my spouse? Not through
pension income splitting. CPP isn't
eligible. But, CPP has its own pension
sharing program through Service Canada
for couples who are both at least 60.
Ask them about it. Do I need a
disability to claim the home
accessibility tax credit? No. Being 65
or older is enough. Can my medical
travel really count? Yes, if you travel
at least 40 km for care not available
closer. At 80 km or more, meals and
lodging can count, too. Keep a log. Is
donating shares really better than
donating cash? Generally, yes, if
they've grown in value. The capital gain
usually isn't taxed when you donate them
directly, and you still get a receipt
for the full value. I missed these in
past years. [clears throat] Is it too
late? Often not. You can ask the CRA to
adjust previous returns, and many
refunds can go back up to 10 years.
Let's bring it all together. Seven
things the CRA lets you do after 65.
One, claim the age amount and watch the
income line where it starts to shrink.
Two, claim the pension income amount
including on RRIF withdrawals after 65.
Three, split pension income with your
spouse and have the best split
calculated every year. Four, claim the
home accessibility tax credit where
being 65 is the whole test. Five, use
the multi-generational credit if your
family builds a suite to bring you home.
Six, get more from the medical expense
credit with the best 12-month period,
the lower income spouse, and medical
travel. And seven, give to charity with
investments in kind and consider a
charity on your RRIF. Because here's the
heart of it, friends. The CRA isn't your
enemy at 65. It's actually written a
whole set of rules in your favor and
then left it entirely up to you to find
them. So, take this list to whoever does
your taxes this year and go through it
line by line. The worst you'll hear is,
"That doesn't apply to you." The best is
a smaller tax bill every year for the
rest of your retirement and perhaps a
check for the years you missed. One
honest note, this is general information
to help you understand what's available.
It is not legal, financial, or tax
advice and I'm not an accountant.
Credits, amounts, and eligibility depend
on your income, your province, your
family, and your own situation and they
change every year. So, always confirm
the specifics for your own case with the
Canada Revenue Agency, the official
canada.ca website, and a qualified tax
professional or free tax clinic before
you act on anything here. If this helped
you, subscribe because I explain the
rules nobody else spells out for
Canadian seniors in plain English before
they cost you. And please, do one thing
for me. Share this with one retired
couple who file their taxes separately
and have never split their pension
income.
That one conversation could be worth
more than a thousand dollars a year to
them.
Take care of yourself, watch out for
your money, and I'll see you in the next
one.

title: Every Canadian Senior Must Know The Real October Changes Hitting CPP, OAS And Savings Or Lose Out

segments.text: Every Canadian senior must know the real
October changes hitting CPP, OAS, and
savings or lose out. Hello, friends. The
title of this video isn't clickbait.
October is the busiest month of the year
for a Canadian senior's money, and
almost nobody treats it that way. In a
single month, your old age security
changes, your guaranteed income
supplement changes, a credit you receive
four times a year arrives under a new
name, the Bank of Canada makes a
decision that reaches straight into your
savings, and the last pension payment
before winter lands, sometimes smaller
than people expect. And on top of all
that, a countdown starts that decides
how much you'll receive next year. Miss
it and you lose out. Not because anybody
took anything, because the month moved
faster than you did. Now, let me be
straight with you right away, because I
will never lie to you. Nobody is cutting
your pension in October. There's no new
law reducing CPP or OAS, and there's no
reason for anyone to move their cash in
a panic. In fact, if you ever hear that
phrase from someone on the phone, it's
almost certainly a scam, and I'll come
back to that. Your money is safe in the
bank, but safe and working for you
aren't the same thing. And October is
the month where the difference shows.
So, today, the five real October
changes, what each one means for your
money, and exactly what to check before
the month is out. Stay with me for
number four, because it explains why
some of you will open your October
deposit and find the increase you were
promised has quietly disappeared. Let's
get into it. Let me tell you why a
single month matters so much on a fixed
income. Your income is set by rules that
run on calendars, quarters at Service
Canada, benefit years that run July to
June, tax years that end on December
31st, and eight rate decisions a year at
the Bank of Canada. Most of those
calendars happen to turn in October or
point straight at the end of the year.
When you know the dates, you can act.
When you don't, the rules decide for
you, and they rarely decide in your
favor. And before we go on, do one quick
thing for me. Subscribe to this channel.
I'm not asking just to ask. I'll cover
the Bank of Canada's decision and the
January pension numbers as soon as
they're announced, and nobody at Service
Canada is going to phone you to explain
them. The people who are subscribed stay
ahead of it. Hit subscribe, tap the
bell, and let me keep watch over your
money with you. All right, change number
one. A quick word before we go on. There
are more of these dates, rules, and
quiet changes than I could ever fit into
one video. The things Service Canada,
the CRA, and your bank never bothered to
spell out. I gathered the whole of it in
plain English into one handbook at
waltercanada.com.
The video is the short version. The
handbook is the whole of it. If you want
it, it's there. I won't bring it up
again.
Change number one. On the 1st of
October, your OAS and your GIS went up,
and so did the line for qualifying. Old
Age Security and the Guaranteed Income
Supplement are adjusted for the cost of
living every 3 months. For October
through December, the increase is 1.4%,
and OAS has risen about 3% over the past
12 months. That part is automatic, and
it's good news. But the part most
seniors miss is what happens to the GIS
income cutoffs. When the amounts rise,
the maximum income you can have and
still receive some GIS rises, too. So, a
senior who was told in the summer that
their income was just slightly too high
may now be just under the line. That
answer was accurate in July and can be
wrong in October and nobody sends a
letter to say so. For a single senior,
the line is roughly $22,000 of income a
year, not counting OAS, and it keeps
creeping up each quarter. And two
related checks while you're thinking
about it. If you turn 75 this year, your
OAS should be permanently 10% higher,
automatic, but sometimes missed. And if
your income dropped this year because
you retired, lost a pension, or lost a
spouse, your GIS can be calculated on
your current income instead of last
year's, using the statement of estimated
income form ISP-3041.
You ask for it by number. Action. If you
were ever refused the GIS for being
close to the line, or your situation has
changed, call Service Canada at
this month and ask them to look again.
Change number two. A credit arrived in
early October under a new name, and it
only reached people who'd done two
things. For years, it was called the
GST/HST
credit. Since July, it's been called the
Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit.
It's paid four times a year, it's
tax-free, it doesn't reduce your GIS,
and since July, it's about 25% bigger
than last year. An increase that
continues for 5 years. For a single
senior on a modest income, it can be
worth up to about $950 a year. Here's
the catch, and it's why some of you
didn't see it. Two things have to be
true for it to reach you. First, your
tax return has to be filed because the
credit is calculated from it, even if
you owe nothing. Second, the Canada
Revenue Agency has to have your banking
information because since January, the
CRA no longer mails checks for most
payments, and your pension direct
deposit doesn't count. That's Service
Canada, a separate department with
separate records. And a note for
couples, because it causes needless
worry every quarter. If you're married
or living common law, only one of you
receives this benefit. It's calculated
on your combined income and paid to one
spouse, usually whoever's return was
processed first. So, if it's not in your
account, check your spouse's before you
assume anything has gone wrong. The
amount is for the household. It simply
arrives under one name. Check your bank
statement for a deposit in the first
days of October. If it's there and
larger than last October's, the increase
is working. If it isn't there at all,
walk into your bank and ask them to set
up direct deposit with the Canada
Revenue Agency. Most banks do it in
about 10 minutes, and make sure your
last return was filed. Payments that
were held are released once both are in
place. And if you received an invitation
this fall from the CRA to file using
Simple File, often just by phone, use
it. And now, change number three. The
28th of October, when the Bank of Canada
decides on interest rates, and why it
reaches your savings. The Bank of Canada
has held its policy rate at 2 and a
quarter percent for most of this year,
seven decisions in a row as of
September. On the 28th, it decides
again. Nobody knows what it will do, and
I'm not going to pretend I do. But
whatever it decides, it reaches your
money in two ways. If you live on
interest from savings and GICs, rates
have already come down a long way from
their peak a couple of years ago, and
many savings accounts now pay less than
inflation.
If the bank cuts again, the next GIC you
buy will likely pay less than the last
one. If it holds, things stay roughly
where they are. And if you carry a home
equity line of credit or a variable rate
mortgage, those move with the prime rate
within days of any change. And let me be
clear about one thing, because rate
decisions bring out frightening
headlines. Your deposits are not at risk
because of an interest rate decision.
Eligible deposits at member banks are
protected by the Canada Deposit
Insurance Corporation up to $100,000 per
category, per institution. And your own
accounts, joint accounts, TFSA, RRSP,
and RRIF are separate categories. So,
most seniors are protected far beyond
$100,000. Credit unions are covered by
provincial insurers, often with broader
limits. The only reason to move money is
to earn more on it, or to stay inside
those limits, never because of a scare.
Here's what you can control, regardless
of the decision. First, check whether
any of your savings accounts were on a
promotional rate that has quietly ended.
Banks often pay a high rate for a few
months, and then drop it close to
nothing without a letter you'd notice.
Second, if a GIC is maturing, don't let
it renew automatically at the bank's
posted rate. Call and ask for their best
rate, and compare one other institution.
Third, if you're on the GIS, keep your
savings in a TFSA where possible,
because interest earned there doesn't
count against your supplement. Action.
Before the 28th, look at what every
account is actually earning today. That
one look is worth more than any guess
about the decision.
Change number four, the one I told you
to stay for, the October deposit on the
29th, and why your raise may not show up
in it. Your CPP, OAS, and GIS arrive
together on the 29th of October in two
deposits, one for your CPP, and one for
your OAS and GIS combined. And for a
good number of seniors, the OAS increase
from the 1st of October won't appear the
way they expect. Here's why.
First, the OAS recovery tax, the
clawback. If your net income for 2025
was above roughly $93,454,
part of your OAS is deducted at source
from every monthly payment from July to
next June at 15 cents for every dollar
above the line. The increase is applied
to the full amount, but the deduction
comes off, too. So, the deposit may
barely move. If your income this year is
lower than last, a one-time sale or
withdrawal last year, for example, you
can ask the CRA to reduce that deduction
using form T1213
OAS.
Second, overpayment recovery.
If you were paid more than you should
have been earlier because your income
came in higher than estimated, your
marital status changed, or a spouse's
payments continued after their death,
Service Canada can recover it by quietly
deducting from your future payments.
You're entitled to an explanation, to
ask for a reconsideration within 90 days
of the decision letter if you think it's
wrong, and to ask for a smaller
repayment schedule if it causes
hardship. And third, your own tax
withholding. If you ask Service Canada
to withhold tax from your CPP or OAS as
a percentage, it rises when your pension
does. That's normal, but if your
situation has changed, you may be having
more withheld than you need. You can
change it with forms ISP-3520-CPP
and ISP-3520-OAS.
Action. When the October deposit lands,
compare it with September's line by
line. If it's not what you expected, log
in to your My Service Canada account or
and ask, "Is there a deduction on my
payment and what is it for?"
Change number five, snowbird season and
the six-month rule.
October is when thousands of Canadian
seniors head south and there's a rule
many snowbirds have never had explained.
The Guaranteed Income Supplement depends
on living in Canada. If you're outside
the country for more than six months in
a row, your GIS stops until you come
back and if you've lived in Canada for
fewer than 20 years as an adult, your
OAS stops after six months away, too. If
nobody tells Service Canada, the
payments keep coming and when it's
discovered later, every one of them
becomes an overpayment that's recovered
from your future checks. And there's a
second clock that matters even more,
your provincial health coverage. In
Ontario, you generally need to be
physically present for at least 153 days
in any 12-month period and an absence of
more than 212 days may mean reapplying
for OHIP. Every province has its own
rule. Lose provincial coverage and your
travel insurance may not cover you,
either. Action. If you're leaving, count
your months and days before you book the
return. Tell Service Canada if you'll be
away more than six months. Arrange for
someone to open your government mail or
sign up for online mail so you don't
miss a letter with a 90-day deadline.
And check your travel medical insurance
carefully, including the medical
questions before you go. Now the or lose
out part because there's a countdown
running underneath all five of these.
From the 1st of October, you have 92
days until December 31st and everything
you earn and withdraw before then
becomes your income for this tax year,
which decides two things from next July.
How much GIS you receive and how much
OAS is clawed back. After December 31st,
it's locked. So, October is when to
plan, not December. If you're on the
GIS, keep RRIF withdrawals to what you
need and take extra money from a TFSA
instead because TFSA withdrawals don't
count as income. If your income is
higher, think about the timing of any
large withdrawal or sale so it doesn't
stack on top of everything else in one
year. If you're married, pension income
splitting can move up to half of
eligible pension income to the lower
income spouse. And if you turn 71 this
year, your RRSP has to be converted to a
RRIF by the end of December, a hard
deadline with no flexibility.
Action. Book your tax preparer or a free
tax clinic for a short planning
conversation in November, not April. A
conversation in November can change next
year's numbers. A conversation in April
can only report them. So, let me put it
all on one page. Your October checklist
in the order the month runs.
This week, check your bank statement for
the groceries and essentials payment and
if it's missing, set up direct deposit
with the CRA and confirm your return was
filed. Before the 28th, look at what
every savings account and GIC is earning
and call about any promotion that's
ended or any GIC that's maturing. If you
were ever turned down for the GIS or
your income has dropped, call Service
Canada and ask them to look again.
On the 29th, compare your deposit with
September's line by line and ask about
any deduction you don't understand.
Before you leave for the winter, count
your months away, tell Service Canada if
it's more than six, and arrange for your
mail. And before the end of November, a
short planning conversation about your
RRIF, your TFSA, and your income for the
year. Six items, one month, and you'll
be ahead of almost everyone you know.
And the warning I promised. Because
October is peak season for fraud aimed
at seniors. When there's real news, a
rate decision, a renamed credit, pension
changes, the scammers use it. Bank of
Canada alert. Move your savings to a
protected account before October 28th.
Your groceries and essentials payment is
on hold. Update your banking details.
Your OAS increase requires verification.
Every one of those is a scam. No bank
and no government agency will ever ask
you to move your money to a safe or
protected account. The CRA and Service
Canada never text you links to update
banking information. Never charge fees
and never take gift cards. Action. If
anyone tells you to move your cash, hang
up. Call your bank on the number printed
on the back of your own card or Service
Canada yourself at 1-800-277-9914.
And if you've already given something
away, call your bank first, then your
local police, then the Canadian
Anti-Fraud Centre at 1-888-495-8501.
Let me make this real with a quick
story. Picture a couple. Call them Len
and Marjorie. Both 73, living on two OAS
pensions, two modest CPP pensions, a
small RRIF, and about $60,000 in a
savings account at their bank. Each
October, they leave for Arizona until
mid-April. Last October, three things
went wrong at once, and they didn't
notice any of them until spring. Their
savings had been moved onto a high
promotional rate two years earlier and
the promotion had quietly ended. Their
60,000 had been earning almost nothing
for 18 months. Their GST credit had
stopped coming in January because the
CRA no longer mailed checks and they'd
never set up direct deposit with the
CRA. And they'd stayed in Arizona a week
past 6 months. So Marjorie's small GIS
should have stopped and in the spring a
letter arrived saying the overpayment
would be recovered from her future
payments. This October, before they
left, they did it differently. They
called their bank, asked what their
savings were really earning, and asked
for the best rate available. The bank
raised it on the spot. They moved what
they could into their TFSAs so the
interest wouldn't count against
Marjorie's GIS. They set up direct
deposit with the CRA and the held
credits came through larger than before
because of this year's increase. They
booked their return flight for 5 months
and 3 weeks. And they signed up for
online mail so nothing from Service
Canada sits unopened in their mailbox
all winter. Same couple, same Arizona
sun, but this year October worked for
them instead of against them. Be a Len
and Marjorie, this year's version.
Let me answer the questions I know
you're thinking. Is my pension being cut
in October? No. OAS and GIS went up 1.4%
on the 1st of October, but deductions
like the clawback or an overpayment
recovery can make the deposit look
smaller. Should I move my cash before
the Bank of Canada decision? Not in a
panic and never because someone phoned
you. Instead, check what your accounts
are earning, avoid automatic GIC
renewals at posted rates, and keep
savings in a TFSA where you can. Is my
money safe in the bank if rates change?
Yes. A rate decision doesn't put your
deposits at risk. Eligible deposits are
insured up to $100,000 per category per
institution. Do I need to do anything to
get the October OAS increase? No, it's
automatic. Just check it appeared and if
you turn 75 this year, check the higher
rate appeared, too. Why didn't I get my
GST credit this month? It's now called
the Canada groceries and essentials
benefit. If it didn't arrive, your
return may not be filed or the CRA may
not have your direct deposit. Your
pension direct deposit doesn't cover the
CRA.
I was turned down for the GIS. Should I
try again? Yes, if you were close to the
line. The cutoffs rose on October 1st
and if your income dropped this year,
ask for form ISP-3041.
Why is my OAS lower than my neighbor's?
It could be the clawback deducted at
source, an overpayment recovery, fewer
years living in Canada, or the fact that
your neighbor is 75 or older and on the
higher rate.
I'm going south for the winter. What
should I know? More than 6 months
outside Canada in a row stops your GIS
and your OAS, too, if you've lived here
fewer than 20 years as an adult. Check
your province's health coverage rule, as
well.
What should I do before December 31st?
Plan your RRIF withdrawals, use your
TFSA, consider pension income splitting,
convert your RRSP if you turn 71, and
book a tax planning conversation in
November. Someone called saying the Bank
of Canada wants me to move my savings.
Is that real? No, that's a scam. Hang up
and call your bank on the number on your
own card.
Let's bring it all together. Five real
October changes. One, OAS and GIS went
up 1.4% on the 1st and the GIS income
cutoffs rose with them. Two, the Canada
groceries and essentials benefit arrived
in early October, 25% bigger, but only
for people with a filed return and
direct deposit with the CRA. Three, the
Bank of Canada decides on the 28th, so
check your rates, promotions, and GIC
renewals now. Four, the October 29th
deposit may not show your raise because
of the clawback, overpayment recovery,
or tax withholding. And each of those
can be checked and sometimes reduced.
And five, snowbirds. More than 6 months
away stops your GIS, and your provincial
health coverage has its own clock. And
underneath it all, the 92-day countdown
to December 31st, which sets next year's
GIS and clawback. Because here's the
heart of it, friends. October isn't a
month to panic in. It's a month to pay
attention in. Nobody is coming for your
pension, and there's no reason to move
your money because of a headline. But a
month this full of dates rewards the
seniors who look, and quietly costs the
ones who don't. One afternoon this
month, your bank, a phone call to
Service Canada, and a glance at what
your savings are earning, and you'll go
into the winter knowing exactly where
you stand.
One honest note. This is general
information to help you manage your
money wisely. It is not legal,
financial, or tax advice. Rates,
amounts, and rules change. The Bank of
Canada's decision hasn't been made yet,
and your own situation depends on your

And nearly every transit system has a
senior fare. While many parks, museums,
and theaters have a senior rate that's
never posted at the window. The rule for
all of them is the same. Before you pay,
ask, "Is there a senior rate or a
program that covers this?" And whatever
you're still paying out of pocket for
health, the drug deductible,
co-payments, dental work the plan
doesn't fully cover, glasses, hearing
aids, keep the receipts because they can
count toward the medical expense tax
credit on your return. Once your
eligible medical costs for any 12-month
period ending in the tax year pass a
threshold, roughly 3% of your net income
or a fixed amount of a little under
$3,000, whichever is less, the amount
above it earns you a credit. On a modest
retirement income, 3% is a low bar, and
a couple can usually combine their
medical expenses and claim them on the
return of the spouse with the lower
income. Ask your pharmacy for an annual
printout of everything you've paid. Most
will print it free.
And two pieces that sit alongside
turning 65 and save people from a costly
gap. First, make sure your old age
security actually starts. Service Canada
enrolls many people automatically and
sends a letter around the time they turn
64, but not everyone. If you didn't get
that letter, you need to apply, and you
can apply up to 11 months before you
want it to begin.
People who wait for something that was
never coming lose months of pension.
When you apply, you can also be
considered for the guaranteed income
supplement if your income is low.
Second, if you're on the GIS and your
spouse is between 60 and 64, ask about
the allowance. It's a monthly benefit
for exactly that situation, the younger
spouse of a GIS recipient, and it's one
of the least known benefits in the
system. Both start with one call to
Service Canada at 1 800 277 9914.
And for the tax return itself, free tax
clinics run right across the country for
seniors and lower-income Canadians,
staffed by trained volunteers. If you've
been paying someone to file a simple
return, that's one more bill that can go
to zero. Here's the simplest way to make
sure none of this slips past you. Take
one sheet of paper and write five lines
on it. Pharmacy, dentist, taxes, CPP
contributions, bank. Beside each one,
write the question you'll ask and the
date you asked it. Then, tick them off
over the next month. It sounds almost
too simple, but the reason most seniors
miss these isn't that they're hard, it's
that there are five different places to
ask and nobody ever gives you the list.
Now you have it. If you're helping a
parent, do it with them, one line at a
time.
Now, a word of warning because lists
like this are exactly what scammers feed
on. Nobody legitimate charges you a fee
to sign you up for any of these
programs. Nobody calls to say you've
been approved for a seniors benefit and
needs your banking details or your
social insurance number to release it.
No government agency is ever paid in
gift cards. The pharmacy, the dental
plan, the bank, and the CRA all work
through their own official channels and
they're happy for you to hang up and
call them back on a number you look up
yourself. Action. If anyone calls
offering to unlock senior benefits for a
fee, hang up. And if you've already
given something away, call your bank
first, then your local police, then the
Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre at
Let me make this real with a quick
story. Picture a man, call him Ken, 67,
a retired school custodian in a small
Ontario town with his OAS, his CPP, a
modest workplace pension, and three
mornings a week driving for a local part
supplier because he likes to keep busy.
When Ken turned 65, as far as he was
concerned, nothing changed. And that was
the problem. He was still paying the
dentist out of his own pocket because
his old work plan ended when he retired
and he assumed that was that. His
part-time paycheck still had CPP
contributions coming off every 2 weeks,
even though he'd been collecting his CPP
pension for 2 years. He was paying 16.95
a month for a bank account he'd had
since 1984.
And he was taking his blood pressure
medication on the standard drug program
without realizing that he and his wife
together were under the co-payment
threshold. His daughter-in-law, who
works in a pharmacy, sat down with him
one Sunday with a pad of paper and they
went through it like a checklist. The
pharmacy put them both on the seniors
co-payment program. They applied for the
Canadian dental care plan and Ken
finally got the crown he'd been putting
off. He gave his employer a CPT134
and his take-home pay went up the
following month. He walked into his bank
and asked the one question and his fee
went to zero. And their tax preparer,
once asked, confirmed they'd been
splitting his pension income but hadn't
been claiming his wife's age amount
correctly. That was fixed, too. Same
man, same pension, same three mornings a
week, but well over a thousand dollars a
year back in his pocket. And not one of
those changes required him to give
anything up. Nobody had told Ken. Nobody
had to. Be a Ken, but don't wait for a
daughter-in-law. Let me answer the
questions I know you're thinking. Is
everything free once I turn 65? No. Some
of these depend on your income, your
province, and whether you're working.
But for most seniors on an ordinary
retirement income, several of these
bills drop sharply or disappear. Do I
have to apply for drug coverage at 65?
In Ontario, no. You're enrolled in the
Ontario drug benefit automatically. But
the seniors co-payment program, which
cuts it to $2 a prescription, does need
an application. Who qualifies for the
dental plan? Seniors 65 and older
without access to private dental
insurance and with adjusted family net
income under $90,000.
Under 70,000, there's no co-payment. You
have to apply.
Will I really owe no tax? Many seniors
living on OAS, GIS, and a modest CPP
don't once the basic personal amount and
age amount are counted. But, you still
need to file because your benefits
depend on it.
I work part-time and get my CPP. Can I
stop paying into it? If you're between
65 and 70, yes, with form CPT 30. The
trade-off is that you won't earn the
small post-retirement benefit. At 70,
contributions stop automatically.
Can my bank really give me a free
account? Many seniors qualify for a
no-cost account, especially GIS
recipients, and many banks waive fees
for older customers. You have to ask.
Does any of this happen without me
asking? Some of it. Ontario drug
coverage at 65 and the end of CPP
contributions at 70. The rest, the
co-payment program, the dental plan, CPT
30, the bank account, the tax credits,
you have to ask for or claim. Do I have
to apply for Old Age Security? Many
people are enrolled automatically and
get a letter around 64. If you didn't
get one, apply up to 11 months ahead of
when you want it to start so you don't
lose months of payments. Can I claim my
prescriptions and dental bills on my
taxes? Yes, through the medical expense
tax credit once your total eligible
costs pass the threshold. Keep every
receipt or ask your pharmacy for an
annual printout. I'm not in Ontario.
Does this apply? The dental plan, the
tax credits, CPP, and the bank accounts
are national. Drug plans, eye exams, and
device programs are provincial. So, ask
your pharmacist and your province what
applies where you live.
Let's bring it all together. Five bills
that shrink or disappear after 65. One,
prescriptions. In Ontario, drug coverage
starts automatically and the seniors
co-payment program drops it to $2 a
prescription with no deductible if your
income qualifies. Two, the dentist. The
Canadian Dental Care Plan covers seniors
without private insurance under 90,000
in family income, fully under 70,000.
But you have to apply. Three, federal
income tax. The basic personal amount,
the age amount, and the pension income
amount mean many seniors owe nothing,
but you must still file. Four, CPP
contributions.
Working seniors from 65 to 70 who
already collect CPP can stop them with
form CPT30.
And five, the bank fee. A no-cost or
low-cost account is very likely yours
for the asking. Because here's the heart
of it, friends. Turning 65 isn't a bill.
It's a change of rules, and a good
number of those rules were written in
your favor. But the system was built on
the assumption that you'd find out on
your own, and most people don't. So take
this list to the pharmacy, the bank, and
whoever does your taxes and ask every
question on it. The worst answer you'll
get is no. The best is a couple of
thousand dollars a year for the rest of
your life.
One honest note. This is general
information to help you claim what you
may be entitled to. It is not legal,
financial, or tax advice, and
eligibility, amounts, and programs
depend on your income, your province,
your employment, and your own situation,
and they change every year. So always
confirm the specifics for your own case
with your pharmacist, your bank, the
Canada Revenue Agency, Service Canada at
and the official canada.ca website
before you act on anything here.
If this helped you, subscribe because I
explain the rules nobody else spells out
for Canadian seniors in plain English
before they cost you. And please, do one
thing for me. Share this with one person
who's just turned 65 or is about to
because the year you turn 65 is the best
possible year to hear this and almost
nobody does.
Take care of yourself, watch out for
your money, and I'll see you in the next
one.

title: The Bank of Canada Just Issued a WARNING to Every Canadian With a Savings Account

segments.text: The Bank of Canada just issued a warning
to every Canadian with a savings
account. Hello, friends. The title of
this video isn't clickbait. If you're a
Canadian senior with money in a savings
account, there's something happening to
it right now that most people never
notice because it doesn't arrive as a
letter or a fee. It arrives as a number
on your statement that's a little
smaller than it should be, month after
month, year after year. Nobody takes
anything from you. Your balance never
goes down. And yet, quietly, your
savings are buying less every year. And
for a great many seniors, the bank
that's holding the money is part of the
reason. Now, let me be straight with you
right away because I will never lie to
you. The Bank of Canada isn't warning
that your savings are in danger, and
your money in an ordinary bank account
isn't about to vanish. Eligible deposits
at member institutions are protected by
the Canada Deposit Insurance
Corporation, and nobody is freezing
anybody's savings. If you've seen a
version of this story built to frighten
you into moving everything, please
ignore it. Panic is how people make
expensive mistakes. The warning I'm
talking about is quieter and more
useful. At the start of September, the
Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2
and 1/4% for the seventh time in a row.
And what that means for a saver,
together with a trick the banks use on
savings accounts that almost nobody
notices, is costing seniors real money.
So, today, five warnings for anyone with
a savings account. What each one costs
you, and exactly what to check this
week. Stay with me for number two
because that one is happening to a great
many of you right now, and you'd never
know it unless you looked. Let's get
into it. Let me tell you why this
matters so much on a fixed income. When
you were working, your savings were
something you added to. Now, they're
something you live on, and you have to
make them last a length of time nobody
can tell you. That changes everything
about how a savings account should be
judged. It isn't enough for it to be
safe. It also has to keep up because a
dollar that buys a loaf of bread today
has to buy one in 10 years, too. And you
can't go back to work if it doesn't. A
savings account that pays almost nothing
isn't safe in the way that matters to a
retiree. It's just slow. And before we
go on, do one quick thing for me.
Subscribe to this channel. I'm not
asking just to ask. The Bank of Canada
makes another decision at the end of
October, and nobody at your bank is
going to phone you to explain what it
means for your savings. The people who
are subscribed stay ahead of it. Hit
subscribe, tap the bell, and let me keep
watch over your money with you. All
right. Warning number one. A quick word
before we go on. There are more of these
rules, rates, and quiet traps than I
could ever fit into one video. The
things your bank and the CRA never
bother to spell out. I gathered the
whole of it in plain English into one
handbook at waltercanada.com.
The video is the short version. The
handbook is the whole of it. If you want
it, it's there. I won't bring it up
again. Warning number one. Your savings
may be earning less than inflation,
which means you're losing money without
seeing a loss. Here's what's happened.
When the Bank of Canada was raising
rates a few years ago, savings accounts
and GICs paid more than they had in a
decade. Seniors who'd been earning
almost nothing suddenly saw real
interest. Then the bank started cutting.
And over the past year and more, it's
held its policy rate at 2.25%.
Savings rates followed it down. The big
banks' everyday savings accounts often
pay a tiny fraction of a percent. Even
many high-interest accounts now pay a
modest rate. Now compare that to prices.
Your old age security was raised about
3% over the past year because the cost
of living rose roughly that much. So
picture a senior with $40,000 in an
account paying half a percent. That's
$200 of interest a year before tax. But
if prices rose around 3%, that same
$40,000 now buys what about 38,800
would have bought a year ago. The
balance went up by $200. It's buying
power went down by about a thousand.
That's the real warning and it's why I
don't like the word safe for money
sitting idle. The deposit is safe. The
value isn't. Action. Look at your last
statement and find the interest rate
you're actually being paid on each
account. Not what you think it is, the
number on the paper or in your online
banking. Write it down. If it's below
about 2%, your savings are almost
certainly falling behind prices right
now. Warning number two, the one I told
you to stay for. The promotional rate
that quietly ends. Here's how it works
and I'd bet a fair number of you are
caught in it right now. Banks compete
for deposits by advertising a high rate
on savings accounts, sometimes several
percent. But read the fine print and the
high rate is very often a promotional
rate. It lasts a few months, three,
four, five, and then without a phone
call, without a letter you'd notice, the
account drops back to its regular rate
and the regular rate can be a small
fraction of the promotional one. Let me
make it concrete. A senior moves $60,000
into a new account advertised at a
bright, attractive rate. For four
months, it earns well. Then the
promotion ends and the rate falls to
something close to nothing. The senior
never notices because the balance keeps
going up a little each month. Two years
later, that money has been sitting at a
token rate for 20 of the 24 months, and
the difference between what it earned
and what it could have earned somewhere
sensible can easily be over a thousand
dollars. The banks aren't hiding this.
It's in the terms. They're counting on
the fact that almost nobody goes back to
check. Action. And this is the most
valuable thing in this video. Call your
bank or check online and ask three
questions about every savings account
you hold. What rate is this account
earning today? Is that a promotional
rate? And if so, when does it end? And
what's the best rate you can offer me on
this money right now? That last question
matters because banks will often match a
better rate to keep you, but only if you
ask. And then, put a reminder on your
calendar for the date any promotion
ends. Warning number three, the tax and
benefit bite on your interest, which
most seniors never connect. Here's the
part that makes a savings account more
expensive than it looks. Interest is the
most heavily taxed kind of investment
income in Canada. It's taxed in full at
your ordinary rate every year. Your bank
sends you a T5 slip if you earn $50 or
more in interest, but you're required to
report all of it, even if it's less than
50 and no slip arrives. And for seniors,
there's a second bite. If you receive
the guaranteed income supplement,
interest earned in a regular savings
account counts as income for the GIS
test, and the GIS falls by roughly 50
cents for every dollar of other income.
So, a lower income senior earning a few
hundred dollars of interest in an
ordinary account can lose a meaningful
part of that to a smaller supplement. At
the other end, for higher income
seniors, interest adds to net income
that can push you toward the old age
security recovery tax, which begins
around $95,300
this year. Now, here's the fix, and it's
the single most useful thing a senior
saver can know. Interest earned inside a
tax-free savings account isn't taxed,
isn't counted for the GIS, and isn't
counted for the OAS recovery tax. The
same money earning the same rate inside
a TFSA instead of an ordinary account
simply keeps all of its interest.
Action. Ask your bank how much TFSA
contribution room you have, or check it
in CRA My Account. Many seniors have
tens of thousands of dollars of unused
room they've never touched. Your savings
cushion can usually sit inside a TFSA in
a high-interest savings account or a
GIC, just as safe and far more
efficient. Warning number four. Know
exactly how much of your money is
protected, so you never panic. Here's
how deposit insurance works, because
fear about bank safety leads people to
make bad moves. The Canada Deposit
Insurance Corporation protects eligible
deposits at member institutions up to
but per category, per institution, not
per person. Deposits in your own name
are one category. Joint deposits are
another. TFSA deposits, RRSP deposits,
and RRIF deposits are each separate
categories, too. So, a senior with
100,000 in their own savings, 100,000 in
a TFSA, and 100,000 in a RRIF at the
same bank is fully protected for all
Two cautions, so you're accurate rather
than just comfortable. First, protection
covers eligible deposits, savings
accounts, checking accounts, and GICs.
It doesn't cover mutual funds, stocks,
ETFs, or cryptocurrency, even if you
bought them through your bank, because
those aren't deposits. Second, if you
bank at a credit union, you're generally
covered by your province's deposit
insurer rather than CDIC. And in several
provinces, that coverage is broader.
Action. If you genuinely have more than
a hundred thousand dollars in one
category at one institution, that's the
one case where spreading it across two
institutions makes sense. Otherwise, you
don't need to move anything for safety.
And anyone urging you to move money
because a bank is about to collapse is
someone to hang up on.
Warning number five, the forgotten
account and the fraud that targets
savings. Two quieter problems and both
cost seniors money. The first is the
account you've forgotten. When a
Canadian bank account sits with no
activity for 10 years and the bank can't
reach the owner, the balance is
transferred to the Bank of Canada as an
unclaimed balance. And there's well over
a billion and a half dollars sitting
there right now. A savings account
opened decades ago, a small GIC that
matured and was forgotten, a parent's
account nobody knew about. Action. Go to
the Bank of Canada's own unclaimed
balances website. It's free to search
and free to claim. And search your name,
older versions of your name, and the
names of a spouse or parent whose
affairs you handle. Anyone who offers to
find it for a fee is running a scam.
The second is fraud. And savings
accounts are a favorite target precisely
because seniors keep their largest
balances there. The most effective scam
in this country right now is a phone
call claiming to be your bank's security
department saying your savings are at
risk and must be moved to a safe account
to protect them. There is no such thing
as a safe account. Every single version
of that call is a crime.
Action. If anyone calls about your
savings and asks you to move money,
confirm a code, or give account details,
hang up and call the number on the back
of your own bank card yourself.
And ask your bank to add a trusted
contact person to your account. It costs
nothing, gives that person no access to
your money, and simply means the bank
has someone it's allowed to call if it
sees something that looks like fraud or
confusion. Now, let me give you the
shape of a sensible setup as general
information rather than advice because a
lot of seniors ask me where savings
should actually sit. Think of it as
three pockets. The first is your
checking account for the month, enough
for your ordinary bills and a little
extra, and not much more because
checking earns essentially nothing, and
it's the account most exposed to card
fraud and e-transfer scams. The second
is your cushion, several months of
expenses plus enough for a genuine
emergency like a furnace or a roof. In a
high-interest savings account, you can
reach the same day. Ideally, inside a
TFSA, so the interest doesn't count
against you. And the third is money you
won't need for a while, which some
people put into GICs, often split across
different maturity dates, so something
comes due every year. The two things to
avoid are leaving large sums idle in
checking and locking up money you might
need into a term you can't break. And if
you hold GICs, there's a cousin of the
promotional rate trap you need to know
about, the automatic renewal. When a GIC
matures, the bank sends you a notice. If
you don't respond, it very often renews
automatically, frequently into a term
you didn't choose at the bank's posted
rate, which is usually lower than the
rate you'd get by simply asking.
That letter looks like routine
paperwork, it goes into the pile, and
another year of interest is decided by
silence.
Action.
Write the maturity date of every GIC you
own on your calendar with a two-week
warning. When the notice arrives, open
it that day. And before you sign
anything, call and say, "What's the best
rate you can actually offer me on this
renewal? Not the posted rate." Then call
one other institution and ask the same
question. 15 minutes, twice a year, and
it's some of the best-paid time a
retired person can spend.
And one more piece for couples, because
it's good news. Each spouse's own name
deposits are a separate insurance
category from the others, and your joint
deposits are a category of their own.
So, a married couple banking at one
institution can hold a great deal more
than a hundred thousand dollars there
with all of it protected. Once you count
each person's own accounts, the joint
account, and each of your TFSAs and
RRSPs. If you've been anxious about
having too much in one bank, it's very
likely that you're covered far more than
you thought. Ask your bank to walk you
through your own coverage category by
category. They're required to know it.
And while you're thinking about all of
this, notice the date. The Bank of
Canada's next rate decision is the 28th
of October. Nobody knows what it will
be, and I'm not going to pretend I do.
But, it means this month is a good time
to check your rates, your promotions,
and your renewals. Because whatever
happens on the 28th, the seniors who've
already sorted their accounts won't need
to react. Let me make this real with a
quick story. Picture a man. Call him
Leonard. 78, widowed, sharp, and
careful. With about ninety thousand
dollars in savings and a small GIS on
top of his OAS and CPP. Two years ago,
during the high rate years, he moved
most of his savings into a new high
interest account his bank advertised at
an excellent rate. He was proud of that.
He'd done his homework. What he didn't
notice was the word promotional and the
four months beside it. The promotion
ended, the rate fell to almost nothing,
and Leonard's money sat there for nearly
two years at a token rate while he
assumed it was still earning what the
poster had promised. And because it was
an ordinary account, not a TFSA, the
little interest it did earn counted
against his GIS. He was being quietly
taxed by his own supplement on interest
that wasn't even keeping up with prices.
His granddaughter, who works at a credit
union, asked to see his statement one
Sunday. It took about an hour to fix.
They called his bank, asked what the
account was really earning, and asked
for their best rate. The bank offered
more on the spot to keep him. They
opened a TFSA and moved his savings
cushion into it, using the room he'd
never touched, so the interest stopped
counting against his GIS. They put the
longer-term money into GICs, split
across three maturity dates. They
searched the Bank of Canada site and
found a small account of his late wife's
from 1994,
and they added his granddaughter as his
trusted contact. Same $90,000,
same careful man, but money that's
finally working. A supplement no longer
being eaten, and a reminder on his
calendar every spring to ask the same
three questions. Be a Leonard, but be
him before the promotion runs out. Let
me answer the questions I know you're
thinking. Is my money in the bank safe?
Eligible deposits at CDIC member
institutions are protected up to
$100,000 per category, per institution.
And own name, joint, TFSA, RRSP, and
RRIF are separate categories. Credit
unions are covered by provincial
insurers. Is the Bank of Canada warning
that banks will fail? No. The real issue
for savers is low rates and the hidden
costs of idle savings, not bank failure.
Anyone urging you to move money out of
fear is someone to be wary of. What's a
promotional rate? A higher rate a bank
pays for a limited time, often a few
months, before the account drops to its
much lower regular rate. Check whether
any of your accounts are on one and when
it ends. Can I ask my bank for a better
rate? Yes, ask what's the best rate they
can offer you on that money today,
especially if you mention you're
comparing. Banks often match to keep a
deposit, but only when asked. Do I pay
tax on my savings interest? Yes,
interest is taxed in full at your
ordinary rate. You'll get a T5 slip if
it's $50 or more, but you must report
all of it. Does savings interest affect
my GIS? Yes, if it's earned outside a
TFSA, the GIS falls by roughly 50 cents
for every dollar. Interest inside a TFSA
doesn't count at all. How much should I
keep in checking? As a general rule,
enough for the month's bills and a
little extra. More than that earns
nothing and is the most exposed to
fraud. Wouldn't it be safer to keep my
savings in cash at home? No, cash at
home isn't insured, it earns nothing
while prices rise, a fire or a break-in
takes it entirely, and home insurance
usually covers only a small amount of
cash. It's also the first thing targeted
when someone with access to your home
takes advantage. Is a GIC better than a
savings account? They do different jobs.
A savings account is for money you may
need quickly. A GIC usually pays more,
but locks money up for a term. Many
seniors keep their cushion in savings
and only money they won't need for a
while in GICs. I think I have an old
account I've forgotten. How do I find
it? Search the Bank of Canada's
unclaimed balances website. It's free to
search and free to claim. Never pay
anyone to find it for you. How often
should I check my rates? At least twice
a year and anytime a promotion ends or a
GIC matures. Put the dates on your
calendar the day you open the account so
you're never relying on memory or on the
bank to remind you. Someone from my bank
called saying I need to move my savings
to a safe account. Is that real? No,
that's always a scam. Hang up and call
the number on the back of your own card.
Let's bring it all together. Five
warnings for anyone with a savings
account. One, with rates held at 2 and
1/4% many savings accounts now earn less
than inflation. So your balance rises
while its value falls. Two, the
promotional rate that quietly ends.
Check what every account is really
earning today when any promotion ends
and ask for the best rate available.
Three, interest is fully taxed and
outside a TFSA cuts your GIS and adds to
your OAS clawback income. So your
cushion belongs inside a TFSA. Four,
deposit insurance covers 100,000 per
category per institution. So you rarely
need to move anything for safety. And
five, search the Bank of Canada's free
unclaimed balances site and never move
money because of a phone call. Because
here's the heart of it, friends. The
danger to a senior savings isn't a bank
collapsing. It's money left sitting
unexamined at a rate somebody chose for
you and stopped telling you about.
Nobody's stealing it. It's just slowly
leaking to inflation, to taxes, to a
supplement that shrinks, to a promotion
that ended without a word. And all of it
is fixed by the same small habit. Once
or twice a year, look at the number and
ask the question. That's the whole
