segments.text: Social Security has already worked out your new amount for next year.
It is sitting in a file with your name on it.
There is no rule anywhere that requires anybody to show it to you before the
middle of December.
One date changes that, and it is the eighteenth of November.
On one side of that date you read your own figure in late November.
On the other side you wait for an envelope, and by the time it reaches your
table your January bills are already decided.
Three weeks. The same money either way.
The difference is whether you spend the most expensive six weeks of the year
knowing your number or guessing at it.
Before I start, one word in the comments.
Does your yearly letter reach you on paper, or on a screen.
Paper or screen, nothing else.
I will give you the date and what is decided on it, the two settings that put
you on one side or the other, what is inside that message besides the raise,
and what those three weeks actually take from you.
Everything here comes from the agency itself
and the sources are in the description.
Number one. The eighteenth of November.
What is decided that day, and by whom.
Nothing about your money changes on the eighteenth.
Your payment does not move. Your raise does not grow or shrink.
What changes is who gets to read it early.
The agency posts the figures for next year into the message area of its own
website in late November. If your account is set up and set to receive notices
without paper, yours appears there.
If it is not, your copy is printed and posted, and printing and posting takes
until December.
So the eighteenth is not a benefits deadline.
It is a sorting date. It decides which pile you are in.
And here is the part worth sitting with.
Nobody is going to write to you to warn you about a date that only matters
if you already know about it. There is no letter telling you to set up the
thing that would have stopped the letter being necessary.
That is the whole shape of it.
I want to be straight about what this is and is not.
Missing the eighteenth does not cost you a dollar directly.
You are not fined and you do not lose the raise.
Anybody telling you otherwise is selling something.
What it costs you is time, at the exact point in the year when time is the
thing you need, and I will show you why in the last item.
Number two. The account. Four minutes, and it has to be opened by you.
The account is free. It is on the agency website and nowhere else.
It takes about as long as filling in a form at a doctor office.
Now the part that stops people, and it is not the form.
It is the identity check. The system asks you questions pulled from your own
financial history, old addresses, an old loan, a card you had years ago.
People get one wrong, get locked out, and decide the whole thing is not for
them. If that happens, you are not finished.
You can complete the check in person instead, at a local office or at many
post office branches, and the person behind
the counter does it in a few minutes
with your identity document.
Two things to be hard about. Nobody else should open this for you.
Not a helpful neighbor, not a man who called offering to set it up.
The account is the single place that shows your payment details and the single
place they can be changed, and an account somebody else controls is worse than
no account at all. And nobody charges for this.
If a website asks for a card number to create it, you are on the wrong website.
There is one address and it is in the description.
Number three. The setting almost everybody misses after opening it.
This is the one that catches people who did everything right.
Opening the account is not enough.
An account on its own still gets you a posted letter.
There is a separate choice inside it, under the settings for how they contact
you, where you say you want your notices delivered without paper.
That is the switch. Until it is on, you are still in the December pile.
So somebody who opened an account two years ago, who logs in now and then,
who would tell you confidently that they are sorted, is very often not.
They have the account and not the setting.
Go and look. Open the account, find the part about communication preferences,
and make sure notices without paper is turned on.
While you are there, add your cell number or your email so the system can tell
you the moment something lands.
That alert is the difference between reading your figure on the day it appears
and finding it three weeks later when you happen to log in.
One honest caution. Turning off paper means turning off paper.
If you are the kind of person who files letters in a drawer and finds them
later, decide now where the screen version gets written down, because there
will not be a second copy arriving.
Let me put a face on it. Picture a man I will call Delroy, seventy one, who
opened his account the year he retired because his daughter sat with him and
did it. He logs in twice a year.
He would tell you, with complete confidence, that he is on the list.
He is not. Nobody ever showed him the second screen, and no letter has ever
mentioned it, because the letter is the thing he is still getting.
Two years of waiting for post he did not have to wait for, and not once did
anything arrive to tell him so.
Number four. What else is inside that message besides your raise.
Everybody is quoting the raise.
Three point six percent, and for a worker on the average retirement payment
it moves the monthly amount from two thousand and ninety five dollars to two
thousand one hundred and seventy.
That reaches about seventy six million people counting both programs, and it
begins with the January payment.
That part is settled. You do not apply for it and nobody can take it.
But the raise is not the only number in that message, and the second one decides
what actually lands in your account.
Medicare takes its monthly charge out of your payment before the deposit is
made. This year that charge is two hundred and two dollars and ninety cents.
It never appears as a bill. It is simply gone before the money is yours.
The figure for next year has not been published.
Not by anybody.
The official projection sits around two hundred and nine dollars and fifty
cents, and a projection is a forecast written down, not a decision made.
It is normally announced in the middle of November, which is to say in the
days right around the date this whole video is about.
So understand what that message in late November actually contains.
Not the average raise everybody is quoting.
Your gross amount, and the Medicare figure coming out of it, and the difference
between them, which is the only number that matters to your bank.
And when somebody tells you with confidence what your January deposit will
be, ask them where the second number came from.
If it was published, they can name the day.
If they cannot, they are reading a forecast out loud and calling it a fact.
Number five. The three weeks. What they actually cost at this time of year.
Here is where I stop being gentle about it.
Between late November and the middle of December you are deciding things that
lock for a year, and here is what that looks like on a kitchen table.
The Medicare plan choice closes on the seventh of December and after that you
live with it until the following January.
Insurance renewals land. Heating runs at its highest.
People decide what they can give at Christmas.
Every one of those decisions is better with your real figure in front of you
and worse with the average figure off the news.
The average is not your number.
Your work history is not the average work history, your Medicare charge may
not be the standard charge, and the gap between what you expect and what arrives
is exactly the gap people spend January trying to understand.
There is a second cost, and it is the one nobody mentions.
If the figure is wrong, and figures are sometimes wrong, the clock on sorting
it out starts when you see it.
See it in late November and you have the whole of December to query it before
the first payment of the year.
See it in late December and you are making that call in January, after the
money has already landed short, and the people answering the phone are at their
busiest of the year. Picture a widow I will call Esther,
seventy eight, living on one payment.
In early December she is looking at a plan renewal, a heating bill that has
already turned, and a figure she heard on the news.
She picks the cheaper plan because the news figure told her she had room.
Her own number arrives on the twentieth of December and it is lower than the
news figure, because her Medicare charge is not the standard one.
The plan window shut on the seventh.
She carries that choice for twelve months.
Nothing was hidden from Esther.
The figure existed in November.
She was simply in the pile that reads it last.
One last thing, because it happens every single year at exactly this point.
When the figures are announced, the calls start.
Somebody rings, says they are from the agency, says your raise needs confirming
or your account needs verifying, and asks for your number or your bank details.
The raise is automatic. It needs nothing from you.
The agency does not call people to hand them money.
Put the phone down, and if you want to check anything, you call them on the
number in the description rather than the number that called you.
So here is all of it in one breath.
The eighteenth of November does not change your money, it changes when you
are allowed to see it. Open the account yourself, on the agency website, and
open it nobody else. Then turn on notices without paper, because the account
alone leaves you in the December pile.
What arrives is two numbers, not one, and the second has not been published
yet. And the three weeks you save are the three weeks you spend deciding a
plan, a renewal and a Christmas on either a real figure or a borrowed one.
If you have already done all of this, say so in the comments, because somebody
reading them has not and will believe you before they believe me.
None of this is advice about your own record.
Your own work history and your own state decide what you see.

title: Seniors: 5 Pieces of Good News Are Coming, and One Is Worth $2,400 a Year

segments.text: Here is some good news for a change.
Starting in January, five things change for your money.
Four of them you will hear about on the news, and they are real.
The fifth one almost nobody claims.
For the people who qualify it is worth about two thousand four hundred dollars
a year.
Hold that number against the raise everybody is talking about, because it is
three or four times larger than the raise will be for the same person.
I am going to take all five one at a time.
For each one I will tell you the real number, what it does to your deposit,
and the one thing you do about it.
Four of them need nothing from you at all.
One of them will sit there untouched for the rest of your life if you never
raise your hand. Stay to the end for number five, because it is the one nobody
is going to mail you a letter about.
Every figure here comes from the agencies themselves, and the sources are in
the description.
Number one. The raise lands by itself.
Nobody has to ask.
Social Security confirmed the increase for next year at three point six percent.
It reaches about seventy six million people, and it starts with the January
payment. On an average retired worker check that is roughly seventy five dollars
more a month. On a thousand dollar check it is about thirty six dollars.
On a fifteen hundred dollar check it is about fifty four.
Run your own number and you will know what to expect before the letter arrives.
In December the agency posts your exact new amount.
If you have an account on their website it appears in your message center.
If you do not, it comes by mail.
Read that notice instead of filing it.
It shows your new gross payment and it
shows what is being taken out for Medicare.
Put it beside the letter from last year and compare the two lines.
That one habit catches errors that otherwise ride along for years.
Now one warning that costs people money every single year.
The week a raise is announced, the phone calls start.
Somebody says they can get you a larger increase, or that you have to confirm
your details to receive it. You do not.
The raise is automatic.
Nobody needs your number to give you something you already have.
And there is one number missing from all of this, which is the reason I am
not going to tell you your net increase.
Medicare has not published the Part B premium for next year yet.
The trustees project about two hundred and nine dollars and fifty cents, up
from two hundred and two dollars and ninety cents, but a projection is not
a published figure. It normally arrives in the middle of November.
Until it does, nobody on this website can tell you what your deposit will actually
be in January, and anybody who says a precise figure is guessing.
There is a rule that stops the Part B increase from pushing your payment below
what it was the year before, and for most people it holds.
It does not cover you if you are new to Medicare this year, if your premium
is billed to you directly rather than taken from your payment,
or if you pay the higher charge that applies at higher incomes.
Roughly three in ten people sit outside that protection.
Number two.
Medicare Advantage premiums go down next year, not up.
This one surprises people because it runs against everything else they hear.
At the end of September, Medicare released the figures for next year.
The average monthly premium on a Medicare Advantage plan is expected to fall
from fourteen dollars and thirty seven cents to twelve dollars.
That is a drop of about sixteen and a half percent.
The part of that premium that pays for your prescriptions falls further.
It goes from about eleven dollars and thirty two cents down to about seven.
That is a drop of nearly forty percent.
Medicare also estimates that about eight in ten people on a Medicare Advantage
plan will be able to stay exactly where they are next year at the same premium
or a lower one.
Now here is the honest limit of that, and I would rather you heard it from
me. An average is only an average.
Your own plan can fall, hold still, or rise.
And the premium is the smallest part of what a plan costs you.
What you pay at the doctor, what you pay at the pharmacy, and the most you
can be charged in a single year all matter more than the premium does.
Here is the move.
Find the envelope your plan sent you called the annual notice of change.
It is the one most people throw out.
It tells you exactly what is changing for you, not for the average.
Then compare it against the other plans where you live before the seventh of
December, because that is when your choice locks for the whole year.
One caution before you move. If you have original Medicare with a supplement
today, a cheaper premium is not on its own a reason to switch to an Advantage
plan.
In most states, once you give up that supplement you may not be able to buy
it back without answering health questions.
That door closes quietly behind you.
Number three.
Six thousand dollars off your taxable income, and what that saves you.
The tax law passed last year created a deduction that exists only for people
sixty five and older. It is six thousand dollars for each person.
For a married couple where both of you are over sixty five, that is twelve
thousand. What makes it different from almost every other break is that it
stacks.
It sits on top of the standard deduction, and on top of the extra amount people
over sixty five have always received.
You get it whether you take the standard deduction or itemize.
Most deductions make you choose one or the other.
This one does not. It shrinks at higher income.
It starts coming down above seventy five thousand dollars for a single filer,
or one hundred fifty thousand for a couple, and it disappears entirely well
above that.
Now the part nobody puts a number on.
A deduction is not a check. What it saves you depends on your tax rate.
If your top rate is twelve percent, six thousand dollars off your income saves
you about seven hundred and twenty dollars.
For a couple where both qualify, about fourteen hundred and forty.
That is every year through the twenty twenty eight tax year.
And here is the honest limit. This only puts money back in your hand if you
owe federal income tax in the first place.
If your income is almost entirely Social Security and you already owe nothing,
this changes very little for you.
You may also have heard that Social Security is no longer taxed at all.
That is not what the law did. It created a deduction, and it put an end date
on it. So do not stop having tax withheld from your payments until somebody
has actually run your numbers.
Number four. The January payment arrives on the last day of December.
This one is small and it catches people out every year, so it is worth the
ninety seconds.
If you receive Supplemental Security Income, the federal amount goes up in
January. For one person it moves from nine hundred and ninety four dollars
to one thousand twenty nine. For a couple it moves from one thousand four hundred
and ninety one to one thousand five hundred and forty four.
Now the timing.
The first of January is a federal holiday, so the January payment does not
arrive in January. It is sent on the thirty first of December instead.
That means two payments land in the same calendar month, December, and none
arrives on the first of January.
Every year people see that and assume
something has gone wrong, or that a payment
has been missed. Nothing has gone wrong.
It is the calendar, not the agency.
Write that date down somewhere you will see it, and if you know somebody who
panics when a deposit does not appear, tell them now rather than on the holiday
itself, when nobody is answering the phone.
Number five. Your state can pay your Part B.
That is two thousand four hundred a year.
Now the one I promised you, and the reason I made this.
If you are on Medicare, more than two hundred dollars a month is coming out
of your Social Security before the deposit ever reaches your bank.
The standard Part B premium this year is two hundred and two dollars and ninety
cents. You never see that money.
It is gone before the payment is a payment.
Over a year it is more than two thousand four hundred dollars.
There is a set of programs, run by your own state, that take over that payment
entirely. They are called Medicare Savings Programs.
When you qualify, the premium stops being deducted.
Your deposit is larger by that amount every month, for as long as you qualify.
Hear what that is, because people mishear it.
It is not a refund at the end of the year.
It is not a credit.
The deduction simply stops. There are three levels.
The most generous one also covers your Medicare deductible and your share of
the cost when you see a doctor, which means the bills that arrive three weeks
after an appointment stop arriving.
The other two cover the premium itself.
And there is a second thing that comes with it.
If you qualify for any of these, you are automatically given a separate program
that lowers what you pay for prescriptions.
You do not file for it twice. It follows you.
It does not run in reverse, which is why there are people today getting help
with medicine while still paying their Part B out of their own payment.
Now the income lines, and this is where people talk themselves out of it.
For the most generous level, a single person can have monthly income up to
about one thousand three hundred and fifty dollars,
and a couple up to about one thousand eight hundred and twenty four.
The middle level reaches about one thousand six hundred and sixteen for one
person and two thousand one hundred and eighty four for a couple.
The third level goes up to about one thousand eight hundred and sixteen for
one person and two thousand four hundred and fifty five for a couple.
Read those against your own situation and be honest about something.
Those lines are higher than you assumed.
Almost everybody assumes they are lower.
There is a savings limit as well.
About nine thousand nine hundred and fifty dollars for one person, and about
fourteen thousand nine hundred and ten for a couple.
And here is what gets left out of that count.
The house you live in does not count.
Your car does not count. Your furniture and your belongings do not count.
It is bank accounts and investments they are looking at.
So the person who looks around at a paid off house and a working car and decides
they are far too comfortable for this has just ruled themselves out over two
things that were never being counted.
Some states also set their lines higher than the federal ones, and some do
not apply the savings test at all.
That varies by where you live, which is exactly why you cannot answer this
at your own table. Nobody is coming to tell you.
There is no office reviewing your income and posting you a letter.
These programs pay out on application, not on eligibility.
The agency has your income and your age and it will sit on that information
for the rest of your life if you never apply.
Here is the move, and you can start it this week.
Call your state Medicaid office and
ask for the Medicare Savings Program application
by name. Or call the free counselling service in your state and they will help
you fill it out. If you do not know the number, call Medicare and ask them
for your state office. It is free to apply.
If somebody asks you to pay to file it, you are being taken.
And if you were turned down in an earlier year, that answer has expired.
The income lines move almost every year.
Ask again.
One more thing about applying, because people assume the clock starts the day
they are approved. For some of these, coverage can reach backward, and months
you have already paid for can be picked up.
Ask about that specifically when you call, because nobody volunteers it.
So here is all five in one breath.
The raise is three point six percent and it needs nothing from you.
Medicare Advantage premiums fall next year, but check your own notice rather
than the average.
The six thousand dollar deduction stacks on everything else, and it is worth
real money only if you owe tax.
Your January payment arrives on the thirty first of December, and nothing is

which is worth more than two thousand four hundred dollars a year and is the
only one of the five that waits for you to ask.
Four of them find you. One of them does not.
If your situation has something in it I did not cover, a public pension, a
spouse still working, a state with its own rules, tell me in the comments.
I read them and they decide what I look at next.
This is general information and not advice about your own record.
Your own income and your own state decide your figures.

Number two. Born in nineteen sixty.

Sixty seven, flat, with nothing attached to it.

Think about how narrow that line is.

Two months of birthday, and one of them waits two extra months for the same
unreduced payment. And there is a detail inside that line which catches people
every year. If you were born on the first day of January, the agency treats
you as though you were born in December of the year before.
So a person born on the first of January, nineteen sixty, is handled as a nineteen
fifty nine birth.
One day decides which side of the line you stand on, and nobody at a field
office is going to volunteer that to you.
There is a second thing about this group that gets missed.
Being first means there is nobody ahead of you to watch.
Every birth year before yours could look at the group in front and see how
it went. Yours cannot.
The field offices have processed this exact situation before, because the rule
was written in nineteen eighty three and the schedule has been public the whole
time, so this is not uncharted ground for them.
It is only new to you. Now the honest limit of this item.
Reaching sixty seven does not mean money arrives.
It means that if you file at that age you get your whole payment with nothing
taken off for being early. Filing is still your decision, and the next item
is about what that decision is actually worth.
Number three. The three numbers to look at before you file.
This is the one thing in this video you can act on this week, and it costs
nothing. Open your own account on the agency website.
If you do not have one, make one, because an account you control is one that
nobody else can open in your name.
Inside it, your estimated payment is shown at different ages.
Put three of them side by side and look at them together.
Sixty two.
Your full age. Seventy.
Here is what you are looking at.
If your full age is sixty seven and you file at sixty two, the payment is cut
by roughly thirty percent, and it is cut for the rest of your life.
Not for a year. Not until you reach sixty seven either.
For good. The reduction is built into the amount and it never comes back.
If you wait past your full age, the opposite happens.
The agency adds roughly eight percent for every year you delay, up to seventy.
Wait the whole way and the payment is about one hundred and twenty four percent
of what it would have been at sixty seven.
Same person, same record, same work history.
Only the start date changed.
Now the gap between the two ends.
Filing at sixty two against waiting to seventy is not a small difference.
On the same record it is the difference between seventy percent and one hundred
and twenty four percent. That is the number that stops people in their tracks
when they finally sit and look at it, and almost nobody looks until the month
they file.
And notice what that gap is actually made of.
It is not a reward the agency hands out for patience.
It is arithmetic that was built into the system from the beginning, designed
so that whenever you start, the total you collect over an average lifetime
comes out roughly similar.
The system is not trying to trick you into filing early.
It is also not trying to talk you into waiting.
It is indifferent, and that is exactly why nobody calls to advise you either
way. I am not going to tell you which one to pick, because the right answer
depends on things I cannot see from here.
Your health. Whether you have a spouse.
Whether you have anything else to live on in the meantime.
Plenty of people need the money at sixty two and that is a real answer, not
a mistake. But look at the three numbers before you decide, not after.
Once you file, that reduction is attached to you.
Number four. Born between nineteen sixty one and nineteen sixty six.
Same age, later year. If this is your group, your full age is also sixty seven.
Exactly the same as the group before you.
The only thing that differs is the year you get there.
So nothing on this list is aimed at you specifically.
What you should be paying attention to instead is the thing that affects you
right now, while you are still working, because most of this group still is.
If you are under your full age for a whole year and you are drawing a payment
while you work, the agency holds back one dollar for every two you earn above
a yearly line.
Next year that line is twenty five thousand five hundred and sixty dollars.
In the year you actually reach your full age the arithmetic softens.
The hold back becomes one dollar for every three, the line jumps to sixty seven
thousand nine hundred and twenty dollars, and only what you earn in the months
before your birthday month counts at all.
And the day you reach your full age the limit disappears completely.
Earn whatever you like. Nothing is held back from that point forward.
Now the part that keeps people from panicking, and almost nobody is told it.
The money held back is not a fine.
It is not gone. Once you reach your full age the agency recalculates your payment
upward to account for the months it held back, and you get it returned to you
over time. It feels like a punishment while it is happening.
It is a delay.
What that means for your group is simple.
If you are in your early sixties, still working, and thinking about filing
because you heard something changes, understand that filing early while you
are still earning can mean a permanent reduction and a temporary hold back
at the same time. That is the one combination worth avoiding.
Number five. Born in nineteen sixty seven.
The year everyone is naming. Now the year I promised you, and the reason I
made this video.
Search this website right now and you will find videos telling you that Social
Security just changed for anyone born before nineteen sixty seven.
I counted fourteen of them while I was writing this.
So let me be direct about it. There is no line at nineteen sixty seven.
Your full age is sixty seven, the same as every birth year back to nineteen
sixty.
Nothing special begins for that group, nothing is taken from it, and no rule
singles it out. The staircase stopped climbing at nineteen sixty and it has
not moved since. I am not saying that to make anybody look bad.
I am saying it because if you were born in that year and you have been worrying
for a week about something landing on you, it is not landing.
But do not click away, because something real does happen to that group next
year, and it is the reason the year keeps getting mentioned at all.
If you were born in nineteen sixty seven, you turn sixty next year.
Sixty is the earliest age at which a widow or a widower can claim a payment
on the record of a husband or a wife who has died.
Not sixty two.
Sixty.
And the vast majority of people have no idea that door opens that early, because
it is the one age in this whole system that nobody advertises.
There is a cost to walking through it at sixty rather than waiting, and you
should know it before you do anything.
Claimed at sixty, a survivor payment is about seventy one and a half percent
of what the person who died was receiving or had earned.
Wait until your own full age and it rises toward the whole amount.
So for that group,
nineteen sixty seven matters, but not for the reason fourteen videos are telling
you. It matters because of a door at sixty that most people walk past without
seeing it. So here is the whole thing in one breath.
The staircase is finished. It stopped at sixty seven and it stopped for everybody
born in nineteen sixty or later.
If you were born in nineteen fifty nine or earlier, your step is lower and
you are already standing on it.
If you were born in nineteen sixty, you are the first group to reach the top,
and you reach it next year. If you were born between nineteen sixty one and
nineteen sixty six, the top is the same, you just get there later, and the
thing to watch is the earnings line while you are still working.
And if you were born in nineteen sixty seven, nothing lands on you, but a door
opens at sixty that nobody mentions.
One group moves. The rest of you were told otherwise.
Here is what I would do this week.
Open your account. Look at the three numbers together, not one at a time.
Write down your own full age and the year you reach it, on paper, where you
will find it again.
And if a husband or a wife has died and you are anywhere near sixty, find out
what a survivor payment on their record is worth before you assume you have
to wait.
If your situation has a twist I did not cover, a public pension, a divorce,
a year you barely worked, tell me in the comments.
I read them and they decide what I look into next.
This is general information and not guidance about your own record.
Your own earnings history and your own birth date decide your figures.

title: Banks Are Now Watching Direct Deposits Into Your Bank Account: Check Yours Now

segments.text: Since June, your direct deposit is looked at twice before you can spend it.
Once by the Treasury before the money leaves Washington.
Once by your own bank the moment it lands.
The second one is new. Every bank and every credit union in this country now
has to watch money arriving, not just money leaving, and hunt for the signs
that somebody redirected a payment to themselves.
Here is what that means on a Wednesday morning.
Your bank can hold the money after it posts.
And nobody has to write to you first.
You find out at the counter, or you find out when the mortgage bounces.
Now the part nobody says out loud.
There is no rule aimed at Social Security.
Nobody wrote a list with retirees on it.
Nothing starts in January.
What actually happened is quieter than that, and it does not end.
The signs these systems hunt for are
the ordinary money life of a retired household.
Three similar payments in one week.
An account you just opened. An account you have not touched in a year.
None of that is wrong. All of it is on the list.
And one of those two checks, your bank cannot fix at all.
If the Treasury stops your payment before it is sent, your branch can do nothing
for you. Only Social Security can, and only in person.
So one question for the next 15 minutes.
If your payment did not land tomorrow morning, do you know which office to
call first?
Most people call the wrong one and lose a week on it.
Five things to check before your next payment day.
Number three is the one sentence to say at the counter.
Numbers four and five are two free blocks at Social Security, and almost nobody
has been offered either one.
Everything here comes from the rule books.
Nacha, the Treasury, Social Security, and the federal regulations that govern
your account.
Every source is in the description.
My examples are invented. The rules are not.
Before we start, tell me in the comments.
Has a deposit of yours ever been late, short, or held, even for one day?
Number one. The name on the account.
Start here, because this is the one the new checks were built to catch, and
it is the one honest families break without knowing.
Under the Treasury rules, a federal benefit payment has to go into an account
in the name of the person receiving it.
Your own account meets that. A joint account with your daughter, with your
name on it, meets that. An account in your daughter name alone does not.
That sounds like paperwork until you see what changed last year.
The Treasury now checks whether the account really belongs to the person being
paid, and those checks became fully operational at the end of September.
In its own report it screened more than a billion federal payments, worth trillions
of dollars, and it stopped thousands that were about to go to people who had
died.
So picture how this happens. A woman in her eighties has a fall.
Her daughter starts handling the bills, and to keep things simple she has the
deposit sent to her own checking account.
Everyone acted out of love. Nothing was stolen.
And an account that belongs to somebody else is exactly the thing an ownership
check is built to notice. Now here is the part that catches people.
The daughter has power of attorney, and she assumed that covered it.
It does not.
Social Security does not recognize a power of attorney for receiving federal
payments. I want to say that again, because almost every family I hear from
gets this wrong. The document your lawyer drew up, the one that lets her sell
the house and talk to the hospital, does not let her receive your benefit into
her own account.
The tool that does exist is called a representative payee.
You apply to Social Security for it.
It is not the same thing and it is not automatic.
So the check before your next payment day is short.
Open your banking app. Read the name on the account.
Then look at your last letter from Social Security and read the name on that.
If they are not the same name, spelled the same way, that is your first phone
call. If you changed your name after a marriage or after losing a husband or
wife, this is where that shows up.
Number two. The four things banks look for.
This is the rule everybody is shouting about, so let me tell you exactly what
it says. The organization that writes the rules for electronic payments is
called Nacha. It is not a government agency, but every bank and credit union
that moves an electronic payment agrees to follow it, and in practice it works
like law. It brought this in over two stages.
From March, it applied only to the largest banks, the ones taking in 10 million
or more of these payments. From June, the size limit disappeared.
Every bank and every credit union now falls under it, down to the smallest
one in your town. What it requires is this.
Each bank must have processes built to spot money coming in that may have been
sent because somebody lied. And they have to review those processes at least
once a year. So this is not a crackdown that fades out.
It is the new normal. Now the four patterns.
These come from the guidance the banks themselves were given.
The first is a payment that does not fit the kind of account it lands in.
The second is a payment that is unusually large for that account.
The third is several similar payments arriving close together, and benefit
payments are named in that example.
The fourth is any of those landing in an account that is brand new, or one
that has been sitting untouched.
Read those four again and think about an honest retired couple.
His payment arrives on the second Wednesday.
Hers arrives on the fourth.
A pension lands on the first.
Their branch closed in the summer, so they opened an account at a credit union
and moved all three across in a single week.
Three similar payments, into an account with no history, in seven days.
Nothing about it is improper. Every piece of it is on that list.
So here is the move, and it is free.
If you are ever changing banks, do not move the deposit first.
Open the new account. Use it for a month, so it has a history.
Then move your deposit over in the days right after a payment has landed, never
in the days before one is due.
That single change in order takes you off three of the four patterns at once.
And if you have an old savings account you never touch, either use it now and
then or close it. A dormant account that suddenly fills up tells a story, whether
the story is true or not.
Number three. Held, or sent back.
This is the one you can actually fix, so if you remember one thing today, remember
this sentence. If your payment is not there, you walk up to the counter and
you ask exactly this. Is my deposit posted and held, or was it returned.
Those are two completely different situations and almost nobody knows there
is a difference.
Held means the money arrived. It is sitting in your account.
The bank has put a stop on your ability to spend it while it looks at something.
The money is still yours and it is still there.
What the bank usually needs is to confirm who you are, so take your identification,
and take a letter from Social Security that shows what they pay you.
You can print that from your own account on their website.
Returned means the money is gone.
The bank sent it back back to the Treasury.
Nothing you say at that counter will bring it back, because it is no longer
in the building.
That is the moment you stop talking to the bank and start talking to Social
Security, because the payment has to be sent out to you again, and only they
can do that. Get those two the wrong way around and you lose days you cannot
afford to lose. Rent does not wait while you learn the difference, and neither
does a car payment. People stand in a bank arguing about money that left the
building on Tuesday, or they sit on the phone to Social Security about money
that is sitting in their own account waiting for a signature.
Now two rules that are on your side, and almost nobody is told either one.
The first. A bank may not hold your money simply because it has not got round
to looking at it. A delay needs an actual reason.
The rule does not require them to check every payment before it posts, and
most of this watching happens after your money is already in your account.
The second. You may have heard that a new account means long holds.
That is true for paper checks.
It is not true for yours.
Under the federal availability rules, an electronic payment like your benefit
generally has to be available by the next business day, even in an account
less than 30 days old.
The long holds on new accounts are about paper.
What can actually slow your deposit is a suspicion, not the age of the account.
So if someone tells you it is held because the account is new, that is the
moment to ask the question again.
Posted and held, or returned. Number four.
The Direct Deposit Fraud Prevention block.
Here is something Social Security will give you for nothing, and will almost
certainly never offer you. Ask for it by its full name and the person on the
phone will know exactly what you mean.
Direct Deposit Fraud Prevention.
Say those four words and nothing else.
What it does is simple and it is strong.
It stops anyone from enrolling you in direct deposit, or changing your address,
or changing where your deposit goes, through the website or through a bank.
Anyone. Including you. That last part is the whole point, so let me explain
why it matters. When you open an account, a lot of banks can sign you up for
direct deposit with Social Security directly, without you ever calling the
agency. It is convenient. It is also a door.
Somebody who has enough of your details can walk through it.
The block closes the door. Once that block is on your record, a change has
to be made in person. You or your representative go to the office.
That is the cost, and I am not going to pretend it is nothing.
If you move house every other year, this will annoy you.
But if your deposit has gone to the same account for years, and you have no
plan to move it, that inconvenience costs you almost nothing and it shuts the
most common way this crime is actually done.
Nobody can quietly redirect a payment they are not allowed to touch.
Number five. The eServices block.
The second block goes further, and it suits a different person entirely.
The eServices block stops anyone from seeing or changing your information online
at all. Not just the deposit. Everything.
This one is for the person who is never going to use that website.
If you do all your business at the office or on the telephone, and you have
no intention of logging in, then an online account in your name is a liability
and not a convenience.
Close the online door completely and the only way to reach your record is in
person.
If you do use the website, this is not your block.
Take the first one instead.
And one last thing, because it is the other side of the same coin.
There is a genuine account you should open, in your own name, before anybody
else does.
An account you control is an account a criminal cannot quietly open pretending
to be you.
Set it up, look at the bank details on file, and check that they are the ones
you expect. While you are in there, look at your payment history and see what
actually arrived, not what you remember arriving.
So that is the five. The name on the account has to be your name, and a power
of attorney does not change that.
Four patterns are being watched for, and the ordinary life of a retired household
hits three of them in a bad week.
If the money is missing, there is one sentence that tells you which office
to call. And there are two free blocks sitting at Social Security that nobody
will offer you. Here is the part I want you to actually do, and it takes one
afternoon.
Open your banking app and read the name on the account.
Compare it with your last letter.
Then call Social Security and ask about the Direct Deposit Fraud Prevention
block by name, and decide whether the in person trade is worth it to you.
Then turn on an alert at your bank for every deposit that arrives, so you know
on the same morning if something is missing, instead of finding out when a
payment bounces.
And write one page and leave it somewhere you will find it.
Your payment date. Your bank fraud department number.
The Social Security number for your local office.
And the name of one person besides you who is allowed to see your accounts.
Nobody is coming to take your check, and I am not going to tell you otherwise
to keep you watching. But the system that moves it has more hands on it than
it had in June, and the people who get their money back quickly are the ones
who knew which door to knock on before they needed to.
If your situation has a twist I did not cover, a payee, a joint account after
a death, a deposit already being held, tell me in the comments.
I read them and they decide what I dig into next.
Everything here is general information, not guidance about your own money.
What your bank does, and what Social Security has on your record, decide what
happens to you.

title: Seniors: The 5 Things That Take Your Money in January, Not the Good News

segments.text: Social Security does not have to tell you what is left of your raise.
Nobody at that agency is required to send you that number.
They gave you 3.6% back in October.
About $75 a month. Both real. Neither one is what lands in your January check.
Five things come for that money on the first of January.
Not one of them needs your permission.
One of them arrives as a letter, and it can take half your check.
Half. There are three forms that stop it and roughly 90 days to send one, and
most people who get that letter sit on it until the money is already gone.
Two of the five have numbers that nobody can give you today.
Not me, not your plan, not the agency.
The figures are not published yet.
The money comes out anyway. No county office.
No number you have to beg someone for.
Five things, in order, and what each one takes.
Before the five, here is where my knowledge stops.
I can tell you what is already decided and signed.
I cannot tell you your own figure, because your plan, your state and your own
record decide that.
Three of these five reach everybody on Medicare.
Two of them reach you only in certain situations, and when we get to those
two I will say so at the top, not at the bottom.
Number one. The Part B premium.
Nobody can tell you the amount yet.
This is the one that reaches your money first.
Before the raise ever shows up in your account, the Part B premium comes out
of it. Right now that is $202.90 every month.
It goes up almost every January, and the amount for next year is not published.
Think about what that means for a second.
They announced your raise in October.
The thing that eats the biggest piece of that raise will not be announced until
the middle of November. So for about a month, every senior in this country
was told a number that nobody could finish.
So the $75 they talked about is not $75.
Part B gets there before you do.
And today nobody can tell you by how much, because the figure is not out.
Here is the part people get wrong.
They think the premium is a bill they pay.
For most people it is not a bill at all.
It is pulled straight out of the payment before the payment reaches the bank.
You never see the money. You never write anything.
There is no moment where you decide.
That is also why the increase is so easy to miss.
A bill that goes up, you notice.
A deduction that goes up inside a payment that also went up in the same month,
you do not notice. The raise and the deduction land together, and the number
in your account looks bigger, so you assume the raise came through.
There is one more thing about this deduction that nobody explains.
It does not come out evenly across the year.
It comes out at the full new amount from the very first payment of January.
So whatever the increase turns out to be, you absorb all of it immediately.
There is no easing in. There is a rule that stops your payment from actually
dropping. If the premium increase would be larger in dollars than your raise,
the increase gets cut back so your payment stays level instead of shrinking.
That sounds like protection, and for that month it is.
What it really means is that you were told about a raise and will receive none
of it. And that rule does not cover everybody.
It reaches you only if the premium already comes out of your Social Security
payment. If you pay Medicare directly instead, you are not covered.
If next year is your first year on Part B, you are not covered.
If your income is high enough that you pay extra for Medicare, you are not
covered at all, not even on the basic amount.
And if your state pays your premium for you, the rule does not reach you either.
Roughly three in every ten people on Medicare sit outside it.
It also does not cover the doctor costs I come to in a few minutes, and it
does not cover any late penalty you are carrying.
What you can actually do about this one is almost nothing, and I am not going
to pretend otherwise.
You cannot refuse it. You cannot pay it later.
You cannot ask for it monthly instead of taken at the source.
The one thing you can do is know the figure the day it comes out, so you can
work out what is really left instead of guessing.
The middle of November. Mark it.
Number two. The first $700 of your medicine.
That part is yours. If you have a drug plan, there is an amount you pay yourself
before the plan pays anything at all.
This year that amount tops out at $615.
Starting the first of January it tops out at $700.
That is $85 more out of your own pocket, and it comes at
the worst possible time of year, because it resets on the first.
Whatever you paid this year is finished.
It does not carry.
On the second of January you are back at the beginning of the ladder.
I want you to see how this collides with the thing I just told you.
Your raise lands in January. Your medicine bill also restarts in January.
If you fill anything in the first week, the money the raise was supposed to
give you is already at the pharmacy counter.
Some plans do not have that starting amount at all, or they have a smaller
one. That is real, and if that is your plan, good.
But the plans with no starting amount usually charge more every month instead,
so you paid it anyway, just spread out.
And here is the piece that makes people angry.
Your plan did write to you about this.
The notice went out at the end of September.
It is a thick envelope that looks like advertising, and it tells you exactly
what your plan is doing in January.
Most people throw it away. I am not going to tell you that is your fault, because
the thing is written to be thrown away.
But the letter exists, and if you still have it, the number is in there.
There is also a trap in the order of events here, and it is worth two minutes
of your life. The window to change drug plans for next year closes on the seventh
of December. The amount you will pay was decided months before that.
So the people who find out in January what their starting amount is are finding
out several weeks after the last day they could have done anything about it.
That is the whole design.
The price is set in the autumn, the warning goes out in an envelope that looks
like junk, the door shuts in early
December, and the money comes out in January.
Nobody breaks a rule anywhere in that sequence.
It just happens in an order that works against you.
So if you are watching this before the seventh of December, you still have
a door.
Compare what you have against what else is offered in your area, and look at
the starting amount, not only at the monthly cost.
A plan that charges you less every month and makes you pay $700 first is not
cheaper. It is just cheaper until you get sick.
Number three. The overpayment letter.
Half your check, and the three forms that stop it.
This is the one that can take the most, and it is the only one on this list
you can actually stop.
So if you remember one thing from today, remember this one.
If the agency decides it paid you more than it should have, at any point, going
back years, it sends a letter.
That letter says you owe the money back.
And unless you answer it, the agency
starts taking the money out of your monthly
payment. There is a number inside that letter that almost nobody knows about.
The amount it takes by default is half.
Half of your monthly retirement, survivor or disability payment, every month,
until the balance is cleared. It used to be a tenth.
For letters sent out since the spring of last year, the standard is half.
Read that again if you need to.
Not half of the extra.
Half of the whole payment. If your check is the thing that pays the rent, the
agency can cut it down the middle while it collects, and it does not need a
judge or a hearing to do it, because the money was never ruled to be yours.
And understand where these letters come from, because it is almost never fraud.
Somebody worked a few months and the earnings got counted late.
A spouse died and two payments crossed in the same month.
A disability review changed a date going backward.
The agency made an arithmetic error years ago and found it in a cleanup.
You did nothing. The letter still comes, and the letter still says you owe.
If what you get is the payment for people with very little income and few resources,
the standard for that one is still a tenth, not half.
That difference matters, so know which payment you receive.
Now the part that actually helps you.
You get roughly 90 days before the money starts coming out.
In that window you can do three things, and all three of them are free.
You can ask them to wipe the debt.
That is the waiver request. You use it when the mistake was not yours and paying
it back would leave you unable to cover your own bills.
You can tell them they are wrong about the money.
That is the reconsideration request.
You use it when you do not believe you were overpaid at all.
Or you can accept the debt and refuse the speed.
That is the request to change the rate.
You tell them what you can actually afford each month, and they lower the amount
they take. Sending any one of those freezes the collection while they look
at it. Sending nothing is what starts the clock.
And that is exactly what most people do.
The letter is long, it is frightening, it uses language nobody speaks, and
it sits on the kitchen table until the first short payment arrives and it is
too late to be gentle about it.
You can start any of the three by calling the agency or by going into your
own account on their website. You do not need a lawyer and you do not need
to pay anybody.
If someone offers to handle it for a fee, that is a person making money from
your fear.
Number four. On the first of January your doctor bill starts over at zero.
There is a second starting amount, separate from your medicine, and this one
is for doctors, tests and outpatient care.
This year it is $283.
It resets on the first of January, and the amount for next year is not published
yet either. So that is two of the five where the figure does not exist today.
What resetting means in practice is simple and it is harsh.
If you had a hard year, if you hit that amount in February and the coverage
carried you through to December, none of that follows you.
The first of January, you owe it again from the beginning.
The calendar does not care that you only finished paying it 11 months ago.
This is the one that catches people who get sick early in the year.
January, February, March is when this bites, because that is when everybody
is starting over at once. And because it is a starting amount and not a monthly
bill, there is no envelope to warn you.
You find out at the front desk.
I am not giving you a way around this one, because there is not one.
What I can tell you is that if you have a choice about when something gets
done, and it is not urgent, the end of a year that you have already paid through
is cheaper than the start of a year you have not.
A test in late December and the same test in early January are the same test

One more thing about this amount, because people assume wrongly.
The rule I mentioned earlier, the one that stops your payment from dropping,

This starting amount can rise every January no matter what your raise was,

The $2,400 line.
Nothing is free until you cross it.
This one reaches you only if your medicine is expensive,
so if your prescriptions are cheap, this is not yours and you can stop worrying
about it right now. For everybody else.
There is a point in the year where you have paid so much for covered medicine

the year.
That point is the best thing in this whole system.
It is also moving further away.
This year that line sits at $2,100.
Starting the first of January it sits at $2,400.
$300 further out. $300 more out of your own money before the protection switches

So if you crossed that line in September and have been paying nothing since,

There is one thing worth knowing here.
Only what you pay for the medicine itself counts toward that line.
The monthly amount you pay for the plan does not count.
People add it up wrong every single year and think they are closer than they

that actually hurts.
The money you pay first went up.
The line where you finally stop paying moved further out.
Both ends moved against you in the same month.
The stretch in the middle where you are paying out of your own pocket got longer

If your medicine costs are anywhere near this, there is help that pays a large

I am putting the page in the description.
Nobody should ever charge you to fill in that form.
If a company calls you offering to get it for you, hang up, because the same

One more, and it only reaches you if you are still working.
Social Security holds back $1 for every two you earn above a yearly line, and

If you reach full retirement age during the year, the line is much higher,

If you are fully retired, this one is not yours.
Add the five together and this is what January actually looks like.
3.6% sounds like a raise. By the time it reaches your hand, Part B has taken

Two of those four numbers are not even published yet, and they will be taken

Four of those five, you cannot stop.
I am not going to dress that up for you.
The fifth one you can stop, and it is the one that takes the most.

Do not let it sit. That is the whole list.
Tell me in the comments which of the five you did not know about, and if you

title: Social Security November 2026: Payment Dates, Early SSI and Who Gets Paid First?

Dates done.

A letter went out by the second of October that told some people their plan

I cannot see your plan, and your plan decides your own answer.

Some Medicare Advantage plans pay part of that back.
Not a discount on the plan. An
actual amount added back into your Social Security
deposit every month. It is written on the plan as a Part B premium reduction,

The amounts are not small. One plan for next year, in northern Indiana, puts

a year, on a plan with no monthly premium of its own.

Nearly two thirds lose it or see it shrink.
UnitedHealthcare is cutting it for about 7% of theirs.
Centene for about 11%. If you chose your plan because of that money, and most

And here is the thing nobody says about this benefit.
Nobody checks your income for it.
Not once. It is not a government program, it is a feature a private plan chooses
to offer, so nobody checks what you earn, nobody counts your savings, and there

So the job this week is one line on one page.
Go to medicare.gov, open the plan comparison tool, put in your own zip code,
and look at each plan for the line that says Part B premium reduction.
If your current plan shows a smaller number for next year than this year, that

ask them directly. Is my Part B premium reduction changing in January, and

Number two. One million plans end in January.
Humana has said that plan exits for next year will affect about 600,000 of
its Medicare Advantage members.
That is roughly 8% of everyone it covers.
UnitedHealthcare has confirmed about 390,000
members are in plans being discontinued,
and most of those are the kind that let you go outside the network.
Together that is close to a million people whose plan stops existing on the
thirty first of December. Let me be accurate about what that does and does
not mean, because the headline has been read wrongly in a lot of places.
It does not mean a million people lose their health coverage.
Humana has said most of its affected members will have another Humana plan
available to them. What it means is that the specific plan you are on, with

Something else replaces it, and the something else is not the same.
That is the part that costs money.
Your doctor may not be in the new network.
Your medicine may sit on a different tier.
The dental or the hearing allowance you were using may be smaller or gone.
Aetna and Centene are pulling back as well.
And the total number of plans across the country barely drops, from about 5,553
this year to about 5,532 next year.
So this is not plans vanishing from the map.
It is plans being closed and reshaped, and the reshaping is where you lose
things. The action is the same page as item one, and you do it before the seventh
of December. Put your own medicines and your own doctors in.
Not the plan name. The doctors and the medicines.
That is the only comparison that tells you anything.
Number three. The counties with no drug plan left.
This one is the hardest number in the
video, and it comes from an outside analysis,
not from a company.
In 193 counties across 16 states, there will be no Medicare Advantage plan

None.
638,000 people live in those counties.
Last year that figure was 399,000 people in 123 counties.
So it has grown by well over half in 12 months, and it is concentrated in rural

That does not leave you without medicine coverage.
It means your route changes. You go to Original Medicare and you buy a standalone

will be one next year. So if you live somewhere rural, do not assume.
Check the plan tool for your own zip code before December,
and if the drug plan list comes back empty, that is not a website fault.
That is the answer, and your next step is a standalone drug plan.
Number four. The letter that came by the second of October.
Every plan that is closing had to mail a notice to its members by the second
of October. It is called a non renewal notice.
Here is why I am giving it a whole item.
It arrives in a plain envelope from your insurance company, in the same month
as a pile of other plan post, and it does not say your plan is being cancelled
in large letters on the outside.
People open the marketing and throw out the rest.
If you threw it away, or if it is still in a pile on the side, you may not
know that your plan ends on the thirty first of December.
And the first time you find out will be at a pharmacy counter or a doctor reception
in January. So go and look. Anything from your Medicare plan that arrived in
the last 4 weeks, open it. You are looking for two phrases.
Non renewal, and will not be offered in your area.
Either of those means your plan is ending.
If you cannot find the mail, telephone the plan and ask one question.
Is my plan being offered in my area next year, yes or no.
They have to tell you. And if you are the son or daughter watching this, this
is the single most useful thing you can do for a parent this month.
Ask to see their Medicare mail from this month.
Not next month. Number five. The window that runs past the seventh of December.
Now the one item that is a right you already hold, not something taken.
Everybody is told that the seventh of December is the last day to change a
Medicare plan. For most people that is true.
But if your plan is one of the ones being closed, it is not true for you.
You get a longer window, and it exists precisely because the plan ended on
you and not the other way round.
That window runs from the eighth of December to the last day of February.
Inside it you can pick a new Medicare Advantage plan, or a standalone drug
plan, and you are not limited to the normal deadline.
Two timing details that matter and that nobody explains.
If you choose by the thirty first of December, your new cover starts on the
first of January, with no gap.
If you leave it until January or February, the new cover starts the first of
the month after you ask, which means you can be left with a gap of weeks.
So the window is real, but using it late costs you.
And there is one more right sitting underneath it.
When a plan is withdrawn from you, that can also open a guaranteed right to
buy a Medigap policy, which is the cover that sits beside Original Medicare,
without being asked a single health question.
Outside those protected windows, a Medigap company can ask about your health
and charge you more for it or turn you down.
Inside one, it cannot.
That right does not apply to every situation, so you confirm yours before you
rely on it. The free advice service in your own state will tell you in one
call, and they do not sell plans.
Ask Medicare to put you through to the free counseling office for your own
state. So that is the five. The give-back being cut.
A million plans closing. 16 states with no Medicare Advantage drug plan.
The letter from the second of October.
And the window that runs to the end of February if your plan was one of the
ones that closed. Four of them are things being taken.
One of them is a right you already have.
And the dates at the top are the easy part.
If you only do one thing this week, find your Medicare mail from the last 4 weeks
and open all of it. That is where you find out whether any of this is yours,
and it costs nothing but 20 minutes at the kitchen table.
This is education and nothing more.
Your plan, your zip code and your
medicines decide your own answer, and I can
see none of the three. And if your mother or father is on one of these plans,

Go and sit with them and open the envelope together.

title: Turn 65? The 5 Bills You Need Not Pay in Any State (Whatever You Earn)

segments.text: I do not get crap in Illinois.
That is a comment under the last video like this one.
Right below it, another comment.
Not in California.
And the comment that more people agreed with than any other was not a complaint
at all. It was a question. What states do all of these apply to.
Somebody watching this paid a bill last month that stopped being theirs years
ago. They will pay it again in 3 weeks.
And the months they already paid are gone.
There is no form for those. Nobody sends them back.
You did not miss a chance. You paid.
That money is spent and you are not getting it back.
So I am answering the state question before I name a single bill.
Most lists like this mix two different things together and never say which
is which.
Some of what they name is the same in every state, on every street in this
country. The rest is run by your county, or your state, or a program with a
waiting list, and whether you get it is decided in an office you have never
been to. So you call, you are told no, and you decide the whole thing was nonsense.
It was not nonsense. It was the wrong half of the list.
That cost you a year. Today I removed the wrong half.
The five bills in this video are the same in Texas, in Illinois, in California,
in all 50 states. Every one of them.
There is no county office in this video and no waiting list.
And not one of the five asks what you earn.
Nobody checks your income, nobody counts what you have saved, and no form asks
what your house is worth. You do nothing and they stop.
The other two keep arriving until you pick up the telephone and ask for them.
No office will call you first.
Every month you wait, you pay those two again.
I am not reading your file and I cannot see your paperwork.
What I can tell you is which of these the law requires and which one depends
on somebody being nice to you.
All five of these are the law.
Number one. The extra deduction at 65.
The day you turned 65, the amount of your income that gets taxed went down.
Permanently. Every year from then on.
The figure for this year is $2,050 if you are on your own.
For a married couple it is $1,650 for each person who is 65 or
older, so if you are both that age it is $3,300.
That is not a refund you claim once.
It is subtracted every single year for the rest of the years you file.
Now the part that makes this item worth more than the money.
There is no income limit on it.
None. You can have a pension, rental income, a paid off house, money in the
bank, and it does not change this figure by one cent.
That matters because there is a second senior deduction, the $6,000 one, and
that one does disappear as your income climbs.
It starts shrinking above $75,000 for one person.
People hear about that one, assume they earn too much, and then assume the
same thing about this one. They are two different lines on two different parts
of the form. This one has no ceiling at all.
And it is not automatic. The number has to be entered.
If somebody prepares your taxes, they almost certainly caught it.
If you fill in your own return and you ticked the wrong box about your age,
you did not get it, and you will not be told.
So here is what to do, and it takes 4 minutes.
Pull out the return you filed last year.
Find the standard deduction line.
If you were 65 or older and the figure you see is the plain amount with nothing
added, it was missed. You can go back and amend a return for 3 years, and that
is 3 years of tax back. If somebody else did your taxes, say this to them.
Confirm my age 65 standard deduction was applied, and show me the line.
Not ask whether it was. Make them show you.
Number two. The shingles shot, and three more like it.
The shingles shot. Two doses, and for years it ran past $200 for the pair,
because it sat on the wrong side of the rules and your drug plan was allowed
to charge you. That ended.
Adult vaccines on the recommended list now cost you nothing under a Medicare
drug plan. No copay. And no deductible, which means you do not have to spend
anything first.
Shingles. The one for the lung virus they now offer to older adults.
Tetanus. Whooping cough. All of them, nothing.
This one is on the list because of how often it goes wrong at the counter,
and it is not your mistake when it does.
There are two different sides to Medicare that can pay for a shot.
One side is your doctor. The other side is your drug plan.
These vaccines are paid by the drug plan side.
If the pharmacy or the clinic sends it to the wrong side, the claim comes back
as not covered, and somebody tells you there is a charge.
So when they tell you there is a charge,
you do not pay it and you do not walk away.
You say this. Please run this through my Part D drug plan, not the medical
side. That one sentence fixes most of them while you stand there.
And if you already paid for a shingles shot after it became free, your plan
can be made to pay you back. Call
them, give them the date, and ask for reimbursement.
Number three. Insulin at $35. If you take insulin, you pay no more than $35
a month for it. Each insulin product.
Not $35 for all of them together, $35 each.
Three things about that number that people get wrong.
It applies no matter which phase of the year your plan says you are in.
It applies even before you have paid your deductible.
And it applies whatever tier your plan has put the insulin on.
There is no version of this where the plan gets to charge you more because
of a tier. Before this rule, people were paying $300 and $400 a month, and
some of them were cutting doses in half to stretch a pen.
That is what this replaced. So the instruction here is short.
Look at what you paid at the pharmacy last month.
If the number is higher than $35 for one insulin, the plan has it wrong, not
you. Call the number on the back of the card and say this.
My insulin was charged above the $35 limit, I want it corrected and I want
the difference back. They will fix it.
They do not fix it on their own.
Number four. Your free yearly visit with the doctor.
Once a year you can sit with a doctor, go through your medicines, your memory,
your balance, your risks, and build a written plan for the year.
You pay nothing for it. Not a copay, and the deductible does not apply.
In your first year on Medicare there is a separate one, a one off visit, and
that is free as well. And the screenings around them are free too.
Colon cancer. Many cancer screenings.
Diabetes checks if you are at risk.
The blood check for heart disease.
A bone density scan when the rules call for it.
Here is the part that catches people, and it catches them every single year.
That yearly visit is not a physical.
It is a planning conversation.
If you walk in and start talking about a knee that hurts, the doctor has to
treat that, and treating it is a different kind of visit that does get billed.
Same chair, same day, two different things.
So do two things when you book.
Say the words annual wellness visit when you call the office, not check up
and not physical. And at the start of the appointment, say this.
I am here for the free yearly wellness visit.
If anything else needs looking at, tell me first that it will be billed separately.
That sentence costs nothing and it is the difference between a free visit and
a bill in 3 weeks. One honest line.
If a free screening finds something, what happens next is ordinary care, and
ordinary care is billed. The screening is free.
Treating what it finds is not, and nobody should tell you otherwise.
Number five. The donut hole is gone.
For nearly 20 years there was a hole in the middle of Medicare drug coverage.
You paid your share, then at a certain point your plan stepped back and you
paid far more, and then eventually help came back.
People called it the donut hole and planned their whole year around it.
It is gone. It was removed last year.
There is no middle phase any more.
What replaced it is a ceiling.
Once what you have paid out of your own pocket for covered medicines reaches
$2,100 this year, you pay nothing more for those medicines until January.
Not a smaller amount. Nothing.
I am putting this on the list because of what people still do in the autumn.
They skip a refill, or they split tablets, or they put off a new medicine until
the new year, because they are protecting themselves against a gap that no
longer exists. That is not caution any more.
That is paying for a rule somebody deleted.
So the job is to know your own total.
Add up what you have paid at the pharmacy since January.
If it is near $2,100, you are close to the point where the rest of the year
costs you nothing. Keep your receipts, because plans do get the tally wrong,
and if you are still being charged above the ceiling you call them and say
you have reached the yearly limit.
So that is the five. The tax line at 65.
The shingles shot. The insulin ceiling.
The yearly visit. The ceiling that replaced the donut hole.
Three of them need nothing from you.
The vaccines, the insulin price, and the drug ceiling all happen on their own,
and your only job is to notice when a pharmacy gets one of them wrong.
Two of them need you. The deduction has to be on the return.
The wellness visit has to be booked, with the right words.
Not one of the five changes if you move house.
Not one of them asks what you earn.
One last thing, and it is not a sixth item, because it breaks the rule I set
at the start. You may have heard about a one off payment of $90 towards the
Part B premium. That is real. It is going to about 20 million people.
And roughly 40 million others are not getting it, because it only goes to people
on original Medicare who are not on a Medicare Advantage plan, who do not pay
the higher income premium, and who do not already have their premium paid for
them. There is no form and there is no appeal.
Look at your bank record once, and if it is not there, let it go.
I am telling you because somebody will try to sell you help getting it.
Everything here is general education.
I do not know your plan, your income or what is in your file, and those three
decide your own figure.
And if your mother or your father is still paying one of these five, do not
forward them this video. Sit down beside them and read their pharmacy receipt
together.

title: October 30 Warning: 6 Critical Social Security Deadlines Nobody Mails You

segments.text: The thirtieth of October is not a deadline.
Nothing closes on that day. No office
shuts a door, no form stops being accepted,
and nothing is taken out of your account.
If somebody told you to move your money before the thirtieth, ask them to name
the rule. There is no rule.
I will give you the date they should have given you instead, and it sits in
December.
Here is what is true. Six real dates land between now and the first of January.
Every one of them has a number attached to it.
And not one of them arrives with a letter warning you that it is about to close.
The first one is 23 days away.
Miss it and you wait three extra weeks to find out what your own check will
be. Two questions always come first, so I will deal with them before item one.
Does this depend on where I live.
No. All six are exactly the same in every state.
Same in Texas, same in Ohio, same in California.
Not one of them goes through a county office or a state office.
Do you have to be poor. No. Not one of these six asks what you earn, what you
have saved, or what your house is worth.
There is no income line anywhere in this video.
Four of the six ask something of you, and three of those four take under 15 minutes
at your own kitchen table. The other two land whether you act or not, and the
only thing you can do is know the number before it arrives.
Every figure in this video comes from Social Security, from Medicare, or from
the law that set it. What I cannot see is your plan and your paperwork, and
those two decide your own amount.
Number one. November eighteenth.
The notice that comes early. Your raise for next year is 3.6%.
For the average retired worker that moves the check from $2,095 a month to
$75 more.
Almost 72 million people are getting it.
That part is settled.
Nobody can take it and you do not apply for it.
What is not settled is when you find out your own number.
Not the average. Yours. Social Security has set one date for that, and almost
nobody has heard it. If you have an account at my Social Security, and you
have told them you want your notices without paper, your own figure appears
in your message center in late November.
If you have not, your notice comes by post in December.
Three weeks apart. Same money, same raise, three weeks of not knowing.
And the cut off to be on the early side is the eighteenth of November.
Why that matters more than three weeks of waiting.
Your December and January bills are being set right now.
The plan premium, the heating, the insurance that renews in January.
If you know your real figure in late November you are deciding with the true
number in front of you. If you wait for the post you are guessing through the
most expensive six weeks of the year, and then correcting in January.
So this week, go to my Social Security and open an account if you do not have
one. It is free and it takes about 10 minutes.
Then find the setting for paperless notices and switch it on.
That is the whole job. If you already have an account, do not assume you are
covered. Having the account and choosing paperless are two separate switches,
and most people only ever did the first one.
Log in and check the second.
Number two. December seventh. Your plan locks for the whole year.
The window to change your Medicare drug plan or your Medicare Advantage plan
is open right now. The seventh of December is the last day it stays open.
Whatever you are holding on the eighth, you carry all the way to next December.
Here is the part that costs people real money, and it has nothing to do with
whether you like your plan. Your plan is allowed to change its own list of
covered medicines every January.
Not with your permission and not with a phone call to you.
The medicine that cost you a small copay this year can sit outside the list
in January, at full price, and the first you hear of it is at the counter in
the chemist. That is the trap in plain terms.
People check whether they are happy with their plan.
