The question is not whether you are happy.
The question is whether the plan still covers your medicines next year, because
that is the thing that moved. So the job is one visit to medicare.gov, to the
tool that compares plans, with your actual medicines typed in.
Every one of them, by name. Or one call to the number on the back of your card
and the words, is every medicine on my list still covered next year, and what
will each one cost me. If the answer is yes, you do nothing and you are done.
If the answer is no, you switch before the seventh, and the new plan starts
on the first of January. And if you want somebody to sit with you through it
at no charge and with nothing to sell you, every state has a free advice service
for exactly this.
Ask Medicare for the free counselling service in your state.
They do not sell plans. That is the point of them.
Number three. The Part B number nobody actually has yet.
$202.90 comes out of your Social Security every month before the money reaches
you. That is the Medicare Part B premium for this year.
It is not a bill you receive. It is already gone when the deposit lands.
Now listen to this carefully, because it is the single most repeated mistake
in every video about your raise.
The figure for next year has not been announced.
Not by anybody. The people who publish it normally do it in November.
Today it does not exist. The best public estimate is around $209.50,
and that estimate comes from the official projection, not from a decision.
So when somebody tells you with confidence what your Part B premium will be
in January, they are reading a forecast and calling it a fact.
I have watched a video this month that put the figure at $29.50.
That is not a smaller number. That is the real number with a digit dropped,
and the whole video was built on it.
Why you should care about an unannounced number.
Because it comes out of your raise before you see your raise.
$75 arrives, the premium takes its share first, and the figure that actually
lands in your account is the one after that subtraction.
Until the real premium is published, nobody can tell you your January deposit.
Including me. So here is the only honest instruction.
When your own notice appears, late November if you did item one, December if
you did not, read the line for the premium and the line for the net payment,
and compare both against this year line by line.
Not the percentage. The two lines.
One thing that has been announced.
A one off payment of $90 towards the Part B premium is going to more than 20 million
people on Medicare. About 40 million others are not getting it.
If nothing has appeared, you are very likely in the second group, and there
is no form to fill in and no appeal to make.
Check your deposits, then stop looking.
Number four. January to March.
The second window. Now the one that is good news, and the one I almost never
see covered. If January goes badly, you are not locked in until next October.
If you are on a Medicare Advantage plan, you get a second window from the first
of January to the thirty first of March.
One change. You can move to a different Advantage plan, or you can leave and
go back to Original Medicare.
That exists because the people who wrote the rules knew that January is when
you discover what your plan actually does.
Three limits, and I will say them plainly so nobody is caught out.
It is one change, not several.
It only applies if you are already on an Advantage plan, so if you are on Original
Medicare this window is not yours.
And if you use it to go back to Original Medicare, you have to pick up a separate
medicine plan at the same time, or you will have no cover for medicines at
all. Your change starts on the first day of the month after the plan receives
it. So a change made in January starts in February.
What to do with this. Nothing today.
Write the thirty first of March on a piece of paper and keep it with your plan
card. If something goes wrong in January, you take that paper out and you ring
the plan or you ring Medicare.
Most people in that situation believe they have to live with it for a year.
They do not.
Number five. December thirty first.
One form, 4 minutes. The amount of tax held back from your Social Security
check every month was set on the day you first asked for it.
If you have never asked for any to be held back, nothing is being held back.
Either way, that decision is probably out of date.
Your income changed this year.
It changes for most people every year.
If too little is being held back, you get a bill in the spring that you did
not plan for, in the same months the heating bill is at its highest.
If too much is being held back, you have been lending money to the government
at no interest for twelve months, and you get it back slowly, long after you
needed it. The form that fixes both is called W-4V.
You can file it at any time, and you can file it again later to change your
mind or to stop it completely.
You are not choosing an amount.
You choose one of four percentages, and they are seven, ten, twelve and 22 percent
of each payment. No other figure is allowed, so do not spend an evening trying
to work out a custom number. The deadline here is not a rule, it is arithmetic.
The tax year closes on the thirty first of December, so a correction filed
in November or early December still reaches most of this year.
One filed in February reaches none of it.
The paper version goes to your local Social Security office, not to the tax
office. Or you can ask for the change by telephone or on the website, which
is faster. The whole job is one page and 4 minutes.
Number six. December eleventh.
The real next date. This is the date that should have been in every video you
watched about the thirtieth of October.
The law that is keeping the federal government funded runs out on the eleventh
of December. That is not a forecast.
It was signed at the start of September and the date was written into it.
Now the part you need, because the fear around this is sold hard and it is
sold wrong. Your Social Security payment is not funded by that law.
It does not stop on the twelfth of December.
It did not stop the last time, it has not stopped in any previous one, and
nobody has to pass anything for your deposit to arrive.
The same is true of your Medicare cover.
What does slow down is service.
Offices, telephone lines, new
applications, appeals, replacement cards, the
paperwork that needs a person at a desk to move it.
Which turns the eleventh of December into the real reason to finish items one,
two and five this month rather than next.
Every one of those three needs a working office or a working helpline.
In the first week of December those lines are at their busiest in the year
anyway, and that is before you add any disruption on top.
So that is the calendar. The eighteenth of November for your own figure.
The seventh of December for your plan.
The thirty first of December for the form.
The eleventh of December for the waiting line.
January to March if January goes wrong.
And the Part B figure, which nobody can give you yet and which decides what
actually lands. Not one of those six is the thirtieth of October.
Two of the six happen with no help from you.
Your raise lands, and the Part B premium takes its share.
Four of them need you, and three of those four are shorter than this video.
If you only do one thing this week, open my Social Security and turn on paperless
notices before the eighteenth.
It is free, it is 10 minutes, and it is the difference between knowing your
own number in November and finding it out after Christmas.
This is education and not advice about your own position.
Your plan, your income and your paperwork decide your own answer.
And if your mother or your father is living on this money alone, do not forward
them this video. Sit down beside them and open the account together.

title: ⚠️ Every Senior Should Check These 7 Benefits for January 2027 — 5 Are Automatic

segments.text: Starting in January the average retired worker gets $75 more every month.
That is $900 over the year, and you do not fill in a single form to get it.
And that is the smallest of the seven things I am going to give you today.
I know what the last few months have sounded like.
Prices up,
Medicare plans dropped, warnings about your savings and your check.
Some of that was real and I covered it here.
Today is the good side. Before we start, two things, because they are the two
questions I get under every video like this one.
The first. Does this apply where I live.
Six of these seven are exactly the same in all 50 states.
Same in Texas, same in Illinois, same in California.
Only one of them goes through your own state office, and I will tell you which
one when we get to it. The second.
Do you have to be poor for any of this.
Only two of the seven ask what you earn.
The other five do not ask at all.
They do not look at your income, they do not look at your savings, and they
do not care that your house is paid off.
If you have been ruling yourself out, you have been ruling yourself out of
the wrong five. Here is the shape of it.
Five of the seven arrive on their own.
You do nothing and the money moves.
The other two do not, and those two are the biggest ones.
Nobody writes to you about those.
Nobody telephones. So that is where we start.
Every number here comes from Social Security, Medicare or the tax office.
I cannot see your income, your state or your paperwork, and those three decide
your own figure.
Number one.
The Medicare Savings Program. Right now
$202.90 comes out of your Social Security every month before you ever see it.
That is your Medicare Part B premium.
Your state will pay it for you.
Not part of it. All of it. That is $2,434 a year back in
your hand.
Most people never apply because they hear a program for seniors and decide
they earn too much. So here are the actual lines, and they have names you can
say on the telephone.
The first is called QMB. One person up to $1,350 a month.
It pays the premium and it also wipes out most of what you hand over at the
doctor and the hospital. The second is called SLMB.
Up to $1,616 a month. It pays the premium.
The third is called QI. Up to $1,816 a month.
It pays the premium too. Read that top number again.
$1,816 a month. That is most retired people in this country.
Now the part that costs people the most, and almost nobody says it out loud.
They do not count every dollar you bring in.
$20 a month is set aside before they start, and if you still work, another
$65 of your wages is set aside on top of that.
So the number on your bank statement can sit above the line and you still get
in. Say that plainly. A single person bringing in $1,900 a month can still
land inside the third level, because 85 of those dollars were never counted
in the first place.
Your savings count, but the line is higher than you think.
$9,950 for one person.
$14,910 for a couple. Your home does not count.
One car does not count. And here is the part that makes it worth more than
the premium. The moment you are in any of these three, you automatically get
a second one called Extra Help, and that cuts what you pay for your medicine
on top.
One warning. That third level, QI, is paid out of a pot of money that is fixed
for the year and handed out in the order people apply.
When it is gone, it is gone until January.
So call your state Medicaid office and ask for the Medicare Savings Program
application by name. Your state, not Medicare.
Ask them whether your state uses higher limits than the federal ones, because
many do. And do not decide for yourself that you are over the line.
Let them tell you. Number two.
The $6,000 deduction. If you are 65 or older you can take an extra $6,000 off
the income you are taxed on. 12,000 for a couple when you both qualify.
This did not exist two years ago.
It runs through 2028 and then it is gone.
Here is what I need you to hear clearly, because the videos get this wrong.
Nobody made your Social Security tax free.
What this does is lower the income the tax office counts against you.
For a great many people on a modest income the result is that the tax on the
check comes out at nothing anyway.
Same ending, different road, and knowing which road you are on is what stops
the form being filled in wrong.
It also shrinks once your income passes 75,000 for one person, or 150,000
for a couple. And it is not automatic.
It has to be on your return.
If somebody else does your taxes, say the words extra deduction for age 65
and over, and make them show you the line.
Number three. Your raise. 3.6%, from January.
The average retired worker goes from $2,095 a month to $2,170.
$75 more. Over the year, $900.
This one needs nothing from you.
It lands on its own. Two things to watch when your notice arrives in the post.
Compare it line by line with last year, because the Medicare premium comes
out before the raise reaches you, and the number you actually receive is the
smaller of the two. And the Medicare
figure for next year has not been announced
yet, so anybody quoting it to you today is guessing.
Number four. 15 medicines get a new price.
On the first of January the price Medicare pays for 15 of the most expensive
drugs drops, and the second round is bigger than the first.
One example tells you the size of it.
The diabetes and weight medicine that carried a list price near $960 for a
month now sits at $274.
The prostate cancer one falls by nearly half.
You do not apply for this. If you take one of the 15, your price simply changes
in January. What to do is small and it matters.
In January, telephone your plan and ask what you pay now for each medicine
on your list. The price moved, but your plan will not write and tell you it
moved.
Number five. The ceiling on what medicine can cost you.
$2,400. That is the most you can be made to pay out of your own pocket for
covered medicine in the whole of next year.
Once you reach it, you pay nothing more until January comes round again.
The amount you pay before the plan starts helping is capped too, at $700.
Nobody has to tell you when you cross that ceiling, and plans do not always
get it right. Keep your pharmacy receipts for the year, and if you are still
being charged after $2,400,
telephone the plan and say you have reached the yearly cap.
Number six.
The earnings limit, if you are still working.
If you took your Social Security early and you are still working, they hold
back a dollar for every two you earn above a line.
From January that line goes up to $25,560.
In the year you reach your full age the line jumps to $67,920, and they only
count what you earn before your birthday month.
And here is the piece almost nobody is told.
The money they hold back is not taken from you.
When you reach your full age they work it out again and give it back to you
in a higher monthly payment for the rest of your life.
People turn down hours they needed because they thought the money was gone.
It was never gone. Number seven.
Your January payment lands in December.
If you are on the extra payment for people with very little income, your January
money arrives on the 31st of December, because the first falls on a holiday.
So you get two deposits in December and nothing at all on the first of January.
Every year people see that second December deposit, decide the government sent
something extra, and spend it.
By the middle of January the account is empty.
Write the word January on your calendar beside the 31st of December.
That deposit is next month, handed to you one day early.
So that is the seven. Five of them arrive on their own.
Your raise, the 15 medicines, the ceiling, the earnings limit and the December
payment. You do nothing and they happen.
Two of them do not. The $6,000 deduction has to be on your tax return.
The Medicare Savings Program has to be applied for at your state office.
Those two are the biggest money on the list, and they are the two nobody will
ever contact you about. If you only do one thing this week, make it the telephone
call. Your state Medicaid office, the Medicare Savings Program application,
by name. A refusal costs you nothing and takes 20 minutes.
Not asking costs you $2,400 every single year you stay quiet.
This is education and not advice about your own situation.
Your income, your state and your paperwork decide your own answer.
And if your mother or your father is living on Social Security alone, do not
send them this video. Sit beside them and make that call together.

title: Congress Just Passed a Social Security Bill — 5 Changes, One Is a Mistake

segments.text: You heard that Congress passed a Social Security bill.
That part is true. It cleared the Senate on the 29th of September, and the
House passed it before that.
Here is the part nobody is leading with.
Not one dollar of your check changes.
Not the amount, not the day it lands, not who qualifies.
Nothing about the money moves.
What moves is three words. And before those three words were written into a
bill, they were tested on people.
Around three and a half thousand of them were sat down and shown two versions
of the same information.
One group read the words the government uses today.
The other group read the words that are about to replace them.
Nobody in that room was told what was really being measured.
It worked. The people who read the new words said they would wait longer before
claiming, by about 10 weeks on average.
And the people it moved the most were the ones who understood money the least.
Read that last part again, because it is the whole thing in one line.
The new words did not do much to people who already knew how the system works.
They worked on the people who did not.
Those are the people who most need the letter to be straight with them, and
they are the ones the wording moves.
So this is not a bill about your benefit.
It is a bill about the three words that sit between you and the biggest money
decision of your life, and somebody checked first that the new words would
change your mind. I cannot see your birth year, your work record or your health,
and those three decide what you should actually do.
What I can do is give you all five changes, tell you which one is honest, and
show you the one that has a mistake buried inside it.
Number one.
62 is now the minimum.
30% less, forever. Today the government calls 62 the early eligibility
age.
Early tells you something. It warns you.
The new name is minimum monthly benefit age.
Minimum sounds like a floor. A floor is a safe place to stand.
People hear minimum and they think of the smallest thing they are entitled
to, the thing that is theirs no matter what.
It is not a floor. It is the earliest door, and it is the most expensive one
in the building.
Here is the number nobody puts next to that word.
If your full age is 67 and you start at 62, every monthly payment is about
a third smaller. Not for a year.
Not until you reach 67. For the rest of your life, and then for your widow
or your widower after you. That is not a fine you pay once and finish.
It is the price of every single month that comes after.
And this already happens without the new word.
In the most recent year counted, about one in four people who started their
retirement benefit started it at 62.
More than half started before they reached their full age.
Number two. 65 is called standard, and your full age may be 67.
This is the one with the mistake inside it, and I want you to hear it slowly.
The bill removes the words full retirement age and normal retirement age.
In their place it puts standard monthly benefit age.
And the age the bill attaches that word to is 65.
Now hold that against the law as it stands today.
Your full retirement age is not 65.
It was 65, back when Social Security started in the 1930s.
Congress raised it in 1983, one slice at a time, and for anybody born in 1960
or later it finished at 67. So a man born in 1962 turns
65 in 2027. Under the new wording he reaches the standard age.
Under the actual rules he is two years short of his full one, and if he claims
there his check is permanently smaller.
Standard is the most dangerous word in this bill.
It sounds like the setting everything arrives on.
It sounds like the one you get if you do nothing and ask nobody.
Nothing arrives on a standard setting.
You still have to apply, and the age that matters for your money is the one
tied to the year you were born, not the one tied to the new word.
And look at who this lands on hardest.
65 is already the age burned into everybody over 70,
because for forty odd years that was the real number.
It is also the age Medicare starts, so it is the one age people are certain
about. Put the word standard on it and you have taken the age people already
half believe in and handed it an official sounding title.
A woman born in 1962 will turn 65 and see standard on her letter.
She signed up for Medicare that same year, so the number already feels correct.
If she claims there, she takes a permanent cut she never agreed to, and nothing
in that letter will have told her so.
I want to be careful here, because this is the one place I could mislead you.
The bill does not change her full age.
Her full age is still 67.
What the bill changes is which number carries the word that sounds final.
Number three. 70 is now the maximum.
The biggest check there is. I will be fair about this one, because one change
in this bill helps you.
Today the government calls the extra money you get for waiting the delayed
retirement credit.
Say that out loud to somebody at a kitchen table and watch their eyes.
It sounds like paperwork. It sounds like something that happens to other people.
The bill deletes that phrase and names 70 the maximum monthly benefit age.
That is the first time the government will have put the word maximum anywhere
near the number 70. Waiting until 70 pays the largest monthly amount the system
will ever pay you, and after 70 it stops growing, so there is no reason to
wait past it. For years that has been the best kept open secret in the whole
system, written down in public and understood by almost nobody.
The new word says it in one breath.
So yes.
One of the three is honest. Number four.
Every letter they send you changes by January.
The bill gives the agency a deadline.
Every piece of material has to use the new words no later than 12 months after
the bill becomes law, or the first of January 2027, whichever comes later.
That means the statement you get once a year, the letters, the pages on the
website, the booklet in your drawer.
All of it changes language. So the paper that lands in your mailbox next year
will not read the way the one in your drawer reads now.
Same system, same rules, same money, different words.
And nobody is going to post you a note explaining why.
If you keep your old letters, keep them.
When the new ones arrive you will want something to hold them against.
Number five. A second law was signed, and that one does something.
This is the part almost nobody has mentioned,
and it is the only thing in either
bill that changes what actually happens to a person.
A separate bill went through on the same run and it was signed on the seventh
of October.
It deals with identity theft. If somebody steals your Social Security number
and uses it, you know what happens now.
You telephone, you explain the whole thing, you are passed along, and the next
time you call you start the story again from the beginning with somebody who
has never heard it. Under the new law the agency has to give you one named
person who handles your case from one end to the other.
They have 180 days to set it up.
That is a smaller headline and a bigger change than anything in the wording
bill. So that is the five. Now the part I owe you, because it is the thing
everybody in the comments is saying and it deserves a straight answer rather
than a nod. The suspicion is simple.
They tested the words, the words made people wait, waiting means the government
pays out later, and some people will not be here to collect.
So the whole thing is a trick to keep your money.
Here is the honest version. The study measured what people said they would
do, not what they actually did.
A person in a survey saying they would wait 10 weeks longer is not a person
who waited. Nobody has the real numbers yet and will not have them for years.
But the rest of the suspicion is not wrong, and I am not going to pretend it
is. They did run a test. They did find words that moved people.
They did then put those words into law.
Whatever the intention, that sequence is exactly what happened, and you are
allowed to feel how you feel about it.
Here is what I would hold on to.
A word is not a rule. The claiming ages have not moved.
62 still pays less, your own full age still pays full, 70 still pays the most,
and all three of those were true last month and will be true next year.
The only thing that changed is which of them sounds safe when you read it quickly.
So this week, do one thing. Find out your own full retirement age, the real
one, tied to the year you were born.
Not 65 because a new word says standard.
Not 62 because a new word says minimum.
Yours. It takes one telephone call or one page on the government website, it
costs nothing, and once you know that number no wording on any letter can move
you. This is education. It is not advice about your own situation.
Your birth year, your health and your work record are three things I cannot
see, and those three decide your answer.
And if your son or your daughter is somewhere near 60, tell them this one.
They are the ones who will read the new letters first, and minimum is going
to be the first word they see.

title: Never Keep More Than This in One Bank Account Over 65 — 5 Hands Can Freeze It

segments.text: Two men, both 68. Same town, same bank, close to the same money
sitting in the same kind of account.
One of them woke up on a Tuesday and could not buy food.
$14,000 of his own money was still sitting there.
He could see it on the screen.
He simply could not touch a cent of it.
He had broken no law. He had missed no payment on anything he knew about.
Nobody had to warn him. Not the bank, not the court, not the person who started
it. The letter that explains it arrives after the money is already locked,
and by then the rent has bounced and the pharmacy has turned him away.
Here is the part that decides which of those two men you are.
It was not how much money they had.
It was how many places they kept it, and whether the money arriving every month
arrived the right way.
Five hands can reach into an account like that and stop you using it.
I am going to name all five. Two of them need no judge at all.
And at the end I will give you the one amount that stays yours no matter which
hand arrives, and the one condition you have to meet to keep it.
None of these five is a secret.
Every one of them is written down, in public, on a government website that
costs nothing to open.
They do damage for one reason only.
Each one is learned on the day it happens, by the person it happens to, standing
at a counter.
Hand number one. Your own bank, and it needs no permission but its own.
This is the one almost nobody sees coming, because it does not feel like a
stranger.
If you owe that same bank money on a car loan, a personal loan, or an overdraft,
the bank is allowed to reach into your checking or savings account at that
same bank and take what you owe.
No court. No hearing. No letter first.
It is written into the account agreement you signed, and most people signed
it without reading the page it sits on.
The bank calls it a right of setoff.
What it means in plain language is that money in one building can pay a debt
in the same building, and the building decides when.
Now here is the line the banks do not put in large print.
They are not allowed to do this for a credit card balance.
That is a federal rule and it is specific.
A card company cannot take money out of your checking or savings account to
cover what you owe on their card, and it cannot simply freeze that account
to squeeze you either.
Under the rule, freezing counts as taking.
Think about how much that one sentence is worth.
Card debt is the debt most people over 65 actually carry, and it is the one
debt that cannot reach your account this way.
So if a bank tells you it has taken your money for a card debt, that is the
sentence to repeat back to them, in writing, that day.
And notice what the whole thing depends on.
The loan and the account have to be at the same bank.
If they are not, this hand cannot reach you at all.
Hand number two. The government, and this one also skips the courtroom.
If you owe back taxes, the tax office does not have to sue you first.
It can send an order straight to your bank, and your bank must hold the money.
Here is the piece almost nobody is told.
The bank holds it for 21 days before it sends it anywhere.
That is not a formality. That is a window, and it is the only one you get.
Most people spend the first two weeks of it frightened and silent, and then
it closes.
There is a second version of this that never touches your bank at all, because
it takes the money before it ever arrives.
If you owe a federal debt, such as a student loan that went into default, the
government can take a slice out of your monthly benefit at the source.
The rule puts a ceiling on it.
It is the smaller of three figures, and one of those figures is the amount
by which your monthly benefit rises above $750.
So a benefit of $850 loses $100, not the 15% people
fear. That floor exists. Almost nobody quoting the 15% number mentions it.
Hand number three. A debt collector, and this one does have to go through a
judge.
A collector cannot simply order your bank to freeze anything.
First it has to sue you and win.
Then it takes that judgment to a court and gets an order, and that order goes
to your bank.
So far that sounds like protection.
Here is why it is not, for a great many people.
If you are sued and you do not answer, the court can rule against you anyway.
You lose without ever walking into a room.
Most of the frozen accounts I read about did not come from a fight that was
lost. They came from an envelope that was never opened.
If you are ever handed court papers about a debt, the one thing that matters
is that you respond by the date on the paper.
Even a simple response keeps the door open.
Silence closes it. And notice what gets frozen.
Not you. The account. Every dollar in it stops at the same moment, including
the money that has nothing to do with the debt, including the money your wife
put in, including the money set aside for the funeral.
One account means one switch.
Hand number four. A support order for a former wife or a child.
This one surprises people because they assume old family matters cannot follow
a retirement check. They can.
Social Security retirement and disability payments can be reached for child
support or spousal support that is owed.
But there is a line here that is worth knowing by name.
The extra payment for people with very little income, the one that arrives
on top of a small Social Security check, is treated differently.
That payment cannot be taken for support, and it cannot be taken for a government
debt either. It is protected in a way the ordinary retirement check is not.
So two people can sit at the same table, both over 65, both with a bank account,
and the same order reaches one of them and bounces off the other.
The difference is which payment they live on.
Hand number five. The other name on the account.
If somebody else is named on your account, their debts walk in through your
door.
A company your son owes money to can win in court against him, and then go
after the account he is named on, even if every dollar in it came from your
pension. He never touched it. His name on the paperwork was enough.
What happens next depends entirely on where you live.
In some states the law assumes the money is split evenly between the two names.
In other states the whole balance can be taken, and it is on you to prove,
with records going back years, which part was yours.
A dozen or so states give married couples a particular form of joint ownership
that keeps one spouse debts away from the other.
I cannot tell you which rule your state follows and I am not going to guess
at it in front of you. What I can tell you is that adding a name to an account
for convenience, so somebody can help with the shopping, is not a small act.
There are other ways to let somebody help you that do not hand your balance
to the people they owe. So that is the five.
Now the part I promised, and it is the part worth writing down.
When a court order arrives at your bank, the bank is required to look back
through two months of your account history first.
Whatever you received in Social Security, disability, veterans benefits, railroad
retirement or federal retirement in those two months is protected and stays
available to you. The bank does this on its own.
You do not have to ask, you do not have to file anything, and you do not have
to know the rule exists. Say you receive $1,000 a month.
Your bank sees $2,000 of benefits in the last two months.
$2,000 stays yours to spend, that day, while everything above it may be frozen.
Here is the condition, and it is the whole video in one sentence.
That protection only exists if the money arrives by direct deposit.
If your benefit comes as a paper check and you walk it into the bank yourself,
the bank is not required to protect anything.
Not two months. Not one month.
Not a dollar. The entire balance can be frozen, and then it is on you to go
to a court and prove where the money came from, while the rent is due.
Same person. Same amount. Same bank.
One of them keeps $2,000 and one of them keeps nothing, and the only difference
is how the money walked in the door.
That is the difference between the two men at the start.
So here is what this week looks like.
Find out how your benefit arrives.
If it is a check, switch it to direct deposit, and that is one phone call.
Look at whether your loan and your main account sit at the same bank, because
that is the only way hand number one can reach you.
Look at whose name is on your account beside yours.
And if court papers ever arrive, answer them by the date printed on the page,
even if you have nothing to pay with.
Treat this as education and not as advice about your own money.
Your state, your account and your own paperwork are three things I cannot see,
and those three decide your answer.
And if your mother or your father still gets a paper check, do not send them
this video. Sit down beside them, telephone the office together, and switch
it while you are in the room. The two months only protects the people who did
that before the order arrived.

title: Should Seniors Move Money Out of Their Bank Account? 5 Things Most Never Hear

segments.text: On the thirtieth of October a payment lands in a great many bank accounts.
In a great many houses it will be gone before the eighth of November.
Then nothing arrives for twenty eight days.
That is not a guess. That is the calendar, and it is already decided.
Now the thing you were told. Move your money before the first of November.
I went looking for that rule. It is not there.
Nothing changes at your bank that day.
No law takes effect. And not one person telling you to move your money has
ever shown you the rule, because there is no rule to show.
So there is your answer. Nothing changes on the first of November.
But five things are real, and every one of them is already set.
The first one empties a month.
I cannot see your account and I am not going to pretend that I can.
What I can do is tell you which of the five reach you.
Two of them touch only people on one kind of payment.
Three touch everybody over 65.
None of this is hidden. Every number here sits on a government website, free,
for anybody who looks.
It works badly for people only because nobody posts it to you.
Number one. The money that lands on the thirtieth of October is November money.
Spend it and November is empty.
Here is why it comes early. The first of November falls on a Sunday this year.
Payments do not go out on a Sunday.
So they go out on the working day before, and that day is Friday the thirtieth
of October.
This is the extra payment for people with very little income, the one that
arrives on top of a small Social Security check.
If that is you, two deposits land in October.
One at the start of the month, and one on the thirtieth.
Now the part that empties a house.
That second deposit is not a bonus.
It is not back pay. It is not extra.
It is November, handed to you two days early.
There is no payment at all in November.
The next one is the first of December.
So the money in your hand on the thirtieth of October has to carry you to the
first of December. That is 32 days.
Every year some people see that deposit, decide the government sent something
extra, and spend it. By the middle of November the account is empty and the
rent is still due. If you get the ordinary Social Security retirement payment,
none of this touches you. Your date does not move.
You are paid on a Wednesday that depends on your birthday, and the thirtieth
of October is not your date. Mark the thirtieth of October on your calendar
today and write one word beside it.
November. Number two. Your savings decide whether the government pays your
Medicare bill. One dollar over and it stops.
Most people rule themselves out on income.
They hear there is help, they think about what they earn, they decide they
earn too much, and they never ask.
That is the wrong number. There are two tests, not one.
Income is the first. What is sitting in the bank is the second, and almost
nobody is told about it. Take the program that cuts what you pay for medicine.
It is called Extra Help. This year the income line is $23,940 a year
for one person, and $32,460 for a married couple living together.
Those lines are higher than most people guess.
The savings line is $18,090 for one person, and $36,100 for
a couple.
Now the hard part. It is not a slope.
It is a cliff. Under the line the help continues.
Over the line it stops. Not reduced.
Stopped. So a man who sells a car in November, puts the money in his savings
account and leaves it sitting there, can lose help he has had for years, and
nobody will telephone to tell him what he did.
Your home does not count. One car does not count.
What counts is money in accounts.
Add your own accounts up once, this week, on paper.
Then ask. A refusal costs you nothing.
Not asking costs you every single month.
Number three. The price of your medicine next year is already set.
It went up, and nobody wrote to tell you.
Two numbers moved, and both are decided.
They are not proposals. They are not projections.
They are published. The amount you pay yourself before the plan pays anything
goes from $615 to $700. That is $85 more out of
your pocket, and most of it lands in January when money is already tight.
The most you can be made to pay in a whole year goes from $2,100 to $2,400.
If you take expensive medicine you reach that ceiling every year, so that is
$300 more on top. Here is what nobody says out loud.
Your plan is allowed to change its list of covered medicines every January.
It can move your medicine into a group that costs you more.
It can change which pharmacies it works with.
None of that needs your permission, and the letter that tells you arrives in
an envelope most people throw away.
The window to change plans is open now and it shuts on the seventh of December.
After that your price is fixed for the whole of next year.
Go to medicare.gov, or telephone 1-800-MEDICARE.
Put in every medicine you take, with the dose, and your own pharmacy.
Then look at the total for the year, not the monthly price.
A cheap monthly price very often hides an expensive medicine.
Number four. Your Medicare payment for next year has not been announced, and
anybody telling you the number is guessing.
Right now it is $202.90 a month.
It comes out of your Social Security check before the money ever reaches you.
You never touch it. For next year there is a projection.
The people who run the numbers put it near $209.50.
A projection is not a price. The real figure comes out in November, and until
it does, nobody has it. So when you see a video with next year number in the
title, you are watching somebody guess.
Ask where they got it, because there is nowhere to get it yet.
Here is why it matters more than it sounds.
You were told your raise is 3.6%.
That is true. But this payment comes out before the raise reaches your bank,
and it has climbed every year.
Last year it jumped almost $18 in one step, and every cent of that climb came
out of the raise people were given.
So the raise you were promised and
the money that lands are two different numbers,
and the second one is not finished.
Do not plan your winter on the headline.
Plan it on the smaller of the two.
If the bigger number lands, you are ahead.
If you planned the other way round, January is where you find out.
Number five. On the first of November the government sets the savings bond
rate, and it locks for six months.
This is the savings bond built to keep pace with prices.
The government sets a new rate twice a year, on the first of May and the first
of November. The rate running now is 4.26%.
It holds until the thirty first of October.
On the first of November a new rate is set, and whatever it says that morning
is the rate you are locked into for six months if you buy after it.
That new number has not been announced either.
Anybody quoting it to you today is guessing, the same as the Medicare one.
Here is the part that costs people.
Most have never heard of this, so they leave every dollar in a bank account
that pays almost nothing. And the bank is not required to tell them when that
almost nothing gets smaller. It does not write.
It does not telephone. It simply pays less, and the money that stops arriving
never shows up as a loss.
You buy these straight from the government at treasurydirect.gov.
There is no salesman and there is no fee.
The one rule to know is that your money stays in for at least a year, so this
is for savings you will not need next month.
And this is the only one of the five where waiting a few days may be the right
move. If you were going to buy this week, the rate on the first of November
is worth seeing first. That is the five.
Now look at what they have in common.
Not one of them is a new rule.
Not one of them is a change on
the thirtieth of October or the first of November.
Every one of them was decided months ago by somebody who was never going to
write to you. The people telling you to move your money by Friday have the
date right and the reason wrong.
The date is real. What happens on it is a payment arriving early and a rate
being set. That is all of it. So treat this as education and not as advice
about your own money. Your plan, your state and your own account are three
things I cannot see, and those three decide your figure.
If you take one thing from this, take the first one.
If a deposit lands on the thirtieth of October and you are on the extra payment
for people with very little income, that money is November.
Write the word November beside it on your calendar, and make it last to the
first of December.
And if your mother or your father is on that payment, do not send them this
video. Sit down beside them, open the calendar, and write it there yourself.
By the middle of November it is already spent.

title: ⚠️ Every Senior Has 7 Pieces of Good News Waiting in January (Most Don't Know)

segments.text: In January seven good things become available to people over 65.
Five of them are the same in every state.
Not one of them will be posted to you.
You heard about the raise last week.
3.6%. That one arrives on its own, and it is the only thing on this list that
does.
These seven sit and wait for somebody to ask.
Two of them depend on your county.
Five do not. I will tell you which is which every time.
And the biggest is worth $6,000 off the income you are taxed on.
Each. I am saving that one for last, because it is also the one most people
get wrong. One line before we start.
I cannot see your state, your income, or your paperwork, and those three decide
your answer. So I will give you the rule, the number the rule uses, and the
office that holds it. Anybody handing you an exact figure for your own house
today is guessing.
None of this is hidden. It is on government websites, free, for anybody who
looks. It works badly for people only because every one of these offices is
built to answer. Not one of them is built to ask.
Number one. Your county will take money off your property tax bill, and it
will never once tell you that you qualify.
This is the one that costs the most and gets claimed the least.
Nearly every state has something for older owners.
It is not automatic. Nobody checks your age and applies it for you.
You file a form at the county assessor or the appraisal district.
Until you file, you pay the full amount.
The ages and the amounts are set by your state, and often by your county.
So I cannot tell you yours. I can tell you how far apart they are.
In Texas, an owner of 65 gets $60,000 taken off the value
the school tax is worked out on.
In Texas, age is enough.
In one Georgia county, Cobb County, an owner of 62 has the whole school part
removed, with no income limit.
The statewide Georgia rule is much smaller.
In Florida, Illinois and New York there is an income limit.
So the answer is not a number.
The answer is a telephone call.
Ask for each one by name. Say this.
I am over 65, and I want the homestead exemption, the senior exemption, and
any freeze you have. Then ask for the deadline.
Write it down while they are still on the line.
Number two. There is a program that pays most of your medicine costs, and the
income line is far higher than people believe.
Same in every state. It is called Extra Help, and it works on the medicine
side of Medicare.
This year the line is $23,940 a year for one person.
For a married couple living together it is $32,460.
Read those again, because this is where people take themselves out.
They hear the word help and decide it is for somebody poorer.
$23,940 a year is about $1,995 a month.
A good many people listening are under that and have never applied once.
If you are a little over, apply anyway.
Some of what you own and receive does not count the way you expect, and the
office works that out, not you.
A refusal costs you nothing. Not applying costs you every month.
You apply through Social Security.
Online, or by telephone. It is free, and nobody should ever charge you to fill
it in. Number three. In January there is money waiting for your heating bill,
and in most places it runs out before the winter does.
This is federal money, handed out by your own state.
That is why somebody two states away gets a different answer.
Your state sets its own income line.
But it is not allowed to go below 1.1 times the poverty figure for a household
of your size. That is the floor, and you can hold them to it.
Here is the part that costs people real money.
It is handed out in the order people ask.
In a cold January it is gone by February in a great many counties.
Being eligible is not the same as being paid.
The people who get it are the people who asked early.
Ask your county office for the home energy assistance program.
In the same call, ask whether they run a crisis fund for a shut off notice.
That is usually a separate pot with its own money.
Number four. A funeral home must hand you a price list before it shows you
a single casket, and it cannot charge you for using a casket you bought somewhere
else. Same in every state, and almost nobody knows it.
Most funeral homes are covered by a federal rule called the Funeral Rule.
It says three things.
First, you can telephone and ask the prices, and they have to tell you.
You do not have to give your name.
You do not have to give your address.
And if you walk in, they must hand you a written list of everything they sell
and what each item costs.
That list is yours to keep. Second, you can buy the casket wherever you like.
From another supplier, or online.
A fraction of what the same box costs in the room with the curtains.
Third, and this is the one that saves the money.
If you bring your own, they cannot charge you a handling fee.
Not a storage fee, not a receiving fee, nothing.
If anybody tells you different, what they are telling you is not true.
So do this on an ordinary afternoon, when nobody has died and nobody is in
a hurry. Ask three funeral homes for the price list.
Put them in a drawer, and tell one person in your family which drawer.
Number five. A nursing home cannot make your son or your daughter promise to
pay the bill as the price of letting you in.
Same in every state, for any home that takes Medicare or Medicaid.
That is very nearly all of them.
The rule is plain. They may not require a third person to guarantee payment
as a condition of admitting you.
They may not require it to let you stay either.
What they can do is ask somebody who already handles your money to pay the
bill out of your own funds. That is a different thing, and the difference is
everything. One asks your daughter to stand behind your bill with her own money.
The other asks her to pay your bill out of your account.
The first they cannot require.
The second they can. So when a form is pushed across a desk in the worst week
of your life, and somebody calls it a formality, ask this out loud.
Am I signing as the person responsible for this bill, or am I signing to handle
money that belongs to my mother.
Ask them to point to the sentence on the page.
Number six. There is a line under which no federal tax at all is taken from
your Social Security, and it has not moved since 1983.
Same in every state. Take half of what Social Security pays you in a year.
Add everything else that comes in.
A pension, wages, interest, money drawn from a retirement account.
If that total is under $25,000 for one person, no federal tax is due on your
Social Security.
For a married couple filing together the figure is $32,000.
There is a ceiling at the other end people do not know about.
However high your income climbs, the most of your Social Security that can
ever be taxed is 85%. 15% of it is never reachable.
Now the hard part, and I am not going to dress it up.
Those two numbers are not tied to the cost of living.
They were set in 1983 and they have stayed where somebody put them, while everything
else in your life went up. That is why people who sat comfortably under that
line twenty years ago sit above it now, without having done anything differently.
Work your own total out once, on paper, before you file.
Number seven, and this is the big one.
If you are 65 or over, an extra $6,000 comes off the income you are taxed on.
Each. So a married couple where both of you are over 65 is $12,000.
It is here for this year and the three that follow, and then it ends.
Same in every state, because it is federal.
Three things people get wrong, and the third matters most.
First. It shrinks if your income is high.
Above $75,000 for one person, or $150,000 for a couple, it starts
coming down. Most people listening are nowhere near that and get the whole
of it. Second. You do not have to itemize to take it.
It sits on top of the ordinary deduction.
People who have never itemized anything still get every dollar.
Third, and listen closely, because there are videos telling you otherwise.
This does not make your Social Security tax free.
It is a deduction. A deduction takes money off the amount you are taxed on.
It does not declare one kind of income untouchable.
If somebody told you Social Security is no longer taxed, they were wrong.
Number six is where the truth about that lives.
You do not apply for this one.
Whoever fills in your return claims it.
So say it out loud to them. I am over 65 and I want the extra deduction for
my age. That is the seven. And the same shape sits under every one.
Not one of these offices is going to write to you.
The county will not mention the exemption.
Social Security will not telephone you about Extra Help.
The funeral home will not open with the price list.
The rule exists, the money exists, and the whole system waits with its hands
folded until somebody asks.
Treat this as education, not as advice about your own money.
Your state sets its own figures and its own deadlines, and yours may sit higher
or lower than anything said here.
Two of the seven depend on where you live.
Number one and number three. The other five are the same in every state in
the country. And if one of your parents is living on a fixed amount this winter,
they do not need this explained.
They need two telephone numbers and the word deadline.
Sit beside them, find the county office and find Social Security, and let them
make the calls themselves.

title: Cash Kept at Home the Day You Die — 6 Things Most Never Know

segments.text: There is money in your house right now that nobody else can prove exists.
The day you die, every account in your name locks.
The bank is told, the account freezes, the safe deposit box is sealed shut
with a court order waiting on it.
That is the part people know. Here is the part they do not.
In this country a drawer stays exactly as you left it.
So does a closet shelf, a coffee tin, an envelope taped under a mattress.
The law reaches the bank in an afternoon.
Your bedroom it leaves alone entirely.
So the money you kept at home because you wanted it close, because you wanted
it out of their hands, because you remember what happened to your parents,
sits there with the house full of people and no record anywhere that says how
much it was. Before you decide this is about somebody wealthier than you.
$2,000 in a drawer behaves exactly the same way as $200,000.
The amount changes nothing about what follows.
And this reaches the families who get on well, the same as the ones who do
not.
Six things start moving the day you die, and four of them arrive whoever is
standing in the room.
Six things. I will say each one out loud as we come to it, and the sixth is
the one with a clock running on it.
Two words I will use. A payable on death form is the slip your bank keeps that
says who gets the account.
Probate is the court process that decides where everything else goes.
Thing number one. The freeze reaches the bank.
It does not reach your house.
Work out what that means in a real room.
The bank learns you have died, usually within days.
From that moment the account is closed to everybody.
Your daughter cannot draw from it.
Your husband cannot draw from it unless his name is on it.
The box in the vault is sealed, and in most states it takes a court order and
a bank officer standing there to open it.
Every one of those protections exists because the money is somewhere the law
can see. Now walk down the hall to the bedroom.
The drawer answers to nobody. It stays exactly as you left it, and the only
people who will ever count what is inside are the ones standing in that room
with the door shut. The protection you have been reading about for years, the
freeze, the seal, the court order, all of it was built around a bank.
You kept your money out of the bank on purpose.
So you kept it out of all of that on purpose too, and that half of the bargain
was left out of the conversation.
The first thing that happens to the money in your house is this.
It sits. Everything else in your estate gets a lock, a seal or a form, and
your cash gets a room full of people.
That is the problem, and the five that follow all grow out of it.
Thing number two. Someone has to sign a list of everything you owned, under
oath. This is the part most families have never heard of until they are inside
it. Whoever takes charge of your estate has to file a sworn inventory with
the court. Not a rough idea. A list, signed under oath, valued at what it was
worth on the day you died. In Texas it is due within 90 days of their appointment.
In California it is 4 months. In New York it is 9 months.
The deadlines move from state to state.
The duty does not. Now hold that against a drawer full of cash.
They have to swear to a number they have no way of knowing.
If you kept $12,000 and they find nine, the list says nine, and that becomes
the official truth of what you owned.
If they never open the drawer at all, the list says nothing, and the money
leaves your estate without ever entering it.
And in Texas there is a line that should stop anybody who agrees to do this
job. If estate property is lost or stolen because the person in charge failed
to secure it, that person, or the bond they posted, repays the value to the
estate out of their own pocket.
Read that as what it is. You are handing somebody you love a legal duty to
account for money you never told them the amount of.
Thing number three. Your payable on death form stops at the bank door.
A great many people have done one thing to prepare, and this is it.
They filled in a payable on death form at the bank.
Good. That form works. On the day you die, the account named on it passes straight
to the person named on it, with no court involved, sometimes within a week.
Here is what that form is. It is an instruction attached to an account.
The bank holds it because the bank holds the account.
Cash in a drawer is not in an account.
There is no institution holding it, so there is no form that can be attached
to it, and no instruction anybody can follow.
Which means every dollar you kept at home travels the slow road.
It goes into the estate, through probate, in front of a judge, on a public
record, and it can be argued over by anybody with standing to argue.
So the very money you were most careful about, the money you wanted to pass
quietly, is the only money in your life that cannot pass quietly.
The account you were careless about moves in a week.
The drawer takes months and is read aloud in open court.
Thing number four. Any one of them can
take that list to a judge and say something
is missing.
Here is where a family comes apart.
Once that sworn list is filed, anybody with an interest in your estate can
file a written complaint with the court saying property was left off it.
They do not need proof. They need a belief and a filing fee.
The court can then order a second list.
In Texas the order gives 20 days to produce it.
Think for a moment about what gets argued over.
The house is on the deed. The car is on a title.
The accounts have statements going back years.
None of that is worth fighting about, because all of it can be checked.
The cash is the only thing in your entire estate with no paper anywhere.
So it is the only thing that can be claimed and denied with nothing to settle
it. One of them says there was always money in that drawer.
Another remembers it differently.
There is no document to open, no officer to telephone, no record to pull, and
no third person alive who looked inside.
By then the argument has stopped being about money.
It is about which of them you trusted, and they will carry it to their own
graves. Thing number five. If Medicaid paid for your care, the state has a
claim on what is left. This one is not a family matter and it does not care
what anybody agreed to. If you were 55 or older and Medicaid paid for long
term care, nursing home care or care
brought to you at home, federal law requires
your state to come back to your estate for that money after you die.
Cash is personal property. Personal property is part of an estate.
So the money in the drawer is inside the claim.
And here is the turn that catches people.
While you were alive, that cash was
counted against you when they decided whether
you qualified for help at all.
After you die, the same cash is counted again, this time to pay the bill.
The same dollars, twice, and in
both directions it works against your household.
There are real limits on this, and I will give them to you straight rather
than let you worry about something that may not apply.
If your husband or wife is still living, your estate is exempt while they are
alive. If the estate is worth less than what is owed, the state cannot chase
your children for the difference.
Some states exempt small estates outright, Georgia at $25,000 and under.
States also run a hardship process, and it is worth asking about in writing.
Thing number six.
The house goes empty, and the policy starts counting.
This is the one with the clock, and almost nobody sees it coming.
Nearly every ordinary home insurance policy
in America contains a vacancy clause.
It says that once the house sits
unoccupied for a set stretch, usually 30 days,
sometimes 60,
cover for certain kinds of loss stops.
Some policies go further and treat the whole thing as void.
The day you die, the clock starts.
Not when probate finishes. Not when the family gets around to it.
From that day. And somebody driving over once a week to collect the post and
check the taps does not stop it.
Occupied means lived in. A house nobody sleeps in is empty, whatever anybody
tells the agent.
So picture the stretch of weeks that follows a funeral.
The family is scattered. The house sits dark.
Day 30 passes, or day 60, and the cover thins or goes.
Then a pipe bursts in February, or somebody notices the post piling up on the
step, and whatever was in that drawer was uninsured for weeks before anyone
opened the policy to look. The one thing to do about it is a telephone call,
and it has to happen in the first month.
The insurer has to be told there has been a death.
Ask them two questions and write the answers down.
How many days before the vacancy clause applies.
And what has to be done to keep cover in force while the estate is settled.
Underneath all six is one thing, and it is the whole reason this video exists.
Everything that protects money in this country was built to protect money the
government can already see. The freeze.
The seal. The court order. The form at the bank.
Every one of those arrived because an institution was holding the money and
a record existed.
You kept cash at home to stay outside all that.
It worked. You are outside all of it.
Here is where my ground runs out.
I do not know your family and I cannot see your estate.
Probate deadlines, what counts as your estate, and how the vacancy clause reads
are set in your own state and your own policy.
What any of this means for your household is a matter for a lawyer in your
state, and most counties have a free legal aid office for people over 60.
Six, in order, before you go. The freeze reaches the bank and stops there,
because nothing locks a drawer.
Someone must swear to a list of what you owned, in 90 days in Texas, 4 months
in California,
9 months in New York, and in Texas they repay from their own pocket what goes
missing on their watch.
Your payable on death form reaches an account and cannot reach a drawer, so
that money goes the slow way, through probate, in open court.
Any one of them can tell a judge the list is short, and the cash is the only
thing in your estate with no paper to settle it.
If Medicaid paid for your care after 55, the state has a claim on what is left,
and the same dollars that were counted against you while you lived are counted
again after. And the house empties the day you die, with 30 or 60 days before
the policy thins out. If somebody telephones offering to protect your estate
for a fee, put the handset down.
No service and no payment changes a single thing on that list.
And if your mother or your father is keeping money in the house, do not ask
them how much. Ask them who knows where it is.
If the answer is nobody, you already know what happens.

title: Social Security Just Announced Your 2027 Raise — Most Never See What November Takes

segments.text: This morning Social Security told you your raise for next year.
They did not tell you what lands in the bank.
That is a different number. It does not exist yet.
The office that sets it does not meet until November.
Here is yours. Take your check, the full amount, before anything comes out
of it. For every $1,000 in that check, this raise adds about $35.
A $1,500 check goes up about $53.
$2,000 goes up about $70.
Work out your own and hold on to it.
Now the part that costs people.
That number is not what arrives.
Something comes out of it first, and the amount has not been set yet.
So if you have already decided where this money goes, the heating bill, the
grocery run, the one bill you keep pushing to next month, wait.
You are spending a number nobody has finished.
Before you decide this is somebody else problem.
Some of you hear Medicare and stop listening, because you are not on it yet.
Some of you hear raise and stop listening, because you already know what yours
went up by. Both of you are in this.
Five things sit between this morning and the day your money arrives.
Two of them you can still change.
One of them closes tomorrow.
And if you get a payment on the thirty first of December, stay with me.
That one is the trap.
Number one. Your Medicare premium.
This is the one that eats the raise, and the number is not out yet.
Right now the standard premium is $202.90 a month.
It comes out of your check before you ever see it.
You never touch that money. It is gone before the deposit lands.
Twelve months ago that same premium was $185.
So it climbed almost $18 in a single year, and every cent of that climb came
out of the raise people were given last October.
For next year, nobody knows. The people who run the numbers for Medicare put
it near $209.50. That is a projection, not the real figure.
Some private forecasters say they are being too hopeful and put it between
$216 and $219. So take the number you worked out at the start.
Then take $6 off it. Then take $16 off it.
Your real raise sits somewhere between those two, and you will not know which
until November. Write both numbers on the same piece of paper.
Plan your winter on the smaller one.
If the bigger one arrives, that is a good surprise.
The other way round is a bad month.
Number two. Your drug plan price.
This is the one you can still change, and the window opens tomorrow.
From tomorrow until the seventh of December, you can move to a different drug
plan or a different Medicare plan.
After the seventh of December it shuts, and your price is fixed for the whole
of next year. It does not open again until next October.
Here is why it matters more than the premium.
Three things are moving at once on the drug side.
The amount you pay first, before the plan pays anything, goes from $615 to
That is $85 more out of your pocket, and most of it hits in January when
money is already tight.
The most you can be made to pay in a year climbs from $2,100 to $2,400.
If you take expensive medicine, you reach that ceiling every year, and that
is $300 more. And a discount that has been holding standalone drug plan prices
down runs out at the end of this year.
When it goes, those monthly prices go up about $16.
Add those together and the drug side can take more than the whole raise.
Switching plans can hand it back.
Your move.
Go to medicare.gov, or call 1-800-MEDICARE, and compare.
It is free.
When you compare, look at three numbers and not one.
The monthly price. The amount you pay first.
And what your own medicines cost under that plan.
The cheapest monthly price very often hides the most expensive medicine.
Number three. The letter with your real number.
Some time in December a plain white envelope arrives from Social Security.
A lot of people never open it.
It is the only place your real figures are written down.
Three of them. Your new full check.
What comes out for Medicare. And what actually reaches your bank.
Everything in this video is me telling you how the gap works.
That letter tells you your own gap, in your own dollars.
Now the part that catches people a year later.
Keep it. Put it somewhere safe the day it arrives.
When you renew food help, or Medicaid, or housing help, or the program that
pays your Medicare premium, the office asks for that letter.
People who threw it out spend weeks getting another one.
And if January looks wrong, that letter is your proof.
Without it you are arguing from memory.
You can also read it online.
Sign in to your account on the Social Security website and look in the message
center. It usually shows up there in early December.
Your move. When the white envelope comes, open it the same day.
Write the third number, the one that reaches your bank, on your calendar for
January. Then put the letter somewhere you will find it in a year.
Number four. Two payments in December, none in January.
This one surprises people every single year, and it empties a whole month.
The first of January next year is a holiday.
Payments do not go out on a holiday.
They go out the working day before.
That day is the thirty first of December.
So if your money normally lands on the first of the month, this is what December
looks like for you. One payment at the start of December.
Then a second payment on the thirty first.
Two payments in one month. And then nothing at all in January.
Here is who this hits.
People who get the payment for those with very little income.
And people who get paid on the third of the month, which is usually anybody
who started Social Security before May of 1997.
Every year some of those people see money arrive on New Year Eve and think
it is extra. A bonus. A gift for the new year.
So they spend it. Then January comes and the account stays empty, and the rent
is still due. It was never extra.
It was January money, handed over one day early.
Everybody else is on a different schedule.
Their January money comes on a Wednesday that depends on their birthday.
Born between the first and the tenth, the thirteenth of January.
Between the eleventh and the twentieth, the twentieth.
Between the twenty first and the thirty first, the twenty seventh.
Your move. If you are paid on the first or the third, mark the thirty first
of December on your calendar right now and write one word next to it.
January. That money has to carry you to the start of February.
And if your mother or your father or a neighbor is on the payment for people
with very little income, tell them this week.
By January it is already spent.
Number five. The check that goes down.
There is a rule that is supposed to stop this happening, and three groups of
people fall outside it.
The rule works like this. If the Medicare premium climbs by more than your
raise, your check would shrink.
For most people the law does not allow that.
Your check is held where it was.
It can stay flat. It cannot drop.
Everybody tells you that part.
Here is the part they leave out.
It leaves out anybody who is only starting Medicare this year.
It leaves out anybody who pays a higher premium because of what they earned
two years ago. And it leaves out anybody who pays the premium by bill instead
of having it taken out of the check.
If you are in one of those three groups, your check can come out smaller next
year than it is this year. In a year everybody was told their money went up.
That second group catches people who stopped work recently.
Medicare looks at what you earned two years back.
So somebody who retired last year, or somebody whose husband or wife died last
year, can still be charged on an income they no longer have.
There is a form for that. You tell Medicare your money dropped and why, and
they look again at what they charge you.
Most people never hear it exists, so they pay the higher amount for years.
Your move. If your income fell because you stopped work, or because you lost
a husband or a wife, call Social Security and say one sentence.
My income has gone down and I want my Medicare charge looked at again.
They will tell you which form to fill in.
The same shape sits under all five.
The raise and the cost are set
by two different offices, in two different months,
and the two offices never speak to each other.
October hands you a percentage.
November hands you a price. The job of putting them together is left to you.
That is why the letter in December matters so much.
It is the only document in this
whole chain where somebody has done the arithmetic
for you. They are not hiding any of it.
The numbers go up on
public websites, free, for anybody who looks.
Careful people still miss it, because nothing arrives to tell you the first
number has changed.
Here is the line where my own knowledge stops.
Your check, your plan and your state are three things I cannot see, and those
three decide your figure. I can show you how the pieces move.
The figure itself belongs to you.
The premium for next year has not been set, so anybody handing you an exact
number today is guessing at it.
Your real answer sits in that December letter, and with the people who run
your plan. All five, one last time.
Take a screenshot of this. One.
The premium is $202.90 now, and next year is set in November.
Plan on the smaller outcome. Two.
Your drug plan window opens tomorrow and shuts on the seventh of December,
and the drug side can take more than the whole raise.
Three.
The white envelope in December holds your real number.
Open it and keep it. Four. If you are paid on the first or the third, two payments
land in December and nothing lands in January.
Five. The rule that stops your check dropping leaves out three groups, and
one form can help the second group.
Now the phone, and treat this as a rule.
Social Security will never telephone you about your raise.
It arrives on its own. There is no form to send, nothing to confirm, nothing
to pay. So if a voice asks you to confirm your details to receive your increase,
put the phone down. That call is a scam every single time.
And if one of your parents is paid on the first or the third of the month,
hand this to them in person.
Sit beside them, find the thirty first of December on their calendar, and write
January next to it.
That one minute is worth more than everything else here.

title: 6 Senior Benefits Unlock at Age 62 (Not 65) — Most Never Claim Them

segments.text: That is the age, and almost nobody uses it.
Six doors open on your 62nd birthday, and almost every one of you is going
to sit through three more years without touching them, because 65 is the number
everybody repeats.
Here is the one thing to do, and it takes an afternoon.
Write down the month you turn 62.
Then go through the six on this list and find which ones your state and your
county actually run. That is all of it.
65 is a Medicare number. It got into everybody heads as the retirement number
because Medicare is the loudest letter that ever arrives, and the rest of the
system never corrected it. Before you decide you are too young for this.
If you are 62, 63 or 64 right now, every day you wait is money
that was sitting there. And if you are already past 65, you want this for a
different reason:
You may have paid three years of something that stopped being required when
you turned 62, and nobody sent the refund.
Six doors. I will name each one out loud as we come to it.
The fifth one is a door that opens at 62, and I am going to tell you to walk
past it. Two names you will hear.
A county assessor is the office that decides what your house is worth for tax.
Section 202 is the name of the federal program that builds housing for older
people.
Door number one. Georgia stops taxing $35,000 of your retirement income at
Start with the one that moves the most money.
Georgia law takes retirement income out of state tax by age, in two steps.
From 62 to 64, each person takes up to $35,000 out.
At 65 it goes up to $65,000.
Retirement income here means what you would expect.
A pension. Money drawn from a retirement account.
Interest, dividends, rent. Capital gains when you sell something.
Read the next part carefully, because this is where couples lose money.
The exclusion belongs to each person separately.
It does not pool.
A husband of 66 and a wife of 63 do not share one pot.
He takes $65,000 against his own income.
She takes $35,000 against hers.
If the income is all in his name, hers goes unused.
One limit, said plainly.
No more than $5,000 of that exclusion can come from wages.
So if you still work, the wage part is capped, and everything else still counts.
And it has nothing to do with whether you stopped working.
A 63 year old still on the job qualifies on age alone.
Do this one first.
Find out whose name the pension and the accounts are in.
If it is all in one name and one of you is past 62, that is a conversation
with whoever does your return, this year, not next.
Door number two. In some Georgia counties the whole school tax comes off at
Now the biggest line on your property tax bill, and most people have never
looked at it separately. Your property tax is not one charge.
It is a stack, and in most of this country the school district takes the largest
slice of it. The rest is county, city, and whatever special districts you sit
inside.
In Cobb County, Georgia, a homeowner of 62 or older has the entire school portion
removed. Not reduced. Removed.
It covers the school general tax and the school bond tax, and your income never
enters into it. Hear that last part again, because it is the opposite of what
people assume. A retired teacher and a retired surgeon get the same answer.
Now the trap, and it is a date.
You have to be 62 on or before the first of January of that tax year.
Turn 62 on the fifteenth of January and you wait until the following year.
Two weeks of birthday costs a whole year of school tax.
And it does not arrive on its own.
You file for it, and in Cobb the deadline is the first of April.
Go and find your own bill. Look for the line that says school.
That number is what is on the table, and whether your county does what Cobb
does is one telephone call to the tax commissioner.
Door number three.
The federal parks pass costs $80 once, at 62.
A small one, and it is the easiest thing on this list to actually get.
At 62, a citizen or permanent resident can buy a lifetime pass to the federal
recreation sites. $80, once, for the rest of your life.
There is a yearly version at $20 if you would rather.
What it covers is wider than people think.
It admits the holder and everybody else in the same vehicle.
So the grandchildren in the back seat come in on your pass.
It also takes half off some of the fees you pay once you are inside.
Camping. Swimming. A boat launch.
Your income never comes into it, and there is nothing to be approved for.
Age and citizenship, and that is the list.
This is the one on here you can finish this week.
Proof of age, proof of citizenship, $80, done.
And at 62 rather than 65, that is three extra years of something you already
paid for through taxes your whole working life.
Door number four. Federal senior housing opens at 62, and the waiting list
is the reason to start now. Here is the one with the longest clock on it.
Section 202 is federal housing built specifically for older people.
One person in the household has to be 62.
Household income generally has to sit at or below half of what is normal for
your county.
What you pay is the part worth hearing.
Rent is set at roughly 30% of your adjusted income.
Not 30% of a market rent. 30% of what you actually have coming in.
Now the part that decides whether this is any use to you.
There is no national waiting list.
You apply at each individual property, one at a time, to the people who manage
that building. And those lists run long, sometimes years.
Which is exactly why the age matters.
62 is when your name is allowed on the list.
If you wait until 65 because that is the number you had in your head, you have
put yourself three years further back in a queue that moves slowly.
