Two honest limits. This is housing, and housing only.
Assisted living and nursing homes run on an entirely separate system.
And at 60 or 61 there are other doors open to you, just a different set.
Door number five. The reverse mortgage door opens at 62, and I want you to
walk past it. Here is the one I promised you, and it is the only item on this
list where my advice is to do nothing.
The federally insured reverse mortgage requires the youngest borrower to be
62. Not 62 when you apply. 62 on the day the loan closes.
So the door is open. That is a fact, and it belongs on a list about 62.
Now the part the advertisements leave at the end.
How much you can draw is set partly by your age, and younger borrowers get
a smaller share of the house. At 62 you are at the bottom of that scale.
You are borrowing against the house at the worst rate the product offers, and
interest runs on it for the longest stretch of your life.
And if your husband or wife is under 62, they cannot be a borrower.
There are protections for them, and those protections cut the amount you can
take. So understand what 62 means here.
It is not the age this becomes a good idea.
It is the earliest age the paperwork will let you do it, which is a different
thing entirely. If you are being telephoned about this, the person ringing
you works on commission. Whether a reverse mortgage ever makes sense for your
household is a question for a counsellor approved by the housing department,
and that counselling is required anyway.
Go to it before anybody sells you anything.
Door number six. Two states let you stop paying property tax at 62 and settle
it later. The last one, and it is the one people confuse with an exemption.
California runs a property tax postponement programme.
You have to be 62 or older. For the current cycle, household income has to
be $57,002 or below, and you generally need at least 40% equity in the home.
Several Missouri counties do something similar at 62.
Saint Charles and Clay both use that age, measured as of the first of January.
Now the word postponement, because it is doing real work in that sentence.
The state pays the bill for you and puts a claim on the house.
It comes back when the house is sold or when the estate settles.
The money is not forgiven. It is moved.
That makes this the right answer for exactly one situation.
You are house rich and cash poor, the tax bill is what is squeezing you every
year, and you would rather your heirs settle it out of the sale than lose the
house now. And it makes it the wrong
answer if your family is counting on inheriting
the house clear. Either way, the age is 62, and the deadline is annual.
You apply every year, and missing the window means missing that year.
The same shape sits under all six.
Every one of them waits for you to arrive.
The parks office stays silent.
The county reads its own records and your birthday is in somebody else files.
The housing list grows from applications, and yours has to be one of them.
The Georgia exclusion sits on a form in your own handwriting.
And every one of them was built with a different age in mind by a different
body, which is why they do not line up with each other and why nobody ever
handed you a single list.
65 is not the retirement age. It is the Medicare age, and those two things
got confused somewhere around 1965 and have stayed confused ever since.
Here is the edge of what I can tell you.
I do not know your state, your county or your income, and those three decide
most of what is above. The Georgia figures and the California income line come
from tax guides rather than from the state offices themselves,
so check your own number before you rely on it.
What any of this means for your household is a matter for whoever prepares
your return and for your own county office.
The six doors, in order, before you go.
Georgia takes $35,000 of retirement income out of state tax from 62, and it
belongs to each person, not to the couple.
In Cobb County the entire school portion of the property tax comes off at 62
with no income limit, but you must be 62 by the first of January and you must
file by April.
The federal parks pass is $80 once, for life, and it admits everybody in your
car.
Section 202 housing opens at 62 and rent is about 30% of your income, which
is why the waiting list is the reason to apply now rather than later.
The reverse mortgage door opens at 62 and that is the earliest age, not the
right one. And California and some
Missouri counties let you postpone property
tax from 62, which moves the bill rather than cancelling it.
All of it sits on public pages, free, for anybody who goes looking.
It catches careful people anyway, because nothing arrives in the post telling
you a door has opened. Now the telephone, and this part is not optional.
If somebody rings offering to claim any of these for you for a fee, put the
handset down. Every one of them is free to apply for, and the offices that
run them do not use salespeople.
And if one of your parents is 62, 63 or 64 right now, do not send them this.
Sit beside them with their tax bill and find the school line together.
It takes an afternoon, and the three years they are about to lose do not come
back.

title: 5 Bills You Legally Stop Paying After 65 — Most Pay Them Anyway, Not Knowing

segments.text: Born before 1961?
Then you stopped owing a stack of bills the day you turned 65.
You probably paid every one of them again this year.
Turning 65 did not just hand you Medicare.
It moved you into a different class of taxpayer.
The federal government, your state and your county are all required by law
to treat you differently now.
Nobody is going to call you about it.
The tax office stays quiet.
So does Medicare, and so does the state.
Every one of them is paid to collect, and that is where their job ends.
The law says you are off the hook.
Being off the hook and keeping the money are two different things.
One form stands between them, and it never arrives in your mailbox.
Before you wave this away as somebody else business.
Some of you hear a break for seniors and think you have to be poor.
Your home is paid off, so you stop listening.
Others think this is for people with an accountant.
You live on Social Security and a small pension, so you stop listening too.
Both of you are wrong. I will tell you which group each one helps.
And if you rent, stay. One of these five decides how fast your rent is allowed
to rise.
Five bills. I will name the form and the office for every one.
Bill number one. Your property tax.
This is the big one, and it is not one break.
It is three, stacked on top of each other, and almost nobody has all three.
The first one knocks money off the value the county puts on your house, before
they work out the bill.
Most places call it a homestead break, and that is all it is.
In most states it is one page, filed once, and it is not automatic.
The second sits on top of the first.
A separate break just for being 65.
And here is where the paid-off house crowd walks away, because they hear a
break for seniors and assume somebody will check their income.
In more than half the states that offer this, there is no income check at all.
Age is the whole qualification.
The third is the one worth the most over time.
A freeze. Once you qualify, the number your house is counted at stops moving.
Your neighbors watch theirs climb every year.
Yours sits still. And in some counties it goes further than a discount.
In Cobb County in Georgia, a homeowner of 62 gets the entire school portion
of the bill removed. Not reduced.
Removed. No income limit.
The school part is usually the biggest piece of the whole bill.
Now the part that costs people a year at a time.
You must be the right age by the first of January, and in Cobb the deadline
to file is the first of April.
A birthday two weeks into January costs you the whole year.
Your move. Call the county tax assessor and ask three things.
What breaks do I get now that I am 65.
Is there a freeze and how do I lock it in.
And what is the last day to hand the form in this year.
Bill number two. Your Medicare Part B premium.
The number in your head is out of date.
For this year the standard Part B premium is $202.90 a month.
It comes straight out of your Social Security payment before you ever see it.
Last year it was $185.
That is a jump of nearly 10% in one year.
Here is what almost nobody is told.
If your income sits under a line, your state pays that premium for you.
Not a discount. The whole thing, every month, going forward.
There are three levels and the numbers are exact.
The first level pays the whole monthly charge, and it wipes out most of what
you hand over at the doctor and the hospital as well.
The monthly income line is $1,350 for one person, $1,824
for a couple.
The second level pays the premium only.
$1,616 for one person, $2,184 for a couple.
The third level also pays the premium only, and it goes higher.
$1,816 for one person, $2,455 for a couple.
Now two things that nobody mentions, and both of them cost people money.
The first $20 of your monthly income does not count.
Neither does the first $65 of anything you earn from work.
So your income on paper can sit above those lines and you can still qualify.
People read the number, do the sum in their head, and rule themselves out on
a figure that was never the figure.
The second is about that third level.
Congress puts a cap on how much money goes into it each year, and it is handed
out in the order people apply.
When the money is gone for the year, it is gone.
Make this call. Call your state Medicaid office and ask for the Medicare Savings
Program application. It is the state that runs it, not Medicare.
Bill number three. The tax on your own Social Security check.
Here is how they work out whether your benefit gets taxed, and it is simpler
than people think.
Take half of your Social Security for the year.
Add everything else you have coming in.
A pension. Money out of a retirement account.
Wages. Interest. That total is the number they measure.
Under $25,000 on your own, none of your benefit is taxed.
Married and filing together, that line is $32,000.
Go over it and up to half your benefit starts getting taxed.
Go higher, past $34,000 on your own and $44,000 married, and it can reach 85%.
Hold on to one thing there. Even at the very top, 15% of your Social Security
is never taxed. That part is yours no matter how high your income goes.
When people sign up for Social Security they are handed a form asking whether
they want federal tax taken out automatically.
Plenty tick the box without doing the sum.
If your total sits under those lines, you are handing money to the government
every month that you were never going to owe, and you wait until the following
spring to get it back.
Do the sum once, tonight, with the figures from last year.
If you come out under the line and they are still taking tax out every month,
the form that stops it is a W-4V, and it goes to Social Security.
Bill number four. A deduction that did not exist two years ago.
This one is a gift, and it is the newest thing on this list.
Starting with the 2025 tax year there is a new one just for people 65 and older.
$6,000 each, taken straight off the income they tax you on.
It replaces nothing. It sits on top of what you already had.
Stack the whole lot and look at what it comes to.
The IRS does not tax every dollar you bring in.
A set amount comes off the top first, and everybody gets it.
This year that set amount is $16,100 on your own, $32,200 if you are married.
On top of that, everyone of 65 gets more.
$2,050 on your own. $1,650 each if you are married and file together.
And now the $6,000 stacks on as well.
A married couple, both over 65, lands somewhere around $47,500 in deductions
before one single receipt is counted.
For a lot of people living on Social Security and a modest pension, that number
alone takes the federal tax bill to nothing.
Two things to know. If you are both 65 and blind, that extra amount is counted
twice. On your own that comes to $4,100.
And the $6,000 is temporary. It runs through the 2028 tax year and then it
is gone unless the law is changed.
One question for whoever prepares your return.
Did you take the new senior deduction on my last return.
If the answer is no, that return can be amended.
Bill number five. Your phone, your internet and your heat.
Smaller money, easier to get, and the one most people never bother with.
There is a federal program called Lifeline.
It takes $9.25 a month off a phone bill or an internet bill.
On tribal land it is $34.25. One per household, and
it is one or the other, not both.
Here is the part worth hearing.
If anyone in the house receives food assistance, Medicaid,
Supplemental Security Income, federal housing help or a veterans pension, you
qualify on that alone. No income check at all.
Separately there is a program that helps pay the heating bill itself, and it
runs on a different application.
In a lot of states it opens on the first of October for households with someone
60 or over, a month before everybody else.
Read that again, because it is the part that matters.
60 or over gets in a month early.
That head start exists because the people who run it know that a cold house
kills older people first. Most of the households it was built for apply in
November with everybody else and find the money already committed.
And getting one of these two usually means you get the other.
People apply for the phone discount, get it, and never learn the heating one
was sitting in the same drawer.
Now the thing that quietly ends both of them.
You have to confirm you still qualify once a year.
Miss that, and the discount stops.
No warning, no letter, and the bill simply goes back to full price.
People think they lost it. They did not lose it.
Nobody reminded them. Last thing on this one.
Lifeline is applied for free, and anybody asking you for a fee to do it is
lying to you. For the heating program, call your local community action agency
and ask when applications open in your state.
One thing runs underneath all five of these.
Every one of them exists on a form, and every one waits for you to arrive.
The county assessor has your birthday on file and sits on it.
The state knows your income to the dollar and sits on it.
Social Security knows exactly how much tax it is taking out of you every month,
and sits on that too.
They are not hiding anything.
The paperwork sits on public websites, free, for anybody who looks.
Careful people still miss it, because a door opening makes no sound.
Here is where my ground gives out.
I cannot see your return, your county or your income, and those three decide
most of what is above.
Property tax rules and the income lines for state programs are set where you
live, and they move. For your own
household the answer sits with whoever does
your return, and with the county office that sends the bill.
The five, one more time. Your property tax comes off in three layers, the freeze
is worth the most, and the deadline is in the spring.
Your Part B premium is $202.90 a month and your state will pay it if your income
sits under one of three lines, with the first $20 not counted.
The tax on your Social Security starts at $25,000 on your own and $32,000 married,
and 15% of it is never taxed at all.
There is a new $6,000 deduction for being 65, it stacks on everything else,
and it ends after 2028. And the discount on your phone and your heat needs
confirming once a year or it quietly stops.
Somebody calls offering to claim any of this for you, for a fee.
That person is working you.
All five are free to apply for, and the offices behind them have never once
used a salesman.
And if one of your parents is over 65 and has never filed a single one of these,
do not send them this.
Sit beside them with the tax bill from last year and start with the county.

title: Born Before 1966? 6 Social Security Changes Hitting Age Group In 2027 (Share With Family)

segments.text: If you are on your own, that is the line.
$32,000 if you are married. Go $1 past it and the government starts taxing
The Social Security you already paid for.
Nobody writes to tell you where you stand against that number.
Not the agency that sends your check, not the office that takes the tax, not
The people who announce the raise every October.
Here is the gap that costs people money every January.
Being under that line and believing you are under it are two different things,
Because the number they test you with is larger than the number in your head.
And the one thing that decides it is a calculation you can do at your own table
In four minutes.
$25,000. $32,000 if you are married.
Hold those. Now, before you decide this does not reach you.
This is not about wealthy retirees.
A single person with a modest pension and an ordinary Social Security check
Is already close to that line, and in some households already past it.
And it is not only about people who are comfortable either.
The line has stayed in the same place since the law was written, and your check
Has gone up every single year since.
The two were always going to meet.
Six things to check, and I will tell you which part is yours as we go.
The last one is the one most people have already got wrong this year, because
A new rule arrived and it does less than the headlines said.
Two names, said once.
Social Security is the check. A Roth is a retirement account that was already
Taxed when the money went in.
Check number one. $25,000. Cross it and your own check starts getting taxed.
Here is the rule as it sits today.
If you file on your own, the first line is $25,000.
If you are married and file together, it is $32,000.
Underneath those lines, none of your Social Security is taxed.
Above them, up to half of your benefit becomes taxable.
And there is a second line higher up, $34,000 on your own and $44,000 married,
Where the share rises to as much as 85%.
Read those four numbers again, because they decide whether a letter arrives
In April.
Now the part that matters more than the numbers themselves.
Not one of those four figures has ever been raised.
Not for inflation, not for wages, not once.
They were written into law in 1983, the tax began in 1984, and the numbers
Have sat exactly where they were put.
Think about everything else in that stretch of years.
Bread. Petrol. A doctor visit.
Your own check, which has had a raise in almost every one of them.
Everything moved except the line.
A woman named Ruth retired in 1991 on a check that was nowhere near $25,000
A year. She never paid a dollar of tax on it.
The same woman, with the same job behind her and the same modest life, retiring
Today would be over the line in her first year.
So write the two numbers on the back of an envelope.
$25,000 on your own. $32,000 married.
Everything that follows is measured against those.
Check number two. Half of your own Social Security gets added in before anything
Else does. This is where almost everybody miscounts, and it is the whole reason
People think they are safe.
When they work out whether you are over the line, they do not look at your
Pension and your interest and stop there.
They start by taking half of your Social Security benefit and putting it on
The pile.
Say that out loud, because it is strange and it is true.
Your Social Security is counted against you to decide whether your Social Security
Gets taxed. So the sum has three parts.
Half of your yearly benefit. Then
Everything already taxed, which means a pension,
A withdrawal from a regular retirement account, wages if you still work, and
Savings interest. Then one more piece that catches people out, interest from
Municipal bonds.
Those are sold as tax free, and for most purposes they are, except this one.
Add those three together and that is the figure they hold against $25,000.
A man named Clarence counted his pension at $18,000 and his bank interest at
$400, decided he was $8,000 under, and never thought about it again.
His benefit was $22,000 a year.
Half of that is $11,000. His real figure was $29,000, $4,000 over the first
Line, and he found out in a letter.
What to do. Take the benefit statement from last year.
Halve the yearly amount. Then add your pension, any withdrawals, any wages,
Your interest, and any municipal bond interest.
That total, not your income as you usually think of it, is the number that
Decides this. Check number three.
The raise goes in. Half of the raise is used to push you over.
Now put the two pieces together, because this is the part that lands in the
Middle of October.
Every autumn, Social Security announces the raise for the following year.
People hear the percentage and work out what it adds to the monthly check.
That is as far as most of it goes.
Follow it one step further. A bigger benefit means a bigger half.
That bigger half goes onto the pile from check number two.
The pile gets closer to the line, or crosses it.
So the raise that is announced to help you is also the thing moving you toward
The tax.
Both of those are true at once, and nobody says the second half out loud.
And nothing in the system warns you.
The letter in December tells you the new monthly amount.
It carries no mention of the line, no mention of where you now stand against
It, and no suggestion that anything about your tax has changed.
A widow named Pearl went over the first line by $600 in a year when her only
Change was the raise. She had done nothing differently.
She had earned nothing extra. The system had simply moved her, and the first
She knew of it was the following April.
What to do. When the new amount comes in December, redo the sum from check
Number two with the new figure.
Four minutes, once a year, and you will know in December instead of April.
Check number four. In 1984 it caught 1 in 10.
It now catches half. Here is what those frozen numbers have actually done.
When the tax started in 1984, fewer than 1 in 10 people receiving Social Security
Paid anything on it. It was written for the small number at the top.
The figure for this year is 48%.
Just under half of everybody receiving a benefit.
That happened without a single vote.
Congress stood still, and standing still was the whole mechanism.
A number that stays put while every check rises will swallow more people each
Year, by arithmetic alone. And it keeps going.
The line sits in the same place next year and the year after.
Your check moves. The only question is which year you cross, and for many people
Watching, that year has already gone.
Comfortably underneath is a temporary condition.
Check number five. Money out of a Roth never gets added in.
Most people have none. Here is the one real lever, and I want to be straight
About how narrow it is. Money taken out of a Roth account stays off the pile.
It was taxed on the way in, years ago, so it has already done its turn.
Your figure holds steady, and either line stays where it is.
That makes it the only kind of
Retirement money that is invisible to this calculation.
Everything else counts. A regular retirement account counts.
A pension counts. Wages count.
Savings interest counts. Now the hard part.
Most people over seventy hold little or nothing in a Roth.
These accounts did not exist for most of their working lives, and converting
Into one means paying the tax up front, in one year, at an age when that is
Rarely the right move. So it is a real lever that is already closed for most
Of you. I am telling you anyway, because a few of you have one and have been
Drawing from the wrong account for years.
What to do. Find out whether any account in your name has the word Roth on
The statement. If one does, that is the account to think about drawing from
First, and that is a conversation with whoever does your return, with your
Own numbers in front of them. Check number six.
The new deduction lowers your tax.
It does not move the line. This is the newest piece and the one being described
Wrongly almost everywhere. There is a new deduction for people 65 and older,
Up to $6,000 a person. It is real, it reduces what you owe, and it is worth
Claiming. What it does not do is help you here, and the reason is where it
Sits in the order. They work out your figure first.
That is the sum from check number two.
Then they compare it with $25,000 and
Decide how much of your benefit is taxable.
Only after all of that is the new deduction applied.
So it arrives too late to change the answer.
It makes the bill smaller. It leaves the line exactly where it was and leaves
You on exactly the same side of it.
I have heard it said this year that the deduction means seniors no longer pay
Tax on Social Security. That is wrong, and anyone repeating it has skipped
The order of the sum. What to do.
Claim it, because it is real money.
But do your check number two sum as though it did not exist, because for that
Purpose it does not.
One thing runs underneath all six of these.
Every part of this was already in motion before you retired.
The lines were set, and every step since has been arithmetic doing what arithmetic
Does. An announcement would require somebody to have decided something.
Nobody did. That is why it catches careful people.
There is nothing to notice, right up until the year there is a letter.
Now the edge of what I can tell you.
I cannot see your return and I do not know what you were paid.
These are the federal rules. States have their own and a number of them tax
Benefits as well, which is a separate question with a different answer in every
State. What any of this means for your household is a matter for whoever prepares
Your return, with your own figures in front of them.
The six, said quickly. The line is $25,000 on your own and $32,000 married,
With a second line at $34,000 and $44,000.
Half of your Social Security is added in before anything else, along with your
Pension, your withdrawals, your wages and your interest, including municipal
Bond interest. The raise lifts that half and moves you toward the line.
In 1984 fewer than 1 in 10 paid this and today it is 48%, with no new
Law behind the change.
Money from a Roth is the only kind that never gets added in.
And the new $6,000 deduction arrives after the sum, so it lowers the bill while
Leaving the line alone.
None of this is hidden. All of it sits in a federal publication, free, for
Anybody who goes looking. It catches older people anyway, because it is written
For somebody who already suspects there is something to look for.
One last thing. If somebody rings you offering to keep your Social Security
Out of the tax, put the telephone down.
No service, no product and no payment changes where that line sits.
The only things that move your figure are which accounts you draw from and
How much, and those are decided at your own table.
And if your mother or your father is on a fixed income and has never once done
This sum, do it for them in December when the new amount arrives.
It takes four minutes, and the alternative is that they find out the way Pearl
Did.

title: If Your Spouse Dies, These 3 Things Happen to the Joint Account — Half of It Loses Cover

segments.text: Six months.
That is how long the bank keeps treating the account the way it did when both
of you were alive.
Nobody starts that clock in front of you.
Nobody writes to you on the day it runs out.
It runs anyway, and on the morning it finishes, a protection you have had for
forty years is simply smaller.
Most people spend those six months doing the hardest things they will ever
do. Sorting papers. Answering calls.
Learning how to be one person in a house built for two.
The clock does not wait for any of that.
Three things happen to a joint bank account when a husband or a wife dies.
The costliest one is first, and it costs quietly, without a letter, without
a call, without anybody at the bank being required to raise it.
Who this lands on. If your name and one other name are both on a bank account,
all three belong to you. No income test.
Nobody asks what you own. The size of the balance changes nothing, except that
the first one gets more expensive as the number climbs.
Two names, said once.
The protection on your deposits comes from the FDIC, which is the federal body
that insures money in banks.
The account itself is called a joint account, which just means two names on
one account.
Number one. Six months. Then half of it is not covered.
Here is the rule as it stands today, and almost nobody over sixty five has
heard it out loud. A joint account is insured for $250,000 per owner.
Two names on the account, $500,000 protected.
That is how it works while both of you are living, and it is why couples with
real savings were told for years to keep the money jointly.
When one owner dies, the FDIC does
something that sounds generous and is actually
a countdown.
For six months it goes on treating the account exactly as it was.
The person who died is counted as though he were still alive.
$500,000 stays protected.
Then the six months end. On that day the account becomes yours alone in the
eyes of the insurance,
and yours alone means $250,000.
Not per name. Not as it was. One limit, for one person, across
everything you hold in your own name at that one bank.
The FDIC writes this out plainly in its own example.
A joint account holding $500,000.
One owner dies. Nothing is changed within the six months.
$250,000 is now uninsured.
That is not a penalty and nobody did it to you.
It is arithmetic.
Two names bought two limits. One name buys one.
Think about who is standing inside those six months.
A woman of seventy three who has never moved money between banks in her life,
because her husband did that. A man of eighty who could not tell you which
of the two local branches holds the bigger account.
A widow who was told at the funeral to change nothing for a year, which is
kind advice for a will and expensive advice for this.
And here is the part that makes it worse.
The FDIC does not know your husband died.
It is not sent a death certificate.
It does not read obituaries. The clock starts from the date of death whether
or not anybody at the bank has been told, so the six months can be partly spent
before the bank even updates its records.
Two more pieces of this that matter and are never mentioned together.
The six months is not given if giving it would make your cover smaller.
The rule exists to protect you, not to trap you, so if the ordinary arithmetic
would already protect you better, the ordinary arithmetic is what applies.
And there is no six months at all when the person who dies is a named beneficiary
rather than an owner. If you have an account that pays out to a named person
on your death, and that person dies first, the cover can drop that same day.
No window. No countdown.
What to do with this one. Write down every bank where you hold money, and next
to each one write what is in it.
If any single bank holds more than $250,000 in your name alone, that is the
number to deal with, and the answer is usually boring.
Move part of it to a second bank.
The FDIC has a free calculator on its own website called EDIE that tells you
exactly what is covered, and it costs nothing and asks for no personal details.
Do it inside the six months. After that you are not protecting money, you are
hoping.
Number two. Close that account and you cannot open it again.
This is the one that comes from doing the right thing.
A sensible person wants the paperwork finished.
The account has his name on it, the name hurts to read, and closing it feels
like one task taken off a list that has thirty tasks on it.
Here is what is still moving through that account on the day you close it.
Money is still coming in. A pension payment that runs a month behind.
A refund from a company that was told about the death in March and processes
it in May. An insurance payment that was filed weeks ago.
A final wage, a dividend, a rebate on a policy nobody remembered.
Money is still going out. The electricity.
The water. The mortgage or the property tax.
The house insurance, which is the
dangerous one, because an insurance premium
that fails to come out does not send you a letter the same day.
It lapses quietly, and you find out about the lapse at the worst possible moment,
which is after something has already happened to the house.
Close the account and every one of those stops at once.
Payments coming in are returned to the sender and begin a chain of letters.
Payments going out fail, and each failure has to be chased, re-authorised and
explained to somebody who has never heard of you.
And a closed account does not come back.
You cannot reopen it. You open a new one, with a new number, and then every
single person who was paying into it or taking out of it has to be told again,
one at a time, by you, in the same month you buried him.
A woman named Eleanor closed her husband's side of things four weeks after
the funeral because her son said it was tidy.
Her car insurance was on that account.
She did not know, because she had never been the one to look.
She found out in July.
What to do with this one. Keep the account open and keep it funded for at least
six months. Do not treat it as finished.
Sit down once, write a list of every payment that goes in and every payment
that comes out, and then deal with them one at a time, deliberately, over months.
The electricity stays. The gym membership goes.
Nothing is closed until the list is empty.
Number three. Two names kept you out of court.
Now there is one. This is the thing almost nobody says out loud, and it is
the reason this item is last. Most joint accounts between husband and wife
carry something called right of survivorship.
Three words on a form you signed decades ago and never looked at again.
What they mean is that when one of you dies, the account passes to the other
one directly, without a judge, without a court, without the months of waiting
that other things go through. That is real and it works and it is the reason
the first weeks are survivable.
But stop and ask where that protection actually came from.
It came from the second name. Not from the bank being kind.
Not from the account being special.
The account skipped the court because there was somebody else already on it,
waiting to take it. The second name is gone.
What you have now is an account with one name on it, and an account with one
name on it does not skip anything.
When your turn comes, that money stops.
It waits.
Your daughter cannot touch it to pay for the funeral, your son cannot use it
for the house, and nobody gets near it until a court appoints somebody and
says so in writing. That can take months, and in some places longer.
So the protection that carried you through this did not transfer to you.
It died with the second name, and nothing replaced it.
The fix takes about ten minutes and it is free.
Ask the bank for a payable on death form.
Some banks call it a beneficiary form.
You write down who should receive the account when you die, you sign it, and
the account skips the court again, the same way it just did for you.
No lawyer. No fee. No court. A man named Howard sat in a branch for twenty
minutes doing exactly this, four months after his wife died, because somebody
told him to. It cost him nothing and his two daughters will never know how
much it saved them, because the thing it prevented will simply never happen.
While you are there, ask the same question about every other account in your
name. The current account. The savings.
The certificate. Each one is separate and each one needs its own form.
There is one thread running through all three of these, and once you see it,
they stop being three separate problems.
Every single one of them is about a second name that is no longer there.
Two names bought you twice the insurance.
Two names kept the money out of court.
Two names meant somebody else knew which bank held what, and which payment
went out on the fourteenth.
The accounts did not change when he died.
The arithmetic underneath them did, all at once, on a date nobody marked.
And none of it generates a letter.
The bank is not required to tell you the insurance limit has moved.
No office is required to say the protection has gone.
The only notification any of this produces is the moment something goes wrong,
and by then the window has closed.
Here is the honest limit on everything I have just said.
I cannot see your accounts and I do not know which words are on them.
Banks differ in what they ask for and how fast they do it.
Some states handle these accounts differently,
and a few handle them very differently.
Everything above is the general federal rule on deposit insurance and the ordinary
shape of how these accounts work.
Your own case is decided by paperwork sitting in a drawer at your branch.
The three, said quickly. The insurance on a joint account holds for six months
after one owner dies, then falls to $250,000 for one person, and
the FDIC's own example has a quarter of a million dollars going uninsured.
Closing the account is the common mistake, because money is still arriving
and bills are still leaving, and a closed account cannot be opened again.
And the protection that kept this money out of court came from the second name,
so with one name left you need a payable on death form to put it back.
None of this is secret. All three sit on government pages, free, where anybody
can read them. They catch older people anyway, because they are written for
somebody already looking, and nobody who has just buried a husband is looking
at a deposit insurance page. One last thing, since this is the season when
these calls go out. No official body telephones a widow to help her reorganise
her accounts. If somebody rings offering to help move money to keep it protected,
that call is not coming from the FDIC, and it is not coming from your bank's
fraud department either. Put the phone down and ring the number printed on
your own statement.
And if you know a woman who buried her husband this year, do not send her this.
Sit down beside her, find out which banks hold what, and count the six months
from the date on the certificate.
She has probably already lost two of them.

title: ⚠️ 7 Things They Can't Take From Seniors After 65 — The IRS Needs a Judge to Take

segments.text: When a senior dies, almost everything handed to the people left behind arrives
whole. The government does not get a share of it.
Nobody tells the family that, so they wait for a bill that never comes.
And one thing does carry a bill.
It arrives quietly, with a clock already running, and the people who inherit
it usually find out years late.
Seven things pass on. Six are out of reach.
One is not. All seven are below, and the one that costs money comes last.
Before any of it, one line, because the two get mixed up everywhere.
This is about tax on income. It is not about the separate tax a very large
estate can face, which almost no household in this country ever meets.
Number one. The money itself is not income.
Nothing is owed on what was left to you.
This is the one people get wrong before anything else happens.
A son gets forty thousand dollars from his mother.
He spends the first week asking how much of it he has to hand back.
The answer is none of it. Not a dollar.
Property handed over as a gift, as a bequest, or by inheritance is not counted
as income.
That is the rule as written. So the money clears and the amount is yours.
There is no form for it. There is no line on a return where you report it.
People go looking for that line, cannot find it, and assume they have missed
something. They have not. It is not there because there is nothing to report.
The thing to do is nothing at all.
Spend a week being certain of that instead of worried about it.
Number two. A policy pays the full sum to whoever is named on it.
When a life policy pays because somebody has died, that payment is not treated
as income. Say the policy is a hundred and fifty thousand dollars.
A hundred and fifty thousand reaches the person named.
Not a hundred and twenty. Not a hundred and thirty five after something is
taken out. The whole of it. And this does not depend on who that person is.
A wife. A son. A daughter. A neighbor.
A church. The rule does not change based on the relationship.
So if there is a policy in the house, the useful thing is to know whose name
is written on it, and whether that name is still correct.
A name written down thirty years ago is the name that gets paid, whatever has
happened since.
Number three. A veteran benefit keeps its shield after death.
No tax, no collector.
Money paid for a veteran's service carries three protections at once.
It cannot be signed over to somebody else.
It is out of reach of people chasing a debt.
And it is not taxed.
Those protections do not fall away when the veteran dies.
They stay attached to the money.
This matters more than people expect, because debt is the thing families fear
most in that first month. A collector telephones, speaks with confidence, and
the widow assumes the money in question is fair game.
If the money came from a veteran's service, it was never fair game.
Say that out loud on the telephone and the conversation usually ends.
Number four. The house is valued from the day they died, not the day it was
bought. This one quietly saves families the most, and almost nobody understands
it until a house is sold. A father buys a house in nineteen seventy eight for
thirty thousand dollars. He dies, and it is worth four hundred thousand.
The daughter inherits it and sells it the following year for four hundred and
five thousand. Her gain is not three hundred and seventy five thousand dollars.
It is five thousand. The clock resets on the day of the death.
Everything the house gained while he was alive goes untouched.
Only what it moves afterwards is counted.
People sell fast, frightened, certain a huge bill is coming.
Some sell cheap to get it over with.
The bill they are frightened of does not exist, and the fear costs them real
money. So before anybody signs anything, find out what the house was worth
on the day of the death. That single figure is the one that decides everything
that follows.
Number five. What the money earns after it reaches you is counted, and people
miss this. Here the direction changes.
Everything so far arrives clean.
What happens next does not. The inheritance is not income.
But once it is yours and it starts earning, the earnings are income like any
other. Forty thousand dollars sits in an account and pays interest.
The interest is counted. Shares pay a dividend.
The dividend is counted. An inherited house gets rented out.
The rent is counted. The money came in free.
What it produces from that day forward does not.
This is where an honest family gets caught, because nothing about it feels
like a change. Same money, same account, same house.
But the law draws a line on the day it became yours, and everything after that
line is ordinary income. So keep the paperwork from that first year.
Not for the inheritance. For what it earned.
Number six. Take the policy in pieces instead of one sum and part of it becomes
taxable. The gentlest-looking choice here is the one with the trap in it.
An insurance company will often offer two ways to pay.
The whole amount now, or the same amount spread across years, which sounds
safer to somebody who has never held that much money.
Choose the whole amount and nothing is owed.
Choose the payments spread out and the company holds the balance while it pays
you. That balance earns while it waits.
The original sum stays untaxed.
The earnings stacked on top are counted, year after year, the whole time it
runs.
Nobody at the company is required to explain that.
They offer two doors and both look safe.
If somebody is offering you a choice like that, ask one question before you
choose. Ask how much of each payment is the policy and how much is interest.
They have that number. They will give it to you if you ask.
Number seven. One account arrives with a bill and a clock already running.
Here is the one. A retirement account is different from everything else on
this list, because the person who built it never paid tax on the money going
in. That was the arrangement. Tax waits until it comes out.
Death does not cancel the arrangement.
It hands it to you. So money leaving an inherited retirement account counts
as income for whichever year you pull it out.
Not the whole account at once.
The part you withdraw, in the year you withdraw it.
And there is a clock. If you are not the husband or wife, the account generally
has to be empty by the end of the tenth year after the death.
Now the part that catches people, and it is why this one sits at the end.
Whether you also have to take something out every single year in between turns
on one thing you had no part in.
It rests on the age of the person who died, and whether the law had already
made them start drawing it down.
If they had not reached it, you can leave the account alone and empty it by
year ten. If they had reached it, you are meant to take something out every
year along the way.
Miss those years and there is a penalty waiting, and most people who inherit
are never told the question exists.
A husband or wife has their own options and is treated differently.
A child who inherits young gets more time, until twenty one, and then the ten
years begin.
So the question to ask, and ask it early, is this.
How old was the person when they died, and had they already started taking
money out? The answer decides whether your clock needs attention this year
or in nine years.
Now the line that joins all seven.
Six of these arrive whole because the tax was either already settled or never
owed. The seventh arrives with the tax still unpaid, because that was the deal
when the account was opened. That is all it comes down to.
Not fairness, not family. Only whether the tax had been settled yet.
Let me be straight about where this stops being useful.
I cannot tell you about your own situation.
States add their own rules on top, a few charge something of their own on what
passes between people, and the paperwork differs everywhere.
If there is a retirement account involved, that is the point to pay somebody
for an hour of their time, because the clock is the part that costs money to
get wrong.
So, the seven, one more time. What was left to you is not income.
A policy pays its full face to the name on it.
A veteran's money keeps its protection after death.
A house is measured from the day of the death, not the day of the purchase.
What any of it earns afterwards is counted.
Spreading a policy over years adds interest, and interest is counted.
And a retirement account comes with tax owing and a ten year clock.
None of this is hidden. It is printed, it is free to read, and it has been
settled for years. Families get it wrong because the month it matters is the
worst month of their lives, and nobody sits them down.
One last thing, because these calls come.
Nobody official telephones a grieving family about an inheritance.
If a voice offers to release money for a fee, or needs a card number to start
the process, that is somebody who read a death notice.
Hang up. And if a death in your family is still being sorted out, do not ask
what anybody is getting. Ask one thing.
Is there a retirement account in it, and has anyone looked at the clock?

title: Every Senior Must Know The Real October Changes Hitting Social Security And Savings — Or Lose All

segments.text: The first of October came and went.
Your payment did not change. Your health card still works.
The amount taken out for your health cover did not move by a single cent.
If somebody told you otherwise, they were either wrong or they were relying
on you not to check.
What the date actually did was wind up a clock.
Four of them, and every one lands on a different day between now and the middle
of November, on a different set of people, and not one of them arrives with
your name on an envelope.
On the fourteenth of this month you will be handed one number.
Three more numbers move the same morning and no newsreader will say them out
loud. And the figure that decides how much of that raise ever reaches your
bank is not released until the middle of November.
When it comes out, nothing is mailed to you.
You find out because the deposit is smaller.
Four things. The one that takes the most money is last.
Before any of it, who it lands on.
Receive Social Security and all four are yours.
Receive the monthly payment for people with very little and the third one is
yours twice over. Not one of the four has an income test, and not one of them
asks what you own. Three names, said once.
Social Security. The health cover is Medicare,
and the piece of it taken straight
out of your payment is called Part B.
The monthly payment for people with almost nothing is called Supplemental Security
Income, and most people just call it the supplement.
Number one. The first of October changed nothing on your payment, and that
is the part being sold to you wrongly.
Every autumn the same wave of noise arrives.
Rules changing on the first. Money stopping on the first.
None of it touched your payment.
What the first of October is, is day one of the money year the government runs
on. Their books turn over. Their new spending year opens.
For you it is an accounting date and nothing more.
The reason it matters is not what happened that day.

changed, at the counter, in front of other people, being asked for a sum they
were not expecting.
The bill is at its heaviest in exactly the month when the heating is at its
heaviest.
Your own number is printed in the letter your plan sent you.
Not the ceiling. Yours. Find the page that says what you pay before the plan
starts paying, and read it before the fifteenth of October, because after that
you are choosing under time pressure.
Number three. Three letters, three colors, three different messages, and people
read the first line of each and stop.
The government sends these. They are colored on purpose, and the color tells
you which one you are holding.
The orange one says you still qualify for help with drug costs automatically.
People read that and feel relief and put it down.
The relief is where they stop.
The second half of that letter says the amounts you hand over at the counter
change on the first of January.
Same help, different price, and the price is in the part nobody finishes.
The grey one says the opposite.
From the first of January you no longer qualify automatically.
You are allowed to apply again.
Nobody applies for you, nobody telephones to ask why you have not, and if you
do nothing the help simply stops and the full price starts.
The blue one arrives in November and it is the one people misread worst.
It does not ask you anything. It tells you your drug plan is leaving Medicare
and that you have already been moved to a different one.
Not a suggestion. Done. A plan you did not choose, with its own list of medicines
and its own prices, unless you pick for yourself before the end of December.
Hold that for a second. A letter arrives, you do not open it, and in January
you are inside a plan you never agreed to.
That is allowed, it is the system working as designed, and the only thing standing
between you and it is whether you opened an envelope in November.
Look at the color before you look at anything else.
Orange, read to the end. Grey, you have lost something and you have to ask
for it back. Blue, a decision has already been made for you.
Number four. The letter from the job you left, and the one question it answers.
Somewhere there is an old employer or an old union still sending you one piece
of paper a year. It has to reach you before the fifteenth of October.
It is required.
It looks like nothing. It reads like the pension paperwork you have been filing
without reading for a decade.
It answers one question. Does the drug cover you already have count as good
enough? That is the whole letter.
One word, buried in a page of language built by people who were not thinking
about your eyesight. If it counts, you are fine, and you can keep what you
have and ignore the rest of this.
If it does not count, you are standing next to the most expensive mistake in
this video. And you do not know it.
Nothing on the envelope says so, and nobody is going to telephone and explain.
Find that letter. Find the sentence that says whether your drug cover counts.
If the letter is gone, telephone the number on your old plan card and put the
question in those exact words.
Somebody on that line knows, and the answer takes them ten seconds.
Number five. The charge that is never taken off, and it has just been made
bigger. Here is the one. If you go sixty three days in a row with no drug cover
that counts, a charge is added to what you pay every month.
Not a fine you settle once. Not a bill you argue about.
It is built into your monthly price from then on, and it stays there for as
long as you hold drug cover under Medicare.
You can change plans every single year and it follows you to each one.
This is how it is worked out. One percent of a national figure, for every full
month you were without cover, added on top.
Two years without, and it is a quarter more every month, forever.
Now the part that has not been reported anywhere, and it is why this item sits
at the end. That national figure is not fixed.
It is reset every year. This year it is thirty eight dollars and ninety nine
cents. Next year it is forty one dollars and thirty three cents.
So the charge is calculated from a bigger number in January.
Which means every person already paying it pays more next year.
They did nothing. They made no choice.
No letter is going out to tell them.
The amount simply grows, quietly, on a line they have stopped reading, and
it will grow again the year after
that. That is the difference between this and everything else here.
The other four cost you a year.
This one gets larger while you are not looking, and it does not end.
Here is the line joining all five.
Every one of them reaches you on paper, in October or November, dressed as
junk. Nothing follows up. No second copy comes in December.
No voice checks that the envelope was ever opened.
One delivery is the entire warning, and that is all anybody is obliged to give
you. Now the edge of what I can do for you.
Your own figures are not in this video and I will not pretend otherwise.
Your plan, your state and your own history decide what is printed on your page.
The amounts here are the national ones for next year, and those are settled.
What your plan does underneath them sits in your envelope and nowhere else
on earth. Five things, said quickly.
What you pay from your own pocket before the year goes quiet moved from two
thousand one hundred to two thousand four hundred.
The most a plan may take before it pays anything moved from six hundred and
fifteen to seven hundred.
Three letters arrive in three colors and only one of them is good news, and
even that one has a price change in the second half.
A letter from an old job, due before the fifteenth of October, answers whether
your drug cover counts. And sixty three days without cover that counts fixes
a charge onto your monthly price for as long as you live on Medicare, calculated
from a figure that just went up.
Nothing here was kept from you.
All of it is printed, all of it is free, and all of it was settled months before
your envelope was sealed. It beats older people anyway, for one reason only.
It comes as paper, once, in the same handful of post as the advertisements,
and not one person in the whole
arrangement is paid to find out whether you
understood a word of it. One more thing, because these calls run through every
October. No official body telephones you about open enrollment.
If a voice offers to sort your plan out there and then, or wants your Medicare
number before anything can move, you are talking to somebody reading off a
bought list. Hang up on them.
Send this to one person over sixty five who still has post sitting unopened.
Do not ask whether they have read their letters, because they will say yes.
Ask something narrower.
Ask whether anything came this month that was orange, grey or blue, and whether
it is still sealed.

title: New Food Assistance Rules for Every Senior Start October — the Denial in Your File Is Out of Date

segments.text: There is one number that decides whether you get food help.
Your own doctor bills are meant to come off that number before anybody looks
at it. No one at that counter is obliged to ask for them.
So the no you were given was worked out on a figure that was never yours.
It sits in a file. Nobody reopens it and works it a second time.
Four things change that figure once somebody sixty or over lives under your
roof. Most people hear the word medical, think of hospitals, and say nothing
at all. I will name the program once so you know what we are talking about.
It is called SNAP. Most people still call it food stamps.
The money lands on a card each month, and you buy groceries with it.
And let me deal with who this covers, since that question arrives under every
one of these videos.
Limits exist, and the figures are below.
But the whole point of today is that the amount being weighed is not the amount
sitting in your head. Number one.
In this program old starts at sixty.
Not sixty five. Read that again, because it costs people five years.
The government writes it down plainly.
In this program you are elderly at sixty.
Not at sixty five, not at retirement, not when your card arrives.
Sixty. And the moment somebody sixty or over lives in your house, one whole
test gets dropped. Here is what that means in practice.
A normal household gets measured twice.
Once on the whole amount arriving, with nothing subtracted yet.
Then again on whatever survives after certain costs are removed.
And the first measurement is precisely where people stop.
It is the headline amount. The one printed at the top, the one that sounds
like wages. Somebody says it out loud, decides it is far too much, and the
form never gets filled in. That measurement does not apply to you.
It never did. Nobody at any counter has ever been required to mention that.
The one that counts is the number left after your costs come off.
For one person that line sits at one thousand three hundred and thirty dollars
a month. For two it is one thousand eight hundred and four.
And those are the figures for the year that started this month.
So here is the small move, and it costs you nothing.
Lead with the age, not the income.
Tell them somebody under your roof is sixty or over, say you want to file,
and leave the sums to the people employed to do them.
Number two. Every dollar past thirty five a month comes off before they judge
you. Thirty five dollars. That is the floor.
Understand how low that is. It is not an operation.
It is not a week on a ward. It is the pills on repeat.
It is getting to the appointment, and getting home again.
It is the dentist. The glasses.
The small items you lift off a shelf without a second thought.
Almost nobody over sixty spends less than thirty five dollars a month keeping
themselves well. It is simply what the month costs.
Everything past that first thirty five is subtracted before they weigh you
at all. There is a limit on it, and you should hear it plainly.
Only what you pay yourself counts.
If the insurance paid it, or a son or daughter paid it, that part is theirs,
not yours. And only the amount over thirty five comes off, not the whole thing.
So before you call anyone, pick one month and put it on paper.
Every health cost you covered yourself in those four weeks.
Most people have never added that column up in their lives, and the total surprises
them. Number three. What counts is wider than medicine.
Dentures, nursing care, the ride there.
Of the four, this is the one least often explained to anybody, and it moves
the most money. People hear medical and they think of pills.
The list the government actually publishes is far longer than that.
Doctor bills. Prescriptions. Things from the drugstore shelf, when a doctor
has said to take them. Dentures.
A stay in hospital and treatment that does not need a stay.
Nursing care. Somebody who comes in to help you.
And two more that people miss every single time.
The cost of getting there. The journey to the appointment counts.
And the health insurance you pay for.
That takes in the Medicare premium removed from your Social Security before
any of it reaches a bank. No check was written.
Nothing was approved. It counts all the same.
Sit with that one, because for most houses it is the largest single line on
the whole sheet. It leaves every month.
It leaves on its own. And it sits on almost nobody's form.
Think about how that happens. A cost you never chose, never approved, and never
watched go, is still a cost you carry.
The office has no way of knowing it unless you say it.
And nothing on that form tells you to.
There is a second one people walk past.
If a husband and wife both have a premium coming out, both of them count.
Two people, two premiums, every month of the year.
That alone has moved households from refused to accepted.
So when you make that sheet of paper, start with the premium.
Then the pills. Then the dentist.
Then the
journeys. A woman of seventy four with a bad knee and a car she pays somebody
else to drive is carrying several hundred dollars a month, and she has been
telling the office she has no medical costs.
Number four.
One thing people claim never counts, and it gets the file refused.
Special food does not count. Ever.
If a doctor has told you to eat a certain way, and that way costs you more,
every instinct says it should come off.
It does not. The rule names it and excludes it.
Put it on the form and you have given them a reason to reject the whole thing.
And there is a second rule that goes with it.
You need proof. Receipts, statements, the paperwork from the insurer.
A number you say out loud is not enough.
Some states let you claim one flat amount instead of listing every item.
Some do not. Ask which one yours is, and ask it in those words, because it
changes how much paperwork you carry.
Here is the thread tying the four together.
Every one of these moves the same number.
Not what arrives. What is left, after what you pay to stay well.
And not one counter anywhere rings an older person to ask what their health
is costing. The form has a box.
The box sits empty. The empty box becomes a figure, and the figure becomes
a no. Here is the arithmetic the government prints in its own rulebook, so
you can see the size of it. Two people, sixty or over, twelve hundred dollars
a month coming in. Take off two hundred and seventeen that every household
gets. Take off three hundred in doctor bills.
Take off what the roof costs above half of what is left.
The number they finally judge is four hundred and twenty four dollars and fifty
cents. The food help that comes back is four hundred and thirty four dollars
a month. Leave the doctor bills off that same form and the number they judge
jumps by three hundred.
Same house. Same income. Same month.
Over ninety dollars a month gone, because one box was empty.
Now a word on the limits of what I have given you.
I am not able to settle your case from here.
States administer this separately, each with its own forms.
Some set their limits higher than the federal ones.
The numbers here are the national ones for the year that opened this month.
Your state lays its own rules over the top of those.
What holds in every state is the shape.
You are weighed on one figure, your doctor bills belong inside it, and no one
is coming to your door to collect them.
So, the four, one more time. In this program you are old at sixty, not sixty
five, and that alone drops a whole test.
Anything you pay for health past thirty five dollars a month comes off before
they judge you. What counts is far wider than medicine, and the biggest piece
of it is the premium already leaving your check.
And special food never counts, no matter how fair that feels.
The name for all of this in the rulebook is the excess medical expenses deduction.
Say that line when you telephone
and whoever answers will understand the request
at once. You will not have to explain anything else.
None of this is secret. It is printed, it has been printed for decades, and
anyone may read it. It fails older people for one reason only.
Those counters are staffed to answer what is put to them, and nothing in them
was ever designed to raise a question first.
One last thing, and it comes around every year.
Honest offices do not ring you about food help.
If a call offers to work out your benefit for a fee, or wants a card number
before anything can go ahead, put the telephone down.
Applying costs nothing. Asking costs nothing.
And if this was refused to someone in your family, say nothing about their
earnings.
Ask them something else entirely.
Did anyone, at any point, ask to see what their health costs them?

title: ⚠️Every Senior Must Do This Before October 14: The 2027 COLA Raise You Don't Actually Get

segments.text: Two weeks from now a number gets fixed for you.
You are not asked, you are not written to, and by the time it reaches you the
work behind it is already months old.
That number is your raise for next year.
And before one dollar of it reaches your account, five other numbers have already
been moved, and not one of them was moved on your say so.
Here is what nobody puts in the same place for you.
The raise is announced on one day.
The cost that comes out of it is announced on a different day.
The limits that decide what help you keep moved on three more days, all of
them different, and one of them has not moved since nineteen eighty three.
Five numbers. Five separate days.
Not one of them is the day you find out.
Let me settle one question before anything else, because it is asked every
single time. Part of this depends on what you have coming in each month.
Part of it does not. The rise does not.
The deduction does not. Those two reach every person on Medicare regardless
of income. The last three do carry limits, and I will give you the figures
and the place to check them. There is no pretending here that you qualify for
something you do not.
Number one. Your COLA is set on the fourteenth of October.
You get no say in it. The full name is cost of living adjustment, and almost
everyone just says COLA. It is the yearly rise added to Social Security, and
it is worked out from a list of prices gathered in July, August and September.
Those three months are finished.
The readings are already taken.
The last one goes public before breakfast on the fourteenth, and from that
moment the figure is locked for the whole of next year.
Estimates right now sit near three and a half percent, with one or two a shade
above it. Last year's was two point eight.
On a payment of about two thousand dollars a month, that works out at roughly
seventy dollars more.
Now hold on to the part that matters.
The list those prices come from is built on what working age people in cities
buy. It is called the price index for urban wage earners.
Urban wage earners.
That is who is measured, and that is who sets your raise.
A woman of seventy eight does not spend like a thirty five year old with a
commute. She spends on heating, on the roof over her, and on medicine.
Those are the three that have risen hardest, and they are the three carrying
the least weight on the list she is judged by.
So the raise is real, and it was never measured on you.
Number two. Medicare Part B takes its cut first, and that number comes out
later. Part B is the part of Medicare that pays doctors and outpatient care,
and for most people the cost of it is taken straight out of the Social Security
payment. Not billed. Not asked for.
Taken, before the money moves.
This year that amount is two hundred and two dollars and ninety cents every
month. The trustees project it rising to around two hundred and nine dollars
and fifty cents next year. That is six dollars and sixty cents a month gone,
close to eighty dollars across the year.
Now put the two dates side by side, because this is the whole of it.
Your raise is announced in October.
The Part B figure is not made official until November.
So for about four weeks every retiree in this country is walking around with
a number in their head that is not the number.
The rise is public. The deduction is not.
And when the deduction is finally
published, there is no second announcement,
no letter, no correction.
Seventy dollars of raise. Seven of it gone before you see it.
You were told the first figure on a Tuesday morning and the second one three
weeks later with no headline at all.
Number three. Your SNAP limits already moved.
They moved before your raise existed.
SNAP is food stamps. Same thing, different name, and the official one is the
one the office uses. Here is the trap in it.
SNAP runs on the government's own year, and that year rolled over at the start
of this month. The income ceilings and the deduction amounts all changed then.
They changed two weeks before your raise even exists as a number.
So a household that is refused in November is refused against ceilings set
in October, measured against income that includes a raise announced after those
ceilings were written.
The two numbers were never designed to meet.
And people do not go back.
They hold on to the refusal and let go of the year it came in.
A no from two winters back was measured against figures that have since been
replaced twice. So call the benefit office in your own state and ask for the
ceiling that applies to the year beginning this month.
Those words, that year.
Whatever figure comes back down the line, it will not match the one sitting
in your memory. Number four. Medicaid and the Medicare Savings Programs judge
you on last year's line until spring.
Of everything in this video, this is the piece fewest people have ever been
told, and it carries the largest sum.
Three programs exist that cover Medicare costs for people on lower incomes,
and their names are nothing but letters.
QMB covers your premium and also the money you pay across a doctor's desk.
SLMB covers the premium by itself.
QI covers that same premium, at a higher income ceiling.
Read those letters out on the telephone and whoever answers will know immediately
what you are asking for. This year the monthly income lines sit at about one
thousand three hundred and fifty dollars for one person on the first, around
one thousand six hundred on the second, and around one thousand eight hundred
on the third. What you have in savings is capped near nine thousand nine hundred
dollars for one person. Your home does not count.
One car does not count. Household goods do not count.
A burial plot does not count. And here is the timing, which is the point of
this whole video.
Your raise lands in January.
The poverty guidelines that set those income lines are not published until
the middle of January or into February, and most states do not start using
the new ones until March or April.
So for two or three months your income is the new one and the line is the old
one. People get letters in that window saying they no longer qualify.
A rule covers this.
States have to leave the rise out of the sum for those three programs, at least
until the fresh guidelines are in use.
It exists because somebody noticed the dates do not meet.
Hardly a soul has been told about it.
So if a letter turns up in February telling you that you have gone over, that
rule is the thing you name back to them.
One more thing before you hang up.
Acceptance into any of those three puts you onto the help with prescription
costs by itself. The name of it is Extra Help.
No second form, no second interview.
One yes, two things. Number five.
The IRS line never moves at all.
It was set in nineteen eighty three.
Everything so far moves. Badly timed, measured on the wrong people, but it
moves. This one does not. Social Security became taxable in nineteen eighty
three, and the line went in at twenty five thousand dollars for a single person,
thirty two thousand for a couple.
Read those out loud and then read what they are now.
Identical. Four decades, and the pen has never gone near them.
Think about what every raise does against a line that is nailed down.
Each year the raise lifts you slightly.
The line does not move to meet you.
So a payment that was below it becomes a payment above it, and nothing about
your life changed except that they gave you the rise they said was to keep
up with prices. That is the shape of the whole thing.
They move the money a little. They leave the line exactly where it is.
And the gap closes on you from one side only.
Now a word about the limits of what I have given you, because nothing here
should go further than the evidence does.
Your own answer is not mine to give.
Each state runs these health programs its own way and writes its own forms.
Next year's Part B amount stays a
projection until November puts it in print.
The rise stays an estimate until the fourteenth makes it real.
What holds regardless of your state and regardless of your figures is the shape
of it. The day your money changes and the day the lines change are different
days, and the ground between those days is where people quietly lose help they
were never disqualified from. So, the five, one more time.
Your raise is fixed on the fourteenth of October from prices measured on younger
people in cities. Part B takes its share first and that figure is not official
until November. The food stamp ceilings moved on the first of October, before
the raise existed.
The health programs go on judging you against last year's line until spring,
and there is a rule that is supposed to protect you in that gap.
And the tax line has not moved since nineteen eighty three and will not move
now.
One last thing, and it turns up on schedule every year at this point.
No honest office rings you about your rise.
A voice offering to calculate your new amount, or to safeguard your benefits
for a small charge, or wanting the long number off a card before it can go
ahead, is a voice to hang up on.
Checking costs nothing. Applying costs nothing.
Anyone asking you for money is somebody who had no business dialling your number.
And where there is a relative living on a set amount, leave their income out
of it. Which month did they turn you down?

title: NEW Income Rules for Seniors Begin October 1  — Your Old Refusal Still Says No

segments.text: Three days ago the government threw away every income limit it had been using
since last autumn.
Every deduction. Every benefit amount.
All of it, replaced overnight.
Nobody wrote to tell you. Nobody is required to.
So a refusal you were handed this spring was worked out with numbers that stopped
existing on the first of October.
Nobody goes back and runs that decision again.
It sits in a file, still saying no, against figures nobody uses any more.
Three things changed that week, and every one of them moves in your direction
if there is somebody sixty or over living in your house.
They never announce the ones that help.
They announce the ones that take.
The first is an income test they simply do not run on you.
The second is a cost that comes off your total with no ceiling on it, and you
are the only household that gets that.
The third is the one limit that did not move at all, and the reason that is
good news.
None of this is new money. All of it has been sitting there, and the only thing
keeping people out is that they decided the answer themselves before anybody
looked.
Number one. They never test your gross pay at all, and nobody tells you that.
Here is how it works for most households.
There are two income tests. The first looks at everything coming in before
anything is taken off. The second looks at what is left after certain costs
are subtracted. A normal household has to pass both.
Yours does not.
That first test is not applied.
It is skipped entirely. Only the second one counts, and the second one is the
one measured after your costs come off.
The number that stops most people is the big one.
It is the number at the top of the page.
The one that looks like a wage.
Somebody reads it out loud and says that is too much, we would never qualify.
That number is not the test for you.
It was never the test for you.
And here is where it costs real money.
People do not apply. They sit at a kitchen table with a bank statement.
They look at the top line. They compare it against a figure they half remember
from two winters ago, and they decide.
No form filled in. No call made.
The decision is made in the kitchen by a person who has not read the rule,
and it is made against the wrong number.
I want to be plain about who this catches, because it is not who you would
think. It is not the person who cannot be bothered.
It is the careful one. It is the woman who has never taken a thing she was
not owed. She would rather go without than ask for something that turns out
not to be hers. She is the one who looks at that top line and rules herself
out, and she is the one the rule was written for.
The office does not want your opinion of your own income.
Deciding is the job they are paid to do.
That is the whole of the work.
So the instruction for this one is small and it does not cost anything.
Put in the application. Do not lead with what you earn.
Do not explain your figures on the telephone before anybody has asked.
Say that you want to apply, and let them do the arithmetic they are employed
to do.
There is one more thing about that first test worth knowing.
It is not a kindness and it is not a special case.
It is written into the law itself, and it has been there for decades, for one
reason. A person of seventy living on a fixed amount has costs a working household
does not, and whoever wrote the rule understood that.
So when somebody tells you that you earn too much, ask them which test they
are talking about. Most of the time they cannot tell you, because they are
repeating what somebody told them.
Number two. Your housing costs come off with no ceiling.
Everybody else has one. This is the one almost nobody has heard of, and it
is worth the most. What you pay to keep a roof over you counts.
The rent or the mortgage payment.
The property tax. The insurance.
The heat, the power, the water, the Trash.
Add all of it together. Now take half of what comes in each month.
Anything you spend on the roof above that half comes off your total before
they judge you.
For most households there is a ceiling on that.
Seven hundred and sixty nine dollars, and that is a new number as of the first
of October. It used to be seven hundred and forty four.
In your house, with somebody sixty or over under the roof, there is no ceiling
at all. Hear that twice. No ceiling.
Not a higher one. None at all.
This is the only place in the whole program where a cost comes off without
a limit on it, and it exists for one reason.
Older people spend a larger share of what they have on the house and on keeping
it warm, and somebody wrote that into the rules.
Then nobody told anybody.
Think about what that does to a real household.
A woman of seventy four with a house that is paid for still owes the tax on
it, the insurance on it, and the cost of heating it.
In a cold state that can run to hundreds of dollars a month before a single
item of food is bought. Every dollar of that above half her income comes off
the figure they judge her on. She has no idea.
She thinks the house being paid off counts against her.
And notice the shape of this, because it is the shape of everything in this
video. The rule is generous. The rule is written down.
The rule is old. What is missing is anybody telling the people it was written
for.
