If the Treasury ever reaches into the joint account, the money in the account
with only your name on it is not part of that reach.
Now a word about the people who appear at exactly this moment.
The death of a spouse is public.
It is in the notices, it is in the court file, and there is an industry that
reads both. Within weeks a widow
gets telephone calls and visits about annuities,
about trusts, about moving the money somewhere safer.
Nothing in this video requires a product, a policy or a fee.
Asking your bank how an account is titled is free.
Asking a pension plan for a copy of a form you signed is free.
Applying for a card in your own name is free.
If somebody arrives offering to solve all of it at once, and the solution involves
moving your money into something they sell, that is the moment to say you will
decide nothing for ninety days.
So that is the whole of it, laid out once more.
The Social Security payment for the month he died is not his and not yours,
it comes back out of the whole account, and if it is already spent the debt
follows you personally. A card where you are only an authorized user closes
when he does, and the years of history on it stop working for you.
His pension may have been chosen to end with him, but that choice required
your signature, and if the signed consent cannot be produced, the choice can
be challenged. And whether the account passes to you at all comes down to the
wording on the signature card, which you can find out this week and cannot
find out on the day. Every one of these four sits in a rule that a bank, a
pension plan or a government office will explain to anybody who asks them.
They stay unknown for one reason.
There is no moment in an ordinary life when somebody is required to raise them
with you, and by the time they matter,
three of the four can no longer be changed.
So telephone the bank this week and ask how the account is titled.
And if your mother is widowed and still carrying a card with your father name
printed on it, look at that card tonight.

title: Seniors Over 65: 6 Ways to STOP Paying Property Tax (Most Never Ask)

segments.text: The house is paid off and you still owe money on it every single year.
Fall far enough behind and the county sells it out from under you.
That is your property tax. It is the bill that keeps arriving long after the
mortgage is gone.
Six charges on that bill can come off after sixty five.
The number the county guessed about your house.
The mistakes on the paper the county keeps.
The veteran exemption that takes the bill down to nothing.
The exemption that does not die with your husband.
The exemption that drops off the record without a word.
And the exemption that stays behind at the old house when you move.
Not one of the six happens by itself.
Not one is ever offered to you.
The office that sends the bill is the same office that decides whether to mention
them, and it does not.
Six charges. What each one is, and what the silence has cost you already.
Number one is the number the county guessed about your house.
Your property tax is not a price anybody set for you.
It is a percentage.
Somebody decides what your house is worth, and the tax is a slice of that figure.
So the whole bill rests on one number, and that number is a guess.
Nobody walks through your house.
Nobody measures your rooms.
A county office looks at what houses near you sold for, applies a formula,
and prints a figure. If three houses on your street sold high last year, your
figure rises, even though nothing about your house changed.
You are allowed to fight that figure.
Every state has a way to do it.
Very few homeowners over sixty five ever do, and there is one reason.
The clock does not start when the bill arrives.
The county sends you a paper before the bill.
It is not a bill. It asks you for nothing.
It says what they have decided your house is worth this year.
Most people look at it, see that no payment is due, and set it aside.
That paper is the starting gun.
In most places you have thirty to forty five days from the date printed on
it, and the deadline is printed on that same paper.
Not on the bill. On the sheet that came months earlier and wanted no money
from you.
So the year runs like this. The paper comes in the spring and you ignore it,
because it is not a bill.
The bill comes in the fall and now you are angry.
You telephone the county to argue, and whoever answers tells you the window
shut four months ago and you may not challenge anything until next year.
That is a full year of paying on a figure you never agreed with.
And a guess left unchallenged becomes the starting point for the guess after
it. It builds against you every year you wait for a bill to argue about.
Number two is the paper the county keeps on your house, and the mistakes sitting
on it. Behind that guess is a record.
The county holds a sheet on your property listing what they believe is there.
How many square feet. How many bedrooms and bathrooms.
Whether there is a garage or a finished basement.
You are allowed to see it and it costs nothing.
Most counties put it on a website now, and if yours does not, you may telephone
and ask for a copy of the record on your property.
Very few homeowners over sixty five have ever asked to see theirs.
The errors are more common than people expect.
County records carry the wrong square footage far more often than homeowners
believe. Sometimes the builder reported it wrong forty years ago.
Sometimes an office estimated instead of measuring.
Sometimes a shed was taken down twenty years ago and is still sitting on the
record, still being taxed. Every one of those errors has been on your bill
every year since it was made. And this is the strongest kind of challenge there
is, because it is not an opinion.
Arguing that your house is worth less than the county says is a judgement,
and a judgement can be waved away.
Showing that the county has you down for four hundred more square feet than
the house actually has is a fact.
Nobody can argue with a measurement.
Many counties will correct a clear
measurement error without any formal hearing.
You telephone, you show them, they fix it.
And in some places the correction reaches backwards.
Where the mistake counts as a clerical error rather than a difference of opinion,
some states return money for prior years, not only for the year you caught
it. Number three is the veteran exemption that takes the bill down to nothing.
This is the largest amount of money in this video, and the one most often missed,
because the families who qualify assume it must be a small discount.
Twenty two states charge no property tax at all on the home of a veteran rated
totally and permanently disabled by the Veterans Administration.
Not a reduction. Not a percentage off.
Nothing. The bill goes to zero.
Texas, Florida and Virginia are among them, and in most cases the rating has
to be one hundred percent. Now the part that gets lost, and it is why this
item sits so high. In most of those states the exemption does not end when
the veteran dies. It passes to his widow.
In Texas, the surviving spouse of
a veteran rated totally and permanently disabled
keeps the full exemption for life on that same home.
In Florida she keeps it until she sells or marries again.
Virginia works the same way. What happens if she marries again differs by state,
and that is worth asking directly.
But she has to ask. It does not carry over on its own.
Nobody reads a death certificate and adjusts the account.
So think about the woman this happens to.
Her husband served.
He was rated totally disabled.
For fifteen years the house was taxed at nothing.
He dies. And a bill arrives that she has not seen in fifteen years, for thousands
of dollars, in the month she buried him.
She assumes it is correct. She assumes the break was his and died with him.
So she starts paying, out of a widow
pension, on a house that was never supposed
to be taxed at all.
If that is your house, or the house your mother lives in, make that call this
week.
Number four is the ordinary age exemption, and the same trap underneath it.
Set the veterans aside now, because this one reaches many more households.
Almost every state gives homeowners a break on property tax once they reach
sixty five.
Some call it a senior exemption.
Some call it a freeze, which locks the taxable value where it stood the year
you signed up, so your bill stops climbing while every other house on the street
keeps rising.
Almost no household knows the next part.
In many of them only one name holds the break.
Whichever spouse turned sixty five first applied, and the break sits under
that name alone. When that spouse dies, the county drops it.
Not out of malice. The account simply loses the person it was attached to,
and the next bill comes at full price.
But the law in many states says she keeps it.
In Texas, a surviving spouse who is fifty five or older on the day her husband
dies may keep his over sixty five exemption on that same home.
New Jersey uses the same age. Washington lets a surviving spouse qualify for
the freeze at fifty seven instead of the usual age.
Fifty five. Not sixty five.
A woman of fifty eight who has just buried her husband is old enough to keep
his break, and she will almost certainly never be told so.
What she must do is file a new application in her own name.
It is not automatic. And the year she spends not knowing is a year she pays
a full bill on an income that has just lost half of itself.
If you are widowed and your bill jumped after your husband died, that jump
has a name and it may be reversible.
Telephone the county, ask whether his age exemption can be continued in your
name, and say your age when you ask.
Number five is the exemption that drops off the record without a word.
Most people believe that once an exemption is on the house it stays there.
For the most part that is true.
In most places you apply once and you are not asked again every year.
But there is a check underneath it that nobody explains.
County offices are required to review their exemption records on a cycle.
In Texas the appraisal districts must audit every five years to confirm the
people claiming exemptions still qualify.
If the office cannot confirm it from what they hold, they are required to ask
the owner to apply again.
That request goes out in the post.
If it is missed, the exemption comes off.
Think about who misses post. Someone who spent three weeks in hospital.
Someone who spent a winter at the home of a daughter.
The break falls away and nothing announces it.
The next bill is simply larger.
And that is exactly how it gets read.
Taxes went up again. It goes on the pile with everything else that costs more
this year.
There is one place it does announce itself,
and you have to know where to look.
When a county removes or denies an exemption they send a notice, and the time
to challenge that removal is short.
In Gwinnett County in Georgia it is forty five days from the date on that notice.
So this is the check to run this month.
Find your last property tax bill and look down it for a line that says exemption,
and for the amount taken off. If that line is missing, or the amount is smaller
than last year, something came off your account and nobody told you.
Number six is the exemption that stays behind at the old house.
This one catches people at the worst possible moment, because it catches them
while they are downsizing. The children are gone.
The stairs are hard. So the big house is sold and a smaller one is bought,
sometimes on the same side of the same town.
And every single person assumes the break comes along.
It does not. The exemption belongs to the house, not to the person.
When you buy a new home it does not transfer with you.
It stays on the property you left.
You have to apply again, on the new address, as though you had never had one.
And there is a deadline.
In Florida the new application is due by the first of March in the first year
after you move.
Miss it and you pay a full unreduced bill on the new house for a year, at the
exact moment you have just paid for a move and given up the old house.
Ask one further question while you are on that call.
Some states let you carry the savings across, not only the exemption.
Florida lets a homeowner move a large part of the built up tax benefit from
the old home to the new one. It has to be requested on the same application.
So if you have moved house in the last two years, check this before anything
else in the video.
What to do, and a note first.
This video describes the general shape of these rules across the country.
Property tax is written at state level and run at county level, so the detail
where you live will differ.
Check anything here with your county before acting on it.
Then do these things. Find your last
property tax bill and look for the exemption
line. Note whether there is one and what it took off.
If there is nothing there, you are paying the full amount, and you have been.
Telephone your county and ask for the office that decides what your house is
worth.
Use these words.
My age is over sixty five and this house is where I live.
Which exemptions can I hold, and which of them are missing from my account
now.
Then ask for a copy of the record on your property, and check the square footage
and the room count against the house you are standing in.
Then ask when the paper comes out that says what my house is worth, and how
many days I have to challenge it.
Put that date on a calendar. That single date decides whether you may argue
at all. And if your husband has died, ask this separately, because it will
not come up on its own.
My husband held the over sixty five exemption.
I am fifty five or older. Can it be continued in my name.
Note the date of that call, and who answered it.
If any of this is disputed a year from now, that note is all you will be holding.
Now a warning about the people who will find you once you start asking.
The moment a senior starts asking about property tax, companies appear.
Some offer to challenge your value for a share of whatever they save you.
But nobody has to be paid to file the exemptions in this video.
Every one is a free form at your own county, and the county will tell you which
ones you qualify for at no cost.
If somebody telephones you first, before you contacted anyone, treat that as
the warning. Counties do not ring homeowners to offer exemptions, so anybody
who does has a reason for finding you.
And no honest service needs your Social Security number to look up a property
record. Run through the six one last time.
The bill is a percentage of a figure the county guessed, and the days to challenge
it start from the paper that comes before the bill, not from the bill.
The county holds a record on your house that may be wrong.
You may see it for nothing, and a wrong measurement is the hardest error to
dismiss. A veteran rated totally and permanently disabled pays no property
tax at all in twenty two states, and in most of them the widow keeps that.
The over sixty five exemption does not have to end when your husband does,
and fifty five is old enough to keep it.
An exemption can come off your account in a five year review with nothing said,
and it shows up only as a bigger bill.
And when you move house it stays behind, and you must file again.
None of the six is hidden. Every one is written in public rules at your own
county office. They stay unknown because nobody in that office is paid to tell
you, and there is no penalty anywhere for the silence.
So telephone your county this week and ask what you are not getting.
And if your mother is widowed and still in the house, make that call for her
tonight.

title: What the IRS Cannot See in Your Bank Account After 65 — 4 Places It Never Looks

segments.text: The bank sends one form about you to the tax office each year.
It is a single page. It says how much interest your money earned.
Ten dollars, forty dollars, whatever it was.
That is the whole of it. Nowhere on that page is the number that is actually
in your account, and there is no second form that carries it.
Nobody has told you this, because the not telling is worth money.
Fear about your own bank account sells guides and courses and videos, and the
people selling them need you to believe that somebody is reading your balance.
Four things sit in your account right now that are never reported to anyone.
Not the balance. Not a check of any size.
Not money your family gives you.
Not what your daughter sends through her phone.
This is each one, and what believing the opposite has already cost you.
Number one is the amount of money sitting in your account.
Say you have eighty thousand dollars in savings.
You have had it a long time. You worry about it, and part of the worry is a
feeling that somebody official knows it is there and is thinking about it.
Nobody knows it is there. There is no report.
There is no file. The bank does not send a yearly statement of your balance
to the tax office and there is no law that asks it to.
What the bank does send is one small form, once a year, and it is triggered
by ten dollars. If your money earned ten dollars or more in interest across
the year, the bank must send that form.
Below ten dollars, it does not even have to do that.
And look at what is printed on it.
The amount of interest. That is the number the tax office receives.
Eighty thousand dollars sitting in an
account earning half of one percent produces
a form that says four hundred dollars.
The eighty thousand does not appear anywhere on it.
So the tax office knows what your money earned.
It does not know what your money is.
Those are two completely different facts and almost everybody has them mixed
up.
Now think about what that mix up has cost people.
I have heard from someone who kept eleven thousand dollars in cash in the house
for two years because they did not want a bank to know they had it.
Two years of a burglary risk, two years of fire risk, and not one dollar of
insurance on any of it, all to hide a number from a form that was never printed.
I have heard from someone who refused to move their savings to an account paying
better interest, because moving it felt like being noticed.
They lost several hundred dollars a year in interest for nothing.
And some people do the most damaging thing of all, which is to divide a deposit
into smaller pieces so it looks smaller going in.
That one is not just pointless.
It is against the law in its own right, and people have been prosecuted over
money that was completely honest.
Every one of those decisions came from the same wrong belief.
Somebody is watching the balance.
Nobody is watching the balance.
And notice who this belief lands on hardest.
It is not the person with an accountant, because somebody already told them.
It is the person who did their own taxes for forty years, who trusts what they
hear, and who has nobody to ask.
The fear is aimed at exactly the people least able to check it, and that is
not an accident. It is a market.
One more thing about that little form, because it is worth being exact.
If your money earned less than ten dollars in the whole year, the bank does
not have to send it at all. So a person with a few thousand dollars in an ordinary
account may go year after year with nothing whatever being sent about them,
and never know that is what silence means.
Number two is what the tax office actually looks at, and what it never does.
Let me set out the whole list, because it is much shorter than people imagine,
and the shortness is the point.
Your bank tells the tax office how much interest you earned.
That is the first thing and it is the ordinary one.
Your bank files a separate report when somebody moves more than ten thousand
dollars in cash.
Notice the word cash.
Paper money, handed across a counter, or taken out across a counter.
That report is not about you being suspected of anything.
It is automatic, it happens thousands of times a day, and if the money is yours
and honest, nothing follows from it.
And your bank files a third kind of report if a member of staff believes something
about the account looks wrong.
You are never told when that happens.
That is written into the law, and it is the one thing in this list you have
no visibility of. That is the list.
Three things. Interest, large cash, and staff suspicion.
That third one deserves a moment, because it is the only one with real teeth
and almost nobody explains it properly.
A member of bank staff who thinks something looks unusual can file a report,
and the law forbids them from telling you they did it.
Not discourages. Forbids. There is a penalty attached to telling you.
Understand what that means and what it does not mean.
It means you will never be warned.
It does not mean anything happens afterwards.
The overwhelming majority of those reports are filed, stored, and never acted
on by anybody, because they are a net, not an accusation.
The thing that gets a senior into that net is almost always the same thing,
and it is behaviour that looks like hiding, not the size of the money.
Now hold on to what is not on it, because this is where the fear lives.
Your balance is not on it. The tax office is not sent a figure for what you
hold. Your ordinary spending is not on it.
Nobody receives a list of what you bought.
Your transfers between your own accounts are not on it.
Moving your own money from savings to checking creates nothing, because you
have not earned anything and nothing has left your hands.
And a check is not on it, at any size.
This is the one that surprises people most, so I want to be very plain.
The ten thousand dollar report is about cash.
If you sell a house and a check for two hundred and forty thousand dollars
is deposited into your account, no report of that kind is filed.
The money is traceable, of course, because a check is a piece of paper with
names on it. But the automatic report people are frightened of does not apply
to it. Number three is the money that comes in.
People treat every deposit as if it carries a tax question with it.
Most of them carry nothing at all.
A deposit is not income.
Those are separate ideas and the difference decides everything.
Income is money you earned or were paid.
A deposit is simply money arriving in an account, and money arrives for all
sorts of reasons that have nothing to do with earning.
You sell a car. The money for the car is not income, because you already owned
the car. You are turning one thing you own into another thing you own.
You move money from one bank to another.
Not income. Your daughter pays you back the four hundred dollars she borrowed.
Not income. She is returning your own money to you.
You take money out of a savings account you already paid tax on years ago.
Not income now. An insurance company pays for the damage to your roof.
Not income.
Every one of those lands in your account looking exactly like every other deposit,
and not one of them creates a tax bill or a report.
And here is where it does the most harm.
Somebody in their seventies sells the old car for six thousand dollars and
then decides not to deposit it at all, because six thousand dollars appearing
in the account feels like it will start something.
So the money sits in a kitchen drawer instead, uninsured, until it is spent
or lost or taken. Nothing would have started.
It was money from their own car.
And this is the pattern under every example.
The money was never the problem.
The hiding was.
A large deposit with a clear reason behind it is the most ordinary thing a
bank sees all day. A pattern of
small deposits from a person who suddenly changed
how they bank is the thing that gets looked at.
So the very act people take to feel safer is the one act that creates the attention
they were afraid of.
Number four is money from your family, and money that arrives through a telephone.
This one has two halves and both of them are simpler than people think.
The first half. If your son or your daughter gives you money, that money is
not income to you. It does not go on your return.
You do not report it and you do not pay tax on it.
That is true whether it is two hundred dollars or twenty thousand.
There is a line, and the line matters, but notice which side of it you are
on. If one person gives another person more than nineteen thousand dollars
in a single year, the person who gave it may have to file a form about it.
The person who received it files nothing.
Not a form, not a note, nothing.
The paperwork, if there is any, belongs to the giver.
So when your daughter helps you with a large bill, or your son covers a hospital
cost, that is not a thing you must report, and the amount does not change your
side of it. The second half is the telephone.
More and more people your age receive money through an application on a phone,
because that is how their children send it now.
When that money is a family payment, when your granddaughter is paying you
back or sending you something for your birthday, it is not reportable at all.
Not at any amount.
The forms that apply to those applications are for business payments, for people
selling things. And the limit on that business reporting recently moved, in
the direction nobody expects. For a while there was talk of it dropping to
six hundred dollars, and a great deal of fear was sold on that number.
It did not happen. The limit is now twenty thousand dollars in a year, and
it also requires more than two hundred separate payments.
Both conditions. Not one. If you have
heard a lower figure from anybody, including
from me in an older video, that figure has been overtaken.
Twenty thousand dollars and two hundred payments is where it stands, and it
applies to selling, not to your family.
What to do now, and a caution first.
Everything above describes rules that apply across the country.
Your own account, your own state and your own tax position can differ, so read
what your bank sends you and ask them directly before you act on anything here.
Then do these four things.
Put the money back in the bank.
If you have been holding cash at home because of any of this, that decision
is costing you and protecting you from nothing.
Cash in a house is not insured.
Money in a bank is insured, and no report is going to be triggered by walking
it in, unless it is over ten thousand dollars in paper money, in which case
a routine form is filed and nothing happens to you.
Stop dividing deposits. If somebody told you to make two trips instead of one,
they gave you advice that can be prosecuted.
Make one deposit. If it is large, bring whatever paper explains where it came
from, and that is the end of it.
Move your savings to wherever it earns more.
The move creates no report and no tax event.
You are moving your own money between your own accounts.
And while you are doing it, look at what the old account actually paid you
last year. Find the little form, or find the line on your December statement.
If the number is under ten dollars, you have learned two things at once.
Your money earned almost nothing, and nothing at all was sent about you.
People carry a fear of being watched while holding an account so quiet that
no paper about it exists. And keep every piece of paper that explains a large
arrival. The car sale. The house closing.
The insurance settlement.
Nobody is likely to ask. But if anybody ever does, one sheet of paper closes
the question in a single sentence.
One warning, and it belongs in this video more than in most.
The people selling fear about your bank account are the ones who benefit from
your not knowing this. If somebody offers you a paid guide to protect your
account from a rule they will not name, or tells you the tax office is watching
a balance, they are selling you a problem you do not have.
Anything real about your account is written down and free to read.
Run through the four a final time.
The amount of money in your account is not reported to anyone.
What is reported is interest, large
amounts of paper cash, and staff suspicion,
and that is the whole list. Money arriving in an account is not income, so
a car sale, a repayment and a transfer between your own accounts create nothing.
And money from your family, in the hand or through a telephone, is not yours
to report at any amount.
None of this was hidden from you by any office.
It sits in public rules that anybody can read.
It stayed unknown because there is money in your believing the opposite, and
no money at all in telling you the truth.
So go and look at what that belief has cost you.
If somebody in your family is keeping cash in the house because they believe
a bank will tell on them, ring them this evening and read them what is actually
printed on that form.

title: Seniors: Your Bank Account Freezes When You Die Unless You Filed That Free Form Everywhere

segments.text: Your first wife is still named on your work  retirement account. You are already telling
yourself that doesn't matter because there is  a will and the will names the children. The
will does not decide this one. The people who  pay that money out are required to follow the
paper they are holding. And the paper they are  holding has her name on it. You did everything
asked of you at the bank. You requested the  form. You wrote your children on it. That form
is real and it works. It works on one account.  It does not reach the account where your shares
are kept. It does not reach the small business  you run in your own name. It does not reach that
work retirement account. And it stops working on  the day the person you named dies before you do.
If you never wrote a second name underneath four  accounts, your children are named on none of them.
This is where each one stops and the words you  use this week to close it. Number one is the
account where the person you named died before you  did. You wrote one name on that form. Your son,
your daughter, your husband, one name, and you  never went back because why would you? It was
done. Then that person dies first. It happens more  than people allow themselves to think about. A son
goes at 61. A husband goes at 74. And on the day  it happens, nobody at the bank telephones you to
say that your form has just stopped working  because that is what happened to it. The form
names a person who is no longer alive. There is  nobody left on it to receive anything. And a form
with a dead name on it protects nothing at all.  So the money goes where money goes when no living
name is attached. It goes to your estate, which is  another way of saying it goes to a court. and your
family waits while a judge decides who gets what  and when. That is the same court you filled the
form in to avoid. You did the work. You avoided  nothing. The fix takes one line. When you fill
that form in, you write a second name underneath  the first. The bank has a place for it. Most
people leave it blank because nobody points at it  and nobody explains what it is for. That second
name does nothing at all while the first person  is alive. It sits there. It costs you nothing.
But on the day your first choice dies before  you, that second name steps in and the account
still passes straight to a living person with no  court, no waiting, no lawyer. And understand what
it means that this is the fix. The most common way  a beneficiary form fails is not that the form is
wrong. It is that the form was right on the day  you signed it and the world moved afterwards and
nobody is employed to tell you. Go and look at  your form. If there is one name on it, it is one
death away from doing nothing. And think about who  that catches hardest. Somebody who did this early
in their 60s while they were well and putting  their affairs in order. They filled it in 20
years ago and they have been carrying the comfort  of it ever since. The person who never filled
the form in at all knows they have a problem. The  person who filled it in perfectly in 2006 does not
and will never be told. Number two is the account  where your shares are kept. If you have money in
shares or funds, that money is not sitting in your  bank. It is held at a different company, a broker,
and it lives under a different set of rules  entirely. The form you signed at your bank does
not reach it. Not partly, not eventually. It has  no effect there at all. Your bank cannot instruct
that company. And that company has never seen your  bank form. That account needs its own paperwork,
and it is not even called the same thing. At a  bank, it is payable on death. at a broker. It
is a transfer on death registration and you have  to ask that company for it by that name. And this
next fact is the reason this one catches so many  families. Whether that company offers it at all
is up to them. Some firms simply do not. There  is no law forcing every broker to give you this.
And if yours does not, then the only route your  shares can take is through the court. Read that
again because it is unusual. On this one, doing  everything right may still not be enough. And
the only way to find out is to ask them directly.  So, put the question to them in these words. Do
you offer transfer on death registration on this  account? And if you do, send me the form. If the
answer is no, you have learned something today  that most people learn after they are gone. And
you have time to move that money somewhere that  does offer it. And do not assume it is handled
because someone helped you set the account  up years ago. The person who sold you those
funds was paid to sell you those funds. Naming who  receives them was not part of that conversation.
Number three is the account for the small business  you run in your own name. A lot of people over 65
have one. You cut lawns. You do books for two  neighbors. You sell what you make. You opened
an account so the money stayed separate from the  household. and the bank put the business name on
it. What that account actually is will surprise  you. If the business is just you with no company
registered behind it, then in the eyes of the  law, that business does not exist as a separate
thing. It has no life of its own. It is you with a  different name printed on the checks. Which means
the money in it is your personal money. And when  you die, it does exactly what your personal money
does. It stops. It waits for the court and it  is worse than an ordinary account for a reason
that catches families offguard. Nobody can step in  and keep the business running while they wait. The
invoices are not paid. The supplier is not paid.  Whatever was owed to you stays owed and whatever
you owed keeps growing and none of it can be  settled from an account nobody can reach. I have
heard from families who watched a small business  die in the 8 weeks after a funeral. Not because
the business was failing, but because the only  account it had was frozen and there was no name
on it. So, if you have an account with a business  name on it, go and ask one question. Can I add
a beneficiary to this account? And if not, what  would let my family reach it? Some banks allow it,
some do not, and will tell you the account has to  be restructured first. Either answer is useful.
Not asking is the only wrong move. Number four  is the work retirement account with a name on
it from a marriage that ended. Check this one  tonight. It holds more money than anything else
most people leave behind. And its paperwork is  the oldest thing in the house. You filled that
form in decades ago. You were married then. You  wrote your wife on it because of course you did.
Then the marriage ended and you dealt with the  house and the lawyers and the children and nobody
in that room ever said the words retirement  account beneficiary form. Here is the rule and
it is harder than people expect. Those plans are  required to pay according to the plan documents
they hold. Not your will, not the divorce papers,  not what everyone in the family knows you would
have wanted, the form. So the money goes to a  person you have not spoken to in 20 years and
your children receive nothing from that account  and there is nobody to be angry with because
every single person involved did exactly what they  were required to do. I want to be accurate with
you here because this one has moving parts. Some  plans do cancel a former spouse automatically when
a divorce comes through. Many do not. It depends  entirely on the wording of the plan you are in,
which means you cannot assume it either way. And  the only way to know is to ask. And if you married
again, your current wife has rights of her own  in most workplace plans, which can change the
answer completely. That is another reason to ask  rather than guess. So telephone the plan and say
this. I want to know who is currently named  as beneficiary on my account and I want it in
writing. Then if the name is wrong, ask for the  form to change it and send it back the same week,
not the same month. There is no penalty for doing  it today and no way to fix it afterwards. Number
five is not an account. It is a limit that changed  and almost nobody has been told. You may have
heard that naming more people protects more of  your money. It used to work more generously than
it does now. That changed in the spring of 2024,  and it changed for accounts that already existed,
not just new ones. The rule, as it stands now, is  this money. An account with beneficiaries named on
it is protected up to $250,000 for each person you  name, and it stops counting at five people. Five
names, $1,250,000. And that is the ceiling for  you at that one bank. So if you name six children,
the sixth name adds nothing. If you named eight  grandchildren, believing each one carried its own
protection, five of them do, and three of them  are carrying nothing at all. And it applies to
accounts you opened years ago, and to money locked  in a certificate, whatever the date on it says.
Nobody wrote to tell existing customers that the  arithmetic under their account had changed. The
rule simply started and the money above the  line stopped being covered the same day. Now
most people watching this are nowhere near  that ceiling. And I am not going to pretend
otherwise. But some of you sold a house. Some of  you have one bank holding everything because it
is the bank you have used since 1970. If that  is you, the money above that line is sitting
there with nothing behind it and moving part of  it to a second bank fixes it in an afternoon.
Now the steps and one line before them. This is  general information about how these systems work,
not advice about your own situation. So read your  own paperwork and ask your own bank and your own
plan. This week, make four telephone calls and  make them in this order. Largest money first.
Call the work retirement plan. Ask who is named  right now and ask for it in writing. That is the
biggest amount and the oldest paperwork. So,  it is where the worst surprise is likely to
be waiting. Call the company that holds your  shares. Ask whether they offer transfer on
death registration on your account. If they say  yes, ask them to send the form. If they say no,
write that down because you now have a  decision to make about where that money lives.
Go to your bank in person if you can and ask to  see the beneficiary form on every account you
hold there. Not one account, everyone. Then look  for the second line, the one under the first name,
and put a name in it. And if you have an account  with a business name on it, ask what can be done
for that one because the answer is different at  different banks. Write down the date of every call
and the name of every person you speak to. You  will not remember in March which of these four
you finished and the one you skip is the one that  costs. Now the warning and it belongs here because
you are about to start telephoning about money and  death and there are people who watch for exactly
that. Nobody from a bank or a retirement plan will  telephone you first about your beneficiaries. If a
call comes in and the person on the line already  seems to know who your children are, hang up.
ring the number printed on your own statement  instead. Nothing about this is urgent enough
to be settled with a stranger who called you. So  there they are one last time and every one of them
is a place where the form you already signed does  not reach. The account where the person you named
died before you did and there was no second name  underneath. The account where your shares are kept
which needs its own paperwork and may not offer it  at all. the account for the small business you run
in your own name, which the law does not treat as  separate from you, and the work retirement account
still holding a name from a marriage that ended,  where the plan is required to follow the paper and
not your will. None of this is hidden, and none  of it is unfair. Every rule here is written down,
and every one of them was followed. The whole  thing works this way because filling in a form
once was treated as the end of the job and  nobody was ever given the task of telling you
when it stopped working. Go and look at your forms  tonight. And if your mother or your father filled
one in 20 years ago and has never looked at it  since, telephone them and ask them one question.

title: Seniors Over 65: Your Bank Just Changed 3 Things About Your Checking Account — Never Told You

segments.text: Two hundred dollars can leave your
checking account without your card, without
your signature, and without anyone telephoning you.
You have sixty days from the day your statement is sent to report it.
Report it in time and you owe nothing.
Miss that day and the two hundred is still yours to reclaim, but everything
taken afterwards is not.
Four hundred more goes out on day sixty one, you speak on day sixty two, and
that four hundred can be charged to you in full.
That is not my example.
That is the example the regulator prints in its own rulebook.
Most people over sixty five open
a statement when something already feels wrong,
and by then the sixty days are spent.
This is how the money goes out, what your bank is forced to do once you speak,
and the deadlines that decide how much of it you carry yourself.
Number one is the thing almost nobody gets right, and getting it wrong costs
people money every single week.
There are two completely different situations, and they run on two different
sets of rules. The first situation is a card or a personal number that is lost
or stolen. Somebody has the physical thing, or the numbers off the front of
it, and they use it. The second situation is money pulled straight out of your
account with no card involved at all.
A company sets up a payment. Someone who got your account number off a check
arranges a withdrawal.
Nothing was taken from your pocket.
The money simply goes out. Now hold on to the difference, because this is where
people lose money they never had to lose.
In the first situation, the one with the card, there are two early deadlines
with two amounts attached.
Tell your bank within two business days of finding out, and the most you can
be made to carry is fifty dollars.
Wait longer than two business days and
that ceiling rises to five hundred dollars.
In the second situation, the one with no card, those two amounts do not exist
at all. The rulebook says it in plain words.
Those first two limits do not apply to money taken without a card.
So what protects you in the second situation.
One thing. Sixty days. And this matters more for you than for anybody else,
because the second situation is the common one after sixty five.
Very few people your age are having a card snatched from their hand at a cash
machine. What happens instead is a company that keeps drawing money after being
told to stop, or a payment arranged by somebody who got your account details
off a piece of paper you threw out.
Which means most older people are protected by exactly one deadline, and it
is the one nobody has ever told them about.
Number two is that deadline, and I want you to be exact about where it starts,
because people get this wrong and it costs them everything that follows.
Sixty days is counted from the day your bank sends the statement.
Not the day it lands on your table.
Not the day you open it. The day they send it.
So every day the statement sits closed is a day off your sixty.
A person who opens their statement once a quarter has already spent the whole
period before they look.
Now the part that decides the money.
If you report inside those sixty days, you carry nothing for that theft.
Not fifty dollars, not five hundred, nothing.
The money goes back. If you go past sixty days, the first theft is still yours
to reclaim. Missing the deadline does not erase it.
What it does is remove the ceiling on everything taken afterwards.
The rulebook gives its own example, and I am reading it to you the way it is
written. Two hundred dollars is taken from an account without permission and
without a card. If the person reports it within sixty days of the statement
being sent, they have no liability at all.
But if four hundred more is taken on day sixty one, and the person does not
speak until day sixty two, they may be liable for the full four hundred.
Sit with that for a moment. The first two hundred was never really the danger.
The danger was the second theft, the one that only happened because the first
one went unreported. That is what the sixty days is actually protecting you
from. Not the money already gone.
The money still coming. And thieves know the pattern.
Somebody who takes two hundred dollars and sees nothing happen for two months
has learned that nobody is watching this account.
The second withdrawal is always bigger than the first.
Number three is what your bank is forced to do the moment you speak, and most
people have no idea how strong this is.
Once you tell them, they must begin looking into it straight away.
They are not allowed to sit and wait for you to put it in writing first.
A telephone call starts the clock.
They then have ten business days to finish looking and tell you what they found.
If they cannot finish inside ten business days, they are allowed more time,
up to forty five days, but only on one condition.
They must put the money back into
your account first, while they carry on looking.
Read that again, because it is the part that changes how the telephone call
feels. The money goes back into your account before they have decided anything.
You get the full use of it during the whole investigation.
And within two business days of putting it back, they have to tell you the
amount and the date they did it.
If they decide an error did happen, they must correct it, and that includes
giving back any fees they charged you and any interest you lost because the
money was missing.
And when they give you their answer, they must put their findings in writing,
and they must tell you that you have the right to ask for the documents they
relied on. If a bank tells you on the telephone that they investigated and
found nothing, you are entitled to see what they looked at.
Ask for it by those words. The papers you relied on.
There are longer periods in a few narrow cases, such as a payment that started
outside the country or an account opened in the last thirty days.
Those are the exceptions. For an ordinary checking account that has been open
for years, ten business days or provisional money back is the rule.
And notice what none of this depends on.
It does not depend on the branch liking you.
It does not depend on how long you have banked there, or on whether the person
answering the telephone believes your story.
These are steps a bank is required to take once it has been told, and the requirement
starts from the words you say, not from a decision anybody makes about you
afterwards.
Number four will surprise you, and it is written into the rules in a single
hard sentence.
Being careless cannot be used against you.
If you wrote your personal number on the card itself, or on a slip of paper
in the same wallet as the card, that does not increase one dollar of what you
owe. The rulebook states it directly.
Carelessness by the customer cannot be used as a reason to make that customer
carry more than the limits allow.
I want you to hear why that sentence exists.
Banks used to argue exactly this.
You were careless, so this is your own doing, so you are paying for it.
That argument was taken away from them and written out of the rules on purpose.
So if you telephone your bank and somebody suggests that you brought this on
yourself, that person is either mistaken or hoping you will accept it and hang
up.
What you owe is decided by one thing only.
How quickly you reported it. Nothing else.
Not your age, not your habits, not where you kept the card.
The same section says something else worth carrying.
No agreement you signed with your bank can make you liable for more than these
limits. If there is a paragraph in your account paperwork that says otherwise,
it does not stand. And if your state has a law that gives you better protection
than this, the better one applies.
Number five was written for exactly the thing that happens to people your age,
and almost nobody knows it is in there.
If the reason you could not report in time was outside your control, the bank
is required to give you longer.
Not may. Is required to. The rules name the circumstances, and the two named
in the official text are being in hospital and being away from home for an
extended period. A person who spends three weeks in a hospital bed and comes
home to two months of mail nobody sorted is precisely the person that sentence
was written for. So if you missed the sixty days because you were ill, or in
a care setting, or away, say so, and say it early in the call.
Those exact circumstances require the bank to extend the period to a reasonable
one. And there is a second protection sitting beside it.
Somebody else can report it for you, and it counts as if you did it yourself.
If you are in a hospital bed and cannot make the call, your daughter can make
it, and the law treats that as your notice.
The bank may ask her to show she is acting for you, but the notice stands from
the moment she speaks. One more thing in that same part, and it removes the
last excuse people give themselves for not calling.
You do not need the account number.
You do not need the card number.
If you can identify the account well enough for them to find it, by the name
on it and the type of account, your notice counts.
People put off calling because they cannot find the paperwork.
The paperwork is not required to start the clock.
Here are the steps, and one note before them.
Everything in this video is general information about rules that apply across
the country. It is not advice about your account, so read your own agreement
and speak to your own bank, because banks differ in what they offer beyond
the minimum. Go and get your last two statements today.
Not this week. Today.
Look at every line that left the account and put a mark next to anything you
cannot name. You are not looking for large amounts.
You are looking for small ones you do not know, because that is how it starts.
A thief takes four dollars first to see whether anybody notices, and when nobody
does, they come back for the rest.
If you find one, telephone the bank the same day and use plain words.
There is a payment on my account that I never agreed to, and I am reporting
it now. Say the date it came out and the amount.
Then write down the date you called, the time, and the name of the person you
spoke to. That note is what proves when your sixty days stopped running, and
if there is ever an argument about it, it is the only thing you will have.
Then ask one question before you hang up.
When will I receive your findings in writing.
That single question tells the person on the line that you know there is a
deadline, and it changes the call.
If more than ten business days pass and no money has come back and no answer
has arrived,
telephone again and say the words provisional credit.
That is the phrase for money returned to you while they are still looking.
And put a date in your calendar for the day each statement arrives from now
on. Ten minutes, once a month, is the whole defense.
Now the warning, and this one is aimed at the exact moment you are in right
now. Nobody from your bank will ever telephone you and ask you to move your
money to a safe account. There is no such thing as a safe account.
That call is the crime itself, and it is aimed at people who have just been
told to watch their statements.
Your bank does not need your personal number to look at your own account.
If a caller asks for it, hang up and telephone the number printed on your own
card. So there they are, one last time.
Money taken with a card and money taken without one run on different rules,
and after sixty five you are almost always in the second one.
Sixty days from the day the statement is sent, and it protects you from the
second theft more than the first.
Once you speak, they have ten business days or they must put the money back
while they keep looking. Being careless cannot be used to make you carry more.
And if you were ill or away, they are required to give you longer, and somebody
else can speak for you. None of this is hidden.
It is printed in the rules that every bank in this country already follows.
It works the way it does because the burden of noticing was put on you, and
nobody was given the job of telling you that.
Go and look at your statements tonight.
If somebody in your family has not opened a bank statement in two months, telephone
them and ask them to open it while you are on the line.

title: 4 Bills You Stop Paying the Day You Ask After 65 — and the Government Will Never Tell You

segments.text: Every month, money you are not required to pay leaves your account anyway.
Not by mistake. Not by fraud. The
rule already exists, your name already qualifies,
and nobody turns it on, because nobody is paid to turn it on for you.
The county does not telephone.
Your state does not write.
Social Security does not go through your file and fix it.
Every one of these stops the day you ask, and not one day sooner.
The years you did not ask are gone, and no one pays them back.
Four bills. Four places to ask.
Here they are, and who you say them to.
Number one is the extra amount Medicare charges you for money you no longer
earn. Here is how it works, and it catches almost everybody who retires.
The amount taken out of your Social Security for Medicare is not set on what
you earn now. It is set on your tax return from two years ago.
Two years. So the year you stop working, the year the salary ends, you carry
on being charged as though you were still on it.
That is not a mistake in their system.
That is the system. It looks back two years because two years is the most recent
return they hold, and nobody at Social Security opens your file and thinks,
this person retired, we should look at this again.
There is no such person and there is no such review.
Think about who that catches hardest.
Somebody who worked right up to sixty seven, on a decent wage, and stopped.
Their income falls off a cliff in one week.
Everything else in their life adjusts within a month or two.
This one does not adjust for two years unless they make it, and those are exactly
the two years when the money is tightest and every dollar is being counted.
But there is a form, and it exists precisely for this.
It is called form S S A forty four, and it is a request to have that amount
recalculated because your life changed.
Stopping work counts as one of those changes.
So does the death of a spouse, a divorce, losing a pension, or a business that
closed. You fill in what happened and when, you show something that proves
it, and you send it to a Social Security office.
A letter from an employer saying you retired.
A death certificate. Whatever fits the event.
If your income really did fall, the amount they take can come down, and it
comes down in the money that lands in your account every month.
And be clear about the size of this one, because it is not small.
The base amount most people pay for
Medicare is a little over two hundred dollars
a month. Anyone charged the higher amount because of an old salary can be paying
well above that, month after month, out of a payment that was meant to cover
their living. Now hear the part that should annoy you.
That form has existed for years.
It sits on their own website. And a person who never hears about it goes on
paying an amount calculated from a salary they have not earned since the day
they walked out of the building, sometimes for years, and every single one
of those months is money gone.
Number two is the phone and internet discount that drops you without a word.
There is a federal discount for older people on a low income that cuts a set
amount from what you pay for phone or internet every month.
That much a good many of you already know.
Here is the part almost nobody knows, and it is where the damage is done.
That discount is not permanent.
Once a year your eligibility has to be confirmed.
A lot of the time that happens
automatically in the background and you do nothing,
which is the way it should work.
But when it does not happen automatically, a letter is sent to you asking you
to confirm. From that point you have sixty days.
Answer it and the discount continues.
Do not answer it, for any reason at all, and you are dropped from the program
entirely.
Think about what that letter looks like arriving at your house.
It is an official looking envelope about a phone discount.
It sits in the pile with the advertisements.
And there is no follow up, no telephone call, and no second warning at day
fifty nine. On day sixty one the discount is simply gone, your bill goes up,
and nothing on the bill explains why.
I have heard from people who assumed the company had raised the price.
They rang and complained about the price.
Nobody at the company mentioned that a letter had gone unanswered, because
the person answering the telephone has no idea either.
So if your phone or internet bill went up and you never found out why, that
is the first thing to go and check, and it costs nothing to check it.
And notice the shape of this one, because you will see it again and again.
The benefit is not taken from you.
It is allowed to lapse.
Nobody decided you should lose it and nobody had to sign anything.
A letter went out, sixty days passed, and a computer removed you.
There is no argument to have with anybody, because nobody did anything wrong.
That is what makes it so hard to get angry at, and so easy to miss.
Number three is the heating money that runs out before winter does.
There is federal money that helps older people pay to heat and cool their homes,
and your own state runs it. Most people who have heard of it think of it the
way they think of Social Security, as something that is simply there when you
need it. It is not. It is a fixed pot of money, and when the pot is empty the
program stops for the year. Many states hand it out first come, first served,
and it is common for programs to run out of money before the season is over.
Applications open in the fall, most states in October or November, and the
people who apply in the first weeks get paid while the ones who wait until
January are told there is nothing left.
Sit with that, because it is not how anybody expects a benefit to work.
It is not that you did not qualify.
You did qualify. You still qualify.
The money went to people who asked earlier, and you asked in February.
Nobody rings to tell you the pot is emptying.
No notice arrives in October telling you the doors are open.
The people who know, know, and they apply, and the rest find out when it is
too late to matter. And it is worth saying who usually knows.
Somebody in the family works in an office where this comes up.
A neighbor mentions it over a fence.
A church runs a session about it in September.
It is passed between people, not sent out by anybody, which means the person
living alone with no one to mention it is the person least likely to hear,
and often the person who needs it most.
So the action is simple and the timing is everything.
Telephone your state energy assistance office now, before the cold weather,
and ask when applications open and what you need to have ready.
Do that in September and October, not in December when your house is already
cold and you are frightened by the bill.
Number four is the one search that finds everything you are entitled to at
once. Everything I have given you so far is a separate door with a separate
person behind it. Social Security for one.
Your phone company for another.
Your state for a third. Nobody holds a list of all of them for you, and no
office looks at your situation and says, here is everything you are owed.
There is one place that comes close, and let me be exact about what it is.
It is a free service run by a national charity for older people, not a government
office and not connected to any of them.
You put in your zip code and some basic details about your income and situation,
and it tells you which programs in your state you are likely to qualify for.
It is called Benefits Check Up, run by the National Council on Aging.
It takes about ten minutes and it does not ask for a payment or a card.
What it gives you back is a list, and that list is the thing you cannot get
anywhere else, because the programs are run by different offices at different
levels of government who do not talk to one another about you.
One more thing about this one.
It will show you programs you have never heard of and did not think applied
to you, and the first reaction most people have is that it must be for somebody
worse off. Read the numbers before you decide that.
The income limits on a good many of these are far higher than people assume,
and a person on an ordinary Social Security payment qualifies for more than
they expect. And do it with somebody if you can.
A daughter, a son, a neighbor who is comfortable with a computer.
Not because you cannot do it, but because two people reading a list catch more
than one, and the list is longer than most people expect.
Now let me be plain about what to actually do this week, and I should say that
everything here is general information and not advice about your own case,
so do check your own position, because states and situations differ.
Start with the Medicare one, because it is the largest amount and the slowest
to move. If you or your husband or your wife stopped working in the last two
years, look up form S S A forty four, fill it in, and send it with something
that proves the date.
That single form has the biggest number attached to it of anything in this
video. Do not write a letter for that one.
Telephone.
A letter to a Social Security office can sit for weeks, and you will not know
whether it arrived.
On the telephone you get a name and a date, and that is worth more than anything
you post. Then telephone your phone or internet company and ask one question.
Am I still on the low income discount, and has anything been sent to me that
I have not returned. Write down the date you called and who you spoke to.
Then telephone your state energy
assistance office and ask when applications
open for the winter. Put the date in your calendar the same day you are told
it. Then sit down for ten minutes with Benefits Check Up and read what comes
back.
And write all four on one sheet of paper before you start.
The date you called. Who you spoke to.
What they said. Not because anybody is going to argue with you, but because
these things take a second telephone call more often than a first one, and
the person you get the second time will not know anything about the first.
If any of that feels like a lot at once, do them in that order and do one a
day.
Monday the form. Tuesday the phone company.
Wednesday the state office. Thursday the search.
By Friday every one of the four is moving, and not one of them needed permission
from anybody.
Four things. None of them costs anything.
All four can be started this week, and the whole list takes less time than
one afternoon. One warning before I finish, because these people follow videos
like this one. If somebody telephones you offering to claim benefits on your
behalf for a fee, or asking for a payment to check what you qualify for, hang
up. Every single thing in this video is free.
The form is free. The discount is free to apply for.
The heating money is free to apply for.
The search is free.
Anybody asking to be paid to stand between you and money you are already owed
is not helping you. So there are the four, one last time.
The Medicare amount charged on a salary you no longer earn, which form S S
A forty four exists to correct.
The phone and internet discount that drops you after sixty days of silence.
The heating money that runs out before winter ends, which is why you apply
in the fall and not in January.
And the one free search that finds the rest.
And there is a pattern under all four that is worth carrying with you after
this video ends. None of these systems is designed to find you.
They are designed to answer you.
That is a completely different thing, and once you see it you will spot it
everywhere, in every office and every bill and every letter that arrives.
Not one of those switches itself on.
Not one office in this country is going to look at your file, notice what you
qualify for, and put it right without being asked.
That is not cruelty and it is not a conspiracy.
It is simply how it is built, and it is built that way because the money stays
where it is when nobody asks. You know what to ask for now, and you know who
to ask.
If somebody in your family retired in the last two years and has never heard
of that form,
telephone them tonight and tell them the number.
Every month they wait is a month nobody gives back.
