understand that completely because it
was how I was raised, too.
But, this is not making a fuss. It is
answering a question that nobody thought
to ask you. Number five is a free
complaint that your bank must answer
within 15 calendar days. Before I
explain it, please treat everything here
as general information and not as legal
or financial advice.
Banks differ, states differ, and only
somebody looking at your actual account
can tell you how your case will go.
There is a federal office whose entire
job is to take complaints about banks
from ordinary people. You do not need a
lawyer to use it. You do not pay
anything at all.
You fill in a form on their website or
you telephone them and you describe what
happened in your own words.
It takes about 10 minutes.
What makes it work is not the form
itself.
Your complaint goes directly to your
bank and your bank is expected to
respond within 15 calendar days.
Not to you at the window where nobody is
keeping score, to a federal office that
writes down whether they answered, when,
and what they said. Almost every
complaint that comes in is routed to the
company that way and you can feel the
difference in how you are treated
afterwards. The person who telephones
you back is not the one from the window.
It is somebody whose job is to close
that file properly
and closing it properly nearly always
means giving you your money and an
explanation.
So, this is the order to do it in
and the order matters more than any
single step. First, before you complain
to anybody, gather three things. The day
you made the deposit or the day you were
first refused, the amount,
and the name of every person you have
spoken to.
If you were given the written notice,
keep it with them.
This takes 10 minutes at your kitchen
table and it is the whole difference
between a complaint somebody reads
properly and one that gets filed away.
Second, telephone the branch manager
once by that title and say three things.
How much is being held and under which
exception? I would like the notice in
writing. And this is the day I need the
money, and this is why. Third, if that
does not fix it, make the complaint.
Do not spend 2 weeks hoping it sorts
itself out, because the 15 days do not
begin until you send it in. Every day
spent hoping is a day nobody is
counting.
And one more thing, because it decides
whether the rest of this works. Keep
everything on paper. A cheap notebook
beside the telephone, the date, the
time, the name, and one line about what
was said.
I have watched people win these because
they could say, on the 11th of the month
at 10:02, a man named David told me it
would be released on Friday. There is
one more thing to be careful about, and
it arrives at exactly this point in the
story.
A stranger telephones, or an
advertisement finds you, promising to
unlock your account for you.
Sometimes they call it a recovery
service. Sometimes they say they know
somebody inside the bank. What they
always want is a cut or a fee up front.
And what they are selling is the
10-minute form you have just been shown.
Understand why they come now.
A person whose account has been blocked
is frightened, in a hurry, and not
thinking clearly, and that is the
easiest person in the world to sell
something to. The federal office charges
nothing.
Your bank charges nothing. Anybody who
wants paying to stand between you and
your own money is not helping you. So,
let me set the five down one final time.
Most of your money is not allowed to be
kept from you, and $275
of it must be there the next business
day.
Your bank must tell you in writing why
it is keeping the rest. It must tell you
the exact day you get it back. Telling
your bank what the money is for can move
it faster. And a free complaint must be
answered within 15 calendar days.
Not one of those five is a kindness.
Not one of them is something your bank
hands you because you were patient
enough or polite enough.
They are rules that already exist,
written down, sitting there waiting for
somebody to point at them.
The only reason they go unused so often
is that the person they were written to
protect was never told they were there.
And I want to leave you with the reason
this matters more than the money in any
one account.
A person who knows the rules stops being
afraid of the letter, the telephone
call, and the counter.
You stop hoping somebody will be kind to
you, and you start asking which rule
applies.
That is a different way to walk into a
bank. And once you have done it once,
you never go back to the other way. You
have been told now. If somebody you care
about has money tied up at their bank
tonight and is sitting at home waiting
for a telephone call, send this to them.
Waiting is the one thing that never
works, and it is the only thing most
people try.

title: Banks Can Take Your Savings After 65 if You Leave It Alone Too Long

segments.text: When did you last take money out of your savings account yourself.
Not the interest going in. Not a statement arriving.
Something you did. Because your state has a rule.
If nobody touches an account for three to five years, your bank must close
it and pass the money to your state.
And the account most at risk is not the one you use every week.
It is the account you set aside on purpose and made a point of leaving alone.
And this is the thing good, careful people never see coming.
The interest the bank adds each month does not count as touching it.
The statement it mails you does not count.
Even a fee it takes out does not count.
None of it came from you. To this rule, an account only the bank touches is
an account nobody is watching.
I will give you four things that decide whether this reaches your money, and
then two ways to stop it. The second way takes about a minute.
And if your money has already gone, it is not lost, and asking for it back
is free.
Number one is what actually counts as using your account.
Only something you do. A deposit you make.
A withdrawal you take. Signing in to look at the balance on a computer or a
telephone. A letter you write asking about the account.
Any one of those tells your bank that the person who owns this money is still
here and still paying attention.
Now hear what does not count, because this is where good people lose money
they were being careful with. The interest the bank adds each month.
The statement that arrives in your post.
A monthly fee the bank takes out.
A notice about new terms and conditions.
None of that is you. All of it is the bank moving numbers around inside its
own building, and every state in the country treats it the same way.
It proves nothing about whether the owner is still there.
I want you to sit with how strange that is.
Your balance can change every single month for five years.
Money can go in. Money can come out for fees.
The paperwork can arrive at your house on time, every time.
And at the end of those five years your account can still be counted as one
that nobody has touched, because not a single one of those movements came from
your own hand. There is a reason the rule was built that way, and it is not
a foolish reason. If a bank could keep an account alive simply by adding a
penny of interest to it, then no account would ever be reported, and money
that truly had been abandoned would sit in banks forever with nobody looking
for the owner. So the people who wrote this decided that only the owner can
prove the owner is there. That is fair enough.
The trouble is that nobody explains it to the owner.
Number two is how many years it takes before your bank must act.
Three to five, depending on where you live.
Your state decides it. Not your bank, not the manager at the branch, and not
the person who opened the account for you twenty years ago.
That matters more than it may sound, and this is why.
If you telephone your branch and ask them to make an exception for you, they
cannot.
If you explain that you are saving that money on purpose and you would rather
it sat still, it changes nothing.
The bank is not choosing to do this.
The bank is being told to do this, and if it fails to do it, the bank itself
is the one in trouble. So nobody at that counter can protect you, however much
they might want to. And
notice which accounts this catches.
Not the everyday account with your Social Security going in and your bills
going out. That one gets touched constantly.
It catches the savings account you opened for an emergency.
The account holding money for a grandchild.
The small account at the second bank you stopped using when you moved.
The certificate of deposit that renews itself every year without anybody looking
at it. In other words, it catches the money you were being most careful with,
for the exact reason that you were being careful with it.
That is the cruelty of it, and I do not use that word lightly.
The person who spends everything is never caught by this.
The person who saved, and set money aside, and had the discipline to leave
it alone for a rainy day, is the only kind of person this can happen to.
Doing the right thing is what puts you in front of it.
Number three is where your bank sends the warning letter.
Before any of this can happen, the bank is required to write to you and give
you the chance to say you are still there.
That sounds like a real protection, and it would be, except for one thing.
That letter goes to the last address the bank has for you.
Think about the last ten years of your life.
If you sold the house and downsized.
If you moved closer to your children.
If you went to live with family for
a while, or into care, or spent long stretches
with a son or a daughter. If you told the main bank about the new address but
never thought about the small account at the other bank, because why would
you. In every one of those cases, the one letter that could have saved your
money is sitting in a hallway you no longer walk through.
And the person now living at that address has no idea what it is.
It looks like ordinary bank post.
It gets thrown away, or it gets sent back, and the bank writes down that it
tried. The requirement has been met.
The clock keeps running. Nobody has broken any rule, and your money still leaves.
I want to be fair to the banks on this one point, because it is not laziness.
They are told to write to the address on file, and that is what they do.
But you and I both know that an address on file at a bank you have not visited
in nine years is no longer an address.
It is old history sitting in a computer.
And that old history is standing between you and every dollar in that account.
Number four is what happens to your money and to your safe deposit box.
I want to be exact here, because most people picture the wrong thing entirely.
They picture the account being frozen, sitting there locked but waiting for
them, the way a bank freezes an account after somebody dies.
That is not what this is. The account is closed.
It stops existing. The money is sent to your state, and your state holds it
under your name. The box is worse, and almost nobody knows this part.
A safe deposit box that goes untouched runs on the same kind of clock.
When it runs out, the box is forced open in front of witnesses.
What is inside is written down, and then it is sold.
The rings that belonged to your mother.
The watch that belonged to your father.
The coins somebody in your family put away one at a time over forty years.
All of it sold at auction, and only the money from that sale is kept for you.
Read that again, slowly.
You do not get the ring back.
There is no drawer somewhere holding what belonged to your family until you
come and ask for it. There is a sum of money, and the ring is now on the hand
of a stranger. That is the part I would most want a member of my own family
to hear, because a box is exactly the kind of thing a careful person leaves
alone for years on purpose. The whole point of a box is that you do not open
it. That is what it is for. And a box is where the things live that cannot
be replaced. Money can be replaced.
A wedding ring worn by a woman who is no longer here cannot.
The rule cannot tell the difference between the two, and it was never built
to. Now let me hand you the two ways to stop it, and I should say plainly that
what follows is general guidance and not legal or financial advice, so do check
the number of years in your own state, because it is not the same everywhere.
Number five is the one action that makes the counting start over.
Take out one dollar. Put in one dollar.
Do it yourself, at the counter or on a computer, on each account you hold.
That is the whole protection. One movement made by you, and your bank writes
down a new date, and the years begin again from that day.
So this is what I would do this week, and it is a short list.
Write down every account with your name on it.
Not just the one you use. The old savings account.
The account at the bank you stopped using.
The certificate that renews on its own every year and that you have not looked
at since. The box, if you have one.
Then touch each of them once. A dollar in or a dollar out, done by you.
Then put a note in your calendar to do exactly the same thing next year on
the same day. And while you have that list in front of you, do the other half
of the job, because it is the half people skip.
Telephone each bank and make sure the address they hold for you is the one
you actually live at now. That is the single most valuable telephone call in
this whole video.
One version of that letter reaches you in time.
The other version reaches somebody you have never met.
If getting to a branch is hard, this can all be done from a chair.
Most banks will let you move a dollar between two of your own accounts over
the telephone, and that counts.
Signing in on a computer or a telephone to look at the balance counts in most
states as well. And if you would rather have it on paper, write a short letter
to the bank asking for a statement on that account and keep a copy.
A written request from the owner is one of the clearest signals there is.
Number six is how to get your money back after your state has taken it.
Because a good many of you are going to go and look, and some of you are going
to find that this already happened, perhaps years ago, to an account you had
genuinely forgotten about. This next part should ease your mind.
It is still yours. Your state does not spend it and does not keep it.
It holds it under your name, and no deadline ever runs out on you.
Money handed over thirty years ago is still claimable today by the person who
owned it, and if that person has died, by the family who inherited it.
You will have to show who you are, and if you are claiming for a parent you
will have to show that as well, but the money is sitting there waiting.
And one warning matters here, because these people find the newly bereaved
and the newly retired first. If somebody contacts you offering to recover money
in your name in exchange for a share of it, understand what they are actually
selling. They are selling you a search that you are able to do on your own,
at no cost, in about ten minutes.
Every state runs its own office for exactly this purpose.
Never hand a stranger a percentage of your own money for giving it back to
you. So let me set the six down one final time, plainly.
What counts as using your account, which is only ever something you do yourself.
How many years it takes, which is three to five and decided by your state.
Where the warning letter goes, which is the last address the bank was given.
What actually happens, which is the account closed and the box sold.
The one action that starts the counting over, which is a single dollar moved
by your own hand. And how to get back money that has already gone, which costs
you nothing at all. Nobody is going to telephone you about this.
Your bank has no reason to, and your state has no way of finding you if the
address it was handed is wrong.
The whole thing runs on paperwork, in silence, and it was never designed to
be cruel. It was designed for money that truly had been abandoned by somebody
who was never coming back.
It simply cannot tell the difference between an account that was abandoned
and an account that was being guarded.
You are now able to tell the difference, and that was the whole point of the
last twelve minutes. If somebody in your family has an old account or a box
they have not touched in years, send this to them tonight and ask them one
question. When did you last move a dollar in that account yourself.
If they cannot answer it, they have their job for the week.

title: 6 TYPES OF MONEY THE IRS DOES NOT COUNT AGAINST SENIORS AFTER 65

segments.text: Every year the government adds up your money to decide whether it is allowed
to tax your Social Security check.
Your pension goes into that sum.
Your withdrawals go in. Your interest goes in.
Even half of the Social Security check itself goes in.
And the closer that total climbs, the more of your own check becomes taxable.
But six kinds of money never go into that sum at all.
Not a penny of them. You can receive every one of them, use every one of them,
and the total the government looks at does not move by a single dollar.
Most people over sixty five have never been told that even one of these exists,
and several of them are sitting in accounts those same people already own.
I will give you all six. And before that, I want to tell you why this sum reaches
you at all, because that part is the thing almost nobody knows and it will
change how you feel about the rest of it.
The first one is the year the numbers were frozen.
When Congress wrote this rule, it picked two amounts.
Twenty five thousand dollars for a person on their own, thirty two thousand
for a married couple.
Under those amounts, your Social Security could not be taxed at all.
Over them, part of it could. And the year they picked those amounts was nineteen
eighty four.
Now consider what nineteen eighty four money was worth.
Twenty five thousand dollars a year was a comfortable retirement then.
It was the sort of income that put a person well above ordinary.
And that was the whole idea.
This rule was built to reach
the wealthiest retirees in the country, roughly
the top ten percent, the people who had real money coming in on top of their
check.
Everybody else was meant to be left completely alone.
Then the government did something that costs older Americans money every single
year since. It never adjusted those two amounts again.
Not once. Almost everything else in the tax system moves a little each year
to keep pace with the cost of living, but these two numbers were set down and
left exactly where they were. So the rule stayed still while the world moved
past it. Twenty five thousand dollars today is a modest retirement, and in
many places it is a tight one.
A rule aimed at the richest ten percent now reaches about half of everybody
drawing a Social Security check, and it reached them without one vote ever
being taken. That is the part worth holding onto.
Nothing about you changed. The rule did not change either.
The money simply moved underneath both of you, and nobody was ever sent a letter
about it. So when you hear that part of your check is taxable, understand that
you did not do anything wrong and you did not become wealthy.
You stayed exactly where you were while a frozen number came to find you.
Which is why the six that follow matter so much.
Every one of them keeps money out of that sum entirely, and each one of them
is perfectly ordinary.
Nothing here is a scheme and nothing here is clever.
These are simply the kinds of money the rule was written to leave alone, and
knowing which is which decides whether your check gets taxed or gets left alone.
The second one is money from a Roth account.
When you take money out of a Roth, it does not enter the sum.
Not the amount you put in years ago, not the growth on top of it, not any part
of it, as long as the account has been open the required length of time and
you are old enough. As far as
the government is concerned, that money is simply
not there. It never appears in the sum, in any year, in any amount.
And it does not matter what you spend it on afterwards.
You can put a new roof over your head with it, or help a grandchild through
a difficult year, and the sum stays exactly where it was.
Take a moment on this one, because it might be the most useful thing here.
Two people can take the very same ten thousand dollars out in the very same
week. The one who takes it from an ordinary retirement account may push their
total up and make part of their Social Security taxable.
The one who takes it from a Roth changes nothing at all.
Same money, same week, same person even, and a completely different answer,
decided by nothing more than which account it came out of.
The third one is money you give straight to a charity from your retirement
account. Once you are seventy and a half years old, you may send money straight
from that account to a church, or to any charity you choose, instead of taking
it yourself.
It goes from the account to them without ever passing through your hands.
And you do not have to wait until the government starts making you take money
out each year. This one opens for you earlier than that.
Here is why that is worth knowing.
Once you are old enough that
the government does require a yearly withdrawal,
a gift sent this way still counts as that withdrawal, so the government is
satisfied. But because the money never came to you, it never enters the sum
that decides how your Social Security is treated.
Most people give to their church out of the money already sitting in their
bank account, and doing it that way helps them not at all.
The same gift, to the same place, sent the other way round, keeps their total
lower for the entire year. The fourth one is money from a life insurance policy.
When a policy pays out after somebody dies, that money comes to the person
named on it without going into the sum.
The size of the payment makes no difference.
Whether it arrives all at once or
in pieces over several months makes no difference
either. The part that is the payout itself simply is not counted.
A widow who receives a payout in the same year she is already worried about
her check does not have to worry about that particular money making things
worse. It does not count. It never did.
I mention it because this is exactly the year when a person is least able to
work anything out. Somebody has just died.
The paperwork is arriving faster than anyone can read it.
And in the middle of that, a large amount of money lands in the account and
the fear arrives with it. That fear is not needed here.
That money is not part of the sum, and nobody at the insurance company is likely
to say so, because it is not their job to explain your Social Security to you.
The fifth one is your own money coming back to you.
If you cash in a savings bond, or close an account, or sell something for roughly
what you paid for it, the part that was always yours does not go into the sum.
Only the growth does. People get this wrong constantly and frighten themselves
badly over it.
They see a large amount land in the bank and assume the whole of it will be
counted against them, when in truth most of it was their own money simply returning
home.
I have heard of people leaving a bond sitting untouched for years past the
day it stopped earning anything, purely because they were afraid of what cashing
it in would do to their check.
The fear cost them more than the tax ever would have.
The same is true when you sell something at a loss or break even.
Nothing is there for the government to count, because nothing was gained.
Only profit enters the sum.
Your own money, coming back to you after years of sitting somewhere, is not
income and was never treated as income.
A person who sells a bond they bought for ten thousand dollars and receives
eleven thousand back has one thousand dollars entering the sum, not eleven.
The other ten thousand was always theirs.
It went out of their pocket years ago and it has simply come home.
The sixth one is money you take in a different year.
This one is not an account and it is not a rule.
It is timing, and it is the one you have the most control over.
The sum is worked out one year at a time.
So a large withdrawal taken all at once can push you over the amounts for that
entire year, while the very same
withdrawal split across December and January
can leave you under them in both years.
Nothing clever is required here.
You do not need an adviser, or a strategy, or anything complicated at all.
You need only to know that the year matters, and to ask the question before
the money moves rather than in March when the return is being filled in.
Once a withdrawal is made it counts, and there is no putting it back afterwards.
This is the reason I would rather you heard all of this in August than in April,
because in August you can still decide when the money moves, and in April you
can only write down what already happened.
Here is what to do with all of this.
I should say up front that what follows is general information and not tax
advice, so please check your own position with somebody who can see your actual
numbers. Start by working out roughly where you stand.
Take last year. Add up everything that came in, and then add on half of what
Social Security paid you. If that total sits comfortably under twenty five
thousand dollars on your own, or thirty two thousand as a couple, then none
of your check is being taxed and you can put this down.
If you are close to those amounts, or a little over them, that is exactly where
the six things I have just given you turn into real money.
A person sitting two thousand dollars above
the amount can often get back underneath
it by changing where one withdrawal comes from, or which year it happens in,
and nothing else about their life needs to change at all.
Then, before you take money out of any account this year, ask yourself one
question. Which account is this coming from, and does that account go into
the sum.
Those are two different questions and the second one is the one nobody asks.
That single question, asked before the money moves, is worth more than anything
you can do afterwards.
And if you are not sure, the free tax help programs for older people will run
the whole thing for you in an afternoon without charging you a penny.
They exist in every state, they are
staffed by people trained for exactly this,
and they see this question so often that they will not think it is a small
one. So let me put the six in front of you one more time, plainly.
The year the numbers were frozen, which is nineteen eighty four, and they have
never moved since.
Money from a Roth account, which never enters the sum.
Money given straight from a retirement account to a charity.
Money from a life insurance policy.
Your own money coming back to you when something is cashed in.
And money taken in a different year, which is the one you control completely.
The government will not write to you about any of this.
There is no letter that arrives explaining which of your money counts and which
of it does not. You have heard it now, though, and that puts you ahead of nearly
everybody who gets the same check.
If somebody you care about is about to take money out of a retirement account
this year, pass this along before they do it.
Five minutes now is worth more than anything they will learn from a tax return
in the spring.

title: 7 Types of Property the IRS Cannot Touch — Even When a Senior Owes

segments.text: This is a real case, and it was decided in the United States Tax Court in December
of two thousand nine.
Kathleen Vinatieri had fourteen dollars in cash.
Eight hundred dollars came in every month, and eight hundred dollars went straight
back out, so there was nothing left over at the end of it.
Her car was worth three hundred dollars,
and she needed it to get to work.
The government looked at all of that, and moved to take her wages anyway.
And she had no defense. She had not filed her tax returns.
She knew it, and they knew it.
She should have lost everything she had.
She did not. Because there are seven things the government is never allowed
to take from you, no matter how much you owe.
Kathleen had every one of them working for her, and she did not even know it.
Almost nobody is ever told these seven exist.
I will tell you how her case ended.
Here are the seven. The first one is your house.
I want to start here because this is the fear that keeps people awake at two
in the morning. You owe money, and you picture somebody knocking at your door
with paperwork, telling you to pack up and leave your own home.
So let me tell you what really has to happen.
Before the government can take the home you live in, a federal judge has to
sign for it, in writing, by hand.
It cannot be a supervisor in an office, and it cannot be a collections officer
working down a list. It has to be a judge, sitting in a courtroom, and that
judge has to be shown three things before he will sign anything.
He has to be shown that the money is truly owed.
He has to be shown that every step was done properly.
And he has to be shown that there is no other sensible way to collect it.
That is not a form to fill in.
It is a court hearing, and you have every right to be in the room while it
happens. You can be represented too, and in a few minutes I will tell you how
to be represented without paying anyone a penny.
Think about how rare that makes it.
Somebody has to want your house badly enough to build a whole court case around
taking it, and then convince a judge who gains nothing either way.
And underneath that sits a second protection, simpler and even stronger.
If you owe five thousand dollars or less, your home is off the table completely.
With a judge, without a judge, it does not matter.
That door is shut. That matters more than it sounds.
A great many tax debts in this country are small ones.
A few thousand dollars left over from a year when somebody fell behind after
an illness, or a death in the family, or a job that ended.
For a debt that size the house was never on the table, and never had been.
The letters will not tell you that.
Letters are written so that everything sounds equally final.
The second one is your Social Security check.
You are getting the whole truth on this one, including the half you will not
enjoy hearing.
They can take part of that check, and the amount is fifteen percent.
It happens through an automatic system, which means a computer matches a list
of debts against a list of payments and acts on its own.
No person reads your file. Nobody stops to ask whether fifteen percent is the
difference between heating the house in January and sitting in a cold one.
That is the part people find hardest to forgive, and I do not blame them.
Now hear the rest, because the rest is better.
Fifteen percent is a ceiling, not a starting point.
They cannot decide on twenty, and they cannot take half.
And it cannot start without warning you first.
A letter has to arrive, and from the day it lands you have thirty days before
a single dollar moves.
One more thing here, and it counts for a lot.
Where the income is low enough, that automatic system is supposed to skip you
completely. There is an income line built into it, set against the poverty
guidelines, and below that line the computer is meant to leave you alone.
It is only meant to, though, and that is exactly why somebody has to speak
up, and I will show you how at the end.
The third one is Supplemental Security Income.
This is the payment that goes to people who have almost nothing left.
This is the one they cannot touch at all.
They cannot take fifteen percent of it, they cannot take one dollar of it,
and they cannot ever take any of it.
Think about how strange that is.
It is the same government and the same person, but two different checks, and
one of them they can reach into while the other they cannot go near.
Nobody ever sits an older person down and explains the difference, so people
assume the worst about both and stop opening their letters altogether.
That is how a small problem turns into a very large one.
If Supplemental Security Income is what you live on, that money is yours.
It does not matter what you owe.
It does not matter how old the debt is.
The fourth one is a set amount out of every payment you get.
When money is being pulled out of a payment, they are not allowed to take all
of it. An amount has to be left behind for you, every single time, and that
floor is written into the law.
Nobody in an office gets to decide it.
It is worked out from the standard deduction, spread across your pay periods,
so the exact figure depends on your own situation.
What matters is that the floor is there, that it cannot be argued away, and
that no collections officer anywhere has the power to go below it.
Somebody put that floor there on purpose, a long time ago, so that collecting
a debt could never be the thing that finished a person off.
The fifth one is your furniture and the things inside your home.
That covers your bed and your chairs,
the coat on the hook by the door,
the fuel that heats the house through winter, and the food in your kitchen
right now.
Six thousand two hundred fifty dollars worth of all that is protected, and
the figure creeps up a little each year with prices, which is where it stands
today.
I include this one because of what frightened people do when nobody has told
them the truth. Families move furniture out to a garage belonging to a cousin.
Somebody sells a dining table worth nine hundred dollars for two hundred, because
they want it gone before anyone comes to the door.
None of that was ever needed.
All of it was already safe. Nobody had told them, and the fear did the rest.
The sixth one is disability payments for military service.
If you were hurt serving this country, and you get payments because of that
injury, the government cannot take that money.
They cannot take fifteen percent of it, and they cannot take any of it.
I say that plainly because a lot of confusion sits around this one.
A military pension and a service
disability payment are two different things,
and the law treats them differently.
It is the disability payment for a service injury that is protected.
If that is you, and somebody has told you otherwise, they were wrong.
The seventh one is workers compensation.
If you were hurt at work and you get payments because of it, that money is
protected too, for the same reason as the one before.
Payments like that are not really income.
They are money handed over for something that was already taken from you once.
And one more belongs beside it, so I will give it to you here.
The tools you need for your work.
If you still work, or you do a little repair, or a trade on the side to keep
things going, those tools are protected up to three thousand one hundred twenty
five dollars.
They are not allowed to take away the very thing you use to earn the money
they say you owe.
Even the government could see the sense in that one.
Now, before I tell you how the case ended, I want to give you one more fact,
and this is not my opinion. It comes from the watchdog that sits inside the
tax system itself.
The Taxpayer Advocate is an office that reports to Congress on how ordinary
people are treated. And what that office has written down is this.
Money is routinely taken from people
through levies without anyone first working
out whether that person can afford to lose it.
Nobody checks. That same office has now asked Congress to force a check to
happen, by building something that finds the people who cannot survive a collection
before the collection ever starts.
That request is sitting in front of
Congress right now, which tells you plainly
that it is not happening yet. So the protection is real.
But it does not switch itself on.
Somebody has to raise a hand and say out loud what their life actually costs
to live.
That somebody is you. Which brings me back to Kathleen Vinatieri.
She filled in a financial statement.
What came in each month, what went out each month, the fourteen dollars in
cash, and the car she needed to reach her job.
The collections office read all of it and said the levy would go ahead anyway,
because she had not filed her returns.
So she took it to the United States Tax Court.
And the court said no. The judges held that when taking money would leave a
person unable to cover their basic living costs, the government is required
to stop. It is not encouraged to stop, and it is not merely allowed to stop
if it feels like it. It is required to stop.
Then they went further, and said that requirement does not depend on whether
you have filed your returns. That is exactly what the agency had argued, and
the court told them plainly they had gone beyond their own powers.
A woman with fourteen dollars and a stack of unfiled returns walked out of
that courtroom with the levy lifted off her.
She did not win because she was clever.
She did not win because she found
a loophole, or knew somebody, or hired anyone
expensive.
She won because the protection was already sitting there in the law, waiting,
and she was the one who finally pointed at it.
That ruling still stands today.
It is the law this morning, while you are listening to me, and every collections
officer in this country is bound by it, whether they mention it to you or not.
Now to the part that actually helps you, and I should say first that this is
general information rather than legal advice, so do check your own situation.
I know some of you heard the word form a few minutes ago and felt your shoulders
drop. You thought about paperwork, and numbers, and one more thing to work
out alone at the kitchen table.
So let me give you the easy way first.
There is something called a Low Income Taxpayer Clinic, and hardly anyone has
heard of it. These are real lawyers and real tax people who will take your
case and deal with the government for you.
They do not advise you from a distance.
They represent you, in your own name, in front of the very people sending you
the letters. And they do it for free.
They are not part of the collections office, and they do not answer to it.
If your income is under about two and a half times the poverty line you qualify,
and that is most people living on a Social Security check.
The amount in dispute needs to be under fifty thousand dollars, which covers
nearly everybody listening to this.
Every state has at least one clinic, and many states have several.
Ask for publication four one three four, which is the list of them, or telephone
the Taxpayer Advocate and ask which one is nearest to you.
That is the whole job. One phone call, and somebody else carries the rest.
If you would rather do it yourself, it comes down to two pieces of paper.
Form twelve one five three asks for a hearing, and sending it in stops the
levy where it stands while a real person looks at your case properly.
Form four
three three F is the money statement.
What comes in, what goes out, nothing more complicated than that.
It is the same form Kathleen filled in.
But the one thing you cannot skip is the thirty days.
From the day that letter arrives, you have thirty days.
After that your strongest protections are gone, and every step becomes harder
and slower than it needed to be.
Make the phone call in the first week, and then let somebody else carry it.
So let me put the seven in front of you one last time.
Your house needs a federal judge before anyone can take it.
Your Social Security check has a ceiling of fifteen percent.
Supplemental Security Income is something they cannot touch at all.
A set amount has to be left out of every payment you get.
Six thousand two hundred fifty dollars of your furniture and household things
is safe.
Disability payments for military service are safe.
And so is workers compensation, along with the tools you work with.
Seven things, and not one of them applies itself.
That is the real lesson of Kathleen Vinatieri.
She had no lawyer at the start.
She had not done everything right.
She was owed no favors by anybody in that building.
She simply wrote down what her life actually cost her to live, and the law
did the rest of the work for her.
The government is not going to read you this list.
It has no reason to. But you have heard it now, and that means you can be the
person in your family who knows.
If somebody you care about has a letter sitting unopened in a drawer, send
them this before their thirty days run out.
That drawer is where nearly all of the damage happens.

title: Never Tell Your Bank These 3 Things After 65 — It Can Freeze Your Own Money

segments.text: I would like to keep this under ten thousand dollars.
Ten words.
Said politely, at a bank counter, by someone who has never broken a law in
their life.
And those ten words can freeze your account, put a report with your name on
it into a federal system that you are never allowed to see, and in the worst
cases cost you the money itself.
Not because you did anything wrong.
Because of how you said it. And this is what catches good people off guard.
Your bank is not only a place that holds your money.
By law, it is also required to watch it, and to report certain things about
you, and it is forbidden from telling you when it does.
So the words you choose at that counter matter far more than anyone ever explains.
There are three sentences in particular that older people say all the time,
believing they sound careful and responsible,
and every one of them can turn
an ordinary transaction into a problem that takes weeks to undo.
So I am going to give you all three, tell you exactly what the person behind
the counter hears when you say them, and give you the plain words to use instead.
And I want to start with the first one, because it is the only one where the
sentence itself is the offense.
Let me say it again. I would like to keep this under ten thousand dollars.
Now here is what almost nobody understands.
There is a rule that says when more than ten thousand dollars in cash moves
through your account in a single day, the bank files a routine report.
Millions of these are filed every year.
For an honest person, that report goes into a file and absolutely nothing ever
comes of it. It is paperwork. It is not an accusation, and it is not an audit.
But the moment you deliberately arrange your money to stay underneath that
line, you have crossed into something entirely different.
Breaking up your own money into smaller amounts to avoid that report is, by
itself, a federal crime. It has a name in the law, and it carries penalties
of up to five years in prison.
And I want you to hear the cruelest part of this clearly.
It does not matter one bit that the money is clean.
It can be money you earned, money you inherited,
money your own children gave you.
If you split it up to stay under the line, the splitting is the crime, all
on its own. And it is not only a criminal matter.
The government can seize that money through
a process that does not even require
them to charge you with anything.
Let me show you what that looks like with a real person, because this is not
a hypothetical.
In Iowa, a woman named Carole Hinders ran a small Mexican restaurant for nearly
forty years.
Cash business.
She did not take credit cards.
So she deposited her daily cash takings at the bank, and because a small restaurant
does not make ten thousand dollars in a day, her deposits naturally came in
under that line, day after day, year after year.
She was not hiding anything. She was simply banking what she earned.
One morning, federal agents came to her home and told her they had taken every
dollar in her business account.
Roughly thirty three thousand dollars.
Her life savings from that restaurant.
She was never charged with a crime, because she had not committed one.
The deposits themselves, the pattern of them, was the entire case.
It took a legal fight and a great deal of public attention before that money
was returned to her, and in the meantime she had to borrow to keep the restaurant
open. And she was not alone.
Hers was one of a number of cases where ordinary people, farmers, shop owners,
a family running a small convenience store, all had their accounts emptied
for the same reason. Not one of them was accused of selling anything illegal,
or hiding income, or cheating anyone.
In every case the government looked at a long row of deposits that happened
to fall under the line and decided that the pattern itself was proof enough.
The lesson those families learned the hard way is the lesson I want you to
have for free. It is not the amount that draws attention.
It is any sign that you were thinking about the line at all.
She did nothing wrong. Her only mistake was a pattern that a computer found
interesting. So here is your rule, and it is simple.
Never say anything about staying under a limit.
Never ask how to avoid the report.
And never split a large sum into smaller trips.
What you say instead is the plain truth.
I would like to withdraw twelve thousand dollars.
I am paying a contractor for a new roof.
That is it. Say the real amount, in one transaction, and let them file whatever
routine paperwork they need to file, because that paperwork has never hurt
an honest person.
That report is harmless.
The avoiding is what is dangerous.
Walk in honest and open, and you are simply a customer moving your own money.
Now the second sentence, and this one has become the most common of the three,
because the world has changed.
Someone told me to send it. Or, it is for a friend I met online.
Or, they said I need to move it right away to keep it safe.
When a teller hears any version of that from an older customer,
something specific happens behind the counter.
Banks now have rules and training built around protecting older people from
being cheated.
If they reasonably believe an older customer is being taken advantage of, they
are allowed to put a temporary hold on the money.
Not for an hour. It can run for days, and with an extension, longer.
Now I want to be fair about this, because it is not the villain it sounds like.
That rule exists because thousands of older Americans really are talked out
of their savings every year by people who are very good at it.
That hold has saved people from losing everything they had.
But it does not know the difference between a stranger running a scheme and
your own daughter asking for help.
It hears the shape of the sentence.
Someone else is directing this money.
That is the trigger. So think of a man sending money to his own son who is
buying a first house.
If he says at the counter, my son told me to send this today, he has said the
exact shape of the sentence the training is built to catch.
Someone told him. It is urgent.
It is going out fast. Nothing about it is wrong, and it can still put a hold
on the money, and now the closing is at risk.
What you say instead is the relationship and the reason.
I am wiring money to my son for the down payment on his house.
Or, this is going to my granddaughter for her tuition.
Name the person, name their relation to you, and name what the money buys.
That single change turns a warning sign into an ordinary family transaction.
And if the person behind the counter still asks you a few more questions after
that, do not take it as an insult, and please do not let it fluster you.
They are following a script that somebody in an office wrote for them, and
they are asking every older customer the same things.
Answer them the same calm way, in ordinary words, and you will be on your way.
The customers who run into real trouble are almost never the ones who answered
plainly.
They are the ones who got angry, or went vague, or changed their story halfway
through, because the questions made them feel accused.
And there is one more piece of this worth carrying with you.
If anyone, on a telephone or a screen, ever tells you to move your money and
not to tell your bank what it is really for, that is not advice.
That is the scheme itself. No honest person will ever ask you to lie to your
own bank.
Now the third sentence, and this is the smallest one, but it does the most
damage in the moment. I would rather not say.
You are perfectly within your rights to feel that way.
It is your money.
Nobody enjoys being questioned about their own savings by a stranger half their
age, and I understand exactly why an older person, asked what the money is
for, feels their back go up. It is undignified.
It should not be necessary. But here is what happens the second those words
are spoken. The person in front of you now has to write something.
And when the field for the reason is left empty, or the customer declined to
explain, that is what goes into the record.
To the reviewer who reads it later, refusing to answer looks far worse than
any answer you could have given.
There is no ordinary explanation that raises more suspicion than no explanation
at all. So do not fight the question, and do not let it wound your pride.
Answer it in one boring sentence, and move on.
I am buying a car. It is for medical bills.
I am helping my daughter. That is all it takes, and the whole thing ends right
there at the counter.
And now let me give you the two things that stop nearly all of this from ever
starting. The first is to call ahead.
If you know a large withdrawal or transfer is coming, telephone your branch
a few days before, tell them the amount and what it is for, and ask them to
make a note of it on your account.
A transaction the bank is expecting is a transaction the bank does not stop.
It turns what could be a week of held money into a five minute conversation
you already had.
The second is to name a trusted contact on your account.
This is a free form. It is a
person the bank is permitted to telephone if something
about your account ever worries them.
Naming a son, a daughter, or an old friend does not give that person one penny
of access, and it does not let them move your money.
It simply gives the bank a human being to call instead of locking the account
and waiting. It costs nothing, it takes about ten minutes at the branch or
on the telephone, and for a person who lives alone it is one of the most useful
pieces of paper you will ever sign.
That one form is the difference between someone picking up the phone and someone
freezing your money.
So let me put the three of them together, simply, one last time.
Never talk about staying under a limit.
Say the real amount and let them file their paperwork.
Never say that someone told you to send it.
Name the person, name the relationship, name what it is for.
And never refuse to explain. Give one
ordinary sentence and the matter is closed.
Everything I have told you today comes down to a single idea.
The money is not the problem. Your money is fine.
The pattern and the wording are what get read, by people and by computers,
and they are read by strangers who do not know you and will never meet you.
So give them nothing to wonder about.
Be the plainest, most boring customer in the branch, and you will walk out
with your own money and never think about any of this again.
And if you know someone who is planning a large withdrawal soon, for a car,
for a roof, to help one of their children, please send this to them before
they go.
Five minutes of the right words is all that stands between an ordinary morning
at the bank and a very long month.

title: If You Use A Credit Card, These 3 New Rules Could Affect Every Senior in 2026

segments.text: Forty one dollars.
That is what one late payment on a credit card can cost you right now.
Not forty one dollars a year. Forty one dollars for being a single day late,
one time, on one card.
And if you thought that number was supposed to come down this year, you are
not imagining things. It was. There was a rule written to cut it down to eight
dollars, and most people still believe that rule is in place today.
It is not. A court threw it out, and almost nobody was told.
That is one of three changes moving through the credit card world right now,
and two of them are already touching your account, whether you have noticed
or not.
One is costing older people money every single month.
One is showing up on your credit report in a way it never used to.
And the third one is a protection you already have, that hardly any older person
knows to use, and it can stop a bank from turning you down for a card because
of your age. So let me walk you through all three, in order, in plain words,
and tell you exactly what to do about each one.
The third one is the one I most want you to remember, because it is the one
that works in your favor. Let me start with that late fee, because it is the
one taking money out of pockets today.
For years, credit card companies charged whatever they liked when a payment
came in late. Thirty dollars.
Thirty five.
Forty one.
It became one of the most profitable things a bank could do, because a late
payment costs them almost nothing to process.
So the consumer protection agency in Washington wrote a rule to stop it.
That rule would have capped the late fee at eight dollars, and it was set to
save households billions of dollars every year.
The banks took it to court. And in the spring of last year, a federal judge
in Texas threw the rule out completely.
It never took effect. Not for one single day.
So here is where that leaves you.
Late fees are right back where they were, running about thirty to forty one
dollars at most major banks.
And if you are one of the many people who heard the news back when the eight
dollar cap was announced, and assumed the problem had been solved, this is
your correction. Nothing changed.
The fee that hits your account is the full amount, same as always.
Now, what do you actually do about it.
Two things, and both of them work.
The first is the one that surprises people the most, because it is so simple
that it feels like it should not work.
If you get hit with a late fee, call the number on the back of your card and
ask them to remove it. That is the whole script.
I noticed a late fee on my account, this is not usual for me, would you please
remove it.
Most of the large banks will waive that fee, especially the first time, and
especially for a customer who has been with them for years.
They do not advertise this. There is no button for it on the website.
But the person on the phone very often has the authority to take it straight
off, and they will do it if you ask kindly.
One phone call, thirty five dollars back, and it takes less time than reading
the statement did.
And do not talk yourself out of making that call.
So many older people feel it is somehow rude to ask, or that a big bank would
never bend for one person. It is not rude, and they bend all the time.
Think of a man who had carried the same card for over twenty years, never missed
a payment in his life, and then landed in the hospital for a week and came
home to a late fee sitting on his statement.
He nearly paid it out of embarrassment.
Instead he called, explained what had happened in two sentences, and the woman
on the phone removed it before he had finished speaking.
Twenty years of loyalty was the whole argument, and he did not even have to
make it. He only had to ask. The second thing is to make sure it never happens
again, and this is the part that protects people whose memory is not what it
once was, or who simply have too many due dates to track.
Set up an automatic payment for the minimum amount only.
Not the full balance, unless you want that.
Just the minimum. That way, even in a month when you are unwell, or traveling,
or something slips, the payment goes out on its own and the late fee never
lands. You can always pay more by hand on top of it.
This one setting, and it takes about five minutes on the telephone with your
bank, closes that door for good.
Now let me give you the second change, and this one is newer, and plenty of
people have walked straight into it without ever realizing.
You know those payment plans that appear now when you buy something online.
Pay in four easy payments. Nothing due today.
They show up at the checkout on almost every website, and on things as ordinary
as a pair of shoes or a refrigerator.
They are called buy now, pay later, and for the last few years they lived in
a strange gap where they were not really reported anywhere.
Take one, pay it late, and your credit report never knew.
That has now changed. The major
credit bureaus have begun accepting this information,
and at least one of them is already allowing it to affect your credit score.
So those little four payment plans, the ones that never felt like real debt,
are becoming part of your permanent credit record.
And here is why this matters more than it looks.
A recent study found that nearly half of the people using these plans had paid
late at least once in the past year.
Nearly half.
Not because they are careless, but because the payments are small, they come
out on odd dates, and it is honestly hard to keep track when you have three
or four of them running at the same time.
When these were invisible, a late one cost you a small fee.
Now it can follow you onto your credit report, and that is a different thing
altogether. And there is a second thing about them worth knowing.
Because they are not treated like an ordinary credit card, the protections
you are used to may not all be there.
If the item arrives broken, or never arrives at all, sorting that out can be
far messier than a simple charge dispute on a normal card.
So for anything expensive, or anything from a seller you do not know well,
the plain old credit card is still the safer way to pay.
So if you use these, or if a son or daughter or grandchild set one up on your
account to help you buy something, do two things this week.
Write down every one of those plans you currently have running, along with
the day each payment comes out.
And if the option is there, link them to automatic payment so they cannot be
missed.
That is it. I am not going to tell you never to use them.
For some purchases they are honestly useful.
Just do not let them be invisible anymore, because the credit bureaus have
stopped treating them that way.
And now the third one, which is the one I truly want you to carry with you,
because this one is on your side.
There is a federal law that makes it illegal for any bank or lender to turn
you down for credit because of your age.
Not at sixty five. Not at seventy five.
Not at ninety five. Your age, all by
itself, cannot be the reason you are denied
a credit card, a loan, or a line of credit.
That is the law, and it has been the law for a long time, and hardly any older
person knows it well enough to use it.
Now why does this matter more today than it used to.
Because a lot of older people are being turned down, and they assume it is
simply what happens when you get older.
They stop applying. They accept worse terms on the cards they already carry.
Or they let a family member add them onto an account instead of holding one
in their own name, which weakens their own credit standing over the years.
And that assumption is backwards.
Here is a fact that ought to make you sit up.
People over sixty five have the highest average credit score of any age group
in this country. The highest. Not the lowest.
Older Americans are, as a group, the most reliable borrowers in America, and
and the numbers say so. So if you ever apply for a card or a loan and you are
turned down, do not simply accept it and feel small about it.
The lender is legally required to tell you the specific reason for that denial,
in writing, if you ask. Ask for it.
If the reason given has anything to do with your age, or with being retired,
or with the fact that your income comes from Social Security or a pension rather
than a paycheck, that is worth
challenging, because income from Social Security
and a pension is perfectly legitimate income under that law.
You can file a complaint with the consumer protection agency, at no cost, and
you would be surprised how quickly a bank revisits a decision once a complaint
is on file. And there is one more piece of this that catches people out.
If your spouse handled all the credit for the whole of your marriage, and every
card was in their name, then your own credit history can be far thinner than
you would expect, even at eighty years old, and even with a lifetime of paying
every bill on time. That is not
age discrimination, it is simply how the record
works. So if that describes you, the fix is to hold at least one card in your
own name, use it lightly for something ordinary like the groceries, and pay
it off each month. That builds a record that belongs to you alone, and it matters
a great deal if you are ever left on your own.
So let me put the three of them back together, because each one asks something
different of you.
The late fee cap was struck down, so those fees are still full price.
If one lands, call and ask them to take it off, and put your minimum payment
on automatic so it never happens again.
Those pay in four plans are now going onto your credit report, so write down
the ones you have and get them on automatic too.
And your age cannot legally be used against you.
If you get turned down, ask for the reason in writing, and challenge it if
age or retirement income is anywhere in that answer.
Two of these three are the kind of thing nobody sends you a letter about.
The rule that would have helped you was reversed in a courtroom, and the payment
plans changed how they report you without any announcement at all.
That is simply how it works now.
The changes that cost you money arrive in silence, and the protections that
help you go unmentioned. But now you know all three, which puts you ahead
of almost everyone your age. So take the small step first.
Go and set up that automatic minimum payment this week.
It is five minutes on the phone, and it closes the door on the most expensive
of the three for good. And here is my challenge to you.
Make that call about the late fee, and then tell one person what happened.
Not a warning, not a lecture. Just tell them what you got back with one phone
call.
That is how this kind of thing actually spreads, one person at a time, at a
kitchen counter or over a cup of coffee, long after the banks have stopped
hoping anyone would find out.

title: The Paid-Off House Is Not the Safest Thing You Own — Here's What Actually Protects It

segments.text: Go and find the deed to your house. I am
serious. Before you finish this video,
put your hands on that piece of paper
because most people have not read it
since the day they signed it. And there
is one line on it that a surprising
number of older homeowners have wrong.
But first, you need to understand what
changed the day you made that last
payment. For 30 years, a bank was
watching that house. They checked that
your insurance was real and still in
force. They made sure the property taxes
were being paid. They had their own
money riding on that roof. So, they
watched it like a hawk every single
year, whether you knew it or not. And
the morning you paid them off, they
closed the file and walked away. From
that day forward, not one person on this
earth has been watching over the biggest
thing you own. Only you. That is why the
paidoff house is not the safest thing
you own. It is the least watched thing
you own. And those two are not the same.
Nobody is going to send you a letter
when something slips. Nobody calls. The
house just sits there worth more than
everything else you have put together
with no one keeping an eye on it but
you. So, let me walk you through the
handful of things that actually protect
it. Not fear, not what could go wrong,
but the real protections in order.
Starting with the one that costs nothing
and takes about 15 minutes at your
county office. Let me begin with that
deed because it is the single most
important document you own and hardly
anyone reads it twice. In most states,
you are allowed to file a short form
that tells the county exactly who your
house goes to when you pass without the
courts ever getting involved. Depending
on where you live, it may be called a
transfer on death deed or a beneficiary
deed. And in a handful of states, it
goes by an odd little name, the Ladybird
deed. Different names, same purpose. You
keep complete control while you are
alive. You can sell the house tomorrow.
You can rent it out. You can change your
mind and name somebody else next year.
Nothing about your ownership changes at
all. But the day you pass, the house
moves to the person you named without a
courtroom, without a judge, and without
a year of legal bills eating into what
you left behind. Now, think about what
happens without it. Your house does not
simply go to your children. It goes into
probate, which is the court process for
sorting out what a person left behind.
And that can stretch on for months and
sometimes well past a year. During all
that time, somebody still has to pay the
taxes and keep the insurance active on a
house nobody is allowed to sell yet.
Families have lost homes in exactly that
gap, not because anyone did anything
wrong, but because the money ran out
before the court was finished. And a
will does not spare you from it. This is
where so many people are caught out. A
will does not avoid probate. A will is
the instruction manual. of the probate
court reads. If your entire plan for the
house is a will in a drawer, then your
plan is the courthouse. So, call your
county recorder office. Ask whether your
state allows a transfer on death or
beneficiary deed and ask what it costs
to file one. In most places, you are
talking about a small filing fee and an
afternoon. Let me put a face on that
because the difference is not small.
Think of two men on the same street,
both widowers in their 80s, both with a
paidoff house and both with a will
tucked in a drawer. One of them, a few
years back, had a neighbor mentioned
this deed to him, and he went down to
the county office one Tuesday morning
and filed it. The other never heard of
it. When the first man passed, the house
was in the name of his daughter inside
of a few weeks. She sold it when she was
ready on her own terms. When the second
man passed, that house sat in the court
process for over a year. His son had to
keep paying the taxes and the insurance
on a home he was not yet allowed to sell
out of his own pocket. And by the end,
the legal costs had taken a serious bite
out of what his father had spent a
lifetime building. Same street, same
kind of house. One filing at the county
office in about 15 minutes was the whole
difference. Now, the second protection,
and this is the line I asked you to go
and look for. Read how you and anyone
else are named on that deed. There are
two ways two people can own a house
together, and they sound almost
identical, but they behave in completely
opposite ways when one person dies. If
it says something close to joint tenants
with right of survivorship, then when
one of you passes, the other simply owns
the whole house, clean and quiet. But if
it reads tenants in common, that is a
different animal altogether. Each person
owns a share, and when one of them dies,
their share goes to their own heirs, not
automatically to the person still living
in the house. Widows have found
themselves owning half of the home they
live in with the other half belonging to
a stepchild or an in-law they barely
speak to. There is a second thing to
check while you have it in front of you.
Look at whether a name on that deed no
longer belongs there. A husband or wife
who passed years ago, a child you added
back when it seemed like a tidy idea.
Because once another living person is on
your deed, their troubles become
troubles for your house. if they are
sued, if they go through a divorce, if
they owe money they cannot pay, a claim
can land on your home. So read those
names out loud if it helps. And if
something on there is out of date or
does not sit right with you, that is a
conversation worth having with an
attorney sooner rather than later. The
third one is the protection almost
nobody thinks about, and it is the one
that hits paidoff owners harder than
anyone else in the country, your
homeowner's insurance. And before you
wave that off as boring, let me tell you
why it matters far more to you than to
your neighbor down the street who still
has a mortgage. Their bank forces them
to carry proper coverage. It checks. It
will not allow the policy to lapse. So
there is nobody checking anything. And
that means two things can go wrong
without a single warning. The first is
that your insurance company may simply
decide not to renew you. That has been
happening across the country, especially
on older homes and older roofs, and the
letter often arrives looking so ordinary
that people set it aside for later. If
that renewal lapses and a fire or a
storm comes through, the entire value of
your house is standing there uncovered.
The second one is harder to spot and it
catches even careful people. Your policy
may still be active, but the amount it
pays out has not kept up with what it
now costs to rebuild. Construction
prices have climbed hard these last few
years. So, a house insured for what it
would have cost to rebuild some years
back can now be short by a great deal.
And you would not find out until the
very worst day of your life. So, do
this. Take out your policy, find the
number listed for the dwelling, and call
your agent and ask one question. If this
house burned to the ground tomorrow,
would this amount actually rebuild it at
the prices builders charge today? If
they hesitate, you have your answer. And
ask them a second question while you
have them on the telephone. Ask whether
your policy pays what it would cost to
rebuild the house or only what the house
is worth today after all the years of
wear. Those are two very different
numbers, and the second one can leave
you far short of a finished home. If you
are on the wrong one, ask what it would
cost to change it. For most people, it's
a smaller difference in the monthly
amount than they fear. And it's the
difference between rebuilding and
walking away. The fourth one surprises
people the most because it seems
impossible that something so small could
touch something so big. A house worth3
owned free and clear can be forced to
sail over a debt of a few thousand. Not
a mortgage since you no longer have one.
Unpaid property taxes. unpaid homeowners
association dues if you live somewhere
that has them. A contractor who did work
on your home never got paid in full and
filed a claim against the property. Even
a city fine that sat ignored long enough
to become a lean. Each one of those
attaches itself to the house and in a
number of states the holder can
eventually push it toward a sale to
collect. And this is what catches good
people. It rarely happens because
someone refused to pay. It happens
because a bill went to an old address or
because the person opening the mail was
unwell or because a spouse who always
handled the paperwork passed away and
nobody knew that particular envelope
mattered. So once a year, call your
county treasurer and ask one plain
question. Is there anything owing on my
property? And is there any lean recorded
against it? That call costs you nothing
and it is the closest thing there is to
an alarm system for the biggest thing
you own. And if you ever do find
something owing, do not panic and do not
ignore it either. These things almost
always have a long runway before
anything serious happens. And counties
will very often set up a payment
arrangement with an older homeowner who
calls them first. The danger is never
the bill itself. The danger is the
silence around it. And the fifth is
short, but it protects everything we
have talked about so far. Never leave
the house looking empty for long. A
hospital stay, a long winter with a son
or daughter in a warmer state. The
months after a spouse passes when nobody
can face the place. That is exactly when
trouble arrives. Because an empty house
with no lender and no one collecting the
mail is the easiest target there is for
someone filing false paperwork or moving
in and claiming rights. And there is a
detail here that catches almost
everyone. Most homeowners insurance
policies have a vacancy clause buried in
them. If the house sits empty beyond a
set stretch of time, often around 30 or
60 days, your coverage can be cut back
or refused altogether. So, if you're
going to be away, tell your insurance
company, ask what your policy says about
vacancy, and have somebody real collect
the mail and walk through the rooms. Not
a favor you ask once, someone you
actually count on. So, let me put the
whole of it back together because the
thread through every one of these is the
same. You did the hardest financial
thing a person can do. You paid off a
house. And the reward for finishing was
that the last set of eyes watching over
it, closed the file, and went home.
Everything I have given you today is
simply a way of putting eyes back on it.
The deed filed so the courts stay out of
it. The names on that deed read
carefully and corrected. Insurance that
would truly rebuild what you own. One
call a year to be certain that nothing
has attached itself to it. And a house
that never looks empty for long. Not one
of those costs much of anything.
Together they do the job the bank used
to do for you. Only now it is being done
by the one person who actually cares
about that house. So start today with
the smallest step. Go find the deed.
Read the names on it and read how it
says you own it. That one piece of paper
sitting in a drawer or a folder
somewhere in your home right now is
holding up everything you spent 30 years
building. And if you know someone else
who has paid off their home and believes
that means the work is finished, share
this with them. They have almost
certainly never been told that the
