authorization denials begin to arrive.
Now the best hospital for that exact
illness turns out not to be covered. So
they tried to do the sensible thing and
move back to plain Medicare with a
supplement. And only then at the worst
possible moment of their life do they
discover that the supplement company can
say no because of the very illness they
are fighting. They are left paying out
of their own pocket or driving hours for
care that counts as in network. Trapped
inside the plan that once looked like
such a bargain. Not because they did a
single thing wrong, but because no one
ever told them. The door only swings one
way. Now, here is how you keep that door
open, because you hold far more power
than the sales pitch lets on. First,
know your one guaranteed window. When
you first join a Medicare Advantage plan
at 65, you have what is called a trial
right. If you leave it within the first
12 months, you can go straight back to
plain Medicare and buy a supplement with
no health questions asked, fully
guaranteed. That first year is your
safety net. So, use it to judge the plan
carefully while the door is still wide
open. Second, if a plan ever pulls out
of your area or drops out of Medicare,
which forced millions of people into
brand new plans just this year, that
also opens a guaranteed window. usually
of 63 days to pick up a supplement
without any underwriting at all. Third,
appeal every denial every time because
you now know that almost all of them are
overturned. And fourth, before you ever
choose between Medicare Advantage and
plain Medicare with a supplement, talk
it through with someone who has nothing
to sell you. Every state runs a free
counseling service built for exactly
this, staffed by trained people who are
no commission. And they will walk
through your own situation with you for
nothing at all. This is general
information to help you understand how
these plans truly work. And it is not
insurance or medical advice because the
rules shift from stateto state and every
situation is different. Before you make
any change at all, check your own plan
and your own state or sit down with that
free counselor so that the choice
actually fits your own life and not what
a salesperson is trying to sell you. So
understand this clearly because it
matters. Medicare Advantage is not a
scam and for a great many healthy
people, it works well for years on end.
The point here is not fear. The point is
to walk in with your eyes wide open,
knowing exactly where the door is and
knowing how to keep it open behind you.
Because the difference between a plan
that serves you and a trap that holds
you is almost always just one thing.
Knowing the rules before you need them
instead of after. Well, now you have
those rules. Keep that first year in
mind. Appeal every no and never sign a
thing until you have spoken to someone
who has paid to help you and not to sell
to you. And if you know anyone who is
turning 65 or choosing a plan this fall,
please share this with them before they
decide because this is the kind of trap
you can only avoid from the right side
of the door.

title: The Verification Step That Stops a Voice Impersonation Scam From Draining Your Bank Account

segments.text: There is one simple question, only a few words long, that can stop
a thief from emptying your bank account, even when the voice on the phone sounds
exactly like someone you love.
That is not an exaggeration, and I am going to prove it to you.
Right now, criminals are using a frightening new kind of technology to copy
the voice of your own child, your grandchild, and even the voice of your bank,
and they are using that stolen voice to talk careful older people into handing
over everything they have saved.
It works because it does not feel like a scam at all.
It feels like family in trouble.
It feels like your own bank calling to protect you.
But there is a single verification step, one you can set up today in about
five minutes, that shuts the whole thing down cold.
So let me walk you through exactly how this scam drains a bank account, and
then I am going to hand you the one question, and the one calm habit, that
stop it every single time. Let me show you how it happens, because once you
truly see it, you can never be fooled by it again.
These criminals now have tools that can copy the voice of a real person from
only a few seconds of sound. That is all it takes.
A short video your grandchild posted online.
An old voice message. A clip from a birthday party.
From as little as three seconds of talking, the machine builds a copy of that
voice so real that it can be made to say anything at all, in the exact tone
of the person you love.
Then, one evening, the phone rings in your kitchen.
It is late, and the voice on the other end is crying.
It is your grandson, and he says he has been in a car accident, or that he
has been arrested, and he is terrified, and he needs money right now, tonight,
or something terrible is going to happen to him.
And it sounds just like him. Because in a cruel way, it is him.
It is his own voice, stolen and copied.
Your heart drops through the floor, and every part of you wants to help him,
and that flood of panic is the exact thing these thieves are counting on.
Here is the coldest part of how the trick is built.
Every single piece of it is designed to stop you from thinking clearly, and
to stop you from checking.
The caller will tell you there is no time.
They will beg you not to hang up the phone.
Sometimes a second voice comes on the line, pretending to be a lawyer, or a
police officer, adding weight and fear to the whole story.
They will tell you not to tell anyone else in the family, because it is embarrassing,
or because talking about it will somehow make the trouble worse.
And then they will push you, gently at first and then harder, toward the money.
They may ask you to wire it. They may tell you to drive to the bank and take
out cash while they stay on the phone in your ear the entire time.
They may even send someone to your front door to collect it.
Notice what every one of those has in common.
Each one is a way to move the money out of your bank account and into their
hands, fast, before a single person who loves you has the chance to stop it.
And there is a second version of this same trick that aims even more directly
at your bank account, so you need to know this one too.
In this version, the phone rings and the voice says it is calling from your
own bank, from the fraud department.
They sound calm, and polite, and completely professional.
They tell you there has been suspicious activity on your account, that a criminal
is trying to steal your money at this very moment.
And then comes the trap.
To keep your money safe, they say, you need to move it right away into a new,
secure account that they will kindly help you set up.
It sounds like they are rescuing you.
They are doing the opposite.
That new account belongs to them.
And here is the one fact that gives this away every time, so please hold on
to it tightly.
Your real bank will never, ever call you and tell you to move your money into
a safe account.
No true bank does this. No real government agent does this.
The very moment anyone tells you to move your money in order to protect it,
you are talking to a thief. That one sentence, remembered, will save some of
you everything you own. So now, the part you came here for.
The verification step that stops all of this, no matter how perfect the fake
voice sounds. It is simple, it is free, and you can do it this week.
Sit down with your family, your children and your grandchildren, and together
choose a secret word. A family safe word.
Pick something that no stranger could ever guess, and that is written down
nowhere online. Not a birthday.
Not the name of a pet. Not a street you once lived on.
Choose something private, a little bit odd, and easy for your family to remember.
Maybe a silly word from an old family joke.
Then you all agree to one firm rule.
If anyone ever calls in an emergency asking for money,
the very first thing you do, before anything else, is ask them for the safe
word.
That is the whole shield. A real grandchild will know it in a heartbeat.
A copied voice, run by a criminal on the far side of the world, cannot possibly
know it, because that word lives only inside your family, and no machine can
ever steal a word that was never spoken online.
If the voice cannot give you the word, you hang up.
And just like that, with nothing more than one private word, you have defeated
a scam that has emptied the life savings of thousands of good people.
Let me show you just how simple that is in the moment it matters most.
Picture the phone ringing at eleven at night, and the voice sobbing on the
other end of the line is your granddaughter, telling you she has been in a
terrible accident, that she is now in trouble with the police, and that she
needs money wired to a lawyer before the morning or she will be kept in a cell.
A year ago, a call like that might have frozen your heart and made you forget
everything you know in a single moment.
But not now, because now you have your word.
So through all of that fear, you take one slow breath, and you say four calm
words. What is our safe word. And the line goes quiet.
The crying stops. The pleading stops.
Because the machine on the other end does not have your word, and it never
will. In that sudden silence, you already know the whole truth, and you gently
set down the phone, and you call your granddaughter directly, and she answers,
half asleep in her own bed, completely fine.
That one small silence is the entire difference between a family that loses
tens of thousands of dollars in a single terrible night, and a family that
loses nothing at all. And here is the calm habit to pair with that word, the
one that covers every version of this, including a call that claims to be your
own bank.
Whenever a phone call brings sudden fear, and urgency, and a push toward your
money, you hang up. You do not argue with them.
You do not explain yourself. You simply hang up the phone.
Then you take one slow breath, and you reach out yourself, using a number that
you already know is real. Call your grandchild back on the number you have
always had for them. Call your bank using the number printed on the back of
your own card, or on your paper statement, and never a number that the caller
gives you. Nine times out of ten, your grandchild will answer, safe and sound
and a little confused, and you will feel your whole body finally relax.
The thief depends on you staying on their line, inside their panic, moving
at their speed. The instant you hang up and check for yourself, at your own
pace, their entire game collapses.
They simply cannot survive you taking five quiet minutes to make one honest
phone call. There are a few smaller steps that add another wall of protection,
and every one of them is worth your time.
Call your bank yourself, on a day when nothing is wrong, and ask them to add
what many of them call a trusted contact to your account, a person they are
allowed to reach if they ever see something that looks strange.
Ask them what alerts they can place on large withdrawals and transfers, so
that a big amount of money can never quietly slip out without you knowing.
Be a little more careful about how much of your voice, and the voices of your
grandchildren, sits out in the open on social media, because that is exactly
the sound these thieves need to copy a voice.
And most important of all, simply talk about this.
Call your children and your grandchildren this week, and set up that safe word
out loud, together.
The families who beat this scam are almost always just the ones who talked
about it before the phone ever rang.
The ones it destroys are nearly always the ones who had never once heard that
such a thing was even possible.
This is general information to help you protect yourself and the people you
love, and it is not legal or financial advice.
If you believe you have already been targeted, or you have lost money to a
call like this, you can report it to the authorities, and there is a national
elder fraud helpline, staffed by real people, who can walk you through exactly
what to do next. It is never too late to reach out and ask for help, and you
have absolutely nothing to be ashamed of, because these criminals fool careful,
sharp, intelligent people every single day of the week.
So here is what I want you to carry with you after this.
The technology behind this scam is frightening, and the honest truth is that
it is only going to get better at sounding real.
But the thing that beats it is not more technology.
It is something no machine will ever have.
It is the private trust between you and the people you love.
One secret word that lives only inside your family.
One calm habit of hanging up and checking for yourself.
A stolen voice can cry, and beg, and sound exactly like your own grandchild
on the worst night of his life.
But it cannot know your word, and it cannot stop you from setting down the
phone and calling the real one.
So set up your family safe word this week, before you need it.
And if you know someone, a friend, a neighbor, anyone at all who could be caught
off guard by a call like this, share this with them today, because the people
who hear about it in time are the ones who never lose a thing.

title: A Stroke Can Freeze Your Bank Account and Lock Your Family Out — Even With a Power of Attorney

segments.text: There is a single day that can quietly take away nearly everything you have
worked for, and it is not the day you die.
It is the day you can no longer manage your own money.
A stroke. A bad fall. The slow fog of memory that far too many families
come to know. In a single moment, you are still alive, your savings are still
sitting in the bank with your own name on the account, and yet the people who
love you most, your husband, your wife, your own children, may not be able
to touch a single dollar of it to help you.
Not to pay your bills. Not to keep your home.
Not even to care for you. And here is the part that shocks families the most,
and the reason I am making this video.
Even the families who did everything right, who sat down and signed the legal
papers years ago, often walk into the bank and find the door slammed in their
face anyway. Let me explain how this happens, because almost nobody sees it
coming until it is far too late.
The money in your bank account belongs to you, and only to you.
That sounds so obvious it is hardly worth saying, but it carries a hard edge
that people never stop to think about.
It means that in the eyes of the law, no one else on this earth has the right
to touch that account but you.
Not the wife you have been married to for fifty years.
Not the son who drives you to every doctor visit.
To the bank, they are strangers to that account.
As long as you are healthy and can walk in and sign your own name, none of
this ever matters. But the day you cannot, the day you are lying in a hospital
bed unable to speak, or sitting at home no longer able to make sense of a bank
statement, that account simply freezes in place.
A few automatic payments may keep going for a little while, but no one can
step in.
No one can move money to cover a new bill.
No one can do the hundred small things that keeping a life running quietly
requires.
Your money is right there, with your name on it, and it might as well be locked
in a vault at the bottom of the sea.
And think for a moment about everything that does not stop just because you
can no longer sign your name. The mortgage or the rent is still due.
The electric bill and the water bill keep arriving.
The property tax does not wait.
The insurance must be paid or it quietly lapses.
And on top of all of it, there is now the enormous cost of your care, the aide,
the medicine, the hospital, all of it landing at once.
Your family stands there watching these bills stack up on the kitchen table,
knowing full well there is more than enough money in your account to cover
every last one of them, and being told, again and again, that they are not
allowed to touch it. That is not a small inconvenience.
That is a family being pushed toward ruin while sitting right on top of a fortune
they cannot reach. Now, you may be thinking, that is exactly what a power of
attorney is for. And you would be right.
A power of attorney is a simple legal paper in which you name a person you
trust, usually your spouse or one of your children, and you give them the authority
to handle your money for you if the day ever comes that you no longer can.
It is one of the most important pieces of paper an older person can ever have.
But here is the cruel surprise that catches so many well prepared families
completely off guard.
The bank can still refuse it. It happens every single day in this country.
A frightened, grieving family walks into the branch holding a valid power of
attorney that a lawyer drew up years ago, and the bank looks at it and says
no.
Sometimes they claim it is too old.
Sometimes they insist you must use the special in house form the bank keeps
behind the counter, the one you can no longer sign because by now you are already
too ill to hold the pen. And sometimes, because banks have grown so afraid
of elder fraud, they simply refuse to trust the document at all.
But the very worst kind is something called a springing power of attorney.
That is one written so that it only springs to life once a doctor certifies,
in writing, that you can no longer manage your own affairs.
It sounds careful and wise. It is a trap.
Because now your family has to track down a doctor willing to put that certification
on paper, fight through medical privacy laws that block them from even speaking
to that doctor, and then pray the bank accepts it once they are finally done.
Weeks slip by. Bills go unpaid.
And the whole time, your money sits there, untouchable.
And this is not some rare misfortune that only strikes careless people.
It happens constantly, to the most careful families there are.
People who planned. People who paid a lawyer.
People who did every single thing they were ever told to do, and still found
that the paperwork alone was not the finish line, because no one had ever warned
them that the real test is getting the bank to actually honor it when the day
finally comes. So what happens to a family that gets that door slammed in their
face?
They are forced down the one road nobody ever wants to travel, and it is called
guardianship, or in some states, conservatorship.
It means going to court, hiring a lawyer, and standing before a judge to ask
for the legal right to manage the money of the person you love.
It is slow, often dragging on for months while the unpaid bills pile higher
and higher.
It is expensive,
frequently costing thousands of dollars, money that comes straight out of the
very savings you were all trying to protect.
And it strips away dignity in a way that is hard to describe until you have
watched it happen to someone you love.
A judge, a complete stranger who has never met your family, now sits in charge
of your money. In some cases the court hands control to a professional guardian,
another stranger entirely, who charges fees to manage your life and answers
to no one but the court. The quiet dignity of handling your own affairs, and
of having your family gently handle them for you when you no longer can, is
simply gone, traded for hearings and forms and permission slips.
And all of it, every bit of that heartache and every dollar of that cost, just
to reach money that was yours the entire time, sitting in an account with your
own name printed right on the front.
And it does not simply end when the judge finally signs the order.
In many states, the guardian must return to that court year after year, filing
reports, asking permission for the larger expenses, accounting for every dollar
spent, as though your whole lifetime of careful saving had suddenly fallen
under suspicion.
A choice as ordinary as selling a car, or moving you into a better care home,
can now require a hearing, a lawyer, and weeks of waiting.
Your spouse, the one person who knew your wishes better than anyone alive,
is reduced to filling out forms and hoping a stranger agrees.
It is a slow and grinding indignity, and the cruelest part of all is that it
was almost always completely avoidable.
Now here is the good news, and there is a great deal of it, because nearly
every part of this nightmare can be prevented with a little bit of paperwork
done ahead of time, while you are still well, and it costs almost nothing.
Let me tell you exactly what to do.
First, have a proper durable power of attorney drawn up, and hold on tight
to that one word, durable.
A durable power of attorney is one that stays in full effect even after you
become unable to manage things yourself, which is the entire point of having
it.
And do not use the springing kind that waits on a signed note from a doctor.
Have it written so that the person you trust can use it the moment they truly
need to. Second, and this is the step that almost everybody misses, take that
power of attorney down to your bank now, today, while you are healthy, and
ask them to accept it and keep it on file.
A great many banks will also want you to fill out their own in house form,
so sit down and do that too, while your hand is still steady enough to sign
it.
Getting the bank to bless the paperwork today is what guarantees there is no
locked door tomorrow.
Third, ask your bank about naming what they call a trusted contact, a person
they are allowed to reach out to if something ever looks wrong on your account.
It adds one more quiet layer of protection, against both fraud and a freeze.
And fourth, keep every one of these papers current, because a document that
is twenty years old is exactly the kind a nervous bank loves to reject.
And if your savings or your home are worth a real amount,
it is worth sitting down just once with a lawyer who works with older families,
the kind sometimes called an elder law attorney, who can make sure the paperwork
is written in a way your own bank and your own state will honor without a fight.
It costs far less than most people fear, and it is a tiny fraction of what
a guardianship would later cost the people you love.
And understand this clearly. None of these steps asks you to give up a single
ounce of control today.
You still run your own money, exactly as you always have.
All you are doing is making certain that on the day you no longer can, the
right person can step in gently, without ever having to beg a judge for permission.
This is general information to help you know what to ask for, and it is not
legal advice, because the exact rules are a little different in every state.
So here is the truth of it, laid out plainly.
This is one of the very few dangers in your whole life that costs almost nothing
to prevent, and very nearly everything to ignore.
One quiet afternoon with the right form, while you are well and clear headed,
is all that stands between your family stepping in to help you the moment you
need them, and your family standing helpless at a bank counter while your own
money sits just out of their reach.
So do not leave this one for someday.
Someday is the exact thing that takes it away.
Handle it now, while it is still easy, while the choice is still yours to make.
Do it, and you will have handed the people you love the one thing that matters
far more than any dollar in that account.
The power to help you, on the day you finally need them most.

title: The Real Danger to a Fully Paid Off Home in Retirement — and How Seniors Keep It

segments.text: The house you are sitting in right now is very likely the biggest thing you
own. You worked for years to pay it off.
You raised a family in it, or grew old in it, and somewhere along the way you
decided it was finally safe. It is yours.
Nobody can take it now. But that is not quite true, and it is the reason I
am making this video. Every single year, older people lose the very home they
already own. Not because they wanted to sell it.
Not because they did anything wrong.
They lose it slowly. To a property tax bill that keeps climbing.
To an insurance bill that doubles.
To a loan that sounded like a good idea at the time.
And in some cases, to a thief who never once sets foot on the porch.
And here is the cruelest part of it.
For nearly every one of these, there was help sitting right there that could
have stopped it, and no one ever told them it was there.
There are five of them. Five ways the home you own can be taken out from under
you. I want you to know every one of them by name, because the danger you can
name is the danger you can stop.
So let us take them one at a time.
The first one is the bill that has quietly forced more older people out of
their paid off homes than almost anything else, and that is your property tax.
Here is the cruel thing about it.
You can own your home free and clear, owe not one penny to a bank, and still
lose it, because the property tax never stops coming,
and it climbs every year as your home is valued higher, even while your income
stays flat. For someone living on a fixed check, a tax bill that grows from
two thousand dollars to five thousand over the years can become the thing that
finally breaks them.
But most people have never heard of the one program that can stop it completely.
It is called a property tax deferral.
In most states, once you reach a certain age, usually sixty five, you can ask
the state to simply pause your property tax.
You pay nothing now. The state covers the bill for you and waits.
You keep living in your home, year after year, without paying that tax out
of your own pocket at all. The bill does not vanish.
It waits quietly until the day you sell the home or pass it on, and then it
is settled out of the value of the house, usually with only a small amount
of interest added.
Think about what that really means.
Instead of lying awake every autumn, afraid that this is the year the tax bill
finally forces you out the door, you pay nothing, you stay in your own home,
and the bill simply waits in the background until the house is one day sold
or passed down. For a great many older people, that single program is the one
thing standing between them and losing everything they spent a lifetime building.
For an older person being squeezed out of a home they already own, this can
be the difference between staying and leaving.
The call that starts it is to your county tax office, and the question is simple.
Do you have a property tax deferral for seniors, and how do I apply.
The second one is a bill that has been climbing faster than almost any other
in the last few years, and that is your homeowners insurance.
If you still have a mortgage, you are required to carry it, and even if your
home is fully paid off, losing it to a fire or a storm without insurance would
cost you everything.
So you pay it, and you watch it rise, sometimes doubling in just a few years,
until it begins to eat into the money you need for food and for medicine.
Most people simply accept it and assume there is nothing to be done.
That is not true. There are several ways to bring that bill down that the insurance
company will never once volunteer.
A great many insurers offer a discount for older homeowners, or for people
who have stayed with them a long time, or who have not filed a claim in years,
and you usually have to ask for it by name.
If your bill has jumped, you have every right to shop it with other companies,
because the price for the very same house can differ far more than people realize.
And if your area has become hard to insure at all, many states run what is
called a fair plan, a state backed option that can cover you when the regular
companies will not.
So the call to make is to your own insurance company first, to ask what discounts
you qualify for and to have them price your policy again, and then to one or
two others to compare.
An afternoon on the phone can quietly save an older homeowner hundreds of dollars
a year. The third one is not a bill at all.
It is a deal that is sold to older people as a way to stay in their home, and
for some it quietly becomes the very thing that costs them the home instead.
It is called a reverse mortgage.
The pitch sounds wonderful. You are told you can turn the value built up in
your home into cash, live there for the rest of your life, and never make a
monthly payment.
And for the right person, in the right situation, it can be a fair tool.
But here is what the friendly advertisement does not make plain.
A reverse mortgage is still a loan against your home, and it comes with rules
that can trip up an older person who was never properly warned.
You are still required to keep paying your property taxes and your insurance,
and to keep the home in good repair, and if you fall behind on any of those,
even by accident, the lender can begin to take the home.
The debt also grows larger over time instead of smaller, which can leave little
or nothing for the family you hoped to pass it on to.
So before you ever sign one, sit down with a housing counselor approved by
the government, whose help is completely free, and who works for you and not
for the lender. They will walk you through whether it is truly right for you,
and what safer choices you may have, before you ever put the roof over your
head on the line. The fourth one is for the moment many older people fear the
most and almost never speak about, and that is the moment you fall behind.
Maybe a health crisis drained your savings.
Maybe a husband or a wife passed away, and with them went half the income,
but not half the bills.
Whatever the reason, you find yourself behind on the mortgage, or behind on
that property tax, and the letters begin to arrive, and the worry keeps you
awake at night. Here is what you must know.
Falling behind does not mean you have already lost, and reaching out early
changes everything. The first place to turn is a housing counselor approved
by the government, and their help is completely free.
They will get on the phone with your lender for you, work out a plan, and know
about help you would never find on your own.
They can often get a lender to pause your payments for a while, stretch them
out over more time, or move what you owe onto the end of the loan, so you can
catch your breath and stay right where you are.
Lenders will often agree to these things when a counselor asks, even when they
would never offer the same to a frightened homeowner calling in alone.
One of those is called the Homeowner Assistance Fund, money set aside to help
homeowners who fell behind catch up on their mortgage, their property tax,
even their insurance.
In some states that fund is still open, though it is closing soon, so if this
is you, the time to call is now, today, and not next month.
The one thing you must never do is stay silent out of shame and wait, because
the help begins to disappear once things go too far.
Reach out early, and you have every chance to keep your home.
And the fifth one is the strangest and the most frightening of them all, because
it is a thief who steals your home without ever coming near it.
It is called home title theft.
Here is how it works.
A criminal forges your signature on a document, files it with the county, and
on paper makes it look as though your home now belongs to them.
They can then try to borrow money against your house, or even sell it, all
without you knowing a single thing, until the collection notices, or the strangers
at your door, begin to appear.
And older people are the favorite target.
Federal investigators found that while seniors were only a small share of the
people who reported this crime, they lost nearly half of all the money that
was stolen.
They are chosen on purpose. An older person who owns a home free and clear,
and who may not think to check the county records or their credit very often,
is exactly the kind of quiet, trusting target these criminals go looking for.
Now here is the good news, and it will cost you nothing.
You do not need to buy one of those services you see advertised on television
that charge you every month, because those do not actually stop the theft,
they only tell you after it has already happened.
Your own county offers the very same warning for free.
Most county recorder offices now let you sign up for a property alert, so that
the moment anyone files any document against your home, you get a notice right
away and can stop it before any real harm is done.
It takes about fifteen minutes to set up.
Call your county recorder, or look them up online, and ask to sign up for property
fraud alerts.
It is free, and it is the single best lock you can put on the home you worked
your whole life for. This is general information to help you know what to ask
for, and it is not legal or financial advice, because the exact rules are a
little different in every state.
That is all five. And look at what they share.
Every one of them is quiet.
Every one of them is counting on you not knowing it is there.
And every single one of them can be stopped, if you move before it happens
instead of after.
You do not have to handle all five today.
Just pick the one that worried you the most while you were sitting here, the
one that made you think, that could be me, and take care of that one this week.
Make the one call. Ask the one question.
That is enough to begin. This is the home you worked your whole life for.
These walls held your family. Your whole life is in the memories here.
Of everything you own, this home may be the one thing that is still truly yours.
And keeping it that way, for as long as you want to live in it, is worth an
afternoon of your time. You earned this home.
Now go and keep it.

title: 5 Bills Seniors Over 65 Are Still Paying That Quietly Ended Years Ago — and How to Stop Every One

segments.text: You know the feeling, even if you have never put words to it.
You look at what is left in your account, and it is less than it should be,
and you cannot quite say where it went.
You were careful. You did not spend foolishly.
You watched the big ones, the groceries, the medicine, the light bill.
And still, somehow, there is less at the end of the month than there ought
to be. That feeling is not you losing track, and it is not in your head.
For a great many older people, a real part of that missing money is being pulled
quietly out of their account every single month, for things that stopped existing
years ago. A service you cancelled and thought was long finished.
A warranty on something you no longer even own.
A tax you may no longer owe at all.
Each one is small enough that you have trained yourself to skip right past
it on the statement.
But added up, over a year, they can quietly take more than a thousand dollars
that was yours to keep, and they will do it again next year, and the year after
that, unless you catch them. And here is the part that should truly frighten
you. These charges do not ever stop on their own.
No letter comes in the mail to warn you.
No one calls. Nothing on your statement lights up to say, you do not have to
pay this anymore. The money simply keeps leaving your account, quietly, month
after month, and every single month you do not catch it is another month of
the money you worked your whole life for staying in the hands of a company
instead of staying with you.
And left alone, it does not fade away.
It keeps draining, silently, for the rest of your life, until one single person
finally reaches in and shuts it off.
That person is never going to be them.
It can only ever be you. There is good news, though, and it is the reason this
is the year to finally catch it.
In twenty twenty six, this exact problem has grown so widespread that the people
whose job it is to protect consumers are cracking down hard, forcing these
companies to make their charges far easier to escape.
So there has never been a better moment than this year to hunt yours down and
shut them off for good.
Stay with me all the way to the end, because the fifth one is not a company
at all. It is money pulled straight out of your Social Security check every
single month, for a reason that may have quietly stopped being true years ago.
The first one hides inside your own bank or credit card statement, and it is
that small monthly charge you no longer remember agreeing to.
A subscription. Maybe it was a free trial you signed up for once, years ago,
and never got around to canceling.
Maybe it is antivirus software on a computer you barely turn on anymore, quietly
renewing itself every year at a hundred dollars or more.
Maybe it is a streaming service, a news site, a club, or an app you have not
opened in a year.
On their own, each one looks far too small to bother with.
Nine dollars here. Twelve dollars there.
But added together, for the average household, they come to well over a hundred
and fifty dollars a year, poured straight down the drain for things nobody
is even using.
And the companies design it that way on purpose.
It is called set it and forget it, and they are betting everything on the forget.
The way to stop it is simple, but you are the one who has to do it.
Sit down with a single month of your bank statement and read every charge on
it, line by line. Any charge you do not recognize, or do not use anymore, call
the number on the statement and cancel it.
If a company makes it hard to cancel, and some of them will, that is exactly
the behavior regulators are cracking down on this year, so be firm and keep
asking until it is done. If they give you the runaround, know that the law
is finally on your side. The second one is a fee your cable or internet company
has been charging you, month after month, for a piece of equipment, usually
the modem or the box that brings the signal into your home.
Now here is what almost no one realizes.
If you bought your own equipment, or if you returned theirs and they kept charging
you anyway, that fee is not merely unfair, it is against the law.
A federal law passed a few years ago made it illegal for these companies to
bill you for equipment you are not actually renting from them.
And yet the charge, often fifteen dollars a month, which comes to a hundred
and eighty dollars every year, keeps showing up, because their system quietly
kept it running. Look at your cable or internet bill and find the line that
says equipment, or rental, or gateway.
Then call and ask one plain question.
Am I being charged to rent equipment, and do I actually own it, or did I already
return it.
If it turns out you own it, tell them to take the fee off, and then ask them
to pay you back for what they wrongly charged.
A great many people get months of that money returned with a single phone call.
The third one is a warranty, or a service contract, the kind you were sold
on a car, an appliance, or a piece of electronics, promising to cover repairs
down the road.
Here is the quiet trap.
A great many of these renew themselves automatically, year after year, long
after the item is gone or the coverage has already run out.
People keep paying for a warranty on a car they sold two years ago, or on a
refrigerator that broke and was replaced, simply because the charge kept renewing
and nobody ever stopped it.
And even when the item is still sitting in your home, these contracts are well
known for being nearly impossible to actually use when the day comes to file
a claim. So if you are paying for one, ask yourself just two questions.
Do I still own the thing it is supposed to cover, and have I ever once actually
been able to use it. If the answer to either question is no, call and cancel
it, and ask whether you are owed money back for the part you never used.
Very often, you are. The fourth one is a monthly charge for something called
credit monitoring, or identity protection.
So many people signed up for one of these years ago, often right after a store
or a bank sent a letter saying their information might have been exposed, and
it came with a few free months at the start.
Then those free months ended, the monthly charge quietly began, and it has
been running ever since, sometimes for years, at fifteen or twenty dollars
a month. And here is what stings.
For most people it is money spent on something you can do yourself, for free.
You are allowed to freeze your own credit at no cost at all, and that freeze
is stronger protection than most of these paid services will ever give you.
Look on your statement for any charge with words like protection, monitoring,
or secure in the name. If you are not truly using it, cancel it, and put a
free freeze on your credit instead.
And the fifth one, the one I promised would be different, is not a company
at all. It is a piece of money pulled straight out of your Social Security
check, or your pension, every single month, and handed to the government as
income tax.
Now, at some point in the past, a great many people chose to have this tax
taken out on purpose, just to be safe, so they would not face a big bill in
the spring. And back then, that may have made perfect sense.
But here is what quietly changes as you get older, and what almost no one ever
goes back to check. Each year past sixty five, the slice of your income the
government does not tax grows larger, and with the newer deductions written
for seniors, a great many older people living on Social Security and a modest
amount more now owe little or nothing at all in federal income tax.
And yet the withholding just keeps going.
Every month, month after month, tax is pulled out of your check for a bill
you may no longer owe, and the government simply holds your own money all year
long, handing it back, without a single penny of interest, and only if you
remember to file for it. Think for a moment about someone who has had that
tax taken from every check for the last five or six years, never once stopping
to ask whether they still owe it, quietly handing over money that was theirs
to keep the entire time. If that might be you, you do not have to guess about
it. A free tax counselor for seniors can look at your income in a few minutes
and tell you plainly whether you owe any federal tax at all.
And if the answer is that you do not, you can stop the withholding with one
short form, handed to Social Security, or to whoever pays your pension.
It is a simple voluntary withholding request, and turning it off means that
money finally stays in your check, where it belonged all along, starting with
your very next payment.
For someone stretching a modest check to cover the month, that can be more
than a thousand dollars a year handed back, money they could have been living
on the whole time. Now step back and look at what all five of these share,
because it is the very same quiet thread running through every one.
Each of them is a charge that kept running on its own, long after the reason
for it had ended. And not a single one of them will ever stop by itself.
The company will not stop it. The government will not stop it.
The only person on this earth who can switch these off is you.
But that also means the power is entirely in your hands,
and switching them off costs you nothing but a little time and a few phone
calls this week.
So here is exactly what to do.
First, pull one month of your bank and card statements, and read every charge,
line by line. Second, cancel any subscription or service you no longer use.
Third, call your cable or internet company about that equipment fee, and ask
for a refund.
Fourth, cancel any warranty or credit monitoring you are not using, and ask
for your money back. And fifth, if tax is being taken out of your Social Security
or your pension, have a free senior tax counselor check whether you even still
owe it, and if you do not, file the one form that stops it.
Every one of these is free to do, and together they can put hundreds, and for
some people well over a thousand dollars a year, back where it belongs.
This is general information to help you know what to look for, and it is not
tax or legal advice, because every situation is a little different.
I have put where to start for each one of these in the description just below
this video. And before you go,
think of one person who is quietly paying for things that ended long ago, and
has no idea it is still happening.
A friend. A parent. A neighbor living on a fixed check.
Send them this video. One hour with their bank statement this week could hand
them back money they never knew they were losing.
Then go and check your own, and help someone you love check theirs.

title: 3 Reasons Seniors Over 65 Should Never Share a Joint Bank Account (Do This Instead)

segments.text: If your name is on a bank account with anyone else, a husband or a wife, an
adult child, a brother or a sister, I need you to hear this before you do one
more thing. Because the very step that so many good and careful people take
to protect themselves in their later years, adding a trusted person to their
bank account, is the same step that can quietly wipe out everything they have
spent a lifetime saving. Not because they did anything wrong.
Not because the person they trusted is a bad person.
But because of the way a shared account works under the law, in ways the bank
will never once sit you down and explain.
I am going to give you three reasons a shared bank account can go very wrong
for someone over sixty five, in plain words, with nothing dressed up and nothing
left out. And I want you to stay with me all the way to the third one, because
it is the one that quietly tears families apart, brother against sister, long
after a parent is gone, over money that was never divided the way that parent
wanted. Then, at the very end, I will show you three safer ways to get the
exact same help, with almost none of this risk.
So as we go, keep a picture in your mind of every account you own, and whose
name is sitting on it beside yours.
First, let me be clear about what we are even talking about, because the words
matter more than you would think.
A joint account is any bank account with more than one name on it, where each
person is a full owner of all the money.
Not a helper. Not an assistant.
A full owner, with the very same complete right to every dollar as you have.
And most people over sixty five who share an account did it for one simple,
loving reason. So that someone could help them.
Help pay the bills if they land in the hospital.
Help manage things if their memory starts to slip.
Step in if something ever happens to them.
It comes from the best place in the heart.
But here is the hard truth. The moment you add that second name as a joint
owner, in the eyes of the bank and the law, that money is just as much theirs
as it is yours. And that single fact is where all three of these dangers begin.
The first reason is this. Once someone is a joint owner, they can take every
dollar in that account, at any time, for any reason, and they never need to
ask your permission to do it. Not half of it.
All of it. They can walk into the bank, or tap a few buttons on a phone, and
move the entire balance into an account that only they control, and there is
nothing the bank is allowed to do to stop them, because the law says the money
is theirs too. Now, you may trust that person with your whole heart, and you
may be completely right to. But here is the part that has nothing to do with
trust.
Their troubles are now your troubles.
If that person is ever sued, the people suing them can go after the money sitting
in your account. If they run up a debt they cannot pay, the company they owe
can reach in and take it. If they go through a divorce, their husband or wife
can try to claim part of it. And if that person ever owes back taxes, the government
can freeze the account and pull the money out, right down to the last dollar,
even though every cent of it came from you and you alone.
In some states they can take the entire account.
Sit with that for a moment. Your life savings, left wide open to a lawsuit,
a divorce, or a tax bill that was never yours.
And none of this requires that anyone did a single thing wrong.
A lawsuit after an ordinary car accident, a small business that quietly fails,
a marriage that falls apart,
any one of these can reach into a joint account through the other person, with
no warning to you at all. The account does not know whose money it was.
It only sees two names, and the law treats every dollar in it as fair game
for the troubles of either one.
That is why this has nothing to do with how much you love or trust the person.
It has to do with everything life might throw at them, and now at you.
The second reason is one that almost nobody sees coming, and it is written
into the very bones of how a shared account works.
Most joint accounts come with something the bank calls the right of survivorship.
In plain words, it means this.
The moment you pass away, whoever else is on that account becomes the sole
owner of every dollar in it, instantly and completely.
And here is the part that stuns families.
That rule beats your will. It does not matter what your will says.
It does not matter if your will states, in black and white, that everything
you own should be split evenly among all of your children.
The money in that joint account does not follow your will at all.
It goes, entirely, to the one person whose name was sitting on the account.
Let me make this real, because it happens in ordinary, loving families every
single day. Picture a mother who adds her oldest daughter to her checking account,
for one reason only, so that daughter can help pay the bills as she gets older.
Her will could not be clearer.
Split everything equally among all four of my children.
But when that mother passes, the law hands the whole account to the one daughter
whose name was on it. The other three children are legally entitled to nothing
from it. Now that one daughter holds all of it, and even in a close and loving
family, that is a heavy and cruel weight to lay on a person.
The mother never meant to do any of it.
She thought she was simply being organized and wise.
Instead, without ever knowing, she quietly wrote three of her children out
of a part of their inheritance, and lit a fire between them that may burn for
the rest of their lives. The third reason strikes at the very worst moment,
the moment you need your money the most, and need help the most.
If the day ever comes that you need long term care, a nursing home, or help
in your own home, a great many people turn to a program called Medicaid to
help pay for it, because that kind of care can cost more than five thousand
dollars a month. But when you apply, that program looks very closely at your
bank accounts. And here is the trap.
If your name is on a joint account, the program can count the entire balance
as yours, even the money the other person put in, and that can push you over
the limit and delay or deny the very help you are desperate for.
Worse still, if you added that person within the last five years, it can be
treated as though you gave your money away, and you can be penalized for it,
and made to wait months before any help will begin.
And there is one more quiet danger.
If that joint owner passes away before you do, or falls into a legal fight
of their own, the account can be frozen or tangled up at the exact moment you
were counting on it to pay for your care.
The very account you set up to make life easier can become the thing standing
between you and the help you need.
Now, I promised you this would not be only a list of fears, and I meant it,
because here is the good news.
Every single reason a person adds someone to their account, help with the bills,
help if their memory fades, making sure the right person receives the money
in the end, can all be handled in a safer way, without ever making another
person a joint owner. Let me give you three.
The first is called an authorized signer, sometimes called a convenience account.
This lets the person you trust write checks and handle the account for you,
and do all the day to day helping you could ever need, but they are not an
owner. Their debts cannot touch the money.
It does not override your will.
It simply lets them help, and nothing more.
The second is called a payable on death beneficiary.
You simply tell the bank who should receive the money when you are gone.
Until that day comes, the money is completely yours, and yours alone.
The person you named cannot touch a single penny while you are alive, and their
troubles can never reach it. But the moment you pass, the money goes straight
to the person you chose, quickly and privately, exactly as you wanted.
The third, and the strongest, is a durable power of attorney.
This is a legal paper, drawn up just once, that names a person you trust to
manage your money for you if the day ever comes that you cannot.
They must act for your benefit, never their own.
They never become an owner of your money.
And it protects you fully if your health ever fails.
For a great many people, a payable on death beneficiary and a power of attorney
together will do everything a joint account was ever meant to do, with almost
none of the danger. So here is the thread that runs through all three of these.
A joint account quietly hands away your control, your protection, and your
final wishes, all at once, and it does it in silence, until the day something
goes wrong and it is far too late to undo.
But you have time to check, right now, today.
This week, do three simple things.
First, find out whose name is truly on each of your accounts, and whether the
bank has you down as joint owners.
Second, call your bank and ask about adding an authorized signer, and about
naming a payable on death beneficiary, and tell them plainly that you do not
want to add a joint owner. And third, if your savings or your home are worth
protecting, sit down just once with a lawyer who works with older families,
and set up a power of attorney the right way.
And please do not let the words scare you off.
You do not need to understand every legal term.
You only need to walk into your bank, or pick up the phone, and say one simple
sentence. I want to help someone manage my account, and I want the right person
to receive it when I am gone, but I do not want to make anyone a joint owner.
That one sentence points them to the safe tools, and it protects everything
you have built. This is general information to help you know what to ask about,
and it is not legal advice, because the exact rules are a little different
in every state. I have put where to start in the description just below this
video. And before you go, think of one person who has quietly added a child,
or a brother, or an old friend to their bank account, believing with all their
heart that they were being wise and safe.
Send them this video. It could protect the savings they worked a lifetime for,
and it could keep their family whole after they are gone.
Then go and check your own accounts this week, and help someone you love check
theirs.

title: One Phone Call Can Wipe Out 6 Bills Seniors Are Overpaying This Summer

segments.text: Right now, somewhere in your home, there is a small stack of bills you have
paid so many times that you barely even look at them anymore.
The power company. The pharmacy.
The county tax office. You open them, you pay them, and you move on, the way
you have done for years.
But here is something that almost no one your age is ever told.
Six of those bills can be cut down, and a few of them wiped out completely,
with nothing more than a phone call to the right place.
The money is real. It is already set aside for people in exactly your situation.
And the only reason you are still paying the full amount is that not one of
those companies will ever call you first to say you have been paying too much.
So do one thing for me before we start.
Find your phone, and keep it right next to you while you watch this.
Because by the end, you are going to have a short list of calls that could
put thousands of dollars a year back into your pocket.
I will take you through all six, one at a time, in plain words.
What each bill is, who gets to stop paying it, and the exact call that fixes
it. And I am saving the biggest one for the very end, because it is the largest
check most of you write all year, and the call that brings it down takes about
ten minutes. The first bill is the one climbing the fastest right now, in this
heat, and that is your home energy bill, the cost of keeping your house cool.
And in these hot months, there are two things working in your favor that most
people never hear about. First, a growing number of states have made it against
the rules for the power company to shut off your electricity during the hottest
part of the summer, so if you have fallen behind, they cannot leave an older
person without cooling in dangerous heat.
Second, there is a program, paid for by the government and run by your own
state, that helps older people pay their heating and cooling bills, and it
will even help cover a fan or a window air conditioner.
It is called the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program.
Older people are moved right to the front of the line for it.
But here is the part that makes this a call for this week and not someday.
The money set aside for summer cooling is smaller than the winter fund, and
it runs out in the middle of the season, so the people who call early are the
ones who actually get it. The phone call that fixes this one is to your state
energy assistance office, and the question is, what cooling help and what shutoff
protection is there for a senior on my bill.
The second bill is the one you hand over at the pharmacy counter.
As of this year, there is a hard limit, written right into federal law, on
how much you can be made to pay out of your own pocket for your covered prescriptions
in a whole year. That limit is about two thousand one hundred dollars.
Once what you have paid for your covered medicine reaches that number, you
are done for the rest of the year, and your drug plan has to pay for all of
it after that. If you take an expensive medicine, the kind that used to cost
people ten or fifteen thousand dollars a year, that can simply never happen
to you again. And there is more.
If money is tight for you, there is a program called Extra Help, run through
Social Security, that lowers what you pay for your medicine, your copays at
the counter, and even your drug plan premium, often down to just a few dollars.
Nobody should be splitting pills in half to save money while help worth thousands
of dollars sits there with their name on it.
But it will not come to you. The phone call that fixes this one is to your
drug plan, or to Social Security, and the question is simple.
Am I signed up for Extra Help, and how does the yearly cap on my medicine work.
That one call can change what you pay all year long.
The third bill comes straight out of your Social Security check every single
month, so quietly that most people forget they are even paying it.
That is your Medicare Part B premium.
This year it is about two hundred and three dollars a month, which comes to
more than two thousand
four hundred dollars a year, taken out of your check before you ever see a
penny of it. But here is what almost no one knows.
If you get by on Social Security and not a lot more, there are programs, called
the Medicare Savings Programs, that will pay that whole premium for you.
The money that has been disappearing from your check every month goes right
back into it, for the rest of your life.
A great many people never even check, because they decide on their own that
they must earn too much to qualify, and they are very often wrong.
The limits are higher than most people expect.
The phone call that fixes this one is to the office in your state that handles
Medicaid, and the question is, do I qualify for a Medicare Savings Program
to pay my Part B premium.
If the answer is yes, that is more than two thousand
four hundred dollars a year put back in your pocket.
The fourth bill is not one that comes in the mail at all.
It is the money quietly taken out of your own bank account, in fees, every
single month.
A charge just for having the account.
Another charge when a payment goes through and your balance is running low.
For an older person living on a fixed check, these can add up to well over
a hundred dollars a year, pulled straight out of your own savings, for nothing
at all. And here is what the bank will never tell you.
Almost every bank has an account with no monthly fee, and many now offer one
built just for older customers, with the fees waived.
They simply do not move you over to it, because those fees are money in their
pocket.
The phone call that fixes this one is to your own bank, and the question is,
do you have an account with no monthly fee, and will you switch me to it today.
One short call can stop money from leaking out of your account for the rest
of your life. The fifth bill is one almost nobody thinks to question, and that
is your phone and your internet.
For a great many older people, this has quietly become one more bill eating
into a fixed check every month.
But there is a federal program, called Lifeline, that takes a set amount straight
off the cost of your phone or your internet every single month, for people
who qualify.
And most older people living mainly on Social Security do qualify.
It is not a fortune, but it is money off the same bill every month, month after
month, for as long as you keep the service.
On top of that, many phone and internet companies have their own low cost plans
for older customers that they do not advertise, because they would rather you
keep paying full price.
The phone call that fixes this one is to your phone or your internet company,
and the question is, do you have the Lifeline discount, or a low cost plan
for seniors, and how do I sign up.
A few minutes on the phone, and your bill is smaller every month from then
on. And the sixth bill, the biggest check most of you write all year, is
your property tax. If you own your home, this is very often the single largest
bill you face, and it keeps climbing as your home is valued higher, even while
your income stays flat. But nearly every state gives people sixty five and
older a way to fight back, and there are two separate ways to do it.
The first is a freeze. The day you qualify, the value your home is taxed on
is locked in place, so even as the houses around you keep rising and your neighbors
watch their bills grow, yours stays frozen for as long as you live there.
The second is a rebate, an actual check sent back to you for part of the property
tax you already paid, and in a number of states those checks are going out
to seniors this very summer.
Depending on where you live, that check can be worth several hundred dollars,
and in some places well over a thousand.
Let me make this one real for a moment.
There are people all over this country who have lived in the same paid off
house for forty years, on nothing but a Social Security check, watching a property
tax bill climb past four or five thousand dollars, and growing more frightened
every single year of losing the very home they already own, over a bill for
taxes. If they simply picked up the phone and asked for the freeze, or filed
for the rebate, that weight would lift, and much of that money would either
stop growing or come straight back to them.
But no one at the county has ever once called to tell them the programs were
there. The phone call that fixes this one is to your county, and the question
is, do you have a property tax freeze, an exemption, or a rebate for seniors,
and how do I apply. It may be the most valuable phone call you make all year.
Now step back and look at what all six of these share, because it is the very
same thread running through every one of them.
The help is real. The programs already exist, paid for and running, written
for exactly your situation. And not a single one of them will ever come looking
for you. The power company stays quiet.
The county does not knock. The drug plan does not call.
The bank says nothing.
They are all counting on your silence, and on a lifetime of habit that tells
you to just pay, and just cope, and never ask.
But that is your money, earned over a whole lifetime of work, and keeping it
can be as simple as a few phone calls this week.
So here is your list, six calls to make this week.
One. Call your state energy assistance office and ask about summer cooling
help and shutoff protection for a senior.
Two. Call your drug plan, or Social Security, and ask about Extra Help and
the yearly cap on your medicine.
Three. Call the office in your state that handles Medicaid and ask about the
Medicare Savings Programs that pay your Part B premium.
Four. Call your bank and ask to be switched to an account with no monthly fee.
Five. Call your phone and internet company and ask about the Lifeline discount
and any low cost plan for older customers.
And six. Call your county and ask about the senior property tax freeze, exemption,
or rebate. Every one of these is free to ask about, and the exact rules are
different in every state, so let each one tell you what you qualify for.
This is general information to help you know what to ask for, and it is not
legal or tax advice.
And I have put where to start for each one of these in the description just
below this video.
And before you go, think of one person who is quietly overpaying every one
of these bills without ever knowing there was another way.
A parent. A neighbor. An old friend getting by on a small check.
Send them this video. It could put thousands of dollars a year back in their
pocket.
Then go and make one of these calls for yourself this week, and help someone
you love make theirs.

title: 5 Home Bills and Repairs Seniors Over 65 Never Have to Pay (Most Seniors Never Ask)

segments.text: There are five costs tied to your own home that the government, and programs
already built for exactly this, will quietly help you lower, wipe out, or pay
for once you turn
sixty five. I am not talking about a small senior discount.
On some of these, the right answer is not a reduced bill, it is a bill of nothing
at all, or a check for thousands of dollars to fix your home that you never
pay back. And here is the part that should make you angry.
Nobody whose job it is to collect that money, or to hand out that help, has
the slightest reason to pick up the phone and tell you.
The city will not tell you. The county will not tell you.
The programs sit there, funded and waiting, quietly, in the hope that you never
learn they exist and keep paying out of a lifetime of habit.
The people who scroll right past a video like this keep on paying.
The ones who stay are the ones who stop quietly handing thousands of dollars
away every year, and sometimes it is the difference between keeping the home
and losing it. Because that is what this is really about.
Keeping the home you worked your whole life to pay for, and staying in it safely,
instead of losing it to bills you did not have to pay or repairs you could
not afford.
Let me take you through all five, one by one, in plain words, what each one
is, who qualifies, and the one quiet mistake that keeps this help sitting on
the table year after year. Wait for the last two, because they can put thousands
of dollars toward fixing your home, and almost no one has ever heard of them.
The first one is a bill that lands every month or two, and you have probably
never once thought to question it, and that is your water, your sewer, and
your trash. Most people assume these are fixed, that everyone pays the same,
and that there is nothing to be done about it.
That is not true.
A great many cities and towns in this country offer a senior discount on water
and sewer service, and often on trash pickup too, once you reach a certain
age, usually sixty five, and sometimes with a modest income limit.
In some places that discount takes twenty five or thirty percent straight off
the bill. In others, the sewer charge is dropped entirely.
On a bill you will pay for the rest of your life, month after month, a discount
like that quietly adds up to hundreds of dollars a year.
But your water company will not put a note in the mailbox telling you to apply.
You have to call them, or your city hall, and ask one simple question.
Do you offer a senior discount on my water, my sewer, or my trash, and how
do I apply for it. That single phone call is worth making this week.
The second one is the biggest bill in your home in the cold months and the
hot ones, and that is your energy bill.
Now, you may have heard of programs that help pay a heating bill in an emergency.
This one is different, and in many ways better, because it does not just pay
a single bill, it makes every future bill smaller, for free.
It is called the Weatherization Assistance Program.
It is a federal program, run through your own state, and here is what it actually
does.
It sends workers to your home, at no cost to you, to seal the leaks, add insulation,
and repair or replace an old furnace or air conditioner, so the money that
has been leaking out of your walls and windows for years finally stops.
For an older person on a fixed income, that can cut a heating and cooling bill
dramatically, and permanently.
And here is the part written right into the rules.
The elderly are given priority.
If your income is modest, and the limit is more generous than most people expect,
you move toward the front of the line simply because of your age.
You apply through your state's weatherization office.
It costs you nothing, and it keeps paying you back every single month for years
to come. The third one is the repair you have been putting off because you
cannot see how you would ever pay for it.
The leaking roof. The broken furnace.
The step that is no longer safe.
If you own your home, you are sixty two or older, your income is modest, and
you live in a smaller town or a rural area,
there is a program from the Department of Agriculture that will simply give
you the money to fix it.
Not a loan you have to pay back.
A grant.
As the program stands now, it can provide up to ten thousand dollars, over
your lifetime, to remove health and safety hazards from your home.
Ten thousand dollars, to repair the very things that might otherwise force
you out of the house you own. And if you need more than that and can handle
a small payment, the same program offers a loan of up to forty thousand
dollars at just one percent interest, far below anything a bank would ever
offer you. Most people who qualify have never once heard of it.
You apply through your local Department of Agriculture Rural Development office,
and you ask about the five oh four home repair program.
For the right person, it is the difference between staying in your home and
losing it. The fourth one decides, for a great many seniors, whether they get
to stay in their own home at all.
As we grow older, the ordinary house we have lived in for decades can slowly
turn against us. A tub you can no longer safely step into.
Stairs that have started to frighten you.
A doorway too narrow for a walker.
And here is the cruel result.
People leave homes they fully own, and move into care that costs a fortune,
not because they truly had to, but because a few simple changes to the house
were never made. Now here is what almost no one knows.
Those changes, grab bars, a walk in shower, a ramp, a raised toilet, a
wider doorway, can very often be done for free.
If you are on Medicaid, there is a special part of it, called a home and community
based waiver, that exists for exactly this.
It pays for the modifications that let you stay in your home instead of entering
a nursing home, for the simple reason that keeping you at home costs the government
far less than paying for that home.
And whether or not you are on Medicaid, your local Area Agency on Aging can
point you to the programs in your area that do this work.
Think for a moment about how much this one quietly decides.
A single slip stepping over the side of the tub, and all at once a family is
sitting around the kitchen table talking about a care home that costs more
than five thousand dollars a month, pulling someone out of the only place they
have ever felt safe, not because they truly had to leave, but because a walk
in shower and two grab bars were never put in.
And those grab bars, that shower, would have been installed for nothing, by
a program built for exactly this, if only someone had said out loud that it
existed.
That is the whole weight of this one.
Not a small repair. The difference between a person keeping the home they own
and losing it to a facility. So before you ever let anyone convince you that
you have to leave your home, make one call to your Area Agency on Aging
and ask, what help is there to make my home safe enough for me to stay in it.
And the fifth one is for every single person who heard those last two and thought,
that sounds wonderful, but I am not in a rural area, or I am not on Medicaid,
so none of it is for me. This one is for you.
Across this country there are national charities whose entire purpose is to
repair and modify the homes of older people who cannot afford to do it themselves,
and they do the work for free.
One of them, called Rebuilding Together, sends skilled volunteers to fix roofs,
repair heating, and make a home safe again.
Another, Habitat for Humanity, runs a program built specifically for aging
in place, installing ramps, grab bars, and safer bathrooms for homeowners who
are sixty two or older with a modest income.
You do not need to be on any government program at all to qualify.
You simply have to find the group that serves your area, and ask.
Search the name of the charity along with the name of your town, or ask your
Area Agency on Aging to point you toward them.
For a senior who has been staring at a repair they cannot afford, quietly wondering
how much longer they can stay in their own home, this is the door almost no
one ever knows to knock on. Now step back and look at what all five of these
share, because it is the very same thread running through every one of them.
The money is real. The programs already exist, funded and running, written
for exactly your situation.
And not a single one of them will ever come looking for you.
The city does not call to offer you the discount.
The county does not knock to hand you the grant.
They are counting on your silence, and on a lifetime of habit that tells you
to just pay, and just cope, and never ask.
But this is your home. The single biggest thing you ever worked for and paid
for. Protecting it, keeping it affordable, and keeping it safe enough to stay
in, is one of the most important things you will ever do with a few phone calls.
So here is your list for this week.
One. Call your water company or your city hall and ask about a senior discount.
Two. Call your state's weatherization office and apply.
Three. If you live in a smaller town, call the Department of Agriculture and
ask about the five oh four home repair grant.
Four. Call your Area Agency on Aging and ask what help exists to make your
home safe. And five. If you need another door, find Rebuilding Together or
Habitat for Humanity in your area.
Every one of these is free to ask about, and the rules and income limits are
different in every place, so let each program tell you exactly what you qualify
for.
This is general information to help you know what to ask for, and it is not
legal or financial advice. And I have put the names of every one of these programs,
and where to start, in the description just below this video.
And before you go, think of one person who is quietly worried about their home.
A parent afraid of the next repair bill.
A widow who no longer feels safe in her own bathroom.
A neighbor paying full price for everything because no one ever told them there
was another way. Send them this video.
It could be the very thing that lets them keep the home they love.
Go and make one of these calls this week, and help someone you love make theirs.

title: The IRS Quietly Watches These 3 Things in Your Bank Account After 65 — and No One Has to Tell You

segments.text: There are three things the IRS can quietly do to the money sitting in your
bank account right now, and it is counting on one thing above all else.
That you will go your whole life never learning that any of them exist.
It does not send a letter to explain them.
Your bank will never warn you.
And two of the three can happen without a single judge ever signing off on
it.
One of these rules decides how much tax you owe on money you already earned.
One of them can turn an ordinary, honest deposit into a federal investigation.
And the last one, the one I truly want you to stay for, can freeze every single
dollar in your account in one quiet afternoon, before you even know it is happening.
Here is the part that catches good, honest people.
Not one of these three rules is a trap because it is complicated.
Each one is simple.
What destroys careful retirees is the one small mistake they make the moment
they find out the rule exists, because they react out of fear instead of knowledge.
So stay with me, because I am going to walk you through all three in plain
language. Exactly what each rule is, who it touches, and the quiet mistake
that turns a harmless rule into a disaster.
By the end, you will understand your own bank account better than most people
ever will.
Let me start with the first rule, because it is the one that touches every
single person watching, and it has quietly gotten more expensive in the last
two years. It is this. Every dollar of interest your bank pays you is reported
straight to the IRS, and every dollar of it is taxable income.
For years this barely mattered, because banks paid almost nothing on your savings.
But interest rates climbed, and now that ordinary savings account you keep
for emergencies is actually paying you real money.
For some of you that is a few hundred dollars a year.
For others with more set aside, it is well over a thousand.
And here is what most seniors do not realize.
The moment your account pays you ten dollars or more in interest across the
year, your bank sends a form to the IRS with your name on it and the exact
amount you were paid. You might get a copy in the mail.
The IRS always gets its copy, every time.
And this is exactly where honest people get caught.
They forget about that small bit of interest.
Or the form never arrived, or it slipped behind other mail, so they leave it
off their tax return believing it does not matter.
But the IRS already has the number.
Its computers quietly match what your bank reported against what you actually
filed, automatically, and when the two do not match, a letter arrives months
later asking for the tax you missed, plus interest on it, plus a penalty, all
on money you barely remembered earning.
Understand the rule and it is nothing.
Ignore it and it becomes a bill.
And there is a sharper edge to this first rule that almost nobody knows about.
If the name or the Social Security number on your account does not perfectly
match the government's records, or if the IRS has flagged you, the bank is
required to hold back twenty four percent of your interest and send it straight
to the IRS, before a single dollar of it ever reaches you.
That is called backup withholding, and it happens automatically.
So the first rule is simple to live with.
Every dollar of interest is seen.
Report all of it, even a few dollars, even when no form arrives, because they
