all the way to the largest pool of forgotten money in the entire country.
That last one is sitting in a government account right now,
it may very well have your name on it,
and checking it takes about two minutes and costs you nothing.
Stay with me until then, because people who were sure they had nothing waiting have
pulled thousands of dollars out of that final one.
Let me begin with the newest, because new is exactly what makes it dangerous.
People miss it for the simple reason that last year it did not exist.
Starting with the twenty twenty five tax year,
there is a brand new deduction written into the law just for people who are
sixty five and older.
It is worth up to six thousand dollars for a single person,
and up to twelve thousand dollars for a married couple where both husband and wife
have turned sixty five.
This sits on top of your regular standard deduction,
and on top of the extra amount that seniors already receive.
And here is the part that catches everyone.
You do not have to itemize to get it.
You can take the plain standard deduction and still claim this on top.
Most people who lose this one lose it for two reasons.
Either they never heard it existed, or they heard about it and assumed it was
only for the wealthy.
It is the opposite.
The full amount goes to seniors with income under seventy five thousand dollars for a
single person, or one hundred fifty thousand dollars for a couple,
and it only starts to shrink above those lines.
It runs all the way through the twenty twenty eight tax year.
That means there are four full years of this money on the table,
and every year you do not claim it is a year of it gone for
good.
Think about what six thousand dollars actually is in a retired person's life.
It is months of groceries.
It is a year of a Medicare supplement.
It is the cushion that lets you keep the heat on without flinching at the
bill.
For a couple, twelve thousand dollars is even more than that.
This is not pocket change, and it is not a loophole.
It is a deduction the law wrote specifically with you in mind.
If a person prepares your taxes, this is the first thing you should ask them
about this year.
And if you file your own, do not let the form move past it without
stopping to claim it.
Number two is much older, but you would be amazed how many people still walk
right past it.
The moment you turn sixty five, the I R S gives you a bigger standard
deduction than younger taxpayers get.
For a single person that is well over a thousand extra dollars of your income
that is never taxed at all, and for a married couple where both of you
are sixty five, it stacks once for each of you.
This one is supposed to be automatic, but automatic only works if the return is
done correctly.
Every year, people who rush through their own taxes,
or who let old software default to the younger amount,
quietly hand back money the law set aside for them.
If someone else files for you, ask them one plain question this season.
Did you apply my age sixty five standard deduction.
You have every right to know.
Number three is not a deduction at all,
and that is what makes it so powerful.
It is a credit.
A deduction only lowers the income you get taxed on.
A credit comes straight off the tax you owe,
dollar for dollar.
It is called the Credit for the Elderly or the Disabled,
and it has been sitting on the books for decades,
and almost nobody claims it.
It is built for older Americans living on a modest income,
and depending on your filing status it can be worth between three thousand seven hundred
and fifty dollars and seven thousand five hundred dollars.
The income limits on this one are low,
which means it is aimed squarely at the seniors getting by on Social Security and
a small amount on top, the very people who can least afford to overpay a
dime.
If that sounds like you, or like someone you love,
the form is called Schedule R.
And here is a gift that goes with it.
The I R S runs a program of free tax help staffed by trained volunteers,
built specifically for older people, and they will sit with you and fill out forms
exactly like this one at no charge.
You do not have to pay anyone to claim what is yours.
Number four moves away from the federal government and down to your own state and
your own county, and this is where some of the very largest unclaimed money of
all is hiding in plain sight.
Nearly every state gives older homeowners a way to lower their property tax,
and a stunning number of people never file for it.
Some states cap your property tax at a small percentage of your income,
so that when the tax bill climbs faster than your income does,
the state pays back the difference.
That kind of program is often called a circuit breaker,
and in some states the refund runs to well over two thousand dollars in a
single year.
On top of that, most places offer what is called a homestead exemption,
which simply lowers the value your home is taxed on before the tax rate is
ever applied.
And many states add an extra exemption just for homeowners who are sixty five and
older, which in some places knocks tens of thousands of dollars off the taxable value
of the house.
But there is a catch, and it is a cruel one.
You almost always have to file for these,
and they are usually not retroactive, which means if you miss the window this year,
that year of savings is gone for good.
One phone call to your county tax office,
asking what exemptions a homeowner over sixty five can claim,
can lower a bill you pay every single year for as long as you live
in that home.
That is not a one time refund.
It is money back in your pocket year after year.
Let me show you how big this can get.
Picture a man who is sixty eight and has owned his home for thirty years.
His house has climbed in value, so every year his property tax climbs with it,
even though his income has not moved at all.
He assumes there is nothing he can do.
But his state has a homestead exemption, an extra exemption just for owners over sixty
five, and a program that will not let his tax climb past a set share
of his income.
He qualifies for all three, and has for years.
He has simply never filed the one page form at the county office.
The difference, once he files, is well over a thousand dollars every single year.
That is more than ten thousand dollars he has handed over across the last decade,
because nobody at the county was ever going to knock on his door and tell
him to ask.
And now the last one, the one I asked you to wait for,
because it is the largest pool of forgotten money in the whole country,
and it has nothing to do with how you filed your taxes.
Right now, spread across all fifty states, the government is holding more than seventy three
billion dollars in what is called unclaimed property.
This is ordinary money that belongs to ordinary people and was simply lost track of
over the years.
An old bank account from a bank that merged into another one.
A final paycheck that never got cashed.
A deposit refund from a utility company.
A dividend check that was mailed to a house you moved away from twenty years
ago.
By law, when a company cannot find you,
that money is eventually turned over to the state,
and the state holds it for you, sometimes for decades,
waiting for you to come and ask.
It is estimated that one in every ten Americans has money sitting and waiting like
this.
And for older people, who have lived in more homes,
opened more accounts, and worked for more employers across a long life,
the odds are even higher than that.
So here is exactly how you check, and please pay close attention to this next
part, because there are companies that will try to charge you for something that is
completely free.
Go to the official website called Missing Money,
which is run by the state governments themselves,
and type in your name.
You can also go straight to the unclaimed property office of any state you have
ever lived in and search there.
If money comes up, you file the claim directly with the state,
and it does not cost you a thing.
Never, ever pay a finder who calls or writes offering to recover it for a
percentage.
You do not need them, and you should not give them a cent.
The money is already yours.
Claiming it is free.
Now step back with me and look at what all five of these share,
because the pattern is the entire lesson.
Not one of them shows up in your mailbox with your name on it and
a friendly note that says please come and claim me.
The new deduction is not applied unless your return is done right.
The credit sits untouched unless someone fills out the form.
The property tax break expires unless you file for it on time.
The money the state is holding stays locked in a government account until the day
you walk up and ask for it.
Every single one of these was built around the quiet assumption that you will not
know about it, will not ask about it,
and will not file for it.
That is how thousands of dollars slip away from honest,
careful people every year.
Not through any fault of their own, but through a system that simply never tells
them what they are owed in the first place.
So here is what I am asking you to do,
and it is small.
Pick just one of these five this week.
Only one.
Maybe it is the two minute search on the Missing Money website tonight,
before you go to bed.
Maybe it is one phone call to your county tomorrow about the property tax exemption.
Maybe it is one question to whoever handles your taxes about the new deduction for
people over sixty five.
You do not have to chase down all five at once and wear yourself out.
You only have to open one of those doors,
because the money waiting behind it has belonged to you the whole time.
And if you will do one last thing,
do this.
Picture one person you know who is older and careful with every dollar,
the kind of person who would never in a hundred years imagine that the government
might be sitting on cash with their name on it.
Send this to them today.
It costs you nothing, and it may be the one message that puts a few
thousand dollars back into their hands this year.
Money that was always theirs.
Money that was only ever waiting on the far side of a question that nobody
had told them to ask.

title: The IRS Rewrote the Rules for Retirees in 2026 — and Nobody Told You

segments.text: The Internal Revenue Service made a series of quiet changes this year that directly
affect how much of your retirement money you get to keep, and almost none
of it was announced in a way you would ever notice.
There was no letter in your mailbox, no warning on your statement, no phone call.
The rules simply changed underneath you, and the people who do not find out
until tax time are the ones who lose the most.
Some of these changes can save you thousands of dollars if you know to use them.
Others can quietly cost you thousands if you do not see them coming.
I am going to walk you through five specific changes the I R S
put in place that hit retirees this year, exactly what each one means for
your money in plain English, and what you need to do about it.
Stay to the end, because the last one is a change to inherited accounts
that can hand your children a tax bill they never saw coming, and it
is the one almost nobody is talking about.
The first change is a new deduction that can push your tax bill all
the way down to zero, and most seniors have no idea it exists.
Starting with this tax year and running through twenty twenty eight, every person who
is sixty five or older gets a brand new senior bonus deduction of up
to six thousand dollars, and for a married couple where both spouses are sixty
five or older that is twelve thousand dollars.
This stacks on top of the regular standard deduction and on top of the
extra deduction seniors have always gotten for being over sixty five.
When you add it all together, a single senior can now shelter well over
twenty thousand dollars of income from federal tax, and a married couple can shelter
close to forty thousand.
For millions of retirees living on Social Security plus a modest pension or a
small withdrawal, that means a federal tax bill of zero.
But here is the catch the I R S does not advertise.
It only lasts through twenty twenty eight unless Congress extends it, and it starts
to shrink for higher incomes, so this is a claim it every single year
while it lasts situation.
Do not leave six thousand dollars sitting on the table.
The second change is connected to the first, and it has quietly created a
window that the smartest retirees are using right now.
Because the standard deduction keeps rising, in twenty twenty six it is sixteen thousand
one hundred dollars for a single person and thirty two thousand two hundred dollars
for a married couple, and because the senior deductions stack on top, there is
now a larger amount of income you can pull out of a traditional retirement
account each year and pay little or no tax on it.
This is the low tax window, and it exists in the years after you
stop working and before forced withdrawals begin.
The change in the deduction made that window wider this year.
The retirees who understand this are moving money out of their traditional accounts at
almost no tax cost, while the ones who do not understand it leave the
money sitting there to be taxed harder later.
The rule change handed you a gift. Most people will never open it.
The third change is a trap, and it is the one that punishes you
for something you did two years ago.
It is the Medicare income surcharge, the extra amount added to your Medicare premiums
when your income passes a certain line, and the line and the lookback both
matter this year.
In twenty twenty six that surcharge kicks in once your income passes roughly one
hundred and nine thousand dollars for a single person or two hundred and eighteen thousand for a married couple.
But here is the cruel part.
Medicare does not look at this year's income.
It looks at your tax return from two years ago.
So a one time spike in your income two years back, from selling a
house, from a large withdrawal, from a Roth conversion you did without planning, can
raise your Medicare premiums this year by hundreds or even thousands of dollars, long
after you have forgotten what caused it.
The change you need to know is that if your income has dropped since
then because you retired, you can file a form and ask them to recalculate
based on what you actually earn now.
Most people pay the surcharge for years without ever knowing they could appeal it.
The fourth change is the one the I R S is counting on you
to ignore, the required withdrawal.
The government does not let you leave money in a traditional retirement account forever.
At a certain age it forces you to start pulling money out and paying
tax on it whether you need the money or not.
For most people that age is now seventy three, and if you were born
in nineteen sixty or later it is seventy five.
Here is what changed and what bites people.
Your very first required withdrawal can be delayed until the first of April of
the following year, but if you delay it, you are then forced to take
two withdrawals in that same year, and stacking two years of income together can
shove you into a higher tax bracket and even trigger that Medicare surcharge we
just talked about.
And if you simply miss a required withdrawal, the penalty is twenty five percent
of the amount you were supposed to take, cut down to ten percent only
if you fix it quickly.
That is a penalty on top of the tax, just for being late.
Know your age, know your deadline, and never miss it.
The fifth change is the one that almost nobody is talking about, and it
is the one that reaches past you and lands on your children.
It is the new rule for inherited retirement accounts.
It used to be that when your children inherited your I R A, they
could stretch the withdrawals out over their entire lifetime, taking a little each year
and keeping the tax small. That is gone.
Under the current rules, when a child or other non spouse inherits your traditional
retirement account, they generally have to empty the entire account within ten years.
And the final version of this rule, now in full effect, says that if
you had already started your own required withdrawals before you passed, your children must
also take a withdrawal every single year during that ten year window, not just
empty it at the end.
What that means in real life is brutal.
Your children are usually in their forties, fifties, or sixties when they inherit, often
in their peak earning years and their highest tax brackets, and now they are
forced to pull this money out and pay tax on it on a tight
schedule, at the worst possible rates of their lives.
A lifetime of your careful saving can be handed to the I R S
in a single decade.
The move that softens this is to consider converting some of that traditional money
to a Roth account while you are alive, because a Roth passes to your
children without that yearly tax bill.
But you have to know the rule exists before you can plan around it,
and most people find out only after it is too late.
Let me bring all five together, because the thread is the same one that
runs through everything the I R S does.
A new deduction that can take your tax to zero, but only if you claim it.
A wider low tax window, but only if you use it.
A Medicare surcharge that punishes you for income from two years ago, but that you can appeal.
A forced withdrawal with a brutal penalty for being late.
And a new inheritance rule that quietly hands your children's inheritance to the government over ten years.
Not one of these came with a warning.
The system changed the rules underneath you, said nothing, and is waiting to see
who notices and who does not.
Nobody from the government is going to call and walk you through how these
changes affect your money.
The I R S processes what you file and stays silent about the rest.
The only person who can use the changes that help you and defend against
the ones that hurt you is you, and for most of this, the move is the same.
Sit down with your real numbers before the end of the year, and if
any of it is complicated, talk to a fee only fiduciary adviser who can
run your specific situation.
I will put the form numbers and the things to ask about in the description below.
So do one thing for me right now.
Send this to one person you care about who is retired or getting close,
and who still has money in a traditional retirement account.
A parent, a sibling, a friend, someone at church who has no idea the
rules just changed underneath them.
The odds are very good that at least one of these five changes is
about to cost them or save them real money, and they have never heard
a word about any of it.
One share from you could be worth thousands of dollars to them and to their children.
That is what we are here for.
I will see you in the next one.

title: Banks Are Quietly Freezing Senior Accounts — Here's How to Protect Yours

segments.text: There is a phone call happening in this country every
single day that goes something like this.
A woman in her seventies walks into her bank to
move some of her own money, to help a grandchild,
to pay for a new roof, to send a deposit
on a place she is moving to.
And instead of handing her the money, the bank pulls
her into a back office, asks her a series of
questions, and then tells her the transaction is on hold.
Her own money, in her own account, frozen.
And she did absolutely nothing wrong.
This is happening to seniors more than to anyone else,
and the reason is something almost nobody has explained to
you. The bank now has the power to freeze your
account, hold your transfer, or block your withdrawal, sometimes for
weeks, and in some cases it is legally forbidden from
telling you exactly why. I am going to walk you
through the six reasons a bank will freeze a senior's
account, why you are a bigger target than you think,
and the exact steps you can take right now so
that your money is never locked away from you when
you need it most. Stay to the end, because the
last step is the one that keeps your account open
even when everyone else's is getting frozen.
The first reason is the one that surprises people the
most, because it was created to protect you.
In the last few years, banks and investment firms were
given the power to put a temporary hold on the
account of anyone sixty five or older the moment they
suspect that senior is being financially exploited.
The hold can last fifteen business days, and it can
be extended even longer than that.
It was written with good intentions, to stop a scammer
from draining a grandmother's life savings before anyone notices.
But the very same rule means that a perfectly sharp,
perfectly capable senior who walks in to take out twenty
thousand dollars to help her own daughter buy a home
can be questioned, doubted, and made to wait while the
bank decides whether to release her own money.
The bank does not have to be right.
It only has to be suspicious.
The second reason is a sudden change in your normal
pattern. The software your bank runs watches every account quietly,
and it is looking for anything that breaks your usual
habits. If you have taken out three hundred dollars a
week for fifteen years and you suddenly ask for eight
thousand, that is a pattern break, and it can trigger
a hold while a human reviews it.
The system does not know you are putting a new
roof on the house. It does not care.
It sees something different from your history, and different is
exactly what it is built to flag.
The third reason is any sign that you might be
the victim of a scam, and this is where seniors
get caught in the trap the most.
Banks are now trained to treat large transfers by older
customers as possible scams. So when a senior tries to
send a wire, especially to a person or a place
the account has never sent money to before, the teller
is trained to slow it down, ask who the money
is for, ask whether anyone instructed you to send it,
ask whether you met someone new online.
If your answers make the bank uneasy, even if everything
is completely legitimate, they can hold the transfer.
The irony is painful. The rule meant to protect you
from losing your money can stop you from using your
money. The fourth reason is one most people never see
coming, and it is doing nothing at all.
It is called a dormancy or inactivity freeze.
If you have a savings account or an old checking
account that you simply leave sitting there untouched, after a
period of time the bank can flag it as dormant,
restrict it, and in some states eventually hand the balance
over to the state government as unclaimed property.
Money you forgot about, money you were saving for later,
can be locked up or swept away simply because you
were not moving it around enough to satisfy the bank.
The fifth reason is the one the bank can never
explain to you, and it is a suspicious activity review.
Federal rules require banks to watch for transactions that look
unusual, and when something gets flagged, the bank can freeze
the account while it investigates, and it is legally prohibited
from telling you that this is what happened.
So you could walk in one day and find your
card declined, your transfer blocked, your account restricted, and the
person at the counter genuinely cannot tell you why, because
the law forbids it. You did nothing illegal.
The system simply scored your activity as worth a second
look, and you are the one who pays for that
with frozen access to your own money.
The sixth reason hits at the worst possible time, and
it is the death of a co-owner.
If you share a joint account with a spouse and
that spouse passes away, the bank can freeze the account
the moment it learns of the death, until the paperwork
is sorted out and ownership is confirmed.
A grieving widow can find herself locked out of the
very account she needs to pay for the funeral, simply
because the name on the account is now in question.
It is cruel, it is common, and almost nobody plans
for it. So now you understand why it happens.
Here is what you actually do about it, because every
one of these freezes can be prevented or shortened if
you take a few simple steps before the trouble starts.
The first step, and the most powerful one, is to
add a trusted contact to your account.
Most banks and investment firms now let you name a
person they are allowed to call if they ever suspect
something is wrong with your account.
When you name that trusted contact, you give the bank
someone to verify with instead of simply freezing you out.
This one step, which takes five minutes and costs nothing,
is the single best protection against the elder exploitation hold,
because it gives the bank a faster path than locking
your money away. The second step is to warn your
bank before you do anything large.
If you know a big withdrawal or a big transfer
is coming, call the branch a few days ahead, tell
them the amount and what it is for, and ask
them to note it on your account.
A transaction the bank is expecting is a transaction the
bank does not freeze. The freeze happens when you surprise
them. Take the surprise away. The third step is to
keep every account active. Do not leave money sitting in
an account you never touch. Set up one small automatic
transaction, even a few dollars moving in or out each
month, so that no account of yours ever gets flagged
as dormant and swept away. The fourth step is to
keep your paperwork ready. If you sell a car, receive
a gift, move an inheritance, or cash in a policy,
keep the document that proves where that money came from.
When the bank questions a deposit or a withdrawal, a
single piece of paper that explains it can be the
difference between a five minute conversation and a fifteen day
hold. And the fifth step is the one I told
you to wait for, and it is the one that
protects you no matter what any single bank decides to
do. Do not keep all of your money in one
account at one bank. Spread it across more than one
institution, keep a reasonable cushion in each, and move the
bulk of your savings into your own name in accounts
that are not sitting under the watchful eye of a
single branch. Because here is the truth.
If one bank freezes one account, a senior with everything
in that one place is completely cut off, with no
way to buy groceries or pay a bill.
But a senior whose money is spread across two or
three places still has access, still has cash, still has
control, no matter what any one bank does on any
given day. The freeze that destroys one person is barely
an inconvenience to another, and the only difference between them
is that one of them planned ahead.
Let me bring this together, because the thread is the
same one that runs through everything.
The bank can freeze your account to protect you, and
freeze it because you broke a pattern, and freeze it
because it suspects a scam, and freeze it because you
left it alone too long, and freeze it for a
reason it cannot legally share, and freeze it the day
a co-owner dies. Six different doors, all leading to the
same place, your own money locked away from you.
And not one of these freezes comes with a warning.
The bank does not call you the week before to
explain how to avoid it. The system is built so
that the freeze happens first and the questions come later,
if they come at all. Nobody at that bank is
going to sit you down and teach you how to
keep your account open. The only person who can protect
your access to your own money is you, and every
step I just gave you can be done this week
with a few phone calls. Name your trusted contact.
Warn them before the big moves.
Keep your accounts active. Keep your paperwork.
And never, ever keep everything in one place.
I will put a checklist of these steps and the
exact things to ask your bank in the description below.
So do one thing for me right now.
Send this to one person you love who is over
sixty and keeps most of their savings in a single
account at a single bank. Your mother, your father, a
friend, the widow down the street who would be completely
stranded if her one account were frozen tomorrow.
The odds are very good that they have never named
a trusted contact and have never been warned that this
can happen to them at all.
One share from you could be the reason their money
is still in reach on the day they need it
most. That is what we are here for.
I will see you in the next one.

title: Stop Paying These 8 Bank Fees (They Won't Tell You)

segments.text: I want you to picture a woman named Dorothy.
She is seventy one years old, she lives alone in the same
house she raised her children in, and she has banked at the
same branch on the same corner for almost forty years.
Every month her statement arrives in the mail, she glances at the
balance on the first page, and she files it away in a
kitchen drawer without ever once reading the middle of it.
And every single month, buried in that middle, her bank quietly takes
a little more of her money in fees she does not even
know she is paying.
Over the last ten years, Dorothy has handed that bank close to
three thousand dollars for nothing, and not one time did anyone there
pick up the phone to tell her she could make it stop.
Dorothy is not careless and Dorothy is not foolish.
She is exactly like millions of good, careful people who simply assume
that fees are the normal price of having a bank account.
They are not.
Every one of these charges is pure profit for the bank, and
the whole system is built on one quiet bet, that you will
not read your statement closely and you will not call to ask
about it.
Because almost every one of these fees can be removed with a
single phone call or a single switch, and the bank will never
be the one to volunteer that to you.
So today I am going to walk you through eight fees your
bank is very likely charging you right now, exactly why each one
exists, and the precise words to say to make each one disappear.
Stay with me to the end, because the last one is not
even printed on your bank statement.
It is hidden somewhere else entirely, and it quietly costs retirees more
money than all seven of these fees put together.
Fee number one is the monthly maintenance fee, sometimes called a service
fee, and it is the most common one of all.
It is a charge, often around fourteen dollars a month, simply for
the privilege of keeping your account open.
Fourteen dollars does not sound like much, but that is well over
a hundred and sixty dollars a year, every year, draining quietly out
of your account for nothing in return.
Now here is the good news.
Almost every major bank offers a senior account with no monthly fee
at all, some starting as young as fifty five and most by
the age of sixty or sixty two.
So the first thing you do is call your bank and say
these exact words.
I would like to switch to your no monthly fee account for seniors.
If they tell you they do not have one, you say this.
Then please tell me how to get this monthly fee waived.
And almost every bank will waive that fee the moment you have
a regular direct deposit going into the account, and your Social Security
payment counts as that direct deposit.
If they still refuse, that is your answer to leave, because an
online bank or a local credit union will give you the very
same checking account with no monthly fee, ever.
Fee number two is the overdraft fee, and this is the one
that does the most damage, because it strikes at the exact moment
you are already short on money.
If you spend even a few dollars more than you have, the
bank quietly covers it and then charges you around thirty to thirty
five dollars for the favor, and they can do it more than
once in a single day.
So a five dollar cup of coffee can end up costing you forty dollars.
Now I need you to hear something important.
Regulators recently tried to cap this fee at just five dollars, but
that rule was overturned in twenty twenty five, so the banks are
once again free to charge the full amount, and they are.
The way you protect yourself is to call your bank and say this.
I want to opt out of overdraft coverage completely.
When you do that, if a payment would ever overdraw your account,
the bank simply declines it at the register, and you pay nothing
at all instead of thirty five dollars.
You would far rather have a card quietly declined for a moment
than pay thirty five dollars for a gallon of milk.
Fee number three is the out of network cash machine fee, and
it is sneaky because you actually get charged twice.
Once by the machine you are standing in front of, and once
again by your own bank, and together those charges now average close
to five dollars just to take out your own money.
Do that a couple of times a week and you have handed
away hundreds of dollars a year in cash you already owned.
The fix could not be simpler.
Only use the cash machines that belong to your own bank, and
when there is not one nearby, do this instead.
At almost any grocery store or pharmacy, when you pay with your
debit card, the cashier will ask if you would like cash back,
and you can take out your cash right there at the register
completely free.
No machine, no fee, your own money in your hand.
Fee number four is the wire transfer fee.
Any time you send money to family, or to a title company
when you buy or sell a home, or even between your own
accounts, and you let the bank send it as a wire, they
charge you somewhere between twenty five and thirty five dollars to push
a button.
For the vast majority of transfers you will ever make, you do
not need a wire at all.
You can send the money for free using a standard electronic transfer
between banks, or through one of the free transfer apps your bank
already offers right inside its phone application.
A wire is only for the rare, truly urgent, same day situation.
For everything else, the free option does the exact same job and
the money simply arrives a day or two later.
Fee number five is the paper statement fee.
More and more banks have quietly begun charging you a few dollars
every month just for mailing you a paper copy of your statement,
the very thing they sent you for free your entire life.
You have two ways to kill this one.
You can switch to electronic statements, which you can always print at
home any time you want a paper copy, and the fee vanishes.
Or, if you genuinely want that paper statement mailed to you and
you are living on a fixed income, you call and say this.
I am a senior on a fixed income and I would like
this paper statement fee waived.
Many banks will waive it the moment you ask, because they would
much rather keep you than lose you over a few dollars a
month.
Fee number six is the inactivity fee, also called a dormancy fee,
and this one is almost insulting once you understand it.
It is a fee the bank charges you for not using an account enough.
If you have a savings account or an older checking account that
you simply leave sitting there, some banks will begin draining it with
a monthly charge for the crime of doing nothing.
The fix is to either set up one small automatic transaction, even
a few dollars moving in or out each month, so the account
stays active, or to simply close any account you are not really
using and move that money somewhere it is not being nibbled away
while you sleep.
Fee number seven is the minimum balance fee, and this is the
one that feels like a trap, because it is one.
The bank promises you free checking, but only if you keep a
certain amount of money sitting in the account at all times, and
the one month your balance dips below that invisible line, even for
a single day, even by a single dollar, they hit you with
a fee.
The answer is to stop playing their game entirely.
Move your money into an account that has no minimum balance requirement
at all, which nearly every online bank and nearly every senior account
now offers, so that a low month or one unexpected expense never
costs you an extra penny on top of it.
Fee number eight is the foreign transaction fee, and it catches people
who do not even realize they left the country.
If you traveled abroad, or even just bought something online from a
company based in another country, your bank quietly adds a charge of
around three percent on top of everything you spent.
On a single trip that can add up to real money for nothing.
Many cards built for travel and most credit unions charge nothing at
all for this, so if you ever spend across the border, even
online, call and ask your bank one question.
Do you charge a foreign transaction fee, and if so, what card
can I use that does not.
Then carry that card whenever your money is leaving the country.
Now here is the bonus I promised you, the fee that is
not on your bank statement at all and that quietly dwarfs every
single one of the eight I just gave you.
It is the fee you pay to have your money managed and
invested for you.
If you have someone managing your retirement savings, and they charge you
what sounds like a tiny one percent a year, I want you
to really hear what that means in actual dollars.
On a nest egg of five hundred thousand dollars, one percent is
five thousand dollars every single year, coming out of your savings whether
your money grew that year or shrank.
And over a long retirement, with that money compounding year after year,
that one small sounding percent can quietly cost you well over a
hundred thousand dollars across your lifetime.
And that is before you count the separate yearly fee that the
funds your money sits inside often charge on top, a fee you
never see on any statement.
So here is what you do.
You ask whoever manages your money one direct question, and you do
not let them answer in percentages.
What am I paying you in total every year, in actual dollars.
And then you ask whether there is a simpler, lower cost option
that does the same job.
That one conversation can be worth more than all seven bank fees combined.
Now let me make the phone call itself easier, because I know
that is the part most people quietly dread, and it is the
real reason these fees go unchallenged for years.
You do not need to argue and you do not need to be rude.
You simply call the number printed on the back of your card,
and when a real person answers, you say this.
I have been a loyal customer for many years, and I would
like to review the fees on my account and have them removed
or waived.
Then you go down your circled list one charge at a time.
If the person on the phone says they cannot help you, you
do not give up and you do not hang up.
You say five simple words.
May I speak with a supervisor.
Because a supervisor is allowed to waive charges that the first person
on the line is not.
Stay calm, stay friendly, and stay on the line until you get
a real answer.
Fifteen quiet minutes on the phone, just once, can save you hundreds
of dollars every year for the rest of your life.
Let me bring this together, because the thread running through every one
of these is the same.
The monthly fee, the overdraft fee, the cash machine fee, the wire
fee, the paper statement fee, the inactivity fee, the minimum balance fee,
the foreign transaction fee, and the management fee hiding off your statement.
Every one of them is your money, leaving your account for nothing,
month after month, year after year.
None of it is illegal.
The bank is allowed to charge every cent of it.
But you are also allowed to say no, and the only difference
between the person who pays all of these and the person who
pays none of them is simply knowing they exist and being willing
to make one phone call.
Nobody at the bank is ever going to call you and offer
to lower your fees.
The whole system is built so those small charges keep flowing quietly
out of your account for as long as you allow it.
The only person who can turn them off is you.
So this week, do one simple thing.
Pull out your most recent bank statement, sit down at the kitchen
table, and read it line by line from top to bottom.
Circle every charge you do not understand.
Then pick up the phone and ask about each one, using the
exact words I gave you today.
Most of these will be gone within a week.
And think back to Dorothy.
The day she finally read one statement line by line and made
three short phone calls, she stopped paying almost every fee on this
list, and she put real money back in her pocket every month
for the rest of her life.
It was never that she could not afford to fix it.
It was only that nobody had ever told her she could.
So do one thing for me right now.
Send this video to one person you care about who has had
the same bank account for decades and has never once questioned the
fees on it.
A parent, a sibling, a friend, someone at your church living on
a fixed income where every single dollar matters.
The odds are very good that they are paying at least three
of these fees right now for absolutely no reason, and one share
from you could put real money back in their pocket every month
for the rest of their life.
That is what we are here for.
I will put a full checklist of these fees and the questions
to ask in the description below.
I will see you in the next one.

title: The IRS Is Watching Your Bank Account — Here's How Much Cash Is Too Much

segments.text: If you have more than a certain amount of money
sitting in your regular checking or savings account right now,
I need you to understand something. You are quietly losing
that money in three different ways at the exact same
time, and the most dangerous of the three is the
one your bank will never, ever warn you about. The
moment your balance crosses a certain line, the Internal Revenue
Service begins paying attention to you, your own money quietly
begins shrinking, and a piece of it stops being protected
at all. And the bank that holds it has no
reason to tell you any of this, because every one
of those three dangers makes money for them and costs
it to you. So today I am going to give
you three things. The exact amount of money that is
too much to leave in a normal bank account. The
three quiet dangers of keeping more than that. And then
the five specific places that careful retirees actually move the
rest of their money, so that it is safe, it
is protected, and it is finally earning something instead of
sitting still. Stay with me to the end, because that
last part is the part nobody explains to you for
free, and it is where the real money is. Let
me start with the first danger, the one that surprises
people the most, which is that once you hold a
large amount of money in one account, you are being
watched. Under federal law, any time more than ten thousand
dollars in cash moves through your account in a single
day, the bank is required to file a report about
it with a federal agency, and that report goes into
a government database with your name on it. But it
does not stop at cash. The software your bank runs
is watching your balance and your habits all the time,
quietly looking for anything that breaks your normal pattern. A
sudden large deposit, a sudden large withdrawal, money moving in
a way it has not moved before. You do not
have to do anything wrong to get flagged. You only
have to do something different. And the bigger the pile
of money sitting in that account, the more attention it
draws. The simplest way to stop being watched so closely
is to stop keeping so much sitting in the one
place that is doing the watching. The second danger is
the one that is purely mathematics, and it is robbing
you every single month whether anyone is watching or not.
It is inflation, and right now it is running at
a little over four percent a year. That means the
cost of everything you buy is rising by about four
percent every year. Now here is the cruel part. The
average regular savings account in this country today pays you
less than half of one percent in interest. Read that
again. Your money is losing more than four percent of
its buying power every year to rising prices, and your
bank is paying you almost nothing to make up for
it. So if you have fifty thousand dollars sitting in
a normal savings account, that money is quietly losing close
to two thousand dollars of real spending power every single
year, and you did nothing wrong to cause it. You
just left the money where the bank wanted it. Meanwhile,
that same bank is taking your money and lending it
back out to other people at far higher rates and
keeping the difference. Your money is doing all the work,
and the bank is keeping all the reward. The third
danger is the one almost nobody checks until it is
too late, and it is about protection. Every account at
every bank is insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation,
the F D I C, but only up to two
hundred and fifty thousand dollars per person, per bank. If
you have more than that amount in a single bank,
and that bank fails, every dollar above the line is
not protected, and you can simply lose it. People think
bank failures are something from their grandparents' time, but in
the year twenty twenty three this country had three of
the largest bank failures in its entire history within the
span of a few weeks. The people who were under
the limit were made whole. The people who were over
the limit had to wait and worry and hope. You
never want your life savings to depend on hope, when
staying protected is so easy to arrange. So now the
question you have been waiting for. How much is actually
too much to keep in a normal bank account. The
honest answer that careful planners give is this. Keep three
to six months of your regular living expenses in your
checking and everyday savings, and not very much more than
that. For most retirees, that lands somewhere between fifteen thousand
and twenty five thousand dollars. That is your cushion, your
emergency money, the cash you can reach in a moment.
Everything above that number does not belong in an account
that is watching it, shrinking it, and barely protecting it.
Everything above that number should be moved somewhere better, and
here are the five places that careful people actually move
it. The first place is a high yield savings account
at an online bank. These are real, fully insured savings
accounts, run by well known institutions that simply operate online
instead of on a street corner, and because they are
not paying for a fancy branch on Main Street, they
pass that savings to you in interest. Right now these
accounts are paying around four percent, sometimes a little more.
That is roughly ten times what your regular bank is
paying you on the very same money, with the very
same federal insurance protecting it. The money stays completely liquid,
which means you can move it back to your checking
account in a day or two whenever you need it.
Opening one takes about ten minutes from your kitchen table.
The second place is a Treasury bill. A Treasury bill
is simply a short term loan that you make directly
to the United States government, and it is considered one
of the safest places on earth to put money. You
can buy them in small amounts directly from a government
website called Treasury Direct, and right now the short term
ones are paying in the range of three and a
half to four percent. Here is the part most people
do not know. The interest you earn on a Treasury
bill is free from state income tax, so if you
live in a state that taxes income, a Treasury bill
can quietly put more money in your pocket than even
a high yield savings account paying the same rate. You
can set them up to mature every few weeks, so
you always have money coming available. The third place is
a series I savings bond, which is built for exactly
this moment in time, because it is designed to keep
pace with inflation. The interest rate on these bonds adjusts
along with the cost of living, so by design your
money does not lose its buying power the way it
does sitting in a regular account. You buy them from
that same government website, up to ten thousand dollars per
person each year. The one rule to know is that
you need to leave the money in for at least
a year, so this is for savings you will not
need right away, not for your emergency cushion. The fourth
place is a brokered certificate of deposit. Now you may
already know about regular certificates of deposit at your local
bank, where you lock your money up for a set
time in exchange for a fixed rate. A brokered one
simply means you buy it through an investment account, which
lets you shop the rates of hundreds of banks across
the country all at once, and pick the best ones.
And here is the powerful part for anyone with a
larger amount to protect. Through one single account, you can
spread your money across several different banks, twenty five thousand
here, two hundred thousand there, so that every dollar stays
under that two hundred and fifty thousand dollar insurance line
at each bank, all of it fully protected, all of
it earning a solid fixed rate. The fifth place is
a money market fund, held inside an investment account. This
is not the same as the money market account at
your bank. A money market fund holds very short term,
very safe government backed debt, and it currently pays in
the range of four to five percent. It is completely
liquid, so you can move the money back to your
checking account in about a day, there is no lock
up period, and there are no penalties for taking your
money out whenever you want it. For a retiree, it
is one of the simplest places to park larger amounts
of cash while still earning a real return on every
dollar. Now let me tie this all together, because the
thread running through every piece of it is the same.
Keeping a large pile of money in a normal bank
account does three things to you all at once. It
puts you under a watchful eye you never agreed to.
It lets inflation quietly eat your savings while the bank
pays you almost nothing. And above a certain line, it
leaves your money unprotected entirely. The fix for all three
is the very same simple move. Keep a few months
of expenses in your everyday account, and move everything above
that into your own name, into accounts that are safer,
fully protected, and actually paying you. You are not taking
on risk by doing this. You are taking risk off
the table, and getting paid properly for the first time
in years. The Internal Revenue Service is never going to
call you and explain how to draw less of its
attention. Your bank is certainly never going to call you
and explain how to earn ten times more on your
money somewhere else, because that money leaving is money it
loses. The only person who can decide to move it
is you, and the move itself is far simpler than
the bank wants you to believe. Most of these accounts
can be opened from your own home in less time
than it takes to drive to the branch. I will
put the names of these account types and the steps
to set them up in the description below. So do
one thing for me right now. Send this video to
one person you love who is over sixty and still
keeps most of their savings sitting in a single checking
or savings account at one bank. A parent, a sibling,
a friend, someone at church who worked hard their whole
life and was simply never told that their own money
could be both safer and earning more at the same
time. That one share could save them a fortune in
lost interest, protect every dollar they have, and quietly take
their name off a list they never knew they were
on. That is what we are here for. I will
see you in the next one.

title: Homeowners: You're Legally Exempt From This IRS Tax (Most Don't Know)

segments.text: If you own your home,
there is a tax sitting quietly in the
background that almost every homeowner gets wrong,
and getting it wrong costs real money.
Some people overpay it without ever realizing they
had a choice.
Others are so frightened of it that they
will not sell a house that has become
too big, too expensive, and too much to
keep up, so they stay trapped for years
to avoid a bill that, for most of
them, does not even exist.
And almost nobody has ever sat them down
and explained the one break, written right into
federal law, that wipes this tax out for
the vast majority of homeowners.
That is the quiet unfairness of it. The
break is enormous, it is sitting there waiting
for you, and nobody whose job touches your
money has any reason to explain it before
you make an expensive mistake. I am going
to walk you through exactly what the I
R S really takes when a home is
sold, the break that erases it for most
people, the special window that protects widows,
the rule that resets the tax to almost
nothing when a home is inherited,
and the well meaning move that hands your
children a giant tax bill instead of saving
them one. Stay to the end, because the
last point quietly does the most damage,
and good people make it every single day
thinking they are being smart. Number one is
the break that wipes out the tax, and
once you understand it you may feel the
fear lift right off your shoulders.
When you sell the home you have lived
in, federal law lets you exclude a huge
amount of the profit from tax entirely.
A single person can exclude two hundred and
fifty thousand dollars of gain,
and a married couple filing together can exclude
five hundred thousand dollars of gain, completely tax
free. The only requirement is that you owned
the home and lived in it as your
main home for at least two of the
last five years.
For the ordinary retiree who bought a house
decades ago and lived in it ever since,
that exclusion covers the entire profit,
and the tax bill they were so afraid
of comes out to zero.
Number two is the single most important word
in everything I just said, and it is
the word gain.
The exclusion is not about the price you
sell for. It is about your profit, and
your profit is only the amount above what
you originally paid for the house plus the
money you put into improving it.
Most people hear that their house will sell
for four hundred thousand dollars and they panic
thinking they owe tax on four hundred thousand
dollars. You do not. If you bought it
for one hundred thousand dollars decades ago,
your gain is the difference, not the whole
sale price, and then the exclusion sits on
top of that to wipe most or all
of it away.
And here is a detail that saves real
money. Every major improvement you ever made, a
new roof, a kitchen remodel, a room addition,
a new furnace, all of it gets added
to what you originally paid, which lowers your
gain even further.
So keep those records, because the more improvements
you can show, the smaller the taxable profit
becomes. Number three is a special protection
for widows that the government will never go
out of its way to explain.
When one spouse dies,
the survivor needs to know about a two
year window. If you sell the home within
two years of your spouse's death,
you can still claim the full five hundred
thousand dollar exclusion,
not the smaller two hundred and fifty thousand
dollar amount that applies to a single person.
That is a difference of a quarter of
a million dollars of protected profit,
and it disappears the day that two year
window closes. A widow sitting in a home
that has gained a great deal in value
needs to understand this clearly,
because waiting too long to sell can turn
a tax free sale into a taxable one
for no reason other than not knowing the
clock was running.
Number four is connected to that, and it
is one of the most powerful and least
understood rules in the entire tax code.
It is called the step up in basis.
When you inherit a home,
or when you inherit your spouse's share of
the home you owned together,
the value of that home is reset, for
tax purposes, to whatever it was worth on
the day that person died.
All the gain that built up over all
those years simply vanishes.
So a widow who inherits the family home
and then sells it often owes little or
nothing, because her starting point is no longer
what the couple paid in nineteen seventy five,
it is what the home was worth the
day her husband passed away.
In the states that treat property as community
property, the entire home gets that reset,
not just half.
This one rule is why patience and proper
planning around a home can save a family
a fortune. Number five is the well meaning
mistake I warned you about,
and it is the opposite of everything I
just described. Out of love,
a parent decides to put a child's name
on the deed,
or to give the house to the children
outright, or even to sell it to them
for one dollar while still alive,
thinking this avoids hassle and passes the home
on cleanly. It does the reverse.
When you give your home to your children
during your lifetime,
they do not get that step up in
basis. They inherit your original low starting point
instead. So when they eventually sell, they
get taxed on decades of gain that would
have completely disappeared if they had simply received
the house after you passed away.
You can turn a tax free inheritance into
a huge taxable event with one trip to
the courthouse. And on top of that, the
moment you put a child on the deed,
you give up control.
If that child gets divorced, the house can
be pulled into the divorce.
If that child is sued or owes money,
a creditor can come after the home you
still live in.
The instinct to be generous and proactive ends
up costing the very people you were trying
to protect. Number six is permission,
and I want you to really hear this
one. Do not let a tax you probably
do not owe keep you trapped in a
house that no longer serves you.
So many seniors stay in a home that
is too big and too dangerous and too
expensive purely out of fear of a bill
that the exclusion and the step up would
erase. If the house has become a burden,
run the real numbers with someone who knows
them, and you will very likely find that
selling and moving somewhere smaller, safer, and cheaper
to run costs you little or nothing in
tax and gives you back money and peace
every single month.
The home is supposed to serve your life.
Your life is not supposed to be held
hostage by the home.
Number seven is for the small number of
you whose gain is so large that it
does go beyond the exclusion,
and even here there is a way to
soften it. The tax on a home sale
profit above the exclusion is a long term
capital gains tax,
and that tax has a zero percent rate
in years when your other income is low.
So if you are in one of those
lower income years,
especially in the early part of retirement
before forced withdrawals begin,
timing your sale into that year can put
part of the taxable gain in the zero
percent bracket and shrink the bill even further.
The sale you cannot avoid being taxed on
can still be timed to be taxed as
gently as possible.
Let me bring it all together,
because the thread here is the same one
that runs through everything.
The home sale exclusion is enormous
and it is sitting right there waiting for
you. The tax is only on the gain,
not the price.
Widows get a two year window worth a
quarter of a million dollars. Inheriting at death
resets the gain to nothing.
Gifting during life throws that reset away and
hands your children the bill. And the fear
of a tax that, for most seniors, does
not exist, is quietly trapping people in homes
that are wearing them down.
Not one of these rules is hidden.
They are all right there in the law.
But nobody whose job touches your money has
a reason to sit you down and explain
them before you make an expensive mistake.
Nobody is going to call you and tell
you the exclusion exists, or that the widow's
window is closing,
or that putting your daughter on the deed
will cost her more than it saves.
The only person who can use these rules
in your favor is you, and the time
to learn them is before you sell or
sign anything, not after.
Find a fee only fiduciary adviser or a
tax professional who can look at your actual
numbers, and bring them every one of these
points. I will put the things to ask
about and the details in the description below.
So do one thing for me.
Send this to one person you care about
who owns their home and is either thinking
about selling, thinking about putting a child on
the deed, or staying stuck in a house
that is too much for them out of
fear of the tax.
A parent, a brother, a sister, a neighbor,
the widow down the street rattling around in
a house that is wearing her out.
The chances are very good that she is
afraid of a tax she does not even
owe, and one share from you could give
her back her freedom and save her family
a fortune. That is what we are here
for. I will see you in the next
one.

title: 7 Social Security Deductions Most Retirees Don't Know Are Shrinking Their Check

segments.text: Social Security is the one check that almost every American will lean on for the
rest of their life, and most people quietly accept whatever the government decides to send
them. They assume the amount is fixed, that it is simply calculated by a computer
somewhere and there is nothing to be done about it.
That is the most expensive assumption in retirement.
The truth is that the size of your check is the result of a series
of choices, and the wrong choices can cost you tens of thousands of dollars that
you earned and were owed, every year, for the rest of your life.
Almost nobody is shown how these choices work, because the Social Security Administration will pay
you exactly what you ask for, and not one dollar more, even when you are
leaving money on the table by accident.
I am going to walk you through seven things that decide how big your check
is, and how to make sure you are collecting every dollar you are entitled to.
Stay with me to the end, because the last one is a brand new change
in the law that is putting hundreds of dollars a month back into the pockets
of more than three million people, and many of them still have no idea it
happened. Number one is the single biggest lever you control, and it is the age
you start. You can claim as early as sixty two, but if you do, you
lock in a permanent cut of around thirty percent for the rest of your life.
Your full retirement age, the age where you get your complete benefit, is sixty seven
for everyone born in nineteen sixty or later.
And here is the part most people never use.
For every year you wait beyond your full retirement age, up until seventy, the government
adds about eight percent to your check, and that increase is permanent.
Waiting from sixty two to seventy can leave you with a monthly check that is
more than seventy percent larger for the rest of your life.
Now, claiming early is the right move for some people, especially if you are in
poor health or you truly need the income.
But it should be a decision you make on purpose with the real numbers in
front of you, not a default you fall into because you did not know waiting
was worth that much.
Number two is the rule that scares people into claiming at the wrong time, and
it is misunderstood almost universally.
It is called the earnings test.
If you claim Social Security before your full retirement age and you keep working, the
government withholds one dollar of benefits for every two dollars you earn above a yearly
limit, and in twenty twenty six that limit is twenty four thousand four hundred and
eighty dollars. People hear that and panic and think their benefits are being taken away
forever. They are not.
That money is not lost.
The day you reach full retirement age, the government recalculates your benefit and gives it
back to you in the form of a higher check going forward.
So the earnings test is not a penalty, it is a delay, and understanding that
one fact stops people from making a rushed, permanent decision based on a temporary withholding
they were always going to get back.
Number three costs people real money and it takes ten minutes to fix.
Your benefit is calculated from your own earnings history, the record of what you made
every year that you worked.
And that record contains mistakes more often than you would think.
An employer reports the wrong amount, a year of income goes missing, your name or
number gets entered wrong, and every one of those errors quietly lowers the check you
will collect for the rest of your life.
You can create a free account on the Social Security website and pull up your
entire earnings record and check it year by year against your own memory and your
old tax forms.
If you find a gap or a wrong number, you can have it corrected.
Nobody at the agency is going to catch these for you.
The record is yours to check, and the money lost to an uncorrected error is
yours to lose.
Number four is connected to that record, and it is the thirty five year rule.
Social Security calculates your benefit by taking your highest thirty five years of earnings and
averaging them together.
Here is the catch that hurts people.
If you worked fewer than thirty five years, the government does not just use the
years you have.
It fills in the missing years with zeros, and those zeros drag your average down
hard. So if you are close to retirement and you only have thirty two or
thirty three years of solid earnings, working even one or two more years, or replacing
an early low earning year with a higher one now, can raise your benefit for
life. A single zero replaced with a good year can be worth more than people
ever realize. Number five is the benefit that millions of people, especially women, never claim,
and it is the spousal benefit.
If you are married, you are entitled to a benefit based on your own work
record or up to half of your spouse's full benefit, whichever is higher.
So if you spent years out of the paid workforce raising a family, or you
simply earned less than your husband or wife over your career, your own check might
be small, but you may be entitled to as much as fifty percent of theirs
instead. A lot of lower earning spouses claim their own tiny benefit and never find
out they could have had a much larger one based on their partner's record.
It is not automatic.
You have to know to ask for it.
Number six is the money that grieving and divorced people leave behind without ever knowing
it was theirs.
If your spouse passes away, you are entitled to a survivor benefit that can be
as much as one hundred percent of what they were receiving, and for many widows
that is significantly more than their own check.
And here is what almost nobody knows.
If you were married for at least ten years and then divorced, you can claim
a benefit based on your former spouse's record, even if they have remarried, and claiming
it takes nothing away from them or their new family.
There are billions of dollars in survivor and divorced spouse benefits going unclaimed every year,
simply because people do not know these benefits exist or assume they would not qualify.
If you have lost a spouse, or you were married for a decade or more
and then divorced, it is worth one phone call to find out what you are
owed. Number seven is brand new, and if it applies to you, it could be
the most valuable thing in this entire video.
For decades, there were two rules that cut the Social Security benefits of people who
had earned a pension from a job that did not pay into Social Security.
This hit teachers, firefighters, police officers, and certain federal and government workers especially hard, slashing
their own benefits and in many cases wiping out their spousal and survivor benefits entirely.
At the very end of twenty twenty four, Congress passed the Social Security Fairness Act,
and in twenty twenty five those two rules were repealed.
More than three million people are now entitled to larger checks, and because the change
reaches back to January of twenty twenty four, many are owed a one time back
payment on top of the higher monthly amount going forward.
The increases are real, averaging a few hundred dollars a month for the workers themselves
and in some cases over a thousand dollars a month for affected spouses and survivors.
If you, or your late spouse, ever worked as a teacher or a firefighter or
a police officer or a government employee with a pension and you were told your
Social Security would be reduced, you need to make sure the Social Security Administration has
your current information so your corrected payment reaches you.
This is money that is now legally yours.
Before I tie this together, here are two quick safety nets most people never hear
about. If you claimed your benefit within the last twelve months and you now realize
you started too early, you can formally withdraw your application, pay back what you received,
and reset as if you never claimed, which lets you start over and claim a
larger amount later.
And separately, once you reach full retirement age, even if you are already collecting, you
can ask the government to suspend your benefit and let it grow by that eight
percent a year until seventy.
Two different doors, both of which let you undo an early decision, and almost nobody
knows either one exists.
Let me bring all seven together, because the thread is the same one that runs
through everything. The claiming age sets the size of your check for life.
The earnings test is a delay, not a loss.
Your earnings record may contain errors that are costing you right now.
Missing work years drag your benefit down with zeros.
A spousal benefit may be worth far more than your own.
Survivor and divorced spouse benefits are sitting unclaimed by the people who earned them.
And a brand new law is owed to millions who spent their lives serving their
communities. Not one of these is a loophole.
Every one of them is money you earned, sitting inside a system that pays you
what you ask for and stays silent about the rest.
Nobody from the government is going to call you and tell you that you claimed
too early, or that your record has a missing year, or that you qualify for
a benefit on a former spouse, or that the law just changed in your favor.
The Social Security Administration processes what you submit.
The rest is on you to know and to ask for.
So before you claim, and even if you have already claimed, sit down with your
earnings record and the real numbers, and if it is at all complicated, talk to
a fee only fiduciary adviser who can run your specific situation.
I will put the things to ask about and the details in the description below.
So do one thing for me.
Send this to one person you care about who is on Social Security or getting
close to it.
A parent, a sibling, a friend, the widow down the street, the recently divorced woman
at church, the retired teacher who was always told her benefit would be cut.
The chances are very good that at least one of these seven things applies to
them right now, and one share from you could put real money back where it
belongs, in their hands, for the rest of their life.
That is what we are here for.
I will see you in the next one.

title: The Widow's Penalty — 6 Tax Traps That Hit the Year After Your Spouse Dies (Most Don't Know)

segments.text: There is a moment that almost every married couple in this country will face, and
the tax code is waiting for it.
The day one spouse dies, the surviving one becomes poorer almost overnight, and then the
federal government does something that feels impossible to believe.
It raises their taxes.
Less income coming in, and a bigger share of it going out.
It has a name among the few advisers who are honest about it.
They call it the widow's penalty, and it quietly takes tens of thousands of dollars
from grieving spouses every single year, mostly women, because women tend to outlive their husbands.
Almost nobody is warned about it until the first tax return comes due and the
number on the page makes no sense.
I want to walk you through exactly how this trap works, because once you see
the machinery you can disarm it, but only while both spouses are still alive.
Everything I am about to show you has to be done before the funeral, not
after. After, the door is closed.
I am going to give you the seven moving parts of the widow's penalty and
then the moves that protect against each one.
Stay with me to the end, because the last move is the one that saves
the most money and the one the fewest people ever make.
Let me start with the engine that drives the whole thing, and it is something
most people have never thought about.
The I R S decides your filing status by where you stand on the thirty
first of December.
For the year your spouse actually passes away, you are still allowed to file married
filing jointly one final time.
But the very next year, you file as a single person.
There is one narrow exception called qualifying surviving spouse that lets you keep the married
rates for two more years, and it only applies if you have a dependent child
living in your home.
For the vast majority of seniors whose children are grown and gone, that exception does
not exist. So one year you are taxed as a couple, and the next year,
while you are still grieving, you are taxed as a single person on almost the
same income. That single switch is what sets off everything that follows.
Number one is the bracket collapse, and this is the heart of the trap.
The tax brackets for a married couple are exactly twice as wide as the brackets
for a single person.
In twenty twenty six, a married couple stays in the twelve percent bracket all the
way up to ninety six thousand nine hundred and fifty dollars of taxable income.
A single person crosses out of twelve percent and into twenty two percent at just
forty eight thousand four hundred and seventy five dollars, less than half as far.
So the moment a survivor files single, income that used to be taxed at twelve
percent gets taxed at twenty two percent, even though not a single thing about that
income has changed.
The brackets did not move.
The person simply lost the spouse who doubled the width of every one of them.
Number two is the standard deduction getting cut almost in half.
In twenty twenty six a married couple filing jointly gets a standard deduction of thirty
two thousand two hundred dollars.
A single person gets sixteen thousand one hundred dollars, exactly half.
There is still a small additional deduction for being sixty five or older, and there
is still the new senior bonus deduction of up to six thousand dollars that runs
through twenty twenty eight, and those help.
But the core deduction that shields your income from tax shrinks by half the year
the survivor files alone.
Less shield, narrower brackets, same income.
You can already see where this is going.
Number three is the one that feels the cruelest, because it is the income actually
going down. When one spouse dies, Social Security does not keep paying both checks.
The survivor keeps the larger of the two benefits and the smaller one stops completely.
So if one of you was collecting two thousand dollars a month and the other
was collecting fourteen hundred, the survivor does not get thirty four hundred anymore.
The survivor gets two thousand.
That fourteen hundred dollar check is simply gone, which can be fifteen or sixteen thousand
dollars a year vanishing from the household at the exact moment everything else is getting
more expensive to face alone.
Number four is that more of the Social Security that remains becomes taxable.
Whether your Social Security is taxed depends on something called provisional income, and here is
the quiet unfairness built into it.
For a married couple, the income thresholds where Social Security starts getting taxed are thirty
two thousand and forty four thousand dollars.
For a single person, those same thresholds drop to twenty five thousand and thirty four
thousand. They are lower for one person than they were for two.
So the survivor, living on less money, often finds that a larger percentage of her
Social Security is now exposed to tax than when there were two people and two
checks in the house.
Number five is the required minimum distribution crossfire, and this one catches people who think
they can simply spend less to stay safe.
Starting at age seventy three, the I R S forces you to pull a minimum
amount out of every traditional I R A and four oh one k you own,
whether you need the money or not.
That forced withdrawal counts as taxable income no matter what you do with it.
While both spouses were alive, that distribution was absorbed inside the wide married brackets.
After one spouse dies, the very same withdrawal, often on a very similar account balance,
gets pushed up into the narrower single brackets and taxed harder.
The survivor cannot turn it off.
The law requires the money to come out, and the law requires it to be
taxed at the single rate.
Number six is the Medicare surcharge, and most people do not even know it is
hiding here. It is called I R M A A, the income related monthly adjustment
amount, and it is an extra charge added to your Medicare premiums once your income
passes a certain line.
And just like everything else, the line for a single person is half of the
line for a couple.
In twenty twenty six the surcharge starts at around two hundred and eighteen thousand dollars
of income for a married couple, but only around one hundred and nine thousand for
a single person.
A survivor whose income looks modest as half of a couple can suddenly find herself
over the single line, paying hundreds or even thousands of dollars a year in higher
Medicare premiums. And because Medicare looks at your tax return from two years earlier, the
bill often arrives long after the loss, when she has no idea what triggered it.
So there it is.
The filing status flips to single.
The brackets collapse to half their width.
The standard deduction is cut in half.
One Social Security check disappears.
More of the remaining check gets taxed.
The forced retirement withdrawals get taxed harder.
And the Medicare surcharge waits at a line set half as high.
Six blades, and they all fall at once, on the person least equipped at that
moment to fight back.
That is the widow's penalty, and now you know why the tax bill makes no
sense to the person sitting at the kitchen table holding it.
Now let me give you the part nobody puts in the title, which is what
you actually do about it, because the tax code that built this trap also contains
every escape hatch.
The work has to happen while both spouses are alive and both are healthy enough
to sign documents and make changes.
Here is where the real money is saved.
The most powerful move is to slowly convert money out of your traditional I R
A and into a Roth I R A during the years you are still married
and still filing jointly.
This is move number seven, and it is the one most people never make.
While you are a couple, you can move money out of that traditional account and
fill up those wide twelve percent and twenty two percent married brackets at a known,
reasonable tax rate.
You pay the tax now, while the brackets are wide, and that money becomes a
Roth account that is never taxed again.
There are no forced withdrawals from a Roth, the growth is tax free, and when
one spouse passes, the survivor inherits an account she can draw from without it adding
a single dollar to her taxable income or pushing her toward that Medicare surcharge.
You are taking a lifetime of future taxes that would have landed on a grieving
single filer and paying a smaller, controlled amount now while there are still two of
you to share the wide brackets.
This takes several years to do well, which is exactly why you cannot wait.
The second protective move is about your regular brokerage account and how it is titled,
because of something called the step up in basis.
When a spouse dies, the investments the survivor inherits get their cost reset to whatever
they are worth on the day of death, and all the built up gain before
that simply disappears for tax purposes.
A stock or a fund that was bought decades ago for very little can be
inherited and sold the next day with little or no capital gains tax at all.
But this only works if the account is titled correctly for your state, and the
