Compounded at something close to the
market's usual long-run pace,
today turns into somewhere around
by the time you'd realistically be
shopping for its replacement anyway.
That's a rough estimate, and rough is
plenty.
You set the box back on the shelf and
walk out with nothing. No consolation
purchase, no smaller version to feel
good about instead.
That part is somehow harder than buying
something would have been.
By the following spring, you've
genuinely forgotten you ever wanted the
laptop at all,
and it isn't until Jake mentions his is
already showing its age that you
remember you were ever tempted, which
tells you more than the math did. Your
restaurant group offers you a regional
trainer position the year you turn 30.
$9,000 more a year, but 3 weeks of
travel a month and weekends twice a
quarter.
Your manager expects an answer on the
spot, the way people usually give one
for a $9,000 raise, and looks visibly
thrown when you ask for the weekend
instead.
You spend most of that weekend not
thinking about the money at all, but
about which specific Tuesdays you'd be
trading away for it. Jake's birthday
dinner, your mother's Sunday calls, the
ordinary unremarkable evenings that
don't sound like much until you picture
actually losing a dozen of them a year.
You turn it down Monday morning. The
$9,000 was real. It just turned out to
be smaller than 12 Tuesdays once you
actually weighed them against each
other.
Jake asks you for the first time, the
year you turn 31, to put money into
something of his directly. Not a stock
this time, a friend's food truck. $5,000
to be a founding investor, paid back
with interest within a year, he
promises, already half pitching before
you said anything.
You love him too much to make it a
lecture, so you just tell him you don't
have it liquid right now, which isn't
true, and he doesn't push.
The food truck lasts 8 months. You never
bring up the fact that you said no, and
he never asks why you were right, too.
The account crosses $140,000
the year you turn 32, and Jake, between
jobs again, this time because the
startup he finally joined as an early
employee ran out of runway, calls you,
not asking for anything, just talking,
the way people do when they're circling
something.
You ask if he's okay for rent. He says
he's fine, too quickly.
You transfer him $1,800
the next morning without telling him
beforehand first, an amount that would
have wiped out your entire savings at
22, and now doesn't even register as a
dip on the balance.
He pays you back in 11 months in three
installments, and you never bring it up
either time.
Something in how he talks to you shifts
a little after that anyway.
A half second of hesitation before
certain topics, like he's recalculating
something about who you are.
You understand for the first time that
being underestimated by your own family
wasn't just convenient. Some of it, it
turns out, is its own particular flavor
of isolation, one nobody thinks to
mention beforehand.
It occurs to you once, stopped at a red
light on the drive home from Jake's,
that the 22-year-old splitting a tip
envelope down to the exact dollar might
have actually known her own life better
than you do now. Back when nothing in it
was too big to notice.
You don't chase the thought any further
than that. The light turns green.
Your mother, that same winter, needs a
procedure her insurance mostly, but not
entirely, covers. $3,400
out of pocket.
3 years earlier, this would have meant a
family group chat, a spreadsheet, an
uncomfortable conversation about who
could contribute what, Jake offering an
amount he didn't quite have, and you
quietly covering the difference without
saying so.
Now, you just pay it quietly before
anyone finishes suggesting a payment
plan.
Your mother hugs you twice on your way
out, which is once more than usual. The
kind of gratitude that assumes you had
to sit down and think about whether you
could afford it. You didn't.
That specific gap between what she
pictures you deciding and what actually
happened, which is nothing, is the whole
distance you've traveled in 11 years,
condensed into a hallway hug.
She asks, almost as an afterthought,
whether you're sure you can spare it.
You tell her you're sure.
She doesn't ask again, but you notice
her looking at you a beat longer than
usual, like she's recalculating
something she thought she already knew
the shape of.
Around this time, you notice you've
quietly given up trying to correct
anyone about money at all. It isn't
really a decision, more a habit you fell
into, because there's no way to say the
real number out loud that doesn't come
out sounding like either false modesty
or a boast wearing modesty's clothes.
So, you just stop offering it up.
When Jake vents about a $400 truck
repair, some part of you still remembers
precisely what $400 used to cost a
paycheck.
These days, the number registers
distantly, like weather in a city you
used to live in. You can describe the
feeling accurately without actually
feeling it anymore. Frank stops coming
into the diner the spring you turn 33.
Not the diner you still work at by then.
You'd moved into managing it 2 years
earlier.
But you hear it from one of the old
regulars. A stroke. Recovering. Mostly
fine. Moved in with his daughter two
states over.
You never got the chance to tell him
what that offhand sentence at the
counter turned into, 11 years and one
habit later.
He probably wouldn't even remember
saying it if you had.
It cost him nothing to say, which might
be exactly why it cost you nothing to
hear it. No lecture attached, no
ceremony, just a fact stated flatly over
a coffee refill.
You send a card to his daughter's
address, care of the diner's old
regulars phone tree, and don't expect
anything back.
Three weeks later, a short note arrives
in handwriting you don't recognize. His
daughter's. Thanking you. Mentioning
that he still tips the home care aide
the same exact 20% to the penny, like
it's a formula rather than a feeling.
You keep the note in a kitchen drawer
you don't open often, mostly so you know
exactly where it is.
You think, more than once, about driving
the two states to see him, and don't.
Not because you don't want to, but
because you're not sure what you'd
actually say once you got there.
Some debts are easier to keep than to
settle.
That October, at a cousin's engagement
dinner, Jake, three drinks in, entirely
sincere, turns to the table and says,
"Honestly, out of the two of us, she's
the one who actually figured it out. I
just make more noise about it."
Everyone laughs, including you, and your
mother says something about how you've
always been the sensible one, which
isn't quite the same compliment, but
lands close enough.
Nobody at that table has the faintest
idea what the real figure actually is.
You let the moment pass without adding a
single correction to it.
What stays with you afterward isn't the
compliment itself.
It's that this is the first time in 11
years anyone in your family has landed,
even by accident, closer to the truth
than they realize.
You turn 33 the same month your account
crosses $500,000.
And the same month Jake, steadier now at
a job he stayed in for two full years,
pays you back a small loan early without
you asking and says, almost sheepishly,
that he's finally opened a retirement
account of his own.
Boring index funds like you'd probably
do.
You tell him that's exactly right and
don't say anything else about it.
You didn't lecture him into it. He just
watched you for over a decade be quietly
fine no matter what happened. And
eventually that did more arguing than
you ever could have.
Tuesday dinner at your mother's still
looks the same on the surface.
A different Tuesday now, years further
into the story.
Jake's phone is face down on the table
this time. The coin from years ago long
forgotten. One of a dozen things he
doesn't bring up anymore.
Your mother asks, out of nowhere,
whether you ever think about buying a
bigger place.
You tell her you're happy where you are,
which is true.
You could say, if she asked, that the
account passed $718,000
four days ago.
You haven't opened the app since and you
don't need to.
Nobody in this kitchen would guess it,
including some days, the version of you
standing here right now, who still
mostly just feels like the sister who
waitressed too many doubles and never
quite grew out of counting exactly
what's left until Thursday.
At some point, you simply lost count of
how wrong everyone's assumptions about
you actually were
because keeping score of it would have
cost you more of your own life than the
assumptions themselves were worth.
You were the boring one over and over
for 11 years.
And if there's a punchline in any of it,
it's that nobody ever had to find out
otherwise.
Not because you hid it,
because there was never a single
dramatic enough moment to reveal it in.
Just $25 pulled out before you could
miss it, week after week, for long
enough that the counting stopped being a
decision somewhere along the way and
turned into simple identity instead.
Not something you were doing anymore,
just who you were.
A man at a diner counter told you once
that nobody had to guess what he was
worth by looking at his car.
It took a folded-up food truck, a
startup that ran out of runway, and a
chart that climbed for exactly one
season before you understood he'd never
been talking about the car at all.
Jake still drives a truck.
A newer one now, paid off this time,
which he mentions more than once, like
the paying off is the part he's proudest
of.
You think that's probably true, and you
think it probably should be. None of
this needed an audience to work, and the
next one won't either.
But if you'd like to be around when it
posts, there's a quiet way to make sure
of that, and you already know what it
is.
If any part of this sounded like your
own life, say so in the comments. Not
for my sake, just so you've said it once
out loud to someone.
Either way, I'll be here.

title: POV: You Quietly Became the Old Money Friend Nobody Knew How

segments.text: It's 9:14 on a Saturday morning, and
you're standing at the counter of
Whitfield's, a consignment shop three
blocks from your apartment, holding a
wool coat you've owned for eight years
while the woman who runs the place sews
a button back on for free because she
likes you, and because, in her words, "A
coat this well-made doesn't get
replaced, it gets repaired."
Your phone buzzes on the counter, a
group chat. Bree, mid-thread, has just
sent a link to a bachelorette weekend
Airbnb. $2,140
for three nights, split six ways, plus
flights.
Someone else in the thread sends a
crying-laughing emoji about their half
of rent this month. You type back,
"Count me in." And put the phone face
down.
Mrs. Whitfield finishes the button,
bites the thread off with her teeth
instead of reaching for scissors, and
slides the coat back across the counter
like she's done it a hundred times,
because she has.
You are not worried about the $357
that's about to leave your account for a
trip you haven't packed for yet. You
know, roughly, without opening the app,
that your brokerage account crossed
two weeks ago. Nobody in that group chat
knows that.
Bree, who you've known since college,
who drives a leased Audi she updates
almost every two years, would probably
assume you're stretching to make the
trip work, the same way she is. You let
her assume that. You've been letting
people assume that for a long time now.
This isn't a story about being cheap, or
about coats, or about a consignment
shop. It's a story about what happens
when you stop needing the people around
you to know what you're actually worth,
and about how, somewhere in the middle
of not telling anyone, you turned into
the kind of person other people start
describing, without quite knowing why,
as old money.
Rewind 15 years. You're 23, eight months
out of college, working the front desk
at a dental office for $34,000 a year,
splitting a two-bedroom with a roommate
who's always exactly 4 days late on her
half of $1,150
rent.
Your checking account, most Fridays
before payday, sits around $180.
You've never had a savings account with
more than $400 in it in your entire
adult life, and you don't think about
that as a crisis. You think about it as
Tuesday.
The coat you're getting mended right
now, the one from the opening scene, you
bought it that year, too, second-hand
for $22 because the department store
version you'd actually wanted was $190
and you couldn't justify it.
You remember being a little embarrassed
carrying the consignment shop bag out
past the mall's other, shinier stores.
Nobody warns you that the thing you're
embarrassed about at 23 is the exact
thing that ends up mattering most 15
years later.
Your roommate that year worked retail,
too, at a different store, and the two
of you had a running, half-joking system
for splitting the exact cost of a
rotisserie chicken down to the cent
because it was cheaper per pound than
almost anything else in the store, and
neither of you wanted to say out loud
how much that math actually mattered.
You didn't feel poor, exactly. You felt
like everyone you knew was doing the
same quiet arithmetic in their own
kitchen, and nobody filmed any of it, so
it never occurred to you to think of it
as a story worth telling.
Mrs. Whitfield, the same woman sewing
your button back on right now, 15 years
younger then, already running the shop,
rang you up that day and said something
you didn't think about again for almost
2 years.
You'd apologized a little for buying
second-hand instead of new.
She looked at you like the apology was
the strange part.
"Quality doesn't care whether you're the
first person to own it," she said,
folding the coat into tissue paper.
Most people spend their whole lives
paying extra just to be first.
Then the next customer stepped up, and
that was it. No music swelled. You
didn't write it down. You just carried
the bag home.
Three weeks later, on a whim you
couldn't fully explain, you opened a
brokerage account at your kitchen table
around midnight. Laptop brightness
turned all the way down so the light
wouldn't show under your roommate's
door.
You funded it with $40. Money that had
been sitting in your checking account
earmarked, loosely, for a haircut you
kept postponing.
$40 into a total market index fund. That
was the whole event. Nothing about your
apartment changed. Nothing about your
roommate's late rent changed. But the
following payday, you did it again. $40.
It wasn't a plan yet. It was barely a
habit. It was just a number that left
before you could talk yourself out of
keeping it.
By that December, the account held $612.
You checked it more than you'd admit to
anyone. Not because it was growing fast,
it wasn't, but because it was the only
number in your entire financial life
that only ever moved in one direction.
Brie, that same year, leased her first
car, a Volkswagen, $289
a month. The week after her own first
real paycheck cleared.
She wasn't reckless. She's never been
reckless.
She worked hard for that job. And for
two years, that car made her genuinely
happy pulling into the office parking
lot.
You never once resent her for it. Not
then, and not later.
You're not performing that generosity
for anyone. It's just true.
You just quietly kept doing the
unremarkable thing every two weeks,
while she did a different unremarkable
thing every 2 weeks, and neither of you
discussed it because there was nothing
dramatic enough yet to discuss.
Two years pass the way most years do. No
single day that feels like a turning
point. You get a raise, $2,600
a year, and you do the boring thing. You
raise your contribution by exactly that
amount before it ever touches checking.
$40 becomes $95.
You never feel the difference because
you never let yourself see it.
At 26, the account crosses $14,600.
That same spring, a market correction
wipes 11% off it in about a month.
becomes roughly $13,000 before it
stabilizes.
You check it the way you'd check a wound
you'd been told to leave alone.
Once in the morning, once before bed,
telling yourself each time is the last.
It isn't the dollar figure that gets to
you. It's watching the number visibly
shrink in real time on a Tuesday
afternoon, like something alive losing
weight in front of you.
You don't sell anything. You don't have
a dramatic reason not to. You just don't
get around to it. And by the time you
think about it seriously, the account
has already climbed back past where it
started.
At 29, the number is $52,000.
And this is the year Bree gets engaged
and starts talking more than she used to
about how everyone in her life seems to
be doing better than her financially
without trying.
You never correct her.
There isn't a version of that
conversation that doesn't sound like
bragging or like lying. So, you just let
her keep thinking you're all more or
less in the same place.
You're not unkind about it. You just
don't say anything.
That same year, your ancient
refrigerator dies. Not slowly, just gone
one Tuesday morning. Milk already
turning by the time you notice.
A replacement, delivered same day, runs
Three years earlier, that number would
have meant a credit card and a payment
plan, and several bad weeks of avoiding
your own balance.
Now, you pay it outright and don't think
about it again until the delivery truck
shows up.
It's an inconvenience with a delivery
window, not an emergency.
At 31, you almost buy a watch. Not a
flashy one, which is exactly what makes
it dangerous.
An estate sale two towns over is selling
a woman's vintage gold watch. Thin band,
no logo anyone would recognize, for
And it's exactly the kind of quiet,
well-made thing Mrs. Whitfield would
approve of.
You stand in the estate sale's dining
room for 11 minutes with it in your hand
before you do the math on your phone in
the parking lot.
invested instead,
left untouched for 25 years, and allowed
to grow at something like the market's
long-term historical pace,
becomes something in the neighborhood of
Not guaranteed, not linear,
but the shape of it is enough.
You put the watch back in its box and
buy a $40 teapot instead, because you'd
actually use the teapot.
You think about the watch on and off for
almost a year.
You never regret not buying it, which
surprises you more than buying it would
have.
At 32, your company offers you a
promotion, office manager, $11,000 more
a year, but also weekend call coverage
and a 45-minute longer commute.
3 years earlier, you'd have taken it
without thinking twice.
You sit with the offer for 6 days, which
surprises your boss more than the answer
eventually does.
You turn it down.
$11,000 is real money and no part of you
pretends otherwise,
but your account, sitting at $180,000
that spring, is quietly generating
something close to $9,000 a year on its
own.
And somewhere along the way, weekends
stopped being negotiable in a way raises
never quite are.
Walking out of that meeting, you realize
you've started weighing job offers
against Saturdays instead of against
each other. And Saturdays keep winning.
Daniel, you've been together 3 years by
now, notices before you say much about
it.
He's known you long enough to remember
the version of you that flinched at a
$60 dinner.
One night, after you tell him you turned
down the promotion, he asks, half
joking, why you still drive the Corolla
when he knows, because you finally told
him the actual number, sitting on the
couch, almost apologetically, like you
were confessing something.
You tell him the car stopped being about
money a while ago. Somewhere in the last
several years, it turned into something
closer to a boundary,
proof that you get to decide what your
life looks like instead of the number in
your account or somebody else's opinion
of it deciding for you.
He doesn't fully get it that night. He
gets it 4 months later when his hours at
the shop get cut for a stretch. And for
the first time in his adult life, a bad
month doesn't become a crisis because
your accounts can absorb the gap without
either of you discussing it twice.
At 35, the account crosses $410,000.
And an old friend from your first
apartment, someone you haven't talked to
in 3 years, reaches out after a job loss
that isn't his fault.
You help quietly, a number that would
have felt impossible at 23, and now
barely moves the account.
Something in the friendship shifts
afterward anyway. He gets a little more
distant. You get more careful about what
you mention.
You start to realize letting people
misjudge what your worth isn't just an
advantage. Sometimes it's a small,
specific kind of lonely that nobody
warns you about.
Bree's wedding that October cost
Venue, dress, a videographer she found
through Instagram.
You help her steam her dress in the
hotel room the morning of, and you
notice, almost with surprise, that
you're not running any numbers at all.
Not the 20-year version, not any
version.
For the first time in over a decade, a
big number just gets to be someone
else's big number, uncomplicated by what
it could have become.
You zip the dress bag and tell her she
looks incredible, and you mean it
completely.
That winter at 36, Daniel's father needs
emergency dental surgery not covered by
insurance. $4,100
due before the procedure.
3 years earlier, that number would have
meant a credit card and a quiet, tense
conversation about how to split it.
Now it means a transfer from savings and
a phone call to confirm the appointment.
Daniel doesn't ask if you're sure.
He stopped needing to ask that question
the same way you stopped needing to
check your balance before saying yes to
anything under five figures.
You start noticing around this time that
you've mostly stopped bringing up money
at all. Not because you're hiding it
exactly, but because every version of
saying it out loud now lands wrong.
Too little sounds like a humble brag.
Too much sounds like a lecture nobody
asked for. So, you just stop reaching
for the topic.
When Bree complains about a $300 car
repair, you remember exactly what $300
used to feel like. You just can't access
the panic the same way anymore. And
pretending you can feels dishonest.
Mrs. Whitfield closes the shop the
spring you turn 37. Not because business
was bad, she tells you ringing up your
last purchase there, a plain gray
sweater, $14,
but because she's old enough now to just
enjoy the coats she already owns.
You ask her, half joking, whether she
ever regretted running a second-hand
shop instead of something flashier.
She laughs, actually laughs, and says
the thing that sends you back instantly
to that parking lot 15 years earlier.
I never once regretted being the person
nobody had to guess about. Guessing is
expensive. I just let people guess
wrong.
She hands you the bag.
You don't tell her what that sentence,
and the one from 15 years ago, actually
did to the rest of your life.
You're not sure she'd even remember
saying either of them.
That August at Bree's bachelorette
weekend, the one from the group chat,
Airbnb, you're sitting on the porch the
last night and one of the other women,
half drunk and entirely sincere, says
out of nowhere, "You're kind of the old
money friend of the group, you know
that? Like, you never buy anything new.
You never talk about money and somehow
you're always fine."
Everyone laughs. Bree laughs, too, and
says, "You've always been like that."
Nobody at that table knows the actual
number.
You laugh along with them and don't
correct it, the same way you never
correct anything.
You just quietly notice that it's the
first time anyone's put a name to what
you've apparently become and that the
name, as it turns out, is more accurate
than any of them realize.
At 39, your account crosses $850,000
the same month Daniel proposes on a
Tuesday in your kitchen with a ring that
costs less than Bree's did. On purpose,
both your choices together.
You say yes before he finishes the
sentence. Later that night, half
serious, he asks whether you're going to
tell people the actual number now that
you're engaged, now that there's a
shared future with paperwork attached to
it.
You tell him probably not.
Not because it's a secret, exactly, but
because you've never found a version of
saying it out loud that doesn't change
how people look at you afterward. And
you like, more than you expected to,
being looked at the same way you've
always been looked at. It's 9:14 on a
Saturday morning again, a different
Saturday, back at what used to be
Whitfield's, which is a small plant shop
now run by someone else entirely. You
still walk past it most weekends out of
habit. Your phone buzzes. Another group
chat, another trip, another split cost
you'll agree to before you've even
finished reading the thread. You know,
without opening the app, that the
account crossed $961,000
two weeks ago.
You're wearing the same coat, the one
Mrs. Whitfield mended for you more times
than either of you ever counted.
You catch your reflection for half a
second in the shop's old window as you
pass. Same coat, same unhurried walk,
nothing about the image asking to be
believed. Nobody passing you on the
sidewalk this morning has any idea, and
for the first time in 15 years, that's
not something that happened to you. It's
something you built, one unremarkable
Friday at a time, long after it stopped
feeling like a choice.
Somewhere in there, you stopped keeping
a running tally of what people assumed
about you, because there were too many
wrong assumptions to correct, and not
enough hours in a life to spend
correcting them.
You chose to be underestimated over and
over for 15 years.
And the strangest part is how invisible
that choice turned out to be.
No renovation, no reveal, no
announcement, just a $40 habit repeated
until the math changed, and then
repeated a while longer after that,
because by then it wasn't really a
decision anymore. It was just who you'd
become.
Somebody eventually put a name to it,
and the name was old money, and the
truth underneath the name was a lot less
romantic and a lot more repetitive than
anyone at that table imagined.
15 years of unremarkable Fridays, and
one woman at a consignment shop who told
you, twice, 15 years apart, that quality
doesn't care whether you're the first
person to own it.
If any of this hit a little close to
home, that's the whole point. Like this
one and subscribe, there's another
already in the works.
Here's what I actually want to know.
What's the boring, unremarkable thing
you're doing right now, quietly, that
your future self is going to be really
glad nobody talked you out of?
Drop it below. I read every one. Catch
you in the next one.

title: POV: You Quietly Became the Rich One and Nobody Noticed

segments.text: Your landlord raises the rent for the
fourth time in 2 years, and at the
mailbox, he tells you about it like
you're both in the same fight. You're
not. It's 6:14 a.m. and before you've
even made coffee, you do the thing you
do every payday. Four taps on your
banking app. Not checking a balance,
moving money before it has the chance to
turn into a coffee run.
By the time you're pouring your coffee,
that money is already somewhere you
don't casually touch.
He doesn't know your portfolio cleared
back in the spring on an ordinary
Tuesday.
Neither of you has ever said a real
number out loud.
This is the story of how four taps a
paycheck quietly built that number, and
it starts 9 years earlier with
considerably less than zero.
You're 24. Your checking account has
$340 in it on a good week, less on a bad
one, and this is a bad one.
You've just left a job that didn't work
out. Not fired, exactly. More like a
mutual understanding that arrived a few
months too late.
The apartment is $780 a month, which
felt reasonable until you actually live
there and discovered the radiator only
works if you hit it twice with your
palm, and the neighbor upstairs runs a
washing machine at 2:00 a.m. for reasons
nobody's ever explained.
You're doing the math on rent, and the
math isn't generous.
Your last paycheck, after everything
comes out, leaves you with about $210 to
make it to the next one.
You've gotten good at a specific kind of
arithmetic. How many days a jar of
peanut butter actually lasts, whether
the gas light is a real emergency or a
psychological one.
You remember your mother at a grocery
register once, years earlier, quietly
asking the cashier to remove an item
after the total came back higher than
she expected. The person behind her
sighed loud enough to be heard. Your
mother didn't react. She just paid and
left calm, like it happened every week,

the travel credit button." Use the same
word from number four, "refund." Here is
what to keep in your purse or your
wallet. Write these down. "I would like
wheelchair assistance to the gate and on
my connection. I am not flying. I would
like a pass to take my mother to her
gate." Look at the date on your license.
"I would like a refund to my card, not a
credit." Call TSA Cares 3 days before.
"Can I be screened sitting down? May I
board first? This is a medical device.
It does not count as a carry-on. Was
this delay caused by the airline? I
would like to speak to the complaints
resolution official." None of it is a
secret. None of it is a favor. It is
already there, waiting for the person
who says the words. What you just heard
is general information for education. It
is not legal advice. Airline policies
change, and some of these are the
airlines' own promises, not the law.
Check with your airline before you fly.
The people described here are made up to
show how the rules work. Safe travels,
and save me a window seat.

title: 2027 Social Security COLA Is 3.6% — Every Senior Must Do This Before January

segments.text: It is official. Next year, Social
Security, SSDI, and SSI go up 3.6%.
That is the number on every channel
today. But, it lands very differently
depending on which check you get. If you
are on both Social Security and SSI,
your Social Security raise does not add
a single dollar to what you have. If
your check is small, there is one rule
that stops Medicare from eating the
raise, and a lot of people are not
covered by it. And if you are a veteran
on disability, the percentage you heard
today is still waiting on a vote. Here
is what the 3.6% means for your own
check. One, what 3.6% looks like in
dollars. A percentage is hard to feel,
so turn it into money. On a check of
$1,000 a month, 3.6% is about $36 more.
On 1,500, about $54. On 2,000, about
$72. Social Security says the average
retired worker will get about $2,170
a month after the raise. Now, picture a
married couple, both retired. He gets
1,000 800 a month, she gets 1,200. Each
check gets its own 3.6%. His goes up
about $64.80.
Hers, about $43.20.
Together, about $108 a month more before
Medicare takes its part from each check.
To find yours, take the amount that
lands in your bank today, add back your
Medicare premium if it comes out of the
check, and multiply by 3.6%. That is
your raise before anything comes back
out of it. And something does come back
out of it. The first part of that is
Medicare. Two, Medicare and the rule
that protects small checks. The Part B
premium for next year has not been
announced yet. It comes separately from
Medicare, usually in the fall. Right
now, you pay $202.90 a month. Medicare's
own trustees expect about $209.50 next
year, $6.60 more. For most people, that
comes straight out of the raise. But,
there is a rule in the law for people
with small checks. It is called hold
harmless. If the Part B increase would
make your Social Security deposit
smaller than it was before the raise,
your premium increase is cut down, so
your deposit does not go down. Picture a
widow whose own Social Security is very
small, a few hundred dollars a month. On
a check that size, her raise is only a
few dollars. If Part B goes up by more
than her raise, her deposit would
shrink. Hold harmless stops that. Her
deposit does not go down. Now the part
most people never hear. Hold harmless
does not cover you if you are new to
Part B next year. If you pay the higher
premium because of your income, or if
your premium is paid by your state, and
it only works if your Part B premium
comes out of your Social Security check
in both December and January. If you pay
Medicare by a separate bill, it does not
protect you. So if your check is small,
the way you pay Medicare matters as much
as the raise. And there is one more
group the rule leaves out, and they
often do not see it coming. Medicare
looks at your income from 2 years back
to decide if you pay the higher premium.
This year, that line starts at $109,000
for one person, and $218,000 for a
couple. Picture a widow who sold her
late husband's rental property last
year. One year of high income from one
sale. Two years later, Medicare can
charge her the higher premium for it,
and hold harmless will not protect her
raise from it.
If you had a year like that, look
closely at your premium notice this
fall. And if you are on SSI as well as
Social Security, the raise works in a
way that catches almost everyone off
guard. Three. On Social Security and SSI
together. This is the part almost nobody
explains. SSI is worked out from your
other income. Social Security ignores
the first $20 of it and takes the rest
off your SSI. So when your Social
Security goes up, your SSI goes down by
the same amount. The new SSI amount for
next year is $1,029 a month for one
person, and $1,544
for a couple. That is $35 more for one
person than this year. Now picture a man
who gets $600 a month in Social Security
and SSI on top.
In January, his Social Security goes up
by about $21.60.
And in that same January, Social
Security counts that raise against his
SSI straight away. His SSI side shrinks
by exactly that amount. So, what does he
actually gain? Only the SSI raise. His
total goes from $1,014
to about $1,049.
That is $35 more, the same as a person
on SSI alone. The Social Security raise
he heard about on the news never adds to
what he has. He does not need to do
anything to get it, but he does need to
know it because if he plans January
around the bigger Social Security
number, he is planning with money he
will not have.
And that $20 Social Security ignores has
a story of its own. Four, two numbers
that have not moved in over 50 years.
The $20 of income SSI ignores goes back
to the start of the program in 1974.
So does the $65 of a paycheck that it
ignores. Social Security's own advisory
board wrote that these amounts have
never been increased. Every year, the
SSI amount goes up with prices. These
two do not. So every year, they protect
a little less. Here is what that means
if you work. Say you are on SSI. You
have no other income. And you earn $465
a month at a part-time job. Social
Security ignores the first $85, then
half of what is left. So $190 comes off
your SSI. $465 earned, $190 taken back.
That is still more money in your pocket
than not working. But know the sum
before you take extra hours and report
your pay every month. If you are on SSDI
instead of SSI, the line that matters is
a different one and it moved today.
Five, if you are on SSDI and you work,
today Social Security published next
year's work limits. The first is
substantial gainful activity. Next year,
it is $1,770
a month, or $2,950
if you are blind. Earn above it, and
Social Security can decide you are able
to work. The second is the trial work
amount. Next year, any month you earn
more than $1,270
counts as a trial work month. Those
months add up. You get nine of them
within any 5-year stretch, and they do
not have to be in a row. Once the nine
are used, Social Security starts looking
at whether your work is substantial, and
that is where the first number comes in.
So, every month just over the trial line
uses one up, even if it was only one
busy week. Write those two numbers down
today, and put them next to your work
schedule. A woman on SSDI who cleans
offices three nights a week plans her
hours around this year's limit. If she
does not know next year's, a busy
January can push her over a line she
never saw move. And there is a second
group whose paycheck line changed today.
Six, if you took Social Security early
and you still work. Claim before full
retirement age and keep a job, and your
paycheck has a ceiling. Go over it, and
part of your Social Security is held
back. Next year, that limit is $25,560
a year. Earn more than that, and Social
Security holds back $1 for every $2
over. In the year you reach full
retirement age, the limit is $67,920,
and it only counts what you earn before
the month you reach it. Over that, they
hold back $1 for every three. Picture a
63-year-old man who drives for a
delivery company. If he earns $4,000
over next year's limit, $2,000 of his
Social Security is held back. It is not
lost forever. Once he reaches full
retirement age, Social Security raises
his monthly check to give him credit for
the months it held back, but it is gone
from the year he was counting on it.
Once you reach full retirement age, the
limit is gone, and you can earn any
amount. And there is the tax line, and
that one has not moved at all. Seven,
the tax line that was never raised. Part
of your Social Security can be taxed if
your income is over line. Take half of
your Social Security for the year and
add your other income. If that comes to
more than $25,000 for one person, or
32,000 for a married couple, part of
your Social Security becomes taxable.
Above 34,000 or 44,000 for a couple,
more of it does. Those lines took effect
in 1984 and 1994, and they have never
been raised. Social Security's own
research says it plainly, because the
lines are not tied to prices or wages,
the share of people paying tax on their
benefits has risen over time.
In 1984, fewer than one in 10 paid it.
So, every raise pushes some people a
little closer to that line, or a little
further over it. Here's how close it can
be.
Picture a married couple with $36,000 a
year in Social Security between them and
15,000 from a small pension.
Half of their Social Security is 18,000.
Add the pension, and they are at 33,000,
just over the line for a couple. Now,
the raise adds about $1,300 a year to
their Social Security, and half of that,
about $650, goes straight into the sum.
Every year, a little more of their check
becomes taxable, while their grocery
bill eats the rest of the raise. There
is a newer rule on your side, though,
and a lot of people have not used it.
For the tax years 2025 through 2028,
anyone 65 or older can take an extra
deduction of $6,000,
12,000 for a married couple who both
qualify. You do not have to itemize to
get it, and a married couple has to file
jointly. It shrinks once income is above
75,000 for one person or 150,000 for a
couple. If you file a return, make sure
it is on there. Veterans have their own
numbers, and they do not all move the
same way. Eight, if you are a veteran.
The VA pension rises automatically by
the same 3.6%
on the 1st of December. For a veteran
alone with no extra help for being
housebound or needing aid and
attendance, this year's top pension is
a year. At 3.6%, that is about $18,069
next year. The pension net worth limit
rises by the same percentage. It should
be about $169,592
from the 1st of December. Disability
compensation works another way. Every
year, its raise needs its own bill from
Congress. Last year's was signed on the
25th of November, less than a week
before the new rate was due to start. If
this year's passes the same way, a
veteran rated 100% with no dependents
would go from $3,938
a month to about $4,080.
So, if you are on disability
compensation, today gave you the
percentage. Congress still has to give
you the raise. Watch for that bill in
November. The same goes for a surviving
spouse on the VA's survivor payment
called DIC. This year, the basic amount
a month. If the bill passes, it would be
about $1,760.
Picture a widow whose husband served 30
years. She hears 3.6% on the news this
morning and assumes it is settled. For
her, it is not settled until Congress
votes. And whichever one you get,
December's VA deposit is still
November's money at the old rate. The
higher amount shows up in the deposit on
New Year's Eve. Nine, when each raise
actually lands. For SSI, the raise rides
in on the deposit of the 31st of
December. That deposit is January's,
paid a day early for the holiday. Treat
it as January. For Social Security and
SSDI, the raise starts with the January
payment. If your birthday is between the
1st and the 10th, that is the 13th of
January. Between the 11th and the 20th,
the 20th. After that, the 27th. And if
your Social Security normally comes on
the 3rd, January's arrives on the 31st
of December. So, a woman who heard 3.6%
this morning will not see a penny of it
for about 3 months. Plan November and
December on this year's check. 10, how
to check that you got the right amount.
Social Security will send you a notice
with your exact new amount. Last year,
people with a My Social Security account
could read theirs in the message center
from late November, and paper copies
were mailed through December. For anyone
on Medicare, the amount on that notice
already had the new premium taken out.
When it comes, put it next to your
January deposit. They should match. If
they do not, call Social Security at
and have the notice in your hand.
Picture a man whose January deposit
comes in lower than the notice he was
sent. The first thing to look at is what
else comes out of that check. A drug
plan premium or a Medicare Advantage
premium can be taken out of Social
Security, too. And next year's price
comes out of the same raise. If that is
not it, then it is a question for Social
Security, and the notice is your proof
of what they told you. And remember who
will not be calling you. Social Security
does not offer to increase your benefits
in exchange for money. And you never pay
a fee to get the raise. The raise is
automatic. If someone calls about it
today, hang up. 11. Your own number
worked out. Take a sheet of paper. Write
your check before Medicare comes out.
Multiply by 3.6%.
That is your raise. Take off about 660
for Part B, unless your state pays your
premium or hold harmless covers you. If
you get food stamps, take off about 30
cents of every new dollar. If you get
SSI as well as Social Security, cross
out the Social Security raise and count
only the SSI raise of $35. What is left
is what January really looks like.
Picture the widow on 1,500 a month. Her
raise is about $54. If Part B goes up as
projected, she keeps about $47.40
of it. Now she knows in October what
most people will only find out when the
January deposit lands. 3.6% is the
number on the news. Your number is the
one on that sheet of paper. Everything
here is educational content and general
information only. It is not legal, tax,
or benefits advice. Some of these
figures are projections. Some depend on
Congress, and the examples are
simplified. Confirm your own amounts
with Social Security, the VA, Medicare,
or a tax professional. Take care of
yourself. Thanks for watching. See you
next time.

title: These Senior Benefits Start at Age 60 (Not 65) — Many Seniors Never Claim Them

segments.text: Do not wait for 65. A lot of the help
you are owed starts at 60 and nobody
calls to tell you. A widow who thinks
social security makes her wait until 65
can go 5 years without a check she could
have had at 60. In Illinois and Iowa,
heating help opened on October 1st for
people 60 and older. Everyone else has
to wait until November. In Iowa, it is
first come, first served. And at 60, a
lawyer paid for under a federal law can
take your case about your benefits or
your home and the law says the state
cannot charge you a cent for it. Here
are 15 benefits that start at 60 or even
sooner. Most people find out about them
at 65 or never. And the last one does
not save you money. It pays you by the
hour. One, the widow's check at 60. If
your husband or wife has died, social
security survivor benefits can start at
60, not 62, not 65, 60. If you have a
disability, they can start as early as
50. You had to be married at least 9
months. At 60, the check is 71 and a
half percent of your late spouse's
benefit. Every month you wait, it goes
up until it reaches the full amount at
what social security calls your full
retirement age for survivor benefits.
That is 66 or 67 and it is not always
the same age as the one on your own
record. One thing to know, if your
spouse started their own check early,
your survivor check is based on that
smaller amount. Picture a woman of 61
whose husband was getting $2,000 a month
when he died. Her sister told her,
"Widows wait until 65." At 60, 71 and a
half percent would have been about
a month. Taking it early or waiting for
more is her choice to make. But she
cannot make a choice she was never told
about. If your spouse worked for the
railroad, the Railroad Retirement Board
has its own version. A A or widower
annuity there is also payable at 60. The
board says the average one awarded in
the 2024 fiscal year was $2,848
a month. And if you remarry after 60,
you can still get part of it. And if you
were thinking about marrying again, the
next one decides whether that check
stays. Two, marry again after 60 and
keep it. If a widow or widower remarries
before 60, the survivor benefit from the
first spouse is usually off the table.
But Social Security says a remarriage at
60 or later does not stop it. 50 or
later if you have a disability. And at
62 or older, if your new spouse's record
would pay you more, you can take that
one instead. There is also a second
chance most people never hear about. If
you remarried before 60 and that
marriage has ended, you may be able to
get the survivor benefit from your first
spouse back. Picture a widower of 63 who
has been seeing a woman from church for
2 years. They have not married because
he is sure the wedding would cost him
his late wife's benefit. At 63, it does
not. And this next one is for people who
think a divorce cut them out for good.
Three, a survivor check for an ex. If
you were married 10 years or more and
your former spouse has died, you may get
survivor benefits on their record
starting at 60, 50 if you have a
disability. It does not matter that they
married someone else. And what you get
does not take a cent from their widow or
their children. Social Security says a
surviving divorced spouse does not
affect the other survivor's amounts.
Picture a woman of 62 who was married
for 22 years before the divorce. Her
ex-husband died last spring and his
second wife now gets a widow's check.
She assumed there was nothing for her.
She may be entitled to her own check on
his record and the second wife loses
nothing. Now, if you qualify for a
survivor check and a check of your own,
the order you take them in matters.
Four, take one check now and switch
later. You do not get two checks added
together. Social Security pays you the
higher one, but you can choose the
order. Social Security gives this
example on its own website. Start with
the survivor benefit, then change to
your own retirement benefit at 70, when
it is at its highest. And under Social
Security's own rules, taking the
survivor check does not count as filing
for your own. Your own keeps growing
while you collect the other. If you
already get your own retirement check,
call Social Security and ask whether you
would get more as a survivor. If you
would, they pay you a combination that
equals the higher amount, but you have
to fill out the application. Nobody
switches it for you. There is also a
one-time payment of $255
that can go to a surviving spouse. You
have to apply within 2 years of the
death. And if you were a teacher, a
police officer, or anyone with a
government pension, the next one may
have changed your answer. Five, the
pension rule that is gone. For years, a
widow with her own government pension,
like a retired school teacher, could
have her Social Security survivor
benefit cut because of that pension. The
rule had a name, the government pension
offset. The Social Security Fairness Act
ended it. It was signed on January 5th,
2025. And Social Security says the
change applies to survivor benefits,
too. So, if you were told years ago that
your pension wiped out what you could
get on your late husband's record, that
answer may no longer be true. Ask again,
and ask in writing. Now, the money that
matters this month. Heat. Six, heating
help that opens early at 60. The heating
help program is federal money that each
state hands out. In the government's own
reports, any home where a person is 60
or older counts as an older household,
and the law tells states to make sure
those households know the help is there.
In Illinois, applications opened October
1st for people 60 and older. All other
households can start on November 1st. It
runs until August, or until the money
runs out. In Iowa, it also opened
October 1st for households with someone
60 or older or disabled. It is first
come, first served, and household income
can be up to 200% of the poverty line.
Take a widow of 74 in Peoria who keeps
the thermostat at 62 all winter because
the gas bill scares her. She does not
have to wait for November with everyone
else. She could have applied 2 weeks
ago. Other states set their own dates
and limits, so call. There is a national
line that tells you where to apply in
And keep this in mind when you apply.
The government says the program does not
charge a fee. If anyone asks you for
money to get heating help, that is not
the program. And the same age puts you
near the front of a second line for the
house itself. Seven, fixing the drafts.
With you at the front of the line, the
weatherization assistance program does
work on homes with lower incomes so they
cost less to heat and cool. Under the
federal rule, a person 60 or older
counts as elderly. And elderly people
are the first group named on the
priority list. By the energy
department's count, a home that gets
this work saves an average of at least
a year on energy. Picture a couple of 68
in an old house where the wind comes in
around every window. Their heating bill
is the biggest check they write each
winter. Being 60 and over puts them at
the front of that list, not the back.
When you call about heating help, ask
where to apply for weatherization, too.
Next is help inside the house, and the
question they are not allowed to ask
you. Eight, help at home and no one
checks your bank account. Under the
Older Americans Act, 60 is the line. The
law defines an older person as anyone 60
or older. At 60, the Agency on Aging
where you live can send a homemaker or
an aide. Someone who calls or stops by
to check on you, help with chores, adult
daycare so a family member gets a break
and small changes to your home that help
you keep living in it. Here is the part
most people get wrong. The federal rule
says means testing is prohibited. They
are not supposed to use your income or
your savings to turn you down. They may
ask for a donation and some services can
have a sliding fee, but the rule is
plain. A service cannot be denied to you
because you will not pay or because you
cannot. What is offered depends on where
you live. Picture a retired nurse of 68
with some savings and a bad hip. She
never asked for help because she thought
it was only for people with nothing. The
agency does not ask what is in her
account. It asks what she needs. And one
of the services under that same law is a
lawyer. Nine, a free lawyer at 60. Legal
help under the Older Americans Act is
for people 60 and older and it is in
every state. And for legal help, the law
does not allow the state to charge you
anything. No sliding fee, nothing. These
lawyers are told to put certain cases
first, income and benefit,
health care and long-term care, housing
and utilities, abuse and neglect, age
discrimination and defending you if
someone tries to put you under a
guardianship. Picture a man of 70 who
opens a letter saying Social Security
overpaid him $2,000 and that they will
take it out of his check. He cannot
afford a lawyer, so he was going to let
it go. That letter is exactly the kind
of case these lawyers handle. To reach
one, ask your local agency on aging for
its legal help program. And there is one
more free professional at 60 and this
one comes from the IRS. 10, free tax
help at 60. The IRS runs a program
called Tax Counseling for the Elderly.
In the agency's own words, it offers
free tax help to individuals who are age
60 or older. It runs during tax season
from January 1st to April 15th. Picture
a couple in their late 60s with two
Social Security checks, a small pension
and a little interest from the bank.
Every year they pay a storefront tax
office to file a return that takes an
hour. That is the kind of return these
volunteers do every day. So, if you paid
someone to do a simple return last
spring, put this on next year's calendar
now. That fee may be money you never
have to spend again. Now, the states. In
some of them, 60 means you can go back
to college without paying tuition. 11.
College classes without the tuition. In
Virginia, residents 60 and older who
have lived there a year can audit up to
three courses a term without tuition. If
your taxable income is $23,850
or less, you can take them for credit,
too. South Carolina lets residents 60
and older attend for credit or not
without tuition. Arkansas's flagship
university offers free tuition for
credit at 60. Rhode Island does, too, if
household income is under three times
the poverty line. Delaware lets
residents 60 and older who are admitted
to a degree program take classes without
the usual fees. Maryland community
colleges waive tuition at 60. And in
Ohio and Wisconsin, you can sit in on
classes without credit, free of tuition.
Florida state schools are allowed to
waive the fees for that, too. Books and
lab fees usually still cost money. And
it is always when there is space in the
class. Picture a retired mechanic of 64
who always wanted to learn Spanish to
talk with his grandkids. Sitting in on a
class at the college 10 minutes from his
house would cost him nothing but the
book. And a few states cut your taxes or
your fees at 60. 12. Tax breaks at 60
and a free license for life. In
Washington state, homeowners can get a
senior property tax exemption starting
at 61 if income is under the county's
limit. Starting with 2027 taxes, that
limit goes up to $101,000 a year in King
County and 85,000 in Pierce and Clark
counties. And at 60, Washington lets you
defer your property taxes, which means
put them off if you qualify. In
Delaware, at 60, up to $12,500
of pension and retirement income is not
taxed by the state if you have lived
there at least 3 years. Under 60, the
pension amount is 2,000. And in Alaska,
residents 60 and older can get a
permanent hunting, sport fishing, and
trapping card free of charge. One card
good for life. If you live somewhere
else, call your county assessor and your
state tax office and ask one question.
At what age does a senior break start
here? Do not assume it is 65. And if you
ride the bus, ask that same question
about the fare. 13. The bus at 60. Under
federal rules, bus systems that get
federal money have to give a reduced
fare to riders 65 and older, but some
start younger. In Orange County,
California, the senior bus fare starts
at 60. 75 cents a ride, and with their
Wave card, a whole month of riding is
capped at $22.25.
In Las Vegas, the Regional Transit
Commission gives a reduced fare to
riders 60 and older with a reduced fare
photo ID. So, call your transit agency
and ask what age their senior fare
starts. It is a 2-minute call that can
cut the cost of every ride. And the
stores start even earlier than that. 14.
Store discounts that start at 55. These
start at 55, so at 60, you already
qualify. At Walgreens, on the first
Tuesday of every month, My Walgreens
members 55 and older get 20% off
eligible regular price items in the
store. Prescriptions do not count, and
the membership is free. Walgreens says
the day can move when there is a
holiday, so check before you go. At
Michael's, it is 10% off your whole
purchase, sale items included, every
day, once you register through their
rewards account. And at Ross, shoppers
55 and older get 10% off on Tuesdays.
Not one of these is printed on the price
tag. You have to ask or sign up. And the
last one does not save you money. It
pays you. 15. Paid by the hour to help.
AmeriCorps Seniors runs two programs,
Foster Grandparents and Senior
Companions. Foster Grandparents work
with children. Senior companions help
other older people stay in their own
homes. Once you are 55, if your income
is up to 200% of the poverty line, you
can serve from 5 hours a week up to
about 40. The stipend is $4 an hour and
some local programs can add to it. And
here is why it matters. The federal rule
says that stipend is free of tax. It
also says it cannot lower or end what
you get from any government program.
Picture a widow of 66 who reads with
second graders three mornings a week.
She gets out of the house. The children
get a grandmother who listens and she
has a little extra each month that does
not count against her. Write these down
before you forget them. If your spouse
has died, call social security and ask
about survivor benefits at 60 and about
the order you take your checks in. If
you are divorced after 10 years or more,
ask about your ex's record. If you have
a government pension, ask again. Call
about heating help now and ask about
weatherization on the same call. Call
your area agency on aging at home and
for a lawyer. Ask your state and county
what age their tax breaks start. Ask the
bus company the same. And at the store,
ask. Nobody hands you these at 60. You
have to ask for them. What you just
heard is general information for
education. None of it is legal, tax, or
benefits advice. Ages, income lines, and
dates can change and every state does it
a little differently. The people
described here are made up to show how
the rules work. Confirm your own
situation with social security, your
state, or your area agency on aging.
Take good care of yourself. Thanks for
watching.

title: Never Keep More Than This in Cash at Home After 65 — 14 Numbers (Most Don't Know)

segments.text: After 65, do not keep your savings in
cash at home. Keep a small amount for an
emergency and nothing more. If your
house burns down tonight, a standard
insurance policy pays $200 for the cash
inside. Not $2,000, $200 for all of it.
If you get SSI and you have more than
$2,000 on the first of the month,
counting the bills in your drawer,
Social Security can take that whole
month's check back. And if a man on the
phone tells you to gather your cash so
his courier can keep it safe, the money
is gone the second you open the door.
Keeping cash at home is legal, but these
14 numbers decide how much of it is
safe. Get one wrong and you lose a
check, a benefit, or everything in the
box. And the last one is a date at the
end of this month. One, the courier who
comes to the door. The FBI's newest
report on internet and phone crime says
people 60 and older filed more than
201,000 complaints last year and
reported about 7.7 billion in losses.
The average loss was about $38,500.
One version is built for people who keep
cash. The voice on the line claims to be
your bank, a federal agency, even the
police. Something is wrong with your
accounts. The answer, he says, is to
pull out cash, add what is already in
the house, and hand it to someone he is
sending over. Picture a retired teacher
of 71 who gets a call on a Tuesday
morning. The voice says her bank card
was used in another state and that her
cash at home is safer with the bank's
own security team. By lunch, a man in a
clean shirt is at her door with an
envelope. Everything she kept in the
cookie tin goes into it. When a scammer
tries to move money out of a bank, a
teller can ask questions and a fraud
team can stop it. Cash in a box has no
fraud department. Once it leaves your
hand, it is gone. In the words of the
Federal Trade Commission, "No one from
the government will ever tell you to
move your money or give cash to anyone."
So, if a phone call ends with someone
coming to your door for money, put the
phone down. If this has already happened
in your family, the Justice Department
runs a free line for it. 833728311.
Weekdays 10:00 in the morning to 6:00 at
night Eastern time. And if you get SSI,
the next number matters even if no
stranger ever calls. Two, $2,000 counted
on the first of the month. If you get
supplemental security income, the most
you can own in countable resources is
$2,000 for one person or 3,000 for a
married couple. Social Security's own
manual says that limit has not changed
since January of 1989. Cash is part of
that. A bank balance and the bills in a
cookie tin are added together. Here's
the part that trips people up. Social
Security counts what you own at the
first moment of each month. If the total
is above the limit at that moment, you
are not eligible for SSI for that month.
And money paid for a month you are not
eligible can be asked back. That is
called an overpayment. Picture a man of
73 on SSI who sells his old truck for
$900 and keeps the money in a coat
pocket in the closet. With what is in
his checking account, on the first of
the next month, he is at $2,400.
He did nothing wrong by selling it. But
on that morning, he is $400 over. So on
the last day of each month, add up the
bills at home and what the bank
statement says. Put that one number on
the calendar. And if you are getting
close, there are things you are allowed
to spend it on that do not count at all.
Three, what SSI does not count. The
house you live in is left out. So is one
car. So are the things inside the house,
like the furniture and the dishes. And
here is one most people never hear
about. You can set aside up to $1,500
for your own burial. And that money does
not count against you. A burial plot, a
casket, or a headstone you already own
does not count no matter what it cost.
If you have life insurance, that is not
counted. That 1,500 can be smaller. So
ask Social Security how it works for
you. You can also spend the extra on
things you need at a fair price. a new
mattress, a repair to the house, a pair
of glasses. But do not hand the extra to
your children to get under the limit.
Social Security says giving money away
for less than it is worth can cost you
up to 36 months of SSI. So if you are
close to the limit, call Social Security
or a legal aid office near you before
the first of the month, not after. Now,
even if you never get SSI, there is a
number in your insurance policy that
decides what happens if the house burns.
Four, $200. Many home policies are built
on the same standard form. Buried in it
is a list called special limits. It caps
what the company pays for a few kinds of
things, however much of them you had. On
that standard form, the limit for money,
banknotes, and coins is $200 for all of
it together, wherever it is in the
house. Picture a couple of 80 who keep
$8,000 under the floor of the hall
closet. A pipe bursts while they are
away for the weekend, and the closet
sits in water for 2 days. The insurance
pays to dry the house and fix the floor.
For the $8,000, the line on the claim
says 200. Your own policy may be
different, so check it. Call your agent
and ask one question. What is the
special limit for money on my policy?
And what would it cost to raise it? Some
insurers let you raise it with an
add-on. One thing can still be saved.
Burned or wet bills that are not
completely gone can be sent to the
Treasury's Bureau of Engraving and
Printing, which checks them at no
charge. When clearly more than half of a
note is left, they pay you its value.
Leave the bills as they are, stuck
together if they are stuck, and pack
them carefully. Expect to wait 6 months
or more, sometimes up to three years.
And if you get food stamps, there is a
number that went up on October 1st. Five
Food stamps have a limit on what a
household can own, too. And cash at home
counts toward it. On October 1st, the
government raised that limit. For a
household with someone 60 or older or
someone disabled, it is now $4,750.
It was $4,500. For other households, it
is 3,000. But here is what most people
do not know. Most states use a rule that
drops the federal asset test for most
households. A few of those states still
set a limit of their own. Texas,
Indiana, and Idaho, for example, use
$5,000. So, call your state food stamp
office and ask two questions. Does my
state count what I have saved? And if it
does, what is the limit? If it does not
count savings at all, the cash in this
number does not affect your food stamps.
And if Medicare is taking a bite out of
your check every month, the next limit
is much higher than most people think.
The Medicare savings programs can pay
your part B premium and for some people
more of your Medicare costs. That
premium is $22.90
a month this year. to get help. Medicare
says what you own can be up to $9,950
for one person or $14,910
for a couple. And Social Security says
some states have no limit at all. Cash
at home counts toward it, but that is a
lot more room than most people think
they have. Picture a widowerower of 71
who never applied because he has $6,000
put away and assume that was too much.
He was under the limit the whole time.
And there is a second program with an
even higher number for your medicines.
Extra help lowers what you pay for
prescriptions under Medicare. For this
year, Medicare says the resource limit
for one person or $36,100
for a married couple. Cash counts toward
that, too. If you are under it, ask. You
apply through social security, and you
can do it by phone. But one program
counts your cash much more strictly, and
it is the one families panic about.
Eight, 60 months. When a nursing home
stay uses up the savings, Medicaid is
usually what pays next. To qualify,
there is an asset limit set state by
state. In many states, it is about
$2,000 for one person. The cash at home
is part of it. And on the application,
Medicaid checks the last 60 months, five
full years, for gifts. Money handed away
in that window can mean a waiting period
before Medicaid pays a scent. Picture a
man of 82 who the year before he goes
into care gives each of his three
grandchildren $5,000 in cash at
Christmas. It was a kind thing to do. To
Medicaid, it is $15,000 given away
inside the 5 years. So, if a nursing
home is a real possibility, leave the
cash where it is and see an elder law
attorney before anything changes hands.
There are legal ways to plan. Guessing
is not one of them. Now, here is a
number for people who do not get any of
these programs. Nine zero. If you get
Social Security retirement or disability
and not SSI, your check does not depend
on what you have saved. Social Security
says the interest from your savings does
not lower your retirement benefit. And
its disability guide says other
resources do not affect your payment.
So, if you have been keeping cash at
home because you were afraid the bank
balance would cut your social security,
that fear is costing you. Your check is
not watching your savings. But there are
people who are watching your cash at
home and you know them. 10 40%. In 2024,
the Treasury's Financial Crimes
Enforcement Network published a study of
a full year of bank reports about money
taken from older people. When the person
who took it was someone the senior knew,
adult children were behind nearly 40% of
those cases. After them came caregivers,
and the Treasury says this kind of theft
is likely under reportported. Money
taken out of an account leaves a paper
trail. Bills taken out of a tin leave
nothing but a smaller pile. So keep a
sheet of paper with the cash. Each time
money goes in or out, write the date and
the new total and tell as few people as
possible where it is. And when you
decide to move that cash into the bank,
there is a right way and a wrong way.
11. $10,000. Bring more than $10,000 in
cash to the bank on the same day and the
bank sends the treasury a short report.
That is normal. It happens all day,
every day for ordinary people. You show
your ID. The form is the bank's job. The
trouble starts when people try to dodge
that report. Splitting the money into
smaller deposits to keep each one under
the line is called structuring. Under
federal law, that is its own crime, even
when the money is completely honest. The
penalty can be up to 5 years in prison.
Picture a widow of 76 who finds $18,000
her late husband kept in the garage. A
neighbor tells her the bank reports
anything over 10,000, so she should
bring it in a little at a time. That
advice is the one thing that could turn
honest money into a problem. So take it
in on one day in one trip and let the
form be filed. Jot down how you came to
have the cash and keep that page with
your papers. And once it is in the bank,
here is the number that protects it. 12.
At a bank with FDIC insurance, your
deposits are covered up to $250,000 per
person per bank for each kind of account
ownership. The FDIC says no depositor
has lost a penny of insured money since
it was founded in 1933. Federally
insured credit unions have the same
protection up to the same amount. But
there is one place at the bank that is
not covered. The FDIC says the contents
of a safe deposit box are not insured.
If the box is robbed or flooded, the
FDIC says do not expect the bank to pay
you back. And it says the bank may limit
what you keep in the box and that can
include cash. So cash goes in an insured
account, not in the box. The box is for
papers. But even money that nobody
touches has one enemy left. 13. 3,850.
Say you put $5,000 in a tin in January
of 2020. Count it today and it is still
5,000. But using the Labor Department's
consumer price index, it now buys what
about $3,850
bought back then. Prices have gone up
almost 30% since that January and 3.4%
in the last year alone. More than $1,100
of buying power gone with the lid still
on. So split the cash in two piles. What
you would truly need for a storm or an
outage stays. The rest is losing value
every month that sits there. Which
brings us to the date at the end of this
month. 14 October 31st. Series 1 savings
bonds from the Treasury pay 4.26% right
now. Bonds bought by October 31st get
that rate for their first 6 months. On
November 1st, the Treasury sets a new
rate. It could be higher or it could be
lower. You buy them at
treasurydirect.gov.
You can buy up to $10,000 a year per
person. You cannot cash them in for the
first 12 months. And if you cash them
before 5 years, you give up the last 3
months of interest. So, this is not for
your emergency money. It is for cash
that has been sitting in a box for years
doing nothing. So, here is your list for
the kitchen table. Keep a small amount
of cash at home in small bills for a
storm or a power outage. Ready.gov, the
government's emergency site, says the
same thing. If you get SSI, keep
everything that counts under $2,000 on
the first of every month. If you get
food stamps, ask if your state counts
savings and what its limit is. If
Medicare costs are eating your check,
you can have up to 9,950
and still get help. Call your insurance
agent and ask for your special limit for
money. Never hand cash to a courier.
Never split deposits. Never put cash in
a safe deposit box. And for the rest,
use an insured account or look at the
bonds before October 31st. None of these
numbers will be mailed to you. You have
to ask. This is educational content and
general information only. It is not
legal, tax, or financial advice. Limits
and rules change and can vary by state
and by policy. The people in the
examples are illustrations. Check with
Social Security, your state office, your
insurance agent, or Treasury Direct
before you act. Take care of yourself.

title: If You're Over 60, Amazon Will Give You These 14 Things (If You Ask)

segments.text: If you get SSI, SSDI, Medicaid, or food
stamps, Amazon has a version of Prime
that costs less than half the regular
monthly price. Same shipping, same
movies, same everything. Most people who
qualify are still paying full price
because nobody at Amazon will ever bring
it up. That is only the first one. There
is a card in a lot of seniors wallets
that Amazon will take for groceries and
cold medicine. There is a $5 a month
plan for medicines and there is a way
for two people in one house to pay for
Prime only once. Here are 14 things
Amazon will give you after 60, but only
if you ask. None of them depend on your
age. They depend on what you already get
or what you already pay for. Stop before
the one that fits you and you keep
paying full price. One Prime for less
than half the monthly price. It is
called Prime Access. Regular Prime costs
a month. Prime Access costs $6.99.
Amazon says it comes with all the same
benefits as the full price membership.
Here is who qualifies. If you get SSI,
SSDI, Medicaid, food stamps, help with
your heating bill through LEH, a VA, or
survivors pension, or you live in
federal public housing, you can qualify.
If your social security comes on a
direct express debit card, that card is
on the list, too. And if none of those
fit, you can still qualify if your
household income is at or below 200% of
the federal poverty line. Be clear about
one thing. Ordinary Social Security
retirement by itself is not on Amazon's
list. It is the programs and the income
test that open the door. You start with
a 30-day free trial. Amazon asks for a
document like your benefits letter dated
within the last 12 months. Some checks
take up to seven business days and your
Prime works while you wait. Once a year,
Amazon emails you to check again.
Picture a widow of 73 on SSI who has
paid full price for Prime for 4 years
because her son set it up and nobody
looked again. At $8 a month less, that
is $96 a year she has been handing over
for nothing. To ask for it, go to
amazon.com/qualify.
Pick the program you are on and upload a
clear picture of your letter. If you
have trouble with the upload, a son, a
daughter, or a neighbor can do it with
you at the kitchen table in a few
minutes. It is your letter and your
account, so they are only helping you
press the buttons. And Prime Access is
not a smaller version of Prime. It is
the whole thing. The free shipping, the
movies, the photo storage, and the free
restaurant delivery further down this
list all come with it. And if you get
food stamps, Prime is not even the first
thing to check. Two, your food stamps
work on Amazon. You can use your EBT
card to buy groceries on Amazon in every
state, and you do not need Prime to do
it. But there is a catch that surprises
people. Amazon says your food stamp card
cannot be used to pay for shipping fees,
delivery fees, or tips. Those have to
come from another card. Here is where it
adds up. On Amazon Fresh, delivery is
free on orders of $100 or more. Under
that, there is a fee. Up to $9.95
on small orders. So, a man of 70 who
orders $30 of groceries three times a
month can pay more in fees than he
thinks. The fix is to order less often
and order more each time or pick it up.
Amazon says pickup is free. There is one
more thing about the card. If your state
gives you cash benefits on the same EBT
card, Amazon says that Cash Part can buy
almost anything on the site in 22 states
in Washington DC, not just food. And
remember that since the start of this
year, some states no longer let food
stamps buy soda and candy. That rule
follows you onto Amazon, too. If those
items will not go through, that is why.
And if you get food stamps, Amazon also
offers its grocery delivery plan for
a month instead of $9.99. It covers
delivery on grocery orders over $35. And
there is a different card in a lot of
seniors wallets that Amazon also takes.
Three, your Medicare Advantage card for
over-the-counter items. Many Medicare
Advantage plans give members a card with
money on it every month or every quarter
for over-the-counter items. things like
pain relievers, vitamins, bandages, and
cold medicine. Some plans cover
groceries, too. Amazon accepts some of
these cards. It works with cards on the
OTC network from plans that have
approved Amazon. Amazon's list includes
plans from Etna, Health First, Oscar,
and TUS. You also need a backup card on
your account in case an item is not
covered. Picture a woman of 78 whose
plan loads $50 a quarter onto that card.
She does not drive anymore, so the money
expires unused every 3 months. If her
plan works with Amazon, she can spend it
from her kitchen table and have it at
the door. To check, call the number on
the back of your card or Amazon's
helpline for these cards at 1888-284331
and find out when your card's money runs
out. On many plans, whatever you do not
spend by the end of the month or the
quarter is gone. Write that date on your
calendar and order what you need the
week before. And if it is your
prescriptions that cost too much, the
next one is a flat price. Four, $5 a
month for your generic medicines. It is
called RX Pass from Amazon Pharmacy. For
$5 a month, you can get as many of the
generic medicines on its list as your
doctor prescribes. The list has more
than 50 common medicines. And since June
of 2024, Amazon says people on Medicare
can sign up. You need Prime and it is
not available if you are on Medicaid. It
also does not ship to every state, so
check yours. Picture a man of 68 on
Medicare who takes three generic
medicines on that list and pays a co-ay
for each one every month. If those
co-pays add up to more than $5, RX Pass
can cut his bill. If they come to less,
it does not help and he should not
switch. Amazon says you can cancel RX
Pass anytime and you will not be charged
again. Still, the safe way is to compare
your last month's pharmacy receipt with
the list first and ask your doctor
before you switch where your
prescriptions come from. Moving a
prescription is easy, but your doctor
and your current pharmacy should both
know so nothing is missed between the
two. Now, if two people in your house
both pay for Prime, one of you is paying
twice. Five. Two adults, one Prime.
Amazon calls it Amazon family. One Prime
member can share with one other adult
who lives at the same home address. The
second person gets the free shipping,
Prime Video, the books, the photo
storage, and grocery delivery without
paying for a second membership. Picture
a married couple who each signed up for
Prime years ago on their own accounts.
That is two memberships, close to $300 a
year. One of them can cancel and join
the other's household instead. And if
either of you shops at Whole Foods,
Prime members get an extra 10% off
hundreds of sale items there. One rule,
it is one other adult, not a whole
family of grown children. And Amazon
asks that you live at the same home
address. And there is a membership you
may already have for free without
knowing. Six, free food delivery from
restaurants. Prime members get GrubHub
Plus at no extra cost for as long as
they stay Prime. Amazon says it is
normally $9.99
a month. GrubHub is a service that
brings food from local restaurants to
your door. With GrubHub Plus, Amazon
says there is no delivery fee on
eligible orders. That matters on the
days you are sick, it is icy out, or you
just cannot face cooking. And Amazon
says it comes with Prime Access, too.
You have to switch it on yourself from
your Prime account. It does not start on
its own. And if you still drive, the
next one is at the pump. Seven. 10 cents
off a gallon of gas. Prime members can
save 10 cents a gallon at more than
7,500 gas stations. You link your Prime
account through a free program and the
discount comes off when you pay. 10
cents does not sound like much, but on a
15gallon fillup once a week, that is
about $78 a year. Again, it does not
happen until you link it. Now, the
things you buy every month can cost
