less, too. Eight. Up to 15% off the
things you buy every month. It is called
subscribe and save. Pick the things you
always buy like coffee, paper towels,
vitamins, or dish soap and have them
sent on a schedule. Amazon says you save
up to 15% when five or more products
come in one delivery to one address.
Shipping is always free and you can skip
or cancel anytime. And Amazon says the
price will never be higher than the
price in your reminder email. Picture a
woman of 70 who buys the same coffee,
the same vitamins, and the same toilet
paper every month. Set them to arrive
together, five items at once, and she
gets the biggest discount without
leaving the house. Check each reminder
email. If a price jumps, skip that
month. And if packages arriving every
other day confuse you or worry you about
theft from the porch, there is a free
setting called Amazon Day. You pick one
day of the week and Amazon sends your
orders together that day in fewer boxes
when it can. One day to watch the door
instead of six. And when something is
wrong, sending it back is easier than
most people think. Nine. Returns with no
box and no label. Most things on Amazon
can be returned within 30 days of
delivery. And at a lot of drop off
places, you do not need a box, tape, or
a printer. You bring the item and a code
on your phone or on paper. Amazon says
it has more than 10,000 drop off
locations, including Whole Foods,
Kohl's, the UPS store, Staples, and
FedEx Office, and it says four out of
five customers have one within 5 miles.
In a small number of cases, the UPS
store can charge a $1 fee. Picture a man
of 80 who orders shoes in the wrong
size. He does not have to find a box or
fight with a printer. He drives to the
Kohl's he already shops at and hands
them over. And if your house is full of
family pictures, there is a free place
to keep everyone. 10. Unlimited photo
storage. Prime members get unlimited
full resolution photo storage with
Amazon photos, plus 5 GB for videos. For
grandparents, that is every picture of
every grandchild kept safe in one place,
even if the phone is lost or breaks.
Picture a grandmother whose phone keeps
telling her it is full, so she has been
deleting pictures of her grandchildren
to make room. With Amazon photos, she
can save them all and stop deleting. And
there is free reading inside Prime, too.
11. Free books, magazines, and music.
Prime Reading lets Prime members read as
much as they want from a selection of
ebooks, magazines, and audiobooks at no
extra cost. You can read them on a
tablet, a phone, or a Kindle, where you
can make the letters as big as you like.
Amazon Music comes with Prime 2 at no
extra cost with music and podcasts and
no ads. There is a bigger paid version,
but you do not need it to start
listening. For someone who used to buy
three magazines at the grocery store
each month, that is money back in the
purse. Now, for things you need, but do
not need brand new. 12. Used and open
box with the same returns. Amazon Resale
sells used, open box, and pre-owned
products for less. Each one is graded
from like new down to acceptable, and
Amazon says they can be returned within
30 days, just like new items. Picture a
woman of 74 who needs a microwave. A
like new one that someone sent back on
open costs less. And if it does not
work, she returns it the same way. And
if something you ordered never shows up,
you are not stuck. 13. The A Toz
guarantee. Many things on Amazon are
sold by other companies, not Amazon
itself. If one of those never arrives or
comes damaged or is not what was
described, Amazon's a Toz guarantee
covers you. If it does not arrive 3 days
after the latest delivery date, contact
the seller. If they do not answer within
48 hours, you can file a claim with
Amazon. You have 90 days. Picture a man
who orders a heater in November from an
outside seller and it never comes. He
does not have to argue with a stranger
forever. He gives them 2 days then goes
to Amazon. And the last one protects
every single thing on this list. 14.
Amazon will never ask for a gift card.
Scammers love to pretend to be Amazon.
The Federal Trade Commission has found
Amazon among the most impersonated
companies. In its 2021 report, it found
people 60 and older lost a median of
$1,500 to these impersonators, compared
with $814 for younger people. Amazon
says it will never ask for your
password, your onetime code, gift card
details or bank card details over the
phone. And Amazon says it is okay to
hang up. So, if a caller says there is a
problem with your Amazon order and you
need to pay with gift cards, hang up.
Open the Amazon app or website yourself
and check your orders there. So, here is
your list for the kitchen table. If you
get SSI, SSDI, Medicaid, food stamps,
heating help, or your income is low, ask
for Prime Access. If you get food
stamps, use them on Amazon and order
bigger and less often to beat the fees.
If you have a Medicare Advantage card
for over-the-counter items, ask your
plan if it works on Amazon. If you take
generic medicines, compare your co-pays
with RX Pass. If two of you pay for
Prime, share one. Then switch on GrubHub
Plus, the gas savings, in the photo
storage. Set up subscribe and save for
the things you buy every month. And
never pay anyone with a gift card. None
of this comes to you on its own. Amazon
will not mention it at checkout. You
have to ask. This is educational content
and general information only. We are not
affiliated with or sponsored by Amazon.
Prices, programs, and rules change and
can vary by state. The people in the
examples are illustrations. Check the
details on Amazon's own pages with your
Medicare plan or with your state food
stamp office before you act. Take care
of yourself.

title: You Could Lose Food Stamps Even If You Still Qualify — Seniors, Do This Before the 15th

segments.text: More than five million people have lost
their food stamps in the last year. And
a lot of them still qualified. They did
not earn too much. They did not break a
rule. They missed a phone call. A form
came back too late. Or a letter told
them they had missed an interview that
had not even happened yet. One woman
wrote online that she got a notice on
the 23rd of September saying she had
missed her phone interview. The
interview was set for the 28th. Here are
11 things that keep your food stamps
from being cut off when you still
qualify. Miss one and you can lose
months of groceries over a piece of
paper. One, how many people are losing
it? The government's own numbers tell
the story. In July of last year, about
41.6 million people were on food stamps.
By June of this year, it was about 36.4
million. That is more than 5 million
fewer people, a drop of almost 13% in
under a year. Some of those people
really did stop qualifying. But a
research group called the Center on
Budget and Policy Priorities, which
looks at these programs, studied three
states and found that nearly one in
three renewals was denied for paperwork
reasons, not because the person stopped
qualifying, and older people were among
them. It is also getting harder for the
offices themselves. Since the 1st of
October, states have to pay 3/4 of the
cost of running their food stamp
offices, up from half, and the
government's own reports show that some
states take far too long. In Georgia,
only about 61% of new applications were
handled on time last year. Picture what
that means at a kitchen table. A man of
70 living alone on a small social
security check has been getting food
stamps for 4 years. Nothing in his life
has changed. Same check, same apartment,
same medicine. In one month, the card is
declined at the register for a loaf of
bread and a carton of milk. He did not
get a letter he understood. He did not
know a renewal was due. He just found
out at the checkout with people waiting
behind him. So the question is not
whether you deserve it. It is whether
your paperwork survives the system. In
plain words, food stamps are not forever
once you are approved. Every so often,
often every 6 months or a year, the
office makes you prove all over again
that you still qualify. That is called a
renewal. You fill out a form, you do an
interview, you send papers, miss any
piece of it, and the food stops, even if
nothing in your life changed. And it all
starts with one letter that a lot of
people throw away. Two, the letter that
starts the clock. Before your food
stamps run out, your state has to send
you a notice. It is called a notice of
expiration. For most people, it has to
be sent before the first day of the last
month of your benefits. That letter
tells you two dates that matter more
than anything else on it. The date your
benefits end and the date you have to
turn in your renewal by if you want your
food stamps to keep coming without a
gap. Picture a widow of 73 in Florida.
She gets a lot of mail. A plain envelope
from the state looks like the last one,
which only said her amount went up $8.
She puts it in the pile. That envelope
was her notice. The date to renew was
inside. So, from today, open every
envelope from your state's food stamp
office the day it comes. Write the two
dates on your calendar in big letters.
And if you have moved, even across town,
tell the office your new address in
writing right away. A notice mailed to
your old apartment is still a notice the
office counts as sent. If you have not
received anything and you think your
renewal is coming up, call and ask for
the dates. Do not wait for a letter that
may never reach you and one of those
dates is earlier than most people think.
Three, the 15th. For most households,
the rule is this. If you turn in your
renewal by the 15th day of the last
month of your benefits, it counts as on
time. That matters because on time is
what protects you from a gap. Turn it in
on the 25th and you may still be
approved, but your next month's food can
come late or not at all for a while.
Picture a man whose benefits end on the
30th of November. He thinks he has until
the end of November, but to be on time,
his renewal should be in by the 15th of
November. Two weeks early is the
difference between food on the 1st of
December and a hungry wait. If your
renewal is due, do not wait for the last
week. Turn it in and get proof that you
did. Picture a married couple who both
get social security. They usually do
everything together at the kitchen table
on a Sunday. This time, the husband is
sick for 2 weeks and the form sits on
the counter until the 20th. They are not
cheating anyone. They are just late. And
late is what the system punishes. Then
comes the step where most people
actually get cut off. Four, the
interview and the missed interview
notice. Most renewals need an interview.
The rule says the appointment letter can
allow for either an in-person or a
telephone interview, and the state has
to schedule it, so you have at least 10
days afterward to send in any papers
before your benefits end. Here is what
happens to a lot of seniors. The phone
call comes while they are at the doctor,
in the bathroom, or the caller ID shows
a number they do not know. So, they do
not answer. If you miss your interview,
the state has to send you a notice of
missed interview. And here is the part
almost nobody knows. If a household
misses its scheduled interview and asks
for another one, the rule says the state
shall schedule a second interview. So,
think of the woman whose letter said she
missed an interview that had not even
happened yet. She does not have to
accept it. She calls the office, says
she did not miss it, and asks for her
interview to be scheduled again or done
right then on the phone. and she writes
down the date, the time, and the name of
the person she talked to. And if the
phone is the problem, say so. Picture a
man of 79 who wears hearing aids and
cannot follow a caseworker on a bad
phone line. He asks the office if his
interview can be done in person instead
or if his daughter can be on the call
with him. Many people never ask because
they do not know they can. And when they
do call, there is one thing to have
ready. Five, the papers and the 10 days.
After the interview, the office may ask
for proof. Your income, your rent, your
medical bills. The rule says the state
must give you at least 10 days to
provide it. The danger is not the 10
days. It is that papers get lost. You
mail them, they never reach your file,
and the case closes as if you never sent
anything. Picture a man in Texas who
mails his bank statement and his
Medicare letter. 3 weeks later, a
closing notice says he did not provide
verification. He did, it just never got
scanned. So, do three things. Ask how
they want the papers by upload, fax,
mail, or in person. Keep a copy of
everything you send. And if you can,
hand them in at the office and ask for a
receipt with the date on it. Or take a
picture of the papers next to the
mailbox with the date showing. The
papers they ask for are usually the same
few things. Your social security or
pension letter for this year. A recent
bank statement, your lease or rent
receipt, or your property tax bill, your
utility bills, and if you have medical
costs, your pharmacy printout, and your
Medicare letter. Keep those together in
one folder so when the letter comes, you
are not hunting through drawers with 10
days on the clock. But what if the
deadline already passed? Six. If your
renewal was late, you may still have 30
days. This rule saves a lot of people
and almost nobody hears about it. If you
turned in your renewal before your
benefits ended, but missed a step, like
the interview or a paper, the rule says
you have 30 days after the end of your
benefits to finish. If you finish within
those 30 days, the state has to reopen
your case. Your benefits restart from
the day you finished the missing step.
Picture the widow in Florida again. She
sent her renewal on time, but she was in
the hospital the week of her interview.
Her food stamp stopped on the 30th. On
the 10th of the next month, she calls,
does the interview, and sends her
papers. She has not lost everything. Her
case can be reopened with benefits from
that day forward. So, if your food
stamps just stopped, do not wait and do
not assume it is over. Call the office
the same week. And here is why speed
matters so much. Benefits restart from
the day you finish the missing step, not
from the day they stopped. Every day you
wait is a day of food you do not get
back. A woman who calls on the third day
loses 3 days. A woman who waits until
the 29th loses almost a month. And if
your food stamps are cut in the middle
of your benefits, there is a different
protection. Seven, 10 days to keep your
benefits coming. If the office wants to
reduce or stop your food stamps in the
middle of your benefit period, it has to
send you a notice first with at least 10
days before the change takes effect. And
here is the protection. If you ask for a
fair hearing within the time the notice
gives you and your benefit period has
not ended, the rule says your food
stamps continue at the old amount while
you wait for the hearing. Picture a
woman who gets a notice that her food
stamps will stop at the end of the month
because the office says her income
changed. It did not. If she asks for a
hearing right away inside the notice
period, her food keeps coming while the
mistake is sorted out. If she waits a
month to complain, it stops and she has
to fight to get it back. Here is a
simple way to remember it. A notice to
cut your food stamps is not the end. It
is a countdown. If you act before the
countdown ends, the food keeps coming
while you argue. If you act after, you
argue with an empty cupboard. So, when a
notice comes, read the date on it the
same day. The clock is short on purpose.
And if you have already lost it and the
cupboard is empty, there is a faster
door. Eight, emergency food stamps
within 7 days. If you are applying or
applying again and you have almost
nothing, you may qualify for what the
rule calls expedited service. You can
qualify if your monthly income is under
$150 and you have $100 or less in cash
and in the bank or if your income plus
your cash in the bank is less than your
rent or mortgage plus utilities. If you
qualify, the rule says the state has to
put benefits on your card no later than
the seventh day after you apply. Picture
a man of 68 whose case closed by mistake
and whose social security does not come
for two more weeks. His rent is due. His
account has $40 in it. When he
reapplies, he says the words, "I need
expedited food stamps." 7 days, not 30.
Normally, the office has 30 days to
decide on an application. For a
household with nothing left, 30 days is
a very long time to wait for groceries.
That is exactly why this faster track
exists. In plain words, expedited means
rushed. The office still has to finish
the rest of the application afterward,
and you still have to send the papers
they ask for. But the first food arrives
within the week, so you are not going
without while the paperwork catches up.
So if you are in that spot, ask for it
by name. And there is a way to make all
of this happen less often. Nine, fewer
renewals, fewer chances to be cut. Many
states run a simpler version of food
stamps for households where everyone is
older and nobody earns a paycheck. The
rule allows no interview at renewal time
and up to 36 months between renewals.
Every renewal is a chance for a letter
to go missing or a phone call to be
missed. Going from a renewal every year
or even every 6 months to one every 3
years means far fewer chances to lose
it. As of the latest government list, 24
states in Washington DC offered it,
including California, Texas, Florida,
New York, and Georgia. Ask your office
if your household qualifies. Picture a
retired couple in Georgia, both in their
70s, living on social security only.
Every year, they dreaded the renewal
phone call. On the simpler program, they
might go 3 years without that call. Over
those 3 years, that is two fewer
renewals and two fewer chances for a
letter to get lost. Now, the one thing
that protects you in every one of these
steps, 10, your paper trail. Every one
of these rules helps you only if you can
show what happened. Keep a folder. Every
letter from the office goes in it with
the envelope because the date it was
mailed matters. Every time you call,
write down the date, the time, the name
of the person, and what they said. Every
paper you send, keep a copy. Picture two
neighbors who are both cut off the same
week, both for a missed interview. One
has a notebook that says she called on
the 20th at 10:00 in the morning and
talked to a worker named Linda. The
other has nothing. At a hearing, the
first one has a case. The second one has
a memory. And if keeping up with all of
this is too much on your own, ask your
office whether a family member or a
friend can be named as your authorized
representative. That is someone you
trust who can help with the forms and
the interview on your behalf. It means
one more person is watching the mail and
the calendar for you. And here is how to
put it all together. 11. your food stamp
calendar today. Find your last notice
from the office. Look for the date your
benefits end. If you cannot find it,
call and ask. Write the 15th of your
last month on the calendar. That is your
ontime date. When the interview letter
comes, write the date on the calendar.
Keep your phone with you that day and
answer numbers you do not know. When
they ask for papers, send copies within
the 10 days and get proof you sent them.
If you get a notice of missed interview
you did not miss, call and ask for a
second interview. If your food stamps
stop, call within the 30 days. If a
notice says your food stamps will be
cut, ask for a fair hearing inside the
notice period so the food keeps coming.
And if your covered is empty, ask for
expedited food stamps. 5 million people
lost their food stamps this year. Not
all of them had to. The difference was
usually a date on a calendar and a copy
in a folder. This is educational content
and general information only. It is not
legal or benefits advice. Food stamp
rules, deadlines, and notices vary by
state and can change. And the examples
here are simplified. Check your own case
with your state food stamp office or a
legal aid office before you act. Take
care of yourself.

title: Get PAID to Care for a Loved One at Home!Most Families Never Know

segments.text: If you are caring for your mother, your
father, or your husband at home and you
are doing it for free, you may be doing
a job that your state already pays
people to do. And the families who do
get paid often walk straight into a
trap. A daughter on disability takes the
caregiver paycheck and a year later,
Social Security says she owes money
back. A son cares for his father for
years and after the funeral, the state
sends a claim against the house. Here
are 12 things every family caregiver
needs to know. You may not need all 12,
but skip the one that fits your family
and you keep doing for free what the
government would pay for or you lose the
house you cared for them in. One, the
rule almost everyone gets backwards.
When people hear that Medicaid can pay
family caregivers, they ask, "Do I
qualify?" That is the wrong question. It
is the person being cared for who has to
qualify. Your mother, your father, your
husband. In most of these programs, they
need to be on Medicaid, and they need to
need a certain level of help with daily
life, like bathing, dressing, or getting
out of bed. Many programs use the same
test as a nursing home. In Florida's
long-term care program, for example, the
person has to be found to need nursing
home level care. your own income, your
job, your savings, those are not what
decide it. Picture a daughter of 58 who
works part-time and owns a small house.
She assumes she could never qualify for
anything, so she never asks. But it was
never her who had to qualify. It was her
mother, 84, living on a small social
security check, who cannot bathe or
dress on her own. her mother may well
qualify and her mother's program may be
allowed to pay her daughter. So the
first call is always about the person
who needs the care. Now here is how the
paying part actually works. Two, how
Medicaid pays a family member. Most
states have Medicaid home care programs
where the person getting care can hire
their own worker. The government calls
this self-direction. In plain words,
Medicaid hands the hiring to the person
getting the care and their family. The
person or someone helping them recruits
the worker, hires them, and supervises
them. And Medicaid pays the worker's
wages. And that worker can often be
family. A 2025 survey by KFF, a health
research group, found that every state
that answered pays family members or
friends through at least one of these
programs. Florida did not answer that
survey. There are limits. Spouses are
harder. Under the regular Medicaid home
care benefit, federal rules do not allow
paying a spouse. But the same KFF survey
found 44 states allow it through at
least one of their special programs,
usually only for care beyond what a
husband or wife would normally do
anyway, like bathing, lifting, or
roundthe-clock care. And these programs
usually do not pay for every hour of the
day. A social worker or nurse comes out,
looks at what help the person needs, and
sets the number of hours. That is why
some families get paid for only a few
hours a day, even when the real job is
all day. It is not full pay for
full-time love. It is pay for the hours
the program decides are needed. Picture
a son who quit his job to care for his
father with Parkinson's. If his father
qualifies and the program sets 20 hours
a week, the son gets paid for 20 hours a
week. The rest he still does for free,
but 20 paid hours is a lot more than
none. Now, the details depend on your
state. Here is how it works in the
states where most of you live. Three,
California inhome supportive services.
In California, the program is called
inhome supportive services. The state
says the care providers can include
family members, friends, and neighbors.
The person getting care has to be a
California resident, have a medical
eligibility determination, live at home,
and turn in a healthcare certification
form. A county social worker comes to
the home to decide how much help is
needed. The pay is an hourly rate set
county by county because the wages are
negotiated in each county. The state
issues the checks. To apply, you fill
out an application and send it to your
county's inhome supportive services
office. Picture a woman in Sacramento
caring for her aunt who raised her. She
had no idea she could be paid. Her aunt
applies, a social worker visits, hours
are approved, and the niece is hired as
the provider. She is doing the same work
she did last month. Now there is a
paycheck with it. New York works
differently and it changed just last
year. Four, New York, the
Consumerdirected Personal Assistance
Program. In New York, it is called the
Consumerdirected Personal Assistance
Program. The state says the worker can
be a friend or a family member as long
as they are not the Medicaid member's
spouse, not the person officially named
to make decisions for them, and not the
parent of someone under 21. So, in New
York, an adult son or daughter can be
paid. A husband or wife cannot picture a
retired couple in Buffalo. She has
advanced dementia. He does everything
for her all day. In New York, he cannot
be her paid worker because he is her
husband. But their daughter who drives
over every evening and on weekends can
be. So the family's question is not can
dad be paid. It is who else in the
family is already doing the work. There
have been big changes. Every person in
this program must now work with one
company the state chose to handle the
payroll. Public partnerships. Their
number on the state's page is
And since the 1st of September 2025, new
applicants must show they need a certain
level of help with daily activities. If
you are already in the program before
that date, the state says the new
minimum needs rule does not apply to
you. The other big states each do it
their own way. Five. Texas, Florida,
Georgia, and a few others. In Texas,
Medicaid has an option called
consumerdirected services, which lets
people who get services from Texas
Medicaid hire and manage the people who
provide them. The state's home care
program for people who would otherwise
need a nursing home is part of Star
Plus. You can apply for Medicaid online
or by calling 211. If you want a family
member to be the worker, ask about
consumerdirected services and ask
directly whether your family member can
be hired. In plain words,
consumerdirected means the person
getting care chooses the worker instead
of an agency sending a stranger. That is
exactly the door a family member walks
through. In Florida, the long-term care
program is for people 65 and older on
Medicaid who need nursing home level
care or younger people with a
disability. The first step is a phone
screening through the elder helpline at
Florida keeps a waiting list and the
state says release from it is not based
on how long you have waited. It is based
on need. So call early and call back if
things get worse. In Georgia, there is a
service called structured family
caregiving inside the state's waiver for
older and disabled people. A relative by
blood or marriage who lives with a
person can be paid a daily stipen
through an agency. Spouses and legal
guardians cannot. To apply, contact
Georgia's aging and disability resource
connection. Picture a granddaughter in
Mon who moved in with her grandmother
after a stroke. She cooks, bathes her,
and gets her to every appointment. Under
Georgia's program, a living relative
like her can be paid a daily amount for
exactly that. And in Indiana, a spouse
can be the paid caregiver under that
state's structured family caregiving.
Now, if the person you care for is a
veteran, there is a separate program and
it pays very differently. Six, veterans,
a monthly payment to the family
caregiver. The VA has a program called
the program of comprehensive assistance
for family caregivers. It pays a monthly
stipen directly to the main family
caregiver. The veteran needs a VA
disability rating of 70% or higher, a
serious injury or illness from the line
of duty, and a need for at least 6
months of continuous in-person care. The
veteran has to be enrolled in VA
healthcare. The caregiver has to be at
least 18 and either a family member or
someone who lives full-time with the
veteran. Since October of 2022, it is
open to veterans of every era. The
amount is not a flat number. The federal
rule ties it to a federal pay grade for
the area where the veteran lives. The
caregiver gets 62.5% of that monthly
amount or the full amount if the VA
decides the veteran cannot live safely
in the community without that care. You
apply with VA form 1010 CG and the VA's
caregiver support line is 1855-260-3274
Monday through Friday 8:00 in the
morning to 8 at night Eastern time.
Picture a wife caring for her husband, a
Gulf War veteran with a high disability
rating who can no longer dress or bathe
himself. Before October of 2022,
veterans of his era were not covered.
Now they are. If she has never applied,
the form is the first step, but most
veterans will not meet that 70% rating,
and there is help for them, too. Seven,
two more VA doors for veterans who do
not fit that program. The 70% rating
rules out a lot of veterans. So, there
are two more things to ask about. The
first is veteran directed care. The VA
helps the veteran set a spending plan
and hire workers. And the VA says those
workers might include their own family
member or neighbor. It is only available
in certain locations and there may be a
co-ay. Ask the social worker at your VA
medical center whether yours offers it.
The second is the general caregiver
support program. It does not pay a
stipend. It gives you training,
coaching, phone support, peer mentoring,
and referrals. There is no formal
application and the caregiver does not
need to be a relative. Picture a man
caring for his brother, an army veteran
with a 40% rating. He does not qualify
for the monthly stipend, but the general
program can teach him how to lift his
brother safely, connect him with other
caregivers, and give him someone to call
on the hard nights. That is not money.
It is help that keeps him going. Now,
here is the trap waiting for every
family caregiver who is on disability.
Eight, if you are on disability, the
paycheck can cost you your check. If you
get Social Security disability, SSDI,
and you take a paid caregiver job,
Social Security treats that pay as
earnings from work, it does not matter
that the person you care for is your own
mother. You are being paid to do a job.
That matters because SSDI has limits on
work. This year, if you earn more than
in a month, that month counts as a trial
work month. and earnings over $1,690
a month can lead Social Security to
decide you are able to work. Social
Security's own manual tells its staff to
look closely at earnings from family
employment. Picture a daughter of 55 on
SSDI. Her mother qualifies for home care
and the daughter becomes the paid
provider for 30 hours a week. She thinks
of it as helping mom, so she never tells
Social Security. A year later, a letter
arrives saying she was overpaid and
asking for the money back. The fix is
simple. Before you take the job, call
Social Security, tell them about the pay
and ask how it will affect your check.
Then report the pay every month in
writing and keep copies. And there is
one more money rule that can work in
your favor. Nine, the pay may be free of
federal income tax if you live there.
The IRS has a special rule for some
Medicaid caregiver payments. If you are
paid through one of the Medicaid
programs that pays for care at home
instead of in a nursing home and the
person you care for lives in your home
with you, those payments can be left out
of your federal taxable income. And your
home can be their home. The IRS gives
the example of a provider who moves into
her mother's house to care for her
because that is where she lives. It
counts. But if you keep a separate home
of your own and go over each day to care
for them, the IRS says you cannot leave
the payments out. If this applied to you
in past years and you paid tax on it
anyway, the IRS says you may be able to
file an amended return for years that
are still open. Ask a tax preparer about
IRS notice 20147. Many tax preparers
will know it by that number. Here is
what that can look like. Two sisters are
both paid to help their mother. One
moved into mom's house. The other lives
10 minutes away and drives over every
morning. The one who moved in may be
able to leave that pay out of her
federal taxable income. The one who
drives over cannot. Same mother, same
work, different tax bill only because of
where they sleep. And then there is the
question every caregiver eventually
asks. What happens to the house? 10.
Will the state take the house after they
die? This is the fear that keeps a lot
of families from ever applying. In plain
words, a state recovery means this.
After someone dies, the state can ask to
be paid back from what they left behind
for some of the care Medicaid paid for.
Here is the federal rule. For people who
were 55 or older when they got Medicaid
long-term care, including home care, the
state must try to recover those costs
from their estate after they die. But
there are protections written into the
law. The state cannot recover while a
surviving spouse is still alive. It
cannot recover when there is a surviving
child under 21 or a child who is blind
or disabled. And every state must have a
way to cancel the claim when it would
cause serious hardship. Ask your state
what it counts as hardship. And there is
one more protection for exactly the
children who give up years to care for a
parent. If your parent ends up in a
nursing home and the state places a
claim on the house, the law protects a
son or daughter who lived in that home
for at least 2 years before whose care
allowed the parent to stay at home
instead of an institution and who still
lives there. Picture a son who moved
back in with his mother for 6 years. She
ends up in a nursing home in the end.
The state's claim on her house is not
the end of the story. if he can show he
lived there and that his care kept her
home all those years. Keep proof of it,
the mail with your name at that address,
the doctor's notes, the care schedule.
Rules differ by state, so before you
apply, call a legal aid office or an
elder law attorney and ask how a state
recovery works where your parent lives.
And if your family has no Medicaid and
no veteran, you are not completely out
of options. 11. If you have no Medicaid
and no VA, a lot of family caregivers
are in the middle. too much income for
Medicaid, no military service, and still
doing the work. First, if you support
your parent and can claim them as a
dependent, the IRS credit for other
dependents can be worth up to $500 a
year, depending on your income. Second,
if you work, the Family and Medical
Leave Act can give you up to 12 weeks of
unpaid job protected leave a year to
care for a parent or spouse with a
serious health condition if your
employer and your job are covered.
Third, some states pay you while you
take that time off. In California, paid
family leave can pay up to 8 weeks in a
year to care for a seriously ill family
member from 50 to $1,765
a week. In New York, paid family leave
can pay up to 12 weeks at 67% of your
pay up to a cap. And it covers caring
for a parent, a parent-in-law, or a
grandparent. And fourth, the National
Family Caregiver Support Program funds
help for people caring for someone 60 or
older. It does not give you a paycheck.
It gives you respit care so you can rest
plus counseling and training. You reach
it through your local agency on aging.
Picture a wife who has cared for her
husband alone for 3 years and has not
had a full day off in all that time.
Respit care means someone comes in for a
few hours or a day so she can sleep, see
a doctor herself, or simply sit in a
coffee shop. A caregiver who never rests
can end up sick, too. And there is one
last thing families get wrong about your
parents own check. 12. handling their
money and where to start. If your parent
can no longer manage their own social
security, there is one thing families
often get wrong. A power of attorney is
not enough. Social Security's own page
says the Treasury Department does not
recognize power of attorney for federal
payments. So, you must apply to be their
representative payee. And as a family
member, you cannot charge a fee for it.
You can only be repaid for real
out-ofpocket expenses. In plain words,
the payee is the person Social Security
trusts to receive the check and pay the
rent, the food, and the bills with it.
Picture a son who has had power of
attorney for his mother for years. He
calls Social Security about her check,
and they will not deal with him. Not
until he applies to be her payee. So,
here is where to start. Call the elder
care locator at 1 8006771116.
Ask for your local agency on Aging and
ask which programs in your area pay
family caregivers. If the person you
care for is a veteran, call the VA
caregiver support line at 18552603274.
If you are on disability, call Social
Security before you accept any pay and
before you sign anything, ask how estate
recovery works in your state. You are
already doing the work. The only
question is whether you keep doing it
for free. This is educational content
and general information only. It is not
legal, tax, or benefits advice.
Programs, eligibility, and pay rates
vary by state and change over time. And
the examples here are simplified. Check
your own situation with your state
Medicaid office, the VA, Social
Security, a tax professional, or a legal
aid office before you act. Take care of
yourself.

title: If You're Over 60, Aldi Will Give You These 14 Things (If You Ask)

segments.text: If you are over 60 and you shop at Aldi,
there are things the store will give you
that almost nobody at the register will
ever mention. Not because they are
secret, because Aldi runs a store with a
handful of workers, no service desk, and
a phone that nobody answers. If you do
not ask, nobody offers. One of them
gives you your money back and the food
again, both for something you simply did
not like. One of them cuts a grocery
delivery membership in half if you are
on food stamps. And one card a lot of
people on Medicare carry gets refused at
the register and they find out in front
of a line of people. Here are 14 things
Aldi gives you. Not all of them will
matter to you, but skip the one that
does and you keep paying full price for
something the store was ready to give
you. One, your money back and the food
again. Aldi calls it the twice as nice
guarantee. In Aldi's own words, "If for
any reason you are not 100% satisfied
with the quality of any product, we will
gladly replace the product and refund
your money. Not one or the other, both."
Here is what that means in a real
kitchen. A woman tries an Aldi coffee
instead of the name brand she has bought
for 30 years. She does not like it. She
takes the bag back to the store with
what is left in it and she walks out
with her money back and a new bag of
coffee or something to replace it. You
bring the packaging and whatever is left
of the product back to the store. If you
have the receipt, you get the refund in
the way you paid. If you do not, Aldi
gives you a store credit card for the
current price. So keep your Aldi
receipts in one envelope in the kitchen
drawer. There are a few things it does
not cover. Non-food items from the
special buys aisle, national brand
alcohol, a product you already got as a
replacement, and problems that are not
about quality. And it only applies to
things you bought in the store, not
online. For someone on a fixed income,
this This the end of the fear of trying
something cheaper. If you do not like
it, the store pays for the mistake, not
you. And it is not only for things that
taste bad. Picture a man who buys a
frozen lasagna, cooks it, and finds it
dry and tasteless. He eats two bites. He
keeps the box and the rest of the tray
in the freezer, takes it back on his
next trip, and gets his money and
another frozen dinner. Opened, half
eaten, it does not matter. What matters
is that he brought back the packaging
and what was left. And if getting to the
store is the hard part, the next one is
for you. Two, if you get food stamps,
groceries delivered for less. You can
use your food stamp card at Aldi in the
store. But a lot of people do not know
you can also use it to order Aldi
groceries online for delivery or pick up
through Instacart. Instacart lists Aldi
among the stores where food stamp
customers can pay for online orders. And
here is the part almost nobody tells
you. Instacart offers food stamp
customers 50% off its Instacart Plus
membership for 1 year. To get it, you
have to have placed a food stamp order
on Instacart in the past 6 months. The
membership gives you no delivery fee on
eligible Aldi orders of $10 or more,
though service fees still apply. One
thing to know before you start, food
stamps can only pay for the food. You
also need a regular debit or credit card
on the account for fees, taxes, and
tips. Picture a man of 74 with a bad
hip. In January, when the parking lot is
ice, he is not going to push a cart.
With his food stamp card on Instacart,
the groceries come to his door. Now
picture a couple on a small fixed income
who order every 2 weeks. With the
delivery fee gone on their orders over
$10, the only extra they pay is the
service fee and the tip. For them, that
can be cheaper than the gas and the
afternoon it takes to get to the store
and back. But if the app itself is the
problem, there is a phone number for
that. Three, a real person who will help
you order. Aldi stores do not answer the
phone. Aldi says so itself. Rather than
hire extra staff to answer phones, its
workers stay focused on shoppers in the
store. But Instacart, which runs Aldi's
online orders, has a line for older
customers. Instacart says it offers
senior and specialized support for
customers who need extra help setting up
an account or placing an order. The
Every day from 8:00 in the morning to
11:00 at night Eastern time. Picture a
widow who has never ordered anything
online. Her daughter lives three states
away. One phone call and a live person
walks her through it. She does not need
to understand the app. She needs to say,
"I am a senior. I have never done this
and I want to order all the groceries
for pickup." The person on the line
takes it from there. Write that number
on the inside of a kitchen cabinet door
where you will find it again. And if you
would rather pick it up yourself, that
is cheaper, too. Four, pickup brought to
your car. If you order online and choose
pickup, Aldi says pickup fees start at
And every online order has to be at
least $10. You drive to the store, park
in the pickup spot, and someone brings
it out to you. Picture a woman who uses
a walker. Getting from the parking lot
to the door, through the store, back to
the car with a loaded cart takes
everything she has. With pickup, she
never leaves the driver's seat. She pops
the trunk and the groceries are in it.
There is a catch with online orders. On
top of the pickup or delivery fee,
service fees can apply. So, for a big
weekly shop, walking in may be cheaper.
Check the total on the screen before you
confirm. For a bad weather week or a bad
knee week, a couple of dollars can be
worth it. And if it is your very first
time ordering, the fees can be lower
still. Five, first time ordering? The
first deliveries can come with no
delivery fee. On its food stamp page,
Instacart says new customers get no
delivery fee on their first three
grocery orders. Read the conditions on
the screen before you order because fees
and service charges are not the same
thing. But, if you are trying delivery
for the first time, those first three
orders are the time to test it. Picture
a woman who has never had groceries
delivered in her life. She uses her
first order for the heavy things only.
Water, cat litter, the big bag of
potatoes, the laundry soap, the things
that hurt her back. Then, she decides
whether it is worth keeping. Now, there
is something you need to know before you
ever reach the register. Six, the
grocery card Aldi refuses at the
register. Some Medicare Advantage plans
give members a card with money on it for
groceries or health items. Aldi says it
does not accept insurance health
spending cards, and it names United,
Aetna, and Humana cards. Picture a woman
who drives across town because her
plan's card has $60 on it. Fills her
cart at Aldi and gets told no at the
register with a line of people behind
her. Do not let that be you. Use that
card at a store your plan lists. Aldi
also does not accept checks, and it does
not accept WIC. What it does accept is a
long list. Cash, most debit cards, Visa,
MasterCard, Discover, American Express,
food stamp cards, and tap to pay with
Apple Pay or Google Pay. So, if your
plan gives you a grocery card, keep it
for the stores that take it and bring
your regular card or your food stamp
card to Aldi. A 2-minute call to the
number on the back of your plan card
tells you exactly which stores take it.
And there is one more thing you can get
at that register. Seven, cash back at
the register. When you pay with a
qualifying card, Aldi offers cash back
at checkout in amounts of 10, 20, 40, or
$100. For a lot of people over 60, cash
is still how the week works. Money for
the hairdresser, the church plate, a
birthday card for a grandchild. If you
are making a separate trip to an ATM or
paying a fee at a machine that is not
your bank's, ask for cash back while you
pay for your groceries instead. Say it
before you pay, "I would like $40 cash
back, please." Picture a widower who
used to drive to his bank every Friday
for $40 in cash. He buys his groceries
on Friday instead, asks for the $40 at
the register, and that is one less trip
in his week. And while you are thinking
about change in your pocket, there is a
quarter you always get back. Eight, your
quarter comes back. Aldi carts are
locked together and you put in a quarter
to unlock one. Aldi's own words are
simple, "Lend us a quarter and we will
lend you a cart." When you bring back
the cart, you get your quarter back.
That quarter is not a fee, it is how
Aldi avoids paying someone to chase
carts around the parking lot. And that
saving is part of the shelf price. If
walking the cart back is hard for you,
hand it to someone walking in. They give
you their quarter, you give them the
cart, and you are done. The next one is
about the price on the shelf. Nine,
price drops and this fall's price cuts.
Aldi runs a program it calls price
drops, extra low prices on certain
items. And in late September, Aldi
announced a round of price cuts for the
fall. In its announcement, honeycrisp
apples were $1.99 for a 2-lb bag and
family packs of chicken breast were
$1.99 a pound. Aldi itself says prices
can vary by store. Picture a couple who
buy chicken every week. At that price, a
family pack bought on the right week and
split into the freezer is three or four
dinners for the cost of one meal at a
drive-thru. Look for the price drop
signs in the store and check the weekly
ad. In plain words, look for that price
drops tag on the things you already buy
every week. A lower price on something
you buy every week is money saved every
week for as long as that price lasts.
And the price drops are only half it.
The other half changes every single
week. 10. A new weekly ad and the
special buys aisle. ALDI puts out a
weekly ad with its deals, and the middle
aisle carries what ALDI calls ALDI
Finds. Products available for a limited
time only and not always food. A space
heater one week, slippers the next. Here
is the rule to remember. Food from that
aisle is covered by the Twice as Nice
Guarantee. Non-food items from that
aisle are not. So, for anything electric
or anything you wear, keep the box and
the receipt and read the return terms at
the store. Picture a woman who buys a
small space heater from that aisle in
November. It stops working after a few
weeks. If she threw the box and the
receipt away on the first day, she has
made it much harder for herself. If they
are on the shelf in the closet, she
takes it back and asks for a refund or
an exchange. And watch out for deals
that say ALDI, but are not from ALDI at
all. 11. Coupons that are real and the
ones that are scams. ALDI does not offer
online coupons. In ALDI's own words,
"Any coupon found online or through
social media is not a legitimate ALDI
coupon." Real ALDI coupons are printed
and handed out in the store or mailed to
you. So, if a post on Facebook says,
"Click here for a $50 ALDI coupon," it
is not from ALDI. And a fake coupon is
often a way to get your name, your
email, or your card number. Picture a
grandmother who sees a post from a
friend saying ALDI is giving away $100
coupons to seniors this week. All she
has to do is fill in a short form. That
form is the scam. ALDI [clears throat]
has already told you where real coupons
come from, the store or your mailbox.
The same goes for text messages that say
you won an ALDI gift card or that your
ALDI order is on hold and you need to
click a link. If you did not order
anything, there is no order. Delete it.
And if you want to give ALDI as a gift,
there There a better way. 12. gift cards
with no fees that never expire. Aldi
sells gift cards in its stores from $5
up to 100. Aldi says there are no fees
and the balance never expires. One thing
to know, they cannot be used for online
orders. For a grandparent on a budget,
an Aldi gift card is a practical gift
for a grown grandchild who is just
starting out. And for yourself, it is a
way to set your grocery money aside on
payday, so it is there at the end of the
month. And there is one page on Aldi's
website worth knowing about before the
next food scare. 13, a recall list you
can check. Aldi keeps a product recalls
page on its company website. If you hear
on the news that a food was recalled,
that is where you check whether it was
an Aldi product. And if you bought it,
follow the recall notice for how to
return it or get your money back.
Picture a man who hears on the radio
that a brand of spinach was recalled. He
does not remember if his bag came from
Aldi or somewhere else. Two minutes on
the recall page or one question to a
grandchild with a phone tells him
whether to throw it out. And one last
thing about the calendar. 14, the days
the doors are closed. Aldi stores are
closed on New Year's Day, Easter Sunday,
Thanksgiving Day, and Christmas Day.
Hours otherwise vary by store. That
matters more than it sounds. Picture a
man who plans to pick up his
Thanksgiving rolls on Thanksgiving
morning because it is close by. The
doors are locked. Shop the day before
and go early because everyone else will
have the same idea. So, that is the
list. What Aldi does not give you is a
senior discount. Aldi says it does not
offer discounts at its stores, it does
not do rain checks, and it does not
price match. Its argument is that the
low price on the shelf is the discount
everyday for everyone. But the things on
this list are real. Your money back and
the food again. Food stamp delivery for
less. A phone line with a real person.
And a register that will not take your
plans grocery card, so you know before
you get there. Write down the three that
matter to you and use them on your next
trip. This is educational content and
general information only. It is not
financial advice and it is not
affiliated with or endorsed by Aldi or
Instacart. Policies, prices, fees, and
offers can change and vary by store.
Confirm anything here with your local
Aldi store or on the official Aldi and
Instacart websites before you rely on
it. Take care of yourself.

title: BREAKING: Medicare Is Sending $90 to 20 Million Seniors on October 8 — Who Gets It and Who Doesn't?

segments.text: On or around the 8th of October, about
21 million people on Medicare get $90
dropped into their bank account. And a
lot of seniors are going to check their
account that morning and find nothing.
Not because something went wrong,
because the rules left them out before
the first dollar was sent. If you are on
Medicare Advantage, you are left out. If
your state pays your Medicare premium,
you are left out. And the people who are
left out are the ones the scam callers
will go after first with a voice on the
phone that says it can fix it for you.
Here are the 11 things you need to know
about this $90. Skip one and you could
be waiting for money that is never
coming or handing your Social Security
number to someone who promised to get it
for you. One, what this payment is. It
is a one-time payment of $90 for people
on Medicare Part B. The government calls
it a premium rebate. The White House
says it is meant to help people pay
their Part B premium and the paper
checks will even say what it is for. $90
to offset the October premium. The money
comes from something called the Medicare
Improvement Fund. Congress set it up in
2008 with $2 billion to make
improvements to traditional Medicare.
According to the White House, this is
the first time that fund has been used
to send money straight to people on
Medicare. You do not apply for it. If
you qualify, it comes on its own. It is
one payment, one time. Nothing in the
official announcement says there will be
another one. In plain words, it works
like this. Every month, most people on
Medicare pay a premium for Part B, the
part that covers doctor visits. For most
people, it is taken out of Social
Security before the check lands. This
$90 is meant to cover part of what you
paid for October. It is $90 per person.
So, a married couple who both qualify
would get $90 each. So, the real
question is not what it is. It is
whether it is coming to you. Two, who
gets it? According to Medicare's own
question and answer page, the payment
goes to people in original Medicare Part
B who meet three conditions. You live in
the United States. You do not get help
with your premium from Medicaid. And you
do not pay the higher premium that is
charged to people with higher incomes.
That comes to about 20.8 million people.
Picture a retired mailman of 72. He has
original Medicare, a supplement plan,
and his Part B premium comes out of his
Social Security every month. His income
is ordinary. He fits every condition.
His $90 should land on or around the
8th. If you are not sure which kind of
Medicare you have, look in your wallet.
If the card you show at the doctor is
your red, white, and blue Medicare card,
and maybe a separate card for a
supplement plan, you are most likely on
original Medicare. If the card you show
has an insurance company's name on it
and says Medicare Advantage, or it
covers your drugs, dental, and doctor
all on one card, you are most likely on
Medicare Advantage. When in doubt, call
Medicare and ask. But a lot of seniors
do not look like him. And the first
group left out is a very big one. Three,
left out if you are on Medicare
Advantage. If you get your Medicare
through a Medicare Advantage plan, the
private plans you see advertised on
television all fall, you do not get the
$90. Medicare's own page says it
plainly, "Beneficiaries enrolled in
Medicare Advantage are not eligible."
That surprises people because they still
pay a Part B premium. Picture a woman
who signed up for a Medicare Advantage
plan 3 years ago because it had a $0
premium and dental. Her Part B premium
still comes out of her check every
month, the same as her neighbor's. Her
neighbor, on original Medicare, gets
$90. She gets nothing. It can even split
a married couple. He stayed on original
Medicare with a supplement. She moved to
an Advantage plan for the dental. Same
house, same kitchen table, and only one
of them gets $90. And here is the trap.
Medicare open enrollment starts on the
15th of October. Some people will think,
I will just switch to original Medicare
and get the $90. It does not work that
way. Changes you make in open enrollment
take effect on the 1st of January. This
payment is going out in October.
Switching plans now does nothing for
this payment and you should never change
your health coverage over $90. And watch
for this. Open enrollment is when the
sales calls pick up. Picture a man who
gets a call in the 3rd week of October.
The caller says, switch your plan with
me today and you will get your $90. That
is not how this payment works. Anyone
who ties your $90 to signing up for a
plan is selling you something. Hang up
and if you want to compare plans, do it
yourself on Medicare's own website or
with your free state health insurance
counselor. The second group left out is
the one that surprises low-income
seniors most. Four, left out if your
premium is paid for you. If Medicaid
helps pay your Medicare premium, you do
not get the $90. That includes many
people whose state pays their Part B
premium through what is called a
Medicare Savings Program. Picture a
widow on $1,200 a month in Social
Security. Two years ago, her state
started paying her Part B premium. She
hears $90 on the news and waits for it.
It does not come. Here is what that
widow needs to understand. She was left
out because she already gets something
bigger. Her state pays her $202.90
every single month. That is more than
a year. The $90 was meant to help people
who are still paying that premium
themselves. How do you know if your
state pays your premium? Look at your
Social Security letter or your bank
deposit. If $202.90
is not being taken out of your check for
Part B, someone else is paying it. For
most people in that position, it is the
state. Here is how it usually looks in
real life. A woman applied for help with
her Medicare costs last year. A few
months later, a letter came saying her
Part B premium would now be paid by the
state, and her Social Security deposit
went up by about $200.
She was happy, and then she forgot all
about it. Now she hears $90 on the news
and thinks it is coming to her. It is
not, and the reason is that letter in
her drawer. She is already getting more
help than the $90 every single month.
So, if you were in this group, do not
call around trying to get the $90. And
if your income is low and you are still
paying the premium yourself, the bigger
money is in applying for that state
program. It is worth far more than this
payment. The third group is the opposite
end. Five, left out if you pay the
higher premium. People with higher
incomes pay more for Part B. That extra
charge has a long name, the
income-related monthly adjustment
amount. If you pay it, you do not get
the $90. This year, that higher premium
starts for people whose income is above
for a married couple. And Medicare looks
at your income from two years back. So,
picture a widow who sold her late
husband's rental property two years ago.
One year of high income from one sale.
Her Medicare premium went up because of
it, and now that same sale also keeps
her out of the $90. She is not rich
today. Her tax return from two years ago
says she was. That two-year look-back
catches people every year. A one-time
sale, a large retirement account
withdrawal, a year when a spouse was
still working. The income is gone, but
the record of it is still deciding what
you pay, and now whether you get this
payment. And there is one more group,
smaller, but it catches people. Six,
left out if you live outside the United
States. The first condition on
Medicare's list is that you live in the
United States. If you have retired to
another country and still have part B,
this payment is not for you. Picture a
retired teacher who moved to Costa Rica
to make her pension go further. She kept
her part B in case she ever comes home
for treatment and the premium still
comes out every month. She hears about
the $90 from her sister in Texas. Under
Medicare's own conditions, she is not on
the list because she does not live in
the United States. Now, if you do
qualify, here is how and when it
actually reaches you. Seven, when it
comes and how. Medicare says most people
will get a direct deposit of $90 on or
around the 8th of October. After that,
in the middle of October, most will get
an email or a letter from the president
about it. Some people will get a paper
check instead from the United States
Treasury later in October. The check
will carry a message that reads Medicare
Improvement Fund Payment. $90 payment to
offset October premium. Picture a man
who qualifies, checks his bank on the
8th and sees nothing. He panics and
thinks he was cut off. He may simply be
in the group getting a paper check and
it is still in the mail. On or around
the 8th is not a promise of the exact
day and later in October means later in
October. Now picture a woman who does
not use direct deposit at all. For her,
the $90 is likely to come as a paper
check from the United
So this month, she opens every envelope
from the Treasury before anything goes
in the trash. It is easy to throw a real
check out with the junk mail, especially
when you were not expecting one. So if
it does not show up on the 8th, the
first thing to do is nothing. Wait. And
if you and your spouse both qualify, do
not be surprised if the two payments do
not land on the same day or come in
different ways. Each person is paid
separately. But if October ends and
still nothing has come, here is who to
call. Eight, what to do if it never
comes. There are two numbers for two
different questions. If you are not sure
whether you qualify, call Medicare. The
number is 1-800-MEDICARE,
If you know you qualify and the money
has not arrived, Medicare says to call
Social Security starting on the 15th of
October. That number is 1-800-772-1213.
Before you call, have three things
ready. Whether your Part B premium comes
out of your Social Security, whether you
are on original Medicare or a Medicare
Advantage plan, and whether your state
pays any part of your premium. Those
three answers will tell you almost
immediately whether the $90 was ever
meant for you. Picture a woman who calls
Social Security on the 20th of October.
She says, "I am on original Medicare. My
premium comes out of my check. I live in
Ohio and I have not received the $90
payment." That one sentence gives them
everything they need. Write it down
before you call so you do not have to
think on the phone.
And here is the warning that matters
more than the $90. Nine, the phone call
that will come with it. Every time money
is in the news, the scam calls follow
and this one is perfect for them.
Millions of people are expecting a
payment. Millions more are confused
about why they did not get one. Here's
how the call will sound. A friendly
voice says, "Your $90 Medicare payment
is on hold. There is a problem with your
file. To release it, they just need to
confirm your Medicare number, your
Social Security number, or your bank
account." Every part of that is false.
The White House says there is nothing to
apply for. If you qualify, it comes on
its own. Social Security's own Inspector
General has warned that Social Security
does not offer to increase benefits in
exchange for money. Nobody needs your
number to send you a payment you already
qualify for. So, if anyone calls about
the $90, hang up. Then, call the
official number yourself, the one on
your Medicare card or the Social
Security number, never a number the
caller gives you. And it will not only
be phone calls, expect text messages
with a link that says, "Click here to
claim your Medicare payment." Expect
emails that look official. Nothing in
the official announcements asks you to
do anything to get this payment. So, if
a message asks you to click, pay, or
send your numbers, treat it as a scam
and delete it. Picture a grandmother who
gets that phone call while she is home
alone. The man is polite, he knows she
is on Medicare, and he says her $90 will
be canceled today if she does not
confirm her Social Security number. She
is scared of losing it, so she almost
says it. Here's the simple rule to give
her and to give anyone you love who is
on Medicare. A real payment never needs
you to confirm anything on a phone call
you did not make. If someone is in a
hurry to get your numbers, that hurry is
the scam. And there is one more thing
about this $90 that nobody is saying out
loud. 10. What $90 is really worth next
to the premium. This payment is to
offset one month's premium, but the
premium itself is going up. Right now,
Part B costs $202.90
a month. Medicare's trustees project
about $209.50
next year. That would be $6.60
more every month. Over a full year, that
So, of the $90 you get once in October,
the projected increase takes back $79.20
over the next 12 months. It is a real
payment, just do not count it as a
raise. Count it as one month of help.
For a married couple who both qualify,
it is the same math doubled, $180 in
October. And if the projection holds,
more in premiums over the next year
between the two of them. And here is why
that matters for planning. A lot of
people will see $90 in October and treat
it like extra spending money. That is
fine. It is yours. But in January, when
the new premium starts coming out of the
check, nobody will send a payment to
cover that. If money is tight, put this
$90 toward January, not toward the
holidays. And the actual raise is
announced on the 14th of October, when
Social Security publishes next year's
cost of living increase. The new Part B
premium comes separately, usually in the
fall. So, here is exactly what to do
this week. 11. What to do this week.
First, find out which group you are in.
Look at your Social Security letter or
your bank statement. Is your Part B
premium coming out of your check? Are
you on original Medicare or a Medicare
Advantage plan? Does your state pay your
premium? Second, if you qualify, watch
your bank account around the 8th. If
nothing comes, wait for a paper check
through the end of October. Third, if
October ends with nothing, call Social
Security at 1-800-772-1213.
Their line for this opens on the 15th.
Fourth, if your income is low and you
are still paying your own premium, ask
your state about a Medicare Savings
Program. That is worth more than $2,400
a year, not 90. And fifth, if anyone
calls you about this payment, hang up.
$90 is going to 21 million people. The
ones who get hurt by it are the ones
waiting for money that was never coming
to them. And the ones who believe the
voice on the phone. This is educational
content and general information only. It
is not legal, tax, or benefits advice.
Details of this payment come from
Medicare and the White House and can
change. Check your own case with
Medicare at 1-800-633-4227
or with Social Security. Take care of
yourself.

title: Free Food Benefits Start at Age 60 (Not 65) — Many Seniors Never Claim Them

segments.text: At 60, a different set of food rules
starts working for you, and nobody mails
you a letter about it. A widow can be
turned down for food stamps and still
qualify for a box of food every single
month. A man who cannot pay a cent can
still get a hot meal brought to his
door, and the law says he cannot be
refused. And a mother living in her
son's house can be counted on her own.
Every month you are not signed up is
food you never get back. Nobody pays you
for the boxes you never asked for. Here
are 11 free food programs for people 60
and older. You may not qualify for all
11, but if you stop watching before the
one you do qualify for, you keep paying
for food you could have gotten free.
One, a box of food every month with a
much higher income limit. It is called
the Commodity Supplemental Food Program.
Most people just call it the senior food
box. You have to be 60 or older, and
your income has to be at or below 150%
of the poverty line. Here's what that
means in dollars. Using this year's
figures, that is up to about 1,000
$1,995 a month for one person, and about
for a couple. Some states set their line
a little lower, so check yours. Now,
compare that with food stamps. For food
stamps, the income that counts, after
deductions, has to be at or under $1,330
a month for one person. So, there is a
whole group of seniors who are told no
for food stamps, and never hear that the
food box line is far higher. Picture a
widow with $1,600 a month in social
security and a paid-off house. Her food
stamp application comes back denied, and
she decides there is nothing out there
for her. But at $1,600, she is well
under the food box line. Or take a
married couple with $2,400 a month
between them. Too much for food stamps,
they were told. Under the food box line
for a couple by about $300. Each of them
can get a box. And what comes in the box
is real food, milk and cheese, juice,
oats, cereal, rice, and pasta, peanut
butter and dry beans, canned meat,
chicken, or fish, canned fruit and
vegetables. It comes every month. It is
meant to add to what you buy, not
replace all of it. But, it is food you
do not have to pay for month after
month. Two things to know. The program
runs in parts of all 50 states, but not
in every county. So, you have to ask
locally. To sign up, you usually fill
out a short form with the local agency
that hands out the boxes, and show your
age and your income. A social security
letter often covers both. And the
federal rule lets you name someone, a
family member or a neighbor, to pick the
box up for you. And you can get the food
box and food stamps at the same time. In
fact, if you already get food stamps,
the federal rule lets your state accept
that as proof of your income for the
box. The food box has an income line.
The next one has no income line at all.
Two, a hot meal with no income test.
Under a federal law called the Older
Americans Act, there are meal programs
for anyone 60 or older. You can sit down
to a hot meal at a senior center, a
church hall, or a community site,
usually at lunchtime, with other people
your age. And here is the part almost
nobody believes. There is no income
test. The law says these programs shall
not means test. They may ask for a small
donation, but it is voluntary. And the
rule says they cannot turn you away
because you will not or cannot pay. Your
spouse can come, too, at any age. If you
are 65 and your wife is 58, she eats
with you. Picture a retired man who
still has a small pension and some
savings. He would never apply for food
stamps. He thinks of himself as
comfortable. But, he lives alone, he
eats crackers for dinner most nights,
and he has not had a real conversation
in a week. A senior meal site does not
ask what he has in the bank. It asks if
he is hungry. You You not bring pay
stubs or bank statements. You show up,
or you call ahead if the site asks you
to, and you sit down. Some sites serve
lunch every weekday, others a few days a
week. The way to find out is one free
phone call, and that number comes at the
end. If getting there is the problem,
ask the site whether it can help with a
ride. But what if you cannot get out of
the house at all? Three, meals brought
to your door, even if you cannot pay.
The same law pays for home-delivered
meals. Many people know them as Meals on
Wheels. They're for people 60 or older
who have trouble getting out, shopping,
or cooking for themselves. Each provider
sets its own details, so the first call
is to find who serves your area. The
same protection applies. Programs paid
for under that law cannot means test,
and cannot refuse you because you do not
pay. A donation is welcome. It is not
required. Picture a woman of 82 home
from the hospital after a fall. She
cannot stand at the stove, and her
daughter lives two states away. A meal
arrives at her door, and the person who
brings it is also the one who notices if
she does not answer. For a lot of people
who live alone, that knock is the only
one all day. Now, the food stamp rules
change at 62, and they change in your
favor. Four, food stamps after 60 play
by different rules. Once someone in your
household is 60 or older, three things
change. First, only one income test
applies, the one that looks at your
income after deductions. The gross
amount on your check is not the test.
Second, the savings line is higher.
Starting this October, it is $4,750
of countable savings for a home with
someone over 60, and some states have
dropped the savings test altogether.
Third, a lot of what you own does not
count. Your home does not count, and
your retirement accounts do not count. A
401k, a traditional IRA, a Roth IRA, and
pension plans are all left out by the
federal rule. That last one matters
because people get it wrong all the
time. Think of a retired bus driver and
his wife. They own their small house
outright. He has an IRA from the transit
authority and they keep a little in
checking. They are sure the IRA
disqualifies them. The office is not
even allowed to add it in. And picture
what the single income test does for a
widow on $1,500
a month. Younger households face two
tests and the first one looks at the
full check. She skips that one. The
office goes straight to her income after
her rent and medical costs are taken off
and that is the number that decides it.
And here is how many people this misses.
In the government's latest count, only
about 55% of older adults who were
eligible for food stamps actually got
them. Close to half were leaving it on
the table. And it was worst for people
living with family. Older people who
lived alone signed up far more often,
about 71% of those eligible. Those who
lived with others signed up much less.
If you live with your children, the odds
are good nobody ever looked at whether
you qualify on your own. But getting
approved is only half of it. The other
half is how much you get. Five, if your
card is close to empty, look at what is
in your file. At 60 and older, your food
stamps can be raised by the costs you
pay. Medical costs above $35 a month
count. And that includes the Medicare
premium that comes out of your social
security. Rent or the property tax and
insurance on a house you own counts,
too. And for older households, there's
no limit on how much of it. If the
office does not have those costs, it
works out your food stamps as if you had
none. That is how so many seniors end up
on the smallest amount the program pays.
So when you apply or the next time you
hear from the office, bring proof of
what you pay. Your Medicare letter, your
pharmacy printout, your lease or your
property tax bill and homeowner's
insurance. And if you live with your
children, there is a rule that can
change the whole picture. Six, living
with family and still counted on your
own. Normally, if you live with your
grown children and you buy food
together, food stamps count everyone's
income together. Your son's paycheck can
push the whole household over the line,
but there is a special rule. If you are
60 or older and you cannot buy and cook
your own food because of a permanent
disability, you and your spouse, if you
have one, can be counted as a separate
household. There is a limit. The income
of the others you live with cannot be
above 165%
of the poverty line. Picture a mother of
76 with severe arthritis and a
disability her doctor has documented
living in her son's house. Counted with
him, she gets nothing. Counted on her
own, her own small check is what the
office looks at. It does not happen
automatically. You have to tell the
office about the disability and ask for
it, but it is in the federal rule and it
is worth asking. And once you are on
food stamps, there is a way to stop
dreading the paperwork. Seven, a simpler
way to keep your food stamps. Many
states run an easier track for homes
where every member is older and nobody
earns a paycheck. It is called the
elderly simplified application project.
What it does is take away the two things
people hate most. No interview when it
is time to renew and instead of renewing
every year or so, you can go up to 36
months. As of the latest government
list, 24 states in Washington D.C.
offered it including California, Texas,
Florida, New York, and Georgia. The age
it starts can be 60 or 65 depending on
the state. So, ask your office if your
household qualifies. Picture a man of 70
who gave up his food stamps last year,
not because he stopped qualifying, but
because he missed one phone interview.
Three years between renewals and no
interview is exactly what keeps that
from happening. Now, in some states,
food stamps do something most people
never hear about. Eight, in some states,
your card works at a restaurant. It is
called the restaurant meals program. In
the states that run it, people on food
stamps who are 60 or older, disabled, or
homeless can use their card for a hot
meal at participating restaurants. Right
now, nine states run it. Arizona,
California, Illinois in some areas,
Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, New
York, Rhode Island, and Virginia. There
is one rule that catches people.
Everyone in the food stamp household has
to qualify as someone 60 or older,
disabled, homeless, or the spouse of
someone who qualifies. A couple who are
both over 60 can use it. A grandmother
whose working grandson is on the same
case may not. If you qualify, the state
turns it on for your card. If standing
at the stove is getting harder, find out
from your office whether your state
offers it and get the list of
restaurants near you. And when the
weather turns, there is fresh food, too,
if you know where to look. Nine. Fresh
fruit and vegetables from the farmers
market. There is a federal program
called the Senior Farmers Market
Nutrition Program. It is for people 60
or older with income up to 185% of the
poverty line. Right now, that is up to
about $2,461
a month for one person and about 3,337
for a couple. It gives you vouchers for
fresh, local fruit, vegetables, honey,
and herbs at approved farmers markets
and farm stands. It is not a lot of
money, usually between 20 and 50 dollars
a year, but it is seasonal and the
vouchers go to people who signed up in
time. Ask your local agency on aging
when your state opens the list. And if
you are on food stamps, some farmers
markets go further. They match your food
stamp dollars for fruit and vegetables.
So, 10 dollars from your card can buy 20
dollars of produce. Not every market
does it, so ask at the market's
information table. Picture a woman who
walks to a Saturday market in July with
her vouchers and her food stamp card.
The vouchers cover a bag of tomatoes,
peaches, and green beans. The card,
matched at the market, covers the rest.
She leaves with more fresh food than she
could have bought at the store for the
same money. And for the weeks when the
money simply runs out, there is one more
door. 10. The food pantry and the meals
with no questions. Food banks and food
pantries hand out food from a federal
program called the Emergency Food
Assistance Program. Each state sets its
own income guidelines for the groceries
you take home. And for prepared meals,
like a soup kitchen, people are presumed
to be low income and are not put through
an income test at all. There is no age
limit on this one, and you do not have
to be on any other program. It is there
for the last week of the month. Picture
a man whose Social Security lands on the
third Wednesday. By the second week of
the month, the cupboard is getting bare.
A pantry visit that week is not charity
he has to earn. It is what the program
is for, and his tax dollars helped pay
for it. So, that is the whole list.
Here's how to get it without a computer.
11. One phone call to start all of it.
There is a free national number that
connects you to your local agency on
aging, and they can point you to the
