food box, the senior meals, the home
delivered meals, and the farmers market
vouchers where you live. It is called
the Elder Care Locator, and the number
When you call, ask four things. Is the
senior food box available in my county,
and how do I sign up? Where is the
nearest senior meal site? Can I get
meals delivered to my home, and when
does the farmers market voucher list
open? Then call your state food stamp
office and ask four more. What do you
count as my income and my costs? Does my
state have the simplified program for
older households. Does my state run the
restaurant program? And if you live with
family and have a disability, ask
whether you can be counted as your own
household. Picture the widow from the
beginning, the one turned down for food
stamps. One phone call and she has a
food box on its way every month, a lunch
table on Tuesdays, and her name on the
voucher list for next summer. She did
not earn a dollar more. She just found
out what turning 60 already gave her.
Write the number down before this video
All of this is educational content
and general information only, and none
of it is legal or benefits advice. What
is offered in the income lines change
from
state to state and county to county, and
they can change over time. The people in
these examples are simplified. Your
local agency on aging or your state
office can confirm your own case. Take
care of yourself.

title: Every Senior Getting $25 in Food Stamps Must Do This to Get Up to $306 Before January

segments.text: If you get $25 a month in food stamps,
you are very likely being shorted. Not
because you have too much money, because
the office never counted what you pay
out. One widow was getting $25 a month,
same check, same rent, and she was owed
about 180, more than seven times as
much. Nobody at the office told her.
They will not tell you, either. And in
January, when the Social Security raise
is fed in, they run your numbers again.
If your costs are not in your file by
then, you start the new year at $25
again. Here is what they are not
counting. One, what $25 actually means.
$25 is the floor. For a household of one
or two people, it is the least you can
get once you qualify. So, if that is
what you get, the office decided you
qualify, and then decided you have
almost no costs. Here is how the sum
works in plain words. The government
sets a top amount. Right now, that is
$306 a month for one person. Then the
office takes your income, takes off
whatever costs it is allowed to, and
looks at what is left. For every dollar
left over, your food stamps go down by
about 30 cents. At 60 or older, only
that leftover income is tested. The
bigger number on your check is not what
decides it. Now, picture the widow. She
is 71, she lives alone, and her Social
Security is $1,250
a month. Every household gets the same
starting deduction of $217.
So, the office counts 1,033.
Take 30 cents of each of those dollars,
and you get about 310, which is more
than the top amount of 306. So, on
paper, she gets nothing, and the floor
lifts her to 25. That is what her file
says when the only thing in it is her
check. The first thing missing from her
file is a cost she pays every single
month and never even sees. Two, the
Medicare premium that comes out before
the check lands. Most people on Social
Security have their Medicare Part B
premium taken out before the money
reaches the bank. This year, that is
$202 and 90 cents a month. Because it
never passes through their hands, a lot
of people never think of it as a bill.
But for food stamps, it is a medical
cost. And at 60 or older, whatever you
pay for medical care beyond the first
$35 each month is taken off your income.
So, for the widow, about $168 comes off.
Put that in her file, and her card goes
from $25 to about 46.
>> One line on a form, $21 more a month.
And she has not even reached the big one
yet. For a married couple, it doubles.
Two Medicare premiums, both taken out
before the checks land, and about $370 a
month of medical cost that never made it
into the file. Three, your rent or the
costs of the house you own. For a
household with someone 60 or older,
there is no ceiling on the housing
deduction. Younger households are
capped. You are not. Here's the simple
version. The office looks at the income
it is counting and asks one question.
Does your rent eat more than half of it?
If it does, every dollar of rent above
that half comes off your income, too.
The widow pays $700 a month in rent.
Half of the income the office is
counting is about 433.
Her rent is $267 more than that. So,
$267 more comes off. Add the rent, and
her card goes from $46 to about 127.
From 25 to 127, and she has only listed
two things.
>> If you own your home, the rule still
works for you. A paid-off house still
has costs. The federal rule counts
property taxes, state and local
assessments, and insurance on the house
itself. If you still have a mortgage,
that counts. So do condo and association
fees. What does not count is separate
insurance on your furniture or
belongings. Picture a widower in a
paid-off house. He thinks he has no
housing costs because there is no
mortgage. But his property tax is 2,400
a year and his homeowner insurance is
That is $300 a month he has never once
put on a food stamp form. And there is a
cost tied to the house that most people
never connect to food stamps at all,
heating. Four, the heating payment that
unlocks a bigger deduction. For heating
and cooling, most states do not add up
your actual bills. They use one fixed
amount for everybody called the utility
allowance. And for a lot of seniors, it
is the second biggest deduction they can
get after rent. And there is a way to
get the full amount that most people
have never heard of. If your household
has someone 60 or older or disabled and
the household gets a heating or cooling
payment of more than $20 from LIHEAP,
the energy assistance program, the
office has to give you the full heating
and cooling allowance. The new federal
law took that shortcut away from younger
households. It left it in place for
yours. California makes it automatic. If
someone in the household is over 60 or
disabled,
the county sends that small energy
payment on its own. In other states, do
not assume it comes by itself. Ask. And
if it does not, apply for heating help
yourself because even a small payment
can unlock the bigger deduction. And it
is not small money. From the 1st of
October, the heating and cooling
allowance is $464
a month in Texas, 445 in Florida and 686
in California. Take the widow at $127
before anything else is added. If she
lives in Texas and that allowance goes
into her file on top of her rent, her
food stamps go to about 266.
In California, she reaches the top
amount, 306. One thing was taken away.
Under the same law, internet service can
no longer be counted as a housing cost.
If it used to be in your file, it is
gone now. So ask your office two
questions. Did my household get any
heating or cooling help this year? and
am I getting the full heating and
cooling allowance? If the answer to
either one is no, apply for heating help
as soon as your state opens it this
fall. Five, the one-time bill that
people think does not count. This is
where a lot of seniors lose money
without knowing it. Picture a woman who
paid $600 for new glasses. She mentioned
it to the office and was told it did not
count because it was not a monthly bill.
That is not what the rule says. The
federal rule lets you choose. A one-time
medical bill can come off all at once in
the month it is due, or it can be spread
over the months left before your next
review. And a bill counts in the month
you are billed, even if you have not
paid it yet. So, if the widow had those
same glasses and spread the 600 over 10
months, that is $60 a month more in
medical costs. Her food stamps go from
127 to about 154. Now, say the bill is
bigger. A man needs new dentures, and
the dentist bills him $1,800
in March. He can ask for the whole thing
to come off in March. For that one
month, his countable income can drop to
almost nothing, and his food stamps can
jump to the top amount. Or, he can
spread it and get a smaller lift every
month until his next review. It is his
choice, and nobody will offer it to him
unless he asks. There is one catch. Old
medical debt that keeps getting carried
forward from earlier bills does not
count, even if you finally pay it. What
counts is what is billed now. And
glasses are only one item on a much
longer list. Six, the full list. And
most people only know two things on it.
Here is what the federal rule counts as
a medical cost for anyone 60 or older or
disabled. Doctor and dental bills,
including the part you pay after
insurance. Hospital and outpatient
bills. Nursing care. Prescription drugs.
And over-the-counter medicine, including
insulin, when a doctor or other licensed
health professional has approved it.
Medical supplies and equipment you buy
or rent, like a walker, a hospital bed,
or an oxygen machine. Insurance
premiums, not just Medicare, a Medigap
policy, a dental plan, a drug plan
premium, dentures, hearing aids,
prosthetics, eyeglasses prescribed by an
eye doctor or optometrist, a seeing eye
dog or a hearing dog, including its food
and its vet bills, the cost of getting
the treatment, rides, gas, and even a
hotel room if you have to stay overnight
for care, and help at home, an
attendant, a home health aide, or a
homemaker when you need it because of
age or illness. Picture a diabetic man,
his insulin, his test strips, his
lancets, the shoes his doctor ordered.
He has been paying for all of it for
years, and his food stamp file shows
none of it. He is not hiding anything.
Nobody ever asked him, and he never knew
to say. Go back to the widow one more
time. Her prescription co-pays come to
about $40 a month, and a neighbor
charges her $20 in gas money to drive
her to the doctor. That is $60 more. Her
food stamps go from 154 to about 181.
$25 to about 181. Her income never
changed. Her file did. And in about half
the states, there is a rule that makes
the medical part even easier. Seven, the
flat medical amount if your state has
one. Some states do not make you add up
every receipt. If your medical costs are
over $35 a month, they give you a set
amount instead, and you only claim your
actual costs if they are bigger. In
California, if your costs fall between
35 and $185 a month, you get 150 taken
off. In Texas, the set amount is 135. In
Georgia, it is 161. Florida and New York
do not use a set amount. So there, every
real cost you show them is what counts.
Here is who this helps most. Picture a
woman in Texas whose state already pays
her Medicare premium. All she has left
is about $50 a month in co-pays. Counted
the normal way, only $15 of that comes
off. With the Texas set amount, 135
comes off. Same woman, same co-pays. Her
food stamps go from about $58 to about
112. She only has to show that her costs
are over $35. One pharmacy printout can
do it. But a lot of people never even
ask for any of this because they are
afraid of one question on the form,
"What do you have in the bank?" Eight,
your savings, your house, and your
retirement account. This fear keeps more
seniors off food stamps than any rule
does. From October, a household with
someone 60 or older can have up to
in savings. And the home you live in
does not count toward that. Neither does
your retirement account. Some states
have dropped the savings test for most
households altogether. So picture a
couple with a paid-off house, an IRA,
and $3,000 in the bank. They assume they
are too well off to ask. On paper, they
may be well under the line. And if
everyone in your household gets SSI,
food stamps do not look at your savings
at all. So the bank account is not a
reason to stay at $25. The next question
is what you have to show them. Nine,
costs you know are coming count, too.
You do not have to wait for a bill to
arrive. The federal rule says the office
should count the medical costs you have
now and the ones you can reasonably
expect before your next review. So if
you take the same medicine every month,
or you know you have a dental
appointment coming, or your Medicare
drug plan premium is going up in
January, say so. The office does need
proof. For medical costs, it has to see
it before it counts it. So, gather it
now. Ask your pharmacy for a printout of
what you paid this year. They print it
at the counter. Keep the receipts from
the dentist and the eye doctor. Your
Social Security letter shows the
Medicare premium coming out. Your lease,
your property tax bill, and your
insurance bill show the house. If you
report a cost and they ask for proof,
you get at least 10 days to bring it.
Now, most people think they have to wait
for their yearly review to do any of
this. They do not. 10. You can report it
today and the clock starts. You can tell
the office about a new cost at any time.
You do not have to wait for your review.
And the federal rule puts a clock on
them. When a change raises your food
stamps, it has to show up no later than
the first payment issued 10 days after
you report it. Report a new medical cost
in the middle of a month and it can be
in the very next month's food stamps.
Picture a woman who sends her pharmacy
printout and her Medicare letter on the
3rd of November. 10 days later is the
13th. Her December food stamps should
already reflect it. If December comes
and nothing changed, she has the date on
her copy to prove when she told them.
One caution. If the office already gives
you a medical deduction and you report
that it went up, some states are allowed
to hold that increase until later,
closer to your next review. But a brand
new deduction, one that is not in your
file at all, they cannot sit on. So,
report in writing, keep a copy, and
write down the date. And if they still
get it wrong, there is a step most
people never take. 11. If the number
still looks wrong, you have the right to
a fair hearing. You can ask for one on
anything the office did in the last 90
days. And the rule goes further than
that. At any time before your next
review, you can ask for a hearing just
to say the amount is wrong. You do not
need a lawyer. You ask your state SNAP
office for a fair hearing, in writing if
you can, and you bring your papers. The
widow walks in with her Medicare letter,
her lease, her glasses receipt, and her
pharmacy printout. Those papers are the
whole case. At a hearing, someone
outside the office looks at the same
numbers. If the costs were real, and
they were reported, and the office left
them out, the hearing is where that gets
fixed. Asking out loud counts. The
federal rule says the request can be
spoken or written. So, saying, "I want a
fair hearing" on the phone is enough to
start it, though a letter gives you
proof. And you can have a relative or a
friend present your case for you. Many
legal aid offices help seniors with this
for free. Ask. And there is one date
that makes all of this more urgent than
it looks. 12. Why it has to be done
before January. The new Social Security
raise is announced in the middle of
October. In January, that raise is fed
into everyone's food stamps at once. The
federal rule allows it as late as the
second payment after the raise takes
effect, and the office has to tell you
if your amount goes down. But, only by
the day the smaller amount is issued.
That recalculation uses what is in your
file. If your Medicare premium, your
rent, your glasses, and your rides are
on file, the raise takes a few dollars.
If they are not, you start the new year
at the floor again, and the raise can
push you off the floor entirely.
So, here is the list, in order. This
week, write down every cost on the list
from this video that you pay, with the
amount. Before the end of October, ask
your pharmacy for a printout, and gather
your Medicare letter, your lease or
property tax bill, and your insurance
bills. Before the end of November, send
copies to your SNAP office, never the
originals. Ask in writing for the
medical and housing deductions to be
added, and keep a copy with the date on
it. When your next notice comes, check
that those costs are on it. If they are
not, ask for a fair hearing. $25 is not
the amount you are worth to the program.
It is the amount your file says you are
worth. Change the file. Everything here
is educational content and general
information only, and none of it is
legal or benefits advice. Deductions and
amounts differ from state to state and
can change. The widow's numbers are
rounded to keep them simple. Confirm
your own case with your state SNAP
office or a legal aid office. Take care
of yourself.

title: Every Senior Must Do This Before October 14: The 2027 COLA Raise Nobody Explains

segments.text: On the 14th of October, the raise for
social security, SSDI, SSI, and VA is
announced. And for a lot of people, it
will not be what it sounds like. One
widow will hear $50 on the news and keep
barely more than half. On SSI, the first
raised deposit comes with a catch. Most
people only find in January. On SSDI, if
you work even a few hours, a number you
live by changes that same morning, and
the phone calls start before lunch. and
two dates around the 14th decide how
much of that raise you actually keep.
One, what happens on the 14th of October
at 8:30 in the morning Eastern time, the
government publishes the September
inflation figure. That is the last piece
Social Security needs. And every year
from 2019 through last year, Social
Security announced the new raise on the
very same day. The raise is not a
decision by Congress. It is a formula.
Social Security compares prices over
July, August, and September with the
same three months a year earlier. And
however much prices rose, that is your
raise. September is the last piece,
which is why nobody can tell you the
number before that morning. And the
formula only goes one way. If prices did
not rise, the law says there is no raise
at all that year. It has happened
before. One number covers almost
everyone. retirement benefits, SSDI, the
disability benefit you earned by
working, survivors benefits, and SSI,
veterans are tied to it, too. The VA's
own words are plain. We are required by
law to match the percentage of cost of
living adjustments made to Social
Security benefits. But for disability
compensation, there is one catch, and it
sits with Congress. So on the 14th, you
will hear one percentage on every news
channel. Do not trust any number you
hear before that morning. Until Social
Security publishes it, anything you see
is a guess, but the percentage on the
news is not what reaches your bank. The
first bite comes out before you ever see
the check. Two, Medicare takes part of
it back, and that number comes later.
The raise is announced in October, but
the Medicare Part B premium for next
year is announced separately by a
different agency, usually in the fall
and in recent years in November. And for
most people on social security, that
premium comes straight out of the check
before it lands. This year, the premium
a month. The official projection for
next year is $29.50.
That would be $6.60 more taken out every
month. So say your raise works out to
$50 a month. If part B goes up as
projected, you keep about $43.40.
The headline says 50, the bank says 43.
There is one way around it. If your
state pays your Medicare premium for you
through a Medicare savings program, that
cut does not touch you at all. And
neither does the $22 you are paying now.
This year, if you live alone and your
income is under about $1,816
a month or about $2,455
for a couple, you may qualify for help
with the Part B premium. Some states go
higher, and there are savings limits,
too, so ask. Here is the date that
matters. Your state can take up to 45
days to decide. Apply after Christmas
and you can still be waiting when
January's premium comes out of your
bigger check. Apply this month and you
give yourself a real chance to have it
in place first. That is the first date.
The second one starts the very next
morning. On the 15th of October,
Medicare open enrollment begins and it
closes on the 7th of December. If your
drug plan or your Medicare Advantage
plan takes a premium out of your check,
next year's premium comes out of the
same raise. Your plan has already mailed
you its changes for next year. Look at
them and compare before the 7th of
December. After that, most people stay
in the plan they have for the whole
year, whatever it costs. And if you get
food stamps, Medicare is only the first
bite. Three, food stamps take another
part, and the warning can come with the
cut. If you get food stamps, the raise
is fed into your food stamp amount early
in the new year. The federal rule lets
the state adjust everyone at once
automatically, and it can be as late as
March. The state does have to tell you
if your amount goes down, but the rule
only requires that notice by the day the
smaller amount is issued. So for a lot
of people, the letter and the smaller
balance arrive together. Food stamps
take back roughly 30 cents of every new
dollar of counted income, a little more
if you also claim housing costs. On a
$50 raise, that can be around $15 a
month less in food stamps. Now add it up
for the widow from the start. Her raise
is $50. Medicare takes about 660. Food
stamps take about 15. She is left with
something close to $28 of the 50 she
heard about on the news. What softens it
is the same thing every time. Make sure
every cost that counts is on file with
your SNAP office before the end of
December before the new numbers are run.
Your Medicare premium, your pharmacy
bills and dental work, your rent or
property tax, insurance and heating.
Every one of those dollars on file give
some of it back. And even the $28 does
not arrive when most people expect it.
Four, when the raise actually reaches
your bank, the raise does not arrive on
the 14th. It arrives at different times
for different checks. If you get Social
Security Retirement or SSDI, the raise
starts with your January payment. Most
people are paid on a Wednesday and your
birthday picks which one. Birthdays
early in the month, the 1st to the 10th,
are paid on the 13th of January.
Birthdays in the middle, the 11th to the
20th, on the 20th of January. Birthdays
late in the month on the 27th. A smaller
group is paid on the 3rd of each month.
Mostly people who began collecting long
ago and people who receive SSI as well.
For them, January's raised payment lands
early on New Year's Eve because the 3rd
of January is a Sunday. If you get VA
disability compensation or a VA pension,
the new rates take effect on the 1st of
December, but the VA pays a month
behind. So, the December check is still
the old amount. The first payment at the
new rate arrives on New Year's Eve
because the 1st of January is a holiday.
Here is a woman on SSDI born on the
15th. She hears the raise on the 14th of
October and expects it in her next
check. It is not in November. It is not
in December. Her first bigger payment
comes on the 20th of January. Knowing
that ahead of time saves her 3 months of
wondering whether something went wrong.
And if you are on SSI, the date is where
the catch is. Five. If you get SSI,
here's what changes for you. This year,
the SSI federal amount is $994 a month
for one person and $1,491
for a couple. On the 14th, Social
Security will publish next year's
amounts raised by the same percentage.
The first SSI deposit with the raise in
it lands on New Year's Eve. It looks
like December money with a little extra
on top. It is not. It is January's money
paid early and it has to last all of
January. Spend it on the holidays and
there is nothing more until February.
And one thing stays frozen while your
check grows. The SSI savings line has
been 2,000 for a single person and 3,000
for a couple since 1989. And no raise
has ever moved it. A slightly bigger
check left to pile up reaches that line
a little sooner every year. If you are
near it, look at your bank before each
new month starts, not after. If you are
on SSDI instead, your trap is not the
deposit, it is your paycheck. Six, if
you get SSDI and you work a little. If
you are on SSDI and you earn some money,
there are two numbers you live by, and
both change every year. The first is
called substantial gainful activity.
This year it is $1,690
a month or $2,830 if you are blind. Earn
above that and Social Security can
decide you are able to work. The second
is the trial work amount. This year, any
month you earn more than $1,210
counts as a trial work month. Both of
those are published again on the 14th.
So, if you work part-time on SSDI, the
14th matters to you twice. Once for your
raise and once for the line you have to
stay under. Here is the trap. A man on
SSDI picks up extra shifts in December
because the store is busy. He did the
math against this year's limit. In
January, the limit changes. If he does
not know the new number, he can cross it
without meaning to write the new numbers
down on the 14th and check your hours
against them before January. And there
is a second group with a paycheck line
that moves the same morning. Seven, if
you are under full retirement age and
still working, if you started Social
Security early and you are still
working, there is a limit on what you
can earn before Social Security holds
some of your check back. This year, if
you are under full retirement age for
the whole year, the limit is $24,480.
In the year you reach full retirement
age, it is 65,160
counted only on what you earn before
your birthday month. Both limits are
published again on the 14th. Picture a
64year-old woman who took Social
Security early and works part-time at a
pharmacy. She earns about 23,000 a year
safely under this year's line. Her boss
offers her more hours in January. Before
she says yes, she should know next
year's limit because the raise in her
check does not move the line on her
paycheck. The new limit does. Once you
reach full retirement age, the limit
disappears and you can earn any amount.
Veterans have a line of their own and it
moves on a different date. Eight, if you
are a veteran, the VA pension rises
automatically. The law ties it to the
social security raise, so it goes up by
the same percentage on the 1st of
December. Disability compensation and
the payment to surviving spouses is
different. Those rise only when Congress
passes a bill for that year. Last year,
that bill was signed on the 25th of
November, 6 days before the raise was
due. This year's bill was still sitting
in committee in early October. So, if
you are on disability compensation, the
14th tells you the percentage you should
get. It does not guarantee it. Watch for
that bill in November. If it passes in
time, the new rate starts on the 1st of
December and the first check at that
rate arrives on New Year's Eve. If you
are on a VA pension, there is another
number to watch. The pension has a limit
called the net worth limit. And net
worth here is not only your savings. The
VA adds what you own to your income for
the year after certain medical costs are
taken off. Your home does not count and
neither does the family car. From the
1st of December last year to the 30th of
November this year, the limit is
A new limit takes effect on the 1st of
December. Picture a widow of a veteran
on a survivor's pension. Her house does
not count. Her savings have slowly grown
to about $140,000
and her income for the year is about
$18,000. Add them and she is at 158,000
under this year's limit, but only just.
If she gets a small inheritance or sells
something the VA did not count and puts
the cash in the bank, she can cross a
line she did not know was there. The new
limit on the 1st of December decides
where that line sits for the next year.
And if you also get social security or
SSI, your veterans check and your social
security can change in different months.
Write them down side by side so you can
see which month each one moves. Now,
most people plan to wait for the letter.
That is the mistake. Nine, how you will
be told and when. Social Security sends
a notice with your new amount. Last
year, the notice showed up online in the
My Social Security account in late
November, and the mailed letters went
out starting in early December. If you
are on Medicare, the exact amount you
will actually get after the premium came
with that December notice. You can also
choose to get that notice online instead
of on paper. Last year, the deadline to
switch was in the middle of November.
Think of a couple on two Social Security
checks. The letter arrives in December
and by then the holidays are on top of
them. The January rent is due and the
pharmacy has already raised its prices.
If they had written the percentage down
in October, they would have known their
January number for 2 months already.
That is what the 14th gives you if you
use it. But the 14th also brings
something else to your phone. 10. The
phone calls that arrive with every
announcement. The same morning the raise
is announced. The phones start ringing.
A voice says your raise has been
approved, but there is a problem with
your file and they need your social
security number to release it. Or they
can get you a bigger raise or get it to
you early for a fee. Social Security's
own inspector general warned about
exactly this in September. Social
Security does not offer to increase
benefits in exchange for money. Picture
how it goes. A woman in her 70s picks up
the phone the morning after the
announcement. The man is polite and
knows her name. He says her raise is
ready, but her file is missing a
verification. And he only needs her
social security number and date of birth
to release it. She has just heard about
the raise on the news, so it sounds
real. That timing is the whole trick.
They call when the raise is on the news
because that is when you are expecting
to hear about it. The raise is
automatic. You do not apply for it. You
do not pay for it. Nobody needs your
number to give it to you. If anyone
calls about your raise, hang up and call
Social Security yourself at 1
11. Three people, one raise. The same
percentage lands very differently
depending on who you are. A man on SSI
only, his raise comes on New Year's Eve
and it belongs to January. Medicare is
often paid for people on SSI through
their state, so the Part B change may
not touch him. But if he also gets food
stamps, part of his raise comes back out
of his card in the new year and his
savings line stays at 2,000. A woman on
SSDI who works a few shifts. Her raise
arrives with her January Wednesday
payment. Medicare takes its share from
her check. And on the 14th, she gets two
new numbers to watch, her raise and her
new work limits. If she plans her
December and January shifts against the
old limits, she can cross the new ones
without knowing it. A widow on
retirement benefits who also gets food
stamps. Her raise comes in January.
Medicare takes a few dollars of it. Food
stamps take more. She hears $50 on the
news and keeps a little more than half.
Three people, one announcement, three
different Januaries. So, here is how to
work out yours. 12. your own number at
the kitchen table before the 14th. Get a
sheet of paper and write three things at
the top. Your check this month, your
Medicare premium this month, and your
food stamps this month if you get them.
Next to them, leave a blank for the
raise. On the 14th, fill in the
percentage and turn it into dollars.
Last year, the raise was 2.8%. On a
check of $1,400,
2.8% is about $39 a month. Take your own
check and multiply by whatever
percentage is announced. then take off
what comes back out. About 660 if part B
goes up as projected and about 30 cents
of every new dollar if you get food
stamps. What is left is what you will
actually have in January. Then put the
dates on the wall by the phone. This
month, if your income is low, apply for
a Medicare savings program so it has
time to be in place before January.
Between the 15th of October and the 7th
of December, open the letter from your
drug plan and compare it with the
others. Before the end of December, send
your SNAP office every cost that counts
in writing and keep a copy. On the 14th,
if you are on SSDI or still working
before full retirement age, write down
the new work limits before you plan your
December shifts. In November, if you are
on VA disability compensation, watch for
the bill in Congress that carries your
raise. On the 1st of December, if you
are a veteran on a pension, the new net
worth limit takes effect. Know it. And
on New Year's Eve, if you are on SSI,
the deposit with the raise in it is
January's money. Put January aside
first. The 14th of October is the day
you hear the number. January is the day
you find out what it was really worth.
The difference between the two is what
nobody explains. This is educational
content and general information only,
not legal, tax, or benefits advice.
Amounts and dates are announced each
year and can change. And the examples
here are simplified. Check your own
numbers with Social Security, the VA,
Medicare, or your state office before
you act.

title: No SSI Check in November — Do This Before October 30

segments.text: There will be no SSI check in November.
The November money comes early on the
30th of October. Spend it as if it were
extra and the next payment does not
arrive until the 1st of December. That
is more than a month with nothing coming
in. And on the first of every month,
Social Security looks at what is sitting
in your bank. Leave too much there and
it can cost you a month of SSI. Here is
exactly how the payments fall between
now and January. What counts against you
and what does not, and what to do before
the 30th. One, the calendar as social
security printed it. SSI is paid on the
first of the month. When the first lands
on a weekend or a holiday, it is paid on
the business day before. The 1st of
November this year is a Sunday. So, the
November payment goes out on Friday the
30th of October. That means two SSI
deposits in October, one on the 1st and
one on the 30th, and none at all in
November. Then it happens again. The
December payment comes on the 1st of
December as normal. But the 1st of
January is a holiday. So January's
payment goes out on Thursday the 31st of
December. Two deposits in December and
none in January. There are two more
shifts worth knowing. If you were born
between the 1st and the 10th of the
month and your social security comes on
the second Wednesday, November's payment
arrives a day early on Tuesday the 10th
because the 11th is Veterans Day. And if
you get both social security and SSI or
you started social security before May
of 1997, your social security is paid on
the 3rd of the month. In December, that
group gets January's social security on
the 31st as well, the same day as
January's SSI. Two deposits, one day,
and both of them meant for January.
Picture a man who sees two deposits on
New Year's Eve and treats it as a good
month. Both of those were for January.
There will be nothing more until
February. Two, it is not extra money. It
is next month's money. Social Security's
own words are plain. Getting two SSI
payments in one month does not mean you
are receiving a duplicate payment. It is
the next month's payment early, and you
do not need to call them to report it.
Here's how people get caught. A man on
SSI sees two deposits in October and
feels for once a little ahead. He
catches up on a bill, buys his grandson
a birthday present, fills the freezer.
On the 1st of November, he checks his
account out of habit, and there is
nothing new. There will be nothing new
until the 1st of December. Count the
days. From the 30th of October to the
1st of December is 32 days. The payment
on the 30th has to cover all of
November, exactly as it always would
have. So before the 30th, do one simple
thing. Take your November bills, rent,
phone, electric, the pharmacy, and write
them down with the dates they are due.
When the money lands on the 30th, set
aside what covers them first. Treat that
deposit as if it said November on it
because it does. And the same in
December. The 31st of December deposit
is January's money. If you spend it on
the holidays, January is empty. Three,
the $2,000 line and when Social Security
checks it. This is the part that can
cost you far more than a tight month. To
get SSI, what you own that counts has to
stay at or under $2,000 for one person
or 3,000 for a couple. Those limits were
set on the 1st of January 1989. And they
have not moved since. And the federal
rule says Social Security makes that
check as of the first moment of the
month. Not the average, not the end, the
first moment. Whatever counts that is
sitting in your bank at that instant is
what they measure. Think of it as a
photograph of your bank account taken 1
second after midnight on the first of
every month. It does not matter that you
will pay the rent on the 3. It does not
matter that the money was only passing
through. What is in the picture is what
they see. So what happens to that early
payment on the 1st of November. Here is
the good news and it comes from Social
Security's own rule book. A payment that
arrives early because of a weekend or a
holiday is treated as the month it was
meant for. It is not counted as savings
on the 1st of November. It is first
looked at as savings on the 1st of the
month after which here is the 1st of
December. So the 30th of October deposit
does not put you over the line on the
1st of November. But whatever is left of
it on the 1st of December does count and
any money left over from earlier months
counts on the 1st of November as normal.
Picture a woman who is careful with
money. She gets $994 a month in SSI and
over the years she has put aside about
On the 1st of November, she is fine. Her
savings are under the line and the early
deposit is not counted. But say she
barely touches that early deposit in
November because she is used to living
on less. On the 1st of December, what is
left of it joins her savings. If $900 is
still there, she now has about $2,600 in
the bank that counts. That is over the
line and for that month, she is not
eligible. The fix is not to hide money.
It is to know your number before the
first of each month. If you are close to
2,000, spend what you need on things you
need. Keep the receipts and ask Social
Security or a legal aid office what you
can do before the first, not after.
Four, what does not count toward the
2,00. A lot of people on SSI are
frightened of that line for the wrong
reasons. They think everything they own
is added up. It is not. The federal
rules list what is left out. And the
list is longer than most people expect.
Your home does not count. And the rule
says regardless of its value, the house,
the land it sits on, the shed out back,
one car does not count. Again,
regardless of its value, as long as it
is used for transportation for you or
someone in your household, your
household goods and personal things do
not count. The furniture, the
television, the wedding ring, burial
spaces do not count. A plot, a
headstone, a vault, an earn, and money
set aside for burial expenses can be
left out up to $1,500.
Life insurance does not count if the
total face value of all the policies on
a person is $1,500 or less. And if
Social Security ever pays you a lump sum
of back benefits from SSI or regular
Social Security, the unspent part of it
is left out for 9 months after the month
you get it. So go back to the woman with
$1,700 in the bank. If she has been
meaning to pay for her burial plot or
the headstone for her husband's grave,
that money moves from the bank where it
counts into something that does not.
That is not a trick. It is how the rules
are written. What does count is mostly
cash, checking, savings, cash at home,
and things you could turn into cash like
a second car or stocks. That is the pile
social security looks at on the first of
the month. And for a couple, the line is
3,000, not four. A married couple who
both get SSI with 2,800 in the bank is
fine on the first of the month. If the
October 30th deposits are still mostly
sitting there on the 1st of December,
they can be over without spending a cent
more than usual. Five. What the early
payment does to your food stamps. If you
also get food stamps, the double deposit
does not double your income in October.
The federal rule says monthly income
shall not be varied merely because
weekends or holidays cause additional
payments to be received in a month. So,
your SNAP office should not count two
SSI payments in October against you.
Picture a widow who gets SSI and food
stamps. In November, a letter arrives
saying her food stamps will go down
because her income in October looked
twice as high. She did nothing wrong and
neither did her money. That letter is
the mistake and the rule is on her side.
There is one more piece of good news for
SSI households. If everyone in your
household receives SSI, food stamps do
not look at your savings at all. The
savings test is skipped for you. But if
you get a letter that seems to count two
payments in October, do not let it
stand. Call your SNAP office and ask
them to apply the rule on payments moved
by weekends and holidays. Six, if your
Medicaid is tied to SSI. For many people
on SSI, Medicaid follows the same rules
as SSI, the same income rules and the
same savings rules. So, the $2,000 line
on the first of the month can matter for
your health coverage, too, not only for
your check. Another reason to know your
balance before the first. Seven, the
raise and when SSI actually gets it. On
the 14th of October, Social Security
announces next year's raise. For SSI,
the federal amount this year is $994 a
month for one person and $1,491
for a couple. Next year's amounts will
be this year's raised by that
percentage. But the first SSI payment
with the raise does not arrive in
January. It arrives on the 31st of
December because that is January's
payment paid early. Here is the trap. A
woman sees the bigger amount land on the
31st of December and thinks it is her
December money with a bonus on top. It
is not. Her December money already came
on the 1st of December. The 31st is
January's money with January's raise in
it. Spend it in December and January is
empty again. Eight. The scam calls that
come with the raise. Every time a raise
is announced, the calls start. On the
21st of September, Social Security's own
Inspector General put out a warning. It
is titled, "Do not pay for promises of
increased social security benefits." The
warning describes it exactly. An
unsolicited call, advertisement, letter,
text, or social media message claiming
someone can boost, unlock, or maximize
your Social Security for an upfront fee.
And it is just as exact about the truth.
Social Security does not offer to
increase benefits in exchange for money.
Here is how the call sounds. A friendly
voice says the new raise has been
approved for you and you can have it
early or have it doubled for a small
processing fee of $49 paid with a gift
card. Every part of that is false. The
raise needs no fee, no form, and no
phone call. It simply arrives. So, if
anyone asks you to pay to raise your SSI
or to claim the new raise early, hang
up. If you want to check anything, call
Social Security yourself at 1
Nine. If you work, report it every
month. This one is for anyone on SSI who
earns a little, a few hours at a store,
some babysitting, a part-time job. In
September, the Inspector General
reported that it found 417,291
SSI recipients with at least one pending
earnings alert. It estimated Social
Security had paid about $1 billion it
should not have to 333,800
people. And it said about $344 million
of that can still be collected back.
Here's what that looks like at the
kitchen table. A man works a few shifts,
does not report the pay because it seems
too small to matter, and a year later, a
letter arrives asking for money back
that he already spent. The way to never
get that letter is simple. Report your
wages to Social Security every month,
even when it is a small amount. Keep
your payubs. If they ever ask, you can
show you told them. 10. Veterans, your
check moves, too. If you get a monthly
payment from the VA, federal law moves
it the same way when the first lands on
a weekend or holiday. So, VA payments
due on the 1st of November should arrive
on the 30th of October and January's on
the 31st of December. Think of a veteran
and his wife. His VA payment and her SSI
both land on the 30th of October, the
same Friday. It feels like a good week.
It is actually the whole of November,
arriving at once for both of them. The
same rule applies. Those are next
month's money. Budget them that way. 11.
Your calendar from now to February, one
date at a time. Put these on the wall by
the phone. The 14th of October, the
raise is announced. Nothing changes in
your bank that day. Write the new SSI
amount down when you hear it so you know
what to expect at the end of December.
The 30th of October, November's SSI
arrives. Before you spend a dollar of
it, set aside November's rent,
utilities, and medicine. If you get VA,
that payment should arrive the same day,
and it is November's, too. The 1st of
November. No SSI arrives. This is the
morning people panic. You will not
because you already set November aside.
Check your balance anyway. Whatever was
left over from before the 30th is what
counts on this day, the 10th of
November. If you are born between the
1st and the 10th and your Social
Security comes on the second Wednesday,
it arrives on this Tuesday instead
because of Veterans Day, a day early,
not a day extra, the 1st of December.
December's SSI arrives as usual. And
today is the day what is left of that
October 30th money starts to count
toward the $2,000 line. Check your
balance before this morning, not after.
The 31st of December, January's SSI
arrives with the new raise in it. If you
also get social security on the 3rd of
the month, January's social security
arrives today, too. Set January aside
the same way you set November aside. The
1st of January, nothing arrives. Again,
this is expected. The 1st of February,
SSI comes on the 1st as normal, and the
calendar goes quiet again. If you get
food stamps as well, January is also
when the raise is fed into your food
stamp amount. So, watch that balance,
too. So, here is what to do before the
30th of October. Write down every
November bill and its due date. When the
30th of October deposit lands, set those
amounts aside first. Check what you have
in the bank and make sure what counts
will be under $2,000 or 3,000 for a
couple on the 1st of December. If you
get food stamps and a letter counts two
payments in October, call and ask for
the weekend and holiday rule. If you
work, report your pay every month. And
if anyone offers to raise your benefits
for a fee, hang up. If you are close to
the line, remember what does not count.
Your home, one car, your household
things, a burial plot, and up to $1,500
set aside for burial. Then do the same
again before the 31st of December
because that deposit is January. The
money is not extra. It is just early.
The people who come out short are the
ones nobody told. This video is
educational content and general
information only. It is not legal or
benefits advice. Payment dates, limits,
and rules can change and your situation
may be different. Check your own case
with Social Security, your state
Medicaid or SNAP office, or a legal aid
office before you act. Take care of
yourself.

title: New Food Stamp Rules for Seniors — Do This Before They Hit

segments.text: New food stamp rules are on the way and
some of them are already on the
calendar. Your social security rays can
quietly shrink your food stamps and the
law says the state does not have to send
you a warning letter first. In some
states, the card will start saying no at
the register on the 1st of November. If
your benefits are stolen, Washington no
longer pays them back. And after the
11th of December, February's benefits
depend on Congress. Here is what is
coming, how it touches your own card,
and what to do before each one reaches
you. One, your raise can cut your food
stamps and nobody has to warn you. On
the 14th of October, Social Security
announces next year's raise. It arrives
in your check in January, and because
food stamps are worked out from income,
the raise is fed into that same sum. The
federal rule is written plainly. The
state adjusts everyone at once
automatically, and a notice of adverse
action shall not be used for these
changes. In other words, the amount on
your card can go down in January or
February, and the first you hear of it
is the balance. Here is why in plain
words. Almost every rule on this list
works through the same simple sum. The
government sets a top amount from
October, that is $36 a month for one
person and $562 for a couple. Then it
works out your income after certain
costs are taken off. That figure is
called your net income. And your food
stamps are the top amount minus 30% of
that net income. So every dollar of
income that counts takes about 30 cents
off your food stamps. And every dollar
of cost that is taken off your income
puts about 30 cents back. That is why
the costs you report matter so much.
Here are two households. Take a widow
living alone. Social Security pays her
$1,100 a month. Her rent is $650 and her
Medicare PartB premium, $22.90,
comes out of her check before she sees
it. First, everyone gets a standard
deduction, $217.
That leaves $883.
Now, her medical costs for someone 60 or
older, what you pay yourself for medical
care above $35 a month comes off. Her
Medicare premium alone takes about $168
off. That leaves about 715. Now her
rent, anything her housing costs more
than half of what is left comes off too.
And for older households, there is no
cap on it. Half of 715 is about 358. Her
rent is 650. So about 292 more comes
off. Her net income is now about $423.
30% of that is about $127. Take that
from 306 and her food stamps come to
about $179 a month. Now run the same
widow without telling the office about
her Medicare premium or her rent. Her
net income stays at $883. 30% of that is
about $265 and her food stamps come to
about $41. Same woman, same check, same
rent, $179 a month or 41 depending on
what is written in her file. Now a
married couple, both on social security.
$2,200 a month between them. Their house
is paid off. Property tax, insurance,
and heating come to about 500 a month,
and they each have a Medicare premium
taken from their checks. After the
standard deduction, they are at 1,983.
The line for a couple is 1,84.
If nobody counts their Medicare
premiums, they are over it and get
nothing. Count the two premiums and
about $371 comes off. They drop to about
under the line. Their housing is less
than half of that, so nothing more comes
off there. 30% of their net income is
about $484. Take that from 562 and they
receive about $78 a month. The
difference between nothing and $78 a
month was two Medicare premiums on a
form. These are rounded examples, and
your state may count some costs a little
differently, but the shape is the same
everywhere. What you report is what you
get. Go back to the widow. Say her raise
comes to $35 a month. Her income goes up
by 35. Half of her income goes up, too.
So, a little less of her rent comes off.
Run the sum again and her food stamps
drop by about $16. A $35 raise and about
16 of it comes straight back out of her
groceries. That is roughly a third of
the raise and a little more when you
also claim housing costs. It is not the
whole raise, but it is money gone from
her groceries every month for a year.
And nobody tells her why her card is
lighter. What you can do is make sure
every cost that lowers your income is on
file before the new figures are run.
Your Medicare premium, pharmacy bills,
dental work, glasses, hearing aids, the
cost of getting to appointments, rent or
mortgage, property tax, insurance on the
house, heating. If any of those went up
this year and your office does not know,
tell them now in writing before January.
That is what softens the drop. Two, the
$20 heating shortcut, and it now works
only for older households. This one is
good news and almost nobody knows it. If
your household receives more than $20 in
heating or cooling help from the energy
assistance program called lie heap, you
automatically get your state's full
utility allowance in that sum. That
allowance is a fixed amount the state
sets for heating and cooling and it can
take a large bite off your countable
income. Under the new law, younger
households lost that shortcut
completely. Only households with someone
elderly or disabled can still use it.
So, for you, a small heating payment can
lead to a bigger food stamp amount every
month. California makes it automatic. If
your household includes someone over 60
or with a disability, the county still
sends a small energy payment on its own,
so the shortcut applies. California also
changed the rule for younger households
back in November of last year. So, if
you hear a younger neighbor complain
that their utility deduction
disappeared, that is why, and it does
not apply to you. In other states, ask
your SNAP office two questions. Did I
receive a heating or cooling assistance
payment this year? And are you using the
full utility allowance for my household?
If the answer to the second one is no,
ask why? And ask how to apply for the
heating help that unlocks it. Three,
your internet bill no longer counts.
Some households used to have their
internet costs counted with their
housing costs. The new law ends that.
Counting internet costs now violates
federal law in the government's own
words. For most people, the chain shows
up at their next reertification, the
regular review of their case. If your
housing costs included internet, they
can come in lower, and so can your
benefit. So, when you are asked about
housing costs, list everything that
still counts. A lot of older people
write the rent and stop. Rent or
mortgage, property tax, home insurance,
heating and cooling, electricity, water.
Every one of those can move the sum.
Four. In some states, the card says no
to soda and candy. Starting on the 1st
of November, five more states stop
allowing food stamps to buy certain
drinks and sweets. Montana, North
Dakota, Ohio, South Carolina, and
Virginia. Montana's list goes further
than the others with high sugar drinks,
energy drinks, candy, and prepared
desserts. Ohio covers sugar sweetened
drinks, and all fountain drinks.
Virginia covers sweetened drinks.
Several states already did this earlier
in the year. Texas started on the 1st of
April with sweetened drinks and candy.
Florida started on the 20th of April
with soda, energy drinks, candy, and
prepared desserts. Indiana, Utah, Idaho,
Oklahoma, Louisiana, and Arkansas are in
as well. Wyoming, Kansas, and Missouri
follow in February, and Hawaii in April.
A federal court stopped the plans in
Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska, Tennessee, and
West Virginia. In California, New York,
and Georgia have no such rule. Here is
how it plays out. A man in Texas puts a
bag of oranges, a loaf of bread, and a 2
L bottle of soda on the belt and swipes
his card. The soda is not covered. He
either pays for it separately or puts it
back with the line waiting behind him.
Nothing else changes. Fruit, vegetables,
meat, eggs, milk, bread, coffee, all
still covered. If you live in one of
those states, keep those few items to
one side at checkout and have a little
cash or another card for them. Five, the
store you walk to may stop taking your
card. Stores that accept food stamps now
have to carry more variety of basic
foods, seven kinds in each of four
staple categories. They have until the
4th of November to meet it. The small
corner store, the little market near
your apartment, the place you can reach
on foot when you no longer drive may
decide it is easier to stop taking the
card. So ask them this week, are you
still taking EBT after November? If they
are not sure, find your second store
now, not on the day you are standing
there with a full basket and a card they
will not take. Six, November, December,
and January are paid. February is the
question. In September, Congress passed
a short-term funding law that runs to
the 11th of December. It keeps food
stamps going, and it has a clause that
lets payments due within 30 days after
that date go out, too. That covers the
1st of November, the 1st of December,
and the 1st of January. The first month
not covered yet, is February. Whether it
arrives on time depends on Congress
passing the next funding bill. So, from
January, if you can, keep a little extra
food in the cupboard, the things that
last. rice, beans, canned fish, peanut
butter, and watch the news around the
11th of December. Your SNAP office will
not call you about it. Seven, if your
benefits are stolen, Washington will not
pay them back. Thieves hide card readers
on store machines, copy EBT cards, and
drain the balance the day it lands. For
a while, the federal government replaced
stolen benefits. That ended on the 20th
of December, 2024, and it has not come
back. Picture two women, one in
Sacramento and one in Houston, both
robbed the morning their benefits
arrive. The woman in California can be
paid back. California moved to chip
cards reports theft down about 83% and
its counties still replace stolen
benefits, mostly with state money. The
woman in Texas has no federal
replacement to fall back on. So,
wherever you live, check your balance on
the day your benefits arrive. And look
at the card reader before you swipe. If
anything looks wrong, report it to your
state SNAP office that same day. Eight.
The work rule now reaches 64 and stops
at 65. Under the new law, adults up to
age 64 can be asked to work, train, or
volunteer about 80 hours a month to keep
food stamps beyond a short time limit.
Before that rule stopped much younger.
If you are 65 or older, you are exempt.
If you are between 60 and 64, there are
still exceptions. for example, a
disability or caring for a child under
14. States are rolling this out on their
own timing. California began on the 1st
of June. Here is who this catches. A
62-year-old man retired early after a
bad back living on a small pension. A
letter arrives about work requirements.
He assumes it cannot mean him and puts
it in a drawer. That is how people lose
benefits they were entitled to keep. If
that letter comes, do not ignore it.
Call and ask to be screened for an
exemption and send in anything that
shows a health condition, a doctor's
note, a disability award letter. Nine,
the easier application for older
households. Many states run a simpler
version of food stamps for households
where everyone is older. The federal
name is the elderly simplified
application project. It removes the
reertification interview and stretches
the time between reviews to 36 months.
Georgia calls its version senior snap.
If you dread the phone interview every
year, this is how you stop having it.
Ask your office whether your state
offers it and whether your household
qualifies. 10. In some states, you can
use your card at a restaurant. There is
a program that lets older people, people
with disabilities, and people without a
home use food stamps at participating
restaurants. It is called the restaurant
meals program, and only some states run
it. There is one rule people miss.
Everyone in the household has to
qualify. So, everyone has to be 60 or
older, disabled, or without a home. A
couple where both are 60 or older can
use it. A grandmother living with her
working son may not. If cooking has
become hard, ask your office whether
your state runs it, and which
restaurants near you take part. 11. What
counts as income and what does not.
Social Security counts. So, does a
pension, VA payments, SSI, and money
from a part-time job. All of it goes
into that sum. Your savings are
different. For a household with someone
60 or older, the savings limit from
October is $4,750,
and your home does not count toward it,
and neither do your retirement accounts.
Some states set the savings test aside
for most people altogether. So, if you
have a paidoff house and an IRA, you
have not ruled yourself out. Apply and
let the office do the sum. And one floor
worth knowing, if you qualify and your
household is one or two people, your
food stamps cannot drop below $25 a
month. 12. How to get your costs on file
before January. Knowing the costs count
is only half of it. They have to be on
paper in your file before the new
figures are run. Gather the proof first.
The letter from Social Security that
shows your Medicare premium being taken
out. A print out from your pharmacy of
what you paid this year, which you can
simply ask for at the counter. Dental
and eye bills, your lease or a rent
receipt, your property tax bill, your
home insurance, your heating and
electric bills. Then send copies, never
the originals, to your SNAP office in
the way your state accepts, online, by
mail, or in person. Keep a copy of
everything you send and write down the
date in the name of anyone you speak to.
And ask for one thing in return, a
written confirmation that your costs
were received and added to your case. If
your benefit drops in January and you
know your costs were on file, you have
something to point to. If they were
never on file, there is nothing to argue
with. Think of the widow again. The
difference between $41 a month and $179
was not her income. It was a pile of
papers she either sent or did not send.
So, here are the dates. The 14th of
October, the raise is announced. The 1st
of November, the soda and candy rules
start in five more states. The 4th of
November, stores must meet the new
stocking rule. The 11th of December, the
funding law runs out. In January, when
the raise is paid and your food stamps
are worked out again. Before January,
put every cost that still counts in
writing with your SNAP office. Ask about
the heating shortcut. Check that your
store is still taking the card. Check
your balance on the day it lands. And if
you are 60 to 64, answer every letter.
The raise is announced on the 14th of
October. Get your cost on file before it
is paid in January because after that,
the sum has already been run without
them. This video is educational content
and general information only. It is not
legal or benefits advice. Rules,
amounts, and dates vary by state and can
change. The examples here are rounded
and simplified. Check your own case with
your state SNAP office before you act.
Take care of yourself.

title: Something Is Changing at Costco — What Seniors Need to Know First

segments.text: Costco changed the rules this fall, and
most members are finding out at the
door. Send your daughter in with your
card, and she can be stopped at the
scanner. Order something through Costco
Next, and Costco is no longer the one
who handles it. Choose the wrong
prescription discount, and you can pay
more than you had to. Nobody mails you a
letter about any of it. Here is what
changed, what it can cost you if you
miss it, and what your card still gets
you. One, the card at the door is now
checked. At the entrance of many
warehouses, you now scan your card or
the barcode in the Costco app before you
can go in. Your card carries your photo,
and Costco's own rules say it plainly,
only Costco members may buy. So, the old
habit of handing your card to a son, a
neighbor, or a grandchild to pick
something up is exactly what the scanner
is built to stop. They can be turned
away, and it is not the clerk being
difficult. It is the rule. Picture how
it happens. You have a bad knee this
week, so your grandson takes your card
to pick up paper towels and your pills.
The card scans, but the photo on it is
you. He is standing at the door holding
a card that is not his, and the answer
can be no. He drives home with nothing,
and you still need the pills. The fix
costs nothing. Every membership comes
with a free household card for one
person 16 or older who lives at your
address. They go to the membership
counter, have their photo taken, and
from then on, they shop on your
membership with a card that has their
own face on it. If someone in your home
does your shopping for you, get them
that card before their next trip, not on
the day you need them. Two, Costco Next
is gone. Costco Next was the part of the
Costco website where you could buy
straight from outside brands, things the
warehouse never carried on its shelves.
In September, Costco closed it. Its own
customer service page now says, "Access
to Costco Next storefronts is no longer
available, and to contact the vendor
directly." Here is why that matters. Say
you ordered a suitcase through Costco
Next in August, and a wheel broke on the
first trip. The habit is to carry it
back to the warehouse because Costco
takes almost anything back. This one, it
will not. Costco's own page now sends
returns and warranty questions for those
orders to the company that sold them.
So, find the order email, find the name
of the company that shipped it, and deal
with them. Costco's own page lists those
companies and how to reach them. Costco
has said the most popular items will
move onto its regular app and website.
So, the next time you see them there,
they are sold by Costco itself. Three,
your groceries can come to your door. If
driving to the warehouse has become
hard, this is the change that matters
most. On its September earnings call,
Costco said its Uber Eats delivery is
growing from 17 states to the entire
country, and its DoorDash delivery is
expanding across the United States as
well. Think about what that means in
practice. Somebody who gave up driving
last winter used to wait for a son on a
Saturday or go without. Now, the paper
towels, the water, the chicken, and the
coffee can be ordered on a phone and
brought to the door. Two things to know
before you order. DoorDash asks for a
valid Costco membership at checkout.
Uber Eats does not. So,
>> a daughter who lives in another town or
a neighbor without a card can place the
order for you. It is still rolling out,
so not every warehouse offers it yet.
And the price you see on a delivery
screen is not always the warehouse
price. Look at it before you tap order
and compare it with what the warehouse
charges. For a few heavy items, paying a
little more to have them carried to your
door can be worth it. For a full cart,
it adds up. Know which one you are
doing. the warehouse stock check before
you leave home. The Costco app can now
show you whether your local warehouse
has an item and what it costs there.
Costco says the information can be up to
30 minutes behind, and items that are
out of stock are not shown at all. So,
if something does not appear, it is not
there today. Here's how that saves a
wasted trip. You want the same bag of
coffee you always buy. Before, you drove
over, walked the whole building, and
found an empty pallet. Now, you type the
name into the app at the kitchen table.
If it shows up, you know your warehouse
has it and what it costs. If it does not
show up, you stay home and try tomorrow.
And if you checked in the morning and
are leaving after lunch, check once more
before you get in the car because the
shelf can change in a few hours. Five,
the early hour and whether it pays for
itself. Executive members now get in
before everyone else. 9:00 to 10:00 in
the morning on weekdays and Sundays and
9:00 to 9:30 on Saturdays. Gold Star
members come in after that. For a lot of
older shoppers, that first hour is the
whole point. Fuller shelves, shorter
lines, a quiet parking lot, and time to
walk slowly without a crowd behind you.
The executive membership costs $130 a
year, 65 more than Gold Star. It pays 2%
back on most of what you buy up to
a year. So, add it up for your own
house. If you spend about $3,250
a year at Costco, that 2% comes to $65
and the upgrade has paid for itself.
Spend $5,000 a year and the 2% is $100.
So, you are $35 ahead with the quiet
hour on top. Spend $2,000 and the 2% is
$40. So, the upgrade costs you 25 more
than it gives back. Then it comes down
to whether that early hour is worth $25
a year to you. And if you try it and it
is not worth it, Costco refunds the
membership fee at any time. You can also
move back down to Gold Star and get the
upgrade fee back less any reward you
have already been paid. So, trying it
for a year carries very little risk.
Six, a doctor on your phone at a Costco
price. Costco members get member pricing
from Sesame, an online health service. A
video visit with a primary care doctor
is $29. A checkup is 72. A therapy
session is 79. And members get 10% off
Sesame's other services. You prove your
membership when you sign up. Picture
when it helps. It is a Saturday. Your
regular doctor's office is closed, and
you have a question that cannot wait
until Monday, but is not an emergency. A
video visit from your own chair for $29
can be the answer. It is a cash price.
So, before you use it, check whether
your own plan already covers a video
visit with your regular doctor for less.
And for anything that feels like an
emergency, that is still 911, not an
app. Seven, the prescription choice you
have to make. The Costco pharmacy is
open to everybody, member or not. And
Costco members can join the Costco
member prescription program at no extra
charge, which lowers the price on many
medicines. Here is the catch that costs
people money. That program cannot be
combined with Medicare or Medicaid on
the same prescription. It is one or the
other, and the choice is made one
prescription at a time. So, say you take
three medicines. For the first, your
Medicare drug plan might be the cheaper
way. For the second, especially if it is
a common generic, the Costco program
might be cheaper. You are allowed to use
Medicare for one and the Costco program
for another. What you cannot do is use
both on the same one. At the counter,
ask the pharmacist to price each
prescription both ways, and pick the
lower one for each. It takes a few
minutes, and nobody will do it for you
unless you ask. Eight, Costco is moving
into Medicare, but not yet. In August,
Costco and SCAN Health Plan, a Medicare
plan, announced a partnership for older
adults. They said they will launch a
range of senior insurance products over
the coming years, and that what they
offer is pending regulatory review and
approval. They did not name the states,
and they did not give a start date. So,
if a phone call or an advertisement this
fall offers you a Costco Medicare plan,
be careful. The announcement itself says
it is still coming. And Medicare's own
rule is simple. Medicare will never call
you to sell you anything. If somebody
calls saying they are from Costco or
from Medicare about a new plan, hang up
and look it up yourself. Medicare open
enrollment runs from the 15th of October
to the 7th of December. If a Costco plan
is ever offered where you live, it will
appear in the official Medicare plan
finder at medicare.gov. Until it does,
do not sign anything over the phone. And
ask your free SHIP counselor before you
change your coverage. So, here's the
list for your next trip. Get a household
card for whoever shops for you. If you
ordered through Costco next, contact the
company that shipped it. Try delivery if
the drive has become hard, and check the
price first. Use the app to check the
shelf before you go. Work out whether
the executive hour pays for itself at
what you spend. And at the pharmacy,
have every prescription priced both
ways. Costco got stricter at the door
and easier from home. And none of it was
announced to you personally. Now you
know which is which. This video is
educational content and general
information only. It is not financial,
medical, or insurance advice. And it is
not affiliated with or endorsed by
Costco. Policies, prices, hours, and
services change and can vary by
warehouse and state. Confirm anything
here on Costco.com
or with the membership desk at your own
warehouse before you rely on it. Take
care of yourself.

title: The FED Just Raised Rates — Seniors, Move Your Savings Before October 31

segments.text: On the 16th of September, the Federal
Reserve raised interest rates. Here is
what that does to you. The savings you
set aside for the roof, the car, and the
hospital bill keep losing value, while
your statement tells you they grew. Your
bank starts earning more on your money,
and nothing makes it pass a cent of that
to you. If you carry a card balance, it
can start costing you more within days.
Nobody is required to warn you. And the
people who made this decision expect to
do it again before the year is out. What
to do about it is simple. And one date,
the 31st of October, matters this month.
One, what this decision does to your
money. The day after the decision, what
the Fed pays banks on the money they
park with it went up to 3.9%. The
national average your savings account
pays you is still 3700s of 1%. Take a
retired couple with $60,000 in savings.
It is the money for the roof, the car,
the hospital bill nobody plans for. They
do not touch it. At the national
average, that 60,000 earns them about
$222 this year, but prices rose 3.4% in
the last year. So, the same 60,000 now
buys about $2,040 less than it did. They
lost more than $1,800 and their bank
statement shows a bigger balance than
last year. Now, look at the other side
of the counter. Their bank can leave
spare money at the Fed and earn $3.9% on
it. On $60,000, that is about $2,340
a year. The couple sees 222. Nobody is
required to tell them about the
difference. And it is not finished. The
Fed raised its target to between 3 and
3/4 and 4% because in its own words,
inflation remains elevated. 16 of the 18
people who set that rate expect at least
one more increase this year. They meet
again on the 27th and 28th of October
and the 8th and 9th of December. Every
increase can make that gap wider and
none of it has to reach the couple
unless they move. Pull out your last
statement and find three letters A, P,
Y. That is what you are being paid. Hold
that number next to the 3.9%.
The difference is your money working for
somebody else. Two, a high yield savings
account at a bank or a credit union.
This is for the money you want to reach
the same day. Online banks and many
local banks advertise savings rates far
above the national average and the APY
is printed before you open anything.
Compare it and check that the bank is
FDIC insured before you move a dollar.
Credit unions work the same way. They
are insured by the NCUA, the Federal
Agency for Credit Union unions, up to
just as the FDIC insures a bank. Three,
certificates of deposit and the latter.
ACD pays a fixed rate for a fixed time,
3 months, 6 months, a year. The average
is 1.73% and plenty of banks pay a great
deal more, so compare before you sign.
The worry with a CD is being locked out
of your own money. If you take it out
early, the bank charges a penalty. The
law does not set how much. Each bank
sets its own, and it has to tell you in
writing before you open the account. Ask
for that page and read it. A ladder
takes most of that worry away. Say you
have $40,000 you will not need this
year. Instead of one CD, you buy four.
10,000 for 3 months, 10,000 for 6,
10,000 for 9, and 10,000 for a year.
Every 3 months, one of them comes due.
You can spend it or roll it into a new
one-year CD at whatever rate is being
paid. Then if rates keep rising, you
catch them and you are never more than 3
months from cash. Four, treasury bills
bought straight from the government. A
treasury bill is a loan to the United
States government for as little as 4
weeks or as long as one year. You can
buy them yourself at treasurydirect.gov
from $100. To open an account, you need
a social security number, an address in
the United States, a checking or savings
account, and an email address. And you
have to be 18 or older. You can also buy
them through a bank or a broker. They
pay what the market is paying that week.
And you see the rate before you buy. And
for anyone in a state with an income
tax, this part matters. The interest on
a Treasury bill is taxed by the federal
government, but it is exempt from all
state and local income tax. interest
from your bank is not five Ibonds before
the 31st of October. An Ibond pays a
rate that follows inflation and the rate
you start with depends on when you buy.
Bonds bought through the end of October
pay 4.26% for their first 6 months and
part of that 90 hundredths of 1% is
fixed for the life of the bond. On the
1st of November, a new rate is announced
and nobody knows yet what it will be.
The bond earns interest from the first
day of the month it is issued and it is
issued when your purchase goes through.
So do not leave it to the last day. Buy
it a few business days before the 31st
at treasurydirect.gov.
Now the limits $10,000 per person per
year. So a married couple can buy 20,000
between them. You cannot cash it for the
first 12 months. And if you cash it
before 5 years, you give up the last 3
months of interest. So, this is for
money you will not need for at least a
year. Six, how a couple keeps well over
250,000 insured at one bank. Bank
deposits are insured up to $250,000 per
person per bank for each kind of account
ownership. Most people hear the first
half of that sentence and stop. The
second half is where the room is. An
account in your own name is one kind.
Your husband or your wife has their own
single account limit, another 250,000. A
joint account is a different kind again,
and each of you is covered up to 250,000
for your share. So, a couple's joint
accounts at one bank are covered up to
500,000. And an IRA is its own kind,
$250,000 for each of you. Add that up
for one married couple at one bank. Two
single accounts, one joint account, and
two IAS. That is up to $1.5 million
fully insured in one building. At a
bank, a trust account is covered up to
250,000 for each beneficiary, up to 1.25
million per owner. Credit unions have
their own rules for trust accounts, so
ask yours directly. Seven, what you owe
goes up, too, so pay that first. Most
credit cards and home equity lines
charge a variable rate tied to an index,
usually the prime rate. On the 25th of
September, the prime rate stood at 7%.
When that index goes up, the rate on a
variable credit card goes up with it.
And for that kind of increase, the card
company does not have to warn you in
advance. Your savings rate did not move.
Your card rate can move the same week.
So if you carry a balance, the order
changes. Paying down a card that charges
you 20% or more is a better return than
any savings account in the country. Pay
the variable rate debt first, then move
your savings. Eight, the extra interest
and your social security. Interest is
taxable income and your bank sends you a
form for it, the 1099 int. And when the
IRS decides whether part of your social
security is taxed, it adds half your
benefits to all your other income.
Interest is part of that other income.
So earning more is the right move and it
can nudge you toward that line. Two
things to know before you make it. The
new $6,000 senior deduction lowers your
taxable income, but it does not lower
the figure used for that test. So it
will not stop extra interest from
counting. and interest from treasury
bills is still federal income, so it
counts toward that test, too, even
though your state does not tax it. If
you are close to the line, that is a
conversation to have with a tax
prepareer before the end of December,
not in April. Nine, if your savings are
small, the bigger money is somewhere
else. If you do not have much sitting in
the bank, a better savings rate will not
change your year. These two programs
might. A Medicare savings program can
pay your part B premium for you. This
year, that premium is $22.90 a month.
