taken out of your social security before
you ever see it. Your SHIP counselor or
your state Medicaid office can tell you
in one call whether you qualify and
extra help lowers what you pay for
prescriptions. Next year, if you
qualify, your drug plan premium and
deductible can be zero. And each
prescription is at most $5.80 for a
generic and $14.40 for a brand name. You
apply at ssa.gov/extrahelp.
Here's what the moves can look like with
$70,000. Sitting in savings at the
national average, it earns about $259 a
year. Keep 20,000 where you can reach it
the same day in a high yield savings
account. Put 40,000 into a ladder, four
pieces of 10,000 in CDs or treasury
bills coming due every 3 months. And
10,000 goes into an Ibond a few days
before the end of October. If that money
earns around 4%, the same 70,000 brings
in something like $2,800 a year instead
of $259. Every dollar is insured, backed
by the government, or both. The only
thing that changed is where it sits. So,
here is the week. Find the APY on your
statement. If you carry a card balance,
pay that first. Move the money you need
close at hand into a high yield account.
Put the money you will not touch for a
year into a ladder or treasury bills. If
you want an Ibond at 4.26, 26% buy it a
few business days before the 31st of
October and check that every account is
inside the insurance limits. Three dates
to keep the 14th of October when the new
inflation figure comes out and social
security announces next year's raise.
The 27th and 28th of October when the
Fed meets again and the 31st of October
when the Ibond rate you can lock in
today ends. The Fed moved on the 16th.
What it pays the banks moved the next
day. Your savings are the only thing
still sitting where they were. This
video is educational content and general
information only. It is not financial,
investment, tax, or legal advice. And it
is not a recommendation to buy any
product. Rates change often, and your
situation is your own. Check the current
rates and terms with the bank, credit
union, or treasury directly, and speak
with a qualified professional before you
move your money. Take care of yourself.

title: 14 Programs. One Call. Most Seniors Never Hear About Them

segments.text: Your state has money set aside this year
for people your age. Help at home. Your
prescriptions, your heating bill, your
rent, rides to the doctor, meals. It is
already budgeted and the offices are
open. None of it is mailed to you. It
goes to whoever asks for it by name and
most people over 60 have never heard the
names. Here are 14 of them and one phone
call that screens you for all of them.
One, getting a family member paid to
take care of you if you need help at
home with bathing, dressing, meals, or
medicine. Medicaid can pay for that care
at home instead of in a nursing home and
in most states it can pay somebody you
choose, a daughter, a son, a niece, a
neighbor. It is called self-directed
care. You or the person acting for you
recruit the helper, hire them, and
supervise them and the state pays them.
In a national survey of state Medicaid
programs in 2025, every state that
answered allowed payment to family and
friends through at least one program.
Alaska was the one state with no
self-direction at all. A husband or a
wife is harder. 44 states allow a spouse
to be paid in some programs when the
care goes beyond what a spouse would
normally do. Indiana spells it out. It's
structured family caregiving program
lets a spouse be the paid caregiver.
Georgia runs the same kind of program
where a family member who lives with you
is paid to care for you. Here is the
part that stops people who should not be
stopped. The income and savings test is
applied to the person who needs the
care, not to the child doing the caring.
Your daughter's salary does not come
into it and there are waiting lists in
many states, which means the day you put
your name down matters more than
anything else about this program. If the
person who needs care is a veteran,
there is a second door. The VA pays a
monthly stipend directly to a family
caregiver for veterans with a service
connected rating of 70% or more who need
at least 6 months of personal care.
Since October of 2022, that is open to
veterans of every era. And in some
locations, the VA runs veteran directed
care where the veteran hires their own
family member or neighbor. Two, one team
for all of your care. PACE. PACE stands
for the Program of All-inclusive Care
for the Elderly. Your doctors, your
therapy, your medicines, your daycare,
your rides to appointments, and your
care at home, all run by one team
instead of build in pieces. You have to
be 55 or older, live in a PACE service
area, be certified by your state as
needing the level of care a nursing home
gives, and be able to live safely in the
community with PACE's help. If you have
Medicaid, Medicare's own website says
you will not pay a monthly premium for
PACE. PACE runs in 33 states in
Washington, D.C. At last count, there
was no PACE program in Alaska, Arizona,
Connecticut, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho,
Maine, Minnesota, Mississippi, Montana,
Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota,
Utah, Vermont, West Virginia, or
Wyoming. Everywhere else, the question
for your call is simple. Is there a PACE
program that covers my zip code? Three,
a way back home from a nursing home. If
you or your parent has been in a nursing
home and wants to come home, there is a
program built for exactly that. It is
called Money Follows the Person.
Medicaid money that was paying the
facility follows you home and pays for
the help that lets you live there. And
the transition support runs for a full
year. You need to have been in the
facility for at least 60 days in a row,
and short rehabilitation stays now
count. It runs in most states. At the
last federal update, six had closed
theirs. Delaware, Michigan, Mississippi,
Nebraska, Oregon, and Virginia. A family
that was told two years ago that the
move was permanent may have a road back
that nobody at the facility had any
reason to mention. Four, protection for
the husband or wife who stays at home.
When one spouse needs long-term care and
Medicaid is paying, the law protects the
one still at home. From the 1st of July,
2026, the spouse at home is guaranteed
an income floor of at least $2,705
a month. And they keep a share of the
couple's savings, between $32,532
depending on the state and the couple's
assets. The house is generally
protected, too, while the spouse is
living in it. Nobody going into care
should be told the family has to spend
everything first. Ask for the spousal
protections by name. Five, help with
your prescriptions. There are four doors
here, and most people only know one. The
first is extra help. If your income is
limited, this federal program can bring
your drug plan premium and your
deductible down to zero next year, and
cap each prescription at $5.80
for a generic and $14.40
for a brand name. You apply at
ssa.gov/extrahelp.
The second is your state. A handful of
states run their own prescription
program for older people on top of
Medicare. New York has EPIC for people
65 and older. New Jersey has PAAD, where
a prescription costs $5 for a generic
and seven for a brand name. Pennsylvania
has one also called PACE, with PACENET
beside it, and it is not the same PACE
as number two. Wisconsin has Senior
Care, Vermont has VPharm, Maryland,
Indiana, Delaware, Maine, Rhode Island,
and Missouri have programs, as well. In
most other states, the only state drug
program is for HIV medicines. Medicare
keeps the list state by state at
go.medicare.gov/spap.
The third is the drug company itself.
Many of the big manufacturers run
assistance programs for people with
Medicare drug coverage who meet their
requirements. Medicare lists those at
go.medicare.gov/pap.
The fourth is a community health center.
They set their fees by your income and
family size. Many have their own
pharmacy with discounted prescriptions,
and they serve everyone, even people who
cannot pay. You find the nearest one at
findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov.
Six, help paying the heating and cooling
bill. It is called the low income home
energy assistance program, LIHEAP for
short. It pays toward your heating or
cooling bill directly, and older adults
get priority. Many states also have an
emergency piece for a furnace that fails
in February or a dangerous heat wave.
The money comes to each state as a
block, and in many places it runs out
before the season does. Apply early, not
when the bill arrives. Seven, getting
your house fixed so the bill stays low.
This is separate from the bill program,
and it is worth more. The weatherization
assistance program sends people to your
home to seal it, insulate it, and make
the heating system safe, and the program
pays for the work. The Department of
Energy says it saves a household $372 or
more every year every year you live
there. You qualify with income at or
under twice the poverty line, or if you
receive SSI, and older people are given
priority. And for the roof, the rotten
steps, and the broken furnace, if you
are 62 or older, own your home, have a
very low income, and live in a rural
area, the USDA Section 504 program gives
grants of up to $10,000 over your
lifetime for repairs and safety fixes.
It also lends up to $40,000 at 1% over
20 years. Eight, your own utility and
phone company. Most gas and electric
companies run their own discount for
lower income or older customers and very
few advertise it. Call them and ask two
questions. Do you have a discount
program and am I on it? And the federal
Lifeline program takes up to $9.25
a month off a phone or internet bill for
households at or under 135% of the
poverty line or on programs like
Medicaid, SNAP, or SSI. Nine, a rent
rebate if you rent. Almost everything
you hear about help for older people is
aimed at homeowners, but your landlord's
property tax is built into your rent and
a number of states pay part of it back
to you. Most of these pay you a check
even if you owe no income tax at all.
Here is where they are. Pennsylvania
pays up to $1,000 to renters 65 and
older. Minnesota and Maine both have
one. New Jersey pays renters 65 and
older $700 and seniors are not filed for
automatically. You have to file the form
yourself before the state's deadline.
Connecticut pays up to $700 single and
900 married for renters 65 and older.
New York pays up to $375
when someone in the home is 65 if your
rent and income are low. North Dakota
pays up to $600 at 65. Montana starts at
62 and Michigan, Wisconsin, Vermont,
Colorado, Missouri, Massachusetts, Rhode
Island, Iowa, Utah, Arizona, New Mexico,
and Washington D.C. all have their own
versions. California has a renter's
credit, too, but it only lowers tax you
owe. If you owe nothing, it pays you
nothing. Most of these are claimed once
a year on a state form, which is why
renters miss them. They live with the
tax forms, not the benefit offices. 10,
food. For a household with someone 60 or
older, SNAP only counts your income
after deductions. Medical costs you pay
above $35 a month come off first, and
that includes your Medicare premium.
There is also a monthly box of groceries
for people 60 and older, the commodity
supplemental food program for incomes up
to 1 and 1/2 times the poverty line. And
in most states, there is a seasonal
program that gives you between 20 and
$50 a year to spend on fresh produce at
farmers markets. It is small and almost
nobody claims it. 11, rides. Your area
agency on aging funds transportation for
people 60 and older. Rides to the
doctor, the pharmacy, the grocery store,
dialysis, sometimes a van, sometimes a
volunteer driver, sometimes a voucher.
If you have Medicaid, your state has to
make sure you have a way to and from
your medical appointments. That is
written into federal rules. And if you
have a Medicare Advantage plan, ask your
plan whether rides are one of its extra
benefits. Giving up the car is not
really about the car. It is about having
to ask for a favor every time. A
scheduled ride does not need anybody's
favor. 12, meals. There are two kinds.
Meals delivered to your home for
somebody who has trouble getting out,
and meals at a senior center or
community site where you sit down and
eat with other people. Both are funded
under the Older Americans Act for people
60 and older. You may be asked for a
donation. The federal rule is plain.
Services shall not be denied because you
will not or cannot make a contribution.
For somebody who lives alone, a seat at
a table on a set day where somebody
notices if you do not turn up is worth
more than the lunch. 13, help for the
family member doing the caring. If your
son or daughter is looking after you,
there's a federal program for them. The
National Family Caregiver Support
Program. It pays for respite, which
means somebody comes and stays with you
so they can leave the house. It also
covers counseling, support groups, and
training. Adult day programs are often
funded through the same channels. And
this one does not use Medicaid's income
and savings tests. Programs under the
Older Americans Act are forbidden from
means testing. If your parent was told
they make too much for Medicaid, this
door is still open. 14, getting paid to
work or to volunteer. If you are 55 or
older, out of work, and your family
income is at or under 125% of the
poverty line, the Senior Community
Service Employment Program pays you to
work part-time at a local nonprofit or
public agency, about 20 hours a week on
average, at the highest the federal,
state, or local minimum wage while you
train for the next job. If the name
draws a blank on the phone, say title
five. It runs in every state. The number
And if you would rather volunteer, the
Senior Companion and Foster Grandparent
programs pay volunteers 55 and older
with incomes up to twice the poverty
line a stipend of $4 an hour. By federal
rule, it is not taxed and it does not
reduce or end any government benefit you
receive. These programs were cut back
and then restored in many states, so ask
whether there is one near you. Now the
people, they cost you nothing. Your
state's SHIP office gives free
one-to-one help with Medicare. You find
yours at shiphelp.org. Free legal help.
Under the same federal law, every state
funds legal assistance for people 60 and
older for things like a benefit denial
or a landlord problem. You can also
search for legal aid near you at
lsc.gov.
The Long-Term Care Ombudsman. Every
state has one. If anybody in your family
is in a nursing home or assisted living,
this is an advocate who investigates
complaints on their behalf and does not
work for the facility. And one more that
is a long road, so start early. HUD
Section 202 housing is for very
low-income households with someone 62 or
older, and the rent is generally set at
30% of your adjusted income. The waiting
lists are long and the only way in is to
be on one years early. Now the call.
Monday to Friday, 8:00 in the morning to
9:00 at night Eastern time. You can also
find them at eldercare.acl.gov.
Say this, "I am in my 60s or my 70s. I
live in this county. I live on about
this much a month. I own or I rent.
Please screen me for these programs."
Then read them the 14 names. At the end,
ask one more question. "Is there
anything else in this county that
someone in my situation usually
qualifies for that I have not asked
about?" No list can cover every county.
The person on the phone knows theirs.
Write down the name of the person you
spoke to and the date. And if the answer
is no, ask for the reason in writing.
That one page tells you exactly what to
fix. Most of these programs have an
appeal and the window is often short. So
read the date on the letter the day it
arrives. The people who end up with
these benefits are the ones who came
back after the first no. Look at how
this is built. The money is set aside,
the offices are open, and there is
nobody whose job it is to come and tell
you. So it reaches the people with a
daughter who knows the words and it
misses the people living alone who are
exactly who it was written for. Make the
call this week. Read the list. Write
down who you spoke to. This video is
educational content and general
information only. It is not legal,
financial, medical, or benefits advice.
Programs, income limits, amounts, and
waiting lists vary by state and county
and change often. Check your own
situation with your area agency on
aging, your state agency, or an official
government source before you act. Take
care of yourself.

title: Seniors: Don't Miss This September 30 Medicare Deadline — It Could Cost You All Year

segments.text: By the 30th of September, by law, a
letter has to be in your hands. It lists
every change your Medicare plan is
making for next year. Do nothing and
each one becomes your coverage on the
1st of January. Nobody will ask whether
you agree. Saying nothing counts as yes.
It comes from your plan, not from
Medicare, and it goes to everyone in a
Medicare Advantage plan or a drug plan.
Here are 10 things to check. Most
expensive first. One, find the letter or
get another one. It is called the annual
notice of change. It can look like any
other mail from your insurance company,
and that is how it ends up in the
recycling. It can come on paper or, if
you signed up for it, by email. If it
has not come or it went out with the
flyers, you are not out of luck.
Medicare's own handbook puts it in one
line. If you do not get these documents,
contact your plan. Call the member
services number on the back of your plan
card and ask them to send it again. And
by the 15th of October, your plan has to
give you a second document, the evidence
of coverage. The letter is the summary
of what changed. The evidence of
coverage is the whole contract for next
year. Every benefit spelled out. On
original Medicare alone, no letter
comes. What usually arrives instead is
the thick Medicare and You handbook. If
you are on original Medicare with a
supplement and no separate drug plan,
most of what follows is about your
neighbor, not you. Hold on for number
seven. That one is about you. Two, your
medicines. Every drug plan keeps a list
of the medicines it covers. That list is
rewritten every single year, and there
are four things that can happen to a
pill you take every morning. It can come
off the list, then the plan does not pay
for it at all. It can move to a higher
tier. Same pill, same pharmacy, same
doctor, and your share of the price goes
up because the plan moved it to a more
expensive shelf. This is the most common
change and the one people find out about
at the counter in January. It can pick
up a prior authorization. That means the
plan will not pay until your doctor
sends in a reason and the plan approves
it. Or it can pick up step therapy. That
means the plan wants you to try a
cheaper medicine first and only if that
one fails, will it pay for the one you
are already on. Somebody who has been
steady on a medicine for years can be
told to go back and try something else
first. There is one protection here.
Plans have to cover nearly all the drugs
in certain protected groups, like
medicines for cancer, HIV, depression,
psychosis, and seizures. And the ones
that stop a transplanted organ being
rejected. So do not skim this page. Take
the actual bottles out of the cabinet,
every one of them, and find each one on
next year's list. Look at the tier and
look for those two phrases, prior
authorization and step therapy. 10
minutes with those bottles is worth more
than anything else on this list. Three,
your doctors. If your plan uses a
network, the list of doctors and
hospitals inside it can change every
year. And it can change in the middle of
the year as well. The doctor you have
seen for 11 years can be out of the
network on the 1st of January. There is
no phone call. You find out at the front
desk when the receptionist tells you
they no longer take your plan. On
original Medicare, there is no network.
Any doctor who takes Medicare takes you,
anywhere in the country. In a Medicare
Advantage plan, the network is the
product. An HMO generally keeps you
inside the network and asks for a
referral before you see a specialist. A
PPO lets you go outside the network and
you pay more when you do. Find out which
kind you are in. Very few people know.
Here is the part that saves people real
grief. Do not trust the directory alone.
Directed fall out of date. Call each
office yourself, including the
specialist you only see twice a year,
and ask one question. Are you in the
network for this exact plan next year?
The person at the front desk will know
before the website does. Four, the most
you can be made to pay in a bad year.
Every Medicare Advantage plan has a
ceiling. Once you have paid that amount
for covered care in a year, the plan
pays the rest. It is a real protection.
But that ceiling can move every year,
and each plan sets its own. For 2027,
federal rules cap it at $9,850
a year for care inside the network, and
a plan is free to set it lower. Original
Medicare on its own has no ceiling at
all. Medicare's own handbook says there
is no yearly limit on what you pay out
of pocket. That is why most people on
original Medicare buy a supplement. So,
when you compare two plans, the premium
is the wrong number to look at. Add up
what you pay every month for a year,
then add the most you could be made to
pay if the year goes badly. A plan with
a tiny premium and a high ceiling is a
bet, and you are betting with your own
health. Five, your premium and your
deductible. The monthly premium and the
deductible can both change. So can what
you pay each time you see the doctor,
the specialist, or the hospital. On the
drug side, there is one number that is
on your side next year. Your total out
of pocket spending on covered drugs is
capped. For 2027, the cap is $2,400.
Once you reach it, you pay nothing more
for covered drugs for the rest of that
year. And the highest deductible any
drug plan is allowed to charge next year
is $700. And insulin stays capped at $35
for a month's supply of each covered
insulin with no deductible. Six, the
dates. The 30th of September is when the
letter has to reach you. That is not
your deadline. It is the plans. From the
1st of October, you can start comparing
next year's plans on the Medicare
website. On the 15th of October, the
window opens. From that day, you can
change plans, move between original
Medicare and a Medicare Advantage plan,
join a drug plan, or drop one. On the
7th of December, it closes. Anything you
change by then starts on the 1st of
January. After the 7th, the ordinary way
to change is gone until next October.
There is one more window and it only
works for some people. From the 1st of
January to the 31st of March. If you are
already in a Medicare Advantage plan,
you get one change. One. You can move to
a different Medicare Advantage plan or
go back to original Medicare and pick up
a drug plan. If you are on original
Medicare in January, that window is not
yours. Seven. The one door that may not
open again. Everything above can be
undone. You can change plans every
autumn for the rest of your life. This
cannot always be undone. Going from
original Medicare into a Medicare
Advantage plan is easy. Going back is
easy, too, on paper. The hard part is
the supplement you need once you are
back. When you first had part B at 65 or
older, you had a 6-month window when any
supplement company had to sell you a
policy, no health questions asked. That
window happens once. It does not come
back every year.
>> Outside it, unless your state gives you
more,
>> the company can ask about your health,
charge you more for it, or turn you
down. Medicare's own guide says there is
no guarantee an insurance company will
sell you a policy if you do not meet
their medical underwriting requirements.
So, picture somebody who chose a
Medicare Advantage plan at 65, which is
a perfectly reasonable choice. At 76,
their health has changed and they they
to go back. The reason they want to
leave is the very reason they can be
refused. There are ways through. If you
joined a Medicare Advantage plan for the
very first time, and it has been less
than 12 months, you are holding a trial
right. You can go back to original
Medicare on any day of the year, and the
supplement companies have to sell to
you. If you dropped a supplement to try
Medicare Advantage for the first time,
the same 12 months can get you your old
policy back if that company still sells
it. If your plan leaves your area or
ends its contract, that opens the door,
too. And some states give you more than
the federal rules do. New York,
Connecticut, and Massachusetts make
companies sell a supplement all year,
whatever your health. Several other
states let people who already have a
supplement switch around their birthday.
Your state's free counseling office can
tell you which rules are yours. If you
have ever thought you might want
original Medicare with a supplement one
day, find out now whether you are inside
a trial right. Not in 5 years when the
answer may be no. Eight, when the plan
says no. A denial is not the end of it.
There are three tools, and almost nobody
uses them. The first is the transition
supply. When you join a new plan, or
your plan changes its list, and a
medicine you already take is not
covered, the plan generally has to give
you a one-time fill of at least a month
supply within your first 90 days.
So, if the pharmacy tells you in January
that a medicine is not covered, do not
pay the full price at the counter. Ask
for the transition fill by name, and use
that month to sort out the rest. The
second is an exception. If a medicine
you need is not on the list, or it sits
on a tier you cannot afford, or it has a
step your doctor says is wrong for you,
your doctor can ask the plan for an
exception. Once the plan has your
doctor's statement, it has to decide
within 72 hours, or within 24 hours if
waiting could seriously harm your
health. The third is the appeal. If the
answer is still no, you have 60 days
from the day you receive the written
decision to appeal. The plan has to
answer a drug appeal within 7 days or
within 72 hours on the fast track. In a
Medicare Advantage plan, your doctor can
ask for a fast decision on medical care
as well. And if the plan still says no,
the appeal can go further to a reviewer
outside the plan entirely. So, when a
plan says no, do not accept it quietly
and pay. Call your doctor's office, ask
them to file, and ask for the fast track
if waiting would hurt you. Nine, the
phone calls and who to trust. From the
middle of October, the advertising does
not stop. Television, mail, phone calls.
A lot of it is dressed up to look
official and it is not. Here is the
rule. Medicare will never call you to
sell you anything and it will never turn
up at your door. Plans and agents are
not allowed to cold call you, send robo
calls, or text you about a plan unless
you ask them to. So, a call you did not
ask for is somebody breaking the rules
or somebody who is not an agent at all.
Nobody legitimate needs your Medicare
number or your bank details on a call
you did not make. If the phone rings,
hang up. If you want to talk, you call.
Use the number on the back of your plan
card or 1-800-MEDICARE, which is
An agent is paid by the plan you join.
That does not make every agent
dishonest. It does mean the incentive is
there. And the advertisements with the
cards full of money and the extra
allowances are describing real features
of real plans. What they leave out is
the network, the permission rules, and
what happens in a bad year. Those never
fit in 30 seconds. There is one place to
get advice with nothing for sale. Every
state has a free Medicare counseling
office called SHIP. You find yours at
shiphelp.org. It calls itself a trusted
unbiased source, and it costs you
nothing.
They will sit down with your list of
medicines and your list of doctors and
run the comparison with you.
If you are a veteran, two things. With
Tricare for Life, you need Part A and
Part B to keep your Tricare, and you do
not need a separate Medicare drug plan.
With VA drug coverage, there is no
penalty for waiting on a Medicare drug
plan as long as you joined within 63
days of losing that VA coverage. Bring
your card to the SHIP meeting either
way. 10. The money you may be leaving on
the table.
There is a federal program called Extra
Help. For people with limited income, it
lowers what you pay for your drug plan.
Next year, if you qualify, your drug
plan premium and deductible can be zero,
and each prescription is at most $5.80
for a generic and $14.40
for a brand name. If a purple letter
from Medicare has ever arrived at your
house, you already qualify
automatically. Separately, your state
runs Medicare Savings Programs, which
can pay your Part B premium for you.
You can apply for both at any time of
year. They are not tied to October. You
start at ssa.gov/extrahelp,
and the same application can start the
state program as well. And once you have
Extra Help, the calendar loosens for
you. You can change your drug coverage
once a month all year, including leaving
a Medicare Advantage plan to go back to
Original Medicare with a standalone drug
plan. And one more. For anyone paying
the higher Part B premium because of
income from 2 years ago, if that income
has since stopped because you stopped
working, cut back your work, or lost
your husband or your wife, there is a
form called SSA-44.
It asks Social Security to use your
income now instead. Divorce, marriage,
and losing a pension count, too. So,
here is the work, and it is one
afternoon. Take one sheet of paper and
write three lists. Every medicine you
take with the dose,
every doctor you actually see, including
the ones you see once a year, and what
you paid this year in premiums and
deductibles. With that one sheet, the
comparison is quick on the Medicare Plan
Finder at medicare.gov, or you can do it
sitting next to a FreeShip counselor.
Put in your real medicines and the
pharmacy you really use, and compare
what each plan costs you, not just the
monthly premium. Two plans with the same
premium can land a long way apart once
your own prescriptions go through them.
And the pharmacy matters. Many plans
charge less at their preferred
pharmacies, so the same plan can cost
you less just by changing where you
fill. Then do the rest before the 7th of
December. Now, look at how this is
built. The letter goes out on time. It
is written in the language of a
contract. It comes in an envelope that
looks like junk mail, and it lands in a
month when you have no deadline of your
own. The plan has done its legal duty
the day it goes in the mail. Somebody
with a son or a daughter who handles
this does fine. Somebody living alone at
82 opening that envelope at the kitchen
table is the one it catches. And every
year, silence is taken as agreement to
changes nobody explained. Doing nothing
is the easiest thing you can do in
October. It is also the most expensive.
That combination is not a coincidence.
Find the letter, fill in the sheet, get
it done before the 7th of December,
because on the 8th, whatever is written
in that envelope is your next year.
This video is educational content and
general information only. It is not
medical, insurance, legal, or financial
advice, and it is not a recommendation
about any plan or company. Every plan is
different, and the rules and amounts
change every year. Before you change
anything, check your own situation with
your plan on the official Medicare
website, by calling 1-800-Medicare, or
with your state's free SHIP counselor.
Take care of yourself.

title: New Food Assistance Rules for Seniors Starting This October 1 (One Erases Your Old Denial)

segments.text: If you are 60 or older, and you were
ever turned down, told your income was
too high, that answer was measured
against numbers that expire at midnight
on the 30th of September. Apply in
October, and your household is measured
against the new ones. The new numbers do
not care what the old ones said. On the
1st of October, every number that
decides whether you get help with
groceries is thrown out and replaced
with a bigger one. And the office that
turned you down will not ring you on the
1st of October to tell you the line
moved. The program is SNAP. Most people
still call it food stamps. From October,
a person living alone can receive up to
$306 a month on a card, and a married
couple up to $562.
For one person, that is $3,672
across a year. That is a winter of
heating. That is a year of car
insurance. Fewer than four in 10
Americans over 65 who qualify for it are
collecting it. If you ever walked out of
that office feeling foolish for asking,
that feeling came from a chart that was
never written for you. Here are the
rules that change on the 1st of October,
and the ones that have always leaned
your way once you turn 60. Not one of
them is applied unless you ask for it.
One, the old denial does not follow you.
A SNAP decision is not a verdict on you.
It is the answer to one question asked
with one year's numbers. Every October,
those numbers are replaced by law. And
when they are, your household can be
measured again from the beginning. A
denial for income is not a penalty. It
does not sit in a file waiting to count
against you. You can walk in and apply
again, and the application is weighed
against the numbers in force on the day
you file. And if your no arrived
recently, you have a second route. The
federal rules give you 90 days to ask
for a fair hearing on any action taken
on your case. The 90 days run from the
action, not from the day you finally
opened the envelope. If there is a
denial letter in a drawer, look at the
date on it this week. Two, you are
measured once, not twice. Most
households applying for SNAP have to
pass two income tests. The first looks
at everything coming in before a single
dollar is taken off. That is the gross
test. The second looks at what is left
after the deductions. That is the net
test. Fail either one and a younger
household is If anyone in your household
is 60 or older, the gross test does not
apply to you. The federal rule says it
in one sentence. Households which
contain an elderly or disabled member
shall meet the net income eligibility
standards. The net one. Only the net
one. So, the income chart you found on a
website, the figure your neighbor
quoted, the number that made you decide
not to bother, may well be the gross
chart. And the gross chart is not your
chart. From the 1st of October, the net
limit rises to $1,330
a month for one person and $1,804
for a couple. And that is measured after
everything that follows has come off.
Three, your medical bills come off your
income. This is the rule that moves more
older households from no to yes than any
other. And it is the one people claim
the least. Once someone in your
household is 60 or older, what they
spend out of their own pocket on medical
care above $35 a month comes straight
off the income you are measured on. And
the list of what counts is long. Doctor
visits and dental work, prescriptions,
over-the-counter medicine when a doctor
or another qualified health professional
has approved it, insulin, dentures and
hearing aids, eyeglasses from an eye
doctor or an optometrist, medical
supplies and equipment, nursing care and
a home health aid, the cost of getting
to your appointments and back, and one
line almost everybody misses, Medicare
premiums. Your Part B premium comes out
of your Social Security before the
deposit ever reaches the bank. You never
hold that money, so you never think of
it as something you spend. The program
counts it anyway. It is named in the
federal rule in two words, Medicare
premiums. For 2026, the standard Part B
premium is $202.90
a month. That one line on its own clears
the $35 for almost everybody on Medicare
before a single pharmacy receipt is
counted. Four,
your housing costs come off with no
ceiling.
Rent or mortgage, property taxes,
insurance on the house, heating,
cooling, electricity, water. When those
costs add up to more than half of what
is left of your income after the other
deductions, everything above that half
comes off as well. For most households,
there is a hard limit on how much. From
the 1st of October, that limit rises to
$769 a month. Spend more than that on
keeping a roof over your head, and the
rest simply does not count. For a
household with someone 60 or older,
there is no limit. None. The federal
rule applies the cap only to households
that do not contain an elderly or
disabled member. Every dollar of the
excess comes off. Think of an older
house in a cold state with a heating
bill that doubles every January. The
young family two doors down stops
getting credit at $769.
The house with a 67-year-old in it keeps
going. Every dollar of that January bill
is counted in its favor. Five, you can
keep more savings and your biggest
assets were never counted at all. From
the 1st of October, the savings limit
for a household with someone 60 or older
rises from $4,500
For everyone else, it stays where it was
at 3,000. And look at what is left out
entirely, your home and the land around
it, retirement accounts, the IRA and the
401k, the cash value of a pension. So,
somebody who owns their house outright
and has a pension behind them, can sit
comfortably inside that limit. The
program is not measuring what you built
over a lifetime. It is measuring what is
in the checking account this month. Some
states go further and set the savings
test aside for most applicants
altogether. Your state office can tell
you which kind of state you live in with
one phone call. Six, a bigger slice
comes off the top. Before anything else
is counted, every household gets a
standard deduction. From the 1st of
October, it rises to $217
a month for a household of one, two, or
three people. It comes off
automatically. You do not have to prove
a thing to get it. Seven, the benefit
itself goes up. The most a single person
can receive rises from $298 a month to
306. For a couple, from 546
And the smallest amount a qualifying
household of one or two people can
receive becomes $25 a month. Here is
what those seven rules do to one
household, a married couple, 72 and 70.
Between two social security checks and a
small pension from the county, $2,600
comes in every month. Somebody glances
at that and says they are over the line.
For a younger couple, they would be. The
gross limit for two people from October
But, they are not a younger couple, and
the gross test is not theirs. Take off
the standard deduction, $217.
They are at 2,383.
Now the medical costs, two Part B
premiums, a little over $400 between
them, $60 of prescriptions, around $466
in all. Everything above $35 comes off,
and they are down to about 1,952.
Now the house, property tax, insurance,
and the winter utility bills come to
a month. Half of what is left of their
income is about $976.
Everything above that, about $424,
comes off. They are now measured at
around $1,528
a month. The line for a couple is
They qualify. The same two checks, the
same pension, the same bank account. The
only thing that changed is that somebody
finally took the deductions. When
somebody tells you that you earn too
much, what it usually means is that
nobody ever subtracted anything. So,
here is the work, and none of it takes
more than an afternoon. First, fill one
envelope. Every pharmacy receipt, the
notice that shows your Medicare premium,
dental bills, the receipts for hearing
aids and glasses, what it costs you to
get to appointments. That envelope is
the single thing that moves most
households from over the line to under
it. Second, apply through your own state
SNAP agency. Not a website offering to
check for you. Every state runs its own
application, and only the state's own
office can say yes. Third, if getting
there is hard, name somebody to do it
for you. The federal rules let a person
from outside your household act as your
authorized representative, fill in the
application, and carry it through on
your behalf. That is written into the
rules. It is not a favor anybody is
doing you. Fourth, when you apply, say
these words out loud. Someone in this
household is 60 or older. Then ask two
questions. Was the medical deduction
taken, and were our housing costs
counted without the cap? Ask to see the
figures on paper. Fifth, if you were
turned down in the last 90 days, find
that letter and read the date. You may
still be inside the window to ask for a
fair hearing. And whether you are or
not, an application in October is
measured against the new numbers. The
calendar is on your side this time. On
the 30th of September, a household
sitting just over the line is over it.
On the 1st of October, the same
household, the same checks, the same
bills, is measured against a higher
line, a bigger deduction, and a higher
savings limit. A "No" you were given
last year was an answer to last year's
numbers. Those numbers are gone. This is
general information, not legal or
benefits advice. The figures here are
the federal numbers for the 48 states
and Washington, D.C. for the year that
begins on the 1st of October 2026.
Alaska and Hawaii use their own, and
your state may add rules of its own.
Confirm your figures with your state
SNAP office before you apply or appeal.
Somebody you know was told they make too
much for this. Send them this video
today.

title: NEW TAX RATES WILL SHOCK AMERICA IN 2027 — And Seniors Are The Target

segments.text: Hello friends. Every number in the
federal tax code moves every year. The
brackets move, the standard deduction
moves, the extra amount you get for
turning 65 moves. Congress wrote that
into the law on purpose so that
inflation does not quietly raise your
taxes while you are standing still. They
indexed all of it except for four
numbers and those four decide whether
your Social Security gets taxed. They
were set in 1983 and 1993.
Ronald Reagan was in the White House for
the first pair. They have never been
adjusted. Not once, not for inflation,
not for anything through every
administration since. I want to say
something before I show you how it
works. If you are 65 or older and you
have ever sat at your kitchen table with
a form in front of you and felt like
this whole system was built to confuse
you on purpose, I want you to know that
the feeling is not you getting slower.
There is a line in the tax code that
proves it and I'm going to show it to
you in a moment. Today I'm going through
three things. The four numbers that have
not moved in 40 years, how to work out
in five minutes which side of them you
are standing on and the three things
that can still be done before the 31st
of December, which is the last day
anything about this year can be changed.
Let us start with what happens every
January. One, what happens every
January? Your cost of living adjustment
arrives. Your Social Security check goes
up. That adjustment exists for one
reason. To keep you level. To make sure
that when bread and gas and electricity
go up, your check goes up with them. So
you are standing in the same place you
were standing the year before. That is
what it is for. Now, here's the question
nobody asks about it. Your check went
up, so did the tax brackets, but they
are calculated from different things at
different times by different formulas
and nobody ever designed them to match.
Most years they do not match. When your
check rises faster than the brackets do,
a piece of your income ends up above a
line it was not above last year. Nobody
will write to you about it. There is no
letter and no phone call. You did not
get a raise, your rent did not fall,
your groceries did not get cheaper.
Nothing about your life improved. A cost
of living adjustment arrived, which
exists to keep you level, and it moved
you into territory where more of your
money is taxable. Nobody has to vote for
that. Nobody has to announce it. There
is no bill with anybody's name on it.
Three. And now the part that belongs to
you and to nobody else. Everything I
have just described happens to your
children, too. Their brackets move,
their income moves. It works the same
way for them. This next part does not
touch them at all. Whether your Social
Security is taxed does not depend on the
brackets. It depends on a separate
figure called provisional income. Your
adjusted gross income plus any
tax-exempt interest plus half of your
Social Security. If that total is over
$25,000 as a single person or over
32,000 as a married couple, part of your
benefit becomes taxable. And there is a
second line above that one, which almost
nobody mentions. Cross 25,000 as a
single person and up to half your
benefit becomes taxable. Keep going past
34,000 and it rises to 85%. For a
married couple, the second line sits at
44,000. 85% of a benefit you paid into
out of every paycheck you ever earned
for 40 or 50 years with money that was
already taxed the first time. And I want
to be exact about what that means
because it is the thing people get wrong
and it changes the number in your head.
It does not mean 85% of your check
disappears. It means up to 85% of your
benefit gets added to the pile of income
they tax you on. What you actually pay
on that pile depends on your bracket.
So, the damage is real and it is smaller
than the panic. Know which one you are
dealing with before somebody sells you
something to fix it. Now, hear the date
on those numbers. $25,000 was set in
Ronald Reagan was in the White House.
The 32,000 and the higher pair came in
Not one of them has been adjusted since.
Not once. Not for inflation, not for
anything. Every other figure in the tax
code moves every year automatically
because Congress wrote that into the
law. The brackets move, the standard
deduction moves, the extra amount you
get for turning 65 moves. Congress
indexed all of it. They did not index
the one line that decides whether your
benefits get taxed. So, every year your
cost of living adjustment arrives. Half
of it counts toward provisional income
and the line it is measured against sits
exactly where it sat when a stamp cost
20 cents. That is not an accident that
lasted 40 years. Four, find out where
you are standing. Nobody is going to
tell you this. The Social Security
Administration will not write to you
about it. Your bank will not mention it.
So, you are going to work it out
yourself at your own table and it takes
5 minutes. Pull out last year's tax
return. Your adjusted gross income is on
the front page. Add any tax exempt
interest. Look for it rather than assume
there is none because that is the line
people miss. Then add half of what
Social Security paid you for the year.
That figure is on the form they send
every January, the one marked SSA-1099.
That total is your provisional income.
Single, the line is $25,000.
Married filing jointly, 32,000. Now,
look at the distance between your number
and that line. That distance is your
entire margin and next year's adjustment
eats into it automatically without
anybody asking you. Somebody who sat
$400 under that line last year maybe
over it this year. Nothing will arrive
in the post to tell them. They will find
out when the return is prepared and by
then the year is closed. Let me put a
real person through it because the
numbers sound harmless until you watch
it happen to somebody. A widow lives
alone, Social Security pays her a little
over $22,000 a year. She also has a
small pension from the school district
she worked at, about 14,000. So, she
takes the 14,000 of pension. She adds
half the Social Security, which is
11,000. Her provisional income is
25,000. She is standing exactly on the
line. She has done nothing wrong. She is
not wealthy. She did not take a
windfall. She worked, she retired, and
she is living on what those two decades
of paperwork produced. Now, the cost of
living adjustment arrives in January.
Her benefit goes up. Half of the
increase lands in provisional income and
she is over. Nobody informed her. There
was no notice, no letter, no phone call.
The first she will hear of it is when
somebody prepares her return and tells
her that a piece of her Social Security
is now taxable income. That is what this
looks like in a real house and there are
millions of her. And there is one more
reason that line matters more than the
tax on it. Adjusted gross income is not
only used to decide whether your
benefits get taxed. It is the same
number Medicare looks at to set what you
pay for part B and part D. They look
back two years. So, the income you
report for this year sets your Medicare
premium two years from now. That means
one decision made in December, a
withdrawal taken in the wrong year, a
conversion done without looking can move
two separate things at once. What you
owe in April and what Medicare takes out
of your check in two years time. Most
people never connect those two. They are
the same number, five. Three things that
can still be done before the 31st of
December. The first, the timing of any
withdrawal you control. If you are
taking money from an IRA or a 401K
beyond your required minimum, the year
you take it decides which year's
provisional income it lands in. December
and January are two different tax years.
That is a decision, and today you still
own it. The 2nd, where your interest is
sitting. Interest from an ordinary
savings account counts toward
provisional income. So does tax-exempt
interest, and that catches people
because exempt means exempt from tax,
but it is still counted when they decide
whether to tax your benefits. If you are
near the line, where the money sits is
the whole difference. And if you are 70
and 1/2 or older, and you give to a
church or a charity at all, there is a
route most people over 65 have never
been told about. It is called a
qualified charitable distribution.
Instead of taking money out of your IRA
and then writing a check, the money goes
straight from the IRA to the charity. It
never passes through you. Two things
happen. It counts toward the required
minimum distribution you have to take
anyway, and on your return, the taxable
amount of that withdrawal is entered as
zero, which means it never enters your
adjusted gross income. And so it never
enters your provisional income, and so
it cannot push you over either of those
lines. You give exactly the same money
you were giving anyway. You simply route
it so it never touches the number that
decides whether your benefits get taxed.
There is an annual limit, and your own
custodian will tell you what it is this
year. If you are already giving, and you
are anywhere near that line, this one is
free money, and almost nobody uses it.
There is one more, and it is the only
move on this list that solves the
problem permanently instead of managing
it. Money coming out of a traditional
IRA counts, every dollar. It lands in
adjusted gross income, it lands in
provisional income, and it pushes you
toward those lines every year for the
rest of your life. Money coming out of a
Roth does not. A qualified Roth
distribution is not included in gross
income at all. It never reaches adjusted
gross income. It never reaches
provisional income. It cannot push you
over anything. And a Roth has no
required minimum distribution while you
are alive. The Internal Revenue Service
puts it plainly. If you are the original
owner of a Roth, you do not have to take
distributions regardless of your age.
So, converting money from a traditional
account into a Roth means paying the tax
now in a year you choose at a rate you
can see instead of having that money
show up in provisional income every
single year until you die. It cost you
tax this year. What you buy is that
those dollars never count against you
again. This is not a move to make on
your own off a video. Mine included. It
has a five-year rule attached, and the
amount you convert can push you up a
bracket on its own. But, if you are
sitting near one of those lines with a
traditional IRA behind you, it is the
conversation to have before the 31st of
December because a conversion has to be
done inside the calendar year. The
third. If you are anywhere close, have
somebody go through it with you before
the year ends. Not in April. April is
only the report. Every decision that
matters was made before the 31st of
December. Six. Free help from people who
are not selling you anything. VITA, the
Volunteer Income Tax Assistance Program,
and TCE, Tax Counseling for the Elderly,
both run through the Internal Revenue
Service. Both free. TCE exists
specifically for people over 60. Find a
site at irs.gov.
And AARP Foundation Tax Aid. You do not
need to be a member of anything. One
last thing, and it is the one I most
want you to hear. A great many of you
are counting on the new $6,000 senior
deduction to keep you out of this. It
was in the big tax bill, it is real, and
if you are 65 or older, you should be
claiming it, but it will not save you
here. That deduction reduces your
taxable income. It does not reduce your
adjusted gross income. And provisional
income is built from adjusted gross
income. So, it can lower your tax bill
once you are already over the line. It
cannot keep you under it. If you have
been told otherwise, you have been told
wrong. And it is the kind of wrong that
only shows up when the return is already
filed. So, add it up this week, your
return, your SSA-1099, one sheet of
paper. Find out which side of that line
you are on while there is still a year
left to do something about it. This is
general information, not tax advice. The
figures change every year, and yours
depend on your own situation. Check
anything here with a tax professional or
with one of those two free services
before you act on it. Take care of
yourself.

title: Every Senior Must Check This Before October 15 — The Medicare Switch You Cannot Undo

segments.text: Between now and December, you are going
to be told you can switch out of your
Medicare Advantage plan anytime you
like. That part is true.
What nobody is going to tell you is that
leaving is not the hard part. Getting a
supplement afterwards is. An insurance
company is allowed to open your medical
history, find the diabetes, the heart
condition, the cancer you beat 6 years
ago, and refuse you. Or, take you and
charge you double for it. Here is
Medicare's own guide, word for word.
There is no guarantee that an insurance
company will sell you a Medigap policy
if you do not meet their medical
underwriting requirements. They may deny
you a policy unless you have a
guaranteed issue right. And that matters
more than it sounds because without a
supplement, you pay 20% of the Medicare
approved amount, and in Medicare's own
words, there is no yearly limit on what
you pay out of pocket. No limit. 20% of
a cancer treatment. 20% of a heart
operation. 26% of whatever comes next.
Now, read that quote again. Unless you
have a guaranteed issue right. There is
a list, a short list, of situations
where the insurance company has no
choice at all, where they must sell to
you, must cover the conditions you
already have, and are not permitted to
ask you a single medical question. Most
of the people standing on that list have
no idea they are on it. One of them
applies to anybody in their first 12
months of Medicare Advantage, and it
lets you leave on any day of the year,
not just in October. By the end of this,
you will know which of the 15 applies to
you, and what to do this week if none of
them do. Biggest first. One, the
12-month trial right. If you joined a
Medicare Advantage plan for the very
first time, and it has been less than 12
months. You are holding the strongest
right in this entire video. There are
two versions of it. The first version,
you joined a Medicare Advantage plan the
moment you became eligible for Medicare
at 65. If you switch to original
Medicare within 12 months of that
enrollment, you can buy any Medigap
policy sold by any company in your
state. Not a short list, any of them.
The company cannot ask about your health
and cannot charge you more because of
it. The second version, you already had
a Medigap policy. You dropped it to try
Medicare Advantage for the first time
and you want to come back. Inside 12
months, you can have your old policy
back if the same company still sells it.
If they do not sell it anymore, you can
buy certain other standard policies
instead. And here is the piece that
changes what you do this week. If you
are inside that trial period, you do not
have to wait for October 15th at all.
Federal regulation gives you a special
enrollment period that lets you leave
your first Medicare Advantage plan and
go back to original Medicare on any day
of the year. Any day, not a season, not
a window, any day. The 12 months runs
from the date your Medicare Advantage
coverage actually started, not from
January, not from the day you first
noticed something was wrong, from the
effective date of the enrollment itself.
Go and find that date. It is on your
enrollment letter and your plan will
confirm it over the phone if you ask
them directly for your effective date of
coverage. I want to be honest about one
limit on this. Both versions require it
to be your first time. The first version
means the first time you took Medicare
Advantage when you became eligible at
65. The second version means the first
time you ever left a supplement to try
Advantage. A second attempt at Medicare
Advantage years later is not a trial
right. The law says first and it means
it. There is one small mercy written
into it. If your first Advantage plan is
terminated involuntarily inside those 12
months through no decision of yours and
you enroll with another one straight
away, that new enrollment can be treated
as the initial one and your clock starts
again. That forgiveness has an outer
wall of 2 years from when you first
enrolled. Two, the 63-day clock that
sits inside the first one. This is the
detail that quietly costs people the
right they already earned and it is why
item one is not as simple as 12 months.
The trial right says you may leave
inside 12 months, but the Medigap
application itself has its own deadline
and it is much shorter. You have from 60
days before your coverage ends until 63
days after it ends. That is the whole
window for the application to land. So,
somebody can do everything right, leave
the plan in month 11, feel no urgency,
take 4 months to shop for a supplement,
and lose a right they genuinely had. The
12 months was satisfied, the 63 days was
not. Apply while the old coverage is
ending, not after you have had a rest,
and keep every letter. Medicare's
guidance here is unusually specific.
Keep copies of letters, notices, emails,
or claim denials that have your name on
them as proof your coverage was
terminated and keep the postmarked
envelope they arrived in as proof of
when it was mailed. You may need to send
copies of those papers with your Medigap
application to prove you have the right.
No proof, no right. So, do not throw
away the envelope. Three, the 6-month
window most people did not know they
used. This is the main Medigap door and
it explains why the others matter so
much. Your Medigap open enrollment
period is 6 months long. It begins on
the first day of the first month in
which you are both 65 or older and
enrolled in Medicare Part B. During
those 6 months, an insurance company
cannot refuse to sell you any policy
they offer and cannot charge you more
because of your health. It is one time
only. It does not come back every year.
Medicare's guide says exactly that. It
is a one-time only 6-month period and it
does not repeat every year. Most people
pass through it without noticing because
they were healthy or because they joined
an Advantage plan and never thought
about supplements at all. One useful
exception. If you delayed Part B because
you were still working and covered by an
employer plan, your 6 months has not
started yet. It starts when Part B
starts. If that is you, you are still
holding the best window there is. Four,
the list where they must sell to you.
Outside those 6 months, federal law
still names a set of situations where an
insurance company must sell you a
Medigap policy, must cover your
pre-existing conditions, and cannot
charge you more for your health.
Medicare calls these guaranteed issue
rights or Medigap protections. Here is
the list. Your Medicare Advantage plan
is leaving Medicare or it stops offering
care in your area or you move out of its
service area or its network changes
significantly. Your employer or retiree
or union coverage that paid after
Medicare is ending. You had Medicare
Select and you moved out of its service
area. Your Medigap company went bankrupt
or your coverage ended through no fault
of your own. You left a plan because the
company broke its own rules or misled
you when they sold it. And the two trial
rights we already covered. If more than
one of these fits you, Medicare says you
may choose whichever one works best for
your situation. Read that list again and
notice what is not on it. Simply
deciding during October 15th to December
7th that you would like to leave
Medicare Advantage and return to
original Medicare with a supplement is
not there. Open enrollment lets you
change your Medicare coverage. It does
not oblige any insurance company to sell
you a Medigap policy. Medicare's own
guide states it plainly. There is no
guarantee that an insurance company will
sell you a Medigap policy if you do not
meet their medical underwriting
requirements. They may deny you a policy
unless you have a guaranteed issue
right. So, the order of operations
matters enormously. Find out whether a
supplement will accept you before you
give up the plan you have, never the
other way round. And one related
protection while we are here. If you are
in a Medicare Advantage plan and
somebody tries to sell you a Medigap
policy, that is not an opportunity. It
is illegal unless you are in the act of
switching back to original Medicare.
Medicare says to report it to your state
insurance department. A supplement
cannot begin until your Advantage
coverage has actually ended. So, there
is never a legitimate reason to be
paying for both at once. Five, if your
plan is leaving, you have more time than
you think. If your plan is not
continuing next year, your coverage ends
after December 31st, and your plan has
to send you a letter explaining your
options. You get three separate things.
You can choose another plan between
October 15th and December 7th, starting
January 1st. You have a special right
under federal law to join another
Medicare health plan until the last day
in February, and you may have the right
under federal law to buy certain Medigap
policies within 63 days after your plan
coverage ends. That last one is a
guaranteed issue right. A plan leaving
Medicare is one of the situations where
they must sell to you. Six, the second
chance in January. If December 7th goes
past and you are still unhappy, you are
not locked in for the year. Most people
believe they are. Between January 1st
and March 31st, if you are in a Medicare
Advantage plan, you may switch to a
different Advantage plan or drop it and
return to original Medicare and pick up
a separate drug plan. Your change takes
effect on the first day of the month
after the plan receives it. There are
real limits. You get one change, not
several, and it only works if you are
already in an Advantage plan. You cannot
use this window to move from Original
Medicare into Advantage, and you cannot
use it to switch from one drug plan to
another if you are on Original Medicare.
One more thing you should hear clearly,
because it is the same trap as before.
This January window does not carry a
Medigap guaranteed issue right, either.
It gets you back to Original Medicare.
It does not make anyone sell you a
supplement. Seven, the five-star window
almost nobody uses. Medicare rates plans
from one to five stars. If a plan with a
five-star rating is available where you
live, there is a special enrollment
period that lets you move to it. The
window is enormous, and almost nobody
knows it exists. It runs from December
8th all the way through November 30th of
the following year. You can use it once
in that period. Two cautions that are
worth more than the window itself. If
you move from an Advantage plan that
includes drug coverage to a standalone
drug plan, you will be disenrolled from
the Advantage plan entirely, including
the health benefit, and returned to
Original Medicare. And if you move to a
five-star Advantage plan that has no
drug coverage, you can lose your drug
coverage and face a late enrollment
penalty later. So, check the stars and
check what you are giving up to reach
them. Eight, the escape from a plan that
keeps failing. If your plan has had a
star rating of less than three stars for
the last three years, you can switch to
another Medicare Advantage plan or a
Medicare drug plan at any time you are
in that low-performing plan. Not in a
season, any time you are still in it. Be
clear on what that one does and does not
do. It moves you to another plan. It is
not a route back to Original Medicare
with a supplement, and it carries no
right to buy Medigap. But, if you are
sitting in a plan that has been rated
poorly 3 years running. You are not
required to wait until October to get
out of it. Nine, the letter that should
already be in your house. Every Medicare
Advantage and drug plan has to send you
an annual notice of change and federal
regulation requires it to reach you no
later than September 30th. So, it is
already there. It is in the pile of mail
you have been ignoring all month and it
is the single most useful piece of paper
you will touch this fall. It lists
exactly what is changing in January. The
premium, the deductible, the drugs
covered, the doctors in network. Your
evidence of coverage is a separate
thicker document and that one has to
reach you by October 15th. If you did
not get them, that is not a dead end.
Call the plan and ask. They are required
to provide them. 10, October 1st, not
October 15th. Here is a genuine head
start that costs nothing. Medicare's key
dates for this year say October 1st,
2026. Start comparing your current
Medicare health or drug coverage with
options for next year before open
enrollment starts. Next year's plan
information goes up two full weeks
before anyone is allowed to enroll. So,
you can sit down with your own list of
medicines, compare every plan in your
county, and know exactly what you intend
to do before the enrollment lines even
open. 11, once you are in, they cannot
push you out. This one is pure
reassurance and it is worth saying
because the rest of this video has been
about doors closing. Every standardized
Medigap policy bought after 1992 renews
automatically every year, even if you
have health problems. Your company can
only drop you if you stop paying the
premium or you were not truthful on the
application or the company itself goes
out of business. So, the difficulty is
getting in. Once you are in, your health
cannot be used against you again. 12,
the cap on what your drugs can cost you.
In 2027, your out-of-pocket costs for
covered drugs are capped at $2,400.
Once you reach that, you pay nothing for
your covered Part D drugs for the rest
of the year. This year, the number is
So, the ceiling is rising, and it is
worth knowing where it sits before you
choose a plan. 13, the most a deductible
can be. No Medicare drug plan may have a
deductible of more than $700 next year.
This year, that limit is $615.
Many plans have no deductible at all.
When you are comparing, that is one of
the honest differences between them. 14,
extra help if money is tight. If your
income and savings are modest, there is
a program that pays most of your drug
costs. With extra help next year, the
plan premium is nothing, the plan
deductible is nothing, and you pay no
more than $5.80 for a generic and $14.40
for a brand-name drug. Once your total
drug costs reach $2,400,
you pay nothing at all. For this year,
the limits were a yearly income under
for a single person with savings under
For a married couple living together,
income under $32,460
and savings under $36,100.
Next year's limits have not been
published yet, so use those as your
guide and apply anyway if you are close
because the limits are higher if you
still work or have dependents living
with you. Your home, your car, your
household goods, and your burial plot do
not count as savings. You apply at the
Social Security website, and the same
application can start you on a Medicare
savings program at the same time. And if
you already have full Medicaid or
Supplemental Security Income, you do not
apply at all. You qualify automatically,
and Medicare mails you a purple letter
to tell you so. 15, free help from
someone who is not selling anything.
Every state has a state health insurance
assistance program. Medicare's handbook
describes it as free personalized help
with appeals, buying other insurance,
choosing a health plan, buying a Medigap
policy, and your Medicare rights. They
do not sell plans. They do not earn
commission. You can put your own
situation in front of a person and get
an answer. You will find your state's
number in the back of the Medicare and
You handbook or at shiphelp.org.
You can also call 1-800-MEDICARE
anytime, day or night. Before I let you
go, two things. The first, everything I
have described is the federal floor.
Your state may give you considerably
more. Several states require companies
to sell you a Medigap policy at times
federal law does not, and some let you
switch policies around your birthday
every year. That is state law. It varies
a great deal, and your state insurance
department is the place to ask. If you
are in one of those states, the door I
have been describing may be open far
wider than you think. The second, I do
not sell insurance. I have no plan to
recommend to you and no stake in what
you choose. What I would do this week is
find two dates. The date your Medicare
Advantage coverage started because if
that is under 12 months ago, you are
holding the strongest right there is,
and you can use it on any day of the
year. And the date on the letter your
plan sent you by the end of September
because that tells you what changes in
January. Two dates. Then decide. And if
you decide you want to leave Medicare
Advantage for original Medicare and a
supplement, ask the supplement first.
Get the acceptance in writing before you
let go of what you have. That is the
whole difference between a switch you
can undo and one you cannot. One last
thing, and then I will let you go. This
is general information, not insurance
advice, and I am not an insurance agent.
Rules, plans, and prices change every
year, and yours depend on your state and
your own situation. Before you change
anything, check it with your state
health insurance assistance program or
call 1-800-MEDICARE.
Both are free. Take care of yourself.

title: Seniors! Your State Will Pay Your $202 Medicare Premium

segments.text: Your state will pay your Medicare
premium for you. The whole thing. $22 a
month straight to Medicare. And it stops
coming out of your Social Security
check. Not a discount, not a coupon you
have to find. And it does not stop at
the premium. There are 14 Medicare costs
you may not have to pay at all. And more
than four and 10 people who are allowed
to have this were never signed up
because nobody has to call and tell
them. One of them is worth more than all
the others put together. and it is the
third on the list. Here they are. The
biggest money first one, the monthly
premium. Every month, Medicare takes $22
out of your Social Security check. You
never touch that money. It is gone
before the deposit lands in your
account. There is a program that pays it
for you instead. It is called a Medicare
savings program. Your state runs it. And
here is the part that confuses people,
so hold on to it. It is run by your
state's Medicaid office. Even though the
bill it pays is a Medicare bill.
Medicaid office. Medicare bill. Two
different words, one program. And that
mixup is one reason so many people never
apply. They hear Medicaid and they think
that is not me. When you are on it, the
state sends that money to Medicare every
month in your place. Nothing changes
about your doctors. Nothing changes
about your card. The only thing that
changes is your social security check,
which goes up by the full amount over
one year. That is about $2,400 that
stays with you instead. Think about what
that looks like on the first of the
month. The deposit that lands is bigger.
Not by a few dollars, by the whole
premium. For most people, that is the
largest single change they can make to
their monthly income without earning
another penny. And you do not lose
anything to get it. You keep original
Medicare. You keep your doctors. You
keep your hospital. Your red, white, and
blue card still works the same way it
did yesterday. Two, the yearly
deductible. Medicare has a deductible on
part B. That is the amount you pay out
of your own pocket each year before
Medicare starts paying its share. For
this year, it is $283.
The state pays that, too. You do not
meet it. You do not save up for it. It
is simply covered. This is the part
people miss when they add up what the
program is worth. They count the premium
and stop there. But the deductible is
real money. And for anyone who sees a
doctor in January, it is money that
would have come out of savings. If the
word deductible has always been fuzzy,
here is the plain version. It is the
amount you pay first on your own each
year. Medicare does not pay its share
until you have paid that. So, it hits
you hardest in January and February,
right after the holidays when money is
already tight. On this program, that
first bill is not yours. Three, the 20%.
This is the one I told you about. It is
worth more than everything else on this
list combined, and almost nobody talks
about it. Original Medicare does not pay
all of your bill. It pays 80% of the
approved amount for most services and
you pay the other 20%. There is no cap
on that 20%. On a big year, a hospital
year, a cancer year, that number can get
frightening. The state covers that 20%
as well, the co- insurance, the
co-ayments. Think about what that means.
The premium gone, the deductible gone,
and the share of every bill that used to
be yours gone. Let me put it in an
ordinary year. You see your doctor a few
times. You have some blood work, maybe a
scan. Each of those leaves you with 20%
to pay. Separately, they look small.
Together, over 12 months, they are not.
Now, put it in a bad year, a fall, a
hospital stay, weeks of followup. That
20% is the number that keeps people
awake at 3 in the morning. That is why
this one matters more than the premium.
The premium is a fixed amount you can at
least plan around. The 20% has no
ceiling at all before the next one. I
have put all of this into a written
guide and there is a good deal in it
that will not fit inside a video. The
worksheet you fill in before you
telephone so you are not hunting for
papers while somebody waits on the line.
The call written out word for word
including what they will ask you back. A
page to log what you were told and the
date and who you spoke to. What to do if
the first answer comes back no. and
every income and savings figure in one
table you can keep beside the phone.
Large print throughout. The link is
under this video and pinned in the
comments or point your phone camera at
the square on the screen. Now, the next
two are the ones people never see
coming. Four, the hospital deductible.
Most people think of part A as the free
half of Medicare. It is premium free for
nearly everybody, but it is not
costfree. If you are admitted to
hospital, there is a deductible for that
stay. This year, it is $1,736.
That is not a yearly charge like the
part B one. It can come around again in
the same year if enough time passes
between stays. On the top level of this
program, that is covered. One hospital
admission and this single item has
already paid you back more than the
premium does in a year. Five, the
nursing facility daily charge. If you go
from hospital into a skilled nursing
facility, Medicare covers the first 20
days in full. Then from day 21 to day
100, there is a daily amount you owe.
This year, that is $217
a day. Sit with that number for a
moment. A person who needs 80 days of
rehabilitation after a broken hip is
looking at a bill in the tens of
thousands on a benefit they thought was
already paid for. That daily charge is
part A cost sharing. And on the top
level, the state covers it. Now, before
the rest of the list, the thing that
decides which of these you get, there
are three levels to this program. And
this is where people fall away. The top
level covers everything I have just
described. The premium, the deductible,
the 20%, the hospital, the nursing
facility. It has the lowest income line.
It is called QMB. And those letters
stand for qualified Medicare
beneficiary. You do not need the
letters. you need to know it is the one
that covers all of it. If your income
sits above that line, you have not run
out of options. You have moved to the
next level. The second level pays the
Medicare premium. It does not pay the
deductible or the 20%. But it pays that
$22 a month every month, the same as the
top level does. That is still about
$2,400 a year back in your hands. It is
called SLMBB.
And this is where a lot of people land.
They check the top level. They see they
are over the line by $50 or $100 a
month. Then they walk away thinking they
missed it. They did not miss it. They
just belong on a different rung. There
is a third level above that. Same
benefit, the full monthly premium paid
for you. Two things to know about this
one. You have to apply again each year.
So, put it on the calendar. And it is
funded from a set pot each year. First
come, first served. So, applying early
beats applying late. There is also a
fourth level almost nobody mentions. It
is for people under 65 who went back to
work after a disability and lost their
free hospital coverage because of it.
The income line for that one is far
higher. Over $5,000 a month. If that
describes you or somebody in your
family, ask about it by name. And here
is the thing that matters most about all
of this. The three levels are not three
separate applications. You make one
application. Your state looks at your
income and puts you where you belong.
You are not choosing. You are not
guessing. They sort it. Six. The income
line. You think you failed. The numbers
I am about to give you are the national
floor. That is the important word floor.
Your state is allowed to be more
generous and many states are. For one
person, the top level sits at about
a month in income. The second level
about 1,600.
The third about 1,800
for a married couple. Each of those is
higher. Some states have raised those
lines well above the national floor. So
if you look at those numbers and think
you are over, you may not be over at all
in the state where you actually live.
How much does your state matter? A study
of who is actually enrolled found a very
wide gap. In one state, nearly 3/4 of
the people who qualify are signed up. In
another, it is closer to 4 in 10. Same
program, same country. The difference is
how hard your state works to tell
people. You cannot control which state
you retired in. You can control whether
you ask. Seven, the savings test. There
is also a limit on savings at the
national level. A little under $10,000
for one person, about 15,000 for a
couple. Your house does not count. Your
car does not count. And here is the part
worth knowing. Medicare says it plainly
on its own page. Some states do not
count certain kinds of savings or
certain amounts when they decide. So
what you have in the bank may not be
part of the conversation at all where
