this.

title: If You're Over 60, Your Credit Card Owes You These 14 Free Things

segments.text: If you are over 60 and you carry a
credit card, you are already paying for
14 things you have almost certainly
never once used. They are not rewards.
They are not points you have to collect.
They are protections that came with the
card the day it arrived. And the only
reason you do not have them is that
nobody has ever told you they are there.
Some of them are worth more in a single
afternoon than the card costs you in a
year. And before we start, one number
because it explains everything that
follows. 87% of people over 65 carry a
credit card. That is the highest of any
age group in the country. And across all
card holders, $33 billion
in benefits and rewards is sitting
unclaimed. Nearly one in four people
never claim anything at all. Here is
what you are sitting on. One, your
telephone is already insured and you are
probably paying somebody else to insure
it. If you pay your monthly phone bill
with the right credit card, the phone
itself is covered. Accidental damage,
theft, on most of the cards that carry
it. That is up to $600 or $800 per
claim. And you can usually make two
claims in a 12-month period. So the
annual cover runs to about $1600 on the
more generous cards. You do not sign up.
You do not pay a premium. You just pay
the phone bill with the card and the
cover switches on. Think about what most
people over 60 are doing instead. Paying
the phone company seven, eight,
sometimes $15 a month for a protection
plan. That is $180 a year for something
the card in your wallet may already be
doing for nothing. Two things to know.
And I am telling you both because I am
not going to make this sound better than
it is. There is a deductible, usually 25
or $50 a claim. So it is cover, not a
blank check. On a broken screen, that
still leaves you a long way ahead. And a
phone that is being financed or rented
or borrowed may not be covered. It
generally has to be a phone you own on a
bill you pay with that card. So the
question to ask is simple. Which card is
my phone bill going out on and does that
card cover the phone? Two, somebody will
come out to your car and it is already
arranged. Most cards include a roadside
dispatch service. You telephone one
number, you tell them where you are and
what has happened and they send
somebody. A flat tire, a dead battery,
locked out with the keys sitting on the
seat, out of fuel, towed. The number for
Visa roadside dispatch is
Write that down or better, put it in
your telephone now under roadside. Now,
I'm going to be straight with you about
this one because I am not going to tell
you a thing is free when it is not. The
dispatch service is included with the
card. The service call itself is charged
to you at a flat rate that is usually
somewhere between about 60 and 80
dollars depending on who issued your
card and they tell you the price before
they send anybody. What you are getting
is not a free tow. What you are getting
is somebody who answers at any hour who
has your location and sends a vetted
driver at a price agreed in advance
instead of whatever a stranger on the
roadside decides to charge a person of
your age at 11:00 at night. For a lot of
people, that is the whole value, not the
money. The not being alone with it.
Three, if your flight is delayed, they
pay for the night. If you are delayed
long enough, the card pays for the
hotel, the meals, and the things you
need to buy because your bag is on an
aircraft and you are not. On a Chase
Sapphire Reserve, that starts at 6
hours. On a Sapphire Preferred, it
starts at 12. Up to 500 dollars per
person per trip and it covers your
immediate family traveling with you, not
just you. You must have paid for the
flight with that card. That is the
condition and it is the one people get
wrong. Here is the part that matters at
our age. When a flight goes at 9:00 at
night and the next one is at 6:00 in the
morning, the airline hands you a voucher
for a sandwich and points at the floor.
Younger people sleep across three chairs
and laugh about it. You cannot do that
and you should not have to. There is a
hotel 2 miles away and the card will pay
for the room. Keep the receipts. That is
all the claim is. Four, you can refuse
to pay a charge and the law is on your
side. This is the big one. This is not a
card benefit. This is federal law, the
Fair Credit Billing Act, and it applies
to every credit card in the country. If
there is a charge on your statement you
did not authorize, or you were billed
twice, or you paid for something that
never arrived, or what arrived was
broken and the company will not make it
right, you can dispute it. Here is
exactly how it works, and these details
are the whole thing. You have 60 days
from the date of the statement, not 60
days from the purchase. 60 days from the
bill. You must do it in writing, and you
must send it to the address for billing
inquiries, which is not the address you
send your payment to. Those are two
different addresses, and they are both
on your statement. Sending a dispute to
the payment address is the single most
common way people lose this. Your
liability for an unauthorized charge is
capped by law at $50, and in practice
almost every major issuer now charges
you nothing at all. Once you have
disputed, they must write back within 30
days to say they have it. They must
finish investigating within two billing
cycles, and no more than 90 days. And
this is the part nobody tells you. While
that investigation is running, you do
not have to pay the disputed amount. You
do not have to pay interest on it, and
they cannot report you late or touch
your credit over it until it is decided.
Read that again if you need to. A
company has taken money from you, and
the law says you stop paying, they
cannot charge you interest, and they
cannot damage your credit while somebody
else investigates it for you. I have
watched people your age pay a charge
they knew was wrong because it felt
easier than arguing. You were never
arguing. You were exercising a right
that is written down. Five, when the
price drops, the card gives you the
difference. You buy something, two weeks
later the same shop has it cheaper, or
you see it advertised at a lower price
somewhere else. On cards that still
carry this, you claim the difference and
they pay it. The window is usually
between 60 and 120 days. It is not
automatic. Nothing happens unless you
file. You will need your card statement
showing the purchase, the original
itemized receipt, and the advertisement
or the online listing showing the lower
price. I will be honest with you about
this one because it is the benefit that
has been disappearing. A number of
issuers have dropped price protection in
the last few years. So, this is one to
check on your own card rather than
assume. But, on the cards that still
have it, most people have never claimed
it once. Six, if it is stolen or broken
in the first few months, the card
replaces it. Purchase protection covers
a new item against theft and accidental
damage. Usually for 90 to 120 days from
the day you bought it. The coat taken
from the restaurant, the tablet that
went off the arm of the chair onto a
tile floor in week three, the thing that
was stolen out of the car. Most people
absorb those. They treat it as their own
carelessness and they quietly replace
it. It was covered. Seven, the
manufacturer gave you 1 year, your card
quietly added another. Extended warranty
takes the manufacturer's warranty and
adds a year or more on top of it. So,
the television that came with 12 months
of cover has 24. The washing machine
that failed in month 14, 3 weeks after
the warranty ran out, was not actually
out of warranty. You file within 60 to
90 days of the thing going wrong. The
contact details are in a document called
your cardholder benefits guide, which is
the booklet that came with the card and
which almost nobody opens. If you have
thrown it away, it is on the issuer's
website and the number on the back of
your card will get you to it. Two things
to be clear about because I am not going
to oversell it. It covers what the
original warranty covered, which means
manufacturing defects. It does not cover
theft or you dropping it. And it is the
benefit issuers have been trimming, so
check your own card. City for one took
it off the Costco cards back in 2023.
Now, here is the statistic that tells
you why this item is in the video at
all. Consumer Reports found that 55% of
people who bought an extended warranty
never filed a single claim on it. Among
people who bought extended cover for a
laptop, only 15% of Windows owners and
7% of Apple owners ever used it. People
pay for cover and then never claim. And
the cover that came free with the card
is claimed even less than that. Eight,
say no at the rental car counter. When
you hire a car, the person at the desk
will offer you a damage waiver. It is
usually somewhere around $30 a day and
they are trained to make declining it
sound reckless. If your card carries
rental car cover, you decline theirs and
you are covered for damage and theft up
to the value of the vehicle. Two
conditions and they both matter. You
must decline the rental company's waiver
and you must pay for the entire rental
on that card. There is one distinction
worth knowing. Primary cover pays first
without involving your own motor
insurance at all. Secondary cover pays
only after your own insurance has paid,
which means a claim on your policy and
possibly a higher premium next year.
Primary is the better one and premium
travel cards are where you usually find
it. On a 10-day hire that is $300 you
were about to hand over at a counter for
something you already had. Nine, you are
not liable for a charge you did not
make. Zero fraud liability. If somebody
uses your card without your permission,
you do not pay for it. That is standard
now across the major issuers and the
major networks. I'm putting this next to
the dispute rights on purpose because
together they are the answer to
something a lot of people your age
genuinely worry about. The fear of being
cleaned out by a stranger with your card
number is real and it is the reason some
people keep using cash for everything. A
debit card takes the money out of your
account first and you argue about it
afterwards with your rent money already
gone. A credit card is the bank's money
until you pay the bill. The dispute
happens before you are out of pocket,
not after. That is the practical
difference and it is the one nobody
explains. 10, if your bag does not
arrive, the card buys what you need.
Baggage delay cover. If your checked bag
is delayed or misdirected for more than
6 hours, the card pays for the
essentials. On a Chase Sapphire
Preferred, that is up to $100 a day for
up to 5 days, so $500 in total.
Toothbrush, clean shirt, and for a lot
of people over 60, the thing that
actually matters, which is the
medication that was in the case. Two
deadlines, and they are tight, so write
them down. You have to contact the
benefits administrator within 20 days of
the bag being delayed, and get your
documents in within 90 days. Keep every
receipt. That is what the claim is built
on. 11, your credit score, free and the
full report with it. Most issuers now
give you your credit score at no cost.
American Express, through a service
called My Credit Guide, gives you your
FICO score, your full Experian credit
report, alerts whenever something on the
report changes, and a simulator that
shows what would happen to your score if
you did a particular thing. None of that
costs anything, and here is the part
worth knowing. You do not need to be an
American Express card holder to use it.
Their own wording is that it is a free
service whether you hold an American
Express card or not. One honest limit.
It reads Experian only. There are three
credit bureaus, and this shows you one
of them. So, it is not the whole
picture, but it is a free look at a
third of it, updated with alerts. And
the alerts are the part that matters at
our age. If somebody opens an account in
your name, that is where it shows up,
and it shows up early. That is worth
more than the score itself. 12, there
are discounts sitting in the app,
switched off. American Express and Chase
both run personalized offers for their
card holders. So, do others. A certain
shop, a certain restaurant, a certain
amount back. Here is the catch, and it
is the entire reason most people never
get a penny from this. You have to
activate the offer before you shop. It
sits there in the app or on the website
with a button next to it. And if you do
not press the button, you spend the
money and nothing comes back. It takes
about 2 minutes. Once a month, open the
app, look at the offers, and switch on
the ones for shops you actually use.
That is the whole job. If somebody in
the family set the app up for you, and
you have never opened it since, that is
where these are. 13. The insurance you
did not know was on the ticket. Travel
accident insurance covers death or
dismemberment while you are traveling as
a passenger on a common carrier, which
means a scheduled aircraft, a train, a
bus, a ship. On some premium cards, that
runs as high as a million dollars. You
have to have bought the fare with the
card. I am not going to dress this one
up. It is not a benefit anybody enjoys
thinking about, but if you are the
person in your family whose name is on
things, and somebody is going to have to
sort out paperwork one day, this is one
more place they should be told to look.
Put it on the list you keep with your
papers. 14. The second card is free, and
your wife or your husband should have
one. On most cards, you can add another
person to your account at no cost at
all. American Express allows up to four.
Capital One does not charge on most of
its cards. Most issuers do not charge
anything. They get their own card in
their own name on your account. The
exception is the expensive travel cards,
the ones with a big annual fee. Those
sometimes charge $75 or more for an
additional card. So, ask before you
assume. But on an ordinary card, which
is what most of us carry, it costs
nothing. And there is a reason this one
is last. A great many couples have run
one card between them for years, because
that is how it was always done, and
because nobody ever mentioned the second
one was free, which means one of you
carries the card, and the other one
carries nothing. And if the person with
the card is in hospital, the other one
cannot buy petrol. One telephone call,
no charge. Do it this week. So, that is
14, and every one of them is attached to
a card you already carry. Now, two more
that are worth knowing about, and that I
am keeping separate, because they do not
belong to most of us. The first is
concierge service. On premium cards,
there is a number you can call at any
hour and a person will make a booking,
find a thing, sort out a reservation. It
is real and it is good and it exists
almost entirely on cards with a large
annual fee. If you carry an ordinary
card, you do not have it. The second is
the AARP Essential Rewards Mastercard
from Barclays. It is one of very few
cards that pays extra rewards on medical
expenses, which for a household our age
is not a small category. But it is a new
card, not a thing you already own and
applying for a card is a decision rather
than a gift. It belongs at the end of
the list, not inside it. Now go back
over the 14 because there is a pattern
in them. The phone cover, the dispute
rights, the price difference, the extra
warranty year, the free second card. Not
one of them arrives on its own. Not one
of them is paid out automatically. Every
single one of them requires the same
thing from you, which is that you notice
and you claim. The card company will not
telephone to say the price dropped. The
warranty will not extend itself out
loud. Nobody at the bank is going to
ring and mention that your husband could
have had his own card free for the last
11 years. And there is a reason it works
that way and it is not a conspiracy. It
is simpler than that. These are written
down in a booklet that came in an
envelope with the card and almost nobody
reads the booklet. That booklet has a
name. It is called the cardholder
benefits guide and that is the phrase to
use. You can telephone the number on the
back of your card and say, "I would like
to know what benefits my card includes.
Please send me the benefits guide." They
will do it. It takes about 4 minutes and
it is their job. $33 billion sits
unclaimed because of an envelope people
did not open. Go and open yours.
Benefits vary by card and by issuer and
issuers change and withdraw them. So
check your own cardholder benefits guide
or telephone the number on the back of
your card before you rely on any of
this. This channel has no affiliation
with any bank, card issuer, or network.

title: If You're Over 60, Costco Owes You These 15 Free Things

segments.text: If you are over 60 and you carry a
Costco card, you are paying for 15
things you are almost certainly not
using. They are not coupons. They are
not a sale you have to catch on the
right week. They are services that come
with the card already in your wallet.
And the only reason you do not have them
is that nobody at that door has ever
told you they exist. Some of them are
worth more in a single year than the
membership costs. Here they are. One,
free technical support on your
electronics for as long as you own them.
Costco runs a service called concier
services. If you bought a television, a
computer, a laptop, a tablet, a camera,
or a major appliance there, you get free
technical support on it by telephone.
Not for the first 90 days, for the life
of the product. Think about what you do
now instead. You wait for a grandchild
to visit. You pay a man $40 or $50 to
come out and press four buttons. or the
television sits on the wrong input for a
year and you stop watching the programs
you liked. The number is 1-866861450.
They are open 5 in the morning until 10
at night, 7 days a week. And there are
agents in English and in Spanish. Have
your receipt or order number ready
because that is what they will ask for.
And do not talk yourself out of calling
because the problem feels too small. The
most common calls they take are exactly
those. The remote stopped working. The
picture went dark. It will not connect
to the internet anymore. You are not
wasting anybody's time. Two, a second
year of warranty you already own and
never paid for. Costco extends the
manufacturer warranty to 2 years from
the date of purchase on select items and
on every television it sells. The
industry standard is one year. You have
two. That is the thing to remember the
next time somebody at another shop leans
across the counter and offers to sell
you an extended warranty. On the Costco
television, you already have that second
year included. Three, tire service for
as long as you own the tires. Buy tires
at Costco and the installation is
included. And after that, so is the
maintenance for the life of those tires.
Rotation, balancing, flat repair,
inflation, pressure checks, nitrogen
inflation. There is also a 5-year road
hazard warranty on them. For a lot of
people over 60, this is the difference
between looking after the tires and

30 days. Most people never check and

title: NEW Medicare Bill To Cover Caregiving at Home — And the Catch Is Not What You Think

segments.text: 93% of Americans think Medicare should
pay for care at home, and most of them
believe it already does. It doesn't. It
never has. And that gap wasn't an
oversight. It was written into the law
on purpose in 1965
by people who knew exactly what they
were leaving out. This month, there's a
bill in Congress that would finally
change it. 20 hours a week of real
hands-on help at home, paid for by
Medicare. Bathing, dressing, getting
someone out of a chair, meals. But
there's a catch in how it gets paid for,
and it's the same catch that got the
most powerful man in Congress chased
across a Chicago parking lot by a crowd
of older women in 1989. Here's what I'm
going to do. I've read the bill, all
seven pages of it. I'll tell you exactly
what Medicare covers at home today and
what it doesn't. I'll tell you what this
bill actually says, not the headlines.
I'll tell you who pays for it. And then,
I'm going to tell you four things that
are sitting inside those seven pages
that almost nobody covering this bill
has mentioned. One of them is the date,
because even if this passed tomorrow,
nobody receives a single hour of this
care before 2029.
If someone you know is caring for a
parent or a spouse right now, send them
this one. Let's get into it. Start with
what Medicare actually does today,
because this is where families get hurt.
Medicare does cover care at home. That
part is true. What it covers is skilled
care, a nurse, a physical therapist, a
speech therapist. The trap is the home
health aid, the person who actually
helps your mother into the bath. That
person is only covered as a helper. You
can only get the aid if you also need
the nurse or the therapist. And there
are two more locks on that door. You
have to be homebound, which means
leaving the house takes what the rules
call considerable and taxing effort. And
the care has to be part-time or
intermittent. So, watch what happens to
a real family. Your father has a stroke.
Medicare sends a physical therapist. An
aid comes three mornings a week and gets
him washed and dressed. Eight weeks in,
the therapist writes one word in the
file, plateaued. The therapy ends, and
the aid, the only person in that house
actually keeping him clean and safe,
walks out the same day. His stroke
didn't reverse. His abilities didn't
come back. His needs didn't shrink by
one minute. The coverage did, and now
it's you, or it's your money. That word
the discharge planner uses for what just
disappeared is custodial care, and
Medicare has never paid a dollar of it.
So, why not? Here's the part I think is
worth knowing, because it explains
everything that follows. On the 30th of
July, 1965, Lyndon Johnson didn't sign
Medicare in Washington. He flew to
Independence, Missouri, to the Truman
Library, and signed it in front of Harry
Truman, who had fought for national
health insurance 20 years earlier, and
been beaten so badly the idea was
considered dead. Truman was 81. Johnson
handed him Medicare card number one.
Beautiful theater. But, look at what was
actually in the box. Medicare was built
on the model of working-age hospital
insurance. Hospitals, doctors,
surgeries. Acute illness, the kind where
you get it, and then you either recover
or you don't. Long-term care doesn't
behave like that. Custodial care isn't
an event. It's a condition that doesn't
end. Insuring it looks less like
insurance and more like a pension. So,
the people writing that bill left it out
and told themselves it could be added
later. Later is now, 61 years later. So,
here's the bill. In the house, it's
House Bill 10,020, introduced on the 3rd
of August, 2026, by Representative
Debbie Dingell of Michigan. In the
Senate, it's Senate Bill 5,270,
introduced two days after that by
Senator Andy Kim of New Jersey. It
amends Title 18 of the Social Security
Act, the section that created Medicare,
and it creates the benefit under Part B,
not Part A, the hospital side, part B,
the outpatient side. Hold on to that
because it decides who pays. The benefit
is up to 20 hours a week, help with
activities of daily living, which the
bill lists as bathing, dressing,
toileting, transferring, and eating.
Plus, what the law calls instrumental
activities of daily living, meaning meal
preparation, medication reminders, and
light housekeeping directly related to
your health and safety. To qualify, a
doctor has to certify that you need help
with at least two of the daily
activities or two of the instrumental
ones or one of each. There's no income
test. There's no asset test. You don't
have to be poor and you don't have to
spend down anything. And now the part
that I think matters most and the part
the headlines keep missing. This benefit
is not attached to skilled care and it
is not attached to the homebound rule.
Go back to your father. Under today's
law, he loses the aid the moment he
stops improving. Under this bill,
functional need alone is the trigger.
The question stops being, is he getting
better, and becomes, can he bathe
himself? That is a genuine structural
change and it is the strongest thing in
this bill. Now, how much is 20 hours?
It's about 3 hours a day. It is not
around-the-clock care. It is not a
substitute for a nursing home for
someone with advanced dementia who
wanders at night. Full-time home care
runs closer to 40 hours a week, so this
covers a little under half of that,
which brings us to the question
everybody skips. Who pays for this? You
do. The bill says the Secretary of
Health and Human Services shall adjust
the monthly part B premium to reflect
the added cost. Part B is the piece
already coming out of your Social
Security check every month. Now, I want
to be fair about this because it gets
garbled constantly. About a quarter of
part B is funded by those premiums. The
rest comes from general tax revenue. So,
a new part B benefit means two things at
once. Premiums go up for everyone who
has part B and the federal deficit
absorbs the the
It does not touch the hospital trust
fund you hear about running short in the
news. That's part A. This is part B,
which gets refilled every year by law.
The real concern is that everyone's
premium goes up, including the many
people who will never qualify for this.
Remember the gate? You need two deficits
certified by a doctor. How much does it
go up? Nobody knows. There is no
Congressional Budget Office score, and
the bill doesn't even ask for one up
front. It asks the chief actuary to
estimate the premium impact within 180
days after it becomes law. I think
that's backwards, and I think you should
notice that it's backwards. What we do
have is outside modeling of a similar
benefit, not of this bill. The Brookings
Institution costed a conservatively
designed home care benefit at roughly
$40 billion a year, which is in the
range of a 4% increase in Medicare
spending. And the Kaiser Family
Foundation put about 15 million
beneficiaries
in range of qualifying. Now, hold on to
one detail there, because I think it
matters more than the headline number.
That Brookings design assumed enrollees
would pay part of the cost themselves.
This bill does not say whether they
will. There's a real argument on the
other side of that ledger. 3 hours a day
of help is associated with fewer falls,
better medication adherence, fewer
emergency room visits, and delayed
nursing home placement. And a nursing
home costs the public purse far more
than this would. Some of the money comes
back. There's also a criticism with a
name, the Woodwork effect. Millions of
families do this work for free right
now. Start paying for it, and people
come out of the woodwork. I don't think
that's fraud. I think that's real unmet
need finally becoming visible. But it
does mean actual usage could run well
past the projections. Now, here are the
four things inside those seven pages
that I have not heard anybody say out
loud. This is the part I'd want my own
family to know. The first one is the
date and it's the big one. The benefit
applies on or after the first day of the
first plan year beginning more than two
years after the date of enactment. And
the department gets a full year from
enactment just to write the regulations,
work that through.
If this bill were signed this afternoon
and it will not be signed this
afternoon,
not one person receives a single hour of
this care before 2029.
If your mother needs help this winter,
this bill is not the answer. And anyone
presenting it as relief that's coming
soon is not reading the last page. The
second thing is what the bill doesn't
say. There is no cost-sharing language
in it. None. It doesn't create a copay.
It also doesn't waive the Part B
deductible and it doesn't waive the
standard 20% coinsurance that applies to
most Part B services. I'm not going to
tell you that you'll owe 20% of your
care because the text doesn't say that.
What I'm telling you is that the text
doesn't say you won't. On a benefit of
this size, that is not a small blank to
leave in a bill and it's the blank I'd
watch as this thing moves through
committee. The third thing, the plan of
care has to be in the bill's words
established and periodically reviewed.
Periodically is not defined. That
interval gets set later in regulation
and regulation is historically where
benefits get narrower, not wider.
Whoever writes that rule decides how
often your father has to prove all over
again that he still can't bathe himself.
And the fourth thing is one nobody
mentions because it isn't about
beneficiaries at all. The bill requires
that payment reflect a reasonable wage
floor for home care workers and it gives
the department one year to write
standards for worker qualifications.
Home care aids have some of the highest
turnover of any job in this country.
There is no benefit without somebody to
show up and deliver it and that clause
is the part of this bill trying to solve
that. One more, and I think it's the
sharpest irony in the whole thing. No
income test, no asset test, nobody has
to be poor. But if you're already
receiving the same services through
Medicaid, you can't double dip. So the
families with the least money, the ones
who already spent everything down to
qualify for Medicaid, are the ones
carved out. Now let me tell you why the
funding line is the part that decides
whether any of this survives. It has
happened twice before.
>> In 2010, tucked inside the Affordable
Care Act, there was a long-term care
program called the CLASS Act. It was
Senator Ted Kennedy's life's work,
passed months before he died. It was
voluntary. You'd pay in and later draw a
cash benefit. Before the law was even
signed, Medicare's own chief actuary
warned of a serious risk of adverse
selection. Meaning, if it's voluntary,
mostly sick people sign up, costs rise,
premiums rise, healthy people leave,
costs rise again. A death spiral. By
late 2011, the secretary said she
couldn't find a viable path forward. By
January 2013, Congress repealed it. This
bill is built to dodge that exact
bullet. It isn't voluntary. It's built
into part B, which nearly everyone on
Medicare already has. And universal
enrollment is the only real cure for
adverse selection. But there's a second
graveyard, and this one isn't about
actuaries. It's about anger. In 1988,
Congress passed the Medicare
Catastrophic Coverage Act. Real
benefits, a cap on hospital costs, the
first outpatient drug coverage Medicare
ever had, signed by Ronald Reagan. And
funded by a surcharge on higher income
seniors. Seniors read their bills, and a
great many of them decided they were
being charged for something they hadn't
asked for, and in many cases already
had. On the 17th of August, 1989, Dan
Rostenkowski, chairman of the House Ways
and Means Committee, and one of the most
powerful men in Washington left a
meeting in his own Chicago district and
was surrounded by protesters, most of
them older women. They followed him
shouting. He got to his car and a woman
ended up on the hood of it. He got out
and walked away on foot while the car
was driven around the crowd. Those
photographs ran in every paper in the
country. On the 22nd of November, 1989,
the repeal was signed.
That law had been on the books about 17
months. It is still the only major
entitlement expansion in American
history undone almost immediately after
it was passed. Now, read this new bill's
funding line one more time. Adjust the
Part B premium. The ghost of 1989 is
sitting in that sentence. And anybody
who tells you the fight over this is
manufactured hasn't read the history.
So, what are the honest odds? So far,
exactly one other member of Congress has
signed on to the House version back on
the 31st of August. In the Senate, not a
single one has. No score. Seven pages.
Both sitting in committee. And the bills
that came before this one, the home care
money in Build Back Better, the Wish
Act, the Better Care Better Jobs Act,
all died. Two things to watch: a
Congressional Budget Office score and
members from both parties signing on in
the double digits. Until both of those
appear, this is agenda-setting
legislation. It matters, but it is not
imminent, and it may be a thing
politicians want to be seen introducing
before an election, which is exactly why
the next 2 minutes are worth more to you
than everything I just said. Because
there are things that exist right now,
today, while this bill sits in a
committee room. Start with the elder
care locator, 1-800-677-1116.
It's federally funded and it connects
you to your local area agency on aging,
which runs the National Family Caregiver
Support Program, respite, counseling,
training, free. You can also dial 211.
Then your SHIP, the State Health
Insurance Assistance Program, free,
trained, unbiased Medicare counseling.
and there is one in every state. Not a
broker, not a sales call.
Consumer-directed Medicaid. In many
states, a family member can be paid to
provide the care. Not every state and
not for everyone, so ask your own state
Medicaid office that exact question and
make them answer it. If there's a
veteran in the family or a surviving
spouse of one, look at Aid and
Attendance and the Veterans Affairs
Caregiver Support Program. Both are
badly underused. For dementia
specifically, there's a program Medicare
runs that provides care navigation. A
helpline that operates around the clock
and up to $2,500 a year of respite care
at no cost to the beneficiary. It runs
through a few hundred participating
organizations across most states. One
catch worth knowing before you spend an
afternoon on the phone. To join it, you
have to be on original Medicare, parts A
and B. If you're on a Medicare Advantage
plan or already in PACE, you are not
eligible for it. And PACE, for people 55
and older who qualify for a nursing home
level of care but can live safely at
home. It runs in about 33 states. One
caution, if you're on Medicare Advantage
and you saw an advertisement about
in-home help, those benefits are real,
but they're often thin. Plans are now
required to send a mid-year notice of
the benefits you haven't used, precisely
because they get marketed hard at
enrollment and quietly forgotten after.
Call your plan and make them tell you in
writing what you're actually entitled
to. And one last set of numbers for the
next time somebody tells you a benefit
like this is too expensive to
contemplate. The median cost of a home
health aide in 2024 was $77,792
a year. A private room in a nursing home
Meanwhile,
59 million Americans are providing this
care for nothing. Nearly 50 billion
hours of it, worth just over $1 trillion
a year. That is the equivalent of about
24 million full-time workers, roughly
17% of the entire American workforce
working for free. It's being paid for.
It's just being paid in lost wages, lost
promotions, lost social security
credits, and lost sleep. So, will this
bill pass? It might, and it'll probably
need to be rewritten first. But, go back
to that room in Missouri in 1965. Truman
fought for this in 1945 and lost so
badly people called the idea dead for a
generation. 20 years later, he was
sitting in a chair watching a president
sign it and hand him the first card.
Long-term care has been sitting outside
that room for 61 years waiting to be let
in. If somebody in your life is doing

title: Half the Medicare Drug Plans Are Gone. Here Is What Happens to Yours in January 2027.

segments.text: Your Medicare drug plan might not exist
in January. In 2024, there were 709
standalone Medicare drug plans in this
country. In 2025, there were 464.
This year, there are 360. Half of them
are gone in 2 years, and the federal
money holding down the price of the one
still standing expires on the 31st of
December. Your 2027 plan has already
been priced without it. Before you go
any further, find out whether this is
about you because it is not about
everyone on Medicare. And the difference
matters. This is about standalone drug
plans. That means original Medicare part
A and part B with a separate
prescription drug plan bought from a
private insurer. That separate plan is
what people call a part D plan or a PDP.
If your drug coverage comes bundled
inside a Medicare Advantage plan, this
particular change does not apply to you.
Your plan may change for other reasons,
and it may change a great deal, but not
because of what expires in December. If
you are in the first group, there are
about 24.9 million of you, and by most
estimates around three quarters of you
are expected to pay more next year. Here
is what is actually expiring. In 2024,
the federal government created something
called the Part D Premium Stabilization
Demonstration. The name is bureaucratic,
and the purpose was simple. Congress had
just redesigned the Part D benefit.
Insurers were facing costs they had not
priced for, and the government was
worried that standalone drug plans would
either raise premiums sharply or leave
the market altogether. So, the
government paid them not to. Each
participating plan received extra
federal money per member per month, and
in exchange, there was a ceiling on how
much the plan could raise your premium
in a single year. Watch the latter
because the latter is the whole story.
In 2025, participating plans received
$15 per member per month, and the most
any plan could raise a premium was $35.
In 2026, this year, the support dropped
to $10 and the ceiling loosened to $50.
the support is zero and that ceiling is
gone with it. Across those two years,
the program cost about $9.8 billion.
That money is now leaving the system and
it was money that sat between the true
cost of your plan and the number printed
on your bill. Now, a fact that most
coverage of this story leaves out and
leaving it out is how you get an
audience that stops trusting you.
Stand-alone drug plan premiums did not
rise this year. On average, they fell
from about $39 a month to about 36. The
demonstration is one of the reasons they
fell. So, nobody should tell you your
premium has already gone up. That is not
what happened and if you have not felt
anything yet, you are not imagining it.
What happened is that the support
holding that number down was scheduled
to shrink and then stop and the final
step happens on the 31st of December.
The government has already published the
figures your 2027 plan is being built
from. The national bid amount for 2027
The base beneficiary premium is $41.33.
Those are not predictions. Those are the
numbers the plans are pricing against
right now while you are watching this.
Now, the part that cost people the most
money and it is not the premium. Look
again at the plan counts. 709 then 464
then 360. Those are not plans that got
more expensive. Those are plans that
stopped existing. The insurers did not
leave out of malice. They left because
the redesigned benefit made the
stand-alone drug plan market
unprofitable for a lot of them,
particularly the smaller ones. And a
company that cannot make the numbers
work stops offering the product. That is
an ordinary commercial decision. It is
also the one that lands hardest on you
because a premium increase is something
you can look at and weigh. A plan that
no longer exists is not a choice you get
to make. It is worth understanding why
the economics turned because it explains
why this is not a one-year problem. For
most of the history of Part D, once a
person spent enough in a year, the
federal government picked up the
overwhelming majority of the cost above
that point. The insurer carried very
little of it. That arrangement is what
made a low premium drug plan possible in
the first place. The redesign changed
two pays. There is now a hard annual
limit on what you can be charged out of
pocket for covered drugs, and once you
hit it, you pay nothing more that year.
That cap is genuinely good for anybody
taking expensive medication, and it is
the reason the old coverage gap, the
thing everybody called the donut hole,
no longer exists. But, the money did not
stop being spent. It moved. A much
larger share of the cost above the cap
now sits with the insurance company,
rather than with the government. So, a
stand-alone drug plan is now carrying
risk it did not carry before on a
product whose entire appeal was a low
monthly premium. For a large insurer
with millions of members, that is
survivable. For a smaller one, it is
not. And the smaller ones are the ones
that left. That is why the demonstration
existed. It was a temporary bridge
across the years when the new economics
arrived, paid for so that the market
would not empty out all at once while
people were still adjusting. The bridge
ends in December. The economics that
made it necessary do not, and nobody can
yet tell you the count for 2027. Those
numbers arrive in late September when
plans publish for the coming year.
Anybody telling you today how many drug
plans will exist next year is guessing.
So, here is the sequence that will
actually happen to people, and it is
worth following it exactly. Late in
September, an envelope arrives. It is
called the annual notice of change, and
plans are required to send it by the
30th of September. It is dull, it is
long, and it is the single most
important piece of mail a person on a
stand-alone drug plan will receive this
year. It tells you what your plan is
doing in 2027. The new premium, the new
deductible, which of your drugs are
still covered and at what tier? And
whether the plan is continuing at all.
Most people put it in a pile. Then from
the 15th of October to the 7th of
December, the enrollment window is open.
That is the period in which you can
change plans. Outside it, for most
people, you cannot. Then on the 1st of
January, the new prices take effect and
the old plans are gone. If you do
nothing across that whole sequence, one
of two things happens. If your plan
still exists, you are renewed into it
automatically at whatever the 2027
premium turns out turns With whatever
its 2027 drug list turns out to be.
Nobody phones to check that you meant
to. Silence is treated as agreement. If
your plan does not still exist, you do
not automatically land somewhere good.
Depending on your circumstances, you may
be moved into another plan chosen for
you. Or you may find yourself in January
with no drug coverage at all, standing
at a pharmacy counter being asked for
the full price of a medication you have
taken for years. And there is a second
cost that is worse because it does not
end. If you go without creditable drug
coverage for 63 days or more, Medicare
can apply a late enrollment penalty.
That penalty is added to your premium
and for most people, it stays there for
as long as they have part D. Not for a
year, for the rest of your life on the
program. It is worth knowing how that
penalty is actually calculated because
in the abstract, it sounds survivable
and in practice, it compounds quietly.
The penalty is worked out as roughly 1%
of the national base beneficiary premium
multiplied by the number of full months
you went without creditable coverage.
For 2027, that base premium is $41.33.
So each uncovered month adds a little
over 40 cents to your monthly premium.
Go a year without coverage and you have
added roughly $5 a month. Then you pay
it in February and in March and every
month after that for as long as you have
drug coverage. It is also recalculated
each year against the new base premium.
So it does not stay frozen at the number
you first saw. And one word in that rule
does a lot of work, creditable. Coverage
counts only if it is at least as good as
standard Medicare drug coverage. Some
retiree plans and some employer plans
qualify. Some do not. Your plan is
required to tell you in writing once a
year which one it is. And that notice is
another piece of mail that people file
without reading. If you are relying on
coverage from a former employer or a
union, find that notice and confirm in
writing that it is creditable. Assuming
it is and being wrong is one of the more
expensive assumptions available in this
system. That is the actual risk in the
story, not that a premium goes up by
some dollars a month, that someone stops
reading their mail in September and pays
for it permanently. There are two other
numbers coming in 2027 that belong in
the same envelope of your attention. The
Part D out-of-pocket cap rises to
That is the most you would pay for
covered drugs in the year. And having a
cap at all is new few years. The
standard deductible rises to $700, which
is the amount you pay before the plan
starts paying. Both of those are worth
knowing before you compare plans because
a plan with a low premium and a high
deductible is not the cheaper plan for
somebody who takes several medications.
The advertised number and the number you
actually pay are two different things.
And the plans know which one you will
look at first. So, what do you do?
First, when the annual notice of change
arrives in late September, open it that
day. Do not put it in a pile. Look for
three things, the new premium, whether
the plan is still being offered, and
whether your medications are still on
its covered drug list at the same tier.
Second, do not assume that staying put
is the safe choice. It is simply the
choice you make by not choosing. In a
year when half the market has already
disappeared and the price support has
ended, the plan that suited you in 2025
may be the wrong plan and may not be a
plan at all. Third, compare on total
annual cost, not on premium. Add the
premium for the year, plus the
deductible, plus what your own
prescriptions will actually cost under
that plan. The official plan finder on
the Medicare website will do this
arithmetic for you if you enter your
medications. A plan that looks expensive
by premium is often the cheaper one for
somebody with several regular
prescriptions. It is worth doing that
arithmetic on paper once because the
result surprises people. Take a plan
advertising a premium of $10 a month
with a $700 deductible against a plan
advertising $40 a month with no
deductible. On premium alone, the first
plan looks like it saves you $360 over
the year. Now add the deductible.
Somebody with several regular
prescriptions will clear a $700
deductible early in the year, and they
pay all of it themselves before the plan
contributes anything. The first plan
costs 120 in premium plus 700 before
coverage begins, which is 820. The
second costs 480 and starts paying from
the first prescription. The plan with
the smaller number on the front of it is
the more expensive one by a wide margin
for that person. For somebody taking one
inexpensive generic, the answer reverses
completely. This is why there is no such
thing as the best drug plan, only the
best plan for your specific list of
medications. Anybody who tells you which
plan to pick without asking what you
take is not advising you. They are
selling. Fourth, check the pharmacy.
Plans have preferred pharmacies, and the
same drug at a non-preferred pharmacy
can cost noticeably more. If you have
used the same pharmacy for 20 years,
confirm it is still preferred under the
plan you are considering. Fifth, if your
plan is ending, do not wait for someone
to sort it out for you. Choose a new
plan inside the enrollment window. That
is the whole protection against the
permanent penalty, and it expires on the
7th of December. Nobody is going to call
and walk you through this. There is no
advisor assigned to you. The mail will
arrive, the window will open, the window
will close, and at no point will anyone
check whether you understood what was
happening. There is free help, and you
should use it rather than paying for it.
Every state runs a counseling service
for exactly this, called the State
Health Insurance Assistance Program,
known as SHIP. The counselors are
trained, they are unbiased, and they do
not sell insurance, which means they
have nothing to gain from which plan you
choose. Your local Area Agency on Aging
can also help. The contact details are
in the description below, along with the
official Medicare number and website. Be
careful about who else you take advice
from between now and December. This is
the season when the calls start. Anyone
who telephones you unprompted, claims to
be from Medicare, and asks for your
Medicare number or your bank details, is
not from Medicare. Medicare does not
cold call people to sell them plans.
Hang up. One last thing, and it is the
thing to hold on to. The government did
not hide any of this. The demonstration
was always temporary. The end date was
published, and the figures your 2027
plan is being priced from are already
public. Nothing here was done in the
dark. That is precisely why nobody will
come and tell you. It has already been
announced. As far as the system is
concerned, you have been informed. The
letter in September is the notice. The
window from October to December is the
remedy. And if you miss both of those,
the system will record that you had the
opportunity and did not take it. This is
general information only, and it is not
legal, financial, or medical advice.
Medicare rules vary, and they change.
Plan details for 2027 are still being
published, and figures should be checked
against the official Medicare website or
a qualified professional before you make
any decision about your coverage. If you
know one person on a stand-alone
Medicare drug plan, send this to them
before the end of September. The
envelope that decides their next year is
already in the post, and the only thing
that makes it useless is not opening it.

title: Turns Out, Medicare DOES Cover Long-Term Care — But Only If the Hospital Admits You

segments.text: 70% of Americans turning 65 will need
long-term care. You've seen this number.
It shows up in insurance ads, in
retirement articles, in the mail that
comes to your house, and it makes it
sound like most of us are headed for a
nursing facility with a six-figure bill
attached. Here's the problem. That
statistic is technically true, and it's
almost universally misunderstood. Today,
I want to do three things. First, I'm
going to show you what that 70% actually
includes because it isn't what the
headlines imply. Second, I'll show you
how it gets stretched into something
scarier than the research supports, and
who benefits from that. And third, I'm
going to walk you through what Medicare
really pays for here because most people
have no idea it covers a meaningful
chunk of this. And then, I'm going to
show you the one sentence in your
hospital file that decides whether you
get any of it. That part's missing from
every other video on this subject,
including the good ones. So, let's get
into it. Start with the definition
because how it gets presented isn't
really accurate. When researchers talk
about long-term care in this context,
they're usually talking about something
called long-term services and supports.
And that phrase covers an enormous range
of situations. It could be somebody
doing your grocery shopping for 2 weeks
after a surgery. It could be a short
stay in a rehab facility after a hip
replacement. It could be hiring someone
to help around the house with cooking
and cleaning. And yes, at the far end of
the spectrum, it could be a full-time
stay in a nursing facility. That 70%
figure traces back to a research brief
from the Department of Health and Human
Services. It estimates that 56% of
Americans turning 65 will develop a
condition requiring some form of
long-term services and supports. Other
methodology puts that number closer to
70%. Now, that number isn't saying seven
in 10 retirees will end up in a nursing
facility. It isn't saying seven in 10
will need permanent custodial care. It's
describing an entire spectrum, and the
overwhelming majority of that spectrum
is short-term, in the home, and often
provided by a family member. It probably
doesn't make you panic in quite the same
way if we say you might need some help
for a week after a minor surgery."
compared to saying, "You're more likely
than not to end up in a facility." So,
this really isn't a minor technicality.
So, how does a careful research finding
turn into a panic headline? Honestly, I
think there are two explanations, and I
don't think most of it is bad faith. The
first is incentives. Fear drives clicks,
and when the organization repeating that
statistic also happens to sell long-term
care insurance, well, the scarier it
sounds, the more urgent their product
feels. You'll find the number quoted
correctly in one paragraph and then used
to mean something much narrower two
paragraphs later on the same page
selling the same policy. The other
explanation is simpler, carelessness. A
writer sees a scary number, doesn't
trace it back to the actual methodology,
and figures out the best headline they
can make from it. Either way, the effect
on you is the same. You end up planning
your whole retirement around the
worst-case in the range instead of the
common one. Okay, now the part that
actually matters. There's a sentence
everybody knows. Medicare doesn't cover
long-term care. A national survey last
year found that 58% of adults believe
exactly that, and it's half right. The
half that's wrong is worth a lot of
money to you. So, long-term care splits
into two kinds, and Medicare treats them
completely differently. The first kind
is driven by aging. You slowly lose the
ability to handle daily tasks or a
memory condition shows up, Alzheimer's
or another dementia, and eventually
there's a move into a facility or a
memory care unit. For that, the sentence
is correct. Medicare pays nothing, not a
dollar. If your only need is ongoing
help with daily living, Medicare isn't
your safety net, and it was never built
to be. The second kind is tied to a
medical event, a fall, a broken hip,
skilled nursing after a hospital stay,
home health after surgery, hospice.
And Medicare covers a lot of that. So,
let's walk through an example, and these
are the current figures for this year.
Someone falls and breaks a hip. A few
days in the hospital, which is pretty
common at this age, and then a move to a
skilled nursing facility for rehab. For
the first 20 days in that facility,
Medicare covers the stay. She pays the
inpatient hospital deductible, which is
and nothing more. For days 21 through
100, she pays $217 a day, and Medicare
covers the rest. The typical stay after
a hip fracture is 1 to 5 weeks. So, her
real out-of-pocket cost lands somewhere
between about $1,700
and about $5,000. And even a full
100-day stretch runs around $19,000 out
of pocket, rather than the high 30,000s
to low 50,000s it could cost with no
coverage at all. Here's something a lot
of people don't know. You don't get one
stretch of 100 days for life. If you
leave the facility and you're out for 60
days, that 100-day period starts over.
So, Medicare has a real impact here.
It's a lot more than the people
repeating that one sentence realize.
But, everything I just described, every
dollar of it, gets switched on or off by
one thing. And it happens back in the
hospital before anybody mentions a
nursing facility. Medicare only pays for
skilled nursing after a qualifying
hospital stay of at least three
consecutive days as an admitted
inpatient. Three days as an inpatient.
And here's the thing. A hospital doesn't
have to admit you as an inpatient to
keep you in the building. It can hold
you under something called observation
status, which is an outpatient category.
Under observation, you're in a bed.
You're on a ward. You've got the gown.
You've got the wristband. Nurses are
coming and going. Meals are showing up.
From where you're lying, it is
identical. But, those nights are
outpatient nights. They don't count
toward the three days. So, somebody can
spend four nights in a hospital, move to
a skilled nursing facility to recover,
and find out afterward that Medicare
won't pay any of it because on paper
they were never admitted. And that's not
some rare edge case. It's common enough
that it has its own name and its own
federal notice requirement. Let me put
two people side by side because this is
the clearest way to see it. Same
hospital, same night, same broken hip.
The first one gets admitted as an
inpatient the evening she arrives. Three
nights later she transfers to a skilled
nursing facility. Medicare covers it.
She pays her deductible, and if she's
there past 20 days, $217 a day. The
second one gets held under observation
for the first 2 nights, then admitted on
the third. She's been in that building
just as long. Same injury, same surgeon.
But she's got one qualifying inpatient
night, not three. So, Medicare pays
nothing toward her nursing facility
stay, and that bill comes in at $300 to
$500 a day. Same hospital, same injury,
same week. The difference is a clerical
category, and nobody's required to walk
over and explain it to her while it's
happening. There's a second sting, too.
While you're under observation, the
regular medications you take at home for
your own chronic conditions get treated
as self-administered drugs in an
outpatient setting. They're generally
not covered, and the hospital can bill
you for them at its own price. So, what
do you do about this? First, you're
entitled to be told. Federal law
requires the hospital to give written
and spoken notice to any Medicare
patient kept under observation more than
24 hours. The form's called the Medicare
Outpatient Observation Notice, and
people in the system call it the MOON
notice. There's a revised version that
took effect this April. If it's been
more than a day and nobody's handed you
one, that's your cue to start asking.
Second, ask the question directly and
ask it early. Day one, not the day of
discharge. Ask this: Is the patient
formally admitted as an inpatient or is
the patient an outpatient under
observation? And if they say inpatient,
ask them to point you to the physician's
admission order. That's it. One question
asked while it can still be changed. And
the answer decides whether a nursing
facility stay costs you a deductible or
costs you thousands. Third, know that
this is being looked at. Starting the
1st of January this year, running
through the end of 2030, CMS is running
a limited demonstration that waives the
3-day requirement for patients getting
one of five specific surgical
procedures. It's narrow. It won't apply
to most people, but it's the first real
movement on this rule in a long time.
And it's worth asking whether your
procedure is on the list. Now, if you're
on a Medicare Advantage plan instead of
original Medicare, the rules shift
again. And this gets left out of almost
everything on this topic. A lot of
Advantage plans waive the 3-day
inpatient requirement completely, which
sounds like good news, and partly it is.
But they swap in something else, prior
authorization. The plan has to agree
ahead of time that the nursing facility
stay is warranted. As of this year,
about 95% of Medicare Advantage members
are in a plan that requires prior
authorization for a skilled nursing
stay. A federal watchdog report out this
June found the average denial rate on
those requests runs about 12%, and it
varies wildly between insurers. Under 1%
at some, over 20% at others. But here's
the number I really want you to hold on
to. When those denials get appealed,
about 95% of them are overturned. 95%.
Which tells you most of those refusals
didn't hold up, and that the families
who just accepted the letter paid for a
stay they were entitled to have covered.
There are new deadlines this year, too.
Plans have to decide a standard request
within 7 days, an urgent one within 72
hours, and they have to give you the
specific reason for a denial instead of
something vague. So, if you're on an
Advantage plan and you get a refusal,
understand what you're actually looking
at. That's a first answer, not a final
one, and the odds on appeal are strongly
in your favor. There's one more belief
that costs families money, and it gets
repeated inside facilities by people who
genuinely think it's true. You'll be
told your mother has plateaued, that she
isn't improving anymore, and that
because she isn't improving, Medicare
stops paying. That's not the law, and it
hasn't been the law since 2013. There
was a nationwide class action called
Jimmo against Sebelius that settled that
year. People had been denied coverage on
the grounds that they weren't getting
better. The settlement confirmed that
coverage depends on whether skilled care
is needed, not on whether the person is
improving. And CMS went back and rewrote
its own manuals to take that suggestion
out. Skilled nursing and skilled therapy
can be covered when they're needed to
maintain someone's condition, or to slow
down how fast it declines, not just when
they're getting better. That's called
the maintenance standard, and more than
a decade after it was settled, families
are still being told the opposite by
staff who are just repeating what they
were taught. So, if somebody tells you
coverage is ending because there's no
more progress, that's your moment to ask
for it in writing and appeal. You're
entitled to a written notice before
coverage ends, and you have the right to
a fast review by an independent quality
improvement organization. Fast means
days, not months, and you can start it
over the phone. Okay, let's zoom out to
the national numbers because the
individual figures don't show you the
scale. The Congressional Research
Service tracked total spending on
long-term services and supports for
2023. That number was 564 billion
dollars. Medicare covered 18% of it,
roughly 102 billion dollars, for
services that supposedly aren't covered
at all. That's more than the 81 billion
dollars households paid straight out of
pocket, which was only 14% of the total.
And the pattern holds when you break it
down. In 2024, Medicare spent about 47
billion dollars on nursing home care,
which is roughly 3/5 of what Medicaid
spent in that same category. On home
health, Medicare spent about 56 billion
against Medicaid's 38 billion. Here's
another one. A Department of Health and
Human Services projection estimates that
91% of seniors will spend less than
$100,000 on long-term services and
supports across their entire retirement.
And about 2/3 will spend nothing out of
pocket at all. One more. Based on
national spending and tax data, seniors
spend about 2% of their income on
out-of-pocket nursing and long-term care
in 2023. Back in 1970, that was closer
to 4%. So, it's coming down. Largely
because Medicare, Medicaid, and private
insurance are absorbing more of it. So,
let's get really clear on this. Medicare
will not pay for an open-ended stay in a
facility that you need because you're
aging. If the move is driven by dementia
or by needing help with daily living or
by choice, Medicare covers none of it.
But, if the need is triggered by a
hospitalization, a surgery, a medical
event, and a lot of long-term care
genuinely is, then Medicare covers a
real portion. And it's a lot more
generous than most retirement content
suggests. That payment is gated behind
three inpatient nights, though. And
whether you get those nights comes down
to a hospital's paperwork, not your
condition. Now, here's the piece that
the coverage of this topic tends to
leave alone, and it's the reason this
channel exists. What happens after day
100? Because those 100 days do end, and
for the aging-driven kind of care, they
never started. At that point, the payer
isn't Medicare, it's you. Until you have
almost nothing, and then it's Medicaid.
That's a different program with
different rules. To qualify for
long-term care Medicaid, most states
hold you to an asset limit around
$2,000. The program looks back 5 years
at anything you gave away. And after you
die, federal law requires the state to
try to recover what it spent from your
estate. For most families, that means
the house. None of that is a reason to
panic today. It's a reason to know which
program you're dealing with. Because
people lose enormous amounts of money
confusing the two. They assume Medicare
will carry them and it stops at 100
days. Or they assume nothing's covered
at all, hand money to their kids in a
panic, and create a Medicaid penalty
they never needed. So, here's what I'd
actually take away from this. Don't plan
your retirement around the 70% headline.
It doesn't mean what the ad wants you to
think it means. Don't plan around the
opposite mistake, either, that nothing's
covered. Because Medicare is paying
about a hundred billion dollars a year
in this space. Learn the split. Medical
event, Medicare pays a lot. Aging,
Medicare pays nothing. And Medicaid is
the road after that. And on the day this
actually happens, when someone you love
is in a hospital bed and a nursing
facility is getting discussed, ask the
one question that decides the money.
Inpatient or observation? Ask it on day
one. Ask for the admission order. Ask
again the next morning. That one
sentence in the file is worth more to
your family than any statistic in this
video. If someone in your family has
been through this and you're comfortable
sharing, tell me about it below. It
helps other people more than you'd think
and I read them. This is general
information, not legal, financial, or
medical advice. Medicare and Medicaid
rules vary and they change. And Medicare
Advantage plans can apply their own
requirements. Figures are current for
2026. Talk to a qualified professional
or call your state health insurance
assistance program, which is free.

title: Single With No Children? Medicaid Takes the House and the State Gets What Is Left Unless You Do This

segments.text: If you are single, if you have no
children, and if your home is paid off,
there is a question you have probably
already asked and never had a straight
answer to. If Medicaid ever pays for
your care, what happens to that house?
And who ends up deciding? Here is the
short version. Every protection built
into the Medicaid rules requires a
husband, a wife, or a child. Every
single one of them. If you do not have
one, almost none of them reach you.
There is one document. It is not a
trust, it is not a deed, it does not
cost thousands of dollars, and it does
not need a five-year head start. You can
sign it in an afternoon, and it is the
only thing in this entire subject that
you cannot go back and do later.
Everything else on this list stays
available until the day you apply for
care. This one closes the moment your
health does. You will hear this document
sold as though one signature protects
your savings. It does not. What it
protects is something else, and for you,
it is worth more. It only makes sense
once you can see where it sits. There
are three stages. The first one takes
your accounts while you are alive. The
second one takes the house after you are
gone, and the third one is not Medicaid
at all. It is the one almost nobody
covers. It is the one that document
actually solves, and for someone in your
position, it is bigger than the other
two put together. Start with the first
stage while you are very much alive. To
have Medicaid pay for long-term care,
you must spend your countable assets
down to your state limit. Countable
means your bank accounts, your
certificates of deposit, your stocks and
brokerage accounts, a second property,
and the cash value sitting inside a
whole life insurance policy. In most
states, that limit for a single person
is around $2,000. A handful of states
are far more generous, and a few are
even tighter than that. California is
the outlier. It brought its own asset
test back at the start of this year at
for a single person, and that figure is
temporary. It is scheduled to fall to
about $21,000 in the middle of next
year. So, if you are in California, the
number you are planning around today is
not the number you will be planning
around then. Some things are left alone
while you are alive. Your primary home,
up to an equity limit that runs from
roughly $750,000
in most states to a little over 1
million in the highest value states. One
vehicle, your personal belongings, a
burial plot, and certain prepaid funeral
arrangements. Term life insurance, which
has no cash value to reach. Now, here is
where being single changes the
arithmetic completely. When a married
person needs this care, federal law
protects the husband or wife still at
home. That spouse keeps the house. That
spouse keeps a vehicle. That spouse
keeps a substantial share of the
couple's savings. So, that caring for
one of them does not leave the other
with nothing. Look closely at what that
is. It is a protection for a spouse. It
is not a protection for a person. If
there is no spouse, nobody is standing
in that position, and nothing is being
sheltered on your behalf. The rule is
not being applied harshly to you. The
rule has no place to attach. The same is
true of every other door people talk
about. Transferring the home to a
husband or wife is fully exempt, and
that needs a spouse. The caregiver child
exemption lets you hand the home to an
adult child who lived with you and cared
for you for 2 years, and that needs a
child. There is a protection for a blind
or disabled child of any age, and that
needs a child. A spouse, a child, a
child. Hold that pattern because you are
about to see it again. That is the money
gone. The house is still standing at
this point, which brings us to the
second stage, the one everybody has
heard of and almost everybody gets the
timing wrong on. It is called estate
recovery, and it happens after you die.
Federal law requires every state to seek
repayment from the estates of people
aged 55 and older who received long-term
care through Medicaid. Not some states,
all of them. And the home is very often
the only thing left to recover from for
a reason that is almost circular. The
home was left alone the whole time you
were alive, so it is still there. The
law does place shields on this. A state
may not recover while there is a
surviving spouse. It may not recover
while there is a child under 21. It may
not recover while there is a blind or
disabled child of any age. There is that
pattern again, a spouse, a child, a
child. If none of them exist, nothing
defers it and nothing pauses it. There
is one exception that does exist for
some people in your position. It is
called the sibling exception. If you
have a brother or a sister who already
owns part of your home and who lived in
it with you for at least a year before
you went into care, the home can pass to
them. That is a real door. But count
what it needs all at once. A living
sibling who co-owns the property, who
moved in, who stayed a full year before
you needed care. For most people hearing
this, that door is closed by
circumstance rather than by law. So the
honest summary is not that you have zero
options. It is that almost every
protection in this system was built
around a family. And if you do not have
one, most of them never reach you. Now,
everything I have described so far
happens to your property. The third
stage happens to you while you are alive
to experience it. And this is the one
that document actually solves. Ask
yourself what happens if you lose the
ability to make your own decisions. Not
when you die, before that. A stroke, a
fall, dementia arriving quietly across a
year of small moments nobody outside
your house ever sees. If you have a
spouse, they step in. If you have adult
children, one of them steps in. If you
have neither and you have not named
anyone in advance, somebody still has to
be given legal authority over your
money, your home, and your medical care.
And the only body that can grant that
authority is a court. So a judge
appoints a guardian. In many cases, that
is a professional or a public guardian,
which means a person you have never met
appointed to a caseload, now deciding
what happens to your money, what happens
to your house, what medical care you
receive, and where you live. This is
where the subject usually gets
exaggerated. So, here is the fair
version. Most guardians are not
villains, and courts do supervise them.
But, supervision is not the same as
choice. The point is not that something
criminal happens to you. The point is
that the most personal decisions of your
life get made by whoever the court could
find, rather than by whoever you would
have picked. And notice the step before
all of it. A court only reaches for that
power when there is nobody already
holding it, which means the whole thing
turns on one question. Did you name
somebody, or did you not? So, here is
the document. It is a durable power of
attorney for your finances, paired with
a healthcare proxy for your medical
decisions. Two pages doing two halves of
the same job. You name a person you
trust, a friend, a niece or a nephew, a
neighbor you have known for 20 years,
anyone you choose, rather than anyone a
court can find. The word that matters is
durable. A plain power of attorney can
stop working at the exact moment you
become incapable, which is the moment
you need it most. A durable one keeps
working. If you take one piece of
vocabulary from this video, take that
one and ask for it by name. The
healthcare proxy is the other half, and
people skip it. That is the one that
says who speaks for you about treatment,
about surgery, about a feeding tube,
about whether you go home or into a
facility. The financial document does
not cover any of that. You want both.
Why this rather than something more
clever? Because of four things that are
true of nothing else in this subject. It
cannot be done later, once capacity is
gone. It has no waiting period and no
5-year clock, so it works the day it is
signed. It costs less than any other
option here, and it is the only one that
decides who is standing beside you while
everything else plays out. Now, the
limit, and it is a real one. Naming
someone does not stop the spend down. It
does not stop estate recovery. Anybody
telling you that one signature protects
your savings from long-term care costs
is not being straight with you. Real
protection of assets is a years-long
process, usually built around an
irrevocable trust signed well before you
ever apply. In most states, the
look-back on transfers runs a full 5
years. California currently runs a
shorter one, which is one more reason
the answer here depends on where you
live. Either way, it needs a qualified
elder law attorney and far more warning
than most people get. A revocable living
trust does not do it. If you have that
runway, use it. And that is a different
conversation than this one. What naming
someone does is decide two things that
are otherwise decided for you. Who holds
authority over your life while you are
still living it? And who receives
whatever is left when it is over? That
second one matters more than people
expect. Somebody wrote this under the
last video on this channel. I live in
New Jersey, no living relatives.
Medicaid said if I have no living
relatives, they want their money back.
Anything I can do so I can leave the
money to my friend's kid? The answer to
that question is yes. With no spouse and
no children, the law does not simply
stop. It works outward through your
family tree. And if it finds nobody at
all, what is left goes to the state. You
are allowed to interrupt that. And most
people in your position have never been
told so. You can name a friend. You can
name a friend's child. You can name a
neighbor, a church, or a cause you cared
about. And two of the ways you do it are
free and need no lawyer at all. Ask your
bank for a payable on death beneficiary
on your accounts. Ask your brokerage for
a transfer on death designation. Both
are forms. Both cost nothing. You keep
complete control while you are alive.
The person you name has no access until
you are gone. And the money passes
straight to them without going through
probate. A will does the same job for
everything those forms do not cover. And
it is where you name who settles your
affairs. For the house itself, some
states allow a transfer on death deed
and a handful allow what is called a
ladybird deed. Whether that is available
to you depends entirely on your state
and whether it survives a state recovery
also depends on your state. So, that is
a question for an attorney rather than a
video. There is an objection under every
video on this subject and it deserves an
answer rather than a comment fight.
Somebody always asks why a person with
assets should have any of this paid by
other people. It is a fair question. So,
here is a fair answer. Nothing I have
described avoids a bill. The spend down
still happens. The recovery still
happens. What we have been talking about
is not whether you pay. It is who
decides for you when you no longer can
and who receives what is left when it is
over. Those decisions get made by
somebody either way. The only question
is whether it is somebody you chose. One
honest word before I go. I am not a
lawyer and I am not describing your
particular situation. These rules move
from state to state. The asset limits
change. The equity limits change and a
state recovery reaches further in some
states than in others. Use your own
state Medicaid office for the numbers
and a qualified elder law attorney for
anything that touches your home. What I
have laid out is the shape of the thing,
not advice about your life. And if you
take one step this week, make it the
smallest one. A durable power of
attorney and a health care proxy. Not
because it saves your savings because it
will not. Because it is the only piece
of this that expires without telling
you. Then think of one person who needs
to hear this. Someone living alone with
no children who has never signed a paper
naming anyone and who assumes that
because there is nothing to fight over,
there is nothing to plan. Send this to
them. Almost nobody in this situation
loses control because they made a bad
decision. They lose it because nobody
ever told them a decision was theirs to
make.

title: America Had No 401(k) Until 1978 — So How Did People Retire?

segments.text: In 1930, an old man in a coal town had
three ways his life could end. He could
work until his body gave out and he died
on the job. He could move in with his
grown children and hope they could
afford one more mouth at the table. Or,
if he had no children and no savings and
no strength left, he could be carried to
the poorhouse to wait for the end among
strangers. There was no fourth option.
There was no monthly check waiting for
him. No account with his name on it. No
plan. The idea that a person had earned
the right to simply stop working and
live out their final years in peace did
not exist for most of American history.
It had to be invented. And the strange,
accidental way it finally arrived tells
you almost everything about why your
retirement today rests so completely on
your own shoulders. Right now, more than
60 million Americans put a piece of
every paycheck into a 401k. It is so
woven into how people picture growing
old that most assume it has always been
there, like some permanent feature of
the country. But the 401k did not exist
until 1978, and no one actually used one
until 1980. That means the people who
raised you and the people who raised
them grew old in a completely different
world, a world with no employer match,
no target date fund, no account to roll
over. So, if none of that existed, how
did people retire at all? The honest
answer is darker than most people
expect, and it explains how the risk of
growing old quietly moved off the
shoulders of companies and the
government and landed squarely on yours.
Go back far enough and the truth is
blunt. Across almost the entire span of
