that child's entire life.
If your son runs up a credit card debt,
if your daughter is sued, if either of
them goes through a divorce, or falls
behind on a car loan or a medical bill,
the money in that shared account can be
treated as partly theirs. Which means a
creditor of your child can reach into
the account and take money that you
spent a lifetime saving.
You did nothing wrong, and your savings
can still be pulled into someone else's
financial trouble.
And there is a second layer to this one
that catches families completely off
guard. If you ever need long-term care
and apply for Medicaid, the way that
account is titled matters enormously.
When a child is added to what is called
an and account, Medicaid can treat the
entire balance as a gift to that child
on the day the name was added.
That gift can trigger a penalty period,
a stretch of time where Medicaid simply
will not help pay for your care at the
exact moment you need it most.
The very act meant to make your life
easier can quietly disqualify you from
the help you were counting on.
There is even a detail in how the
account is worded that most people never
notice.
An account joined by the word and can be
treated very differently from one joined
by the word or.
That one small word can change whether
adding a child is counted as a gift and
whether both people must sign to move
money.
It sounds like a technicality,
yet families have lost real protection
over which tiny word a bank happened to
print on the paperwork. I want to be
fair because there is a right way to get
help with your bills.
There are safer ways to let someone
assist you,
such as a proper power of attorney or a
different account arrangement that do
not expose your money or trip the
Medicaid rules.
The point is not that you should never
accept help. The point is that walking
into the bank and adding a name is not
the harmless little favor it appears to
be. Now, let me get to the second
mistake, and this is the one that tears
families apart because it goes against
everything you thought your will would
do.
Most people believe their will is the
final word on who gets what. You wrote
it carefully. You divided things evenly
among your children. You feel settled.
But a joint bank account does not listen
to your will at all. Almost every joint
account comes with something called the
right of survivorship.
In plain terms, it means that when one
owner dies, the money in that account
passes automatically and immediately to
the surviving owner.
It does not go through your will. It
does not get divided the way your will
says. It goes straight to whichever
person shares the account, and it is
theirs completely. So, picture a parent
with three children who adds only one of
them to the account, again, just for
convenience.
That parent may have a will that splits
everything three ways. It will not
matter.
On the day that parent passes, the money
in that account belongs entirely to the
one child whose name was on it.
The other two can be left with nothing
from that account.
And there is often little anyone can do
about it. Sometimes that child chooses
to share it fairly.
Very often in the grief and confusion
that follows a death, they do not. And
it becomes the thing that turns siblings
into strangers for the rest of their
lives.
A single name on a single account can
override a whole lifetime of intentions.
And the person who wrote those
intentions is no longer here to explain
what they truly wanted.
That is why this mistake is so much
bigger than it looks.
And why the fix I am about to give you
matters even more than you might think.
So, stay with this, because what is
coming is the part that actually
protects the people you love.
Which brings us to the third mistake,
and this one is the opposite problem.
It is what happens when there is no
joint owner and no plan at all.
Say a person keeps their account
entirely in their own name.
No second owner and no one named to
receive it.
It feels clean and private, and in a way
it is.
But here is what happens on the day they
die. That account freezes. No one can
touch it. Not a spouse, not a child, no
one, until the account passes through a
court process called probate. Probate
can take months.
Sometimes it drags on far longer.
It can involve court filings and legal
fees. And all the while, the money just
sits there, locked, while the family is
trying to pay for a funeral and keep the
lights on.
The savings meant to protect them
becomes unreachable at the precise
moment they need it.
A lifetime of careful saving sealed
behind a courtroom door. And it is often
a surviving spouse who feels this the
hardest.
Two people who shared everything for 40
years,
and yet as that account sat in one name
alone,
the one left behind can be locked out of
it for months,
made to wait on a court to release money
that the whole marriage already treated
as theirs. Now, here is the free step
that quietly solves this, and it is the
reason I asked you to keep listening.
You can ask your bank to add what is
called a payable on death designation.
Some banks call it a beneficiary.
It is a simple form. It costs nothing,
and it does something powerful.
It lets you name the person who should
receive that account when you are gone.
And when that day comes, the money
passes straight to them, directly,
without freezing, and without ever going
through probate. You keep complete
control while you are alive. The person
you name has no access at all until you
pass.
You can change it whenever you like.
And unlike adding a joint owner, a
payable on death beneficiary does not
expose your money to that person's debts
or divorces while you are living. It is
the control you want without the door
you do not. And there is one more quiet
advantage that almost no one mentions.
That same payable on death form can
actually increase how much of your money
is protected by federal deposit
insurance.
The FDIC, the agency that insures your
bank deposits, covers up to $250,000
per owner at a bank.
But when you name beneficiaries, your
account is insured as a trust, and the
coverage can rise to $250,000
for each person you name up to a much
higher ceiling.
So the same free form that keeps your
money out of probate can also keep more
of it safe if your bank ever fails.
Let me put that in plain numbers because
it is easier to feel that way.
Imagine a person with $300,000 in a
single bank in an account with no
beneficiary named.
50,000 of those dollars would be sitting
beyond what federal insurance would
cover if that bank ever failed.
Now imagine that same person names three
people to receive the account.
The coverage can stretch to well past
that balance, and every last dollar is
protected. Same money, same bank, one
free form, and a completely different
outcome if the worst ever came.
Let me tie this together because once
you see the pattern, all three mistakes
are really the same mistake wearing
three different faces. Every one of them
comes from letting a bank account be
decided by accident instead of on
purpose.
Adding a name for convenience feels like
a small thing, but it can hand your
money to a creditor or to one child
instead of all of them.
Leaving no plan at all falls private,
but it can lock your savings behind a
courtroom for months.
And in every case, the harm lands after
you are gone on the people who can least
afford it at the worst possible time.
The good news is that it is genuinely
simple to get right.
You do not need to be wealthy, and you
do not need a lawyer to take the first
step. So, here is what I would gently
encourage you to do this week.
Call your bank or walk in and ask a few
plain questions.
Ask exactly how each of your accounts is
titled and who would receive the money
if something happened to you.
Ask whether you have a payable on death
beneficiary on file, and if you do not,
ask to add one.
And if you have already added one of
your children as a joint owner,
ask what your safer options are before
you assume it is the only way. And then,
think of one person who needs to hear
this.
Someone who has quietly added a child to
their account
or who has never named a beneficiary in
their life
and has no idea what waits on the other
side of that choice.
Share this with them.
Most families do not lose money here
because anyone did anything wrong.
They lose it because no one ever sat
them down and explained how a simple
bank account really works. One honest
word before I go.
I am not a lawyer, and I am not speaking
about your particular family
because these rules do bend from one
state to the next and one bank to the
next. And the difference between and and
account and or account and a beneficiary
can change everything.
So, use your own bank, and if your
situation is at all complicated, a
qualified elder law attorney to get the
answer that fits your life.
The reason I lay all of this out is not
to worry you.
It is so that the money you worked so
hard for ends up exactly where you want
it, with the people you love, and not
lost to a rule that nobody ever bothered
to explain.

title: If You Own or Rent a Home After 62 — 5 Programs Most Seniors Never Claim

segments.text: If you are a senior living on a fixed
income and the house you live in is
starting to cost more than it should,
either to fix, to heat, or simply to
stay in,
I need you to hear something. There is
real money set aside by the government
right now whose entire purpose is to
help older Americans keep a safe roof
over their heads. Grants that do not
have to be paid back. Programs that cut
your bills. Housing help that caps what
you pay.
And the reason you have probably never
heard of any of it is not that you do
not qualify. It is that no office is
paid to come find you and tell you. So,
let me be the one to tell you. I am
going to walk you through the real
programs. The ones with actual names you
can look up that help seniors pay to
repair a home, to heat it, and to afford
the rent. I will tell you roughly who
qualifies for each and a single place to
call to begin.
None of this is a scheme and there is
nothing to buy.
It is help that already exists, funded
and waiting for people in exactly your
situation.
Let me begin with the one that surprises
people the most because it comes from a
place you would never expect. If you own
your home and it needs repairs to stay
safe, a roof that leaks, a furnace that
has quit, steps that are no longer safe
to climb, there is a federal program
that will actually give qualifying
seniors money to fix those hazards. It
is run, of all places, through the
United States Department of Agriculture
because it was built for homeowners in
rural and small-town America.
For homeowners who are 62 or older with
a low income, it offers a grant, and a
grant means money you do not repay, of
specifically to remove health and safety
hazards from your home.
And if you also need a larger repair,
there is a low-interest loan of up to
at just 1% stretched over many years
that can be combined with the grant. The
main requirements are simple.
You own and live in the home, your
income is modest, and the home is in an
eligible area, which covers far more of
the country than most people assume.
To start, you call your local United
States Department of Agriculture Rural
Development Office, and you ask about
the Home Repair Program for Seniors.
That one call is the whole beginning.
The second program tackles the bill that
quietly drains a fixed income all winter
and all summer long. And that is your
energy bill.
There is a long-standing federal effort
whose entire job is to make your home
cost less to heat and cool.
And it does this not by handing you a
check, but by sending trained workers to
your home to seal it up properly. They
add insulation, they seal the drafts and
the leaks, they check that your heating
is running safely and efficiently. And
in many cases, they will repair or
replace a dangerous old furnace. And
here is the part that matters most.
For those who qualify, this work is done
completely free.
It is meant for households with modest
incomes.
And if you already receive certain kinds
of assistance,
you may qualify automatically. The
savings are not a one-time thing. A
properly sealed home costs less to heat
every single winter for as long as you
live in it.
To begin, you contact your state or
local weatherization office. And many
people find it fastest to simply dial
211, the free national helpline, and ask
who handles home weatherization in their
county.
There is a third cost that hits
homeowners hardest of all, and it is the
one that keeps climbing even after the
mortgage is long gone. Here is what a
great many seniors never realize.
Almost every state has a program that
will either freeze your property tax so
that it can never rise on you again
or directly lower what you owe once you
reach a certain age and if your income
is modest.
In some places, it can cut that bill
nearly in half.
For a homeowner on a fixed income, that
is hundreds and in many places well over
a thousand dollars staying in your
pocket every single year for as long as
you live in that home.
But this one carries a trap that is easy
to fall into.
You almost always have to file for it
with your county by a specific deadline,
often early in the year.
Miss that window and in most places you
lose the entire benefit for that whole
year with no refund.
So, the two questions to ask your county
assessor are simple.
Do I qualify for the senior property tax
freeze or exemption? And what is the
deadline to apply?
And there is one more kind of help that
matters enormously if what you truly
want is to stay in your own home safely
as the years go on.
If climbing the stairs or stepping over
the side of the tub or getting through a
narrow doorway has become hard, there
are programs, including some run through
Medicaid for those who qualify, that
will actually pay to modify your home
for you.
A ramp at the front step, grab bars in
the bathroom, a walk-in shower in place
of the tub, a sturdy rail along the
stairs. These are not luxuries. They are
the exact changes that let a person go
on living in their own home instead of
being pushed into care that costs many
times more.
And that is the very reason the money
exists to pay for them.
Now, if you rent
or if the house itself has simply become
too much to keep up,
there is help built for that, too. There
is a federal housing program built for
one group and one group only,
older adults.
It is designed specifically for seniors
62 and over with low incomes.
And in these buildings, instead of
paying whatever the market demands, you
generally pay only around 30% of your
income toward the rent. And the
government quietly covers the rest. Many
of these communities are built for aging
comfortably with things like shared
meals, transportation, and staff who
help connect residents to services.
Alongside it, there is a separate and
more widely known program, a rental
voucher that helps low-income seniors
afford a home in the regular private
market. Again, by capping what you pay
at roughly 30% of your income. I will be
honest with you about one thing because
I would rather you hear it from me.
These programs are in high demand and
the waiting list can be long, sometimes
a year or more.
That is exactly why the right time to
get your name on a list is now, long
before you feel you urgently need it,
not the week you do.
And there is a fourth piece that ties
these together, the free guide that most
people never use. In nearly every county
in this country, there is an office
called the Area Agency on Aging.
Its entire reason to exist is to help
older adults find and apply for exactly
the kinds of programs I have just
described along with help for property
taxes, food, and medical costs.
They do not charge you. They do not sell
you anything, and they will sit with you
and sort out which of these you actually
qualify for.
If everything else I have said feels
like too much to chase down one by one,
then let this be the only phone number
you write down today.
Search for the Area Agency on Aging in
your county, and let them do the hard
part with you. Now, I want to be
straight with you about how all of this
works because there is a pattern to it.
And once you see the pattern, you will
never be caught by it again. Not one of
these programs is automatic.
No one at the government cross-checks
your age, and your income, and your
address, and mails you the help.
In every single case, the money sits
there, real and funded, and it waits for
you to raise your hand and ask. The
homeowner who never calls
keeps paying for the repair out of
savings they could not spare.
The renter who never gets on the list
keeps paying a rent that eats them
alive.
And the whole system runs quietly on the
assumption that most people will never
make the call.
Every month you do not is a month the
help simply goes to someone else, or
goes unspent.
And when you do make that call, one
small thing will save you a great deal
of frustration.
Have a few papers within reach before
you dial. Something that shows your age,
a recent statement of your income,
whether that is social security or a
pension, and proof that you own or rent
the home.
Almost every one of these programs turns
on those same three facts. Your age,
your income, and your address. And
having them in front of you turns a
confusing phone call into a short one.
You do not need to prepare a case. You
just need to be ready to answer plainly.
I also want to be fair and careful
because programs like these can change.
their funding can shift from year to
year, and the exact income limits and
rules vary from one state and one county
to the next.
So, please do not take any single number
I have given you as the final word for
your own home.
Take it as proof that the help exists
and as the reason to pick up the phone
and get your own real answer from the
office that runs it.
So, here is what I am asking you to
actually do this week. You do not have
to chase all of these at once. Pick the
one that matches your situation.
If you own your home and something in it
needs fixing to stay safe, call your
local United States Department of
Agriculture Rural Development Office and
ask about the Senior Repair Grant.
If your heating and cooling bills are
crushing you, dial 211 and ask about
weatherization. If the rent has become
impossible or the house has become too
much, contact your local housing
authority and ask to get on the list
today.
And if you're not sure where to even
begin, call the Area Agency on Aging in
your county and let them point you. And
then do one more thing.
Picture someone you know, a parent, a
neighbor, an old friend who is quietly
struggling in a home that costs a little
more than they can carry,
and who would never in a hundred years
think to ask the government for help,
share this with them.
Most people are not missing out on this
because they do not qualify.
They are missing out because no one ever
sat them down and told them the help was
theirs to claim. One last thing,
plainly, I am not with any of these
agencies and I am not selling a service,
and the details really do depend on
where you live and what you earn. So,
use the official offices, the ones
ending in .gov, or the free help at your
area agency on aging to check your own
eligibility.
All I want is for you to know that if
the home you live in has started to feel
like a weight you cannot carry alone,
you do not actually have to carry it
alone.
There is help, it is real,
and it has been waiting the whole time
for you to ask.

title: Seniors! Never Keep This Much Money in One Bank Account

segments.text: My mother almost lost $250,000,
a lifetime of saving nearly gone, all
because of one ordinary mistake that
millions of seniors are making right now
without knowing it. Here is exactly what
she did so it never happens to you. That
one mistake was simple. She kept a large
amount of money in one account at one
bank, the way most people are taught to
their whole lives. And doing that
quietly exposes your money to three
specific risks at the very same time. I
want to walk you through all three using
what happened with my mother as a real
example, because once you understand
them, every one of them is simple to
check and simple to fix. Let me start
with her situation because it will sound
familiar. My mother was never wealthy.
She had just done everything right for
50 years. She paid her bills, she
avoided debt, and she slowly built a
cushion so that she would never have to
be a burden to anyone. When she sold her
home, all of it came together into one
number in one account. And every month
that number on her statement gave her a
sense of relief. The problem is that the
feeling of safety and the fact of safety
are not always the same thing. And in
her case, they had quietly drifted
apart. The first risk is the one most
people find hardest to believe because
it feels impossible that their own bank
would leave them exposed.
So let me give you the rule plainly.
Federal Deposit Insurance protects the
money in your bank account only up to a
limit. Right now, that limit is $250,000
per person per bank in each ownership
category. Any money you hold above that
limit in a single bank is not insured.
If the bank fails, and banks do fail,
the insured portion is returned to you
quickly and in full. The uninsured
portion is not guaranteed. You become a
creditor of the failed bank standing in
line behind others, and you may recover
some of it or none of it, and it can
take years. Here is what that meant for
my mother. A large share of her savings
sat in one account well above that line.
As a simple example, if a person keeps
$400,000 in one account at one bank,
roughly 150,000 of that is completely
uninsured. That money sat exposed for 4
years, and no one at the bank had any
obligation to mention it because being
over the limit does not break any rule.
It was simply a risk she was carrying
without knowing it existed. The good
news is that this one is easy to solve,
and it is worth understanding how
because the same rule that creates the
risk also hands you the fix. That
$250,000 limit applies for each
ownership category, and there are
several categories that stack on top of
one another at the same bank. An account
in your own name is one category. A
joint account with a spouse is a second.
A properly set up trust account naming
the people you want the money to go to
is a third. Each one carries its own
separate $250,000
of coverage. So, a single person using
an individual account and a trust
account can protect far more than the
basic limit. And a married couple using
individual, joint, and trust categories
can be fully insured on well over a
million dollars at just one bank. And if
you simply move some of the money to a
second or third bank, the protection
begins again from zero at each new bank.
There is also a free tool offered by the
agency that runs the insurance that lets
you type in your accounts and see
exactly how much of your money is
currently protected and how much is
exposed. It takes about 10 minutes, and
most people have never once used it. My
mother had never heard of it. The second
risk is quieter, and it affects almost
everyone, not just people with large
savings. Money sitting in a checking
account or in a basic savings account
usually earns very little interest,
often a fraction of 1%. Meanwhile, the
cost of living rises every year. When
the interest you earn is lower than the
rate at which prices are climbing, the
real value of your money, its actual
buying power, falls each year, even
though the balance on your statement
never changes. This is the part that
fools careful people, and it fooled my
mother completely. She watched the
number, the number held steady, and so
she assumed nothing was being lost. But
consider what happens over time. If
prices rise even a few percent a year,
and your money earns almost nothing,
then a large sum sitting idle for 4 or 5
years can quietly lose thousands of
dollars in what it can actually buy,
without the statement ever showing a
single dollar leaving. The fix here is
not to gamble the money in the stock
market, which carries its own risks that
most retirees do not want. It is to move
the money you do not need for daily
living into options that are still safe,
but that at least keep pace with rising
prices. A high-yield savings account, a
money market account, and a certificate
of deposit are all still covered by the
same federal deposit insurance. And
United States Treasury products are
backed directly by the federal
government. Any of them can protect your
money while it earns a reasonable
return, instead of letting it sit still
and slowly shrink. The third risk is the
one that can turn a simple mistake into
a genuine legal problem. So it is worth
understanding exactly. By law, banks are
required to report any cash transaction
over $10,000 to the federal government.
That report is automatic, and for honest
money, it is nothing whatsoever to worry
about. The danger is in what some people
do to try to avoid it. Breaking a large
deposit or withdrawal into smaller
amounts, specifically to stay under that
$10,000 line, is a federal crime. It has
a name. It is called structuring, and it
is illegal regardless of whether the
money itself is completely legitimate.
The penalties are serious, including
heavy fines and even the possibility of
prison, because the law treats the act
of deliberately hiding the transaction
as the offense, entirely separate from
where the money came from. My mother
nearly did exactly this. When she needed
to move a large sum to help one of her
grandchildren, a well-meaning friend
advised her to split it into several
smaller amounts over a couple of weeks
to avoid the paperwork and the
attention. She was not trying to hide
anything from anyone, but the pattern of
splitting a transaction to stay under
the line is precisely what the law looks
for. And ordinary, honest people have
had their accounts frozen and
investigated over it. The correct
approach is simple and completely safe.
Move large sums in the open in a single
transaction and let the automatic report
happen. Honest money has nothing to fear
from that report. It only creates a
problem when it looks like it is being
hidden. So, let me put the three fixes
together plainly because this is the
part you can actually act on. To close
the insurance gap, spread money across
more than one bank or use the separate
ownership categories at a single bank
and use that free coverage tool to
confirm that every dollar is protected.
To stop the quiet loss of value, move
money you do not need for daily expenses
out of a near zero interest account and
into safe, insured, or government-backed
options that keep pace with rising
prices. And to avoid the reporting
problem, never split a transaction to
stay under the limit. Move money openly
in one piece and there is nothing to
worry about. There is one more point
that is easy to miss and it matters.
This is not something you set up one
time and then forget. Insurance coverage
can change if you move money, add a name
to an account, or if your bank merges
with another one. Interest rates shift
over time, so an account that was
reasonable two years ago may be paying
almost nothing today. For that reason,
it is worth doing a simple review about
once a year. Check where your money sits
against the insured limit, confirm it is
still fully protected, and check whether
it is still keeping up with the cost of
living. It takes a few minutes and it is
the difference between setting up a plan
and actually keeping one. The thread
that runs through all three of these
risks is the same and it is the reason I
wanted to lay them out so clearly. None
of them are the result of doing
something wrong. They are the result of
doing the ordinary careful thing,
keeping a large amount of money in one
place without knowing the specific rules
that quietly apply to it. And the
institutions involved have very little
reason to explain those rules to you
because in each case, the very
arrangement that puts you at risk is the
same one that works in their favor and
against yours. So, here is the practical
takeaway I hope you will act on this
week. Look at how much of your money or
your parents money is held in one
account at one bank and check just two
things, whether any of it is sitting
above the insured limit and whether the
money you are not actively using is
earning less than the rate that prices
are rising. Both are quick to check and
both are straightforward to fix. And if
this was useful to you, please pass it
along to someone who keeps their savings
in a single account because the reason
this keeps happening to careful people
over and over is simply that no one ever
took the time to explain it to them. A
brief closing note. This is general
educational information and the specific
limits and rules can change over time
and can depend on your own
circumstances. So, use your bank, the
official insurance tool, or a qualified
professional who has no stake in where
your money sits to confirm exactly where
you stand. The goal here is only to make
sure you know which questions are worth
asking before another year goes by.

title: Never Keep This Much Money in One Bank Account — and the Innocent Mistake That Can Freeze It

segments.text: If you keep more than a certain amount
of money sitting in one ordinary
checking or savings account, something
is quietly working against you right
now. And the bank that holds your money
has no reason in the world to warn you
about it. In fact, it quietly profits
from your silence because the moment
your money crosses a certain line, three
separate things begin happening to it at
the very same time. The first one is
slowly shrinking it month after month
without a single number on your
statement ever changing. The second one
leaves a large part of it completely
unprotected so that if your bank ever
failed, and banks do fail, you could
simply lose it. And the third one, the
most dangerous of the three, can put a
freeze on your account or a federal
report with your name on it over a
completely innocent move that millions
of careful, honest seniors make every
single month without ever realizing it
can be treated as a crime. You did
nothing wrong. You stole nothing. You
broke no rule even recognize as a rule,
but the system does not care about that.
It only sees the pattern, and the
pattern is what it acts on. I went
through the federal banking rules, the
deposit insurance limits, and the
reporting laws that most people over 60
have never once had explained to them in
plain English. And I am going to give
you three things clearly and simply. The
exact line where your own money quietly
starts working against you. The three
hidden dangers of leaving more than that
sitting in a normal account. And then,
the specific, completely legal ways that
careful retirees keep their money safe,
protected, and finally earning something
instead of sitting still and exposed.
One of these three is going to surprise
you because the innocent little thing
people do to avoid it is the exact thing
that gets them into trouble. Let me
start with the danger that is the
easiest of all to miss because it
happens so slowly that you never once
feel it. The first danger is the quiet
one, and it is already happening to
almost everyone watching this.
Money that simply sits in a regular
checking account or in a basic savings
account paying you almost nothing is not
standing still. It is shrinking.
Every year the cost of everything you
buy climbs a little higher. Your
groceries, your medicine, your electric
bill, your property taxes.
You do not need anyone to name it for
you. You feel it every time you stand at
the register and the total is higher
than it used to be for less in the bag.
Now, here is the part that matters, and
it is the part the bank will never say
out loud. If your money is earning
almost nothing while the world around it
gets more expensive every year, then the
real value of that money, what it can
actually buy, is falling steadily month
after month, even though the number on
your statement never moves. $10,000 left
untouched in a no interest account does
not stay $10,000 in any way that
actually matters. In buying power, a few
short years from now, it is worth
noticeably less than it is today. And
the bank is perfectly content to let it
sit there because while it sits, they
are lending your money out and earning
on it and handing you back almost
nothing for the privilege. So, this
first danger is not loud. There is no
freeze, no letter, no knock at the door.
It is just a slow, silent leak in the
bottom of the bucket. And the more you
keep in that account, the bigger the
leak grows. Do not comfort yourself with
the idea that a tiny bit of interest
fixes this either. If your account pays
you a fraction of 1% while prices climb
several percent a year, you are still
losing ground every single month. The
only real question is how fast. The
second danger is the one that can turn a
lifetime of careful saving into a gamble
you never agreed to take.
There is a federal insurance program run
by an agency known as the FDIC,
and it protects the money you keep in a
bank if that bank should ever fail. And
most seniors assume, very reasonably,
that all of their money is fully
covered. It is not.
That protection stops at a line. As of
right now, that line is $250,000
for each person at each bank in each
ownership category. And here is the part
almost no one is told. Every single
dollar you keep in one bank above that
line is not insured. It is exposed. If
that bank were to fail, the insured
money comes back to you quickly and
completely. But the money sitting above
the line becomes something you can only
hope to recover from whatever is left
behind. And you might get some of it, or
you might get none of it. Now, picture a
couple who sold their home, or received
an inheritance, or spent 40 patient
years building a nest egg, and placed
all of it into one account at one bank,
because keeping it together in one place
simply felt safe. The very thing they
did to feel safe is the thing that
quietly left a large part of their life
savings uninsured. And their bank had no
obligation whatsoever to warn them,
because sitting above the line breaks no
rule at all. It is simply your risk to
carry silently, whether you understand
you are carrying it or not. And what
makes this one worse is that almost no
one ever checks. They see one big,
reassuring number on the statement, and
assume the entire thing is protected.
The right day to find out where your
money sits against that line is a calm
afternoon this week, not the morning the
news says your bank is in trouble. And
now the third danger, the one I promised
would surprise you. Because the trap is
not in having the money at all. It is in
how you move it. For more than 50 years,
there has been a federal law that
requires your bank to file a report with
the government anytime you move more
than $10,000 in cash in a single day.
Not because you did anything wrong. It
is completely automatic. A cash deposit,
a cash withdrawal, any movement of
physical currency over that $10,000 line
and a report is quietly filed with your
name on it. Now, that report by itself
is not a crime and it is nothing at all
to fear if your money is honest, which
for nearly everyone watching this, it
is. But, here is exactly where good,
careful people walk straight into
trouble without ever meaning to. Someone
hears about that $10,000 line and they
decide to be clever and careful. So,
instead of depositing $12,000 at once,
they bring in 6,000 one day and 6,000 a
few days later just to stay under the
line and avoid the paperwork and the
attention. That feels careful. It feels
private. It feels responsible. And it is
also, under federal law, a crime. It
even has a name. It is called
structuring. And it is illegal whether
or not the money was earned in the most
honest way imaginable. Deliberately
breaking a deposit into smaller pieces
to stay under that reporting line can
carry very serious penalties, including
heavy fines and even prison time.
Because the law treats the act of hiding
the transaction as the offense all on
its own, completely separate from where
the money actually came from. So, the
single most dangerous mistake in this
entire video is the one that feels the
very safest. Trying to quietly slip
under the radar is the exact thing that
puts you on it. Honest people have had
their accounts frozen and their money
seized over this. Not because they were
criminals, but because the pattern
looked like hiding and the pattern is
all the system sees. So, what do careful
retirees actually do about all three?
Not the wealthy with teams of advisers,
just ordinary people who took a little
time to learn this before it cost them.
The answer to all three dangers turns
out to be one single idea.
Do not let large amounts of money sit
still, exposed, and idle in one ordinary
account. For the insurance danger, you
spread it. Because the protection is
counted for each bank, and for each
ownership category, the same money split
across two or three banks can be made
completely insured instead of partly
exposed. And even within one single
bank, different ownership categories
each carry their own separate
protection. An account in your name
alone, a joint account with your spouse,
a retirement account, and a properly set
up trust account naming your loved ones,
each one can carry its own coverage so
that a careful arrangement protects far
more than that single $250,000
line ever could. For the shrinking
danger, money you do not need for your
day-to-day living does not belong in a
no interest account at all. There are
options that are still completely safe
and still federally insured or federally
backed, like a money market account, a
certificate of deposit, or United States
Treasury products, that will protect
your money and let it earn at the very
same time. Instead of quietly bleeding
value while it sits. And for the
reporting trap, the rule that keeps you
perfectly safe is beautifully simple.
Never, ever break up a deposit or a
withdrawal to slide under a line. If you
are moving a large sum honestly, move it
in the open, all at once. Let the
ordinary report be filed without a
second thought, and you have absolutely
nothing to fear. The only people that
law is built to catch are the ones
trying to hide. So, simply never look
like you are hiding. And please, do not
treat any of this as something you
arrange one time and then forget
forever. Interest rates change,
insurance categories get quietly
misunderstood, and the single most
common way honest people still get
flagged is by getting clever with one
large transfer years after they were
sure they understood all the rules. So,
on the very day you rearrange your
money, write down plainly how each piece
is protected and why, and then look at
it again once every year. Because the
people who end up lying awake over this
are almost never the ones who did
something wrong. They are the ones who
did something quietly and never stopped
to check whether quiet and legal were
actually the same thing. Step back for a
moment and look at the shape of all
three together. Your money, sitting in
one ordinary account, is quietly
shrinking, partly unprotected, and one
innocent-looking move away from a
federal report with your name on it. And
not one part of that is because you did
anything wrong. It is because the system
is built to keep running in the
background whether you are paying
attention or not. And the bank that
holds your money has no reason at all to
stop and explain any of it to you
because every piece of it works quietly
in their favor and against yours. But
every single one of these dangers has a
calm, simple, completely legal answer.
And now you know what all three of them
are. So, here is the one thing I am
asking you to do.
Sometime this week, look honestly at how
much you are keeping in one account at
one bank, and ask yourself two plain
questions.
Is any of my money sitting above the
insured line unprotected? And is the
money I do not need right now quietly
losing its value while it sits there
earning nothing? And then think of one
person you love, a parent, a neighbor, a
friend,
who worked and saved their whole life
and keeps every dollar of it in one
place
because no one ever once told them there
was any risk in that at all.
Send this to them today. It may be the
one thing that keeps their savings safe,
whole, and growing instead of exposed
and shrinking for the rest of their
life. One honest word before you go.
The insurance limits, the reporting
rules, and the safest places to keep
your money can all change over time, and
no two people are in exactly the same
situation. So, please take this as the
push to go look closely at your own
accounts and not as personal financial
or legal advice. A few quiet minutes
with your bank or with someone you trust
who has no reason at all to profit from
where your money sits can tell you
exactly where you stand. None of this is
worth losing a night of sleep over. It
is worth one calm afternoon of checking
before another year slips by with your
money quietly working for everyone
except the person who earned it.

title: Married and Over 65? The Bank Freezes Your Account When You Die — Unless You File This One Free Form

segments.text: If you are married, there is something

freeze your account. Not for an hour,
not for a day, but for months. And the
husband or the wife left behind, the
very person you spent a lifetime trying
to protect, may not be able to reach a
single dollar of your shared money at
the exact moment they need it most. It
sounds impossible, yet it happens to
ordinary, careful couples every single
week. And almost none of them ever saw
it coming. Here is the good news. By the
end of this video, you will know the
four simple moves that make sure this
never happens to the person you love,
and every one of them can be done in a
single afternoon. But first, let me tell
you how I learned that this can happen
to almost anyone. Margaret had been
married for 41 years. Three days after
her husband passed, she drove to the
bank on a gray Tuesday morning to pay
for the funeral out of their savings.
The savings they had built together
their whole lives. She had the death
certificate in her purse. She had their
account number. She had done nothing
wrong. The teller was kind and lowered
her voice, but the answer did not
change. The account was frozen. Margaret
could not touch a single dollar. Not for
the funeral, not for the mortgage, not
for the electric bill that was already
past due. She stood there, 73 years old,
holding the counter, locked out of her
own family's money on the worst week of
her life. What happened to Margaret is
not rare, and it is not a mistake by the
bank. It is exactly how the system is
built to work. And most married seniors
have no idea it is quietly waiting for
them. Here's the truth that almost
nobody explains until it is too late.
When a bank account is held in only one
person's name, and that person dies, the
bank is legally required to freeze that
account the moment it learns of the
death. It does not matter that you were
married for decades. It does not matter
that the money was always meant for the
survivor. Once the bank is notified,
usually by the death certificate, its
duty is no longer to the family. Its
duty is to the estate, and the money is
locked until the courts sort everything
out through a process called probate.
Let me explain what probate really means
because the word gets used a lot and
understood very little. Probate is the
legal process where a court confirms the
will, appoints someone to manage the
estate, pays off any debts and taxes,
and only then releases what is left to
the people who inherit it. It is slow by
design. It can take several months in a
simple case, and it can stretch beyond a
year when things are complicated. And
every single day of that wait, the
frozen account just sits there
untouchable. While the family waits, the
bills do not wait. The funeral home
wants to be paid. The mortgage is due on
the first, the car payment, the
insurance, the property tax, the
everyday cost of simply staying in your
home, all of it keeps coming. And the
surviving spouse can be left with no
legal way to reach the very money that
was supposed to protect them in this
exact moment. Now, here's the part that
should make you sit up straight. This
does not only happen to the wealthy, it
happens to ordinary retirees with one
modest checking account and a small nest
egg. If that account is in one name, it
can be frozen. The comforting news, and
the reason I am making this video, is
that everything I am about to show you
can be set up in a single afternoon. And
it can spare the person you love most
from ever standing at that counter the
way Margaret did. The first move is the
simplest one, and for most couples, it
solves the biggest part of the problem
by itself. Turn your main accounts into
joint accounts with what is called right
of survivorship. When two people own an
account this way, and one of them
passes, the account belongs fully and
immediately to the survivor. There is no
freeze. There is no waiting. Your spouse
keeps access from the very first day.
You can usually add a spouse to an
existing account with one short visit to
the bank. The second move is to name a
beneficiary directly on the account. On
a checking or savings account, this is
called payable on death, and you may
hear it spoken as POD. On an investment
or brokerage account, it is called
transfer on death or TOD. You simply
fill out a short form naming the person
who receives the money when you pass.
That money then goes straight to them
and skips the frozen estate entirely. It
does not go through probate. It costs
nothing and it takes only a few minutes
to set up. The third move is for
families with a home and more to
protect, and that is a revocable living
trust. When your accounts and your house
are placed inside a living trust, they
are no longer trapped in probate when
you pass. Control moves quietly to the
person you chose without the courts and
without the long freeze. This is the
step where sitting down with an estate
planning attorney is genuinely worth the
money because a trust has to be set up
and funded correctly or it will not do
its job. The fourth move is one that
people forget and it matters far more
than they expect. Keep a separate,
reachable pool of money that your spouse
can always touch on their own, in their
own name or in a joint account. Even
with everything else in place, having an
emergency account with enough to cover a
few months of bills means your loved one
never has to borrow or beg or wait
during the hardest weeks of their life.
Think of it as a bridge that carries
them across until the rest is settled.
And there is a fifth thing that costs
nothing at all. Tell your spouse where
everything is. The accounts, the online
passwords, the insurance papers, the
name of your attorney if you have one.
So much of the pain that families go
through is simply not knowing what
exists or where to find it. One quiet
conversation at the kitchen table can
lift an enormous weight before it ever
lands. Let me show you the other side of
this because it is just as real. A
couple I heard about, the Hansons, had
done these very things years earlier.
Their accounts were joint. Their
beneficiaries were named. When the
husband passed, the wife did not lose
access to a single dollar. She paid the
funeral home that week. She kept the
house running without missing a beat.
She was able to grieve instead of fight
the bank. That is the whole difference.
Same loss, two completely different
weeks. Now, let me say something
important, especially if you are in your
50s or 60s and thinking this is a
problem for later, it is not. The best
time to set these things up is long
before anyone needs them, while both of
you are healthy and clear-headed and can
make these decisions together calmly at
your own pace. Waiting is the one move
that never once helps anybody. Think
about what we covered. A joint account
with right of survivorship, so your
spouse is never locked out. A payable on
death or transfer on death beneficiary,
so the money skips the frozen estate. A
living trust for families who want the
fullest protection. A reachable
emergency account for the hard weeks.
And one honest conversation, so nobody
is ever left in the dark. Any one of
these helps on its own. Together, they
can mean the difference between your
spouse grieving in peace and your spouse
standing at a teller's window being told
they cannot touch their own family's
money. If this helped you, send it to
one married person over 65 who has never
set this up. It may quietly turn out to
be the most important thing they do all
year. This video is for general
education only and it is not legal or
financial advice. Every state has
different rules. Please speak with a
licensed estate planning attorney about
your own situation before you make any
changes.

title: Over 65 With a Paid-Off Home? Here's What Medicaid Does to It the Day You Need Care

segments.text: If you are over 65 and you own your
home, the government can take it to pay
for a nursing home. Most families never
see it coming until it is too late to
stop it. I'm talking about the home you
spent 30 or 40 years paying off. For a
great many families, when a parent
eventually needs full-time care, that
home ends up being sold to cover the
bills and very little is left to pass on
to the children. This happens to
careful, hard-working people all the
time and the hard part is that it is
almost always avoidable when you plan
ahead. So, stay with me because I am
going to show you how these costs
actually work, why Medicare will not
cover them, the one rule that decides
whether your family keeps your home, and
the four moves a homeowner over 65 can
make to protect what they spent a
lifetime building. The fourth move
starts a clock and the sooner you start
it, the more it can protect. Let me
start with the misunderstanding that
catches most families off guard. Most
people assume that Medicare will pay for
a nursing home. In most cases, it will
not. Medicare, the program you paid into
out of every paycheck for 40 years,
covers very little long-term care. It
will pay for a short rehabilitation stay
after a hospital visit, usually up to
100 days and only while you are still
improving. Once you are no longer
improving, Medicare coverage ends. It
does not pay for the daily help that
long-term care really means, such as
help with bathing, dressing, and staying
safe. That kind of help is called
custodial care and it is one of the most
expensive services in the country. In
many areas, a nursing home now costs
between $10,000 and $15,000 a month.
That is not a year, that is every month.
So, if Medicare will not pay, who does?
For most families, the answer is
Medicaid and this is the part that
surprises people. Medicaid will pay for
long-term care and it will pay for as
long as you need it. But Medicaid is a
needs-based program. So to qualify, your
savings generally have to be spent down
to a very low limit first. In many
states, a single person is allowed to
keep only around $2,000 in countable
assets before Medicaid will help. The
savings you protected your whole life
often have to be used up before any
coverage begins. Now, here is the part
that turns a difficult moment into a
much bigger loss.
You usually cannot simply give your
money or your home to your children at
the last minute. When you apply for
Medicaid, most states review five full
years of your finances. Every account,
every large withdrawal, every gift,
every transfer. This is called the
five-year look-back.
If you gave away money or moved your
home during those five years, it can
create a penalty period where Medicaid
will not pay yet, and the family ends up
covering the cost out of pocket for a
while. And there is one more step many
families do not see coming. There is a
federal program called the Medicaid
Estate Recovery Program. You will often
see it written as MERP.
Every state is required to have one.
Here is what it does in plain terms. The
care Medicaid pays for is recorded, and
after a person passes away, the state
can file a claim to recover those costs
from their estate. In many cases, that
means a claim against the home, which
has to be settled before the house can
pass cleanly to the children. So, a home
worth a few hundred thousand dollars can
end up leaving very little behind once
that claim and the usual selling costs
are paid. None of this happens because
anyone did something wrong. These rules
are complicated, they are different in
every state, and they have been getting
stricter over the years. Most families
simply never learn about them until they
are already in the middle of a crisis.
That is the real problem. And the good
news is that it is one you can plan for
well ahead of time. So, let me walk you
through the four moves that protect a
family. Move one, understand the
difference between living in your home
and legally owning it. These are not the
same thing. The approach that protects
families is to move the home out of your
personal name while keeping your full
right to live in it for the rest of your
life. You do not lose your home. You do
not move out. You simply change who
legally owns it so that it is better
protected. Move two. Use the right legal
structure to do it. The tool many elder
law attorneys use is called a Medicaid
asset protection trust. You will often
see it written as MAPT. It is a trust
that cannot be changed once it is set up
and that is exactly what allows it to
work. Your attorney names one of your
adult children, rather than you, to
manage it and names your children as the
ones who will inherit. You keep the
right to live in your home for life.
When you pass, the home can move
directly to your children without going
through probate. Move three. Place the
right assets into that protection. There
are usually three. First, the home,
which is almost always the largest and
the most important. Second, the savings
you do not need for everyday living, so
it is not all spent down if you need
care. Third, any regular investment or
brokerage account. When this is done
correctly, moving these assets into the
trust does not create a tax bill because
it is not the same as selling them. Move
four. And this is the one that decides
everything. Start the clock as early as
you can. Remember the five-year look
back. The protection becomes fully
effective five years after you move the
assets in. That means time is the single
most important factor. A family that
sets this up five years and one day
before care is ever needed can protect
the entire estate. A family that waits
until care is already needed has very
few options left. Every year you wait is
a year on the wrong side of that window
and the clock only starts once you act.
Let me make this real with two examples
because the difference is striking.
Picture two neighbors, both 78, both
with a paid-off home worth $400,000 and
$200,000 in savings. Both eventually
need full-time care for several years.
The first neighbor did no planning. The
savings are used up in a little over a
year and Medicaid only begins to help
once almost everything is gone. After he
passes, the state files its claim, the
home is sold to repay it, and his three
children are left with very little. A
lifetime of work mostly gone in the
final chapter. The second neighbor
planned 5 years earlier. She paid a few
thousand dollars to an elder law
attorney to set up the trust and move
her home and savings into it. She kept
living in her home the whole time.
When she later needed care, those assets
were already outside the 5-year window,
so they did not count against her.
Medicaid helped. When she passed, there
was nothing left in her estate for the
state to claim, and her home and
savings, around $600,000, passed
straight to her three children.
The difference between the two neighbors
was a few thousand dollars in legal fees
and 5 years of time. That is the whole
point. Same income, same home, same
children. The only real difference was
planning early. And this is why I want
to speak for a moment to anyone who is
not yet in their 70s or 80s.
Because of that 5-year clock, the people
who end up fully protected are almost
always the ones who set this up early,
often in their 50s and 60s, long before
there is any health problem at all. If
you own a home and you are still
healthy, this is exactly the right time
to act while every option is still open
to you. And if it is your parents who
own the home, this is the conversation
to have with them this year, gently and
early, not after a stroke or a fall when
the clock has already run out. Planning
ahead is the entire difference between
keeping the home and losing it. Now, I
want to be very clear with you. This is
general education, not legal advice.
Every state has different rules, and
some, such as California, have recently
changed theirs in important ways. A
structure like this has to be set up
correctly by a professional, or it will
not protect you. So, the real step today
is simple. If you are over 65 and you
own your home, talk to a licensed elder
law attorney in your state and ask
specifically about a Medicaid asset
protection trust and the 5-year
look-back where you live. I am putting a
link in the description to help you find
one. The best time to do this is while
you are healthy because these rules
reward the families who plan ahead. Here
is what I want to stay with you after
this video ends. Families do not lose
their homes because they did something
wrong. They lose them because no one
explained these rules in time. Medicare
covers very little long-term care.
Medicaid asks you to spend down almost
everything first and the state can
recover its costs from your estate
later. But a family that moves the right
assets into the right structure 5 years
before care is needed can protect all of
it. The one thing standing between those
two outcomes is time and the clock
starts the day you decide to act. So, if
you own a home and you want it to go to
the people you love, please send this
video to one person over 65 who has not
made a plan yet. One share takes 10
seconds. For the right family, those 10
seconds could help them keep a home that
took a lifetime to build.

title: 7 Benefits Seniors Get in January 2027 (Some Only If You Ask)

segments.text: Next January, millions of retirees are
going to open their bank statements and
find a little more money than they
expected. The average retired worker
will see about $75 more every month. A
typical retired couple will see roughly
$117 more.
And here is the part that surprises
people. That raise is not even the
biggest piece of good news waiting for
you in January. If you have been
following the headlines lately, I
understand why you might be tired. For
months, nearly everything aimed at
retirees has sounded gloomy.
Rising prices, changes to Medicare
plans, warnings about taxes, warnings
about savings.
Some of that is real, and we have talked
about it here before.
But today, I want to give you something
different. I'm going to walk you through
seven genuine pieces of good news that
take effect around January, all of them
backed by federal law and published by
Social Security, Medicare, and the IRS.
For every single one, I will tell you
the number, who it helps, and the one
simple step that makes sure it actually
reaches you. And please stay with me
until the very end because the seventh
item is the one that can put roughly
$2,400 a year back into your pocket.
Millions of people are eligible for it
right now and have never applied. Some
of them assume they earn too much.
Others simply never heard the name of
the program. I will explain exactly who
qualifies and which phone call gets it
started. One quick note before we begin.
Every [clears throat] figure I share
comes from a federal agency. The people
in my examples are made up, so please do
not go looking for them, but the rules
and the dollar amounts are real. Now,
why does this matter so much? Because
some of this money arrives on its own
with no effort from you at all, while
other pieces only reach you if you ask
for them. And nobody is going to phone
you to remind you. The government is
excellent at announcing increases and
not so excellent at explaining how to
claim the ones that require a request.
So treat this video like a checklist. By
the time we finish, you will know which
benefits are already on their way to you
and which you need to go out and
collect. Let us begin with the one
everybody has heard about because there
is more to it than the headline. The
first piece of good news is the cost of
living raise. Every October, Social
Security measures how much prices
climbed over the previous year and then
it raises benefits to keep pace. That is
the cost of living adjustment, often
shortened to COLA. For 2027, the agency
announced it on October 14th and the
number is 3.6%
the largest increase in several years.
Here is what that means in real dollars
using Social Security's own estimates.
The average retired worker currently
receives about $2,095 a month. Starting
in January, that becomes about $2,170.
That is $75 more each month or $900
across the year. For a retired couple
where both people collect, the raise
works out to about $117 a month, which
is $1,404 over 12 months. And if you are
a widow or widower living on a single
check, you can expect roughly $70 more
each month. Let me introduce you to
Harold and Gloria. Harold is 74 and
spent 30 years driving a bread delivery
truck. Gloria is 71 and worked in a
school kitchen. Together, their benefits
land very close to the average couple's.
In January, their deposit grows by about
Across the year, that is $1,400 they did
not have before and they never filled
out a form or made a call to get it. Now
here is what most people overlook. You
do not need to apply for this raise, but
you should absolutely check it. Before
the year ends, Social Security sends a
notice showing your new benefit amount.
If you have a My Social Security account
online, it appears in your message
center. If you do not, it arrives in the
mail. When it comes, do not toss it in a
drawer. Set it beside last year's letter
and compare the two line by line. Look
at the gross benefit and look at what is
being deducted for Medicare. If anything
looks off, you have every to ask Social
Security to explain it. That one small
habit catches errors that could
otherwise cost you money for years. But
many seniors have a nagging worry right
now, which is that Medicare will quietly
take that raise right back.
And that leads us to the second piece of
good news. The second piece of good news
is a protection called the hold harmless
rule.
Most people on Medicare have their part
B premium taken directly out of their
Social Security check before the money
ever reaches the bank.
In 2026, the standard part B premium is
a month.
For 2027, Medicare's trustees projected
it will rise to about $209.50.
That is an increase of roughly $6.60.
The official figure is usually announced
in the fall, so keep an eye out for it.
So the natural question is, will
Medicare eat my raise?
For the great majority of people, the
answer is no, and there is a law behind
that answer.
The hold harmless provision is part of
the Social Security Act. It says that
for most beneficiaries, a rise in the
part B premium cannot make your Social
Security payments smaller than it was
the year before. If the premium jumps by
more than your raise, the premium
increase is limited so that your check
does not shrink.
This year, it is not even a close call.
If the average retiree gets $75 more and
the premium goes up about $6.60,
that person still comes out a
>> Most people forget a video within a
week, and that is exactly when a missed
rule, form, or deadline can cost them
real money.
That's why I created the Senior Money
Guide. It's one complete book, 156 pages
in large print [music] with the exact
forms, the right questions to ask, and
step-by-step checklists all in one
place.
Scan the QR code on your screen or visit
richardretires.shop.
Clear, plain English and nothing
complicated.
>> Now come back to the hour video. Head by
roughly $68 every month. Think about
Dolores. She is 78 and lives on one
check.
For years, every December she has braced
herself for the letter. Certain Medicare
would swallow her raise. This time, her
raise is about $70 and the premium
increase is only a sliver of that. the
hold harmless rule stands behind her no
matter what.
Now, here comes the twist, and I need
you to listen closely. That protection
does not cover everyone. It does not
apply if you are new to Medicare this
year. It does not apply if your premium
is not deducted from your Social
Security check. And most importantly, it
does not apply if you pay the higher
income surcharge known as IRMAA.
IRMAA is an extra charge added on top of
your Part B premium when your income was
above certain levels. And here is the
trap. Medicare does not look at what you
earned today. It looks at your tax
return from two years ago. That means a
one-time event, like selling a house,
cashing out an account, or taking a
large required withdrawal, can trigger a
surcharge long after that money has been
spent. If that describes you and your
income has since dropped because you
retired, lost a spouse, or stopped
working, you are allowed to ask Social
Security to use your newer, lower income
instead. The form is called SSA-44.
It costs nothing and it can reduce your
surcharge, sometimes all the way to
zero. How can you tell whether you are
paying IRMAA?
Look at the Medicare line on your
notice. If the amount being taken out is
higher than the standard premium, the
difference is almost always IRMAA.
Social Security also mails a separate
letter that explains it and tells you
which year of income they used. So, if
your Medicare deduction looks too high,
do not simply accept it. Ask whether you
are paying IRMAA and if your income has
dropped, file the SSA-44.
Medicare is not the only January worry,
though. If you are still working, there
is a rule that has been quietly holding
back your money, and it just loosened.
The third piece of good news is for
retirees who still earn a paycheck. Here
is the situation. If you claim Social
Security before your full retirement age
and keep working, social security can
withhold part of your benefit once your
earnings pass a certain amount. This is
called the earnings test. In 2026, the
limit is $24,480.
In 2027, it rises to $25,560.
That gives you $1,080 of additional
earnings before social security touches
a single dollar of your benefit. Above
that limit, social security holds back
$1 of benefits for every $2 you earn
over it. So the higher limit means more
of your work income is safe and less of
your check is held back.
In the calendar year when you actually
reach full retirement age, the limit is
far more generous. It climbs to $67,920
and the withholding drops to $1 for
every $3 over the line. If you were born
in 1960 or later, your full retirement
age is 67. For those born a little
earlier, it comes a few months sooner.
And here is the best part. The moment
you reach full retirement age, the
earnings test disappears entirely. No
limit at all. You can earn as much as
you like and keep every dollar of your
benefit. Consider Frank. Frank is 63.
He started social security early, got
restless at home, and took a part-time
job at a hardware store.
Last year, he earned slightly over the
limit and social security held back part
of his check.
Frank was furious. He assumed that money
had vanished. But here is what hardly
anyone tells people. That money is not
lost.
When Frank reaches full retirement age,
social security recalculates his benefit
and credits him for every month they
withheld payment. His monthly check
becomes larger from then on. So if you
are working while collecting early, look
at the new limit and plan your hours
around it. And if some of your benefit
has been held back, please do not panic.
It comes back to you later in the form
of a bigger check.
Now let us move away from work because
the next item has to do with taxes and
the filing season that opens soon is
when many seniors will discover just how
large it is. The fourth piece of good
news is that seniors are heading into
tax season with the biggest deductions
they have ever had. First, let me clear
up some confusion because you may have
seen this online.
Social Security did not become tax-free.
If your income is high enough, part of
your benefit can still be taxed. But
Congress did create something that for
many seniors gets them to a very similar
place. When you file your 2026 return in
early 2027, you can claim three separate
breaks simply for being 65 or older. The
first is the regular standard deduction,
which is $16,100
for a single filer. The second is the
additional amount for age, which is
$2,050 for a single filer. Wait, to be
exact, it is $2,050.
And the third is the brand new senior
deduction of $6,000 for every person 65
or older available through the year
2028. Add those together and a single
senior can subtract $24,150
from income before the IRS taxes a
single cent. For a married couple where
both spouses are over 65, the standard
deduction is $32,200
+ $1,650 each for age + $6,000 each for
the senior deduction. That totals
And here is what makes the senior
deduction special. You can claim it
whether you take the standard deduction
or itemize. Almost every other deduction
forces you to choose. This one does not.
Think about Lorraine. She is 68 and a
widow with a small pension, a little
interest from savings, and her social
security.
Since her husband passed, she has paid a
modest amount of income tax every year.
This year, with all three breaks stacked
together, much of her taxable income
simply disappears. Depending on her
exact numbers, she may owe far less than
last year or nothing at all.
There is a catch, however. The senior
deduction begins to shrink when your
income goes above $75,000
for a single filer or $150,000 for a
married couple.
And it only helps if it truly lands on
your return.
I have seen seniors rely on bargain tax
software or a rushed preparer or skip a
question about their age and then miss
out on money that was rightfully theirs.
The IRS is not going to call you to say
you forgot something. So when you file
this winter, look for the senior
deduction by name.
Make sure the extra amount for age
appears for every person on the return
who is 65 or older. And if you would
like someone to double check your work
for free, the IRS runs a program called
Tax Counseling for the Elderly.
You can find the closest site by calling
Taxes are only one bill getting smaller.
The next one shows up at the pharmacy
counter. The fifth piece of good news is
that on January 1st, the prices Medicare
pays for 15 more expensive drugs fall.
For the first time in history, Medicare
was permitted to negotiate directly with
drug companies. The first round of
negotiated prices took effect this year,
and the second round begins on January
1st, 2027, covering 15 additional

Under the 2026 formula, Social Security

a month. So, the five zeros cost him

If Social Security will cover most of
your bills, it matters a lot. That's the

you leave. There's a second cost to
retiring at 55 that people don't think

In those early years, you might have
