title: Retirees: 8 Money Risks Nobody Warns You About After Age 65

segments.text: Eight things can drain a retirement, and
seven of them are the kind that make
headlines. A market crash, a big medical
bill, a scam. You've heard about all of
those, but one item on this list is
different because it doesn't just cost
you money by itself. It makes every
other item on the list bigger. And the
number that connects all of them is one
that most people guess wrong, usually by
about 10 years. I'll tell you which one
it is at the very end. First, I want to
walk you through all eight with the
actual figures for 2026 and 2027, and
one thing you can do about each. I am
Richard, and on this channel I read the
official numbers, the Medicare tables,
the IRS rules, and the Social Security
data, so you get the real figures before
they show up as a surprise in your
mailbox. Let's start with the one that
arrives in your mailbox every month, and
it isn't the one most people expect. The
first risk is the part of your
healthcare bill that Medicare doesn't
cover. Original Medicare, meaning parts
A and B, has no yearly limit on what you
can pay out of pocket. In 2026, the Part
B deductible is $283.
After you meet it, you generally pay 20%
of the Medicare-approved amount for
doctor visits, outpatient care, and many
tests, and there is no ceiling on that
20%. For a routine year, that's
manageable. But in a year with a knee
replacement, a cancer treatment, or a
long hospital stay, 20% of a very large
bill can reach into the thousands, and
it keeps going. On top of that, you pay
a premium. The standard Part B premium
a month, up from 185. For 2027, the
Medicare Trustees report projects it
will rise to about $209.50,
although as I record this, the official
2027 figure has not been announced, so
please check medicare.gov for the final
number. Then there's the income-related
surcharge called IRMAA.
In 2026, it applies if your income is
as a single filer or $218,000 as a
married couple filing jointly. And it's
based on your tax return from two years
earlier. So, a large retirement account
withdrawal or a big taxable gain from
selling a home can raise your Medicare
premiums two years later. Drug costs are
the other piece. Part D now has a yearly
cap on what you pay out of pocket for
covered drugs. In 2026, that cap is
In 2027, it rises to 2400 and the
standard deductible rises from $615
to 700. So, how do people protect
themselves from the 20% with no ceiling?
There are two main routes. One is a
Medigap policy, also called Medicare
supplement, which pays some or all of
what original Medicare leaves behind.
That usually costs more each month, but
you can generally see any doctor who
accepts Medicare. The other is a
Medicare Advantage plan, which has a
yearly out-of-pocket maximum up to
in 2026 for in-network care.
Those plans often cost less up front,
but they use networks and can require
prior approval. Both have trade-offs and
neither is right for everyone. There's
also a timing rule that matters. Your
best chance to buy a Medigap policy is
the 6-month window that begins when
you're 65 or older and enrolled in Part
B. After that, in most states, an
insurer may be allowed to ask health
questions and may turn you down or
charge more. And right now, we're in
Medicare's annual open enrollment
period, which runs from October 15th to
December 7th. If you have a Medicare
Advantage plan or a Part D plan, this is
when you can change it for next year.
Plans change their networks, their drug
lists, and their costs every year. And
some are pulling out of certain areas,
so don't assume that your plan next year
will look like this year's.
I want to pause here for a second. If
this is the kind of rule-by-rule
breakdown you find useful, tap subscribe
because I do one of these every week.
And drop your state in the comments
right now and tell me which of these
eight risks worries you most. I read
those comments, and your answers help me
decide what to cover next.
Now, let's keep going, because the next
one is the most expensive on the list.
The second risk is long-term care. A lot
of people assume Medicare will cover it.
It generally doesn't, at least not the
kind most people picture. Here's what
Medicare actually does. After a hospital
stay of at least 3 days as an admitted
patient, original Medicare can cover a
stay in a skilled nursing facility. The
first 20 days cost you nothing. Days 21
through 100 cost you $217 a day in 2026.
After day 100, you pay everything. And
it has to be skilled care, like therapy
or nursing, not help with bathing,
dressing, or eating, which is what most
long-term care really is. Medicare's
home health benefit works the same way.
It's part-time skilled care for people
who are home-bound, not an aid who comes
every day. Now, the price tag. According
to the 2025 CareScout Cost of Care
Survey, the national median for a
private room in a nursing home is about
a year. A semi-private room is about
And a non-medical caregiver at home
comes to about $80,000 a year, based on
44 hours of care a week.
One thing to know about that source,
CareScout is owned by Genworth, which
sells long-term care insurance. And the
federal government doesn't publish a
single national price like this. So,
treat these as useful benchmarks, not
exact quotes. Prices vary a lot by
state. How likely is it that you'll need
care? The Federal Administration for
Community Living says someone turning 65
today has almost a 70% chance of needing
some type of long-term care services in
their remaining years.
On average, that need lasts about 3
years. For women, it's about 3.7 years,
and for men, about 2.2.
About 1/3 of people never need it, but
roughly 20% will need it for more than 5
years. So, there are four main ways
people pay. You can pay from savings.
You can buy a traditional long-term care
insurance policy. You can buy a hybrid
policy that combines life insurance or
an annuity with long-term care benefits.
Or, you can rely on Medicaid, which can
pay for nursing home care if you meet
your state's income and asset rules. And
that may mean spending down some of your
savings first. And be careful with
gifts. Medicaid looks back 60 months at
transfers of money or property. And if
you gave assets away during that window,
you can face a penalty period before
Medicaid pays. Rules vary by state. So,
this is a case where a conversation with
an elder law attorney can be worth the
fee. Each option has a catch.
Traditional policies can raise their
premiums after you buy them, and you pay
for coverage you might never use. Hybrid
policies usually lock in the premium and
pay a death benefit if you don't need
care. But, they cost more up front. Both
require you to be healthy enough to
qualify, which is much easier at 60 than
at 75. And if you have substantial
savings, paying your own way can make
more sense than paying premiums for
years. If you have very little, Medicaid
may be the realistic path. Insurance
tends to fit in the middle. The point
isn't that one answer is right. It's
that deciding at 65 gives you choices
you may not have at 80. The third risk
is inflation, and it doesn't arrive as
one bad day. It arrives as a little less
every year for decades. Social Security
adjusts for it. The cost of living
increase for 2026 was 2.8%
and the Social Security Administration
announced on October 14th that the
increase for 2027 will be 3.6%,
which averages about $75 more per month.
But, a lot of other income doesn't
adjust. A pension without a cost of
living clause stays the same. So does a
fixed annuity, and so does interest from
a certificate of deposit. Here's what
even moderate inflation does. At 3% a
year, a $1,000 of monthly spending
becomes about $1,344
in 10 years and about $1,806 in 20. In
other words, the same life that cost
$1,000 a month at 65 costs almost twice
that at 85, even though nothing about
how you live has changed. And there's a
second way inflation works against you
through the tax rules. The income
thresholds that decide whether your
Social Security is taxed, $25,000 for a
single filer and 32,000 for a married
couple, were set in 1983.
A second set of thresholds, 34,000 and
44,000, was added in 1993.
Neither has ever been adjusted for
inflation. So, every year more retirees
cross those lines without any real raise
in their lifestyle. Most people forget a
video within a week, and that is exactly
when a missed rule, form, or deadline
can cost them real money.
That's why I created the Senior Money
Guide. It's one complete book, 156 pages
in large print with the exact forms, the
right questions to ask, and step-by-step
checklists, all in one place.
Scan the QR code on your screen or visit
richardretires.shop.
Clear, plain English, and nothing
complicated. What helps? Income that
rises with prices, starting with Social
Security itself, and investments that
are meant to keep up, such as Treasury
Inflation-Protected Securities, called
TIPS, and Series I Savings Bonds. And
some money invested for growth. But
growth means living with market ups and
downs, which brings us to the next risk.
The fourth risk is when the market
falls, not just whether it falls. Let me
show you with a simplified example.
Imagine two retirees. Each starts with
$900,000 and withdraws $45,000 at the
start of every year for 10 years. I'm
keeping the withdrawals flat to keep the
math clear. Both of them earn exactly
the same 10 annual returns, a loss of
20% in 1 year and a gain of 8% in each
of the other nine. Same returns, same
average, same withdrawals. The only
difference is the order. The first
retiree takes the 20% loss in the very
first year and then gets nine good
years. After 10 years, that retiree has
The second retiree gets nine good years
first and then takes the 20% loss in
year 10.
After 10 years, that retiree has about
That's a gap of roughly $157,000
with identical returns. Why? Because
when the loss comes early, you're
selling shares at low prices to pay your
bills and those shares are gone before
the recovery arrives.
Researchers call this sequence of
returns risk. Two things can soften it.
One is keeping a cushion of cash and
bonds. So, in a bad year, you spend from
that pile and leave your stocks alone to
recover. The other is flexible spending,
meaning you take a little less in a down
year, skip the big trip, or delay buying
a new car. Both help and both have a
cost. Cash and bonds earn less over
time. So, if the bad years don't come
early, that cushion will have cost you
some growth. As always, it's a
trade-off, not a free fix.
The fifth risk affects married couples
and it's one almost nobody talks about
until it happens. When the first spouse
passes away, the household's income
usually drops, but not by half. Start
with Social Security. The surviving
spouse generally keeps the larger of the
two benefits and the smaller one goes
away. But then, the taxes change. In the
year after the death, the survivor
usually files as a single filer, unless
there's a qualifying dependent child.
And in 2026, the standard deduction for
a married couple is $32,200.
For a single filer, it's $16,100.
That's half. The 22% tax bracket starts
of taxable income for a married couple,
but at $50,400 for a single filer. Also
half. And the Medicare IRMAA line drops
So, you can have the same pension, the
same retirement account withdrawals, and
the same required distributions, but
smaller deductions and narrower
brackets. That's often called the
widow's penalty, though it affects
widowers just as much. One break. The
surviving spouse can still file a joint
return for the year the spouse passes
away and the switch to single filing
comes the following year.
Here's why some people look at Roth
conversions while both spouses are still
alive. You'd pay tax at joint rates now
instead of at single rates later, but
that's not right for everyone because a
conversion means paying tax today on
money you may not need for years. If
both of you have modest retirement
accounts, the widow's penalty may be
small and a conversion may not pay off.
The right move is to run the numbers
both ways as a couple and as a survivor,
ideally with a tax professional.
The sixth risk is losing money to a scam
or a bad decision. As we age, managing
money gets harder and scammers know it.
According to the FBI's Internet Crime
Complaint Center, Americans age 60 and
older filed 201,266
complaints in 2025 and reported losses
of about 7.7 billion dollars, up 59%
from the year before. The average loss
per victim was about $38,500
and more than 12,000 people in that age
group lost over $100,000 each. And those
are only the losses people reported.
Many people are too embarrassed to say
anything. The biggest dollar losses came
from investment fraud, about 3 and 1/2
billion dollars, much of it involving
cryptocurrency and fake trading
platforms.
Next were tech support scams at about 1
billion, then confidence and romance
scams at about 584 million.
And the FBI is now tracking scams that
involve artificial intelligence, such as
cloned voices in so-called grandparent
scams.
The warning sign is almost always the
same. A real bank or government agency
will not ask you to move your money to
keep it safe and they will not ask you
to pay with gift cards or
cryptocurrency. If someone does, that
request is the red flag. Hang up and
call the institution using a number you
look up yourself. There are three moves
that can help. First, use the free
yearly wellness visit under Medicare,
which includes a review for cognitive
impairment at no cost if your doctor
accepts Medicare assignment. Second,
name a trusted contact at your bank and
your brokerage. Brokerage firms are
required to ask you for one, though you
aren't required to name someone. That
person can't touch your money, but
they're the person the firm can call if
something looks wrong. Third, consider a
durable power of attorney for your
finances while you're still healthy. If
you wait until it's needed, it may be
too late to sign one. And if you or
someone you know is targeted, you can
report it at ic3.gov
or call the Justice Department's
National Elder Fraud Hotline at
The seventh risk gets a lot of
headlines, so let me keep it in
proportion. It's the fear that Social
Security will be cut. The 2026 Trustees
Report projects that the retirement
trust fund, the Old Age and Survivors
Insurance Fund, will run short of
reserves in the last quarter of 2032. If
nothing changes, incoming payroll taxes
would still cover about 78% of scheduled
retirement and survivor benefits.
If you combine the retirement and
disability funds, the date moves to 2034
with about 83% payable.
That's not the end of Social Security.
It's an automatic reduction that would
follow if Congress took no action. And
Congress has changed Social Security to
address shortfalls before, and there are
several options on the table. I mention
this because fear is one of the biggest
reasons people claim early. When AARP
asked people 50 and older who claimed
earlier than planned why they did it,
worry about the program's future was the
top reason.
But claiming early locks in a
permanently smaller check. So, if you're
tempted to claim sooner because of the
headlines, it's worth running the
numbers first.
Now, the last risk, the one I told you
ties all the others together. It's
living longer than your plan. Most
people build a plan around an average
life expectancy. Under the period life
table used in the 2026 Social Security
Trustees Report, a 65-year-old man can
expect to live about 18 more years, and
a 65-year-old woman nearly 21. But,
that's the middle, not the end. About
24% of men and 35% of women who reach 65
go on to reach 90. For a married couple,
that works out to roughly even odds that
at least one of them sees 90. And about
8% of men and 14% of women reach 95. So,
a plan that ends at 84 leaves a lot of
people short. And the longer you live,
every other risk on this list gets
bigger.
There are more years of inflation
compounding, more years of premiums and
out-of-pocket medical costs, a higher
chance that you'll need care, a higher
chance that one spouse will be living
alone with a single filer's tax bill,
and more years of exposure to someone
targeting you. There's a flip side, and
I want to be fair about it. If your
health or family history points to a
shorter life, planning to 95 could lead
you to spend too little right now. So,
think of your own health as one piece of
information, not the final answer.
What can you do? One answer is income
that can't run out before you do, such
as Social Security, a pension, or an
annuity. For many couples, that includes
having the higher earner delay Social
Security because each year you wait past
full retirement age adds about 8% until
age 70. And that larger payment becomes
the basis for the survivor benefit, so
delaying can protect the spouse who
lives longer. So, how do you put all
this together? Here's what I'd do.
First, build an income floor that lasts
as long as you do. Cover your basic
expenses with income that can't run out,
and think carefully about when to claim
Social Security. Second, decide how
you'd pay for long-term care, whether
that's savings, a traditional or hybrid
policy, or Medicaid while you still have
options. Third, protect your decisions.
Name a trusted contact, sign a durable
power of attorney, and use your free
yearly wellness visit. Fourth, run your
numbers two ways, as a couple and as a
survivor, so you can see what the
widow's penalty would look like for you.
Fifth, keep enough in cash and bonds to
ride out a bad market without selling at
the bottom. And sixth, this fall, use
open enrollment to review your Medicare
coverage for next year. Let me bring it
together. The eight risks are the part
of your health bill Medicare doesn't
cover. Long-term care, inflation, a
market drop early in retirement, the
loss of a spouse, scams, Social Security
fear, and the one that multiplies them
all, a long life. The good news is that
almost all of them are easier to handle
while you're healthy, while you and your
spouse can make the decisions together,
and well before the bill arrives.
One more thing. Everything in this video
is educational, and it isn't financial,
tax, or legal advice. The examples are
simplified illustrations, and your own
numbers, your state, and your health
will change the answers.
Please check the official sources, like
medicare.gov, ssa.gov, and irs.gov, and
talk with a qualified professional
before making big decisions. Now, I'd

And if you have a question you'd like me

title: 3 Social Security Rules Just Changed — Here's What's Actually True

segments.text: Right now, there's a change sitting
inside the Social Security payment
system that touches your account
directly. Not a rumor, not a maybe
someday. A real set of rules already in
effect that can hold your payment, delay
it, or reroute it to a paper check you
never see coming until it's too late.
Let me get straight to it because the
rules themselves matter more than the
buildup. There are three things worth
knowing. One, a name mismatch between
your bank and your social security
record can hold a payment. Two, direct
deposit changes now process faster than
they used to, which cuts both ways.
Three, representative payee accounts
have specific titling rules that a lot
of families get wrong, and the oversight
on this has actually gotten thinner, not
stricter. I'll walk through each one in
plain terms, correct a couple of things
being reported inaccurately elsewhere,
and give you a straightforward checklist
at the end. And if you're thinking,
"I've been retired for 20 years. None of
this touches me." Here's why it might
anyway. Rule one applies to anyone whose
name has ever changed since they opened
their bank account, regardless of how
long ago you retired. Rule three applies
if you're a representative payee for a
spouse or adult child, or if someone is
one for you. And the scam pattern tied
to all of this targets people
specifically because they've been on
direct deposit a long time and have
stopped thinking about it, which makes
longtime recipients a common target, not
an exception. This applies whether
you're living on SSI or SSDI and
counting on every deposit landing on
time, or whether you're collecting a
full retirement check and feel
financially comfortable. It applies
whether you've been on direct deposit
for 30 years or you switched over last
spring. I want to be upfront about
something before we go further because a
lot of what's circulating online about
this topic right now is either
exaggerated or flatout backwards. I
checked the actual current policy
against what's being repeated in a lot
of videos and posts and at least one
widely shared version of this story has
a central claim completely reversed.
I'll walk through exactly where that
happened and what the real picture looks
like because getting it right matters
more here than getting it dramatic.
Let's start with what actually changed
and why. The Social Security
Administration didn't tighten its direct
deposit rules because it wanted more
paperwork in your life. Federal
oversight bodies flagged real
weaknesses. identity fraud, banking
fraud aimed specifically at
beneficiaries, and processing gaps
inside the SSA's own systems. Fraudulent
direct deposit redirections, where
criminals reroute someone's payment into
an account they control, became one of
the AY's highest volume fraud categories
in recent years. The response was a
genuine security overhaul that began in
2025, and it's still settling into its
current form. That overhaul is where all
three of today's rules come from. Rule
one, a mismatch between the name on your
bank account and the name on your social
security record can hold up a payment.
This is the most common and most
avoidable of the three. And it isn't
some exotic new database. It's a basic
reality of how electronic payments get
matched between two systems that were
built independently and have rarely been
reconciled against each other. Here's
what commonly triggers it. A married
woman who legally changed her name, but
whose bank account still carries her
maiden name because she opened it
decades ago and never updated it. A
person whose SSA record lists a full
legal name, while their bank account
uses a shortened version, a nickname
that stuck. A hyphenated surname
recorded one way at the SSA and a
different way at the bank. And often
overlooked, anyone whose legal name
changed after a divorce and who updated
one record but never got around to the
other. Let me tell you about a woman
I'll call Patricia. She's 71, a retired
postal worker from outside Memphis,
Tennessee, and she'd been receiving her
retirement benefit by direct deposit for
6 years without a single hiccup. Her
bank account, held at the same
institution since 1989, was registered
under the name Pat, the name she'd gone
by her whole life. Her SSA record
carried her full legal name. Those
aren't the same string of characters.
And when a routine verification check
ran against her account, it flagged. Not
fraud, not anything she did wrong, just
two systems that had operated
independently for decades suddenly being
compared against each other. Her
payments sat delayed for over a week
while a mortgage due date came and went.
The fix starts with knowing the actual
recorded strings, not what you assume
they are. Log into your bank account,
not last month's paper statement, the
live account screen, and look at the
exact name displayed. Then log into your
Social Security account online and look
at the name on file there. Compare the
two character by character. If they
don't match, that's worth correcting
proactively rather than waiting for it
to cause a delay. There are three real
pathways to fix a mismatch like this.
The first is through your online my
social security account. Log in,
navigate to your payment section, then
direct deposit information, and the
system shows you what's currently on
file. If a discrepancy shows up, you can
start a correction from that same
screen, and it's worth screenshotting
the confirmation since that becomes your
record of when you made the change. The
second pathway is the SSA's phone line.
When you call, be specific. Say you need
to verify your direct deposit account
ownership information against your
current record. That freezing gets you
routed more usefully than a general
question would. The third pathway is an
in-person visit to your local field
office. The slowest option, but the most
thorough since a representative can
compare both records side by side in
real time. Bring a governmentissued
photo ID, a bank statement dated within
the last 30 days showing the exact name
on the account, and a recent SSA benefit
verification letter. Now, rule two, and
this is where I need to directly correct
something. A lot of what's being shared
online right now describes a new 30-day
lockout on direct deposit changes,
framing it as a fresh trap that catches
people who recently switched banks
completely offguard. Here's the problem
with that. The 30-day hold was the old
system. It's the rule Social Security
moved away from, not toward. As part of
that same 2025 security overhaul, the
agency replaced the roughly 30-day
processing hold with next business day
processing once your identity is
verified through your online account or
in person. If you've seen a video
confidently telling you a 30-day lockout
is a new danger, that video has the
timeline backwards. Here's the real
current trade-off worth understanding.
because there is one. It's just not the
one getting repeated. Faster processing
is genuinely more convenient if you're
the one making a legitimate change.
You're not stuck waiting a month
anymore. But faster also means less time
exists for anyone, including you, to
catch a fraudulent change before money
actually moves. That's exactly why
stronger identity verification now sits
in front of the process. It's also why
the agency has scaled back how much can
be changed through an unverified phone
call alone. Identity sensitive changes
increasingly require going through your
verified online account or an in-person
visit rather than a phone call where the
person on the other end can't be fully
confirmed as you. This is a real problem
for a specific group of people. Anyone
who genuinely cannot navigate the online
verification system and doesn't live
near a field office. If that's your
situation or a parent's situation, know
that in-person help does exist
specifically for this. And it's worth
scheduling that visit ahead of time
rather than discovering the gap on the
day you need to make an urgent change.
There's a scam pattern that rides
directly on top of both of these first
two rules. And it's worth pausing on
because it's specifically built to
exploit the general anxiety around
banking changes. Investigators who track
this fraud describe a predictable
sequence. First, a caller claims to
represent Social Security or a related
federal office. Second, they manufacture
a problem. Your benefits are suspended.
Your account's been flagged, something
that sounds entirely plausible given
everything we just covered. Third, they
apply pressure with an artificial
deadline, usually 24 to 48 hours,
insisting you act immediately or lose
your payment. Fourth comes the actual
ask. Your account number, your social
security number, or a one-time
verification code sent to your phone.
The Social Security Administration does
not call, text, or email you to confirm
your banking details. If a call, text,
or email ever follows that four-step
pattern, don't engage with it. Hang up.
Close the message. And if you want to
check whether anything is genuinely
wrong, call the SSA back using a number
you already have on an old benefit
statement. Never one a caller or text
message gives you. Let me tell you how
close this can actually come to working.
A retired school teacher, I'll call
Helen, 69, living outside Tulsa,
Oklahoma, got a call from someone who
already knew her full name and the last
four digits of her social security
number. Information that made the whole
thing sound legitimate right out of the
gate. The caller told her that her
direct deposit information had been
flagged for review and that her payment
would be suspended within 48 hours
unless she confirmed her banking details
right then on the phone. Helen almost
gave it to him. What stopped her was
remembering that the SSA doesn't call to
confirm banking details ever. She told
the caller she'd called the agency back
herself and hung up. When she called the
real number printed on an old benefit
statement, there was no flag on her
account, no review pending, nothing
wrong with her payment at all. The
scammer hadn't needed to know everything
about Helen, just enough to sound
convincing, paired with a deadline built
to keep her from thinking it through.
The same four-step pattern shows up in
texts and emails, too. Now, often
dressed up to look official, complete
with a government style seal and a link
that appears to lead to a real
government site, but actually leads
somewhere else. If a message like that
lands in your inbox, don't tap anything
inside it. Type the social security
website into your browser yourself
rather than trusting any link the
message provides.
Now, rule three, and this is the one
where accuracy really matters because
the version circulating online gets the
underlying facts wrong in a way that
changes the entire picture. This
concerns representative payee accounts
for anyone managing social security
benefits on behalf of a parent, spouse,
or family member who can't manage them
independently due to age, disability, or
a medical condition. Here's the claim
you may have heard that Social Security
launched an aggressive new
reverification crackdown on joint
accounts and representative pay
arrangements, catching longtime
functioning setups offguard and
rerouting payments to paper checks.
When I checked this against Social
Security's actual published rules for
representative payes, the underlying
premise doesn't hold up the way it's
being told. A representative pay account
is not supposed to be an ordinary joint
account in the first place where the pay
and the beneficiary share equal
ownership. Social Security's own rules
require the account to be titled
specifically to show the fiduciary
relationship. Something like Jane Smith,
representative pay for John Smith, not a
standard joint account. Using a regular
joint account for this purpose is
actually one of the most common issues
flagged when Social Security does review
a pay arrangement, which is a different
problem than a sudden new crackdown on
accounts that were previously fine. So,
if a family story about this involves a
payee and a beneficiary sharing a true
joint account that had worked for years,
the more likely underlying issue is that
the account was never titled correctly
to begin with, which is worth fixing
directly with your bank, regardless of
whether a review ever happens. Here's
something else worth knowing because it
cuts against the crackdown narrative
entirely. In October of 2025, members of
Congress, including Senators Gillibrand
and Widen, sent a formal letter raising
concerns that pay oversight reviews have
actually fallen behind schedule,
specifically because of staffing
reductions at the Social Security
Administration.
Advocacy groups working with vulnerable
beneficiaries echoed that concern. So,
the honest current picture isn't a
system aggressively reverifying every
arrangement and catching people off
guard. It's closer to the opposite.
Fewer reviews happening than there used
to be, which means more responsibility
falls on families to get the account set
up correctly and keep their own record
straight because you can't count on a
timely outside review to catch a
problem. Either way, if you are a
representative payee or you're setting
up that arrangement for a parent, here's
what's actually worth doing. Confirm
with your bank that the account is
titled to clearly reflect the fiduciary
relationship, not as a standard joint
account. Keep the beneficiaries funds
completely separate from your own money
in that account. Coming funds is the
single most common issue flagged in an
actual SSA pay review. And keep basic
records of how funds are used since if a
review does eventually happen, having
your own documentation ready makes it a
formality rather than a scramble.
There's a related legal distinction
worth understanding here too because
families often get it wrong at exactly
the moment it matters most. The
difference between a representative
payee and someone holding power of
attorney. A representative payee is
designated specifically to receive and
manage social security benefits. Power
of attorney is a separate legal
instrument set up through an attorney
that can grant someone broader authority
over a person's finances. Depending on
how it's written, one doesn't
automatically cover the other. And
assuming it does has caused real
problems at bank counters and SSA
offices when someone believes they have
authority and finds out on the spot that
they don't. If you're setting up either
arrangement, it's worth having both
conversations separately. While we're on
the subject of where money sits in these
arrangements, it's worth a quick mention
of FDIC insurance since this tends to
surface during the same life events that
prompt a payee arrangement or an account
consolidation.
Standard FDIC coverage protects up to
per depositor per insured bank per
ownership category. A checking account
and a savings account held the same way
at the same bank share that single
limit. They don't each get separate
coverage. If an account was recently
consolidated or a lump sum like an
inheritance landed in the mix, it's
worth checking whether your total
balance at that one bank now exceeds
what's actually insured and whether
restructuring ownership or adding a
payable on death beneficiary would
restore full protection. Let's talk
about who's actually most exposed across
these three rows in order of how much it
matters. First, anyone who's updated
their banking information recently and
hasn't confirmed the change actually
completed since the faster processing
means a small error can still surface
quickly rather than sitting hidden for a
month. Second, SSI recipients with a
representative payee since SSI amounts
sit at the income floor for the most
financially exposed recipients and even
a brief delay has immediate consequences
for food, rent, and medication.
Third, anyone whose legal name on file
doesn't exactly match their bank account
name. The largest group by far and the
one most likely to assume this doesn't
apply to them until a payment doesn't
show up. Fourth, anyone who's received a
notice from the SSA in the last 30 days
and hasn't opened it yet. The agency
does send physical notices when
something needs attention, but they're
written in dense bureaucratic language
that buries the urgency. If there's a
piece of SSA mail sitting on a counter
somewhere, open it today. One honest
note about calling the SSA directly. If
a representative tells you your account
is fine, that answer might be completely
accurate, or it might be incomplete
simply because phone representatives
aren't uniformly trained on every detail
of every recent policy change, and the
person you reach may not have visibility
into every layer of your file. That's a
training and access gap inside a large
federal agency, not necessarily a
mistake on their part. When you call,
it's worth asking for four specific
things. Have them read back the exact
name on your SSA record, character by
character. Ask whether there are any
pending flags or verification holds on
your account. Ask whether your account
is classified as individual, joint, or
representative pay, and confirm that
classification is accurate. and ask them
to log the call with a confirmation
number. If something goes wrong later
and you need to file a formal request
for reconsideration, that record becomes
your foundation. One more tool worth
setting up while you're already logged
in and it takes about 2 minutes. Look
for the notification preferences section
inside your online social security
account. You can turn on email or text
alerts for specific account activity, a
change to your direct deposit
information, an update to your mailing
address, or a new representative payee
being added. Turning this on means that
if anyone ever tries to alter your
banking details, including a scammer
who's somehow gotten partial access some
other way, you find out the moment it
happens rather than weeks later when a
payment simply fails to land. It's one
of the few genuinely proactive steps
available here and it costs nothing.
Here's your action checklist. Five
things you can do today. One, check the
exact name on your social security
record against the exact name on your
bank account character by character and
correct any mismatch through your online
account or a field office visit. Two, if
you're updating direct deposit
information, do it through a verified
channel, your online account or in
person, understanding it now typically
processes in about a business day rather
than the old month-long wait. Three, if
you or a family member serves as a
representative payee, confirm the
account is titled correctly as a
fiduciary account, not an ordinary joint
account, and keep the beneficiaries
funds separate from your own. Four, if
you manage benefits for someone else or
have both a representative payee and a
power of attorney situation in your
family, make sure everyone understands
those are two separate legal tools, not
interchangeable ones. Five, open any SSA
mail sitting around from the last 30 to
60 days. A routine looking envelope may
have a response deadline attached that's
easy to miss. One habit worth building
alongside all of this costs nothing and
takes less than a minute of
conversation. If you have a spouse, an
adult child, or a trusted friend who
helps keep an eye on your finances, tell
them which bank your payment goes to and
agree in advance that if either of you
gets a call, text, or email claiming to
be from Social Security, you talk to
each other first before doing anything.
That single agreement closes the door on
almost every version of the scam
described earlier because it relies on
isolation and urgency working together.
The moment you introduce even one other
person into the decision, whether that's
a spouse across the kitchen table or an
adult child a phone call away, the
pressure loses most of its power. Let me
talk to my daughter first ends almost
every one of these calls immediately
because a real representative has no
objection to that at all. while someone
running a script very much does. If
you're watching this because you're
looking out for a parent rather than
yourself, the best way to help isn't to
take the whole process over for them.
Sit down together, walk through the same
checks side by side, the exact name on
file against their bank account, whether
their pay account is titled correctly,
if that applies, and whether there's any
SSA mail sitting around unopened. Let
them do the typing and confirming
themselves. if they're able to with you
guiding rather than doing it for them so
they'll remember how to check it
themselves next time and so they keep a
sense of control over their own money
which matters enormously at this stage
of life. Here's the truth underneath all
three of these rules. None of them exist
to make your life harder on purpose.
They exist because real fraud against
Social Security beneficiaries has been a
genuine growing problem. And the AY's
response, however imperfectly explained
to the public, is trying to close real
gaps. But the honest version of that
story is less dramatic than what tends
to circulate. It's not a sudden
crackdown catching everyone offg guard.
It's a slow, uneven roll out where speed
increased in one place, verification
tightened in another, and oversight in a
third area has actually fallen behind
rather than intensified. Knowing which
is which is the entire difference
between reacting to a rumor and actually
protecting your own payment. This is
general educational information, not
personal legal or financial advice.
Always confirm your own specific
situation directly with the Social
Security Administration.

The risk isn't the new system itself.

>> Here's exactly where this turns from a

So, here's step one for everyone

title: One Bank Mistake Erases Your VA Check Protection

segments.text: There is money sitting in your bank
account right now that a creditor cannot
legally take from you. Not after a court
order, not after a judgement, not at
all.
If you draw VA disability compensation,
federal law puts a wall around that
money.
And here's the part almost nobody knows.
That wall does not come down when the
money lands in your account. It follows
the money in.
A veteran at 100% is drawing $3,938
a month. At 70%, it's over $1,800.
Whatever your number is, that money is
protected by a statute most veterans
have never heard of and could not name
if you asked them.
But there's a catch, and it's the reason
for this video.
There is one completely ordinary thing
veterans do at the bank every single day
without thinking about it for a second.
It does not cancel the protection on
paper, but it makes that protection very
hard to actually use when you need it.
So, here are three things we're covering
today.
One, the law itself, word for word, so
you know exactly what it says and
exactly how strong it is.
Two, the bank mistake, and why it turns
a clear protection into an argument you
have to win.
Three, the honest list of exceptions,
because there are real ones and anybody
who tells you this protection is
absolute is lying to you.
Let's start with the statute. It's title
38 of the United States Code, section
and here's the operative sentence
exactly as Congress wrote it.
Payments of benefits due or to become
due under any law administered by the
secretary shall not be assignable except
to the extent specifically authorized by
law. And such payments made to or on
account of a beneficiary shall be exempt
from taxation, shall be exempt from the
claim of creditors, and shall not be
liable to attachment, levy, or seizure
by or under any legal or equitable
process whatever, either before or after
receipt by the beneficiary.
Let me take that apart, because every
clause in it is doing work. Exempt from
taxation. Your VA compensation is not
taxable income. Most veterans know that
one.
Exempt from the claim of creditors. A
creditor cannot make a claim against it.
Not a credit card company, not a
hospital, not a collection agency that
bought your old debt for pennies.
Not liable to attachment, levy, or
seizure. Those are the three legal tools
somebody uses to take money out of an
account, and all three are off the
table.
By or under any legal or equitable
process whatever.
That word whatever is doing something
specific. It means it doesn't matter
what kind of proceeding it is or what
court it came from.
And then the line that matters most.
Either before or after receipt by the
beneficiary.
That's Congress saying in plain language
that the protection does not stop at the
moment of deposit. It doesn't only cover
the money while the VA is holding it.
It covers the money after it arrives in
your hands, and after it arrives in your
account.
I want to sit on that, because it's the
single most misunderstood thing about
this whole subject.
Most veterans assume that once the money
hits the bank, it's just money. It mixes
in with everything else. It stops being
VA money and becomes fair game like any
other dollar.
That is not what the statute says.
The statute says the exemption travels
with it.
So, why do veterans still end up with
frozen accounts and drained balances?
That brings us to the mistake.
Here's the ordinary thing. A man has one
checking account. His VA compensation
goes in, his social security goes in. If
he still works part-time, his paycheck
goes in. His wife's money goes in.
Everything lands in the same place, the
way it has for 40 years, because that's
just how a bank account works.
That's called commingling, mixed funds.
And here's the problem it creates.
The protection in section 5301 attaches
to VA money. It does not attach to your
account. It attaches to those dollars.
So, when a creditor comes after the
account, the question stops being is
this money protected and becomes which
of these dollars are the VA dollars?
If every deposit for the last 5 years is
sitting in one pot, that's a genuinely
hard question to answer, and the burden
of answering it is not on the creditor.
It's on you.
Let me put it as plainly as I can.
The law is on your side. But, a right
you cannot prove is a right you have to
fight for, and fighting for it costs
time and usually costs money.
The veterans who have the easiest time
with this are the ones who can point at
an account and say, "That one. Nothing
goes in there but the VA. Every dollar
in it came from the Department of
Veterans' Affairs, and I can show you
the deposits."
That's the whole difference. Not a
loophole, not a trick, just a clean
record.
Now, here's the part that changes this
from a legal fact into something that
actually helps you, and it's the reason
direct deposit matters more than anybody
tells you.
There's a federal banking rule that sits
on top of the statute.
It's Title 31 of the Code of Federal
Regulations, Part 212, and it was
written jointly by Treasury, the Social
Security Administration, the Department
of Veterans' Affairs, the Railroad
Retirement Board, and the Office of
Personnel Management. Five agencies, one
rule.
Here's what it makes your bank do.
When a bank gets a garnishment order
against your account, it is not allowed
to just freeze everything and let you
sort it out. It has to run what the rule
calls an account review first. In that
review, the bank looks back two months.
It goes through the deposits and asks
one question. Did a federal benefit
payment come into this account in that
window? And if the answer is yes, the
rule requires the bank to immediately
calculate a protected amount, ensure the
account holder has full and customary
access to it, and not freeze it. Then
comes the line I want you to actually
remember because it's the whole point.
The account holder has no requirement to
assert any right of garnishment
exemption prior to accessing the
protected amount. No requirement to
assert. You don't have to file anything.
You don't have to call anybody. You
don't have to prove you're a veteran or
explain what the money is. The bank has
to do it automatically before it freezes
a dollar. That's a genuinely strong
piece of consumer protection, and most
veterans have never heard of it.
But look carefully at what triggers it
because this is where it connects back
to everything else. It applies to
benefit payments deposited into the
account directly by the agency. An
electronic payment the bank can identify
as coming from the VA.
Two months of direct deposited VA money
is protected automatically.
Everything past that two-month window
and anything that came in some other way
goes back to the ordinary situation
where the statute still protects it, but
somebody has to establish which dollars
those are. So, the picture is really
three layers. Layer one, the statute.
Your VA compensation is exempt from
creditors before and after you receive
it. That's always true.
Layer two, the banking rule. Two months
of direct deposited benefits get
protected automatically with no action
required from you at all.
Layer three, everything else. Still
protected by law, but you're the one who
has to show it. And that's far easier
from a clean account than from a pot
everything has been going into for
years.
Let me make this concrete with two
examples because I've seen this go both
ways.
Two veterans, same rating, same money,
same old hospital bill that eventually
turned into a judgment.
The first has his VA compensation going
into one account by direct deposit and
nothing else goes into it.
When the garnishment order lands, the
bank runs its two-month review, sees VA
deposits, calculates the protected
amount, and he keeps access to it. He
doesn't file anything. He doesn't even
know the rule exists. It just works
because the bank is required to make it
work.
The second has everything landing in one
account going back nine years. VA money,
a part-time paycheck, his wife's money,
a tax refund, cash from selling a truck.
When the order lands, the bank protects
the two months of VA deposits it can
identify and freezes the rest of the
balance.
Everything above that two-month line is
money the law still says is exempt, but
he's the one who has to establish it
dollar by dollar out of nine years of
mixed deposits.
Same law, same rating, same protection
on paper. The difference is entirely in
what a bank could see in two minutes.
Now, the part that makes this video
honest, the exceptions.
You'll find people online telling you
that VA compensation is untouchable,
full stop. Nobody can ever get at it.
That is not true. And if you believe it,
you can get hurt.
The statute itself names the first one.
Right after the sentence I read you, it
says, "The preceding sentence shall not
apply to claims of the United States
arising under such laws."
Read that again. Claims of the United
States.
The protection is against creditors. It
is not against the government itself.
So, if the VA overpays you and wants
that money back, the shield you have
against a credit card company doesn't
point at them.
VA overpayment recovery is its own
process with its own rules, and this
statute is not what stops it.
Second exception, court-ordered child
support and alimony.
Family court is treated differently from
ordinary debt, and VA compensation can
be reached for those obligations in ways
it cannot be reached for a hospital
bill.
Third, where compensation replaces
military retired pay.
If you waived retired pay to receive VA
compensation, the portion tied to that
waiver can be treated differently in a
divorce division because of how those
two payments interact. Fourth, federal
tax.
An IRS levy is a claim of the United
States, and it does not sit behind the
same wall a private creditor does.
And there's one more line in the statute
worth knowing because it catches people
out, and almost nobody mentions it. It
says, "The exemption as to taxation
shall not extend to any property
purchased in part or wholly out of such
payments."
In plain English, the money is exempt
from tax. What you buy with the money is
not. Use your compensation to buy a
house, and that house is ordinary
taxable property like anybody else's.
The protection covers the payment, not
everything the payment ever turns into.
So, let's put the whole picture
together. Your VA compensation is exempt
from taxation, exempt from the claim of
creditors, and cannot be attached,
levied, or seized by any legal process
whatever before or after it reaches you.
That's a genuinely powerful protection,
stronger than most veterans believe.
It does not protect you from the
government's own claims, from
court-ordered family support, or from
the IRS.
And it protects dollars, not accounts,
which means the practical strength of it
depends on whether anybody can tell your
VA dollars apart from the rest.
Here's what to actually do with this. If
you ever get a letter, a call, or a
notice about a judgment or a frozen
account, do not assume the money is
gone, and do not just accept it.
There is a federal statute that says
that money is exempt. It's short, and
you can read the whole thing yourself.
Section 5301
of Title 38. And get somebody qualified
in front of it. A veteran service
officer costs you nothing, and every
state has them.
For a bank or court matter specifically,
many states also run free legal aid for
veterans, and there are law school
clinics that do this work for free.
One more thing worth being blunt about.
Anybody who charges you money to prepare
a VA claim without accreditation is
breaking federal law, and outfits have
been shut down over exactly this.
Free help exists. Use it before you pay
anybody.
The thing I want you to take away is
smaller than the whole statute.
Most veterans think the money stops
being protected the second it hits the
bank. It does not.
Congress wrote before or after receipt
on purpose, and it's still sitting there
in the law today.
Knowing that one freeze is the
difference between a man who assumes he
has no options and a man who knows
exactly what to point at.

title: September Brings 10 Changes for Seniors — Most Don't Know Any of Them

for anyone receiving Social Security,
Medicare, or a federal benefit.

deadlines, some tied to legislation,

that spelled out in plain language what
you personally need to do.
So, let's go through it, piece by piece.
Number one, paper checks.
The federal government has been moving
toward electronic-only benefit payments
since 2025,
and the Social Security Administration
has said it intends to complete that
transition before the end of this year.

The original hard deadline was pushed

people who genuinely can't make the

automatic. You still have to act, not
wait.
If you're still receiving a paper check

will simply arrive to walk you through

through your My Social Security account

doing nothing and assuming you're
covered.

coverage has its own September deadline

change laying out everything shifting in
your plan for next year, which
medications are being moved to a more

And whether your premium is about to
climb.
What most people get wrong is treating
this letter like junk mail. Compare your
current medications against the new
list.
First, a drug shifting from a lower tier

your monthly cost without you noticing
until the charge shows up. Then check

in network since those changes take

increase. Even 15 or 20 extra dollars a

SHIP counselors are available in every

And September, before the open

and this one looks smaller, but it can
put real money back in your pocket.

disappears at the same time. If your
plan includes an over-the-counter
allowance, many of these run on a
quarterly basis, meaning your balance
covering July through September can
expire on September 30th. It doesn't
roll into the next quarter. It doesn't
show up later as a credit. It simply
vanishes. This is a common structure
across a meaningful number of Medicare
Advantage OTC benefits, and it costs

unused balances. The fix takes a few

your Medicare card, ask what your
current balance is, and use it before
the deadline hits. Now, stay with me
because the next one is the one most
people never see coming, a threshold
buried in the tax code that hasn't moved
in over 40 years, and it's about to
catch more seniors than ever. Number
four, and it connects directly to the
next piece.
The Social Security cost of living
adjustment for 2027. September is the
final month of the three-month data
window used to calculate next year's
COLA. July and August numbers are
already in, and whatever the Consumer
Price Index does, this September
finishes the calculation. The official
figure gets announced in October.
But as of the most recent inflation
data, independent projections are
converging around 3.4%
to 3.6% on an average benefit of roughly
a month,
which could mean somewhere around $70 to
$75 more starting in January.
That sounds like straightforward good
news, but here's the catch. The income
thresholds where Social Security
benefits become taxable, $25,000 for
single filers, $32,000 for married
couples filing jointly,
have not been adjusted since 1983
They don't move with inflation, and they
don't move with COLA increases. So, a
larger benefit check can be the exact

line for the first time, even though
their overall financial situation hasn't
really changed. If your income outside
of Social Security, plus half your
annual Social Security benefit
sits within a couple thousand dollars of
those thresholds,
it's worth recalculating once the
official Cola number comes out in

senior deduction can help offset some of

your situation. Number five, the
deadline for senior property tax relief.
In most states, applications for senior
exemptions, assessment freezes, or tax

programs exist in virtually every state,

with no way to get that money back
retroactively. Your county assessor's
phone number is printed right on your
property tax bill, and a 5-minute call
is enough to find out what you might be
eligible for. Number six,
the quarterly estimated tax deadline on
September 15th. If part of your income
doesn't have automatic withholding IRA
withdrawals, pension distributions,
rental income, self-employment earnings,
you may be required to send in a
quarterly payment. Missing it triggers a
penalty that runs at roughly 8%
annualized.
If you haven't recalculated your
payments to reflect the new $6,000
senior deduction, this deadline is the
moment to do it. Depending on your
income, you might be overpaying, or you
might need to increase your payment to
avoid a penalty when you file next
spring. Number seven, and this one has
nothing to do with deadlines and
everything to do with speed. The Social
Security Administration recently
expanded its Compassionate Allowances
program, adding 14 new serious medical
conditions to the list that qualifies
for expedited disability approval,
bringing the total to over 300
conditions.
Normally, a disability claim can take
several months or longer to process. A
claim flagged under Compassionate
Allowances can be approved in days or
weeks instead. If you or someone in your
family has received a serious diagnosis
recently or has an application sitting
in a lengthy review queue, it's worth
checking the updated list on the Social
Security Administration's website to see
if the condition now qualifies.
The wrong option is assuming the faster
process happens automatically. It
doesn't. If it does qualify, that
designation needs to be requested
specifically. Number eight, there's one
more layer connecting almost everything
above. A lot of the pressure behind
these September deadlines traces back to
the same source.
Federal agencies tightening up programs
that have existed for years but were
loosely enforced. The push to eliminate
paper checks isn't new.
It's been in motion since 2025, but the
actual follow-through, the part where a
missed deadline really can interrupt
your payment, is what's different about
this particular stretch. The same is
true for the annual notice of change
requirement. Insurers have technically
had to send these letters for years,
but scrutiny over whether seniors
actually understand what's in them has
increased,
which is part of why so many people are
hearing about formulary and network
changes for the first time. None of this
is a coincidence. It's a pattern of
older rules finally getting real teeth,
and September happens to be where
several of them converge.
The wrong response is panic. The right
response is attention. Number nine.
If you're on a fixed income and any part
of your Medicare or prescription costs
feels heavier than it used to, this is
also a good month to check whether you
qualify for a Medicare savings program
or the extra help program for
prescription drug costs.
These aren't new for 2026, but they're
chronically underused. Millions of
seniors who qualify never apply.
Often because they assume their income
is too high or the paperwork is too
complicated. Medicare savings programs
can cover your part B premium, and
depending on income, your deductibles
and co-insurance as well.
Extra help can bring prescription costs
down to just a few dollars per
medication. Both are worth a phone call
to your state Medicaid office or SHIP
counselor while you're already dealing
with your annual notice of change. Since
the two conversations naturally overlap.
Number 10. It's also worth keeping an
eye on state-level relief that sometimes
rides alongside these federal deadlines.
A number of states run their own senior
rebate or utility assistance programs
with enrollment or renewal periods that
happen to fall in the same August
through October stretch as property tax
exemption deadlines. These aren't
federal programs, so they won't show up
in anything the Social Security
Administration or Medicare sends you.
Which makes them easy to miss unless you
ask directly. When you call your county
assessor about property tax relief, it
costs nothing extra to ask what other
senior programs the county or state
currently run. Put together, that's
what's landing this September.
Paper checks continuing their move
toward electronic only with real support
still available if you need it.
Your Medicare notice arriving with
changes you need to read carefully and
over the counter benefit
quietly expiring on some plans. A cola
calculation wrapping up with a decades
old tax threshold hiding behind it.
Property tax relief windows closing
county by county. A quarterly tax
deadline for anyone with non-withheld
income.
And a faster path to disability approval
for newly added medical conditions.
None of these pieces were designed to be
confusing on purpose, but taken together
they add up to a month where paying
attention actually pays off.

title: If Your Spouse Dies Tomorrow, Your Bank Account Could Be Frozen — Here's Why

segments.text: If you have a joint bank account with
your spouse, I want you to picture this
for a second.
It's the worst day of your life. You've
just lost your husband or your wife, and
somewhere in the middle of the funeral
arrangements, the phone calls, the
paperwork,
you have to walk into a bank and figure
out what happens to the money you've
shared for maybe 30, 40, 50 years.
Here's what most people don't know. What
happens next depends entirely on three
little words that were decided the day
that account was opened. Words most
couples never even noticed on the
paperwork. Today, I want to walk you
through exactly what happens to a joint
bank account after a spouse dies. What
transfers automatically, what doesn't,
what the bank will ask you for, and the
one document almost every widow and
widower wishes they'd set up years
earlier.
This isn't meant to scare you. It's
meant to make sure that if this day
comes, or if it's already come,
you're not standing at that bank counter
confused and alone. The good news first,
right of survivorship.
Let's start with the good news, because
there is some. Most joint bank accounts
between spouses are set up with
something called rights of survivorship.
That's the three words I mentioned a
minute ago. If your account has this,
here's what it means in plain English.
When one spouse dies, the surviving
spouse automatically becomes the sole
owner of everything in that account. Not
eventually, not after a court process,
automatically. The moment your spouse
passes, that account does not become
part of your spouse's estate.
It does not go through probate, the long
court-supervised process that other
assets often have to go through. And
here's something that surprises a lot of
people. Even if your spouse's will says
something different about that money,
the survivorship right on the account
usually overrides the will. The account
transfers by operation of law, not by
what's written in the will. So,
practically speaking, what do you
actually need to do?
You'll need to bring the bank a
certified copy of the death certificate,
not a photocopy, an actual certified
copy. And I'd recommend ordering several
extras
because you'll need them for other
accounts, too. Once the bank has that,
they update the account into your name
alone, and you continue using it. In
most cases, the account isn't even
frozen during this process.
It's a name change, not a lockout.
That's the part that should bring you
some relief, but I want to walk you
through the exceptions because they
matter just as much. When it's not that
simple, here's where it gets more
complicated, and this is the part most
explainers skip over. Exception one,
community property states. If you live
in Arizona, California, Idaho,
Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas,
Washington, or Wisconsin, your joint
account might be titled as community
property instead of having a right of
survivorship. If that's the case, only
50% of the account may automatically
belong to you as the surviving spouse.
The other 50% could be treated as part
of your spouse's estate, meaning it
might need to go through probate
or be distributed according to the will.
If you're in one of those nine states,
this is worth checking on directly with
your bank or an estate attorney
because the paperwork isn't always
obvious at a glance. Exception two,
large estates and estate tax.
For most families, this next part won't
apply, but I want you to have the full
picture.
As of 2026, the federal estate and gift
tax exemption is $15 million per
individual and $30 million for a married
couple
using portability, a significant jump
from the $13.99
million exemption that applied in 2025,
made permanent under recent federal tax
legislation. So, the vast majority of
Americans
won't owe a dime of federal estate tax
on a joint account. But, and this is
important, a number of states plus
Washington, D.C. have their own estate
or inheritance taxes. And some of those
state thresholds are dramatically lower
than the federal one.
In states like Massachusetts, Oregon, or
Maryland, a threshold as low as $1
million is possible. If you live in one
of these states and your total estate is
anywhere near that range, this is a
conversation worth having with a tax
professional, not something to guess at.
Exception three, interest earned after
the date of death.
One detail that catches people off
guard, the funds themselves aren't
treated as taxable income to you as the
surviving spouse. You already had an
ownership interest in that account, so
receiving full ownership isn't income.
But, any interest the account earns
after the date of death is reportable,
and it belongs to you going forward, not
your spouse's estate. What to do in the
first 30 days.
I want to give you a simple checklist
because I know that during grief,
checklists are sometimes the only thing
that keeps you moving. Step one,
order eight to 10 certified copies of
the death certificate from the funeral
home or county vital records office.
You'll use these far more than you'd
expect. Banks, Social Security,
insurance, pensions, the DMV. Step two,
bring one certified copy to every bank
where you and your spouse held joint
accounts.
Ask them directly, "Can you confirm this
account has right of survivorship? And
what do you need from me to transfer it
into my name alone?" Step three, ask
about any accounts that were not joint,
meaning they were only in your spouse's
name.
Those accounts do not transfer
automatically. They typically go through
the estate and you may need to work with
an executor or go through probate,
depending on how they were set up. Step
four, this is the one most people skip
and I really want you to hear this part.
Once your joint account becomes solely
yours,
go back and update your own estate plan.
If that account was part of how you and
your spouse avoided probate together,
it's no longer serving that purpose now
that you're the sole owner.
Consider adding what's called a payable
on death or POD beneficiary to the
account. This is a simple form at your
bank, often free, that lets the account
pass directly to whoever you choose
without probate when it's eventually
your turn. It takes 15 minutes and it
can save your children or your family
months of court process later. Step
five, review your will with an estate
planning attorney to make sure it
reflects your new financial reality. A
will written when there were two of you
managing shared accounts often needs
updating once you're managing everything
alone.
One more thing worth knowing. If your
joint account wasn't with your spouse,
say it was set up with an adult child to
help manage your finances. The rules
shift slightly.
The IRS may look more closely at who
actually contributed the money to that
account. If your child withdrew funds
from an account you funded entirely,
those withdrawals could in some cases be
treated as taxable gifts.
Though the annual gift tax exclusion,
which stands at $19,000 per recipient in
or $38,000 for a married couple gift
splitting, covers most everyday
situations. This is a much narrower
situation than the spousal scenario
we've been talking about. But if it
applies to your family, it's worth a
quick conversation with an accountant
just so there are no surprises. Losing a
spouse is one of the hardest things a
person can go through. And the very last
thing you should have to worry about in
that moment is whether the bank is going
to make it harder than it needs to be.
Here's what I want you to remember.
If your account has right of
survivorship, the money is already
yours. The bank just needs a death
certificate to make it official on
paper. If you're in a community property
state, check your titling. And once
things settle, take 15 minutes to add a
POD beneficiary. So the next generation
doesn't have to go through this same
uncertainty.
If this helped you, or if you know
someone who's navigating this right now,
please share it with them. Sometimes,
the kindest thing you can do for a
grieving friend is send them clear
answers instead of one more thing to
research alone.

of them doesn't. The difference is fixed
costs. The dentist's life costs him
almost $14,000 a month to keep running.
Ray's costs about 3,000. When you have a
big number but a bigger monthly bill,
money still owns you. When your monthly
bill is small, the same number sets you
free. Level five, the binder. There's a
retired couple on Birch Street, the
Okonkwos, married 44 years. A 1956 ranch
house with a garden that takes up the
whole backyard. They've never once
called your emergency line. Not in 12
years. Every September, Mr. Okonkwo
calls to schedule maintenance. When you
arrive, he hands you a binder. Every
service you've ever done, every part,
every price, with your notes from last
year highlighted. He told you once that
he runs his money the same way. A
binder, checked every quarter. Nothing
exciting. They have about $2 million,
mostly in boring index funds, and they
live on less than 3% of it each year.
Their portfolio pays their life. Their
pensions are extra. At level five, money
stops being a worry and turns into
maintenance. Like a furnace. You don't
think about it every day. You just take
care of it once a year, so it takes care
of you all winter. Mr. Halverson laughs
at that one. He likes the binder. "Is
there a level six?" he asks. There is.
You've been inside a few of those
houses, too. A 12,000 square foot place
up on the ridge with six furnaces, two
pool heaters, and a house manager who
calls you instead of the owner. The
owner is worth about $40 million. You've
met him twice. Both times, he was on the
phone with a lawyer. He has more money
than anyone you've ever worked for. He
also has more people who need things
from him. More property to protect, more
staff to manage, and more ways to be
sued. He's not broke. He's just never
off duty. Above level five, more money
doesn't buy more freedom. It mostly buys
more things to take care of. Then he
asks, "And what level am I?" You look
around the basement, the 26-year-old
furnace he won't replace, the workbench
with tools older than you, the
paint-stained sweatshirt. "Honestly,
sir, I think you stopped worrying a long
time before this house." He nods slowly,
and then he tells you something you'll
think about for the rest of your career.
"Money stopped being a worry for me at
about $400,000," he says. "1987. The
house was paid off. I had a year of
expenses saved, and I owed nobody
anything. That was the day I was free.
Everything after that," he says, "was a
hobby. Some years it was a fun hobby.
Some years it was a stressful one, but
it was never the thing that made me
free. You sit there with your hot
chocolate getting cold because that's
exactly what you've seen in 11,000
basements. The people who are fine
aren't the ones with the biggest number.
They're the ones where a $3,000 surprise
is a nuisance, not a disaster. The ones
with low fixed costs. The ones who
expect things to break. Freedom isn't at
the top level. It's way down the ladder,
much earlier than people think. Most
people just keep climbing past it. Then
Mr. Halvorson asks you one more
question. So, what level are you in,
Maya? You think about it. Your 1978
house, paid off, the old van, the index
funds you fed every month since you were
24. Maya's binder, which is just a
spreadsheet with color coding. Level
five, you say. Maybe a little past it,
but we live like level three, on
purpose. He smiles like that's the right
answer. A month later, your boss calls
you into his office. A charity none of
you has ever heard of has prepaid for 40
furnace replacements. Free installs for
families who can't afford them. They've
asked for one specific technician to
choose the homes. You. You know exactly
whose idea it was. He never says a word
about it. When you call to thank him, he
says, "Don't know what you're talking
about, Nate. Furnace still runs great,
by the way." The first house on your
list is a small apartment with the
thermostat set to 58°. Marcus opens the
door. His twin girls are four now. He
doesn't understand at first. A new
furnace, paid for, nothing to sign
except the work order. He cries a
little. He apologizes for crying. You
tell him not to. Before you leave, you
write something on the back of your
business card and hand it to him. Step
one, $1,000. Don't touch it. He tapes it
to his fridge. Six months later, he
texts you a photo. The card is still on
the fridge. Next to it is a bank
screenshot. $1,040.
He's at level two now. And the best
part? The furnace in that photo isn't
the thing he's proud of. So, here's what
11,000 basements taught you.
Level one is when every surprise is a
disaster. Level two is a big paycheck
with no cushion. It looks better than
level one, and it worries just as much.
Level three is when emergencies turn
into errands. Level four is where fixed
costs decide whether you're rich or just
busy. Level five is when money becomes
maintenance, and everything above that,
like an old plumber told you at midnight
in his basement, is a hobby. Most people
are trying to get to the top of the
ladder, but the freedom is a lot closer
to the bottom than anyone tells you.
Somewhere around $1,000, a paid-off
roof, and a furnace you service every
October, whether it needs it or not.

title: POV: Your Coworkers Think You Got Demoted — You Actually Chose a 2-Day Work Week at 41

segments.text: It's 10:40 on a Wednesday morning, and
you're standing in the cereal aisle at
the grocery store when your old
coworker, Lenny Dawson, spots you from
the end of the row. He's in his work
shirt. He's on his lunch break. And his
face changes the second he sees you in
jeans and a hoodie on a weekday. "Nate,"
he says, way too gently. "Man, I heard.
I'm so sorry." Heard what? He lowers his
voice like you're at a funeral. "That
they let you go. Big Mike said you're
only coming in Mondays and Tuesdays now.
Part-time. At your age, man, that's
rough. You need me to put in a word
somewhere?" You look at the cereal in
your hand. You look at Lenny. And you
decide, for some reason, not to correct
him. "I'm doing okay," you say. "You
need anything, you call me," Lenny says.
He actually squeezes your shoulder. Then
he leaves, shaking his head. By Friday,
the story at the shop is that Nate got
demoted. By the following Monday, a guy
you barely know has asked if you'd want
to do some side jobs for cash to help
you out. Your boss's wife sent Maya a
casserole. Here's what none of them
know. Nobody let you go. You asked for
this. Three months ago, you walked into
your boss's office and asked to cut your
schedule to two days a week. You took a
pay cut on purpose. 60% of your paycheck
gone. And you've never been less worried
about money in your life. Because the
money you already saved is doing the
rest of the work. You just don't have to
touch it. And 3 weeks from now, the same
Lenny Dawson who squeezed your shoulder
in the cereal aisle is going to sit at
your kitchen table and ask you to
explain exactly how it works. Because
he's 54, and he just found out his own
retirement plan has a hole in it the
size of a truck. To understand how a
furnace guy cuts to two days a week at
41 without being rich, you have to
understand one idea. It has a funny
name. Coast. Most people think about
retirement as a single finish line. You
work full-time until you have enough to
never work again. And then you stop. All
or nothing. But there's a point before
that finish line where something quietly
changes. The point where the money
you've already invested, if you just
leave it alone, will grow into enough
for a normal retirement by 65, without
you adding another dollar. When you hit
that point, you don't have to save for
retirement anymore. You only have to
earn enough to pay this month's bills.
That point is called Coast FI, financial
independence, but coasting. You're not
done, you're just done pushing. Here's
how you found yours. You and Maya sat
down last winter with a pencil and a
spreadsheet. First, what you'd need in
retirement. Your house is already paid
off. Your expenses are about $4,200 a
month, about 50,000 a year. Social
Security for both of you would cover
maybe half of that. So, your investments
need to cover about 25,000 a year. Using
a common rule of thumb, where you plan
to withdraw about 4% a year, 25,000 a
year needs a pile of about $625,000
by 65. Let's call it 700,000 to be safe.
Then the second question, what do you
have right now? Between your 401k, your
Roth IRA, and Maya's accounts, about
Third question, if you never add another
dollar, what does 340,000 become in 24
years? Nobody knows the future, but if
the market does something like it's
long-term average after inflation, say
grows to roughly 1.3 million in today's
money terms. Even at a cautious 4%, it's
Either way, more than 700,000. You and
Maya looked at that number for a long
time. So, we're done, Maya said. We're
done saving for being old, you said.
We're not done working, we just have to
cover today. And today costs about the
same, 50,000 a year. Maya's job as a
nurse covers about 34 of it, which means
you only need to bring in about $16,000
a year to cover the gap, plus a buffer.
Two days a week of furnace work covers
that with room to spare. So, you asked
for two days. Your boss Phil thought you
were sick at first. When you explained,
he leaned back in his chair and said,
"You're telling me you could just stop
working full-time on what we pay you?"
"On what you've paid me for 19 years,"
you said, "if I hadn't spent most of
it." He gave you Mondays and Tuesdays
and the emergency on-call list on
weekends, which pays time and a half and
which you actually like. Here's what
those three months have looked like. You
fixed the back porch you'd been ignoring
for six years. You coached your nephew's
Little League team. You drove Maya to
work every morning and picked her up
after every night shift, which she says
is the most romantic thing you've ever
done. You read 11 books. You started
teaching a free Saturday class at the
community center on how to maintain your
own furnace. And people, it turns out,
absolutely hate it. Not your friends,
just people who see a man at the grocery
store on a Wednesday and decide
something must be wrong with him. Big
Mike at the shop told everyone you'd
been demoted for a mistake on a job.
Your neighbor asked Maya if things were
okay at home. Somebody at church prayed
for your season of unemployment out
loud. You let it go. It isn't their
business. But you'd be lying if you said
