business, if you're new here, please hit
subscribe. This channel is still small
and every single subscriber genuinely
helps me keep making these stories. Now,
let's go back 10 years.

title: POV: You Won the Lottery the Morning After Your Ex Left You

segments.text: It's 7:12 on a Sunday morning in Tampa,
Florida, and you're sitting on the floor
of your apartment because there's no
longer a couch to sit on.
There's a rectangle of cleaner carpet
where it used to be.
There are four dents where its legs
pressed down for 2 years.
Your girlfriend took it last night along
with the TV, the good towels, the air
fryer, and the framed photo of the two
of you on Clearwater Beach. She left the
frame's hook still stuck in the wall.
You didn't sleep. Your eyes are burning.
Your phone is face down next to you, and
on the screen are three texts you sent
her at 1:00 a.m. that she never
answered.
In the kitchen drawer under the takeout
menus, there's a small velvet box with a
$3,200 ring inside. You'd been saving
for it for 11 months. You were going to
propose in 2 weeks.
You don't really know why you do what
you do next. Maybe you just need
something to do with your hands. You
pull a crumpled lottery ticket out of
your work jacket, the one you bought
Friday at the gas station near the
hardware store because the jackpot was
big and a coworker dared you. You open
the lottery app. You type in the
numbers. The first number matches, then
the second, then the third. Your heart
starts pounding so hard you can hear it.
The fourth, the fifth, the Powerball.
The screen goes green. A little cartoon
of confetti falls across it, and under
the confetti is a number you have to
read four times before your brain will
accept it. 186 million. You sit on the
floor of your empty apartment in the
exact spot where your couch used to be,
and you laugh.
Then you cry. Then you laugh again so
hard your neighbor bangs on the wall. 12
hours ago, the woman you love told you
that you'd never be enough. This morning
you're worth more than everyone she's
ever met.
Before we go any further, if you're new
here, hit that subscribe button. This
channel is still small, and every single
subscriber genuinely helps me keep
making these stories. Now, let's go back
12 hours to the night everything fell
apart.
Your name is Ben Alvarez. You're 29
years old.
You're the assistant manager of a
family-owned hardware store on the north
side of Tampa, where you've worked since
you were 19.
You make $52,000 a year. You know where
every bolt, hinge, and paint chip in the
building is.
When old men come in with a broken part
in a sandwich bag and no idea what it's
called, they ask for you by name.
You've been with Kayla for 2 and 1/2
years.
Kayla was 28, gorgeous, and ambitious.
She worked as an assistant at a real
estate brokerage that sold waterfront
condos in South Tampa.
Every day, she showed $3 million homes
to people who arrived in Range Rovers.
And every night, she came home to a
one-bedroom apartment next to a highway
with a guy who smelled like sawdust and
paint thinner.
At first, she said she loved that you
were real. She loved that you could fix
anything. She loved that you remembered
her coffee order and kept her car
running for free.
But somewhere along the way, it changed.
She started following a lot of
influencers who filmed themselves on
yachts.
She started showing you listings for
houses you couldn't afford. She started
saying things like, "My broker's
boyfriend just bought a boat." And then
waiting for you to say something.
Saturday night, she came home from a
friend's engagement party at a rooftop
bar downtown.
The friend's fiance had given her a
4-carat ring and a trip to the Amalfi
Coast. Kayla sat down at the kitchen
table and didn't take off her heels.
"Ben," she said, "where do you see
yourself in 5 years?"
You told her the truth.
Store manager, maybe. A small house, a
dog, her.
She nodded slowly, like she'd already
known the answer and just needed to hear
it out loud. "You're a good guy," she
said. "You really are. But good doesn't
pay for a house in South Tampa. I'm 28.
I don't want to wait 10 years for a life
I could have now."
You asked if there was someone else.
She didn't answer that.
Which was an answer.
An hour later her brother showed up with
a pickup truck.
They took the couch, the TV,
the air fryer, and the photo from the
wall.
Kayla hugged you at the door.
A quick, polite, finished kind of hug.
"I hope you find someone who wants the
same simple life." she said.
Then she was gone and you were alone
with a velvet ring box and a bare wall.
So there you were, Sunday morning on the
floor with a hundred eighty-six million
dollars on a crumpled piece of paper.
Your first instinct was to call Kayla.
You actually had her name pulled up.
Your thumb was hovering over it.
Then you thought about what she'd said.
"Good doesn't pay for a house."
And you realized something that made
your stomach turn.
If you called her right now, she'd come
back. Of course she would. And you'd
spend the rest of your life wondering
why.
You put the phone down.
Instead you drove an hour east into Polk
County to the only person you trusted
completely.
Your grandfather. Walt Alvarez was
eighty-four years old and lived alone in
a small cinder block house surrounded by
orange trees.
He'd been a citrus farmer his whole
life.
In nineteen eighty-five, a brutal freeze
killed every tree on his three hundred
acres in a single night.
And he lost almost everything.
He spent the next twenty years quietly
buying back small pieces of land and
replanting.
One row at a time.
He drove a nineteen ninety-four Ford
pickup and still wore a straw hat he
bought for six dollars at a feed store.
You found him on the porch peeling an
orange with a pocket knife.
You sat down next to him and handed him
the ticket without saying a word.
He read it. He read it again.
Then he set it on the little table
between you.
Finished peeling his orange and handed
you half.
"That's a lot of oranges."
You laughed for the first time since
Saturday.
Then he got serious.
"Ben, I've watched a lot of men come
into money. Land deals, inheritances,
insurance checks after hurricanes. I'll
tell you what I've learned. Big money
arrives loud.
Your whole job is to make it sit down
and be quiet.
He gave you four rules that afternoon on
the porch.
You wrote them on the back of a feed
store receipt.
One, don't spend a single dollar on
yourself for 1 year.
Two, take care of family first, but only
their debts, not their wants.
Three, put most of it somewhere boring
where you can't touch it and forget it
exists.
And four, the last one, he said slowly
looking right at you.
Pay attention to who shows up before
anyone knows. Those people came for you.
Anyone who shows up after came for the
money.
You knew exactly who he was talking
about.
If you think Walt gave the best advice
in this whole story, let me know in the
comments.
And if you haven't yet, please hit

this small channel more than you can
imagine. Because the next 90 days
changed everything.
Here's something most people don't know.
In Florida, when you win a jackpot that
big, the state gives you a 90-day window
before your name becomes public record.
After that, anyone can find out.
90 days, that was your head start.
You used every one of them.
You hired a lawyer and a flat-fee
financial advisor in St. Petersburg who
had been recommended by your
grandfather's banker of 40 years.
You took the lump sum.
After taxes, about 57 million landed in
an account.
Then you followed Walt's rules exactly.
You paid off your mother's mortgage and
her car.
You paid off your little sister's
nursing school loans. You paid the back
taxes on Walt's farm that he'd never
mentioned to anyone. You didn't buy your
family boats or cars or vacations, just
their debts, gone. Your mother cried on
the phone for 20 minutes.
Then you put 50 million into boring,
steady investments your advisor promised
you'd hate because they were so dull.
Index funds, treasury bonds, nothing you
could post about. And you went back to
work at the hardware store. Monday
morning, 7:00 a.m., like nothing had
happened.
That Monday is the day that matters most
in this story, because when you walked
in, red-eyed and exhausted, still nobody
knew about the ticket. And the only
person in the whole world who noticed
something was wrong with you was Tess.
Tess Morales was 30. She ran the paint
counter. She was a single mom to a
7-year-old boy named Leo, who spent
Saturday mornings at the store
organizing the paint chips by color.
She'd work next to you for 4 years, and
you'd never once thought of her as
anything but a friend.
She took one look at you and said,
"Kayla."
You nodded. She didn't say anything
else. She just covered your register for
the rest of the morning, so you could
hide in the stockroom.
At lunch, she brought you a Cuban
sandwich from the place across the
street and wouldn't let you pay her
back.
That night, she texted you a photo of
Leo holding a drawing of a frowning
stick figure with a hammer. Under it,
he'd written, "Feel better, Mr. Ben."
She did that every day for a week. Not
because you had money. You had a velvet
box of failure and a sad, empty
apartment. And as far as she knew, that
was it.
Over the next 2 months, you started
eating lunch together every day, then
dinner once a week at her tiny apartment
with Leo explaining dinosaurs to you.
Not because you were testing her, but
because for the first time in years,
money just didn't feel like the most
important thing in the room. We're about
halfway through, and if you're still
watching, thank you. Seriously.
Tap like and subscribe, so you don't
miss the next one. Because on day 91,
Ben's name went public, and someone he
never expected to see again came
knocking.
On day 91, at 6:40 in the morning, a
local news site published a short
article.
Tampa hardware store manager revealed as
$186 million Powerball winner.
By 8:00 a.m., your phone had 214
notifications. Cousins you hadn't heard
from in a decade. High school friends
with business ideas. A guy you'd sold a
lawnmower to in 2019.
Three financial advisers you'd never
met, a pastor from a church in Ohio,
and at 11:52 a.m., one text that made
you stop breathing.
Kayla, "Hey stranger, I've been thinking
about you a lot lately. Can we talk?"
You didn't answer. Walt's fourth rule
was ringing in your ears.
Two days later, she showed up at the
hardware store. She walked in wearing a
white sundress and the perfume you used
to love, carrying a little bag from your
favorite bakery.
Customers turned to look. At the paint
counter, Tess froze with a can of primer
in her hands. Kayla smiled at you like
nothing had ever happened. "I brought
those guava pastries you like," she
said. "Can we talk somewhere? Just for a
minute?" You walked outside with her to
the parking lot. She talked for 10
minutes about how she'd made a mistake,
about how she'd been confused and
stressed at work, and how her friends
had put ideas in her head.
How she'd realized that what you two had
was real.
How she missed you. How she'd never
stopped loving you.
She was crying by the end, real tears.
And here's the strange part, you didn't
think she was lying. You think she
believed every word. When she finished,
you asked her just one question. Kayla,
"When did you start missing me?"
She opened her mouth, then she closed
it. You watched her try to find an
answer that wasn't the truth.
You watched her realize there wasn't
one. She hadn't called on day one, or
day 10, or day 90.
She'd called on day 91 at 11:52 a.m., 5
hours after a news article went up.
"That's not fair," she whispered. "I
know," you said gently. "I'm not trying
to be unfair. I just needed to know."
You told her you weren't angry. You told
her you hoped she'd find what she was
looking for. And then you said the
hardest, truest thing you've ever said
to anyone.
"You were right that night. I'm just a
simple guy who wants a simple life. The
money didn't change that. It just
changed who wants to share it with me."
She left the pastries on the hood of
your truck and drove away.
When you walked back inside, Tess was
still standing at the paint counter. She
looked at you carefully. "You okay?" she
asked. "Yeah." you said. And then,
because you suddenly realized you should
have done it weeks ago, you asked her if
she wanted to get dinner. Just the two
of you. A real date. She raised an
eyebrow. "Is this because you're rich
now?" "No." you said. "It's because you
brought me a Cuban sandwich when I
wasn't." She laughed so hard a customer
dropped a box of screws.
"Okay, I have to ask. Did Ben make the
right call? Tell me in the comments. I
genuinely want to know. And if you're
enjoying this story, take 2 seconds to
subscribe. It helps a small channel like
this one more than you know." That was 5
years ago. You kept working at the
hardware store for another year, just
like Walt said. When the owner decided
to retire, you bought the store, kept
every single employee, and gave everyone
a raise.
Then you opened two more locations.
Old men still bring in broken parts in
sandwich bags and ask for you by name.
You spent your second year buying back
land. Every acre your grandfather had
lost in the 1985 freeze, you tracked
down and bought piece by piece.
On his 87th birthday, you drove Walt out
to the edge of the property and handed
him a folder with all the deeds inside.
He didn't say anything for a long time.
He just walked out into the rows of
young orange trees and stood there with

That evening on the porch, he peeled an
orange and handed you half, the same as

The boring investments did exactly what

Your $50 million is now worth a little

You've never bought a yacht, a

You married Tess 2 years after that

orange trees.

thing, the old feed store receipt with

are. Timing does.
Pay attention to who shows up before

those are the only ones who came for
you.

sitting in the break room of a cold

how people do it, man. I really don't."
You nod. You tell him it'll work out.
You mean it more than he knows.
Because 10 years ago almost to the day
you won $47 million in the lottery.

and in 10 years you've told exactly one
person.
Not Benny, not your friends, not your
cousins, not even your mom.
You still work three days a week on a

2013 Honda with a cracked tail light.
Most of your co-workers think you're a
nice guy who's careful with money.

warehouse. It pays $18.75 an hour, about
You wear thermal gloves in July because

in medical bills from a surgery last

You don't know much about money yet, but

Her name is Margaret Hollis.

She helps you set one up. She introduces

She's proud of you. She tells her

But every time she worries about money,

You hold her and tell her you'll figure

pay the mechanic in cash and tell her

You propose in year five on a hiking
trail with a simple ring. She says yes
before you even finish the question.
The night before the wedding, you sit

Then you slide a folder across the

Then she starts laughing.
Not a nervous laugh, a real one. Tears
running down her face.
She tells you that for two years, she's
been secretly worried you were saving
every penny because you were in some
kind of trouble.
She'd even started putting money aside
to help you.
Then, she pushes the folder back to you
unopened. She says she fell in love with
the guy who walks the dogs nobody else
wants. That's who she's marrying
tomorrow.
The rest is just paperwork. She only
adds one condition. Rule four stays. You
keep helping people and you keep it
quiet. Together.
In year six, the stock market crashes.
Over a few terrifying months, the
trust's investments fall from 27 million
to 19 million.
$8 million gone on paper.
More money than most people will earn in
10 lifetimes.
You can't sleep. You stare at the
numbers at 3:00 in the morning. The news
channels all say it's going to get
worse. You call your advisor. He asks
you one question. Are you planning to
spend 19 million this year?
You laugh and say no. Then, nothing has
actually happened to you yet. Don't make
it happen by selling.
You don't sell.
Elena reminds you that you're still
living on a forklift driver's paycheck,
and that paycheck hasn't changed at all.
Two years later, the account is back
above 30 million.
Then, in year seven, the warehouse
almost closes. The parent company
announces they're selling the building
and moving operations out of state. 140
people are going to lose their jobs,
including Benny, who has a daughter
starting high school, and a guy named
Luis, who has worked the loading dock
for 26 years.
The break room goes silent for weeks.
Benny tells you he doesn't know what
he'll do.
Before I tell you what you decided to
do, if you haven't subscribed yet, now's

All right, here's what happened next.
You go home and talk to Elena. Then, you
call Margaret. Six weeks later, a

buys the warehouse and the business for

The new owners announce that every
employee will keep their job. Everyone

They pick Benny.

would take a chance on this old place.
He wonders out loud who the mysterious
new owners are. Some rich guy in another
state, probably.
You clap along with everyone else. Then,
you put on your orange vest and go back
to the forklift.
In year eight, you and Elena quietly set
up something else, a scholarship fund at
the local high school for kids whose

tuition, books, housing, everything. You
name it after your dad, the Tom Novak
Memorial Scholarship. Nobody at the

know the checks always arrive on time.
Which brings you back to tonight. The
high school gym is packed and hot.
Folding chairs on the basketball court,
balloons tied to the bleachers, proud
parents waving phones in the air. You
sit with Elena, Benny, and your mom, who
has baby sat Sophie since she was in
diapers and wouldn't miss this for
anything. Near the end of the ceremony,
the principal announces the scholarship
awards. He tells you he applied to
everything Sophie could find, but he
isn't getting his hopes up.
Then, the principal says, "This year's
recipient of the Tom Novak Memorial
Scholarship, covering full tuition,
housing, and books for 4 years, is
Sophie Ramirez." Benny makes a sound
you've never heard a grown man make. He
stands up, then sits down, then stands
up again.
Sophie walks across the stage with her
hands over her mouth. The whole gym
applauds.
You didn't choose her. A committee of

But you can't stop smiling. Then you
feel your mom's hand grip your arm.
She's staring at the printed program in
her lap, at the name Tom Novak, her

You don't say anything. You just give

After the ceremony in the parking lot,

She tells you that your father used to

Benny never finds out. On Monday

listening to Benny tell everyone about

looking out for you.
10 years ago, you won $47 million. The
money changed a lot of lives,

exactly the way you wanted it.

would you tell?

title: POV: You Pretended to Be Broke on Your First Date—She Paid for Dinner

segments.text: The check lands on the table between
you, in a little black plastic folder
with a peppermint on top.
You're sitting in a red vinyl booth at a
taco place on Colfax Avenue in Denver,
the kind with paper napkins, a jukebox
that only plays country, and a neon sign
in the window with one letter burned
out. It's 8:15 on a Thursday night in
March.
Across from you sits a woman named Maya.
She has dark, curly hair pulled into a
messy bun, a paint stain on her left
thumb, and a laugh so loud that the
couple at the next table turned around
twice. This is your first date.
You're wearing a faded flannel shirt
with a frayed collar, old jeans, and
work boots with dried drywall dust on
the toes. You drove here in a 2009
Subaru Outback with a cracked taillight

under job, you wrote building
maintenance. All of that is true. What

taxes and a few quiet investments,
you're worth a little over $70 million.

toolbox.

something you've never done before in
your entire life. You reach for it
slowly, wince a little, and say,
"Would you mind if we split it? Payday's
not until Friday." It's a test. You know
it's a test, and you hate yourself a

Maya looks at you for a second, then she

Your name is Will Carter and you grew up
in a trailer outside Grand Junction,

with a dad who fixed furnaces and a mom
who worked the register at a hardware
store.

calls when you were a kid.

So, at 24, while working as a

For 5 years, it was just you, a laptop

Then plumbing companies. Then some of

At 31, a large software company bought

and that's when everything got strange.

Your photo was on page 34. Within a

Two old high school friends pitched you
business ideas over beers. Your landlord
tried to sell you his building at double
its value.
And then there was Brooke.
You'd been engaged to Brooke for a year
before the sale.
After the magazine article, she changed.
Slowly at first. She started sending you
links to houses in Cherry Creek. She

One night you found her on the phone

Within a week, a woman you'd never met
messaged you a link to the magazine

On your third date with someone else,

Mostly. So, you deleted everything. For

You kept the Subaru. You kept her dad's

You kept your money invested in boring

And one night, at 34, lonely and tired
of eating dinner alone, you made a new
dating profile.
No last name. No mention of Root Wise.
Job, building maintenance.
You told yourself it wasn't lying.
It just wasn't the whole truth.
Two days later, a woman named Maya sent

If you've ever wondered whether someone

After that first night, you kept your

And slowly, date by date, you got to

Maya Torres was 32.
She taught seventh grade science at a

Every time she reached for a check, a

You called the one person who knew the

Janet was quiet. Then she said, "Will,
you're not testing her anymore. You're

yourself you'd tell Maya soon, next
week, after her school's science fair,
after her birthday.
You kept finding reasons.
Quick favor. If you're enjoying this

Because what happened next tested Will
in a way he didn't see coming. In June,
3 months after that first taco night,
the Subaru finally broke down. It wasn't
a test this time. It was real.
The transmission started slipping on
I-25 on the way to pick Maya up for a
hike, and you limped it into a gas
station with smoke coming out from under
the hood.
The mechanic said it would cost $1,800
to fix.
Maya was in the passenger seat. You saw
her doing the math in her head.
A building maintenance guy, $1,800, the
end of the month.
That evening, she knocked on your
apartment door. You lived in a small
one-bedroom in one of your own buildings
on purpose.
She was holding a white envelope.
"Don't be weird about this," she said,

It's not much. It's just to help with

You stood there holding the envelope.

from. It was the money she saving for a

Maya, I can't take this.
You can and you will, she said. You do

She kissed you on the cheek and left

You closed the door and sat down on the

For the first time since you sold

Not because of who you were, but because

That night you didn't sleep. You sat at

This wasn't a test anymore.
Maya had passed every test you never
should have given her.
The only person still failing was you.
You put the envelope in the top drawer

You'd tell her everything in person at

picked a date, the following Saturday.
You never got the chance.
We're about halfway through this story
and if you're still here, you're exactly

for.
If you haven't subscribed yet, now's a

On Thursday night, two days before you

friend Priya.
Priya's boyfriend worked in private
equity downtown.
The party was in a big house in the

You wore your flannel.
Maya held your hand and introduced you
to everyone as Will, he fixes buildings,

A few of the quarter-zip guys nodded

And then Priya's boyfriend, a guy named

"No way." He said, way too loudly. "No

The conversation around you stopped. A

"You passed a test you should never have

Maya's mom cried through the whole

title: POV: You Turned Grandpa’s Failing Business Into a $650 Million Empire

segments.text: It's 7:40 on a Thursday morning and
you're standing in line at a hardware
store.

one arm and a bag of fittings in your
other hand.

asks if you want the contractor
discount. You say, "Sure."
He has no idea that 40 minutes ago, you
were on a video call with a team of
investment bankers in New York.
They spent 6 weeks going through every
invoice your company has ever sent.
At the end, the senior partner leaned
toward his camera and said the number
slowly.
$650 million.
You said, "Thank you." Closed the laptop
and drove to the hardware store because
a pipe is leaking under your own kitchen
sink and you'd rather fix it yourself.
Most people in your life think you run a

decided you'd been handed a joke.

a year.

The company owes $212,000 to a bank, a

You spend 2 weeks learning where the

The business isn't dying because people

it.
The problem is that Walter Haskins was a
brilliant technician and a terrible
businessman. He was still charging
prices from the early 2000s.
He had nearly $90,000 in unpaid invoices
sitting in a shoebox because he didn't

And he never sold a single maintenance

Customers only called when something

You call every customer who owes money

600 customers join the Comfort Club. The

isn't a talker, but one evening, wiping

to say you had the steadiest flashlight
