title: 7 Types of Income the IRS May Not Tax After 65 — Most Seniors Miss These

segments.text: There are seven kinds of income. The IRS
is legally not allowed to touch after
the age of 65. And one of them can
shield as much as $500,000
from federal tax in a single afternoon.
Yet almost every senior in this country
knows about only one of the seven and
quietly hands the government money that
was never entitled to take. Think about
that. Not a loophole, not a scheme, not
some gray area a clever accountant
whispers about behind a closed door.
Seven categories of money that the tax
code itself in plain black and white
says you get to keep in full.
And the reason you were never taught
them is simple. Nobody profits when you
keep your own money. There is no
industry built around telling a widow on
a fixed income that the check in her
hand was tax-free the whole time. Before
I go 1 in further, I want you to hold on
to two promises because they're the
whole reason to stay till the end. There
is one type of income on this list that
can protect the single largest amount
far more than the rest. And I'm going to
name it and show you the exact dollar
figure. And there's one specific move,
one decision you make with your own
money that determines whether the IRS
gets to tax your Social Security check
at all. Or whether it stays completely
untouched. I'll give you both before
we're done. But the second one only
works if you understand the first six.
So stay with me all the way through. Let
me start with the one type almost
everyone already half knows because it's
the doorway to understanding all the
others. Most seniors have heard
somewhere along the way that Social
Security is not fully taxed.
And that part is true. What they never
learned is exactly how much of it is
protected. And that's where thousands of
dollars slip through the cracks every
single year. Here's the hard rule
straight from the tax code. No matter
how high your income climbs, the
absolute most of your social security
the government can ever tax is 85%.
That means at least 15% of every social
security dollar you receive is exempt
from federal income tax for everyone at
every income level always. It cannot be
touched. But that's only the ceiling and
for a great many seniors the real number
is far better than that.
Whether the government taxes your
benefits at all depends on something
called your provisional income and the
thresholds are lower than most people
fear and higher than they hope. If
you're single and your provisional
income sits below $25,000
then 0% of your social security is
taxable. None of it. If you're married
and filing jointly and that number sits
below $32,000
again 0% is taxed. Above those lines up
to half becomes taxable. And only once a
single filer passes $34,000 or a married
couple passes $44,000
does that 85% ceiling ever come into
play?
So the truth almost no one tells you is
this. A large number of seniors living
on modest fixed incomes are paying tax
on social security they never actually
owed simply because no one showed them
where those lines are drawn. And here's
the quiet cost of not knowing it. Every
single year a great many seniors sit
down with their tax paperwork or hand it
to someone in a hurry. And they include
social security income the government
was never entitled to tax.
Because nobody ever showed them the
$25,000 and $32,000 lines they overpay
by a few hundred here, a thousand
dollars there year after year and it
adds up over a retirement into real
money.
It's not a dramatic robbery. It's a slow
leak and a slow leak sinks a boat just
as surely as a hole.
The tragedy is that it's completely
avoidable and it starts with knowing
that the one rule everyone half
remembers has real numbers attached to
it.
Now, I'm Mark and on this channel we do
one thing. We take the rules that were
written to protect you. The ones that
got buried under jargon and silence
and we drag them back into the daylight
where you can use them. And today might
be the most valuable list I've ever
handed you because this isn't about
clawing back one small fee. This is
about seven separate rivers of money
that can flow to you and your family
without the federal government ever
dipping its hand in you know, one of
them. Now, let me give you the other six
and I promise the biggest one is still
coming. The second type of income the
IRS cannot touch is the money that comes
out of a Roth account. A Roth individual
retirement account or a Roth version of
a workplace plan is funded with dollars
you already paid tax on. And because you
already paid, the deal the government
made with you is permanent. Once you're
past the age of 59 and a half and the
account has been open for at least 5
years, every single dollar you withdraw
comes out completely free of federal
income tax. Not the money you put in,
not the growth, not the gains that built
up over 20 or 30 years.
All of it tax-free. Picture a retiree
who put money away quietly for decades
and now has a Roth with $200,000.
When she draws on it, she owes nothing.
Her neighbor pulling from an ordinary
retirement account pays tax on every
withdrawal. Same money saved, two
completely different outcomes. The
difference is which bucket it sat in and
there's a hidden second gift buried
inside that Roth. One that almost no one
talks about because those withdrawals
aren't counted as income. They don't
push up that provisional income number
that decides whether your social
security gets taxed. So a senior who
pulls from a Roth can cover her expenses
without accidentally dragging her social
security into the taxable zone. There's
a cruel little trap in the tax code that
professionals quietly called the tax
torpedo, where pulling money from the
wrong account raises your income just
enough to start taxing your social
security on top of it. So you get hit
twice from one withdrawal. The Roth is
one of the few tools that lets you step
around that torpedo completely. That's
why which bucket your money sits in is
not a small detail. It can decide your
tax bill for the rest of your life.
Therefore, the type of account your
money lives in matters just as much as
how much money you have. And this is
where the third category comes in
because it's the closest thing to true
magic the tax code allows. It's called a
health savings account. Money you put
into one of these was never taxed going
in. It grows without being taxed. And
when you pull it out to cover a
qualified medical expense, so it comes
out without being taxed, either. That's
three separate tax breaks stacked on a
single account, which exists nowhere
else in the entire code. And here's the
part built for seniors specifically.
Before the age of 65, if you pull that
money out for something other than
medical care, the government hits you
with a 20% penalty on top of the tax.
But the day you turn 65, that penalty
vanishes. And from that day forward, you

all. And if you use it for medical
costs, and seniors face a mountain of
medical costs, it's still 100% tax-free.
Let me make this a real person for a

people stay with you. Picture a man,
I'll call him Walter, 68 years old,
careful with a dollar his whole life.
Walter quietly built a health savings
account up to $40,000 over his working
years. Now in retirement, every
prescription, every doctor visit, every
pair of glasses, hearing aid, and dental
bill, he pays straight from that
account. Not one cent of it is ever
taxed. His brother, who never opened
one, pays for the identical care out of
a taxable account and loses a slice to
the government every time. Same
illnesses, same bills, and one brother
handing money to the IRS, the other
keeping all of it. Walter was never
smarter. He was just shown the door, and
he walked through it. But the three
we've covered so far, Social Security,
Roth, and the health savings account,
are all about income you arranged for
yourself. The fourth type is different
because it arrives at the worst moment
of a family's life, and the tax code for

to their spouse or their children, that
money, the death benefit, is generally
not counted as taxable income at all. A
A $4 million policy pays $4 million,
and the beneficiary doesn't report it as
income and doesn't lose a piece of it to
federal income tax. In a season of
grief, when a widow is trying to figure
out how to keep the lights on, that full
untouched check can be the difference
between keeping the house and losing it.
And most families brace themselves for a
tax bill on it that, in the ordinary
case, simply never comes.
I've watched families sit frozen over a
life insurance letter, afraid to cash
it,
whispering to each other that the
government is going to take a third of
it, so they'd better set money aside.
And they set aside money they didn't
need to set aside, and they lived
smaller than they had to in a hard year
over a tax that was never going to
arrive. So, hear me clearly. In the
ordinary case, when a policy pays out
because someone died, that money reaches
the beneficiary whole. That's one way
you can lift off the shoulders of the
people you love just by telling them the
truth about it while you still can. Now,
I want you to lean in because we've
reached the fifth type, and this is the
giant I promised you at the very
beginning. This is the one that can
shield the largest single amount of
money from the IRS in one move. And it
sits inside something almost every
senior watching me owns, your home.
When you sell your main home, the profit
you made on it, the gain, would normally
be taxable. But, the tax code hands you
an exemption so large that most seniors
sell and owe absolutely nothing. If
you're single, you can exclude up to
of gain from tax. And if you're married
and filing jointly, you can exclude up
Half a million dollars of profit on your
own home completely invisible to the
IRS, as long as you owned it and lived
in it as your main home for at least two
of the last five years. Think about what
that means for people who bought a
modest house decades ago for $30,000 or
and now it's worth $400,000 or $500,000.
That's an enormous gain on paper. The
kind of number that would terrify anyone
into thinking the tax bill will swallow
half of it. And yet, because of this one
rule, a married couple can walk away
from that sale with half a million
dollars of profit and hand the
government nothing. This is the one out
of all seven that can protect the most.
And it's the one seniors most often
forget they even have because they only
think about it in the one year they
finally sell.
There's one condition you have to meet,
and it's worth saying plainly so no one
gets caught out. You have to have owned
the home and lived in it as your main
home for at least two of the last five

lived in the same house for 20 or 30

if you're thinking about selling a place
you moved into only recently, or a
second home, or a rental, the rules are
different. And that's exactly the kind
of thing worth checking before you sign
anything, not after. Because getting
this one right can be the single largest
tax decision of your entire retirement.
And getting it wrong can cost you tens
of thousands of dollars the law would
happily have let you keep. Let me stop
here at roughly the middle of everything
I have to tell you. Because up to this
point, you might think these are just
seven nice little breaks, a bit of money
saved here and there. They're not.
Stacked together, they can shape whether
you spend your final decades comfortable
or squeezed, and whether your children
inherit something whole or something the
government took a bite out of first. So,
lean in because the sixth type reaches
past your own lifetime and into what you
leave behind. And it's one of the most
misunderstood rules in the entire code.
The sixth type of income the IRS cannot
touch is an inheritance. When you
receive money or property from someone
who has died, that inheritance is
generally not treated as taxable income
to you at all. There's no federal
inheritance tax reaching into an
ordinary family's pockets. And there's a

than most people ever realize, called

When you inherit an asset, say a house
or shares of stock the person bought
long ago for very little, the tax value
of that asset resets to what it's worth
on the day they died. So, if your mother
bought a home for $40,000 and it was
when she passed, and you inherit it and
sell it,
the decades of gain in between are wiped

and the tax on all that growth simply
disappears. Let me put a real picture on
that stepped-up basis, because it's

generous rules in the whole code. Say
your father bought shares of a company

If he had sold them himself the day

But people hear the words estate tax and

with a real number. Because this is
where families torture themselves for no
reason.
The federal estate tax, the one everyone

until the estate is worth more than
per person. $13 million and change. For
the overwhelming majority of seniors
watching me right now, that tax will
never ever apply. You've been frightened

down the the from your house. The
inheritance you leave and the
inheritance you receive in almost every
normal family passes free of that tax

you've spent a lifetime paying off can
move to your children far more intact
than you were ever led to believe.
Which brings me to the seventh type on
the list.
And this one is quieter than the rest
because it doesn't arrive as a windfall
or a sale or a death benefit. It arises
as steady trickle of interest month
after month and the government agreed
long ago to keep its hands off it.
Entirely. I'm talking about the interest
paid by municipal bonds. When you've
lend money to a state, a city, a county,
or a local school district by buying
what people call a muni bond, the
interest that bond pays you back is
exempt from federal income tax.
It's one of the oldest bargains in the
entire code.
The government wanted towns to be able
to build roads and schools and hospitals
cheaply. So, it made the interest on
those bonds tax-free to the people who

in municipal bonds can collect that

because I'll never hand you half a

So, it's a powerful tool, but it's not a

here and not listening to someone
selling you something. Now, before I
give you the action steps, I promised

and it still counts toward the required

completely untouched. Exactly as I
promised at the very beginning. Now, let

their names. The first neighbor knows

The second neighbor draws from a Roth

of gain, gives to her church straight

basis that wipes out decades of gain.
Same money, same streets. One family

$250,000 of gain protected if you're

a year keeps that money off your tax

Say that back to yourself so it sticks.

title: 5 Types of Debt Relief Seniors Should Know About After Age 65

segments.text: There are five bills that the government
itself says you may no longer have to
pay once you turn 65. Not a smaller
amount, not a discount, shaved off the
top. The whole bill gone, wiped away by
a rule that already exists and already
has your name on it. And here is the
part that should make you angry. Nobody
whose job it is to collect that money
from you has the slightest reason to
pick up the phone and tell you that you
are allowed to stop.
The hospital will not tell you, the
county will not tell you, not even the
government office that runs the program
will call to say you qualify. It is all
left sitting there quietly in the hope
that you will keep on paying out of a
lifetime of habit. Thank you for
stopping here because most people scroll
right past a video like this and it
quietly cost them thousands. So today
I'm going to walk you through all five.
Exactly which ones, who qualifies, and
the one quiet mistake that keeps this
money draining out of your account year
after year.
Stay with me all the way to the end
because the last one is the largest of
them all and it is the one almost nobody
has ever heard of. The first one is a
hospital bill. Most of the hospitals in
this country are non-profit hospitals
and in exchange for paying no taxes at
all, the law requires every one of them
to run a program that forgives the bills
of patients whose income is modest. It
is not charity in the way you are
picturing it and it is not a favor. It
is a condition of the enormous tax break
the hospital receives every single year.
If your income is below a certain line
and that line is far more generous than
most people expect, the hospital must
reduce your bill and in a great many
cases it must erase the entire thing.
This is true whether you have insurance
or not because even an insured senior
can be left with thousands of dollars
that Medicare did not cover.
But here is the catch, the same catch
that runs through all five of these. The
hospital does not have to offer it to
you. You have to ask for it by name. You
call the billing department and you say,
"I want to apply for your financial
assistance program." And by law, they
must hand you the application. To give
you a sense of how wide this reaches, at
many hospitals, a single person earning
under roughly $30,000 a year, or a
couple under about 40,000, can have the
entire bill wiped away. And even well
above those numbers, the bill is often
cut by half or more. Picture a woman who
spends 5 days in the hospital and comes
home to a bill for $30,000 that she has
no idea how she will ever pay.
She may never learn that the hospital
was required, by the terms of its own
tax break, to erase most or all of it,
if only she had asked. So, the bill sits
on her kitchen table, and she quietly
starts skipping her own medicine to make
the payments on a debt she may never
have owed at all.
The second one is what you hand over at
the pharmacy counter. As of this year,
there is now a hard limit written into
federal law on how much be made to pay
out of your own pocket for your covered
prescriptions in a single year.
That limit is $2,100.
Once your spending on covered
medications reaches that number, you are
finished for the rest of the year, and
your drug plan must pay the entire cost
of everything after that.
For someone taking an expensive
medication for cancer or for a heart
condition, the kind of drug that used to
cost people 10 or 15,000 dollars a year,
that can no longer happen to you. The
government capped it. And there is a
second step almost nobody uses. You can
ask your drug plan to spread that amount
across the whole year in small monthly
pieces, so it never lands on you all at
once. Think for a moment about what this
used to mean. Before this cap existed, a
senior on a fixed income could open the
mailbox and find a pharmacy bill for
$8,000 for a single cancer drug, and be
forced to choose between the medicine
keeping her alive and the money she
needed to eat. That cruel choice is now
gone. The law drew a line and said, "No
further." But your plan will not send
you a letter celebrating it. You have to
know the line is there
and know that once you cross it, you can
stop worrying. The third one is the
largest bill most homeowners face all
year, and that is your property tax.
Now, you may have heard that seniors can
freeze their property tax or take an
exemption to lower it. This is something
different and far more powerful for
anyone who is truly stretched. In most
states, once you reach 65, you can apply
to defer your property tax entirely. To
defer it means you do not pay it now at
all. Not a reduced amount, none of it.
The state quietly steps in and pays the
bill for you year after year and simply
records what it has paid as a line
against your home to be settled much
later when the house is eventually sold
or passes to your family, usually with a
low rate of interest that in most states
does not climb above 5%.
For a senior on a fixed income being
crushed by a property tax bill of three,
four, or five thousand dollars a year,
that is money that stays in your own
pocket for the rest of your life in that
home. And like all the others, it is
never automatic. You apply for it
through your county and you have to ask.
Let me put a real face on it. Picture a
widower in his late 70s who has lived in
the same paid-off house for 40 years.
The house where he raised his children.
His only income now is his social
security check and the property tax has
climbed to five thousand dollars a year,
more than a month and a half of
everything he receives. Every year he
grows a little more afraid of losing the
home he already owns over a bill for
taxes. If he simply applied to defer it,
the state would carry that bill for him
quietly for the rest of his life in that
home and the fear would be gone. But no
one at the county has ever once told him
the program exists.
The fourth one is a protection so strong
that almost no one believes it is real
until they see it in writing.
There is a program run by your own state
called the Qualified Medicare
Beneficiary Program. If your income is
modest and you qualify for it, two
things happen. The state pays your
Medicare costs for you, and this is the
part that stuns people. It becomes
against federal law for a doctor, the
hospital, or a pharmacy to bill you for
the deductibles, the co-pays, or the
co-insurance that Medicare would
normally leave you to pay. Against the
law. If you are in this program and a
provider sends you a bill for those
costs, they have broken federal law, and
you do not owe it.
Congress wrote this protection decades
ago and strengthened it in recent years,
and it is fully in force right now.
Yet doctors' offices send these bills by
mistake all the time, and the people who
receive them, not knowing the law,
quietly pay for costs they never owed.
So, how do you know if this is you? The
income limits are modest. They are aimed
at seniors who live mostly on social
security with a little on top, and they
are adjusted every year. There is also a
limit on savings and other resources,
and it varies from state to state. That
is exactly why the honest mistake is to
assume you earn too much and never
check. Checking costs you nothing.
Here is how to find out. Contact your
state Medicaid office, the same office
that handles health coverage for people
with limited income.
You can also call 1-800-MEDICARE,
or look up your state health insurance
assistance program, called SHIP, where
trained counselors will go through the
application with you for free. Once you
are approved, keep your notice from the
state and show your Medicare card at
every appointment and every pharmacy.
If a bill still arrives for a
deductible, a co-pay, or co-insurance,
do not pay it. Call the billing office.
Tell them you are a qualified Medicare
beneficiary, and ask them to remove the
charge.
If they push back, call 1-800-MEDICARE
or your SHIP counselor, and they will
step in. And if you are already enrolled
and you find old bills you paid, gather
the statements and ask for a refund in
writing.
A provider who billed you in error is
supposed to give it back. That brings us
to the fifth one, the biggest of all,
and the one almost nobody has heard of.
It is not for everyone, but if it is for
you, it can be worth more than the other
four combined.
If you served in the military during a
wartime period, or you are the surviving
spouse of someone who did, there is a
benefit from the Department of Veterans
Affairs called Aid and Attendance. It is
an extra amount added on top of the VA
pension for veterans and survivors who
need help with daily life,
like bathing, dressing, eating, or
managing medications, or who live in a
nursing home or assisted living
facility. The numbers are not small.
Right now, it can pay a single veteran
more than $2,400
a month. A married veteran closer to
$2,900 a month. And a surviving spouse
more than $1,500 a month. The money is
tax-free. It arrives every month, and it
continues for as long as you remain
eligible. The amounts adjust each year,
so check the current rates on va.gov.
You do not have to have been wounded,
and you do not have to have seen combat.
Generally, you need at least 90 days of
active duty with at least one day during
a recognized wartime period, and a
discharge that was other than
dishonorable. On top of that, you need a
medical need for care, and your income
and net worth have to fall under the
limits the VA sets each year.
Here is the part people miss. The VA
does not simply look at your income.
It subtracts your out-of-pocket medical
costs, and that includes what you pay
for assisted living, in-home care, and
Medicare premiums. So, a senior who
looks to well-off on paper may still
qualify once those costs are counted.
Now, one warning. The VA looks back 36
months at any assets you gave away or
moved. Do not give away money or
property in an attempt to qualify.
It can trigger a penalty period and
delay your benefit, and be very careful
who you trust.
Accredited Veteran Service Officers at
groups like the VFW, the American
Legion, and Disabled American Veterans,
and at your county veterans office, will
help you file for free. Be wary of
anyone who asks for an upfront fee, or
who pushes you to restructure your
finances. To get started, call the VA
benefits line at 1-800-827-1000
or visit va.gov and ask about the
Veterans Pension with Aid and
Attendance. Gather your discharge
papers, called a DD214,
your income and medical expense records,
and the form your doctor fills out about
your care needs. If you are not ready to
file, ask about filing an intent to
file, which can protect your start date
for up to a year. The process can take
months, but an approved claim can often
be paid back to that start date. I think
about the widows most of all. A woman
whose husband served in a war a lifetime
ago, who is now spending her thin
savings on help just to bathe, dress,
and cook with no idea that the
government may owe her more than $1,500
a month for exactly that care because of
what her husband did in his 20s.
That money could change her entire life,
and it has been sitting there unclaimed
the whole time. If that is you, or your
mother, or a widow you know from church,
that one phone call is worth making
today. Now step back and look at what
all five of these share because it is
the whole reason they stay hidden in
plain sight. Not one of them switches
itself on. The hospital will not erase
your bill until you ask. Your drug plan
will not send you a letter about your
spending cap. The county will not knock
on your door and offer to defer your
property tax. The doctor who bills you
by mistake will not confess it. And the
VA will not call the widow to say she
has been for years. Every one of these
was written into the law to help you,
and everyone was wrapped in just enough
silence that most people never claim it.
The system is not exactly lying to you.
It is simply counting on you to stay
quiet and to keep paying. Before you
make those calls, a few quick reminders
that tie all of this together. For the
hospital, ask for an itemized bill and a
copy of the financial assistance policy,
which the hospital must make available
to you. For the pharmacy, call your drug
plan and ask about the Medicare
prescription payment plan so your costs
are spread across the year in small
monthly pieces. And for every program,
write down the date you applied, who you
spoke to, and what they told you. A
simple notebook keeps everyone honest.
Many seniors also need a hand with the
phone calls. So, if you are a son or
daughter watching this, sit down with
your parent and make them together.
So, here's what I want you to do, and it
is not a someday task. It is a this week
task. Pick the one that fits your life
and go claim it. If you are holding a
hospital bill, call and say the words
financial assistance program before you
pay a cent of it. And ask them to hold
off on collections while your
application is reviewed. If your
property tax is crushing you, call your
county and ask about deferral.
If your income is modest, contact your
state Medicaid office and ask about the
qualified Medicare beneficiary program.
And if you or your husband or wife ever
served in a time of war, make the call
about aid and attendance because that
single phone call has been worth tens of
thousands of dollars to people exactly
like you. One important note before we
close, everything in this video is
general information, not legal, medical,
or financial advice.
Income limits, dollar amounts, and rules
change every year and differ by state
and by hospital. So, please confirm your
details with the office that runs each
program. You do not have to chase all
five at once and wear yourself out. You
only have to open one door because
behind each of them is money that may
have been yours the whole time. Quietly
kept just out of reach by a system that
was hoping you would never ask. So, ask.
And if this video helped you, please
share it with one person over 65 you
care about and subscribe so you do not
miss the next one. Then let yourself
feel what it is to finally take back
something that was always meant to be
yours.

title: New US Laws Taking Effect in Fall 2026: What They Could Mean for Your Money

segments.text: On September 30th, you will go to sleep
in one America and wake up on October
1st in a different one because at
midnight five new laws take effect that
will directly change how you buy a car
and how you keep your home, how you
drive on the highway, and how you vote.
And almost no one is talking about what
happens if you miss the deadline that
expires on September 30th. If you live
in California, Maryland, Connecticut,
Alabama, or if you ever drive through or
have family in those states, what I'm
about to tell you will save you money,
protect your rights, and prevent a
costly mistake in October. And even if
you live nowhere near these states, stay
with me until the end because the last
change I will cover is federal. It
affects every single American with
health insurance, social security, or a
bank account. And the window to act on
it closes on September 30th as well.
Before we walk through each new law,
what it says in plain English, who it
helps, and exactly what to do before the
clock strikes midnight. Please hit the
like button and subscribe with the bell
on. It is the only way you will get the
October update the moment these laws
actually go live, and it helps this
channel keep translating legal language
into real dollars and real protections
while there is still time to use them.
Let us start with the biggest change,
and it affects the most populous state
in the country, California. Effective
October 1st, the California Car Act,
also known as Senate Bill 766,
completely rewrites the rules for buying
a vehicle in California. And if you are
shopping for a used car, this single law
gives you a right you have never had
before. For years, car dealers in
California could advertise one price
online and then add thousands of dollars
in fees, add-on products, and hidden
markups once you were sitting in the
finance office. That practice is now
under the new law. Every dealer must
disclose the true total price of the
vehicle upfront, including all mandatory
fees, taxes, and add-ons.
They cannot hide charges in the fine
print or charge you for products you did
not ask for and will not benefit from.
But, the most powerful part of this law
is for used car buyers. Starting October
1st, if you buy a used vehicle in
California, you have a 3-day right to
cancel the purchase after you sign the
contract and 72 hours to change your
mind and return the vehicle for a full
refund. This has never existed before in
California for car sales. It applies to
used cars purchased from a licensed
dealer on or
after October 1st, and it gives you
three full business days to have the car
inspected by your own mechanic, review
the financing, or simply decide the deal
was not right. If you are planning to
buy a used car in California,
do not sign before October 1st, if you
can wait. That 72-hour protection is
worth waiting a few days for. And if you
already bought a used car in late
September and feel pressured, know that
this new right does not apply
retroactively. So, the timing of your
signature matters. Our second October
1st law takes us to the East Coast, to
Maryland, and this one is about keeping
your home. Starting October 1st,
Maryland has new tax sale protections
for homeowners who have fallen behind on
property taxes due to serious illness,
financial hardship, or other qualifying
circumstances. Under the old system, if
you fell behind on property taxes, your
county could sell your tax debt to a
private investor who could then charge
high interest and eventually take your
home. The process moved quickly, and
many vulnerable homeowners,
especially seniors on fixed incomes,
lost their homes over relatively small
tax balances. The reforms that take
effect October 1st expand eligibility
for assistance through the state tax
sale ombudsman and establish priority
support for the most vulnerable
homeowners. If you own a home in
Maryland and you have fallen behind on
property taxes because of a medical
crisis, a loss of income, or another
hardship, you now have stronger options
to stop the sale, request a payment
plan, and get a dedicated advocate
assigned to your case. This is not
automatic. You must contact the
ombudsman if you or a family member in
Maryland has received any notice about
the delinquent taxes or a pending tax
sale, call the state tax sale ombudsman
immediately. The new protections that
exist on October 1st did not exist in
September and waiting even a few weeks
could mean the difference between
keeping your home and losing it to an
investor. Change number three takes
effect on the highways of Connecticut
and it will affect anyone who drives
Interstate 95 or Interstate 84 this
fall.
Effective October 1st, Connecticut has a
new left lane law. Driving in the left
lane of a multi-lane highway without
actively passing another vehicle is now
a ticketable offense.
The left lane is now legally a passing
lane only, not a cruising lane.
For a first offense, the fine is $88.
With administrative costs, the total can
reach up to $142.
The Connecticut Department of
Transportation has already begun
installing new signs that say, "Pass on
the left. Drive on the right along major
highways." Police can now pull you over
simply for staying in the left lane when
the right lane is open, even if you were
driving the speed limit. This matters
whether you live in Connecticut or are
just driving through from New York to
Massachusetts or to Rhode Island. If you
normally set your cruise control and
stay in the left lane to avoid merging
traffic on the right, you will need to
change that habit on October 1st. Stay
in the right or center lane unless you
are overtaking pass and then move back
over. It is a simple change that saves
you a ticket and keeps traffic flowing
as the law intends. Change number four
is about voting and it takes effect in
Alabama on October 1st. Starting October
1st, Alabama will no longer accept
digital or mobile identification for
voting.
Voters must present a physical printed
form of approved photo identification at
the polls. A photo on your phone, a
digital copy in an app, or a screenshot
of your license will not be accepted
even if it is issued by the state. This
change comes just 5 weeks before the
midterm elections on November 3rd, 2026
where every seat in the House of
Representatives and about 1/3 of Senate
seats are on the ballot. If you live in
Alabama or have parents or grandparents
there who vote, check right now that
they have a valid physical ID, a current
unexpired Alabama driver's license, a
state-issued non-driver ID, a United
States passport, or another approved
physical form. If that ID is expired,
lost, or only available digitally, get a
physical replacement before election
day. Do not wait until November 3rd to
discover at the polling place that a
phone screen is no longer enough. The
law is effective October 1st and will be
enforced for the November election. Now,
change number five is the one that
affects every American no matter what
state you live in and it is the reason
September 30th itself is a hard
deadline.
September 30th is the last day of the
federal fiscal year.
At midnight, the government must have a
new funding agreement or face a
shutdown. First, if you get health
insurance through the federal
marketplace or state exchange, about 40
million Americans do, the enhanced
premium tax credits that have kept
marketplace premiums affordable for the
last several years are in legislative
uncertainty right now. Congress is
negotiating whether to extend them into
2027 and whether they continue in their
current form will determine what you pay
every month starting January 1st.
You cannot control that vote, but you
can control this. Verify your income
projection and subsidy eligibility
before the marketplace opens on November
1st. And do not assume next year's
subsidy will be identical to this
year's. For seniors between age 60 and
64 who are not yet on Medicare, this
matters more than for anyone else.
You are in the age range where
marketplace premiums are highest and
subsidies are most valuable. The
difference between the right plan and
the wrong plan can be thousands of
dollars for the year. Mark December 15th
on your calendar. That is the real
deadline. If you enroll or change plans
between November 1st and December 15th,
your new coverage begins January 1st. If
you wait until after December 15th, your
coverage does not begin until February
1st, meaning you have no coverage for
the month of January. Second, September
30th is your final warning for the
December 31st tax deadlines that will
determine your 2026 return. You have
exactly 92 days from October 1st to
December 31st to execute the moves that
the wealthiest retirees do every fall.
Missing your RMD can trigger a penalty
of 25% of the amount you were supposed
to withdraw. That penalty can be reduced
to 10% if you correct the mistake
quickly and file form 5329
with a reasonable cause explanation. But
the better strategy is to avoid the
mistake altogether. Check with your
financial institution now and confirm
that your required distributions have
been satisfied across all of your IRA
accounts. Do not assume that one account
automatically covers what is required
from another.
If you are 70 and 1/2 or older and you
normally give money to charity, consider
qualified charitable distribution. You
can transfer up to about $18,000
directly from your IRA to a qualifying
charity.
The transfer can count toward your RMD
without being included as taxable
income. If you were already planning to
donate, this can make the transaction
more tax efficient than taking the
distribution as ordinary income and
donating what remains after taxes. There
is another December 31st deadline that
can matter if you are considering a Roth
conversion. Moving money from a
traditional IRA into a Roth IRA is a
taxable transaction.
But completing the conversion before
December 31st makes it part of the 2026
tax year. Waiting until January 1st
moves that conversion into 2027
instead. That means the decision is not
something to leave for the act last week
of the year. And then there's the $6,000
senior deduction created by the one big
beautiful bill act. This deduction
applies for tax years 2025
through 2028.
If you are 65 or older,
it can reduce adjusted gross income by
or by $12,000 when both spouses are 65
or older.
The important point is that this is a
deduction you need to account for when
planning your tax situation. It is not
money that simply appears in your bank
account. If your income is close to the
thresholds where Social Security becomes
taxable or close to the levels where
Medicare related IRMAA surcharges can
become relevant, every part of your tax
picture deserves attention. The
deduction could affect where your income
lands, but you should calculate your
individual situation rather than
assuming the full benefit will apply
automatically. So, before September 30th
passes, do not focus only on the
headline about October 1st. Use the
deadline as a reminder to organize the
decisions that come next.
First, review your health insurance
situation. If you receive coverage
through the marketplace, verify your
expected income and subsidy information
and be prepared to review your options
when enrollment opens on November.
First, remember that the amount you pay
for coverage in 2027 may not be
identical to what you paid this year. If
you are between 60 and 64 and are not
yet on Medicare, pay especially close
attention to this review. Marketplace
premiums can be significant at these
ages and changes in subsidy eligibility
can materially change what you are pay.
Mark December 15th as an important date
if you want coverage beginning January
1st and do not wait until the final day
to compare your options. Third, keep the
new state rules in mind. If you're
buying a used car in California,
remember the new 3-day cancellation
protection and the requirement for
dealers to show the true total price. If
you are dealing with delinquent property
taxes in Maryland, contact the tax sale
ombudsman and ask about the hardship
protections available to you.
If you drive in Connecticut, remember
that the left lane is for passing rather
than cruising. And if you vote in
Alabama, make sure your approved
identification is physical rather than
relying only on a digital copy. That is
why September 30th should be treated as
a planning checkpoint, not as a day to
panic. Write down what applies to you
and confirm the official requirements.
Here is the simple checklist. Before
September 30th, review your health
insurance and your expected income for
the coming year. Review your retirement
accounts and identify any RMD, QCD, or
Roth conversion decisions that need to
be completed before December 31st. On
October 1st, remember the California
used car protections, the Maryland
property tax assistance, the Connecticut
left lane rule, and the Alabama physical
ID requirement. Then, during the final
months of the year, keep your December
deadlines visible.
December 15th matters for marketplace
enrollment if you want January coverage.
December 31st matters for RMDs, QCDs,
Roth conversions, and year-end tax
planning. And remember one final thing,
information is useful only when you have
it before the decision.
Most people hear about a car protection
after they have already signed the
contract. They hear about a property tax
assistance program after the situation
has already become urgent. They learn
about a traffic rule after receiving a
ticket. They discover an identification
requirement after arriving at the
polling place. You now have the
opportunity to prepare earlier. Take a
screenshot of this checklist, keep it
somewhere you will see it, and share it
with anyone who may need it, especially
family members in California, Maryland,
Connecticut, or Alabama, and anyone
approaching an important year-end,
retirement, or tax deadline. Thank you
for watching. If this October 1st update
helped you understand what is changing
and what deadlines are coming next,
subscribe and turn on the bell so you
can follow the official updates as new
numbers and rules are released. The
October 14th Cola announcement and the
mid-November Medicare premium numbers
will be important updates to watch.
Until then, do not wait for a headline
to remind you about something you could
have prepared for today. Check your
documents, mark your deadlines, verify
the rules that apply to you, and make
your decisions before the calendar makes
them for you. I will see you in the next
video with the official numbers and
updates as they are released.

else is looked at. Then the medical
spending goes on the table. And in the
AY's own example, it takes another $300
off. That household is now being
measured at a little under 700 a month,
and housing costs have not even been
touched yet. Two people, one bank
account, the same deposits arriving
every month. One version of that
household is over the line and the other
is under it. The only difference is
whether anybody bothered to do the
subtractions. So, when you say you earn
too much, what you usually mean is that
nobody has ever subtracted anything from
what you earn. Here's the third way the
counting changes, and this one is about
savings rather than income. There is a
limit on what you can have in the bank
and still qualify. For most households,
that ceiling is $3,000. Once somebody in
the house is 60 or older, it rises to
And the things that most older people
actually own do not count toward it.
Your home does not count. The lot it
sits on does not count. Most retirement
and pension accounts do not count. That
last one stops people. Somebody with a
pension behind them owning their house
outright can still sit inside the
resource limit. The program is not
measuring what you built over a
lifetime. It is measuring what is
sitting in a checking account this
month. There is one more thing worth
knowing about that ceiling. States are
allowed to set their own limits above
the federal ones and most of them have
done exactly that. A household sitting
over 45,500
can still be inside the line where
actually the lives and the published
guidance says so in plain terms. So the
honest answer to whether savings
disqualify you is that it depends on
your state. The only way to find out is
to ask the state agency that holds the
file and the ceiling itself is on the
list that gets rewritten on the 1st of
October. The fourth difference is the
one that costs the most and gets
explained the least. So stay with me
through this one. Your housing costs
come off your income, too. Rent counts,
mortgage interest counts, and so do the
property taxes on the place you live in.
heating, cooling, electricity, water,
and the basic fee on one telephone all
count. Anything you spend on shelter
above half of what is left after the
other subtractions comes off as well.
For most households, there is a cap on
how much of that can come off.
Whatever the heating bill actually came
to, for a household of somebody 60 or
older, there's no cap. The whole excess
comes off. Take a moment with what that
does. Picture an older household in a
cold state, in an old house with a
heating bill that doubles in January.
Every dollar of that comes off the
income the state agency counts. A
younger household, one street over,
stops subtracting at 744.
Two homes, two different arithmetics,
and only one of them gets told about it.
And that is the reason I sit here and do
this. My work on this channel is to take
the rules that sit between an older
household and its own money. I say them
out loud in words you can use before
they cost you anything. SNAP and the
programs beside it get their limits
rewritten every single year. And no
state agency writes to tell you when
yours changed. Subscribing is how the
people who catch it in time catch it in
time. That is four separate provisions
inside one program. and every one of
them exists only for households like
yours. The resource limit alone puts
most of them out of reach for a younger
household. Nobody at any office is
required to walk you through them. The
application never asks whether the
senior rules should be applied to you.
The form assumes you already know. I
went through a whole video not long ago
on the nine benefits older Americans can
still claim and almost never ask about.
Food help under the senior rules was one
line on that list. It carries a set of
rules that could never fit in one line
and that is why it gets a whole night to
itself here. Now let me come back to the
date because everything we have talked
about is about to move. The published
page for the current numbers says the
information covers the 1st of October
last year through the 30th of September
this year. That is the window we are
standing in and it closes at the end of
next month. A new set of standards takes
its place on the 1st of October. The
important point is that you are not
being measured against a permanent
number. The standards are updated on the
schedule. The income limits move, the
deductions move, the benefit amount is
recalculated, and the figures used for
one year's eligibility calculation do
not simply remain in place because
nobody personally called you to announce
that they changed. The income limits go
up with the annual adjustment. The net
monthly figure for a single person
household sits just over $1,300 right
now. And the figure for two people is
just under $1,700
under the numbers described here. Those
are the numbers the current file was
measured against. They are replaced when
the new standards take effect with the
adjustment tied to the cost of living.
And there is a second change happening
at the same time. The deductions go up
as well. The standard deduction is taken
from household income before the rest of
the calculation is completed and that
amount changes with the annual
standards. The shelter calculation
changes too for households subject to
the shelter cap. Then there is the
benefit itself. The maximum monthly
amount is recalculated every June and
takes effect on the 1st of October. So
this is not one isolated number moving
on the calendar. The income standard,
the deductions used in the calculation,
and the maximum benefit are all part of
the yearly update. The important part is
what happens next. The state office does
not automatically reopen every closed
file just because October arrives. A
case can remain closed until the
household contacts the agency and starts
a new application or we uses whatever
review process is available for the
existing decision. In practical terms,
the person who needs the benefit may
have to be the person who puts the case
back in motion. A new application after
the 1st of October is not simply the
same application sitting on a desk. It
is a household being measured under a
new set of standards. So, what should a
household actually do with this
information? First, gather the medical
spending before you apply.
Do not wait until someone asks you for a
receipt that you threw away 3 months
ago. Keep the pharmacy receipts
together. Keep the Medicare premium
notice. Keep dental bills, vision
expenses, hearing related costs,
insurance premiums, transportation to
medical appointments, and other
qualifying medical spending in one
place. If an over-the-counter medicine
was recommended by a doctor to keep the
documentation that connects the expense
to that recommendation, one envelope is
usually enough to create order out of a
pile of small expenses. The point is not
that one receipt magically guarantees
eligibility. The point is that every
qualifying expense the agency is allowed
to consider needs to be documented and
reported. A household that reports
nothing can be measured very differently
from a household with the same income
that documents its allowable expenses.
Second, apply through your own state
agency. Do not assume that a federal
information page is the place where your
application will actually be processed.
The federal program establishes the
framework, but states administer
applications and cases. Use the official
state channel that handles SNAP in your
state. Third, say the important fact out
loud when you apply. Tell the office
that someone in the household is 60 or
older. Then ask for the rules for an
older household to be applied to the
file. Do not assume the person on the
other end of the phone can see every
detail you have in your head. Give them
the information that changes the
calculation. Ask whether the medical
expense deduction has been taken. Ask
whether the Medicare premium has been
included, if applicable.
Ask whether the housing costs were
counted and whether the shelter
calculation was handled under the rule
that applies to an older household.
Those questions are not clever tricks
and they are not aggressive. They are
simply questions about how your case was
calculated. The form may not ask them in
the exact words you would use, so you
have to provide the facts yourself.
Fourth, pay attention to timing. An
application filed after the 1st of
October is measured under the standards
that apply during that new period rather
than automatically using the numbers
that turned you down before. If your
household is sitting close to the line
right now, the calendar may change the
arithmetic even if your income is not
changed. That does not mean everyone who
was denied will automatically qualify in
October. It means the old decision
should not be treated as a permanent
answer when the standards in your
circumstances can be different. There is
another part people often overlook. What
happens after the form goes in. Waiting
is where many households give up. You
submit the application, days pass,
nobody calls, and you begin to think
that nothing is happening. But there is
a process behind that silence. Your
state office generally has a standard
processing period, often up to 30 days,
to process an application and issue a
decision with faster handling available
for households that meet the criteria
for expedited service. There is normally
an interview as part of the process,
often conducted by telephone, depending
on the state's procedure. That interview
is another opportunity to make sure the
case worker has the information needed
to calculate the household correctly and
keep the date you submitted the
application. That date matters. When
benefits are approved, the effective
date is generally tied to the
application date under the applicable
rules rather than simply starting on the
day the approval notice arrives. That is
one reason it can be important not to
delay an application while waiting for
the perfect moment. One last piece, and
this matters if you have already been
turned down. If the denial notice is
recent, look at the date printed on that
notice. There is a window to challenge
an adverse decision and the appeal
period is counted according to the rules
stated in the notice. Do not assume the
clock begins when you happen to open the
envelope. Read the notice carefully
because a deadline can be tied to the
date on the notice or the date the
agency considers the notice received
depending on the applicable procedure.
Appeals can go through several levels.
The handbook lays them out one at a time
along with the language and steps used
at each stage. If you believe an
allowable expense was missed, the wrong
household rule was used, or the case was
decided using information that was
incomplete, those are the kinds of
details you would want to identify and
document during a review process. So, go
back to the four things we covered. The
first is the income test. If someone in
the household is 60 or older, the gross
income test that applies to many
households does not work the same way
for that household. The second is
medical spending.
Qualifying out-ofpocket medical costs
above the applicable amount can reduce
the income that is counted, which means
documentation can change the
calculation. The third is resources. The
federal resource figures described here
are different for households with an
older member and states may use
different limits or policies. Your state
rules are the ones that determine what
happens to your actual case. The fourth
is shelter. Rent, mortgage interest,
property taxes, utilities, and other
qualifying shelter expenses can affect
the calculation. And the treatment of
excess shelter costs is different for at
households with an old a member. Then
put the date beside those four points.
The annual standards change on the 1st
of October. That means an old number you
saw online, an old denial you received
months ago, or an old calculation
someone made for you should not
automatically be treated as the answer
for the new period. If you are going to
do only one thing after watching this,
take the denial letter or your last
application information and put it
beside a fresh list of your current
income, medical expenses, housing costs,
and resources. Then contact the state
agency that actually handles SNAP and
ask them to evaluate the household under
the rules that apply to an older
household. You do not need to guess your
eligibility from a headline. You do not
need to rely on a neighbor's income or a
number from an old website. And you
should not assume that one denial closes
the door forever. The rules are written
in numbers, deductions, dates, and
procedures. Your job is to make sure the
facts of your household actually make it
into that calculation. If your state
office has never once heard from you
because some number on a website
convinced you not to bother, this week
is a good one to change

title: 7 Assets Seniors May Be Able to Protect From Creditors and the IRS

segments.text: There are seven things the law says no
creditor, no debt collector, and no
nursing home can take from you after the
age of 65, no matter how much you owe.
And the biggest one on that list is the
single thing most seniors lie awake at
night afraid of losing, the roof over
their head worth hundreds of thousands
of dollars. Think about that for a
moment. Not a loophole, not a trick, not
some gray area a clever lawyer whispers
about behind a closed door. Seven
categories of money and property that
federal and state law and plain black
and white put behind a wall that the
people coming after you cannot climb
over. And the reason almost no senior
knows the full list is simple. There's
an entire industry built on making you
afraid, on making you believe that one
lawsuit, one hospital bill, one long
stay in a care home, and everything you
spent a lifetime building is gone. That
fear is profitable. The truth is not.
Before I go 1 in further, I want you to
hold on to a single promise because it
is the whole reason to stay till the
very end. There is one thing on this
list that is protected more fiercely
than all the others. The thing you are
most afraid a nursing home or Medicaid
will swallow. And I'm going to show you
exactly why in most cases it cannot be
taken from you while you are alive. And
the specific rule that keeps it in your
family. It is the last one I will name
because it is the most important. And it
only makes sense once you understand the
six that come before it. So stay with me
all the way through.
Let me start with the one almost
everyone half knows because it is the
doorway to understanding all the rest.
Most seniors have a vague sense that
social security is somehow safe, that
nobody can just take it. That instinct
is correct and it is written directly
into federal law. Under a section of the
United States Code, social security
benefits are protected from execution,
levy, attachment, garnishment, and any
other legal process. In plain English,
that means a credit card company, a
hospital, a debt collector, or any
private creditor who takes you to court
and wins a judgment against you still
cannot garnish your social security
check. They can win the case and still
walk away with nothing from that
benefit. It sits behind a federal wall.
But, you have to know the honest
exceptions because half a truth in this
area can hurt you. That same protection
does not stop everyone. The federal
government can still reach your social
security for a few specific debts. The
IRS can levy up to 15% of your benefit
for unpaid federal taxes. Your check can
be tapped for child support or alimony
you owe. And a defaulted federal student
loan can reach it. So, the honest rule
is this, against a private creditor,
your social security is a fortress.
Against the federal government itself,
for those few specific debts, it is not.
Knowing which is which is the difference
between panicking over a threat that is
empty and acting on one that is real.
Let me make that real with a person
because a rule floats away, but a face
stays with you.
Picture a woman I will call Ruth, 71
years old, living on a social security
check of $1,900 a month and not a dollar
more. An old credit card balance from a
hard year finally catches up to her. The
company sues and it wins a judgment
against her in court. The letters start
arriving, thick with threats, warning
that they will take what she owes, and
Ruth stops sleeping. She is certain that
next month the check will not come, that
she will have to choose between her
heart medication and her electric bill.
But, the first of the month arrives and
so does her check, whole, exactly as it
always has. That judgment has no power
over her social security. The creditor
spent good money to win a case that
bought them nothing from that benefit.
Ruth spent 3 months of her life in
terror over a threat the law had already
answered before it was ever made.
That is the real cost of not knowing
this. It is not only the money, it is
the fear that eats the years you have
left over dangers that were never
coming. And here is the second thing
they cannot take. And this one surprises
almost everyone because it happens
automatically and no one ever told you
it exists. When money is deposited into
your bank account, you might think that
if a creditor freezes the account,
everything in it is frozen, including
your benefits. That is not true. Federal
rules require your bank, the moment it
receives a garnishment order, to
automatically protect the last two
months of federal benefits that were
directly deposited into that account.
Two full months of Social Security or
Veterans benefits or a federal pension
are walled off before the bank hands a
single dollar to the creditor. You do
not file anything. You do not call
anyone. The bank is required by law to
do it for you. But, and this matters, it
only works for benefits that arrive by
direct deposit, which is one more reason
every senior watching should have their
benefits deposited straight into the
account and never taken by paper check.
Therefore, the money the government
sends you is protected both while it
travels and once it lands. And that
brings us to the third thing they cannot
touch, which for many of you is the
largest pile of money you will ever
have, your retirement savings. Money
held in an employer plan, a traditional
pension, or a workplace retirement
account carries a powerful federal
shield written into the law that governs
those plans. That shield means the funds
generally cannot be assigned to a
creditor or seized to pay a judgment,
even in bankruptcy. A creditor can win a
lawsuit against you and still cannot
force open your workplace retirement
account. Picture a man who spent 40
years paying into a plan and built it up
A lawsuit lands on him at 70, and he is
terrified that account will be drained
overnight. In the ordinary case, it
cannot be.
That federal wall was built on purpose,
so that a person could not be stripped
of the very savings meant to carry them
through old age. But, there is a
distinction inside this you need to hear
plainly because it is where people get
caught. An individual retirement
account, an IRA, is protected a little
differently from a workplace plan. In
bankruptcy, your IRA is shielded up to a
very high federal limit, currently more
a ceiling that is adjusted every few
years. Outside of bankruptcy, how well
your IRA is protected from a regular
creditor depends on the state you live
in. And some states guard it completely,
while others guard it less. So, the
workplace plan is the stronger fortress,
and the IRA is strong, but with a
footnote. Both are far safer than the
ordinary savings account most people
fear for, but the exact wall around your
IRA is one worth checking for your own
state before you ever need it.
Now, I am Mark, and on this channel we
do exactly one thing. We take the
protections that were written to shield
you, the ones buried under legal jargon
and quiet neglect, and we drag them back
into the daylight where you can actually
use them. And this list today may be the
most important I have ever handed you,
because it is not about clawing back one
small fee. It is about the wall around
everything you have left. You know three
of the seven now. Let me give you the
other four, and remember, the biggest
and most protected one of all is still
coming.
Now, before I give you the fourth, I
want to stop for one moment and raise
the stakes on everything you are
hearing, because it is easy to nod along
and forget why this matters so urgently
right now. The people who profit from
your fear are not sitting still. Every
single year, more seniors are frightened
into signing away their homes, cashing
out protected retirement accounts, and
handing over money they never had to
surrender, because a phone call scared
them, or a smooth salesman promised to
shield them from a danger that was never
real in the first place. The protections
I am naming today are only as strong as
your willingness to stand on them. A
wall does you no good at all if a
stranger can talk you into walking
around it. So, as we move into the
biggest protections on this list, hold
on to this single thought. Knowing the
rule is step one. Refusing to be
frightened out of it is step two. And
step two is the one that actually keeps
the house in your name. The fourth thing
they cannot take is the set of benefits
earned by the men and women who served
this country. Veterans benefits carry
their own federal protection, written in
plain terms. They are not assignable.
They are exempt from the claims of
creditors, and they are exempt from
taxation. That means veterans disability
compensation
and it is not counted as taxable income
at all. A veteran living on that
compensation does not report it on a tax
return the way wages are reported, and a
debt collector cannot garnish it. And
because those benefits usually arrive by
direct deposit, they also get that same
2-month automatic bank protection I
described a moment ago. So, for a
veteran, the protection stacks, one wall
on top of another, exactly as it should
for someone who already paid their
price.
Therefore, the money you earned in
service is guarded coming and going, and
that leads us to the fifth thing they
cannot take. One that arrives at the
hardest moment a family ever faces. When
a person dies and leaves a life
insurance payout to a spouse or a child,
that death benefit is generally not
counted as taxable income. A $100,000
policy pays the beneficiary the full
A quarter million-dollar policy pays a
full quarter million dollars. The person
receiving it does not report it as
income and does not lose a slice of it
to federal income tax. In a season of
grief, when a widow is trying to figure
out how to keep the lights on, that
whole untouched check can be the
difference between keeping the home and
losing it. And here is a second layer
many never learn.
The cash value that builds up inside a
life insurance policy or annuity while
you are still living is protected from
creditors in many states. So, the very
savings tucked inside that policy can
sit behind a wall, too. It varies from
state to state, so it is worth
confirming where you live. But for a
great many seniors, that money is far
safer than they ever realized.
I have watched families sit frozen over
a life insurance letter afraid to even
open it, whispering to each other that
the government is going to take a third
of it, so they had better set money
aside for the tax bill. And they set
aside money they did not need to set
aside, and they lived smaller than they
had to in the hardest year of their
lives over a tax that was never going to
arrive. So, hear me clearly. In the
ordinary case, when a policy pays out
because someone has died, that money
reaches the beneficiary whole, and the
savings built up inside it can be
shielded, too. Telling the people you
love that simple truth while you still
can is one way you can lift off their
shoulders before you ever go.
Now, lean in because we have reached the
sixth, and it sounds humble, but it
protects your dignity in the worst case.
Both federal and state exemption laws
reserve a floor of basic property that
no creditor and no bankruptcy can strip
from you. Your household goods and
furniture, your clothing, the tools you
use for work, and equity in a car
protected under federal bankruptcy law
at around $4,450,
with many states protecting far more
than that. The reason this matters is
simple and human. The law does not allow
a creditor to leave an older person with
nothing sitting in an empty house with
no way to get to a doctor. There is a
line beneath which they cannot reach, a
reserved set of the basics of a life,
and most people never know that line is
drawn in their favor until the day they
desperately need it. Think of what that
means in practice.
A creditor cannot come into your home
and haul away your bed, your kitchen
table, your refrigerator, or the coat on
your back. They cannot take the reliable
car you need to get to the pharmacy and
the doctor. The law treats those things
not as prizes for a creditor to seize,
but as the floor of a dignified life
that a person is entitled to keep. And
in most states, that floor is higher
than the federal minimum, protecting
more of your property, not less. So,
even in the very worst case, the picture
sure of an older person left with
absolutely nothing is not what the law
allows. It draws a line, and it draws it
on your side. But, everything I have
named so far, the benefits, the
retirement accounts, the life insurance,
the basic property, all of it circles
around the one thing you have been
waiting for, the thing you are most
afraid of, and this is the promise I
made you at the very start. The seventh
thing they cannot take is your home, and
I need you to hear this clearly because
the fear around it has been sold to
seniors for years, and it is mostly a
lie. The story goes like this. You get
old, you need long-term care, you go
into a nursing home, and the nursing
home takes your house. So, families
panic. They rush to give the house away.
They make expensive mistakes, all to
stop something that in most cases, the
law already stops for them. Here is the
truth. A nursing home is a private
business. It bills you for care. It
cannot take your house. It has no power
to seize your property.
The real question is about Medicaid, the
program that pays for most long-term
care. And even there, the protections
are far stronger than the fear suggests.
While you are alive, your home is what
the rules call an exempt asset for
Medicaid purposes. Up to a home equity
limit that runs, depending on your
state, from roughly $700,000
to over $1 million.
That means you can qualify for the help
you need and still keep your home. And
the protection is even stronger than
that. If your spouse lives in that home,
or a child under 21, or a blind or
disabled child of any age, the home is
fully exempt with no dollar limit at
all. Your husband or wife is not going
to be put out on the street so the state
can be paid. The law specifically
protects the spouse who still lives
there. So, while you are alive, in the
ordinary case, that house stays yours.
Let me put a face on this, too, because
this is the one that matters most.
Picture a couple, married 50 years, in
the house they raised their children in.
A house worth maybe $400,000 today that
they bought for almost nothing decades
ago. The husband has a stroke and needs
long-term care, and a well-meaning
relative tells the wife she has to sell
the house immediately or the state will
take it. She is 78 years old and
terrified, and she nearly signs a paper
handing the home to someone else in a
panic. But, she does not have to sell,
and she must not sign anything. Because
her husband needs Medicaid to pay for
his care, does not mean the home is
lost. She lives there. As the spouse
living in that home, her house is fully
exempt with no dollar limit at all while
she is alive. The very thing the
relative told her to give away in fear
was the thing the law was already
holding safe in her hands.
Therefore, the thing you feared most is
in fact the most protected item on this
entire list, and the only piece left to
understand is what happens after you are
gone, because that is where the last of
the fear lives. After death, a state may
seek repayment for the long-term care
Medicaid paid through something called a
state recovery, and that can involve the
home. But even here, the law is full of
doors left open on purpose. There is no
recovery while a surviving spouse is
alive. There is no recovery while a
child under 21 or a blind or disabled
child is living. And there are specific
protections for a child who moved in and
cared for you and kept you out of a
nursing home for years. And for a
sibling with an ownership interest who
lived in the home. These are not
accidents. They are protections Congress
built into the law, and they exist
precisely so that the home can stay in
the family.
The tragedy is that most families never
learn them until after a crisis, when
the expensive mistakes have already been
made. Learn them before, and in most
cases the house is exactly where it
belongs.
Now, let me be honest with you about
what this video can do and what it
cannot, because you deserve straight
talk. Everything I have told you is real
federal and state law, but every one of
these seven protections has conditions,
and none of them is truly automatic in
the sense that you can ignore it and
assume it works. The bank protection
happens on its own, yes, but only for
direct deposit. The homestead protection
and the Medicaid rules depend heavily on
your own state and your own numbers, and
states differ enormously. What I have
given you is the map, the knowledge that
the walls exist and roughly where they
stand. What I cannot do in one video is
fill in the exact form for your county,
your state's exact homestead figure, or
your family's specific situation. For
the people who want that, the exact
forms, the state-by-state numbers, and
the full checklist of every protection,
I put it all together in the Senior
Exempt Playbook, and the link is in the
description.
But you do not need to buy anything to
act on what you learned today. You just
need to stop being afraid of threats
that the law already blocks, and stop
confirming the ones that are real. So,
here is exactly what to do in order.
First, make sure every federal benefit
you receive, your Social Security, your
veteran's benefits, your pension,
arrives by direct deposit into your bank
account, because that single choice
unlocks the automatic 2-month protection
we talked about. Second, if a debt
collector ever threatens to take your
Social Security, your retirement
account, or your veteran's benefits,
know that against a private creditor,
those are protected, and do not let a

They were not required to call you. They
