became possible. And millions of account
holders, most of them over 60, had no
idea that the rules they thought
governed their money had been quietly
rewritten. This is not speculation. The
changes are documented. The policy
updates are real. They're active right
now at banks across the country. And the
reason you've probably not heard about
any of them in plain clear language is
that nobody with an interest in your
understanding sat you down and explained
what changed, what it costs, and what
you need to do about it. That is exactly
what is about to happen in the next few
minutes. Three rules, all of them
already in effect. All of them affecting
your checking account right now if you
are over 60. By the time we are done,
you will know what each one does, how it
can hurt you if you stay unaware, and
the specific steps you can take this
week to protect yourself. Before we get
into the rules, you need to understand
what triggered all of them in the first
place. Because if you understand the
cause, the rules stop feeling random.
Elder financial exploitation is now the
fastest growing category of financial
crime in the United States. According to
the Federal Trade Commission's most
recent protecting older consumers
report, adults over 60 reported fraud
losses of approximately 2.4 billion in
2024 alone. That number has quadrupled
since 2020. The losses come from scams,
from wire fraud, from fake investment
schemes, and critically from what
regulators call undue influence.
Situations where a family member, a
caregiver, or an outside party pressures
an older account holder into making
transactions that benefit someone else
at their expense. The Consumer Financial
Protection Bureau has documented these
losses extensively. The Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation has issued updated
guidance to banks multiple times in
recent years, specifically focusing on
how financial institutions should handle
accounts belonging to older customers.
That guidance is not legally binding the
way a federal statute is, but banks
follow it anyway because the alternative
is a compliance examination that creates
enormous problems for the institution.
The result has been a wave of internal
policy changes at banks large and small.
New monitoring systems, new protocols
for reviewing transactions by holder
account holders, new requirements around
who can be contacted about your account,
new fee structures following a major
federal regulatory fight over overdraft
rules that ended with Congress stepping
in and reversing the protection that had
been created. None of these changes
arrived with a press conference or a
news segment that explained them in
language a normal person could act on.
They arrived buried in paperwork. So let
us go through all three one at a time in
plain English. Rule number one is called
the trusted contact requirement. Of the
three rules, this is the most visible
one because many banks are now actively
asking customers to designate a trusted
contact either during a branch visit
through an online account update or
during account renewal. When a bank asks
you for a trusted contact, what they're
asking for is the name and phone number
of a person they are authorized to reach
out to if they have a concern about your
account. That is the version they will
describe to you. What they will not
describe in equal detail is exactly what
that means in practice. Under Federal
Rule 4512, financial institutions are
required to make reasonable efforts to
collect trusted contact information from
customers. For brokerage and investment
accounts, this is a formal regulatory
requirement with no exceptions. For
checking accounts at commercial banks,
it remains guidance rather than statute,
but the vast majority of major
institutions have adopted it as standard
practice. The bank is authorized to
contact your trusted contact if they
believe you may be experiencing
diminished mental capacity, if they
suspect you're being financially
exploited by someone, or if they have
been unable to reach you and have a
concern about activity on your account.
Critically, under FINRA rule 21-65,
financial institutions are also
permitted to place a temporary hold on a
dispersement of funds from your account
for up to 15 business days if they
reasonably believe financial
exploitation has occurred or is being
attempted. During the hold, they can
notify your trusted contact. All of that
can happen without your explicit
permission at the moment it occurs. Here
is the catch that most people never hear
about. The trusted contact has zero
legal authority over your account. They
cannot make transactions. They cannot
override your decisions. They cannot
instruct the bank to do anything, but
they can be told that the bank is a
concern and that conversation can happen
before anyone calls you to explain what
is going on. The bank makes its own
internal assessment of your transaction
patterns and decides on its own terms
when to make the call. If the person you
named as your trusted contact is someone
who does not know your financial
situation, someone who tends to panic or
someone who was never told they were
listed, the result of that phone call is
chaos rather than protection. A routine
transaction you made with completely
clean documentation can set off a family
emergency that never needed to exist,
and you end up spending your time and
energy managing someone else's anxiety
instead of your own estate business.
Here's the real upside, though. If you
take control of this process yourself,
the trusted contact policy can work
entirely in your favor. The mistake
people make most often with this rule is
one of two things. Either they name
someone without ever telling that person
or they let the bank prompt them to name
someone in a stressful moment without
thinking through who is actually the
right choice. The right trusted contact
is someone who understands your finances
well enough not to panic if a bank calls
who knows they have been named and who
knows exactly what a trusted contact is
and is not authorized to do this week.
Call your bank or log into your account
and ask two direct questions. First, do
you currently have a trusted contact on
file for this account? and if so, who
was listed? Second, when was that
information last updated? If no trusted
contact is on file, request the form and
set the terms yourself on your own
timeline, not the banks. Take the
conversation off the table before the
bank decides to have it for you. Rule
number two is the one running quietly
right now inside your bank system every
time you make a transaction. Banks have
viewed automated monitoring software for
decades. What changed over the past
several years is the specificity of what
triggers a human review when the account
holder is over 60. internal compliance
guidance updated at major institutions
added what banks internally call
enhanced monitoring parameters for older
account holders. This is not publicly
disclosed. You will not find it on your
bank's website. It lives in training
documents and compliance frameworks that
banks are under no obligation to share
with you. In practical terms, what this
means is that your account may sit under
a lower threshold for triggering the
human review than a younger account
holder with an identical balance in
history. It's a transaction that
generates an automated flag and nothing
else in a 35-year-old's account may
generate an actual hold or call back
requirement to yours. This is entirely
legal. The Equal Credit Opportunity Act
prohibits age discrimination and lending
and credit decisions, but it does not
prohibit applying enhanced monitoring
protocols as a protective measure for
older account holders. The specific
behaviors that trigger a flag under
these systems include a withdrawal
significantly above your historical
average, a wire transfer sent to an
account that has never received money
from you before, multiple cash
withdrawals within a short window, a
sudden shift in your deposit pattern in

falls outside your normal pattern. Any
single one of these may generate a
monitoring note in your file. two or

almost certainly generate a hold that
freezes access to your funds until the
bank is satisfied. As of January 2026,
the situation has become more
significant because over half of US
states have now enacted what are called
hold laws, legislation that gives banks
explicit legal protection to delay
dispersements when they have reasonable
cause to believe a senior account holder

American Bankers Association, nearly 60%
of bankers now report feeling confident
in their legal immunity when they freeze
a transaction involving an older account

incentive to hold first and ask
questions later has increased, not
decreased. The bank faces less legal
risk by freezing your money than by

the situation. This brings up one of the
most important and least understood
dangers connected to this rule. When

large transactions, the instinct for
many is to break a large deposit or

drawing attention. That instinct has a
name under federal law structuring.
Under title 31 of the United States
Code, section 5324,
deliberately splitting a financial

deliberately broke a transaction into
pieces to avoid scrutiny, that is an

prove your innocence while your money

Never structure a transaction for any
reason. If the money is legal, deposit
it in a single transaction with
documentation prepared in advance. The
documentation step is the most
protective thing you can do under this
rule. If you are planning a transaction
that is significantly larger than your
typical activity, whether that is an
inheritance coming in, proceeds from a
property sale, a large gift, or a
consolidation from another account,
write a onepage summary of the source

from, the amount, and your contact

The currency transaction report that

completely different situation and can
cost you your money, your time, and
months of your life while you sort it

the one most account holders have not

customers with a typical household that

In early 2025, Congress introduced

unless specifically authorized by future
legislation. JP Morgan Chase and Wells
Fargo each collected approximately $1

According to an analysis by the National
Consumer Law Center, the CFOPB rule is
gone. Overdraft fees at large banks are
no longer count. And the trend that had

Higher thresholds for fee waiverss,

branchb-based banks is now around $13.95
per month according to 2026 data for
money rates. That is roughly $167 per

If you're paying a monthly maintenance

whether they offer senior checking
account with no monthly fee and no

Complete legitimate transactions
honestly and maintain appropriate

If you want another person to have

account. In fact, the goal is the

The goal is to replace uncertainty with

unusual activity.

avoid an interruption. The story sounds
real, which is exactly why it works. The
DWP will not text you asking for your
bank details. If a call sounds official,
hang up, wait a minute, and ring back on
a number you looked up yourself. If
someone claims to be your bank, dial 159
and you will be put through to your real
bank. Forward scam texts to 7726.
And if you are ever tricked into sending
money, call your bank the moment you
realize. Most victims of this kind of
scam can now be reimbursed up to 85,000
pounds if they report it within 13
months. But the faster you call, the
more likely the money is still sitting
there. Checking your pension is free.
Never pay a company a fee to recover a
missing payment, and be wary of anyone
who offers to do it for a percentage.
Now I want to be direct. If you have
done your banking the same way for long
break 20 years, I am not here to
frighten you. I am here to show you that
a few small changes made on a calm
afternoon can stop a bad morning ever
happening.
So here is what I want you to do, and
this is the part to write down. Step
one. Read the name on the account your
pension goes into. Then read the name on
your last letter from the DWP. Make sure
they match. If you changed your name
after a marriage or divorce, make sure
the bank and the DWP have the same one.
Step two. Turn on an alert in your
banking app, or ask your bank for a text
for every payment coming in. That way
you know the same morning if a payment
is missing or held. Step three. If you
ever change banks, open the new account
first, use it for a month or two, then
move your pension right after a payment
arrives, never in in days just before
one. Step four. write one page at your
kitchen table, your payment day, your
amount, your bank's fraud number, the
Pension Service number 08 long break 100
731 0469, and the name of one person
besides you who can see your accounts.
If anything ever goes wrong, that one
page turns a frightening morning into
three phone calls. This is the part I
want to stay with you after this video
is over. The DWP is not your enemy, and
neither is your bank. Most of these
checks exist to protect people exactly
like you, but the systems are enormous,
they make mistakes, and they do not
explain themselves. The only person who
sees the whole journey of your money is
you, and the only way to spot a problem
early is to look. So, before you close
this video, do three things. Read the
name on your account, write down the
Pension Service number, and send this
video to one person you love who gets a
state pension, especially a parent whose
son or daughter helps with the bills, or
someone who has just changed banks
because their branch closed. One share
takes 10 seconds, and it could stop a
payment going missing. If you want the
whole journey in one place, the story,
the rules in plain language, the exact
figures, the step-by-step plan, the
phone scripts, the watch out warnings,
and the do this today list, it is all in
chapters 21, 24, and 25 of my book, The
UK Pension and Benefits Playbook.
Chapter 26 gives you a 7-day plan to get
it done. The link is in the description,
and it is the only link there. Nothing
in this video replaces the official
guidance on gov.uk, and the book does
not either. This has been education, not
financial advice. I am Arthur Penrose.
Look after yourselves, and I will see
you in the next one.

title: The HMRC Doesn’t Want You to Understand This New Bank Rule

segments.text: That is the amount HMRC says it will
always leave across your bank accounts
if it ever takes money from them.
And this week, the Chancellor may change
the rules about when it starts. Let me
tell you about a man I will call Bill.
He is 72, a retired caretaker, and he
owed HMRC 1,350
pounds from an old tax bill that nobody
had ever explained to him. He left four
letters unopened. He did not answer the
door to a visit. Then his bank account
was put on hold. Bill had not stolen
anything. He had simply ignored the
post. I will tell you how his story
ended and the one phone call that would
have changed it before this video
finishes.
Before we go further, type your age in
the comments and subscribe if you have
not already.
I read every comment and it tells me
what to cover next. My name is Arthur
Penhaligon and I read the rules so you
do not have to. If you want the forms
and phone scripts in one place, my book,
the UK Pension and Benefits Playbook is
in the description. So go and check it
out.
Everything here comes from gov.uk,
HMRC's own published briefing, the House
of Commons Library, and news reports
that I will name as reports.
This is education, not advice about your
own money. Here is what you will leave
with. What HMRC can already do to your
bank account today. What is only
reported and not yet a rule. The
American 10,000 pound myth that
frightens people over here. The one
sentence to say if a letter or a frozen
account ever lands. And why the real
danger this week is not HMRC at all. It
is a phone call from someone pretending
to be HMRC. Let me start with the myth
because it explains why so many people
are afraid of the wrong thing.
Millions of people in Britain believe
there is a magic number, 10,000 pounds,
and that the moment you cross it, a form
is fired off to the government. That is
an American rule. We do not have it.
There is no automatic report in the
United Kingdom triggered by an amount of
cash.
What we have instead is more
discretionary. Banks and building
societies must report to the Crime
Agency if they suspect money may be the
proceeds of crime. It is called a
suspicious activity report. goes to the
National Crime Agency, not to HMRC.
And there is no minimum amount.
A report can follow £200 if the behavior
looks wrong, and a well-explained
£50,000 can pass without a murmur. It is
the story the money tells, not the size
of it. I will come back to that because
it is where honest people get caught.
But first, the rule that this video is
really about and the one safeguard most
people do not know exists. HMRC already
has a power called direct recovery of
debts. It lets HMRC instruct your bank
or building society to pay unpaid tax
straight from your account, including a
cash ISA, without going to court first.
It sounds frightening, so let me give
you the safeguards one at a time because
they matter.
First, the debt must be £1,000 or more.
Second, it must be an established debt,
meaning it is due and you have no appeal
still open. Third, before your case is
even considered, HMRC says you will get
a face-to-face visit from its agents. A
letter is not enough.
Fourth, anyone it identifies as
vulnerable is not supposed to be
considered at all. Fifth, HMRC must be
able to take the debt and still leave at
least £5,000 across your accounts
combined. If you have less than that in
total, this power cannot be used. And
sixth, when HMRC puts a hold on the
money, you have 30 days to object and
nothing is transferred during those 30
days. If your objection is rejected, you
can appeal to the county court and
hardship is one of the grounds. In
England, Wales, and Northern Ireland,
that is the process. Scotland has a
separate route. A joint account matters,
too. Anyone with an interest in an
account, including a joint holder, can
object if they think the money is not
the debtor's. Now, why does this exist?
HMRC says it is for people who can
afford to pay and choose not to. That is
the honest answer and it is also why
Bill was in danger, not because he was
rich, because he went silent. So, what
do you do with that? Action number one.
If you owe HMRC anything, ring them
before they ring you. Ask for a payment
plan. HMRC's own guidance says that if
you cannot pay or you dispute the bill,
you should contact them to talk about it
and they will discuss an affordable time
to pay arrangement. Action number two.
Open every letter from HMRC the day it
arrives, even the ones that look boring.
Every letter has a date on it and your
rights are counted from that date.
And if a hold is ever placed on your
money, do three things the same day.
Write down the date on the notice, ring
HMRC and ask how to object
and get free help from Citizens Advice
or from Tax Help for Older People, a
charity that gives free tax advice to
older people on lower incomes. Here is
the part that is making the headlines.
On Sunday, The Independent, quoting The
Times, reported that Chancellor John
Healey may announce a change in the
budget on the 28th of October. The
report says the government is
considering wider deductions from
current and savings accounts for people
who repeatedly ignore HMRC payment
requests and possibly a lower minimum
debt before the power can be used. The
Treasury told The Times it would not
comment on rumor, speculation, or
proposals before a budget.
So, let me be very clear. That is a
reported plan. It is not a confirmed
rule. The background is real, though.
The National Audit Office has reported
HMRC is chasing tax debt of about £43.8
billion,
which is why it wants sharper tools. No
new threshold, no start date, and no
final set of safeguards has been
announced.
But there is something official behind
the speculation.
In June, HMRC launched a consultation
called Tackling Lower Value Tax Debts.
It asked for views on extending direct
recovery to smaller debts for people who
can afford to pay but keep ignoring
HMRC. The idea was to collect manageable
monthly installments rather than one
lump sum after normal contact had
failed. The consultation said debts in
scope were not expected to be more than
including added charges and penalties,
and that the final limits had not been
decided. It closed on the 28th of
August, and the government says it will
publish a summary of the responses later
this year.
So when the Chancellor stands up, here
is what to listen for.
Who qualifies? The minimum debt. How
affordability is assessed. What notice
you get. How you object. Until you hear
those five things, anything you read
online about the new rule is a guess.
Now, who does this realistically touch
among people over 65?
HMRC expects about 9.58 million people
over state pension age to pay income tax
this year. So this is not a small group.
Most of you will never see this power
used on you. If your tax is collected
through your tax code and you keep your
letters, you are in the safe group.
Trouble tends to start in four places. A
small private pension that brings you
just over the personal allowance.
Savings income that pushes you over your
allowance. An old self-employed tax
bill. Or a tax credit overpayment that
nobody explained. In every case, the
pattern is the same.
A bill, a letter that goes unopened, a
reminder, another reminder, and then a
visit.
At every one of those steps, a single
phone call can stop it.
So here is the five-minute check. Log in
to your personal tax account on gov.uk.
Look at your tax code and ask why if it
has changed. Look for any letter called
a tax calculation and any demand called
a simple assessment. If you see a figure
you do not recognize, ring HMRC and ask
them to explain it. Do not pay in panic
and do not ignore it either. The middle
path is a phone call. Here is the
sentence to say. I want to arrange a
payment plan and this is what I can
afford each month. It is that simple. It
starts a conversation. And a
conversation is what this whole system
is designed to wait for.
Now back to what I promised, the other
bank power, because people mix the two
up and the difference changes what you
should do. When a bank suspects money is
not clean, it files a suspicious
activity report to the National Crime
Agency. Most reports go nowhere. They
sit in a database as intelligence,
but a few lead to something far harder
to deal with,
an account freezing order.
Police, the National Crime Agency, and
HMRC can all apply for one. They apply
to a magistrate's court, not a Crown
Court. They need only reasonable grounds
to suspect the money may come from
unlawful conduct. They do not need a
charge or a conviction. They can apply
without telling you. The account must
hold more than a minimum amount, and an
order can last up to two years in total.
The first you know of it may be a card
declined at the supermarket, and your
bank will not be able to explain why.
Tipping off a customer about a suspicion
report is a criminal offense for the
bank worker, so the kind person on the
phone is gagged, not unhelpful. So what
puts honest people at risk? One thing
above all, splitting money into pieces.
3,000 on Monday, 2,000 on Thursday,
another three next week at different
branches. It feels careful. The software
sees a shape, and the shape it hunts for
is somebody hiding. It cannot tell that
you sold a caravan. So never split a
lump to avoid attention. Pay it in once
with paperwork.
A receipt for the car, a letter from the
solicitor for the inheritance, a note
from your daughter for the boiler. And
if the cashier asks, say one sentence.
This is the sale of my car, and I have
the receipt. Say it calmly and bring the
paper. Now the warning I most want you
to hear this week because it is where
people actually lose money. Whenever
there is news about HMRC and bank
accounts, scammers move first. You get a
call or a text. It says HMRC is about to
freeze your account or has already, and
you must move your money to a safe
account or pay a fee by gift cards or
read out a code. Every word of that is
false. The real process starts with
letters and a face-to-face visit.
HMRC will never ring you and tell you to
move your money to protect it, and
neither will your bank.
If a call like that arrives, put the
phone down. Then find the number
yourself on gov.uk or on the back of
your bank card and ring that. If you are
unsure whether a message is real, log
into your personal tax account yourself
through gov.uk, not through a link in a
text, and see whether a bill or message
appears there.
So let me bring it together.
HMRC can already take unpaid tax of
£1,000 or more from your accounts, but
only after letters and a visit, only if
£5,000 stays behind and with 30 days to
object.
A wider version has been reported ahead
of the budget, but nothing is confirmed.
The American £10,000 rule does not exist
here. Suspicious activity reports go to
the National Crime Agency, and splitting
money is the mistake that gets honest
people frozen. And the real risk this
week is a scam call.
Here is your folder, and it takes 5
minutes. One envelope for HMRC letters
kept in date order,
a note of where any large deposit came
from with the receipt, your tax code
written down with the date you checked
it, and the phone number for HMRC copied
from gov.uk stuck on the fridge. And
Bill?
He finally picked up the phone. He told
HMRC what he could afford, agreed
monthly payments, and with more than
£5,000 left in his account, nothing was
taken. One phone call instead of four
unopened letters, and he kept the notice
dated in his folder
in case anyone ever asked. If this
helped, subscribe because I will cover
what the Chancellor actually announces
the day it lands. And if you want every
form and phone script in one place, my
book, The UK Pension and Benefits
Playbook, is in the description. So go
and check it out. This has been
education, not financial advice, and I
will see you in the next one.

title: If Your Spouse Dies, These 3 Things Happen To Your Joint Bank Account (UK Pensioners Must Know)

segments.text: Picture the worst morning of your life.
You have just lost your husband or your
wife.
Somewhere between ringing the doctor,
ringing the family, and trying to
remember whether you have eaten anything
at all, you are going to have to walk
into a bank and work out what happens to
money you have shared for 20, 30, maybe
50 years.
Here is what almost nobody tells you
before you walk through that door.
What happens to that account was decided
years ago on a form most couples signed
in about 30 seconds and never thought
about again.
The good news is that for most of you,
that form worked in your favor.
The bad news is that three things
surround it that nobody explains, and
one of them catches thousands of couples
out.
Before we go on, type in the comments
whether you and your partner have ever
checked how your joint account is held.
And subscribe if you have not already,
because I cover the rules that nobody
explains.
My name is Arthur Penrose, and I read
the rules so you do not have to.
If you want every form and phone script
in one place, my book, The UK Pension
and Benefits Playbook, is in the
description, so go and check it out.
Everything here comes from gov.uk, HMRC,
and the published guidance of the banks
and the courts.
This is education, not legal or
financial advice, and I will tell you
where you need a solicitor.
Here are the three things.
One, in most of the UK, your joint
account becomes yours automatically.
Two, accounts that were only in your
spouse's name do not, and Scotland works
differently.
Three, the tax, which does not bite now,
but does bite later, and the form that
decides who gets what.
This is not meant to frighten you.
It is meant to make sure that if this
day ever comes, you are not standing at
that counter confused and exhausted.
Stay with me to the end, because the
detail in the middle is the one that
catches thousands of retired couples,
and most of them only find out when it
is too late to fix quietly.
Let us start with the part that works in
your favor because you deserve the good
news first.
Thing one.
In England, Wales, and Northern Ireland,
the great majority of joint accounts
held by married couples and civil
partners are held as joint tenants.
That word tenant has nothing to do with
renting a flat.
It is old legal language and what it
means is simple.
When one account holder dies, the
survivor automatically becomes the sole
owner of everything in that account.
Not eventually.
Not after months of paperwork.
Automatically, the moment your spouse is
gone.
Here is the detail that surprises people
most.
That account is not part of your
spouse's estate.
It does not need probate.
The principle is called the right of
survivorship and it means the money
passes to you by law, outside the will
altogether.
Even if your late husband's or wife's
will said something different about that
money, the survivorship rule generally
wins because the account was never half
his and half hers in a way a will can
touch.
It was owned by both of you in full and
now it is owned in full by the one who
is left.
Picture a man in Bristol whose wife died
very suddenly.
No warning at all.
In the days that followed, while he was
still taking in what had happened, he
had to pay the funeral director, cover
that month's rent, and keep the heating
on.
Because their joint account had been set
up properly decades earlier, as almost
all joint accounts are, none of the
money was frozen.
He took a death certificate into his
local branch and within days the account
was fully his, running exactly as it
always had, without £1 caught up in
probate.
So, what actually happens at the bank or
these days often over the phone with a
bereavement team?
You will need an original death
certificate or a certified copy.
Order several extra copies when you
register the death, five or six at
least.
In England, Wales, and Northern Ireland,
you normally register within 5 days and
in Scotland within 8.
Banks, pension providers, the DVLA, your
council, and sometimes your mortgage
lender will all want to see one.
Once the bank has seen it, most simply
remove your spouse's name and the
account carries on in yours.
Most high street banks have a dedicated
bereavement service.
Ask for it by name rather than waiting
in a general queue.
It is a change of name, not a lockout.
And before you leave the registrar, ask
about Tell Us Once.
It is a free service in most of the UK
that passes the news to the Department
for Work and Pensions, HMRC, the
council, and others in one go, so you do
not have to repeat the worst news of
your life 20 times.
One practical warning.
If your husband or wife was receiving a
state pension, anything paid after the
date of death will be taken back, so do
not spend it.
Now, thing two, and this is where people
get caught.
Thing two,
anything held only in your spouse's name
does not pass automatically at all.
A sole account, an old savings account,
a pension pot paid into a single name.
Those normally form part of the estate.
They are usually frozen and will need
probate or confirmation in Scotland
before the money can be reached,
depending on how much is involved and
what else the estate contains.
Each bank has its own limit below which
it will release a small balance without
probate, and those limits vary a great
deal, so ask.
And here is the part that helps.
Most banks will pay the funeral director
directly from a frozen account if you
send them the invoice on headed paper.
You do not have to pay it from your own
pocket and wait to be repaid.
So, the first job in the first week is
to make a list.
Every account, in whose name, and
whether it is joint or sole.
If you cannot find the paperwork, ask
each bank to confirm in writing how each
account is held.
Do not rely on a decade-old memory of
what you think you signed.
Then there is the part of the UK that
works differently.
If you or your spouse live in Scotland,
or the account is held with a Scottish
bank, the rules underneath work a little
differently, and it genuinely surprises
people.
Scotland has its own succession law,
entirely separate from England and
Wales.
Whether the survivor takes a joint
account depends on how it was set up, in
particular whether the account mandate
carries a survivorship destination.
Many Scottish banks do treat a joint
account as passing to the survivor, and
will re-register it on seeing the death
certificate.
But Scotland's rules also include
something called legal rights.
Even where there is a will, a surviving
spouse and children can have an
automatic entitlement to part of the
movable estate, which means cash and
investments, whatever the will says.
It does not usually reach a
straightforward joint account with a
survivorship destination.
But where there are larger holdings, an
investment account, or an account
recently put into joint names, Scottish
law can produce an outcome very
different from the one someone in Kent
or Cardiff would expect.
So, if Scotland is in the picture, do
two things this week.
Ask your bank in writing to confirm
exactly how each joint account is held.
And speak to a Scottish solicitor about
how legal rights might apply to your
estate.
Get it confirmed now, while there is no
crisis attached to asking.
Now, thing three, the tax.
Thing three.
For the current tax year, the
inheritance tax nil rate band is 325,000
pounds.
If the family home passes to children or
grandchildren, there is an extra
residence nil rate band of up to 175,000
pounds.
Both bands are frozen until April 2031.
That means more and more ordinary
households are being pulled towards
inheritance tax, simply because property
values rise while the threshold stands
still.
Here is the good news, and it is worth
pausing on.
Assets left to a spouse or civil partner
are exempt from inheritance tax,
whatever the size of the estate, as long
as you are both treated as UK-based for
tax purposes.
So, the money in that joint account
coming to you will not trigger an
inheritance tax bill when your spouse
dies.
Where inheritance tax tends to catch
families out is later, when the
surviving spouse dies and the whole
combined estate is measured against
those thresholds.
And there is another quiet help.
Any unused part of your late spouse's
allowances can be passed on to you.
A couple can pass on up to £1 million
between them if the home goes to direct
descendants.
If your estate, home, savings, and
pensions included comes anywhere near
that, it is worth a conversation with a
solicitor or tax adviser.
One more change that is coming.
From April 2027, most unused pension
pots will count towards your estate for
inheritance tax.
So, the nomination form on your pension
matters more than it used to.
There is one more tax detail, and it
catches careful people.
The balance in the account is not
treated as new income to you, because
you already had a genuine ownership
interest in it.
Becoming the sole owner is not a taxable
event.
But from the date of death, anything the
account earns is yours alone, and it
belongs on your tax record from that
date, not on your late spouse's final
return.
It counts towards your own allowances.
The personal savings allowance is £1,000
for a basic rate taxpayer, 500 for a
higher rate taxpayer, and there is also
a starting rate band of up to £5,000 if
your other income is low enough.
Most people stay inside those limits.
But if your late spouse's income is gone
and yours rises as the account grows,
check where you now stand.
Now, here is your checklist for the
first 30 days.
During grief, a clear list is sometimes
the only thing that keeps a person
moving on the hardest days.
Step one,
order several certified copies of the
death certificate when you register the
death and ask about Tell Us Once.
Step two,
take a copy to every bank or building
society where you and your spouse held a
joint account and ask the bereavement
team to confirm that it carries a right
of survivorship and what they need to
put it into your sole name.
Step three,
ask about every account that was only in
your spouse's name because those do not
transfer automatically.
Find out the bank's limit for releasing
money without probate and ask them to
pay the funeral invoice directly.
Step four is the one people skip most,
so please hear this clearly.
Once the joint account becomes yours
alone, think about your own plan for it.
Unlike some other countries, UK bank
accounts do not normally have a form
naming who receives the money when you
die.
So this is the moment to update your own
will with a solicitor and to check the
nomination forms on your pensions and
any workplace death benefits.
Those forms often sit outside your will
entirely and they are usually the
fastest way to pass money to your family
without probate delays when your own
time comes.
It takes one appointment and it can save
your family months.
Step five,
review your will with a solicitor or a
regulated will writing service.
A will written when there were two of
you managing money together often needs
real changes once you are managing
everything alone, particularly who your
executors are and who benefits.
Now one more situation, a little
narrower but worth knowing.
If your joint account was not with a
spouse, say you set it up with an adult
son or daughter to help manage your
money as you got older, the rules shift.
HMRC may look closely at who actually
put the money in.
If that account is later treated as part
of your estate for inheritance tax,
having your child's name on it does not
automatically remove it because the
spouse exemption does not apply between
parent and child.
There is an annual gift allowance of
£3,000 a year, which covers many
everyday situations, but not a whole
account balance.
Larger gifts can still be counted if you
die within 7 years.
If this applies to your family, one
conversation with a solicitor can save
your children surprises later.
Losing a spouse is one of the hardest
things a person can go through, and the
very last thing you should worry about
in that moment is whether your own bank
will make it harder than it has to.
So, here is what I want you to take
away.
If your account carries a right of
survivorship, which the great majority
of joint accounts do, that money is
already yours.
The bank only needs a death certificate
to make it official on paper.
Anything held only in your spouse's name
does not pass automatically, so make a
list in the first week.
If you or your spouse are in Scotland,
check how your accounts and wider estate
are held, because succession law there
works differently.
And once things settle, update your will
and your nominations, so the next
generation does not learn all of this
the hard way.
This is general education for a UK
audience, not personal legal, tax, or
financial advice.
Joint account rules, Scottish succession
law, and inheritance tax thresholds can
change, and every family is different.
Please confirm your own position with
your bank and a qualified solicitor or
advisor before assuming anything about
how your accounts are held.
If this helped, or you know someone, a
friend or neighbor, who is going through
exactly this, please share it with them.
Sometimes the kindest thing you can do
for someone who is grieving is hand them
clear answers, rather than one more
thing to research alone.
Subscribe, because next time I will
cover what happens to a jointly owned
house when a spouse dies, and where the
survivorship rule does and does not
apply to property.
And if you want every form and phone
script in one place, my book, The UK
Pension and Benefits Playbook, is in the

title: If You Have a Current Account, These 3 New Rules Could Affect You Right Now

segments.text: Hello friends. On the 27th of April this
year, a man of 81 opened a letter from
his bank and read that his account would
close in 2 months. His pension went into
that account, his rent came out of it.
The very next day, on the 28th of April,
the law changed for every account opened
from that date on, and almost nobody has
been told. That man could not use the
new rules because his account was older.
But every account opened since runs on
new rules, and they are already sitting
in your bank's small print. Not one bank
will ring you to explain them.
Here is how little it takes to go wrong.
One letter, a pension with nowhere to
land, a rent payment that bounces,
direct debits failing one after another,
each with its own fee. By the time the
panic ends, the credit file is bruised
for 6 years. All of it for a decision
the customer never got to question.
Before anything else, type your age in
the comments, because these rules matter
most to people over 60, and I read every
comment. My name is Arthur Penrose, and
I read the rules so you do not have to.
If you want the practical side in one
place, my book, the UK Pension and
Benefits Playbook, is in the
description. So go and check it out. And
if your money matters to you more than
the bank's convenience, subscribe now,
because these rules keep moving, and I
cover each one the as it lands. Here are
my two promises. First, by the end of
this video, you will know what your bank
can and cannot do to your current
account.
Second, you will learn the one question
to ask at the counter that makes your
bank tell you where you stand. It costs
nothing to ask. Everything here comes
from published sources, gov.uk, the
Financial Conduct Authority, the
Financial Services Compensation Scheme,
the Financial Ombudsman Service, and the
House of Commons Library. Every source
is in the description. This is
education, not advice, and I have no
connection to HMRC, the DWP, or any
bank. Confirm anything that affects your
money with a qualified advisor.
Three rules. The first changes how your
account can end. The second changes why
it can end. The third protects the money
inside it. Let us take them in the order
they landed. Rule one arrived on the
28th of April.
For accounts opened on or after that
date, your bank must give you at least
90 days written notice before closing
it. That is up from 2 months, and the
letter must come with a detailed
specific reason. Older accounts still
carry the old 2 months with no duty to
explain, though some banks are choosing
to extend the new terms to everyone. So,
the first thing to find out is when your
account was opened. Let me show you why
this matters. A man I will call Clive
got 10 days to move his money because
his letter arrived over Christmas when
nobody could reach anybody.
His pension landed in a closed account
for weeks afterwards. 90 days is enough
to redirect a pension, rebuild your
direct debits, and use the current
account switch service, which moves
everything in 7 working days and
redirects payments for 3 years. 10 days
gives you none of that. The gap between
10 and 90 is the gap between a bad week
and a ruined year. One honest note,
there are exceptions. If the bank
suspects fraud or financial crime, or
cannot complete its legal checks, or the
customer has been abusive, the notice
can be shorter. But for the ordinary
quiet closures, 90 days is now the
floor.
There is also a contrast with America
worth knowing because American videos
about a trusted contact frightened
people over here.
In the United States, many firms ask you
to name someone they can ring. In
Britain, there is no such rule. If you
want someone able to speak to your bank,
the tools are a third-party mandate,
which many banks offer free, or a
lasting power of attorney, which costs
92 pounds to register in England and
Wales and takes months to come back.
Consider Gwen, 79. After her hip
operation, her daughter set up a mandate
in one branch visit and paid her bills
while she was in hospital.
2 years later, when Gwen's memory faded,
the mandate was no longer enough. The
families who wait until it is needed are
the families who cannot. If a closure
letter ever lands, ask for the reasons
in writing. Note the date on the letter
and the date it arrived. If the
explanation is thin, complain because
the Financial Ombudsman Service can
review the closure and Citizens Advice
will help free. If you have followed me
this far, type the word account in the
comments because rule two explains the
part banks dislike most. Rule two comes
from the same change and it answers a
question that started the whole debate.
Can your bank close your account because
of your lawful opinions? The answer is
no. Banks may not discriminate against
customers over their political views or
beliefs when providing a payment
account. What is new is that for
accounts opened from the 28th of April,
the bank must now put its reason in
writing so a closure can be checked and
challenged. Listen to the word lawful
because it cuts both ways. If a bank has
concerns under the money laundering
rules, those concerns come first and it
may not even tell you the details
because tipping off a customer is itself
a criminal offense.
So, here is the practical version, the
one that keeps accounts open. Large cash
deposits draw questions and banks add up
smaller deposits that look connected.
Splitting money into pieces to avoid
that conversation is the mistake, not
the cash itself.
Bring paperwork. A house sale, an
inheritance, a gift, a car you sold.
Dorothy sold her late husband's caravan
and paid the cash in that afternoon. Her
account froze within a day. She spent
three weeks treated like a suspect
because the sale was private and nothing
was in writing.
One receipt signed by the buyer would
have ended it in a phone call. The bank
was not wicked, it was blind and
paperwork cures blindness. Nobody
respectable will ever ask you to move
money in small pieces. If a caller says
your bank wants that, hang up. Rule
three is the quiet one. On the 1st of
December 2025, the protection limit rose
from 85,000 pounds to 120,000 pounds per
person, per authorized bank or building
society. It is in force today. A couple
with a joint account is protected up to
pounds because the limit belongs to each
person, not the account. And a large
lump from a life event, such as a house
sale, an inheritance, a redundancy, or a
pension lump sum, gets its own shield.
Temporary high balances are protected up
to 1.4 million pounds for 6 months from
the day the money lands.
Take a couple I will call Walter and
Joan, both 77, who sold their bungalow
in May for 310,000 pounds. It sat in
their only account at their only bank.
The shield covered it until November.
In October, they spread the money across
other institutions and it stayed
protected. Nobody at the bank suggested
it. 6 months is a countdown and that is
the part people miss. Sell a house in
March and that money needs a plan before
September. Two cautions. First, the
limit is per authorized institution. Two
brands under one banking license share
one limit and the scheme's own checker
tells you which is which. Second, it
protects you if a bank fails, not if a
scammer fools you. Scams run on
different rules. Since October 2024, if
you are tricked into sending money to a
fraudster, your bank must reimburse you
up to 85,000 pounds and it should decide
within five working days, longer only
for complicated claims.
If a bank tells you that you were
careless and sends you away, do not let
a rejection letter end it. You can
complain and then go to the ombudsman.
Three things are not happening. Your
account is not being moved anywhere
against your will. Your bank cannot
lawfully close your account because of
your age. And the 120,000 limit is not a
rumor, it is live. If anyone tells you
your savings are only safe to 85,000,
they are quoting last year's rules.
And one more rule worth knowing, since
branches keep closing. Under the cash
access regime that began in September
2024, the largest banks must assess cash
access when a branch shuts, and the
regulator can require a banking hub.
Small rules, but they add up to a bank
that has to tell you things. Why do
banks not shout about any of this?
Notice is expensive, closure is cheaper.
A bank that explains your rights is a
bank that expects you to use them. So,
where do the three rules leave you? 90
days and a real reason for new accounts,
no closure for lawful opinions, and
120,000 pounds of protection per person,
per institution, with a 6-month clock on
large lumps. Here is what I would do
this week. First, find out when each of
your accounts was opened and which
banking license sits behind it.
Second, check your balances against
120,000 pounds per institution. Third,
if a lump from a life event is sitting
in your account, look at the date it
arrived.
Fourth, ask your bank at the counter,
"What notices and protections currently
apply to my account?" Do not ask whether
you are safe, ask what applies, and have
them point to it.
Fifth, set up a free third-party mandate
now, or register a power of attorney
while you are well, because nobody can
register one after capacity has gone.
Sixth, keep every letter, every
reference number, and every date,
because files with dates move and files
without them stall.
Pension Wise offers free guidance on the
pension side, and Citizens Advice will
sit with you through the paperwork, also
free. If this made sense, subscribe now
before the rules change again, because a
budget is coming.
And my book, The UK Pension and Benefits
Playbook, is in the description, so go
and check it out. This has been
education, not financial advice.
My name is Arthur Penrose, and I will
see you in the next one.
