intended prosecution must reach the
registered keeper within 14 days, which
means the first you know about it is a
letter.
The penalty for using a handheld phone
while driving is £200 and six penalty
points.
If you passed your test within the last
2 years, six points means your license
is revoked. You go back to a provisional
license and have to pass both the theory
and practical tests again.
For everyone else, six points is halfway
to 12 and 12 points within 3 years
usually means a ban.
Here's the part most people miss. The
same camera can pick up both offenses
from a single image. That means two
separate penalties from one journey.
£200 and six points for the phone, plus
a £100 fixed penalty for the seatbelt.
In England and Wales, the seatbelt
offense carries no points and if it goes
to court, the fine can be higher. But
for a new driver, those six phone points
alone are enough to lose the license.
The camera never pulls you over. It
records you, reads your number plate,
and the letter follows. Change number
two. Average speed cameras are no longer
just a roadworks thing. For years,
average speed cameras meant motorway
roadworks. You slowed down, drove
through, then sped up again. Now,
permanent average speed systems are
fitted on many A roads and trunk roads
with a history of speeding and more are
being added.
Cameras at the start and the end of a
measured stretch record your number
plate at each point. The system divides
the distance by your time and works out
your average speed. If it is above the
limit, a notice follows. There is no
camera in the middle to slow down for.
The ones that matter sit at the entrance
and the exit and you often cannot see
them as you drive in. Slowing down for
one camera is no longer enough because
the whole stretch counts, every mile.
This is why a driver who eases off
beside one camera and then speeds up
again can still be caught by the stretch
between them. The sums are done by
machine, so the figure is either under
the limit or it is not.
Change number three. Stealth cameras on
smart motorways enforce speed limits
that can change within seconds. Smart
motorway sections include parts of the
M1, M3, M4, M6, M20, M25, and M62. Many
of them are enforced by HADECS 3
cameras. They are gray, much smaller
than the yellow Gatso cameras drivers
know, and they are built into the gantry
structure above you. At motorway speed,
most people cannot spot them even when
they know to look. On a smart motorway,
the limit on the gantry can drop within
seconds from 70 to 50 or from 60 to 40,
set by a control room responding to
congestion, an incident, or the weather.
When that limit is shown in a red
circle, it is a legal limit, and the
camera enforces whatever the gantry
above you shows at that exact moment.
Picture this.
It is early morning, the road is almost
empty, and you are doing 58. The gantry
above you shows 50, while the signs
before and after show 60. There is no
queue and no visible reason. The limit
was set and the camera enforced it.
Gantry limits exist to manage traffic
flow, so they can look odd on an empty
road, but legally the number you see is
the number you must follow. The minimum
penalty for speeding is £100 and three
points.
In serious cases, a court can impose a
fine of up to £2,500
on a motorway and a driving ban. Change
number four. Driving in a red X lane can
now be caught automatically. A closed
lane on a smart motorway is marked by a
red X on the gantry above it. Driving in
that lane has always been illegal. What
has changed is how easily it is
detected. Cameras on the gantries can
now spot vehicles passing under a red X
without an officer standing there. The
penalty is £100 and three points, which
police check and send out by post.
National Highways has been blunt about
it. No excuse, do not ignore the red X.
That X could be showing because of a
breakdown, debris, or an incident just
ahead that you cannot see yet. Driving
under it is not a small slip. It is a
danger to whoever is stopped in that
lane.
If you see a red X, move into another
lane as soon as it is safe to do so.
And those three points stay on your
license for 4 years.
Change number five, Op Snap. Other
drivers can now report you straight to
the police. This is the change most
people have not factored in at all.
Operation Snap is run by most police
forces across England and Wales, each
with its own online portal. It lets
members of the public upload dashcam,
phone, or other footage of driving
offenses. An experienced officer reviews
the footage, and if it meets the
standard, the result can be a notice of
intended prosecution, a fixed penalty, a
court summons, or an offer to attend a
driver awareness course,
depending on how serious it was. The
offenses most often reported include
running red lights, phone use,
tailgating, dangerous overtaking, and
careless driving.
It costs nothing, and it is open at any
hour.
Footage can come from a dashcam in the
car behind you, one in front, or a
passenger filming from the next lane.
Because police usually have to serve a
notice within 14 days, most forces ask
for footage within 7 to 10 days, so it
can arrive quickly.
Most people who receive one of these
notices had no idea they were being
recorded. Check your own police force's
website to see how its Op Snap scheme
works.
On any public road in 2026, assume a
serious driving offense could be filmed
by someone you will never see in a car
you will never identify.
Change number six, the insurance tail.
This is why every one of these is
measured in years, not pounds. Most
penalty points stay on your license for
4 years from the date of the offense,
and insurers usually ask about
convictions going back 5 years.
You have to answer honestly at every
quote and every renewal. A single
speeding conviction can push your
premium up noticeably, and a phone
conviction with six points usually hits
harder. Now, imagine one speeding
notice, one phone notice, and one red X
notice inside 12 months. That is 12
points, enough to put you in front of a
totting up ban hearing with higher
premiums following you for years.
Premium rises vary by insurer, age, and
area. So, the safest rule is to avoid
the points in the first place. The fine
on the letter is not the real cost. The
insurance tail is. So, here is the full
picture for every driver on the M25 and
every major road in Britain this autumn.
AI cameras can flag a phone and a
missing seatbelt in the same image. So,
one pass can mean two penalties.
Average speed cameras now sit on
permanent stretches beyond roadworks.
So, slowing for one camera no longer
works. Stealth cameras enforce limits
that can change within seconds. And the
gantry above you is the one that counts.
Red X lanes can be caught automatically
at £100 and three points. Op Snap means
any driver with a dashcam can send your
offense to the police.
And every set of points carries an
insurance tail that costs far more than
the fine itself.
The enforcement system on British roads
in 2026 does not need to pull you over.
It records you, identifies you, and
sends a notice to your door. Subscribe.
Share this with anyone you know who
drives a motorway this winter. I will
see you in the next one.

title: Every UK Retiree With a Savings Account Needs to Move This Money — Here’s Why

segments.text: Hello friends. Two men, both 70, both on
the full new state pension, both with a
small workplace pension of about £3,000
a year. One has paid around £400 more
tax than he should over two years. The
other has paid exactly what he owed. The
difference was not a clever investment
or a better pension provider. It was one
short code on one piece of paper that
nobody had ever explained to either of
them. That is what this video is about.
Not stocks, not shares, nothing risky.
It is about how HMRC taxes your pension
and the mistakes in your tax code that a
great many retired people never notice.
Nobody from HMRC will write and explain
it. Your pension provider certainly will
not. So, I will. Before I start, type
your age in the comments and subscribe
if you have not already. My name is
Arthur Penrose and I read the rules so
you do not have to. And if you want
every limit and every phone script in
one place, check out my guide book, the
UK Pension and Benefits Playbook. The
link is in the description.
Everything here comes from published
government and HMRC rules.
I am not a financial advisor and I am
not an accountant. This is education,
not advice for your own circumstances.
Let me start with a number because it
explains almost all of this.
and 40p. That is the entire gap this tax
year between the full new state pension,
and your tax-free personal allowance of
Your state pension has used up your
whole allowance to within a few pounds.
It arrives with no tax taken off, which
is why it never feels like taxable
income, but HMRC counts it first. So,
every pound of other income you receive
sits above the allowance and on its own,
that would mean tax on all of it. That
is where most people stop and assume the
worst. Except HMRC has a way of
collecting it, and it hides in your tax
code. Here is how it works.
Because your state pension is paid in
full, HMRC collects the tax on it from
your other pension. It does that by
shrinking the tax-free allowance in the
code on your workplace or private
pension.
So, your code may look tiny, or your
pension may be taxed at the basic rate
on almost every pound. For a pensioner
with a state pension and a small second
pension, that is normal. In plain
numbers, with a workplace pension of
£3,000 a year, nearly all of it is
taxable, which is about £600 of tax. So,
the code on that pension matters, and it
is worth getting right.
What is not normal is a code that is
wrong. And a wrong code does not feel
like a mistake. It just feels like your
pension is a bit smaller than it should
be.
Where do mistakes come from? Your code
is built from estimates. Your state
pension forecast, your workplace
pension, any other income HMRC thinks
you have. If an estimate is out of date,
you pay too much or too little, and it
can take a year or two to show.
The letter that tells you, called a
notice of coding, is the one most people
throw away. Do not. You can also see
your code and the income figures HMRC is
using in your HMRC online account. If a
figure looks wrong, ring HMRC and say
these words. Please check the income
figures used in my tax code because I
think my state pension estimate is out
of date. Imagine a man we will call
Derek. He is 68. He draws the full new
state pension and has a small workplace
pension of £3,000 a year.
For 2 years, his tax code assumed his
state pension was higher than it really
was because it was based on an old
forecast. He was overtaxed by about £200
a year, and nothing in his life told
him. One call to HMRC, one corrected
figure, and a refund for the years back.
And do not pay anyone a share of a
refund to claim it for you. You can do
it yourself for free. If that might be
you, check your code against your real
figures. You can usually claim back
overpaid tax for up to four tax years.
Now, the other side. Let me tell you
about a woman I will call Sheila. She
was 74, recently widowed. When her
husband died, his workplace pension
passed to her, her income rose, and her
tax code was never updated. Then a
letter arrived from HMRC saying she owed
She had never had a tax bill in her
life. She had assumed, reasonably, that
because nobody had ever mentioned it, it
was fine. That assumption is the most
expensive one in retirement. How HMRC
collects an underpayment depends on the
size of the bill. Small amounts, usually
under £3,000, are collected by changing
your tax code, so a little more comes
off your pension each month. Larger
amounts come as a formal demand called a
simple assessment. If one lands, do not
just pay it. Check the income figures
HMRC has used against your own pension
statements, because mistakes do happen.
You usually have 60 days to challenge,
so open that envelope the same day.
There is one more place where pensioners
lose money, and it is the biggest. If
you take a lump sum from a defined
contribution pension, your provider
often has no proper tax code for you
yet. So, it uses an emergency code,
which treats your one-off withdrawal as
though you will take the same amount
every month for the rest of the year.
You can be overtaxed by hundreds of
pounds, or more, on the spot. Usually up
to a quarter of your pot can be taken
tax-free, and the rest is taxed at your
real rate for the year.
If you were overtaxed, you can reclaim
it. There is a form for it. It is called
a P55 if you took part of your pot, a
P53Z if you emptied it and carry on
working, and a P50Z if you emptied it
and stopped working. Your pension
provider can tell you which one applies.
Who does this hit? Everyone.
The modest pensioner taking a small sum
to fix the boiler is hit just as hard as
the one moving a larger amount.
Now, put all of this beside what is
coming because almost nobody has joined
it up. The personal allowance is frozen
until at least 2031. Meanwhile, the
state pension is expected to rise by
around 3.9% next April to about £13,000
a year. That takes it past the allowance
by roughly £466.
The government has said that people
whose only income is the full state
pension will not have to pay income tax.
But anyone with a second pension or any
other income will find the margin for
error gets thinner every year. That is
exactly why checking your code matters
more now than it did 5 years ago. What
about money you will not need for a long
time? Some people use a stocks and
shares ISA. You can put in up to £20,000
each tax year and the growth and income
inside it are free from tax. Some people
choose diversified funds that screen out
harmful industries. But please hear this
clearly. Investments can fall as well as
rise. They are only for money you will
not need for at least 5 years, never
your emergency pot. And everyone's
situation is different, so get free
guidance before you act.
So, let me leave you with six things.
First, find your tax code. It is on your
pension payslip or your notice of
coding. Second, check the income figures
HMRC is using and ask for a correction
if they are wrong. Third, if you took a
pension lump sum, check whether you were
taxed on an emergency code and reclaim
the overpayment. Fourth, if you have
overpaid in previous years, claim it
back because you can usually go back
four tax years. Fifth, if you receive a
simple assessment, check it and
challenge it within 60 days. Sixth, keep
every letter from HMRC in one place and
set one reminder each April to check
your code again. One last warning, HMRC
will never ask for your bank details by
text or email, and it will never ask you
to pay a fee to get a refund.
If a message says otherwise, it is a
scam. If you want to work through your
own position, Tax Help for Older People,
Pension Wise, and Citizens Advice all
offer free help. If this made sense,
subscribe now before the rules change
again because the allowance freeze is
already in law. And if you want every
limit and every phone script in one
place, my guidebook, The UK Pension and
Benefits Playbook, has its link in the
description. This has been education,
not financial advice, and I will see you
in the next one.

title: 7 Types of Income HMRC Can’t Touch After 65 (Most Seniors Only Know One)

segments.text: Hello friends.
Seven kinds of money that the law itself
says HMRC cannot touch after 65.
Not one loophole.
Not a scheme you have to pay somebody
for. Seven categories written into the
legislation in plain black and white,
and almost every retiree in this country
knows only one of them. So, they quietly
hand over tax they never owed. Here are
the two promises I am making you before
we start. One type on this list protects
a bigger amount on its own than all the
others put together. And I will name it
and give you the exact figure. And there
is one decision about your own money
that decides whether HMRC taxes your
state pension at all or never gets near
it. I will give you both before we
finish. But, the second one only works
once you understand the first six. So,
stay with me. Before I start, type your
age in the comments. I read everyone and
it tells me what to cover next. My name
is Arthur Penrose and I read the rules
so you do not have to. If that is
useful, subscribe now because these
rules keep moving and I cover each
change as it lands. Everything here
comes from published sources.
gov.uk
HMRC, the House of Commons Library, and
research published by Parliament. Every
source is in the description below. I am
not a financial advisor and I am not an
accountant. This is education, not
advice for your own circumstances. Let
me start with the one you probably
already know because it is the doorway
to the other six. When you build up a
private pension pot over your working
life, the rule is simple. Up to 25% of
it can be taken as tax-free cash up to a
limit of 268,275
pounds. You paid in from income that was
already taxed, so the law lets you take
a quarter out tax-free. From age 55 and
57 from April 2028, that door opens.
Here is what most people get wrong. They
hear 25% and think it means 25% of each
withdrawal. It does not. It is a quarter
of the whole pot. And if you take it in
pieces, you can easily lose track of how
much of your tax-free share you have
already used. 200,000 pounds in the pot
means 50,000 pounds that HMRC cannot
touch in one payment if you want it. And
here is the detail almost nobody
mentions because it matters more than
the money itself. Tax-free cash does not
count as income. Remember that phrase
because it is the key to the last part
of this video. It does not count as
income, so it does not push anything
else into a tax bracket. Write that
down. Let me put a face on why this
matters because a rule you have never
used feels like a rule that does not
exist. A woman I will call Joan, 71,
took her 25% as one payment the week she
retired and her advisor marked it as
tax-free on the paperwork. Her neighbor
did the same thing two years later, but
his paperwork was filled in carelessly,
the box was marked wrong, and it took
him 11 months and a stack of letters to
get the tax back. Same money, same rule.
The only difference was knowing what the
25% actually was and insisting it was
honored. Type two is the one the law
protects most completely and it is the
quiet river running underneath
everything else. The individual savings
account, the ISA.
Whatever an ISA earns is outside the tax
system entirely. No tax on dividends, no
tax on gains if you sell something at a
profit, and nothing to report because
there is nothing to report.
Every year you can put away 20,000
pounds and whatever that pile earns, it
earns clean. And there is a change
coming that protects this audience
specifically. From the 6th of April
2027, the cash limit inside an ISA drops
to 12,000 pounds for anyone under 65.
But if you are 65 or over, your full
20,000 pounds a year stays open to you.
That protection is written into the
policy for exactly the people watching
this. This video does not tell you what
to hold inside your ISA. That choice is
yours and it should suit your own
circumstances. Type three is the most
underused one on this list, the
rent-a-room scheme. If you let out a
furnished room in your own home, the
first 7,500 pounds a year of that rent
is completely free of tax. Not
discounted, free. If you share the
income with a partner or someone else,
the limit is 3,750
pounds each. And if you earn less than
the limit, the exemption is automatic.
No form, no reporting, nothing to claim.
Plenty of retirees have a spare bedroom
and never think about it. And if this is
the first video where somebody has
actually laid the list out for you, type
the word new in the comments because it
tells me this is working. This is the
moment to do it. Now, let me pause on
the honest part because I will never
give you half a truth.
Rent-a-room means a lodger living in
your home. For some people, that is a
fair trade for tax-free rent and for
others, it is not. It only covers
furnished rooms in the home you live in,
not a separate flat. Check with your
mortgage lender, your home insurer, and
your benefits advisor first. That is a
judgment only you can make. On with the
list. One more comparison before I move
on because the numbers are the part that
sticks.
Put 7,500 pounds of rent from a lodger
beside 7,500 pounds of rent from a flat
you let out. The lodger rent is yours,
every penny, and no letter ever arrives.
The flat rent goes on your tax return
and HMRC taxes what is left after costs.
Same street, same year. One pile is
invisible to the taxman and the other is
on a list with your name on it. Type
four arrives at the worst moment of a
family's life and the law, for once,
shows mercy. When somebody dies, the
family often has to sell what is left
behind. The car, the jewelry, the
furniture, the tools in the shed. Most
families brace themselves for a tax bill
on that money and in the ordinary case,
it simply never comes. A private car is
exempt from capital gains tax, whatever
it sells for, and any personal
possession, a watch, a painting, a piece
of furniture, is exempt if it sells for
£6,000 or less.
I have seen people set aside a third of
what they raised for a tax that was
never going to arrive and live on less
than they had to in the hardest year of
their lives because nobody told them
about one condition. The £6,000 limit
applies to each item, but a matching set
counts as one. Split a pair of vases or
a set of silver to stay under the limit
and the rule treats it as a single sale.
Above that, ask a professional before
you sell. Keep the receipts and write
down the date the person died and what
each item was worth then. Same
belongings, one rule, no tax bill. Type
five is the giant I promised you at the
start and it is sitting inside something
nearly everybody watching owns.
Your home. When you sell a second
property, the profit is normally
taxable, but your main home is different
and it is different in a way that
surprises people who learn the rules
from American videos. In the United
States, a couple can shield around half
a million dollars of profit from a home
sale. Here, the rule is stronger than
that. If the house you are selling has
been your only or main home, private
residence relief removes the entire gain
from capital gains tax. Not the first
half million, all of it. A couple who
bought a house for £30,000 40 years ago,
worth 400,000 today, hands over nothing
on that £370,000
profit as long as it has been their home
throughout. There is one condition and
one warning. The condition is that it
was your main home and generally your
only one.
The warning is for people who have
recently moved out. Since 2020, the
grace period after you stop living there
is nine months, not the 18 months older
guidance mentions. If you are selling a
home you moved out of, or a second
property, or somewhere you let to
tenants, the rules are different and
that check belongs before you sign
anything, not after.
Because the right decision here can be
the single biggest tax number in your
whole retirement. Type six reaches past
your own lifetime, and it is the most
misunderstood rule in the entire system.
When you inherit money or property, you
do not pay income tax on it. Not on the
cash, not on the house. It is not your
income, and HMRC has no claim on it as
income. And there is a second layer
worth more than most people realize.
When somebody dies, the value of
everything they own is reset to the
market price on the day they died for
tax purposes. So, if your mother bought
a house for 40,000 pounds decades ago,
and it was worth 400,000 when she died,
all those years of growth simply vanish
for tax.
It is as if you inherited it at 400,000.
Sell the next day, and there is nothing
to tax. A lifetime of gains crosses to
the next generation wiped clean. It is
one of the main reasons an ordinary
family can pass on a home at all. Now,
let me deal with the fear, because
people hear the words inheritance tax
and panic. Your estate only pays
anything above 325,000
pounds, with a further 175,000
on top, when a home goes to direct
descendants. That is up to 500,000 each,
and a million for a couple, and both
bands are frozen until April 2031.
Anything left to a spouse or a civil
partner passes free entirely, and so
does anything left to charity. For the
overwhelming majority of families
watching, that charge never applies.
But there is a change coming, and I
would be failing you if I skipped it.
From the 6th of April 2027, most unused
pension pots and pension death benefits
fall inside the estate for inheritance
tax. That is a real shift. It means the
old idea that a pension is automatically
the cleanest thing to leave behind is no
longer automatically true. If you are
leaving a large pot to your children,
this is the one to check with a
professional. Which brings me to type
seven. The quiet monthly river that most
retirees collect without ever being told
it is protected. Certain benefits are
completely tax-free. The two that matter
most after 65 are attendance allowance
and personal independence payment. If
you receive either, every pound of it is
yours. No tax, no reporting. A tax-free
payment every month for life is worth
more than its face value because none of
it ever feeds a tax bill.
So, there are the seven.
Your pension is tax-free quarter, your
ISA, your rent-a-room income, the sale
of a loved one's belongings, the whole
gain on your family home, your
inheritance and the reset at death, and
your tax-free benefits. And now, as
promised, the one decision that decides
whether HMRC taxes your state pension at
all. It is the order you withdraw from
things. Your full state pension sits
just below the personal allowance of
pounds. So, on its own, it triggers
almost no tax. But every taxable pound
you draw on top eats into what is left
of that allowance. Withdraw spending
money from your tax-free cash or your
ISA or your rent-a-room income and
nothing counts as income. So, the wall
around your state pension stays
standing. Withdraw the same spending
money from a taxable pension pot and you
can drag your other income into the
taxable zone at the same time.
One decision, two completely different
tax bills every year for the rest of
your life. So, here are your steps and
they are short. Check how much of your
25% tax-free cash you have already used.
Check what your ISAs hold and use this
year's allowance before the 6th of April
because an unused allowance is gone. If
you have a spare furnished room, check
whether rent-a-room could work for you.
If you are selling belongings after a
death, keep the paperwork. If a sale of
your home is anywhere ahead, confirm the
relief before you sign. And if If pot is
heading to your children, take advice
about the April 2027 change this year.
Not after it bites. Now, let me be clear
about three things this list is not. It
is not avoidance, and it is not a gray
area. Every one of these seven is
written into the legislation for you to
use. It is not hidden, either. HMRC
publishes all of it, though I have never
once seen a letter arrive to explain it.
And it is not going to stay still.
Figures freeze, thresholds shift, and
April 2027 is already loaded with
changes. If you want to work through
your own pension position properly,
Pensionwise offers free and impartial
guidance, and you reach it through
MoneyHelper. Use them. That is what they
are there for. And if this made sense to
you, subscribe now before the rules
change again. Because they are already
moving for April 2027. Everything I have
quoted comes from gov.uk,
HMRC, the House of Commons Library, and
research published by Parliament. Every
source is in the description below. This
has been education, not financial
advice, and I will see you in the next
one.

title: 3 Banking Changes to Watch in 2026 That Could Affect Your Current Account

segments.text: Hello friends.
Two men, both 72, both retired, both
banking with the same high street name.
One of them can move his money this
afternoon. The other had his current
account frozen for 11 days, and he had
done nothing wrong at all. Same bank,
same sort of balance, same age. The only
difference was that one of them knew
what his bank had changed this year, and
the other one never opened the letter.
That letter arrived for both of them.
Your bank changed the terms on your
current account, and nobody called you
about it. They did not have to. They
posted a notice, and under the rules
that counts as telling you. So, the
changes came in quietly, and a great
many people over 65 have still not
noticed. So, today I will walk you
through three of those changes in plain
English. Change number two decides
whether your bank has to give your money
back after a scam.
Change number three is quietly costing
people money every single month.
Before we start, type your age in the
comments. I read everyone, and it tells
me what to cover next. My name is Arthur
Penrose, and I read the rules so you do
not have to. If that is useful,
subscribe now because more of these
rules land in 2026 and 2027. And I will
cover each one as it arrives.
Everything here comes from published
sources, gov.uk, HMRC, the Financial
Conduct Authority, the Payment Systems
Regulator, the Financial Ombudsman
Service, and research published by
Parliament. Every source is in the
description below. And one thing before
we begin. I am not a financial advisor,
and I am not a lawyer. This is
education, not advice. Your
circumstances are your own, so before
you move serious money, speak to
somebody qualified.
Let me start with why any of this is
happening. Because once you understand
the cause, the changes stop feeling
random. Fraud is now the most common
crime in this country, and most of it
moves through bank payments rather than
through burglary or a stolen wallet. The
Payment Systems Regulator and the
Financial Conduct Authority have both
been pushing banks to act, and the
result has been a wave of new payment
rules, new name checks, and new duties
to refund customers. Some of those
changes are firmly on your side. A few
of them are not, and almost none of them
arrived with an explanation you could
actually use.
Change number one is called Confirmation
of Payee, and it is the one you have
probably already met without knowing its
name. Here is how it works. When you set
up a new payment to somebody, or when
you change the details on an existing
payee, your bank checks the name you
typed against the name actually held on
the receiving account. If the name
matches, the payment goes through as
normal.
If the name is close, but not exact,
your bank shows you a warning and tells
you the name that is really on that
account. If the name does not match at
all, you get a much stronger warning,
and you are asked to think again before
sending anything.
This is the single most useful
protection in British banking right now,
because most scams die at exactly this
moment. A fraudster can copy a bank's
logo, copy its phone number, and copy
its letters. What a fraudster cannot do
is put your son's name on an account
that is not your son's.
For a long time, this check only applied
to the biggest banks, and only to some
payments. That has changed. Since
October 2024, many more firms handling
faster payments and CHAPS have had to
offer it. And in July 2026, the
regulator consulted on removing the end
date on that direction, and on bringing
in the firms that offer the check
voluntarily. More than 300 firms now
offer it, so almost every payment you
make in Britain should pass through a
name check first. Here is the catch, and
it matters enormously. You can override
the warning. You can look at a red
screen that says the name does not
match, and press send anyway. Your bank
will let you, but if you override the
warning, and you are then scammed, you
have made your own life much harder.
Because the bank will argue you were
warned in clear terms and chose to
ignore it. So, the habit to build is
simple. Treat a name mismatch as a full
stop, not a speed bump. Stop, phone the
person on a number you already had, and
confirm the account details with your
own ears before a single pound leaves.
There is a second thing worth knowing.
Because banks now check names, some
payments take a moment longer. If a
family member gives you new account
details, ask them to confirm the name
held on it. It is the difference between
sending money to your grandson and
sending it to a stranger.
There is one more thing about this
change. In America, many financial firms
ask you to name a trusted contact they
can phone if they suspect you are being
exploited. Britain does not have a rule
like that yet. What Britain has instead
is third-party access,
where you can formally nominate somebody
you trust to see and discuss your
account with the bank. And there is a
lasting power of attorney, registered
with the Office of the Public Guardian,
which gives a named person real legal
authority over your money if you ever
lose the ability to manage it. Those two
things are not the same, and neither is
automatic.
Ask your bank this week whether
third-party access is available on your
account, and who is currently nominated.
Change number two is the one I promised
you, and it is the biggest single change
to British banking in a generation.
It is called mandatory reimbursement for
authorized push payment fraud. Push
payment fraud is the polite term for a
very rude crime. Nobody hacks your
account, nobody steals your card.
Instead, somebody convinces you to send
the money yourself. They pretend to be
your bank, or the police, or an
investment firm, or a builder you have
actually hired.
You authorize the payment, which is why
the old rule said it was your problem.
That changed on the 7th of October 2024.
Under rules set by the Payment Systems
Regulator, if you are tricked into
sending money by a scam through faster
payments, your bank must reimburse you
unless you were grossly negligent. Both
the sending bank and the receiving bank
share the cost equally, so the bank that
accepted the scammed money can no longer
sit back and shrug. The maximum you can
claim is 85,000 pounds per claim. There
is a five working day deadline for the
bank to refund you in most cases, and up
to 35 working days for more complicated
claims that need investigation. And this
is the part that changed the
relationship between you and your bank.
The bank now has to prove gross
negligence. You do not have to prove
your innocence. Meet Doreen. She is 79,
lives on her own, and got a call that
looked like her bank's fraud line on her
phone screen. The caller knew her name,
her branch, and the last four digits of
her card. She moved 11,000 pounds to a
so-called safe account. Under the old
rules, that money was simply gone.
Under the rules that now apply, her bank
had to replace it because she had not
been grossly negligent. She had been
deceived by somebody who had done their
homework. But, and this is the part
nobody explains properly,
this protection is not automatic in
every situation. Reimbursement applies
to faster payments, which covers most
everyday transfers. Other payment
methods are treated differently, and the
gross negligence test is real. If you
ignored multiple clear warnings from
your own bank, or if you refused to take
part in a scam check the bank was
required to carry out, you can lose the
protection.
So, the correct behavior is not to stay
silent and hope. It is to engage, answer
the questions honestly, and write down
everything. And here is the hardest
thing about this change. Because the
bank now pays when you are scammed, the
bank now has a real incentive to stop
payments before they leave. That is good
in most cases, but it also means your
own perfectly legitimate payment can be
held while the bank makes inquiries, and
it can take longer than you expect. If
that happens, ask one direct question.
Ask whether this is an automated
security check or a formal hold, and ask
what you need to provide to release it.
Those are two completely different
situations, and you deserve to know
which one you are in. Change number
three is the money one, and it went the
opposite way to America. So, let me be
honest with you about that, because you
may have seen American videos saying the
overdraft protections were scrapped. In
Britain, the protections were kept. Back
in April 2020, the Financial Conduct
Authority banned the old system of fixed
daily and monthly overdraft charges.
Banks were told they could only charge a
simple annual interest rate, the same
rate for arranged and unarranged
borrowing, with no separate fees stacked
on top. That rule still stands. If your
bank is charging you a flat fee for
going overdrawn, that is worth
questioning. Here is what has quietly
changed instead. Because the banks lost
their fee income, they went looking for
it elsewhere. Some accounts that used to
be free now carry a monthly fee. Some
free accounts have become harder to keep
free because the conditions changed.
Some accounts that were open to anybody
now require a minimum monthly deposit.
And some charges that were once waived
for older customers are no longer waived
automatically, because the waiver
depends on the account you actually
hold, not on your age. Here is what to
do. And it takes one phone call.
Ask your bank three questions. What is
my current account called, exactly? What
does it cost me each month? And what do
I have to do every month to keep that
cost at zero? Write the answers down,
and then compare them with your last
three statements.
Look at every line that is not a payment
you made yourself. While you are on that
call, ask one more thing.
Ask whether your bank offers a basic
bank account, because British banks
offer a no-frills account with no
monthly fee and no overdraft, and it is
available even to people with a poor
credit history. Many people are paying a
monthly fee for an account they were
never told they could switch away from.
Ask for the notice period you will get
if your bank ever closes your account.
New rules push that to at least 90 days,
up from 2 months. Now, one more change
that is coming straight for your
savings, and it is not a banking rule at
all. It is a tax one, and it works
quietly in the background. After the 5th
of April each year, your bank and
building society tell HMRC how much
interest they paid you. You do not
report it, and you do not fill in a
form.
HMRC already has it. If the interest on
your record does not match what HMRC
expected, you can receive a letter
asking you to explain the difference.
Those letters are not accusations, but
they are not junk mail, either, and they
should never go in the bin. Why does
this matter more than it used to?
Because your personal allowance has been
frozen at 12,570
pounds since April 2021, and is now
frozen until at least April 2031. Your
personal savings allowance is frozen,
too, at 1,000 pounds of interest for
basic rate taxpayers, and 500 above
that. And from the 6th of April 2027,
the tax on savings interest outside an
ISA rises from 20 to 22% from 40 to 42,
and from 45 to 47. So, interest you earn
this year can create a tax bill later,
long after you have spent the interest.
Three things that are not happening, so
you can stop waiting for them. No bank
is required to telephone you before it
changes your terms, because a posted
notice is legally enough. No
reimbursement under the scam rules is
automatic in every type of payment,
because it depends on how you paid and
on how you behaved. No fixed overdraft
fee is legal in Britain. So, if you are
being charged one, that charge itself is
worth challenging. So, here is your list
for this week. Turn on confirmation of
payee warnings, and decide in advance
that you will never override one. Phone
your bank and confirm the exact name
held on any account you pay money to.
Keep a written note of what you would do
if a caller claiming to be your bank
asked you to move money, and put it next
to the phone. Ask your bank what your
current account costs, and what would
make that cost zero. Ask specifically
about a basic bank account with no
monthly fee. Read every letter from your
bank about terms, even the ones that
look like advertising, because one of
them will be a real change. Check your
savings interest against your personal
savings allowance before it surprises
you. And if you have been scammed,
report it the same day, because the
clock on your claim starts immediately.
Turn on transaction alerts if your bank
offers them. An alert telling you the
moment money leaves your account turns a
6-month problem into a 6-minute one. One
last thing, and it is free. If you are
over 50 and you have a defined
contribution pension, you are entitled
to free guidance from Pension Wise, part
of the Money and Pension Service. It is
a real conversation with a trained
person about your options, and it is not
a sales call. Take it before you make a
decision you cannot undo. A current
account is not something you open once
and then forget for a decade. The terms
change, the fees change, the security
systems change, and the law changes with
them. The people who get caught are not
the careless ones. They are the ones who
trusted that everything stayed the same.
My name is Arthur Penrose, and I read
the rules so you do not have to.
Subscribe before it changes.

title: Never Keep More Than This in the Bank After 65 — Most Seniors Miss These

segments.text: Hello friends. Two men, both 67, both
retired last year, both keeping their
life savings in one bank account. One
sleeps perfectly well at night. The
other lost access to 11,000 pounds of
his own money, and he had done nothing
wrong. The difference between them is
one rule that almost nobody over 65 has
been told about. It is not the bank's
fault, and it is not the government's
fault. It is just how the law is
written. This country has a small number
of money limits sitting quietly in the
background. They are not secret, but
they are buried in documents most people
never read. And the moment your balance
crosses one, somebody else gets a say
over your money. The government, a
creditor, the court, or your own bank.
So today I will walk you through seven
of those limits one at a time in plain
English.
Some are amounts.
Some are dates.
One lets a bank reach into your savings
without asking you first. And number
five can freeze every penny you have,
and you may not find out until your card
is declined at the checkout. By the end,
I will give you the exact amount to keep
in the account where your pension lands,
and why. And it is not my opinion.
It falls out of the way British courts
and British banks actually behave. The
people in my examples are made up, built
from situations, advice, charities
describe.
Before we start, type your age in the
comments. I read everyone, and I use
them to decide what I cover next. Most
people watching are between 60 and 80,
and most will cross at least one of
these lines without knowing the line was
there.
My name is Arthur Penrose, and I read
the published rules so you do not have
to. If that sounds useful, subscribe
now, because several of these rules
change in 2027, and I will cover each
change as it lands. Everything here is
built on published sources. gov.uk,
HMRC,
the Department for Work and Pensions,
the Financial Conduct Authority, the
Financial Services Compensation Scheme,
and the Bank of England, plus research
published by Parliament. Every source is
in the description below. And one thing
before we begin, I am not a financial
advisor and I am not a lawyer. This is
education, not advice. Your
circumstances are your own. So, before
you move real money, speak to somebody
qualified. Number one,
16,000 pounds.
This is the harshest line here because
crossing it does not trim your help, it
switches it off completely. If you claim
housing benefit or council tax reduction
and you do not receive the guarantee
part of pension credit, then once your
savings pass 16,000 pounds, you are
generally not entitled to that help at
all. Not a smaller amount, nothing. If
you do receive the guarantee part, this
limit does not apply to you. Meet
Maureen. She is 76, lives alone and has
12,000 pounds in savings. Then she sells
her late husband's car for 4,000 pounds
and leaves the money in her account
while she decides what to do. A small
gift from her daughter takes her over
16,000 and the council writes to say her
reduction has stopped. Her income did
not change, one deposit did. And there
is a second trap inside this one. If you
give money away to get under a limit,
the council or the Department for Work
and Pensions can treat you as though you
still have it. It is called deprivation
of capital.
Number two has nothing to do with
savings at all.
But it decides whether the money landing
in your account is really yours to keep.
Number two, 12,570
pounds.
That is the personal allowance, the
amount you can have each year before you
pay income tax.
It is frozen until at least the 5th of
April 2031. The full new state pension
this tax year is 241 pounds 30 a week,
which is 12,547
pounds 60 a year. Just 22 pounds 40
under the allowance. So, the pension
alone only just fits and anything on top
pushes you into the tax system. That is
exactly what is happening. Around 9.58
million pensioners are expected to pay
income tax this year, roughly half a
million more than last year. About 1.1
million of them pay 40% or more. These
are not wealthy people. The threshold
stays frozen while the pension rises, so
more people cross the line without a
real pay rise. Your state pension is
paid with no tax taken off. HMRC
collects the tax by changing the code on
your other pension. So, the bill appears
as a smaller payment with no new money
to explain it.
And from the 6th of April 2027, tax on
savings income outside an ISA goes up by
two percentage points, from 20 to 22, 40
to 42, and 45 to 47%.
Number three, £10,000.
This is where pension credit starts
counting your savings as income. If you
are over state pension age and claim
pension credit, housing benefit, or help
with council tax, the first £10,000 is
ignored. Above that, for every £500 you
hold, or part of 500, you are treated as
having £1 a week of extra income. Back
to Maureen. With £12,000, she is four
lots of 500 over the line, so £4 a week
of income she does not have is counted
against her.
At £20,000, it would be £20 a week.
Pension credit has no upper savings
limit, which is good news. This tax
year, it tops your weekly income up to
£238 if you are single, or £363.25
for a couple.
And it is a doorway, not just a top-up.
It can open a free TV license at 75, the
warm home discount, cold weather
payments, and help with prescriptions,
dental treatment, and glasses. So, even
a small award is worth claiming.
Hold on to that, because number four
surprises people more than any other,
and it involves your own bank. Number
four, any amount at a bank where you owe
money.
Most people think their bank is a safe.
In law, it is a business and you may
have more than one contract with it.
Banks have a right called set-off. If
you fall behind on a debt, they can take
money from an account of yours that is
in credit to clear it. Meet Harold. He
is 73 with 12,000 pounds in savings and
an unpaid balance at the same bank. He
goes into hospital for 2 months and the
payments are missed. When he gets home,
3,600 pounds has gone from his savings.
No phone call, no court. The bank paid
itself.
But there is a real protection most
people have never heard of. It is called
the first right of appropriation. When
money is paid into your account, you
have the right to tell your bank how you
want it used. Write to them and say,
"This money is for my rent, my council
tax, my energy bills and my food." If
you do that, the bank should not sweep
it away to settle something else.
You can even invoke it after they have
taken the money. Write that letter
before you need it. And keep your spare
money in a separate account with a
provider where you owe nothing at all.
Before I show you number five, if this
is useful so far, hit subscribe. Now,
number five. Number five, a county court
judgment and then a third-party debt
order.
If someone wins a judgment against you,
they can go back to court and apply for
an interim third-party debt order. Your
bank is the third party. The order tells
the bank to freeze your account up to
the amount you owe. It can happen within
days and you may not hear about it until
you try to pay for something. Meet
Beryl. She is 78 and her state pension
goes straight into her current account.
Years ago, after her husband's illness,
she fell behind on a bill and the
creditor got a judgment for about 6,000
pounds. She forgot about it. Meanwhile,
she had moved 14,000 pounds of savings
into the same account because one
account felt simpler. The order arrives.
Her pension is now mixed in with her
savings, and untangling it takes time
she does not have because her rent is
due. So, what can you do? The order is
not final straight away. The final
hearing is at least 28 days after the
first, and you can object. And if the
freeze leaves you unable to pay for food
or heating, you can ask the court for a
hardship payment order using form N244.
But, the honest lesson is simpler. Do
not keep your life savings where your
pension lands. Two more lines, and the
last one is a big one. Number six, 15
years of silence.
An account goes quiet. Nobody logs in,
no money moves, and statements keep
going to an old address. Under the
dormant asset scheme, an account
untouched for 15 years can be treated as
dormant, and the balance can go to
Reclaim Fund Limited. Your money is
never taken from you, and you can
reclaim it anytime for free, but you
have to know it is there. Meet Edna. She
kept a rainy day account with 9,000
pounds and never touched it. Then, she
moved in with her daughter, and the
statements went to the old house. She
got the money back, but it took months
of paperwork. So, put one reminder in
your calendar each year. Log in to every
account you own, or move a small amount
in and out. Update your address with
every bank when you move. And if you
lose track of an account, use My Lost
Account, the free tracing service.
Now, the last line, the biggest sums on
the list. Number seven, 120,000 pounds.
If you learned the old figure of 85,000,
it has changed. For any bank, building
society, or credit union that fails
after the 30th of November 2025, the
Financial Services Compensation Scheme
covers you up to 120,000 pounds per
eligible person per institution. A joint
account gets that protection for each of
you, so a couple is covered up to
240,000 pounds at one firm. And there is
a clock hidden inside this rule. It is
called temporary high balance
protection.
When a large sum lands from a life
event, such as selling your home or an
inheritance, the scheme can protect up
to 1.4 million pounds, but it lasts 6
months from the day the money was paid
in. After that, cover drops back. Meet
Ken and Pauline. They sell their home
and 410,000 pounds sits in one joint
account while they look for somewhere to
live. 6 months later, the cover falls
away and 170,000 pounds is unprotected.
They never made a mistake, they just did
not know the clock existed. So, those
are the seven lines. 16,000 pounds for
means-tested benefits, 12,570
pounds where your pension meets the tax
system, 10,000 pounds where pension
credit counts your savings as income,
any amount in a bank where you owe
money, a court judgment and a frozen
account, 15 years of silence, and
120,000 pounds per person per bank with
a 6-month clock inside it. Now, the
amount you came here for. How much
should sit in the account where your
pension lands? The honest answer is that
British law does not shield a fixed sum.
There is no magic number a creditor must
leave alone. What you have instead is a
set of habits. Keep about 1 month of
bills in the account your pension is
paid into. Enough to run the month and
little left to argue about. Move
everything above that to a separate
account with a provider where you owe
nothing, and check that every pound
there sits inside the compensation
limit. And if a large sum ever lands,
write the 6-month date in your diary the
day it arrives. Say Don and Linda
receive their state pension into one
joint current account, about 2,000
pounds a month. They keep roughly 2,000
pounds there for the monthly bills.
Their other money sits in a separate
account with a provider where they owe
nothing. Each of them is inside the
compensation limit. Nothing they own
sits outside the safety net. Three
things are not happening, so you can
stop waiting for them. No letter arrives
before a bank uses set-off because the
money is simply gone from your
statement. No automatic protection
follows your state pension once it is
mixed with other money. And no warning
is issued before the 6-month clock runs
out. So, here is your list for this
week. Write down one number, 12,570
pounds, and remember your state pension
sits just under it. Check whether any
benefit you claim has a capital limit,
and add up honestly what you hold. Move
your savings away from any bank where
you owe money, and if you cannot, use
your first right of appropriation. Put
one yearly reminder in your calendar to
log in to every account and update your
address. Check your compensation cover
bank by bank, remembering the 240,000
pound figure for a couple. And if a
large sum ever arrives, write the
6-month date in your diary the same day.
One last thing, and it is free. If you
are over 50 and you have a defined
contribution pension, you are entitled
to free guidance from Pension Wise, part
of the Money and Pensions Service. It is
a real conversation with a trained
person, not a sales call. You do not
need to remember all seven lines.
Remember three: 12,570
pounds, 120,000 pounds, and 1 month of
bills where your pension arrives. Get
those three right, and most of these
traps will never touch you. My name is
Arthur Penrose, and I read the rules so
you do not have to. Subscribe before it
changes.

title: Never Keep This Much Money in Bank   HMRC Sees It All in 2026 UK

segments.text: There is an amount of money you should
never leave sitting idle in your bank
accounts in 2026.
Not because the bank will lose it, and
not because anyone will take it. It is
because your bank reports on your
accounts to the tax office every year,
and nobody ever tells you it is done it.
Before I go any further, I need to clear
up a misunderstanding that stops most
pensioners from hearing the rest of
this.
Some of you will think, this is only for
people with big savings, so it is not
for me. If you have a few thousand put
by for bills and a rainy day, you may
feel the tax office could not possibly
be interested in you. And some of you
will think the opposite. If you have
built up a decent pot over a lifetime of
careful saving, you may feel this is a
warning for people on benefits, not me.
You are both wrong. Genuinely, both of
you.
Whether your savings would fit in a
biscuit tin or fill several accounts,
the system treats you in exactly the
same way. On some of these points, it is
the modest saver who gets the nasty
surprise. On others, it is the
comfortable saver who quietly loses out.
I will tell you on every point who needs
to listen hardest, so nobody gets to
say, not me.
My name is Arthur Penrose, and on this
channel I explain UK pensions, benefits,
and tax in plain English, with no jargon
and no waffle. Today, I am going to take
you through five parts. What your bank
actually tells the tax office. Why 2026
is different. How much cash is the right
amount to keep. The benefits trap that
catches thousands of people, and where
to keep anything above that line safely.
Please stay to the end, because the last
part is the one that helps people most,
and it can be sorted in an afternoon.
Here is the idea that holds everything
together. The tax office does not see
your balance. It sees a photograph that
your bank sends once a year, and a
photograph can be old or incomplete or
wrong.
Being sensible with your money is not
about hiding it. It is about making sure
the photograph matches the real picture.
And I want to say something that nobody
says out loud. Wanting your money to
feel safe is not foolish. You worked for
it for decades. But safe from thieves
and sensible are two different things,
and the gap between them is where people
lose money without noticing.
So, let us start with what the tax
office actually sees because most people
have this backwards.
Part one is that your bank tells the tax
office about your accounts, and it never
tells you it has done it.
Many pensioners still believe this
system works like this. You add up
everything yourself at the end of the
year, you tell the tax office if you owe
anything, and if you say nothing,
nothing happens. That is not how it
works anymore.
Banks and building societies report
information about the income your
accounts produce to HMRC automatically
after the end of each tax year.
You do not sign anything. You do not get
a copy. There is no letter saying, "We
have told the taxman about your
accounts." It just happens with
computers talking to computers.
HMRC then uses that information to
adjust your tax code for the next year.
If it thinks your savings will produce
the same taxable income again, it can
lower your tax-free pay to collect the
tax in advance straight out of your
pension. Now, who does this hit? Both of
you in different ways.
If you are on a modest income, a state
pension, and a small workplace pension,
this can be frightening
because you assume you are too small to
be noticed. You are not. If you are more
comfortable with money spread across two
or three accounts, it can hit harder
because HMRC adds the accounts together.
Three small amounts from three different
banks become one larger figure in its
computer.
Imagine a woman we will call Norma. She
is 71 with four savings accounts she
opened over the years, each at a
different bank. She never added them up.
Her banks did. The following year, her
tax code changed, and her monthly
pension went down. She had not had a pay
