67. For people born a little earlier, it
is a few months sooner.
Now, here is the best part. Once you
reach full retirement age, the earnings
test disappears completely. There is no
limit at all. You can earn as much as
you want and keep every dollar of your
Social Security. Meet Hank. Hank is 63.
He took Social Security early, then got
bored, and went back to work part-time
at a hardware store. Last year, Hank
earned a little over the limit, and
Social Security held back part of his
check. Hank was furious. He thought that
money was just gone. But, here is what
almost nobody tells you. That money is
not lost. When Hank reaches full
retirement age, Social Security
recalculates his benefit and gives him
credit for every month they held money
back. His check goes up from then on.
Therefore, if you are working and
collecting early, look at the new limit
and plan your hours around it. And if
money has been held back, do not panic.
It is not gone. It comes back to you in
a higher check later. But, the next
piece of good news has nothing to do
with work. It has to do with taxes, and
the filing season that opens in January
is the first time a lot of seniors will
see how big it really is.
Number four, tax season opens in
January, and seniors get the biggest
deductions they've ever had. Let me
clear something up first, because there
is a lot of confusion out there. Social
Security did not become tax-free. You
may have heard that on the news or seen
it online. It is not true. If your
income is high enough, part of your
Social Security can still be taxed. But,
here is the good news. Congress created
something that for a lot of seniors gets
them to the same place.
When you file your taxes for 2026,
starting in late January, you get three
separate breaks just for being over 65.
First, the regular standard deduction.
For a single filer, that is $16,100.
Second, the extra amount for being 65 or
older. For a single filer, that is
$2,050 more. And third, the brand new
senior deduction. That is $6,000 for
every person 65 or older, and it runs
through 2028. Add those up, and a single
senior can subtract $24,150
from their income before the IRS taxes a
single penny.
For a married couple who are both over
plus $1,650 each for age, plus $6,000
each for the senior deduction. That is
And here's what makes the senior
deduction different from almost every
other tax break. You get it whether you
take the standard deduction or itemize.
Most deductions make you choose. This
one does not. Meet Betty. Betty is 68
and a widow. She has a small pension,
some interest from her savings, and her
social security. She has been paying a
little income tax every year since her
husband passed. This year with all three
of these breaks stacked together, a lot
of her taxable income simply disappears.
Depending on her exact number, she may
owe much less than last year or nothing
at all. But, there is a catch. The
senior deduction starts to shrink if
your income is above $75,000 for a
single filer or $150,000 for a married
couple. And it only helps you if it
actually ends up on your return. I have
seen seniors use cheap tax software or
rush preparer or skip a question about
their age and miss money they were
entitled to. The IRS is not going to
call you and say you forgot something.
Therefore, when you file this winter,
look for the senior deduction by name.
Make sure the extra amount for age is
there for every person on the return who
is 65 or older. And if you want someone
to check it for free, the IRS runs a
program called Tax Counseling for the
Elderly. You can find the nearest site
by calling 800-906-9887.
But, taxes are only one bill that gets
smaller in January. The next one shows
up at the pharmacy counter and for some
people, it is the biggest drop of all.
Number five. On January 1st, the price
Medicare pays for 15 of the most
expensive drugs drops. For the first
time ever, Medicare was allowed to
negotiate directly with drug companies.
The first round of lower prices started
this year. The second round starts on
January 1st, 2027, and it covers 15 more
drugs.
Here are a couple of examples from
Medicare's own numbers. Ozempic, along
with Wegovy and Rybelsus, had a list
price of about $959 for a 30-day supply.
The new negotiated price is $274.
Trelegy, a common inhaler for breathing
problems, goes from $6,000 or to $75.
The full list includes drugs for
diabetes, cancer, breathing problems,
and more, including Xtandi, Ibrance,
Linzess, Breo, Tradjenta, Janumet, and
Otezla. Medicare estimates people on
drug plans will save about $685 million
out of their own pockets.
Now, I want to be honest with you. Your
exact copay depends on your plan.
A lower price for Medicare does not
automatically mean the same discount for
you at the counter, but a lower
negotiated price pushes everything in
your direction. And there is another
protection that keeps working in
January. Your out-of-pocket costs for
covered drugs on the Medicare drug plan
are capped. For 2027, the cap is $2,400
for the whole year. Once you hit it, you
pay nothing more for covered drugs until
the year starts over. And insulin is
capped at $35 a month.
Meet Ray. Ray is 70 and takes three
brand-name medications, one of them on
the negotiated list. A few years ago,
there was no cap at all, and Ray was
spending thousands of dollars a year at
the pharmacy. Now, his worst case for
the whole year has a ceiling, and one of
his drugs just got a lot cheaper for
Medicare to buy. Therefore, if you take
any of these drugs, look at your plan's
notice for next year, and call your plan
in January to ask what your copay is
now.
And if you are still deciding on a plan,
you have until December 7th to compare
and switch. Plans change their drug
lists every single year, so a drug that
is covered today may not be covered next
year.
5 minutes on the phone now can save you
a very expensive surprise in January.
But the next piece of good news is for
the people who need it most, and it
arrives before January even starts.
Number six, SSI goes up, and the January
payment arrives early. SSI stands for
supplemental security income. It is a
separate program from regular social
security, and it is for people 65 and
older or disabled who have very little
income and very few assets. A lot of
seniors get both a small social security
check and an SSI payment on top of it.
In January, the federal SSI payment goes
up. For an individual, it from $994 a
month to $1,029.
For a couple, it goes from $1,491
till $544.
And here is a little bonus. Because
January 1st is a holiday, the January
SSI payment is actually sent out on
December 31st. So, the raise shows up
before the new year even begins. Now,
here is the part that matters most. A
lot of seniors who qualify for SSI have
never applied because they think they
own too much. The limit is $2,000 in
countable resources for an individual
and $3,000 for a couple. But the home
you live in generally does not count.
One car generally does not count. Many
personal belongings do not count. Meet
Marie. Marie is 81. Her Social Security
is small because she spent years at home
raising five children. She owns her
little house, an old car, and has about
$1,500 in the bank. But Marie always
assumed owning a home meant she could
not qualify for anything. She was wrong.
Therefore, if your income is very low
and your savings are under those limits,
not counting your home and car, call
Social Security and ask to apply for
SSI. The number is 1-800-772-1213.
Even a small SSI payment can open the
door to other help, including help with
medical bills. But the biggest piece of
good news on this list is not SSI. It is
the one I promised you at the beginning,
the one worth about $2,400 a year.
Number seven, a program that pays your
Medicare premium for you. Remember that
Part B premium I talked about? Easy 202
dollars 90 cents a month taken right out
of your Social Security check. Over a
year, that is $2,434.80.
There is a set of programs that will pay
that premium for you.
They're called Medicare Savings
Programs. When you qualify, the premium
stops coming out of your check and that
money goes straight back into your
pocket. That is the $2,400 a year I
promised you.
And here is why most people never apply.
They think these programs are only for
people with almost no income. That is
not clear as a throat true. There are
three main levels. The first, called
QMB, pays your Part B premium and also
your deductibles, coinsurance, and
copays.
For this year, the income limit for an
individual is about $1,350 a month. The
second, called SLMB, pays your Part B
premium. The income limit is about
a month for an individual. And the
third, called QI, also pays your Part B
premium. The income limit is about
a month for an individual or $2,455
for a couple. Think about that. A single
person with about $1,800 a month of
income can still qualify to have their
Medicare premium paid. That is a lot of
retirees. There is usually an asset
limit, too, about $19,950 for an
individual and $14,910 for a couple. But
your home and your car generally do not
count. And some states set the limits
higher or drop the asset test
completely. But wait, because it gets
better. If you qualify for any of these
Medicare Savings Programs, you
automatically qualify for another
program called Extra Help, which lowers
what you pay for prescription drugs. In
2027, the standard deductible on a
Medicare drug plan can be as high as
$700. With Extra Help, your deductible
is zero and your copays are capped at
$5.80 for a generic and $14.40 for a
brand-name drug.
Let's go back to Marie. Her income is
well under those limits. Once she
qualifies for a Medicare Savings
Program, $202.90
a month stops coming out of her Social
Security check. On top of her raise,
that adds about $2,400 a year back in
her pocket plus a $0 drug deductible
from Extra Help. And for a married
couple where both spouses qualify, the
premium savings can be close to $4,900 a
year. That is real money. That is
groceries, a car repair, a gift for the
grandkids, or simply not worrying about
the next bill. Therefore, if your income
is anywhere near those limits, apply. Do
not decide for yourself that you are
over. Let them tell you. Medicare
Savings Programs are run through your
state Medicaid office and you can apply
even if you've never been on Medicaid
and never will be. When you call, ask
for the Medicare Savings Program
application by name and ask whether your
state uses higher limits than the
federal ones. If you are turned down,
ask for the reason in writing because
mistakes happen and you can appeal. So,
let's put all seven together. Here is
your January checklist. One, your Social
Security goes up 3.6% automatically.
When the notice comes, compare it line
by line with last year's.
Two,
the hold harmless rule protects most
people from Medicare shrinking their
check. If you pay the IRMAA surcharge
and your income has dropped, file form
SSA-44.
Three, if you are working and collecting
early, the earnings limit rises to
Money held back is not lost, it comes
back later.
Four, when you file your taxes, make
sure the $6,000 senior deduction and the
extra amount for age are on your return.
Five, if you take one of the 15
negotiated drugs, call your plan in
January and ask what you pay now. Your
yearly drug costs are capped at $2,400.
Six, if your income and savings are very
low, apply for SSI even if you own your
home.
Seven, if your income is under about
$1,800 a month, apply for a Medicare
Savings Program. It can put about $2,400
a year back in your check and it opens
the door to extra help. You can call
Social Security at 1-800-772-1213.

title: Every Senior Should Do These 7 Things in November — Or Pay More in 2027

segments.text: Some of the money you have already paid
this year is about to disappear. Not
stolen, not lost, reset. At midnight on
New Year's Eve, a set of counters you
have been filling up since January goes
back to zero. What you have paid toward
your Medicare costs, what you have spent
toward your drug plan's yearly limit,
the amount you are allowed to give each
person you love without a single form,
the new tax breaks in the law signed
last summer, the yearly room in the new
accounts the government just opened for
your grandchildren. Every one of them
starts over on the 1st of January, and
whatever you did not use is simply gone.
And here is what makes November the
month that matters. Most of these
counters cannot really be used in
December. Even if you are bucked to
paperwork, it takes weeks and the
offices close for the holidays. So,
today I am going to walk you through
each counter, how to see where your
stands right now, and what to do before
the 30th of November. And there is one
counter in this video that never resets
at all. It runs for 5 years, and it is
the one that can turn a Christmas gift
into a $70,000 bill.
Why the 30th of November and not the
31st of December? Because almost
everything on this list needs somebody
else to do something first. A doctor has
to write a prescription, a surgery
center has to find an opening, a
retirement account company has to
process a request, and most of them set
their own cutoff dates well before New
Year's Eve. Medicare's own enrollment
window closes on the 7th of December.
And the last week of the year is
Christmas week when doctors' offices,
pharmacies, and account companies run on
holiday hours and skeleton staff. If you
treat the end of November as your
deadline, you finish with room to spare.
If you treat the end of December as your
deadline, you are relying on everybody
else being fast in the busiest month of
their year. Every source used here is
listed in the description, so you can
check it yourself. This is education,
not personal advice, and some of it
depends on your state and your plan. The
first counter is your health hour, and
for most people watching, it is really
three counters. The first is your Part B
deductible. In 2026, it is $283.
Once you have paid it, Medicare pays 80%
of covered doctor and outpatient care
for the rest of the year. Now, if you
have a supplement like plan G, that
supplement usually pays the other 20. In
January, it starts over and Medicare's
trustees project it will rise to about
The second is the limit on your drug
costs. This year, the most anybody in a
Medicare drug plan can pay out of pocket
for covered drugs is $2,100.
Once you reach that line, your covered
prescriptions cost you nothing for the
rest of the year, zero. On the 1st of
January, the counter resets and next
year the limit rises to 2,400
with a deductible of up to $700 before
your plan starts sharing the cost. The
third counter is for anybody in a
Medicare Advantage plan. Every one of
those plans has a yearly maximum
out-of-pocket for covered care in its
network. In 2026, Medicare allows plans
to set it as high as $9,250.
And according to KFF, the average is
around 5,400.
Once you reach your plan's maximum, the
plan pays 100% of covered care in its
network for the rest of the year.
Every office visit, every scan, every
outpatient procedure, and then at
midnight on New Year's Eve, it all
starts again from nothing.
If your plan is a PPO, it actually has
two maximums, one for care inside the
network and a higher one for care inside
and outside combined. So, ask which one
you're close to.
If you have the high deductible version
of plan G, you have one more counter of
your own just under $3,000 and it resets
the same night. There is one Medicare
counter that does not follow the
calendar and people get it wrong in both
directions. The part A deductible, the
one for a hospital stay, is $736 this
year.
But, it is not charged once a year. It
is charged once per benefit period,
which starts when you are admitted and
ends after you have been out of the
hospital and out of skilled nursing care
for 60 days in a row. So, a hospital
stay in December and another in February
can mean two deductibles if they fall in
separate benefit periods and two stays a
month apart can mean only one. New
Year's Day has nothing to do with it.
Ma reached her plan's maximum in
September. A fall in the spring, a
broken wrist, surgery, and weeks of
therapy, and by the end of summer she
had paid $5,900,
the most her plan could charge her.
In October, her eye doctor told her she
was ready for cataract surgery in both
eyes. The scheduler offered two dates,
the 18th of December or the 8th of
January. Ma picked January so the
holidays would be quiet. Nobody in that
office mentioned her counter because
nobody in that office knew about it. In
January, her counter was back at zero.
The surgery center co-pays, the
follow-up visits, and the specialist
charges added up to about $1,100.
In December, the same two surgeries
would have cost her nothing.
Ma did not choose wrong. She chose
without one piece of information that
her plan had and her surgeon's office
did not. The scheduler was thinking
about the calendar, the plan was not
going to call, and Ma had no reason to
know that a single date on that calendar
was worth $1,100. So, here is how to
read your own health counters this week.
For a Medicare Advantage plan, log in to
your plan's website or call the number
on your card and ask one question.
How much have I paid toward my maximum
out-of-pocket this year? They have the
number. For a drug plan, look at the
monthly statement your plan mails you,
usually called an explanation of
benefits. Somewhere on it is a line for
your total out-of-pocket cost so far
this year. If it says $2,100,
you are at the limit. And if you change
drug plans partway through this year,
the amount you paid under your old plan
generally follows you to the new one for
the rest of the year. So, do not assume
you started over. For part B, your
Medicare Summary Notice or your account
on Medicare's website shows whether your
deductible has been met.
Then, if you are at or near any of those
limits, think about what you've been
putting off. A procedure your doctor has
already said you need. A scan? Physical
therapy? Hearing tests? New glasses if
your plan covers them? Not care you do
not need. Care you were going to get
anyway, just in January. Call this month
because surgery centers and specialists
often book 4 to 6 weeks out. And if your
plan requires permission in advance,
that approval can take time, too.
The drug counter needs a little more
care because there are rules about
refills. If you have reached the limit,
ask your doctor this month to write your
regular prescriptions for a 90-day
supply if that is appropriate for you.
Most plans let you refill once you have
used most of your current supply, often
somewhere around three power meds. So,
time your last refill of the year to
land before the 31st, and you can carry
several months of medicine into January
at no cost. I want to be precise about
what that does. If your drug costs land
you near the limit every year, moving a
few months of medicine into a year you
have already paid for can genuinely
lower what you pay next year. If your
costs are far above the limit every
year, you will probably reach next
year's limit anyway. So, it mostly
changes when you pay rather than how
much. But even that helps because
January is when the new deductible hits
all at once. And if you are switching
drug plans on the 1st of January, check
whether your new plan covers the same
drugs before you stock up, so you are
not left mid-supply on a medicine your
new plan treats differently.
One more health counter, and this one
belongs to people in Advantage plans
with extras. Dental allowances, vision
allowances, hearing aid allowances, and
those cards loaded with money for
groceries or over-the-counter items.
Those almost never roll over. If you
have $500 of dental coverage left, that
cleaning and filling are worth now.
Dentists fill up in December for exactly
this reason. Now, a word for anybody who
is about to leave for the winter because
November is when a lot of you pack the
car and head south. Original Medicare
works with any doctor or hospital in the
country that takes Medicare.
A Medicare Advantage plan usually does
not work that way.
Many Advantage plans, especially the
ones called HMOs, cover routine care
only inside your home network.
Away from home, they generally cover
emergencies and urgent care and not much
else. So, before you leave, call your
plan and ask what it covers in the state
where you'll be spending the winter and
whether it has a travel or visitor
program.
Ask your drug plan whether your pharmacy
chain is in network down there or set up
mail order to your winter address.
And if you are traveling outside the
country for the holidays, know that
original Medicare generally does not pay
for care abroad.
Several supplement plans, including plan
G and plan N, include a foreign travel
emergency benefit and some advantage do,
too. Find out before you board, not in a
foreign emergency room. The second
counter is the one people misunderstand
most and it is the one that comes out in
December. Gifts. Every year the IRS lets
you give a certain amount to any one
person without filing anything at all.
For 2026, that amount is $19,000 per
person. A married couple can each give
it, so together you can give $38,000
each child, each grandchild, anyone you
like without a single form. And that
allowance does not carry forward. If you
give nothing this year, you do not get
to give $38,000 next year. On the 1st of
January, the counter resets. Two things
almost nobody tells you about that
number. First, going over it does not
mean you owe tax. It means you file a
gift tax return, form 709, and the extra
is subtracted from a lifetime amount.
Under the law President Trump signed
last summer, that lifetime amount is $15
million per person starting this year.
Very few families will ever pay a dollar
of gift tax.
Second, there are payments that do not
count toward the 19,000 at all. If you
pay a grandchild's college tuition
directly to the school or pay someone's
medical bill directly to the hospital or
doctor, there is no limit for gift tax
purposes. The money has to go straight
to the school or the provider, not to
the grandchild. And if you are helping a
grandchild with college, one rule
changed recently in your favor. On the
newer financial aid form, money that a
grandparent pays out of a college
savings plan is no longer counted as the
student's income.
For years, a grandparent's generosity
could quietly shrink a grandchild's aid.
That trap is largely gone. There is also
a way to use 5 years of the gift
allowance at once, but only for college
savings. You can put up to 5 years worth
into a grandchild's college savings plan
in a single year, $95,000 from one
person, or $190,000 from a married
couple, and spread it across 5 years on
your gift tax return.
Hold that thought because of what I am
about to tell you about the counter that
never resets.
One timing detail about the gift counter
itself, a gift by check generally counts
in the year the check is deposited and
paid, not the year you wrote it. A check
written on the 28th of December and
cashed on the 3rd of January can land in
next year's counter. If the year
matters, give early or ask the person to
deposit it right away.
Now, the newest place grandparents can
give, and it opened only weeks ago. The
law signed last summer created a new
kind of account for children, officially
called Trump accounts.
On the 1st of October, the Treasury
announced it had automatically opened
accounts for more than 60 million
children under 18.
Treasury Secretary Scott Besant put it
this way, "Over 60 million more eligible
children now have an account ready to be
claimed."
>> Ready to be claimed is the important
part.
>> The account cannot receive a dollar from
anyone until a parent claims it in the
Trump accounts app or on the official
website by verifying who they are and
that the child is theirs.
And there is money waiting in the system
that many families are going to miss.
A child who is a United States citizen
born from the beginning of 2025 through
the end of 2028 can receive a $1,000
deposit from the government, but it is
not automatically deposited. A parent
has to choose it, usually on a form
called form 4547 or through the online
system.
Before the Treasury stepped in, only
about 5.6 million sign-up forms had been
processed for more than 70 million
eligible children. So, if you have a
grandchild born last year or this year,
the single most valuable thing you can
do this Thanksgiving may be to ask your
son or daughter one question, Have you
claimed the account and did you elect
the $1,000? If they have, family and
friends can contribute up to $5,000 a
year per child combined and that limit
resets every January, too. The money
must be invested in low-cost funds that
track the American stock market until
the child turns 18. Two honest cautions.
Your contribution is not tax deductible
for you and the Treasury is still
finishing some of the rules including
how gifts of stock will work. So, some
advisors suggest starting small until
the final rules are written. A modest
holiday contribution is a fine way to
begin. A very large one can wait for the
details. And if your grandchild is a
little older, born from 2016 through
2024, check one more thing. Michael and
Susan Dell pledged $6.25 billion to put
$250 into the accounts of about $250
into the accounts of about 25 million
children that age in zip codes where the
typical household earns under $150,000 a
year.
No application is needed, but the
account still has to be claimed before
anyone can see it. The money generally
cannot come out until the year the child
turns 18 and after that it follows rules
much like an IRA. Now, here is the
counter that never resets and it is the
one that turns all of that generosity
into danger.
Medicaid.
If you or your husband or wife ever need
long-term care in a nursing home and
apply for Medicaid to help pay for it,
the state looks back at every gift you
made during the previous 5 years. In
California, it is shorter, 30 months,
and California brought its asset test
back this year. But for most of the
country, it is 5 years and here is the
sentence I most want you to hear today.
The $19,000 IRS allowance means nothing
to Medicaid. Nothing. A gift can be
perfectly fine with the IRS and still
count fully against you for Medicaid.
The same is true of tuition you pay
directly to a college. Medicaid
generally treats it as a gift and so is
that 5-year lump sum into a college
savings plan.
One generous afternoon at the bank can
sit inside the look back window for the
next 5 years.
The penalty works like this. The state
adds up the gifts made inside the look
back window. Then it divides that total
by what a month in a nursing home costs
in your state, a figure each state sets.
The answer is the number of months
Medicaid will refuse to pay for your
care, and here's the cruel part. That
penalty does not start the day you made
the gift. Under federal rules, it starts
only when you are already in care, your
savings are already spent down, and you
would otherwise qualify. It lands at the
worst possible moment on the people
least able to absorb it. And notice the
difference between giving and spending.
Medicaid penalizes transfers for less
than their value. It does not penalize
you for spending your own money on
yourself, repairing your own roof,
paying off your own mortgage, buying a
reliable car you will use. In most
states, prepaying your own funeral
through an arrangement that cannot be
canceled within the state's limits.
Those are generally not gifts.
Giving a grandchild the money to fix
their roof is. Josephine gave each of
her four grandchildren $19,000 two
Christmases ago. A teller at her bank
told her that was the legal limit, and
she believed she was being careful.
$76,000 to four young people she adored
for houses and school and fresh starts.
Last spring she had a stroke. After
rehab, she needed full-time care. Her
savings went quickly, and when her
daughter applied for Medicaid, the case
worker found the four gifts. In her
state, a month in a nursing home was
counted at about $11,000.
$76,000 became almost 7 months with no
Medicaid payment for her care. Her
family had two choices, ask four
grandchildren to return the money or
find $76,000 themselves. Josephine did
everything she was told. The problem is
that she was told about the wrong rule.
The IRS line and the Medicaid line are
two different lines written by two
different parts of the government, and
nobody at the bank counter was ever
going to explain the second one.
So, what should you actually do?
First, be realistic about your own odds.
If you are in good health, your savings
are large enough to pay for years of
care, or you have long-term care
insurance, the lookback may never touch
you.
If your savings are modest, and your
health is uncertain, it matters a great
deal.

One day of birth, $6,000 of deduction.

And here is the connection almost nobody

For marketplace help, the income they

title: Every Senior Should Check These 6 Things Before October Is Over

segments.text: October is the busiest month of the year
for anyone on Social Security and
Medicare, and this year it is busier
than usual. In the space of 31 days,
there is a new federal budget year, a
new set of food assistance rules, an
announcement that sets your income for
next year, the opening of the window
that sets your health costs for next
year, a tax deadline that a lot of
retirees forget, and a quiet deadline
for anyone with money in savings. And
alongside the real changes, there is a
flood of noise. Videos and messages
claiming your Social Security is being
cut in October, that you must verify
your account or lose your benefits, that
a new rule will take your savings. Most
of that is wrong, and some of it is
designed to frighten you into handing
over information. So, this video is a
calendar. I am going to walk through
October date by date. For each date, I
will tell you what is actually changing,
who it reaches, and the one thing to do.
And I will finish with three things you
may have heard about that are not
happening this October, so you can put
them down and stop worrying. My name is
Franklin. I have spent years helping
seniors and their families work through
rules like these. I am not your lawyer,
your accountant, or your financial
advisor, and this is general education,
not advice for your situation. If this
is useful, subscribe and send it to
someone who has been getting frightening
messages about October.
On the 1st of October, the federal
government's new financial year began.
That date matters for three groups of
people. The first group is anyone who
receives food assistance through SNAP.
Every year, on the 1st of October, the
program's numbers reset. This year, the
most a single person can receive rose to
$36 a month in the lower 48 states. The
standard deduction for small households
rose to $717, and the savings limit for
households with someone 60 or older, or
with a disability, rose from $4,500 to
A handful of quiet rules decide who
keeps their money in retirement. There
is also a rule change many people in
their late 50s and early 60s have not
heard about. Under last year's federal
budget law, SNAP's work requirement now
reaches adults up to age 64 who do not
have dependent children and do not
qualify for an exemption. If that is
you, you generally need to work,
volunteer, or train for 80 hours a month
to keep benefits beyond 3 months in a
3-year period. People 65 and older are
completely exempt, and there are
exemptions for people who are unable to
work or who are caring for someone who
cannot care for themselves. But those
exemptions usually have to be claimed
and shown. And here is the SNAP rule I
most want older viewers to know. If you
are 60 or older, you can deduct out of
pocket medical costs above $35 a month,
including your Medicare Part B premium.
Many older people on SNAP never report
those costs, and they receive far less
than they are entitled to. The second
group is certain lawfully present
immigrants, such as refugees and people
granted asylum, who under the same
budget law generally stop qualifying for
Medicaid from the 1st of October, unless
they are lawful permanent residents or
fall into certain protected groups. If
you are a citizen, this does not reach
you.
And the third group is everyone on
Medicare, because the 1st of October was
the day insurance companies were allowed
to begin marketing next year's plans.
That means your phone, your mailbox, and
your television are about to fill up.
Remember one rule, a legitimate agent
generally may not call you out of the
blue. If they came to you, be careful.
If you went to them, you are usually
fine.
And there is one more thing tied to the
new federal year. Heating assistance for
the coming winter through the program
called LEAP Heat starts its new year on
the 1st of October. Many states open
applications in October or around the
1st of November. And in a lot of places,
the money is handed out as applications
arrive until it runs out. If you need
help with heating bills, apply early.
Dial 211 to find where to apply. On the
14th of October, Social Security is
scheduled to announce next year's cost
of living adjustment on the same morning
the September inflation figures are
published. Here is where the estimate
stand. ARPE estimates 3.6%, the Senior
Citizens League estimates 3.5, the
analyst Mary Johnson estimates 3.4. On
the average retirement benefit of
a raise of 3.5% is about $72 a month,
but the raise is not the only number
announced that day. Social Security also
announces the new earnings limit for
people under full retirement age who are
still working, which this year is
It announces the new maximum amount of
wages subject to Social Security tax,
which this year is $184,500.
It announces the new SSI payment
amounts, which this year are $94
for an individual, and it announces the
maximum benefit.
Here is what to do with the raise. Do
not write down the percentage, write
down the dollar amount of your raise.
Then wait for the Medicare Part B
premium for next year, which is usually
announced in November. The Medicare
trustees projected it at about $29.50,
up from $22.90, and although some
analysts expect it to come in higher.
Subtract the premium increase from your
raise. What is left is your real raise.
Let me tell you about a woman I will
call Bonnie. Bonnie is 70, a retired
dental assistant in Oregon. Every year
she tells her children the raise
percentage on the day it is announced,
and every January she is disappointed
when her check goes up by less. This
year she is going to wait for the
premium and do the subtraction first. It
sounds small, but it changes the
conversation from why did I get less
than they said to here is exactly what I
will have.
The 15th of October is a date with two
completely different deadlines attached,
and retirees tend to remember only one.
The first is the opening of Medicare
open enrollment season.
Subtract the premium increase from your
raise. What is left is your real raise.
Let me tell you about a woman I will
call Bonnie. Bonnie is 70, a retired
dental assistant in Oregon. Every year
she tells her children the raise
percentage on the day it is announced,
and every January she is disappointed
when her check goes up by less. This
year she is going to wait for the
premium and do the subtraction first. It
sounds small, but it changes the
conversation from why did I get less
than they said to here is exactly what I
will have. The 15th of October is a date
with two completely different deadlines
attached, and retirees tend to remember
only one. The first is the opening of
Medicare open enrollment. From the 15th
of October to the 7th of December, you
can change your Medicare Advantage plan,
change your drug plan, or move between
Medicare Advantage and Original
Medicare. This year it matters more than
usual. Insurers are pulling back. One
large insurer says its plan exits will
affect about 600,000 members, and
analysts estimate about one in 10
Medicare Advantage members will need a
new plan. Many plans that continue are
cutting extras like dental coverage and
the money some plans paid back toward
your Part B premium. And on the drug
side, two numbers are already set for
next year. The highest a standard drug
plan deductible can be rises from $615
to $700, and the most you can pay out of
pocket for covered drugs in a year rises
from $2,100 to $2,400. So, the action is
this. Open the annual notice of change
your plan sent you. Check whether your
plan is continuing. Check your doctors
and your drugs, and compare the total
yearly cost on the plan finder at
medicare.gov or with your state's free
ship counselors who sell nothing. The
second deadline on the 15th of October
has nothing to do with Medicare. It is
the deadline to file your tax return if
you asked the IRS for an extension back
in April. A surprising number of
retirees request an extension because a
corrected tax form arrived late or
because a spouse died and the paperwork
was complicated and then lose track of
the October date. If you filed an
extension and have not yet filed your
return, the 15th of October is the day.
And while you are thinking about that
return, here is something to check. Last
year's tax law created an extra
deduction of up to $6,000 for each
person 65 or older for the tax years
2025 through 2028. If you were eligible
for 2025 and it was not claimed, it may
be worth asking your preparer about
amending your return. Let me tell you
about a man I will call Hector. Hector
is 76, a retired bus mechanic in New
Jersey. His wife died in February and
his tax paperwork was the last thing on
his mind in April. So, his son filed an
extension. In September, the son
realized the October deadline was close.
When they finally sat down with the
preparer, they found that Hector
qualified for the new senior deduction
and that he and his late wife could
still file jointly for the year she
died. The return they filed was far
better than the one they had feared.
Now, the savings part of this video,
because October has a quiet deadline for
anyone with money set aside. If you buy
United States Series I Savings Bonds,
the inflation-linked bonds sold by the
Treasury, their interest rate resets
twice a year on the 1st of May and the
1st of November.
A bond bought by the end of October
keeps the current rate for its first 6
months. A bond bought in November gets
the new rate. Nobody can tell you in
advance whether the new rate will be
higher or lower. So, I am not telling
you to rush, but if you were planning to
buy I bonds anyway, it is worth checking
the current rate and the forecast before
the end of the month. The same thinking
applies to certificates of deposit. If
you have a CD maturing this autumn, do
not let it roll over automatically into
whatever the bank offers. Banks often
renew a maturing CD at a rate lower than
their best advertised rate. Look at what
your bank and other banks and credit
unions are offering before it renews and
compare with Treasury bills whose
interest is exempt from state income
tax. And here is the part almost nobody
connects to their social security.
Interest from savings, CDs, and Treasury
bills counts as income and income
affects your social security in two
ways. It counts toward the calculation
that decides how much of your social
security is taxed using lines that have
not changed since the 1980s and 90s and
it can raise your Medicare premiums 2
years later through the income-related
surcharge. For most people with modest
savings, earning more interest is still
clearly worth it. But, if your income is
close to one of those lines, the timing
of when interest lands, December or
January, can matter. Let me tell you
about a woman I will call Wilma. Wilma
is 73, a retired librarian in Wisconsin.
For 10 years her savings earned almost
nothing. In the last 2 years her CDs
renewed at much better rates. And this
spring for the first time part of her
Social Security was taxable. She thought
she had made a mistake. She had not. Her
savings were finally earning something
and that pushed her across the line that
has not moved since 1984. The new senior
deduction helps a great deal, but she
now looks at the whole picture before a
CD renews. October is also the right
month to start two-year end tasks
because both have a hard deadline of the
31st of December and both get harder the
longer you wait. The first is your
required minimum distribution. If you
are 73 or older and have a traditional
IRA or an old 401k, the IRS requires you
to take a minimum amount out each year.
Miss it and the penalty is 25% of the
amount you should have taken, reduced to
10% if you correct it in time.
Financial companies get very busy in
December. So ask yours now whether this
year's distribution has been taken or
scheduled.
The second for anyone who gives to a
church or charity and is 70 and a half
or older is a qualified charitable
distribution. Instead of writing a check
from your bank account, you ask your IRA
custodian to send the gift directly to
the charity. That money counts toward
your required distribution, but it is
not added to your taxable income. For
many people that is a better deal than
any deduction because it keeps your
income lower, which can reduce the tax
on your Social Security and help keep
you below the Medicare surcharge lines.
The paperwork takes time, so start in
October. One more date belongs on this
calendar even though it falls just after
October. If you or your spouse are
retired but not yet 65 and you buy
health insurance through the
marketplace, open enrollment for next
year begins on the 1st of November. This
matters more than usual.
The extra premium help that many
marketplace buyers received from 2021
through 2025 expired at the end of last
year.
Premium help is once again limited to
households with incomes up to 400% of
the federal poverty level, and many
people saw their premiums rise sharply
this year. Insurers have proposed
further increases for next year. If you
are an early retiree, look carefully at
your options in November, and remember
that the income you report decides your
help. So, the timing of withdrawals and
Social Security can matter a great deal
before 65.
There is one more thing worth doing in
October, and it takes 10 minutes. Social
Security has said it will finish moving
everyone off paper checks by the end of
this year.
Fewer than 1% of beneficiaries still
receive paper checks, but if you or a
parent are among them, do not wait for a
final notice. Set up direct deposit or
ask for the Direct Express prepaid debit
card if you do not have a bank account.
And whether you get a paper check or
not, set up your own My Social Security
account online if you have not already.
Criminals have been creating accounts in
other people's names and redirecting
their payments. The best protection is
to create your own account first. In
early December, your notice showing next
year's benefit and deductions will also
appear there, often before the paper
letter.
There is one particular scam aimed at
savings that rises every autumn, and I
want to describe it word for word
because it works on careful people. It
starts with a call, a text, or a pop-up
on your computer saying, "There is a
problem with your bank account." or that
your identity has been used in a crime.
You are passed to someone claiming to be
from your bank's fraud department or
from a federal agency. They tell you
your savings are at risk, and you must
move them to a safe account, or withdraw
cash, or buy gold and hand it to a
courier for safekeeping.
They tell you not to tell anyone, not
even your bank, because the bank staff
may be involved.
Every part of that is a lie. No real
bank and no government agency will ever
ask you to move your money to protect
it, withdraw cash for a courier, or keep
it secret from your family. Your
deposits are already protected by
federal deposit insurance up to $250,000
per depositor per bank for each
ownership category.
If anyone asks you to move money to keep
it safe, stop, hang up, and call your
bank on the number on your card or call
a family member first.
Now, as I promised, three things you may
have heard about that are not happening
this month. First, your Social Security
benefit is not being cut in October.
There is no rule that reduces your check
this month. Your benefit rises in
January with the cost of living
adjustment. Second, there is no
automatic 4% Medicare cut coming from
last year's budget law. You may have
heard that one. When the law added to
the deficit, an old budget rule could
have triggered automatic cuts, including
up to 4% to Medicare payments to doctors
and hospitals. Last November, Congress
cleared that effect away as it has every
time before. It is not happening, and
even if it had, it would have reduced
payments to providers, not your benefit.
Third, Social Security is not running
out of money this year. The trustees
report from June projects that the
retirement trust fund will run short in
late 2032. If Congress did nothing at
all before then, benefits would
continue, but at about 78% of the
scheduled amount. That is a serious
problem that Congress needs to fix, and
the earlier it does, the better. But, it
is not an October problem, and anyone
telling you your benefits are
disappearing this autumn is wrong. Every
October brings the same scams. A caller
text says your Social Security will be
suspended unless you verify your account
or claim your 2027 raise, or your
Medicare card is being replaced and you
must confirm your number. None of those
are real. The raise is automatic. There
is no new Medicare card. Social Security
will not call you out of the blue asking
for your Social Security number or bank
details. Hang up and call Social
Security yourself at 1-800-772-1213
or Medicare at 1-800-MEDICARE. Here is
what I think about October. Almost
nothing that matters this month is a
threat. Most of it is a decision. The
raise is a number to plan with. Open
enrollment is a chance to fix your
coverage. The tax deadline is a chance
to claim a deduction you may have
missed. The savings deadline is a chance
to earn more on money you already have.
The danger in October is not that
something will be taken from you. It is
that you will be so busy reacting to
frightening headlines that you miss the
decisions that are actually yours to
make.
One, if you are on SNAP and 60 or older,
report your medical costs including your
Medicare premium. Two, if you need help
with heating this winter, apply for
LIHEAP early. Dial 211.
Three, on the 14th of October, write
down your dollar raise, not the
percentage, and wait for the Medicare
premium before you plan.
Four, between the 15th of October and
the 7th of December, check whether your
Medicare plan is continuing and compare
plans by total cost.
Five, if you filed a tax extension, file
by the 15th of October and ask about the
senior deduction. Six, before the end of
October, look at any maturing CDs and if
you buy I bonds, the current rate.
Seven, set up your own My Social
Security account and hang up on anyone
who calls you about your benefits. If
you have a question about your own
situation, leave it in the comments. I
read them and they decide what I cover
next. Bonnie will finally know her real
raise before January. Hector filed a
better return than he feared. Wilma
learned that good news on her savings
came with a tax line attached. October
is loud. Most of the noise is about
things that are not happening. The real
changes are quieter and every one of
them comes with something you can do.
Take the calendar one day at a time.
Thank you for watching and I will see
you in the next.

segments.text: If you're on Medicare, there's a date
eight days from now that most people
will walk straight past October 15th.
It's the day open enrollment begins, and
it's also the deadline for a letter from
an old employer or union that quietly
decides whether you could be paying a
penalty for as long as you're on
Medicare.
At the same time, the drug cost numbers
for 2027 are already locked in, and they
all moved in the wrong direction. In the
next 12 minutes, I'll show you what
changed, what's real, what's being
exaggerated online, and exactly what to
do this week. Stay till the end because
the last step is the one that saves
people the most money.
One honest thing before we start. Some
videos make it sound like everything
hits every person on Medicare. It
doesn't. The drug cost changes apply if
you have a Part D plan or a Medicare
Advantage plan with drug coverage. The
colored letters I'll explain later only
go to people who get extra help. I'll
tell you who each item affects, so you
don't lose sleep over the wrong one.
Change number one, the $2,400 cap. Part
D has a yearly limit on what you pay out
of your own pocket for covered drugs.
Once you hit it, covered drugs cost you
nothing until January. In 2026, that
limit is $2,100.
In 2027, it's $2,400 higher. People hear
cap and think protection, but think of
it as a finish line. It tells you how
far you have to run before the help
kicks in, and they moved it back. Let me
make it real. Say you take one brand
name drug that costs $900 a month.
Under the standard benefit in 2026,
you'd pay your deductible and then 25%
of the cost each month, and you'd reach
the cap around August. In 2027, same
drug, same price, you'd reach it around
September. That's roughly a month more
of paying at the counter and $300 more
out of your pocket. Who does this
affect? If you take one cheap generic,
probably nobody. You'll never get near
the line. But if you take several
medications or even one expensive one,
this is your number. Change number two,
the $700 deductible. In January, the
maximum deductible goes from $615 to
$700. That's the amount you can be asked
to pay in full before the plan starts
sharing costs. Two details matter here.
First, it's a maximum.
Many plans charge less and some have no
deductible on certain drug tiers and
most generics are usually excluded.
Second, the deductible hits in January
when you're already paying heating bills
and holiday bills. Your own number isn't
in this video. It's in a document your
plan was required to send you by the end
of September. It's called the annual
notice of change or A.
Find the page that says what you pay
before the plan starts paying. That's
yours. And if January is where it hurts,
ask your plan about the Medicare
prescription payment plan. It lets you
spread drug costs across monthly
payments instead of one big hit at the
pharmacy. It doesn't lower what you owe,
but it can make it livable.
Now premiums. The national base premium
goes from $38.99
That's about 6% and by law it can't grow
faster than that, but hear this. That
cap protects the base number, not your
plan's premium. A temporary federal
subsidy that held down stand-alone drug
plan premiums ends after 2026. So 2027
is the first year in a while that
insurers price plans without it. I can't
tell you your premium will jump. Plans
vary. What I can tell you is that last
year's plan being cheap doesn't mean
next year's plan will be, which is
exactly why you compare. Before the next
part, a quick note. Everything I'm
covering today is one piece of a bigger
picture. Medicare premiums, Social
Security taxes, required withdrawals
from your IRA, the Medicare surcharge
called IRMAA, the new $6,000 senior
deduction, even how your house deed is
written.
>> These rules all affect each other and
almost nobody explains how. That's why I
wrote my ebook, The Retirement Ambush:
12 Hidden Money Traps and How to Fight
Back. It's written in plain English.
Each chapter has a real-life example,
the current numbers, and action steps

all expenses. Some investors will do
much better. Others will do much worse.
Real estate depends heavily on the
market that you buy in, the tenants you
attract, and how well you manage the
property.
Lucas has experienced a very different
20 years. His original $50,000
investment has quietly continued
compounding. Every month, another $200
has been invested automatically. Nothing
exciting, just consistency.
Assuming the market delivers its
long-term average return of around 10%
per year, his portfolio has grown to
approximately $518,000.
Over those 20 years, Lucas has
personally contributed $98,000.
The remaining more than $420,000
came purely from compound growth. No
debt, no tenants, no repair bills.
When you compare their net worth after
20 years, the result surprises most
people. Ethan finishes with
approximately $505,000
in total wealth. Lucas finishes with
approximately $518,000.
Two completely different paths, almost
the same destination, Yet, the journey
couldn't have been more different.
Ethan built his wealth through leverage.
Lucas built his through compounding.
Ethan accepted concentration risk. Lucas
accepted market volatility.
Ethan invested time alongside his money.
Lucas invested patience.
Neither approach is automatically
better. They're simply different.
At this point, it might sound like the
stock market is the obvious choice. But,
that wouldn't be a fair conclusion
either. Stocks come with risks that are
every bit as real. They're just easier
to ignore.
Market crashes can be brutal. In 2008,
broad stock indexes fell by nearly 40%.
During the early months of 2020, they
plunged by more than 30% in just a
matter of weeks.
Imagine opening your investment account
and watching years of savings disappear
almost overnight. That can be
psychologically devastating.
Stocks also don't produce meaningful
monthly income for most investors. Yes,
index funds pay dividends, but the yield
is relatively small. A portfolio worth
might generate only around $250 per
month. Useful, but nowhere near enough
to replace a full-time income.
Leverage is another major difference.
Lucas used $50,000 to buy $50,000 worth
of investments. Ethan used the same
$50,000 to control a $250,000
property. When property prices rise,
that leverage magnifies the gains. The
stock market simply can't replicate
that.
So, which investment actually wins?
That's the wrong question. Ethan
believed buying property was the proven
path to wealth. Lucas believed the stock
market would quietly do all the work.
Both were only partially right. The real
winner wasn't determined by the
investment. It was determined by
understanding everything that came with
it. The money, the time, the stress, the
risk, and the opportunity cost.
The truth is, there isn't one perfect
investment. Only the one that's right
for your goals, your temperament, and
the life you want to build.
So, the next time someone tells you that
real estate always beats the stock
market, or the stock market always beats
real estate, ask them one simple
question.
Did you include everything?
Because the answer that includes

matters.

segments.text: Meet Daniel and Ryan. They are both 22

Month three arrives.

He spends another $3,000 during the
month.

Ryan still feels in control. After all,
he's making every payment the bank asks
for.
But something is quietly changing.

minimum payment.
Month one, $90. Month two, $179.05.
Month three, $267.15.
Now, let's jump forward. By month five,

He pays $2,955.60
and his balance remains under $3,000.
His total interest paid over the first
five months is only $185.28.
Ryan's situation looks very different.
By month five, his balance has climbed
almost the entire credit limit.
His interest charged that month alone is
His minimum payment has risen to
And despite making every payment on
time, he is now dangerously close to his
credit limit.

back. Ryan cannot continue spending
$3,000 every month while making only
minimum payments.

Month six becomes the turning point.

His balance now sits at $14,529.68.

credit on a card with a $15,000 limit.
For the first time, Ryan cannot continue
spending the way he normally does.
He wants to put another $3,000 of
monthly expenses on the card, but the
limit will not allow it.
The minimum payment is no longer the
problem. The credit limit is.
Ryan is now forced to make a much larger
payment.
He decides to pay exactly $2,529.68.
Not because he wants to reduce the debt,
but because he needs to free up enough
room to continue using the card for
another $3,000 of spending.
That is a very different type of
payment. Daniel pays large amounts to
stay in control. Ryan pays a large
amount because he has run out of room.
And from this point forward, the
situation becomes even more expensive.
Once Ryan reaches the $15,000 limit, his
monthly interest charge stabilizes at
$300 every month.
Think about that. Every month, before
groceries, before fuel, before
subscriptions, before life, the bank
takes $300.
Now, let's jump to the end of the year.
Daniel spent exactly $36,000
on his credit card, the same as Ryan.
Not $1 less, not $1 more.
Over the course of the year, Daniel paid
a total of $609.79
in interest. His ending balance is
Ryan also spent exactly $36,000.
The same purchases, the same lifestyle,

But Ryan paid $2,660.76
in interest. More than four times what

This is the part most people never

That money is gone forever. It didn't

Millions of people around the world use

The mathematics doesn't care which side

Month after month, year after year. And

title: Why Millennials Think About Money So Differently

segments.text: David graduated college in 1985.
Ryan graduated college in 2015.
They both wanted the same things: a good
job, a house, a family, and enough money
to retire someday without worrying about
bills.
Neither one dreamed of becoming a
millionaire. They just wanted financial
security. But if you listen to how they
talk about money, you'd think they grew
up on different planets.
David believes hard work solves most
financial problems. Ryan believes the
system is stacked against him.
David sees a house as the foundation of
wealth. Ryan sees a house as an
impossible dream.
David trusts long-term investing. Ryan
trusts flexibility.
One generation believes ownership
creates wealth. The other believes
ownership creates risk.
And the strange part is that both have a
point. Because over the last 40 years,
the rules changed. But some of the
beliefs that changed with them maybe
creating a new problem nobody is talking
about.
Let's start at age 22. David graduates
His first job pays about $22,000 a year.
It isn't glamorous, but it doesn't need
to be.
A modest house in his city costs roughly
three to four times his annual income.
Within a few years, home ownership feels
realistic. Student debt exists, but it
isn't crushing. Most people aren't
carrying six-figure balances before they
earn their first paycheck.
Retirement feels simple. Work, save,
invest, repeat. Nobody is talking about
passive income. Nobody is building
personal brands. Nobody is starting side
hustles from their phone.
The formula isn't exciting, but it feels
reliable.
Now, let's look at Ryan. He graduates in
2015. His salary is higher than David's
was. Much higher.
But so are the costs. Housing prices
have risen faster than wages for years.
Student loans follow him into adulthood.
Healthcare costs more. Rent consumes a
larger percentage of income. And every
day he opens social media and sees
people claiming to make money in ways
nobody talked about in 1985.
Trading, crypto, online businesses,
influencing.
Ryan doesn't just compare himself to his
neighbors. He compares himself to
millions of people every day.
And that's where the first major
difference appears.
David grew up believing wealth was built
slowly.
Ryan grew up watching people get rich
overnight. Or at least that's what it
looked like.
>> By age 30, the gap becomes even larger.
David has been working for 8 years. He's
purchased a house. He's building equity.
Every mortgage payment increases his
ownership.
His retirement account isn't exciting,
but it's growing.
Nothing about his financial life feels
dramatic, which is exactly why it works.
Ryan reaches 30 and faces a completely
different reality.
Housing prices have risen again. Many of
his friends still rent. Some are living
with roommates. Others moved back home
for a period. A few bought homes. Most
didn't.
Ryan starts asking a question David
never had to ask. What if ownership
isn't worth it?
What if flexibility is better?
What if renting is smarter?
What if the traditional path doesn't
work anymore?
And to be fair, some of those questions
are completely reasonable. The math
really did change. Housing became less
affordable. Debt became larger. Job
security became weaker.
Millennials didn't invent these
problems. They inherited them.
But this is where something interesting
happens.
A reasonable observation slowly becomes
a dangerous belief.
Because when people believe something is
harder, they often stop pursuing it
entirely.
Ryan sees home ownership becoming
difficult, then gradually convinces
himself it doesn't matter.
He sees investing becoming confusing,
then gradually convinces himself it's
rigged.
He sees wealth taking longer to build,
then gradually convinces himself it
can't be built at all.
The economy changed, but some of the
conclusions changed, too. And not all of
them were correct.
Let's talk about investing.
David's generation had fewer options,
much fewer. Most people invested through
retirement accounts, mutual funds,
pensions, basic stock portfolios.
It wasn't exciting, but it forced
patience.
Ryan has infinite options, stocks, ETFs,
crypto, forex, private investments,
thousands of opinions, millions of
predictions.
At first, more options sounds like an
advantage, but often it creates the
opposite effect, paralysis.
Ryan spends years researching the
perfect investment. David spent years
invested. One generation feared making
mistakes, the other fears making
decisions.
And while Ryan is learning, researching,
optimizing, and waiting, compounding is
quietly passing him by.
Because the stock market doesn't reward
certainty, it rewards time.
The uncomfortable truth is that many
millennials understand investing better
than previous generations, yet often
invest less. Not because they're lazy,
because they are overwhelmed.
The amount of financial information
available today is staggering. And
information isn't always the same thing
as wisdom.
And this is where the consequences start
showing up.
By age 40, another difference emerges.
David's wealth doesn't look impressive.
His house appreciated slowly. His
retirement account grew slowly. His
salary increased gradually. Nothing
about the journey looked extraordinary.
But over 20 years, ordinary decisions
compound.
And compounding has a habit of making
average decisions look brilliant in
hindsight.
Ryan is now entering his prime earning
years.
His income may exceed what David earned
at the same age after adjusting for
inflation.
But something strange happens.
Higher income doesn't automatically
create higher wealth.
Lifestyle inflation arrives.
Subscriptions, travel, experiences,
upgrades. Every increase in income
creates new expenses.
And because modern culture celebrates
consumption far more than ownership,
many millennials become trapped in a
cycle David rarely experienced.
They earn more, spend more, earn more,
spend more.
The lifestyle improves, the balance
sheet doesn't. And that's the second
major belief that quietly hurts wealth
building.
The belief that income matters more than
assets.
Income helps, assets create freedom.
Those are not the same thing.
A person earning $200,000 with no assets
may be less financially secure than
someone earning $90,000 with significant
investments.
The paycheck feels powerful. The asset
quietly does the heavy lifting.
This brings us to the biggest difference
of all. Risk.
David's generation often viewed
investing as risky.
Ryan's generation often views not
investing as risky.
And both perspectives make sense.
David saw market crashes. Ryan saw
housing bubbles, crypto collapses,
layoffs, inflation, economic
uncertainty.
But here's the irony. The people who
fear risk the most often become exposed
to the greatest risk of all. Doing
nothing.
Because inflation doesn't care how
cautious you are. It slowly attacks
cash. Every year, every decade, every
generation.
And the longer money sits still, the
harder it becomes to build wealth later.
This is why some millennials find
themselves in a frustrating position.
They understand the problems better than
previous generations. They understand
debt. They understand inequality. They
understand economic pressure. But
understanding a problem doesn't
automatically solve it. And eventually
every generation faces the same reality.
Assets still matter. Ownership still
matters. Compounding still matters.
The tools may change. The economy may
change. The technology may change. But
those principles remain remarkably
consistent.
The truth is that millennials think
differently about money because they had
to. They entered a different world.
Higher housing costs, higher debt,
greater uncertainty, more information,
more complexity.
Many of their concerns are completely
justified. But some of the beliefs
created by those challenges became
obstacles of their own.
The belief that investing can wait. The
belief that ownership is optional. The
belief that perfect decisions matter
more than consistent ones.
David's generation wasn't right about
everything. Ryan's generation isn't
wrong about everything.
Both made mistakes. Both adapted to the
world they inherited. And both can learn
from each other.
Because wealth has never been about
predicting the future perfectly. It's
about consistently acquiring assets that
grow over time.
That's true in 1985. It's true in 2015.
And it will probably still be true 30
years from now.
The economy changes. The principles
rarely do.
And that's the part every generation
eventually discovers for itself.
>> [music]

title: The Smartest Order To Invest Your Money Step By Step

segments.text: Theo and Maya earn the same salary. They

paper, Theo starts investing months
before Maya does. So, why, 10 years
later, is Maya $16,140
ahead? Because there is an order to
this, and most people do it backwards.
We're going to climb it one step at a

kind of debt has to die before you

nothing but a few minutes of paperwork.

Maya fills the pot in three months. Theo

more than it should. Step two is the one

the most valuable step on the whole

becomes $200 in her account. That's a

Theo never fills in the form. He's still
on the minimum and his employer is

First checkpoint, one year in. Maya is
better off than the day she started.

Credit cards, store cards, overdrafts,

in. Maya is $12,843
ahead of where she started. Theo is at
and remember, he's the one who started

was for. Quick question before we go on.
The first time you had money left over
at the end of the month, what did you do
with it first? Start investing or deal
with the debt? Drop it in the comments.
I'm curious how many of us were Theo.
Now, here's a twist that surprises
people. Not every debt deserves the same
treatment. A simple rule of thumb,

is the engine room. What goes inside
that account? For most people, the
